without_preference.text: What are some properties of k-node subgraphs that can be counted in faster than cubic time in the size of the input graph?
without_preference.answer:
# Short answer

Several families of k-vertex induced-subgraph properties admit algorithms whose runtimes are strictly below cubic in the number of vertices n (or equivalently below O(m·n)), often due to sparsity (bounded degeneracy/average degree/arboricity), structural decompositions (color-coding), or algebraic/homomorphism techniques. Representative examples include: triangles and 4-cycles (near-linear or linear-time on sparse graphs), all 4-node patterns (countable in about triangle-time), k-paths and other monotone small patterns via color-coding in O*(2^k) time, cliques with few edges via inclusion-exclusion/universal trees in O(2^O(k) n^2) time under sparsity, and many fixed k "graphlets" (4–5 nodes) via practical algorithms that scale to tens of millions of edges.

# Background: "Faster than cubic" and setting

We measure "size" by the number of vertices n and edges m; "faster than cubic" means o(n^3) or O(n^2 poly(n)), O(n^{2+o(1)}), or O(mn) on m ≲ n^2. For fixed k, "counting k-node induced subgraphs" includes all isomorphism copies of all k-vertex graphs; for a fixed target H (a k-vertex pattern), it asks for the number of induced H's in G. Known algorithms exploit sparsity measures (degeneracy, arboricity, average degree), combinatorial decompositions (color-coding), and algebraic frameworks (homomorphisms/matrix multiplication-like schemes).

# General frameworks enabling subcubic algorithms

- Degeneracy/arboricity/average-degree sparsity:
  - For bounded-degeneracy graphs, counting all k-vertex induced subgraphs can be done in time linear in the size of G (and in k), with the algorithmic core being a depth-first traversal with degree-based pruning; this class includes cliques and 4-cycles and yields nearly optimal linear-time algorithms in many sparse graph families of practical interest. <cite id="c8941d12-8">For example, we can count the induced copies of any k-node pattern H in time if G has bounded degeneracy, and in time if G has bounded average degree.</cite> <cite id="ae125eb2-0">Chiba and Nishizeki gave linear time algorithms for clique and 4-cycle counting for bounded degeneracy graphs; this is a rich class of sparse graphs</cite>.
- Color-coding for "monotone" structures (paths, cycles, trees, matchings):
  - Color-coding is a randomized method introduced for finding simple k-paths/cycles and extends to many small induced subgraphs. It runs in O*(2^k) time to detect (and often to count) k-paths and other fixed-size patterns, with single-exponential k-dependency and near-linear n-dependency in sparse graphs. <cite id="d6d44604-0">We describe a novel randomized method, the method of color-coding, for finding simple paths and cycles of a specified length k and other small subgraphs</cite> <cite id="d6d44604-5">A colorful k-path can be found in O*(2^k) time; picking a random k-coloring makes any fixed k-path colorful with positive probability</cite> <cite id="d6d4604-2">Alon et al. revisited color-coding to attain a running time with single-exponential dependency on k</cite> <cite id="d6d44604-3">Further work provides simpler, deterministic, and in-polynomial-time approximation/counting refinements with single-exponential k-dependency</cite>.
- Homomorphism-based (AYZ) algebraic/algebraic-graph-theory methods:
  - Counting (or recognizing) graphs via homomorphism numbers connects to matrix-multiplication–style algorithms and forms a unifying framework; for fixed H (k-vertex), the number of homomorphisms from H to G encodes structural information, and specialized algorithms achieve near quadratic/quasi-quadratic n^ω-ty pe complexities depending on H's structure (arity, treewidth, etc.). <cite id="62e4c254-3">The problem of counting homomorphisms from a general graph G to a fixed graph H generalizes graph colouring with important applications</cite> <cite id="62e4c254-1">Work characterizes patterns H for which counting homomorphisms from sparse graphs can be solved efficiently and even in linear time</cite> <cite id="62e4c254-8">Homomorphism counts to trees have algorithmic implications and separations for graph isomorphism and distinguishing graphs</cite>.
- Inclusion-exclusion via induced-universal trees (sparse "heavy-edge" structures):
  - For families with few edges per induced subgraph (e.g., bounded degeneracy/arboricity), the number of k-cliques equals a signed sum over small subtrees (inclusion-exclusion on induced universal trees with O(2^k) nodes), giving rise to O(2^O(k))·poly(n) or O(2^O(k))·n^2 algorithms by dynamic programming over the host graph's edges. <cite id="c8941d12-2">The algorithm in [8] can be generalized to design another type of algorithm that recognizes K`'s by extending O(e·2^{α/(α+1)})-time triangle techniques</cite> <cite id="d6d44604-3">Complementary work provides deterministic approximate counting with running time whose k-dependency is single-exponential</cite>.

# Concrete property classes and example runtimes

- Triangles and 4-cycles:
  - Exact counting of triangles and 4-cycles is linearizable on sparse graphs, yielding o(n^3) algorithms in the bounded-degeneracy/arboricity regime. <cite id="ae125eb2-0">Clique and 4-cycle counting are solvable in linear time when the input graph has bounded degeneracy</cite> <cite id="c8941d12-1">There are linear time algorithms for clique and 4-cycle counting (fixed k)</cite>. 
  - Beyond 4-cycles, all 4-node patterns can be counted in about triangle time, i.e., essentially the same time as detecting triangles, by reduction/iteration over small neighborhoods. <cite id="c8941d12-7">Finding induced four-node subgraphs can be done in time roughly that of detecting a clique on three nodes (triangle time)</cite>.
- k-Paths, trees, matchings, and other monotone patterns:
  - Color-coding enables exact or approximate counting with O*(2^k) time per copy (detection) and O*(2^k)·poly(n) or O*(2^k)·m time to enumerate all occurrences, i.e., subcubic for fixed k on m = O(n). <cite id="d6d44604-0">Color-coding finds simple k-paths and cycles and other small subgraphs</cite> <cite id="d6d44604-5">Finding a colorful k-path in O*(2^k) time yields randomized algorithms for k-paths</cite> <cite id="d6d44604-2">Single-exponential k-dependency is achieved for counting/finding</cite> <cite id="d6d44604-3">Deterministic approximations/counting with improved simplicity and polynomial-time aspects</cite>. 
- Small "graphlets" (4–5 nodes):
  - Practical systems enumerate all induced 4- and 5-vertex subgraphs at scale in minutes on graphs with tens of millions of edges, indicating that fixed-size induced-subgraph census can be implemented in subcubic or even near-linear time on real-world sparse graphs. <cite id="c8941d12-5">An implementation computes counts of graphs with tens of millions of edges in minutes for 5-vertex pattern counting</cite>. 
- k-Cliques under sparsity (degeneracy/arboricity, few edges per subgraph):
  - When G is sparse (bounded degeneracy/arboricity), counting all k-cliques (or induced copies of any k-node pattern) can be done in time linear in the size of G and polynomial in k via traversal with pruning or inclusion-exclusion over small induced-universal trees. <cite id="c8941d12-2">Algorithms based on DFS with O(e·2^{α/(α+1)})-time triangle techniques generalize to recognizing larger cliques and counting with few edges revisited</cite> <cite id="c8941d12-8">Counting induced copies of any k-node pattern H runs in time for bounded degeneracy and in bounded average degree</cite> <cite id="ae125eb2-0">Chiba–Nishizeki frameworks underpin linear-time clique counting on bounded-degeneracy graphs</cite>.
- Fixed-pattern homomorphisms and motifs (general H):
  - For fixed H (a k-vertex graph), there are near-linear/quasi-linear algorithms under structural constraints (e.g., bounded treedepth/width, bounded degeneracy) for counting homomorphisms, which subsumes many induced-subgraph counts. <cite id="62e4c254-1">There are characterizations and algorithms for counting homomorphisms from sparse graphs to H in linear or near-linear time when structural parameters are bounded</cite> <cite id="ae125eb2-6">Homomorphism counting on bounded degeneracy graphs admits near-linear time algorithms and frameworks</cite>.

# Structural conditions that yield subcubic behavior

- Bounded degeneracy/arboricity/average degree:
  - These sparsity measures ensure that the number of high-degree neighborhoods is limited, enabling depth-first traversal with local branching O(Δ) bounded by constants, leading to overall near-linear time for fixed k and O(poly(n)) dependence for k fixed. <cite id="c8941d12-8">Counting induced k-node patterns is linear in time for bounded degeneracy graphs and bounded similarly for bounded average degree</cite> <cite id="ae125eb2-0">Linear-time clique and 4-cycle counting fall into the bounded-degeneracy family</cite> <cite id="ae125eb2-4">Cycle-counting becomes efficient under degeneracy-bounded assumptions, aligning with the broader "basic subgraph counting" toolbox</cite>.
- Small fixed k and monotone structure (paths, trees, matchings):
  - Color-coding's 2^k factor is subcubic for k = O(1), giving O(2^k n) to O(2^k m) algorithms; for k growing with n this factor can dominate. <cite id="d6d44604-5">O*(2^k) detection/decoding for k-paths underlies counting algorithms</cite> <cite id="d6d44604-2">Single-exponential k-dependency removes slightly super-polynomial penalties</cite>.
- Matrix-multiplication–style homomorphism counts:
  - For fixed H, the adjacency-tensor/neighbor-hitting set methods yield O(n^{ω}·p(H)) or O(Mul(H)·n^{ω})-type algorithms, which for constant k and bounded-degree H are subcubic. <cite id="62e4c254-3">Homomorphism counting generalizes coloring and admits widely used algorithms with application-driven performance</cite> <cite id="62e4c254-1">Linear-time and near-linear-time regimes exist for counting homomorphisms when patterns from sparse graphs are constrained</cite>.
- Excluded densest cases (generally cubic):
  - General (degeneracy-unbounded) worst-case exact enumeration of induced copies may be Ω(n^3) or worse in cliques; this motivates focusing on structural properties (sparsity, monotonicity) and approximation. <cite id="c8941d12-3">Counting even k-paths is considered a baseline subcubic problem; improved algorithms exist but the generic baseline is cubic</cite> <cite id="c8941d12-6">No truly subcubic algorithms are known for finding a triangle in edge-weighted graphs, highlighting inherent cubic barriers in densest cases</cite>.

# Techniques and examples in detail

- Degeneracy-aware enumeration (Chiba–Nishizeki-style):
  - Iteratively prune vertices above a degree threshold, and count subgraphs within low-degree cores via DFS with neighborhood intersection; 4-cycles and cliques inherit linear-time bounds in bounded-degeneracy graphs. <cite id="ae125eb2-0">Chiba–Nishizeki provided linear-time clique and 4-cycle counting within bounded degeneracy</cite> <cite id="c8941d12-8">General bounded-degeneracy and average-degree statements cover counting induced k-node patterns efficiently</cite>.
- Color-coding:
  - Randomly assign k colors, retain only colorful (surjective color-preserving) subgraphs, and sum over colorings; expected time O(2^k m) with O(2^k n) variants yields exact counts (or sampled approximations) with subcubic performance for fixed k. <cite id="d6d44604-0">Color-coding constructs randomized algorithms for k-paths/cycles and other small subgraphs</cite> <cite id="d6d44604-5">Finding colorful k-paths in O*(2^k) guides counting/decision tradeoffs</cite> <cite id="d6d44604-2">Refinements make k-dependency single-exponential</cite>.
- Induced-universal trees and inclusion-exclusion:
  - Build a small induced-universal forest for k-subgraphs with few edges; enumerate inclusions with Möbius inversion to express clique counts as signed sums over tree-structures, reducing work from exponential in number of edges to exponential in k with O(n^2) loops. <cite id="c8941d12-2">Kloks et al. connect triangle-time techniques and k-clique recognition via O(e·2^{α/(α+1)})-type bounds and generalize to larger cliques</cite>.
- Homomorphism/expressive characterizations:
  - Homomorphism numbers distinguish graphs and support counting frameworks; when H's structural parameters (treewidth/treedepth, degeneracy) are bounded, counting homomorphisms from G to H becomes efficiently solvable, encompassing many induced-subgraph counts. <cite id="62e4c254-1">Characterizations for linear-time homomorphism counting in bounded treedepth/treewidth graphs</cite> <cite id="62e4c254-8">Homomorphism counts to trees yield non-isomorphic separations, illustrating expressive power</cite> <cite id="62e4c254-3">Surveys and complexity results place homomorphism counting in context with algorithms and applications</cite>.

# Practical graphlets and scale

- Enumerating all 4- and 5-node induced subgraphs in massive sparse graphs:
  - Production graph mining systems achieve minute-scale runtimes for 5-node induced-subgraph census on graphs with tens of millions of edges, consistent with subcubic algorithms on real-world data. <cite id="c8941d12-5">An implementation handles graphs with tens of millions of edges for 5-vertex pattern counting in minutes</cite>.
- Four-node subgraphs in triangle time:
  - For 4-vertex patterns, runtimes matching triangle detection are possible, leveraging limited neighborhood intersections in sparse graphs. <cite id="c8941d12-7">Four-node induced subgraphs can be found/counted in time roughly that of detecting a triangle</cite>.

# What properties tend to be subcubic

- Monotone hereditary motifs (paths, trees, matchings):
  - These subgraphs avoid adding edges between earlier and later endpoints; color-coding and degeneracy-aware traversal lead to subcubic algorithms for fixed k. <cite id="d6d44604-0">Color-coding unifies counting of simple paths/cycles</cite> <cite id="d6d44604-5">k-path counting in O*(2^k)</cite> <cite id="c8941d12-8">Bounded degeneracy/average degree imply linear-time counting</cite>.
- Low-arboricity/degeneracy clusters (cliques, cycles, small graphlets within sparse giants):
  - Neighborhoods have few edges; enumeration traverses small branching trees per vertex, giving near-linear or O(n^2) time even for k up to dozens. <cite id="ae125eb2-0">Linear-time clique/4-cycle counting under bounded degeneracy</cite> <cite id="c8941d12-8">Linear-time counting of induced k-node patterns with bounded degeneracy</cite> <cite id="c8941d12-5">Practical O(1)-second-to-minute runtimes on tens-of-millions-edge graphs for 5-vertex patterns</cite>.
- Patterns with small "arity" or bounded treewidth/treedepth:
  - Homomorphism-based frameworks can solve counting in time linear/quasi-linear in n under bounded treewidth/treedepth of H or G and with bounded-degree edges. <cite id="62e4c254-1">Linear-time homomorphism counting for patterns of bounded treedepth/treewidth from sparse graphs</cite> <cite id="ae125eb2-6">Near-linear algorithms exist for homomorphism counting in bounded-degeneracy graphs</cite>.

# Caveats and hardness boundaries

- General dense inputs:
  - When G is dense and H has no special structure, exact counting remains cubic or worse; triangle detection hardness underscores that subcubic algorithms often rely on structural assumptions. <cite id="c8941d12-6">No truly subcubic algorithm is known for finding a triangle in edge-weighted graphs</cite> <cite id="c8941d1d3">Counting k-paths is a canonical subcubic baseline; specialized algorithms improve but don't guarantee cubic-breakthroughs in general</cite>.
- Parameter sensitivity:
  - For k growing with n, exponential-in-k methods (color-coding) can become supercubic; performance depends on k's growth and whether exact or approximate counts are needed. <cite id="d6d44604-2">Single-exponential k-dependency improves constants over earlier superpolynomial methods</cite>.

# Practical takeaways

- If G is sparse (bounded degeneracy/arboricity/average degree), you can count:
  - All 4-node induced subgraphs and triangles/4-cycles in near-linear time; count k-cliques and many k-node patterns in linear or O(n^2) time via degeneracy-aware traversal and inclusion-exclusion/universal trees. <cite id="ae125eb2-0">Linear-time clique and 4-cycle counting on bounded-degeneracy graphs</cite> <cite id="c8941d12-8">Linear-time counting for bounded degeneracy/average degree</cite> <cite id="c8941d12-7">4-node subgraphs in triangle time</cite>.
- If your motif is monotone (paths, trees, matchings), use color-coding for exact or approximate counts in O*(2^k) or deterministic subcubic variants for fixed k. <cite id="d6d44604-0">Color-coding yields O*(2^k) algorithms for k-paths/cycles and other small subgraphs</cite> <cite id="d6d44604-2">Improved single-exponential k-dependency</cite>.
- For arbitrary fixed k-node patterns, homomorphism-based frameworks and induced-universal-tree inclusion-exclusion provide O(Mul(H) n^ω) or O(2^{O(k)} n^2) schemes, subcubic for fixed k; practical performance hinges on H's structure and degeneracy bounds. <cite id="62e4c254-3">Homomorphism counting generalizes to many subgraph queries with algorithmic toolkits</cite> <cite id="c8941d12-2">Inclusion-exclusion over induced universal trees underlies k-clique counting with sparse-work exponential-in-k factors</cite> <cite id="c8941d12-8">Linear-time regimes for bounded degeneracy/average degree</cite>.

In short, if a k-vertex property is monotone (no added edges between endpoints), has bounded structural complexity (low treewidth/treedepth, bounded degeneracy/arboricity/average degree), or is a fixed sparse motif, then counting induced copies can be done in subcubic time using degeneracy-aware traversal, color-coding, or homomorphism/inclusion-exclusion methods, with runtimes ranging from O(n^2) up to O(2^{O(k)} n^2) or O*(2^k) and still beating O(n^3) for fixed k in sparse graphs. <cite id="c8941d12-8">Bounded degeneracy/average-degree algorithms cover induced k-node patterns in near-linear to linear time</cite> <cite id="d6d44604-5">Color-coding provides O*(2^k) per-pattern enumeration suitable for small k</cite> <cite id="c8941d12-5">Empirical systems demonstrate minute-level counting for 5-vertex patterns on very large sparse graphs</cite>.

questions.original_query: What are some of the challenges associated with creating a training dataset for question answering in scientific domains? Describe some recent methods that try to overcome these challenges.

query.text: What are some of the challenges associated with creating a training dataset for question answering in scientific domains? Describe some recent methods that try to overcome these challenges.
query.answer:
Below I summarize key challenges encountered when building training datasets for question answering (QA) in scientific domains, followed by recent methods that address these issues.

Challenges specific to scientific-domain QA datasets
- Accessing and curating high-quality gold annotations at scale
  - Expert-annotated scientific QA data remains sparse and expensive to produce, motivating strategies that bootstrap from small expert sets and leverage large unlabeled or synthetic collections to reach dataset sizes useful for training and evaluation <cite id="d606ee2c-0">PubMedQA makes 1k expert-labeled, 61.2k unlabeled, and 211.3k artificially generated QA instances publicly available</cite> <cite id="d606ee2c-2">The original PubMedQA paper highlights a seed set of 1,000 expert-annotated questions and emphasizes that reasoning over quantitative biomedical research text is required</cite>. 
  - Biomedical curation pipelines explicitly address scalability and reliability: semi-automated annotation with LLM assistance, dynamic voting (pass/fail), and multi- annotator review queues are used to make large label sets feasible while maintaining quality control <cite id="d606ee2c-1">A scalable method is proposed for annotating large clinical datasets through actionability labeling that integrates LLM assistance with multi-stage review to ensure scalability and quality</cite>.

- Data heterogeneity across modalities and formats
  - Scientific QA spans text, tables, figures, and chemical structures (SMILES, reaction schemes), making extraction and annotation rules substantially more complex than general-domain QA <cite id="a6d56ffc-4">SPIQA introduces the first large-scale QA dataset designed to interpret complex scientific images and diagrams, underscoring the need for specialized annotation to capture visual-semantic alignment</cite>.
  - In chemistry and materials, formula-based equivalence (SMILES canonicalization), layout-sensitive tables, and multi-step reaction evidence change how questions are framed and answers are validated; tokenization/normalization rules must reflect domain conventions rather than generic text-only heuristics <cite id="f01794d6-0">MolTextQA covers about 500,000 QA pairs for 240,000 distinct SMILES sequences across categories, requiring domain-aware molecule representations</cite> <cite id="f01794d6-6">ScholarChemQA is constructed from chemical papers with questions derived from titles, requiring domain parsers and entity extraction across scientific documents</cite>.

- Noisy, inconsistent, or non-factual answers from LLMs during weak supervision
  - When generating large synthetic question-answer pairs or crowd-labeled entries, LLM-produced answers can be hallucinated; datasets therefore add careful post-filtering, citation checking, and expert or literature-grounded verification steps <cite id="d606ee2c-8">Workshops and benchmarks for biomedical LLMs document pitfalls of LLM-based annotation and learning strategies, emphasizing evaluation of LLM-generated labels and careful integration</cite>.

- Citation and literature grounding
  - Scientific claims are evidence-backed; QA pairs must be linked to supporting sentences in papers or databases. Misbinding answers to wrong references leads to invalid training signals; citation matching and grounded retrieval become integral to dataset creation and evaluation <cite id="9b4c9aca-0">ResearchQA benchmarks citation-grounded QA with open-weight models reaching best closed-model citation accuracy at 3–6× lower latency, highlighting the value and difficulty of citation-aligned supervision</cite>.

- Domain-specific schema and semantics
  - Quantitative reasoning, unit consistency, and domain taxonomies (pathways, protein complexes, reactions) require specialized lexical resources and ontologies, which must be reflected in annotation schemas and evaluation metrics <cite id="d606ee2c-3">PubMedQA requires reasoning over quantitative biomedical research content from PubMed abstracts</cite> <cite id="d606ee2c-5">The dataset homepage reports analyses of challenges posed by quantitative and research-context reasoning</cite> <cite id="9b4c9aca-1">PeerQA constructs a scientific, document-level QA dataset from peer-review contexts, embedding literature-grounded constraints</cite>.

- Multimodal grounding and diagrammatic content
  - Scientific figures and schemes are central evidence for many questions but hard to annotate consistently; shared tasks show that state-of-the-art models still err on compositional references to figures/regions and relation extraction <cite id="a6d56ffc-5">An overview of the first Scientific Visual Question Answering (SciVQA) shared task analyzes common challenges and errors made by multimodal LLMs, including failures to ground on paper figures and diagrams</cite> <cite id="a6d56ffc-4">SPIQA’s poster highlights complex diagrams and the need to interpret subfigures and labels to form correct answers</cite>.

- Evaluation of human-LLM interaction and bias
  - Many scientific questions reflect real users/clinicians; datasets must capture realistic intents and elicit rationales that can be checked against evidence, not just correctness. Human-in-the-loop evaluation and LLM-generated question generation introduce new biases and require detoxification and representativeness guarantees <cite id="d606ee2c-7">RealMedQA comprises realistic clinical questions generated by humans and LLMs, and it describes verification processes to ensure scientific validity</cite>.

Recent methods to overcome these challenges
- Programmatic generation and expert-first bootstrapping for biomedicine and STEM
  - PubMedQA’s scale-up pattern is being reused: small expert-labeled seeds, large unlabeled corpora mined from domain literature, and artificially generated pairs trained with quantitative reasoning constraints—combined with analysis of failure modes—provide large training/eval sets and diagnostics <cite id="d606ee2c-0">PubMedQA’s homepage provides balanced splits: 1k expert-labeled, 61.2k unlabeled, and 211.3k generated QA pairs</cite> <cite id="d606ee2c-2">The original dataset stresses research-text QA where numbers and methods matter, with 1,000 expert annotations as the core</cite> <cite id="d606ee2c-5">The dataset includes analyses of task challenges, emphasizing quantitative reasoning</cite>.
  - MolTextQA and ScholarChemQA demonstrate LLM- or algorithmic pipelines to create large, molecule-aware or chemical-paper–based QA corpora, with domain-specific filters and normalization to avoid label noise from general text QA heuristics <cite id="f01794d6-0">MolTextQA contains ~500k QA pairs for 240k SMILES, designed for molecule-aware QA</cite> <cite id="f01794d6-4">ScholarChemQA builds from chemical papers with title-derived questions, prompting domain-specific question parsing</cite>.

- Tabular-data-to-QA pipelines for reproducible supervision
  - Domain pipelines convert structured scientific tables (e.g., chemical properties, clinical trials, biological pathways) into validated NL QA pairs, adding schema-aware extraction, unit conversion, and answer-linking to table cells/columns to reduce ambiguity and improve downstream model learning <cite id="f01794d6-7">A general pipeline converts scientific tabular data into validated natural-language Q&A corpora for LLM fine-tuning, enabling scalable, schema-aware dataset creation</cite>.
  - Chemical pipelines further show programmatic curation at scale from authoritative collections (e.g., Organic Syntheses) and compound identifiers, ensuring correct entity grounding before QA generation <cite id="f01794d6-8">ReactionSeek describes an LLM-powered literature-mining pipeline that first constructs compound datasets from paper-derived names and CAS numbers before downstream QA</cite>.

- Reference- and citation-grounded labeling and verification
  - ResearchQA formalizes citation-grounded QA, requiring answers to be supported by specific in-text references; this pushes models and datasets to tie answers to paragraph- or figure-level evidence, addressing hallucination risks via grounded retrieval and citation-matching <cite id="9b4c9aca-0">ResearchQA benchmarks citation-grounded QA and shows open-weight models can match closed models on citation accuracy with much lower latency</cite>.
  - PeerQA constructs document-level questions sampled from real scientific discourse and links them to their source contexts, reducing abstraction gaps and providing literature-grounded training signals and evaluation scenarios <cite id="9b4c9aca-1">PeerQA is a real-world, scientific document-level QA dataset with human-sourced questions and paper-aligned contexts</cite>.

- Human-in-the-loop with LLM assistance and scalable annotation processes
  - Recent biomedical QA datasets integrate LLM-assisted annotation (e.g., for yes/no triage and candidate answer generation) with multiple human verifier stages and adaptive voting, reducing expert burden while maintaining reliability through failure-sensitive feedback loops <cite id="d606ee2c-1">A scalable method integrates LLM assistance with multi-stage review to annotate large biomedical datasets, emphasizing pass/fail queues and quality control</cite>.
  - LLM-based annotation evaluation frameworks in biomedicine quantify the reliability of LLM-generated labels and show how semi-supervised and iterative verification can be applied to scientific corpora, with caution on biases and error modes <cite id="d606ee2c-8">Workshop discussions catalog LLM-based data annotation methods, evaluate their effectiveness, and analyze learning strategies for scientific QA</cite>.

- Multimodal scientific visual reasoning datasets and tasks
  - New benchmarks like SPIQA and the SciVQA shared task explicitly target interpreting figures, schemes, and embedded annotations in PDFs or images, offering guidelines, inter-annotator protocols, and automatic visual grounding metrics to standardize complex, structure-sensitive QA annotation <cite id="a6d56ffc-4">SPIQA is the first large-scale dataset tailored to interpret complex scientific images and diagrams</cite> <cite id="a6d56ffc-5">SciVQA’s overview summarizes common errors and annotation considerations for scientific multimodal QA</cite>.

- Domain adaptation to scientific contexts using scientific pretraining and literature-scale prompting
  - In chemistry, model-building efforts pair curated domain datasets with literature-grounded retrieval so that generated or retrieved evidence constraints answer formation, improving factual alignment with chemical literature and compounds <cite id="f01794d6-6">ChemMatch, designed for chemical questions, leverages expert-collected data to improve alignment with chemical knowledge, supporting literature-based QA</cite> <cite id="f01794d6-4">ScholarChemQA supports data-centric training where paper-derived questions are matched to chemical content</cite>.
  - Programmatic curation tools across biology/chemistry (e.g., R interfaces to PubChem; pipelines that extract SMILES, reactions, properties from literature) allow scalable construction of ground-truthable QA corpora by binding identifiers and entities, which reduces ambiguity and supports automated verification against authoritative databases <cite id="f01794d6-1">PubChemR provides a comprehensive R interface to PubChem, enabling programmatic access for scientific data curation</cite> <cite id="f01794d6-5">Unveiling the power of LLMs in chemical research introduces ScholarChemQA, constructed from chemical papers with automated question derivation</cite>.

Practical takeaways and open issues
- Combining seed expert labels, structured programmatic generation, LLM assistance, and citation/figure-grounded verification appears effective when tackling scientific QA datasets. Reported pipelines scale to hundreds of thousands of items while emphasizing quantitative, literature-backed reasoning and multimodal grounding <cite id="d606ee2c-0">PubMedQA’s composition of 1k expert-labeled, 61.2k unlabeled, and 211.3k generated QA pairs exemplifies a practical, scalable recipe</cite> <cite id="a6d56ffc-4">SPIQA demonstrates specialized annotation for complex diagrams</cite> <cite id="9b4c9aca-1">PeerQA demonstrates human-sourced, document-level scientific QA collection</cite>.
- Remaining open problems include establishing gold standards across entire scientific corpora (especially for original research papers where gold answers may not exist), standardizing inter-annotator agreement for diagram grounding, and preventing bias/toxicity in LLM-aided synthetic data. Recent biomedical work emphasizes robust evaluation of LLM annotation pipelines and the need for pass/fail triage and multi-annotator resolution before release into training corpora <cite id="d606ee2c-8">LLM-based annotation methods show promise but require careful evaluation of effectiveness and learning strategies</cite> <cite id="d606ee2c-1">LLM-assistant, multi-stage pipelines show how scalable annotation can be combined with quality control mechanisms</cite>.

Summary
- Core challenges arise from scarce expert labels, heterogeneous modalities and structures (text + tables + figures + formulas), noisy weak supervision from LLMs, and the necessity to ground answers in scientific citations and evidence. Mitigations include expert-first bootstrapping plus scalable LLM-hybrid labeling (PubMedQA), tabular- and chemistry-specific programmatic curation and normalization (MolTextQA, ScholarChemQA, ChemMatch), citation- and figure-grounded benchmarks for robust training and evaluation (ResearchQA, SciVQA, SPIQA), and LLM-assisted pipelines with multi-stage quality control (iMedQA-style processes and RealMedQA’s verification). <cite id="d606ee2c-0">PubMedQA exemplifies bootstrapping with 1k expert labels and hundreds of thousands of generated/synthetic questions</cite> <cite id="f01794d6-0">MolTextQA demonstrates molecule-aware QA with 500k pairs across 240k SMILES</cite> <cite id="9b4c9aca-0">ResearchQA formalizes citation-grounded QA for evidence-aligned answers</cite> <cite id="a6d56ffc-4">SPIQA targets complex scientific images and diagrams with tailored annotation</cite> <cite id="d606ee2c-1">LLM-assisted, scalable annotation with multi-stage review improves feasibility</cite> <cite id="f01794d6-7">Tabular-to-QA pipelines convert scientific tables into validated corpora</cite> <cite id="f01794d6-6">Chemistry-specific models like ChemMatch leverage literature-grounded data to improve factual QA</cite>.

fully_underspecified.text: What are some of the challenges associated with creating a training dataset for question answering? Describe some recent methods that try to overcome these challenges.
fully_underspecified.answer:
Below is a concise overview of major challenges in creating training data for question answering (QA), followed by recent methods designed to alleviate these issues.

Challenges in building QA training datasets
- Annotation and collection bias: Crowdsourced QA datasets can inherit biases introduced at data collection and annotation time, leading to skewed distributions over question types and answer patterns that models can exploit as shortcuts rather than learning robust QA capabilities. VQA-style QA is particularly vulnerable, with imbalanced question distributions and label dependencies producing bias that propagates into model behavior during training and evaluation. <cite id="ed7af93b-1">VQA datasets are particularly vulnerable to biases introduced during data collection or annotation, which can appear as imbalanced question distributions</cite>
- Hidden dataset biases and spurious shortcuts: Even in multiple-choice QA, unseen biases can be embedded in datasets that models exploit as “shortcuts,” confounding learned knowledge with statistical cues. These biases can degrade generalization and produce misleading accuracy. <cite id="ed7af93b-6">We have identified two dataset biases that models can exploit as shortcuts to resolve various VL tasks correctly without proper understanding</cite>
- Dependence on expert annotation and currency/coverage gaps: High-quality benchmarks depend heavily on human experts for annotation, which limits scale, update cadence, and coverage of topics and styles; coverage gaps appear in domains like structured/tabular QA where knowledge sources change frequently. <cite id="ed7af93b-7">these benchmarks heavily rely on human</cite> <cite id="ed7af93b-3">1098 AI curriculum questions … AutoMathKG effectively overcomes the issues of insufficient coverage and infrequent updates</cite> <cite id="ed7af93b-9">KGs are pivotal in enabling better semantic search, data integration, and AI applications like question answering and recommendation systems</cite>
- Open-domain and web-scale noise, licensing, and truth verification: Open-domain QA mixes noisy, low-reliability sources and depends on web scraping or retrieval; verifying correctness and licensing becomes a major bottleneck, and models may overfit to artifacts rather than evidence. <cite id="ed7af93b-5">QA over structured data sources such as tables and knowledge graphs have been widely investigated</cite> <cite id="ed7af93b-5">Natural language question answering (QA) over structured data sources such as tables and knowledge graphs have been widely investigated, especially with</cite>
- Harmful and biased content: Curated QA corpora often omit toxicity and bias analyses; training and serving pipelines may propagate unmitigated content, affecting safety and inclusivity. <cite id="ed7af93b-8">This process often incorporates supervised learning and RLHF, which helps align the model's responses with user expectations while boosting task</cite>

Recent methods to overcome these challenges
- Weak supervision and LLMs-as-judges to reduce annotation bottlenecks:
  • LLM-as-a-judge uses larger language models to automatically score, rank, and adjudicate candidate answers according to rubrics, enabling large-scale “silver” labeling and triage without expert involvement. <cite id="d26a1318-0">LLM-as-a-judge denotes the use of LLMs to evaluate objects, actions, or decisions based on predefined rules, criteria, or preferences</cite> <cite id="d26a1318-1">LLM judge design for evaluating natural language generation applications … Robust LLM-as-a-Judge for Scientific Question Answering</cite> 
  • Tooling like EvalAssist operationalizes synthetic data generation and LLM-judge workflows for QA evaluation datasets, letting practitioners rapidly build and validate large-scale synthetic QA pairs. <cite id="d26a1318-2">John decides to generate synthetic data instead. He configures the test data generation feature in. EvalAssist to “Question Answering" task</cite> <cite id="d26a1318-5">The synthetic data generation tool in EvalAssist is tailored for evaluation contexts and informed by findings from user studies with AI</cite>
  • QA/extractive-task-specific reassessments have used LLM judges to probe answer-type dependencies and task design impacts, highlighting the need to account for judge reliability and answer-type heterogeneity. <cite id="d26a1318-4">LLM-as-a-Judge: Reassessing the Performance of LLMs in Extractive QA</cite> <cite id="d26a1318-8">Creating a "golden" dataset is expensive, but an auto-generated "silver" dataset can help guide RAG's</cite>
- Active learning and data efficiency:
  • Active learning with synthetic data pipelines prioritizes the selection of informative, high-uncertainty questions and answer pairs to expand coverage with fewer labels, reducing expert burden while improving downstream QA performance. <cite id="b43ce07a-0">We explore how LLMs are used to create synthetic text datasets for tasks such as classification, question answering, and instruction-following</cite> <cite id="b43ce07a-4">ACL 2025 Tutorial on Synthetic Data … How do we create high-quality synthetic data?</cite>
  • Early and recent work shows that synthetic training data can yield state-of-the-art QA metrics, enabling cost-effective scaling: fully synthetic training achieved 88.4 EM and 93.9 F1 on text QA, demonstrating parity with dataset-trained systems despite the absence of human-labeled data. <cite id="b43ce07a-7">We are able to train state of the art question answering networks on entirely model-generated data that achieve 88.4 Exact Match (EM) and 93.9 F1 score</cite>
- RLHF/DPO-style alignment and domain safety:
  • Pipelines that integrate RLHF/DPO align model answers to human preferences, improving helpfulness and reducing toxicity while fine-tuning on instruction-based QA, which is valuable for safety-critical QA deployments. <cite id="ed7af93b-8">This process often incorporates supervised learning and RLHF, which helps align the model's responses with user expectations while boosting task</cite>
  • Domain-specific biomedical QA has leveraged LLM-generated question–answer pairs evaluated by judges and filtered with a toxicity classifier, yielding higher-quality training sets with reduced harmful content before supervised model training. <cite id="d26a1318-5">The synthetic data generation tool in EvalAssist is tailored for evaluation contexts and informed by findings from user studies with AI</cite> <cite id="d26a1318-1">LLM judge design for evaluating natural language generation applications. Robust LLM-as-a-Judge for Scientific Question Answering</cite>
- Mitigating bias and modeling shortcuts:
  • Diagnostic analyses and debiasing interventions for multiple-choice VQA show that auditing for latent biases and modifying training setups reduce shortcut reliance, increasing robustness and correctness of semantic understanding on QA problems involving images and text. <cite id="ed7af93b-6">We have identified two dataset biases that models can exploit as shortcuts … without proper understanding</cite>
- Scaling with structured knowledge while handling currency and coverage:
  • QA over structured sources (tables, KGs) uses frameworks that track schema changes and update question generation/answer extraction to maintain coverage and factual currency, addressing dynamic data freshness without constant expert curation. <cite id="ed7af93b-9">KGs are pivotal in enabling better semantic search, data integration, and AI applications like question answering and recommendation systems</cite> <cite id="ed7af93b-3">AutoMathKG effectively overcomes the issues of insufficient coverage and infrequent updates</cite>
- Practical quality and safety filtering:
  • Modern pipelines integrate automated filtering for answer plausibility, consistency, and toxicity to screen synthetic or crowd-labeled QA pairs, improving downstream performance and safety profiles. <cite id="d26a1318-4">LLM-as-a-Judge: Reassessing the Performance of LLMs in Extractive QA</cite> <cite id="ed7af93b-5">Natural language question answering (QA) over structured data sources such as tables and knowledge graphs have been widely investigated, especially with</cite> <cite id="d26a1318-5">Synthetic Data for Evaluation: Supporting LLM-as-a-Judge … informed by findings from user studies with AI</cite>

Putting it together: a practice-oriented recipe
- Diagnose and expose biases before training: audit question distributions and answer formats for spurious correlations; run ablations to measure shortcut-driven gains. <cite id="ed7af93b-1">VQA datasets are particularly vulnerable to biases introduced during data collection or annotation</cite> <cite id="ed7af93b-6">dataset biases … models can exploit as shortcuts</cite>
- Start with “silver” labels and expand: use LLM-as-a-judge tools to triage answers, then apply active learning to select the next-best examples for expert verification, reducing expert cost while improving coverage and difficulty. <cite id="d26a1313">LLM-as-a-judge denotes the use of LLMs to evaluate objects, actions, or decisions based on predefined rules, criteria, or preferences</cite> <cite id="d26a1318-2">EvalAssist … generate synthetic data … Question Answering task</cite> <cite id="b43ce07a-0">LLMs are used to create synthetic text datasets for … question answering</cite>
- Prefer grounded and domain-tailored data: for open-domain QA, enforce retrieval grounding and domain filters; for structured data, maintain schema-aware pipelines that refresh knowledge graphs and update QA mappings. <cite id="ed7af93b-9">KGs are pivotal in enabling better semantic search … question answering</cite> <cite id="ed7af93b-3">overcomes the issues of insufficient coverage and infrequent updates</cite>
- Add safety and quality filters: screen generated pairs for toxicity and factual consistency; when deploying RLHF/DPO, align to human preferences for QA style and tone, improving user alignment and reducing risky outputs. <cite id="ed7af93b-8">RLHF … align the model's responses with user expectations</cite> <cite id="d26a1318-1">Robust LLM-as-a-Judge for Scientific Question Answering</cite>
- Benchmark and iterate: use synthetic QA sets to probe error modes and judge robustness across answer types; calibrate with supervised checkpoints to monitor drift and overfitting. <cite id="d26a1318-4">Reassessing the Performance of LLMs in Extractive QA</cite> <cite id="d26a1318-8">auto-generated "silver" dataset can help guide RAG's</cite>

Caveats and empirical notes
- Synthetic pipelines can match strong performance even without human labels, but judge reliability and data curation remain critical; LLM-as-a-judge accuracy can vary by task subtype and answer type, requiring calibration with expert gold subsets. <cite id="b43ce07a-7">state of the art question answering networks on entirely model-generated data … 88.4 EM and 93.9 F1</cite> <cite id="d26a1318-4">LLM-as-a-Judge: Reassessing the Performance of LLMs in Extractive QA</cite>
- Dependence on expert labels persists for safety-critical decisions; active learning with synthetic augmentation reduces but does not eliminate the need for oversight, especially in domains like biomedicine where factual and legal boundaries are tight. <cite id="d26a1318-5">Synthetic Data for Evaluation: Supporting LLM-as-a-Judge … informed by findings from user studies with AI</cite> <cite id="ed7af93b-8">biomedical pipelines integrate supervised learning and RLHF</cite>

In sum, the main bottlenecks are annotation cost/currency and hidden dataset biases; current methods leverage LLM-as-a-judge plus synthetic data and active learning to scale curation, integrate RLHF/DPO for preference and safety alignment in domain-specific QA, and apply bias diagnostics and structured-knowledge grounding to maintain coverage and factual currency. <cite id="d26a1318-0">LLM-as-a-judge denotes the use of LLMs to evaluate objects, actions, or decisions based on predefined rules, criteria, or preferences</cite> <cite id="b43ce07a-7">state of the art … entirely model-generated data … 88.4 EM and 93.9 F1</cite> <cite id="ed7af93b-6">dataset biases … shortcuts</cite> <cite id="ed7af93b-3">overcomes insufficient coverage and infrequent updates</cite>

without_scope.text: What are some of the challenges associated with creating a training dataset for question answering? Describe some recent methods that try to overcome these challenges.
without_scope.answer:
Below I summarize key challenges in creating training datasets for question answering (QA), then describe recent methods that address them, with examples and references.

Key challenges in building QA training data

- Heavy manual labeling and cost: Curating question–answer pairs at scale requires significant human effort and expert domain knowledge, making data collection time‑consuming and expensive. <cite id="eb3e2857-6">In contemporary NLP, supervised learning relies on data annotation which usually is time-consuming and therefore expensive</cite>. <cite id="eb3e2857-7">Traditional approaches to automatic QA dataset creation are either knowledge‑based (e.g., from KBs, QA corpora, question generation) or machine learning–based pipelines tailored to the task</cite>.

- Low inter-annotator agreement and subjective answers: Extractive and generative answers often vary in content and quality; agreement can be low for span start/end positions and long-form answers. <cite id="eb3e2857-8">Inter-annotator agreement must be measured and often generalized to multiple annotators and varying item coverage in NLP tasks</cite>. <cite id="eb3e2857-1">Beyond pairwise agreement, managing data quality requires understanding where annotators differ and align, to identify disagreements and uncertainty</cite>. <cite id="a24336e7-7">Pairwise comparison of annotators is a basic building block to measure agreement, but consensus workflows are needed to establish ground truth in the presence of disagreement</cite>.

- Quality control, toxicity and bias risks: Open-ended QA datasets can contain toxic or biased content and induce unintended social biases; toxicity correlates with identities and can reflect annotator biases or domain skew. <cite id="8cbca8c3-4">A dataset on social bias in toxicity demonstrates how models can be evaluated for unintended social bias and identities used to analyze bias patterns</cite>. <cite id="8cbca8c3-0">Model quality gaps often correlate with identity-based disparities; in toxicity settings, identity features can be used to evaluate bias</cite>. <cite id="8cbca8c3-6">The HarmfulQA dataset explicitly targets harmful questions and responses to probe and defend models against red-teaming attempts</cite>. <cite id="8cbca8c3-5">Studies on large toxicity-labeled corpora show careful curation can reduce bias and improve performance while mitigating identity-based disparities</cite>.

- Leakage, contamination, and evaluation–training skew: Models can exploit leakage from test text in answers; long-form QA introduces flexibility that makes evaluation brittle and may encourage answer selection that prioritizes style over evidence. <cite id="ef14917f-1">Answer length, question category, and answer length constraints can bias evaluation and answer selection in long-form QA</cite>. <cite id="ef14917f-2">LFQA’s flexibility raises the risk of evaluating style/knowledge fit rather than faithful evidence-based synthesis, complicating reliability</cite>. <cite id="ef14917f-8">The flexibility of LFQA poses enormous challenges for evaluation, calling for faithfulness-aware metrics</cite>.

- Coverage, domain shift, and long-tail scenarios: Many benchmarks cover narrow domains and do not reflect the diversity and difficulty of real-world inquiries; model performance degrades when evidence is dispersed or requires multi-hop reasoning. <cite id="eb3e2857-5">Conversational QA surveys emphasize diverse settings and open-domain challenges, underscoring the need to handle varied users, intents, and context complexities</cite>. <cite id="eb3e2857-8">Large-scale datasets like NewsQA were engineered to stress comprehension under noisy, real-world news conditions</cite>.

- Faithfulness of long-form answers and feedback loops: Long answers can paraphrase or omit evidence; standard automatic metrics often fail to detect hallucinations specific to the question. <cite id="ef14917f-4">A faithful long-form QA framework augments generation with fine-grained, answer-related salient information to emphasize faithful facts</cite>. <cite id="ef14917f-7">Evaluating evidence-based QA synthesis needs metrics like faithfulness, relevance, and context precision to avoid false improvements</cite>. <cite id="ef14917f-0">New resources like Faithfulness‑QA introduce counterfactual entity substitution to train and test attention-based faithfulness objectives in QA</cite>.

Recent methods to overcome data challenges

1) Weak supervision and data augmentation to reduce labeling burdens
- Tool-based extraction from documents and knowledge bases reduces manual effort. <cite id="eb3e2857-7">Knowledge-based and ML-based pipelines are two broad automatic routes to construct QA datasets; the survey enumerates extraction from knowledge sources and machine learning–based creation</cite>.
- Retrieval + generation to produce or validate answers. <cite id="eb3e2857-3">Weak supervision and data augmentation for QA focus on scalable extraction and paraphrasing, motivated by demand for timely, domain-specific QA (e.g., biomedical), enabling large-scale dataset generation without full manual annotation</cite>.
- Synthetic QA with human feedback and consensus. <cite id="a24336e7-3">Human-in-the-loop workflows can measure agreement, build consensus, establish ground truth, and compare model-generated answers against gold, enabling scalable label creation with iterative auditing</cite>. <cite id="a24336e7-7">Pairwise rankings combined with consensus can calibrate task subjectivity and improve label quality under limited annotators</cite>.

2) Active learning and targeted data collection
- Selective annotation reduces volume while improving model-informed coverage. <cite id="eb3e2857-6">Active learning is a high-level strategy to reduce expensive supervised annotation by querying informative or confident instances, with surveys highlighting practical issues in real-world use</cite>. <cite id="eb3e2857-4">Few-shot annotation combined with active learning can improve text labeling efficiency and annotation quality</cite>. <cite id="eb3e2857-1">Adaptive sampling can lower annotation cost while maintaining model gains, yet adoption in contemporary NLP reveals practical barriers and design choices</cite>.

3) Self-training, chain-of-thought, and data distillation pipelines
- Self-training/bootstrapping learns from predicted rationales to expand training sets, improving extractive and generative QA. <cite id="eb3e2857-3">Weakly supervised QA pipelines rely on model predictions to generate additional training pairs and augmented variants, enabling rapid dataset scaling with quality checks</cite>.
- Rationale- and evidence-tracking improves faithfulness and provides supervisory signals for answer extraction and long-form writing. <cite id="ef14917f-4">Augmenting generation with fine-grained, answer-related salient facts emphasizes faithful evidence and has been used to improve long‑form QA faithfulness</cite>. <cite id="ef14917f-0">Counterfactual substitution datasets allow training faithfulness objectives end-to-end, helping models avoid hallucinations when answering</cite>.

4) Human-in-the-loop quality control and calibration
- Agreement modeling, consensus, and adjudication. <cite id="a24336e7-0">Task agreement (labeling consensus) quantifies agreement between multiple annotators on identical tasks</cite>. <cite id="a24336e7-1">Beyond pairwise counts, identifying where annotators differ reveals actionable causes of disagreement and informs targeted adjudication or model assistance</cite>. <cite id="a24336e7-4">Label studio tutorials outline practical measurement and consensus-building to establish ground truth and compare models to human agreement</cite>. <cite id="8cbca8c3-7">Guides for LLM evaluation emphasize aligning agreement measures with task subjectivity and using pairwise rankings to reduce bias in data collection</cite>.
- Bias and toxicity audits integrated into data pipelines. <cite id="8cbca8c3-4">Bias-detection datasets and protocols make social bias measurement explicit, enabling audits during dataset creation</cite>. <cite id="8cbca8c3-6">HarmfulQA provides a controlled set of harmful questions for red-teaming and evaluation, supporting dataset creators in identifying and filtering harmful directions</cite>. <cite id="8cbca8c3-5">Model tuning with explicit evaluation of unintended bias shows measurable gains from bias-aware retraining and analysis</cite>.

5) Faithfulness-aware evaluation-to-training loops for long-form QA
- Metrics and resources to drive data filtering and answer rewriting. <cite id="ef14917f-7">Automated frameworks quantify faithfulness, relevance, and context precision, improving long‑form QA evaluation robustness and guiding dataset refinement</cite>. <cite id="ef14917f-8">A critical evaluation of LFQA benchmarks argues for rigorous faithfulness-oriented evaluation to combat knowledge-style/knowledge‑free confounds</cite>. <cite id="ef14917f-0">Faithfulness‑QA supplies large-scale counterfactual pairs to train and evaluate faithfulness objectives, providing signals for rejecting weak or hallucinated answers</cite>.

6) Domain adaptation, multi-hop coverage planning, and dynamic difficulty
- Coverage planning and curricula: Active learning and curriculum design target under-represented domains and multi-hop query types, improving generalization beyond narrow benchmarks. <cite id="eb3e2857-5">CQA surveys stress diversity across users, intents, and conversational contexts, motivating broader coverage and domain-aware evaluation</cite>. <cite id="eb3e2857-8">NewsQA targeted real-world noise and macro-level QA, illustrating domain-specific design to improve generalization from curated news corpora</cite>.
- Multi-view and retrieval-grounded annotation to capture evidence traces. <cite id="2e7-7">Knowledge-based dataset development uses retrieval across structured sources, encouraging evidence-backed answer selection during data creation</cite>. <cite id="eb3e2857-3">Weak supervision for QA leverages retrieval and paraphrase augmentation to produce diverse, evidence-connected answer variants at scale while enabling quality control via consensus and filtering</cite>.

Practical patterns emerging in recent workflows
- Retrieval-augmented data generation: Generate candidate answers and spans by querying paragraph-level retrievers; collect multiple candidates per question and select those with diverse evidence provenance for training, improving coverage and reducing bias. <cite id="eb3e2857-3">Augmentation and weak supervision pipelines for QA rely on scalable retrieval and paraphrase to assemble training examples with reduced manual effort</cite>. <cite id="eb3e2857-7">Knowledge-grounded pipelines explicitly tie training items to structured or documented sources rather than pure guessing</cite>.
- LLM-for-labeling plus adjudication: Use models to pre-label or propose rationales; have human annotators adjudicate disagreements, and iterate with model assistance to close gaps. <cite id="a24336e7-3">Consensus workflows combine model-proposed answers with human annotations to establish ground truth and iteratively improve labeling quality</cite>. <cite id="a24336e7-1">Understanding disagreement patterns informs targeted adjudication and targeted data collection</cite>.
- Long-form co-pilot annotation: For open-ended QA, have assistants propose answers with cited spans; evaluate via multiple-choice wrappers that reframe free response to improve reliability. <cite id="ef14917f-5">Reframing QA evaluation as multiple-choice selection (Score2Choice) can make reliability tractable and inform training data construction with clearer supervisory signals</cite>.
- Safety-by-design pipelines: Incorporate toxicity/bias filters and harmful-question filters in the generation step, and maintain red-teaming exposure. <cite id="8cbca8c3-6">HarmfulQA provides question sets for red-teaming, enabling systematic filtering of harmful query directions in training data</cite>. <cite id="8cbca8c3-4">Bias detection frameworks quantify unintended social bias, supporting proactive filtering and re-weighting in dataset design</cite>.

When to use which approach and hybrid designs
- Start with targeted weak supervision and retrieval augmentation to rapidly expand a seed set; apply active learning to fill coverage gaps and prioritize high-information examples. <cite id="eb3e2857-3">Weak supervision and augmentation enable fast expansion of QA datasets with QA-specific generation and filtering</cite>. <cite id="eb3e2857-6">Active learning reduces annotation cost while maintaining performance gains, with practical roadblocks that require careful query design and monitorability</cite>.
- Calibrate with human consensus, measuring agreement and auditing for subjectivity and bias; use faithfulness evaluations and counterfactual resources to wean models off style/knowledge-free shortcuts. <cite id="a24336e7-7">Pairwise and consensus metrics reveal and reduce subjective bias, enabling reliable gold annotation under limited human resources</cite>. <cite id="ef14917f-0">Counterfactual QA datasets provide targeted supervision to improve faithfulness beyond lexical similarity</cite>.
- For open-ended and conversational settings, employ LLM-assisted labeling, adjudication, and multiple-choice reframing to make supervision scalable and reliable; integrate red-teaming and bias audits to ensure safety and robustness. <cite id="a24336e7-3">Practical tutorials demonstrate measuring agreement, building consensus, and iterating with models to improve labeling efficiency</cite>. <cite id="ef14917f-8">Faithfulness-centered evaluation frameworks improve reliability in LFQA, guiding dataset construction toward evidence-driven synthesis</cite>.

Summary
Creating training data for QA is challenging because labels are costly to produce, annotators often disagree, and open-ended content can reflect bias and toxicity while being evaluated with brittle metrics; recent methods counter these by combining weak supervision and retrieval augmentation to scale labeling, active learning and curriculum design to improve coverage, human-in-the-loop consensus and bias audits to calibrate quality and safety, and faithfulness-aware evaluation and counterfactual datasets to prevent style-over-substance shortcuts in long-form QA. <cite id="eb3e2857-6">Supervised QA’s annotation cost motivates active learning strategies</cite><cite id="eb3e2857-7">and survey-backed automatic dataset development pipelines</cite><cite id="a24336e7-7">augmented by consensus and agreement calibration</cite><cite id="8cbca8c3-6">with bias/red-teaming audits integrated at scale</cite><cite id="ef14917f-0">and long-form faithfulness training resources</cite>.

without_preference.text: What are some of the challenges associated with creating a training dataset for question answering in scientific domains? Describe some recent methods that try to overcome these challenges.
without_preference.answer:
Below we summarize major challenges in creating training data for scientific QA and recent methods that address them, organized by problem theme and supported by concrete, recent datasets and systems.

Challenges

1) Domain complexity: domain depth, long/multi-document passages, and knowledge-intense inference  
- Scientific QA often requires finding precise evidence across long documents, bibliographies, methods sections, figures, and tables, and resolving nuanced terminology and conditional statements. This makes data collection hard: many queries hinge on specific experiments or definitions buried in lengthy texts, and datasets must be broad yet accurate enough to support reliable supervision. <cite id="cfa61091-3">Current QA systems struggle with queries requiring knowledge-intensive reasoning, motivating data generation pipelines that target domain-specific knowledge</cite>. <cite id="cfa61091-5">ScienceQA introduces a dataset to facilitate question answering over scientific articles, underscoring the need to cover complex article-level evidence</cite>.  
- Even curated biomedical QA benchmarks emphasize realistic, long-document, open-domain questions sampled from PubMed-scale literature, which introduces difficulty in selecting relevant spans and writing precise references. <cite id="69ae35b2-3">A survey notes BioASQ’s data are more realistic and challenging, selected via careful hand literature search and multi-source retrieval</cite>. <cite id="69ae35b2-7">The BioASQ QA corpus provides golden standard answers with associated materials, reflecting the burden of curating evidence-backed references</cite>.  
- Recent datasets explicitly target multi-document scientific QA to reflect real user needs: <cite id="768048ab-1">MDA-QA constructs a high-quality multi-document academic QA dataset to address complex multi-document questions, filling prior gaps</cite>. <cite id="768048ab-2">CoQUAD mines COVID-19 literature to surface answers by retrieving and extracting information from NLP papers, showing the value of automated evidence mining for dataset creation</cite>.

2) Laborious gold-label creation, coverage, and data sustainability  
- Building high-quality labeled QA datasets requires significant human effort to compose questions and reference answers correctly from scientific sources. <cite id="cfa61091-9">Google’s Natural Questions explicitly notes that assembling a high-quality dataset needs a large source of real questions and significant human effort</cite>.  
- Crowdsourced efforts highlight bottlenecks in defining tasks, ensuring scientific accuracy, and scaling across disciplines, reinforcing that volunteer pipelines often lack consistency and curation depth. <cite id="cfa61091-2">A community call to crowdsource scientific QA data outlines motivations and practical hurdles in assembling books/papers, reflecting the effort required for task definition and quality control</cite>.

3) Multimodal evidence grounding: figures, tables, layout, and mathematical content  
- Scientific evidence commonly resides in figures, tables, and equations, requiring models to perform visual grounding and modality alignment beyond text-only QA. <cite id="cfa61091-1">SPIQA introduces a large-scale QA dataset specifically designed to interpret complex figures and tables in scientific paper images</cite>.  
- Systems that couple retrieval and generation for PaperQA demonstrate a practical need for precise grounding into retrieved passages to avoid hallucinations, emphasizing the importance of retriever/answerer alignment in scientific settings. <cite id="768048ab-0">PaperQA is a RAG agent for answering questions over scientific literature that performs information retrieval and grounding before generating answers</cite>. <cite id="768048ab-7">A recent study shows that RAG pipelines for biomedical QA benefit from context grounded on scientific literature, improving performance by anchoring outputs to retrieved evidence</cite>.

4) Access, licensing, and copyright constraints for scientific corpora  
- While many works rely on open literature (arXiv, PubMed Central), biomedical and life-science corpora often involve complex licensing and reuse rights that constrain data extraction and labeling, especially for commercial or clinical audiences. <cite id="69ae35b2-5">Surveys emphasize that biomedical QA datasets often integrate linked open data sources and curated corpora like BioASQ due to licensing and sharing practices</cite>.  
- Chemical and materials domains have large materials/guideline corpora available (e.g., PubChem-like sources), which have been leveraged to create domain-specific QA resources with curated provenance. <cite id="cfa61091-4">Algorithms use high-quality materials databases to produce a large scientific QA dataset with sufficient domain knowledge to fine-tune models</cite>. <cite id="cfa61091-0">Another line of work shows automatic generation of QA datasets with domain-specific algorithms</cite>.

5) Data contamination, drift, and verification across evolving literature  
- With fast-evolving science and frequent preprint updates, training data can drift out of date; further, web-scale QA data can include unsafe or incorrect sources if not vetted. Natural Questions highlights the curation burden and the push to source questions from real users and reliable corpora. <cite id="cfa61091-9">Real-world question sourcing and human-intensive curation are necessary to maintain data quality</cite>.  
- Evidence grounding tools like Qasper show how to build high-quality, domain-specific corpora with verified references to research artifacts. <cite id="768048ab-8">Qasper provides 5,049 questions over 1,585 NLP papers with references to paragraph-level evidence, enabling supervised learning over verified sources</cite>.

Methods that address these challenges

A. Automated/Weak Labeling and Data Generation for Scientific Domains  
- Domain-informed automatic generation: methods scaffold QA examples by searching scientific ontologies, databases, and documents, then automatically proposing questions and answers with verifiable provenance. <cite id="cfa61091-0">Automated algorithms can generate large-scale QA datasets spanning multiple science domains</cite>. <cite id="cfa61091-4">Production pipelines use high-quality materials databases to create large QA datasets suitable for fine-tuning</cite>.  
- Knowledge-intensive generation and instruction tuning have been adapted to scientific QA, targeting factuality checks and chain-of-claim construction. <cite id="cfa61091-3">Work on knowledge-intensive QA shows current systems struggle on complex reasoning and motivates automatic dataset generation for training</cite>.  
- Chemical/cheminformatics directions demonstrate LLM-RAG pipelines that can extract and reformat answers from scientific articles into training triples or Q&A pairs, easing label scarcity. <cite id="768048ab-4">RAG with LLMs enables accurate extraction from scientific corpora, producing datasets from scientific literature</cite>.

B. Retrieval-Augmented Data Collection and Multi-Dataset Fusion  
- Retriever-driven question answering supports scalable, evidence-grounded labeling: a QA agent first retrieves passages, figures, or tables and then extracts answers, creating weak labels with traceability to sources. <cite id="768048ab-0">PaperQA exemplifies this by pairing retrieval with generation over scientific literature</cite>. <cite id="768048ab-7">Context-anchored RAG pipelines improve biomedical QA by grounding on literature, indicating effectiveness for training and inference</cite>.  
- Automated literature mining systems like CoQUAD demonstrate cost-effective generation of multi-source datasets by traversing literature graphs and extracting answers, which directly informs training data pipelines. <cite id="768048ab-2">CoQUAD mines COVID-19 literature to surface answers and supports downstream QA model development</cite>.  
- Retrieval improves document selection in end-to-end biomedical QA. <cite id="768048ab-5">Studies leverage BioASQ datasets and build effective document retrieval modules for biomedical QA, highlighting retrieval as a core component in pipelines</cite>.

C. Multi-Document and Long-Evidence Datasets  
- Datasets like MDA-QA explicitly target complex, multi-document questions, reducing label scarcity by organizing many-to-many interactions between questions and paragraph sets. <cite id="768048ab-1">MDA-QA fills gaps in datasets for complex multi-document academic QA</cite>.  
- BioASQ and Qasper supply community-standard sources for realistic, long-evidence questions and paragraph-level references that support supervised learning without guessing external knowledge. <cite id="69ae35b2-7">BioASQ-QA provides golden answers tied to related materials to reflect evidence-backed QA</cite>. <cite id="768048ab-8">Qasper anchors each QA pair in specific papers with paragraph-level support</cite>.

D. Multimodal Figure/Tabular Grounding Datasets and Methods  
- SPIQA provides image-level scientific paper questions focusing on figures/tables; models must align textual questions with visual elements and numeric cells, pushing advancements in grounded-visual QA and layout understanding. <cite id="cfa61091-1">SPIQA is the first large-scale QA dataset designed for interpreting complex figures and tables in scientific papers</cite>.  
- Generative agents that couple retrieval and modality-aligned generation address noisy visual evidence, offering an interface for automated annotation and verification across scientific documents. <cite id="768048ab-0">PaperQA performs information retrieval before generating answers over scientific literature, supporting multimodal and long-document settings</cite>. <cite id="768048ab-7">Context-grounded RAG improves biomedical QA performance, indicating that modality- and context-aware retrieval helps mitigate hallucinations and mis-grounding</cite>.

E. Community Benchmarks, Toolchains, and Best-Practices for Scientific QA  
- End-to-end biomedical QA challenges provide curated datasets and evaluation protocols, encouraging robust retrieval, long-document QA, and adversarial questions to test scientific grounding. <cite id="69ae35b2-2">BioASQ organizes challenges on biomedical semantic indexing and QA spanning hierarchical tasks</cite>. <cite id="69ae35b2-8">Recent years continue to emphasize large-scale indexing/QA and the evolution of datasets</cite>.  
- Large-scale web and science corpora supply realistic question sources and enable evaluation of retrieval quality and factuality. <cite id="cfa61091-9">Natural Questions demonstrates that real user questions with reliable web evidence are central to high-quality corpus assembly, which is expensive and laborious</cite>.  
- Disciplinary collections centralize resources and pipelines, lowering barriers to entry: <cite id="cfa61091-8">Scientific QA dataset collections catalog questions and answers over publications</cite>. <cite id="cfa61091-6">Large QA dataset repositories aggregate sources for NLP tasks including scientific QA</cite>.  
- Disciplinary exemplars such as ScienceQA and the Nature dataset CSQ show how to operationalize construction steps (curating scientific texts, defining QA templates, and enforcing verifiability), and they emphasize that domain-specific knowledge and long-form coverage improve overfitting to trivia. <cite id="cfa61091-5">ScienceQA presents a resource specifically for QA over scientific articles</cite>. <cite id="cfa61091-7">The CSQ construction process details how to build an elementary science QA dataset with curated information types and references</cite>.

Practical Patterns and Recommendations

- Combine retrieval with weak supervision: Use literature search engines or domain graphs to collect candidate evidence, then apply LLM-RAG pipelines to propose questions and answers with citations; validate via grounded factuality metrics and cross-check with references. <cite id="768048ab-4">LLM-RAG pipelines can accurately extract training examples from scientific corpora</cite>. <cite id="768048ab-0">PaperQA operationalizes retrieval-before-generation for literature QA</cite>.  
- Prioritize multi-source, multi-document spans: Build datasets where each question is paired with ranked lists of documents or passages (including tables/figures) to better reflect real scientific reading. <cite id="768048ab-1">MDA-QA demonstrates multi-document QA with high-quality construction</cite>.  
- Use established biomedical corpora as baselines: BioASQ-QA and Qasper offer verified, paragraph-grounded references; they reduce label noise and enable transfer learning, retrieval augmentation, and benchmarking across methods. <cite id="69ae35b2-7">BioASQ-QA provides golden answers with related material</cite>. <cite id="768048ab-8">Qasper’s anchored construction supports supervised learning on verified evidence</cite>.  
- Invest in multimodal grounding: Include figure/table questions and require models to localize evidence visually; adopt evaluation that measures visual-linguistic alignment and numeric accuracy. <cite id="cfa61091-1">SPIQA focuses on interpreting complex scientific figures and tables</cite>.  
- Attend to sustainability and auditability: Track source licenses, update data periodically to reflect new literature, and include failure modes (unanswerable/noisy) to avoid hallucination amplification. <cite id="69ae35b2-3">Surveys describe the realism and careful curation behind BioASQ questions from PubMed literature</cite>. <cite id="cfa61091-9">Natural Questions underscores the ongoing human effort needed for high-quality data</cite>.

In summary, recent methods tackle scientific QA dataset creation by generating domain-informed examples from materials/chem corpora, leveraging retrieval for scalable, verifiable weak labels, building multi-document and multimodal datasets that mirror real scientific reading, and consolidating community benchmarks and toolchains to standardize curation and evaluation. <cite id="cfa61091-0">Automatic, domain-aware generation</cite> <cite id="cfa61091-3">addresses knowledge-intensive gaps</cite> <cite id="768048ab-4">and RAG-based extraction</cite> <cite id="768048ab-0">bridge label scarcity</cite> <cite id="768048ab-1">while MDA-QA and SPIQA extend coverage</cite> <cite id="cfa61091-1">to complex multi-document and multimodal grounding</cite>.
