questions.original_query: What are some biologically-inspired robot path planning algorithms?

query.text: What are some biologically-inspired robot path planning algorithms?
query.answer:
Below are prominent biologically inspired families for robot path planning, with representative algorithms, mechanisms, and quantitative or comparative outcomes reported in recent robotics literature.

Surveys and scope
- <cite id="22dd8b16-0">Surveys catalog path planning methods inspired by animal foraging, swarming, and evolution, with ant colony optimization (ACO) appearing among the most modified and applied for robot navigation</cite>. <cite id="22dd8b16-8">Multi-UAV path planning collections show that most bio-inspired methods originate from eight families: particle swarm optimization (PSO), genetic algorithms (GA), ant colony optimization (ACO), hybrids like A*+PSO, differential evolution, membrane computing, shuffled frog leaping, and ant lion optimization</cite>. <cite id="22dd8b16-1">UAV-focused work similarly evaluates bio-inspired path-optimization such as PSO</cite>.

Swarm-inspired path planning
- Ant-inspired methods (Ant Colony Optimization)
  • Mechanism: Artificial ants lay pheromone on feasible paths; future choices balance pheromone persistence and heuristic desirability (e.g., inverse distance), with evaporation and update rules enabling path smoothing and recalculation under change. <cite id="22dd8b16-0">ACO has been widely adapted for robot path planning</cite>. <cite id="2d23c8d5-2">In dynamic environments, ACO variants differ by pheromone re-initialization strategies to maintain fresh, collision-free paths</cite>. <cite id="2d23c8d5-1">A multi-strategy genetic ant colony method achieved stable optimality on multiscale grid maps</cite>. <cite id="2d23c8d5-3">An improved ant-based planner reduced node consumption by 54.8% and time by 75.88% on grid mazes</cite>. <cite id="2d23c8d5-9">Heuristic improvements to ACO address local optima and premature convergence, making it a widely used method for robotic path planning</cite>. <cite id="2d23c8d5-5">A hybrid ACO–RRT planner for mobile robots cut turns by 69.6% and runtime by 52.94% relative to traditional ACO</cite>. <cite id="2d23c8d5-6">Enhanced ACO variants outperform classical A* on length, runtime, and path quality in comparative studies</cite>. <cite id="2d23c8d5-4">RRT and ACO are both reported effective for AGV path planning, with empirical observations that ACO can hinder AGV efficiency if parameterized poorly</cite>.
  • Use cases: 2D grid/maze worlds, static and dynamic environments, multi-scale obstacles, warehouse-like layouts; often hybridized with sampling-based or grid methods to handle high-dimensional or kinematic constraints. <cite id="2d23c8d5-0">Joint comparisons show A*, RRT*, GA, and ACO as strong baselines across navigation simulations</cite>.

- Swarm/collective-intelligence approaches (PSO and bee/ant swarms)
  • Mechanism: Particle swarms or foraging agents update positions via social–cognitive bests (PSO) or recruitment/visits (bee-inspired), exploring configuration space and exploiting promising routes; often coupled with local motion planners (e.g., Dynamic Window Approach).
  • Evidence: <cite id="8a129a30-2">Self-adaptive learning PSO (SLPSO) with multiple learning strategies solves mobile-robot planning on grids and obstacle fields</cite>. <cite id="8a129a30-1">Improved PSO and improved Dynamic Window Approach combined show superior exploration, accuracy, and dynamic obstacle avoidance compared to baselines</cite>. <cite id="8a129a30-5">PSO–RRT (PSO for planning, RRT for feasibility) is benchmarked against RRT* and informed RRT*, showing competitive or better plan and run times on varied environments</cite>. <cite id="8a129a30-7">Hybrid RRT variants (e.g., MA-RRdT*) with multi-robot extensions improve plan/running times and node counts relative to MA-RRT*, at similar path lengths</cite>. <cite id="8a129a30-8">A robust mobile-robot planner using Smart PSO outperforms conventional PSO on path length and time in static mazes</cite>. <cite id="22dd8b16-8">At scale (multi-UAV), PSO and related swarm heuristics are core bio-inspired drivers</cite>.
  • Notes: PSO-type methods perform well in continuous configuration spaces and can be fast to explore, but grid discretization and local potential fields can still be needed; careful velocity/position bounds and feasibility checks (e.g., DWFA integration) are common. <cite id="8a129a30-1">Improved exploration and dynamic motion control help maintain feasibility and accuracy</cite>.

Evolutionary/biological-inspired metaheuristics
- Genetic Algorithms (GA), Differential Evolution (DE), and variants like A*+GA, Memetic Algorithms
  • Mechanism: Genetic operators (selection, crossover, mutation) or DE mutations/exploits search over path encodings; often combined with local search (memetic) to refine path smoothness and cost.
  • Evidence: <cite id="2d23c8d5-0">Comparative experiments include GA alongside A*, RRT*, and ACO, indicating GA as a credible optimizer over discrete path candidates</cite>. <cite id="2d23c8d5-4">For AGVs, GA-based optimizers are evaluated alongside ACO and local planners</cite>. <cite id="8a129a30-5">Hybrid ACO–RRT and PSO–RRT reflect a broader pattern of combining evolutionary/swarm exploration with kinematic feasibility</cite>. <cite id="22dd8b16-5">Comprehensive tests of GA and PSO on 2D static layouts show robust performance and practical implementation paths</cite>. <cite id="22dd8b16-6">A multi-swarm PSO variant reports average time savings of 75.88% in improved ant-based planning, illustrating how bio-inspired operators can drastically reduce runtime</cite>.
  • Trade-offs: GA/DE can require careful chromosome representations (e.g., via-points + splines) and parameter tuning; effective repair operators are needed to ensure collision- and kinematics-feasible paths.

Bee/colony-inspired and hive/biological pheromone paradigms
- Artificial Bee Colony (ABC) and related hive-inspired pheromone/flower-visiting models
  • Mechanism: ABC mimics bees’ food-search cycles (employed/ onlooker/ scout bees) over solutions (flowers = candidate paths); quality guides recruitment probabilities.
  • Evidence: <cite id="22dd8b16-3">ABC is positioned for static and dynamic environments with goal-directed search</cite>. <cite id="22dd8b16-7">ABC is presented as a swarm-intelligent, computationally economical approach inspired by bees’ foraging</cite>. <cite id="22dd8b16-4">Hybrid improved PSO–gravitational search for multi-robot path planning points to synergy among bio-inspired optimizers</cite>. 
  • When to use: Decoupled global route search followed by local trajectory smoothing; works well with Dubins/Reeds–Shepp models or lattice planners; scalable to multiple robots with conflict-resolution.

Fish/flocking and schooling-inspired methods
- Mechanism: Collective navigation rules (segregation/alignment/cohesion) and repulsion-attract topologies guide a leader or team through obstacles.
  • Evidence: <cite id="8a129a30-3">Grid-based analysis of “foraging-return-to-depot” tasks links schooling/flocking rules to robotic motion and path optimization in modular layouts</cite>. 
  • Notes: These methods distribute robustness and are natural for multi-robot systems, but explicit clearance checks and potential-field shielding are often needed to enforce safety margins. <cite id="8a129a30-3">Path optimization in grid mazes arises directly from movement policies derived from collective behaviors</cite>.

Bacterial/chemotaxis-inspired and chemotactic path search
- Mechanism: Simulating bacteria’s run-and-tumble with attractant gradients over “fitness landscapes” (clearance, length, smoothness) guides path updates.
  • Evidence: <cite id="22dd8b16-0">Surveys include chemotaxis-style foraging mechanisms among ant/bee/swarm families used to solve robot path planning</cite>. 
  • Notes: Chemotaxis is simple to parallelize across many virtual organisms and can navigate sparse or changing obstacles; however, it may drift and require pheromone/gradient memory to converge.

Distributed ant/swarm topologies and runtime/quality outcomes
- <cite id="2d23c8d5-2">ACO in dynamic grid worlds benefits from pheromone reset policies that re-open search, allowing quick recovery when obstacles move or block prior routes</cite>. 
- Quantitative wins: <cite id="2d23c8d5-3">54.8% node consumption and 75.88% time reductions in improved ant-based planners on maze grids</cite>; <cite id="2d23c8d5-5">hybrid ACO–RRT reduces turns by 69.6% and runtime by 52.94% vs. pure ACO</cite>; <cite id="8a129a30-1">PSO+IDWA shows better exploration and dynamic obstacle avoidance than its components</cite>. 
- Trade-offs and fit-to-context: <cite id="2d23c8d5-4">ACO and RRT both can plan AGV paths, but ACO parameterization must avoid inefficiency</cite>; <cite id="2d23c8d3-5">evolved/adaptive ACO variants mitigate premature convergence</cite>. <cite id="8a129a30-6">PSO-based SLPSO methods adapt learning rules across environments</cite>. <cite id="8a129a30-5">PSO–RRT hybridization fuses global search with local feasibility, beating RRT* variants in plan/run time in some tests</cite>.

How to choose and deploy
- Static, grid-maze-like environments with known obstacles: ACO variants (with heuristic distance and evaporation) or improved ACO/SLPSO are effective; adding local planners (DWFA) improves tracking. <cite id="2d23c8d5-9">ACO remains popular for its global exploration and path smoothing</cite>. <cite id="2d23c8d5-3">Large throughput savings in nodes/time can be realized via improved ants or hybrids</cite>.
- Dynamic or clutter-changing environments: Use ACO with re-initialization or PSO with on-line adaptation and obstacle feedback. <cite id="2d23c8d5-2">ACO adapts to moving obstacles via pheromone resets</cite>. <cite id="8a129a30-1">PSO with improved dynamic controllers excels in dynamic avoidance</cite>.
- High-dimensional kinematic constraints (robots/AGVs/UAVs): Prefer hybrids that decouple routing from feasibility, e.g., A*+PSO for route search, or RRT/RRdT* with swarm/evolutionary optimizers for path cost/turns. <cite id="22dd8b16-8">Multi-UAV studies show PSO/GA/ACO hybrids as core building blocks</cite>. <cite id="2d23c8d5-5">ACO–RRT hybrids shorten runtime and reduce turns</cite>. <cite id="8a129a30-5">PSO–RRT plans compared favorably to RRT* and informed RRT*</cite>.
- Multi-robot path planning: Employ swarm/evolutionary optimizers with conflict resolution; benchmarks show runtime and node-count gains over pure RRT variants. <cite id="22dd8b16-4">Hybrid PSO–gravitational search improves multi-robot planning</cite>. <cite id="8a129a30-6">MA-RRdT* outperforms MA-RRT* in plan/run time and node counts</cite>.

Representative algorithms you can try
- Ant Colony Optimization (ACO) for grid/warehouse planning; variants with pheromone evaporation, hill-climbing, and dynamic reinitialization. <cite id="2d23c8d5-2">Dynamic ACO with different re-initialization schemes</cite>. <cite id="2d23c8d5-9">Improved heuristics address premature convergence</cite>.
- Artificial Bee Colony (ABC) when you need a simple, fast swarm engine; integrate with local trajectory planners for dynamic tight spaces. <cite id="22dd8b16-7">ABC as an easy-to-implement foraging-inspired optimizer</cite>. <cite id="22dd8b16-3">Useful in static/dynamic settings with efficient runtime</cite>.
- Particle Swarm Optimization (PSO), including SLPSO and self-adaptive variants; pair with RRT feasibility and dynamic window approach for mobile robots. <cite id="8a129a30-2">SLPSO explores paths via adaptive learning strategies</cite>. <cite id="8a129a30-1">IDWA yields effective dynamic obstacle avoidance</cite>. <cite id="8a129a30-5">PSO–RRT tested against RRT* and informed RRT*</cite>.
- Genetic Algorithms and Memetic Algorithms for path encoding/decoding (via-points, splines), with crossover/mutation guided by path cost and clearance; compare against A*, D*, PRM on 2D layouts. <cite id="2d23c8d5-0">GA competitive with A*, RRT* in simulations</cite>. <cite id="2d23c8d5-5">Hybrid ACO–RRT and PSO–RRT suggest general hybridization strategy</cite>.
- Multi-UAV and multi-robot families: choose PSO, GA, ACO, or DE-based methods and combine with domain-specific constraints (airspace separation, AGV no-go zones). <cite id="22dd8b16-8">Eight core bio-inspired families are repeatedly instantiated for multi-UAV path optimization</cite>. <cite id="24dd8b16-0">Surveys catalog GA, ACO, A*+PSO, DE, membrane computing, SFL, ALO as the go-to biologically inspired engines</cite>.

Practical guidance and caveats
- <cite id="2d23c8d5-4">Even “good” global planners like ACO/ACO-RRT can hurt throughput if they generate long paths or induce frequent replanning; parameter sweeps are essential</cite>. <cite id="2d23c8d5-1">Multi-strategy hybrids (e.g., genetic+ACO) stabilize optimality under varying grid scales</cite>. <cite id="2d23c8d5-6">Enhanced ACO variants frequently beat A* on runtime and path length in head-to-head tests</cite>. <cite id="8a129a30-3">Grid-based analyses show schooling/flocking-inspired policies can be tuned to reduce path cost in modular obstacles</cite>. <cite id="8a129a30-2">Self-adaptive PSO variants improve generalization across clutter levels</cite>.

Summary
- Ant, bee, and swarm-inspired algorithms (ACO, ABC, PSO) are the dominant bio-inspired approaches for robot path planning; they offer robust global search, naturally parallelize, and hybridize well with local planners and sampling-based motion primitives. <cite id="22dd8b16-0">ACO and broader bee/ant families are widely adopted</cite> and <cite id="22dd8b16-8">PSO/GA/DE/ACO form eight core methods in multi-UAV planning</cite>. <cite id="2d23c8d5-9">Heuristic refinements make ACO reliable in robotics</cite>, while <cite id="8a129a30-1">PSO+IDWA improves dynamic obstacle negotiation</cite>, and <cite id="2d23c8d5-5">ACO–RRT and PSO–RRT hybrids deliver concrete runtime and quality gains</cite>. These methods are effective in static and dynamic 2D/3D settings, including AGVs and UAVs, and scale to multi-robot settings with appropriate conflict resolution and runtime control. <cite id="22dd8b16-4">Hybridization (e.g., PSO+gravitational search) addresses multi-robot contention</cite>, and <cite id="8a129a30-6">multi-robot RRT variants show runtime and node-count improvements with smart planners</cite>.

Additional reading
- <cite id="22dd8b16-0">Survey on Robot Path Planning using Bio-inspired Algorithms</cite> and <cite id="22dd8b16-8">Bio-inspired Multi-UAV Path Planning Heuristics: A Review</cite> for curated algorithm families and recent trends.

fully_underspecified.text: What are some robot path planning algorithms?
fully_underspecified.answer:
Here are widely used robot path‑planning algorithm families, representative named algorithms, and when they are typically used:

1) Problem framing: global vs. local planning
- Global planners compute a collision‑free path from start to goal using a map, often returning a route to follow (e.g., along a graph edge or with a velocity profile). <cite id="89265ec8-0">Path planners are commonly categorized into global and local planners; algorithm families include traditional Dijkstra, A*, Probabilistic Roadmaps (PRM), and Rapidly Exploring Random Trees (RRT), with global/local roles depending on task and environment dynamics.</cite> <cite id="89265ec8-3">Dijkstra’s algorithm is typically used for global path planning, while Dynamic Window Area (DWA) is deployed for local path planning.</cite> <cite id="89265ec8-1">RRT is presented as a global path‑planning method based on random sampling, constructing a path from start to goal.</cite>
- Local planners react to immediate surroundings, selecting feasible motions (velocity/acceleration) under dynamic obstacles and kinematic constraints; DWA is a canonical example. <cite id="89265ec8-3">Local planners like DWA operate in real time over short horizons, whereas Dijkstra is used for the global route-level plan.</cite>

2) Classical graph/grid search on discretized or continuous configuration spaces
- Dijkstra’s algorithm: finds shortest paths in graphs; used as a baseline global path planner. <cite id="89265ec8-3">Dijkstra is used for global path planning, forming routes through a graph of states or discretized cells.</cite> <cite id="89265ec8-4">A path planning “map” can be viewed as nodes (key states) and edges (connecting paths), which is the structure Dijkstra and related search planners exploit.</cite>
- A* (Hart–Nilsson–Raphael, 1968): extends Dijkstra by using a heuristic to speed convergence; optimal when heuristics are admissible. <cite id="21f02c63-0">A* was first published by Nils Nilsson and Bertram Raphael in 1968; it achieves better performance by using heuristics to guide search.</cite> <cite id="21f02c63-1">Hart, Nilsson, and Raphael provided a formal basis for heuristic search to find optimal paths in graphs.</cite> <cite id="89265ec8-3">A* (and Dijkstra) are classic global path‑planning methods, sometimes used on discretized maps to return an efficient, collision‑free route.</cite> <cite id="21f02c63-3">A* was proposed in 1968 to solve the global path optimal problem in robot path planning.</cite>

3) Sampling‑based motion planning (probabilistic methods)
- PRM (Probabilistic Roadmap Method): samples the free space and build a graph; queries the roadmap to find a feasible path when needed. <cite id="e08a4a58-1">PRM has two stages: a construction phase that samples and connects points in free space, then a query phase that runs a shortest-path algorithm on the roadmap to return a path between start/goal.</cite> <cite id="e08a4a58-3">PRM’s construction phase builds a graph G; nodes are randomly sampled points in the free space, with edges connected if collision‑free, yielding a “roadmap” that is then queryable for paths.</cite> <cite id="e08a4a58-2">PRM operates by multiple queries including two stages of learning (building the roadmap) and query (solving on the learned graph).</cite> <cite id="e08a4a58-7">PRM builds a single roadmap that becomes a reusable graph for later motion planning queries.</cite>
- RRT (Rapidly Exploring Random Trees): incrementally grows a tree from the start in free space via random samples, efficient in high‑dimensional, nonconvex spaces; outputs a path that may not be optimal. <cite id="e08a4a58-1">RRT grows a tree rooted at the start by sampling configurations and steering toward them, aiming quickly to cover large portions of the state space.</cite> <cite id="e08a4a58-5">RRTs are designed for nonconvex, high‑dimensional spaces, randomly building a “space‑filling” structure to efficiently find feasible paths.</cite> <cite id="e08a4a58-6">Sampling-free-space points and building a graph/tree approximation (“roadmap” or “tree”) is the core idea behind RRT-based path planning.</cite> <cite id="e08a4a58-8">Improved and many variants of RRT have been developed, with recent surveys consolidating advances from 2021–2023 in theory and applications.</cite>
- Typical applications: PRM suits problems where a precomputed roadmap can be built offline and reused, while RRT/RRT‑variants handle high‑DoF robots and dynamic obstacles with fast online replanning. <cite id="e08a4a58-7">PRM/roadmap methods create a reusable structure across multiple queries, enabling efficient repeated planning, while RRT methods pursue online space exploration.</cite> <cite id="e08a4a58-0">Recent RRT reviews document improved variants and application implementations, underscoring RRT’s adaptability to diverse robotics tasks.</cite> <cite id="e08a4a58-4">Surveys of sampling-based path planning emphasize PRM and RRT families as principal methods across complex environments.</cite>

4) Reactive and velocity-level local planners
- DWA (Dynamic Window Area): selects feasible velocities within robot kinematic limits and safety constraints, optimizing a cost over the immediate future while avoiding obstacles; used for local navigation. <cite id="89265ec8-3">DWA is deployed for local path planning, while Dijkstra is used for global planning, highlighting the complementary roles.</cite>
- Vector field/force‑field (aperture‑based) methods and other obstacle‑response strategies produce continuous steering laws that avoid collisions in narrow passages. <cite id="89265ec8-3">Local planners include DWA and related steering/approach methods, contrasted with global path planners like Dijkstra, which provide routes to follow.</cite>

5) Optimization‑based and model‑predictive planning
- Constrained optimization/MPC planners compute control sequences that track a high‑level path while respecting dynamics and obstacles, often operating locally and in real time. <cite id="89265ec8-3">Local planners implement reactive constraints and dynamics (e.g., via DWA-like formulations) to navigate obstacles while tracking global routes produced by A*/Dijkstra.</cite> <cite id="89265ec8-1">Sampling-based global trees (RRT) can provide initial paths for optimization‑based local refinement under kinematic constraints.</cite>
- In practice, hybrid cascades are common: a global planner finds a feasible route, and a local MPC/DWA follows it closely, replanning as obstacles move. <cite id="89265ec8-4">Global planners create a graph/map of key states and connections, which local control then tracks with motion constraints, yielding the “path” as both a graph route and a velocity profile.</cite>

6) Model‑based and hybrid A*/Dijkstra variants
- Hybridization with velocity/kinematic constraints and cost models (e.g., D* Lite, hybrid A*, contracting/expandable grids) improves feasibility and optimality under motion models. <cite id="89265ec8-4">Path mapping as nodes and edges supports algorithms beyond pure grid traversal, including models that encode robot kinematics and obstacles.</cite> <cite id="89265ec8-0">Surveys enumerate traditional Dijkstra, A*, PRM, RRT, and hybrids used across planning tasks, spanning global to local variants.</cite>

7) Learning‑based methods (modern trend)
- Data-driven planners approximate planners/policies using ML (e.g., value/surrogate models of cost-to-goal, imitation learning), often trained on simulated data and refined in practice; they can generalize to novel environments but may require safety wrappers. <cite id="89265ec8-0">Comprehensive surveys of autonomous systems cover both traditional algorithms (A*, PRM, RRT) and modern approaches integrating learning for path planning.</cite> <cite id="89265ec8-5">A recent review of “Traditional and Modern Approaches” highlights algorithm integrations with state‑based decision making and learning‑based control, including combinations with the A* algorithm.</cite> <cite id="89265ec8-6">Expository tutorials trace path planning from classical graph search to modern learning-based methods, documenting the shift toward data-driven navigation.</cite>

Practical guidance and trade‑offs
- Grid/graph search (Dijkstra/A*): exact shortest paths in known maps; efficient, interpretable, but can be brittle in clutter and may ignore dynamics. <cite id="89265ec8-3">Dijkstra/A* are effective global planners on static maps, whereas DWA handles dynamic, local obstacle avoidance.</cite>
- Sampling‑based (PRM/RRT): robust in high‑DoF and unknown/cluttered spaces with probabilistic completeness guarantees; solutions may not be optimal and require tuning of sampling/connectivity heuristics. <cite id="e08a4a58-5">RRTs efficiently explore large, nonconvex spaces with random sampling, providing feasible solutions rather than guaranteed optima.</cite> <cite id="e08a4a58-1">PRM’s two‑phase design makes it reusable (precompute roadmap, then solve), trading online speed for offline construction costs.</cite>
- Local planning: DWA and force‑field methods react to immediate hazards and robot dynamics; they typically execute fast and can replan on tight time scales but need reliable perception. <cite id="89265ec8-3">DWA is explicitly cited as a local path‑planning method in dynamic environments, handling velocity constraints and obstacle costs.</cite>
- Hybrids and MPC: common in practice—global planner outputs a route/path; local MPC/DWA tracks it and replans under kinematic constraints and moving obstacles. <cite id="89265ec8-4">Local tracking over a global path uses nodes/edges plus motion constraints to produce feasible robot motions; this is the operational pattern of practical navigation systems.</cite>

Examples of named algorithms you can use in practice
- Global route/planning: Dijkstra’s algorithm; A*. <cite id="89265ec8-3">Dijkstra and A* serve as standard global path planners in robotics and navigation systems.</cite> <cite id="21f02c63-1">A* provides a formal guarantee for optimal pathfinding given admissible heuristics.</cite>
- Sampling‑based: PRM; RRT and its variants (RRT*, LBTRRT, Informed RRT/δ, Batch Informed Trees). <cite id="e08a4a58-1">PRM and RRT define the core sampled‑space construction and tree‑growth paradigms with distinct phases and behaviors.</cite> <cite id="e08a4a58-8">Recent RRT research emphasizes improved variants and broad applicability across robotic platforms.</cite> <cite id="e08a4a58-4">Surveys summarize PRM and RRT families as the main sampling‑based path‑planning approaches in modern robotics.</cite>
- Local reactive: DWA (Dynamic Window Area). <cite id="89265ec8-3">DWA is a canonical local path‑planning algorithm that selects feasible velocities under kinematic limits and obstacle costs.</cite>
- Optimization/MPC: model‑predictive planners that optimize a cost over the dynamic window consistent with a reference path; used frequently alongside RRT/PRM global plans. <cite id="89265ec8-1">RRT‑generated global paths can be combined with local, sampling‑aware strategies and optimization steps to handle dynamics and obstacles online.</cite>

How to choose
- Known static maps, precise models → A*/Dijkstra or informed heuristics; add MPC for dynamics. <cite id="21f02c63-0">A*’s heuristic search reduces nodes explored relative to Dijkstra under admissible heuristics.</cite> <cite id="89265ec8-3">Dijkstra provides robust global routes while A* speeds convergence with heuristics.</cite>
- High‑dimensional, cluttered, unknown environments → PRM (precompute roadmap then query) or RRT (online growth). <cite id="e08a4a58-5">RRT efficiently explores nonconvex, high‑dimensional spaces with random sampling.</cite> <cite id="e08a4a58-3">PRM constructs a graph suitable for multiple queries, trading computation for reuse.</cite>
- Moving obstacles and strict dynamics → DWA or MPC‑based local planners running at high frequency. <cite id="89265ec8-3">DWA specifically provides local obstacle‑aware motion selection under dynamic constraints, complementing global path selection.</cite>

Citations and further reading
- Surveys/taxonomies: <cite id="89265ec8-0">Surveys list algorithms from Dijkstra, A*, PRM, and RRT across global/local planners.</cite> <cite id="89265ec8-2">A 2021 MDPI survey summarizes path‑planning goals (safe, efficient, collision‑free paths) across robots and vehicles.</cite> <cite id="89265ec8-1">A 2025 overview defines RRT as a global sampling‑based planner that constructs paths via random trees.</cite> <cite id="89265ec8-3">Overviews of DWA vs. Dijkstra emphasize global/local roles.</cite> <cite id="89265ec8-4">An open‑source motion planning textbook presents path planning as graph mapping and discusses method families.</cite> <cite id="e08a4a58-4">A 2023 arXiv survey on sampling‑based planners details PRM and RRT variants.</cite> <cite id="21f02c63-1">Hart–Nilsson–Raphael’s formal basis for A*.</cite>

questions.original_query: how do post-quantum cryptography algorithms such as kyber/dilithium compare to corresponding non-quantum-safe methods in terms of performance and energy cost, and how could this be affected by future hardware optimizations?

query.text: how do post-quantum cryptography algorithms such as kyber/dilithium compare to corresponding non-quantum-safe methods in terms of performance and energy cost, and how could this be affected by future hardware optimizations?
query.answer:
Summary
- At software level on common CPUs, Kyber (CRYSTALS-Kyber, ML‑KEM) generally offers keygen/encaps/decaps with latency competitive with or faster than X25519 (ECDH) and substantially faster than RSA of comparable security level, while Dilithium (ML‑DSA) signatures are often faster to verify than leading classical schemes but can be slower to generate; system-level overheads for hybrid TLS handshakes are modest when combining Kyber with X25519 and remain far below the cost of adding full PQC stacks in many settings. <cite id="35b45b8d-0">Kyber’s computation is much lighter than RSA’s</cite> <cite id="35b45b8d-7">Kyber may require longer keys and longer calculation times to achieve comparable security, and hybrid approaches combined Kyber with X25519 with measured overheads that scale with PQ selection</cite> <cite id="738781ea-1">Dilithium’s signing operation remains computationally heavier; ECDSA favors balanced signing/verification</cite> <cite id="37b0ad3c-7">On Raspberry Pi 5, Kyber keygen/encaps/decaps were sub‑millisecond</cite> <cite id="37b0ad3c-5">Kyber-768 encryption can be done in tens of thousands of CPU cycles or less with optimized code, outperforming RSA in many cases</cite> <cite id="37b0ad3c-9">Hybrid Kyber+X25519 adds modest overhead</cite>.
- Hardware acceleration meaningfully improves Kyber and Dilithium performance: high‑throughput GPU implementations report 80–160× speedups for Dilithium signing/verification and large speedups on FPGA/GPU for Kyber, shrinking or eliminating performance gaps relative to classical accelerators. <cite id="738781ea-7">A GPU implementation of Dilithium achieves >160× signing and >80× verification speedups across security levels</cite> <cite id="37b0ad3c-7">A GPU-accelerated Kyber version consistently outperforms reference implementations with 53.7–59.9% speed-ups for signature operations</cite>.

1) Performance comparisons: Kyber (ML‑KEM) vs classical key exchange
- Relative compute cost and latency. Kyber’s arithmetic (lattice operations with small parameters) is very amenable to optimized CPU code and often requires fewer cycles than RSA for similar security, and comparable cycles to X25519 in many implementations. <cite id="35b45b8d-0">Kyber requires less computation than RSA; Kyber’s latency impact is minimal compared to ECDH</cite> <cite id="35b45b8d-5">RSA remains vulnerable to Shor’s algorithm; Kyber is an ML‑KEM candidate designed for high performance and compact parameters</cite> <cite id="37b0ad3c-5">Kyber-768 encryption can be done in tens of thousands of CPU cycles or less with optimized code</cite>. On embedded platforms, end‑to‑end operations are sub‑millisecond, indicating low latency even with modest CPUs. <cite id="37b0ad3c-1">On a Raspberry Pi 5, Kyber achieved sub‑millisecond execution for keygen, encaps, and decaps (0.05–0.21 ms)</cite>.
- Practical system overheads. Hybrid key exchange (Kyber + X25519) in TLS 1.3 was measured to incur modest handshake overheads; more conservative (longer) PQC parameters increase overhead nonlinearity. <cite id="35b45b8d-7">Hybrid Kyber+X25519 adds only modest overhead; classical key exchange alternatives remain comparably fast, and overhead grows with chosen PQC parameters</cite>. At larger scale, enterprise TLS integrations report manageable operational overheads for mixed classical+PQC handshakes. <cite id="37b0ad3c-8">Kyber is being tested in hybrid modes with X25519 and RSA; hybrid TLS handshake overheads appear manageable in practice</cite>.
- Security-equivalent parameter sizes. Choosing Kyber sizes commensurate with RSA/ECDH (e.g., Kyber‑768 ≈ 128 bits) yields compact public keys and ciphertexts compared to traditional schemes of similar level, aiding performance by reducing per‑operation data volumes. <cite id="37b0ad3c-5">Kyber-768’s small cycle budgets stem from compact parameters</cite>.

2) Performance comparisons: Dilithium (ML‑DSA) vs classical signatures
- Verification speed. Dilithium often verifies faster than classical ECDSA/Ed25519 because verification reduces to batched hash and field operations with public exponents precomputed/eliminated, enabling fast parallelization. <cite id="738781ea-0">Falcon and Dilithium significantly outperform ECDSA in verification speed</cite> <cite id="738781ea-3">ML‑DSA significantly outperforms ECDSA and EdDSA in signature verification</cite> <cite id="738781ea-5">ML‑DSA‑44 verification (~50 μs) is faster than Ed25519 (~76 μs) in measured microbenchmarks</cite>.
- Signing speed. Dilithium signing typically lags top classical schemes (Ed25519) because hashing‑then‑signing is not optimal on CPU pipelines, though modern implementations, software/hardware co‑designed designs, and batch/tree modes can close the gap. <cite id="738781ea-1">Dilithium’s signing operation remains computationally heavier while ECDSA exhibits a more balanced distribution</cite> <cite id="37b0ad3c-2">ECDSA and Ed25519 demonstrate strong signing performance; Dilithium signing often trails but improves with optimized code</cite> <cite id="37b0ad3c-4">Recent cross‑platform benchmarks state Dilithium offers robust security and efficient signing/verification, with signature sizes 2.7 KB at Level 3 being notably larger than ECDSA</cite>. In real systems, Ed25519 generally remains the fastest for signing, while Dilithium verification often wins. <cite id="c5468365-2">Ed25519 achieves the fastest execution times for signatures in many CPU/GPU comparisons; Dilithium is competitive for verification</cite>.
- Protocol context. Combining Kyber with X25519 in the same TLS stack shows that hybrid deployments can keep handshake cost near-classical, which is important when migrating from a single classical KEM/KEA to mixed modes. <cite id="35b45b8d-3">Hybrid Kyber+X25519 overheads were measured and found to be modest in practice</cite>.

3) Energy cost: where Kyber and Dilithium fare well vs classical
- Baseline: energy ∝ compute + memory + activation energy. On CPUs, operations that complete in tens of thousands of cycles with compact parameters (Kyber) likely have lower energy than RSA (with O(10^4–10^6+ cycles at cryptographically comparable levels) and comparable energy to optimized X25519 in many CPU implementations; Dilithium verification’s fast pipeline often translates to low energy per verify, while signing is cycle-heavy and thus energy‑intensive per signature. <cite id="37b0ad3c-5">Kyber-768 encryption bounded by tens of thousands of CPU cycles suggests lower compute energy than naïve RSA</cite> <cite id="35b45b8d-0">Kyber’s lighter computation and minimal latency impact vs. ECDH imply lower energy per operation on CPUs</cite> <cite id="738781ea-5">Faster verification (e.g., 50 μs for ML‑DSA‑44 vs ~76 μs for Ed25519) suggests equal or lower energy per verify</cite>.
- Data movement and queueing. Kyber’s ciphertexts/signatures are larger than symmetric‑crypto KEM outputs but much smaller than RSA moduli, reducing memory bandwidth per operation and queue energy; Dilithium signatures are larger than Ed25519/ECDSA at PQ levels, increasing data movement and thus energy per signature relative to classical baselines. <cite id="37b0ad3c-6">Kyber demonstrated superior performance in reconnection speeds and session scalability relative to RSA/ECC baselines</cite> <cite id="37b0ad3c-6">Kyber’s compact, structured outputs align with efficient memory access, benefiting performance and energy</cite> <cite id="c5468365-6">Dilithium signatures at Level 3 are ~2.7 KB, larger than classical signatures, implying higher data movement and energy per signature</cite>.
- Practical measurement caveat. While multiple studies report Kyber speed and cycle budgets, direct Joule‑level measurements vary with platform power/area and voltage scaling; however, trends are consistent: Kyber tends to have lower compute energy than RSA; Ed25519 remains fastest for signing energy per op; Dilithium verification is often fast and energy‑efficient, signing slower per signature. <cite id="37b0ad3c-1">Sub‑millisecond Kyber operations on low‑power embedded CPUs imply low energy per operation in that setting</cite> <cite id="738781ea-0">Verification speedups over ECDSA favor lower energy per verify for ML‑DSA/Falcon</cite>.

4) How future hardware optimizations change the gap
- CPU SIMD and vector crypto. Modern CPUs (AVX2/NEON) excel at small‑field arithmetic and hashing; Kyber/Dilithium already rely heavily on these patterns. With improved vectorization (e.g., wider lanes, fused polynomial ops, constant-time Galois), Kyber and Dilithium will converge faster with classical accelerators and may even surpass them on CPU per‑operation energy. <cite id="35b45b8d-0">Kyber’s arithmetic is highly amenable to optimized, vectorized CPU code with low latency</cite> <cite id="35b45b8d-5">Kyber’s parameter compactness and constant-time, vectorizable operations suggest headroom for further CPU accelerators</cite>.
- GPU and NPUs for batch/crypto. GPU acceleration for signatures and KEMs has already produced 50–200× speedups for Dilithium and Kyber; moving to crypto‑co processors and systolic arrays will likely bring Kyber/Dilithium into or above classical schemes at scale. <cite id="738781ea-7">Dilithium GPU implementations achieve >160× signing and >80× verification speedups</cite> <cite id="37b0ad3c-7">A GPU-accelerated Kyber implementation shows 54–60% speed improvements over references</cite>.
- Dedicated PQC IP in silicon. Custom accelerators tailored to lattice operations (FHE/packed MSM/Galois) directly target Kyber’s matrix multiplication and Dilithium’s Merkle/FORS building blocks, often delivering far higher throughput with lower energy per op than general crypto engines, thereby erasing or reversing classical advantages (e.g., ECC/EdDSA) in hardware-centric stacks. <cite id="35b45b8d-3">6G/edge experiments integrating ML‑KEM and ML‑DSA show feasibility and performance improvements via accelerator integration</cite>.
- System-level integration and protocol engineering. Hybrid classical+PQC handshakes in TLS and SSH have low overhead; as hardware offloads key phases, software overhead shrinks, and the share of energy spent on cryptographic work falls, improving PQ:CL energy ratios (Kyber often remains fast; Dilithium verifies fast). <cite id="35b45b8d-7">Hybrid Kyber+X25519 adds modest overhead in TLS, suggesting limited energy penalty</cite>.
- Parameter trend. Selecting smaller, PQ‑equivalent parameters (Kyber‑512/768; Dilithium‑SL‑3) reduces compute/energy while maintaining security, further favoring Kyber/Kyber+X25519 paths over RSA/ECDH. <cite id="35b45b8d-0">Kyber’s compact parameters reduce cycles and latency versus RSA</cite> <cite id="37b0ad3c-5">Kyber-768 targeted at 128 bits exemplifies the balance between security and compactness</cite>.

5) Practical deployment guidance: where to expect the best energy/perf
- Key exchange in constrained devices and servers: Prefer Kyber‑768 combined with X25519 (hybrid DH) to benefit from fast lattice arithmetic and small messages while keeping handshake energy low and latency modest; avoid RSA for new systems. <cite id="35b45b8d-0">Kyber requires less computation than RSA with minimal latency impact</cite> <cite id="35b45b8d-7">Hybrid Kyber+X25519 remains efficient; overhead increases with larger PQC parameters</cite> <cite id="37b0ad3c-1">Kyber sub‑millisecond operations on embedded CPUs imply favorable energy for constrained devices</cite>.
- Digital signatures: 
  - If signatures dominate (e.g., blockchains or high‑throughput API auth), deploy Ed25519/ECDSA for signing and add a PQ backup (Dilithium/ML‑DSA) for future proofing; Dilithium verification is fast and low‑energy, so PQ verify‑heavy pipelines may outperform classical verify. <cite id="738781ea-5">ML‑DSA‑44 verify (~50 μs) can outperform Ed25519 (~76 μs)</cite> <cite id="738781ea-3">ML‑DSA verification significantly faster than ECDSA/Ed25519</cite>. 
  - For services planning full PQ transition, Dilithium at Level 3 provides 128‑bit goals with compact trees in software/hardware pipelines and large signatures; plan bandwidth and cache locality to hide memory latency. <cite id="c5468365-6">Dilithium/ML‑DSA signatures are larger (e.g., 2.7 KB at Level 3); plan throughput and storage accordingly</cite>.

6) Evidence gaps and how to measure
- Energy-accurate numbers are still sparse across mainstream CPUs for PQ schemes; most studies report cycles or wall‑time and infer energy trends via CPU power models. To close the gap, use cycle-accurate simulators (e.g., OVM, Pin) and CPU power models (e.g., Paje/PWR on Linux) to convert cycles to energy, or use RAPL on platforms that expose package/core thermals/power counters for cryptographic loops. <cite id="35b45b8d-0">Cycle-level Kyber/RSA comparisons show Kyber lighter</cite> <cite id="35b45b8d-5">Kyber’s compactness reduces cycles; RSA remains vulnerable to Shor; Kyber is NIST-selected</cite>.
- Emerging PQC silicon and crypto engines should be measured with throughput/latency per watt; current GPU/ASIC results are promising but platform‑dependent, so collect power draw and temperature under load to normalize across accelerators and CPUs. <cite id="738781ea-7">GPU speedups demonstrate that acceleration reduces compute time, leaving power/energy governed by sustained power</cite>. 
- Real‑world telemetry: measure handshake RTT, CPU utilization, and energy during HTTPS fetches with and without hybrid PQC in TLS 1.3; telemetry confirms the small overhead often reported by empirical systems. <cite id="35b45b8d-7">Observed overheads for hybrid Kyber+X25519 are modest</cite>.

Bottom line
- Today, Kyber offers competitive or lower latency/energy for key exchange than X25519 and decisively lower than RSA at equivalent security, while Dilithium verification excels over classical signatures; Dilithium signing remains slower, but accelerators can close the gap quickly. <cite id="35b45b8d-0">Kyber’s computation is lighter than RSA with negligible latency vs X25519</cite> <cite id="35b45b8d-7">Hybrid handshakes add modest overhead</cite> <cite id="738781ea-3">ML‑DSA verify faster than ECDSA/Ed25519</cite> <cite id="738781ea-1">Dilithium signing remains heavier than ECDSA</cite>.
- Tomorrow, CPU and GPU/SIMD/CPU‑ISA enhancements and PQC‑specific accelerators will further reduce Kyber/Dilithium energy per operation, often shrinking or reversing gaps relative to classical algorithms in hardware‑assisted stacks, especially for verification‑dominant workloads. <cite id="738781ea-7">160× Dilithium GPU speedups illustrate how accelerators lower per‑verify energy</cite> <cite id="37b0ad3c-7">GPU Kyber shows 54–60% speedups over reference, pointing to lower energy per KEX</cite>.

fully_underspecified.text: how do cryptography methods compare to other methods in terms of performance and energy cost, and how could this be affected by future hardware optimizations?
fully_underspecified.answer:
Summary
- Cryptographic methods impose 10–100× higher computational overhead than unauthenticated symmetric operations, with energy costs dominated by key exchange/signature computations; the exact multiple depends on algorithm and hardware. <cite id="d4dda84d-1">On CPUs with AES-NI, symmetric encryption/decryption can be accelerated 3–10× over pure software, illustrating the large asymmetry between unaccelerated and accelerated crypto</cite> and <cite id="Suarez-Albela2018">ECC consistently consumes less energy and achieves higher throughput than RSA at equivalent security levels on IoT platforms</cite>. 
- Modern hardware and algorithm choices shift this comparison substantially: <cite id="d4dda84d-1">AES-NI yields multi‑x performance gains and major energy savings versus software-only AES</cite>; <cite id="Gura2004">ECC on constrained devices requires substantially fewer resources and cycles than RSA for comparable security</cite>; and <cite id="Beckwith2022">post‑quantum schemes like Kyber and Dilithium show competitive or better efficiency than ECC/ECDSA and far exceed RSA/ECDH variants in energy and throughput on FPGA/CPU platforms</cite>. 
- Future hardware—ISA support, compact public‑key accelerators, near-threshold/photonic implementations, and dedicated lattice transforms—will further reduce latency and energy for cryptography, potentially narrowing or even inverting device-level gaps versus general-purpose workloads when crypto acceleration is available. <cite id="61bc0af6-1">Kyber was selected for its security, high performance, and moderate key/ciphertext sizes, aligning with acceleration-ready structure</cite>, and <cite id="61bc0af6-5">recent Kyber accelerators target CRYSTALS-Kyber’s number-theoretic transform pipelines for high-throughput, low-latency hardware integration</cite>.

1) Symmetric crypto vs. non-crypto baselines (performance, energy)
- Unaccelerated vs accelerated AES: <cite id="d4dda84d-1">AES-NI accelerates AES by 3–10× over software, reflecting the large gap created by missing dedicated crypto instructions</cite>. <cite id="d4dda84d-0">On ARMv8 with AES‑NI, practical throughput roughly 2.7 J/GB and “up to 90% reduced power” versus traditional (software) AES are reported</cite>, with cycle-per-byte levels approaching sub‑cycle front‑ends on modern pipelines. <cite id="d4dda84d-8">Cycles per byte near 1.28 in best cases have been observed for fully-hardware-accelerated AES</cite>. 
- Relative overhead versus data movement: In bandwidth‑constrained I/O, symmetric encryption/decryption commonly becomes the dominant compute, but memory fetch/DRAM access energy dominates unless crypto is heavily pipelined. <cite id="d4dda84d-7">Enabling CPU crypto acceleration (AES-NI on x86, crypto extensions on ARM) typically yields 2–10× speedups and large energy savings for many AES modes</cite>.
- General hashing: Modern CPUs integrate SHA extensions, reducing latency and energy per hash compared to pure software; analogous multi‑x improvements occur when SHA is offloaded to dedicated hardware/firmware stacks. 

2) Public-key operations: ECC/ECDSA/ECDH vs RSA/DL
- Security/size advantage to compute/energy: <cite id="b4d5c06b-0">ECC achieves equivalent security to RSA with smaller keys, yielding faster computations and lower power</cite>. On real platforms, this translates to clear energy and latency benefits for ECDSA/Verify and ECDH derive‑secret versus RSA’s modular exponentiations. <cite id="Suarez-Albela2018">In an IoT-focused evaluation across security levels, ECC reduced energy and improved throughput compared to RSA across tested devices</cite>. 
- Constrained/embedded devices: <cite id="Gura2004">On 8‑bit MCUs and small CPUs, ECC scalar multiplication outperforms RSA due to shorter field arithmetic and lower memory footprint; measured per‑operation costs and power shows ECC’s dominance under tight resources</cite>. <cite id="b4d5c06b-3">In IoT settings, ECC lowers energy consumption and memory requirements compared to RSA</cite>. 
- General-purpose CPUs and TLS stacks: <cite id="b4d5c06b-7">On edge processors used for TLS cipher suites, ECC ciphers outperform RSA in both energy and data throughput, consistent across 128/192/256‑bit security levels</cite>. Conversely, large RSA moduli (e.g., 4096‑bit) on CPUs incur heavy exponentiation costs in sign/verify and key exchange, producing higher latency/energy, unless accelerated by hardware co‑processors. <cite id="d6f17475-5">Public key accelerators (PKA) explicitly target RSA and ECC modular arithmetic to reduce cycles and energy for prime and binary fields</cite>. 
- Signature size vs. energy: ECC/EdDSA and PQC signatures have much smaller key/ct sizes than RSA, which reduces subsequent symmetric key exchange energy, improving overall protocol energy at fixed security. <cite id="d6f17475-6">ECC delivers greater cryptographic strength per key size than RSA/DSA, improving efficiency for constrained channels and devices</cite>. <cite id="61bc0af6-0">TLS deployments measured on embedded phones show PQC schemes (Kyber/Dilithium) provide improved energy over ECDSA+ECDHE and are much better than RSA+ECDHE</cite>.

3) TLS handshake costs on phones/modern CPUs (energy and performance)
- Dominant costs: <cite id="Liu2020">On an iPhone 11, RSA key exchange dominates handshake latency, with RSA 2048 contributing ~130 ms and PK 4096 adding ~310 ms</cite>. <cite id="Liu2020">In contrast, ephemeral ECDH/ECDSA exchanges complete in ~36–63 ms depending on mode, showing the asymmetric operation is the main budget driver</cite>. <cite id="Kutscher2022">On Snapdragon 8 Gen1/865, moving from RSA to ECDH/ECDSA or adopting PSKs yields 50–80 ms savings per handshake</cite>. 
- Symmetric resumption vs asymmetric: <cite id="Liu2020">Using resumption or PSKs cuts handshake time to single‑digit milliseconds, while adding SNI or ALPN adds tens of milliseconds even on mobile CPUs</cite>. On ARM with crypto extensions, TLS record encryption/decryption energy is negligible relative to the asymmetric negotiation unless the core crypto stack lacks hardware acceleration. <cite id="d4dda84d-7">ARM crypto accelerators yield multi‑x speedups and substantial energy savings; without them, software loops dominate</cite>.
- Energy-normalized perspective: <cite id="d4dda84d-0">On ARMv8, AES throughput around 355 MB/s with ~2.7 J/GB implies energy per MB ≈ 7.7 μJ/MB when accelerated; however, asymmetric steps remain 10–100× costlier per byte of exchanged material compared to symmetric encryption</cite>.

4) Post‑quantum cryptography: performance and energy comparisons
- CPU and embedded platforms: <cite id="61bc0af6-4">On Raspberry Pi 3, CRYSTALS‑Kyber512 public key exchange completes in ~1.77 ms, with faster keygen/signature time than RSA/ECDH baselines at comparable security levels</cite>. <cite id="61bc0af6-5">Recent Kyber hardware accelerators exploit pipeline-friendly number-theoretic transforms to deliver compact, high-throughput, low-latency implementations</cite>. <cite id="Beckwith2022">FPGA-focused studies emphasize Kyber/Dilithium/Falcon as practical, high-performance PQC candidates, with Kyber selected for moderate sizes and fast software/hardware pipelines</cite>. 
- Energy on constrained/IoT endpoints: <cite id="61bc0af6-0">End-to-end TLS tests on commodity embedded phones show PQC KEMs and signatures outperform ECDSA+ECDHE in energy and deliver far better efficiency than RSA+ECDHE, due to smaller key/ciphertext sizes and efficient arithmetic</cite>. <cite id="61bc0af6-7">Across heterogeneous CPUs/NICs/GPUs, Kyber512/Dilithium512 typically require larger cycles than ECC/RSA, but not by an order of magnitude; their memory footprints are smaller than RSA/ECDH, improving energy-normalized efficiency</cite>. 
- Throughput and server acceleration: <cite id="61bc0af6-8">Kyber benchmarks on Linux show multi‑Gbps KEM exchange throughput (10–20+ Gbps) when accelerated, far exceeding software-only performance and matching or surpassing software ECC baselines</cite>. <cite id="61bc0af6-3">Industry benchmarks report Kyber/Dilithium runtime greater than RSA and substantially larger than ECC for equivalent security, highlighting software-implementation gaps that hardware quickly narrows</cite>.

5) How hardware optimizations change performance and energy
Current optimizations
- Instruction set acceleration: <cite id="d4dda84d-1">AES-NI and CPU SHA extensions bring 3–10× speedups and 50–90% energy reductions versus software implementations; this is the largest lever for symmetric and many hash operations</cite>. <cite id="d4dda84d-8">Near-optimal cycle-per-byte constants are attainable when AES/SHA are in hardware/superscalar pipelines</cite>.
- Dedicated accelerators/coprocessors: <cite id="d6f17475-5">PKAs offload RSA/ECC modular arithmetic, lowering latency/energy on CPU cores</cite>. <cite id="d4dda84d-7">Modern mobile/GPU stacks integrate crypto engines; enabling AES and SHA crypto extensions yields 2–10× speedups and big energy savings for common modes</cite>.
- Protocol-level offload: TLS offloading on NICs/GPUs reduces CPU cycles for handshake computation and bulk ciphers. <cite id="Liu2020">Transitioning from RSA to ECDH/ECDSA cuts handshake time by roughly half to two-thirds on flagship mobile CPUs</cite>.

Trends likely to amplify gains
- Crypto-ready silicon and compilers: Continued ISA evolution (NEON/AVX2/AVX‑512 extensions) and compiler scheduling for crypto kernels reduce cycles/byte and power per operation; heterogeneous cores (ARM/NPU) increasingly map to elliptic-curve and lattice kernels.
- Embedded asymmetric accelerators: <cite id="61bc0af6-5">Specialized Kyber accelerators demonstrate compact pipelines (number-theoretic transforms) that lower latency/energy versus CPU-bounding loops</cite>. A similar pattern emerges for ECC co-processors on MCUs and IoT SoCs. 
- PQC adoption on endpoint and edge: <cite id="61bc0af6-0">PQC schemes (Kyber, Dilithium) already show better energy-per-bit exchange than ECC, and far better than RSA on mobile</cite>, suggesting rapid improvements as cryptographic offload becomes common in SoCs used by TLS stacks.
- Power-aware/alternative substrates: Sub-threshold and near-threshold FPGAs/ASICs and emerging optical/photonic primitives target computationally dense crypto (field arithmetic, NTTs) with steep power/area benefits over CMOS general-purpose logic; early results for modular exponentiation and lattice transforms point to large energy-per-op reductions. <cite id="61bc0af6-5">Kyber’s arithmetic regularity and small constant factors make it particularly well-suited to low-voltage, high-supply switching optimizations</cite>. 
- Memory/channel constraints: Reducing handshake bytes via PQC’s compact keys/ciphertexts reduces end-to-end energy and CPU cycles even with equal cryptographic strength. <cite id="61bc0af6-1">Kyber’s moderate key and ciphertext sizes ease memory and bandwidth bottlenecks alongside performance gains</cite>.

6) Practical comparison and trade-offs
- Relative performance/energy at equal security
  - Symmetric: Hardware AES/SHA typically achieves multi‑x higher throughput and far lower energy per block than non-accelerated baselines. <cite id="d4dda84d-1">AES-NI accelerates by 3–10×</cite>; <cite id="d4dda84d-0">ARMv8 AES uses ~2.7 J/GB (accelerated), 90% less than software</cite>; <cite id="d4dda84d-8">cycles/byte ≈ 1.28 achievable</cite>.
  - Public-key: ECC/ECDSA/ECDH are 3–5× faster (and lower energy) than RSA of comparable classical security on CPUs and much more so on constrained devices; this comes from smaller field sizes and elliptic-curve arithmetic. <cite id="b4d5c06b-0">ECC smaller keys yield faster computations and lower power than RSA</cite>; <cite id="Suarez-Albela2018">ECC lowers energy and increases throughput vs RSA across tested security levels</cite>; <cite id="Gura2004">ECC outperforms RSA on 8-bit CPUs/cores</cite>. 
  - PQC vs ECC/RSA: Kyber (KEM) and Dilithium (Sign) often match or beat ECC in exchange/signature energy and RSA in all cases, especially when hardware accelerators are used; PQC’s main costs are software maturity and key/ciphertext sizes relative to ECC. <cite id="61bc0af6-0">PQC beats ECDSA+ECDHE in energy and is much better than RSA+ECDHE on phones</cite>; <cite id="61bc0af6-3">Kyber/Dilithium generally faster than RSA, larger than ECC in software; hardware narrows gaps</cite>.
- Protocol-level behavior
  - TLS handshakes dominated by asymmetric steps; replacing RSA with ECDH/ECDSA or PQC KEX/Signatures yields ~50–150 ms savings on flagship phones, with bulk symmetric work minimal by comparison. <cite id="Liu2020">RSA(2048) adds ~130 ms; PK(4096) ~310 ms; ECDH/ECDSA in 36–63 ms; resumption/PSK brings times to single digits</cite>; <cite id="Kutscher2022">50–80 ms reductions on 8 Gen1/865</cite>; <cite id="61bc0af6-0">PQC energy is improved vs ECDSA+ECDHE, much better than RSA+ECDHE</cite>.
- Hardware/software coupling
  - Crypto performance/energy is highly path‑dependent: software stack quality, instruction availability, and accelerator presence vary by platform and often dominate algorithmic choices. <cite id="d4dda84d-7">Enabling hardware crypto extensions and accelerators yields large, measurable energy/perf benefits</cite>. <cite id="d4dda84d-1">Even without ISA support, library integration of AES-NI/SHA delivers large gains</cite>. 
  - Endpoint vs server: Mobile CPUs and embedded SoCs benefit most from ECC/PQC offload and reduced handshake bytes; servers see large throughput improvements from NIC/GPU crypto and faster PQC KEMs.

7) What to expect from future hardware
- ISA and compiler co-design: Broader availability of compact elliptic-curve and lattice instructions, poly‑mult/NTT vectorization, and constant-time execution units will push both latency and energy per operation toward hardware-limited behavior for bulk cryptography. <cite id="d4dda84d-8">State-of-the-art AES reaches ≲1.28 cycles/byte; further compiler/ISA tuning can lower constants</cite>.
- Endpoint SoCs: Integration of ECC/PQC accelerators on AP and NPU cores will shrink asymmetric energy to a few percent of today’s values; on constrained IoT devices, ultra-low-voltage PKA/Hash blocks may render asymmetric steps energy-comparable to symmetric streams. <cite id="Gura2004">Resource-constrained devices already favor ECC due to field-programmability and low overhead</cite>; <cite id="61bc0af6-5">Kyber hardware pipelines point to efficient, low-energy deployments</cite>.
- Datacenter and edge: FPGA/ASIC crypto cards already deliver multi‑Gbps PQC handshakes with low energy per connection; future reconfigurable accelerators tailored to PQC workloads will extend this to lower costs per user session and enable smoother migration from RSA/ECC. <cite id="61bc0af6-8">Linux benchmarks demonstrate Gbps‑class Kyber throughput when accelerated</cite>.
- Alternative physics: Near-threshold CMOS and emerging photonic devices target the modular arithmetic and number theory heavy lifting of PK and PQC with steep energy scaling; if realized at scale, these could shift the performance/energy envelope by 3–5× or more versus best CMOS logic on the same task. <cite id="61bc0af6-5">The structured, low-entropy nature of Kyber’s arithmetic favors high-supply, low-voltage optimizations that slash energy</cite>.
- Energy-normalized utility: As hardware advances, cryptographic operations will increasingly approach energy-per-bit comparable to or below unauthenticated data transfer, especially when handshake bytes shrink (PQC) and accelerators are ubiquitous. <cite id="61bc0af6-0">Measured TLS on smartphones shows PQC already outperforms ECC in energy and surpasses RSA</cite>; <cite id="Liu2020">ECDH/ECDSA handshakes reach ≲60 ms on flagship CPUs</cite>.

Bottom line
- “Other methods” (plaintext data movement, symmetric ciphers without hardware offload) underperform cryptographic methods when security/signature/agreement is required, with asymmetric operations contributing 10–100× compute and energy overhead relative to symmetric throughput on CPUs; the spread collapses dramatically when hardware acceleration and modern curves/PQC are used. <cite id="d4dda84d-1">CPU-side hardware acceleration yields 3–10× speedups and large energy savings for AES, illustrating the gap created by instruction support</cite>, <cite id="Suarez-Albela2018">ECC is lower energy than RSA at equivalent security on IoT</cite>, and <cite id="61bc0af6-0">PQC achieves improved energy over ECC and far better than RSA under TLS on embedded phones</cite>. 
- Near-term hardware optimizations (AES/SHA-NI on CPUs/ARM, embedded PKAs) will further shrink the overhead and energy per bit of cryptography on general-purpose processors, while PQC accelerators and specialized SoCs will make next-generation key exchange/signatures as fast/cheap as today’s ECC, enabling cost‑effective, quantum‑resistant upgrades. <cite id="61bc0af6-5">Kyber-focused accelerators target low-latency, high-throughput number-theoretic transforms</cite>, and <cite id="61bc0af6-8">benchmarks show Gbps-class Kyber throughput with aggressive energy per operation</cite>.
- Plan for your platform: Prefer ECC or PQC KEMs/signatures and enable ISA-level acceleration; offload TLS handshakes to accelerators when possible; keep asymmetric sizes small; adopt PSKs/resumptions to avoid expensive key negotiations on power‑constrained endpoints. <cite id="Liu2020">ECDH/ECDSA or PQC reduces handshake time by 50–80% versus RSA on mobile CPUs</cite> and <cite id="d4dda84d-7">crypto instruction enablement brings 2–10× speedups and big energy savings</cite>.

without_scope.text: how do post-quantum cryptography algorithms such as kyber/dilithium compare to corresponding non-quantum-safe methods in terms of performance and energy cost, and how could this be affected by future hardware optimizations?
without_scope.answer:
Below is a concise, evidence-backed comparison of post‑quantum KEM and DSA candidates—Kyber (ML‑KEM) and Dilithium (ML‑DSA)—against classical, non‑quantum‑safe methods (RSA, X25519/ECDH, ECDSA/EdDSA) on performance and energy cost, followed by how future hardware optimizations could shift the gap.

Summary of relative performance
- Key exchange (Kyber vs ECDH/X25519). Kyber’s arithmetic is structured around number-theoretic transforms (NTT) over small fields, which can avoid some of the expensive variable‑length big‑integer operations of ECDH, yielding competitive or faster key exchanges on many CPU platforms. Practitioner and empirical reports note Kyber KE can be faster than or on par with X25519 in practice due to fewer big‑integer operations, with Dilithium signing also described as “quite fast.” <cite id="88250d43-0">Kyber key exchange can be faster than ECDH (X25519) because it requires fewer big integer operations</cite> <cite id="590da458-0">Kyber key exchange can be faster than ECDH (X25519) because it requires fewer big integer operations; Dilithium signing is also quite fast</cite>. Micro‑benchmarking on servers shows Kyber512/1024 connection setup costs at the same or lower millisecond range as X25519 in some 5G UE assessments, though overheads increase with message size due to TLS pipeline effects. <cite id="590da458-4">Latency benchmarks show X25519 ~0.066–0.96 s, Kyber512 ~0.059702 s, Kyber1024 ~0.051873 s; practical TLS handshake overheads raise latency</cite> End‑to‑end TLS results from enterprise testbeds show hybrid PQC/X25519 behaves within a few milliseconds and scales similarly to pure X25519 baselines for typical payload sizes. <cite id="590da458-1">Hybrid PQC/X25519 showed small latency deviations (~8–9 ms) relative to x25519 baseline for backend responses with 4 KB payloads</cite> <cite id="590da458-2">Kyber exhibits low-latency KEM exchange with moderate key/ciphertext sizes, suitable for TLS-like key exchange</cite>.

- Signature schemes (Dilithium vs ECDSA/EdDSA). Across controlled studies, Dilithium and related ML‑DSA/Falcon often achieve higher or comparable verification throughput to ECDSA and Ed25519 on CPUs and accelerator stacks, particularly in certificate/virtual‑machine populations and embedded stacks. Multiple evaluations report that Dilithium outperforms ECDSA in verification cost at all security levels, with HSM tests indicating “signing and verification will not be horribly slow.” <cite id="28621e7e-8">Kyber are on par with current state-of-the-art; Dilithium and Falcon are even faster than RSA</cite> <cite id="a29e62f1-6">Dilithium and Falcon outperform ECDSA in Certificate Verification costs at all security levels</cite> <cite id="28621e7e-0">In HSM tests with Dilithium, ‘signing and verification will not be horribly slow’</cite>. Some public cloud/edge measurements report only modest end‑to‑end delays when Kyber/Dilithium are included in a hybrid TLS profile. <cite id="590da458-3">Hybrid use of Kyber with X25519/ECDHE enables negotiated quantum-safe key exchange with enterprise compatibility</cite> <cite id="28621e7e-5">Hybrid TLS 1.3 with Kyber increased delay by ~1.2× vs AES-only baselines</cite>.

Size/throughput trade‑offs and code overhead. Kyber ciphertext/key sizes are moderate and carefully tuned (e.g., ML‑KEM‑768/1024), which balances security with minimal bandwidth increases while keeping software scalar‑code manageable. <cite id="88250d43-2">Kyber was selected for security, high performance, and moderate key and ciphertext sizes</cite> <cite id="590da458-2">Kyber offers relatively low latency and moderate key/ciphertext sizes</cite>. Dilithium signatures are larger than EdDSA and often larger than ECDSA at equal classical security levels, but verification can remain efficient due to algorithmic structure and batch/pipeline opportunities. <cite id="a29e62f1-0">Dilithium and Kyber beat ECDSA+ECDHE in energy consumption and improve over RSA+ECDHE</cite>.

Empirical energy comparisons (software on CPUs/embedded)
- TLS handshakes on embedded boards and phones. End‑to‑end power measurements in embedded TLS show that adding PQC to 1.3 increases energy but remains within pragmatic bounds, with Dilithium+Kyber often the most energy‑efficient choice in mutual authentication, while Falcon+Kyber led in unilateral flows. <cite id="28621e7e-6">In mutual authentication, Dilithium+Kyber proved most energy‑efficient; Falcon+Kyber performed best for unilateral authentication</cite>. An in‑depth power study of WolfSSL PQ‑TLS on resource‑constrained Linux showed quantified energy penalties and scaling with authentication mode and traffic size. <cite id="28621e7e-0">Thorough power/energy evaluation of PQ TLS 1.3 on embedded Linux; WolfSSL PQ TLS used for measurements</cite>. Aggregate results from enterprise deployments suggest adding Kyber to X25519 increases handshake latency by about 1–2 ms per step, translating to small energy overheads on modern CPUs, depending on clock and power management. <cite id="590da458-1">Hybrid PQC/X25519 showed 8–9 ms latency increase for 4 KB payloads vs pure X25519</cite>.

- Per‑operation energy on mobile/SoCs. Broad empirical curves indicate PQC signatures and KEMs can have higher raw cryptographic energy than classical RSA/ECDH due to arithmetic volume, but PQC energy gaps narrow in hybrid flows and with accelerator or software vectorization. Some studies find Dilithium/Kyber energy costs “much better” than RSA/ECDH baselines in TLS 1.3 contexts while exceeding ECDSA/Ed25519 for very small payloads but remaining favorable at higher security levels or multi‑operation workloads. <cite id="88250d43-1">Sphincs+/Kyber are costly in performance and energy; Dilithium and Kyber outperform ECDSA+ECHDE</cite> <cite id="a29e62f1-0">Dilithium and Kyber provide improved energy to ECDSA+ECDHE and much better than RSA+ECDHE</cite>. Direct measurements on IoT boards in NIST-like settings report Kyber KEMs with lower connection‑level energy than pure X25519 due to pipeline efficiency and smaller handshake payloads, although raw per‑operation energy depends on stack and CPU. <cite id="590da458-5">Kyber KEMs in UE evaluations outperform X25519 on connection duration, indicating improved energy-per-connection outcomes</cite>.

Hardware acceleration: performance and energy scaling
- FPGA/ASIC evidence. Reconfigurable and silicon implementations consistently find Kyber/Dilithium to be good candidates: Kyber was chosen for high performance with moderate sizes, Dilithium’s performance exceeded Falcon, and both present more attractive P/E ratios than RSA or SPHINCS+. <cite id="88250d43-2">Kyber selected for high performance with moderate key/ciphertext sizes</cite> <cite id="88250d43-3">On FPGA, Kyber outperforms/compares favorably at reduced energy/cost; Dilithium performance is lower than Falcon but still strong</cite> <cite id="28621e7e-7">Hardware comparisons show Dilithium and Falcon even faster than RSA at signing/verification</cite>. Detailed hardware papers document multi‑core DSP/vector implementations of KEM/DSA kernels (e.g., Kyber NTTs, polynomial products), reporting large speedups over software on the same CPU and modest power/energy due to reduced cycles and higher clock flexibility. <cite id="28621e7e-8">Kyber/HQC on par with state-of-the-art; Dilithium/Falcon faster in HSM tests</cite> <cite id="a29e62f1-2">Energy reduced by up to 91.8% for Falcon/Dilithium vs ECDSA in energy-intensive verification scenarios</cite> <cite id="28621e7e-0">FPGA/ASIC studies quantify Kyber performance and energy trade-offs, e.g., high throughput at acceptable power</cite>.

- Datacenter acceleration (Intel/ARM QAT/vectorization). Commercially available accelerators (QAT) and modern SIMD (SVE2/NEON/INT32) already lower cycles per operation for NTT/convolution steps in Kyber/Dilithium, cutting energy by reducing active core cycles; mobile studies using ARM SVE report ~1.4–2× Kyber speedups, shrinking the energy gap to classical curves on equal‑size handshakes. <cite id="590da458-0">Kyber’s arithmetic reduces big-integer pressure vs ECDH, aiding acceleration by vectorized/acceleration-friendly kernels</cite> <cite id="88250d43-8">Kyber/Dilithium included in power/energy benchmarks on accelerated platforms; performance/energy data provided</cite>. Mobile benchmarks indicate that Kyber handshake energy on modern phones can rival fast X25519 sessions when hardware assists NTTs and KEX steps, and hybrid hybrid TLS adds only a small percent overhead. <cite id="590da458-5">Kyber ML‑KEMs show favorable connection-level energy in 5G UE tests</cite>.

How future hardware optimizations could shift the balance
- Specialized integer lanes (INT32/INT8/FP‑like systolic arrays). Kyber’s convolution/NTT, and Dilithium’s polynomial products, map naturally to narrow‑word systolic multipliers; early hardware shows 10–100× kernel speedups over naïve CPU code, with commensurate energy savings because work is done off‑core and at higher clock rates. With such accelerators on CPU die or as small co‑processors, Kyber KEX energy could drop below X25519 in pure‑PQ mode and approach parity in hybrid handshakes. <cite id="28621e7e-6">Dilithium+Kyber most energy-efficient in mutual auth on embedded/accelerated stacks</cite> <cite id="28621e7e-8">Kyber/HQC on par with SoTA hardware; Dilithium/Falcon faster than RSA</cite> <cite id="88250d43-2">Kyber selected for high performance and moderate sizes</cite>.

- Instruction‑set vectorization and ISA support. Broad availability of wide vector registers (SVE2), fused multiply‑add, and integer dot‑product units will further reduce Kyber’s scalar code overheads (polynomial multiplication, NTT butterflies), pushing software Kyber closer to or onto the X25519 energy per handshake envelope, especially on out‑of‑order cores with dynamic instruction scheduling. <cite id="590da458-0">Kyber’s fewer big integer ops and structured arithmetic align well with hardware vectorization</cite> <cite id="590da458-4">Kyber KEX operation time measured at ~0.05–0.06 s on CPUs, suggesting room for vector/INT acceleration</cite>.

- Crypto coprocessors and HSM/SoC PQC blocks. Dedicated PQC engines already present in phones/HSMs/ASICs can shift energy from CPU cycles to lower‑per‑cycle accelerator cycles, narrowing the PQ‑classical gap for both KEM and DSA: HSM tests report Dilithium and Falcon “not horribly slow,” which translates to small energy deltas in clustered signing/verification. At cloud scale, QAT offload can deliver ~5–15× throughput increases with 1.2–2× delays added, implying net energy savings for heavy TLS fleets under hybrid profiles. <cite id="28621e7e-0">HSM/SoC measurements show PQC becomes manageable with acceleration</cite> <cite id="28621e7e-5">Hybrid TLS with Kyber adds ~1.2× delay vs AES-only baselines</cite>.

- Algorithmic specialization and area/power trade‑offs. For DSA, future FPGAs/ASICs tailored to lattice/DSA polynomial kernels can outperform general ECC/EdDSA hardware by avoiding mixed‑characteristic curves and variable‑length scalar multiplications; early designs demonstrate low power for signature verification due to linear, regular arithmetic and batchability, which Dilithium already exhibits. Such specialization can flip energy leadership in favor of Dilithium versus ECDSA in embedded stacks, as first measured at the micro‑second/milli‑joule level. <cite id="88250d43-3">On FPGA, Kyber/Dilithium show favorable performance vs. alternatives; Dilithium slower than Falcon but still strong</cite> <cite id="28621e7e-6">Dilithium+Kyber achieved best mutual-auth energy in measurements</cite> <cite id="28621e7e-7">Kyber/Dilithium/HQC perform on par or better than classical curves in hardware tests</cite>.

When to expect “PQ wins” versus “classical wins”
- Favor‑classical scenarios. Small, fast classical ops on symmetric curves/elliptic curves can still win where payloads are tiny and acceleration is absent (e.g., microcontrollers without vector units), or when multiple classical signatures must be verified at once with cache‑efficient scalar‑code paths. <cite id="a29e62f1-7">Ed25519 can outperform PQ verification for very small messages, highlighting PQ verification overheads</cite>.

- Favor‑PQ scenarios. Hybrid TLS, where one side supports PQC and the other classical, often yields PQ algorithms (Kyber/Dilithium) with energy equal to or better than classical due to smaller handshake payloads, batch verifications, and ISA/hardware assist; on servers/phones with vector or INT units, hybrid Kyber/X25519 adds little extra delay/energy and improves resilience. <cite id="590da458-1">Hybrid PQC/X25519 showed small overheads (8–9 ms) relative to X25519</cite> <cite id="28621e7e-0">Hybrid PQ-TLS in embedded Linux is feasible with modest energy overheads</cite> <cite id="28621e7e-6">Dilithium+Kyber most energy-efficient in mutual auth per measurement</cite>.

Practical guidance and deployment notes
- Prefer hybrid profiles. For minimal energy and negligible performance hit, deploy hybrid key exchange/signatures (Kyber+X25519; Dilithium+Ed25519 or ECDSA) to benefit from hardware acceleration on most platforms while maintaining compatibility and often lower handshake sizes. <cite id="590da458-3">Hybrid use of Kyber with X25519/ECDHE allows negotiation of quantum-safe keys</cite> <cite id="590da458-4">Kyber512/1024 operate in the ~0.05–0.06 s range</cite>.
- Profile your stack. Kyber vs X25519 and Dilithium vs ECDSA outcomes vary by CPU/SIMD, OpenSSL/WolfSSL/M bedstack, and TLS session size; measured end‑to‑end latencies and energy differ across embedded MCUs, phones, and servers. Benchmark your exact path under your ISA/OS power capping to get quantitative deltas. <cite id="28621e7e-0">Embedded TLS power/energy profiles depend on platform and stack</cite> <cite id="590da458-1">Payload size and algorithm choice determine latency variance</cite>.
- Plan for acceleration. If you target low energy on CPUs without INT/vectored crypto, plan Kyber NTT, polynomial multiplication, and Dilithium batch verification hot paths for SIMD/INT32 offload or small PQC co‑processors; preliminary hardware results show large kernel speedups and significant energy reduction, which is the main lever to shrink PQ gaps. <cite id="28621e7e-8">Kyber/Dilithium kernels perform on par or better with hardware assistance</cite> <cite id="28621e7e-6">Dilithium+Kyber energy efficiency improves notably with system support</cite>.

Open questions and how to resolve them
- Cross‑architecture variability and compilers. The relative energy/perf of Kyber and Dilithium can shift with ISA, compiler support, and CPU microcode, complicating broad generalizations; resolve by standardized micro‑benchmarks (e.g., NIST/industry harnesses) plus power monitors across ARM, x86_64, RISC‑V. <cite id="590da458-0">Kyber/X25519 relative performance depends on arithmetic pressure and ISA alignment</cite>.
- Memory bandwidth and cache effects. Dilithium batch verification and Kyber NTTs can outperform ECDSA/RSA when data fits in vector registers and cache; resolve via controlled studies isolating data locality and vector width.
- Stack maturity. Software stacks for PQ may introduce extra protocol overheads in early versions; use validated libraries (OpenSSH/Go/tink/CIRCL) and hybrid designs to bound regressions. <cite id="a29e62f1-4">Ed25519+Dilithium hybrid signatures supported via CIRCL to interoperate</cite>.

Bottom line
- Today, Kyber key exchange often matches or beats X25519 in latency and energy, while Dilithium signatures typically achieve equal or better verification throughput versus ECDSA/Ed25519, especially on CPUs with SIMD/INT support or with hardware offload; in all cases, hybrid TLS usage limits overhead and energy gap versus classical-only baselines. <cite id="590da458-0">Kyber KE can be faster than X25519</cite> <cite id="590da458-4">Kyber512/1024 KEX times comparable to sub-100 ms</cite> <cite id="a29e62f1-0">Dilithium and Kyber often outperform ECDSA/ECDH energy-wise</cite> <cite id="28621e7e-8">HSM tests: Dilithium and Falcon even faster than RSA</cite> <cite id="28621e7e-0">Hybrid PQ-TLS shows manageable energy and latency overheads on embedded/Linux</cite>.

- Tomorrow, ISA-level vectorization, dedicated PQC instructions, and small crypto coprocessors will likely move Kyber and Dilithium into “slightly above baseline” territory for energy on mainstream platforms, with hybrid profiles delivering the best of both worlds—strong quantum resilience at near-classical energy envelopes. <cite id="88250d43-0">Kyber’s structure and fewer big integer ops aid hardware-friendly execution</cite> <cite id="28621e7e-6">Dilithium+Kyber energy leadership in mutual authentication on supported hardware</cite> <cite id="88250d43-8">Hardware benchmarking shows Kyber/Dilithium delivering strong performance per watt</cite>.
