without_preference.text: What are leading methods for generating hard examples of the boolean satisfiability problem, and what are their strengths and weaknesses?
without_preference.answer:
Below are leading methods for generating hard Boolean satisfiability (SAT) instances, grouped by strategy, with mechanisms, strengths, and weaknesses.

1) Random k-SAT near the phase transition
Mechanism and rationale:
- Random k-SAT instances generated by sampling clauses uniformly tend to have a sharp satisfiable/unsatisfiable transition; instances around the transition (near the “critical” clause-to-variable ratio) are typically hardest in practice for resolution- and local-search–style solvers <cite id="fe1f17db-3">The performance of popular SAT solvers on random problems and the problem of generating hard instances with solutions are considered; a family of hard random k-SAT instances is described</cite> <cite id="55891bdf-6">In the classic Achlioptas–Naor–Peres framework, random k-SAT instances are obtained by sampling m = r·n clauses uniformly and independently; phase transitions in hard optimization problems occur at specific clause-to-variable ratios</cite> <cite id="55891b7d-2">Phase transition is clearly evident in the hardness of random k-SAT instances as the clauses-to-variables ratio varies</cite>.
- Algorithmic hardness persists even when restricting solution algorithms: recent results quantify the “algorithmic” phase transition and lower bounds for low-degree polynomial algorithms on random k-SAT <cite id="55891bdf-4">For uniformly random k-SAT formulas Φ with n variables and m clauses, the algorithmic task of finding a satisfying assignment exhibits a sharp transition; rigorous hardness is proved at certain α values for stable algorithms</cite> <cite id="55891bdf-5">Rigorous hardness for random k-SAT is shown at α = 4.911 for certain algorithm classes</cite> <cite id="55891bdf-7">Work on phase transitions in random SAT explains how critical-region hardness relates to solver difficulty</cite>.

Strengths:
- High reproducibility and tunability via clause density and k; practitioners can precisely calibrate difficulty along empirically known hard regimes and benchmark solver scaling <cite id="55891bdf-2">Phase-transition hardness provides a systematic way to tune instance hardness via clauses/variables ratio</cite>.
- Provides clean tests of general-purpose heuristics (unit propagation, clause learning, restarts) without built-in domain structure confounds <cite id="fe1f17db-3">Classical analyses focus on solver behavior on random problems and hard instance construction</cite>.
- Empirical studies compare top solvers across many random instances, yielding transparent performance curves and insights into solver limitations near the transition <cite id="55891bdf-0">Systematic empirical study of solver running times on random 3-SAT at the phase transition across solvers and scales</cite>.

Weaknesses:
- Structural “blandness”: uniform randomness may not stress solver components that are effective on structured industrial or cryptographic benchmarks; community/scale-free structure can make instances easier by preserving local search basins <cite id="fe1f17db-5">Community-structured k-SAT instances can preserve subformula properties from random k-SAT yet induce distinct hardness patterns in practice</cite>.
- Lack of domain realism; phase-transition instances may not reflect real-world encodings (e.g., cryptographic constraints) that have complex algebraic dependencies and exploitable structure for specialized cryptanalytic methods <cite id="55891bdf-1">Theoretical/experimental analyses emphasize solver success patterns but also highlight the role of problem structure in tractability, motivating realistic benchmarks</cite>.

2) Planted-solution (hidden-solution) SAT: planted k-SAT and hidden k-SAT
Mechanism:
- Generate a target assignment uniformly or by design, then sample clauses that are satisfied by it (planted satisfiable); alternatively hide the solution by sampling clauses with few conflicts (hidden satisfiable) or deliberately unsatisfiable hidden structures <cite id="fe1f17db-1">Tools for generating hard SAT formulas with a planted solution support benchmarking of SAT solvers</cite> <cite id="fe1f17db-2">New generators produce multiple-solution random k-SAT instances and control hardness, outperforming p-hidden and q-hidden baselines in producing harder instances</cite>.
- Connections to Ising physics and integer-derived constraints yield modern planted families used for SAT and optimization solver benchmarking <cite id="fe1f17db-4">Planted-solution SAT/Ising benchmarks derived from integer models provide a principled way to embed known hard structure into satisfiable instances</cite>.
- Hard satisfiable construction is linked to one-way function hardness: creating hard forced satisfiable instances relates to the difficulty of inverting one-way functions <cite id="fe1f17db-6">A simple model builds hard satisfiable instances and links the hardness to open problems like computing one-way functions</cite>.

Strengths:
- Guaranteed satisfiable targets enable stress-testing search and learning without solver-side unsatisfiability artifacts; useful for core algorithmic comparisons and for constructing worst-case instances under distributional assumptions <cite id="fe1f17db-1">Planted-solution benchmarks explicitly target hard satisfiable instances for solver evaluation</cite> <cite id="fe1f17db-4">Integer-derived planted benchmarks allow controlled embedding of hard structure across SAT/Ising</cite>.
- Hidden-solution variants can mimic “secret key” scenarios and produce hard-to-find solutions; modern designs better target hardness than simple p/q-hidden methods <cite id="fe1f17db-2">Compared with p- and q-hidden, a new approach generates harder k-SAT and allows controlled hardness tuning</cite>.
- Tunable via number of clauses, noise level (clause conflict rate), and variable/domain coupling, enabling targeted evaluation of resolution and message-passing methods <cite id="fe1f17db-6">Hard satisfiable construction emphasizes how coupling strength relates to solver intractability</cite>.

Weaknesses:
- Hardness is relative to the planted distribution; planted low-density or very highly constrained instances may admit easy structure (e.g., long chains of implications) not present in adversarial objectives, especially if solvers can detect or exploit plantedness <cite id="fe1f17db-2">The method explicitly outperforms p/q-hidden baselines as a generator of harder instances, suggesting that naive hidden variants can be too easy</cite>.
- Over-satisfaction guarantees do not ensure cryptographic robustness; SAT-specific planting may be reverse-engineered by statistical learning on clause distributions <cite id="fe1f17db-4">Benchmarks bridge SAT and Ising but still rely on controllable structure that can be exploited</cite>.

3) Expander-graph (graph-theoretic incidence) generators
Mechanism and theory:
- Build a bipartite incidence graph between variables and clauses that is an expander; then convert to k-SAT. The SAT instances are provably hard for large-resolution-width proofs, and empirical studies show resistance to CDCL solvers <cite id="fe1f17db-7">Constructing the incidence graph as an expander yields hard k-SAT instances with theoretical and practical evidence of difficulty for CDCL</cite>.
- Community-structured generators can preserve “local-to-global” properties of random k-SAT while adding structural cues; subformula properties carry over to the structured ensemble, supporting hardness inheritance <cite id="fe1f17db-5">Subformula-inherited properties transfer from random k-SAT to community-structured distributions, underpinning empirical hardness</cite>.

Strengths:
- Theoretical justification via expander mixing and width lower bounds in resolution yields confidence that certain instances are proof-complex; empirically, CDCL solvers struggle on these encodings <cite id="fe1f17db-7">Expander-based SAT instances are hard for CDCL in practice and justified by bipartite incidence construction</cite>.
- Modular generation from expander graphs allows tuning spectral expansion and clause/variable degrees to match target solver behaviors and proof complexity <cite id="fe1f17db-7">The incidence-graph construction gives handle on clause/variable interconnectivity and derived hardness</cite>.

Weaknesses:
- Dependence on combinatorial design may limit realism for cryptanalysis; practical ciphers exploit differential/linear structure that expanders don’t capture.
- Some sub-classes discovered by modern solvers (e.g., XOR, bounded-arithmetic reasoning) can create weak points; instances with hidden structure may be easier than general random k-SAT at equal clause density <cite id="fe1f17db-7">Empirical results show hardness but also show solver progress that can affect different structured families</cite>.

4) Structural realism: cryptographic encodings (AES/SHA/RSA) and algebraic (ANF/XOR) formulations
Mechanism:
- Encode cryptographic primitives or cryptanalytic tasks into CNF or ANF over GF(2), preserving complex algebraic/structural constraints used in practice (e.g., substitution-permutation networks, hash pipelines, modular arithmetic) <cite id="0030a55d-0">SAT-based security evaluation of SHA-3 finalists involves full CNF encoding of the primitive and analysis of solver behavior</cite> <cite id="0030a55d-7">ANF-based SAT formulations of plaintext–ciphertext relations admit algorithmic simplification that enhances key decryption, showing exploitability of algebraic structure</cite>.
- Empirical performance shows modern SAT solvers already handle large industrial-like instances; encodings of RSA and related problems are used to build SAT instances reflecting realistic computational challenges <cite id="0030a55d-1">Modern SAT solvers routinely solve very large SAT instances from industry/academia, motivating use of large, realistic encodings</cite> <cite id="0030a55d-4">Fast reduction from RSA to SAT motivates constructing SAT instances corresponding to cryptographic hardness tasks</cite>.

Strengths:
- High external validity: constraints mirror real cryptanalysis, testing solver robustness and deployment readiness for security analyses and certification <cite id="0030a55d-0">End-to-end CNF generation and evaluation of SHA-3 finalists operationalize realistic hardness</cite>.
- Rich structure can require diverse reasoning (algebraic equivalence, cancellation, case analysis), probing hybrid solver capabilities (e.g., CDCL+lookahead+XOR) <cite id="0030a55d-7">ANF simplification algorithms take advantage of plaintext/ciphertext structure to accelerate key solving</cite>.
- Benchmarks support reproducible stress tests for solver advances in cryptanalysis, with public instances (e.g., AES/SHA) used widely across the community <cite id="0030a55d-6">NIST SHA-3 standardization and evaluation provides standardized materials for algorithmic stress-testing</cite>.

Weaknesses:
- Solvers exploit domain-specific patterns (e.g., Gaussian elimination for XOR constraints, ANF reductions); these shortcuts can create variance in difficulty that is less reflective of pure logical hardness, and progress in cryptanalysis can render some families easier <cite id="0030a55d-7">Key-solving algorithms simplify ANF instances using plaintext/ciphertext, indicating exploitable structure</cite>.
- Instance generation can be brittle: encoding errors or modeling omissions (e.g., omitted propagation in cryptographic steps) can make instances artificially easier or lose algorithmic relevance; benchmarks require ongoing curation and updates <cite id="0030a55d-0">CNF generation pipelines require careful HDL-to-CNF compilation and synthesis to preserve hardness</cite>.

5) Controlled structural operators: community/scale-free and cycle-suppression (No-Triangle)
Mechanism:
- Generate variable/variable graphs with community structure and embed clauses to preserve intra-community density but limit inter-community edges, transferring random-like hardness while making local search navigate many weakly connected clusters <cite id="fe1f17db-5">Community-structured SAT inherits subformula properties from random k-SAT and yields empirically hard instances</cite>.
- No-Triangle generator explicitly reduces small cycles (triangles) in the interaction graph; empirical comparisons show these instances are harder and provide a knob via clustering control that correlates with solver difficulty <cite id="fe1f17db-8">No-Triangle SAT suppresses triangles to raise hardness; empirical comparisons show it is harder than triangle-preserving baselines</cite> <cite id="fe1f17db-2">The generator claims to control hardness beyond simple hidden-variable schemes</cite>.

Strengths:
- Graph-level control yields reproducible hardness variation and a direct link to empirical hardness trends related to clustering and modularity; useful to test solvers’ community-aware behavior and clause-learning robustness across scales <cite id="fe1f17db-5">Empirical hardness trends carry over subformula properties from random to community-structured graphs</cite> <cite id="fe1f17db-8">Controlling cluster coefficient via triangle suppression produces systematically harder instances</cite>.
- Adds realism absent from pure uniform randomness (communities, modularity) and can reflect characteristics of some real-world problem graphs <cite id="fe1f17db-5">Community-structured models preserve key properties from random k-SAT while adding structural realism</cite>.

Weaknesses:
- Graph-level hardness does not guarantee logical proof lower bounds; some families remain vulnerable to structural breaking (e.g., aggressive backtracking, symmetry exploitation) not captured by clause graphs <cite id="fe1f17db-5">Despite preserved properties, practical solver techniques can differentiate random- and community-structured cases</cite>.
- Choice of operator may not cover all failure modes; for example, triangle suppression may not stress XOR-rich or highly functional (arithmetic) structures effectively <cite id="fe1f17db-8">No-Triangle emphasizes clustering-induced difficulty but does not address algebraic structure</cite>.

6) Adaptive/perturbative and algorithmic-configuration generation
Mechanism:
- Use automated algorithm configuration and performance modeling to tune instance parameters (e.g., clause-to-variable ratio, literal bias, conflict rates) so that produced formulas induce solver bottlenecks; also applied to planted-solution generators to locate “hard” parameter regions empirically <cite id="fe1f17db-1">Algorithm configuration tools are used to generate hard SAT formulas with a planted solution, enabling solver-independent hard instance discovery</cite> <cite id="fe1f17db-2">A configured, multi-solution generator targets harder-than-hidden variants with tunable hardness</cite>.
- Some recent generators learn or enforce multi-solution behavior to shift difficulty versus unique-solution regimes that can be easier to exploit via unit propagation or symmetry effects <cite id="fe1f17db-2">Compared with p- and q-hidden, a multi-solution generator produces harder K-SAT instances and controls hardness continuously</cite>.

Strengths:
- Maximizes practical difficulty for a given solver or solver class via data-driven search; produces adversarially calibrated benchmarks for fairness in solver evaluations <cite id="fe1f17db-1">Tools for generating hard planted instances are shown useful for benchmarking SAT solvers</cite>.
- Flexible: can incorporate planted solutions, clause-graph constraints, conflict diversity, etc., to exercise both local and global search <cite id="fe1f17db-2">Hardness control and multi-solution design explicitly outperform traditional hidden variants</cite>.

Weaknesses:
- Generative models can overfit to specific solver strategies; resulting instances may show brittleness when tested against broader method families or future advances <cite id="fe1f17db-2">Demonstrated superiority versus naive hidden baselines suggests sensitivity to modeling choices, which can also be a failure mode for new methods</cite>.
- Lacks provable complexity guarantees unless combined with hardness-preserving structure (e.g., expansion, cryptographic hardness) <cite id="fe1f17db-7">Expander integrations provide theoretical anchors; purely configured models may lack such guarantees</cite>.

Cross-cutting properties and selection guidance
- Inheritance of random-hardness properties: when constructing structured variants from random k-SAT (community structure, expander incidence), key properties like subformula complexity and typical algorithmic hardness can carry over, enabling principled structured hard instances <cite id="fe1f17db-5">Hardness-related properties of random k-SAT subformulas transfer to instances drawn from community-structured distributions</cite>.
- Provable vs. empirical hardness: expander-based and theoretical phase-transition results offer lower bounds/anchors for proof complexity, whereas planted/random methods yield high-reproducibility empirical hardness without general proof barriers <cite id="55891bdf-5">Hardness proved for random k-SAT at specific clause-density thresholds for stable algorithms</cite> <cite id="fe1f17db-7">Expander-based generators provide both theory and empirical solver difficulty</cite>.
- Realism and domain validity: cryptographic encodings deliver the most domain-realistic stress tests but can embed exploitable algebraic structure; security benchmark suites (e.g., SHA-3) demonstrate their role in evaluating solver/cryptanalysis toolkits <cite id="0030a55d-0">SAT encodings used to assess SHA-3 finalists</cite> <cite id="0030a55d-6">NIST SHA-3 evaluation process established standardized hard-instance material</cite>.
- Generative trade-offs: planted and hidden models allow worst-case/one-way-function links and clean tunability; community/cycle-suppression adds realism and modularity to the interaction graph; expander/incidence provides theoretical difficulty; cryptographic realism adds algebraic depth—choose one family per evaluation goal and combine when possible to diversify stressors <cite id="fe1f17db-6">Links to one-way function hardness inform choice for theoretical stressors</cite> <cite id="fe1f17db-8">Graph operator control offers a practical knob for solver hardness</cite>.

Practical recommendations
- For general algorithm development and scaling studies near “typical” SAT hardness: use random 3-SAT at clause activity near the empirically hardest regime, augmented with planted hiddenness to avoid trivial satisfiability signals; add community overlays for realism <cite id="55891bdf-0">Empirical scaling of top solvers on random 3-SAT at the phase transition</cite> <cite id="fe1f17db-3">Survey highlights random k-SAT and hard instance construction for benchmarking</cite> <cite id="fe1f17db-5">Community-inherited properties connect to structured difficulty</cite>.
- For testing clause-learning and restart heuristics under provable barriers: generate expander-based incidence k-SAT; if cryptographic features are desired, overlay small AES/DES s-box ANF gadgets while preserving expansion properties to maintain proof-complexity <cite id="fe1f17db-7">Expander-based generators yield hard CDCL instances</cite> <cite id="0030a55d-7">ANF reductions exploit algebraic structure; embed modestly to stress learning</cite>.
- For security and cryptanalysis readiness: use standardized cryptographic SAT/ANF encodings (e.g., AES/SHA-3 materials) and measure solver or hybrid toolkits’ progress over time; where helpful, add hidden-solution targets to quantify search difficulty independent of side-channel realism <cite id="0030a55d-0">SAT-based security margin evaluation for SHA-3 finalists via CNF</cite> <cite id="0030a55d-6">SHA-3 selection based on rigorous evaluations</cite>.
- For realistic industrial/complex structure without cryptographic semantics: use community-scale-free generators with controlled triangle content to probe solver behavior on clustered constraint landscapes and evaluate hybrid solvers with decomposition, symmetry handling, and ML guidance <cite id="fe1f17db-5">Community structure preserves random-like subformula properties and induces solver difficulty</cite> <cite id="fe1f17db-8">Triangle suppression increases empirical hardness</cite>.

Key limitations and open challenges
- Lack of universal theory: beyond expander and phase-transition backings, “hardness” remains largely empirical; planted and community-based generators can be tuned to appear hard but may admit solver-specific shortcuts <cite id="fe1f17db-2">Generators surpass simple hidden variants because naive planting/hiddenness can be too easy</cite> <cite id="fe1f17db-5">Differences in subformula properties across structures reveal solver-specific vulnerabilities</cite>.
- Evolving difficulty: algorithmic and ML advances (XOR reasoning, ANF simplification, learning-from-examples) change which instance families are “hard,” requiring continual benchmark refresh and multi-method evaluation to avoid stagnation artifacts <cite id="0030a55d-7">ANF-based key solving shows how algebraic structure can be exploited</cite> <cite id="0030a55d-1">SAT solvers have solved increasingly large real-world instances, shifting what constitutes a “hard” challenge</cite>.

In summary, leading hard-instance generators span random/phase-transition baselines (tunable, theoretically grounded), planted/hidden-solution families (controlled satisfiability/unsatisfiability with one-way-function connections), expander/incidence encoders (provably resistant to narrow classes), realistic cryptographic/ANF encodings (domain-valid but structure-exploitable), and structured graph operators (community and cycle control to transfer and modulate hardness). The best choice depends on whether you need theoretical guarantees, cryptographic realism, or solver-agnostic empirical stress tests; combining multiple families often yields the most robust evaluation battery <cite id="fe1f17db-3">Survey tying random k-SAT, hard instance construction, and solver behavior</cite> <cite id="fe1f17db-5">Community-structured inheritance of random hardness properties</cite> <cite id="fe1f17db-7">Expander-based generation with both theory and empirical difficulty</cite> <cite id="fe1f17db-8">Cycle-based, graph-statistic control to increase hardness</cite> <cite id="fe1f17db-6">Planted-solution links to one-way functions and hard satisfiable construction</cite> <cite id="0030a55d-0">Cryptographic SAT encodings for standardized benchmarking</cite> <cite id="0030a55d-7">ANF-based reductions demonstrate practical solver-side structure exploitation</cite> <cite id="55891bdf-6">Phase-transition definitions and rigorous hardness in random k-SAT</cite> <cite id="55891bdf-4">Algorithmic phase transition and hardness results at specific α for k-SAT</cite>.

ambiguity_judge.evidence: The response directly answers the question with a full taxonomy of methods and their strengths/weaknesses, without asking for clarification or stating any assumptions about what “leading methods” should mean.

questions.original_query: What datasets and methods are used to pre-train models on table specific tasks?

query.text: What datasets and methods are used to pre-train models on table specific tasks?
query.answer:
Below is a synthesis of the datasets and learning methods commonly used to pretrain and finetune models for table-specific tasks. For each component, I summarize what the data contains, how it is typically used, and representative examples.

1) Datasets used for pretraining and finetuning on tables

- WebTables/Wiki-derived multi-table corpora. Early and widely used sources provide massive collections of relational tables scraped from the web. <cite id="95684960-0">The Web contains an estimated 154 million HTML tables, with Wikipedia alone containing 1.6 million high‑quality relational tables, which motivated WebTables and related resources for extracting structured, high‑quality tables</cite>. <cite id="95684960-8">WebTables is a long‑running effort to exploit the large and diverse set of online HTML tables as casual databases</cite>.

- Task‑oriented table corpora (QA, data-to-text). <cite id="95684960-3">Open‑WikiTableQA composes 67,023 questions with 24,680 tables for open‑domain QA where the answers are derived from multi‑column, semi‑structured tables</cite>. <cite id="95684960-2">WikiTableT provides a large‑scale data‑to‑text corpus mapping Wikipedia tables to article sections, enabling table summarization and data‑to‑text pretraining/finetuning</cite>. <cite id="c9e99e03-1">WikiTableQuestions is a large-scale dataset for question answering over semi-structured tables, used to fine-tune QA capabilities grounded in tabular evidence</cite>.

- Source‑code and structured data tables. <cite id="95684960-1">GitTables is a 1M‑table corpus extracted from GitHub CSVs, intended for tasks like QA that depend on table contents</cite>, and <cite id="95684960-5">is suitable for QA over relational tables at scale</cite>.

- Text-to-SQL datasets (schema + questions). <cite id="c12acabc-4">Spider provides 10,181 questions across 5,693 complex, cross‑domain SQL queries with multi‑step subgoals, allowing models to be pretrained/finetuned on schema-grounded reasoning and generation</cite>. <cite id="c12acabc-6">Spider‑Realistic has been used as an evaluation resource in structure‑grounded pretraining for text‑to‑SQL generation</cite>.

- Table understanding and detection (visual tabular inputs). <cite id="c12acabc-0">TableBank is an image‑based table detection and recognition dataset built with weak supervision from Word/LaTeX documents on the internet</cite>, and <cite id="c12acabc-3">was created to provide a large set of high‑quality labeled tables for robust training of neural models for table detection/recognition</cite>, which pairs with downstream text/table grounding tasks when models read table images or layouts.

- Instructional and dialog-style table datasets. <cite id="c9e99e03-6">A SemEval‑2025 paper demonstrates instruction‑following NL‑to‑SQL with LLMs (GPT‑4o, DeepSeek), showing how models are prompted to act over database schemas via structured tools and queries</cite>. While not a pretraining corpus, this pattern motivates using instruction-style dialog data with tabular schemas as inputs during tuning.

2) Pretraining and finetuning methods for tables

- Structure‑aware text understanding with table structures. Because tables combine text cells with row/column semantics, pretraining and finetuning leverage both textual content and structural signals. <cite id="c12acabc-6">Structure‑grounded pretraining for text‑to‑SQL uses Spider‑Realistic to align model representations with SQL operators and schema keys, improving downstream SQL generation over unseen schemas</cite>. This approach emphasizes grounding tokens such as table/column names and operators in the model’s hidden state prior to fine-tuning.

- Task‑specific generative pretraining on tabular data. <cite id="95684960-2">WikiTableT supports pretraining/finetuning for data‑to‑text generation from tables to paragraph sections in Wikipedia articles</cite>, enabling models to learn mapping between tabular facts and fluent prose grounded in table content. <cite id="95684960-0">Leveraging millions of tables from Wikipedia/Web reduces noisy tables and can provide higher‑quality data for pretraining tasks that need reliable entities and relations</cite>.

- Table QA pretraining over evidence tables. <cite id="95684960-3">Open‑WikiTableQA provides question→table→answer tuples where the answer is read directly from the table cells, enabling masked LM‑style QA over tabular evidence</cite>. <cite id="c12acabc-8">TabFact introduces language inference over tables with mixed symbolic and linguistic reasoning, supplying finetuning signals for models to extract facts and justify them with table facts</cite>.

- Visual and layout‑aware pretraining. For scenarios where tables are provided as images/tables, <cite id="c12acabc-0">TableBank’s labeled table images and cells</cite> can be used to pretrain vision‑language encoders to detect tables, rows, and cells, which then serve as inputs to text encoders that read cell content—effectively fusing structure and text.

- Reinforcement learning and verifier‑based distillation. Although more common in text QA/SQL, RL can guide table models toward higher‑confidence, verifiable outputs. <cite id="c9e99e03-6">At inference, agentic setups (e.g., NL‑to‑SQL with tool use) allow iterative query planning and execution with feedback from executed SQL results, which can be framed as reward signals to retrain policy models</cite>. In practice, RL‑based finetuning over Spider‑style datasets improves exact SQL matching; the same pattern transfers to table reasoning tasks where an execution verifier for cells or relations provides feedback.

- Instruction tuning and agent prompting. LLMs specifically trained or fine‑tuned to accept tabular inputs as part of instructions benefit from large instruction corpora that include table schemas or samples as context. <cite id="c9e99e03-6">Empirically, using GPT‑4o/DeepSeek with explicit NL‑to‑SQL tools yields substantial gains on table tasks, which can be replicated by instruction‑tuning with large corpora that include database schema examples and table‑aware prompts</cite>.

3) End-to-end workflows used for table tasks

- Table QA and structured reasoning. <cite id="95684960-3">Open‑WikiTableQA shows how to read tables directly as evidence for QA</cite>, while <cite id="c9e99e03-1">WikiTableQuestions supplies question→table→answer examples for large‑scale QA over semi‑structured data</cite>. <cite id="c12acabc-8">TabFact frames inference over tables as natural language inference, requiring derivation of textual statements from table facts with justifications</cite>. <cite id="c9e99e03-6">SemEval‑2025 demonstrates the effectiveness of instruction‑driven NL‑to‑SQL for tables when coupled with a SQL engine as a verifier</cite>, which generalizes to other table tasks like attribute search and comparative reasoning.

- Data-to-text and table summarization. <cite id="95684960-2">WikiTableT trains data‑to‑text models to generate coherent sections from tables, capturing nested relations and hierarchical summaries</cite>. <cite id="95684960-0">Using Wikipedia/Web tables helps ensure consistency and high-quality content for abstractive summaries</cite>.

- Table grounding and VLM+LLM fusion. <cite id="c12acabc-0">TableBank enables pretraining vision‑language models to detect and recognize tables in documents</cite>, which can be combined with language‑only encoders that read cell content and perform QA or summarization over the parsed table structure.

- Schema‑grounded generation (text‑to‑SQL) as a canonical table task. <cite id="c12acabc-4">Spider’s complexity and cross‑domain coverage make it a staple for pretraining and finetuning schema‑aware reasoning and generating correct SQL over novel databases</cite>. <cite id="c12acabc-6">Structure‑grounded pretraining improves robustness by aligning generated SQL with relational operators and table/column embeddings before task‑specific finetuning</cite>.

4) Practical training recipes (how people combine datasets and methods)

- Web/Wikipedia‑quality text‑table pretraining. Combine a Web/Wikipedia‑derived multi‑table corpus (e.g., WebTables) with masked LM over cells, plus structure‑aware tasks (row/column permutation prediction) and QA examples from WikiTableQ datasets; then finetune on task‑specific datasets like Spider (SQL) or Open‑WikiTableQA for table QA. <cite id="95684960-0">Large, high‑quality table corpora from Wikipedia provide reliable data to bootstrap pretraining</cite> and <cite id="c12acabc-4">Spider supplies challenging cross‑domain evaluations for generative tasks aligned to SQL</cite>.

- GitHub/CSV‑style tabular data for QA and NL reasoning. <cite id="95684960-1">GitTables provides a 1M‑table corpus in CSV/structured text suitable for QA and schema‑based NL tasks</cite>, where models can be pretrained on masked filling of attribute cells and then finetuned on question answering with multi‑table retrieval over repository READMEs and docs.

- Data‑to‑text pipelines. <cite id="95684960-2">Use WikiTableT to pretrain an encoder‑decoder that converts tables into article sections, then fine‑tune on domain‑specific tables</cite>. Add table structure supervision (e.g., aligning header spans and nested cells) from TableBank or LaTeX/Word sources to improve macro‑structure fidelity. <cite id="c12acabc-0">Structure annotations in TableBank assist in learning how to parse and respect hierarchical tabular layouts</cite>.

- Instruction‑tuned agents over tables. <cite id="c9e99e03-6">Pretrain or tune a base LLM on large instruction corpora, then specialize with table‑aware prompts that present schemas or sample tables as inputs; at inference equip with tools (e.g., SQL execution, web table lookup) to verify outputs</cite>. This yields strong performance on QA, extraction, and NL‑to‑SQL without extensive table‑specific pretraining, mainly due to tool feedback and retrieval over table data.

- Reinforcement and distillation loops. For tasks with a clear correctness oracle (SQL, factual QA), <cite id="c9e99e03-6">use the execution result as a reward signal</cite>—e.g., run sampled generations over a validation set of Spider or WikiTableQA, filter by successful queries, and update the model or its policy; <cite id="c12acabc-6">structure‑grounded pretraining</cite> further stabilizes learning by pre‑aligning text to schema structures.

5) Additional resources and trends

- Foundational corpora and surveys. <cite id="c9e99e03-0">Recent surveys catalog pretraining corpora categories and acquisition channels, highlighting domain‑specific tables as key vertical data</cite>. <cite id="c9e99e03-2">Curated “awesome pretraining” repositories keep track of open datasets and data methods, including table corpora and masking strategies</cite>.

- Visual table understanding. <cite id="c12acabc-1">Recent “visual table understanding” datasets emphasize robust representation of tabular layouts for tasks spanning detection, recognition, and reasoning</cite>, supporting multimodal pretraining where a model reads table images and then maps cells to text.

Putting it together, state‑of‑the‑art table‑trained models typically combine:
- A large multi‑table corpus (Web/Wikipedia/GitHub) as the primary pretraining source, often with masked LM and structure‑aware objectives. <cite id="95684960-0">Web/Wikipedia tables provide high‑quality, scalable supervision</cite>; <cite id="95684960-1">GitHub‑derived tables supply noisy‑but‑representative real‑world schemas and data</cite>.
- Task‑specific datasets (e.g., Spider for SQL; WikiTableQuestions/QA; TabFact for structured inference) for finetuning and evaluation, sometimes with RL/verifier feedback. <cite id="c12acabc-4">Spider provides realistic evaluation for generated SQL</cite> and <cite id="95684960-3">WikiTable datasets give QA signals directly tied to table facts</cite>; <cite id="c9e99e03-6">tool‑assisted RL patterns improve factual correctness</cite>.
- Instruction/agent‑style finetuning and inference that explicitly surface tables, schemas, and tools (e.g., SQL execution) for robust out‑of‑distribution performance. <cite id="c9e99e03-6">LLMs guided by tools show strong transfer to new databases and tables</cite>.

If you share your target task (e.g., SQL generation vs. multi‑table QA vs. table summarization), I can map this to a concrete recipe (data mix and training objective sequence) with suggested checkpoints and evaluation baselines.

fully_underspecified.text: What datasets and methods are used to pre-train models on tasks?
fully_underspecified.answer:
# Overview

Pre-training equips models with general-purpose capabilities by learning from large, unlabeled corpora using objectives that capture syntax, semantics, and world knowledge. In natural language and vision–language models, the dominant pre-training methods are masked language modeling (MLM) and next-token prediction (NTP), often implemented as generative pre-training followed by task-specific fine-tuning. <cite id="371ccf8a-4">Next-token prediction trains a language model by turning tokenized text into shifted input–target pairs and updating weights to predict the next token at each position</cite>. <cite id="0b290751-2">BERT introduced deep bidirectional representations by pre-training a Transformer encoder with an MLM objective jointly conditioning on left and right context</cite>. Across domains, pre-training data typically aggregate broad web text, books, Wikipedia, and curated benchmarks or multilingual resources; recent “data compendia” synthesize multi-trillion-token pipelines for reproducibility and policy guidance. <cite id="dd0fb0e9-0">Standard pipelines collect and process hundreds of billions to trillions of tokens from sources like Common Crawl, web corpora, books, and Wikipedia</cite>. 

Below are canonical datasets and methods used to pre-train models for language and structured tasks, followed by common downstream task pre-training resources.

# Core Pre-training Objectives and Methods

1) Next-Token Prediction (NTP, autoregressive LM)
- Method: Train a decoder-only or encoder-decoder autoregressive model to predict the next token given the history; widely used to initialize parameters for supervised fine-tuning. <cite id="371ccf8a-4">NTP converts text into sliding input–target pairs and updates the model to minimize prediction error</cite>. <cite id="0b290751-5">OpenAI’s “Improving Language Understanding by Generative Pre-Training” uses a language modeling objective on unlabeled data to initialize a neural network, then adapts via supervised fine-tuning</cite>. 
- Variants and scaling: Research evaluates how sequence length N and maximum sequence length affect generalization in NTP; multimodal extensions extend NTP to images and audiovisual inputs. <cite id="371ccf8a-0">The generalization ability of NTP pretraining depends on the number of token sequences and the maximum length</cite>. <cite id="371ccf8a-1">Next-token prediction serves as a powerful paradigm for large multimodal models, enabling scaling beyond language</cite>. 
- Empirical alternatives: New objectives (e.g., multi-token prediction) and non-autoregressive training have been proposed as alternatives to strictly one-step prediction. <cite id="371ccf8a-6">Multi-token prediction pre-trains by predicting the next k tokens at each position, offering an alternative to standard autoregressive objectives</cite>. <cite id="371ccf8a-2">A survey of alternatives spans multi-token, latent-space, and non-autoregressive training for text generation</cite>. 

2) Masked Language Modeling (MLM, denoising/unsupervised)
- Method: Randomly mask a fraction of input tokens and train a model to reconstruct the missing tokens, learning bi-directional context. <cite id="0b290751-2">BERT jointly conditions on both left and right context during pre-training via an MLM objective</cite>. <cite id="0b290751-6">BERT’s MLM masks 15% of tokens and trains a bidirectional encoder to predict them</cite>. 
- Objectives and theory: Analyses and laws describe how MLM shapes contextualized embeddings and scaling behavior. <cite id="371ccf8a-3">A quantitative “law” governs the learning of contextualized token embeddings through intermediate representations during pre-training</cite>. <cite id="0b290751-7">MLM directly addresses the need for bidirectional understanding by masking tokens and training the model to reconstruct them</cite>. 
- Contrastive/contrastive language modeling: Unsupervised contrastive approaches learn sentence- or text-level representations by contrasting positive/negative pairs, a lineage connecting Siamese/InfoNCE-style objectives to vision-language pre-training and to text-only sentence encoders. <cite id="371ccf8a-1">Multimodal NTP builds on contrastive paradigms that scale general-purpose pre-training to vision–language</cite>. 

3) Sequence-to-Sequence (seq2seq) Unified Pre-training (Text-to-Text, T5-style)
- Method: Frame all text problems as unconditional text generation and pre-train a Transformer decoder on denoising tasks to convert inputs like [“translate english to german” “Hello world”] → “Hallo welt”. <cite id="3b10bf74-8">T5 reframes diverse NLP tasks as text-to-text, enabling a single model and loss across generation, translation, and comprehension</cite>. <cite id="3b10bf74-0">T5 pre-trained on C4 achieves state-of-the-art results across many NLP benchmarks</cite>. <cite id="3b10bf74-3">T5 is trained on C4 with a denoising objective, supporting wide-ranging NLP tasks in a unified format</cite>. 
- Training data: 
  - C4 (Colossal Clean Crawled corpus) is a multilingual, filtered Common Crawl derivative built from books and web text; Books1M/Books2 are large book collections; Wikipedia and other web corpora are common sources. <cite id="dd0fb0e9-0">Modern LM pipelines combine Common Crawl–derived corpora, Wikipedia, and books at hundreds of billions to trillions of tokens</cite>. <cite id="dd0fb0e9-4">Recent data-compilation work considers Wikipedia, OpenWebText2, and RedPajama-books as reference positive data sources with reference pipelines</cite>. <cite id="dd0fb0e9-1">Practical tokenizer pipelines train on mixtures sampled from Common Crawl, Wikipedia, and Books to learn high-quality subword vocabularies</cite>. 
  - TEDTalks-based T0 exemplifies multilingual pre-training for transfer across tasks and languages. <cite id="dd0fb0e9-4">RedPajama-books (Books1M/Books2) appears alongside Wikipedia and OpenWebText2 in contemporary pre-training resource lists</cite>. <cite id="3b10bf74-1">T5’s unified framework converts all text-based tasks into text-to-text using token-level templates, with pre-training on large corpora like C4</cite>. 

4) Generative Pre-training and Unified Initialization (GPT-style)
- Method: Pre-train autoregressive Transformer decoders on large web and book corpora to initialize models for supervised fine-tuning on classification, question answering, etc. <cite id="0b290751-5">Generative pre-training learns a language model on unlabeled data and then adapts via supervised fine-tuning</cite>. <cite id="dd0fb0e9-5">Transformer decoders are trained autoregressively to produce sequences, then adapted to downstream tasks</cite>. 
- Data sources: Large-scale corpora are built from Common Crawl, curated web text (WebText/WebText2), books (Books1M/Books2), and Wikipedia; pipelines now standardize multi-source concatenations and filtering. <cite id="dd0fb0e9-6">GPT-3 was pretrained on five datasets: Common Crawl, WebText2, Books1, Books2, and Wikipedia</cite>. <cite id="dd0fb0e9-0">LM pre-training now commonly trains on hundreds of billions of tokens drawn from Common Crawl, Wikipedia, books, and other web sources using standardized pipelines</cite>. <cite id="dd0fb0e9-4">Contemporary references track comparable corpora (Wikipedia, OpenWebText2, RedPajama-books) when designing new training data</cite>. 

# Datasets and Mixtures Used in Practice

1) Foundational monolingual English corpora
- Books and web:
  - Books: Books1M/Books2 (unpublished books), BookCorpus (11M words from 11k books), and Wikipedia passages. <cite id="0b290751-5">BERT was trained on BookCorpus (11,038 unpublished books, ~2,500M words from Wikipedia passages)</cite>. <cite id="0b290751-8">Findings emphasize that BERT differs from scientific literature; it is pre-trained on BooksCorpus and Wikipedia rather than domain-specific books</cite>. 
  - Web: Common Crawl, WebText/WebText2, and arXiv/StackExchange-style corpora; these are widely used for broad coverage and new word forms. <cite id="dd0fb0e9-6">GPT-3 mixed Common Crawl, WebText2, and Wikipedia with two large books datasets</cite>. <cite id="dd0fb0e9-1">Tokenizer training often samples from Common Crawl, Wikipedia, and Books for robust subword splits</cite>. 
- Wikipedia and academic text: Used to cover formal writing, terminology, and QA-relevant facts. <cite id="0b290751-5">BERT’s Wikipedia-derived passages supply diverse, high-quality text</cite>. <cite id="dd0fb0e9-0">Modern compendia catalog Wikipedia alongside web and books as a core LM-building block</cite>. 

2) Multilingual and filtered crawl mixtures
- C4 (Colossal Clean Crawled): A filtered Common Crawl subset used in T5-style models and multilingual tasks; often paired with CCMatrix or OPUS parallel corpora for translation. <cite id="3b10bf74-0">T5, pre-trained on C4, achieves strong cross-task results</cite>. <cite id="371ccf8a-1">Large multimodal models extend NTP across languages using massive crawl-derived corpora</cite>. 
- RedPajama/OpenCompass-style mixtures: Books1M/2, OpenWebText2, and Wikipedia compilations used as pre-training corpora and evaluation references. <cite id="dd0fb0e9-4">Data-compilation work enumerates Wikipedia, OpenWebText2, and RedPajama-books as standard positive data sources</cite>. 
- Multilingual benchmarks as pre-training material: T0/other TED-style corpora and CCMatrix/OPUS for translation and cross-lingual transfer. <cite id="3b10bf74-1">T5’s unified framework applies to generation, translation, and comprehension using monolingual and multilingual corpora</cite>. <cite id="dd0fb0e9-4">Contemporary pipelines include multilingual sources (OpenWebText2; books) to broaden coverage</cite>. 

3) Domain-specific and safety-filtered corpora
- Code: Pre-training on code repositories (GitHub, Stack Overflow) improves code generation and completion; modern efforts emphasize license compliance and deduplication. <cite id="dd0fb0e9-7">Work on Cross-lingual CodeGPT and code completion highlights dataset design and evaluation for token-level code tasks</cite>. 
- Safety: Curated “positive” web, book, and Wikipedia data are promoted over raw internet crawl to reduce contamination; the field is moving toward auditable, reproducible pipelines. <cite id="dd0fb0e9-4">Reference positive data often draw from Wikipedia, OpenWebText2, and RedPajama-books with increasing attention to quality control</cite>. <cite id="dd0fb0e9-3">A 2-trillion-token dataset pipeline documents collection, processing, and publication choices for reusable LM pretraining</cite>. 
- Multimodal: Web-scale image–text pairs (COCO, CC3M, LAION-style) are used to pre-train vision–language models and multimodal NTP; NTP extends to pixels and audio in emerging systems. <cite id="371ccf8a-1">Large multimodal models show that NTP generalizes to non-text modalities, scaling beyond language</cite>. 

4) Tokenizer training resources
- Tokenizers often train on mixtures to learn quality subwords: <cite id="dd0fb0e9-1">subword tokenizers are trained on samples from Common Crawl, Wikipedia, and Books to balance coverage and efficiency</cite>. 

# Downstream Task Pre-training and Fine-tuning Datasets

1) General-purpose ability datasets
- English Wikipedia and BookCorpus provide broad coverage and support QA and understanding-style tasks when used for pre-training or as knowledge banks; they are commonly combined with web crawl and books. <cite id="0b290751-5">BERT’s original pretraining on BookCorpus and Wikipedia passages builds strong general representations</cite>. <cite id="0b290751-8">Differences between domain corpora and scientific literature motivate using domain-specific pre-training corpora when targeting scientific tasks</cite>. 
- Massive web-and-book mixtures improve generalization and few-shot performance, serving as the backbone for transfer to many tasks. <cite id="dd0fb0e9-0">Trillions of tokens across web, books, and Wikipedia underpin modern LMs, enabling general-purpose reasoning and generation</cite>. 

2) Supervised fine-tuning tasks
- Text classification, NLI, QA, summarization, translation, and generation are typically solved by freezing or partially freezing a pre-trained LM and fine-tuning on labeled sets. <cite id="3b10bf74-8">T5 shows the same model and loss can be applied to generation, translation, and comprehension tasks through unified text-to-text framing</cite>. <cite id="0b290751-5">GPT-style models pre-train generatively and then adapt via supervised fine-tuning to downstream tasks</cite>. 

3) Canonical benchmark datasets used for task-oriented pre-training/fine-tuning
- QA and reading comprehension: SQuAD, MultiNLI/MNLI, AX (Analogy), and LAMBADA/OpenBookQA exemplify reasoning and knowledge-transfer; pre-training on broad corpora plus fine-tuning on these datasets yields strong gains. <cite id="371ccf8a-0">Sequence-length and data-scale choices in pre-training affect generalization on downstream QA-like tasks</cite>. 
- Named-entity recognition and NLP pipelines: CoNLL-03/05, WNUT/ACE for NER; pre-training with MLM/NTP followed by task-specific layer adapters is standard. <cite id="dd0fb0e9-4">Reference data sources (Wikipedia, OpenWebText2, RedPajama-books) supply background knowledge for such task layers</cite>. 
- Translation and MT: Tatoeba, OPUS, and CCMatrix often serve as fine-tuning corpora for seq2seq adapters on top of T5/GPT-encoder-decoder backbones. <cite id="3b10bf74-0">T5 trained on C4 attains strong performance on translation when adapted to target languages</cite>. 
- Summarization: CNN/DailyMail, xSum, PubMed; pre-training learns cross-attention and context compression, then fine-tuning aligns to source–target pairs. <cite id="3b10bf74-1">The unified text-to-text framing supports conditional generation for summarization</cite>. 
- Cross-lingual tasks and evaluation: XNLI, XGLUE, mDiverse; pre-training on multilingual C4/T0 and then cross-lingual fine-tuning. <cite id="3b10bf74-1">T5’s multilingual coverage via C4/TED-style corpora supports cross-lingual transfer</cite>. 

# Representative Model Families and Their Pre-training

- BERT/DeBERTa/MLP-encoders: <cite id="0b290751-2">Bidirectional Transformers with MLM on BooksCorpus and Wikipedia build bidirectional context and zero-shot transfer</cite>. 
- GPT/LLaMA-like: <cite id="0b290751-5">Generative pre-training on unlabeled web/books/Wikipedia, then supervised fine-tuning for tasks</cite>. <cite id="dd0fb0e9-6">GPT-3’s five-source mix (Common Crawl, WebText2, Books1/2, Wikipedia) illustrates standard practice</cite>. 
- T5/TinyT5/MT5: <cite id="3b10bf74-0">Decoder-only T5 trained on C4 unifies encoding and decoding for conditional text generation</cite>. <cite id="3b10bf74-3">C4 denoising objective enables transfer across NLP tasks</cite>. 
- Multimodal (CLIP/Mask2Former/MMDIT): Pre-train on image–text pairs with contrastive and masked prediction objectives; NTP and masked objectives generalize to pixels and audio. <cite id="371ccf8a-1">Next-token prediction paradigms extend to multimodal inputs, enabling cross-modal scaling</cite>. 
- Code: StarCoder/Codex/CodeLM train on GPL’d code corpora plus docs/web-code, improving code completion and synthesis; evaluation emphasizes test-based and contamination checks. <cite id="dd0fb0e9-7">CodeGPT work formalizes token-level code completion evaluation and setup</cite>. 

# Practical Data Composition Choices and Emerging Trends

- Composition and filtering: Pipelines increasingly combine web (Common Crawl/OpenWebText/WebText2), books (Books1M/2), and Wikipedia, with deduplication, safety filters, and language coverage; data compendia document the provenance and licenses. <cite id="dd0fb0e9-0">Modern reports detail collection, processing, and publication of hundreds of billions to trillions of tokens</cite>. <cite id="dd0fb0e9-4">Commonly tracked positive data include Wikipedia, OpenWebText2, and RedPajama-books</cite>. 
- Tokenizers: Trained on mixtures to balance coverage and compression; modern subword schemes affect how models see data. <cite id="dd0fb0e9-1">Tokenizer training commonly draws from Common Crawl, Wikipedia, and Books in one-to-many pipelines</cite>. 
- Objectives beyond MLM/NTP: Non-autoregressive multi-token training and latent-space methods seek efficiency and better density. <cite id="371ccf8a-6">Multi-token prediction trains models to predict k future tokens at each position</cite>. <cite id="371ccf8a-2">Surveys catalog alternative decoding and training objectives beyond NTP</cite>. 
- Curriculum and length: Curriculum scheduling and careful sequence-length choices improve generalization and stability; analyses quantify learning laws and sequence-length effects. <cite id="371ccf8a-0">NTP performance depends quantitatively on N and max sequence length</cite>. <cite id="371ccf8a-3">Quantified laws describe how contextualized embeddings are learned during pretraining</cite>. 
- Auditable and ethical datasets: Recent work emphasizes standardized, reproducible, and ethically sourced data with public documentation. <cite id="dd0fb0e9-3">A two-trillion-token dataset lays out collection, processing, and publishing with governance</cite>. <cite id="dd0fb0e9-0">Community-reusable trillion-token sources are cataloged with quality controls and policy guidance</cite>. 

# Minimal Examples: Putting It Together

- MLM (BERT-like): Pre-train a bidirectional encoder on BooksCorpus + Wikipedia using 15% random masking; then fine-tune for NER on CoNLL-03 or QA on SQuAD. <cite id="0b290751-2">BERT uses bidirectional LM pre-training to capture left/right context</cite>. <cite id="0b290751-6">Masked 15% of tokens to enforce bidirectionality</cite>. 
- NTP (GPT-like): Pre-train an autoregressive decoder on WebText + Books1M + Common Crawl; fine-tune with prompt-learning or adapters for classification/QA/summarization. <cite id="0b290751-5">Generative pre-training then supervised fine-tuning adapts to tasks</cite>. <cite id="dd0fb0e9-6">Use Common Crawl/WebText2/Books/Wikipedia as base sources</cite>. 
- T5-style seq2seq: Pre-train a decoder on C4 (multilingual) with a denoising objective; fine-tune to translation with OPUS and summarization with CNN/DailyMail. <cite id="3b10bf74-0">C4-trained T5 achieves state-of-the-art across benchmarks</cite>. <cite id="3b10bf74-3">C4 denoising supports conditional generation tasks</cite>. 

# Takeaways

- Objectives: Two dominant paradigms drive pre-training—masked language modeling (bi-directional reconstruction) and next-token prediction (autoregressive prediction)—with emerging non-autoregressive and multi-token alternatives. <cite id="0b290751-2">BERT popularized deep bidirectional MLM</cite>; <cite id="0b290751-5">OpenAI showed generative pre-training followed by supervised fine-tuning</cite>; <cite id="371ccf8a-6">multi-token prediction offers an alternative objective</cite>. 
- Data: Effective pre-training mixes large-scale web, books, and Wikipedia, increasingly supplemented by multilingual C4/OPUS and domain-specific corpora (code, science) along with safety filters and standardized pipelines. <cite id="dd0fb0e9-6">GPT-3 combined Common Crawl, WebText2, Books1/2, and Wikipedia</cite>; <cite id="0b290751-5">BERT combined BookCorpus and Wikipedia passages</cite>; <cite id="dd0fb0e9-4">modern compilations list Wikipedia, OpenWebText2, and RedPajama-books as canonical sources</cite>. 
- Downstream tasks: Pre-training supplies general capability; fine-tuning on task datasets such as SQuAD, CoNLL-03, MNLI/AX, and translation/summarization corpora yields strong performance across QA, NER, NLI, MT, and summarization. <cite id="3b10bf74-8">T5 demonstrates unified pre-training across generations and understandings</cite>. 
- Multimodal/code: The same principles scale to vision–language and code LMs via appropriate input modalities and data sources (image–text pairs; code repositories), with growing emphasis on auditable, high-quality corpora. <cite id="371ccf8a-1">NTP extends to multimodal models, enabling cross-modal scaling</cite>; <cite id="dd0fb0e9-7">code LMs emphasize token-level completion and evaluation</cite>.

without_scope.text: What datasets and methods are used to pre-train models on table specific tasks?
without_scope.answer:
Below is a synthesis of datasets and methods that have been used to pre-train models for table‑specific tasks (e.g., structured-data understanding, multi-table QA, table manipulation), with concrete examples, data curation patterns, and architectural tricks.

Overview of “table-specific pretraining”
- Pretraining for tables typically adapts language modeling to the tabular structure: headers/rows/cells, schema types, column dependencies, and cross-table links, rather than treating tables as plain text. <cite id="d59c04cb-0">Recent work explicitly constructs datasets spanning both numerical and textual columns to cover real‑world scenarios and learn across mixed data types</cite>. <cite id="3b99ee1b-0">Challenges include generalizing across diverse table formats (“cross‑table hurdle”), so pretraining data must cover heterogeneous schemas, layouts, and missing values</cite>.

I. Datasets used to pretrain on tables
1) Massive Web table corpora (text–table parallel data)
- TaBERT-style data: <cite id="18943e37-2">pretraining on a massive corpus of 26M Web tables paired with associated natural‑language context</cite> enables joint representations over cells and sentences (table–text parallel examples). <cite id="18943e37-4">The model “jointly learns representations for NL sentences and (semi‑)structured tables,” with training on 26M parallel table–text examples</cite>. <cite id="3b99ee1b-5">The masking objectives extend to columns, with a “Masked Column Prediction” (MCP) objective that recovers names and data types of masked columns</cite>.
- Source diversity and schema coverage: <cite id="d59c04cb-0">curated collections that span numerical and textual columns provide broad coverage of real‑world tabular scenarios and allow models to learn structured patterns across heterogeneous data</cite>.

2) Curated tabular benchmarks and single-/multi-table collections
- Tabular benchmark suites and multi-table collections are increasingly used as pretraining corpora or for transfer. <cite id="d59c04cb-1">A recent model and training dataset for transfer learning on tabular data achieved strong zero‑/few‑shot accuracy across 300 tabular benchmarks</cite>, indicating the availability of structured datasets and aligned targets suitable for pretraining and transfer.
- Large-scale LLM evaluations and pretraining over tabular data also leverage diverse Kaggle-/domain datasets. <cite id="d59c04cb-6">One survey-style resource benchmarks models over 19 real‑world datasets with tens of thousands of rows across multiple tables</cite>, highlighting the use of structured relational samples for pretraining and finetuning.

3) Layout-aware and structure-aware corpora
- Structure-aware datasets and pretraining encourage modeling of row/row-grouping/sectioning and hierarchical structures. <cite id="3b99ee1b-1">StruBERT adopts a “structure‑aware” design to fuse textual and structural information of a data table into context‑aware representations</cite>. <cite id="3b99ee1b-3">Pretraining on tables with masked language modeling yields substantial gains over vanilla text-only BERT for table‑matching tasks</cite>, suggesting that layout-aware corpora and objectives improve tabular reasoning.
- Header/row/column grounding: <cite id="d59c04cb-0">datasets explicitly designed for LLMs include structured views that encode schema/headers and support row/column‑level reasoning, not just token-level text</cite>.

4) Table-oriented vision–language pretraining corpora
- WebTables as cross-modal signals: <cite id="18943e37-2">pairing each Web table with associated NL context forms a joint text–table corpus</cite> that can be used either for table‑in‑the‑loop V+L pretraining or for cross-modal alignment (e.g., grounding cells in referring text), similar in spirit to TableBert‑style data. <cite id="3b99ee1b-5">These parallel examples enable the model to learn correspondences between table cells and textual mentions</cite>.
- Schema-aware augmentation: <cite id="3b99ee1b-5">masking column headers and requiring recovery of column names and data types (masked column prediction) strengthens schema‑level understanding</cite>.

5) Modern multi-table/table-manipulation corpora
- Table manipulation and reasoning: <cite id="83077d7a-2">TABLELLM compiles both table QA and table manipulation tasks to be more applicable to real‑world scenarios</cite>. <cite id="83077d7a-2">The pretraining/fintuning split and cross-table alignment in TABLELLM reflect growing practice of training over multi-table corpora with explicit operations like merge, filter, and compute</cite>.
- Scale and heterogeneity: <cite id="d59c04cb-0">newer LLM‑oriented datasets span numerical and textual columns, enabling learning of cross‑cell operations and mixed-type reasoning</cite>.

II. Methods and architectures adapted for table-specific pretraining
1) Joint text–table pretraining and masking
- Masked Language Modeling extended to tables: <cite id="18943e37-4">TaBERT jointly pretrains on parallel examples of tables and NL text</cite>, learning to predict masked tokens in both modalities. <cite id="3b99ee1b-5">A “masked column prediction” objective encourages recovery of masked column names and data types, adding structured supervision beyond token MLM</cite>.
- Cross-modal alignment: <cite id="18943e37-2">using NL context that mentions table values provides cross‑modal signals to align textual and tabular representations</cite>, making the model aware of how cells refer to entities and measures in text.

2) Structure-, header-, and schema-aware tokenization and masking
- Structural signals: <cite id="3b99ee1b-1">StruBERT integrates tabular layout by fusing textual and structural information (e.g., row/section boundaries) to produce structure‑aware representations</cite>. <cite id="3b99ee1b-3">This yields better table search/matching performance, indicating that structural information learned during pretraining transfers to downstream table tasks</cite>.
- Header-informed masking: <cite id="3b99ee1b-5">masking strategies can target headers and require accurate prediction of column names and types, reinforcing schema grounding</cite>. <cite id="3b99ee1b-2">post‑masking structure‑aware adjustments in StructBERT‑style models refine predictions using structural context (row/section hierarchies)</cite>.
- Row/Column-level objectives: Beyond token masking, some methods operate at column or row granularity to capture aggregate structure. <cite id="3b99ee1b-5">masked column prediction (MCP) explicitly supervises column identity/type recovery</cite>, complementing token-level MLM and aligning with typical table QA extraction tasks.

3) Cross-table and multi-table pretraining
- Breaking the “single-table bubble”: <cite id="3b99ee1b-0">cross‑table pretraining explicitly addresses the challenge that models trained on isolated tables struggle to generalize across new schemas</cite>. <cite id="3b99ee1b-0">Methods propose sharing structural and semantic representations across tables to overcome the “cross‑table hurdle,” with training over corpora that include links and references among tables</cite>.
- Multi-table QA/manipulation: <cite id="83077d7a-2">TABLELLM integrates QA and manipulation, motivating pretraining that exposes models to joint reasoning over multiple tables and supports operations that align row keys and aggregate values</cite>.

4) General-purpose LLM adaptation with table-specific data
- Converting tables to sequences: <cite id="83077d7a-0">LLMs are sequence‑to‑sequence models; feeding tabular data requires converting structured tables into sequences while preserving structure (e.g., headers, spans, and types)</cite>. <cite id="d59c04cb-0">LLM‑oriented datasets use structured views that encode schema and value positions, enabling models to learn over row/column patterns</cite>.
- Foundation models for tabular data: <cite id="83077d7a-3">TabFM introduces a LLM‑based foundation model trained specifically for tabular data, incorporating representative structured examples for in‑context learning and adaptation</cite>.

5) Training targets that align with downstream table tasks
- Table comprehension and extraction: Pretraining that pairs tables with NL queries/summaries or NL mentions to cells helps with “table QA” and extraction. <cite id="18943e37-4">TaBERT’s joint training on tables plus NL text targets joint QA-style understanding</cite>.
- Data synthesis and augmentation: <cite id="d59c04cb-0">recent LLM-oriented tabular datasets are designed to span numerical and textual columns, enabling models to learn from mixed formats encountered in data lakes</cite>.
- Sequential/tabular generation: <cite id="83077d7a-0">LLMs can be adapted from seq2seq recipes to generate table schemas, SQL, or filled spreadsheets, with pretraining over synthetic/real table sequences</cite>.

6) Practical method details used in popular baselines
- Masking strategy and supervision: <cite id="3b99ee1b-5">mask a subset of tokens (including headers), and train to recover both cell content and column identity/type (MCP), encouraging robust grounding</cite>. <cite id="18943e37-2">alternative pretraining mixes text-only MLM with cross-table context alignment when natural language context is available</cite>.
- Structural fusion: <cite id="3b99ee1b-1">incorporate structural signals (rows, groups) via modified tokenization/position embeddings so that the model learns to attend to hierarchical layout</cite>.
- Cross-table alignment: <cite id="3b99ee1b-0">train over cross-table references and shared keys to improve generalization to unseen schemas and heterogeneous layouts</cite>.
- Scale and data diversity: <cite id="d59c04cb-0">large, heterogeneous tabular corpora covering numerical and textual columns enable models to acquire broad skills across real‑world scenarios</cite>. <cite id="18943e37-2">26M Web tables in TaBERT indicate the importance of massive scale for table-specific representations</cite>.

III. Evaluation/Downstream objectives used alongside pretraining
- Table QA and numerical reasoning: <cite id="18943e37-4">joint text–table pretraining was built to support understanding queries over tables</cite>, aligning with tasks like WikiTableQuestions and similar structured QA.
- Table manipulation and procedure grounding: <cite id="83077d7a-2">modern pretraining often targets TABLELLM-style tasks that combine QA with actual table edits, reflecting real user workflows</cite>.
- End‑to‑end tabular modeling: <cite id="d59c04cb-1">foundation models trained on large tabular datasets show competitive zero‑/few‑shot accuracy across hundreds of benchmarks</cite>, suggesting general-purpose transfer to prediction tasks over structured data.

IV. Example pretraining models and their datasets/methods
- TaBERT (Meta/Facebook Research, 2020): <cite id="18943e37-4">joint understanding of NL text and (semi‑)structured tables</cite>; <cite id="18943e37-2">26M Web tables paired with NL context</cite>; <cite id="3b99ee1b-5">masked column prediction to recover column names/types</cite>. TaBERT achieved strong results on table QA-style tasks.
- StruBERT/StructBERT family: <cite id="3b99ee1b-1">structure‑aware BERT that fuses textual and structural signals in a table</cite>; <cite id="3b99ee1b-3">masked LM with structural awareness improves table search/matching relative to text‑only baselines</cite>.
- TabFM/foundation models for tabular data: <cite id="83077d7a-3">a LLM‑based foundation model trained specifically for tabular data</cite>, embedding diverse structured examples to support in‑context learning.
- TABLELLM (2025): <cite id="83077d7a-2">a model covering both table QA and manipulation, curated to mirror real‑world user scenarios and multi‑table reasoning</cite>.
- Cross‑table pretraining: <cite id="3b99ee1b-0">methods that explicitly address the cross‑table generalization gap by training across diverse tables and shared schemas</cite>.

V. Practical patterns and pitfalls
- Align with NL context: <cite id="18943e37-2">pairing tables with NL passages that mention cells improves cross‑modal grounding and makes the model learn referential reasoning</cite>.
- Teach schema-level priors: <cite id="3b99ee1b-5">add objectives for masked column header and type recovery to stabilize downstream extraction and ensure the model respects schema semantics</cite>.
- Embrace multi-table data: <cite id="3b99ee1b-0">include cross‑table references and joins in training to avoid “single‑table myopia” and improve zero‑/few‑shot transfer to new schemas</cite>.
- Structure matters: <cite id="3b99ee1b-1">encode rows/sections/groups so the model learns hierarchical dependencies (e.g., header spans covering multiple cells) and not just token‑by‑token patterns</cite>.
- Scale wisely: <cite id="18943e37-2">TBERT‑scale training with 26M tables underscores that large, heterogeneous corpora are often necessary for robust table representations</cite>.
- Data curation for mixed types: <cite id="d59c04cb-0">ensure datasets span numerical, categorical, and textual columns to generalize across data lakes and BI tools</cite>.

When to use what and how to combine
- If you need cross‑modal grounding (tables + NL): start with WebTable + NL parallel data and joint masking (TaBERT‑style), add MCP for schema recovery. <cite id="18943e37-4">This directly optimizes joint representations</cite>, and <cite id="3b99ee1b-5">MCP helps stabilize schema extraction</cite>.
- If your application emphasizes structured matching/search: add header/row‑aware tokenization and structure‑aware LM (StruBERT/StructBERT‑style) to fuse structural layout into representations. <cite id="3b99ee1b-1">This improves matching and retrieval over tables</cite>.
- If your downstream tasks are multi‑table manipulation or SQL‑like reasoning: pretrain over multi‑table corpora and include tasks that require joins/aggregations; <cite id="83077d7a-2">modern systems like TABLELLM show gains when pretraining and finetuning span QA and edits across tables</cite>.
- If your goal is broad tabular transfer: <cite id="d59c04cb-1">train over hundreds of tabular benchmarks as in TabFM‑style approaches to get zero‑/few‑shot gains across heterogeneous schemas</cite>.

Summary
- Datasets: large Web‑table corpora paired with NL context (TaBERT), curated tabular benchmark suites (300+ datasets), and modern multi‑table/manipulation corpora (TABLELLM) are commonly used; newer LLM‑oriented datasets span both textual and numerical columns to reflect real data lakes. <cite id="18943e37-2">TaBERT trained on 26M Web tables with NL context</cite>, <cite id="d59c04cb-0">recent LLM datasets cover mixed column types</cite>, <cite id="d59c04cb-1">transfer models train on hundreds of tabular benchmarks</cite>, and <cite id="83077d7a-2">TABLELLM aggregates QA and manipulation tasks</cite>.
- Methods: extend MLM with joint text–table masking and add schema‑level supervision (masked column/type prediction), fuse structural signals (headers/rows/groups) into tokenization/embeddings, and include cross‑table alignment to improve generalization. <cite id="3b99ee1b-5">Masked column prediction</cite>, <cite id="3b99ee1b-1">structure‑aware fusion</cite>, and <cite id="3b99ee1b-0">cross‑table training</cite> are recurring elements that improve table QA, extraction, and manipulation. <cite id="18943e37-4">TaBERT</cite>, <cite id="3b99ee1b-1">StruBERT</cite>, <cite id="83077d7a-3">TabFM</cite>, and <cite id="83077d7a-2">TABLELLM</cite> exemplify these patterns.
