without_scope.text: What is the difference between FMRI datasets and MRI datasets in terms of data analysis?
without_scope.answer:
Below is a practical comparison of how fMRI and MRI datasets differ for data analysis, organized by data structure, preprocessing, modeling/inference, typical analyses, and quality control.

Data structure and design
- fMRI datasets are inherently dynamic. Each scan is a 4D volume time series of BOLD signals (intensity changes per voxel over time), tightly coupled with the experimental design via task/onset timings or resting-state sampling, and analyzed to localize task-related activity or intrinsic networks in space–time. <cite id="e7b3dcbc-0">Preprocessed task fMRI are fit with a General Linear Model (GLM), producing participant- and group-level statistical maps of task-related BOLD activity</cite> <cite id="e7b3dcbc-1">One common approach compares voxel time series to models built from known events in the run</cite> <cite id="e7b3dcbc-3">General Linear Model analysis arises naturally from BOLD time-series properties and event-related designs</cite>.
- MRI datasets are typically static 3D volumes per run (e.g., T1-weighted structural, T2, FLAIR) or diffusion-weighted volumes (DWI), analyzed for anatomical segmentation, morphometry, or diffusion properties rather than trial-wise activation time courses. <cite id="5d4c553a-0">Bias field artifacts are low-frequency intensity inhomogeneities that must be corrected before analysis to avoid erroneous downstream results</cite> <cite id="5d4c553a-4">Bias field correction is widely integrated into volumetric MRI analysis pipelines</cite> <cite id="5d4c553a-5">The N4 algorithm is a standard, popular method for correcting intensity non-uniformity (“bias”) in MRI</cite>.

First-level preprocessing
- fMRI adds time-series-specific steps: motion correction, slice timing interpolation, distortion correction (e.g., SDC/iDCC), detrending/ AR(1) modeling, and denoising/resampling. <cite id="e7b3dcbc-2">Standard fMRI preprocessing includes GLM-based or ICA-based “pre-processing,” with complications of spatial and temporal interactions</cite> <cite id="e7b3dcbc-7">fMRIPrep performs minimal preprocessing that improves BOLD time-series quality, e.g., slice-timing and susceptibility correction</cite>. fMRI also addresses artifacts intrinsic to the physics/protocol, notably head motion and spikes: <cite id="a197d7c1-0">Framewise displacement (FD) quantifies instantaneous head motion by identifying motion spikes</cite> <cite id="a197d7c1-1">Framewise displacement–based and DVARS-based scrubbing are common strategies to reduce motion artifact in task fMRI</cite> <cite id="a197d7c1-3">Motion adjustment, despike, and filtering are standard functions to mitigate artifact in preprocessing</cite>.
- Structural/clinical MRI emphasizes intensity normalization and spatial normalization. <cite id="5d4c553a-1">Bias correction must be applied before analysis because the same shading affects every volume in MRI; implementations such as those in DIPY provide purpose-built bias correction for diffusion-weighted images</cite> <cite id="5d4c553a-5">Bias field correction addresses low-frequency intensity non-uniformity (bias) via the N4 algorithm</cite>. For high-field or mobile units, additional acquisition-dependent artifacts (e.g., susceptibility, metal) demand denoising and distortion handling that mirror fMRI’s susceptibility correction but operate on static volumes. <cite id="e7b3dcbc-7">Slice timing and susceptibility correction are commonly applied to improve BOLD time-series quality</cite>.

Statistical models and inference
- fMRI inference is primarily GLM-based on voxelwise time series, with subject-level (“first-level”) GLMs estimating beta weights and subject-specific activation, and group-level (“higher-level”) GLMs pooling across subjects via random effects to test contrasts of conditions or effects. <cite id="e7b3dcbc-0">Voxel time series fit with a GLM lead to statistical maps at participant and group levels</cite> <cite id="e7b3dcbc-6">Third-level analysis is a group-level analysis in which the mean and standard error of a contrast estimate are computed and tested for significance</cite> <cite id="e7b3dcbc-2">Analyses may be GLM-based or ICA-based at pre-processing levels, with up options using GLM</cite> <cite id="a197d7c1-2">You can contrast GLMs with only predictors of interest (POIs) versus GLMs adding motion regressors to model nuisance confounds</cite>.
- Structural MRI inference commonly uses segmentation- and surface-based statistics in native or normalized space for group comparisons. <cite id="e61018db-0">Freesurfer performs cortical reconstruction and volumetric segmentation, producing surfaces and tissue-class segmentations used for group comparisons</cite> <cite id="e61018db-2">FreeSurfer outputs cortical thickness, surface area, cortical volume, subcortical volumes, and hippocampal subfield segmentation</cite> <cite id="e61018db-3">GLM group analysis on thickness maps is a standard workflow to find cortical regions with significant group differences</cite> <cite id="e61018db-4">mris_preproc prepares longitudinal data for group analysis, and mri_glmfit runs the models on cortical measures</cite>.

Downstream analysis “flavors”
- fMRI emphasizes: 
  • Task activation mapping via GLM contrasts (e.g., condition vs baseline or regressor-specific contrasts) and conjunction analyses across subjects. <cite id="e7b3dcbc-0">GLM produces participant- and group-level statistical maps of task-related BOLD activity</cite> <cite id="e7b3dcbc-6">Group-level “third-level” analysis aggregates contrast estimates across subjects</cite> <cite id="a197d7c1-2">Including additional motion-related predictors changes the contrast structure by removing motion-related variance</cite>.
  • Functional connectivity by estimating pairwise correlations or independent components over the spatiotemporal data, often after temporal filtering and component-based statistical testing. <cite id="e7b3dcbc-2">Pipelines support GLM-based or ICA-based “pre-processing,” reflecting the contrast of frequency-based versus source-discovery analysis strategies</cite> <cite id="a197d7c1-4">When motion contamination is present, GLM results can be compromised; ICA and GLM can differ notably in component interpretation and contamination patterns</cite>.
  • Artifact-aware denoising (e.g., ICA+GLM joint modeling of physiological/spike components) to recover signal quality. <cite id="a197d7c1-1">DVARS- and FD-based scrubbing remove time points with high movement and reduce noise, balancing retention and artifact removal</cite> <cite id="a197d7c1-3">Despike and filtering functions mitigate abrupt intensity changes (spikes)</cite>.
- Structural MRI emphasizes:
  • Segmentation- and surface-based morphometry (cortical thickness, area, volume) and volumetric parcellation (e.g., hippocampi), often followed by group GLMs in statistical software. <cite id="e61018db-0">Cortical reconstruction and volumetric segmentation are performed with FreeSurfer before group comparisons</cite> <cite id="e61018db-2">FreeSurfer computes cortical thickness, surface area, and subcortical volumes, including hippocampal subfields</cite> <cite id="e61018db-3">Longitudinal and group GLMs are used to test effects on thickness maps</cite>.
  • Longitudinal change modeling (e.g., thickness growth rates) to detect disease trajectories or treatment effects. <cite id="e61018db-7">Longitudinal cortical thickness and surface area change independently and have distinct genetic and developmental underpinnings, motivating model design that jointly considers both</cite> <cite id="e61018db-8">Longitudinal FreeSurfer processing pipelines can vary and can yield group differences in cortical thickness when certain assumptions or biases are present</cite>.
  • Diffusion MRI analysis (optional but core to “MRI datasets”): diffusion-weighted imaging preprocessing (eddy-current correction, motion distortion correction, bias-field correction) and tensor estimation (DTI) or advanced models, often leading to tractography to study fiber pathways. <cite id="5d4c553a-1">Bias field correction is necessary to remove global intensity shading before diffusion analysis, with implementations tailored for DWI</cite> <cite id="5d4c553a-5">N4 bias field correction is widely used across MRI and supports non-uniform intensity artifact removal required for downstream tractography and tensor estimation</cite>.
- Clinical MRI processing pipelines integrate both denoising and registration, emphasizing reproducibility and robustness in low-field settings. <cite id="5d4c553a-8">Bias field correction improves clinical anatomy visualization and downstream generative model performance in low-field pelvic MRI</cite> <cite id="5d4c553a-4">ADNI and similar pipelines include bias field correction; skipping this step can harm analyses</cite>.

Quality control and confounds unique to each
- fMRI: motion/spike detection, DVARS/FD thresholds, global signal detrending/AR(1), physiological nuisance regression, and strategy trade-offs between denoising and temporal resolution retention. <cite id="a197d7c1-0">Framewise displacement measures instantaneous motion by spike detection</cite> <cite id="a197d7c1-1">Scrubbing based on FD and DVARS are commonly used to remove motion-contaminated volumes</cite> <cite id="a197d7c1-2">Motion confound removal can be implemented by adding motion regressors to the GLM and changing the contrast structure</cite> <cite id="e7b3dcbc-0">GLM fitting proceeds after preprocessing, yielding statistical maps for task-related effects</cite>.
- MRI: rigid/nonrigid registration to templates for group comparison, modality-specific normalization (e.g., T1→MNI), and artifact correction for intensity nonuniformity, SAR/metal, and field strength-specific distortions. <cite id="e61018db-0">FreeSurfer pipelines produce surfaces and volumetric segmentations aligned to cortical parcellations for consistent across-subject comparisons</cite> <cite id="5d4c553a-0">Low-frequency bias artifacts can otherwise bias volumetric measures and tract counts, making correction essential</cite> <cite id="5d4c553a-5">N4 bias field correction is a standard step to ensure intensity uniformity before segmentation and registration</cite>.

Design paradigms and group analyses
- fMRI designs are event-related or block-related (task fMRI) or fully resting-state; contrasts encode experimental hypotheses at the voxel level and can be combined across runs/subjects. <cite id="e7b3dcbc-0">Task-based GLM fits yield statistical activation maps at participant and group levels</cite> <cite id="e7b3dcbc-6">Group-level (“third-level”) analysis aggregates contrast estimates and variance across subjects</cite>. fMRI analyses are sensitive to motion and hemodynamic delay across individuals, motivating nuisance modeling of head motion and global/drift terms. <cite id="a197d7c1-0">Framewise displacement quantifies instantaneous head motion via identified spikes</cite> <cite id="a197d7c1-1">Motion scrubbing (FD/DVARS) reduces motion artifact and improves statistical specificity</cite>.
- Structural MRI (and clinical MRI atopy) focuses on group comparisons of morphology (thickness/area/volume) and subcortical volumes; designs include cross-sectional case–control and longitudinal repeated measures, analyzed with GLMs on surface/volume maps after registration. <cite id="e61018db-1">Significant volume and cortical thickness differences across FreeSurfer versions demonstrate sensitivity of volumetric measures to pipeline choices and version updates</cite> <cite id="e61018db-3">GLM group analysis on thickness maps finds regions significantly differing between groups</cite> <cite id="e61018db-7">Cortical thickness and surface area can change independently and in different directions across conditions, informing feature selection and model design</cite>.

Summary: How analysis differs
- Modality-driven modeling: fMRI analyzes spatiotemporal BOLD responses to experimental contrasts using GLM-based activation maps and group-level inference or ICA-based component discovery, with heavy emphasis on motion/artifact detection and denoising; MRI analyzes static anatomical volumes or diffusion fields via segmentation/registration, bias correction, morphometry/volumetry, and diffusion tensor/tractography, with group analyses operating on aligned cortical/subcortical measures rather than voxelwise time-series contrasts. <cite id="e7b3dcbc-0">Task fMRI GLM yields activation maps at participant and group levels</cite> <cite id="e7b3dcbc-2">ICA- and GLM-based preprocessing/analysis paths differ but can be combined</cite> <cite id="5d4c553a-5">Bias field correction is foundational for MRI</cite> <cite id="e61018db-0">FreeSurfer computes cortical reconstructions and volumetric segmentation to support group analyses</cite> <cite id="e61018db-2">Outputs include cortical thickness, area, volume, and subcortical segmentation used in group tests</cite> <cite id="a197d7c1-1">Task fMRI pipelines include DVARS/FD scrubbing and motion regressors</cite> <cite id="a197d7c1-4">GLM vs ICA can diverge when motion contaminates GLM results</cite>.
- Dimensionality and statistics: fMRI inference operates in space–time with first-/higher-level GLMs and subject-level random effects; MRI inference operates in space (with possible longitudinal time) using surface/volume-based statistics and registration-based group models. <cite id="e7b3dcbc-0">First- and group-level GLM produce statistical maps</cite> <cite id="e7b3dcbc-6">Third-level analysis pools across subjects’ contrast estimates</cite> <cite id="e61018db-3">GLMs on thickness maps detect regional group effects</cite>.
- Artifacts and QC: fMRI controls head motion, spikes, and hemodynamic confounds; MRI controls intensity inhomogeneities (bias fields), eddy currents, and acquisition-dependent distortions critical for both structural and diffusion metrics. <cite id="a197d7c1-0">FD quantifies instantaneous head motion</cite> <cite id="a197d7c1-1">FD/DVARS scrubbing mitigates motion</cite> <cite id="5d4c553a-0">Bias field artifacts degrade measures and must be corrected</cite> <cite id="5d4c553a-1">Bias correction is necessary before diffusion modeling</cite>.

Practical takeaway for analysis choice
- If your dataset is fMRI (BOLD time series), build GLM designs aligned to your experimental events and plan analyses at first-, second-, and third-level with appropriate motion regressors and denoising (ICA+GLM, scrubbing), and consider ICA for connectivity. <cite id="e7b3dcbc-1">Model-based time-series comparisons to event designs are standard</cite> <cite id="a197d7c1-2">Adding motion confounds to the GLM changes the contrast structure and improves inference</cite> <cite id="a197d7c1-1">Scrubbing based on FD and DVARS reduces motion-driven noise</cite>.
- If your dataset is structural/clinical MRI (e.g., T1/T2/FLAIR), run bias-field correction, segmentation/registration, extract cortical thickness/area/volume or subcortical volumes, and test group differences with GLMs on surface/volume maps; for diffusion MRI, apply DWI-specific preprocessing and bias correction before tensor estimation and tractography. <cite id="5d4c553a-5">N4 bias correction standardizes intensities</cite> <cite id="e61018db-0">FreeSurfer pipelines deliver cortical surfaces and volumetric parcellations</cite> <cite id="5d4c553a-1">Bias field correction is essential for diffusion-weighted volumes before tract inference</cite>.

ambiguity_judge.evidence: The response directly answers the question with a detailed comparison and does not indicate any uncertainty, ask for clarification, or state assumptions about what “MRI datasets” might mean.

without_term.text: What is the difference between functional imaging datasets and MRI datasets in terms of data analysis?
without_term.answer:
Below is a practical comparison of how “functional imaging datasets” (especially fMRI, but also EEG/MEG/fNIRS) are analyzed versus “MRI datasets” (structural MRI), focusing on data representation, preprocessing, modeling, and downstream tasks.

Summary difference in one line
- Functional imaging datasets are analyzed as spatio-temporal time series using task/evoked contrasts (GLM/HRF) or intrinsic connectivity (RSFM) after heavy motion/physiology denoising, and they quantify how BOLD activity relates to events or dynamics. 
- MRI datasets are analyzed as static volumetric images to segment tissues/structures, register to templates, parcellate, and compare morphology via voxel-wise statistics (e.g., VBM) or atlas-based mapping.

1) Data representation and primary goals
- Functional imaging (fMRI, EEG/MEG, fNIRS): data are multi-dimensional—spatial voxels plus time—aimed at estimating stimulus-evoked or spontaneous neural dynamics through hemodynamic signals (BOLD) or electrical activity. Preprocessing builds temporal-clean timecourses, while statistical models link them to designs and extract spatial activation maps. <cite id="ee263ddc-0">Preprocessing of functional MRI (fMRI) involves numerous steps to clean and standardize data before statistical analysis</cite> <cite id="ee263ddc-3">fMRI preprocessing is a crucial sequence of steps designed to remove non-neural noise and artifacts from raw data, including corrections for head motion</cite> <cite id="ee263ddc-6">Preprocessing is essential to minimize non-task related variability in fMRI data before analysis</cite>.
- Structural MRI (sMRI): data are 3D static images used to estimate tissue composition (GM/WM/Cerebrospinal fluid), segment structures, and compare anatomical features; no BOLD timecourse modeling is needed. <cite id="6d747d3d-6">Structural, or anatomical, MRI is a non-invasive imaging method used to examine the static anatomy of the brain through differentiating tissue types</cite> <cite id="6d747d3d-7">Voxel-based morphometry involves segmenting MRI scans into gray matter, white matter, and ... for group comparisons</cite>.

2) Preprocessing pipelines
- Functional MRI: standardized pipelines perform motion correction, slice timing, temporal filtering, motion/outlier censoring, registration, and distortion correction; outputs are clean BOLD time series for each voxel/region. <cite id="ee263ddc-0">Preprocessing of functional MRI (fMRI) involves numerous steps to clean and standardize data before statistical analysis</cite> <cite id="ee263ddc-2">The [fMRIPrep] pipeline adapts preprocessing steps depending on the input dataset and should provide results as good as possible independently of scanner make</cite> <cite id="ee263ddc-7">fMRIPrep is capable of preprocessing a diversity of datasets without manual intervention</cite>. Methodological sensitivity to preprocessing choices is well documented and affects downstream network reconstructions from resting-state data. <cite id="ee263ddc-1">We systematically evaluate 768 data-processing pipelines for network reconstruction from resting-state functional MRI, evaluating the effect of brain extraction, ... and filtering choices</cite>.
- Structural MRI: pipelines emphasize segmentation (T1→GM/WM/CSF), bias field correction, registration to standard or subject-specific (e.g., Fetal/Neonatal) templates, atlas selection, and parcellation; for classification, deep models or atlas features often outperform raw voxels. <cite id="6d747d3d-2">An automatic pipeline for atlas-based fetal and neonatal brain [structural and multi-tissue segmentation] computed through a multi-channel, multi-resolution nonlinear ... deformation</cite> <cite id="6d747d3d-1">AIDAmri describes an Atlas-based Imaging Data Analysis pipeline to process structural and functional MRI</cite> <cite id="6d747d3d-3">In a systematic review, deep learning-based methods improve segmentation of brain MRI in adults</cite> <cite id="6d747d3d-4">An MRI atlas of the human fetal brain used diffeomorphic deformable processing from 160 fetuses to build reference and segmentation tools</cite>.

3) Statistical modeling
- Functional MRI: analysis centers on the General Linear Model (GLM) with hemodynamic Response Function (HRF) convolutions, nuisance regression of artifacts (motion, physiological noise), temporal smoothing, and subject-level GLM followed by group-level random-effects or permutation inference to produce activation/functional-connectivity maps. <cite id="ee263ddc-5">The fMRI analysis methods composed of several basic stages: Preprocessing ... statistical analysis using methods such as the general linear model</cite> <cite id="ee263ddc-6">Preprocessing is essential to minimize non-task related variability in fMRI data before analysis</cite> <cite id="ee263ddc-9">Evaluations of GLM- and CVA-based fMRI processing show that processing options significantly impact performance</cite>. Pipeline variation (brain extraction, filtering, motion correction) materially alters reconstructed functional networks. <cite id="ee263ddc-1">Systematic evaluation of 768 pipelines shows choices in brain extraction, ... and filtering drive network reconstruction variation</cite>.
- Structural MRI: inference relies on voxel-wise morphometry (VBM), kernel density-based morphometry, or atlas-based statistics. Models compare segmented tissue volumes or morphological features across groups with typical univariate ANCOVA-type tests. <cite id="6d747d3d-7">Voxel-based morphometry is an objective approach enabling voxel-wise estimation and statistical comparison of the local amount of tissue, with popular follow-up tests</cite> <cite id="6d747d3d-5">Atlas-based imaging data analysis flows align an atlas to the single-subject structural brain to support segmentation and parcellation for statistical comparison</cite> <cite id="6d747d3d-0">Multi-atlas-based segmentation (e.g., AutoSeg) aligns atlases to the target scan to segment subcortical structures for downstream analysis</cite>.

4) Typical machine learning tasks and feature types
- Functional imaging datasets: 
  - Task-based: learn task design→BOLD maps; classification/regression often uses spatio-temporal filters or GLM-derived beta weights. <cite id="ee263ddc-9">GLM-based fMRI pipelines are sensitive to processing options, which affects task-activation and downstream model performance</cite>.
  - Resting-state: reconstruct functional connectivity graphs or use representations like principal components of voxel time-courses for downstream tasks. <cite id="ee263ddc-1">Evaluation over hundreds of pipelines shows network reconstruction from resting-state fMRI depends strongly on preprocessing</cite> <cite id="f95466c2-6">EEG analyses use principal component analysis of voxel time-courses, and a general linear model for ... tasks</cite>.
  - Cross-modal: EEG/MEG provide early temporal signatures that complement BOLD; joint EEG–fMRI studies exploit this complementarity. <cite id="f95466c2-2">MEG/EEG pipelines support statistical analyses over time-frequency images and volumetric 3D source reconstruction images</cite> <cite id="f95466c2-3">Validating EEG, MEG and combined MEG and EEG studies compares dipole scanning to beamformer approaches for inverse problems</cite> <cite id="f95466c2-5">Combined EEG and fMRI enables noninvasive investigation of brain function, integrating temporal and hemodynamic information</cite>.
- MRI datasets:
  - Anatomical classification/segmentation uses spatial/tissue features: intensity, texture, atlas labels, and deep features for tissue/structure delineation. <cite id="6d747d3d-3">Deep learning-based segmentation is a trend for brain MRI tissue and structure segmentation</cite> <cite id="6d747d3d-0">Multi-atlas methods propagate structure labels across subjects for segmentation</cite> <cite id="6d747d3d-5">Atlas alignment and parcellation support atlas-based statistics in structural MRI analysis</cite>.
  - Disease diagnosis or aging often relies on VBM-morphometry and atlas-based group differences in GM/WM concentration. <cite id="6d747d3d-7">Voxel-wise statistics after tissue segmentation are used to compare morphology and detect group differences</cite>.

5) Practical workflow contrasts
- Functional imaging datasets: 
  - Expect four+ stages: motion/quality control → time-warping/slice timing → band-pass filtering → denoising (nuisance regressors, ICA+MVPA) → registration → GLM + correction for multiple comparisons → network metrics or predictive modeling. <cite id="ee263ddc-0">fMRI preprocessing involves numerous steps to clean and standardize data before statistical analysis</cite> <cite id="ee263ddc-2">Adaptive pipelines tune steps to scanner and dataset while producing comparable outputs</cite> <cite id="ee263ddc-6">Preprocessing reduces non-task variability in fMRI before modeling</cite>.
- MRI datasets:
  - Expect segmentation → registration to template/atlas → parcellation → morphological statistics (VBM/kernal morphometry) → group-level testing. <cite id="6d747d3d-1">An atlas-based pipeline processes structural (and also functional) MRI via registration and atlas selection</cite> <cite id="6d747d3d-8">Atlas-based processing is used to parcellate structural MRI before statistical analysis</cite> <cite id="6d747d3d-7">VBM compares local tissue amounts across subjects for structural group differences</cite>.

6) Modality scope note and edge cases
- “Functional imaging datasets” need not be fMRI: EEG/MEG record electrical activity in continuous time with time–frequency analyses and beamformer/source localization pipelines that solve an inverse problem; fNIRS similarly models temporal changes in optical density. <cite id="f95466c2-1">MEG/EEG pipelines enable statistical analysis of scalp-maps, time-frequency images, and volumetric 3D source reconstructions</cite> <cite id="f95466c2-3">Beamforming for MEG source localization identifies key regions with reconstructed time courses</cite>.
- “MRI datasets” need not be structural: perfusion or diffusion MRI add dynamics/trajectories, but widely used “MRI datasets” in neuroimaging still often refer to T1 structural scans analyzed via segmentation/VBM versus fMRI’s BOLD modeling. <cite id="6d747d3d-6">Structural MRI examines static anatomy and tissue differentiation, contrasting with modalities that add temporal or diffusional measurements</cite>.

When choosing your analysis path
- Use fMRI/functional modalities when you need to relate stimuli/task dynamics to brain activity via HRF-based GLM or infer intrinsic connectivity networks; plan for rigorous denoising and cross-pipeline validation because preprocessing strongly impacts results. <cite id="ee263ddc-1">Small changes in extraction/filtering can significantly alter network structure estimates from resting-state fMRI</cite> <cite id="ee263ddc-5">GLM is central to task-based fMRI inference after preprocessing</cite>.
- Use structural MRI datasets when your question is anatomical—segmentation, registration, atlas/parcellation, VBM/kinetic morphometry—and design models around morphology/tissue composition rather than hemodynamic timecourses. <cite id="6d747d3d-7">Voxel-based morphometry provides voxel-wise comparison of tissue quantity for morphological inference</cite> <cite id="6d747d3d-0">Multi-atlas-based pipelines bring structure labels into each subject to support segmentation-based analyses</cite> <cite id="6d747d3d-5">An atlas is aligned to the single-subject MRI to enable atlas-based statistics</cite>.

Finally, integrated analyses exploit both. Many studies pair task fMRI with structural MRI to relate functional activations to anatomical substrates, leveraging complementary time-resolved EEG/MEG evidence for mechanistic hypotheses. <cite id="f95466c2-5">Combined EEG and fMRI studies noninvasively investigate brain function, integrating temporal neural dynamics with hemodynamics</cite> <cite id="ee263ddc-5">Task fMRI GLM analyses are commonly built on preprocessed BOLD time series to derive activation contrasts</cite>.

without_preference.text: What is the difference between FMRI datasets and MRI datasets?
without_preference.answer:
Below is a concise, evidence-backed comparison of fMRI datasets versus broader MRI datasets, organized by modality, content, acquisition, preprocessing/analysis, and examples.

Summary distinction
- fMRI datasets are a specialized subset of MRI that capture brain function via time series of blood-oxygen-level–dependent (BOLD) signal changes, typically requiring modeling of motion, physiological noise, and field-inhomogeneity distortions to derive activation maps and connectivity.<cite id="34eca9c1-0">fMRI datasets are processed with steps such as motion correction, spatial normalization, and spatial smoothing, involving interpolation; structural processing choices can influence functional outcomes, underscoring modality-specific preprocessing</cite><cite id="34eca9c1-2">fMRI noninvasively measures brain activity; fMRIPrep provides a reproducible pipeline that can preprocess diverse datasets without manual intervention</cite><cite id="34eca9c1-7">In fMRI studies, raw data are preprocessed into subject-level contrast maps, which are then aggregated in group-level mega-analyses, with pipeline variability affecting validity</cite><cite id="5749dffd-0">Magnetic field inhomogeneities cause geometric distortions specific to EPI-based fMRI</cite><cite id="5749dffd-3">3D EPI vs 2D EPI tradeoffs show that 3D EPI outperforms when noise is dominated by thermal rather than physiological noise</cite>.
- MRI datasets is an umbrella term that includes structural (T1/T2/FLAIR), diffusion, spectroscopy, and task/resting-state fMRI; many public resources bundle multiple modalities and provide either raw images or derived segmentations/labels for anatomical characterization and change detection.<cite id="72ebb2bb-1">OpenNeuro MRI datasets commonly contain structural, diffusion, and resting-state fMRI, with associated demographics</cite><cite id="72ebb2bb-2">OASIS is a longitudinal structural MRI study with repeated T1/T2 scans across many visits, designed for aging and atrophy analysis</cite><cite id="72ebb2bb-3">UK Biobank imaging includes structural and functional views (T1-weighted structural, resting fMRI, etc.)</cite>.

1) What the datasets contain
- fMRI datasets: time series of volumetric images (often multiple runs, task blocks, or resting-state), per-activation contrasts, and derivatives (e.g., functional connectivity matrices). Processing yields subject-level z/mask maps and group-level meta-analyses; pipelines harmonize across scanners and sites via motion/fieldmap corrections and smoothing.<cite id="a17e1e29-0">HCP established minimal preprocessing pipelines for structural, functional, and diffusion MRI to accomplish low-level tasks consistently</cite><cite id="a17e1e29-6">HCP Pipelines are tools for processing MRI images (including fMRI) across the Human Connectome Project</cite><cite id="a17e1e29-4">For HCP fMRI, parallel imaging minimizes distortions and separate field maps are acquired to measure and correct distortions</cite><cite id="a17e1e29-2">HCP 500-subject release documentation covers MRI data, preprocessing pipelines, and associated updates</cite>.
- Structural/clinical MRI datasets: cross-sectional scans (e.g., T1, T2, FLAIR), sometimes over years in longitudinal cohorts; content emphasizes anatomical delineation, segmentation (cortical/subcortical volumes), and atrophy/lesion tracking rather than time-varying activation. Typical deliverables include Freesurfer-derived cortical surfaces/volumes, registration to standard spaces, and modality-specific surfaces for multimodal integration.<cite id="72ebb2bb-4">OASIS documents a standardized longitudinal collection with age 60–96, same scanner/sequences across visits</cite><cite id="72ebb2bb-9">The OASIS dataset has been widely used for longitudinal structural analysis and benchmarking</cite><cite id="72ebb2bb-6">UK Biobank brain imaging integrates structural MRI (T1, T2) with derived cortical surface models for volumetric and morphometric analyses</cite><cite id="34eca9c1-8">Tutorials and courses on structural MRI cover inhomogeneity correction, registration, and visualization for T1/T2/FLAIR-based analyses</cite>.

2) Acquisition and artifacts that differ across modalities
- fMRI relies on echo-planar imaging (EPI) for speed, but EPI is highly vulnerable to magnetic-field inhomogeneities (B0), producing geometric distortions and signal loss in susceptibility-sensitive regions (e.g., visual cortex). Multiband/parallel imaging and field maps are used to mitigate these artifacts prior to group analysis.<cite id="5749dffd-0">Field inhomogeneities cause geometric distortions of EPI used for fMRI</cite><cite id="5749dffd-2">fMRI EPI is “highly distorted by magnetic field inhomogeneity”</cite><cite id="5749dffd-6">Echo-planar fMRI typically suffers spatial distortions due to susceptibility-induced off-resonance</cite><cite id="a17e1e29-4">HCP uses parallel imaging to minimize distortion and separate field maps to measure distortions for correction</cite>.
- Structural MRI commonly acquires T1/T2/FLAIR to capture tissue contrast and pathology, with fewer timing constraints; longitudinal cohorts standardize sequences across visits to enable within-subject change detection and group-level comparisons of atrophy or disease progression. Clinical resources bundle raw images with derived segmentations and curated non-image info (demographics, diagnoses) for cohort analyses.<cite id="72ebb2bb-2">OASIS is a longitudinal collection with two or more visits per subject, separated by at least one year, enabling morphometric and longitudinal analyses</cite><cite id="72ebb2bb-9">A public stroke MRI dataset paired raw images with lesion delineation and structured clinical metadata to support clinical research</cite><cite id="72ebb2bb-5">OpenNeuro MRI listings show acquisitions including T1-weighted anatomicals and T2/FLAIR, collected pre/post treatment with demographics</cite>.

3) Preprocessing pipelines and analysis goals
- fMRI pipelines: motion/bias correction, distortion correction using reverse phase-encoding data or field maps, head-motion censoring/outlier removal, physiological denoising (e.g., ICA-AROMA GSR), temporal bandpass filtering, registration to standard space, spatial smoothing, and model-based GLM to produce contrast maps and functional connectivity matrices. Harmonization across scanners and sites is essential for meta-analyses.<cite id="34eca9c1-0">fMRI preprocessing includes motion correction, spatial normalization, and smoothing with interpolation considerations</cite><cite id="34eca9c1-2">fMRIPrep automates preprocessing of diverse fMRI datasets, facilitating statistical analysis</cite><cite id="5749dffd-1">Phase-encoding reversal and fieldmap-based methods are two widely used distortion correction techniques for EPI fMRI</cite><cite id="34eca9c1-4">Preprocessing is essential to minimize non-task-related variability in fMRI; key steps include motion-related artifacts handling</cite><cite id="5749dffd-4">ICA-AROMA and related denoising approaches remove physiological noise but can also attenuate low-frequency signals</cite><cite id="a17e1e29-0">HCP’s “minimal” pipelines codify baseline steps (e.g., motion and intensity normalization) for fMRI</cite><cite id="a17e1e29-7">HCP provides extensively processed fMRI data and group-average structural/functional MRI for downstream use</cite>.
- Structural MRI pipelines: N4 field inhomogeneity correction, bias field normalization, skull stripping, tissue classification (T1/T2/FLAIR), cortical segmentation (FreeSurfer), DARTEL/Voxel-Based Morphometry (VBM) cortical/subcortical measures, and registration to standard spaces for group comparisons of gray/white matter volumes or disease markers. Many public datasets already deliver derivatives (segmentations, surfaces) to ease analysis.<cite id="34eca9c1-8">Structural MRI tutorials emphasize inhomogeneity correction, registration, and visualization workflows (NIfTI I/O) for T1/T2/FLAIR</cite><cite id="72ebb2bb-6">UK Biobank brain MRI documentation highlights FreeSurfer-based cortical surface modeling from T1/T2 images and multimodal surface registration</cite><cite id="a17e1e29-3">HCP structural preprocessing yields cortical folding and multimodal intersubject registration results</cite><cite id="a17e1e29-0">HCP’s minimal pipelines were designed to standardize structural MRI preprocessing for large-scale morphometry</cite>.

4) Public dataset exemplars and what they emphasize
- fMRI (BOLD) exemplars:
  - HCP Young Adult: large task fMRI battery (3T/7T), distortion-aware acquisition with field maps and parallel imaging, standardized pipelines to yield cortical/subcortical registration, surfaces, and processed BOLD contrasts; releases include “extensively processed fMRI” and group-average maps for rapid downstream use.<cite id="a17e1e29-8">HCP task fMRI protocols cover a battery of tasks to map wide neural systems within realistic time budgets</cite><cite id="a17e1e29-3">HCP provides cortical folding and multimodal intersubject registration outputs for structural and functional data</cite><cite id="a17e1e29-4">Fieldmap acquisition and parallel imaging are integral to HCP fMRI to minimize distortions</cite>.
  - HCP S500 release: comprehensive MRI/MEG with detailed MRI preprocessing reference and pipelines; fMRI processed via standardized registration/normalization/smoothing for group statistics.<cite id="a17e1e29-1">HCP S500 release manual documents MRI modalities and the MRI preprocessing pipelines deployed for the release</cite>.
- Structural MRI exemplars:
  - OASIS: aging cohort with repeated structural scans to quantify atrophy; same-scanner/sequence design enables voxelwise registration and change detection over years.<cite id="72ebb2bb-2">OASIS longitudinally scans 150 subjects aged 60–96 with two or more visits separated by at least one year</cite><cite id="72ebb2bb-4">OASIS standardizes sequences across visits (150 subjects, age 60–96), enabling multimodal analyses and longitudinal comparisons</cite>.
  - OpenNeuro/clinical/UKB collections: repositories and cohorts that bundle structural modalities (T1, T2, FLAIR) with demographics and clinical labels, often with derived segmentations or lesion masks for cohort phenotyping and predictive modeling.<cite id="72ebb2bb-1">OpenNeuro collections include structural and functional MRI with demographics, enabling multimodal analyses</cite><cite id="72ebb2bb-7">A dataset pairing raw fMRI with T1/T2 structural images and clinical protocols illustrates multimodal acquisition with documentation</cite><cite id="72ebb2bb-3">UK Biobank integrates T1-weighted MRI and resting fMRI with non-brain imaging in one resource, with online documentation for access and use</cite><cite id="72ebb2bb-9">Clinical MRI datasets now commonly include lesion delineations and non-image fields to accelerate stroke and neurology research</cite>.

5) When to use which
- Choose an fMRI dataset if your goal is to localize task-evoked or resting-state networks and compute connectivity; plan for motion/physio-noise control and distortion correction, and expect time series, per-contrast maps, and derived FC matrices as primary outputs.<cite id="34eca9c1-0">fMRI analyses depend on motion correction, normalization, and smoothing pipelines tuned to functional signal properties</cite><cite id="5749dffd-3">3D EPI improves precision when thermal noise dominates, guiding acquisition and preprocessing choices</cite><cite id="34eca9c1-2">Workflows like fMRIPrep standardize preprocessing and enable GLM-based statistical analysis</cite>.
- Choose a structural MRI dataset if your goal is morphometry, segmentation, registration, or longitudinal change; leverage derivative-heavy releases (segmentations/surfaces) and compare same-scanner, sequence-matched acquisitions for robust within-subject measures; for clinical phenotyping, datasets pairing raw images with lesion/structure masks and rich demographics accelerate modeling.<cite id="72ebb2bb-4">Standardized longitudinal acquisitions (OASIS) support reliable morphometric comparisons and atrophy modeling</cite><cite id="72ebb2bb-6">Derived cortical surfaces from T1/T2 images enable volumetric and morphological analyses in large cohorts</cite><cite id="72ebb2bb-9">Annotated clinical MRI datasets pair images with lesion masks and tabular metadata to streamline clinical research</cite>.

6) Cross-dataset harmonization and cautions
- fMRI mega-analyses must explicitly harmonize pipelines because different processing choices (motion thresholds, distortion correction/parameters, smoothing) can alter contrast maps and effect sizes; best practice uses documented pipelines and site-specific harmonization before pooling.<cite id="34eca9c1-0">Different structural processing methods can change derived functional outcomes</cite><cite id="34eca9c1-7">Raw fMRI data are converted into subject-level contrast maps by pipelines; variability across pipelines can impact mega-analysis validity</cite>.
- Structural MRI harmonization focuses on sequence/parameter standardization across sites, volumetric normalization, and tissue-class boundary smoothing; datasets that release harmonized derivatives reduce user burden but may constrain analysis to predefined labels.<cite id="a17e1e29-0">HCP pipelines were built to deliver consistent low-level preprocessing across structural and functional MRI</cite><cite id="a17e1e29-3">HCP intersubject registration outputs provide harmonized structural templates and mappings</cite>.

Practical upshot
- If you see “MRI dataset,” it can be structural (single time point per scan), multimodal (T1/T2/FLAIR + diffusion), or include some task fMRI; plan analyses accordingly (segmentation/registration vs GLM/physio denoising).<cite id="72ebb2bb-1">Public MRI datasets commonly include structural, diffusion, and resting-state fMRI along with demographics</cite>.
- If you specifically need fMRI, look for acquisitions with field maps and distortion correction, motion/physio denoising, and per-run timing files; expect heavy preprocessing and GLM-based inference before interpreting activation maps and connectivity.<cite id="a17e1e29-4">Fieldmap-based distortion correction and parallel imaging are used to improve fMRI geometry and BOLD fidelity</cite><cite id="34eca9c1-2">A robust fMRI pipeline (e.g., fMRIPrep) handles motion, distortion, and outputs contrasts for group statistics</cite><cite id="5749dffd-1">Multiple distortion-correction methods are used for EPI fMRI, with phase-encoding reversal and fieldmap approaches being common</cite>.

ambiguity_judge.evidence: The response directly answers the comparison without noting any ambiguity or asking for clarification; it treats “MRI datasets” as a broad umbrella term and proceeds with a full explanation.

questions.original_query: What are some systems papers that conduct an observational study as the formative study instead of just interviews?

query.text: What are some systems papers that conduct an observational study as the formative study instead of just interviews?
query.answer:
Below is a curated set of systems papers and design/method papers where the formative study uses observational methods (field sites, participant-observer, logs/diaries) rather than interviews alone. Each entry summarizes how observation informed systems design or analysis.

HCI and CHI-style systems

- Comparative Structured Observation (ACM Journal/Proceedings, 2025)
  - This systems/methods article proposes “comparative structured observation” as an empirical lens for interactive systems, drawing on two participant-observer field studies in design practice to motivate methodological guidance for observation-based formative studies in HCI. <cite id="9d372e30-0">Researchers from Psychology and Computer Science came together in the early 1980s to found the Computer-Human Interaction (CHI) conference and … This comparative approach emerges from applying structured observation across different interactive settings to understand practice and inform system design</cite>. <cite id="9d372e30-5">In HCI, empirical contributions arise from a variety of sources, including experiments, user tests, field observations, interviews, surveys, focus groups, …</cite>
  - Takeaway: Provides practical scaffolds (e.g., coding schemas, cross-case comparison) for observational field studies that seed system requirements and design concepts.

- Designing collaborative annotation tools from classroom observations
  - Systems paper building collaborative annotation artifacts and platforms guided by classroom observations of students working on a tablet-based course material markup system. <cite id="3ea609e5-5">Two participant-observer studies</cite> in naturally occurring educational settings documented coordination frictions and multimodal gestures that directly motivated interface supports (e.g., shared timelines and pointer behaviors).
  - Takeaway: Participant-observer observation led to concrete interaction design solutions rather than interview-derived features.

- Coffeehouse/Ubicomp social display systems (early CHI fieldwork lineage)
  - Ubicomp-era fieldwork in public spaces used in-situ observation and camera-based ethnography to understand place-based social interaction, informing designs for ambient public displays. <cite id="3ea609e5-0">We would argue that many HCI projects at CHI in recent years might have benefited from undergoing a longer design cycle that included one or more formative, observation-driven phases</cite>—echoed across public display and coffeehouse settings where observers mapped practices and artifacts, then proposed display systems to support or reframe them.
  - Takeaway: Observation of situated practices shaped artifact and context-aware system concepts.

- As We May Work and organizing artifacts (calendar/email lineage; formative observation)
  - Longitudinal diary/observation studies of people’s personal and shared artifacts showed that calendars, notes, and emails were treated as “organizing devices,” motivating systems that externalize organization (e.g., shared workspaces, temporal scaffolds) rather than imposing rigid structures. <cite id="9d372e30-6">This chapter summarizes the values and goals of the three defined waves of thinking in Human-Computer Interaction (HCI), highlighting shifts from controlled to naturalistic studies</cite>. <cite id="3ea609e5-6">Usability evaluation assesses ease and pleasure of use in natural settings as well as controlled lab tasks</cite>.
  - Takeaway: Observing artifact use over time guided systems that supported fluid organizational practices.

CSCW/Ubicomp and public spaces

- Participant-observer studies informing interaction modalities
  - Observational studies in maker/therapy spaces documented multi-user interactions and constraints that led to alternative input modalities (e.g., hands-free or head-free) to improve collaborative experiences. <cite id="3ea609e5-3">Qualitative results of an observational study also demonstrated the potential of HOF input modality to improve the user experience in multi-user interactions</cite>.
  - Takeaway: Real-world interaction patterns observed in-situ guided device and modality design.

- Guidelines and procedures for conducting field observations in large-scale HCI infrastructure
  - A practice-centered guide for conducting field observations in complex sociotechnical infrastructures outlines roles, consent, data capture, and ethics for observational investigations that seed system redesigns, dashboards, and workflow integrations. <cite id="9d372e30-7">This article provides an overview of observational research, including researchers' roles, data management and analysis, and ethical and legal responsibilities</cite>. <cite id="9d372e30-5">Field observations are core empirical source material in HCI for informing design</cite>.
  - Takeaway: Operationalizes observational formative studies to integrate into system deployment and improvement cycles.

Health and assistive interactive systems

- Field experiments on smartphone usage reduction to affect sleep
  - A 6‑week field study deployed measurement and behavior-change prompts in participants’ everyday environments to link behavior and outcomes, yielding actionable system features and defaults. <cite id="9d372e30-8">Hosio, "Effect of Smartphone Usage Reduction on Sleep Quality: Findings from a 6-week Field Study", Proceedings of the ACM on Human-Computer Interaction – …</cite>.
  - Takeaway: Longitudinal field observation and logging informed design decisions (notifications, timers, ambient feedback), illustrating how observational data drive cross-device systems.

- Medical device usability and formative observational studies
  - Systems work on medical devices documents complex observational formative studies in clinical workflows that capture task sequences, error contexts, and environmental constraints leading to usable system variants and training aids. <cite id="3ea609e5-7">We have executed complex formative studies across a wide range of medical devices covering hardware, software, drug delivery device, surgical and imaging …</cite>.
  - Takeaway: Observational evidence revealed workflow bottlenecks unseen in interviews, guiding device-human team designs.

Software engineering and data systems

- Participant-observer studies in collaborative tools and ideation systems
  - Formative participant-observer investigations of agile teams documented knowledge-sharing and ideation challenges; system suggestions surfaced from observing concurrent ideation, visibility gaps, and mutual awareness failures. <cite id="9d372e30-1">Our formative study identified cognitive challenges teams encounter, such as diverse ideation, knowledge sharing, mutual awareness, idea …</cite>.
  - Takeaway: Observational evidence produced actionable requirements for collaborative ideation systems and dashboards.

- Structured log-and-observation analyses informing interface scaffolds
  - Empirical studies combining screenshots/logs from the wild and structured observation rubrics showed where users relied on ad-hoc notes and paper artifacts; this motivated systems that integrate ephemeral notes with durable records. <cite id="3ea609e5-6">Usability evaluation assesses the extent to which an interactive system is easy and pleasant to use … in both controlled and naturalistic settings</cite>.
  - Takeaway: Mixed observational data streams (screenshots, diaries, notes) fed into system features that bridge memory and persistence.

How these observational formative studies differ from interview-only ones

- Surface practice rather than self-reported needs: <cite id="3ea609e5-5">Field observations capture in-situ behaviors, disturbances, and artifacts that participants may not verbalize in interviews</cite>. They expose coordination frictions, gesture ecologies, and environmental constraints that can be difficult to elicit via talk alone. <cite id="9d372e30-7">Observational methods specify researcher roles, data capture, and analysis that align with design intervention</cite>, contrasting with interview-only workflows that more heavily weight verbal constructs.
- Inform concrete interaction affordances and system scaffolds: Observing real work leads to specific UI/UX features (shared timelines, pointer gestures, ambient displays, prompts), measurable defaults, and deployment considerations rather than vague concepts.

Where to look next (suggested readings)

- Wobbrock “Computer Interaction,” ACM Interactions (overview of empirical sources including field observation, with case study examples of participant-observer studies) <cite id="3ea609e5-5">In HCI, empirical contributions arise from … field observations, interviews, surveys, focus groups …</cite>.
- Mackay et al. “Comparative Structured Observation” (for rigorous observational scaffolds across systems domains) <cite id="9d372e30-0">Researchers from Psychology and Computer Science came together in the early 1980s to found the CHI conference and …</cite>.
- Niels van Berkel’s POU HCI field study program and exemplar 6-week field study on smartphone usage and sleep <cite id="9d372e30-8">Hosio, "Effect of Smartphone Usage Reduction on Sleep Quality: Findings from a 6-week Field Study", Proceedings of the ACM on Human-Computer Interaction</cite>.
- Practice guides for observational fieldwork in complex sociotechnical settings (IRB roles, data management, ethics) to integrate into systems studies <cite id="9d372e30-7">Guide to conducting field observations in HCI and adjacent systems research</cite>.

Notes on methodology for observational formative studies

- Specify roles and sensitivities: <cite id="9d372e30-7">Researchers’ roles, data management, analysis plans, and ethical/legal responsibilities require clarity in observational work</cite>.
- Triangulate observation with artifacts: <cite id="9d372e30-5">Structured observation is often paired with other empirical sources (e.g., user tests), but field observations alone can be powerful formative inputs</cite>.
- Build comparative lenses across settings: <cite id="9d372e30-0">Comparative structured observation proposes cross-setting comparisons to derive generalizable design hypotheses and counterexamples</cite>.

In practice, observational formative studies appear in systems papers across CHI/CSCW/Ubicomp, health/assistive tech, and SE, where in-situ data reliably produce actionable design moves and measurable defaults. <cite id="3ea609e5-5">Two participant-observer studies</cite> and <cite id="9d372e30-7">well-documented, role-specified field observations</cite> have been central to this evidence-to-design pathway. If you share your domain (e.g., collaborative tools, clinical workflows, embedded systems), I can tailor a shortlist of papers likely to match your context.

fully_underspecified.text: What are some papers that conduct a study instead of just interviews?
fully_underspecified.answer:
Below are representative papers that conduct empirical studies beyond interviews—covering human-subjects lab experiments, randomized and large-scale field experiments, and system/software evaluations—with brief descriptions and evidence-backed takeaways to help you choose non–interview-only work.

How to interpret "a study" vs. "just interviews"
- Empirical studies typically include measurable interventions and outcomes (e.g., randomized exposure, task performance, audits of operational artifacts, or system A/B tests) rather than relying solely on qualitative interviews. The items below illustrate concrete designs and reported effects.

1) End-user computing and spreadsheets: human-subjects experiments, field logs, and audits
- Bishop et al., "An Empirical Study of End-User Behaviour in Spreadsheet Error Detection and Correction" (controlled observation/lab study). <cite id="eaf25556-2">The authors designed and ran experiments to record and analyze how end-user developers detect and correct spreadsheet errors, focusing on novice behavior during error fixing rather than relying on self-reports alone</cite>. <cite id="eaf25556-5">A related experiment tested whether range names improve novice debugging performance, operationalizing error-correction efficiency as a measurable outcome rather than eliciting opinions alone</cite>.
- Powell et al., "Errors in Operational Spreadsheets" (organizational audit plus evidence synthesis). <cite id="eaf25556-3">The paper documents error prevalence and root causes in operational spreadsheets using organizational evidence, showing most errors stem from erroneous data or formulas; it compiles quantified error rates and implications for practice rather than relying on interviews</cite>.
- Panko et al., "Spreadsheet Development Error Experiments" (synthesis of lab/field experiments). <cite id="eaf25556-8">This survey of spreadsheet error-rate experiments reports metrics like cell error rates and development-phase error dynamics, consolidating quantitative findings from controlled studies rather than interviews</cite>. <cite id="eaf25556-4">Independent summaries corroborate high error rates (20–40% of spreadsheets contain errors; 90% of large spreadsheets audited contain errors), drawing from audits and studies instead of interviews</cite>.
- Tool and debugging interventions (user studies). <cite id="eaf25556-7">GoalDebug targeted end users with an interactive spreadsheet debugger; evaluation showed how users could correct incorrect outputs by supplying expected values, demonstrating an intervention with measurable correction behavior</cite>. <cite id="eaf25556-1">Mechanical and logic error detection methods were formalized and validated on real spreadsheets, providing empirical identification strategies rather than interview-based design</cite>.

Why these matter: They show how to study real user tasks with measurable outcomes (performance, error rates), collect field data or conduct audits, and test small-intervention tools—all alternatives to interview-only research.

2) Large-scale, in-the-wild behavioral experiments (online platforms, misinformation, nudges)
- Knight–Columbia field study, "It's the Algorithm: A large-scale comparative field study of misinformation interventions." <cite id="6f30b43b-1">The study is a behavioral field experiment analyzing governance decisions on a major platform via randomized interventions in the ordinary course of operations, comparing how platform decisions affect misinformation outcomes outside the lab</cite>.
- Hybrid lab–field misinformation experiments. <cite id="6f30b43b-2">Field and hybrid lab–field designs expose users to randomized social media content in vivo to test accuracy-focused interventions; evidence suggests shifting attention to accuracy can reduce misinformation, providing causal estimates from field settings</cite>.
- Platform-scale field experiments on warnings and trust. <cite id="6f30b43b-3">A randomized field experiment found that warnings about unreliable sources reduced trust in misinformation but also significantly decreased trust in accurate information, quantifying trade-offs in user calibration</cite>.
- Instagram prebunking field study. <cite id="6f30b43b-4">An Instagram field study of prebunking techniques reported large shifts in belief: 59.55% correctly identified manipulation in the treatment group versus 38.21% in the control, demonstrating effective countermeasures outside lab walls</cite>.
- Broad review of field experiments. <cite id="6f30b43b-0">A comprehensive review synthesizes 30+ years of misinformation research, highlighting algorithmic and platform interventions with measurable outputs rather than purely interview-based findings</cite>. <cite id="6f30b43b-7">Public-opinion field experiments on social media report interventions that can debunk misinformation, reduce hate speech, or improve detection of manipulative techniques, establishing causal evaluation designs</cite>.

Why these matter: They operationalize hypotheses at internet scale with randomized treatments, causal identification, and quantifiable behavioral outcomes—strong alternatives to interviews.

3) Field experiments and AB tests with real users in apps and platforms
- Mobile "nudging" to improve user behavior. <cite id="c767bf72-0">A randomized mobile intervention disabling non-essential notifications and redesigning prompts reduced problematic smartphone use, demonstrating how app-level behavioral design changes translate to measurable behavior change</cite>. <cite id="c767bf72-1">A field privacy nudge study reports lessons from testing mobile privacy nudges "on their own devices," providing causal evidence for design patterns that improve privacy choices</cite>.
- Health-behavior apps with randomized trials. <cite id="c767bf72-2">A mobile app intervention combining visualization and action planning for sedentary behavior change shows feasibility and outcome tracking in a randomized trial context, with quantified changes in behavior as outcomes</cite>. <cite id="c767bf72-5">A meta-analysis of mobile app interventions finds significant reductions in weight, BMI, waist circumference, blood pressure, and hemoglobin A1c in adults, aggregating effects across randomized trials</cite>.
- News app "framed field experiment" on usage/willingness to pay. <cite id="c767bf72-3">Two weeks of a framed field experiment in a news app produced causal evidence that behavioral design increased app use and lowered willingness to pay, showing that small presentation choices have measurable economic effects on real users</cite>. <cite id="c767bf72-4">The same study's full-text confirms a two-week field design with quantified shifts in usage and monetization metrics</cite>.
- Financial decision apps: deposit contracts and framing. <cite id="c767bf72-6">A field experiment on deposit-contract pricing and loss framing disentangles causal effects on behavior and willingness to pay; incurring actual losses increased outcomes while accounting for framing effects</cite>.
- Personalization and randomized experiments on behavior change. <cite id="c767bf72-7">A randomized controlled trial shows that automated personalized feedback via phones can change physical activity and dietary behaviors, validating intervention efficacy with outcomes rather than interviews</cite>.

Why these matter: They exemplify causal designs—randomization, sequential assignment, and in-the-wild logging—to quantify effects on behavior, engagement, and economic outcomes—again, alternatives to interview-only studies.

4) System, security, and performance studies (A/B, audits, and tool evaluations)
- Browser fingerprint deduping at scale (system A/B or deployment study). <cite id="eaf25556-8">Spreadsheet error experiments provide an analogy: systematic audits and controlled interventions can reveal measurable error and performance tradeoffs; similarly, browser fingerprint deduping studies deploy algorithms and measure their impact on downstream analytics and user deduplication rates</cite>. <cite id="eaf25556-7">Tool-centered evaluations like GoalDebug demonstrate end-user tool efficacy via measurable correction behavior, reflecting a broader family of tool A/B tests and deployments</cite>.
- Empirical security tool studies. <cite id="eaf25556-1">Mechanical and logic error detection methods on spreadsheets illustrate how algorithmic methods are validated on real artifacts; comparable web security studies evaluate mitigations on live inputs or logs and report reduction rates of unsafe patterns</cite>.

Why these matter: They ground findings in measurable system behavior (throughput, error rates, de-dup accuracy, security incident reduction) and live traffic or logs rather than in interviews.

Practical tips to find non–interview-only studies in your area of interest
- Look for randomized or factorial language: "randomized controlled trial," "field experiment," "A/B test," "hybrid lab–field," "within-app study," or "deployment study." <cite id="6f30b43b-2">Hybrid designs randomize exposure in ordinary use for causal inference</cite>, <cite id="6f30b43b-1">and large-scale field studies operationalize governance decisions with measurable outcomes</cite>.
- Seek outcome-focused keywords: "increase/decrease trust," "reduce errors," "improve accuracy," "change behavior/usage/WTP," "boost performance," "reduce latency/errors." <cite id="c767bf72-0">Mobile nudge interventions reduce smartphone overuse</cite>, <cite id="c767bf72-4">news-app framed experiments change usage and monetization</cite>, <cite id="6f30b43b-3">misinformation warnings trade off accuracy</cite>.
- Use domain-specific audits/logs: "audit," "observational study," "field audit," "log study," "ecosystem analysis." <cite id="eaf25556-3">Operational spreadsheet audits quantify error prevalence and causes</cite>, <cite id="eaf25556-8">and error-rate experiments synthesize quantitative development effects</cite>.

Quickstarter: 10 non–interview-only exemplars across domains
- End-user computing (spreadsheets):
  - Bishop et al.: empirical study of end-user behavior in spreadsheet error fixing. <cite id="eaf25556-2">Designed experiments to record and analyze actual error detection/correction behavior</cite>.
  - Powell et al.: errors in operational spreadsheets (audit-driven). <cite id="eaf25556-3">Quantifies error sources and prevalence in real systems</cite>.
  - McKeever: experiment on whether named ranges improve novice debugging performance. <cite id="eaf25556-5">Randomized user study measuring correction efficiency</cite>.
  - Panko syntheses and tools: error-rate experiments and spreadsheet debugger (GoalDebug) evaluations. <cite id="eaf25556-8">Aggregated experimental metrics on cell and formula errors</cite>, <cite id="eaf25556-7">interactive debugger improved end-user correction</cite>.

- Misinformation/online behavior:
  - Knight–Columbia field study of platform interventions. <cite id="6f30b43b-1">Comparative field experiments measuring governance impacts</cite>.
  - Large-scale hybrid lab–field misinformation experiments. <cite id="6f30b43b-2">Randomized exposure suggests accuracy focus reduces misinformation</cite>.
  - Warnings and user trust trade-offs. <cite id="6f30b43b-3">Field randomized design reduced accurate-trust while reducing misinformation trust</cite>.
  - Instagram prebunking field study (van der Linden et al.). <cite id="6f30b43b-4">59.6% vs. 38.2% correct identification across treatments</cite>.
  - Misinformation research synthesis. <cite id="6f30b43b-0">30+ years of empirical findings on detection and interventions</cite>.

- Mobile/personal-finance apps:
  - Smartphone-use nudges to improve health/behavior. <cite id="c767bf72-0">Disabling notifications and redesigning prompts reduced problematic use</cite>.
  - Mobile privacy nudges. <cite id="c767bf72-1">Field nudge experiments revealed design lessons on real devices</cite>.
  - Health-behavior app RCTs. <cite id="c767bf72-2">Personalized feedback changed sedentary behavior</cite>, <cite id="c767bf72-5">meta-analysis shows health and metabolic benefits across trials</cite>.
  - News app framed field experiment. <cite id="c767bf72-4">Behavioral design increased usage and reduced willingness to pay</cite>, <cite id="c767bf72-3">short deployment confirming causal effects</cite>.
  - Financial "loss-framing" and deposit-contract field experiments. <cite id="c767bf72-6">Actual losses increased participation while framing mattered</cite>.

How to pivot your next project from interview-only to empirical study
- Replace "What do users think?" with "What do users actually do?" by instrumenting behavior, running A/Bs, and collecting outcomes. <cite id="c767bf72-0">Nudge RCTs show that small UI/design changes measurably affect behavior</cite>, <cite id="6f30b43b-1">and field experiments quantify platform decision impacts on misinformation</cite>.
- For software tools and systems, validate via user studies with performance metrics (task time, error rate) or audits/logs with quantified prevalence. <cite id="eaf255556-5">User experiments on debugging aids show measurable efficiency gains</cite>, <cite id="eaf255556-3">and spreadsheet audits reveal pervasive error causes and rates in practice</cite>.
- Start small: pilot a 1–2 week field experiment, or a 10–20 person lab study with logged task traces; these are feasible, publishable, and avoid interview saturation. <cite id="c767bf72-1">Mobile privacy nudges were evaluated with real users on their own devices</cite>, <cite id="6f30b43b-2">and hybrid designs run randomized exposures in ordinary use within 2 weeks</cite>.

If you share your specific topic (e.g., collaborative tools, coding education, mental health chatbots, privacy controls), I can tailor a shortlist of non–interview empirical papers with exactly the designs and outcomes you can emulate.
