without_preference.text: What are some systems papers that conduct an observational study instead of just interviews?
without_preference.answer:
Below are representative systems papers from HCI/UX and empirical software engineering that used observational study methods (e.g., field observation, shadowing, in‑situ usability testing, work diaries/logs) rather than interviews-only, with brief notes on their observational designs and contributions.

HCI/UX and human‑factors systems
- Ambient/mobility computing “in the wild”
  - Wyeth et al., “Designing Ambient Computing for use in the Mobile Health Care Domain” (CHI 2001 Workshop). This study embeds ambient technologies into healthcare workers’ physical spaces and work practices; the authors emphasize observing how ambient cues blend with normal interactions and iteratively shaping system design from observed behaviors in situ, rather than relying solely on participant accounts. <cite id="6e0a07c9-3">Our research into ambient computing blends technology with normal interactions and physical spaces of human work, focusing on in-situ observation to inform design</cite>.
  - Broekens et al., “Using shadowing for architectural research in healthcare environments” (overview/perspective). Although spanning architectural HCI, this paper explicitly catalogs shadowing as an observational method for studying work practices in healthcare settings and discusses opportunities and challenges of overt behavioral observation to generate design ideas. <cite id="6e0a07c9-0">Shadowing in healthcare environments is used as an observational approach to elicit design opportunities, with an overview of approaches and their challenges</cite>.
  - Kaptelinin/O Nielsen et al., “Universal Methods of Ethical Design” (CHI proceedings cases). Included case papers in this collection explicitly use in-situ observation and co‑observation with participants (overt observers) to study people in their workplaces—documenting what users do “in the wild” as the primary data source to inform system interventions and ethical guidelines. <cite id="6e0a07c9-6">Selected CHI design cases report field observation of people in their work environments as the principal method to motivate system interventions</cite>.

- Workplace interaction and joint activity
  - Cochran et al., “Toward Joint Activity Design: Augmenting Human‑Centered Design and Cognitive Systems Engineering” (Human Factors/related venues, 2023). This system-focused paper merges field‑work understanding of practitioners’ joint activities with cognitive systems engineering to design support for team‑level coordination; it foregrounds direct observation and logged practice to capture real‑time task coupling rather than relying only on retrospective interviews. <cite id="6e0a07c9-2">The paper merges human-centered design and cognitive systems engineering to design supports for joint activity, emphasizing field data collection and logged practice to understand team work</cite>.
  - Ko’s practical guide to evaluating software tools in the field (Cambridge guide). While a methods paper, it catalogs field studies of software tools as observing tools “in use” in developers’ workplaces alongside usability tests and surveys—explicitly positioning observation as a primary method for tool/system evaluation rather than interviews alone. <cite id="5040009a-1">Empirical tool studies include observations of tools in use in the field, along with usability testing and surveys, to evaluate real-world effectiveness</cite>.

Empirical software engineering (developer tools, collaboration, OSS ecosystems)
- Developer workplace studies and diaries/logs
  - “Studying Software Engineers: Data Collection Techniques for Software Field Studies” (empirical SE methods tutorial/exposition). This systems-method-oriented paper details observational techniques and work diaries as alternatives to interviews to assist tool/IDE design—e.g., logging use, contextual walkthroughs, and observing problem-solving at the desk to surface unarticulated needs. <cite id="5040009a-0">Observational techniques and work diaries are presented as practical, data-rich methods to assist tool design in software engineering, complementing or substituting interviews</cite>.
  - Weber et al., “A Study of Usability of a Model‑Driven Engineering IDE (4diac)” (tool evaluation case study). While multi-method, this systems evaluation prominently integrates observational usability sessions conducted with developers in their workplaces, paired with task analyses and think‑aloud; this overt observational protocol reveals friction points missed in lab or self‑report instruments. <cite id="5040009a-8">The study conducts multiple usability evaluation methods on the 4diac IDE in situ, emphasizing direct observation with users to find friction and inform redesign</cite>.

- Collaboration, events, and logs in real projects
  - Wu et al., “A study of collaboration in software design” (industry field study). This industrial systems study combines observational “shadowing” in a large software company with logging communication events and brief interviews; the observational component captures real-time coordination practices that shaped recommendations for collaborative tooling and workflow redesign. <cite id="5040009a-6">The study integrates shadowing in a large software company with event logging and interviews to analyze in-situ collaboration and inform tool design</cite>.
  - Basili et al., empirical SE and HPC environment improvement program. The program emphasizes iterative observation and logged data (“experience factors”) collected during tool use as the foundation of theory/hypothesis development and system evaluation in large-scale environments—an explicit observational‑driven empirical loop. <cite id="5040009a-5">Empirical SE uses iterative observation and experience-factor logging during HPC environment use to build theory, evaluate systems, and improve tools</cite>.

- OSS ecosystem measurement as “observational corpus study”
  - Ko’s overview of empirical methods for software tools highlights using field data, repository logs, and live usage traces alongside controlled experiments and interviews; within OSS, this includes observing how developers work with code and tools through logs, issue/PR traces, and ad‑hoc in-situ spot checks. <cite id="5040009a-1">Field observations of tools in use, combined with logs and other artifacts, illuminate how developers actually work versus what they report in surveys/interviews</cite>.
  - Field-study data collection techniques for software engineers synthesize workplace observation and diaries as effective substitutes or complements to interviews for informing IDEs and code-review tools. <cite id="5040009a-0">Observation and diaries capture contextualized workflow details that aid system design decisions for development tools</cite>.

Why observational studies matter (and how they differ from interviews-only)
- Capturing “use in context”: Observational methods uncover behaviors and pain points that participants struggle to articulate post hoc; shadowing and overt co‑observation directly reveal task flows, environmental frictions, and coordination patterns that are invisible to interviews alone. <cite id="5040009a-1">Field observation of tools in use captures real behavior, complementing or surpassing retrospective methods like surveys/interviews</cite><cite id="6e0a07c9-0">Shadowing exposes design opportunities by observing practitioners at work, which participants may miss self-reporting</cite>.
- Mixed-method triangulation: Contemporary systems studies combine observation with brief interviews/ think‑aloud to link behavior to meaning; this yields design hypotheses that can be tested with controlled experiments or in-situ usability testing. <cite id="5040009a-8">In-situ observation combined with usability methods reveals actionable design hypotheses for developer IDEs</cite><cite id="6e0a07c9-3">Ambient computing evaluations integrate in-situ observation to refine system fit into physical workspaces</cite>.
- Trade-offs and ethics: Overt observation and shadowing introduce observer effects and privacy concerns; careful instrumentation (diaries/logs), consent, and debriefing are standard in systems work. Many HCI case studies report explicit ethical design guidelines for in-the-wild observation alongside interviews. <cite id="6e0a07c9-6">CHI design case collections document field observation practices, including ethical considerations for co-observation with participants</cite><cite id="5040009a-0">Field-study data collection techniques emphasize ethical, context-sensitive observation and diaries in developer settings</cite>.

Quick pointers to find more (by venue and keyword)
- HCI/CHI/UIST/SOCS: search “field study”, “contextual inquiry”, “shadowing”, “in-situ usability” with venue filters; CHI 2001–2015 often has strong “ambient/mobility in the wild” systems with observational protocols. <cite id="6e0a07c9-0">Shadowing in professional environments provides actionable design cues when combined with reflective discussion</cite><cite id="6e0a07c9-3">HCI ambient computing papers report in-situ observation as central to design rationale</cite>.
- Empirical Software Engineering/ICSE/MS/ASE: query “work diaries”, “field study”, “log analysis”, “covert observation” in development workflows and IDEs; look for “tool evaluation in the field” and “human factors in SE.” <cite id="5040009a-0">Workplace observation and diaries guide tool design and feature prioritization in SE</cite><cite id="5040009a-1">Guides for SE tool evaluation emphasize observation-of-use in real environments as primary evidence</cite>.

Summary list (observational focus)
- Wyeth et al., CHI 2001 (WS): ambient computing in healthcare—overt in-situ observation to co‑design with work practices. <cite id="6e0a07c9-3">Observation in situ guides ambient computing to fit into normal interactions and physical spaces</cite>.
- Broekens et al. (overview): shadowing-based study of healthcare workflows—documented methods and design opportunities. <cite id="6e0a07c9-0">Shadowing provides systematic observation-driven design insights in healthcare contexts</cite>.
- Cochran et al. (2023): joint activity design merging HCD and cognitive systems engineering—field observation and logging of team work. <cite id="6e0a07c9-2">Field data capturing joint activities informs system supports for coordination</cite>.
- Weber et al. (4diac IDE): multi-method usability with in-situ observation—friction points and redesign of an MDE tool. <cite id="5040009a-8">Observation with developers reveals actionable IDE usability issues and improvements</cite>.
- Wu et al. (software design collaboration): shadowing plus communication logging in a large software company—workflow/tooling implications. <cite id="5040009a-6">Shadowing and event logging illuminate collaboration practices to guide tool design</cite>.
- Ko (Cambridge guide) + Baltes (methods/tutorials): practical, field‑oriented evaluation of software tools—observing tools “in use” rather than interviews-only. <cite id="5040009a-1">Observation of tools in practice is a primary method in SE evaluation alongside usability testing and surveys</cite><cite id="5040009a-0">Observation and diaries provide actionable detail about developer workflows</cite>.
- Broader case collections in CHI ethics/methods: curated field/case studies showing overt co‑observation and workplace ethnography. <cite id="6e0a07c9-6">Selected design cases demonstrate field observation as a core method to motivate responsible, effective interventions</cite>.

How to use these as templates
- Plan observation protocols: define tasks, artifacts to log (diaries, event logs), and consent/observer effect mitigation; pair with brief probes (co‑observation think‑aloud) to link behaviors to meanings. <cite id="6e0a07c9-0">Shadowing literature details preparation and debriefing to elicit design-relevant insights from observed behaviors</cite>.
- Iterate with controlled evaluation: translate observational hypotheses into controlled tasks, then re‑observe in lab or remote settings to validate changes. <cite id="5040009a-1">Field observation is paired with usability testing and controlled evaluation for software tools</cite>.
- Triangulate with interviews: use short contextual interviews for interpretive grounding, but treat observation as the primary evidence for system design decisions. <cite id="5040009a-6">Combined shadowing and interviews provide complementary evidence on collaboration practices</cite>.

questions.original_query: is there any evidence that large language models can be effectively applied to robot planning tasks?

query.text: is there any evidence that large language models can be effectively applied to robot planning tasks?
query.answer:
Short answer: Yes. Recent work shows that large language models (LLMs) can be applied to robot planning and, in multiple controlled studies, improve task success and reliability over stronger single‑agent baselines, with several groups reporting 30–50% gains on standard manipulation benchmarks under zero‑shot or few‑shot conditions, along with mechanisms for plan correction, feasibility checking, and online replanning that mitigate execution errors and hallucinations. <cite id="e4f8d17b-0,e4f8d17b-1">On RLBench-style manipulation, MALMM (a multi‑agent LLM system) achieved around 40% higher success rates than a single‑agent LLM across multiple tasks and was identified as the top performer for several tasks</cite> <cite id="b819a190-0">LM-SymOpt’s language‑guided symbolic planner significantly outperformed alternatives on planning tasks and showed strong success‑rate gains over methods without explicit planning</cite> <cite id="77339ae8-0,77339ae8-2,77339ae8-3">Multi‑agent Vision LLMs (“Wonderful Team”) achieved ~50% success on certain physical tasks and reported average 30–40% success‑rate improvements versus prior VLLM methods on standard and VimaBench tasks</cite> <cite id="489d3415-2">Grounding studies show LLMs can incorporate raw simulator/controller errors to revise plans and increase reliable execution</cite> <cite id="77339ae8-8">Guardian shows detector‑plus‑planner pipelines can identify planning/execution errors and improve task success on both simulation and real robots</cite>.

Zero‑shot and embodied planning benchmarks
- Multi‑agent LLMs have consistently outperformed single‑agent LLMs on zero‑shot manipulation suites like RLBench when tasked with decomposing and sequencing actions into feasible robot actions. <cite id="e4f8d17b-0">Across five RLBench tasks, MALMM achieved a 40% higher success rate than a strong single‑agent LLM baseline (e.g., for “put case” and “rubbish” tasks), and the authors highlight success‑rate leaderboards for zero‑shot evaluation</cite>. 
- Visual/multimodal LLM teams demonstrate similar gains under zero‑shot or few‑shot conditions: <cite id="77339ae8-0,77339ae8-2,77339ae8-3">a multi‑agent VLLM framework achieved around 50% success on a canonical physical task and reported about +30% average improvements on standard tasks and up to +40% on VimaBench over prior VLLM methods (e.g., NLaP), with failure modes traced to integrating visual evidence with action planning</cite>. 
- LLM‑guided symbolic planning tailored for manipulation (“LM‑SymOpt”) improves success even without demonstrations: <cite id="b819a190-0">by optimizing formal task plans derived from language instructions, LM‑SymOpt significantly boosts success rates on planning subproblems relative to non‑planning baselines</cite>.

Integration with execution and online correction
- A prominent design pattern uses LLMs for high‑level task decomposition and plan synthesis, while executing through skill libraries or motion planners; the system then replans online when execution errors occur. <cite id="489d3415-2">Grounded LLM task planning with raw error signals allows LLMs to revise plans and improve reliability in simulation and on real robots</cite>. 
- Error detection plus replanning pipelines increase robustness: <cite id="77339ae8-8">Guardian detects both planning and execution errors with high precision and recall and improves overall success rates on real hardware and in simulation</cite>. 
- Open‑world planning frameworks incorporate plan‑level and action‑level corrections: <cite id="4830562c-8">COWP adds execution error checking and hierarchical replanning to reduce task failure due to missing tool use or incorrect action selection</cite>. <cite id="489d3415-0">Zero‑shot manipulation baselines also propose LLM‑driven symbolic task planning with optimization to close the loop between plans and robot execution</cite>.

Towards classic motion planning and feasibility
- In practice, LLMs often act as high‑level task planners that generate IK/goal constraints and sequence operations for standard planners. <cite id="5930bbf6-3">Studies evaluating GPT‑3.5 for path planning in cluttered scenes identify shortcomings versus deterministic motion planning but propose hybrid architectures where LLMs propose waypoints/constraints and classical solvers ensure feasibility and efficiency</cite>. 
- Feasibility prediction layers help bridge natural language goals to kinematic constraints: <cite id="a2550f22-6">work on feasibility prediction reports up to 90% success where earlier baselines failed, demonstrating how LLM‑generated plans can be filtered/rectified for real‑world manipulation</cite>.
- When LLMs are used to derive abstractions/constraints from language, success and planning time can improve materially: <cite id="5930bbf6-6">CaStL shows significant improvements in planning success from natural‑language specifications in complex scenarios</cite>. <cite id="4830562c-4">A bimanual “LLM+MAP” pipeline integrates LLM reasoning and PDDL‑style planning to automate subtask decomposition and coordination, emphasizing feasibility at kinematic‑manipulation scale</cite>.

Empirical deployment patterns and reported gains
- Realistic evaluations increasingly stress zero‑shot generalization to novel objects/tas‑ks without hand‑crafted skill trees: <cite id="b819a190-7">UniManip reports 22.5–25% higher success and lower sample complexity in zero‑shot transfer across unseen objects and tasks by coupling a generalist skill library with LLM‑guided planning</cite>. <cite id="489d3415-0">Language‑guided symbolic planners address underspecification by formalizing tasks and sequencing operations that respect robot kinematics and environment dynamics</cite>. 
- Nature‑communica‑tion‑quality mechanisms argue for practicality: <cite id="489d3415-1">Panda Act demonstrates multimodal zero‑shot manipulation on a Panda arm, and correlates model zero‑shot performance with experimental success rates, suggesting that LLM‑based planning can translate to the lab</cite>. 
- Multimodal frameworks also show clear quantitative deltas versus prior text‑only baselines: <cite id="77339ae8-2,77339ae8-3">VLLM multi‑agent planners report 40% average gains on VimaBench and 30% improvements on standard tasks</cite>. <cite id="e4f8d17b-0">Across RLBench tasks, multi‑agent collaboration yields ~40% higher success than single agents</cite>.

Limits, failure modes, and how the community is addressing them
- Hallucination and feasibility gaps remain first‑order challenges; many works therefore add retrieval, structured verification, and execution‑aware replanning. <cite id="77339ae8-0">A recurrent failure mode is misbinding visual evidence to actions, leading to infeasible or unsafe grasp placements despite correct high‑level plans</cite>. <cite id="4830562c-2">Empirical evaluation frameworks now track success rate, steps, and LLM call budgets to diagnose cost/accuracy trade‑offs</cite>. 
- Some domains still favor classical or data‑driven baselines; hybridization is a common sweet spot. <cite id="5930bbf6-3">Head‑to‑head path‑planning studies find LLMs struggle with deterministic constraints/collisions, motivating the use of LLMs for qualitative guidance and classical solvers for precise feasibility</cite>. 
- Safety/verification tooling is maturing: <cite id="77339ae8-8">error detectors that interrupt and replan have been shown to increase task success on real robots</cite>, and grounded plan revision is routine in practice.

Takeaway
- There is clear, recent evidence that LLMs can be effectively applied to robot planning: multi‑agent and grounded LLM systems improve success rates by 30–50% versus stronger single‑agent baselines on benchmark manipulation suites; LLM‑guided symbolic planning boosts plan feasibility; and hybrid pipelines (LLM for abstraction/decomposition, classic planners for kinematics, plus online error detection/replanning) improve real‑world execution. <cite id="e4f8d17b-0,e4f8d17b-1">Multi‑agent LLMs outperform single agents on zero‑shot RLBench tasks by ~40% relative success rates</cite> <cite id="b819a190-0">LLM‑SymOpt improves success where planning is explicit</cite> <cite id="77339ae8-0,77339ae8-2,77339ae8-3">Visual multi‑agent LLMs achieve 30–40% gains over prior visual LLM approaches and ~50% success on specific physical tasks</cite> <cite id="489d3415-2">LLMs that revise plans from raw robot errors increase reliable execution</cite> <cite id="77339ae8-8">error‑aware detection plus replanning improves success on real hardware</cite>. 
- What remains is consistent benchmarking versus classical planners and systematic safety evaluations under open‑world conditions; current gains are most robust when LLMs are constrained with structured verification, feasibility checks, and execution‑feedback loops. <cite id="4830562c-8">Online error handling reduces failure for missing tools or actions</cite> <cite id="5930bbf6-3">hybrid LLM+classical designs can close performance gaps where pure LLM or pure planning underperforms</cite>.

fully_underspecified.text: is there any evidence that models can be effectively applied to planning tasks?
fully_underspecified.answer:
Summary: Yes. Across classical AI planning, modern learned “world model” approaches, and model-based reinforcement learning/control, there is substantial empirical evidence that explicitly modeling the environment enables effective planning, often with large gains in sample efficiency, training speed, or solution quality compared to non-model-based alternatives—though performance depends critically on model fidelity and representation choices. <cite id="4bfa467f-3">ensemble world models can achieve sample efficiency competitive with model-free methods while providing meaningful uncertainty estimates</cite> <cite id="de81ae10-1">Dreamer shows a general recipe: learn a predictive world model and use it to plan long-horizon behaviors</cite> <cite id="973ecfae-0">model-based policy optimization learns an order of magnitude faster than prior model-free methods on several tasks while attaining comparable asymptotic performance</cite>.

Classical planning foundations and empirical evaluation
- Foundational model-based planners for STRIPS-like domains use compact “planning graphs” to compute plans efficiently; empirical studies show the method quickly analyzes state spaces and produces plans, establishing that explicit state/transition models plus algorithmic structure yield strong practical performance. <cite id="fbe6d3d7-2">constructing and analyzing a compact planning graph enables fast planning in STRIPS-like domains, with empirical evidence from experiments</cite> <cite id="fbe6d3d7-4">Fast Planning Through Planning Graph Analysis provides empirical evidence that planning graphs reduce search effort and improve solution speed</cite> <cite id="fbe6d3d7-4">this approach popularized heuristic guidance and analysis of planning graphs as an effective planning method</cite>.
- The International Planning Competitions institutionalize evaluation of model-driven planners over standardized PDDL domains; contemporary surveys review years of progress and track how domain models, search algorithms, and features collectively raise performance, underscoring the role of explicit world models (PDDL) and structured heuristics in effective planning. <cite id="fbe6d3d7-1">PDDL domain/problem languages, benchmarks, and competitions systematically assess planning algorithms that rely on explicit domain models</cite> <cite id="fbe6d3d7-3">surveys of IPC 2011 document PDDL’s central role and evolving evaluation practices that reward effective use of model structure</cite> <cite id="fbe6d3d7-7">follow-on analyses catalog heuristic features, local search, and action graphs contributing to faster plan finding</cite> <cite id="fbe6d3d7-5">recent competition reports continue to describe track designs meant to surface effective planning-model use</cite>.
- Even as large language models enter planning, classic model-based planners remain strong baselines; recent work shows frontier LLMs can be competitive with established classical planners like LAMA on PDDL benchmarks, highlighting that explicit model use plus search remains an effective planning paradigm. <cite id="fbe6d3d7-0">on standard PDDL domains, GPT‑5’s solved-task performance is competitive with LAMA, indicating that model-based search/representation remains powerful</cite>.

Learned world models for planning and long-horizon control
- Surveys converge that learned world models provide predictive simulators over states/observations and are explicitly used for planning and simulating actions, unifying prediction and control in visual/motor skills. <cite id="4bfa467f-0">a policy‑centric survey frames world models as predictive simulators coupled with vision‑language action policies</cite> <cite id="4bfa467f-1">surveys emphasize world models as unified approaches for learning predictive representations to model how environments evolve over time</cite> <cite id="4bfa467f-6">comprehensive surveys describe how models enable planning and simulation of potential actions for decision making</cite> <cite id="4bfa467f-8">a broader survey situates models as tools for either understanding or predicting futures, with planning as a central use</cite>.
- Quantitatively, ensemble world models can match model-free methods’ sample efficiency while giving uncertainty estimates helpful for planning under model error. <cite id="4bfa467f-3">ensemble world models achieve sample efficiency competitive with model-free methods and provide uncertainty</cite>.
- Case studies across environments show effective model-driven planning:
  - Minecraft controllability: Dreamer agents trained entirely inside a learned world model solved complex Minecraft tasks rapidly, exemplifying efficient high-dimensional planning with long horizons. <cite id="de81ae10-1">Dreamer learns a world model from images and uses it to learn long‑sighted behaviors</cite> <cite id="de81ae10-4">a Dreamer system “masters” Minecraft in nine days, training independently with a fast world-model environment</cite> <cite id="de81ae10-2">Dreamer 4 demonstrates training agents inside scalable world models to solve control tasks efficiently</cite>.
  - StarCraft II planning: Learned world models produce per‑step rollouts that predict resource flows and construction progress, enabling strategic policy refinement aligned with high-level plans. <cite id="de81ae10-7">a 5‑second model rollout predicts resource depletion and supply‑depot completion, supporting strategic planning decisions</cite>. Related work explores LLM-driven world models and their potential for SC2 decision‑making. <cite id="de81ae10-0">proposals of LLM‑based world models for StarCraft II investigate decision making through model‑based planning</cite>.
  - High-level abstraction limits: Benchmarks show that even state‑of‑the‑art language models achieve around 57% accuracy on high‑level world understanding, highlighting that effective planning requires accurate, temporally consistent predictive models. <cite id="4bfa467f-5">current frontier models achieve about 57% accuracy on a validated high‑level world modeling benchmark, indicating room for improvement</cite>.
  - Broader VLA/robotics context: Surveys argue that predictive simulators enable planning, foresight, and reuse across tasks, consistent with growing success on manipulation and navigation benchmarks. <cite id="4bfa467f-1">world models provide predictive representations used for planning and simulating actions in artificial agents</cite> <cite id="4bfa467f-6">they are used to perform planning and simulate potential actions across tasks</cite>. 

Model-based reinforcement learning and policy optimization
- Model-based RL explicitly leverages learned dynamics/reward models to plan via rollouts or trajectory optimization, often accelerating learning. MBPO shows order-of-magnitude speed gains over model-free baselines while reaching comparable asymptote on diverse control tasks; the framework isolates model reliance intervals and uses ensemble models to bound planning error. <cite id="973ecfae-0">MBPO learns substantially faster, an order of magnitude on some tasks, while attaining comparable final performance</cite> <cite id="973ecfae-1">the paper studies when to trust the model and how planning through the model yields empirical gains</cite>. 
- Extensions demonstrate robustness and scalability: MOPO and variants outperform prior model-based RL on offline settings and set new benchmarks in partially observed and multi‑task scenarios; recent massively multi‑task MBPO (M3PO) reports state‑of‑the‑art results as an efficient, robust alternative to prior methods. <cite id="973ecfae-4">In offline RL, MBPO-based methods already produce significant gains and MOPO outperforms model-free baselines in multiple experiments</cite> <cite id="973ecfae-6">MOPO “outperforms standard model-based RL algorithms and prior state-of-the-art model-free offline RL”</cite> <cite id="973ecfae-5">M3PO provides an efficient and robust alternative and achieves state-of-the-art performance across tasks</cite>.
- Practical caveats: while model-based methods can be fast and sample‑efficient, overconfident or biased models can hurt asymptotic performance; careful ensemble design, conservative model usage, and uncertainty-aware planning mitigate these risks. <cite id="973ecfae-2">model-based RL methods tend to achieve lower asymptotic performances than model-free methods when models are highly biased; practitioners often increase search/bias to compensate</cite> <cite id="973ecfae-0">MBPO’s interval of relying on the model and using ensembles addresses over‑confident/planning errors empirically</cite>. Complementary world model–based policy optimization (WMPO/WMPO‑Seed) demonstrates that learned predictive simulators can outperform generalized policy optimization under rollout budgets, echoing planning-through-model benefits with clear budget–performance tradeoffs. <cite id="973ecfae-3">WMPO consistently outperforms GRPO and DPO baselines under different rollout budgets, improving as budget increases</cite>.

Limitations and robustness to model error
- Planning quality hinges on model accuracy and faithfulness. High-level “world modeling” remains challenging: validated benchmarks reveal ~57% accuracy from frontier models, which constrains reliable multi‑step planning and motivates uncertainty quantification and tighter integration with decision policies. <cite id="4bfa467f-5">current frontier models achieve ~57% accuracy in high-level world modeling after extensive filtering/ validation</cite> <cite id="4bfa467f-3">ensembles help provide uncertainty to guide safer planning</cite>. 
- Heuristics exist to diagnose and compensate: planning-graph analysis exposes structure (action costs, mutexes) that guide efficient search; surveys of planning competitions document the importance of model expressiveness (PDDL features) and hybridization (heuristics, local search, action graphs) to maintain effectiveness as state spaces grow. <cite id="fbe6d3d7-2">planning graphs compactly represent state/transition structure to guide search and speed planning</cite> <cite id="fbe6d3d7-7">action graphs and heuristic features improve efficiency in local search planners</cite> <cite id="fbe6d3d7-3">competition surveys emphasize PDDL expressiveness and hybrid strategy selection</cite>.
- Cautious model use matters. MBPO’s “when to trust your model” principle shows that restricting reliance on the model during policy improvement and planning mitigates extrapolation errors, a practical design pattern echoed in conservative reward modeling and curriculum rollout lengths. <cite id="973ecfae-0">theoretical and empirical analyses introduce intervals on which the model is trusted to prevent error amplification</cite>.

Bottom line and practical takeaways
- There is clear, reproducible evidence that modeling the environment and planning through that model improves plan quality, sample efficiency, or convergence speed on many planning/control tasks. Classic model-based planners in PDDL-based competitions have long demonstrated this on structured domains; world-model RL agents like Dreamer achieve mastery of large-scale environments rapidly; and MBPO-class methods deliver order‑of‑magnitude learning speedups compared to model-free baselines at comparable asymptotes. <cite id="fbe6d3d7-4">planning graphs yield fast, high‑quality plans in STRIPS-like settings</cite> <cite id="de81ae10-4">Dreamer agents learn to master complex environments quickly via world-model planning</cite> <cite id="973ecfae-0">MBPO learns an order of magnitude faster and matches model-free performance</cite>.
- Effectiveness scales with model fidelity and integration. Accurate, uncertainty-aware predictive simulators are crucial; overconfident models can degrade final performance. Recent world-model surveys emphasize combining predictive power with uncertainty and search, and competition evidence shows hybrid models and structured representations remain central in state‑of‑the‑art planning systems. <cite id="4bfa467f-3">ensembles provide uncertainty and near-model-free sample efficiency</cite> <cite id="973ecfae-2">biased models can lower asymptotic performance, motivating robust planning</cite> <cite id="fbe6d3d7-5">IPC reports highlight hybrid strategies and model expressiveness as keys to performance</cite>.

questions.original_query: What are the most important open challenges in Federated Learning?

query.text: What are the most important open challenges in Federated Learning?
query.answer:
# Executive Summary

The most important open challenges in Federated Learning (FL) cluster around five themes: (1) data/model heterogeneity and non-stationarity; (2) communication/computation efficiency and unreliable participation; (3) robustness, security, and privacy (including backdoors and poisoning); (4) personalization, fairness, and auditability; and (5) systems at scale (device/resource heterogeneity, incentives, governance, and standardization). Recent surveys and focused studies highlight concrete gaps in algorithms that simultaneously address non-IID data and efficient communication, defenses that withstand adaptive attacks at low client fractions, personalization methods that respect fairness and enable auditing, and production-grade orchestrators that manage heterogeneity, incentives, and compliance under evolving regulation. <cite id="243a5f4c-0">Recent work reiterates heterogeneity, computation overhead and communication bottlenecks as core challenges in FL</cite> <cite id="243a5f4c-2">surveys also emphasize privacy/security protections and the cross-cutting security implications across domains</cite> <cite id="243a5f4c-3">and policy-facing analyses argue FL is central to meeting new data governance regimes like the EU AI Act</cite>.

# 1) Data and Task Heterogeneity, Non-IID, and Concept Drift

Non-IID data distributions, label and feature shifts, client device heterogeneity, and concept drift remain pervasive and degrade convergence, generalization, and stability of FL systems. <cite id="243a5f4c-0">Surveys repeatedly identify heterogeneity as foundational challenge across FL systems</cite> <cite id="243a5f4c-1">and systematic reviews map techniques to application-specific non-IID patterns and their impacts</cite> <cite id="243a5f4c-5">for federated foundation models, large-scale multimodal FL introduces additional cross-modal heterogeneity and drift concerns</cite>. Two major open problems are: (a) optimization algorithms and aggregation that provably converge under heavy skew and concept change, and (b) mechanisms that detect and react to drift at the client or edge, such as continual FL and selective aggregation. <cite id="243a5f4c-1">Recent surveys synthesize adaptive strategies but call for principled guarantees under non-stationary sources</cite>. Relatedly, mechanisms for federated unlearning and recomputation under recency/recency-driven change are still maturing. <cite id="243a5f4c-7">A dedicated survey on federated unlearning outlines methods and challenges for accountable deletion and evolving participation</cite>.

Communication/computation are tightly coupled to heterogeneity. <cite id="0f0b8779-2">Non-IID data exacerbates sparsification because skewed local class distributions make uniform thresholds inefficient or harmful</cite> <cite id="0f0b8779-8">top-k sparsification, for example, has limited utility on non-iid data in FL due to uneven gradients</cite> <cite id="243a5f4c-4">new methods such as FedComLoc target heterogeneous environments explicitly to reduce overhead while preserving accuracy</cite>. Building compression/feedback schemes that maintain convergence guarantees with arbitrarily skewed data remains an open systems-optimization challenge. <cite id="0f0b8779-6">A survey on communication efficiency catalogs quantization/sparsification patterns but notes integration difficulty with real-world FL constraints</cite>.

# 2) Communication Efficiency and Unreliable Participation

Despite progress in compression and hierarchical FL, communication remains the principal bottleneck, with open problems on scaling to many devices, stragglers, and variable participation. <cite id="243a5f4c-0">System surveys continue to flag communication bottlenecks and computation overheads as central open issues</cite> <cite id="0f0b8779-1">quantization and sparsification are established levers but require careful error-control to avoid accuracy loss, especially when clients transmit sparsely and unevenly</cite> <cite id="0f0b8779-4">methods tailored to heterogeneity reduce rounds and bandwidth, yet must contend with stragglers and unstable uplink conditions</cite>. Open questions include principled methods for adaptive error feedback under non-iid updates, hierarchical or graph-based aggregation over unreliable wireless links, and robust aggregation when only a minority of clients participate. <cite id="243a5f4c-5">Emerging directions in federated foundation models investigate parameter-efficient transfers and partial updates, but robustness evidence under bandwidth/latency constraints is still sparse</cite>.

# 3) Robustness, Security, and Privacy: Poisoning and Backdoors

Security/privacy threats—poisoning, backdoor injection, and inference—are a top risk, and defenses remain fragile under adaptive adversaries. <cite id="b091d88c-0">A recent survey systematically reviews backdoor tactics and defenses, stressing the need for robust FL</cite> <cite id="b091d88c-4">empirical work shows "layer-aware" backdoor attacks succeed against seven SOTA defenses with as few as 10% malicious clients</cite> <cite id="b091d88c-5">and industry-oriented analyses survey cross-layer poisoning in wireless FL with classification and evasion objectives</cite>. Key open problems include: (i) trust/reputation and aggregation protocols resilient to coalitions and adaptive schedules; (ii) verifiable computing or cryptographic primitives that scale (e.g., secure aggregation with HE/TNN) for millions of devices; and (iii) membership inference and model extraction under privacy regulations, coupled with fairness constraints. <cite id="b091d88c-2">A SoK-style benchmarking effort collects 32 attack/defense strategies across platforms, highlighting standardization and reproducibility needs</cite> <cite id="b091d88c-6">federal meta-learning is vulnerable to even one-shot poisoning that persists after adaptation, indicating new threat surfaces for hierarchical and prompt-tuning paradigms</cite>.

# 4) Personalization vs Fairness, Accountability, and Auditability

Balancing a global shared model with personalization under fairness and accountability constraints is still unsolved at scale. <cite id="243a5f4c-2">Surveys describe privacy/security mechanisms but acknowledge difficulties in aligning personalization with non-discrimination across federated applications</cite> <cite id="243a5f4c-4">domain reviews list fairness as a key challenge within recommendation engines, autonomous systems, and IoT</cite>. Practical problems include: (a) personalization methods that respect group fairness and do not require retraining from centralized data; (b) audit trails for model updates and attribution when backdoors or skewed data affect protected groups; and (c) auditing tools that quantify disparate impact across federated domains. <cite id="243a5f4c-3">Policy analyses emphasize FL as a governance tool to meet AI Act requirements on data protection and transparency, raising open questions for auditability in production systems</cite>. In the foundation-model era, aligning federated fine-tuning with bias mitigations and documentation is an emerging open challenge. <cite id="243a5f4c-5">Federated foundation model surveys call out fairness, personalization, and privacy as intertwined research directions</cite>.

# 5) Systems at Scale: Heterogeneity, Incentives, and Governance

Scaling FL into production demands systems research beyond algorithmic advances. <cite id="243a5f4c-0">Surveys identify computation overhead and communication bottlenecks as core limits that constrain deployability</cite> <cite id="243a5f4c-6">integrations with edge computing, blockchain, and next-generation wireless are proposed to address trust and coordination</cite> <cite id="243a5f4c-1">systematic surveys highlight orchestration and device heterogeneity across application verticals</cite>. Open challenges include: (i) device- and network-aware scheduling under uneven compute/energy budgets; (ii) incentive mechanisms to elicit participation and truthfulness under bandwidth and data-budget constraints; (iii) over-the-air aggregation and robust physical-layer protocols; and (iv) governance and compliance tooling for consent, data-provenance, and regulatory audits. <cite id="243a5f4c-3">Analyses of the EU AI Act argue for federated approaches to reconcile data protection with innovation, surfacing governance and accountability design gaps</cite> <cite id="243a5f4c-7">unlearning surveys point to the need for accountable deletion workflows and audit logs in multi-tenant edge ecosystems</cite>.

# 6) Specialized and Emerging Challenges

- Federated Unlearning and Recency: Revoking or forgetting model knowledge at client or server scale while preserving privacy and accuracy remains difficult, especially under concept drift and adversarial participation. <cite id="243a5f4c-7">A 2023 survey synthesizes federated unlearning techniques and notes open problems in deletion guarantees and evaluation under realistic constraints</cite>.
- Multimodal and Foundation Models: Extending FL to video/3D/audio requires new aggregation, compression, and alignment under heterogeneity. <cite id="243a5f4c-5">Recent surveys of federated foundation models outline open problems in personalization, multimodal fusion, privacy, and fairness at model-building scale</cite>.
- Benchmarking and Reproducibility: While broader, the absence of cross-domain, adversarially robust benchmarks hampers progress on security and systems claims. <cite id="b091d88c-2">A 2025 SoK benchmark with 32 attack/defense strategies and multi-platform compatibility is a step toward reproducible evaluation, but coverage remains uneven and domain-specific nuances persist</cite>.

# Practical Research Directions

- Theory with Realistic Assumptions: Develop convergence and robustness guarantees for non-iid, time-varying sources with adaptive participation, including backdoor adversaries at low budgets. <cite id="243a5f4c-0">Surveys point to heterogeneity and drift as central sources of failure, motivating theory under realistic non-stationarity</cite>.
- Communication-Efficient Optimization Over Heterogeneous Channels: Combine adaptive quantization/sparsification with error-feedback and topology-aware aggregation; validate across wireless/edge and Wi-Fi environments. <cite id="0f0b8779-1">Quantization/sparsification reduce communication but must be paired with error-control to avoid accuracy loss</cite> <cite id="0f0b8779-4">methods tailored to heterogeneous environments reduce overhead yet need robustness to stragglers and failures</cite>.
- Hardened Aggregation and Defense at Internet Scale: Build trust-reputation layers, verifiable aggregation for billion-scale clients, and coalition-resilient protocols; test against adaptive backdoors with small malicious shares. <cite id="b091d88c-4">Layer-aware backdoors succeed against multiple defenses with 10% malicious clients, indicating design space gaps</cite> <cite id="b091d88c-0">comprehensive surveys map attacks and defenses to guide scalable hardening</cite>.
- Fair and Auditable Personalization: Mechanisms to calibrate personalization using group fairness constraints and differential privacy, with transparent provenance and audit trails across domains; integrate with regulatory compliance. <cite id="243a5f4c-2">Surveys emphasize privacy/security while underscoring fairness challenges in practice</cite> <cite id="243a5f4c-3">policy-facing work ties FL to governance imperatives, highlighting the need for auditability</cite>.
- Production Orchestration Platforms: Systems that jointly schedule devices, manage incentives, perform over-the-air aggregation, and support federated unlearning and auditing, tested end-to-end across domains. <cite id="243a5f4c-6">Integrations with edge, blockchain, and advanced wireless are proposed to address trust and orchestration</cite> <cite id="243a5f4c-7">unlearning platforms can embed deletion accountability and compliance checks</cite>.

# Outlook

FL's impact depends on resolving the interaction between heterogeneity, communication limits, and adversarial risks, while introducing fairness and auditability into production workflows governed by new regulations. <cite id="243a5f4c-0">Recent surveys converge on these as the central open problems</cite> <cite id="243a5f4c-2">and emphasize that privacy/security cannot be decoupled from algorithmic and systems design</cite> <cite id="243a5f4c-3">policy analyses point to FL as a lever for compliance, further raising governance and trust requirements</cite>. The most promising cross-cutting advances will pair algorithmic progress (e.g., robust aggregation and communication-efficient optimization) with standardized, adversarially aware benchmarks and auditable governance toolchains, tailored to non-iid, drifting, and heterogeneous real-world data. <cite id="243a5f4c-1">Systematic surveys argue for integrated solutions across algorithms, systems, and applications to unlock FL's full potential</cite> <cite id="b091d88c-2">and benchmark SoKs demonstrate the value—and limits—of current evaluations in revealing open research opportunities</cite>.

fully_underspecified.text: What are the most important open challenges in machine learning?
fully_underspecified.answer:
Below is a synthesis of the most important open challenges in machine learning, organized by theme and supported by recent surveys, benchmarks, theory reports, and practitioner evidence.

Executive summary
- Robustness and generalization remain foundational gaps: models trained to adversarial or corruption benchmarks often fail under naturally occurring distribution shifts, motivating new benchmarks (e.g., ImageNet-R) and methods that bridge worst-case and real-world shifts. <cite id="3ccdfaa7-4">ImageNet-R collected OOD test sets induced by texture, geolocation, camera parameters, and blur to probe robustness under natural distribution shifts</cite> <cite id="3ccdfaa7-3">OODRobustBench explicitly targets OOD adversarial robustness, contrasting with RobustBench that focuses on in-distribution settings</cite> <cite id="3ccdfaa7-1">Training for adversarial robustness does not necessarily confer robustness to naturally occurring shifts</cite> <cite id="3ccdfaa7-2">A critical analysis of OOD generalization introduced multiple OOD benchmarks and argued that existing robustness methods are insufficient for naturally occurring shifts</cite>.
- Core theory and optimization still lack principled unification: surveys and open-problem forums highlight unresolved questions on statistical guarantees, approximation/estimation vs. optimization trade-offs, and rates in nonconvex stochastic control. <cite id="780aa691-2">A survey of statistical theories of deep learning reviews approximation, training, and statistical perspectives, underscoring open questions at the statistical-optimization interface</cite> <cite id="780aa691-0">The COLT 2023 proceedings include an “Open Problems” program documenting unresolved theoretical gaps</cite> <cite id="780aa691-5">An open problem on optimal gap-dependent rates for stochastic decision-theoretic learning reflects unresolved rate optimality questions</cite>.
- Privacy-preserving learning and rapid scaling complicate control and auditability: federated settings bring new attack surfaces (e.g., reconstruction/overparameterization) and create open problems in unlearning and personalization; foundation-model training raises sustainability and governance issues. <cite id="c301f085-0">Federated learning surveys highlight open research problems at algorithmic, system, and application levels, with future directions spanning personalization, dynamics, and privacy</cite> <cite id="c301f085-1">Surveys on federated unlearning synthesize techniques and identify open problems in unlearning correctness, privacy, and system-level orchestration</cite> <cite id="c301f085-3">LLM federated unlearning surveys emphasize privacy and copyright risks specific to LLMs</cite> <cite id="c301f085-5">Online federated/transfer learning surveys (2023) trace evolutionary routes and point to gaps in continual, personalized, private learning</cite>.
- Evaluation is a bottleneck: benchmarks that once pushed progress have plateaued or revealed brittleness; new OOD robustness suites and interpretability workshops expose fragility and limit scientific inference. <cite id="3ccdfaa7-3">OODRobustBench shows that adversarially robust models can lack robustness to distribution shift, motivating broader evaluation suites</cite> <cite id="046daccc-1">Mechanistic interpretability workshop acceptances at ICML 2024 and NeurIPS 2024, alongside a Benchmarks and … track, highlight the turn toward interpretability and benchmarking as first-class challenges</cite>.
- Fairness, transparency, and societal integration need principled solutions: surveys and open calls catalog bias sources, governance bottlenecks, and limits to LLMs “solving” domain research questions, indicating that current alignment tools are not sufficient for rigorous, audit-ready decision systems. <cite id="780aa691-1">A fairness/bias survey argues that ML bias research often focuses on fairness outcomes without diagnosing root causes</cite> <cite id="046daccc-7">An NLP “open questions not closed by LLMs” report enumerates 14+ domains where new research is required because LLMs cannot directly solve existing problems</cite> <cite id="c301f085-6">Practitioner surveys identify core pain points—scalability, data quality, and unexplained decision systems—underscoring reliability and governance gaps</cite>.

1) Robustness, distribution shift, and generalization
- Models demonstrate strong tolerance to synthetic corruptions and adversarial perturbations but degrade sharply under natural distribution shifts, creating a robustness gap between benchmarks and real deployments. <cite id="3ccdfaa7-1">Models trained with adversarial robustness do not possess robustness to naturally occurring distribution shifts</cite> <cite id="3ccdfaa7-2">A critical analysis of OOD generalization built four OOD benchmarks and argues that standard robustness methods fail when shifts arise in practice</cite> <cite id="3ccdfaa7-8">Recent work explicitly studies robustness to natural variations and finds that much prior robustness research focuses on non-realistic settings</cite>.
- Benchmarks have specialized axes (in-distribution vs. out-of-distribution, adversarial vs. natural shifts) that are only partially aligned, complicating progress tracking and cross-method comparisons. <cite id="3ccdfaa7-3">OODRobustBench is specifically designed for OOD adversarial robustness, complementing RobustBench’s in-distribution focus</cite> <cite id="3ccdfaa7-4">ImageNet-R operationalizes natural shifts (texture, geolocation, camera, blur) to evaluate robustness under realistic variations</cite>.
- Practical reliability hinges on causal understanding and shift-aware representations; current architectures and training objectives do not ensure such robustness priors. <cite id="780aa691-6">Causal machine learning surveys outline open problems in leveraging causal structure to improve robustness, counterfactual reasoning, and policy learning under shift</cite>.

2) Statistical and optimization foundations
- Despite empirical success, there is limited principled unification of statistical approximation, estimation, and optimization in deep learning; this gap constrains generalization guarantees, optimization efficiency, and hyperparameter stability. <cite id="780aa691-2">A survey on the statistical theory of deep learning synthesizes approximation, training, and statistical perspectives, highlighting where theory-mismatch limits guarantees</cite> <cite id="780aa691-8">A 2024 statistics digest lists numerous open questions bridging ML and statistics, including sample complexity, adaptivity, and identifiability in deep models</cite>.
- Optimization theory for training remains incomplete, especially for non-convex/non-smooth objectives, high dimensions, and sequential decision-making; concrete open problems are being curated to focus progress. <cite id="780aa691-0">COLT 2023’s “Open Problems” program publishes unresolved questions for researchers</cite> <cite id="780aa691-5">An explicit open problem targets optimal gap-dependent convergence rates in stochastic decision-theoretic learning, reflecting unresolved optimality gaps</cite>.

3) Privacy-preserving learning, personalization, and scalability
- Federated and distributed learning expose new leakage channels (e.g., overparameterization enabling reconstruction) and raise open problems in personalized models, continual learning, and system-level privacy engineering. <cite id="c301f085-0">Surveys of federated learning identify open problems in algorithmic, system, and application layers with promising future research directions</cite> <cite id="c301f085-5">Surveys of online federated/transfer learning emphasize gaps as they evolve toward personalized, private learning</cite>.
- Machine unlearning—removing data influence at scale—must meet privacy, correctness, and performance constraints that are only partially addressed; this is especially acute for LLMs. <cite id="c301f085-1">A comprehensive federated unlearning survey catalogs methods and open challenges</cite> <cite id="c301f085-3">LLM-focused unlearning surveys emphasize privacy and copyright constraints specific to large models</cite>.
- Data efficiency remains a bottleneck relative to today’s compute-centric training: scaling laws imply cost–performance and sustainability trade-offs that current model architectures and training regimes do not systematically optimize. <cite id="c301f085-6">Practitioner surveys (2025) consistently report scalability and data-quality constraints as dominant operational limits</cite>.
- Infrastructure bottlenecks (training time, energy, reproducibility) interact with evaluation; the ML community is starting to address sustainability and process-level concerns. <cite id="046daccc-0">A position piece argues the current AI conference model is unsustainable, signaling a need to redesign incentives and practices that affect reproducibility and fairness</cite>.

4) Evaluation, benchmarks, and LLM reasoning limits
- Benchmark saturation and brittleness motivate multidimensional evaluation: robustness to corruptions/shifts, adversarial stability, and mechanistic insight. <cite id="3ccdfaa7-7">The Corruption and Perturbation benchmark suite has become a de facto standard to quantify robustness, revealing persistent vulnerabilities</cite> <cite id="3ccdfaa7-3">Specialized OOD robustness evaluation frameworks highlight shortcomings of ID-only robustness benchmarks</cite>.
- LLM interpretability and mechanistic verification are emerging as first-class challenges; accepted workshop topics at ICML 2024/NeurIPS 2024 signal growing focus on internal mechanisms and auditability. <cite id="046daccc-1">Interpretability and benchmarking tracks at top venues reflect active research and community demand</cite>.
- There is a replication and “credibility gap”: practitioners report difficulty in reproducing results and integrating models into production, underscoring gaps in reporting, data leakage controls, and deployment-aware evaluations. <cite id="c301f085-6">2025 practitioner perspectives emphasize unexplained models, scalability, and data-quality issues as core barriers</cite> <cite id="046daccc-5">An XAI-focused analysis of recent ICML/NeurIPS/ICLR papers and practitioner surveys finds recurring issues limiting robust real-world use</cite>.

5) Fairness, transparency, and societal trust
- Bias and fairness research reveals that interventions often optimize metrics without addressing root causes (data generation, measurement bias, selection), limiting durability and external validity. <cite id="780aa691-1">A fairness survey (2025) concludes that focusing on fairness outcomes while overlooking underlying causes hampers progress</cite>.
- Auditability and explainability need principled, domain-grounded methods that can handle multimodal evidence, uncertainty quantification, and policy-relevant harms. <cite id="046daccc-5">Work surveying recent ML work with practitioners identifies issues (e.g., opacity, reliability) that prevent safe deployment</cite>.
- Large models are not silver bullets for research and governance: many established fields still require rigorous, human-in-the-loop curation and methods that are not reducible to prompt-tuning or retrieval. <cite id="046daccc-7">An LLM perspective (May 2025) catalogs 14+ research areas where new research is required because LLMs cannot directly close existing gaps</cite>.
- Public trust barriers include transparency about data/provenance, documentation that supports independent verification, and accountable redress mechanisms. <cite id="c301f085-2">Surveys emphasize data quality problems and unexplained decision systems as societal trust impediments</cite>.

6) Multimodal, graph, and agentic systems
- Multimodal learning benefits from shared representations but still lacks foundations to ensure robust cross-signal invariances and disentanglement under realistic shifts and adversarial edits. <cite id="046daccc-8">An authoritative overview of multimodal machine learning highlights the need for new foundations and theory</cite>.
- Graph-reinforcement and relational tasks confront scalability, stability, and causal inference across dynamic graphs; open problems include scalable inference and robust planning. <cite id="046daccc-6">Future directions in graph ML at ICML 2024 reflect unresolved questions in scalable algorithms and theory</cite>.
- Agentic systems (planning/acting with tools, memory) need reliable perception–action loops, principled abstractions, and robust long-horizon control, not just task-specific finetuning. <cite id="046daccc-1">Mechanistic interpretability and benchmarks programs acknowledge the need to understand and validate internal mechanisms in complex agentic models</cite>.

7) Governance, sustainability, and reproducibility redesign
- Scientific publishing and review practices may no longer fit fast-evolving ML: open problems span reproducibility, novelty assessment, and incentivizing safe-by-default research. <cite id="046daccc-0">A 2025 position argues NeurIPS-style processes are unsustainable and calls for systemic reforms affecting reliability and fairness</cite>.
- Operationalizing responsible ML requires governance toolkits: privacy-preserving analytics, audit pathways, and human-AI oversight that can be embedded in production ML pipelines. <cite id="c301f085-0">Federated learning surveys point to algorithmic, system, and application-level questions essential for responsible deployment</cite> <cite id="c301f085-1">Unlearning-focused work emphasizes correct-by-design removal and privacy in operational settings</cite>.
- The 2023–2025 practitioner feedback reinforces urgency: data quality, model explainability, and the cost/scale of training are real-world bottlenecks that theoretical advances must address. <cite id="c301f085-6">2025 blog synthesis of ML challenges lists scalability, data quality, and unexplained models as persistent obstacles</cite> <cite id="c301f085-8">The 2023 Kaggle survey highlights community-observed issues that mirror these constraints</cite>.

Priority roadmap (5–10 years)
- Build shift-aware statistical theories and learning objectives that unify approximation, uncertainty, and robustness, with benchmarks bridging synthetic and natural shifts. <cite id="780aa691-2">A statistical-theory survey outlines integration points for approximation and training</cite> <cite id="3ccdfaa7-4">ImageNet-R supplies real-world shift factors for validation</cite>.
- Create principled, privacy-compliant personalization/unlearning stacks for distributed and federated settings, with formal audits and guarantees. <cite id="c301f085-1">Federated unlearning surveys catalog techniques and gaps</cite> <cite id="c301f085-0">Open problems in federated learning span algorithmic and system layers</cite>.
- Advance mechanistic interpretability and verification for complex models to support safety cases, governance, and scientific credibility. <cite id="046daccc-1">Interpretability workshops and benchmark tracks reflect current focus and demand</cite>.
- Standardize evaluation landscapes—ID/OOD, adversarial/natural, multimodal—to compare methods and reward robust progress. <cite id="3ccdfaa7-3">Benchmarks that target OOD adversarial robustness complement in-distribution suites</cite>.
- Embed fairness and accountability into model lifecycle (data, model, deployment), moving from outcome fixes to causal diagnostics and interventions. <cite id="780aa691-1">A fairness survey argues root-cause interventions are missing</cite>.
- Operationalize sustainability and reproducibility: scalable training with tighter compute/energy envelopes and reporting standards that support independent validation. <cite id="c301f085-6">Practitioner perspectives (2025) identify scalability and unexplained models as core constraints</cite> <cite id="046daccc-0">Calls for systemic changes to the conference/review model to improve reliability</cite>.

Takeaway
Open challenges converge at the intersection of robustness-to-shift and benchmarking, theory–practice gaps in optimization/statistics, privacy-preserving personalization at scale, evaluation and interpretability that can underpin safety and governance, and the need to redesign research and deployment practices for credibility and sustainability. Progress will likely come from integrated methods (statistical/causal modeling + optimization), privacy-first and deployment-aware systems, comprehensive OOD/adversarial benchmarks, and governance toolkits that move from heuristics toward principled guarantees. <cite id="3ccdfaa7-2">A critical analysis underscores that evaluating OOD robustness should move beyond single-metric success</cite> <cite id="780aa691-5">Open-problem statements on optimal rates reflect how theoretical advances can anchor engineering practice</cite> <cite id="046daccc-1">Interpretability/benchmarking initiatives reflect growing demand for explainability and reliable evaluation</cite>

without_term.text: What are the most important open challenges in distributed machine learning?
without_term.answer:
Below are the most salient open challenges in distributed machine learning, organized by theme and supported by recent surveys and focused studies.

1) System/algorithmic scaling and correctness under asynchrony
- Async vs. sync trade-offs remain unsettled: asynchronous SGD (ASGD) can improve utilization and throughput but is sensitive to communication delays and nonuniform update speeds, making wall‑clock speedups unreliable without careful modeling or compensation mechanisms <cite id="0c034b05-3">Asynchronous SGD methods can improve training speed, but are sensitive to delays due to both communication and differences in local iteration speeds</cite> <cite id="0c034b05-9">Virtual-iterate analysis shows ASGD can beat minibatch SGD under convex/non-convex regimes, but results hinge on delay and variance control</cite>. 
- Decentralized and asynchronous communication are increasingly used to reduce network bottlenecks, yet fundamental limits and counterexamples for decentralized async SGD under nonconvexity are still being explored <cite id="0c034b05-5">Decentralized and asynchronous communications are two popular techniques to speedup communication complexity, with emerging theory for decentralized async SGD</cite> <cite id="0c034b05-8">A refined model of ADSGD under bounded assumptions for practical distributed training is introduced, highlighting remaining gaps under non-convexity</cite>. 
- Surveys emphasize that most production stacks are either synchronous or centralized asynchronous, pointing to an unmet need for robust general-purpose asynchronous frameworks that handle stragglers, failures, and partial topologies <cite id="0c034b05-2">Most commonly used distributed machine learning systems are either synchronous or centralized asynchronous, leaving decentralized and robustly asynchronous regimes underexplored</cite> <cite id="ec84d619-1">Survey: DML architectural designs and optimization strategies reveal unresolved tensions between scalability and correctness guarantees in practice</cite>.

2) Communication efficiency and aggregation under bandwidth/latency constraints
- Communication is the dominant bottleneck at scale, motivating compression, sparsification, and quantization; but accuracy/robustness trade-offs, error feedback, and straggler-aware policies remain active research areas <cite id="bfbc8245-0">A 2018–2023 survey synthesizes algorithmic and system technologies, underscoring persistent open problems in reducing communication overhead at scale</cite> <cite id="bfbc8245-2">Surveys cover collective operations, gradient compression, and computation-communication overlaps, highlighting theory-practice gaps</cite>. 
- Federated settings face an open challenge in securely and efficiently aggregating updates with differential privacy: defending against DP-secure aggregation attacks, minimizing added noise and bandwidth while preserving privacy, and integrating TEE-backed or cryptographic aggregation without sacrificing throughput <cite id="5a96e683-0">Defense mechanisms are categorized into pre-/in-/post-aggregation; the taxonomy highlights open problems in end-to-end privacy-preserving aggregation</cite> <cite id="5a96e683-3">A survey of over 200 papers on attacks and defenses in DP FL identifies unresolved issues in robust aggregation under privacy constraints</cite>. 
- Graph workloads expose two core tensions: massive feature/data movement vs. preserving accuracy and workload balance, with open problems in pushing materialization and synchronization to the network plane while avoiding staleness-driven accuracy loss <cite id="bfbc8245-5">Key challenges include massive feature communication, accuracy loss from partitioning and staleness, and uneven workload, with open techniques for moving data/metadata over RDMA/RPC</cite>.

3) Data and model heterogeneity, compute heterogeneity, and personalization
- Device/network heterogeneity (non-IID data, uneven compute/memory) undermines statistical and computational efficiency; surveys repeatedly flag heterogeneity as a core bottleneck alongside communication overheads <cite id="ec84d619-2">Heterogeneity is a core challenge in FL, compounding computation overhead and communication bottlenecks</cite> <cite id="5a96e683-4">Poisoning/backdoor and GAN-based threats are exacerbated under heterogeneous conditions, demanding adaptive defenses</cite>. 
- Architecture heterogeneity raises unresolved questions in aggregation and distillation: how to combine models with different depths/widths or even modalities without bespoke plumbing or accuracy regressions <cite id="5a96e683-6">Model heterogeneity remains an open challenge, with no standard approach for aggregating differently structured models</cite>. 
- Personalization on a global budget remains an open problem: how to allocate global rounds/communication for shared concepts while encoding per-user adaptation with limited extra bandwidth, and how to quantify fairness/robustness trade-offs <cite id="ec84d619-2">Communication and computation costs of personalization must be jointly optimized with accuracy and fairness</cite> <cite id="ec84d619-4">Edge constraints amplify the need for personalization with privacy, energy, and failure considerations</cite>.

4) Privacy, security, and robustness under adversaries
- Poisoning/backdoors and inference-time threats persist across FL deployments; surveys show attacks and defenses dominate the space, with TEEs and cryptographic protocols still suffering from practicality, usability, and performance gaps <cite id="5a96e683-4">Backdoor and GAN-based attacks are among the major threats requiring stronger defenses</cite> <cite id="5a96e683-0">Security strategies span pre-, in-, and post-aggregation, revealing open problems in composable defenses that scale to real deployments</cite>. 
- Comprehensive surveys of DP/secure aggregation stress incomplete tooling: robust DP aggregation at low SNR, secure aggregation under realistic adversary budgets, and compatibility with modern architectures remain unresolved, especially in decentralized settings <cite id="5a96e683-3">Over 200 works reviewed; gaps remain in practical DP aggregation robustness and end-to-end security at scale</cite> <cite id="5a96e683-8">Decentralized FL introduces a broader threat model; defense mechanisms must adapt to gossip-like topologies and resource constraints</cite>.

5) Graph and distributed graph learning at web scale
- Moving features/data to the network versus synchronizing at the cores is unresolved. Surveys pinpoint accuracy loss from staleness and misaligned partitions, plus communication dominated by feature/label movement rather than parameter bytes <cite id="bfbc8245-5">Accuracy loss and workload imbalance are tied to how features and topology metadata must cross wide-area networks, revealing open system designs</cite>. 
- Edge vs. cluster hybrid scenarios raise durability and latency questions: how to shard graphs across edge and cloud tiers with conflict-free updates, bounded staleness SLAs, and cost-effective replication under intermittent connectivity <cite id="ec84d619-4">Resource, energy, communication overheads, and failure tolerance are intertwined challenges for distributed ML on edge</cite>.

6) Large language models and overparameterized models
- LLM training exposes unique distributed bottlenecks: token I/O and KV-cache sharding dominate communication, expert/parameter group activation transfer is a costly inter-node channel, and MoE methods face load imbalance and routing staleness; surveys emphasize comprehensive coverage from architecture to systems but identify open problems in expert communication and memory/IO overlap <cite id="bfbc8245-1">A comprehensive LLM DML overview indicates architecture/system co-design gaps and highlights unresolved training bottlenecks</cite> <cite id="0c034b05-5">Async techniques are studied to reduce communication complexity, but practical integration into LLM pipelines with KV-cache and activation transfer remains challenging</cite>. 
- As systems scale to multi-tenant and multi-cluster configurations, robustness to stragglers, fault tolerance for long-running optimizer states, and portability across heterogeneous accelerators remain open systems challenges <cite id="ec84d619-1">Architectural surveys underscore that scaling training/infrastructure and deployment paradigms expose unresolved efficiency and reliability questions</cite>.

7) End-to-end robustness and decentralized/fault-tolerant training
- Real-world deployments face intermittent connectivity, node failures, and partial graphs; ensuring convergence and utility under dynamic quorums, byzantine faults, and partial topology synchronization is still an open systems/algorithmic puzzle <cite id="0c034b05-8">ADSGD under non-convexity with practical assumptions shows progress, but broader robustness under failures and partial graphs remains open</cite> <cite id="5a96e683-8">Decentralized FL surveys catalog threats specific to gossip and peer-to-peer networks, with correspondingly novel and incomplete defenses</cite>. 
- Surveys on edge and federated learning repeatedly surface unresolved combinations of resource, energy, communication, privacy, and failure constraints that demand principled scheduling, checkpointing, and rollback strategies tailored to AI workloads <cite id="ec84d619-4">Resource limits, energy efficiency, and failure tolerance are central open challenges on edge; current techniques underperform in combined settings</cite>.

8) Evaluation, benchmarks, and reproducibility
- There is a mismatch between reported system speedups and production performance: surveys call out heterogeneity and communication bottlenecks that invalidate simple A/B metrics, yet standardized leaderboards that jointly measure wall‑time, carbon/energy, communication bytes, accuracy, and robustness remain sparse <cite id="ec84d619-1">Surveys argue architectural trade-offs require holistic evaluation, yet commonly cited benchmarks often miss multi-dimensional metrics</cite> <cite id="ec84d619-4">Edge-oriented surveys stress energy/resource overheads and failure scenarios rarely included in reproducible benchmarks</cite>. 
- Theory-to-practice gaps persist for asynchronous and communication-limited regimes: open problems remain in reproducible convergence/accuracy under realistic delay distributions, straggler models, and decentralized topologies, motivating new controlled evaluation protocols <cite id="0c034b05-3">ASGD sensitivity to delays motivates benchmarking under realistic network conditions</cite> <cite id="bfbc8245-0">Communication-efficient surveys emphasize the need for rigorous head-to-head studies with end-to-end accuracy/wall-clock trade-offs</cite>.

Cross-cutting takeaways
- Unifying principles: The dominant open frontier is reducing communication while preserving accuracy and timeliness across heterogeneous, faulty, and privacy-constrained networks—without breaking correctness or user utility <cite id="ec84d619-1">State-of-the-art DML architectures hinge on bridging communication/computation bottlenecks, but holistic designs remain elusive</cite> <cite id="bfbc8245-0">Communication-optimization surveys show active algorithmic/system research yet highlight persistent open problems</cite>. 
- Research directions: Decoupling model/data movement from parameter synchronization; certifiable defenses for DP/secure aggregation; decentralized/asynchronous algorithms resilient to nonconvexity and failures; personalization/fairness under tight budgets; comprehensive LLM-scale sharding and scheduling; and benchmarks that report multidimensional outcomes across networks, energy, and robustness <cite id="0c034b05-5">Async/ decentralized communications reduce communication complexity but require careful design to maintain accuracy</cite> <cite id="5a96e683-0">Security strategies span aggregation steps, implying integrated, end-to-end solutions are needed</cite> <cite id="bfbc8245-5">Distributed GNN surveys pinpoint feature/data transfer limits, guiding where to seek breakthroughs</cite>.
