questions.original_query: What strategies are used to improve robustness and safety of quadrotor UAVs in extreme weather conditions?

query.text: What strategies are used to improve robustness and safety of quadrotor UAVs in extreme weather conditions?
query.answer:
Below are evidence-backed strategies to improve the robustness and safety of quadrotor UAVs in extreme weather, organized by problem domain, control/estimation techniques, sensing/navigation, mechanical/icing protection, gust prediction and load alleviation, and operational/safety procedures.

1) Model, disturbances, and failure-aware control/estimation
- Robust, disturbance-tolerant, and fault-tolerant control frameworks explicitly target time-varying wind, gusts, payload changes, and actuator faults to maintain tracking and stability margins in high winds and turbulence. <cite id="104e61f4-2">A composite disturbance-tolerant control framework for quadrotors is presented to enhance robustness under external disturbances</cite>. <cite id="104e61f4-3">Wind disturbances and payload variations motivate multi-stage control strategies for trajectory tracking</cite>. <cite id="104e61f4-4">Fixed-time control methods improve quadrotor trajectory tracking under time-varying wind disturbances by guaranteeing convergence within a finite and a priori bounded time</cite>. 
- Disturbance observers integrated with model predictive or sliding-mode controllers provide online disturbance estimation and feedforward to counter gusts and parameter drift. <cite id="ae1862ff-6">A nonlinear model predictive position controller that uses a disturbance observer adapts to changing weather conditions and landmark drift</cite>. <cite id="d912b763-1">A frequency-based nonlinear disturbance observer estimates wind gusts as input disturbances to quadrotors</cite>. <cite id="d912b763-2">A high-gain disturbance observer augments observer-based adaptive neural control to handle wind gusts and uncertainties</cite>. <cite id="d912b763-3">Predictive sliding mode control is proposed to track trajectories subject to wind gusts and uncertainties</cite>. 
- Wind-adaptive perception–planning systems adjust control authority and trajectories based on estimated wind fields, reducing risk of over-reaching in gusty conditions. <cite id="104e61f4-0">A comprehensive review details exogenous atmospheric disturbances (wind, precipitation) affecting UAV operations</cite>. <cite id="104e61f4-1">WESPR integrates geometric perception and local weather data to estimate wind fields and adjust control strategies</cite>. <cite id="104e61f4-7">A ground-based LiDAR approach predicts wind gusts to enable wind-aware landing and disturbance mitigation</cite>. <cite id="d912b763-5">Lidar-based wind field estimation fits linear, free-form models of vertical wind speed to inform control</cite>. <cite id="d912b763-8">Lidar-derived vertical wind estimates enable feedforward gust load alleviation control</cite>. <cite id="d912b763-7">NASA’s CLASP toolchain simulates gust/turbulence encounters for UAM and VTOL concepts to design robust responses</cite>.

2) Sensing, perception, and navigation in precipitation, fog, and GNSS-degraded conditions
- Multi-sensor fusion with uncertainty quantification increases perception robustness during rain/snow/fog and improves safety margins without excessive conservatism. <cite id="ae1862ff-0">Multi-sensor fusion for robust perception in rain, fog, and snow can improve detection accuracy (e.g., up to 7.2% gains in adverse conditions for an Edge AI model)</cite>. <cite id="ae1862ff-1">An uncertainty-aware multi-modal fusion framework integrates LiDAR and RGB under heavy snow and dense fog</cite>. <cite id="ae1862ff-8">A systematic survey assesses weather-induced influences on sensors and surveys solutions for adverse conditions</cite>. 
- For navigation under precipitation and high winds, resilient fusion of GNSS, visual odometry, inertial sensors, and augmentation mitigates drops and noise. <cite id="ae1862ff-3">A robust UAV navigation system fuses GPS, visual odometry, inertial measurements, and/or magnetic data with Kalman filtering for GPS-degraded/denied environments</cite>. <cite id="ae1862ff-4">Uncertainty-aware fusion and adaptive receding-horizon planning improve localization and safety margins, with robustness during GNSS dropouts and higher average speed</cite>. <cite id="ae1862ff-9">GNSS augmentation and carrier-phase methods mitigate atmospheric/ionospheric errors and improve integrity and continuity in degraded conditions</cite>. <cite id="ae1862ff-6">Disturbance-observer-aware MPC improves position control when weather degrades GNSS and vision cues</cite>. 
- Precipitation can degrade vision and LiDAR via droplet scattering and snow clumping; designing perception pipelines to detect and quantify performance degradation enables switching to robust sensors or planning modes. <cite id="ae1862ff-5">UAV-AWID quantifies vision-based detection performance degradation under adverse weather and image distortions</cite>. <cite id="ae1862ff-8">A broad survey details sensor degradation mechanisms and countermeasures for inclement weather</cite>.

3) Icing, aerodynamics, and thermal/mechanical protection
- Quantifying icing effects on propulsion and control is essential to set safe operating envelopes and power reserves. <cite id="60dcf838-0">Icing degrades aerodynamic performance and disrupts airflow over lifting surfaces, adversely affecting UAV control</cite>. <cite id="60dcf838-1">For rotorcraft, ice accumulation reduces lift and thrust, increases drag and torque, degrading performance and risking overload</cite>. <cite id="60dcf838-7">Experimental icing tests show near-instantaneous thrust loss as soon as conditions are encountered; thrust decreased by more than 10% in under a minute during climate wind-tunnel tests</cite>. <cite id="60dcf838-6">Loss of thrust is observed almost immediately after icing onset in propeller tests</cite>. <cite id="60dcf838-9">An experimental quadcopter study (25 kg class) evaluates icing impacts and power/thermal loads</cite>. 
- Hardware-level anti/de-icing strategies should be considered in addition to environmental avoidance. <cite id="60dcf838-2">Active anti/de-icing (AAD) and passive protection are core building blocks of aircraft icing protection systems, with design strategies for power/weight trade-offs</cite>. <cite id="60dcf838-5">HeatCoat anti-icing technology demonstrated in-flight anti-icing and de-icing in wind-tunnel tests for UAVs</cite>. <cite id="60dcf838-8">Electrothermal anti-icing/de-icing experiments on UAVs quantify heat loads and inform protection system design</cite>. <cite id="60dcf838-4">UAV icing protection programs emphasize anti-icing design test of aero-engine inlets and integration methods for small vehicles</cite>. 
- On the vehicle level, icing-aware safety constraints include monitoring rotor torque/thrust margins, limiting sustained high-power operation in known icing regions, and enabling emergency climb-out or diversion to warmer air. <cite id="60dcf838-1">Icing’s torque increase and thrust loss raise risk of overloading rotors and exceeding power margins</cite>. <cite id="60dcf838-7">Ice accretion can cause abrupt power consumption increases that threaten mission safety</cite>. 
- For snow/ice environments, increase redundancy and sealing on critical electronics, and use temperature/relative humidity sensors to proactively engage de-icing and heating if needed. <cite id="104e61f4-0">Reviews enumerate precipitation mechanisms and environmental loads that degrade standard UAV operation</cite>. <cite id="60dcf838-8">UAV icing lab work documents control surface and actuator heat-load data to support protective system scheduling</cite>.

4) Gust prediction, airwake avoidance, and load alleviation
- Exogenous wind reviews motivate strategies that pre-emptively adjust speed, altitude, and heading, and that allocate larger control authority buffers during gusty or snowy/icy conditions. <cite id="104e61f4-0">Comprehensive analyses link wind characteristics to UAV controllability and energy margins</cite>. <cite id="104e61f4-7">Ground LiDAR can predict landing-site gusts to trigger evasive maneuvers and reduce collision risk</cite>. <cite id="d912b763-5">Lidar-based vertical wind estimation supports feedforward control to reduce gust-induced loads</cite>. <cite id="d912b763-8">Two-degree-of-freedom control using lidar-based vertical wind enables gust load alleviation</cite>. 
- On the flight deck: weather-aware path planning reduces exposure to cumulonimbus updrafts and shear, and uses predictive controllers that anticipate gust-induced accelerations. <cite id="104e61f4-1">Wind-adaptive perception–planning reduces control aggressiveness and adjusts setpoints using local weather data</cite>. <cite id="104e61f4-4">Fixed-time controllers limit transient excursions under wind, constraining peak accelerations during gusts</cite>. 
- VTOL/UAM concepts use simulation and aeroservoelastic models to design stall/spin-resistant responses and VTOL-glide fallback modes. <cite id="d912b763-7">NASA CLASP simulates gust/turbulence time-domain responses for VTOL/UAM concepts to derive robust control laws and safe envelopes</cite>. <cite id="d912b763-0">Ground LiDAR-based gust prediction is applied to quadrotors to improve resilience</cite>.

5) Emergency and safety procedures for extreme conditions
- Fail-safe behaviors: monitor margins and trigger Return-Home/Force-Land if winds exceed safe limits; reduce altitude to minimize gust sensitivity; and avoid climbing through cumulonimbus towers. <cite id="ae1862ff-4">Adaptive planning with uncertainty-aware fusion improved safety margins and maintained higher average speeds during GNSS dropouts, illustrating robust fail-safe operations</cite>. <cite id="ae1862ff-6">Disturbance-observer MPC under GNSS-degraded and windy conditions shows how adaptive controllers maintain performance within safety envelopes</cite>. 
- Tethered operations and power constraints: for persistent adverse weather, tethered UAVs can extend loiter time and reduce need for aggressive power reserves. <cite id="104e61f4-8">Tethered UAVs can leverage ground-based sensing and power to enhance resilience in wind and gust environments</cite>. 
- Icing safety: enforce icing-avoidance routes; maintain power margins and heating if required; and pre-program emergency descent and thermal shedding (e.g., reduce rotor rpm with adequate descent) if protection system failure occurs. <cite id="60dcf838-1">Ice-induced torque and thrust changes necessitate conservative power allocation and airspeed management</cite>. <cite id="60dcf838-7">Abnormal power/thermal signatures under icing should trigger automated recovery behaviors</cite>. 
- Operator-in-the-loop constraints: use ground LIDAR to forecast local gusts, prioritize safe landing sites, and coordinate emergency landings outside severe wind fields. <cite id="d912b763-0">Ground LiDAR gust prediction at the landing site improves quadrotor resilience against sudden wind changes</cite>. <cite id="104e61f4-7">A lightweight pipeline predicts gusts to adjust controller gains and path planning at the last minute</cite>.

6) Environmental mitigation and vehicle hardening for precipitation and cold
- Reduce supercooled droplet exposure via heating/anti-icing of leading edges and power management; use sealed connectors and drains; schedule pre-flight icing checkouts in cloud/rain forecasts. <cite id="60dcf838-2">Active anti-icing and passive strategies form the basis of protection system construction, guiding where to allocate mass/power for reliable de-icing</cite>. <cite id="60dcf838-5">Electro-thermal anti-icing demonstrated in UAV wind-tunnel tests provides in-flight protection with measurable performance benefits</cite>. 
- Perception hardening: use radar fusion with camera/LiDAR to reduce rain/snow-induced occlusion errors. <cite id="ae1862ff-0">Radar and camera fusion improves detection accuracy in fog/rain/snow, supporting safe planning under visibility loss</cite>. <cite id="ae1862ff-1">Heavy snow and dense fog degrade RGB-only perception, motivating multi-modal fusion and uncertainty management</cite>. 
- GNSS resilience in precipitation-induced ionospheric scintillation and multipath: use carrier-phase augmentation and cross-validated solutions; if lost, fall back to inertial/visual fusion with integrity monitors. <cite id="ae1862ff-9">Advances in adverse weather GNSS cover atmospheric and ionospheric errors; carrier-phase augmentation and integrity design reduce dropout risks</cite>. <cite id="ae1862ff-3">Robust GPS/VO/IMU fusion provides continuous relative navigation during GNSS outages</cite>. 
- Thermal management: ensure battery insulation/canopy ventilation, and use pre-flight warm-up cycles or inductive heating for cold climates to preserve discharge capability. <cite id="60dcf838-9">Experimental icing work in a 25 kg quadcopter includes energy/heat balance aspects relevant to battery and actuator thermal management</cite>. <cite id="60dcf838-1">Increased drag and torque from ice drive higher energy consumption, demanding thermal-aware power strategies</cite>.

7) Overall architecture and autonomy that integrate weather-awareness
- Sense-estimate-plan-control stacks should fuse meteorological sensors with physics models and uncertainty-aware optimization. <cite id="104e61f4-1">A lightweight pipeline jointly estimates wind fields and adapts control/plan to maintain safety margins</cite>. <cite id="ae1862ff-4">Uncertainty-aware multi-sensor fusion with adaptive receding-horizon planning yields improved localization and safety margins during GNSS dropouts</cite>. <cite id="ae1862ff-0">Multi-sensor fusion improves detection accuracy by up to 7.2% under adverse conditions, directly improving perception reliability</cite>. 
- Redundancy and graceful degradation: prioritize safe modes when sensor authority collapses (e.g., visual-only to inertial fusion), and constrain trajectory curvature/speed proportional to wind and icing risk. <cite id="ae1862ff-3">MAV navigation systems that fuse GPS/VO/IMU/magnetic data offer graceful degradation under GPS loss</cite>. <cite id="104e61f4-4">Fixed-time controllers bound tracking errors in wind, providing graceful performance degradation with bounded risk</cite>. 
- Icing and weather avoidance constraints: integrate icing and wind risk maps into trajectory planning; schedule vertical separation from severe weather and limit crosswind components. <cite id="60dcf838-2">Icing protection system construction strategies provide guidance for embedding weather-avoidance constraints into autonomy</cite>. <cite id="104e61f4-0">Wind disturbance analyses inform planning constraints (e.g., speed limits, no-fly zones within gust cores)</cite>. 
- Ground-truthed weather: use ground LIDAR/radar to provide local gust forecasts and airwake maps to the onboard autonomy, enabling risk-aware path planning and landing site selection. <cite id="d912b763-0">Ground-based LiDAR gust prediction enhances quadrotor landing safety and mitigates wind disturbances</cite>. <cite id="d912b763-5">Lidar-derived vertical wind fields can be used online for feedforward load alleviation</cite>.

Practical checklist for operations in extreme weather
- Pre-mission: avoid forecasted severe convective cores; if unavoidable, increase margin of safety (power reserve, glide/descent reserves), inspect for sealing/anti-icing readiness, and schedule pre-takeoff de-icing. <cite id="60dcf838-7">Icing can cause abrupt power consumption increases, requiring pre-mission protective measures</cite>. <cite id="60dcf838-2">Active/ passive protection system selection should be aligned with mission icing risk</cite>. 
- Climb and cruise: maintain an icing-avoidance ceiling, use climb-out to warmer air if conditions worsen; manage airspeed to keep stall margin and limit crosswind exposure. <cite id="60dcf838-1">Icing elevates torque and reduces thrust and lift, necessitating conservative airspeed and power management</cite>. <cite id="60dcf838-0">Airflow disruption from ice degrades controllability</cite>. 
- Turbulence: use predictive/sliding-mode controllers plus disturbance observers to anticipate gusts; if turbulence persists, reduce airspeed and climb to smooth wind layers. <cite id="d912b763-3">Predictive sliding mode control improves quadrotor tracking under wind gusts</cite>. <cite id="d912b763-2">High-gain disturbance observers augment control under gusts</cite>. <cite id="ae1862ff-6">Disturbance-observer MPC maintains performance under wind and degraded GNSS</cite>. 
- Perception in precipitation: enable radar fusion; add GNSS augmentation; if GNSS drops, trigger fused VO/IMU navigation with reduced plan update rate; land safely if dropout persists. <cite id="ae1862ff-4">Adaptive, uncertainty-aware fusion and planning improved safety margins during GNSS outages</cite>. <cite id="ae1862ff-0">Radar fusion boosts detection reliability in rain/fog/snow</cite>. 
- Icing in-flight: if sensors detect ice forming, engage de-icing; if protection fails, execute icing contingency (autorotation-like descent using maximum endurance, immediate diversion to unprepared site supported by ground team). <cite id="60dcf838-5">UAV electrothermal anti-icing demonstrated effective in-flight de-icing</cite>. <cite id="60dcf838-7">Rapid thrust loss indicates ice accretion; immediate action is required</cite>. 
- Landing: use ground LiDAR to verify touchdown area and winds at the final approach; prefer gust-sheltered orientations; increase flare altitude and reduce power late if a strong gust is predicted. <cite id="d912b763-0">Ground LiDAR gust prediction supports wind-aware landing and disturbance mitigation at the landing site</cite>. <cite id="104e61f4-1">Wind-aware perception and control strategies adjust landing approach</cite>.

Summary
- To improve robustness and safety in extreme weather, combine weather-informed autonomy that fuses exogenous wind/precipitation information with robust controllers that are resilient to time-varying disturbances; add icing-aware constraints and protective systems; harden perception and GNSS with multi-sensor fusion and augmentation; and implement fail-safe procedures and emergency behaviors triggered by real-time and ground-truthed weather measurements. <cite id="104e61f4-0">Exogenous disturbance analysis guides design choices for wind/precipitation resilience</cite>. <cite id="104e61f4-1">Wind-adaptive perception–planning adjusts control/plan based on wind field estimates</cite>. <cite id="ae1862ff-0">Multi-sensor fusion improves adverse-weather perception accuracy</cite>. <cite id="ae1862ff-4">Uncertainty-aware fusion and adaptive planning yield improved safety margins during GNSS dropouts</cite>. <cite id="d912b763-5">Lidar-based gust estimation enables feedforward alleviation and improves control authority</cite>. <cite id="60dcf838-1">Icing increases drag/torque while reducing thrust, requiring anti-icing/de-icing design and conservative envelopes</cite>. <cite id="60dcf838-7">Icing leads to rapid thrust loss and power spikes, demanding robust emergency procedures</cite>. <cite id="d912b763-0">Ground LiDAR gust prediction directly enhances quadrotor resilience via site-aware decision-making</cite>. Together, these strategies reduce failure probability and enable safe recovery when adverse weather conditions exceed nominal operating envelopes.

fully_underspecified.text: What strategies are used to improve robustness and safety in extreme weather conditions?
fully_underspecified.answer:
# Framing: What "robustness and safety" mean under extreme weather
Improving robustness and safety involves moving beyond hazard-focused "control" to a risk-based, layered approach that combines prevention, protection, preparedness, and rapid response, while explicitly planning for uncertainty and cascading system failures. <cite id="4a585376-1">Extreme weather interacts with infrastructure and health systems, producing cascading impacts that require coordinated, risk-informed responses rather than single-damage-reduction fixes</cite>. <cite id="4a585376-0">Military and critical facilities illustrate the security and continuity stakes when infrastructure cannot cope with extremes</cite>. <cite id="4a585376-3">Practitioner tools such as FEMA's Resilience Analysis and Planning Tool (RAPT) operationalize multi-hazard exposure and risk mapping for planning and investment</cite>. <cite id="4a585376-4">Health system analyses indicate that floods, storms, heatwaves, cold spells, and wildfires strain services across the care continuum, underscoring the need for robust backstops</cite>.

# Cross-cutting Strategy: Early Warning Systems and Preparedness
Effective early warning reduces loss of life and economic damage when coupled with investable communication, response, and governance capacity. <cite id="1965b8ee-0">Early warning systems comprise risk knowledge, monitoring/warnings, warning dissemination/communication, and response capacity; strengthening any weak link increases impact</cite>. <cite id="1965b8ee-1">Independent analysis of the Global Commission on Adaptation shows that adding roughly a day's forecast lead time can reduce damage by about 30%</cite>. <cite id="1965b8ee-2">Evaluations report that with strong governance and inter-agency cooperation, early warning systems can cut disaster deaths by roughly 60%</cite>. <cite id="1965b8ee-9">Authoritative syntheses affirm that early warnings reduce loss of life, injuries, and economic losses when delivered with appropriate response protocols</cite>. <cite id="4af91acf-6">Digital twin and sensing advances now allow testing of infrastructure resilience and response strategies before events, optimizing operations and long-term mitigation</cite>. 

For operational preparedness, organizations should: <cite id="4a585376-9">complete risk assessments, ensure reliable and interoperable warning communications, raise public awareness, and pre-test coordination and sheltering/evacuation plans</cite>. <cite id="4a585376-2">Site-specific vulnerability assessments for exposure, severity, and response capability are foundational to prioritizing resilience investments</cite>, and <cite id="4a585376-3">community-level risk mapping guides where to deploy protective measures and emergency services</cite>.

# Hazard-Specific Strategies

## Flooding and Coastal Storm Surge
Resilience mixes structural, ecological, and operational tools tailored to local hydrology and floodplains. <cite id="4af91acf-0">Flood management research has evolved from "control" to "risk management," emphasizing upstream catchment measures, floodplain protection, and multi-objective planning</cite>. <cite id="4af91acf-1">Green infrastructure mitigates floods by slowing and storing stormwater, reducing runoff to drainage systems and waterbodies</cite>, and <cite id="4af91acf-3">urban reviews show that green infrastructure meaningfully contributes to urban flood resilience when integrated across watersheds and corridors</cite>. <cite id="22013ec5-8">Urban heat island mitigation strategies (e.g., greening, shading) complement flood adaptation by reducing peak loads on power during storm events</cite>. 

Economic and governance safeguards are essential. <cite id="4af91acf-9">Federal flood adaptation spending yields an average damage reduction of $2–$3 per dollar, indicating high cost-effectiveness across projects</cite>, and <cite id="4af91acf-7">economics work finds green infrastructure projects to be cost-effective, durable, and adaptable in flood-risk settings</cite>. Operational tools include: <cite id="4af91acf-6">model-based testing of response scenarios and infrastructure resilience to identify shutdown/surge management options and strengthening priorities</cite>, and <cite id="4af91acf-5">restoring and protecting floodplains under regulatory constraints to accommodate natural flows and reduce downstream damages</cite>. 

## Hurricanes, Severe Storms, and Wind Hazards
Buildings, lifelines, and communities harden via codes, materials, and correct installation, with targeted retrofits for existing stock. <cite id="d9be399e-0">Recent hurricane-driven code enhancements emphasize exterior envelopes, roof systems, and installation details that limit damage from wind and rain-driven failures</cite>. <cite id="d9be399e-1">Using higher-than-code-minimum, wind-rated products and following correct installation methods reduces damage during windstorms</cite>. <cite id="d9be399e-4">Newer engineering-based standards produce buildings that perform well structurally under hurricane loads</cite>, and for existing homes, <cite id="d9be399e-2">manuals outline wind-retrofit packages (e.g., roof anchorage, openings protection) that improve survivability and reduce repair costs</cite>. Portfolio-level retrofits show value: <cite id="d9be399e-5">even basic and intermediate retrofit packages can reduce damage and downtime in high-wind zones even if they do not address all structural failure modes</cite>. 

Community-level strategies include managed retreat, phased elevations, and flood-resilient urban design. <cite id="4af91acf-0">Risk-based planning prioritizes combinations of structural defenses, floodplain restoration, and non-structural measures (e.g., elevating critical infrastructure)</cite>, while <cite id="4a585376-8">resilient building credits encourage designs that resist reasonably expected hazards like flooding and high winds with minimal damage</cite>. For continuity of operations, <cite id="bc32e180-4">microgrids that can island and serve critical loads improve resilience of emergency response and communication nodes during outages</cite>.

## Extreme Heat
Urban-scale cooling and equity-focused planning reduce mortality and service strain. <cite id="22013ec5-0">Urban green–blue–grey infrastructure (parks, wetlands, engineered greening, reflective surfaces, water features) mitigates urban overheating</cite>. <cite id="22013ec5-1">Re-integrating vegetation reduces the urban heat island and provides cooling while delivering co-benefits such as air quality and stormwater management</cite>. Policy packages and operations matter: <cite id="22013ec5-2">combining multiple policies (cool roofs/roads, tree canopies, urban hydrology, and equitable access) strengthens resilience and ensures equitable adaptation</cite>, and <cite id="22013ec5-3">C40 guidance emphasizes simple, cost-effective technologies and strategies (e.g., reflective surfaces, shade structures, cooling centers) that cut heat-related impacts</cite>. At the service level, <cite id="4a585376-3">RAPT and GIS can target siting of cooling centers and identify populations with limited access during heatwaves</cite>. For energy resilience, <cite id="22013ec5-6">cool building technologies and urban heat mitigation reduce energy use and thermal stress, decreasing strain on power systems during peak loads</cite>. 

## Wildfire Perimeter Threats and Community Safety
A layered strategy combining landscape fuel management, ignition-resistance, evacuation, and sheltering is essential. Risk-based siting and treatment prioritize life-safety. <cite id="4a585376-2">Assessing exposure to wildfires and vulnerabilities at sites guides investments in fuel breaks, perimeter hardening, and emergency access</cite>. Fuel management reduces incident severity, while ignition-resistant building practices limit house-to-house spread. <cite id="1965b8ee-9">Operationalizing early warning with robust dissemination and response is critical: warnings save lives only when communities can receive, understand, and act</cite>, and <cite id="1965b8ee-1">extending warning lead times reduces damages; this logic applies to wildfire smoke (air quality forecasts) where early alerts enable sheltering and evacuation</cite>. For agencies, <cite id="4a585376-9">investing in reliable communications and interoperable systems for evacuation coordination and public awareness</cite> complements structural protections. 

## Energy Continuity and Critical Services
Microgrids, distributed energy resources (DERs), storage, and resilient design harden continuity during storms, heat, and floods. <cite id="bc32e180-1">Microgrids can mitigate extreme-weather-induced outages, though their cost-effectiveness depends on local generation mixes and avoided interruption value</cite>. <cite id="bc32e180-5">Resilience frameworks emphasize de-energization and DER coordination, targeted hardening, and restoration prioritization under natural hazards</cite>, and <cite id="bc32e180-4">operating microgrids to island and support critical nodes improves reliability during grid disturbances</cite>. System-level reviews show the need for metrics, redundancy, and real-time controls. <cite id="bc32e180-0">Recent reviews detail resilience metrics and enhancement strategies for power systems and microgrids under extreme events</cite>, while <cite id="bc32e180-7">state-level summaries synthesize policies to improve reliability and resilience as extreme weather threatens the grid</cite>.

# Governance, Equity, and Trade-offs
Resilience is not a one-off project; it requires iterative planning, investment, and governance. <cite id="4af91acf-0">Risk management stresses integrating upstream measures, floodplain protection, and adaptive management, shifting from purely structural "control" to systemic approaches</cite>, and <cite id="4a585376-3">RAPT's access to hazard and asset data supports participatory, data-driven planning</cite>. Investments deliver outsized benefits. <cite id="4af91acf-9">Flood adaptation spending reduces expected damages at ~$2–$3 saved per dollar</cite>, and <cite id="1965b8ee-1">a day's extra warning can cut damages by ~30%</cite>, underscoring the value of communications and forecast investments. Limits and failures matter. <cite id="1965b8ee-2">EWS may not reduce deaths by 60% unless governance, cooperation, and response capacity are adequate</cite>, and <cite id="d9be399e-1">code-compliant materials must be installed correctly to realize damage reductions</cite>. Wildfire risks are also sensitive to vegetation management timelines and ignition pathways. <cite id="1965b8ee-9">Effective EWS hinge on risk knowledge, monitoring, dissemination, and response; bottlenecks in any component undermine outcomes</cite>.

# A Practical Playbook

1) Measure and plan at multiple scales
- Use GIS and risk tools (e.g., RAPT) to inventory exposures, vulnerabilities, and critical assets. <cite id="4a585376-3">RAPT provides open access to hazard, exposure, and resilience indicators to guide planning</cite>. 
- Conduct hazard-vulnerability profiles for buildings, lifelines, and services to rank interventions. <cite id="4a585376-2">Methodical exposure/vulnerability assessments prioritize resiliency actions</cite>.

2) Invest in layered defenses and green/nature-based infrastructure
- For floods: preserve/restore floodplains, implement green stormwater infrastructure, and integrate urban greening and blue-grey features to reduce runoff and peak flows. <cite id="4af91acf-1">Green infrastructure slows and reduces stormwater runoff and protects floodplains</cite>; <cite id="4af91acf-3">urban reviews validate green infrastructure for flood resilience</cite>; <cite id="22013ec5-0">green–blue–grey measures mitigate urban overheating during wet extremes</cite>.
- For coastal hazards: elevate and protect critical infrastructure, enforce and locally adapt building codes, and consider managed retreat for high-risk assets. <cite id="d9be399e-0">Building code enhancements target wind-prone envelope systems</cite>; <cite id="d9be399e-1">wind-rated products with correct installation reduce storm damage</cite>.

3) Make the built environment more heat- and wind-robust
- Extreme heat: cool roofs/roads, expand tree canopy and urban hydrology, site cooling centers equitably, and design for thermal comfort; combine with microgrids to sustain operations during peaks. <cite id="22013ec5-1">Vegetation-based strategies mitigate heat islands</cite>; <cite id="22013ec5-2">policy mixes support equitable adaptation</cite>; <cite id="22013ec5-6">cool building technologies reduce energy use and indoor heat stress</cite>; <cite id="bc32e180-4">microgrids sustain critical loads during heat-driven outages</cite>.
- Wind hazards: pre-approve wind-rated materials, create construction checklists, and offer retrofit subsidies (roof anchorage, window protection, exterior wall bracing). <cite id="d9be399e-1">Higher-than-minimum, properly installed wind-rated products reduce storm damage</cite>; <cite id="d9be399e-2">wind retrofit guides provide actionable procedures for existing homes</cite>.

4) Build robust early warning and response systems
- Invest in forecast lead time (model resolution; river/road network assimilation), and closing the "last mile" of communication (SMS, sirens, social media, interoperable agencies). <cite id="1965b8ee-1">More lead time reduces damages; funding for warnings pays off</cite>; <cite id="1965b8ee-0">effective warnings require all four components</cite>; <cite id="1965b8ee-2">adequate governance doubles as multiplier on warning benefits</cite>.
- Pre-train, pre-stage, and digitally rehearse evacuations, sheltering, and surge staffing plans. <cite id="4a585376-9">Reliable communication, interoperability, and awareness are essential operational levers</cite>.

5) Secure energy supply and critical services
- For high-hazard locations, design for islanded microgrid operation, DER coordination, and staged restoration; harden transformers and intake structures for floods/snow. <cite id="bc32e180-4">Microgrids operate reliably and mitigate disturbances</cite>; <cite id="bc32e180-5">resilience frameworks prescribe targeted hardening and DER coordination</cite>; <cite id="bc32e180-9">state policy syntheses outline steps to improve reliability against extreme weather</cite>.

6) Manage trade-offs and equity
- Favor measures with demonstrated cost-effectiveness (e.g., flood adaptation; timely warnings) and design benefits that reduce inequities in exposure (cooling centers in heat-vulnerable neighborhoods; elevating first-floor utilities in floodplains). <cite id="4af91acf-9">Flood adaptations save ~$2–$3 per dollar in expected damages</cite>; <cite id="1965b8ee-1">forecast improvements yield ~30% damage reductions when actionable</cite>; <cite id="22013ec5-2">equity requires combining multiple cooling strategies and policies</cite>. 
- Accept limits: warnings only save when communication/response capacity is strong; building retrofits need correct installation and maintenance to perform. <cite id="1965b8ee-2">Warnings reduce deaths by ~60% only with adequate governance and cooperation</cite>; <cite id="d9be399e-1">materials and methods must be installed per wind-resilience guidance</cite>.

# Illustrative Outcomes to Date
- Flood adaptation investments in the U.S. have returned ~$2–$3 saved per dollar in expected damages across programs and places, supporting large-scale adoption of green and grey measures. <cite id="4af91acf-9">Spending for flood adaptations reduces expected damage by an average of $2 to $3 per dollar spent</cite>.
- Extended forecast lead times substantially reduce damages in water hazards; early warning system effectiveness in saving lives hinges on the quality of communication and response governance. <cite id="1965b8ee-1">Twenty-four hours of advance warning can reduce damage by 30 percent</cite>; <cite id="1965b8ee-2">EWS can decrease death tolls by 60% when governance and cooperation are adequate</cite>.
- Wind- and flood-resilient building codes, wind-rated products, and retrofits reduce structural damage and downtime, with codes especially influential for new construction and retrofits for existing stock. <cite id="d9be399e-0">Modern building codes focus on exterior envelope performance for hurricanes</cite>; <cite id="d9be399e-1">higher-than-code materials and proper installation reduce windstorm damage</cite>.
- Urban cooling strategies and microgrids reduce heat-related strain on health and energy systems and sustain emergency operations during peaks. <cite id="22013ec5-0">Urban green–blue–grey infrastructure mitigates overheating</cite>; <cite id="bc32e180-4">microgrids help mitigate grid disturbances with reliable operation</cite>.
- Digital planning tools (e.g., RAPT) and nature-based flood defenses are increasingly central to resilience portfolios for communities, enabling targeted interventions and continuous updating. <cite id="4a585376-3">RAPT provides accessible GIS mapping to support resilience decisions</cite>; <cite id="4af91acf-0">risk-based flood management expands the toolkit beyond control structures</cite>.

In sum, robustness and safety in extreme weather improve when jurisdictions adopt a layered, risk-based portfolio: upstream nature-based flood control and urban cooling, robust building codes and targeted retrofits, resilient energy architectures, high-quality early warning with reliable outreach, and adaptive planning governance that continuously updates investments to local hazards and equity goals. <cite id="4af91acf-0">The move from control to risk management under changing hazards is central</cite>, and <cite id="1965b8ee-2">the dividends of early warning and resilient systems are large when governance and communications are strong</cite>.

ambiguity_judge.evidence: The response directly answers the question with a detailed list of strategies and does not indicate any uncertainty, ask for clarification, or state assumptions about what “robustness and safety” or “extreme weather conditions” might mean.

without_scope.text: What strategies are used to improve robustness and safety of quadrotor UAVs?
without_scope.answer:
Below are evidence-backed strategies to improve robustness and safety of quadrotor UAVs, organized by function and cross-cutting safeguards. Where possible, we highlight concrete mechanisms, constraints, and evaluations.

Control and Estimation Strategies for Robustness
- Robust and fault-tolerant flight control: Composite and adaptive robust controllers (sliding mode, super-twisting, prescribed performance) explicitly handle matched/unmatched disturbances, parameter uncertainty, and actuator faults while enforcing safety constraints on attitude/position and control authority.<cite id="6705aeea-3">This paper presents a composite disturbance-tolerant control framework for quadrotor unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs), tailored to handle large uncertainties and faults without controller switching</cite><cite id="60ed0cef-0">This work addresses prescribed-time attitude tracking for quadrotors under unknown disturbances and actuator faults, showing robustness and boundedness guarantees</cite><cite id="60ed0cef-4">A super-twisting sliding-mode FTC design mitigates actuator faults via second-order sliding mode and observer-based estimation, yielding practical bounds on tracking error</cite><cite id="60ed0cef-5">A super-twisting observer is combined with FTC to retain reliability and safety under thrust-loss faults, illustrating observer-FTC co-design patterns</cite><cite id="60ed0cef-1">A nonlinear-observer-based sliding-mode FTC is validated in hardware-in-the-loop and recovers full control for motor faults up to 40% while maintaining tracking performance</cite>.
- Constraint-handling and performance certification: Prescribed performance and prescribed-time sliding-mode methods confine tracking error within user-specified bounds over a预定 time, providing safety margins against excursions due to faults or disturbances.<cite id="60ed0cef-0">Prescribed-time sliding-mode FTC guarantees attitude tracking within a fixed-time horizon despite unknown disturbances and faults</cite><cite id="60ed0cef-6">A uniform FTC handles a complete rotor failure without controller switching, improving fail-operational robustness</cite>.
- Active fault diagnosis integrated with control: Online fault estimators (e.g., higher-order sliding-mode or L1 adaptive estimators) detect and isolate actuator faults and thrust loss to trigger controller reconfiguration, maintaining stable flight envelopes under partial-loss scenarios.<cite id="60ed0cef-5">A super-twisting observer design for thrust-loss faults improves safety by accurately estimating and accommodating actuator degradations</cite><cite id="60ed0cef-8">L1 adaptive control has been used as an FTC baseline for quadrotors, enabling robust tracking with actuator faults and facilitating reconfiguration</cite><cite id="60ed0cef-1">A nonlinear observer-based sliding-mode FTC experimentally recovers control with up to 40% motor faults</cite>.

Planning and Perception-Aware Avoidance
- Perception-aware replanning under limited sensory/communication: RAPTOR provides robust, perception-aware trajectory replanning that fuses semantic perception and metric tracking of dynamic obstacles to ensure fast, safe flight despite sensing ambiguities and failures, explicitly allocating trust to perception and enforcing collision and boundary constraints.<cite id="4fd3d7be-7">RAPTOR frames robust replanning for quadrotors by combining perception and tracking, allocating perception trust while enforcing safety constraints to achieve fast and safe flight</cite><cite id="4fd3d7be-2">A vision-based planning system integrates dynamic obstacle tracking and prediction to yield efficient and reliable navigation in cluttered environments</cite>.
- Perception-agnostic operation in GNSS-challenged environments: Monocular/event-camera based obstacle avoidance enables safe navigation without stereo/LiDAR, reducing reliance on sensors that can saturate or fail; this improves robustness when GPS is limited or denied and supports safe setpoint generation and replanning margins from visual priors.<cite id="4fd3d7be-4">A monocular event-camera method achieves static-obstacle avoidance for quadrotors using only onboard computation, highlighting robust, lightweight perception for safety-critical avoidance</cite><cite id="4fd3d7be-3">A vision suite can eliminate GPS dependence for navigation, supporting GNSS-denied missions with coordinate extraction from imagery</cite>.
- Observability-aware planning: Planning algorithms that account for state and environmental observability degrade gracefully when features are scarce, maintaining safety margins and avoiding unsafe maneuvers due to unobservable states.<cite id="4fd3d7be-1">Observability-Based Path Planning quantitatively evaluates how observability shaping affects planning reliability relative to Monte Carlo planning</cite>.

Hardware and System-Level Redundancy/Fail-Safe Design
- Rotor-level redundancy and uniform FTC: Coaxial dual-rotor and dedicated FTC under a uniform control law avoid abrupt controller switches during rotor failure, preserving controllability and preventing unsafe tumbling or divergence in the presence of single-rotor outages.<cite id="60ed0cef-6">A uniform fault-tolerant controller for a quadcopter maintains control without controller switching when one rotor fails completely</cite>.
- Active FTC architectures in HIL: Observer-based sliding-mode FTC with hardware-in-the-loop validation provides practical confidence that actuator faults (e.g., thrust loss) can be accommodated within safety limits during real-time operation, guiding safe payload and envelope limits for field use.<cite id="60ed0cef-1">Hardware-in-the-loop experiments show effective recovery of control up to 40% motor faults with FTC, supporting safe operational envelopes</cite>.
- Broad survey context: Quadrotor-specific surveys catalog configurations, modeling uncertainties, control methods, collision avoidance, fault diagnosis, and tolerant control, providing a taxonomy for selecting robustness-enhancing components for safety-critical applications like inspections and emergency response.<cite id="6705aeea-1">A quadrotor survey synthesizes configurations, modeling, control, collision avoidance, fault diagnosis, and tolerant control, supporting resilient autonomy architectures</cite><cite id="6705aeea-7">A quadrotor survey highlights accurate, efficient operation and emphasizes robustness and fault-tolerant design for safety</cite>.

Operational Safeguards and Flight Management
- Safety-first autonomy architecture: Multi-layer autonomy that couples planning and control with explicit safety monitors improves safety margins by coordinating conservative planning (goal re-routing), safe control layer (constraint enforcement), and run-time diagnostics to avoid unsafe states under uncertainty.<cite id="6705aeea-1">A resilient, multi-layer autonomy architecture improves planning and control safety for UAV inspections, indicating cross-layer safety coordination</cite>.
- Perception uncertainty and trust allocation in replanning: Vision-based planning with explicit dynamic obstacle prediction and perception trust management reduces the likelihood of unsafe replanned contacts or collisions when sensors intermittently fail or are occluded.<cite id="4fd3d7be-2">Combining tracking and trajectory prediction with dynamic obstacles yields reliable planning under uncertainty</cite><cite id="4fd3d7be-7">Perception-aware replanning allocates trust to perception and enforces safety constraints, improving robustness to sensing limitations</cite>.
- GNSS-denied strategies and fallback modes: Vision-based Raptor-like systems and monocular/event-camera methods provide coordinate estimates and collision avoidance when GPS is unreliable, complemented by conservative replanning and geofencing logic to prevent boundary violations in degraded GPS modes.<cite id="4fd3d7be-3">Vision-based navigation eliminates GPS dependence for quadrotors and provides coordinates for safe operation in GNSS-denied missions</cite><cite id="4fd3d7be-4">Event-camera-based avoidance works with onboard, monocular input, enabling robust fallback avoidance without bulky sensors</cite>.
- Safety certification and operational practices: Surveys on fault diagnosis and FTC frame fault-tolerant design choices that align with certification-oriented safety goals such as detect–isolate–accommodate (DIA) for actuator faults, safety-of-life constraints, and envelope guarding; these motivate design for fault detection latency and controller reconfiguration with bounded performance guarantees.<cite id="6705aeea-0">A survey of fault diagnosis and FTC summarizes DIA pipelines and reconfiguration strategies to maintain safety under faults, informing certification-aligned design</cite><cite id="6705aeea-5">A robust adaptive FTC for six-DOF quadrotors targets bounded performance under faults, a typical requirement for safety certification</cite>.

Learning-Based and Data-Driven Safety Components
- Deep RL for obstacle avoidance with safety layers: In unknown/constrained environments, deep reinforcement learning for navigation and avoidance can be paired with safety layers (e.g., collision avoidance constraints) to maintain safety while exploring risky trajectories; operational deployments use conservative inner loops for safety-critical maneuvers.<cite id="4fd3d7be-5">Vision-based autonomous navigation with deep reinforcement learning studies safe navigation and obstacle avoidance in unknown, constrained environments</cite>.
- Adaptive FTC with L1 methods: L1 adaptive controllers offer robustness to large uncertainty/faults with guaranteed transient performance if adaptation limits are respected, giving a clear safety envelope and enabling fail-safe defaults (e.g., coast-to-a-hover) if adaptation fails.<cite id="60ed0cef-8">An L1 adaptive controller for quadrotors is evaluated as an FTC baseline, providing robust tracking with actuator faults</cite>.

End-to-End Evaluation and Simulation-to-Real Practices
- High-fidelity simulation and HIL validation: Robust planning and FTC methods are increasingly validated with hardware-in-the-loop, rapid-prototyping HIL, and realistic fault injection to bound performance under actuator degradation, wind gusts, and sensor noise before field deployment.<cite id="6705aeea-0">FTC frameworks emphasize validation and integration with fault diagnosis for reliable operation</cite><cite id="60ed0cef-1">HIL experiments validate FTC recovery under significant motor faults, supporting safe deployment within specified limits</cite>.
- Barrier/MPC-based safety filters: Constraint-enforced trajectory optimization (model predictive trajectory tracking) with robustness-aware cost shaping and explicit collision/ boundary constraints can be paired with perception-aware trust metrics to provide safe setpoints under uncertainty, complementing vision-based planning and FTC loops.<cite id="4fd3d7be-7">Perception-aware replanning enforces safety constraints at replanning time, a pattern compatible with MPC-style safety filters</cite>.

Putting It Together: A Practical Safety/Robustness Blueprint
- Control/Estimation Core: Choose an observer-augmented robust controller (e.g., super-twisting sliding-mode or prescribed-time FTC) with constraint enforcement and actuator power/authority limits; integrate a high-order fault estimator for early detection/Isolation of motor/thrust faults and degrade gracefully (e.g., switch to a certified fail-safe profile).<cite id="6705aeea-0">FTC surveys provide the DIA workflow and reconfiguration safeguards to maintain safety with faults</cite><cite id="60ed0cef-5">Super-twisting observer plus FTC yields safe operation during thrust-loss faults by estimating and accommodating losses</cite><cite id="60ed0cef-0">Prescribed-time sliding-mode FTC guarantees bounded tracking within a fixed time despite unknown disturbances and faults</cite>.
- Planning/Avoidance Layer: Use perception-aware planning that fuses semantic and metric perception, tracks dynamic obstacles, and allocates perception trust; enforce collision and boundary constraints; and provide GNSS-denied fallback using event/monocular vision or event-based sensing to avoid unsafe GPS-dependent maneuvers.<cite id="4fd3d7be-7">RAPTOR’s perception-aware replanning with safety constraints supports fast, safe flight under sensing uncertainty</cite><cite id="4fd3d7be-4">Monocular event cameras enable robust static-obstacle avoidance on-board</cite><cite id="4fd3d7be-3">Vision-based Raptor provides GNSS-denied navigation with imagery-derived coordinates</cite>.
- Hardware/Failsafe: Add rotor redundancy (e.g., dual-rotor pairs or hybrid VTOL morphing) and run uniform FTC without controller switching during single-failure modes; define certified operational envelopes (e.g., max payload, wind class, altitude) and trigger auto-landing/hold protocols beyond these bounds.<cite id="60ed0cef-6">Uniform FTC tolerates a complete rotor failure without switching, improving fail-operational safety</cite><cite id="6705aeea-1">Surveyed multi-layer architectures for quadrotors support coordinated planning, control, and fault handling for inspections, where safety envelopes are critical</cite>.
- Run-Time Safeguards: Enforce geofencing and altitude/boundary limits, implement perception uncertainty-aware replanning with conservative corridors, and deploy HIL-backed fault modes (e.g., hover-and-communicate) with finite-time guarantees to bound risk during degradation events.<cite id="60ed0cef-1">HIL results quantify acceptable fault severities and controller recoveries in real time</cite><cite id="4fd3d7be-7">Perception-aware replanning enforces fast, safe flight with bounded collision risk using explicit safety constraints</cite>.
- Validation Practices: Combine closed-form safety guarantees (prescribed performance, barrier-style constraint tightening) with sim-to-real testing using HIL and fault-injection, and field-prove FTC under realistic actuator faults to support certification-ready claims.<cite id="60ed0cef-0">Prescribed-time FTC provides fixed-time guarantees useful for certification-style safety margins</cite><cite id="60ed0cef-1">HIL experiments with up to 40% motor faults demonstrate real-time FTC viability</cite><cite id="6705aeea-0">FTC/DFD surveys advocate integrated validation and deployment practices to maintain safety under faults</cite>.

Open Challenges and Trade-offs
- Sensing reliability vs. performance: Vision-only strategies can be lighter and more robust when GPS is degraded, but they may fail under rain/fog or featureless backgrounds; blending with GNSS (RTK/PPK) and using event cameras helps, but safety margins must budget perception uncertainty explicitly.<cite id="4fd3d7be-7">Perception-aware replanning addresses sensing uncertainty by allocating trust and enforcing constraints</cite><cite id="4fd3d7be-3">Vision-based coordinate extraction enables GNSS-denied navigation but relies on imagery quality</cite>.
- Actuator limits and safety envelopes: FTC can mask faults but cannot violate physical limits; designers must set conservative adaptation rates and power limits, verified via HIL and wind/fault injection, to ensure certified safe behavior during reconfiguration.<cite id="60ed0cef-1">HIL evidence quantifies the maximum acceptable actuator fault magnitude and controller recovery</cite><cite id="6705aeea-0">FTC/DFD frameworks formalize detect–isolate–accommodate pipelines to respect safety constraints</cite>.
- Cross-layer coherence: Safety requires coordination across planning/perception and control/estimation; observer-based FTC should be paired with perception trust metrics so that both layers converge to safe, consistent setpoints during failures.<cite id="6705aeea-1">A resilient multi-layer autonomy architecture improves planning and control safety by coordinating layers</cite><cite id="4fd3d7be-2">Perception- and prediction-aware planning improves reliability of quadrotor navigation under uncertainty</cite>.

Summary
In practice, robustness and safety of quadrotors are improved by combining robust/fault-tolerant control with accurate fault diagnosis, perception-aware planning under explicit safety constraints, GNSS-denied navigation and fallback sensing, hardware-level redundancy and uniform FTC, and rigorous validation via HIL and fault-injection within certified safety envelopes; these components are supported by surveys and studies that report quantitative performance and operational limits, enabling deployment with bounded risk in dynamic, partially observable environments.<cite id="6705aeea-0">Surveys of fault diagnosis and FTC provide design patterns—detect–isolate–accommodate and reconfiguration—that preserve safety during faults</cite><cite id="60ed0cef-1">Observer-based sliding-mode FTC with HIL shows effective recovery of control under up to 40% motor faults</cite><cite id="4fd3d7be-7">Perception-aware replanning (e.g., RAPTOR) yields fast, safe flight under limited/uncertain perception by enforcing safety constraints</cite><cite id="4fd3d7be-4">Monocular event-camera avoidance provides lightweight, robust onboard collision avoidance in challenging conditions</cite><cite id="60ed0cef-6">Uniform FTC handles rotor failure without switching, improving fail-operational robustness</cite><cite id="60ed0cef-0">Prescribed-time sliding-mode FTC guarantees bounded, fixed-time tracking under disturbances/faults, offering certification-relevant safety margins</cite>.

without_term.text: What strategies are used to improve robustness and safety of unmanned aerial vehicles in extreme weather conditions?
without_term.answer:
Below is a structured overview of strategies to improve UAV robustness and safety in extreme weather, organized by sensing, control/estimation, airframe/aerodynamics, planning/operations, and verification/testing. Each strategy is paired with examples of methods, quantitative or operational guidance, and known trade-offs.

Sensing, Detection, and Environmental Awareness
- Hazard-aware mission design and avoidance: Real-time weather observation and route planning can reduce exposure to severe convective environments; studies and guidelines emphasize anticipating turbulence/shear and avoiding core storm regions to minimize risk and maintain controllability, with proposed weather-avoidance rules tailored to high-altitude UAVs such as NASA’s Global Hawk to improve target coverage while avoiding significant turbulence and hail regions <cite id="99cd4016-7">Weather avoidance rules for high-altitude UAV missions emphasize avoiding significant turbulence near tropical storms to reduce hazard exposure</cite> <cite id="99cd4016-9">Adapted Global Hawk weather avoidance guidelines prioritize avoiding significant turbulence, which is the most probable hazard when flying above tropical storms</cite> <cite id="99cd4016-0">Modern flight systems are designed to withstand turbulence, but the best operational strategy remains anticipating meteorological events and avoiding them when possible</cite> <cite id="99cd4016-8">Advances in real-time weather sensing and machine learning classification of hail/lightning/turbulence improve situational awareness and enable proactive avoidance strategies</cite>.
- Icing detection and environmental measurement: Electro-thermal icing systems require timely detection and control policies; flight tests have validated closed-loop solutions integrating icing detection, anti-icing, and de-icing procedures, demonstrating airborne operation and autonomy feasibility <cite id="3650c7ce-1">Autonomous icing protection solutions with integrated detection/anti-icing/de-icing procedures have been validated via test flights</cite>. Small UAV systems employ microwave-based icing detectors for airborne measurement, enabling real-time accretion assessment during flight; complementary airborne icing measurement systems estimate liquid water content, drop size, density, and phase to guide protection strategies <cite id="3650c7ce-4">A microwave resonator unit icing detection system has been developed and flight-tested for real-time accretion measurement</cite> <cite id="3650c7ce-5">Airborne Icing Measurement System (AIMS) measures cloud liquid water content, drop size, density and phase for icing threat assessment</cite>. Reviews document UAV applications of detection and de-icing, including electrothermal approaches and their power/thermal implications for small vehicles <cite id="3650c7ce-0">UAV applications for environmental ice detection and de-icing have been reviewed, emphasizing potential roles of UAVs in monitoring and mitigating icing hazards</cite>.
- Perception robustness in precipitation and turbulence: In adverse visibility, integrating multi-sensor fusion (e.g., scanning LiDAR, radar, vision) and robust state estimation improves obstacle avoidance and navigation. Adaptive MPC frameworks have been proposed to handle external disturbances and model uncertainty in quadrotor obstacle avoidance, enabling safe trajectories amidst wind-induced motion perturbations and clutter <cite id="ae3b8d1a-7">Adaptive MPC for quadrotor obstacle avoidance addresses external disturbances and model uncertainty to maintain safe navigations among obstacles</cite>. Preview-based wind sensing (e.g., LiDAR) offers a pathway to improve disturbance rejection and tracking in windy environments, supporting robust perception–control loops that anticipate gusts rather than react after impact <cite id="ae3b8d1a-1">Wind-preview-based MPC for multi-rotor UAVs uses remote LiDAR wind measurements to improve disturbance rejection and trajectory tracking</cite>.

Robust Control, Estimation, and Guidance
- Robust model-predictive and adaptive control: To maintain stability and tracking under gusts and model uncertainty, dual cascade or robust H∞-enhanced MPC can guarantee stability while exploiting multi-timescale dynamics; these approaches reduce overshoot and settling time in quadrotor attitude and thrust regulation under external disturbances <cite id="ae3b8d1a-0">A robust H∞ dual cascade MPC approach for quadcopter attitude control maintains stability under disturbances via nested MPC layers</cite> <cite id="ae3b8d1a-4">A robust H-infinity controller retains stability amid system model uncertainty and external disturbances, demonstrating suitability for wind-buffeted UAVs</cite>. Hierarchical cascaded MPC has been proposed to optimize performance in turbulent environments, explicitly targeting resilience to wind-induced disturbances through nested predictive layers and state estimation <cite id="ae3b8d1a-2">A hierarchical cascaded MPC framework addresses quadrotor performance in turbulent environments through multi-layer predictive control</cite>. Beyond single-aircraft cases, adaptive topology and reduced-order models for UAV flocking under wind gusts enable resilient coordination with online model updates and consensus control despite transient gusts <cite id="ae3b8d1a-3">Adaptive topology and model reduction MPCs for UAV flocking in wind gusts maintain consensus and robustness using online model updates</cite>.
- Disturbance-aware trajectory optimization and NMPC: Nonlinear and stochastic NMPC methods with explicit wind disturbance models improve trajectory tracking and ride quality in high-density wind environments such as urban air mobility (UAM), reducing lateral/vertical excursions during gust encounters compared to conventional regulators <cite id="ae3b8d1a-8">Nonlinear MPC for UAM aircraft with gust models improves trajectory tracking and ride quality under uncertain, gusty wind fields</cite>. Wind disturbance observers integrated with MPC can reject disturbances and restore tracking accuracy, validated on quadrotors via flight test data analysis and energy/actuator constraints assessments <cite id="3650c7ce-6">Wind disturbance rejection approaches for quadrotors demonstrate resilience to wind using disturbance observer–based MPC and flight test data</cite>.
- Operational notes from fixed-wing UAS: Fixed-wing UAVs often tolerate higher gust intensities due to larger rotor diameters/airframes but can suffer from icing in contaminated clouds; this motivates careful weather screening and cloud penetration planning and the use of robust attitude hold controllers tuned for gust-laden conditions <cite id="99cd4016-1">Fixed-wing RPAS typically tolerate gusty winds with larger coverage, but icing during cloud penetration remains a key hazard requiring robust control and planning</cite>.

Airframe and Aerodynamic Design
- Anti-icing and de-icing power/thermal design: Electro-thermal leading-edge heating and surface zone control are validated on UAVs; studies quantify required heat loads and heating durations to achieve safe ice shedding without catastrophic power draw, informing energy-efficient IPS sizing and duty-cycle strategies <cite id="3650c7ce-7">Experimental tests quantify required heat loads and heating periods for ice shedding, guiding efficient electrothermal de-icing on UAVs</cite>. Thermal imaging of anti-icing configurations shows continuous leading-edge heating producing uniform energy distribution; system analyses link energy consumption to ambient temperature and flight speed for small UAV airframes, supporting duty-cycle selection and thermal management plans <cite id="3650c7ce-2">Continuous leading-edge heating in anti-icing tests yields uniform surface energy distribution</cite> <cite id="3650c7ce-3">Energy consumption analyses for UAVs under ambient and icing conditions inform anti-icing/de-icing system sizing and efficiency trade-offs</cite>.
- Airframe icing-aware operations and shielding: Small UAV icing lab work and field programs propose testing and operational protocols for natural icing encounters, including flight-test areas that explicitly generate icing to establish safety/ reliability baselines and parameterize protection strategies for different mission envelopes and airframe geometries <cite id="3650c7ce-8">An advanced diagnostic and forecast system for icing (IFIRE) targets UAV safety and reliability via a dedicated natural-icing flight-test area</cite>. Design practices include vertical takeoff/landing or ground-effect operations to minimize exposure to supercooled droplets in icing threats, and shielding via leading-edge radius/ fences/vortex generators to delay accretion; research emphasizes leading-edge suction and powered film cooling as promising avenues to inhibit accretion on UAV leading edges <cite id="3650c7ce-0">UAV icing mitigation reviews discuss airframe geometry and system-level strategies with an emphasis on reducing accretion via design and electrothermal systems</cite>.
- Rotor/wing protection in precipitation: Rotorcraft are susceptible to reduced rotor performance and inflow disruption in rain/hail; UAV-specific studies emphasize selecting rotors with larger tip clearances, pitch-servo damping, and higher power margins for wet operations and using arming/mission constraints to avoid executing beyond specified weather thresholds <cite id="99cd4016-1">Fixed-wing operations tolerate gusts but icing during cloud/precipitation remains a primary risk, motivating airframe and operation constraints during precipitation</cite>.

Perception, Navigation, and Obstacle Avoidance in Adverse Conditions
- Multi-sensor fusion and robust state estimation: Robust obstacle avoidance and multi-modal perception pipelines integrate LiDAR/radar/visual and inertial sensors with adaptive MPC planning to tolerate wind-induced position drift and false positives in poor visibility, maintaining collision avoidance guarantees under disturbances and model mismatch <cite id="ae3b8d1a-7">Adaptive MPC for aerial platforms provides robust obstacle avoidance under external disturbances and model uncertainty, enabling resilient navigation in cluttered environments</cite>. For rotorcraft, GNSS degradation in heavy rain/ice can be compensated with INS/LiDAR fusion and integrity monitoring; research emphasizes terrain-relative navigation and visual-mapping fallbacks to sustain safe flight outside GPS-denied precipitation regimes <cite id="99cd4016-6">Strong winds degrade stability and control, increasing the need for robust perception and multi-sensor fusion to maintain safe trajectories</cite>.
- Turbulence-aware perception and decision making: Storm hazard classification and probabilistic downburst/wind-shear models feed into perception-triggered path planning and emergency maneuvers; operations research on weather-avoidance logic for UAV and UAM platforms recommends pre-mission weather screening, mid-flight hazard detection, and dynamic replanning to reduce encounter likelihood and severity <cite id="99cd4016-8">Real-time machine learning-based storm classification aids avoidance decisions for hazards (hail, lightning, turbulence, heavy rain)</cite> <cite id="99cd4016-7">Weather-avoidance rule modifications improve science target access while avoiding hazardous storm regions</cite>.

Mission Planning, Routing, and Operations
- Weather-informed routing and constraint management: Control-oriented routing uses forecast wind fields and gust climatology to choose energy-efficient yet weather-robust corridors; NMPC and robust MPC planners incorporate wind disturbance bounds to maintain safety margins and ride quality in gust-prone regions <cite id="ae3b8d1a-8">NMPC with gust-aware models improves UAM trajectory quality and ride comfort when planning under wind uncertainty</cite>. Operational policies include dynamic mission envelopes—ground-station pre-mission thresholds by wind speed/temperature/dewpoint; in-flight uplink of severe weather advisories triggers hold patterns, vertical separation, or diversion to avoid dangerous cells <cite id="99cd4016-7">Adaptive weather avoidance rules adjust flight plans to avoid hazardous storm features and preserve controllability</cite> <cite id="99cd4016-0">Anticipating and avoiding meteorological hazards is a primary strategy for maintaining safety in adverse weather</cite>.
- Downlink-dependent safe mode management: Fleet operators can enforce “weather-safe mode” policies—reducing speed/altitude, increasing buffer distances, activating de-icing, or landing when thresholds are exceeded—guided by predictive models of storm evolution and hazard probabilities <cite id="99cd4016-8">Real-time weather and hazard analytics enable proactive flight safety decisions and avoidance triggers during operations</cite>.

Verification, Testing, and Human-in-the-Loop
- Grounded-in-data avoidance logic and HIL/SIL validation: UAV weather-avoidance logic and control laws can be validated in hardware-in-the-loop or simulation using measured wind fields and icing conditions; studies of aircraft gust alleviation provide templates for flexible models and H∞ control law synthesis, transferable to UAV scale for gust load mitigation and robust stability margins <cite id="ae3b8d1a-5">H-infinity optimal control law design for gust load alleviation on flexible aircraft demonstrates design and validation pathways applicable to UAV gust-robust flight control</cite>. For icing, autonomous protection strategies have been validated via controlled flight tests with detection, anti-/de-icing control procedures, establishing operational feasibility and identifying energy/actuator limits to inform safe mode constraints <cite id="3650c7ce-1">Autonomous icing protection procedures integrated detection, anti-icing, and de-icing, validated through test flights</cite> <cite id="3650c7ce-7">Flight tests quantify heat loads and shedding times to inform IPS design and safe duty cycles</cite>.
- Constructive airworthiness envelopes and run-way choice: Extreme weather requires conservative selection of launch/recovery sites, clearances, and pre-mission weather screening to avoid microbursts, downbursts, and mountain-wave gusts; fixed-wing operations in harsh weather benefit from longer runways and turbulence-tolerant profiles, while rotorcraft may rely on VTOL clearances and immediate hover margins to mitigate sudden wind/shear events <cite id="99cd4016-1">Fixed-wing UAVs survey gusty conditions but require careful planning for icing and wind-laden operations, including runway and profile selection</cite> <cite id="99cd4016-6">Strong winds degrade stability and control, reinforcing the need for conservative mission parameters and safe recovery geometry</cite>.

Cross-Cutting Trade-offs and Implementation Guidance
- Energy and mass budgets for icing protection: Electro-thermal anti-/de-icing on UAVs demands careful thermal/power sizing; flight-test analyses quantify energy needs vs. ambient and speed conditions, and recommend on-demand heating on leading edges with shedding-assist to preserve mission endurance and avoid excessive actuator loading <cite id="3650c7ce-3">Energy consumption analyses for UAV icing systems inform anti-icing/de-icing sizing and duty cycles under ambient and operational conditions</cite> <cite id="3650c7ce-7">Required heat loads and heating periods must be matched to mission energy budgets to enable safe ice shedding</cite>.
- Detection latency and false-negatives in storms: Sensor-based hazard detection can be error-prone in complex storms; combining multi-sensor inputs and predictive hazard models with operator override and emergency protocols reduces risk of undetected penetration into severe cells <cite id="99cd4016-8">Real-time hazard analytics improve classification accuracy for storm cells and support proactive avoidance in operations</cite>.
- Control conservatism vs. performance: Robust H∞/MPC strategies can introduce conservative thrust/actuator schedules in benign segments; wind-preview can reduce conservatism by anticipating disturbances, and adaptive topology/flocking control reduces inter-aircraft stress during gusts by dynamically reconfiguring formations <cite id="ae3b8d1a-1">Wind preview from LiDAR improves disturbance anticipation over reactive control, enabling less conservative MPC scheduling</cite> <cite id="ae3b8d1a-3">Adaptive topology in UAV flocking adjusts inter-UAV distances to reduce gust-induced stress</cite>.
- Cost of avoidance: Post-mission analysis on storm-exposed platforms shows that avoiding hazardous weather preserves controllability and reduces incident rates; operational strategies may increase latency but lower accident probability and repair costs, aligning with industrial guidance that avoidance is the preferred tactic when feasible <cite id="99cd4016-0">The best operational strategy to improve safety is to anticipate hazards and avoid them when feasible</cite> <cite id="99cd4016-7">Weather-avoidance rule modifications improve safety margins without unduly sacrificing mission utility</cite>.

Summary

Paths are computed using RRT*, and a distribution of path qualities/usage of narrow routes is observed over 10,000 trajectories</cite>.

What to change:
- Recognize that effective samples are boundary/bridge points rather than interior tree nodes in corridors; steer toward walls/exits and sample from corridors when detectable. <cite id="3a2602f5-4">RBB avoids sampling near interior free space and instead emphasizes bridge points where passages connect components</cite>.
- Use problem-specific geometric cues (wall normals, corridor cross-section estimates) to bias step direction and next-query selection once near a candidate passage. <cite id="d3b77974-3">Narrow passages impede progress due to step-size constraints in free space</cite>.

2) Boundary-first and region-specific sampling strategies
- Hybrid/near-boundary sampling in PRM-like pipelines (RBB) increases success by avoiding uniform free-space sampling and focusing on bridge points that connect wide space into a corridor. <cite id="3a2602f5-4">A hybrid sampling strategy samples near bridges to find paths through narrow passages by avoiding unnecessary interior samples</cite> <cite id="2b2e07f8-8">Narrow Passage Sampling for PRM: hybrid sampling around bridges yields efficiency gains by not sampling near wide open areas</cite>.

- Adaptive step sizes and local reparameterization near suspected corridors. <cite id="d3b77974-3">A critical challenge in sampling-based planners is the narrow passage problem, where fixed step sizes prevent efficient traversal of constrained corridors</cite> <cite id="3a2602f5-0">A modification of RRT with improved ability to find a collision-free path for a flexible agent in narrow environments via boundary-informed sampling and steering was introduced</cite>.

Practical recipe:
- Start broad; once a sample lies within distance ε of a corridor edge or a “potential bridge”, switch to a boundary-local coordinate frame and bias steps along the wall (small step size h in the corridor; hysteresis reverts to global once far). <cite id="3a2602f5-4">Sampling near bridges improves connection probability through narrow channels compared to uniform free-space sampling</cite> <cite id="3a2602f5-3">Runtime improves when sampling probability in passages is increased (1–2× improvements reported)</cite>.

3) Iterative/detailed sampling on obstacles’ edges (NP-RRT* and relatives)
- Iteratively refine sampling near obstacles to increase the probability of hitting narrow entrances/exits and then tunneling through. <cite id="d3b77974-8">Options to solve the narrow passage problem include more detailed sampling around obstacles, such as NP-RRT*, or combinations of planning levels and local optimization</cite> <cite id="3a2602f5-6">Narrow passage methods include enhanced sampling near obstacles with iterative RRT-like strategies</cite>.

- When you detect you’re inside a corridor, freeze transverse DoF and control along the wall with a small step size; once near the exit, re-introduce transverse motion. <cite id="2b2e07f8-6">Exploring from inside to outside a narrow passage is easier than finding the entrance; DoF reduction and local control aid completion</cite>.

Methods that adapt RRT sampling and local search report improved success in tight passages and fewer redundant joints or waypoints compared to vanilla RRT, yielding straighter, higher-quality paths in corridors and channels.<cite id="cdf153dc-0">This line of work re-examines how sampling points drive tree expansion and refines RRT to favor progress along under-explored directions</cite><cite id="cdf153dc-2">Improved sampling yields fewer redundancy points, straighter paths, and higher path quality in constrained environments</cite><cite id="cdf153dc-3">Sampling-based planners with tailored strategies for narrow passages effectively solve corridor routing under various constraints</cite><cite id="cdf153dc-4">Dynamic, region-biased PRM-like sampling finds feasible paths through narrow corridors where basic methods often fail</cite><cite id="cdf153dc-5">Collision-constrained interpolation provides continuity and feasibility in narrow passage problems across industrial and household settings</cite>.

2) Account for robot kinematics and obstacle avoidance while traversing pathways
- Use collision-avoidance constraints or narrow-passage formulations in the steering function and connection checks. RRT variants that explicitly constrain motion planning in narrow corridors report improved success and path quality by enforcing inter-obstacle and wall clearances during tree growth and edge validation.<cite id="cdf153dc-1">A narrow-passage paradigm tailored to rigid-body robot kinematics provides effective sampling and steering to succeed where unmodified RRT may fail</cite><cite id="cdf153dc-3">Sampling-based planners augmented for narrow passages address various constraints and efficiently solve corridor routing</cite><cite id="cdf153dc-5">Collision-aware interpolation ensures connectivity with clearance during interpolation through narrow regions</cite>.

RRT-Dijkstra hybrids and occupancy-grid–aware RRT constraints illustrate how to integrate collision-avoidance inequalities and dynamic updates so that a global RRT graph is pruned/updated as the environment evolves, maintaining feasible, time-efficient routes along pathways.<cite id="4673270c-6">An RRT-Dijkstra-based strategy uses occupancy grids with collision avoidance constraints to update paths in real time and deliver feasible plans</cite><cite id="4673270c-2">State-of-the-art reviews and challenges highlight planning–control tight coupling for autonomous vehicles, where RRT-based planning integrates with control to maintain safe paths on roads</cite><cite id="4673270c-1">Autonomous driving planners update or replan around obstacles, demonstrating efficient receding-horizon path updates at scale</cite>.
