- For single-occupant corridors or hallways with predictable foot traffic, use online reservations or temporal logic constraints to “book” time windows on the path segment, reducing conflicts and replanning overhead. Multi-robot surveys and frameworks propose decentralized assignment and localized RRT that allocate tasks and paths while coordinating at intersections and shared segments to avoid collisions.<cite id="c9a7da40-4">In multi-robot path planning, the objective is collision-free, efficient, and coordinated trajectories in a shared workspace</cite><cite id="c9a7da40-5">Decentralized task and path planning decomposes coordination into task allocation and localized planning, enabling conflict-free traversal along shared routes</cite><cite id="c9a7da40-7">Task-and-path frameworks schedule robot motions at intersections through prioritization and coordination (e.g., CPAD/CPOM) as new information arrives</cite>.
- When human-shared pathways are unknown or dynamic, equip RRT with human-motion priors or online collision avoidance policies. Recent methods combine RRT exploration with learned or MPC-based avoidance in real time to handle unpredictable pedestrians, effectively keeping the robot within safe offsets from pathways while maintaining progress to the goal.<cite id="c9a7da40-2">A multi-policy RRT for human-shared environments with unknown human motions improves path finding by integrating planning with online safety policies</cite><cite id="4673270c-7">Path following with obstacle avoidance via NMPC shows robust local collision handling compatible with planning-based path definitions</cite>.
- Practical multi-robot systems often mix global RRT roadmaps with local prioritization and reservation at predicted intersections, switching priority based on urgency or deadline to keep latency low along shared corridors.<cite id="4673270c-8">Hybrid planners combine lattice/curvature constraints and lazy collision repair to reduce conflicts at narrow or shared junctions</cite><cite id="c9a7da40-3">Recent reviews show real-time multi-robot path planning approaches that reduce congestion and improve efficiency through coordination</cite><cite id="c9a7da40-1">A warehouse MRPP study introduces congestion relief via scheduling to improve throughput, illustrating pathway coordination in practice</cite>.

Add collision-aware interpolation to maintain clearance along path segments.<cite id="cdf153dc-1">Narrow-passage planning tailored to rigid bodies improves success via dedicated sampling/steering</cite><cite id="cdf153dc-5">Collision-constrained interpolation preserves feasible, collision-free connections across narrow regions</cite>.

  - Decouple RRT-based path planning from a tracking layer that enforces lane/sidewalk offsets and right-of-way. Use grid/occupancy costmaps to penalize entering crosswalks or no-parking zones, and trigger local replanning when obstacle density or traffic light states change.<cite id="4673270c-0">Path planning plus path tracking achieves lane keeping and collision avoidance in practice</cite><cite id="4673270c-6">Collision avoidance constraints integrated with RRT-style updates yield feasible paths in real time</cite>.
- Shared hallways/corridors among robots/agents:
  - Build a reservation graph over key waypoints and corridor bottlenecks; assign time windows via scheduling/consensus, then run localized RRT only within each agent’s window. Employ decentralized task and path allocation to maintain collision-free trajectories and minimize waiting at intersections.<cite id="c9a7da40-5">Decentralized task and path planning modules localize planning and allocate tasks to avoid collisions</cite><cite id="c9a7da40-7">CPAD-style mechanisms coordinate motions at intersections, assigning priorities as information evolves</cite><cite id="c9a7da40-3">Real-time multi-robot reviews show that coordination reduces congestion and improves path efficiency</cite>.
- Dynamic or risky environments:
  - Use chance-constrained RRT* variants with risk budgets per corridor segment; when the solver’s confidence falls below threshold, trigger replanning using the latest door/motion predictions. Validate feasibility with a local MPC or avoidance policy to bridge between global plans while uncertainties resolve.<cite id="4673270c-5">Chance-constrained RRT* gives probabilistic guarantees on path safety, useful for dynamic urban environments</cite><cite id="4673270c-2">Vehicle planning/control integration is essential to maintain safe following under uncertainty</cite>.
- Heuristics that accelerate convergence in corridors:
  - Employ corridor-aware RRT variants (e.g., region-biased or dual-tree) and hybrid RRT variants (VD–RRT) that bias search toward free space along the path’s medial axis and attach drivable primitives; this cuts runtime and path cost in narrow environments.<cite id="cdf153dc-0">Sampling-driven improvements alter expansion dynamics to make RRT more effective near narrow regions</cite><cite id="cdf153dc-4">Dynamic, region-biased sampling improves narrow passage search efficiency</cite><cite id="4673270c-8">VD–RRT hybrids improve feasibility and smoothness by matching motion primitives to terrain constraints</cite>.
- Post-processing and optimization:
  - After RRT* finds a tentative path, apply geometry-aware smoothing that respects corridor widths and clearance zones; also consider RRT-Dijkstra retraction toward shortest collision-free routes where corridor geometry has already been validated.<cite id="cdf153dc-2">Improved RRT variants reduce redundant waypoints and straighten paths in constrained corridors</cite><cite id="4673270c-6">RRT-Dijkstra strategies use collision avoidance constraints to refine and shorten feasible paths</cite>.
  - Prefer mixed RRT variants (e.g., RRT* + Dijkstra, PRM/roadmaps hybridized with local potential fields) to leverage global reach and local feasibility in pathways; these hybrids often converge faster in constrained settings than pure sampling in high-dimensional configuration spaces.<cite id="4673270c-6">RRT-Dijkstra hybrids in occupancy grids provide collision-aware shortest paths</cite><cite id="cdf153dc-4">PRM-based, region-biased sampling finds connections through narrow corridors efficiently</cite><cite id="4673270c-3">Recent RRT surveys highlight improved algorithms and application implementations across domains</cite>.

- Domain constraints: define corridor geometry, bounds, and constraints (footprint, height, steering angle, max speed) plus dynamic events (door times).
- World model: occupancy grid or occupancy field with time-stamped door/motion predictions; maintain a local corridor graph seeded by static obstacles.
- Global planner: corridor-aware RRT* with footprint-inflated collision models and edge cost that penalizes overstepping bounds; integrate a hybrid repair step (VD–RRT/lazy collision repair) to ensure feasibility.
- Local controller: lane/sidewalk-keeping PID/MPC enforcing offset from path and avoiding obstacles; trigger replanning when crosswalk/pedestrian density or predicted door state changes.
- Temporal coordination: if shared pathways, maintain a reservation manager assigning time windows at bottlenecks; in dynamic cases, enforce chance constraints on corridor traversal success and replan when risk exceeds budget.
- Runtime optimizations: use region-biased or dual-tree sampling to accelerate growth into under-explored corridor segments; apply post-smoothing that respects wall clearances; and adopt RRT-Dijkstra retraction to improve path length where feasible.

Summary: RRT can be adapted for efficient pathway traversal by combining corridor-aware sampling and steering, hybrid global–local planning with avoidance constraints, reservation- and time-aware coordination for shared routes, and chance-constrained or MPC-augmented safety layers for dynamic elements like doors and people. These adaptations have been validated across narrow passages, sidewalks/roads, and multi-robot corridors, yielding higher success rates, smoother and shorter paths, and improved timeliness under uncertainty.<cite id="cdf153dc-0">Sampling-aware RRT variants improve expansion in narrow regions</cite><cite id="cdf153dc-1">Narrow-passage-specific formulations leverage robot kinematics for better success</cite><cite id="cdf153dc-5">Collision-aware interpolation maintains clearance and connectivity through tight spaces</cite><cite id="4673270c-0">Plan–track pipelines realize lane keeping with collision avoidance</cite><cite id="4673270c-6">RRT-Dijkstra hybrids update collision-avoidance constrained paths in real time</cite><cite id="c9a7da40-5">Decentralized task and path planning enables collision-free coordination on shared routes</cite><cite id="c9a7da40-7">Reservation/prioritization mechanisms coordinate robot motions at intersections</cite><cite id="4673270c-5">Chance-constrained RRT* provides probabilistic safety guarantees under uncertainty</cite><cite id="4673270c-8">Hybrid VD–RRT with lazy repair improves constrained-path feasibility and smoothness</cite>.

without_term.answer:
Below is a practical, evidence-backed recipe for adapting path-planning methods to efficiently handle narrow pathways (corridors/lanes where robot footprints must fit with clearance). We synthesize techniques across sampling-based, decomposition/graph-search, and optimization-based planners, and include deployment tips and trade-offs.

Problem framing for narrow passages
- Narrow pathways constrain valid configurations to thin regions of the free space; feasibility depends on robot footprint and maneuver clearance, and paths may snake through bottlenecks. Methods must bias sampling and search toward corridor axes, preserve resolution completeness if needed, and coordinate in multi-robot settings where doorways become contention points. <cite id="0b912f6f-0">Corridor checks can guide sampling to produce reliable narrow-passage samples</cite> and <cite id="0b912f6f-2">visibility-based PRM is related to the narrow passage problem and reduces unnecessary nodes by checking visibility</cite>. <cite id="62ea2c14-8">Narrow corridors of width 1 (doorways) are an explicit challenge, and experience-based multi-agent path finding is tailored to this setting</cite>.

Adaptation 1: Sampling and graph construction tailored to corridors
- Hybrid sampling in PRM: Use a bridge-based strategy to insert samples inside corridors. The “bridge test” hybridizes grid-like sampling outside narrow regions with targeted exploration inside by connecting boundary samples across bottlenecks, enabling small roadmaps to succeed in narrow passages; it is a sampling strategy with resolution-complete behavior under mild assumptions and improves success probability at moderate sizes <cite id="e9df3059-0">The visibility-based PRM is related to the narrow passage problem</cite><cite id="e9df3059-1">This paper presents a hybrid sampling strategy in the PRM framework for finding paths through narrow passages</cite><cite id="e9df3059-2">A hybrid sampling strategy in PRM to find paths through narrow passages efficiently is presented</cite><cite id="e9df3059-3">Key to the new strategy is enabling relatively small roadmaps to succeed in narrow passages by controlling sampling density inside narrow passages</cite>. 
- Visibility/bridge points to expose corridor channels: Visibility graphs and bridge-point methods connect road segments via points-of-view across bottlenecks to create a path-oriented graph that is efficient for corridor navigation <cite id="e9df3059-0">The visibility-based PRM reduces unnecessary nodes via visibility checks and is related to narrow passage handling</cite><cite id="0b912f6f-2">The visibility-based PRM is related to the narrow passage problem</cite>.
- Narrow-region detection to bias sampling: Preprocess the map to detect narrow regions/doorways and bias sampling or exploration toward their axes; recent work uses occupancy grids and visibility to deterministically identify narrow regions before planning <cite id="0b912f6f-8">A novel narrow region detector uses occupancy grid maps and visibility</cite><cite id="e9df3059-8">Finding Narrow Passages with Probabilistic Roadmaps shows PRM can work in high-dimensional C-space and outlines how to locate bottlenecks</cite>.
- Task-specific samplers for corridor geometry: For microrobot-like settings, exploit long thin free-space “tunnels” with a graph search that decouples global coverage from local corridor guidance, and use local planning to thread the needle through narrow segments <cite id="0b912f6f-3">An efficient path-planning algorithm for microrobots passing through narrow passages uses planning tailored to long and narrow free-space corridors</cite>. 
- Anytime reinforcement of bottlenecks: If a planned path requires a narrow passage, run an iterative refinement (e.g., local search or PRM reinsertion) that focuses on the bottleneck segment to resolve deadlocks. <cite id="e9df3059-5">Enhanced PRM increases the number of sampling points in narrow passages, leading to better paths</cite>, and <cite id="0b912f6f-4">optimizing PRM for narrow corridors reduces waypoint discrepancies in bottlenecks</cite>. 
- Alternative samplers (Lévy flights and neural guidance): Move samples with heavy-tailed Lévy steps or neural field guidance to preferentially land in narrow regions where uniform random sampling fails; these strategies have improved narrow-region coverage and success in C-space <cite id="e9df3059-7">A Lévy-flight based narrow passage sampling method generates key samples in narrow C-space regions to increase success</cite> and <cite id="0b912f6f-0">bridge points guided neural motion planning uses corridor checks to generate reliable samples inside narrow passages</cite>.

Adaptation 2: Graph/cell decomposition and corridor-aware search
- Corridor-aware cell/graph decomposition: Use narrow-passage detection to define cells or subgraphs aligned with corridors and doorways (portals/sections), then search over these high-level corridors. <cite id="62ea2c14-0">A GNN predicts portal scores on a cell adjacency graph to bias corridor search toward near-optimal regions while preserving completeness</cite> and <cite id="62ea2c14-2">a natural cell decomposition arises from narrow passage detection, which is exploited in sampling and planning</cite>. 
- Section/portal patterns for high-dimensional bottlenecks: In high-dimensional configuration spaces (manipulators or vehicles), partition the space into sections and connect via portals (corridors), enabling resolution-complete or near-complete planners to efficiently navigate bottlenecks <cite id="62ea2c14-1">Section patterns efficiently solve high-dimensional narrow passage motion planning problems</cite>.
- Hybridization with A* and geometric funneling: Integrate topological corridors discovered by sampling with A*/D* tiebreaks and local funnel adjustments to maintain low-level feasibility and clearance as the graph is traversed. Experience-based and potential-field–guided hybrid approaches improve narrow-corridor throughput by aligning robot motion with corridor axes <cite id="58369d8b-1">ASCON couples improved artificial potential field directional guidance with global search to handle narrow corridors</cite>.
- Narrow-corridor multi-agent coordination: For multiple robots, pre-arrange sequencing at doorways and allocate corridors to avoid conflicts; specialized experience-based multi-agent path finding handles doorways (narrow passages of width 1) by sharing experiences and prioritizing corridor reservations <cite id="62ea2c14-7">An experience-based multi-agent algorithm specifically addresses narrow corridors of width 1 (doorways)</cite><cite id="62ea2c14-8">Experience-based multi-agent path finding with narrow corridors expands path planning to contention-limited channels</cite>. 
- Domain-specific graph planners: In long, linear subterranean environments, combine global graph guidance with local planning to snake through narrow parts; this hybrid style reliably guides robots through long and narrow structures <cite id="0b912f6f-8">GBPlanner operated by mostly engaging the local planning stage, guiding robots through long and narrow parts of environments</cite>.

Adaptation 3: Optimization/trajectory-level planners with robot footprint and clearance
- Embed 2D collision and clearance constraints directly: Formulate planning as convex optimization over trajectories with explicit distance-to-obstacle constraints and robot footprint envelopes, yielding paths that stay within corridor clearances and resolve narrow bottlenecks without relying solely on probabilistic sampling density. <cite id="58369d8b-0">Narrow passage path planning is prevalent; a collision-constraint formulation integrates robot footprint and obstacle clearances to find feasible paths in tight spaces</cite> and <cite id="58369d8b-2">autonomous trajectory planning via convex optimization (SOCP) enables handling nonlinear constraints typical of clearance-limited motion</cite>.
- Hybrid state-space A*/graph global search with 2D local control: Extend A* with continuous 2D state for position/orientation and a local controller (e.g., funnel/trajectory adjustment) to maintain clearance as the path snakes through corridors; reported advantages include maneuver-level feasibility and robustness in cluttered spaces when the hybrid state space incorporates geometric constraints <cite id="58369d8b-7">Hybrid-state A* directly formulates path planning as non-linear optimization and manifests its main advantage in maneuvers in narrow and cluttered spaces</cite>.
- Anytime improvement with repulsion/attraction hybrids: Couple a global search for corridors with potential fields that penalize walls and reward corridor centerlines to drift away from narrow-passage deadlocks and fine-tune trajectories iteratively <cite id="58369d8b-1">ASCON improves success in narrow corridors by combining global path planning with directional potential-field guidance</cite>.

Engineering checklist: Practical steps to adapt a planner
- Preprocess to surface bottlenecks: Run a narrow-region detector (occupancy + visibility/line-of-sight) to identify passageways/doorways and compute corridor axes; use these to seed start-goal corridors and bias global search <cite id="0b912f6f-8">Narrow region detector for sampling-based planning based on occupancy grids and visibility</cite><cite id="e9df3059-3">Sampling density control and hybrid strategy inside narrow passages reduces roadmap size while preserving success</cite>.
- Teach sampling to love bottlenecks: Replace pure uniform sampling with: (a) boundary-to-boundary bridging across detected passages; (b) visibility-bridging to insert key points; (c) Lévy-flight perturbations; (d) neural guidance conditioned on corridor features. <cite id="e9df3059-0">Visibility-based PRM relates to and reduces nodes in narrow passages</cite><cite id="e9df3059-7">Lévy-flight sampling places key points in narrow regions to improve feasibility</cite><cite id="0b912f6f-0">Bridge-points guided neural motion planning uses corridor checks to sample reliably inside narrow passages</cite>.
- Construct corridor-aligned graphs: Create a high-level “corridor graph” whose nodes are corridor endpoints/bridges and edges represent passable bottlenecks, then run A* over this graph with 2D local planning to resolve tight turns; add section/portal patterns for higher-dimensional state <cite id="62ea2c14-0">GNN-prioritized portal scoring biases corridor search while preserving completeness</cite><cite id="62ea2c14-1">Section patterns efficiently solve high-dimensional narrow passage problems</cite><cite id="62ea2c14-2">Narrow passage detection naturally defines a cell/portal decomposition guiding sampling</cite>.
- Enforce 2D clearance and kinematics: Use convex trajectory optimization to impose distances-to-obstacles, footprint constraints, and turning radii; integrate with a local funnel/motion-primitive executor to maintain feasibility as the path is traversed. <cite id="58369d8b-0">Collision-constraint path planning addresses the common narrow passage problem with explicit feasibility checks</cite><cite id="58369d8b-2">SOCP-based trajectory planning encodes nonlinear constraints for autonomous motion</cite><cite id="58369d8b-7">Hybrid-state A* formulates planning as nonlinear optimization with maneuver-level constraints in clutter</cite>.
- Anytime/local repair for bottlenecks: After an initial plan, run a local search that focuses on the narrowest segments (e.g., corridor-aware RRT/PRM reconnection, potential-field nudges) to unstick paths that fail due to insufficient clearance or kinematic feasibility <cite id="e9df3059-5">Enhanced PRM increases samples in narrow passages, improving plan quality and feasibility</cite>.
- Multi-robot handling: If multiple agents need doorways, enforce ordering/experience sharing; use narrow-corridor-aware multi-agent planners that prevent conflicts and schedule corridor usage using learned experiences <cite id="62ea2c14-7">Experience-based multi-agent path finding addresses narrow corridors of width 1 via shared experiences</cite><cite id="62ea2c14-5">Narrow corridors of width 1 (doorways) require coordination to avoid conflicts</cite>. 
- Domain tailoring: Microrobot or subterranean settings benefit from decoupling global corridor graph traversal from local “threading” controllers that exploit funnel geometry to navigate tight sections <cite id="0b912f6f-3">Efficient algorithms for microrobot passage through narrow corridors exploit corridor structure</cite><cite id="0b912f6f-8">Local planning guided through long, narrow parts improves success in subterranean exploration</cite>.

Trade-offs and choosing a method family
- Sampling-based (PRM/LazyPRM/bridge): Fast to code and scalable in high-dimensional spaces; success depends on corridor-aware sampling and density. <cite id="e9df3059-3">The bridge strategy lowers sampling density in free space and focuses it in bottlenecks, enabling small roadmaps to succeed in narrow passages</cite>, and <cite id="e9df3059-4">hybrid sampling in PRM enables relatively small roadmaps with high success in narrow passages</cite>. For multi-robot narrow corridors, a PRM with bridge/narrow-detection guidance plus a sequenced reservation protocol performs well <cite id="62ea2c14-8">Experience-based multi-agent algorithms tailor to narrow corridors</cite>.
- Decomposition/graph-search: Most complete when decomposition is exact and corridor connections (portals) are reliable; useful for global route planning over buildings/subterranean networks with many doorways. <cite id="62ea2c14-1">Section/portal patterns efficiently handle high-dimensional narrow passages</cite> and <cite id="62ea2c14-0">GNN-guided portal scoring steers search while preserving completeness</cite>.
- Optimization/trajectory planning: Strong when you can encode collision-cylinder and kinematic constraints; often returns globally optimal or near-optimal trajectories and is robust in clutter. <cite id="58369d8b-0">A collision-constraint formulation targets the narrow passage problem with integrated footprint/clearance</cite> and <cite id="58369d8b-7">hybrid-state A* integrates 2D geometry into a nonlinear optimization framework</cite>. For applications where footprints and turning radii must be respected (e.g., differential-drive platforms), this family yields fewer re-plans once a feasible path is found <cite id="58369d8b-2">Convex optimization for trajectories embeds constraints that otherwise require costly replanning</cite>.

Putting it together: A modular pipeline
- Precompute narrow passages and corridor skeletons; seed two graphs: a coarse “corridor graph” (endpoints/bridges) and a fine “roadmap/trajectory graph” over 2D states. <cite id="62ea2c14-2">Narrow passage detection naturally yields a cell/portal decomposition used in sampling and planning</cite>.
- Sample hybridly: uniform away from corridors plus bridge/visibility and Lévy flight targeting within detected passages. <cite id="e9df3059-3">Bridge sampling focuses density in narrow passages to improve success at small roadmap sizes</cite><cite id="e9df3059-7">Lévy flights place key samples in narrow C-space regions, improving success</cite>.
- Search globally: A* or hybrid-state A* over the corridor graph with 2D local optimization/constraints to ensure clearance; add bidirectional search from start and goal to find corridor overlaps quickly. <cite id="58369d8b-7">Hybrid-state A* directly encodes geometric constraints and maneuvers, improving performance in narrow, cluttered spaces</cite>.
- Local repair and multi-robot coordination: After planning, run any-time corridor-focused local search; in multi-robot scenarios, enforce corridor sequencing and experience sharing to resolve door bottlenecks <cite id="62ea2c14-7">Experience-based multi-agent path finding addresses narrow corridors by leveraging shared experiences</cite><cite id="e9df3059-5">Enhanced PRM increases sampling in narrow passages and yields better plans</cite>.

When to prefer which adaptation
- Unknown/complex geometry with high dimensionality: Prefer decomposition + bridge/visibility sampling and hybrid A*, since it maintains completeness where possible and reduces reliance on blind sampling density <cite id="62ea2c14-1">Section patterns improve efficiency in high-dimensional narrow passages</cite><cite id="e9df3059-0">Visibility-based PRM reduces unnecessary nodes and is tailored to bottlenecks</cite>.
- Tight time budgets and fast prototyping: Use a sampling-based base (RRT/PRM) with bridge/Lévy flight sampling and potential-field repulsion/attraction to bias into corridors; add a post-local optimization pass to enforce clearance <cite id="e9df3059-7">Lévy-flight sampling efficiently places key corridor points</cite><cite id="58369d8b-7">Hybrid-state A* yields maneuver-feasible paths under constraints</cite>.
- Robustness to footprints/kinematics and deterministic feasibility: Encode a collision-constraint or convex trajectory optimization with a footprint envelope and corridor-aware cost; use funnel-like local controllers to navigate hairpin turns in narrow lanes <cite id="58369d8b-0">Collision-constraint planning integrates robot footprint and narrow passage feasibility</cite><cite id="0b912f6f-3">Microrobot algorithms specifically exploit long thin free-space corridors</cite>.
- Multi-robot logistics: Add experience-based corridor reservation and sequencing; prioritize allocating different robots to parallel narrow passages and resolve contention at doorways using shared narrow-corridor policies <cite id="62ea2c14-8">Experience-based multi-agent narrow-corridor algorithms coordinate doorways</cite><cite id="62ea2c14-5">Narrow corridors are prone to conflicts among multiple robots</cite>.

Common pitfalls and fixes
- Sampling misses the corridor: Use boundary/visibility checks to expose corridors and bias sampling toward detected channels <cite id="0b912f6f-8">Visibility-assisted narrow region detection guides sampling into corridors</cite><cite id="e9df3059-0">Visibility-based PRM uses visibility checks to avoid useless nodes outside passages</cite>.
- Kinematics clip against walls: Augment graph edges with motion primitives that respect minimum turning radii; enforce Minkowski-erosion (footprint) in collision checks within the optimization <cite id="58369d8b-0">Embedding collision constraints with footprint models addresses narrow passage feasibility</cite>.
- Bottlenecks cause deadlock: Run targeted re-sampling in the bottleneck, add potential-field soft constraints or staged reservations for multi-robot use; or switch to corridor-aligned graph search with bidirectional A* to find overlapping channels <cite id="e9df3059-5">More samples in narrow passages increase feasibility</cite><cite id="62ea2c14-1">Section patterns provide alternative routes in high-dimensional bottlenecks</cite>.

Summary
Efficiently handling narrow pathways hinges on (i) exposing corridor structure via visibility/detection and using bridge/Lévy sampling to place critical points, (ii) organizing a corridor graph with portal/section connections and hybrid A* search constrained by footprint/kinematics, and (iii) adding local optimization and multi-robot coordination to resolve bottlenecks. These adaptations directly target the geometry of narrow passages, focusing sampling and constraints where the problem is hardest and borrowing lessons from microrobot navigation and multi-agent corridor routing. <cite id="e9df3059-2">Hybrid sampling strategies in PRM efficiently find paths through narrow passages with small roadmaps</cite><cite id="62ea2c14-2">Cell/portal decompositions derived from narrow-passage detection guide sampling and planning</cite><cite id="58369d8b-0">Collision-constraint path planning with robot footprints addresses the core narrow passage problem</cite><cite id="62ea2c14-8">Experience-based multi-agent planning is purpose-built for narrow corridors and doorways</cite>.

without_preference.text: how can RRT-based path planning be adapted to handle narrow pathways
without_preference.answer:
Below are concrete ways to adapt RRT-style planners to find paths through narrow passages, organized by mechanism and supported by recent evidence and design principles.

1) Why narrow passages are hard for RRT
- Sampling degeneracy: In a corridor, the “onion-like” shell of free space near walls shrinks with robot footprint; the chance that a random sample lies in the thin pass becomes vanishingly small, inflating search time and stalling progress. <cite id="495417a8-5">Narrow passages induce a higher runtime, because the chance to sample them becomes vanishingly small.</cite> <cite id="495417a8-0">This paper re-examines the role of sampling points in RRT to better explore near walls when expanding the tree.</cite>
- Consequence: Standard uniform sampling wastes many iterations probing far from bottlenecks; biasing schemes and geometric awareness are required to reduce commute time across narrow bottlenecks. <cite id="7a42caae-7">Narrow passages induce a higher runtime, because the chance to sample them becomes vanishingly small; we can use biased sampling methods.</cite>

2) Core adaptation levers

2.1 Sampling strategy and biasing toward walls/bridges
- Bridge sampling and hybrid sampling: Direct samples toward candidate bottleneks (“bridges”) or along on-the-fly candidate walls, and only stochastically fall back to uniform sampling. <cite id="7a42caae-1">Narrow passages: Consider bridge sampling or adaptive sampling.</cite> <cite id="495417a8-0">RJ-RRT focuses on the role of sampling points and how the tree expands toward samples to improve exploration near passages.</cite>
- Narrow passage detection and constraint-aware bias: Detect passages and bias samples to respect kinematic/joint limits so that expansions hit walls rather than wander in wide areas. <cite id="7a42caae-2">A sampling-based motion-planning algorithm for narrow passages includes narrow passage detection and sampling bias for kinematic constraints.</cite> <cite id="7a42caae-3">The 2021 narrow-passage paradigm introduces a rigid-body robot model targeting corridor planning.</cite>

2.2 Collision checking and representation
- Footprint/robot model inflation: Construct the free space using a Minkowski sum or ellipsoidal/convex robot footprint to make collision checking conservative and visible corridor boundaries explicit. <cite id="495417a8-2">Efficient path planning for robots with ellipsoidal footprints specifically targets narrow passages by encoding the robot’s swept volume.</cite>
- Lazy collision checking to reduce wasted checks: Defer detailed collision checks until promising edges are formed; this reduces overhead in early tree growth in wide areas and accelerates corridor search when a viable edge is near. <cite id="7a42caae-4">Lazy-PRM* and Lazy-RRG* eliminate most collision checks with lazy strategies, improving runtime.</cite> <cite id="7a42caae-8">Edge-lazy RRT can improve runtime by adopting a lazy collision-checking approach.</cite>
- Perimeter sampling around obstacles: Sample along obstacle edges at a fixed offset to ensure candidate expansions probe wall-following corridors, which increases the odds of connecting segments in a narrow maze. <cite id="7a42caae-0">RRT is probabilistically complete with collision-free sample checking; perimeter-probing sampling improves feasibility in narrow channels.</cite>

2.3 Steering and motion model
- Steering kernels tailored to corridors: Use repulsive/gradient forces from walls (e.g., potential fields) to bias steering toward free-wall trajectories inside the passage (complementary to sampling bias). <cite id="7a42caae-1">In narrow passages, domain-guided steering and sampling bias are recommended to reduce aimless wandering.</cite>
- Kinodynamic feasibility: Select steering functions that respect velocity/curvature/joint-limits so that tree steps “fit” through bottlenecks rather than overshoot and clip. <cite id="7a42caae-2">Sampling-bias for kinematic constraint is an integral part of handling narrow passages.</cite>

3) Variants and hybrids that improve corridor success

3.1 Biased RRT families (RJ-RRT, improved RRT)
- RJ-RRT (Randomized Jump RRT): Revisits how new samples are chosen so that expansions systematically carve into narrow channels by placing samples closer to likely bottlenecks or along walls, improving success earlier in the search. <cite id="495417a8-0">RJ-RRT re-examines the role of sampling points; the tree expands toward samples to better explore narrow passages.</cite>
- General biased RRT: Combine uniform sampling with on-demand wall/border sampling and “bridge” queries between nearby segments to bridge the gap across bottlenecks. <cite id="7a42caae-1">Narrow passages: Consider bridge sampling or adaptive sampling.</cite> <cite id="495417a8-5">Biased sampling methods help overcome the vanishing sample chance in passages; runtime increases with passage narrowness and dimensionality.</cite>

3.2 RRT-Connect/RRT*-style global guidance
- RRT-Connect with narrow-aware steering: Build trees from both ends (start and goal), using corridors/midline sampling to guide edges across passages and reducing search time compared to single-tree RRT. <cite id="7a42caae-5">RRT*-Connect (IRRT*-Connect) is tailored for narrow environments with multiple obstacles, improving manipulator path planning under corridor constraints.</cite>
- Optimality and feasibility trade-offs: If near-optimal length is not essential, use RRT/Connect variants with corridor-biased sampling to get feasible paths rapidly; if needed, switch to RRT* with incremental rewiring and hybrid sampling to improve path quality. <cite id="7a42caae-6">RRT* is asymptotically optimal but often spends more time avoiding collision checks than feasibility-first planners.</cite>

3.3 Preprocessing and geometric abstractions for corridors
- Visibility graphs and narrow-roadmaps: Preprocess corridors to build a graph of corridors and vertices at wall intersections or endpoints, then use this roadmap to bias RRT’s state space and reduce the tree’s commute in bottlenecks. <cite id="7a42caae-9">Explicit Corridor Maps compute shortest or clearance-maximizing paths using corridors, guiding search to structurally feasible solutions.</cite>
- Domain-specific microrobot roadmaps: For micro/nano-scale passages, construct geometric roadmaps (offset walls, capillaries) and integrate them into RRT sampling to avoid persistent aimless search. <cite id="495417a8-4">RRT planning through narrow passages suffers from aimless path searching; domain roadmaps mitigate this.</cite> <cite id="495417a8-1">An efficient path-planning algorithm for microrobots through narrow passages demonstrates roadmap-guided strategies.</cite>

4) Narrow-escape-aware runtime management
- Runtime scaling with bottleneck sharpness: The worse the passage, the slower progress due to low sampling probability; compensate with adaptive sampling density, hybrid MCMC/bridge steps, or hierarchical planners that route to the corridor first and then refine. <cite id="495417a8-5">Narrow passages increase runtime because sampling chances become vanishingly small; biased sampling can mitigate, but time remains higher than in wide spaces.</cite>
- Multi-level or hierarchical decomposition: Plan at coarse scale to locate the narrow passage, then switch to a narrow-specific subspace with inflated footprints and biased sampling to thread the needle. <cite id="7a42caae-7">Use biased sampling methods when solving hierarchical or multilevel motion planning problems involving narrow passages.</cite>

5) Putting it together: Practical recipe for narrow-path RRT
- Robot/footprint modeling: Inflated Minkowski footprint or ellipsoid; conservative collision predicate; perimeter samples along obstacles/bridges. <cite id="495417a8-2">Ellipsoidal-footprint modeling improves corridor planning.</cite> <cite id="7a42caae-4">Lazy collision checking reduces overhead as paths are assembled.</cite>
- Sampling and steering: 
  - Bias 60–80% of samples along obstacle edges at several wall-offset distances, and 20–40% uniform; 
  - Use a wall-normal repulsive potential to steer queries toward free-wall trajectories when inside a corridor. <cite id="7a42caae-1">Bridge and adaptive sampling address aimless search in narrow passages.</cite> <cite id="7a42caae-2">Sampling-bias tailored to kinematic constraints is part of a complete solution.</cite>
- Search architecture: 
  - Start with RRT-Connect(-*) dual-tree growth using corridor-aware sampling/steering to get a feasible skeleton quickly, then apply RRT* rewiring for smoothing/length reduction; 
  - If manipulators, use IRRT*-Connect with joint-space constraints. <cite id="7a42caae-5">IRRT*-Connect adapts RRT*-Connect for narrow environments and multiple obstacles.</cite> <cite id="7a42caae-6">LQR-RRT* and RRT* provide asymptotically optimal frameworks once collision checking is efficient.</cite>
- Preprocessing: 
  - Compute explicit corridor graphs/maps and feed corridor midlines/vertices as anchors for initial samples and goal biasing; 
  - In microfluidic-like domains, precompute micro-roadmaps. <cite id="495417a8-9">Explicit Corridor Maps expose the structurally valid corridors and support shortest/clearance queries.</cite> <cite id="495417a8-1">Microrobot algorithms emphasize domain-specific preprocessing for narrow channels.</cite>
- Runtime control: 
  - Use lazy collision checking; 
  - Add MCMC/rejection-sampling “bridge moves” between corridor anchors to accelerate escape from wide regions; 
  - Switch to narrow-specific settings when corridor width < 1.5× footprint diameter. <cite id="7a42caae-4">Lazy planners reduce collision checks and improve throughput.</cite> <cite id="7a42caae-7">Biasing and hybrid strategies directly address narrow-passage bottlenecks.</cite>

6) When to choose which adaptation
- Fast feasibility in tight corridors: RJ-RRT or improved RRT with wall/bridge sampling and lazy collision checking. <cite id="495417a8-0">RJ-RRT targets sampling to drive quick corridor penetration.</cite> <cite id="7a42caae-8">Lazy edge checking accelerates early-stage growth.</cite>
- Near-optimal paths across many narrow channels: RRT*-Connect(-Cubic/steering) with preprocessing (explicit corridor maps/visibility) and corridor-aware sampling. <cite id="7a42caae-5">IRRT*-Connect improves manipulator paths in narrow, cluttered spaces.</cite> <cite id="495417a8-9">Corridor maps guide RRT* towards shortest, high-clearance routes.</cite>
- Ultra-tight micro/nano passages: Microrobot-style planning using ellipsoidal/convex footprints and roadmap-guided sampling, possibly with domain-potentials. <cite id="495417a8-2">Planning for ellipsoidal rigid-body footprints is tailored for narrow passages.</cite> <cite id="495417a8-1">Microrobot narrow-path planning shows algorithmic efficacy in extreme bottlenecks.</cite>

7) Known limitations and empirical guidance
- Success vs. runtime frontier: The probability of successfully sampling a corridor is inversely related to its width relative to footprint; expect many more samples and longer runtimes in sharp bottlenecks, even with biasing. <cite id="495417a8-5">Narrow passages cause higher runtime due to vanishing sampling probability; biased sampling improves success but not asymptotically.</cite>
- Dimension and kinematics: High-dimensional manipulators benefit from RRT*-Connect with narrow-aware joint biasing; naive RRT struggles to reach feasible joint corridors. <cite id="7a42caae-5">IRRT*-Connect for robotic arms explicitly targets narrow obstacles and multiple degrees of freedom.</cite> <cite id="7a42caae-2">Sampling bias for kinematic constraints is essential to find feasible paths in narrow channels.</cite>
- Guarantees and heuristics: Standard RRT is probabilistically complete with exact collision checking; adding lazy checking and heuristic biasing improves speed but breaks formal completeness guarantees, so validate with periodic exact checks. <cite id="7a42caae-0">Sampling-based RRT is probabilistically complete with collision-free sample checking; integrate this safely with practical optimizations.</cite>

Summary: To make RRT handle narrow pathways, bias samples and steering toward walls/bridges, inflate/accurately model the robot footprint and use lazy collision checking; then choose an RRT variant—RJ-RRT or RRT*-Connect(-*) tuned for corridors—with corridor roadmaps (explicit corridor maps/visibility) for global guidance. In ultra-tight domains, adopt microrobot-style footprint/roadmap strategies and kinematic-aware sampling. Expect slower runtime and more iterations as bottlenecks narrow, and trade some optimality or completeness for reliable corridor threading. <cite id="495417a8-5">Narrow passages increase runtime and call for biased sampling.</cite> <cite id="7a42caae-1">Bridge and adaptive sampling directly address aimless search in narrow corridors.</cite> <cite id="7a42caae-5">IRRT*-Connect demonstrates corridor-tuned RRT for narrow, obstacle-stacked environments.</cite> <cite id="495417a8-9">Explicit corridor maps expose passable channels to guide shortest/maximum-clearance paths.</cite> <cite id="495417a8-2">Footprint-aware models (ellipsoidal/convex) support accurate collision checking in narrow spaces.</cite>

query.text: what are some datasets used for evaluating variable type inference for decompiled binaries?
query.answer:
Below are commonly used datasets and resources for evaluating variable type inference on decompiled binaries. I group them into curated benchmark suites, model/training datasets tied to decompilers (Ghidra/IDA/Binarynoodle), and tool/data resources used to annotate or evaluate typed decompilations.

1) Curated benchmark suites for decompiler type inference
- sefcom/decompiler-types-benchmark (GitHub)
  - What it is: A full-stack benchmark including binaries, extraction/evaluation scripts, extracted type data, and published results for “Benchmarking Binary Type Inference Techniques.” It targets variable- and function-level type recovery across multiple decompilers and exposes typed data for reproducible evaluation. <cite id="5858aa98-2">This repository contains the binaries, extraction and evaluation scripts, extracted type data and the results of the paper “Benchmarking Binary Type Inference”</cite> <cite id="5858aa98-0">This paper presents a benchmark study of five decompilers, focusing on their ability to infer types at both the function and variable levels</cite> <cite id="5858aa98-9">A benchmark study of five decompilers, focusing on their ability to infer types at both the function and variable levels, allowing us to assess decompiler …</cite>
  - How to use: Directly run the provided extraction/eval scripts to map decompiled functions/variables to ground-truth types; the included typed dataset and leaderboards help compare a baseline decompiler’s type annotations versus learned augmentation methods. <cite id="5858aa98-2">This repository contains the binaries, extraction and evaluation scripts, extracted type data and the results of the paper “Benchmarking Binary Type Inference”</cite>

- DecompileBench family (systematic, multi-task evaluation)
  - What they are: “DecompileBench,” “Decompile-Bench-Eval,” and related arXiv/ACL Findings entries propose comprehensive end-to-end evaluations of decompiler fidelity that explicitly include the recovery of variable/function types as a decompilation signal. <cite id="5858aa98-3">We present DecompileBench, the first comprehensive framework that enables effective evaluation of decompilers in reverse engineering workflows</cite> <cite id="5858aa98-7">This task is challenging because compilers remove key information during compilation, such as variable types and control structures</cite> <cite id="5858aa98-4">Decompilation transforms the compiled binaries into high-level source code, helping engineers analyze program behaviors, uncover vulnerabilities, study malware</cite> <cite id="5858aa98-8">Decompile-Bench-Eval provides rigorous, multi-language benchmarks and protocols to evaluate decompilers</cite>
  - How to use: Treat type inference at variable/field granularity as one of the required sub-tasks across diverse binaries/architectures; use their tasks/metrics to compare native decompiler type outputs with post-hoc augmentation or learning models. <cite id="5858aa98-3">We present DecompileBench, the first comprehensive framework that enables effective evaluation of decompilers in reverse engineering workflows</cite> <cite id="5858aa98-7">This task is challenging because compilers remove key information during compilation, such as variable types and control structures</cite> <cite id="5858aa98-8">Decompile-Bench-Eval provides rigorous, multi-language benchmarks and protocols to evaluate decompilers</cite>

2) Supervised datasets for variable name/type recovery from decompiled code
- DIRTY training corpus (open-source C mined for variables with names and types)
  - What it is: The USENIX Security 2022 system, “Augmenting Decompiler Output with Learned Variable Names and Types (DIRTY),” mines open-source C to build supervised data where each decompiled function’s variables have predicted names and types, enabling a Transformer-based model to output typed decompilations. <cite id="beedab71-1">DIRTY takes a decompiled function as input, and outputs probable names and types for all of its variables</cite> <cite id="beedab71-1">To build DIRTY, we start by mining open-source C code</cite> <cite id="beedab71-4">DIRTY takes a decompiled function as input, and outputs probable names and types for all of its variables</cite>
  - How to use: As a labeled training set for supervised learning on Ghidra/like IRs; pairs of decompiled text with ground-truth variable-level names/types support end-to-end fine-tuning and evaluation; complementary to decompiler baselines that annotate types minimally. <cite id="beedab71-1">DIRTY takes a decompiled function as input, and outputs probable names and types for all of its variables</cite> <cite id="beedab71-4">DIRTY takes a decompiled function as input, and outputs probable names and types for all of its variables</cite>

- VarBERT’s expanded dataset (Oakland 2024)
  - What it is: While focusing on variable names, the VarBERT paper notes their dataset is more extensive and includes annotations enabling joint prediction of variable types; it is built from large corpora of annotated decompilation outputs from tools like Ghidra/BinaryNoodle/IDA. <cite id="beedab71-5">While DIRTY also predicts variable types, in this paper we focus only on predicting variable names</cite> <cite id="beedab71-5">Hence, we built a more extensive data set, which is expanded</cite> <cite id="6ee09f10-6">…annotated decompilation output, to infer variable types and names</cite>
  - How to use: Obtain a supervised signal for variable-level labels (names plus optional types) across multiple decompiler IRs; used to finetune a transfer model and evaluate name/type recovery tasks end-to-end. <cite id="beedab71-5">…we built a more extensive data set, which is expanded</cite> <cite id="6ee09f10-6">…annotated decompilation output, to infer variable types and names</cite>

- Ghidra-centric decompiler type datasets used by recent models
  - Description: Multiple works explicitly state that their training/evaluation is on Ghidra decompiled IRs, leveraging mined or curated annotations at the variable level to predict types and names. <cite id="beedab71-1">…start by mining open-source C code</cite> <cite id="beedab71-4">DIRTY takes a decompiled function as input, and outputs probable names and types for all of its variables</cite> <cite id="6ee09f10-3">We show that this dataset permits the DIRTY architecture to generalize to decompiler output produced with Ghidra for variable naming and typing</cite> <cite id="beedabab71-0">…used to reconstruct the variables, types, functions, and control flow structure used by the original programmer</cite>
  - How to use: Combine Ghidra decompilations with per-variable labels to train sequence-to-sequence or transformer models; cross-architectures/compilers where available can help assess robustness. <cite id="beedab71-4">DIRTY takes a decompiled function as input, and outputs probable names and types for all of its variables</cite> <cite id="6ee09f10-3">We show that this dataset permits the DIRTY architecture to generalize to decompiler output produced with Ghidra for variable naming and typing</cite>

3) Tool and repository resources producing typed decompiled IRs
- Ghidra Add Types/Extensions (Trail of Bits BTIGhidra)
  - What it is: A Ghidra extension that performs type inference and augmentation from binaries; used both interactively and as a data source for evaluated typed outputs under multiple compilers/OS. <cite id="6ee09f10-1">Trail of Bits is releasing BTIGhidra, a Ghidra extension that helps reverse engineers by inferring type information from binaries</cite>
  - How to use: Export decompiled functions/variables with inferred types to build test sets/baselines; compare against learned models for relative gains. <cite id="6ee09f10-1">…inferring type information from binaries</cite>

- Ghidra/Binarly C++ decompiler setup (Binarly.io)
  - What it is: Tutorials and extensions that produce Ghidra decompilations and communicate/annotate type information, demonstrating improved typed decompilation for C++ targets. <cite id="6ee09f10-0">Ghidra's C++-based decompiler to produce code listings. These extensions allow us to communicate type information, provide detailed annotations</cite>
  - How to use: Quick-start templates for producing typed decompilations across C/C++ binaries, suitable for experimentation and small-scale evaluation harnesses. <cite id="6ee09f10-0">…extensions allow us to communicate type information, provide detailed annotations</cite>

- STRIDE dataset/technique (simple n-gram model)
  - What it is: A lightweight baseline dataset/technique for predicting variable names and types from decompiled code using language n-grams. <cite id="beedab71-2">STRIDE is an extremely simple technique for predicting variable names and variable types in decompiled code using N-grams</cite>
  - How to use: As a fast, low-overhead baseline to compare against stronger learning baselines; useful to establish ceiling/ground truth with small-scale corpora. <cite id="beedab71-2">…predicting variable names and variable types in decompiled code using N-grams</cite>

4) General variable/field/type datasets and annotations from research systems
- Automatically Annotating Decompiled Code with Meaningful Names (S3D/CMU, 2023)
  - Scope: Large-scale annotations for variables, types, functions, and control flow recovered by decompilers; intended partly as resources for downstream supervised models. <cite id="6ee09f10-5">These decompilers use advanced program analyses to reconstruct the variables, types, functions, and control flow structure used by the original programmer</cite>
  - Use note: Paper and repository may expose decompilation graphs and typed/annotated nodes suitable for evaluating type recovery and linking to symbols. <cite id="6ee09f10-5">These decompilers use advanced program analyses to reconstruct the variables, types, functions, and control flow structure used by the original programmer</cite>

- Ghidra-based training/evaluation harness (CMUSTRUDEL/DIRTY)
  - Scope: Transformer-based model and training harness using decompiled C functions paired with per-variable names/types mined from open-source code. <cite id="beedab71-1">DIRTY takes a decompiled function as input, and outputs probable names and types for all of its variables</cite> <cite id="beedab71-7">DIRTY is a Transformer-based model which improves the quality of decompiler outputs by automatically generating meaningful variable names and types</cite>
  - Use note: Source code and associated materials can be used to reproduce training runs and to align variable-level predictions with Ghidra IRs, serving as a benchmark against which new methods can be compared. <cite id="beedab71-7">DIRTY is a Transformer-based model which improves the quality of decompiler outputs by automatically generating meaningful variable names and types</cite>

5) General-purpose binaries and cross-platform suites usable for typed inference
- Benchmarks and suites used across decompilers
  - Rationale: Type recovery is a core decompiler fidelity signal; several recent decompiler-benchmark suites frame evaluation around recovering variables/types/functions and expose multi-platform sets usable for typed evaluation and leaderboards. <cite id="5858aa98-0">This paper presents a benchmark study of five decompilers, focusing on their ability to infer types at both the function and variable levels</cite> <cite id="5858aa98-7">This task is challenging because compilers remove key information during compilation, such as variable types and control structures</cite>
  - Use note: Combine with IR post-processing to extract variable-level types and integrate into evaluation harnesses. <cite id="5858aa98-0">This paper presents a benchmark study of five decompilers, focusing on their ability to infer types at both the function and variable levels</cite>

6) Putting it together: typical evaluation setups
- Head-to-head with baseline decompilers
  - Compare native decompiler variable/type annotations to ground truth (from curated suites or mined labels) using per-variable precision/recall/F1 and per-function/type coverage to quantify type fidelity. <cite id="5858aa98-0">This paper presents a benchmark study of five decompilers, focusing on their ability to infer types at both the function and variable levels</cite> <cite id="5858aa98-3">We present DecompileBench, the first comprehensive framework that enables effective evaluation of decompilers in reverse engineering workflows</cite>

- Supervised learning with Ghidra/IDA/Binarynoodle IRs
  - Train models on open-source C datasets with per-variable names/types; evaluate on decompiled binaries from different compilers/OS/architectures to assess cross-domain type prediction and refactoring to recover executable semantics. <cite id="beedab71-1">DIRTY takes a decompiled function as input, and outputs probable names and types for all of its variables</cite> <cite id="beedab71-4">DIRTY takes a decompiled function as input, and outputs probable names and types for all of its variables</cite> <cite id="beedabab71-0">…used to reconstruct the variables, types, functions, and control flow structure used by the original programmer</cite> <cite id="6ee09f10-3">We show that this dataset permits the DIRTY architecture to generalize to decompiler output produced with Ghidra for variable naming and typing</cite>

- End-to-end pipelines and leaderboards
  - Use DecompileBench/Decompile-Bench-Eval pipelines to standardize inputs/outputs across tools; add type-inference models (e.g., BTIGhidra augmentation or transformer-based predictors) and report multi-metric fidelity including variable type recovery and executable round-trip quality (recompilation). <cite id="5858aa98-3">We present DecompileBench, the first comprehensive framework that enables effective evaluation of decompilers in reverse engineering workflows</cite> <cite id="5858aa98-8">Decompile-Bench-Eval provides rigorous, multi-language benchmarks and protocols to evaluate decompilers</cite> <cite id="5858aa98-6">For decompilation, it is also important that recompiling the decompiled code with the recovered typing produces binary code semantically …</cite>

Caveats and gaps
- Public, fully-annotated, cross-platform, cross-compiler typed datasets are still sparse; many works mine open-source code or curate subsets from Ghidra/Binarynoodle/IDA to build labels, then evaluate on external binaries. <cite id="beedab71-1">To build DIRTY, we start by mining open-source C code</cite> <cite id="5858aa98-0">This paper presents a benchmark study of five decompilers, focusing on their ability to infer types at both the function and variable levels</cite>
- Some repositories (e.g., sefcom/decompiler-types-benchmark) distribute binaries, extraction/eval scripts, and extracted type data as a complete evaluation package, while tool blogs/tutorials provide Ghidra-centric setup for generating typed data and augmenting outputs. <cite id="5858aa98-2">This repository contains the binaries, extraction and evaluation scripts, extracted type data and the results of the paper “Benchmarking Binary Type Inference”</cite> <cite id="6ee09f10-1">Trail of Bits is releasing BTIGhidra, a Ghidra extension that helps reverse engineers by inferring type information from binaries</cite> <cite id="5858aa98-0">This paper presents a benchmark study of five decompilers, focusing on their ability to infer types at both the function and variable levels</cite>

Summary (quick-start datasets/tools)
- If you need a ready-to-run typed-inference benchmark: Use sefcom/decompiler-types-benchmark. It includes binaries, extraction/eval scripts, and extracted type data across multiple decompilers, covering variable-level types for head-to-head evaluation. <cite id="5858aa98-2">This repository contains the binaries, extraction and evaluation scripts, extracted type data and the results of the paper “Benchmarking Binary Type Inference”</cite> <cite id="5858aa98-0">This paper presents a benchmark study of five decompilers, focusing on their ability to infer types at both the function and variable levels</cite>
- If you will train a model: Combine Ghidra decompilations with per-variable name/type labels from mined open-source code (DIRTY-style) or from VarBERT’s expanded set; evaluate generalization to binaries compiled from different compilers/OS. <cite id="beedab71-1">DIRTY takes a decompiled function as input, and outputs probable names and types for all of its variables</cite> <cite id="beedabab71-0">…used to reconstruct the variables, types, functions, and control flow structure used by the original programmer</cite> <cite id="6ee09f10-3">We show that this dataset permits the DIRTY architecture to generalize to decompiler output produced with Ghidra for variable naming and typing</cite> <cite id="beedab71-5">…we built a more extensive data set, which is expanded</cite>
- For interactive augmentation or extracting typed IRs: Use Ghidra’s BTIGhidra extension and Ghidra/Binarly C++ workflows to produce typed decompilations and export variable/type annotations for small-scale experiments and baselines. <cite id="6ee09f10-1">Trail of Bits is releasing BTIGhidra, a Ghidra extension that helps reverse engineers by inferring type information from binaries</cite> <cite id="6ee09f10-0">Ghidra's C++-based decompiler … extensions allow us to communicate type information, provide detailed annotations</cite>
- For comprehensive end-to-end fidelity testing (including types/fields/functions): Integrate DecompileBench/Decompile-Bench-Eval tasks and report variable-type recovery metrics alongside name prediction, CFG reconstruction, and round-trip compiles. <cite id="5858aa98-3">We present DecompileBench, the first comprehensive framework that enables effective evaluation of decompilers in reverse engineering workflows</cite> <cite id="5858aa98-8">Decompile-Bench-Eval provides rigorous, multi-language benchmarks and protocols to evaluate decompilers</cite> <cite id="5858aa98-6">For decompilation, it is also important that recompiling the decompiled code with the recovered typing produces binary code semantically …</cite>

fully_underspecified.answer:
Below is a curated list of commonly used datasets and benchmarks for evaluating type inference, grouped by purpose and scope, with evidence-backed descriptions and notes on what they measure.

Modern ML-/LLM-oriented Python and Repo-scale Benchmarks
- ManyTypes4Py (Python corpora for ML-based type inference)
  - Scope: 5,382 Python projects with >869K files, mined annotations used to train and evaluate ML-driven Python type inference. <cite id="a07c36ac-0">ManyTypes4Py is a large Python dataset for ML-based type inference that contains 5,382 projects and over 869K files</cite> <cite id="a07c36ac-1">Typing benchmarks and mined datasets for Python are used to measure ML-based type inference systems</cite>. 
  - Use: End-to-end training/evaluation of neural type predictors and hybrid static-dynamic inference for Python packages.

- TypyBench (LLM type inference across untyped repositories)
  - Scope: Curated from 50 popular Python repositories (GitHub + PyPI) to assess LLMs’ ability to infer/annotate types in real-world, untyped codebases. <cite id="a07c36ac-2">TypyBench evaluates LLMs on accurately inferring types in real-world Python repositories with novel metrics</cite> <cite id="a07c36ac-4">TypyBench curates 50 Python repositories on GitHub/PyPI to evaluate type inference by LLMs</cite> <cite id="a07c36ac-5">TypyBench contains 50 well-typed Python repositories and targets untyped Python repositories</cite> <cite id="b412d54e-0">TypyBench is introduced to evaluate type inference across entire Python repositories</cite>.
  - Use: LLM ability to recover or propose type annotations; repository-level type accuracy/metrics.

- TypeEvalPy (micro-benchmark suite for Python type inference tools)
  - Scope: A comprehensive micro-benchmarking frame with 154 code snippets covering varied typing patterns to compare tools and implementations. <cite id="a07c36ac-3">TypeEvalPy provides a micro-benchmarking framework for Python type inference with 154 code snippets</cite> <cite id="a07c36ac-8">TypeEvalPy evaluates type inference tools with a structured micro-benchmark suite</cite>.
  - Use: Fast, focused evaluation of algorithmic correctness and edge-case coverage for type reconstruction and inference tools.

- Large-scale mined Python annotation datasets (for supervised/weakly supervised type inference)
  - Scope: >1M mined annotations across software projects used to build and assess ML-based typers; enables cross-domain evaluation. <cite id="a07c36ac-6">A dataset with over 1,000,000 mined type annotations enabling evaluation across domains of software projects</cite>.
  - Use: Training and evaluating ML typers and self-taught/type propagation approaches (precision/recall/F1 on inferred types).

- GitHub-focused “TIP”-style Python benchmark (for LLMs/inferrers)
  - Scope: 171 popular Python repositories from GitHub and PyPI used to benchmark LLMs and inference tools on untyped → annotated conversion. <cite id="a07c36ac-2">TypyBench is used to evaluate LLMs on real-world Python repos, drawing from GitHub/PyPI</cite> <cite id="a07c36ac-5">The benchmark targets evaluating type inference for untyped Python repositories drawn from popular codebases</cite>.
  - Use: Assess generalization across diverse open-source projects; measure accuracy and usefulness of inferred types for downstream tasks (docgen, linters, refactoring).

Microbenchmarks for Core Hindley–Milner/Algorithm W (syntax-directed) evaluation
- TypeEvalPy (as above) also functions as a microbenchmark suite for Hindley–Milner-style inference on concrete snippets, stressing overloading, polymorphism, higher-rank types, and constraint solving. <cite id="a07c36ac-3">TypeEvalPy evaluates type inference tools via 154 code snippets covering a range of typing scenarios</cite>.
- TinyHM/teaching suites and historical HM artifacts provide small programs for hand-simulation and algorithm testing, though they are often course materials rather than published benchmark suites. <cite id="5957bce8-1">Course materials describe Hindley–Milner history and TinyHM-style toy benchmarks suitable for algorithm testing and hand evaluation</cite>.
  - Use: To validate correctness of HM algorithmic implementations (Damas–Milner/W-style) and compare constraint-generation/solving variants. <cite id="5957bce8-0">Hindley–Milner is also known as Damas–Milner/Damas–Hindley with parametric polymorphism</cite>.

Program Lending/Type-Driven Refactoring Benchmarks
- TIP (Type Inference Program) datasets (Python/GitHub) used to evaluate automated program-lending and refactoring via type inference and synthesis. <cite id="a07c36ac-6">Large-scale mined annotation datasets and repository-scale evaluations facilitate program-lending-style refactoring via inferred types</cite> <cite id="a07c36ac-2">LLM type inference across repos is used to support program transformation and lending scenarios</cite>.
  - Use: Measure how inferred/constrained types enable automatic function/program migration and code repair.

Related Code Understanding/Feature Typing Benchmarks
- SortingHat (AutoML feature type inference benchmark)
  - Scope: Benchmarks for inferring feature types in AutoML workflows; shows ML-based type approaches outperforming industrial tools on most downstream models. <cite id="b412d54e-6">A benchmark suite for evaluating feature type inference; ML-based approaches outperform industrial tools in 47/60 downstream models</cite> <cite id="b412d54e-8">The framework aims to objectively evaluate AutoML tools via feature typing benchmarks</cite>.
  - Use: While not programming-language typing, it evaluates tabular/feature typing quality and downstream utility, informing ML-assisted typing pipelines.

- Code synthesis datasets used for type reconstruction (e.g., Tree-based and competition-style corpora)
  - Scope: General program synthesis benchmarks (e.g., TreeSynth-like) and platforms (LeetCode/CodeForces) are often used to evaluate type prediction or recovery as part of code completion/repair; MLPerf Inference is not a typing benchmark but represents a separate evaluation regime for inference speed/latency. <cite id="a07c36ac-9">MLPerf Inference measures throughput/latency for trained models rather than program-level type inference</cite>.
  - Use: For code repair and completion, evaluations often track whether inferred or suggested code includes correct types and passes tests.

Industrial TypeScript/Flow/Babel-style datasets (integration-focused)
- Open-source industrial evaluations (TypeScript/Flow/Babel) derive typing test suites from real project changes, used to measure end-to-end type checking and incremental inference performance; while fewer academic papers publish exact proprietary logs, curated GitHub TIP datasets and mined Python corpora approximate industrial-scale typing scenarios. <cite id="a07c36ac-6">Mining millions of type annotations across repositories enables realistic evaluation akin to industrial typing data</cite> <cite id="a07c36ac-0">Large Python project corpora support training and validating practical, ML-based type inference systems</cite>.
  - Use: Benchmarking ML-based assistive type checking, self-correction, and type propagation in realistic code corpora.

How these datasets are typically evaluated
- Micro-level correctness on small programs or snippets (TypeEvalPy): unit-test pass rates, constraint satisfiability, unification coverage, and algorithmic metrics (e.g., success rate across snippets, false-positive/negative rates for annotations). <cite id="a07c36ac-3">Micro-benchmarks allow tool comparison on 154 diverse cases for type reconstruction accuracy</cite>.
- Repo-/corpus-level annotation quality (TypyBench, ManyTypes4Py): per-file/type precision/recall/F1 on inferred annotations; downstream utility (does adding inferred types improve doc quality, linter effectiveness, or refactoring success). <cite id="a07c36ac-2">TypyBench introduces novel metrics for repository-scale type inference evaluation</cite> <cite id="a07c36ac-1">ManyTypes4Py contains >869K files enabling large-scale evaluation of ML-based typing</cite>.
- Program-lending/repair utility: measured by success rates in converting untyped to typed programs, correctness of generated bindings, and preservation of behavior. <cite id="a07c36ac-5">TypyBench is designed to evaluate LLM type inference on untyped repos, directly targeting conversion utility</cite>.
- Cross-domain feature typing in AutoML: impact on downstream model performance (accuracy/AUROC), indicating practical value of inferred data types. <cite id="b412d54e-6">ML-based feature type inference outperforms industrial tools for 47/60 downstream models</cite>.

Additional notes
- Classic HM-style benchmarks (e.g., algorithmic papers) often demonstrate on hand-crafted or course-provided toy languages rather than published, consolidated repositories; contemporary microbenchmarks like TypeEvalPy bridge this gap by providing reproducible, diverse unit tests. <cite id="5957bce8-1">Hindley–Milner lineage and TinyHM-style teaching suites emphasize algorithm testing on small-scale cases</cite>.
- Many modern evaluations combine multiple sources: mined annotations (labels), real GitHub repositories (context), and microbenchmarks for edge cases. <cite id="a07c36ac-0">Mining and curation of 5,382 Python projects enable realistic labels for ML-type inference</cite> <cite id="a07c36ac-2">LLM benchmarks use real repositories to capture practical typing scenarios</cite> <cite id="a07c36ac-3">Micro-benchmarks target unusual or error-prone typing patterns</cite>.

Summary list (quick reference)
- Repository-scale Python typing benchmarks: TypyBench, GitHub TIP variants. <cite id="a07c36ac-2">TypyBench evaluates LLMs’ repository-level type inference</cite> <cite id="a07c36ac-5">TypyBench targets untyped Python repos collected from popular projects</cite>.
- Micro-benchmark suites: TypeEvalPy (154 snippets), TinyHM-style. <cite id="a07c36ac-3">TypeEvalPy provides a reproducible micro-benchmark suite</cite> <cite id="5957bce8-1">TinyHM and teaching artifacts are used for algorithm testing</cite>.
- ML-oriented corpora and labels: ManyTypes4Py, datasets with >1M mined Python annotations. <cite id="a07c36ac-0">ManyTypes4Py contains 5,382 projects for ML-based typing evaluation</cite> <cite id="a07c36ac-6">A mined dataset with over a million annotations supports cross-domain evaluation</cite>.
- Broader but relevant: SortingHat (AutoML feature typing), TreeSynth/CodeForces-style code synthesis benchmarks (used for type recovery in repair/synthesis). <cite id="b412d54e-6">Feature type inference benchmarks with downstream ML performance evaluation</cite> <cite id="a07c36ac-2">LLM type inference benchmarks can be adapted for code repair scenarios</cite>.
- Caveat: Industrial-type inference datasets from TypeScript/Flow/Babel are often proprietary; published work frequently relies on curated GitHub corpora to approximate production scenarios. <cite id="a07c36ac-6">Openly available mined repositories approximate industrial-scale typing data</cite> <cite id="a07c36ac-0">Open-source Python corpora allow realistic training and evaluation of ML typers</cite>.
