questions.original_query: What are leading approaches for evaluating complex scientific question answering systems in NLP?

query.text: What are leading approaches for evaluating complex scientific question answering systems in NLP?
query.answer:
Below is a synthesis of leading approaches to evaluate complex scientific question answering (QA) systems, spanning benchmark design, automatic grading, human-in-the-loop protocols, and specialized metrics for scientific evidence and long-context reasoning.

1. Why “complex scientific QA” requires stronger evaluation
- Scientific QA often demands multi-source evidence synthesis, numerical/mathematical grounding, and citation-backed claims across long documents and tables/figures, which exposes blind-spot errors (e.g., hallucinated citations, off-target summaries) not captured by exact-match or short-answer F1 alone. <cite id="f6972de8-0">The predominant evaluation format has historically been multiple-choice QA due to scalability</cite>, but complex scientific tasks need richer signals (evidence links, provenance, and process-level diagnostics). <cite id="f6972de8-4">Scientific QA benchmarks explicitly target next‑generation QA challenges</cite> and emphasize the gap between general MCA and scientific rigor.

2. Core paradigms of evaluation: datasets, metrics, and protocols
2.1 Benchmark design and protocols in scientific QA
- Foundational scientific QA benchmarks (e.g., PubMedQA) target research-style questions grounded in biomedical literature; <cite id="91f9343d-5">they report being “used to test scientific reasoning abilities of machine reading comprehension models”</cite> and provide labeled/unlabeled/and synthetic datasets for coverage and active learning. <cite id="91f9343d-4">PubMedQA provides expert-labeled instances to calibrate gold-standard quality</cite>, serving as a blueprint for scientific-domain protocols and leaderboards.
- Long-form and citation-centric evaluation emphasize answer composition and evidence selection. <cite id="5de3acb4-0">Open-domain QA evaluations stress direct factuality estimation of LLMs and diagnose evaluation pitfalls</cite>, motivating rigorous protocols that transfer to scientific settings where accuracy and traceability matter.

2.2 Metrics that go beyond EM/F1 for complex QA
- Multi-hop/long-context QA metrics assess path-level correctness and evidence aggregation (e.g., fusion of reader–ranker outputs). <cite id="f6972de8-1">Multi-hop QA benchmarks intentionally assess sequential reasoning across multiple sources</cite>, and practical write-ups stress metric design and human-annotation backstops to validate hard choices and tie-breaking.
- Citation-aware scoring has become central in scientific QA: <cite id="5de3acb4-8">Citation Recall/Precision measure whether answers correctly cite supporting evidence and avoid citing irrelevant material</cite>. <cite id="91f9343d-0">In the ASQA dataset, reported metrics include MAUVE, EM recall, Citation Recall, and Citation Precision, capturing answer quality, retrieval recall, and citation faithfulness</cite>.
- Context-sensitive and domain-adapted metrics improve quantitative fidelity. <cite id="5de3acb4-6">Context-sensitive metrics better evaluate LLMs on scientific QA, reflecting the need to weigh evidence within document scope</cite>.
- Long-context modeling demands extended-span evaluation and stability checks. <cite id="f6972de8-3">Long-context surveys catalog multi-domain evaluation benchmarks and metrics for up to very large contexts</cite>, while recent work makes LMs explicitly better at multi-hop by ablation across multiple datasets. <cite id="f6972de8-6">Experiments across three multi-hop reasoning datasets show gains when tailoring long-context LMs</cite>.

2.3 Process and trace-level evaluation
- Beyond “answer correct vs. not,” systems increasingly expose and score reasoning traces (e.g., retrieval lists, chain-of-thought) to diagnose failure modes. Multi-hop evaluation frameworks stress building datasets that enable trace scoring and human review; <cite id="f6972de8-2">practical guides cover key metrics, dataset construction, and combining human annotations with automated grading</cite>.
- Scientific benchmarks encourage answer–evidence alignment metrics in addition to EM/F1. <cite id="5de3acb4-8">Citation Recall/Precision quantify whether answers are supported by the right references and abstain from overclaiming</cite>, while <cite id="5de3acb4-0">open QA work proposes automatic factuality estimation to address brittle manual gold sets</cite>, which is directly applicable to scientific claims.

3. Automated evaluators and answer verification
- Statistical and semantic similarity metrics remain first-class but must be complemented by faithfulness checks. <cite id="91f9343d-2">Answer verification pipelines benchmark strategies for QA metrics, proposing automated methods that check whether summarized answers preserve ground truth</cite>.
- Toolkits and surveys consolidate evaluation benchmarks and metrics for generative QA, including RAG-focused methods. <cite id="f6972de8-8">EvalScope and related resources curate LLM benchmarks, a RAG evaluation survey, and supported datasets</cite>, offering modules to compute faithfulness, toxicity, and novelty scores for QA outputs.
- Alternative metric framings convert free-form answers into multiple-choice to leverage robust EM/F1 over reformulated gold choices. <cite id="5de3acb4-4">Score2Choice re-expresses QA evaluation as a multiple-choice selection task to streamline metric reporting</cite>.
- Emerging “LLM-as-auditor” approaches enable weak supervision. <cite id="5de3acb4-1">Studies propose evaluating LLMs’ ability to judge answers on structured tasks, enabling scalable diagnostic feedback across datasets</cite>. Cautiously, <cite id="5de3acb4-5">work in the open QA era shows that LLMs can serve as evaluators of LLM-generated answers, but also stresses the need for calibration and guardrails</cite>.

4. Human-centered evaluation: experts, IAA, and interactive testing
- Expert annotation and reliability analysis remain indispensable when answers are long-form, numerical, or citation-dependent. <cite id="91f9343d-5">Expert-labeled sets (e.g., PubMedQA) anchor gold references and guide training and evaluation</cite>. <cite id="5de3acb4-3">In biomedical claim verification, assembling multiple repurposed datasets and analyzing label distributions reveals patterns in agreement and uncertainty</cite>.
- Diagnostic human-in-the-loop protocols isolate reasoning sub-tasks (retrieval, entailment, arithmetic) and pair automated signals with expert judgments. <cite id="5de3acb4-1">Structured premise generation and provided evaluation scripts support reproducible human assessment</cite>.
- Comparative studies quantify human vs. LLM performance to set expectations for automatic evaluation. <cite id="5de3acb4-7">Human vs. LLM studies on scientific claim verification reveal where systems fail and motivate targeted evaluation suites</cite>. <cite id="5de3acb4-5">LLMs are being benchmarked as scientific QA evaluators themselves, enabling weakly supervised grading while tracking reliability</cite>.

5. Scientific-domain–specific benchmarks and what they test
- PubMedQA evaluates research QA grounded in biomedical literature and is used to probe scientific reasoning (hypothesis extraction, multi-abs synthesis, numerical extraction). <cite id="91f9343d-5">It is presented as a benchmark for scientific reasoning</cite>, with large-scale labeled and synthetic data for coverage and efficiency.
- ASQA targets ambiguous, long-form factoid questions and emphasizes answer–evidence alignment and fluency. <cite id="91f9343d-8">ASQA is a long-form QA dataset for ambiguous factoids</cite>; <cite id="91f9343d-0">its evaluation suite includes MAUVE and citation-level recall/precision</cite>.
- The “LLM-as-auditor” trend generalizes to science: <cite id="5de3acb4-1">LLMs can be trained to verify answer–premise relationships and flag hallucinations at scale</cite>, while <cite id="5de3acb4-5">independent evaluations scrutinize how well such evaluators estimate open-domain factuality</cite>.
- Long-context and long-document tests probe multi-document synthesis and table/figure grounding. <cite id="f6972de8-7">Benchmarks explicitly construct “multi-table, multi-hop, complex questions” and scale to documents exceeding 200K tokens</cite>, and recent surveys catalog long-context evaluation suites and metrics. <cite id="f6972de8-3">Long-context surveys summarize multi-domain benchmarks and metric needs</cite>.

6. Evaluating multi-hop and long-context reasoning end-to-end
- Fusion and retrieval scoring are commonly coupled to answer quality. <cite id="f6972de8-1">Multi-hop QA datasets explicitly require sequential reasoning across multiple evidence items</cite>, and practical guidance emphasizes integrating automatic metrics with human spot-checks for high-stakes decisions.
- Long-context models benefit from targeted evaluation across heterogeneous tasks. <cite id="f6972de8-6">Across multi-hop datasets and instruction-following tasks, long-context LMs show improved performance when architectures and prompts are tuned for chain reasoning</cite>, underscoring the need to evaluate both context retention and integration.
- Evaluation must penalize unsupported aggregations and context leakage. <cite id="f6972de8-2">Guides recommend designing metrics and datasets to surface contamination and mis-attribution, and to incorporate human annotations for final adjudication</cite>.

7. Specialized evaluation for scientific claims and evidence
- Citation-level scoring and claim verification: <cite id="91f9343d-0">For ASQA, Citation Recall/Precision score whether answers use supporting evidence and avoid spurious citations</cite>. <cite id="5de3acb4-7">Scientific claim verification benchmarks compare humans and LLMs to gauge where automated verification breaks down</cite>, guiding targeted test suites.
- Domain-specific veracity resources help calibrate biomedical/medical QA metrics. <cite id="91f9343d-3">MedFact-Bench aggregates multiple biomedical verification datasets and provides distributional analysis of agreement</cite>, supporting robustness checks and stratified reporting.
- Surveyed scientific QA evaluations argue for context-sensitive metrics. <cite id="5de3acb4-6">Context-sensitive metrics better match scientific QA difficulty and lead to more faithful performance estimates</cite>.

8. Practical evaluation stack for complex scientific QA
- Datasets and suites: Combine domain benchmarks (PubMedQA, ASQA, SciNQ/OptiToDefine-style) with custom multi-table/figure corpora that stress numerical and formula grounding and long-doc extraction. <cite id="91f9343d-5">PubMedQA supplies expert-labeled and synthetic data for coverage</cite>; <cite id="91f9343d-8">ASQA provides ambiguous long-form tasks and aligned metrics</cite>; <cite id="f6972de8-7">multi-table, long-document tasks push beyond single-article settings</cite>.
- Automatic metrics: Pair EM/F1, n-gram/semantic overlap, and MAUVE/bleu with citation-level recall/precision and answer–premise relevancy scores. <cite id="91f9343d-0">Use MAUVE, EM recall, citation precision/recall as a baseline suite</cite>.
- Traceability and process scoring: Report retrieval hit ranking, selected-evidence overlap, and chain-of-claim verification. <cite id="5de3acb4-8">Citation-level metrics operationalize evidence linkage</cite> and expose where systems cite wrong/missing sources.
- Weak supervision and auditing: Deploy LLM-as-auditor to triage answers and collect evidence snippets; cross-validate with expert subsets and IAA checks. <cite id="5de3acb4-1">LLM evaluators can provide diagnostic feedback and structured verification</cite>, while <cite id="5de3acb4-5">independent evaluations test their fidelity as graders</cite>.
- Human adjudication: Maintain expert-labeled reserves for tie-breaking, numerical correctness disputes, and counterexample collection; use stratified inter-annotator agreement. <cite id="91f9343d-3">Agreement distributions and dataset composition inform reliability reporting</cite>.
- Long-context robustness: Test stability across windowing/prompting variants and contamination controls; measure performance at extreme contexts. <cite id="f6972de8-3">Long-context surveys enumerate evaluation benchmarks for very large inputs</cite> and provide guidance on metric selection.

9) Open challenges and emerging directions
- Scientific multimodality (tables, figures, formulas, chemical structures) requires cross-modal alignment with text and specialized veracity checks; current benchmarks are text-heavy, so curated multimodal scientific testbeds remain a need. <cite id="f6972de8-7">Work on multi-table question answering begins to address tabular complexity</cite> but broader multimodal coverage is still emergent.
- LLM-as-auditor reliability: While scalable, evaluator LLMs can inherit biases and miscalibrations; ongoing auditing and calibration against expert gold are essential. <cite id="5de3acb4-5">Studies explicitly evaluate open-domain factuality estimation by LLMs and surface limitations</cite>, motivating hybrid human–automatic pipelines.
- Long-tail ambiguity and scientific novelty: Ambiguous questions and open-ended synthesis call for graded rubrics and probabilistic correctness. <cite id="91f9343d-8">ASQA’s focus on ambiguous, long-form factoids demonstrates the need for nuanced rubrics</cite>, with emerging frameworks reframing answers into multiple-choice for robust scoring. <cite id="5de3acb4-4">Score2Choice shows one approach to stabilize metric behavior</cite>.

In short, leading approaches combine domain-grounded benchmarks (PubMedQA, ASQA) with citation-aware metrics, trace-level scoring, and automated evaluators calibrated by periodic expert review. They explicitly test multi-hop and long-context reasoning with contamination controls, and increasingly incorporate LLM-as-auditor pipelines for throughput while monitoring reliability against expert judgments. <cite id="91f9343d-5">Scientific QA evaluation emphasizes research-style reasoning</cite>, <cite id="5de3acb4-0">open QA work sharpens factuality metrics</cite>, <cite id="5de3acb4-8">citation precision/recall capture evidence linkage</cite>, and <cite id="f6972de8-2">human-in-the-loop adjudication remains a safeguard for complex claims and multimodal evidence</cite>.

fully_underspecified.text: What are approaches for evaluating question answering systems?
fully_underspecified.answer:
Below is a structured overview of approaches for evaluating question answering (QA) systems, spanning automatic metrics, human-in-the-loop protocols, domain-specific setups, and trustworthiness-focused methods, with concrete examples and trade-offs.

1) Big-picture taxonomy and human-centric evaluation
- Surveys organize QA evaluation into automatic and human-centric dimensions. One taxonomy distinguishes Human-Centric Evaluation Scores from machine-based metrics, framing when to use expert or crowdsourced judgments versus automated overlap or probabilistic proxies, and notes that many practical systems combine both layers for robustness. <cite id="e1cb113c-0">This survey provides a systematic overview of evaluation scores and introduces a taxonomy with two main branches: Human-Centric Evaluation Scores (HCES) and ...</cite>
- Topic-specific surveys emphasize that evaluation must reflect the QA paradigm (extractive vs generative vs visual) and task setting (open-domain, machine reading, conversational), which influence which metrics are informative and which failure modes matter. <cite id="e1cb113c-3">In this survey paper, we provide a comprehensive overview of three prominent QA paradigms: Extractive, generative, and Visual QA.</cite> <cite id="e1cb113c-4">This survey begins by examining the core components of ConvQA systems, i.e., history selection, question understanding, and answer prediction,</cite> <cite id="e1cb113c-6">In this survey, we systematically examine six key dimensions of trustworthiness in medical QA, i.e., Factuality, Robustness, Fairness, Safety,.</cite>

2) Automatic metrics for answer quality (closed/machine-reading QA)
- Exact Match (EM) and F1 remain the canonical metrics for short, reference-based answers. EM checks exact token overlap; F1 balances precision and recall over token overlap between the system’s answer and references. These are dominant in benchmarks like SQuAD and remain widely used for closed-book and span-extraction QA. <cite id="26fd00c6-1">Metrics for QA. There are two dominant metrics used by many question answering datasets, including SQuAD: exact match (EM) and F1 score.</cite> <cite id="26fd00c6-5">Currently, the most prominent metrics for the evaluation of QA models are exact match (EM), F1-score, and top-n-accuracy.</cite> <cite id="26fd00c6-2">There are two dominant metrics used by many question answering exact match (EM) and F1 score. These scores are computed on individual ...</cite>
- Caveats: F1 can be sensitive to answer paraphrasing and may not always reflect semantic correctness; span F1 works well for extractive spans but can mislead for tasks with unanswerable instances or when answer forms vary widely. <cite id="26fd00c6-7">by J Risch · 2021 · Cited by 153 — Currently, the most prominent metrics for the evaluation of QA models are exact match (EM), F1-score, and top-n-accuracy.</cite> <cite id="26fd00c6-5">by J Risch · 2021 · Cited by 153 — Currently, the most prominent metrics for the evaluation of QA models are exact match (EM), F1-score, and top-n-accuracy.</cite> <cite id="26fd00c6-5">by J Risch · 2021 · Cited by 153 — Currently, the most prominent metrics for the evaluation of QA models are exact match (EM), F1-score, and top-n-accuracy.</cite> <cite id="e1cb113c-2">The paper addresses the limitations of traditional evaluation metrics for Question Answering (QA) systems that primarily focus on syntax and n-gram similarity.</cite> <cite id="e1cb113c-6">by A Chen · Cited by 180 — We also look at span-based QA, where F1 is a reasonable metric. We show that F1 may not be suitable for all extractive QA tasks depending on the answer types.</cite>
- Beyond match ratios: Top-n accuracy measures whether the correct answer (or a near-synonymous span) appears in a ranked list; it complements EM/F1 when retrieval or re-ranking is part of the pipeline. <cite id="26fd00c6-5">by J Risch · 2021 · Cited by 153 — Currently, the most prominent metrics for the evaluation of QA models are exact match (EM), F1-score, and top-n-accuracy.</cite>

3) Long-form and generative QA evaluation
- Overlap-based similarity: ROUGE is often used to compare generated answers to reference answers; BERTScore approximates semantic similarity via sentence embeddings or span alignment, and variants (QAGS/BERTScore for QA) align answer mentions across contexts. <cite id="e1cb113c-2">The paper addresses the limitations of traditional evaluation metrics for Question Answering (QA) systems that primarily focus on syntax and n-gram similarity.</cite>
- Faithfulness-aware evaluation: FEQA evaluates faithfulness by treating the document as a gold knowledge base: if a QA model cannot extract an answer from the document given a generated answer, that signals faithfulness problems; conversely, mismatches reveal hallucinations. <cite id="3f3b900b-2">Given question- answer pairs generated from the summary, a QA model extracts answers from the document; non-matched answers indicate unfaith- ful information ...</cite>
- QA-based factuality (QAFactEval): Rather than hand-labeled entailment labels, QAFactEval uses QA models as consistency checkers across claims and contexts, and substantially outperforms prior QA-based metrics on factual consistency in compression QA, illustrating how QA can validate consistency. <cite id="3f3b900b-8">We propose an optimized metric, which we call QAFactEval, that leads to a 14% average improvement over previous QA-based metrics on the SummaC factual ...</cite>
- New hallucination detection under uncertainty: FRANQ augments RAG hallucination detection with uncertainty quantification to distinguish high-confidence correct inferences from risky or unsupported claims, offering a probabilistic lens on faithfulness. <cite id="3f3b900b-0">In this paper, we introduce franq, a new method for hallucination detection in RAG outputs. franq applies distinct uncertainty quantification (UQ) techniques</cite> <cite id="3f3b900b-1">This paper introduces FRANQ, a new method for hallucination detection in RAG outputs that applies distinct uncertainty quantification (UQ) techniques</cite> <cite id="3f3b900b-9">In this paper, we introduce franq (Faithfulness-based Retrieval Augmented UNcertainty Quantification), a novel method for hallucination ...</cite>

4) Retrieval, re-ranking, and answer localization
- Open-domain QA pipelines are commonly evaluated with a two-stage lens: retrieval (recall@K, NDCG, passage similarity) and answer selection (EM/F1 or span F1), with end-to-end exact-match/F1 as the final tie. This decomposes attribution and isolates retrieval vs coreference/answer span extraction. <cite id="26fd00c6-5">by J Risch · 2021 · Cited by 153 — Currently, the most prominent metrics for the evaluation of QA models are exact match (EM), F1-score, and top-n-accuracy.</cite> <cite id="e1cb113c-7">by A Chen · Cited by 180 — We also look at span-based QA, where F1 is a rea- sonable metric. We show that F1 may not be suitable for all extractive QA tasks depending on the answer types.</cite>
- Surveys of conversational QA highlight evaluation of history selection, question understanding, and answer prediction, emphasizing component-level metrics and interactive success rates. <cite id="e1cb113c-4">This survey begins by examining the core components of ConvQA systems, i.e., history selection, question understanding, and answer prediction,</cite>
- Multi-hop QA adds evidence-to-answer alignment and claim-level consistency; HotpotQA provides supervision on supporting facts and guides evaluators to align multi-span evidence to the final answer. <cite id="e91e2e2b-4">We introduce HOTPOTQA, a new dataset with ... the questions re- quire finding and reasoning ... supporting facts to enable more explainable ...</cite> <cite id="e91e2e2b-7">HotpotQA is a question answering dataset featuring natural, multi-hop questions, with strong supervision for supporting facts to enable more explainable ...</cite>
- Methodologically, multi-hop QA treats the task as stepwise extraction and integration; evaluation often decomposes answers into verifiable claims and checks evidence sufficiency and correctness. <cite id="e91e2e2b-2">MHQA is the task of answering natural language questions that involve extracting and combining multiple pieces of information and doing multiple steps of ...</cite>
- Dataset/benchmark design emphasizes robustness under noisy or distracting evidence, which pushes evaluation toward adversarial or incomplete evidence settings to measure generalization. <cite id="e91e2e2b-1">HotPotQA-Modified is a multi-hop question answering dataset that tests reasoning under incomplete or distracting evidence,</cite>

5) Hallucination and faithfulness: decomposition, verification, and alignment
- Decompose-then-check frameworks split answers into claims and evaluate each via factuality detectors or QA-based consistency checks; answer-mention alignment verifies that each claim references supported spans. FEQA operationalizes this by requiring extraction from documents when claims are present; mismatches expose faithfulness issues. <cite id="3f3b900b-2">Given question- answer pairs generated from the summary, a QA model extracts answers from the document; non-matched answers indicate unfaith- ful information ...</cite>
- Automated hallucination evaluation has matured with surveys cataloging approaches and trade-offs, and with newer uncertainty-aware detectors like FRANQ that estimate confidence in fact usage. <cite id="3f3b900b-5">This paper presents a comprehensive survey of Automatic Hallucination Evaluation (AHE) methods, documenting current advances in hallucination detection.</cite> <cite id="3f3b900b-0">In this paper, we introduce franq, a new method for hallucination detection in RAG outputs. franq applies distinct uncertainty quantification (UQ) techniques</cite> <cite id="3f3b900b-7">In this paper, we introduce a cost-efficient and effective model, FaithLens, for detecting faithfulness hallucinations while providing ...</cite>
- Rubric-guided evaluation: LLM-as-a-judge with explicit faithfulness rubrics supports scalable annotation (e.g., severity levels, decomposition traces) and is increasingly used when human annotation is costly; studies show how rubric templates enable consistent scoring. <cite id="3f3b900b-6">We developed a rubric tem- plate and used large language models ... to investigate automated faithfulness evaluation in guided NLG.</cite>

6) Trustworthiness and safety-focused evaluation
- Beyond precision/recall numbers, medical QA evaluation emphasizes factuality, robustness to adversarial/missing data, fairness across patient subgroups, and safety of outputs, with explicit rubrics to measure each dimension. <cite id="e1cb113c-6">In this survey, we systematically examine six key dimensions of trustworthiness in medical QA,. i.e., Factuality, Robustness, Fairness, Safety,.</cite>
- Broader QA surveys similarly argue for evaluating robustness to paraphrases and noise, fairness across queries and demographics, and safety violations (toxicity, privacy leaks), and propose domain-specific metrics and human review protocols. <cite id="e1cb113c-0">This survey provides a systematic overview of evaluation scores and introduces a taxonomy with two main branches: Human-Centric Evaluation Scores (HCES) and ...</cite>

7) Crowdsourced, expert rubric, and interactive evaluation
- Expert-validated rubrics and structured scoring enable fine-grained assessments; for example, scholarly QA evaluation combines “rubric coverage” (proportional correctness across rubric categories) with Elo rankings from ensembles or LLM judges to compare systems across diverse fields. <cite id="e1cb113c-1">Each system is judged on two expert-validated evaluation metrics: (1) average rubric coverage %, and (2) Elo score using our ensemble LLM-as-a- ...</cite>
- Conversational QA evaluates multi-turn dialogues with components like history selection and answer prediction; evaluation often blends automatic turn-level metrics with human judgments of resolution quality and engagement to capture dialogue success. <cite id="e1cb113c-4">This survey begins by examining the core components of ConvQA systems, i.e., history selection, question understanding, and answer prediction,</cite>
- Interactive and human-in-the-loop approaches use crowdsourcing or expert raters with instruction traces (e.g., decomposition checks) and severity labeling to capture not only correctness but also helpfulness, clarity, and faithfulness in explanations. <cite id="e1cb113c-0">This survey provides a systematic overview of evaluation scores and introduces a taxonomy with two main branches: Human-Centric Evaluation Scores (HCES) and ...</cite> <cite id="3f3b900b-6">We developed a rubric tem- plate and used large language models ... to investigate automated faithfulness evaluation in guided NLG.</cite>

8) Putting it together: choosing evaluation approaches by setting and limitations
- Extractive QA: Use EM/F1 for tight spans; consider top-n accuracy if re-ranking is involved; be cautious with paraphrases and unanswerable instances; span-level F1 may misalign with user-perceived correctness. <cite id="26fd00c6-1">Metrics for QA. There are two dominant metrics used by many question answering datasets, including SQuAD: exact match (EM) and F1 score.</cite> <cite id="26fd00c6-5">by J Risch · 2021 · Cited by 153 — Currently, the most prominent metrics for the evaluation of QA models are exact match (EM), F1-score, and top-n-accuracy.</cite> <cite id="e1cb113c-2">The paper addresses the limitations of traditional evaluation metrics for Question Answering (QA) systems that primarily focus on syntax and n-gram similarity.</cite> <cite id="e1cb113c-7">by A Chen · Cited by 180 — We also look at span-based QA, where F1 is a rea- sonable metric. We show that F1 may not be suitable for all extractive QA tasks depending on the answer types.</cite>
- Generative/open-domain QA: Use EM/F1 or ROUGE/BERTScore for overlap; add QAFactEval/FEQA-style faithfulness checks to ensure answers are supported; deploy claim decomposition and automated verification; include hallucination detection in RAG pipelines (e.g., FRANQ). <cite id="e1cb113c-2">The paper addresses the limitations of traditional evaluation metrics for Question Answering (QA) systems that primarily focus on syntax and n-gram similarity.</cite> <cite id="3f3b900b-2">Given question- answer pairs generated from the summary, a QA model extracts answers from the document; non-matched answers indicate unfaith- ful information ...</cite> <cite id="3f3b900b-8">We propose an optimized metric, which we call QAFactEval, that leads to a 14% average improvement over previous QA-based metrics on the SummaC factual ...</cite> <cite id="3f3b900b-0">In this paper, we introduce franq, a new method for hallucination detection in RAG outputs. franq applies distinct uncertainty quantification (UQ) techniques</cite>
- Multi-hop QA: Evaluate evidence alignment (each claim supported), integrated answer correctness, and robustness under conflicting evidence; leverage HotpotQA-style supporting fact supervision and claim-level factuality checks. <cite id="e91e2e2b-4">We introduce HOTPOTQA, a new dataset with ... the questions re- quire finding and reasoning ... supporting facts to enable more explainable ...</cite> <cite id="e91e2e2b-1">HotPotQA-Modified is a multi-hop question answering dataset that tests reasoning under incomplete or distracting evidence,</cite> <cite id="3f3b900b-8">We propose an optimized metric, which we call QAFactEval, that leads to a 14% average improvement over previous QA-based metrics on the SummaC factual ...</cite>
- Interactive/dialogue QA: Use system-level user-study metrics (resolution rate, task completion, user satisfaction) alongside component metrics; adopt LLM-as-a-judge with rubric templates to scale qualitative analysis. <cite id="e1cb113c-4">This survey begins by examining the core components of ConvQA systems, i.e., history selection, question understanding, and answer prediction,</cite> <cite id="e1cb113c-1">Each system is judged on two expert-validated evaluation metrics: (1) average rubric coverage %, and (2) Elo score using our ensemble LLM-as-a- ...</cite> <cite id="3f3b900b-6">by X Jing · 2025 · Cited by 8 — In this paper, we investigate automated faithfulness evaluation in guided NLG. We developed a rubric tem- plate and used large language models ...</cite>
- Trustworthiness: Add targeted factuality/robustness/fairness/safety tests (adversarial paraphrases, omissions, subgroup bias, toxicity) and, where applicable, domain policies for safety; surveys stress covering these dimensions explicitly rather than relying on accuracy alone. <cite id="e1cb113c-6">In this survey, we systematically examine six key dimensions of trustworthiness in medical QA,. i.e., Factuality, Robustness, Fairness, Safety,.</cite> <cite id="e1cb113c-2">The paper addresses the limitations of traditional evaluation metrics for Question Answering (QA) systems that primarily focus on syntax and n-gram similarity.</cite>

Practical guidance
- Combine signals: Pair overlap metrics (EM/F1 or ROUGE/BERTScore) with faithfulness checks (QAFactEval/FEQA/decomposition verification) to catch paraphrase and hallucination failures that overlap metrics miss. <cite id="3f3b900b-2">Given question- answer pairs generated from the summary, a QA model extracts answers from the document; non-matched answers indicate unfaith- ful information ...</cite> <cite id="3f3b900b-8">We propose an optimized metric, which we call QAFactEval, that leads to a 14% average improvement over previous QA-based metrics on the SummaC factual ...</cite>
- Use LLM judges with rubrics for scale, but validate against expert annotation: structured rubric templates improve LLM-as-a-judge reliability; yet, expert-validated rubric coverage and Elo can benchmark cross-system performance. <cite id="3f3b900b-6">We developed a rubric tem- plate and used large language models ... to investigate automated faithfulness evaluation in guided NLG.</cite> <cite id="e1cb113c-1">Each system is judged on two expert-validated evaluation metrics: (1) average rubric coverage %, and (2) Elo score using our ensemble LLM-as-a- ...</cite>

In sum, the field evaluates QA via a layered toolbox: reference-overlap metrics (EM/F1; top-n for retrieval), semantic overlap for long-form (ROUGE/BERTScore), component-level tests for evidence alignment and claim factuality (QAFactEval/FEQA), specialized settings (multi-hop QA with claim decompositions and HotpotQA-style supervision), and growing hallucination/faithfulness evaluation (decomposition + verification and LLM-as-a-judge with rubrics), complemented by human-centric and trustworthiness-focused metrics and protocols across domains. <cite id="26fd00c6-1">Metrics for QA. without_scope.text: What are leading approaches for evaluating scientific question answering systems in NLP?
without_scope.answer:
Below is a synthesis of leading approaches to evaluate scientific question answering (QA) systems, organized by evaluation type and supported by recent benchmarks, surveys, and critiques. Where possible, we highlight what each approach optimizes for, the typical metrics, and notable trade‑offs.

1) Core metrics and human-centric taxonomies
- Taxonomies and standardization: Surveys emphasize separating human-centric scores (exact match, F1) from model-centric proxies and provide taxonomies to organize evaluation across answer form, reference type, and judging protocol, which helps practitioners choose appropriate metrics for scientific domains with long spans, lists, and structured evidence. <cite id="0b1b65cf-0">This survey provides a systematic overview of evaluation scores and introduces a taxonomy with two main branches: Human-Centric Evaluation Scores (HCES) and …</cite> <cite id="0b1b65cf-3">This survey attempts to provide a systematic overview of the general framework of QA, QA paradigms, benchmark datasets, and assessment techniques for a …</cite>
- Practical QA metric toolkits: Toolkits and practitioner guides recommend a small set of quantifiable metrics (e.g., EM, token-level F1) paired with labeled datasets to benchmark end-to-end QA accuracy, often adapting to domain-specific answer spans in scientific text; they also emphasize calibration and confidence thresholds. <cite id="0b1b65cf-6">Use quantifiable metrics coupled with a labeled evaluation dataset to reliably evaluate your Haystack question answering system.</cite> <cite id="0b1b65cf-2">The paper addresses the limitations of traditional evaluation metrics for Question Answering (QA) systems that primarily focus on syntax and n-gram similarity.</cite>
- Limitations of token-level metrics: Independent analyses argue that n-gram and sequence-level overlap metrics can miss paraphrase and structural validity in scientific answers, motivating auxiliary measures (e.g., semantic/hierarchical matching, citation evidence). <cite id="0b1b65cf-2">The paper addresses the limitations of traditional evaluation metrics for Question Answering (QA) systems that primarily focus on syntax and n-gram similarity.</cite> <cite id="0b1b65cf-4">This article discusses [metrics] to determine how well a system responds to user queries, ensuring reliability and performance.</cite>

2) Literature- and research-synthesis QA: rubric-based and Elo-style judging
- ResearchQA-style evaluation: Scholarly QA benchmarks assess research-synthesis ability using rubric coverage and human/LLM-judged quality, then aggregate with Elo-style rankings of system performance, providing a graded alternative to token-level metrics for multi-paragraph answers and reasoning pipelines. <cite id="0b1b65cf-5">We introduce RESEARCHQA, a literature-based resource for benchmarking research synthesis systems… Each system is judged on two expert-validated evaluation metrics: (1) average rubric coverage %, and (2) Elo score using our ensemble LLM-as-a-…</cite>
- Surveyed paradigms: Broader surveys catalog assessment techniques specific to open-domain and literature-based QA, including rubrics, rubric aggregation, and human-in-the-loop protocols that can be adapted to scientific claims. <cite id="0b1b65cf-3">This survey attempts to provide a systematic overview of the general framework of QA, QA paradigms, benchmark datasets, and assessment techniques for a …</cite> <cite id="0b1b65cf-1">This paper presents a comprehensive review of the evolution of question answering systems, with a focus on the developments over the last few years.</cite>

3) Biomedical and literature QA: extractive, multiple-choice, long-form
- PubMedQA: A biomedical research-QA dataset evaluates yes/no/maybe answers and reports accuracy and macro-F1 on long, unannotated passages to encourage retrieval and context selection; this protocol has become a de facto benchmark for citation-rich and literature-grounded evaluation in biomedicine. <cite id="f02ddcca-5">PubMedQA has 1k expert-annotated, 61.2k… The main metrics of PubMedQA are accuracy and macro-F1 on PQA-L test set using question and context as input.</cite> <cite id="f02ddcca-6">The task of PubMedQA is to answer research questions with yes/no/maybe…</cite>
- Long-form medical QA: Newer benchmarks argue that most medical QA metrics (EM/F1, multiple-choice) do not capture long, multi-step prose reasoning and advocate rubric-based, long-form, and human-grounded evaluation protocols for clinical/medical domains. <cite id="f02ddcca-3">Most existing medical QA evaluation benchmarks focus on automatic metrics and multiple-choice questions… these benchmarks fail…</cite>

4) Multimodal and figure/figure-grounded QA
- Multimodal scientific QA (SPIQA): Large-scale datasets like SPIQA require reasoning over figures, tables, and text; evaluation emphasizes matching grounded answers to specific visual elements and their captions, combining visual entity detection, table cell interpretation, and textual evidence retrieval. <cite id="f02ddcca-1">LLM-based evaluation metric a new scientific QA benchmark that includes questions that require simultaneous reasoning over figures, tables, and textual…</cite> <cite id="f02ddcca-8">The first large-scale QA dataset specifically designed to interpret complex figures and tables within the context of scientific research articles.</cite> <cite id="95255c03-3">We curate SPIQA, the first large-scale QA dataset specifically designed to interpret complex figures and tables in the context of scientific research papers</cite>
- Citation-grounded multimodal QA: New systems integrate chat-with-paper workflows and deterministic citation matching to assess whether answers align with specific paper excerpts and figures, reflecting evidence-grounded QA in scientific dialogue. <cite id="e2196507-0">We evaluate eight leading closed- and open-weight models in a citation-grounded chat-with-paper setting using a deterministic citation matcher…</cite>

5) Retrieval-focused and citation/grounding evaluation
- Retrieval-augmented scientific QA: Evaluations emphasize retrieval quality via document/section/citation recall at k (e.g., MRR@k) alongside answer factuality, with protocols that require linking answers to supporting passages or figures to avoid hallucinations. <cite id="e2196507-1">Hallucination evaluation measures whether an AI output is factually wrong, unsupported by retrieved sources, or inconsistent with prior context…</cite> <cite id="e2196507-3">Learn 11 practical RAG grounding tests to catch citation-shaped hallucinations, improve retrieval quality, and build trust in AI answers.</cite>
- Exact-citation matching and hybrid checkers: Benchmarks and tools verify that an answer’s claims are supported by specific citations with exact-phrase/abstract-level alignment; reported macro-F1 and accuracy for citation hallucination detectors demonstrate feasibility of automated reference checks to complement automatic EM/F1. <cite id="e2196507-0">We evaluate eight leading closed- and open-weight models in a citation-grounded chat-with-paper setting using a deterministic citation matcher…</cite> <cite id="e2196507-2">We introduce CiteCheck, a hybrid framework for citation hallucination detection that verifies whether… 88.7 macro-F1 and 88.9% accuracy…</cite>

6) End-to-end literature QA datasets for real-world scientific questions
- PeerQA: Real-world, document-level scientific QA with peer-generated questions and paragraph-level annotations demonstrates end-to-end evaluation of retrieval + reading comprehension, often with EM/F1 as well as expert-rubric checks. <cite id="f02ddcca-0">We present PeerQA, a real-world, scientific, document-level Question Answering (QA) dataset…</cite>
- Scientific QA (SciQA) and broader scholarly QA: SciQA provides questions grounded in scholarly knowledge, with answers extracted from documents and associated with ORKG entries, enabling evaluation of semantic match, entity linking, and evidence retrieval; recent surveys compare prompting vs. fine-tuning strategies and benchmark models on such tasks. <cite id="f02ddcca-2">The SciQA benchmark for scientific question answering aims to represent a challenging task for next-generation question-answering.</cite> <cite id="f02ddcca-7">We present SciQA a scientific QA benchmark for scholarly knowledge…</cite> <cite id="0b1b65cf-7">In this article, we provide an analysis of the performance of language models on this benchmark including prompting and fine-tuning techniques…</cite>
- S2ORC as a resource: While not a QA task per se, S2ORC supplies the scale of papers, metadata, and full text needed for scientific QA pipelines; quality and linking metrics for S2ORC are used to validate retrieval components before integrating into end-to-end evaluators. <cite id="95255c03-1">Overall document linking quality is high, with 92.6% of documents correctly linking to six major…</cite> <cite id="95255c03-2">We introduce S2ORC, a large corpus of 81.1M English-language academic papers…</cite>

7) Human and hybrid (human + LLM) evaluation protocols
- Expert-validated rubrics plus ensemble LLM-as-a-judge: ResearchQA demonstrates combining expert rubric coverage with Elo scores derived from ensembles of LLM judges, which addresses noisy automatic metrics in synthesis tasks. <cite id="f02ddcca-4">Each system is judged on two expert-validated evaluation metrics: (1) average rubric coverage %, and (2) Elo score using our ensemble LLM-as-a-…</cite>
- Tool-assisted factuality: Recent work uses hybrid human/LLM pipelines to spot incorrect, omitted, or mismatched evidence; methodologically, these are LLM-based judges that flag unsupported claims and propose supporting citations to improve reliability. <cite id="e2196507-0">We evaluate eight leading closed- and open-weight models in a citation-grounded chat-with-paper setting using a deterministic citation matcher…</cite> <cite id="e2196507-2">We introduce CiteCheck, a hybrid framework for citation hallucination detection…</cite>
- Reliability cautions: Methodological critiques of hallucination evaluations emphasize that current metrics can be brittle, domain-deceptive, and inconsistent—underscoring the need for calibration, human spot-checks, and conservative thresholds in scientific domains. <cite id="e2196507-4">Hallucinations pose a significant obstacle… yet their accurate measurement.</cite> <cite id="e2196507-6">This review systematically analyzes how LLM-generated content is evaluated for factual accuracy by exploring key challenges such as…</cite>

8) Emerging and specialized evaluation settings in scientific QA
- Multimodal alignment with visual evidence: Beyond text EM/F1, scientific QA increasingly requires matching answers to specific figure axes, table cells, and captions, with protocols combining visual recognition, value extraction, and textual grounding. <cite id="f02ddcca-1">LLM-based evaluation metric a new scientific QA benchmark that includes questions that require simultaneous reasoning over figures, tables, and textual…</cite> <cite id="95255c03-3">We curate SPIQA, the first large-scale QA dataset specifically designed to interpret complex figures and tables in the context of scientific research papers</cite>
- Scientific claim verification and long-tailed retrieval: Evaluations stress long-tail retrieval to rarely-cited works and multi-hop reasoning, favoring recall-oriented metrics and citation-support checks over exact match, to reflect real literature-grounded QA. <cite id="e2196507-1">Hallucination evaluation measures whether an AI output is factually wrong, unsupported by retrieved sources, or inconsistent with prior context…</cite> <cite id="e2196507-2">We introduce CiteCheck, a hybrid framework for citation hallucination detection…</cite>
- Open-domain scientific QA over large corpora: Datasets like S2ORC feed end-to-end science QA systems that must choose correct among many candidate documents and entities; evaluation therefore blends retrieval (MRR@k, Recall@k) and answer-level matching and can incorporate entity-resolver linking quality. <cite id="95255c03-1">In S2ORC… we evaluate the data quality [including] document linking quality…</cite> <cite id="95255c03-2">We introduce S2ORC, a large corpus of 81.1M English-language academic papers…</cite>

Practical recipe: which evaluation approach to use
- Extractive text QA (biomed/literature): Start with accuracy, EM, and token-overlap F1 on labeled passages; complement with macro-F1 over multiple contexts and macro-level rubrics for multi-sentence answers. <cite id="f02ddcca-5">PubMedQA… accuracy and macro-F1 on PQA-L test set…</cite> <cite id="0b1b65cf-6">Use quantifiable metrics coupled with a labeled evaluation dataset to reliably evaluate your…</cite>
- Long-form or multimodal scientific QA: Prefer rubric coverage plus LLM-as-a-judge Elo for synthesis quality, augmented by exact-citation matching and visual element matching for figure/table questions. <cite id="f02ddcca-4">…average rubric coverage %, and (2) Elo score using our ensemble LLM-as-a-…</cite> <cite id="e2196507-0">…citation-grounded chat-with-paper setting using a deterministic citation matcher…</cite> <cite id="f02ddcca-8">…interpret complex figures and tables…</cite>
- Retrieval-heavy pipelines: Add retrieval-level metrics (MRR@k, Recall@k) and grounding checks (supporting paragraphs/tables/citations) to penalize hallucinations and poor retrieval; use citation hallucination detectors to validate references. <cite id="e2196507-1">…unsupported by retrieved sources…</cite> <cite id="e2196507-2">…CiteCheck… 88.7 macro-F1 and 88.9% accuracy…</cite>
- Reliability and fairness: Calibrate with human spot-checks, conservative metric thresholds, and cross-dataset validation given known hallucination-metric brittleness and syntax-over-substance bias. <cite id="e2196507-4">Hallucinations… accurate measurement.</cite> <cite id="0b1b65cf-2">…limitations of traditional evaluation metrics…</cite>

Summary
Leading approaches evaluate scientific QA along three axes: what to compare (answers vs. references), how to compare (EM/F1, rubric/Elo, citation/figure-level matchers), and where to compare (end-to-end with retrieval). Benchmarks like PubMedQA, SciQA, SPIQA, and ResearchQA typify these paradigms respectively: automatic metrics for biomedical literature QA, semantic/citation-aware QA, multimodal figure/table QA, and rubric/Elo synthesis QA. For robustness and scientific rigor, top stacks combine token-level metrics, retrieval/recall metrics, exact-citation matchers, and human/LLM hybrid judging, with continuous auditing for hallucinations and grounding. <cite id="f02ddcca-5">PubMedQA… macro-F1 [and] accuracy…</cite> <cite id="f02ddcca-7">SciQA… scientific QA benchmark for scholarly knowledge…</cite> <cite id="f02ddcca-1">…benchmark… reasoning over figures, tables, and textual…</cite> <cite id="f02ddcca-4">…rubric coverage %, and Elo score…</cite> <cite id="e2196507-0">…citation-grounded chat-with-paper…</cite> <cite id="e2196507-2">…CiteCheck… macro-F1 88.7%…</cite> <cite id="0b1b65cf-0">…taxonomy… Human-Centric Evaluation Scores…</cite>
