questions.original_query: what are the most important open challenges in using neural networks in combination with PDE solvers for fluid simulation?

query.text: what are the most important open challenges in using neural networks in combination with PDE solvers for fluid simulation?
query.answer:
Below is a concise synthesis of the most pressing open challenges when combining neural networks (NNs) with PDE solvers for fluid simulation, grouped by problem class and supported with recent evidence.

Summary
• Across physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) and NN-native PDE solvers, common bottlenecks are training stability/constraint enforcement, accuracy/efficiency compared to legacy CFD, generalization over Reynolds numbers and scales, data scarcity/quality, and robust handling of shocks, interfaces, and boundary conditions. <cite id="f4d42fe5-0">Recent reviews emphasize progress in complex fluids (turbulence, multiphase) but persistent limitations</cite> <cite id="f4d42fe5-2">and explicitly note scalability, spectral bias, constraint enforcement, and reproducibility challenges in PINNs</cite> <cite id="f4d42fe5-4">while hands-on reports argue PINNs currently lack the accuracy/efficiency to replace traditional CFD</cite>.

1) Optimization/training stability and constraint enforcement
• Non-convex, implicit residual matching, and ill-conditioning lead to spectral bias and spurious minima; enforcement of conservation/energy and complex boundary conditions remains unreliable at scale. <cite id="f4d42fe5-1">Benchmarks highlight scalability limits and persistent issues with constraint enforcement and reproducibility</cite> <cite id="aca48ad4-8">and practitioner studies reveal that naive PINN training on Navier–Stokes can get stuck in not-so-successful steady states</cite>.
• Physics propagation artifacts can destabilize long-time integration, especially for discontinuities. <cite id="9e4cc49b-7">PINNs can bidirectionally propagate shock information in time, causing non-physical oscillations or incorrect history dependence</cite>.
• Hybridizing architectures with physics-aware discretization can stabilize training. <cite id="9e4cc49b-2">Hybrid finite-difference + PINN (HFD-PINN) has been proposed to restore robustness by anchoring learning to discrete flux balance</cite>.

2) Accuracy vs. legacy solvers and practical efficiency
• Today, PINNs and many NN PDE solvers still struggle to match production CFD accuracy and timestep efficiency without heavy physics-informed discretization or extremely fine grids. <cite id="f4d42fe5-4">Experience reports explicitly state PINNs are not meant to replace existing CFD solvers due to inferior accuracy and efficiency</cite>.
• Even at moderate Reynolds numbers, end-to-end PINN vortex problems require careful design and specialized augmentations to converge credibly. <cite id="aca48ad4-5">A PINN approach for 2-D vortex dynamics illustrates that success often hinges on architecture choices and domain-specific tricks</cite>.

3) Generalization across regimes (Reynolds numbers, scales, turbulence)
• Low-Re demonstrations are common; extending to high-Re, fully turbulent flows remains open. <cite id="aca48ad4-0">Recent PINN applications showcase cylinder flows at low Reynolds numbers without external data, underscoring the gap to high-Re regimes</cite> <cite id="f4d42fe5-2">and reviews note limited success in complex turbulence scenarios</cite>.
• Subgrid-scale modeling via NN closures is an active area, but reliable closure transfer and data conditioning remain major hurdles. <cite id="aca48ad4-7">Perspectives on ML-augmented RANS/LES discuss structured neural networks as substitutes for turbulence closures while stressing open questions in generalization and robustness</cite> <cite id="aca48ad4-1">and a PINN-variational bridge links data assimilation with turbulence modeling objectives</cite>.
• Spectral bias and residual weighting limit learning of high-frequency dynamics critical for turbulence and shocks. <cite id="f4d42fe5-1">Spectral bias and constraint enforcement are repeatedly identified as key unsolved challenges</cite>.

4) Data, labels, and measurement constraints
• Fluid problems involve sparse, noisy, or incomplete measurements; learning from partial fields and boundary tracers is unreliable without physics guidance or strong invariants. <cite id="f4d42fe5-6">Studies report overfitting and high errors in velocity components when PINNs operate under incomplete data conditions</cite> <cite id="aca48ad4-4">noting that experimental data are often sparse and incomplete, complicating end-to-end training</cite>.
• Labeling Navier–Stokes fields at scale is expensive; differentiable surrogates mitigate but do not remove the need for careful initialization, teacher forcing, and validation strategies. <cite id="5a71bc85-4">Recurrent neural operators improve long-term stability by avoiding naive teacher-forcing pitfalls</cite>.

5) Discontinuous flows, shocks, and multiphase interfaces
• Generic PINN architectures have difficulty resolving shocks without tailored numerics or hybrid discretization. <cite id="9e4cc49b-3">Comprehensive studies argue PINNs struggle with shocks and discontinuities unless augmented with high-order, high-resolution schemes</cite> <cite id="9e4cc49b-0">and show sensitivity of PINNs to PDE formulation and shock-capturing design</cite>.
• Operator-learning and mesh-mapping NNs help, but shock reflection, entropy consistency, and interface-capturing fidelity degrade without domain-specific inductive biases and entropy production guidance. <cite id="5a71bc85-6">Fourier neural operators have been used for FSI but still require careful design for interfaces and long-term stability</cite> <cite id="5a71bc85-8">with evidence that hybridizing operators with physics guidance alleviates generalization gaps</cite>.

6) Operator learning for 3D, multiscale, and long-time dynamics
• Neural operators reduce dimensionality but still face generalization across topologies, Reynolds numbers, and time horizons. <cite id="5a71bc85-2">Multiscale neural operators for CFD show promise but emphasize remaining accuracy and scalability gaps</cite> <cite id="5a71bc85-1">and a 3D thesis highlights real-world 3D domain complexities</cite>.
• Hybrid operator-learning + local PINN/FEM-FVM strategies are needed to balance global mapping errors and local conservation. <cite id="5a71bc85-5">Hybrid operator learning (combining data with physics constraints) mitigates generalization challenges</cite> <cite id="aca48ad4-8">and PINN-based multiscale frameworks explore constrained PDE surrogates under variational principles</cite>.

7) Integration with legacy solvers and data assimilation
• Bridging NN surrogates with finite-volume/element Navier–Stokes kernels, AMR, and wall-time budgets requires certified I/O, conservative flux coupling, and robust variational interfaces. <cite id="aca48ad4-1">Recent work explicitly bridges PINN-based data assimilation and variational methods to improve stability and fidelity</cite> <cite id="9e4cc49b-0">with evidence that PDE formulation choices materially affect coupling behavior</cite>.
• In embedded-interface methods (VOF/LS), neural encoders/decoders need to respect geometric consistency and jump conditions over long transients. <cite id="5a71bc85-6">FNO-based FSI solvers demonstrate feasibility but reveal sensitivity to interface representations</cite>.

8) Discretization choices and numerical invariants
• Spectral/hybrid discretizations and adaptive timestepping must enforce discrete mass/energy dissipation and potential dissipation tuning; residual weighting and collocation density control error budgets unevenly. <cite id="f4d42fe5-2">Reviews identify constraint enforcement and spectral bias as central obstacles for reliable invariant preservation</cite> <cite id="9e4cc49b-2">and hybrid finite-difference PINNs illustrate how flux-conservative discretization anchors the NN to physics</cite>.
• Physics-aware regularization and localized linearization can curb shock artifacts but introduce their own hyperparameter and stability trade-offs. <cite id="9e4cc49b-7">Locally linearized PINNs reveal bidirectional shock propagation, motivating one-way boundary handling and localized stabilizers</cite>.

9) Efficiency and memory/compute constraints
• End-to-end NN PDE solvers face training and inference costs comparable to full CFD at fine meshes and variable fidelity across transients. <cite id="f4d42fe5-4">Reports conclude PINNs remain less efficient than established CFD in most regimes</cite> <cite id="5a71bc85-5">and operator-learning literature emphasizes scalability gains must be matched with physics-constrained generalization</cite>.
• Operator models can amortize inference but still require careful handling of periodic/entropy-consistent updates and hierarchical composition. <cite id="5a71bc85-4">Recurrent neural operators are proposed to stabilize long-term prediction by improving temporal consistency</cite>.

10) Benchmarking, verification, and documentation gaps
• Reproducibility remains limited: loss formulations, residual weighting, and domain normalizations can flip outcomes; long-time asymptotics and shock tests are inconsistent across studies. <cite id="f4d42fe5-1">Reproducibility and constraint enforcement are explicitly called out as unresolved challenges</cite> <cite id="aca48ad4-4">with practical documentation of solver constraints and overfitting patterns</cite>.
• For academic benchmarks, standardized suites with entropy filters, shock-tube/regularizations, and uncertainty targets are needed to compare NN-PDE solvers fairly against off-the-shelf CFD at matched grids and budgets. <cite id="5a71bc85-8">Recent overviews argue for augmenting differentiable PDE solvers with NNs but stress rigorous validation against traditional solvers</cite>.

11) Uncertainty quantification, safety, and certification
• Quantifying uncertainty in learned fluxes and operator mapping, and certifying residuals against safety envelopes, is underdeveloped; error sources include discretization, NN approximation, and measurement noise compounding. <cite id="f4d42fe5-1">Reviews highlight the need for robust constraint enforcement that is also uncertainty-aware</cite>.
• Robustness to adversarial residual perturbations, domain shifts (mesh morphing, geometry variance), and Reynolds number drift remains an open threat to deployment. <cite id="5a71bc85-2">Multiscale operator models indicate sensitivity to domain topology that needs uncertainty quantification</cite>.

Where hybrids help now
• Operator learning + PINN/local solvers can cut training time for steady-state and periodic flows, accelerate DNS/LES snapshots, and stabilize long-time integration via recurrent structures and conservative couplings. <cite id="5a71bc85-4">Recurrent neural operators improve long-term stability on standard benchmarks</cite> <cite id="5a71bc85-5">and hybrid operator learning boosts generalization</cite>.
• Data-constrained PINNs and variational assimilation improve accuracy when field data are available, especially for transitional regimes and parameter sweeps. <cite id="aca48ad4-1">A PINN-variational bridge improves data assimilation and stability</cite>.

Practical roadmap
• Define target regime (Re, Mach, turbulence intensity) and compile matched datasets with conservative variables and entropy-consistent labels; quantify current solver baseline errors and budgets. <cite id="aca48ad4-4">Sparse/incomplete measurements make this step critical</cite>.
• Start with hybrid PINN discretizations (finite-volume aware fluxes) and enforce global conservation via penalty terms; add local limiter/tracer filters for shocks and interfaces. <cite id="9e4cc49b-2">Hybrid finite-difference PINNs provide a robust baseline</cite> <cite id="9e4cc49b-7">and locally linearized stabilizers can control bidirectional shock artifacts</cite>.
• For long-term or multiscale dynamics, layer an operator learner (e.g., FNO) to amortize steady/background modes and couple to a PINN turbulence model or conservative closure; validate against spectral baselines and entropy/energy checks. <cite id="5a71bc85-5">Hybrid operator learning mitigates generalization failures</cite> <cite id="5a71bc85-6">and FSI-oriented operator solvers show promising coupling patterns</cite>.
• Establish standardized verification suites with shock-tubes, cavity/turbulence targets, and entropy-consistency tests; report error budgets (conservation residuals, rms fields) and training-time/inference costs at matched mesh resolutions. <cite id="f4d42fe5-1">Reproducibility and constraint enforcement must be part of reporting</cite> <cite id="f4d42fe5-4">and community experience suggests careful benchmarking against CFD is necessary</cite>.

Closing perspective
• The field is transitioning from proof-of-concept to hybrid systems where NNs accelerate or assist PDE solvers rather than fully replace them. <cite id="aca48ad4-8">Reviews of ML-augmented turbulence modeling stress data-driven closures and hybrid variational learning as the near-term path</cite> <cite id="f4d42fe5-2">and comprehensive PINN surveys note persistent barriers to full replacement</cite>. Prioritizing physics-aware discretization, uncertainty-aware training, and rigorous benchmarking will determine which NN–PDE hybrids become reliable, deployable fluid simulators. <cite id="f4d42fe5-1">Scalability and constraint enforcement remain central, but reproducible protocols and conservative enforcement tools are within reach</cite>.

fully_underspecified.text: what are the most important open challenges in using machine learning with equation solvers for simulation?
fully_underspecified.answer:
Below are the most pressing open challenges in combining machine learning (ML) with equation solvers for simulation, grouped by theme and accompanied by representative open problems and pointers to active directions.

1) Predictive fidelity and physics consistency across regimes
- Challenge: Ensuring that ML-accelerated solvers remain accurate and conserve invariants while transferring from training to new PDE regimes, meshes, and boundary/initial conditions remains unsettled. Neural operator and PINN approaches promise mesh-invariance and embedding of physics, but robust guarantees and quantitative generalization bounds are active research needs. <cite id="c86bfa42-4">Neural operators are powerful only when test problems resemble the training distribution, underscoring distribution shift as a core limitation</cite> <cite id="c86bfa42-1">Estimates on generalization error for PINNs approximating PDEs have been developed (IMA J Numer Anal, 2022), indicating that rigorous error control is still maturing</cite>. 
- Open problem: principled certification that ML-enhanced PDE solvers preserve energy/dissipativity and discrete invariants across adaptive discretizations and Reynolds/Weber number regimes.

2) Generalization, transfer, and data scarcity
- Challenge: Data-efficient transfer to unseen operators, boundary conditions, Reynolds numbers, and multi-physics couplings is a bottleneck: operator learning works often evaluate on close relatives of training distributions, limiting applicability to real-world domain shift. <cite id="c86bfa42-4">Neural operators are powerful only when test problems resemble training distribution</cite> <cite id="c86bfa42-0">PINNs embed governing equations into training, enabling ODE/PDE solutions, but challenges include training dynamics, scalability, and theoretical guarantees</cite>.

3) Uncertainty quantification (UQ), calibration, and risk-aware simulation
- Challenge: Many ML-PDE pipelines lack robust UQ calibrated against classical solvers; reduced-order models (ROMs) often lack well-established uncertainty propagation, impeding use in safety-critical design under uncertainty. <cite id="be107966-2">Reduced-order models can efficiently simulate high-dimensional systems, but lack robust uncertainty quantification methods</cite> <cite id="be107966-0">Accounting for data uncertainty in transport simulations materially impacts design outcomes (multi-objective problems), indicating that UQ cannot be ignored in decision-making</cite> <cite id="be107966-1">UQ quantifies influence of uncertain or uncontrolled parameters in industrial numerical simulations</cite>.
- Open problem: principled UQ for hybrid ML/physics solvers with calibrated credible intervals, propagation from simulation/data/model-form uncertainties, and decision-relevant risk metrics matched to classical finite-element baselines.

4) Stability, conservation, and the interplay with iterative solvers
- Challenge: Augmenting Krylov/Newton-style solvers with ML can risk breaking structure-preserving properties if not designed carefully. Recent work emphasizes that success requires respect for invariant subspaces to maintain stability and accelerate convergence. <cite id="dbaa776d-0">Neural Krylov iteration uses invariant subspaces to expedite convergence and enhance stability</cite> <cite id="dbaa776d-1">Using invariant subspaces expedites Krylov convergence and enhances stability</cite>.
- Open problem: systematic design guarantees and diagnostics for ML-guided iterates that preserve contraction/expansion along invariant manifolds and enforce local conservation/circulation bounds during online solve.

5) Data pipelines, data–physics mismatch, and clean-label acquisition
- Challenge: High-fidelity labels for training physics-aware ML are scarce; simulator surrogates often have mismatch between training and deployment physics (e.g., different constitutive laws, numerical fluxes, turbulence models). This yields distribution shift and requires domain translation. <cite id="39494aa0-0">Surveys document PINN/DGM-style approaches that integrate data and first principles, implicitly assuming access to physics-aligned training data</cite> <cite id="be107966-5">A general framework for UQ in data-driven dynamical models frames prediction error from data- and model-centric uncertainties, highlighting data limitations</cite>.
- Open problem: data-centric pretraining and domain adaptation that respects PDE structure (e.g., operator norms), along with self-supervised/physics-aware generative labeling compatible with legacy solvers.

6) Integration with legacy solvers and HPC workflows
- Challenge: Bridging ML-accelerated components (e.g., coarsened operators or learned residuals) with classical discretizations and preconditioners requires faithful fidelity and robust coupling. Communication/compute patterns and checkpointing/AMR integration remain under-specified in many demonstrations. <cite id="39494aa0-6">A paradigm coupling numerical PDE solutions via ML-based methods has been presented, but calls for systematic integration strategies across numerical methods</cite> <cite id="c86bfa42-2">Physics-informed neural networks and neural operators promise flexible scientific simulation, but require careful integration with existing numerical workflows to be practically effective</cite>.
- Open problem: end-to-end composable hybrids where ML modules plug into Krylov/Jacobi–Saul’yev splittings or domain decomposition, with guarantees on preconditioner-learned complements and mesh coarsening trade-offs.

7) Verification, validation, and certification for engineering use
- Challenge: Adapting established V&V frameworks to ML-enhanced solutions is nontrivial; practitioners need reference-free verification of ML solvers against known physics, and validated surrogates with traceable error budgets comparable to those of FEM/FVM. <cite id="be107966-2">Reduced-order models still lack robust UQ methods</cite> <cite id="39494aa0-9">A unifying vision emphasizes robust and reliable modeling and solving of PDEs with ML, underscoring current gaps in rigor for engineering adoption</cite>.
- Open problem: evidence-based validation benchmarks comparing ML-PDE solvers to state-of-the-art classical solvers with matched UQ, plus regulatory-grade documentation linking uncertainty to acceptable risk.

8) Scalability, training dynamics, and hyperparameter sensitivity
- Challenge: PINNs often face stiff optimization, high-dimensional architectures, and sensitivity to physics loss weighting and architectures; while adaptive methods and second-order updates improve convergence, scalable training on PDE manifolds and robust hyperparameter regimes remain open. <cite id="c86bfa42-6">PINNs face persistent challenges in training dynamics, scalability, and theoretical guarantees</cite> <cite id="c86bfa42-7">Second-order methods can enhance PINN training and are being scaled via domain decomposition pipelines, implying substantial remaining engineering hurdles</cite> <cite id="39494aa0-0">Surveys span PINNs, Deep Galerkin, and related approaches that require stable training regimes for predictive accuracy</cite>.
- Open problem: adaptive discretization–training coupling (e.g., hierarchical grids with curriculum learning of operators), along with principled regularization and loss design that maintain well-posedness.

9) Quantifying and controlling solver artifacts in ML-augmented systems
- Challenge: ML surrogates/schur complements or learned preconditioners can introduce spurious modes and numerical artifacts; recent Krylov augmentations explicitly target stability by exploiting invariant structure to avoid divergence. <cite id="dbaa776d-0">Neural Krylov methods improve convergence while explicitly leveraging invariant subspaces for stability</cite>.
- Open problem: diagnostics to detect and mitigate pollution of learned residuals and Jacobians, including invariant-respecting residual normalization and error-localization maps during iterative solves.

10) Data and compute efficiency across the loop
- Challenge: Offline/online data partitioning and compute budgets must jointly optimize accuracy and cost when integrating ML surrogates into simulation loops; robust reduction in wall-clock time without sacrificing UQ standards is an unsolved scaling puzzle. <cite id="c86bfa42-2">Operator-learning and PINN frameworks promise flexible improvements, but their efficiency hinges on matching test-time distributions and scalable training</cite> <cite id="be107966-0">Accounting for data uncertainty materially changes optimal designs, indicating that cost-accurate trade-offs are necessary before deployment</cite>.
- Open problem: systematic co-design of data acquisition campaigns, surrogate granularity (coarse-to-fine operators), and HPC scheduling to deliver certified accuracy within budgets, with ablations vs. classical solvers.

Representative emerging directions and resources
- Surveys consolidate scope and challenge lists across PINNs and neural operators, while also cataloging progress on training stability, scalability, and uncertainty-aware modeling. <cite id="c86bfa42-3">Recent PINN surveys summarize applications and advances, while acknowledging gaps in theory and scalability</cite> <cite id="c86bfa42-5">Surveys on adaptive PINNs identify transfer/meta-learning as responses to poor generalization and outline open points</cite>.
- In solver augmentation, recent “Neural Krylov” designs emphasize stability-preserving mechanisms, pointing an architecture pattern for robust hybrids that respect invariant subspaces. <cite id="dbaa776d-0">Neural Krylov methods leverage invariant subspaces to stabilize and accelerate iterative solutions</cite>.
- For risk-aware adoption, works on UQ-embedded data-driven models and reduced-order UQ stress that credible, decision-comparable uncertainty is the linchpin for industrial deployment. <cite id="be107966-2">Reduced-order models lack robust uncertainty quantification, hampering practical design workflows</cite> <cite id="be107966-5">A general UQ framework for data-driven dynamical models unifies data/model uncertainties to produce decision-relevant error bounds</cite>.

Practical starting points for research and deployment
- Build distribution-shift-aware benchmarks that span mesh/coarsening, boundary/initial perturbations, and regime changes; report predictive error and UQ metrics head-to-head with classical solvers. <cite id="c86bfa42-4">Distribution shift is a primary limit for neural operators</cite>.
- Insert invariant-respecting stabilizers into learned iterations (e.g., Galerkin-consistent residual forms) and develop diagnostics for invariant preservation under mesh morphing. <cite id="dbaa776d-0">Respecting invariant subspaces stabilizes and accelerates neural Krylov iterations</cite>.
- Prioritize UQ co-designed with training: score gradients with measurement UQ, learn conservative flux approximations with entropy dissipation checks, and quantify transfer error from surrogate pretraining distributions. <cite id="be107966-2">ROMs need robust UQ</cite> <cite id="c86bfa42-1">Generalization error theory for PINNs offers a path to quantify transfer risk</cite>.

Summary
The central tensions are data–physics alignment, stability-preserving augmentation, and UQ-calibrated generalization. Progress hinges on distribution-shift-aware training, invariant-preserving solver coupling, and rigorous UQ tied to decision-making. <cite id="c86bfa42-4">Neural operators’ dependence on training–test similarity is a blunt indicator of these limits</cite> <cite id="dbaa776d-0">while stability-aware Krylov augmentations show concrete design patterns</cite>, and <cite id="be107966-2">UQ gaps for ROMs expose the missing piece for high-assurance simulation</cite>. Together, these define an urgent and tractable set of open challenges for the next phase of ML-enhanced equation solving.

without_scope.text: what are the most important open challenges in using neural networks in combination with PDE solvers for fluid simulation?
without_scope.answer:
Below are the most pressing open challenges when combining neural networks (NNs) with PDE solvers for fluid simulation, grouped by theme and supported by recent evidence from PINNs, data-driven closures, reduced-order modeling (ROM), and hybrid/surrogate workflows.

1) Stability, conservation, and energy/entropy compliance
- Neural PDE solvers, including PINNs, frequently struggle to guarantee numerical stability, conservation (mass/momentum/energy), and long-time accuracy without extensive engineering of loss functions and regularization, even for Navier–Stokes problems in complex geometries.<cite id="9cd4ab23-5">An experience report highlights not-so-successful attempts to replace a traditional solver with a PINN, underscoring practical stability and robustness gaps</cite><cite id="96bd04f4-1">A 2025 review emphasizes critical challenges in PINN development around loss design and geometric integration for physics-compliant behavior</cite><cite id="96bd04f4-4">Work on incompressible PINNs explicitly discusses convergence and stability concerns alongside practical deployments</cite>. 
- Early variational frameworks are beginning to provide stability certificates via coercivity and energy-stability arguments, but these are mostly for simplified PDEs and training regimes and are not yet general, plug-and-play guarantees for high-Reynolds compressible turbulence.<cite id="96bd04f4-2">A rigorous stability framework for PINNs grounded in variational analysis and operator coercivity has been developed, but remains a topic under active investigation</cite>.

What would help: general-purpose stability tools that maintain discrete energy/entropy dissipation bounds for high-velocity, shock-capturing regimes; certified training/regularizers that enforce integral conservation properties globally.

2) Geometry, boundaries, and discretization fidelity
- Embedding fluid PDEs into deep learning frameworks runs into loss-weighting, geometric feature integration, and boundary-condition enforcement; naive voxel/coordinate embeddings degrade accuracy near complex interfaces and walls and can violate essential/Robin conditions without careful design.<cite id="96bd04f4-1">Loss function design and geometric information integration are core, open challenges for PINNs</cite><cite id="9cd4ab23-0">A 2025 MDPI review notes PINN progress while highlighting needs like extended formulations for highly heterogeneous and complex geometries</cite><cite id="9cd4ab23-5">Preliminary work proposes discretized PINN architectures, suggesting that traditional finite-volume-like enforcement may improve fidelity compared to naive continuous-space losses</cite>. 
- Physics-motivated discretization choices (flux form for incompressible pressure-velocity coupling; entropy- and carbuncle-stable schemes for compressible flows) are not yet fully integrated into end-to-end neural solvers with consistent error control and shock handling.<cite id="96bd04f4-4">Incompressible PINN work emphasizes practical issues in implementing stable, conservative discretizations</cite>.

3) Generalization and domain transfer beyond training conditions
- The central limitation of data-driven closures and surrogates is out-of-distribution (OOD) robustness: models trained on curated grids, specific Reynolds numbers, or laminar-dominated datasets show large regressions when predicting detached separation, compressible shock structures, or multi-physics regimes.<cite id="bedb9c93-2">Generalizability of ML-based turbulence closures to unseen practical flows remains a key challenge</cite><cite id="bedb9c93-1">Using invariant NN architectures to model Reynolds stresses and fluxes is promising, but transfer must respect symmetries of the dynamics</cite>. 
- ROMs and neural closure models can collapse the state manifold but face regime shift, fidelity-loss, and coverage gaps; time-sequence learners (LSTMs/NODEs) improve latent dynamics, yet principled certification of stability/robustness is lacking.<cite id="4b41f93e-2">Empirical studies compare LSTM and NODE closures for latent dynamics in fluid ROMs, documenting sensitivity to architecture and training regimes</cite><cite id="96bd04f4-1">Design choices like loss weighting and geometric embeddings strongly affect physics fidelity, making robust transfer nontrivial</cite>.

4) Data scarcity, labels, and active learning efficiency for PDE solvers
- High-fidelity labels—DNS/LES snapshots for closure learning—are expensive; practical hybrid strategies require active learning and selective enrichment (boundary layers, separation, shocks) to make NN closures usable in production.<cite id="9cd4ab23-4">Recent PINN reviews and implementations discuss the need for optimal solver constraints and active learning guidance to curate labels efficiently</cite><cite id="9cd4ab23-0">Experience shows PINNs in heterogeneous media benefit from tailored physics-informed formulations and targeted data</cite>. 
- Sparse/collocated collocation is common; obtaining boundary/interfacial truth is harder, and misaligned labels degrade closures and hybrid models if not actively managed.<cite id="9cd4ab23-5">An experience report attributes much of the “unsucces[s]” to inadequate training regimes and data coverage</cite>.

5) Coupling legacy solvers and hybrid workflows: stability and overhead
- Hybrid PDE–NN solvers that couple traditional CFD/FEA with learned closures/ROMs are promising but face stability interfaces, time-step coupling constraints, and communication overheads; rigorous frameworks for closure identification within a computational graph are still immature.<cite id="4b41f93e-1">Scientific ML for closure models explicitly motivates coupling traditional solvers with NN closures using reduced-order techniques</cite><cite id="4b41f93e-6">A survey emphasizes hybrid models that combine physics-based and ML objectives, distinguishing a priori versus a posteriori closure design</cite><cite id="96bd04f4-7">Physics-informed mult-task PINN frameworks are emerging to share structure across related Navier–Stokes subproblems, but scaling and robustness remain open</cite>. 
- Mori–Zwanzig-inspired “neural closure” models introduce memory terms and lagged forcing; reliably learning and stabilizing these nonlocal, non-Markovian components for realistic turbulence remains unsettled, especially in multiscale configurations.<cite id="bedb9c93-5">Koopman-Mori–Zwanzig latent closures are explored with neural learnable terms, but stability and prediction accuracy depend on latent design and training protocols</cite><cite id="bedb9c93-4">Reduced stochastic closures can improve accuracy, but their generalization and uncertainty quantification are open issues</cite>.

6) Uncertainty quantification, robustness, and monitoring
- Fluid PINNs and neural closures often lack calibrated uncertainty and sensitivity analysis; practitioners need quantified aleatory and epistemic uncertainty from limited data, sensitivity to hyperparameters/loss weights, and failure detection when physics is violated in long runs.<cite id="96bd04f4-1">Loss design choices and geometric handling introduce implicit model-form uncertainty; monitoring these choices for physics compliance is difficult</cite><cite id="96bd04f4-4">Practical incompressible PINN work calls out convergence and stability concerns, implying a need for runtime diagnostics and uncertainty</cite>. 
- Robustness to adversarial/perturbational changes in inputs, coefficients, and boundary data is essentially unexplored for PDE-constrained networks in high-Reynolds regimes; certified or verifiably stable perturbation bounds remain largely an open frontier.<cite id="96bd04f4-2">A variational stability framework is a step toward guarantees but offers little on adversarial robustness beyond simplified settings</cite>.

7) Interpretability, physics compliance, and online monitoring
- Because gradients and training objectives do not obviously enforce conserved quantities or entropy conditions, practitioners have no reliable, built-in guardrails to detect drift from physical reality during long training or hyperparameter sweeps; this hampers deployment in safety-critical contexts.<cite id="96bd04f4-1">Reviews stress loss-weighting and geometric integration for maintaining physics compliance within PINNs</cite><cite id="9cd4ab23-5">A negative experience report underscores that naive PINN setups can fail to produce physically consistent Navier–Stokes solutions</cite>. 
- Embedding human-understandable invariants (e.g., Kelvin–Helmholtz circulation, helicity, dissipation balances) into training or monitoring loops is still a research challenge; practical tooling to log and test these invariants at scale is underdeveloped.<cite id="96bd04f4-1">Geometric information must be integrated with loss functions to preserve invariants; current practice lacks standardized guardrails</cite>.

8) Algorithmic/implementation gaps: from research toy problems to production CFD
- Benchmarks that stress real CFD workflows (adaptive mesh refinement, wall-modeled LES, detached separations, compressible shocks and combustion) are sparse; recent studies show PINNs can reproduce Navier–Stokes behavior, but robust, production-ready systems remain elusive, especially for high-speed and transitional regimes.<cite id="9cd4ab23-2">PINNs effectively solve Navier–Stokes in complex geometries, evidencing potential; yet open problems remain for broader applicability</cite><cite id="9cd4ab23-5">Real CFD replacements have not been consistently achieved; systematic solver constraint and training optimization are needed</cite>. 
- Active learning for neural PDE solvers offers promise but needs scalable acquisition strategies that balance global exploration (shock/boundary features) with local refinement, respecting solver coupling time steps and budgets.<cite id="9cd4ab23-4">Active learning for neural PDE solvers is highlighted as a direction to improve efficiency relative to brute-force PDE solution</cite><cite id="9cd4ab23-0">Recent formulations target heterogeneous and complex media, hinting at path-dependent training strategies</cite>.

What’s on the horizon and how to make progress
- Build stability-by-design backbones: combine flux-/entropy-conservative discretizations with variational, energy-stable training or constraints, then validate on compressible/shock-capturing benchmarks before scaling to turbulence.<cite id="96bd04f4-2">Variational frameworks for PINN stability provide a template for guaranteed energy behavior</cite><cite id="9cd4ab23-5">Discretized PINNs suggest finite-volume-like enforcement may improve robustness</cite>. 
- Learn closures that respect Mori–Zwanzig and Koopman structure: enforce memory-term decay and invariant measurement mappings; quantify uncertainty of learned residuals and use conservative aggregation to improve OOD robustness.<cite id="bedb9c93-5">Latent Koopman closures with neural corrections can achieve global linearization while retaining nonlinear residuals</cite><cite id="bedb9c93-4">Stochastic reduced closures improve long-term behavior but need generalizable priors</cite>. 
- Engineer hybrid pipelines with guardrails: use ROMs/PINNs for fast coarse evolution and traditional solvers for validation/feedback; monitor conserved quantities and entropy/energy dissipation, and trigger conservative surrogate fallbacks when violations occur.<cite id="4b41f93e-1">Hybrid scientific ML frameworks explicitly couple traditional and learned closures</cite><cite id="96bd04f4-1">Loss/geometry-aware PINNs help maintain physics compliance under hybrid workflows</cite>. 
- Standardize data/label protocols and benchmarks with uncertainty reporting: curate DNS/LES datasets with boundary/interfacial labels, perform active-learning campaigns with uncertainty-guided sampling, and publish failure modes and invariant checks to catalyze trust and transfer.<cite id="9cd4ab23-4">Active learning for neural PDE solvers can improve efficiency, but systematic protocols are missing</cite><cite id="9cd4ab23-5">Benchmarked experience reports illuminate how solver constraints and training regimes determine success</cite>. 
- For production CFD, prioritize domain-transfer robustness: train closures and PINNs on invariant subspaces (e.g., Lagrangian particle coordinates or streamline/deformation coordinates) and test invariant-score monitors for architecture selection.<cite id="bedb9c93-1">Invariant architectures for Reynolds-stress modeling aim to improve transfer across flows</cite><cite id="4b41f93e-2">Latent dynamics learners (LSTM/NODE) show promise when the feature space respects fluid invariants</cite>.

In summary, the key open problems are: provably stable, conservative, and robust neural PDE solvers; reliable generalization across regimes with physics-consistent training and monitoring; scalable active-learning pipelines that produce usable closure models; stable and interpretable hybrid couplings to legacy solvers; and rigorous uncertainty quantification and robustness diagnostics. The most promising path is to integrate structural stability, invariant-aware geometry/discretization, well-designed loss hierarchies, and uncertainty-informed active learning and hybridization, validated on standardized, physically interpretable benchmarks spanning laminar, transitional, and compressible regimes.<cite id="96bd04f4-1">Loss and geometry integration are central to physics-compliant PINNs</cite><cite id="96bd04f4-4">Convergence and stability issues in incompressible settings point to the need for principled discretizations</cite><cite id="bedb9c93-2">Generalizability of ML turbulence closures to unseen practical flows is a major unsolved problem</cite><cite id="bedb9c93-5">Neural closures informed by Mori–Zwanzig/Koopman offer a principled route but face stability and transfer challenges</cite><cite id="4b41f93e-1">Hybrid scientific ML explicitly targets coupling physics and ML with reduced-order closures, yet stability/overhead remain open</cite><cite id="9cd4ab23-5">Experience reports caution that naive PINN replacements for CFD fall short without careful solver constraints and training strategies</cite>.

without_term.text: what are the most important open challenges in using neural networks in combination with equation solvers for fluid simulation?
without_term.answer:
Below is a structured view of the most important open challenges when combining neural networks (NNs) with equation solvers for fluid simulation. Each challenge is framed by the integration pattern (surrogate/PINN, learned numerical linear algebra, hybrid production coupling), followed by concrete issues and evidence.

Problem framing
- Combining NNs with equation solvers spans: (a) NN surrogates and physics-informed models for PDEs/Navier–Stokes; (b) data-driven accelerators that replace or assist preconditioners, multigrid, and Krylov iterations; and (c) hybrid pipelines (data-driven closures, ROMs, immersed/cut-cell methods) that plug into conventional meshes and time integrators. <cite id="50fdcfdb-0">Recent ML-in-CFD surveys emphasize these directions as primary avenues for accelerating and augmenting CFD workflows</cite>.

Challenge 1: Stability, convergence, and dynamics of training for PDE-informed NNs
- Training instability and slow convergence remain pervasive, especially for strongly nonlinear incompressible flows and high-Reynolds-number regimes, where the optimization landscape and mixed-coupling losses can be ill-conditioned or ill-behaved. <cite id="5470dade-0">PINNs often exhibit training instability and slow convergence when applied to strongly nonlinear fluid problems</cite>. <cite id="5470dade-4">Instability can arise when physics losses destabilize the overall objective in systems with strong nonlinearity, undermining convergence</cite>. Even improved architectures like NSFnets have not fully eliminated these issues in complex regimes. <cite id="5470dade-1">Architectural variants explicitly designed for Navier–Stokes improve practice but do not remove the underlying optimization/convergence difficulties</cite>. Practical evaluations show that robust loss design and careful supervision are still required to reliably solve canonical problems (e.g., lid-driven cavity), underscoring open work on loss engineering and solver-friendly training dynamics. <cite id="5470dade-6">It remains challenging for PINNs with robust loss functions to solve even model Navier–Stokes problems like lid-driven cavity</cite>.

Challenge 2: Physics consistency and generalization (mesh, Reynolds, turbulence, geometry)
- Data efficiency and out-of-distribution generalization remain critical gaps. Building accurate Navier–Stokes surrogates is feasible in narrow regimes, yet covering geometry complexity, mesh variation, Reynolds numbers, and turbulence remains open. <cite id="50fdcfdb-4">PINNs have shown effectiveness in laminar flow demonstrations, highlighting that progress is achievable but context-limited</cite>. Reviews stress that ensuring fidelity in 2D/3D across operating conditions calls for robust inductive biases, scalable architectures, and principled combination with validated discretizations. <cite id="5470dade-2">Reviews of PINNs for incompressible Navier–Stokes emphasize the need for architectures and training strategies that generalize across dimensional scales and Reynolds regimes</cite>. For complex fluids and reactive/combustion flows, PINN foundations must be adapted to non-Newtonian behavior and stiff source terms, where loss weighting and invariances need new design. <cite id="5470dade-4">PINN foundations must contend with complex fluids, where loss instability and convergence problems compound</cite>. Experience reports and surveys consistently flag robustness across unseen geometries and operating points as a key hurdle. <cite id="50fdcfdb-8">Experience reports document not-so-successful PINN attempts to replace traditional solvers across varied CFD tasks, highlighting generalization failures and training pitfalls</cite>.

Challenge 3: Learned preconditioners, multigrid, and Krylov solvers: robustness and integration
- Linear algebra acceleration via learned preconditioners shows promise but faces open questions in robustness to parameter variations, mesh hierarchies, and PDE heterogeneity, as well as seamless integration with production multigrid/Krylov frameworks. <cite id="2f2bf034-1">High-performance preconditioners are hard to design and their quality critically drives CG convergence, motivating learned approximations but raising robustness concerns</cite>. <cite id="2f2bf034-5">Learning matrix factorizations to build preconditioners can improve PCG convergence and is compatible with multigrid hierarchies, yet generalization and reliability remain active concerns</cite>. Novel operator learning and multigrid-augmented approaches demonstrate gains for specific PDEs (e.g., Helmholtz), but scaling to general convection-dominated systems and ensuring mesh- and frequency-robustness is unsettled. <cite id="2f2bf034-6">Deep learning preconditioners augmented with multigrid offer iterative solutions for high-wavenumber Helmholtz, illustrating gains but also highlighting domain-specific limitations</cite>. <cite id="2f2bf034-0">Neural Preconditioning Operators aim to accelerate Krylov methods for large PDE solves, indicating a promising direction while leaving open questions about training data coverage and robustness across regimes</cite>. Practical CFD case studies confirm speedups but emphasize that gains degrade when discretization changes or when Reynolds and Mach numbers move out of training distributions. <cite id="2f2bf034-8">Learned preconditioners in a fluid simulation case study improved CG convergence, yet the study underscores sensitivity to discretization and operating-point shifts</cite>.

Challenge 4: Coupling data-driven models with traditional solvers and physics
- Hybrid pipelines (e.g., ROMs with neural closures, PINNs embedded in partitioned solvers, cut/cell schemes with NN augmentation) must ensure stable coupling, enforce boundary/continuity conditions, and preserve energy/diagram-consistency. Surveys of ML+CFD highlight integration issues: mapping between symbolic PDE form and neural parameterization, preserving invariants, and handling transient multiphysics (aerothermal, fluid-structure interaction). <cite id="50fdcfdb-0">Broad ML-in-CFD overviews emphasize integration with traditional solvers and the importance of stability-preserving couplings</cite>. Operator-learning preconditioners and multigrid hybrids show feasibility paths but still require principled handling of Jacobians, Jacobian-free variants, and nonlinear effects. <cite id="2f2bf034-7">A multigrid preconditioner for Jacobian-free Newton–Krylov methods demonstrates robustness and efficiency building blocks that can be integrated with neural surrogates under controlled assumptions</cite>.

Challenge 5: Data scarcity, curation, and fidelity in physics-informed learning
- Physics-informed and hybrid methods hinge on high-fidelity demonstrations and broad, curated datasets; in CFD, training and validation dataset creation is hard and noisy. Experience reports and studies observe that PINN performance hinges on data diversity and loss design, with collapse or bias if training data miss key flow regimes or boundary-layer physics. <cite id="50fdcfdb-8">Failed attempts to fully replace traditional solvers with PINNs point to gaps in data coverage and training stability</cite>. <cite id="5470dade-4">Losses that poorly weight stiff or singular limits can destabilize training and lead to physically inconsistent states</cite>. Bridging the data gap with uncertainty-aware training, selective-supervision, and physics-guided data augmentation remains an active challenge.

Challenge 6: Uncertainty quantification, verification, and trustworthy simulation
- Lacking certified error bounds and robustness guarantees hinders deployment. Studies attempting “reliable PINNs” for Navier–Stokes report that even with robust loss design, solving benchmark problems remains challenging, motivating verification frameworks and uncertainty quantification. <cite id="5470dade-6">Reliable PINNs for Navier–Stokes simulations: robust loss design still struggles with canonical cases, signaling the need for rigorous verification and trust measures</cite>. Broader experience reports echo pitfalls that threaten falsifiability and reproducibility in scientific computing. <cite id="50fdcfdb-7">Experience reports catalog pitfalls and frustrations in PINN-based fluid simulations, underscoring verification and validation challenges</cite>. For safety-critical applications, quantifying aleatory and epistemic uncertainty across extrapolation regimes, and certifying residual norms and energy balance, is a central open problem.

Challenge 7: Scalability, hardware efficiency, and workflow integration
- Memory/compute scaling, mixed-precision stability, and integration with legacy toolchains complicate practical adoption. Learned preconditioners and operator-learning approaches promise speedups but must demonstrate sustained efficiency on GPU clusters and at mesh sizes comparable to production CFD, including preconditioned conjugate gradients, deflation, and hierarchical multigrid. <cite id="2f2bf034-4">New deflation strategies can accelerate PCG convergence for parametric systems, but practical scaling and hardware-aware deployment remain to be demonstrated</cite>. <cite id="2f2bf034-0">Neural preconditioning operators target large-scale Krylov acceleration, highlighting the need to match solver-level scalability and hardware efficiency</cite>. Surveys stress that end-to-end replacements are not yet production-ready; stability, robustness, and workflow compatibility slow translation. <cite id="50fdcfdb-8">Reports that tried to use PINNs as full replacements show many workflow and robustness issues that hinder current deployment</cite>.

Challenge 8: Extending to turbulence, complex fluids, and multiphysics
- Capturing turbulence and complex fluids without resolving all scales or relying solely on eddy viscosity requires learning closures, adaptive subgrid models, or hybrid RANS-LES-NN strategies; these need to remain stable and generalizable. <cite id="5470dade-4">PINN reviews note that complex fluids call for specialized loss/inductive-bias designs and highlight instability risks</cite>. Approaches that combine PINNs with asymptotic/physical inductive biases have emerged, but rigorous comparison to traditional high-fidelity DNS/LES and generalization to open-jet or conjugate heat-transfer settings is still limited. <cite id="5470dade-5">PINN frameworks integrating symmetries and decay conditions have been proposed to stabilize discovery workflows</cite>. Embedding neural solvers into multiphysics (e.g., combustion, phase change) adds stiffness and non-convexity that challenge optimization and robustness.

High-yield subproblems and research opportunities
- Robust loss and optimizer design for mixed conservative/convective laws (entropy/energy dissipative losses; substep coupling; implicit integrators).
- Domain generalization: architectures and training strategies that transfer across mesh families, Reynolds/Mach numbers, and geometry classes; self-/meta-learning preconditioners that adapt deflation/incomplete factorizations.
- Physics-aware verification: certificates for residual and energy error growth, uncertainty-aware PINNs, and invariant preservation tests.
- Production-grade coupling: certified plug-ins for preconditioners/multigrid within mainstream CFD (OpenFOAM, SU2, FUN3D) that guarantee convergence robustness and error bounds when hybridized with neural closures.
- Data regimes and active learning: targeted data augmentation of critical flow features (shock/boundary-layer interaction, wakes), and uncertainty-guided sampling for complex regimes.

Practical guidance when adopting today’s approaches
- Start with conservative hybridization: use a learned component as a drop-in preconditioner/multigrid smoother or as a residual-aware closure inside a validated discretization, with explicit convergence tolerances and monitoring. <cite id="2f2bf034-5">Learning preconditioner factorizations as drop-in replacements for iterative solvers can improve convergence when integrated carefully</cite>. 
- Favor PINN designs with strong inductive biases and hierarchical supervision, but validate with mesh sequences, Reynolds sweeps, and energy/conservation checks; treat single-dataset laminar demonstrations as insufficient. <cite id="5470dade-2">PINN design must incorporate biases and multi-scale validation to generalize across laminar and turbulent regimes</cite>.

without_preference.text: what are the most important open challenges in using neural networks in combination with PDE solvers for fluid simulation?
without_preference.answer:
Below is a structured view of the most important open challenges when combining neural networks (NNs) with partial differential equation (PDE) solvers for fluid simulation, grouped by problem area and highlighting where theory, algorithms, and systems engineering must jointly advance.

1) Stability, Convergence, and Consistency of Learning-Based Numerical Methods
- A core difficulty is ensuring stable and provably convergent training dynamics for NN PDE solvers. Recent work explicitly treats PINNs as numerical methods and studies their stability and convergence, revealing that ill-conditioning at operator collocation points and constraint enforcement can destabilize optimization and slow convergence if not addressed with improved regularization or architecture choices. <cite id="c6ed5ada-4">Physics Informed Neural Networks is a numerical method which uses neural networks to approximate solutions of partial differential equations</cite> <cite id="c6ed5ada-5">A survey identifies key open challenges where theory and practice intersect for physics-informed approaches</cite> <cite id="c6ed5ada-0">PINNs face persistent challenges in training dynamics, scalability, and theoretical guarantees</cite> <cite id="c6ed5ada-1">Stability and convergence analyses and error estimates for PINNs expose limits that require tailored solvers</cite>.
- Fluid problems are particularly challenging because of stiffness, nonlinear convection, and turbulence; empirical successes exist but PINNs still struggle with stiff fluid systems and discretization artifacts unless careful architectures and constraints are used. <cite id="fbc2476c-1">Although PINNs have proven effective for various fluid dynamics problems, they still have difficulties when applied to stiff problems</cite>.
- Time integration remains fragile. Neural ODE/PINN-style continuous-time formulations promise flexibility but must guarantee consistency with discretized PDE solvers; parareal decomposition and RNN-style step-by-step integration need proof that distributed/truncated trains converge to consistent solutions over long times and high Reynolds numbers. <cite id="fbc2476c-3">An antisymmetric recurrent neural network encodes RK intermediate stages to respect integration structure</cite> <cite id="fbc2476c-8">Neural differential equation approaches provide a promising framework to develop NN PDE solvers</cite>.

2) Generalization: Reynolds/Operating-Point Shifts, Geometry, and Initialization
- Physics-informed approaches often fail to generalize to unseen geometries, boundary conditions, or operating points unless the model learns invariant structures and effective priors. Multiple surveys report slow mixing and poor generalization in high dimensions, calling for better initialization schemes, transfer/few-shot strategies, and meta-learning to reduce sample complexity. <cite id="c6ed5ada-6">PINNs face challenges including convergence issues in high-dimensional problems and long training times due to computational expense</cite> <cite id="c6ed5ada-2">Adaptive PINN surveys study transfer/meta-learning to improve efficiency and adaptability across domains</cite> <cite id="fbc2476c-5">Recent work emphasizes addressing ill-conditioning and new training formulations to improve robustness</cite>.
- Neural operator solvers for Navier–Stokes illustrate both promise and limits. While FNO variants can stabilize long-time, 3D predictions in turbulent channel flow, success depends on operator conditioning, Reynolds number coverage, and the ability to compose implicit U-Nets with stable time updates; open questions remain on robust long-horizon generalization across viscosities and grids. <cite id="02ab559c-1">An implicit U-Net enhanced Fourier neural operator stabilizes long-time, 3D turbulent channel flow prediction</cite> <cite id="02ab559c-4">Neural operators are positioned to augment or replace simulators in CFD, with conditions for viability</cite>.

3) Scalability and Systems Integration: From Miniapps to HPC Couplers
- Solvers for real fluid problems must scale. Current PINNs are limited by per-epoch global communication, expensive Jacobians/inverse solves for constraint enforcement, and slow convergence, which can outpace classical discretizations. Benchmarks on incompressible lid-driven cavity and channel flows show promise but highlight that training time and memory footprint still dominate for production turnover. <cite id="fbc2476c-0">Demonstrations on complex incompressible lid-driven cavity problems show competitive performance but sit within limited-scale studies</cite> <cite id="fbc2476c-1">Fluid PINNs have difficulties with stiff systems, indicating algorithmic and systems challenges</cite> <cite id="c6ed5ada-6">Long training times and high-dimensional convergence issues hinder practical scalability</cite>.
- Integration with legacy PDE tools is nontrivial. For uncertainty quantification, ensemble PINNs and hybrid solvers demand tight coupling with preconditioners, multigrid or domain decomposition—mechanisms absent in vanilla auto-regressive operators. New couplers and hybrid pipelines (e.g., coarse FEM with NN corrections, parareal hybrids) need principled consistency proofs and engineering to exploit GPU/accelerator kernels. <cite id="fbc2476c-4">An RK-structured recurrent PINN indicates the need to encode solver stages in architectures</cite> <cite id="02ab559c-7">Neural operators are being engineered to accelerate scientific simulations and design</cite>.

4) Data Scarcity, Missing Physics, and Hybrid Closure Modeling
- Fluid simulations often rely on partially observed domains; PINNs aim to make use of incomplete physics information and imperfect data, but require explicit strategies to identify missing terms, enforce realizability, and regularize with physically meaningful priors. In practice, reconstruction tasks from sparse measurements show that robustness hinges on combining PDE priors with noise-aware loss and UQ. <cite id="c6ed5ada-3">Physics-informed ML helps NNs learn from incomplete physics information and imperfect data</cite> <cite id="758c5605-0">Flow field reconstruction from noisy data faces challenges that mirror PINN principles, emphasizing PDE-guided inference under uncertainty</cite>.
- Closure modeling remains largely heuristic. Operator learning can approximate linearized Navier–Stokes or laminar flows, but fully turbulent closures across Re ranges require data that span coherent and stochastic modes; current demonstrations often assume stable base flows and limited Reynolds stresses, exposing a gap in learning Reynolds-averaged or large-eddy closures with guarantees. <cite id="02ab559c-1">Fourier neural operators stabilized 3D channel flow at large Reynolds numbers, suggesting viability for reduced-order surrogates</cite> <cite id="02ab559c-4">Neural operator surrogates can augment CFD when operators are trained with appropriate biases</cite>.

5) Time-Stepping, Energy/Entropy Dissipation, and Long-Horizon Dynamics
- Accurate and stable time-stepping for turbulent or shock-dominated flows is open. RNN/neural-ODE formulations can be tuned to emulate Runge–Kutta stages and antisymmetric update rules to respect conservation/entropy principles, but proving fidelity to discrete energy or Kelvin–Helmholtz norms, and ensuring monotonicity for stiff layers, remains unsettled; distributed training strategies also require consistency checks for parallel parareal/overlapping intervals. <cite id="fbc2476c-3">An antisymmetric recurrent neural network that encodes RK intermediate stages improves structural fidelity</cite>.
- Long-horizon prediction and bifurcation tracking require models to resolve unstable solutions and singularities. Reports of “unstable singularities” and deep-learning-guided searches in Navier–Stokes/Euler highlight both potential and hazard: discoveries can reflect spurious NN artifacts or genuinely new dynamics, motivating rigorous verification and continuation workflows. <cite id="02ab559c-3">Neural networks uncovered unstable singularities in fluid systems, emphasizing validation needs</cite> <cite id="02ab559c-5">AI-driven methods have revealed new unstable singularities in Navier–Stokes and Euler equations, framing verification as a Millennium-problem-level challenge</cite>.

6) Uncertainty Quantification, Robustness, and Safety
- Aleatoric and epistemic uncertainties must be propagated alongside fields and parameters, including for Reynolds-averaged or LES closures. Current work proposes deep ensembles, ensemble-based UQ, and newer EFI-style frameworks tailored to PINNs; yet, rigorous error control and calibration under adversarial or noisy inputs remain open, especially for continuous-in-time couplers. <cite id="758c5605-1">Ensemble-based UQ tailored to PINNs enables quantification in PDE systems</cite> <cite id="758c5605-8">PINN solvers increasingly attach uncertainty estimates to fields and inferred parameters, with techniques under active development</cite> <cite id="758c5605-3">Extended fiducial inference provides rigorous UQ for PINNs</cite> <cite id="758c5605-4">Repulsive deep ensembles target PDE systems for scalable UQ</cite>.
- Robustness to adversarial or adversarial-like measurement attacks, missing boundary/initial conditions, and domain shift is limited; PINN-specific adversarial UQ and robust training have emerged but not yet to the standards of CFD certification. <cite id="758c5605-2">A deep learning framework quantifies and propagates uncertainty for nonlinear differential systems using physics-informed neural networks and adversarial UQ concepts</cite> <cite id="758c5605-6">Common challenges include insufficient training data, lack of interpretability, and disregard for physical laws, motivating robust PDE-aware training and validation</cite>.

7) Interoperability and Tooling: From Bench-to-Prod Workflows
- End-to-end pipelines need standard miniapps, regression tests, and metrics to compare PINN, operator, and hybrid solvers; recent benchmark videos and tutorials show rapid progress, but systematic comparisons on manufactured solutions, grid convergence, and Reynolds/Prandtl parameter sweeps are inconsistent, impeding adoption. <cite id="fbc2476c-9">Neural differential equation tutorials outline workflows for developing PDE solvers</cite>.
- Engineering for production: checkpointing, mixed-precision, memory bandwidth, and differentiator stability between forward and adjoint modes are active areas where NNs must interoperate with legacy kernels; operator solvers can compress workloads but require certified composition with preconditioned linear solvers. <cite id="758c5605-7">Quantifying aleatoric and epistemic uncertainties within a unified PINN framework points to the need for production-grade uncertainty-aware training</cite>.

Practical Research Directions to Tackle These Challenges
- Build hybrid multi-level solvers that integrate NN surrogates with classical algebraic solvers: coarse-residual PINNs with FEM/FVM backbones, parareal hybrids where learned coarse propagators respect conserved quantities, and DNNO/FNO corrections to Jacobians/preconditioners. <cite id="c6ed5ada-4">PINNs as numerical methods create a natural coupling point with traditional discretizations</cite> <cite id="02ab559c-1">Stable long-time prediction for turbulent flows suggests operator+time-splitting hybrids are viable</cite>.
- Develop provably stable architectures and training regimes: anti-symmetric RNNs/RK stages for time, constraint enforcement that controls Jacobian condition numbers, and proofs of consistency for parareal decompositions with spectral convergence rates on Navier–Stokes miniapps. <cite id="fbc2476c-3">Architecture choices encoding RK stages align learned updates with numerical stability principles</cite> <cite id="c6ed5ada-1">Generalization error estimates guide when and how to regularize or reweight constraints</cite>.
- Engineer robustness/UQ into the solver loop: combine deep ensembles, Bayesian PINNs, and adversarial training with certified error bounds and energy/entropy monitors; adopt ensemble Kalman-filter-like updates for flow reconstruction to handle noisy sensors. <cite id="758c5605-1">Ensemble-based UQ techniques tailored to PINNs provide practical uncertainty propagation</cite> <cite id="fbc2476c-0">Applications demonstrate feasibility on complex incompressible flows</cite>.
- Create domain-adaptive, meta-learning frameworks tuned by Reynolds, Mach, and operating point; use few-shot or transfer learning from laminar to turbulent regimes with UQ-aware metrics to detect regime mismatch and trigger adaptive re-training. <cite id="c6ed5ada-2">Adaptive PINN surveys show pathways via transfer/meta-learning to improve efficiency and adaptability</cite>.

Summary
The most urgent challenges are stable and scalable optimization, principled time discretization and long-horizon generalization, robust adaptation to unseen regimes and geometry, tight integration with classical linear algebra systems, and production-grade uncertainty quantification and robustness. Progress will require co-designing NN architectures with physics-preserving update rules, embedding uncertainty and safety into the solver loop, and establishing rigorous convergence/UQ guarantees alongside reproducible benchmarks on Navier–Stokes miniapps and canonical turbulent flows. <cite id="c6ed5ada-0">PINNs face persistent challenges in training dynamics, scalability, and theoretical guarantees</cite> <cite id="fbc2476c-1">Fluid PINNs still struggle with stiff problems, indicating open algorithmic and systems challenges</cite> <cite id="02ab559c-1">Neural operators stabilized long-time turbulent channel flow dynamics, pointing to promising but conditional gains</cite> <cite id="758c5605-8">PINN solvers are increasingly coupled with uncertainty estimates, but rigorous certification remains limited</cite>.
