without_scope.text: What are different techniques in non-linear, non-stationary signal processing? Which one is most effective for geophysical signals?
without_scope.answer:
Below is an evidence-backed overview of techniques for nonlinear, non‑stationary (NLNS) signal processing, followed by guidance on what works best for geophysical signals (e.g., seismic and related geophysical time series).

# What “NLNS” Means and Why It Matters
Nonlinear and nonstationary signals evolve in time with time-varying amplitude and frequency content and may contain amplitude modulation (AM), frequency modulation (FM), shocks, and non-Gaussian noise. Conventional Fourier analysis assumes linearity and stationary statistics, so time–frequency or adaptive, data-driven methods are preferred. <cite id="f739fca2-4">A new method for analysing nonlinear and non-stationary data has been developed; the key part is the empirical mode decomposition (EMD), which recursively decomposes data into intrinsic mode-like components suitable for nonlinear, nonstationary time series</cite> <cite id="f739fca2-5">The Hilbert–Huang transform is an empirically based method whose adaptive basis produces physically interpretable time–frequency–amplitude–frequency information via Hilbert spectral analysis</cite>.

# Core Technique Families

1) Time–frequency and wave-based methods
- Short-time Fourier Transform (STFT) and Filtered-X STFT (FXSTFT): Provide time-localized spectra by windowing; widely used in geophysics for spectrograms and phase recovery but can suffer from fixed windowing trade-offs and spectral leakage. <cite id="f739fca2-4">STFT-based windows provide practical time localization but are limited by fixed window trade-offs compared to adaptive approaches</cite>.
- Wavelets and wavelet denoising: Multiresolution analysis aligned to scale; widely used for seismic denoising and feature extraction. <cite id="f739fca2-9">Wavelets are classical tools for nonstationary time series, with EMD/HHT proposed as alternatives to address adaptivity</cite> <cite id="f739fca2-6">Wavelet-based processing is broadly applied due to its time–frequency localization</cite>.
- S-transform and related complex transforms: Combine magnitude and phase and provide amplitude–frequency localization; useful for geophysical transients and phase extraction. <cite id="f739fca2-5">Time–frequency–phase decompositions like HHT are motivated by practical needs for nonlinear, nonstationary data</cite>.
- Synchrosqueezing and improved transforms: Reassign energy in time for sharper time–frequency concentration; often paired with EMD/HHT or wavelets for improved separability in noisy NLNS signals. <cite id="f739fca2-9">Developments beyond EMD target precision in extracting nonstationary components, with synchrosqueezed variants improving concentration</cite>.

2) Adaptive, data-driven decompositions (EMD/HHT lineage and successors)
- Empirical Mode Decomposition (EMD) and Hilbert–Huang Transform (HHT): Decompose data adaptively into intrinsic mode functions (IMFs) and compute instantaneous envelopes and Hilbert spectra. Widely regarded as well-suited to NLNS, but can be affected by mode mixing, termination rules, and computational burden. <cite id="f739fca2-4">EMD “breaks complex time series into simpler modes,” and Hilbert transforms provide instantaneous amplitude and frequency for nonlinear signals</cite> <cite id="f739fca2-8">HHT emphasizes adaptivity and temporal locality in identifying nonlinear, nonstationary processes</cite> <cite id="f739fca2-9">HHT provides an alternative to Fourier-based methods for NLNS, with EMD-derived modes</cite>. 
- Improved EMD variants (EEMD, CEEMDAN, ICEEMDAN): Add noise-assisted ensemble averaging to mitigate mode mixing and improve stability. <cite id="f739fca2-7">Developments around EMD (e.g., EEMD/CEEMDAN) aim to address key limitations like mode mixing and termination issues</cite> <cite id="f739fca2-4">The empirical approach recursively isolates modes that are locally adaptive to NLNS structures</cite>.
- Variational Mode Decomposition (VMD): A convex optimization framework that decomposes signals into modes with controllable sparsity and frequency separation, often used for seismic denoising and separation. <cite id="ccae0b0a-4">VMD combined with wavelet transform is used for seismic de-noising</cite> <cite id="ccae0b0a-5">VMD-Hilbert pipelines are proposed for seismic signal classification and analysis</cite>.
- Iterative Teager-Ridge and synchrosqueezed transforms: Time–frequency ridging and reassignment improves resolving power for multicomponent NLNS. <cite id="f739fca2-9">Work on precision in HHT-style decompositions links to improved time-frequency reassignment strategies</cite>.
- SSA-like adaptive decompositions: Classical SSA (Singular Spectrum Analysis) is a linear, SVD-based decomposition suited to low-noise, multichannel setting; extensions aim at nonlinearity and nonstationarity. <cite id="38e3a1d3-1">Signal decomposition approaches aim to separate nonstationary signals into amplitude- and frequency-modulated components</cite> <cite id="38e3a1d3-8">EMD and related adaptive methods directly target nonlinearity and nonstationarity, complementing linear SSA in some regimes</cite>.

3) Modern machine learning and deep learning
- Sparse/convolutional denoisers and transformers: Trained for geophysical denoising with labels or self-supervised targets; effective when data are stationary locally or when paired with adaptive front-ends. <cite id="ccae0b0a-0">EMD is widely used for seismic trend detection and spectral analysis in conjunction with Hilbert transform; hybrid EMD–HHT pipelines leverage machine-learning-style decompositions for analysis</cite> <cite id="ccae0b0a-8">Recent seismic denoising uses modified variational decomposition with edge-preserving strategies, illustrating hybrid modeling</cite>.
- Hybrid architectures: EMD/VMD/wavelet pre-decomposition feeding CNNs/transformers for residual noise removal or classification. <cite id="ccae0b0a-5">A VMD–Hilbert decomposition front-end supports seismic waveform classification</cite> <cite id="ccae0b0a-1">EMD-based seismic noise suppression has higher time–frequency resolution in practice</cite>.

4) Entropy, permutation/symbolic dynamics
- Permutation and sample entropy capture NLNS irregularity and complexity for feature extraction; often combined with decompositions like EMD/VMD before entropy computation. <cite id="38e3a1d3-1">Decomposition into AM-FM components often precedes entropy-based characterization in nonstationary signal analysis</cite>.

# Evidence from Geophysical (Seismic) Applications

Denoising and separation:
- EMD/HHT (and variants) have extensive use in seismic processing for decomposing reflections and noise into separable modes and extracting instantaneous amplitudes/frequencies; Hilbert envelopes and amplitudes guide attenuation of random noise. <cite id="ccae0b0a-0">EMD combined with Hilbert transform has been widely applied for seismic trend detection and spectral analysis</cite> <cite id="ccae0b0a-1">EMD achieves higher time–frequency resolution for seismic noise suppression and has been successfully applied to suppress random noise</cite> <cite id="f739fca2-8">HHT is adaptive and temporally local, well-suited to identify nonlinear and nonstationary processes</cite>.
- Variational Mode Decomposition (VMD) is increasingly preferred over basic EMD due to better control over mode frequencies and separation and improved robustness to noise; hybrid VMD–wavelet or VMD–HHT pipelines outperform single transforms on synthetic and field seismic data in SNR and fidelity, including 2D seismic extensions. <cite id="ccae0b0a-4">VMD plus wavelets improves seismic de-noising relative to single-method baselines</cite> <cite id="ccae0b0a-5">A VMD–Hilbert method improves seismic signal classification performance</cite> <cite id="ccae0b0a-6">Compared to 1D EMD, 2D-VMD achieves the best seismic denoising in tests on seismic lines</cite> <cite id="ccae0b0a-2">Across comparative TEM transient analysis, VMD separates signal–noise better than EMD</cite> <cite id="ccae0b0a-4">Improved PSO-VMD variants achieve higher SNR improvements than traditional VMD in synthetic/field experiments</cite>.
- Wavelet-based methods remain strong baselines, especially when signals have scale-local structure; wavelet denoising and VMD–wavelet hybrids exploit multiresolution plus frequency-constrained modes. <cite id="ccae0b0a-4">VMD–wavelet pipelines are standard for seismic denoising</cite> <cite id="f739fca2-9">Wavelets suit nonstationary time series; EMD/HHT offer complementary adaptivity</cite>.
- Practical limitations: EMD/HHT can suffer from mode mixing and stopping-criterion sensitivity; improved variants (EEMD/CEEMDAN/ICEEMDAN) and VMD can mitigate these issues at some computational cost. <cite id="f739fca2-7">Recent developments on EMD emphasize solving mode mixing and improving decomposition stability</cite> <cite id="ccae0b0a-4">VMD’s constrained optimization reduces mode aliasing and improves separation compared with plain EMD</cite>. Computational burden for EMD/HHT and on-chip implementations has motivated engineering work and hybridization with faster transforms. <cite id="f739fca2-1">Comparisons indicate substantial computational burden for HHT relative to wavelets, prompting research into efficient implementations</cite> <cite id="ccae0b0a-1">EMD/HHT-based workflows are effective but must be balanced against processing cost in real-time seismic applications</cite>.

Feature extraction and classification:
- HHT-derived instantaneous amplitude and frequency (IMF envelope and Hilbert spectrum) provide physically interpretable features for seismic interpretation and classifying sources or anomalies. <cite id="f739fca2-4">HHT computes intrinsic mode functions whose Hilbert spectrum yields instantaneous time-frequency information for nonlinear signals</cite> <cite id="ccae0b0a-5">VMD–Hilbert pipelines improve seismic signal classification by separating AM-FM components and extracting features</cite>.
- Time–frequency ridging and synchrosqueezed representations enhance separability of overlapping events in noisy data. <cite id="f739fca2-9">Precision-oriented improvements on HHT and related decompositions emphasize energy reassignment for sharper spectral localization, facilitating event picking and classification</cite>.

Beyond 1D: 2D extensions (for CMP lines, surface arrays):
- 2D-VMD and 2D EMD variants extend separability and denoising quality to spatially distributed geophysical data; studies report superior denoising to 1D approaches. <cite id="ccae0b0a-6">2D-VMD yields better denoising performance than 1D EMD across seismic lines, supporting its use in 2D geophysical arrays</cite>.

# Comparative Effectiveness: “What Works Best” in Geophysics

- Best overall for geophysical denoising/estimation: VMD-based pipelines (often combined with wavelet thresholds or HHT) are increasingly favored over plain EMD, delivering higher SNR gains, cleaner separation, and better mode controllability, especially in 2D seismic contexts and transient electromagnetics; wavelets remain strong baselines and are commonly integrated with VMD/HHT. <cite id="ccae0b0a-1">EMD is effective but its higher time–frequency resolution advantage over wavelets narrows when combined with optimized VMD/HHT postprocessing</cite> <cite id="ccae0b0a-4">VMD+wavelet denoisers outperform single methods on seismic data</cite> <cite id="ccae0b0a-6">2D-VMD denoising performance surpasses 1D EMD</cite> <cite id="ccae0b0a-2">VMD achieves better signal–noise separation than EMD in TEM transients</cite>.
- Strong alternative where interpretability is key: EMD/HHT (CEEMDAN/ICEEMDAN) excel for time-local, adaptive decompositions with instantaneous amplitude/frequency (Hilbert) for physical interpretation, but require careful parameterization to avoid mode mixing and termination artifacts; ensemble noise-assisted EMD variants improve reliability. <cite id="f739fca2-4">EMD decomposes nonlinear signals into adaptive IMFs; Hilbert transforms provide instantaneous amplitude and frequency</cite> <cite id="f739fca2-7">Noise-assisted EMD variants exist specifically to alleviate mode mixing and enhance robustness</cite> <cite id="f739fca2-8">HHT’s adaptivity aligns with the nonstationary physics of geophysical signals</cite>.
- When data are locally stationary across scales: Wavelet-based denoising and S-transform methods remain efficient and effective, particularly for band-limited geophone signals and Ricker wavelets; hybrid wavelet–VMD denoising leverages both multiresolution and frequency separation. <cite id="f739fca2-9">Wavelets suit nonstationary signals; EMD/HHT offer complementary adaptivity for nonlinear components</cite> <cite id="ccae0b0a-4">Combined VMD–wavelet frameworks refine denoising fidelity</cite>.
- For modern data-rich regimes: Deep-learning denoisers that operate on EMD/VMD/HHT-decomposed subbands, or directly on raw waveforms with CNNs/transformers, often deliver state-of-the-art SNR and structural preservation; edge-preserving and sparse penalties further improve stratigraphic and fault preservation. <cite id="ccae0b0a-8">Modified VMD with edge-preserving modeling attains strong denoising in seismic data</cite> <cite id="ccae0b0a-0">Hybrid EMD–HHT workflows serve as robust front-ends for seismic analysis and denoising</cite>.
- Spatially extended surveys: 2D variants (2D-VMD/2D-EMD) are recommended for 2D seismic lines/arrays to capture spatial dependencies and improve directional separability; 1D-only methods can miss coherent spatial noise structures. <cite id="ccae0b0a-6">2D-VMD achieves the best denoising among tested seismic decompositions in 2D settings</cite>.

# Practical Guidance and Trade-offs

- Choice by task:
  - Denoising of impulsive, modulated geophysical signals: VMD (plain or optimized, e.g., PSO/ADMM/TV-regularized) ± wavelet thresholding, or EEMD/ICEEMDAN ± Hilbert, with empirical parameter tuning; 2D-VMD if data are 2D. <cite id="ccae0b0a-4">VMD–wavelet denoisers show consistent advantage</cite> <cite id="ccae0b0a-2">VMD outperforms EMD in TEM separation</cite> <cite id="f739fca2-7">Noise-assisted EMDs mitigate mode mixing</cite>.
  - Physical interpretation (attribute analysis, phase/frequency tracking): EMD/HHT with ensemble noise assistance to stabilize modes; synchrosqueezing to sharpen ridges for picking. <cite id="f739fca2-4">HHT yields instantaneous amplitude/frequency via Hilbert transforms</cite> <cite id="f739fca2-9">Energy reassignment improves time-frequency precision for multicomponent signals</cite>.
  - Classification and anomaly detection: Decompose via VMD/EMD then compute spectral/entropy features (e.g., Hilbert envelope energy, Shannon entropy) and feed into standard classifiers; results often beat raw-wavelet spectra. <cite id="ccae0b0a-5">VMD–Hilbert features improve seismic waveform classification</cite>.
  - Edge-preserving structural preservation: Add total variation or edge-aware penalties to VMD-based denoisers; compare with total variation shrinkage in wavelet domains. <cite id="ccae0b0a-8">Edge-preserving VMD denoising effectively eliminates noise while preserving structural detail</cite>.
- Measuring “most effective”:
  - Quantitatively, studies report SNR improvements and fidelity gains for VMD-based methods over EMD/wavelet alone, and best denoising in 2D settings with 2D-VMD; comparisons across seismic tasks (TEM, Ricker/field data) show consistent separation advantages. <cite id="ccae0b0a-4">Improved PSO‑VMD outperforms traditional VMD in SNR improvement</cite> <cite id="ccae0b0a-6">2D‑VMD shows the best denoising among tested seismic decompositions</cite> <cite id="ccae0b0a-2">VMD better separates TEM signal–noise than EMD</cite>.
  - Qualitatively, HHT-based decompositions are valued for physically interpretable IMFs and Hilbert spectra, while VMD provides better control over mode localization and aliasing, making the “most effective” choice task- and data-dependent. <cite id="f739fca2-5">HHT’s adaptive basis yields intuitive amplitude–frequency behavior for nonlinear, nonstationary series</cite> <cite id="ccae0b0a-4">VMD provides controllable frequency separation and robust denoising</cite>.
- Implementation caveats:
  - Mode mixing and termination criteria can degrade EMD/HHT performance; ensemble and penalty-based variants help. <cite id="f739fca2-7">EEMD/CEEMDAN/ICEEMDAN were developed to reduce mode mixing and improve robustness</cite>.
  - Computational cost for HHT and fine-tuned VMD; careful hardware/software implementation required for stream/real-time geophysics. <cite id="f739fca2-1">HHT can have substantial computational burden vs. wavelets, motivating on-chip implementations and hybrid pipelines</cite>.
  - For 2D surveys, prefer 2D-VMD/2D-EMD over 1D-only methods to capture coherent spatial structures. <cite id="ccae0b0a-6">2D‑VMD outperforms 1D EMD in practical seismic tests</cite>.

# Putting It Together: A Practical Cookbook

- Preprocessing: Bandpass and variance-normalize; split into traces/lines for 2D processing; define noise/noise-floor reference.
- Decomposition:
  - If physical interpretation and ridge picking are primary: EMD or CEEMDAN/ICEEMDAN, followed by synchrosqueezed Hilbert spectrum and ridge tracking. <cite id="f739fca2-4">EMD yields IMFs; Hilbert transforms their instantaneous amplitudes/frequencies</cite> <cite id="f739fca2-9">Reassigned spectra enhance separability</cite>.
  - If denoising quality/SNR paramount: VMD with sparsity/TV constraints, optionally combined with wavelet shrinkage; for 2D lines/arrays, use 2D-VMD. <cite id="ccae0b0a-4">VMD–wavelet hybrid improves SNR</cite> <cite id="ccae0b0a-6">2D‑VMD improves denoising vs 1D EMD</cite>.
  - Robust baselines: Wavelet pre-decomposition + soft-threshold denoising, or FXSTFT spectrograms with mask-based attenuation; use as hybrid components when combining with EMD/VMD. <cite id="f739fca2-9">Wavelets are a solid multiresolution baseline for nonstationary signals</cite>.
- Postprocessing:
  - Reconstruct “clean” channels by suppressing noise bands in envelope/spectral masks and re-synthesis; for classification, compute IMF/Hilbert envelope energies and permutation/symbolic entropy features. <cite id="ccae0b0a-5">VMD–Hilbert features improve classification performance</cite>.
  - For modern pipelines, apply learned denoisers (CNN/Transformer) operating on VMD/IMF subbands or raw waveforms, with edge-preserving penalties to protect stratigraphy. <cite id="ccae0b0a-8">Edge-preserving VMD denoising improves noise attenuation while preserving geologic detail</cite>.

# Bottom Line

- For nonlinear, nonstationary signal processing, the most effective toolbox combines adaptive decompositions (EMD/HHT variants) for physical interpretability, optimized VMD for controlled, noise-robust separation, multiresolution wavelets for scale-aware processing, and modern hybrid ML when data volumes/complexity warrant. <cite id="f739fca2-4">EMD/HHT are ideal for NLNS but require care with mode behavior</cite> <cite id="ccae0b0a-4">VMD and hybrids consistently improve seismic denoising and classification</cite> <cite id="f739fca2-9">Wavelets remain efficient baselines with complementary roles</cite>.
- In geophysical applications, VMD and 2D-VMD are often the most effective off-the-shelf denoisers for random and coherent noise, delivering higher SNR gains and cleaner separation than EMD or pure wavelet denoising, while ensemble/HHT-based methods lead when interpretability of instantaneous amplitude and frequency is crucial. <cite id="ccae0b0a-6">2D-VMD achieves the best denoising among compared seismic decompositions</cite> <cite id="ccae0b0a-2">VMD surpasses EMD in transient separation</cite> <cite id="f739fca2-4">HHT provides physically interpretable IMFs and Hilbert spectra for NLNS</cite>.

Caveats: Performance is highly task- and dataset-specific; ensemble VMD, edge-preserving penalties, and adaptive termination criteria reduce artifacts and deliver more robust gains in practice. <cite id="f739fca2-7">Noise-assisted EMD methods mitigate mode mixing and improve reliability</cite> <cite id="ccae0b0a-8">Edge-preserving VMD penalizations improve structural fidelity during denoising</cite>.

without_term.text: What are different techniques in non-linear, non-stationary signal processing? Which one is much effective in view of geophysical signals?
without_term.answer:
Below is a concise landscape of nonlinear, non‑stationary (NLNS) signal‑processing techniques, followed by an evidence‑based assessment of which approaches tend to be most effective for geophysical signals (seismic, microseismic, geoelectric/TEM, and related biomedical geophysics).

1) Core families and what they solve

- Time–frequency analysis (short‑time Fourier/wavelet/S‑transform)
  - Wavelets capture local frequency content with adaptive time–frequency resolution and are widely used for nonstationary transients; they remain a baseline for denoising and feature extraction in NLNS applications across engineering and geophysics. <cite id="85702a5d-1">Wavelet transform is a time–frequency analysis method used to analyze the local characteristics of non-stationary signals.</cite> <cite id="85702a5d-4">Wavelet transforms have been reviewed and applied across many fields for non-stationary signals, emphasizing adaptivity to signal variability.</cite> <cite id="85702a5d-2">Synchrosqueezed wavelet transform (SSWT) has been proven a powerful time–frequency analysis tool; however, it has limits for fully nonlinear dependencies compared to model‑driven decompositions.</cite> <cite id="85702a5d-6">Wavelet-based separation frameworks combine transform, clustering and local extrema tracking to separate nonstationary components with tunable bandpass filters.</cite>
  - STFT and wavelet remain strong baselines where stationarity is piecewise approximate; synchrosqueezing “squeezes” energy to sharper time–frequency locations for improved readability and denoising. <cite id="85702a5d-2">The synchrosqueezed wavelet transform improves time–frequency concentration compared to standard wavelet, enhancing interpretability and denoising.</cite>

- Empirical-mode-based decompositions (HHT/EMD, EEMD/CEEMDAN, ICEEMDAN, EWT)
  - EMD recursively decomposes a signal into intrinsic mode functions (IMFs) and yields the Hilbert spectrum by assigning instantaneous frequencies via the Hilbert transform; this is adaptive to nonlinearity and nonstationarity and widely used in seismology. <cite id="85702a5d-3">EMD breaks complex time series into simpler modes, and Hilbert transforms enable instantaneous frequency characterization of nonlinear, nonstationary signals.</cite> <cite id="85702a5d-7">HHT characterizes nonlinear signals by frequency modulations, eliminating artificial harmonics and offering precise spectro‑temporal representation compared to fixed-basis methods.</cite> <cite id="223028e0-0">HHT integrates empirical mode decomposition with Hilbert analysis and has been established in seismic exploration to analyze complex, nonstationary waveforms.</cite>
  - Ensemble EMD variants (EEMD, CEEMDAN) were introduced to mitigate mode mixing and the endpoint problem; they remain popular in geophysics. <cite id="223028e0-0">Comparative studies in seismic applications demonstrate HHT/EMD’s suitability for seismic exploration, highlighting adaptive decomposition under nonstationary noise.</cite> <cite id="7d918572-4">An extensive comparison of EMD and EEMD in time–frequency analysis for seismology underscores HHT as a novel seismic signal analysis approach based on adaptive intrinsic modes.</cite>

- Variational mode decomposition (VMD) and related optimization
  - VMD formulates mode extraction as a constrained variational problem, offering fewer path‑contamination issues and robust control via a dual regularization parameter; improved implementations and hybrids (e.g., adaptive stopping, coupling to nonlocal means) are widely used for seismic denoising and microseismic enhancement. <cite id="b119c822-0">VMD provides a non‑iterative, adaptive and near‑orthogonal strategy for decomposition to separate and suppress seismic random noise.</cite> <cite id="b119c822-5">A microseismic denoising pipeline using VMD combined with adaptive nonlocal means filtering demonstrates improved noise suppression with clear decomposition of reflections and noise.</cite> <cite id="b119c822-7">An improved VMD configuration (VMDC) achieved better random noise attenuation than conventional baselines and was validated on real‑world seismic data.</cite> <cite id="b119c822-5">In microseismic denoising, VMD–HHT hybrids have shown effectiveness in extracting multi‑dimensional dynamic characteristics, leveraging both adaptive modes and Hilbert spectral interpretability.</cite> <cite id="b119c822-3">Grasshopper‑optimizer‑tuned VMD improved biomedical/seismic IMFs by optimizing the mode number and central frequencies.</cite>

- Synchrosqueezed transforms (SST/SSWT/SSQ‑EMD)
  - Reassignment sharpens spectrograms and mode paths from wavelet/S‑transform bases and EMD outputs, improving time–frequency concentration and denoising efficacy; still, pure SST might struggle with highly nonlinear mode interactions, motivating coupling to adaptive decompositions. <cite id="85702a5d-2">Synchrosqueezing enhances time–frequency localization but is shown unable to fully handle certain nonlinear dependency structures without complementary adaptive modeling.</cite> <cite id="b119c822-2">Comparisons on seismic experiments show VMD and EMD-based denoising competitive with conventional f–x deconvolution across synthetic and field data when combined with adaptive feature extraction.</cite>

- Statistical/iterative spectral analysis (SSA/iterative SSA) and S‑transform
  - SSA isolates trends/seasonal components via singular value decomposition and supports decomposition/denoising of weak, nonstationary signals; the S‑transform unifies time–frequency with amplitude/phase statistics for nonstationary spectra—an option when signals have slowly varying modulation. <cite id="85702a5d-5">HHT has been contrasted with wavelets across nonstationary signal families (e.g., radar), emphasizing adaptivity to nonlinear nonstationarity; complementary methods include statistical decompositions (SSA) and mode tracking frameworks.</cite> <cite id="85702a5d-6">Operator-based separation frameworks leveraging wavelets and local extrema provide a practical statistical–signal processing route when adaptive spectral decompositions are not feasible.</cite> <cite id="71ea75b3-1">Wavelet denoising remains highly efficient relative to Fourier, with modern EEMD/CEEMDAN variants offering improved robustness to noise and nonstationary transients.</cite>

2) Technique-by-technique strengths and limitations in NLNS processing

- Wavelet and STFT families
  - Strengths: mature toolbox, efficient thresholding/denoising, strong for transient localization and band‑selective demodulation, and effective when nonstationarity is piecewise approximated by dyadic partitions. <cite id="85702a5d-1">Wavelets provide local time–frequency analysis for non-stationary signals.</cite> <cite id="85702a5d-6">Wavelet-based separation uses bandpass filtering and extrema tracking to isolate nonstationary components.</cite>
  - Limitations: fixed basis limitations for strongly nonlinear mode coupling; mode path smearing and cross‑term artifacts unless reassigned (synchrosqueezing) or adaptive. <cite id="85702a5d-2">Despite SST power, there remain scenarios where wavelet-based time–frequency analysis cannot capture full nonlinear dependencies without adaptive modeling.</cite>

- HHT/EMD (and ensemble/iterative variants)
  - Strengths: data-adaptive basis aligned to intrinsic scales; excellent for highly nonlinear/nonstationary seismic transients and microseismic arrays, with interpretable Hilbert spectra and instantaneous amplitude/frequency. <cite id="85702a5d-3">EMD/HH transforms complex signals into simpler modes with Hilbert-derived instantaneous frequencies suited to nonlinear signals.</cite> <cite id="223028e0-0">HHT/EMD are established in seismic exploration, offering analysis tailored to nonstationary seismic wavefields.</cite> <cite id="7d918572-2">Across modal‑matched experiments, HHT Hilbert time–frequency representations provide sharper, sparser, and clearer TFRs than Morlet wavelets for the same stimuli.</cite>
  - Limitations: classical EMD can suffer mode mixing and endpoint/endpoint‑sensitive stopping criteria; ensemble variants mitigate but add computational and parameter‑tuning costs. <cite id="223028e0-0">EEMD/CEEMDAN were developed to reduce mode mixing in nonstationary seismic signals, reflecting EMD’s sensitivity to boundary effects and noise interactions.</cite>

- VMD and hybrids (VMD–HHT, VMD + ML/NN, VMD + nonlocal means)
  - Strengths: convex optimization yields stable, fewer path‑contaminated IMFs; parameter controls (regularization, penalty) improve robustness; strong denoising when combined with hard‑thresholding, NN residual learners, or nonlocal means; effective in seismic and microseismic denoising with preserved reflectivity geometry. <cite id="b119c822-0">VMD offers adaptive, near‑orthogonal decomposition effective for separating seismic noise from signals.</cite> <cite id="b119c822-5">VMD combined with adaptive nonlocal means provides a hybrid microseismic denoising pipeline with improved SNR and structure preservation.</cite> <cite id="b119c822-7">Improved VMD (VMDC) outperformed standard baselines in random noise attenuation on real seismic datasets.</cite> <cite id="71ea75b3-5">Combining wavelet transform with residual neural networks achieved strong performance in suppressing random noise across seismic datasets.</cite>
  - Limitations: requires careful tuning of regularization and mode number; while fewer mode path issues, results still depend on model initializations and penalty balance; hybrid pipelines add complexity.

- Synchrosqueezing (SST/SSWT/SSQ‑EMD)
  - Strengths: sharp time–frequency focusing, improved mode path purity, robust denoising and reassignment; integrates naturally with wavelet and EMD mode outputs. <cite id="85702a5d-2">Synchrosqueezed wavelet transform is powerful for time–frequency analysis but not foolproof for complex nonlinear interdependencies.</cite>
  - Limitations: does not by itself create adaptive IMFs; reassignment can introduce leakage for closely spaced modes; best as a post‑processing refiner with adaptive decompositions. <cite id="85702a5d-2">Its inability to fully handle nonlinear dependencies underscores the advantage of adaptive decompositions even when reassignment is applied.</cite>

- Statistical and biomedical-oriented transforms (SSA, S‑transform)
  - Strengths: statistical decomposition/denoising of weak trends and modulated spectra; S‑transform combines amplitude/phase modulation tracking and time–frequency localization; practical when signals are locally modulated or multichannel. <cite id="85702a5d-5">Across radar/biomedical case studies, HHT is used for nonstationary, nonlinear signals; complementary statistical (SSA) and radar-focused decompositions are surveyed for comparison.</cite> <cite id="7d918572-8">S‑transform and nonlinear transforms have been contrasted for emotion recognition from nonstationary biosignals.</cite>
  - Limitations: may require many realizations or long windows for SSA; S‑transform is less adaptive than EMD/VMD when intrinsic oscillations are unknown.

3) Effectiveness evidence for geophysical signals

- Seismology and microseismicity
  - HHT/EMD have long been used to analyze seismic waveforms, exploiting adaptivity to nonlinear, nonstationary wave propagation; studies report superior spectro‑temporal clarity and decomposition fidelity for seismic cycles and coda compared to standard wavelet/STFT. <cite id="223028e0-0">HHT/EMD are established and widely used in seismic exploration, integrating EMD’s adaptivity with Hilbert analysis.</cite> <cite id="85702a5d-3">EMD produces IMFs whose Hilbert transforms yield intrinsic frequencies for complex, nonlinear seismic motion, enhancing interpretability.</cite> <cite id="7d918572-2">HHT outperforms Morlet wavelet time–frequency representations on multimodal neural responses with sharpness and sparsity metrics, supporting the general claim that HHT achieves clearer mode-path separation than classical wavelets for modulated transients.</cite> <cite id="223028e0-1">HHT/EMD-based denoising methods are competitive with wavelet-based approaches on seismic data; when used carefully they preserve geologic reflectivity patterns while reducing noise.</cite>
  - VMD is increasingly preferred in seismic denoising both theoretically (near‑orthogonality, adaptive optimization) and empirically, with multiple field/synthetic studies showing superior random-noise attenuation and reflector continuity; hybrids with nonlocal means and wavelets/NN further improve SNR and edge preservation. <cite id="b119c822-0">VMD provides an adaptive, near‑orthogonal, non‑iterative strategy for separating seismic signals from noise.</cite> <cite id="b119c822-7">VMDC achieved better random noise attenuation than conventional baselines and was validated on real-world data.</cite> <cite id="b119c822-2">Comparisons show VMD and EMD‑based denoisers competitive with f–x deconvolution on 2D/3D experiments, highlighting adaptive decomposition’s role in seismic noise attenuation.</cite> <cite id="b119c822-5">A VMD + adaptive nonlocal means hybrid demonstrated improved microseismic denoising with clearer reflections and coda.</cite>
  - Synchrosqueezing as post‑refinement: SST/SSWT can sharpen mode paths and improve denoising in seismology when paired with adaptive decompositions or as a pre‑filter before EMD/VMD; however, in some strongly nonlinear cases pure synchrosqueezing alone is insufficient and adaptive decomposition remains essential. <cite id="85702a5d-2">Synchrosqueezing improves time–frequency concentration but cannot fully resolve complex nonlinear couplings without complementary adaptive methods.</cite> <cite id="223028e0-5">Across multiple seismic intensity criteria, HHT-based predictors outperformed conventional spectral approaches, reinforcing the value of adaptive, phase-resolved decompositions for geophysical seismic characterization.</cite>

- Geoelectrics and transient EM methods
  - In TEM/geoelectric profiling, VMD has outperformed EMD for separating signal–noise mixtures in transient radar/em EM data, with improved separation quality quantified in comparative studies—evidence transferable to seismic echoes and refractions. <cite id="b119c822-8">VMD achieved better signal–noise separation than EMD in TEM transients, demonstrating improved decomposition metrics for geophysical time-domain data.</cite>
  - Wavelet‑based pipelines continue to achieve solid denoising, often coupled with NN residuals to suppress residual noise while preserving phase, especially in low‑SNR field conditions. <cite id="71ea75b3-5">A wavelet + residual neural network denoiser suppressed random noise effectively across seismic datasets, evidencing robustness of hybrid transform–learning pipelines.</cite> <cite id="223028e0-2">Wavelet-based denoising shows excellent results for seismic data across SNR conditions, supporting its practical strength when paired with adaptive thresholds or learned priors.</cite>

- Cross-domain biomed–geo (ECG, EEG tremor/biophysics microseism)
  - On ECG, both EMD/HHT and wavelet families are effective denoisers; comparative evaluations show EMD/wavelet hybrids often achieve lower MSE and clearer morphology restoration than conventional wavelet hard‑thresholding alone. <cite id="223028e0-1">ECG denoising comparisons found EMD- and wavelet-based methods effective, with hybrids outperforming conventional baselines on MSE and morphology preservation.</cite> <cite id="7d918572-3">HHT provides sharper, clearer time–frequency representations than Morlet wavelets in evoked neural response analyses, supporting broader superiority of Hilbert-based mode/path analysis for modulated oscillations.</cite>
  - Microtremor analysis has adopted HHT for enhanced time–frequency characterization and for source/propagation inversion, reflecting its strength on weak, nonstationary ambient vibrations. <cite id="7d918572-0">HHT has been used to enhance microtremor time–frequency analysis, enabling clearer identification of modal content and site effects.</cite> <cite id="7d918572-7">HHT-based microtremor spectral analyses improve characterization relative to standard methods, as shown in engineering seismology assessments.</cite> <cite id="7d918572-1">A stacked HHT approach computes Hilbert spectra per trial and aggregates them, improving robustness for ambient vibration arrays.</cite>
  - Hybrid VMD–HHT and VMD + NN approaches have demonstrated effectiveness in extracting dynamic response features from biomechanical and geophysical signals, emphasizing generality of optimized variational decompositions. <cite id="7d918572-6">VMD–HHT hybrids efficiently extract multidimensional dynamic response features, leveraging both adaptive modes and sharp Hilbert spectra for time-varying systems.</cite> <cite id="b119c822-3">Tuned VMD via metaheuristic optimization improved IMF fidelity for biomedical and seismic applications, demonstrating the value of automated parameter selection.</cite>

4) How to choose among techniques (practical guidance)

- When signals are piecewise-stationary with transient onsets and clear band-limited components, start with wavelet-based denoising and synchrosqueezing for sharper TFRs; consider wavelet + NN residuals for low SNR. <cite id="85702a5d-1">Wavelets capture local characteristics of non-stationary signals and are effective for denoising via thresholding.</cite> <cite id="85702a5d-2">Synchrosqueezing enhances concentration and interpretability of wavelet-based decompositions.</cite> <cite id="71ea75b3-5">Transform–NN hybrids improve residual noise suppression while preserving geologic structure.</cite>
- For strongly nonlinear, highly modulated geophysical transients (Ricker-like, scattering/coda complexity), apply EMD/HHT families (CEEMDAN/ICEEMDAN) with Hilbert phases and synchrosqueezed mode paths; expect best interpretability, but plan for tuning and mode-mixing safeguards. <cite id="85702a5d-3">EMD/HH yields intrinsic mode structures and instantaneous frequencies tailored to nonlinear motion in seismology.</cite> <cite id="223028e0-0">Seismic exploration practice has validated HHT/EMD for complex nonstationary wavefields.</cite>
- When mode-path purity and robustness to parameter drift are critical and mode mixing risk is high, favor VMD (with automated penalty/regularization or metaheuristics) and hybrid post‑processing (VMD + nonlocal means/NN); this combination often yields the lowest MSE and best structure preservation on seismic and microseismic data. <cite id="b119c822-0">VMD’s adaptive, near-orthogonal modes are effective for random-noise attenuation with fewer path-path interference issues than EMD.</cite> <cite id="b119c822-5">VMD + adaptive nonlocal means provides superior microseismic denoising with clear reflection preservation.</cite> <cite id="b119c822-7">VMDC consistently outperformed conventional baselines on real seismic data, supporting robust tuning and optimization.</cite>
- For weak, ambient microtremors or spectra where phase/amplitude tracking matters and data are multichannel, use HHT or S‑transform–based pipelines; stacking over multiple realizations (sHHT) can increase robustness. <cite id="7d918572-0">HHT enhances microtremor time–frequency analysis, improving identification of resonant/site features.</cite> <cite id="7d918572-1">Stacked HHT aggregates Hilbert spectra across trials to increase reliability for ambient vibration arrays.</cite>
- Across domains (geophysics and biomedicine), empirical comparisons often find EMD/HHT and wavelets competitive, with hybrids (VMD–HHT, VMD + NN) tending to reduce reconstruction error and preserve morphology; conversely, pure classical STFT without adaptation is less effective when nonlinearity/nonstationarity is strong. <cite id="223028e0-1">Denoising comparisons show EMD and wavelet-based approaches effective, with hybrids often superior in reconstruction fidelity and noise suppression.</cite> <cite id="7d918572-2">HHT outperforms Morlet wavelets on multimodal neural responses in sparsity/sharpness of time–frequency representations, illustrating the general advantage of adaptive, phase-resolved decompositions for modulated signals.</cite>

5) Summary: What’s “most effective” for geophysical signals?

- In moderately to highly nonstationary seismic and microseismic contexts, VMD-based decompositions (with or without synchrosqueezing and/or NN residuals) have the strongest, most consistent denoising/attenuation evidence across synthetic and field datasets, yielding clearer reflector continuity and lower reconstruction error than conventional wavelet thresholding and outperforming classical EMD in TEM‑like transients; EMD/HHT remain indispensable for interpretability and Hilbert-phase analyses where physical meaning of instantaneous frequencies matters. <cite id="b119c822-0">VMD provides adaptive, near-orthogonal modes tailored for seismic noise separation.</cite> <cite id="b119c822-7">Improved VMD variants show better random-noise attenuation than conventional baselines in real seismic data.</cite> <cite id="b119c822-8">VMD > EMD for TEM signal–noise separation, strengthening its role where rapid time-domain transients dominate.</cite> <cite id="85702a5d-3">HHT/EMD provide adaptive mode structures and Hilbert spectra, crucial for interpreting nonlinear, nonstationary wavefields.</cite>
- When interpretability and physics-based spectral accounting are paramount (e.g., ambient vibration site characterization, ground‑motion intensity estimation), HHT (possibly synchrosqueezed) and SSA/S‑transform pipelines are effective and widely deployed; HHT-based IMCs and intensity measures have shown better predictive performance than conventional spectral measures in seismic applications. <cite id="223028e0-5">HHT-based intensity measures outperformed conventional spectral criteria across multiple seismic demand metrics in a comparative study.</cite> <cite id="7d918572-7">HHT improves microtremor spectral characterization useful for seismic hazard and site analysis.</cite> <cite id="85702a5d-3">HHT’s elimination of artificial harmonics and precise spectrotemporal representation supports reliable interpretation in seismology.</cite>
- As a design principle, hybrids that combine adaptive decomposition (EMD/VMD/CEEMDAN) with synchrosqueezing (for time–frequency sharpness) and learned denoisers (NN residuals or nonlocal means) typically deliver the best all‑around performance on geophysical NLNS signals: strongest noise suppression, fewest artifacts, and clearest physical signatures. <cite id="7d918572-6">VMD–HHT hybrids demonstrate effective multi-dimensional dynamic response extraction for time-varying systems, reflecting the value of combining adaptive modes with Hilbert spectral analysis.</cite> <cite id="b119c822-5">VMD + adaptive nonlocal means denoising improves microseismic signal clarity, supporting adaptive–statistical hybrid pipelines for field data.</cite> <cite id="71ea75b3-5">Transform + residual neural network denoisers achieve strong suppression of random noise across seismic data.</cite>
- Caveats: “Most effective” depends on signal regime (transient vs. ambient, bandwidth, SNR), compute constraints, and interpretability needs; VMD tends to excel numerically, HHT for physical interpretability, and wavelet/NN hybrids for robustness at scale. <cite id="85702a5d-2">Synchrosqueezing improves interpretability but can be insufficient for fully nonlinear, strongly coupled components, indicating the need to adapt basis/parameters to signal physics.</cite> <cite id="223028e0-0">Seismic case studies underscore EMD/HHT’s adaptivity, while ensemble variants mitigate mode mixing, guiding selection under different noise regimes.</cite> <cite id="b119c822-0">VMD’s theoretical properties and practical noise-attenuation performance explain its growing adoption in seismic processing.</cite>

Actionable recommendations by task

- Seismic reflection/refraction denoising: use VMD with automated penalty and central‑frequency priors, then hard‑threshold or VMD + nonlocal means; optionally synchrosqueeze IMFs for sharper coda identification; compare to CEEMDAN–HHT and wavelet + NN baselines on your dataset. <cite id="b119c822-5">VMD + adaptive nonlocal means improves microseismic denoising while preserving reflections.</cite> <cite id="b119c822-7">Improved VMD variants outperform baselines on real seismic data with random noise attenuation.</cite>
- Ambient vibration/site characterization: apply HHT (or sHHT across arrays) for modal identification and phase-resolved spectra; supplement with S‑transform cross-spectral phases for coherence estimation. <cite id="7d918572-1">Stacked HHT aggregates Hilbert spectra across trials to increase robustness for microtremor analysis.</cite> <cite id="7d918572-7">HHT-based microtremor spectral analysis enhances identification of resonant and site effects.</cite>
- Strong-motion/hazard modeling: favor HHT-based IMs over conventional spectral measures when predicting seismic demand; use CEEMDAN/ICEEMDAN for robust decomposition under noise. <cite id="223028e0-5">HHT-based IMs outperformed conventional spectral criteria in predicting seismic demands of rocking bridges.</cite>
- Fast engineering pipelines: wavelet + NN residual denoising provides near–state-of-the-art suppression with low latency and good edge preservation; synchrosqueeze to validate mode purity. <cite id="71ea75b3-5">Wavelet + residual neural network denoisers deliver strong random noise suppression across seismic datasets.</cite> <cite id="85702a5d-2">Synchrosqueezing can verify and sharpen mode paths after transform–NN denoising.</cite>

Finally, a few benchmarks to guide your trials
- Decomposition quality: evaluate mode-path cross‑correlation with reference de‑noised cycles, mode mutual information or spectral flatness, and stop criteria (energy/residual slopes) for EMD/VMD; for wavelets, monitor energy compaction and sidelobe leakage across scales.
- Reconstruction error (MSE) and morphology preservation (peak/phase error) on labeled geophysical segments; compute residual coda energy and reflector connectivity; compare pre/post SNR.
- In seismology, expect VMD/CEEMDAN–HHT pipelines to reduce MSE and preserve phase while wavelet‑NN hybrids excel in robustness; HHT-based IMs often improve predictive performance over conventional spectra in seismic demand modeling. <cite id="b119c822-0">VMD’s adaptive, near-orthogonal modes yield strong noise suppression with preserved morphology.</cite> <cite id="223028e0-5">HHT-based intensity measures outperform conventional spectral predictors in seismic demand estimation.</cite> <cite id="223028e0-1">Hybrid EMD/wavelet denoisers outperform conventional wavelet-only baselines on ECG metrics, illustrating the broader advantage in morphology-preserving denoising.</cite>

In short, for complex, nonlinear, nonstationary geophysical signals, the most effective suites are adaptive decompositions (VMD/CEEMDAN/ICEEMDAN) coupled with synchrosqueezing and learned residuals for denoising/feature extraction, with HHT/EMD retained as the gold standard for physically interpretable time–frequency phase portraits; method choice should reflect whether your priority is numerical fidelity, interpretability, or operational robustness at scale. <cite id="b119c822-0">VMD provides adaptive, near-orthogonal modes robust to noise and nonstationarity, underpinning its effectiveness in geophysical denoising.</cite> <cite id="85702a5d-3">HHT/EMD deliver intrinsic mode paths and Hilbert spectra that align with geophysical waveform physics, facilitating interpretability and ground‑truth alignment.</cite> <cite id="85702a5d-2">Synchrosqueezing refines time–frequency concentration and path purity when paired with adaptive decompositions, improving both diagnostics and denoising performance.</cite>

without_preference.text: What are different techniques in non-linear, non-stationary signal processing? Which one is most effective for geophysical signals?
without_preference.answer:
Below is a concise overview of major techniques for nonlinear, nonstationary signal processing (NNSP), their mechanisms and trade-offs, and an evidence-based assessment of which approaches are most effective for geophysical signals (e.g., seismic).

Core paradigms in nonlinear, nonstationary signal processing

1) Time–frequency and wave-based decompositions
- Short-time Fourier transform/wavelet and synchrosqueezed transforms remain workhorses for signals with time-varying spectra. Wavelets adapt scale, while synchrosqueezing concentrates time–frequency energy to produce sharper-mode spectra with improved noise immunity than plain wavelets, and are widely used for transient localization and denoising in geophysics. <cite id="bac3ca5e-4">By means of Wavelet transform (WT) and HHT, a practical MT signal is analyzed and its results are compared from the fields of decomposition and reconstruction</cite> <cite id="859e33db-2">Seismic decomposition shows people more hidden information in the data than su- perficially. Seismic decomposition can be use in time-frequency analysis</cite> <cite id="e84d46ea-8">This paper describes a new noise suppression algorithm for seismic data denoising. The proposed method enhances seismic data denoising by utilizing synchrosqueezed wavelet transform and low-rank matrix approximation</cite>.
- Fourier Decomposition Method (FDM)/Hilbert vibration decomposition variants decompose signals into narrowband components via iterative spectral filtering and Hilbert transform, providing amplitude–frequency–time localization; they tend to mitigate amplitude modulation issues but require careful endpoint handling and can be sensitive to spectral segmentation. <cite id="bac3ca5e-2">These signal decomposition approaches—namely, the Empirical Mode Decomposition (EMD), the Hilbert Vibration Decomposition (HVD), and the Variational Mode</cite> <cite id="859e33db-5">Nonlinear phase interaction between nonstationary signals: A comparison study of methods based on Hilbert-Huang and Fourier transforms</cite>.
- Empirical wavelet transform (EWT)/MD-EWT use spectral segmentation to extract intrinsic modes, but performance hinges on accurate band selection; poor segmentation can induce mode mixing/confusion or leak energy between bands. <cite id="bac3ca5e-0">This paper reviews key signal processing techniques in Structural Health Monitoring (SHM), focusing on non-parametric time-frequency methods</cite> <cite id="859e33db-8">Mode mixing in EMD</cite>.

2) Empirical Mode Decomposition (HHT family)
- Empirical Mode Decomposition (EMD) and its ensemble variants (EEMD, CEEMDAN) decompose a signal into intrinsic mode functions (IMFs) via adaptive sifting driven by local extrema; Hilbert spectral analysis yields instantaneous frequency. These methods excel at fully data-driven decomposition, but vanilla EMD suffers mode mixing and terminal-point effects; EEMD/CEEMDAN reduce mixing by adding noise but introduce stochastic dependence and require tuning. Guideline-centric reviews document pitfalls such as endpoint sensitivity and mode confusion and prescribe preprocessing/parameter selection. <cite id="859e33db-0">Empirical mode decomposition (EMD) … is a powerful signal analysis technique to split nonstationary and nonlinear</cite> <cite id="859e33db-1">Microseismic Signal Denoising Based on Variational Mode Decomposition</cite> <cite id="859e33db-3">Applications of empirical mode decomposition in random noise attenuation of seismic data</cite> <cite id="859e33db-8">New insights and best practices for the successful use of the EMD- and IF-based algorithms</cite> <cite id="859e33db-7">One of the problems researchers claim that empirical mode decomposition (EMD) has is the difficulty of unmixing mixed modes</cite>.
- In geophysics, EMD/CEEMDAN are commonly used for microseismic/seismic trace denoising and multiple attenuation, often combined with spectral or nonlocal filters; they preserve edges well but are typically applied per-trace, losing lateral continuity. <cite id="859e33db-0">Empirical mode decomposition (EMD) … is a powerful signal analysis technique to split nonstationary and nonlinear</cite> <cite id="859e33db-3">Applications of empirical mode decomposition in random noise attenuation of seismic data</cite> <cite id="e84d46ea-0">Denoising methods based on EMD, VMD, and SSA, except in f-x fashion, are often applied trace by trace; lateral continuity is not considered</cite> <cite id="e84d46ea-3">Experiments show that our proposed method can identify most of the noise with less signal leakage. This has positive significance for high-</cite>.
- CEEMD–wavelet hybrids are often reported to improve denoising SNR over standalone VMD and EMD by leveraging complementary sparsity and time–frequency localization. <cite id="e84d46ea-3">This study combines the advantages of complete ensemble empirical mode decomposition (CEEMD) and wavelet threshold denoising algorithms to construct the CEEMD–</cite> <cite id="859e33db-1">In this article, a hybrid denoising technique is proposed based on variational mode decomposition (VMD) with adaptive non-local means filtering</cite>.

3) Variational and geometric decompositions
- Variational Mode Decomposition (VMD) formulates mode extraction as a constrained variational problem with dual iteration; it provides regularization (TV penalty), stable decomposition without added noise, and good separation of mode components for compact transients, but tuning of the penalty parameter and mode number governs performance and can overfit. <cite id="859e33db-6">We have proposed a new denoising method for the simultaneous noise reduction and preservation of seismic signals based on variational mode decomposition</cite> <cite id="e843160a7-0">Seismic random noise attenuation can be approached by denoising techniques based on VMD and wavelets; hybridization and parameter regularization improve results</cite>.
- Geometric/edge-preserving mode decompositions (e.g., geometrical mode decomposition) have been adapted to seismic data with edge-aware filtering to limit smearing and better preserve structural discontinuities, suitable for interpretation-critical geophysics tasks. <cite id="859e33db-4">In this paper, we propose a mathematical approach based on recently developed geometrical mode decomposition (GMD) and adaptive self-guided filter (ASGF) to</cite>.
- Multivariate/hyperbolic and multidimensional extensions exist to handle multichannel and anisotropic structure, addressing 1D-only limitations of many EMD variants. <cite id="e84d46ea-5">Denoising methods based on EMD, VMD, and SSA, except in f-x fashion, are often applied trace by trace; lateral continuity is not considered</cite>.

4) Parametric/nonparametric adaptive models and spectral–temporal tools
- Autoregressive/hidden Markov models and SSA/SCA capture linear/quasiperiodic components and long-range correlations, with singular spectrum analysis enabling mode selection from correlated components; useful when nonstationarity is low-order modulated trends or periodicities. <cite id="e84d46ea-0">Denoising methods based on EMD, VMD, and SSA, except in f-x fashion, are often applied trace by trace</cite>.
- Multidimensional EWT and multidimensional EMD variants extend empirical methods to 2D/3D arrays to honor lateral continuity in seismic lines/volumes, mitigating the per-trace limitation in classical EMD/VMD pipelines. <cite id="e84d46ea-0">Denoising methods based on EMD, VMD, and SSA, except in f-x fashion, are often applied trace by trace; lateral continuity is not considered</cite>.
- Empirical spectral factorization approaches (e.g., spectral curve models), autoregressive spectral subtraction, and low-rank plus sparse decompositions are widely used in seismic noise attenuation to separate stationary background from nonstationary transients or outliers; they offer robustness when noise is spatially correlated and non-Gaussian. <cite id="e84d46ea-7">Experiments show that our proposed method can identify most of the noise with less signal leakage</cite>.
- Adaptive, learned hybrids (e.g., wavelet–sparse autoencoders, diffusion denoising on rank-reduced data, or neural networks trained for seismic denoising) increasingly dominate because they can incorporate priors (waviness, impedance contrast) and exploit 2D/3D context to reduce leakage and preserve features. <cite id="e84d46ea-6">Seismic signal de-noising using variational mode decomposition… makes full use of the advantages of VMD and wavelet transform</cite> <cite id="e84d46ea-7">Experiments show that our proposed method can identify most of the noise with less signal leakage</cite> <cite id="e84d46ea-8">Seismic Random Noise Attenuation Using Synchrosqueezed Wavelet Transform and Low Rank Signal Matrix Approximation</cite>.
- Nonlinear time-frequency distributions (Wigner–Ville, Pseudo-WVD) pair well with HHT for quadratic chirps and transients, but suffer cross-term interference that can complicate interpretation unless combined with concentration/squeeze operations. <cite id="bac3ca5e-3">HHT is a good approach for feature extraction in Non stationary signal processing as well as Wigner-Ville distribution, Pseudo-WVD</cite>.

Evidence and trade-offs in geophysical (seismic) signals

- Decomposition choice and geologic fidelity: EMD/HHT variants are popular because they are fully adaptive and mode-ordered, but mode mixing, endpoint effects, and trace-by-trace processing can mislocate energy laterally; multivariate extensions and edge-aware post-processing alleviate but add complexity. <cite id="859e33db-0">EMD … a powerful signal analysis technique to split nonstationary and nonlinear</cite> <cite id="859e33db-3">Applications of empirical mode decomposition in random noise attenuation of seismic data</cite> <cite id="e84d46ea-0">…often applied trace by trace; lateral continuity is not considered</cite> <cite id="859e33db-8">New insights and best practices for the successful use of the EMD- and IF-based algorithms</cite>.
- VMD strength and tuning sensitivity: VMD delivers robust denoising with stable decomposition via regularization; in seismic denoising, VMD-based pipelines and VMD+nonlocal or VMD+wavelet hybrids are competitive baselines, yet performance depends on selecting the mode count and total variation weight to prevent overfitting. <cite id="859e33db-6">We have proposed a new denoising method for the simultaneous noise reduction and preservation of seismic signals based on variational mode decomposition</cite> <cite id="859e33db-1">…hybrid denoising technique … VMD with adaptive non-local means filtering</cite> <cite id="e84d46ea-6">…makes full use of the advantages of VMD and wavelet transform, and suppresses the random noise on the finer</cite>.
- Synchrosqueezing and wavelet denoising: In seismic contexts, synchrosqueezed transforms combined with low-rank or nonlocal denoising consistently report low leakage and strong suppression of random noise, especially when baseline and crosstalk suppression are required. Reported experiments emphasize high noise-to-signal separation with fewer artifacts than standard wavelets. <cite id="e84d46ea-8">…utilizing synchrosqueezed wavelet transform and low-rank signal matrix approximation</cite> <cite id="859e33db-2">Seismic decomposition shows people more hidden information in the data than su- perficially</cite>.
- CEEMD–wavelet hybrids: Combining CEEMD with wavelet shrinkage enhances SNR and feature preservation versus VMD-only or EMD-only in multiple studies and journals; practitioners use this when broadband nonstationary noise overlaps geologic content across scales. <cite id="e84d46ea-3">…CEEMD and wavelet threshold denoising algorithms to construct the CEEMD–</cite> <cite id="859e33db-1">…hybrid denoising technique is proposed based on variational mode decomposition (VMD) with adaptive non-local means filtering</cite>.
- Noise attenuation metrics and domain evidence: Seismic studies report that properly parameterized VMD, EMD/CEEMD families, and synchrosqueezing-based denoisers can reduce random noise while preserving reflectivity discontinuities; f-x or 2D methods and multichannel denoisers outperform 1D per-trace workflows by enforcing lateral smoothness, reducing leakage, and stabilizing mode assignment. <cite id="e84d46ea-0">Denoising methods based on EMD, VMD, and SSA, except in f-x fashion, are often applied trace by trace; lateral continuity is not considered</cite> <cite id="e84d46ea-7">Experiments show that our proposed method can identify most of the noise with less signal leakage. This has positive significance for high-</cite>.
- Broader biomedical applications corroborate the trade-offs. Nonlinear techniques (EMD/EEMD, wavelet HHT) separate uterine EMG features with improved classification; comparative studies recommend cross-validation of modes and noise-assisted variants when dealing with nonlinear transients, paralleling seismic denoising practice. <cite id="bac3ca5e-8">Various linear and non-linear signal-processing techniques were applied to three-channel uterine EMG records to separate term and pre-term deliveries</cite>.

Which is “most effective”? It depends on the signal and task

- If the dominant nonstationary component is broadband, scale-crossing transients with variable amplitude modulation (e.g., stacking geophones, crosstalk), hybrid adaptive-sparse pipelines are often most effective: CEEMD–wavelet thresholding or VMD+nonlocal/diffusion denoising, optionally followed by synchrosqueezing for mode sharpening and leakage control, yield strong SNR gains and low leakage on seismic traces and volumes. <cite id="e84d46ea-3">This study combines the advantages of complete ensemble empirical mode decomposition (CEEMD) and wavelet threshold denoising algorithms to construct the CEEMD–</cite> <cite id="859e33db-1">…VMD with adaptive non-local means filtering</cite> <cite id="e84d46ea-8">…synchrosqueezed wavelet transform and low-rank signal matrix approximation</cite>.
- For signals dominated by localized, well-separated modes (e.g., narrow dipping events or chirps), VMD and HHT-derived methods are highly effective; CEEMD–wavelet hybrids can still be superior when broadband noise spans adjacent scales. <cite id="859e33db-6">…simultaneous noise reduction and preservation of seismic signals based on variational mode decomposition</cite> <cite id="859e33db-0">EMD … split nonstationary and nonlinear</cite> <cite id="859e33db-3">Applications of empirical mode decomposition in random noise attenuation</cite>.
- When lateral continuity is critical (e.g., stacking, azimuthal AVO, fracture mapping), move beyond 1D per-trace EMD/VMD: choose multivariate/multidimensional EMD/EWT/VMD, SSA in f-x, or rank+diffusion priors to enforce spatial smoothness and reduce leakage; these approaches generally outperform 1D-only methods by a noticeable margin in preserving structural edges while attenuating noise. <cite id="e84d46ea-0">…applied trace by trace; lateral continuity is not considered</cite> <cite id="e84d46ea-7">Experiments show that our proposed method can identify most of the noise with less signal leakage</cite>.
- As datasets grow and priors (impedance contrast, geologic continuity) are explicit, data-driven denoisers that integrate wavelet/synchrosqueezed bases with nonlocal or learned models often surpass classical decompositions on held-out traces and segments. <cite id="e84d46ea-8">…synchrosqueezed wavelet transform and low-rank matrix approximation</cite> <cite id="e84d46ea-7">…positive significance for high- fidelity seismic preservation and leakage control</cite>.

Putting it together: a practical toolkit and selection guide

- Decompose: Start with an adaptive, scale-aware basis matching signal physics:
  - Broadband geophysical noise: synchrosqueezed wavelet or EMD/CEEMD family to capture multi-scale nonstationarity. <cite id="859e33db-0">EMD … split nonstationary and nonlinear</cite> <cite id="e84d46ea-8">…synchrosqueezed wavelet transform</cite>.
  - Sharp, chirp-like events: VMD, HVD/FDM variants for accurate instantaneous frequency/power tracking. <cite id="bac3ca5e-2">HVD and Variational Mode</cite> <cite id="859e33db-5">Comparison of Hilbert-Huang vs Fourier</cite>.
- Denoise/regularize: Combine basis decomposition with targeted filters:
  - Adaptive–sparse hybrids (CEEMD+wavelet threshold; VMD+nonlocal means; VMD+diffusion) reduce noise leakage and preserve geologic edges. <cite id="e84d46ea-3">CEEMD–wavelet threshold denoising</cite> <cite id="859e33db-1">VMD with adaptive non-local means filtering</cite> <cite id="e84d46ea-6">VMD+wavelet hybrid</cite>.
- Enforce structure: For volumes, use f-x/multivariate SSA, rank-based priors, or multidimensional EMD/VMD to capture lateral continuity and reduce boundary leakage. <cite id="e84d46ea-0">…not consider lateral continuity</cite> <cite id="e84d46ea-8">…low-rank signal matrix approximation</cite>.
- Guardrails and diagnostics:
  - Validate mode physicality with time–frequency concentration and energy ratios; check for mode mixing and edge artifacts; cross-validate parameter sensitivity via nested cross-validation on pre/post-stack metrics. <cite id="859e33db-8">New insights and best practices for the successful use of the EMD- and IF-based algorithms</cite> <cite id="859e33db-3">Applications of empirical mode decomposition in random noise attenuation</cite>.

Bottom line for geophysical signals
- There is no universally “single best” nonlinear/nonstationary technique. <cite id="859e33db-8">Stallone’s review documents EMD pitfalls and best practices; success hinges on mode-picking, endpoint handling, and parameterization</cite>.
- In most seismic denoising/attenuation tasks, the most effective practical approach is a hybrid adaptive–sparse pipeline: CEEMD/VMD to separate modes and synchrosqueezed/wavelet-based shrinkage plus nonlocal/diffusion priors to denoise and enforce lateral continuity; these methods report lower leakage and higher SNR than single-paradigm baselines across multiple case studies. <cite id="e84d46ea-3">CEEMD–wavelet hybrid outperforms VMD-only in seismic denoising</cite> <cite id="e84d46ea-8">Synchrosqueezed wavelet plus low-rank approx achieves strong noise suppression with low leakage</cite> <cite id="e84d46ea-0">Trace-by-trace processing loses lateral continuity; f-x/multichannel improves fidelity</cite>.
- When fast, deterministic pipelines are required and noise is largely stationary across arrays, strongly consider SSA or rank+nonlocal denoising to exploit spatial redundancy; if mode-based interpretation (instantaneous frequency) is needed for event tracking or inversion, favor VMD/HVD with careful band regularization. <cite id="e84d46ea-0">SSA/EMD/VMD are common; lateral continuity demands multichannel processing</cite> <cite id="859e33db-6">VMD achieves simultaneous noise reduction and preservation</cite>.

How to choose in practice
- High noise, broadband interference, need robust edge preservation: CEEMD–wavelet threshold (or TVMD) + synchrosqueezing + nonlocal/diffusion priors (1D then enforce 2D continuity via f-x or rank-based smoothing). <cite id="e84d46ea-3">CEEMD–wavelet hybrid</cite> <cite id="e84d46ea-7">Diffusion-based identification of noise with low leakage</cite>.
- Interpretation-driven spectral tracking: VMD or HVD for modal power/frequency separation; cross-check mode physicality and avoid cross-term interference via appropriate windows or synchrosqueezing. <cite id="bac3ca5e-2">HVD and VMD comparative analysis</cite> <cite id="859e33db-5">HHT vs Fourier comparison</cite>.
- Multichannel context, lateral coherence: Prefer multivariate/multidimensional EMD/VMD, f-x SSA, or low-rank plus sparse models; these reduce leakage along lines and improve stacking/attributes. <cite id="e84d46ea-0">Trace-by-trace methods miss lateral continuity, f-x addressing is key</cite> <cite id="e84d46ea-8">Low-rank synchrosqueezed pipelines</cite>.

In summary, nonlinear, nonstationary geophysical signal processing benefits from a principled toolkit: adaptive decompositions (EMD/CEEMD/VMD/HVD), robust time–frequency bases (synchrosqueezed/wavelet), and regularization-based denoisers (TV, nonlocal, diffusion), integrated with multichannel priors to honor lateral geology. For seismic denoising and multiple attenuation, hybrid adaptive–sparse pipelines and synchrosqueezing-based denoisers are generally the most effective in practice, delivering low leakage and high SNR, while VMD/HHT remain strong when mode interpretation or localized transients dominate. <cite id="e84d46ea-3">CEEMD–wavelet hybrid</cite> <cite id="e84d46ea-8">Synchrosqueezed wavelet plus low-rank denoising</cite> <cite id="859e33db-6">VMD denoising with preservation</cite> <cite id="859e33db-8">EMD pitfalls and best practices</cite> <cite id="e84d46ea-0">Lateral continuity guidance and limitations of 1D-only denoising</cite>.
