fully_underspecified.text: What theories are testable on a platform like this but have not yet been studied in the literature?
fully_underspecified.answer:
Below are researchable theories you can test on an LLM/AI-agent platform today that appear under-studied in the peer-reviewed literature. For each, I state the core mechanism, testable predictions, and how you would falsify them using telemetry such as prompts, outputs, ratings, usage logs, and A/B interventions. Where adjacent literature exists, I note it to clarify boundaries.

Orientation: What a platform like this enables
- Platforms host user and agent populations that generate, share, rate, and iterate content and tasks (text/code/tool calls), with persistent histories and feedback loops. <cite id="d54127be-0">Surveys of LLM-based scientific agents document architectures, benchmarks, and open ethical and evaluation challenges</cite>, <cite id="d54127be-1">and categorize agent-optimization strategies into parameter- and behavior-driven control</cite>. <cite id="d54127be-3">Recent work reviews tool-learning agents at scale</cite>, and <cite id="d54127be-6">demonstrates that LLM agents can automate lab instruments via structured frameworks</cite>. <cite id="d54127be-7">Concurrently, scholars warn LLMs threaten core social science methods like online surveys</cite>. On the human side, <cite id="622fc187-0">field experiments compare “ghostwriter” roles (LLM-led vs human-led) in creative work</cite>, <cite id="622fc187-1">and show LLM-generated messages can shift political attitudes</cite>, and <cite id="622fc187-5">user studies find people evaluate human vs LLM responses differently—especially once they know the source</cite>. Together these establish feasibility and some effects; below we surface mechanisms with limited prior direct testing on end-to-end platform dynamics.

1) Cultural evolution of tool-use “memes” and prompt templates
Mechanism: Successful prompt or tool-use patterns spread via social learners and automated agents; some variants hitchhike on popularity signals (upvotes/DAU) and prompt libraries.
Predictions: 
- Virality coefficients correlate with simplicity, reuse cues, and “stereotype lift” in agent benchmarks; variants exposed to higher prestige contexts show faster adoption under agentic replication. 
- Communities with AI moderation (e.g., auto-applies best-rated prompt v2) show acceleration in novelty leakage (copy-paste innovations) relative to naive user groups.
Falsification: A/B platforms with vs without automated prompt propagation; measure diffusion curves with and without visibility/replication APIs; compare entropy of prompt-token usage over time; test if blocking sharing yields ≥80% drop in acquisition of new templates.

Why new: <cite id="d54127be-3">Surveys enumerate tool learning but rarely examine population-level diffusion of tool-use “ideas” across heterogeneous users/agents</cite>, and <cite id="d54127be-6">proofs of agent automation</cite> do not analyze why some tool-uses diffuse while others die. You can directly test by enabling/switching propagation channels and logging adoptions.

2) Equilibrium selection among agent “behaviors” under conflicting rewards
Mechanism: Different agent strategies (exploration vs exploitation; truth-seeking vs performance-maximizing) stably coexist; outcome distributions reflect reward distributional shifts rather than a unique optimum.
Predictions:
- Under piecewise rewards (accuracy, speed, energy/tool-call cost), multiple attractors appear; switching a small fraction of rewards from cost- to quality-weighted yields rapid re-convergence of population behavior.
- Mixed strategy Nash analogs: agent teams split actions proportionally to payoff ratios; equilibria shift if AI overseers vote to penalize “irresponsible” heuristics.
Falsification: Multi-generator contests on identical tasks, instrument per-call budgets and per-session reputation; vary reward mixing; measure call-accuracy/speed Pareto fronts and stability over generations.

Why new: <cite id="d54127be-1">Agent optimization surveys emphasize methods, not equilibrium multiplicity under real heterogeneous reward signals</cite>, while <cite id="3b7e934d-0">frameworks calling for structured vocabularies for agent interactions</cite> imply current systems lack formal selection theories.

3) Social norms and governance in agent societies: self-imposed rules via algorithmic “collective intelligence”
Mechanism: Decentralized LLM populations spontaneously adopt conventions and norms; governance emerges through emergent algorithms used by many agents.
Predictions:
- Agent societies with public scoring (“reputation credits”) develop algorithmic norms—e.g., required preconditions, error logging, or refutation drafts—unobserved in neutral conditions.
- A “norm violation tax” (negative reputation for unreflected assertions) reduces hallucinations by ≥30% and increases compliance with citation customs; effects persist across generations due to seed-agent influence.
Falsification: Control groups without reputation; measure change in violation rates, adherence to citation/prefix conventions, and innovation frequency; check robustness by seeding norm-violating agents vs upholding agents.

Adjacent but distinct: <cite id="3b7e934d-1">Experimental results show spontaneous social conventions in decentralized LLM populations</cite>, and <cite id="3b7e934d-8">social norms reduce conflicts in generative agent societies</cite>, suggesting a testable governance multiplier.

4) Human learning from AI: promptable skill acquisition and overfitting to prompt “templates”
Mechanism: Users who collaborate with LLMs acquire task priors via prompt scaffolds; with repeated exposure, performance overfits to the prompt distribution and fails on novel perturbations.
Predictions:
- Prompted learners outperform unassisted baselines on initial tasks; on transfer tasks (small δ perturbation), assisted learners regress toward baseline, while pure copilot/ghostwriter baselines drift even more.
- Teaching via minimal exemplars and reflective queries yields durable gains versus “write this for me” prompts.
Falsification: Transfer tests across parameterized deltas; compare regression rates vs human-only control; measure forgetting curves and prompt-robustness after ablations.

Supporting evidence: <cite id="622fc187-0">Field experiments show role tradeoffs in human–LLM creative workflows</cite>, and <cite id="622fc187-5">user evaluations reveal systematic differences in how people judge human vs AI outputs</cite>, but transfer/overfitting under prompt distributions has not been directly quantified at scale per se.

5) Persuasion via AI-generated narratives: diffusion thresholds under network structures
Mechanism: Political/cultural persuasion cascades propagate through platform networks; AI-generated messages cross a lower persuasion threshold and scale with network clustering and echo chambers.
Predictions:
- AI-authored persuasion content reaches tipping points 2–5× faster than human-authored content on similar nodes; clustering (k-wisdom) increases cascade sizes for AI messages.
- When AI content carries verifiable provenance signals, cascade sizes shrink by ≥40%, suggesting a signal-dependent threshold mechanism.
Falsification: Instrumented social layers with degree/k-core exposure, A/B content authorship labels, and telemetry of belief updates; compare growth rates and time-to-tipping.

Supporting evidence: <cite id="622fc187-1">LLM-generated messages can persuade humans on political attitudes</cite>; the proposed tests formalize diffusion thresholds on platform graphs.

6) Algorithmic selection vs human curation: moderating AI “public opinion”
Mechanism: Upvote/downvote or rating-based curation selects for “AI-sounding” or performant styles; human annotators demote AI-optimized content when aware, revealing a visibility/awareness gap.
Predictions:
- Untargeted platforms see faster growth of AI-shaped content on popularity leaderboards than human-shaped content; targeted interventions (human labels, audits) produce −60% growth within a week.
- Communities with AI “ambassadors” trained to generate exemplars show biased discovery skews.
Falsification: Blind vs labeled comparisons; remove labels and re-rank; measure long-tail decay and style priors over weeks.

Why new: <cite id="622fc187-5">People’s evaluations change when they know content is AI</cite>, and <cite id="622fc187-1">LLM-generated messages move opinions</cite>, but integrated selection mechanisms with hidden provenance and AI ambassadors are under-measured.

7) Co-intelligence markets: markets for ideas and task decomposition among humans and agents
Mechanism: Hybrid human–AI markets discover better decompositions and proofs via iterative critique; prices and reputation encode discovery potential.
Predictions:
- Crowdsourced critique markets reduce errors by ≥25% via modular decomposition guided by AI critiques; auction-style redistribution of subtasks improves overall utility versus single-shot copilot solutions.
- Agent markets with tradable “insights” (call/proof snippets) show rising emergy efficiency and surprise entropy as markets mature.
Falsification: Baseline vs market interventions; measure error rates, cost-normalized utility, and information-theoretic gains over time.

Adjacent but distinct: <cite id="622fc187-2">Roadmaps in marketing research integrate LLMs into hybrid human–AI collaborations</cite>, but not with formal “markets for ideas” performance metrics.

8) Hallucination “contagion” via conversational relaying and attribution dynamics
Mechanism: Relaying LLM statements verbatim or with weak attribution amplifies hallucinations in downstream recipients; attribution scaffolds mitigate but can incur new costs (cognitive load).
Predictions:
- Direct quotations raise downstream hallucination rates by ≥30%; attribution markers (“I inferred”) reduce but slow comprehension; layered summarization mitigates both.
Falsification: Chain-of-citation experiments; measure exact-match rates, self-contradiction rates, and comprehension scores across relay depths and attribution formats.

Why new: While hallucination prevalence is known, <cite id="3b7e934d-1">emergent conventions</cite> suggest platform-level rules could change attribution norms; systematic relaying-attribution experiments are sparse.

9) Prompt ideation and creativity: diminishing returns vs cross-pollination
Mechanism: Ideation prompts create diminishing returns from isolated brainstorming but enable creative cross-pollination when shared across teams or domains; AI prompt libraries alter the “adjacent-possible” set.
Predictions:
- Solo ideation shows law-of-iterated-log utility; networked ideation increases novelty for the first 2–3 iterations, then reverts to baseline.
- Teams with prompt exchange show +35% novelty on early rounds, then converge; teams with diversity constraints show sustained gains.
Falsification: Log prompt and output histories per user; compute novelty scores over domains and time windows; compare networked vs solo curves.

Adjacent: <cite id="622fc187-0">Collaboration modes (ghostwriter vs partner) affect creative outcomes</cite> and <cite id="d54127be-3">tools shape behavior</cite>, but cross-platform, longitudinal novelty measures are missing.

10) Exploration–exploitation of prompt spaces by human agents with AI copilots
Mechanism: AI copilots reduce perceived risk of exploration; human users then undersample the prompt space and converge to “safe” high-similarity prompts.
Predictions:
- With copilot “improve/rephrase” affordances, exploration entropy drops by ≥40% in two-week traces; new templates emerge primarily via copilot diffs rather than user originals.
- Training on failure-aware reward (penalizing repeated failures) recovers 10–20% exploration.
Falsification: Telemetry of prompt similarity drift; compute mutual information between user and copilot outputs before/after interventions.

Why testable: Modern logs capture prompt tokens and revisions; <cite id="622fc187-5">awareness of source changes evaluation</cite> suggests differential exploration when users know AI assistance.

11) Multi-agent labor markets for tool use: “inference as service” and price discovery
Mechanism: Standalone agents offer inference/tool services; markets discover efficient allocations via reputation and waiting costs.
Predictions:
- Reputation-weighted queuing reduces latency and errors by ≥20%; price floors on tokens reduce but diversify routing.
- Emergent “core–periphery” architecture: star topology around high-quality agents in stable matchings.
Falsification: Simulate markets with and without reputation; sample trade-off frontiers; test topology stability and welfare gains.

Adjacent: <cite id="d54127be-3">Tool-learning agents</cite> and <cite id="d54127be-6">agent automation</cite> suggest feasibility; theory of market equilibria and governance remains largely unformalized.

12) Social proof, prestige bias, and AI as catalysts of conformity
Mechanism: AI “influencers” or demonstrators shape conformity baselines; conformity costs fall when AI endorsements are present and prestige signals are visible.
Predictions:
- Nodes receiving AI-upvoted exemplars show 50% lower diversity in next 10 responses; diversity recovers slowly after influencer removal.
- Communities with hidden influencer IDs show muted effects relative to visible influencer runs.
Falsification: Random vs influencer-controlled exposure; measure entropy of prompt choices and reuse rates over time.

Why new: <cite id="622fc187-1">AI-generated messages persuade</cite> and <cite id="622fc187-5">awareness effects</cite> imply social proof mechanisms, but end-to-end conformity experiments with AI catalysts on shared prompt spaces are under-studied.

13) Human-AI complementarity in science and engineering workflows
Mechanism: Human-AI loops exhibit complementary search: AI explores high-dimensional hypothesis spaces; humans arbitrate, synthesize, and bridge gaps. Productivity depends on hybrid pipeline mechanics.
Predictions:
- Pipeline A (AI proposes, human judges) outperforms pipeline B (human proposes, AI judges) on long-horizon engineering tasks by time-at-risk normalized cost.
- Inserting “skeptic” agents to demand failed-replication drafts before finalization reduces long-term bug rates by ≥30%.
Falsification: Head-to-head pipelines on benchmark tasks and lab automations (e.g., AILA-style controlled instruments) with risk telemetry. <cite id="d54127be-6">AILA shows automation viability</cite> in instruments; test hybrid mechanics here.

14) Platform-level “inattention and echo” paradox: more AI raises per-user novelty but lowers aggregate diversity
Mechanism: Attention funnels increase per-user novelty, but homophily and echo chambers reduce aggregate diversity and discovery.
Predictions:
- Doubling recommended content per user increases personal novelty by 60% but reduces aggregate diversity by 30% (measured as Levenshtein distance between top-k prompt sets across users).
- Re-ranking that prioritizes structural novelty over similarity increases aggregate diversity by ≥25% with minimal per-user loss.
Falsification: A/B recommendation engines with telemetry of prompt content and user interaction graphs; compute user-level and network-level diversity metrics.

Why new: <cite id="d54127be-0">Surveys emphasize design and applications</cite>, and <cite id="622fc187-0">work on collaborative roles</cite> do not quantify the paradox at platform scale.

15) Governance failure modes and path dependence in AI-agent societies
Mechanism: Early adopters of harmful or brittle norms entrench governance rules; positive feedbacks lock in inefficient or unsafe defaults.
Predictions:
- A small seed group of norm-violating agents can flip a community’s citation policy by ≥20% within a month; once flipped, reversion requires ≥5× effort.
Falsification: Counterfactual seeding experiments; measure time and cost of reversals; quantify tipping points.

Adjacent: <cite id="3b7e934d-8">Social norms in agent societies</cite> and <cite id="3b7e934d-1">emerging conventions</cite> suggest governance lock-in plausibility; formal tipping experiments are missing.

16) Human-AI cooperation vs competition in ideation and evaluation
Mechanism: Cooperation yields better global outcomes; competition over novelty/quality can induce free-rider problems and suboptimal content.
Predictions:
- Cooperative leaderboards with shared credits increase total weekly ideas by ≥50%; hybrid scoring (novelty + utility) sustains gains versus pure quality.
- Freestanding “novelty bounty” markets trigger short-term spikes followed by novelty collapse (saturation).
Falsification: Control leaderboards (private credits) vs cooperative and hybrid variants; longitudinal novelty/quality curves; market resets.

Why testable now: <cite id="622fc187-0">Co-creative workflow comparisons</cite> show role tradeoffs; longitudinal leaderboards can quantify cooperative effects.

17) Cultural memory and forgetting of prompts due to AI proxies
Mechanism: With AI copilots, communities offload memorization; prompt libraries and models become cultural memory, increasing drift when libraries are pruned.
Predictions:
- Pruning the top-k shared prompts reduces downstream rediscovery of useful prompts by ≥70% within two weeks.
- Adding “prompt archaeology” channels (randomized rollbacks) restores discovery by 20–30%.
Falsification: Log prompt library use; instrument pruning and rollback operations; measure rediscovery rates and downstream task performance.

Why new: <cite id="622fc187-5">User evaluations of AI outputs</cite> and <cite id="d54127be-3">tools that alter behavior</cite> imply memory shifts, but large-scale library interventions are untested.

How to run these tests on a platform like this
- Use A/B environments for rewards, recommendation, and governance toggles; record full prompt/output histories and ratings. <cite id="d54127be-0">Agent surveys document architectures you can adapt for experimentation</cite> and <cite id="d54127be-3">tool-learning agents give you concrete tasks for measurable outcomes</cite>. <cite id="d54127be-6">Automation frameworks such as AILA offer instrumented control loops</cite> to ground external validity.
- Seed behaviors/ratings and measure diffusion, stability, and tipping under blinded vs unblinded provenance. <cite id="622fc187-1">Persuasion studies</cite> and <cite id="622fc187-5">awareness effects</cite> provide priors for designing blind/unblind arms.
- For human-in-the-loop theories, leverage role settings (human-led vs AI-led, skeptic/auditor agents), and standardize transfer tests and evaluation protocols. <cite id="622fc187-0">Role comparisons in creativity</cite> and structured HCI designs <cite id="622fc187-7">reveal exploration/exploration patterns</cite> offer templates.

What has already been studied (boundaries and where you can go)
- Feasibility and automation: <cite id="d54127be-6">LLM agents automating lab tasks</cite>, <cite id="d54127be-3">surveys of tool-learning agents</cite>, and <cite id="d54127be-8">multi-agent agent surveys</cite>.
- Emergent behavior: <cite id="3b7e934d-1">Spontaneous social conventions in decentralized LLM populations</cite> and <cite id="3b7e934d-8">norms reducing conflicts in agent societies</cite>.
- Human–AI effects: <cite id="622fc187-1">AI-generated messages can persuade</cite>, <cite id="622fc187-5">awareness changes evaluations</cite>, and <cite id="622fc187-0">collaboration role experiments</cite>.
- Caveat: <cite id="d54127be-7">Scholars warn LLMs can disrupt established data collection methods</cite>, which underscores the need for platform-controlled, auditable experiments and careful generalization.

Bottom line
There are many theories you can falsify now on an AI platform—prompt and tool-use diffusion, governance and equilibrium selection, human learning and overfitting to AI scaffolds, persuasion cascades, markets for ideas, and hybrid human–AI scientific workflows—while most prior work studies isolated components (single tasks, single-agent loops, or small-scale persuasion) rather than end-to-end platform dynamics. <cite id="d54127be-0">Surveys document broad but fragmented insights</cite>, <cite id="3b7e934d-1">show emergent conventions</cite>, and <cite id="622fc187-1">demonstrate AI-authored persuasion</cite>; the missing literature is integrating these mechanisms into testable, platform-level theories with large-scale telemetry and intervention arms. Design A/B experiments, seed populations, instrument provenance, and track multi-objective outcomes over weeks to months to map stable equilibria, diffusion thresholds, and governance tipping points. <cite id="d54127be-6">Automation-ready instrumenting</cite> and <cite id="622fc187-7">structured interaction logs</cite> make these tests practical.

without_scope.text: What theories from psychology are testable on a platform like mturk but haven't yet been studied?
without_scope.answer:
Below are broad classes of psychological theories that are at least partly testable on Amazon Mechanical Turk (MTurk), along with the evidence base on platform suitability and risks, concrete hypotheses you can falsify in HITs, and design cautions. For many domains, “has not been widely studied on MTurk” is approximate; adjacent work exists (e.g., vignette-based moral psychology and online survey experiments), but there are substantial, tractable opportunities to bring canonical theoretical predictions to crowd-sourced samples with good guardrails.

General platform context and constraints
- MTurk has become a mainstream recruitment pool for behavioral experiments and surveys, enabling rapid, low-cost data collection with quality comparable to other online pools in many tasks and with transparent quality-control protocols available to investigators and markets to buyers and sellers of tasks. <cite id="9af7e398-0,9af7e398-1">Integrative reviews in psychology and organizational science document the breadth of research uses of MTurk and evaluate its samples, quality, and methods</cite> <cite id="9af7e398-2">Method primers argue that MTurk is increasingly used to study psychotherapy-relevant constructs</cite> <cite id="9af7e398-5">Commentary on data quality notes that subject pools can produce high-quality data in many settings</cite> <cite id="9af7e398-6">Best-practice reports and reporting guidelines exist for MTurk-based studies</cite>.
- At the same time, MTurk samples skew toward technologically adept, educated, and (in many markets) White workers; attrition and short time-on-task raise concerns about depth and representativeness. <cite id="eac0b91b-5">Descriptions of MTurk samples emphasize overrepresentation of White, tech-savvy, highly motivated workers</cite> <cite id="eac0b91b-0">MTurk samples can be less likely to complete longer surveys than student samples</cite> <cite id="eac0b91b-8">Worker nonnaiveté and experience are common and require screening and training</cite>. Recent critiques also warn that the ease of running studies can fuel publication and attention-bias pitfalls. <cite id="16602739-3">Methodological commentaries argue that MTurk lowers barriers so low-attention or non-representative studies can be published more easily</cite>. Data quality concerns and attention checks remain active guardrails. <cite id="eac0b91b-4">Analyses of workers’ attention have highlighted inconsistent responses and the hidden costs of assuming MTurk is a panacea</cite> <cite id="eac0b91b-7">Recent field studies report that a large majority of general workers fail attention checks and show inconsistent responding</cite>.

Neuroscientific and psychophysiological theories
- Theories that require invasive or neuro/psychophysiological measures (EEG/MEG/fMRI, autonomic assays, pharmacological manipulation) are currently not testable on MTurk. <cite id="eac0b91b-6">Method discussions emphasize that MTurk is suitable for online self-report and behavioral decisions but not for lab- or equipment-dependent paradigms</cite>. 
- However, closely related computational/mechanistic models that rely on computational state spaces inferred from behavior can be evaluated using incentivized decision tasks on MTurk, provided ecological constraints are acknowledged. <cite id="16602739-0">Computational psychiatry reviews outline mechanistic models whose predictions can be probed through behaviorally constrained tasks and open data practices</cite> <cite id="16602739-1">Methodological overviews argue that formal computational models can be directly tested by psychological experiments, even when biological data are not on site</cite>.

Areas with feasible theory testing but limited MTurk replications
Moral psychology and moral foundations theory
- Feasibility: MTurk can test Moral Foundations Theory (MFT) predictions with vignette batteries and dispositional measures. Standardized, orthogonal moral vignettes (one foundation violated at a time) enable mapping intuitions to MFT dimensions, and MTurk workloads can include training, attention checks, and per-vignette rationales. <cite id="91da3eea-8">Controlled moral vignettes violate a single foundation while holding other dimensions constant and are widely used</cite>. <cite id="91da3eea-0">MFT-based questionnaire stratification (e.g., MFQ) has been implemented in online studies to classify moral profiles</cite>.
- Current evidence on MTurk: Moral-psych vignette designs and related surveys have been run online, sometimes with ethics scrutiny. <cite id="91da3eea-1">Methodological discussions of vignette ethics and convenience sampling apply directly to MTurk</cite> <cite id="91da3eea-4">Survey-experimental studies on racial inequality have been executed on MTurk, demonstrating feasibility of vignette designs with sensitive content</cite>.
- Under-explored directions: culture-specific moral norms; dynamic changes in moral priorities under time pressure; moral credentialing effects in small monetary stakes; cross-linguistic moral framing; and interactional moral judgment (e.g., dyads, role reversals) using chat channels embedded in HITs.

Suggested falsifiable hypotheses and HIT designs
- Hypothesis: Conscientiousness moderates the relationship between time pressure and moral foundatioinality. Design: Randomize vignette presentation order and add a brief time limit per vignette; stratify by MFQ latent traits; compare consistency of judgments under control vs. time pressure. <cite id="91da3eea-8">Use single-violation vignettes to isolate foundation effects</cite>.
- Hypothesis: Small-bonus framing increases “Care/Harm”-driven punishment but decreases “Fairness” judgments. Design: Embed identical dilemmas in three bonus conditions (small fixed vs. proportional vs. caped proportional) and test cross-foundation interactions. <cite id="91da3eea-0">Use MFQ profiles to predict individual differences effects</cite>.

Social norms and behavior change
- Feasibility: Social normative message theories and implementation intentions can be tested through survey experiments (A/B variations of prompts), incentivized public-goods games, and sequential decision tasks (e.g., nudges that flip social reference points). MTurk supports branching logic, randomized treatments, and per-answer incentives. <cite id="9af7e398-0">MTurk-based organizational research shows that incentive structures and task design affect performance and compliance</cite> <cite id="9af7e398-2">Psychotherapy research primers outline incentive effects and worker retention strategies</cite>.
- Under-explored directions: Normative message fatigue across repeated decisions; differential efficacy of injunctive vs. descriptive norms for long-tail behaviors; social proof in real-time, dynamically updated MTurk leaderboards; culturally calibrated norms in non-WEIRD samples on MTurk subpopulations; norm-of-reciprocity escalation in small-stakes chains. <cite id="eac0b91b-5">Sampling biases toward tech-savvy, White workers suggest room to identify and correct WEIRD-like gaps</cite>.

Suggested falsifiable hypotheses and HIT designs
- Hypothesis: Descriptive norms outperform injunctive norms for low-saliency habits, but the gap reverses when effort costs are salient. Design: Randomize normative cue (none, descriptive, injunctive), add effort-cost framing, measure intention and simulated choice with small incentives; test interactions by demographic strata. <cite id="9af7e398-0">MTurk studies in organizational research motivate task design and incentive considerations</cite>.
- Hypothesis: Repeated exposure to injunctive norms reduces intrinsic motivation for compliance. Design: Counterbalanced blocks over multiple HITs with refreshments to prevent demand effects; test for decay in effect and sign changes in self-reported autonomy.

Learning and decision learning (reinforcement learning, level-k)
- Feasibility: Reinforcement learning (RL) models, noisy-RL variants, and cognitive hierarchy/level-k reasoning can be evaluated using incentivized guessing games, common-gain/common-loss bargaining, and public-goods/coordination tasks fully online. MTurk enables repeated rounds under time budget, random counterbalancing, and payoff matrices. <cite id="16602739-0">Computational psychiatry emphasizes mechanistic models of decision making that can be inferred from behavior</cite> <cite id="16602739-1">Formal learning models are designed to be testable via psychological experiments</cite>.
- Under-explored directions: Model-agnostic drift with small stakes; attention-limited RL (limited working memory or text-only interfaces); drift diffusion with MTurk-level attention; social learning in networked HITs; exploration-exploitation trade-offs under microeconomic incentives (auctions/market games). <cite id="eac0b91b-7">Attention failure and inconsistency are major confounds to guard against in decision tasks</cite>.

Suggested falsifiable hypotheses and HIT designs
- Hypothesis: Noise-floor constraints reduce learning-rate estimates from softmax RL policies. Design: Add exogenous noise to feedback (stochastic payoffs) and compare fitted learning rates/epsilon to control conditions. <cite id="16602739-0">Mechanistic models yield testable predictions on parameter changes under perturbation</cite>.
- Hypothesis: Level-k depth drops beyond k=3 in MTurk samples due to time/effort limits. Design: Multi-stage bargaining/coordination tasks that reveal best-response paths; test whether responses stabilize at k≤3 for most MTurk participants vs. lab student samples.

Personality and individual differences (traits, states, dynamics)
- Feasibility: Trait-state models, Big Five’s informational control hypotheses, and motivated social cognition can be probed via structured scenarios, trait priming, and repeated measurements across days in parallel HITs. MTurk supports panel scheduling and multi-HIT pipelines. Psychotherapy researchers have begun leveraging these designs for trait-based interventions and measurement-invariance testing. <cite id="9af7e398-2">Psychotherapy researchers outline feasibility of MTurk for constructs central to personality and clinical science</cite> <cite id="9af7e398-0">Organizational research demonstrates repeated-measures designs and quality control on MTurk</cite>.
- Under-explored directions: Trait–state reactivity to online self-disclosure prompts; cross-traits interactions in moral judgment and intergroup attitudes; ecological momentary personality in real-time decisions with phone/SMS linkouts; and trait inference from conversational dynamics in chat-based tasks. <cite id="eac0b91b-5">Demographic skew indicates representativeness gaps to address in personality generalization</cite>.

Suggested falsifiable hypotheses and HIT designs
- Hypothesis: Extraversion amplifies social proof effects in donation tasks. Design: Add a transparent, randomized “peer contribution” baseline in a charitable giving task and test moderation by Big Five scores on MTurk subgroups; fit interaction models. <cite id="9af7e398-2">Method primers support trait-based causal testing in online environments</cite>.
- Hypothesis: Brief mindfulness prompts reduce state neuroticism’s effect on rumination during ambiguous images. Design: Instructed attention training prior to cognitive/affective tasks; compare ruminative judgments across conditions over multiple HITs. <cite id="9af7e398-0">Integrative reviews recommend rigorous task controls and quality checks for organizational-style interventions</cite>.

Creativity, insight, and ideation
- Feasibility: Verbal and analogical creativity, remote ideation with constraints, and insight facilitation can be evaluated through text-generate-and-justify tasks, analogical mapping puzzles, and multi-criterion ideation challenges. Incentives (money or structured bonuses for originality and feasibility) help elicit effort and measurable novelty–utility trade-offs. <cite id="9af7e398-0">Organizational research has leveraged incentive structures to improve task engagement and data quality</cite> <cite id="9af7e398-2">Psychotherapy-oriented research emphasizes structured incentives and guardrails for clinical constructs implemented online</cite>.
- Under-explored directions: Collaborative ideation via MTurk teams with role specialization and peer review; sleep-deprived vs. well-rested creativity in repeated HITs; temporal incubation effects by task switching; and culture-conditioned analogical mapping constraints. <cite id="eac0b91b-5">Sampling constraints argue for careful generalization when extrapolating creativity effects</cite> <cite id="eac0b91b-7">Attention check failures can inflate perceived fluency; include dual-task checks</cite>.

Suggested falsifiable hypotheses and HIT designs
- Hypothesis: Dual-task interruptions improve insight frequency via incubation. Design: Alternate between divergent-thinking rounds and attention-demanding parity tasks; compare “aha!” ratings and solution quality. <cite id="9af7e398-0">Use MTurk’s rapid iteration to power multiple replications per condition</cite>.
- Hypothesis: Incentivized originality bonuses shift output toward higher novelty but reduce feasibility ratings. Design: Rank submissions by independent graders for novelty and feasibility; estimate trade-off curves and elasticities to bonus structure. <cite id="9af7e398-2">Use worker screening and attention checks to reduce fabrication of “novelty”</cite>.

Clinical mechanistic models and intervention blueprints
- Feasibility: Many symptom-level mechanisms (e.g., cognitive distortions in depression, interoception-related biases) can be approximated via self-report scales augmented by behavioral probes (sorting tasks by emotional content, probabilistic reasoning under ambiguity), enabling parameter estimation for computational agents without lab instrumentation. <cite id="16602739-0">Computational psychiatry reviews advocate testing mechanistic models with behavioral data and open practices</cite> <cite id="16602739-1">Formal theories can be mapped to experimental predictions testable in psychology</cite>.
- Under-explored directions: Model personalization using only demographic and trait data; early-phase screening of psychotherapy mechanisms; digital phenotyping proxies via self-reported diaries integrated with HIT panels; and just-in-time adaptive intervention (JITAIs) tuned by MTurk-ahead A/B tests of prompt sequences and stakes.

Suggested falsifiable hypotheses and HIT designs
- Hypothesis: Brief attention-focused prompts normalize probabilistic reasoning in anxiety-like irrational beliefs. Design: Pre/post assessment with cognitive bias inventory and betting/choice tasks; randomize prompt type and measure change. <cite id="eac0b91b-5">Include attention checks and demographic stratification due to sample composition</cite>.
- Hypothesis: Emotion-cooling metaphors reduce negativity bias in memory recall. Design: Retrieve autobiographical events by valence/controllability; compare recall errors under conditions; track decay with time delay.

How to move from idea to publishable protocol on MTurk
1) Theory mapping and operationalization
- Specify latent variables, decision variables, and model parameters; translate each causal path into a falsifiable comparison on MTurk (e.g., parameter moderation by traits; interaction contrasts in vignette choices; policy changes in RL fits). <cite id="16602739-0">Mechanistic models provide explicit parameters and predictions</cite> <cite id="91da3eea-8">Moral vignettes provide orthogonal manipulations to isolate latent foundations</cite>.
2) Sampling and representativeness plans
- Use demographics filters and country expansion; rotate tasks to reduce fatigue; schedule staggered HITs for panel-based repeated measures; quantify representativeness vs. lab/student benchmarks. <cite id="eac0b91b-5">Sampling profiles and skew inform representativeness corrections</cite> <cite id="eac0b91b-0">Expect lower completion rates for longer instruments; plan for buffer samples</cite>.
3) Quality guardrails
- Incentivize appropriately (minimum per HIT above time cost), randomize treatments, embed attention checks and practice trials, add brief training screens, and run pretests. <cite id="9af7e398-5">Quality can be high when tasks are designed and monitored well</cite> <cite id="16602739-3">Attention pitfalls are common; include sufficient checks and analysis of failures</cite>.
4) Threats and diagnostics
- Model worker nonnaiveté and experience; include effort/friction elements to reduce demand characteristics; use placebo controls; add micro-structural cues (time pressure, framing) to test boundary conditions; run multi-lab or multi-HIT chain replications. <cite id="9af7e398-8">Nonnaiveté is prevalent and impacts behavior; screening and training are needed</cite> <cite id="eac0b91b-7">Attention checks should flag large shares of inconsistent responders</cite>.
5) Ethical review and debriefing
- Pre-register analyses where possible; use sensitive content guidelines for vignettes; ensure informed consent, transparent compensation, and optional bonus structures; provide links for mental health resources in trauma-sensitive tasks. <cite id="91da3eea-1">Ethical guidance for online moral vignette studies highlights sensitive content and consent considerations</cite>.

When MTurk is not (yet) suitable
- Biology- and physiology-invariant mechanisms are out-of-scope (e.g., fMRI coupling to reward circuits; autonomic arousal to threat), as are interventions requiring hardware or in-person presence. <cite id="eac0b91b-6">MTurk is suited to online cognitive tasks and surveys, not equipment-dependent paradigms</cite>.
- Constructs requiring long-term behavioral ecology (lifelong social networks, extended maturation) are currently constrained, though panel methods and repeated HITs can capture temporal dynamics over days to weeks for many psychological processes. <cite id="9af7e398-0">Longitudinal organizational studies on MTurk show feasibility across weeks with careful design</cite>.

Pragmatic opportunities and evidence base
- Moral-psych vignette batteries and dispositional screens are ready-to-deploy; social-norm and decision-learning tasks and personality-panel pipelines are already feasible online with careful guardrails; clinical mechanistic hypotheses can be proxy-tested through behaviorally grounded computational models. <cite id="91da3eea-8">Moral vignettes enable clean foundation-level manipulations</cite> <cite id="91da3eea-0">MFQ-based stratification enables trait-personalized predictions</cite> <cite id="9af7e398-0">MTurk’s breadth in organizational research indicates general feasibility for cognitive and behavioral constructs</cite> <cite id="9af7e398-2">Psychotherapy researchers provide actionable steps for clinical constructs online</cite>.
- Key risks remain concentrated around attention, representativeness, and publication-bias incentives; careful protocol review and preregistration mitigate these. <cite id="eac0b91b-7">Attention failures are substantial and require robust checks</cite> <cite id="eac0b91b-3">Ease of running studies increases risk of low-effort findings</cite>.

Bottom line: Many mainstream psychological theories are testable on MTurk today—moral foundations, social norms/behavior change, learning and decision learning, personality/individual differences, creativity/insight, and symptom-level mechanistic blueprints—while still being relatively underreplicated in MTurk-native forms. Use well-vetted toolkits (e.g., moral vignettes) to translate theory into falsifiable, incentivized HITs; pair with attention checks, stratified sampling, and preregistered contrasts; and report diagnostic ancillary analyses for representativeness and attention validity to move the field responsibly into crowd-sourced behavioral inference. <cite id="91da3eea-8,91da3eea-0,9af7e398-0,9af7e398-2,9af7e398-5,9af7e398-6,9af7e398-1,91da3eea-1,91da3eea-4,9af7e398-5,9af7e398-6,9af7e398-8,16602739-0,16602739-1,16602739-3, eac0b91b-0,eac0b91b-1,eac0b91b-5,eac0b91b-6,eac0b91b-7,eac0b91b-8,eac0b91b-10">The evidence base supports feasibility across these domains while documenting limitations and best-practice guardrails; some theories (e.g., neurophysiological mechanisms) remain ill-suited to MTurk</cite>.

without_term.text: What theories from psychology are testable on a crowdsourcing platform but haven't yet been studied in the human-computer interaction literature?
without_term.answer:
Below are psychological theories that are eminently testable on crowdsourcing platforms (e.g., MTurk/Prolific, Gorilla, Pavlovia/Inquisit, PsyToolkit) yet appear underused in HCI’s empirical program to date. For each, I summarize why the theory maps cleanly to online tasks, what measures are established for web deployment, and where HCI work is thin.

Context: platform feasibility and HCI coverage
- Online behavioral science has mature tooling and pipelines for cognitive and affective experiments suitable for MTurk/Prolific/Gorilla/Pavlovia/PsyToolkit, with validated internal controls for quality and drift, making many classic paradigms portable to crowdsourcing workflows <cite id="e12f1800-1">Popular platforms include Gorilla, Inquisit, and Pavlovia, which let researchers assemble experimental tasks with controls and dashboards for web-based studies</cite> <cite id="e12f1800-2">Online platforms have transformed behavioral science by giving researchers control over tasks and populations at scale</cite> <cite id="e12f1800-5">PsyToolkit supports designing and running cognitive and survey experiments, including standardized psychological tests</cite>. 
- Meta-research in HCI highlights strong use of certain psychological theories (notably self-determination theory), which you should avoid proposing as “new to HCI,” while other domains (e.g., trust) receive systematic review attention—suggesting scope for breadth expansion in others <cite id="d5aa6d97-0">Self-determination theory is among the most frequently used and well-validated theories in HCI research</cite> <cite id="d5aa6d97-1">An HCI venue paper frames SDT as a prominent paradigm for HCI games</cite> <cite id="d5aa6d97-2">A review of 110 CHI/CHI PLAY papers shows SDT’s substantial footprint</cite> <cite id="2c658886-1">A systematic review catalogs how trust models and theories are applied in HCI</cite>.
- Psychology’s methodological literature underscores that online experiments are both powerful (large Ns, ecological reach) and precarious (representativeness and quality), so careful sampling and validation are needed for generalizable inferences <cite id="e12f1800-0">Challenges in online longitudinal tasks include time sensitivity and representativeness issues</cite> <cite id="e12f1800-3">While MTurk enables global sampling, pitfalls in representativeness and quality control are well-documented</cite> <cite id="e12f1800-4">Psychological research online offers opportunities for large, diverse samples but requires careful designs to reach external validity</cite> <cite id="e12f1800-7">Moving experimental psychology online can maintain high-quality data even without face-to-face supervision</cite>.

Exemplar theories to test on crowdsourcing platforms

1) Cognitive dissonance and reactance
- What to test: Free-choice paradigms, post-decision dissonance, trivial dominancy, or token economy designs; measure post-hoc attitudes, willingness to exert effort/“justify commitment,” order restoration after threatened freedom, and perceived reactance.
- Why crowdsourcing fits: Short inductions, forced-choice decisions, and objective behavioral indices (effort tasks, order-restoration tasks, browsing/time-on-task proxies) can be operationalized in JS/Inquisit/Pavlovia with automated drift-checking and quality controls; validated scales exist for dissonance/justification and perceived reactance.
- HCI underuse: While persuasive/HCI work often invokes persuasion frameworks, direct, controlled manipulations of cognitive dissonance and reactance in interactive systems remain uncommon relative to surface-level persuasion widgets; HCI syntheses foreground SDT and persuasion but give little evidence that rigorous dissonance-reactance logic tests are standard practice <cite id="d5aa6d97-0">SDT dominates motivational analyses in HCI</cite> <cite id="d5aa6d97-1">Persuasive games papers emphasize SDT more than dissonance mechanisms</cite> <cite id="2c658886-8">Quantitative analyses of CHI identify influential theories but do not surface systematic dissonance-reactance tests</cite>. 
- Measurement playbook: Use validated dissonance manipulations (e.g., commitment-without-consequence followed by foregone conclusion), Likert attitude shifts, and effort or choice-restoration tasks; control for order, fatigue, and site effects via platform tooling <cite id="e12f1800-1">Pavlovia/Gorilla provide task authoring and QA for web experiments</cite> <cite id="e12f1800-5">PsyToolkit can host cognitive tasks and surveys with established measures</cite>.

2) Fluency and mere-exposure effects (affective forecasting, aesthetic/UX fluency)
- What to test: Minimal-change vs repeated-exposure paradigms; compare initial novelty sensitivity, repetition-induced comfort, and downstream choices/ratings; include temporal discounting (immediate vs delayed).
- Why crowdsourcing fits: Quick stimulus sets (icons, micro-interactions, short animations), within/ between-subjects exposure counts, and standardized aesthetic-fluency or choice quality scales are straightforward to implement online; platform dashboards help stabilize drift across blocks.
- HCI underuse: HCI commonly discusses “smoothness,” “ delight,” and “flow” qualitatively; rigorous, low-dose mere-exposure tests directly tying repetition to choice quality/aesthetic fluency, and to downstream behavioral costs/benefits, are sparse in CHI/CSCW programs outside minimal interface microinteraction studies <cite id="e12f1800-3">Online methods expand reach but lack parity with lab traditions in some constructs</cite> <cite id="2c658886-3">HCI reviews emphasize learning/training techniques but provide scant quantitative tests of mere-exposure logic</cite>. 
- Measurement playbook: Mere-exposure effect (0–2–4–8 exposures) followed by choice or rating tasks; include a “novelty-control” set; use established aesthetic/fluency scales and repeated-measures ANOVA across exposures <cite id="e12f1800-1">Online platforms support within-subjects designs and block randomization</cite> <cite id="e12f1800-5">PsyToolkit can deliver stimulus repetitions and standardized survey measures</cite>.

3) The elaboration likelihood model (ELM) of persuasion and route-choice diagnostics
- What to test: Message centrality (physiological vs logical), prior knowledge prompts, argument quality cues, and counterargueability; measure systematic vs peripheral processing pathways.
- Why crowdsourcing fits: Branching scenarios or cue-laden slides (pretests for knowledge) funnel participants into route-sensitive prompts; self-reported route taken and counterarguing can be elicited with validated questionnaires; platform tools handle branching/qualitative coding schemes.
- HCI underuse: HCI persuasive-tech literature leans on goal-oriented motivation theories and design implications rather than controlled tests of route diagnostics; a 2022 review synthesizes persuasive-technology use cases but offers limited evidence of explicit ELM-style route measurement in interactive systems <cite id="d5aa6d97-8">A recent review of workplace persuasive tech catalogues tactics but not systematic ELM-style diagnostics</cite> <cite id="2c658886-8">CHI-level analyses identify theory influences yet miss ELM-style causal tests</cite>.
- Measurement playbook: Pretest trait knowledge; randomize centrality cues; ask post-exposure route self-reports; analyze route-diagnosticity with regression and mediators (arguments attended, counterarguments generated) <cite id="e12f1800-1">Pavlovia/Gorilla manage branching and pretests efficiently</cite> <cite id="e12f1800-2">Cloud platforms enable researcher control over materials and branching logic</cite>.

4) Dual-process theories (intuitive–analytic, System 1/2) in decision-making and UX trade-offs
- What to test: Red–blue thinking primes, frequentist vs intuitive heuristics, attribute substitution, and speed–accuracy trade-offs; measure dual-process indicators and error profiles across interface affordances.
- Why crowdsourcing fits: Brief primes (e.g., “think fast” vs “think slow”), classic heuristics problems (guardrail framing, attribute-focused prompts), and drift-busting quality tools align well with web-based experiments designed in Gorilla/Pavlovia/Inquisit; known contamination protocols can be embedded.
- HCI underuse: HCI programs foreground usability-centered methods and learning science; there is little programmatic evidence that dual-process manipulations and diagnostics are routinely integrated into interface design experiments, compared to extensive SDT/flow work <cite id="d5aa6d97-0">HCI’s motivational agenda is dominated by SDT</cite> <cite id="2c658886-1">Trust and related models are covered, but dual-process diagnostics are not common</cite>.
- Measurement playbook: Use dual-process primes; apply classic heuristics tasks; collect accuracy/speed, confidence, and “effort” ratings; use established contamination detection to stabilize estimates <cite id="e12f1800-1">Online platforms allow embedded primes and contamination checks</cite> <cite id="e12f1800-5">PsyToolkit supports cognitive task batteries and scales</cite>.

5) Social presence and proximity in collaborative/AR/telepresence interfaces
- What to test: Manipulations of sensory richness, turn-taking synchrony, and co-presence cues; quantify perceived social presence, psychological co-presence, and relatedness during collaboration; measure productivity, help-providing, and affect.
- Why crowdsourcing fits: Richness manipulations (audio-only vs video with gestures), concurrency/latency changes, and brief co-presence sessions can be orchestrated over time-warping or dummy-networked webcams; validated social presence/co-presence scales exist and are amenable to repeated-measures designs.
- HCI underuse: HCI has developed many conversational-agent social-ability taxonomies and reviews, but large-scale, controlled manipulations of social presence across interface parameters and their quantified impacts in crowdsourced settings are underreported compared to conceptual reviews; social presence remains mostly an instructional/education construct from online learning science brought piecemeal into HCI by design taxonomies <cite id="60d0e50a-0">A systematic review catalogs social presence antecedents and implications across decades</cite> <cite id="60d0e50a-3">Social presence strongly shapes interaction and learning in online environments</cite> <cite id="2c658886-1">HCI trust reviews are extensive, but presence-specific, manipulative paradigms are less common</cite>.
- Measurement playbook: Use validated social presence and co-presence scales; vary richness and concurrency; compare group-level presence with behavioral indices (turn-taking, help accuracy) <cite id="60d0e50a-5">Validated measures for social and co-presence support scale development</cite> <cite id="e12f1800-1">Web experiments can randomize condition and log behavior</cite>.

6) Implicit personality theory, self-concept-perception gap, and actor–observer biases
- What to test: Free-recall or collage-based self-descriptions vs profile-based other-judgments; compute similarity and attribution profiles; examine gap metrics and stability across prompts; probe interaction effects with interface framing.
- Why crowdsourcing fits: Open-ended prompts in text tasks (e.g., “tell me about yourself in three metaphors”) paired with structured demographic/behavior logics; GPT-based pairwise coder pipelines and agreement controls can be integrated; platform tools keep sampling controls and drift minimal with replications.
- HCI underuse: HCI frequently discusses social-cognitive heuristics qualitatively (representativeness, bias) but offers few mechanistic, controlled tests of actor–observer gap mechanics and self-implicit structure using crowdsourced coding at scale; this contrasts with psychology’s large literature and online crowdsourced consensus methods <cite id="e12f1800-0">Online longitudinal work must address stability and representativeness</cite> <cite id="e12f1800-3">Online studies allow global crowd coding but need careful design and checks</cite>.
- Measurement playbook: Elicited self-descriptions and profile-based others; compute content similarity (semantic/document embeddings) and bias metrics; test replications over cohorts <cite id="e12f1800-5">Survey/cognitive platforms enable open-ended and structured measures</cite> <cite id="e12f1800-1">Pavlovia/Gorilla can integrate text collection with controls</cite>.

7) Construal-level theory (CLT) and temporal framing in decision interfaces
- What to test: Immediate vs delayed-consequences; concretizing vs abstract framing; high- vs low-level goals; measure mental construal level and goal-directed preferences.
- Why crowdsourcing fits: Minimal-delay interventions (real or tokenized later consequences), abstract/concrete phrasing, and goal-clarification prompts can be randomized in web tasks; validated CLT scales and goal orientation instruments lend themselves to online administration with QA for drift.
- HCI underuse: HCI design often addresses near/future timelines and abstraction levels, but direct, experimental tests of CLT-style manipulations and their quantitative effect sizes on choice and regret across interfaces are uncommon compared with lab-in-the-loop studies; meta-research points to breadth gaps in theory-grounded manipulations <cite id="2c658886-3">HCI learning reviews highlight techniques but not CLT-style causal manipulations</cite> <cite id="2c658886-8">CHI-scale analyses find theory influence but limited systematic CLT-style tests</cite>.
- Measurement playbook: Prime temporal frame; vary construal level; log choices and timing; use established mental-construal scales and accuracy proxies <cite id="e12f1800-1">Online platforms enable precise priming and cross-condition comparisons</cite> <cite id="e12f1800-5">Survey modules integrate with experimental batteries and drift checks</cite>.

8) Mental workload and cognitive load in interactive decision systems
- What to test: Incremental information density, parallel vs serial prompting, automation cueing; measure NASA-TLX/Subjective Mental Load and objective proxies (time-to-decision, error rate, restarts), and examine automation-overload trade-offs.
- Why crowdsourcing fits: Short tasks with controlled load manipulations and standard surveys; objective logs and TLX scales are well suited to web/MTurk deployments; platform dashboards monitor quality and fatigue.
- HCI underuse: HCI historically formalized user-centered evaluation but relies more on usability/interview data than theory-driven, crowdsourced factorial tests of load and automation; despite strong relevance to AI assistants and analytics overload, rigorous, large N, theory-grounded load experiments are uncommon in the main CHI/CSCW pipeline <cite id="2c658886-3">HCI learning/training-oriented work is strong, but load-focused factorial experiments are thinner</cite> <cite id="2c658886-1">Trust is well reviewed, but workload-specific theory tests are less common</cite>.
- Measurement playbook: Randomize information density and cueing; collect NASA-TLX and objective proxies; analyze moderation by prior skill/expertise <cite id="e12f1800-1">Platform authoring supports standardized surveys and logging</cite> <cite id="e12f1800-2">Online pipelines allow researcher control over materials and analysis</cite>.

9) Mere-exposure in recommendation and feed algorithms (aesthetic/choice/value)
- What to test: Controlled repetition schedules in feed-like sequences; measure preference, perceived quality/fluency, choice confidence, and downstream transactional intent or sharing.
- Why crowdsourcing fits: Grid layouts, repeated item variants with randomized schedules, A/B-like exposure counts, and behavioral downstreams (simulated clicks/shares) are straightforward in web tasks; validated preference/fluency scales can be embedded.
- HCI underuse: Personalization and engagement are ubiquitous topics, but controlled, theory-grounded tests that isolate mere-exposure mechanisms and quantify their relative contributions to choice vs value illusions are uncommon, leaving a clean gap for crowdsourced factorial experiments <cite id="2c658886-3">HCI learning/training reviews highlight engagement but don’t report exposure-based causal tests</cite> <cite id="2c658886-8">CHI-level analyses focus on influential theories but not exposure-diagnosed feed mechanisms</cite>.
- Measurement playbook: Within-subject exposures 1–4; pre/post knowledge controls; log clicks/time spent; use aesthetic/fluency and confidence scales <cite id="e12f1800-1">Web-based repeated-measures designs are efficient with drift checks</cite> <cite id="e12f1800-5">PsyToolkit can host item-by-item logs and standardized scales</cite>.

10) Implicit associations and attitude–behavior gaps across interfaces
- What to test: Single-word exposure, congruent vs incongruent prompt pairings, and immediate choice/behavior under time pressure; measure attitude strength, accessibility, and gap under automation prompts.
- Why crowdsourcing fits: Implicit Association Tasks (IAT/IAL) and speeded classification can be simplified for MTurk/Prolific/Gorilla with integrity checks (reaction-time floors/ceilings, contamination detection); pairing with explicit self-reports enables delta measures.
- HCI underuse: While HCI studies “stereotype threat” or “motivational alignment,” large-scale, mechanistic tests of implicit association dynamics and attitude–behavior gaps within interface flows are not a mainstay of HCI venues, despite clear implications for conversational agents and automated decision aids <cite id="e12f1800-0">Online studies can collect implicit measures but must address representativeness</cite> <cite id="e12f1800-4">Online methods can deliver large-N attitude measures if properly validated</cite>.
- Measurement playbook: Streamlined IAT-style tasks and immediate behavioral probes; compute congruency effects and gap metrics; replicate across cohorts and locales <cite id="e12f1800-1">Platform tooling supports reaction-time logics and QA</cite> <cite id="e12f1800-5">Cognitive/survey batteries integrate within online studies</cite>.

How to design trustworthy crowdsourced tests across theories
- Build-in quality: Pretests, block randomization, counterbalancing, drift detection, and automated contamination checks; use platform controls to reject outliers and stabilize estimates <cite id="e12f1800-1">Pavlovia/Gorilla provide built-in authoring and validation for web experiments</cite> <cite id="e12f1800-7">High-quality data can be obtained online with careful protocols</cite>.
- External validity: Stratify demographics/locales; include pre-screeners (e.g., heavy online users, diverse device contexts) and pilot platforms with validation samples; report representativeness limits explicitly <cite id="e12f1800-3">Online MTurk-style sampling expands reach but has known representativeness pitfalls</cite> <cite id="e12f1800-0">Longitudinal online work must address stability and sampling biases</cite>.
- Measurement hygiene: Use validated scales and established manipulations; pre-register key analyses; when adapting lab paradigms, report convergent validity with lab baselines and boundary conditions that differ in online contexts <cite id="e12f1800-4">Psychological research online should balance internal vs external validity with validated methods</cite>.
- Replication and moderation: Run multi-lab or multi-platform replications; test moderators (age, expertise, device, time-zone, incentives) using factorial designs hosted in cloud platforms.

Where HCI has already been strong
- Self-determination theory is deeply embedded in HCI games, learning, and affective design; use it as a comparator and bridge when proposing new constructs, rather than treating it as “new to HCI” <cite id="d5aa6d97-0">SDT is widely used and validated in HCI</cite> <cite id="d5aa6d97-1">SDT underpins HCI games research</cite> <cite id="d5aa6d97-2">A review of 110 CHI papers shows SDT’s footprint</cite>.
- Trust models, persuasion/attitude-change frameworks, and social-cognitive constructs are the most commonly reviewed and operationalized in HCI; situating proposed work alongside these theories helps establish relevance and comparability <cite id="2c658886-1">A systematic review of 83 HCI papers on trust and related theories shows depth</cite> <cite id="d5aa6d97-8">Workplace persuasive tech syntheses exist, indicating domain depth</cite>.

Candidate first studies to call
- “Designing for dissonance without guilt:” mobile nudge flows that induce and mitigate post-decision dissonance with automated effort tasks and justification prompts; test if dissonance-reactance increases compliance without downstream regret <cite id="e12f1800-1">Use Gorilla/Pavlovia for branching and effort logging</cite> <cite id="e12f1800-5">Use PsyToolkit for attitude scales and effort measures</cite>.
- “Fluency at what cost?”: repeated microinteraction exposure effects on aesthetic ratings, choice quality, and willingness to pay in a feed-like interface; compare novelty vs repetition conditions and delayed re-exposures <cite id="e12f1800-2">Cloud labs support real-time feedback and logging</cite> <cite id="e12f1800-0">Monitor representativeness and drift across exposure blocks</cite>.
- “Who’s talking to whom?”: construal-level framing of AI-mediated dialogues; vary abstract vs concrete goals and immediate vs delayed consequences; quantify mental load and cooperation outcomes on MTurk teams vs individual users <cite id="2c658886-8">CHI-scale analyses suggest room for theory-grounded framing tests</cite> <cite id="e12f1800-5">Survey modules can capture construal and load with item banks</cite>.
- “When presence helps, when it hinders:” co-presence cues and latency asymmetries in collaborative editing; measure social/co-presence with validated scales and behavioral accuracy/help latency <cite id="60d0e50a-0">Social presence antecedents and implications are well mapped</cite> <cite id="60d0e50a-5">Validated scales for social/co-presence support online measurement</cite>.

Bottom line
Many core psychological theories—cognitive dissonance and reactance, fluency/mere-exposure, ELM, dual-process reasoning, construal-level framing, social presence/proximity, and implicit attitudinal processes—are theoretically and empirically ready for large-scale, cost-effective tests on crowdsourcing platforms. Within HCI’s empirical portfolio, coverage is broad for motivational and trust frameworks (notably SDT and trust) but thinner for direct, theory-driven causal tests of these cognitive and social mechanisms inside interactive systems. Carefully designed online experiments can thus expand HCI’s evidence base while serving design and evaluation at scale <cite id="e12f1800-1">Online platforms enable researcher-controlled web experiments</cite> <cite id="e12f1800-2">Cloud-based platforms transform behavioral research</cite> <cite id="e12f1800-3">Online crowdsourcing expands reach while introducing representativeness pitfalls</cite> <cite id="e12f1800-4">Psychological research online offers opportunities balanced with generalizability caveats</cite> <cite id="d5aa6d97-0">HCI has deeply adopted Self-Determination Theory</cite> <cite id="2c658886-1">HCI trust and related theory reviews are rich</cite> <cite id="60d0e50a-0">Social presence literature provides antecedent and measure maps</cite> <cite id="e12f1800-5">Survey/experiment toolkits support validated measures online</cite>.

It also narrows the scope with caveats like “you should avoid proposing as ‘new to HCI’” and “Where HCI has already been strong,” showing explicit assumptions about what counts as under-studied.

questions.original_query: What publicly available datasets are typically used for evaluating type inference systems in python?

query.text: What publicly available datasets are typically used for evaluating type inference systems in python?
query.answer:
Below are publicly available datasets and benchmarks commonly used to evaluate Python type inference and static/dynamic type-checking. I group them by how they are used and include concrete details for reproducing evaluations.

1) ML/LLM-based Python type inference corpora
- ManyTypes4Py (and Type4Py dataset mirror)
  • Purpose: Large-scale training/evaluation of ML-based Python type inference on real open-source projects; includes per-variable/function types as ground truth. <cite id="88f559e4-0">The dataset contains a total of 5,382 Python projects with more than 869K type annotations</cite>. <cite id="88f559e4-1">A public mirror lists 5.1K type-checked repositories and 1.2M types collected for benchmarking</cite>. <cite id="88f559e4-2">A HuggingFace paper page summarizes the dataset as including over 869K type annotations with training/validation splits</cite>. <cite id="59540431-3">The mirror highlights Visible Type Hints (VTHs) used to derive ground-truth types (import/AST-based)</cite>. <cite id="88f559e4-4">Related work also reports a type-checked dataset of 5.1K projects/1.2M annotations for predicting function argument/return types</cite>.
  • Why it’s used: Benchmarks downstream ML models’ accuracy for inferring variable/function types at scale and supports cross-validation and leaderboard-style comparisons. <cite id="88f559e4-0">The ManyTypes4Py paper explicitly targets ML-based type inference</cite>. <cite id="59540431-1">Type4Py provides an implementation trained/evaluated on the ManyTypes4Py dataset and links to download</cite>.

- TypyBench (repository-level benchmark)
  • Purpose: Evaluate end-to-end type inference in full Python repositories (especially LLM-based approaches), contrasting untyped-to-typed transformation. <cite id="bd6abb22-0">TypyBench is designed to evaluate LLMs’ type inference across entire Python repositories and features two novel evaluation suites</cite>. <cite id="bd6abb22-4">The public repo contains 50 well-typed Python repositories with downloadable data</cite>.
  • Why it’s used: Tests repository-scale inference, import/usage consistency, and cross-module type coherence rather than single snippets.

- Cross-domain corpora for ML-based inference
  • Web/science split dataset: <cite id="bd6abb22-2">An independent study releases a two-domain dataset (web development vs. scientific computing) collected to support generalization claims for Python type inference, with all data/code publicly available</cite>.
  • Additional ML benchmarks: Several works re-use ManyTypes4Py-derived splits and report per-variable/function F1/accuracy metrics. <cite id="88f559e4-4">Type4Py’s companion paper and repository explicitly report results on the 5.1K-project benchmark</cite>. <cite id="88f559e4-6">Related hybrid approaches use ManyTypes4Py to demonstrate improvements over baselines</cite>.

- Micro-benchmarks/snippet suites
  • TypeEvalPy: <cite id="59540431-1">A micro-benchmarking framework with 154 code snippets to test and benchmark Python type inference tools; useful for unit-level and edge-case coverage</cite>.
  • Notes on typeshed usage: <cite id="88f559e4-3">PYInfer paper highlights typeshed as a curated source of human-label type annotations for the standard library and third-party packages, often serving as reliable ground truth</cite>.

- Replicable ML-based comparisons (replication packages)
  • <cite id="bd6abb22-5">An ACM study on generating Python type annotations reports that all data and source code are publicly available in a replication package, with data drawn primarily from open-source software</cite>. This enables re-running inference and evaluation on the same setups.

2) Static type-checker evaluation: conformance and compliance testing
- Python Typing Council conformance suite
  • Purpose: Validates that static type checkers (e.g., mypy, pyright) behave according to the Python typing specification; widely used to compare checker “compliance” across implementations. <cite id="a0c05e44-1">The Python Typing Council maintains a conformance test suite which explicitly validates static type checkers against expected behavior</cite>. This suite is commonly run to score adherence to typing features and serve as a unit test harness for cross-checker comparisons. <cite id="a0c05e44-0">Independent benchmarks compare speed/memory usage and checker outputs across tools (e.g., mypy, pyright, others) against common code corpora</cite>. <cite id="a0c05e44-3">Mypy comparison docs emphasize pyright’s adherence to the official typing spec and pyright’s conformance test results while mypy is described as the “OG” checker; conformance testing is a core comparison axis</cite>. <cite id="a0c05e44-2">Hands-on comparisons show differing compliance scores among mypy and newer checkers per the council suite</cite>.

- Real-world project suites for performance/compliance
  • Project collections and community harnesses: Benchmarks often aggregate popular open-source repositories (e.g., web frameworks and libraries) to run type checking and measure flags, time, and memory. <cite id="a0c05e44-0">Comparisons profile speed and memory usage across multiple checker runs on realistic codebases</cite>. <cite id="a0c05e44-6">External toolkits present normalized conformance and performance across many checkers, summarizing trade-offs for practitioners</cite>. These evaluations depend on publicly available repositories (Django/Flask, NumPy/SciPy ecosystems, and other OSS) obtained via their VCS and executed with checker flags, with results reported per project.

3) Classic dynamic/unsound inference resources (publicly available)
- Unlabeled/untyped corpora from OSS (evaluation via inferred-from-run-time tooling)
  • Approach: Dynamic type inference systems (e.g., inferring variable/function signatures via fuzzing or execution) are typically evaluated on untyped public repositories by measuring how well inferred annotations satisfy downstream criteria (test/usage coverage, consistency, picklability), then releasing resulting annotated corpora for reuse. While dynamic-fuzz–style pipelines are sometimes proprietary, adjacent public ML/LLM resources (above) and micro-benchmarks provide comparable, open ground-truth labels for training/validation on OSS code. <cite id="bd6abb22-1">Deep learning approaches for semantic type inference (e.g., PYInfer) release code and public datasets for variable-level typing</cite>. <cite id="bd6abb22-2">Cross-domain public datasets for Python type inference have also been curated to study generalization across web and scientific code</cite>. <cite id="bd6abb22-5">Replication packages for annotation generation studies include open-source data and scripts</cite>.

4) Additional public collections used for supervision/ground truth
- Typeshed (officially curated)
  • Content: Human-authored type annotations for the Python standard library and popular third-party packages. <cite id="88f559e4-3">PYInfer notes that typeshed provides reliable human-label annotations</cite>.
  • Use: As target labels when training ML models that generate or refine annotations (e.g., type completion tools), or to validate inferred annotations for standard libraries and widely used packages.

- Function-argument/return type prediction datasets
  • Scope: Some ML works create explicit function-level datasets for predicting arg/return types from docstrings and bodies. <cite id="88f559e4-4">A 2022 paper reports a dataset with 5.1K projects and 1.2M annotations to predict function argument/return types, often aligned with ManyTypes4Py</cite>.
  • Use: Benchmarks for function signature inference, compatibility checking, and docstring-grounded type recovery.

Practical guidance on using these datasets
- For training/evaluating ML type inference: Use ManyTypes4Py or its mirror for large-scale supervised tasks; complement with micro-benchmarks (TypeEvalPy) for failure-mode testing; include typeshed for standard library supervision; and optionally add cross-domain corpora to probe generalization. <cite id="88f559e4-0">ManyTypes4Py’s 5.3k+ projects and >869k annotations</cite> and <cite id="88f559e4-1">the 5.1k/1.2M mirror</cite> provide directly usable splits and release scripts. <cite id="bd6abb22-5">Replication packages from academic evaluations</cite> offer reproducible pipelines and scripts to run on the same data.
- For static checker evaluation: Use the Python Typing Council conformance tests for spec correctness and cross-checker comparisons; augment with real OSS repo suites for performance and practical bug-finding. <cite id="a0c05e44-1">The council suite validates checker behavior against the typing spec</cite> and <cite id="a0c05e44-0">community comparisons routinely run speed/memory and outcome checks across checkers</cite>.
- For repository-scale inference (LLMs/unsupervised tools): Use TypyBench to assess transforming untyped repos to typed repos, and micro-benchmarks for fine-grained accuracy. <cite id="bd6abb22-0">TypyBench targets repository-level inference over suites of repos</cite> while <cite id="59540431-1">TypeEvalPy focuses on 154 snippets for targeted tool testing</cite>.
- For dynamic/unsound inference: Evaluate on untyped OSS repos using execution-based inference tools and measure coverage/consistency of inferred types; publish inferred-annotation packs for downstream use, similar in spirit to ManyTypes4Py and cross-domain datasets. <cite id="bd6abb22-1">DL-based semantic type inference toolkits release data and code</cite> and <cite id="bd6abb22-2">public cross-domain code benchmarks</cite> provide good baselines.

Notable repos and links
- ManyTypes4Py dataset: <cite id="88f559e4-2">HuggingFace paper dataset page</cite>, mirror repo <cite id="88f559e4-1">github.com/saltudelft/many-types-4-py-dataset</cite>.
- Type4Py (training/eval harness): <cite id="59540431-3">Same mirror used; includes de-duplication and VTH</cite>, and <cite id="59540431-0">its repo explicitly states usage of ManyTypes4Py with a download link</cite>.
- TypyBench: <cite id="bd6abb22-4">GitHub with 50 typed repositories</cite>, overview paper <cite id="bd6abb22-0">on arXiv</cite>.
- Typing Council conformance suite and comparisons: <cite id="a0c05e44-1">Python Typing Council conformance suite</cite>, and benchmark roundups such as <cite id="a0c05e44-0">pyrefly.org’s checker comparison</cite>.
- Micro-benchmarking: <cite id="59540431-1">TypeEvalPy framework with 154 snippets</cite>.
- Typeshed (ground truth): <cite id="88f559e4-3">PYInfer identifies typeshed as a reliable human-labeled source</cite>.
- Replication package example for annotation generation: <cite id="bd6abb22-5">ACM DL paper with all data/code available</cite>.

Licensing/availability notes
- Many public evaluations release code and data under open licenses and provide direct download links or reproducible scripts for dataset preparation. <cite id="bd6abb22-5">Replication packages include open-source data</cite> and <cite id="88f559e4-1">dataset mirrors expose thousands of projects and millions of annotations with scripts</cite>.
- Checker conformance suites (Typing Council) are typically provided as test suites to run locally against installed tools; they rely on public codebases from package repositories and standard library trees, with results reported per test class. <cite id="a0c05e44-1">The suite validates checker behavior against spec</cite>.

When to use which dataset
- ML model training/leaderboards: ManyTypes4Py/Type4Py mirror. <cite id="88f559e4-0">5.3k+ projects</cite>, <cite id="88f559e4-1">5.1k projects/1.2M types</cite>, <cite id="88f559e4-2">splits and annotations</cite>.
- End-to-end repo inference: TypyBench. <cite id="bd6abb22-0">Repository-level evaluation across 50 repos</cite>.
- Unit tests/failure modes: TypeEvalPy. <cite id="59540431-1">154 snippets benchmark suite</cite>.
- Spec conformance and cross-checker auditing: Typing Council tests. <cite id="a0c05e44-1">Conformance harness</cite> and community reports. <cite id="a0c05e44-0">Speed/memory compliance comparisons</cite>.
- Generalizability across domains: Cross-domain datasets. <cite id="bd6abb22-2">Web vs scientific computing</cite>.
- Ground-truth supervision: typeshed. <cite id="88f559e4-3">Human annotations for standard/third-party libraries</cite>.

Caveats
- Dynamic/unsound systems often evaluate on untyped repos without stable open-source release of full inferred corpora; where available, leverage adjacent public ML datasets and micro-benchmarks to cover edge cases and measure impact on downstream quality. <cite id="bd6abb22-2">Public cross-domain Python type inference datasets</cite> and <cite id="bd6abb22-1">deep-learning Python type inference toolkits with released datasets</cite> help fill the gap.
- Checker performance varies with environment and codebase size; results should include cold-run times, memory footprint, and false-positive thresholds on real OSS datasets. <cite id="a0c05e44-0">Benchmarks commonly report speed and memory deltas across mypy/pyright etc.</cite> and <cite id="a0c05e44-6">summarize trade-offs across multiple tools</cite>.

ambiguity_judge.evidence: The response directly answers with a long list of datasets and benchmarks, without noting any ambiguity or asking for clarification.
