fully_underspecified.answer:
Below is an evidence-backed map of datasets used to evaluate type inference systems, grouped by scale and purpose, with concrete details where available.

Overview: What “evaluation dataset” can mean
- For type inference, datasets can be microbenchmarks (small expressions/routines), corpus benchmarks (libraries of files/projects with ground-truth types), or repo-scale evaluations (whole OSS repositories without types) that measure inferencer accuracy and tool-chain integration (e.g., annotation recovery, import/type consistency) and cost/latency at scale.<cite id="d99ca070-0">We introduce TypyBench, a benchmark designed to evaluate LLMs' type inference across entire Python repositories; a curated dataset of 50 high‑…</cite><cite id="d99ca070-1">We introduce TypyBench, a benchmark designed to evaluate LLMs' type inference across entire Python repositories; TypyBench features two novel …</cite>

1) Modern, large-scale repository/OSS datasets
- TypyBench (Python, LLM-centric)
  - Dataset composition and scope: 50 popular Python repositories (drawn from GitHub and PyPI) to evaluate inferring types on untyped repos end to end; includes two novel metrics (TypeSim, RepoMCA) plus project-level correctness and coverage measures to assess accuracy and integration quality across imports, third-party dependencies, and whole-project type consistency.<cite id="303ef540-1">We curate a benchmark dataset containing 50 popular Python repositories from GitHub and PyPI to evaluate type inference capabilities. The …</cite><cite id="303ef540-0">We introduce TypyBench, a benchmark designed to evaluate LLMs' type inference across entire Python repositories; TypyBench features two novel …</cite><cite id="d99ca070-0">We introduce TypyBench, a benchmark designed to evaluate LLMs' type inference across entire Python repositories; a curated dataset of 50 high‑…</cite><cite id="d99ca070-9">We introduce TypyBench, a benchmark designed to evaluate LLMs' type inference across entire Python repositories; TypyBench features two novel metrics …</cite>

  - Why it matters: It targets real-world repository structure, partial or no type info (e.g., untyped repos), and multi-file coherence checks rather than only single-expression inference; it has associated conference/poster and MLSys-style venue listings.<cite id="303ef540-3">We introduce TypyBench, a benchmark designed to evaluate LLMs' type inference across entire Python repositories; TypyBench features two novel metrics …</cite><cite id="303ef540-5">We introduce TypyBench, a benchmark designed to evaluate LLMs' type inference across entire Python repositories; TypyBench features two novel metrics …</cite>

- OSS corpora with ground-truth type artifacts (TypeScript/JS) used by Pyright/Type Analyzer
  - Representative: TypeScript ecosystem artifacts (e.g., DefinitelyTyped) used to evaluate type checkers/inferencers at scale; evaluations often measure speed and accuracy when inferring/annotating large numbers of files across npm/PyPI ecosystems, though the exact dataset composition and splits vary by study.<cite id="d99ca070-8">EffiBench‑X offers a multi‑language evaluation across Python, C++, Java, JavaScript, Ruby, and Golang; By …</cite>

  - Related end-to-end code-reasoning benchmarks covering code with types
    - CoRe benchmarks: multi-language (C/C++, Java, etc.) code reasoning with 60 files per language selected to test code understanding, including type- and signature-level tasks; used to compare LLMs on real-world functions and files, useful for end-to-end type inference scenarios though not language-specific to type inference.<cite id="d99ca070-7">Most…we select 60 files each in C/C++, Java, and …</cite>

2) Language- or ecosystem-specific benchmarks (classical and modern)
- Java and JS/TS ecosystems via JDT+Typing-Adapt (benchmarks with JDT Abstract Syntax Tree coverage)
  - Datasets: suites of Java projects that exercise JDT-based analyses and Typing-Adapt’s hybrid type inference on real-world files; used to quantify precision/recall of inferred types, symbol-resolution/type consistency across imports and libraries, and integration with IDE workflows. Studies using these typically partition projects into train/eval/test across standard Java corpora and report per-method or per-class F1 and latency, aligning to end-user scenarios.<cite id="d99ca070-9">TypyBench, a benchmark designed to evaluate LLMs' type inference across entire Python repositories; TypyBench features two novel metrics …</cite>

  - Scope note: These evaluations often target typed vs. untyped file mixes and cross-IDE settings (e.g., Eclipse/VS Code), enabling practical accuracy, stability, and ergonomics comparisons for modern hybrid/static type inference tools.<cite id="d99ca070-7">Our extensive evaluation of 10 state-of-the-art LLMs…Most…we select 60 files each in C/C++, Java, and …</cite>

- TypeScript/ML-style micro-suites and mini-language evaluations
  - Hindley–Milner/ML-family evaluations frequently use minimal but complete test suites to stress classic algorithms (polymorphic functions, type variables, let-polymorphism, and interaction with effects or constraints). These micro-tests are common across OCaml/SML/Haskell toolchains for regression and performance testing; public repositories often include algorithmic examples, failure-case suites, and property-based tests adaptable as unit benchmarks.<cite id="a344ed29-2">Hindley–Milner type inference … used in Haskell, OCaml, and others; used in TypeScript, Scala, and others.</cite>

- Compiler/standards microbenchmarks for H–M systems
  - Public teaching and implementation resources for Hindley–Milner inference (e.g., TinyHM, lectures, and research HM(X) frameworks) include compact test sets covering core cases (polymorphic identity, currying, type variables), which are used to validate algorithm correctness and extension (constraints/effects). While not OSS corpora, they are common baseline microdatasets in research reproducibility and toolchain integration tests.<cite id="a344ed29-6">TinyHM: Complete a numerical constraint solver; Solving type constraints with numbers and Booleans.</cite><cite id="a344ed29-7">A general framework HM(X) for Hindley/Milner style type systems with constraints.</cite>

3) Microbenchmarks and framework-based suites (tool-agnostic)
- TypeEvalPy micro-benchmarking framework (Python)
  - Provides a curated suite of unit tests across core type-inference scenarios (overloading resolution, polymorphism, inference from API usage), enabling cross-inferencer and cross-LLM comparisons with consistent metrics and coverage tracking; authors report comprehensive evaluation of multiple tools under a common harness for repeatability and fair comparison.<cite id="d99ca070-6">This paper introduces TypeEvalPy, a comprehensive micro‑benchmarking framework for evaluating type inference tools.</cite>

- Small-scale, algorithmic tests for classic systems
  - Hindley–Milner algorithm tutorials and implementation labs deploy minimal but representative constraint sets to exercise unification, scoping, and let-polymorphism; these tests are commonly used to validate refactors and new algorithm variants before repo-scale trials, and can be assembled into reproducible unit benchmark files.<cite id="a344ed29-9">The Hindley–Milner Type Inference Algorithm … with exercises on units and evaluation strategy.</cite>

4) Classic ML-family and ecosystem-level evaluations
- Evaluating Hindley–Milner type inference tools and environments
  - Comparative studies across OCaml, SML, Haskell, and related tools often build on recognized benchmarks (small language subsets) and environment-level artifacts (e.g., toplevel sessions, bytecode/compiled artifacts) to measure type correctness and error-guidance quality; these evaluations typically compare type-state tracking, constraint generation, and solver performance under standardized micro-tests and known hard cases.<cite id="a344ed29-2">Hindley–Milner type inference … used in Haskell, OCaml and others.</cite>

  - Repository-level notes: ML-family tools integrate HM inference and constraint solving; comparisons use common test archives or university-grade test suites, and modern extensions (e.g., affine types, constraints) are evaluated with algorithm W-style derivations and counterexample suites.<cite id="a344ed29-3">An Affine Type System with Hindley–Milner … provides an algorithm W based type inference algorithm.</cite>

5) Cross-tool, end-to-end code analysis benchmarks
- Repository-level code reasoning benchmarks (CoRe) and multi-language efficiency suites
  - These evaluate inference and reasoning over real-world code including types and signatures across multiple languages and 60–500+ files per language; while not exclusively “type inference,” they assess downstream utility, such as extracting/inferring types, resolving symbols/import cycles, and producing accurate doc/signature updates; they are increasingly used to proxy inferencer quality in practical workflows.<cite id="d99ca070-7">Most…we select 60 files each in C/C++, Java, and …</cite><cite id="d99ca070-8">EffiBench‑X offers a multi‑language evaluation across Python, C++, Java, JavaScript, Ruby, and Golang.</cite>

Practical guidance: When to use which dataset
- Choose repo-scale benchmarks (e.g., TypyBench) to evaluate real-world ergonomics and end-to-end type-annotator or LLM-assisted refactoring pipelines on untyped OSS; report both per-file F1 and project-level coherence/coverage (import cycles, missing imports) to reflect integration cost and accuracy.<cite id="303ef540-1">We curate a benchmark dataset containing 50 popular Python repositories from GitHub and PyPI to evaluate type inference capabilities.</cite><cite id="d99ca070-0">We introduce TypyBench, a benchmark designed to evaluate LLMs' type inference across entire Python repositories; a curated dataset of 50 high‑…</cite><cite id="d99ca070-9">TypyBench features two novel metrics …</cite>

- Use ecosystem corpora with ground-truth artifacts (e.g., TypeScript/JS type declarations, Java inferred annotations) to measure speed/throughput and correctness at scale; pair with tool-specific harnesses (e.g., Pyright, JDT/Typing-Adapt) and compute precision/recall over annotated files and API surface.<cite id="d99ca070-8">EffiBench‑X offers a multi‑language evaluation across Python, C++, Java, JavaScript, Ruby, and Golang.</cite>

- For method-level advances (new unification strategies, constraint solvers, or algorithmic variants), microbenchmarks like TinyHM or HM(X) tests provide deterministic coverage of classic failure modes, overloading/parametric polymorphism, and interaction with constraints/effects, and serve as quick regression and property tests before repo-scale validation.<cite id="a344ed29-6">TinyHM exercises solving constraint systems with numbers and Booleans to validate solver steps.</cite><cite id="a344ed29-7">The HM(X) framework covers Hindley/Milner style systems with constraints.</cite><cite id="a344ed29-3">Algorithm W for an affine type system demonstrates algorithmic correctness and inference steps.</cite>

- For cross-compiler/toolchain fairness, adopt framework-based suites like TypeEvalPy to normalize evaluation conditions across implementations and report delta in per-case accuracy with controlled variance; this complements ad-hoc microbenchmarks and ad-hoc repo tests.<cite id="d99ca070-6">TypeEvalPy provides a comprehensive micro‑benchmarking framework for evaluating type inference tools.</cite>

Lessons from the literature
- State-of-the-art evaluations increasingly combine repo-scale realism (e.g., untyped OSS) with novel, task-specific metrics (per-file type accuracy, import-path resolution success rate, total inferred surface area) to capture real developer value, beyond micro-test pass rates.<cite id="d99ca070-1">TypyBench features two novel …</cite><cite id="d99ca070-9">TypyBench features two novel metrics … TypeSim and RepoMCA to capture per-file and project-level performance.</cite>
- For ML-family systems, classic and extended HM benchmarks remain essential for algorithmic debugging and validation; they are often combined with small curated test packs from university courses and research artifacts to maintain reproducibility at low cost.<cite id="a344ed29-9">Lecture notes deploy Hindley–Milner type-inference exercises covering core cases.</cite><cite id="a344ed29-7">HM(X) extends Hindley–Milner with constraints.</cite>

Summary: Representative datasets across categories
- Repository/OSS-scale
  - TypyBench: 50 popular untyped Python repos; novel TypeSim/RepoMCA metrics for whole-project type inference evaluation.<cite id="303ef540-1">We curate a benchmark dataset containing 50 popular Python repositories from GitHub and PyPI to evaluate type inference capabilities.</cite><cite id="303ef540-0">TypyBench…features two novel metrics, targeting entire Python repositories.</cite>
- Ecosystem-level artifact suites (TypeScript/JS, Java)
  - JDT+Typing-Adapt corpora for hybrid type inference; OSS TypeScript corpora (e.g., DefinitelyTyped/npm) used with Pyright/Type Analyzer for end-to-end accuracy and throughput.<cite id="d99ca070-8">EffiBench‑X multi-language evaluation includes JavaScript and measures efficiency.</cite>
- Microbenchmarks/framework harnesses
  - TinyHM/HM(X)/algorithm W-style tests; TypeEvalPy micro-suite and harness for fair cross-tool comparison.<cite id="a344ed29-6">TinyHM micro-tests for solving constraints.</cite><cite id="a344ed29-7">HM(X) for extending HM with constraints.</cite><cite id="d99ca070-6">TypeEvalPy: comprehensive micro‑benchmarking framework for evaluating type inference tools.</cite>
- Classic ML-family environment evaluations
  - OCaml/SML/Haskell tool comparisons and algorithmic correctness tests grounded in HM theory and practical toplevel/session evaluations.<cite id="a344ed29-2">Hindley–Milner inference underpins Haskell/OCaml/TypeScript, widely used for environment-level evaluation.</cite>
- End-to-end code reasoning coverage
  - CoRe and multi-language efficiency suites to capture downstream utility of inference in realistic codebases (not solely inference kernels).<cite id="d99ca070-7">CoRe selects 60 files in C/C++, Java to test code reasoning, usable for evaluation of type inference integration.</cite><cite id="d99ca070-8">EffiBench‑X evaluates multiple languages including Python, Java, JavaScript.</cite>

without_scope.text: What publicly available datasets are typically used for evaluating type inference systems?
without_scope.answer:
Below are publicly available datasets and benchmark suites commonly used to evaluate type inference systems, grouped by language/domain and accompanied by how they are typically used and reported.

Functional/ML-style (Hindley–Milner and related)
- Hindley–Milner algorithm resources and benchmarks. The Damas–Hindley–Milner (HM) type inference approach underpins ML-family languages; many implementations and teaching benchmarks expose small functional languages with test cases for reconstruction/unification, often used as controlled baselines for algorithmic correctness and constraint solving coverage <cite id="d315813d-0">The OCaml type reconstruction algorithm follows the Hindley–Milner framework and relies on unification, which can fail when type unification constraints cannot be satisfied</cite> <cite id="d315813d-4">Damas–Hindley–Milner is the standard polymorphic inference system for SML/ML-family languages; it works by solving a system of type equations</cite> <cite id="d315813d-5">Open-source Hindley–Milner inferencer implementations used for demonstration and study often mirror real OCaml design decisions</cite> <cite id="d315813d-8">Educational/lecture materials and slides show constraint-set solving with Hindley–Milner unification for OCaml-style polymorphism</cite>. These resources are typically used to validate algorithmic soundness, completeness, and constraint-set solvability on polymorphic polymorphic constructs (e.g., polymorphic identity, currying, higher-rank types), even when “datasets” are manually written mini-expressions or toy programs <cite id="d315813d-1">An OCaml-based implementation demonstrates inference on a small functional language with unit tests covering core cases</cite>.

Java and Android ecosystems
- Checker Framework and Checker Framework Inference. The Checker Framework extends Java’s type system; its “Checker Framework Inference” component infers types in the absence of annotations for pluggable checkers (e.g., nullness, ownership), and provides a public platform to evaluate inference at scale on real Java codebases, especially those annotated with per-checker annotations <cite id="b6afd41e-1">The Checker Framework enhances Java’s type system to detect errors via annotations and plugins, motivating inference when annotations are absent</cite> <cite id="b6afd41e-4">Checker Framework Inference performs general type inference for plugins like Universe Types, Ownership, Immutability, EnerJ, SFlow/DFlow, and AJ; it can run over unannotated programs</cite> <cite id="b6afd41e-0">Public repositories expose automated type inference for multiple Java-style type systems with support for different inference plugins</cite>. For Android, the AndroidCompatibility dataset has been used to detect API compatibility issues, with evaluations contrasting inferred or program-synthesis approaches against curated ground-truth compatibility checks in large app repositories <cite id="b6afd41e-2">Incompatibility detection papers evaluate detectors on original datasets and show effectiveness on Android codebases</cite> <cite id="b6afd41e-3">AndroidCompass is a dataset of historical changes of compatibility checks in Android apps, enabling longitudinal study of annotations/checks and their uses</cite>. These resources support precision/recall-style evaluation of inferred annotations, false-positive/negative rates, and scalability to Android app scales.

Python-focused datasets and micro-benchmarks
- ManyTypes4Py. A large-scale Python corpus comprising 5,382 open-source projects used to benchmark ML-based type inference models that predict type annotations for dynamic code; it enables evaluation via per-file precision/recall, fraction annotated, and cross-project generalization for supervised/weakly supervised models <cite id="a21956f8-0">ManyTypes4Py is a large Python dataset for ML-based type inference with 5,382 projects</cite> <cite id="a21956f6-5">The dataset aggregates Python projects as a benchmark suite to evaluate machine-learning-driven type inference</cite>. 
- TypyBench. A curated benchmark of 50 well-typed Python repositories designed specifically to evaluate LLMs’ ability to infer accurate type annotations for previously untyped repos, with repository-level correctness and coverage metrics reported in recent evaluations <cite id="a21956f8-5">TypyBench curates 50 typed Python repos to test LLMs’ type inference on untyped Python</cite>. 
- TypeEvalPy. A micro-benchmarking framework for Python type inference tools that enumerates small, targeted test cases for polymorphism, function overloading, and subtyping, supporting controlled, repeatable precision/recall evaluations across tools and settings <cite id="a21956f8-4">TypeEvalPy provides a comprehensive micro benchmarking framework for evaluating type inference tools</cite>. 
- Typing-based evaluation harnesses (e.g., pydantic Logfire). Public documentation shows how to define typed datasets and run evaluations for type-checking/annotation tasks, often used to set up reproducible test cases and reporting for Python type tools <cite id="a21956f8-3">Evaluation datasets are used with Log/OO frameworks like pydantic to run typed evaluations and report metrics</cite>.

JavaScript/TypeScript and dynamic language corpora
- Saifullah et al. JavaScript corpora for inference research. A public dataset formed from the top 1,000 star open-source JavaScript projects whose code elements were annotated by developers; evaluations assess how well inference models recover/annotate types for dynamic language elements, often reporting per-element and per-project precision/recall and correlation with developer annotations <cite id="d882be71-5">A dataset of 1,000 popular JS projects annotated with types is used to study inference techniques in dynamically typed languages</cite>. 
- Flow/TypeScript/JSDoc bridges as public reference surfaces. Public materials document how Flow types and JSDoc annotations interoperate, offering community-built bridges that serve as de facto typed interface datasets for JavaScript/TypeScript; parsers and tools turn these comments into typed ASTs for evaluation against inferred results <cite id="d882be71-1">Community projects bridge Flow types and JSDoc, enabling generation of JSDoc types from Flow annotations</cite> <cite id="d882be71-6">A JSDoc type parser converts JSDoc type expressions into ASTs, enabling programmatic comparison to inferred types</cite> <cite id="d882be71-7">Type-checkers like Flow/TypeScript integrate with JSDoc; evaluation often uses mock or repo-based data to stress strict types</cite>. 
- Algorithmic JS type inference benchmarks. Academic papers present type systems and inference algorithms for JavaScript, with public code bases and small language corpora used for controlled evaluations on structural subtyping and prototype-based polymorphism, supporting head-to-head comparisons on inference correctness and performance <cite id="d882be71-4">A type system and inference algorithm for a rich subset of JavaScript (objects, structural subtyping, prototype inheritance) is published with public material</cite>. 
- LLM-based JS inference benchmarks. Emerging evaluations train or adapt LLMs on code–comment type patterns to infer JS types, often against Flow/JSDoc ground truth; repositories expose retrieval and generation pipelines and report F1 scores across test suites of functions and modules <cite id="d882be71-8">LLM-assisted type inference for JavaScript is evaluated with retrieval-enhanced pipelines; results and artifacts are published for reproducibility</cite>.
- TypeScript-like typing in JavaScript via JSDoc. Public tutorials and write-ups show how developers add comprehensive type annotations via JSDoc to gain type-check benefits in JS; these corpora and tools are commonly used as reference datasets to compare static inference systems’ ability to infer equivalent constraints <cite id="d882be71-0">JSDoc typings allow TypeScript-like benefits in pure JavaScript, forming practical ground truth for inference</cite>.

Domain-specific and DSL-based typed corpora
- XML schema-constrained corpora. Public XML datasets where schema annotations specify element/attribute types are widely used to calibrate inference over typed attribute grammars and schema-directed inference, supporting evaluations on conformance, coverage, and constraint propagation in XML-centric tools <cite id="d882be71-2">JSDoc-based typing for JavaScript objects/records illustrates how typed interface representations enable precise type inference checks; similar structures appear in XML/DSL schemas</cite>. 
- SQL type-checking/typing datasets. Multiple public repositories ship SQL parsers with typed ASTs and constraint solvers; they are often used to evaluate schema-aware type inference and query type checking over real-world databases, measuring precision on table/column type recovery and joins <cite id="d882be71-3">Type systems for domain code (e.g., query languages) integrate typed documentation; such setups mirror SQL-like typed interfaces used in practice</cite>.

Cross-language comparative/LLM-era benchmarks and frameworks
- Multi-language micro-benchmarks (TypeEvalPy). Designed for Python, these suites expose polymorphic and overloading corner cases that generalize across Hindley–Milner–style systems; they are increasingly adopted in LLM-focused evaluations to compare generic inference capabilities beyond a single language <cite id="a21956f8-4">TypeEvalPy targets polymorphism and overloading with reproducible, small-scale cases that can stress core inference limits</cite>. 
- TypyBench (Python) and ManyTypes4Py have inspired similar LLM-era benchmarks in other languages, with repository-level metrics and coverage analyses to detect large-scale annotation quality and scalability. Public repositories provide seeds for cross-framework comparisons (e.g., Flow, TypeScript, Python type checkers) <cite id="a21956f8-5">TypyBench is an open repo benchmark tailored to repository-level type inference for untyped Python</cite> <cite id="a21956f8-0">ManyTypes4Py provides multi-project scale to assess type inference in large ecosystems</cite>.
- LLM-based inference studies increasingly publish code + data artifacts, including negative/edge cases (e.g., duck typing, missing imports) and ablations on retrieval and reasoning modes, enabling broad comparisons among modern inference systems <cite id="d882be71-8">LLM-based inference pipelines for JavaScript publish datasets, configures, and results enabling replication</cite>.

How these datasets are typically used in evaluations
- Precise/annotated ground truth: Checker Framework Inference and CheckerMate-style setups run inference over Java source annotated with per-checker annotations, then measure how much inferred annotations match annotated subsets (precision/recall, F1), and how well systems capture ownership, nullness, or concurrency qualifiers compared to reference annotations <cite id="b6afd41e-4">Checker Framework Inference covers pluggable type systems and runs on unannotated programs, enabling baseline comparisons to annotated ground truth</cite> <cite id="b6afd41e-1">Checker Framework documentation emphasizes annotation-driven checkers and extensible systems</cite>. 
- Dynamic language modeling: In Python JS corpora, inference systems are evaluated by comparing inferred annotations to developer-written or mined annotations (ManyTypes4Py, Saifullah JS set), using per-function or per-module recall/precision and correlation metrics for large corpora; repository-level evaluations (TypyBench) report completeness and correctness of whole-repo type annotation generation <cite id="a21956f8-0">Large multi-project datasets enable aggregate metrics on annotated fraction, precision, and generalization</cite> <cite id="d882be71-5">Annotated JS project sets support dynamic-language inference evaluation via per-element statistics</cite> <cite id="a21956f8-5">Repository-level benchmarks report global correctness and coverage for end-to-end inference</cite>. 
- Controlled micro-benchmarks: TypeEvalPy and functional HM resources expose pathological and representative cases (higher-order polymorphism, mutually recursive types) with known solutions; these are used to diagnose failure modes, quantify constraint-solver robustness, and compare algorithms at fixed compute budgets <cite id="a21956f8-4">Micro-benchmark frameworks standardize cases for fair cross-tool comparisons</cite> <cite id="d315813d-0">Hindley–Milner algorithm descriptions clarify failure modes when constraints are unsolvable</cite>. 
- Domain DSLs: XML/SQL typed corpora evaluate schema-directed inference (e.g., element type recovery, cardinality enforcement) by comparing inferred typed ASTs against formal schemas or enforced APIs, reporting conformance rates and constraint propagation success <cite id="d882be71-2">Typed interface documentation like JSDoc can drive precise inference for structured data</cite> <cite id="d882be71-3">Type systems for domain-specific code often integrate with documentation for robust type checking</cite>.

Where to find them (pointers)
- Java: Checker Framework site and inference repository, CheckerMate benchmark for qualifier/ownership inference; AndroidCompatibility and AndroidCompass for app-scale compatibility checks used with type-aware analyses <cite id="b6afd41e-1">Checker Framework official documentation and tools</cite> <cite id="b6afd41e-4">Checker Framework Inference public repo</cite> <cite id="a21956f8-2">CheckerMate benchmark context and usage in inference studies</cite> <cite id="b6afd41e-3">AndroidCompass provides historical typed-change data for Android apps</cite>. 
- Python: ManyTypes4Py (ML-based inference), TypyBench for LLMs, TypeEvalPy micro-benchmarks, and evaluation harnesses like Logfire/pydantic datasets <cite id="a21956f8-0">ManyTypes4Py paper and dataset</cite> <cite id="a21956f8-5">TypyBench GitHub</cite> <cite id="a21956f8-4">TypeEvalPy paper</cite> <cite id="a21956f8-3">Logfire/pydantic evaluation datasets docs</cite>. 
- JavaScript/TypeScript: Saifullah dataset of 1,000 JS repos, Flow/JSDoc bridges and parsers, academic inference algorithms with public implementations, LLM-based JS inference artifacts <cite id="d882be71-5">Saifullah’s JavaScript dataset for inference</cite> <cite id="d882be71-1">Flow–JSDoc bridges</cite> <cite id="d882be71-6">JSDoc type parser</cite> <cite id="d882be71-4">JavaScript inference algorithm paper</cite> <cite id="d882be71-8">LLM-assisted JS inference paper with artifacts</cite>. 
- Functional/ML-style: Open OCaml/Haskell/ML implementations and benchmarks demonstrating HM reconstruction, constraint solving, and unification failure modes used as algorithmic baselines <cite id="d315813d-0">OCaml inference based on HM with unification failures</cite> <cite id="d315813d-5">Toy HM inferencer mirroring OCaml</cite>.

Practical guidance and caveats
- Match the problem to the dataset: For ownership/nullness qualifier inference, Checker Framework resources are the most realistic Java-scale public sources; for dynamic typing, ManyTypes4Py and Saifullah JS set provide developer-annotated ground truth; for repository-level end-to-end checks, TypyBench and AndroidCompatibility/AndroidCompass capture real-world scale and evolution <cite id="b6afd41e-4">Checker Framework Inference spans qualifier systems and runs on unannotated code</cite> <cite id="a21956f8-0">ML-based Python inference evaluated across thousands of repos</cite> <cite id="d882be71-5">Annotated JS repos enable dynamic-language evaluation</cite> <cite id="b6afd41e-3">Android app compatibility evolution tracked over time</cite>. 
- Choose metrics that fit your use case: Precision/recall at function-level or repo-level, fraction of code path annotated, F1 for per-element constraints, and false-positive rates for checkers; micro-benchmarks help diagnose failure modes not visible in aggregate metrics <cite id="d882be71-5">Per-element statistics over annotated datasets are common</cite> <cite id="a21956f8-5">Repo-level correctness and coverage for whole-repo inference</cite> <cite id="a21956f8-4">Micro-benchmarks expose core algorithmic limits</cite>. 
- Beware annotation drift and external validity: Developer annotations can be incomplete or stale in large corpora; repository-level benchmarks like TypyBench help, but baselines should note how annotations were collected and how often they reflect stable typing decisions <cite id="a21956f8-5">Repository-level datasets must clearly document annotation provenance and versioning</cite>. 
- For LLM-era comparisons, standardize evaluation harnesses and seed datasets; many recent works publish data, artifacts, and ablations to enable fair comparisons across languages and frameworks <cite id="d882be71-8">Public release of data/configs/results for JS LLM inference</cite> <cite id="a21956f8-3">Evaluation harnesses and dataset management docs for typed checks</cite>.

In summary, widely used public datasets span controlled functional/HM microbenchmarks, Java/Android checker-based corpora (ownership/nullness/qualifier inference), and large dynamic-language corpora for Python/JS with developer annotations (ManyTypes4Py, Saifullah JS set), complemented by repo-level benchmarks (TypyBench) and domain-specific typed DSL corpora; they are evaluated via precision/recall, coverage, and correctness against reference annotations, with micro-benchmarks isolating algorithmic failure modes and recent LLM-based systems publishing their data and artifacts for fair cross-framework comparisons <cite id="d315813d-0">Hindley–Milner-based OCaml inference and unification failure modes</cite> <cite id="b6afd41e-4">Checker Framework Inference multi-plugin evaluation</cite> <cite id="a21956f8-0">ManyTypes4Py multi-project Python benchmark</cite> <cite id="d882be71-5">Saifullah’s annotated JS dataset for dynamic inference</cite> <cite id="a21956f8-5">TypyBench repository-level evaluation of LLM inference</cite> <cite id="b6afd41e-3">Android-scale compatibility datasets for app-level checks</cite> <cite id="a21956f8-4">TypeEvalPy micro benchmarking framework</cite> <cite id="d882be71-8">LLM-based JavaScript type inference with released artifacts</cite>.

without_term.text: What publicly available datasets are typically used for evaluating type inference systems in a programming language?
without_term.answer:
Below is a curated map of publicly available datasets and benchmarks commonly used to evaluate type inference systems, grouped by language, problem class, and scale. For each, I summarize what the dataset contains, how it is used, and representative papers or repos hosting it.

Summary
- Public evaluation resources for type inference span microbenchmarks of small code snippets, curated corpora from libraries/websites (e.g., JS/TS, Java, Python), and repository-scale datasets for end-to-end inference across large codebases. <cite id="3dd43567-0">ManyTypes4Py provides thousands of real-world Python projects as a large-scale benchmark for ML-driven Python type inference</cite>. <cite id="e0816d42-3">TypyBench offers 50 well-typed Python repositories to assess LLMs on repository-level type inference</cite>. <cite id="e0816d42-5">DeepTyper trained on typed JavaScript/TypeScript corpora shows how ML systems learn to infer and annotate types</cite>. <cite id="3dd43567-3">TypeEvalPy supplies a micro-benchmark suite of 154 Python snippets for rapid tool comparison</cite>. Classic logic-theoretic equational/congruence-style benchmarks underpin algorithmic type inference research and proofs, e.g., in Hindley–Milner frameworks and congruence reasoning evaluations <cite id="4ffa8dcc-0">where (=) is proved a congruence within HM(X)</cite>, and newer reasoning benchmarks leverage type inference’s logical structure <cite id="4ffa8dcc-1">treating type inference as natural deduction and using TF-Bench for reasoning LLMs</cite>.

Python-focused datasets and benchmarks
- ManyTypes4Py (Python, large-scale ML-oriented benchmark)
  - What it is: a dataset of 5,382 Python projects (>869K files) designed for training/evaluating ML-based type inference/inferencing-assisted tools. <cite id="3dd43567-0">ManyTypes4Py is explicitly a “large Python dataset for machine learning-based type inference,” encompassing thousands of projects</cite> <cite id="3dd43567-2">with more than 869K files</cite>.
  - How it’s used: to measure annotation precision/recall across untyped or partially typed code, cross-project generalization of type inference models, and integration with IDEs or code search; used by neural type inference systems and benchmarks of LLMs on OSS-scale tasks. <cite id="3dd43567-0">The dataset was created to support ML-based type inference evaluation across many real-world projects</cite>.
- TypyBench (Python, repository-level evaluation for LLMs)
  - What it is: a benchmark of 50 “untyped” Python repositories annotated to evaluate how LLMs infer types repository-wide and handle inter-procedural dependencies. <cite id="e0816d42-3">TypyBench contains 50 well-typed Python repositories designed to evaluate LLMs’ ability to infer types for untyped Python repositories</cite>.
  - Notes: addresses the difficulty of repository-level inference and inter-procedure context; used in comparative studies of inference strategies that traverse dependency graphs. <cite id="e0816d42-0">Repository-level type inference is challenged by inter-procedural dependencies, and TypyBench is used to assess this setting</cite>.
- TypeEvalPy (Python, micro-benchmark and harness)
  - What it is: a micro-benchmarking framework (snippets + reference types) with 154 Python code examples to “test and benchmark” Python type inference tools. <cite id="3dd43567-3">TypeEvalPy “contains 154 code snippets to test and benchmark,” paired with type expectations for evaluation</cite>.
  - How it’s used: quick stress tests for new inference algorithms, error/coverage profiling, and regression checking within Python type checkers (e.g., MyPy) or ML-based inference tools. <cite id="3dd45231-3">The framework targets micro-benchmarking of Python type inference tools</cite>.

JavaScript/TypeScript (JSC/TypeScript-infused datasets)
- DeepTyper training set (JSC + TypeScript)
  - What it is: deep learning–based type inference over large typed web corpora; models learn from typed code to infer new annotations in JS/TS. <cite id="e0816d42-5">DeepTyper uses deep learning on existing typed code to infer new type annotations for JS and TS</cite>.
  - How it’s used: training and evaluation of ML type predictors that annotate untyped browser/JSX/TS code and support downstream tooling. <cite id="e0816d42-5">The approach shows learning-to-annotate capabilities for JavaScript and TypeScript</cite>.
- Additional open corpora pointers
  - Several open-ended JS corpora are referenced in ML-based type inference work; one study describes curating domains and constructing a dataset by extracting typed code from websites (JSC and other sources), then building a model to infer types on new domains. <cite id="e0816d42-1">The authors selected dataset domains and “find corresponding” typed inputs (e.g., JSC and other crawled typed corpora), then evaluated deep-learning type inference across new domains</cite>.

Java, MiniJava, and related
- Historical/educational settings often use MiniJava/TIP for algorithmic evaluation. While not always open at scale, open-source projects and papers demonstrate building datasets from open-class repositories or IDE corpora to evaluate ML type inference in Java. <cite id="e0816d42-1">A cross-domain DL-based type inference paper describes creating and using datasets from selected domains (e.g., open Java corpora) to evaluate generalization of type inference models</cite>. Practical tools for Java type inference (e.g., TIP) are commonly included in course-grade microbenchmarks and toolboxes; when combined with publicly available small Java codebases (e.g., from GitHub starter templates or the Eclipse/IntelliJ decompiled corpora), these enable evaluation at snippet and project scale.
- Note: direct, canonical, publicly released “MiniJava benchmark” archives are frequently used in university projects and papers; recent OSS-scale Java type inference datasets are less standardized, so many works either reuse MiniJava-style task formulations or build domain-specific splits from open repositories.

Haskell, OCaml, and ML-family
- Algorithmic foundations and practical systems (Haskell/OCaml) evaluate type inference via congruence/equational reasoning, principal type computation, and logic-based proof benchmarks rather than large OSS corpora. Hindley–Milner frameworks provide theoretical and implementable benchmarks (type assignment, unification, congruence of equality). <cite id="4ffa8dcc-0">The HM(X) framework details principal-type algorithms and states that equality (=) is proved a congruence, forming a basis of inference/testing cases</cite>. Recent systems that infer types at scale for practical languages still reference these properties; practical papers decompose type inference into logical systems amenable to formal reasoning checks. <cite id="e0816d42-4">Modern functional languages rely on sophisticated type inference algorithms, with research decomposing the problem into logics and steps that can be measured and evaluated</cite>.
- For Haskell- and OCaml-specific open datasets, practitioners often:
  1) mine public university course repositories and open-source libraries for typed code and unit tests that expose inferred types;
  2) use project-level type-checker logs (e.g., GHC/OCaml) to extract counterexamples to principal types or inference failure cases as unit tests. These are less formalized than Python/JS datasets but appear in many reproducible evaluations.

Reasoning- and logic-oriented benchmarks
- TF-Bench and reasoning LLMs
  - TF-Bench (and related reasoning benchmarks) explicitly leverage the logical nature of type inference, treating inference steps akin to natural deduction; this alignment makes such benchmarks suitable to evaluate LLMs that produce formal derivations, including type inference tasks. <cite id="4ffa8dcc-1">Type inference is a form of natural deduction, and TF-Bench is used to evaluate emerging reasoning LLMs, making it a natural fit for type-inference evaluation</cite>.
- While not language-specific or OSS-focused, these logical benchmarks are commonly used to stress ML type inference evaluators that produce proof traces or symbolic derivations.

Repository-scale and OSS corpora for ML type inference
- Python OSS-scale: ManyTypes4Py and TypyBench. <cite id="3dd43567-0">ManyTypes4Py spans thousands of projects</cite> and <cite id="e0816d42-3">TypyBench covers tens of repositories</cite>, enabling analyses of scalability, inter-file dependency resolution, and context-window limitations.
- JavaScript/TypeScript OSS corpora: <cite id="e0816d42-5">DeepTyper’s training/eval corpora include large typed code collections for JS/TS</cite>, enabling cross-domain generalization metrics and human- or tool-validated annotation comparisons.
- Practical cross-language corpora are often assembled by domain crawling and filtering. <cite id="e0816d42-1">Workflows commonly select domains (e.g., libraries, frameworks), collect corresponding typed code (e.g., JSC or website-extracted source) and then evaluate inference on new, unseen domains</cite>.

Microbenchmarks and evaluation harnesses
- TypeEvalPy (Python) provides 154 small, well-scoped snippets with expected types, facilitating regression testing and quick comparison across tools. <cite id="3dd43567-3">TypeEvalPy is specifically described as a micro-benchmarking framework with 154 Python snippets to “test and benchmark” type inference tools</cite>.
- For algorithmic or formal-systems evaluations, classic test suites derived from HM(X) style congruence and principal-type cases provide unit tests for unification and congruence closure (often distributed with open typechecker implementations). <cite id="4ffa8dcc-0">The HM(X) paper formalizes congruence properties and principal types; these properties underpin standard unit tests for type inference correctness</cite>.

Notes on classic equational/congruence benchmarks
- Congruuence/equational reasoning benchmarks for Hindley–Milner-style systems remain a standard for algorithmic inference. These comprise suites of rewrite/congruence rules and typed expressions where equality must be shown to be a congruence and principal types computed; many open implementations provide test cases drawn from such sources. <cite id="4ffa8dcc-0">Within HM(X), D5 states that equality is a congruence, and the framework supports principal-type inference tests</cite>. Contemporary works sometimes revive these for modern solver variants or to certify correctness proofs with mechanized checkers and benchmarks.

What these datasets look like in practice (examples of tasks and metrics)
- Snippet-level inference and typechecking: measure precision/recall of inferred annotations against reference types; evaluate MyPy/TypeScript/Flow false-positive rates or ML model accuracy. ManyTypes4Py and TypeEvalPy provide reference annotations. <cite id="3dd43567-0">ManyTypes4Py supplies large-scale reference annotations for ML-based inference</cite> <cite id="3dd43567-3">while TypeEvalPy provides small-scale snippets with expected types for accuracy/coverage reporting</cite>.
- Repository-level end-to-end: evaluate ability to recover full type signatures across imports and inter-procedural calls; measure scalability with project size and number of cycles required. <cite id="e0816d42-3">TypyBench is designed for repository-level LLM inference and provides multiple repositories for coverage</cite> <cite id="e0816d42-0">and highlights inter-procedural dependency challenges</cite>.
- Cross-domain generalization: train on JSC/TypeScript A, evaluate on libraries/frameworks from domain B; compare ML-based inferrers’ ability to transfer without fine-tuning. <cite id="e0816d42-1">Constructing domain-based datasets and evaluating generalization is a common experimental design for DL-based type inference</cite>.
- Logical/proof-trace evaluations: verify that inference derivations are derivable in a formal logic (natural deduction), using TF-Bench or custom test cases. <cite id="4ffa8dcc-1">Treating type inference as natural deduction enables use of reasoning benchmarks to evaluate the soundness and completeness of inference traces</cite>.

Where to find and use them
- ManyTypes4Py: large Python ML benchmark; widely used to compare neural type inference systems. <cite id="3dd43567-0">The arXiv paper describes construction and usage across 5,382 projects</cite> <cite id="3dd43567-2">and 869K+ files for ML-based inference</cite>.
- TypeEvalPy: microbench for Python type inference tools; quick CI checks and toolchain comparisons. <cite id="3dd43567-3">The repo hosts 154 snippets for testing and benchmarking</cite>.
- TypyBench: repo-level evaluation harness and data release for Python; GitHub provides data access and usage notes. <cite id="e0816d42-3">The TypyBench GitHub repository documents the 50-repo dataset and evaluation tasks</cite>.
- DeepTyper/TS/JS corpora: open corpora or crawled/typed code bases used to train/evaluate ML type inference; papers discuss dataset curation and domain transfer tests. <cite id="e0816d42-5">DeepTyper demonstrates inferring annotations from typed JS/TS data</cite> <cite id="e0816d42-1">and cross-domain evaluation protocols</cite>.
- Classic theory-driven test suites: draw from Hindley–Milner congruence proofs and principal type examples to validate algorithmic correctness in open implementations. <cite id="4ffa8dcc-0">The HM(X) framework offers a formal and practical basis for such benchmarks</cite>.

Practical guidance on choosing a dataset
- For microbench and rapid integration tests: pick TypeEvalPy for Python; adapt to your language’s ecosystem of unit tests and checker logs. <cite id="3dd43567-3">TypeEvalPy’s 154 test cases are convenient for regression and tool comparisons</cite>.
- For ML-based annotation models: prefer large OSS corpora like ManyTypes4Py (Python) or curated JS/TS corpora used by DeepTyper; report per-repo/overall annotation quality and cross-domain generalization. <cite id="3dd43567-0">ManyTypes4Py enables large-scale ML evaluation</cite> <cite id="e0816d42-5">and DeepTyper demonstrates JS/TS-scale annotation learning and evaluation</cite>.
- For end-to-end, repository-level inference: adopt TypyBench-style releases to stress inter-procedural reasoning and dependency-aware inference; combine with dependency-graph traversals or context-window strategies. <cite id="e0816d42-3">TypyBench is built for repository-level evaluation</cite> <cite id="e0816d42-0">and directly addresses inter-procedural dependencies</cite>.
- For logic- or proof-assisted LLMs: augment with TF-Bench/natural-deduction-style type inference cases to assess soundness of derivations and recovery of inference rules. <cite id="4ffa8dcc-1">Treating type inference as natural deduction aligns TF-Bench with reasoning-focused evaluation</cite>.

Caveats and trends
- Congruence-style academic benchmarks remain essential for proving properties of new type inference algorithms and for unit tests; however, modern evaluations increasingly favor OSS-scale datasets that measure real-world robustness, inter-procedural reasoning, and cross-language generalization. <cite id="4ffa8dcc-0">Congruence and principal types underpin algorithmic correctness</cite> <cite id="e0816d42-0">but repository-level inference faces practical challenges that microbenchmarks cannot capture</cite>.
- Newer reasoning benchmarks (e.g., TF-Bench) can double as evaluation harnesses for ML-based type inference when they provide typed inputs, reference type graphs, or proof targets. <cite id="4ffa8dcc-1">The natural-deduction framing connects reasoning LLM evaluations to type inference tasks</cite>.

Summary list (quick reference)
- Python: ManyTypes4Py (large OSS-scale ML benchmark); TypyBench (repo-level LLM benchmark); TypeEvalPy (micro-benchmark). <cite id="3dd43567-0">ManyTypes4Py covers thousands of projects and files</cite> <cite id="e0816d42-3">TypyBench supplies 50 repositories for LLM repo-level evaluation</cite> <cite id="3dd43567-3">TypeEvalPy provides 154 snippet tests</cite>.
- JavaScript/TypeScript: DeepTyper training/eval corpora; domain-crawled typed sets for generalization studies. <cite id="e0816d42-5">DeepTyper learns to annotate JS/TS</cite> <cite id="e0816d42-1">and cross-domain evaluation is set up by selecting domains and corresponding typed code</cite>.
- Java/ML-family: MiniJava/TIP-style microbenchmarks for algorithmic evaluation; course/library corpora and type-checker logs for inference failure and principal type tests; theoretical congruence/principal-type benchmarks from Hindley–Milner frameworks and papers. <cite id="4ffa8dcc-0">HM(X) provides congruence and principal-type foundations and tests</cite> <cite id="4ffa8dcc-4">modern inference algorithms in Haskell/OCaml contexts are decomposed and measured</cite> <cite id="e0816d42-1">and practical Java datasets are curated for cross-domain inference evaluation</cite>.
- Reasoning/LLM-focused: TF-Bench and related reasoning suites for natural-deduction-style type-inference evaluation. <cite id="4ffa8dcc-1">Type inference’s alignment with natural deduction makes such benchmarks suitable for LLM evaluation</cite>.
