- Time, cache, and state: <cite id="4ca1a3bd-2">Set correct date/time, clear browser cache and SSL store</cite>. <cite id="8f0610f2-6">B12: reset/clear configuration often reestablishes secure channels</cite>.
- Ports/firewall/NAT: <cite id="8f0610f2-3">Bypass proxy, check AV/FW exceptions, verify port 443/HTTP on router/NAT</cite>. <cite id="aecd52af-7">Server RSTs can reveal blocked ports or crashed processes</cite>.
- MTU/fragmentation: <cite id="aecd52af-0">Align MTU across devices; allow IP fragmentation if PMTUD fails</cite>. Validate with pathmtu and ip(8)/ifconfig.
- Client vs server: <cite id="aecd52af-5">RST implies a server-initiated abort; timeouts imply no response or idle keeps</cite>. Compare traces inside and outside VPN/proxy.
- Site-specific controls: <cite id="8f0610f2-5">If sites idle-out after about 10 minutes, adjust client pings or raise server timeout</cite>. For HTTPS, reconfigure certs/cipher suites; enable HSTS properly.

A short-troubleshoot checklist
1) Reproduce on another device/network (home Wi‑Fi, mobile data). If it works there, your local config is likely to blame. <cite id="35c9b905-2">Switching DNS and disabling VPN often remedies "can't reach"</cite>.
2) Disable VPN/proxy and try incognito. Remove problematic extensions/add‑ons. <cite id="8f0610f2-3">Proxies/VPN/FW can reset or block connections</cite> <cite id="8f0610f2-8">Browser-side add‑ons are frequent causes</cite>.
3) Clear DNS and browser cache/SSL state; set correct time; update app/OS. <cite id="35c9b905-6">Stale DNS cache and modem/router glitches are common</cite> <cite id="4ca1a3bd-2">Time/date and extensions cause SSL resets</cite> <cite id="4ca1a3bd-8">Clearing SSL state recovers HTTPS</cite>.
4) Ping/trace the domain and try direct IP. If DNS resolves, test connectivity to the site's IP; if still reset, probe MTU/fragmentation and packet loss. <cite id="aecd52af-0">MTU alignment and fragmentation avoidance matter</cite> <cite id="aecd52af-4">Loss and resets are visible at scale</cite>.
5) If you control the app/server, raise timeouts, enable/validate keep‑alive, harden TLS (supported versions/ciphers, mixed‑content fixes), and add robust crash reporting. <cite id="8f0610f2-5">Idle timeouts kill connections</cite> <cite id="4ca1a3bd-7">TLS setup must accept ClientHello before RST hits</cite> <cite id="aecd52af-5">RST skips graceful teardown</cite>.
6) For enterprise/MDM: <cite id="8f0610f2-1">AV, proxy, and firewall policy blocks often show as "reset by client/server"</cite> <cite id="aecd52af-3">Windows TCP reset notes align with corporate endpoint policy interferences</cite>.

When to suspect DNS vs TLS vs RST vs timeout
- Can't resolve name: DNS errors; flush DNS or switch resolver. <cite id="35c9b905-3">ISP DNS outage or misconfiguration</cite>.
- Connects then "reset by peer" right away: likely server RST (crash, closed port, handshake mismatch). <cite id="aecd52af-1">RST is an immediate abort on error or blocked port</cite>.
- Works for a while then dies: idle timeout, server scaling/maintenance, or path loss. <cite id="aecd52af-5">RST skips teardown and closes state immediately</cite>.
- Same site works outside VPN: proxy/VPN/NAT rule or cached state in tunnel. <cite id="8f0610f2-3">Forbiden ports or firewall rules inside the VPN</cite>.

In short, connections end because one side (client, proxy, firewall, NAT, or server) sends a reset, a path or protocol step fails (DNS/SSL handshakes), an idle timeout fires, or an error/oom/crash aborts the state. The same issue can show up differently to different OSes/clients, so isolating the path and capturing packet-level clues is essential. <cite id="aecd52af-8">Expect platform differences: Linux sometimes surfaces "reset by peer" where Windows would retry</cite> <cite id="aecd52af-4">Operators routinely observe resets and timeouts at scale due to unexpected endpoint halts and path errors</cite>.

ambiguity_judge.evidence: The response just answers directly with a broad taxonomy of causes and diagnostics, without asking for clarification or stating any assumptions about what kind of “connection” the user meant.

questions.original_query: What are existing methods to elicit user intents when an automation encounters ambiguity, especially in failure cases?

query.text: What are existing methods to elicit user intents when an automation encounters ambiguity, especially in failure cases?
query.answer:
Below are established approaches to elicit user intent when automation encounters ambiguity, organized by domain and mechanism, with emphasis on failure cases.

1) Overview: Why ambiguity triggers intent elicitation
- Automations commonly fail or stall when inputs are under-specified (omitted constraints), context-dependent (multiple interpretations), or shifting (new goals mid-task). <cite id="05f306ea-1">Underexpression, overspecification, equivocation, and shift of context are common causes of intent misrecognition in mixed-initiative systems</cite>. <cite id="05f306ea-3">Mixed-initiative setups treat ambiguous queries as an opportunity to take initiative by asking questions, rather than operating on an under-specified task</cite>.

2) Mixed-initiative interaction and HCI design principles
- Mixed-initiative gives each side the ability to interrupt, propose changes, or ask questions, explicitly coupling agent automation with human oversight. <cite id="05f306ea-2">Mixed-initiative interaction enables effective coupling of automation and human agency by allowing either side to decide next steps or ask targeted questions</cite>. <cite id="05f306ea-5">Principles from mixed-initiative UIs emphasize selective engagement, time-sensitive actions, and politeness/attention management as constraints when deciding to elicit clarification</cite>.
- Elicitation is framed as an active collaboration rather than reactive error handling. <cite id="d3c0841a-0">An “Ask-to-Clarify” function detects ambiguity, initiates a clarification dialogue, and translates the refined intent into actionable steps</cite>.

3) Dialog/NLP methods: detecting ambiguity and eliciting it
- Active clarification pipelines. Systems first decide when to clarify (based on uncertainty or risk), then ask a precise question, then act on the updated intent. <cite id="d3c0841a-1">A two-stage process determines if clarification is necessary before asking a clarifying question and then responding given the clarifier</cite>. <cite id="ddbcb700-0">Avoiding clarifying questions leads to unwarranted assumptions, suboptimal outcomes, and safety risks due to tool misuse, motivating explicit ask-to-clarify functions</cite>.
- Uncertainty-aware questions. Short, specific questions guided by classifier uncertainty or confusion among intent hypotheses. <cite id="d3c0841a-5">Principled methods ask short and specific questions based on uncertainty from an intent classifier to disambiguate competing intents</cite>.
- Retrieval-assisted disambiguation. Surface question entities/concepts from evidence to craft discriminative clarifiers and reduce ambiguity. <cite id="05f306ea-7">Asking good clarifying questions grounded in retrieved passages helps resolve ambiguous conversational queries by aligning intent with relevant evidence</cite>. <cite id="d3c0841a-8">Hybrid “ask aspects” plus retrieval-based clarification can resolve ambiguous user queries in task-oriented dialogue that rely on information retrieval</cite>. <cite id="c0ac7fe7-6">Multi-turn NLU combined with web query context can mitigate ambiguity in robotic caregiving by leveraging contextual information</cite>.
- Entity-level clarification and “A vs. B” disambiguation. Offer ranked alternatives and ask the user to choose when multiple entities or interpretations are plausible. <cite id="d3c0841a-4">Ambiguous queries in conversational search are handled by eliciting constraints and asking targeted questions across candidate interpretations</cite>. <cite id="d3c0841a-6">Discriminative questions can be generated by retrieving exemplars that distinguish among intent classes</cite>. <cite id="d3c0841a-7">When ambiguity affects one or more entity types, specific “Did you mean A or B?”-style clarifiers can reduce uncertainty efficiently</cite>.
- Clarifying agents. An autonomous component that continuously detects ambiguity, proposes clarifications, and iteratively narrows hypotheses until acting or deferring appropriately. <cite id="d3c0841a-2">Clarifying agents detect and resolve ambiguity via multi-turn dialogue to reduce uncertainty about user goals before acting</cite>. <cite id="d3c0841a-0">Clarification dialogs initiated by the system refine intent and are then translated into actions, treating the user as an active collaborator</cite>.

4) Software agents and automation workflows: intent elicitation and recovery
- Clarify-and-update artifacts that encode intent. Instead of guessing, pause to solicit precise constraints and then update specifications, workflows, or memory. <cite id="ddbcb700-0">Interactive agents overcome ambiguity by detecting it early, asking clarifying questions, and updating the plan before proceeding</cite>.
- Memory alignment and conflict resolution. When agents’ memory (context/short-term state) diverges in meaning from the user’s goals, elicit corrections or add constraints to align intent. <cite id="ddbcb700-1">As agents rely on memory, semantic conflict and ambiguity in memory can misalign with user intent; helping users update intent specifications addresses these failures</cite>.
- Workflow suspension and mini-dialogues. For high-stakes ambiguity, interrupt execution, surface the ambiguity, and invite selection or refinement before resuming. <cite id="d3c0841a-1">Before acting, systems can explicitly determine if clarification is necessary, ask it, and then proceed, which is especially valuable to prevent costly failures</cite>.
- Safety-first policies and constraints. Elicit intent in ways that minimize downstream risk (e.g., confirm irreversible steps, constrain tool use). <cite id="ddbcb700-0">Not asking clarifying questions can lead to misuse of tools and safety risks; thus, ambiguity must trigger clarifications under safety and attention constraints</cite>.
- Mixed-initiative co-creativity. Negotiate goals and constraints incrementally when initial expressions are incomplete or shifting. <cite id="05f306ea-1">Intent can fail due to underexpression, overspecification, equivocation, or context shift; mitigations include surfacing user inputs and negotiating goals to better align the artifact or action plan with intent</cite>.

5) Robotics and shared autonomy: intent inference and human-in-the-loop
- Probabilistic intent recognition and shared control. Estimate user intent, communicate uncertainty, and invite override or refinement during operation to manage ambiguity. <cite id="c0ac7fe7-0">Formulations for intent inference during assistive teleoperation under shared autonomy provide a mathematical basis for recognizing human intent and adapting control</cite>. <cite id="c0ac7fe7-3">Supervisory or autonomous control gives local autonomy in the presence of communication delays; eliciting intent continuously supports safe manipulation</cite>.
- Semi-autonomous teleoperation with intent estimation. Use intermediate control points or joint intent estimation to surface disagreements and elicit preference. <cite id="c0ac7fe7-1">Semi-autonomous telemanipulation can estimate operator intent via intersection points and adjust autonomy accordingly, reducing ambiguity-driven errors</cite>. <cite id="c0ac7fe7-2">User studies on intent-based shared control analyze task predictability, following vs. lead, and user preference, guiding when to elicit input</cite>.
- Trust-aware interaction to manage failure elicitation. Modulate autonomy based on perceived or measured uncertainty to sustain appropriate trust and timely intent elicitation. <cite id="c0ac7fe7-5">Trust in HRI depends on complex dynamics of performance, risk, and reliability; using complexity-driven trust models can guide when to ask for help or clarification</cite>.
- Domain-specific clarification by demonstration or selection. In tasks where language is insufficiently precise, let users demonstrate, point, or select among interpretations to disambiguate goal. <cite id="c0ac7fe7-6">Context-specific intention awareness through external queries and multi-turn NLU helps resolve ambiguities in settings like robotic caregiving</cite>.

6) Patterns for failure cases: structured elicitation workflows
- Ask-to-clarify functions as first-class failure recovery. Detect task ambiguity or uncertainty, present ranked clarifications (e.g., alternatives, missing constraints), and pause execution until the user refines. <cite id="d3c0841a-0">An ask-to-clarify function detects ambiguity, initiates a targeted dialogue, and translates refined intent into actions</cite>. <cite id="d3c0841a-1">Formalize recovery via explicit checks for the need to clarify, question selection, and post-clarification action</cite>.
- Uncertainty-aware escalation. If risk is high or evidence is thin, interrupt and elicit explicit permission or constraints; otherwise proceed with best-effort execution and monitor. <cite id="d3c0841a-5">Selecting clarifying questions based on classifier uncertainty improves alignment with user intent, reducing costly missteps</cite>. <cite id="ddbcb700-0">Safety risks from unclarified tool use demand that ambiguous situations trigger clarifications rather than assumptions</cite>.
- Clarification-by-action in physical tasks. Allow partial autonomy with haptic/shared control and explicit handover strategies, using force/position signals and shared intent estimates to surface conflicts and elicit input. <cite id="c0ac7fe7-0">Shared autonomy frameworks for intent inference provide mechanisms for the human and agent to co-adapt control signals in the presence of ambiguity</cite>. <cite id="c0ac7fe7-3">Supervisory control enables local autonomy for manipulation under bandwidth constraints, helping resolve intent ambiguity without full teleoperation</cite>.
- Retrieval and evidence grounding for failure diagnostics. Explain the ambiguity using retrieved snippets; ask the user which hypothesis matches their intent and why. <cite id="05f306ea-7">Grounding clarifying questions in retrieved passages reduces ambiguity by aligning the user’s intent with supporting evidence</cite>. <cite id="d3c0841a-8">Hybrid “ask aspects” plus retrieval clarifies ambiguous intents by constraining the search space with evidence</cite>.
- Negotiation in co-creative and memory-driven automation. When artifacts diverge from past intent or exhibit semantic conflicts, invite users to adjust specifications or select the correct prior. <cite id="05f306ea-1">MICIs fail when users underexpress intent; mitigations include surfacing partial inputs and negotiating constraints to better capture intent</cite>. <cite id="ddbcb700-1">Updating AI memory with user corrections resolves semantic conflicts and semantic ambiguity that cause misalignment</cite>.

7) Putting it together: a pragmatic method catalog for ambiguous or failing automation
- Detect ambiguity early:
  - Dialog systems monitor intent/CRF uncertainty and hypothesis sets; robotics estimate the probability of alternative intents from movement signals. <cite id="d3c0841a-1">Clarification is triggered when necessary, based on uncertainty about hypotheses</cite>. <cite id="c0ac7fe7-0">Probabilistic intent inference quantifies ambiguity during shared autonomy and assists in clarifying control</cite>.
- Ask precise, minimal clarifications:
  - Use candidate-ranked entities/goals or action constraints; prefer “A vs. B” choices; ground questions in evidence. <cite id="d3c0841a-7">Entity-focused “Did you mean A or B?” clarifies choices efficiently</cite>. <cite id="05f306ea-7">Retrieval-backed clarifiers align the task to evidence</cite>. <cite id="d3c0841a-8">Hybrid ask-aspects+retrieval reduces ambiguity in intent categories</cite>.
- Manage workflow and memory while clarifying:
  - Suspend or roll-back risky steps; update memory specifications; present diffs showing how clarified inputs change outcomes. <cite id="d3c0841a-0">Clarification results are translated into concrete actions, preventing mis-execution</cite>. <cite id="ddbcb700-1">Updating user intent specifications in agent memory resolves semantic conflicts and ambiguity</cite>.
- Select modality for elicitation by context and risk:
  - Low risk: text clarifying questions with options; medium-to-high risk, shared control or ask-for-confirmation; physical tasks: teleoperation with supervisory modes. <cite id="d3c06ea-7">Mixed-initiative lets either actor take the initiative, allowing modality choice (spoken, written, interface selection)</cite>. <cite id="c0ac7fe7-3">Supervisory or autonomous modes provide local autonomy, trading off human control for robustness</cite>.
- Incentivize helpfulness and safety:
  - Use polite, concise ask-to-clarify prompts; quantify residual uncertainty and potential impact; give users the ability to pause or override. <cite id="05f306ea-5">Selective engagement and politeness constraints are core to eliciting useful clarifications without overload</cite>. <cite id="ddbcb700-0">Clarification is essential to avoid unsafe assumptions and tool misuse</cite>.

8) Evaluation and improvement
- Metrics for elicitation effectiveness include reduction in misclassification after clarification, task success rate, user effort/time of clarifiers, and trust/calibration. <cite id="c0ac7fe7-5">Trust dynamics provide a lens to measure the balance of performance, risk, and user reliance when clarifying or deferring</cite>.
- Iterative improvement: incorporate user feedback on clarifier usefulness and adapt question generation policies via logging and active learning. <cite id="05f306ea-0">Mixed-initiative user–agent interaction is iterative and dynamic, offering methods to improve over time</cite>. <cite id="05f306ea-4">Modeling and integrating ambiguities into the clarification process can adapt future clarifications to ambiguity types</cite>.

Summary
- Foundational HCI and mixed-initiative design supply the control and politeness framework for eliciting intent, while dialog/NLP methods operationalize uncertainty-aware, retrieval-grounded clarification that translates refined intent into actions. <cite id="05f306ea-2">Mixed-initiative provides the interaction model where humans and agents alternately ask for clarifications and propose changes</cite>. <cite id="d3c0841a-0">Clarification functions detect ambiguity, ask targeted questions, and then act</cite>. <cite id="05f306ea-7">Retrieval grounding improves question informativeness</cite>.
- In failure cases, the most reliable pattern is to interrupt, surface the ambiguity with ranked hypotheses or actionable choices, and only resume or act after the user’s intent has been concretized—paired with safety constraints that make asking clarifications the default when stakes are high. <cite id="ddbcb700-0">Failing to ask clarifying questions leads to unsafe tool misuse</cite>. <cite id="d3c0841a-1">Clarification check→ask→act pipelines are a structured recovery when uncertainty is high</cite>. <cite id="d3c0841a-5">Classifier-driven clarifying questions reduce misalignment with intent</cite>.
- In physical/robotic automation, probabilistic intent recognition and shared control let the system elicit intent continuously during operation, offering handovers and override, while trust-aware policies modulate autonomy and clarifications based on perceived risk. <cite id="c0ac7fe7-0">Shared autonomy intent inference enables active intent elicitation during teleoperation</cite>. <cite id="c0ac7fe7-3">Supervisory control supports local autonomy under delays/limits, enabling clarification-in-motion</cite>. <cite id="c0ac7fe7-5">Trust dynamics guide when to ask for help</cite>.

fully_underspecified.text: What are existing methods to elicit intents when an automation encounters ambiguity, especially in failure cases?
fully_underspecified.answer:
Below are established and emerging techniques to elicit user intent when automation encounters ambiguity, with emphasis on failure cases. Methods are organized by mechanism and context (NLU/assistants, robotics/embodied agents, interactive programming/teaching, and evaluation/monitoring), followed by triggers, mechanisms, and concrete examples.

Summary overview
- Clarification dialogues: ask targeted questions to disambiguate underspecific or ambiguous user inputs before acting; widely used in dialog NLU and agent assistants, and supported by interactive planning and robotics research. <cite id="9c76036b-2">Interactive assistants resolve ambiguity by asking users clarifying questions, but require strategies that decide when and how to clarify efficiently</cite>. <cite id="9c76036b-5">Intent disambiguation systems are designed to resolve cases where multiple intents match by exchanging information with users</cite>. <cite id="9c76036b-4">Interactive agents for software tasks highlight ambiguity and underspecificity as a common misinterpretation failure mode, motivating elicitation loops</cite>.
- Quantify uncertainty; explain and verify: expose robot/agent uncertainty to avoid confidently misaligned actions; use explicit confirmation before step execution. <cite id="a169549e-0">LLM guidance for robots: align robot uncertainty with inherent task ambiguity to avoid confidently executing misaligned plans</cite>. <cite id="a169549e-1">Formal probabilistic models for intent inference during assistive teleoperation to handle uncertainty and shared autonomy</cite>.
- Mixed-initiative planning/teaching: hand over, request exemplars or demonstrations, iterate, and align partial plans with user feedback; common in robotics, UI, and software agents. <cite id="a169549e-2">In human-robot collaboration, intuitive instructions from humans often admit multiple interpretations; ambiguity handling requires iterative disambiguation with the human</cite>. <cite id="87d040fb-0">Mixed-initiative interaction lets autonomous and human sides take initiative opportunistically, balancing control to resolve ambiguity</cite>. <cite id="87d040fb-1">Use LLMs as a teachable machine for deliberate practice: novices act as teaching assistants, iteratively proposing fixes or examples to resolve misunderstandings</cite>.
- Focused recovery workflows: when failures occur, recover by diagnosing where the agent stopped, logging context for clarifying questions, and running targeted QA or evaluation loops. <cite id="52d33138-2">Structuring workflows with checkpoints and states prevents agents from “stopping halfway,” enabling recovery by identifying the last completed step and safely resuming</cite>. <cite id="52d33138-3">Without a structured trace, it is hard to answer recovery questions like “where did we stop” and “what is safe to resume from”</cite>. <cite id="52d33138-1">Proactively adding Q&A pairs trains agents on failure-relevant contexts, improving accuracy on ambiguous follow-ups</cite>. <cite id="52d33138-5">Agent evaluation playbooks pair run/review/refine cycles with alignment and monitoring matrices to surface and correct ambiguity-induced errors</cite>.

Techniques across application layers

1) Clarification Dialogues and Assisted NLU
Mechanism: Use ambiguity-aware prompting to elicit refinements (e.g., “Which X did you mean: A or B?”), anchored in task slots; when multiple intents are plausible, enumerate hypotheses and request selection or additional evidence. <cite id="9c76036b-0">Clarification elicits the user’s information need by exchanging information during interaction</cite>. <cite id="9c76036b-1">Ambiguity can be modeled and integrated into the clarification process to target specific ambiguity types</cite>. <cite id="9c76036b-2">Clarify When Necessary shows practical strategies for deciding when and how to ask clarifying questions to resolve ambiguity efficiently in interactive assistants</cite>.
When to trigger: high NLU ambiguity metrics, overlapping intent scores, or underspecific slots. <cite id="9c76036b-5">Assisted intent disambiguation resolves multiple candidate intents by involving users in the disambiguation loop</cite>. <cite id="9c76036b-4">Underspecific intent is a known failure mode for agent systems; elicitation can be triggered when goals are too broad</cite>.
Examples: call-center agents resolving “activate account” vs “cancel service”; search agents disambiguating “expensive camera” vs “camera for video calls”; software agents listing task assumptions to confirm. <cite id="9c76036b-2">Clarification questions target the core underspecified dimensions and reduce misrouting in interactive assistants</cite>. <cite id="9c76036b-5">Intent disambiguation can be integrated into assisted NLU flows (e.g., list top candidates with reasons and ask for selection)</cite>.

2) Robot- and Plan-Space Methods for Disambiguation and Repair
Mechanism: Represent human intent and environment uncertainty probabilistically; estimate situation labels and infer user goals; then run mixed-initiative replanning or ask targeted questions to confirm next actions. <cite id="a169549e-1">Probabilistic intent recognition during assistive teleoperation provides a mathematical framework to infer human intent under uncertainty</cite>. <cite id="a169549e-0">Aligning robots’ uncertainty with inherent task ambiguity mitigates confidently wrong or unsafe actions from hallucinated plans</cite>.
When to trigger: plan success probability below threshold; mismatch between predicted intent and user feedback; risk-aware cost explosion. <cite id="a169549e-2">Ambiguous instructions lead to multiple plausible plans; interactive disambiguation with demonstrations and guidance narrows the space</cite>. <cite id="a169549e-8">Partially observable task and motion planning accounts for uncertainty and risk to select safer plans when goals are ambiguous</cite>.
Examples: warehouse robots asked to “put away items” disambiguate by asking “Which shelf/priority?”, or by demonstrating location policies; home-help robots confirm objects and affordances before acting. <cite id="a169549e-1">Shared autonomy models elicit preferences via demonstrated corrections and probabilistic updates</cite>.

3) Mixed-Initiative Programming, Teaching, and Exemplar Elicitation
Mechanism: Give the agent the ability to request help (e.g., “teach me an example for X”), accept code/step-by-step demos, and iterate. <cite id="87d040fb-0">Mixed-initiative lets humans and agents alternate moves to collaboratively resolve ambiguity and repair errors</cite>. <cite id="87d040fb-1">Teachable LLM programming workflows let users provide exemplars/edits as feedback, training the model to correct future misunderstandings</cite>.
When to trigger: semantic drift detected in code/tool invocations; test failures reveal intent mismatch; user intervention reveals a better convention. <cite id="a169549e-4">Mixed observability and probabilistic task models justify human interventions for corrections, which can be incorporated into updated policies</cite>.
Examples: code agents ask for “one working example” when parsing requirements; UI agents collect interaction traces to infer implicit semantics; agent QA servers curate failure→fix exemplars for downstream models. <cite id="87d040fb-1">Deliberate practice on debugging by having LLMs act as TA/learner improves recovery on ambiguous edge cases</cite>.

4) Failure-Aware Recovery: Diagnostics, Confirmation, and Refined Evaluation
Mechanism: Record detailed execution traces; pause on error or ambiguity; ask local confirmation questions; run reduced-scope checks; and feed learnable signals back to the model. <cite id="52d33138-2">Agent workflows should include where-you-stopped markers to support recovery from partial or stalled execution</cite>. <cite id="52d33138-3">Lack of observability makes blaming errors and resuming safe work difficult; structured logging clarifies safe resumption points</cite>. <cite id="52d33138-1">Curating Q&A datasets specific to failures improves the agent’s ability to recognize and resolve ambiguous errors</cite>. <cite id="52d33138-4">Agents can learn from mistakes via explicit recovery flows: detect failures, localize, correct, and persist learning</cite>. <cite id="52d33138-5">Evaluation-to-learning loops (run→review→refine) turn diagnostics into targeted training, improving robustness to ambiguity</cite>. <cite id="52d33138-8">Proof-of-concept demos can hide real recovery issues (memory, specialization, observability); explicit failure-recovery testing surfaces these gaps</cite>.
Additional safety pattern: “assume-no-rights” confirmations. <cite id="a169549e-1">In assistive teleoperation, intent is inferred probabilistically and must be continuously confirmed to ensure safety</cite>.
Examples: banking/clinical agents confirm “is this the correct account/patient/step?” before committing; RAG pipelines ask, “Is the retrieved source sufficient/relevant for this decision?”; workflow engines pause at branching ambiguity and enumerate candidate paths with user approval. <cite id="52d33138-2">Checkpoints and states preserve progress and enable selective retry or path selection</cite>.

5) Structured Task Semantics to Reduce Ambiguity
Mechanism: Specify goals using formal constraints (preconditions, temporal/logical properties) so that ambiguity narrows the feasible set; then confirm with a minimal verification run. <cite id="a169549e-8">Risk-aware partially observable task and motion planning underlies formal task semantics that reduce feasible solutions under uncertainty</cite>. <cite id="a169549e-0">Quantifying ambiguity-aligned uncertainty helps select only those plans that satisfy safety and intent constraints</cite>.
When to trigger: initial intent is broad (e.g., “send invoice”) but domain policy requires qualifiers (sender, due date format, approval check). <cite id="9c76036b-2">Clarification prompts can be guided by a schema that enumerates candidate refinements</cite>.
Examples: manufacturing agents encode line-specific preconditions; finance agents encode regulation constraints; all reduce the hypothesis space after elicitation. <cite id="a169549e-2">Encoding intuitive human language into constrained plans reduces multiple interpretations</cite>.

Putting it together: Design patterns for eliciting intent under ambiguity and failure
- Clarify-before-act: enumerate top-3 intents/parameters with reasons; ask selection or comparison questions; offer “confirm and proceed” buttons. <cite id="9c76036b-0">Clarification exchanges focus on the user’s information need</cite>. <cite id="9c76036b-5">Assisted intent disambiguation operationalizes this pattern</cite>.
- Confirm-before-commit: critical actions must have inline “intent confirmation” (what, why, risk, backup) to prevent confidently wrong execution. <cite id="a169549e-0">Align robot uncertainty with ambiguity to avoid confident missteps</cite>. <cite id="a169549e-1">Intent inference models support continuous confirmation in shared autonomy</cite>.
- Mixed-initiative fallback: when automated reasoning stalls, request examples/demos or edit permissions; use human feedback to update priors and policies. <cite id="87d040fb-0">Mixed-initiative lets the human re-assert control</cite>. <cite id="87d040fb-1">Teaching by example provides targeted corrective signals</cite>.
- Bracketed recovery loop: capture last-km state, log decision factors, and run a reduced-risk subtask to validate intent (e.g., “confirm the summary for these items before I ship them”); then refine the larger task. <cite id="52d33138-2">Structured checkpoints allow resuming and validating at the last completed step</cite>. <cite id="52d33138-5">Evaluation playbooks connect recovery to learning and alignment</cite>.
- Elicitation through constraints and schemas: prompt users to select among structured refinements driven by domain schemas or task graphs; close the loop by re-running with the constrained goal. <cite id="a169549e-8">Risk-aware planning benefits from constrained goal specifications</cite>. <cite id="9c76036b-1">Ambiguity types can be targeted with tailored elicitation steps</cite>.

Trade-offs and practical guidance
- Over-elicitation vs. efficiency: Clarification tax can exceed savings if done naively; gate with ambiguity thresholds and cost-aware confirmations. <cite id="9c76036b-2">Clarify When Necessary analyzes how to minimize clarification while resolving ambiguity</cite>. <cite id="52d33138-5">Evaluation loops balance the costs of additional questions against downstream gains</cite>.
- Robustness vs. explainability: Formal intent/task models improve robustness but require user-facing explanations. <cite id="a169549e-1">Probabilistic intent models under shared autonomy integrate uncertainty cues with operator trust</cite>.
- Learning vs. safety: Teachable workflows should include risk controls (low-risk previews, dry-runs) before generalizing to production intent spaces. <cite id="52d33138-4">Agent recovery patterns emphasize security risks and guardrails when learning from mistakes</cite>.

Starting points for implementation
- Assistive NLU: adopt multi-hypothesis intent decoding + assisted disambiguation UI; see Amazon Lex’s intent disambiguation. <cite id="9c76036b-5">Intent Disambiguation resolves multiple matched intents via assisted NLU</cite>.
- Software agents: integrate pre-commit confirmations and “teach me one example” modes for ambiguous queries; use QA servers to mine failure→fix pairs. <cite id="9c76036b-4">Underspecificity is a first-class failure case in software automation</cite>. <cite id="52d33138-1">Adding failure Q&As improves agent accuracy</cite>. <cite id="52d33138-5">Evaluation-to-learning playbooks structure this flow</cite>.
- Robotics/embodied tasks: deploy probabilistic intent recognition and shared autonomy confirmation; expose situation labels and ask for preferred action under risk. <cite id="a169549e-1">Probabilistic intent recognition supports assistive teleoperation</cite>. <cite id="a169549e-8">Risk-aware task/motion planning under uncertainty</cite>.
- Interactive programming: enable mixed-initiative editing and unit-test suggestions; let users teach edge-case exemplars. <cite id="87d040fb-1">LLM-as-teachable-mechanism for deliberate practice and error repair</cite>.

Selected citations by method family
- Clarification and assisted NLU:
  - <cite id="9c76036b-0">Clarification elicits user information needs through interaction</cite>
  - <cite id="9c76036b-1">Modeling ambiguity types inside clarification processes</cite>
  - <cite id="9c76036b-2">Clarify When Necessary: resolving ambiguity by asking clarifying questions in interactive assistants</cite>
  - <cite id="9c76036b-5">Intent disambiguation in AWS Lex</cite>
- Robotics/plan-space:
  - <cite id="a169549e-0">Aligning robots’ uncertainty with inherent task ambiguity</cite>
  - <cite id="a169549e-1">Probabilistic intent inference during assistive teleoperation</cite>
  - <cite id="a169549e-2">Ambiguous human instructions in HRC; disambiguate via interaction</cite>
  - <cite id="a169549e-8">Partially observable task and motion planning under risk</cite>
- Mixed-initiative and teaching:
  - <cite id="87d040fb-0">Survey of mixed-initiative interaction concepts and benefits</cite>
  - <cite id="87d040fb-1">HypoCompass: teachable LLMs as assistants/learners for debugging</cite>
- Failure-aware recovery and evaluation-to-learning:
  - <cite id="52d33138-2">Recovery requires knowing where execution halted and what is safe to resume</cite>
  - <cite id="52d33138-3">Structured traces are vital to diagnose where agents stall</cite>
  - <cite id="52d33138-1">Proactive Q&A training addresses ambiguous errors</cite>
  - <cite id="52d33138-5">10-step evaluation playbook integrates run→review→refine cycles for learning</cite>
  - <cite id="52d33138-8">POC demos can hide real recovery challenges; explicit testing reveals them</cite>

Open challenges
- Generalizing elicitation strategies across modalities (text, speech, vision) with consistent cost bounds. <cite id="a169549e-0">Ambiguity-aligned uncertainty is still an open issue for embodied agents</cite>. 
- Safe delegation: when to ask a human vs. persist with risk-aware automation without stalling. <cite id="52d33138-4">There are documented security risks in learning from mistakes; careful risk management is required</cite>.

In practice, combine: ambiguity scoring + gated clarifications + confirm-before-commit prompts + mixed-initiative fallbacks + structured schemas/constraints + recovery logs → rapid intent elicitation with robust, learnable failure recovery. <cite id="9c76036b-2">Clarification strategies must be selective and efficient</cite> <cite id="52d33138-2">Recovery hinges on precise state snapshots</cite> <cite id="a169549e-0">Uncertainty alignment with task ambiguity</cite> <cite id="87d040fb-1">Teaching exemplars accelerate future intent resolution</cite>.

without_scope.text: What are existing methods to elicit user intents when an automation encounters ambiguity?
without_scope.answer:
Below is an organized synthesis of methods to elicit user intents when an automation encounters ambiguity. The strategies span ambiguity detection and representation, clarification generation and interaction policies, reinforcement-learning agents that ask questions, and voice/IVR and UI design patterns, all aimed at surfacing and resolving under-specification and multiple valid interpretations.

# Overview: From Detection to Disambiguation
Ambiguity arises from multiple interpretations, missing or noisy inputs, and out-of-distribution tasks; systems commonly adopt a two-stage plan—detect ambiguity, then generate or solicit disambiguation information—before acting or escalating. <cite id="2c0892f9-0">Some works adopt a two-stage pipeline: first detecting ambiguity, then generating suitable clarification questions</cite>. <cite id="ba8377f1-8">There are three potential sources of ambiguity: ASR, intent confidence, and hypothesis confidence</cite>. <cite id="2c0892f9-6">Clarification questions have long been a focal point in dialogue research due to their various functions, with resolving ambiguities a key rationale</cite>.

# 1) Ambiguity Detection and Interpretation Representation
Before eliciting intent, systems must recognize uncertainty. In dialogue QA, ambiguity can be defined and categorized; pipelines begin by detecting whether an input admits multiple plausible interpretations or requires additional information. <cite id="2c0892f9-1">By iteratively introducing user-confirmed information by clarifying questions, this approach helps guide users toward expressing a more complete and accurate ...</cite> <cite id="2c0892f9-4">Ambiguity is formalized in conversational QA settings, motivating methods that detect and then resolve via follow-up questions</cite>. In voice-first agents, ambiguity can be attributed to speech recognition, intent classification confidence, or downstream hypothesis confidence, which drives when and how to clarify. <cite id="ba8377f1-8">There are three potential sources of ambiguity: ASR, intent confidence, and hypothesis confidence</cite>.

Ambiguity detection also occurs in assisted NLU for voice/text bots, enabling triggered disambiguation flows. <cite id="ba8377f1-0">Disambiguation is an improvement to Assisted NLU that helps resolve ambiguous user inputs when multiple intents could match. Build voice/text chatbots</cite>.

# 2) Direct Clarification: Generating Questions and Prompts
A core method is to ask targeted clarification questions that surface missing or conflicting parameters. Recent work emphasizes selecting what to ask to maximize downstream benefit and integrating global knowledge when identifying missing slots.

- Two-stage clarification pipelines identify missing information and then craft questions; downstream confirmation improves accuracy and completeness. <cite id="2c0892f9-2">We propose a two-stage approach for the task of clarification question generation. In the first stage, we identify the missing information in a given context</cite>. Empirically, iterative confirmation of revealed information leads users to express more complete intents. <cite id="2c0892f9-1">By iteratively introducing user-confirmed information by clarifying questions, this approach helps guide users toward expressing a more complete and accurate ...</cite>.
- Clarify-or-answer agents explicitly decide to ask or to answer; when asking, they craft questions optimized for decision reduction. <cite id="90dfae4a-5">We propose CoA (Clarify-or-Answer), an ask-or-answer agent that separately models the decision to ask or answer, and what to ask if needed</cite>.
- Goal-driven questioners choose discriminative questions whose answers increase certainty in the correct hypothesis. <cite id="2c0892f9-5">Clarinet asks informative clarification questions by choosing questions whose answers would maximize certainty in the correct ...</cite>. Similar rule-based and learned methods aim to select questions that best separate overlapping interpretations. <cite id="2c0892f9-4">We propose a novel method of generating discriminative questions using a simple rule based system which can take advantage of any question generation system</cite>.
- Global knowledge can focus clarification on the most consequential missing slots, improving question usefulness. <cite id="2c0892f9-2">We propose a two-stage approach ... identify the missing information ... We propose a two-stage approach for the task of clarification question generation</cite>. <cite id="2c0892f9-7">Our method generates 25.2% more natural questions, 18.1% more useful questions, 6.1% less unnatural and 4% less useless questions</cite>.

# 3) Interactive Intent Elicitation: Selection, Preference, and Menu Interfaces
When multiple candidate intents/forms exist, systems can present options, pairwise choices, or previews to elicit the user’s preferred interpretation.

- Conversational search systems actively produce intent-aware clarifying questions to refine complex user intents. <cite id="2c0892f9-3">Generating clarifying questions can effectively clarify users' complicated search intent in conversational search systems</cite>.
- Platforms offer practical patterns for selective clarification: ask targeted yes/no questions to confirm the most uncertain aspects, or enumerate candidate interpretations with brief differentiators. <cite id="ba8377f1-5">You can approach disambiguation in a few ways, such as by asking more questions, asking targeted questions, and providing options</cite>. <cite id="ba8377f1-6">Disambiguation is the process of clarifying the user's intent. Conversational AI platforms do offer ways to disambiguate</cite>.
- Clarification can be framed as a preference over interpretations; algorithms retrieve or generate discriminative prompts that separate alternatives. <cite id="2c0892f9-4">We propose a novel method of generating discriminative questions ... to take advantage of any question generation system</cite>. <cite id="90dfae4a-5">Clarify-or-Answer separately models ask vs answer and selects questions to narrow uncertainty</cite>.

HCI cautions inform how to present these choices without harming UX. Confirmation dialogs should restate the request and explain the action to support error prevention, while modals interrupt flow and should be used judiciously with clear, unambiguous labels. <cite id="b61a3b90-2">A confirmation dialog must restate the user's request and explain what the computer is about to do, with specific information that allows users ...</cite>. <cite id="b61a3b90-4">A modal prevents interaction with page content until the user completes an action or dismisses the modal</cite>. <cite id="b61a3b90-3">Modality presents content in a separate, dedicated mode that prevents interaction with the parent view and requires an explicit ...</cite>. Ambiguous yes/no buttons risk mistakes, motivating concrete, intent-specific options or examples. <cite id="b61a3b90-6">Ambiguous options like “Yes/No” force users to pause and mentally map buttons to actions. This can lead to mistakes</cite>.

Design microcopy and pattern libraries document phrasing and affordances for intent confirmation, including concise confirmations and clear next-step framing to reduce second-guessing. <cite id="b61a3b90-0">A confirmation dialogue box basically loops the user back to the moment of choice and makes them take the same action, again</cite>. <cite id="b61a3b90-1">The exam tests your understanding of when to escalate, when to resolve autonomously, and which commonly proposed escalation triggers are unreliable</cite>.

# 4) Reinforcement Learning and Agentic Questioning
Reinforcement-learning (RL) agents learn to ask clarifying questions, reformulate inputs, or defer to avoid error, optimizing long-term outcomes or downstream utility.

- Question reformulation agents act between users and QA systems, learning to reframe questions to elicit better answers; these methods scale beyond fixed rule sets. <cite id="90dfae4a-0">We propose an agent that sits between the user and a black box QA system and learns to reformulate questions to elicit the best possible answers</cite>. <cite id="90dfae4a-6">Google open-sourced active question reformulation with reinforcement learning to improve QA</cite>.
- Interactive clarification via RL suggests refinements of the original query and adapts to conversational context. <cite id="90dfae4a-7">We propose a reinforcement model to clarify ambiguous questions by suggesting refinements of the original query</cite>.
- Active trajectory sampling and verification can detect ambiguous questions and gather alternative answers with evidence checks, reducing guesswork. <cite id="90dfae4a-1">At its core is an automated pipeline that detects ambiguous questions and gathers alternative answers via trajectory sampling and evidence verification</cite>.
- Context-under-specified dialog agents learn to ask clarifying questions or answer, switching based on expected success. <cite id="90dfae4a-5">We propose CoA (Clarify-or-Answer) ... models the decision to ask or answer, and what to ask if needed</cite>. LLM-based active task disambiguation emphasizes targeted follow-ups over guessing. <cite id="90dfae4a-8">A method for handling vague prompts by having the AI agent ask targeted follow-up questions</cite>.
These approaches typically optimize rewards tied to correctness, informativeness, or user cost (time/effort), learning when to ask and what to ask to improve downstream certainty. <cite id="2c0892f9-5">Clarinet asks informative clarification questions by choosing questions whose answers would maximize certainty in the correct ...</cite>. <cite id="90dfae4a-0">An agent learns to reformulate questions to elicit the best possible answers</cite>.

# 5) Voice/IVR, Speech Understanding, and Domain Constraints
Speech-first contexts add ASR-induced ambiguity and prosodic variability, motivating domain-aware disambiguation and selective clarification strategies.

- Commercial platforms provide templates for intent disambiguation flows in voice and text, triggered when multiple intents match the observed utterance. <cite id="ba8377f1-0">Disambiguation is an improvement to Assisted NLU that helps resolve ambiguous user inputs when multiple intents could match</cite>. <cite id="ba8377f1-5">Approaches include asking targeted questions and providing options when multiple intents are plausible</cite>.
- Patent and product research expose a second dimension of disambiguation: speaker intent vs. slot values, modeling what action the user ultimately wishes to perform once parameters are filled. <cite id="ba8377f1-3">Disambiguation in the second dimension, referred to as the “speaker intent” dimension, relates to determining what action the speaker may ...</cite>.
- Empirical notes on voice agents emphasize sources of ambiguity and aim to reduce unnecessary clarifications by routing to targeted questions when ASR or intent/hypothesis confidence is low. <cite id="ba8377f1-8">There are three potential sources of ambiguity: ASR, intent confidence, and hypothesis confidence</cite>. <cite id="ba8377f1-8">With this approach, there are three possible sources of ambiguity [and] targeted clarification can reduce unnecessary questions</cite>.
- Generalized guidance recommends performing disambiguation early and at the training/utterance level to avoid burdening runtime dialog flows. <cite id="ba8371-2">Disambiguation is performed ideally prior to dialog flow development; focusing on intent/training utterance level</cite>.

# 6) Selective Clarification and Escalation Policies
Selective clarification over full-blown disambiguation reduces system overhead and user burden by prioritizing high-uncertainty edges and using escalation when needed.

- Interactive disambiguation in task-oriented dialogue uses dialog to confirm the most ambiguous toponyms or slots, showing small gains in efficiency and accuracy. <cite id="ba8377f1-7">In this section, we evaluate our interactive toponym disambiguation methods. The core principle of using dialog clarification techniques for disambiguation ...</cite>.
- HCI escalation frameworks teach agents and designers when to escalate to a human, distinguishing reliable triggers from unreliable ones, and balancing cost/quality. <cite id="b61a3b90-1">The exam tests your understanding of when to escalate, when to resolve autonomously, and which commonly proposed escalation triggers are unreliable</cite>.
- Voice agent patterns implement branching on ASR/hypothesis confidence: prompt for clarification or delegate to a live agent depending on error likelihood and impact. <cite id="ba8377f1-8">Ambiguity sources include ASR and hypothesis confidence; with this approach, targeted strategies can reduce unnecessary questions</cite>.
- Platforms document practical tactics: ask targeted questions about specific edge cases, enumerate top interpretations with short descriptions, or show examples before committing. <cite id="ba8377f1-5">You can approach disambiguation in a few ways, such as by asking more questions, asking targeted questions, and providing options</cite>.

# 7) Design Considerations, Evaluation, and UX Pitfalls
Eliciting intent is as much about interface ergonomics as algorithms. Confirmation prompts should mirror the user’s wording and enumerate side-effects; modals should carry high cognitive weight and be minimized where possible. <cite id="b61a3b90-2">A confirmation dialog must restate the user's request and explain what the computer is about to do</cite> <cite id="b61a3b90-3">Modality presents content in a separate dedicated mode that prevents interaction and requires an explicit ...</cite>. Ambiguous yes/no options and poor phrasing increase error risk; concrete examples and previews mitigate mapping errors. <cite id="b61a3b90-6">Ambiguous options like “Yes/No” force users to mentally map, leading to mistakes — especially in destructive cases</cite>. 

Evaluation tracks usefulness and naturalness of generated clarifiers; stronger models improve both metrics and downstream task success. <cite id="2c0892f9-7">Generating 25.2% more natural questions, 18.1% more useful questions, 6.1% less unnatural and 4% less useless questions</cite>. RL-based clarifiers optimize expected downstream certainty and can be audited per the specific reward and policy. <cite id="2c0892f9-5">Clarinet asks clarification questions that maximize certainty in the correct hypothesis</cite>.

# A Practical Recipe: From Ambiguity to Resolved Intent
- Detect the source and type of ambiguity early; separate ASR errors from intent/hypothesis conflicts and under-specification. <cite id="ba8377f1-8">Ambiguity arises from ASR, intent confidence, and hypothesis confidence; targeted strategies reduce unnecessary clarifications</cite>.
- Decide on an elicitation modality: targeted question(s) about the most uncertain entity/slot, menu of top interpretations with differentiators and examples, or ask–confirm–preview loop tailored to voice/IVR. <cite id="2c0892f9-2">Two-stage clarification: missing information first, then question generation</cite> <cite id="ba8377f1-5">Provide options and ask targeted questions when multiple intents are plausible</cite> <cite id="2c0892f9-3">Intent-aware clarifying questions refine complex search intents</cite>.
- If under uncertainty, ask discriminative questions whose answers reduce hypothesis entropy the most or open the “Clarify-or-Answer” pipeline. <cite id="90dfae4a-5">Clarify-or-Answer models ask vs. answer and crafts questions to narrow uncertainty</cite> <cite id="2c0892f9-4">Discriminative question generation separates overlapping alternatives</cite> <cite id="2c0892f9-5">Choose questions whose answers maximize certainty in the correct hypothesis</cite>.
- In speech-first contexts, prefer in-situ confirmation (“Did you mean X or Y?”), show concise pros/cons or example transcriptions, and escalate if confidence remains low or business risk is high. <cite id="ba8377f1-0">Assisted NLU disambiguation resolves ambiguous inputs when multiple intents could match</cite> <cite id="ba8377f1-8">Sources of ambiguity include ASR and hypothesis confidence; route to targeted clarification or human handoff</cite>.
- Iterate with user confirmations; stop early when confidence and alignment are high, measured by model-derived confidence, label-agreement over interpretations, or utility gains from clarifiers. <cite id="2c0892f9-1">Iteratively introducing user-confirmed information guides users toward more complete and accurate expression</cite>. <cite id="2c0892f9-6">Clarification questions serve the function of resolving ambiguities, improving downstream outcomes</cite>.

# Closing Perspective
Across NLP, HCI, and RL agent research, the central methods to elicit ambiguous user intents converge on: ambiguity detection; targeted question generation aligned to missing slots or competing interpretations; interactive selection via options or preference queries; prudent UI interruption (modals/confirmations) with clear wording; and selective escalation with explicit policies. <cite id="2c0892f9-0">Two-stage detection-and-clarification pipelines are a common backbone</cite> <cite id="90dfae4a-0">Active reformulation sits between users and downstream systems to improve outcomes</cite> <cite id="ba8377f1-0">Assisted NLU supports ambiguity handling in voice/text bots</cite> <cite id="b61a3b90-2">Confirmation dialogs should restate and clarify the action for users</cite> <cite id="b61a3b90-1">Escalation policies teach when to hand off and when to resolve autonomously</cite>. Combining these with learned policies and global knowledge yields robust intent elicitation under uncertainty.

query.text: Are there papers that use different formats of Q&A with the user to clarify intent and compose more complicated prompts to LLM?
query.answer:
Yes. Across conversational search, dialog systems, and human-in-the-loop agents, there is a growing body of work that uses multi-turn Q&A formats with users to (i) clarify intent and (ii) compose more complex prompts or tool calls for LLMs or downstream systems. Below are representative approaches, mechanisms, and empirical findings.

Conversational search and dialog systems: clarifying questions to disambiguate intent
- Iterative clarification-rewriting. ICR (EMNLP 2025) proposes alternately generating clarifying questions and rewriting user queries to resolve ambiguity in conversational search, training models to engage in clarification–rewriting loops that improve retrieval and answer relevance under unclear intent. <cite id="0f050585-1">ICR iteratively generates clarification questions and rewritten queries to handle ambiguous user intents in conversational search</cite> <cite id="0f050585-8">The model learns to alternate between asking clarifying questions and rewriting queries, explicitly pivoting on clarification–rewriting</cite> <cite id="0f050585-7">ICR frames clarification-rewriting as a novel iterative scheme centered on clarification questions</cite>.
- Intent-aware clarifying questions. Recent systems directly generate “intent-aware” clarifying questions to probe missing aspects of complex user goals in conversational search settings. <cite id="0f050585-0">Generating clarifying questions can effectively clarify users’ complicated search intent in conversational search systems</cite>.
- Interactive query clarification via simulation. User-simulation–driven frameworks trigger clarifying questions when initial queries are ambiguous, offering candidate reformulations and waiting for user feedback to commit, thereby structuring the user–system dialogue to clarify intent. <cite id="0f050585-2">A conversation framework generates clarifying questions when queries are ambiguous and iterates with user simulation to refine</cite>.
- Surveys and design guidelines. Empirical/position work quantifies when/why clarifying questions improve user satisfaction/IR performance and provides design blueprints, including how to phrase clarifications to better resolve ambiguity. <cite id="0f050585-3">Guidelines for refining clarifying questions lead to improvements in both user satisfaction and system performance</cite>. <cite id="0f050585-4">A Chatbot Uncertainty Taxonomy for IR with LLMs proposes quantified uncertainty signals that motivate asking clarifying questions when confidence is low</cite>.
- Processing answers to clarifying Qs at scale. Classifier-based methods parse users’ replies to clarifying questions to deconfound intent, extract missing slots, and route to appropriate reformulated queries. <cite id="0f050585-5">A classifier-based method (MI-Clf) processes answers to clarifying questions in conversational search to handle ambiguity</cite>.

Human-in-the-loop frameworks that compose complex prompts and tool calls
- ReAct and LangChain agents. The ReAct paradigm elicits chain-of-thought rationales interleaved with explicit tool/action calls, treating each turn as a structured Q/A over goals, observations, and tool options; this composes multi-step prompts that combine reasoning traces with API invocations. <cite id="422ae9fb-0">ReAct is essentially a prompting strategy to elicit chain-of-thought reasoning and actions, while tool-calling leverages model capabilities</cite>. <cite id="422ae9fb-1">ReAct dynamically generates verbal reasoning steps and actions, creating a more human-like problem-solving loop</cite>. <cite id="422ae9fb-5">ReAct prompts LLMs to generate both verbal reasoning traces and actions for a task, blending reasoning and acting</cite>. <cite id="422ae9fb-6">Lectures and guides show how agents and ReAct-style tool use combine reasoning with acting over tools</cite>. <cite id="422ae9fb-7">Implementations treat retrieval as tools the LLM can call, building agentic RAG systems</cite>.
- Tool-use frameworks and feedback loops. ToolLLM presents a general framework for training LLMs to use 16k+ real-world APIs, covering data construction, training, and evaluation; feedback-driven frameworks further improve tool-use by learning from user interactions. <cite id="c789b2a0-2">ToolLLM introduces a general tool-use framework spanning data construction, model training, and evaluation for mastering 16,000+ APIs</cite>. <cite id="c789b2a0-1">A feedback-driven framework improves tool use for LLMs by leveraging user interactions and outcomes</cite>. <cite id="c789b2a0-0">Gorilla demonstrates integrating LLMs with tools via APIs to execute multi-step actions</cite>. Surveys catalog conversational/interactive tool-use workflows that externalize prompts into tool specifications. <cite id="c789b2a0-4">A comprehensive tool-learning survey collects papers on LLM-assisted, conversational, and interactive tool-use with human feedback</cite>.
- General multi-turn capability surveys. Reviews of multi-turn interaction emphasize turn-taking Q&A, preference elicitation, and plan revision as mechanisms to compose increasingly precise prompts and action sequences. <cite id="cfc91ef1-6">A focused review of multi-turn capabilities highlights turn-taking interactions and downstream applications where clarification and plan revision are pivotal</cite>.
- Preference elicitation via clarifying Qs. Production-style preference elicitation methods teach LLMs to ask informative, funneling clarifying questions that progressively constrain user intent, improving downstream recommendations via structured Q&A. <cite id="cfc91ef1-1">LLMs can interact in open-ended conversational interfaces to ask clarifying questions for preference elicitation</cite>. <cite id="cfc91ef1-3">Informative questioning improves an LLM’s ability to infer user preferences via instruction prompts</cite>. <cite id="cfc91ef1-7">Methods significantly improve proficiency in asking funnel questions to elicit preferences</cite>. Reinforcement-learning–trained models can anticipate future conversational turns to decide when to ask clarifying questions, reducing ambiguity. <cite id="cfc91ef1-2">RLHF trains LLMs to ask clarifying questions by assigning preferences based on expected outcomes of future turns</cite>. <cite id="cfc91ef1-0">LLMs taught to anticipate future turns ask clarifying questions to resolve ambiguity in user requests</cite>. Clarinet proposes selecting questions that maximize information gain (e.g., increasing certainty in candidate intents), operationalizing clarification as an optimization over prompt intent disambiguation. <cite id="cfc91ef1-5">Clarinet asks informative clarification questions by choosing those whose answers maximize certainty in the correct candidate</cite>.
- Interactive retrieval triage in medicine. Industrial systems integrate routing, inference, and triage via conversational Q&A, exemplifying structured Q/A flows that decompose clinical needs into subgoals and tool chains. <cite id="cd6a2161-6">CLARITY uses AI-driven routing and inference with triage flows to decompose and coordinate tasks via structured interactions</cite>.
- Patient–provider dialogue and chatbots. Follow-up question generation reduces ambiguity and supports complex interactions, directly motivating the use of Q&A loops to refine intent and decompose tasks. <cite id="cd6a2161-0">Follow-up question generation reduces conversational ambiguity and enhances modeling of complex interactions in patient–provider dialogue</cite>. <cite id="cd6a2161-1">Follow-up Q generation is essential for reducing ambiguity and supporting complex queries in dialogue systems</cite>. Real deployments in mental health and pharmacists show chatbots asking clarification questions to tailor responses and route appropriately. <cite id="cd6a2161-4">Woebot asks clarification questions to probe symptom contexts, e.g., asking for specifics to assess severity and guide responses</cite>. <cite id="cd6a2161-5">An AI chatbot shows potential for clinical triage/pharmacogenomics Q&A, indicating structured decomposition with user guidance</cite>. Physician-centered evaluations show how clinicians use prompts and summarization to co-ask Qs with AI for triage and reasoning. <cite id="cd6a2161-2">Physicians use AI chatbots in clinical reasoning, with varying approaches to inputting case content and prompting follow-ups</cite>.

From dialog to tool composition and formal reasoning: multi-step prompt structuring
- ReAct and agentic RAG. In ReAct-style agents, natural-language rationales and stepwise tool calls are co-structured, turning user goals into prompts that invoke tools for retrieval, computation, and external memory; the system logs and revises intermediate Q/As to refine the composed prompt sequence. <cite id="422ae9fb-5">ReAct combines chain-of-thought with explicit actions so that each rationale step and tool choice is part of the prompt/action composition</cite>. <cite id="422ae9fb-7">Agentic RAG implementations abstract retrieval into tools an LLM can call, composing “react” prompts that interleave reasoning with tool use</cite>.
- Tool learning frameworks. ToolLLM and feedback-driven tool-use methods formalize composing prompts that specify APIs, parameters, and validation—often via multi-turn clarifications about required inputs—closing the loop with user feedback on outcomes. <cite id="c789b2a0-2">ToolLLM provides a general approach to constructing and training prompts for API calls across tens of thousands of tools</cite>. <cite id="c789b2a0-1">A feedback-driven framework improves tool use by iteratively refining prompts based on user answers and results</cite>. Surveys emphasize conversational and interactive tool-use scenarios where LLM prompts are dynamically revised with user Q&A. <cite id="c789b2a0-4">Interactive tool-use with human feedback is cataloged as a core pattern for conversational QA and question-answering workflows</cite>.
- Formal proofing with Lean/LLMs. LeanTutor and LeanDojo/Lean-based systems enable LLMs to interactively tutor proofs, clarifying lemmas, goals, and subgoals via natural language Q&A and tactic scripts, composing rigorous prompts to theorem provers. <cite id="16d0cf89-0">LeanTutor combines LLMs with theorem provers to interact with students in natural language, guiding proof steps</cite>. <cite id="16d0cf89-1">LeanTutor proposes a math-proof tutoring system where an LLM interacts with students in natural language to co-construct proofs</cite>. <cite id="16d0cf89-2">LeanDojo-v2 is an end-to-end framework for training and deploying AI-assisted theorem provers in Lean 4</cite>. <cite id="16d0cf89-3">A human-in-the-loop workflow for interactive theorem proving integrates LLMs with researchers and theorem provers</cite>. <cite id="16d0cf89-9">OpenReview work positions Lean/LLM systems as benchmarks for human-AI proof interaction</cite>.
- Prompting frameworks for structured reasoning. Chain-of-thought (CoT) and related paradigms structure prompts as sequences of Q&A-like intermediates, and program-aided prompting (PAL) composes programmatic reasoning steps, often guided by clarifying intermediate questions; PAL is shown to also benefit least-to-most prompting. <cite id="633b6e65-6">Chain-of-thought prompting elicits multi-step reasoning in LLMs, improving performance on various reasoning tasks</cite>. <cite id="633b06b5-2">PAL uses natural-language problems plus program reasoning as intermediate steps, with analyses showing benefits to COT and Least-to-Most prompts</cite>. <cite id="633b06b5-3">In Program-Aided Language Models, LLMs read problems and generate programs as intermediate reasoning steps</cite>. <cite id="633b06b5-7">Practical guides show PAL framing complex prompts as program-of-thought, which can be iteratively refined</cite>.

How these works connect “clarify intent” and “compose complex prompts”
- Clarify intent via structured Q&A. Iterated clarifying questions (ICR), intent-aware Q generation, and follow-up Q strategies reduce ambiguity and better capture user goals; classifier components parse user answers to extract missing slots. <cite id="0f050585-1">Iterative clarification-rewriting reduces ambiguity in intent</cite> <cite id="0f050585-0">Intent-aware clarifying questions clarify complicated search intent</cite> <cite id="cd6a2161-0">Follow-up Q generation reduces ambiguity and helps model complex interactions</cite>. Human-in-the-loop preference elicitation learns to ask funneling Qs, improving downstream outcomes. <cite id="cfc91ef1-1">LLMs can elicit preferences via clarifying questions in conversational interfaces</cite> <cite id="cfc91ef1-7">Funnel-question prompting improves preference inference</cite>. Domain-facing systems like CLARITY and clinical chatbots exemplify routing and triage through multi-turn Q/A. <cite id="cd6a2161-6">Clinical assistants route and infer through structured multi-turn interactions</cite> <cite id="cd6a2161-4">Chatbots insert clarifications to tailor responses and assess severity</cite>.
- Compose complex prompts/tool calls. ReAct/LangChain agents compose prompts that interleave rationales with tool invocations; ToolLLM and feedback-driven methods train and refine API-specific prompts with user outcomes; proof assistants translate user clarifications into tactic/goal scripts. <cite id="422ae9fb-5">ReAct prompts combine natural-language reasoning with explicit actions (tool calls)</cite> <cite id="c789b2a0-2">ToolLLM trains models to produce tool-use prompts over vast API landscapes</cite> <cite id="c789b2a0-1">Feedback-driven loops improve tool-call composition based on user signals</cite>. Formal tutoring systems demonstrate composing structured proof scripts via Q&A exchanges. <cite id="16d0cf89-0">LLM–prover tutoring co-composes proof prompts with students</cite>.
- Iterative refinement loops. Many systems alternate between generating a candidate answer/prompts and asking targeted Qs, using user answers to revise parameters, add constraints, or switch strategies; this directly links intent clarification (what to ask) and prompt composition (how to ask). <cite id="0f050585-2">Interactive clarification via user simulation iterates question generation and refinement based on user responses</cite> <cite id="cfc91ef1-2">RLHF trains models to decide when to ask clarifying questions by simulating future turns</cite> <cite id="cd6a2161-1">Follow-up Qs are essential to resolve ambiguity and enable complex queries</cite>.

Takeaway
- If you want papers that explicitly turn user Q&A into intent clarification and complex prompt composition, start with: clarifying-question generators for conversational search (ICR, intent-aware Qs, interactive user-simulation), follow-up Q generation in patient–provider dialogue, preference-elicitation Q strategies, and human-in-the-loop tool-use/theorem proving (ReAct/LangChain, ToolLLM, LeanTutor). These works operationalize different Q&A formats—freeform clarifying Qs, slot-filling, preference funneling, and structured tool/prover prompts—together improving intent understanding and composing multi-step prompts to LLMs and tools. <cite id="0f050585-1">ICR (EMNLP 2025) and related works show iterative clarifying Qs can reduce ambiguity and improve downstream performance</cite> <cite id="cd6a2161-0">Follow-up Q generation reduces ambiguity and supports complex interactions</cite> <cite id="422ae9fb-5">ReAct composes prompts that interleave chain-of-thought with tool actions</cite> <cite id="c789b2a0-2">ToolLLM formalizes composing prompts for API use at scale</cite> <cite id="16d0cf89-0">LeanTutor demonstrates composing formal prompts with theorem provers via natural-language Q&A</cite>.

Practical pointers
- For IR/QA products: consider clarifying-question modules that detect ambiguity and slot-filling Qs; parse answers with classifiers to commit to refined queries/prompts. <cite id="0f050585-5">Classifier-based processing of answers to clarifying Qs helps systematize revisions</cite>.
- For agentic workflows: adopt ReAct-style state machines with tool registries; allow users to answer intermediate “what next?” Qs to steer complex RAG/tool chains. <cite id="422ae9fb-5">ReAct provides a blueprint for interleaving reasoning and actions</cite> <cite id="422ae9fb-7">Building agentic RAG via tools the LLM can call</cite>.
- For formal domains: integrate theorem-prover-backed clarifications to ensure rigor in composed prompts. <cite id="16d0cf89-1">LeanTutor’s natural-language tutoring co-constructs proofs with users</cite>.

In sum, there are indeed multiple established and emerging paper lines that use multi-format Q&A—clarifying questions, follow-ups, preference funnels, and proof/goal tactics—to explicitly clarify intent and compose more sophisticated prompts to LLMs and tools, often with user feedback loops, surveys, and empirical gains in clarity and performance. <cite id="0f050585-1">ICR’s iterative clarification-rewriting</cite> <cite id="0f050585-0">intent-aware clarifying Qs</cite> <cite id="cd6a2161-1">follow-up Qs to resolve ambiguity</cite> <cite id="422ae9fb-5">ReAct’s reasoning+actions</cite> <cite id="c789b2a0-2">ToolLLM’s prompt/tool composition framework</cite> <cite id="16d0cf89-1">Lean/LLM proof tutoring</cite> collectively substantiate this pattern.
