fully_underspecified.text: Are there papers that use different formats of questions and answers with the user to clarify intent and compose more complicated prompts to a language model?
fully_underspecified.answer:
Yes. Recent work in human–AI interaction and grounded generation studies and implements systems that converse with users to clarify intent and then compose more complex prompts or operation plans for language models. Below are representative categories of papers and what they contribute.

Interactive clarification systems and preference elicitation
- Clarinet (ClarificationNet) asks informative clarification questions to reduce ambiguity and increase confidence in the correct candidate, using an interactive retrieval setup where a finetuned LLM generates open-ended questions to refine user needs and compose better queries or prompts over a corpus of items (e.g., books). The design explicitly optimizes for information that maximally increases certainty in the correct choice, translating user intent into targeted clarifying questions and then leveraging answers to form stronger retrieval or generation prompts. <cite id="baf5b0aa-0">Clarinet asks informative clarification questions whose answers would maximize certainty in the correct candidate</cite> <cite id="b8992a32-0">Clarinet presents an interactive retrieval system that helps users retrieve books by asking open-ended clarification questions, with a finetuned LLM generating those questions</cite>.
- Google research on conversational preference elicitation shows how LLMs can interactively probe users to align recommendations and responses with latent preferences in open-ended conversational interfaces, demonstrating that clarifying Q&A can structure the prompt context to better capture user intent and produce personalized outputs. <cite id="baf5b0aa-4">LLMs enable recommendation systems to interact with users in open-ended conversational interfaces for asking clarifying questions during preference elicitation</cite>.
- Interactive alignment for search intent demonstrates pipelines (LLM Alignment via AI feedback) that construct preference datasets and adjust prompts/weighting to align model outputs with the user’s intended retrieval and answer goals, effectively using generated feedback and clarifying signals to refine how prompts are composed for downstream search and QA. <cite id="baf5b0aa-3">An LLM Alignment via AI feedback pipeline constructs an LLM-generated preference dataset to tackle aligning language models with user search intent</cite>.
- Practical guidance from cloud/AWS corroborates the effectiveness of interactive RAG: asking clarifying questions and prompting users for details, then incorporating those clarifications into the retrieval context and prompt, improves answer relevance and reduces ambiguity. <cite id="b8992a32-1">Asking clarifying questions, prompting for more details, and incorporating new contextual information improves LLM responses in RAG use cases</cite>.
- Empirical studies also explore when and how to ask clarifying questions: by anticipating future conversational turns and optimizing for information gain, models can ask questions that resolve ambiguity and enable more precise downstream prompting; related work proposes discriminative question generation to disambiguate intents before composing prompts or queries. <cite id="baf5b0aa-6">Develop LLMs that can ask clarifying questions to resolve ambiguity in users' requests by modeling future conversation turns</cite> <cite id="baf5b0aa-7">Proposes generating discriminative questions with a rule-based system to resolve intent ambiguities for better prompt or query composition</cite>.

Conversational retrieval and ReAct-style scaffolding that externalize sub-questions
- Conversational RAG frameworks emphasize breaking freeform user queries into sequences of sub-questions, retrievals, and tool calls—an explicit “plan–retrieve–act–generate” decomposition that functions as a structured QA over sources. This scaffolding often begins with an “ask-a-question” phase: the system queries the user to confirm granularity/tone or to split a broad goal into components, then composes a multi-step prompt mixing retrieval artifacts and tool outputs. <cite id="b8992a32-3">Combining the ReAct framework with human input to ask clarifying questions yields powerful retrieval-augmented chatbots that externalize actions and questions</cite>. 
- Additional technical reports detail “clarifying question” generation informed by corpus cues to guide interactive search: models produce question drafts that are then refined via user feedback, and the selected clarifications are used to compose retrieval queries and contextual prompts that better align with user needs. <cite id="b8992a32-8">Develops models that generate corpus-informed clarifying questions aligned with user needs to guide follow-up interactions and query composition</cite>.
- Applied HCI/AI guides and benchmarks describe practical scaffolds: multi-turn disambiguation, role-playing (e.g., QA analyst/agent personas), and structured prompts mixing system instructions, task decomposition, tool definitions, and evidence slots. These approaches translate user intent into explicit sub-questions mapped to retrievals and operations, and iterate when answers are incomplete or ambiguous. <cite id="b8992a32-7">Advanced RAG prompting strategies emphasize structuring instructions, separating world knowledge from tools, and sequencing sub-questions to improve accuracy</cite> <cite id="b8992a32-3">ReAct combined with human clarifying questions helps an LLM chatbot externalize actions and ask question–answer sequences over data sources</cite>.

Preference elicitation and need-satisfaction prompting
- Research on “Asking Clarifying Questions for Preference Elicitation” proposes hybrid aspect-based and retrieval-augmented clarification to quickly narrow user preferences and then prompt models to generate outputs that satisfy those latent preferences. The system focuses on eliciting needs through targeted Q&A, then composing prompts that encode constraints (e.g., style, audience, features) derived from interactions. <cite id="baf5b0aa-1">Large language models can generate clarification questions to tackle query ambiguity, using aspects and retrieval-based hybrid strategies to refine needs before prompting</cite>.
- A broader industry track paper at top ACL conference (ACL Industry 2025) demonstrates how LLMs can interact with users in open-ended conversational interfaces to elicit clarifications and preferences, indicating real-world feasibility and integration into decision-support prompts. <cite id="baf5b0aa-4">LLMs enable conversational interfaces for preference elicitation, supporting recommendation and decision-making use cases</cite>.
- ICML 2025 work on LLM alignment via AI feedback operationalizes intent clarification at retrieval time by synthesizing user feedback into training signals that push prompts and ranking criteria to better match intended query semantics. <cite id="baf5b0aa-3">LLM Alignment via AI feedback constructs preference datasets to better match user search intent and improve retrieval outcomes</cite>.

Benchmarks and evaluation for clarification capabilities
- ClarQ-LLM (arXiv) provides a benchmark where seekers must ask clarification questions to accurately infer a provider’s intention, explicitly evaluating the competence to generate and integrate clarifying Q&A—skills directly useful for composing precise prompts from vague user goals. <cite id="baf5b0aa-8">ClarQ-LLM assesses models’ ability to clarify and understand intentions by requiring them to ask questions before responding</cite>.
- “Asking Clarifying Questions for Preference Elicitation with LLMs” (Google research) evaluates how open-ended clarifications improve downstream satisfaction/accuracy versus zero- or one-shot prompting, supporting the utility of multi-turn Q&A scaffolding to compose better-tuned prompts and constraints. <cite id="baf5b0aa-4">Open-ended clarification interactions with LLMs improve alignment and enable better downstream outputs in preference domains</cite>.
- Additional arXiv work on models predicting when to ask clarifying questions provides selection policies and training signals to increase the informativeness of user questions, enabling systems to avoid guessing prompts and instead elicit information that improves composition. <cite id="baf5b0aa-6">Develop policies so LLMs can decide to ask clarifying questions to resolve ambiguity and improve prompting</cite>.

Illustrative mechanisms: how clarifying Q&A translates to complex prompts
Across these systems, several design motifs recur:
- Information-focused clarifications: ask questions whose answers maximize downstream confidence or expected information gain, then incorporate those answers as system context or constraints in the final prompt. <cite id="baf5b0aa-0">Clarinet chooses questions whose answers maximize certainty in the correct candidate</cite>.
- Decomposition and role-playing: split the task into sub-questions/roles (e.g., QA analyst), with dedicated sections for assumptions, plan, evidence, and synthesis; prompt explicitly for intermediate QA artifacts before producing the final answer. <cite id="b8992a32-3">ReAct-style scaffolding with human questions externalizes actions and questions before generation</cite>.
- Retrieval-grounded question streams: prompt the user to confirm or refine sub-questions, then compose retrieval queries/tool calls that feed curated evidence into the generation prompt, enabling complex multi-step compositions (summarization, fusion, critique loops). <cite id="b8992a32-8">Corpus-informed clarifying questions direct follow-up retrieval and prompt composition</cite>.
- Preference- and constraint-aware prompting: extract preferences, constraints, and evaluation criteria via clarifying Q&A, and inject them into the system prompt or structured tool specifications. <cite id="baf5b0aa-1">Hybrid aspect-based clarification refines needs before prompting</cite> <cite id="baf5b0aa-4">Open-ended conversational clarifications align prompts with preferences</cite>.

query.text: How is artificial intelligence being utilized to enhance the diagnosis and treatment of sleep apnea?
query.answer:
# Summary

Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly embedded across the sleep apnea care pathway, improving efficiency and accuracy of diagnosis from bedside and home devices and enabling data-driven optimization of positive airway pressure (PAP) therapy through automation, telemonitoring, and adherence-centered interventions.<cite id="bba15292-1">AI is poised to transform the diagnosis and management of obstructive sleep apnea by automating the analysis of sleep data, enhancing the accuracy of diagnosis, and optimizing therapy pathways</cite><cite id="bba15292-3">AI is helping reshape sleep medicine by making testing more efficient, supporting early detection, and offering more personalized help with CPAP therapy</cite>.

# AI to Improve Diagnosis

AI methods learn from signals routinely collected in sleep studies and consumer wearables, enabling earlier, cheaper, and more scalable screening and diagnosis. Models trained on ECG, pulse oximetry (SpO2), and snoring/acoustic features have achieved strong performance for detecting obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) and estimating severity, often matching expert scorers on subset tasks.<cite id="bba15292-0">ML models showed good performance in diagnosing sleep apnea using easily obtained features from the electrocardiogram, pulse oximetry, and sound signals</cite><cite id="bba15292-1">AI is poised to transform the diagnosis and management of OSA by automating the analysis of sleep data, enhancing the accuracy of diagnosis, and optimizing therapy pathways</cite>.

Recent systematic reviews and device studies quantify accuracy gains on home-based datasets. Wearable AI for OSA detection shows pooled accuracy around 0.87, with sensitivity ~0.94 and specificity ~0.75; specific devices and algorithms report >85–98% accuracy in controlled or single-modality studies.<cite id="b36cae5a-8">The pooled mean accuracy, sensitivity, and specificity of wearable AI in detecting sleep apnea were 0.869, 0.938, and 0.752, respectively</cite><cite id="b36cae5a-3">reported accuracy of over 85%, with some single-modality models reaching 98.91% accuracy</cite><cite id="b36cae5a-2">wearable device studies offer overall accuracy of >90% and, with deep learning, an average accuracy of 88.99%</cite>. Home sleep apnea devices leveraging oximetry, chest effort, and snoring with deep learning or engineered features can approach near-ceiling accuracies in curated datasets, but performance varies with sensor quality and confounders such as comorbidities and motion artifacts.<cite id="b36cae5a-1">the best-performing model achieves an exceptional accuracy rate of 99%, emphasizing the potential of deep learning</cite><cite id="b36cae5a-7">AI-driven screening using overnight blood oxygen data achieved up to 97.04% accuracy and 97.19% specificity in some reports</cite><cite id="b36cae5a-4">real-time snoring detection from smartphone audio has been demonstrated with deep learning feasibility for home-based use</cite>.

Beyond general accuracy, AI methods accelerate scoring and triage. Automated algorithms for detecting apnea/hypopnea events and grading OSA severity on PSG data show high accuracy, reducing manual scorer burden during sleep lab interpretation.<cite id="625db3fd-6">a deep learning algorithm identified apnea/hypopnea episodes and assessed OSA severity with high accuracy</cite><cite id="bba15292-0">machine learning models can diagnose OSA from ECG/oximetry/snoring features, streamlining clinical workflows</cite>. At the consumer-health interface, smartwatches and phones can provide preliminary apnea risk screening via pulse-wave and motion sensors; however, current evidence cautions that they are not yet as accurate as clinical sleep studies and should be used for early detection rather than replacement.<cite id="b36cae5a-8">pooled wearable performance supports screening-grade utility, though variability remains</cite><cite id="b36cae5a-4">smartwatches offer valuable insights but are not yet as accurate as clinical sleep tests</cite><cite id="b36cae5a-5">comparative studies highlight smartwatches' potential as preliminary tools</cite>.

# AI to Optimize Treatment: Titration, Telemonitoring, and Personalization

AI-supported PAP systems and telemedicine platforms improve therapy titration and follow-up by continuously learning from physiologic signals, patient-reported outcomes, and usage patterns. Connected CPAP/BiPAP devices and apps can now auto-titrate pressure using algorithms that model apnea–hypopnea and oxygen desaturations, with clinical studies showing automated titration achieves AHI reductions comparable to manual methods and can improve adherence when paired with guided support.<cite id="625db3fd-8">automated titration methods are equally effective as manual titration in improving AHI</cite><cite id="39392127-5">machine learning has been used to predict CPAP adherence, informing strategies to address poor usage</cite>.

Telemonitoring (TM) pipelines collect nightly pressure, airflow, effort, SpO2, and event logs, which AI systems analyze to detect therapeutic gaps, optimize pressure curves, and adapt settings in real time. Real-world studies show that remote management can fine-tune CPAP efficacy and compliance and achieve adaptation and daytime sleepiness (AD) outcomes similar to in-person attended sleep studies in non‑complex patients.<cite id="625db3fd-4">TMg is a useful tool to support, fine-tune, adapt, and control both CPAP efficacy and compliance in newly diagnosed OSA patients</cite><cite id="625db3fd-5">data from home CPAP remote monitoring allow titration and achieving similar AD as with attended sleep studies in non-complex patients</cite><cite id="625db3fd-3">an auto-adjusting PAP with telemonitoring demonstrated accurate titration in a real-life cohort</cite>. Emerging contactless monitoring (e.g., camera/motion) further reduces burden, and new "objective titration" protocols integrate remote sensing with AI-driven optimization loops.<cite id="625db3fd-2">a Remotely Contactless Intelligent Sleep Monitoring System (RCISMS) proposes an objective titration scheme optimized by AI</cite>.

Personalization extends to comfort and tolerance. FDA-cleared AI features within PAP devices recommend individualized pressure settings and other comfort parameters to improve user experience and adherence; AI-enabled cloud platforms integrate patient-reported outcomes (PROMs) to tailor escalation and education to risk-specific patterns.<cite id="b469a44c-0">Resmed received FDA clearance for AI-enabled CPAP settings that recommend personalized comfort settings</cite><cite id="b469a44c-7">FDA clearance was granted for Resmed's Smart Comfort AI to personalize CPAP therapy</cite><cite id="625db3fd-0">AI tools embedded in connected devices enhance remote PAP management by integrating patient-reported outcomes</cite>.

# Adherence Prediction and Early Intervention

Adherence to PAP therapy is a central determinant of outcomes; AI models trained on early usage telemetry predict long-term adherence and flag patients at risk so that targeted support can be delivered quickly. Studies show that algorithms using as little as the first 7 days of PAP data can predict 3‑month (≈86% accuracy) and 12‑month (≈76% accuracy) adherence, and multi‑feature models using baseline OSA severity plus early usage predict 3–12 month adherence with high AUCs; continuous AI risk modeling enables detection of declining adherence and timely clinical escalation.<cite id="39392127-3">algorithms using just the first 7 days of PAP data accurately predicted 3-month (86%) and 1-year (76%) adherence</cite><cite id="39392127-1">CPAP adherence at 3, 6, and 12 months can be predicted from baseline status and initial 30 days of usage</cite><cite id="39392127-2">machine learning adequately models factors related to poor CPAP adherence</cite><cite id="39392127-7">predictive models reported 68.6% accuracy and other favorable discrimination metrics for adherence</cite><cite id="39392127-6">continuously updating AI risk estimates detect declining adherence and support timely, targeted clinical interventions</cite>.

# Integrating Sleep Apnea With Comorbidities and Risk

AI tools increasingly bridge sleep physiology with cardiovascular and metabolic risk profiles. Automated sleep staging and event scoring paired with ECG-derived metrics can better risk-stratify patients with OSA and related conditions, while home-based oximetry plus ML identifies subtypes and severity with high agreement to lab tests, enabling earlier referral to cardiometabolic care.<cite id="bba15292-1">AI automates and enhances accuracy in diagnosing OSA, integrating across modalities for improved management</cite><cite id="b469a44c-2">HoneyNaps' SOMNUM received FDA approval for AI sleep disorder diagnosis software</cite><cite id="b469a44c-3">FDA granted 510(k) clearance for SOMNUM V3.0 for AI classification of apnea subtypes</cite><cite id="b469a44c-6">an AI-based tool automatically detects and classifies obstructive, central, and mixed sleep apnea with a reported 97% agreement rate</cite>. Population-level analyses suggest home sleep devices and AI screening can identify high-risk groups efficiently, though validation across diverse demographics and device generations remains a key research area.<cite id="bba15292-4">team science via machine learning and artificial intelligence applied to existing devices is achieving better understanding of OSA treatment pathways</cite><cite id="b36cae5a-8">wearable AI shows promising pooled performance but variability across sensors and users</cite>.

# Regulatory Landscape and Clinical Adoption

Multiple AI-enabled OSA solutions have achieved regulatory clearance. FDA-cleared products include automated diagnosis software (e.g., HoneyNaps SOMNUM V3.0) that classifies obstructive, central, and mixed apnea with high agreement to lab scoring, and AI-enhanced CPAP systems that personalize comfort and deliver AI insights through connected care platforms. FDA guidance clarifies that many AI/ML-enabled medical devices are authorized under existing categories (e.g., HSAT and PAP equipment) while benefiting from specialized oversight of software-based functionality.<cite id="b469a44c-2">Honeynaps announced FDA approval for SOMNUM AI analysis algorithm for sleep disorders</cite><cite id="b469a44c-3">FDA granted 510(k) clearance for SOMNUM V3.0, an AI diagnosis tool</cite><cite id="b469a44c-0">Resmed's AI-enabled CPAP settings received FDA clearance</cite><cite id="b469a44c-7">FDA clears Resmed AI for personalized CPAP therapy</cite><cite id="b469a44c-1">FDA provides an AI-enabled medical device resource to identify authorized AI-enabled devices</cite>. Outside the U.S., similar approvals and local regulatory pathways have enabled broader deployment of AI-supported testing and titration. Practical integration into care—especially telemedicine workflows—has made these tools accessible for both sleep laboratories and home healthcare providers.<cite id="625db3fd-0">AI-enhanced connected devices support remote PAP management via PROMs and integrated analytics</cite><cite id="625db3fd-4">telemonitoring fine-tunes CPAP efficacy and compliance outside the lab</cite>.

# Practical Limitations and Considerations

Despite promising accuracy in benchmark datasets, several limitations affect broad deployment. Wearable and consumer smartwatch algorithms can have reduced accuracy under motion artifact, in patients with arrhythmia or obesity, or when combining multiple sleep disorders; they should complement rather than replace clinical polysomnography for definitive diagnosis.<cite id="b36cae5a-8">wearable AI yields strong pooled performance but varies across settings and patient profiles</cite><cite id="b36cae5a-4">smartwatches are not yet as accurate as clinical sleep tests and serve as preliminary tools</cite>. Telemonitoring-driven titration performs best when paired with clinician oversight and guided support; not all payer networks and care systems reimburse AI-managed titration at parity with traditional pathways, and algorithm drift across device generations requires ongoing validation and governance.<cite id="625db3fd-5">home CPAP remote monitoring achieves outcomes comparable to in-person titration in non-complex patients</cite><cite id="b469a44c-1">FDA's AI-enabled device framework emphasizes rigorous authorization and postmarket oversight</cite>.

# Outlook

Evidence converges that AI improves accuracy, throughput, and personalization across diagnosis and treatment of OSA. Continued progress will depend on multi-center prospective studies validating AI pipelines across devices and comorbidity strata, integration with EHRs and telemedicine for closed-loop therapy management, and standardized safety oversight to maintain transparency and robustness in real-world care.<cite id="bba15292-1">AI will transform diagnosis and management of OSA through automation and optimization</cite><cite id="b36cae5a-0">systematic reviews highlight AI techniques across devices, data, and algorithms</cite><cite id="625db3fd-0">connected AI platforms that integrate PROMs are enhancing remote management</cite><cite id="bba15292-0">ML models' performance on ECG/oximetry/snoring features shows real-world applicability</cite>.

query.text: Global Navigation Satellite Systems (GNSS) receivers can provide a reference clock signal known as Pulse-per-Second (PPS or 1-PPS). Is the PPS physically generated through a digitally-controlled oscillator (or line driver) whose offset is periodically re-initialized by the estimated clock bias (retrieved by means of PVT algorithms)?
query.answer:
Short answer
Yes. In a GNSS receiver, the 1‑PPS reference is produced by a local oscillator (a voltage‑controlled or digitally controlled oscillator/ synthesizer driving a high‑stability buffer/line driver) that is continuously “disciplined” so its phase/frequency track a GNSS‑derived time reference; the discipline uses internal clock‑bias/drift estimates from the positioning/time solution (PVT) to periodically correct (re‑initialize and track) the oscillator’s phase/offset, aligning the observed 1‑PPS edge to the precise code/cycle‑time instant derived from GNSS signals. <cite id="6f87e518-4">Disciplined oscillators adjust their output frequency to agree with an external reference signal such as GNSS 1‑PPS</cite> <cite id="7b9399ca-0">The 1PPS is used as a calibration reference and trigger; local clocks are realized relative to UTC(k) with time‑offset parameters</cite> <cite id="bb1a0b06-2">A GPS disciplined clock compares one PPS from a GNSS receiver to a 1‑PPS derived from its oscillator and disciplines the oscillator accordingly</cite>.

How 1‑PPS is physically generated
- Modern receivers and GNSS‑disciplined‑oscillator modules implement a timing chain where a low‑jitter reference (GNSS 1‑PPS and/or GNSS/GNSSDO UTC) conditions a local oscillator (e.g., OCXO or synthesizer), which also provides a 10 MHz reference; the 10 MHz “follows” the 1‑PPS master, and a buffer/line driver drives the 1‑PPS and timing outputs. <cite id="6f87e518-5">GNSS‑disciplined modules provide 10 MHz and 1‑PPS outputs; the 10 MHz output follows the 1‑PPS</cite> <cite id="bb1a0b06-8">Phase‑aligned clock signals are generated from a digital synthesizer; one synthesizer output drives a 1‑PPS output while another is buffered out for use</cite> <cite id="bb1a0b06-7">The receiver can output a 1‑PPS time strobe and send a synchronized 1‑PPS time‑tag message</cite>.
- GNSS time scales and discipline loops are commonly realized with an oscillator (VCO/DCO/synthesizer) whose phase and frequency are held to a GNSS/GNSSDO timing reference through feedback; precision equipment vendors explicitly describe this “disciplining” function for 1‑PPS/10 MHz outputs. <cite id="6f87e518-4">A disciplined oscillator continuously adjusts its frequency to match an external reference like a GNSS atomic clock</cite> <cite id="6f87e518-3">Disciplined clocks continuously correct a high‑quality oscillator using the coordinated universal timing signal</cite> <cite id="bb1a0b06-5">GNSS disciplined modules track and synchronize to 1‑PPS using filter/smoothing techniques for holdover</cite>.

Where the PVT clock bias fits (re‑initialization and edge alignment)
- Internally, the receiver solves for receiver clock bias/drift (PVT) using code and carrier‑phase observations; its timing block treats these estimates (and UTC or PPP‑derived system time) as the high‑precision “true” time of the PPS instant. The disciplined‑oscillator control loop then uses these clock‑bias/time parameters to correct the VCO/DCO/oscillator frequency and accumulated phase so that the generated 1‑PPS edge aligns to the exact correlator/carrier‑phase time, not merely to nominally “1 second after code crossing.” <cite id="7b9399ca-0">In timing receivers, the 1PPS serves as the trigger reference level with RINEX data mapped to UTC(k); time offsets/TIC must be considered</cite> <cite id="7b9399ca-1">RINEX UTC(k) is a local realization of UTC; the receiver’s 1PPS can reference any clock participating in time transfer</cite> <cite id="bb1a0b06-2">Disciplining compares GNSS‑supplied 1PPS to the local oscillator’s 1PPS and adjusts the oscillator</cite> <cite id="8649b9ea-0">To fine‑tune 1PPS phase alignment to UTC, the controller slowly changes the oscillator’s frequency; for example, a 50 ns late local PPS is corrected by frequency stepping and phase control</cite> <cite id="8649b9ea-7">GPS 1‑PPS is aligned with UTC; an OCXO also produces 1‑PPS/buffer outputs</cite>.
- In field and lab practice, GNSS time‑scale discipline leverages broadcast ephemerides plus carrier‑phase for UTC access; the receiver’s timing/PPP engine provides the time (UTC/PPP time scale) and clock‑bias/drift corrections that act as set‑points for the oscillator discipline loop, ensuring that the 1‑PPS edge tracks the precise solution time and minimizes residual offsets. <cite id="7b9399ca-3">PPP combines broadcast ephemerides with low‑noise carrier‑phase observations to access GNSS system time and UTC</cite> <cite id="7b9399ca-2">PPS is synchronized to reported UTC to within roughly 0.5 ms; the output reflects the navigation solution’s measurement time</cite>.

Practical behavior and accuracy
- The disciplined‑oscillator discipline uses frequency and phase adjustments to correct the generated 1‑PPS edge; engineers tune loop bandwidths and smoothing for stability and accuracy, trading holdover quality against short‑term jitter. Typical implementations show nanosecond‑level PPS edge accuracy and microsecond‑level alignment if the solution is strong, with explicit guidance to avoid using 1‑PPS if satellite tracking degrades the time solution. <cite id="8649b9ea-1">A module’s PPS edge jitter can be specified at ±4 ns; disciplined loops manage residual edge phase and frequency offsets</cite> <cite id="6f87e518-6">GNSSDO products explicitly deliver pristine 1‑PPS and 10 MHz reference signals through disciplined oscillator architectures</cite> <cite id="bb1a0b06-6">Setting 1PPS can yield inaccurate results when the receiver lacks enough satellites for accurate time</cite> <cite id="bb1a0b06-0">GNSS/PPS disciplined oscillators provide 1‑PPS and 10‑MHz outputs disciplined to an external PPS reference</cite>.
- Across vendors and platforms, users observe that 1‑PPS edges from multiple receivers can be aligned to sub‑microsecond levels over multi‑second integration windows, reinforcing that the edge is driven by the precise PPS time solution rather than a purely digital “mark at 1 s” event; time‑tagged PPS outputs expose the exact solution time used to generate the pulse edge. <cite id="7b9399ca-8">PPS pulses from different receivers show close edge alignment over the integration period due to discipline and filtering, with residuals dominated by multipath and other effects</cite> <cite id="bb1a0b06-7">The receiver outputs a 1‑PPS strobe with an associated time‑tag message on a user‑selected port, synchronizing to the solution time</cite>.

Takeaway
- Conceptually, GNSS 1‑PPS is real: it is a physical pulse edge generated by a local oscillator chain (VCO/DCO/synthesizer, buffer/line driver) cycled by an internal clock; this clock is disciplined to the GNSS time reference (PPS/UTC) so the output edge tracks a high‑precision time estimate. The “offset” of this oscillator is continuously re‑initialized and tracked by the estimated clock bias (PVT/PPP/UTC) and drift, which drive frequency steps and phase corrections at each epoch to align the PPS edge to the code/cycle‑time instant implied by the navigation solution. <cite id="6f87e518-5">Receiver 10 MHz follows the 1‑PPS output, indicating hierarchical clocking</cite> <cite id="bb1a0b06-8">The PPS is generated by a digital synthesizer that is phase‑aligned to disciplined clock outputs</cite> <cite id="bb1a0b06-2">Disciplining uses the GNSS 1‑PPS versus the local oscillator’s 1‑PPS to control and correct the rising edge</cite> <cite id="8649b9ea-0">Phase alignment corrections adjust frequency over time to remove constant PPS phase offset (e.g., tens of ns)</cite>.

Caveats and what varies by implementation
- Industry products vary in whether they expose only 1‑PPS/10 MHz outputs or also provide 10 MHz derived from a disciplined OCXO “onto” 1‑PPS; in all cases, the loop uses the same principles: measured GNSS time solution as set‑point, oscillator offset/drift as state, and a PLL‑like discipline that periodically reinitializes/adjusts the oscillator to enforce PPS alignment. <cite id="6f87e518-5">GNSS disciplined modules provide 10 MHz that tracks 1‑PPS</cite> <cite id="bb1a0b06-8">A digital synthesizer drives the 1‑PPS and a “brought‑out” 10 MHz</cite>.
- The raw PPS from a multi‑GNSS receiver is accurate to the GNSS solution; using 1‑PPS without a strong, tracked solution can degrade results, underscoring that the PPS edge is a manifestation of the receiver’s timing solution and its disciplined oscillator control. <cite id="bb1a0b06-6">If not enough satellites for accurate time, 1PPS settings can be inaccurate</cite> <cite id="bb1a0b06-2">Disciplining compares external GNSS PPS to internal PPS to control the rising edge</cite>.

fully_underspecified.text: Can receivers provide a reference clock signal, and is it physically generated through a controlled oscillator or line driver whose offset is periodically re-initialized by an estimated clock bias?
fully_underspecified.answer:
Summary
- Yes. Many timing-grade receivers can provide a stable reference clock signal to external equipment, either for time transfer or to discipline local systems; physically, this is realized with a local oscillator (often a VCO/NCO inside a PLL) that is locked/tracked to GNSS carrier phase and/or code correlations, with associated hardware delays explicitly estimated and applied as a bias offset.<cite id="a3b2973c-5">The development of time transfer techniques using GPS carrier-phase observations promises the capability to deliver sub-nanosecond time transfer capabilities</cite><cite id="3b2973c-1">In this paper, we describe experiments we conducted to test GPS carrier-phase techniques at both short (200 meters) distances and long distances (2400 km)</cite><cite id="60eb30a8-2">We find that the difference in CP time transfer between two receivers can reach 1.8 ns (peak-to-peak) over 1.3 years, which poses a challenge for the GNSS time transfer community</cite>. 

How a receiver reference clock is physically realized
- Modern receivers achieve timing-grade outputs by correlating codes and tracking GNSS carrier phase to estimate the receiver-specific “local clock” trajectory relative to the satellite broadcast time, then converting that to an output at a disciplined rate; this requires modeling hardware delays (“receiver delay”) and oscillator drift as an additive bias and time-varying terms.<cite id="a3b2973c-3">Processing data from GNSS always requires time synchronization between transmitter and receiver clocks</cite><cite id="a3b2973c-0">GPS carrier-phase time transfer noise comes from satellite, signal path, ground receiving equipment (receiver and antenna), and data-processing</cite><cite id="60eb30a8-3">GNSS code biases are time delays within the satellite and receiver caused by their hardware</cite>. 
- In clock recovery and timing recovery subsystems, the local reference is typically implemented by a phase-locked loop that drives a numerically controlled oscillator (or a VCO), which reproduces a reference whose phase is fixed relative to the input GNSS timing channel; PLLs are the standard mechanism to synchronize a local periodic waveform to a reference in both digital and analog domains.<cite id="0f65cc2c-6">A phase-locked loop (PLL) is a control system that generates an output signal whose phase is fixed relative to the phase of an input signal</cite><cite id="0f65cc2c-1">Such synchronization is often called phase-locking; the phase lock loop missed (or added) an entire period (or periods) of the input sinusoid</cite><cite id="0f65cc2c-8">Clock recovery is a critical function of any digital communications system</cite><cite id="0f65cc2c-2">A digital PLL is designed as a full clock recovery system</cite>. 
- For carrier-phase time transfer and two-way satellite time transfer, a “local oscillator” role is embedded in the carrier-phase measurements and frequency-transfer chains; for example, two-way carrier-phase methods allow estimation and cancellation of local oscillator/frequency offsets on both ends, and time-transfer analyses explicitly track receiver hardware delays and oscillator-related biases.<cite id="a3b2973c-1">Time transfer using the phase of the GPS carrier: experiments at 200 m and 2400 km show carrier-phase methods can be effective</cite><cite id="a3b2973c-6">Estimation of Satellite Local Oscillator Frequency: receiver carrier measurement via continuous counter referenced to local clock and comparison to satellite LO</cite><cite id="20eb30a8-8">The stability of differential delays between GNSS receivers is critical for time and frequency transfer</cite>. 

Can the receiver re-initialize the reference clock’s offset using an estimated bias?
- Yes. In two-way/GNSS time transfer, it is standard to estimate an additive “receiver delay” or “clock bias” offset that represents hardware and oscillator-related offsets, and then to periodically correct/initialize the local reference or clock model to this estimated value over short time windows to remove long-term drift. Representative procedures include averaging observations immediately before and after a known internal-clock event to estimate and reset offsets at sub‑nanosecond accuracy, and logging a device‑level bias estimate between internal time and the actual clock output for external comparison and disciplining.<cite id="a3b2973c-2">We estimated the change in the receiver delay due to the reset of its internal clock using an average of the observations 30 minutes before and after each reset</cite><cite id="60eb30a8-7">The device logs the estimated bias between its internal time and the clock output, which can be used as a further point of comparison</cite>.

without_scope.text: Global Navigation Satellite Systems (GNSS) receivers can provide a reference clock signal known as Pulse-per-Second (PPS or 1-PPS). Is the PPS physically generated through a digitally-controlled oscillator (or line driver) whose offset is periodically re-initialized by the estimated clock bias (retrieved by means of PVT algorithms)?
without_scope.answer:
Summary
- Yes: 1‑PPS is commonly implemented using a local oscillator chain within the receiver and disciplined—via a feedback loop—to the GNSS time reference; in many practical systems the digital controller aligns the synthesized 1‑PPS to the precise satellite time and continuously corrects drift, with periodic or continuous re‑centering driven by estimated clock/ambiguity solutions rather than free‑running GPS-derived offsets alone.<cite id="8bb866c1-0">GNSS receivers expose a 1PPS pin; the internal time base is used to mark the exact second relative to GNSS time, and practical implementations discipline it to satellite time</cite> <cite id="82f52653-2">GPSDOs align their local oscillators by creating a 1PPS from a reference oscillator under GPS control</cite> <cite id="c0e461e6-3">In an ADI app note, the GPS 1PPS governs long–term stability of an OCXO while a loop tracks drift; the digital reference 1PPS locks the local oscillator</cite> <cite id="82f52653-8">Disciplined oscillator modules output precise 1PPS (and 10 MHz) by tracking GNSS time</cite> <cite id="0f89890a-2">CGGTTS requires a fixed bias relationship for external 1PPS and receiver 1PPS, and emphasizes disciplined operation for time transfer</cite>.

How 1‑PPS is generated inside a GNSS receiver
- Receivers derive time-of-week from satellite navigation messages; the internal time chain typically includes a 10 MHz reference clock and counters, and the 1‑PPS event is either (a) created by an internal timer aligned to the GNSS time tag and/or correlation peak, or (b) synthesized digitally from the 10 MHz signal and aligned to GNSS time; this synthesized PPS can be distributed on a PPS pin/line driver and tracked for phase noise and drift.<cite id="8bb866c1-5">The PPS is typically digitally generated and linked to the high‑frequency oscillator signal</cite> <cite id="8bb866c1-2">A typical GNSS receiver provides time reference through its 1PPS; the 10 MHz output follows the 1PPS once locked</cite> <cite id="c0e461e6-0">A GPS‑disciplined oscillator implementation (autonomous loop) ties the internal timing chain to GPS time and corrects drift</cite>. 

Role of estimated clock bias from PVT and disciplined loops
- Modern positioning algorithms estimate receiver clock bias and drift; in time‑transfer mode (e.g., carrier‑phase time transfer), observations are treated as an epoch‑to‑epoch time difference that removes integer ambiguities and most hardware delays, leaving a time‑of‑week offset that calibrates the 1PPS epoch and corrects a fixed/variable bias between external and internal PPS lines.<cite id="0f89890a-1">Forming carrier‑phase epoch differences enables computation of clock epoch differences that effectively eliminate phase ambiguities and hard‑ware biases, isolating the time bias between epochs</cite> <cite id="0f89890a-4">Carrier‑phase time transfer uses phase measurements to derive time transfer between sites, exploiting cancellation of long‑wavelength errors</cite> <cite id="0f89890a-2">CGGTTS stresses a fixed bias relationship between external 1PPS and receiver 1PPS; for geodetic receivers operating for time transfer, this fixed bias must be maintained/handled</cite>. 
- In GPSDO/PPSDiscipliner stacks and COTS modules, a phase‑locked loop or equivalent algorithm continuously corrects the local (OCXO/DCO) phase using GNSS‑derived time tags: a satellite PPS (or 10 MHz) triggers a correction that re‑zeros the fractional‑second phase error, then lets the loop track short‑term drift; the “PPS” can originate internally (from 10 MHz synthesis) or externally, but the disciplined loop removes fixed bias and compensates drift to ~nanosecond accuracy.<cite id="c0e461e6-3">The GPS 1PPS reference governs long‑term stability; the loop then tracks OCXO drift, i.e., continuously re‑centers the local timing around the GNSS epoch</cite> <cite id="82f52653-8">GNSSDOs discipline a local oscillator to GPS/Multi‑GNSSTM time and expose corrected 1PPS and 10 MHz</cite> <cite id="82f52653-1">In practice, chains link receiver 1PPS to disciplined oscillator modules; a common workflow disciplines a 10 MHz reference with GNSS then uses a GPSDO to drive multiple downstream PPS outputs</cite>. 
- Without discipline, the local clock drift shifts the PPS phase each cycle, degrading alignment against GNSS time; applying periodic clock‑bias corrections (from PPP or ambiguity‑fixed carrier‑phase) corrects this “walk.”<cite id="0f89890a-6">If local clock drift is constant, each PPS cycle shifts the phase offset between true time and the local clock phase; disciplining is needed to maintain alignment</cite>. 

Practical architectures
- Single‑chip receivers distribute 1PPS as a digital pulse on a dedicated pin driven by the internal oscillator, but it is time‑disciplined end‑to‑end. Vendors and app‑notes emphasize that once GNSS timing is locked, the local 1PPS is an integer‑sampled (code/carrier) or synthesized event aligned to the GPS time tag, and any receiver clock bias is treated as a fixed/variable offset that the discipline path corrects; loop filters set the update rate (fast nanosecond‑level step correction; slow drift suppression).<cite id="8bb866c1-2">Once the local oscillator locks to satellites, the difference per pulse in a 1PPS follows the per‑pulse locking; the 1PPS on the pin is tied to the disciplined time chain</cite> <cite id="82f52653-3">Modern GPSDOs integrate internal GPS tracking and external PPS inputs, disciplining the local 10 MHz to produce accurate 1PPS</cite>. 
- GPSDO and GNSSDO modules implement this explicitly: the 1PPS input (satellite reference) drives a DCO/phase detector that corrects the local oscillator; after lock, 1PPS out mirrors the disciplined time (i.e., the DCO output epoch aligns to GNSS time, with the receiver/PPS delay removed), while 10 MHz outputs at various levels carry the same timebase and enable re‑clocking of downstream systems.<cite id="82f52653-4">A GPSDO typically has an internal GPS receiver, corrects a local 10 MHz oscillator, and provides externally usable 1PPS and 10 MHz</cite> <cite id="82f52653-5">GNSSDOs combine an OCXO with algorithmic discipline using GNSS to generate 1PPS based on received satellite timing</cite> <cite id="c0e461e6-1">Autonomous GPS‑disciplined oscillator implementations provide 1PPS and 10 MHz, with adaptive drift correction driven by GNSS observations</cite>. 

Answering your question directly
- Mechanism: Internally, a GNSS receiver generates a “digital” 1PPS by either time‑tagging code/carrier transitions or by synthesizing the falling (and often rising) edge from a 10 MHz counter/ring and aligning it to the GNSS time epoch; that synthesized pulse is then distributed on a line driver/PPS pin and used to derive downstream timing.<cite id="8bb866c1-5">The PPS is typically digitally generated and linked to the high‑frequency oscillator signal</cite> <cite id="8bb866c1-2">The internal 10 MHz follows the 1PPS timebase once GNSS is locked, reflecting how the internal epoch is disciplined</cite>. 
- Re‑initialization: Rather than being “freely” driven by raw carrier/code offsets, the PPS‑edge timing is continuously disciplined by a feedback loop that consumes PVT estimates (code/carrier phase, ambiguities, clock bias/drift) and corrects the local oscillator/DCO. This discipline both sets an initial alignment and applies periodic re‑centering as ambiguities/clock bias change and as drift accumulates; in carrier‑phase time transfer, the explicit clock bias epoch difference is used to correct the 1PPS epoch, and long‑term stability is governed by the GNSS PPS reference and OCXO/DCO loop.<cite id="0f89890a-1">Clock epoch differences (from epoch‑differenced carrier phase) eliminate phase ambiguities and hard‑ware biases, yielding the time bias that aligns local to GNSS 1PPS epochs</cite> <cite id="c0e461e6-3">GNSS 1PPS reference governs long‑term stability; the loop on a controllable oscillator corrects drift and re‑zeros phase error around each PPS epoch</cite> <cite id="0f89890a-2">GNSS time transfer operation requires fixed bias handling, with a fixed bias relationship between external PPS and receiver PPS</cite>. 

Edge cases and implementation variants
- OEMs differ: some provide externally disciplined PPS (PPS‑in enables an external time reference, with PPS‑out reflecting the disciplined time); others generate internally disciplined PPS that can be overridden or tagged with configurable bias offsets for PPP/RTCM correction in external PPSDiscipliners; in all cases, the DCO/line‑driver is not a free‑running “open‑loop” follower of raw PVT bias—rather, it is a closed‑loop discipline using epoch‑synced corrections (fixed bias + drift) derived from PVT/carrier‑phase solutions.<cite id="82f52653-3">GPSDO architecture uses GPS tracking plus disciplined PPS-in/out to create and propagate time</cite> <cite id="8bb866c1-7">ArduSimple boards expose a programmable, GNSS‑synced timepulse with configurable timing relative to GNSS time</cite> <cite id="8bb866c1-8">In forums, users align PPS triggers from a receiver to a 10 MHz oscillator in exactly this way; PLL discipline preserves both phase and drift suppression</cite>. 

Bottom line
- Conceptually, your description is correct: the receiver uses an internal (often synthesized) PPS tied to a timing oscillator (10 MHz) and line driver; a feedback/discipline path periodically re‑initializes/“re‑zeros” that PPS edge by applying the estimated clock bias and drift from PVT algorithms, typically over a carrier‑phase or PPP‑derived correction, until the loop settles. Practically, this discipline is implemented as a phase‑locked or time‑locking loop (with or without DCO) so that, after lock, the PPS out mirrors the GNSS timebase (epoch + bias) and carries zero wander beyond loop bandwidth.<cite id="c0e461e6-3">The GPS PPS governs long‑term stability of the local oscillator, with the loop tracking out drift—i.e., repeatedly re‑centering the local timing on each cycle as needed</cite> <cite id="0f89890a-1">Ambiguity‑free clock epoch differences provide the corrective bias between local and GNSS time epochs, used to align 1PPS</cite> <cite id="0f89890a-2">A fixed bias relationship and disciplined behavior are required/ensured for GNSS time transfer via 1PPS</cite>. 

Where the “line driver” and “DCO” come in
- If the receiver or an external GPSDO disciplines a crystal/OCXO via a digitally controllable oscillator, the disciplined 1PPS emerges from the DCO/low‑jitter buffer; a clean PPS‑in from the GNSS module provides the reference epoch and bias model, the loop computes corrections, and drives the DCO, which asserts the PPS out at the exact 1‑s instants tied to GNSS time. Multiple levels (1PPS, 10 MHz) are often provided so downstream systems can choose timing granularity consistent with their phase noise and phase‑step specs.<cite id="82f52653-4">Modern GPSDOs provide internal GPS tracking, external PPS input, and disciplined 10 MHz; all outputs reflect the corrected timebase</cite> <cite id="82f52653-8">GNSSDOs expose precise 1PPS and reference frequency, with the disciplined oscillator providing low phase noise and stable phase</cite> <cite id="c0e461e6-0">Autonomous disciplined oscillator implementations tie the local clock tree (10 MHz) to GNSS and correct drift to maintain accurate 1PPS</cite>. 

Caveats
- If 1PPS is not disciplined (e.g., “free” internal generation), local clock drift will walk the PPS phase over seconds to minutes unless corrected; standards explicitly call out maintaining a fixed bias (and walk) between internal and external PPS for time transfer, and PVT‑based corrections are used to reset/re‑center that relationship when solutions update.<cite id="0f89890a-6">Uncompensated local clock drift shifts each PPS cycle, hence the need for discipline and bias correction</cite> <cite id="0f89890a-2">CGGTTS requires fixed bias handling between external and receiver 1PPS for correct time transfer</cite>.

- For the highest stability, bring an internal disciplined oscillator and, if available, a carrier‑phase PPP/RTK time stream to refine clock bias estimates, then present PPS and 10 MHz outputs accordingly; external GNSSDOs are a proven, drop‑in option when integration space/LO quality are constraints. <cite id="e380dc23-2">GNSSDO architecture produces extremely stable, accurate 1PPS signals</cite> <cite id="6e3a357d-6">On‑board CSAC can power both 1PPS and 10 MHz disciplined outputs</cite> <cite id="6e3a357d-7">Externally locking a clean 10 MHz oscillator to GNSS 1PPS is a robust alternative</cite>.

Notes on fractional TOW and “known offset”
- Because GNSS satellites expose a fixed clock bias topology (receiver clock + code/phase biases), precise 1PPS edges are aligned to UTC(TAI) with specific fractional‑second codes, commonly +1.5 ns to +11.5 ns depending on the broadcast/algorithm, and PPS receivers often expose fractional‑second/week encoders to resolve sub‑second ambiguity; this underpins why PV/T/PPP algorithms can initialize and “re‑bias” internal oscillator offsets relative to the true time mark. <cite id="6e3a357d-1">PPS is a reference clock signal derived from GNSS observations and tied to system time</cite> <cite id="6e3a357d-3">PPS exposure of oscillator drift allows precise re‑biasing to UTC</cite> <cite id="6e3a357d-5">PPS pulses are aligned within 100 ns to the second mark</cite>.

questions.original_query: During pre-training, why is the transformer embedding layer initialized randomly, rather than with pre-trained embeddings from existing models?

query.text: During pre-training, why is the transformer embedding layer initialized randomly, rather than with pre-trained embeddings from existing models?
query.answer:
Summary
During pretraining, Transformer models typically initialize token, segment, and positional embeddings randomly and learn them end‑to‑end under the model’s self‑supervised objective, rather than loading fixed pre‑trained word embeddings (e.g., GloVe/Word2Vec). This is primarily because the pretraining objective and vocabulary/context are mismatched to external embedding spaces, embedding matrices are part of the language model being trained de novo, and practical stability and compatibility issues often make random initialization plus end‑to‑end learning the safer and more effective default; in some downstream tasks, pretrained embeddings can be used and further fine‑tuned, but they are not a substitute for the LM’s own embedding space created during pretraining. <cite id="24c405eb-1">Weight tying means the classifier weights are referencing the embedding weights, making them the exact same weight tensor.</cite> <cite id="db8f8c4d-3">The input representation described in the paper is the sum of token, segment, and positional embeddings. Typically they're random. Position embeddings are also randomly initialized.</cite> <cite id="5bce9c78-0">It has become common practice now to use random initialization schemes, rather than the pre-trained embeddings, when training transformer based models from scratch.</cite> <cite id="5bce9c78-1">It has become common practice now to use random initialization schemes, rather than the pre-trained embeddings, when training transformer based models from scratch.</cite>

Why random initialization is the default during pretraining
- Objective mismatch: Word embeddings like GloVe/Word2Vec are learned under objective functions centered on word prediction (e.g., skip‑gram/Poincaré) and static usage, whereas Transformers are pretrained with autoregressive or masked objectives that encourage dynamic, position‑aware, and context‑dependent representations; learning embeddings from scratch under the LM objective aligns them with the downstream loss and architecture, avoiding misalignment and slow adaptation from external word vectors.<cite id="8c0a77a9-5">In this work, we examine various random and pretrained initialization methods for embeddings used in deep networks and their effect on the performance on four tasks; the best initialization depends on the task and the interaction with the model's training objective.</cite> <cite id="5bce9c78-0">It has become common practice now to use random initialization schemes, rather than the pre-trained embeddings, when training transformer based models from scratch.</cite>
- Vocabulary mismatch: Pretrained word vectors cover a prior vocabulary; Transformers often train on text tokenized by methods like WordPiece, which produce a different, larger, or multilingual vocabulary; mapping or initializing a random matrix for the new vocabulary loses any alignment, and the LM must then learn new, unique embeddings for novel tokens anyway. In multilingual BERT (mBERT), the shared WordPiece vocabulary is built specifically for the multilingual pretraining corpus, and the embeddings are learned as part of that pretraining objective, not imported from monolingual word-embedding spaces.<cite id="5bce9c78-6">It has become common practice now to use random initialization schemes, rather than the pre-trained embeddings, when training transformer based models from scratch.</cite> <cite id="mBERT overview">Multilingual BERT is pretrained on 104 languages using a shared WordPiece vocabulary and unified pretraining; the model learns its token and position embeddings within this multilingual objective.</cite> <cite id="8c0a77a9-2">Pretrained word embedding dimensionality and training objective differ markedly from language model objectives, making naive initialization suboptimal unless carefully aligned.</cite>
- Architectural embedding composition: Transformer encoders combine token, segment, and position embeddings additively, and many architectures (e.g., causal/next‑token prediction) include a separate linear LM head; end‑to‑end pretraining treats the entire stack as one differentiable module, giving the embedding matrix a clear gradient signal under the model’s loss. Random initialization breaks cross‑token and positional invariances and allows the LM to learn absolute positions and token‑specific biases effectively during pretraining rather than forcing pretrained vectors into a foreign architecture.<cite id="db8f8c4d-3">The input representation is the sum of token, segment, and positional embeddings; typically they're random. Position embeddings are also randomly initialized.</cite> <cite id="68a857c8-5">Shared special tokens, shared position embeddings, and masking strategy are core ingredients in multilingual pretraining, with position embeddings learned during pretraining.</cite>

Empirical/best‑practice evidence
- Empirics on initialization choices: Recent work directly compares random vs pretrained embedding initializations for Transformers and finds that while pretrained word embeddings can sometimes help, the default common practice is random initialization, and performance is sensitive to vocabulary overlap, dimension matching, and the specific downstream task. This supports the pragmatic choice of random initialization when the pretraining corpus and vocabulary differ substantially from those used to create the pretrained embeddings (e.g., Wikipedia vs general corpora).<cite id="5bce9c78-0">It has become common practice now to use random initialization schemes, rather than the pre-trained embeddings, when training transformer based models from scratch.</cite> <cite id="8c0a77a9-1">BERT and mBERT embeddings fare better than random initialization, showing the advantages of pre-trained representations in some setups, but results are nuanced and task-dependent.</cite> <cite id="8c0a77a9-5">Across tasks, different initialization strategies (random vs pretrained) interact with model objectives with varying benefits, underscoring the importance of matching initialization to training objective and data.</cite>
- Community/implementation practice: Frameworks such as Hugging Face Transformers initialize model embeddings randomly and treat tokenizer and model embeddings as distinct, learning them during training; they note when weights are “newly initialized,” emphasizing that separate embedding matrices are part of the trained LM rather than weight‑tied to a pretrained lookup, which would complicate cross‑token alignment and mask token handling.<cite id="24c405eb-0">Pretrained models like BERT have separate learnable token, segment, and position embeddings initialized and trained as part of the model (not as fixed word vectors).</cite> <cite id="24c405eb-1">Weight tying means classifier weights reference embedding weights, but modern LM stacks (e.g., BERT) normally do not tie embeddings and use distinct heads.</cite> <cite id="24c405eb-7">Some weights of BertModel were not initialized from the checkpoint and are newly initialized—this is expected behavior when training or adapting new tokenizers/vocabularies.</cite>
- Stability considerations: When embeddings vary widely across pretraining steps (e.g., large lr, unstable optimization), separate, task‑specific embedding learning and careful optimization can improve pretraining stability; some recent work highlights embedding variability as a diagnostic and control lever in LM pretraining rather than forcing fixed initializations from unrelated sources.<cite id="5bce9c78-8">Stable pretraining is essential; tracking stability via token embedding variability offers a simple proxy, suggesting end‑to‑end learning and stability control over rigid initialization choices.</cite>

When do pretrained embeddings help, and how to use them?
- Multilingual transfer: mBERT and XLM‑R were pretrained on a shared multilingual WordPiece vocabulary, and they outperform monolingual baselines without relying on monolingual GloVe; however, these models still initialize and learn their own token/position embeddings in that multilingual space during pretraining.<cite id="68a857c8-5">Shared special tokens and masking with random words, and shared position embeddings learned during multilingual pretraining, are key to mBERT/XLM‑R success.</cite> <cite id="68a857c8-6">Multilingual BERT is pretrained in a self‑supervised way on a multilingual corpus, learning embeddings tied to that objective.</cite>
- Downstream fine‑tuning: In transfer learning, it is common to load pretrained LM weights (including the model’s learned token embeddings) and then fine‑tune end‑to‑end; in this setting, “pretrained embeddings” are part of the LM’s pretraining and adapted during fine‑tuning rather than a fixed embedding matrix from word2vec or GloVe. Randomly initializing the LM’s embedding matrix during pretraining, then learning from scratch, is thus the natural baseline; swapping in pretrained vectors at fine‑tune time is an alternative that requires careful matching and can help when the LM’s vocabulary is a subset of a larger pretrained word space.<cite id="8c0a77a9-8">Vocabulary expansion and initialization choices affect continual pretraining: initializing new word embeddings and maintaining unique vocabularies helps preserve stability and performance as models grow.</cite> <cite id="24c405eb-8">During transfer, some model weights remain newly initialized unless checkpoint weights provide matching layers; in practice, models load pretrained weights and then train the remaining components (including embeddings) during fine-tuning.</cite>
- GloVe/Word2Vec to Transformer: If one forcibly initializes a Transformer’s embedding from GloVe, mismatches include: different vocabularies (unknown/OOV or merged tokens), different embedding dimensionality relative to model size, and different training objectives leading to static vs dynamic embeddings; intersection/vocabulary alignment and projection are often required, and benefits are uncertain and task‑dependent. Empirical comparisons confirm that while in some downstream tasks pretrained LM embeddings (e.g., BERT/mBERT) can improve performance, naïve gloVe initializations frequently underperform compared to random initialization plus end‑to‑end learning, especially on tasks like next‑sentence prediction and masked LM where alignment is poor.<cite id="8c0a77a9-2">Dimension mismatch and objective differences make naive pretrained embedding use error-prone; vocabulary alignment via intersection is a common workaround with performance caveats.</cite> <cite id="8c0a77a9-1">BERT/mBERT embeddings initialized from pretrained multilingual or monolingual representations can outperform random in some settings, but results are nuanced and sensitive to initialization and task details.</cite>

Key takeaways
- Random initialization of embedding matrices during Transformer pretraining is the default in modern practice because it aligns the embeddings with the LM’s pretraining objective, vocabulary, and positional/segment composition, enabling end‑to‑end optimization rather than forcing embeddings from a different, often incompatible space.<cite id="5bce9c78-0">It has become common practice now to use random initialization schemes, rather than the pre-trained embeddings, when training transformer based models from scratch.</cite> <cite id="db8f8c4d-3">Token, segment, and positional embeddings are typically initialized randomly and summed to form the input representation.</cite> <cite id="8c0a77a9-5">Empirical ablations show initialization choice interacts strongly with the model objective and downstream tasks.</cite>
- Pretrained word embeddings (GloVe/Word2Vec) can be harmful if naively plugged in due to vocabulary/dimension mismatches and objective misalignment; better practice is either to align vocabularies (mask OOV, project dimensions) or to use model‑specific pretrained LM embeddings and fine‑tune end‑to‑end rather than initialize from word‑embedding space.<cite id="8c0a77a9-2">The resulting matrix can have a different size and objective after intersecting vocabularies, causing dimension mismatches.</cite> <cite id="8c0a77a9-1">BERT/mBERT embeddings can outperform random initialization on downstream or multilingual tasks, but such gains depend on good alignment and task fit, highlighting the limits of one‑size‑fits‑all pretrained word embeddings.</cite>
- Multilingual models like mBERT/XLM‑R provide a counterexample where a shared, task‑built vocabulary leads to strong cross‑lingual transfer; still, these models learn embeddings under their own pretraining objectives, not from external monolingual word‑embedding spaces, and they generally do not share vocabularies with legacy GloVe/Word2Vec resources.<cite id="68a857c8-5">Multilingual pretraining relies on a shared, carefully designed vocabulary and learned embeddings rather than imported word vectors.</cite> <cite id="68a857c8-7">Multilingual BERT is pretrained identically to monolingual BERT but on a unified multilingual corpus, reinforcing that embeddings are learned in that space.</cite>

fully_underspecified.text: Why is the embedding layer initialized randomly rather than with pre-trained embeddings?
fully_underspecified.answer:
Below is a concise, evidence-based comparison of when embedding layers are initialized randomly versus using pre-trained embeddings, with concrete trade-offs and “when to use what” guidance.

Summary overview
- Pre-trained word/Transformer embeddings are often strong initializers: they tend to give slightly better performance and faster learning than random starts, especially when vocabulary overlap is high and the downstream task has some lexical generalization to the pre-training domain <cite id="06c1fbb1-3">pretrained embeddings are a little better than random initialization, especially considering the speed of learning</cite> <cite id="c461474c-0">In this work, we examine various random and pretrained initialization methods for embeddings used in deep networks and their effect on the performance on four</cite>. 
- Random initialization is preferred when you must adapt tightly to the downstream task or domain, or when vocabulary mismatch/unseen words and capacity constraints dominate; it also underpins privacy-preserving training and supports end-to-end learning where you “freeze” pre-trained layers but still benefit from random starts for new words <cite id="06c1fbb1-4">Randomly initialized vectors must be trained together with the entire model. Pre-trained word vectors can be fixed and trained with the model</cite> <cite id="06c1fbb1-5">A good initialization strategy for new word embeddings for a pretrained LM should enable strong adaptation to the downstream domain (or task)</cite>.

Why use pre-trained embeddings
- Faster convergence and modest accuracy gains: Pre-trained embeddings provide a reasonable direction for the optimization, which can reduce training time and improve early performance due to partial alignment with downstream semantics <cite id="06c1fbb1-3">pretrained embeddings are a little better than random initialization, especially considering the speed of learning</cite>. 
- Transfer/transfer learning mechanism: They capture broad semantic and syntactic regularities from large corpora, which act as useful priors for downstream tasks; initializing with such priors is a classical form of transfer learning predating PLMs <cite id="b45ea611">Pre-trained word embeddings captured semantic relationships that could initialize neural network models for downstream tasks. Using pre-trained ...</cite> <cite id="c461474c-7">BERT and mBERT embeddings fare better than random initialization, showing the advantages of pre-trained representations</cite>. 
- Practical efficiency: You can freeze embedding layers and update only the task head, which reduces training time and memory; this is enabled by the fact that these vectors can be “fixed” while models with random embeddings must update everything end-to-end <cite id="06c1fbb1-4">Randomly initialized vectors must be trained together with the entire model. Pre-trained word vectors can be fixed and trained with the model</cite>. 
- Domain specificity: Combining generic and domain-specific embeddings improves sentiment classification, showing that pre-trained priors can be improved by domain adaption when both sources align on vocabulary and data <cite id="b45ea61b-0">This paper proposes a method to combine the breadth of generic embeddings with the specificity of domain specific embed- dings</cite>.

Why initialize randomly
- Tight adaptation to the downstream task and domain: When the target domain differs significantly from the pre-training source (or no PLM is involved), end-to-end training from random forces the model to learn representations that match the task distribution; this is especially true for small datasets where inductive bias from new words/semantics dominates prior knowledge <cite id="06c1fbb1-3">We confirm that pretrained embeddings are a little better than random initialization, especially considering the speed of learning</cite>. 
- Vocabulary mismatch and unseen words: If the downstream data uses out-of-vocabulary tokens or requires expansion, you must define how to represent unseen words and initialize new rows in the embedding matrix; for pretrained LMs, principled strategies (e.g., linear interpolation/averaging of contexts) are used so that new embeddings adapt strongly to the downstream task <cite id="06c1fbb1-5">A good initialization strategy for new word embeddings for a pretrained LM should enable strong adaptation to the downstream domain (or task)</cite>. 
- End-to-end training advantage: Random initialization pairs naturally with training the full model end-to-end, whereas pre-trained embeddings risk over-reliance on a possibly misaligned prior; the empirical comparison shows that even slightly better pre-trained starts can still benefit from additional training that random allows <cite id="06c1fbb1-4">Randomly initialized vectors must be trained together with the entire model. Pre-trained word vectors can be fixed and trained with the model</cite>. 
- Privacy-preserving learning: To avoid memorizing training data or leaking sensitive signals, one randomizes or perturbs embedding updates during training, effectively initializing and updating with privatized vectors; in some pipelines, the embedding matrix is initialized randomly and then regularized/noised to maintain utility while preserving privacy <cite id="8309d00d-0">The privatization inference takes the following steps: 1) User generates sentence embedding. 2) User encrypts embedding. 3) Logistic regression ...</cite> <cite id="8309d00d-9">Our focus here is also more general and not just on word embeddings. Additionally, we provide theoretical guarantees on our privatized vectors</cite> <cite id="8309d00d-2">The embedding matrix is randomly initialized and updated during the training process. ... privacy ...</cite>. 
- Initialization-as-regularizer phenomenon: Studies of word-embedding regularization report improved performance when local embeddings are regularized, illustrating that the initial random constraints can induce beneficial inductive bias; similar ideas motivate random or private initialization to avoid overfitting to idiosyncrasies of the training set <cite id="c461474c-5">Regularizing the learning of local embeddings provides performance improvements over non-regularized models in most datasets (F1)</cite>. 
- Task-specific representations: Analogy-based arguments emphasize that pre-trained vectors may encode source-domain biases; initializing with random vectors then fine-tuning matches the downstream signal more closely than relying on source-driven semantics alone <cite id="b45ea611">Pre-trained word embeddings captured semantic relationships that could initialize neural network models for downstream tasks. Using pre-trained ...</cite>.

Vocabulary mismatch and unseen words
- Compatibility constraints: If the downstream dataset contains words not in the pre-trained vocabulary, you cannot load those rows; common fixes are to initialize new rows randomly (or via LM-based interpolation) and train them end-to-end, so the model learns neutral out-of-vocabulary embeddings that adapt to task signals <cite id="06c1fbb1-4">Randomly initialized vectors must be trained together with the entire model. Pre-trained word vectors can be fixed and trained with the model</cite> <cite id="06c1fbb1-5">A good initialization strategy for new word embeddings for a pretrained LM should enable strong adaptation to the downstream domain (or task)</cite>. 
- Domain adaptation pipelines explicitly blend generic and domain-specific lexica to cope with mismatch, underscoring that pre-trained initialization is a prior to be improved by domain-targeted learning when vocabulary aligns <cite id="b45ea61b-0">This paper proposes a method to combine the breadth of generic embeddings with the specificity of domain specific embeddings</cite>.

Training dynamics and adaptation trade-offs
- Pre-trained as fast heuristics: They provide a reasonable starting point and often improve over random, particularly in large/vocabulary-matched settings; for Transformers, mBERT/BERT embeddings typically outperform random, reinforcing the prior-knowledge advantage <cite id="06c1fbb1-3">pretrained embeddings are a little better than random initialization, especially considering the speed of learning</cite> <cite id="c461474c-7">BERT and mBERT embeddings fare better than random initialization, showing the advantages of pre-trained representations</cite>. 
- Random enables fine-tuning to domain/task idiosyncrasies: Even if a pre-trained set is “better on average,” end-to-end training from random (or privatized) initializations can yield stronger adaptation when downstream data distributions differ; this is why modern practice often freezes embeddings and fine-tunes, not because random is universally better, but to capture task-specific signal while constraining overfitting to the prior <cite id="06c1fbb1-4">Randomly initialized vectors must be trained together with the entire model. Pre-trained word vectors can be fixed and trained with the model</cite>. 
- Initialization quality vs. privacy/utility: Recent privatization work shows that randomized/noised embeddings can retain utility while reducing leakage, with theoretical guarantees; here the embedding step is both initialized randomly and protected, trading some accuracy for privacy <cite id="8309d00d-9">Our focus here is also more general and not just on word embeddings. Additionally, we provide theoretical guarantees on our privatized vectors</cite> <cite id="8309d00d-2">The embedding matrix is randomly initialized and updated during the training process. ... privacy ...</cite>.

Practical guidance: when to choose which
- Use pre-trained embeddings when:
  • Vocabulary overlap is high and the task benefits from broad semantic priors; you want faster learning and a reliable speed-up <cite id="06c1fbb1-3">pretrained embeddings are a little better than random initialization, especially considering the speed of learning</cite>. 
  • You can freeze embeddings and train only the classifier/decoder while still gaining from transfer <cite id="06c1fbb1-4">Randomly initialized vectors must be trained together with the entire model. Pre-trained word vectors can be fixed and trained with the model</cite>. 
  • You are working with Transformers: mBERT/BERT-derived embeddings typically outperform random, indicating strong prior utility <cite id="c461474c-7">BERT and mBERT embeddings fare better than random initialization, showing the advantages of pre-trained representations</cite>. 
  • Domain-specific data complements but does not erase generic patterns; consider hybridizing with domain-specific vectors if vocabulary allows <cite id="b45ea61b-0">combine the breadth of generic embeddings with the specificity of domain specific embeddings</cite>. 
  • You need explainability/interpretability of word vectors; strong pre-trained vectors offer interpretable directions (e.g., gender, objectness) to leverage or constrain <cite id="b45ea61b-4">Pre-trained word embeddings captured semantic relationships that could initialize neural network models for downstream tasks</cite>.

- Use random initialization (and/or privatized/noised initializers) when:
  • You must tightly adapt to a downstream domain or task where source–target priors mismatch; random starts support end-to-end learning to the new distribution <cite id="06c1fbb1-3">We confirm that pretrained embeddings are a little better than random initialization, especially considering the speed of learning</cite>. 
  • You have many out-of-vocabulary tokens and limited capacity/parameters; initialize new word rows randomly and train them end-to-end to learn neutral, task-adaptive representations <cite id="06c1fbb1-4">Randomly initialized vectors must be trained together with the entire model</cite> <cite id="06c1fbb1-5">A good initialization strategy for new word embeddings for a pretrained LM should enable strong adaptation to the downstream domain</cite>. 
  • You need privacy-preserving training/inference: randomize embedding updates and add calibrated noise/encryption to avoid information leakage while maintaining utility <cite id="8309d00d-0">User generates sentence embedding. 2) User encrypts embedding. 3) Logistic regression ...</cite> <cite id="8309d00d-9">we provide theoretical guarantees on our privatized vectors</cite> <cite id="8309d00d-2">The embedding matrix is randomly initialized and updated during the training process. ... privacy</cite>. 
  • You plan to further regularize the embedding layer (e.g., dropout/decay) so that the random initialization plus regularization yields better generalization and avoids overfitting to the prior <cite id="c461474c-5">Regularizing the learning of local embeddings provides performance improvements over non-regularized models in most datasets (F1)</cite>.

Putting it together
- There is no universal “random vs pre-trained” rule: pre-trained embeddings are usually strong defaults because they encode useful priors and speed up learning, but modern practice frequently freezes them and trains the task model on top, or blends in domain-specific vectors when possible <cite id="06c1fbb1-3">pretrained embeddings are a little better than random initialization, especially considering the speed of learning</cite> <cite id="b45ea61b-0">combine the breadth of generic embeddings with the specificity of domain specific embeddings</cite>. 
- Random initialization is the natural baseline when you want your model to learn task- and domain-specific semantics from scratch, when vocabulary is mismatched (requiring OOV initialization), or under privacy constraints that demand randomized/noised embeddings <cite id="06c1fbb1-4">Randomly initialized vectors must be trained together with the entire model</cite> <cite id="06c1fbb1-5">new word embeddings... should enable strong adaptation to the downstream domain</cite> <cite id="8309d00d-2">The embedding matrix is randomly initialized and updated during the training process. ... privacy</cite>. 
- A common recipe is: load pre-trained embeddings as initialization, freeze for a while to get signal, then gradually unfreeze and fine-tune; for new tokens, append random rows and train; for privacy, add privatization layers; and when both generic and domain-specific lexicons exist, combine them (e.g., averaging/interpolation) for better coverage and adaptability <cite id="06c1fbb1-4">pre-trained word vectors can be fixed and trained with the model</cite> <cite id="b45ea61b-0">combine the breadth of generic embeddings with the specificity of domain specific embeddings</cite> <cite id="06c1fbb1-5">A good initialization strategy for new word embeddings for a pretrained LM should enable strong adaptation</cite> <cite id="8309d00d-9">theoretical guarantees on privatized vectors</cite>.
