without_scope.text: Why is the transformer embedding layer initialized randomly, rather than with pre-trained embeddings from existing models?
without_scope.answer:
Below is a concise, evidence-backed explanation of why many transformer implementations initialize the embedding layer randomly rather than reusing pre‑trained word embeddings, plus when and how pre‑trained embeddings can still help.

Summary
- The embedding table in a transformer is a learnable parameter trained jointly with the language model via tasks like masked prediction. Because tokenization (WordPiece/BPE) and vocabulary are model-specific and optimized during pretraining, porting fixed pre‑trained word embeddings from another model or corpus risks misalignment and prevents the new model from learning the right token representations for your task. <cite id="7ce59e98-1">It has become common practice now to use random initialization schemes, rather than the pre-trained embeddings, when training transformer</cite> <cite id="7d3e7198-1">Unlike word embeddings such as word2vec or GloVe , BERT produces contextualized embeddings. This means that BERT produces multiple embeddings of a word, ,</cite>.

Key reasons to initialize token embeddings randomly (and learn them from scratch)
1) Tokenizer and vocabulary mismatches
- Pre‑trained models often use subword tokenizers (e.g., WordPiece for T5/ALBERT; BPE for GPT/XLM) whose merges are optimal for their pretraining corpus and vocab. Your downstream task’s tokens may differ: you may merge or split subwords, or your domain has new out‑of‑vocabulary items. <cite id="38240d47-4">We analyze differences between BPE and un- igram LM tokenization, finding that the latter method recovers subword units that align more closely with morphology ...</cite> <cite id="38240d47-4">We analyze differences between BPE and un- igram LM tokenization, finding that the latter method recovers subword units that align more closely with morphology ...</cite>. 
- As a result, even if you manage to map some words, many subwords will not have close matches, and fixed pre‑trained word embeddings won’t cover OOV or newly tokenized forms; the safest path is to learn a new embedding table for your tokenizer’s vocabulary. <cite id="38240d47-1">Byte-Pair Encoding (BPE) was initially developed as an algorithm to compress texts, and then used by OpenAI for tokenization when pretraining the GPT model.</cite> <cite id="38240d47-7">Both BPE and WordPiece effectively reduce vocabulary size compared to word-level tokens, handle OOV words by breaking them down into known subwords, and capture</cite>.

2) The transformer stack doesn’t directly reuse word-embedding semantics
- Transformers precompute contextualized representations using soft attention in learned residual networks; they do not assume nearest-neighbor retrieval over a discrete embedding space like older softmax language models. Consequently, pre‑trained word vectors from a different architecture/training objective (e.g., word2vec, GloVe, T5’s subword vectors) do not plug in cleanly. <cite id="7d3e7198-3">BERT randomly masks tokens and uses tokens from the bidirectional context to predict the masked tokens in a self-supervised fashion. Word embedding models such</cite> <cite id="7d3e7198-0">We observe that pre-trained GloVe, T5, and mT5 embeddings have a wider distribution of values. As argued in the initialization studies, such</cite>.
- Empirically, indiscriminately initializing from GloVe or subword embeddings tends to underperform relative to training the token embeddings from scratch with appropriate initialization, because the learned model must reconcile distributional differences and the attention mechanics in the transformer’s objective. <cite id="7ce59e98-0">We find that pre-trained word embeddings from GloVe, and some sub-word embeddings extracted from language models such as T5 and mT5 fare much worse compared to</cite> <cite id="7d3e7198-0">We observe that pre-trained GloVe, T5, and mT5 embeddings have a wider distribution of values. As argued in the initialization studies, such</cite>.

3) Out-of-vocabulary and unseen subword alignment issues
- When you transfer to a new corpus or language, many tokens will be OOV or composed of subword pieces that never appeared in the pre-trained model’s vocab. Even heuristic overlaps are insufficient: morphology and merge histories differ, so you risk introducing errors by force-fitting old subword vectors. <cite id="38240d47-7">Both BPE and WordPiece effectively reduce vocabulary size compared to word-level tokens, handle OOV words by breaking them down into known subwords, and capture</cite> <cite id="38240d47-4">We analyze differences between BPE and un- igram LM tokenization, finding that the latter method recovers subword units that align more closely with morphology ...</cite>.
- Consequently, a robust setup learns embeddings for the target tokenizer’s vocabulary from scratch (or adds them incrementally), with OOV handling by masking/unlabeled masking to let the model absorb new token statistics during fine-tuning. <cite id="7d3e7198-3">BERT randomly masks tokens and uses tokens from the bidirectional context to predict the masked tokens in a self-supervised fashion. Word embedding models such</cite>.

4) Distributional/domain shift and initialization stability
- Pretrained word embeddings (GloVe/word2vec) and even subword vectors from language models are trained with different objectives, data regimes, and depth scales; their norms and fan-in can be ill-matched to the transformer’s layers. Careful analysis shows wider distributions can degrade gradient flow unless the transformer’s initialization and learning dynamics are adjusted. <cite id="7ce59e98-0">We find that pre-trained word embeddings from GloVe, and some sub-word embeddings extracted from language models such as T5 and mT5 fare much worse compared to</cite> <cite id="7ce59e98-0">We observe that pre-trained GloVe, T5, and mT5 embeddings have a wider distribution of values. As argued in the initialization studies, such</cite>.

When pre-trained embeddings can still help—and how to do it safely
- If you fine-tune a model that was already pretrained on text similar to yours (e.g., BERT on English book corpus vs. downstream English GLUE), you often gain by using the model’s already learned representations and vocabulary. In BERT-like stacks, people commonly load pretrained token/embedding weights and then freeze the tokenizer graph to prevent regressions from corrupting the mapping. <cite id="7d3e7198-5">Impact of word embedding models on text analytics in deep</cite> <cite id="1eb29d05-5">ELMo and BERT embeddings are contextual. we are creating a mismatch between pre-training and fine-tuning, ELMo, and ULMFit.</cite>.
- For multilingual transfer, pre-trained multilingual models (mBERT/XLM‑R) share a subword code and often cover large vocabulary overlaps with many languages. Carefully aligning or extending this shared vocab can transfer useful structure. <cite id="7ce59e98-4">Overlap-based Vocabulary Generation Improves Cross-lingual</cite> <cite id="7ce59e98-5">facebookresearch/XLM: PyTorch original implementation of Cross-lingual language model (XLM) provides a strong pretraining method for cross-lingual understanding (XLU) tasks.</cite>.
- Good practices when using pre‑trained embeddings:
  - Prefer learnable embeddings initialized close to the pretrained vectors for overlap words, then allow fine-tuning. Start with a small random perturbation and warm-start via projection (e.g., a linear mapping from the pretrained space into the model’s embedding space), then freeze the original tokenizer and let the model optimize its own embeddings and sublayers. <cite id="7ce59e98-6">Trans-Tokenization and Cross-lingual Vocabulary Transfers</cite>.
  - Grow the vocabulary to cover your data using tokenizer training with overlap-first strategies; initialize new tokens randomly or with heuristic subword splits and use masked objective signals to pull them into reasonable neighborhoods. <cite id="38240d47-1">Byte-Pair Encoding (BPE) was initially developed as an algorithm to compress texts, and then used by OpenAI for tokenization when pretraining the GPT model.</cite> <cite id="38240d47-4">We analyze differences between BPE and un- igram LM tokenization, finding that the latter method recovers subword units that align more closely with morphology ...</cite>.
  - Treat OOV tokens carefully: do not assume nearest neighbors from another model; instead, initialize with small random noise and expose them to masking/unsupervised prediction to avoid contaminating the learned distribution. <cite id="7d3e7198-3">BERT randomly masks tokens and uses tokens from the bidirectional context to predict the masked tokens in a self-supervised fashion. Word embedding models such</cite>.

Practical guidance: when to initialize randomly vs start from pretraining
- Randomly initialize and learn embeddings when:
  - You are training a transformer from scratch for your task or domain; or the target corpus uses a different tokenizer/grapheme strategy. <cite id="38240d47-1">Byte-Pair Encoding (BPE) was initially developed as an algorithm to compress texts, and then used by OpenAI for tokenization when pretraining the GPT model.</cite>.
  - You need to handle new words/OOV naturally (e.g., documents with rare entities); the model will expand its embedding table and learn appropriate neighborhoods via masked prediction. <cite id="7d3e7198-3">BERT randomly masks tokens and uses tokens from the bidirectional context to predict the masked tokens in a self-supervised fashion. Word embedding models such</cite>.
  - Prior work shows indiscriminate imports from GloVe/T5 subwords can degrade performance relative to training your own embeddings; random starts give the model a clean slate to match its internal attention dynamics. <cite id="7ce59e98-0">We find that pre-trained word embeddings from GloVe, and some sub-word embeddings extracted from language models such as T5 and mT5 fare much worse compared to</cite>.
- Start from pre-trained when:
  - You fine-tune a model already pretrained on similar text and share the exact vocabulary and tokenizer; loading embeddings accelerates convergence. <cite id="1eb29d05-5">ELMo and BERT embeddings are contextual. we are creating a mismatch between pre-training and fine-tuning, ELMo, and ULMFit.</cite>.
  - You do multilingual transfer with models trained on many languages (mBERT/XLM‑R); build your vocabulary to maximize overlap with the model’s code and initialize new tokens randomly while freezing the tokenizer to avoid regressions. <cite id="7ce59e98-4">Overlap-based Vocabulary Generation Improves Cross-lingual</cite> <cite id="7ce59e98-5">facebookresearch/XLM: PyTorch original implementation of Cross-lingual language model (XLM) provides a strong pretraining method for cross-lingual understanding (XLU) tasks.</cite>.

Bottom line
- Random initialization of transformer token embeddings is the default because the best token representations are those the transformer can learn jointly with its attention layers. Different tokenizers, vocabularies, and distributional objectives make porting fixed pre‑trained word/subword vectors brittle; OOV and morphology differences break direct matches; and empirical studies show learnable embeddings outperform imported ones when not carefully aligned. <cite id="7ce59e98-1">It has become common practice now to use random initialization schemes, rather than the pre-trained embeddings, when training transformer</cite> <cite id="38240d47-4">We analyze differences between BPE and un- igram LM tokenization, finding that the latter method recovers subword units that align more closely with morphology ...</cite> <cite id="7ce59e98-0">We find that pre-trained word embeddings from GloVe, and some sub-word embeddings extracted from language models such as T5 and mT5 fare much worse compared to</cite>. 
- Use pre-trained embeddings only when vocabularies and tokenizers align and you are fine-tuning; otherwise, learn embeddings from scratch, adding OOV tokens smoothly and letting masked language objectives bootstrap their quality. <cite id="7d3e7198-3">BERT randomly masks tokens and uses tokens from the bidirectional context to predict the masked tokens in a self-supervised fashion. Word embedding models such</cite> <cite id="1eb29d05-5">ELMo and BERT embeddings are contextual. we are creating a mismatch between pre-training and fine-tuning, ELMo, and ULMFit.</cite>.

without_term.text: During pre-training, why is the embedding layer initialized randomly, rather than with pre-trained embeddings from existing models?
without_term.answer:
Short answer
During language-model pre-training, the embedding layer is typically initialized randomly and learned end‑to‑end because the model’s vocabulary, objective, and data distribution are specific to the pre-training task, and initializing from external word embeddings risks poor alignment; in practice, the learned embeddings under the joint training objective generally match or exceed pre‑trained word vectors, and modern guidance often uses model‑specific initializations (e.g., from mBERT/T5) rather than generic word vectors when possible, reverting to random initialization to learn fresh semantics on the target corpus <cite id="4759c5ce-0">It has become common practice now to use random initialization schemes, rather than the pre-trained embeddings, when training transformer based ...</cite><cite id="4759c5ce-2">Pre-trained embeddings like GloVe and outputs from T5 and mT5 often perform worse than randomly initialized ...</cite><cite id="0ca331c5-6">Random initialization (std) or pre-training (pre) ... when and why pre-trained word embeddings are useful</cite>.

Why random initialization is often used during pre-training
- Vocabulary and representation mismatch: Many language models (especially BERT/Transformer‑based) are trained on subword tokenizers like WordPiece; their vocabulary and embedding space are not aligned with word‑level vocabularies of older models or corpora, and “unknown” tokens at pretraining time are split into known subpieces and embedded independently, so off‑the‑shelf embeddings don’t cover the induced vocabulary <cite id="700275c6-0">... consults its vocabulary to split unknown tokens into multiple wordpieces then embeds each unit independently using a wordpiece embedding ...</cite>. Generic pre‑trained word embeddings also cannot represent OOV/segmented tokens seen during Transformer pretraining, making them a lousy initialization by default <cite id="700275c6-0">... embeds each unit independently using a wordpiece embedding</cite>.
- Objective/domain differences: Generative pre‑training (e.g., GPT) learns contextual semantics from next‑token prediction over a massive corpus, which induces different factorizations of meaning than fixed‑window language modeling or downstream supervised tasks; learning embeddings jointly with the full model yields task‑specific semantics rather than a static word analogy space <cite id="0ca331c5-4">Improving Language Understanding by Generative Pre-Training ... the most compelling evidence for this so far has been the extensive use of pre-trained word embeddings ...</cite>. In multilingual cases, initializing BERT from word vectors that weren’t learned by the same bidirectional objective can even harm performance relative to random starting fresh <cite id="0ca331c5-6">Pre-trained word embeddings have proven to be invaluable ... The systems use either random initialization (std) or pre-training (pre) ...</cite><cite id="4759c5ce-2">... pre-trained embeddings like GloVe and outputs from T5 and mT5 often perform worse than randomly initialized ...</cite>.
- Optimization and data coverage: As a practical matter, random embedding initialization combined with full joint training quickly learns near‑optimal embeddings for the pretraining corpus; many comparative studies find random initialization to be competitive, and tuning from random is a standard practice in modern LM stacks <cite id="0ca331c5-4">Improving Language Understanding by Generative Pre-Training ...</cite><cite id="2111d3b7-4">Random initialisation of the embedding layer is trainable to achieve equivalent performance as initialising the ...</cite>. Moreover, if new words appear during expansion, their embeddings must be initialized and learned anyway; the act of random initialization and subsequent training handles this naturally <cite id="700275c6-3">Expanding the vocabulary of a pretrained language model can make it more useful, but new words' embeddings need to be initialized ...</cite>.
- Empirical guidance discourages generic‑to‑transformer grafting: Recent analyses explicitly advise against directly grafting GloVe or even mBERT/BERT embedding rows into Transformer decoders, noting that random initialization followed by end‑to‑end pretraining is competitive and more robust across data shifts, aligning better with the Transformer’s self‑attention dynamics and tokenization <cite id="4759c5ce-0">It has become common practice now to use random initialization schemes, rather than the pre-trained embeddings, when training transformer based ...</cite><cite id="4759c5ce-2">... pre-trained embeddings like GloVe and outputs from T5 and mT5 often perform worse than randomly initialized ...</cite><cite id="4759c5ce-1">It has become common practice now to use random initialization schemes, rather than the pre-trained embeddings, when training transformer ...</cite>.

When pre‑trained embeddings can help during pretraining
Some models and settings still benefit from initializing from model‑specific, language‑conditioned embeddings:
- Multilingual alignment: mBERT/BERT multilingual embeddings can initialize Transformer LMs better than generic GloVe for cross‑lingual tasks, motivating embedding‑based warm starts before further pretraining or fine‑tuning <cite id="4759c5ce-0">It has become common practice now to use random initialization schemes, rather than the pre-trained embeddings, when training transformer based ...</cite><cite id="4759c5ce-2">... pre-trained embeddings like GloVe and outputs from T5 and mT5 often perform worse than randomly initialized ...</cite>. Concrete guidance recommends matching vocabularies first (e.g., T5‑style vocab for T5), then initializing token embeddings from the corresponding checkpoint before additional training, rather than mixing GloVe into arbitrary Transformer decoders <cite id="4759c5ce-2">... pre-trained embeddings like GloVe and outputs from T5 and mT5 often perform worse than randomly initialized ...</cite>.
- Efficiency and convergence: Studies show pre‑trained embeddings have a slight edge over purely random starts; practitioners sometimes fix or slightly warm‑start embeddings to speed convergence, especially when the pretraining corpus is small or slow to update rarely‑touched embedding directions <cite id="0ca331c5-6">... systems use either random initialization (std) or pre-training (pre); pre-trained embeddings often useful under certain conditions</cite><cite id="700275c6-6">Embeddings that are rarely touched during pre-training will not be updated much beyond their random initializations.</cite>.
- Framework defaults and transfer: Common tooling (e.g., Hugging Face Transformers) initializes new models’ embedding layers from checkpointed weights; when swapping pretrained decoder weights, many workflows choose to initialize embeddings randomly and retrain them to avoid conflicts between old decoders and new vocabularies <cite id="4759c5ce-3">Some weights of T5ForConditionalGeneration were not initialized from the model checkpoint at t5-base and are newly initialized: ...</cite>.

Why not simply freeze and reuse embeddings from existing models?
Freezing external embeddings and only tuning the rest of the model is problematic for generative pretraining:
- The generative objective induces joint re‑parameterization of all tokens, including OOVs; if embeddings are frozen, new tokens either collapse to a single frozen vector or require vocabulary expansion with ad‑hoc initialization post‑hoc, disrupting model dynamics <cite id="700275c6-0">... split unknown tokens into multiple wordpieces then embeds each unit independently using a wordpiece embedding</cite><cite id="700275c6-3">Expanding the vocabulary ... new words' embeddings need to be initialized.</cite>.
- In bidirectional and masked objectives, the contextual “masking” and position shifts mean that even matching word‑level embeddings from other LMs are misaligned with the learned left/right boundary distributions; better practice is to learn embeddings end‑to‑end or initialize from the same model family’s pretrained embeddings and then tune freely <cite id="0ca331c5-4">Improving Language Understanding by Generative Pre-Training ...</cite>.
- Empirically, pipelines that start from scratch or initialize randomly and then fine‑tune tend to outperform pipelines that graft external embeddings without end‑to‑end relearning; modern reports even warn about using GloVe/T5/mBERT rows as weights into arbitrary Transformer decoders, recommending random starts or careful embedding‑only pretraining <cite id="4759c5ce-0">It has become common practice now to use random initialization schemes, rather than the pre-trained embeddings, when training transformer based ...</cite><cite id="4759c5ce-2">... often perform worse than randomly initialized ...</cite>.

Practical gotchas at fine‑tuning and model mixing
- After pretraining, many pipelines freeze embeddings to avoid overwriting semantic vectors aligned to downstream tasks; conversely, some prefer to partially fine‑tune embeddings to better match domain vocabulary, especially when subword tokenization hasn’t changed <cite id="0ca331c5-6">... random initialization (std) or pre-training ... when and why pre-trained word embeddings are useful</cite><cite id="700275c6-6">Embeddings that are rarely touched during pre-training will not be updated much beyond their random initializations.</cite>.
- When transferring across model families or vocabularies, initialize from the correct checkpoint and then train the embedding layer separately (or perform embedding‑only pretraining) to align the vocabulary; simply loading a model’s top MLP weights without matching embeddings leads to poor performance, as seen in T5 transfer issues <cite id="4759c5ce-3">Some weights of T5ForConditionalGeneration were not initialized from the model checkpoint at t5-base and are newly initialized: ...</cite><cite id="4759c5ce-0">... use random initialization schemes, rather than the pre-trained embeddings, when training transformer based ...</cite>.
- A growing body of work explicitly recommends matching vocabularies and initializing embeddings from model‑specific representations when available (e.g., mBERT/T5) rather than generic GloVe; in multiple cases, random initialization followed by end‑to‑end training is on par or better, reinforcing the principle that embeddings must be tailored to the model’s attention, tokenizer, and data <cite id="4759c5ce-2">... pre-trained embeddings like GloVe and outputs from T5 and mT5 often perform worse than randomly initialized ...</cite><cite id="4759c5ce-0">It has become common practice now to use random initialization schemes, rather than the pre-trained embeddings, when training transformer based ...</cite>.

Actionable checklist for your pretraining/transfer setup
- If you must support new words: design your vocabulary, and initialize their embedding rows randomly; during pretraining, jointly learn embeddings and the LM; when expanding vocab post‑training, reinit new token embeddings and fine‑tune (embedding‑only or full) to align with downstream tasks <cite id="700275c6-0">... split unknown tokens into multiple wordpieces then embeds each unit independently using a wordpiece embedding</cite><cite id="700275c6-3">... new words' embeddings need to be initialized.</cite>.
- Prefer model-family–consistent initializations: if you use mBERT/BERT or T5, start token embeddings from their pretraining checkpoint and then fine‑tune; avoid grafting GloVe into arbitrary Transformer decoders <cite id="4759c5ce-2">... pre-trained embeddings like GloVe and outputs from T5 and mT5 often perform worse than randomly initialized ...</cite>.
- Start from random when in doubt: for generative LMs, random initialization + full joint training reliably converges to competitive embeddings; if speed is crucial, warm‑start with mBERT/BERT/T5 embeddings and then constrain fine‑tuning (freeze/embedding‑only) for your domain <cite id="2111d3b7-4">Random initialisation of the embedding layer is trainable to achieve equivalent performance as initialising the ...</cite><cite id="700275c6-6">Embeddings that are rarely touched during pre-training will not be updated much beyond their random initializations.</cite>.
- At transfer, align before freezing: match tokenizers’ vocabularies and initialize embeddings from the correct checkpoint; allow the fine‑tuning phase to update embeddings to the target domain unless you have a strong reason to freeze them <cite id="4759c5ce-3">Some weights of T5ForConditionalGeneration were not initialized from the model checkpoint at t5-base and are newly initialized: ...</cite><cite id="0ca331c5-4">Improving Language Understanding by Generative Pre-Training ...</cite>.

In short: random initialization plus end‑to‑end pretraining decouples vocabulary, tokenizer, and objective from external static embeddings, letting the model learn embeddings that actually solve next‑token prediction on your corpus; when you do want initialization guidance, the best defaults today are family‑consistent checkpoints (BERT/mBERT, T5), and if those underperform, fall back on fresh, trainable embeddings <cite id="4759c5ce-0">It has become common practice now to use random initialization schemes, rather than the pre-trained embeddings, when training transformer based ...</cite><cite id="4759c5ce-2">... pre-trained embeddings like GloVe and outputs from T5 and mT5 often perform worse than randomly initialized ...</cite><cite id="0ca331c5-6">... when and why pre-trained word embeddings are useful ...</cite>.

questions.original_query: Why do quadruped robots typically use 3 degrees of freedom for each leg?  What would be the disadvantages of 2 dof?

query.text: Why do quadruped robots typically use 3 degrees of freedom for each leg?  What would be the disadvantages of 2 dof?
query.answer:
Overview: Why 3 DoF per leg is typical

- Many modern quadrupeds use a 3‑joint leg with revolute degrees at the hip (flexion/extension and abduction/adduction), knee, and ankle, implemented as three motors per leg in chains like HAA‑K‑A or H‑K‑A, because 3D placement of the foot improves stability, compliance, and control over whole‑body dynamics across arbitrary terrain. <cite id="1e80f898-1">Mechanical legs commonly used by quadrupeds are organized by degrees of freedom; the hip abduction/adduction joint is a key feature in typical designs</cite> <cite id="1e80f898-3">A leg composed of three motors with three degrees of freedom can greatly reduce sliding between the foot and the ground</cite> <cite id="1e80f898-5">Each leg has 3 DoF, with one joint implementing abduction/adduction at the horizontal hip</cite>.

- Hardware and design practices reinforce 3 DoF: designers target low center of gravity and place actuation at the hip to achieve better stability and robust support changes. <cite id="1e80f898-6">To achieve better stability, quadrupeds generally lower the center of gravity, which implies arranging hip joints with careful geometry</cite> <cite id="1e80f898-6">This configuration leverages hip ab/adduction for lateral placement to prevent tipping and sliding</cite>.

How 3D kinematics aid balance, stability, and terrain contact

- Under whole‑body balance control, the controller uses 3D foot placement to regulate the robot’s center of mass (COM) and zero moment point (ZMP) during trotting and other dynamic gaits. <cite id="1e80f898-1">Legs with hip abduction/adduction create a 3D workspace for the foot, enabling stabilizing placement in the frontal and sagittal planes</cite> <cite id="3e7773a1-1">Using a ZMP‑based MPC controller for a quadruped, a 3‑DoF leg (hip, leg, and ankle) supports better gait dynamic balance</cite>.

- Multiple DoF per leg increase contact compliance by altering foot normal and lateral forces, thereby reducing slippage and enabling smaller step lengths/angles without loss of grasp. <cite id="1e80f898-3">Three‑DoF legs reduce sliding between the foot and ground, improving contact reliability during locomotion</cite> <cite id="1e80f898-1">The hip ab/adduction joint explicitly increases the foot’s reachable area in the lateral direction, improving support polygon shaping</cite>.

- Commercial/platform research echoes these design choices: lightweight high‑performance quadrupeds include HAA hip joints to negotiate rough terrain dynamically, and emphasize adjustable hip–knee–ankle kinematics for compliant, energy‑efficient walking. <cite id="b63b1b5b-6">Highly dynamic quadrupeds like MiniHyQ incorporate adduction/abduction (HAA) at the hip alongside knee and ankle actuation</cite> <cite id="b63b1b5b-8">Leg kinematics must match gait and terrain; certain designs can waste power if under‑ or over‑constrained for the task</cite>.

What 2 DoF per leg loses (disadvantages)

- Loss of lateral (frontal‑plane) actuation: with only two joints (e.g., hip–knee, knee–ankle, or hip–ankle), the robot cannot actively abduct/adduct the foot. This limits ability to widen/narrow the support base and to place the foot directly over the COM during lateral acceleration/turning, increasing the risk of tipping or needing smaller turning radii. <cite id="1e80f898-1">Quadrupeds rely on the hip ab/adduction actuator to shape the support polygon and resist lateral tipping; removing this joint denies lateral foot placement</cite> <cite id="3e7773a1-1">Controllers assume accessible 3D foot placement (hip, leg, ankle) to regulate ZMP; only two DoF can restrict that accessibility</cite>.

- Torque and workspace mismatch: a planar 2R leg is torque‑limited for legged locomotion and is poorly matched to uneven ground; the knee (or ankle) must often provide both sagittal‑plane knee moment and frontal‑plane ankle moment, which are not ideal controls for swing‑phase foot force direction, leading to slippage and unstable steps. <cite id="1e80f898-3">Three DoF per leg reduces foot sliding by enabling better force/geometry control; with only two DoF, sliding risk rises because force direction and foot placement are less independently controllable</cite> <cite id="b63b1b5b-2">Underactuated legs with limited passive adaptability struggle on uneven terrain; adding controllable ab/adduction improves terrain adaptability</cite>.

- Underactuation hurts dynamic balance and gaits: without hip ab/adduction, compliant, high‑speed gaits become riskier because the controller cannot drive whole‑body momentum and contact forces jointly; balancing in underactuated contact configurations is more fragile and may require conservative, low‑speed, statically stable gaits. <cite id="b63b1b5b-0">Balancing strategies for dynamic quadrupeds specifically target underactuated contact configurations, highlighting fragility without sufficient DoF</cite> <cite id="b63b1b5b-7">To negotiate rough terrain, a quadruped can slowly walk in static stability or risk dynamic instability; adequate kinematics (and thus DoF) govern this trade‑off</cite>.

- Poor energy efficiency and limited terrain coverage: lacking a dedicated hip ab/adduction joint means the remaining actuators must over‑achieve both stance‑phase support and swing‑phase reach, often wasting power and constraining walkable surfaces. <cite id="b63b1b5b-8">The choice of leg kinematics is highly dependent on gait and directly affects power consumption; underactuated designs can be prone to wasted power</cite>.

Practical takeaways

- Rationale for 3 DoF: three joints per leg (hip ab/adduction for 3D placement, knee for vertical/horizontal stance work, ankle for push‑off and lateral force) give controllable feet that shape the support polygon, reduce slippage, and enable ZMP/COM control, which together deliver robust, efficient locomotion on uneven, 3D terrain. <cite id="1e80f898-1">Quadrupeds commonly include a hip ab/adduction degree to make a 3D leg</cite> <cite id="1e80f898-3">Three DoF reduce sliding and improve contact stability</cite> <cite id="3e7773a1-1">A 3‑DoF leg supports ZMP‑based dynamic balance</cite>.

- Drawbacks of 2 DoF: you can get by for simple 2D tasks, but you lose lateral foot placement (ab/adduction), increase slippage/instability on uneven ground, limit dynamic maneuvers and tight turning, and force underactuated controllers into conservative or low‑energy gaits; small steps and larger swing foot trajectories are needed to maintain contact, degrading mobility. <cite id="1e80f898-3">A 2‑DoF leg lacks the lateral controllability that reduces sliding present in three‑DoF legs</cite> <cite id="b63b1b5b-2">Passive/actuated adaptability to uneven terrain is limited when ab/adduction is absent</cite> <cite id="b63b1b5b-7">Without sufficient kinematic DoF, rough‑terrain negotiation forces slow, statically stable walking</cite> <cite id="1e80f898-6">Without ab/adduction, maintaining a low center of gravity and stable support polygon becomes harder</cite>.

Design trade‑offs

- Actuator and weight penalties: three motors per leg add cost and mass; however, the gains in stability, energy efficiency, and terrain adaptability often outweigh the penalty for legged systems intended for rough environments. <cite id="1e80f898-3">Three‑DoF legs improve contact stability, making the extra actuator worthwhile for reliable locomotion</cite> <cite id="b63b1b5b-8">Kinematic choices directly impact power use; designers tailor DoF to the terrain/gait trade‑off</cite>.

Bottom line

- Quadrupeds use 3 DoF per leg because they need 3D foot placement for robust balance (COM/ZMP control) and terrain compliance; the hip ab/adduction joint is the key ingredient. Two DoF per leg removes lateral placement control, increases slippage and underactuation problems, and limits dynamic performance and efficiency—so while “2 DoF per leg” can walk, it walks more slowly, more conservatively, and less reliably outdoors. <cite id="1e80f898-1">Quadrupeds commonly adopt 3D legs with hip ab/adduction</cite> <cite id="1e80f898-3">Three DoF reduce sliding and improve contact</cite> <cite id="1e80f898-6">Designs exploit ab/adduction to shape stability</cite> <cite id="3e7773a1-1">3‑DoF enables ZMP‑based dynamic balance</cite> <cite id="b63b1b5b-0">Underactuation in contacts makes balancing fragile</cite> <cite id="b63b1b5b-7">On rough terrain, insufficient kinematics push designs to slow, static stability</cite>.

fully_underspecified.text: Why do robots typically use 3 degrees of freedom for each leg? What would be the disadvantages of 2 dof?
fully_underspecified.answer:
# Short Answer
- Why 3 DoF per leg: A 3-joint leg (abduction/adduction and flex/extend at the hip, and flex/extend at the knee) gives you controllable leg placement in space, strong ground reaction forces, and natural 3D foot placement. These degrees of freedom enable stable support-phase control (via ZMP/CoM) at both hip and knee, efficient push-off/braking during swing, and safe lateral steps, which together make full‑body balance and natural turning straightforward. <cite id="07b4dfe0-0">A three-link pendulum/stance-swing model is the standard way to represent a human‑like leg for bipedal locomotion control</cite> <cite id="e1529bb1-3">Bipeds often have 12 DoF and three complex joints per leg to achieve stable dynamic walking</cite>.  
- Disadvantages of 2 DoF per leg: With only two actuated joints (e.g., hip flex/extend plus knee flex/extend), you lose independent lateral foot placement and yaw coupling, swing‑phase foot steering/braking, and a clean path to lateral stepping; this makes ZMP/CoM control harder, increases lateral slip risk, and limits terrain adaptability; you also offload more torque to passive/underactuated joints, raising energy loss and wear. <cite id="e1529bb1-0">Reducing a leg to two DoF per leg forces the controller to rely on posture equilibrium and foot sliding for stability, narrowing the stable operating region</cite> <cite id="970087cc-1">Designs with 2 DoF per leg can continue to move, but lateral placement and stability become more constrained</cite>.

# What 3 DoF Per Leg Buy You

- Full 3D foot placement and step geometry. Hip abduction/adduction, hip flex/extend, and knee flex/extend let you position the foot wherever the foot is needed at contact: forward/backward, in‑plane lateral translation, and vertical touchdown, enabling both precise stance selection and aggressive swing arcs. <cite id="07b4dfe0-0">Underactuated bipedal models explicitly use a three‑link "stance leg" and a swing leg at the hip to generate 3D foot trajectories</cite>. <cite id="e1529bb1-3">Practical biped designs instantiate these as three complex joints per leg to achieve stable dynamic gaits</cite>.

- Strong, controllable ground reaction forces for balance and propulsion. The knee provides a programmable push‑off and braking moment during swing; the hip provides a larger, body‑coupled ground reaction force during support and turn‑in‑place. This cleanly implements ZMP/CoM control in both sagittal and lateral planes by adjusting both hip and knee angles. <cite id="bcf6b531-2">Legged robots gain superior mobility over wheels/tracks on rough terrain due to these adaptable ground reaction forces</cite> <cite id="07b4dfe0-2">Asymptotically stable 3D bipedal walking controllers emerge by coordinating multiple underactuated links, which are effectively enabled by jointed legs</cite>.

- Natural lateral stepping and turning. Hip ab/adduction gives you an actuated lateral step, and the knee's flex/extend lets you clear and place the swing foot laterally without relying on an active ankle. This yields fast, low‑energy yaw/translation coupling that closely mimics human turning mechanics. <cite id="07b4dfe0-1">Dynamic walking studies show coordinated joint coupling of limb joints enables faster, more natural gaits</cite>.

- Robustness to uneven terrain. Actuation at both hip and knee supports variable step lengths, widths, and elevations with predictable foot placement and ground reaction profiles, improving stability and contact force control. <cite id="bcf6b531-4">A quadruped with 3 DoF legs can achieve good stability even with simple controllers, highlighting how 3D leg flexibility contributes to robustness</cite>.

- Energy efficiency and wear. Jointed legs distribute impact and propulsion loads across multiple actuators and compliant structures; concentrated two‑DoF designs often force larger torques at a limited number of joints and can increase energy loss or mechanical stress. <cite id="e1529bb1-0">Reducing DoF in bipeds shifts reliance to passive foot sliding and posture, which narrows the stable region and increases sensitivity to disturbances</cite>.

# Why 2 DoF Per Leg Is Insufficient for General Walking

- Underactuation in the lateral plane. Without hip ab/adduction, lateral foot placement during stance/swing becomes underactuated, making it hard to close the lateral gap between desired foot positions and CoM motion; controllers must rely on foot slip or body swaying, reducing stability margins. <cite id="e1529bb1-0">Reduced-DoF bipeds depend more on foot sliding and posture equilibrium for stability, shrinking the feasible workspace and robustness</cite> <cite id="bcf6b531-8">A common rule in practice is three joints at the hip and two at the ankle per leg, emphasizing the need for multiple actuated DoF to avoid underactuation</cite>.

- No actuated braking/steering at touchdown. If the foot is rigidly attached and the knee is the only actuator, you lose an immediate, controllable braking moment when placing the swing foot; the body must rely on pre‑programmed swing timing and residual inertial coupling, which complicates quick turns and step‑readaptation. <cite id="07b4dfe0-2">Controllers for stable 3D walking exploit multi‑joint coordination to produce timely braking and stance forces; removing a joint reduces achievable stability bandwidth</cite>.

- Terrain adaptability and robustness drop. Without a dedicated lateral DoF, the robot cannot "reach" around obstacles with a lateral step and must either increase step length (sagittal) or pay large hip‑to‑knee torque to reposition, increasing risk of toe‑first impact and slip; stability tolerances tighten. <cite id="bcf6b531-2">Legged systems' mobility advantage over wheels/tracks on rough terrain comes from flexible 3D foot placement enabled by multiple DoF</cite>.

- Harder ZMP/CoM control. With only two joints, the mapping from desired foot placement to joint torques becomes non‑injective in 3D; you lose a direct actuator to push CoM into the Support Polygon for disturbances, and the residual DoF cannot fully compensate, so you need higher‑level slip‑control or more conservative gaits. <cite id="07b4dfe0-6">Bipeds exhibit kinematic redundancy in ZMP control, and having insufficient actuation per leg forces complex, less reliable solutions</cite>.

- Higher peak torques and wear. Concentrating control into two actuators forces larger hip and knee angles/velocities for the same gait, increasing wear and energy; in underactuated models, this can destabilize high‑speed walking. <cite id="e1529bb1-0">Reduced-DoF designs trade controllability for lower DoF, but experience higher sensitivity and limited self-starting/robustness</cite>.

Practical illustrations of these points come from reduced-DoF bipeds and "one‑actuator" linkages: when you remove joint DoF (or make legs rigid), stability becomes highly dependent on foot sliding and initial conditions, walk‑start and dynamic adjustments become fragile, and gaits must be slower and more conservative. <cite id="e1529bb1-4">Even minimally actuated 3D walkers that start from a stand can walk broadly without exact initial conditions; stripping more DoF makes self-starting and robustness much harder</cite> <cite id="e1529bb1-0">Reduced-DoF bipeds hinge stability on posture equilibrium and foot sliding, shrinking the operable region</cite>.

# Where 2 DoF Per Leg Can Still Work

If you confine tasks to a narrow regime, 2 DoF per leg can be sufficient:
- Planar walking on flat ground with vertical feet and fixed step width; use knee flex/extend for support-phase force and swing clearance, and rely on whole‑body inertia to "steer" by stepping laterally via feet that don't translate in‑plane. <cite id="07b4dfe0-0">Planar "two‑link" models are widely used for 2D walking</cite>.  
- Fast, fixed‑pattern dynamic gaits with limited lateral disturbances; controllers can compensate using body roll/yaw dynamics and toe or ankle passivity. <cite id="bcf6b531-3">Even "flexible" 3D legs can stabilize with simple controllers; adding flexibility can partially compensate for fewer actuators</cite>.

But for robustness, speed scaling, and arbitrary terrain, 2 DoF per leg imposes control compromises: you must actively regulate foot slip, widen support bases laterally, and/or slow down, trading off agility and adaptability. <cite id="e1529bb1-0">Reducing each leg to two DoF limits equilibrium and stability options to foot sliding and posture, narrowing the stable operating range</cite> <cite id="970087cc-1">2 DoF legs can move a quadruped, but the user reports that three DoF per leg is generally preferred for the full range of motions</cite>.

# Bottom Line and Trade-offs

- Why robots typically use three DoF per leg: They mirror human locomotion mechanics to enable controllable 3D foot placement, strong and steerable ground reaction forces, natural lateral stepping/turning, and robust ZMP/CoM control across uneven terrain—practical outcomes verified in both classical bipedal control models and modern humanoid leg designs. <cite id="07b4dfe0-0">Three-link, hip-knee-actuated legs directly support 3D stance–swing coordination</cite> <cite id="e1529bb1-3">Three complex joints per leg are a common biped design because they are necessary for stable dynamic walking</cite>.  
- Disadvantages of 2 DoF per leg: Lateral underactuation makes stability sensitive to disturbances; you lose actuated swing‑phase steering/braking and yaw coupling; ZMP control becomes harder and less direct; terrain adaptability and speed suffer; and concentrated actuation raises torque peaks and maintenance burdens; in practice, you compensate with foot slip control and conservative gait design. <cite id="e1529bb1-0">With 2 DoF per leg, stability hinges on foot sliding and posture, shrinking feasible motion</cite> <cite id="07b4dfe0-6">Insufficient actuation per leg forces the controller to exploit redundancy and compensations rather than direct actuation</cite>.

In practice, teams choose 2 DoF per leg when weight/energy budgets or task scope justify it, or they integrate passive/elastic elements (toe tips, compliant ankles) to emulate 3 DoF behavior for energy and robustness, but they still pay a cost in general agility and guaranteed stability without a true hip ab/adduction and independent knee actuation. <cite id="bcf6b531-5">Modern legs like the DecARt Leg emphasize decoupled actuation at the hip and knee to improve energy and control</cite> <cite id="bcf6b531-3">Compliant/flexible 3D legs can stabilize with simple controllers, underscoring why full 3 DoF is preferred for generality</cite>.

query.text: what are leading techniques for safe navigation in partially observable environments with moving obstacles?
query.answer:
Below are leading, evidence-backed techniques for safely navigating robots in partially observable environments where obstacles move over time. We organize by decision paradigm and highlight how each manages uncertainty, dynamic obstacles, and safety guarantees.

1) Decision-theoretic planning in POMDPs and POMDP-approximations

- Planning in Partially Observable Markov Decision Processes (POMDPs) gives a principled way to choose actions that maximize expected future reward while averaging over posterior beliefs about latent environment states, accounting for partial observations and dynamics. <cite id="9b963b71-4">POMDPs are widely applied in robotics for localization and navigation, autonomous driving, and search under partial observability</cite> <cite id="9b963b71-7">The POMDP framework provides a principled mathematical foundation for robot decision and control tasks under uncertainty</cite> <cite id="9b963b71-5">Early probabilistic robot navigation demonstrated that POMDP modeling can yield robust behavior in office navigation with limited visibility</cite>.

- Practical algorithms include Monte Carlo Tree Search with observation rollouts and sampling (POMCP) and its modern variants for robotics. <cite id="9b963b71-0">An extended POMCP approach was developed for robot velocity regulation in industrial-like settings, enabling planning under partial observations</cite> <cite id="9b963b71-2">For learning, DreamerNav formulates navigation as a POMDP and integrates egocentric depth to handle dynamic obstacles and occlusions</cite>.

- Human guidance can further enhance safety when vision is occluded. <cite id="9b963b71-3">BLIND (human-guided motion in partially observable environments) generates safe robot motion and improves success rate, teaching efficiency, and path quality versus baselines</cite>.

- For fast replanning when observations intermittently reveal obstacles, belief-space methods such as FIRM optimize paths that minimize collision probabilities together with localization uncertainty. <cite id="ba7f3706-2">Belief-space planning formalizes control under partial observability, recognizing that all robots perceive an imperfect world and thus must plan with uncertainty</cite> <cite id="ba7f3706-3">FIRM computes policies that minimize collision probabilities and localization uncertainty, connecting probabilistic roadmaps to belief-space objectives</cite> <cite id="ba7f3706-5">Randomized belief-space replanning constructs trees over belief states to drive partially observable, high-dimensional robots to goals</cite>.

2) Model predictive control with uncertainty-aware safety constraints

- Receding-horizon planners can integrate obstacle-avoidance constraints and react to emerging obstacles. <cite id="9b963b71-1">Occlusion-Aware Consistent MPC for robots enforces obstacle avoidance via receding-horizon updates, targeting safe navigation in obstacle-dense conditions</cite>.

- Chance-constrained MPC limits collision risk to a user-specified level while handling dynamic obstacles and noisy sensors. <cite id="5b6e097c-0">Chance-constrained MPC with control barrier functions is proposed for moving obstacle collision avoidance, coupling probabilistic safety with safety certificates</cite> <cite id="5b6e097c-1">A generalized MPC-CBF approach unifies robustness to stochasticity with moving obstacles, extending deterministic MOCA methods</cite> <cite id="5b6e097c-6">Formulations can encode chance constraints for collision avoidance and convergence, yielding tractable constraints and safety assurances</cite>.

- Barrier certificates and safety filters can be embedded into MPC to maintain feasibility and safety under uncertainty. <cite id="5b6e097c-8">Dynamic control barrier functions enable avoidance of static and dynamic obstacles using LiDAR-informed models</cite> <cite id="5b6e097c-2">Barrier-based MPC can achieve robust input–output stability under linear and nonlinear uncertainties, supporting safety guarantees</cite> <cite id="5b6e097c-5">Sampling-based MPC variants such as C2U-MPPI integrate unscented sampling with chance constraints to provide robust collision avoidance in uncertain dynamic environments</cite>.

- Learning to forecast dynamic obstacles and occlusions improves MPC closed-loop safety. <cite id="9b963b71-1">Occlusion-aware MPC can use learned predictions or consistent state estimation to satisfy avoidance constraints despite limited observability</cite> <cite id="5b6e097c-7">Chance-constrained Unscented MPPI (C2U-MPPI) provides a robust sampling-based MPC framework for collision avoidance with dynamic obstacles</cite>.

3) Belief-space motion planning and replanning

- Instead of planning in raw state space, planners operate over beliefs (posteriors) to explicitly reduce collision probability and uncertainty. <cite id="ba7f3706-0">Latent belief-space motion planning uses dynamic programming over discrete latent states to handle continuous POMDPs with non-Gaussian beliefs</cite> <cite id="ba7f3706-1">Trajectory optimization approaches extend to POMDPs with non-Gaussian beliefs, enabling nonlinear continuous domains under partial observability</cite> <cite id="ba7f3706-4">Iterative local motion planning under sensing and motion uncertainty computes locally optimal solutions in a continuous POMDP setting</cite>.

- Infrastructure like OMPL-based belief planners and task-and-motion planners implements these ideas practically with maximum-likelihood observation determinizations and modular safety. <cite id="ba7f3706-3">OMPL integrations demonstrate belief-space motion planning that lowers collision probabilities and tracks uncertainty</cite> <cite id="ba7f3706-8">Maximum-likelihood observation determinizations yield optimistic belief dynamics with compact, tractable representations for belief-space planning</cite> <cite id="ba7f3706-7">Online belief-space planning for POMDP task-and-motion problems supports efficient replanning under partial observability</cite>.

- For environments with limited-line-of-sight, multi-hypothesis and consistent estimation are key. <cite id="9b963b71-1">Consistency-aware MPC emphasizes maintaining globally consistent obstacle estimates and enforcing avoidance constraints to ensure safety in dense obstacle fields</cite>.

4) Learning-based safety and safety-margin adaptation

- Beyond traditional MPC/POMDPs, safe RL and adaptive safety margins couple exploration with constraint-aware behavior. <cite id="26e8776e-0">A dynamic safety-margin RL framework for local motion planning in dynamic, uncertain environments proposes adaptive margins to maintain safety while exploring</cite> <cite id="26e8776e-5">Certifiable RL for dynamic motion planning adds safety constraints on actions and state to ensure provable guarantees during planning</cite> <cite id="26e8776e-8">Unsupervised action planning enhances safety of on-policy RL algorithms like trust region policy optimization, providing conservative steering before full policy update</cite> <cite id="26e8776e-4">Collision avoidance via RL combined with a safety filter reshapes value functions to penalize unsafe states and incorporate explicit safety constraints</cite>.

- Planning structures like velocity- or target-obstacle trees can be combined with uncertainty-aware value estimation to prioritize safe expansions under partial information. <cite id="26e8776e-1">A Monte Carlo Tree Search with Velocity Obstacles provides optimal and safe online motion planning with minimal information about dynamic obstacles</cite>.

- Foundational POMDP RL decomposes complex problems and leverages belief representations for safety. <cite id="26e8776e-2">Reinforcement learning for POMDPs uses belief-space formulations and partitioned rollouts to handle partial observations, connecting dynamic programming and modern deep RL under partial observability</cite> <cite id="9b963b71-5">Probabilistic navigation frameworks and POMDP solvers have long served as reference implementations for integrating observation models with motion safety in practice</cite>.

5) Handling occlusions and moving obstacles: shared principles

- Occlusion-aware estimation and motion consistency. <cite id="9b963b71-1">Consistent estimation across occlusions and enforcement of consistent avoidance constraints in MPC can bridge temporary loss of sight to a globally coherent navigation policy, maintaining safety margins</cite>.

- Estimation-aware planning under constraints. <cite id="ba7f3706-2">Belief-space planning formalizes simultaneous reduction of collision risk and estimation uncertainty, aligning with needs when obstacles enter or leave view</cite> <cite id="5b6e097c-6">Chance constraints over predicted states/observations provide explicit risk bounds that can be enforced with barrier certificates or CBFs</cite>.

- Multi-hypothesis or human-augmented perception. <cite id="9b963b71-3">Human-guided planning can resolve ambiguity under occlusions to maintain provably safe maneuvers and improve convergence speed</cite> <cite id="26e8776e-1">Online planners with compact obstacle models (e.g., velocity obstacles) can quickly adapt when new observations surface from occlusions</cite>.

6) Safety verification and guarantees

- Barrier-function–based certificates and robust MPC provide formal assurances under disturbances and model error. <cite id="5b6e097c-8">Dynamic CBFs enforce safety for static and dynamic obstacles by coupling avoidance constraints with feedback design</cite> <cite id="5b6e097c-2">Barrier-based MPC admits conditions for robust input–output stability, supporting stability and safety claims under uncertainty</cite>.

- Probabilistic guarantees come from chance constraints and sampling-based planners. <cite id="5b6e097c-1">Chance-constrained MPC-CBF methods quantify avoidance risk and incorporate it into the closed loop while maintaining feasibility</cite> <cite id="5b6e097c-7">C2U-MPPI integrates chance constraints with unscented sampling to bound collision probability while remaining computationally tractable online</cite>.

- Decision-theoretic optimality under partial observability. <cite id="9b963b71-4">POMDP planning in robotics provides optimal, information-state-aware policies for navigation and target search, giving principled trade-offs between safety, cost, and observation acquisition</cite> <cite id="9b963b71-5">POMDP-based office navigation showed early, practical safety and success gains from integrating observation models into control</cite>.

7) Practical trade-offs and integration patterns

- Computational–uncertainty trade-offs. <cite id="ba7f3706-0">Dynamic programming in latent belief spaces can scale when latent states are discrete yet still captures continuous state/action/observation dynamics</cite> <cite id="5b6e097c-6">Tight formulations of chance constraints over predicted obstacles require accurate motion/observation models and may need conservative risk levels for safety, impacting throughput</cite>.

- Hybrid estimation–planning loops. <cite id="9b963b71-1">Occlusion-aware consistent MPC shows that fusing estimation updates with replanning and enforcing constraint consistency can sustain safety despite intermittent observations</cite> <cite id="ba7f3706-5">Randomized belief trees blend sampling-based exploration in belief space with goal-directed replanning under partial observability</cite>.

- Baselines and empirical safety margins. <cite id="9b963b71-3">Human-aware methods like BLIND show measurable safety and efficiency improvements from safely resolving ambiguous, occluded conditions</cite> <cite id="9b963b71-1">Sampling-based and estimation-aware MPC can close loops around blind spots when conservative safety margins and obstacle priors are embedded</cite>.

8) Putting it together: an architecture for safe navigation under partial observability with moving obstacles

- A practical stack combines online state estimation (RGB-D/LiDAR/IMU), belief-updating, and decision-theoretic or MPC safety filters. <cite id="9b963b71-1">Occlusion-aware consistent MPC uses receding-horizon avoidance constraints with consistent obstacle/state estimation to handle dense, moving obstacles</cite> <cite id="5b6e097c-1">Chance-constrained MPC with CBFs integrates stochastic obstacle dynamics and observation noise into safety constraints, maintaining feasibility and safety</cite> <cite id="9b963b71-2">Learning-based belief updates (e.g., DreamerNav) integrate egocentric depth, reducing uncertainty about dynamic obstacles</cite> <cite id="ba7f3706-3">Belief-roadmaps or FIRM-like planners drive collision-probability and uncertainty down at each step, ensuring high confidence</cite> <cite id="26e8776e-0">Dynamic safety margins in RL provide adaptive, online padding that grows when risk rises due to occlusions and shrinks as evidence accumulates</cite>.

- When visual occlusions are severe, hybrid human-in-the-loop corrections and tree-based replanning accelerate recovery with provable safety. <cite id="9b963b71-3">Human-guided planning can provably improve safety and teach efficient behaviors under limited observability</cite> <cite id="26e8776e-1">Velocity-Obstacle MCTS enables safe re-planning with minimal obstacle state knowledge and fast online updates</cite>.

9) Emerging directions and research frontiers

- Deeper integration of learning with belief spaces. <cite id="9b963b71-6">Recent formulations treat navigation as a POMDP and integrate learned perception (e.g., depth) to enable agents to cope with occlusions and moving obstacles</cite> <cite id="ba7f3706-0">Latent belief-space dynamic programming handles non-Gaussian beliefs in continuous domains, pointing toward scalable, differentiable solvers</cite>.

- Certified and risk-aware control. <cite id="5b6e097c-2">Robust stability guarantees for barrier-based MPC broaden the class of plants and disturbances for which safety certificates are available</cite> <cite id="26e8776e-5">Safe RL frameworks and dynamic safety margins emphasize verifiability and runtime robustness for navigation in changing scenes</cite>.

Practical guidance: choose a technique that matches system constraints and uncertainty sources. If you need provable invariance amid sudden obstacle emergence, start with barrier/CBF-constrained MPC and wrap with chance constraints tuned to your risk budget. <cite id="5b6e097c-8">Dynamic CBFs are effective for static and moving obstacles</cite> <cite id="5b6e097c-1">Chance constraints quantify residual risk from forecast/observation error and can be enforced online</cite>. If the scene is highly occluded and you must fuse multiple hypotheses, use belief-space planning and replanning with estimation-aware costs; add human guidance where feasible to break ambiguity quickly. <cite id="ba7f3706-3">Belief-space policies reduce collision probability and uncertainty jointly</cite> <cite id="9b963b71-3">Human guidance yields quantifiable safety gains under occlusions</cite>. When learning dominates perception, combine POMDP-style belief updates with safety-aware MPC or safe RL to retain guarantees while exploiting data. <cite id="9b963b71-2">Learning-based POMDP navigation fuses depth and dynamic obstacle handling</cite> <cite id="26e8776e-0">Dynamic safety-margin RL sustains safety during exploration</cite>.

fully_underspecified.text: what are techniques for navigation in environments with obstacles?
fully_underspecified.answer:
Below is a concise, evidence-backed overview of techniques for navigating robots in obstacle-filled environments, grouped by approach, with trade-offs and when to use them.

1) Problem framing and planner taxonomy
- Navigating amidst obstacles is typically solved with a layered system: a global planner computes a collision-free route from a map, while a local planner/avoider reacts to dynamic obstacles and sensor noise in real time.<cite id="fb74913e-0">Path planning and obstacle avoidance in mobile robotics are distinct but complementary functions: planning focuses on finding feasible routes from map information, while avoidance reacts to immediate collisions when obstacles are detected at runtime</cite> <cite id="fb74913e-7">RRTs compute an initial path while artificial potential fields handle real-time obstacle avoidance and trajectory smoothing</cite>.
- Surveys emphasize unifying frameworks that incorporate kinematic/kinodynamic constraints, cost (terrain, risk), and dynamic obstacles, guiding the choice of algorithm class, and many modern methods blend global and local behaviors via potential fields or layered pipelines.<cite id="fb74913e-5">RRT* variants can be aligned with constraints such as dynamic and kinodynamic, enabling cost- and constraint-aware planning</cite> <cite id="fb74913e-7">Artificial potential field methods are designed for real-time obstacle avoidance and can smooth paths produced by tree/graph search</cite>.

2) Grid/lattice and search-based planning on occupancy/cost grids
- Graph/search planners like Dijkstra’s, A*, and their variants remain core for known or partially known environments discretized into grids or lattices; they guarantee optimality under admissible heuristics and are effective for integrating terrain cost and feasibility constraints.<cite id="fb74913e-3">Classic techniques include Dijkstra’s and related grid-based path finding alongside obstacle avoidance strategies</cite> <cite id="fb74913e-0">Surveys summarize grid- and lattice-based planning methods and their theoretical foundations</cite>.
- Concrete improvements address collisions/feasibility during grid search, yielding faster, safer paths. Examples include prioritized, collision-aware A* variants and open-source search frameworks that implement multiple planners and cost models.<cite id="fb74913e-4">A Collision-Aware Improved A* algorithm enhances classical A* with collision checks to avoid path segments that would lead to collisions in grid environments</cite> <cite id="b9572c6a-2">An improved A* algorithm for grid maps integrates lidar/IMU and refines heuristic/cost integration in 2D grids</cite> <cite id="b9572c6a-6">Smac Planner is a search-based planning framework with multiple algorithm implementations for cost-aware, kinematically feasible planning</cite>.
- Time-extended or hybrid approaches handle nonholonomy and continuous maneuvers. Hybrid A* interleaves discrete graph search over feasible motions with continuous space optimization to plan dynamically feasible, near-optimal trajectories for car- or truck-like robots amid obstacles, and remains popular in outdoor/indoor vehicle navigation.<cite id="b9572c6a-0">Hybrid A* combines discrete grid search with continuous-space optimization to enable feasible, optimized trajectories</cite> <cite id="b9572c6a-1">Hybrid A* has been applied to nonholonomic outdoor robots to plan near-optimal paths in mostly unknown environments</cite> <cite id="b9572c6a-3">Hybrid A* is a widely used path planner for car-like robots, combining sampled and graph-based decisions to manage nonholonomic constraints</cite> <cite id="b9572c6a-2">Improved A* variants can incorporate sensor/terrain costs while remaining efficient on grid lattices</cite>.
- Terrain-aware and 3D-aware planners improve path quality in challenging terrains by integrating elevation/roughness and volumetric obstacles. 3D-RRT* and related cost-aware RRT variants maintain path quality across rugged, obstacle-dense terrains.<cite id="fb74913e-4">3D-RRT* maintains path quality in complex terrains, with terrain-aware metrics significantly improving path quality</cite>.

3) Sampling-based motion planning (RRT/RRT* and variants)
- RRTs are indispensable for high-dimensional configuration spaces and kinodynamic constraints, incrementally building trees toward the goal using random samples and nearest-neighbors; RRT* adds asymptotic optimality via a second phase and informative sampling, trading runtime for near-optimal solutions, and has many kinodynamic and constrained variants (e.g., iDb-RRT, EG-RRT).<cite id="3ab3df87-0">RRT is an incremental, random sampling algorithm designed for high-dimensional space problems; it efficiently handles obstacle avoidance scenarios</cite> <cite id="3ab3df87-1">iDb-RRT combines search and optimization for kinodynamic planning within an RRT framework to efficiently handle nonholonomic constraints and obstacles</cite> <cite id="3ab3df87-2">Sampling-based motion planning is a cornerstone paradigm for generating robot motions under constraints</cite> <cite id="3ab3df87-3">An annual review highlights sampling-based planning as fundamental and demonstrates real-time obstacle avoidance for manipulators, with RRTs finding solutions efficiently to single-query problems</cite> <cite id="3ab3df87-4">Informed RRT* focuses planning via optimal sampling, achieving optimal sampling-based path planning for single-query problems</cite> <cite id="3ab3df87-6">EG-RRT efficiently plans motions for systems with internal dynamics and external environmental obstacles, showing the generality of RRT-style methods</cite>.
- Practical surveys and reviews cover breadth and trade-offs: sampling-based planners handle unknown or changing spaces, kinodynamic feasibility, manipulator obstacle avoidance, and can be tuned for real-time operation; they are often complemented by local potential/field methods for reactive adjustments.<cite id="3ab3df87-0">RRT’s design addresses obstacle avoidance in high-dimensional spaces</cite> <cite id="3ab3df87-3">Sampling-based methods are used for real-time obstacle avoidance and single-query efficiency, underpinning rapid deployment in dynamic environments</cite> <cite id="fb74913e-7">Artificial Potential Field methods are used for real-time obstacle avoidance and smoothing alongside tree-based global paths</cite>.

4) Local reactive and field-based methods for obstacle avoidance
- Reactive navigation methods (e.g., Bug algorithms) provably solve exploration/avoidance by following boundary-following or goal-directed rules when obstacles occlude the global path; they require no prior map but may traverse extra detours in cluttered areas.<cite id="fb74913e-3">Surveys include classic reactive obstacle avoidance like Bug algorithms alongside classic graph-based methods</cite>.
- Vector field and potential field techniques synthesize steering forces to obstacles and the goal for real-time avoidance and path smoothing; they are simple, continuous, and integrate well with perception uncertainties but can suffer from local minima and oscillations without hybridization with search or control.<cite id="fb74913e-7">Artificial Potential Field methods handle real-time obstacle avoidance and trajectory smoothing, often complementing RRT-generated paths</cite> <cite id="fb74913e-0">Surveys highlight vector-field and potential-field obstacle avoidance among fundamental techniques used in practice</cite>.
- Velocity-Obstacle (VO) methods represent obstacles as forbidden velocity sets and compute safe velocity/heading adjustments online; they are effective for known obstacle geometries and kinematics and are closely related to potential-field steering in reactive layers. (See also related survey contexts for reactive and field-based avoidance summarized in Section 1 and specific method overviews in Section 3; these approaches are commonly combined with global search.)

5) Autonomous exploration and frontier-based mapping
- Frontier-based exploration drives robots to maximally informative, reachable borders between known free space and unknown regions; it incrementally expands a map and guides global goals until the environment is fully explored. Classic formulations use Yamauchi frontiers (depth-first frontier selection) and have been refined with improved frontier definitions, prioritization, and deep reinforcement learning to pick exploration goals in unknown or partially unknown maps.<cite id="50dc0e64-6">Frontiers are defined as boundaries between open space and unexplored space; exploring each frontier reveals reachable locations and expands the map</cite> <cite id="50dc0e64-5">The frontier algorithm uses depth-first search to drive a robot to the nearest frontier, enabling efficient exploration and mapping</cite> <cite id="50dc0e64-2">Improved frontier-based exploration uses deep reinforcement learning to select target points, enhancing exploration efficiency</cite> <cite id="50dc0e64-0">A frontier-based exploration algorithm integrates mapping, navigation, localization, and obstacle avoidance to autonomously reach and explore frontiers</cite> <cite id="50dc0e64-3">Frontier-based strategies can be embedded in higher-level control loops for autonomous, comprehensive mapping of unknown environments</cite> <cite id="50dc0e64-1">Frontier-based navigation removes the need for a priori maps by using frontier selection to guide obstacle-avoiding exploration</cite>.
- Integration with A*/heuristic search is common: robots maintain a known map with frontiers prioritized by information (e.g., entropy, reachability) and select the most “valuable” frontier as the next goal, returning to plan and re-optimzie when necessary.<cite id="50dc0e64-6">Frontier-based exploration defines and explores regions along boundaries to map previously unexplored areas</cite> <cite id="50dc0e64-5">Depth-first frontier traversal efficiently connects a robot to successive frontiers as they are created</cite>.

6) Optimization- and control-based planners (including MPC and tube/MPC)
- For robots with accurate kinematic models and short horizons, optimization-based motion planners (including MPC and sampled-constraint MPC/tube MPC) can directly maximize safety and performance subject to obstacle constraints and dynamics; such methods are often paired with sampling-based global replanning to maintain feasibility and robustness to model mismatch and disturbances.<cite id="3ab3df87-3">Surveys note optimization-based, real-time obstacle avoidance settings for manipulators and high-dimensional motion planning</cite> <cite id="3ab3df87-2">Sampling- and optimization-based paradigms are both fundamental; modern frameworks often combine them (e.g., search plus reactive optimization)</cite>.
- Terrain-aware planning cost functions and safe tubes around nominal trajectories, learned or hand-crafted, can keep paths above obstacles and rough terrain while maintaining smooth, dynamically feasible motions; empirical studies show large improvements in path quality over naive planners.<cite id="fb74913e-4">Terrain-aware metrics with 3D-RRT* significantly improve path quality and maintain quality in challenging terrains</cite> <cite id="3ab3df87-1">Kinodynamic RRT variants integrate optimization within the tree growth to maintain feasible, obstacle-avoiding motions</cite>.

7) Multi-robot obstacle coordination and deconfliction
- For multiple robots sharing obstacle-strewn spaces, two main strategies are used: (1) centralized coordination that assigns routes and temporally sequences robots to avoid collisions; (2) decentralized negotiation where robots exchange intentions and replan with mutual avoidance constraints; in both cases, RRT* variants, cost maps, and potential-field repulsion layers are common, sometimes embedded within MAPF (multi-agent path finding) solvers for tight corridors and dynamic environments.<cite id="fb74913e-5">RRT* variants and decision maps align with constraints including dynamic and kinodynamic settings, enabling application to multi-vehicle planning under obstacle avoidance</cite> <cite id="fb74913e-0">Surveys of mobile-robot navigation report diverse obstacle avoidance methods suitable for multi-robot contexts, including tree search and potential-field layers</cite>. 
- These approaches are prevalent in industrial and UAV domains where robots must share 3D volumes; RRT-based planning plus potential-field repulsion yields tractable deconfliction with performance guarantees in single-query regimes, often coupled with runtime collision checking and replanning.<cite id="fb74913e-3">Industrial robot path planning surveys emphasize RRT-based techniques and potential-field avoidance for collision-free shared spaces</cite> <cite id="fb74913e-1">Recent RRT-focused reviews detail how RRT and its variants improve industrial path planning with obstacle avoidance</cite>.

8) Putting it together: practical stacks and selection guidance
- A widely used stack is ROS-integrated Hybrid A*/A* for global paths on grid costmaps, plus a reactive layer (e.g., artificial potential fields or VO) for local obstacle avoidance and differential-drive or car-like controllers for tracking; sampling-based planners are preferred when kinematics/dynamics are complex or spaces are high-dimensional and unknown, with local field/VO for online safety.<cite id="b9572c6a-5">Hybrid A* implementations exist in C++/ROS with visualization for real robot path planning</cite> <cite id="b9572c6a-2">Improved A* on lidar/IMU-equipped platforms shows how sensor-driven cost grids operationalize grid-based planning with obstacle awareness</cite> <cite id="fb74913e-7">Separating path planning from real-time obstacle avoidance is effective, with RRT for global paths and potential fields for local avoidance and smoothing</cite>.
- For mapping and structured environments, combine frontier-based exploration with global search/planning and local avoidance to expand maps efficiently while maintaining safety; in unknown terrains, terrain-aware planners (3D-RRT*) yield superior path quality over naive methods.<cite id="50dc0e64-2">Deep RL frontier selection improves the efficiency of reaching and exploring informative frontiers</cite> <cite id="fb74913e-4">3D-RRT* maintains path quality in rugged, obstacle-rich terrains via terrain-aware metrics</cite>.
- Choice-of-method: 
  • Known/simple geometries: A*/Dijkstra with admissible heuristics and potential-field repulsion layers, or Hybrid A* for car-like robots.<cite id="b9572c6a-1">Hybrid A* plans near-optimal paths for nonholonomic robots in unknown environments</cite> <cite id="fb74913e-0">Grid/lattice A* lies at the foundation of practical obstacle avoidance in mobile robotics</cite>. 
  • High-dimensional/kinodynamic robots or unknown/crowded spaces: RRT/RRT* and kinodynamic variants with local avoidance; integrate with perception via costmaps and dynamic re-planning.<cite id="3ab3df87-1">Kinodynamic planners like iDb-RRT integrate search and optimization within RRT to handle nonholonomic constraints and obstacles</cite> <cite id="3ab3df87-3">Sampling-based planners deliver real-time obstacle avoidance performance and efficient single-query solutions</cite>. 
  • Fast-moving obstacles and reactive safety: Potential fields and VO with obstacle inflation/velocity masks, used in local controllers; combine with global plans from search/sampling for long-horizon goals.<cite id="fb74913e-7">Artificial Potential Fields are used specifically for real-time obstacle avoidance, often paired with global path planners</cite>. 
  • Multi-robot missions: Use RRT* variants with centralized or decentralized conflict resolution (time windows, potential-field social forces) and maintain per-robot safety margins on shared cost grids.<cite id="fb74913e-5">RRT* families and decision maps organize strategies for dynamic/kinodynamic constraints useful in multi-robot obstacle avoidance</cite> <cite id="fb74913e-3">Industrial/mobile-robot surveys report practical obstacle avoidance methods applicable to multi-robot coordination</cite>.

Summary: Effective obstacle navigation uses layered planning—global path search (A*, Hybrid A*, RRT/RRT*), local avoidance (potential/velocity obstacles and reactive strategies), and autonomous mapping (frontier-based exploration)—augmented by cost models for terrain/risk and controller-level safety; sampling-based methods dominate when configuration spaces are high-dimensional or unknown, while search-based planners and field methods remain efficient and interpretable for structured environments. <cite id="fb74913e-0">Surveys consolidate these families and their roles in mobile-robot obstacle navigation</cite> <cite id="fb74913e-3">They document classic search and Bug-like reactive approaches, industrial applications, and trade-offs</cite> <cite id="3ab3df87-2">and establish sampling-based planning as a cornerstone</cite> <cite id="fb74913e-7">with potential fields for real-time avoidance and smoothing</cite> <cite id="50dc0e64-6">and frontier-based exploration for mapping unknown spaces</cite>.
