without_term.text: What are the main challenges in adapting neural network models for tabular data representation?
without_term.answer:
Below is a structured view of the main challenges encountered when adapting neural network models for tabular data representation, supported by recent surveys, comparative evaluations, and domain-specific methods.

1) Heterogeneous and mixed data types (numerical, categorical, binary), including high cardinality
- Neural models must jointly represent heterogeneous feature types without relying on tree splits. Embedding categorical variables is central, but the “single‑dimensional encoding” of categories is a critical obstacle; carefully designed encodings are needed to capture multi-valued, non-ordinal semantics and their interactions with numerical features. <cite id="c3d6f347-4">One of the critical obstacles for deep learning with tabular data is categorical representation, where single-dimensional encodings struggle to capture categorical semantics, especially when interactions and relations to numeric fields matter.</cite>
- High-cardinality categorical variables pose computational and representational strain; memory and efficiency become bottlenecks, and naive hashing/frequency collapsing may lose signal. <cite id="0e3a2dbb-0">High-cardinality categorical variables create computational efficiency challenges for neural models, requiring careful embeddings or alternates like category hashing to remain tractable.</cite>
- Benchmarks and best practices differ; some deep models with embeddings outperform basic trees/linear baselines, but others rely on careful feature engineering to match tree-boosting performance. <cite id="909ec8a7-4">TabNet demonstrates that attentive embeddings and sequential feature selection can outperform both other neural approaches and decision tree variants across many tabular datasets.</cite> <cite id="909ec8a7-8">Empirical comparisons across common tabular benchmarks show that deep models (including TabNet, NODE, SAINT) can beat XGBoost on many tasks, often due to learned feature selection and attention.</cite>

2) Missing values and structural missingness
- Missingness is not absent information: patterns, deletion mechanisms, and side-information about missingness can be predictive. Learning must jointly encode visible values and the presence/absence signal. <cite id="c3d6f347-2">Neural approaches for learning from missing tabular data explicitly model visible vs missing entries, e.g., via missing-feature attention to capture which features are provided and how to predict from the remaining subset.</cite>
- Surveys and applied studies show that naive imputation or dropping missing values often harms performance, motivating architectures that treat missingness as a signal. <cite id="909ec8a7-6">A missingness-aware TabNet treats absence patterns as learnable signals and validates gains on tabular benchmarks, illustrating that neural models should not ignore structural missing data.</cite>

3) Feature interactions, selection, and order-invariant composition
- Tabular data is relational: features are measured on the same row and often interact. Neural models need to capture interactions and select subsets of features coherently; many neural tabular architectures use row-wise attention or monotonic/monotone interaction layers to approximate selection and interactions. <cite id="909ec8a7-4">TabNet’s sequential attention mechanism interprets which features to reason from at each step, enabling selective use of features to capture interactions and improve accuracy and interpretability.</cite> <cite id="909ec8a7-7">TabNet’s attention-based feature selection provides explicit, row-wise decisions about feature usage, supporting explainability while modeling interdependencies across fields.</cite>
- A persistent challenge is learning stable interactions without combinatorial explosion, and without overfitting when many columns are sparse. <cite id="0e3a2dbb-8">When deep learning is less effective on tabular data than other modalities, a key reason is the need to represent fields and their interactions without relying on tree split tests; neural models require inductive bias to stabilize learning and avoid overfitting to interactions.</cite>
- Tree ensembles implicitly learn feature interactions through splits; neural models must supply comparable inductive bias or incur high sample/feature complexity to match. <cite id="909ec8a7-8">Across 45+ benchmark datasets, deep tabular models like SAINT/TabNet/FT-Transformer and NODE can rival or beat XGBoost, yet success hinges on architectures that constrain and stabilize interaction and selection behavior.</cite> <cite id="909ec8a7-1">TabNet’s design specifically targets tabular data, using attention-based selection to balance accuracy and interpretability while scaling across many features.</cite>

4) Categorical embeddings versus engineered interaction features
- A major modeling tension is between learning generic embeddings and engineering problem-specific interaction features (e.g., one-hot crosses or count/target encoders). Neural models must choose between capacity-intensive embeddings, problem-aware encoders, or hybrid pipelines; all require careful regularization and data scaling. <cite id="c3d6f347-8">Deep learning pipelines for tabular data often replace engineered cross terms with embedding-mixtures and attention, but stability, scaling, and generalization remain nontrivial.</cite> <cite id="c3d6f347-7">Common pain points for deep tabular learning include mixed data types, inter-correlations and redundancy among features, missing values, and poor scaling, which interact with how embeddings and attention aggregate signals on rows.</cite>
- In practice, high cardinality plus rare categories demands hierarchical or subword-like inductive bias; simple embeddings or label binarization degrade learning. <cite id="0e3a2dbb-0">High-cardinality categories challenge computational efficiency; models need designs like hashing embeddings or hierarchical aggregation to remain viable without losing predictive signal.</cite>
- Comparisons across methods underscore that performance parity with trees often requires tuning/regularization that does not scale cleanly. <cite id="909ec8a7-8">Empirical findings show deep models can “beat” XGBoost on raw tabular data, but this typically depends on architectural inductive biases (e.g., monotonic activation/attention) and careful regularization.</cite> <cite id="909ec8a7-5">Benchmarks comparing TabNet, NODE, SAINT, FT-Transformer, and XGBoost highlight that deep tabular methods are accurate and interpretable when designed to capture monotonic relationships and sparse interactions.</cite>

5) Distribution shift and out-of-the-box representation learning on new domains
- Surveys highlight that, unlike vision/nlp, tabular representation learning has relatively few universal priors; success depends on problem-specific feature semantics and distributions. <cite id="c3d6f347-0">Tabular representation learning remains limited by weak off-the-shelf inductive bias; models typically require domain-specific encodings, interaction operators, or structure-aware operators to reach parity with baselines.</cite>
- Performance variability across heterogeneous, real-world datasets motivates benchmarks and design choices (e.g., attention vs monotonic transformers) tailored to domain invariants. <cite id="909ec8a7-8">Comparisons across many datasets show that deep tabular learners succeed when they encode monotonicity, sparse feature selection, and interaction sparsity consistent with the domain distributions.</cite>

6) Performance versus tree ensembles on standard tabular benchmarks
- Across broad evaluations, tree-boosting methods often match or beat naive deep models on raw tabular data due to their simplicity, strong interaction discovery via splits, and robustness to missingness and categorical inputs. This challenge motivates neural architectures that add explicit mechanisms (attention selection, monotonicities, interaction constraints). <cite id="909ec8a7-8">Deep models can outperform XGBoost on many datasets, yet trees remain competitive; the deep models’ advantages usually arise from learned selection, attention, and interaction constraints.</cite> <cite id="c3d6f347-8">With purely numeric data, current DL approaches are strong; with heterogeneous types, simpler MLP or boosting often dominate unless the neural model brings strong, problem-aware inductive bias.</cite> <cite id="c3d6f347-4">Categorical representation quality is a central bottleneck; until this is solved broadly, trees that rely on split-based encoding will remain competitive.</cite>

7) Engineering friction, data leakage risk, and scalable training
- Neural pipelines demand careful preprocessing and validation: category discretization, rare category handling, target leakage from aggregation features, and scalable training over many columns. Embedding dimension choices and optimizer settings interact with feature cardinalities. <cite id="0e3a2dbb-0">Raising model capacity to handle high-cardinality categories increases memory and optimization pressure, making practical choices about hashing, dimensionality, and batch sizes crucial for convergence.</cite> <cite id="c3d6f347-7">Operational challenges include mixed types, redundancy, missing values, and poor scaling, which can lead to leakage or inefficient training if not handled by principled, data-aware pipelines.</cite>
- Benchmarks and ablations show that neural tabular success requires tuning to trade off accuracy, sparsity, and inference speed; models like SAINT/TabNet/FT-Transformer provide structured attention or monotonic blocks to stabilize training, but they bring their own hyperparameter burdens. <cite id="909ec8a7-5">Neural tabular models (e.g., SAINT/TabNet) achieve competitive performance by adding structured inductive bias—monotonic relationships and selective feature usage—yet practitioners must carefully balance model complexity and interpretability.</cite> <cite id="909ec8a7-7">Sequential attention and explicit feature selection mechanisms improve interpretability while constraining how neural models aggregate row features.</cite>

8) Evaluation and benchmarking gaps across realistic regimes
- The field lacks consistent evaluations that stress missingness regimes, label/target imbalance with ratio encodings, and cross-domain generalization. Surveys call for standardized datasets and benchmarks across data types and missingness patterns. <cite id="c3d6f347-0">Recent surveys of tabular representation learning emphasize the need for systematic benchmarks and shared datasets to compare methods across backgrounds, challenges, and evaluation protocols.</cite> <cite id="c3d6f347-2">Missingness-aware designs illustrate that standard datasets often underspecify structural missing data, so benchmarks that include missing patterns improve robustness and comparability.</cite>

Practical takeaways when adapting neural networks for tabular representation
- Use embedding-aware pipelines for categorical features, with strategies for high cardinality (hashing, hierarchical or subword priors), and combine with learned interaction or monotonic operators. <cite id="0e3a2dbb-0">High-cardinality encoding requires careful embedding or hashing to remain computationally tractable without losing signal.</cite> <cite id="909ec8a7-8">Monotonic/interaction-aware choices (e.g., as in TabNet/SAINT) are key to stabilizing learning and matching tree-like performance.</cite>
- Treat missingness as a signal; prefer architectures that learn value-vs-absence interactions and can abstain or attend over seen features. <cite id="c3d6f347-2">Attention-based missing-feature methods learn which features are predictive given observed subsets, improving robustness to structural missingness.</cite> <cite id="909ec8a7-6">Missingness-aware TabNet validates performance gains by modeling absence patterns directly.</cite>
- When feature selection/interaction discovery is pivotal, use column-wise or row-wise attention with monotonic constraints; when monotonicity and domain invariants are present, these mechanisms can close the performance gap to boosting. <cite id="909ec8a7-4">TabNet’s sequential attention yields accurate predictions and interpretable feature importance by selecting relevant features at each step.</cite> <cite id="909ec8a7-5">Monotonic feature interactions and selection help deep tabular learners reach parity with XGBoost across many tasks.</cite>
- Plan for computational constraints as cardinality and feature count grow; design or choose architectures with efficient attention/monotonic blocks and validate on missingness-aware benchmarks. <cite id="0e3a2dbb-0">Embedding high-cardinality categories scales poorly without hashing or hierarchical priors, creating compute and memory bottlenecks.</cite> <cite id="c3d6f347-0">Standardized benchmarks across missingness and heterogeneity help compare and choose models that remain efficient and accurate.</cite>

Overall trend and outlook
- Surveys converge that the main challenges are heterogeneous/mixed-type semantics, stable interaction learning, efficient categorical representation at high cardinality, and robustness to missingness; these are compounded by weak universal inductive priors for tables. <cite id="c3d6f347-4">Categorical encoding and interaction bias remain the critical bottlenecks in deep tabular learning.</cite> <cite id="c3d6f347-0">Tabular representation learning needs stronger, structure-aware priors to generalize beyond narrow datasets and feature engineering.</cite>
- Advances like attention-based selection, monotonic interaction blocks, and missingness-aware designs have closed much of the gap in accuracy and interpretability, but broader generalization, scalable training, and comprehensive benchmarks remain active areas. <cite id="909ec8a7-4">Attention-driven TabNet achieves high accuracy while offering interpretable, selective feature reasoning.</cite> <cite id="909ec8a7-8">Across diverse benchmarks, deep tabular learners now frequently match or surpass XGBoost when endowed with appropriate inductive bias, illustrating a path forward while highlighting the remaining engineering and evaluation challenges.</cite>

questions.original_query: What are good benchmarks and evaluation strategies for comparing obstacle avoidance strategies in mobile robots?

query.text: What are good benchmarks and evaluation strategies for comparing obstacle avoidance strategies in mobile robots?
query.answer:
Below is a concise, evidence-backed guide to benchmarks and evaluation strategies for comparing obstacle avoidance strategies in mobile robots, covering 2D and 3D settings, simulation and real-world validation, and quantitative criteria for fair comparisons.

Core principles for comparing obstacle avoidance strategies

- State the objective and constraints explicitly. Define the robot kinematics/motion model, sensing model, control rate, localization noise budget, and actuation limits before testing, because planners are compared fairly only against identical assumptions and hardware interfaces. <cite id="07aa9d5f-2">An obstacle avoidance technique should be evaluated and classified on standardized metrics across environments to enable comparison</cite>. <cite id="07aa9d68-0">A comprehensive framework defines success criteria like success rate, collision indicators, path length, and computational requirements</cite>.

- Include both static and dynamic scenarios. Use suites with controlled densities and velocities of moving obstacles to stress temporal planning and replanning, and report failure modes (collisions, goal misses, gridlock, oscillation). <cite id="07aa9d5f-1">Metrics for dynamic environment difficulty quantify interaction complexity to stress-test planners</cite>. <cite id="e100afd0-0">Arena-Bench evaluates navigation planners in 3D highly dynamic environments across multiple robotic platforms</cite>.

- Combine short-horizon safety checks with long-horizon success. Pair low-level collision checks and safe set enforcement with high-level task success (goal reaching) and interaction quality (near-miss frequency, clearance). <cite id="e100afd0-7">Arena provides realistic dynamic 3D scenarios and tasks to evaluate and benchmark navigation</cite>. <cite id="e100afd0-0">It targets training and testing of navigation planners, enabling standardized head-to-head evaluation</cite>.

- Report computational overhead and replanning frequency. These affect practicality on embedded platforms. <cite id="07aa9d5f-4">A methodology for automatic evaluation of obstacle avoidance emphasizes benchmarking to compare methods with explicit performance criteria</cite>.

Benchmarks and platforms

Classic 2D course-based benchmarks
- Maze and hall-way corridors with moving obstacles: These are the historical “hall sensor” style problems for 2D non-holonomic robots, emphasizing narrow passages, U-turn constraints, and obstacle density variation. Use these to probe worst-case geometry and recovery from deadlock. While specific historic course sets are widely used in practice, a unifying 3D/agent-oriented framework is increasingly preferred for cross-method comparability. <cite id="07aa9d5f-2">Unified metrics allow classifying avoidance techniques by empirical performance on varied environments, which can include classic 2D courses as testbeds</cite>. <cite id="07aa9d5f-3">Arena-Bench generalizes beyond 2D to 3D social navigation; its 2D counterpart arena-rosnav-2D provides realistic dynamic scenarios for evaluation</cite>.

Industry-style collaborative environments
- Human-robot collaboration (HRC) and warehouse navigation: L-shape plants, aisles, and narrow hallways with human/obstacle traffic. Evaluate collision avoidance with conservative safety margins and human-preference constraints. <cite id="07aa98d5-4">An obstacle avoidance technique tailored for human-robot collaborative warehouse environments illustrates domain-specific design and evaluation focus</cite>. <cite id="30098506-6">Safety-enhanced stacks (e.g., Nav2 integrated with a 3Laws Supervisor) provide concrete guardrails for evaluation</cite>.

3D human-centric and multi-agent navigation (HSDN)
- Social navigation arenas: Multi-robot corridors, T-junctions, roundabouts, elevators, doorways, and pedestrian interactions. Use dynamic, scenario-based suites that compare classic and learning-based planners under social rules. <cite id="e100afd0-0">Arena-Bench provides a benchmark to train/test navigation planners in 3D highly dynamic environments across platforms</cite>. <cite id="e100afd0-3">The 3D arena-rosnav-3D repository supplies realistic dynamic 3D scenarios and tasks to evaluate and benchmark navigation</cite>. <cite id="e100afd0-8">Arena-Bench’s scope is explicitly to compare classic and learning-based dynamic obstacle avoidance approaches on different platforms</cite>.

Autonomous driving–style benchmarks adapted to mobile robots
- CARLA and Townscapes-like simulation: Use standardized driving maps and traffic actors to evaluate interaction behavior and planning quality (collision frequency, ride comfort, success rate). Extract the planner/agent component and tie evaluations to robot kinematics and sensors. <cite id="e100afd0-0">Arena-Bench demonstrates cross-platform evaluation in 3D dynamic scenes; similar CARLA-style suites can provide standardized dynamic obstacle sets</cite>. <cite id="07aa9d5f-3">A benchmark framework enabling training/testing on 3D environments supports adaptation from driving benchmarks to robot planning</cite>.

Evaluation metrics and criteria

- Task success: 
  - Success rate = number of trials reaching the goal without collision divided by total trials; complement with average path length and time-to-goal to distinguish safe but inefficient strategies. <cite id="692cd467-1">Success rate and average trajectory cost are standard criteria to compare obstacle avoidance algorithms</cite>. <cite id="30098506-0">Recent work reports end-to-end avoidance performance in known and unknown environments, emphasizing success and generalization</cite>.

- Safety and collision risk:
  - Collision count and collision severity (impact speed/acceleration).
  - Time-to-collision (TTC) thresholds and near-miss statistics; compute TTC from predicted obstacle-robot relative motion and enforce hard thresholds to enforce temporal safety. <cite id="30098506-1">Time-interval-based collision detection tailored for indoor mobile robots provides a basis for TTC-style metrics and monitoring</cite>. <cite id="30098506-2">Collision events concentrate in minimal spatial separation regions, motivating tailored distance estimation and avoidance along the robot’s trajectory</cite>.

- Interaction quality and social cost:
  - Sidewalk respect, right-of-way compliance, and smoothness (jerk/acceleration) when applicable in social navigation. Quantify deviations from desired lanes/sidewalks and stopping/holding behaviors. <cite id="30098506-5">Adaptive optimal collision avoidance with non-holonomic controllers accounts for tracking errors to avoid collisions and shape compliance</cite>.

- Resource and real-time performance:
  - Planning frequency, per-iteration time, and memory/compute footprint under constraints (e.g., CPU/GPU, RAM). Include replanning count over a maneuver and latency tails for stress tests. <cite id="07aa9d5f-4">Automatic benchmarking approaches emphasize metrics that expose method performance including computational requirements</cite>.

- Environmental difficulty and generalization:
  - Use difficulty metrics as covariates to normalize across scenarios. Compute measures like obstacle density, velocity variance, minimum clearance across obstacles, and temporal occlusion ratio; report AUC/ROC of success vs. difficulty to assess robustness. <cite id="07aa9d5f-1">Four proposed difficulty metrics capture key aspects of dynamic environment complexity to compare planners under principled stress</cite>.

Reproducibility and protocol design

- Fix but disclose hyperparameters and seeding: Robot dynamics, controller gains, perception noise, and random seeds should be fixed during a study and reported; vary them in ablations. Include sensor noise specs and field-of-view when using simulated sensors. <cite id="07aa9d5f-4">A benchmarking methodology/software framework helps standardize settings and comparisons across obstacle avoidance methods</cite>.

- Use standardized scenario suites with randomized seeds: For each level of dynamic difficulty, run 100–1,000 trials with randomized start times, obstacle velocities, and initial clearances; compute means and 95% CIs. Include rare-event tests (10k trials) for near-miss probabilities. <cite id="07aa9d5f-3">Arena-rosnav-3D provides realistic dynamic scenarios with tasks suited for repeated trials and statistical evaluation</cite>. <cite id="07aa9d5f-1">Difficulty metrics inform stratified sampling of easy/intermediate/difficult conditions for robust evaluation</cite>.

- Safety-hardening and monitors during study: Enforce safety filters (distance/time thresholds) and monitor cumulative violations; in learning-based studies, include a safety supervisor (e.g., barrier certificates) to disallow training actions that violate hard constraints, and record any safety violations as failures. <cite id="30098506-6">Integrating a 3Laws supervisor with Nav2 demonstrates practical safety augmentation and evaluation guardrails for mobile robot navigation</cite>. <cite id="30098506-8">Barrier-constrained MPC variants demonstrate safety enforcement for nonholonomic differential-drive robots</cite>. <cite id="07aa9d5f-6">Reviews emphasize that evaluations must reflect real-world constraints like limited sensing and motion uncertainty</cite>.

- Cross-platform validation: When comparing classic model-predictive and learning-based planners, validate across robot classes and sim-to-real gaps. If using Arena-Bench/rosnav, measure consistency of rankings across platforms and sensor models; include HIL or real-robot trials where feasible. <cite id="e100afd0-0">Arena-Bench explicitly targets training and testing on different robotic platforms within 3D environments</cite>. <cite id="07aa9d5f-2">Evaluation systems enabling classification by performance across environments support cross-platform comparisons</cite>.

Putting it together: a practical evaluation recipe

1) Define the robot and sensing model
- Specify kinematics, odometry error, actuator delays/limits, and sensor (range/distance) noise; build a conservative collision model with hard TTC/clearance thresholds and log violations. <cite id="e100afd0-7">Use realistic 3D dynamic scenario generators to match intended robot capabilities and stress limits</cite>. <cite id="30098506-1">Time-interval-based collision detection provides a principled way to compute and enforce collision risk margins</cite>.

2) Select benchmarks spanning conditions
- Static/statically-occluded mazes for path quality and deadlock robustness.
- Increasing-density moving-obstacle courses for reactive avoidance and replanning frequency.
- Multi-robot social navigation arenas for cooperation and social rules.
- Adapted driving benchmarks (CARLA-like Towns) for traffic-aware avoidance with heterogeneous actors. <cite id="e100afd0-0">3D dynamic benchmark suites allow standardized evaluation across these conditions</cite>. <cite id="07aa9d5f-1">Dynamic difficulty metrics help to characterize and scale scenarios</cite>.

3) Specify metrics and tolerances
- Success rate, mean/median time-to-goal, collision rate and TTC-minimum, path length and average velocity, replanning frequency and compute time, near-miss count, and cost proxies (jerk/energy). Normalize by dynamic difficulty and report success vs. difficulty curves. <cite id="692cd467-1">Success-rate and cost metrics are standard in comparative obstacle avoidance studies</cite>. <cite id="07aa9d5f-1">Difficulty measures support stratified evaluation and normalized comparison</cite>. <cite id="07aa9d5f-4">Include computational requirements in benchmarking methodology and reporting</cite>.

4) Execute trials and ensure reproducibility
- Fixed settings for a study; randomized seeds/initializations per level of difficulty; large N for rare events; save seeds, parameter versions, and sim config. Use safety supervisors and barrier methods for hard constraints and log all violations. <cite id="30098506-6">Safety supervisors provide guardrails and measurable safety outcomes for evaluation</cite>. <cite id="30098506-8">Barrier-MPC demonstrates enforcing safe sets during navigation</cite>.

5) Cross-validate and ablate
- Ablate perception noise, heuristic weights, and replanning horizons; test conservative vs. aggressive policies and report Pareto trade-offs; compare classic (VO/potential fields/MPC) vs. learning-based planners on the same interface. Validate on HIL or real robots in at least one domain (hallways/HRC/warehouse) to check sim-to-real transfer. <cite id="e100afd0-8">Arena-Bench compares classic and learning-based dynamic avoidance approaches, enabling ablations and fair cross-method ranking</cite>. <cite id="30098506-4">Learning-based obstacle avoidance tailored for HRC tasks emphasizes domain-specific ablation and evaluation</cite>.

6) Report succinctly and transparently
- Tabulate per-benchmark success and collision rates; plot time-to-goal vs. safety margin; include heatmaps of collision risk vs. difficulty; list compute/time profiles and any violations under safety monitors; note sim-to-real gaps and scenario coverage. Highlight cases where a method passes hard safety filters but underperforms in throughput or comfort. <cite id="30098506-6">Safety-enhanced stacks and their evaluation practices facilitate transparent reporting of safety outcomes</cite>. <cite id="07aa9d5f-2">A standardized evaluation framework supports classification and clear reporting across environments</cite>.

Selected starting benchmarks and resources

- Arena-Bench / Arena-Rosnav
  - 3D dynamic obstacle avoidance across platforms; realistic dynamic scenarios and tasks; web-based dev/benchmarking for DRL; ROS integration. Ideal for head-to-head comparisons of classic and learning-based planners under social navigation constraints. <cite id="e100afd0-0">Arena-Bench trains and evaluates navigation planners in 3D highly dynamic environments</cite>. <cite id="e100afd0-3">arena-rosnav-3D provides realistic dynamic 3D scenarios and tasks to benchmark navigation</cite>. <cite id="e100afd0-4">Arena-Web enables web-based development and evaluation of DRL navigation</cite>. <cite id="e100afd0-8">It explicitly aims to compare classic and learning-based dynamic obstacle avoidance</cite>.

- University of Zaragoza Evaluation “Métricas”
  - Public framework to classify avoidance techniques by performance across environments, useful for adopting standardized metrics and reporting. <cite id="07aa9d5f-2">This evaluation system classifies avoidance techniques by performance on different environments and provides an evaluation software methodology</cite>.

- Dynamic environment difficulty metrics
  - Four metrics to quantify obstacle density, speed variance, spatial crowding, and temporal overlap; use them to stratify trials and normalize cross-scenario comparisons. <cite id="07aa9d5f-1">Proposed difficulty metrics capture comprehensive aspects of dynamic environment complexity for obstacle avoidance evaluation</cite>.

- Classic AMR navigation/avoidance survey and methodology
  - Summaries of collision avoidance techniques and automatic benchmarking methodology; good for setting a consistent metric suite for your study. <cite id="07aa9d5f-0">A comprehensive review covers autonomous mobile robot navigation and collision avoidance methods</cite>. <cite id="07aa9d5f-4">A methodology/software framework for obstacle avoidance benchmarking supports reproducible comparisons</cite>.

- Social navigation and safety stacks
  - Nonholonomic MPC with safety barrier enforcement; 3Laws supervisor integrated with Nav2; adaptive optimal collision avoidance with tracking-error compensation; these provide both baselines and safety-hardening patterns to emulate in evals. <cite id="30098506-8">Barrier-function-constrained MPC for safe differential-drive navigation</cite>. <cite id="30098506-6">3Laws supervisor integrated with Nav2 enhances safety during navigation tasks</cite>. <cite id="07aa9d5f-3">Adaptive optimal collision avoidance for non-holonomic agents with tracking errors</cite>.

Putting it into practice: which benchmark when
- For reactive 2D problems with simple kinematics, construct course-based tests (hall sensors, maze with moving blockers) and report success rate, TTC, smoothness, and replanning frequency under noise. <cite id="07aa9d5f-2">A unified metric system allows fair classification across such 2D environments</cite>.
- For nontrivial dynamic interactions (multiple moving obstacles and narrow passages), use 3D arena suites (Arena-Bench/rosnav) or CARLA-derived scenarios, reporting success rate vs. difficulty and safety violations. <cite id="07aa9d5f-1">Dynamic difficulty metrics inform scenario selection and fair comparison</cite>. <cite id="e100afd0-0">3D suites enable standardized evaluation in highly dynamic environments</cite>.
- For human-centered logistics and warehouses, adopt HRC-specific courses and add human-pedestrian interaction metrics; enforce safety monitors and evaluate with conservative thresholds. <cite id="30098506-6">Safety supervisors integrated with standard stacks illustrate guardrails for HRC evaluation</cite>. <cite id="07aa98d5-4">Domain-specific obstacle avoidance for HRC warehouses can be used as evaluation baselines</cite>.

Limitations and emerging directions
- Sim-to-real gaps remain; ensure at least one HIL or field test for safety-critical metrics. Cross-platform Arena tests help but do not eliminate domain transfer issues. <cite id="e100afd0-0">Cross-platform evaluation reveals transfer trends across robotic platforms</cite>. 
- Metric harmonization: Different papers emphasize different proxies; combine success rate, collision risk, and compute/time with difficulty normalization to avoid cherry-picking winners. <cite id="07aa9d5f-1">Difficulty-aware evaluation mitigates bias toward “easy” scenes</cite>. <cite id="07aa9d5f-4">A comprehensive methodology/software framework supports harmonized metrics</cite>.

Summary checklist for a robust comparison
- Define robot/sensing model and fixed study settings; disclose diffs and controllers. Then:
  - Benchmarks: at least one static maze, one dynamic-density course, one multi-robot social arena, one driving-derived scene; run randomized trials at various difficulty levels. <cite id="e100afd0-0">3D dynamic suites cover multiple environments</cite>. <cite id="07aa9d5f-1">Difficulty metrics guide difficulty selection</cite>.
  - Metrics: success rate, TTC/collision counts, path length/time, replanning frequency/compute time, near-miss rate; add social cost when applicable; report stratified by difficulty and compute Pareto (safe vs. fast). <cite id="692cd467-1">Success-rate and trajectory cost provide core comparative criteria</cite>. <cite id="30098506-2">Tailored distance estimation and collision detection support accurate safety metrics</cite>. <cite id="07aa9d5f-4">Include computational requirements per trial</cite>.
  - Safety: enforce hard safety monitors and barrier constraints; log all violations; perform ablations to understand trade-offs and safety margins. <cite id="30098506-6">Supervisor-guarded evaluation quantifies safety improvements</cite>. <cite id="30098506-8">Barrier-constrained MPC defines a safe baseline for comparison</cite>.
  - Reproducibility: seeds, configs, and compute profiles; large-N trials for rare events; cross-platform and HIL validation when possible. <cite id="07aa9d5f-4">Methodology/software frameworks support reproducible comparisons across methods</cite>. <cite id="e100afd0-8">Arena-Bench supports cross-platform ranking</cite>.
