fully_underspecified.text: What are good benchmarks and evaluation strategies for comparing avoidance strategies in robots?
fully_underspecified.answer:
Below is a practical guide to benchmarks and evaluation strategies for comparing robot avoidance strategies, organized by goals, datasets/environments, metrics, protocols, and safety/robustness checks. Each section highlights concrete resources you can deploy today.

Summary of goals and when to use which evaluation
- Core objectives for “avoidance” typically include safety (no collisions), efficiency (short trajectories and time), robustness (tolerance to uncertainty), and adaptability (generalization to new environments and agents). <cite id="c0e50838-7">A structured framework for object-aware controllers should anticipate and alter motion to avoid collisions, enabling the separation of perception–planning–control responsibilities during evaluation</cite>. 
- Decide early whether to run simulation first or directly on robots. Simulation allows controlled gradients of difficulty and repeated trials; field tests reveal sensor noise, slip/odometry errors, and human/obstacle nonrigidity. <cite id="c0e50838-8">An automatic evaluation methodology is needed to assess obstacle avoidance across wide conditions; the steps emphasize domain-general protocols and repeatability</cite>. For dynamic environments, use graded difficulty curricula to expose edge cases. <cite id="c0e50838-0">Difficulty metrics for dynamic environments capture aspects beyond static clutter, supporting the design of curricula that stress-test avoidance controllers</cite>.

Curated benchmarks to compare avoidance strategies
- Arena-Bench (cross-platform 3D obstacle avoidance): Arena-Bench provides a unified suite to train, test, and evaluate navigation and obstacle-avoidance planners across robotic platforms in 3D environments. It emphasizes scenario generation, multi-platform comparability, and reporting of head-to-head results. <cite id="ac978d5b-0">Arena-Bench targets 3D obstacle avoidance across multiple platforms</cite> <cite id="ac978d5b-1">It supports developing and benchmarking navigation approaches with scenario design and evaluation tasks</cite> <cite id="ac978d5b-2">The accepted RA-L paper outlines the benchmark and tools to evaluate approaches under varied conditions</cite>. If your goal is 3D clutter and multi-robot integration, Arena-Bench is a primary choice.
- Difficulty-graded navigation suites (2D basements/rooms): Benchmarks that order environments by predicted difficulty enable ablations on safety–efficiency trade-offs and early-stopping/generalization. <cite id="c2b821ac-4">BARN provides 300 navigation environments ordered by a difficulty metric set, enabling comparison of navigation systems and as a proxy cost function</cite>. <cite id="ac978d5b-4">A concurrent line (NavDiff) likewise defines a benchmark to predict and compare navigation difficulty, supporting selection and comparison</cite>. Use these when you need a standardized way to stress-test planners at increasing interaction complexity.
- Social navigation stacks and domains: For dynamic crowds and multiple agents, use social navigation platforms. <cite id="ac978d5b-3">Arena 3.0 is a comprehensive stack for development and benchmarking of social navigation, integrating simulation and metrics for multi-agent avoidance</cite>. In human-centric settings, also benchmark off-the-shelf local avoidance like DWA and measure the collision metrics they optimize. <cite id="c2b821ac-9">DWA is a collision-avoidance strategy that optimizes direction and velocity toward the goal while maintaining local collision safety; head-to-head comparisons should measure its collision and efficiency trade-offs</cite>.
- Domain-specific and field-centric evaluations: For dynamic sports-like scenarios, robot soccer provides an operational testbed for high-speed collision-avoidance motion planning and reactive control. <cite id="c2b821ac-5">A real-time collision-avoidance motion planner for robot soccer was implemented and evaluated in highly dynamic environments, demonstrating protocol and metric choices under time pressure</cite>. These stress reactive planning more than structured lab mazes.
- Terrain and uneven ground: If your robot operates on rough terrain, benchmarking tools that explicitly target 3D terrain and uneven ground help catch path-following failures that indirectly cause collisions. <cite id="ac978d5b-5">MeshNav3D provides a Python framework to visualize and benchmark motion planning on uneven 3D terrain, addressing the lack of standardized tools</cite>. Combine with slope-induced drift tests to ensure lateral avoidance remains reliable.

Metrics and protocols to compare strategies
- Safety: collisions and clearance margins
  - Primary success metric: task success rate without collisions on a given environment/task. <cite id="c2b821ac-0">Navigation and social navigation metrics provide a structured framework to assess performance, including collision-related indicators, in crowded environments</cite>.
  - Collision frequency/latency-to-collision and minimum collision clearance (radial/temporal headway) expose reactive failures and over-aggressive behaviors; plot CDFs across environments and trials for robustness. <cite id="c2b821ac-0">Structured social navigation metrics allow separation of localization/planning/control and direct collision-risk assessment</cite>.
  - Multi-agent collision margin: in social navigation, compute inter-agent time-to-collision (TTC) and enforce safety envelopes; report mean/percentile TTC and fraction violating safety bounds. <cite id="c2b821ac-3">Social navigation benchmarking emphasizes multi-agent interaction evaluation, enabling computation of collision risk and compliance with social norms</cite>.
- Efficiency: path and control cost
  - Path length/energy and time-to-goal, contrasted with collision-induced replans. <cite id="c0e50838-3">Arena-bench frames evaluation around success at avoiding obstacles while reaching goals, which aligns with measuring goal reachability under safety constraints</cite>.
  - Steering/DWA-style baselines provide a good controlled comparator; measure velocity replanning frequency and local clearance to isolate avoidance overhead. <cite id="c2b821ac-9">DWA trades off goal progress with local collision avoidance via velocity cost terms; evaluate its collision and efficiency tradeoffs against alternatives</cite>.
- Detection and avoidance split (planning and control evaluation)
  - Adopt a detection-vs-avoidance test framework to separate perception/detection limits from avoidance policy competence. <cite id="c0e50838-5">An evaluation framework comprising detection tests and avoidance tests can uncover performance limits and decouple causes of failures</cite>. For reactive methods, include occlusion and long-horizon prediction trials to measure miss-distance and recovery ability.
- Difficulty-aware and curriculum tests
  - Sort environments by predicted or measured difficulty and evaluate monotonic stress tests (easy→hard) to measure learning and generalization curves, including safety adherence across difficulty levels. <cite id="c0e50838-0">Difficulty metrics for dynamic environments enable graded benchmarking that comprehensively captures complexity</cite> <cite id="c2b821ac-4">Difficulty-ordered suites like BARN allow comparing systems across increasingly challenging settings</cite>.
- Multi-robot and human-aware policies
  - Use pair-wise conflict scenarios: point a robot at a moving target while another approaches laterally; measure collision rates, clearance distributions, and negotiation/replanning latencies across communication delays. <cite id="c2b821ac-5">Robot soccer evaluations provide ablations on collision-avoidance algorithms under high dynamic coupling and goal-directed urgency</cite>.
  - In human social navigation, adopt crowd-density sweeps and track compliance with social distance norms alongside collision risk. <cite id="c0e50838-6">Object-aware obstacle avoidance evaluates anticipatory motion to avoid potential collisions, a core dimension in crowded human settings</cite>.
- Human/agent evaluation and realism
  - For human-aware baselines (e.g., DWA), report collision metrics versus human ground truth or safety labels, and examine failure modes near doorways/throngs. <cite id="c2b821ac-9">DWA is widely used as a local collision-avoidance strategy in human-aware navigation; its effectiveness should be quantified with local collision and efficiency metrics</cite>.

Statistical evaluation and reporting
- Replication and variance: report mean success/collision rates with confidence intervals over multiple seeds/environments/trials; for dynamic scenes, evaluate under randomized agent start velocities and sensor noise. <cite id="c0e50838-8">Automatic evaluation emphasizes repeatability across conditions and workloads</cite>. Where applicable, include variance of TTC and clearance distributions to capture tail risks.
- Ablations and feature attribution: isolate perception pruning, collision cost weights, replanning frequency, and horizon length; use nested designs over difficulty-ordered suites to quantify interaction effects. <cite id="c2b821ac-0">Structured navigation metrics support decomposition of perception, planning, and control contributions to collision risk</cite>.
- Distributional checks and safety envelopes: plot collision-free operating regions (e.g., velocity vs. density), and require policies to satisfy TTC or clearance tolerances for a fraction (e.g., 95th percentile) of high-risk scenarios. <cite id="c2b821ac-3">Social navigation evaluation frameworks allow reporting of inter-agent collision risks and compliance</cite>.
- Domain shift: compare simulator-to-robot transfer: measure the drop in collision rate or increase in replan frequency and analyze where localizers or collision functions fail. <cite id="c0e50838-5">A detection-and-avoidance test framework reveals where perception or avoidance limits dominate under new conditions</cite>.

Practical evaluation workflow
1) Define the user scenario and safety contract: specify allowed collision rates, TTC envelopes, and maximum replanning costs under each operating point (density, speed, communication latency). <cite id="c0e50838-5">Detection and avoidance tests allow you to specify and verify limits and constraints on performance</cite>.
2) Select platforms and benchmarks: use Arena-Bench for 3D indoor/obstacle mazes and multi-robot deployment; BARN/NavDiff for difficulty-graded 2D basements; robot soccer league data for dynamic human-agent interactions; MeshNav3D for uneven terrain to expose lateral drift failures. <cite id="ac978d5b-0">Arena-Bench targets 3D, cross-platform obstacle avoidance</cite> <cite id="ac978d5b-1">includes scenario generation and evaluation tasks</cite> <cite id="c2b821ac-4">BARN orders 300 environments by difficulty to compare systems</cite> <cite id="ac978d5b-5">MeshNav3D standardizes 3D terrain benchmarking</cite> <cite id="ac978d5b-3">Arena 3.0 supports social navigation benchmarking and development</cite>.
3) Instrument metrics and logs: log full trajectories, velocities, collision events, sensor observations, and TTCs; compute success, collision rate, clearance CDF, replanning count/latency, and energy/time. <cite id="c0e50838-7">Object-aware controllers benefit from analytics that anticipate collisions and alter motion, enabling metric separation and reproducible evaluation</cite>.
4) Run controlled head-to-head trials:
   - Baselines: DWA, velocity obstacles, force-field steering, MPC-based collision avoidance; reactivate object detectors and semantic filters systematically. <cite id="c2b821ac-9">DWA’s velocity-cost formulation is a strong baseline for local avoidance, suitable for direct comparison</cite>.
   - Difficulty sweeps and occlusion/occlusion-recovery trials. <cite id="c0e50838-0">Dynamic-environment difficulty metrics enable targeted ablations</cite>.
   - Multi-agent TTC enforcement and social-distance trials (crowds). <cite id="c2b821ac-0">Social navigation metric suites provide the constructs to measure crowded-environment performance</cite>.
5) Synthesize with safety-first lenses: report worst-case TTC/clearance under percentile tails, collision-free corridors by density, and replanning costs vs. delivery time; include confidence intervals and variance explanations. <cite id="c2b821ac-5">Real-time soccer planning evaluations demonstrate that under high dynamic coupling, collision avoidance and efficiency tradeoffs are measurable and reportable</cite>.
6) Validate and deploy: run field trials and measure drop in collision rate and increase in replanning overhead; refine perception and localizer robustness, and add safety guards (deadlines and conservative fallbacks). <cite id="c0e50838-8">An automatic, condition-spanning evaluation workflow reveals performance under wide workloads and guides iterative refinement</cite>.

Specialized resources and how to use them
- University of Zaragoza’s obstacle-avoidance benchmarking metrics: Use their environment-level difficulty metrics to curate a test suite and stratify comparisons by collision risk. <cite id="c0e50838-1">The evaluation system classifies avoidance techniques by performance across environments, making the comparison principled and repeatable</cite>.
- Habitat/ObjectNav-style challenges (if indoors with visual maps): ObjectNav and ImageNav provide standardized goals and environments to compare vision- and map-based avoidance policies. <cite id="ac978d5b-6">The Habitat Navigation Challenge 2023 ObjectNav and ImageNav tasks create standardized environments for object/goal-directed navigation evaluation</cite>. Couple with a collision-check module to derive collision-rate envelopes by clutter and view occlusions.
- Terrain navigation: Use NavDiff/BARN as proxies for collision risk when uneven ground induces falls or drifts, then add dedicated lateral-slipping collision courses. <cite id="c2b821ac-4">Navigation difficulty datasets predict and compare system performance, enabling pre-test triage for collision risk</cite> <cite id="ac978d5b-5">MeshNav3D exposes terrain-induced hazards through benchmarking</cite>.

Examples across methods and domains
- Reactive local avoidance (DWA) vs. model-based planners: Compare steering angles, collision margins, and frequency of replanning in dense labyrinths; DWA provides a simple, strong baseline for collision risk, with efficiency tradeoffs captured by time-to-goal and energy. <cite id="c2b821ac-9">DWA maintains collision safety via velocity costs and is suitable as a baseline for head-to-head evaluation</cite>. <cite id="c0e50838-5">A detection-and-avoidance test framework clarifies whether failures arise from detection or avoidance policy gaps</cite>.
- Social navigation and multi-robot collision avoidance: Use multi-agent TTC and collision-risk CDFs; robot soccer evaluations offer protocols and metrics under high dynamic coupling and urgency. <cite id="c2b821ac-5">A real-time collision-avoidance planner evaluated on robot soccer demonstrates avoidance under time pressure with measurable criteria</cite> <cite id="c2b821ac-0">Social metrics frameworks provide definitions for efficiency, obstacle avoidance, and safety compliance in crowded spaces</cite>.
- Safety-tail characterization: Report 1e-3–1e-4 collision tail probabilities at various velocities and densities; compare fallback policies (e.g., stop-and-clear vs. probabilistic steer) for tail-risk reduction. <cite id="c0e50838-3">Arena-bench reports and compares navigation planners’ success at reaching goals while avoiding obstacles, aligning with tail-risk analysis</cite>.

Putting it together: an evaluation pack to compare avoidance strategies
- Benchmarks: Arena-Bench (3D cross-platform), BARN/NavDiff (difficulty-graded 2D), social navigation suites (Arena 3.0), robot soccer data, MeshNav3D for uneven terrain. <cite id="ac978d5b-0">Arena-Bench spans 3D obstacle avoidance across platforms</cite> <cite id="c2b821ac-4">BARN orders environments by difficulty to support comparative evaluation</cite> <cite id="ac978d5b-3">Arena 3.0 provides a comprehensive social navigation stack</cite> <cite id="ac978d5b-5">MeshNav3D standardizes uneven terrain benchmarking</cite>.
- Metrics pack: success rate, collision frequency and latency, minimum headway/clearance, TTC compliance rate, replanning count/latency, energy/time cost, efficiency indices; multi-agent collision matrices (pairwise). <cite id="c0e50838-5">Detection-and-avoidance tests expose and separate limits</cite> <cite id="c0e50838-0">Dynamic difficulty metrics quantify environment stress</cite> <cite id="c2b821ac-0">Social navigation metrics formalize crowded-environment success and safety components</cite>.
- Protocols: randomized initializations and sensor noise; ablate perception pruning and cost weights; density sweep; occlusion and recovery trials; enforce safety envelopes (e.g., 0.5 m TTC buffers) and report compliance; confidence intervals over 100+ seeds; simulator-to-robot transfer checks. <cite id="c0e50838-8">Automatic evaluation across conditions and workloads strengthens comparability</cite> <cite id="ac978d5b-1">Arena-bench provides tools to generate scenarios and evaluation tasks across platforms</cite>.
- Reporting and robustness: include difficulty-normalized cost, collision-tail CDFs, failure heatmaps by density/velocity; show generalization to unseen agents and terrains; include human-in-the-loop preference if social norms matter. <cite id="c2b821ac-0">Structured metrics facilitate interpretation and comparison of trade-offs in crowded settings</cite>.

Selected starting points
- If you need an out-of-the-box 3D benchmark with multi-platform parity and reporting tools: Arena-Bench. <cite id="ac978d5b-0">Arena-Bench trains, tests, and evaluates planners within 3D environments across platforms</cite> <cite id="ac978d5b-1">Its scenario tools make head-to-head comparisons straightforward</cite>.
- To grade and compare planners across many environments by difficulty: BARN/NavDiff for 2D basements/rooms. <cite id="c2b821ac-4">BARN includes 300 difficulty-ranked environments to compare systems and predict difficulty</cite>.
- To test social navigation/crowds and multi-robot conflicts: social navigation benchmarks and robot soccer datasets; add TTC and collision-envelope compliance metrics. <cite id="c2b821ac-0">Social navigation metrics define efficiency, obstacle avoidance, and navigation success under crowding</cite> <cite id="c2b821ac-5">Robot soccer evaluates real-time motion planners under high dynamic coupling</cite>.
- To catch terrain-induced failures that cause collisions: MeshNav3D for uneven 3D terrain benchmarking. <cite id="ac978d5b-5">MeshNav3D fills the need for standardized, reproducible benchmarking on uneven terrain</cite>.

Finally, always include a negative-control protocol (e.g., a planner disabled for avoidance) and a positive-control standard (e.g., DWA) to validate measurement sensitivity, and ensure your metric battery answers the safety–efficiency question for your domain and deployment risks. <cite id="c2b821ac-9">DWA’s explicit collision cost structure offers a transparent baseline for evaluating trade-offs in avoidance</cite> <cite id="c0e50838-8">A domain-spanning evaluation workflow helps you trust the comparisons and prioritize safety-critical improvements</cite>.

ambiguity_judge.evidence: The response goes straight into a full guide and benchmark list without noting any ambiguity or asking for the robot type, environment, or avoidance setting; it treats the query as fully specified.

without_scope.text: What are good benchmarks and evaluation strategies for comparing obstacle avoidance strategies?
without_scope.answer:
Below is a concise, evidence-backed blueprint of benchmarks and evaluation strategies you can use to compare obstacle avoidance strategies across common domains: autonomous driving/simulation, mobile and aerial robots, and multi-agent/social navigation. I group recommendations by domain, then outline a common evaluation checklist; I note where to source data, metrics, and stressors and how to assess statistical and safety guarantees.

High-level guidance
- Choose a domain-true environment that encodes your robot’s kinematic/dynamic constraints (e.g., CARLA for 2D driving with traffic; robot simulators for ground/UAV kinematics). Use standardized scenario libraries so comparisons reflect the same obstacle densities, speeds, and interaction patterns and report scenario-level and aggregate metrics (success rate, cost, safety margins, and time-based performance) normalized by scenario difficulty. Validate with statistical tests across randomized seeds/scenarios and, where needed, ground with physical hardware tests and risk assessments. <cite id="1bd84981-0">Recent surveys emphasize comparing detection–avoidance systems using consistent metrics over representative scenarios to increase security and efficiency in autonomous platforms</cite> <cite id="1bd84981-6">A general AV obstacle avoidance capability assessment proposes standardized dimensions to compare strategies across highway-speed scenarios</cite>.

Domain A: Autonomous driving and aerial/ground robot simulation
Benchmarks and platforms
- Open-source driving simulators with scenario/benchmark modules:
  - CARLA: widely used for AV research and benchmarking; includes a performance metrics module and “Leaderboard”-style evaluations across standardized scenarios <cite id="e1eb7173-0">Open-source CARLA is a common testbed, with Leaderboard benchmarks used for evaluation</cite> <cite id="e1eb7173-4">CARLA exposes computed performance metrics to summarize agent actions across scenarios</cite> <cite id="e1eb7173-2">CARLA introduced interactive real-traffic scenarios as a training/testing ground and benchmark</cite> <cite id="e1eb7173-8">CARLA’s Scenario Runner generates and executes standardized autonomous driving scenarios for evaluation</cite>. 
  - Alternatives/stack complements: AirSim and Gazebo for photorealistic perception and physics; AirSim is often chosen for perception-heavy tasks, while CARLA excels in urban traffic scenarios <cite id="e1eb7173-3">CARLA targets urban traffic, while AirSim leverages high-end graphics for photorealistic perception; both are compared in simulator reviews</cite>.
- UAV/robot obstacle avoidance datasets and methods:
  - ODA_Drone: a real indoor dataset with multi-sensor streams for drone obstacle avoidance; use it to compare reactive and geometric planners under realistic occlusions and motion dynamics <cite id="1c8289ff-2">The Obstacle Avoidance Dataset for Drones provides raw indoor sensor data with adapted sensors to study real-world avoidance</cite>.
  - Comparative UAV method surveys and head-to-head evaluations: recent surveys catalog UAV avoidance approaches and comparison criteria; pair these with your own experiments on collision frequency, recovery time, and energy use in indoor/outdoor corridors and mazes <cite id="1c8289ff-0">A 2025 UAV survey compares obstacle avoidance and path planning methods for UAVs across multiple criteria</cite> <cite id="1c8289ff-5">Velocity-Obstacle analyses provide classical geometric baselines and evaluation points for collision avoidance</cite> <cite id="1c8289ff-9">Learning-based methods are often compared by collision rate and recovery time in indoor avoidance tasks</cite>.
  - Safety-aware planning: combining velocity obstacles with control barrier functions yields certified safety properties; use such methods as safety baselines and measure constraint satisfaction and violation rates under disturbances <cite id="1c8289ff-1">Combining VO with control barrier functions provides a multi-agent collision avoidance framework with formal safety properties</cite>.

Metrics and scoring that work well
- Outcome and safety:
  - Collision rate and near-miss rate (pre-defined safety thresholds on distance/TTC). Track penetration depth and minimum time-to-collision across episodes and aggregate by density/speed band. <cite id="e1eb7173-0">Leaderboard-style evaluations with CARLA report task-level success and performance summaries that can be mapped to collision/efficiency metrics</cite> <cite id="e1eb7173-4">CARLA’s metrics module computes summaries of agent actions over scenarios, enabling collision/efficiency accounting</cite>.
  - Barrier/constraint satisfaction for safety-critical comparisons (e.g., control barrier function residual safety margins) <cite id="1c8289ff-1">Barrier-function–based multi-agent avoidance defines measurable safety constraints for evaluation</cite>.
- Efficiency and user cost:
  - Path/trajectory cost (Euclidean/arc length), energy (if actuator-aware), and time-to-goal or time-to-exit, plus deviation penalties that weigh safety back-offs; for AVs, add highway-lane-keeping effort and comfort measures. <cite id="1bd84981-6">General obstacle avoidance capability assessment frameworks quantify capability across safety and efficiency dimensions in highway AVs</cite> <cite id="1bd84981-7">Unbiased AV benchmarking argues for a complete metric set over diverse scenarios to compare systems</cite>.
- Kinematic fidelity under sensor uncertainty:
  - In sim–reality transfer, add lidar/radar noise and latency; measure robustness via collision rate deltas and recovery time. For drones, evaluate actuator limits and wind disturbances. <cite id="1c8289ff-2">Real indoor datasets with raw multi-sensor streams let you add noise/motion uncertainty to probe robustness</cite>.

Stressors and scenarios
- Drive/multi-agent stressors:
  - Vary obstacle density, speed variance, acceleration bursts, occlusions, and intersection geometries; include cooperative and competitive interactions. <cite id="e1eb7173-2">CARLA’s interactive real-traffic scenarios expose dense, heterogeneous interactions for stress-testing</cite>.
  - For social navigation among humans/robots, use human-robot interaction studies to ground comfort/safety thresholds and validate behavior against user-preference benchmarks <cite id="b073c414-3">User studies identify discomfort factors, grounding social navigation comfort/safety requirements</cite>.
- Formal and statistical validation:
  - Randomize seeds/hardware/comms latency across K>20 runs; report means ± std and paired t-tests or Wilcoxon for paired strategies; include scenario-level bootstrapped confidence intervals for collision-rate and path-length differences. <cite id="1c8289ff-6">A two-sample t-test–based obstacle recognition study illustrates statistical evaluation of avoidance improvements</cite>.
  - Use safety-gap methods or barrier certificates to compute failure risk in distributional terms (e.g., fraction of scenarios violating safety margin) and compare across planners <cite id="1c8289ff-1">Safety margins are formalized and testable in barrier-constrained multi-agent avoidance</cite>.

Domain B: Mobile robots (indoor/warehouse/household) and social navigation
Benchmarks and platforms
- Navigation datasets and environments:
  - Robotic navigation benchmarks: use scenarioized robot environments (e.g., CARLA scenario runner for traffic-like indoor/outdoor maps; BARN-style datasets organize hundreds of environments by difficulty) to compare planners/avoiders across layouts, clutter, and congestion curves. <cite id="e1eb7173-8">CARLA Scenario Runner executes standardized scenarios for evaluation</cite> <cite id="b073c414-4">The BARN dataset provides 300 navigation environments with defined difficulty metrics for benchmarking</cite>.
  - Social navigation benchmarks: social robot datasets and scenario suites (e.g., “crowd” hallways, gathering plazas) from recent surveys/datasets support head-to-head comparisons; also use HRI user-study metrics as ground-truth comfort/safety targets. <cite id="b073c414-0">A benchmarking review in social robot navigation compiles learning-based methods and comparative setups under human coexistence</cite> <cite id="b073c414-1">Curated social navigation resources catalog advances in dynamic/human environments</cite>.
- Multi-agent collision avoidance methods:
  - Velocity/Force Obstacles (VO/OI/SO) and potential fields remain strong baselines; combine with modern control-theoretic safety (e.g., CBFs) and learning (DRL) to form fair ablations. <cite id="1c8289ff-4">Velocity obstacle analyses offer classical baselines for geometric multi-agent collision avoidance</cite> <cite id="1c8289ff-1">VO+CBF blends provide both performance and formal safety testability</cite>.

Metrics
- Trajectory-quality (reactive/local) that capture practical robot costs:
  - Curvature, heading angle error, speed deviation, path length, heading/curvature rates (jerk/comfort) and collision-free duration; aggregate over episodes and normalize by start-to-goal time. <cite id="1bd84981-8">Evaluation for obstacle-avoidance trajectory planning includes curvature, heading angle, and speed measures</cite>.
  - Social cost: distance-to-human, comfort scores from user studies, and interaction frequency; align KPIs with HRI comfort/safety requirements derived from user studies. <cite id="b073c414-3">User studies reveal discomfort triggers and provide requirement grounding for social-robot metrics</cite> <cite id="b073c414-6">Social Force–based navigation integrates interaction dynamics and comfort measures that can serve as evaluation targets</cite>.
- Multi-agent interaction quality:
  - Collision rate, missed-collision rate (if ground truthed), minimum clearance distribution, and time-to-interact (for planning latency sensitivity). <cite id="b073c414-2">Optimization-based multi-agent collision avoidance is evaluated via its fundamental collision metrics under coexistence</cite>.

Stressors
- Human-like motion and occlusions:
  - Embed pedestrian social forces, crossing behaviors, and timed occlusions; compare reactive vs. optimization-based planners’ ability to maintain safety margins and smoothness under dynamic occlusions. <cite id="b073c414-6">Social Force models capture human-robot interaction dynamics used to validate navigation strategies</cite>.
- Noise and partial observability:
  - Inject lidar/radar sparsification, motion noise, and delayed observations to measure robustness trade-offs between safety buffers and path efficiency. <cite id="1bd84981-9">Lidar-based obstacle detection yields uneven point clouds; evaluation should reflect downstream avoidance robustness to such noise</cite>.

Domain C: UAV/underwater vehicles and extreme scenarios
Benchmarks and platforms
- Indoor/outdoor drone datasets and sim-to-sim/hardware-in-the-loop:
  - Use ODA_Drone for realistic indoor avoidance; pair with CARLA-like city scenarios for high-density traffic and aerodynamic constraints; include wind/gust perturbations to test robustness. <cite id="1c8289ff-2">ODA_Drone provides real indoor sensor data and motion for rigorous avoidance testing</cite> <cite id="e1eb7173-0">CARLA supports Leaderboard-style evaluation for complex traffic scenarios</cite>.
- Comparative surveys and controlled head-to-heads:
  - Surveyed UAV methods can be re-evaluated on shared obstacle courses (cone corridors, weave paths, T-maze turns) with time-based and energy/actuator cost accounting; report collision and recovery counts per maneuver family. <cite id="1c8289ff-0">Recent UAV surveys provide comparative criteria for re-evaluating avoidance strategies across obstacles and dynamics</cite> <cite id="1c8289ff-9">Certifiable safe policies are evaluated by safety margin satisfaction and collision rate in multi-robot navigation</cite>.

Metrics and trade-offs
- Kinematic and energy cost:
  - Path length vs. climb/descent energy, vertical and horizontal clearance distributions, rate-of-climb penalties, and time-to-climb penalties; include terminal safety buffer before landing/goal. <cite id="1c8289ff-0">UAV surveys discuss efficiency–safety trade-offs for obstacle avoidance and path planning</cite>.
- Safety and formal guarantees:
  - Check barrier/constraint satisfaction and fallback success rates; measure violation probabilities under bounded disturbances and compare planners’ tolerance margins. <cite id="1c8289ff-1">VO+CBF formulations specify testable constraints for safety evaluation under disturbances</cite>.

Cross-cutting evaluation strategy (agnostic to domain)
1) Choose an environment that matches kinematics/constraints
   - Use CARLA for ground/AV kinematics; robot simulators (including scenario runners) for wheeled robots; AirSim for photorealistic perception; UAV-native datasets/sims for aerial dynamics. <cite id="e1eb7173-3">Select platforms by fidelity: CARLA for urban traffic and AirSim for photorealistic perception, both useful for obstacle avoidance evaluation</cite> <cite id="b073c414-4">Large robot navigation environment suites (e.g., BARN) offer difficulty gradients for standardized comparisons</cite>.
2) Build a scenario library and protocol
   - Curate S scenarios by density, speed, occlusion percentage, and interaction type; randomize initial poses of agents and obstacles; include edge cases (slalom, U-turns, merges). Run K≥20 seeds per scenario; report per-scenario success/collision/clearance and aggregate means/medians with CI. <cite id="e1eb7173-8">CARLA Scenario Runner supports executing curated scenario suites</cite> <cite id="b073c414-4">BARN’s difficulty metrics support stratified benchmarking across obstacles and clutter</cite>.
3) Define metrics aligned to objectives and safety
   - Core: success rate, collision rate, near-miss (TTC<τ) rate, mean time-to-goal, path length/energy cost. Add trajectory smoothness (heading/curvature/speed changes), clearance distributions, and comfort/social cost where relevant. <cite id="1bd84981-8">Trajectory evaluation includes curvature, heading angle, and speed-based measures</cite> <cite id="1bd84981-6">Highway-speed capability assessment stresses safety and efficiency together</cite> <cite id="b073c414-3">HRI comfort/safety requirements inform social navigation metrics</cite>.
   - Safety: minimum clearance over time, time-to-safety after collision avoidance, control barrier residual magnitudes, and failure-rate curves under noise/disturbances. <cite id="1c8289ff-1">Barrier-function residuals provide testable safety margins for avoidance</cite>.
4) Ablate strategy components and learning setups
   - Compare: classical geometric (VO/OI), optimization/constraints (CBF-QP), learning (RL/Diffusion), and hybrid reactive–optimization. Evaluate across scenario difficulty bins; plot efficiency–safety Pareto fronts. <cite id="b073c414-2">Optimization-based multi-agent avoidance is a key ablation baseline with clear metrics</cite> <cite id="1c8289ff-0">UAV surveys provide taxonomy and criteria to re-run ablations</cite>.
5) Statistical and sim-to-reality validation
   - Use paired tests across scenario pairs to test significance; compute scenario-level AUC (e.g., safe operation fraction as obstacle speed/density varies) and rank strategies. Validate sim-to-reality via hardware-in-the-loop or flight tests on a subset of scenarios; check transfer gaps and add domain randomization in sim if gaps appear. <cite id="1c8289ff-6">t-test-based comparisons demonstrate statistical evaluation of obstacle-avoidance improvements</cite> <cite id="1c8289ff-2">Real indoor datasets enable direct transfer checks for drone avoidance strategies</cite>.
6) Document robustness, explainability, and HRI factors
   - For social settings, collect user studies or video-labelers to rate comfort and norm compliance, and correlate with metrics to ensure strategy improvements don’t harm social acceptability. <cite id="b073c414-3">User studies reveal comfort determinants that should be monitored during strategy iteration</cite>.

Good benchmark suites and starting points
- Autonomous driving
  - CARLA simulator and Leaderboard: scenario-based evaluation, photorealistic sensors, metrics module for path actions, and traffic interaction benchmarks; add your collision/efficiency metrics and safety thresholds. <cite id="e1eb7173-0">CARLA is a standard testbed that supports Leaderboard-style comparisons</cite> <cite id="e1eb7173-4">CARLA’s metrics compute summaries over agent actions for scenario scoring</cite> <cite id="e1eb7173-2">Interactive real-traffic scenarios create dense collision-avoidance stressors</cite>.
- Mobile/social robots
  - BARN dataset (300+ robot nav environments with difficulty metrics) plus HRI-focused social benchmarks; evaluate trajectory quality and social safety/comfort jointly. <cite id="b073c414-4">BARN offers scalable, difficulty-graded benchmarks and difficulty-aware evaluation</cite> <cite id="b073c414-0">Social navigation benchmarking reviews compile methods and comparative setups</cite>.
- UAVs
  - ODA_Drone indoor dataset and CARLA aerial scenarios for traffic; add wind/disturbance channels; evaluate collision rate, recovery smoothness, and energy. <cite id="1c8289ff-2">ODA_Drone supplies realistic indoor sensor data for obstacle avoidance</cite> <cite id="e1eb7173-0">CARLA supports AV/traffic interaction evaluation</cite>.
- Classical multi-agent method baselines
  - RVO2/VO-family baselines and CBF-verified baselines for direct comparisons of geometric vs. control-theoretic safety. <cite id="1c8289ff-4">Velocity obstacle approaches dominate classical multi-agent collision avoidance and provide clear evaluation baselines</cite> <cite id="1c8289ff-1">VO+CBF combinations offer formal safety for direct ablation</cite>.
- General evaluation frameworks
  - Comprehensive AV collision-avoidance benchmarks advocate standardized, scenario-based metrics across safety, efficiency, and robustness; use them as templates for your domain. <cite id="1bd84981-0">Surveys argue for standardized evaluation of collision avoidance systems across scenarios</cite> <cite id="1bd84981-6">GOACA proposes a general AV obstacle avoidance capability assessment</cite> <cite id="1bd84981-7">Unbiased metrics frameworks enumerate metrics and scenario coverage to compare AV systems</cite>.

Practical tips and pitfalls
- Pitfall: “Luck on easy scenarios.” Use stratified scenario difficulty and compute per-difficulty performance to avoid spurious wins. <cite id="b073c414-4">BARN’s difficulty metrics enable difficulty-aware ranking and prevent wins on trivial cases</cite>.
- Pitfall: Metric gaming. Avoid single-point collisions-only metrics; include clearance distributions, TTC buffers, effort, and social comfort; when using learned policies, include abstain/brake behaviors and their costs. <cite id="1bd84981-5">Studies find metric gaming and active violations in 30–50% of scenarios when only surface metrics are optimized</cite>.
- Win: Combine domain simulators with datasets that capture real sensor noise and dynamics; pair with safety-guaranteed controllers for a strong safety baseline and fair comparison. <cite id="1c8289ff-2">Real indoor sensor datasets expose noise, occlusion, and dynamics to stress-test avoidance</cite> <cite id="1c8289ff-1">Barrier-function baselines provide safety-grounded comparison points</cite>.
- Win: Use HRI/user-study-derived comfort and norm compliance as auxiliary metrics and constraints in long-horizon deployments. <cite id="b073c414-3">User studies quantify discomfort factors, enabling comfort-aware benchmark targets</cite>.

What to report
- Protocol: environment and robot model, scenario library composition, random seeds, K and compute budgets.
- Metrics tables per scenario: success, collision, TTC-violation, mean time-to-goal, path/energy, trajectory smoothness, and safety-gap statistics.
- Aggregates: per-strategy mean/median success under density/speed strata, Pareto efficiency fronts, statistical significance.
- Safety: safety-residual distributions and violation probabilities; recovery quality after near-misses.
- Sim-to-reality: hardware validation on a subset, transfer gaps, and mitigation (domain randomization). <cite id="1c8289ff-6">Include at least two-sample t-tests to demonstrate statistical significance of improvements</cite> <cite id="1c84981-...">[Continue with domain-agnostic safety/comfort reporting as above.]</cite>.

Selected resources to get you started
- Surveys and frameworks: Autonomous driving collision-avoidance benchmarking and capability assessments; social navigation benchmarking for humans/robots coexisting. <cite id="1bd84981-0">Survey of AV collision avoidance emphasizes security/efficiency and evaluation under diverse scenarios</cite> <cite id="1bd84981-6">General obstacle avoidance capability assessment for AVs at highway speeds provides a benchmark framework</cite> <cite id="b073c414-0">Social robot navigation benchmarking review covers learning-based methods and comparative setups</cite>.
- Simulators/datasets: CARLA simulator with metrics and scenario runner; AirSim and Gazebo comparisons; BARN dataset (300+ robot nav environments) and ODA_Drone dataset for UAV obstacle avoidance. <cite id="e1eb7173-4">CARLA metrics module for quantitative evaluation</cite> <cite id="e1eb7173-8">CARLA Scenario Runner for standardized scenario evaluation</cite> <cite id="b073c414-4">BARN dataset for robot navigation benchmarking</cite> <cite id="1c8289ff-2">ODA_Drone: real indoor avoidance data for UAVs</cite>.
- Methods and safety: VO/OI baselines and VO+CBF safety frameworks; UAV-specific comparisons and unbiased benchmarking of AV systems. <cite id="1c8289ff-4">VO approaches as classical baselines for multi-agent avoidance</cite> <cite id="1c8289ff-1">VO+CBF collision avoidance with formal safety constraints</cite> <cite id="1bd84981-7">Unbiased AV benchmarking with complete metric sets across scenarios</cite>.

Open gaps and how to close them
- Dynamic uncertainty and partial observability: explicitly measure robustness under lidar/radar noise and delay. <cite id="1bd84981-9">Lidar-based detection yields uneven point clouds; evaluation should reflect downstream avoidance robustness</cite>.
- Formal safety in learning: incorporate barrier-function residuals or chance constraints into your objective or acceptance criteria. <cite id="1c8289ff-1">Control barrier formulations provide measurable, testable safety margins for avoidance</cite>.
- Transfer gaps: validate on real robots or HIL with domain randomization; report sim-to-real generalization curves. <cite id="1c8289ff-2">Real indoor drone data enables direct transfer assessment and fine-tuning of avoidance strategies</cite>.

By anchoring your evaluation in a faithful environment, running standardized scenario suites, and reporting a complete metric set (safety, efficiency, smoothness, and social comfort), you can make fair, quantitative comparisons across obstacle avoidance strategies and identify where your method trades safety for efficiency, and where it truly advances robustness and user comfort. <cite id="1bd84981-0">Scenario-based, standardized comparisons are the core of reliable evaluation in autonomous-vehicle collision avoidance</cite> <cite id="b073c414-0">Social navigation benchmarks show how to combine performance and user-centric metrics under human coexistence</cite> <cite id="e1eb7173-4">CARLA’s metrics infrastructure demonstrates how to operationalize these metrics in practice</cite>.

ambiguity_judge.evidence: The response immediately launches into a broad, domain-spanning answer (“Below is a concise, evidence-backed blueprint...”) without noting any ambiguity or asking for clarification.

without_preference.text: What are good benchmarks and evaluation strategies for comparing obstacle avoidance strategies in mobile robots?
without_preference.answer:
Below is a curated guide to benchmarks and evaluation strategies for comparing obstacle avoidance strategies in mobile robots, organized by environment class and the types of metrics that produce fair, reproducible comparisons. Where possible, recommendations include standardized datasets and leaderboards with quantitative scoring.

1) What to optimize and what to measure
- Core objectives for obstacle avoidance include safety (no collisions), efficiency (on-time arrival, minimal detours), smoothness/roll-out feasibility (Dubins/Curvature-bounded motions), and real-time feasibility (computation and sensing budgets). A recent survey emphasizes that standardized benchmarks and metrics are needed and highlights indicators like navigation safety, collision costs, and smoothness criteria to form a holistic scorecard for strategies <cite id="2f9111f9-0">Metrics specifically track obstacle number, size, and velocity to reflect dynamic difficulty and help compare methods under principled conditions</cite> <cite id="2f9111f9-2">Benchmarking in Mobile Robotics synthesizes evaluation methods and metrics, arguing for consistent protocols and measurable indicators (safety, efficiency, smoothness, and computational cost) across tasks</cite> <cite id="61e09bfc-0">Standardized benchmarks and metrics are necessary to fairly evaluate obstacle avoidance strategies; key indicators include navigation safety, collision-related penalties, trajectory smoothness and adherence to kinematic constraints</cite> <cite id="61e09bfc-3">Path planning surveys clarify roles: global plans provide setpoints while local avoidance must handle obstacles and respond to dynamics, motivating metrics on responsiveness and constraint compliance</cite>.

- Robust comparison metrics:
  - Safety: collisions, near-misses, minimum distance to obstacles/agents over time; cost-augmented planners penalize unsafe proximity (typical in dynamic traffic leaderboards) <cite id="2f9111f9-0">Evaluations attribute task difficulty to obstacles’ number, size, and velocity, enabling planners to be compared under varying safety pressure</cite> <cite id="06eb1382-6">The CARLA Leaderboard 2.0 defines infractions with explicit penalties to quantify safety failures over episodes</cite>.
  - Reachability/efficiency: on-time arrival, delay, detour ratio relative to a nominal path; penalty functions that trade off path cost and obstacle risk <cite id="61e09bfc-1">Hybrid planners emphasize reducing aggressive accelerations/decelerations while maintaining avoidance, pointing to velocity smoothness and energy-like objectives</cite>.
  - Smoothness and feasibility: turn radius/curvature compliance, jerk/acceleration variability, dynamic window feasibility; these affect wear, comfort, and real-time roll-out <cite id="61e09bfc-1">Suppressing aggressive acceleration/deceleration while ensuring avoidance provides a smooth velocity space, indicating the role of smoothness metrics</cite>.
  - Computational overhead: per-step runtime, VO/VFO search sizes, MPC QPs size; include time budgets to reflect embedded constraints <cite id="2f9111f9-2">Survey guidance encourages reporting practical constraints like computation time alongside accuracy to reflect real-world deployments</cite>.
  - Environment difficulty: stratify tests with metrics quantifying obstacle density, speed, and arrangement to ensure methods aren’t “measuring through” difficulty <cite id="2f9111f9-0">Dynamic difficulty metrics capture how obstacle number, size, and velocity shape task hardness</cite> <cite id="2f9111f9-5">The BARN dataset orders 300 environments by difficulty metrics to allow controlled comparisons across increasing challenge</cite>.

2) Benchmarks you can use today

2.1 Classic algorithmic and kinematic-oriented testbeds
- Potential/velocity fields (VFO/VO) and hybrid methods: Use grid labyrinths with moving and stationary obstacles to stress VO/VFO limitations (local minima, oscillation), and to quantify overshoot distances or collision radii. Incorporate Dubins/Curvature-bounded maneuver sets to check smoothness and safety corridors; report failure modes and recovery time. Classic papers argue that potential fields have inherent limits (attraction wells, tangling), motivating evaluations that explicitly test such failure cases and recovery efficiency <cite id="61e09bfc-8">Potential Field Methods are limited by local minima and path tangling; the Virtual Force Field approach targets real-time obstacle avoidance on fast robots, but requires tests of real-time feasibility and failure resilience</cite> <cite id="61e09bfc-6">The Obstacle Velocity approach integrates velocity terms to improve avoidance behavior and is useful as a baseline to test gains from hybridization</cite>.
- Dynamic window/DWA-style planners: benchmark on cluttered corridors and narrow passes where slipstreaming and minimum turning radius matter; measure successful passage rate, required slowdowns, and time-to-clear. <cite id="61e09bfc-7">Combining improved Dynamic Window Approach with potential fields improves obstacle avoidance with smoother velocities, indicating that smoothness and kinematic feasibility should be core metrics</cite>.

2.2 Navigation simulation suites (2D/3D, collision-free to dynamic)
- BARN (Benchmark for Autonomous Robot Navigation): Large suite of collision-free navigation environments with precomputed difficulty metrics that let you sweep occupancy and obstacle dynamics at scale, making it ideal to compare algorithmic gains while controlling difficulty strata. Download and reproduce experiments across 300 maps; split by difficulty for cross-validation. <cite id="2f9111f9-1">The BARN benchmark provides 300 navigation environments and a set of difficulty metrics to order tasks by expected challenge</cite> <cite id="2f9111f9-5">BARN’s environments are designed to test collision-free navigation and can be extended to include dynamic elements; difficulty metrics allow principled stratification</cite>.
- Velocity-Obstacle and Dynamic Obstacle method suites: Use sets of 2D/3D scenarios where agents move on Dubins/Curvature-invariant velocity lattices, reporting collision cones and time-to-collision (TTC) before and after planner interventions. Include occlusions to test sensor-based methods. <cite id="2f9111f9-0">Difficulty is tied to obstacle motion; scenarios that vary obstacle speed and density produce reliable discrimination among avoidance strategies</cite>.
- Egocentric perception-plus-navigation datasets (for sensor-driven avoidance): RoboSense offers 133K egocentric frames with dense obstacle annotations in near ranges; pair with perception-to-motion backbones to assess how obstacle detection quality propagates to avoidance success and failure modes under occlusions. <cite id="2f9111f9-7">RoboSense contains over 133K synchronized frames with rich annotations of nearby obstacles, enabling evaluation of perception-driven obstacle avoidance under varying occlusion levels</cite>.

2.3 Dynamic, interactive traffic and multi-agent environments
- CARLA Autonomous Driving Leaderboard: While primarily vehicular, CARLA provides realistic traffic, sensor stacks, and a mature scoring module with penalties for infractions and safety violations; it’s suitable to benchmark obstacle avoidance behaviors for dynamic obstacles and interactive agents, with published evaluation protocols. <cite id="06eb1382-1">The CARLA Leaderboard aims to evaluate driving proficiency in realistic traffic scenarios and aggregates algorithm performance over standard episodes</cite> <cite id="06eb1382-6">Leaderboard 2.0 defines individualized metrics for infractions with penalty coefficients applied per occurrence, enabling quantitative comparison of safety-aware behavior</cite> <cite id="06eb1382-4">CARLA’s performance metrics module computes summaries from agent actions over episodes, facilitating integration with obstacle avoidance metrics</cite>.
- Real Traffic Scenarios in CARLA: Replicate real-world interactions (crosswalks, yield/priority rules) to stress reactive avoidance; evaluate TTC thresholds, lane adherence, and pedestrian right-of-way compliance as part of your scoring. <cite id="06eb1382-3">CARLA introduced real-world-based interactive traffic scenarios, providing realistic interaction patterns for evaluation</cite>.
- Complementary multi-agent benchmarks: Recent work augments CARLA with human-like action benchmarks that integrate official and customized metrics for behavioral realism and interaction quality, which can be adapted to mobile robot pedestrian avoidance. <cite id="06eb1382-2">HABIT introduces a human action benchmark for interactive traffic in CARLA, combining standard CARLA metrics with new behavioral metrics to evaluate interaction quality</cite>.

2.4 Additional domains and sensor realism
- Underwater/marine obstacle detection datasets are not mobile-robot standard but do expose sensor noise and distance aliasing issues; they are useful for stress-testing perception layers and IOU/recall-like evaluation of obstacle footprint handling as part of end-to-end avoidance evaluation <cite id="2f9111f9-4">A marine obstacle detection benchmark provides a dataset, benchmark evaluation scripts, and scripts to measure detection efficiency as a starting point for perception-centric avoidance evaluation</cite>.
- HRC task studies that combine vision/IMU/sonar show evaluation matrices including sensor fusion error metrics and feed-forward time, reinforcing evaluation of the sensing-avoidance loop as a pipeline under bounded compute.

3) How to run a rigorous head-to-head evaluation

3.1 Environment design and stratification
- Mix static and dynamic scenes, and sweep obstacle density, speed, and predictability to measure robustness. Use difficulty metrics to normalize cross-experiment comparisons and to generate stratified k-folds that preserve distributional hardness within each fold <cite id="2f9111f9-1">BARN provides precomputed difficulty features enabling stratified evaluation across 300 environments</cite> <cite id="2f9111f9-0">Difficulty can be quantified from obstacle number, size, and velocity; using these as covariates normalizes comparisons</cite>.
- Include occlusion and sensor noise studies by down-sampling, corrupting, or masking LiDAR/camera channels and measuring the drop in success and safety margins to assess tolerance and redundancy.

3.2 Metrics and scoring functions
- Safety-first scoring: sum discounted collision energy E_col = ∑ τ_t (d_t / d_min)^p over steps; add binary collision as a hard constraint for screening trials; penalize hard infractions in dynamic settings like run-over or rear-end risk <cite id="06eb1382-6">Each infraction type has a configurable penalty in the CARLA evaluation, enabling energy-like safety scoring under a standardized taxonomy</cite>.
- Efficiency: define a time-weighted path cost E_path = ∑ τ_t (||v_t||^2 + λ ||a_t||^2) or detour ratio vs. nominal path; include door/terminal penalties for late arrival or missed goals <cite id="61e09bfc-1">Hybrid planning work shows that reducing acceleration/deceleration while maintaining avoidance yields smoother, likely more energy-efficient trajectories</cite>.
- Smoothness/feasibility: curvature exceedance ratio, jerk magnitude, number of stops; include a time budget C and fail trials that exceed C; report successful clear time and pass efficiency per corridor or maze <cite id="61e09bfc-7">An IDWA+PF method explicitly aims to deliver smooth velocity profiles while avoiding obstacles; smoothness metrics should be included in comparison</cite>.
- Environment-aware normalization: divide raw scores by nominal difficulty scores to compare algorithms across strata; use repeated-measures ANOVA across 10–20 difficulty buckets to check for statistical interaction with difficulty <cite id="2f9111f9-1">BARN’s difficulty metrics provide a ready-made stratification to compare performance trends across increasing difficulty</cite> <cite id="2f9111f9-0">A difficulty model capturing obstacle number, size, and speed helps normalize differences among algorithms</cite>.

3.3 Protocol and statistics
- Environment set: Use 3–5 simulation suites (BARN mazes, CARLA traffic, custom lab scenes) for external/internal-consistency; add 1–2 perception-heavy domains (e.g., RoboSense) for sensing-limited cases.
- Splits: temporal splits across recording days for HRC/field studies; stratified difficulty splits for sim; ablations that mask sensors or alter budgets.
- Significance: apply nonparametric tests (e.g., Wilcoxon) on success rates, safety energies, and travel costs across 100+ trials per setting; report effect sizes and Bayes factors if applicable.
- Reproducibility: publish seeds for sim physics, initial poses, and per-episode randomizers; include hardware/software specs for embedded planners and ROS/Gazebo stack versions.

3.4 Robustness checks
- Noise/occlusion ablations: systematically vary sensor noise and occlusion levels while holding planner parameters constant; evaluate failure rate and safety energy increases to understand graceful degradation and error ceilings <cite id="7393ee8c-2">A tracked mobile robot benchmark with real-world sensor evaluation found Intel RealSense T265 robust under bounded vibrations and low light, suggesting sensor selection and noise tolerance are key to reliable avoidance</cite>.
- Recovery from deadlock: instrument tests for potential-field deadlocks and VO oscillations, with timeouts and adaptive repathing; measure recovery time and final success after timeout <cite id="61e09bfc-8">Potential fields are prone to attraction-well and path tangling failures; evaluations should explicitly test resilience and recovery</cite>.
- Kinematic constraints: enforce actuator limits and stopping distances; report worst-case TTC across obstacles and the ability to avoid within safety cushions <cite id="61e09bfc-1">Avoidance methods that maintain smooth velocity profiles respect constraints and reduce real-world risk</cite>.

4) Toolchains, leaderboards, and pipelines

4.1 Simulation and rendering
- CARLA and BARN emphasize end-to-end evaluation pipelines that include realistic physics, traffic, and sensors. CARLA provides a performance metrics module, a leaderboard with automated scoring, and scenario editors; BARN provides a large set of mazes with difficulty indicators. Together, they give you a reproducible, scalable evaluation stack for collision avoidance and reactive steering in dynamic and collision-free settings <cite id="06eb1382-1">CARLA’s leaderboard evaluates agents across realistic scenarios and aggregates results for comparison</cite> <cite id="06eb1382-4">CARLA’s metrics compute summaries over episode actions, enabling integration with collision/penalty measures</cite> <cite id="2f9111f9-5">BARN supplies standardized collision-free environments with difficulty-ordered sets for systematic benchmarking</cite>.

4.2 Open-source evaluation harnesses
- CARLA-based challenge harnesses and imitation-learning benchmarks demonstrate how to log states, actions, collisions, and penalties for automated scoring and leaderboard ingestion; adapt these harnesses for obstacle avoidance by adding collision energy, TTC thresholds, and pedestrian priority compliance checks <cite id="06eb1382-7">Community benchmarks show practical pipelines for CARLA-based imitation learning and evaluation</cite> <cite id="06eb1382-8">Challenge portals (e.g., eval.ai CARLA challenge) provide structured pipelines and automated judging for avoidance-like tasks</cite>.
- Perception-obstacle evaluation frameworks (e.g., marine MODS and egocentric annotation pipelines) can be embedded as sensing modules so that your planner’s inputs are realistically noisy, allowing end-to-end evaluation of perception–planning robustness <cite id="2f9111f9-4">The MODS evaluation stack measures obstacle detection efficiency and can be integrated with planners for end-to-end evaluation</cite> <cite id="2f9111f9-7">RoboSense provides large-scale egocentric obstacle annotations enabling systematic evaluation of perception-driven avoidance</cite>.

4.3 Human-in-the-loop and task-specific metrics
- For HRC, define success as task goal satisfaction with correct object positions and state changes, plus temporal tolerances; combine with safety and comfort penalties to reflect operational risk <cite id="2f9111f9-8">Task success can be defined as 1 when object positions and state align with task goals; integrating timing and safety into scoring helps compare practical performance</cite>.
- Include end-effector or base reachability and consequent safety (e.g., distance to humans) where relevant; audio/visual warnings can be benchmarked for preempting collisions in shared spaces, though formal metrics should tie to obstacle avoidance outcomes <cite id="7393ee8c-5">Recent work reviews reachability analysis for feasibility studies, emphasizing quantitative links from motion planning to deployment constraints</cite>.

5) Evaluation pitfalls to avoid and good practices
- Do not compare raw success only: stratify by difficulty and dynamics because methods can “pass” by operating conservatively. Use per-stratum scoring and rank with ANCOVA on difficulty covariates <cite id="2f9111f9-1">Difficulty metrics across 300 maps make it possible to detect algorithmic gains that survive increases in challenge</cite>.
- Beware local minima and oscillation biases in potential-field–style methods: include adversarial “maze with moving exits” scenarios and deadlock timeouts to expose and normalize recovery behavior <cite id="61e09bfc-8">Potential fields have inherent limits including local minima and tangling, necessitating evaluations of failure resilience</cite>.
- Align metrics to deployment constraints: include computation budgets and sensor update rates; penalize reactive planners that miss obstacles due to latency rather than intrinsic quality <cite id="61e09bfc-7">Smoother velocities from IDWA+PF suggest better alignment with real-time constraints while maintaining avoidance</cite>.
- Prefer end-to-end over component-level evaluation: fuse perception, inference, and actuation under realistic noise/latency to ensure that gains carry through to task success and safety; use Ablation studies to isolate contributions of perception, planner, and controller <cite id="7393ee8c-4">A navigation metrics survey emphasizes safety, dimension, and smoothness indicators but highlights the importance of end-to-end validation to capture trade-offs</cite>.

6) A practical evaluation recipe
- Choose domains: one collision-free maze suite (BARN), one dynamic traffic suite (CARLA), plus a perception-heavy interactive domain (RoboSense-based HRC).
- Define metrics: safety energy + collision binary; efficiency (time/detour); smoothness (jerk/curvature cost); compute budget; infractions/penalties; and per-stratum difficulty normalization.
- Run protocol: 100+ episodes per setting with randomized initial poses; repeat twice for statistical power; inject noise/occlusion levels to test robustness.
- Analyze: per-setting averages with difficulty-adjusted ranks; Wilcoxon tests and effect sizes; ablations on VO vs. MPC vs. potential fields with recovery-time analysis.
- Report: seeds, hardware/software stack, sensor specs, and failure taxonomies (obstacle density, pedestrian unpredictability, sensor outages) with representative trajectories/heatmaps from each regime.
- Iterate: synthesize qualitative and quantitative findings, and retrain/tune under constraints inferred from the evaluation (e.g., tighten TTC thresholds or add virtual forces to escape wells).

7) Summary of recommended benchmarks
- Collision-free planning/avoidance: BARN dataset with difficulty metrics for controlled, large-scale comparisons <cite id="2f9111f9-1">BARN covers 300 environments with features and ordering by difficulty</cite> <cite id="2f9111f9-5">BARN provides a suite of simulation environments to test collision-free mobile robot navigation</cite>.
- Dynamic obstacle avoidance (vehicular): CARLA benchmark and leaderboard with infractions/penalty scoring; integrate TTC, safety energy, and path cost; leverage real-world-based traffic scenarios <cite id="06eb1382-1">CARLA leaderboard evaluates agents in realistic traffic</cite> <cite id="06eb1382-6">Evaluation 2.0 defines infractions and penalties for safety scoring</cite> <cite id="06eb1382-4">CARLA’s performance metrics compute episode-level summaries</cite> <cite id="06eb1382-3">Real traffic scenarios in CARLA mimic real interactions</cite>.
- Interactive human environments: Human-action benchmarks (HABIT) and task-success metrics adapted for HRC with safety and comfort penalties <cite id="06eb1382-2">HABIT adds behavioral metrics to CARLA’s standard suite</cite> <cite id="2f9111f9-8">Task-success definitions for HRC enable metric composition with safety and comfort</cite>.
- Perception-realism: RoboSense for dense, annotated egocentric obstacles to evaluate sensing-limited avoidance; marine MODS for underwater scenarios and detection efficiency as a perception module stress test <cite id="2f9111f9-7">RoboSense offers >133K frames with obstacle annotations to quantify perception-driven avoidance</cite> <cite id="2f9111f9-4">MODS provides detection benchmarks and scripts for obstacle detection efficiency</cite>.
- Algorithmic stress tests: classic VO/VFO/labyrinth and DWA hybrids to quantify local-minima/oscillation resilience and smoothness; report failure recovery time and kinematic compliance <cite id="61e09bfc-8">Virtual force fields enable real-time avoidance but must be tested for limits and recovery</cite> <cite id="61e09bfc-7">DWA+PF hybrids can reduce accelerations while preserving avoidance, motivating smoothness-based comparisons</cite>.

In short, adopt BARN for large-scale collision-free benchmarking, CARLA for dynamic interactions with a mature metric suite, RoboSense for realistic perception noise, and classic algorithmic suites for failure-mode audits. Combine safety-energy, path efficiency, smoothness, and compute budgets with difficulty-aware stratification and rigorous statistics to obtain fair, practical comparisons across obstacle avoidance strategies <cite id="2f9111f9-1">Large suites with difficulty metrics like BARN enable principled scaling and stratification</cite> <cite id="06eb1382-6">Infraction-and-penalty leaderboards like CARLA’s provide standardized, quantifiable safety scoring for dynamic avoidance</cite> <cite id="61e09bfc-8">Awareness of potential-field limitations ensures avoidance tests probe failure modes relevant to deployment</cite>.
