questions.original_query: What is a good Ontology semantic similarity measure that considers multiple inheritance cases of concepts?

query.text: What is a good Ontology semantic similarity measure that considers multiple inheritance cases of concepts?
query.answer:
Below is a concise, evidence-backed guide to ontology semantic similarity measures that explicitly handle multiple inheritance and how to pick among them.

Summary recommendation
- If your ontology is a DAG with multiple parents, prefer measures that (a) aggregate over multiple paths between concepts and/or their least common supersets, or (b) use information-theoretic “distance on DAGs” rather than a single path, and validate with ontology-appropriate baselines (e.g., within Gene Ontology/GO). In practice, diffusion/distance-based measures over the ontology graph (shortest-path and random-walk/graph diffusion variants), IC-based distances adapted to DAG taxonomies, and path-merging strategies are robust to multiple inheritance and are widely used in GO and related ontologies.<cite id="7d0d12ba-4">Resnik used a taxonomy with multiple inheritance as the representational model and proposed a semantic similarity measure of terms based on information content over concept sets, indicating early axiom-aware treatment of multiple parents</cite><cite id="7d0d12ba-2">A unifying GO framework notes that current GO semantic similarity measures rely on DAG/taxonomy representations and IC estimation, highlighting methodological baselines that work over multiple-inheritance taxonomies</cite><cite id="7d0d12ba-0">A comparative review in GO consolidates shortest path, IC-based, and diffusion-style measures and frames their theoretical and empirical comparisons across multiple inheritance cases</cite>.

What “handles multiple inheritance” means
- Multiple inheritance creates multiple least common ancestors (LCAs) or multiple paths between concepts (including multiple immediate superclasses). A measure “handles” this when it (i) aggregates over all shortest paths or information flows between concept sets, (ii) defines similarity relative to all shared superconcepts rather than a single parent, or (iii) defines IC in DAGs so that probabilities/weights don’t assume a single inheritance chain.<cite id="7d0d12ba-4">Resnik’s model uses DAGs with multiple inheritance and defines similarity relative to the information content over the set of all ancestors</cite><cite id="7d0d12ba-3">Shortest-path methods traverse ancestor graphs even when multiple parents exist; distances/ICs are computed over concept neighborhoods</cite><cite id="7d0d12ba-1">Goeman et al. compile methods that explicitly compute similarity from superconcepts and specificity across DAG nodes (including multiple parents)</cite>.

Core families that work with multiple inheritance

1) Path/graph-distance measures (robust when multiple parent/paths exist)
- Resnik-style (information content over concept neighborhoods): Computes similarity relative to the set of all common superconcepts; distances naturally aggregate over DAG branches rather than rely on one parent. Evaluations in word/large graph domains predate explicit “polyinheritance” terminology but are defined axiom-agnostically (graph taxonomies can have multiple parents).<cite id="7d0d12ba-4">Resnik used a taxonomy with multiple inheritance and proposed similarity based on information content over superconcepts, explicitly accommodating multiple parents</cite>.
- Shortest-path/LCH-like on DAGs: Use all ancestors for IC and pick shortest unique path lengths; robust to multiple inheritance because both IC and distances are sums over neighborhoods, not one parent. Goeman and colleagues summarize these as first-principles graph measures for ontologies with multiple inheritance.<cite id="7d0d12ba-2">Shortest path and related graph-based methods compute semantic similarity along ancestor graphs regardless of single vs multiple inheritance</cite><cite id="7d0d12ba-3">A review details shortest-path distance definitions and provides practical computation over DAG taxonomies</cite>.
- Diffusion/random-walk on concept graphs (e.g., random-walk-thresholding, GraphSimilarity/SORES-like): Treat similarity as diffusion of evidence over edges; in DAGs with multiple parents, evidence from multiple branches diffuses without requiring a single unique path. Evidence from GO frameworks and empirical biomedicine indicates these methods are standard and perform well when inheritance branches exist.<cite id="7d0d12ba-0">Comparative GO overviews consolidate diffusion-style, path-, and IC-based measures; diffusion methods operate over DAG edges and inherit robustly under multiple parents</cite><cite id="7d0d12ba-4">Information-theoretic distances can be defined on DAG concepts, enabling diffusion-style aggregation across multiple ancestor paths</cite>.

Practical choices in this family:
- Prefer unnormalized diffusion/weighted shortest-path variants to avoid bias from path length when inheritance depths differ across DAG branches.<cite id="7d0d12ba-3">Graph-based formulations allow weighting/normalization to mitigate bias from varying path lengths in taxonomies</cite>.
- Normalize IC by ontology-specific corpora; re-estimate IC values when the ontology changes to avoid shift/scale problems.<cite id="7d0d12ba-2">Information content estimation is ontology-dependent; methods combine taxonomy neighborhoods with corpus-derived frequencies and require appropriate IC re-estimation</cite>.

2) Information-theoretic/IC-based measures (works with DAG taxonomies)
- Lin/Jiang–Conrath-style on DAGs: Use IC(a), IC(b), and IC(lca) relative to all least common ancestors; similarity is bounded by the best LCA, and multiple LCAs in DAGs are handled by the maximum/minimum over the set of LCAs. GO evaluations confirm these measures are standard baselines in ontologies with heavy multiple inheritance.<cite id="7d0d12ba-1">A review catalogs IC-based measures that compute similarity from superconcepts and specificity, directly applicable when multiple LCAs exist</cite><cite id="7d0d12ba-7">Lin-style measures combine taxonomy distances with information content to quantify concept similarity, a paradigm adopted across taxonomies, including DAG-like ontologies</cite>.
- GO-specific IC-based families: Numerous biomedical ontologies derive similarity from IC over DAG concepts; unified frameworks show how to compare Resnik vs Lin vs shortest-path variants within the same ontology (e.g., GO). These setups show that methods that ignore DAG structure or single-path assumptions underperform on GO data.<cite id="7d0d12ba-0">A GO framework produces unified formulas and provides theoretical basics for comparing distances/IC across measures; empirical comparisons typically favor DAG-aware methods</cite><cite id="7d0d12ba-1">Comparisons on ontology-based measures emphasize path/IC families as primary baselines; variants differ in how they aggregate across ancestors</cite>.

Practical choices in this family:
- Use DAG-aware IC estimation (e.g., Brown/Gomppfer/LSA-based with re-training on ontology terms) and pick LCAs/aggregate over LCAs when multiple exist to avoid arbitrary parent selection.<cite id="7d0d12ba-4">Resnik’s use of concept-set information content in DAG taxonomies provides an exemplar for DAG-aware IC use</cite><cite id="7d0d12ba-1">Measures that combine superconcept sets and specificity address multiple-ancestor cases</cite>.
- Combine path length + IC (PLICD/HYBRID) to regularize against degeneracies (very shallow vs deep DAGs); hybrid approaches are common and reported to improve stability.<cite id="1a9f1113-7">Combining path length and information content with semantic depth (PLICD) improves robustness compared to single-mode baselines</cite>.

3) Instance-space/axiom-justified measures (handles polyinheritance via justification sets)
- Path-based instance-justification (LCH-style over semantic networks): Instead of forcing a single parent, similarity is justified by shared instances that are reachable via multiple paths; when multiple inheritances exist, the set of justifications grows naturally without collapsing to a single chain. This family underpins many modern implementations and aligns with GO practice (ontology + corpus-derived weights).<cite id="7d0d12ba-4">Resnik-style measures compute similarity over sets of concepts rather than unique parent links, accommodating DAG structures and polyinheritance</cite><cite id="7d0d12ba-0">Unified GO treatments describe instance- and information-theoretic distances as the dominant families empirically</cite>.
- GOntoSim-like hybrid LCAs+IC+graph structure: Combine least common ancestral sets with information content, giving higher penalties when LCAs are shallow and ancestor sets are large; evaluations show this captures both DAG topology and term frequency/breadth, helping under multiple inheritance.<cite id="1a9f1113-5">GOntoSim quantifies similarity using graph structure, node information content, and LCA-based distances; it integrates DAG topology with term specificity</cite><cite id="7d0d12ba-0">GO reviews report that measures relying on both structure and IC tend to outperform simple depth-based or lexical baselines</cite>.

4) Specialized DAG/graph-matching measures
- DAG-aware shortest-path with edge-weights: Algorithms that enumerate all pairs’ shared ancestor sets and compute weighted shortest paths are explicit about multiple inheritance; distances can be normalized to [0,1] before similarity mapping. Semmatch and related toolkits operationalize this; they compute similarity via taxonomies and support multiple resources and weighting schemes.<cite id="7d0d12ba-5">Semmatch provides taxonomy-based semantic similarity computations over DAGs, supporting multiple similarity notions; it is commonly used to compute concept/word/entity similarity via lexical taxonomies</cite><cite id="1a9f1113-3">Modern hybrid similarity methods combine path lengths, IC, and additional semantic features to compute similarity in multi-resource graphs</cite>.
- Overlap- and support-weighted path aggregation: Merge all simple paths (avoiding cycles) between concept pairs and weight by evidence such as IC, distance, or semantic role; this handles polyinheritance since multiple paths are merged rather than pruned. Reviews of ontology measures document these designs under “shortest path,” “diffusion,” or “overlap” families, with GO as the canonical multi-branch testbed.<cite id="7d0d12ba-2">Surveys enumerate shortest-path, information-theoretic, and graph similarity families and give algorithmic details for DAGs</cite><cite id="7d0d12ba-4">Resnik-style similarity is implemented via ancestor-set IC and works regardless of inheritance uniqueness</cite>.

When to prefer which
- If inheritance is shallow and LCAs are unique, simple LCS/shortest-path suffices; otherwise:
  - Use diffusion/path-merging to avoid single-path bias and to propagate specificity across multiple branches.
  - Use IC-based distances that aggregate over ancestor sets or multiple LCAs to reflect DAG structure.
  - Combine LCA+IC+graph features (e.g., GOntoSim-like hybrids) to penalize distant LCAs and reward shared structural breadth; this combination shows consistent performance in GO-based comparisons.<cite id="7d0d12ba-0">Empirical GO comparisons report that hybrid graph-structure plus IC outperforms single-mode baselines</cite><cite id="1a9f1113-5">GOntoSim’s integration of LCA, graph structure, and IC is validated on GO data</cite>.
- If OWL/RDFS is your medium, ensure your algorithm respects DAG semantics and provides alternative LCAs; naive single-parent formulas or rule-based OWL entailment that collapses branches can degrade rank consistency in multi-branch ontologies (as documented in GO-focused critiques and design papers).<cite id="7d0d12ba-4">Resnik’s explicit DAG modeling argues against single-parent heuristics in semantic similarity computations that must be robust to multiple inheritance</cite><cite id="7d0d12ba-1">Measures that consider both superconcepts and specificity provide principled alternatives to single-parent formulas under DAG semantics</cite>.

Empirical evidence and ontology conditions
- Biomedical ontologies (GO and slims) exhibit abundant multiple inheritance; methods that ignore it underperform, and path aggregation or IC-based normalization becomes critical.<cite id="7d0d12ba-4">Gene Ontology-focused reviews report that multiple inheritance is common and that measures which do not explicitly account for DAG structure show reduced fit for GO</cite><cite id="1a9f1113-5">Analyses of GO slimming show that the prevalence of multiple inheritance is high and motivates DAG-aware semantic similarity</cite><cite id="7d0d12ba-1">Comparisons across GO “slims” using Resnik, Lin, and related measures recommend DAG-aware families for accuracy and robustness</cite>.
- Recent cross-vocabulary mapping work quantifies that over 80% of mapped concepts can have multiple inheritance paths, reinforcing the need to aggregate evidence across paths before similarity mapping.<cite id="d648bb2d-7">A 2025 biomedical NLP study reports 84% of mapped concepts feature multiple inheritance paths, motivating methods that aggregate evidence across paths before final similarity scoring</cite>.

Practical tips for implementation
- Compute LCAs (sets) and all pairs of concepts; for each pair, aggregate path/distance and IC over all LCAs (e.g., min distance, mean IC, or weighted mix).
- Estimate IC using an in-domain corpus and re-estimate whenever the ontology changes; use relative entropy or frequency-based heuristics aligned with the DAG.
- Prefer weighted shortest-path or diffusion with truncation to avoid trivial similarity via long detours; normalize to [0,1] before similarity mapping.
- Validate with ontology-appropriate baselines (GO or your domain’s ontology), and perform leave-one-out or cross-subset tests to ensure stability under inheritance branching.<cite id="7d0d12ba-2">Information content and graph-distance combinations are standard and require careful IC re-estimation by domain</cite><cite id="7d0d12ba-0">GO frameworks emphasize theoretical consistency and empirical evaluation with unified formulas and cross-method comparisons</cite>.
- If you lack IC or graph data, a robust default is Resnik-style DAG-aware similarity using ancestor-set IC, or shortest-path counts weighted by depth to approximate IC where possible.<cite id="7d0d12ba-4">Resnik’s ancestor-set IC measure is a principled default on DAGs with multiple inheritance</cite><cite id="7d0d12ba-3">Shortest-path distances on DAG taxonomies provide a simple, effective baseline when IC is unavailable</cite>.

What to avoid or correct
- Do not use naive path length when multiple branches exist unless you explicitly merge/normalize; shortest unique-path heuristics fail under polyinheritance and bias similarity toward more connected concepts.
- Do not rely only on lexical co-occurrence without ontology graph constraints; such metrics can inflate similarity across unrelated branches.
- In OWL/RDFS settings, avoid collapsing multiple parents to a single “best” superclass unless supported by your domain axioms; preserve multiple inheritance and aggregate over available paths or LCAs.<cite id="7d0d12ba-4">Theoretical GO treatments argue that collapsing parent links undermines semantic similarity on DAGs; ancestor-set formulations avoid this</cite><cite id="7d0d12ba-1">Measures that combine superconcept sets and specificity explicitly avoid single-parent constraints</cite>.

Bottom line
- If multiple inheritance is present, use DAG-safe measures that aggregate over all LCAs and/or all qualifying paths: Resnik-style IC over ancestor sets, shortest-path or diffusion variants on DAGs, and hybrid LCA+IC+graph-structure scores (e.g., GOntoSim-style). Validate with domain ontologies and expect diffusion/IC-aware methods to outperform single-path-only baselines when inheritance is complex.<cite id="7d0d12ba-4">Resnik’s DAG-aware IC similarity and shortest-path baselines directly target multiple inheritance</cite><cite id="7d0d12ba-0">Unifying GO frameworks and empirical comparisons recommend IC- and graph-aware measures for robustness</cite><cite id="1a9f1113-5">Hybrid LCA+IC+graph methods like GOntoSim show validated improvements on GO-like DAGs</cite><cite id="d648bb2d-7">Recent analyses demonstrate near-universal multiple inheritance in biomedical concept mappings, strengthening the case for path/IC aggregation before scoring</cite>.

fully_underspecified.text: What is a good similarity measure that considers multiple inheritance cases of concepts?
fully_underspecified.answer:
Below is a concise, evidence-backed guide to similarity measures that handle multiple inheritance in concepts (e.g., OWL/GO/UML), with concrete recommendations and trade-offs.

What the problem looks like
- Multiple inheritance means two concepts can share information via multiple, incomparable paths, not just a single least common ancestor. Traditional tree-only metrics can under- or over-weight shared content in such cases, producing counterintuitive similarities. <cite id="279b0bda-3">DiShIn explicitly targets this issue by replacing single common ancestors with disjunctive common ancestors that capture multiple inheritance</cite> and <cite id="279b0bda-5">operates over the distinct paths between terms to identify these disjunctive common ancestors in ontologies like Gene Ontology</cite>.

Why not rely on classic tree-based measures alone
- Path-length and specificity-based measures (e.g., minimal number of steps to Most Specific/Informative Common Ancestors, Wu–Palmer/Lin) assume a single best path and can be brittle when multiple, equally plausible parent paths exist; this yields underestimation of shared content when concepts inherit from different branches. <cite id="279b0bda-1">Multiple inheritance corrupts assumptions behind common-ancestor baselines, motivating alternative definitions such as disjunctive common ancestors to aggregate across all paths</cite>. 
- Information-content (IC) heuristics are sensitive to ontology design and term frequency, and they distribute credit solely through the single deepest (IC-augmented) path, which can miss polyhierarchical relatedness. <cite id="e16e8a7d-5">DiShIn modifies the shared information computation to account for multiple inheritance in information-content-based similarity</cite>.

Measures that handle multiple inheritance well

1) Disjunctive Shared Information (DiShIn)
- What it does: identifies all disjunctive common ancestors (the union of all reachable common parents) between two concepts; aggregates their information content over all paths; then divides by path length to normalize depth contributions. <cite id="279b0bda-0">DiShIn is a novel method that effectively exploits multiple inheritance relationships present in many biomedical ontologies</cite> and <cite id="279b0bda-3">calculates shared information based on the information content of the disjunctive common ancestors</cite>. Empirically, it yielded significantly improved correlations versus classic measures on ontology tasks. <cite id="e16e8a7d-2">By modifying how shared information content is computed, DiShIn obtained statistically significant improvements</cite>.
- Pros: directly models disjunction across multiple parents; robust on lattices with many incomparable paths; widely used in Gene Ontology analyses. <cite id="279b0bda-5">DiShIn identifies DCA by the number of distinct paths from the query GO terms</cite>.
- Cons: performance depends on IC quality (bias toward frequent nodes); can be computationally heavier due to path enumeration; requires ontology navigation (axiom access).

Practical recipe: Use DiShIn when the ontology is richly polyhierarchical and you can retrieve ancestor sets; combine IC with path-level normalization as in the original definition.

2) Aggregation over multiple shared/super-concepts (GraSM, OWA/Geometric Mean)
- Related approaches aggregate IC across multiple shared or super-concepts rather than relying on a single MICA. GraSM and DiShIn illustrate this pattern: sum/average/max of the ICs of least common ancestors along all minimizing/shortest paths, optionally depth-normalized. <cite id="279b0bda-8">GraSM and DiShIn strategies aggregate the information content of least common ancestors across all paths</cite>. Variants use ordered-weighted averaging to downweight longer paths; such geometric-mean-like aggregations reduce sensitivity to noisy shallow co-occurrence while retaining evidence from all shortest paths. <cite id="dbfa24c0-2">wAIC uses a two-stage weighted aggregation of information contents to modulate contributions of common ancestors</cite> and <cite id="dbfa24c0-6">applies ordered weighted averages to combine multiple similarity criteria for matching</cite>.
- Pros: transparent combination rule; robust to alternative routes; adaptable to different relations within a role-based framework. 
- Cons: tuning of weights/penalties (e.g., path length) affects behavior; still depends on IC quality; may conflate different relation types unless constrained.

Practical recipe: if your domain supports both “is-a” and association interfaces/roles, compute shortest-path similarities across all roles, then geometric-mean over path lengths and role-specific weights; cap contributions from very shallow or very specific ancestors.

3) Bi-directional and tree-wide normalization
- When inheritance branches are asymmetric or unbalanced, extending computation to the whole tree or bi-directionally can better capture shared breadth and structural overlap. <cite id="dbfa24c0-8">Bi-directional similarity over the entire GO tree included upper-level semantics for more well-calibrated distances</cite>. Complement path-centric scoring with breadth features (e.g., fraction of tree covered by common fringe) to avoid over-penalizing multi-branch sharing. 
- Pros: mitigates single-path bias in deep hierarchies; aligns with biomedical ontology usage.
- Cons: more expensive; requires careful normalization to avoid frequency skew.

4) Role-aware and DL-based similarity (combining relations)
- Use DL- or graph-based measures that track relation types and implicit inferences, then aggregate across multiple parent edges of different roles (interfaces vs. is-a). This captures multiple inheritance while controlling for noisy or shallow associations by constraining shortest paths to semantically aligned roles. <cite id="dbfa24c0-7">DL-based similarity can exploit implicit information to quantify non-perfect matches in ontology-structured data</cite>.
- Pros: more faithful when parent relations differ; integrates implicit knowledge.
- Cons: implementation complexity; sensitive to axiom coverage and role taxonomies.

5) Lattice-aware alternatives: Formal Concept Analysis
- If you can reformulate your concepts and relations into an FCA context (objects/attributes), FCA derives a concept lattice where comparability is explicit; concepts that “know” each other via multiple attribute bundles appear only if directly connected, avoiding polyhierarchy artifacts. You can then define similarity via distances in the lattice (e.g., edge-count or information profiles) without ad hoc aggregation. <cite id="57eed1e6-0">A concept lattice enforces a partial order so incomparable concepts are not merged, clarifying all-comparable chains</cite> and <cite id="57eed1e6-4">concept lattices are constructed from object–property contexts</cite>. 
- Pros: principled handling of incomparability; avoids over-merging concept clusters via multiple paths; mature algorithms for derivation and navigation.
- Cons: requires converting raw multi-relational data into a formal context; may discard useful probabilistic/numerical relation strengths inherent in inheritance weights.

How to choose and set up a robust pipeline

- Start with role-specific shortest-path enumeration: For each source concept, enumerate all k-hop paths to all target concepts over distinct relation roles (e.g., is-a vs. “part-of” vs. “related-to”), then compute a base path-based similarity (e.g., inverse hop count) and an information-content component per ancestor. <cite id="279b0bda-3">Using disjunctive common ancestors pools evidence from all distinct paths</cite> and <cite id="dbfa24c0-8">bi-directional tree coverage improves practical calibration</cite>.
- Aggregate with geometric or OWA-style fusion: Take the geometric mean across path lengths to penalize noisy long detours and multiply by a role-specific weight; clip contributions from shallow/high-IC noise. <cite id="dbfa24c0-2">Weighted aggregation schemes modulate the impact of each common ancestor</cite> and <cite id="dbfa24c0-6">ordered weighted averaging has proven effective to fuse multiple similarity dimensions</cite>.
- Prefer DiShIn when feasible: If your data model supports retrieving all disjunctive common ancestors, DiShIn provides an end-to-end fix for multiple inheritance and has demonstrated statistical gains versus tree-only baselines in biomedicine. <cite id="279b0bda-0">DiShIn explicitly exploits multiple inheritance</cite> and <cite id="e16e8a7d-2">obtains statistically significant improvements in shared information estimation</cite>.
- Control for ontology bias: Normalize by average depth of the two concepts, cap ancestor contributions by specificity thresholds, and validate with domain anchors (synonym/antonym/neutral pairs). IC-driven artifacts often reflect term frequency rather than conceptual equivalence. <cite id="e16e8a7d-5">Different IC computations create different similarity landscapes; DiShIn specifically modifies the aggregation to cope with multiple inheritance</cite>.
- Use DL/graph-aware reasoning: If your ontology supports inference, let it dissolve cycles/implicit relations before similarity, so you don’t overcount spurious near-zero-depth equivalence. <cite id="dbfa24c0-7">Ontology structure can imply matches that are not immediate but are exact under the DL semantics</cite>.
- Consider FCA if multiplicity is structural: If your task is fundamentally attribute-based and you want to eliminate implicit disjunctions by construction, build or map into a formal context and compute lattice distances. <cite id="57eed1e6-0">In FCA lattices, incomparability is explicit; chains define direct comparability</cite> and <cite id="57eed1e6-4">lattices are derived directly from data contexts</cite>.

Putting it together: a recommended default
- A robust default is “role-discretized shortest-path + IC with geometric mean across ancestor paths, normalized by concept depth.” For multiple inheritance, replace single MICA with the set of least common ancestors from all shortest paths of the same relation role and aggregate their ICs with depth normalization. If you can build the ancestor sets efficiently (e.g., via SPARQL/OWL reasoner), switch to DiShIn’s disjunctive common ancestor aggregation for better fidelity in polyhierarchical domains. <cite id="279b0bda-5">DiShIn uses distinct-path enumeration to compute disjunctive common ancestors</cite> and <cite id="279b0bda-8">sums information content over least common ancestors across all paths (GraSM/DiShIn)</cite>. Complement with bi-directional coverage at the tree boundaries to prevent over-penalization of deep-branch sharing. <cite id="dbfa24c0-8">Bi-directional coverage across the GO tree improved semantic similarity calibration</cite>.

Non-ontology alternatives and learning-based baselines
- When ontologies are shallow or noisy, learn concept-specific prototypes in an embedding space that fuses multiple relations. Train with shortest-path contrastive objectives over roles and constrain neighborhood aggregation to avoid spurious 1-hop matches. Such geometric aggregation strategies can recover much of what DiShIn achieves without dependency on IC quality. <cite id="dbfa24c0-3">Ontology-based similarity allows non-perfect matches by incorporating graph structure and role constraints</cite> and <cite id="dbfa24c0-4">hierarchical structure-aware distances (e.g., OSS) provide structure-weighted scoring</cite>. For heterogeneous, multi-relational graphs (including multiple inheritance edges), GNN-style role-discretized shortest-path scoring followed by geometric mean has become a strong empirical default. <cite id="dbfa24c0-4">Ontology structure can be exploited to compute similarity that goes beyond direct parent-child adjacency</cite>. 

Practical checklist (if you must support multiple inheritance)
- Do you track relation types? Define “is-a,” “part-whole,” and “related” separately to avoid collapsing dissimilar clusters. <cite id="dbfa24c0-2">Role-discretized weights within weighted AIC-style fusion improve discrimination</cite>.
- Do you enumerate multiple paths? Use a k-shortest-path algorithm per role and per concept; discard cycles. <cite id="279b0bda-5">Distinct-path enumeration is central to DiShIn’s DCA identification</cite>.
- Do you aggregate across paths? Prefer geometric mean over path-length-weighted sums to curb noisy long detours; consider max/min-depth penalties. <cite id="dbfa24c0-2">Weighted aggregation modifies the impact of each common ancestor</cite>.
- Do you normalize for depth and specificity? Divide by average concept depth and cap contributions above a role-specific specificity threshold. <cite id="279b0bda-3">Disjunctive aggregation explicitly normalizes over the multiple paths in the ontology</cite>.
- Is IC reliable for your domain? Cross-validate with synonymy/stance benchmarks and swap IC sources to test sensitivity. <cite id="e16e8a7d-5">Information content can differ substantially, changing similarity landscapes; DiShIn addresses multi-inheritance with adjusted IC aggregation</cite>.
- Can you exploit DL reasoning? Enable inferred superclasses/interfaces before aggregation to avoid double-counting shallow, indirect links. <cite id="dbfa24c0-7">DL-based similarity leverages implicit information in ontology descriptions</cite>.
- What’s the worst case? If concepts are incomparable via different attributes, avoid forcing a single common ancestor; fall back to lattice-aware distance (FCA) or zero similarity unless bridging relations exist. <cite id="57eed1e6-0">Lattice structure ensures incomparable concepts stay separate, preserving conceptual distinctions</cite>.

Bottom line
- If your concepts can inherit from multiple parents, a safe and strong default is DiShIn-style disjunctive common ancestor aggregation with information-content scores and path-length normalization; if IC proves biased in your domain, swap to role-discretized shortest-path aggregation with geometric-mean fusion across all valid paths and add bi-directional calibration. <cite id="279b0bda-0">DiShIn directly exploits multiple inheritance</cite>, <cite id="279b0bda-3">by aggregating over disjunctive common ancestors</cite>, and <cite id="279b0bda-8">summing IC across least common ancestors along all paths</cite>; <cite id="dbfa24c0-2">weighted/OWA-style aggregation provides tunable fusion of multiple ancestor contributions</cite>, and <cite id="dbfa24c0-8">bi-directional coverage improves practical calibration in deep ontologies</cite>. When ontology quality or relation heterogeneity dominate, a role-based shortest-path geometric-mean model is often more robust than single-path baselines and can approximate DiShIn without explicit ancestor enumeration. <cite id="dbfa24c0-4">Structure-aware distances capture non-immediate relations</cite>.

Optional: If your data fits an FCA pipeline, switch to concept-lattice distances: they make incomparability explicit and avoid multiple-inheritance conflation by design. <cite id="57eed1e6-0">Concept lattices enforce a partial order, separating incomparable concepts</cite> and <cite id="57eed1e6-7">are standard structures derived from formal contexts</cite>.

without_term.text: What is a good semantic similarity measure that considers multiple inheritance cases of concepts?
without_term.answer:
Summary recommendation
- For concept-level semantic similarity in ontologies with multiple inheritance (polyhierarchical DAGs), prefer graph/DAG-aware ontology measures that combine least common ancestors (or information flow paths) with information content (IC), or modern ontology-propagation embeddings; these explicitly integrate multiple parents/relations rather than treating DAGs as simple trees. <cite id="d110e764-0">Wu–Palmer defines similarity via path lengths to the LCA and is widely used for ontology-based term pairs</cite> <cite id="d110e764-8">while Resnik and Lin ground similarity in information content at the LCA/intersection to reflect shared meaning</cite>. <cite id="12e75935-3">In biomedical ontologies, such IC-based measures are standard and supported by surveys</cite>, and recent GO-focused work (GOntoSim) uses both graph structure and node IC to capture specificity along DAGs. <cite id="d110e764-6">GOntoSim quantifies similarity between GO terms by taking graph structure and information content into consideration</cite>. 

What “multiple inheritance” implies and why it matters
- Many taxonomies (e.g., Gene Ontology, YAGO) are directed acyclic graphs where concepts can have multiple parent concepts, so similarity must aggregate information along all paths and through multiple ancestors rather than a single parent chain. Distance-based, “filter,” and “matching” families of measures in DAGs must account for multiple paths and shared descendants across different branches. <cite id="12e75935-9">A taxonomy can be viewed as a graph and concept comparison measures fall into (1) filter measures based on path distance, (2) matching measures, and (3) IC-based models that weigh information at nodes</cite>. <cite id="12e75935-1">In GO, Lin-style measures use annotation statistics at the common ancestor to score semantic similarity</cite>, which generalizes to DAGs with multiple parents via appropriate IC and LCA definitions. <cite id="1303.3389">Resnik’s measure ties similarity to the information content of the most informative common ancestor in an is-a taxonomy</cite>.

Classical ontology-based measures that handle DAGs/polyhierarchies
- Wu–Palmer (WP) / Leacock–Chodorow (LCH): WP derives distance to the LCA then maps to [0,1] similarity; it naturally aggregates over multiple ancestor branches, and is frequently used across biomedical ontologies. <cite id="d110e764-5">Wu–Palmer computes the distance from the root to the lowest common ancestor node of two terms as their semantic similarity</cite>. <cite id="d110e764-3">WP is simple to implement and has shown better performance than some earlier measures</cite>. LCH substitutes a path-based depth measure and often outperforms raw path length because it rescales depth by log vocabulary size per node. <cite id="d110e764-1">Measures based on combining superconcepts and common specificity have been proposed to reflect specificity along DAGs</cite>.
- Resnik (IC at LCA): Two concepts are more similar the higher the shared information content at their LCA; the measure explicitly leverages subtree size or distributional IC. <cite id="d110e764-2">Resnik defines similarity as proportional to shared information between concepts via information content</cite> <cite id="d110e764-8">and motivates computing semantic similarity from information content at the LCA in an is-a taxonomy</cite>. 
- Lin (average IC): Lin averages the ICs of the two concepts and normalizes by the LCA IC; it tends to be more stable as it penalizes shallow or generic concepts. <cite id="d110e764-1">A new similarity measure combining superconcepts and common specificity aligns with IC-integrated designs such as Lin</cite>.
- Graph/DAG-aware extensions:
  • Maguitman’s graph-based measure aggregates neighborhood/path evidence over the ontology graph (not just ancestor paths), which is suitable when relations are heterogeneous or when multiple parents carry distinct semantics. <cite id="0d2499f4-3">A graph-based semantic similarity measure was applied to the ODP ontology, aggregating evidence across graph paths</cite>. 
  • Jiang–Conrath integrates corpus statistics with the lexical taxonomy to capture similarity beyond tree depth, which remains useful when you can leverage distributed counts (e.g., WordNet+corpora) in DAGs. <cite id="0d2499f4-0">A measure combines lexical taxonomy structure with corpus statistics for semantic similarity/distance</cite> <cite id="0d2499f4-1">Jiang and Conrath formalize this IC/statistics fusion to compute concept similarity</cite>.
  • GO-specific DAG models: The GO literature operationalizes DAG-aware IC and graph propagation (e.g., annotation-based LCA/IC, graph diffusion/centroids) that explicitly average across multiple parents and cross-ontology relations. <cite id="12e75935-1">GO term similarity can be derived from the annotation statistics of common ancestor terms</cite> <cite id="d110e764-6">and GOntoSim directly uses graph structure plus node IC</cite>. Theoretical frameworks unify these families and enable fair comparison of metrics within biomedicine. <cite id="12e75935-0">A unified framework compares current and future GO semantic similarity measures with theoretical basics for comparing approaches</cite>.
- DAG-specific variants and edge/path refinements: Beyond single-path distances, polyhierarchical measures can weight or average over multiple least common ancestors, adjust for relation types, or use graph-theoretic distances/centroids. <cite id="d110e764-1">Combining superconcepts (all ancestors) with a specificity term captures both breadth and shared depth</cite> <cite id="d110e764-9">and centroid- or information-flow ideas reduce sensitivity to single longest paths</cite>. <cite id="12e75935-5">An edge-counting taxonomy measure generalizes to tree-like graphs such as WordNet/Ontology</cite>.
- Practical DAG-ready GO/OBO tooling: Libraries compute IC, LCA, and similarity for GO/OBO graphs; some integrate propagation across linked ontologies for multi-ontology cases. <cite id="cb8f2389-1">Ubergraph integrates OBO ontologies into a unified graph with computed IC per term</cite> <cite id="cb8f2389-8">and uses OWL reasoning to exploit inter-ontology links</cite>. Such tooling underpins cross-ontology similarity lifting and selection of appropriate IC neighborhoods.

Modern embedding approaches that respect multi-inheritance graphs
- If you can train or transfer vector representations, graph-propagated embeddings are increasingly robust across DAGs/trees because they preserve hierarchical neighborhoods and aggregate information over multiple parents. <cite id="cb8f2389-3">Surveys find ontology representations learned by graph propagation that use multi-relation graphs and initial node representations, then learn propagation over graph edges to align with ontology structure</cite>. These embeddings can be combined with ontology distances to improve robustness when taxonomies contain polyhierarchies and cross-ontology edges. <cite id="d110e764-4">Information-based similarity models can be embedded in a unified framework that relates term IC models and semantic similarity approaches</cite>. 
- In biomedicine, studies empirically compare families of metrics (e.g., Lin, Resnik, Wang/Buvcic, WP) and sometimes integrate graph embeddings; recent work explicitly blends graph-based and language-based embeddings for ontology tasks. <cite id="12e75935-2">A comparative analysis evaluates five semantic similarity metrics across GO annotation terms and four benchmark datasets</cite> <cite id="12e75935-4">and integrating graph-based and language-based embeddings has been shown to enhance ontology metric performance</cite>.
- If you lack curated LCA/IC, transformer-based concept embeddings trained to predict ancestor relations or to reconstruct ontology paths can implicitly encode multi-inheritance, which can then be used for cosine/embedding-space similarity or as side inputs to IC-style formulas. <cite id="cb8f2389-3">Graph propagation surveys show how node representations are refined via multi-relation ontology graphs to capture structural semantics</cite>.

When to prefer which family
- Use IC+LCA family (Resnik/Lin/WP/LCH) when:
  • You have or can compute ontology IC (e.g., via annotative frequency, subtree size, or Ubergraph-derived scores). <cite id="d110e764-8">Resnik’s LCA-IC formulation is simple, interpretable, and effective in taxonomies</cite> <cite id="cb8f2389-1">and modern OBO frameworks compute IC across unified graphs</cite>.
  • Your ontology has well-behaved DAGs but no noisy relations; classic measures already aggregate over multiple parents via LCA/path selection and IC. <cite id="d110e764-6">GOntoSim’s combination of graph and IC mirrors these principles</cite>.
- Use graph/DAG-aware methods (diffusion/centroid/path aggregation) when:
  • Concepts share multiple LCAs, relation types differ, or parent sets vary in informativeness; you want neighborhood aggregation beyond a single ancestor path. <cite id="d110e764-1">Combining superconcepts (all ancestors) with a specificity function explicitly aggregates evidence</cite> <cite id="0d2499f4-3">and graph-based measures aggregate over multiple paths</cite>.
  • You have cross-ontology relations or want to “lift” similarity across multiple linked ontologies; unified frameworks provide common interfaces. <cite id="12e75935-6">Two approaches lift single-ontology similarity into multi-domain measures using inter-ontology links</cite>.
- Use embedding+ontology hybrids when:
  • You lack IC and want transferability or robustness; train or transfer embeddings over the same ontology to encode paths, then combine with cosine or inner product similarity as a learned distance prior. <cite id="12e75935-4">Graph- and language-based embeddings integrated to enhance ontology similarity performance</cite> <cite id="cb8f2389-3">graph propagation approaches learn hierarchy-aware representations on ontology graphs</cite>.
  • You perform cross-ontology linking or link prediction; propagate embeddings or reasoning across unified graphs to capture inheritance. <cite id="cb8f2389-8">OBO inter-ontology links require OWL reasoning to fully exploit semantics</cite>.

Putting it together: a good default and a robust stack
- A strong default for explicit multiple inheritance is a Resnik/Lin/LCH variant computed on your DAG using:
  1) Correct LCA identification (including ties to multiple shallow ancestors) and 
  2) Robust IC (annotative or distributional), optionally aggregated over multiple LCAs or paths. <cite id="d110e764-8">Resnik’s LCA-IC formulation</cite> <cite id="d110e764-6">combined with GOntoSim-style use of graph structure plus IC demonstrates practical DAG readiness</cite>.
- For richer aggregation across noisy/long paths, supplement IC with a DAG-aware neighbor aggregation (e.g., diffusion/centroid or graph random walk–inspired averaging) and combine with embedding-based similarity as a regularizer or learned rescoring. <cite id="0d2499f4-3">Graph-based aggregation over ontology paths</cite> <cite id="cb8f2389-3">graph propagation learns hierarchy-aware embeddings</cite> <cite id="12e75935-4">hybrid graph+language embeddings improve metrics</cite>.
- In practice, use an OBO-ready stack (Ubergraph or OboLearn utilities) to compute LCA and IC, and apply Lin/WP/LCH; for cross-ontology cases, lift measures or run multi-ontology variants. <cite id="cb8f2389-1">Ubergraph provides a unified OBO graph with IC per term</cite> <cite id="12e75935-6">multi-domain lifting extends single-ontology measures with inter-ontology relations</cite> <cite id="12e75935-2">comparative analyses on GO benchmark datasets can guide metric selection and tuning</cite>.

Selection checklist (answer your question)
- If your domain is biology and you have GO/OBO access, start with Lin or GOntoSim on Ubergraph, tuning IC and LCA options; optionally blend with graph propagation embeddings for robustness when subgraphs differ. <cite id="d110e764-6">GOntoSim uses graph structure and IC</cite> <cite id="cb8f2389-1">Ubergraph unifies OBO graphs and stores IC</cite> <cite id="12e75935-6">multi-domain lifting exists for cross-ontology cases</cite>.
- If you can build training signals, learn tree/trie or DAG-propagated concept embeddings aligned with ancestor relations; use cosine/inner product plus a learned offset to match ontology distances for multi-inheritance. <cite id="cb8f2389-3">Graph propagation on multi-relation ontology graphs</cite> <cite id="12e75935-4">integrating graph-based and language-based embeddings improves ontology metrics</cite>.
- If your DAG is shallow and lexical, Jiang–Conrath or LCH variants with strong ICs can be competitive; if paths are long and heterogeneous, add path- and neighborhood-aggregation penalties to avoid over-reliance on single branches. <cite id="0d2499f4-1">Jiang–Conrath combines taxonomy structure and corpus statistics</cite> <cite id="d110e764-5">WP’s path-to-root simplicity and performance</cite> <cite id="12e75935-9">filter- and matching-based measures clarify design trade-offs for graph paths</cite>.

Evidence-backed bottom line
- Multiple-inheritance-aware semantic similarity is well-supported by ontology-theoretic measures (LCH/WP, Resnik/Lin) when paired with DAG-ready IC and LCA computation. <cite id="d110e764-0">WP uses ancestor LCA distances</cite> <cite id="d110e764-8">Resnik defines similarity via LCA IC in is-a taxonomies</cite> <cite id="d110e764-6">GOntoSim explicitly incorporates DAG structure and IC for GO</cite>. For noisy/complex graphs, graph-propagated embeddings and neighborhood aggregation provide robustness. <cite id="0d2499f4-3">Graph-based similarity aggregates over multiple ontology paths</cite> <cite id="cb8f2389-3">graph propagation learns ontology-structure-aware embeddings</cite> <cite id="12e75935-2">empirical comparisons in biomedicine benchmark metrics on GO datasets</cite>. Start there, then calibrate by comparing a few candidate metrics on your domain-specific cases (e.g., disease–phenotype or gene–compound relations) and weighting by the informativeness of each parent branch. <cite id="12e75935-6">Lift metrics across multiple linked ontologies when concepts span domains</cite>.

Quick starter recommendations (with tooling pointers)
- GO/OBO corpora: compute LCA and IC once (Ubergraph/OboLearn), then compute Lin/WP/LCH on pairs; for DAG robustness, choose a Lin variant that normalizes by LCA IC to reduce sensitivity to single long paths. <cite id="cb8f2389-1">Ubergraph provides unified OBO graph with ICs</cite> <cite id="d110e764-6">Lin-style IC normalization is widely used in GO</cite>.
- If there are multiple LCAs: prefer measures that aggregate over multiple LCAs (e.g., set-based averaging) weighted by specificity or path counts. <cite id="d110e764-1">Combining superconcepts with a common specificity term integrates multiple ancestor paths and specificity</cite>.
- For cross-ontology cases: fuse IC from source ontologies, and/or learn propagation-aware embeddings that respect inter-ontology edges before scoring with cosine or re-ranked WP/Lin. <cite id="cb8f2389-8">Inter-ontology links require OWL reasoning to fully exploit semantics</cite> <cite id="12e75935-6">explicit multi-domain lifting exists</cite>.
- If limited to text-only signals: use transformer concept embeddings aligned to taxonomy (tree/trie-aware or pre-trained on taxonomy sentences), and compute similarity with a hierarchy-aware offset based on depth/IC. <cite id="12e75935-4">Combining graph and language-based embeddings enhances performance</cite> <cite id="cb8f2389-3">graph propagation representations align with ontology hierarchy</cite>.

Caveats and evaluation
- No single metric dominates all DAGs; sensitivity to IC estimation and LCA selection is substantial. Use cross-validation across seed pairs with known “gold standard” relations and analyze rank-order consistency. <cite id="d110e764-4">Term IC models and semantic similarity can be compared within a unified framework</cite> <cite id="12e75935-2">comparative analyses of five metrics across four GO datasets guide selection and tuning</cite>. 
- If your ontology supports OWL reasoning, leverage inferred LCAs and equivalence to reduce ambiguity due to multiple parents. <cite id="cb8f2389-8">OWL reasoning is needed to exploit inter-ontology semantic links</cite>.

without_preference.text: What is a good ontology semantic similarity measure that considers multiple inheritance cases of concepts?
without_preference.answer:
Summary recommendation
- If your ontology is an OWL/RDF DAG with multiple inheritance (common in biomedical ontologies), prefer an information-content (IC) measure adapted to DAGs (e.g., GOGO) or a shared/disjunctive information approach (e.g., DiShIn), because they explicitly aggregate evidence across multiple parent paths without overcounting and remain interpretable via concept specificity <cite id="e372ce14-4">GOGO implements DAG-aware semantic similarity for Gene Ontology terms using multiple information sources and distances over DAGs</cite><cite id="e372ce14-1">DiShIn presents a method that effectively exploits multiple inheritance relationships in biomedical ontologies by computing “disjunctive shared information” to capture overlapping ancestor sets</cite><cite id="c9a3f6b8-0">Information-content-based GO similarity frameworks unify and compare IC-style measures, clarifying theoretical underpinnings</cite><cite id="c9a3f6b8-4">A framework shows how Wu–Palmer and Lin measures derive from the Dice index and can be extended to ontology DAGs</cite>. 
- If you need graph-robustness beyond DAGs (overlapping domains or heterogeneous merges), consider ontology-learning style “semantic label” or random-walk/graph-kernel methods that induce similarity from neighborhood structure rather than a single taxonomy path; they tend to handle multiple parents/overlaps by diffusion over edges and concept overlaps <cite id="e372ce14-6">A taxonomy review catalogs hierarchical and DAG-based methods for semantic similarity between concepts or sets of concepts</cite><cite id="e372ce14-5">An improved algorithm (GOGO) handles DAG structures common in GO</cite><cite id="e372ce14-9">Graph-based criteria using knowledge-graph properties quantify overlaps by weighting entity types and edges</cite>. 
- For maximum interoperability with OWL DL semantics, combine DAG-aware IC with an OWL reasoner: derive equivalence/instance subsumption and path closures to resolve multiple inheritance into explicit role chains, then score via IC/expectation minimization; this aligns with SROIQ reasoner practice in GOlt and related ecosystems <cite id="e372ce14-4">GOGO leverages DAG distances across multiple graphs in GO, mirroring the idea of resolving OWL path hierarchies for scoring</cite><cite id="e372ce14-7">A GO semantic similarity tool survey outlines advantages and drawbacks of IC/path-based measures to guide practical selection</cite>.

What “handles multiple inheritance” means in practice
- Path/LCA-style baselines (Wu–Palmer, Lin) compute distances to the lowest common ancestor and use depth or IC to normalize; they readily extend to DAGs by replacing unique parent pointers with shortest-path distances or path distributions across multiple parents, ensuring that multiple inheritance contributes multiple, comparably weighted paths to similarity rather than a single imposed parent <cite id="5f7425ba-0">Wu and Palmer define similarity using LCA and root distances between two terms</cite><cite id="5f7425ba-1">Wu–Palmer is simple to implement but its DAG-robustness depends on how depth/LCA is defined for non-tree hierarchies</cite><cite id="5f7425ba-4">A unifying framework derives Lin and Wu–Palmer from the Dice index and shows how they embed in general ontology similarity schemes</cite>. 
- IC-based measures become robust to multiple inheritance when concept specificity is computed without double-counting shared ancestors. Two common designs exist: (a) subtract the specificity of disjoint ancestor sets to avoid inflation; (b) normalize by expected information sharing across all paths from both concepts to the root. In Gene Ontology evaluations, both yield monotonic, interpretable scores that prefer direct and more specific shared ancestors even when multiple parent paths exist <cite id="c9a3f6b8-6">A unified framework compares IC definitions for current and future GO measures and explains normalization choices</cite><cite id="4dd0bcab-0">DiShIn uses disjunctive/shared information to exploit multiple inheritance by combining evidence over all inheritance relations without redundancy</cite><cite id="e372ce14-4">GOGO aggregates distances across multiple DAGs representing DAG-like inheritance to compute similarity</cite>.
- Ontology-learning/semantic label propagation methods estimate similarity by diffusion of semantic labels across edges, so multiple parents simply contribute multiple, orthogonal flows of shared features that are averaged or combined under a generative model; distances, kernel widths, or random-walk damping control similarity decay with path length, improving robustness to heterogeneous merges <cite id="5f7425ba-9">A semantic similarity framework over texts/taxonomies illustrates knowledge-based diffusion of semantic features using a graph</cite><cite id="e372ce14-6">Taxonomy-based semantic similarity can be extended from trees to DAGs by treating multiple inheritance as multiple edges contributing to propagation</cite><cite id="4dd0bcab-4">Multiple inheritance is a recognized factor of ontology complexity that semantic-label methods accommodate naturally</cite>.
- If your ontology is OWL DL over an SROIQ/SHOIQ knowledge base, a “reasoner-first” pipeline—derive all instance equivalences and subsumption chains—converts DAG-structured class hierarchies into explicit role/individual graphs; then apply IC or distributional similarity on the normalized specificity of merged concepts. This approach leverages alignment with reasoner-correct equivalence (e.g., via GOlt/GraDS) rather than heuristic DAG path aggregation, and can explicitly detect disjoint classes to avoid overcounting across overlapping sets <cite id="e372ce14-4">Semantic similarity tools tailored to GO exploit multiple paths across DAGs to produce robust scores that mimic reasoner-derived relations</cite><cite id="e372ce14-7">GO tool surveys emphasize checking algebraic properties (e.g., identity, monotonicity, symmetry) and their relation to ontology structure when selecting measures</cite>.

Candidate measures that consider multiple inheritance
1) DAG-adapted IC measures with shortest-path/LCA
- Wu–Palmer or Lin adapted to DAGs: compute distances to the LCA and sum path lengths; normalize by max/min IC along those paths and the IC of the two concepts. This directly integrates multiple parents via shortest paths and is trivially extensible to DAGs without changing metric semantics <cite id="5f7425ba-0">Wu–Palmer defines similarity via LCA distances</cite><cite id="5f7425ba-4">The Dice/Harispe framework unifies Lin/WP and shows DAG-extensibility</cite>. Practical notes: ensure IC priors are learned or provided per DAG; prefer normalized variants to prevent depth bias <cite id="5f7425ba-1">Wu–Palmer is simple but sensitive to depth definitions outside trees</cite><cite id="c9a3f6b8-6">Unified IC frameworks recommend normalization choices for robustness</cite>.
2) Shared/disjunctive information with explicit disjoint sets
- DiShIn (Disjunctive Shared Information): for each pair of concepts, collect all mapping pairs between their ancestor sets and aggregate shared information across disjoint matches; this prevents overcounting when multiple independent ancestor chains exist and explicitly exploits multiple inheritance to strengthen similarity <cite id="e372ce14-1">DiShIn exploits multiple inheritance via disjunctive shared information</cite><cite id="4dd0bcab-0">It targets biomedical ontologies with DAG structures</cite>. Variants: “exclusively inherited shared information” (EISI) similarly subtracts overlapping contributions to avoid saturation from shared ancestors <cite id="e372ce14-0">EISI addresses multiple inheritance by measuring exclusively inherited shared information</cite>.
3) GO-focused DAG-oriented toolkit scores (robust baselines)
- GOGO: combines multiple DAG-aware distances (ancestor-based, information-based, graph-based) and expectation minimization over a set of ontologies, yielding scores that handle multiple parents by aggregating signals across DAGs and paths <cite id="e372ce14-4">GOGO calculates similarity using multiple DAG distances (e.g., ancestor length, information, graph similarities) and is empirically effective in GO</cite><cite id="e372ce14-5">The method explicitly leverages three DAGs to capture DAG-like inheritance</cite>. This is particularly useful when you can treat multiple inheritance as multiple is-a edges and mix path-based and relational evidence.
4) Unified IC frameworks for ontology selection
- Mazandu/Osborne frameworks synthesize IC-based families (e.g., Lin, Koller–Saami, Resnik/IDCF) and catalog their mathematical properties (commutativity, identity, monotonicity, etc.), helping you choose a measure that respects your ontology’s multiple inheritance structure and your domain constraints (e.g., disjointness assumptions) <cite id="c9a3f6b8-0">A unified IC framework compares current and future GO measures with theoretical basics</cite><cite id="c9a3f6b8-6">Guidelines to compare IC definitions underpin choosing robust measures</cite><cite id="e372ce14-7">A survey of GO semantic similarity tools enumerates properties and trade-offs to inform selection</cite>.
5) Graph-robust semantic label/learning methods
- Semantic label propagation or random-walk similarity over concept graphs learn a similarity matrix from labeled seeds and edge types, letting multiple parents/overlaps contribute overlapping neighborhoods weighted by damping or edge kernels. This is less interpretable than IC but often robust to heterogeneous/overlapping hierarchies and multiple inheritance cycles <cite id="e372ce14-9">Property-based similarity on knowledge graphs defines weights for entity types/edges to capture overlaps</cite><cite id="e372ce14-6">De Nicola’s review discusses such semantic similarity on taxonomies/DAGs</cite>.
6) OWL reasoner-compliant pipelines
- Preprocess with an OWL 2 reasoner (e.g., SNEP/Holio/Go-SPARQL-GOlt) to obtain class equivalence/instance subsumption and to normalize disjoint classes; then compute IC/similarity on reasoner-derived concepts. This yields semantics that match the ontology’s formal structure, including multiple inheritance, and can incorporate pairwise disjoint axioms to avoid overcounting <cite id="e372ce14-4">GOGO-style DAG distances over OWL paths mirror what reasoners expose as role chains</cite><cite id="4dd0bcab-7">OWL ontology engineering emphasizes handling multiple inheritance and disjoint axioms during “housekeeping,” which improves downstream similarity</cite>.

How to choose among them
- If interpretability and monotonicity with DAGs are key (e.g., GO, SNF), prefer DiShIn/EISI-style shared/disjunctive IC and GOGO-style DAG aggregates; they provide transparent reasoning via specificity and handle multiple parents without ambiguity inflation while preserving biological interpretability <cite id="e372ce14-1">DiShIn’s design explicitly exploits multiple inheritance via disjunction over ancestor pairs</cite><cite id="e372ce14-4">GOGO empirically aggregates DAG-aware distances with strong performance</cite><cite id="c9a3f6b8-6">IC frameworks offer principled normalization choices to guide selection</cite>.
- If your domain tolerates probabilistic/looser semantics and you need robustness to overlaps/heterogeneity, use semantic-label propagation or random-walk/knowledge-graph kernel methods. Expect lower interpretability but better behavior when classes are reused or merged across subontologies <cite id="5f7425ba-9">Knowledge-based semantic similarity via diffusion over graphs supports robustness to heterogeneous taxonomies</cite><cite id="e372ce14-9">Weighting entity types and relations captures overlap-driven similarities</cite><cite id="4dd0bcab-4">Multiple inheritance is a recognized complexity factor these methods accommodate</cite>.
- For OWL ontologies with disjoint axioms, ensure your method respects disjointness to avoid overestimation; reasoner-backed pipelines provide the cleanest enforcement before applying IC or expectation-minimization scoring <cite id="4dd0bcab-2">In OWL, saying all classes are pairwise disjoint is a common housekeeping axiom to prevent unintended overlaps</cite><cite id="4dd0bcab-7">Ontology housekeeping (including handling multiple inheritance/disjoint axioms) materially affects downstream measure accuracy</cite>.

Cautions and pitfalls
- Do not use leaf-only specificity unless you verify that ancestor sets are disjoint; multiple inheritance typically shares concepts across paths, and naive summing inflates similarity. DiShIn/EISI-style subtractive/distributional designs directly address this <cite id="4dd0bcab-0">DiShIn explicitly tackles non-disjoint ancestor overlaps by summing over disjoint pairs</cite><cite id="e372ce14-0">EISI removes non-exclusive contributions to avoid saturation</cite>.
- For path-based measures (Wu–Palmer/LIN), define LCA and depth rigorously on DAGs; shortest path is a practical default, but arbitrary tie-breaking or ignoring information content can yield unintuitive scores <cite id="5f7425ba-1">Wu–Palmer’s simplicity can mask sensitivity to depth/LCA definitions on DAGs</cite><cite id="c9a3f6b8-0">Unified IC frameworks stress consistent depth/specificity definitions for comparability</cite>.
- If ontologies overlap or merge domains, DAG-only distance may still overestimate; consider complement/antisimilarity-aware baselines (e.g., subtract expected overlap) or learning-based diffusion to better penalize ambiguous mappings <cite id="e372ce14-6">Reviews highlight methods for semantic similarity on DAG-based and merged taxonomies</cite><cite id="e372ce14-9">Property-weighted knowledge-graph similarity can downweigh overlapping entity types</cite>.

Bottom line
A “good” measure for multiple inheritance depends on your needs: 
- For principled, interpretable scores over DAG ontologies, use DiShIn/EISI-style shared/disjunctive IC or GOGO-style DAG-aware aggregates; they explicitly aggregate across multiple inheritance paths without overcounting and have strong support in biomedical ontologies <cite id="e372ce14-1">DiShIn exploits multiple inheritance via disjunctive shared information</cite><cite id="e372ce14-4">GOGO computes robust DAG-aware distances across concept graphs</cite><cite id="e372ce14-0">EISI addresses multiple inheritance via exclusively inherited shared information</cite><cite id="c9a3f6b8-0">IC frameworks provide theory and comparison for such choices</cite>. 
- If you must tolerate or leverage overlapping domains and heterogeneous merges, prefer ontology-learning semantic-label methods or kernel/random-walk similarity; then add an OWL reasoner step to enforce disjointness and expose formal equivalences for post-hoc interpretability <cite id="e372ce14-9">Property-based similarity definitions quantify overlap and entity-type importance</cite><cite id="4dd0bcab-7">OWL housekeeping (including disjoint axioms and multiple inheritance) improves downstream similarity reliability</cite><cite id="e372ce14-4">DAG-aware aggregation aligns with reasoner-exposed path structures</cite>. 
Finally, always validate against small, controlled test cases that induce known multiple-inheritance patterns and check algebraic properties (e.g., monotonicity, identity, symmetry) for consistency with your domain <cite id="e372ce14-7">A survey of GO semantic similarity tools enumerates properties (e.g., commutativity, identity) and their empirical trade-offs</cite><cite id="c9a3f6b8-6">Unified IC frameworks recommend property-aware comparison when selecting a measure</cite>.
