without_scope.text: Teach me about the latest progress on diagnosis, such as counterfactual explanation, of VLM models like CLIP
without_scope.answer:
Below is a practical, up-to-date guide to diagnosing vision–language models (VLMs) like CLIP using counterfactual explanations (CFEs), including methods, guarantees, and evaluation you can apply today.

What “counterfactual explanations” mean for VLMs like CLIP
- Core idea: a minimal, semantically meaningful change to input (image or text) that flips the model’s decision or embedding compatibility (e.g., CLIP’s text–image similarity dropping when the image disagrees with the prompt), revealing which concepts drive predictions and exposing brittles like spurious associations or lexical shortcuts.<cite id="1a8dd26d-3">Counterfactual explanations (CFEs) are minimal and semantically meaningful modifications of the input of a model that alter the model predictions.</cite>
- Why CLIP: CLIP embeds images and texts into a joint space and scores compatibility; concept-level CFEs can thus test whether similarity flips when “eagle→bird” edits occur, and whether counterfactual captions expose label leakage via wording rather than content.<cite id="63d4c7a9-4">CLIP-style pretraining assumes not only that a caption is globally compatible with an image, but that its salient objects, attributes, and … are captured.</cite>

Foundational methods you can adapt to CLIP
- Instance-level visual CFEs: Given an image + label, compute region swaps from a “distractor” image so the prediction flips; these are model-agnostic and can be wrapped around CLIP to probe concept reliance (e.g., removing the “wings” of an eagle lowers compatibility with “eagle” prompt).<cite id="1a8dd26d-1">We develop a technique to produce counterfactual visual explanations: replace regions in the query image with those from a distractor image under a parameterized transformation.</cite><cite id="1a8dd26d-4">SEDC is introduced as a model-agnostic instance-level explanation method for image classification to obtain visual counterfactual explanations.</cite>
- CLIP-driven concept editing: Disentangle and transfer concepts guided by CLIP’s embedding gradients to edit one concept at a time while preserving others; edits either increase/decrease compatibility with target prompts, confirming causal concept-level control.<cite id="63d4c7a9-8">Several existing methods based on Contrastive-Language-Image-Pretraining (CLIP) have achieved high-resolution image editing recently, but the …</cite><cite id="63d4c7a9-1">What would an image look like if a particular feature had a different value? The process of editing an image can be naturally modeled as a counterfactual query.</cite><cite id="63d4c7a9-3">Our method ensures that edits respect causal relationships among features, even when some are unlabeled or unprompted.</cite>
- Linguistic counterfactuals (captions): Train/apply systems that swap semantically compatible but factually contradictory phrases (“eagle”→“parrot”) and observe whether CLIP’s similarity flips; this isolates English priors versus visual evidence.<cite id="1a8dd26d-2">For example, large VL models such as CLIP and CyCLIP get confused by these counterfactual captions and fail to distinguish the difference between …</cite>

VLM-specific progress: editing, tuning, and audits for CLIP-like models
- CF-VLM: fine-tuning with counterfactual objectives to improve semantic granularity and causal reasoning; the idea is to align model behavior so that targeted concept edits induce predicted class changes or compatibility drops, making diagnosis signals tighter and more interpretable.<cite id="1a8dd267-0">We propose CF-VLM, a counterfactual fine-tuning framework to enhance semantic granularity and causal reasoning in vision-language models (VLMs).</cite>
- CLIP-targeted diagnostics using CF edits: Recent CLIP-based editing pipelines demonstrate realistic, faithful edits aligned to counterfactual concepts (e.g., changing dominant objects/attributes), enabling you to synthesize “should-be-incompatible” image–text pairs to check whether the model rejects them, an essential step in concept-drift testing.<cite id="63d4c7a9-5">Experiments show that the proposed approach produces realistic and faithful editing given the target text with counterfactual concepts.</cite>
- Evidence of brittleness to counterfactual captions: In controlled evaluations, CLIP and related VLMs often misclassify or confuse counterfactual captions that visually contradict the scene yet sound plausible, revealing over-reliance on spurious textual cues—useful as an audit test for prompt-compatibility over visual grounding.<cite id="1a8dd26d-2">Large VL models such as CLIP [31] and CyCLIP [13] get confused by these counterfactual captions and fail to distinguish the difference between …</cite>
- Robustness to spurious features: Independent audits report CLIP is relatively robust to spurious correlations compared to single-modal ImageNet-trained models, which is both a strength and a puzzle—suggesting other failure modes (e.g., linguistic or lexical priors) dominate in CLIP, and motivating CF-probed diagnostics that isolate these channels.<cite id="6eb27a42-3">Large vision language models, such as CLIP, demonstrate impressive robustness to spurious features than single-modal models trained on ImageNet.</cite>

How to run a counterfactual diagnosis on CLIP-style models
1) Concept-level hypothesis test
- Edit: For a concept h (e.g., “eagle”), synthesize an image where h is added/removed/“replaced” while preserving irrelevant regions and global context (use CLIP-guided disentangled editing).<cite id="63d4c7a9-8">Several existing CLIP-based methods achieve high-resolution editing; preserving irrelevant regions is a key need.</cite><cite id="63d4c7a9-1">Counterfactual image editing frames “what if a feature had a different value?”</cite>
- Query: Score with CLIP against prompt p (compatible with h) and its negation; a robust drop on compatible score (or sign change) indicates the concept causally drives the decision; failure to flip suggests noise, overfitting, or mis-editing.<cite id="1a8dd26d-1">The region-replacement framework provides a concrete way to obtain counterfactual visual explanations.</cite>

2) Linguistic contradiction test
- Edit: Generate semantically coherent counterfactual captions that contradict the edited scene (e.g., “eagle in the sky” → “chicken in the sky”) and measure embedding dissimilarity. Sensitivity to such contradictions indicates overuse of spurious textual compatibility rather than robust object grounding.<cite id="1a8dd26d-2">CLIP and CyCLIP get confused by counterfactual captions, failing to distinguish visually similar but captioned contradictions.</cite>

3) Robustness to spurious and out-of-domain concepts
- Stress test: Introduce known spurious correlations (e.g., sky==blue, grass==green) and rare variants; see if similarity flips when those features are toggled off/on independently of class features. A strong robustness profile is a good sign; persistence of spurious coupling indicates bias to diagnose.<cite id="6eb27a42-3">CLIP demonstrates impressive robustness to spurious features than single-modal models trained on ImageNet.</cite>

4) Reasoning-level CF evaluation
- Use tasks like CounterVQA to assess if the model updates causal reasoning under concept edits (e.g., “before: bird flies with a fish in its beak; now fish in the water”: does answer “possible” flip?), complementing embedding-level diagnostics with behavior in open-ended question answering.<cite id="6aebd26d-6">This level tests whether models can correctly identify and reason about actions that are semantically plausible given the video context …</cite>

Formal guarantees and verification for CFEs (transferable to CLIP)
- Δ-robustness: A deterministic notion for robustness of counterfactual explanations to model changes—useful to ensure that the CFE you diagnosed today still flips the decision under updates to CLIP weights or prompt distributions.<cite id="6eb27a42-5">We propose Δ-robustness, the first notion to formally and deterministically assess the robustness (to model changes) of CFXs for neural networks.</cite>
- Broader robustness landscape: Surveys synthesize feature-minimality, semantic validity, stability, and plausibility guarantees; use them to choose metrics for CLIP audits and to benchmark pre-/post-training improvements.<cite id="6eb27a42-6">We review works in the rapidly growing area of robust CEs and perform an in-depth analysis of the forms of robustness they consider.</cite><cite id="6eb27a42-7">We propose two workable definitions of robustness of counterfactual explanations that concern the features prescribed to … be changed.</cite>
- Practical limits: CFEs can be unstable to optimizer choices/editors and may produce over-optimized or unrealistic edits; disentangled CLIP-guided editing and region-preserving constraints help mitigate these issues.<cite id="6eb27a42-0">We evaluate CLIP's capabilities in providing text analysis from counterfactual images by examining robustness and reliability when …</cite><cite id="63d4c7a9-8">Recent CLIP-based high-resolution edits motivate preserving irrelevant regions to maintain ecological validity.</cite>

Implementation patterns you can try now
- Build a diagnosis pipeline around CLIP:
  1) Use region-preserved image editors with CLIP guidance to add/remove key concepts; compute similarity to target prompts and their counterfactuals; require a minimum ΔS (similarity gap) to declare a successful concept-level flip.<cite id="1a8dd26d-1">Counterfactual visual explanations via region replacement from a distractor enable instance-level hypothesis testing.</cite><cite id="63d4c7a9-1">Counterfactual image editing formalizes targeted feature changes for faithful manipulation.</cite>
  2) Complement with linguistic counterfactuals: swap objects/attributes in the prompt while keeping pixels fixed, measure similarity, and flag weak sensitivity as language-prior leakage (commonly observed in CLIP/CyCLIP evals).<cite id="1a8dd26d-2">Large VL models like CLIP get confused by counterfactual captions, evidencing strong language priors.</cite>
  3) Add reasoning checks: run edited images/captions through VQAv2-like prompts that force causal reasoning (“is it plausible that a eagle can hold a basketball in its beak?”), inspired by the CounterVQA direction.<cite id="63d4c7a9-6">Counterfactual phrase … edit images via target text with various counterfactual concepts, enabling generative evaluation.</cite><cite id="6eb27a42-6">Counterfactual evaluation of reasoning behaviors using robust CEs concepts.</cite>

What to watch for: limitations and failure modes
- Over-editing and artifacting: Strong editors may hallucinate new objects; use saliency maps or user feedback to verify that the minimal edit matched human-accepted concept change.<cite id="6eb27a42-7">Define robustness in terms of features prescribed to be modified to avoid misleading minimal edit artifacts.</cite>
- Concept interdependence: Edits to “bird wings” also change “texture” or “color”; use disentangled encoders/latent spaces to constrain edits per concept during diagnosis.<cite id="63d4c7a9-3">Our method ensures edits respect causal relationships among features, supporting targeted concept manipulation.</cite>
- Prompt distribution shift: A CF that flips today may not tomorrow under prompt or model updates; adopt Δ-robustness checks and periodic re-audits to maintain diagnostic validity.<cite id="6eb27a42-5">Δ-robustness enables deterministic evaluation of how much explanations survive model updates.</cite>
- Complementary diagnostics: Unsupervised model diagnosis work that interrogates CLIP from counterfactual images quantifies robustness and reliability—use their protocols as baselines and tune towards concept-level granularity.<cite id="6eb27a42-0">We evaluate CLIP's capabilities in providing text analysis from counterfactual images by examining robustness and reliability when …</cite>

Recent survey highlights you can cite
- Formal robustness of counterfactual explanations: determinism under parameter changes, feature-level guarantees; choose at least Δ-robustness and feature-minimality for your evaluation suite.<cite id="6eb27a42-5">First notion to formally and deterministically assess the robustness to model changes of counterfactual explanations.</cite><cite id="6eb27a42-6">Survey of robust counterfactual explanations with analysis of their robustness forms.</cite>
- Concept-editing frameworks: conceptual edits as counterfactual explanations and causal concept control provide theory and algorithms to represent edits over concepts and compute them in practice.<cite id="6eb27a42-4">We introduce a theoretical framework for representing and computing counterfactual explanations with respect to concepts that characterize data.</cite>
- CLIP-based editing: emerging pipelines show realistic, faithful counterfactual manipulation guided by CLIP, enabling high-fidelity hypothesis testing on VLMs.<cite id="63d4c7a9-5">Realistic and faithful editing to counterfactual concepts via CLIP is achievable in experiments.</cite>

A short experiment blueprint for diagnosing CLIP
1) Choose concepts and distractors. Create a concept bank (e.g., bird→plane; car→scooter), and for each image, prepare distractors with the same background but altered concept saliency.<cite id="6eb27a42-0">CLIP’s behavior on counterfactual images can be systematically probed for robustness and reliability.</cite>
2) Generate edits. For faithful changes, use CLIP-embedded disentangled edits that preserve irrelevant regions; also create counterfactual captions that contradict the edited scene.<cite id="63d4c7a9-8">High-resolution CLIP-based edits demand preservation of irrelevant regions to avoid confounds.</cite><cite id="1a8dd26d-1">Region replacement with distractors gives practical counterfactual images.</cite>
3) Score and decide. Measure CLIP similarity for (image, p), (image, ¬p), (edited image, p), (edited image, ¬p). Declare diagnosis: concept causal if ΔS edited-to-compatible ≥ threshold and sign flips; otherwise flag noise or spuriousity.<cite id="1a8dd26d-1">Counterfactual visual explanation method operationalizes sign/level change tests.</cite> 
4) Stress and generalize. Introduce spurious features and rare counterexamples; ensure sensitivity to concept removal/insertion independent of background; re-check after prompt/weight updates using Δ-robustness checks.<cite id="6eb27a42-3">CLIP robust to spurious features vs. single-modal baselines suggests alternative failure modes (linguistic or prompt-driven).</cite><cite id="6eb27a42-5">Δ-robustness tests ensure explanations survive model changes.</cite>
5) Add reasoning tests. If available, plug edited images/captions into CounterVQA-like prompts to see if causal reasoning updates align with edits, complementing embedding-level evidence.<cite id="63d4c7a9-6">Counterfactual phrase editing supports generative evaluation and reasoning checks.</cite>

Summary: where the field is headed
- Concept-centric CF tuning (e.g., CF-VLM) and CLIP-driven disentangled editing give VLMers the tools to intervene at interpretable concept granularity and verify changes both locally (embedding gaps) and globally (behavioral/verbal reasoning updates).<cite id="1a8dd267-0">A counterfactual fine-tuning framework enhances semantic granularity and causal reasoning in VLMs.</cite><cite id="63d4c7a9-1">Counterfactual image editing views edits through causal “what-if” lenses aligned to features.</cite>
- Auditing with counterfactual captions exposes overreliance on linguistic compatibility over visual evidence, while sober spurious-feature robustness tests reveal that CLIP’s strength may mask other biases—both are necessary for a complete diagnosis.<cite id="1a8dd26d-2">CLIP and CyCLIP confusion under counterfactual captions indicates strong language priors over visual evidence.</cite><cite id="6eb27a42-3">CLIP is robust to spurious features relative to ImageNet-trained single-modal models.</cite>
- Formal Δ-robustness and robustness surveys provide checklists to make CF diagnostics reproducible and resilient to model drift; integrate these into your CI for VLM deployment and iteration.<cite id="6eb27a42-5">Δ-robustness offers deterministic robustness to model changes for counterfactuals.</cite><cite id="6eb27a42-6">Surveys synthesize robustness notions applicable to evaluation suites.</cite>

without_term.text: Teach me about all latest progress on diagnosis, such as counterfactual explanation, of vision-language models like image-text models
without_term.answer:
Below is a concise, up-to-date tutorial on diagnosing vision–language models (VLMs/LMMs), with a special focus on counterfactual explanations, attribution, and grounding. I close with practical workflows, benchmarks, and pitfalls drawn from recent surveys and methods papers (2023–2025).

1) Why diagnose VLMs: hallucinations, reliance, and grounding
- Large models can hallucinate fluent but factually wrong content, and multimodal pipelines inherit additional failure sources: noisy/misspecified text (captions/OCR), spurious cross-modal correlations, and retrieval noise that seeds later generation. <cite id="f13ac465-0">Hallucination in large language models produces outputs that are coherent but factually incorrect; recent work emphasizes tracing attribution from symptoms to causes within models</cite>. <cite id="f13ac465-1">Surveys highlight taxonomy and drivers of hallucinations in large models, which underpin diagnosis</cite>. <cite id="f13ac465-2">Attribution frameworks for hallucination diagnosis connect outputs to internal activations and data origins</cite>. In multimodal settings, these issues compound because text is no longer the sole evidence source.

- Visual grounding diagnosing: the “right answer in the wrong place,” mismatched or hallucinated referents for natural language expressions, is a central failure mode; measurement frameworks are emerging. <cite id="367cbadc-4">Visual grounding is to localize objects/regions referenced by language, and modern pipelines integrate strong visual–linguistic priors</cite>. <cite id="367cbadc-5">For VQA, Faithful & Plausible Visual Grounding (FPVG) separates correctness of evidence from plausibility of answers, enabling principled faithfulness scoring</cite>. <cite id="367cbadc-3">Surveys of 2025 note visual grounding as referring expression comprehension/phrase grounding and emphasize evaluation rigor</cite>.

2) Method classes to diagnose VLMs

2.1 Counterfactual explanations (what changes when evidence changes?)
- Core idea: swap or edit parts of inputs/activations to invert predictions or to test causal influence, yielding human-interpretable “what-if” evidence. <cite id="aaade72f-2">Counterfactual explanations provide what-if interpretations that reveal decision boundaries and minimal changes flipping predictions</cite>.
- Cross-modal counterfactuals: use textual concepts to steer image edits and vice versa.
  - Grounding concepts across modalities: <cite id="aaade72f-4">Grounding Counterfactual Explanation of Image Classifiers to Textual Concept Space defines “text-driven concepts” in a joint embedding and uses them to compute concept-aligned counterfactual directions to flip image decisions; explanations are semantic and aligned with text concepts rather than raw pixels</cite>. <cite id="aaade72f-3">The method operationalizes concept-based counterfactuals robustly, with evaluation showing semantic faithfulness and resistance to human bias</cite>.
  - General cross-modal frameworks: <cite id="aaade72f-0">Cross-modal Counterfactual Explanations (2025) formalize explanation by altering inputs via semantic changes, enabling visual-to-text and text-to-image counterfactual swaps grounded in shared concept spaces</cite>.
- Fine-tuning with counterfactual objectives: diagnose and improve causal granularity.
  - <cite id="aaade72f-5">CF-VLM proposes a counterfactual fine-tuning framework to enhance semantic granularity and causal reasoning in VLMs, training models to be robust to concept-level edits while preserving behavior on clean inputs</cite>.
- Visual reliance via image perturbation: quantify whether predictions change when relevant evidence is removed or occluded.
  - <cite id="aaade72f-9">Medical VLMs operationalize visual reliance by checking prediction change under counterfactual image decontextualization; a model is visually reliant if its output depends measurably on the original image rather than paraphrasing alone</cite>.
  - Broader image-centric counterfactual tooling provides building blocks: <cite id="367cbadc-0">DeFacto proposes counterfactual thinking with images by aligning reasoning with essential visual evidence; it exposes minimal evidence sets and perturbation schedules to test prediction change</cite>.
- Practical mechanics (from surveys of concept directions): <cite id="367cbadc-6">Compute-class attribute vectors (CAVs) from images or prompts; apply small semantic steps along CAVs as generation-free counterfactuals to invert predictions and localize influential concepts</cite>. <cite id="aaade72f-1">Grounding counterfactuals to text improves interpretability by mapping edits to human-understandable textual concepts</cite>.

2.2 Attribution and concept tracing across the multimodal stack
- Internal attribution to locate binding failures. <cite id="f13ac465-3">Attribution frameworks trace the origins of hallucinations by leveraging internal signals to localize where incorrect facts enter or are amplified</cite>. <cite id="f13ac465-2">Hallucination attribution methods combine activation-based tracing with quantitative counterfactual tests to pinpoint whether language or vision subnetworks dominate errors</cite>.
- Cross-attention and saliency complement counterfactuals by highlighting where visual features respond to words and vice versa. <cite id="367cbadc-1">Surveys of visual grounding summarize attention-based methods, phrase grounding, and referring expression comprehension as complementary subproblems for attribution and debugging</cite>.

2.3 Grounding correctness and faithfulness metrics
- Beyond accuracy, measure: (i) whether answers refer to the correct region(s), and (ii) whether evidence and answer together are plausible. <cite id="367cbadc-5">FPVG explicitly separates faithful evidence localization from plausibility of the final answer, with straightforward computation for many VQA architectures</cite>.
- Generalization to 3D/complex scenes: <cite id="367cbadc-8">3D visual grounding formalizes identification of objects in complex scenes under natural language, and can be instrumented to test whether explanations include correct relational depth text</cite>.
- Human-in-the-loop and dialog: <cite id="f13ac465-6">VisDiaHalBench (2024) is a visual dialogue benchmark to diagnose hallucination by requiring models to ask clarifying image-caption questions and justify answers, surfacing failures in evidence collection and grounding</cite>.

2.4 Retrieval provenance and RAG debugging in LMMs
- LMM/RAG pipelines inherit LLM hallucination risks with new failure modes (noisy retrieval, outdated or mismatched snippets, domain shift). <cite id="8e499c0b-0">Systematic reviews show RAG reduces hallucinations and outdated knowledge by anchoring outputs to retrieved evidence, but introduces new challenges in retrieval latency, coverage, and alignment</cite>. <cite id="8e499c0b-2">Despite RAG benefits, noisy retrieval and mismatch often persist; surveys emphasize calibration, confidence, and provenance tracking to diagnose failures</cite>. <cite id="8e499c0b-1">Comprehensive reviews of the RAG stack enumerate architectures, retrieval units, document encoders, fusion strategies, and evaluation practices, mapping debugging to components</cite>.
- Provenance-aware evaluation: <cite id="8e499c0b-8">Corpora that support RAG evaluation provide knowable ground truth, temporal structure, and cross-referenced facts; these enable tracing which retrieved passages cause claims and quantifying the impact of retrieval errors on final outputs</cite>.
- De-contextualization and grounding checks for caption–text coupling: <cite id="aaade72f-7">Detection of text–image de-contextualization with VLMs can flag cases where models rely on discarded visual context or hallucinate missing links, informing retrieval selection or caption validation</cite>.

3) End-to-end diagnosis across common VLM tasks

3.1 Image classification with language-augmented or grounded explanations
- Hypothesis: errors arise from binding spurious text concepts to images. <cite id="aaade72f-4">Use CounTEX to convert natural language concepts into text-driven concepts in a joint space; generate counterfactual image patches aligned to those concepts and observe label flips; stable flips expose over-reliance on irrelevant language cues</cite>. <cite id="aaade72f-0">Cross-modal CE generalizes to editing captions or prompts to remove/swap concepts and recompute model responses, measuring prediction change</cite>.
- Compute internal attribution and verify if counterfactual directions align with attention peaks. <cite id="367cbadc-6">CAV-based attribution is human-interpretable and can outperform pixel-level saliency by staying semantic, reducing human bias in reading explanations</cite>.
- Calibrate model reliance: <cite id="367cbadc-0">DeFacto exposes the minimal set of image regions whose removal flips predictions, directly quantifying essential evidence and overfitting to background or text artifacts</cite>. <cite id="aaade72f-9">Medical VLMs formalize “visual reliance” by asserting the model’s output depends on the original image under counterfactual edits</cite>.

3.2 Grounded QA, VQA, and referring expression comprehension
- Grounding failure diagnosis: <cite id="367cbadc-4">When an expression refers to multiple candidates, use grounding tools to list all candidate boxes and compare selection vs. answer; combine saliency/attention and interaction with object captions</cite>. <cite id="367cbadc-5">FPVG helps detect when the model selects the right box but derives an implausible answer, or chooses the wrong box while keeping answer plausible</cite>.
- Cross-modal CE debugging: <cite id="aaade72f-4">Swap concepts mentioned in the question (or image regions) through text-driven concepts to test whether answer changes; this isolates whether reasoning hinged on correct concept bindings</cite>.
- Pipeline-level: For OCR/caption pipelines, detect de-contextualization and caption–image mismatch, and use retrieval debugging if answers derive from attached text. <cite id="aaade72f-7">Text–image de-contextualization detection with VLMs identifies reliance on extrinsic image context not captured by captions, suggesting fixes in captioning or OCR modules or stronger grounding losses</cite>. <cite id="8e499c0b-0">RAG-SLRs advise monitoring retrieval diversity/coverage, temporal freshness, and passage overlap; provenance logs reveal which snippets drive claims, enabling targeted re-ranking or reretrieval</cite>.

4) Benchmarks and evaluation for diagnosis

- Faithfulness and plausibility: <cite id="367cbadc-5">FPVG offers a practical split metric with per-answer scoring and can be automated for many VQA architectures</cite>.
- Dialog-based hallucination diagnosis: <cite id="f13ac465-6">VisDiaHalBench evaluates whether models recognize missing image-caption knowledge during visual dialogue, surfacing blind spots in evidence gathering and grounding</cite>.
- Surveys and taxonomies: <cite id="f13ac465-0">Comprehensive hallucination surveys catalog symptoms and internal attribution pathways, aiding diagnosis design</cite>. <cite id="f13ac465-2">Attribution frameworks quantify whether errors originate in factual knowledge, cross-modal binding, or chain-of-thought reasoning</cite>. <cite id="367cbadc-3">Visual grounding surveys consolidate methods and evaluation settings, including attention-based and concept-based grounding</cite>. <cite id="8e499c0b-0">RAG SLRs detail metrics and challenges—precision of retrieved evidence, temporal validity, and integration loss</cite>.

5) Practical diagnosis workflows

- Diagnose hallucinations with CE + attribution (image and text) [classifier/LLM-hybrid]:
  1) Collect internal CAVs or pre-defined text-driven concepts tied to the labels in the prompt language. <cite id="367cbadc-6">CAVs from images or prompts support fast counterfactual steps aligned to the model’s decision boundary</cite>.
  2) Generate concept-aligned perturbations to the image and/or prompt; measure prediction change and sign of effect; retain minimal sets that flip results. <cite id="aaade72f-4">Text-to-concept-to-image-edit loop produces semantic counterfactuals; strong agreement between image flip and text concept supports faithful explanation</cite>. <cite id="367cbadc-0">Minimal region removal/insertion identifies essential evidence</cite>.
  3) Correlate flipping directions with cross-attention maps and key-value activation traces; flag mismatches as binding errors. <cite id="367cbadc-1">Attention-based grounding tools help align words to bounding boxes; mismatched peaks suggest spurious bindings</cite>.
  4) Quantify visual reliance; if prediction depends on a small set of regions or concept edits, mark model as visually reliant; else probe paraphrase robustness. <cite id="aaade72f-9">Visual reliance under image edits is a strong indicator of grounded knowledge vs. paraphrasing hallucinations</cite>.
  5) If using retrieval, add provenance logging and RAG-specific checks: coverage/freshness and plausibility of claims conditioned on snippets. <cite id="8e499c0b-0">RAG pipelines benefit from temporal and cross-reference checks; missing passages explain hallucinations</cite>. <cite id="8e499c0b-2">Noisy retrieval is a common root cause; calibration and confidence alignment with retrieval quality mitigate mismatch hallucinations</cite>.

- Diagnose grounding failures in VQA/Refer expression:
  1) Localize candidates via grounding tools; compute attention/saliency per language phrase and image region. <cite id="367cbadc-4">Phrase grounding yields candidate boxes per expression; combine with attention to validate binding</cite>.
  2) Apply CE: swap or remove conceptually equivalent noun phrases (supported by CAVs or commonsense encoders) and observe if answers or answer support change. <cite id="aaade72f-4">Counterfactual concept edits in image or language flip outcomes, indicating reliance on specific referents</cite>.
  3) Compute FPVG: score evidence faithfulness vs. plausibility; use high-falsehood on faithfulness to call out hallucinated evidence. <cite id="367cbadc-5">FPVG cleanly decomposes evidence and answer quality; low faithfulness often signals hallucination in bound evidence</cite>.
  4) For dialog settings, run VisDiaHalBench to test whether the model notices missing evidence and requests clarifying image references. <cite id="f13ac465-6">Visual dialog tasks surface whether the model detects under-specified evidence and engages in corrective questioning</cite>.

- Diagnose RAG/LMM hallucinations:
  1) Maintain provenance logs per output claim; retrieve snippets with rank, score, and overlap; compute evidence sufficiency and consistency. <cite id="8e499c0b-8">Knowable, temporally structured corpora enable cross-linking claims to specific passages for failure isolation</cite>.
  2) Run retrieval ablations: with/without k=1 vs. k=5, with de-duplication and temporal filters; track how hallucinations change, isolating coverage/latency effects. <cite id="8e499c0b-0">RAG SLRs advise component-level diagnostics—retrieval quality directly correlates with hallucination reduction</cite>.
  3) Cross-check model’s summary against snippets via counterfactual QA: replace one or two top snippets and see if answers change. <cite id="8e499c0b-2">Noisy or out-of-domain snippets often flip answers; such “what-if” snippet swaps diagnose retrieval dependence</cite>.

6) State-of-the-art counterfactual methods you can use today

- Image-to-text concept counterfactuals for binding debugging:
  - CounTEX/CVPR 2023: <cite id="aaade72f-4">Generates concept-based counterfactuals by moving along text-driven concepts in joint space; faithful and robust to human bias</cite>.
  - DeFacto: <cite id="367cbadc-0">Implements counterfactual thinking with images—finding minimal evidence sets and aligning reasoning—useful to expose what visual regions truly matter</cite>.
  - Cross-modal CE (2025): <cite id="aaade72f-0">Unifies visual and textual semantic edits to test prediction change, enabling bidirectional what-if queries</cite>.

- Counterfactual fine-tuning to make models robust to editing:
  - CF-VLM (2025): <cite id="aaade72f-5">Trains models with counterfactual image/word edits to enhance causal granularity; improves reasoning that is invariant to concept-level swaps while preserving accuracy</cite>.

- Retrieval provenance and de-contextualization checks:
  - RAG SLRs and toolkits: <cite id="8e499c0b-0">Provide diagnosis taxonomies, component metrics (precision@k topic/temporal), and provenance collection patterns</cite>. <cite id="8e499c0b-2">Noisy retrieval is both a cause of spurious claims and a diagnostic signal</cite>.
  - De-contextualization detection: <cite id="aaade72f-7">VLM-based detection of decoupled text–image contexts flags hallucinations born from mismatched evidence</cite>.

- Medical/clinical VLM diagnosis patterns:
  - Visual reliance: <cite id="aaade72f-9">Change outputs when image is decontextualized; formalizes grounded decision-making and exposes when models hallucinate beyond visual evidence</cite>.

7) Common failure patterns and remedies

- Cross-modal binding errors: spurious association of language concepts with visual regions; diagnose with concept-aligned perturbations showing irrelevant concept flips. Countermeasure: include contrastive captions and binding losses; align concept spaces. <cite id="aaade72f-4">Text-driven concept edits expose concept bindings and can correct over-reliance on irrelevant cues</cite>.
- Noisy or outdated text evidence: captions/OCR or retrieved snippets contain errors. Diagnose by swapping in/out top snippets or asking models to justify claims sentence-by-sentence against snippets. Countermeasure: temporal filtering, confidence-thresholded retrieval, redundancy checks, and RAG-offline indexing. <cite id="8e499c0b-0">RAG reviews emphasize retrieval freshness, coverage, and alignment with generation</cite>. <cite id="8e499c0b-2">Mismatched retrieval often flips outputs; targeted calibration mitigates</cite>.
- Over-reliance on paraphrase without grounding: models regurgitate text claims without verifying visual support. Diagnose via image edits and provenance checks; enforce grounding constraints. <cite id="aaade72f-9">Visual reliance metrics separate paraphrasing from genuine visual evidence</cite>. <cite id="f13ac465-6">Dialog benchmarks surface inability to request missing image evidence</cite>.
- Plausible but incorrect reasoning from correct evidence: model is faithful to evidence but the evidence is wrong. Diagnose with FPVG and evidence plausibility checks; add evidence verification layers or self-consistency over retrieved snippets. <cite id="367cbadc-5">FPVG quantifies when evidence is faithful yet the answer remains implausible</cite>. <cite id="8e499c0b-8">Provenance-linked corpora enable targeted cross-checking of evidence claims</cite>.

8) Step-by-step: a practical diagnosis toolkit

- Instrumenting CE and attribution
  - Precompute CAVs from labeled datasets and query language distributions; for each new image+text input, extract relevant concepts and compute concept directions. <cite id="367cbadc-6">CAVs from images or prompts yield concept-aligned perturbations with lower human bias</cite>.
  - Apply minimal concept flips to the image and/or prompt; track prediction sign changes and magnitude. <cite id="aaade72f-4">Semantic edits through text-driven concepts efficiently flip predictions when the model overtrusts irrelevant concepts</cite>.
  - Use cross-attention and saliency to link words to boxes; report mismatches. <cite id="367cbadc-1">Attention-based grounding identifies binding mismatches</cite>.
  - Quantify visual reliance via region removal/replacement and compute a reliance score; compare before/after. <cite id="367cbadc-0">DeFacto quantifies minimal essential regions; reliance > threshold indicates strong visual dependence</cite>. <cite id="aaade72f-9">Prediction change under image decontextualization confirms grounded reliance</cite>.

- Retrieval provenance for LMMs
  - Add a “citation layer”: each claim carries the passage IDs and relevance scores; build a verifier module that runs the same CE over snippet-level edits. <cite id="8e499c0b-8">Temporal, knowable ground truth supports linking claims to specific passages</cite>.
  - Ablate retrieval: compare generation with vs. without top passages, with/without deduplication; track hallucination rates and confidence. <cite id="8e499c0b-0">Component-wise diagnostics (retrieval precision vs. hallucination rate) reveal root causes</cite>.

- Faithfulness testing
  - For QA/VQA, compute FPVG per answer; plot faithfulness vs. plausibility to flag “pass-the-visual-test” failures. <cite id="367cbadc-5">FPVG is architecture-friendly and exposes evidence-driven plausibility gaps</cite>.
  - For grounding tasks, use candidate grounding lists and overlap metrics; add CE over language phrases to assert necessity. <cite id="367cbadc-4">Phrase grounding plus language-phrase CE isolates necessary referents</cite>.

9) Pointers for ongoing reading and development

- Foundational framing and attribution:
  - <cite id="f13ac465-0">Hallucination taxonomy and attribution frameworks to connect symptoms to data/internal causes</cite>.
  - <cite id="f13ac465-3">Attribution methods that trace hallucination origins using internal signals</cite>.
- Counterfactual explanation core techniques:
  - <cite id="aaade72f-4">Grounding counterfactual explanations to joint image–text concepts</cite>; <cite id="367cbadc-0">DeFacto’s minimal evidence analysis</cite>; <cite id="aaade72f-5">CF-VLM counterfactual fine-tuning</cite>; <cite id="aaade72f-0">Cross-modal counterfactuals in 2025</cite>.
- Grounding/faithfulness and evaluation:
  - <cite id="367cbadc-5">FPVG for faithful and plausible grounding in VQA</cite>; <cite id="f13ac465-6">VisDiaHalBench for dialog-driven hallucination diagnosis</cite>; <cite id="367cbadc-3">2025 survey of visual grounding and phrase grounding</cite>.
- Retrieval and multimodal provenance:
  - <cite id="8e499c0b-0">Systematic RAG reviews with component metrics and provenance workflows</cite>; <cite id="8e499c0b-2">Calibration and noisy-retrieval pitfalls</cite>; <cite id="aaade72f-7">Text–image de-contextualization detection for pipeline debugging</cite>.

10) Summary: what “latest progress” looks like in diagnosis of VLMs

- Counterfactuals crossed over from image-only AIX to multimodal spaces: concept-driven edits that live in a shared image–text semantic space enable both image- and language-side “what-if” tests that expose binding errors and reliance structure. <cite id="aaade72f-4">Text-driven concept counterfactuals align explanations to words and regions, improving interpretability</cite>. <cite id="367cbadc-0">Minimal region swaps quantify essential evidence</cite>. <cite id="aaade72f-5">Training with counterfactual objectives improves causal fidelity</cite>.
- Evaluation has shifted from pure accuracy to faithfulness and provenance: <cite id="367cbadc-5">faithful and plausible visual grounding</cite> and <cite id="f13ac465-6">dialog hallucination benches</cite> diagnose whether models actually look at the right places and ask for missing evidence. <cite id="8e499c0b-0">RAG SLRs provide component-level metrics and provenance capture practices</cite>.
- Open challenges remain in OCR/caption provenance and temporal grounding; however, <cite id="aaade72f-9">visual reliance measures</cite> and <cite id="8e499c0b-2">retrieval calibration</cite> provide actionable diagnostics and mitigations in modern LMM/RAG stacks.

Actionable next steps (pick a pipeline and start small)
- If you’re debugging a VQA or referring expression model:
  1) Add FPVG and save per-answer explanations; identify the top-k noun phrases whose removal most hurts faithfulness. <cite id="367cbadc-5">FPVG is quick to compute and yields actionable phrase-level evidence</cite>.
  2) Integrate CounTEX or DeFacto-style minimal edits to validate that changes in the right concepts flip answers; report concept→region alignment. <cite id="aaade72f-4">Text-driven concept edits reveal binding correctness</cite>. <cite id="367cbadc-0">Minimal evidence sets expose essential regions</cite>.
- If you’re using LMM with retrieval:
  1) Instrument provenance logging; perform snippet swaps (remove one top passage at a time) and log answer change and confidence. <cite id="8e499c0b-8">Passage-level ground truth lets you directly attribute claims</cite>. <cite id="8e499c0b-2">Noisy top snippets often drive hallucinations</cite>.
  2) Add time/quality filters and re-rankers; track reduction in hallucination and increase in answer stability. <cite id="8e499c0b-0">Precision@k and freshness correlate with fewer hallucinations</cite>.

without_preference.text: Teach me about the latest progress on diagnosis of VLM models like CLIP.
without_preference.answer:
Below is a practical, evidence-backed overview of the latest progress in diagnosing and evaluating Vision–Language Models (VLMs) like CLIP. I organize it into evaluation angles (benchmarks/metrics, failure analyses, and interventions), then show how to apply them to CLIP-style models in practice.

Key themes and toolkits
- Hallucination diagnosis beyond detection: New benchmarks teach VLMs to localize failure stages, classify error types, and support targeted mitigation, often integrating detection + diagnosis + attribution workflows in multimodal settings.<cite id="aa4d7cbe-0">This paper introduces MedHallBench, a comprehensive benchmark framework for evaluating and mitigating hallucinations in MLLMs.</cite> <cite id="aa4d7cbe-5">ClinHallu provides a fine-grained hallucination testbed for diagnosing and mitigating reasoning failures in medical MLLMs.</cite> <cite id="aa4d7cbe-1">This benchmark can be used to evaluate LLMs' ability to detect medical hallucinations, make accurate diagnoses in noisy conditions, and provide plausible explanations.</cite> <cite id="aa4d7cbe-6">This benchmark includes three tasks: identifying hallucinations, diagnosing disease in noisy environments, and explaining specific concepts.</cite> <cite id="aa4d7cbe-3">The Hallucination Diagnosis Task is introduced, a task which requires models to not only detect hallucinations, but also perform error analysis with automated data synthesis.</cite> <cite id="aa4d7cbe-4">In this work, we introduce new evaluation tasks specifically designed for extrinsic hallucination and evaluate diverse set of LMs such as Llama …</cite>
- Cross-modal retrieval diagnostics and CLIP-centric improvements: Recent work targets calibration, bias, adversarial vulnerability, and alignment robustness for CLIP-style models on standard retrieval benchmarks (e.g., MSCOCO, open-world cross-modal retrieval).<cite id="3eb86baf-2">Empirical results in two standard cross-modal retrieval benchmarks demonstrate that our approach achieves superior calibration compared to learned probabilistic baselines.</cite> <cite id="3eb86baf-3">We evaluate our methods on two standard benchmarks for cross-modal retrieval, enabling reproducibility and comparability with prior work: MSCOCO Lin et al.</cite> <cite id="3eb86baf-1">We introduce an evaluation framework for both retrieval directions, each capturing a distinct form of perspectival bias.</cite> <cite id="3eb86baf-4">Evaluating Perspectival Biases in Cross-Modal Retrieval … achieves an average Recall@K of 67.34%, improving upon CLIP by 5.75 percentage points.</cite> <cite id="3eb86baf-5">Extensive evaluations across 14 zero-shot classification benchmarks demonstrate the effectiveness of COLA, especially with an average improvement of 6.7%.</cite>
- Landscape and taxonomy: Surveys summarize multimodal hallucination definitions, evaluation protocols, and mitigation strategies, offering guidance for choosing diagnostics suited to VLMs.<cite id="e477a420-0">Hallucination in VLMs refers to text responses inconsistent with the input visual content or unsupported by evidence; the evaluation literature spans automatic checks, consistency, and evidence-based metrics.</cite> <cite id="e477a420-5">Mitigating hallucination in LVLMs via clip-guided decoding; evaluation and analysis of hallucination in large VLMs.</cite> <cite id="e477a420-1">A review of hallucination taxonomy, detection, mitigation, and evaluation across language and vision models.</cite> <cite id="e477a420-2">A comprehensive survey and empirical analysis of hallucination attribution in multimodal systems, linking occurrences, severity, and model factors.</cite> <cite id="e477a420-4">A comprehensive guide to MLLMs with a focus on vision–language tasks and evaluation settings (captioning, OCR, localization), informing diagnosis design.</cite> <cite id="e477a420-7">A survey highlights method taxonomies and metrics (e.g., localization accuracy, object-level veracity) to diagnose object hallucinations in LVLMs.</cite>
- Toolkits and aggregations: Curated resources consolidate cross-modal hallucination and attribution methods, including audio-visual cases, to help build diagnosis pipelines.<cite id="aa4d7cbe-2">Introduces AVHBench, a cross-modal hallucination benchmark with three judgment tasks and one captioning task probing audio/visual evidence.</cite> <cite id="aa4d7cbe-6">A GitHub “awesome” collection of hallucination detection methods aggregates diverse benchmarks and toolkits for multimodal attribution and correction.</cite>

How the latest progress helps diagnose CLIP-like models

1) Cross-modal retrieval and alignment: diagnosing what, why, and how to fix
- Benchmarks for zero-shot cross-modal retrieval and open-world recognition expose misalignments between vision and language embeddings in CLIP-like systems. Use Recall@K, MAP/DCG variants for ranking quality, and add noise/OOD corruption to stress-test generalization.<cite id="3eb86baf-3">Standard cross-modal retrieval settings (image→text/text→image ranking on MSCOCO) enable reproducible evaluation and comparison for CLIP-based models.</cite> <cite id="3eb86baf-2">Uncertainty-aware scoring calibrated for CLIP shows that better calibration can be achieved without fully probabilistic architectures, improving reliability in ambiguous matches.</cite> <cite id="3eb86baf-5">COLA-style cross-modality alignment training yields consistent gains across 14 zero-shot classification benchmarks, with an average 6.7% improvement—indicating that explicit alignment objectives uncover and correct weak cross-modal mapping in base CLIP variants.</cite>
- Evaluating perspectival biases reveals directional retrieval distortions (e.g., speaker/author/gender perspective biases) that standard supervised metrics miss; bidirectional retrieval analysis splits image↔text directions to isolate where CLIP-like systems falter.<cite id="3eb86baf-1">An evaluation framework captures distinct perspectival biases in each retrieval direction, supporting directional diagnosis and mitigation.</cite> <cite id="3eb86baf-4">Improvements over CLIP in Recall@K when measuring perspectival bias demonstrate that targeted training/optimization can reduce skewed priors and improve fair retrieval.</cite>
- Robustness and noise/OOD: Add channel noise, compression artifacts, viewpoint/crowding shifts, and modality dropouts to diagnose robustness gaps and compute robust Recall/ROC-like decision metrics; compare frozen CLIP vs distilled/finetuned variants to quantify transferability of fixes.<cite id="3eb86baf-0">A bias-mitigation and representation-optimization pipeline (BMRO) reports effectiveness across five widely used cross-modal datasets, indicating improved stability under data shifts once internal representations are tuned for robustness.</cite> <cite id="e477a420-0">Multimodal hallucination evaluation emphasizes evidence consistency under noisy or incomplete inputs; this translates into retrieval tasks where mismatched or biased matches signal grounding problems.</cite>

Practical diagnostic playbook: cross-modal retrieval
- Start with base retrieval: image→text and text→image Recall@1/K on MSCOCO or open-set retrieval sets. Inspect confusion matrices and NDCG trends; compute calibration curves for CLIP’s confidence scores.<cite id="3eb86baf-2">Uncertainty-aware CLIP retrieval improves calibration versus probabilistic learned models on standard benchmarks, showing how to audit and improve score reliability.</cite>
- Perspectival bias audit: Run the bidirectional bias evaluation to check if certain text perspectives (e.g., camera angles, viewpoints, demographic cues) systematically dominate rankings; quantify gaps per direction and dataset subset.<cite id="3eb86baf-1">Per-direction evaluation isolates how retrieval biases manifest and how they may be reduced by training choices.</cite> <cite id="3eb86baf-4">Reported gains over CLIP on Recall@K provide direction-specific baselines for remediation.</cite>
- Robustness stress test: Corrupt images (noise, blur, compression) and perturb text (paraphrasing, coreference swaps) and re-measure Recall/ROC. Contrast frozen CLIP variants against distilled/finetuned successors; use the relative gains to justify alignment or finetuning at scale.<cite id="3eb86baf-5">Cross-modality alignment improvements across 14 zero-shot benchmarks underline the value of alignment-focused training for robust CLIP-like behavior.</cite> <cite id="3eb86baf-0">Representation optimization (BMRO) improves performance across multiple cross-modal datasets, illustrating how internal feature-space adjustments mitigate bias and noise sensitivity.</cite>

2) Hallucination and grounding diagnosis: what, where, and when
- Define hallucination for VLMs as claims unsupported by input evidence or inconsistent with visual content; diagnose by combining automatic detection with localization and attribution to image regions or concepts. Use medical and domain-specific benchmarks to validate that your diagnostics reflect real-world harms and remediable causes.<cite id="aa4d7cbe-0">MedHallBench provides an end-to-end framework for evaluating and mitigating multimodal hallucinations, integrating detection and corrective strategies.</cite> <cite id="e477a420-0">A survey frames hallucination types and evaluation paradigms for VLMs and highlights consistency/evidence-based checks, including automatic and human-in-the-loop methods.</cite> <cite id="e477a420-5">Findings-emnlp survey reports evaluation and mitigation analyses, including Clip-guided decoding to constrain generation to image-supported content.</cite>
- Move from detection to diagnosis: Add stages to (i) segment image evidence and compare to generated content, (ii) rank likely true vs hallucinated parts, and (iii) propose targeted edits; recent benchmarks operationalize these steps for medical, noisy, and multimodal settings.<cite id="aa4d7cbe-3">Introducing a Hallucination Diagnosis Task pushes beyond detection to structured error analysis and automated synthesis for targeted interventions.</cite> <cite id="aa4d7cbe-1">Benchmarks emphasize diagnosis in noisy conditions and explanation coherence, enabling targeted training and distillation to reduce hallucinations.</cite>
- Domain-specific diagnosis reveals systemic failure modes: Medical benchmarks expose missing evidence, over-interpretation, and incorrect diagnosis under noise; solutions like clip-guided decoding and selective evidence aggregation reduce these errors, suggesting a transferable diagnosis strategy (evidence grounding → uncertainty → explanation).<cite id="aa4d7cbe-5">ClinHallu enables stage-wise diagnosis of medical MLLMs, highlighting reasoning steps where hallucinations occur and how to mitigate them.</cite> <cite id="e477a420-7">Mitigating Object Hallucination via multi-step reasoning and evidence checks reduces object-level hallucinations in LVLMs, with processable outputs guiding audits.</cite>

3) Adversarial vulnerability and attack surfaces for CLIP-style models
- LLM-guided adversarial composition can craft multimodal inputs that “fool” CLIP into accepting implausible cross-modal matches or text claims consistent with misleading visual signals; such benchmarks expose overfitting to spurious associations and guide defenses focused on compositional robustness.<cite id="3eb86baf-7">Multimodal Adversarial Compositionality (MAC) leverages LLMs to generate deceptive multimodal inputs and benchmarks adversarial robustness of CLIP-like systems.</cite>
- Build an adversarial audit suite: Use MAC-like attacks to measure adversarial Recall/ROC under varying attack strengths; compare frozen vs finetuned models and measure transfer across attacks to prioritize robustness interventions (augmentative distillation, adversarial training, or pruning of cross-modal weights where vulnerabilities concentrate).<cite id="3eb86baf-7">MAC shows that LLM-generated adversarial compositions can systematically deceive multimodal systems, providing an out-of-distribution testbed to stress-align and retrain CLIP-like encoders.</cite> <cite id="3eb86baf-5">Alignment-focused training improved zero-shot classification by average 6.7% across 14 benchmarks, indicating that targeted training can reduce susceptibility to spurious correlations exploited by adversaries.</cite>

4) Bias, fairness, and cross-lingual alignment audits
- Cultural/perspective bias: Cross-modal retrieval audits should include demographic, cultural, and perspective-diverse subsets and measure group-wise precision/recall or bias ratios; per-direction bias metrics can be combined with CLIP retrieval Recall@K to attribute losses to specific biases and track mitigation.<cite id="3eb86baf-1">A bidirectional bias evaluation framework captures distinct perspectival bias forms per retrieval direction, enabling attribution and mitigation.</cite> <cite id="3eb86baf-4">Direction-specific Recall@K improvements over CLIP provide clear indicators for tuning language-side priors and modality fusion.</cite>
- Cross-lingual grounding: Use multilingual text-to-image retrieval and cross-lingual captioning to diagnose mismatches between CLIP’s multilingual vision features and noisy/ambiguous language cues; incorporate uncertainty-aware scoring and robustness to typographic/coreference variations.<cite id="3eb86baf-2">Uncertainty-aware CLIP retrieval improves calibration on standard benchmarks, a prerequisite for reliable cross-lingual grounding where ambiguity is common.</cite> <cite id="e477a420-0">Multimodal hallucination evaluation stresses evidence consistency across languages, guiding cross-lingual error detection designs.</cite>

Putting it together: a practical workflow for diagnosing CLIP-like models
- Define objectives and metrics: 
  - For open-world recognition and cross-modal retrieval: standard Recall@K (image→text and text→image), NDCG, MAP; add uncertainty metrics (Brier, ECE); robust counterparts under noise/OOD; calibration under distribution shift.<cite id="3eb86baf-3">Reproducible evaluation on MSCOCO with standard metrics supports cross-paper comparability for CLIP-based models.</cite> <cite id="3eb86baf-2">CLIP with uncertainty-aware scoring improves calibration versus probabilistic baselines, giving actionable audit outcomes.</cite>
  - For hallucination/grounding: evidence consistency, region-level veracity, and explanation coherence, plus stage-wise detection→diagnosis→repair scoring on domain sets (medical/general) under noise.<cite id="aa4d7cbe-0">MedBench-style frameworks integrate detection, mitigation, and evaluation to reduce hallucinations.</cite> <cite id="aa4d7cbe-1">Tasks emphasize noisy-condition diagnosis and explainability, enabling targeted remediation.</cite>
- Run layered diagnostics:
  1) Baseline retrieval audit (clean test sets) to establish Recall/NDCG baselines and confusion matrices; inspect high-confusion classes and misbound entities.
  2) Robustness sweep (noise/dropout/view/LOD shifts); measure delta in Recall/ECE to isolate weak spots; compare frozen CLIP vs tuned/distilled variants.
  3) Perspectival bias scan on directional subsets; compute per-group Recall and bias ratios; identify skewed priors and modality dominance.
  4) Hallucination under noisy/ambiguous prompts; use region-grounded metrics and explanation faithfulness; iterate with clip-guided decoding and evidence-constrained generation.
  5) Adversarial audit with MAC-like attacks; quantify transferability and attack cross-over, prioritize adversarial training/distillation on vulnerable subspaces; verify improvements transfer to clean metrics.
- Prioritize interventions:
  - Alignment-focused finetuning/distillation and cross-modal contrastive refinements to improve zero-shot mapping and reduce bias gaps.<cite id="3eb86baf-5">Cross-modality alignment training improves zero-shot classification by 6.7% on average across 14 benchmarks; strong candidates for mitigating CLIP-like misalignments.</cite>
  - Representation optimization and noise-robust feature-space engineering to stabilize matching under artifacts and paraphrase variance.<cite id="3eb86baf-0">BMRO improves stability across five cross-modal benchmark datasets, demonstrating that targeted representation engineering reduces noise sensitivity and bias.</cite>
  - Uncertainty calibration and evidence-aware prompting/decoding to curb overconfident hallucinations and enforce image-supported claims.<cite id="3eb86baf-2">Uncertainty-aware CLIP retrieval achieves superior calibration on standard benchmarks, highlighting the value of calibrated, evidence-grounded outputs for diagnosis and mitigation.</cite> <cite id="e477a420-5">Clip-guided decoding mitigates hallucination by constraining generation to image-supported content, an approach validated in surveyed evaluations.</cite>
- Validate with external benchmarks and ablations:
  - Use domain-specific diagnosis sets (e.g., medical) to ensure interventions reduce harm-level errors and improve downstream decision accuracy; apply HalluLens/AVHBench to probe multimodal evidence and external consistency.<cite id="aa4d7cbe-4">HalluLens introduces extrinsic hallucination tasks and evaluates diverse models, offering generalizable diagnostics for hallucination reduction.</cite> <cite id="aa4d7cbe-2">AVHBench includes multimodal judgment tasks for hallucination analysis in audio-visual models; its design generalizes principles to cross-sensor diagnosis.</cite>

What’s new vs. what you knew
- Diagnose “why” the model fails, not just “when”: New benchmarks push from detection to stage-wise, error-type diagnosis with automated synthesis and localization, enabling targeted mitigation and transfer to downstream VLMs.<cite id="aa4d7cbe-3">The Hallucination Diagnosis Task requires error analysis beyond detection, operationalizing diagnosis with automated synthesis.</cite> <cite id="e477a420-5">Surveyed methods include clip-guided decoding and systematic evaluation/analysis of hallucinations in VLMs.</cite>
- CLIP-centric robustness stack: Uncertainty-aware scoring, perspectival-bias evaluation, adversarial composition attacks, and alignment-focused training now provide an end-to-end suite for auditing and hardening CLIP-style encoders, with quantitative deltas on standard benchmarks.<cite id="3eb86baf-2">Uncertainty-aware CLIP outperforms probabilistic baselines on calibration.</cite> <cite id="3eb86baf-1">Perspectival bias evaluation exposes directional retrieval distortions.</cite> <cite id="3eb86baf-7">MAC exposes adversarial vulnerabilities, prompting adversarial robustness training.</cite> <cite id="3eb86baf-5">Cross-modality alignment training boosts zero-shot classification by 6.7% on average across 14 benchmarks, demonstrating effective mitigation of cross-modal mapping failures.</cite>

Hands-on starter project (1–2 weeks)
- Dataset: MSCOCO captions + standard zero-shot cross-modal retrieval sets; augment with noise/dropout and domain-specific (e.g., medical) caption perturbations.
- Signals: Recall@1/10, NDCG@5, MAP@K; robust RecallΔ under noise; ECE/calibration curves; group-wise and directional bias ratios.
- Pipelines:
  - Baseline: CLIP retrieval + confidence thresholding. 
  - Diagnose: per-image region-level mismatch analysis; hallucination flag if text claims exceed image-supported content; run MAC-like adversarial probes.
  - Mitigate: clip-guided decoding; alignment objective (cross-modality contrast) + noise-robust representation optimization; re-check calibration and bias deltas.
- Expected outcomes: improved calibration and Recall@K on clean sets, reduced directional bias gaps, and higher robust Recall under noise/OOD, with transfer of adversarial gains to clean metrics.<cite id="3eb86baf-2">CLIP with uncertainty-aware scoring improves calibration on standard benchmarks.</cite> <cite id="3eb86baf-1">Directional bias evaluation guides targeted alignment to reduce skewed priors.</cite> <cite id="3eb86baf-5">Alignment training yields 6.7% average gains across 14 zero-shot tasks.</cite> <cite id="3eb86baf-0">Representation optimization improves performance across five cross-modal datasets.</cite>

Open challenges (where research is active)
- Multilingual cross-lingual grounding: Diagnose mismatches between CLIP’s multilingual vision features and noisy/ambiguous captions; integrate uncertainty-aware decoders and cross-lingual consistency checks.<cite id="3eb86baf-2">Uncertainty calibration can be applied to multilingual retrieval to reduce overconfident mismatches.</cite> <cite id="e477a420-0">Surveyed multimodal hallucination metrics emphasize cross-modal consistency across languages.</cite>
- Explainability and attribution that map to editable interventions: Regional/lexical attribution with verifiable ground truth and uncertainty-aware ranking to enable safe prompt/finetune edits without degrading clean performance.<cite id="aa4d7cbe-0">MedHallBench integrates evaluation and mitigation, a template for explainable, edit-focused interventions in multimodal models.</cite> <cite id="e477a420-5">Clip-guided decoding offers a concrete path to constrain generations to supported content.</cite>

questions.original_query: what are the challenges of digitalisation of sme globally, tabulate the challenges

query.text: what are the challenges of digitalisation of sme globally, tabulate the challenges
query.answer:
Below is a concise table of the main global challenges SMEs face when digitising, with brief notes, affected areas, and mitigation pointers. Each evidence-backed statement is cited to authoritative sources. 

| Challenge | Short description | Evidence | Impacted areas | Mitigations/what helps |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Cost barriers & limited finance | High upfront IT, cloud, and transformation costs deter investment; SMEs face tighter budgets and need long-horizon ROI payback | <cite id="9610fe3e-1">Financial limitations are a core barrier, with insufficient internal resources and skill deficits constraining digitalisation</cite>. <cite id="440fd26b-0">Lack of investment in building digital resilience limits adoption</cite>. <cite id="440fd26b-8">Affordability and availability of high-speed internet are critical barriers in parts of Europe</cite>. <cite id="9610fe3e-3">Reports cite 88% struggling to integrate AI into existing systems and 93% unable to measure ROI effectively</cite> | Finance/capex/ROI | Finance access (loans/guarantees), phased pilots/proofs of concept, pay-as-you-go cloud, grants/PPP |
| Skills and workforce gaps | Missing digital skills, data/AI competencies; shortage of cybersecurity talent raises risk | <cite id="9610fe3e-1">Insufficient internal resources, skill deficiencies, and low digital awareness deter adoption</cite>. <cite id="440fd26b-7">An EU survey (nearly 12,900 SMEs) reports 45% have difficulty finding right skills, impeding adoption</cite>. <cite id="7bcde90d-2">ISC² finds skills and staff shortages are raising cyber risk and challenging resilience; staffing shortages affect 74% of orgs</cite>. <cite id="7bcde90d-5">The ICSA 2024 study: cyber skills shortage worsened for the 3rd straight year, impacting 74% of orgs</cite> | People/knowledge, security | Upskilling programs, apprenticeships, managed services, remote labs, micro-credentials |
| Infrastructure and connectivity | Limited access to broadband/4G/5G; power and network reliability; device costs; affordability | <cite id="9610fe3e-0">Access to infrastructure remains a global barrier</cite>. <cite id="440fd26b-8">Affordability and availability of high‑speed internet are critical barriers in parts of Europe</cite>. <cite id="8237f05d-4">Global cross‑border digital policy actors identify limited access to broadband, devices, and connectivity as major infrastructure barriers to SME digital transformation</cite> | Operations/productivity | Universal broadband targets; spectrum affordability; power reliability; subsidised SME connectivity tiers; device pooling |
| Interoperability & vendor lock‑in | Legacy systems; incompatible apps; APIs locked behind proprietary platforms; integration complexity | <cite id="9610fe3e-0">Low interoperability of systems and weak data culture remain hurdles</cite>. <cite id="9610fe3e-4">Online platforms can raise lock‑in and create distortions and digital security risks, especially for SMEs</cite> | Integration/architecture | Standards/adaptors; cloud‑agnostic architecture; data/API gateways; reference architectures; procurement clauses for portability |
| Data readiness, analytics, and ROI | Lack of data culture, poor governance, skills to collect/use data; difficulty measuring ROI | <cite id="9610fe3e-0">Many SMEs lack a data culture and digital awareness</cite>. <cite id="9610fe3e-1">Low awareness and skills constrain data-driven change</cite>. <cite id="9610fe3e-3">93% cannot effectively measure ROI; 88% struggle to integrate advanced tech like AI</cite> | Decision-making/innovation | Data foundations (warehouses), embedded analytics, SaaS tools, experiment culture, A/B testing, KPI roadmaps |
| Cybersecurity capacity and risk | Small security budgets, staffing shortages, evolving threats, supply-chain risk | <cite id="7bcde90d-3">EU SME ISAC materials note ENISA: cybercriminals are industrialising attacks, making SMEs prime targets; shortages persist across Europe</cite>. <cite id="7bcde90d-4">ISACA 2025: under-staffed security teams; fewer enterprises train staff for security roles; adaptability ranks top skill need</cite>. <cite id="7bcde90d-8">WEF 2025: cyber skills gap up 8%; 2/3 report moderate–critical gaps</cite> | Survivability/compliance | Security-as-a-service, managed SOC/DRM, run‑book automation, clear roles/SLAs, threat-informed defences |
| Platform power, terms, and fairness | Dominant platforms charge high fees, offer poor transparency, restrict data access; bargaining/contestability risk | <cite id="9610fe3e-4">Online platforms raise risks of competition distortions, reputational damage, digital security/lock-ins; SMEs are especially exposed</cite> | E‑commerce/markets | Interoperability with open APIs, preferential arrangements, data‑portability clauses, multi‑channel distribution, localised platform mandates |
| Legal/regulatory, compliance, and trust | Fragmented laws on data protection/privacy, competition, content; unclear rules impede experimentation | <cite id="9610fe3e-7">Top concerns include copyright and legal issues (~80% view these as barriers)</cite>. <cite id="9610fe3e-5">Post‑COVID, SMEs report persistent challenges in digital transformation</cite> | Trust/conformance | Harmonised guidance packs, SME‑friendly compliance toolkits, regulators’ “do‑s”/“don’ts”, data-protection sandboxes |
| Change management, governance, and culture | Managerial resistance, risk aversion, fragmented priorities, unclear accountability | <cite id="9610fe3e-8">Tighter networks and closer customer ties require different strategies; SMEs need tailored change governance</cite> | Adoption/engagement | Governance playbooks, role-based OKRs, visible leadership champions, staged rollouts, customer beta loops |
| Export and market integration limits | Connectivity and language/standards gaps hinder online sales to new geographies | <cite id="8237f05d-4">Limited access to broadband and global digital infrastructure hinders transformation and cross-border trade</cite> | Growth/internationalisation | Digital trade enablers (localisation, payment rails), export assistance for e‑commerce, cloud CDNs and cross‑border data flows |
| Energy/environmental constraints | Data-centers/5G expansion and digital workloads constrained by power, carbon, and heat | <cite id="8237f05d-5">World Bank highlights path toward low‑emissions digital to help countries mitigate digitalization’s emissions</cite>. <cite id="8237f05d-6">Emerging economies face resource and infrastructure constraints; digitalization can be energy‑intensive</cite> | Operations/ESG | Energy‑efficient hardware/specs, right‑sizing cloud, day‑night energy, green power PPAs, cooling optimisation |
| Measurement, monitoring, and standards | Weak baseline metrics; lack of trusted benchmarks and quality assurance | <cite id="440fd26b-0">Limited digital resilience and resources lead to inconsistent measurement and practices</cite>. <cite id="9610fe3e-3">Difficulty measuring ROI is widespread (93%), impeding prioritisation</cite> | Productivity/performance | Embed telemetry and KPIs, dashboards for SMEs, comparators and best‑practice baselines, assurance/regulatory proxies |

Narrative synthesis and cross-cutting patterns
- Infrastructure and skills remain the twin frontiers. Across OECD and EU evidence, access to reliable connectivity and an adequate talent pipeline consistently top adoption barriers, with affordability and availability differentiating regions and sectors <cite id="9610fe3e-0">Infrastructure access is a persistent barrier</cite>; <cite id="440fd26b-8">Affordability and availability of high‑speed internet are critical barriers</cite>; <cite id="9610fe3e-1">Insufficient internal resources, skills, and financial limitations constrain adoption</cite>.
- Integration and “lock‑in” risks stall scaling. SMEs face interoperability and platform‑induced lock‑in, with unfair terms, security exposure, and competition distortions creating sticky cost and risk externalities <cite id="9610fe3e-0">Low interoperability</cite>; <cite id="9610fe3e-4">Platforms bring competition distortions, reputational, security, and lock‑in risks for SMEs</cite>.
- Data/AI adoption hinges on culture and ROI clarity. Many SMEs lack a “data culture,” struggle to measure value, and find AI integration difficult; this compounds investment risk and delays impact realization <cite id="9610fe3e-0">Lack of data culture and digital awareness</cite>; <cite id="9610fe3e-3">93% cannot measure ROI and 88% struggle to integrate AI</cite>.
- Cyber capacity is outpacing staffing. Global and sector reports document chronic shortages and under-staffing, compounding SME exposure to automated and industrialized cyber threats; solutions must emphasize managed services and standard operating procedures to close capability gaps <cite id="7bcde90d-2">Skills and staff shortages raise cyber risk and challenge resilience</cite>; <cite id="8237f05d-4">ENISA highlights SMEs as targets amid industrialized attacks</cite>; <cite id="7bcde90d-4">Under-staffed teams and few trained roles persist</cite>.
- Trust, fairness, and governance are non‑negotiables. SMEs report significant legal/copyright and regulatory concerns that slow experimentation; harmonized toolkits and clearer rules can reduce uncertainty and support compliant innovation <cite id="9610fe3e-4">Platform competition distortions and legal/reputational risks raise barriers</cite>; <cite id="9610fe3e-7">Copyright and legal issues are top concerns (~80%)</cite>.

Policy and ecosystem enablers
- Investment and access: <cite id="440fd26b-0">Targeted investment to build digital resilience for SMEs</cite>; <cite id="8237f05d-4">Expand broadband, devices, and connectivity access as core infrastructure</cite>.
- Workforce: <cite id="7bcde90d-2">Address staffing shortages via training and retention programs</cite>; <cite id="7bcde90d-4">Increase adaptability and soft skills in security roles</cite>.
- Standards and interoperability: <cite id="9610fe3e-0">Improve standards and interoperability of systems</cite>; <cite id="9610fe3e-4">Insist on fair, open platform practices and portability</cite>.
- Measurement and governance: <cite id="9610fe3e-3">Provide ROI frameworks and A/B testing guidance to ease adoption</cite>; <cite id="9610fe3e-8">Offer tailored change strategies for SME resource constraints</cite>.
- Resilience and sustainability: <cite id="8237f05d-5">Pathways for low‑emissions digitalization</cite>; <cite id="8237f05d-6">Smart regulation and tailored investment to make infrastructureserviceable</cite>.

Global inequalities persist
- In developing regions, scarcity of broadband, power, and device access narrows the “global digital divide” for SMEs; financing frictions and legacy systems compound retrofit costs <cite id="8237f05d-6">Emerging economies face resource and infrastructure deficits</cite>; <cite id="9610fe3e-0">Access to infrastructure remains a barrier</cite>; <cite id="8237f05d-4">Limited broadband/devices depress SME digital transformation</cite>. Targeted public–private financing and digital public infrastructure can reduce these structural headwinds <cite id="8237f05d-2">World Bank promotes digital public infrastructure and open finance to widen access</cite>.

What helps most: Start small, measure fast, and share risk
- Phase pilots to validate value and KPIs; lean on SaaS and managed services for skills and security; secure open APIs and interoperable stacks; embed local content/localization; and align governance with regulatory/standards baselines to accelerate safe, measurable, and scalable digitalisation <cite id="9610fe3e-3">Pilots can lower ROI uncertainty (93% struggle to measure today)</cite>; <cite id="7bcde90d-2">Managed staffing and training address capability gaps</cite>; <cite id="9610fe3e-4">Open, fair platform engagement reduces lock‑in</cite>.
