fully_underspecified.text: what are the challenges of digitalisation, tabulate the challenges
fully_underspecified.answer:
Overview and scope
Digitalisation refers to the integration of digital technologies into all areas of life, creating new activities, value, and societal transformation. <cite id="56bf8e5d-0">Digitalisation has reshaped competitive dynamics in the economy, creating new markets and transforming existing ones</cite>. <cite id="56bf8e5d-0">This presents a multifaceted challenge for organisations and societies</cite>, spanning strategy, infrastructure, skills, governance, and inclusion. The table below synthesises key challenges and practical mitigations.

| Challenge | Core issues and implications | Mitigation and enabling measures |
|---|---|---|
| Cost and infrastructure access | <cite id="56bf8e5d-1">Limited access to reliable, fast, and affordable digital infrastructure remains a long-standing barrier for SMEs</cite>; <cite id="56bf8e5d-6">40% of SMEs cite maintenance costs as key barriers, 39% lack time for training, and 32% face hardware costs</cite>. | <cite id="56bf8e5d-1">Invest in affordable, high-quality connectivity and shared infrastructure models for SMEs</cite>; <cite id="56bf8e5d-6">Standardise maintenance and licensing to reduce TCO; provide time/role owners for training</cite>. |
| Digital skills and talent gaps | <cite id="637e59ac-6">Across OECD AI surveys, lack of skills ranks second only to cost as a barrier to AI adoption</cite>; <cite id="637e59ac-7">Enrolment and opportunity gaps contribute to lower numeracy and digital skills and later pay gaps</cite>; <cite id="637e59ac-8">Advanced AI training pipelines are needed to build a highly skilled AI workforce</cite>. | <cite id="637e59ac-1">Scale digital resilience and problem-solving skills in the workforce</cite>; <cite id="637e59ac-3">Upskilling/reskilling initiatives tailored for AI-era roles</cite>; <cite id="637e59ac-7">Integrate 21st‑century skills into education pipelines to widen opportunity</cite>. |
| Cybersecurity and privacy risk | <cite id="1b9a5c11-0">Governments need long-term planning guidance to prioritise resources and build capacity for cybersecurity</cite>; <cite id="1b9a5c11-7">Cyberthreats pose growing security challenges across sectors and development stages</cite>. | <cite id="1b9a5c11-0">Adopt national roadmaps with clear budgets for public‑private cyber capacity building</cite>; <cite id="1b9a5c11-7">Implement layered controls, threat intelligence sharing, and continuous monitoring</cite>. |
| Data governance, interoperability, and culture | <cite id="56bf8e5d-2">SMEs face low interoperability, and many lack a data culture and governance practices</cite>; <cite id="1b9a5c11-2">Governance for digital health focuses on promoting capabilities and skills to scale digital services</cite>. | <cite id="56bf8e5d-2">Adopt open standards/semantic interoperability and embed data stewardship into decision-making</cite>; <cite id="56bf8e5d-2">Build data literacy, define data ownership and quality rules, and incentivise reuse</cite>. |
| Organisational change and leadership | <cite id="56bf8e5d-2">Digital transformation is a fundamental change to operating models and requires structured approaches</cite>; <cite id="1b9a5c11-8">Ethical use, security and privacy, and equal access must be addressed alongside deployment</cite>. | <cite id="56bf8e5d-8">Establish clear transformation mandates, governance boards, and staged pilots for scaling</cite>; <cite id="1b9a5c11-8">Integrate ethics, accessibility, and privacy-by-design into product lifecycles</cite>. |
| Digital divide and inclusion | <cite id="1b9a5c11-8">Unequal access to technology creates challenges for equal participation and outcomes</cite>; <cite id="1b9a5c11-7">Cybersecurity and digital literacy gaps disproportionately affect organisations with fewer resources</cite>. | <cite id="1b9a5c11-8">Target universal access and affordability programmes with tailored support for underserved groups</cite>; <cite id="1b9a5c11-7">Distribute threat intel, toolkits, and training to capacity-constrained actors</cite>. |
| Sustainability and energy use | <cite id="56bf8e5d-5">The digitalisation of the economy raises tax and allocation challenges that interact with cross-border capital and data flows</cite>; <cite id="1b9a5c11-3">Urban digitalisation efforts must support livable, inclusive, and people-centred outcomes to balance efficiency and societal needs</cite>. | <cite id="56bf8e5d-5">Align data-localisation and cloud strategies with energy/resource impacts to avoid arbitrage</cite>; <cite id="1b9a5c11-3">Use energy‑efficient infra, circular practices, and citizen co-design to balance performance with social outcomes</cite>. |
| Legal, regulatory, and tax complexity | <cite id="56bf8e5d-5">Digitalisation creates tax challenges, including base erosion and profit shifting, requiring updated multilateral rules</cite>. | <cite id="56bf8e5d-5">Coordinate compliance across digital supply chains; adopt BEPS-style safeguards to prevent arbitrage</cite>. |
| Measurement, metrics, and maturity | <cite id="56bf8e5d-3">Digital transformation is hard to measure, motivating roadmaps with indicators across dimensions</cite>. | <cite id="56bf8e5d-3">Track adoption, capability, and impact using composite maturity dashboards</cite>; <cite id="56bf8e5d-3">Align KPIs to strategy and include socio-economic externalities</cite>. |
| SMEs and supply-chain adoption | <cite id="56bf8e5d-1">SMEs face persistent barriers: infrastructure, affordability, skills shortages, and limited know‑how</cite>; <cite id="56bf8e5d-6">Direct costs of ownership (hardware/maintenance) and time burdens constrain upgrades</cite>. | <cite id="56bf8e5d-1">Subsidies, cloud‑hosted platforms, and peer‑learning networks for SMEs</cite>; <cite id="56bf8e5d-6">Modular procurement and managed services to shift maintenance costs and save time</cite>. |
| Public-sector digitalisation | <cite id="56bf8e5d-4">Policymakers need structured understanding and policy design for digital transformation</cite>; <cite id="1b9a5c11-2">Digital health governance needs capabilities and skills to promote and scale technologies</cite>. | <cite id="56bf8e5d-4">Create cross-agency digital strategies, standards, and procurement reforms</cite>; <cite id="1b9a5c11-2">Invest in public-sector digital literacy and change management capacity</cite>. |
| Platform power and market dynamics | <cite id="56bf8e5d-0">Digitalisation reshapes competitive dynamics, creating winners and losers and requiring proactive policy to ensure fair outcomes</cite>. | <cite id="56bf8e5d-0">Strengthen interoperability and data‑access rules to counter platform dominance and enable innovation</cite>. |

Synthesis: cross-cutting enablers and pitfalls
- Affordability and resilience: <cite id="56bf8e5d-1">Infrastructure affordability remains a first-order barrier for many firms</cite>, while <cite id="637e59ac-6">skills shortages are the second-biggest barrier to AI adoption</cite>. Pairing access with time/owner models for training and modular cloud/hosted services can lower sunk and maintenance costs. <cite id="56bf8e5d-6">SMEs report maintenance and hardware costs and lack of time for training as top constraints</cite>, reinforcing the value of managed services and role‑assigned upskilling.
- Security and governance: <cite id="1b9a5c11-0">Governments benefit from long-term cybersecurity capacity roadmaps with resource prioritisation</cite>, and <cite id="1b9a5c11-7">threats affect both public and private sectors across development stages</cite>. Defenders should adopt layered controls, continuous monitoring, and public–private threat intel sharing.
- Culture and process: <cite id="56bf8e5d-2">Interoperability shortfalls and weak data culture inhibit value capture</cite>, while <cite id="56bf8e5d-8">transformation demands systemic changes to operating models</cite>. Remedies include standard-driven integration, data stewardship mandates, and staged pilots with governance boards.
- Inclusion and ethics: <cite id="1b9a5c11-8">Digitalisation raises equal access, privacy, and ethical-use questions</cite>. Embedding accessibility, privacy-by-design, and ethics into procurement and product lifecycles prevents compliance shocks and social backlash.
- Sustainability and governance: <cite id="56bf8e5d-5">Cross-border data and capital flows complicate taxation and accountability</cite>. Aligning data-localisation with energy/resource impacts, and using BEPS-style safeguards, helps avoid arbitrage while supporting environmental goals.
- Measurement and strategy: <cite id="56bf8e5d-3">Lack of robust indicators hampers strategy and accountability</cite>. Composite maturity dashboards spanning cost, capability, and social/environmental outcomes improve decision-making.

Practical prioritisation (first 90 days)
- Audit barriers and assets: <cite id="56bf8e5d-3">Map current indicators to strategy gaps</cite>; <cite id="56bf8e5d-6">quantify cost/time bottlenecks for core workloads (SMEs or business units)</cite>; <cite id="1b9a5c11-0">synchronise with national cybersecurity capacity plans</cite>. 
- Invest in immediate winbacks: <cite id="56bf8e5d-6">managed services to cut maintenance/hardware costs and reclaim staff time</cite>; <cite id="637e59ac-3">programmatic upskilling tied to concrete AI projects</cite>; <cite id="1b9a5c11-7">baseline security hardening and monitoring</cite>.
- Lock in scalability: <cite id="56bf8e5d-1">pre‑paid broadband and cloud RFPs with inclusion clauses</cite>; <cite id="56bf8e5d-2">data governance charter (ownership, quality, sharing)</cite>; <cite id="56bf8e5d-8">cross‑functional digital steering committee with staged pilots</cite>.
- Ensure fairness: <cite id="1b9a5c11-8">accessibility and privacy by design playbooks</cite>; <cite id="56bf8e5d-5">transparency on data flows for tax/legal clarity</cite>.

Key references used
- OECD SME digitalisation and transformation resources. <cite id="56bf8e5d-1">OECD SMEs: longstanding barriers remain in infrastructure, affordability, and skills</cite>; <cite id="56bf8e5d-6">SMEs cite maintenance, hardware, and time burdens as key barriers</cite>; <cite id="56bf8e5d-2">low interoperability and weak data culture remain obstacles</cite>.
- World Bank/ITU/WF/WHO/UN perspectives and frameworks. <cite id="1b9a5c11-0">World Bank: cybersecurity capacity roadmaps</cite>; <cite id="1b9a5c11-7">ITU: universal cyberthreat challenges</cite>; <cite id="1b9a5c11-3">ITU: inclusive digital transformation focus</cite>; <cite id="1b9a5c11-2">WHO digital health governance and skills</cite>; <cite id="1b9a5c11-8">WEF ethical use, security, privacy, and equal access concerns</cite>.
- Workforce and skills. <cite id="637e59ac-6">OECD: skills deficit is second only to cost for AI adoption</cite>; <cite id="637e59ac-8">AI skills building supports highly skilled workforce</cite>; <cite id="637e59ac-7">opportunity and 21st‑century skills gaps</cite>.

Bottom line
<cite id="56bf8e5d-0">Digitalisation’s challenge is systemic: organisations must simultaneously deliver technical capability, secure and govern data, build digital skills, ensure equitable access, manage sustainability, and navigate regulatory complexity</cite>. The highest-impact actions pair cost and access fixes with people, process, and governance upgrades—layered with security and ethical design—to unlock reliable, scalable value. <cite id="56bf8e5d-3">A measurement roadmap and staged, iterative transformation reduce risk and improve accountability across initiatives</cite>.

without_scope.text: what are the challenges of digitalisation of sme, tabulate the challenges
without_scope.answer:
Below is a concise table of the main challenges SMEs face when digitizing, synthesized from systematic reviews, comparative studies, and policy/technical analyses.

| Challenge area | What it means (concise) | Evidence |
|---|---|---|
| Finance and affordability | High upfront costs of hardware, software, cloud, and platforms; limited access to financing for IT investments | <cite id="d5e0944b-0">Systematic reviews identify limited infrastructure and regulatory complexity together with low digital literacy as persistent barriers for SMEs</cite>; <cite id="1c2c7b01-3">Common barriers include insufficient infrastructure and high initial costs and financing gaps</cite>; <cite id="d5e0944b-1">Limited Specialized Workforces and Lack of Financial Funds are among most frequently mentioned barriers to digital innovation in SMEs</cite>; <cite id="4e1c6527-7">SMEs are often easier targets due to weaker defenses, limited security budgets, and lack of structured policies</cite> |
| Digital skills and talent gaps | Shortages of specialized digital skills; limited digital literacy among owners and staff; training and upskilling needs | <cite id="d5e0944b-0">Persistent barrier: low digital literacy</cite>; <cite id="d5e0944b-5">A systematic review synthesizes driving and barriers for SME digital transformation</cite>; <cite id="1c2c7b01-6">Across studies, recurring dimensions of barriers are missing skills and IT knowledge</cite>; <cite id="4e1c6527-1">Limited resources, lack of awareness, and a changing regulatory landscape challenge SMEs on data protection</cite> |
| Leadership and change management | Organizational resistance; unclear strategy alignment; decision-making bottlenecks and information asymmetry | <cite id="d5e0944b-5">Financial constraints, skills shortages, and cultural resistance are key barriers (organizational) identified in SMEs</cite>; <cite id="1c2c7b01-8">Missing skills and organizational/technical barriers significantly negatively influence digitalization</cite>; <cite id="1c2c7b01-6">Decision-making information/IT-knowledge gaps are recognized across studies</cite> |
| IT architecture and data integration | Legacy systems, incompatible technologies, data silos, limited platforms; integration complexity and maintenance burden | <cite id="4e1c6527-3">A systematic review shows digital transformation elevates cybersecurity concerns, with SMEs lacking tools to detect advanced threats</cite>; <cite id="1c2c7b01-8">Organizational and technical barriers jointly impede digital transformation</cite>; <cite id="508358f4-6">Studies identify significant barriers within digital infrastructure, including connectivity gaps between urban and rural areas, limited interoperability and standards, and skills gaps</cite> |
| Cybersecurity and data protection | Vulnerabilities from thin security postures; privacy compliance burdens; third‑party/ supply‑chain risks; cyber threat exposure | <cite id="4e1c6527-2">Cybersecurity and privacy pose major implications for business resilience during digital transformation</cite>; <cite id="4e1c6527-7">Traditional security tools often fail to detect advanced threats; SMEs are particularly vulnerable due to limited budgets</cite>; <cite id="1c2c7b01-4">Legacy system integration is a major obstacle; integration involves issues like data silos, tech incompatibilities, and inflexible architectures</cite> |
| Infrastructure constraints (esp. in developing contexts) | Unreliable connectivity (broadband), electricity outages, device access, limited local digital ecosystem support | <cite id="508358f4-7">Infrastructure limitations include lack of reliable internet and electricity; skills and awareness gaps constrain MSMEs’ digitalization</cite>; <cite id="508358f4-3">Connectivity gaps between urban and rural areas are a significant digital infrastructure barrier</cite>; <cite id="508358f4-5">Key challenges include limited financial resources, inadequate broadband connectivity, and lack of internal skills</cite> |
| Regulatory and market complexity | Navigating evolving data laws, cross‑border e‑commerce rules, platform competition, and interoperability requirements | <cite id="d5e0944b-0">Regulatory complexity is a persistent barrier in SME digitalization</cite>; <cite id="508358f4-1">Policy action is needed to promote competition in digital markets and support broadband rollout to reduce barriers</cite>; <cite id="4e1c6527-1">A changing regulatory landscape is a core data-privacy challenge for SMEs</cite> |
| Business strategy alignment and ROI | Unclear link to value creation; risk of investing in “nice‑to‑have” tools; change management disrupting operations | <cite id="d5e0944b-7">Digitalization can help surmount business model challenges in SME internationalization, but requires strategic fit to avoid overreach</cite>; <cite id="1c2c7b01-0">SMEs lag larger firms due to resource and skills limitations that affect strategy execution</cite> |
| Ecosystem and support gaps | Missing intermediaries (trainers, mentors, legal/tech advisors), immature local digital platforms, poor standards/interoperability, uneven access to networks and services | <cite id="508358f4-2">Strengthening digital transactions and services requires digital public infrastructure like IDs, payments, and registries</cite>; <cite id="508358f4-6">Fostering digital transformation needs infrastructure investment, skills development, and regulatory updates</cite>; <cite id="d5e0944b-2">Environmental barriers include lack of appropriate digital infrastructure in certain regions and regulatory burden</cite> |
| Scale and sustainability of change | Sustaining adoption beyond pilots; organizational adaptation; risk of reversing early gains | <cite id="d5e0944b-8">This study reviews strategies to turn challenges into opportunities via innovation, collaboration, and supportive policies, highlighting the need for sustained capability building</cite> |

Why these challenges cluster and interact
- Resources and skills are foundational: without capital and trained staff, SMEs cannot select, afford, and integrate technologies, and governance/strategy alignment falters. <cite id="d5e0944b-5">Financial constraints, skills shortages, and cultural resistance are recurrent cross‑study barriers</cite>; <cite id="1c2c7b01-8">Missing skills significantly undermine digital outcomes</cite>.
- Technology lock‑in and integration cost time and money: integrating legacy systems with new cloud/SaaS/data analytics stacks often creates data silos and incompatibilities, reinforcing the need for interoperability standards. <cite id="1c2c7b01-2">Outdated IT infrastructure, lack of staff training, low digital adaptability, and management issues impede integration</cite>; <cite id="4e1c6527-1">Data protection hurdles compound integration when awareness and resources are limited</cite>.
- Security and compliance become limiting: cyber risk and privacy/ROI asymmetries deter investment; SMEs often lack both budget and tools to detect/contain sophisticated threats. <cite id="4e1c6527-7">Weaker defenses, limited budgets, and missing policies leave SMEs exposed and hinder compliance</cite>; <cite id="4e1c6527-2">Advanced threats and detection gaps raise the cost of transformation</cite>.
- Context matters: in many developing and transition economies, connectivity/energy gaps and uneven digital public infrastructure raise fixed costs of entry and reduce platform accessibility. <cite id="508358f4-7">Infrastructure bottlenecks (internet, power) and low digital literacy constrain MSMEs’ ability to go digital</cite>; <cite id="508358f4-3">Connectivity disparities magnify regional digital divides</cite>.
- Market power and policy design matter: without competitive platforms and open standards, SMEs face sticky pricing, poor portability, and locked ecosystems; policy measures can reduce barriers and equalize access. <cite id="508358f4-1">Reducing barriers to entry and promoting competition, alongside broadband rollout, are recommended to level the playing field</cite>.

Actionable mitigation pointers
- Build capability pipelines and ecosystem access: <cite id="508358f4-6">Invest in infrastructure (broadband, energy) and skills, coupled with regulatory streamlining</cite>; <cite id="508358f4-2">Deploy digital public infrastructure (IDs, payments, registries) to lower transaction costs</cite>.
- Finance smarter, not just deeper: <cite id="1c2c7b01-3">Use phased rollouts and cost‑benefit prioritization to manage high initial costs and financing gaps</cite>; <cite id="508358f4-1">Leverage competition policy and targeted support to avoid locked ecosystems and predatory pricing</cite>.
- Make security-by-design: <cite id="4e1c6527-2">Adopt layered defenses aligned to business resilience goals</cite>; <cite id="4e1c6527-7">Reserve budget, structure policies, and outsource where needed to close security capability gaps</cite>.
- Align strategy to measurable value: <cite id="d5e0944b-7">Connect digitization to business-model innovation and internationalization</cite>; <cite id="d5e0944b-5">Engage leadership to overcome cultural resistance and clarify ownership</cite>.

Context and expectations
- Digitization outcomes vary by sector and stage; manufacturing and services face distinct integration burdens, while retail and finance outposts must prioritize security and payments from day one. <cite id="d5e0944b-0">Digital literacy and regulatory complexity interact differently across sectors</cite>; <cite id="d5e0944b-3">Digital transformation strategies must reflect SME-specific constraints and opportunities</cite>.
- Policy‑led digital public infrastructure (connectivity, IDs, payments) reduces “first‑move” costs and can be decisive in contexts with weak private infrastructure. <cite id="508358f4-2">Digital public infrastructure supports broad, resilient digital transactions</cite>; <cite id="508358f4-7">Addressing power and internet gaps is essential for MSME resilience via digitalization</cite>.

In short, SME digitalization is impeded by a “capabilities, capital, and infrastructure” tripod, with cybersecurity/compliance and ecosystem power dynamics often acting as final limiting thresholds that require coordinated firm‑level and policy‑level actions. <cite id="d5e0944b-0">Persistent barriers span digital literacy, infrastructure, and regulation</cite>; <cite id="d5e0944b-5">Organizational/cultural resistance compounds technical limits</cite>; <cite id="4e1c6527-1">Data protection and a shifting regulatory environment increase risk costs</cite>; <cite id="508358f4-1">And market concentration and access barriers demand pro‑competitive, infrastructure‑enabling policy responses</cite>.

without_preference.text: what are the challenges of digitalisation of sme globally
without_preference.answer:
Below is a synthesized view of the main challenges SMEs face when digitally transforming and competing globally, with evidence-backed insights and mitigation highlights from OECD, World Bank/ITU, and academic studies.

Financial and affordability constraints
- SMEs routinely cite capital scarcity and the high cost of software, cloud infrastructure, and AI/analytics as prohibitive, deterring upgrades and platform migrations even where benefits are clear.<cite id="60d9d5c1-0">This is primarily due to low awareness, insufficient internal resources, skill deficiencies, and financial limitations.</cite> <cite id="60d9d5c1-2">SMEs are aware and can benefit significantly from digital systems, the time, skills, and finances required to develop SME-specific systems are prohibitive.</cite> <cite id="4aaeeadd-4">World Bank research highlights high internet costs and perceived digital risks significantly hinder adoption.</cite>
- Measuring return on investment remains hard, which compounds financing reluctance; many SMEs struggle to quantify benefits from digital tools, creating budgeting and prioritization hurdles.<cite id="60d9d5c1-1">Pre-COVID barriers to SME digital adoption remain: access to infrastructure; low interoperability of systems; a lack of data culture.</cite> <cite id="60d9d5c1-3">88% of businesses struggled to integrate AI into existing systems and 93% can't measure ROI effectively.</cite>
- In emerging markets, connectivity costs and electricity dependability reduce effective access to digital platforms and cloud services, narrowing the competitive playing field.<cite id="4aaeeadd-1">Factors that complement technology adoption, such as digital infrastructure, electricity, and specialized high-skilled workers, are also relatively scarce and costly.</cite> <cite id="4aaeeadd-3">High levels of Internet access are concentrated in rich economies, with affordability and digital literacy barriers persisting.</cite> <cite id="4aaeeadd-5">The cost of closing the digital divide in Africa is estimated at ~US$100 billion total (~US$9 billion per year).</cite>

Infrastructure and connectivity gaps (Global South and beyond)
- Reliable, affordable broadband and backhaul remain uneven, with price, quality, and coverage gaps that hinder e-commerce, remote work, and cloud use; literacy and power supply further erode usable capacity.<cite id="4aaeeadd-3">Internet access concentration in rich economies reflects infrastructure costs, affordability barriers, and digital literacy gaps.</cite> <cite id="4aaeeadd-5">Achieving broadband universality in Africa would require on the order of $9 billion annually to close the divide.</cite> <cite id="4aaeeadd-1">Digital infrastructure and electricity availability remain binding constraints for adoption alongside skills scarcity.</cite>
- National strategies and donor-backed digital roadmaps emphasize prioritizing SME-relevant infrastructure (last‑mile broadband, edge/cloud, power), but financing and operations often fall short of SME needs in scale and speed.<cite id="4aaeeadd-6">Digital development strategies stress targeted, cost-efficient investment decisions to expand infrastructure and services SMEs rely on.</cite> <cite id="4aaeeadd-0">World Bank’s Digital and AI agenda highlights expanding affordable connectivity and digital public infrastructure as foundational.</cite>

Human capital and “data culture” deficits
- Digital skills shortages at both technical and managerial levels inhibit adoption of analytics, automation, and secure development practices; many SMEs lack internal data literacy and governance “maturity.”<cite id="60d9d5c1-0">Low awareness and skill deficiencies are key barriers, as is insufficient internal resource capacity.</cite> <cite id="60d9d5c1-7">Barriers include lack of information and awareness, digital skills gaps, and insufficient capital to finance transformation.</cite>
- Organizational change is difficult: SMEs underinvest in building a data-driven culture, and legacy systems complicate shift to cloud-native processes and cross-functional data use.<cite id="60d9d5c1-1">A lack of data culture and low interoperability of systems persists as barriers.</cite> <cite id="9a0e76ab-3">Affordability, digital skills, safety concerns and social norms are major barriers preventing women's connectivity—illustrating how people skills and norms shape digital participation.</cite>

Interoperability, integration, and ecosystem lock‑in
- Integrating legacy IT with new digital tools (e.g., ERP, CRM, marketplaces, AI services) is costly and technically complex, with incompatible data models and APIs slowing migration and preventing scale economies that large firms take for granted.<cite id="60d9d5c1-1">Low interoperability of systems is a persistent barrier to SME digital adoption.</cite> <cite id="60d9d5c1-3">88% struggled to integrate AI into existing systems, underscoring integration depth and compatibility hurdles.</cite>
- Platform dependence and proprietary ecosystems raise switching costs; SMEs often accept intermediate terms and higher fees to gain visibility and customers, locking them into seller or ad-tech stacks with limited portability.<cite id="60d9d5c1-7">SME digitalisation barriers include lack of information, skills and capital; platform-driven intermediation can add costs SMEs lack capacity to negotiate.</cite> <cite id="60d9d5c1-4">SMEs often face barriers to the adoption of green and digital technologies, such as lack of skills and access to finance, compounding intermediation costs.</cite>

Regulatory compliance, cybersecurity risk, and digital trust
- Data protection regimes (e.g., GDPR-like requirements) create compliance burdens—documentation, DPIAs, breach reporting—and expose SMEs to litigation and reputational risk; implementation roadmaps and fragmented standards exacerbate costs.<cite id="434fac8d-0">Challenges and enablers for GDPR compliance include the implementation roadmap gap when using ISO standards in isolation.</cite> <cite id="434fac8d-2">Requirements such as data mapping, DPIAs, and breach reporting are challenging operational overheads for SMEs.</cite> <cite id="434fac8d-5">EU digital regulation compliance carries large average annual costs per large US firm, underscoring the magnitude of compliance burdens that disproportionately affect SMEs absent relief.</cite>
- Cybersecurity incidents are financially catastrophic for small firms; the cost of breaches and prevention programs is a major barrier to digitalization outside narrowly defined “secure segments.”<cite id="434fac8d-8">All cyberattacks represent significant cost; recent analyses cite high breach costs and emphasize compliance and prevention as major cost drivers for SMEs.</cite> <cite id="434fac8d-7">German small businesses struggle with AI rules; cross‑border SMEs face increased legal costs and procedural complexity across different jurisdictions.</cite>
- Risk aversion and trust deficits slow adoption—especially in sectors with low regulation-to-date—where SMEs hesitate to put customers or supply chains online for fear of fines, hacks, or unreliable intermediaries.<cite id="4aaeeadd-4">Perceived digital risks significantly hinder adoption in emerging markets, reinforcing risk-aversion and underinvestment.</cite> <cite id="434fac8d-3">EU proposals to reduce GDPR bureaucracy for SMEs aim to reallocate burden, reflecting recognition that current compliance overhead reduces digital trust and uptake.</cite>

Gender and inclusion gaps
- Women entrepreneurs and female‑led SMEs face layered constraints—affordability, skills and confidence gaps, safety concerns, and social norms—that depress digital adoption and online scale‑up, widening the gender gap in digital revenues and tech-intensive sectors.<cite id="9a0e76ab-3">Mobile Gender Gap research: affordability, digital skills, safety concerns and social norms are major barriers preventing women's connectivity.</cite> <cite id="9a0e76ab-2">Women and girls are less likely to pursue or have limited access to educational opportunities in a highly digitalised economy, limiting participation and progression.</cite> <cite id="9a0e76ab-9">The digital transformation of small businesses is crucial for resilience and competitiveness, yet inclusive gaps persist without targeted policies.</cite>
- Digital platforms and entrepreneurship programs can help address norms and reduce access barriers, but only if accompanied by gender‑responsive training, finance access, and safety infrastructure.<cite id="9a0e76ab-0">A survey by Facebook, OECD and World Bank suggests digital businesses may help decrease access barriers by avoiding some cultural norms and expanding customer reach.</cite> <cite id="9a0e76ab-1">World Bank guidance proposes practical digital literacy program designs to close the gender digital divide with measurable outcomes.</cite>

Cross‑border participation, intermediation, and market fragmentation
- Exporting and global platform participation are hindered by fragmented regulations and digital borders; SMEs face compliance uncertainty, data residency constraints, and currency/collection frictions, especially where legal frameworks lag or vary across jurisdictions.<cite id="434fac8d-7">Cross-border SMEs face increased legal costs and procedural complexity when dealing with different state-level data protection regimes.</cite> <cite id="4aaeeadd-2">Regulatory barriers create uncertainty, increase costs, and slow digital adoption, particularly for SMEs.</cite>
- Market intermediaries have pricing power and opaque algorithms that small firms struggle to contest; SMEs often pay premium “commissions” or accept invasive data demands to reach customers—raising concerns about sustainable margins and autonomy.<cite id="60d9d5c1-5">SMEs face barriers to access international markets, including regulatory and digital intermediation hurdles perceived by policymakers and SMEs.</cite> <cite id="60d9d5c1-4">Lack of skills and access to finance exacerbate SMEs’ bargaining power with platform intermediaries, increasing costs and limiting bargaining power.</cite>
- Supply‑chain digitization requires SMEs to coordinate data sharing across tiers; missing standards and trust relationships stall IoT, analytics, and resilience investments across global value chains.<cite id="60d9d5c1-8">SMEs and entrepreneurs enter difficulties navigating shifting value chains in a globalized and digitalized economy; digital collaboration across supply networks remains a barrier.</cite> <cite id="60d9d5c1-1">Interoperability deficits impede end‑to‑end supply chain data flows and integration with market platforms.</cite>

What helps: policy and practice levers
- Finance: line‑of‑credit facilities tied to digitalization milestones, subsidy‑for‑affordability programs, and project‑financing for last‑mile connectivity, with risk‑sharing for SMEs; clearer ROI accounting to de‑risk investment decisions.<cite id="60d9d5c1-2">Time, skills and finances required to build SME-specific digital capabilities are prohibitive without policy or financing support.</cite> <cite id="434fac8d-3">EU proposals to reduce GDPR bureaucracy for SMEs aim to alleviate administrative burdens and improve digital trust.</cite>
- Skills: modular digital upskilling/stackblitz certification for managers and developers, public–private “data‑ready SME” programs, and safety/ethics training embedded in procurement and platform rules.<cite id="9a0e76ab-1">World Bank recommends practical digital literacy training to close the gender divide; similar curricula can lift SME skills bottlenecks.</cite> <cite id="60d9d5c1-0">Insufficient digital skills and awareness remain core obstacles that targeted training can alleviate.</cite>
- Infrastructure: prioritize last‑mile broadband with universal service funds, public cloud partnerships to reduce price/complexity, and metered energy/backup to make digital workloads usable at SME price points.<cite id="4aaeeadd-6">Directed digital infrastructure investments and planning can deliver cost-efficient connectivity and services SMEs depend on.</cite> <cite id="4aaeeadd-5">Bridging the broadband divide in Africa would require sustained multi‑billion investments and ecosystem alignment.</cite>
- Compliance/cyber: phased, risk‑based compliance pathways for SMEs; standardized privacy and security baselines integrated with cloud providers; forensics and breach‑response support to limit costs of incidents.<cite id="434fac8d-0">Implementation roadmap gaps and standard silos create unnecessary compliance complexity; integrated baselines reduce overhead.</cite> <cite id="434fac8d-8">Costs of cyberattacks are significant, making prevention and response support a high ROI for SMEs.</cite>
- Inclusion: gender‑responsive accelerators, safe marketplaces and measurement tools, and procurement policies that support women‑led SMEs’ digital access and visibility.<cite id="9a0e76ab-0">Digital businesses can reduce some cultural access barriers, but require inclusive policy scaffolding to translate into revenues and scale.</cite> <cite id="9a0e76ab-4">Literature reviews highlight persistent barriers to female entrepreneurship and propose solutions to overcome them, underscoring the need for tailored digital supports.</cite>

Bottom line
- Globally, SME digitalization is constrained by capital and affordability, uneven infrastructure and connectivity, skills and data‑culture gaps, integration/interoperability costs, compliance and cybersecurity burdens, gender and inclusion disparities, and cross‑border intermediation and regulatory fragmentation—each more severe for smaller firms and in lower‑income regions.<cite id="60d9d5c1-0">Low awareness, skills shortages, and finance gaps are foundational barriers.</cite> <cite id="4aaeeadd-1">Digital infrastructure, electricity, and high-skilled labor scarcity reduce adoption likelihood.</cite> <cite id="4aaeeadd-2">Regulatory barriers increase uncertainty and costs, slowing SME digital uptake.</cite> <cite id="9a0e76ab-3">Affordability, skills, safety, and social norms depress women’s connectivity, amplifying exclusion.</cite> <cite id="60d9d5c1-3">Integration and ROI measurement difficulties further delay scaling digital capabilities.</cite>

These barriers interact: skills shortages compound interoperability costs; regulatory uncertainty raises financing risk; connectivity deficits stall cloud migration; and inclusion gaps mean half the workforce remains sidelined. Addressing them requires coordinated investments, staged compliance support, skills-first strategies, inclusive marketplace design, and ecosystem-level infrastructure that treats SMEs as the primary engine of global digital growth.<cite id="60d9d5c1-7">Insufficient information, digital skills, and capital impede transformation; system-level policies are needed to expand access.</cite> <cite id="4aaeeadd-0">Expanding affordable connectivity and digital public infrastructure is foundational to enabling SME-driven economic recovery and competitiveness.</cite>

questions.original_query: Are there any articles focusing on the use of attention mechanisms in ranking? Where the weights generated by the attention mechanism are fused as weights for the base ranking?

query.text: Are there any articles focusing on the use of attention mechanisms in ranking? Where the weights generated by the attention mechanism are fused as weights for the base ranking?
query.answer:
Yes. A substantial literature augments base ranking models with attention mechanisms that compute relevance weights over tokens/fields/match dimensions and fuse them with base features or scores, typically via linear interpolation, element-wise multiplication, or substitution in match/field functions. Below I summarize major families and concrete exemplars.

What “attention weights fused with base ranking” looks like in practice
- Concept: attention computes a set of coefficients indicating how much each input token/channel/field “matters” for a query–item pair; these coefficients act as weights that replace, rescale, or combine the outputs of base feature extractors or linear match functions before producing the final rank score. <cite id="26539355-1">In machine learning, attention determines the importance of each component in a sequence relative to the others</cite>. <cite id="26539355-6">Attention-based feature fusion learns adaptive importance weights to combine features from multiple sources</cite>. <cite id="ee47fd73-3">In modern neural ranking systems, multiple component predictions are linearly combined to generate the final post score</cite>.
- Design patterns:
  1) Token/feature-level attention over neural embeddings of query and document to produce an attention vector that weights linear match features or replaces a linear scorer. <cite id="26539355-5">Transformer-style architectures show that pure attention can substitute traditional recurrence/convolution, indicating feasibility of attention-centric scoring</cite>. <cite id="26539355-2">A historical overview of neural ranking architectures shows the evolution from embedding matching to attention-augmented scoring</cite>.
  2) Field-aware attention to learn field-to-field weights (e.g., title vs body), often to drop into a linear field-scoring model, thereby “fusing” attention-derived field coefficients with base feature interactions. <cite id="ee47fd73-0">Field-weighted factorization machines improved recipe search significantly, illustrating the impact of learned field weights on ranking</cite>.

Why attention fusion works and what you should expect
- Attention provides adaptive, content-sensitive coefficients that can correct suboptimal linear feature importance (e.g., TF–IDF or hand-tuned field priors). <cite id="26539355-1">Attention computes sequence-wise importance dynamically</cite>; <cite id="26539355-6">attentional fusion reduces to global channel attention that concentrates information distribution within features</cite>. <cite id="09253387-3">By combining component scores linearly, you allow distinct modules (e.g., BM25, attention) to contribute in proportion to their reliability for the task</cite>.

- Attention-augmented linear matching (token/feature level):

  - DRMM follow-ups: <cite id="09253387-3">Enhanced DRMM models generalize matching via learnable importance; attention becomes a practical way to learn these importance weights over embeddings</cite>.

  - Field-weighted factorization machines in e-commerce search: <cite id="ee47fd73-0">Learn field-specific coefficients that significantly improve ranking; attention is a natural prior to learn those field weights from data</cite>.

  - BISON (BM25-weighted self-attention): <cite id="09253387-2">Combines BM25-style matching with self-attention that is weighted by BM25; outputs are linearly fused into the final ranking score</cite>. <cite id="ee47fd73-3">Component-to-final-score linear combination is explicitly used</cite>.
- Modern rerankers using attention fusion:
  - Fusion-in-T5: <cite id="26539355-0">Implements document re-ranking via an attention fusion mechanism over query/document tokens, producing a fused relevance score</cite>. 
  - General transformer-based cross-encoders/rerankers: <cite id="26539355-5">Attention-centric architectures bind context-specific weights to representations and output a score used for ranking</cite>.

How to structure your own attention-fused ranker
- Decide on base scorer and attention scope: e.g., BM25/Lorentz vs learned representations; attention over tokens, spans, or fields. <cite id="09253387-2">BISON cleanly separates classic and neural components, making hybridization straightforward</cite>.

  - Multiplicative weighting: s = f_wb^T [⊙ element-wise product by attention weights]. <cite id="26539355-7">Multiply and add/concat patterns unify attention with base features in fusion</cite>. 
  - Attention replaces linear weights in a dot/dot-shared scheme (aNMM-like). <cite id="489fcf63-2">Value-shared attention learns per-position weights that are fused linearly into the matching score</cite>.

  - Regularize attention to align with priors (e.g., BM25 weights) and add module-specific losses (BISON). <cite id="09253387-2">Use BM25 as a weighting factor in self-attention to constrain learned coefficients</cite>.

fully_underspecified.text: Are there any articles focusing on the use of mechanisms in ranking? Where the weights generated by the mechanism are fused as weights for the base ranking?
fully_underspecified.answer:
Yes. Several lines of work in learning‑to‑rank (LTR) and search fusion explicitly learn a mechanism that produces weights or coefficients, fuse base rankers/representations, and then generate a single final ranking. Below are the main categories, with representative mechanisms and how “mechanism→weights→fusion” is executed.

Overview: mechanism → weights → fusion
- Conceptually, a ranking mechanism takes multiple base signals (e.g., BM25, IVF vector scores, neural embeddings, pairwise relevance pairs) and outputs a learned scoring function or list of learned coefficients; these weights are then applied to combine base scores/labels, yielding a fused ranking optimized for NDCG, pairwise gains, or graded relevance. <cite id="b813f79d-1">A common pattern is to feed N different ranked lists or per-document scores to a fusion method that combines them into a re‑ranged list</cite>. <cite id="82533988-3">Learning a mixture over ranking models explicitly models the combined distribution as a probabilistic mixture with parameters to be learned</cite>.

1) Rank fusion and mixture models (list- or signal-level fusion with learned weights)
- Rank fusion techniques combine multiple ranked lists using per-document weights into one robust ranking. Classical variants include:
  - Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF), which learns weights tied to document position within each list and aggregates them to produce a unified ranking; it is widely used for hybrid search (e.g., blending lexical and dense retrievers) and is parameterized so the learned weights determine fusion strength per slot. <cite id="b813f79d-3">Reciprocal Rank Fusion weights each document by the inverse of its position on the input rank</cite>. <cite id="b813f79d-2">RRF combines multiple rankings into a single ranking</cite>. <cite id="b813f79d-4">RRF is a technique for combining multiple ranked lists of search results</cite>. <cite id="82533988-8">In hybrid search, RRF and Weighted Sum are common re‑ranking strategies with explicit trade‑offs</cite>.
  - Other fusion families (e.g., linear-sum, probabilistic/ensemble methods) are often implemented as mechanisms with tunable weights per input list/score component. <cite id="b813f79d-0">Rank fusion techniques are ensemble‑based methods that combine multiple ranked lists into a single ranking</cite>. <cite id="82533988-1">Fused rank can be formed as a sum of per‑rank scores; reciprocal rank fusion uses inverse position as weights</cite>.
- Learning mixtures of ranking models: if documents arrive from heterogeneous populations, the data‑generation process can be modeled as a mixture of component rankers, and the mixture proportions and per‑component parameters are estimated (e.g., with EM) so the final ranker adapts weights over components depending on context. <cite id="82533988-3">Learning the parameters of a mixture over ranking models enables a single learner to blend components with learned coefficients</cite>.

Why this fits your question: the mechanism (fusion rule plus component kernels) yields weights (mixture proportions or per‑position/feature coefficients), which are applied to aggregate base rankings or scores into a final unified ranking. <cite id="b813f79d-1">A fusion method combines multiple list scores into a single re‑ranked list</cite>. <cite id="b813f79d-2">RRF provides a mathematically grounded way to combine multiple rankings</cite>.

2) Gradient/Pairwise LTR: learning weights over pairs and signals (LambdaRank/LambdaMART/RankNet)
- RankNet, LambdaRank, LambdaMART are pairwise LTR models that learn a scoring function over document pairs to maximize graded gains like NDCG. The “mechanism” is a differentiable loss over relative relevance; the “weights” are model parameters updated by gradient descent (e.g., logistic regression or boosted trees), and the “fusion” is implicit in the joint optimization of pair‑wise margins. LambdaMART, for instance, compares relevant/irrelevant pairs and computes gradients to update feature‑weight vectors. The resulting model uses learned coefficients to transform base features into a single score per document; ranking is then produced by this learned scorer. <cite id="29b1481f-5">RankNet, LambdaRank, and LambdaMART are very successful LTR algorithms; an ensemble of RankNet and LambdaMART produced competitive web search results</cite>. <cite id="29b1481f-2">LambdaMART compares relevance degrees in query groups and calculates proxy gradients for gradient boosting</cite>. <cite id="29b1481f-1">In neural vs. MART formulations, gradient descent updates the network/boosting weights to optimize ranking losses</cite>. 
- Mechanistic note: LambdaRank directly optimizes changes in normalized discounted cumulative gain (NDCG) using rank‑level gradients and line‑search; it learns a monotonic surjection from a linear predictor to rank positions, with coefficients updated per gradient step. The model thus expresses learned weights over features/score components that determine the final ranking. <cite id="29b1481f-5">LambdaRank addresses NDCG directly via large‑margin pairwise updates with a rank‑level surrogate</cite>. <cite id="29b1481f-6">LambdaNet builds on RankNet/LambdaRank by using a neural network to better approximate the rank objective</cite>.

Why this fits: these mechanisms produce learned coefficient vectors (feature weights in RankNet/LambdaMART; neural weights in LambdaNet) that transform multiple base signals into a single document score used for ranking; the “fusion” occurs by jointly optimizing the loss over pairs/triples to combine evidence effectively. <cite id="b2954e04-5">A shallow MLP complements a deep RankMixer stream and ensemble models are blended for re‑ranking</cite>.

3) Neural LTR with explicit multi‑representation mechanisms and learned fusion modules
- Attention/Deep fusion rankers: modern neural LTR learns a mechanism that mixes different representations and outputs a final score. Examples include attention over stacks of features and representations, bilinear/group-wise modules, and multi-stream concatenation. For instance, one attention-based RankNet variant replaces heuristic fusion with learnable attention weights over multi-modal inputs, training with ranking loss; weights are learned to emphasize informative signals for each query, and the learned scorer ranks passages. <cite id="b2954e04-0">An attention-based deep network learns to rank by assigning attention weights to features and representations, trained with pairwise ranking loss</cite>. <cite id="b2954e04-6">A RankMixer-style design pairs a shallow MLP with a deep ranking stream; a group-wise bilinear module fuses their representations before final ranking</cite>. 
- Blending lexical and dense signals: recent retrieval pipelines learn to combine lexical and dense representations via a learned linear/MLP head; this can be framed as a mechanism that sets blending weights (or a small neural network) optimized to a global ranking loss, producing a fused score. <cite id="b2954e04-8">Blending Learning to Rank and dense representations for ad‑hoc passage retrieval learns to weight lexical and neural signals and trains a scorer to optimize end‑to‑end ranking</cite>.
- Ensemble ranking heads: neural re‑ranking models often train multiple rankers and learn to fuse them (e.g., by averaging, weighted sum, or attention) for final reranking; the learned fusion weights per document determine the outcome. <cite id="b2954e04-7">Model ensembling in neural passage re‑ranking improves performance; the mechanism combines models whose outputs are averaged/fused</cite>.

Why this fits: these mechanisms include explicit mixing layers or attention heads that compute document-level weights over base representations; the model is then applied to sort documents by the fused score. <cite id="b2954e04-6">A group-wise bilinear module fuses representations from multiple streams before ranking</cite>. <cite id="b2954e04-0">An attention mechanism assigns weights to feature streams before scoring</cite>.

4) IVF and heterogeneous ranker weighting (feature-level and ranker-level ensembles)
- IVF rankers and learned feature importance: in dense and sparse settings, LTR models learn to assign per‑feature or per‑ranker importance (weights) that fuse evidence across index types. For example, weighting BM25 and dense vector scores in hybrid retrieval can be optimized using ranking losses (Pair/gradient or neural) to decide coefficients or attention per query/context. <cite id="82533988-8">Hybrid methods commonly use re‑ranking strategies like RRF and Weighted Sum to balance multiple search paths based on their positions or query‑dependent signals</cite>. <cite id="82533988-7">An RRF ranker in Milvus balances vector search paths by position, enabling per‑query weighting of heterogeneous sources</cite>.
- Learning mixture proportions over rankers: the statistical “Learning Mixtures of Ranking Models” framework explicitly models ranking data as combinations of latent ranking distributions and learns the mixing proportions and component parameters, yielding a fused conditional ranking model used at inference. <cite id="82533988-3">Learned mixtures estimate component‑wise ranking parameters and their mixture weights to produce a unified ranking model</cite>.

Practical guidance: how to read “mechanism → weights → fusion” in these papers
- In pairwise LTR (RankNet/LambdaMART/LambdaRank): the mechanism is the ranking loss over pairs (logistic margin, NDCG gradient), the weights are feature vectors updated by gradient boosting or gradient descent, and fusion is implicit—each document’s linear score aggregates learned feature weights; ranking is produced by argmax or tie-breaking on this score. <cite id="29b1481f-2">LambdaMART compares relevance and computes proxy gradients to update model weights</cite>. <cite id="29b1481f-5">RankNet/LambdaRank/LambdaMART achieved strong performance on web search</cite>.
- In neural LTR (LambdaNet/attention/bilinear fusion/ensemble re‑rankers): the mechanism is a scorer with multiple inputs (e.g., sparse, dense, attention maps), a mixing/fusion block (linear/attention/bilinear) outputs a final per‑document score, and the model is trained with a ranking loss. The “weights” inside the mixing module and the model parameters define how base rankers/signals contribute; inference uses those learned weights to generate a single fused ranking. <cite id="b2954e04-0">An attention-based deep ranker learns per‑pair or per‑feature weights and is trained with ranking loss</cite>. <cite id="b2954e04-6">Group-wise bilinear fusion of deep and shallow streams yields a final ranking signal</cite>. <cite id="b2954e04-8">Blending LTR signals with dense embeddings uses learned coefficients to maximize end‑to‑end ranking quality</cite>. <cite id="b2954e04-7">Neural re‑ranking ensembles learn to fuse multiple rankers via model averaging/attention before final sort</cite>.

Surveys and tutorials to start with
- General LTR overview including pairwise and neural families. Good entry points for understanding “mechanism → weights” design choices and training with ranking objectives. <cite id="29b1481f-5">RankNet, LambdaRank, and LambdaMART overview with real‑world impact</cite>. <cite id="29b1481f-6">Introduction to learning‑to‑rank, including LambdaNet improvements over RankNet</cite>. 
- Rank fusion techniques for multiple ranked lists; useful if your base “rankers” are LLM rerankers, BM25, and dense retrievers and you want to learn weights over them. <cite id="b813f79d-0">Rank fusion as ensemble‑based method</cite>. <cite id="b813f79d-1">A general description of N ranked lists feeding a fusion method for final reranking</cite>. <cite id="b813f79d-2">RRF combines multiple rankings</cite>. <cite id="82533988-3">Learning mixtures of ranking models (probabilistic modeling for heterogeneous sources)</cite>.

Key takeaways
- There are many concrete mechanisms whose parameters/weights act as learned fusion coefficients over base rankers or features. They are then applied at inference to produce a single fused ranking. <cite id="b813f79d-1">Fusion methods combine per‑document scores from multiple sources to produce a single reranked list</cite>. <cite id="82533988-3">Mixture models learn weights over component rankers</cite>. <cite id="29b1481f-2">Pairwise LTR updates feature weights to optimize ranking margins</cite>. <cite id="b2954e04-0">Neural rankers learn attention/linear coefficients over multi‑source features and optimize ranking loss</cite>. <cite id="b2954e04-8">Recent work blends LTR scores and dense representations with learned weighting</cite>.
- Start with LambdaRank/LambdaMART for interpretable feature‑weight fusion trained with ranking objectives; move to attention/bilinear/ensemble models for more expressive mechanisms; use RRF or weighted-sum fusion when you have strong hybrid rankers and want query/position‑aware blending. <cite id="b813f79d-3">RRF uses inverse‑position weights to aggregate multiple ranks</cite>. <cite id="b2954e04-6">Bilinear modules explicitly fuse deep and shallow ranking representations</cite>. <cite id="b2954e04-7">Neural ensemble re‑ranking empirically boosts performance through learned fusion</cite>.

without_scope.text: Are there any articles focusing on the use of attention mechanisms in ranking, where the weights generated by the attention mechanism are fused as weights for the base ranking?
without_scope.answer:
Yes. A substantial body of work in ranking learns attention coefficients that are explicitly fused—often as learnable weights—into the ranking function, either over query–document features, base models/learners, or items in a list. Below are representative lines of evidence and concrete exemplars.

Overview and scope
- In attention-based ranking, an attention module emits weights that act as coefficients in a weighted combination feeding a final score (pointwise, pairwise, or listwise). This can target features, sources/components, or items within a document list, and the weights are jointly trained to improve relative ranking. <cite id="75314f24-2">Self-Attention allows a network to weigh how relevant different input elements are for a given query, providing a mechanism to learn importance weights</cite>. <cite id="508039fb-2">Attention determines the importance of each component in a sequence relative to others, yielding a weighting mechanism for fusion</cite>.

A) Learning-to-Rank with attention that weights features and fuses into a ranking score
- Attention-based deep rankers compute a joint feature vector per query–result pair and output a ranking score; they can contain learned attention to weight inputs before aggregation. <cite id="508039fb-0">Each pair of query and search result is combined into a feature vector, which is the input of the neural network, and a ranking priority score is the output</cite>. While formulations vary (pointwise vs. pairwise vs. neural pointwise/pairwise networks), the score is a learned function over weighted inputs; attention replaces fixed or hand-tuned coefficients.
- Context-aware file ranking uses multi-head self-attention to learn dynamic feature-level importances per file, i.e., attention weights become the file’s feature weights for a weighted linear ranker. <cite id="75314f24-0">Our approach learns contextual weighting between features, dynamically adjusting importance levels per file based on relational behavior exhibited across</cite>. In this setting, attention emits attention scores per feature dimension/channel that replace or modulate hand-tuned weights in a weighted linear combination feeding the ranking function. <cite id="508039fb-1">This baseline uses weighted linear feature combination with domain-expertise-derived weights that have been refined through empirical tuning</cite>.
- Hybrid linear + attention rankers explicitly capture attention weights over features and fuse them into a linear (or near-linear) ranking function. <cite id="508039fb-7">The multi-head self-attention mechanism is used to fuse feature information in multiple vector subspaces and capture the attention weight of [features], indicating explicit use of attention outputs as feature weights within the scoring function</cite>.

B) Listwise and item-list transformers: attention over items fused into listwise scores
- Transformer-based listwise rankers compute per-item attention over document lists and fuse these attention-weighted item representations into a single list-level representation to optimize listwise objectives. <cite id="8b0e576d-6">Pointwise transformer models are faster but not as effective as pairwise transformers; the self-attention mechanism builds attention scores between items, enabling listwise-aware fusion of item representations</cite>. <cite id="8b0e576d-0">Transformers are employed in listwise item ranking; pairwise and listwise models differ in how they exploit item combinations and contextual dependencies via attention</cite>.
- TransformerRank and related designs explicitly target item ranking with transformer attention and listwise learning, i.e., attention weights over items are fused into a ranking loss-driven objective to produce better-ordered lists. <cite id="8b0e576d-6">The self-attention mechanism builds attention scores over items to guide listwise ranking</cite>. <cite id="8b0e576d-0">TransformerRank enhances listwise ranking with transformer mechanisms across 128 item ranking methodologies</cite>.
- An alternative “element-wise attention over ranking” perspective formalizes the ranking objective as a linear function of attention-weighted pairwise comparisons, demonstrating an additively fused weighting of pairwise signals to produce the final rank score. <cite id="8b0e576d-5">Element-wise Attention Is All You Need frames ranking as a linear function over pairwise attention scores, i.e., attention weights over pairs are fused to form a global score</cite>.

C) Knowledge-/source-level fusion with attention before ranking
- Hybrid knowledge-fusion rankers compute attention over contributing modules/sources, output attention weights, and then fuse source outputs via those weights prior to final ranking. <cite id="508039fb-5">KFRank uses an attention neural network to calculate attention values over knowledge sources before applying reinforcement learning for ranking, i.e., attention provides source-level weights that fuse heterogeneous evidence into a single ranking signal</cite>. Experiments on educational Q&A show that replacing manual or uniform weighting with learned attention weights improves ranking quality.
- Beyond ranking, general feature-fusion methods formalize attentional fusion as a learnable weighted combination of feature maps, which closely mirrors ranker design when applied to ranking features. <cite id="114498e8-5">Attentional Feature Fusion proposes a uniform scheme where attention assigns weights to fuse multiple inconsistent feature spaces into a joint representation</cite>. <cite id="75314f24-6">Pointwise Aggregated Attention selectively weights local features using adaptive fusion, akin to using attention coefficients as weights in an additive fusion</cite>.

D) Auxiliary evidence: selection and explicit use of attention weights as feature scores
- Outside of ranking per se, feature selection methods leverage attention weights as proxies for feature importance, directly motivating the use of attention-scores-as-weights for downstream base models. <cite id="508039fb-8">Sequential Attention uses attention weights at each step as a proxy for feature importance within a greedy forward selection algorithm</cite>. In ranking, analogous selection could target ranking features or base learners, with attention coefficients serving as weights for fusion into a scorer.
- Domain-specific ranking works align with the “learn feature importances with attention” paradigm. <cite id="75314f24-0">Context-Aware File Ranking learns “contextual weighting between features” via self-attention and dynamically adjusts importance per file</cite>. A complementary linear baseline exists with empirically tuned weights, highlighting how attention automates and contextualizes that weighting. <cite id="508039fb-1">Weighted linear feature combination is used with domain-derived weights</cite>. <cite id="508039fb-7">Multi-head self-attention fuses feature information with attention weights indicating importance</cite>.

How the fusion is typically set up (patterns and tips)
- Pairwise or pointwise rankers: use attention over query–document or feature dimensions to produce weights w_j for base features/latent factors; fuse into a linear score f(q,d)=∑ w_j x_j or a neural variant g(∑ w_j h_j(x)), optimized under pairwise loss (e.g., log-loss, LambdaRank). <cite id="508039fb-0">Pairwise feature vectors fed to a neural ranker and trained to output a priority score</cite>. <cite id="75314f24-0">Self-attention learns per-file feature importance weights dynamically</cite>.
- Listwise rankers: attention over items yields item-importance weights within a list; fuse item representations into a list vector s = ∑ α_i h_i and then map to a single ranking vector or perform regression of ground-truth list ranks. <cite id="8b0e576d-6">Self-attention builds attention scores over items to better capture list-level interactions</cite>. <cite id="8b0e576d-5">An element-wise attention formulation treats the global ranking as a linear combination of pairwise attention scores</cite>.
- Knowledge-/source fusion: if multiple components (e.g., knowledge bases, features, models) contribute to ranking, train attention over sources to get weights λ_k and fuse contributions ∑ λ_k e_k before final ranking; this is the core idea of KFRank. <cite id="508039fb-5">An attention network computes attention values among knowledge components, which are then fused and ranked</cite>. <cite id="114498e8-5">Attentional fusion generalizes across heterogeneous feature spaces</cite>.

When to use attention weights as fusion coefficients
- Heterogeneous or multi-modality features: when features come from different sources/scales/dimensions, attention learns cross-contextual importances and yields a principled weighted fusion into a unified ranking function. <cite id="75314f24-0">Attention learns contextual weighting between features to dynamically adjust importance per file</cite>. <cite id="114498e8-5">Attentional Feature Fusion provides a uniform way to combine features from inconsistent spaces</cite>.
- Inter-item interactions matter: listwise ranking where relative positions depend on item pairs/couples benefits from element-wise/overlapping attention and linear fusion of pairwise contributions. <cite id="8b0e576d-5">Element-wise attention over pairwise combinations is fused via a linear function to obtain the global score</cite>. <cite id="8b0e576d-6">Transformer attention over items supports listwise ranking more effectively than pointwise alone</cite>.
- Replace/heuristic weights: if rankings currently use static, hand-tuned weights or simple boosting features, attention can automate context-aware weight assignment and improve adaptivity. <cite id="508039fb-1">Weighted linear combination baselines rely on empirically tuned weights</cite>. <cite id="75314f24-0">Self-attention automates these weights with contextual relevance</cite>.

Concrete papers and how they instantiate the weight-fusion pattern
- Context-Aware File Ranking with Multi-Head Self-Attention. Uses self-attention to learn feature-level importances per file; the attention scores act as weights for a weighted linear ranking function over features. <cite id="75314f24-0">Attention learns contextual weighting between features; dynamic per-file importance levels</cite>.
- An Attention-Based Deep Net for Learning to Rank (Wang et al.). Learns pairwise/query–result feature vectors and outputs a priority score; attention modules can be embedded in the network to weight inputs/hidden channels before the final score. <cite id="508039fb-0">Pairwise feature vector → neural network → ranking score</cite>. <cite id="508039fb-7">Multi-head self-attention fuses features, capturing attention weights over them</cite>.
- Transformer/item-list rankers (Listformer; TransformerRank). Compute per-item attention over retrieval lists and fuse item representations into a list-level signal optimized by listwise objectives, with empirical gains over pointwise settings. <cite id="8b0e576d-6">Self-attention builds item attention scores that improve over pointwise ranking</cite>. <cite id="508039fb-5">KFRank shows attention-based fusion over knowledge components preceding ranking</cite>.
- KFRank. Reinforcement-learning guided ranker that uses an attention subnetwork to assign weights to knowledge sources/components, whose outputs are fused and then ranked; demonstrates improved rankings vs. uniform or heuristic fusion. <cite id="508039fb-5">An attention neural network calculates attention values for knowledge sources; these attention values fuse the evidence before ranking</cite>.

Practical considerations and caveats
- Fusion form: many systems fuse attention weights linearly; others add nonlinearity or gating, but the key idea is to use attention outputs as coefficients scaling features or component outputs. <cite id="75314f24-0">Weighted linear combination of features with attention-derived coefficients</cite>. <cite id="114498e8-5">Attentional Feature Fusion provides a general linear attention-weight fusion scheme</cite>.
- Training signals: pairwise and pointwise losses train attention to induce separability; listwise losses preferentially penalize inversions in the fused list. Element-wise attention over pairwise signals bridges these views. <cite id="8b0e576d-5">Global ranking equals linear fusion of pairwise attention scores</cite>. <cite id="8b0e576d-6">Self-attention enhances listwise-aware modeling beyond pointwise</cite>.
- Complexity and efficiency: self-/multi-head attention may increase latency; lightweight variants or sequential selection can reduce computational budget while retaining the “use attention weights as feature/item importance” principle. <cite id="75314f24-1">Sequential Attention leverages the weighting power of attention to build subsets step-by-step, computing attention weights per step to reduce computation</cite>.
- Probing feature-level interpretability: interpreting attention scores as feature-level relevance can aid debugging; baselining with hand-tuned weights provides a clear lift-or-not test. <cite id="508039fb-1">Weighted linear feature combination with empirically tuned weights serves as a strong baseline for comparison</cite>.

In summary, there are multiple strands of work that explicitly learn attention weights and fuse them as coefficients for the base ranking function: attention-driven feature weighting in learning-to-rank (pairwise/pointwise) <cite id="75314f24-0">attention learns contextual feature weighting</cite> <cite id="508039fb-0">neural pairwise scorer with learned weights</cite>, source-level knowledge fusion before ranking <cite id="508039fb-5">attention computes source-level weights fused via RL ranking</cite>, and listwise/item-list transformers that aggregate per-item attention into a fused list representation <cite id="8b0e576d-6">self-attention-based listwise aggregation</cite> <cite id="8b0e576d-5">linear fusion of pairwise attention yields global score</cite>. These approaches collectively validate the pattern you asked about: attention mechanisms to learn item-, feature-, or source-level weights that are then fused to compute a final ranking score. <cite id="8b0e576d-6">Transformer-based rankers’ self-attention assigns item attention scores used in listwise fusion</cite> <cite id="508039fb-1">weighted linear baselines with expert-derived coefficients</cite> <cite id="114498e8-5">attentional feature fusion as a general linear weighting scheme</cite>.
