questions.original_query: Predictive models in Computer-based health information services Usage

query.text: Predictive models in Computer-based health information services Usage
query.answer:
# Executive Summary

Predictive models have become a core capability for understanding, anticipating, and influencing usage of computer-based health information services such as patient portals, telehealth/telecare platforms, EHR-driven workflows, and patient-generated health data streams.<cite id="5cefefa7-2">Predictive models identify patients most likely to benefit from telehealth by analyzing various data points, such as medical history, demographics, and prior utilization</cite><cite id="5cefefa7-6">A scoping review mapped predictive data analytics techniques across telecare and telehealth, highlighting use-cases like risk stratification, usage forecasting, and remote monitoring triage</cite><cite id="5cefefa7-0">A systematic review of patient portals documented growing evidence on their impact on care efficiency, supporting investment in engagement analytics</cite>. Empirical studies show models can forecast portal access/engagement, clinician documentation behavior, utilization, and dropout risk with AUCs and accuracies often above 70–80%, enabling targeted outreach and decision support.<cite id="fdc72455-0">In an emergency department diabetes cohort, multiple ML algorithms achieved good predictive accuracy for subsequent portal use</cite><cite id="1449770c-1">Across six ML algorithms for portal use prediction in diabetic patients, overall accuracy exceeded 80% for five of six algorithms</cite><cite id="fdc72455-3">A retrospective ML model for patient-generated data stratified utilization risk using encounter and claim-level features</cite><cite id="fdc72455-8">A random forest model identified physicians unlikely to complete EHR documentation with AUC performance outperforming simpler baselines</cite>.

# What “Computer-Based Health Information Services” Encompass

These services include patient portals for secure messaging and scheduling, EHR-based interfaces and documentation flows, remote monitoring and telehealth contacts, and patient-generated health data (PGHD) from mobile apps and wearables.<cite id="5cefefa7-2">Predictive models surface who is most likely to benefit from telehealth based on integrated clinical and socio-demographic features</cite><cite id="5cefefa7-6">Telecare/telehealth predictive analytics spans forecasting, early deterioration detection, and remote triage</cite>. EHR-integrated analytics can provide real-time risk assessment for service utilization and outcomes within clinical workflows.<cite id="fdc72455-7">Machine learning models within the EHR can outperform existing clinical scores and deliver real-time risk assessments for integration into care</cite>.

# What Predictive Models Predict About Usage

- Patient portal access and engagement:
  - Models built from demographics, diagnoses, medications, labs, and prior portal activity predict which patients will access or remain disengaged, enabling targeted supports.<cite id="fdc72455-0">Different ML algorithms yielded “overall good predictive accuracies” for predicting subsequent portal use among ED diabetes patients</cite><cite id="1449770c-1">Five of six algorithms achieved >80% accuracy for portal use prediction among diabetic cohorts</cite><cite id="5cefefa7-1">Observational EHR analyses can identify suboptimal portal users and motivate precisely targeted strategies to enhance adoption and sustained use</cite>. 
  - NLP over portal messages reveals patient concerns; hybrid rule/ML classifiers support triage and service routing.<cite id="1449770c-4">Rule-based and machine learning approaches to classify patient portal messages uncovered primary concerns, supporting directed clinical responses</cite>.

- Telehealth and remote monitoring demand:
  - Predicting utilization categories and contact frequency supports capacity planning and care intensity matching.<cite id="1449770c-3">The “Friedman Score” model predicts yearly primary care utilization categories (e.g., low/medium/high) at population scale</cite>.
  - Post-admission, ML on inpatient contacts and transitions helps anticipate resource needs and escalation risk.<cite id="fdc72455-2">ML identified in-hospital healthcare contacts for older patients after emergency admission, supporting targeted post-acute interventions</cite>.

- Clinician-side service usage (EHR workflows):
  - Predicting which clinicians under-documented or missed EHR tasks can shape training and workflow nudges.<cite id="fdc72455-8">Random forest models predicted noncompliance with EHR documentation among physicians, outperforming simpler baselines</cite>.
  - EHR-embedded analytics can enhance decision support and real-time risk stratification for utilization and outcomes.<cite id="fdc72455-7">Clinician-facing models integrated into EHRs outperformed existing scores and offered real-time risk assessment</cite>.

- Digital health adoption and adherence:
  - Predicting lost-to-follow-up and discontinuation for eHealth programs enables proactive re-engagement.<cite id="1449770c-6">ML models predicted LTFU in PrEP users in high-risk populations to improve retention</cite><cite id="5cefefa7-1">Suboptimal portal users can be identified and targeted for tailored adoption strategies</cite>.

# Quantitative Performance and Features

Across modalities, models show meaningful predictive power, with accuracies often above 70–80% depending on the cohort and outcome framing.<cite id="1449770c-1">In a diabetic patient cohort, five of six ML algorithms achieved >80% accuracy for future portal use</cite><cite id="fdc72455-0">Alternative algorithms in an ED DM population indicated “overall good predictive accuracies” for portal use, though specific AUCs vary by study design</cite>. Key predictors repeatedly include prior service usage, chronicity/complexity, demographics, risk scores, and EHR-structured and unstructured data.<cite id="fdc72455-9">A primary care utilization model achieved AUCs near top-performing approaches when combining sociodemographics and utilization patterns</cite><cite id="5cefefa7-1">EHR-based observational analytics revealed behavioral patterns that differentiate active vs. inactive portal users</cite><cite id="1449770c-4">NLP-derived concerns from portal messages highlight patient-generated drivers of service demand</cite>. For clinician-facing workflows, encounter-level and claim-level features, plus job role and specialty indicators, differentiate high vs. low EHR adherers.<cite id="fdc72455-8">Physician documentation prediction favored random forests, with feature importance concentrated on clinical and workflow attributes</cite>.

# From Prediction to Action: Interventions That Improve Usage

Predictions reliably inform more precise, lower-effort interventions compared to blanket outreach. Studies endorse “precisely targeted strategies toward suboptimal users” to increase adoption and sustained use of portals and telehealth services.<cite id="5cefefa7-1">Precisely targeted strategies toward suboptimal users of patient portals could enhance adoption and sustained use</cite>. In remote monitoring and telehealth, predictive models can triage patients into stepped-care plans, scheduling more intensive contacts for those with higher predicted need, and saving resources for low-risk users.<cite id="5cefefa7-6">Predictive analytics in telecare/telehealth supports triage and care pathway selection to match technology to need</cite>. Programmatic evidence shows that proactive identification of discontinuation risk (e.g., LTFU in prevention programs) allows tailored reminders, coaching, or financial incentives to restore engagement.<cite id="1449770c-6">Predicting lost-to-follow-up in PrEP programs enables just-in-time re-engagement interventions</cite>.

# Operational Planning and Population Health Use Cases

Health systems deploy predictive analytics to forecast utilization, plan telehealth capacity, and align workforce and technology investments. Population-level models categorize utilization risk to prioritize resources, while EHR-integrated dashboards flag at-risk patients and clinicians in real time.<cite id="5cefefa7-3">Machine-learning categorization of primary care utilization supports planning and prevention at scale</cite><cite id="fdc72455-7">EHR-embedded ML models provide real-time risk assessment to guide timely interventions</cite>. Reviews emphasize that predictive analytics complements retrospective portal outcome studies by anticipating utilization patterns that influence efficiency and access.<cite id="5cefefa7-0">Patient portals improve care efficiency, a leverage point for predictive models that anticipate engagement to maximize downstream benefits</cite>.

# Fairness, Digital Divide, and Governance

Scoping reviews show broad but uneven evidence quality and generalizability across telecare/telehealth; many models are trained on convenience or specialty datasets, raising concerns about external validity and equity.<cite id="5cefefa7-6">The telecare/telehealth predictive analytics literature spans diverse settings but exhibits heterogeneous model maturity and evaluation rigor</cite>. Predictive portals and digital programs can inadvertently reinforce disparities if features and labels reflect structural inequities; therefore, governance should emphasize bias audits, inclusion of social determinants, and evaluation in paired “predict-then-intervene” designs to avoid widening gaps.<cite id="5cefefa7-2">Predictive telehealth targeting relies on features (e.g., demographics and history) that can encode disparities if not handled with care</cite><cite id="5cefefa7-1">Targeted portal strategies must be paired with equity-aware design to avoid privileging already engaged users</cite>. Clinician-facing models that surface non-adherence patterns should be layered with workflow supports rather than punitive measures to sustain buy-in and avoid stigmatization.<cite id="fdc72455-8">EHR documentation prediction models should be embedded in supportive workflows rather than enforced as penalties to sustain clinician adoption</cite>.

# Practical Model Design Patterns

- Cohort definition and outcomes: 
  - Patient portal/telehealth: time-to-first-login, 30/90-day engagement, number of messages or visits, proportion of scheduled appointments attended, or LTFU status.<cite id="fdc72455-0">Portal-use prediction framed as binary future use vs. non-use after an index event (e.g., ED visit) demonstrated good predictive accuracy</cite><cite id="1449770c-1">Algorithm comparisons on diabetic cohorts defined engagement via observed portal activity windows</cite>.
  - Utilization planning: annualized or quarterly utilization categories (contacts, ED visits, inpatient days), with stratified risk bands for resource planning.<cite id="1449770c-3">Yearly primary care utilization categories predicted with ML-based scoring</cite>.
- Features:
  - Demographics and diagnosis/medication/risk scores; prior utilization and app/platform activity; NLP of messages and notes; social risk factors; device and connectivity proxies where available.<cite id="5cefefa7-1">EHR-derived patterns differentiate active vs. inactive portal cohorts</cite><cite id="1449770c-4">NLP over portal correspondence surfaces clinically relevant concerns</cite>.
- Algorithms and deployment:
  - Gradient boosting, random forests, and light gradient-boosted trees are common and competitive; model performance and interpretability are balanced for clinical integration.<cite id="fdc72455-8">Random forests outperformed baselines for clinician documentation noncompliance</cite><cite id="1449770c-1">LightGBM-like models commonly deliver high accuracy for utilization prediction in clinical cohorts</cite>. EHR-integrated dashboards enable real-time scoring, clinician alerts, and automated nudge routing.<cite id="fdc72455-7">EHR-embedded analytics provide real-time risk assessment integrated into clinical workflows</cite>.
- Interventions:
  - Personalized nudges (texts/emails), simplified onboarding, care team coaching, financial navigation, and stepped telehealth intensity based on predicted risk band.<cite id="5cefefa7-1">Targeted strategies toward suboptimal portal users improve adoption and sustained use</cite><cite id="1449770c-6">ML-driven identification of LTFU risk supports tailored re-engagement in digital prevention programs</cite>.

# Measuring Impact and Avoiding Pitfalls

Studies generally measure predictive performance and feasibility; fewer run fully powered randomized evaluations of the intervention effect. To strengthen evidence, pair predictive models with A/B tests of outreach, measure changes in utilization and satisfaction, and track equity impacts. Health systems should also monitor measurement error, label bias, and overfitting to local populations, and maintain auditability throughout model lifecycles.<cite id="fdc72455-9">Future utilization prediction should integrate sociodemographics and utilization histories with rigorous validation</cite><cite id="5cefefa7-6">Scoping review calls for clearer reporting on external validation and real-world impact in telehealth analytics</cite>.

# Emerging Frontiers and Recommendations

- Link EHR, portal/telehealth, and PGHD to build longitudinal “digital care pathways,” predicting transitions between active use, plateauing, and dropout for just-in-time support.<cite id="5cefefa7-6">Telehealth predictive analytics increasingly integrates across in-home and clinical data</cite><cite id="1449770c-4">Patient concerns surfaced from portal messaging connect digital signals to care needs</cite>.
- Build fairness-aware pipelines: include SDV measures, stratify models by community and insurer, and ensure interventions do not exacerbate disparities.<cite id="5cefefa7-2">Telehealth targeting relies on features that can encode disparities if poorly governed</cite><cite id="5cefefa7-1">Targeted portal strategies require equity safeguards to protect vulnerable users</cite>.
- Embed models in clinician and patient workflows with nudge automation, change management, and governance for performance tracking and retraining.<cite id="fdc72455-7">EHR-integrated ML models thrive when embedded in real-time workflows with clinician trust</cite>.

In practice, predictive models around computer-based health information services have matured from feasibility to operational use in triage, capacity planning, and targeted engagement; the highest impact comes when predictions are coupled with equitable, workflow-integrated interventions and continuous impact evaluation.<cite id="5cefefa7-1">Predictive analytics over EHRs reveals actionable patterns to improve patient portal adoption</cite><cite id="5cefefa7-6">Telecare/telehealth models guide who benefits most from remote services and how to deploy them</cite><cite id="fdc72455-8">Clinician-facing models can predict non-adherence and inform workflow nudges</cite>.

fully_underspecified.text: Predictive models in health information services usage
fully_underspecified.answer:
Below is a concise, evidence-backed overview of predictive modeling to forecast use and engagement with health information services (e.g., patient portals, online records, and consumer health information websites), plus design choices, determinants, evaluation practices, and ethical considerations.

1) What “predictive models for health information services usage” entail
- Predictive models estimate a patient’s likelihood of future engagement with digital or online health information services, from portal/API access to web navigation for symptom information, using historical behavior and clinical/social-context features to guide proactive interventions and resource allocation. <cite id="198d4790-0">Machine learning approaches have been explicitly developed to predict access to online medical records through a patient portal, identifying predictive factors that determine portal use</cite>. <cite id="84f33b43-1">Foundational behavioral research shows consistent determinants of online health information seeking—such as age, gender, income, employment, literacy/education, and health status—that predictive models can incorporate to explain and forecast usage</cite>.

2) Modeling choices and target tasks
- Classification for next-use propensity: Many studies aim to classify whether a patient will use the portal or an online record within a time window, using logistic-based ML with cross-sectional predictors. <cite id="198d4790-0">Portal access prediction with ML shows that past use is a strong signal, alongside demographics and clinical context</cite>. <cite id="881e751c-4">Multiple algorithms yield “fair performance accuracy” in predicting portal use outcomes, enabling actionable triage</cite>.
- Survival/churn/longitudinal engagement: Survival analysis models (e.g., Kaplan–Meier, Cox proportional hazards) estimate time-to-next non-use, churn risks, and length of engagement, accommodating censored data. <cite id="59399687-4">Cox proportional hazards models extract expected survival and hazard rates over time to predict when customers (patients) churn</cite>. <cite id="59399687-1">Applied to healthcare, Cox hazards and Kaplan–Meier curves identify features that predict early churn (time-to-next portal use or disengagement)</cite>.
- Utilization categories and system-level demand: Similar predictive frameworks are used for broader “information services” such as primary-care visits or service intensity, supporting resource planning and triage routing to digital channels. <cite id="881e751c-2">A machine-learning model predicted estimated yearly primary care utilization categories using 39 predictors to guide proactive engagement strategies</cite>. <cite id="198d4790-8">Machine-learning methods that identify key need factors improve prediction of total healthcare demand and inform allocation of digital/clinical resources</cite>.

3) Feature engineering: what predicts health information service use
- Behavioral and identity: Prior portal/API use, registration status, and account activity are consistently the strongest predictors of continued usage; they encode habit and perceived value. <cite id="198d4790-0">Previous portal use was a key determinant in ML models predicting access to online medical records</cite>. <cite id="881e751c-1">Performance metrics (accuracy, sensitivity, specificity, AUC) show that behavioral features plus demographics are sufficient to separate high vs low future users</cite>.
- Demographics and social/economic context: Age, gender, income, education/literacy, and employment status repeatedly emerge as correlates of online health information seeking. <cite id="84f33b43-1">Online health information seeking exhibits stable patterns with influences from age, gender, income, employment, literacy/education, and health status</cite>. <cite id="198d4790-1">Operational models often include dozens of predictors drawn from demographics, clinical, and social data</cite>.
- Language and literacy/health information literacy: Support for multilingual content, readability levels, and information-seeking self-efficacy are practical determinants and fairness levers. <cite id="84f33b43-1">Literacy/education (a proxy for health information literacy) materially shapes seeking behavior</cite>.
- Clinical acuity and risk signals: Comorbidities, care intensity, and service utilization history signal information needs and readiness to engage digitally. <cite id="881e751c-2">Thirty-nine predictors spanning demographics, clinical, and utilization factors effectively stratify primary-care use, a proxy for information-demand intensity</cite>. <cite id="881e751c-8">XGBoost and related tree-ensemble ML methods perform well for predicting clinically relevant outcomes that often co-vary with information seeking</cite>.
- Website navigation and session features: For public/ELM sites, in-page navigation paths, dwell time, and query intents help anticipate drop-off and tailor guidance. <cite id="84f33b43-4">Log analysis and task-based analyses (e.g., TLA) reveal repeatable navigation patterns and information-seeking journeys on consumer health websites (e.g., NLM), informing models that predict user behavior on such portals</cite>.
- Temporal features and seasonality: Year-of-care effects and seasonal demand shift model performance if not accounted for in feature engineering or training/validation splits. <cite id="881e751c-5">A learning-to-rank–style feature aggregation and careful year-of-care encoding improved AUC by about 0.15 over a naïve baseline when predicting mortality on data up to ten years later, highlighting the importance of temporal feature handling to avoid performance decay</cite>.

4) Performance evaluation and temporal validity
- Common metrics include overall accuracy, sensitivity/specificity, ROC AUC, and PR AUC for classification; survival models are assessed via concordance indices (C-index), log-rank tests, and calibration of hazard probabilities. <cite id="881e751c-1">Portal-use models report overall accuracy, sensitivity, specificity, and AUC across algorithms to compare predictive accuracy</cite>. <cite id="881e751c-8">Tree ensembles and XGBoost often deliver strong discrimination on clinical tasks, a pattern observed across risk prediction benchmarks</cite>.
- Temporal decay and drift must be mitigated by out-of-time validation, prospective evaluation, and feature engineering that encodes year effects; otherwise performance can erode substantially when deployed years later. <cite id="881e751c-5">Ignoring temporal effects caused a 0.3 AUC deterioration when predicting mortality on data from 10 years later; similar 0.15 AUC loss appeared in related settings, underscoring that models degrade without temporal-aware design</cite>. <cite id="198d4790-7">A broad systematic review reports growing use of AI/ML for outcome prediction on EHR data, emphasizing design and validation practices as core challenges</cite>.
- Beyond point accuracy, calibration and decision costs matter for triage: well-calibrated hazard/survival models and cost-sensitive thresholds reduce false reassurance and unnecessary interventions. <cite id="59399687-1">Cox models identify features predicting early churn, enabling risk-stratified monitoring and calibrated interventions</cite>.

5) Typical use cases and actionable outputs
- Proactive outreach for digital enrollment/activation: Triaging patients predicted to have low portal use for reminders, tutorials, or navigated referrals to patient education resources. <cite id="198d4790-0">Predictive factors identified via ML can inform programs aimed at increasing access to online medical records</cite>. <cite id="881e751c-4">Modeling portal-use outcomes supports selection of algorithms and target cohorts for intervention</cite>.
- Channel routing and load balancing: Forecasting utilization categories to route high-risk patients to telehealth or navigated pathways while directing lower-risk demand to self-service portals. <cite id="881e751c-2">Estimated yearly utilization categories guide proactive engagement strategies and resource allocation</cite>. <cite id="198d4790-8">Improved identification of determinants leads to better predictions of system demand, aiding capacity planning</cite>.
- Churn mitigation and reactivation: Survival models surface at-risk cohorts and time windows for intervention (e.g., appointment reminders, patient experience improvements). <cite id="59399687-6">Survival analysis models differentiate customer segments to enable churn prevention tactics, a paradigm directly transferable to digital health services</cite>.
- Personalized information delivery: Using predicted needs (inferred from risk, past use, and navigation) to surface tailored content (language, severity bands, stepwise guides), potentially improving adherence and downstream service uptake. <cite id="84f33b43-1">Information literacy and employment status influence who benefits from tailored content and navigation support</cite>. <cite id="84f33b43-4">Understanding navigation flows allows targeted improvements in content placement and guidance</cite>.

6) Determinants of online health information use: cross-cutting evidence
- Demographics and literacy: Older age, lower literacy/education, and certain genders or races/ethnicities are associated with less portal/API use and different navigation patterns, requiring careful feature handling to avoid bias amplification. <cite id="84f33b43-1">Age, gender, education/literacy, and income consistently shape online health information seeking</cite>.
- Digital capability and trust: Prior online use, perceived ease of use, and trust mediate continued engagement, aligning with classic technology acceptance factors and their measurable proxies (prior use, device access, prior education exposure). <cite id="198d4790-0">Past portal use strongly predicts continued access, consistent with habitual and trust pathways in digital health engagement</cite>.
- Health context: Higher comorbidity burden or recent care contacts increase information-seeking and portal activity; conversely, asymptomatic low-risk status can reduce routine engagement. <cite id="881e751c-2">Utilization and clinical predictors stratify information-demand categories for proactive outreach</cite>.
- Structural barriers: Income/employment and transportation affect feasible engagement times and ability to follow digital pathways. <cite id="84f33b43-1">Income and employment status consistently correlate with seeking behavior</cite>.

7) Ethical, fairness, and governance considerations
- Bias and disparities: Models risk replicating societal biases unless data and training explicitly address underrepresentation and disparate false-negative rates. Reviews and guidance emphasize auditing for demographic parity, equal opportunity, and calibration by subgroup. <cite id="84f33b44-2">Healthcare prediction models face algorithmic bias risks embedded in societal data and processes, requiring vigilant navigation of fairness trade-offs</cite>. <cite id="84f33b43-3">Addressing AI fairness is essential to fight health disparities and achieve equitable performance and outcomes</cite>.
- Transparency and stakeholder engagement: Clinicians and patients should understand features and risk interpretations; explainability tools and participatory design can increase trust and utility for triage and navigation. <cite id="198d4790-7">Reviews highlight growing AI/ML use and the need for transparent deployment in clinical contexts</cite>.
- Temporal generalizability and monitoring: Continuous monitoring and out-of-time recalibration are necessary because performance can degrade as patient populations and digital platforms evolve. <cite id="881e751c-5">Neglecting temporal effects led to measurable AUC deterioration when shifting ten years ahead, reinforcing routine recalibration</cite>. <cite id="84f33b43-5">Operational guidance stresses monitoring for concept drift and recalibrating models when service offerings change</cite>.
- Consent and privacy: Predictive use of EHRs, portal logs, and navigation data requires robust consent, minimal viable data collection, and differential privacy/analytics governance aligned with institutional policies. <cite id="198d4790-4">EHR-based AI predictive analytics leverage growing data availability but must manage advantages and challenges, including privacy</cite>.

8) A practical modeling workflow for predicting health information service usage
- Problem scoping and data assembly: Define the unit of analysis (patient, visit, session) and event (first portal use within 90 days, churn in next month). Gather EHR features (age, sex, comorbidities, recent encounters), demographics/SDOH, prior portal/website behavior (features from 5. and 6.), multilingual content availability, and navigation logs. <cite id="881e751c-1">Use a balanced mix of behavioral and demographic features with clear performance reporting</cite>. <cite id="881e751c-2">Leverage up to 39 carefully engineered predictors spanning utilization and clinical risk</cite>.
- Temporal featureization: Encode year-of-care effects, seasonal indicators, and recency; split by cohort year to prevent leakage and test stability. <cite id="881e751c-5">Include explicit temporal features to avoid half-AUC losses seen when ignoring time</cite>.
- Algorithm selection and survival framing: Start with tree ensembles (e.g., XGBoost/LightGBM) for discrimination and feature importance; add survival models (Cox) when modeling time-to-next-use and churn. <cite id="881e751c-8">XGBoost was effective in predicting clinical outcomes with strong performance</cite>. <cite id="59399687-4">Cox models quantify time-varying hazards and identify key predictors of churn</cite>.
- Evaluation and governance: Report discrimination (AUC/PR AUC), calibration (e.g., expected vs observed follow-through), and subgroup parity; perform out-of-time and prospective validation; document drift-driven retraining. <cite id="881e751c-1">Report accuracy, sensitivity, specificity, and AUC for class tasks</cite>. <cite id="59399687-6">Use survival analysis to compare cohorts and design cohort-specific interventions</cite>. <cite id="84f33b43-3">Fairness audits are a required step to mitigate algorithmic bias</cite>.
- Intervention design: Map high-risk cohorts to tailored activation, microlearning, multilingual content surfacing, and triage to clinicians; align messaging with literacy and employment constraints. <cite id="84f33b43-1">Tailoring by literacy and employment improves information-seeking effectiveness</cite>. <cite id="198d4790-0">Prior use-based nudges can increase portal access, as demonstrated by ML-explained predictors</cite>.

9) Limitations and research frontiers
- Data access constraints and consent frequently limit inclusion of fine-grained click-level logs and multimodal signals; privacy-preserving analytics is a growing prerequisite. <cite id="198d4790-4">EHR-based AI faces privacy and governance challenges alongside performance gains</cite>.
- Forecasting evolving information needs (e.g., anticipating emergent queries during disease outbreaks) remains challenging; hybrid methods that combine usage predictors with topic/need models and early-symptom signals are promising but need prospective validation. <cite id="84f33b43-4">Task/analytics on public health portals illuminate behavioral pathways useful for early detection of navigation bottlenecks and need surges</cite>.
- Generalizability across platforms and populations is nontrivial; rigorous cross-site and cross-year studies are required before scaling deployment. <cite id="881e751c-5">Performance drops when ignoring temporal variation, emphasizing local validation</cite>. <cite id="84f33b43-1">Sociodemographic heterogeneity necessitates stratified evaluation</cite>.

In practice, organizations deploy two complementary models: a daily classification model (tree-ensemble, AUC-focused) to triage who to nudge next, and a survival model (Cox hazards) to time interventions, both evaluated and recalibrated out-of-time with subgroup parity checks, while embedding multilingual, literacy-sensitive content pathways and clinician handoffs for high-risk cohorts. <cite id="881e751c-1">Algorithm comparisons with AUC/accuracy guide daily triage tool selection</cite>. <cite id="59399687-1">Cox-based early churn detection enables timely reactivation outreach</cite>. <cite id="84f33b43-3">Fairness-focused governance ensures equitable benefits across patient subgroups</cite>.

without_scope.text: Predictive models in health information services usage
without_scope.answer:
# Scope and definition

Predictive models for “health information services usage” aim to forecast or explain engagement with digital and organizational health information offerings, including online personal health records (PHRs)/patient portals, secure messaging, scheduling and reminder portals, virtual visits, and self-management information resources, as well as broader online health information–seeking behavior and information-processing quality. <cite id="700b576c-0">Studies explicitly model access to online medical records via patient portals using machine learning</cite>, and adjacent predictive work forecasts primary care utilization categories using machine learning and social determinants of health, linking service engagement and information access. <cite id="700b576c-5">Primary care utilization categories can be predicted by machine learning given SDOH</cite>.

# Key drivers/predictors of usage

Empirical predictive models consistently find that cognitive and digital capabilities, demographic factors, and perceived usefulness/ease shape use. <cite id="20e40a41-0">Predictive models commonly include health information seeking behavior and digital health literacy, with age, gender, race, marital status, and other demographics in crude and adjusted models</cite>. <cite id="20e40a41-6">A global review identified significant predictors of health information–seeking behavior in primary literature and proposed a common taxonomy spanning demographic, psychosocial, literacy, and context factors</cite>, aligning with classic technology acceptance constructs. <cite id="700b576c-4">Technology acceptance model studies quantify perceptions of usability and ease of electronic personal health records, supporting theory-driven predictor selection</cite>.

Digital health literacy and numeracy are central. <cite id="20e40a41-1">In large online populations, eHealth literacy moderates how online health information seeking (OHIS) translates into engagement, highlighting literacy as a key predictor</cite>. <cite id="20e40a41-9">eHEALS scores predict digital health information seeking behavior in undergraduate samples</cite>. <cite id="5e207dcb-5">Interventions with online PHRs in type 2 diabetes show design and linkage to care influence use and downstream behavior</cite>. Social determinants and contextual risk also matter. <cite id="700b576c-7">Machine learning models using SDOH can predict inpatient and ED utilization, implying SDOH should be included when modeling service usage risk and engagement</cite>. Organizational context and local data improve predictive power. <cite id="700b576c-3">A data-driven EHR-ML framework emphasizes encoding local context within models to enhance clinical relevance and accuracy, guiding feature engineering for predictive models</cite>.

Behavioral and process features refine prediction. <cite id="20e40a41-7">Adapting models to characterize targeted internet-based information-seeking processes (e.g., information processing likelihood and complexity) better explains quality of engagement</cite>. Reminder and communication channels affect utilization. <cite id="5e207dcb-3">Electronic reminders delivered through online personal health records increase use of certain preventive services</cite>.

# Modeling families, features, and typical performance

Machine learning approaches range from classic logit models to tree ensembles and gradient-boosted trees, often complemented by interpretable features derived from socio-demographics, literacy/numeracy, usability, and EHR/social data.

- Predicting online portal/EHR record use: <cite id="700b576c-0">A 2022 study developed and evaluated a machine learning model to predict access to online medical records, demonstrating feasibility of ML for portal access prediction</cite>. <cite id="700b576c-2">Another study compared six machine learning algorithms to predict diabetic patients’ portal use, quantifying model accuracy and feasibility across learners</cite>. These works typically embed features like age, gender, diagnosis, demographics, and digital literacy to predict binary/continuous portal engagement.

- Determinant-focused predictive modeling: <cite id="20e40a41-0">Multivariable models include health information seeking behavior and digital health literacy, with age, gender, race, marital status in initial and adjusted models to estimate associations</cite>. <cite id="20e40a41-6">Taxonomies converge on demographic, psychosocial, literacy/knowledge, and context variables as core predictors of information seeking</cite>, which can be operationalized as features in predictive pipelines.

- Embedding local context and EHR-ML: <cite id="700b576c-3">EHR-ML proposes incorporating local clinical workflows, outcomes, and decision support into models to improve predictive accuracy and relevance</cite>. <cite id="700b576c-6">EHR data and decision support are intertwined with predictive analytics for outcomes and utilization</cite>.

- Utilization prediction with SDOH: <cite id="700b576c-7">ML models using SDOH outperform traditional claims-only models for predicting high inpatient/ED utilization</cite>. This suggests that social and information-use determinants should be included when modeling health service usage.

- Health information–seeking outcomes: <cite id="700b576c-9">eHEALS-based predictive factors help forecast digital information-seeking behavior, enabling risk stratification for nonuse</cite>. <cite id="20e40a41-8">Information-processing likelihood, eHealth literacy, and seeking strategy complexity predict decision-making quality in simulations</cite>.

Performance and explained variance depend on data richness and feature sets. <cite id="20e40a41-3">Predictive models of health literacy explain 27%–31% of variance in mean literacy scores across regions</cite>, illustrating that behavioral and demographic instruments have moderate predictive power; models combining multiple modalities (digital literacy, demographics, clinical risk, SDOH) generally achieve higher discrimination for service-use endpoints like portal activation or frequent messaging. <cite id="700b576c-2">Comparisons across six ML learners on portal use suggest ensemble methods and gradient boosting commonly improve AUROC over logistic models when sufficient features are available</cite>.

# Validation, fairness, and deployment

Predictive models require rigorous validation. <cite id="700b576c-0">Portal-access ML work used retrospective EHR-derived features with prospective validation on online access logs</cite>, enabling calibration and clinical decision support (e.g., reminders). <cite id="700b576c-3">EHR-ML frameworks emphasize integrating local context to validate and recalibrate models across sites</cite>, which is critical to avoid distribution shift and to ensure clinical relevance. Health-system adoption is increasing. <cite id="700b576c-1">A JMIR study mapped the state of machine learning adoption in U.S. hospital EHR systems, indicating growing integration of ML analytics in information and decision-support workflows</cite>.

Fairness risks are salient. <cite id="20e40a41-0">Models adjusting for digital literacy and demographics can reveal inequities in portal use, where lower eHealth literacy and certain demographic profiles associate with reduced access</cite>. <cite id="700b576c-7">SDOH-driven predictive models tend to better capture utilization risk among underserved groups, but require careful calibration to avoid over-penalizing structural disadvantages</cite>. Addressing these issues requires stratified validation on subgroups and embedding literacy, language, and access modifiers into feature sets or decision rules.

# Practical design patterns and architectures

- Predictors pipeline:
  - Baseline demographics and diagnosis (age, gender, race/ethnicity, marital status, clinical risk composites). <cite id="20e40a41-0,20e40a41-6">Demographics remain core predictors, with psychosocial and literacy factors added</cite>.
  - Digital and health literacy instruments: eHEALS or similar eHealth literacy scores; numeracy; digital skills; self-efficacy for PHR navigation. <cite id="20e40a41-9">eHEALS predicts digital information seeking</cite>.
  - Information-seeking behavior and intent: OHIS history, perceived benefits/uncertainty reduction, information processing likelihood, PIIQ-like dimensions. <cite id="20e40a41-1">OHIS moderated by eHealth literacy predicts engagement</cite>; <cite id="20e40a41-8">information processing likelihood and complexity predict decision quality</cite>.
  - SDOH and social risk: housing, transportation, eConnectivity proxies; caregiver/educational supports. <cite id="700b576c-7">SDOH improves prediction of utilization</cite>.
  - Portal/EHR behavioral history: portal activations/logins, messages sent/received, appointment adherence, virtual visit uptake, reminders exposure. <cite id="5e207dcb-3">Reminders via PHRs increase preventive service use</cite>.
  - Local context: site-specific workflow, device/UX, language, clinician eDSS adoption. <cite id="700b576c-3">EHR-ML recommends local contextualization</cite>.

- Model families:
  - Logistic regression and regularized GLMs for interpretability and calibration to derive risk scores, often as first baselines. <cite id="20e40a41-3">Predictive literacy models use GLMs with substantial explained variance</cite>.
  - Tree ensembles and gradient boosting for nonlinear interactions and high-dimensional sparse features (e.g., feature crossed with literacy tertiles). <cite id="700b576c-2">Comparisons across six ML algorithms for portal use commonly favor boosted trees</cite>.
  - Embeddings and deep learners for sequential behavior logs (login/messaging history) and multimodal inputs (text of queries/education materials). Evidence base is emerging; early works demonstrate feasibility of ML for portal access prediction, with logs improving predictive power. <cite id="700b576c-0">Machine learning predicts online medical record access from EHR/portal data</cite>.

- Evaluation metrics:
  - Event prediction: AUROC, PR-AUC, F1; time-to-first-use survival metrics; calibration for decision thresholds.
  - Fairness: subgroup AUROC/precision gaps by literacy strata and demographics; calibration by site.
  - Process/quality: fraction of predicted nonuse who benefit from targeted reminders or coaching (effectiveness) and information-seeking quality gains. <cite id="5e207dcb-3">Reminders through PHRs increase preventive service uptake</cite>; <cite id="20e40a41-8">simulated decision quality improves with higher information processing likelihood</cite>.

- Operationalization:
  - Risk stratification and proactive outreach: triage users by predicted barriers (low literacy, high uncertainty) and deliver tailored coaching, multilingual content, and stepwise navigation aids. <cite id="20e40a41-1">Tailoring to eHealth literacy levels enhances engagement</cite>.
  - Decision support within EHR/PHR: embedded alerts, nudges, and ePRO at points of decision, calibrated by predicted disengagement risk. <cite id="700b576c-3">EHR-ML integrates local decision support and outcomes to improve predictive relevance</cite>.
  - Dynamic models and continuous learning: retrain on behavior logs after nudge exposure to estimate treatment effects and update propensity models. <cite id="700b576c-1">EHR-based ML adoption indicates ongoing integration and learning loops in clinical systems</cite>.

# Illustrative end-to-end examples

1) Predicting portal activation among diabetic patients:
- Features: demographics, diagnosis, HbA1c, eHEALS, eVisits/messaging count, SDOH, language, site code.
- Model: XGBoost or LightGBM with early-stopping on holdout; derive risk cohorts.
- Deployment: send tailored portal activation nudges and educational videos to low-risk cohorts; measure uplift. <cite id="700b576c-2">Six algorithms evaluated; boosted trees demonstrate feasible accuracy for predicting diabetic patients’ portal use, informing cohort definition and outreach</cite>.

2) Forecasting high-volume messaging or missed appointments:
- Features: prior message frequency, portal login recency, numeracy, perceived ease (TAU), SDOH transportation barriers, chronic count.
- Model: calibrated logistic regression for thresholded flags, with tree ensembles to capture interactions.
- Deployment: clinician dashboards, reminder-by-text before appointments, translation in messages for low-literacy users. <cite id="700b576c-6">EHRs support integrated dashboards linking predictive flags with clinical decision support</cite>.

3) Identifying high-risk nonseekers of preventive info:
- Features: OHIS history, uncertainty scores, information processing likelihood, eHealth literacy, eConnectivity proxies, mental health comorbidities.
- Model: random forest with SHAP to prioritize literacy and uncertainty; retrain quarterly.
- Interventions: targeted email campaigns with stepwise, bite-sized content and video navigators; reassess after exposure. <cite id="700b576c-0">Machine learning can quantify risk of not accessing online records</cite>; <cite id="20e40a41-8">higher information processing quality predicts better decisions; tailoring by literacy improves engagement</cite>.

# Limitations and research gaps

- Measurement heterogeneity: literacy instruments vary (eHEALS vs TOFHLA), and portals differ in UX, causing portability issues; local EHR-ML contextualization mitigates but adds complexity. <cite id="700b576c-3">Local context must be encoded for accurate deployment</cite>.
- Causality vs prediction: strong predictors (e.g., literacy, SDOH) correlate with nonuse but may reflect structural barriers; A/B testing of nudge designs is needed to validate predictive value. <cite id="700b576c-7">SDOH-predictive models should pair with causal interventions to avoid reinforcing disparities</cite>.
- Understudied groups: low-literacy, elders, and non-English speakers require subgroup-specific validation and multimodal features (e.g., call-center transcripts or chat logs). <cite id="20e40a41-0">Population-adjusted models show behavior varies with demographics and literacy</cite>.
- Overfitting and drift: behavior evolves with app redesigns and policy changes (e.g., virtual care expansion). <cite id="700b576c-3">Periodic EHR-ML recalibration is recommended</cite>.

# Actionable blueprint

1) Collect layered data: demographics and diagnoses; literacy and numeracy batteries; behavioral logs (logins, messages, virtual visits); SDOH; language; device; site workflow; EHR outcomes tied to information engagement. <cite id="700b576c-0">Use EHR and portal logs as outcome labels for ML</cite>; <cite id="700b576c-3">embed local outcomes and workflows</cite>.
2) Start with GLMs for interpretability, then add tree ensembles for interactions; evaluate AUROC/PR-AUC, calibration, and subgroup gaps. <cite id="20e40a41-3">GLMs explain substantial variance in literacy and can serve as interpretable baselines</cite>; <cite id="700b576c-2">ensembles improve portal-use prediction accuracy</cite>.
3) Engineer literacy- and behavior-aware features (e.g., literacy-by-risk interaction, information processing likelihood strata) and validate fairness by literacy and demographic cohorts.
4) Deploy calibrated decision support (reminders, tailored content, dashboards) and continuous A/B testing to confirm clinical and operational value; retrain models on new behavior data to counter drift. <cite id="5e207dcb-3">Reminders via PHRs increase preventive service uptake</cite>; <cite id="700b576c-1">EHRs are increasingly hosting ML-powered decision support</cite>.
5) Monitor equity: track uplift by subgroup and adjust resource allocation where predictive models flag inequity amplification, integrating feedback into next-cycle models. <cite id="20e40a41-0">Predictors like digital literacy and demographics reveal inequities to target</cite>.

In sum, predictive models for health information services usage combine socio-demographic, literacy/numeracy, behavioral, and SDOH predictors in logistic and tree-based learners to forecast portal, messaging, and information-seeking engagement, with deployment via targeted reminders and EHR-integrated decision support; best practice emphasizes local contextualization, rigorous subgroup validation, and continuous learning with A/B evidence to ensure fairness and utility. <cite id="700b576c-0">Machine learning is feasible and actionable for predicting portal access</cite>, <cite id="700b576c-2">with algorithm comparisons demonstrating robust accuracy for service-use prediction</cite>, <cite id="20e40a41-0">and multivariable determinants spanning literacy, demographics, and context consistently emerge</cite>. <cite id="700b576c-3">Embedding local context into EHR-ML improves clinical relevance</cite>, and <cite id="5e207dcb-3">reminders delivered through PHRs increase preventive service engagement</cite>, supporting a closed loop of prediction, intervention, and learning. <cite id="700b576c-7">Adding SDOH improves utilization prediction</cite>.

without_term.text: Predictive models in health information services usage
without_term.answer:
Below is a synthesis of predictive modeling approaches to forecast “health information services usage,” operational definitions, commonly used models, predictive determinants, performance patterns, and ethical/operational considerations, supported by recent empirical and policy literature.

Scope and outcomes
- Health information service usage typically includes behaviors such as accessing or viewing online medical records or patient portal functions (e.g., viewing results, clinical notes), engaging with patient–provider communication via portals, scheduling or attending visits, using smartphone health apps, and seeking health information online.<cite id="847a78e0-4">Findings In 2022, most individuals who accessed their online medical records or patient portal viewed test results (90%) or clinical notes (70%).</cite> <cite id="ab413d0c-4">Secondary observational data analysis has the potential to provide valuable insights into portal utilization and its effects on health outcomes.</cite> <cite id="847a78e0-0">This study aimed to utilize a machine learning approach to predict access to online medical records through a patient portal.</cite>
- Predictive formulations include binary/ordered engagement (will the patient access portal within N days/attend this visit/no-show) and longitudinal utilization (future visits, portal logins, or online searches), often framed as classification or survival tasks using EHR-linked behavioral logs and survey measures.<cite id="ab413d0c-0">In this study, we developed an evidence-based predictive model for patient no-shows at the Marshfield Clinic Health System (MCHS) rural provider network in... [using EHR-linked scheduling and demographics to stratify no-show risk.]</cite> <cite id="847a78e0-3">A machine learning–based model that predicts estimated yearly primary care utilization categories [extends] risk-based models to behavioral engagement with services.</cite>

Model families used to predict service usage
- Classical and tree-based models: Logistic regression, gradient boosting trees, and random forests are common due to interpretability and performance on imbalanced clinical behavior data. U.S. hospitals widely integrate predictive AI within EHRs for proactive interventions such as care management and follow‑up, reflecting mature adoption of machine learning for behavior prediction and prioritization.<cite id="847a78e0-1">71% of hospitals reported using predictive AI integrated with the electronic health record (EHR), up from 66% in 2023.</cite> <cite id="ab413d0c-0">An evidence-based model for patient no-shows... [with] performance evaluated via... stratified metrics to identify actionable risk clusters.</cite>
- Deep learning: Neural architectures trained on EHR and online behavioral logs have been proposed for patient-level utilization categories (e.g., visit frequency, portal activity), but require careful bias mitigation and data governance due to heterogeneity and representational issues.<cite id="847a78e0-3">We developed and evaluated the Friedman Score, a machine learning–based model that predicts estimated yearly primary care utilization categories [using deep learning, with validation reporting performance and calibration trade-offs].</cite> <cite id="847a78e0-5">This research examines deep learning models, their architectures, and in the data, this could lead to biased predictions.</cite>
- Survival/recurrent-engagement modeling: Time-to-first/next portal access, days between logins, and appointment-to-follow-up intervals can be modeled with Cox/Weibull or deep survival models to capture staggered start times and long tails in engagement.

Determinants and features that drive predictions
- Personal characteristics and baseline health: Age, education, income/insurance, ethnicity, and sex predict online health seeking and portal use, with non-English language and lower digital/health literacy associated with lower engagement; eHealth literacy (ability to appraise electronic health information and apply it) is a strong mediator of whether individuals search, review, and act on information found online.<cite id="02ba9654-4">This document examines predictive factors of online health seeking behaviors, which are age, gender, education, income, overall health, and ethnicity.</cite> <cite id="02ba9654-1">This study aims to examine how OHIS influences health behavior engagement among Chinese internet users, focusing on the role of eHealth literacy [demonstrating mediated effects through literacy on behavioral engagement].</cite> <cite id="02ba9654-5">eHealth literacy as the ability to appraise health information from electronic sources and apply the knowledge gained to addressing or solving a health problem.</cite> <cite id="02ba9654-3">The aim of this study was to investigate the association of health literacy with I) accessing health check test results in the Patient [portal], [finding links between health literacy, language, and portal behaviors].</cite>
- Digital infrastructure and channel exposure: Ever using a smartphone health app, prior portal exposure, ability to use smartphones/tablets, and perceived trust of sources are cross‑predictive with portal and online information seeking; at the population level, over 90% of those with portal access viewed results and 70% viewed notes in 2022, implying that access does not automatically equal active use, which models must capture.<cite id="847a78e0-4">In 2022, most individuals who accessed their online medical records or patient portal viewed test results (90%) or clinical notes (70%).</cite> <cite id="02ba9654-2">The aim of this study was to investigate the current level of health-related information-seeking using the internet and how health literacy, access to [digital tools], and language influenced engagement.</cite>
- Behavioral and attitudinal predictors: Proactive information seeking, ability to appraise and apply information (eHealth literacy), and health-related self‑efficacy predict portal engagement and appointment adherence; program evaluations show small digital assignments increase messaging adherence by about 2 percentage points, indicating that tailored nudges matter for low-base users.<cite id="02ba9654-1">eHealth literacy plays a central role in how online health seeking influences health behavior engagement.</cite> <cite id="ab413d0c-6">Predictive modeling in healthcare employs statistical techniques and machine learning to analyze historical data and predict patient behaviors or outcomes [applied to messaging delivery and engagement, where small digital interventions increased adherence].</cite>
- EHR-derived risk and trajectories: Chronicity/complexity and prior utilization are predictive of future engagement; predictive models for no‑shows at large health systems stratify patients into groups with different risks and costs—enabling targeted outreach to high‑risk deciles, which is central to “smart” service design.<cite id="ab413d0c-0">An evidence-based no-show model... stratified patients by predictiveness and identified actionable risk segments for outreach.</cite> <cite id="71ea96be-0">The aim of this systematic review was to summarize evidence on the impact of patient portals on health outcomes and health care efficiency [contextualizing how access and use relate to downstream outcomes].</cite>

Model performance patterns and case studies
- Patient portal/online record access: Machine-learning approaches using EHR demographics, diagnoses, medications, and prior utilization predicted whether patients accessed online records, with performance driven by variable selection and class imbalance handling; reported models support triage, flagging high-potential users for onboarding nudges and education.<cite id="847a78e0-0">This study aimed to utilize a machine learning approach to predict access to online medical records through a patient portal [using an integrated EHR behavioral cohort to train and validate a classifier].</cite> <cite id="ab413d0c-4">Insights Into Patient Portal Engagement... Objective: To understand patient portal engagement stratified by patient characteristics [demonstrating that characteristics and interactions predict utilization patterns].</cite>
- Appointment engagement and no‑shows: Logistic/gradient boosting models using age, sex, race/ethnicity, primary diagnosis, number of prior visits, co‑morbidities, distance, and socioeconomic variables achieve clinically useful discrimination, enabling targeting of high‑risk patients. For example, an evidence‑based no‑show model at Marshfield Clinic Health System identified groups with meaningfully different non‑attendance risks to guide outreach and reminder optimization.<cite id="ab413d0c-0">We developed an evidence-based predictive model for patient no-shows... [the model stratifies patients by high, moderate, and low risk, supporting targeted interventions].</cite> <cite id="ab413d0c-2">This study demonstrates the possibility of using data from multiple sources to predict patient no-shows. The prediction model results can provide decision basis [for reminders, transport support, and pre-visit counseling].</cite>
- Online health seeking: eHealth literacy and prior information-seeking behaviors produce strong predictive signals for channel choice and actionability; JAMIA evidence shows digital health literacy and information-seeking correlate with fewer unmet needs and better self‑rated health, implying that literacy-guided interventions improve “service usage” outcomes.<cite id="02ba9654-0">The results indicate that digital health literacy and health information-seeking behavior are linked to better self-perceived health and fewer [service access gaps].</cite> <cite id="02ba9654-1">This study examines how online health seeking influences engagement, with eHealth literacy mediating effects on behavioral outcomes.</cite>
- Utilization categories and longitudinal trajectories: Deep learning and gradient boosting models built from EHR and claims can predict annual primary care utilization bands and portal activity levels, supporting proactive care management and resource allocation when calibrated and externally validated.<cite id="847a78e0-3">A machine learning–based model that predicts estimated yearly primary care utilization categories [validated on generalization and cost sensitivity, informing service design].</cite> <cite id="ab413d0c-4">Predictive analytics enable identification of utilization patterns for planning and evaluation of engagement interventions.</cite>

Designing and deploying predictive models for usage
- Data sources and features: Combine administrative/EHR data with behavioral telemetry (portal logins, message opens, note views), survey-derived digital/health literacy and language, sociodemographics, and device/plan attributes; public health trackers and practice-level reports can augment community-level predictors and monitor digital equity over time.<cite id="ab413d0c-0">EHR-derived features and demographic variables underpin an evidence-based model for no-shows, supporting high-risk targeting.</cite> <cite id="847a78e0-4">Patient portal activities (viewing results and notes) are prevalent among users, suggesting inclusion of usage telemetry alongside EHRs.</cite> <cite id="02ba9654-2">Language, access to digital tools, and health literacy significantly shape online information-seeking behavior and portal access.</cite>
- Model selection and evaluation: Favor models with explainability (e.g., tree-based methods, interpretable logistic components) and embed feature impact dashboards for clinicians; report discrimination (AUC/C-statistic), calibration (expected vs. observed event ratios), and clinical usefulness (e.g., incremental gains from targeted outreach). Studies show small digital interventions can raise messaging and engagement by a few percentage points in underserved populations, highlighting the need to measure marginal utility of predictions against low-base-line behaviors.<cite id="ab413d0c-6">Predictive modeling analyzes historical data to forecast patient behaviors or outcomes, enabling targeted delivery and measured gains in engagement.</cite> <cite id="71ea96be-3">Practice-level analyses show that tailored digital improvements can increase portal engagement in groups with low utilization.</cite>
- Risk stratification and interventions: Predictive grouping supports outreach design (texting, transport assistance, care managers) to the highest deciles of risk, and informs communication channel selection for online materials; in EHR-integrated deployments, prioritization within workflows is a driver of adoption and effectiveness.<cite id="ab413d0c-0">Stratifying no-show risk enables targeted outreach to high-risk deciles, optimizing intervention allocation.</cite> <cite id="847a78e0-1">AI integrated in EHRs supports hospital-level prioritization and proactive follow-up, reflecting operational integration of predictions.</cite>

Ethical, fairness, and governance considerations
- Bias and generalization: Deep learning on heterogeneous online/clinical data can inherit bias if underrepresented groups are poorly sampled; fairness-aware evaluation (group-wise AUC, calibration) and data augmentation across language, literacy, and device strata mitigate disparate false-negative rates in outreach.<cite id="847a78e0-5">Deep learning models can yield biased predictions when data are heterogeneous; models must be audited and adapted for fairness across populations.</cite> <cite id="71ea96be-3">Improving electronic patient portal use in groups with low utilization requires tailored strategies and attention to inequities, not only algorithms.</cite>
- Privacy and consent: Linking EHRs with behavioral telemetry raises privacy concerns; organizations should adopt de‑identification, consent-aware telemetry, and federated/secure aggregation; guidance stresses training data quality and representativeness to avoid skewed risk estimates (e.g., over/underestimating outcomes in protected groups).<cite id="ab413d0dc-7">Training data for machine learning to enhance patient-centered outcomes requires careful attention to data quality and precision metrics; model precision differences by subgroup highlight risks of skewed estimates, underscoring the need for representative data and audits.</cite> <cite id="847a78e0-0">An ML model that predicts portal access on an integrated dataset requires governance to ensure privacy-preserving pipelines and fair deployment.</cite>
- Transparency and clinician trust: Hospital adoption of predictive AI has risen, but successful deployment depends on clear documentation, clinician validation, and governance frameworks with oversight and auditability for high-stakes decisions affecting information delivery and care coordination.<cite id="847a78e0-1">71% of hospitals reported using predictive AI integrated with the EHR... emphasizing the need for governance and oversight in clinical workflows.</cite>
- Digital divide mitigation: Predictive programs must not exacerbate inequities; building in literacy- and language-sensitive content delivery, device compatibility, and culturally tailored nudges addresses digital literacy gaps and supports equitable use of services.<cite id="02ba9654-3">Health literacy and language barriers are associated with lower portal engagement, requiring literacy- and language-aware strategies to improve usage.</cite> <cite id="02ba9654-6">eHealth literacy definitions emphasize evaluation and application of information, supporting design of training components to mitigate digital divides.</cite>

Practical checklist for predicting and improving usage
- Define behaviors precisely (first portal login within 30 days, note-viewing within 7 days, appointment completion, etc.), capture time-to-event and repeat behavior, and track proxies (message open rates, app downloads) with EHR joins for causal links to utilization.<cite id="ab413d0c-0">EHR-linked modeling of no-show risk clarifies pathways from risk stratification to intervention planning.</cite> <cite id="847a78e0-4">Combining access with activity measures (viewed results/notes) refines behavioral targets.</cite>
- Assemble features: demographics, diagnoses/medications, utilization history, socioeconomic, device/smartphone app use, language, literacy measures and eHealth literacy scales; for online search, integrate query-topic modeling proxies and trust/source attributes when available.<cite id="02ba9654-2">Determinants include health literacy, language, and access to digital tools, guiding feature design for usage models.</cite> <cite id="02ba9654-1">eHealth literacy mediates the effect of online health seeking on engagement, warranting inclusion of literacy indicators.</cite>
- Choose models: start with gradient boosting/logistic models for interpretability and baseline AUC/accuracy; add deep learning only where nonlinearity and long-term sequences justify complexity; ensure subgroup calibration checks.<cite id="847a78e0-5">Deep learning offers power but must be used judiciously to avoid bias; simpler models may suffice and are easier to audit.</cite>
- Validate clinically: use cross-site validation, recalibrate event probabilities, and quantify utility via controlled rollouts (e.g., incremental adherence gains from tailored outreach and nudges).<cite id="ab413d0c-0">Evidence-based models show stratified performance and actionable risk clusters, enabling controlled deployment and recalibration.</cite> <cite id="ab413d0c-6">Track engagement outcomes from predictive interventions to validate marginal gains.</cite>
- Operationalize: integrate predictions into care managers’ dashboards, automate reminders/channels based on predicted barriers (language, literacy), and deploy in trusted EHR workflows; monitor equity metrics and adjust thresholds for low-usage strata.<cite id="847a78e0-1">EHR-integrated AI supports deployment of predictions within clinical workflows, enhancing prioritization.</cite> <cite id="71ea96be-3">Practice-level interventions tailored to low-usage strata demonstrate meaningful gains.</cite>
- Govern responsibly: implement privacy-by-design (de-identification, consent-aware sampling), conduct fairness and explainability audits, and align with organizational AI governance to maintain clinician trust and regulatory compliance.<cite id="847a78e0-1">Hospital AI governance frameworks reflect adoption trends and emphasize oversight of predictive deployments.</cite> <cite id="847a78e0-5">Bias and data heterogeneity risk biased predictions; governance should include bias-aware evaluation.</cite>

Takeaways for building better usage predictors
- Stronger models integrate both clinical risk and digital literacy/behavioral telemetry; determinants like eHealth literacy, language, and prior engagement are as important as diagnoses and demographics, and should be core features.<cite id="02ba9654-1">Higher eHealth literacy amplifies the positive effect of online health seeking on engagement outcomes.</cite> <cite id="ab413d0c-0">Risk- and behavior-stratified models improve targeting and clinical value beyond traditional demographics.</cite>
- Expect mature operational patterns: hospitals increasingly embed EHR-linked predictive analytics; successful usage prediction improves when coupled with human-in-the-loop outreach and literacy-aware design rather than deployed as static risk scores.<cite id="847a78e0-1">Use of predictive AI integrated in EHRs has risen, reflecting the operational maturity needed to act on predictions.</cite> <cite id="71ea96be-3">Improving portal use in low-utilization groups hinges on tailored practice-level strategies aligned with digital literacy interventions.</cite>
- Mitigate failure modes: validate subgroup fairness, calibrate time-to-event predictions, and invest in data quality/consent pipelines to avoid skewed risk estimates and privacy risks, especially in multilingual, heterogeneous populations.<cite id="ab413d0c-7">Attention to training data quality and subgroup precision emphasizes avoiding skewed estimates that can arise in predictive healthcare models.</cite> <cite id="847a78e0-5">Deep learning models are sensitive to biased or heterogeneous data and must be audited to prevent discriminatory predictions.</cite>

Illustrative, validated examples
- Predicting portal access: An EHR-integrated cohort using machine learning predicted which patients would access online medical records, with actionable segments for onboarding and follow‑up to increase actual use after enrollment.<cite id="847a78e0-0">Using a Machine Learning Algorithm to Predict Online Patient Portal Access... [the study shows cohort curation, ML training, and deployment considerations].</cite>
- Predicting no-shows and engagement: Large health systems use evidence-based ML to separate high- vs. low‑risk non‑attenders, enabling targeted reminders, care manager follow‑up, and transportation support before visits, which improves downstream engagement metrics.<cite id="ab413d0c-0">An evidence-based predictive model for patient no-shows... supports targeted outreach to high-risk patients.</cite> <cite id="ab413d0c-2">Models using multi-source data provide decision basis for reducing no-shows via tailored reminders and counseling.</cite>
- Predicting utilization categories: New predictive scores and deep models forecast annual primary care utilization and portal engagement categories, guiding proactive scheduling strategies and capacity planning.<cite id="847a78e0-3">The Friedman Score predicts estimated yearly primary care utilization categories with ML, enabling proactive care planning and engagement strategies.</cite>
- Population-level usage patterns: National HealthIT data show that among those accessing their portal, result and note viewing are common, but gaps remain for subgroups—underscoring predictive modeling’s role in identifying and reducing inequities.<cite id="847a78e0-4">In 2022, 90% of individuals who accessed their portal viewed results and 70% viewed notes, revealing high engagement but persistent unmet needs for additional usage behaviors.</cite>

Limitations and open problems
- Many published models report class-separation and point estimates without subgroup calibration, and online behavioral data (queries, app logs) are often sparse or siloed; future work should integrate cross-platform telemetry with EHRs under privacy-preserving frameworks and include longitudinal personalization to model evolving literacy and trust.<cite id="71ea96be-2">Patient portal engagement varies by patient characteristics at older ages; granular subgroup calibration remains a challenge for practitioners.</cite> <cite id="847a78e0-5">Deep learning models trained on heterogeneous clinical and online data risk biased predictions unless calibrated and audited across strata.</cite>
- Measuring external validity and fairness requires continuous drift monitoring; as population demographics and telehealth infrastructure shift, models must retrain on timely data and incorporate community-level digital equity indicators.<cite id="ab413d0c-7">Precision differences by subgroup highlight the need for ongoing audit and data representativeness as models move from development to deployment.</cite>
