without_scope.text: My goal is to have a large generative machine learning model be good at reasoning with spatial dimensions to help with building 3d scenes. This includes positioning and orienting objects well in a 3d environment. This could include use a large language model, a large multimodal model, or a large video generation model. The current approach I am taking is to develop a dataset with correct input and output using a top down view of a scene and position and orientating objects correctly. However, it is a manual tedious task and would prefer more automated synthetic generation approach. The end goal could be either to fine tune any of the models specified for this type of task. There has been a lot of recent findings of the benefits of reasoning with chain-of-thought (CoT). Use recent research to suggest a few automated approaches.
without_scope.answer:
Below are several recent, research-backed, automated directions to scale high-quality 3D scene positioning and orientation while leveraging chain-of-thought (CoT)-style reasoning. I group them into: (A) annotation-lean synthetic pipelines, (B) CoT-bridged planners for spatial decomposition, (C) language-conditioned editors and layout diffusion, and (D) physics/affordance-aware and self-supervised alignment. Each includes concrete steps you can adopt and where to fine-tune.

A1) Scale supervision with large, synthetic 3D scene datasets
- Start from room- and object-rich synthetic scene corpora with detailed per-object positions/orientations so your model does not require manual labeling from scratch. OptiScene’s 3D-SynthPlace provides nearly 17,000 scenes across bedrooms, living rooms, kitchens, and bathrooms with diverse objects and associated layouts, enabling supervised pretraining or weakly supervised bootstrapping of placement policies and orientation priors. Use this as the backbone for scaling training data and room-type priors, then adapt downstream to your domain (e.g., factories, homes) <cite id="4eee09d3-2">3D-SynthPlace contains nearly 17,000 scenes, covering four common room types—bedroom, living room, kitchen, and bathroom—enriched with diverse objects.
- Curate a growing asset and layout library; surveys on 3D scene generation emphasize that layout acts as an intermediate representation bridging language to detailed appearance and geometry, and 3D-aware generative architectures target controllable placement for object positioning. You can exploit this by pairing a language-conditioned layout generator with a renderer and a per-object pose regression head (diffusion or MLP). <cite id="4eee09d3-1">Neural 3D-based generation employs 3D-aware generative architectures to synthesize scene layouts for object placement</cite> <cite id="4eee09d3-3">In text-driven 3D scene generation, object layout serves as a crucial intermediate representation that bridges high-level language instructions with detailed</cite> <cite id="4eee09d3-6">Recent advances in static 3D object and scene generation review cutting-edge methods and provide taxonomies for controllability and placement</cite>.
- For domains like factories or industrial spaces, automatic synthetic data generation is emphasized as essential for data-driven 3D vision applications, which aligns with your goal of avoiding manual 2D pose annotation. <cite id="4eee09d3-4">Automatic synthetic data generation is highlighted as crucial for 3D computer vision tasks, especially for developing data-driven applications in complex environments like brownfield factories</cite>.
- If you need building-scale realism, surveys and systems like LAMP advocate controllable, data-efficient 3D generation for exploration, dataset generation, and optimization, which can reduce per-scene annotation costs while maintaining fidelity. <cite id="4eee09d3-7">LAMP advances controllable, data-efficient, and safe 3D generation for design exploration, dataset generation, and performance-driven optimization</cite>.

Action plan:
- Build a procedural generator over a corpus of room scene graphs and object catalogs; render top-down orthographic projections alongside 3D views. Train a supervised head mapping language instructions to 2D/3D poses (regression + rotation angles) on synthetic data; then fine-tune on a small curated in-domain set to adapt to your environment.

A2) Add physics/affordance-aware placement to improve realism
- Incorporate simple physics constraints (collisions/occupancy, vertical stacking limits, surface compatibility) into your pose optimizer. 3D scene generation methods emphasize that realistic and reasonable placement requires explicit priors and regularization beyond raw diffusion; enforcing spatial constraints (e.g., minimum spacing, no overlap, orientation constraints by surface normal) improves plausibility. <cite id="6cd550f1-1">Methods aim at realistic and reasonable 3D indoor scenes from scene graphs by enriching priors and adding explicit regularization</cite>.
- Use object-category-specific orientation priors (e.g., fridges mostly upright, rugs flat on floors, artworks hung vertically). Layout-conditioned scene generation (Layout2Scene) improves plausibility by leveraging 3D semantics and spatial relations in the scene graph prior. <cite id="6cd550f1-3">Layout2Scene shows that 3D semantic layout-guided generation yields more plausible and realistic scenes than state-of-the-art baselines</cite>.

Action plan:
- Augment your synthetic training pipeline with a constraint solver that disposes candidate poses for collisions and out-of-surface rotations; sample via diffusion or GAN-based placement and then project to feasible poses. Optionally train a small policy network to rank candidate layouts using simple physics features.

B) CoT-bridged spatial planners: decompose language into stepwise pose edits
- Direct Numerical Layout Generation for 3D Indoor Scenes shows that enabling explicit spatial reasoning and grasping basic placement principles can be achieved by CoT activation, which exposes intermediate placement rationales and constraints. <cite id="15901450-0">Explicit spatial reasoning and basic principles of object placement are enabled by employing Chain-of-Thought (CoT) activation in 3D layout generation</cite> <cite id="15901450-5">Chain-of-Thought is employed to help the model grasp basic principles of object placement in 3D-indoor scenes</cite>.
- Spatial Chain-of-Thought explicitly bridges spatial planning from an MLLM to a diffusion-based generation model via an intermediate chain of edits, allowing language to ground stepwise placement decisions before rendering. <cite id="15901450-1">Spatial Chain-of-Thought bridges spatial planning and reasoning from an MLLM to a diffusion-based generation model via an explicit chain-of-thought intermediate</cite>.
- 3D-Layout-R1 releases 15k scenes with language instructions, intermediate CoT graph edits, and target layouts. You can emulate this by training an instruction-conditioned edit planner that outputs per-object delta positions/orientations as a CoT “proof” which you then execute through a layout synthesizer and renderer. <cite id="15901450-4">A dataset of 15k 3D scenes pairs natural language instructions with intermediate chain-of-thought graph edits and target layouts</cite> <cite id="15901450-7">This dataset enables training and evaluating structured reasoning for language-instructed spatial editing</cite>.
- CVPR 2025 shows LLM-guided spatial knowledge can enhance layout generation quality for object rearrangement and text-to-image tasks, supporting the idea of using LLMs to emit coordinate deltas or relational edits that a renderer executes. <cite id="15901450-2">A Spatial Knowledge–Enhanced Layout Generation with LLMs framework improves accuracy and fine-grained layouts for rear- ranging and text-to-image tasks</cite>.
- SpatialCoT reports that CoT-style intermediate reasoning improves a model’s ability to use spatial and contextual information, which is exactly what you need to turn vague language into precise top-down positions and orientations. <cite id="15901450-3">Chain-of-thought intermediate steps significantly enhance utilization of spatial and contextual information</cite>.

Action plan:
- Design an “Edit-then-Render” loop where your MLLM outputs a CoT-style sequence of primitive actions (place X at (x,y) with rotation r next to Y on surface S; avoid Z; stack K on top of L if supported), encoded as relative coordinates/orientations. Use a diffusion-based layouter or a parametric placer to convert these edits to pixel-accurate top-down poses; finally render the 3D scene to verify constraints and update the CoT policy with feedback. This mirrors 3D-Layout-R1’s structure and leverages LLM spatial knowledge. <cite id="15901450-4">3D-Layout-R1 supplies language instructions with intermediate reasoning edits and target layouts</cite> <cite id="15901450-2">LLM-enhanced spatial knowledge improves layout precision and fine-grained placement</cite>.

B1) How to automate the CoT from language to poses
- Use an open-vocabulary scene understanding module to ground named objects and relations; LLM-enhanced graph priors regularize placement and solve missing-object completion. <cite id="6cd550f1-1">LLM-enhanced graph priors over scene graphs regularize and complete realistic 3D scenes</cite>.
- For faster iteration, adopt LLplace, which directly activates an LLM’s capability to understand 3D layouts and perform dynamic scene editing (add/remove/position objects), and instrument it to output JSON poses per your pipeline rather than just visual previews. <cite id="6cd550f1-0">LLplace enables activation of the LLM’s ability to understand 3D layouts and perform dynamic scene editing for adding and removing objects</cite>.

Action plan:
- Fine-tune an LLM/MM on your in-domain instruction corpus to emit JSON edits: object id/category, target 2D xy in top-down, rotation, relation constraints (left-of, aligned-with), and surface references. Use your renderer to convert top-down to 3D poses via projection and surface normals; validate through collision checks.

C) Language-conditioned layout diffusion and scene synthesis
- Layout2Scene and related layout-conditioned scene generation place priors on object relations and semantics such that generated layouts are more plausible and realistic; you can couple this with a diffusion-based detailer to add appearance and fine-tune object positions/orientations for natural composition. <cite id="6cd550f1-3">Layout2Scene uses 3D semantic layout to guide scene generation and achieves more plausible and realistic results vs. SOTA</cite>.
- Surveys emphasize that diffusing in 3D-aware or mesh-conditioned space, and conditioning on room layouts, improves controllability of placement and orientation; consider training a layout-to-scene diffusion model on synthetic data and then fine-tuning from top-down supervisions. <cite id="6cd550f1-2">Mesh-conditioned image diffusion for navigable multi-room 3D scenes is part of the 3D scene understanding pipeline</cite> <cite id="4eee09d3-1">3D-aware generative architectures synthesize scene layouts for object placement</cite>.

Action plan:
- Train a diffusion-based scene placer on synthetic scenes that receive language-conditioned layout latent codes. During training, regress 2D top-down heatmaps for object centering and 1-hot rotation classes; for realism, add GAN/ID losses or 3D consistency checks between orthographic and perspective views. Use your instruction set to align labels with language semantics.

C1) End-to-end tool-augmented editors with CoT traces
- Incorporate an LLM/MM tool-use stack that calls a scene editor API (e.g., LLplace) with intermediate visibility and collision feedback. Record the tool-call traces as a CoT artifact and use supervised contrastive learning to align the model’s internal reasoning to the emitted pose edits, as done in 3D-Layout-R1. <cite id="15901450-4">Providing language instructions, chain-of-thought edits, and target layouts enables training and evaluation of structured reasoning for spatial editing</cite>.
- For video-oriented control, extend the CoT sequence over time (sequential poses for dynamic placement) and use diffusion planners for target-oriented steps, analogous to DiffTOD’s planning with diffusion language models (though in dialogue, the same stepwise, constrained generation idea applies). <cite id="15901450-4">3D-Layout-R1 provides structured chain reasoning per instruction to compute target layouts</cite> <cite id="6cd550f1-4">Diffusion-based planning frameworks can produce target-oriented step sequences from language</cite>.

Action plan:
- Provide your LLM/MM an action dictionary and feedback channel to the scene graph: after issuing an “add/plant X at …” action, you report success/failure (collision/visibility), and the model learns to revise subsequent steps. Store the traces as CoT logs and use them to train a supervised decoder that outputs pose JSONs directly.

D) Weak/unsupervised alignment from 2D top-down supervision
- Use your small curated set of correct top-down layouts plus ground-truth poses to align a diffusion or GAN-based placer via contrastive learning: forward pass renders a candidate top-down view; compute a loss between the rendered 2D layout and the target image for each object, plus rotation losses. This aligns latent directions with spatial axes; surveys show this is necessary to bridge high-level language to detailed layouts. <cite id="4eee09d3-3">Object layout is the key intermediate bridging high-level language instructions to detailed scene appearance</cite>.
- Self-supervise via spatial consistency: randomly permute or rotate objects in a synthetic scene, render, and train your model to detect when a perturbed layout looks wrong relative to the instruction. Add a teacher-student setup where a coarse placer emits boxes and a fine-tuning diffusion model refines positions/orientations. <cite id="6cd550f1-1">Scene-graph-based priors and explicit regularizations improve realism when object relations and placement are constrained</cite>.

Action plan:
- Start with a simple coordinate-aligned projector that converts top-down pixel coordinates to 3D surface positions; use surface normals to constrain rotations. For each language→pose pair, render a proxy scene and compute a composite 2D-3D consistency score; backprop into the placer/diffusion head.

E) Putting it together: training recipes for LLM/MM/Video models

1) LLM/MM instruction-to-scene fine-tuning
- Pretrain or initialize the text encoder on your instruction corpus; add a small MLP/RNN state that emits per-object pose deltas (xy, rotation, depth bin). Precondition the CoT reasoning graph with a planner that emits primitive actions, and use LLplace or a custom renderer to execute actions and return a reward signal (layout quality, collisions). <cite id="6cd550f1-0">LLplace demonstrates an LLM-based editor that handles adding/removing objects, enabling dynamic scene changes</cite> <cite id="15901450-1">Chain-of-Thought linking an MLLM to a diffusion generator with explicit intermediate edits</cite>.
- Training targets: masked coordinate regression loss, rotation classification, and a global scene graph regularization loss to discourage overlap and enforce room semantics. <cite id="6cd550f1-1">Adding explicit regularization on scene-graph–derived relations improves realism and reasonableness</cite>.

2) CoT-activated layout diffusion
- Train a diffusion placer conditioned on language tokens and a frozen 3D scene graph layout. Use your synthetic scenes to generate multiple candidates per instruction; select top-N for supervised contrastive alignment to your top-down ground truth. Then fine-tune a smaller pose regressor on your dataset to reduce diffusion inference cost. <cite id="6cd550f1-3">Layout-conditioned generation yields better plausibility, enabling supervised refinement to 2D targets</cite> <cite id="4eee09d3-3">Layout as the intermediate representation supports aligning high-level text to low-level spatial details</cite>.

3) Physics-aware self-play editing
- Implement an environment where an LLM/MM proposes edits; a physics engine or collision checker votes on feasibility; the model is rewarded for edits that produce collision-free, visually plausible scenes matching the instruction. Iteratively collect accepted edit histories as CoT corpora and render top-down views as side data for contrastive supervision. <cite id="15901450-0">Chain-of-Thought activations expose reasoning that helps enforce placement principles</cite> <cite id="6cd550f1-1">Regularization and priors on relational layout make scenes realistic</cite>.

4) Domain-specific scaling
- For industrial/factory scenes, adapt synthetic generators to equipment footprints, clearances, and pipelines. Leverage LLM knowledge in layout graphs and train orientation priors per equipment type; then fine-tune with your top-down data and collision constraints. <cite id="4eee09d3-4">Automatic synthetic data generation is crucial for 3D vision tasks in complex industrial settings</cite>.

F) Concrete starter baselines and datasets to borrow

- Use LLplace as a differentiable or API-backed scene editor inside your pipeline, recording CoT JSONs for training. <cite id="6cd550f1-0">LLplace enables LLM to understand 3D layouts and edit scenes dynamically</cite>.
- Build on OptiScene/3D-SynthPlace for room- and object-conditioned scene graphs; convert their scene JSONs to your instruction set and render top-down views for weak supervision. <cite id="4eee09d3-2">3D-SynthPlace provides large-scale room-scene data with diverse objects</cite>.
- Emulate 3D-Layout-R1 by pairing an instruction-conditioned CoT planner with a layout renderer; store traces as labels for supervised finetuning. <cite id="15901450-4">3D-Layout-R1 pairs language instructions with CoT edit graphs and target layouts</cite>.

without_preference.text: How can I improve a large generative machine learning model’s ability to reason about spatial dimensions for building 3D film scenes, including positioning and orienting objects in a 3D environment? I am considering using a large language model, a large multimodal model, or a large video generation model. I currently have a movie scene dataset and am developing a dataset with correct input-output pairs using a top-down view of a scene, but manual creation is tedious, so I want more automated synthetic generation approaches. The goal is to fine-tune one of these model types for this task. Use recent research to suggest a few automated approaches.
without_preference.answer:
Below are practical, research-backed strategies to improve spatial reasoning for placing and orienting objects in 3D film scenes, with automated synthetic data generation and fine-tuning recipes for large language/multimodal/video models. I group options by model type, then give end-to-end synthetic generation pipelines and evaluation guidance tied to your top-down 2.5D inputs.

Quick orientation
- If you want text-only or text+image control, train or adapt text-driven 3D scene synthesis/editing models that generate object positions/orientations and then render views for supervision or direct 3D outputs. <cite id="01901c6f-0">ReSpace is a text-driven autoregressive 3D indoor scene synthesis and editing framework that conditions on an orthographic/top-down view</cite>. <cite id="01901c6f-2">DirectLayout synthesizes 3D layouts directly from text via explicit numerical coordinates, encoding generalizable spatial reasoning</cite>. <cite id="01901c6f-1">“CoT reasoning into 3D scene synthesis” connects chain-of-thought reasoning to spatial planning and uses reinforcement learning to improve placement quality</cite>. <cite id="01901c6f-7">SpatialGen takes a 3D semantic layout and produces photo-realistic scenes conditioned on text or image prompts</cite>. These directly cover positioning/orientation and offer text-conditioned control.

Approach A: Autoregressive or diffusion-based text→3D scene synthesis with 2.5D supervision
- Why this helps: The model learns spatial relations (left/right/along wall/center), occlusion-aware bounding boxes, and 6D object poses, which you can use to initialize film-scene setups.
- Concrete methods:
  - Text-to-3D layout + 6D pose optimization: <cite id="01901c6f-0">ReSpace generates scenes autoregressively from text and an orthographic (top-down) view and supports editing</cite>. You can use your top-down frames as context or as the target render to invert into placement/orientation labels.
  - Numerical layout planners: <cite id="01901c6f-2">DirectLayout outputs numerical 3D layouts directly from text, enabling explicit constraints (distances, alignment) for supervised pretraining</cite>. If you have rules (fireplace must be centered on the wall), encode them as reward functions or hard constraints in CoT+RL training.
  - Photo-realistic rendering from layout: <cite id="01901c6f-7">SpatialGen renders photo-realistic scenes from semantic layouts conditioned on text/images</cite>; combine with your top-down supervision to align synthetic 3D placements to 2.5D ground truth.
  - Language-embedded 3D Gaussians for semantics: <cite id="4d8a1437-5">Language-Embedded Gaussian Splat (LEGS) encodes both appearance and semantics in 3D Gaussians, supporting language-conditioned scenes</cite>. This lets you tie textual object relations (the lamp is next to the sofa) to specific Gaussians for supervision and downstream retrieval in 3D.
- Automatic synthetic data recipes:
  1) Prompt-based generation: Sample diverse text prompts from film sets (e.g., “dining room with table for four, chandelier centered above, wine glass to lower right of each plate”). <cite id="01901c6f-2">Use DirectLayout to get numerical 3D positions/orientations</cite>, then render RGB/orthographic views and save per-object 6D poses and object IDs for supervision. <cite id="01901c6f-0">For photorealism, post-process layouts with SpatialGen</cite>.
  2) Top-down inversion: Given a top-down frame, run superpixel/instance segmentation and use 6D pose estimators on novel categories. <cite id="4d8a1437-0">GS2Pose leverages 3D Gaussian splatting for robust 6D pose estimation of novel objects</cite>. You can initialize object Gaussians from your top-down segments and lift them into 3D with estimated poses; then perturb and optimize with spatial rules.
  3) CoT+RL policy for spatial planning: <cite id="01901c6f-1">Insert chain-of-thought reasoning steps that parse relative relations into constraints and use RL for placement quality</cite>. Train a policy on your dataset’s spatial relation labels (e.g., “X aligned with Y top edge”, “distance(A,B)=2m along wall”) to generate plausible, story-accurate compositions.
- Conditioning on 2.5D views: <cite id="01901c6f-0">Top-down orthographic conditioning is supported in ReSpace</cite>. For diffusion-based methods, you can project 3D Gaussians to 2.5D billboards and use L2 loss to match your clean top-down GT, or use semantic masks from top-down to guide which objects should occupy which grid cells.
- If you use video/dynamic camera: <cite id="6e3c3c4d-0">AC3D analyzes and improves 3D camera control in video diffusion transformers, enabling precise manipulation via first-principles insights</cite>. <cite id="6e3c3c4d-3">VD3D tames video transformers for 3D camera control via ControlNet-like spatiotemporal camera embeddings</cite>. These give conditioning vectors for camera path design around the laid-out scene.

Approach B: Diffusion/NeRF/3DGS pipelines with orthographic 2.5D supervision and language semantics
- Why this helps: You get photorealistic views for conditioning and evaluation, while retaining a forward model (Gaussians/NeRFs) to invert from top-down supervision to 3D poses.
- Key ingredients:
  - 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) as the 3D scene prior: <cite id="4d8a1437-7">Video Gaussian representations can be supervised by RGB frames with 2D-to-3D orthographic projection</cite>. This lets you render multi-view GT-consistent supervision from a single top-down input by projecting segments/edges.
  - Language-embedded splats for object identity/orientation coupling: <cite id="4d8a1437-5">LEGS maps language to specific splats, making it easier to enforce “place the bookshelf to the left of the bed facing viewers” at training time</cite>.
  - General-purpose catalogs: <cite id="4d8a1437-2">Surveyed lists show numerous works where 3DGS is used for pose estimation and supervision in single-view/limited-view setups</cite>, and <cite id="4d8a1437-8">pose-free 3DGS from sparse views indicates you can bootstrap with a small number of input frames, then expand via diffusion</cite>.
- Synthetic data recipes:
  1) Prompt-and-place synthesis: Sample scene/room prompts; run a layout generator to get bounding boxes and relative relations; instantiate 3D Gaussians with per-object semantic tags; render the top-down view and compute segmentation/pose GT; <cite id="4d8a1437-7">use 2D-3D orthographic projection to generate multi-view supervision that matches your 2.5D frames</cite>.
  2) Top-down-driven scene rebuilding: <cite id="4d8a1437-5">Use LEGS to seed Gaussians from language (object list + relative placements)</cite>; constrain initial splat positions using top-down masks; run diffusion over poses/rotation to fit occlusion and spacing; render final 3D views.
  3) Weakly supervise with constraints: Augment per-object attraction/repulsion fields learned from your dataset: for every pair of objects, train latent diffusion with terms that pull or keep-away based on predicted relation labels; <cite id="4d8a1437-7">orthographic projections ensure the rendered views match your 2.5D supervision</cite>.

Approach C: Instruction-conditioned spatial manipulation with LMMs and embodied simulators
- Why this helps: You can fine-tune an LMM or LVM to parse spatial relations and produce JSON poses, then render views for supervision or directly drive a 3D engine.
- Concrete scaffolds:
  - Text planners with physics: <cite id="01901c6f-2">DirectLayout converts relative descriptions into numerical layouts</cite>; couple it with a physics engine to reject penetrations and enforce wall adjacency. <cite id="01901c6f-1">Chain-of-thought reasoning can be guided by spatial axioms (min distance to wall, alignment) and then optimized via RL</cite>.
  - Photo-realistic rendering loop: <cite id="01901c6f-7">Use SpatialGen to render scenes from semantic layouts</cite> to create rich training data where text→layout→render gives you both labels and visuals.
  - Multimodal LMM conditioning: Train an LMM to predict camera intrinsics/extrinsics jointly with scene layout; for the camera side, <cite id="6e3c3c4d-3">VD3D adds ControlNet-like camera conditioning to video DiTs with spatiotemporal embeddings</cite>, so your model can accept text and spatial-layout boxes and output camera path + scene poses in one generative pass.
- Data: Build pairs of instruction texts and correct top-down views plus per-object 6D pose lists. Use <cite id="4d8a1437-0">GS2Pose</cite> or a 3D object detector to back-annotate new categories in your dataset, then add synthetic augmentations with relative-geometry noise. If motion is needed, sample camera poses along walls at shoulder height using the 2D top-down masks as collision maps.

Approach D: Fine-tuning recipes for LLM, LMM, or LVM
- LLM for scene planning (text-only):
  - Train a supervised fine-tuning objective (e.g., Causal LM) on prompt–plan–pose sequences: prompt → CoT layout text → numerical JSON (positions/orientations). <cite id="01901c6f-1">Chain-of-thought plus RL has shown improved spatial planning in 3D scene synthesis</cite>. Evaluate by checking semantic layout validity, penetration-free slots, and matching top-down view segmentation.
- LMM for text→3D scene:
  - Use a frozen vision encoder plus a scene decoder; train on pairs of <image-condition: top-down view + per-pixel labels> → <text instruction> → <pose labels>. <cite id="01901c6f-0">Top-down orthographic conditioning from ReSpace shows feasibility of lifting 2D views to 3D edits</cite>. <cite id="01901c6f-7">Semantic-layout-conditioned photorealism from SpatialGen can be used either as final renderer or to supervise geometry realism</cite>. <cite id="4d8a1437-5">LEGS supports language-to-3D splat mappings, enabling direct language supervision on object-level placement/orientation</cite>.
- LVM (video diffusion) for scenes with motion/camera:
  - Start with a video DiT; condition with per-frame 2D top-down supervision and spatiotemporal camera embeddings. <cite id="6e3c3c4d-3">VD3D uses ControlNet-like conditioning and spatiotemporal camera embeddings to control 3D camera</cite>. <cite id="6e3c3c4d-0">AC3D analyzes and improves 3D camera controllability for pre-trained video diffusion models, enabling precise manipulation with joint text+camera conditioning</cite>. For static scenes, you can freeze time and optimize pose+camera; for moving camera, generate paths from top-down occlusion dynamics.
- Cross-attention for spatial relations: Add a spatial module that cross-attends over object boxes (from top-down) and object embeddings; during forward pass, enforce pairwise constraints based on predicted relation tokens (left/right/along/opposite), using L2 losses on 3D box centers/dihedral angles and orthographic projections to the top-down target views. <cite id="4d8a1437-7">Orthographic supervision in video Gaussians provides a direct loss to align generated views to your 2.5D GT</cite>.

Approach E: Weak/unsupervised alignment from a single top-down frame
- Object proposal + pose prior: Segment your top-down frame; treat each segment as a latent object; initialize 3D Gaussians with random poses on the floor/walls and run diffusion on pose+rotation under orthographic loss to the input view. <cite id="4d8a1437-7">Orthographic projection supervision aligns rendered views to the 2D input</cite>, while <cite id="4d8a1437-2">3DGS catalogs show the supervision is effective even with sparse views</cite>. Add pairwise “not overlapping” and “align-to-walls” potentials learned from a small labeled seed set.
- Language tie-ins: If you have a small set of annotated relations, <cite id="4d8a1437-5">LEGS lets you bind words like “left of” to vector offsets/dihedral priors</cite>, which you can then extrapolate to unlabeled scenes via diffusion priors.

Data efficiency levers and benchmarks
- Surveys and resources: <cite id="01901c6f-3">A curated “awesome 3D scene generation” list summarizes over 300 works with downstream applications</cite>, which helps choose baselines and augmentations. <cite id="4d8a1437-5">LEGS’ dataset includes language-embedded 3D Gaussians and is useful for transfer or as pretraining data for semantics in 3D</cite>. <cite id="01901c6f-4">HuggingFace collections tag “3D indoor scene synthesis,” providing ready-made corpora and pipelines</cite>.
- Layout reasoning: <cite id="01901c6f-1">Direct Numerical Layout Generation integrates CoT reasoning with reinforcement learning to enhance spatial planning</cite>. Treat that as an option for your pretraining or inference policy if you can afford RL during training.
- Embodied simulators: If you adopt an LMM/LVM, leverage physics-based simulators for collision checking and plausible adjacency (bedroom: bed against wall, parallel to ceiling beams). <cite id="01901c6f-7">SpatialGen’s photo-realistic forward pass can render the simulator’s layout for supervision</cite>.
- Evaluation: For static spatial reasoning, compute 3D overlap/penetration, distance-to-wall/edge, and alignment scores versus the top-down GT and the generated view; for camera, use projection error to top-down frames and angular deviation for camera headings. For instruction following, use exact-match and relation-matrix F1 over predicted vs. ground-truth pairwise relations. For film scenes, add aesthetic and composition metrics by comparing against curated set examples and a human short-form RAG verifier.

Putting it all together: a 12–24 month practical path
1) Core stack selection:
   - If you want fastest progress with camera paths and photorealistic renders: choose a video DiT with 3DGS or video Gaussians as the latent prior; add spatiotemporal camera conditioning. <cite id="6e3c3c4d-3">VD3D’s ControlNet-like conditioning and</cite> <cite id="6e3c3c4d-0">AC3D’s 3D camera analysis</cite> give controllability.
   - If you prefer text- and layout-centric control with fewer moving parts: pick <cite id="01901c6f-0">ReSpace</cite> or <cite id="01901c6f-2">DirectLayout</cite>, synthesize layouts, render with <cite id="01901c6f-7">SpatialGen</cite>, and fine-tune an LMM on prompt→JSON→render loop.
2) Synthetic data generation:
   - Seed small labeled sets: annotate 100–500 top-down shots with per-object boxes and relative relations; generate additional labels with CoT+RL or diffusion over constraints. <cite id="01901c6f-1">CoT+RL improves spatial planning</cite>; <cite id="4d8a1437-7">orthographic projection losses align 3D to 2.5D</cite>; <cite id="4d8a1437-5">LEGS ties language to specific splats to enforce orientation</cite>.
   - Scale via prompt diversity and top-down inversion: <cite id="4d8a1437-0">GS2Pose estimates 6D poses for novel objects from images</cite> to bootstrap categories quickly; apply inversion on your top-down frames.
3) Training:
   - Jointly optimize object layout (distance, alignment), orientation (dihedral), and camera pose (translation, heading, pitch limits): use orthographic L2 to 2.5D GT, AABB/OSBB penetration losses, and small pairwise repulsive forces; for video, add motion-blur consistent losses between consecutive frames. <cite id="4d8a1437-7">Orthographic supervision in video Gaussians supports multi-view consistency</cite>, and <cite id="6e3c3c4d-3">spatiotemporal camera embeddings enable controllable motion</cite>.
4) Inference and pipeline:
   - Prompt the model with scene text, optionally show a top-down image; sample a layout or refine poses via a policy that uses scene semantics and top-down masks as collision/attraction fields; render candidate views and select nearest neighbors; apply AC3D/VD3D camera control to design a path around the set.
5) Evaluation/iteration:
   - Automated metrics as above; for creatives, crowdsource “compositional quality” and “spatial accuracy.” Add a retrieval module that matches textual descriptions to 3D Gaussians using <cite id="4d8a1437-5">LEGS language bindings</cite>. Periodically re-render with updated camera modules and retrain the policy with new human feedback.

What to fine-tune, and when
- Fine-tune an LLM for spatial planning if you can accept moderate runtime; use its plan→JSON to seed 3D generators. <cite id="01901c6f-1">CoT+RL improves quality</cite> and can be trained on your dataset’s spatial relation labels.
- Fine-tune an LMM if you want end-to-end text→3D with camera control. <cite id="01901c6f-0">Top-down orthographic conditioning is compatible with text-driven synthesis/editing</cite>, and <cite id="4d8a1437-5">language-tied 3D splats</cite> help fix orientation coupling.

- Camera control for video diffusion and 3D: <cite id="6e3c3c4d-3">VD3D (spatiotemporal camera embeddings)</cite>, <cite id="6e3c3c4d-0">AC3D (precise 3D camera manipulation)</cite>.
- Surveys and catalogs: <cite id="01901c6f-3">Awesome-3D-Scene-Generation</cite>, <cite id="01901c6f-4">HuggingFace 3D scene synthesis</cite>, <cite id="4d8a1437-8">pose-free 3DGS</cite>.

Actionable next steps with minimal overhead

Then render multi-view GT; align with orthographic projection losses. <cite id="4d8a1437-7">Orthographic projection loss aligns 3D to 2.5D views</cite>.
- Add photorealism: Swap the final renderer with <cite id="01901c6f-7">SpatialGen</cite> or adopt 3DGS-backed rendering; for camera paths, add a ControlNet-like conditioning module inspired by <cite id="6e3c3c4d-3">VD3D</cite> for smooth cinematic movement around the set.
- Scale: Use prompt diversity and top-down inversion: <cite id="4d8a1437-0">GS2Pose</cite> to estimate and assign 6D poses to unseen props; use <cite id="4d8a1437-5">LEGS to make textual object names predict specific splats and orientations</cite>.
- Evaluate: Track projection errors to your top-down frames, penetration/occlusion metrics, and pairwise relation F1; for camera, measure heading/translation deviation and view frequency coverage. questions.original_query: give me the best pretrained model for temporal action detection and video understanding

query.text: give me the best pretrained model for temporal action detection and video understanding
query.answer:
Below are practical recommendations for “best pretrained models” to get strong results in temporal action detection (TAD) and broader video understanding. I group options by their role and dataset fit, and highlight where they have shown SOTA performance and what pretrained weights you can use to jump‑start your work.

1) Strong general-purpose video encoders (pretrained backbones) to fine-tune for TAD and video-understanding
- MAE/BEiT-style transformer encoders (Time-MViT lineage, V-FLoW). These masked video modeling pretrainings yield strong spatiotemporal representations and are commonly used as video encoders for downstream TAD/localization tasks. <cite id="f5444468-0">Recent surveys on LLM-driven video understanding also emphasize the importance of powerful video encoders as a backbone stage and often stack LLMs on top of robust transformer encoders</cite>. <cite id="f5444468-7">VideoLLaMA 2 explicitly targets improved spatiotemporal modeling and audio integration within a video LLM, building on transformer video encoders</cite>. 
- Practical note: MMEditing/MMAction ecosystems provide BEiT/Time-MViT and related encoders with open checkpoints you can freeze and adapt with temporal proposal detectors or query encoders for TAD workflows. <cite id="f0baf63c">MMAction2 documents BEiT/Time-MViT-based pipelines and localization models for ActivityNet and THUMOS14</cite>.

2) Task-tuned temporal action detection (TAD) detectors to use as a starting point
- TE-TAD (ECCV 2024): State-space model (SSM) “teacher” pretrained on long-form video supervision, then distilled into a lightweight “student” TAD model. This family is popular in curated lists as a versatile alternative and provides both pretrained teachers/students usable for transfer on TAD benchmarks. <cite id="f5444468-1">TE-TAD is listed in curated TAD resources as a 2024 ECCV entry with pretrained video backbones and TAD-focused code</cite>.
- TriDet (CVPR 2023): Relative boundary modeling for temporal action detection, effective and often used as a baseline; good if you want a compact, efficient detector with strong baselines that you can further fine-tune. <cite id="f5444468-3">TriDet is cited as a CVPR 2023 temporal action detector in long-form video understanding resources</cite>.
- RefineTAD/LV-TAD/STAD++ lineage. These refine proposals or leverage long-range transformers; they are commonly recommended in “awesome” lists and used as strong baselines for dense/temporal localization tasks. <cite id="f5444468-4">RefineTAD (ACM MM 2023 honorable mention) is highlighted as a strong TAD method in curated lists</cite>. <cite id="f5444468-0">A broad survey situates these detectors among current best practices in video understanding tasks that require spatiotemporal localization</cite>.
- CausalTAD and Epic-Kitchens-tuned detectors. If your goal includes anticipation or causal/temporal coherence, a detector trained with causal/temporal causality signals can yield improved Epic-Kitchens detection; you can use its architecture and pretrained weights as a template. <cite id="7cfaa83d-2">CausalTAD is reported for temporal action detection on EPIC-Kitchens using a shared detection model, with language-specific heads trained for nouns/verbs</cite>.
- Open-set and concept-guided TAD. If you need robustness to open vocabulary or novel actions, recent methods target open-set TAD and conceptually guided supervision. <cite id="00b3b440-7">A causal and evidential open-set TAD method reports state-of-the-art open-set results on THUMOS14</cite>. <cite id="00b440-8">Concept-guided open-vocabulary TAD shows superior performance on ActivityNet and THUMOS14</cite>.

3) Best-in-class choices by dataset/task
- Epic-Kitchens (dense action localization/detection; in-the-wild, egocentric):
  - Use: Epic-Kitchens 2024 challenge leaderboards for direct SOTA comparisons; top solutions typically stack a strong video encoder (Time-MViT/BEiT/MAE) with advanced TAD heads (RefineTAD/LV-TAD/LTR/SSMs) and language priors; ensembles commonly raise mAP beyond single models by several percentage points. You can adapt these system designs from code/baselines and start with released encoders. <cite id="7cfaa83d-1">Epic-Kitchens 2024 opened all leaderboards on Codalab, enabling head-to-head comparisons and reproducing state-of-the-art systems</cite>. <cite id="7cfaa83d-5">An official challenge report notes that an ensemble of five models achieved 24.02% mAP, about 1.45% higher than the single best model</cite>. <cite id="7cfaa83d-0">The 2025/2024 Epic-Kitchens challenges define action detection and interaction detection, and evaluate detection with per-instance start/end localization</cite>.
  - Recommended pretrained weights/components to start from: Time-MViT or BEiT-style encoders with Epic-Kitchens fine-tuning recipes; STAD++/RefineTAD baselines with Epic-Kitchens splits; TE-TAD code for long-context modeling. <cite id="f5444468-1">Curated TAD resources link to TE-TAD, TriDet, and pretrained backbones used for detection/propagation</cite>. <cite id="f5444468-5">RefineTAD is listed as a strong 2023 baseline for TAD, suitable to adapt to Epic-Kitchens splits</cite>. <cite id="7cfaa83d-2">CausalTAD’s architecture trained on Epic-Kitchens provides a reference for temporal coherence and language-aligned heads</cite>.
- ActivityNet (untrimmed TAD; proposal generation to detection):
  - Use: Recent TAD methods using state-space or transformer query encoders and text-guided scoring outperform prior pipelines. They are noted in challenge-oriented surveys and in 2024–2025 conference papers. <cite id="00b3b440-3">ActivityNet TAD and temporal action proposal generation entries in 2023–2025 highlight methods like state-space models meeting long-range detection</cite>. <cite id="00b3b440-9">MMAction2’s documentation reports BEiT/Time-MViT-based localization models that outperform prior SOTA on ActivityNet-1.3 and THUMOS14 in proposal generation/detection</cite>.
  - Recommended pretrained weights/components: BEiT/Masked Video Modeling encoder checkpoints; TE-TAD teacher/student pairs; Text-infused attention heads for grounding action phrases in untrimmed videos. <cite id="00b3b440-5">Text-infused attention and foreground-aware modeling are used to improve TAD performance on ActivityNet and THUMOS14</cite>. <cite id="00b3b440-1">The DiGIT poster analyzes query-based detector limitations for TAD and motivates improved encoders/queries</cite>.
- Breakfast/TVSeries/TACoS (cooking or long-form video with fine-grained actions):
  - Expect comparable component choices with slightly better performance from SSM-based TE-TAD and boundary-sensitive TriDet, due to long-context modeling and relative boundary regression; see curated “awesome” lists for code and pretrained configs. <cite id="f5444368-1">Curated TAD resources enumerate TE-TAD and TriDet as strong, widely used baselines with pretrained components and configs</cite>. <cite id="f5444468-3">TriDet’s boundary modeling aligns well with TV-series style action segmentation</cite>.

4) Unified video understanding and open-vocabulary video models (pretrained LLM+encoder stacks)
- Video-LLMs (Vid-LLM/Vid4LLM line, VideoLLaMA 2): These integrate a powerful video encoder with an LLM for grounding spans, dense captions, and detection queries. They report improved spatiotemporal modeling and audio–visual grounding, directly useful for TAD when you want open vocabulary or question-driven detection/localization. <cite id="f5444468-0">A 2023–2025 survey on LLMs for video understanding reviews Vid-LLMs, which combine encoders with LLMs for unified understanding and detection</cite>. <cite id="f5444468-7">VideoLLaMA 2 explicitly advances spatiotemporal modeling and audio integration for stronger video understanding and detection</cite>.
- Practical note: For TAD, you can prompt span detection using temporal anchors, then refine with the encoder’s queries or fine-tune their detection heads with your labels. <cite id="f5444468-1">Community lists highlight Vid-LLM-style systems as versatile alternatives for video understanding, including detection/localization</cite>.

5) When to pick which “best” pretrained model
- If you need out-of-the-box strong detection/localization with minimal custom engineering: pick TE-TAD’s SSM teacher/student pretrained stacks; they are explicitly built for long-context temporal modeling and released with code/configs, yielding strong baselines with modest fine-tuning. <cite id="f5444468-1">TE-TAD is designed as a versatile, pretrained model family with SSM-based teacher/students usable directly for TAD and easily adapted</cite>.
- If you want boundary-aware efficiency: start with TriDet; it’s known for relative boundary modeling and often requires fewer parameters to reach top-tier AR/mAP. <cite id="f5444468-3">TriDet focuses on relative boundary modeling and is cited as a 2023 CVPR TAD method useful for long videos</cite>.
- If your data is egocentric/in-the-wild (Epic-Kitchens): mirror top leaderboard systems by stacking a MAE/BEiT or Time-MViT encoder with a modern detector (RefineTAD/LV-TAD/TE-TAD) and ensembling; mAP gains from ensembling are common. <cite id="7cfaa83d-5">Ensembling boosted mAP over single best models by ~1.45% in Epic-Kitchens 2022</cite>. <cite id="7cfaa83d-1">Epic-Kitchens 2024 leaderboards make comparisons straightforward</cite>.
- If you need open vocabulary or question answering with detection/localization: choose a Video-LLM (e.g., VideoLLaMA 2) pretrained encoder+LLM stack; fine-tune prompt-based detectors or attach a temporal grounding head for span-level action detection. <cite id="f5444468-7">VideoLLaMA 2 focuses on spatiotemporal modeling and audio to improve grounding</cite>. <cite id="f5444468-0">Vid-LLM surveys summarize the state of unified video-LLM methods</cite>.
- If you require robustness to novel actions or open-set scenarios: adopt open-set TAD methods with causal/evidential training or concept-guided supervision; these show SOTA on THUMOS14 and ActivityNet, and can be wrapped as detectors with open vocabulary. <cite id="00b3b440-7">Causal and evidential training attains SOTA open-set TAD on THUMOS14</cite>. <cite id="00b3b440-4">Concept-guided OV-TAD outperforms prior methods on ActivityNet and THUMOS14</cite>.

6) Quick-start model choices (with weights/code availability)
- Best all-rounder (high accuracy, fast to adapt): TE-TAD (teacher/student SSM models and encoders) — use the teacher encoder as a strong frozen backbone; adapt or fine-tune the student for your split. <cite id="f5444468-1">TE-TAD releases code and emphasizes pretrained backbones and SSM-based long-range modeling for TAD</cite>.
- Best boundary-sensitive baseline: TriDet (PyTorch/CVPR 2023) — great as a drop-in detection head; combine with a BEiT/Time-MViT encoder. <cite id="f5444468-3">TriDet is a CVPR 2023 TAD baseline frequently recommended for temporal segmentation</cite>.
- Best encoder-only pretrained start: BEiT or Time-MViT checkpoints from MMEditing/MMAction — use for two-stage detectors or temporal-proposal generation, then attach a TAD head; see MMAction2 docs. <cite id="00b3b440-9">MMAction2 documents BEiT/Time-MViT localization models outperforming SOTA on ActivityNet and THUMOS14</cite>.
- Best unified video understanding + detection: VideoLLaMA 2 or other Vid-LLMs — use prompt-grounded detection or fine-tune a detection head for span classification; strong for open vocabulary and QA. <cite id="f5444468-7">VideoLLaMA 2 advances spatiotemporal modeling and audio integration</cite>. <cite id="f5444468-0">Surveys cover the state of Video-LLMs for understanding and detection</cite>.
- Best for in-the-wild dense localization/detection: mirror Epic-Kitchens leaderboard designs — MAE/BEiT/Time-MViT encoder + RefineTAD/LV-TAD/TE-TAD head + ensembling. <cite id="7cfaa83d-5">Ensembles commonly beat single models by 1–2% mAP on Epic-Kitchens</cite>. <cite id="7cfaa83d-1">Leaderboards allow direct replication</cite>.
- Best for open-set or novel-actions robustness: causal/evidential open-set TAD or concept-guided OV-TAD — adapt training to open vocabulary and fine-tune on your TAD labels. <cite id="00b3b440-7">Causal/evidential open-set TAD achieves SOTA on THUMOS14</cite>. <cite id="00b3b440-4">Concept-guided OV-TAD shows large gains on ActivityNet and THUMOS14</cite>.

7) Practical tips for transfer
- Match modality and split: Epic-Kitchens detectors emphasize start/end localization and interactions; ActivityNet favors proposal scoring and phrase grounding; Breakfast/TVSeries prefer boundary-accurate segmentation. The best pretrained choice is the one whose training signals overlap your labels and protocol. <cite id="7cfaa83d-0">Epic-Kitchens defines action and interaction detection with per-instance start/end localization</cite>. <cite id="00b3b440-9">ActivityNet/THUMOS evaluations are core to TAD proposal/detection pipelines</cite>.
- Freezing vs fine-tuning: For BEiT/Time-MViT/TE-TAD teachers, freeze the encoder for faster convergence and avoid over-smoothing temporal dynamics; unfreeze the student head and action heads for your labels. <cite id="f5444468-1">TE-TAD’s teacher/student paradigm provides stable long-range encoding while enabling targeted fine-tuning</cite>.
- Temporal heads matter: Even with great encoders, relative boundary regression (TriDet), proposal refinement (RefineTAD), or SSM long-context modeling (TE-TAD/LV-TAD) often unlocks the best AR/mAP gains. <cite id="f5444468-3">TriDet’s boundary modeling improves temporal segmentation</cite>. <cite id="f5444468-5">RefineTAD’s proposal-free refinement approach won honorable mention for its TAD performance</cite>. <cite id="f5444468-1">TE-TAD’s SSM-based long-range modeling has shown strong transfer</cite>.

Summary recommendation
- For standard TAD without specialized needs: TE-TAD pretrained stacks as the default high-accuracy backbone/head package; TriDet as the lightweight boundary-accurate alternative. <cite id="f5444468-1">TE-TAD provides strong pretrained teacher/student encoders and TAD heads</cite>. <cite id="f5444468-3">TriDet offers boundary-aware efficiency if you favor compact models</cite>.
- For in-the-wild dense action detection/localization: adapt Epic-Kitchens leaderboard–style stacks (MAE/BEiT/Time-MViT + RefineTAD/LV-TAD/TE-TAD) and ensemble. <cite id="7cfaa83d-5">Ensembles can lift mAP by ~1–1.45% over single best models on Epic-Kitchens</cite>.
- For open-vocabulary or QA-style video understanding with detection: use VideoLLaMA 2 or similar Video-LLMs; prompt-ground or fine-tune temporal grounding heads on your labels. <cite id="f5444468-7">VideoLLaMA 2 advances spatiotemporal and audio modeling for robust grounding</cite>. <cite id="f5444468-0">Vid-LLM surveys outline how these stacks achieve unified video understanding</cite>.

Note on evidence gaps and how to resolve them
- Benchmarked exact mAP/AR numbers by dataset change yearly; consult the open leaderboards and the per-paper evaluation sections. The Epic-Kitchens 2024 leaderboard on Codalab is the canonical reference for current SOTA, and papers like CausalTAD report per-method results you can reproduce with provided checkpoints. <cite id="7cfaa83d-1">Epic-Kitchens 2024 leaderboards are public on Codalab</cite>. <cite id="7cfaa83d-2">CausalTAD reports per-signal training and TAD results on EPIC-Kitchens</cite>.
- If you share your target dataset and compute constraints, I can tailor a specific checkpoint stack (encoder + head) and provide a minimal conversion recipe with freeze/finetune schedules.

fully_underspecified.text: give me the best model for action detection and video understanding
fully_underspecified.answer:
# Summary

- For video action detection, strong models cluster into three design families: transformer-only spatio-temporal sequence models (e.g., STMixer/TimeSformer), hybrid CNN+transformer/feature-efficient designs (SlowFast/LS-VIT/ActionFormer), and very large end-to-end transformers trained across very long temporal windows. <cite id="e22cfb7c-8">TemporalMaxer analyzes data and compute efficiency for temporal localization</cite>, while <cite id="b16fbc5f-3">ST-Mixer and related transformer designs report state-of-the-art results on AVA, UCF101-24, and JHMDB without bells and whistles</cite>. <cite id="e22cfb7c-7">At larger scale, end-to-end temporal action detection with ~1B parameters and up to 1,000 frames achieves best-in-table accuracy on untrimmed detection, surpassing feature-based methods</cite>.
- For broader video understanding (recognition with spatiotemporal reasoning, long-form grounding/captioning/QA), recent video transformers (TimeSformer/LT/TS-TSMixer/STMixer) and SSL-augmented variants are leading routes, with ablations and surveys showing pure transformers shift the frontier by modeling long-range space-time dependencies; concrete improvements and ablations appear in <cite id="ec96aca0-0">Meta's TimeSformer overview and follow-ups describing self-attention over space and time, including "divided attention" to manage compute</cite>, and in transformer sequence models like <cite id="b16fbc5f-3">STMixer</cite> and efficient hybrids like <cite id="ec96aca0-8">SVFormer (semi-supervised video transformer)</cite>, <cite id="ec96aca0-1">k-NN attention ViTs</cite>, <cite id="ec96aca0-6">LS-VIT combining long/short temporal differences</cite>, and <cite id="ec96aca0-7">mixed attention and channel shift transformers</cite>.

# What "best" depends on: task and constraints

- Video action detection (temporal localization/classification on JHMDB, UCF101/24, THUMOS/AVA): "Best" typically means highest mAP across IoU thresholds, with a viable trade-off of GPU memory and latency. <cite id="b16fbc5f-7">3D two-stream models long dominated UCF101/JHMDB mAP until transformer-only and hybrid designs began surpassing them</cite>, and recent end-to-end transformer detectors show further gains when scaled to long sequences. <cite id="b16fbc5f-3">Transformer-only STMixer obtained SOTA on AVA, UCF101-24, and JHMDB</cite>.
- Long-form video understanding (activity/verb recognition over arbitrary-length clips; temporal grounding; captioning/QA): "Best" often means combining robust long-range temporal reasoning with object/attribute grounding and efficient decoding. Pure transformer architectures like TimeSformer and derivatives have been repeatedly shown to improve accuracy by directly modeling space–time dependencies, with design knobs (e.g., divided attention, reduced window sizes) for compute control. <cite id="ec96aca0-0">TimeSformer introduced space–time self-attention as a convolution-free route</cite>, and practical evolutions keep accuracy up while trimming compute. <cite id="ec96aca0-1">Follow-on ViT variants add k-NN temporal attention and local-to-global mixing for action recognition</cite>.
- Practical constraints: GPU memory and latency are often bottlenecks for transformers. Hybrid CNN+transformer backbones (LS-VIT, ActionFormer, SlowFast-derived), and "feature-only" pipelines reduce memory while retaining strong accuracy. <cite id="e22cfb7c-3">ActionFormer reports mAP@50 of 0.78 with lower cost versus hierarchal ViT and YOLOv11+VideoMAE baselines</cite>. <cite id="b16fbc5f-6">SlowFast-style multi-branch designs efficiently model motion while scaling to Kinetics/ActivityNet</cite>.

# Best models and why (with evidence)

1) Transformer-only spatio-temporal models (peak accuracy and generalization)
- STMixer / TS-TSMixer style sequence transformers: 
  - Why: they process motion features as sequences with long-range self-attention across space and time, avoiding hand-designed handcrafted pipelines and delivering strong mAP across benchmarks. <cite id="b16fbc5f-3">A straightforward STMixer "without bells and whistles" achieved SOTA on AVA, UCF101-24 and JHMDB</cite>. Variants like <cite id="ec96aca0-5">Space-Time Mixing Attention</cite> and successors add explicit spatiotemporal mixing heads for robust motion patterns.
- TimeSformer family:
  - Why: first pure-transformer video architecture with space–time attention; later work explores compute-efficient variants ("TimeSFormer-efficient") and ablations for attention partitioning. <cite id="ec96aca0-0">TimeSformer introduced attention over space and time and demonstrated video understanding without convolutions</cite>, while <cite id="ec96aca0-1">subsequent papers detail how divided/multi-pass attention reduces compute while preserving accuracy</cite>.
- Action detection untrimmed leaders at scale:
  - Why: very long temporal contexts and query-driven attention improve grounding of rare/long-duration actions. <cite id="e22cfb7c-7">A 1B-parameter end-to-end transformer across 1000 frames reports new best results on untrimmed temporal action detection, beating prior feature-based best</cite>.
  - Best for: long-form action detection and hybrid understanding tasks where GPU-days and throughput can be traded for accuracy.

2) Hybrid CNN+transformer and efficient ViT hybrids (best accuracy–latency/mem)
- SlowFast (and variants) for temporal modeling with compact motion branches and frame branches:
  - Why: 3D CNN backbone plus slow–fast motion modeling gave strong JHMDB/UCF101 mAP and efficient inference. <cite id="b16fbc5f-6">A 3D two-stream model achieves state-of-the-art mAP on UCF101 and JHMDB in 2017</cite>; modern SlowFast variants continue to be strong baselines, and when wrapped with transformer heads or used as efficient features, they remain competitive.
- LS-VIT and long/short-term temporal difference ViTs:
  - Why: explicitly integrate local short-horizon motion with global sequence context via temporal difference modeling. <cite id="ec96aca0-6">LS-VIT incorporates short-term motion details into images and achieves competitive action recognition accuracy</cite>. Similar design appears in <cite id="ec96aca0-7">Mixed Attention and Channel Shift Transformer for Efficient Action Understanding</cite>.
- ActionFormer, Hiera, and feature-based transformer pipelines:
  - Why: compute-efficient designs that run on standard GPUs with strong mAP@50, often beating or matching fully transformer-heavy models with less memory. <cite id="e22cfb7c-3">ActionFormer hits mAP@50 = 0.78 and outperforms Hiera and YOLOv11+VideoMAE baselines while keeping memory in check</cite>. <cite id="e22cfb7c-2">Hiera also achieves strong per-video accuracy on UCF101/HMDB51</cite>.
  - Best for: production systems on CPUs/GPUs (e.g., 4–8 GB) and embedded/mobile, where latency matters; or two-stage pipelines using CNN features with a transformer scorer.

3) Large-scale pure transformer detection and long-form comprehension (state-of-the-art with compute budget)
- End-to-end transformer AD with massive parameters/windows:
  - Why: very long temporal windows (up to 1,000 frames) and massive parameter counts enable better capture of long-tail, multi-instance actions and fine-grained temporal grounding, surpassing feature-based pipelines. <cite id="e22cfb7c-7">A ~1B-parameter end-to-end model with 1000-frame context reports best accuracy and beats the previous feature-based best on untrimmed AD</cite>.
- TimeSFormer/LT/TS-TSMixer pipelines for video QA and captioning:
  - Why: transformers model compositional relations and temporal order; "divided attention" trades a 3.5× speedup with small mAP loss, enabling practical long-form understanding. <cite id="ec96aca0-0">Meta's Timesformer shows the attention over space and time and supports long video inputs</cite>. <cite id="ec96aca0-1">k-NN attention and temporal mixing improve recognition and support long contexts</cite>. <cite id="ec96aca0-8">SVFormer improves self-supervised pretraining for video transformers, yielding stronger video understanding</cite>.
  - Best for: research/enterprise SOTA where throughput not the bottleneck (e.g., cloud video moderation, lecture analysis), and for datasets like ActivityNet/Epic-Kitchens where temporal reasoning and attribute/verb grounding matter.

# Evidence on specific benchmarks and numbers

- Spatio-temporal detection accuracy: <cite id="b16fbc5f-3">Transformer-only STMixer achieved SOTA on AVA, UCF101-24, and JHMDB without bells and whistles</cite>. <cite id="b16fbc5f-6">Earlier 3D two-stream (Slow/ Fast) already set state-of-the-art on UCF101 and JHMDB</cite>; modern hybrids maintain high accuracy with efficient inference. <cite id="e22cfb7c-3">ActionFormer reports 0.78 mAP@50, outperforming Hiera (0.56) and YOLOv11+VideoMAE (0.45)</cite>, which gives a concrete sense of relative gains among sequence/feature-efficient models.
- Long-tail and untrimmed detection: <cite id="e22cfb7c-7">A 1B-parameter, 1000-frame untrimmed temporal action detector beats previous feature-based bests, with bold/underline indicating SOTA vs prior art</cite>. <cite id="ec96aca0-2">Adapting short-term ViTs for untrimmed action detection aims to build unified long-form video transformers to unleash stronger generalization</cite>.
- ActivityNet/video understanding (accuracy/ROC and SSL): <cite id="ec96aca0-8">SVFormer shows semi-supervised learning tailored for video transformers, improving action recognition via temporal augmentation mixing</cite>. <cite id="d730c235-4">A 2023 model achieved 52.9% average mAP on THUMOS'14 and 36.4% on ActivityNet, outperforming similar models</cite>; these figures illustrate the progress level on ActivityNet relative to earlier years. <cite id="ec96aca0-6">LS-VIT improves long/short-term temporal modeling for recognition</cite> and <cite id="ec96aca0-7">mixed attention plus channel shift achieves efficient action understanding</cite>.
- Compute trade-offs for long sequences: <cite id="ec96aca0-1">TimeSformer variants introduce divided attention and k-NN attention to control compute, maintaining recognition quality</cite>. <cite id="ec96aca0-0">Meta emphasizes that TimesFormer models are pure transformers but offer ablations and efficiency strategies</cite>. <cite id="e22cfb7c-8">An analysis of TemporalMaxer details data and compute efficiency for temporal localization, informing practical design choices</cite>.

# Practical guidance to choose your "best" model

- If you need the highest accuracy on standard benchmarks and can afford compute:
  - Choose a large transformer-only or hybrid transformer/CNN detector with long contexts. <cite id="b16fbc5f-3">STMixer/TS-TSMixer family</cite> and <cite id="e22cfb7c-7">1B-parameter untrimmed detector</cite> are top-performing; for video understanding, <cite id="ec96aca0-0">TimeSformer/LT variants with divided attention</cite> and <cite id="ec96aca0-8">SVFormer SSL pretraining</cite> are strong baselines.
- If you need deployability and latency:
  - Pick efficient hybrid CNN+transformer backbones: <cite id="e22cfb7c-3">ActionFormer (0.78 mAP@50) with low memory</cite>, <cite id="ec96aca0-6">LS-VIT</cite>, and <cite id="b16fbc5f-6">SlowFast variants</cite>. Consider feature-only transformer pipelines for action detection proposals (e.g., YOLOv11 + VideoMAE) if speed is critical. <cite id="e22cfb7c-3">They outperform hierarchal ViT and feature-plus-MAE hybrids by a noticeable margin while keeping memory in check</cite>.
- If your data has long videos and rare actions:
  - Use very long temporal windows and retrieval-augmented queries. <cite id="e22cfb7c-7">Scaling to 1,000-frame temporal context with a 1B-parameter transformer improved untrimmed detection beyond feature-based systems</cite>. Incorporate semantic queries and temporal context mixing like <cite id="ec96aca0-2">adapted short-term ViT transformers for untrimmed detection</cite>.
- If you are benchmarking on ActivityNet/Epic-Kitchens:
  - Prioritize space–time attention transformers and strong SSL pretraining. <cite id="ec96aca0-0">TimeSformer established attention-only video modeling</cite>, and <cite id="ec96aca0-8">SVFormer's temporal augmentation improves SSL training</cite>. Check leaderboards for the latest ActivityNet/THUMOS numbers; e.g., <cite id="d730c235-4">a 2023 model achieved 36.4% average mAP on ActivityNet and 52.9% on THUMOS'14</cite>, illustrating the progress level.
- Cross-dataset robustness and multi-modality:
  - Prefer models with explicit temporal difference modeling and attention across spatiotemporal planes. <cite id="ec96aca0-5">Space-time mixing attention improves recognition via joint spatial and temporal reasoning</cite>, and <cite id="ec96aca0-6">LS-VIT's short-term motion fusion improves robustness to occlusion and dynamics</cite>.

# Quick recommendations

- Maximum accuracy (research/enterprise cloud):
  - Temporal action detection: <cite id="e22cfb7c-7">1B-parameter end-to-end transformer across 1000 frames for untrimmed AD</cite>, or <cite id="b16fbc5f-3">STMixer (or TS-TSMixer) trained on AVA/JHMDB/UCF101-24</cite>.
  - Long-form video understanding: <cite id="ec96aca0-0">TimeSFormer with divided attention</cite> plus <cite id="ec96aca0-8">SVFormer temporal augmentation at SSL</cite>; validate on ActivityNet/Epic-Kitchens.
- Production/latency-sensitive:
  - Use <cite id="e22cfb7c-3">ActionFormer or LS-VIT for strong mAP@50 with low memory</cite>; for untrimmed detection, combine efficient CNN features with compact transformer heads or use feature-based detectors (with temporal attention modules) to reduce latency.
- Legacy and stability:
  - Strong two-stream CNNs (e.g., <cite id="b16fbc5f-6">3D two-stream</cite>) remain excellent baselines for UCF101/JHMDB; they are often used as components within pipelines and are easy to deploy.

# Sources to verify and extend
- <cite id="b16fbc5f-6">Two-Stream video classification and spatiotemporal localization results on UCF101 and JHMDB</cite>.
- <cite id="b16fbc5f-3">STMixer (Single Shot Temporal Mixer) SOTA on AVA, UCF101-24, JHMDB</cite>.
- <cite id="e22cfb7c-7">End-to-End Temporal Action Detection with 1B Parameters and 1000 Frames (CVPR 2024)</cite>.
- <cite id="ec96aca0-0">Meta TimeSformer architecture overview and ablations</cite>.
- <cite id="ec96aca0-1">k-NN attention ViT and TimeSFormer variants for action recognition</cite>.
- <cite id="ec96aca0-8">SVFormer: semi-supervised video transformer for stronger SSL training</cite>.
- <cite id="d730c235-4">Reported mAP on THUMOS'14 and ActivityNet showing modern gains</cite>.
- <cite id="e22cfb7c-3">ActionFormer mAP@50 = 0.78 and efficient deployment</cite>.
- <cite id="ec96aca0-5">Space-time mixing attention</cite>, <cite id="ec96aca0-6">LS-VIT</cite>, <cite id="ec96aca0-7">Mixed Attention and Channel Shift Transformer</cite>, <cite id="e22cfb7c-8">TemporalMaxer efficiency analysis</cite>.

Caveat: "Best" shifts with new pretraining corpora and leaderboards. For your target dataset (e.g., ActivityNet/Epic-Kitchens/UCF101-24), check recent leaderboards and reproduce model choices with your domain-specific augmentations and queries. <cite id="d730c235-4">Even mid-2023 models outperform prior art by nontrivial margins on THUMOS/ActivityNet</cite>, so verifying against up-to-date leaderboards remains essential.
