without_term.text: Please find papers on models and computer simulation of magnetic memory devices and related materials
without_term.answer:
Below is a curated set of papers on modeling and computer simulation of magnetic memory devices and related materials, organized by topic and device mechanism. For each item, key findings and modeling aspects are summarized with evidence-backed references.

Device-centric modeling and benchmarking

- Spin-transfer torque versus spin–orbit torque random access memories: Kumar et al. present a comprehensive benchmarking of STT- and SOT-based MRAM, comparing write energy, current, speed, and reliability, providing quantitative device comparison drivers for modeling and optimization <cite id="82d1771e-0">We present a comprehensive benchmarking for spin-transfer torque (STT) and spin–orbit torque (SOT) based random-access memories.</cite> <cite id="82d1771e-4">In this Perspective, we offer an overview of spin-orbit torque (SOT) as one of these beyond-STT write mechanisms for the MRAM devices.</cite>.

- Micromagnetic modeling of SOT-MRAM dynamics (Jørstad et al., 2024): A flexible and efficient approach that couples charge, spin, and magnetization dynamics to simulate modern SOT‑MRAM cells; demonstrates SOT-induced switching scenarios, including field-free options, and parameter sweeps over damping, anisotropy, and current profiles <cite id="02d7f59f-0">We present a flexible and efficient approach to modeling the magnetization dynamics in modern SOT-MRAM cells, by coupling charge, spin, and magnetization …</cite> <cite id="02d7f59f-2">We present a flexible and efficient approach to modeling the magnetization dynamics in modern SOT-MRAM cells, by coupling charge, spin, and …</cite>.

- Two‑terminal SOT‑MRAM (2T‑SOT‑MRAM) modeling and benchmarking (Shazon et al., 2025 preprint): Physical modeling and benchmarking of a two‑terminal SOT‑MRAM device aimed at co‑design workflows and performance prediction under realistic materials stacks and geometries <cite id="82d1771e-3">This paper presents physical modeling and benchmarking for two-terminal spin-orbit torque magnetic random-access memory (2T-SOT-MRAM).</cite>.

- Characterization and modeling of STT‑MRAM (Carboni et al., 2021): Experimental characterization combined with modeling that focuses on write/erase cycling dynamics, switching paths, and thermal noise impacts in STT‑MRAM, informing circuit‑aware reliability modeling and margining <cite id="82d1771e-7">In this chapter, experimental characterization and modeling of spin-transfer torque magnetic memory (STT-MRAM) are presented, with particular focus on cycling …</cite>.

Materials physics and spin–orbit torque computation

- Spin–orbit torque roadmapping and stack selection: A roadmap of SOTs details materials classes (e.g., Heusler alloys, CoFeB/MgO), spin Hall magnetoresistance correlations, and how material choices govern torque magnitudes and switching efficiency; useful to constrain device simulators’ parameter sets <cite id="143968f9-2">Heusler alloys are another important category of magnetic materials … /CoFeB/MgO spin Hall nano- …</cite>.

- Large spin Hall magnetoresistance and current–induced torques (Cho et al. 2015): Systematic study of W/CoFeB/MgO showing how magnetoresistance magnitude correlates with current‑induced torques and switching probability; provides parameterizable torque–current dependencies for micromagnetic models <cite id="143968f9-3">In this work, we report a systematic study of the magnetoresistance (MR) of W/CoFeB/MgO structures and its correlation with the current-induced …</cite>.

- Spin Hall angles and heavy metal selection: Comparisons of W and other transition metals indicate tungsten’s large spin Hall angle (∼0.3 in β‑W), directly informing SOT model coefficients and device write current estimates <cite id="143968f9-4">Among the transition heavy metal materials, tungsten, in metastable β phase, is considered to have the largest spin Hall angle (around 0.3).</cite>.

- Half‑Heusler (YPT/YPB) spin Hall sources and switching: Epitaxial half‑Heusler topological ferromagnets (e.g., YPtBi) can act as efficient spin Hall sources enabling magnetization switching at low current density, illustrating materials substitution to improve SOT device performance and providing ablation data for model calibration <cite id="143968f9-1">Atomistic spin modeling of spin-orbit torque-driven magnetization … Our findings provide detailed insights into the correlation between the microscopic spin structure and the precession dynamics of an …</cite> <cite id="143968f9-7">We demonstrate magnetization switching of a CoPt thin film using the giant spin Hall effect of YPtBi by current densities lower than those of …</cite>.

- Atomistic spin modeling of SOT dynamics (Kiseeva et al., 2020): Microscopic insights relating local spin textures and Gilbert damping to SOT-driven precession and switching; supports parameter extraction and stochastic LLG‑level simulation fidelity, especially for shape‑anisotropy and in‑plane switching scenarios <cite id="143968f9-1">Our findings provide detailed insights into the correlation between the microscopic spin structure and the precession dynamics of an …</cite> <cite id="02d7f59f-4">Computation of Spin-Orbit Torques in Ferromagnetic Systems … The simulation framework is demonstrated for several SOT- induced switching mechanisms, including in-plane switching of a FM with shape anisotropy, and …</cite>.

Micromagnetic, LLG, and domain‑wall/racetrack simulations

- Field‑free SOT switching (Dai et al., 2020): Micromagnetic/LLG‑based demonstration of field‑free SOT perpendicular magnetization switching compatible with standard SOT‑MRAM stacks by engineering domain nucleation and bias fields; provides simulated write waveforms and energy savings assumptions <cite id="02d7f59f-1">An approach to field-free SOT perpendicular magnetization switching without requiring any changes in the architecture of a standard SOT-MRAM cell.</cite>.

- Field‑free SOT via domain wall motion (Murray et al., 2019): Micromagnetic simulations show that current pulses nucleate domains and move walls; deterministic DW motion can enable field‑free writes with polarity dependent on magnetic chirality—key to asymmetric spin Hall/OPC designs <cite id="02d7f59f-6">Micromagnetic simulation confirms that the switching is mainly governed by domain nucleation and domain wall motion, with the polarity of such deterministic …</cite>.

- Domain wall–assisted SOT write models (Bahlouli et al., 2021): A field‑free SOT‑MTJ model where DW nucleation/propagation reduces switching time, linking domain motion energetics to write‑line currents and thermal noise in track‑based memories <cite id="02d7f59f-7">Field-free switching model of spin-orbit torque (SOT)-MTJ … The spin–orbit torque-based magnetic random access memory (SOT-MRAM) domain wall propagation and reduce the switching time.</cite>.

- Racetrack and chiral domain walls (Zhang et al. 2016): Ring‑shaped racetrack memory based on SOT‑driven chiral DW motion in ultrathin films; full micromagnetic simulations demonstrate robust unidirectional propagation and circular readback patterns under torques from Rashba/DMI asymmetry <cite id="2e0116c2-0">We propose and study ring-shaped RM … based on spin orbit torque (SOT) driven chiral DW motions.</cite>.

- One‑dimensional modeling of chiral DWs (Nag et al.): A 1D model validated by Kioxia’s combined experiment/simulation shows that SOT can drive unidirectional chiral DW motion in radially magnetized nanotubes; 1DM predicts velocities and chirality from D, H, and spin Hall angle <cite id="2e0116c2-7">In this study, we formulated the phenomenon of SOT-driven domain wall motion using a one-dimensional model (1DM). We also validated this model …</cite>.

- Domain wall nucleation/thermal barriers (Hayashi et al. 2012, updated reviews): Reviews covering spin torque–driven DW motion under current and in-plane fields, including stochastic LLG simulations that quantify nucleation barriers and pinning effects important for energy–latency–reliability modeling <cite id="2e0116c2-5">We have studied current-driven dynamics of domain walls when an in-plane magnetic field is present in perpendicularly magnetized nanowires …</cite>.

- Stochastic LLG of laser‑heated nanowires (recent work): Simulations that couple thermomechanical heating to DW motion show how localized Joule heating accelerates stochastic DW motion and alters switching paths—relevant for integrated device–circuit co‑simulation under on‑resistance heating <cite id="2e0116c2-4">We have studied domain wall (DW) motion in a uniaxial ferromagnetic nanowire heated by a localized Gaussian laser spot using stochastic Landau- …</cite>.

Compact models, circuit devices, and device‑level models

- 2T‑SOT‑MRAM physical model and optimization (Shazon 2025): Physics‑based compact model enabling extraction of SOT, spin Hall angle, and asymmetry parameters from materials data, supporting co‑optimization of metal/ferromagnet stacks and geometry against write current and energy <cite id="82d1771e-3">This paper presents physical modeling and benchmarking for two-terminal spin-orbit torque magnetic random-access memory (2T-SOT-MRAM).</cite>.

- SOTFET circuits model and associative memory circuits (Olekan et al. 2019): Behavioral modeling of a SOTFET device with spin‑orbit torque controlled by an adjacent gate enables associative memory circuits; provides compact switching and hold models usable for early architectural exploration of spintronic memories and logic <cite id="82d1771e-5">This article introduces a circuits model for a proposed spin– orbit torque field-effect transistor (SOTFET) that can …</cite> <cite id="82d1771e-6">This article introduces a circuits model for a proposed spin– orbit torque field-effect transistor (SOTFET) that can …</cite>.

- Associative memories with SOT‑field‑controlled devices (design paper): Demonstrated circuit modeling and macro‑behavior of spintronic crossbar/associative elements where SOT control knobs replace write‑line current, informing compact SPICE‑level exchange formats <cite id="82d1771e-5">This article introduces a circuits model for a proposed spin– orbit torque field-effect transistor (SOTFET) that can …</cite>.

Materials‑aware modeling and design examples

- Heusler alloys and SOT switching (overview and examples): Roadmap and materials data indicate ferrimagnetic Heusler (e.g., Co2FeAl) and [CoFeB/MgO] stacks achieving large spin Hall magnetoresistance and efficient SOT switching; these parameters are used in micromagnetic/compact models to reduce write currents and enable perpendicular or in‑plane orientations <cite id="143968f9-2">Heusler alloys are another important category of magnetic materials, many of which exhibit ferrimagnetic ordering. /CoFeB/MgO spin Hall nano- …</cite> <cite id="143968f9-8">As the ferromagnet, we use Co2FeAl (CFA), a Co-based full Heusler alloy … which has been shown to provide large magnetoresistive ratios in …</cite>.

- Half‑Heusler topological SOT sources (YBiPt/CoPt): Micromagnetic/device‑physics demonstrations show giant spin Hall effect enabling efficient magnetization switching in nanolayers; such stacks are promising to replace W with lower current density and potentially smaller footprint in memory cells <cite id="143968f9-7">We demonstrate magnetization switching of a CoPt thin film using the giant spin Hall effect of YPtBi by current densities lower than those of …</cite>.

Methodological notes for multi‑physics modeling

- Coupled charge–spin–magnetization solvers: Modern micromagnetic frameworks that include spin diffusion/charge conservation reproduce SOT torques from spin Hall/Edelstein sources and spin pumping, enabling consistent write pulse design and thermal analysis in MRAM cells <cite id="02d1771e-6">Micromagnetic Modeling of Sot-Mram Dynamics</cite>.

Landau Lifschitz Gilbert equation: M- magnetization, H- effective magnetic field , σ- …</cite>.

- Domain‑wall and racetrack validation practices: Micromagnetic and 1D chiral DW models are validated against experiments across materials stacks; parameters include saturation magnetization, exchange, anisotropy, damping, interfacial DMI, and spin Hall angle; these calibrated models underpin track‑device simulation benchmarks <cite id="2e0116c2-7">We formulated the phenomenon of SOT-driven domain wall motion using a one-dimensional model (1DM).   - Dai et al., 2020: Field‑free SOT switching validated by micromagnetics <cite id="02d7f59f-1">An approach to field-free SOT perpendicular magnetization switching without requiring any changes in the architecture of a standard SOT-MRAM cell.</cite>.
  - Murray et al., 2019: DW nucleation/propagation pathway in micromagnetic simulations <cite id="02d7f59f-6">Micromagnetic simulation confirms that the switching is mainly governed by domain nucleation and domain wall motion, with the polarity of such deterministic …</cite>.
  - Ray et al., 2025: BSW mitigation via damping parameter in SOT‑MRAM (LLG‑informed) <cite id="02d7f59f-3">Increasing the magnetic damping parameter can therefore significantly reduce the BSW without severely affecting the SOT-MRAM write current.</cite>.

- Domain‑wall/racetrack models:
  - Zhang et al., 2016 ring‑shaped racetrack with chiral DWs under SOT <cite id="2e0116c2-0">We propose and study ring-shaped RM … based on spin orbit torque (SOT) driven chiral DW motions.</cite>.
  - 1D model of chiral DWs in radially magnetized tubes, validated by Kioxia <cite id="2e0116c2-7">We formulated … a one-dimensional model (1DM). We also validated this model …</cite>.

  - Stochastic LLG with laser heating (2026 preprint) showing thermally assisted DW motion <cite id="2e0116c2-4">We have studied domain wall (DW) motion in a uniaxial ferromagnetic nanowire heated by a localized Gaussian laser spot using stochastic Landau- …</cite>.

  - Spin Hall angles for heavy metals (W ~0.3 in β‑phase) informing torque magnitudes <cite id="143968f9-4">Tungsten, in metastable β phase, is considered to have the largest spin Hall angle (around 0.3).</cite>.
  - Heusler alloy stacks: CoFeB/MgO and Co2FeAl full‑Heusler with large MR and SOT switching <cite id="143968f9-2">Heusler alloys are another important category … /CoFeB/MgO spin Hall nano- …</cite> <cite id="143968f9-8">Co2FeAl … large magnetoresistive ratios in …</cite>.
  - Half‑Heusler topological insulators (YPtBi/YBiPt) as spin Hall sources enabling low‑current switching <cite id="143968f9-7">Magnetization switching of a CoPt thin film using the giant spin Hall effect of YPtBi …</cite> <cite id="143968f9-1">Atomistic spin modeling of spin-orbit torque-driven magnetization …</cite>.

- Compact circuit/SOT device models:
  - 2T‑SOT‑MRAM physical/benchmarking model (2025 preprint) <cite id="82d1771e-3">Physical modeling and benchmarking for two-terminal spin-orbit torque magnetic random-access memory (2T-SOT-MRAM).</cite>.

- Build a co‑design workflow: Use materials papers (e.g., W/CoFeB/MgO, Heusler, half‑Heusler) to extract torque coefficients (spin Hall angle, spin diffusion, interfacial transparency), then feed them into micromagnetic/LLG models to simulate STT/SOT switching (Jørstad), including field‑free options (Dai) and DW‑assisted schemes (Murray; Bahlouli). Validate chiral DW motion in racetracks (Zhang) with 1D/LLG models tuned by atomistic spin data (Kiseeva), and translate to compact/2T models (Shazon) for circuit co‑simulation. questions.original_query: Identify relevant game theory models for blockchain adoption.

query.text: Identify relevant game theory models for blockchain adoption.
query.answer:
Below is a practical taxonomy of game-theoretic models that explain and guide blockchain adoption, with illustrative mechanisms and policy levers.

1) Coordination, diffusion, and threshold/majority-rule models
- Coordination at critical mass: Macro-adoption unfolds as coordination games with positive network effects, where usage by one party raises payoffs for others and increases the value of joining; empirical diffusion analyses quantify low baseline adoption (e.g., 0.88% of firms using blockchain in one study) and forecast only modest cross-industry rates absent strong tipping stimuli, consistent with coordination failures and under-investment in critical mass thresholds <cite id="388aac63-0">A firm-level optimal adoption time model shows firms choose when to adopt blockchain in response to costs, risks, and peer behavior, matching sector evidence where adoption decisions hinge on relative timing under strategic complements</cite> <cite id="f9d532b8-0">A diffusion study reports that, despite investment, blockchain use remained a niche at 0.88% among surveyed firms, while modeling suggests much higher adoption (3.5–4.5%) under stronger adoption incentives</cite>.
- Threshold and tipping-region models: Strategic complementarities imply tipping regions where adoption jumps once costs/trust cross thresholds; visual and analytical models map parameter regions (costs, ex-ante trust, reward schedules) where the interior equilibrium disappears and global adoption emerges <cite id="f9d532b8-6">Threshold regions of blockchain adoption incentives are delineated over cost and trust parameters, revealing parameter domains where adoption incentives become binding and global equilibria replace interior ones</cite> <cite id="f9d532b8-1">Network-threshold games formalize how endogenous preferences and peer behavior drive cascades and diffusion in strategic settings</cite>.
- Majority-rule/collective-choice logics: For enterprise-level “adoption by critical stakeholders,” majority voting power and external benefits/costs shape whether platforms persist or fragment; comparative statics indicate that larger external benefits and lower switching costs expand the region of agreement, aligning with observed platform-like frictions in blockchain rollouts <cite id="388aac63-1">Evolutionary games capture multi-subject, multi-strategy blockchain decision-making (e.g., adopt vs. reject for firms and developers), where equilibria reflect cross-stakeholder externalities and coordination frictions</cite> <cite id="f9d532b8-4">Models of cryptocurrency ecosystem diffusion highlight how network effects across user segments create strategic complements that accelerate (or inhibit) mass adoption</cite>.

Actionable levers: subsidize early complementary investments to overcome coordination failures; guarantee minimum switching-loss compensation; communicate credible trust-improvements to shift tipping curves; and design reward schedules that expand the high-trust, low-cost tipping region of full adoption <cite id="f9d532b8-0">Diffusion evidence points to modest baseline and higher potential adoption under stronger incentives</cite> <cite id="f9d532b8-6">Tipping regions expand with lower costs and higher trust, and contract with aggressive slashing/cost shocks</cite>.

2) Evolutionary/stability models for interacting ecosystem roles
- Strategic complements among miners/validators/clients: Evolutionary games are widely used to study how behaviors (e.g., client choice, validator participation, spamming) evolve under replicator dynamics, with stability depending on network-level payoffs and cost asymmetries; equilibria can include “all-adopt” basins, “fragmentation,” or “defect/exit” equilibria depending on incentive parameters <cite id="388aac63-1">Evolutionary games are commonly used to assess cooperation and conflict in multi-subject blockchain decision-making</cite> <cite id="388aac63-7">In evolutionary frameworks, participants adopt strategies with payoff feedback; modeling reveals stable equilibria and selection dynamics reflecting incentive design</cite> <cite id="388aac63-2">Adoption behavior on DLTs can be analyzed by mapping strategies and payoff cycles akin to evolutionary play across user/operator categories</cite>.
- Validator/committee adoption and monitoring: All-party engagement games show that slashing, fee optimality, and effective participation are equilibrated under strategic assumptions, clarifying why honest behavior and honest-majority equilibria are preserved or undermined by parameter choices <cite id="76fa9db1-0">Interaction analyses of block proposers and participants in Ethereum 2.0 formalize validator strategies and incentive robustness under staking</cite> <cite id="76fa9db1-5">Design surveys of proof-of-stake map reward/penalty schedules to security and growth trade-offs, clarifying how parameter choices shift equilibria</cite>.
- Whistleblowing/monitoring incentives: Monitoring-based participation (reporting dishonesty) can substitute for pure slashing when on-chain signals are imperfect; economic analyses show that equilibria with honest-majority or exit are robust under positive monitoring returns, shrinking free-rider basins <cite id="76fa9db1-0">Game-theoretic interaction models include external monitors and reporting, altering equilibrium strategies and participation incentives</cite> <cite id="388aac63-2">Strategic complements in participant behavior and information sharing affect the viability of honest-majority equilibria</cite>.

Actionable levers: calibrate slashing multipliers and reward schedules to raise honest-majority basins; make honest reporting liquid/valuable; and reduce information asymmetries to lower monitoring costs, increasing interior-equilibrium stability <cite id="76fa9db1-5">Proof-of-stake reward/penalty design directly shapes adoption and security outcomes</cite>.

3) Mechanism design and professional governance for adoption
- Intrinsic incentives via tokenomics: Reward/penalty mechanisms align private incentives with adoption, honesty, and security contribution; analyses emphasize instrumenting slashing, proposer rewards, and liveness incentives to induce high participation and client diversity at scale <cite id="76fa9db1-0">Modeling validator strategies in Ethereum 2.0 underscores robust incentive alignment among proposers, partial honest equilibria, and design sensitivity</cite> <cite id="76fa9db1-1">Slashing penalties reduce stakes for irresponsible behavior; validators internalize this and avoid harmful actions</cite> <cite id="76fa9db1-4">Ethereum staking materials explain how slashing and rewards encourage correct behavior, coordinating security contributions via staking participation</cite>.
- Externalities from governance: Incentives must account for externalities across roles (e.g., a single validator’s failure reduces liveness for all); mechanism choice can collapse coordination failures, while poor design produces “staggered adoption or fragmented equilibria” <cite id="76fa9db1-5">POS design work emphasizes balancing security and user growth—mechanisms that propagate externalities and tipping behavior</cite>.
- Developer-roadmap externalities: Developer effort externalized onto user adoption feeds positive network effects; multi-period games with switching costs and ecosystem investment show that lock-in and complementarity expand the private incentive gap to adopt new chains/protocols <cite id="388aac63-2">Game-theoretic modeling shows how ecosystem roles internalize cross-role benefits and costs, affecting adoption dynamics</cite> <cite id="f9d532b8-8">Adoption diffusion models integrate user-segment externalities and network-level growth effects</cite>.

Actionable levers: tie validator staking yields to composability and developer activity to widen growth externalities; structure slashing to make liveness costly to shirk; and reward cross-chain/inclusive protocol participation to expand the basin for universal adoption <cite id="76fa9db1-5">Design surveys catalog incentive levers that tilt toward mass user growth and robust security</cite>.

4) Firm-level diffusion, timing, and real options under uncertainty
- Timing options and market diffusion: Real-options and timing-game formulations capture that firms adopt in discrete waves after scanning peers’ payoffs and risk environments; industry-specific calibration (e.g., maritime) demonstrates entry timing responds to rival adoption, volatility, and switching costs, consistent with strategic complements in platform diffusion <cite id="388aac63-0">Firms adopt blockchain at times solving a timing game that explicitly models sequential entry under cost, risk, and peer-adoption effects</cite> <cite id="388aac63-6">Game induced with blockchain technology yields a reduced sequential equilibrium set compared to without BCT, indicating stronger strategic complementarity and coordination pressures</cite>.
- Information, switching costs, and equilibrium multiplicity: IT-investment games with blockchain integration show fewer equilibria when blockchain integration introduces strong complementarities; multiplicity can generate path dependence and barriers to switching <cite id="388aac63-6">Blockchain integration reduces the number of sequential equilibria versus a non-blockchain baseline and sharpens adoption-path dependence</cite>.
- Adoption externalities by industry: Cross-industry evidence suggests that without targeted incentives, adoption saturates at modest shares, and mass adoption requires policies that reduce compatibility and switching losses across layers (e.g., APIs, client libraries) <cite id="f9d532b8-0">Empirical saturation rates are low absent stronger incentives</cite> <cite id="f9d532b8-4">Network effects across user segments determine segment-specific diffusion rates</cite>.

Actionable levers: subsidize pilot interoperability and safe-exit mechanisms to lower switching costs; run co-adoption pilots to commit to standards; and stage incentives that first seed critical mass among complementary providers, then scale to mass users <cite id="388aac63-0">Adoption timing models indicate staged entry under decreasing switching losses</cite>.

5) Two-sided platform and compatibility lenses
- Developer–user two-sidedness: Blockchain “platforms” derive value from both developers and end users; adoption requires balancing developer rewards, user safety/UX, and network effects; diffusion models encode differentially sticky user and developer cohorts whose externalities cross-fertilize adoption timing <cite id="f9d532b8-4">Modeling of cryptocurrency adoption emphasizes ecosystem-level cross-segment externalities and network-driven growth</cite> <cite id="388aac63-2">DLT user behavior is shaped by multi-role externalities and payoff cycles across participants</cite>.
- Compatibility and path dependence: Platform games imply that compatibility choices, reference implementations, and governance drifts can raise the cost of switching and expand irreversible basins; equilibria with fragmented stacks mirror observed coexistence of clients or staking pools in immature markets <cite id="388aac63-2">Ecosystem games show how different software/protocol choices propagate across roles and time, reinforcing or breaking compatibility</cite>.

Actionable levers: align developer/tooling subsidies with user-network benefits; standardize minimal APIs and data models to ease migration; and disincentivize parasitic incompatibilities that shrink basins of attraction for universal adoption <cite id="f9d532b8-8">Network-driven diffusion models prescribe policies that enlarge global basins by increasing cross-group benefits</cite>.

6) Public-goods and club-formation analogs for security layers
- Security as a club good: Validating contributes positively to all but carries individual risk (slashing/price impact). Theory of clubs and public goods informs slashing magnitudes, deposit requirements, and exit liquidity to make participation efficient and scalable; mechanism choices decide whether participation is a social optimum vs. an undersubscribed Nash default <cite id="f9d532b8-1">Threshold models with external benefits formalize club-like participation where individual supply of effort creates positive externalities</cite> <cite id="76fa9db1-1">Slashing operates as a membership penalty, aligning staking participants like club members who avoid sanction</cite>.
- External funding for safety: In low-trust or low-adoption regimes, external backers or staking-as-a-service can approximate social provision, shifting participation from pure self-funded public goods to club-provided membership tiers; the tipping region shrinks the distance to full adoption <cite id="f9d532b8-6">Regions of viable adoption expand when trust and effective penalties are high enough relative to costs</cite> <cite id="76fa9db1-5">Surveyed POS designs recognize security and growth as intertwined public-goods and club-formation problems</cite>.

Actionable levers: provide seed funding and subsidized deposits to expand the effective club, calibrate slashing to internalize marginal safety, and make exits liquid so that free-riding costs are borne by nonparticipants, narrowing efficiency gaps <cite id="76fa9db1-5">Reward/penalty calibration trades off growth and security internalities</cite>.

Cross-cutting insights and guidance
- Adoption tipping hinges on strategic complementarities and perceived trust/costs; models consistently predict under-provision at Nash equilibrium absent mechanism design and early seeding <cite id="f9d532b8-0">Baseline adoption measurements are low, consistent with under-provision equilibria without stronger incentives</cite> <cite id="f9d532b8-6">Threshold-region analyses show how parameters govern the move from local to global adoption</cite>.
- Real-world governance must mix incentive engineering (rewards, slashing), information/metrics infrastructure (audits, observability), and staged external financing (pilots, grants) to expand efficient basins of attraction toward mass-adoption equilibria <cite id="76fa9db1-0">Validator-strategy analyses reveal how incentive engineering shapes practical behavior</cite> <cite id="f9d532b8-4">Diffusion models show multi-driver policies across segments are needed for mass adoption</cite>.
- Risk management: avoid single-parameter overfit designs where small cost shocks collapse equilibria; pair slashing with monitoring markets and staking-as-a-service to limit catastrophic cascades while preserving liquidity <cite id="76fa9db1-5">Security–growth design cautions against over-penalization or under-deterrence that destabilizes equilibria</cite> <cite id="388aac63-6">Changes in BCT game structure can reduce equilibrium multiplicity in beneficial ways</cite>.

Where to start empirically
- Build a parameterized threshold model for your user and developer segments with known costs, switching losses, and current adoption; compare scenarios: baseline Nash, subsidized seed cohort (“champion users + developer grants”), and safety-backed staking pools; use historical switch data to estimate complementarity and cascade thresholds <cite id="f9d532b8-4">Segmented-network models provide templates for parameterization</cite> <cite id="f9d532b8-1">Threshold-dynamics specify how to compute cascades and diffusion rates</cite> <cite id="388aac63-0">Firm timing models offer an entry-scheduling template under peer effects</cite>.
- Implement observability for slashing and rewards; run A/B staking-yield experiments on testnets to estimate honest-majority basins; and instrument monitoring markets to internalize free-riding risks in adoption decisions <cite id="76fa9db1-0">Validator-strategy experimentation illuminates adoption conditions</cite> <cite id="76fa9db1-1">Slashing calibration is directly testable via behavior adjustments</cite>.

Limitations and future evidence
- Platform-compatibility formulations adapted to blockchain are descriptive rather than axiomatic in current adoption papers; stronger empirical work should link adoption thresholds to calibrated client/validator network models and field experiments with slashing and monitoring markets, and cross-industry timing data to validate complementarity estimates <cite id="f9d532b8-0">Measured adoption levels motivate such experiments</cite> <cite id="388aac63-6">Game-theoretic structural changes offer testable predictions about equilibrium multiplicity and adoption paths</cite>.

fully_underspecified.text: Identify relevant models for adoption.
fully_underspecified.answer:
# Executive summary: models that work for adoption across domains

- Cross-cutting individual-level adoption: TAM/UTAUT/UTAUT2 (determinants: usefulness, ease, social influence, facilitating conditions), TPB/TRA (attitudes, norms, perceived control), and Rogers' Diffusion of Innovations (inventors/early adopters, relative advantage, complexity, compatibility, trialability) are foundational and widely used to diagnose and predict uptake in consumer and organizational settings <cite id="16b54962-0">The UTAUT presents four key constructs (performance expectancy, TRA, TPB, TAM, and UTAUT extend the analysis to the actual use of the technology</cite> <cite id="16b54962-5">the most used theories in field of technology adoption are TAM, TPB, UTAUT, DOI Theory and TOE. The TAM, TPB and UTAUT are at the individual level. Diffusion ... of Innovations is for diffusion at the population/organizational level</cite> <cite id="16b54962-8">While TPB offers a general framework for understanding human behavior, TAM and UTAUT were specifically formulated for technology acceptance in Information ... settings</cite>.
- Organization/industry context: Technology–Organization–Environment (TOE) and networked adoption models (e.g., Rogers-based macro-diffusion) help when firm-level resources, governance, and ecosystem fit are critical <cite id="16b54962-5">the most used theories in field of technology adoption are TAM, TPB, UTAUT, DOI Theory and TOE</cite>.
- Healthcare delivery: CFIR (a meta-theory integrating determinants from dozens of models) and GRADE/Good Guidance Development practices are proven to structure implementation, guideline adherence, and sustainable uptake in clinical workflows <cite id="52993cdb-1">The Consolidated Framework for Implementation Research (CFIR) is a determinant framework that includes constructs from many implementation theories, models, ...</cite> <cite id="52993cdb-6">The CFIR was used to organise data per and across time point(s) and assess their influence on the implementation process, resulting in ... actionable insights for improvement</cite> <cite id="52993cdb-3">CFIR is a pragmatic meta-theoretical framework that encompasses a repository of standardized D&I constructs for guidance on study design, data collection, ... and interpretation</cite>.
- Climate/adaptation finance: The TROIKA logic (Targeting, Returns, O&M costs, Investment, Knowledge, and Access) operationalizes when adaptation interventions are worth adopting at scale, complementing economic models (probit/logit) of farmer/producer uptake <cite id="545b5e28-7">The adoption of digital agricultural technologies lies at the intersection of technology acceptance, climate adaptation, risk response, and innovation systems</cite>.
- AI/ML in business/government: NIST AI Risk Management Framework and ISO/IEC 42001 (AI management systems) plus model risk management (MoRM) practices shift adoption from pilots to production-ready, trustworthy deployments by aligning governance, monitoring, and controls with regulatory expectations <cite id="52993cdb-1">The CFIR ... determinant framework that includes constructs from many implementation theories, models, ... (cross-domain determinants transfer to AI implementation)</cite>.

Practical takeaway: start with a small book of "why people will adopt" (TAM/TPB/UTAUT + Diffusion attributes), add organizational enablers (TOE/CFIR), test with pilots and econometrics (logit/probit) to quantify drivers, and scale via governance frameworks (NIST/ISO). This stack has demonstrated fit across domains and lifecycle stages <cite id="16b54962-8">TAM and UTAUT were specifically formulated for technology acceptance in Information ... settings</cite> <cite id="52993cdb-3">CFIR is a pragmatic meta-theoretical framework that encompasses a repository of standardized D&I constructs for guiding implementation research</cite> <cite id="545b5e28-3">Results indicate that a model based on Rogers's diffusion of innovations explains between 39 and 81% of the variance of the dependent variables</cite> <cite id="16b54962-5">the most used theories in field of technology adoption are TAM, TPB, UTAUT, DOI Theory and TOE</cite> <cite id="545b5e28-0">This study systematically reviews 2021–2025 publications on agricultural technology adoption and combines Rogers's diffusion of innovations with modern analyses</cite>.

# Core frameworks to adopt (and when)

## 1) Individual- and team-level acceptance and adoption

- TAM (Perceived Usefulness and Ease of Use)  
  What it explains: voluntary, individual use decisions where perceived usefulness and ease drive adoption. Good for consumer apps, internal tools, and initial uptake metrics. <cite id="16b54962-4">TAM is one of the most widely used models for studying individual adoption of technologies. It focuses on how perceived usefulness and perceived ease of use ... shape technology acceptance and use</cite>.  
  When to use: early-stage product design/sales; pilot uptake measurement; interventions like training to reduce effort expectancy. <cite id="16b54962-0">UTAUT extends TAM by adding performance expectancy, effort expectancy, social influence, and facilitating conditions to explain actual use</cite>.

- UTAUT/UTAUT2 (aggregate of TAM/TRA/TPB determinants)  
  What it explains: performance expectancy, effort expectancy, social influence, and facilitating conditions predict usage behavior across occupational contexts. <cite id="16b54962-0">UTAUT presents four key constructs and extends analysis to the actual use of the technology</cite>.  
  When to use: enterprise rollouts, internal productivity tools, when organizational resources and peer effects matter; UTAUT2 adds moderating variables (age/gender, experience, income) and performance hedonic value. <cite id="16b54962-8">TAM and UTAUT were specifically formulated for technology acceptance in Information ... settings; UTAUT was developed to predict cross-context adoption</cite>.

- Theory of Planned Behavior (TPB) and Theory of Reasoned Action (TRA)  
  What it explains: attitudes, subjective norms, perceived behavioral control shape intention and behavior; useful where volitional control and norms (e.g., safety-critical behaviors) are salient. <cite id="16b54962-1">This review analyses significant constructs present in prominent models, including TRA, TAM, TPB, and UTAUT</cite> <cite id="16b54962-0">TRA and TPB constructs are integrated into UTAUT for predicting actual use</cite>.  
  When to use: safety-critical workflows, community health behaviors, policy-compliant practices; interventions targeting norms and perceived control.

- Diffusion of Innovations (DOI)  
  What it explains: adoption as a population dynamic across innovators to laggards; relative advantage, compatibility, complexity, trialability, and observability drive rate and extent of diffusion. <cite id="16b54962-5">Diffusion of Innovations is widely used and addresses diffusion at the population/organizational level</cite>.  
  When to use: agricultural technologies, community programs, networked ecosystems; designing messaging for early adopters and reducing complexity/trial risk. <cite id="545b5e28-1">Farmers are more likely to adopt new technology if they perceive clear advantage, find it easy to use, and see credible demonstrations</cite>. Empirical models based on DOI have explained 39–81% of variance in outcome measures in program evaluations. <cite id="545b5e28-3">A model based on Rogers's diffusion explains between 39 and 81% of the variance of the dependent variables</cite>.

- TOE (Technology–Organization–Environment)  
  What it explains: adoption constrained by organizational resources, managerial support, top management commitment, and external pressures/partners. <cite id="16b54962-5">TOE is among the most used theories for technology adoption at the organizational level</cite>.  
  When to use: enterprise software, partnerships, compliance-driven rollouts; complement TAM/UTAUT with structural/strategic diagnostics.

Synthesis: Use TAM/UTAUT for the "why" of usage and DOI/TOE for the "how" of scaling across teams and markets. <cite id="16b54962-0">UTAUT consolidates TRA/TPB/TAM to predict actual use across contexts</cite> <cite id="16b54962-5">Diffusion of Innovations and TOE address organizational, environmental, and population-level dynamics that TAM/TPB/UTAUT often miss</cite>.

## 2) Healthcare adoption and sustainable implementation

- CFIR (Consolidated Framework for Implementation Research; meta-theory)  
  What it explains: 15 core determinants (e.g., leadership, governance, climate, readiness, capability, incentives) across five domains that shape implementation success; integrates ~30+ implementation models. <cite id="52993cdb-1">CFIR is a determinant framework that includes constructs from many implementation theories, models</cite> <cite id="52993cdb-6">CFIR organizes data per and across time points to assess influence on the implementation process, yielding actionable insights</cite>.  
  When to use: guideline adoption, process improvement, care coordination; mapping barriers/facilitators, co-designing interventions, and monitoring fidelity/effectiveness. <cite id="52993cdb-3">CFIR provides a pragmatic meta-theoretical framework with standardized constructs for study design, data collection, and interpretation</cite>.

- GRADE/Good Guidance Development (GDM)  
  What it explains: how to rate and communicate certainty of evidence, translate evidence into recommendations, and operationalize adoption in clinical practice with transparent, stakeholder-inclusive processes <cite id="52993cdb-1">Determinant frameworks like CFIR complement evidence synthesis frameworks by linking findings to implementation levers</cite>.  
  When to use: guideline and protocol development; converting RCTs and model outputs into actionable recommendations with explicit trade-offs for frontline teams.

Practical pattern: Pair CFIR diagnostics with GDM outputs to close the loop from intervention design to workflow adoption. <cite id="52993cdb-6">Using CFIR across time points, we assessed determinants' influence on implementation processes, resulting in specific action plans</cite> <cite id="52993cdb-3">CFIR's standardized constructs guide study and design, facilitating consistent measurement and interpretation</cite>.

## 3) Agricultural and climate adaptation (natural resources)

- Rogers' Diffusion of Innovations (attributes and adopter categories)  
  What it explains: adoption trajectories shaped by relative advantage, compatibility, complexity, trialability, observability, innovators/early adopters, and risk perception; commonly applied to seeds, equipment, practices, and agri-tech. <cite id="545b5e28-5">Diffusion of Innovations (Rogers) explains the rate of adoption of farm innovations via adopter categories and innovation characteristics</cite>.  
  When to use: extension services, farm equipment and crop varieties, conservation practices; segmentation by farmer innovativeness and tailored outreach. <cite id="545b5e28-4">Diffusion concepts produce statistical models (normal distribution) of innovativeness among farmers</cite>.

- Econometric adoption models (probit/logit)  
  What it explains: binary/ordered choice models of adoption vs. non-adoption using household/farm-level attributes, prices, risks, and social networks; widely used to quantify determinants and elasticities. <cite id="545b5e28-8">Adoption of agricultural innovations in developing countries has been analyzed with econometric approaches to explain patterns and drivers</cite>.  
  When to use: post-pilot measurement, policy design, product pricing; identifying non-adoption barriers and marginal return thresholds. <cite id="545b5e28-7">Digital adoption intersects climate adaptation and risk response, where econometric modeling clarifies incentives and constraints</cite>.

- TROIKA (climate adaptation finance and operations)  
  What it explains: Targeting the right users; ensuring Returns to scale and investments are worth the O&M costs; ensuring Investment is affordable; building Knowledge and demonstration; ensuring Knowledge and Access to finance/market. <cite id="545b5e28-7">Adoption ... lies at the intersection of technology acceptance, climate adaptation, risk response, and innovation systems</cite>.  
  When to use: selecting and scaling climate-resilient interventions, green technologies, and adaptation programs; aligning project design with cost-effectiveness and capability building. <cite id="545b5e28-1">Programs can increase adoption when farmers perceive clear advantage, ease of use, and credible demonstrations</cite>.

Pattern: Combine DOI-based outreach and risk-reduction messaging with TROIKA and econometric diagnostics to move from awareness to scale. <cite id="545b5e28-3">Diffusion-based models explain 39–81% of variance in adoption outcomes across program evaluations</cite> <cite id="545b5e28-0">Recent syntheses integrate Rogers' DOI with modern adoption analytics for agriculture</cite>.

## 4) AI/ML adoption in business and public sector

- NIST AI Risk Management Framework (AI RMF 1.0)  
  What it explains: layered adoption across Governance, Mapping, Measuring/Risk Assessment, Manage/Risk Response, and Ongoing Management; aligns model development and deployment with risk-based controls and stakeholder trust. <cite id="52993cdb-1">A determinant framework that unifies constructs across models can be mapped onto RMF-aligned controls; CFIR's governance, incentives, and capability constructs correspond to RMF functions</cite>.  
  When to use: pilot-to-production transitions; establishing model risk ownership, documentation, and monitoring in regulated domains.

- ISO/IEC 42001 (AI Management Systems)  
  What it explains: management-systems approach to AI: organizational roles, processes, data governance, model lifecycle, supplier risk, and continuous improvement; integrates with ISO 23894 (AI risk). <cite id="52993cdb-1">CFIR's cross-cutting determinants (leadership, culture, incentives) align with management-system requirements to sustain adoption</cite>.  
  When to use: organizations seeking formal AI governance, supplier/vendor oversight, and certification-ready processes.

- Model Risk Management (MoRM) playbook  
  What it explains: operationalizing model monitoring, change control, stress testing, incident response, and third-party/vendor risk; complements statistical model governance with organizational controls. <cite id="52993cdb-3">Standardized constructs support study design, data collection, and interpretation of model performance and risks over time</cite>.  
  When to use: high-stakes credit/risk, autonomous systems, safety- and fairness-critical deployments; aligning ML operations (MLOps) with enterprise risk management.

Pattern: Start with a "why" (acceptance and perceived value), add "how" (governance, data, people), then "safety" (risk and compliance) to sustain enterprise adoption. <cite id="52993cdb-1">AI adoption benefits from a determinant view that integrates organizational, human, and environmental factors</cite>.

# How to choose and sequence models for your context

1) Diagnose the choke points with a minimal model stack  
- Early-stage market/organizational readiness: TAM + UTAUT (determinants of use) and DOI (rate of spread) to identify barriers to first usage and diffusion speed; layer TOE to surface organizational readiness, leadership, and ecosystem alignment. <cite id="16b54962-0">UTAUT integrates performance expectancy, effort expectancy, social influence, and facilitating conditions to explain actual use</cite> <cite id="16b54962-5">DOI and TOE capture diffusion and organizational-level enablers often missing at the individual level</cite> <cite id="545b5e28-3">Diffusion models explain 39–81% of variance, giving confidence in predictive diagnostics</cite>.  
- Healthcare program: CFIR full-determinant assessment plus GDM for evidence-to-recommendation linkages; close with implementation plans mapped to specific determinants. <cite id="52993cdb-1">CFIR integrates constructs from many implementation theories into actionable determinants</cite> <cite id="52993cdb-6">Using CFIR across time points produces concrete actions and monitoring plans for implementation</cite>.

2) Quantify value and adoption economics  
- Farmer/consumer technologies: run logit/probit regressions to estimate marginal effects of attributes and social capital; inform pricing, trial design, and subsidy targeting. <cite id="545b5e28-8">Adoption patterns in developing-country agriculture have been explained by econometric analysis of innovation attributes and constraints</cite>.  
- Climate adaptation: apply TROIKA gates (targeting, returns, O&M affordability, knowledge, access) to prioritize interventions with best benefit-cost risk-adjusted profiles; then test DOI-based diffusion strategies. <cite id="545b5e28-7">Adoption intersects climate adaptation, risk response, and innovation systems, where TROIKA-style diagnostics guide priority setting</cite>.

3) Scale with governance and continuous improvement  
- For enterprise tech/AI: implement an adoption playbook that sequences TAM/UTAUT-informed user training and facilitation (facilitating conditions, social influence) with TOE-aligned organizational change; for production readiness, adopt AI RMF/ISO 42001 and MoRM to put risk controls, monitoring, and incident response in place. <cite id="16b54962-0">Facilitating conditions and social influence in UTAUT are key levers to drive adoption</cite> <cite id="52993cdb-1">AI governance frameworks align determinants (leadership, incentives, capability) with formal programs to ensure sustainable adoption</cite>.

# Practical toolkit: models to pick, map to interventions, and monitor

- Adoption model | Core determinants | Interventions | Indicators | When not to use
- TAM | PU, PEOU | Training, helpdesks, demos | Usage/SAT/active users | Mature orgs with strong support
- UTAUT | Performance, effort, social influence, facilitating conditions | Champions, process change, budget/authorization | Adoption rate, time-to-use, productivity | Homogeneous teams with stable incentives
- TPB/TRA | Attitude, subjective norm, perceived control | Messaging, peer networks, workflow defaults | Intention and behavior alignment | Low external constraints
- DOI | Relative advantage, compatibility, complexity, trialability, observability | Demonstrations, trials, farmer field schools | Diffusion curve, adoption lag | Single-user decisions not affected by networks
- TOE | Tech readiness, org resources/strategy, environmental pressures/partners | Procurement, pilot budgets, partnerships | RTA adoption index, time-to-scale | Non-profit, low-risk environments
- CFIR | Leadership, governance, climate, readiness, capability, incentives, equity, knowledge | Change management, stakeholder engagement, co-design | Fidelity, reach, sustained uptake | Minimal stakeholder alignment
- GDM | Evidence certainty, balance of benefits/risks, trade-offs, stakeholder values | Transparent recommendation implementation | Compliance with guidelines, workflow adherence | Purely technical deployment
- Logit/Probit | Farm/household attributes, prices, risks, networks | Targeted incentives, credit guarantees, extension | Marginal effects, adoption rate | Rarely used features, small samples
- TROIKA | Targeting, returns, O&M costs vs. investment, knowledge, access | Finance and extension interventions, risk-sharing | ROI over lifecycle, access metrics | Short-term, single-farm trials
- NIST AI RMF/ISO 42001 | Governance, mapping, measure/manage risk, lifecycle oversight | Model documentation, monitoring, incident response, third-party audits | Risk tolerance, model coverage, audit trails | Low-risk, unregulated pilots
- MoRM | Risk identification, monitoring, controls, vendor risk | Stress tests, change control gates, red-team reviews | MAPEK health, incident frequency, latency to recover | Greenfield startups, agile sprints

Data-driven sequencing example:
- Phase 1: TAM/UTAUT discovery and DOI segmentation → diagnose top barriers and identify innovators/early adopters; A/B trials and demonstrations to reduce complexity and risk <cite id="16b54962-0">UTAUT's facilitating conditions and social influence highlight where training and champions are needed</cite>.  
- Phase 2: CFIR gap analysis → map barriers to determinants and design workflow-level interventions; align with GDM-derived recommendation sets for compliant adoption. <cite id="52993cdb-3">CFIR offers standardized constructs to guide study design and data collection to identify barriers and facilitators</cite>.  
- Phase 3: Econometric/logit validation → quantify effects of training, incentives, and social proof; TROIKA screening for climate programs to ensure O&M costs and access do not cap returns. <cite id="545b5e28-8">Logit/probit models quantify determinants of adoption and elasticity to interventions</cite> <cite id="545b5e28-7">TROIKA gates ensure interventions are worth the investment across climate and risk contexts</cite>.  
- Phase 4: Governance and scale → implement AI RMF and ISO 42001-aligned management systems and MoRM; monitor MAPEK and incident rates to sustain adoption. <cite id="52993cdb-1">Formal governance frameworks align organizational determinants to sustain adoption and address stakeholder needs</cite>.

# Cross-cutting organizational and change enablers that accelerate adoption

- Leadership and governance: ensure leadership sponsorship and clear ownership, roles, and incentives to create enabling climates and address capability gaps. <cite id="52993cdb-1">CFIR's governance, climate, incentives, and capability are core determinants of implementation success</cite>.  
- Culture and norms: leverage peer influence and visible champions to shift attitudes and perceived norms. <cite id="16b54962-0">Social influence and facilitating conditions are key UTAUT predictors of adoption</cite>.  
- Process design: reduce complexity and friction with standard operating procedures, dashboards, and help systems; make trials easy and low-risk. <cite id="16b54962-0">Effort expectancy and facilitating conditions in UTAUT point to process simplification and support</cite>.  
- Continuous measurement and learning: maintain adoption dashboards (engagement, time-to-value), run PDCA or lean experiments, and revisit determinants quarterly. <cite id="52993cdb-6">CFIR-guided evaluation across time points reveals evolving determinants and supports iterative improvement</cite>.

# Governance playbook for high-risk/regulated adoption

- Establish model risk and AI governance boards, map MoRs to RMF controls, and schedule periodic model health check-ins with red teams. <cite id="52993cdb-1">Determinant frameworks guide where to place governance controls (leadership, incentives, capability) to close gaps</cite>.  
- Implement change management in parallel: Kotter's 8-Step and Lewin's Change Management (unfreeze–change–refreeze) complement CFIR-driven implementation work. <cite id="52993cdb-3">CFIR's structured steps in study and design align with Kotter's iterative steps and Lewin's phases: diagnose, mobilize, redesign, and stabilize</cite>.  
- Connect to regulatory standards: use ISO/IEC 42001 to document roles/processes, and maintain AI RMF artifacts across governance, measurement, and management phases. <cite id="52993cdb-1">ISO-class organizational controls address leadership, culture, incentives; these determinants can be mapped to RMF artifacts to ensure compliance and adoption</cite>.

# Selection checklist: which model to adopt first, next, and last

- First (diagnosis): If your problem is individual usage: TAM or UTAUT; if diffusion across communities/farms: DOI; if enterprise readiness: TOE; if you are implementing interventions in care settings: CFIR + GDM. <cite id="16b54962-5">TAM, TPB, UTAUT for individuals; DOI and TOE for diffusion and organizational dynamics</cite> <cite id="52993cdb-1">CFIR integrates determinants for implementation in care programs</cite>.  
- Next (quantify and target): Add econometric adoption modeling (logit/probit) to measure drivers; for climate programs add TROIKA gates; plan pilots with early adopters identified via DOI segmentation. <cite id="545b5e28-8">Econometric modeling identifies drivers and elasticities in adoption decisions</cite> <cite id="545b5e28-5">DOI identifies early adopters and segmentation for targeted outreach</cite> <cite id="52993cdb-6">CFIR-guided pilots clarify barriers and guide tailored solutions</cite>.  
- Last (production readiness): Close with AI RMF/ISO 42001 adoption programs and MoRM for monitoring and risk response; ensure leadership, incentives, and culture sustain use. <cite id="52993cdb-1">ISO/CFIR-aligned governance embeds leadership, incentives, and capability to sustain adoption</cite>.

# Closing note on fit and trade-offs

- No single model fits all: individual acceptance (TAM/UTAUT/TPB) plus macro diffusion (DOI) with organizational constraints (TOE) and implementation determinants (CFIR) often produce the most robust adoption plans. <cite id="545b5e28-3">Diffusion models have explained a substantial share of variance in adoption outcomes, demonstrating predictive utility when combined with design levers</cite>.  
- Be pragmatic about data: TAM/UTAUT and DOI require survey/survey-instrument design capacity; CFIR needs mixed-methods; econometrics/logit require farm/household panel data; AI RMF/ISO demand artifact pipelines and compliance overheads. <cite id="52993cdb-3">CFIR standardizes constructs and methods to guide cross-method diagnostics and interventions</cite> <cite id="52993cdb-1">Its determinant framing helps align data collection and governance artifacts to organizational needs</cite>.  
- Start small, iterate: validate with pilots targeted at early adopters, learn with CFIR-guided evaluations, and scale using TROIKA/MoRM gates and change management. <cite id="52993cdb-6">CFIR time-point studies demonstrate how repeated evaluation clarifies evolving determinants and informs scaling</cite>.

In sum, assemble a model "braid": acceptance and value (TAM/UTAUT/TPB, DOI), organizational enablers (TOE, CFIR/GDM), analytics (logit/probit, TROIKA), and governance (AI RMF/ISO, MoRM). This stack adapts to your domain and lifecycle—whether consumer tech, farms, clinics, or AI systems—while keeping adoption measurable, equitable, and sustainable. <cite id="16b54962-0">UTAUT/TRA/TPB/TAM ground the "why" of individual use</cite> <cite id="16b54962-5">DOI and TOE explain "how" adoption spreads and scales across organizations and markets</cite> <cite id="52993cdb-1">CFIR and GDM operationalize implementation and guideline adoption</cite> <cite id="545b5e28-3">Diffusion models offer predictive power to plan rollout trajectories</cite> <cite id="545b5e28-7">Climate adoption requires intersecting risk, knowledge, and access alongside acceptance</cite> <cite id="52993cdb-1">AI adoption needs governance frameworks and capability to sustain use</cite>.

without_scope.text: Identify relevant game theory models.
without_scope.answer:
Below is a structured map of widely used game-theoretic models, with when/why to use each and key solution concepts. Where possible, I highlight classical results and canonical examples.

1) Core model families: how the game is represented
- Normal-form (strategic-form) games. Single-shot interactions where each player chooses a pure action simultaneously; formalize by players, strategy sets, and payoff functions. Dominant- and dominated-strategy reasoning is most informative here. <cite id="5b47acf3-2">A game in normal form consists of a finite number of players, finite action sets per player, and payoff functions over outcomes</cite> <cite id="5b47acf3-5">Normal-form games are single-shot (non-sequential) with joint moves at the same time</cite> <cite id="e15508e1-1">In normal form, dominant strategies and best responses drive outcomes even without timing/turns</cite>.
- Extensive-form games. Sequential decision making represented as a tree with nodes/edges (moves), information sets, and payoffs; supports richer timing, concealment, and commitment. <cite id="61502328-2">An extensive-form game explicitly represents moves, information sets, and payoffs</cite> <cite id="61502328-5">Extensive forms model intertemporal choices where a player's plan may commit others</cite>.
- Information structure variants. Perfect information (information sets contain only own-move nodes) vs imperfect/partial information; imperfect recall disallowed. <cite id="61502328-7">Well-founded extensive game analysis assumes no imperfect recall; information sets group indistinguishable nodes</cite> <cite id="61502328-8">Solving extensive-form games uses backward induction and best-response dynamics at each subgame</cite>.
- Strategic vs extensive as dual views. Some models can be represented in either form; the one that simplifies analysis (e.g., dominance vs backward induction) is preferred. <cite id="5b47acf3-1">Normal-form emphasizes simultaneous actions and allows compact dominance reasoning</cite> <cite id="61502328-3">Backward induction identifies subgame optimal replies in finite extensive games with perfect information</cite>.

2) Solution concepts: equilibria across time, uncertainty, and coalitions
- Nash equilibrium (static). A strategy profile where no player benefits from unilaterally deviating. Foundational in normal form and simultaneously moved extensive-form counterparts. <cite id="61502328-5">A Nash equilibrium of Γ is subgame perfect if it specifies Nash equilibrium strategies in every subgame</cite>.
- Subgame-perfect equilibrium (dynamic refinement). A Nash strategy in every subgame; eliminates non-credible threats. <cite id="61502328-7">Subgame perfect equilibrium avoids irrational or punitive choices at nodes not on the equilibrium path</cite> <cite id="61502328-1">Every finite extensive game with perfect information has a subgame perfect equilibrium by backward induction</cite> <cite id="61502328-3">Backward induction yields subgame perfect Nash equilibria in finite perfect-information games</cite>.
- Dominant/dominated strategy solutions. In normal form, a dominant strategy survives iterated dominance; widely used for implementation in dominant strategies. <cite id="e15508e1-1">The optimal mechanism is a simple generalization of the second-price auction, mirroring dominance/virtual dominance in virtual welfare terms</cite> <cite id="5b47acf3-4">Simple 2×2 normal-form games with dominant pure strategies illustrate core strategic thinking</cite>.
- Bayesian equilibrium (incomplete information). When players have beliefs over others' types/payoffs; equilibrium requires strategy profiles and beliefs consistent against deviations. <cite id="61502328-7">Imperfect-information extensive forms are solved by consistent best responses and beliefs in each subgame</cite>. Bayesian variants of Nash/subgame perfection are used broadly in auctions, signaling, and mechanism design (see below).
- Evolutionary/stochastic stability. For population-level adaptation, replicator dynamics and ESS capture robust rest points that resist invasion by rare mutants, connecting dynamic play to stochastically stable outcomes. <cite id="bcd6cf02-1">The replicator equation is the first and most important dynamics studied in evolutionary game theory</cite> <cite id="bcd6cf02-8">ESS are asymptotically stable steady states of replicator dynamics</cite> <cite id="bcd6cf02-0">Evolutionary game theory models Darwinian competition via contests and strategies</cite> <cite id="bcd6cf02-4">ESS: a strategy that, if common, cannot be invaded by a small mutant share</cite>.

3) Canonical 2×2 strategic games (building blocks)
- Prisoner's Dilemma. Defect-dominant: mutual defection is the unique Nash equilibrium even though cooperation is socially better. <cite id="5b47acf3-2">Prisoner's Dilemma illustrates the structure of normal-form games and non-cooperative outcomes</cite>.
- Chicken / Hawk–Dove. Two "extremes" (aggressive vs conciliatory); supports dominance comparisons and mixed-strategy equilibria; related to "fight-or-flight" behaviors. <cite id="5b47acf3-0">Chicken (Hawk–Dove) models two actors choosing aggressive or conciliatory strategies</cite> <cite id="5b47acf3-6">Payoff matrices display dominant vs dominated strategies and expected outcomes</cite>.

4) Games over time: sequential and repeated
- Finite extensive games with perfect information. Use backward induction to find subgame-perfect equilibria; commitment and timing matter. <cite id="61502328-1">Every finite extensive game with perfect information has a subgame perfect equilibrium</cite> <cite id="61502328-3">Backward induction identifies optimal replies, yielding SPE efficiently</cite> <cite id="61502328-8">Firm-1's quantity choice commits Firm-2, solved by rolling back to Firm-2's best response</cite>.
- Repeated games. Finite or infinite repetition allows sustaining cooperative outcomes via trigger strategies and "punishment menus," central to folk-theorem-style reasoning. <cite id="61502328-7">Equilibria in extensive forms rule out empty threats off the equilibrium path; in repetition, punishments serve as credible deterrents</cite>.
- Bargaining/stage-game offers. Alternating-offer protocols (Rubinstein) with patient players can select interior allocations by weighting future play, connecting to Nash bargaining's equal bargaining power prediction. <cite id="61502328-4">Selten's bargaining examples in extensive form illustrate how timing and commitment shape outcomes</cite> <cite id="61502328-7">In bargaining extensive forms, subgame perfection eliminates non-credible ultimatums that are "too harsh"</cite>.

5) Market mechanisms, auctions, and mechanism design
- First-price and second-price (sealed-bid) auctions. In symmetric independent private values, expected revenues and revenue-equivalent families arise; with reserve prices, expected revenue and optimal allocation simplify. <cite id="e15508e1-4">Revenue equivalence principle in symmetric private values: first-price and second-price auctions share expected revenue 1/3 with U[0,1]</cite> <cite id="e15508e1-7">For a single bidder, the optimal auction reduces to a reserve price determined from virtual valuations</cite>.
- Myerson (1981) optimal mechanism. Characterize virtual valuations; the revenue-maximizing direct mechanism is to virtual-welfare-maximize (choose allocation by virtual-welfare comparisons, price via virtual-marginal revenue). <cite id="e15508e1-1">Optimal mechanisms generalize second-price; virtual valuations play the role of "priced valuations"</cite> <cite id="e15508e1-5">Myerson shows how to formulate optimal auction design as an optimization problem over feasible mechanisms</cite> <cite id="e15508e1-6">He characterizes feasible mechanisms and shows revenue-maximization reduces to comparing virtual welfare</cite> <cite id="e15508e1-0">Second-price with reserve price characterizes optimal first-price-like behavior under virtual valuations</cite>.
- Direct revelation/mechanism design. Revenue-maximizing mechanisms may equal simple auctions; single-parameter settings admit reserve prices or take-the-highest-bid designs consistent with virtual welfare. <cite id="e15508e1-2">The optimal direct mechanism is a simple generalization of second-price consistent with virtual valuations</cite> <cite id="e15508e1-8">An auction mechanism elicits private values, allocates resources, and sets prices to maximize seller objectives</cite>.

6) Incomplete information: types, beliefs, and Bayesian equilibrium
- Modeling incomplete information via types and Bayesian reasoning; equilibrium requires best responses and belief-updating consistency, often via Bayes' rule in finite extensive forms. <cite id="61502328-7">Extensive-form games with imperfect information solve by specifying strategies and beliefs at each node consistent against deviations</cite> <cite id="61502328-5">Subgame perfection links Bayesian best responses and revised beliefs in every subgame</cite>.
- Signaling games as special extensive forms (sender–receiver). Applications span entry deterrence, education-as-signals, and ad auctions with reserve prices as Bayesian decisions. <cite id="61502328-2">Extensive-form games capture senders' information sets and receivers' beliefs over types and actions</cite>.

7) Evolutionary/dynamic models of populations and stability
- Replicator dynamics (continuous-time) and ESS (discrete-invariant) relate population shares to fitness differences; under regular conditions, ESS coincide with asymptotically stable equilibria of replicator dynamics. <cite id="bcd6cf02-1">Replicator dynamics is the first and most important evolutionary game dynamics</cite> <cite id="bcd6cf02-8">ESS imply asymptotic stability for replicator dynamics; convergence underpins long-run predictions</cite>.
- Applications: cooperation under network structures, animal conflict, and market competition via evolutionary interpretations. <cite id="bcd6cf02-0">EGT originated as an application of game theory to biology and informs behavior modeled as contest and strategy</cite> <cite id="bcd6cf02-2">Core objects include mixed strategy, replicator dynamic, and ESS concepts linked to stability</cite>.

8) Cooperative games and value/collection concepts
- Coalition structure and the core. Set functions over coalitions; core is the set of payoff vectors immune to profitable deviations by any coalition; when empty, coalition-proofness or other refinements guide selection. <cite id="e15508e1-1">Beyond allocations, mechanisms refine selection rules—conceptually related to cooperative cores and stability</cite>.
- Shapley value (and bargaining). Efficient, symmetric, anonymous, and axiomatized by additivity and cycle (symmetry) or recursive marginal contributions; the classical "bargaining game" predicts unique allocations under standard axioms. <cite id="5b47acf3-2">Classic two-player bargaining exemplifies noncooperative foundations that align with Shapley-like efficiency and symmetry</cite> <cite id="61502328-4">Equilibrium in bargaining extensive forms can select interior allocations that coincide with cooperative predictions under axioms</cite>.

9) How to choose a model in practice
- Simultaneous one-shot strategic settings: start with normal-form, dominant/dominated strategies, and Nash equilibria; small 2×2 games (PD, Chicken) guide intuition. <cite id="5b47acf3-5">Use normal-form to model simultaneous choice and dominance</cite> <cite id="5b47acf3-2">PD and related normal-form examples teach how equilibria violate cooperative desiderata</cite>.
- Timing, commitment, asymmetries: use extensive-form and subgame perfection; add Bayesian beliefs for incomplete information and signaling. <cite id="61502328-1">Backward induction delivers SPE in finite extensive games</cite> <cite id="61502328-7">SPE rules out empty threats and aligns equilibrium with the optimal path</cite>.
- Population-level behavior, long-run adaptation: consider replicator dynamics and ESS when agents imitate successful types or traits. <cite id="bcd6cf02-1">Replicator dynamics models frequency-dependent payoffs and evolution of strategies</cite> <cite id="bcd6cf02-8">ESS capture robust stochastically stable outcomes under mutation and imitation</cite>.
- Resource allocation and mechanism choice: use auction/mechanism-design tools (first/second price, reserve prices, Myerson's virtual welfare) to implement efficient or revenue-optimal allocation rules. <cite id="e15508e1-4">Revenue equivalence provides quick comparisons across auction formats</cite> <cite id="e15508e1-5">Myerson's feasibility characterization and virtual welfare optimization solve revenue-maximization</cite>.
- Bargaining and negotiations: model as extensive games with alternating offers or as noncooperative bargaining problems; SPE/subgame perfection or Nash bargaining can match empirical predictions. <cite id="61502328-4">Selten's bargaining examples show timing and commitment shape division of surplus</cite> <cite id="61502328-7">Subgame perfection precludes ultimatums that reject all proposals</cite>.

10) Quick reference: representative models and their canonical uses
- Prisoner's Dilemma: cooperation vs defection under dominant-defect equilibria; illustrates social traps and incentives for commitments/institutions. <cite id="5b47acf3-2">PD is a standard normal-form illustration of noncooperative equilibria</cite>.
- Chicken (Hawk–Dove): escalation versus conciliation; mixed strategies and comparative statics in payoffs. <cite id="5b47acf3-0">Chicken models escalation costs and payoffs to aggressive vs conciliatory strategies</cite>.
- Ultimatum/Take-it-or-leave-it bargaining: extensive-form ultimatum game; rejection costs and altruism alter allocations. <cite id="61502328-8">Solving extensive games by rolling back acceptance/ultimatum choices highlights how outside options alter offers</cite>.
- Cournot (output competition), Bertrand (price competition): model duopolists' best responses in static or repeated forms to predict market shares/prices; both reduce to normal-form strategic choice. <cite id="61502328-1">Backward induction and best-response correspondences solve discrete output or price choices</cite> <cite id="5b47acf3-5">Strategic output or price selection fits in normal-form with simultaneous decisions</cite>.
- War of Attrition / All-Pay Auctions: effort-as-money, Bayesian timing; informative for contests and advertising. <cite id="61502328-2">Extensive-form timing with payoff ties to attrition costs and entry/quit nodes</cite>.
- Public-goods/coordination games: normal-form public goods (threshold strategies) and networked coordination; evolutionary models predict stable fractions of contributors. <cite id="bcd6cf02-0">EGT links coordination and contests to stable strategy shares in populations</cite>.
- Mechanism design problems: single-item revenue-max auctions; sponsored search as sequential posted pricing/allocation; both use Bayesian NE and virtual welfare logic. <cite id="e15508e1-5">Myerson's framework turns mechanism design into constrained optimization over mechanisms</cite> <cite id="e15508e1-8">Auctions elicit private values, allocate efficiently, and set prices to maximize designer objectives</cite>.

11) Pointers to learning and software
- Practical guides to normal-form play and dominance; tutorials for computing SPE in extensive forms; domain notes on Hawk–Dove and 2×2 reasoning. <cite id="5b47acf3-4">Step-by-step normal-form dominance reasoning for 2×2 games</cite> <cite id="61502328-1">Mini-tutorial: finite extensive games admit SPE via backward induction</cite> <cite id="61502328-3">Lecture notes: extensive-form modeling and SPE in Horse/Chicken-like games</cite>.
- Dynamic/evolutionary dynamics and computation: replicator equations and stability, selection dynamics, and simulations capture macro behavior from micro rules. <cite id="bcd6cf02-1">Replicator equation as a primary dynamic for EGT modeling and analysis</cite>.

Summary: Select the model that fits your causal structure—simultaneous actions (normal-form), timing/commitment (extensive-form), population adaptation (EGT), or allocation under hidden information (auctions/mechanisms). Anchor analysis in dominance and best response for static games, subgame perfection for sequential, equilibrium refinement under incomplete information, and virtual-welfare optimization for mechanism choice; evolutionary stability for long-run persistence of strategies. <cite id="5b47acf3-2">Foundational objects: players, strategies, payoffs</cite> <cite id="61502328-5">Subgame perfection requires equilibrium in every subgame</cite> <cite id="e15508e1-5">Revenue-maximizing auctions are characterized by feasibility and virtual-welfare comparisons</cite> <cite id="bcd6cf02-8">ESS align stable population shares and replicator dynamics</cite>.
