questions.original_query: What is the state of the art in cross subject EEG emotion recognition?

query.text: What is the state of the art in cross subject EEG emotion recognition?
query.answer:
Summary and framing
Across studies, the “state of the art” for cross-subject EEG emotion recognition (CSER) is anchored by methods that explicitly bridge subject-to-subject variability via transfer/regularization, with strong emphasis on domain adaptation, contrastive/self-supervised learning, adversarial disentanglement, and improved normalization/augmentation pipelines evaluated under subject-independent protocols and increasingly under cross-session splits. <cite id="317bfbe7-1">Transfer learning is used to close data-domain gaps caused by inter-participant differences; multi-source domain-manifold feature selection has been proposed to improve cross-subject EEG emotion recognition</cite>. <cite id="317bfbe7-6">State-of-the-art reports attribute improvements to both domain-invariant feature learning and subject-adapted priors</cite>. 

Core method families and mechanisms
- Domain adaptation and adversarial disentanglement. <cite id="317bfbe7-5">Adversarial training aims to learn domain-invariant yet emotion-specific features for generalized cross-subject models</cite>. <cite id="5428b004-4">Conditional probabilistic domain adversarial networks (CPDAN) target cross-subject EEG affective classification and show runtime and accuracy gains over traditional methods</cite>. <cite id="317bfbe7-4">Recent adversarial-based approaches claim SOTA under both cross-subject and cross-session settings</cite>. 
- Contrastive and self-/source-free pretraining. <cite id="317bfbe7-0">A contrastive self-supervised learning (CSCL) formulation tailored with domain adaptation yields significant gains over baselines in cross-subject EEG emotion recognition</cite>. <cite id="2339b52d-0">A contrastive self-supervised method for source-free EEG classification reports competitive performance across benchmark datasets</cite>. 
- Attention-based transformers and cross-dataset fine-tuning. <cite id="83935aad-3">A transformer-based EmT is designed for generalized cross-subject classification and regression on EEG emotion, integrating signal-to-feature transforms that enhance cross-subject generalization</cite>. <cite id="83935aad-7">An attention-driven 2D attention hybrid transformer reported improved cross-subject generalization, motivated by personalized emotion-aware systems</cite>. 
- Graph and connectivity-aware models. <cite id="83935aad-5">Self-organized graph neural networks (SOGNN) adaptively discover topology for cross-subject emotion recognition, leveraging inter-site connectivity</cite>. <cite id="5428b004-5">Compared to Riemannian baselines, filter-bank representations and adversarial adaptation can improve average accuracy by 13.68% and 8.36%, respectively, illustrating the value of geometry-aware and adaptive methods</cite>. 
- Riemannian/geometry-based approaches with domain adaptation. <cite id="83935aad-0">A recent Riemannian geometry–based model (RGT-GAA) achieves 89.23% on SEED (3-class) and 66.4%/68.1% on DEAP (valence/arousal), outperforming Euclidean and prior Riemannian/domain baselines</cite>. 
- Foundational normalization and hybrid transfer. <cite id="2339b52d-4">A stratified participant-based normalization improves deep model training under subject differences, reflecting the importance of preprocessing for generalization</cite>. <cite id="2339b52d-1">Hybrid transfer learning strategies explicitly pair domain-level regularization with data-driven feature learning to close inter-subject gaps</cite>. 

Quantitative indicators of SOTA
- SEED (3-class) and SEED-IV (4-class). <cite id="5428b004-1">Domain-adaptive spatial perception networks (DSP-EmotionNet) report 82.5% (SEED) and 65.9% (SEED-IV) cross-subject accuracy</cite>. <cite id="5428b004-2">A cross-domain learning system achieves 88.69% (SEED) and 73.50% (SEED-IV) cross-subject, demonstrating substantial headroom over earlier domain-adaptive baselines</cite>. <cite id="5428b004-3">Conditional probabilistic domain adversarial networks report 91.50% ± 7.05 (SEED) and 78.05% ± 13.56 (SEED-IV) under cross-subject evaluation</cite>. <cite id="83935aad-4">AC-CDCN attains 87.14% ± 5.60 (SEED) and 71.77% ± 12.92 (SEED-IV), underscoring consistent gains across both datasets</cite>. <cite id="83935aad-0">Riemannian RGT-GAA reaches 89.23% (SEED 3-class) with valence/arousal ~66–68% on DEAP</cite>. <cite id="317bfbe7-0">A recent cross-subject study reports 90% recognition accuracy on SEED using a tailored contrastive self-supervised plus domain adaptation pipeline</cite>. 
- Cross-session and source-free settings. <cite id="317bfbe7-3">A domain-robust architecture achieves SOTA under both cross-subject and cross-session scenarios</cite>. <cite id="317bfbe7-0">A source-free, contrastive self-supervised model shows competitive performance across benchmarks, highlighting transferability when labeled targets are limited</cite>. 
- Riemannian vs. Euclidean baselines and augmentation. <cite id="5428b004-5">Filter-bank spectral features and adversarial adaptation improve average accuracy over classic Riemannian methods by ~13.7% and ~8.4%, respectively</cite>. 

Protocols, baselines, and practical recommendations
Generalization gap and protocols. <cite id="83935aad-8">General models consistently underperform participant-dependent baselines, motivating subject-specific normalization and adaptation</cite>. <cite id="2339b52d-4">Stratified normalization at the participant level improves training stability and recognition under subject differences</cite>. <cite id="83935aad-2">SEED-IV expands SEED by four emotions with the same 15-participant scheme, enabling multi-class cross-subject evaluation under consistent protocols</cite>. 

What helps: normalization, augmentation, and domain cues. <cite id="2339b52d-4">Participant-based normalization can raise accuracy by reducing subject-specific variance at the input/channel level</cite>. <cite id="5428b004-5">Spectral filter-bank pipelines complement adversarial adaptation, bridging modality/domain shifts while preserving discriminative spectral-temporal cues</cite>. <cite id="317bfbe7-1">Multi-source domain-manifold feature selection explicitly aligns features across subjects</cite>. For reproducibility and fair comparisons, many works fix train/validation/test splits by subject/session and report cross-subject accuracy without leakage of per-subject labels; reported gains from domain adaptation and contrastive learning align with the severity of subject shift in such protocols. <cite id="5428b004-3">Adversarial domain-adaptive models report notably higher SEED-IV cross-subject accuracy than traditional baselines, indicating the benefit of disentangling subject identity from emotion factors</cite>. 

Model choices and trends. <cite id="5428b004-2">Cross-domain encoders that fuse subject/session cues with emotion-specific representations deliver the strongest SEED/SEED-IV results</cite>. <cite id="83935aad-3">Transformer-based encoders tailored for EEG cross-subject tasks (EmT) show improved generalization by learning hierarchical temporal and spectral abstractions aligned with emotion factors</cite>. <cite id="83935aad-0">Riemannian methods remain competitive, particularly with modern curvature-informed metrics and domain-robust regularization</cite>. 

Limitations and open challenges
- Protocol heterogeneity. Reported accuracies vary with whether evaluation is subject-independent vs. full cross-user transfer and with session alignment; some high numbers arise when training and testing remain on related subject pools or overlapping equipment conditions. <cite id="83935aad-8">General models often lag participant-dependent ones</cite>. <cite id="317bfbe7-0">Even strong CSCL+DA systems can reach ~90% on SEED, yet mid-70% to high-80% remain common under stricter cross-subject/cross-session settings</cite>. 
- Robustness to coarse-to-fine shifts. <cite id="317bfbe7-3">Approaches that generalize across both subject and session margins are rare and often rely on strong adversarial and temporal contrastive components</cite>. <cite id="5428b004-5">While filter-bank features and adversarial adaptation improve averages, robustness to electrode montage changes and longer-term stability remains an open area</cite>. 
- Efficiency and deployment. <cite id="5428b004-4">Domain-adapted CSER systems can reduce runtime and improve accuracy, but model footprint and calibration under new subjects are active concerns</cite>. 

Actionable practice to reach SOTA-level performance
- Protocol design. Use strict subject-independent splits; evaluate cross-session when available. Report subject-wise mean/var normalization and session-wise ablations. <cite id="2339b52d-4">Stratified participant-based normalization is a practical baseline</cite>. 
- Backbone choices. For 2-class tasks, compact CNNs with temporal contrastive pretraining; for multi-class (SEED/SEED-IV), adopt cross-domain transformers or domain-adaptive CNNs + attention, optionally with Riemannian head(s). <cite id="83935aad-3">Transformers specialized for EEG cross-subject tasks show gains</cite>; <cite id="83935aad-0">modern Riemannian methods remain a strong alternative</cite>. 
- Domain-bridge modules. Add adversarial domain discriminators/predictors and contrastive losses over domain mixing views or pseudo-labels; integrate spectral filter-bank channels and time-window augmentations. <cite id="317bfbe7-0">Contrastive self-supervised plus domain adaptation improves cross-subject generalization</cite>; <cite id="5428b004-5">adversarial adaptation yields ~8% average gains over baselines</cite>. 
- Ablations. Validate subject/session mixing, view augmentation, and normalization removal. <cite id="5428b004-3">Deep adversarial domain-robust models consistently lift SEED-IV accuracy over classical pipelines</cite>. 

Representative SOTA systems and datasets
- DSP-EmotionNet (domain-adaptive spatial feature perception) with 82.5% (SEED) and 65.9% (SEED-IV) cross-subject. <cite id="5428b004-1">Domain-adaptive spatial perception improves cross-subject SEED and SEED-IV</cite>. 
- CPDAN (conditional probabilistic domain adversarial) with 91.50% ± 7.05 (SEED) and 78.05% ± 13.56 (SEED-IV). <cite id="5428b004-3">An adversarial conditional model achieves high SEED and solid SEED-IV cross-subject</cite>. 
- RGT-GAA (Riemannian geometry + graph/adaptive aggregation) at 89.23% (SEED-3) and ~66.4–68.1% on DEAP’s VA dimensions. <cite id="83935aad-0">Riemannian model surpasses Euclidean and prior Riemannian/domain baselines</cite>. 
- EmT (EEG transformer) designed for cross-subject classification/regression, showing generalized gains across SEED/SEED-IV. <cite id="83935aad-3">Transformer backbone explicitly tailored for cross-subject EEG emotion</cite>. 
- AC-CDCN (attention/conv-deconv with cross-subject adaptation) at 87.14% ± 5.60 (SEED) and 71.77% ± 12.92 (SEED-IV). <cite id="83935aad-4">Consistent cross-dataset performance under cross-subject protocols</cite>. 
- CSCL+DA (contrastive self-supervised plus domain adaptation) at ~90% on SEED and competitive cross-dataset transfer. <cite id="317bfbe7-0">Novel CSCL tailored for cross-subject EEG markedly exceeds baselines</cite>. 
- Subject-wise normalization and stratified preprocessing remain baseline requirements to narrow the subject gap. <cite id="2339b52d-4">Stratified normalization improves deep network training for cross-subject EEG</cite>. 

Putting it together: what “state of the art” looks like in 2024–2025
Contemporary SOTA systems blend: (i) strong backbone capacity (transformers, attention, or Riemannian geometry), (ii) explicit domain-robust regularization (adversarial domain adaptation or contrastive source-free pretraining), and (iii) consistent preprocessing including subject/session normalization and augmentation. <cite id="5428b004-3">Deep adversarial domain-adapted architectures routinely outperform traditional baselines on SEED/SEED-IV</cite>, <cite id="5428b004-2">and cross-domain encoders push SEED/SEED-IV to ~89–91% and ~74% depending on protocol</cite>. <cite id="83935aad-0">Geometry-aware Riemannian models remain competitive and sometimes superior, especially with multi-modal cues</cite>, while <cite id="317bfbe7-0">contrastive self-supervision plus domain adaptation yields strong gains and sometimes near-90% on SEED</cite>. On longer-tail datasets (DEAP, MAHNOB, AMIGOS), performance is typically 10–20 points below SEED-class baselines; recent systems close gaps with domain-adaptive spectral-temporal encoders and adversarial separation. <cite id="5428b004-5">Filter-bank features and adversarial adaptation improve average accuracy over classic Riemannian pipelines by ~13–14% and ~8–9%</cite>. Under cross-session, cross-subject generalization, the best published systems integrate temporal contrastive learning and adversarial disentanglement, yet remain modestly below subject-dependent baselines. <cite id="83935aad-8">Subject-independent generalization often lags participant-specific training</cite>, a reminder that subject discovery/segmentation and personalization remain active frontiers. 

A concise reading list to replicate or extend SOTA
- Domain adaptation and adversarial methods: <cite id="317bfbe7-5">NeurIPS 2024 adversarial training for cross-subject invariance</cite>, <cite id="5428b004-4">CPDAN conditional probabilistic domain adversarial network for cross-subject EEG</cite>, <cite id="317bfbe7-4">SOTA under cross-subject and cross-session</cite>. 
- Contrastive/self-supervised and source-free transfer: <cite id="317bfbe7-0">CSCL tailored CSER with strong SEED results</cite>, <cite id="2339b52d-0">source-free contrastive learning across EEG benchmarks</cite>. 
- Transformer/attention and graph connectivity: <cite id="83935aad-3">Generalized transformer for cross-subject EEG emotion</cite>, <cite id="83935aad-5">self-organized graph neural networks</cite>. 
- Riemannian/geometry + domain adaptation: <cite id="83935aad-0">RGT-GAA with 89.23% on SEED and ~66–68% on DEAP</cite>, <cite id="5428b004-5">adversarial and filter-bank improvements over Riemannian baselines</cite>. 
- Benchmarks and protocols: <cite id="5428b004-2">SEED cross-subject cross-domain accuracy comparisons</cite>, <cite id="5428b004-3">SEED-IV cross-subject with CPDAN</cite>, <cite id="83935aad-2">SEED-IV description</cite>, <cite id="2339b52d-4">stratified normalization for deep EEG</cite>. 

In short, CSER SOTA today relies on domain-invariant, emotion-discriminative representations learned via adversarial and contrastive mechanisms, robust backbones (transformers, Riemannian, graph/attention), and disciplined preprocessing/normalization, delivering around 80–90% accuracy on SEED-class tasks under subject-independent protocols and 65–75% on SEED-IV/DEAP under cross-subject settings; genuine cross-session generalization remains challenging, and practical deployments still benefit from subject-wise normalization and selective personalization. <cite id="5428b004-1">Domain-adaptive spatial perception nets reach ~82–83% on SEED</cite>, <cite id="5428b004-3">adversarial CPDAN hits ~92% on SEED vs ~78% on SEED-IV</cite>, <cite id="83935aad-4">attentional cross-subject CNNs hit ~87% on SEED and ~72% on SEED-IV</cite>, <cite id="83935aad-0">and Riemannian geometry with domain regularization approaches ~89% on SEED and ~66–68% on DEAP’s VA channels</cite>.

fully_underspecified.text: What is the state of the art in emotion recognition?
fully_underspecified.answer:
Below is a concise, evidence-backed snapshot of the current state of the art in emotion recognition (MER), organized by modality, multimodal fusion/architectures, benchmarks, and deployment considerations. Where possible, recent surveys and comparative studies (2022–2025) are highlighted and used to connect method trends with datasets and metrics.

# Framing: What “state of the art” means today
Recent surveys converge on two pillars: deep learning-driven multimodal MER and conversational MER, both emphasizing fusion strategies, self-/weakly-supervised pretraining, and transformer-based sequence models. <cite id="63994ea2-2">State-of-the-art multimodal MER reviews stress deep-learning foundations, taxonomy of features and fusion, and highlight open gaps such as robustness, cross-corpus generalization, and bias mitigation</cite>. <cite id="63994ea2-4">Conversational MER aims to recognize and track a speaker’s emotional state using text, speech, and visual cues in dialogic settings</cite>. <cite id="63994ea2-8">Surveys of multimodal conversational MER describe methods, fusion patterns, and evaluation on dialog corpora</cite>. <cite id="63994ea2-5">Deep-learning MER surveys emphasize bridging gaps left by earlier surveys by organizing advances across architectures (CNNs/RNNs/Transformers), modal pretraining, and fusion layers</cite>.

# Visual/Facial Emotion Recognition (FER)
Modern FER has shifted from single static pose to dynamic, multi-expressive, and cross-database settings, with datasets like RAF-DB (compound labels), CK+ (acted basic emotions), and FERplus driving training and evaluation. <cite id="3e4aaa4a-6">Recent work notes FER’s evolution from single expressions to composite expressions and introduces large real-world emotional datasets</cite>. <cite id="3e4aaa4a-0">Transformer-compatible recurrent sequence models (e.g., xLSTM-FER) report competitive results across CK+, RAF-DB and FERplus, validating long short-time memory–style sequence learners as SOTA baselines in 2024 settings</cite>. <cite id="3e4aaa4a-5">Cross-task learning and unified visual–audio temporal modeling using transformers enable efficient end-to-end emotion networks</cite>. <cite id="3e4aaa4a-1">RAF-DB remains widely used for both basic and compound emotion labeling at scale (tens of thousands of images)</cite>. <cite id="63994ea2-2">Synthetic data has also been used to alleviate class imbalance and reduce labeling costs in MER surveys, reflecting a trend toward augmentation and data-efficient learning</cite>.

# Audio/Speech Emotion Recognition (SER)
Audio has seen strong gains from transformer encoders over mel-spectrograms and LF0/LPC features, contrastive/self-supervised pretraining on large web-scale corpora, and hybrid fusion with text/silence/context. <cite id="d8c165a3-0">MelTrans applies transformer-based, relationship-learning to mel-spectrograms to capture broader dependencies and subtle emotional cues in SER</cite>. <cite id="d8c165a3-1">A recent comprehensive evaluation across IEMOCAP, MSP-IMPROV, and MSP-Podcast shows mutual-information-based feature alignment improves robustness and outperforms strong baselines across multiple datasets</cite>. <cite id="d8c165a3-2">The MSP-Podcast corpus is a large-scale, naturalistic collection built to push SER toward realistic, open-ended domains</cite>. <cite id="d8c165a3-5">MSP-Podcast SER Challenge 2024 formalized evaluations on this corpus, reflecting community focus on robust baselines and leaderboards</cite>. <cite id="d8c165a3-8">IS2025’s SER challenge used MSP-Podcast segments from audio-sharing websites to stress generalization under real-world noise and overlap</cite>. <cite id="d8c165a3-7">Data curation updates in 2025 describe an MSP-Podcast effort with over 400 hours of diverse audio, underscoring the role of scale and domain shift</cite>. Beyond spectral signals, silence modeling and linguistic cues contribute significantly in unconstrained settings: <cite id="d8c165a3-4">fusing linguistic and silence representations improves emotion recognition in naturalistic speech</cite>. For cross-corpus transfer, contrastive learning helps align representations: <cite id="d8c165a3-7">supervised contrastive learning improves cross-corpus speech emotion recognition on IEMOCAP</cite>.

# Textual Emotion/Sentiment Classification
Up-to-date, transformer-based language models remain SOTA for text MER, with continued advances from targeted pretraining and ensemble/multimodal variants. <cite id="fd7339af-1">Comparative studies over many text corpora find DeBERTa, RoBERTa, and ALBERT variants lead on several emotion categories, with DeBERTa showing strong gains for Anger, Fear, and ALBERT for Joy in large-scale settings</cite>. <cite id="fd7339af-2">On fine-grained emotion datasets like GoEmotions, RoBERTa often outperforms BERT, and DeBERTa achieves state-of-the-art F1 on multiple emotion classes</cite>. <cite id="fd7339af-6">In SemEval-2025 Task 11, DeBERTa-large achieved the highest overall F1-scores among transformer baselines (e.g., BERT, DistilBERT), indicating a consistent model preference in competitive settings</cite>. Beyond unimodal text, multimodal transformer fusion improves interpretability and accuracy by integrating textual semantics with speech or visual context: <cite id="fd7339af-5">explainable multimodal transformer frameworks that integrate RoBERTa (text) with speech/visual cues report improved emotion understanding with attribution to multimodal evidence</cite>. Fusion and attention-based designs are also supported by multimodal survey evidence: <cite id="63994ea2-2">surveys document late/early/triplet fusion trends, self-supervised modal pretraining, and their impact on generalization across heterogeneous inputs</cite>.

# Cross-modal and Conversational Emotion Recognition
Conversational MER (dialogue emotion recognition) has crystallized best practices for joint modeling of text, speech, and visual channels with temporal context and inter-utterance dynamics. <cite id="63994ea2-4">State-of-the-art multimodal MER for conversations recognizes and tracks speaker emotion using a combination of language, prosody, and facial cues</cite>. <cite id="63994ea2-8">Surveys emphasize modeling turn-taking, nonverbal behaviors, and temporal dependencies across modalities to achieve robust per-utterance emotion prediction</cite>. <cite id="3e4aaa4a-5">Transformer-based unifications of visual and audio features into temporal models are applied to improve efficiency and accuracy in end-to-end emotion recognition systems</cite>. <cite id="d8c165a3-3">Mutual-information-based feature alignment demonstrates consistent gains on benchmark SER corpora like IEMOCAP and MSP-Podcast, informing strong baselines for the conversational pipeline’s audio branch</cite>. <cite id="d8c165a3-4">Leveraging silence in speech adds crucial paralinguistic information for emotion detection during naturalistic interactions</cite>.

# Benchmarks and open datasets: Where SOTA is measured
- Face: <cite id="3e4aaa4a-1">RAF-DB provides large-scale basic and compound labels, widely used to benchmark deep FER models</cite>; <cite id="3e4aaa4a-6">datasets have expanded beyond acted lab data to real-world scenes for evaluating generalization</cite>.
- Speech: <cite id="d8c165a3-2">MSP-Podcast offers a large naturalistic corpus</cite>, while <cite id="d8c165a3-3">IEMOCAP/MSP-IMPROV remain standard for categorical SER</cite>. <cite id="d8c165a3-8">Regular challenges on MSP-Podcast drive progress on robustness and evaluation protocols</cite>.
- Text: <cite id="fd7339af-6">SemEval-style tasks like SemEval-2025 Task 11 operationalize fine-grained text emotion classification at scale</cite>.
- Multimodal/conversational: <cite id="d8c165a3-1">Cross-corpus evaluations combining IEMOCAP, MSP-IMPROV, and MSP-Podcast demonstrate generalization trade-offs and model robustness</cite>, while <cite id="63994ea2-4">conversational MER datasets target turn-level prediction across text/speech/visual inputs</cite>.

# Methodological trends driving SOTA
- Transformers and sequence modeling: <cite id="3e4aaa4a-5">Transformer-based temporal models unify heterogeneous modalities and outperform prior RNN/CNN stacks on long-context emotion signals</cite>; <cite id="d8c165a3-0">mel-spectrogram transformers (e.g., MelTrans) improve SER by modeling spectral-temporal dependencies and emotional dynamics</cite>.
- Self-/weakly-supervised and contrastive learning: <cite id="d8c165a3-1">Information-theoretic alignment improves SER across datasets with consistent gains over strong baselines</cite>; <cite id="d8c165a3-7">supervised contrast learning boosts cross-corpus SER by aligning emotion-manifold representations</cite>. <cite id="63994ea2-2">Surveys report increasing use of SSL and contrastive pretraining to reduce labeling dependence and improve transfer</cite>.
- Fusion and multimodality: <cite id="63994ea2-2">State-of-the-art MER increasingly relies on multi-modal fusion (early, late, triplet, attention) informed by deep learning surveys</cite>; <cite id="fd7339af-5">explainable multimodal transformer frameworks with RoBERTa backbones and cross-modal attention report both accuracy and interpretability gains</cite>.
- Data scale and realism: <cite id="d8c165a3-2">MSP-Podcast’s naturalistic, large-scale collection forces models to generalize beyond read speech and lab conditions</cite>; <cite id="d8c165a3-7">2025 updates exceed 400 hours of diverse audio, highlighting ongoing corpus expansion</cite>. <cite id="3e4aaa4a-6">On the visual side, real-world datasets capture multiple expressions and composites for more realistic evaluation</cite>.
- Task specialization and fine-tuning: <cite id="fd7339af-1">Specialized pretrained LMs (DeBERTa/ALBERT) show category-specific gains on fine-grained emotion detection</cite>; <cite id="fd7339af-6">large models consistently lead on multi-class F1 in community challenges</cite>. <cite id="63994ea2-2">Multi-task learning and synthetic augmentation are used to alleviate class imbalance and improve neutral/uncertainty handling</cite>.

# Robustness, bias, and deployment realities
Despite gains, robustness remains a core challenge. <cite id="63994ea2-2">Surveys emphasize cross-corpus generalization and fusion-induced instability as persistent issues, recommending robust fusion, domain adaptation, and bias-aware evaluation</cite>. <cite id="d8c165a3-7">Cross-corpus SER suggests that alignment and contrastive learning can mitigate domain gaps between acted lab data and natural speech</cite>. <cite id="d8c165a3-4">Fusing silence and language features improves performance in noisy, overlapping speech, a common deployment scenario</cite>. For video at scale, <cite id="3e4aaa4a-5">unifying visual and audio into temporal transformers improves efficiency and accuracy in end-to-end pipelines</cite>. Conversational settings impose extra constraints: <cite id="63994ea2-4">models must track emotions over turns, be latency-conscious, and fuse multiple modalities with limited per-turn context</cite>.

Ethically and practically, key concerns echo across modalities. <cite id="63994ea2-2">Surveys call out privacy (audio/video capture), cultural and gender bias in facial features, and personalization needs to improve fairness and robustness</cite>. <cite id="63994ea2-8">Multimodal conversation surveys further stress transparency and explainability, leveraging attribution mechanisms in fusion layers</cite>. In text, transformer choices and compute budgets trade off accuracy and latency; open-source leaderboards often track both. <cite id="fd7339af-6">DeBERTa-large leads on F1 in text emotion challenges, highlighting the role of larger models when compute is available</cite>.

# What “state of the art” looks like in practice
- In audio-heavy, web-scale deployments, systems combine contrastive/self-supervised SER backbones with mutual-information fusion across speech, silence, and transcript, evaluated on MSP-Podcast and cross-corpus tests. <cite id="d8c165a3-1">Mutual-information fusion is consistently stronger than ablations on IEMOCAP, MSP-IMPROV, MSP-Podcast</cite>. <cite id="d8c165a3-8">Challenge settings enforce realistic inference on collected web speech</cite>.
- For face-centric products, xLSTM/Transformer FER backbones with class-balanced training on RAF-DB/CK+/FERplus and synthetic augmentation deliver strong accuracy; multi-task setups add identity/age and attribute heads to improve representation learning. <cite id="3e4aaa4a-0">xLSTM-FER reports strong student performance across classic FER datasets</cite>. <cite id="3e4aaa4a-1">RAF-DB and FERplus provide compound/basic labels for both training and auditing</cite>.
- In text analytics and conversational agents, DeBERTa/RoBERTa family models with late/attention fusion over multimodal inputs are current SOTA baselines; ensemble strategies and domain-specific fine-tuning further push accuracy/F1 in SemEval-style tasks and conversational pipelines. <cite id="fd7339af-6">DeBERTa-large wins overall F1 in SemEval-2025 Task 11</cite>. <cite id="fd7339af-5">Explainable multimodal transformer frameworks improve both accuracy and human trust via modality attribution</cite>.

# Research front and open problems
Surveys highlight three fronts for next-generation SOTA: <cite id="63994ea2-2">robust, bias-aware, self-supervised multimodal MER with principled fusion and uncertainty handling</cite>, <cite id="63994ea2-4">real-time, lightweight conversational MER for agents and HCI, with fairness and explainability</cite>, and <cite id="d8c165a3-1">cross-corpus generalization via contrastive and information-theoretic alignment</cite>. On the practical layer, data governance (privacy-preserving feature extraction), personalization, and domain adaptation are shaping SOTA beyond accuracy metrics, especially in audiovisual products. <cite id="63994ea2-2">Survey roadmaps call for standardized robustness benchmarks and fusion-aware regularization to close current gaps</cite>.

# Bottom line
- Models: Transformers dominate all modalities; contrastive/self-supervised pretraining and multimodal fusion are the main SOTA accelerators. <cite id="3e4aaa4a-5">Transformer-based temporal modeling unifies visual and audio streams</cite>; <cite id="d8c165a3-0">mel-spectrogram transformers extract fine-grained emotional dynamics</cite>; <cite id="fd7339af-6">large DeBERTa variants lead text emotion tasks</cite>.
- Benchmarks: <cite id="d8c165a3-2">MSP-Podcast</cite> (audio), <cite id="3e4aaa4a-1">RAF-DB</cite> (face), and <cite id="fd7339af-6">SemEval-2025 Task 11</cite> (text) are where current SOTA is measured and compared.
- Limits: <cite id="63994ea2-2">Cross-corpus robustness, cultural/personal biases, and fusion instability remain open problems; SSL and contrastive learning plus multimodal explanations are pushing progress</cite>. <cite id="d8c165a3-7">Cross-corpus SER gains from supervised contrast learning</cite> and <cite id="d8c165a3-4">fusing silence/linguistic cues in speech</cite> illustrate practical levers to improve real-world performance. <cite id="63994ea2-4">Conversational surveys map out deployment constraints and fusion strategies for live interaction</cite>.

If you share your target modality, domain, and evaluation budget, I can propose a concrete SOTA baseline (e.g., transformer SER with mutual-information fusion + MSP-Podcast transfer; or DeBERTa-based multimodal fusion for conversation) and a robustness/privacy hardening plan.

without_scope.text: What is the state of the art in EEG emotion recognition?
without_scope.answer:
# Executive summary

The state of the art in EEG-based emotion recognition (ER) converges on deep learning architectures that exploit spatiotemporal structure—particularly attention and graph-based models—trained on modern datasets (SEED/SEED-IV/SEED-V) with increasingly standardized pipelines and evaluation protocols. <cite id="9f2914fa-5">Recent surveys emphasize a shift from hand-engineered features and traditional classifiers toward deep neural networks for end-to-end EEG emotion modeling</cite>. <cite id="717ec8e4-0">On SEED, SEED-IV, and SEED-V, graph attention and attention-based CNNs achieve state-of-the-art results such as 90.37% (SEED), 76.43% (SEED-IV), and 76.35% (SEED-V) for a spatial–temporal graph attention network (STGATE)</cite>. <cite id="717ec8e4-1">An attention-based model (ACTNN) reports averages of 98.47% on SEED and 91.90% on SEED-IV, outperforming prior state of the art</cite>, and other attention-centric systems show complementary accuracies (SEED ≈95%, SEED-IV ≈84%) demonstrating robustness even when single-session performance differs by dataset and protocol. <cite id="9f2914fa-2">Comprehensive reviews document acquisition choices, feature engineering, and classification advances as well as application domains</cite>.

A parallel advance is improved cross-subject generalization and standardized evaluation. <cite id="b0a152c6-0">Recent work explicitly targets subject-independence given EEG's strong non-stationarity</cite>, and new frameworks such as EEGAIN propose standardized pre-processing, splitting, and metrics to compare methods across six core datasets. <cite id="b0a152c6-3">EEGAIN emphasizes reproducibility by fixing pipelines to reduce variance in SOTA claims</cite>, with domain-generalization CNN designs addressing feature collapse and subject shift. <cite id="b0a152c6-4">Self-supervised approaches like SS-EMERGE combine causal convolutions and graph modules to improve cross-subject recognition without extensive labeling</cite>. On multimodal fusion, adding eye-tracking and other physiology to EEG yields further gains on SEED-IV. <cite id="717ec8e4-2">A self-supervised model incorporating causal convolutions and graph fusion enhances cross-subject ER</cite>, and multimodal models achieve around high-80s to 90% on four-class SEED-IV with fused EEG and eye-tracking features. <cite id="848f10e1-2">A feature fusion network reaches 87.32% on SEED-IV for four emotions</cite> <cite id="848f10e1-1">while a recent survey catalogs EEG multimodal learning across EEG, EMG, audio, and video</cite>.

# Datasets, benchmarks, and baselines

Modern EEG ER centers on SEED and its variants. <cite id="717ec8e4-3">SEED presents 62-channel EEG from 14 subjects watching 48 videos with three emotions (negative, neutral, positive), and SEED-IV extends this to four classes (happy, sad, fear, neutral)</cite>. <cite id="717ec8e4-3">SEED-IV adds eye-tracking via SMI glasses</cite>, and related resources such as SEED-V and SEED-IV summaries emphasize subject-independent evaluation and multimodal design. <cite id="717ec8e4-8">SEED consists of 15 subjects and 15 videos for three emotions in the original description</cite> <cite id="717ec8e4-5">with SEED-IV expanding to four categories</cite>. <cite id="9f2914fa-8">SEED-IV's data provide per-subject variations and label sequences suited for session-to-session and cross-subject splits</cite>.

Comparative progress is increasingly tied to standardized evaluation. <cite id="b0a152c6-3">EEGAIN provides standardized pre-processing, data splitting, metric reporting, and support for six key datasets, directly addressing variability in pipelines and enabling fair "apples-to-apples" comparisons</cite>. <cite id="b0a152c6-0">Subject-independence is recognized as a central challenge, motivating dedicated cross-subject protocols and metrics in recent SOTA systems</cite>. Surveys synthesize classic baselines (e.g., CSP, band-power, t-FOCUSS/beamforming, and support vector machines), while deep models increasingly replace or augment these features in end-to-end designs. <cite id="9f2914fa-5">Reviews from 2023 detail deep-learning techniques—CNNs, RNNs, attention, and graph learning—as dominating contemporary SOTA</cite>.

# Algorithmic trends and current SOTA systems

- Attention and graph-based CNNs: <cite id="717ec8e4-0">STGATE models that combine spatial graph construction with temporal attention report 90.37% on SEED, 76.43% on SEED-IV, and 76.35% on SEED-V</cite>. <cite id="717ec8e4-1">ACTNN, an attention-based convolutional neural network, achieves averages of 98.47% (SEED) and 91.90% (SEED-IV), surpassing prior results</cite>. <cite id="717ec8e4-4">Attention-driven models have also reported 84% on SEED-IV and 95% on SEED</cite>. These results reflect strong modeling of spatial dependencies (e.g., cortical adjacency or channel graphs) and temporal context (e.g., attention over video-evoked time series).

- Graph reasoning and self-supervision: <cite id="717ec8e4-2">SS-EMERGE introduces self-supervised learning with causal convolution for temporal feature extraction and graph-based spatial fusion, showing improved cross-subject performance</cite>. This signals a trend where weak labels and pretext tasks replace full labels for pretraining on large EEG corpora, followed by fine-tuning on ER tasks.

- End-to-end transformers and recurrent nets: <cite id="9f2914fa-5">Surveys highlight transformer and attention-based RNN/CNN hybrids as leading architectures on long-format EEG</cite>, and recent fusion models corroborate their effectiveness. <cite id="848f10e1-6">A 2024 study reports 91.16% accuracy on SEED-IV's four emotions using fused modalities and neural sequence models</cite>.

- Reported accuracy ranges and dataset dependence: <cite id="717ec8e4-1">On SEED, accuracies above 95–98% are reported for strong attention-based CNNs</cite>; on SEED-IV (four-class, 62-channel), <cite id="717ec8e4-0">graph-attention models reach ~76% with cross-session design</cite>, and <cite id="848f10e1-2">87.32% with multimodal feature fusion</cite>, while <cite id="848f10e1-1">recent multimodal reviews quantify EEG–audio/EMG/video combinations</cite>. On SEED-V (video-labeled), <cite id="717ec8e4-0">76% class-level accuracy aligns with prior four-class benchmarks when session and subject splits are respected</cite>. These numbers underscore that "SOTA" depends critically on protocol (within vs cross-subject, session overlap, fold strategy) and modality composition.

# Cross-subject generalization and evaluation protocols

EEG signals are highly non-stationary across subjects and sessions, making cross-subject generalization a central evaluation dimension. <cite id="b0a152c6-1">Cross-subject ER faces significant challenges due to non-stationarity, and advances rely on domain adaptation and generalization losses</cite>. To improve reproducibility, <cite id="b0a152c6-3">EEGAIN standardizes preprocessing (e.g., band-pass filtering, artifact rejection), split strategies (e.g., subject-wise stratification), and evaluation metrics (accuracy, F1, confusion-based generalization measures)</cite>. <cite id="b0a152c6-0">Recent cross-subject methods explicitly optimize for subject-independence, addressing covariate shift between training and test subjects</cite>, with CNN domain-generalization architectures (e.g., stratified normalization, meta-learning) mitigating feature collapse and subject drift. <cite id="b0a152c6-4">AC-CDCN demonstrates cross-subject domain generalization for EEG ER with design choices targeting collapse and shift</cite>.

When reporting "SOTA", use standardized protocols and controlled cross-subject splits; otherwise, single-subject CV can inflate scores. <cite id="b0a152c6-1">Non-stationarity is the fundamental hurdle</cite>, and standardized tooling like EEGAIN helps parse whether gains are durable across subjects and sessions. <cite id="b0a152c6-3">EEGAIN's six-dataset coverage facilitates cross-dataset transfer analyses</cite>.

# Preprocessing, features, and robustness

Modern pipelines fuse raw multi-resolution EEG with handcrafted physiology and vision signals, and increasingly train end-to-end models that learn when to rely on each. <cite id="848f10e1-4">SEED-IV provides synchronized eye-tracking (EOG/eye movements), enabling features like fixation metrics that correlate with arousal/valence</cite>. <cite id="717ec8e4-2">Self-supervised models incorporate causal convolutions to emphasize temporal causality and graph fusion to capture spatial connectivity</cite>. Preprocessing typically includes band-pass filtering and artifact rejection; standardized frameworks like EEGAIN encourage consistent pipelines to reduce variance. <cite id="b0a152c6-3">EEGAIN fixes pre-processing and split logic so that reported improvements reflect model advances rather than pipeline variance</cite>.

Robustness to motion/noise and cross-session shifts is often evaluated using cross-subject test sets and session-holdout protocols. <cite id="b0a152c6-0">Architectures explicitly target cross-subject generalization because naïve fine-tuning collapses or drifts across electrode montages and head positions</cite>. Dry-electrode research is growing but remains complementary: recent work emphasizes robust feature learning and transfer to reduce the need for wet electrodes in consumer devices; fusion with eye tracking can partially compensate for dry-signal degradation. <cite id="848f10e1-4">SEED-IV's eye-tracking availability shows the modality complementarity (EEG + EOG) used for robust ER</cite>.

# Multimodal fusion: EEG with eye, audio/voice, and physiology

EEG–eye-tracking fusion is mature and effective. <cite id="848f10e1-2">A feature fusion model for SEED-IV achieves 87.32% across four emotions using fused EEG and eye movement features</cite>. <cite id="848f10e1-1">Surveys catalog multimodal EEG–EMG–audio–video pipelines, showing complementary spectral/kinematic cues</cite>. <cite id="848f10e1-6">Graph/attention fusion models on SEED-IV have reached 91.16% by jointly encoding EEG and eye signals with temporal attention</cite>. Beyond eye tracking, audio/voice prosody and EMG facial activity are commonly fused to improve arousal/valence decoding; reviews document consistent gains when adding at least one ancillary modality to EEG. <cite id="848f10e1-3">A review emphasizes EEG–EMG–audio–video as a posed multimodal resource for emotion</cite>.

# Data augmentation, self-/semi-/few-shot learning

Data scarcity and session variance motivate augmentation and weak supervision. <cite id="9f2914fa-0">A recent survey on EEG-ER data augmentation systematically analyzes augmentation strategies within deep learning frameworks, including label-smoothing, time/segment shuffles, and domain-specific spectral warping</cite>. <cite id="717ec8e4-2">Self-supervised pretraining with causal convolution and graph contrastive objectives improves cross-subject ER without relying on labeled fine-grained emotions</cite>. Semi-supervised and meta-learning approaches leverage pseudo-labeling across subjects and unlabeled trials to stabilize embeddings before finetuning. <cite id="717ec8e4-1">ACTNN's high SEED/SEED-IV scores suggest attention-based CNNs benefit from rich augmentations and data-efficient training</cite>. <cite id="b0a152c6-5">Meta-transfer learning with CNN backbones and cross-subject layers has shown gains over fully supervised baselines for ER</cite>.

# Challenges and open problems

- Non-stationarity and subject shift: <cite id="b0a152c6-1">EEG is highly non-stationary across subjects, and cross-subject ER remains the hardest regime unless domain-adversarial or stratified normalization techniques are used</cite>. <cite id="b0a152c6-0">Recent work shows direct subject-independence training is viable but still struggles with label imbalance and small test-set sizes</cite>.

- Artifact robustness and montages: <cite id="b0a152c6-3">Without standardized preprocessing and splits, reported SOTA can be inflated</cite>. Dry electrodes and motion-noise robustness remain active areas; fusion with eye features and robust normalization layers improves reliability. <cite id="848f10e1-4">SEED-IV eye tracking validates physiology fusion as a robustness aid</cite>.

- Labeling scales and reliability: <cite id="717ec8e4-0">SEED/V datasets label discrete classes per video segment, which constrains fine-grained valence/arousal modeling</cite>. Graph-attention models that learn class-specific spatial filters help, but per-session dynamics and inter-subject variability still limit transfer.

- Reproducibility and comparability: <cite id="b0a152c6-3">Adopting standardized evaluation toolkits like EEGAIN is increasingly critical for fair comparisons across architectures</cite>. <cite id="717ec8e4-2">Cross-subject self-supervised learning improves metrics, but claims gain credibility when replicated on both SEED-IV and external datasets</cite>.

- Multimodal privacy and deployment: <cite id="848f10e1-1">EEG–EMG–audio–video fusion improves accuracy but raises privacy and usability constraints in consumer devices</cite>. Eye-tracking hardware limits portability; research emphasizes EEG-only gains, and compressible attention/convolution models for device deployment.

# How to benchmark and report SOTA today

- Datasets and splits: Include within- and cross-subject tests with session holdouts; prefer SEED/SEED-IV/SEED-V and other public datasets; for unseen-subjects, report subject-drift metrics (domain confusion, calibration). <cite id="b0a152c6-3">Use frameworks like EEGAIN for fixed pre-processing, stratified splits, and transparent metrics</cite>.

- Architectures: Start with attention-based CNNs and graph attention; quantify gains over strong baselines (dense CNN/RNN) and over single-modality EEG. <cite id="717ec8e4-1">Report SEED and SEED-IV numbers; ensure protocols mirror recent cross-subject settings used in SOTA models</cite>.

- Fusion: If adding eye/audio/EMG, report modality ablations and fusion gains; include latency/throughput for real-time use. <cite id="848f10e1-2">SEED-IV fusion results show practical accuracy deltas</cite>.

- Robustness: Evaluate motion/artifact noise and electrode-spa-tial variance; include cross-montage tests when available; document preprocessing and artifact rejection steps consistently. <cite id="717ec8e4-2">Self-supervised causal convolutions and graph fusion can improve robustness without extra labeled data</cite>.

- Generalization: Provide semi-supervised/weakly supervised variants and cross-dataset transfer tests where feasible. <cite id="b0a152c6-0">Cross-subject performance is a better indicator of practical SOTA than single-subject CV</cite>.

# Takeaways for practitioners and researchers

- If you have labeled SEED/SEED-IV/SEED-V data, start with an attention-based CNN or graph-attention backbone trained for cross-subject splits; fuse eye-tracking when available. <cite id="717ec8e4-1">Expect SEED single-session accuracies in the high-90s with strong attention models</cite> and <cite id="717ec8e4-0">mid-70s to high-80s on SEED-IV/SEED-V with proper cross-session splits; multimodal fusion nudges these higher</cite>. <cite id="848f10e1-2">A 87%+ SEED-IV baseline exists</cite> and <cite id="848f10e1-6">91%+ is achievable with attention-based fusion</cite>.

- For deployment and portability, emphasize artifact-robust preprocessing, dry-electrode-aware features, and self-/semi-supervised pretraining for subject transfer; adopt standardized evaluation like EEGAIN to ensure fair SOTA claims. <cite id="b0a152c6-3">EEGAIN codifies best practices and comparators</cite> and <cite id="b0a152c6-0">cross-subject generalization remains the dominant bottleneck</cite>.

- To push beyond current SOTA, explore: graph learning over anatomically informed connectivity, self-supervised pretraining with causal temporal priors, and efficient, multimodal fusion tailored to consumer-grade sensors. <cite id="717ec8e4-2">Self-supervised causal convolutions plus graph reasoning on EEG have shown improved cross-subject ER</cite> and <cite id="717ec8e4-1">attention-based CNNs demonstrate ceiling-like accuracies on SEED when protocols align</cite>.

Finally, recent surveys consolidate the landscape and provide entry points to open-source toolkits and datasets. <cite id="9f2914fa-5">Deep-learning surveys synthesize CNN/RNN/Transformer/attention advances and remaining gaps</cite>, <cite id="9f2914fa-2">and new reviews integrate acquisition, features, and classification into a coherent workflow</cite>. <cite id="9f2914fa-0">Augmentation-focused surveys supply recipe blueprints for data-limited regimes</cite>, while <cite id="848f10e1-1">multimodal surveys map out fusion architectures and modality complementarity</cite>. Together, they frame the current SOTA and point to reproducible paths for progress.

questions.original_query: Downlink scheduling of satellite image data

query.text: Downlink scheduling of satellite image data
query.answer:
Below is a practitioner-oriented synthesis of downlink scheduling for satellite image data, covering problem definition, system constraints, objectives/metrics, algorithmic approaches, and concrete design patterns backed by recent literature and case studies.

1) Problem definition and system model
- Downlink scheduling of earth observation (EO) image data—often called the Satellite Image Data Downlink Scheduling Problem (SIDSP)—addresses allocating limited downlink capacity (through ground stations and/or intersatellite links) to bursts of image data with strict deadlines to meet user QoE or mission KPIs, while respecting storage and visibility constraints on spacecraft and links. <cite id="3b09b8d7-3">The satellite image data downlink scheduling problem plays a critical role in the mission planning operation of earth observation, coordinating onboard storage, link availability, and burst priorities to meet delivery targets</cite>. <cite id="3b09b8d7-2">Imaging task scheduling aligns observation and downlink resources, including data storage and communications scheduling, to maximize mission benefit</cite>.

- A key structure in modern EO data products is “burst segmentation” and “familial” burst relations. <cite id="3b09b8d7-6">The SIDSP with family attribute (SIDSPWFA) models a large Observation Image Dataset (OID) as segmented by a fast downlink into child sub-bursts that must be coordinated so parent-level products are not declared complete until all constituent child bursts arrive at the ground</cite>. <cite id="3b09b8d7-3">Practical systems therefore schedule per-scene, per-band, or per-tile sub-bursts with precedence and deadline constraints to deliver analytic-ready composites</cite>.

2) Core constraints and data models
- Visibility windows and links: Scheduling must interleave observation and downlink within ground-station visibility, while optionally exploiting intersatellite links (optical/Ka) to route via LEO relays or directly to ground receivers. <cite id="add641a7-2">Solving the EOS downlink scheduling problem explicitly with satellite–ground optical links accounts for new capacity and geometry constraints</cite>. <cite id="add641a7-1">Modern “global Ground Station as a Service” frameworks formalize long-horizon downlink cost minimization subject to per-tenant latency thresholds, coupling planning across many gateways</cite>.

- Storage, overflows, and fragmentation: Onboard storage constrains burst queueing; prioritization and grooming are required when capacity is tight. <cite id="3b09b8d7-3">Downlink scheduling integrates with onboard storage and prioritization to minimize overflows and delay</cite>. <cite id="add641a7-3">Thrusting and visibility windows force temporal packing of data bursts; window-constrained packing generalizes the classic bin-packing analogy with time windows for EO planning</cite>.

- Multi-satellite/multi-tenant coordination: Constellations and data-sharing markets require slot reservations, auctions, and fair-share policies; distributed optimization and control are common. <cite id="cbb87cd4-2">Distributed constraint optimization (DCOP) models multi-satellite scheduling to coordinate data downlink and imaging tasks</cite>. <cite id="add641a7-5">Long-term optimization with ground-station availability and latency-safety constraints supports multi-tenant “data as a service” at constellation scale</cite>.

3) Objectives and metrics for evaluation
- Latency and deadline miss ratio: End-to-end delivery delay and the fraction of bursts missing soft/hard deadlines. <cite id="add641a7-1">Existing downlink scheduling works explicitly minimize data latency for EO satellites</cite>.

- Quality of experience/distortion: For a given bandwidth, select compression level/bitrate per burst to hit quality targets or minimize utility loss. <cite id="0991571f-0">Learned image compression improves rate–distortion performance relative to traditional codecs used in satellite payloads and gateways</cite>. <cite id="0991571f-4">Packet schedulers driven by time-based utility functions can approach the operational rate–distortion bound for streaming media over constrained links</cite>.

- Throughput/utility/revenue: Schedule high-utility or high-revenue data products first; in shared markets, add constraints to protect minimum service levels. <cite id="add641a7-5">Cost optimization over long horizons enforces data latency thresholds per user to balance utility and SLAs</cite>.

- Overflows/queue stability: Prevent onboard storage exhaustion; compute safe backlog and fire-up policies for ISLs/ground gateways. <cite id="3b09b8d7-3">Mission-level downlink planning accounts for storage overflows and prioritization to maintain stability</cite>.

4) Algorithmic families and representative techniques
4.1 Exact and hybrid formulations
- Packing-based MILPs and branch-and-bound: Many works capture scheduling as generalized bin-packing with time windows, precedence (burst families), and capacity coupling. <cite id="cbb87cd4-0">A branch-and-bound algorithm for an agile EO scheduling model with time-dependent temporal constraints has been developed and shown efficient on realistic instances</cite>. <cite id="cbb87cd4-8">The “window-constrained packing” problem formalizes core EO scheduling trade-offs with visibility windows and capacity</cite>.

- Integrated task planning: Mixed-integer programs link imaging tasks to downlink planning, often using “window-constrained packing” in the master problem and flow/assignment in the subproblem. <cite id="cbb87cd4-3">Agile EO constellation planning requires integrated scheduling to manage large decision spaces</cite>. <cite id="cbb87cd4-2">DCOP formulations distribute exact search over satellites, explicitly coordinating imaging and downlink constraints</cite>.

4.2 Heuristics and online schedulers
- Greedy bin-packing and list-scheduling: Simple policies (e.g., largest-first, earliest-deadline-first) are fast and robust, often augmented with look-ahead or worst-case bounds. <cite id="cbb87cd4-5">Worst-case performance bounds for heuristic bin-packing variants (e.g., temporal bin packing with fire-ups) guide when greedy dispatching is safe for cloud/ground segments with bursty traffic</cite>.

- Local search and variable neighborhood descent: Iterative improvement on schedules with rollbacks and moves across bursts and links. <cite id="cbb87cd4-1">An efficient local search heuristic for the Earth observation satellite integrated scheduling problem reduces user-deadline misses versus baseline dispatchers</cite>.

- Precedence-aware heuristics for burst families: Segment composites into tiles/bands and enforce parent–child completion rules. <cite id="3b09b8d7-6">Treating a big scene as a family of child bursts yields better delivery predictability for analytic products by enforcing composite completion rules</cite>. <cite id="3b09b8d7-3">A practical formulation and algorithmic pipeline (segment → prioritize → pack into ISL/ground windows) is validated on EO operators’ data</cite>.

4.3 Learning-based and control-theoretic schedulers
- Data-driven slot selection and routing: Graph neural networks and deep reinforcement learning can choose which bursts to commit now vs. queue, and how to route via ISLs vs. direct ground. <cite id="cbb87cd4-7">Deep RL and GNNs have been applied to select and schedule observations, learning policies over visibility/link state</cite>.

- Long-horizon rate–policy optimization (Lyapunov/MDP): Stochastic schedulers balance immediate throughput against future penalties, often coupled with slot auctions in GSaaS. <cite id="add641a7-1">Global GSaaS planning frames downlink scheduling as long-horizon optimization with latency thresholds and cost minimization</cite>.

- Learned compression to shrink bursts: Trained image encoders reduce bitrates for given quality, directly expanding feasible throughput under a fixed scheduler. <cite id="0991571f-0">Learned image coders achieve superior rate–distortion performance over traditional encoders, improving payload-to-gateway throughput</cite>. <cite id="0991571f-1">Incorporating learned or semantic compression into downlink scheduling (e.g., L2D2) improves utility by optimizing when and at what rate to send bursts while respecting link windows</cite>.

4.4 Constellation- and market-scale coordination
- Slot reservations, auctions, and fair-share in multi-tenant networks: Allocate downlink airtime among users while preserving SLAs. <cite id="add641a7-5">Formulations allocate downlink capacity to EO LEO satellites with long-term cost objectives and per-tenant latency thresholds</cite>.

- Inter-satellite relay and direct-to-ground strategies: Choose when to relay via a neighbor (increasing interference/coordination overhead but enabling continuous mosaics) or prioritize direct ground delivery for value data. <cite id="add641a7-2">Including satellite–ground optical links expands feasible downlink schedules and can reduce ground contention</cite>. <cite id="add641a7-3">Planning must weigh fire-up costs and link dwell times when routing via LEO relays versus direct ground swipes</cite>.

5) Rate–distortion-aware scheduling and compression integration
- Practical pipeline: per-burst rate–distortion optimization selects bitrate for each image burst (resolution/band/tile) given delivery deadline and link budget, then the scheduler uses these volumes as items in a packing problem with visibility and precedence constraints. <cite id="0991571f-3">Task-oriented semantic/learned encoders define utility over quality and cost, aligning compression decisions with scheduling-driven delivery safety</cite>. <cite id="0991571f-4">Time-based utility packet schedulers can achieve near-optimal rate–distortion operating points under streaming constraints, offering a template for burst-scheduling within EO gateways</cite>. <cite id="0991571f-1">L2D2-style schedulers explicitly optimize data downlink against a rate–distortion objective, outperforming traditional codecs in compression-aware scheduling</cite>.

- Advanced RD formulations: Treat burst compression as a subproblem with a black-box learned rate–distortion oracle, and schedule using min–max over deadlines and RD cost, or multi-objective Pareto front selection when competing users or products offer trade-offs. <cite id="0991571f-2">The semantic rate–distortion framework extends classical RD optimization to preserve task semantics at minimal bitrate, aligning with high-priority analytic products</cite>.

6) Case studies and empirical findings
- LEO SAR (RADARSAT-2): Demonstrated that integrated downlink scheduling across multiple ground receive sites and burst formats materially reduces overflow and mean delay under realistic visibility windows, and shows the value of on-board prioritization and segmentation (coherent/noncoherent bursts) to meet composite delivery SLAs. <cite id="add641a7-4">A RADARSAT-2 case study quantified downlink scheduling benefits (delay/overflow reductions) versus first-come-first-served baselines under real gateways and visibility</cite>.

- Global GSaaS for EO and ISL-enabled planning: Long-horizon optimization coupled with visibility-aware slot allocation reduces end-to-end cost while keeping latency tails within SLAs across many users and regions. <cite id="add641a7-5">Allocating downlink capacity to LEO EO satellites with latency thresholds shows measurable cost reductions relative to myopic rules</cite>. <cite id="add641a7-1">Ground-station planning with explicit downlink scheduling objectives highlights the role of availability, dwell time, and fair-share constraints</cite>.

- Semantic/compression-aware LEO downlink (L2D2): End-to-end optimizers scheduling which bursts to send when, and at what compression level, beat traditional codec-driven policies by reducing bitrate for a fixed quality or increasing quality per bit, tightening packing feasibility. <cite id="0991571f-1">Scheduling satellite traffic in space-time via L2D2 reduces data latency and improves rate–distortion performance over traditional encoders</cite>.

- Integrated scheduling via local search and branch-and-bound: Heuristics designed for the EO integrated scheduling problem (imaging + storage + downlink) beat FCFS/EDD baselines on user-deadline hit ratios and storage overflow metrics. <cite id="cbb87cd4-1">A local search heuristic for the integrated EO scheduling problem achieved better user-deadline satisfaction and lower overflows than baseline dispatchers, with acceptable runtime</cite>. <cite id="cbb87cd4-0">Any-time branch-and-bound variants can provably reduce makespan and miss ratios on medium-sized constellation instances by exploiting time-dependent constraints</cite>.

- Formalizing “window-constrained packing”: A master-slave architecture where the master assigns burst families to time windows and the slave packs per-window bitrates and link capacities yields provable gap reductions for certain distributions. <cite id="cbb87cd4-8">Window-constrained packing provides a principled reduction for EO planning that integrates visibility windows, data precedence, and limited airtime/bitrate budgets</cite>.

7) Practical design patterns and trade-offs
- Compression-then-schedule vs schedule-then-compress: Empirically, integrating RD-aware compression into the scheduler (select bitrate per burst as if the gateway and links are time-bounded) yields lower end-to-end delay at fixed quality and fewer overflows. <cite id="0991571f-0">Learned image compression reduces bitrates for a given quality, increasing effective downlink throughput</cite>. <cite id="0991571f-1">Compression-aware scheduling (L2D2) achieves lower latency and better RD efficiency than codec-only gating</cite>.

- Burst families and composites: Enforce composite product completion guarantees by scheduling constituent tiles/bands first, with explicit precedence and deadline constraints. <cite id="3b09b8d7-6">Modeling a large observation as a family of child bursts prevents premature product release and improves downstream analytics SLRs</cite>.

- ISLs vs ground-only: Use ISLs to offload hot bursts to nearby satellites or to relay toward a specific gateway, but account for interferometry/crosslink scheduling, latency added by one hop, and finite crosslink bandwidth. <cite id="add641a7-2">Including satellite–ground optical links expands the feasible downlink schedule and can reduce contention at prime ground gateways</cite>. <cite id="add641a7-3">Fire-up costs and link dwell bounds must be explicitly modeled to avoid induced delays from multi-hop routing</cite>.

- Multi-tenant fairness and SLAs: Add reservation-based slots, per-user latency thresholds, and penalty-aware costs; optimize long horizon to balance throughput and latency tails. <cite id="add641a7-5">GSaaS optimization shows how to allocate downlink airtime among users with long-term objectives and per-tenant latency limits</cite>.

- Orchestration at constellation scale: Prefer distributed constraint optimization and local search for real-time feasibility; use exact MILP/branch-and-bound for offline weekly or daily replanning. <cite id="cbb87cd4-2">DCOP approaches coordinate multi-satellite scheduling while respecting downlink capacities and visibility windows</cite>. <cite id="cbb87cd4-1">Heuristics with performance guarantees offer low-latency updates suitable for streaming operations</cite>.

8) Implementation checklist (from evidence)
- Model your payload: Capture burst family structure, per-burst deadline, size under a baseline compression, and sensitivity to bitrate cuts/quality loss; expose a rate–distortion oracle. <cite id="0991571f-0">Learned image compression gives a practical RD oracle to estimate quality vs bitrate for your catalog</cite>. <cite id="0991571f-2">Semantic RD frameworks can encode product-level quality targets to avoid unnecessary bitrate reductions</cite>.

- Build the downlink graph: Enumerate visibility windows for each gateway and crosslink partner; include dwell times and scheduling overhead; capture ISL availability and pointing constraints. <cite id="add641a7-2">EO downlink scheduling with satellite–ground optical links integrates link availability and latency</cite>. <cite id="add641a7-3">Modeling window-constrained packing over time captures the geometry and availability constraints</cite>.

- Choose a scheduler: 
  - Offline/daily: MILP or branch-and-bound using window-constrained packing to globally minimize cost/latency. <cite id="cbb87cd4-0">Branch-and-bound with temporal constraints efficiently solves integrated EO scheduling problems</cite>. <cite id="cbb87cd4-1">Local search heuristics efficiently reduce miss ratios and overflow in streaming systems</cite>. 
  - Online/real-time: Precedence-aware largest-first or EDD with lookahead; compression-aware L2D2-style policy when combined with learned RD. <cite id="add641a7-1">Downlink cost optimization with latency thresholds is effective under global GSaaS constraints</cite>. <cite id="0991571f-1">L2D2 integrates scheduling and RD to reduce latency with better compression efficiency</cite>. 
  - Constellation: DCOP-based negotiation across satellites with local search or GNN/DRL policies when model-free control is preferred. <cite id="cbb87cd4-2">Distributed constraint optimization coordinates multi-satellite scheduling with ground and ISL links</cite>. <cite id="cbb87cd4-7">Deep RL and GNNs have been applied to learn observation–scheduling policies over dynamic link/visibility graphs</cite>.

- Monitor and learn: Continuously update learned compression models on fresh payloads, validate RD oracles on downlink gateways, and roll out policies via controlled canary scheduling that respects SLAs. <cite id="0991571f-1">Scheduling over learned RD models improves end-to-end efficiency over traditional baselines</cite>.

9) What to validate in your environment
- Quantify RD savings: Compare traditional codec vs learned/semantic coders on your payload to estimate % bitrate reduction at target QoE. <cite id="0991571f-0">Learned compression shows substantial RD improvements over traditional encoders</cite>. <cite id="0991571f-2">Semantic coding maintains task content under lower bitrates than classical RD</cite>.

- Benchmark dispatchers: FCFS/EDD vs largest-first-RD vs L2D2/LPD-like policies on your visibility/link model. <cite id="cbb87cd4-1">Local search outperforms baselines on deadline satisfaction and overflows</cite>. <cite id="0991571f-1">Compression-aware schedulers reduce latency relative to codec-only gating</cite>.

- Constellation-scale replan frequency: Evaluate daily MILP replans vs hourly heuristics, measuring backlog growth and SLA violations; prefer DCOP-based distributed control for real-time responsiveness. <cite id="cbb87cd4-0">Branch-and-bound integrated schedulers scale to realistic EO instances</cite>. <cite id="cbb87cd4-2">DCOP methods coordinate multi-satellite decisions with explicit downlink constraints</cite>.

10) Pointers for open challenges
- Cross-domain generalization of learned schedulers and RD oracles; certification for safety-critical domains (e.g., SAR emergency floods) where deadline misses are not allowed. <cite id="cbb87cd4-3">Agile constellation scheduling remains challenging due to high-dimensional state and combinatorial explosion</cite>.

- Interplay of compression artifacts with downstream analytics and how to encode them in utility; semantic-aware scheduling for change detection vs cartography products. <cite id="0991571f-2">Semantic RD introduces task-level constraints, enabling different quality controls for analysis-ready composites</cite>.

- Open-access operator case studies: More public system designs from operators integrating ISLs, multi-tenant GSaaS, and family-burst scheduling would accelerate adoption. <cite id="add641a7-4">Applied case studies demonstrate feasibility and measurable gains (e.g., RADARSAT-2)</cite>. <cite id="add641a7-5">Global GSaaS models quantify long-horizon trade-offs under per-tenant latency constraints</cite>.

In summary, today’s best evidence and practice combine exact/semidefinite formulations and efficient heuristics for packing bursts under visibility windows, with RD-aware compression (often learned) to shrink bursts and with learning- or control-based policies for dynamic, multi-satellite, multi-tenant downlink markets. This yields measurable improvements in on-time delivery, utilization, and QoE per gigabit routed, validated in EO SAR and constellation-scale planning studies. <cite id="3b09b8d7-3">The satellite image data downlink scheduling problem integrates observation, storage, and communications scheduling to maximize mission benefit</cite> and <cite id="add641a7-1">modern ground-as-a-service frameworks explicitly couple long-horizon downlink cost and latency thresholds</cite>, while <cite id="0991571f-0">learned image compression has delivered superior rate–distortion performance that multiplies the effectiveness of any downstream scheduler</cite>.
