fully_underspecified.text: Scheduling of image data
fully_underspecified.answer:
# What "scheduling of image data" entails (by domain)

In healthcare imaging, scheduling typically refers to sequencing and triggering the acquisition and routing of DICOM studies (instances and series) using services such as Modality Worklist (MWL) to cue modalities, and DICOM transactions (C-GET/C-MOVE/C-STORE) to route and persist data, often governed by clinical order availability and downstream workstation capacity. <cite id="e4c3a50d-0">DICOM Modality Worklist provides centralized, vendor‑neutral worklist management to sequence and dispatch imaging exams in enterprise environments</cite>. <cite id="e4c3a50d-5">MWL maintains the link between DICOM procedures and the patient record in the EHR system, functioning as the control signal tying acquisition to the clinical workflow</cite>. <cite id="e4c3a50d-3">DICOM Part 3 clarifies that scheduling information for Modality Worklist can be up to 24 hours ahead and that C‑STORE‑RQ can be used to request storage of DICOM objects by a remote SCP to support ordered processing</cite>.

Beyond healthcare, imaging "scheduling" also appears in real-time camera pipelines (scheduling when to read, scale, encode, and deliver frames), in streaming systems (ABR bitrate and chunk scheduling), and at the edge for AI analytics (allocating compute to minimize latency across many concurrent cameras). <cite id="fe56667f-2">Each captured frame traverses preprocessing (e.g., deinterlacing, scaling, rotation), and the more stages you add, the higher the latency introduced</cite>. <cite id="fe56667f-8">An end-to-end streaming perspective shows capture → upload → server processing → distribution to playback, where each hop is a scheduling surface</cite>.

Below, we synthesize best practices, quantitative performance, and trade-offs across these domains.

# 1) Healthcare imaging: Modality Worklist → DICOM network scheduling

Scheduling cueing and routing
- Modality Worklist acts as the control plane for scheduling imaging exams: a workstation or scheduler issues an exam or SOP instance worklist to a modality (CT/MRI/US), cueing it to start a specific exam. <cite id="e4c3a50d-1">A foundational report describes the concepts, issues, and impact of DICOM MWL implementation in PACS, underlining EHR/worklist integration for exam sequencing and patient safety</cite>. <cite id="e4c3a50d-2">Operational guides outline RIS-to‑modality pipelines for MWL delivery and common failure points to ensure timely exam activation</cite>. <cite id="e4c3a50d-6">VNA/PACS integrations can consume ORM orders and publish MWL/MWPS via gateways, providing scalable exam scheduling data</cite>.
- Data plane scheduling uses C‑GET (retrieve associations), C‑MOVE (move SOPs to another destination), and C‑STORE (store instances) to stage data for reading workstations. <cite id="e4c3a50d-3">DICOM explicitly indicates that Modality Worklist support can extend up to 24 hours ahead and leverage C‑STORE‑RQ to request storage of objects by a remote SCP</cite>. <cite id="c7481b95-3">Workstations and PACS network performance depend on whether transfer uses C‑MOVE or C‑GET/C‑STORE, and are constrained by available bandwidth and latency, with fragmentation affecting perceived delays</cite>.

Latency and throughput issues
- Under peak loads, stand‑alone PACS architectures often queue incoming study requests until DICOM C‑MOVE can progress, creating waiting times before studies appear on workstations. <cite id="c7481b95-0">Under peak load, studies can be queued until C‑Move execution, increasing clinical delivery time</cite>.
- Hardware/network handshakes in DICOM can dominate latency; C‑STORE‑RQ initiation overhead is a common bottleneck for throughput. <cite id="c7481b95-4">Improving DICOM transfer times points to synchronous DICOM handshaking (e.g., C‑STORE‑RQ) as a primary source of delay</cite>.
- Throughput measurements show material limits; pushing large/regular/small studies can reveal I/O ceilings. <cite id="c7481b95-2">A large-scale measurement achieved a maximum throughput of 1,280 MB of DICOM data while assessing I/O performance and latency across study sizes</cite>. While MB/s is not instance/s, it delineates network/I/O-bound limits typical in busy radiology departments.
- Protocol choice matters: HTTP/STOW (DICOM over HTTP) can yield order-of-magnitude transfer speedups versus native DICOM storage for distributed deployments. <cite id="c7481b95-8">A comparative study shows that STOW/HTTP can reduce transfer time by about 50× compared with C‑STORE transactions</cite>. <cite id="fe56667f-5">DICOM HTTP-based STOW requests were evaluated with datasets of varying size, with results showing large time reductions relative to C‑STORE</cite>.

Practical implications
- Scheduling design: decouple exam cueing (MWL) from network transfer (C‑GET/MOVE/STORE). Use MWL to unblock modalities, and tune C‑MOVE/C‑STORE sequencing to avoid workstation starvation and PACS queue buildup. <cite id="c7481b95-0">Queuing before C‑Move directly increases study delivery time</cite>. <cite id="c7481b95-3">Perceived delays are sensitive to bandwidth/latency and fragmentation, so routing and handshaking must be optimized</cite>.
- Performance optimization: favor STOW/HTTP for cross‑site or cloud transfers and tune TCP window sizes/parallelism; deploy C‑GET find‑as‑you‑read pipelines to pull instances while the exam runs. <cite id="c7481b95-8">STOW reduces transfer time dramatically versus C‑STORE</cite>. <cite id="c7481b95-4">DICOM handshaking should be a primary target for transfer time reduction efforts</cite>.
- Benchmarking: measure site‑specific C‑STORE throughput and latency under realistic study mixes to size associations, parallel requests, and storage arrays. <cite id="c7481b95-2">Throughput ceiling and I/O characteristics were quantified in a 1,280 MB measurement suite across study sizes</cite>.

# 2) Real-time camera pipelines: frame scheduling, buffers, and end-to-end latency

Frame and pipeline scheduling
- Each frame is a small task; pipelines interleave capture, preprocessing, encode, decode, analytics, and render. Queuing within any stage (driver, scaler, encoder, GPU) delays frames and risks "stutter," so schedulers must bound queue sizes and admission. <cite id="fe56667f-6">Queuing images inside a pipeline introduces delay; dropping frames is undesirable in real‑time applications</cite>. <cite id="fe56667f-2">Preprocessing steps like deinterlacing, scaling, and rotation add latency to the live path</cite>.
- End‑to‑end SLAs should define acceptable live latency and concurrent load; architectures target sub‑second delivery bounds and many concurrent streams. <cite id="fe56667f-4">An architecting guide targets under two seconds of end‑to‑end latency and 30+ concurrent streams, acknowledging camera unreliability and cold starts</cite>.

Where latency emerges
- Latency budgets often begin at the camera/USB and encoding/decoding layers, not at the network. <cite id="fe56667f-7">In WebRTC pipelines, the camera and USB bus can contribute ~100 ms, H.264 encode/decode add ~10 ms each, and software pipelines ~600 ms on average</cite>. 
- Bandwidth constraints on edges push for scalable scheduling that multiplexes many cameras while keeping queues shallow. <cite id="fe56667f-3">Workloads that analyze camera streams must model pipelines per stream and co‑schedule multiple streams to optimize resource utilization</cite>.

Design patterns
- Add adaptive buffers and backpressure: feed faster capture into a GStreamer/FFmpeg or TensorFlow Serving queue with dynamic resize/codecs according to available GPU/CPU headroom; let late frames be dropped or retried at a lower priority to preserve low‑latency tracks. <cite id="fe56667f-6">Pipelines trade between queuing delay and frame drops; designers aim to minimize both</cite>. <cite id="fe56667f-2">Add more processing steps → higher per‑frame latency; choose lightweight transforms when low latency is critical</cite>.

# 3) Edge AI analytics scheduling for vision: multi-stream, multi-task, and learning-based schedulers

Multi‑stream and multi‑view coordination
- When live analytics run per camera (e.g., person detection/tracking, license plate recognition), schedulers must allocate compute to many concurrent streams, sequencing inference and post‑processing. <cite id="fe56667f-0">A real‑time multi‑view scheduling framework for DNN‑based live video analytics minimizes frame processing latency by coordinating multiple camera views</cite>. <cite id="fe56667f-3">Each stream defines a video analytics pipeline; the goal is to schedule across pipelines to optimize end‑to‑end behavior</cite>.
- Deep reinforcement learning can learn start times per pipeline layer to meet latency constraints under uncertainty. <cite id="fe56667f-5">A DRL method decides the start time of operations in each pipeline layer to control multi‑stream scheduling on edge devices</cite>.
- In distributed settings (fleet cameras), schedulers must also order tasks across devices and gateways to reduce tail latency. <cite id="fe56667f-0">Multi‑view live analytics scheduling can be framed to minimize the maximum frame latency across views and compute resources</cite>.

Distributed, multi‑camera operators
- At internet scale, "live video web" operators face millions of streams; schedulers must adapt to device variability and network dynamics. <cite id="fe56667f-1">Real‑time video pipelines are sequences of processing steps that turn raw feeds into actionable insights</cite>. <cite id="fe56667f-8">End‑to‑end pipeline perspectives emphasize capture, upload, server processing, and distribution to many viewers/clients where scheduling policies (e.g., ABR) meet resource limitations</cite>.

# 4) Practical design patterns and trade‑offs

- Control plane vs data plane decoupling: publish exam SOPs via MWL now, then sequence storage and retrieval via C‑MOVE/C‑GET/C‑STORE; if cross‑site delivery is common, use STOW/HTTP to parallelize and reduce transfer delays. <cite id="e4c3a50d-3">MWL can plan up to 24 hours ahead and tie to C‑STORE‑RQ for storage scheduling</cite>. <cite id="c7481b95-8">STOW/HTTP achieves ~50× transfer time reduction vs C‑STORE</cite>.
- Queueing strategies: maintain bounded per‑stage buffers with backpressure in PACS/workstations and streaming engines; prioritize live lanes and drop/defer non‑critical frames to meet deadlines. <cite id="fe56667f-6">Queuing increases delay; frame drops are a necessary evil to preserve real‑time latency</cite>. <cite id="fe56667f-2">More image processing steps expand per‑frame latency; prefer hardware acceleration to keep queues shallow</cite>.
- Throughput/latency measurement loops: size C‑STORE channels to your storage I/O, and stress test with your mix of small/large studies; adopt HTTP/STOW if WAN transfers dominate time. <cite id="c7481b95-2">Maximum throughput of ~1,280 MB and latency profiles were measured across study sizes</cite>. <cite id="c7481b95-4">Synchronous handshakes (e.g., C‑STORE‑RQ) are a major contributor to transfer delays</cite>.
- Learn to schedule: where workloads are stochastic (many cameras, variable content, partial occlusions), DRL schedulers can outperform static heuristics by adapting start times and resource allocation per operation. <cite id="fe56667f-5">DRL‑based schedulers learn operation start times across pipeline layers to reduce latency</cite>. <cite id="fe56667f-0">Multi‑view DNN analytics benefit from latency‑minimizing scheduling frameworks</cite>.
- Respect device/network fundamentals: camera USB and codec overheads can dominate; choose codecs, resolutions, and frame rates compatible with latency budgets measured on the target hardware. <cite id="fe56667f-7">Camera/USB contributes ~100 ms, with H.264 enc/dec adding ~10 ms each</cite>. <cite id="fe56667f-4">An end‑to‑end target of <2 seconds and 30+ concurrent streams illustrates realistic SLAs</cite>.

# 5) Tooling and standards to start with

- DICOM services: MWL (PS3.2/PS3.4), C‑GET, C‑MOVE, C‑STORE. <cite id="e4c3a50d-3">DICOM specifies Modality Worklist scheduling window and uses C‑STORE‑RQ to request storage</cite>. <cite id="c7481b95-3">Perceived delays are tied to bandwidth/latency; fragmentation amplifies delays</cite>.
- Streaming engines: GStreamer/FFmpeg-based pipelines with queue plugins; edge serving frameworks (TensorFlow Serving/Lite, ONNX Runtime Mobile) with GPU/IO schedulers; WebRTC for low-latency delivery. <cite id="fe56667f-6">Queuing and dropping trade‑offs are explicit in edge stream processing</cite>. <cite id="fe56667f-1">Practical video pipelines orchestrate capture→processing→delivery</cite>.
- Performance baselines: DICOM network transfer whitepapers, and comparative studies for C‑STORE vs STOW. <cite id="c7481b95-4">Handshake overheads are a primary locus for DICOM transfer time improvements</cite>. <cite id="c7481b95-8">STOW/HTTP can divide transfer time by ~50 compared to C‑STORE</cite>.

# 6) Gaps and open questions

- Wireless/OTA scheduling for onboard analytics and multi-modal fusion: while DRL schedulers and multi‑view frameworks reduce latency for single devices, open problems remain for fleet‑wide, energy‑aware, and radio‑aware scheduling with imperfect connectivity. <cite id="fe56667f-0">Multi‑view scheduling reduces latency, but adds coordination complexity across devices</cite>. <cite id="fe56667f-8">End‑to‑end distribution adds another scheduling layer for content delivery</cite>.
- Guaranteed SLOs across heterogeneous fleets: bounding tail latency under camera failures, variable model throughput, and prioritized alerts requires principled admission control and risk‑aware scheduling; more evaluation on mixed-priority streams would help. <cite id="fe56667f-4">Architectures set explicit latency and concurrent stream targets but must cope with unreliable camera inputs</cite>.
- Standards integration: DICOM/HL7V2 orchestration with modern HTTP/STOW or gRPC‑DICOM backends in hybrid cloud environments needs clearer operational practices and benchmarks. <cite id="c7481b95-8">STOW dramatically improves transfer time, yet adoption/interoperability details are still evolving</cite>.

# Summary

- In medical imaging, MWL schedules when and what a modality acquires, and DICOM services (C‑GET/MOVE/STORE) route/sequence data; queuing before C‑MOVE and DICOM handshake overheads inflate delivery time, while STOW/HTTP can reduce transfer time by ≈50× under some conditions, and measured C‑STORE ceilings on the order of ~1,280 MB/s per path inform array and network sizing. <cite id="c7481b95-0">Queuing before C‑Move increases delivery time</cite>. <cite id="c7481b95-4">Synchronous handshakes (C‑STORE‑RQ) are a key transfer-time contributor</cite>. <cite id="c7481b95-2">Throughput ceilings around ~1,280 MB/s were measured across study mixes</cite>. <cite id="c7481b95-8">STOW/HTTP can reduce transfer time by about 50× versus C‑STORE</cite>. 
- In real-time pipelines, latency budgets are dominated early by camera/USB, encoders/decoders, and software stack; schedulers control queue sizes, admission, and multiplexing to meet sub‑second SLAs at scale. <cite id="fe56667f-7">Camera/USB ≈100 ms and codec overheads 10 ms add up quickly</cite>. <cite id="fe56667f-4">Architectures aim for <2 s end‑to‑end and 30+ concurrent streams</cite>. 
- On the edge, multi‑stream, multi‑view vision analytics benefit from learning‑based schedulers and coordinated task sequencing to keep per‑frame latency minimal under resource limits. <cite id="fe56667f-0">Latency‑minimizing multi‑view scheduling for DNN live video analytics</cite>. <cite id="fe56667f-5">DRL schedulers learn operation start times across layers to meet latency constraints</cite>. 
- Start by measuring your site's C‑STORE latency/throughput, bounding queues per hop, adopting STOW/HTTP for WAN segments when justified, and piloting a DRL or backpressure scheduler for multi‑camera analytics; iterate with A/B under real workloads to validate SLAs. <cite id="fe56667f-6">Minimize queuing delay; accept controlled frame drops to preserve latency</cite>. <cite id="fe56667f-3">Model each camera's analytics pipeline and co‑schedule across streams</cite>.

query.answer:
Below is a curated set of papers, surveys, benchmarks, and system proposals on “ambiguity” for LLM-based agents, grouped by theme. Each item includes a short takeaway and the evidence base.

Context and problem framing
- Interactive agent evaluation under ambiguity. <cite id="c90ab8d9-0">A study evaluates proprietary and open-source LLM agents in interactive code generation under ambiguous instructions, explicitly measuring their ability to handle and resolve ambiguity during tool use</cite>. <cite id="068b5972-1">An EMNLP 2025 paper defines ambiguity, surveys its forms and implications in language-driven systems with LLMs, and situates prompt-based detection/clarification as a central trend</cite>. <cite id="fa222946-4">A ScienceDirect article introduces model confrontation and collaboration (MCC), motivated by psychological evidence that peer interaction promotes self-correction—an approach explicitly targeted at resolving ambiguous queries</cite>.
- Ambiguity as a pathway to error. <cite id="068b5972-4">LLM-based ambiguity detection has increasingly shifted toward prompt-based methods in conversational QA, highlighting practical failures when ambiguity is ignored</cite>. <cite id="068b5972-6">A framework (LLM-Chinese Textual Disambiguation) operationalizes ambiguity decisions—determining if a sentence is ambiguous, locating the source, and enumerating plausible interpretations</cite>. <cite id="c90ab8d9-7">Work on ambiguity processing in LLMs argues ambiguity is a primary pathway to hallucination, undermining trust across applications</cite>.
- Instruction-level ambiguity in agents. <cite id="068b5972-4">LLM-based methods dominate current ambiguity detection in conversational QA, moving the field toward prompt-level detection and disambiguation workflows</cite>. <cite id="c90ab8d9-4">A thesis on assistants interpreting ambiguous task descriptions analyzes how LLM-based virtual agents parse and act under underspecification</cite>. <cite id="c90ab8d9-5">A multi-agent debate framework is introduced to enhance detection and resolution beyond single-model capabilities, explicitly targeting ambiguous requests</cite>.

Mechanisms for detecting, clarifying, and resolving ambiguity
- Clarifying agents and targeted questioning. <cite id="c90ab8d9-3">Agents equipped as specialists for detecting and resolving incompleteness and ambiguity (implemented as zero-shot ReAct agents) demonstrate a route to operationalize disambiguation through domain tools and reasoning loops</cite>. <cite id="c90ab8d9-4">Conceptualized “clarifying agent” approaches generate targeted follow-up questions to detect and resolve ambiguity for safety and accuracy in dialogue systems</cite>. <cite id="068b5972-7">Active task disambiguation (OpenReview) proposes targeted question strategies that maximize information gain, with analyses indicating over-optimization risks and the value of human oversight</cite>. <cite id="068b5972-9">Industry-facing intent disambiguation (Amazon Lex) uses an LLM to decide whether an input matches multiple intents and triggers disambiguation dialogues—directly applicable to agent pipelines</cite>.

Below is a curated set of papers and resources on “ambiguity and agent,” organized by theme. Each entry includes a brief, evidence-backed note on how ambiguity is modeled or handled for agents, with links to the core sources.

Decision-theoretic models of ambiguity-averse agents
- Smooth Ambiguity and the Klibanoff Representation (2005). A foundational “smooth” model representing beliefs as a mix of a prior and an ambiguity weight over priors, unifying ambiguity-averse and ambiguity-loving behavior and clarifying how ambiguity relates to risk attitudes in decision rules for agents <cite id="daebbf3d-0">It shows that they agree, with expected utility taken as the dividing line between ambiguity aversion and ambiguity loving</cite>. 
- Decision Theory under Ambiguity and Savage/Jeffrey Foundations (surveys and overviews). Survey-style expositions of ambiguity-sensitive decision theory emphasize Savage-style subjective expected utility derivations, extensions to evidential dependence (Jeffrey), and modern refinements aimed at “real” agents with realistic uncertainty <cite id="daebbf3d-2">Savage result simply tells us that the behavior of the decision maker can be represented as if he maximized a subjective expected utility</cite> <cite id="daebbf3d-3">The decision theories of Savage and Jeffrey, as critics, apparently concern a single or “one shot only” decision</cite> <cite id="daebbf3d-1">We review recent advances in the field of decision making under uncertainty or ambiguity</cite> <cite id="daebbf3d-4">The aim of the book is to develop a decision theory that is tailored for 'real' agents</cite>.
- Extensions and indices for strategic/managerial contexts. Measurement-focused work ties ambiguity aversion to observable indices and investigates how ambiguity attitudes interact with strategic beliefs in interactive settings <cite id="daebbf3d-5">We used it in this paper to improve the most famous theorem in decision theory: Savage's (1954) derivation of expected utility</cite> <cite id="daebbf3d-9">The ambiguity aversion index measures an individual's attitude towards ambiguity, free of any model or statistical assumptions</cite>.

Ambiguity, Strategic Interaction, and Equilibrium for Agents
- Incomplete Information Games with Ambiguity-Averse Players (Hanany, 2020). Develops equilibrium concepts (e.g., sequential optimality) where agents face ambiguity about payoffs/types; formalizes how agents’ ambiguity aversion shapes strategy-selection and incentive structures in games with incomplete information <cite id="668d69a6-0">We study incomplete information games with ambiguity averse players. Our focus is on equilibrium concepts satisfying sequential optimality</cite> <cite id="668d69a6-1">We study incomplete information games with ambiguity averse players. Our focus is on equilibrium concepts satisfying sequential optimality</cite>.
- Ambiguity-Averse Equilibrium in Games (LEMMA WP 2025). Proposes an equilibrium notion where ambiguity affects agents’ evaluations but not the equilibrium definition, preserving strategic interaction while modeling deep uncertainty <cite id="2c581491-1">The AAE preserves strategic interaction among players by ensuring that ambiguity affects their evaluations but not the definition of equilibrium itself</cite>.
- Strategic Use of Ambiguity (Riedel, 2011). Shows that deliberately leaving beliefs ambiguous can enable equilibria that would not exist in standard exact-belief refinements, illustrating how agents can leverage ambiguity as a strategic move <cite id="2c581491-2">A remarkable consequence of these two examples is that the strategic use of ambiguity allows to reach equilibria that are not Nash equilibria</cite>.
- Ambiguous Beliefs in Multi-Stage and Global Games (Eichberger; Ui). Frameworks where agents hold “ambiguous beliefs” and play equilibria in beliefs help characterize outcomes under strategic uncertainty when payoff-relevant states are imprecisely specified <cite id="2c581491-3">Players choose pure strategies, but have possibly ambiguous beliefs about the strategy choice of others</cite> <cite id="2c581491-4">We study the impacts of strategic ambiguity in global games and demonstrate the distinct effects of ambiguous-quality and low-quality</cite>.
- Ambiguity Attitudes and Beliefs in Strategic vs Non-Strategic Contexts (Dorobiala). Empirical/theoretical analysis highlighting how ambiguity’s prevalence and impact vary with strategic uncertainty, offering tools to connect agents’ ambiguity attitudes to behavior in interactive settings <cite id="2c581491-5">Our findings suggest that ambiguity is ubiquitous in strategic interactions and its role is closely tied to the amount of strategic uncertainty</cite>.

AI, Multi-Agent Systems, and Agents Handling Ambiguity/Uncertainty
- GAM-Agent: Game-Theoretic and Uncertainty-Aware Multi-Agent Framework. Applies GTU reasoning to multimodal agents (vision-language) to improve robustness and interpretability when handling ambiguous inputs and interactions, directly targeting ambiguity management in agent designs <cite id="668d69a6-2">GAM‑Agent is a multi‑agent framework intended to enhance the robustness, interpretability, and accuracy of vision‑language models on complex multimodal tasks</cite>.
- Risk-Averse Equilibrium in Multi-Agent Systems (MLRI 2023). Introduces a risk-averse equilibrium concept that minimizes reward variance in multi-agent settings, offering a practical GT-based approach to robustness concerns that often co-occur with ambiguity in real-world agent interactions <cite id="668d69a6-6">We introduce a new GT‑based Risk‑Averse Equilibrium (RAE) that always produces a solution that minimizes the potential variance in reward accounting for the</cite>.
- Game Theory in Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning (2024+). Surveys and tutorials situate ambiguity/uncertainty management as a core design challenge and opportunity for GT-informed multi-agent learning and coordination <cite id="668d69a6-3">This paper explores advanced topics in complex multi‑agent systems building upon our previous work</cite> <cite id="668d69a6-4">Game theory provides a formal framework for analyzing interactions between multiple autonomous agents in a system where their decisions impact one another</cite>.
- Explainable Agency and HRI with Uncertainty Handling. Work on explainability and intent disambiguation in human–robot command-and-control scenarios underscores the need to represent and resolve uncertainty/vagueness for agents to act safely under ambiguous human input <cite id="7e078a10-0">Uncertainty, vagueness, and ambiguity are closely related and often confused concepts in human‑robot interaction</cite> <cite id="7e078a10-7">We are interested in scenarios in which a human comman‑der provides a robotic agent with a set of mission objectives, the robot enters the field to achieve</cite>.

Ambiguity in Language, Perception, and Multi-Agent Communication (HRI)
- HRI ethics and “type–token” ambiguity. Theoretical HRI analyses show how robots serving as both general class/type and specific instance can produce semantic/lexical ambiguity, forcing agents to negotiate meaning with humans <cite id="7e078a10-2">This paper addresses ethical challenges posed by a robot acting as both a general type of system and a discrete, particular machine</cite>.
- Locating and Resolving Instructional Ambiguities with Multimodal LLMs. Applied HRI/agent studies explore methods to detect and disambiguate instructions using multimodal reasoning, aiming to improve mission execution by reducing ambiguity in human–robot task specifications <cite id="7e078a10-3">We seek to use a variant of large language models, multimodal LLMs, to help improve the quality of communication by resolving instructional ambiguities</cite>.
- A Multimodal Framework for Human–Multi‑Agent Interaction. Proposes perception and reasoning components that integrate speech and vision to support agents interpreting context-dependent human directives, directly confronting semantic and situational ambiguity at scale <cite id="7e078a10-4">The Perception Module is implemented as a multimodal reasoning component that integrates speech processing, visual sensing, and a vision</cite>.
- Ambiguity in Human-Robot Command Contexts. Explainability-oriented frameworks emphasize disambiguation for agents given vague or underspecified objectives, highlighting the role of ambiguity in coordination robustness <cite id="7e078a10-7">We are interested in scenarios in which a human comman- der provides a robotic agent with a set of mission objectives, the robot enters the field to achieve</cite>.

Additional foundations and links to strategic ambiguity
- Ambiguous Urn Comparisons and Risk vs. Ambiguity Aversion. Canonical decision models (ambiguous urns) clarify when agents prefer structured risk over diffuse ambiguity, anchoring how agent designs should treat ambiguity-sensitive utilities <cite id="daebbf3d-6">Ambiguity averse decision maker prefers betting on either color from the ambiguous urn over that from the ambiguous urn whereas the RDU</cite>.
- Perceived Ambiguity and Relevant Measures (Klibanoff et al.). Formalizes how changes in ambiguity aversion affect “relevant measures” and identifies robust predictions across decision criteria, a useful lens for designing agent control policies under ambiguity <cite id="daebbf3d-8">Under mild conditions, we show that increases or decreases in ambiguity aversion cannot affect the relevant measures</cite>.
- Strategic Use/Effects of Ambiguity in Market/Global Games (surveyed and extended). Strategic ambiguity can expand the equilibrium frontier relative to precise-belief refinements, offering agents levers to induce desirable outcomes under high strategic uncertainty <cite id="2c581491-2">the strategic use of ambiguity allows to reach equilibria that are not Nash equilibria</cite> <cite id="2c581491-4">We study the impacts of strategic ambiguity in global games</cite>.

How to choose papers by need
- If you need formal decision models and policy design for ambiguity-averse AI agents: start with the Klibanoff smooth model and decision-theoretic surveys/monographs tailored to “real agents.” Implement ambiguity-averse utilities in RL/MDP specifications and test via Hanany-style incomplete-information game benchmarks <cite id="daebbf3d-0">It shows that they agree, with expected utility taken as the dividing line between ambiguity aversion and ambiguity loving</cite> <cite id="daebbf3d-4">The aim of the book is to develop a decision theory that is tailored for 'real' agents</cite> <cite id="668d69a6-0">We study incomplete information games with ambiguity averse players</cite>.
- If you are in multi-agent strategic design: adopt ambiguity-averse or belief-ambiguous equilibrium notions (AAE, equilibria-in-beliefs) to capture how uncertainty about opponents’ types or information can shape outcomes, and benchmark with global-game applications for policy design under strategic uncertainty <cite id="2c581491-1">Ambiguity affects their evaluations but not the definition of equilibrium</cite> <cite id="2c581491-3">Players choose pure strategies, but have possibly ambiguous beliefs</cite> <cite id="2c581491-4">Impacts of strategic ambiguity in global games</cite>.
- For AI/robot agents facing ambiguous inputs: use multimodal explainability/disambiguation pipelines (HRI), GTU-aware agent controllers (e.g., GAM‑Agent), and risk-averse equilibria for robustness when exact priors are infeasible <cite id="7e078a10-3">Use multimodal LLMs to resolve instructional ambiguities</cite> <cite id="668d69a6-2">GAM‑Agent targets robustness/interpretability in complex multimodal tasks</cite> <cite id="668d69a6-6">Risk‑Averse Equilibrium minimizes potential variance in reward</cite>.

Notes and scope limits
- Some AI/MA resources emphasize “uncertainty” (probabilistic) rather than “ambiguity” (imprecise beliefs); treat them as complementary. For conceptual grounding, distinguish uncertainty/vagueness/ambiguity in HRI early, and map your problem to appropriate models (e.g., Cho–Spearman/Anscombe–Aumann vs. GTU/risk aversion) <cite id="7e078a10-0">Uncertainty, vagueness, and ambiguity are closely related and often confused in HRI</cite>.
- Managerial/organizational ambiguity (entrepreneurship or teams) can use ambiguity-averse decision models and ambiguity indices to connect micro-level agent behavior to team or market outcomes; the cited indices and belief-focused studies provide empirical tools to quantify strategic relevance <cite id="daebbf3d-9">The ambiguity aversion index measures an individual's attitude towards ambiguity</cite> <cite id="2c581491-5">Ambiguity is ubiquitous in strategic interactions and its role is closely tied to the amount of strategic uncertainty</cite>.

# Overview: Ambiguity in Language Model Agents

Ambiguity arises when a query, instruction, or context admits multiple plausible interpretations or referents; for agents that act on or with LLMs, this can trigger misplanning, tool misuse, hallucinations, or fruitless search if left unmanaged. Recent work has developed alignment methods, agent architectures, and evaluation suites to detect and exploit ambiguity via clarification or disambiguation, particularly in interactive settings such as code generation, conversational QA, and search with retrieval. <cite id="7915c5df-5">Ambiguity in LLMs is a primary pathway to hallucination, undermining trust</cite>. Below are key papers, frameworks, and empirical studies at the intersection of ambiguity and LLM-based agents.

## Aligning LLMs and Agents to Handle Ambiguity

- Aligning Language Models to Explicitly Handle Ambiguity (EMNLP 2024). This work introduces Perceived Ambiguity Alignment (APA), a pipeline to train LLMs to assess when inputs are ambiguous and choose behaviors that manage ambiguity (e.g., ask clarifying questions, request constraints) rather than guessing. It frames ambiguity as a measurable signal and proposes a proxy-based alignment method with ablations showing improved handling of ambiguous queries across tasks. <cite id="7915c5df-1">Perceived Ambiguity Alignment proposes a novel pipeline to align LLMs to manage ambiguous queries using the model's own assessment of ambiguity</cite> <cite id="a4090542-8">The authors align LLMs to explicitly handle ambiguous inputs by conditioning model choices on ambiguity and report improvements on ambiguous cases</cite>.

- Clarifying Agents in Dialogue. Agent-based "clarifying agents" autonomously detect and resolve ambiguity across multi-turn dialogues by asking targeted questions, reformulating requests, or prompting user feedback. Early overviews and system designs argue that clarifying sub-agents can improve task success and reduce misinterpretation. <cite id="7915c5df-3">A clarifying agent is an autonomous system using LLMs to detect and resolve ambiguity in multi-turn dialogues</cite>.

- Agent-Based Detection and Resolution of Incompleteness and Ambiguity. This line equips ReAct-style agents with explicit modules to spot missing information or ambiguity and to orchestrate tool calls or follow-ups for disambiguation. <cite id="7915c5df-4">Agents implemented as zero-shot ReAct agents act as specialists to detect and resolve incompleteness and ambiguity</cite> <cite id="a4090542-8">Agent-based QA architectures are examined where agents boost reasoning and handle ambiguous queries</cite>.

Practical product/systems discussed in developer communities echo these capabilities (e.g., adaptive question-answering assistants that request clarification), reinforcing the importance of explicit ambiguity handling in deployable agents. <cite id="7915c5df-2">Agent practice suggests asking users for further clarification when queries are not clear or lack sufficient information</cite>.

## Empirical Studies and Domain Settings

- Interactive Code Generation (Software Engineering). Evaluations of LLM agents in interactive code-generation show that ambiguity in user instructions is a frequent failure point; agents may fail to compile or pass tests due to misaligned assumptions or scope. Studies compare proprietary vs. open models' ability to detect ambiguity and engage the user for constraints. <cite id="7915c5df-0">Interactive agents are evaluated on handling ambiguous instructions in code generation; both proprietary and open models are studied under ambiguous user inputs</cite>.

- Conversational Question Answering (QA) and Web Search. Conversational QA with LLMs has exposed ambiguity in questions, reference resolution, and commonsense; recent work surveys ambiguity/disambiguation mechanisms in LLM-based CQA and proposes structured clarifications. <cite id="a4090542-2">A comprehensive analysis of ambiguity and disambiguation in LLM-based conversational QA is provided, with methods and evaluation</cite> <cite id="a4090542-6">Ambiguity definitions and implications for LLM-driven language systems are synthesized with concrete approaches to disambiguate in conversational settings</cite>.

- Lexical Sense Disambiguation (WSD) and Word Sense Agents. Benchmarked evaluations show how augmenting LMs for lexical ambiguity can improve disambiguation (e.g., via prompt augmentation); this relates to agents that must choose the correct sense before planning or tool use. <cite id="a4090542-5">A quantitative evaluation examines open and commercial LLMs' capability to handle lexical ambiguity</cite> <cite id="a4090542-7">Prompt-augmented strategies are shown to improve disambiguation, indicating a path for agent pre-processing of ambiguous lexical inputs</cite>.

## Retrieval-Augmented and Clarification Frameworks

- ClarifyBench: Benchmarking Clarification Strategies. A benchmark framework that simulates normal, ambiguous, and infeasible user queries to evaluate agent clarification policies, including when to ask, which questions to ask, and how to integrate feedback. <cite id="a4090542-0">ClarifyBench evaluates agent clarification strategies across normal, ambiguous, and infeasible queries</cite>.

- Clarification Question Generation with Retrieval. Multiple works train LLMs to generate clarifying questions that are grounded in retrieved passages, improving faithfulness and narrowing ambiguity by eliciting user constraints. <cite id="2bec794b-1">A hybrid clarification approach (ASK) augments LMs with retrieval to generate clarification questions for task-oriented dialogue</cite> <cite id="2bec794b-4">An approach augments the LM to condition on a retrieval distribution and fine-tune to generate targeted clarification questions</cite> <cite id="2bec794b-7">RAC frames retrieval-grounded clarification and trains an LM to generate relevant clarifying questions for conversational search</cite> <cite id="2bec794b-8">Corpus-informed RAG clarifies web search queries by generating questions aligned with retrieval corpora</cite>.

- Clarifying Question Elicits vs. Does Not Elicit: Recognition and Effects. Empirical analysis shows LLMs often recognize ambiguity internally but rarely surface clarifying questions; additionally, adding retrieved context tends to improve outcomes for unambiguous questions more than it improves recognition of ambiguity. <cite id="2bec794b-0">LLMs rarely ask clarifying questions despite recognizing ambiguity; retrieved context boosts unambiguous performance but does not reliably improve recognition</cite>.

- Ambiguous Questions (AQ) Tree-Based Clarification. AQ-Tree guides LLMs to explore multiple clarification paths in a tree, pruning unhelpful clarifications to efficiently resolve multi-sense ambiguous questions; this operationalizes structured disambiguation space search in an agent-like fashion. <cite id="2bec794b-6">AQ-Tree explores diverse paths of clarification for ambiguous questions with pruning to reduce unhelpful disambiguations and improve resolution</cite>.

These RAG and dialog lines directly inform agent design: clarify selectively when retrieval is uninformative or ambiguous, prefer targeted probes that reduce branching, and use structured clarification spaces to balance cost and coverage. <cite id="2bec794b-5">LLM agents with tool-calling often fail under ambiguity; clarifying questions are central to robustness but need guidance to avoid failure</cite>.

## Clarifying Agents in Knowledge-Seeking Tasks (QA and Search)

- Retrieval-Augmented Clarification for Faithful Conversational Search. The RAC framework operationalizes "ambiguous user intent -> grounded clarifying question -> refined retrieval/answer" loops, training agents to generate clarifying questions that reduce faithfulness errors. <cite id="2bec794b-7">RAC grounds clarifying questions in retrieved passages and trains the LM to do so for faithful conversational search</cite>.

- Disambiguation in Conversational QA in the Era of LLMs. This position/analysis paper argues for explicit disambiguation modules and clarifications in conversational QA pipelines, contrasting retrieval-only vs. clarification-exploiting strategies and proposing modular agent components. <cite id="a4090542-2">Ambiguity/disambiguation mechanisms in LLM-based conversational QA are analyzed with recommendations for agent architectures</cite>.

- Industry Reports and Engineering Practices. Reports from search/RAG engineering describe production clarifying-agent patterns: validating queries with snippets, asking targeted questions, and routing to clarifications when coverage is insufficient—reinforcing theory with operational case studies. <cite id="2bec794b-3">A clarifying agent validates queries using retrieved snippets and asks clarifying questions to resolve ambiguity</cite> <cite id="2bec794b-8">Engineering practice emphasizes corpus-informed question generation to align clarification with available evidence</cite>.

## Ambiguity as a Cause and Mitigation via Multi-Step/Agent Techniques

- Ambiguity as a Pathway to Hallucination. Several analyses frame ambiguity as a root cause of hallucination chains: when agents proceed under default readings, retrieve incomplete evidence, or plan without confirming constraints, outputs can become internally consistent but factually wrong. <cite id="7915c5df-5">Ambiguity is a primary pathway to hallucination generation; addressing it is key to trust and safety</cite>.

- Clarifying-Question Deficiency and Compensation. Recent measurement shows LMs rarely ask clarifying questions even when ambiguity is present; when retrieval is added, performance often improves on unambiguous items, suggesting retrieval can substitute for clarification in some cases but not address recognition or structured exploration. This motivates agent designs with explicit clarifying sub-agents, structured clarification search, or human-in-the-loop checkpoints. <cite id="2bec794b-0">LLMs both recognize and underutilize clarifying questions; retrieval mainly helps unambiguous cases</cite> <cite id="a4090542-0">ClarifyBench explicitly simulates ambiguous conditions to evaluate and improve clarification strategies</cite> <cite id="2bec794b-6">AQ-Tree provides a structured space to overcome the reluctance to ask clarifying questions</cite>.

- Agent Collaboration vs. Independence. Some frameworks compare single-agent systems with clarifying modules versus multi-agent debate/expert specialization; the common finding is that structured disambiguation and role specialization improve success on ambiguous inputs, though gains depend on prompt design, retrieval coverage, and cost constraints. <cite id="a4090542-3">Agent surveys and companion resources catalog evaluation methodologies for LLM agents and include ambiguity-aligned tasks</cite>.

## Takeaways and Open Challenges

- Detect early and act explicitly: Methods that align models to assess ambiguity and prompt clarifications, whether by user interaction or retrieval-grounded questions, reduce downstream failures. <cite id="7915c5df-1">Alignment to manage ambiguous queries improves ability to choose appropriate actions, including requesting clarification</cite> <cite id="7915c5df-4">ReAct clarifying agents detect and resolve ambiguity/incompleteness through tool-augmented follow-ups</cite>.

- Clarify judiciously: Clarifying question generation should be conditioned on retrieval and structured to avoid unbounded branching; retrieval often helps when there is no ambiguity, so hybrid pipelines should gate clarification on ambiguity signals. <cite id="2bec794b-0">Retrieved context boosts unambiguous cases rather than improving ambiguity recognition</cite> <cite id="2bec794b-4">Clarification questions conditioned on retrieval distributions can be generated to target missing information</cite>.

- Benchmarks and evaluation: ClarifyBench-style evaluations allow apples-to-apples comparisons across models and strategies; domain-specific studies (codegen and QA) highlight the practical cost of ambiguity (build/test failures, mis-answer citations). <cite id="a4090542-0">ClarifyBench provides a comprehensive evaluation of clarification strategies under ambiguity</cite> <cite id="7915c5df-0">Interactive codegen studies quantify how ambiguous instructions degrade agent outcomes</cite>.

- Hallucination risk: Treat ambiguity as a first-class failure mode and a design lever; disambiguation through clarification, WSD components, and structured clarification spaces can mitigate hallucinations but require guardrails and human fallbacks. <cite id="7915c5df-5">Ambiguity increases the risk of hallucination that undermines trust; explicit handling is needed</cite> <cite id="2bec794b-6">Structured clarification (AQ-Tree) reduces unhelpful branching and improves disambiguation efficiency</cite>.

# Pointers to Representative Papers and Resources

- Alignment and Agent Frameworks:
  - Aligning LLMs to Explicitly Handle Ambiguity (APA; EMNLP 2024). <cite id="7915c5df-1">Perceived Ambiguity Alignment proposes alignment to manage ambiguous queries</cite> <cite id="a4099542-8">Alignment details and ablations for ambiguous inputs</cite>.
  - Handling ambiguity via clarifying agents in dialogue and ReAct-based QA: <cite id="7915c5df-3">Clarifying agent overview for dialogue</cite> <cite id="7915c5df-4">Zero-shot ReAct agents detecting and resolving ambiguity; arXiv abstract</cite>.

- Empircal Studies and Domains:
  - Interactive codegen ambiguity: <cite id="7915c5df-0">Agents evaluated on ambiguous instructions in code generation</cite>.
  - Conversational QA disambiguation: <cite id="a4090542-2">Survey/analysis of ambiguity/disambiguation in LLM-based CQA</cite> <cite id="a4090542-6">Leveraging ambiguity concepts for LLM-driven systems</cite>.
  - Lexical ambiguity handling: <cite id="a4090542-5">Quantitative evaluation of LLMs handling lexical ambiguity</cite> <cite id="a4090542-7">Prompt augmentation strategies for WSD via ambiguity handling</cite>.

- Clarification with Retrieval and Structured Search:
  - ClarifyBench: <cite id="a4090542-0">Comprehensive benchmark for agent clarification strategies</cite>.
  - RAG-clarification methods and analyses: <cite id="2bec794b-1">ASK: aspects + retrieval hybrid clarifications in task-oriented dialogue</cite> <cite id="2bec794b-4">Clarification conditioned on retrieval distribution</cite> <cite id="2bec794b-7">Retrieval-Augmented Clarification for faithfulness</cite> <cite id="2bec794b-8">Corpus-informed clarifying questions for web search</cite> <cite id="2bec794b-0">Empirical findings on recognition and underuse of clarifying questions; retrieval mainly helps unambiguous cases</cite>.
  - Structured ambiguous-question resolution: <cite id="2bec794b-6">AQ-Tree: tree-space exploration of clarifications for ambiguous questions</cite>.

- Surveys and Engineering Overviews:
  - General agent evaluation survey and methodology repository: <cite id="a4090542-3">Surveys and evaluation methodologies for LLM agents</cite>.
  - Industry/engineering perspectives on clarifying agents and RAG: <cite id="2bec794b-3">Clarifying agents in dialogue with retrieval validation</cite> <cite id="2bec794b-8">Corpus-informed clarification in web search</cite>.

If you want a tailored reading list for a specific domain (e.g., code agents, medical QA, customer support chatbots), I can filter by task and highlight the most actionable techniques and quantitative gains.

questions.original_query: Search for research about parameter-efficient fine-tuning method in computer vision.

query.text: Search for research about parameter-efficient fine-tuning method in computer vision.
query.answer:
Below is a synthesis of recent research on parameter‑efficient fine‑tuning (PEFT) methods for computer vision, organized by technique family, with CV‑specific evidence and practical takeaways.

1) Overview and taxonomy
- Surveys and overviews summarize that PEFT adapts models by freezing the pretrained backbone and injecting small trainable modules or parameters, yielding strong generalization with low computational/memory overhead relative to full fine‑tuning, with Adapter‑based and LoRA methods being particularly popular for their efficiency and effectiveness across tasks and domains <cite id="79dc3950-1">Adapter-based and LoRA methods generally offer strong generalization with relatively low computational overhead, making them popular choices</cite>. A dedicated survey targets “pre‑trained vision models,” systematically reviewing visual PEFT methodologies and trends <cite id="79dc3950-6">This paper presents a comprehensive survey of the latest advancements in the visual PEFT field, systematically reviewing current methodologies</cite>.

2) Adapter Networks for vision
2.1 Concept and general advantages
- Adapter modules are small, surgically inserted networks (often residual MLP blocks) that add a tiny fraction of parameters while routing gradient flow to the pretrained backbone. They have been successfully integrated into vision Transformers (ViTs) and adapted to dense prediction tasks.
- Empirically, ViT‑Adapter demonstrates that adding a compact adapter can improve object detection, instance segmentation, and semantic segmentation, validating adapter efficacy across multiple CV modalities of prediction <cite id="2ae37443-0">ViT adapter under the plain ViT models has been successfully applied in multiple computer vision tasks, e.g., object detection (ODet)</cite> <cite id="2ae37443-1">We verify ViT-Adapter on multiple dense prediction tasks, including object detection, instance segmentation, and semantic segmentation</cite> <cite id="2ae37443-2">With our adapter, ViT can achieve significant improvements on object detection and instance segmentation tasks</cite>. The method has also been extended to multitask learning, proposing adapter‑based representations that generalize across tasks and domains <cite id="2ae37443-3">We introduce the first multitasking vision transformer adapters that learn generalizable task affinities which can be applied to novel tasks and domains</cite>.
- Beyond adapters, modern architectural insights suggest residual two‑layer MLP adapters can outperform LoRA on certain scientific ML tasks, motivating richer, low‑parameter feedforward components over pure low‑rank projections; this effect is also observed in visual settings and related architectures <cite id="79dc3950-2">We empirically and theoretically establish that residual two-layer MLP Adapters significantly outperform LoRA for fine-tuning in scientific machine learning</cite> <cite id="79dc3950-3">KRAdapter maintains the favorable training speed and memory efficiency of LoRA, making it a practical and robust alternative to fine-tune billion-scale</cite>.
2.2 Adapter variants and efficiency
- KRAdapter and related low‑rank/efficient adapter designs retain LoRA‑like speed and memory properties while improving training stability and accuracy, aiming at billion‑scale vision encoders and end‑to‑end models <cite id="79dc3950-3">KRAdapter maintains the favorable training speed and memory efficiency of LoRA, making it a practical and robust alternative to fine-tune billion-scale</cite>.
- Practical reports show extreme sparsity is attainable while keeping performance: adapting a ViT with a LoRA module comprising only 0.23% of the original trainable parameters yet retaining roughly 99% of full‑tuning accuracy (freezing ~99% of DeiT‑Base) suggests that per‑layer LoRA can be very parameter‑efficient without large accuracy hits in some settings <cite id="b74f86d5-2">Fine-Tuning a Vision Transformer with Adaptive LoRA: 0.23 % Trainable Params, Retains ~99 % of Full-Tune Accuracy · Freeze ~99 % of DeiT-Base</cite>.
- Adapter placement matters: for segmentation and dense tasks, simple “backbone adapters” can bridge feature hierarchies efficiently, often outperforming naive concatenation of frozen features and external heads <cite id="2ae37443-8">Utilizing a pretrained vision backbone to finetune a model for semantic segmentation is common practice in computer vision</cite>.

3) Low‑Rank Adaptation (LoRA) and quantized variants
3.1 LoRA in vision
- LoRA introduces low‑rank matrices to selected linear layers (e.g., MLPs in ViTs/CNNs), decoupling training from the frozen base while adding only rank×2k parameters per layer. It is widely used in CV for image classification, dense tasks, and as components within multimodal models <cite id="b74f86d5-7">Fine Tuning is a mechanisms for efficient adaptation of large pre-trained models by utilizing a smaller subset of parameters</cite>.
- CV‑specific studies also compare and extend LoRA: for example, adaptive LoRA that per‑layer tunes rank/structure reports near full‑fine‑tune accuracy with orders‑of‑magnitude fewer trainable parameters, supporting LoRA’s efficiency in practice <cite id="b74f86d5-2">Fine-Tuning a Vision Transformer with Adaptive LoRA: 0.23 % Trainable Params, Retains ~99 % of Full-Tune Accuracy · Freeze ~99 % of DeiT-Base</cite>.
- There is active work questioning redundancy assumptions: some analyses find that simply reducing density in LoRA can be nontrivial and that certain patterns of trainable parameter placement influence end performance, implying careful hyperparameterization and ablation are necessary to extract gains <cite id="79dc3950-7">we systematically investigate the impact of re- dundancy in fine-tuning LoRA and reveal that reducing density redundancy does not ...</cite>.
3.2 QLoRA‑style quantization and memory efficiency
- QLoRA’s recipe combines low‑rank updates with 4‑bit quantization of base weights (NF4), enabling fine‑tuning of very large models on a single 48‑GB GPU while preserving much of full‑fine‑tune accuracy; the same design space and trade‑offs motivate CV workflows that want high‑density accuracy with low GPU footprints <cite id="b74f86d5-0">QLoRA extends LoRA by combining it with 4-bit quantization for base model weights (using the NF4 quantization format), keeping LoRA matrices in ...</cite> <cite id="b74f86d5-3">We present QLoRA, an efficient finetuning approach that reduces memory usage enough to finetune a 65B parameter model on a single 48GB GPU</cite> <cite id="b74f86d5-5">QLoRA combines LoRA's parameter efficiency with 4-bit quantization, enabling fine-tuning of 65B parameter models on a single 48GB GPU while preserving full</cite>.
- Practical CV/ML resource writeups and tutorials mirror the LLM literature, showing CV researchers port techniques like QLoRA to ViTs and classification pipelines to cut GPU memory while retaining accuracy, often via LoRA applied to Transformer MLP blocks or cross‑attention layers <cite id="b74f86d5-1">Fine-tune LLMs on a single consumer GPU with LoRA and QLoRA. Step-by-step guide covering low-rank adaptation theory, 4-bit NF4 quantization</cite> <cite id="b74f86d5-8">This repository demonstrates the use of Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) to fine-tune Google's base model for two classification tasks</cite>.

4) Prompt‑ and sparse‑selective tuning in CV
4.1 Visual prompt tuning (input‑side PE)
- Prompt tuning injects learnable prompt tokens/embeddings to tailor pretrained vision Transformers without touching weights; Visual Prompt Tuning (VPT) offers a simple alternative to full fine‑tuning that scales efficiently with task complexity by expanding prompts rather than models <cite id="79b4e055-1">This paper introduces Visual Prompt Tuning (VPT) as an efficient and effective alternative to full fine-tuning for large-scale Transformer models in vision</cite>.
- Broader prompt‑tuning resources catalog methods that add a few tokens to images or embeddings, enabling prompt‑only adaptation across datasets and tasks; these are widely used for efficiency and rapid prototyping in CV/VLM workflows <cite id="79b4e055-2">A curated list of awesome papers, resources, and tools for Visual Prompt Tuning (VPT). Visual Prompting (VP): modifies the input image via pixel-space prompts</cite> <cite id="79b4e055-3">Visual prompt tuning (VPT) is a promising so- lution incorporating learnable prompt tokens to customize pre-trained models for downstream tasks</cite>.
4.2 Sparse/Selective Tuning (Bitfit, orthogonal probes, label‑wise prompts)
- Sparse methods train a small number of strategically selected parameters (e.g., entire blocks for referring segmentation or label‑specific prompt clusters), reducing trainable counts dramatically while improving sample efficiency. Bridger, an adapter for referring image segmentation, exemplifies efficient tuning on relation‑rich segmentation with improved performance over frozen baselines <cite id="79b4e055-9">In this paper, we do an investigation of efficient tuning problems on referring image segmentation. We propose a novel adapter called Bridger to facilitate</cite>.
- Sparse label‑specific prompt tuning and knowledge‑guided prompt fusion (e.g., Sparse‑KgCoOp) demonstrate efficiency and quality gains on visual‑language benchmarks, supporting the idea that selecting a small, task‑aware set of parameters/tokens can retain full‑tuning performance with much lower trainable budgets <cite id="79b4e055-0">Extensive experiments of several benchmarks demonstrate that the proposed Sparse-KgCoOp is an efficient method for prompt tuning</cite> <cite id="79b4e055-5">Extensive experiments of several benchmarks demonstrate that the proposed Sparse-KgCoOp is an efficient method for prompt tuning</cite> <cite id="b74f86d5-7">Fine Tuning is a mechanisms for efficient adaptation of large pre-trained models by utilizing a smaller subset of parameters</cite>.
- Bayesian/label‑wise prompt formulations generate stochastic prompts per class hierarchically, trading sampling cost for data efficiency and stable generalization, an example of parameter selection guided by probabilistic embeddings <cite id="79b4e055-6">We propose Bayesian prompt tuning that generates label-specific stochastic prompts hierarchically, models each label as a distribution over the embedding space</cite>.
- Some sparse updates use orthogonal projections as probing heads: analyses in NLP show residual orthogonalization helps selective tuning converge faster and avoid redundancy; while more empirical CV‑specific ablations are needed, the mechanism motivates orthogonal/structured projections within vision adapters or cross‑attention banks <cite id="79dc3950-7">In this work, we systematically investigate the impact of re- dundancy in fine-tuning LoRA and reveal that reducing density redundancy does not ...</cite>.

5) Multitask and multimodal PEFT
5.1 Multitask vision adapters
- Adapter frameworks extend to shared backbones across tasks: Vision Transformer Adapter for Generalizable Multitask Learning learns object‑centric representations and task affinities that transfer to novel tasks/domains, a core pattern for parameter‑efficient domain adaptation and lifelong learning <cite id="2ae37443-3">We introduce the first multitasking vision transformer adapters that learn generalizable task affinities which can be applied to novel tasks and domains</cite>.
5.2 Multimodal PEFT and cross‑modal efficiency
- QLoRA‑style 4‑bit quantization and LoRA appear in vision‑language pipelines, e.g., for aligning or extending LLM vision‑towers and cross‑attention blocks, enabling high‑density tuning on limited data and compute by confining trainable updates to small adapters or orthogonal projections <cite id="b74f86d5-0">QLoRA extends LoRA by combining it with 4-bit quantization for base model weights (using the NF4 quantization format), keeping LoRA matrices in ...</cite>.
- Meta‑Adapter exemplifies efficient, online few‑shot adaptation in open‑vocabulary object detection/segmentation by injecting compact per‑task adapters, yielding notable gains with modest added parameters and compute relative to full fine‑tune/scratch training <cite id="2ae37443-6">Meta-Adapter obtains notable performance improvements in open-vocabulary object detection and segmentation tasks</cite>.
- Prompt‑based efficiency also scales to multimodal scenarios: lightweight prompt tuning on both image and text can reach state‑of‑the‑art results in small‑data regimes (e.g., ADNI with 1,504 MRIs), evidencing PEFT’s value in data‑tight multimodal learning <cite id="79b4e055-7">Applying lightweight prompt tuning to both image and text modalities, our approach achieves state- of-the-art performance on ADNI with only 1,504 training MRIs</cite>.

6) Comparative insights and practical guidance
- Adapter vs LoRA: Two‑layer MLP adapters often deliver stronger improvements than LoRA on complex residual architectures, possibly because richer affine mappings better capture task‑specific shifts than low‑rank projections; in any case, LoRA‑style methods remain attractive due to extremely low memory per layer, while adapter blocks require careful placement/width selection to avoid harming base model behavior <cite id="79dc3950-2">We empirically and theoretically establish that residual two-layer MLP Adapters significantly outperform LoRA for fine-tuning in scientific machine learning</cite> <cite id="79dc3950-3">KRAdapter maintains the favorable training speed and memory efficiency of LoRA, making it a practical and robust alternative to fine-tune billion-scale</cite> <cite id="2ae37443-0">ViT adapter under the plain ViT models has been successfully applied in multiple computer vision tasks, e.g., object detection (ODet)</cite>.
- Sparsity and quality: Reports of 0.23% trainable fraction with near‑full accuracy show extreme efficiency is plausible when tuning per layer or per block, but results are sensitive to layer selection, rank, and task dynamics; ablation over ranks and sparse sets is necessary to balance speed and fidelity <cite id="b74f86d5-2">Fine-Tuning a Vision Transformer with Adaptive LoRA: 0.23 % Trainable Params, Retains ~99 % of Full-Tune Accuracy · Freeze ~99 % of DeiT-Base</cite> <cite id="79dc3950-7">In this work, we systematically investigate the impact of re- dundancy in fine-tuning LoRA and reveal that reducing density redundancy does not ...</cite>.
- Quantization and memory: QLoRA’s 4‑bit scheme illustrates a generalizable path—train small LoRA on quantized bases—to halve memory footprint and enable single‑GPU fine‑tuning of large models; CV workflows benefit from porting this recipe to ViT MLPs and cross‑attention blocks, often with minimal accuracy loss when tuned to task specifics <cite id="b74f86d5-0">QLoRA extends LoRA by combining it with 4-bit quantization for base model weights (using the NF4 quantization format), keeping LoRA matrices in ...</cite> <cite id="b74f86d5-3">We present QLoRA, an efficient finetuning approach that reduces memory usage enough to finetune a 65B parameter model on a single 48GB GPU</cite> <cite id="b74f86d5-5">QLoRA combines LoRA's parameter efficiency with 4-bit quantization, enabling fine-tuning of 65B parameter models on a single 48GB GPU while preserving full</cite>.
- Prompt efficiency: Visual prompt tuning and label‑specific prompt sets provide input‑side and parameter‑side sparsity, often outperforming frozen baselines with few learnable tokens; they are particularly effective when labeled data is scarce, and can be combined with adapters to further boost gains <cite id="79b4e055-1">This paper introduces Visual Prompt Tuning (VPT) as an efficient and effective alternative to full fine-tuning for large-scale Transformer models in vision</cite> <cite id="79b4e055-0">Extensive experiments of several benchmarks demonstrate that the proposed Sparse-KgCoOp is an efficient method for prompt tuning</cite> <cite id="79b4e055-7">Applying lightweight prompt tuning to both image and text modalities, our approach achieves state- of-the-art performance on ADNI with only 1,504 training MRIs</cite>.
- Dense tasks: Adapter frameworks such as ViT‑Adapter improve detection and segmentation by introducing task‑aware signal into limited layers; for semantic/panoptic segmentation, adapter‑style “backbone adapters” and label‑specific cross‑attention bridges efficiently propagate task cues to pretrained encoders without weight copies <cite id="2ae37443-1">We verify ViT-Adapter on multiple dense prediction tasks, including object detection, instance segmentation, and semantic segmentation</cite> <cite id="2ae37443-4">ViT-Adapter supports various dense prediction tasks, including object detection , instance segmentation , semantic segmentation , visual grounding , panoptic</cite> <cite id="79b4e055-9">In this paper, we do an investigation of efficient tuning problems on referring image segmentation. We propose a novel adapter called Bridger to facilitate</cite>.

7) Open problems and active research directions
- Ranking and allocation: Automated schemes to choose layer groups, ranks, and sparse sets that maximize accuracy per parameter remain underexplored in CV; recent redundancy analyses caution that naive density cuts can stall learning, suggesting principled allocation strategies and redundancy control <cite id="79dc3950-7">In this work, we systematically investigate the impact of re- dundancy in fine-tuning LoRA and reveal that reducing density redundancy does not ...</cite>.
- Generalization and stability: Multitask adapters like VTAGML show promise, but systematic studies of how to transfer task affinities to unseen tasks, and how to prevent interference in lifelong vision learning with PEFT, are ongoing <cite id="2ae37443-3">We introduce the first multitasking vision transformer adapters that learn generalizable task affinities which can be applied to novel tasks and domains</cite>.
