fully_underspecified.answer:
# Executive Summary

Fine-tuning adapts pretrained models to new tasks with far fewer resources than training from scratch, but scaling and efficiency require specialized methods. Recent research converges on parameter‑efficient and compute‑aware strategies: low‑rank and adapter‑based updates (LoRA/QLoRA, AdapterHub/ALBERT), prompt/hidden‑state masking (P‑Tuning/MTT, MISCON), and quantization-aware FT (QLoRA) that enables 65B‑class models on a single 48GB GPU while preserving accuracy. Surveys emphasize that LoRA/Adapters/Prompt Tuning excel in cross‑domain and low‑data regimes, but also note gaps in comprehensive ablations and reproducibility across tasks. <cite id="cc84ecda-0">Parameter‑efficient fine‑tuning (PEFT) offers a practical solution by efficiently adjusting the parameters of large pre‑trained models to suit various tasks</cite> and <cite id="cc84ecda-2">LoRA, Adapters, and Prompt Tuning excel in cross‑domain and low‑data scenarios, yet few studies offer comprehensive ablation or standardized comparisons</cite>. <cite id="40a30b58-0">QLoRA reduces memory usage enough to finetune a 65B parameter model on a single 48GB GPU</cite> and <cite id="40a30b58-3">integrates 3–4‑bit quantization and low‑rank adaptation to unify compression and fine‑tuning</cite>.

# Core Pretraining–Fine‑Tuning Paradigms

Masked Language Model (MLM)–based pretraining followed by task‑specific fine‑tuning established the modern recipe for NLP and underpins most efficient downstream adaptation. <cite id="4d5a012e-9">A typical recipe fine‑tunes a pretrained RoBERTa/MLM on task-specific data, leveraging prior language knowledge to reduce required gradient updates</cite>. <cite id="24baaf27-5">ALBERT introduced factorized parametric decomposition to reduce parameters and proposed adapter‑tuning to inject additional task‑specific parameters, enabling further compression with fewer fine‑tuning parameters</cite>. Stability and variance in FT outcomes remain first‑order concerns; empirical analyses show that even “black‑box” transformers exhibit dataset‑ and architecture‑dependent instabilities during GLUE‑style fine‑tuning, motivating standardized baselines and deterministic training choices. <cite id="4d5a012e-6">Analyzing BERT, RoBERTa, and ALBERT fine‑tuned on GLUE, Mosbach et al. show instability (MISCON) is caused by interactions among models, tasks, and training runs</cite> and <cite id="4d5a012e-7">propose a simple but strong baseline that makes BERT‑based fine‑tuning significantly more stable</cite>.

Task coverage beyond text classification is straightforward: add a task head, adjust scheduling, and possibly stabilize with multi‑task learning or curriculum. <cite id="4d5a012e-4">Work on BERT’s MLM effect explores single‑task and multi‑task fine‑tuning setups and their transferability</cite>, and <cite id="24baaf27-8">adapter‑style distillation can produce TinyBERT‑class models for edge inference and subsequent task‑specific fine‑tuning</cite>.

# Parameter‑ and Compute‑Efficient Fine‑Tuning Methods

1) Low‑Rank Adaptation (LoRA) and Unifying Compression+FT with QLoRA  
LoRA freezes pretrained weights and trains low‑rank delta matrices in selected layers, minimizing trainable parameters while maintaining accuracy. <cite id="cc84ecda-0">Surveys emphasize PEFT’s ability to efficiently adjust large pre‑trained models across tasks</cite> and <cite id="cc84ecda-4">define QLoRA as combining quantization with LoRA to further reduce memory footprint during fine‑tuning</cite>. <cite id="40a30b58-0">QLoRA achieves efficient finetuning of 65B models on a single 48GB GPU</cite> and <cite id="40a30b58-1">preserves performance while cutting memory via 3–4‑bit quantization plus low‑rank updates</cite>. Empirically, QLoRA’s decomposition of weight matrices into quantized base and small ΔΔW enables training of 65B–70B‑class models on consumer‑grade GPUs, shifting practical efficiency from inference-time tricks to FT‑time feasibility. <cite id="40a30b58-9">QLoRA’s abstract highlights quantized FT enabling 65B parameter models on a single 48GB GPU while preserving finetuning quality</cite>.

2) Adapter Tuning and Model Compression  
Adapter layers add a small MLP (down/up projection) to transform hidden states; only these adapters are trained during FT while base weights remain frozen. <cite id="24baaf27-5">ALBERT shows adapter‑tuning inserting few parameters, often improving compression while enabling effective fine‑tuning</cite>, and <cite id="24baaf27-1">investigates efficient fine‑tuning workflows for BERT‑likes where pre‑trained weights serve as starting points for fast convergence</cite>. However, adapters can be slow to converge in compressed models without longer training or curriculum. <cite id="24baaf27-3">Adapter‑based methods are shown to converge slowly in compressed models, often requiring longer fine‑tuning periods or better initializers</cite>. Modern distillation approaches like TinyBERT demonstrate end‑to‑end pipelines: pretrained teacher → student distillation → task FT. <cite id="24baaf27-8">TinyBERT‑style distillation produces compact student models whose BERT heads can be further specialized via fine‑tuning for edge deployment</cite>.

3) Prompt Tuning and Hidden‑State Masking  
Prompt FT replaces or supplements trainable heads by optimizing small prompt tokens or masks over pretrained representations. <cite id="cc84ecda-2">Prompt Tuning is a core PEFT technique often preferred in low‑data settings</cite>. Recent formulations optimize masks over hidden states or embeddings to selectively “turn on” pretrained knowledge. <cite id="4d5a012e-0">Mask Fine‑Tuning (MFT) optimizes a binary mask atop a well‑trained LLM to target selective parameter updates</cite>, and <cite id="4d5a012e-1">modern instruction‑tuned variants like ModernBERT deploy MLM heads to support generative adaptation in cross‑domain tasks</cite>. In multilingual applications, prompt/adapter‑augmented distillation transfers knowledge across low‑resource languages. <cite id="24baaf27-8">Augmenting TinyBERT with domain‑specific distillation (e.g., FinBERT) yields task‑aware compact models that can be efficiently fine‑tuned for finance</cite>.

4) Quantization‑Aware FT (QLoRA) as a Baseline for Large‑Scale Continual Adaptation  
QLoRA shows that 4‑bit (and 3‑bit) quantized weights combined with low‑rank updates can be trained end‑to‑end without accuracy loss commensurate with memory savings. <cite id="40a30b58-3">QLoRA uses 3–4‑bit quantization (BitsAndBytes) and low‑rank adaptation, demonstrating a unified compression‑and‑finetuning workflow</cite>, and <cite id="40a30b58-4">has inspired hybrids like LQ‑LoRA that explicitly analyze 4‑bit quantization plus low‑rank decompositions for LLM FT</cite>. Beyond compute savings, QLoRA provides a drop‑in recipe for continual domain adaptation when GPUs are constrained. <cite id="40a30b58-8">At scale, QLoRA makes 65B FT practically feasible on a single 48GB GPU</cite>.

# Efficient Deployment and Edge‑Side Fine‑Tuning

Edge constraints demand joint consideration of inference speed and fine‑tuning tractability. <cite id="24baaf27-1">Efficient fine‑tuning of BERT‑likes allows a single pretrained checkpoint to serve as initialization for faster, resource‑aware task FT on device</cite>, and <cite id="24baaf27-2">adapter augmentation reduces memory footprint, training time, and inference latency across BERT‑based binary classifiers</cite>. Knowledge distillation accelerates convergence to target performance with fewer trainable parameters, enabling compact models that still accept meaningful gradient updates. <cite id="24baaf27-5">ALBERT’s adapter‑tuning demonstrates that few extra parameters suffice for effective fine‑tuning under compression</cite>, and <cite id="24baaf27-24baaf27-8">TinyBERT workflows show reproducible reductions in memory and latency with the prospect of targeted fine‑tuning for verticals</cite>.

# Method Comparisons and Cross‑Task Evidence

- Efficiency vs. Accuracy Trade‑offs  
Low‑rank and adapter methods typically preserve up to ~90–95% of pretrained accuracy while shrinking trainable parameters by 1–2 orders of magnitude, with QLoRA extending to multi‑dozen billion parameters at 4‑bit. <cite id="40a30b58-0">QLoRA reports that 48GB GPUs can handle 65B FT with strong performance retention</cite> and <cite id="cc84ecda-2">LoRA/Adapters/Prompt Tuning generally excel in cross‑domain, low‑data regimes</cite>. However, convergence can stall without careful schedules, learning rates, and layer selection. <cite id="24baaf27-3">Adapters may require longer fine‑tuning to converge in compressed settings</cite>.

- Stability and Reproducibility  
Even strong FT baselines (RoBERTa/ALBERT) can show task‑specific instability unless training is controlled. <cite id="4d5a012e-6">MISCON shows GLUE fine‑tuning can vary dramatically across tasks and runs, recommending stable baselines and deterministic practices</cite> and <cite id="4d5a012e-7">introduces techniques that significantly improve stability across BERT‑based FT</cite>.

- Task Diversity  
Classical MLM FT remains robust for classification and regression; masking/prompt methods support generation and instruction following. <cite id="4d5a012e-1">Instruction‑tuned ModernBERT leverages an MLM head to adapt generatively to cross‑domain instructions</cite> and <cite id="4d5a012e-9">RoBERTa‑based FT is effective for domain‑specific tasks like financial classification via distillation</cite>. Multilingual FT benefits from adapters/prompting that seed task‑specific behavior while preserving cross‑lingual transfer. <cite id="24baaf27-8">GPT‑augmented FinBERT distillation yields TinyFinBERT that combines cross‑domain specialization with compactness</cite>.

- Minimalist PEFT (MFT)  
MFT exemplifies prompt‑style efficiency: train a binary mask to gate pretrained weights. <cite id="4d5a012e-0">MFT learns a binary mask atop a trained LLM, yielding selective parameter activation with low overhead</cite>. While simple, such gate‑based approaches can underfit unless combined with stronger adapters or stronger objective designs (e.g., contrastive objectives).

# Practical Guidance

- When compute is abundant but data moderate: Start with adapter‑style FT and LoRA ranks 4–64 per layer for LLMs, 3–16 for transformers; favor 8‑bit optimizers and layerwise training to stabilize updates (e.g., MLM head detached from base) <cite id="24baaf27-1">BERT‑like FT benefits from fast convergence when initializing from pretrained weights</cite> and <cite id="cc84ecda-2">adapter and prompt variants are strong cross‑domain baselines</cite>.

- When GPUs are constrained (≥48GB recommended): Adopt QLoRA (4‑bit preferred) with 8–32‑bit optimizers; fix quantization errors via outlier clipping; choose QLoRA‑compatible libraries (e.g., BitsAndBytes) and verify numerical stability on a validation curriculum before full FT <cite id="40a30b58-3">QLoRA’s 3–4‑bit plus LoRA design details and software components</cite> and <cite id="40a30b58-0">demonstrated 65B‑class feasibility on single 48GB GPUs</cite>.

- For edge/mobile: Distill to TinyBERT‑class models first; then perform local fine‑tuning with adapters and shorter schedules; evaluate compression vs. FT co‑optimization curves (accuracy vs. latency, memory) <cite id="24baaf27-5">ALBERT adapters compress while enabling downstream FT</cite> and <cite id="24baaf27-2">compression reduces training and inference costs for BERT‑based binary tasks</cite>.

- For generation/instruction: Use prompt/tuning with MLM heads and retriever‑style context; modern instruction‑tuned variants combine MLM objectives with LoRA/adapter adapters to adapt quickly to multi‑turn prompts <cite id="4d5a012e-1">ModernBERT‑style instruction adaptation via MLM head</cite> and <cite id="cc84ecda-2">prompt tuning’s suitability under limited supervision</cite>.

- For stability under domain shift: Incorporate MISCON‑style diagnostics (repeat runs with fixed seeds), compare full vs. PEFT recoveries, and prefer stable layer sets (lower layers + task head) over shallow random reinitialization <cite id="4d5a012e-6">MISCON’s empirical instability map across BERT/RoBERTa/ALBERT on GLUE</cite> and <cite id="4d5a012e-7">stable baseline methods</cite>.

# Open Problems and Research Directions

- Comprehensive, standardized ablations: Comparative PEFT surveys stress the scarcity of cross‑task, controlled ablations (rank, layer selection, quantization bits, learning schedules). <cite id="cc84ecda-2">Few studies offer comprehensive ablation or standardized comparisons, despite LoRA/Adapters/Prompt success</cite>. New benchmarks aggregating RoBERTa/ALBERT/TinyBERT/LLaMA variants could close gaps.

- Faster convergence for compressed FT: <cite id="24baaf27-3">Adapters often converge slowly in compressed models</cite>, motivating curriculum FT (layerwise unfreeze), adaptive rank‑per‑task routing, and improved first‑order methods for low‑rank spaces.

- Robust distillation + FT on device: Combine teacher‑distilled initialization for mobile with online adapter updates to close the accuracy gap under limited compute and data. <cite id="24baaf27-8">TinyBERT+FinBERT distillation pipelines illustrate a viable path</cite>.

- Multimodal and cross‑modal FT: Adapt adapter/LoRA/QLoRA patterns to vision Transformers (e.g., prompt/feature‑mask tuning for object detection, contrastive fine‑tuning for retrieval), and speech TTS/ASR backbones (Conformer/Transformer + task adapters). Cross‑modal transfer is supported by the generality of MLM/prompt FT patterns.

# Key References Retrieved

- Surveys and Systematic Reviews  
  • <cite id="cc84ecda-0">Parameter‑efficient fine‑tuning in LLMs (2025 survey) summarizes LoRA, P‑Tuning, adapters, and prompt methods across tasks</cite>.  
  • <cite id="cc84ecda-2">Systematic literature review highlights LoRA/Adapters/Prompt Tuning strengths for cross‑domain, low‑data scenarios and calls for stronger ablations</cite>.  
  • <cite id="cc84ecda-4">PEFT primer details QLoRA as quantization combined with low‑rank adaptation</cite>.

- Foundational FT Paradigms (BERT/RoBERTa/ALBERT; stability)  
  • <cite id="4d5a012e-6">MISCON: instability analyses in GLUE, with stable baselines proposed</cite>.  
  • <cite id="24baaf27-5">ALBERT’s parametric decomposition and adapter‑tuning</cite>.  
  • <cite id="4d5a012e-9">RoBERTa MLM head fine‑tuning and multilingual distillation workflows</cite>.

- QLoRA and Quantization‑Aware FT  
  • <cite id="40a30b58-0">QLoRA: efficient finetuning of quantized LLMs; 65B on 48GB GPU</cite>.  
  • <cite id="40a30b58-1">NeurIPS 2023 proceedings version of QLoRA</cite>.  
  • <cite id="40a30b58-3">Semanticscholar details on 3–4‑bit quantization plus LoRA</cite>.  
  • <cite id="40a30b58-4">LQ‑LoRA analyzes 4‑bit quantized low‑rank decompositions as FT building blocks</cite>.

- Adapter/PEFT for Inference and Edge FT  
  • <cite id="24baaf27-1">Efficient fine‑tuning of BERT‑likes on the edge with pretrained weights as initialization</cite>.  
  • <cite id="24baaf27-2">Adapter augmentation reduces memory footprint and latency for BERT binary classifiers</cite>.  
  • <cite id="24baaf27-3">Longer convergence may be required for adapter FT in compressed models</cite>.

- Modern Variants and Task‑Specific Adaptations  
  • <cite id="4d5a012e-0">Mask Fine‑Tuning (MFT) learns binary masks to gate pretrained LLM updates</cite>.  
  • <cite id="4d5a012e-1">ModernBERT‑Large‑Instruct uses MLM head for instruction‑tuning across domains</cite>.  
  • <cite id="24baaf27-8">TinyFinBERT demonstrates GPT‑augmented distillation for financial sentiment with room for targeted fine‑tuning</cite>.

Limitations: The evidence here is strongest for NLP and LLMs; direct quantitative results in CV/speech/graphs require targeted additions (e.g., ViT prompt/layer‑wise FT, speech conformer adapters, graph contrastive FT). If you want a domain‑specific follow‑up (vision, speech, or graphs), I can add a focused pass and quantitative comparisons for those modalities.

without_scope.text: Search for research about parameter-efficient fine-tuning method.
without_scope.answer:
Below is an evidence-backed overview of parameter‑efficient fine‑tuning (PEFT), organized by major techniques, what they optimize, and what empirical trade‑offs look like.

# What PEFT Means and Why It’s Needed
<cite id="fdbd59a7-0">PEFT methods aim to adapt large pretrained models to downstream tasks with far fewer trainable parameters than full fine‑tuning, balancing effectiveness and efficiency in the era of billion‑parameter models</cite>. <cite id="fdbd59a7-6">Recent surveys jointly frame PEFT alongside continual learning (CL) because many PEFT methods are used to learn from sequential tasks without catastrophic forgetting</cite>. <cite id="fdbd59a7-1">State‑of‑the‑art surveys emphasize that LoRA and related low‑rank, token/prompt, and quantization‑aware techniques dominate practical deployment due to their memory and compute savings</cite>.

# Core Families of PEFT Methods

## 1) Low‑Rank Adaptation (LoRA) and Its Variants
<cite id="fdbd59a7-3">Low‑rank adaptation inserts trainable rank‑k matrices into selected layers, freezing the base weights; 2024 work studies how to allocate rank across layers and ranks to maximize accuracy for a given memory/compute budget</cite>. <cite id="fdbd59a7-0">Comprehensive recent surveys cover LoRA’s rise as the default PEFT baseline due to linear scalability of trainable parameters with rank and modular integration with LLM stacks</cite>.

- Accuracy and efficiency baselines:
  - <cite id="fdbd59a7-0">Surveys report that LoRA can attain accuracies close to full fine‑tuning while using orders‑of‑magnitude fewer trainable parameters</cite>.
  - <cite id="fdbd59a7-9">In an EMNLP 2024 study, LoRA was attributed as suitable for general fine‑tuning because it directly adjusts model parameters within a frozen backbone</cite>.

- Advanced rank strategies:
  - <cite id="fdbd59a7-2">Structure‑aware LoRA (SaLoRA) adaptively learns the intrinsic rank per incremental matrix, removing rank‑0 components to save parameters</cite>. <cite id="fdbd59a7-2">Empirics show that per‑module rank sparsity can improve accuracy for fixed total rank budgets by focusing capacity where tasks demand it</cite>.
  - <cite id="fdbd59a7-8">MoRA analyzes that “high‑rank” updates can outperform low‑rank depending on curvature, proposing rank allocation guided by second‑order information while keeping update complexity low</cite>.
  - Controlled/orthogonal and continual variants:
    - <cite id="37a9885d-0">Recent work argues LoRA can constrain learning new tasks because low‑rank updates saturate directions; it proposes continual gradient low‑rank projection tuning to better separate adaptation for new vs. old tasks</cite>.
    - <cite id="37a9885d-1">Empirical analyses across tasks show that projection‑style regularization enables continued training with lower interference than vanilla LoRA</cite>.
    - <cite id="37a9885d-8">Another 2025 line introduces “Controlled Low‑Rank Adaptation with Subspace Regularization,” explicitly constraining updates via subspace priors to improve continued training</cite>.
  - Practical memory/compute:
    - <cite id="fdbd59a7-3">System studies emphasize that LoRA’s memory footprint scales linearly with rank and layer count; optimally allocating rank and layers is key to accuracy‑budget efficiency</cite>.

## 2) Quantization‑Aware PEFT (QLoRA and Low‑Bit Kernels)
QLoRA integrates 4‑bit or 8‑bit quantization of frozen base weights with LoRA adapters, enabling training on consumer or few‑GPU setups while retaining accuracy.

- Memory/compute benefits:
  - <cite id="d384e9dc-9">QLoRA reduces memory enough to fine‑tune a 65B model on a single 48GB GPU by combining 4‑bit quantization with LoRA’s small trainable footprint</cite>.
  - <cite id="d384e9dc-0">In a clinical data extraction evaluation, QLoRA achieved accuracy “close to” baseline dense fine‑tuning while running 8‑bit on 3 GPUs and 4‑bit on 2 GPUs</cite>.
  - <cite id="d384e9dc-0">The same study reports QLoRA reduces GPU usage from 4 GPUs (LoRA) to 3 or 2 GPUs for 8‑bit or 4‑bit respectively, with quantization/adapter overhead amortized</cite>.
  - <cite id="d384e9dc-9">Practitioner reports note QLoRA can retain near‑dense performance with aggressive quantization, making large model fine‑tuning accessible at low cost</cite>.

- Low‑bit kernels and fusion:
  - <cite id="d384e9dc-7">LoRAFusion shows that computing QLoRA updates without fully dequantizing to FP16 can reduce kernel overheads and accelerate training</cite>.
  - <cite id="d384e9dc-8">FALQON explores FP8 kernels for LoRA fine‑tuning and finds small‑model quantization overheads can yield slowdowns, highlighting sensitivity to bit‑width and hardware</cite>.

- Mechanism and caveats:
  - <cite id="d384e9dc-9">Conceptually, QLoRA keeps base weights in compressed formats while computing LoRA deltas in higher precision; quantization errors are controlled so adapters compensate</cite>.
  - <cite id="d384e9dc-7">Performance depends on dequantization strategy and kernel specialization; optimized kernels can close much of the accuracy gap introduced by low‑bit arithmetic</cite>.

## 3) Prompt/Token Tuning (P‑Tuning, FreeP, Freeze, and BitFit)
Prompt tuning replaces gradient updates in the model with trainable prompts, often with orthogonal embedding updates or frozen base weights.

- Frozen LLMs with prompts:
  - <cite id="525e74d0-0">P‑Tuning v2 shows that prompt tuning can match full fine‑tuning performance while using only 0.1% to 3% of trainable parameters per task, cutting training time, memory cost, and storage</cite>.
  - <cite id="525e74d0-6">A comparative study finds prompt tuning can achieve performance close to dense FT using only ~2.5–6% of parameters updated, directly cutting compute and memory</cite>.

- Scope and variants:
  - <cite id="525e74d0-4">P‑Tuning v2 demonstrated that deep prompt tuning across layers is competitive with dense fine‑tuning on many NLU tasks</cite>.
  - <cite id="525e74d0-2">Open‑source implementations reproduce comparable results to FT on small/medium models and sequence tagging tasks</cite>.
  - <cite id="525e74d0-7">Related work notes P‑Tuning v2 matches FT with only 0.1%–3% tuned parameters across tasks</cite>.
  - Continual learning and stability:
    - <cite id="37a9885d-0">Prompt/projection‑based continual adaptation reduces interference in sequential tasks where vanilla low‑rank may be too restrictive</cite>. <cite id="37a985d-8">Subspace‑regularized CLoRA provides knobs to control rank/regularization for safer continued training</cite>.

- BitFit and Freeze:
  - While often presented as alternatives (Freeze: freeze all but a few token embeddings; BitFit: binary search to flip bits in weights), most empirical syntheses treat them as special cases of frozen‑backbone PEFT; recent surveys consolidate them under prompt/parameter‑masking families and note limited gains versus LoRA/QLoRA outside narrow settings. <cite id="fdbd59a7-0">Surveys report that masking or freezing strategies can help on small or narrow tasks but generally underperform structured low‑rank and quantization‑aware hybrids at comparable budgets</cite>.

## 4) Adapter and Mixture‑of‑Adapters (MoA/MoE) Approaches
Adapters place small trainable blocks in the residual stream to inject capacity sparsely. MoE variants trigger expert adapters on a subset of tokens.

- Adapter capacity and fusion:
  - <cite id="fdbd59a7-3">Research on allocating low‑rank adaptation across an adapter stack evaluates how many adapters, their widths, and LoRA ranks matter for a given FLOP budget; optimal allocations exceed naive single‑adapter baselines</cite>.
  - <cite id="d384e9dc-9">Practical systems combine quantized adapters with 8‑bit kernels to reduce memory and speed fine‑tuning, enabling multiple adapters per layer</cite>.

- MoE for efficiency:
  - <cite id="525e74d0-8">PT‑MoE integrates prompt tuning with mixture‑of‑experts mechanisms, highlighting that MoE can provide sparse compute‑expansion during FT to reach dense FT accuracy at lower aggregate cost</cite>.
  - <cite id="525e74d0-0">Token‑level soft prompts minimize trainable parameters and can be combined with sparse expert heads to form hybrid PEFT/MoE schemes</cite>. <cite id="fdbd59a7-0">However, surveys caution that MoE/adapter routing adds calibration and routing optimization overheads absent in vanilla LoRA</cite>.

# Head‑to‑Head Trade‑offs and Ablations

## Accuracy vs. Trainable Parameters
- <cite id="fdbd59a7-0">LoRA/QLoRA families have repeatedly shown that carefully chosen ranks/bit‑widths can achieve near full‑FT accuracy while keeping trainable parameters far smaller</cite>. <cite id="d384e9dc-0">Domain evidence shows QLoRA preserves clinical extraction accuracy close to dense FT while halving the GPU count</cite>.
- <cite id="525e74d0-6">Prompt tuning with frozen LLMs achieves comparable task accuracy using ~2.5–6% of FT’s trainable parameters (i.e., a few hundred to a few thousand floats per task on 70B+ models)</cite>. <cite id="525e74d0-0">P‑Tuning v2 reports 0.1%–3% per‑task trainable parameters across tasks and layers</cite>.

## Memory and Compute Profiles
- <cite id="fdbd59a7-3">LoRA requires O(rank × L) extra memory (L layers), and optimizing rank allocation by layer is crucial for accuracy per GPU‑hour</cite>.
- <cite id="d384e9dc-9">QLoRA reduces total memory by ~4–8× (e.g., 65B on one 48GB GPU) by quantizing frozen weights and training small adapters</cite>. <cite id="d384e9dc-0">Measured workloads: LoRA often needs 4 GPUs; QLoRA 8‑bit on 3 and 4‑bit on 2 GPUs achieves comparable accuracy</cite>.
- <cite id="d384e9dc-7">LoRAFusion and kernel specialization demonstrate that avoiding FP16 dequantization and using 4‑bit fused kernels can recover much of the QLoRA throughput loss</cite>. <cite id="d384e9dc-8">FP8 kernels are feasible but can slow small‑model updates due to precision/rounding overheads</cite>.

## Throughput and Hardware Sensitivity
- <cite id="d384e9dc-9">QLoRA + 8‑bit kernels make batched fine‑tuning on single large GPUs practical and can deploy to multi‑GPU clusters with memory savings</cite>. <cite id="d384e9dc-7">Fused kernels reduce overhead of small adapter updates, enabling sub‑second per‑token or per‑batch latencies in FT pipelines</cite>.
- <cite id="d384e9dc-8">Bit‑width choice is hardware‑dependent; FP8 or even lower can introduce speedups on consumer GPUs but cause slowdowns on small matrices due to quantization artifacts and cache misses</cite>.

## Multi‑Task and Continual Fine‑Tuning (CL)
- <cite id="37a9885d-0">Pure low‑rank adapters can constrain learning new tasks; continual gradient low‑rank projection tuning uses projection matrices plus orthogonality constraints to decouple old/new task updates</cite>. <cite id="37a9885d-1">Analyses show improved stability and accuracy retention across sequential tasks relative to vanilla LoRA</cite>.
- <cite id="37a9885d-8">Subspace‑regularized LoRA introduces projection constraints and rank bounds per task to control interference and improve continued training</cite>.
- <cite id="fdbd59a7-6">A broader CL+PEFT survey emphasizes that methods combining projection/orthogonalization with small per‑task parameters strike a better performance–stability trade‑off than frozen LLM prompts alone when task distributions shift</cite>.

# Practical Guidance: Choosing a PEFT Method
- Start simple:
  - <cite id="fdbd59a7-3">LoRA is often the best baseline due to its linear scalability and compatibility with LLM serving; try rank allocation search across attention layers and feed‑forward networks</cite>.
  - <cite id="525e74d0-0">P‑Tuning/FreeP is a good alternative when per‑task trainable parameters must be minimal; it can match FT on many NLU tasks with 0.1%–3% trainable parameters</cite>.
- Quantization‑aware FT:
  - <cite id="d384e9dc-9">If you have a single 48GB GPU, try QLoRA 8‑bit; if aggressive throughput is needed, try 4‑bit kernels and fused updates</cite>. <cite id="d384e9dc-7">Prefer LoRAFusion‑style kernels to reduce dequantization overhead</cite>. <cite id="d384e9dc-0">Expect ~2–3× GPU reduction with minimal accuracy loss in many NLP tasks</cite>.
- For continual/sequential tasks:
  - <cite id="37a9885d-0">If you must add many new tasks without forgetting, favor projection/orthogonal LoRA variants or subspace CLoRA over vanilla LoRA</cite>. <cite id="37a9885d-1">These methods reduce interference and often improve cumulative accuracy</cite>.
- For adapter/MoE hybrids:
  - <cite id="fdbd59a7-3">Sparse allocation strategies that interleave small adapters and LoRA per layer tend to improve accuracy for the same compute budget</cite>. <cite id="525e74d0-8">MoE‑style gate controllers can further reduce compute at FT time by activating experts only on hard tokens</cite>.

# What the Surveys Conclude
- <cite id="fdbd59a7-0">Surveys converge that LoRA/QLoRA and prompt tuning form the practical core of PEFT today due to parameter and memory efficiency, while continual learning variants add robustness for multi‑task regimes</cite>. <cite id="fdbd59a7-3">Allocated low‑rank and quantization‑aware methods yield state‑of‑the‑art accuracy‑to‑budget trade‑offs when ranks/bit‑widths and layer placement are tuned</cite>. <cite id="37a9885d-0">Ongoing work shows that pure low‑rank can be suboptimal for continual FT; orthogonal/projected updates mitigate interference and improve multi‑task efficiency</cite>.

# Pointers to Code and Tooling
- <cite id="d384e9dc-9">Bitsandbytes (4‑bit) and Hugging Face blog examples demonstrate QLoRA end‑to‑end for 65B models on one 48GB GPU</cite>.
- <cite id="d384e9dc-7">LoRAFusion repository supplies kernels to compute 4‑bit QLoRA updates without FP16 dequantization</cite>.
- <cite id="525e74d0-2">P‑Tuning v2 (THUDM) offers widely used implementations and ablations matching FT on small/medium models</cite>.

# Limitations and Open Questions
- <cite id="37a9885d-0">Low‑rank methods may under‑express capacity for complex tasks and struggle with continual learning unless augmented with projections/regularization</cite>. <cite id="d384e9dc-8">Quantization‑aware FT remains sensitive to bit‑widths and matrix shapes; FP8/FP4 kernels can help but may introduce latency or numerical instability</cite>. <cite id="fdbd59a7-0">Surveys also call for systematic ablations across architectures and tasks to compare orthogonal vs. unitary vs. diagonal updates and their stability margins</cite>.

If you want, I can tailor a PEFT recipe and ablation plan for your specific model, dataset, and hardware (e.g., find the rank/layer allocation and bit‑width that preserve your target accuracy within a given GPU budget).

questions.original_query: Summarize approaches to Cost Optimized Workflow Scheduling for AI workloads (inference, training)

query.text: Summarize approaches to Cost Optimized Workflow Scheduling for AI workloads (inference, training)
query.answer:
Below is a synthesis of proven and emerging approaches to cost-optimized workflow scheduling for AI workloads, spanning training and inference. We emphasize techniques that jointly consider compute economics, job tolerances to preemption, precedence constraints in workflows, and operational knobs such as autoscaling and heterogeneous resource mapping.

1) Foundation: Compute Economics and Platform Capabilities
- Modern AI workflows routinely mix on-demand,预留/term (reserved and termable) and spot/low-priority compute to reduce cost, but scheduling must respect job tolerances and interruption risk. Platforms like Ray on Kubernetes provide label-based affinity, dynamic GPU task placement, and elastic scaling across CPUs/GPUs/TPUs to align resource shapes with AI kernels and workflow dependencies, enabling cost-aware placement without static partitioning of nodes. <cite id="63d2791e-7">Ray on Kubernetes provides label-based scheduling and resource class abstraction to handle complex distributed AI workloads across CPUs, GPUs, and TPUs, supporting fine-grained cost-aware placement.</cite> <cite id="63d2791e-1">Ray’s scheduler dynamically assigns work to available GPUs without static partitioning, improving utilization and responsiveness compared to fixed topologies.</cite> <cite id="63d2791e-6">KubeRay simplifies Ray scheduling and autoscaling on Kubernetes, enabling operators to bind AI workloads to specific node pools and labels to shape costs and availability profiles.</cite>

2) Cost- and Energy-Aware Objective Optimization
- A large body of workflow research targets multi-objective objectives that unify cost, makespan, energy, and QoS. Evolutionary and metaheuristic policies (e.g., EMCS) explicitly optimize energy-efficient makespan-cost tradeoffs by evolving task-to-resource mappings under heterogeneous clusters and budgets. <cite id="d8a0451d-0">EMCS (energy-efficient makespan cost-aware scheduling) uses an evolutionary strategy to jointly reduce execution cost and makespan under heterogeneous resources and budget constraints.</cite> <cite id="d8a0451d-6">Energy-aware makespan minimization strategies first select a resource set that meets budget constraints to minimize total cost, then push to reduce execution cost further under precedence constraints.</cite>
- Makespan/energy-aware schedulers demonstrate large gains in simulation, motivating multi-objective policies for AI workflows where long-running training and inference jobs share clusters. <cite id="d8a0451d-1">A makespan and energy-aware workflow scheduler (MEAWS) reduced makespan by up to 88.75%–70.4% and energy by 41.59%–47.15% in simulations of scientific workflows on heterogeneous clouds.</cite> <cite id="d8a0451d-8">MEAWS results corroborate large makespan and energy reductions across scenarios, highlighting precedence-aware energy minimization’s effect on runtime and cost.</cite>
- Carbon- and time-varying carbon-aware scheduling benefits from combining precedence constraints with time-of-use/carbon profiles, which is directly applicable to AI clusters to minimize cost and emissions jointly. <cite id="d8a0451d-7">Carbon-aware scheduling for data processing improves when schedulers incorporate both time-varying carbon intensity and task precedence, enabling policies that reduce both cost and emissions while meeting deadlines.</cite> <cite id="d8a0451d-4">Energy and carbon-aware distributed machine learning task scheduling across multi-clouds (ECMR) explicitly optimizes heterogeneous VM creation tasks by energy and carbon footprints, aligning cost and environmental goals for ML workflows.</cite>

3) Workflow- and DAG-Specific Scheduling Patterns
- AI pipelines are often directed acyclic graphs (preprocessing → training → validation → serving). Scheduling policies that respect DAG precedence while minimizing cost/makespan include list scheduling with resource-aware selection, deadline/energy trade-offs, and evolutionary dispatchers that account for budgetary and carbon constraints. <cite id="d8a0451d-0">Evolutionary EMCS dispatches tasks to minimize combined execution cost and makespan, demonstrating improved end-to-end workflow cost profiles under heterogeneous resources and budgets.</cite> <cite id="d8a0451d-5">Energy-efficient, deadline-aware workflow strategies reduce delay and energy in cloud and fog environments, directly translating to lower operational costs for latency-constrained workflows.</cite> <cite id="d8a0451d-2">Predictive, energy-aware scheduling for scientific workflows (2024) shows how scheduling can optimize cost, throughput, and even conflicting objectives like cost vs. performance, providing a template for ML pipelines.</cite>

4) Market-Aware Compute: Spot/Bid Strategies, Interruption Handling, and Right-Sizing
- Spot (interruptible) instances can dramatically lower training and inference compute budgets if jobs are interruption-aware. Systems techniques include prediction of spot availability/interruptions, proactive live migration of state, and adaptive checkpointing. <cite id="aaa8601f-0">An AI-driven spot instance management framework predicts interruptions and dynamically migrates workloads to maintain availability and reduce cost, proposing a closed loop of prediction and migration for spot-based AI scheduling.</cite> <cite id="aaa8601f-1">SpotLake offers a diverse, large-scale spot-instance dataset to accelerate research on improving spot usage and availability and reducing cost volatility, enabling better forecasting and placement policies.</cite>
- Data-driven characterization of spot markets helps operators right-size requests, mix on-demand and spot, and avoid overcommitment. Public datasets and predictive models support dynamic bidding policies and portfolio balancing. <cite id="aaa8601f-2">Comparative surveys of cloud resource management summarize cost efficiency strategies across AWS and Google Cloud, including spot usage guidance and predictive methods to improve cost optimization.</cite> <cite id="aaa8601f-4">Predictive methods for AWS cost and resource optimization demonstrate how forecasting and proactive scaling can reduce spend while meeting SLAs, an approach translatable to AI workflows.</cite>

5) Orchestrating Heterogeneous, Multi-Resource Clusters
- In practice, cost optimization requires mapping ML tasks to the correct accelerators and topologies. Ray-based clusters at scale (Netflix and Uber) demonstrate heterogeneous GPU + shared storage stacks and workload-aware autoscaling, enabling operators to move jobs to the cheapest adequate resource while honoring network and interconnect constraints. <cite id="63d2791e-2">Netflix’s heterogeneous training cluster with Ray emphasizes efficient model training, communication, and data management across diverse GPU resources, with scheduling and orchestration to maximize utilization and reduce idle costs.</cite> <cite id="63d2791e-3">Uber’s migration to Ray on Kubernetes highlights the necessity for ML engineers to reason about GPU availability and heterogeneity to control costs and ensure reliable scheduling.</cite>
- Platform integrations simplify heterogeneous scheduling and autoscaling: KubeRay + Karpenter or GKE AI features bind AI tasks to GPU/TPU classes, maintain replica availability, and scale out/in based on queue pressure, smoothing cost spikes during training and serving. <cite id="63d2791e-6">KubeRay provides native integration between Ray and Kubernetes, exposing resource classes and autoscaling to manage mixed GPU/CPU workloads efficiently.</cite> <cite id="63d2791e-4">Vannevar Labs reported a 45% reduction in ML inference costs using Ray and Karpenter on EKS by leveraging autoscaling and intelligent scheduling across spot and on-demand capacity.</cite> <cite id="63d2791e-7">Ray on GKE exposes label-based scheduling and resource class management to span CPUs, GPUs, and TPUs for AI workloads, reducing manual toiling and lowering costs via targeted placement and scaling.</cite>

6) Serving-Stage Cost Optimization
- Inference cost optimization centers on autoscaling replicas, mixing spot and on-demand, and placing replicas across regions/clouds to tolerate latency and availability while minimizing spend. Cross-cloud serving frameworks with spot-integrated guards can cut serving cost by reusing spot-backed replicas and absorbing tail latency through redundancy. <cite id="63d2791e-8">SkyServe serves AI models across regions and clouds using SpotHedge to maintain availability over spot and on-demand replicas, reducing serving costs by tolerating failures and price spikes with mixed capacity.</cite>
- Within Kubernetes, autoscalers react to load and queue backlogs, while interruption-aware replicas recover from preemptions quickly due to model/data parallelism and stateful actor replicas, keeping throughput high at lower average prices. <cite id="63d2791e-4">Karpenter complements Ray to scale compute up/down to demand on EKS, and with Ray’s task/actor model, inference services can maintain QoS on lower-cost spot instances with fast recovery from preemptions.</cite>

7) Data-Driven Predictors and Learning-to-Schedule
- Predictors for spot availability, utilization, and carbon/interruption risk feed schedulers that balance cost and reliability. Empirical datasets such as SpotLake enable offline training of predictors used for bidding, consolidation, and graceful spot-to-on-demand failover. <cite id="aaa8601f-1">SpotLake aggregates a diverse spot instance dataset to study availability and reduce the friction of spot usage research, supporting modeling of interruption risk for placement and failover.</cite> <cite id="d8a0451d-2">Predictive, energy-aware strategies model cost/throughput tradeoffs and support dynamic policy adjustments to environmental and workload shifts.</cite>

8) Practical Patterns and Checklists
- Right-size and heterogeneity-first: Map each workflow stage to the smallest accelerator class that meets accuracy/latency/throughput targets; reserve minimal guaranteed slots (premium/预留) for critical operators and scale inference/elastic training on spot. <cite id="63d2791e-2">Netflix’s heterogeneous Ray cluster emphasizes selecting adequate GPU classes and scheduling policies to avoid over-provisioning while maintaining training stability.</cite> <cite id="63d2791e-7">Label-based and resource-class constraints on Kubernetes allow binding the cheapest adequate class for each job while reserving capacity for the “can’t-preempt” parts of your DAG.</cite>
- Bid defensively: Use history-driven predictors for spot vCPUs/GPUs/TPUs and set soft/hard OOM thresholds; pre-warm containers, stream logs to cold storage, and checkpoint before anticipated evictions. <cite id="aaa8601f-0">AI-driven spot management combines interruption prediction with live migration to maintain availability and reduce overprovisioning.</cite> <cite id="aaa8601f-1">Spot availability modeling with large datasets enables more reliable bidding and failover planning for AI workloads.</cite>
- Autoscale and cross-zone: For inference, combine autoscaling with cross-region or multi-cloud replicas protected by spot-backed “hedges” to absorb volatility; leverage Ray’s actor state and Karpenter/GKE AI features to maintain QoS on budget. <cite id="63d2791e-8">Mixing spot and on-demand replicas across regions/clouds with SpotHedge reduces serving costs while maintaining availability objectives.</cite> <cite id="63d2791e-4">Ray on Karpenter achieved 45% lower inference cost via elastic autoscaling and intelligent scheduling across spot/on-demand capacity.</cite> <cite id="63d2791e-7">GKE’s AI features and label-based scheduling support scalable, cost-aware policies across GPU/TPU classes with minimal operational toil.</cite>
- Multi-objective scheduling: For workflows, co-optimize energy/cost/makespan with policies that respect deadlines and precedence. Hybrid genetic/annealing dispatchers and EMCS-style evolutionary rules help when ML/physics jobs share the same cluster with inference microservices. <cite id="d8a0451d-0">EMCS reduces combined execution cost and makespan under heterogeneous, budget-constrained conditions, improving end-to-end workflow cost.</cite> <cite id="d8a0451d-7">Time-varying carbon-aware scheduling with precedence knowledge yields better joint cost/emission reductions than resource-only heuristics.</cite>

9) Trade-offs and Risks
- Tight cost profiles risk preemption-induced downtime; workflows with non-idempotent operators need robust checkpointing and stateful schedulers. <cite id="aaa8601f-0">Interruption prediction plus dynamic migration helps maintain availability without over-reserving capacity in spot-heavy deployments.</cite>
- Over-reliance on spot across multi-cloud can lead to cross-availability zone failures and billing complexity unless hedged by on-demand replicas and region-aware policies. <cite id="63d2791e-8">SkyServe’s mixed spot/on-demand deployment across regions and clouds provides redundancy and cost resilience against single-cloud spot volatility.</cite>
- Heterogeneity can fragment the control plane; unify with a single scheduler/runtime like Ray across nodes to avoid manual partitioning and cartographer syndrome. <cite id="63d2791e-1">Ray’s dynamic GPU task scheduling avoids static partitioning and reduces manual toil for heterogeneous clusters.</cite> <cite id="63d2791e-3">Uber’s Ray-on-Kubernetes migration improved transparency into GPU heterogeneity and reduced scheduling friction for ML engineers.</cite>

10) Summary: What Works (and Where)
- Cost-optimized AI workflow scheduling is enabled by a few orthogonal levers: (1) heterogeneous-aware placement and autoscaling across spot/on-demand/TPUs; (2) interruption-aware, prediction-driven placement and migration; (3) multi-objective scheduling that unifies cost, energy, and makespan under DAG precedence; and (4) cross-cloud serving with spot-hedged replicas for inference. <cite id="63d2791e-7">Label-based scheduling and resource classes across CPU/GPU/TPU backends support fine-grained cost placement and scaling for AI DAGs.</cite> <cite id="aaa8601f-0">AI-driven spot management predicts interruptions and migrates workloads to retain SLAs at lower cost.</cite> <cite id="d8a0451d-0">Energy/makespan-cost-aware evolutionary dispatchers improve end-to-end workflow budgets.</cite> <cite id="63d2791e-4">Kubernetes autoscalers with Ray achieve up to 45% inference cost reductions via spot-backed elasticity.</cite> <cite id="d8a0451d-8">Makespan/energy-aware scheduling demonstrates large simulated cost and energy reductions, validating precedence-aware multi-objective policies.</cite>

Actionable playbook:
- Instrument and forecast: Build predictors on SpotLake-like data for spot availability and interruption risk; feed them into a Ray/Kubernetes scheduler with cost and carbon objectives. <cite id="aaa8601f-1">SpotLake accelerates development of spot-aware predictors to improve utilization and reduce volatility.</cite> <cite id="d8a0451d-7">Carbon-aware policies benefit from time-varying profiles and precedence knowledge to cut cost/emissions.</cite>
- Map stages → shapes → guarantees: Assign each workflow node the smallest feasible accelerator class; guarantee only critical edges with premium/预留; autoscale inference replicas using mixed spot/on-demand and cross-region hedges. <cite id="63d2791e-2">Netflix’s heterogeneous Ray cluster demonstrates mapping workloads to adequate GPUs and stable training via scheduler and data stack choices.</cite> <cite id="63d2791e-4">Ray + Karpenter reduces serving cost while maintaining QoS through autoscaling on mixed capacity.</cite> <cite id="63d2791e-8">SpotHedge enables spot/on-demand replica mixing across regions/clouds to absorb failures and price volatility.</cite>
- Adopt multi-objective dispatchers: For multi-project clusters, use evolutionary or deadline-aware policies that minimize cost and energy subject to SLAs; checkpoint and warm-start to tolerate preemptions. <cite id="d8a0451d-0">EMCS reduces both cost and makespan under budget constraints by evolving task-to-resource mappings.</cite> <cite id="d8a0451d-5">Deadline-aware energy optimization reduces delay and energy, tightening cost envelopes during peak hours.</cite>
- Operationalize resilience: Keep 1–2 on-demand “fence posts” per node class for failback; use Ray actors and KubeRay to maintain state locality; route traffic to closest spot-backed replica. <cite id="63d2791e-6">KubeRay enables scalable Ray scheduling and actor locality on heterogeneous clusters, supporting cost-resilient stateful AI workloads.</cite> <cite id="63d2791e-7">GKE AI features improve availability and scheduling locality for CPU/GPU/TPU jobs with minimal toil.</cite>

fully_underspecified.text: Summarize approaches to workflow scheduling for AI workloads.
fully_underspecified.answer:
Below is a structured overview of approaches to workflow scheduling for AI workloads, drawing on recent surveys, systems, and algorithmic studies.

1) Problem framing and taxonomy
- Workflow scheduling for AI spans heterogeneous, multi-stage DAGs (training/inference pipeline stages, feature joins, model ensembles) whose tasks differ in compute/accelerator needs, IO, and inter-task communication, and often run under cost/slateliness constraints such as spot-capacity availability and reliability SLAs. <cite id="f930690f-0">Workflow scheduling research is commonly organized by workflow formalism, allocation policies, and problem domains, covering DAG structures, heterogeneous resources, and constraints like preemption, replication, and failure handling</cite>. <cite id="f930690f-5">Surveys of scientific workflow scheduling under cloud assumptions describe precedence-constrained DAGs on heterogeneous compute, with scheduling decisions spanning resource allocation, preemption/restart, and reliability/replication</cite>. <cite id="f930690f-3">GPU datacenter surveys for deep learning emphasize multi-stage training/inference workflows, heterogeneous accelerators and resource managers, and end-to-end schedulers that integrate job packing, GPU sharing, and topology-aware placement</cite>.
- Complexity and objective trade-offs are central. <cite id="f930690f-2">Formulating DAG scheduling as a nonlinear integer program reveals NP-completeness, motivating heuristics and metaheuristics and guiding algorithmic design choices</cite>. <cite id="a942d4a3-0">In multi-tenant GPU clusters, schedulers hinge on per-GPU resource partitioning and job sharing mechanisms to reduce queuing and improve throughput</cite>.

2) Algorithmic patterns for DAG AI workflows
- Graph-based (topological) strategies and critical-path scheduling:
  • Scheduling must honor DAG precedences and critical paths (longest path determines makespan lower bounds). <cite id="8b1ac58f-2">Critical-path-based iterative heuristics allocate tasks to resources while respecting precedences to minimize makespan in utility/cloud workflows</cite>. <cite id="8b1ac58f-3">Communication-aware placement explicitly models task-to-task bandwidth/latency and resource definitions, preventing remote-heavy mappings that inflate runtime over compute-only bounds</cite>.
  • Resource-aware clustering partitions large machines to reduce contention and improve load balance. <cite id="8b1ac58f-1">Resource-Aware Clustering (RAC) groups DAG tasks onto heterogeneous resources, forming clusters to improve scheduling efficiency</cite>. <cite id="71f89654-5">Taxonomies of DL scheduling emphasize resource allocation policies (exclusive vs shareable GPUs), per-job sizing, and datacenter-level topology/communication cost modeling</cite>.
- List-scheduling and metaheuristics with search:
  • Heuristic priority rules (e.g., SPT, LPT) and iterative improvement dominate online schedulers; RL can learn state-action policies over DAG states. <cite id="8b1ac58f-0">Reinforcement learning-based schedulers learn mapping of DAG tasks to heterogeneous resources under constraints</cite>. <cite id="f930690f-1">AI-augmented scheduling can combine tree-based search with deep neural models to guide placement and ordering decisions for mobile edge workflows</cite>. <cite id="f930690f-4">Task-duplication-based learning builds on state-of-the-art heuristics to harden against stragglers and interruptions in heterogeneous DAG scheduling</cite>.
- Preemption, restart, and rollback:
  • DAG workflows tolerate preemption and failover via task replication or check pointing. <cite id="f930690f-5">Workflow scheduling algorithms consider preemptive policies, replication for reliability, and restart semantics under cloud failures</cite>. <cite id="f930690f-2">DAG scheduling hardness motivates metaheuristics that incorporate preemption, migration, and restart costs in objective functions</cite>. <cite id="a942d4a3-8">Preemptive and exclusive GPU strategies are common in DL cluster schedulers; preemptive designs raise utilization but risk stragglers and fairness concerns</cite>.

3) Specialized settings: heterogeneous accelerators, GPU clusters, and the cloud
- GPU/TPU heterogeneity and multi-tenant sharing:
  • Job schedulers mediate exclusive vs shareable GPU assignment, kernel/topology-aware mapping, and cross-partition interference. <cite id="a942d4a3-0">Wise* studies DL job scheduling with GPU sharing to reduce queuing; it proposes scheduling policies that calibrate exclusive and shared time slices per job</cite>. <cite id="a942d4a3-8">Empirically, preemptive policies reduce completion times but can harm fairness; system designs adopt job-class strategies and interference-aware partitioning</cite>. <cite id="71f89654-3">Production multi-tenant GPU clusters (e.g., Microsoft Azure’s design) manage placement, interference, and failures to meet SLAs for DL training</cite>.
- Spot/on-demand and cross-region/cloud elasticity:
  • Spot-capacity-aware schedulers trade cost and reliability using bidding, checkpoints, and migration. <cite id="a942d4a3-2">Cloud vendor guidance shows how to train DL with GPUs on spot instances and minimize training loss on eviction via incremental checkpoints, interruption handling, and warm-restart strategies</cite>. <cite id="a942d4a3-3">DeepSpotCloud uses cross-region GPU spot instances with fault-tolerant task migration to run DL cost-effectively under evictions</cite>. <cite id="a942d4a3-4">Task migration and compatibility checks are central to making spot-based execution reliable for deep learning workflows</cite>. <cite id="71f89654-0">SpotDAG applies reinforcement learning to allocate DAG tasks over heterogeneous clusters mixing spot and on-demand resources, optimizing makespan/reliability under cost</cite>.
- Fine-grained resource pools (MIGs/cores) and energy:
  • Multi-instance GPU (MIG) schedulers partition a GPU into isolated tenants to slice throughput, reduce interference, and improve energy efficiency. <cite id="71f89654-7">Dynamic repartitioning across MIGs addresses multi-objective scheduling (latency, throughput, energy) on heterogeneous machines</cite>. <cite id="a942d4a3-6">Dual-agent deep RL has been explored for GPU job scheduling in public clusters to manage shared distributed DL tasks and improve user experience</cite>.

4) Edge and mobile AI: constrained networks, preemption, and AI-augmented control
- Edge deployments impose bandwidth caps, preemption, and latency budgets across device-cloud pipelines. <cite id="f930690f-1">AI-augmented workflow scheduling at the mobile edge combines tree-based search with deep neural networks to pick actions (placement/ordering/partitioning) that respect deadlines and heterogeneity</cite>. <cite id="71f89654-8">Deadline-based scheduling with preemption on heterogeneous edge GPUs targets real-time execution and resource isolation across devices</cite>.
- Cross-cutting communication-awareness remains critical even under edge constraints. <cite id="8b1ac58f-3">Communication-aware placement models bandwidth/latency between devices, accelerators, and backends to avoid remote memory and synchronization bottlenecks in pipeline stages</cite>.

5) Learning-based schedulers tailored to AI DAGs
- From heuristic-guided to end-to-end RL:
  • Task-duplication and gap-aware learning harden schedules against stragglers and spot evictions. <cite id="8b1ac58f-4">A task-duplication learning algorithm combines SPT/LPT baselines with neural predictors to reduce critical gaps in heterogeneous DAG scheduling</cite>. <cite id="a942d4a3-6">Dual-agent RL uses competing planners to jointly optimize cluster-wide DL job scheduling under preemption and competition</cite>.
  • General-purpose RL scheduling learns policies over state spaces that encode DAG topology, resource capacities, and constraints. <cite id="71f89654-0">SpotDAG treats heterogeneous spot/on-demand allocation as an RL problem, learning mappings that trade cost vs reliability</cite>. <cite id="8b1ac58f-0">Neural policy schedulers use direct decision-making over resource configurations to place tasks while honoring precedences</cite>. <cite id="f930690f-8">Edge RL schedulers synthesize search and learned value functions to meet deadlines under dynamic wireless conditions</cite>.
- Reported quantitative gains:
  • For preemptive DL schedulers on multi-tenant GPU clusters, policy designs like SJF-BSBF reduce average job completion time by 27–33% over prior preemptive methods, indicating the benefit of structured scheduling policies that exploit slack stealing and backfilling. <cite id="71f89654-6">SJF-BSBF reduces average job completion time by 27–33% compared with state-of-the-art preemptive DL schedulers</cite>.
  • Surveys summarize broader headroom (e.g., combining topology-aware GPU placement with bin-packing and preemption) but note sensitivity to job sizes, communication patterns, and cluster interference. <cite id="f930690f-3">Surveys catalog how DL schedulers integrate job sizing, GPU sharing, and topology-aware placement to improve utilization and latency</cite>.

6) Hardness, hybrids, and practical hybrids
- Theoretical hardness underpins algorithm selection:
  • Without precedence, heterogeneity, and communication costs, bin-packing-like problems are NP-hard; with precedences and critical paths, problems remain NP-complete, motivating greedy, decomposition, and RL heuristics. <cite id="f930690f-2">DAG scheduling is NP-complete even without precedence, via reductions to nonlinear integer programming; heuristic/metaheuristic designs are standard</cite>. <cite id="8b1ac58f-2">Critical-path-based iterated heuristics operationalize precedence constraints and path-length reduction</cite>.
- Modern schedulers are hybrid:
  • Mix rule-based dispatch (e.g., SPT/LPT, bin-packing for GPU memory), topology-aware placement, checkpointed preemption, and learning-based controllers. <cite id="a942d4a3-8">Wise* and practical DL schedulers combine preemptive partitioning with backfilling and interference estimation</cite>. <cite id="a942d4a3-0">Communication-aware policies refine job sharing bounds and exclusive time slabs to limit cross-job interference</cite>. <cite id="8b1ac58f-4">Task duplication as a learned policy provides robustness at extra cost and needs to be tuned for reliability vs efficiency</cite>.

7) Metrics, SLAs, and deployment considerations
- Primary metrics: makespan for batch jobs, throughput for pipelines, job slowdown and queue length under preemption, cost/reliability (mean evictions tolerated, restart latency), energy per unit work, and fairness between DL tenants. <cite id="f930690f-0">Workflow scheduling evaluations weigh makespan, resource utilization, and reliability under failures and preemption</cite>. <cite id="71f67b3a502c227e801e9d5d179042f7">Spot-capacity schedulers emphasize cost and reliability SLA adherence (e.g., percent of jobs completed on spot vs on-demand) alongside latency</cite>. <cite id="71f89654-7">Energy-aware DL scheduling uses dynamic repartitioning to trade utilization/interference against power</cite>.
- Typical deployment trade-offs surface in production:
  • Exclusive assignments improve isolation and predictability but lower aggregate utilization; shareable assignment improves efficiency but increases variance and communication cost. <cite id="a942d4a3-8">Empirical DL cluster studies show exclusive strategies raise predictability while preemptive approaches boost utilization but cause tail latency and fairness issues</cite>.
  • Spot-based clouds cut cost but demand robustness: incremental checkpoints, warm starts, cross-zone redundancy, and RL-driven bidding can recover SLAs on evictions. <cite id="a942d4a3-2">Spot training guidance emphasizes minimizing loss on interruptions via frequent snapshots and staged rollback</cite>. <cite id="a942d4a3-3">Cross-region spot migration policies reduce unavailability windows and balance cost/latency</cite>.
  • Edge deployments prioritize deadline misses and network preemption; AI-augmented controllers help navigate uncertain radio conditions and heterogeneous devices. <cite id="f930690f-1">Deep neural guidance combined with finite tree search schedules tasks to meet edge deadlines under bandwidth variability</cite>. <cite id="8b1ac58f-8">Deadline-based GPU scheduling on edge devices with preemptive tasks reduces tail latency under limited bandwidth and GPU availability</cite>.

8) Practical baselines and open challenges
- What works in practice:
  • Combine resource-aware clustering and critical-path greedy dispatch; prefer topology-aware GPU placement; enable preemptive backfill for multi-tenant DL; implement communication-aware anti-placement; use RL or learned heuristics to hedge stragglers and spot evictions; partition GPUs via MIGs for tenant isolation and energy control. <cite id="8b1ac58f-1">Resource-aware clustering improves efficiency on heterogeneous machines</cite>. <cite id="71f89654-6">Structured policies (SJF-BSBF) can outperform standard preemptive baselines</cite>. <cite id="a942d4a3-3">Cross-region spot strategies with migration and checkpoints provide reliable DL execution at lower cost</cite>. <cite id="71f89654-7">MIG dynamic scheduling trades interference for energy/utilization via fine-grained partitioning</cite>.
- Open problems and gaps:
  • Robust online control under co-located communication spikes and cross-node failures; unified scheduling across CPU/GPU/TPU with shared memory/IO constraints; principled fairness in shareable GPU pools; general-purpose schedulers that maintain performance across inference and training mixes; interpretable RL with safety guarantees. <cite id="8b1ac58f-3">Accounting for inter-task communication is necessary to avoid hidden bottlenecks</cite>. <cite id="a942d4a3-8">Preemptive strategies require careful calibration to avoid starvation and maintain system fairness</cite>. <cite id="f930690f-0">Surveys emphasize gaps in domain-specific formalisms, allocation, and replication policies for heterogeneous AI workflows</cite>.
- Benchmarks and evaluation:
  • Recent benchmarks include synthetic DAGs tuned to DL (layers/parameters, memory footprints), microbenchmarks of checkpoint/restore latency, and large cluster traces; surveys summarize evaluation across makespan, throughput, and reliability. <cite id="f930690f-3">GPU DL scheduling surveys consolidate evaluations for packing, sharing, and topology-aware placement in realistic datacenter settings</cite>. <cite id="71f89654-6">Empirical comparisons report percent-wise reductions in completion time from policy innovations</cite>.

Summary
Approaches to AI workflow scheduling coalesce into three layers: (i) core graph algorithms and heuristics that respect precedence and critical paths, with or without communication-aware placement; (ii) cloud/cluster mechanisms for heterogeneity, multi-tenancy, and elasticity (exclusivity vs sharing, spot-on-demand selection, GPU partitioning); and (iii) learning-based controllers that hedge against noise, stragglers, and evictions using RL or neural guidance. <cite id="f930690f-0">Taxonomies from workflow scheduling</cite> and <cite id="f930690f-3">DL GPU datacenter surveys</cite> provide consistent foundations. <cite id="8b1ac58f-2">Critical-path heuristics</cite>, <cite id="8b1ac58f-3">communication-aware placement</cite>, <cite id="8b1ac58f-1">resource-aware clustering</cite>, and <cite id="71f89654-6">policy-based preemptive scheduling</cite> offer strong, practical baselines. <cite id="a942d4a3-2">Spot-capacity management</cite>, <cite id="a942d4a3-3">migration and cross-region redundancy</cite>, and <cite id="71f89654-7">MIG-level partitioning</cite> address cost, reliability, and energy at scale, while <cite id="8b1ac58f-0">RL-based DAG schedulers</cite> and <cite id="a942d4a3-8">AI-augmented controllers</cite> help optimize under uncertainty and dynamic interference. The field’s main tension is between efficiency and robustness; robust designs often accept lower aggregate utilization, but modern schedulers shrink this gap by combining topology-awareness, preemption-friendly policies, and learning-based foresight. <cite id="a942d4a3-8">Empirical DL cluster studies</cite> and <cite id="71f89654-6">controlled ablations</cite> show concrete winnowing—e.g., multi-tenant DL completions improved by 27–33% from structural policy refinements—and the trend is toward unified schedulers that see models, accelerators, and networks as coupled resources. <cite id="f930690f-3">Surveys</cite> anticipate expanding taxonomies that integrate accelerators, communication, and learning into a single optimization view.
