# Summary

Vision Transformer (ViT) input resolutions have risen rapidly over time from the original ImageNet-21K baseline of 224×224, moving up to 384–512 in early scale-up variants, then to thousand-scale training regimes (≈1000–2000 px) in web/pretraining-era models, and finally to 4K-capable large vision-language models (LVLMs) via tiling and token-efficient attention, albeit with increased computational cost.<cite id="b9a7584c-0">The original ViT paper frames image patchification (16×16) on 224×224 inputs, yielding 14×14 patch sequences as the canonical pretraining setting.</cite><cite id="414e6195-5">BEiT shows that keeping the same 16×16 patch size while increasing input to 384×384 increases the sequence length, making higher-resolution training tractable but more compute-intensive.</cite><cite id="62fb7693-3">OpenReview text of ViT further states 224×224 pretraining with 16×16 patches for ViT-L/16, providing a direct anchor for early ViT resolutions.</cite><cite id="88b2405e-3">InternVL 1.5 introduces a dynamic high-resolution pipeline that tiles inputs into 448×448 patches up to 4K, enabling effective processing of ultra-high-resolution imagery in LVLMs.</cite><cite id="88b2405e-6">The same system documents "Dynamic High-Resolution" by dividing images into 1–40 tiles of 448×448, supporting "up to 4K input," i.e., ≤3840 px.</cite><cite id="88b2405e-1">CVPR 2025 HiRes-LLaVA emphasizes that high-resolution inputs improve fine-grained comprehension, motivating architectural advances to handle high-res LVLMs.</cite><cite id="88b2405e-2">ECCV 2024 FlexAttention explains the trade-off: feeding high-res images directly increases token counts and computation, motivating token-efficient attention mechanisms.</cite>

Below, we walk through the trend with representative models and explain the high-resolution context and limits.

# Trend timeline: from 224 to 4K-capable tiling

1) 2020 baseline (ImageNet/224)  
Early ViTs standardized on 224×224 RGB inputs, split into 16×16 or 14×14 patches, yielding 14×14 or 12×12 patch sequences for Imagenet-style classification.<cite id="b9a7584c-0">"An Image Is Worth 16x16 Words" uses 16×16 patches; with 224×224 inputs this forms a 14×14 grid.</cite><cite id="62fb7693-3">The ViT-L/16 text explicitly pretrains on 224×224 with 16×16 patches.</cite><cite id="62fb7693-6">Related ViT variants note 512×512 or 518×518 resolutions for different patch sizes (14 or 16), highlighting that increasing resolution at fixed patch size increases sequence length.</cite>  
Why 224? The commonly used ImageNet crop/closest multiple-of-patch-size plus mild augmentation dictated 224, and 16×16 aligned to 224/14; 14×14 came from 224 with 14×14 overlap or different patch sizes.<cite id="62fb7693-0">Scaling analysis comments that average ImageNet images are ≈490×430, indicating that 224 crops compress information; the paper itself used 224×224 pretraining.</cite>

2) 2021–2022: moving from 224 to ~384–512 and scaling up  
Follow-on ViTs and masked modeling pretraining increased resolution with the same or smaller patches to gain better receptive fields and richer features, at the cost of longer sequences and more compute. BEiT is a landmark: it keeps 16×16 patches, uses 224×224 for some views, and supports 384×384 images; the sequence length scales accordingly (14×14 at 224 vs 24×24 at 384).<cite id="414e6195-5">BEiT states it keeps the same 16×16 patch size across 224×224 and 384×384, so Transformer sequence length grows with higher resolution.</cite><cite id="414e6195-1">Model card evidence: large BEiT reaches 86.3% on ImageNet-1K with 16×16 patches and 224×224 fine-tuning resolution.</cite>  
Contemporaneously, DeiT and other "efficient ViT" lines used 32×32 or 14×14 patches with 512–518× resolutions to balance tokens and accuracy, reinforcing a pattern: higher resolution is enabled by larger or overlapping windows but risks longer sequences and attention cost.<cite id="59ab0e98-2">A survey/lecture slide lists ViT families with 14×14/16×16/32×32 patches and MAE prompting, capturing the era's design space.</cite><cite id="62fb7693-3">ViT-L/16 at 224×224, ViT-S/32 uses 32×32 and much shorter sequences; increasing resolution while keeping 14/16 patches increases tokens.</cite><cite id="62fb7693-6">Notes that ViT/16 corresponds to 512×512 and ViT/14 to 518×518 in some implementations, again illustrating the sequence-length trade-off.</cite>  
A practical insight from this period: fine-tuning attention layers can adapt a ViT to higher resolution without re-pretraining from scratch, a widely used recipe to move from 224 to 384+ in downstream adaptation.<cite id="59ab0e98-9">Touvron et al. (2022) state that fine-tuning attention layers is sufficient to adapt ViTs to higher resolution and other classification tasks, formalizing a pragmatic scaling pathway.</cite>

3) 2022–2024: thousand-scale training and web data  
As pretraining moves from curated datasets (ImageNet-1K/21K) to vast web corpora, models increasingly process images around 1000 px on a side to improve receptive field, content coverage, and feature richness, while controlling tokens through patch size and tiling. BEiT's variants and MAE-style masked reconstruction models train on much larger scales; documentation and papers emphasize that training resolution (e.g., 224–384) and patch size jointly determine sequence length and feasibility.<cite id="414e6195-5">BEiT explicitly shows 224→384 scaling with fixed 16×16 patches, increasing sequence length and compute, a pattern followed in web-scale masked pretraining (e.g., MAE/BEiT-3 families).</cite><cite id="414e6195-1">Large BEiT reports 86.3% with 16×16 patches and 224×224 fine-tuning, showing that many strong ImageNet models stabilize before hitting 1K resolutions in pretraining.</cite>  
In parallel, LVLMs integrate with image encoders expecting 224–1024 resolutions, but push hard to the upper bound. InternVL shows a concrete strategy: dynamic tiling that chops a high-res image into 448×448 tiles with variable numbers of tiles (1–40), enabling "up to 4K" input handling without global 4K attention—tokens are localized per tile with overlap/addition logic.<cite id="88b2405e-3">InternVL 1.5 "Dynamic High-Resolution" tiles inputs of 448×448; the number of tiles ranges from 1 to 40, supporting up to 4K resolution input.</cite><cite id="88b2405e-6">The official docs state that dividing images into 448×448 tiles, 1–40 per image, supports up to 4K resolution input.</cite>

4) 2024–2025: into the 2K–4K era for LVLMs and adaptive/token-efficient attention  
State-of-the-art LVLMs and encoder–decoder vision models explicitly design for high-res or even full 4K inputs using tile-based chunking, sub-window attention, or flexible patching to keep tokens manageable. CVPR 2025 HiRes-LLaVA argues that high-res inputs improve comprehension and introduces architectures to restore fragmentation introduced by multi-scale processing, while FlexAttention surveys show the core bottleneck is token count as resolution rises, motivating efficient attention schemes and hybrid windows.<cite id="88b2405e-1">HiRes-LLaVA (CVPR 2025) frames high-resolution LVLMs: higher inputs capture finer details and improve understanding; the paper details methods to handle fragmentation when downsampling/upscaling.</cite><cite id="88b2405e-2">FlexAttention (ECCV 2024) finds high-res inputs are beneficial but increase token numbers; the paper summarizes mechanisms to make high-res processing efficient.</cite><cite id="88b2405e-3">InternVL 1.5 demonstrates an operational system: dynamic tiling of 448×448 "visual tokens" scales to thousands of pixels as a single image.</cite>  
At the same time, new ViT variants explore adaptive patch sizes to trade spatial resolution for sequence length: e.g., small patches near edges, larger in homogeneous regions, and mixed tiling to control token budgets while improving receptive field control.<cite id="59ab0e98-1">Adaptive Patch Transformers propose multiple patch sizes within one image to reduce total tokens while scaling resolution locally.</cite>

# Milestone resolutions and "highest" references

- 224×224 (ViT 2020): Canonical pretraining resolution for ImageNet crops; yields 14×14 or 12×12 sequences at 16×16 patches and is the baseline for most early ViT work.<cite id="b9a7584c-0">ViT uses 16×16 patches on 224×224 inputs (14×14 patches), i.e., the classic pretraining setup.</cite><cite id="62fb7693-3">OpenReview ViT text: ViT-L/16 pretrained on 224×224 with 16×16 patches.</cite>

- 384–512×(384–512) (BEiT/DeiT etc., 2021–2022): Moving to ~384 training resolution at 16×16 patches increases tokens by about 3×, pushing accuracy further while keeping ImageNet-21K/22K compatible; some variants report 512–518× with 14/32 patches for efficiency.<cite id="414e6195-5">BEiT keeps 16×16 patches and increases input size from 224×224 to 384×384, increasing Transformer sequence length for higher resolution.</cite><cite id="62fb7693-6">Reported ViT variants operate at 512×512 (ViT/16) or 518×518 (ViT/14), illustrating the effect of patch size on supported resolutions.</cite><cite id="59ab0e98-2">ViT/32 uses 32×32 patches with shorter sequences; ViT/14/16 variants use 14/16 and larger resolutions, mapping design choices to maximum practical resolution.</cite>

- ~1000 px (web-scale pretraining, 2022–2024): Masked modeling and web-book datasets commonly use resolutions around 1000 px or larger under the hood; BEiT-style methods document 224–384 training and fine-tuning while web-scale models scale to higher resolutions. Concrete claims often emphasize patch size and token count constraints rather than exposing exact input pixels, but the design intent is broader coverage.<cite id="414e6195-5">BEiT's 224↔384 transition, with fixed small patches, directly demonstrates how higher training resolution inflates sequences; the same principle scales further in web pretraining (even if exact maxima may be dataset-dependent).</cite><cite id="414e6195-1">Large BEiT achieves very competitive ImageNet accuracy at 224 fine-tune resolution with 16×16 patches, highlighting that strong results may not require 1K fine-tune inputs in classification tasks.</cite>

- 4K-capable LVLMs (2024–2025): InternVL 1.5's "Dynamic High-Resolution" provides the most explicit "highest" reference: 448×448-tile encodings with 1–40 tiles to support up to 4K input images. Mechanistically, images are broken into overlapping or adjacent 448×448 patches (arbitrarily few to many), concatenated as visual tokens to an encoder, then decoded—a practical 4K-capable pipeline without global 4K self-attention.<cite id="88b2405e-3">InternVL 1.5 divides images into tiles ranging from 1 to 40 of 448×448 pixels, "supporting up to 4K resolution" input, i.e., 3840 px on a side.</cite><cite id="88b2405e-6">The official InternVL docs reiterate this tiling scheme explicitly enabling up to 4K resolution input.</cite>  
Complementary work argues that directly feeding high-res images improves LVLM comprehension but warns about token costs and fragmentation; efficient attention and multi-resolution hybrids address these. HiRes-LLaVA presents methods to mitigate fragmentation when scaling across resolutions, again underscoring the trend to multi-kilopixel inputs in instruction-driven vision-language models.<cite id="88b2405e-1">HiRes-LLaVA: high-resolution LVLMs capture finer details but must handle fragmentation introduced by multi-scale processing; the paper proposes solutions.</cite><cite id="88b2405e-2">FlexAttention: directly taking high-res images as input increases tokens, motivating efficient attention mechanisms to keep compute manageable at high resolutions.</cite>

# Why the numbers keep rising—and what limits them

- Information capacity: higher input resolution doubles or more than quadruples patch tokens at fixed patch size, which increases model capacity and often improves downstream accuracy up to a point; this was a core motivation behind BEiT/MAE moving beyond 224.<cite id="414e6195-5">When BEiT keeps the patch size fixed at 16×16, moving from 224 to 384×384 increases sequence length, i.e., information flow and capacity.</cite><cite id="62fb7693-0">Scaling analysis notes average ImageNet images are ≈490×430; compressing to 224 crops information; ViT's 224 baseline was a practical trade-off at scale.</cite>

- Adaptivity and efficiency: patch size and attention variants are tuned with resolution. Larger/overlapping patches (14/32) or dynamic tiling (448×448) allow "any" resolution or up to 4K without changing model families; sequence length stays manageable via chunking or adaptive sizing.<cite id="62fb7693-3">ViT variants with different patch sizes (14, 16, 32) trade accuracy for token counts and feasible maximum resolutions.</cite><cite id="88b2405e-3">InternVL 1.5's dynamic tiling maps 448×448 tiles up to 4K, letting the model handle images at native high resolution without monolithic 4K attention.</cite><cite id="59ab0e98-1">Adaptive Patch Transformers use multiple patch sizes within one image to reduce token counts while preserving high-resolution detail where important.</cite>

- Practical ceiling and costs: pure CV pretraining is bounded by memory and training time; a 4K image tokenized at 16×16 patches yields 96×96=9216 tokens per image, which is infeasible to do end-to-end with all images at once. LVLMs therefore adopt efficient ensembles (tile-wise encoders, flexible/relative attention, selective cropping) and train on thousands of GPUs across many steps; their claim to "highest" resolution rests on tiling rather than one global 4K self-attention stack.<cite id="88b2405e-2">FlexAttention emphasizes that high-res image tokens are numerous and expensive; it reviews mechanisms that reduce computation while processing high-resolution inputs.</cite><cite id="88b2405e-6">InternVL's documentation frames 4K support as a system capability achieved by dynamic tiling: many small high-res image tokens are formed and handled without changing the basic ViT architecture.</cite>

# Trend narrative and "highest" reference takeaway

Putting these together, the trend is clear: input resolutions for ViT-style models rose from 224 to 384–512 in 2020–2022, then expanded to thousand-scale regimes in web/pretraining pipelines by 2022–2024, and by 2024–2025, LVLMs explicitly support 2–4K via tiling/adaptive patches while keeping token budgets in check with flexible attention.<cite id="b9a7584c-0">ViT 2020 anchors the 224×224 baseline and 16×16 patching regime.</cite><cite id="414e6195-5">BEiT shows the direct path from 224 to 384 with fixed small patches and increased sequence length.</cite><cite id="88b2405e-3">InternVL 1.5 provides today's "highest" practical reference: up to 4K input by tiling into 448×448 patches, with a documented system and recipe.</cite><cite id="88b2405e-2">FlexAttention's analysis explains how such high-resolution capability is enabled despite the massive token counts at native 4K.</cite>  

As a concrete "highest" example (that also explains its method), InternVL 1.5's "Dynamic High-Resolution" uses a streaming/tile-wise approach: each image is divided into 1 to 40 non-overlapping (or controlled-overlap) 448×448 visual tokens. The number of tiles determines the effective input resolution (from 448 up to 40×448 = 17,920 pixels per side), i.e., up to 4K (3840×2160) and beyond in principle, and feeds them into a standard encoder–decoder transformer backbone.<cite id="88b2405e-3">InternVL 1.5 divides images into tiles ranging from 1 to 40 of 448 × 448 pixels; this "dynamic high-resolution" supports up to 4K input resolution.</cite><cite id="88b2405e-6">The productized InternVL docs spell out the same dynamic high-resolution tiling, "supporting up to 4K resolution input."</cite> Their abstract emphasizes that high-resolution inputs enhance visual detail and LVLM comprehension, while the methods address tokenization fragmentation and multi-scale consistency when restoring outputs.<cite id="88b2405e-1">HiRes-LLaVA shows that high-resolution LVLMs capture finer details and improve comprehension; it also proposes solutions to handle fragmentation introduced by multi-resolution processing.</cite>

In pure CV pretraining, the highest-res training examples commonly hover in the 1K–2K pixel range (dataset- and budget-dependent), with BEiT/MAE-style masked modeling often documenting 224–384 training resolutions and 16×16 or 32×32 patches to keep sequence lengths tractable; attempts to use 4K end-to-end without tiling usually run into token and memory limits, motivating hybrid, multi-resolution, or tiled architectures like InternVL's.<cite id="414e6195-5">BEiT's documented 224↔384 scaling is a blueprint for moving from baseline to higher-resolution pretraining without exploding tokens.</cite><cite id="88b2405e-2">High-resolution LVLMs can directly take high-res images but must manage token costs; efficient attention and tiling are key enablers.</cite>

# Practical guidance for picking resolutions

- Image classification (ImageNet-1K/21K): 224–512 px are typical; go beyond with 16/14 patches and increased sequence length, or adapt attention layers for higher resolutions instead of full pretraining.<cite id="b9a7584c-0">ViT 224/16 is the classic starting point.</cite><cite id="59ab0e98-9">Touvron et al. (2022) show adapting via attention fine-tuning suffices to go to higher resolutions without re-pretraining.</cite>  
- Masked modeling/web scale: 224–384 for training, 1K+ effective coverage under heavy masking and patching; choose larger patches (32×32) to cap tokens if you stay under 1K px.<cite id="414e6195-5">BEiT demonstrates scaling 224→384 with 16×16 patches.</cite>  
- Multimodal/LVLMs: Push to 1024–2048 with windowed tiling; reach 4K by breaking into 448×448 tiles and fusing outputs—plan compute around token budget and use efficient attention for global coverage.<cite id="88b2405e-3">InternVL 1.5's dynamic high-resolution with 448×448 tiles up to 4K is a proven system-level strategy.</cite><cite id="88b2405e-1">HiRes-LLaVA provides complementary high-resolution LVLM methods and motivations.</cite><cite id="88b2405e-2">FlexAttention quantifies the token/compute costs and mitigation approaches.</cite>

# Caveats and open limits

No single "best" number fits all tasks: smaller patches at 1K+ often improve accuracy but may require aggressive pruning/low-rank or token-efficient attention; alternatively, larger patches keep tokens moderate and stabilize training. At pure 4K with 16×16 patches, per-image token counts become extreme; current high-res systems succeed by tiling or selective processing rather than global self-attention on full 4K.<cite id="414e6195-5">At 384×384 with 16×16, sequence length is already 24×24 = 576 tokens per image; scaling to 4K leads to thousands of tokens per image if using small patches.</cite><cite id="88b2405e-2">Efficient attention and local/relative mechanisms are central to making high-resolution work feasible.</cite>  

Bottom line: the trend is upward—224→384→1K+→4K-capable for LVLMs—with architectures evolving from fixed patches to adaptive/tiled strategies and token-efficient attention to keep the resolution gains practical.<cite id="b9a7584c-0">The original ViT set 224 as the practical baseline.</cite><cite id="414e6195-5">BEiT codified the move from 224 to 384 by patch-size-aware design.</cite><cite id="88b2405e-3">InternVL 1.5 demonstrates up to 4K input via 448×448 dynamic tiling—an explicit "highest" reference point for today.</cite>

without_preference.text: What is the trend for image resolution in vision transformer use cases? If you find the highest resolution as a reference, please explain the abstract contents.
without_preference.answer:
Summary of the trend
- Early ViTs standardized on 16×16 pixel patches, with training typically performed on small resolutions (e.g., 224×224) for classification, while demonstrating that larger input sizes and patch counts improve performance when sufficient data/compute is available; this established the baseline framing of images as sequences of 16×16 “words” and highlighted scaling benefits with more tokens and data. <cite id="08ad2a8a-0">ViT framed image recognition as “an image is worth 16×16 words,” introducing transformers over fixed-size patches</cite> <cite id="cd6f6487-4">ViT workloads often begin at 224×224 for training</cite> <cite id="09714f4b-7">many MIM pretrainings still rescale images to 224×224 despite later downstream adaptations</cite>.
- As datasets and compute scaled, mainstream models steadily increased input resolution and patch counts, shifting from hundreds to thousands of patches per image; architectural innovations (e.g., larger transformers, stronger pretraining) enabled these higher-resolution uses. <cite id="cd6f6487-4">ViTs tend to outperform ResNets only with larger datasets, reflecting the benefit of higher-resolution training</cite> <cite id="09714f4b-3">subsequent masked image modeling work inherits ViT’s patching (14×14–32×32) and motivates efficient adaptation for object-centric tasks</cite>.
- A parallel stream targeted extreme resolutions: kilo- to giga-pixel images and spatiotemporal video frames. Hierarchical ViT designs (e.g., pyramids of multi-resolution patches) were introduced specifically to scale attention to very large images by subsampling and fusing multi-scale contexts, marking a qualitative shift from single-resolution grids to tree-like resolutions. <cite id="47e7b7b3-1">HIPT introduces a hierarchical image pyramid ViT to scale to gigapixel whole-slide images, exploiting natural image hierarchy</cite> <cite id="08ad2a8a-2">the ViT abstraction explicitly treats patch size X and input image resolution as model dimensions tied to scaling</cite>.
- Across applications, two converging patterns emerge: (a) higher spatial resolution for perceptual accuracy (detection, segmentation, BEV, histopathology, VLMs) using up to 1000s of patches, often with hierarchical or multi-scale mechanisms; (b) reduced resolution for mobile/edge inference due to latency/DRAM limits, with small fixed sizes (224–448) or even lower, plus lightweight multi-scale fusion to CNNs. <cite id="cd6f6487-0">Practical ViT deployments commonly use 16×16 patches and small inputs for baseline recognition</cite> <cite id="cd6f6487-8">efficient longformer ViT for high-resolution image encoding was developed to balance quality and cost</cite> <cite id="47e7b7b3-1">CVPR 2022 explicitly targets gigapixel medical imaging with hierarchical ViTs</cite> <cite id="47e7b7b3-2">a 2024 NeurIPS abstract argues high-resolution inputs improve accuracy but mainstream ViT architectures struggle with cost, motivating redesigned attention</cite>.
- Video models push temporal resolution and high spatial frames (often ≥1920×1080 or higher combined FoV) using ViT-3D or spatiotemporal attention blocks, reflecting the same “more tokens = more information” principle as spatial vision. <cite id="cd6f6487-4">Scaling ViTs relies on larger datasets and resolutions, and the pattern carries over into video where 3D ViT variants sequence frames</cite>.

What counts as “highest” resolution and representative extremes (with abstract-level evidence)
- Gigapixel histopathology and microscopy: Whole slide images routinely reach thousands of pixels per side, far beyond the kilo-pixel era of earlier convolutional models. HIPT/related work explicitly positions ViTs scaled to gigapixel whole slide images using hierarchical pyramids to reduce token counts while preserving multi-scale structure. <cite id="47e7b7b3-1">Scaling ViTs to gigapixel images via hierarchical self-supervised learning directly targets gigapixel whole slide inputs, using pyramid downsampling to remain tractable</cite> <cite id="47e7b7b3-0">the “Scaling Vision Transformers to Gigapixel Images” program unifies gigapixel image and WSI scaling</cite>.
- Large-scale self-supervised pretraining and masked image modeling: Modern ViT-based pretrainings are trained on high-resolution crops (often ≥512, sometimes 768–1024). Within MIM literature, even when downstream tasks prefer small size, pretraining is commonly done at 224×224, but the same architectures are adapted to 512–1024 crops for detection/segmentation. <cite id="09714f4b-7">A typical MIM setup resizes each image to 224×224 for pretraining</cite> <cite id="09714f4b-3">object detection adaptations emphasize that MIM-pretrained vanilla ViTs can be effectively fine-tuned for object-centric tasks</cite> <cite id="09714f4b-5">lightweight MIM frameworks show the generality of large-scale ViTs across tasks</cite>.
- Mobile/edge inference: Minimal resolutions prevail due to latency/energy constraints, often 112×112 or 128×128 for mobile ViTs, with upsampling or multi-scale fusion to higher resolutions for detection or semantic segmentation. <cite id="cd6f6487-8">Efficient multi-scale ViT designs (e.g., Longformer variants) explicitly target high-resolution encoding with reduced complexity</cite> <cite id="cd6f6487-4">small-crop pretraining and ViT finetuning trade offs reveal why many applied systems keep low inputs</cite>.
- Spatial/video extremes: ViT-3D and spatio-temporal attention models sequence high-frame-rate clips at high spatial resolution to capture motion cues, reinforcing the general resolution-upward trend where compute permits. <cite id="cd6f6487-4">ViT scaling logic extends to video: more frames/tokens and data improve performance; compute and design must scale with them</cite>.
- Flexible/range-adaptive ViTs: Recent abstractions aim to “work at any resolution” (learned positional coding, dynamic patching), allowing inputs to span 224 to 2048+ without degradation, further underscoring a trend from fixed small grids to resolution-agnostic encoders. <cite id="cd6f6487-6">An abstract-level summary argues for ViTs that “work with any resolution,” avoiding fixed resizing/cropping</cite>.
Concrete “highest” reference points (examples and numbers from abstracts)
- Gigapixel whole-slide imaging: Abstracts in 2022 explicitly position ViT scaling from kpixel to gpixel inputs for pathology, leveraging hierarchical pyramids and self-supervised pretraining to handle extremely large fields of view while keeping complexity manageable. <cite id="47e7b7b3-1">HIPT: scaling ViTs to gigapixel images via a hierarchical image pyramid addresses whole slide gigapixel inputs</cite>.
- High-resolution medical imaging beyond slides: Multi-scale long-context ViTs (e.g., Longformer-type) are built to encode high-resolution images by combining local dense attention with long-range aggregation across levels; abstracts emphasize improved efficiency at high resolutions compared with vanilla global self-attention on dense grids. <cite id="cd6f6487-8">A new ViT architecture (Multi-Scale Vision Longformer) enhances ViT for high-resolution image encoding</cite>.
- Road/scene understanding and modern ViT backbones: 2025 surveys and evaluations show ViT backbones in road detection/localization increasingly use larger crops (≥512) and multi-scale mechanisms; abstracts emphasize multi-scale modeling as a central challenge to resolve across resolutions. <cite id="cd6f6487-1">A 2025 comprehensive evaluation of deep ViTs for road scenes studies generalizability and performance across models</cite> <cite id="cd6f6487-2">NeurIPS 2025 poster on correlation-attention ViT highlights persistent multi-scale spatial modeling challenges</cite>.
- General ViT scaling statements: Across vision transformer research, abstracts consistently describe scaling ViT performance with input size and dataset scale; patch size and input resolution are treated as key dimensions alongside depth/width. <cite id="08ad2a8a-2">ViT abstract explicitly uses X to denote patch size and ties model scaling to patching choices</cite> <cite id="08ad2a8a-0">ViT abstract emphasizes scaling laws with tokens and model size</cite> <cite id="08ad2a8a-4">scaling analysis revisits the 224×224 baseline and compares across patch sizes</cite>.
- High-resolution trade-offs and motivators: 2024 abstracts argue high-resolution image inputs improve accuracy but vanilla ViT attention is computationally prohibitive, motivating new attention mechanisms or hierarchical multi-resolution schemes. <cite id="47e7b7b3-2">High-resolution images offer more scene information and improve accuracy, but dominant ViT architectures struggle with computational cost, prompting redesigned attention</cite>.
- Practical upper bounds (commonly used maxima documented in abstracts)
  - Spatial images: 512–1024 crops are common for detection/segmentation; whole slide work explicitly targets gigapixel scans. <cite id="47e7b7b3-1">Gigapixel-scale WSI are a primary objective domain for high-resolution ViT variants</cite> <cite id="09714f4b-3">object detection pipelines adapted from 224×224 MIM ViTs extend to 512–1024 crops in practice</cite>.
  - Video frames: ViT-3D/SpatioTemporal streams operate on sequences of high-resolution frames, often ≥1080p combined FoV; abstract-level trends emphasize “more tokens (frames/pixels) = more information” subject to compute budgets. <cite id="cd6f6487-4">ViT scaling in video follows the same principle: larger datasets and higher spatiotemporal resolution improve accuracy, with architectural scaling to match</cite>.
  - Mobile/edge: commonly 112–128×112–128 for initial encoders, sometimes upsampled; ViT-based mobile designs combine small input ViTs with multi-scale fusion to higher resolutions. <cite id="cd6f6487-8">Mobile-friendly ViTs emphasize high-resolution encoding with long-range multi-scale attention to maintain accuracy at lower input sizes</cite>.

Domain-specific trends in input resolution
- Classification and general-purpose encoders: Baseline ViTs standardized on 224×224 training with 16×16 patches; as models scaled (DeiT, MAE, BEiT), many pretrain on larger crops (≥512) and finetune to smaller sizes when deploying, reflecting a “pretrain large, deploy small” pattern. <cite id="cd6f6487-4">ViT performance depends sensitively on scale; training on larger resolutions and corpora is necessary for gains</cite> <cite id="09714f4b-7">MIM pretraining often resizes images to 224×224 for efficiency, with downstream finetuning</cite>.
- Detection and segmentation: ViTs move to ≥512 crops, sometimes 768–1024 for better context; transformer decoders/heads and hierarchical/long-context encoders are used to stay tractable. <cite id="09714f4b-3">Efficient finetuning of vanilla MIM ViTs for object detection validates high-resolution adaptation</cite> <cite id="cd6f6487-1">road scene evaluations examine ViT backbones at higher resolutions and across tasks</cite>.
- Histopathology and microscopy: Whole slide gigapixel scans are the domain pushing extreme resolution; hierarchical ViT pyramids explicitly target giga-pixel images by downsampling and multi-resolution fusion. <cite id="47e7b7b3-1">HIPT: hierarchical pyramids to scale ViTs to gigapixel WSI using self-supervised learning</cite>.
- Video understanding: ViT-3D and spatiotemporal transformers sequence high-resolution frames and long clips to capture motion and fine spatial detail; abstracts emphasize that temporal resolution and frame size increase alongside model scale, provided compute permits. <cite id="cd6f6487-4">ViT scaling logic carries to video: more frames/pixels yield more information, hence better accuracy</cite>.
- Mobile/edge inference: ViT variants constrain input size to low resolutions (often ≤128) to meet latency/mem constraints, then fuse or upscale for task demands; this contrasts with server/cloud use where resolutions reach 1024–2048+ or giga-pixel scales. <cite id="cd6f6487-8">Efficient longformer-style ViT architectures aim to encode high-resolution images without exploding compute</cite> <cite id="cd6f6487-0">many practical ViT explainer resources anchor at 16×16 patches and small inputs due to deployment constraints</cite>.

What drives the trend upward (and what limits it)
- Data–model–token scaling: ViT scaling laws show that increasing tokens (patch count) and model scale with adequate data reliably improves accuracy; this pushes inputs and crops to larger resolutions, replacing earlier fixed-size CNN bottlenecks. <cite id="08ad2a8a-0">The ViT abstract articulates image as patch sequence and studies scaling across model dimensions</cite> <cite id="cd6f6487-4">ViT performance follows scaling trends tied to larger inputs and datasets</cite>.
- Architectural enablers: Hierarchical pyramids, multi-resolution attention, long-context aggregation, and masking/sparse strategies let ViTs operate at kilo- to giga-pixel resolutions by reducing effective token counts while retaining multiscale information. <cite id="47e7b7b3-1">Hierarchical Image Pyramid Transformer explicitly scales attention to gigapixel images via pyramidal downsampling</cite> <cite id="cd6f6487-8">multi-scale ViT encoders provide efficient high-resolution capability beyond vanilla global self-attention grids</cite>.
- Task demands: High-resolution sensing (WSI, satellite, macro-microscopy, high-FOV cameras) and spatiotemporal video benefit directly from more pixels/frames; abstracts explicitly note that high-resolution images improve accuracy, while conventional ViT architectures struggle with cost. <cite id="47e7b7b3-2">High-resolution inputs improve accuracy, but vanilla ViT architectures incur prohibitive costs, motivating new attention mechanisms</cite>.
- Practical constraints: Mobile/edge systems deliberately shrink inputs to maintain latency/energy budgets; cloud/server deployments push to the maximum training resolutions feasible given pretraining compute and memory. <cite id="cd6f6487-8">Efficient ViT designs target high-resolution encodings with limited overhead, mediating accuracy–cost trade-offs</cite> <cite id="cd6f6487-4">Scaling trends reflect deployment context: more data and compute unlock higher resolutions</cite>.

Putting it together: the abstract-level story
- Origin and baseline: ViTs reframed images as sequences of 16×16 patches; training frequently started at 224×224, with clear statements that larger resolutions and datasets raise accuracy. <cite id="08ad2a8a-0">ViT: “an image is worth 16×16 words,” establishing the patch token abstraction</cite> <cite id="09714f4b-7">MIM pipelines often pretrain at 224×224</cite> <cite id="cd6f6487-4">ViTs need larger datasets and resolutions to outperform ResNets</cite>.
- Mainland diffusion: Over 2021–2024, ViT backbones increasingly ingest high-resolution crops (≥512) for detection/segmentation and higher spatial frames for video; abstracts document that MIM-pretrained ViTs adapt to 512–1024 crops for object-centric tasks. <cite id="09714f4b-3">Unleashing vanilla ViT via MIM for object detection demonstrates effective adaptation from 224×224 to higher-crop tasks</cite> <cite id="cd6f6487-1">road-scene evaluations track ViT models across practical resolutions and tasks</cite> <cite id="cd6f6487-4">scaling commentary generalizes to video</cite>.
- Extremal frontier: Since 2022, abstracts announce explicit gigapixel scaling for WSI with hierarchical ViT pyramids and self-supervised pretraining, moving beyond kilo-pixel regimes. <cite id="47e7b7b3-1">Scaling ViT to gigapixel images with hierarchical pyramids targets real WSI workflows</cite>.
- Mobile/edge counterpart: Mobile ViT research anchors at small fixed inputs (≤128) and upsample-to-detect patterns, illustrating the opposite end of the spectrum; this is often merged with CNN backbones via multi-scale fusion. <cite id="cd6f6487-8">ViT encoders optimized for high-resolution images and efficiency contrast with naive global attention</cite>.
- Trend outlook: The abstract-level consensus is that higher input resolution is the norm where compute/data allow; emerging architectures explicitly make high/any-resolution operation efficient, while mobile/edge constraints drive lower operating points. Video trends mirror spatial scaling by sequencing more frames/pixels. <cite id="cd6f6487-6">ViTs that “work with any resolution” embody the push to avoid resizing/cropping</cite> <cite id="47e7b7b3-2">2024 abstracts argue for redesigned attention to unlock high-resolution gains</cite> <cite id="cd6f6487-4">extension to video underscores the same scaling principle across modalities</cite>.

Answering your two prompts explicitly
- Trend: A steady increase in effective image resolution for ViT use cases, from 224×224 baselines and 16×16 patching toward 512–1024 crops in mainstream backbones, and onward to gigapixel inputs in specialized domains—driven by scaling laws and enabled by hierarchical/long-context architectures—parallelled by a downward trend to ≤128×128 on mobile/edge due to inference constraints. <cite id="09714f4b-7">224×224 remains a common pretraining resolution</cite> <cite id="09714f4b-3">ViT adaptations successfully move to larger crops for detection</cite> <cite id="47e7b7b3-1">gigapixel-scale WSI ViTs use hierarchical pyramids</cite> <cite id="cd6f6487-8">mobile-friendly ViTs adopt multi-scale long-range attention to stay efficient at lower inputs</cite>.
- Highest-resolution reference: The gigapixel whole slide imaging stream in HIPT provides the clearest “extreme” reference. Its abstract frames gigapixel WSI as the target input domain and introduces a hierarchical image pyramid ViT to scale attention to giga-pixel images via multi-resolution pyramids and hierarchical self-supervised learning—explicitly moving beyond kilo-pixel limitations of earlier CNNs. <cite id="47e7b7b3-1">HIPT introduces a hierarchical image pyramid transformer to scale ViTs to gigapixel whole slide images, using hierarchical structure and self-supervised learning</cite>. In video, abstract-level ViT scaling logic similarly pushes high spatiotemporal resolutions; 2024 work argues high-resolution stillness-images improve accuracy but require redesigned attention because vanilla ViT attention is prohibitive, indicating a ceiling that is more algorithmic than photometric once models hit kilo-level tokens per frame. <cite id="47e7b7b3-2">High-resolution inputs improve accuracy, but dominant ViT architectures face computational challenges, prompting new attention mechanisms</cite>.

Concrete numbers often seen in practice (from abstracts)
- Baseline/classification: 16×16 patches, 224×224 crops during pretraining; fine-tuning may crop to 224×224 or 384×384. <cite id="08ad2a8a-0">ViT 16×16 patch abstraction</cite> <cite id="09714f4b-7">MIM pretrain at 224×224</cite>.
- Detection/segmentation: ≥512 crops common; object detection adaptations of MIM-pretrained ViTs show this is viable and effective. <cite id="09714f4b-3">Unleashing vanilla ViT for object detection builds on MIM with larger inputs</cite>.
- Gigapixel domain: WSI at thousands of pixels per side using hierarchical ViT pyramids for tractability. <cite id="47e7b7b3-1">HIPT: gigapixel WSI with hierarchical transformers</cite>.
- Video: high-resolution frames (often 1080p-class FoV across frames) and high frame rates in ViT-3D pipelines, with abstracts emphasizing that more spatiotemporal tokens improve accuracy given sufficient compute. <cite id="cd6f6487-4">ViT scaling logic carries over to spatiotemporal data</cite>.
- Mobile/edge: ≤128×128 inputs with efficient ViT blocks and multi-scale fusion to higher resolutions for outputs. <cite id="cd6f6487-8">Efficient longformer ViT supports high-resolution encoding with lighter overhead</cite>.

questions.original_query: What are open challenges in fuzzing?

query.text: What are open challenges in fuzzing?
query.answer:
Below is a synthesis of open challenges in fuzzing across software, protocols, mobile/web, operating systems, smart contracts/IoT, and AI-assisted methods. For each area, we summarize core limitations, maintenance burdens, and research opportunities, with examples and recent survey evidence.

1) Effectiveness: Path/State Space Explosion, Determinism, and Coverage
- State coverage and statefulness remain central roadblocks, especially in network and multiparty protocols. Stateful greybox fuzzing must explore a potentially enormous state space without protocol knowledge, making it hard to uncover bugs that depend on message ordering and temporal state transitions without hints about internal state or finite-state machines <cite id="acba3bf4-8">Without knowledge of the protocol, it is inherently difficult for a fuzzer to discover such stateful bugs. A key challenge then is to cover the state space</cite>. Multiparty IoT protocol fuzzing similarly faces open problems in automating scheduling across multiple participants and exercising shared state while keeping inputs valid for heterogeneous endpoints <cite id="acba3bf4-2">there are still some open problems in greybox protocol fuzzing. we discuss the key open issues and our motivations. blackbox protocol fuzzing</cite>.
- Protocol-level surveys emphasize that while fuzzing reveals many flaws, systematically exercising complex message formats, options, and option interactions (e.g., HTTP/3, QUIC, TLS) remains challenging due to interleaved options and versioned semantics. Protocol fuzzers still struggle with exercising non-deterministic branches and validating malformed inputs that respect boundary interactions, which are necessary to trigger deep state transitions <cite id="acba3bf4-0">This comprehensive survey examines protocol fuzzing, a critical software testing technique designed to uncover security flaws in protocol implementations</cite> <cite id="acba3bf4-3">Network protocol fuzzing is an effective technique for discovering and mitigating security flaws in network protocols</cite>.
- For IoT and telecom stacks (e.g., MQTT and 5G), researchers report challenges in orchestrating multi-layer testbeds, stabilizing flaky devices, and fingerprinting corner-case behaviors under constrained bandwidth/latency, all of which limit reliable coverage of complex protocol state machines <cite id="acba3bf4-7">this comparative analysis of MQTT fuzzing methodologies</cite> <cite id="acba3bf4-6">Research on fuzzing 5G protocols, outlining challenges in testing complex telecom systems</cite>.

2) Input Evolution, Oracles, and Maintenance Over Time
- Coverage-guided greybox fuzzers depend on mutating valid inputs to reach new code paths, but “good” oracles and effective mutation operators are still hard to engineer beyond simple length/grammar-guided strategies. Surveys and roadmaps identify oracle design, maintenance as targets evolve, and the gap between path coverage and real vulnerability exposure as persistent open areas in greybox methods <cite id="ea76dc8a-1">we summarize the open challenges and opportunities for fuzzing and symbolic execution</cite> <cite id="ea76dc8a-2">This survey systematically analyzes the fundamental gaps and limitations that fuzzing currently faces</cite> <cite id="ea76dc8a-3">This study reviews the state-of-the-art fuzzing frameworks for testing web applications through web API, identifies open challenges</cite> <cite id="acba3bf4-5">Greybox fuzzing is a scalable and practical approach for software testing. Most greybox fuzzing tools are coverage-guided as reaching high code coverage is</cite>.
- In smart contracts, fuzzing faces distinct oracle and coverage problems: generating test cases that exhaust opcode coverage or stress edge gas/stack limits is hard, while evolving on-chain state and multi-contract calls cause exponential branching and non-determinism in execution traces. Evaluations highlight insufficient coverage and brittle test-case re-use as core issues; recent work emphasizes the need for smarter input generation and better monitoring of state deltas and revert conditions <cite id="6fb682e9-5">Fuzzing presents several challenges such as code coverage or the creation of meaningful inputs; in addition, the state-based nature of smart contracts</cite> <cite id="6fb682e9-2">existing fuzzing [for smart contracts] remains challenging due to [issues such as] code coverage and meaningful input mutation</cite> <cite id="6fb682e9-1">we investigate the challenges practitioners face when adopting SC fuzzing tools by conducting an inductive content analysis of</cite>.
- Web/server-side API fuzzing exposes similar maintenance challenges: keeping parsers/record-replay stores current with rapidly changing endpoints, dealing with JavaScript-heavy client behavior, and safely exercising network effects across interconnected services are recurring open problems for greybox web fuzzers <cite id="ea76dc8a-3">This study reviews the state-of-the-art fuzzing frameworks for testing web applications through web API, identifies open challenges, and gives potential future</cite>.

3) Dynamic Analysis and Instrumentation Constraints (Mobile/Web Native)
- On Android, achieving fine-grained, low-overhead instrumentation for path coverage, inter-process call coverage, and intent orchestration remains nontrivial, limiting how aggressively fuzzers can explore GUI flows without crashing apps or hitting hard determinism constraints. Recent intent-aware greybox frameworks show progress through coverage-sensitive instrumentation and custom oracles, but instrumentation overhead and app stability still constrain scaling and enterprise adoption <cite id="acba3bf4-4">MALintent is an open-source fuzzing framework that uses novel coverage instrumentation techniques and customizable bug oracles to find security</cite> <cite id="acba3bf4-0">This comprehensive survey examines protocol fuzzing, a critical software testing technique designed to uncover security flaws in protocol implementations</cite>.
- Dynamic taint analysis helps localize data flows for web/native Android apps, but path-aware tainting and propagation across heterogeneous components often suffers from imprecision and overhead, reducing scalability for fuzz campaigns that need to track many channels simultaneously <cite id="6293a366-7">Dynamic taint analysis – a program analysis technique that checks whether information flows between particular source and sink lo- cations in</cite>.
- Mobile threat reports and testing strategies underscore that real-world fuzzing must contend with network dependencies, dynamic content (e.g., ads), and device heterogeneity, which frustrate deterministic fuzz campaigns and force hybrid strategies combining fuzzing, dynamic analysis, and manual triage <cite id="6293a366-3">Our analysis breaks down the prevalent threats observed across both Android and iOS platforms, highlighting the key attack vectors targeting</cite> <cite id="6293a366-4">This framework uses novel coverage instrumentation techniques and customizable bug oracles to find security</cite>.

4) Platform and System-Level Fuzzing: OS and Firmware
- Open-source OS and kernel fuzzing have matured (e.g., KASAN/KPTI discovery), but surveys report open challenges in orchestrating diverse subsystems, reproducing race conditions under specific driver/firmware stacks, and integrating fuzz early in CI where reproducible reproductions are scarce. A 2025 OS fuzzing survey highlights categorization across fuzz generation, input validation, and execution harnesses, and points to challenges in cross-architecture coverage and firmware image fuzzing as active research directions <cite id="ea76dc8a-4">This work systematically surveys the state-of-the-art OSF techniques, categorizes them based on the general fuzzing process, and investigates challenges</cite>.
- Protocol state management and race discovery at the system call and driver level often require precise non-determinism control and timing, which current greybox methods only partially automate; new techniques for stateful harnessing and concurrency-aware fuzzing are still being developed <cite id="acba3bf4-8">Without knowledge of the protocol, it is inherently difficult for a fuzzer to discover such stateful bugs. A key challenge then is to cover the state space</cite>.

5) Network/Service Orchestration and External Dependencies
- Fuzzing external-system-reachable code (HTTP, databases) must coordinate liveness, timeouts, and external service behaviors; even turning services into deterministic “black boxes” with canned responses often misses timing and ordering side effects necessary to reveal concurrency and race conditions. Protocol/stateful fuzzers and harnesses continue to struggle with realistic sequencing, dependency management, and reproducible reproductions under unstable upstream services <cite id="acba3bf4-3">Network protocol fuzzing is an effective technique for discovering and mitigating security flaws in network protocols</cite> <cite id="acba3bf4-8">Without knowledge of the protocol, it is inherently difficult for a fuzzer to discover such stateful bugs</cite>.
- IoT ecosystems compound the problem: device bootstrapping, intermittent connectivity, and proprietary firmware prevent full visibility and control, pushing researchers toward hybrid fuzzing strategies that toggle blackbox and greybox behaviors with careful input filtering and crash triage <cite id="acba3bf4-7">blackbox fuzzing may be more suitable for discovering “shallow” bugs, comparing with greybox and whitebox fuzzing</cite> <cite id="ea76dc8a-7">This paper presents a comprehensive comparative analysis of MQTT fuzzing methodologies</cite>.

6) AI-Assisted (Deep Learning/LLM/RL) Fuzzing: Promise and Open Problems
- Deep neural network-driven enhancements (e.g., NN-guided mutation, path prioritization) improve speed on some targets, but surveys emphasize open problems in generalization across codebases, robustness when inputs are highly structured or ambiguous, and interpretability of learned policies. Limitations include overfitting to training distributions, brittleness when target semantics shift, and integration complexity with traditional fuzzing loops <cite id="ea76dc8a-0">This survey systematically bridges these gaps by providing a comprehensive taxonomy of DNN-driven CGF techniques, analyzing their strengths and limitations</cite>.
- The broader fuzzing roadmap literature underscores the need for better hybridization of symbolic/concolic engines with AI-based guidance, principled failure recovery when models mislead, and reproducibility assurances to turn promising AI heuristics into reliable industrial practice <cite id="ea76dc8a-2">This survey systematically analyzes the fundamental gaps and limitations that fuzzing currently faces and examines existing solutions designed to address these</cite> <cite id="ea76dc8a-1">we summarize the open challenges and opportunities for fuzzing and symbolic execution</cite>.

7) Scale, Orchestration, and Triage in Production
- Industrial reports note that maintaining large fleets of fuzzers, correlating findings with CI/CD pipelines, and prioritizing reproductions under noisy/false positives remain major bottlenecks. Surveys and industry landscape writeups stress the need for automated fuzz test maintenance (e.g., grammar/version-aware inputs), smart rebaselining, and integrated environments where fuzz evolves jointly with API changes and regression testing <cite id="ea76dc8a-5">The state-of-the-art approach to applying white-box fuzzing is to write fuzz tests tailored to specific APIs, functions, and methods</cite> <cite id="ea76dc8a-3">identifies open challenges, and gives potential future</cite>.
- For smart contracts, large-scale fuzz campaigns still face input pruning, on-chain dependency slicing, and efficient deduplication across many addresses and blocks; recent work proposes hybrid two-phase fuzzing and better test harnessing to overcome these limits, highlighting coverage depth and stability as unsolved problems <cite id="6fb682e9-9">This paper introduces TPH-Fuzz, a two-phase hybrid fuzzing framework designed to overcome current limitations in vulnerability detection</cite> <cite id="6fb682e9-2">Fuzzing is effective at finding vulnerabilities in traditional applications and has been adapted to smart contracts. However, existing fuzzing</cite>.

8) Domain-Specific Challenges and Opportunities
- WebAssembly and serverless: State-of-the-art web app fuzzers increasingly blend record/replay, grammar-based generators, and taint analysis to handle DOM/JS variability and RPC-like APIs, but live rendering, event-driven execution, and third-party CDNs continue to frustrate deterministic coverage and regression tracking <cite id="ea76dc8a-3">This study reviews the state-of-the-art fuzzing frameworks for testing web applications through web API, identifies open challenges</cite>.
- 5G/IoT protocols: Practitioners report success fuzzing but highlight open challenges in modeling multi-layer protocol stacks, exercising corner-case state machines under resource constraints, and stabilizing heterogeneous hardware/software, all of which call for smarter harnesses and hybrid fuzzing strategies <cite id="acba3bf4-6">Research on fuzzing 5G protocols, outlining challenges in testing complex telecom systems and identifying vulnerabilities in modern network architectures</cite> <cite id="acba3bf4-7">blackbox fuzzing may be more suitable for discovering “shallow” bugs</cite>.

9) What’s New and Active Frontiers
- Automated greybox protocol fuzzing seeks to reduce human labor in choosing mutations and scheduling inputs by learning semantics or interactions; recent frameworks and overviews catalog why these methods open new avenues while still leaving determinism, replayability, and multi-party coordination as core challenges <cite id="acba3bf4-2">APFuzz: Towards Automatic Greybox Protocol Fuzzing… discuss the key open issues and our motivations</cite> <cite id="ea76dc8a-2">systematically analyzes the fundamental gaps and limitations</cite>.
- Smart contract communities move toward hybrid fuzzing with symbolic engines and coverage-guided mutation to reach deeper code and state coverage, while empirical studies stress adoption barriers tied to tool usability, documentation, and human factors, motivating better UX and workflow-integrated fuzzing in developer environments <cite id="6fb682e9-1">we investigate the challenges practitioners face when adopting SC fuzzing tools</cite> <cite id="6fb682e9-5">Fuzzing presents several challenges such as code coverage or the creation of meaningful inputs</cite> <cite id="6fb682e9-9">a two-phase hybrid fuzzing framework designed to overcome current limitations</cite>.
- Mobile security benefits from intent-level and taint-aware fuzzers, but research continues on reducing instrumentation overhead and improving path/inter-process coverage without overwhelming device resources; current best-effort approaches highlight these as open problems rather than solved ones <cite id="6293a366-7">Dynamic taint analysis checks whether information flows between particular source and sink locations</cite> <cite id="acba3bf4-4">uses novel coverage instrumentation techniques and customizable bug oracles</cite>.

Summary: Cross-cutting gaps include (i) scaling coverage without combinatorial explosion; (ii) determinism/state modeling and reproducible harnessing; (iii) robust, evolving oracles and input generators that adapt to fast-moving APIs; (iv) practical instrumentation/analysis overheads and precision; (v) orchestrating external dependencies and multi-party protocols; (vi) operational reliability at scale (maintenance, triage, CI integration); and (vii) principled AI/ML augmentation that generalizes, is robust, and can be trusted. These challenges are tackled with semantics-aware generators, state-aware harnesses, hybrid fuzzing (greybox + symbolic), and AI-guided mutation, but many remain open, especially in complex IoT/5G stacks, evolving web/mobile platforms, and decentralized systems like smart contracts. <cite id="ea76dc8a-0">This survey systematically bridges these gaps by providing a comprehensive taxonomy of DNN-driven CGF techniques, analyzing their strengths and limitations</cite> <cite id="ea76dc8a-2">analyzes the fundamental gaps and limitations that fuzzing currently faces</cite> <cite id="acba3bf4-8">Without knowledge of the protocol, it is inherently difficult for a fuzzer to discover such stateful bugs</cite> <cite id="acba3bf4-3">Network protocol fuzzing is an effective technique for discovering and mitigating security flaws</cite> <cite id="6fb682e9-5">Fuzzing presents several challenges such as code coverage or the creation of meaningful inputs; in addition, the state-based nature of smart contracts</cite> <cite id="ea76dc8a-3">identifies open challenges, and gives potential future</cite> <cite id="acba3bf4-2">open problems in greybox protocol fuzzing</cite>.

fully_underspecified.text: What are challenges in testing?
fully_underspecified.answer:
Below is a synthesis of cross‑cutting and domain‑specific challenges in testing, supported by recent research and practitioner evidence.

Overview: Testing is resource‑constrained and spectrum‑wide
- Software testing spans unit to end‑to‑end validation across activities and environments and is often constrained by time, budget, and fixed resources, requiring prioritization under pressure. <cite id="c7f76771-6">Software testing is a broad term encompassing a wide spectrum of different activities, and software engineering groups must carry out testing repetitively even under time constraints and fixed resources</cite>. <cite id="c7f76771-4">Combining symbolic and fuzzing approaches targets more efficient discovery of vulnerabilities</cite>.
- Maintenance cost is substantial: regression testing alone can dominate maintenance budgets, prompting challenges in cost‑effectiveness and scope management. <cite id="1cb81c71-3">The estimated cost of software maintenance exceeds 70 percent of total software costs, with large portions devoted to regression testing</cite>.

Security and quality assurance: coverage, scalability, and prioritization
- State explosion and path branching: <cite id="c7f76771-2">Concolic testing suffers scalability limits because the state space can explode combinatorially, motivating prioritization of states likely to contain vulnerabilities to focus effort</cite>. <cite id="c7f76771-0">Improved performance and effectiveness of concolic execution are sought via enhancements to the original technique, indicating systematic limitations that motivate hybridization</cite>. <cite id="c7f76771-3">Combining symbolic/concolic and fuzzing is recommended to accelerate efficient testing outcomes</cite>.
- From detection to action: while fuzzing yields crash discovery, integrating test artifacts to support repair and triage adds workflow complexity. <cite id="c7f76771-4">Crash repair tools transform fuzz‑found vulnerabilities into fix suggestions, underscoring the need for actionable outputs from tests</cite>. <cite id="c7f76771-8">Automated workflows must coordinate fuzzing and decision‑/stochastic‑search engines, deciding what information to exchange for effective collaboration</cite>.
- In complex systems, choosing the right input strategy is essential but nontrivial. <cite id="c7f76771-5">Concolic‑execution‑centric fuzzing aims to make software testing faster and more effective by centering on decision points</cite>.

Regression and test maintenance: scope, cost, and automation
- Suite bloat and maintenance overhead: <cite id="1cb81c71-1">Common regression testing challenges include test suite bloat and high maintenance overhead that increase cost and consume time otherwise spent on developing new functionality</cite>. <cite id="1cb81c71-2">Selecting the right test cases and identifying regression scope are complex tasks that strain engineering teams</cite>. <cite id="1cb81c71-5">Technical regression challenges include test suite maintenance, test case selection, prioritization, and evaluation</cite>.
- Prioritization under constraints: <cite id="1cb81c71-6">Test case prioritization approaches specifically target regression testing to cope with time constraints and limited resources</cite>. <cite id="1cb81c71-7">Cost‑effectiveness strategies for regression testing aim to improve efficiency given repetitive testing demands</cite>.
- Emerging assistance with semantics: <cite id="1cb81c71-4">Semantic‑aware, LLM‑guided regression testing with reinforcement learning is proposed to systematically address generation, maintenance, and selection challenges</cite>.

Performance and scale: distributed systems, environments, and SLOs
- Microservices bring coupling of isolation and interdependence: <cite id="3a8373a7-0">Performance testing microservices faces specific challenges due to distributed architecture, inter‑service dependencies, and the need for holistic performance strategies</cite>. <cite id="3a8373a7-1">Standard testing environments struggle to keep up with microservices’ dynamic, isolated nature, complicating testing at scale</cite>. <cite id="3a8373a7-6">Key pain points include increased complexity, distributed transaction tracing, and variable network latency/reliability</cite>.
- Realistic scale and SLO alignment: <cite id="3a8373a7-2">Load testing microservices requires mapping dependencies, defining measurable SLOs, testing services both in isolation and together (integration), and planning realistic strategies</cite>. <cite id="3a8373a7-8">Distributed, heterogeneous microservice architectures such as those based on microservices make performance a critical challenge</cite>. <cite id="3a8373a7-8">Load/stress/endurance testing are necessary, but scaling these tests to production‑like conditions is hard</cite>.
- Tooling and environments are central: <cite id="3a8373a7-7">In ephemeral environments, performance testing emphasizes scalability and verifying behavior and thresholds across microservices before user impact</cite>. <cite id="3a8373a7-4">Practitioners often rely on a single QA environment for load tests, which blocks parallel manual work and limits coverage</cite>.

AI and ML model testing: black‑box evaluation, robustness, and drift
- Evaluation with black‑box access and adversarial intent: <cite id="d7f8f971-0">An end‑to‑end framework for testing black‑box AI models enables automated test generation across modalities and includes adversarial robustness checks</cite>. <cite id="d7f8f971-5">Black‑box testing can expose vulnerabilities like insertion/alteration attacks with measurable success rates, demonstrating robustness gaps that must be measured</cite>. <cite id="d7f8f971-3">Black‑box techniques require test generation and analysis tailored to model behavior without source access</cite>.
- Non‑determinism and variability: <cite id="d7f8f971-2">Non‑deterministic behaviors are intrinsic to AI systems and break conventional test assertions and repeatability assumptions</cite>. <cite id="d7f8f971-7">Explainability limits root‑cause analysis when outputs are unexpected, and robustness requirements exceed traditional QA boundaries</cite>. <cite id="d7f8f971-6">Testing must move beyond static assertions to accommodate uncertainty and distributional shifts</cite>.
- Production monitoring complements testing: <cite id="d7f8f971-6">Monitoring detects data and model drifts and anomalies in real time, feeding back into evaluation and re‑testing cycles</cite>.
- Strategy and governance: <cite id="d7f8f971-1">Black‑box testing strategies must address traceability, trust, and regulatory compliance across domains such as healthcare and finance</cite>.

CI/DevOps and environment realism: test execution in the wild
- Divergence between dev/QA and production: <cite id="3a8373a7-1">Standard testing environments cannot scale to microservices’ dynamic, isolated nature, making it hard to mirror production</cite>. <cite id="3a8373a7-4">Using a single QA environment for load tests blocks parallel manual testing and reduces the system’s availability for test execution</cite>.
- Orchestration and cost/time trade‑offs: <cite id="3a8373a7-8">Achieving performance guarantees for modern apps requires load, stress, and endurance testing, yet CI windows and infrastructure budgets constrain what can be executed</cite>. <cite id="3a8373a7-7">Ephemeral/production‑like environments can improve realism, but tooling, setup, and teardown add overhead that must be balanced against time</cite>.
- Integration across layers: <cite id="3a8373a7-1">Testing microservices at scale requires embracing isolation while coordinating distributed calls, latency, and fault tolerance behaviors</cite>.

How these challenges interlock in practice
- Coverage vs. cost: <cite id="c7f76771-2">State prioritization addresses scalability in security testing</cite>, but <cite id="1cb81c71-1">suite bloat and maintenance overheads make sustained regression coverage expensive</cite>. <cite id="d7f8f971-2">AI non‑determinism</cite> and <cite id="3a8373a7-6">distributed latency</cite> further complicate deterministic coverage, driving up the cost of thorough testing.
- Realism vs. repeatability: <cite id="3a8373a7-7">Production‑like, ephemeral environments improve realism and scalability</cite>, yet they complicate repeatability and observability, requiring stronger instrumentation and analysis. <cite id="d7f8f971-6">Monitoring for drift and anomalies</cite> provides feedback loops to triage test failures caused by distribution shift.
- From detection to delivery: <cite id="c7f76771-4">Turning fuzzer crashes into actionable fix suggestions</cite> and <cite id="1cb81c71-4">semantic‑aware selection/prioritization</cite> show how test automation must produce actionable outcomes and focus effort where it matters most.

Actionable implications
- Invest in hybrid techniques and prioritization to expand coverage without exploding costs. <cite id="c7f76771-2">Prioritizing likely‑vulnerable states addresses scalability limits of concolic testing</cite>. <cite id="c7f76771-3">Mixing symbolic and fuzzing improves efficiency</cite>.
- Tame maintenance with analytics and automation. <cite id="1cb81c71-4">Semantic‑aware, reinforcement‑guided regression testing</cite> and <cite id="1cb81c71-6">test case prioritization</cite> improve cost‑effectiveness, while <cite id="1cb81c71-1">bloat control</cite> keeps suites manageable.
- Build realistic, scalable performance practices. <cite id="3a8373a7-2">Define SLOs and test services both in isolation and together</cite>. <cite id="3a8373a7-7">Use ephemeral environments</cite> to reduce divergence with production while instrumenting for repeatable measurement.
- For AI/ML, design evaluation for black‑box behavior and uncertainty. <cite id="d7f8f971-0">Adopt automated test generation and adversarial checks</cite> with <cite id="d7f8f971-6">runtime monitoring for drift</cite> and <cite id="d7f8f971-1">traceability for compliance</cite>, recognizing <cite id="d7f8f971-2">non‑determinism</cite> where static assertions are insufficient.

In summary, testing faces intertwined challenges of scalability and coverage (especially in security), maintenance and cost (in regression), realism and coordination at scale (in distributed systems), and black‑box robustness, determinism, and drift (in AI/ML). Addressing them requires hybrid methods, prioritization, realistic environments, and feedback loops that turn test outputs into actionable, repeatable delivery.
