- Transformers and Hebbian local rules: There is active interest in grafting Hebbian local plasticity onto modern transformers for vision, but most head‑to‑head SOTA numbers still favor ViTs/ConvNeXts trained by backprop. Early hybrids demonstrate how to inject Hebbian updates into feed‑forward or self‑attention sublayers and report competitive features for tasks like linear probing on ImageNet‑100 when combined with data curricula, showing promise yet to be matched by full transformer+Hebbian end‑to‑end finetuning on standard ImageNet with current reports <cite id="322ccf77-5">Linear probing accuracy on ImageNet-100. Our data curriculum pipeline matches DINOv2 performance while achieving a 1.44× convergence speed-up.</cite> <cite id="322ccf77-8">The research presented in this paper advances the integration of Hebbian learning into Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) for image processing.</cite>.

- Tooling and frameworks: Practical barrier reductions include PyTorch/TF operators and optimizers that implement local Hebbian updates stabilized by normalization, curvature guidance, and sparsity/orthogonality constraints; these allow users to plug Hebbian plasticity into CNN modules for ablations and to compare against SGD+cross‑entropy baselines with matched compute <cite id="3a81f974-0">Comparison of Hebbian Learning and Backpropagation for ...</cite> <cite id="3a81f974-8">Hebbian convolutional neural networks with modern deep ...</cite>.

Comparison to mainstream SOTA and limitations
- Against modern CNNs/Transformers: On standard public benchmarks, CNNs/Transformers trained fully by SGD+cross‑entropy still tend to be SOTA on ImageNet and CIFAR for end‑to‑end accuracy and latency/throughput under matched hardware. - Global‑direction Hebbian updates: A 2026 paper argues that incorporating global direction into Hebbian adjustments yields features competitive on ImageNet and narrows the performance gap to standard backpropagation, suggesting that principled hybridization can achieve strong practical outcomes without abandoning local plasticity <cite id="322ccf77-7">datasets like ImageNet, our framework achieves the competitive results and significantly narrows the gap with standard backpropagation.</cite>.

- Mechanistically, deep Hebbian image recognition models are feasible: combine Hebbian local plasticity in lower layers with supervised backprop in higher layers, or use hybrid local learning without explicit feedback targets. fully_underspecified.text: what is the latest about neural networks in image recognition?
fully_underspecified.answer:
Below is a concise, evidence-backed snapshot of the latest (2023–2025) advances in neural networks for image recognition, organized by theme.

Architectural landscape: transformers vs CNNs and hybrids
- Recent comparative reviews conclude vision transformers (ViTs) and convolutional neural networks (CNNs) remain the two main pillars, with hybrid ViT–CNN designs proliferating as a design pattern in 2023–2025 surveys and benchmarks. <cite id="1c581c02-0">This 2024 literature review contrasts ViTs and CNNs with practical guidance for feature extraction and classification</cite>; <cite id="1c581c02-1">a 2023 survey presents a taxonomy of ViTs and hybrid ViTs in depth</cite>; <cite id="1c581c02-5">an accompanying 2023 survey emphasizes hybrid transformer architectures, reflecting deployment-driven design trends</cite>.
- Empirically, ViTs have shown advantages under occlusion and distance for face recognition and general vision tasks, while CNN-derived families (ConvNeXt) close the gap via modernization of residual blocks, global/local attention, and scaling. <cite id="1c581c02-2">ViTs outperform CNNs in accuracy and robustness against distance and occlusions for face recognition</cite>; <cite id="1c581c02-0">comparisons highlight architecture-specific trade‑offs for feature extraction and classification</cite>.
- In detection/segmentation, both paradigms are active; 2025 review work shows CNN- and ViT-based detectors each have representative advances with growing convergence via hybrid token/conv kernels. <cite id="1c581c02-3">A 2025 review surveys object detection developments spanning CNN and ViT-based methods</cite>; <cite id="1c581c02-4">surveys of ViT variants explicitly catalog hybrid designs</cite>; <cite id="1c581c02-8">a 2024 transformer survey covers transformer backbones for downstream vision tasks</cite>.

Scaling, benchmarks, and long-tail
- ImageNet‑1K results illustrate parity and surpassing: modern ViTs and ConvNeXt variants reach state of the art; head-to-head comparisons probe behaviors beyond top‑1. <cite id="93a5f812-2">An ImageNet‑1K leaderboard shows best “pure ConvNet” entries like ConvNeXt V2 Huge as current SOTA among CNNs</cite>; <cite id="93a5f812-0">an analysis compares ConvNet vs Transformer and supervised vs CLIP “beyond ImageNet accuracy,” emphasizing calibration, OOD robustness, and fairness</cite>; <cite id="93a5f812-3">the MLR proceedings formalize this broader evaluation perspective</cite>.
- CNNs remain competitive thanks to architectural refinements; reports cite ImageNet‑1K accuracy around the high‑80s for strong ConvNeXt models. <cite id="93a5f812-5">Narrative summaries report ConvNeXt reaching ~87.8% ImageNet accuracy and strong detection results</cite>; <cite id="93a5f812-4">public forecasting threads reference ~88.9% claims circa early 2023 and note leaderboard evolution</cite>.
- Resolution scaling and training regime changes continue to lift top‑1 accuracy curves; updated curves show ViTs and CNNs interlocking as size/resolution increase. <cite id="93a5f812-6">A comparative figure relates ImageNet‑1K top‑1 vs model size at 224×224, showing strong performance for both families</cite>.

Training and data efficiency: self‑supervision, distillation, and data‑free methods
- Knowledge distillation (KD) and teacher–student pipelines are widely used to transfer representation quality from large teachers (supervised or self‑supervised) to smaller students, improving accuracy/latency trade‑offs. <cite id="7e719389-0">A 2025 KD approach targets transparency in medical image tasks, illustrating KD’s clinical uptake</cite>; <cite id="7e719389-1">teacher–student collaborative KD for image classification improves model performance</cite>.
- Self‑distillation and contrastive/self‑supervised paradigms bolster representation learning with little labeled data or even no labels, and are applied across vision tasks. <cite id="7e719389-3">Self-Supervised Self Distillation (WACV 2023) constructs a teacher on unlabeled images to induce strong visual representations</cite>; <cite id="7e719389-8">the accompanying WACV entry details self-teacher training without labels</cite>; <cite id="7e719389-9">SEED (2021) framed self- and teacher-driven distillation to transfer representation quality</cite>.
- Data‑free and embedding‑based distillation let students learn from large pretrains without access to data, growing in popularity for privacy/ops constraints. <cite id="7e719389-7">A 2024 paper notes data‑free distillation trains lightweight students from a pre‑trained teacher without teacher data</cite>; <cite id="7e719389-6">distilling from self-supervised teachers via embedding space alignment improves downstream representation quality</cite>.

Efficiency, quantization, and deployment
- 8‑bit quantization is mainstream for latency/size reduction with post‑training and quantization‑aware training (QAT) improving vision accuracy preservation. <cite id="e7b443d2-1">Clipping‑based post‑training 8‑bit quantization reduces model size and improves CPU latency</cite>; <cite id="e7b443d2-2">Google AI Edge notes post‑training quantization reduces model size and accelerates CPU and accelerator inference</cite>; <cite id="e7b443d2-0">comprehensive quantization surveys catalog CNN quantization methods including 8‑bit</cite>.
- ViT quantization has matured from fringe to core: recent CVPR 2025 work provides Fisher‑informed post‑training quantization (FIMA‑Q) validated on classification and detection, and industrial guidance is available. <cite id="e7b443d2-4">FIMA‑Q (CVPR 2025) shows post‑training ViT quantization via Fisher information guidance on multiple ViT architectures for classification and detection</cite>.
- Practical deployment often combines pruning, quantization, and KD: edge‑AI roundups emphasize quantization error analysis and best practices across CNNs and Transformers. <cite id="e7b443d2-3">A 2024 edge‑AI survey reviews quantization techniques and error analysis with best‑practice guidance</cite>.

Robustness, generalization, and evaluation beyond accuracy
- Beyond top‑1 ImageNet accuracy, recent studies compare calibration, robustness to occlusion/distance, and OOD behaviors for ViT vs CNN backbones. <cite id="93a5f812-0">Comparative analyses examine model behaviors beyond ImageNet accuracy for ConvNet vs Transformer</cite>; <cite id="1c581c02-2">face verification/occlusion/distance stress tests reveal ViT robustness advantages</cite>.
- Detection/segmentation evaluations mirror classification trends: hybrid architectures and multi‑scale fusion are used to balance accuracy with robustness to occlusion, scale variance, and domain shifts. <cite id="1c581c02-3">CNN vs ViT object detectors are reviewed in 2025, reflecting converging design patterns for robust inference</cite>.
- In domains like medical imaging, KD and robust evaluation emphasize reliability and transparency, aligning recognition performance with clinical acceptance criteria. <cite id="7e719389-0">KD has been applied to medical image models to improve transparency and potentially generalization</cite>.

Multimodality and rising hybridization
- Vision transformers have become a backbone for cross‑modal alignment (e.g., CLIP/Flamingo), which in turn drives new zero‑shot recognition and improves discriminative tokenization. While not all multimodal specifics appear in the retrieved snippets, broader surveys and detector reviews reflect the trend toward hybrid CNN–Transformer backbones and attention‑augmented CNNs for richer feature semantics. <cite id="1c581c02-1">A 2023 survey catalogs hybrid ViTs as dominant in modern architectures</cite>; <cite id="1c581c02-8">a 2024 transformer survey classifies transformer backbones for downstream image tasks</cite>; <cite id="1c581c02-3">a 2025 object detection review spans CNN and ViT methods with hybridization patterns</cite>.
- Empirically, occlusion/distance robustness—a known challenge for early ViTs—has improved through design tweaks and hybrid token mixing, reinforcing their utility in real‑world recognition pipelines. <cite id="1c581c02-2">ViTs’ robustness to occlusion/distance for face recognition has been empirically demonstrated</cite>; <cite id="1c581c02-0">comparative analyses highlight robustness–accuracy trade‑offs that hybrid designs can mitigate</cite>.

Open trends and what to watch next
- Resolution and scale scaling continue to lift top‑1 and improve generalization, with careful calibration and OOD evaluation recommended to avoid overfitting to training resolution and labels. <cite id="93a5f812-6">Top‑1 vs size curves with increasing resolution illustrate how both families improve together</cite>; <cite id="93a5f812-0">beyond‑accuracy comparisons argue for robustness and calibration, not just clean‑set top‑1</cite>.
- Transformer specialization: ViTs win on long‑range context and cross‑modal transfer; CNN/ConvNeXt routes win on memory‑efficiency and inductive biases aligned to local textures; hybrids bridge both. <cite id="1c581c02-2">ViTs show robustness gains under occlusion/distance</cite>; <cite id="1c581c02-5">surveys underline the prevalence and benefits of hybrid designs</cite>.
- Data‑aware distillation and privacy‑preserving training/data‑free transfer will further accelerate deployment at low precision and on constrained devices. <cite id="7e719389-7">Data‑free distillation enables student learning without teacher data</cite>; <cite id="e7b443d2-2">post‑training 8‑bit quantization reduces size/latency for CPU and accelerators</cite>; <cite id="e7b443d2-4">FIMA‑Q validates post‑training ViT quantization at scale</cite>.

Actionable takeaways for 2025 image recognition
- Model choice and hybridization: Favor ViT‑based or hybrid CNN+Transformer backbones when occlusion, distance, and cross‑domain robustness matter; pick ConvNeXt/efficientnet‑style families for latency‑bounded, label‑hungry settings or when you need strong ImageNet accuracy with compact models. <cite id="1c581c02-2">ViT strength under occlusion/distance</cite>; <cite id="93a5f812-5">ConvNeXt accuracy figures indicate competitive accuracy at reasonable scales</cite>.
- Train smarter, deploy leaner: Self‑supervised or KD‑assisted pretraining, then prune+quantize (8‑bit post‑training or QAT) and retrain small students for production; for confidential data, explore data‑free distillation. <cite id="7e719389-3">Self-distillation from unlabeled data builds strong representations</cite>; <cite id="e7b443d2-2">quantization improves latency/size while preserving accuracy</cite>; <cite id="7e719389-7">data‑free distillation transfers knowledge without exposing data</cite>.
- Evaluate robustly: Include OOD splits, occlusion/augmentation tests, and calibration metrics; compare ViT vs CNN variants head‑to‑head beyond top‑1. <cite id="93a5f812-0">Comparative analyses beyond top‑1 emphasize calibration and OOD behavior</cite>; <cite id="1c581c02-2">empirical occlusion/distance evaluations favor ViTs in some settings</cite>.

Summary
From 2023–2025, image recognition has converged on hybrid ViT–CNN architectures scaled to higher resolutions, evaluated not only by top‑1 accuracy but by robustness, calibration, and OOD behavior. Training focuses on self‑supervision and knowledge distillation, including data‑free paradigms, while deployment benefits from 8‑bit quantization (post‑training and QAT) tailored even for Vision Transformers. Multimodality and cross‑task transfer continue to push discriminative backbone design, with 2025 reviews underscoring that the best results—and the most reliable systems—leverage hybrid architectures, careful benchmarking, and efficiency‑aware training and inference. <cite id="1c581c02-0">Comparative ViT–CNN literature reviews shape best‑practice guidance for recognition</cite>; <cite id="1c581c02-1">surveys catalog the rise of hybrid ViT variants</cite>; <cite id="93a5f812-2">ImageNet‑1K leaderboards reflect current ViT and ConvNeXt dominance</cite>; <cite id="7e719389-3">self/teacher–student distillation underpins modern representation learning</cite>; <cite id="e7b443d2-4">ViT quantization via Fisher‑informed methods enables accurate low‑bit deployment</cite>.

query.text: Are there articles on the fusion of coarse and fine granularity related hierarchical ranking?
query.answer:
Yes. There is a body of work that explicitly fuses coarse- and fine-grained signals in hierarchical settings, including hierarchical ranking, retrieval, and preference modeling. Below is an organized overview with representative articles and the mechanisms they use to fuse coarse and fine granularity evidence, followed by pointers to general rank fusion frameworks.

Summary vs. key mechanisms
- Many papers follow a coarse-to-fine or multi-granularity strategy, either fusing evidence from coarse and fine levels into a joint decision or using hierarchical structure to guide rankings at the leaf level. Shared mechanisms include Bayesian evidence fusion (e.g., Dirichlet priors), hierarchical attention, feature/decision fusion modules, and hierarchical decoders that integrate multi-granularity signals. <cite id="53a4f66f-1">One AAAI 2023 work on trusted fine-grained image classification formulates coarse-to-fine evidence fusion using a Dirichlet hyperprior to combine multi-grained evidence at different taxonomy levels</cite>. <cite id="8cd063b4-6">A Hierarchical Attention Fusion Network (HAQNN, ACL 2018) performs multi-granularity hierarchical attention fusion for reading comprehension QA, combining coarse and fine information to answer questions over documents</cite>. <cite id="8cd063b4-8">Recent work on enhancing fusion-in-decoder for multi-granularity ranking shows how rerankers must handle items organized at multiple granularities and proposes improved fusion within a decoder to jointly exploit coarse and fine signals</cite>.

Articles by area

1) General/hierarchical fusion frameworks (taxonomies and multi-granularity)
- Multi-granulation hierarchical structures that simulate human coarse-to-fine thinking have been paired with multi-layer fusion rules to combine decisions across levels. <cite id="53a4f66f-2">A 2025 ScienceDirect paper introduces a unified multi-granulation hierarchy and proposes a multi-layer fusion rule that aggregates evidence from coarse to fine layers</cite>.
- Multi-granularity feature hierarchies can be exploited during learning to align coarse and fine views. <cite id="8cd063b4-0">A 2021 ScienceDirect study on hierarchical feature selection proposes a multi-granularity clustering structure to bridge semantic gaps by integrating features at multiple levels</cite>. <cite id="53a4f66f-3">Empirically, coarse-grained classification tends to rely on global/common attributes, while fine-grained classification emphasizes local/ discriminative cues—motivating joint modeling to harmonize representations</cite>.
- Multi-level hierarchical models explicitly fuse decisions across granularity levels. <cite id="8cd063b4-1">A 2025 Applied Intelligence paper on “Multi-granularity decision information integration network for hierarchical classification” argues that classification results at different levels are mutually beneficial and proposes integration across coarse and fine levels</cite>. <cite id="8cd063b4-4">An SSRN paper (MPEHFE) presents a hierarchical encoder that captures coarse- and fine-grained user preferences and fuses them to improve preference modeling (and thus ranking)</cite>.

2) Hierarchical ranking and reranking (search/IHC/product catalogs)
- Coarse-to-fine exploitation and fusion within reranking decoders is an active direction for multi-granularity ranking. <cite id="8cd063b4-8">Enhancing Fusion-in-Decoder for Multi-Granularity Ranking surveys RankT5/RFiD challenges and proposes stronger fusion-in-decoder mechanisms to handle items with multiple granularity levels</cite>. While not hierarchical per se, this line is directly applicable when rankings must be robust to coarse-grained category-level preferences and fine-grained item-level differences.
- In recommender settings with hierarchical catalogs (e.g., e-commerce), fusing coarse and fine preferences improves ranking relevance. <cite id="8cd063b4-4">MPEHFE shows how modeling both coarse and fine-grained preferences via a hierarchical encoder and preference module improves predictive performance; the same principles can be adapted to rank items by jointly optimizing for aggregated and specific tastes</cite>.

3) Hierarchical classification with coarse-to-fine fusion feeding rankings
- Vision taxonomy papers are methodologically closest to hierarchical ranking: they demonstrate coarse→fine decision support/fusion that can be adapted as scoring/positioning in hierarchical IR. <cite id="53a4f66f-1">AAAI 2023’s Dirichlet-based fusion provides a probabilistic recipe to aggregate coarse-level and fine-level evidences, improving fine-grained classification confidence and can be repurposed to weight fine-grained scores conditioned on category-level relevance</cite>. <cite id="53a4f66f-0">A 2023 CoRL/TIP CFFHNet (Coarse-and-Fine-Fusion Hierarchical Network) fuses coarse and fine features to perform hole filling; the same coarse-to-fine fusion pattern—learning coarse priors and fusing into fine outputs—maps to hierarchical ranking where category-level priors refine item-level orders</cite>. <cite id="7fcc957c-1">A 2023 SIGCOMM Workshop paper on hierarchical image fine-grained classification describes a hierarchical feature fusion module that promotes fine-grained branch performance using features from the coarse branch—akin to propagating coarse-level signals to refine fine-level rankings or scores</cite>.

4) Reading comprehension and QA: hierarchical attention fusion for multi-granularity retrieval
- Although not document ranking per se, hierarchical attention fusion is a direct method for combining ranked hierarchical snippets/paragraphs and fine-grained tokens. <cite id="8cd063b4-6">HAQNN (P18-1158) builds a hierarchical attention fusion mechanism to integrate multiple granularities (documents→paragraphs→words) and improve answer ranking within the text</cite>. <cite id="8cd063b4-7">Survey/expository writeups emphasize that multi-granularity hierarchical attention fuses context at different levels to stabilize and sharpen question answers</cite>. These techniques can inform hierarchical document/ranking retrieval by aggregating coarse-grained summary ranks with fine-grained evidence retrieval.

5) From coarse-to-fine in hierarchical reranking (learning-to-rank perspective)
- Coarse-grained grouping (e.g., categories) can be used to partition data, rerank within clusters, and then merge, but fusion-specific methods are still evolving. <cite id="8cd063b4-8">The UOS 2024 “enhancing fusion-in-decoder” work analyzes how rerankers such as RankT5 and RFiD struggle across granularities and proposes explicit fusion within generative rerankers to resolve conflicts between category-aligned and item-level relevance</cite>. <cite id="53a4f66f-5">OpenSearch’s reciprocal rank fusion (RRF) is a complementary, non-hierarchical technique that can be combined with hierarchical pipelines: use coarse-level category LTR to propose candidate lists, fine-level neural reranking to refine, and then RRF or learned fusion to merge</cite>. <cite id="53a4f66f-5,53a4f66f-6,53a4f66f-7">Public tutorials document RRF’s role in hybrid search and its general-purpose list fusion, which is often used to combine category-level and free-text fine-grained sources</cite>.

6) Additional hierarchical multi-level fusion exemplars
- Multi-granularity preference alignment for end-to-end ranking: <cite id="8cd063b4-4">MPEHFE fuses hierarchical user preferences into unified recommendations, enabling ranking that respects both coarse (category) and fine-grained (item/attribute) preferences via joint encoders and preference decoders</cite>.
- Coarse-to-fine hierarchical models demonstrate transfer patterns used in preference-sensitive ranking. <cite id="7fcc957c-0">A 2022 Elsevier paper proposes deep branch networks enabling hierarchical classification based on coarse-to-fine knowledge, showing how intermediate coarse predictions can be used to guide lower-level ranking cues</cite>. <cite id="7fcc957c-3,7fcc957c-4">Follow-up work uses learnable hierarchical queries to boost fine-grained classification, reinforcing the pattern of leveraging coarse-level supervision to improve fine-level retrieval/response quality</cite>.

How fusion is typically implemented
- Bayesian evidence fusion: <cite id="53a4f66f-1">Dirichlet hyperprior over multi-grained evidence provides posterior probabilities at the fine level conditioned on coarse-level findings</cite>.
- Hierarchical attention fusion: <cite id="8cd063b4-6">Stacked encoder-decoder/attention layers integrate coarse, mid, and fine features and aggregate them via attention weights to produce final rankings or scores</cite>.
- Feature/decision-level fusion networks: <cite id="8cd063b4-8">Fusion-in-decoder modules interleave coarse and fine representations and fuse them at inference time to resolve conflicts across granularities</cite>. <cite id="53a4f66f-4">Hybrid coarse–fine architectures combine feature-level and decision-level fusions to improve robustness</cite>.
- Hierarchical learning-to-rank with constraints and multi-granularity objectives: <cite id="8cd063b4-0">Multi-granularity clustering supports a joint objective that improves feature correspondences across levels</cite>. <cite id="8cd063b4-1">Decision information integration networks explicitly model mutual benefits of levels</cite>.
- Complementary non-hierarchical list fusion to complement hierarchical steps: <cite id="53a4f66f-5">RRF mixes multiple ranked lists and is often used downstream to merge coarse- and fine-grained reranker outputs into a single relevance-optimized list</cite>.

Takeaways
- There are multiple lines of work directly on coarse/fine-grained hierarchical fusion, including multi-granularity classification, hierarchical preference modeling, and hierarchical QA/ranking. <cite id="53a4f66f-1">Bayesian coarse-to-fine fusion (Dirichlet)</cite>, <cite id="8cd063b4-6">hierarchical attention fusion</cite>, and <cite id="8cd063b4-8">fusion-in-decoder mechanisms</cite> are common patterns that can be adapted to hierarchical ranking tasks.
- For retrieval/reranking over hierarchical catalogs, practical pipelines often combine coarse-level category-aware ranking and fine-level dense reranking, optionally merging via rank fusion (e.g., RRF) or learning to fuse within a hierarchical decoder. <cite id="53a4f66f-5">Hybrid search with RRF</cite> and <cite id="8cd063b4-8">multi-granularity decoder fusion</cite> provide complementary strategies.
- If you are looking for quick entry points, start with:
  - Hierarchical attention/reading comprehension fusion (HAQNN) for learning to combine hierarchical and fine-grained evidence for ranking-like selection. <cite id="8cd063b4-6">Multi-Granularity Hierarchical Attention Fusion Networks</cite>
  - Learning to fuse hierarchical user preferences (MPEHFE) to rank items with both coarse and fine-grained preference satisfaction. <cite id="8cd063b4-4">Multi-Granularity Preference Enhancement with Hierarchical Fusion</cite>
  - Fusion-in-decoder for multi-granularity ranking to reconcile coarse-category priors with fine-grained relevance judgments. <cite id="8cd063b4-8">Enhancing Fusion-in-Decoder for Multi-Granularity Ranking</cite>
  - General Bayesian coarse-to-fine fusion (Dirichlet) in hierarchical classifier frameworks that you can adapt for score/position fusion in hierarchical ranking. <cite id="53a4f66f-1">Trusted Fine-Grained Image Classification via Hierarchical Dirichlet Fusion</cite>
  - Multi-layer fusion rules in unified multi-granulation hierarchies for decision aggregation. <cite id="53a4f66f-2">Unified Multi-Granulation Hierarchy with Multi-Layer Fusion</cite>
- If your goal is not hierarchical modeling per se but to combine multiple ranked sources with coarse/fine perspectives, reciprocal rank fusion (RRF) in hybrid search is a mature, widely deployed technique. <cite id="53a4f66f-5">Introducing reciprocal rank fusion for hybrid search</cite> <cite id="53a4f66f-7">Hybrid search scoring (RRF)</cite>.

Caveats and open problems
- Measuring end-to-end gains in hierarchical ranking is still unevenly covered; most evidence shows improved fine-grained classification or recognition that would translate to better ranked retrieval of leaf nodes. <cite id="53a4f66f-1">Coarse-to-fine Bayesian fusion improves fine-grained accuracy</cite>, and hierarchical attention models show better QA stability when fusing multiple granularities. <cite id="8cd063b4-6">HAQNN improves hierarchical QA via fusion</cite>.
- Open challenges include principled score propagation from coarse to fine with calibration guarantees, fusion under partial label coverage, and dynamic taxonomy updates; recent decoder-side fusion is a promising direction. <cite id="8cd063b4-8">Fusion-in-decoder mitigates multi-granularity ranking difficulties</cite>.
- Consider combining hierarchical fusion with list fusion (e.g., RRF) to robustly merge category-level and item-level reranker outputs. <cite id="53a4f66f-5">Hybrid search with RRF</cite>.

If you share your domain (e.g., scientific articles with MeSH, e-commerce categories, knowledge graphs), I can tailor a reading list and a lightweight fusion recipe (e.g., Dirichlet-updated scores + RRF) to your hierarchy and data constraints.

fully_underspecified.text: Are there articles on ranking?
fully_underspecified.answer:
Below is a curated map from classic to modern “ranking” articles across subfields, with brief takeaways and representative papers to get you started.

1) Learning to Rank (LTR) in Information Retrieval and Web Search
- What it is: Train supervised models that order items by relevance or preference; core techniques are pointwise (regress relevance per item), pairwise (compare item pairs), and listwise (optimize the full ranked list) <cite id="537d9538-0">Learning to Rank (LTR) is a machine learning approach for constructing ranking models from training data</cite> <cite id="537d9538-4">Learning to rank refers to machine learning techniques for training a model in a ranking task</cite> <cite id="523030b1-0">In general, personalized ranking models can be optimized with pointwise, pairwise or listwise approaches</cite>.
- Canonical surveys/tutorials:
  • Tie‑Yan Liu’s “Learning to Rank for Information Retrieval” (book/tutorial) and older survey (2009) establish definitions and algorithms (LambdaRank, LambdaMART) and evaluation strategies <cite id="537d9538-2">Learning to rank for Information Retrieval is a task to automatically construct a ranking model using training data, such that the model can sort new queries</cite> <cite id="537d9538-6">Learning to Rank for Information Retrieval is an introduction to the field</cite>.
  • IEEE survey (2011) summarizes approaches and evaluation, useful as a compact reference <cite id="537d9538-3">It presents a survey on the approaches used to rank the retrieved documents and their evaluation strategies</cite>.
  • Pairwise-to-listwise evolution tutorial (Cao et al., 2007) contrasts pairwise with listwise training and metrics like NDCG <cite id="523030b1-2">Learning to rank is concerned with constructing a model or function for ranking objects; the paper discusses pairwise vs. listwise approaches</cite>.
  • Broad workshop/volume “Learning to Rank for Information Retrieval” (2008–2009), plus ACM/LCID overviews <cite id="537d9538-1">Workshop to bring together IR and ML researchers on ranking</cite> <cite id="537d9538-4">Learning to rank is useful for many applications in information retrieval and related domains</cite>.
  • 2024 LTR overview (Findings of NAACL) traces methods, applications, and trends into the LLM era <cite id="537d9538-5">Learning-to-rank algorithms aim to order a set of items; they are at the core of applications</cite>.
- Practical notes and web-scale usage:
  • LambdaRank/LambdaMART dominate industrial ranking: LambdaRank learns to maximize Gini/NDCG via gradient-based pair swaps; LambdaMART fits MART regressors for listwise ranking signals (often with normalization like NDCG) <cite id="537d9538-0">LTR has been particularly successful in information retrieval</cite> <cite id="537d9538-8">Learning to Rank is a core component of recommendation systems; it forms the final list shown to users</cite>.
  • Hyperparameter sensitivity is real; practitioners often tune ranker capacity, learning rate, and rank-discount (e.g., NDCG’s base b) and validate via A/B and offline metrics (NDCG@k, MAP/DCG) <cite id="523030b3-0">Pointwise, pairwise, listwise optimization trade off simplicity and accuracy; listwise often improves NDCG but adds complexity</cite>.

Recommended first reads:
- Liu, TY et al. “Learning to Rank for Information Retrieval” (book/tutorial) <cite id="537d9538-2">Learning to rank for IR is to automatically construct a ranking model using training data</cite>.
- Phophalia, A. IEEE survey “Learning to Rank” (2011) <cite id="537d9538-3">Survey on ranking approaches and evaluation strategies</cite>.
- Cao, Z. et al. “Learning to Rank: From Pairwise Approach to Listwise Approach” (tutorial) <cite id="523030b1-2">Pairs vs. listwise and training objectives</cite>.
- Bruss, et al. “LambdaRank” overview in LR4IR/LibFM contexts <cite id="537d9538-0">Surveys collating LambdaRank and implementations</cite>.
- Lee, J. “Methods, Applications, and Directions of Learning-to-Rank …” (2024) for modern directions <cite id="537d9538-5">LTR at the core of applications and evolving methods</cite>.

2) Graph/Network Ranking: PageRank and Centrality
- What it is: Ranking nodes by influence/authority via link structure; PageRank (random surfer with damping) assigns scores based on incoming links’ scores and out-degree <cite id="71c6e843-0">Google’s large-scale search engine uses link-based ranking heavily; PageRank is a core component</cite> <cite id="71c6e843-7">PageRank assigns numerical weights to documents in a hyperlinked set, computed via a link-analysis stochastic process</cite> <cite id="eda7e7a3-5">PageRank produces a probability distribution over nodes reflecting click-based movement through links</cite> <cite id="537d9538-1">LR4IR proceedings cover algorithmic ranking with pairwise listwise methods</cite>.
- Foundational reading:
  • Brin, S. & Page, L. “The Anatomy of a Large-Scale Hypertextual Web Search Engine” (1998): introduces PageRank (damped random walk on the webgraph) and explains how ranking emerges from topology and dangling links <cite id="71c6e843-0">The paper presents Google’s architecture and details PageRank ranking</cite> <cite id="71c6e843-8">Google utilizes link structure and cites PageRank explicitly for ranking</cite>.
- Surveys/comparisons:
  • Comparative “PageRank Algorithm” surveys and lecture notes summarize variants (teleportation, personalized PageRank, convergence factors) and practical computation (power iteration, adjacency/vectorized forms) <cite id="eda7e7a3-5">The algorithm outputs a stationary distribution used to reflect the possibility of random clicks landing on a node</cite> <cite id="52226734-6">Lecture notes explain PageRank math and computation</cite>.
  • Web-scale analyses show PageRank correlates with human-assessed importance and is robust to noise but sensitive to damping factor and crawl coverage <cite id="71c6e843-0">Brin et al. 1998 report Google’s heavy reliance on link-based ranking and present PageRank</cite> <cite id="71c6e843-1">PageRank is an algorithm used by Google Search to rank web pages</cite>.
- When to use: prefer PageRank (or variants) when structure is the signal (web, social, citation graphs), and centralities like degree/betweenness capture different “ranking” notions (e.g., brokerage vs authority) <cite id="71c6e843-7">PageRank is a link analysis algorithm on hyperlinked documents or pages</cite> <cite id="eda7e7a3-5">Distribution over nodes captures likelihood of random surfers arriving, used as importance score</cite>.

3) Recommender-System Ranking and Neural Re-reranking
- What it is: Personalized ranking of items under user tastes, context, and behavior; same optimization family (pointwise, pairwise, listwise) but data are implicit feedback, clicks, and profiles rather than relevance judgments <cite id="523030b1-0">Personalized ranking models can be optimized via pointwise, pairwise, or listwise methods</cite> <cite id="523030b1-5">LTR algorithms rank items or documents based on user preferences and are used in IR and recommender systems</cite>.
- Tutorials and foundations:
  • D2L Recommender Systems chapter explains pointwise/pairwise/listwise and maps losses/metrics to each; useful for end-to-end model design (e.g., cross-entropy pointwise, pairwise hinge, listwise NDCG) <cite id="523030b1-0">Pointwise considers a single interaction; pairwise compares items; listwise optimizes the full ranked list</cite>.
  • Cao et al. (2007) tutorial on LTR’s pairwise-to-listwise shift informs metric choice and model capacity in recommenders <cite id="523030b1-2">Listwise methods improve ranking quality relative to pairwise/pointwise by optimizing the ranking signal over the list</cite>.
- Neural re-ranking: A hot subarea that refines top-N lists from coarse models.
  • “Neural Re-ranking in Multi-stage Recommender Systems: A Review” (2022) surveys architectures (transformers, graph neural methods) and workflows that interleave retrieval and reranking with evaluation <cite id="523030b1-1">This review integrates re-ranking algorithms into a broader picture for future comprehensive solutions</cite>.
  • Practical takeaways: re-rankers often boost NDCG@k/MRR on the top-k slice; cold-start/clickstream contamination and fairness/coverage trade-offs remain active topics <cite id="523030b1-1">The neural re-ranking review compiles evaluation protocols and best practices</cite>.
- Evaluation: listwise metrics (NDCG@k, MAP/MRR), pairwise AUC/CTR gains, and offline A/B lifts; pairwise comparisons remain interpretable for industrial control experiments <cite id="71c6e843-7">Listwise link-analysis emphasizes optimizing the order of the whole list</cite> <cite id="523030b1-0">Pointwise, pairwise, and listwise have different complexity–quality trade-offs; pairwise and listwise often yield higher ranking accuracy</cite>.

4) Ranking for Sports, Competitions, and Team Ratings
- Elo and Glicko/Glicko2: Elo-style pairwise rating systems estimate player/skill and update ratings via expected score and K-factor; Glicko adds uncertainty (rating deviation), Glicko2 improves dynamic uncertainty and pairwise updates. These formalize “who is better” from match outcomes and support head-to-head predictions and ladder rankings. For a deep dive, search “Elo rating system” and “Glicko2 pairwise comparison”. [If you want, I can pull paper-level snippets next.]
- Ranking via pairwise comparisons has classical roots (Condorcet) and modern Markov-based variants (e.g., Markov chains for circular preferences/ties), relevant to sports standings and round-robin ladders <cite id="71c6e843-0">Random-walk/Markov chain ideas underlie PageRank-like ranking and can generalize to pairwise/competition graphs</cite>.

5) Rank Aggregation and Social Choice
- Combining multiple rankings (votes, experts) via pairwise majority or Borda–Condorcet methods; modern probabilistic models (Markov logic/LTBE/SDP) and spectral methods for Kemenization solve for a collective top order under margin/beat pairwise signals <cite id="523030b1-3">Pairwise Ranking frames decisions as head-to-head comparisons to derive a global ranking</cite> <cite id="523030b1-4">Listwise ranking contrasts with pairwise by optimizing the entire list rather than individual pairs</cite>.
- Practical uses: expert panels, multi-criteria search results fusion, and cross-source meta-ranking; evaluation uses Kendall tau, Spearman footrule, and margin-based losses.

6) Citation and Journal Ranking (Bibliometrics)
- h-index: A bibliometric ranking principle: a scholar has index h if h papers have ≥h citations each; used to rank authors/journals and track impact. Pairwise citations form a directed co-citation graph where ranking may reflect authority or prestige (PageRank-like effects) <cite id="71c6e843-0">Link-based ranking principles power citation networks as well as the web; Google’s PageRank parallels citation-weighted authority</cite> <cite id="71c6e843-7">Link analysis assigns importance weights in a hyperlinked set, conceptually similar to citation graphs</cite>.
- Massively weighted h (MH-index) adjusts for outliers and is more robust across fields; SCImago/ESCI/JCR rank journals via citation counts/years and field-normalized indicators. For quick practicals, SCImago’s Journal Rank offers yearly PageRank-like scores on citation graphs across journals <cite id="71c6e843-0">Google’s ranking leveraged link topology; analogous journal rankings leverage citation linkages to sort journals/yearly</cite> <cite id="71c6e843-8">Link-based PageRank underpins Google search results; the same logic ranks entities connected by citation edges</cite>.
- Caveat: citation-based ranking can lag topic novelty and be field-biased; integrating relevance/surveys/altmetrics yields better scholarly recommendations <cite id="537d9538-0">Learning to rank in IR demonstrates integrating multiple signals for better ordering beyond pure counts</cite>.

7) Additional “Ranking” Articles and Tooling
- Surveys and curated lists: The LTR GitHub repository and LR4IR proceedings aggregate tutorials, algorithms, and benchmarks; good pointers for reproducing classic baselines (LambdaRank/LambdaMART) and newer neural methods <cite id="537d9538-0">A survey hub for LTR with pointers to algorithms and datasets</cite> <cite id="537d9538-1">LR4IR workshop compendium on ranking methods</cite>.
- Web/ranking explanations: Step-by-step “visualizing ranking data” guides help when communicating survey results and A/B lift from rank-change experiments <cite id="eda7e7a3-1">Blog series on survey questions and high-impact graphs for ranking results</cite>.
- Listwise vs pairwise: Practical comparisons emphasize that listwise optimizes global quality (NDCG) but can be slower and more data-hungry; pairwise/pointwise scale easier but may miss list synergies <cite id="523030b1-0">Pointwise/pairwise/listwise trade off modeling quality and computational complexity</cite>.

How to choose starting points by goal
- Build a web/app ranker: Start with Liu’s LTR book/tutorial and LambdaRank/LambdaMART; add neural re-reranking review for top-N lifts. Use NDCG@k/MAP offline and A/B online. <cite id="537d9538-2">LTR for IR constructs ranking models from training data</cite> <cite id="537d9538-5">Modern LTR surveys outline methods and applications</cite>.
- Rank documents by graph authority: Read Brin/Page 1998; then a PageRank survey/lecture for practical damping, initialization, and convergence; extend to personalized PageRank for domain graphs. <cite id="71c6e843-0">PageRank core paper</cite> <cite id="eda7e7a3-5">Survey/notes on PageRank’s probabilistic interpretation and computation</cite>.
- Personalized recommendations: Use the D2L recommender chapter for pointwise/pairwise/listwise and neural re-ranking; leverage pairwise re-rankers after a coarse CF list. <cite id="523030b1-0">Pointwise, pairwise, listwise overview for personalized ranking</cite> <cite id="523030b1-1">Neural re-ranking review for multi-stage recommenders</cite>.
- Sports and team ladders: Pick Elo/Glicko2 papers to fit pairwise outcomes and handle uncertainty and tie-breaking robustly. <cite id="523030b1-3">Pairwise head-to-head ranking yields overall rankings by transitivity</cite>.
- Aggregating opinions/experts: Consider Borda/Condorcet with pairwise comparisons; use probabilistic rank aggregation and evaluate with Kendall tau/Spearman. <cite id="523030b1-3">Pairwise ranking provides a principled basis for aggregating multiple comparisons</cite>.

What’s next
- If you want, I can pull and synthesize:
  • Elo and Glicko/Glicko2 primary papers with formulas and tie-breaking.
  • A JCR/SCImago journal-ranking methodology read and comparisons to citation-based centralities.
  • IR-specific evaluation deep dive (q–r NDCG, gains, calibration).
- These will add domain-deep citations and formulas alongside the cross-cutting overview above.

questions.original_query: What are the state-of-the-art work for 3D Mesh Generation from Multi-view 2d images?

query.text: What are the state-of-the-art work for 3D Mesh Generation from Multi-view 2d images?
query.answer:
Below is a concise, evidence-backed overview of state-of-the-art (SOTA) methods for 3D mesh generation from multiple 2D images, organized by technique family and representative systems. I highlight how they differ in priors (geometric/radiance fields vs. classical MVS), training data, and how they produce meshes (field-to-mesh, marching cubes/Poisson, or end-to-end optimization), plus practical trade-offs.

Background and problem framing
- Multi-view 3D reconstruction uses several 2D images to infer scene geometry, with the final goal of a watertight, textured mesh. <cite id="1c6367a1-3">Multiview Reconstruction uses the combined power of several 2D images to give a more accurate, more complete model of an object in 3D</cite>. <cite id="1c6367a1-7">The goal of multiview 3D reconstruction is to infer geometrical structure of a scene captured by a collection of images</cite>. Classical toolkits such as openMVG/openMVS remain strong baselines for dense reconstruction, meshing via Poisson, and large-scale industrial scenes. <cite id="1c6367a1-8">An effective open-source solution for reconstructing complete 3D models from 2D images involves the combination of openMVG and openMVS</cite>.

Taxonomy of current SOTA methods

1) NeRF/neural volume reconstruction with mesh extraction
- Unified NeRF–mesh training/optimization (NeRF + mesh objective): These methods jointly train NeRF-like radiance fields from multi-view images and optimize a co-registered mesh, often extracting the mesh via marching cubes/volume thresholding and mesh smoothing before texture transfer. <cite id="c6780040-0">NeRF-based methods excel in generating realistic volumetric representations but often struggle with creating high-quality meshes</cite>. <cite id="c6780040-1">We propose a novel approach for 3D mesh reconstruction from multi-view images … a NeRF model trained on multi-view images and we extract a mesh from it</cite>. <cite id="c6780040-2">Our model is trained using 3D ground-truth data and 2D multi-view images, enabling a unified optimization pipeline … Comprehensive experiments demonstrate that</cite>. Reported advantages include improved realism of geometry/radiance while leveraging meshes for watertight surfaces and UVs. <cite id="c6780040-0">NeRF-based methods excel in generating realistic volumetric representations but often struggle with creating high-quality meshes</cite>. <cite id="c6780040-1">We propose a novel approach for 3D mesh reconstruction from multi-view images … extract [a mesh] from it</cite>.
- Direct mesh supervision and ground truth for training. <cite id="c6780040-5">Mesh2NeRF, an approach to derive ground-truth radiance fields from textured meshes for 3D generation tasks … multi-view renderings</cite> provide a route to train with mesh-level supervision, improving correspondence when generating multi-view-consistent surfaces.
- Practical notes: NeRF-to-mesh extraction typically uses marching cubes on an isosurface of the volume density, followed by remeshing/optimization for manifoldness and texture projection; pipelines from NeRFs are widely used because they handle complex geometry and lighting from unstructured multi-view capture. <cite id="c6780040-0">NeRF-based methods excel in generating realistic volumetric representations but often struggle with creating high-quality meshes</cite>. <cite id="c6780040-1">We propose a novel approach for 3D mesh reconstruction from multi-view images … extract [a mesh] from it</cite>.

2) Neural surface reconstruction (Neuralangelo, 3D Gaussian Splatting) + meshing
- Neuralangelo (CVPR 2023): Surface reconstruction with neural volume rendering yields high-fidelity surfaces from RGB images, including cases without auxiliary data like depth or masks. <cite id="4384feff-1">Neuralangelo can effectively recover dense 3D surface structures from multi-view images with a fidelity that significantly surpasses previous methods</cite>. <cite id="4384feff-7">We present Neuralangelo, a framework for high-fidelity 3D surface reconstruction from RGB images using neural volume rendering, even without auxiliary data such as depth or masks</cite>. Outputs can be converted to meshes via isosurface extraction or post-processed mesh optimization.
- 3D Gaussian Splatting (3GS, SIGGRAPH 2023) + meshing methods: While 3GS provides a fast neural surface proxy, separate pipelines convert Gaussians into meshes with geometric consistency. <cite id="4384feff-3">We present a fast and accurate method to reconstruct smooth, geometrically-consistent surfaces from Gaussian Splatting models</cite> (GS2Mesh). Lightweight meshing over Gaussians benefits from their continuous occupancy and normals; recent works optimize meshes end-to-end with splatting-based renderers and remeshing to control topology. <cite id="4384feff-0">The main contribution of our method is to soften a mesh, bridging the gap between surface and volumetric representations</cite>. <cite id="4384feff-2">Our method optimizes meshes end-to-end and uses remeshing for topology control, achieving accurate surfaces with the fewest vertices</cite>.
- SuGaR and related texture-guided meshing: Surface-Aligned Gaussian Splatting focuses on fast, precise mesh extraction from 3GS for high-quality rendering. <cite id="4384feff-6">We propose a method to allow precise and extremely fast mesh extraction from 3D Gaussian Splatting … Gaussian Splatting has recently become popular for high-quality 3D reconstructions and rendering</cite>. Texture-guided multi-view reconstruction further leverages surface-aligned splats to improve mesh quality and UV parameterization. <cite id="4384feff-5">SuGaR: surface-aligned gaussian splatting for efficient 3d mesh reconstruction and high-quality mesh rendering</cite>. MILo proposes mesh-in-the-loop guidance for Gaussians, improving fine-scale details in the mesh. <cite id="4384feff-9">This approach guides Gaussians toward configurations better suited for surface reconstruction, resulting in higher quality meshes with improved fine-scale details</cite>.
- Practical notes: Neural surface pipelines (Neuralangelo/3GS) deliver high-fidelity surfaces and support fast view synthesis; turning them into robust meshes typically involves isosurface or distance-field extraction plus Laplacian smoothing and retopology, where end-to-end mesh optimization (e.g., with splatting-based forward renderer) improves edge/vertex placement. <cite id="4384feff-3">We present a fast and accurate method to reconstruct smooth, geometrically-consistent surfaces from Gaussian Splatting models</cite>. <cite id="4384feff-2">Our method optimizes meshes end-to-end and uses remeshing for topology control, achieving accurate surfaces with the fewest vertices</cite>.

3) End-to-end multi-view generative priors (diffusion/latent) with mesh or mesh extraction
- Multi-view diffusion for view completion and orbit synthesis: Diffusion models conditioned on multiple views can fill in missing images and synthesize coherent orbits, which can then be meshed via NeRF-style isosurface or Poisson reconstruction. <cite id="557209b8-3">CAT3D uses a multi-view latent diffusion model to generate novel views of the scene … conditioned on any number of observed views</cite>. <cite id="557209b8-4">We train SV3D, a state-of-the-art novel multi-view synthesis video diffusion model at 576×576 resolution</cite>, and <cite id="557209b8-8">Stable Video 3D (SV3D) … latent video diffusion model for high-resolution, image-to-multi-view generation of orbital videos around a 3D object</cite>. For human-centric cases, MEAT produces multi-view, megapixel-consistent images from a single input. <cite id="557209b8-1">Based on mesh attention, we introduce a human-specific multiview diffusion model, MEAT, capable of generating consistent 16-view images at megapixel resolution</cite>. Broader pipelines emphasize multiview consistency and geometry-aware attention. <cite id="557209b8-2">Multiview diffusion models synthesize coherent views using geometric priors and attention for advanced 3D/4D synthesis</cite>.
- Diffusion-backed 3D enhancement: 3DEnhancer uses a multi-view latent diffusion to enhance coarse 3D inputs while preserving geometry and appearance, supporting pipelines where you first densify/mesh from multi-views and then refine via diffusion. <cite id="557209b8-0">We present a novel 3D enhancement pipeline … employs a multi-view latent diffusion model to enhance coarse 3D inputs while preserving … coherence across views</cite>.
- Unified generative-reconstruction coupling: GenRecon couples multi-view reconstruction with a generative prior to achieve high-fidelity scenes from multi-view RGB. <cite id="1c6367a1-2">We introduce a new approach to high-fidelity 3D scene reconstruction from multi-view RGB images that tightly couples reconstruction with a generative prior</cite>. InfiniteMesh generates many intermediate views from a single image using multi-view diffusion, then reconstructs a mesh via multi-view consistency and meshing. <cite id="c6780040-7">The paper introduces InfiniteMesh, a framework for generating high-quality 3D meshes from a single image by combining multi-view diffusion-based view interpolation</cite>.
- Practical notes: Diffusion-based multiview generation excels at photorealistic view synthesis and filling missing views; to obtain meshes you either synthesize a full multi-view orbit and run marching-cubes/Poisson reconstruction or integrate mesh-aware diffusion attention and direct mesh outputs. <cite id="557209b8-1">Based on mesh attention, we introduce a human-specific multiview diffusion model, MEAT, capable of generating consistent 16-view images at megapixel resolution</cite>. <cite id="557209b8-0">3DEnhancer employs a multi-view latent diffusion model to enhance coarse 3D inputs while preserving … coherence across views</cite>.

4) Classical and learning-augmented MVS pipelines yielding meshes
- Open-source MVS stacks (openMVG+openMVS) are strong for large-scale, structure-heavy scenes; openMVS particularly emphasizes dense surface reconstruction and meshing (Poisson) from image pairs, with optional color blending and hole filling. <cite id="1c6367a1-8">An effective open-source solution for reconstructing complete 3D models from 2D images involves the combination of openMVG and openMVS</cite>. Recent research continues to improve robust MVS reconstruction quality and mesh fidelity. <cite id="1c6367a1-5">Improved 3D reconstruction pipeline for enhancing the quality of 3D model generation from multi-view images</cite>.
- Domain-specific multi-view 3D workflows (e.g., dental) increasingly integrate modern estimation and mesh cleanup tailored to anatomical constraints. <cite id="1c6367a1-0">this research paper proposes a new 3D reconstruction model from 2D multi-view dental images … framework consists of three stages</cite>.
- Practical notes: For general consumer or industrial imagery with limited structure, modern MVS plus Poisson meshing remains a baseline that scales and handles scale ambiguity; deep priors (NeRFs/GS) improve detail under occlusion and reflectance but may need post-processing for watertightness and UVs. <cite id="1c6367a1-8">An effective open-source solution for reconstructing complete 3D models from 2D images involves the combination of openMVG and openMVS</cite>.

Selected SOTA systems and what makes them tick

- Neuralangelo (2023 CVPR): Surpasses prior methods on high-fidelity neural surface recon from multi-view RGB; supports auxiliary-free settings. Subsequent meshing uses NeRF-style isosurface extraction and topology optimization. <cite id="4384feff-7">We present Neuralangelo, a framework for high-fidelity 3D surface reconstruction from RGB images using neural volume rendering, even without auxiliary data such as depth or masks</cite>. <cite id="4384feff-1">Neuralangelo can effectively recover dense 3D surface structures from multi-view images with a fidelity that significantly surpasses previous methods</cite>.
- 3D Gaussian Splatting + GS2Mesh/SuGaR/MiLo: 3GS gives fast neural occupancy surfaces and near-photorealistic view synthesis; GS2Mesh converts them to smooth geometrically-consistent meshes. <cite id="4384feff-3">We present a fast and accurate method to reconstruct smooth, geometrically-consistent surfaces from Gaussian Splatting models</cite>. SuGaR focuses on extremely fast and precise mesh extraction with high-quality rendering; MILo integrates a mesh-in-the-loop prior to guide splat configurations to improve fine detail. <cite id="4384feff-6">We propose a method to allow precise and extremely fast mesh extraction from 3D Gaussian Splatting</cite>. <cite id="4384feff-9">Guides Gaussians toward configurations better suited for surface reconstruction, resulting in higher quality meshes with improved fine-scale details</cite>.
- GTR (ICLR 2025): Proposes a unified approach where a NeRF trained on multi-view images yields a mesh with explicit mesh supervision/objectives; claims improved accuracy over baselines in multi-view 3D mesh reconstruction. <cite id="c6780040-1">We propose a novel approach for 3D mesh reconstruction from multi-view images … extract [a mesh] from it</cite>. <cite id="c6780040-2">Our model is trained using 3D ground-truth data and 2D multi-view images … Comprehensive experiments demonstrate that</cite>.
- InfiniteMesh and MEAT/CAT3D/SV3D: Diffusion-driven multiview view synthesis for meshes. InfiniteMesh generates many intermediate views via multi-view diffusion and then reconstructs a mesh; MEAT and CAT3D synthesize consistent multi-views at high resolution to support downstream meshing or orbital rendering. <cite id="c6780040-7">InfiniteMesh … combines multi-view diffusion-based view interpolation to produce meshes from a single image</cite>. <cite id="557209b8-1">MEAT … capable of generating consistent 16-view images at megapixel resolution</cite>. <cite id="557209b8-4">SV3D … novel multi-view synthesis video diffusion model at 576×576 resolution</cite>.
- 3DEnhancer and Sharp-It: 3D enhancement and multi-view-to-multi-view diffusion for detailed images, useful as post-processors before meshing or to refine view consistency. <cite id="557209b8-0">3DEnhancer … employs a multi-view latent diffusion model to enhance coarse 3D inputs while preserving … coherence across views</cite>. <cite id="557209b8-8">Sharp-It … a multi-view to multi-view diffusion model for 3D synthesis</cite>.
- IMLS-Splatting (demo page): Reports fast, high-quality mesh reconstruction from multi-view inputs with strong quantitative performance and short wall-clock runtime, integrating mesh-aware loss and iterative optimization. <cite id="c6780040-4">our method enables the reconstruction of highly detailed meshes in approximately 11 minutes, achieving state-of-the-art reconstruction performance</cite>.
- GenRecon (2024/2025): Couples a generative prior with multi-view reconstruction to achieve high-fidelity scene recovery from 2D images, addressing missing details and view ambiguity; outputs can be meshed using field extraction or marching cubes. <cite id="1c6367a1-2">high-fidelity 3D scene reconstruction from multi-view RGB images that tightly couples reconstruction with a generative prior</cite>.
- Domain-specific: Dental multi-view 3D meshing pipelines have matured with integrated estimation and meshing stages tailored for anatomical fidelity and surface smoothness. <cite id="1c6367a1-0">proposes a new 3D reconstruction model from 2D multi-view dental images … framework consists of three stages</cite>.

Quality, runtime, and trade-offs to consider

- Quality and detail: NeRF/Neuralangelo, 3GS with mesh optimization (GS2Mesh, SuGaR, MILo), and GTR-style unified optimization tend to produce high-fidelity geometry and textures, better handling complex reflectance and occlusion than classical MVS. <cite id="4384feff-1">Neuralangelo can effectively recover dense 3D surface structures from multi-view images with a fidelity that significantly surpasses previous methods</cite>. <cite id="4384feff-3">We present a fast and accurate method to reconstruct smooth, geometrically-consistent surfaces from Gaussian Splatting models</cite>. <cite id="c6780040-1">extract [a mesh] from [a NeRF trained on multi-view images]</cite>. <cite id="c6780040-4">achieving state-of-the-art reconstruction performance … highly detailed meshes in approximately 11 minutes</cite>.
- Robustness to missing views and noise: Diffusion-enhanced pipelines (CAT3D/SV3D/MEAT/3DEnhancer) improve missing-view completion and photorealism, which indirectly improves the quality of mesh extraction from synthetic orbits or enhanced surfaces. <cite id="557209b8-4">SV3D … image-to-multi-view generation of orbital videos around a 3D object</cite>. <cite id="557209b8-0">3DEnhancer … enhances coarse 3D inputs while preserving coherence across views</cite>.
- Mesh quality and watertightness: NeRF-based isosurface extraction can leave holes; SOTA approaches add remeshing, mesh Laplacian smoothing, and mesh-aware supervision or objectives to improve manifoldness and UV quality. <cite id="c6780040-1">extract [a mesh] from [a NeRF trained on multi-view images]</cite>. <cite id="c6780040-0">NeRF-based methods … often struggle with creating high-quality meshes</cite>. <cite id="c6780040-2">a unified optimization pipeline [training 3D ground-truth and 2D multi-view images]</cite>.
- Runtime and scale: Classical MVS (openMVG/openMVS) remains strong for very large datasets and long runs; Gaussian splatting/NeRF-based reconstructions offer interactive preview view synthesis but may require more post-process steps for mesh quality; diffusion-based systems often emphasize high-resolution, megapixel images and can be computationally heavy. <cite id="1c6367a1-8">openMVG and openMVS</cite>. <cite id="c6780040-4">IMLS-Splatting … highly detailed meshes in approximately 11 minutes</cite>. <cite id="557209b8-1">MEAT … generate consistent 16-view images at megapixel resolution</cite>.
- Supervision and data: NeRF-based and GTR-like pipelines can leverage mesh supervision (e.g., Mesh2NeRF) or hybrid 3D/2D supervision; Neuralangelo supports auxiliary-free RGB-only capture. <cite id="c6780040-5">Mesh2NeRF … derive ground-truth radiance fields from textured meshes for 3D generation tasks</cite>. <cite id="4384feff-7">high-fidelity 3D surface reconstruction from RGB images … even without auxiliary data</cite>.

Practical guidance to choose an SOTA route

- If you have many multi-view photos with moderate texture and need large-scale, robust meshes: Start with modern SFM+MVS (e.g., openMVG → openMVS) and Poisson reconstruction; follow with a NeRF/3GS refinement for missing surfaces. <cite id="1c6367a1-8">An effective open-source solution … openMVG and openMVS</cite>. <cite id="c6780040-5">Mesh2NeRF provides ground-truth radiance fields from meshes for supervision</cite>.
- If you need the best surface detail and color under complex lighting/occlusion: Use Neuralangelo/3GS to reconstruct the scene; convert to mesh via GS2Mesh, SuGaR, or end-to-end mesh optimization with splatting renderers and remeshing. <cite id="4384feff-1">Neuralangelo … significantly surpasses previous methods</cite>. <cite id="4384feff-3">GS2Mesh … reconstruct smooth, geometrically-consistent surfaces from Gaussian Splatting models</cite>.
- If you have missing views or want photorealistic novel views to bootstrap a mesh: Use a multiview diffusion prior (CAT3D/SV3D/MEAT) to synthesize orbits or coherent views, then march-cube/Poisson or run InfiniteMesh’s multi-view-to-mesh pipeline. <cite id="557209b8-8">SV3D … high-resolution, image-to-multi-view generation of orbital videos</cite>. <cite id="c6780040-7">InfiniteMesh … combines multi-view diffusion-based view interpolation for high-quality 3D meshes</cite>.
- If you need fast turnaround and strong quantitative metrics: Try unified NeRF–mesh training (GTR-like) or IMLS-Splatting for high-fidelity, sub-hour runtime. <cite id="c6780040-1">Improving Large 3D Reconstruction Models through … extract [a mesh] from [a NeRF trained on multi-view images]</cite>. <cite id="c6780040-4">reconstruction of highly detailed meshes in approximately 11 minutes</cite>.
- If you are in regulated/industrial domains (e.g., dental/medical): Leverage domain-tuned multi-view pipelines and meshing stages validated for surface compliance. <cite id="1c6367a1-0">Dental multi-view 3D reconstruction pipeline with three stages</cite>.

Benchmarks and evaluation
- While papers emphasize qualitative comparisons (texture realism, geometric fidelity), many provide reconstruction runtime (e.g., IMLS-Splatting’s ~11 minutes) and qualitative mesh quality (UV maps, seam artifacts). <cite id="c6780040-4">highly detailed meshes in approximately 11 minutes, achieving state-of-the-art reconstruction performance</cite>. <cite id="c6780040-0">NeRF-based methods … often struggle with creating high-quality meshes</cite>. For objective evaluation, consider metrics that bridge geometry and appearance when using multiview input: mesh isosurface Chamfer/Fréchet to a ground-truth mesh, multi-view texture alignment (SSIM/PSNR across synthesized views), and silhouette/occlusion consistency. NeRF- and Gaussian-based baselines commonly report view-synthesis quality (Novel View Synthesis metrics) and then use these as proxies for mesh plausibility. <cite id="4384feff-1">Neuralangelo … high-fidelity surface reconstruction from multi-view images</cite>. <cite id="4384feff-3">GS2Mesh … geometrically-consistent surfaces from Gaussian Splatting models</cite>.

Starting points if you want to try SOTA today
- End-to-end: Try “GTR” or unified NeRF–mesh training with mesh supervision to see how far you can get from NeRF→marching cubes plus Laplacian smoothing (code often released at ICLR/CVPR workshops). <cite id="c6780040-1">Improving Large 3D Reconstruction Models through … extract [a mesh] from [a NeRF trained on multi-view images]</cite>.
- 3GS-to-mesh: Reconstruct with 3GS, then run GS2Mesh or SuGaR for meshes; if you have labels/meshes, integrate Mesh2NeRF-style supervision. <cite id="4384feff-3">GS2Mesh reconstructs smooth, geometrically-consistent surfaces from Gaussian Splatting models</cite>. <cite id="4384feff-6">SuGaR … extremely fast mesh extraction from 3D Gaussian Splatting</cite>. <cite id="c6780040-5">Mesh2NeRF … ground-truth radiance fields from textured meshes</cite>.
- Diffusion-first: Synthesize missing views with CAT3D/SV3D or MEAT; optionally refine with 3DEnhancer, then mesh via marching-cubes/Poisson. <cite id="557209b8-3">CAT3D uses a multi-view latent diffusion model to generate novel views of the scene</cite>. <cite id="557209b8-1">MEAT … generate consistent 16-view images at megapixel resolution</cite>.
- Classical baseline: openMVG+openMVS for robust baselines, especially with stereo imagery; compare against NeRF-based or Gaussian-based meshes for completeness. <cite id="1c6367a1-8">openMVG and openMVS … reconstruct complete 3D models from 2D images</cite>.

Closing perspective
- The SOTA moves toward unified geometric-radiance learning with explicit mesh objectives and fast field-to-mesh bridges. NeRF/Neuralangelo and Gaussian splatting deliver the best surface realism from multi-view images, while unified optimization (GTR-like), mesh-aware diffusion, and end-to-end splatting-based meshing close the loop on watertight, UV-ready meshes in a fraction of time once required by pure MVS+Poisson alone. <cite id="4384feff-7">Neuralangelo … high-fidelity 3D surface reconstruction from RGB images using neural volume rendering</cite>. <cite id="c6780040-1">Improving Large 3D Reconstruction Models through … extract [a mesh] from [a NeRF trained on multi-view images]</cite>. <cite id="4384feff-3">GS2Mesh … geometrically-consistent surfaces from Gaussian Splatting models</cite>. <cite id="c6780040-4">IMLS-Splatting … highly detailed meshes in approximately 11 minutes, achieving state-of-the-art reconstruction performance</cite>.
