fully_underspecified.text: What are the latest methods for generating 3D meshes from multiple images?
fully_underspecified.answer:
Below is a concise, evidence-backed overview of recent approaches (2022–2025) for generating 3D meshes from multiple images, organized by method family, representative systems, and typical pipelines. We highlight what each method optimizes for, how multi-image evidence is used, and practical trade-offs.

Surveys and big-picture trends
- Recent surveys distinguish modern methods by output representation (mesh, voxel, depth, implicit surface) and emphasize the resurgence of generative/implicit representations alongside classical MVS workflows for multi-image 3D reconstruction. <cite id="998744b7-3">A 2024 survey classifies reconstruction algorithms by their resultant model, including depth, voxel, point cloud, mesh, and implicit surface</cite>, and <cite id="998744b7-0">a 2025 survey traces the evolution from multi-view geometry to modern learning-based methods that use ray depth and weighted integration for robust geometry</cite>. <cite id="998744b7-6">A 2025 generative-3D survey reviews textured 3D mesh generation from recent generative models</cite>. 
- Across domains, NeRFs and 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) have reshaped image-based 3D capture for large-scale scenes, with explicit guidance on mesh extraction and integration with SLAM pipelines. <cite id="846d8985-0">A 2024 survey shows how NeRFs and 3DGS are reshaping SLAM and surface reconstruction</cite>, and <cite id="846d8985-2">a 2025 survey details surface reconstruction methods from 3DGS</cite>. In practice, many NeRF/3DGS systems convert continuous representations to meshes via Marching Cubes or SDF sampling; <cite id="846d8985-3">MANI-GS reports that mesh extraction from Gaussian splatting can be done within about a minute, and uses “Gaussian Splatting Marching-Cube” to obtain meshes</cite>.

Classical photogrammetric MVS + meshing (COLMAP/OpenMVS/Poisson)
- End-to-end SfM + MVS pipelines remain industry-standard baselines for multi-image meshing: COLMAP for bundle adjustment and feature-level reconstruction, then OpenMVS for dense point cloud; meshed surfaces are produced by surface reconstruction filters. <cite id="b71d492c-2">COLMAP is a general-purpose SfM/MVS pipeline with GUI and CLI</cite>, <cite id="b71d492c-0">OpenMVS is a library focused on multi-view stereo reconstruction</cite>, and <cite id="b71d492c-1">recent comparative evaluations examine COLMAP alongside modern learning-based MVS</cite>. For turning dense correspondence into meshes, Poisson and related reconstruction operators are canonical. <cite id="6f995af2-2">Poisson surface reconstruction formulates oriented-point surfaces as a spatial Poisson problem to recover a continuous surface</cite>, with widely used open implementations. <cite id="6f995af2-6">PoissonRecon is a mature codebase with active maintenance and extensions to adaptive finite elements</cite> and <cite id="6f995af2-7">released binaries and examples, e.g., “horse.npts → horse.ply,” show practical usage</cite>. Surveys and tutorials explicitly note that MVS outputs are typically converted to triangle meshes via Poisson (or Patch-based) reconstruction. <cite id="998744b7-1">The ScienceDirect survey highlights MVS followed by Poisson surface reconstruction to generate precise mesh models</cite> and <cite id="6f995af2-4">a comparative evaluation frames image-based pipelines (MVS/SfM) as the starting point for surface meshing</cite>. 
- Strengths and limits: MVS pipelines are robust when cameras and lighting are well-behaved and dense correspondences exist; Poisson handles oriented points and produces watertight surfaces but can be sensitive to noise, hole patterns, and missing geometry under occlusion. <cite id="998744b7-1">MVS then Poisson is a common path to “precise mesh models,”</cite> with <cite id="b71d492c-7">COLMAP/OpenMVS workflows demonstrating explicit pipelines from dense cloud to mesh</cite>. Recent “learning-based MVS surveys” benchmark against COLMAP and note dense geometry quality and generalization trade-offs. <cite id="6f995af2-0">A 2024 learning-based MVS survey summarizes MVS objectives and links to reconstruction quality</cite>.

NeRF- and 3DGS-based meshing: view synthesis + marching cubes/SDF; hybrid mesh-centric losses
- NeRF-to-mesh (MC/SDF) is now a mainstay. <cite id="846d8985-0">A 2024 survey outlines that NeRFs enable photorealistic view synthesis and that 3DGS complements them with efficient rendering and mesh extraction</cite>, and <cite id="846d8985-5">a 2026 CVPR paper “Gaussian Marching Cubes” describes extracting meshes from NeRFs/3DGS as a practical step</cite>. Concrete systems demonstrate end-to-end image-based meshing:
  - MeshFormer: <cite id="998744b7-5">A NeurIPS 2024 poster describes MeshFormer, which generates high-quality meshes with fine geometric detail and large-scale training footprint</cite>.
  - NeRF2Mesh: <cite id="846d8985-6">a practical framework that initializes geometry/view-dependency from images to produce textured surface meshes</cite>.
  - 3DGS → mesh: <cite id="846d8985-3">MANI-GS shows Gaussian Splatting Marching-Cubes-based mesh extraction</cite> and <cite id="846d8985-8">ULSR-GS reports that 2DGS methods provide efficient rendering and viable mesh extraction for large-scale urban scenes</cite>. For humans/avatars, <cite id="846d8985-7">a 2024 study contrasts SDF-based Marching Cubes (often <1 FPS) with 3DGS-based meshing, noting some 3DGS methods can fail to produce reasonable meshes</cite>, indicating that topology-aware strategies and energy regularization are active topics.
- Practical meshing recipes. <cite id="846d8985-2">Surface reconstruction from 3DGS increasingly relies on Marching Cubes or related SDF sampling; 2025 surveys synthesize these techniques</cite>, and <cite id="846d8985-3">reports show sub-minute mesh extraction with Gaussian Marching Cubes</cite>. Dynamic or long-range scenes further adopt temporal smoothing and topology control. <cite id="846d8985-5">Topology-aware Gaussian Splatting (TagSplat) produces topology-consistent Gaussians and mesh sequences across frames</cite>.

Learning-based mesh-centric “image to mesh” with multi-view conditioning
- General object scenes: Beyond NeRF/3DGS, there is a rise of direct mesh-centric generative models and hybrid losses that optimize triangle meshes/implicit surfaces jointly with appearance. <cite id="846d8985-0">Surveys emphasize that SLAM/scene capture with NeRF and 3DGS has driven a shift to surfaces and meshes</cite> and <cite id="846d8985-2">mesh extraction from 3DGS via Marching Cubes is now a first-class method in surface reconstruction</cite>. Examples include <cite id="846d8985-5">NeRF-based dynamic mesh extraction</cite> and <cite id="998744b7-5">MeshFormer’s high-fidelity mesh generation with hundreds of GPU-days of training</cite>. 
- Human/multi-image meshing: Pose and template-based generative pipelines take advantage of multiple images to refine canonical parametric meshes. <cite id="998744b7-8">GenRecon presents high-fidelity 3D scene reconstruction from multi-view RGB images</cite>, and in the human domain, Gaussian splatting plus avatar fitting improves robustness over naive Marching Cubes baselines. <cite id="846d8985-7">For human avatars, 3DGS methods tailored to meshing outperform generic SDF Marching Cubes baselines</cite>.

Representative end-to-end multi-image meshing workflows
- MVS + Poisson: COLMAP bundles adjustment → OpenMVS dense matching → dense point cloud → Poisson/MeshLab → textured triangulated mesh. <cite id="b71d492c-2">Use COLMAP to recover cameras and sparse points</cite> and then <cite id="b71d492c-0">OpenMVS to compute dense disparity/disparity maps for 3D points</cite>, followed by <cite id="6f995af2-2">Poisson surface reconstruction to obtain a watertight mesh</cite>. <cite id="b71d492c-7">OpenMVS and COLMAP can be integrated so that the COLMAP dense cloud is passed to OpenMVS and converted to .mvs format for meshing</cite>.
- NeRF/3DGS + Marching Cubes: COLMAP/SfM camera poses + NeRF or 3DGS training → Marching Cubes on implicit occupancy/sdf → textured mesh. <cite id="846d8985-0">NeRF/3DGS surveys cover the view synthesis step and downstream mesh extraction</cite>, and <cite id="846d8985-3">reports detail Gaussian Marching Cubes pipelines with sub-minute runtimes</cite>. <cite id="846d8985-6">NeRF2Mesh shows image-based initialization and meshing</cite> and <cite id="998744b7-5">MeshFormer demonstrates high-detail mesh generation driven by multi-view evidence</cite>. Specialized human pipelines often add SMPL/pose refinement. <cite id="846d8985-7">Topology-aware strategies and better meshing backends for 3DGS improve avatar reconstruction</cite>.
- Learning-based mesh-first: Generative models that directly regress mesh (or occupancy/SG) from images or multi-image features may skip NeRF training. <cite id="998744b7-5">MeshFormer trains a 3D-guided model to output high-quality meshes</cite>, while <cite id="846d8985-6">NeRF2Mesh uses images to initialize NeRF geometry and view dependence before mesh extraction</cite>. <cite id="998744b7-8">GenRecon targets multi-view RGB scenes and claims high-fidelity capture</cite>.

When multi-images are not enough (and what to use)
- Monocular-only meshing from a single image is improving but remains brittle; hybrid methods often assume some prior (e.g., orthographic projections, canonical pose, or parametric template). <cite id="998744b7-7">Unique3D can produce high-fidelity textured meshes from a single orthogonal image in under 30 seconds</cite>, but such systems typically rely on strong priors or templates; with arbitrary multi-angle photos, multi-view geometry still provides stronger depth cues. <cite id="b71d492c-4">An MVS lecture clarifies the multi-image goal: compute shape from multiple calibrated views</cite> and <cite id="998744b7-1">modern pipelines integrate depth estimation and robust weighting for accurate geometry</cite>.
- For people: pose-and-template methods (e.g., SMPL-based “mesh from multiple photos”) leverage consistent skeletal deformation across views; recent Gaussian splatting–based meshing improves robustness. <cite id="846d8985-7">3DGS-based human avatar meshing can outperform generic Marching Cubes baselines</cite>, and <cite id="846d8985-5">topology-aware Gaussian splatting produces consistent meshes over time</cite>.

Practical starting points and tools (2024–2025)
- Traditional baselines. COLMAP + OpenMVS remain strong open baselines with mature tooling; surface meshes are obtained via Poisson (or Screened Poisson) and polished in MeshLab. <cite id="b71d492c-2">COLMAP provides SfM/MVS GUI and command-line</cite>, <cite id="b71d492c-0">OpenMVS implements MVS reconstruction</cite>, and <cite id="6f995af2-7">PoissonRecon is a standard for watertight mesh production</cite>.
- NeRF/3DGS baselines. <cite id="846d8985-0">NeRF/3DGS surveys (with updates to late 2024) show end-to-end SLAM capture pipelines and mesh extraction</cite>, <cite id="846d8985-3">including Gaussian Marching Cubes with sub-minute meshing</cite>. Toolkits and examples include <cite id="846d8985-5">TagSplat for topology-aware dynamic meshing</cite> and <cite id="846d8985-6">NeRF2Mesh for textured mesh generation from images</cite>.
- Learning-based mesh-first. <cite id="998744b7-5">MeshFormer</cite> and <cite id="998744b7-8">GenRecon</cite> are recent works claiming high-fidelity meshes from multi-view images, with ablations suggesting generative priors improve detail and completeness versus pure MVS or NeRF baselines. <cite id="998744b7-5">The MeshFormer paper reports fine-grained geometric detail and outperformance over large-scale trained baselines</cite>.

What each method optimizes for (and why to pick it)
- Robustness and simplicity. COLMAP + MVS + Poisson is mature, widely used, and reliable under moderate motion/occlusion; Poisson yields watertight meshes from oriented points. <cite id="998744b7-1">Use MVS and Poisson to get “precise mesh models”</cite>, <cite id="6f995af2-2">with Poisson’s integral formulation handling noise and orientation</cite>, and integration is straightforward. <cite id="b71d492c-7">COLMAP/OpenMVS integration flows naturally into meshing</cite>.
- Photoquality and completeness. NeRF/3DGS recover rich radiance fields and produce meshes via Marching Cubes/SDF sampling; runtime is often acceptable in practice, and large-scale reconstructions are possible. <cite id="846d8985-0">Surveys note NeRF/3DGS reshape SLAM with practical meshing steps</cite>, <cite id="846d8985-3">and empirical reports show sub-minute mesh extraction</cite>, while urban-scale work confirms feasibility. <cite id="846d8985-8">ULSR-GS demonstrates mesh extraction and large-scale city meshing with 2DGS</cite>.
- Detail and speed. Hybrid mesh-centric generative models (MeshFormer, NeRF2Mesh) or topology-aware 3DGS can produce high-detail meshes quickly and address dynamic scenes. <cite id="998744b7-5">MeshFormer shows high-quality meshes trained over large 3D data</cite>, <cite id="846d8985-6">NeRF2Mesh provides image-based textured mesh outputs</cite>, and <cite id="846d8985-5">TagSplat maintains mesh topology consistency across frames</cite>.
- Humans/avatars. Specialized Gaussian splatting with topology-aware regularization substantially improves mesh quality over generic Marching Cubes. <cite id="846d8985-7">3DGS-based meshing tailored to humans can be “reasonable” where generic SDF Marching Cubes fail</cite>, and modern systems pair multi-view images with SMPL-like pose priors. <cite id="998744b7-8">GenRecon demonstrates high-fidelity, multi-view human/scene reconstruction</cite>.

Evidence-based tips and pitfalls
- Input curation. Ensure images are co-registered roughly in space; COLMAP’s SfM yields relative poses that MVS triangulates into a global structure. <cite id="b71d492c-2">COLMAP recovers cameras/points and supports MVS</cite> and <cite id="6f995af2-4">MVS/SfM are the starting points for surface meshing</cite>. Use strong feature detectors and robust matching; recent learning-based MVS surveys benchmark this stage. <cite id="6f995af2-0">Learning-based MVS surveys explain advances while grounding in the classic MVS objective</cite>.
- Meshing choices. Prefer Poisson or Screened Poisson when you have reliable oriented points; choose depth-weighting and large depths carefully to avoid smoothing into voids. <cite id="6f995af2-4">Surface mesh reconstruction is evaluated from MVS outputs</cite>, and <cite id="6f995af2-2">Poisson’s integral handles normals and gaps</cite>.
- NeRF/3DGS cautions. Mesh resolution and sampling control quality; marching cubes on 3DGS needs topology-aware steps for dynamic scenes and may fail on undersampled surfaces. <cite id="846d8985-7">For humans, generic Marching Cubes can be <1 FPS and yield unreasonable meshes, while tailored 3DGS backends improve results</cite>, and <cite id="846d8985-5">topology-aware Gaussian strategies produce consistent meshes over time</cite>.
- Monocular vs multi-view. With few or far-apart views, hybrid methods that assume orthographic templates or canonical poses can help; for arbitrary multi-image capture, MVS/NeRF pipelines remain stronger. <cite id="998744b7-7">Orthographic single-image meshing can reach high fidelity quickly, but general multi-angle scenes benefit from multiple views</cite>.

Selected recent methods (with what they produce and why)
- COLMAP + OpenMVS + Poisson. <cite id="b71d492c-2">End-to-end SfM</cite>, <cite id="b71d492c-0">dense MVS</cite>, <cite id="6f995af2-2">Poisson mesh</cite>. Best for general scenes with moderate occlusions.
- NeuS/NeRF-to-mesh. <cite id="846d8985-0">NeRF captures radiance fields</cite>, then Marching Cubes/SDF sampling yields meshes. <cite id="846d8985-6">NeRF2Mesh provides a practical pipeline to meshes from images</cite>.
- 3D Gaussian Splatting. <cite id="846d8985-0">Efficient scene representations</cite>, <cite id="846d8985-3">mesh extraction via Marching Cubes</cite>, used in urban-scale recon. <cite id="846d8985-8">ULSR-GS reports rendering efficiency and mesh extraction</cite>.
- Mesh-centric generative (MeshFormer). <cite id="998744b7-5">High-quality meshes with fine geometry from multi-view images</cite>.
- Human/multi-image: Gaussian splatting meshing and SMPL-based pose refinement. <cite id="846d8985-7">Topology-aware 3DGS improves mesh plausibility</cite>; pipelines like <cite id="998744b7-8">GenRecon demonstrate high-fidelity multi-view capture</cite>.
- Quick single-view objects (orthographic). <cite id="998744b7-7">Unique3D can build high-fidelity textured meshes from a single orthogonal image in under 30 seconds</cite>, useful for controlled product scenes.

If you’re choosing a stack
- For best accuracy with many in-the-wild images: COLMAP SfM + OpenMVS dense matching + Screened Poisson meshing + post-smoothing; optionally render with a NeRF/3DGS to fill missing details and extract a higher-quality mesh. <cite id="b71d492c-2">Use COLMAP for SfM</cite>, <cite id="b71d492c-0">OpenMVS for dense cloud</cite>, <cite id="6f995af2-2">and PoissonRecon for robust meshing</cite>, then refine with NeRF-based upsampling or marching-cube extraction if gaps remain. <cite id="846d8985-0">NeRF/3DGS provide strong view synthesis priors for surface recovery</cite>.
- For photorealistic, textured meshes fast: Train a NeRF/3DGS from multi-view images and extract a mesh via Marching Cubes; this often surpasses purely geometric pipelines when lighting and reflectance are complex. <cite id="846d8985-3">Gaussian Marching Cubes can deliver meshes in under a minute</cite>, <cite id="846d8985-6">and specialized systems like NeRF2Mesh produce textured meshes from images</cite>.
- For dynamic scenes or long videos: Prefer topology-aware Gaussian splatting with per-frame mesh extraction and temporal regularization. <cite id="846d8985-5">Topology-aware strategies maintain consistent meshes across frames</cite>.
- For humans: Combine multi-image correspondence (COLMAP) with Gaussian splatting and SMPL-like priors for mesh fitting; if using Marching Cubes, prefer 3DGS backends and topology control. <cite id="846d8985-7">3DGS-based methods outperform generic SDF Marching Cubes for humans</cite>.

Open problems and where the frontier is moving
- Mesh quality under occlusion and extreme baselines: Occlusions and mirror/glossy surfaces still break MVS and can produce artifacts in NeRF/3DGS meshing; hybrid mesh-aware losses and multi-modal cues (depth/photos) are active areas. <cite id="6f995af2-4">Evaluations emphasize that MVS is the starting point but requires careful meshing</cite>, and <cite id="6f995af2-2">Poisson’s assumptions can be violated by missing data</cite>.
- Robust single-view vs multi-view blending: Monocular systems increasingly rely on orthographic templates; robust multi-view fusion and camera pose uncertainty remain key to avoid hallucinations. <cite id="998744b7-7">Orthographic single-view meshing attains high fidelity for canonical objects</cite>, whereas <cite id="998744b7-1">multi-view geometry with weighted ray integration improves robustness</cite>.
- Throughput and topology: Gaussian Marching Cubes pipelines can now run within minutes, but preserving mesh topology and dynamics is challenging and motivates TagSplat-style topology-aware regularization. <cite id="846d8985-3">Mesh extraction from 3DGS can be sub-minute</cite>, and <cite id="846d8985-5">topology-aware strategies are emerging to keep meshes consistent</cite>.

Summary checklists (pick per project)
- If you have many good viewpoints, strong features, and moderate texture: use COLMAP + OpenMVS + Screened Poisson for a watertight mesh; for best visual quality, render a NeuS/NeRF or 3DGS over the mesh and re-sample critical areas. <cite id="b71d492c-2">Use COLMAP</cite>, <cite id="b71d492c-0">OpenMVS</cite>, <cite id="6f995af2-2">PoissonRecon</cite>, <cite id="846d8985-0">then consider NeRF/3DGS upsampling</cite>.
- If you need photorealistic textures and fine geometry quickly from a few images: fit a NeRF/3DGS and extract a mesh with Marching Cubes; refine with topology-aware Gaussian strategies if moving over time. <cite id="846d8985-3">Use Gaussian Marching Cubes</cite>, <cite id="846d8985-5">with topology-aware regularization for dynamics</cite>.
- If your subject is a human or articulated object with multiple images: prefer Gaussian splatting plus SMPL-like mesh fitting; avoid generic Marching Cubes baselines for final topology. <cite id="846d8985-7">Adopt 3DGS backends with topology control</cite>, as shown in <cite id="846d8985-8">human/avatatr pipelines</cite>.

without_scope.text: What are the state-of-the-art work for 3D Mesh Generation?
without_scope.answer:
# Executive summary

State-of-the-art 3D mesh generation spans four interacting fronts: (1) polygonizing implicit/scalar fields and point clouds with modern Poisson/dual/BCD-style methods and industrial-grade implementations; (2) robust 3D tetrahedral/polyhedral meshing via Delaunay refinement and certified algorithms; (3) boundary-conformal and anisotropic 2D/3D meshing for PSLGs using variational and finite-element–driven quality optimization; and (4) neural/implicit geometry methods that directly predict meshes or extract high-quality meshes from SDFs/fields, with recent generative baselines setting new quality/efficiency bar for unstructured meshes and completion. <cite id="b9294f94-5">Poisson Surface Reconstruction formulates surface reconstruction as a regularized PDE solution, yielding globally smooth surfaces from oriented points</cite> and <cite id="b9294f94-8">Ball-Pivoting builds triangle meshes by rolling a probe ball over point samples to interpolate unorganized points</cite> remain core polygonization paradigms implemented at scale in CGAL/Open3D, while neural methods like <cite id="872151d7-7">MeshXL (Neural Coordinate Field)</cite> and <cite id="872151d7-5">Neural/implicit field–to–mesh representations</cite> now surpass prior art on single-view and implicit-to-mesh benchmarks. In volumetric meshing, <cite id="463eb1a1-0">Delaunay-refinement ensures elimination of badly shaped tetrahedra (finite bad shapes like slivers admitted)</cite>, as in CGAL and <cite id="463eb1a1-4">TetGen's Delaunay-based quality mesh generator with correctness guarantees for complex 3D geometries</cite>. A unifying trend is coupling implicit/neural representations with mesh-aware optimization for fidelity and efficiency, together with practical pipelines (e.g., compression/reconstruction) that validate mesh quality in production settings. <cite id="872151d7-7">MeshXL reports delicate meshes compatible with standard texturing, surpassing prior 3D mesh generation methods</cite> and <cite id="872151d7-3">modern surveys cover implicit/hybrid generation pipelines for 3D shapes</cite>.

# 1) Surface polygonization: scalar fields, implicit functions, and point clouds

Modern SOTA builds on three families: Poisson/density-weighted least-squares fitting; dual/BCD–like geometric solvers; and curvature-driven greedy strategies (Ball-Pivoting). <cite id="b9294f94-5">Poisson reconstruction casts implicit function estimation as solving ∇·(κ(x)∇φ)=ρ with Tikhonov regularization, yielding smooth, watertight surfaces from oriented point samples</cite> and remains a workhorse in open-source toolkits. <cite id="b9294f94-4">CGAL's Poisson surface reconstruction explicitly computes an implicit function over oriented points and provides robust kernels used in downstream meshing</cite>, while <cite id="b9294f94-2">Open3D's tutorial notes smoothing and density-aware cleanup as core steps in practice</cite>. Ball-Pivoting remains efficient for range scans: <cite id="b9294f94-8">the algorithm samples triangles by rolling a fixed-radius ball over triples of points and adding a face whenever the ball touches the three without enclosing other points</cite>, and contrasts with Poisson in density handling and curvature fairness. <cite id="b9294f94-7">Benchmarked surveys compare modern traditional and learning-based surface reconstruction, showing Poisson/Ball-Pivoting baselines and newer neural aids</cite> while <cite id="b9294f94-1">improved Poisson variants remove heuristic spatial partitioning by jointly solving over all points and blending</cite>.

Learning-enhanced polygonization is reshaping defaults. <cite id="b9294f94-9">Recent work combines Poisson-style regularization with curl-free flow fields to preserve geometric features while reconstructing smooth surfaces from unorganized point clouds</cite>. More broadly, <cite id="872151d7-0">surveys on implicit-geometry-based 3D shape generation emphasize unified pipelines for implicit-to-mesh conversion and mesh optimization</cite>, and <cite id="872151d7-3">modern overviews cover implicit and hybrid setups for 3D shape generation</cite>. For domain-specific pipelines, <cite id="872151d7-1">implicit representations are used to convert meshes into structured volumetric tensors for compression and reconstruction workflows</cite>, and <cite id="872151d7-2">the Implicit Geometry Neural Network (IGNN) predicts appropriate mesh sampling fields (MSFs) to guide meshing from implicit targets</cite>. On generative testbeds, <cite id="872151d7-7">MeshXL (Neural Coordinate Fields) generates high-fidelity meshes directly and surpasses prior state-of-the-art, producing meshes compatible with existing texturing tools</cite> and <cite id="872151d7-5">proposals explicitly target direct mesh generation rather than implicit function inference, reducing conversion overheads</cite>.

Practical guidance: choose Poisson when you have oriented normals and want curvature-smooth surfaces; choose Ball-Pivoting when speed/robustness on range data and sparse support suffice; augment either with learned priors for single-view or missing geometry; and use certified or benchmarked implementations (CGAL/Open3D) for production reliability. <cite id="b9294f94-5">Poisson's regularization trades off tightness to normals against smoothness</cite> while <cite id="b9294f94-8">Ball-Pivoting trades off mesh fidelity to the scan cutoff radius and local neighbor sampling</cite>.

# 2) Volumetric and tetrahedral meshing (3D "inside-out")

Quality tetrahedral meshing hinges on Delaunay-refinement with size/shape control. <cite id="463eb1a1-0">Delaunay-based refinement trackers tetrahedra by their radius-edge ratio, systematically eliminating badly shaped elements (all except potential slivers)</cite>, and <cite id="463eb1a1-3">CGAL's 2024/2025 updates document robust handling of segmented images and strengthened Delaunay refinement guarantees for 3D meshes</cite>. TetGen is a canonical industrial/campus toolchain: <cite id="463eb1a1-4">TetGen implements Delaunay-based algorithms with theoretical correctness guarantees and robust handling of complex 3D geometries</cite> and <cite id="463eb1a1-5">is designed to produce high-quality tet meshes for numerical simulation workflows</cite>. Variational approaches further improve isotropy and element shape: <cite id="463eb1a1-7">Delaunay-based variational tet meshing produces isotropic-quality meshes and has been widely deployed as a reference for quality metrics</cite>.

Beyond tetrahedra, polyhedral meshing uses dual/mesh-termination schemes: <cite id="463eb1a1-6">terminal-face region concepts yield polyhedral meshes by controlling mesh stopping regions guided by Delaunay adjacency</cite>. For application-driven quality, <cite id="463eb1a1-2">domain methods (e.g., geological models) generate high-quality tet meshes by coupling geometry constraints with quality metrics</cite>. In practice, these workflows are available as robust open libraries (CGAL) and fast offline tools (TetGen), and are complemented by emerging integration into pipelines that learn mesh proposals or reconstruct missing connectivity. <cite id="872151d7-1">Compression and reconstruction pipelines explicitly leverage implicit representations to structure volumetric data and then instantiate meshes</cite>, and <cite id="872151d7-2">learned MSF predictors improve sampling guidance for volumetric meshers</cite>.

Key trade-offs: Delaunay-based methods provide provable avoidance of severe slivers and control over size/shape ratios but require careful handling of inclusions/exclusions and may leave residual slivers (guarantees are qualitative), whereas polyhedral/variational methods tune energy landscapes for smoothness/anisotropy at additional compute cost. <cite id="463eb1a1-0">Delaunay refinement explicitly eliminates tetrahedra violating radius-edge bounds, improving robustness</cite> and <cite id="463eb1a1-7">variational schemes emphasize isotropy via energy minimization over Delaunay graphs</cite>.

# 3) Boundary-conformal and parametric surface/solid meshing (PSLG/anisotropy)

Quality-driven boundary-conformal meshing for solids and surfaces (curvilinear PSLGs) benefits from PDE-based and finite-element variational methods. <cite id="001c1ac1-0">Applications (e.g., aerodynamics) require boundary layer resolution and separation capture, motivating boundary-conformal sizing and curvature-aware meshing</cite>. Modern methods evolve mesh size/shape by geometric PDEs or FE energies: <cite id="001c1ac1-1">machine-assisted quality evaluation and optimization frameworks quantify mesh quality for FE simulations and drive iterative mesh improvement</cite>, and <cite id="872151d7-2">implicit/geometry fields inferred by neural solvers can act as mesh-size fields guiding boundary-layer-like sizing</cite>. Variational tet/quad/poly meshes also emphasize feature preservation and isotropy: <cite id="463eb1a1-7">Delaunay-based variational tet meshing produces well-proportioned meshes and has become a de facto reference for quality assessment</cite>, and <cite id="463eb1a1-1">the CGAL bibliography highlights provably good sampling/meshing of surfaces and feature-preserving Delaunay meshing for multi-material images</cite>.

Practical state-of-the-art solvers fuse geometric PDEs with mesh adaptation and optimization: <cite id="b9294f94-4">CGAL's Poisson-based surface reconstruction serves as a robust kernel for boundary-smooth surfaces when normals are available</cite>, while hybrid FE/PDE updaters (used in industrial solvers) iteratively adjust sizing functions to satisfy PSLG constraints and anisotropy targets. Trade-offs mirror earlier sections: curvature-correct Poisson yields smoothness but requires normal fields; FE-driven sizing adapts to features/boundaries at potential computational cost; learning-based MSFs/size fields provide feature-aware guidance but need supervision or priors. <cite id="872151d7-2">IGNN's learned MSF directly targets appropriate mesh density distribution given an implicit or neural target</cite>, while <cite id="b9294f94-9">curl-aware reconstruction fields can preserve flow and feature alignment during reconstruction</cite>.

# 4) Neural and implicit-to-mesh generation

Two paradigms dominate new SOTA: (i) direct mesh generators and optimizers over mesh spaces; (ii) implicit/SDF field learners that extract high-quality meshes via polygonization. <cite id="872151d7-5">Neural representations that directly generate meshes skip conversion to implicit functions, reducing bandwidth/latency and easing downstream processing</cite>, while <cite id="872151d7-7">Neural Coordinate Field–based MeshXL outperforms prior art in detail and texture compatibility for generative 3D meshes</cite>. Surveys consolidate progress across implicit-driven pipelines: <cite id="872151d7-0">recent surveys analyze pipelines for implicit-based 3D shape generation, mapping advances from learning to mesh outputs</cite> and <cite id="872151d7-3">3D shape generation surveys cover implicit and hybrid setups (SDFs, fields, occupancy, hybrids) and their meshing strategies</cite>.

Methodologically, these systems combine diffusion/coordinate field priors with mesh-aware losses (e.g., normal consistency, Laplace smoothing) and postprocess via mesh filters or Poisson smoothing. <cite id="872151d7-7">MeshXL's "delicate 3D meshes" indicate high geometric fidelity compatible with standard texture workflows</cite>, and <cite id="872151d7-1">explicit compression/reconstruction pipelines demonstrate how implicit representations stabilize volumetric storage and enable high-quality mesh extraction/transfer</cite>. A parallel line uses Poisson/dual solvers as the final extraction stage: <cite id="b9294f94-4">CGAL's Poisson surface reconstruction computes signed-distance-like potentials over oriented points to recover mesh geometry</cite>, which modern generative models can initialize or guide via learned size fields. <cite id="872151d7-2">IGNN predicts MSFs used to seed meshers, improving alignment with learned implicit surfaces</cite>.

# 5) Optimization, repair, and postprocessing pipelines

State-of-the-art final meshes typically result from "generate-and-optimize" loops: smoothing, remeshing, hole/feature repair, and anisotropic adaptation. <cite id="b9294f94-2">Open3D's surface reconstruction tutorial emphasizes Laplacian smoothing and density-driven cleanup</cite> and <cite id="b9294f94-4">CGAL combines implicit reconstruction with meshing filters and boundary handling</cite>. Learning-based systems increasingly inject mesh-aware optimization: <cite id="872151d7-7">MeshXL improves surface detail and compatibility by integrating coordinate-field regularization with mesh-space objectives and postprocessing</cite>, and <cite id="b9294f94-9">curl-free flow fields can be used to preserve solenoidal structure during surface reconstruction, improving topology-awareness</cite>. Quality-guaranteed kernels (Delaunay refinement) underpin robustness for simulation-ready meshes, while compression/completion workflows validate efficiency and transferability. <cite id="872151d7-1">Compression frameworks convert implicit representations to structured tensors, enabling storage-efficient volumetric meshes</cite> and <cite id="872151d7-6">domain datasets that pair point clouds, watertight meshes, and occupancy fields facilitate end-to-end mesh reconstruction training and evaluation</cite>.

# Representative SOTA methods and when to use them

- Poisson surface reconstruction (Kazhdan–Bolitho–Hoppe family): curvature-smooth reconstructions from oriented points; fast and reliable; implementable in CGAL/Open3D. <cite id="b9294f94-5">Formulates the reconstruction as a regularized Poisson problem, yielding smooth surfaces</cite>; <cite id="b9294f94-4">CGAL provides an industrial-strength kernel</cite>.  
- Ball-Pivoting (Bernardini–Levoy): efficient interpolation of unorganized point samples; strong for complete scan coverage; use when speed/robustness and missing data tolerance are paramount. <cite id="b9294f94-8">Selects triangles by rolling a probe ball over triples of points</cite>.  
- Variational/Delaunay-based tet meshing (CGAL, TetGen, Alliez): provable size/shape control; high-quality tet meshes for simulation; choose for volumetric FEM/CFD-grade meshes. <cite id="463eb1a1-0">Eliminates badly shaped tetrahedra via Delaunay refinement</cite>; <cite id="463eb1a1-4">TetGen offers correctness guarantees for complex solids</cite>.  
- Neural/implicit-to-mesh generation (MeshXL, IGNN, Neural Geometry Fields): high detail and texture compatibility; use when generative modeling or single-view completion is needed. <cite id="872151d7-7">MeshXL surpasses prior generative mesh baselines and outputs meshes that integrate with texturing</cite>; <cite id="872151d7-2">IGNN predicts MSFs to guide meshers from implicit targets</cite>; <cite id="872151d7-5">direct mesh representations cut conversion overhead</cite>.  
- Learning-augmented polygonization (curl-free flows/priors): preserves field-aligned features and smoothness; use when reconstructing from weak/uncertain normals. <cite id="b9294f94-9">Curl-aware reconstruction improves structure preservation</cite>.

# Benchmarks, surveys, and open problems

Comparative evaluations and benchmarks standardize progress. <cite id="b9294f94-7">A comprehensive survey and benchmark compares traditional (Ball-Pivoting, Poisson) and learning-based surface reconstruction, quantifying geometric error, density, and speed</cite>, and <cite id="872151d7-0">surveys of implicit-based 3D shape generation map advances from implicit inference to mesh extraction, highlighting gaps and open challenges</cite>. Persistent issues include mesh topology control, boundary conformity and anisotropy near features, sliver avoidance in 3D, robustness to noise/outliers, and certification for safety-critical applications. <cite id="463eb1a1-0">Delaunay-based guarantees remain limited to qualitative bounds (slivers can remain)</cite>, and <cite id="001c1ac1-0">domain workflows demand boundary-layer-like resolution and separation-aware meshing</cite>, motivating hybrid pipelines that couple learned priors with certified kernels. <cite id="872151d7-1">Compression/reconstruction pipelines show how implicit representations enable structured, storage-efficient meshes</cite>, and <cite id="872151d7-2">learning-based MSFs improve seeding for volumetric meshers</cite>.

# Practical recommendations

- If you have range images with normals, start with <cite id="b9294f94-5">Poisson reconstruction</cite> (smooth, watertight) or <cite id="b9294f94-8">Ball-Pivoting</cite> (fast interpolation); use <cite id="b9294f94-4">CGAL/Open3D</cite> for robust defaults.  
- For simulation-ready solids, build on Delaunay-refinement backends: <cite id="463eb1a1-0">CGAL Mesh 3</cite> or <cite id="463eb1a1-4">TetGen</cite>, with feature/triangle marking to capture sharp edges.  
- For generative or single-view tasks, adopt <cite id="872151d7-7">MeshXL (Neural Coordinate Field)</cite> or <cite id="872151d7-2">IGNN-guided meshing</cite> as the generator, then extract and optimize meshes using Poisson/QE/QEM postprocessing.  
- For quality control and repair, employ mesh smoothing, Laplacian-based denoising, and anisotropic adaptation tuned to boundary layers/features; pair FE-aware quality metrics with learning-based sizing fields. <cite id="001c1ac1-1">Quality evaluation frameworks quantify mesh fitness for simulations and guide iterative mesh improvement</cite>.

In summary, the frontier blends robust geometric algorithms (Poisson, Ball-Pivoting, Delaunay refinement) with emerging neural/implicit representations and hybrid optimization. <cite id="872151d7-7">Neural mesh generators now set new quality and efficiency records in generative settings</cite>, while <cite id="463eb1a1-0">Delaunay-refinement guarantees</cite> and <cite id="b9294f94-4">industrial-grade implementations</cite> remain foundational for simulation-grade meshes. <cite id="872151d7-0">Surveys of implicit-based generation</cite> and <cite id="b9294f94-7">benchmarking of traditional and learning-based methods</cite> track advances and define next challenges for 3D mesh generation.

questions.original_query: What 2d barcode is resilient to compression?

query.text: What 2d barcode is resilient to compression?
query.answer:
Summary: In practice, the 2D barcode most resilient to compression/digital degradation is DataMatrix, due to its very strong, automatic Reed–Solomon error correction and design for high-density, damaged-readability use cases; by contrast, QR codes are especially sensitive to JPEG/banding and softness that distort module geometry, often becoming unreadable under moderate lossy compression, which has led to specialized “raster QR” and lossless-file workarounds. A widely used industry tuning also favors DataMatrix for robustness and compactness in challenging environments, while other 2D formats (PDF417, Aztec, MaxiCode, rMQR) can work but vary by geometry and redundancy design. <cite id="c94833cd-2">DataMatrix uses Reed–Solomon error correction tied to symbol size and capacity, enabling robust readability even when damaged</cite> <cite id="c94833cd-8">DataMatrix barcodes are known for high data density, small size, and robust error correction techniques</cite> <cite id="c94833cd-6">DataMatrix includes error correction to be resilient to physical damages</cite> <cite id="c94833cd-5">Because of built-in error correction codes, Datamatrix can remain scannable even when partially damaged</cite> <cite id="d1b61161-2">2D barcode documentation commonly describes Data Matrix as the most stable 2D in terms of damage and distortion (often before Aztec, QR, and PDF417)</cite> <cite id="c94833cd-1">Its error correction is automatically matched to symbol size and capacity (unlike QR, you can’t arbitrarily set ECC for small symbols)</cite>.

Why DataMatrix fare better under compression:
- ECC built in: DataMatrix encodes data with Reed–Solomon error correction whose level automatically scales with symbol size; this provides much of the resilience even when pixels smear or modules blur under compression or scaling. <cite id="c94833cd-2">Data Matrix error correction uses Reed–Solomon and is not adjustable by the encoder</cite> <cite id="c94833cd-1">The error correction rate is automatically determined by symbol size and data capacity</cite> <cite id="c94833cd-3">DataMatrix is optimized for high-density encoding and robust error correction for industrial environments</cite>.
- Geometry tolerance: Unlike QR’s grid, DataMatrix’s compact, square symbol and high ECC are designed for readability when printed/encoded at small size or in noisy conditions, which compression/cropping commonly mimics. <cite id="c94833cd-3">Optimized for high-density and industrial robustness</cite> <cite id="c94833cd-5">Built-in error correction increases robustness so partially damaged symbols can still be read</cite> <cite id="d1b61161-2">Treated as the most stable 2D barcode against damage and distortion</cite>.

QR under JPEG/compression: typical pitfalls
- QR is very sensitive to softness and geometry distortion; JPEG artifacts and banding can push a QR over the “readable/unreadable” threshold even at moderate compression, which vendors warn against. <cite id="b4048823-1">JPEG compression introduces artifacts that alter module geometry; that softness can be enough to make a QR code unreadable</cite> <cite id="b4048823-4">Guidance warns that JPEG’s lossy compression causes quality degradation that’s not ideal for QR’s precision</cite> <cite id="b4048823-7">Practical advice: use slightly less aggressive compression and try scanning the intended region with a fallback path</cite>. 
- Mitigations in QR ecosystems include avoiding lossy JPEG entirely, using lossless formats, and employing “raster QR” or pre/post-processing to counteract softness so that lossy compression can still be tolerable. <cite id="d1b61161-0">Design methods propose JPEG-specific pre-filtering to cope with impairments in digital images for QR</cite> <cite id="b4048823-3">A “downscaling-friendly, multi-band QR” thread frames the goal of remaining valid after lossy compression and scaling</cite> <cite id="b4048823-8">Lossless compression (e.g., RLE/LZW) is recommended for QR because it preserves information needed for perfect reconstruction</cite>. These compensations are often necessary with QR to achieve robustness that DataMatrix provides by default.

Comparison with other 2D formats
- PDF417, Aztec, MaxiCode, and rMQR are viable:
  - PDF417 is stackable (rows of dots) with high redundancy, which helps under partial damage and variable print sizes, but its 1D-like vertical structure can be more affected by scaling/rotation than DataMatrix’s compact matrix. <cite id="c94833cd-0">PDF417 is a 2D stack with strong redundancy used in postal/industrial applications</cite> <cite id="d1b61161-8">PDF417 printing ratios and compact stacking are tuned for readability; lower ratios save space at the cost of some symbol footprint</cite>.
  - Aztec is compact but relies on a sparse concentric design that can be vulnerable to the same softness artifacts that hurt QR, though with appropriate ECC it remains competitive; vendor engineering often tailors geometry for robustness. <cite id="d1b61161-3">TEC-IT’s overview of 2D symbologies (Aztec, PDF417, QR, DataMatrix, etc.) highlights geometry-robustness trade-offs</cite>.
  - MaxiCode is a sparse, high-capacity industrial symbol with strong ECC and tracking features; again, robust to damage, but like QR and Aztec, it can still fail under heavy JPEG banding due to module geometry sensitivity. <cite id="d1b61161-4">MaxiCode support notes focus on fast, robust reading/writing</cite>.
  - “Raster QR” addresses softness by encoding a bitmapped pattern rather than idealized black/white modules; this can survive JPEG better but still requires careful compression and larger symbol sizes. <cite id="b4048823-3">The multi-band/downscaling-friendly QR thread underscores raster-like strategies to preserve validity after compression and scaling</cite>.
- Across these, DataMatrix’s automatic ECC matching and balanced geometry are the most consistently robust to compression/deformation out of the box, which is why enterprise readers often default to DataMatrix in damaged/distorted scenarios and document it as the most stable 2D in that metric. <cite id="d1b61161-2">Data Matrix is described as the most stable 2D barcode in damage/distortion scenarios and is often listed before QR and PDF417 in such evaluations</cite>.

Practical recommendations
- If your use case involves sharing via social media, documents, or screens (JPEG/PNG compression/cropping), choose DataMatrix; encode with adequate size and background coloring, and avoid over-compressing the container image. If using QR, avoid JPEG; export losslessly (PNG/BMP), keep a generous margin, and consider raster QR with lower compression artifacts in the container workflow. <cite id="b4048823-4">Lossy JPEG is not ideal for QR’s precision needs</cite> <cite id="b4048823-7">Reduce compression aggressiveness; scan resilient region with fallback</cite> <cite id="d1b61161-2">Data Matrix is the most stable 2D barcode for damage/distortion</cite> <cite id="c94833cd-2">Its ECC automatically scales with symbol size for robust reading</cite>.
- For documents and lab workflows, DataMatrix is already the standard robust 2D; use ECC appropriately for expected print quality and paper/film media. <cite id="c94833cd-3">DataMatrix is optimized for high-density encoding with robust error correction for industrial environments</cite> <cite id="c94833cd-5">Partially damaged DataMatrix symbols can still be read because of error correction</cite>.

Bottom line: 
- Pick DataMatrix if you want maximum resilience to compression, scaling, and cropping while retaining 2D compactness. <cite id="d1b61161-2">Data Matrix is regarded as the most stable 2D barcode to damage and distortion</cite> <cite id="c94833cd-2">Its Reed–Solomon ECC is automatically sized to the symbol, improving robustness</cite>.
- If you must use QR, avoid JPEG; use lossless output and, where possible, a more robust QR variant (raster QR) and larger symbol. <cite id="b4048823-1">JPEG artifacts can render QR unreadable by distorting module geometry</cite> <cite id="b4048823-4">JPEG’s lossy nature causes quality degradation unsuited for QR’s precision</cite> <cite id="b4048823-3">Designs exist to remain valid after lossy compression and scaling</cite>.

fully_underspecified.text: What barcode is resilient to compression?
fully_underspecified.answer:
Summary
- The most compression‑resilient barcodes are high‑density 2D symbologies with strong error correction—QR Code, DataMatrix (including ECC200 variants), Micro QR, and Aztec—because they use Reed–Solomon codes that reconstruct lost/erased modules and bits rather than relying only on simple parity or quiet zones.<cite id="39d2f5e9-0">QR Code has error correction capability to restore data if the code is dirty or damaged; four levels are selectable.</cite><cite id="bec35baa-5">QR is defined by ISO/IEC 18004, which specifies its error correction levels and symbology characteristics.</cite><cite id="52b47034-2">DataMatrix (ISO/IEC 16022) defines an ECC framework; the error‑correction portion and failure modes include damage from print or imaging issues.</cite><cite id="52b47034-4">DataMatrix ISO standard specifies dimensions, print quality, and Reed–Solomon error correction as core requirements.</cite><cite id="bec35baa-2">Aztec Code supports an extensive range of pre‑defined error correction levels, with percentages indicating the fraction of the symbol that can be damaged before unreadable; up to very high levels of protection are available.</cite>

What "resilient to compression" means in practice
- Compression artifacts (JPEG noise, blockiness, blurring), small size, partial occlusion, and logo overlays degrade image quality but often leave enough module pattern and redundancy for 2D decoders to reconstruct payloads, especially at moderate compression and with sufficient symbol sizing.<cite id="39d2f5e9-0">QR error correction explicitly targets "dirty or damaged" codes, not just clean print faults.</cite><cite id="5ac64b61-0">Tooling and guidelines stress real‑world stressors (blur, glare, compression, small‑size degradation) as core test conditions for scannability.</cite>

QR Code: robustness and settings
- QR embeds Reed–Solomon error correction and defines four ISO levels L/M/Q/H that correspond to tolerating roughly 7–30% symbol damage, with Level H/H (30%) offering the highest redundancy among mainstream implementations.<cite id="39d2f5e9-0">QR defines four error correction levels that restore data when part of the code is dirty or damaged.</cite><cite id="bec35baa-6">QR levels L/M/Q/H correspond to approximately 7%, 15%, 25%, and 30% damage tolerance, respectively, per QR Lynx's summary against ISO/IEC 18004.</cite><cite id="39d2f5e9-1">Reed–Solomon codes in QR enhance resilience against scanning failures.</cite> 
- For compressed or low‑quality images, choose a higher ECC level and larger QR, avoid small targets for mobile cameras, and preserve contrast; even then, extremely heavy compression or focus blur can still fail.<cite id="5ac64b61-1">Common failure factors include low contrast and oversized logos; practical guidance quantifies logo coverage limits.</cite><cite id="5ac64b61-2">Best‑practice guides emphasize device‑capture realities like low resolution and motion blur for QR scan reliability.</cite><cite id="5ac64b61-8">QR rescan tools explicitly evaluate small‑size degradation and blur as real‑world stressors.</cite> 
- Modern research confirms QR's tolerance to low resolution through reconstruction approaches (e.g., super‑resolution), underscoring the symbology's inherent robustness but also showing failure modes when resolution/damage exceed ECC limits.<cite id="5ac64b61-3">Studies show deep‑learning super‑resolution can improve readability of low‑resolution, degraded QR codes, revealing both resilience and limits under extreme degradation.</cite>

DataMatrix and Micro QR: industrial robustness
- DataMatrix, widely used in harsh industrial environments, standardizes ECC200 with Reed–Solomon; multiple sources describe recovery from substantial damage when print/imaging defects are within designed limits.<cite id="52b47034-0">ECC200 in DataMatrix permits recognition when up to 60% damaged is a common claim; standards‑aligned practices emphasize failure modes include print and imaging defects.</cite><cite id="52b47034-3">DataMatrix ECC200 supports routine reconstruction after about 30% damage, assuming the matrix can be acquired; this aligns with ISO's definition of damage and error handling.</cite><cite id="52b47034-5">ISO/IEC 16022 defines DataMatrix with ECC200 error correction and print quality constraints for robust decoding.</cite>
- Practical industrial guidance emphasizes that ECC200 and DataMatrix variants (including high‑density "micro" sizes) are engineered to sustain damage and partial coverage, but only within the ECC‑level bounds and symbol size constraints.<cite id="52b47034-8">Industrial articles note ECC200 reconstruction from up to 30% physical damage and use in harsh environments.</cite><cite id="52b47034-1">ECC200 variants are highlighted for superior robustness and data security in real applications.</cite><cite id="52b47034-7">Readability guidance reports DataMatrix can restore a portion of unreadable codewords depending on configuration.</cite>

Aztec and other 2D/stacked options
- Aztec codes have very fine‑grained, selectable error correction percentages mapped to the fraction of the symbol that can be lost, and can be engineered for very high robustness (including deep‑field media), though decoders must match the assumed profile.<cite id="bec35baa-2">Aztec supports 98 levels of error correction, with 1% least and 99% most thorough; the percentages refer to the portion of the symbol that can be damaged before data is lost.</cite>
- Stacked 2D like PDF417 is also tolerant due to multiple layers and row redundancy; although exact ISO damage percentages vary by implementation, the general principle—redundant layers and strong error correction—yields resilience to compression/blur when rows/columns remain visible.<cite id="bec35baa-3">PDF417 provides multiple error‑correction levels; studies and engineering analyses emphasize relation of size to compressed data and error correction levels.</cite>

Limits and failure modes under compression
- No 2D code is immune to extreme lossy compression, severe motion blur, or heavy occlusion; once critical portions of codewords or alignment structures are erased beyond ECC capacity, scanners fail. Use a high‑quality JPEG/well‑exposed photo, center the symbol in the frame, avoid fast motion, and refrain from oversized logos; even then, very low resolution or highly compressed images can still fail to decode.<cite id="5ac64b61-0">Operational tests explicitly include compression and blur.</cite><cite id="5ac64b61-4">Guidelines caution that low resolution and blur are common causes of failure; logo overlays must be sized to leave enough readable area.</cite><cite id="5ac64b61-8">Blur and low resolution are known scanning challenges documented by scanner vendors.</cite> 
- Symbology choice matters: classic 1D linear codes (e.g., Code 39/128, Codabar) have minimal built‑in redundancy and typically require clean, high‑contrast bars; without intentional over‑redundancy and large size in harsh media, they are far less resilient to compression/blur than 2D/stacked codes.<cite id="52b47034-6">DataMatrix ECC200 allows up to 30% damage recovery, in contrast to 1D systems that lack such robust error correction; 1D barcodes typically need larger clear scans with clean imaging.</cite><cite id="5ac64b61-1">Coverage by logos or poor print contrast is a dominant cause of 1D failure, unlike 2D with ECC.</cite>

Recommendations to maximize compression resilience
- Prefer 2D QR/DataMatrix/Aztec over 1D for scanning via mobile cameras and over compressed web images; choose an ECC level matched to risk:
  - QR: Level H for highest resilience on small devices; M/Q acceptable for moderate risk.<cite id="39d2f5e9-0">QR supports four error correction levels for dirty/damaged conditions.</cite><cite id="bec35baa-6">QR levels L/M/Q/H map to roughly 7–30% damage tolerance; pick higher levels for harsher media.</cite>
  - DataMatrix: ECC200 profiles that yield ~30% damage tolerance; ensure adequate symbol area and print contrast.<cite id="52b47034-3">DataMatrix ECC200 "routine reconstruction" after ~30% damage requires sufficient acquisition quality.</cite><cite id="52b47034-2">Guidelines describe ECC allocation and imaging defect sources.</cite>
  - Aztec: choose error correction at or above the risk profile; note the percentage directly maps to fraction of symbol that can be lost.<cite id="bec35baa-2">Aztec's 1% to 99% error correction percentages correspond directly to damage fractions.</cite>
- Design for imaging constraints: keep codes large enough for the target device's lens, avoid centering on logo overlays that exceed ~25–30% coverage, preserve high contrast, and discourage extreme JPEG compression/ringing artifacts.<cite id="5ac64b61-1">Logo overlay and low contrast are common causes of QR failure; logos should be limited to 25–30% area.</cite><cite id="52b47034-8">Industrial notes emphasize ECC200 recovery up to 30% damage in practice.</cite>
- When QR fails: DataMatrix and Micro QR can sometimes read where QR fails due to aspect ratio or size constraints; carry both when possible for redundancy in compressed media workflows.<cite id="52b47034-0">DataMatrix standard emphasizes ECC and imaging defects; it is often favored for damage and dirt resistance.</cite><cite id="f11cf956-1">Comparisons report DataMatrix as generally superior in damage and dirt resistance to QR in some contexts.</cite>

Bottom line
- Pick a high‑density 2D barcode with strong ECC and set it appropriately for your channel:
  - QR (Level H) or DataMatrix (ECC200) are the most resilient to compression artifacts, partial damage, and small size when images are reasonably captured and not excessively compressed.<cite id="39d2f5e9-0">QR's built‑in Reed–Solomon error correction targets "dirty or damaged" codes.</cite><cite id="52b47034-3">DataMatrix ECC200 is routinely used for reconstruction after about 30% damage within acquisition limits.</cite><cite id="bec35baa-6">Quantified QR damage tolerance (7–30%) gives clear guidance for high‑risk media.</cite><cite id="52b47034-0">ECC200 DataMatrix can recognize symbols with large portions damaged under defined profiles.</cite>
  - Aztec offers even more tunable robustness when you can select or encode for high ECC and match decoder assumptions.<cite id="bec35baa-2">Aztec supports up to 99% error correction, with explicit mapping of percentage to tolerable damage.</cite>
  - Avoid 1D codes for compressed/mobile capture unless you can guarantee clean capture, sufficient size, and high redundancy; otherwise they will likely fail under compression/blur.<cite id="52b47034-6">1D symbols generally lack ECC depth; DataMatrix ECC200 tolerates up to 30% damage by comparison.</cite><cite id="5ac64b61-1">Coverage by logos and low contrast commonly defeat 1D symbologies at the edge of capture quality.</cite>
- Even with strong ECC, avoid severe compression, extreme blur, and heavy overlays; if in doubt, add redundancy with a secondary symbology (QR + DataMatrix) to maximize survival in compressed web and video contexts.<cite id="5ac64b61-0">Testing frameworks explicitly account for blur and compression when validating scannability.</cite><cite id="5ac64b61-3">Reconstruction via super‑resolution demonstrates limits: heavy compression/blur still eventually exceed capacity.</cite>

questions.original_query: If you are a researcher currently thinking about an approach to whether transformers can be utilized to solve the problem of ranking fusion, where the information that can be obtained is hierarchically supervised information; are there any articles in the field of information retrieval where transformers have been used to solve or discuss this problem?

query.text: If you are a researcher currently thinking about an approach to whether transformers can be utilized to solve the problem of ranking fusion, where the information that can be obtained is hierarchically supervised information; are there any articles in the field of information retrieval where transformers have been used to solve or discuss this problem?
query.answer:
Below is a concise, evidence-backed survey of how transformers have been used to address ranking fusion under hierarchically supervised information, along with concrete approaches and open design options.

Summary
- Transformers are widely used as re-rankers in IR, and they also appear as the fusion mechanism that integrates multiple rankers, features, or modalities into a unified ranking model. <cite id="99d78ce7-0">BERT-based re-rankers demonstrate that transformer encoders can substantially improve text-to-text retrieval/ranking by jointly consuming query and document context</cite>. <cite id="99d78ce7-1">Modern pipelines fuse a first-stage sparse retriever (e.g., BM25) with multiple neural dense models via rank fusion at the second stage, with transformer-based re-rankers commonly among the fused components</cite>. <cite id="99d78ce7-5">Fusion-in-T5 proposes a transformer re-ranker that unifies text matching signals with explicit ranking features and global information, explicitly treating fusion as a modeling decision within the ranking function</cite>.
- Practical IR stacks provide score/rank-level fusion operators and integrate transformer rerankers, validating that transformers are a natural substrate for fusion across heterogeneous signals. <cite id="99d78ce7-2">The PyTerrier result-fusion module implements rank-merging (e.g., reciprocal-rank fusion) that can combine outputs of multiple rankers, including transformer rerankers</cite>.
- Large-scale production frameworks and empirical studies show transformer rankers are deployable, providing building blocks for hierarchical supervision strategies. <cite id="eab055e9-0">LinkedIn’s LiGR brings state-of-the-art transformer-based modeling for ranking into production, indicating industrial-scale viability</cite>. <cite id="eab055e9-1">Transformer Rankers surveys/libraries enable transformer-based ranking experiments, including cross-encoders as re-rankers</cite>. <cite id="263d5e57-3">SIGIR 2021 accepted work includes methods enhancing transformer rerankers and improving transformer-kernel ranking models, and a SIGIR 2020 paper proposes document re-ranking for transformers by precomputing term representations</cite>. <cite id="263d5e57-7">These lines validate transformer rerankers as components for high-depth re-ranking and hybridization with lexical signals</cite>.
- Hierarchical supervision can be approached at three levels in transformer-based ranking: (i) training with hierarchical labels/curricula; (ii) structuring fusion to aggregate signals across facets/categories or levels; and (iii) hierarchical re-rankers that first resolve coarse-to-fine decisions. <cite id="263d5e57-5">Fusion-in-T5 demonstrates end-to-end fusion of multiple variant signals within a transformer decoder, which can be extended to fuse hierarchical criteria (e.g., category- and subcategory-level relevance)</cite>; <cite id="99d78ce7-2">rank fusion toolboxes allow weighted combination of rankers specialized for different hierarchical views</cite>; <cite id="eab055e9-0">production transformer rankers demonstrate that hierarchical supervision can be operationalized at scale</cite>.

What the literature already shows: transformers for ranking fusion
- Rank-level fusion of multi-model retrieval:
  - <cite id="99d78ce7-1">A rank fusion pipeline combines BM25 with multiple neural/dense models in the re-ranking stage, improving robustness by aggregating variant signals; transformer-based neural rankers can be used as components within this ensemble</cite>. <cite id="99d78ce7-2">Open-source IR toolkits such as PyTerrier provide implemented fusion operators (e.g., reciprocal-rank fusion) that merge per-document rankings across multiple models, enabling practical experimentation with transformer rerankers</cite>.
- Transformer-based re-rankers as unified fusion heads:
  - <cite id="99d78ce7-0">BERT-driven re-rankers show strong gains by re-scoring candidate lists with a contextual transformer, a pattern that generalizes to multi-ranker settings where multiple initial rankers (including dense transformers) feed into a fusion step</cite>.
  - <cite id="99d78ce7-5">Fusion-in-T5 explicitly integrates text matching, ranking features, and global context within a single transformer-based reranker, offering a principled way to fuse heterogeneous signals in one model rather than concatenating multiple lists</cite>. <cite id="263d5e57-3">SIGIR 2021 reports on methods improving transformer-based rerankers (e.g., pairwise training strategies, efficiency tactics), indicating that transformer re-rankers are mature enough to be fused or used as fusion subcomponents</cite>.
- Production-scale integration:
  - <cite id="eab055e9-0">LiGR operationalizes transformer architectures for large-scale ranking, showing that organizations already fuse lexical and neural signals and adopt transformer rankers at scale</cite>. This suggests practical patterns to incorporate hierarchical supervision (e.g., category-aware labels) into transformer ranking objectives and ensembles.

From hierarchical supervision to ranking fusion: design patterns
Given hierarchically supervised information (e.g., labels organized by categories and subcategories, or curriculum from coarse to fine), three transformer-centric strategies are supported by current practice and research:

1) Hierarchy-aware feature and signal fusion with transformers
- Fuse coarse-grained and fine-grained signals inside a transformer decoder/MLP head.
  - <cite id="99d78ce7-5">Fusion-in-T5 shows how a transformer’s cross-attention and fusion head can combine text matching and explicit features; the same idea extends to fusing hierarchical label signals (category-level and document-level relevance) as separate modalities or feature sets inside the same encoder–decoder</cite>.
  - <cite id="eab055e9-0">Production frameworks like LiGR indicate feasibility at scale, enabling you to incorporate hierarchical supervision via label hierarchies or curriculum into the training objective while retaining transformer-based ranking</cite>.
- Combine multiple hierarchical rankers using list-level fusion before final re-scoring.
  - <cite id="99d78ce7-2">Use rank fusion (e.g., reciprocal rank fusion) to merge outputs of specialized rankers trained on different levels of supervision (e.g., category-level first-stage retrieval vs. document-level fine-grained re-ranking)</cite>. <cite id="99d78ce7-1">Empirically, this improves robustness and mitigates label-noise sensitivity at lower levels</cite>.

2) Hierarchical re-rankers and curriculum supervision
- Train a transformer re-ranker with multi-level labels to prioritize coarse-to-fine corrections.
  - <cite id="eab055e9-1">Transformer Rankers provide ablations and training recipes (cross-encoders) for re-rankers; you can add multi-level supervision (higher-level labels as weak supervision guiding lower-level ranking)</cite>.
  - <cite id="263d5e57-7">SIGIR 2020’s “document re-ranking for transformers by precomputing term representations” suggests efficiency patterns for deep re-ranking that can be extended to hierarchical re-ranking steps</cite>.
- Precompute hierarchical cues (category features, taxonomy-aware representations), and fuse them in the reranker’s context.
  - <cite id="99d78ce7-5">Fusion-in-T5’s design of integrating “global context” and ranking features can be adapted to insert taxonomy-derived cues into the transformer’s contextualization</cite>.

3) Multi-signal multimodal fusion tailored for IR
- Fuse content and structure signals under a unified transformer.
  - <cite id="99d78ce7-6">Transformer-based fusion has been applied to align and combine modalities (e.g., knowledge-aligned multimodal transformer) and can be adapted to fuse hierarchical signals (e.g., category-level metadata and document text) via modality-specific encoders with a shared transformer fusion layer for ranking</cite>.

Representative works you can build on
- Learned fusion with transformers:
  - <cite id="99d78ce7-5">Fusion-in-T5 (ACL 2024): a re-ranker that fuses text matching information, ranking features, and global context, achieving competitive end-to-end ranking</cite>. Directly relevant as a template for hierarchical fusion (e.g., per-label hierarchy).
- Rank fusion toolkits and ensembles:
  - <cite id="99d78ce7-2">PyTerrier’s result fusion implements list-level merging (reciprocal rank fusion) across multiple rankers; you can wrap transformer re-rankers (and hierarchical ones) and combine them</cite>. <cite id="99d78ce7-1">Evidence from WSDM/CISPA-style submissions shows consistent performance gains of neural re-ranker fusion at scale</cite>.
- Production transformer ranking:
  - <cite id="eab055e9-0">LiGR: transformer-based modeling at LinkedIn scale</cite>; <cite id="263d5e57-3">SIGIR 2021 includes methods improving transformer rerankers</cite>; <cite id="263d5e57-7">SIGIR 2020’s document re-ranking for transformers</cite>. Together, they show robust, efficient transformer rankers that are good candidates for hierarchical supervision setups.
- General transformer re-rankers:
  - <cite id="99d78ce7-0">BERT for similar-text retrieval/ranking</cite>; <cite id="99d78ce7-8">passage-level transformer re-rankers that re-score relevant vs. truthful content</cite>. These can be wired into fusion or used as hierarchy-aware components.

Practical design advice for hierarchical supervision with transformers
- Data: encode label hierarchies as weak supervision.
  - Use category/subcategory relevance labels to train a hierarchical curriculum loss: coarse levels for quick convergence, then refine with fine-grained labels. <cite id="eab055e9-1">Transformer cross-encoder training pipelines can be adapted to include these labels as weak supervision in re-ranking objectives</cite>.
- Model: choose between list-level fusion vs. learned fusion inside a transformer
  - Start with list-level fusion (RRF or learned list merge) across specialized rankers (category-specialized and general), then add a transformer re-ranker head for final fusion. <cite id="99d78ce7-2">Tools like PyTerrier offer ready-to-use fusion</cite>. <cite id="99d78ce7-1">Studies show consistent robustness gains</cite>.
  - Alternatively, adopt a Fusion-in-T5-style model and add hierarchy-specific encoders/attention heads to inject category signals and fuse them with document text and features. <cite id="99d78ce7-5">Fusion-in-T5 shows how to unify multiple signal types in one transformer head</cite>.
- Training/efficiency: make the hierarchy work for inference
  - <cite id="263d5e57-7">Precompute term representations and use hierarchical grouping for early pruning</cite> to keep latency acceptable while re-ranking many candidates. <cite id="263d5e57-3">SIGIR 2021 reports propose practical improvements (e.g., pairwise strategies) that cut compute while boosting gains</cite>.
- Evaluation: measure per-level and overall gains
  - Track ranking metrics at coarse and fine levels (NDCG@k with hierarchical cutoffs, facet-aware metrics) and compare list-level vs. learned fusion, plus ablations with/without hierarchical supervision.

Related systems and tutorials
- Ecosystems:
  - <cite id="99d78ce7-3">Task submissions combining BM25 with neural re-ranker fusion demonstrate practical pipelines</cite>. <cite id="263d5e57-3">SIGIR 2021 accepted program highlights industrial methods for transformer rerankers</cite>.
- Implementation guides:
  - <cite id="99d78ce7-8">S-BERT’s retrieve-and-rerank application shows a plug-and-play transformer reranker</cite>; <cite id="eab055e9-1">Transformer Rankers library provides end-to-end experiments</cite>.
- Fusion concepts:
  - <cite id="99d78ce7-2">PyTerrier fusion docs define reciprocal-rank fusion and rank-merging</cite>; <cite id="99d78ce7-1">rank fusion over diverse neural rankers</cite>; <cite id="99d78ce7-7">retrieval fusion literature characterizes inputs (rankings, scores, embeddings) and fusion operators</cite>.

Are there papers specifically tying transformers and hierarchical supervision in ranking?
- Not all IR papers explicitly “train transformers with hierarchical labels,” but multiple strands directly support your plan:
  - <cite id="99d78ce7-5">Transformer-based learned fusion of features and signals (Fusion-in-T5)</cite> enables you to fuse hierarchy-derived signals (category-level and subcategory-level) inside one model.
  - <cite id="263d5e57-3">SIGIR 2021 includes transformer-reranker improvements</cite> and <cite id="263d5e57-7">SIGIR 2020 proposes document re-ranking for transformers</cite>, indicating transformer rankers are fit for hierarchical pipelines.
  - <cite id="eab055e9-0">Large-scale production frameworks (LiGR) integrate transformer models</cite>, suggesting practical paths to exploit hierarchical supervision (e.g., label-aware pretraining, curriculum).
  - <cite id="99d78ce7-2">Rank list fusion toolkits operate over multiple rankers</cite>, which you can specialize by hierarchy and then unify with a transformer reranker head.

Concrete starting points for your approach
- If supervision is hierarchical across categories/subcategories:
  - Train two specialized transformer rerankers (one per top-level category) with fine-grained labels; fuse their outputs via list-level fusion (RRF) into a final transformer re-ranker that performs hierarchical tie-breaking. <cite id="99d78ce7-2">Use PyTerrier’s fusion module to implement reciprocal-rank fusion</cite>. <cite id="99d78ce7-5">Alternatively, use Fusion-in-T5 to fuse category-aware features and cross-attention signals into one model</cite>.
- If supervision is weak/noisy at fine levels:
  - Use category-level labels as weak supervision to pre-train or guide a transformer reranker, then finetune with available document-level labels. <cite id="eab055e9-1">Transformer cross-encoder training recipes provide templates</cite>.
- If combining lexical and neural signals:
  - Fuse BM25 with a transformer reranker using learned or rank-level fusion; add category-aware features into the transformer context or fusion head. <cite id="99d78ce7-1">Neural + sparse fusion improves robustness</cite>. <cite id="99d78ce7-2">Rank fusion toolkits support learned weight allocation across rankers</cite>.

Takeaway
- Yes—there are multiple articles and systems in IR where transformers have been used to solve or discuss ranking fusion, both as learned fusion heads within a transformer reranker and as components in list-level fusion pipelines. <cite id="99d78ce7-5,99d78ce7-2,99d78ce7-0,99d78ce7-1">Fusion-in-T5, IR toolkits like PyTerrier, BERT-based re-rankers, and rank fusion of neural models</cite> establish current practice. <cite id="eab055e9-0,263d5e57-3,263d5e57-7">Production frameworks and SIGIR works validate deployability</cite>.
- For hierarchical supervision, the literature suggests two complementary routes: (a) list-level fusion across specialized hierarchical rankers, and (b) learned fusion inside a transformer head that integrates multi-level signals. Start with list-level fusion (fast, modular), then move to end-to-end learned fusion with a transformer head if you need stronger cross-level coherence. <cite id="99d78ce7-2">Implement rank-merging with PyTerrier</cite> and <cite id="99d78ce7-5">adapt Fusion-in-T5 to fuse category- and document-level supervision within a single transformer re-ranker</cite>. If you want more hierarchical alignment, <cite id="99d78ce7-6">knowledge-aligned multimodal transformers</cite> offer a template for fusing structured and unstructured hierarchy-aware cues.
- If you want, we can sketch an experiment blueprint: data encoding of hierarchies, two-stage retrieval, multiple hierarchical rerankers, fusion layer design (learned vs. rank-level), training recipe, and evaluation with facet-aware metrics, grounded in the cited systems and methods.

fully_underspecified.text: Are there any articles where a certain type of model has been used to solve or discuss a problem involving ranking fusion and hierarchically supervised information?
fully_underspecified.answer:
Yes. Below are concrete model families and representative articles where a particular modeling approach has been used to solve or discuss ranking fusion together with hierarchically supervised or structured information.

Overview: Ranking fusion + hierarchical supervision
- Ranking fusion: combine multiple ranked lists (often from different sources or cues) into a single ranking; classic IR papers cast this as a data fusion/global ranking problem solved via probabilistic pairwise models, learned combination rules, or late fusion algorithms. <cite id="2cc6b20e-1">Global ranking via data fusion frames the problem as aggregating pseudo-ranked lists</cite> <cite id="2cc6b20e-6">Rank fusion combines arithmetic functions and machine learning to produce a fused ranking</cite> <cite id="2cc6b20e-4">Hsu et al. give a simulation/analysis framework for data fusion in IR, rank/score combination</cite> <cite id="2cc6b20e-7">Recent work frames fusion of multiple retrievers/rankings to produce robust final rankings</cite>.
- Hierarchical supervision: labels or ratings organized in trees/DAGs, multi-label with parent–child constraints, or multi-rater settings where performance varies by level in a hierarchy. <cite id="d6656d57-0">HANS fuses hierarchical labels with attributed network structure</cite> <cite id="03f434bc-4">Statistical fusion with hierarchical models of rater performance</cite> <cite id="d6656d57-2">Hierarchical multi-label classification uses label hierarchies in supervision</cite>.

1) Probabilistic/Markov-graph fusion models (late fusion for ranks)
- Markov-based pairwise ranking and latent fusion. Markov-chain and Markov-random-field style rankers turn pairwise comparisons into a graph and compute global rankings; such graph models can fuse multiple ranking signals or rankers trained under hierarchical supervision. <cite id="2cc6b20e-3">Markov-based ranking uses chains for pairwise comparisons</cite> <cite id="2cc6b20e-6">A rank fusion algorithm combining arithmetic functions and machine learning outperforms baselines</cite>. Dai et al. show how multiple pseudo-ranked lists (views) from different sources can be fused into a global ranking, highlighting the data-fusion-to-ranking pipeline. <cite id="2cc6b20e-1">As a result, the global ranking problem is transformed into a data fusion problem, aggregating pseudo-ranked lists</cite>.
- Bayesian/statistical fusion with hierarchical supervision. When raters/labels form a hierarchy (e.g., experts vs novices; fine-to-coarse classes), Bayesian hierarchical models estimate per-level performance and fuse outputs accordingly. <cite id="03f434bc-4">A generalized statistical fusion framework with hierarchical models of rater performance provides a principled way to pool uncertainty and supervision across levels</cite>. This approach explicitly uses hierarchical supervision to weight fusion.
- Practical rank-list fusion frameworks. Foundational work in IR formalizes rank- and score-level fusion and shows how late fusion of multiple ranked outputs can achieve better NDCG/precision than a single model. <cite id="2cc6b20e-4">A model for simulation and framework for analysis of data fusion in IR, covering rank/score combination methods</cite>.
- Modern multi-retriever rank fusion. Recent algorithms combine dense and sparse retrievers’ ranked lists under principles like Condorcet to obtain a robust global ranking—illustrating learned/algorithmic fusion of rankings with heterogeneous supervision/quality signals. <cite id="2cc6b20e-7,2cc6b20e-8">Rank-based fusion algorithms assemble rankings from multiple retrieval systems, combining precise matching and semantic richness</cite>.

How the hierarchy factors in: 
- In multi-rater/hierarchical annotation settings, the fusion weights can depend on rater credibility or label position in the hierarchy, producing rankings that reflect structured supervision. <cite id="03f434bc-4">Hierarchical models of rater performance guide statistical fusion</cite>.
