Yes. Several works in information retrieval use transformers to perform, discuss, or generalize ranking fusion under hierarchical supervision. What “ranking fusion” and “hierarchical supervision” mean here
- Ranking fusion refers to combining multiple ranked lists or heterogeneous signals (scores/embeddings/models) into a single ranking to improve end performance. This can be list-level (e.g., RRF) or neural (learning to weight/combine features or predictions) and often occurs before a final reranker or passage/section selector.

without_term.text: If you are a researcher currently thinking about an approach to whether neural network models can be utilized to solve the problem of ranking fusion, where the information that can be obtained is hierarchically supervised information; are there any articles in the field of information retrieval where neural network models have been used to solve or discuss this problem?
without_term.answer:
Summary: Yes—neural network models have been used in information retrieval both (a) to rank with hierarchically/gradedly supervised signals, and (b) to perform ranking fusion (late or early) by combining multiple ranked lists or rankers, often within retrieve–rerank pipelines. Contemporary works show that neural rerankers trained on weak/graded labels inherit hierarchical supervision and that neural “rerank-then-fuse” or “cascade” architectures can combine multiple sources of supervision or rankers, improving over single-run baselines. <cite id="033f7e34-1">Neural ranking models can benefit substantially from weakly labeled data that are plentiful in IR</cite>, and <cite id="033f7e34-5">weak supervision methods produce pseudo-labels to train ranking models in place of manual judgments</cite>. Concurrently, <cite id="76322976-8">score- and rank-based fusion are established tools in IR</cite> and have been explicitly studied in neural reranking contexts, e.g., <cite id="76322976-4">ranking fusion functions within retrieve-and-rerank with Fast-Forward Indexes</cite>.

1) Neural ranking from hierarchical/graded supervision
- Weak/graded supervision for neural ranking models. Several IR papers propose training deep neural rankers when only coarse, hierarchical, or multi-level relevance labels are available. <cite id="033f7e34-1">Neural Ranking Models with Weak Supervision shows how supervised neural rankers benefit from pre-training on large amounts of weakly labeled data typical of unsupervised IR</cite>, and <cite id="033f7e34-3">a broader review notes success of weak supervision in ranking and related IR tasks</cite>. The concept is extended to multi-source weak supervision: <cite id="033f7e34-6">a cascade ranking framework that combines two weakly supervised relevance signals significantly improves deep ranking performance</cite>. Generalized approaches from 2023 emphasize that neural rankers trained with weak supervision can generalize and outperform the weak labelers that generated them, suggesting adaptability to graded/hierarchical supervision schemes. <cite id="033f7e34-0">Generalized Weak Supervision for Neural IR reports that weakly supervised neural ranking models can generalize and surpass weak labelers</cite>. A practical blueprint is also provided by <cite id="033f7e34-5">Weakly-Supervised Deep IR, which describes pseudo-labeling between pseudo-queries and documents to substitute for manual judgments</cite>.

- Hierarchical retrieval and hierarchical supervision. Beyond listwise signals, neural IR has explored explicit hierarchies. <cite id="e4db2d55-7">Learning in Hierarchical Prediction Networks includes “Hierarchical Information Retrieval,” indicating neural models that incorporate hierarchical supervision structures</cite>. <cite id="76322976-8">Textbooks and lecture notes further detail score- vs. rank-based fusion and learning-to-rank, grounding hierarchical decision-making and aggregation methods</cite>.

2) Neural ranking fusion: combining multiple ranked lists or rankers
- Neural reranking with fusion functions. An explicit thread in IR evaluates how to fuse multiple ranked outputs within neural rerankers. <cite id="76322976-4">A Delft master thesis analyzes “Ranking Fusion Functions in Neural Ranking Models” in the context of Fast-Forward Indexes, i.e., directly studying how fusion combines neural rerankers’ outputs</cite>. Complementary surveys emphasize that <cite id="76322976-0">many rank fusion methods have been proposed in IR</cite>, and that simple yet effective fusion like Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF) or Condorcet voting can be wired before a neural reranker or among rerankers trained on different supervision levels (weak vs. strong).

- Classic fusion wired into neural pipelines. Although many fusion rules are non-neural, they are commonly used as components inside end-to-end neural retrieval systems. For example, <cite id="76322976-3">RRF aggregates multiple ranked lists from different systems into a single ranking</cite>, and <cite id="76322976-5">empirical work reports that RRF often outperforms Condorcet and individual rank learners</cite>. These fusion functions can be applied before a neural reranker to boost list quality; conversely, neural rerankers can be trained and then fused with one another or with traditional rankers.

- Cascades and multi-source neural reranking. Neural cascades that jointly exploit multiple sources of supervision are a practical realization of “fusion” at inference. <cite id="033f7e34-6">By combining two weakly supervised relevance signals inside a cascade, researchers report stronger deep ranking performance</cite>. In a hierarchical setup, a coarse neural ranker could be reranked or fused with a fine-grained neural module trained on deeper labels, leveraging both levels of supervision.

3) Examples linking hierarchy to fusion and supervision
- Graded/multi-level relevance supervision feeding neural rankers. Weak supervision frameworks generate multi-level judgments for training, which can be fused at inference when multiple rankers or list sources exist. <cite id="033f7e34-5">Weakly-Supervised Deep IR details pseudo-label construction and its use to train neural rankers</cite>, and <cite id="033f7e34-1">weakly labeled data are emphasized as a core resource for neural ranking</cite>.

- Hierarchical relevance/label taxonomies. While explicit multi-leaf taxonomies like WordNet are not tied in every paper to specific fusion mechanisms, the broader literature supports using hierarchical labels to train listwise neural models and then fuse multiple ranked results. <cite id="e4db2d55-8">Work on hierarchical prediction with neural networks in IR supports modeling hierarchical supervision</cite>, and <cite id="033f7e34-0">neural rankers trained with generalized weak supervision can leverage coarse-to-fine label hierarchies as supervision sources</cite>. At inference, <cite id="76322976-3">RRF-based fusion combines multiple ranked lists</cite>, which can include outputs from hierarchical rankers or modules.

4) Representative papers and takeaways
- Neural ranking with weak/hierarchical supervision:
  - <cite id="033f7e34-1">Neural Ranking Models with Weak Supervision (Dehghani et al., 2016): argues that neural ranking benefits from weak supervision abundant in IR</cite>.
  - <cite id="033f7e34-5">Weakly-Supervised Deep Information Retrieval (MacAvaney et al., 2017): provides a practical blueprint for pseudo-labeling to train neural rankers</cite>.
  - <cite id="033f7e34-6">Investigating Weak Supervision in Deep Ranking (Zheng and Liu): a cascade that combines two weak-label sources improves performance</cite>.
  - <cite id="033f7e34-0">Generalized Weak Supervision for Neural IR (2023): shows generalization and superiority of weakly supervised neural rankers over their weak labelers</cite>.
  - <cite id="e4db2d55-8">Hierarchical Information Retrieval via hierarchical prediction networks (NeurIPS 2019 tutorial/line of work): demonstrates hierarchical supervision in neural IR</cite>.
  These support training neural rankers when supervision is hierarchical or graded, which is prerequisite for hierarchical fusion.

- Ranking fusion inside neural systems:
  - <cite id="76322976-4">Ranking Fusion Functions in Neural Ranking Models (Fast-Forward Indexes): analyzes how to fuse rankers/listwise outputs in a neural retrieve–rerank pipeline</cite>.
  - <cite id="76322976-5">Comparative evidence that Reciprocal Rank Fusion outperforms Condorcet and individual rank learners</cite>.
  - Surveys and overviews: <cite id="76322976-0,76322976-1,76322976-2">rank fusion methods for combining multiple ranked lists are well-established and used across domains</cite>, and are readily integrated with neural rerankers.

5) Design guidance if you plan to use neural models for hierarchical ranking fusion
- Data and supervision
  - Construct or leverage hierarchical/graded label hierarchies (e.g., LDA topics as coarse labels, multi-leaf relevance levels or WordNet-derived labels), then generate weak labels for deep learning using pseudo-querying or hierarchical active learning. <cite id="033f7e34-5">Weak supervision via pseudo-labels is a standard approach to train neural rankers when full manual judgments are scarce</cite>, and <cite id="033f7e34-0">neural rankers trained on generalized weak supervision generalize beyond their labelers</cite>.
  - If multiple sources produce ranked lists (query expansions, cross-lingual, graph signals), compute list-level fusion scores via RRF/Condorcet before a neural reranker or train neural rerankers on each source and fuse via learned or rule-based fusion. <cite id="76322976-5">RRF often outperforms Condorcet and single rankers</cite>, and <cite id="76322976-4">neural reranking frameworks can incorporate fusion functions</cite>.
- Model architectures
  - Two-stage with fusion: BM25/lexical or coarse hierarchical ranker → neural listwise reranker trained on hierarchical/graded labels → list fusion (RRF or neural fusion head). <cite id="76322976-4">Evidence from Fast-Forward reranking studies the effect of fusion functions in neural rerankers</cite>.
  - Neural cascades across supervision levels: coarse neural ranker outputs can be refined by a fine-grained neural reranker trained on deeper labels in the hierarchy. <cite id="033f7e34-6">Combining multiple weak-label streams within a cascade improves ranking performance</cite>.
- Training and objectives
  - Use hierarchical listwise losses and curriculum (coarse-to-fine): train on coarse relevance first, then refine with deeper labels; or jointly learn from multi-level supervision with monotonic aggregation. <cite id="033f7e34-1">Weak supervision principles and pretraining demonstrate robust gains with coarse-to-fine label availability</cite>.
  - Incorporate weak/graded signals directly (BM25-derived graded relevance, TF–IDF importance as weak supervision) and measure transfer to test queries. <cite id="033f7e34-5">Weak-labeling provides practical relevance supervision for training neural rankers</cite>.
- Evaluation plan
  - Check single vs. fused runs: <cite id="76322976-5">RRF frequently improves over single rankers</cite>, and <cite id="76322976-8">both score- and rank-based fusion have established baselines</cite>.
  - Test ablations: replace fusion with single neural reranker; replace neural reranker with classical reweighting; swap fusion rules (RRF vs. Condorcet) to validate marginal improvements.

6) Practical pointers to start
- If your hierarchy is label-side (e.g., categories/WordNet), first train a neural ranker with hierarchical labels (coarse leaves as positives, descendants as weak negatives/irrelevant), then fuse multiple rerankers (lexical + hierarchical) using RRF/Condorcet and evaluate with graded relevance judgments as gold. <cite id="033f7e34-0">Neural models trained with generalized weak supervision can surpass labelers</cite>, and <cite id="76322976-3">RRF aggregates multiple ranked lists into a robust single ranking</cite>.
- If your hierarchy is relevance-side (graded judgments), combine multiple weak supervision sources in a neural cascade and evaluate the fused output. <cite id="033f7e34-6">Evidence from cascaded weak-label supervision shows performance gains</cite>.
- For late fusion, consider a learned fusion layer over neural embeddings of documents/query+document pairs, trained to optimize NDCG@k from combined distributions of multiple rerankers’ scores. <cite id="76322976-4">Analyzing fusion functions in neural reranking provides guidance on how to combine rank outputs within neural pipelines</cite>.

Takeaway: Neural models have already been used to tackle both the supervision and the fusion. Train hierarchical/graded neural rankers with weak supervision, and wire them with rank fusion (RRF/Condorcet or learned) to boost final rankings. Expect solid gains from combining weak/graded supervision with fusion, with concrete exemplars in neural reranking and multi-source cascades. <cite id="033f7e34-1">Weakly supervised neural ranking works well with available IR supervision</cite>, while <cite id="76322976-4">neural reranking studies of fusion functions</cite> and <cite id="76322976-5">classic fusion techniques like RRF</cite> provide proven mechanisms to fuse ranked lists produced by hierarchical or multi-source models.

questions.original_query: Can LLMs learn new information when trained on supervised fine-tuning (SFT)?

query.text: Can LLMs learn new information when trained on supervised fine-tuning (SFT)?
query.answer:
Short answer: Yes. Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) allows LLMs to acquire new behaviors and improve factual and task performance when trained on task-relevant supervision, such as instruction–response pairs or domain corpora—provided the data and objective are appropriate. <cite id="5bd61dd2-2">Instruction tuning refers to further training LLMs in a supervised fashion on (instruction, output) pairs, explicitly teaching the model to recognize and execute requests</cite>. <cite id="5bd61dd2-7">Instruction tuning (IT), or supervised fine-tuning (SFT), gives large language models the ability to execute tasks specified by users</cite>.

What “learning new information” looks like in practice
- Instruction-following and task execution: <cite id="5bd61dd2-0">Instruction tuning addresses the problem of making models recognize and execute requests by fine-tuning on instruction–response pairs</cite>. <cite id="5bd61dd2-7">Empirically, instruction-tuned/continuation-trained models show measurable gains at executing tasks specified by users compared to frozen pretraining-only models</cite>. <cite id="5bd61dd2-4">Google’s FLAN models used instruction tuning to substantially improve performance across many tasks new to the frozen base, demonstrating that targeted supervision can elicit capabilities beyond original pretraining</cite>.
- General aptitude benchmarks: <cite id="1abb09e7-2">Studies of FLAN report instruction-tuning improves performance on a broad set of tasks, including classic aptitude-style benchmarks like MMLU and BBH</cite>. <cite id="21c3ba88-6">Analyses challenge the notion that domain-specific SFT always harms general capabilities, showing it can preserve while improving targeted skills</cite>.
- Instruction-response alignment: <cite id="5bd61dd2-8">High-quality supervised finetuning data are a key ingredient for eliciting strong instruction-following capabilities from pretrained LLMs</cite>.

Evidence across domains and tasks
- Biomedical and clinical domains: <cite id="21c3ba88-0">A 2025 evaluation of biomedically fine-tuned LLMs reports that a base-and-specialist SFT (B-SFT) achieved 54% accuracy, slightly higher than the base model, indicating factual or task gains from domain-specific fine-tuning</cite>. <cite id="21c3ba88-1">Clinical NLP studies find that supervised fine-tuning and related preference-optimization tuning (DPO) improve performance on common clinical natural language tasks relative to base models</cite>. <cite id="21c3ba88-2">Balanced-factuality SFT (BFT) significantly outperforms standard SFT on medical tasks, enabling models to acquire knowledge that standard SFT misses, underscoring data curation and loss functions as key levers for factual learning</cite>. <cite id="21c3ba88-5">Broader biomedical benchmarking across fine-tuning methods shows full/adapter fine-tuning improves over frozen baselines across many NLP tasks, supporting the general pattern that additional gradient updates to internal layers can adapt and specialize models</cite>.
- Domain adaptation and transfer: <cite id="21c3ba88-6">Recent work argues domain-specific SFT does not inherently degrade general capabilities, and can improve targeted domains without catastrophic forgetting, suggesting effective adaptation to new information sources</cite>. <cite id="21c3ba88-7">Two-stage domain fine-tuning frameworks (e.g., summarization of biomedical articles) demonstrate improved domain-specific performance through supervised updates, illustrating transfer from general pretraining to specialized corpora</cite>. <cite id="21c3ba88-8">Domain-augmented fine-tuning improves task performance on domain-relevant subproblems (e.g., health misinformation), highlighting that adding in-domain examples during SFT improves specialization</cite>.

Compared to alternatives: prompt-tuning, preference tuning, and RLHF
- Prompt-tuning and frozen bases: <cite id="5bd61dd2-0">Instruction tuning improves upon prompt-style methods by jointly optimizing the model’s parameters over instruction–response pairs, allowing the model to “execute” requests rather than rely solely on in-context heuristics</cite>. <cite id="5bd61dd2-7">Instruction-tuned models show that supervision enables execution of user-specified tasks that prompt-only models struggle with</cite>.
- DPO/RLHF for alignment: <cite id="21c3ba88-1">In clinical and other domains, preference optimization (e.g., DPO) can improve performance over SFT on tasks measuring alignment or evaluative quality</cite>. <cite id="21c3ba88-2">Balancing factuality during supervised fine-tuning can surpass vanilla SFT on knowledge-heavy tasks, indicating that tailored losses/data weighting can better encode intended knowledge than standard cross-entropy on uncurated data</cite>. <cite id="21c3ba88-0">In biomedical lay summaries, base plus domain SFT achieved measurable gains over the frozen base, but specialized preference or balanced-factuality variants may be needed for optimal alignment and accuracy</cite>.
- Instruction-tuning vs generalization: <cite id="5bd61dd2-4">FLAN’s instruction-tuning phase is specifically targeted at generalization, yielding models that handle many tasks new to the base model, evidencing transfer learning through supervision</cite>. <cite id="1abb09e7-2">Improvements measured across multiple datasets (MMLU, BBH) and “unseen tasks” in the FLAN study support that instruction tuning can induce broad, transferable capabilities beyond original pretraining</cite>.

Mechanisms that make SFT effective (and what can go wrong)
- Data and objectives: <cite id="5bd61dd2-8">High-quality instruction data are crucial; curating well-structured instruction–response pairs elicits stronger instruction-following abilities</cite>. <cite id="21c3ba88-2">Balancing positive and negative evidence during SFT improves biomedical factuality, with BFT outperforming standard SFT on medical tasks</cite>. <cite id="21c3ba88-3">Compared to prompt-only approaches, SFT compares predictions to ground truth and typically yields higher accuracy at the cost of more compute</cite>.
- Trade-offs and pitfalls: <cite id="21c3ba88-6">Domain-specific SFT can introduce overfitting or bias if the objective or data are poorly controlled, but evidence shows it need not harm general capabilities and can yield domain gains when tuned carefully</cite>. <cite id="21c3ba89-0">Analyses of biomedical fine-tuning highlight that naive cross-entropy on contaminated or noisy data can fail to improve factuality, motivating domain-specific data filtering and balanced objectives</cite>. <cite id="21c3ba88-2">Methods that explicitly constrain model updates to preserve external knowledge (e.g., balanced-factuality losses) show SFT can be steered to learn the intended facts rather than the base model’s slop</cite>.

Practical takeaways
- If your goal is to teach the model new behaviors on novel tasks, construct instruction–response pairs with clear criteria and train with SFT; you can expect better task execution than prompt-only baselines and measurable gains on held-out instruction-following and aptitude-style tasks, especially when evaluated on broad benchmarks like MMLU/BBH/HELM. <cite id="5bd61dd2-0">Instruction tuning directly teaches request recognition and execution via supervised updates</cite>; <cite id="1abb09e7-2">instruction-tuned models improved MMLU and BBH overall scores</cite>; <cite id="5bd61dd2-7">SFT enables following user-specified instructions</cite>.
- If your goal is domain-specific factuality and performance, use domain corpora and task labels with quality control, possibly via balanced or contrastive objectives; this outperforms frozen models and can rival or surpass generic SFT on knowledge-critical tasks. <cite id="21c3ba88-0">B-SFT achieved 54% accuracy vs base</cite>; <cite id="21c3ba88-2">BFT significantly outperforms SFT, acquiring knowledge SFT misses</cite>.
- If your goal is preference-aligned outputs (e.g., medical/clinical tone, safety), combine SFT with preference optimization (DPO/RLHF) to improve evaluative quality beyond accuracy alone. <cite id="21c3ba88-1">SFT and DPO improved clinical NLP tasks</cite>; <cite id="21c3ba88-2">BFT shows the role of supervised preference-weighted losses in acquiring better factual behaviors</cite>.

Bottom line
Yes—LLMs can learn new information when supervised fine-tuning is applied to appropriate instruction- or domain-labeled data. Instruction tuning demonstrates that supervised updates can endow models to execute tasks they were not pre-trained to do, and domain-specific SFT improves factual accuracy and task performance beyond frozen pretraining baselines, with stronger results when data quality and objectives are carefully managed. <cite id="5bd61dd2-7">Supervised fine-tuning enables LLMs to execute user-specified tasks</cite>, <cite id="5bd61dd2-0">by jointly optimizing model parameters over instruction–response pairs</cite>, and <cite id="1abb09e7-2">empirically improves broad aptitude benchmarks</cite>, while <cite id="21c3ba88-0">biomedical evaluations show accuracy gains over base models</cite> and <cite id="21c3ba88-2">balanced-factuality SFT can surpass standard SFT in acquiring intended knowledge</cite>. Preference-based tuning (DPO/RLHF) can further refine alignment and evaluative quality where needed. <cite id="21c3ba88-1">Supervised and preference-tuned models outperform base models on clinical tasks</cite>. The key constraints are data quality, loss design, and monitoring to avoid overfitting or knowledge degradation. <cite id="21c3ba88-6">Domain-specific SFT does not necessarily harm general capabilities and can improve targeted skills without catastrophic forgetting</cite>.

fully_underspecified.text: Can models learn new information when trained?
fully_underspecified.answer:
Summary
- Yes. Training changes model parameters so that the model better maps inputs to targets on the current task; that is the core of learning new information from data. However, in neural networks, training on new data can destabilize prior knowledge, so models may simultaneously improve on new tasks while forgetting aspects of old ones unless designed otherwise.<cite id="81cf9b83-0">Catastrophic forgetting occurs when neural networks forget previously learned tasks after being trained on new data or undergoing fine-tuning for specific tasks</cite><cite id="81cf9b83-1">Artificial neural networks tend to rapidly and drastically forget previously learned information when learning something new, a phenomenon central to catastrophic forgetting</cite>.

What "learning new information when trained" looks like
- At a mechanism level, training updates parameters to reduce loss on the current task, which necessarily encodes new statistical structure, categories, or functions into the network's weights; this is the standard supervised or unsupervised gradient update story.<cite id="4666ad57-1">Continual learning frames training over a stream of tasks/domains, where the model must learn new capabilities while retaining prior ones; failure to do so manifests as forgetting</cite><cite id="5ed2f264-0">Task-specific synaptic consolidation lets a model preserve what was learned while learning new tasks</cite>.
- In deep learning, learned representations are distributed, so continual training can overwrite or shift minima relevant to earlier tasks; this "interference" explains observed forgetting even without catastrophic outliers.<cite id="81cf9b83-2">In deep learning, representations are spread thinly across neurons; this architecture can make catastrophic forgetting likely when new tasks overwrite old features</cite>.

Do models "learn" while retaining the old?
- The continual-learning literature studies conditions under which models both learn new information and remember prior tasks. Conceptually, the goal is to regulate which weights are plastic and when, so that new gradients do not erase the past.<cite id="4666ad57-2">EWC quantifies weight importance to previous tasks and penalizes large deviations for important synapses, mitigating catastrophic forgetting</cite>.
- Two influential strategies operationalize this:
  1) Elastic Weight Consolidation (EWC): estimate per-weight importance to previous tasks via a Fisher information matrix, then regularize updates to protect critical parameters; this enables selective plasticity for new tasks while preserving old capabilities.<cite id="5ed2f264-0">Elastic Weight Consolidation mitigates catastrophic forgetting by protecting task-specific synapses; "synaptic consolidation enables continual learning"</cite><cite id="5ed2f264-5">EWC mimics synaptic consolidation by making important parameters less plastic, demonstrating continual learning behavior</cite>.
  2) Synaptic Intelligence (SI): learn a parameterization of "sensitivity-to-gradient" for each weight, and scale gradients inversely to sensitivity (or importance) so updates are larger for unimportant weights and smaller for critical ones, again reducing interference during online training.<cite id="5ed2f264-1">EWC and Synaptic Intelligence protect critical parameters to prevent catastrophic forgetting in continual learning</cite><cite id="5ed2f264-8">SI provides an online approach by consolidating changes in parameters that were important for past tasks, thereby avoiding catastrophic forgetting</cite>.
- Bayesian continual learning reframes updates to be explicitly "metaplastic": maintain uncertainty over weights and balance "learning new information" against "forgetting old" via Bayes' rule, yielding update rules that retain old constraints while adapting to new data at low task-switching cost.<cite id="81cf9b83-7">A metaplastic formulation of Bayes' law balances learning and forgetting, training BNNs to update without catastrophic loss of past information</cite><cite id="5ed2f264-6">EWC-style regularization emerges from the goal of making important parameters less plastic, with demonstrated continual-learning behavior</cite>.
- Memory-augmented models and "nested learning" show that augmenting training with external or hierarchical memory structures helps the model offload fragile information, reducing reliance on overwriting parameters and thereby improving retention of old knowledge while acquiring new.<cite id="81cf9b83-6">Continually updating parameters often leads to catastrophic forgetting; Nested Learning proposes a new paradigm to improve continual learning</cite><cite id="4666ad57-4">Dynamic external memory with neural networks supports continual and one-shot learning by offloading information to an external memory</cite>.

When and how models fail to learn without care
- In the default setting (train on new data), interference causes nonmonotonic performance on old tasks, and the model may forget even when it improves on the new task. This shows that "learning new information" alone is insufficient to guarantee retained prior knowledge.<cite id="81cf9b83-0">Neural networks can forget previously learned tasks after training on new data</cite><cite id="4666ad57-3">Different neural field approaches exhibit varying degrees of catastrophic forgetting; mitigation strategies can reduce interference</cite>.
- Diagnoses and fixes span: curriculum/task scheduling, replay of past data, synaptic plasticity control (EWC/SI), metaplastic Bayesian inference, dynamic external memory, and model architectures with representation plasticity that separates task-discriminative from stable subspaces.<cite id="4666ad57-8">Continual learning is tightly coupled to learning dynamics; improving data and architecture-level dynamics can considerably improve data reuse and retention</cite><cite id="5ed2f264-7">A review situates EWC among core strategies to overcome catastrophic forgetting via weight importance constraints</cite>.

Learning new information in and from models
- Beyond supervised adaptation, training paradigms like knowledge distillation let a "student" acquire the teacher's implicit information by matching soft outputs rather than raw features, enabling transfer of complex behavior into smaller/fast models. Crucially, this shows models can learn new information encoded by another model's training artifacts—loss landscapes, logits, and uncertainties—not just by first-principles data.<cite id="4666ad57-5">Knowledge distillation trains a smaller network to approximate a larger teacher's outputs, reducing memory footprint while preserving behavior</cite><cite id="4666ad57-3">A study analyzes catastrophic forgetting across neural field models and proposes strategies to mitigate it in the context of knowledge transfer, highlighting how distillation interacts with continual-learning constraints</cite>.

Practical takeaway: Yes, but control plasticity
- Models do learn new information during/after training, in the sense that they adjust parameters to better fit new objectives and can generalize to new inputs. Yet, absent continual-learning design, the new learning tends to overwrite or distort old learning. Practitioners therefore balance plasticity via importance-aware regularization, online heuristics like Synaptic Intelligence, Bayesian epistemic constraints, replay/memory augmentation, or nested/hierarchical learners to ensure that learning new information does not erase what was already learned.<cite id="81cf9b83-3">Research community works to counteract catastrophic forgetting when training for new tasks</cite><cite id="5ed2f264-0">Synaptic consolidation provides a unique solution to the continual-learning problem by protecting vital synapses</cite><cite id="81cf9b83-6">Simple continual parameter updates often cause catastrophic forgetting; alternative paradigms are needed</cite><cite id="4666ad57-2">EWC quantifies and constrains weight importance to earlier tasks to mitigate forgetting</cite><cite id="81cf9b83-7">Metaplastic Bayesian update rules explicitly trade off learning and forgetting, improving continual learning</cite>.

Edge cases and caveats
- Deep ensembles and Bayesian uncertainty can diagnose "conflicts" between old and new experience; when a new task contradicts prior data, selective parameter freezing, distillation into a new head, or task-specific subspaces are prudent to preserve the global model while learning a new mode.<cite id="5ed2f264-8">Online consolidation in SI protects important past-parameter changes while enabling further training</cite><cite id="4666ad57-3">Different neural field approaches vary in their proneness to forgetting, motivating tailored mitigation in continual learning pipelines</cite>.
- In distributed representations, the same neurons often participate in multiple tasks; hence, training always trades off some degree of interference. Good initialization, linear separability, and task clustering reduce interference; adversarial or high-capacity settings exacerbate it.<cite id="81cf9b83-2">Because representations are thinly spread, interference is a natural risk in deep networks; this explains observed forgetting</cite>.

Bottom line
- Yes. Models learn new information when trained by updating parameters to fit new objectives, and they can acquire, consolidate, and even distill capabilities from other models. But, without explicit continual-learning mechanisms, this new learning erodes prior knowledge; the field has developed principled methods—EWC, Synaptic Intelligence, Bayesian metaplastic updates, dynamic memory, and nested learning—to learn while retaining.<cite id="5ed2f264-0">Elastic Weight Consolidation protects task-specific synapses, enabling learning while retaining</cite><cite id="5ed2f264-8">Synaptic Intelligence performs online consolidation, avoiding catastrophic forgetting</cite><cite id="81cf9b83-7">Bayesian metaplastic updates explicitly balance learning and forgetting</cite><cite id="4666ad57-4">Dynamic external memory lets models offload fragile information, improving continual learning</cite><cite id="81cf9b83-6">Nested learning frames show parameter-only updates are brittle; architectural/memory strategies help</cite><cite id="4666ad57-5">Knowledge distillation learns behavior from a trained model's outputs, enabling new information transfer</cite>.

without_term.text: Can large language models learn new information when trained on supervised fine-tuning?
without_term.answer:
Summary
Yes. Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) enables LLMs to learn new information, capabilities, and behaviors by adapting pretrained models with task- or instruction-specific prompt–response data, improving downstream task performance and zero‑shot/few‑shot generalization to novel prompts and domains. <cite id="be1e55ce-0">Instruction fine-tuning (SFT) trains models on example prompts and corresponding desired outputs to align them to follow instructions</cite> and <cite id="be1e55ce-9">instruction tuning is a technique that fine-tunes large language models on labeled instructional prompts and outputs</cite>. In practice, SFT can raise human and automated evaluation scores on instruction-following and transfer tasks, and even small-scale instruction-tuned models can match or surpass much larger untuned baselines. <cite id="8d4e02e5-0">Alpaca (7B) achieves comparable human evaluation performance to InstructGPT (175B) and in some comparisons outperforms it</cite> and <cite id="9a1d5e43-0">fine-tuning with human feedback aligns language models with user intent across a wide range of tasks</cite>. However, learning via SFT carries risks: it can amplify memorization of sensitive information, degrade or reshape intrinsic safety behaviors, overfit to training data or domains, and even cause “catastrophic forgetting” of pretraining knowledge if not designed carefully. <cite id="a899372d-1">Fine-tuning on generated data increased success rates of PII attacks by over 50% relative to pre-fine-tuning baselines</cite> and <cite id="a899372d-0">fine-tuned models systematically exhibit unintended memorization of personally identifiable information (PII)</cite>.

How SFT enables learning new information
During supervised fine-tuning, the frozen pretrained language model’s output layer(s) are trained to predict target responses for instruction prompts, aligning model behavior with demonstration data. <cite id="be1e55ce-0">Instruction fine-tuning is a conventional alignment approach that trains models on example prompts and outputs</cite> and <cite id="9a1d5e43-4">the InstructGPT pipeline uses supervised fine-tuning on human demonstrations to learn to generate helpful and safe responses</cite>. Beyond raw accuracy, this process adapts models to follow instructions and perform “out-of-the-box” reasoning aligned with the fine-tuning distribution. <cite id="be1e55ce-4">Fine-tuning a large language model trains it on specific task data to perform best on that task</cite> and <cite id="8d4e02e5-2">instruction fine-tuning improves zero-shot performance on new tasks by enhancing the model’s ability to react to novel instructions</cite>.

Empirical evidence that SFT “learns” new things
SFT has repeatedly produced measurable gains on instruction-following and cross-task generalization, even with relatively small supervised datasets and large pretrained baselines.

- Scale and transfer: <cite id="8d4e02e5-1">Alpaca fine-tunes a 7B LLaMA model on 52K instruction-following demonstrations to attain strong instruction-following behavior</cite>, and <cite id="8d4e02e5-0">in human evaluation, Alpaca (7B) achieves comparable or higher performance than InstructGPT (175B) on certain benchmarks</cite>. <cite id="8d4e02e5-8">Recent survey work shows instruction-tuning methods across open instruction-following datasets improve model instruction-following capabilities</cite>.
- Efficiency and further gains: <cite id="8d4e02e5-3">Recent theory-driven methods argue that fine-tuning on large instruction datasets improves zero-shot and few-shot learning, and report that optimizing the loss over instructions boosts AlpacaEval 1.0 performance by over 100%</cite>. <cite id="8d4e02e5-5">Instruction Tuning With Loss Over Instructions reports win rate improvements on AlpacaEval 1.0 and shows scaling relationships between training examples and relative gains over baseline instruction tuning</cite>.
- Human-preference alignment: <cite id="9a1d5e43-0">InstructGPT demonstrates fine-tuning with human feedback as an effective alignment pathway “on a wide range of tasks”</cite>, and <cite id="9a1d5e43-2">OpenAI describes the technique as using human preferences as a reward signal to fine-tune models for safety and alignment</cite>. <cite id="9a1d5e43-8">In practice, the pipeline consists of supervised fine-tuning on human demonstrations, reward model training from human rankings, and RLHF</cite>.

SFT also interacts with instruction-following safety: <cite id="a899372d-3">Instruction finetuning considerably enhances model performance in zero-shot settings, but the same process can increase safety risks that require careful monitoring and mitigation</cite>.

Caveats: memorization, privacy, intrinsic safety, overfitting, and forgetting
Because SFT learns from example inputs and outputs, it can memorize sensitive details (e.g., personally identifiable information) from training data or demonstrations and leak them in new contexts. <cite id="a899372d-1">Security evaluations show that fine-tuning LLMs using generated data can increase the success rate of PII attacks by more than 50% relative to pre-fine-tuning models</cite> and <cite id="a899372d-0">systematic analysis reveals unintended memorization of PII in fine-tuned language models</cite>. Related work stresses instruction-structure and privacy controls to mitigate leakage during SFT. <cite id="a899372d-3">Fine-tuning without appropriate instructional structure amplifies privacy leakage from pre-training data</cite>.

SFT can also shift intrinsic safety behaviors—for better or worse—by privileging instruction-matched responses over the model’s preexisting knowledge, potentially making models more compliant while introducing new harmful patterns from the training set. <cite id="a899372d-3">Safety-tuning instruction-following models improves capability but can also increase new safety risks that must be audited</cite>. In data-scarce regimes, SFT may overfit to limited examples or domains and fail to generalize robustly; structured surveys emphasize designing fine-tuning regimes that remain effective with little data. <cite id="be1e55ce-2">A practical survey details methods for fine-tuning LLMs with limited data, highlighting performance, training, and dataset construction trade-offs</cite>.

There is also evidence of “catastrophic forgetting” or selective forgetting: when models are strongly fine-tuned to a narrow domain, they may lose calibration or knowledge on broader pretraining tasks, especially if intrinsic safety behaviors are adjusted in the process. Practitioners address this via regularization, mixed-domain objectives, and careful evaluation at domain boundaries. <cite id="be1e55ce-6">A practitioner-oriented review notes that supervised fine-tuning enhances task performance while potentially compromising general instruction-following abilities</cite> and <cite id="c2e87082-0">summarizes lessons from improving safety of instruction-following models as part of broader alignment work</cite>.

Contrast with RLHF and other alignment methods
SFT is typically used as the first stage before reward model training and RLHF to align models with human preferences. <cite id="9a1d5e43-8">In InstructGPT, supervised fine-tuning on human demonstrations is followed by reward model training from human rankings and RLHF</cite>. Compared to purely pretraining or SFT-only pipelines, the multi-stage approach improves safety and intent-following while retaining instruction-transfer capabilities. <cite id="9a1d5e43-0">Stage-wise tuning with human feedback aligns models with user intent across many tasks</cite> and <cite id="9a1d5e43-2">uses preference signals to fine-tune safety and alignment</cite>.

Practical takeaways and best practices
- SFT works: It reliably improves instruction-following, narrow-task accuracy, and zero/few-shot transfer when using high-quality demonstration data, often with small additional parameter counts. <cite id="8d4e02e5-1">Fifty-two thousand instruction–response examples can fine-tune a 7B LLaMA to strong instruction-following</cite> and <cite id="8d4e02e5-0">a 7B Alpaca model can match or surpass much larger InstructGPT baselines on human evals</cite>.
- Guardrails are essential: Prefer high-quality, curated demonstrations; monitor and test for memorization and privacy leakage; include diverse safety prompts and intrinsic safety evaluations. <cite id="a899372d-1">Leakage amplification during fine-tuning demands privacy-aware SFT pipelines</cite> and <cite id="a899372d-3">instruction-structured fine-tuning mitigates leakage risks</cite>.
- Scope and generalization: Tune to targeted tasks or styles, but keep test coverage on out-of-domain and safety-sensitive prompts; beware overfitting and boundary-case failures. <cite id="be1e55ce-6">Instruction tuning can enhance task performance but may reduce general instruction-following without careful design</cite> and <cite id="8d4e02e5-2">improvements in zero-shot capability depend on how instruction-tuning is done</cite>.
- Combine with human preference learning: For safety-critical use, follow SFT with reward modeling and RLHF to calibrate intent and reduce harmful behaviors. <cite id="9a1d5e43-8">InstructGPT’s three-stage process provides a reference for combining SFT with preference learning</cite>.

Open questions
Three questions remain active. First, how broadly and consistently does SFT transfer across distant tasks and modalities without overfitting? <cite id="8d4e02e5-2">Evidence suggests improved zero-shot capability, but transfer quality varies with data curation and objective design</cite>. Second, what scalable methods best prevent or detect memorization and leakage after SFT, especially in federated or private domains? <cite id="a899372d-3">Gradient-free leakage persists, motivating instruction-aware defenses</cite>. Third, how to balance specialization (strong performance on a task) with robust instruction-following and intrinsic safety across a model family. <cite id="be1e55ce-6">Practitioners report tension between task-specific gains and broader instruction-following quality</cite>.

Bottom line
LLMs can and do learn new information when trained with supervised fine-tuning—across tasks, domains, and safety/intent behaviors—providing measurable gains in instruction-following and zero/few-shot performance. <cite id="be1e55ce-0">Instruction fine-tuning trains models on prompts and outputs to align with desired behaviors</cite>, <cite id="9a1d5e43-0">including following human intent across tasks</cite>, and <cite id="8d4e02e5-1">even small, instruction-tuned models can match or exceed much larger untuned baselines on instruction tasks</cite>. Deployers should plan for memorization/privacy risks, safety trade-offs, and overfitting, and consider staged pipelines (SFT then RLHF) and careful evaluation to retain both capability and reliability. <cite id="a899372d-1">Fine-tuning can increase PII attack success, so privacy-aware pipelines are needed</cite>, <cite id="a899372d-0">fine-tuned models often memorize sensitive information</cite>, <cite id="be1e55ce-6">and SFT may compromise general instruction-following unless carefully designed</cite>, <cite id="9a1d5e43-8">with multi-stage methods providing stronger alignment</cite>.

questions.original_query: how do GNNs perform on graphs with billions of nodes?

query.text: how do GNNs perform on graphs with billions of nodes?
query.answer:
Summary
• Billion-scale graphs (billions of nodes, often hundreds of billions of edges) are trainable with GNNs using a combination of mini-batch neighbor sampling, system optimizations for full-batch and distributed training, and simplified architectures that avoid expensive nonlinearities, while facing limits like over-smoothing and communication/feature-materialization overheads. <cite id="4668bbee-6">The graphs used in industry applications are usually massive, with billions of nodes and hundreds of billions or even trillions of edges</cite> <cite id="cad7e845-0">Mini-batch training keeps memory bounded by sampling subgraphs and is recommended for large graphs (100K+ nodes)</cite> <cite id="844e95f0-0">Distributed systems such as DistDGL achieve linear speedup while preserving accuracy</cite> <cite id="1bbf0d64-0">LightGCN simplifies GCNs to pure neighborhood aggregation for billion-scale recommender graphs</cite> <cite id="c2101988-0">Increasing depth commonly leads to over-smoothing, limiting representational power</cite>.

1) What “billion-scale” looks like and benchmarks
• Practice and scale. Industry graphs commonly have billions of nodes and hundreds of billions of edges; hence training must minimize shuffles, maximize data locality, and overlap compute and communication. <cite id="4668bbee-6">The graphs used in industry applications are usually massive, with billions of nodes and hundreds of billions or even trillions of edges</cite>. Recent frameworks explicitly target “billion-scale” graphs in terms of throughput and epoch time. <cite id="844e95f0-3">A system paper reports an epoch on a graph with 100 million nodes completed in 13 seconds</cite>, indicating that practical billion-scale training focuses on both raw speed and fitting the graph in memory (or near-memory). 
• Benchmarks and comparisons. Large-scale benchmarking papers examine end-to-end GNN performance, training regimes, and ablations across datasets and models. <cite id="4668bbee-3">Recent surveys document scalability progress and comparative performance across GNN systems</cite> <cite id="7ab5f7ae-3">A comprehensive benchmarking study surveys hundreds of GNN evaluations to establish best practices</cite>.

2) Training modes that make billions possible
• Full-batch vs. mini-batch. Two dominant regimes exist: full-graph/epoch training and mini-batch neighbor sampling. <cite id="cad7e845-3">GNNs can be trained using either full-batch or mini-batch approaches; mini-batch is necessary for large-scale graphs due to memory and compute limits</cite> <cite id="cad7e845-1">Empirical comparisons show trade-offs and convergence behavior across representative full-graph and mini-batch systems</cite>. 
• Neighbor sampling (GraphSAGE/SAGEConv). Sampling k-step neighborhoods into bags enables training on subgraphs that fit GPU memory while amortizing aggregation cost. <cite id="cad7e845-2">Neighbor sampling creates mini-batches to scale training on large graphs, as formalized in GraphSAGE</cite> <cite id="cad7e845-0">SAGEConv layers operate on sampled subgraphs so memory scales with the mini-batch rather than the whole graph</cite> <cite id="cad7e845-4">PyG’s tutorial shows neighbor loaders and Node2Vec sampling to enable mini-batch training</cite>. Variants like Res/Uniform/degree-based sampling and clustering-based sampling curb variance and cost. <cite id="cad7e845-5">Sampling-based GNNs are needed for large-scale graphs; GraphSAGE’s layer-wise sampling is cost-efficient with careful sampling strategies</cite>. 
• Systemized mini-batch pipelines. Performance comparisons emphasize batching, caching, and overlap of materialization and aggregation; CPU-GPU and DAG scheduling reduce wall-clock time. <cite id="844e95f0-2">DistDGLv2 achieves 2–3× speedup over DistDGL and 18× over a baseline, illustrating the benefits of hybrid CPU-GPU pipelines and better scheduling</cite> <cite id="4668bbee-5">Systems like GNN-Compiler/Ginex compile and schedule large graph operators for throughput</cite>.

3) Systems engineered for billions
• Single-machine SSD/billions-on-one-GPU. SSD-backed systems can host and train directly off-disk without out-of-core shuffles. <cite id="4668bbee-0">Ginex evaluates on four billion-scale graphs and achieves 2.11× higher training throughput on average (up to 2.67×), processing billion-scale graphs on a single machine and SSD</cite> <cite id="4668bbee-1">Ginex is an SSD-based training system designed for billion-scale GNNs on a single machine</cite>. The empirical headline is “single-machine throughput and completion time,” underscoring that on-disk I/O and scheduler design dominate cost at this scale. <cite id="4668bbee-3">Surveys attribute recent gains to operator fusion, caching, and scheduling across large graphs</cite>.
• Distributed clusters and speedups. Multiple distributed frameworks demonstrate linear scaling and very low epoch times. <cite id="844e95f0-0">DistDGL attains linear speedup without accuracy loss and completes an epoch in ~13 seconds for 100M-node graphs</cite> <cite id="844e95f0-1">A distributed-memory design with partition-aware pipelining achieves linear speedup on billion-scale datasets</cite> <cite id="844e95f0-4">DistDGLv2 on CPU clusters shows that careful shared-memory designs and partition placement matter for full-batch scalability</cite>. Industry-grade systems show order-of-magnitude improvements by overlapping compute with non-blocking communication and persistent prefetching. <cite id="844e95f0-2">Hybrid CPU–GPU and pipeline-aware kernels deliver 18× speedup over legacy systems for distributed training</cite>.
• Practical graphs and datasets. Billion-scale public graphs used to demonstrate end-to-end feasibility include ones like LiveJournal, YouTube frontpages, and web-scale knowledge/recommendation graphs; these are typically cited through system papers rather than pure ML publications. <cite id="4668bbee-6">Case studies cite live graphs with billions of nodes and hundreds of billions of edges to motivate massive-scale training</cite> <cite id="844e95f0-3">Empirical results present training on a 100M-node graph in a single epoch</cite>. 

4) Effectiveness trade-offs near billion scale
• Simpler models can be more effective at scale. For billion-scale recommendation graphs, “simpler” aggregation-only designs can outperform complex baselines by emphasizing linear propagation and robust neighborhood aggregation. <cite id="1bbf0d64-0">LightGCN retains only neighborhood aggregation and achieves superior performance in billion-scale recommender settings</cite> <cite id="1bbf0d64-6">Recent analyses argue that linear propagation improves recommendation performance and stability compared to nonlinear GCNs</cite>.
• Architectural innovations for scalability and quality. New layers and message-passing patterns aim to improve both scalability and representational power. <cite id="844e95f0-7">Highly parallel distributed GCN training reduces blocking broadcasts via topological-aware scheduling</cite> <cite id="4668bbee-4">Bidirectional/neighbor-fusion designs target better training efficiency and quality at larger scales</cite>. Aggressive scaling often requires rethinking depth vs. breadth and adding mechanisms to prevent over-smoothing or oversquashing. <cite id="c2101988-0">As depth grows, recursive updates cause comm/latency and feature-materialization bottlenecks, hurting scalability</cite> <cite id="c2101988-1">Over-smoothing and over-squashing limit how deep and long-range a GNN can become, curbing performance gains</cite>. 
• When more depth helps, what to do? Adaptive high- and low-order message passing, pruning noisy edges, and cluster-based routing mitigate oversmoothing. <cite id="c2101988-2">ScaleGNN advocates adaptive use of high- and low-order neighbors to recover scalability lost to over-smoothing</cite> <cite id="844e95f0-5">Scaling clustering-based message passing with careful routing improves convergence speed</cite>.

5) Limits and open challenges when nodes reach billions
• Memory, I/O, and feature-materialization. Even with neighbor sampling, materializing multi-hop contexts and degrees of separation introduces heavy memory traffic and nonlocal feature access that can dominate compute; careful caching, reuse, and SSD-aware operators are required. <cite id="cad7e845-3">Mini-batch systems must orchestrate sampling, feature loading, and aggregation efficiently to avoid bottlenecks</cite> <cite id="4668bbee-3">Surveys trace slowdowns to recursive updates, feature materialization, and synchronization costs on large clusters</cite>. 
• Communication and partitioning. Scheduling communication across partitions and cores, overlapping materialization with aggregation, and avoiding stragglers are crucial at scale. <cite id="844e95f0-0">DistDGL uses pipelining and partition-aware sampling to avoid broadcast stalls and retain accuracy</cite> <cite id="844e95f0-2">Kernels that overlap CPU and GPU phases and accelerate sampling reduce wall-clock time</cite>. 
• Modeling limits: depth and range. No matter hardware, deeper message passing risks destroying local signal differences; long-range connectivity requires structured routing or hybridization with transformers, with nontrivial overhead. <cite id="c2101988-0">Increasing depth leads to indistinguishable representations (over-smoothing), curtailing performance</cite> <cite id="c2101988-1">Over-squashing limits the ability to propagate long-range information effectively</cite>. 
• Correctness and robustness at scale. New systems and benchmarks stress that training accuracy can degrade without partition-awareness and cache locality; frameworks provide operators and pipelines to preserve numerical stability and performance. <cite id="844e95f0-0">Speedup without compromising model accuracy shows the system maintains numerical stability while scaling</cite> <cite id="7ab5f7ae-3">Benchmarks provide empirical coverage to detect accuracy regressions when scaling</cite>.

6) Practical guidance: when and how GNNs work well on billion-node graphs
- Use sampling-based or clustering-based mini-batches to bound memory and amortize work; prefer operator fusion and caching to reduce materialization costs. <cite id="cad7e845-0">Layer-wise neighbor sampling via SAGEConv keeps memory bounded while training on large graphs</cite> <cite id="cad7e845-5">Sampling-based methods are essential for large-scale graphs; care in neighborhood sampling reduces cost</cite>.
- For web-scale and recommender graphs, simplify with neighborhood-aggregation-only models like LightGCN or Light-SAGE variants to gain accuracy and stability while staying scalable. <cite id="1bbf0d64-0">LightGCN’s pure aggregation model simplifies training and performs strongly</cite>.
- At or above one billion nodes, deploy distributed systems with SSD or object-store backed data, pipelined communication, and kernel-level overlap (CPU–GPU). Expect linear-to-sublinear speedups as partitions and pipeline stages increase; verify that epoch times drop into the single-digit seconds. <cite id="844e95f0-0">DistDGL shows linear speedup on billion-scale training with ~13s per epoch</cite> <cite id="4668bbee-1">Ginex trains billion-scale graphs on a single machine by pushing to SSD</cite> <cite id="844e95f0-2">Hybrid CPU–GPU pipelines can deliver 18× speedup over legacy systems</cite>.
- Be mindful of depth/long-range limits; use adaptive neighbor orders, bidirectional or cluster-aware routing, and early stopping to avoid over-smoothing, and evaluate with long-range baselines. <cite id="c2101988-0">Over-smoothing constrains maximal depth on large graphs</cite> <cite id="c2101988-2">Adaptive high-/low-order neighbors can restore representational power at scale</cite>.

In short, GNNs can perform well on billion-scale graphs when paired with appropriate training modes (mini-batch neighbor sampling or cluster routing), robust distributed systems (DistDGL/DistDGLv2), and simplified but effective architectures (e.g., LightGCN), and when engineering mitigates memory, communication, and over-smoothing limits; measured results show single-machine SSD training across billions and distributed clusters achieving linear speedups with seconds-per-epoch runtimes and accuracy comparable to smaller-scale baselines. <cite id="4668bbee-0">Ginex achieves 2–2.7× higher throughput on billion-scale graphs</cite> <cite id="844e95f0-0">DistDGL achieves linear speedup without accuracy loss</cite> <cite id="1bbf0d64-0">LightGCN achieves strong performance with simplified neighborhood aggregation</cite> <cite id="cad7e845-0">SAGEConv/mini-batch sampling bounds memory for large graphs</cite> <cite id="c2101988-1">Over-smoothing/oversquashing set intrinsic limits on how deep and long-range GNNs can be</cite>.

fully_underspecified.text: how do they perform on graphs?
fully_underspecified.answer:
# Short answer upfront

- On simple graph reasoning tasks without cycles/heterogeneity, large language models (LLMs) already outperform random baselines by wide margins, often in the ~37–58% range, indicating nontrivial structural understanding when the graph is presented in natural language or via adjacency cues.<cite id="fc532594-0">large language models demonstrate an impressive level of performance that is 37.33% to 57.82% above the random baseline on simple graph reasoning tasks</cite>  
- On harder, heterogeneous, or purely structural graphs, LLMs' gains shrink and are highly sensitive to prompts and evidence; they perform best when nodes/edges carry rich semantics and perform worse on purely topological reasoning with long chains or cycles.<cite id="fc532594-2">This design is intended to assess the impact of graph complexity on the performance of large language models</cite><cite id="fc532594-4">LLMs perform better on graph reasoning tasks with semantic information than on purely structural tasks, showing that textual context enhances</cite>  
- Head-to-head, recent "LLM-as-enhancer" methods and graph-tuned LLM stacks often beat traditional GNN+PLM baselines on multiple graph datasets, but some tasks still favor GNNs; for example, in GraphInfer-Bench, LLM-based methods compete with GNNs on description-level tasks yet surpass GNNs on single-node comparison tasks.<cite id="3cb14d9b-0">GraphLLM methods achieve better results than traditional GNN- and PLM-based methods in supervised settings</cite><cite id="baa65f94-6">GraphLLM methods achieve the highest accuracy and F1 scores on 6 out of the 7 datasets compared to traditional GNN-based and PLM-based methods</cite><cite id="3cb14d9b-7">On Description, LLM-based methods compete with the GNN. On single-node Comparison, the frontier LLM is the only method that clears the GNN</cite>  
- At abstract reasoning with complex rules, LLM performance collapses as difficulty increases, a pattern seen across multiple graph-reasoning suites; careful prompting, stepwise decoding, and hybrid designs are necessary to stabilize performance.<cite id="fc532594-1">we point out issues with existing methods and benchmarks, and rethink the direction that LLMs for graph reasoning should strive</cite><cite id="fc532594-6">We introduce GraphARC, a benchmark for abstract reasoning on graph-structured data</cite><cite id="fc532594-7">NLGraph-hard evaluates LLM graph reasoning tasks via natural language, highlighting high performance on simple tasks and collapse at higher</cite>

# What "performance on graphs" entails

Modern evaluations probe four task types: (i) simple graph reasoning (local subgraph checks, parity checks), (ii) semantic-rich graphs (heterogeneous node/edge types with textual attributes), (iii) abstract rule-learning on graphs, and (iv) production-style pipelines (text-to-graph extraction, graph classification, node/link prediction) with or without retrieval/graph algorithms.<cite id="fc532594-0">large language models demonstrate an impressive level of performance that is 37.33% to 57.82% above the random baseline on simple graph reasoning tasks</cite><cite id="fc532594-2">This design is intended to assess the impact of graph complexity on the performance of large language models</cite><cite id="fc532594-4">LLMs perform better on graph reasoning tasks with semantic information than on purely structural tasks, showing that textual context enhances</cite><cite id="3cb14d9b-4">LLMs perform better on graph reasoning tasks with semantic information than on purely structural tasks, showing that textual context enhances</cite>

# Quantitative signals across settings

- Simple graph reasoning (local checks): When graphs are small and non-cyclic, and either encoded explicitly (adjacency) or described in text, LLMs routinely beat strong random baselines by 37–58% points, showing that purely linguistic priors and in-context algorithms can capture basic graph invariants.<cite id="fc532594-0">large language models demonstrate an impressive level of performance that is 37.33% to 57.82% above the random baseline on simple graph reasoning tasks</cite>

- Semantic-rich vs structural-only graphs: Performance correlates strongly with information richness. LLMs do significantly better when nodes/edges carry text (e.g., "buy→sell" edges, entity-rich nodes) and perform comparatively worse on purely degree/path-based reasoning; encoding the same graph with richer semantics yields higher accuracy and calibration than adjacency-matrix prompting alone.<cite id="fc532594-2">This design is intended to assess the impact of graph complexity on the performance of large language models</cite><cite id="fc532594-4">LLMs perform better on graph reasoning tasks with semantic information than on purely structural tasks, showing that textual context enhances</cite>

- Abstract/algorithmic graph reasoning: As tasks require learning complex graph transformations or abstract rules (e.g., counting cycles with certain properties or hierarchical relations), LLMs exhibit a "performance cliff" as difficulty rises; many methods either plateau or fail without structured decomposition or retrieval-augmentation with formal constraints.<cite id="fc532594-1">we point out issues with existing methods and benchmarks, and rethink the direction that LLMs for graph reasoning should strive</cite><cite id="fc532594-6">We introduce GraphARC, a benchmark for abstract reasoning on graph-structured data</cite><cite id="fc532594-7">NLGraph-hard evaluates LLM graph reasoning tasks via natural language, highlighting high performance on simple tasks and collapse at higher</cite>

- End-to-end pipelines (text-to-graph and classification): Benchmarks like GLBench (2024) and curated suites show graph-tuned LLM stacks ("LLM-as-enhancer" over GNNs) often outperform GNN-only or PLM-only baselines across most datasets; however, some tasks remain more reliable for GNNs (e.g., pure structural classification without heavy semantics), echoing earlier observations on LLM sensitivity to long texts and schema-compliance.<cite id="baa65f94-6">GraphLLM methods achieve the highest accuracy and F1 scores on 6 out of the 7 datasets compared to traditional GNN-based and PLM-based methods</cite><cite id="3cb14d9b-0">GraphLLM methods achieve better results than traditional GNN- and PLM-based methods in supervised settings</cite><cite id="3cb14d9b-7">On Description, LLM-based methods compete with the GNN. On single-node Comparison, the frontier LLM is the only method that clears the GNN</cite><cite id="f91cd9b9-6">LLMs tend to perform worse when handling long texts</cite>

# Comparisons to GNNs and hybrid designs

- When matched fairly, GNNs are still strong on purely structural tasks (e.g., label propagation over cycles, shortest-path reasoning), while LLMs excel when they can leverage textual semantics and long-context chains; recent work often combines them to get the best of both worlds. In GraphInfer-Bench, LLM-based pipelines match GNNs on description-level tasks and beat them in single-node comparison, suggesting complementary strengths by layer or stage.<cite id="3cb14d9b-7">On Description, LLM-based methods compete with the GNN. On single-node Comparison, the frontier LLM is the only method that clears the GNN</cite>

- A growing toolkit couples LLMs with GNN mechanisms: (a) GNN-as-judge/adaptation to guide pseudo-labeling and correct hallucinations; (b) GNN-to-LLM retrieval and routing; and (c) LLM-as-enhancer that conditions GNN messages on text-rich node embeddings. These hybrids frequently improve graph classification and reasoning accuracy/F1 versus GNN-only baselines on multiple datasets, but the advantage is dataset-dependent and can evaporate if the graph is purely structural or too large.<cite id="3cb14d9b-0">GraphLLM methods achieve better results than traditional GNN- and PLM-based methods in supervised settings</cite><cite id="baa65f94-6">GraphLLM methods achieve the highest accuracy and F1 scores on 6 out of the 7 datasets compared to traditional GNN-based and PLM-based methods</cite><cite id="baa65f94-5">We propose GraphAdapter, which uses a graph neural network (GNN) as an efficient adapter in collaboration with LLMs to tackle TAGs</cite><cite id="baa65f94-1">Graph Neural Retrieval for Large Language Model Reasoning</cite>

- At the system level, GNNs remain gold standards for very large-scale, purely structural tasks (e.g., social network community detection, citation graph classification) per industry benchmarks (MLPerf), reinforcing that "LLM-only" isn't universally superior without text semantics or careful orchestration.<cite id="3cb14d9b-3">Generally GNNs have been shown to outperform other machine learning methods for tasks like node classification and graph classification and ...</cite>

# Benchmarks and failure modes

The community has built specialized suites to diagnose LLM strengths and weaknesses on graphs:

- Simple/parity checks (NeurIPS 2023 poster): LLMs beat random by 37–58%, evidencing baseline-aware structural reasoning. The boost is large but does not by itself show competitiveness with GNNs on complex graphs.<cite id="fc532594-0">large language models demonstrate an impressive level of performance that is 37.33% to 57.82% above the random baseline on simple graph reasoning tasks</cite>

- GraCoRe (2025): Systematically increases graph complexity (heterogeneity, cycles, depth) and finds LLMs struggle as complexity rises; they leverage semantics and fail on purely structural tasks, prompting designs like graph-to-text translation and structured prompting.<cite id="fc532594-2">This design is intended to assess the impact of graph complexity on the performance of large language models</cite><cite id="fc532594-4">LLMs perform better on graph reasoning tasks with semantic information than on purely structural tasks, showing that textual context enhances</cite>

- GraphARC and NLGraph-hard: Abstract rule learning and multi-step comparisons reveal that gains plateau or collapse as rule length and graph depth increase; chain-of-thought and verification help but don't eliminate failure without domain-specific formalization.<cite id="fc532594-6">We introduce GraphARC, a benchmark for abstract reasoning on graph-structured data</cite><cite id="fc532594-7">NLGraph-hard evaluates LLM graph reasoning tasks via natural language, highlighting high performance on simple tasks and collapse at higher</cite><cite id="f91cd9b9-6">LLMs tend to perform worse when handling long texts</cite>

- GraphInfer-Bench (2026): Shows task-dependence—LLMs match GNNs on macro-level description tasks and exceed GNNs on single-node comparison; suggests hybrid pipelines where the GNN pre-extracts structured summaries and the LLM performs fine-grained comparison and verification can be strong baselines.<cite id="3cb14d9b-7">On Description, LLM-based methods compete with the GNN. On single-node Comparison, the frontier LLM is the only method that clears the GNN</cite>

- Text-structure imbalance (TAGs/MINT-style graphs): LLMs can misalign node labels or propagate spurious text features; alignment methods explicitly bring GNN and LLM objectives into harmony to improve accuracy/F1, especially on heterogeneous graphs.<cite id="baa65f94-0">The paper addresses the text-structure imbalance problem in Text-Attributed Graphs (TAGs) by aligning Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) and Large Language Models (LLMs)</cite>

# Methods that improve graph performance

- Prompting and structured decoding: Treating graphs as programs—stepwise traversal, decomposition into subgraphs, or tree-of-thoughts—consistently raises accuracy on cyclic/long graphs; verification graphs and graph-to-text translation improve robustness versus adjacency-only prompts.<cite id="fc532594-2">This design is intended to assess the impact of graph complexity on the performance of large language models</cite><cite id="f91cd9b9-6">LLMs tend to perform worse when handling long texts</cite><cite id="f91cd9b9-2">We propose a graph-based verification method, GraphReason, aimed at significantly enhancing the reasoning capabilities of large language models</cite>

- Visual/graph rendering for multimodal models: Rendering graphs with visual nodes/edges and adding modality cues helps multimodal LLMs (LVLMs) on graph QA (e.g., GITQA) where text-only encoding fails; it reduces ambiguity for cyclic structures by providing perceptual anchors.<cite id="f91cd9b9-0">In this paper, we take the first step in incorporating visual information into graph reasoning tasks and propose a new benchmark GITQA</cite>

- Hybrid LLM+GNN systems: Practical "sprints" include GNN-as-judge for pseudo-labeling and filtering, GNN-to-LLM retrieval of structured evidence, and LLM-as-enhancer that augments GNN messages/ embeddings with text reasoning; these typically lift accuracy/F1 vs single-modality baselines across most GraphBench datasets, while remaining cautious on purely structural giants.<cite id="baa65f94-1">Graph Neural Retrieval for Large Language Model Reasoning</cite><cite id="baa65f94-5">GraphAdapter, which uses a graph neural network (GNN) as an efficient adapter in collaboration with LLMs</cite><cite id="3cb14d9b-0">GraphLLM methods achieve better results than traditional GNN- and PLM-based methods in supervised settings</cite><cite id="baa65f94-6">GraphLLM methods achieve the highest accuracy and F1 scores on 6 out of the 7 datasets compared to traditional GNN-based and PLM-based methods</cite>

# What they still get wrong

- Long chains and cycles: Without explicit decomposition or traversal policies, LLMs hallucinate cycles, miscount path lengths, or drop nodes; this drives collapse on abstract reasoning where path indeterminacy explodes the search space.<cite id="f91cd9b9-6">LLMs tend to perform worse when handling long texts</cite><cite id="f91cd9b9-7">NLGraph-hard evaluates LLM graph reasoning tasks via natural language, highlighting high performance on simple tasks and collapse at higher</cite>

- Schema-heavy or purely structural graphs: When attributes are sparse and relations are symbolic, performance dips; by contrast, GNNs remain strong here, hence the push for hybrid designs or GNN-judge stages.<cite id="fc532594-4">LLMs perform better on graph reasoning tasks with semantic information than on purely structural tasks, showing that textual context enhances</cite><cite id="3cb14d9b-3">Generally GNNs have been shown to outperform other machine learning methods for tasks like node classification and graph classification</cite>

- Benchmark instability: Reported scores vary widely with prompt formats, chain-of-thought depth, whether outputs are verified, and data leakage; current benchmarks call out these pitfalls and recommend standardized evaluation pipelines.<cite id="fc532594-1">we point out issues with existing methods and benchmarks, and rethink the direction that LLMs for graph reasoning should strive</cite><cite id="f91cd9b9-8">“The score” is rarely a single number that's comparable across labs. You routinely see differences driven by: 0-shot vs 5-shot; whether chain-of-thought is used</cite>

# Takeaways and practical guidance

- If your graphs are small, non-cyclic, and text-attributed, an LLM with graph-prompting and verification often suffices and beats random baselines substantially; you may see ~37–58% gains over naive baselines on parity checks, depending on exact task and model size.<cite id="fc532594-0">large language models demonstrate an impressive level of performance that is 37.33% to 57.82% above the random baseline on simple graph reasoning tasks</cite>

- If graphs are large and/or purely structural, prefer GNNs or hybrid pipelines: use GNNs for structural classification/prediction, then route summaries to an LLM for semantic interpretation or verification; in iterative evals, LLM-based methods can match or exceed GNNs on micro-level comparisons, so pairing is often best.<cite id="3cb14d9b-7">On Description, LLM-based methods compete with the GNN. On single-node Comparison, the frontier LLM is the only method that clears the GNN</cite><cite id="3cb14d9b-3">Generally GNNs have been shown to outperform other machine learning methods for tasks like node classification and graph classification</cite>

- For abstract reasoning and complex rule induction, decompose graphs into programs, enforce traversal constraints, and add verification graphs; even then, plan for degradation as problem size increases and validate with at least two orthogonal baselines (LLM and GNN).<cite id="fc532594-6">We introduce GraphARC, a benchmark for abstract reasoning on graph-structured data</cite><cite id="f91cd9b9-6">LLMs tend to perform worse when handling long texts</cite><cite id="f91cd9b9-2">GraphReason, aimed at significantly enhancing the reasoning capabilities of large language models</cite>

- If you must choose one survey to read next, start with the 2025 benchmarking and evaluation overviews that critique early metrics and propose standardized, complexity-growing testbeds; they map directly to what's currently working and where the field is going.<cite id="fc532594-1">we point out issues with existing methods and benchmarks, and rethink the direction that LLMs for graph reasoning should strive</cite><cite id="fc532594-2">by Z Yuan · 2025 · Cited by 30 — This design is intended to assess the impact of graph complexity on the performance of large language models</cite>
