query.text: planning with Large Language Models
query.answer:
# What “Planning with Large Language Models” Means

Planning with LLMs refers to using large language models to generate multi-step strategies, decompose tasks into subgoals, invoke tools or environment actions, and adapt plans based on feedback, often operating as “LLM-as-an-agent.” Recent surveys explicitly treat planning as a core capability and catalog successes and shortcomings across task planning and structured execution settings, including interactions with classical planning methods and external formalisms <cite id="9396b827-0">A recent survey critically investigates the use of LLMs in automated planning, detailing successes and shortcomings</cite> <cite id="9396b827-1">A 2025 survey presents a comprehensive overview of large language models in task planning</cite> <cite id="9396b827-2">A 2025 survey frames LLMs as planning formalizers, leveraging their ability to generate structured outputs such as executable code or formal representations</cite>.

# Core Paradigms and Algorithms

A recurring design pattern is chain-of-thought (CoT), where the model emits intermediate inferences to guide multi-step solutions; its extension “program-of-thoughts” (PoT) disentangles symbolic representation and computation by generating executable code or explicit procedures alongside reasoning <cite id="ecb85585-0">Program of Thoughts prompting disentangles computation from reasoning, using Codex to express the reasoning process via code or structured artifacts</cite> <cite id="ecb85585-2">Program of Thoughts Prompting models the CoT paradigm by explicitly expressing intermediate reasoning artifacts such as code or equations</cite>. CoT and PoT are widely recommended for numerical and tool-using tasks because they make latent steps interpretable and delegable to external evaluators or code executors <cite id="ecb85585-4">Program-of-Thoughts is effective for tasks requiring precise arithmetic, equations, or repeated numerical operations, unlike standard CoT</cite>.

Reflection/self-improvement methods add feedback cycles to refine plans: an agent solves a problem, critiques the solution, and iterates. Self-Refine and Reflexion exemplify this, using either self-generated feedback or “verbal reinforcement learning” to update future behavior, improving reliability on complex tasks but sometimes facing challenges such as inadequate feedback quality or long-horizon instability <cite id="2e83cb5f-0">Self-Refine elicits feedback from LLMs on intermediate reasoning and iteratively refines the solution path</cite> <cite id="525a2b46-0">Reflexion updates the agent’s internal monologue with reflections and action histories to improve subsequent decisions</cite> <cite id="525a2b46-1">Self-Refine and Reflexion enhance problem-solving, though challenges remain with feedback quality and convergence</cite> <cite id="525a2b46-2">Stepwise reasoning with Chain-of-Thought, Self-Refine, and Reflexion supports deeper, more reliable problem solving</cite>. Surveys further discuss distinctions: Self-Refine typically operates within a single session by iteratively polishing the same problem state, while Reflexion spans episodes and builds narrative self-awareness from prior experiences <cite id="525a2b46-4">Self-Refine applies within a single solving session, contrasting with Reflexion, which operates across separate episodes</cite>.

A complementary paradigm is “planning formalization,” where the LLM translates natural-language goals into formal target languages (e.g., PDDL, ASP, SMT, MILP) so that classical or programmatic solvers can compute the plan, which the LLM then interprets into actions <cite id="9396b827-2">LLMs-as-planning-formalizers generate executable code or structured formal models (e.g., PDDL/ASP/SMT/MILP) to bridge NL goals and action spaces</cite> <cite id="9396b827-5">LLM-generated heuristics can improve classical planners, illustrating hybrid synergies</cite>.

# Execution, Tools, and Environment Interaction

LLM planning often proceeds in a loop: deliberate (plan), act (use tools/APIs), observe (get partial/full observations), and repeat. Code-assisted reasoning (PoT) makes computation explicit and checkable, enabling precise arithmetic, data transformation, and program synthesis to serve as planning subroutines or decision procedures <cite id="ecb85585-0">PoT uses code to separate declarative reasoning from computable steps</cite> <cite id="2e83cb5f-0">Self-Refine builds on iterative feedback to refine such code-aided reasoning traces</cite>. Surveys highlight planning-as-execution systems that organize memory, actions, and decision-making through tool-use and environment interaction, with reflective monologues improving policy stability over time <cite id="525a2b46-5">Agents organize memory, action, and decision-making; Reflexion augments with verbal reflection and reinforcement learning from experience</cite>.

General-purpose agent frameworks increasingly split behavior into Thought/Plan → Act/Execute → Critic/Feedback phases, using external tools (search, APIs, code execution) and structured memory, then looping with self-evaluation to reduce error accumulation <cite id="2e83cb5f-1">Agents’ behavior is structured into thought (planning), action (execution), and self-feedback loops</cite>. These design choices explicitly respond to the observation that naive LLMs can mis-specify steps, underspecify assumptions, or hallucinate actions over long horizons; decomposition and explicit feedback reduce brittle failures but still require careful prompt design and guardrails <cite id="9396b827-0">The planning literature emphasizes both successes and shortcomings of LLMs, including mis-specification and hallucination risks</cite>.

# Hybrid and Classical-Planner Integration

Hybrid approaches combine LLM intuition with symbolic optimizers or heuristic search. Surveys describe translation “formalizers” that convert NL into PDDL/ASP/SMT/MILP for classical solvers, then map solutions back to LLM-side action schemas; conversely, LLMs can generate heuristics or domain models to warm-start classical planners and improve efficiency or solution quality <cite id="9396b827-2">LLMs-as-planning-formalizers translate tasks into formal structured models suitable for classical solvers</cite> <cite id="9396b827-5">Classical planning with LLM-generated heuristics demonstrates hybrid gains</cite>. Empirical overviews also note that post-hoc prompting strategies like Reflexion and Self-Refine plug into this pipeline as feedback or policy improvement layers, though convergence and robustness remain open issues <cite id="525a2b46-1">Self-Refine and Reflexion enhance problem-solving with feedback, but face challenges with stability and feedback quality</cite>.

# Benchmarks, Empirical Evidence, and Typical Pitfalls

Contemporary planning research benchmarks include natural-language task suites (e.g., WebShop, ALFWorld) and software-engineering-style repairs/simulators; recent overviews report that CoT/PoT improve arithmetic and tool-use accuracy, while reflective agents reduce failure rates on multi-step problems by catching pre-mature commitments and mis-specifications. However, long-horizon tasks still suffer from drift, myopic subgoals, or brittle tool-use when inputs deviate from training distributions; surveys emphasize systematic evaluation and the need for robust decompositions and verification loops <cite id="9396b827-0">Surveys document that LLMs can succeed where instruction-following suffices yet falter on structured planning due to mis-specification, hallucination, and brittleness</cite> <cite id="ecb85585-0">PoT reduces errors on numerical reasoning by disentangling computation from language, improving disentangling on numeric tasks</cite> <cite id="525a2b46-2">Chain-of-Thought and its reflective variants provide stepwise breakdowns that increase reliability compared to single-shot responses</cite>.

Common failure modes include:
- Under/overspecification: goals are too vague for code; too specific without error handling for classical solvers.
- Hallucination: generated plans reference non-existent APIs or data fields; symbolic formalizations contain unreachable goals.
- Error diffusion: a wrong intermediate tool call contaminates later steps; long chains lose context.
Surveys and practice-oriented lists recommend decomposition, explicit preconditions/effects, code validation, and iterative feedback as mitigations <cite id="9396b827-1">The 2025 task-planning survey stresses decomposition, guardrails, and monitoring of LLM plans</cite> <cite id="9396b827-3">Curated compilations of planning-capability papers highlight decomposition and validation patterns</cite> <cite id="2e83cb5f-0">Self-Refine’s feedback loop targets intermediate errors before final execution</cite>.

# Practical System Designs

- LLM-as-executor with CoT/PoT: Generate step-by-step reasoning and/or code, execute snippets, and validate outputs; repeat. This is effective for math-heavy, tool-accessible tasks and reduces ambiguity by materializing artifacts <cite id="ecb85585-0">PoT explicitly disentangles computation from reasoning via executable artifacts</cite> <cite id="ecb85585-4">Guidelines: use PoT when tasks require precise arithmetic, equations, or repeated operations</cite>.

- Reflective agents (Self-Refine/Reflexion): After each plan segment, summarize partial results, diagnose failure modes, and re-plan. Evidence shows improved reliability but warns about potential feedback loops and oscillation without strong stopping criteria <cite id="525a2b46-0">Reflexion stores reflections and action histories to guide future choices</cite> <cite id="525a2b46-1">Self-Refine and Reflexion boost problem solving, yet challenges persist with feedback quality</cite>.

- Planning-by-formalization: Translate NL goals to PDDL/ASP/SMT/MILP, compute plans with classical solvers, and map back to actions; optionally let the LLM propose abstractions or heuristics. Reports highlight that this leverages LLMs’ structured generation while restoring optimality/completeness guarantees from classical planning where feasible <cite id="9396b827-2">The planning formalizer survey details how LLMs produce formal structured plans</cite> <cite id="9396b827-5">LLM-derived heuristics warmed into classical planners improve performance</cite>.

- Human-in-the-loop checkpoints: Use LLM reflections plus human expert reviews for high-stakes steps, especially when tool landscapes change rapidly or domain knowledge is tacit. Reflective frameworks explicitly target this by maintaining experience-derived monologues for better simulation and safer extrapolation <cite id="525a2b46-5">Reflexion enhances agents with verbal reflection, improving simulation and decision-making</cite>.

# Choosing Among Paradigms: Factors and Trade-offs

- Task structure and data access: If precise computation is needed, prefer PoT/Code-Aided reasoning with sandboxed execution; if the environment has a known API, equip the LLM with tool specs and use reflective acting; if the state space admits formal modeling, use planning formalization to offload to classical solvers <cite id="ecb85585-0">PoT excels when computation can be disentangled from language</cite> <cite id="9396b827-2">Planning formalizers target settings where structured outputs can be offloaded</cite>.

- Safety and verifiability: Decomposition, explicit preconditions/effects, and unit tests on intermediate outputs reduce hallucination risk and enable rollback. Reflection narrows blind spots in the LLM’s self-critique but can be brittle without strong evaluators or bounded recursion <cite id="525a2b46-1">Despite improvements, feedback-based methods can still struggle with convergence and quality</cite>.

- Hybrid pipelines: Combine CoT/PoT for idea generation, classical planners for optimality on formal subproblems, and LLM reflections for global control; let LLMs propose heuristics and formalizers, then validate before deployment. Surveys and workshop notes report strong synergies in practice when these layers are integrated with explicit interfaces between models and tools <cite id="9396b827-5">LLM-generated heuristics improving classical planning exemplifies effective hybridization</cite>.

# Practical Benchmarks and Reproducible Checks

Surveys catalog planning benchmarks and suites, recommending reproducible evaluations that include:
- Stepwise accuracy: correctness of each subgoal and tool call.
- Path efficiency: number of retries, tool calls, or execution time.
- Robustness: performance across perturbations, noisy observations, and domain shifts.
They argue that even if end-task success improves, intermediate verification and failure analysis should be measured to diagnose hallucination and drift, and that reflective methods should be stress-tested for oscillation or reward hacking in sparse-feedback regimes <cite id="9396b827-0">Evaluation must attend to shortcomings like mis-specification and hallucination</cite> <cite id="525a2b46-1">Self-Refine/Reflexion improve outcomes, but feedback challenges necessitate careful evaluation</cite>.

# Recommended Recipe (Evidence-Backed)

- Decompose: Use CoT/PoT to elicit a clear sequence of subgoals and symbolic/algorithmic steps; capture preconditions and measurable checkpoints <cite id="ecb85585-0">Disentangling computation into code artifacts supports precise, testable steps</cite>.

- Execute with safeguards: Run code/tool calls in a sandbox with deterministic I/O, enforcing timeouts; re-plan on errors or assertions <cite id="ecb85585-0">Materializing code/thoughts improves verifiability of steps</cite>.

- Reflect and adapt: Apply Self-Refine/Reflexion cycles per segment or episode to summarize context, critique outputs, and update the plan; limit recursion depth and converge with a strong stopping criterion <cite id="525a2b46-0">Reflexion maintains verbal reflections over contexts and histories to improve decisions</cite> <cite id="525a2b46-1">Self-Refine and Reflexion enhance reliability but require guarding against feedback brittleness</cite>.

- Formalize where helpful: For NP-complete or structured domains, translate to PDDL/ASP/SMT/MILP, solve with off-the-shelf planners, and reconcile results back into action lists; let the LLM propose abstractions, macros, or heuristics to speed convergence <cite id="9396b827-2">LLM formalizers facilitate transfer to classical planners</cite> <cite id="9396b827-5">Heuristics from LLMs can warm-start classical planners</cite>.

- Monitor and human-fall-back: Establish dashboards for parse/plan/act/learn latency, success rates, and error histograms; reserve a human-in-the-loop for semantic anomalies or evolving APIs <cite id="525a2b46-5">Agent frameworks organize memory, action, and decision-making with reflective monitoring</cite>.

# Outlook

Surveys converge that the field is transitioning from “magic” to modular pipelines: LLMs formalize, plan, and teach tools, while classical methods and reflective loops ensure correctness. Open problems include principled long-horizon guarantees, robust feedback acquisition, and seamless multimodal/tool integrations; however, the evidence base of CoT/PoT, self-refinement, and planning formalization already supports practical progress in many domains when paired with rigorous evaluation and hybridization <cite id="9396b827-0">Recent surveys trace progress and shortcomings, motivating principled integrations</cite> <cite id="9396b827-2">Planning formalizers open a path to correctness-preserving LLM-enabled planning</cite> <cite id="525a2b46-2">A broader trend is to break solutions into step-by-step paths, improving reliability</cite>.

# What "Planning with Models" Means

Planning with models refers to an agent's use of an internal or learned model of the environment to choose actions that achieve goals over time. Models can encode state transitions, observations, costs, and dynamics, and can be deterministic or probabilistic (MDPs/POMDPs), finite or infinite horizon, fully observable or partially observable. In the LLM era, "models" also include language-model-based world simulators, program/value function critics, temporal-logic monitors, and memory/retrieval modules that constrain and evaluate plans before or during execution. <cite id="2d7d5df0-0">LLM surveys in transportation note how models are used across analysis, system design, and simulation for planning tasks</cite> <cite id="2d7d5df0-2">and surveys of self-driving decision-making cover model-based knowledge-driven and data-driven planners</cite> <cite id="2d7d5df0-1">as well as broader reviews of LLM-based planning methods</cite> <cite id="2d7d5df0-3">and task-planning with LLMs</cite> <cite id="2d7d5df0-5">with critical assessments of strengths and limitations</cite> <cite id="2d7d5df0-8">including categorizations of generative models as controllers and modelers within decision making</cite>.

# Classical Foundations: MDPs/POMDPs and Solver Algorithms

Model-based planning in classical decision theory is framed as Markov Decision Processes (MDPs) when states are fully observable and as Partially Observable MDPs (POMDPs) when observations are noisy/limited. The canonical solution patterns are dynamic-programming value/policy iteration and learning methods like Q-learning that leverage models for rollouts. <cite id="01b3f3de-2">A standard POMDP lecture explains that value iteration is an exact method over belief states, computing optimal value functions and derived policies; policy iteration alternates policy evaluation and improvement to converge faster</cite> <cite id="01b3f3de-7">a concise MDP framing defines the 4-tuple (S, A, p, R) and links to planning/control algorithms</cite> <cite id="01b3f3de-6">an exposition on Q-learning notes convergence to optimal Q-values and that model-free solutions can work without an explicit transition model when the model is learned online</cite> <cite id="01b3f3de-4">instructional materials show how value iteration computes optimal policies on gridworlds</cite>.

These formal methods address finite- and infinite-horizon problems, incorporate risk/reward via dynamic programming, and provide guarantees under bounded model error or known transition kernels. <cite id="01b3f3de-8">Planning in MDPs and POMDPs yields policies that map (belief) states to actions to minimize expected cost, with belief-state policies central to POMDPs</cite> <cite id="ac85c0b2-0">and modern analyses characterize LLM reasoning as world-model–based planning, where a separate plan/act loop (Reasoning → Action → Plan → …) iteratively refines via feedback</cite>.

Practical deployment often mixes model-based planning with heuristic or domain-specific search, especially when state spaces are large. <cite id="01b3f3de-2">Belief-state value/policy iteration remains exact but can be computationally heavy; thus, approximations and structured relaxations dominate in robotics/robotics-style domains</cite> <cite id="01b3f3de-7">and model predictive control concepts are brought into RL planning by rolling forward with current-model beliefs for receding-horizon decisions</cite>.

# Temporal Logic and Model-Based Synthesis

Many real-world goals are best specified with formal temporal logic rather than fixed terminal costs (e.g., "eventually reach goal, always stay safe"). MDPs with Linear Temporal Logic (LTL) provide a way to synthesize policies that satisfy temporal specifications over infinite horizons. <cite id="eefdaee7-5">Qualitative analysis and synthesis for POMDPs with LTL properties have been developed for robot motion planning, enabling verification of safety/liveness under partial observability</cite> <cite id="eefdaee7-2">LTL-based path planning for robots offers concise, readable, and verifiable mission specs</cite> <cite id="eefdaee7-6">the LTLMoP toolkit operationalizes LTL mission planning from hybrid controllers to execution</cite>.

Solving LTLMDP formulations often involves reduction to automata-based MDPs, quantitative analysis (probabilistic reachability), and optimization to obtain finite-state controllers or structured policies. <cite id="eefdaee7-1">Automated planning pipelines integrate symbolic model checking and MDPs with logic-based goals for schedulability and planning</cite> <cite id="eefdaee7-5">qualitative analysis reduces to solving parity conditions over product MDPs and ω-automata</cite> <cite id="eefdaee7-4">semi-MDPs relax one-step memory to handle unbounded horizons with generalized reinforcement learning</cite>. Recent work also tackles POMDP planning under LTL constraints, providing algorithms that mitigate the curse of dimensionality via structured relaxations and decomposition. <cite id="eefdaee7-3">POMDP planning with finite LTL constraints has been addressed by synthesis methods that build controllers enforcing the temporal properties on partially observed systems</cite> <cite id="eefdaee7-7">with extensions emphasizing scalability and practical verification pipelines for robotics motion planning</cite>.

# LLM-Era Model-Based Planning: Search, Simulation, and Reflection

Large language models expand the toolset for model-based planning by serving as world models, simulators, critics, and planners, enabling explicit search over candidate plans with feedback and reflection. <cite id="ac85c0b2-0">Reasoning with Language Models is Planning with World Models: reasoning can be decomposed into plan generation via search, followed by action execution and learning from outcomes</cite> <cite id="ac85c0b2-1">search-based LLM planners can reach high accuracy on multi-step tasks when search components (e.g., codified by LLM-generated code) efficiently prune the action space</cite>.

Key methodological patterns include:
- Simulated execution loops (program-of-thoughts/PAL): LLMs generate code or action sequences that are executed in a simulator, with intermediate states and errors feeding the next iteration. <cite id="ac85c0b2-5">PAL program-aided LLMs read natural language problems and generate executable programs as intermediate reasoning artifacts</cite>.
- Reflective and grounded search: planners simulate proposed actions in a learned world model, reflect on costs/consistency, and refine subgoals to reach global objectives. <cite id="ac85c0b2-0">RAP-style planning formalizes repeated plan–act–learn cycles, achieving new state-of-the-art on long-horizon and compositional reasoning tasks</cite> <cite id="ac85c0b2-2">and in robotics, plan–act loops with language programs bridge abstract goals to low-level motion planning</cite>.
- Temporal-logic–constrained LLM planning: combining LTL specs with LLM-based search or controllers to ensure safety and liveness. <cite id="ac85c0b2-0">World-model planning supports explicit monitoring and re-planning when temporal properties are violated</cite>.
- Hybrid learning-to-plan: LLMs propose trajectories, which RL with offline simulation and trajectory annotations refines into robust policies. <cite id="ac85c0b2-4">Learning planning-based reasoning via trajectory collection synthesizes process rewards from outcome annotations using offline simulation to bootstrap long-horizon control</cite>.

These techniques often integrate symbolic planning to reduce search in large discrete spaces and to make reasoning artifacts interpretable and verifiable. <cite id="eefdaee7-0">Symbolic transition models can be learned and used to guide hierarchical LRL, enabling decomposition of complex goals and efficient exploration</cite> <cite id="ac85c0b2-1">further accuracy gains are observed when LLMs design the search code, with some pipelines reaching 100% dataset accuracy in constrained settings</cite>.

# Applications and Case Studies

Transport and mobility: LLM planners and world models are increasingly used to analyze and design transport systems, offering scalable simulation, scenario analysis, and agent-based route/activity planning. <cite id="2d7d5df0-0">Surveys find LLMs contribute to transport modeling across analysis, demand forecasting, system design, and scenario planning, leveraging internal models to generate and evaluate plans</cite> <cite id="2d7d5df0-1">and LLM planning reviews detail the breadth of transportation use-cases</cite>.

Autonomous driving: Modern self-driving stacks combine high-accuracy state models and MPC-like receding-horizon controllers with model-based behavior planning under LTL safety goals; knowledge-driven models (maps, localization) and data-driven perception/feedforward models enable robust decisions. <cite id="2d7d5df0-2">Comprehensive surveys of decision-making in autonomous driving cover classical and learning-based model-driven planners, emphasizing verification and uncertainty handling</cite> <cite id="eefdaee7-5">POMDP/LTL frameworks have been applied to robot motion planning with verifiable guarantees</cite> <cite id="ac85c0b2-3">LLM-guided RL (Plan-Seq-Learn) bridges language-level goals and low-level robot motion planning to execute long-horizon tasks</cite>.

Information-seeking and discrete operations: LLM-based agents use web/information memory, retrieval, and simulation to plan multi-step objectives with external evaluators. <cite id="ac85c0b2-4">Trajectory-based planning methods learn from outcome feedback, enabling complex information gathering and tool-use under long horizons</cite> <cite id="ac85c0b2-2">symbolic LLM planning with grounded and reflective search leverages a learned simulator to propose actions, evaluate them, and refine subgoals</cite>. Hierarchical decompositions using symbolic models reduce branching and make progress in structured domains like logistics. <cite id="eefdaee7-0">Learning symbolic transition models supports hierarchical reinforcement learning to scale planning over large action spaces</cite>.

# Design Principles, Trade-offs, and Open Problems

- Model accuracy vs. tractability: Planning with precise dynamics is optimal in MDPs/POMDPs but often intractable on large continuous domains; approximations (symbolic abstraction, factor graphs), rollouts, and sampling-based search are used at scale. <cite id="01b3f3de-2">Exact value/policy iteration over belief states is computationally demanding, motivating approximation and structured decomposition</cite>.
- Model efficiency vs. expressivity: LLM-generated code and planners can dramatically prune search and reach high accuracy, but depend on robust tooling, safe execution, and verification to avoid brittleness. <cite id="ac85c0b2-1">LLM-designed search components can restore full dataset accuracy in benchmarks</cite> <cite id="ac85c0b2-5">PAL shows program synthesis can stabilize reasoning and improve reliability on compositional tasks</cite>.
- Safety and guarantees: LTL-constrained planning and controller synthesis provide formal assurances, but practical deployment must reconcile partial observability and model uncertainty with runtime monitoring and adaptive replanning. <cite id="eefdaee7-5">LTL over POMDPs enables qualitative verification and synthesis for motion tasks</cite> <cite id="eefdaee7-3">finite LTL constraints on POMDPs have dedicated optimal control synthesis methods</cite>.
- Data and learning: Model-based planners benefit from data-driven refinement (Q-learning, plan–seq–learn), trajectory bootstrapping, and hybridization with LLMs. <cite id="01b3f3de-6">Q-learning converges to optimal values when states/actions are sufficiently explored</cite> <cite id="ac85c0b2-4">trajectory-based learning methods derive process rewards from outcome annotations, enabling offline simulation-assisted planning</cite> <cite id="ac85c0b2-3">LLM-guided RL modularly couples abstract goals with low-level execution</cite>.
- Evaluation and benchmarks: LLM and classical planning need standardized, verifiable benchmarks with temporal goals and partial observability to compare planners across domains. <cite id="2d7d5df0-0">Transport planning surveys emphasize simulation and testing as central to model validation and evaluation</cite> <cite id="2d7d5df0-2">autonomous driving surveys call for evaluation under uncertainty and interaction with traffic</cite>.

# Practical Blueprint

- Choose the formalism: use MDPs when states are available/observable; POMDPs with belief states and observation models when only partial information is available. <cite id="01b3f3de-7">An MDP is a tuple hS, A, p, Ri over states, actions, transition and reward</cite> <cite id="01b3f3de-8">solutions are belief-to-action policies minimizing expected cost in POMDPs</cite>.
- Plan or learn: for small/modest state spaces, solve with value/policy iteration or LTL-synthesis; for large spaces, use search over LM-generated actions with a learned simulator, plus LTL monitors for safety. <cite id="01b3f3de-2">Value/policy iteration remains exact in POMDPs</cite> <cite id="ac85c0b2-0">world-model planning loops improve reasoning via iterative act–plan–learn</cite> <cite id="ac85c0b2-1">LLM-crafted search can push accuracy and efficiency to high levels</cite>.
- Integrate memory and reflection: use a world model to run simulations, an LTL interpreter/monitor to check intermediate milestones, and a planner (symbolic or heuristic) to propose next actions. <cite id="ac85c0b2-2">SPIRAL uses a learned simulator for grounded and reflective search over language plans, monitoring goal progress</cite>.
- Validate and certify: test with motion/temporal benchmarks and, where possible, synthesize controllers that guarantee LTL properties over discrete/abstracted models before roll-out. <cite id="eefdaee7-5">Qualitative LTL analysis on POMDPs yields verifiable guarantees for robot motion planning</cite> <cite id="eefdaee7-6">LTLMoP operationalizes hybrid controllers for LTL mission planning</cite>.
- Iterate with data: collect outcomes and use them to update models and rewards, or let trajectory learning bootstrap process objectives for long-horizon tasks. <cite id="ac85c0b2-4">Trajectory-based planning synthesizes process rewards from observed outcomes with offline simulation</cite>.

In sum, planning with models spans classical DP/optimal control on MDP(P)s to modern LLM-driven world-model search with temporal logic and hybrid RL, with strong traction in mobility and robotics. The trajectory from exact DP methods to simulated LLM planning reflects a pragmatic shift: use models to make search tractable, verify safety via temporal logic, and refine solutions with data—closing the loop between model, plan, and execution. <cite id="01b3f3de-2">Dynamic programming gives exact policies in POMDPs over belief states</cite> <cite id="ac85c0b2-0">LLM-based world models support iterative planning/execution loops that improve reasoning performance</cite> <cite id="eefdaee7-5">and LTL-driven synthesis provides a formal lens for planning correctness and safety in robots and vehicles</cite>.

without_term.text: planning with language models
without_term.answer:
Below is a concise, evidence-backed overview of how language models (LLMs) are used for planning, what works, where it breaks, and practical recommendations.

1) What “planning with language models” entails
- Core idea: leverage LMs to generate intermediate goals, decompose tasks, reason over options, and coordinate with tools or simulators to execute multi-step plans and adapt when things fail. <cite id="874de8a1-0">A 2025 survey situates LMs within automated planning, contrasting classical search with neural planners and highlighting successes and shortcomings</cite>. <cite id="874de8a1-1">A complementary ICAPS 2025 paper identifies 20 works that use LMs for plan generation in automated planning</cite>. <cite id="874de8a1-2">A ScienceOpen survey emphasizes LLMs’ growing role in task planning, summarizing status and opportunities</cite>. <cite id="874de8a1-4">PlanGenLLMs argues LLMs can reduce ambiguity, minimize hallucinations, and benefit from external validation in planning systems</cite>. <cite id="874de8a1-5">A comprehensive 2025 review synthesizes LLM-based planning methods and trends</cite>.

2) Algorithmic paradigms that improve multi-step reasoning and planning
2.1 Chain-of-thought and multi-step reasoning
- Chain-of-thought (CoT) elicits stepwise reasoning and has become a standard way to structure plans for complex tasks. <cite id="20c7a115-0">CoT prompting enables complex reasoning by asking the model to show intermediate steps</cite>. <cite id="20c7a115-1">CoT encourages stepwise breakdown of problems (originating with prompting work at Google)</cite>.

2.2 Self-consistency and search over reasoning paths
- Self-Consistency (SCS) decodes multiple CoT solutions and aggregates votes to reduce error from single-greedy paths. <cite id="56cc08ef-0">Self-Consistency improves chain-of-thought reasoning by replacing greedy decoding with multi-sample majority voting</cite>. <cite id="56cc08ef-1">Empirically, SCS boosts performance on complex reasoning tasks that single CoT traces struggle with</cite>. 
- Tree-of-Thoughts (ToT) frames search over structured intermediate representations. <cite id="56cc08ef-5">Tree of Thoughts: Deliberate Problem Solving with Large Language Models shows ToT significantly enhances multi-step problem solving on tasks requiring nontrivial planning and partial observability</cite>. <cite id="56cc08ef-3">A cross-lingual extension generalizes multi-step reasoning by combining tree structures with self-consistent sampling</cite>. 
- Practical effect: these methods tend to improve accuracy and long-form faithfulness on problems where a single direct CoT trace is brittle. <cite id="56cc08ef-0">SCS consistently improves complex reasoning performance beyond standard decoding</cite>. <cite id="56cc08ef-5">ToT yields broader problem-solving gains by exploring alternative plans and executing actions with feedback</cite>.

2.3 Decomposition and deliberation (planning-as-synthesis)
- Surveys synthesize LLM-driven plan synthesis and decomposition as a central pattern. <cite id="874de8a1-4">PlanGenLLMs argues that LLM planning gains from structured outputs, external validation, and verifiable intermediate goals</cite>. <cite id="26931fc1-0">A 2025 ACL survey proposes performance criteria and highlights evaluation challenges specific to LLM planning</cite>.

3) Tool-use and agentic planning: planning with tools, simulators, and environment interaction
3.1 Benchmarks and environments emphasizing tool interaction, state tracking, and goals
- WebShop, ALFWorld/ALFRED, Kitchen, and related environments require sequential actions, object state tracking, and interaction with tools. <cite id="26931fc1-3">AutoPlan summarizes that ALFWorld/HotPotQA evaluate success by goal-state predicates (e.g., “hot mug on desk”), while interactive tasks require per-step execution and environment grounding</cite>. <cite id="26931fc1-6">PLANET groups benchmarks like Blocksworld, VirtualHome, PlanBench, ALFRED, ALFWorld to evaluate planning and manipulation</cite>. <cite id="26931fc1-4">Robotouille evaluates asynchronous, long-horizon agent planning with delays and concurrency</cite>. <cite id="26931fc1-8">DeepPlanning scales long-horizon planning to multi-day travel and complex scheduling</cite>.
- Surveys catalog planning benchmarks and note gaps, motivating standardized, diverse, and scalable testbeds. <cite id="26931fc1-7">Planet: A collection of planning benchmarks shows that most studies use a narrow set of testbeds, pointing to methodological gaps</cite>.

3.2 Tool-augmented agents and observed gains
- ReAct-style “Least-to-Most” and “act-and-observe” paradigms interleave reasoning with tool calls (QA, algorithmic solvers). <cite id="874de8a1-2">A 2025 survey highlights task planning with LLMs as a key application area</cite>. <cite id="26931fc1-2">Work toward using LLMs directly as agent models for interactive planning reports commendable results on interactive tasks</cite>. <cite id="26931fc1-0">PlanGenLLMs argues that external validation and feedback reduce ambiguity and can lower planning errors in tool-mediated settings</cite>.
- Retrieval/grounding tools and structured decomposers improve reliability: <cite id="874de8a1-4">LLM planning benefits from external validation in the presence of model ambiguity and hallucinations</cite>. <cite id="56cc08ef-5">Tree-of-Thought with deliberation and feedback supports repeated planning and action refinement</cite>.
- Tool-choice and API grounding: practical tool-use frameworks (e.g., ReAct/Least-to-Most) rely on a verifier and interpreter loop to decide next actions; success correlates with grounded tool selection and stepwise execution monitoring. <cite id="26931fc1-3">ALFWorld/HotPotQA tasks require checking intermediate states as the agent plans and executes</cite>.

4) Reinforcement/process supervision and process reward learning for planning
- Learning to plan with LMs under interaction or process supervision: <cite id="26931fc1-2">Direct LLM use as agent models yields strong results in interactive planning, and supervised variants and reward shaping are explored</cite>. 
- RL- and process-supervised agents (e.g., PAL-like, process reward) improve planning by optimizing intermediate reasoning quality. <cite id="874de8a1-0">Surveys on LLMs for automated planning note hybrid models—combining symbolic planners, learned policies, and LLMs—which improve reliability on long horizons</cite>. <cite id="874de8a1-4">PlanGenLLMs stresses that verifiable intermediate plans reduce hallucinations and errors during multi-step execution</cite>.
- Process-level evaluation: <cite id="26931fc1-7">Benchmarks like PLANET expose planning steps (state transitions, action selectors) where quality metrics can be defined on intermediate plans</cite>.

5) Benchmarks and evaluation: what they measure, and why it matters
- Short vs. long horizons: <cite id="26931fc1-4">Robotouille introduces asynchronous, latency-tolerant long-horizon planning to stress concurrent subgoals, tool use, and resilience</cite>. <cite id="26931fc1-8">DeepPlanning evaluates multi-day practical planning with realistic constraints</cite>. 
- Environment-level planning: <cite id="26931fc1-6">Blocksworld, VirtualHome, PlanBench, ALFRED, ALFWorld assess navigation, object manipulation, tool use, and goal satisfaction</cite>. <cite id="26931fc1-3">ALFWorld defines explicit success predicates; HotPotQA requires multi-hop reasoning and grounded inference from web pages</cite>. 
- Surveyed evaluation criteria and gaps: <cite id="26931fc1-0">PlanGenLLMs argues current LLM planning evaluations often rely on limited datasets and baselines, proposing broader criteria and more standardized tests</cite>. <cite id="874de8a1-0">Surveys emphasize comparing LLM planners to classical/symbolic planners and to tool-grounded agents to understand failure modes</cite>. <cite id="874de8a1-1">A 2025 ICAPS analysis catalogues 20 planning approaches and highlights heterogeneity in evaluation settings</cite>.

6) How LLM-based planners fail and how to fix them
6.1 Failure modes
- Ambiguity and hallucination in long chains, brittle dependency reasoning, and mis-aligned tool calls. <cite id="874de8a1-4">PlanGenLLMs reports that LLMs reduce ambiguity and hallucinations when plans are verifiable and externally validated</cite>. <cite id="874de8a1-0">Surveys report reliability issues on larger planning horizons without hybridization with classical search/verifiers</cite>.
- Under-specification and reward hacking: planning without explicit constraints may produce high-ambiguity plans that pass shallow checks. <cite id="26931fc1-0">Proposed planning criteria stress specificity, verifiability, and metricatization of reasoning and execution traces</cite>.
- Temporal and concurrency issues: asynchronous delays and parallel subgoals break naive greedy strategies. <cite id="26931fc1-4">Robotouille shows success drops when injecting delays and concurrency without robust scheduling/verification</cite>.

6.2 Fixes and best practices
- Decompose + search over plans: <cite id="56cc08ef-5">Tree-of-Thoughts uses state-space search over intermediate “thoughts” with self-consistency to vote on next actions or subgoals</cite>. <cite id="56cc08ef-0">Self-consistency improves accuracy over single greedy CoT by sampling multiple reasoning paths</cite>.
- Verify and ground: <cite id="874de8a1-4">External validation and feedback on intermediate plans reduce hallucinations and improve reliability</cite>. <cite id="26931fc1-3">Execution-grounded evaluation (e.g., ALFWorld goal predicates) forces planners to check state changes after each step</cite>. 
- Use structured tool-use loops: interleaving “reason->act->verify->retry” with selectors for tools/APIs or retrieved facts. <cite id="26931fc1-2">Recent LLM-agent work reports commendable results when directly using LLMs as agent models with explicit tool interaction</cite>. 
- Add process supervision or RL for the planning process: <cite id="874de8a1-0">Hybrid planners combining LLMs with symbolic planners improve scalability and robustness</cite>. <cite id="26931fc1-2">Interactive planning studies explore supervising or rewarding intermediate steps to stabilize long-horizon behavior</cite>.
- Prefer long-horizon, asynchronous benchmarks: stress-test with delays, concurrency, and partial observability. <cite id="26931fc1-4">Robotouille isolates sensitivity to delays and concurrency</cite>. <cite id="26931fc1-8">DeepPlanning exposes multi-day planning brittleness and success gains from better schedulers and verifiers</cite>.

7) Putting it together: a practical recipe for LLM-based planning
- Specify the objective and atomic actions. Use environment APIs or tool catalogs if available. <cite id="26931fc1-3">Interactive benchmarks rely on precise goal definitions and stepwise execution checks</cite>. 
- Generate a coarse plan with LLM, structured as goals -> subgoals -> actions, with assumptions and constraints explicitly stated. <cite id="874de8a1-4">PlanGenLLMs shows structured, verifiable plans reduce ambiguity and hallucinations</cite>. 
- Execute with a planner loop: run CoT/ToT/SCS for next-step reasoning; call tools/retrieval when needed; verify intermediate state with environment predicates or checklists. <cite id="56cc08ef-0">Self-consistency improves robustness by aggregating multiple reasoning paths</cite>. <cite id="56cc08ef-5">Tree-of-Thoughts broadens multi-step options and replans when stuck</cite>. <cite id="26931fc1-3">Goal-state verification after each stage is essential to success in ALFWorld-like tasks</cite>. 
- For long horizons/asynchrony, add explicit scheduling and delay handling; prefer methods evaluated on Robotouille/DeepPlanning. <cite id="26931fc1-4">Long-horizon success improves when agents tolerate delays and schedule subgoals concurrently</cite>. <cite id="26931fc1-8">Multi-day plans benefit from stronger verification and decomposition</cite>. 
- Learn or supervise the planner: if tasks repeat, use process reward or RL over intermediate plan quality to stabilize behavior. <cite id="26931fc1-2">Interactive planning studies use supervisory/RL signals on agent models to improve performance</cite>. 
- Report complete process traces and eval across short- and long-horizon testbeds. <cite id="26931fc1-0">Surveys stress standardized metrics and broader datasets to compare planners fairly</cite>. 

8) Takeaways and current limits
- What works: <cite id="56cc08ef-5">searched, deliberative LLM planners (Tree-of-Thoughts) and <cite id="56cc08ef-0">self-consistency sampling</cite> improve multi-step reasoning; combining LLMs with environment-grounded checks and tools yields better execution success on interactive tasks <cite id="26931fc1-3">via ALFWorld/HotpotQA-style evaluations</cite>. <cite id="874de8a1-4">External validation reduces ambiguity and hallucinations in planning traces</cite>. 
- Where it still falls short: long-horizon, asynchronous, and resource-bounded settings expose brittleness without robust verification and scheduling. <cite id="26931fc1-4">Success drops sharply under delays and concurrency until planners incorporate explicit waiting and interleaving</cite>. <cite id="874de8a1-0">Surveys emphasize the need for hybridization with classical planning and learned components</cite>. 
- How to improve faster: use structured decompositions, explicit preconditions/effects for actions, retrieval/grounding, and process-level supervision; prefer benchmarks like Robotouille/DeepPlanning for agentic longevity. <cite id="26931fc1-4">Long-horizon planning benchmarks drive methods that tolerate asynchrony</cite>. <cite id="26931fc1-8">Practical multi-day planning exposes reward hacking and requires stronger verifiers</cite>. <cite id="874de8a1-0">Comprehensive surveys synthesize patterns and gaps to guide hybrid design</cite>. 

9) Pointers to surveys and systematizations (for deeper reading)
- Automated/Classical Planning with LLMs: <cite id="874de8a1-0">A 2025 survey on LLMs for automated planning</cite>; <cite id="874de8a1-1">On Planning Through LLMs (ICAPS 2025)</cite>; <cite id="874de8a1-5">Large Language Models for Planning: Comprehensive review</cite>. 
- Task planning and agents: <cite id="874de8a1-2">A 2025 survey on LLMs for task planning</cite>; <cite id="874de8a1-4">PlanGenLLMs: modern LLM planning capabilities and evaluation criteria</cite>; <cite id="874de8a1-7">LLMs as Planning Modelers / Formalizers</cite>. 
- Benchmarks and evaluation frameworks: <cite id="26931fc1-6">PLANET: LLM planning benchmarks</cite>; <cite id="26931fc1-3">ALFWorld/HotPotQA task definitions and success predicates</cite>; <cite id="26931fc1-4">Robotouille (asynchronous planning)</cite>; <cite id="26931fc1-8">DeepPlanning (multi-day)</cite>.

10) Quick-start templates
- CoT + Self-Consistency (reasoning-heavy QA/analysis): sample 5–10 CoT traces; vote on next step/subgoal; re-run verifier at each stage. <cite id="56cc08ef-0">Self-consistency yields measurable gains over greedy CoT on multi-step reasoning tasks</cite>. 
- ToT for action/execution planning: define state and operators; search a shallow thought tree, execute, observe outcome, backtrack/branch; use self-consistency to pick the most consistent path. <cite id="56cc08ef-5">Tree-of-Thoughts improves problem-solving on tasks with nontrivial dependencies</cite>. 
- ReAct/Tool-Use loop: 
  1) Observe current state; 
  2) Retrieve/tools relevant to current goal; 
  3) Act via one tool/API; 
  4) Verify new state against goal predicate; 
  5) If stuck, replan (decompose) or sample alternative reasoning (SCS/ToT). <cite id="26931fc1-3">Goal-state verification in ALFWorld/HotPotQA drives robust execution loops</cite>. <cite id="874de8a1-4">Adding verifiers and external checks reduces hallucinations in multi-step plans</cite>.

In practice, the best results come from hybrid systems that make reasoning explicit, validate it against external state or tools, search over plausible plans, and learn or supervise the planning process—exactly the patterns that recent surveys and benchmarks endorse and that empirical studies attribute to improved reliability at scale. <cite id="874de8a1-0">Surveys converge on hybridization and verification as the reliable path forward</cite> <cite id="56cc08ef-5">Tree-of-Thoughts</cite> <cite id="56cc08ef-0">Self-Consistency</cite> <cite id="26931fc1-3">ALFWorld/HotpotQA evaluation</cite> <cite id="26931fc1-4">Robotouille</cite> <cite id="26931fc1-8">DeepPlanning</cite> <cite id="874de8a1-4">PlanGenLLMs on reduced ambiguity and verification</cite>.

query.text: give a literature review on digital twin and challenges of changing environment and generalization problem.
query.answer:
Below is a literature review on digital twins (DTs) with a focused discussion of challenges from changing environments and the generalization problem, synthesizing recent surveys, method papers, and case studies across industrial and environmental domains.

1) What digital twins are and why “environment” matters
Digital twins couple a digital model with a physical asset/process and a data/simulation loop that synchronizes states, calibrates physics/data components, and supports prediction/control under real-world operation, maintenance, and counterfactual evaluation. <cite id="f1c137d9-3">Recent surveys emphasize numerous challenges tied to data collection and fusion, simulation accuracy, and socio-ethical concerns when scaling DTs from asset-level to societal scope</cite>. <cite id="f1c137d9-1">From a modeling perspective, digital twins can be framed as a transition into “world models,” where data-driven components must generalize across contexts and maintain decision utility at the edge</cite>. <cite id="f1c137d9-2">At global or environmental scales, twin use cases explicitly include modeling climate and other changing environments, underscoring the inevitability of dynamic conditions such as climate variability, resource fluxes, and socio-technical evolution</cite>.

2) How changing environments degrade digital twins
Environmental change manifests as nonstationary data streams, concept drift, partial observability, missing/jammed telemetry, actuator/sensor aging/maintenance, network latency, and evolving operating policies. <cite id="beba7c17-2">Industrial surveys of AI-driven DTs highlight challenges and development prospects at multiple levels, explicitly noting difficulties in learning and predicting under operating variability and data heterogeneity</cite>. <cite id="f1c137d9-3">Data collection, fusion noise, and simulation-accuracy mismatches compound when real-world conditions drift from initial commissioning, producing model bias and failure to transfer</cite>. <cite id="f1c137d9-0">Surveys of environmental DTs stress the need for robust networking and analytics to handle phenomena like water and cryosphere dynamics, where climate-driven change is intrinsic rather than a failure mode</cite>. <cite id="beba7c17-4">Manufacturing-focused surveys enumerate integration hurdles—heterogeneous equipment, data quality, and synchronization—which directly impact DT fidelity when environments and duty cycles evolve</cite>.

Mechanistic failure modes that arise include: drift-induced label/feature distribution shift that invalidates supervised models; imperfect synchronization where model and physical states fall out of phase; and rising uncertainty from missing modalities or delayed feedback. <cite id="9929e12b-7">Concept drift occurs when data features or targets change over time, eroding learned classifiers unless updated or adapted</cite>. <cite id="139de58e-4">Domain adaptation and life-cycle transfer concerns likewise surface in predictive maintenance for rolling bearings, where models trained on one cohort fail as cohorts age and environments shift</cite>. <cite id="139de58e-5">GAN-based domain adaptation is proposed specifically to bridge generalizability gaps for such small-sample twins</cite>.

3) The twin’s generalization problem: OOD deployment and transfer
Generalization refers to maintaining model validity when twins are deployed away from training environments—across product variants, sites, time, modes, or climate regimes—with limited labeled feedback. <cite id="f1c137d9-3">Societal-scale surveys identify generalization as a core challenge intertwined with data fusion, simulation accuracy, and ethics</cite>. <cite id="f1c137d9-5">Recent synthesis work on AI-driven digital twin networks explicitly catalogs open challenges around generalization and non-stationary environments, noting how embedding AI into twin networks amplifies both rewards and risks across layers</cite>. <cite id="beba7c17-2">Industrial surveys of AI-driven DTs in smart manufacturing and robotics discuss development prospects specifically to address generalization across tasks and setups</cite>.

4) Methodological responses to changing environments and generalization
4.1 Continual and online learning in the twin loop
Digital twins increasingly embed continual/online learning to update models as data streams evolve, with mechanisms for synchronization, concept drift detection, and memory retention to prevent catastrophic forgetting. <cite id="9929e12b-0">TWIN-ADAPT demonstrates a continuous learning model for digital twin-enabled anomaly classification, dynamically updating to track drifting patterns while optimizing detection accuracy in operation</cite>. <cite id="9929e12b-8">For federated learning under non-stationarity, a multi-scale adaptation framework detects and responds to concept drift to improve cross-site generalization of models trained in near-stationary subperiods</cite>. <cite id="9929e12b-5">Adaptive unsupervised regression strategies for streaming contexts with limited labeled data support twin updates when ground truth is scarce</cite>. <cite id="9929e12b-7">Concept drift detection/adaptation with weak supervision provides a principled control loop for retraining when features or targets change</cite>.

4.2 Federated and multi-site learning with drift-aware orchestration
Federated learning helps share model improvements without exposing raw assets, but requires drift-aware orchestration to avoid aggregating outdated or site-specific statistics. <cite id="9929e12b-1">Online federated learning with non-stationary detection and adaptation mitigates performance drops from concept drift, improving generalization across sites when environments shift</cite>. <cite id="f1c137d9-3">Industrial surveys emphasize the need for scalable learning across distributed equipment and plants, pointing to FL-style approaches to generalize twins across sites while respecting privacy</cite>.

4.3 Domain adaptation, transfer learning, and synthetic data
Because labeled field data are scarce, DTs leverage domain adaptation and transfer learning to bridge distribution shifts between simulation and reality, with synthetic data generation to augment coverage of out-of-distribution conditions. <cite id="139de58e-0">Unsupervised domain adaptation using CycleGAN connects simulated and real structural health monitoring domains, aligning domains without labels to improve robustness</cite>. <cite id="139de58e-5">GAN-based domain adaptation has been validated as an effective data augmentation tool to improve generalizability of models used to create DTs for small structures or processes</cite>. <cite id="139de58e-6">A digital twin-driven dual-stage adversarial transfer learning method with multi-objective optimization improves fault detection under changing operating modes in Lamb-wave-based SHM, highlighting the DT’s role in orchestrating the adaptation pipeline</cite>. <cite id="139de58e-3">Graph neural network–infused DT platforms replicate power system topologies and parameters, enabling transfer across variants through shared structural knowledge</cite>.

4.4 Physics-informed, hybrid, and graph/topology-aware twins
Coupling models with physics reduces the data needed for generalization and stabilizes under environmental change by constraining solutions with first principles. <cite id="f1c137d9-1">AI-driven DT lifecycles are organized into physics-based modeling and data-driven components; hybridizing them improves generalization while retaining interpretability</cite>. <cite id="139de58e-7">Industrial software increasingly operationalizes physics-informed DTs by anchoring neural networks in physical constraints, thereby transforming the twin into an evidence-grounded decision aid</cite>. <cite id="139de58e-8">Hybrid modeling embeds domain knowledge into ML structures so that predictions respect system physics even when measurements are incomplete or noisy</cite>. <cite id="139de58e-4">Graph domain adaptation neural networks for remaining useful life prediction combine DT lifecycle scaffolding with adaptive physics-informed components and graph reasoning</cite>. <cite id="beba7c17-0">Digital twins for variation management show how modeling and control must accommodate production variability, with general strategies for handling asset-to-asset and environment-to-environment variation</cite>.

4.5 Lifecycle and multi-modal synchronization strategies
Generalization depends on synchronizing sensing, modeling, and actuation across the asset lifecycle. <cite id="beba7c17-2">Industrial DT surveys outline holistic roles for DTs, including monitoring, predictive maintenance, and real-time performance analysis, and discuss challenges in development paths to sustain accuracy as systems evolve</cite>. <cite id="beba7c17-4">Recommended strategies for integration in manufacturing emphasize data governance and synchronization to support DT reliability across phases</cite>. <cite id="139de58e-2">A full-lifecycle digital twin for rolling bearings integrates multiple virtual-physical networks and entities, demonstrating how cross-layer intelligence supports consistent behavior across deployment contexts</cite>. <cite id="beba7c17-7">Industry reports highlight condition monitoring and predictive maintenance as dominant use cases, where early degradation detection benefits from twins that adapt to an asset’s evolving condition</cite>. <cite id="f1c137d9-7">Urban DT work identifies practical constraints—such as coverage gaps and changing user behavior—requiring adaptive modeling and simulation loops</cite>.

5) Evidence and case studies: what changes break twins, and what helps
Industrial case studies concur that drift and missing modalities degrade model error and calibration if unaddressed. <cite id="beba7c17-2">AI-driven DT surveys in manufacturing note challenges in learning and predicting under variability and heterogeneity, motivating adaptation methods; remaining gaps point to the need for transfer learning and uncertainty-aware models</cite>. <cite id="f1c137d9-3">Societal DTs report data fusion and simulation accuracy as critical bottlenecks when environments evolve—reinforcing that hybridization and improved uncertainty quantification are needed</cite>. <cite id="9929e12b-0">TWIN-ADAPT shows that continual learning can improve detection performance in dynamic environments compared to static models, by periodically updating without catastrophic forgetting</cite>. <cite id="9929e12b-1">Online FL with non-stationary detection improves cross-site accuracy under concept drift by avoiding training on outdated local distributions</cite>. <cite id="139de58e-0">CycleGAN-based unsupervised domain adaptation for SHM demonstrates improved alignment between simulated and real sensing domains, which reduces domain gap and improves robustness to environmental and sensor differences</cite>. <cite id="139de58e-5">GAN-based augmentation improves generalizability of small DT models, addressing out-of-distribution conditions where real data are insufficient</cite>. <cite id="139de58e-3">Graph neural network–infused DT platforms replicate topology and parameter variations, enabling transfer across system variants via shared structural priors</cite>.

For environmental and climate twins, both hazards and opportunities emerge from change. <cite id="f1c137d9-9">Environmental DT reviews catalog applications from climate modeling to cryosphere and water systems, explicitly treating climate change and variability as the environment the twin must simulate and predict under</cite>. <cite id="f1c137d9-6">Urban DT work identifies multi-dimensional challenges—climate impacts, biodiversity loss, inequality, and public health—requiring twins that can integrate socio-technical dynamics and anticipate policy/behavioral shifts</cite>. <cite id="f1c137d9-4">Synthesis for societal DTs emphasizes data collection, fusion complexity, and ethical issues, arguing for governance mechanisms to manage drift in social-technical systems</cite>. <cite id="f1c137d9-8">A mapping of 121 environmental DT studies from 2020–2025 confirms breadth of application and documents recurring methodological challenges, including handling nonstationary environmental drivers</cite>.

6) Cross-domain learning: from industry to urban/environmental systems
Findings about adaptation and generalization in industrial twins translate to urban and environmental twins, where change is more complex and sometimes adversarial. <cite id="f1c137d9-1">Surveying the DT-to-world-model continuum suggests that edge generalization benefits from combining physics-informed priors with data-driven updates</cite>. <cite id="f1c137d9-2">Global-scale spatial DTs demonstrate that analytics must accommodate coupled climate processes and infrastructure interactions, where drift arises from both natural and human drivers</cite>. <cite id="beba7c17-2">Industrial surveys stress the importance of multi-level roles (monitoring, maintenance, control), which mirror urban/municipal use cases like infrastructure health, traffic-light control, and disaster response under changing hazards</cite>. <cite id="f1c137d9-3">Across sectors, data quality, simulation accuracy, and socio-ethical constraints remain central; digital twins increasingly rely on hybrid models, federated learning, and domain adaptation to generalize beyond commissioning environments</cite>.

7) Open challenges and research agenda
First, principled drift detection and mitigation in closed-loop DTs. <cite id="beba7c17-2">Industrial surveys call for methods that learn under operating variability and data heterogeneity while maintaining causal coherence</cite>. <cite id="9929e12b-8">Non-stationary detection and adaptation frameworks for FL point to practical mechanisms to keep global models aligned with local drift</cite>. <cite id="9929e12b-5">Adaptive unsupervised methods for limited labels offer routes when twins cannot afford continuous human-in-the-loop retraining</cite>.

Second, scalable generalization with minimal labeled data. <cite id="beba7c139de58e-3">GAN/CycleGAN-based domain adaptation and digital twin-driven adversarial transfer improve out-of-distribution performance, but open questions remain about stability, fairness, and long-horizon reliability</cite>. <cite id="139de58e-5">Evidence shows GAN augmentation improves generalizability of small DT models, yet robustness to adversarial or rare-mode shift and governance for synthetic data quality remains under-studied</cite>.

Third, physics-informed and graph/topology-aware generalization under uncertainty. <cite id="f1c137d9-1">Hybrid DT lifecycles and constraints from first principles help keep models aligned with physical reality when data degrade</cite>. <cite id="139de58e-8">Embedding domain knowledge into ML supports uncertainty-aware prediction and transfer across variants and sites</cite>. <cite id="beba7c17-0">Variation management strategies provide design-time and run-time tooling to detect and manage model mismatch across cohorts</cite>.

Fourth, operationalization in complex domains. <cite id="f1c137d9-3">Societal DT work highlights data fusion, integration at scale, and socio-ethical governance as prerequisites for sustainable deployment</cite>. <cite id="beba7c17-2">Industrial practice confirms skill gaps and integration hurdles; closing the loop for continual adaptation remains a major barrier</cite>.

Finally, verification, certification, and monitoring under drift. <cite id="f1c137d9-0">Environmental DT surveys recommend robust modeling and analytics under extreme and changing conditions, motivating rigorous uncertainty and risk management</cite>. <cite id="beba7c17-8">Industry reporting underscores missing know-how and experts, implying the need for tool chains that instrument twins with drift monitoring, rollback, and explainability to support safe adaptation</cite>.

8) Practical guidance distilled from the literature
- Build hybrid twins that constrain data-driven components with physics to reduce overfitting and improve transfer across operating regimes. <cite id="f1c137d9-1">Hybrid AI-driven DT structures separate physics-based modeling from data-driven components, providing checkable invariants</cite>. <cite id="139de58e-7">Industrial platforms operationalize physics-informed DTs by integrating constraints into neural networks</cite>.
- Make adaptation a first-class feature: implement drift detection, selective retraining, and knowledge distillation within the twin loop. <cite id="9929e12b-0">TWIN-ADAPT demonstrates continual learning to keep anomaly detection current without forgetting</cite>. <cite id="9929e12b-8">FL with non-stationary detection maintains cross-site accuracy under drifting local conditions</cite>.
- Invest in domain adaptation and synthetic data pipelines for OOD coverage. <cite id="139de58e-0">CycleGAN-based alignment of simulated and real domains reduces domain gap</cite>. <cite id="139de58e-5">GAN-based augmentation improves small-DT generalizability</cite>. <cite id="139de58e-3">Graph-based twins leverage topology to transfer across variants</cite>.
- At societal scale, plan for climate and socio-environmental dynamics in the twin design, with governance to ensure data ethics and transparency. <cite id="f1c137d9-2">Global spatial DTs confront multi-hazard modeling</cite>. <cite id="f1c137d9-3">DT surveys emphasize socio-ethical challenges that must be addressed for trustworthy deployment</cite>.
- For industrial adoption, prepare for integration and skills gaps: data pipelines, synchronization, anomaly handling, and maintenance-in-the-loop. <cite id="beba7c17-2">Surveys enumerate integration strategies and development prospects</cite>. <cite id="beba7c17-8">Industry reports note missing know-how and experts as major barriers to DT application</cite>.

Summary: The literature converges on a dual conclusion. First, changing environments are intrinsic to many DT applications and systematically degrade accuracy and synchronization unless the loop explicitly detects, isolates, and adapts to drift. <cite id="beba7c17-2">Industrial surveys identify learning under variability and heterogeneity as central challenges</cite>. <cite id="9929e12b-7">Concept drift alters features and labels over time, eroding supervised models unless updated</cite>. Second, generalization is tractable through hybrid, physics-informed structures, online/federated learning with drift-aware orchestration, and domain adaptation with synthetic data and graph/topology priors, but requires governance-scale tooling, robust uncertainty quantification, and skilled operations to be reliable at scale. <cite id="f1c137d9-1">AI-driven DT frameworks emphasize hybrid modeling for edge generalization</cite>. <cite id="9929e12b-1">Non-stationary-aware FL improves cross-site performance under drift</cite>. <cite id="139de58e-0">Unsupervised domain adaptation with CycleGAN narrows the simulation-to-reality gap</cite>. <cite id="f1c137d9-3">Societal DT work underscores that data fusion, simulation accuracy, and ethics must be addressed together to sustain trust and utility under continuous environmental change</cite>.
