Below is a concise, evidence-backed historical overview of large language models (LLMs), grouped by major eras and pointing to landmark papers you can read first. I also include brief pointers to recent surveys if you want breadth-first coverage.

Surveys and overviews to start
- For a compact, up-to-date survey of architectures, families (GPT, LLaMA, PaLM), and developments, see Large Language Models: A Survey (2024) and A Comprehensive Overview of Large Language Models (2025). <cite id="4be23664-0">This paper reviews prominent LLM families (GPT, LLaMA, PaLM) and their characteristics</cite> <cite id="4be23664-4">This article summarizes architectural and training details of pre-trained LLMs and presents a survey of developments</cite> <cite id="4be23664-1">This 2025 survey reviews LLMs as a major paradigm shift</cite> <cite id="4be23664-3">A curated collection of papers and resources aligned with a recent LLM survey</cite> <cite id="4be23664-6">An interactive timeline tracing evolution from rule-based systems to neural architectures</cite> <cite id="4be23664-5">A 2025 review covering DeepSeek R1 and RLVR, inference-time scaling, benchmarks, and architectures</cite>

Era 1 — Foundations: deep, context-sensitive language models (2013–2018)
- ELMo (Embeddings from Language Models): introduced deep contextualized word representations via a language model, enabling simple fine-tuning adapters to transfer to downstream tasks across NLP. <cite id="6d02f305-5">Deep contextualized word representations model complex characteristics of word use (syntax and semantics) and directly address integration challenges</cite> <cite id="6d02f305-6">ELMo provides contextualized representations easily integrated into existing models for improved downstream performance</cite>
- GPT-1 (Improving Language Understanding by Generative Pre-Training): proposed generative pretraining on a large internet corpus followed by task-specific fine-tuning, demonstrating strong zero/one/few-shot transfer across language tasks with a compact model. <cite id="6d02f305-0">This work presents generative pre-training as a powerful inductive bias, comparing to earlier methods like ELMo</cite> <cite id="6d02f305-7">A single pre-trained model, fine-tuned minimally, could beat purpose-built models across a wide range of language tasks</cite> <cite id="6d02f305-1">GPT-1 laid out pre-training on vast text and task-agnostic transfer, influencing downstream transferability</cite>

Why this era matters: it established that deep LMs pretrained on large text corpora can transfer broadly to many tasks with light fine-tuning, motivating later scaling in parameters and training data.

Era 2 — The Transformer pivot (2017)
- The Transformer (Attention Is All You Need): replaced recurrence/convolutions with self-attention, enabling stable parallelization and state-of-the-art sequence modeling; its encoder–decoder design underpins modern LMs. <cite id="9abef27b-0">The Transformer uses only attention mechanisms, dispensing with recurrence and convolutions</cite> <cite id="9abef27b-1">The 100M-parameter encoder–decoder Transformer was published on 2017-06-12</cite> <cite id="9abef27b-4">Self-attention in the decoder with locality constraints (masking) supports next-token prediction while preserving parallelism</cite>

Why this era matters: attention and positional encoding solved long-range dependency modeling and scaling bottlenecks, making end-to-end neural machine translation competitive and seeding the “scaled transformer LM” era.

Era 3 — Pretraining paradigms and unified objectives (2018–2020)
- Bidirectional masked LM with transformers: BERT (Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers) popularized masked language modeling (MLM) and deep bidirectional context, further improving representation learning before LLMs dominated. <cite id="4be23664-0">Surveys note BERT as a widely adopted LLM precursor and member of the GPT/BERT/LLaMA families with distinct pretraining objectives</cite>
- GPT-2: continued scaling of generative pretraining with Transformer decoders; while not fully open-sourced, it empirically reinforced that larger scale improves general-purpose task performance without task-specific signals. <cite id="b9111461-0">Scaling up language models greatly improves task-agnostic, few-shot performance, sometimes reaching competitiveness with prior SOTA</cite>
- T5 (Text-to-Text Transfer Transformer): advocated a text-to-text framing with discrete tokenizer and unified pretraining tasks (MLM and next-sequence prediction), showing that many NLP tasks can be cast as conditional language modeling, further aligning encoder-decoder Transformers with large-scale pretraining. <cite id="4be23664-0">Surveys highlight T5 as a core architecture in modern LLM families</cite>

Why this era matters: MLM and bidirectionality refined pretraining to capture left-to-right and bidirectional signal, and the text-to-text framing unified diverse tasks under a common training objective—key ingredients for LLMs.

Era 4 — The modern LLM wave: scaling, zero/few-shot, instruction tuning, and RLHF (2020–2023)
- GPT-3: “Language Models are Few-Shot Learners” showed that simply scaling parameter count and data can dramatically boost zero/one/few-shot performance, enabling strong capability without fine-tuning per task. <cite id="b9111461-0">Scaling up language models greatly improves task-agnostic, few-shot performance, sometimes competitive with prior SOTA</cite> <cite id="4be23664-0">GPT is one of the principal LLM families in recent surveys</cite>
- InstructGPT (Supervised Fine-Tuning via Human Feedback): introduced instruction-following by scaling RLHF using curated preference data, yielding instruction-tuned assistants that better align with human preferences. <cite id="4be23664-0">Surveys describe the evolution of GPT-style models and the rise of alignment-focused successors</cite>
- FLAN (xLm-RoBERTa and Flan-T5 variants): instruction-tuned transformer models demonstrating strong cross-task generalization and conversational fluency via large-scale data and distillation; part of the broader shift toward instruction-tuned LLMs. <cite id="4be23664-1">A 2025 survey emphasizes the paradigm shift and catalogs instruction-focused LLM families</cite>
- Alpaca: small-scale supervised fine-tuning using SFT with human prompts and outputs to produce instruction-following assistants from base LMs; popularized low-resource instruction tuning workflows. <cite id="4be23664-5">A 2025 review discusses instruction-based developments and RLVR as continued evolution</cite>

Why this era matters: large-scale pretraining plus instruction tuning and RLHF produced versatile assistants capable of multi-tasking and following natural-language instructions, replacing per-task supervised training in many settings.

Era 5 — Efficiency and reasoning scaffolds, with richer evaluation (2022–2025)
- Parameter-efficient finetuning (PEFT): LoRA (Low-Rank Adaptation) adapts base LMs at far lower rank than full finetuning, enabling high performance with small trainable footprint and broad sharing across tasks. <cite id="4be23664-1">Recent surveys catalog PEFT methods (e.g., LoRA) among the key toolkit for modern LLM development</cite>
- In-context reasoning: Chain-of-Thought Prompting and related methods inject intermediate reasoning steps into the prompt, improving hard reasoning and math; ReAct combines reasoning actions with language grounded in tool use to solve tasks by planning. <cite id="4be23664-1">Surveys describe prompting-based paradigms, including few-shot and chain-of-thought, as central to capability expansion</cite> <cite id="4be23664-5">2025 reviews highlight inference-time scaling and reasoning-centric methods (e.g., RLVR)</cite>
- Evaluation ecosystems: MT-Bench and AlpacaEval benchmark assistants via multi-turn dialog and comparative preference; HELM aggregates diverse metrics across tasks and systems to compare trade-offs; these efforts respond to reproducibility and safety scrutiny. <cite id="4be23664-1">Surveys document benchmarking and evaluation as core to LLM progress</cite> <cite id="4be23664-5">2025 reviews discuss benchmarks (including MT-Bench), evaluation standards, and predictions</cite>

Why this era matters: as models grew, efficiency demands (small memory footprints) and robust reasoning led to PEFT and prompting paradigms, while comprehensive evaluation frameworks compare capabilities and alignment at scale.

How to read this list: a suggested minimal reading path
1) Architectural foundations: Transformer (2017). <cite id="9abef27b-0">The Transformer replaces recurrence/convolutions with attention</cite>
2) Generative pretraining lineage: GPT-1 (2018), ELMo (2018). <cite id="6d02f305-0">GPT-1 proposes generative pretraining and shows broad transfer</cite> <cite id="6d02f305-5">ELMo introduces deep contextualized word representations</cite>
3) Bidirectional MLM and unified pretraining: BERT and T5 (2018–2019). <cite id="6d02f305-6">ELMo highlights the importance of integration-friendly contextualization</cite> <cite id="4be23664-0">BERT and T5 as canonical LLM precursors with distinct pretraining</cite>
4) The scaling shift and instruction-tuned assistants: GPT-3 (2020), InstructGPT/FLAN/Alpaca (2022–2023). <cite id="b9111461-0">Scaling up substantially improves zero/one/few-shot performance</cite> <cite id="4be23664-0">GPT and instruction-tuned successors dominate recent families</cite> <cite id="4be23664-1">Instruction-oriented families and alignment are central today</cite>
5) Efficiency and reasoning: LoRA (2021–2022), chain-of-thought/ReAct (2022–2023), MT-Bench/AlpacaEval/HELM (2023–2024). <cite id="4be23664-1">Surveys summarize LoRA and prompting-based reasoning</cite> <cite id="4be23664-5">Contemporary reviews discuss benchmarks and reasoning-time improvements</cite>

Key milestones and why they matter
- Transformer (2017): attention-only architecture enabled stable training and massive scale, delivering state-of-the-art NMT and seeding all modern LLMs. <cite id="9abef27b-0">Only attention-based mechanisms; no recurrence or convolutions</cite> <cite id="9abef27b-1">Original encoder–decoder release in June 2017</cite>
- GPT-1 and ELMo (2018): demonstrated that deep generative pretraining and shallow adapters can surpass task-specific baselines across many NLP tasks. <cite id="6d02f305-7">A single pre-trained model beats purpose-built models with minimal fine-tuning</cite> <cite id="6d02f305-5">ELMo’s deep contextualization modeled syntax/semantics and integrated easily</cite>
- BERT/T5 (2018–2019): bidirectional masked LM and text-to-text unification refined representations and broadened pretraining tasks, improving cross-task transfer. <cite id="4be23664-0">BERT and T5 are core families; surveys emphasize T5’s unified objectives</cite> <cite id="6d02f305-6">ELMo–BERT comparison highlights integration-friendly contextualization</cite>
- GPT-3 (2020): showed strong zero/few-shot transfer purely from scaling, reframing many tasks as prompt-response rather than model-specific finetuning. <cite id="b9111461-0">Scaling up yields large gains in few-shot performance and competitiveness</cite>
- InstructGPT/FLAN/Alpaca (2022–2023): instruction-tuning and RLHF produce assistants that follow natural language instructions and better align with human preferences, while being transfer-agnostic in prompting. <cite id="4be23664-0">Modern families include instruction-tuned successors of GPT</cite> <cite id="4be23664-1">Surveys emphasize instruction-oriented LLMs and alignment</cite>
- LoRA, CoT/ReAct, MT-Bench/AlpacaEval/HELM (2021–2025): parameter-efficient finetuning, in-context reasoning scaffolds, and multi-dimensional evaluation matured as models scaled, enabling efficient capability expansion and fair comparisons. <cite id="4be23664-1">PEFT, prompting paradigms, and evaluation frameworks are now central</cite> <cite id="4be23664-5">2025 reviews summarize benchmarks and emerging methods (e.g., RLVR)</cite>

What’s next and open problems
- Training compute and costs: scaling laws and inference-time resource scaling remain active areas; new approaches seek better scaling and cost-efficient inference. <cite id="4be23664-5">2025 reviews discuss inference-time scaling and emerging methods</cite>
- Safety, alignment, fairness: RLHF/Constitutional AI and red-teaming pipelines continue to mature. <cite id="4be23664-1">Alignment-focused developments occupy central ground in 2025 surveys</cite>
- Reasoning and tool use: in-context memory, programmatic reasoning, and tool-augmented agents aim to bridge weak and strong reasoning. <cite id="4be23664-5">Reasoning-centric methods and evaluations are a major focus</cite>

Suggested first reads (short list)
- Transformer (2017) — architecture and attention-only design. <cite id="9abef27b-0">Only attention mechanisms</cite>
- ELMo (2018) — deep contextualized word representations. <cite id="6d02f305-6">Contextualized representations that integrate easily</cite>
- BERT (2018/19) — masked LM and bidirectionality. <cite id="4be23664-0">BERT as a core family with masked objectives</cite>
- GPT-1 (2018) — generative pretraining and transfer. <cite id="6d02f305-0">Generative pre-training and broad transfer</cite>
- T5 (2019/20) — text-to-text pretraining. <cite id="4be23664-0">T5 unifies diverse tasks under conditional LM</cite>
- GPT-3 (2020) — scaling yields zero/few-shot power. <cite id="b9111461-0">Task-agnostic few-shot performance improves with scale</cite>
- InstructGPT (2022) and Flan (2022) — instruction tuning and RLHF. <cite id="4be23664-0">Instruction-tuned GPT-family models</cite> <cite id="4be23664-1">Instruction-centric evolution emphasized</cite>
- Alpaca (2023) — low-resource SFT workflow. <cite id="4be23664-5">Instruction-tuning workflows and evaluations</cite>
- LoRA (2021–2022) — parameter-efficient finetuning. <cite id="4be23664-1">LoRA as a key PEFT method in modern toolkits</cite>
- MT-Bench and AlpacaEval (2023–2024), plus HELM — evaluation design space. <cite id="4be23664-1">Contemporary surveys cover benchmarks and metrics</cite> <cite id="4be23664-5">2025 perspectives on benchmarks and progress</cite>

Context-specific background
- If you want a big-picture timeline (from rule-based chatbots to neural LMs) with where GPT, Claude, Gemini fit historically, see curated timelines. <cite id="4be23664-2">A timeline from 1950 to 2025 covering early systems to modern families</cite> <cite id="4be23664-6">An ISSARIce timeline linking early MT/rule-based chat to neural architectures</cite>
- For a structured “what changed and why” narrative with LLM-family characteristics (GPT, LLaMA, PaLM), see dedicated surveys. <cite id="4be23664-0">Prominent LLM families and characteristics are summarized</cite> <cite id="4be23664-4">Architectural and training details are laid out comprehensively</cite>

Citations to key resources
- Surveys and timelines: <cite id="4be23664-0">Large Language Models: A Survey</cite> <cite id="4be23664-1">A Survey of Large Language Models: Evolution …</cite> <cite id="4be23664-2">LLM history timeline</cite> <cite id="4be23664-3">LLMSurvey repository</cite> <cite id="4be23664-4">Comprehensive Overview of Large Language Models (ACM DL)</cite> <cite id="4be23664-5">State of LLMs 2025</cite> <cite id="4be23664-6">ISSARIce timeline</cite>
- Architectural milestone: <cite id="9abef27b-0">Attention Is All You Need</cite> <cite id="9abef27b-1">June 2017 release details</cite>
- GPT-1 and ELMo: <cite id="6d02f305-0">Improving Language Understanding by Generative Pre-Training</cite> <cite id="6d02f305-5">Deep contextualized word representations (ELMo)</cite> <cite id="6d02f305-6">ELMo paper (ACL 2018)</cite> <cite id="6d02f305-7">GPT-1 transferability observations</cite>
- Scaling and Instruct-tuning: <cite id="b9111461-0">Language Models are Few-Shot Learners (GPT-3)</cite>
- Instruction-tuned families: <cite id="4be23664-0">GPT successors in instruction-tuned families</cite> <cite id="4be23664-1">Instruction-oriented evolution and alignment focus</cite>

If you’d like, I can tailor a reading plan by topic and subfield (e.g., dialogue assistants vs. scientific reasoning) and map each step to a hands-on project (finetuning LoRA adapters for your domain with MT-Bench evaluation).

questions.original_query: What benchmarks are there for language models reasoning and what is the state of the art

query.text: What benchmarks are there for language models reasoning and what is the state of the art
query.answer:
Below is a concise map of major benchmarks used to assess reasoning in large language models (LLMs), followed by a synthesis of the current state of the art (SOTA), including where models excel, where they falter, and how evaluations are evolving.

1) Why “reasoning” benchmarks matter and how they’re measured
- Reasoning-oriented benchmarks probe multi-step logic, math/science inference, program synthesis/execution, and real-world commonsense, often requiring chain-of-thought explanations or executable correctness checks rather than mere keyword matching. <cite id="fc65fa57-2">Common LLM benchmarks explicitly include question-answering, language understanding, and especially math problem-solving and coding tasks; widely used suites include HellaSwag, HellaSwag-Reasoning, ARC, and others targeting inference and disambiguation</cite>. <cite id="fc65fa57-7">New meta-reasoning benchmarks such as MR-Ben probe whether LLMs can “evaluate reasoning” itself, covering domains like physics and chemistry</cite>.

2) Core benchmark families and what they test

2.1 Arithmetic, logic, and competition-style math
- GSM8K (Grade School Math 8K): 8,500 grade-school math word problems requiring 2–8 steps of arithmetic; widely used for evaluating chain-of-thought and general numeric reasoning. <cite id="502065f7-8">GSM8K consists of 8.5K linguistically diverse word problems</cite>. <cite id="502065f7-1">Curated variants report 2–8-step problems and aggregate SOTA such as GPT-4.5 at 98.2% pass for GSM8K-style sets</cite>. <cite id="502065f7-2">However, contamination concerns have been raised, with multiple groups finding data leakage/contamination in GSM8K-style evaluations</cite>. <cite id="502065f7-6">Independent discussions note best accuracy well below perfect (≈0.973), motivating harder suites</cite>.
- BIG-bench Hard (BBH): 23 challenging BIG-bench tasks emphasizing multi-step reasoning; CoT methods closed many gaps vis-à-vis zero-shot. <cite id="fa09bb86-0">Chain-of-thought prompting enabled PaLM to surpass average human-rater performance on 10 of 23 BBH tasks</cite>. <cite id="fa09bb86-3">BBH was selected from BIG-bench to focus on complex reasoning and compositional generalization</cite>. <cite id="fa09bb86-1">Follow-ups (e.g., BBEH) argue current BBH may be insufficiently hard and propose BIG-Bench Extra Hard</cite>.
- AIME-style olympiad-level math: Modern AIME 2024/2025 leaderboards evaluate Olympiad-level problems (0–13 points per problem, 30 total). <cite id="d457d0d3-5">AIME 2024 shows top models around 95–96% accuracy per problem under zero-shot settings</cite>. <cite id="d457d0d3-0">AIME 2025 aggregations report near–perfect scores (e.g., Grok-4 Heavy at 1.000) across 114 models</cite>. <cite id="d457d0d3-4">Alternative snapshots report Kimi K2.5 and MAI-Thinking-1 in the mid-90s (96–97%) on AIME 2025</cite>. <cite id="d457d0d3-1">Complementary olympiad-level benchmarks like OlymMATH explicitly target Olympiad difficulty to test deeper mathematical reasoning</cite>.
- Robustness to information gaps: Math-RoB surfaces reasoning failures under missing/uncertain information. <cite id="fc65fa57-3">Math-RoB targets hallucinations and reasoning gaps induced by missing information, aiming to expose brittleness in model chains of reasoning</cite>.

2.2 Graduate-level proof-style reasoning and science domains
- GPQA (Graduate-Level Google-Proof Q&A): Multi-subject questions (bio/physics/chem) designed to foil web lookup and require deep reasoning; GPQA Diamond is the hardest subset. <cite id="9e066c23-1">GPQA comprises 448 expert-authored multiple-choice questions across biology, physics, and chemistry</cite>. <cite id="9e066c23-0">GPQA Diamond is presented as a graduate-level “proof” benchmark, with PhD experts achieving about 65% and models like Gemini 3.1 Pro approaching 94% in curated leaderboards</cite>. <cite id="9e066c23-2">Leaderboards emphasize that Diamond contains the most challenging 198 items, where top models achieve around 94% while PhD experts ~65%, underscoring a ceiling gap</cite>.
- ARC/ARC-PR: Commonsense and real-world reasoning via multiple-choice science items; ARC-AGI variants and ARC Prize continue to push generalization. <cite id="9e066c23-3">ARC Prize (nonprofit) advances open AGI through ARC-style benchmarks and associated challenges</cite>. <cite id="9e066c23-8">Recent ARC Challenge leaderboards place frontier models near 96% accuracy, reflecting progress but leaving room for error</cite>.

2.3 Programming, algorithmic reasoning, and software engineering
- HumanEval and HumanEval+: Code-generation focusing on functional pass@1; EvalPlus augments tests with hidden/online checks and adversarial cases. <cite id="435e6166-8">EvalPlus highlights variants like HumanEval.jl, LiveCodeBench, MHPP, and links to SWE-bench; pass@1 and hidden tests capture stronger generalization</cite>. <cite id="435e6166-4">HumanEval remains a classic 164-problem Python benchmark, with HumanEval+, LiveCodeBench, and SWE-bench Pro referenced on unified leaderboards</cite>.
- LiveCodeBench: Holistic, contamination-aware evaluation of code reasoning, offering a central axis for code LLMs. <cite id="435e6166-3">LiveCodeBench is positioned as an “axis of LLM coding evaluation,” with linked leaderboards across coding tasks</cite>.
- SWE-bench (Lite / Verified / Pro): Repair/agent-oriented benchmarks on real GitHub issues measuring planning, repo-scale navigation, and patch correctness via execution. <cite id="435e6166-0">SWE-bench leaderboards track mini-SWE-agent scores up to 74% on Verified in ~100 lines of Python, indicating real-world issue resolution remains hard</cite>. <cite id="435e6166-6">SWE-bench includes Lite and Verified leaderboards explicitly designed to evaluate LLM-based repair agents</cite>. <cite id="435e6166-2">Aggregated leaderboards show Claude Fable/Mythos/Opus variants leading SWE-bench Verified with high scores (>0.93), reflecting strong agent performance</cite>. <cite id="435e6166-1">Independent coding leaderboards put Claude Mythos around 80.8% on SWE-bench Pro/LiveCodeBench, with GPT-5 variants close behind</cite>. <cite id="435e6166-5">Another source reports GPT-5.5 leading around 88.7% (and Claude Opus tied near 88.6%) on SWE-bench Verified, illustrating leaderboard variability across sources and dates</cite>. <cite id="435e6166-7">Survey-style posts note GPT-5.5 around 88–89% and Gemini 3.1 Pro ~80% on SWE-bench Verified, situating current SOTA within single-digit percentage margins of perfection</cite>. <cite id="435e6166-8">EvalPlus and related leaderboards provide parity updates relative to HumanEval and broader code reasoning suites</cite>.

3) State of the art: where frontier models succeed and where they struggle

3.1 Math and logic: near–human performance on school-level, significant headroom on Olympiad/proof-style reasoning
- Substantially higher scores on GSM8K under CoT and fine-tuning are common; however, contamination debates keep the ceiling imperfect. <cite id="502065f7-1">GPT-4.5 has been reported near 98% on GSM8K-style sets</cite>. <cite id="502065f7-2">Contamination concerns suggest some GSM8K results may be inflated</cite>. <cite id="502065f7-6">Top results remain sub-perfect (≈0.97), reinforcing that unaided “human” performance is the hard target</cite>.
- Olympiad-style AIME shows current best per-problem accuracies around 96–97% under zero-shot prompting in multiple independent leaderboards. <cite id="d457d0d3-5">AIME 2024 leaderboards show GPT-5, Grok-4, and o4-mini topping ~95–96%</cite>. <cite id="d457d0d3-0">AIME 2025 leaderboards list submitters with score reports near 95–100%, depending on snapshot</cite>. <cite id="d457d0d3-4">Alternative snapshots list Kimi K2.5 and MAI variants at ~96.1%</cite>.
- BBH shows that CoT can close many gaps to near-human performance on 10/23 tasks, but not all tasks yield to CoT, underscoring domain-specific limitations. <cite id="fa09bb86-0">Chain-of-thought raised PaLM to exceed average human performance on 10 of 23 BBH tasks</cite>.
- Graduate-level proof-style reasoning (GPQA, Diamond) remains challenging: models close the gap to strong graduate baselines but are not yet reliably surpassing PhD expert parity on the hardest subset. <cite id="9e066c23-2">GPQA Diamond leaderboards show current best models around 94% while PhD experts ~65%, evidencing a persistent ceiling gap</cite>.

3.2 Commonsense and real-world reasoning
- ARC-family tasks report high but not perfect accuracy, reflecting that commonsense remains fragile and transferable only partially. <cite id="9e066c23-8">ARC Challenge leaderboards show frontier models near ~96%, suggesting residual weaknesses</cite>. <cite id="9e066c23-3">ARC Prize’s continued benchmarking reflects a view that real-world generalization remains a bottleneck</cite>.

3.3 Programming and software engineering reasoning
- Agentic coding on real-world issues is advancing rapidly, but solved rates on Verified remain a work in progress. <cite id="435e6166-0">SWE-bench reports mini-SWE-agent scores up to ~74% on Verified in limited code length, indicating only partial resolution</cite>. <cite id="435e6166-5">Different leaderboards place Claude Mythos and GPT-5.6 in the ~80–90% range for SWE-bench Verified, underscoring sensitivity to method and evaluation scope</cite>. <cite id="435e6166-1">Independent coding leaderboards show similar head-to-head orderings (Claude, GPT-5.x, strong open models), with LiveCodeBench and SWE-bench Pro results in the same performance band</cite>.
- Foundational code-generation (HumanEval/EvalPlus) continues to scale, but pass@1 and hidden tests expose brittleness to adversarial cases. <cite id="435e6166-8">EvalPlus highlights improved robustness via hidden/online test cases across HumanEval variants and broader coding suites</cite>.

4) Trends, caveats, and how to read leaderboard numbers

- Trend line: CoT and self-consistency have materially improved reasoning, especially on school-level and many BBH tasks, while Olympiad/proof and software engineering benchmarks reveal tougher ceilings. <cite id="fa09bb86-7">Chain-of-thought prompting elicited multi-step reasoning and improved performance across arithmetic, commonsense, and symbolic tasks</cite>. <cite id="502065f7-1">GPT-4.x/4.5-era models approach 98% on GSM8K-style math via enhanced reasoning strategies and test-time computation</cite>.
- Robustness and contamination: Evaluations are shifting to less-contaminated sets and missing-information stress tests. <cite id="502065f7-2">Scholars argue GSM8K contains contamination and that results may overestimate generalization</cite>. <cite id="fc65fa57-3">Math-RoB isolates reasoning errors under missing information, which many benchmarks overlook</cite>.
- Variability and comparability: Reported “SOTA” can differ by evaluation protocol (few-shot vs. zero-shot), contamination handling, pass@1 vs. majority vote, and whether agents use tools or multi-round repo navigation. Aggregators help normalize comparisons across benchmarks but should be cross-checked against official leaderboards/leaderboard update dates. <cite id="fc65fa57-0">LLM-stats aggregates live leaderboards across reasoning, coding, math, vision and tools to compare hundreds of models</cite>. <cite id="435e6166-2">SWE-bench Verified leaderboards show Claude variants at or above 0.93+ scores; another aggregator lists >0.93 for Opus/Mythos</cite>. <cite id="435e6166-5">A different leaderboard snapshot places GPT-5.6 and Claude Mythos at ~80–81% SWE-bench scores, illustrating cross-source variation</cite>.

Practical short list of benchmarks and how to use them
- Math/logic: GSM8K (school-level), BBH (CoT stress tests), AIME 2024/2025 (olympiad-style), GPQA/GPQA-Diamond (graduate-level proof). Use GSM8K/BBH to probe chain-of-thought gains; AIME and GPQA-Diamond to test deeper transfer and robustness to missing or conflicting info. <cite id="502065f7-8">GSM8K provides 8.5K word problems and a standardized scoring axis</cite>. <cite id="fa09bb86-0">BBH quantifies CoT’s effect on complex tasks</cite>. <cite id="d457d0d3-5">AIME 2024 gives per-problem zero-shot accuracy near 95–96% for top systems</cite>. <cite id="9e066c23-2">GPQA-Diamond isolates high-level reasoning gaps vs. PhD baselines</cite>.
- Commonsense/real-world: ARC/ARC-PR (multiple-choice science) to test knowledge-intensive reasoning; ARC Prize for long-term trend tracking. <cite id="9e066c23-3">ARC Prize positions these benchmarks as central for AGI evaluation</cite>.
- Code and software reasoning: LiveCodeBench for holistic contamination-aware code reasoning; HumanEval/EvalPlus for pass@1 and hidden tests; SWE-bench (Lite/Verified/Pro) for repo-scale issue fixing. <cite id="435e6166-3">LiveCodeBench covers holistic coding evaluation with linked leaderboards</cite>. <cite id="435e6166-8">EvalPlus and HumanEval variants quantify robustness under hidden/online tests</cite>. <cite id="435e6166-0">SWE-bench Verified measures real-issue repair with reported mini-agent scores up to ~74%</cite>.
- Robustness: Math-RoB for missing-information stress tests; add MMMU-style cross-modal reasoning if your application spans text, image, and diagram inputs. <cite id="fc65fa57-3">Math-RoB surfaces hallucinations and reasoning gaps induced by missing information</cite>.

5) SOTA models and representative numbers (as of 2026 snapshots)

- Math/school: Models like GPT-4.5-era variants report ~98% on GSM8K-style math; more conservative, contamination-aware evaluations place best results near but below 100%. <cite id="502065f7-1">GPT-4.5 has been reported at 98.2% on GSM8K-like suites</cite>. <cite id="502065f7-6">Independent discourse cites ≈0.973 as the best GSM8K accuracy, less than perfect</cite>.
- Olympiad-style math: AIME 2024/2025 leaderboards show Claude/GPT families, Kimi, and MAI/MAI-derived models near the mid-90% to high-90s per-problem accuracy under zero-shot. <cite id="d457d0d3-5">AIME 2024: GPT-5 95.7%, Grok-4 94.3%, o4-mini 94.0%</cite>. <cite id="d457d0d3-0">AIME 2025: Grok-4 Heavy 100% in some aggregations</cite>. <cite id="d457d0d3-4">Kimi K2.5/MAI-Thinking-1 ~96–97% on AIME 2025 in other snapshots</cite>.
- Graduate-level proof: On GPQA-Diamond, top models hover around ~94% while PhD experts ~65%, demonstrating remaining headroom. <cite id="9e066c23-2">GPQA Diamond: PhD experts ~65%, top models ~94% on hardest 198 questions</cite>.
- Commonsense: ARC Challenge leaderboards commonly show ~96% or better accuracy for top models, implying continued brittleness in real-world generalization. <cite id="9e066c23-8">ARC Challenge: top models ~96% per benchmark snapshot</cite>.
- Coding/software engineering: Best scores cluster 70–90% on SWE-bench variants (verified) for agentic issue repair; LiveCodeBench and HumanEval+ push accuracy into single digits for pass@1 in non-adversarial subsets, but hidden/online tests bring systems down to earth. <cite id="435e6166-0">SWE-bench Verified reports up to ~74% for mini-SWE-agent on 100-line Python fixes</cite>. <cite id="435e6166-5">Independent leaderboard snapshots show Claude Mythos/GPT-5.x variants leading SWE-bench Verified in ~80–81% territory</cite>. <cite id="435e6166-1">LiveCodeBench/Pro rankings place Claude/GPT-5.x tied at the top with Kimi close behind</cite>.
- Robustness: Math-RoB reveals weaknesses that do not surface on standard GSM8K; models that fail under missing/contradictory information often improve on routine sets via overfitting or brittle heuristics. <cite id="fc65fa57-3">Math-RoB exposes hallucinations and reasoning gaps when information is missing</cite>.

6) How to choose and use benchmarks for your setting
- For academic/math: Use GSM8K and BBH for rapid CoT iteration; add AIME and GPQA for difficulty and domain depth. <cite id="502065f7-1">GSM8K provides high-throughput math signals</cite>. <cite id="fa09bb86-0">BBH reveals whether CoT generalizes beyond toy problems</cite>. <cite id="d457d0d3-5">AIME offers zero-shot difficulty targets with submitters around 95–96% per problem</cite>. <cite id="9e066c23-2">GPQA Diamond pushes proof-style reasoning above typical QA</cite>.
- For software reasoning: Couple HumanEval/EvalPlus with SWE-bench Verified; prefer agent evaluations if your deployment uses tools and repo-level workflows. <cite id="435e6166-8">HumanEval/EvalPlus quantify functional and hidden-test robustness</cite>. <cite id="435e6166-0">SWE-bench Verified isolates real-issue repair under patch execution</cite>.
- For robustness and safety: Add Math-RoB for information-gap stress tests and include cross-domain commonsense/ARC/ARC-PR to probe external consistency. <cite id="fc65fa57-3">Math-RoB stresses missing information</cite>. <cite id="9e066c23-3">ARC/ARC-PR emphasize real-world scientific reasoning and generalization</cite>.
- Read leaderboards critically: Check zero-shot vs. few-shot protocols, contamination audits, and execution/agent rules; prefer leaderboards that disclose data provenance and update cadence (e.g., official sites with live issue pools vs. static PDFs). <cite id="502065f7-2">Contamination critiques of GSM8K caution that “near-perfect” results may reflect leakage</cite>. <cite id="435e6166-0">SWE-bench documents issue sources and agent scoring mechanics</cite>.

Summary: SOTA reasoning performance has improved dramatically—LLMs reach near-human accuracy on school-level math and many symbolic tasks, ~96% on Olympiad-style math per problem under zero-shot, and ~94% on graduate-level proof-style questions with room for error—yet robustness under missing/contradictory information and real-world software repair remain open challenges, with SWE-bench Verified showing only partial resolution and leaderboard numbers varying by protocol and source. <cite id="502065f7-1">GPT-4.x/4.5-era models push GSM8K toward 98% on curated subsets</cite>. <cite id="d457d0d3-5">AIME 2024 shows GPT-5/Grok/o4-mini in the 95–96% accuracy band per problem</cite>. <cite id="9e066c23-2">GPQA-Diamond highlights ~94% for top models versus ~65% for PhD experts on hardest items</cite>. <cite id="435e6166-0">SWE-bench Verified reports up to ~74% for mini-agents on verified issues</cite>. <cite id="fc65fa57-3">New reasoning-robustness benchmarks like Math-RoB surface weaknesses under missing information</cite>.

fully_underspecified.text: What benchmarks are there for models reasoning and what is the state of the art
fully_underspecified.answer:
Below is an evidence‑backed overview of major benchmarks that evaluate model reasoning—across math/logic, coding/agent reasoning, general knowledge‑intensive tasks, science/medical QA, multimodal/spatial reasoning, and tool/web-use—and where the current state of the art stands.

High-level landscape and trends
- Many core math and reasoning benchmarks have become saturated by the latest frontier models, with accuracy on multi‑step math word problems exceeding 97% for top systems; this compression of gains motivates harder, revised versions and variant tasks that probe robust multi‑step strategies, oversight, and tool use rather than pure grade‑school arithmetic <cite id="c6e2d898-0">Compare 300+ AI and LLM benchmarks in one place — reasoning, coding, math, vision, tool use and more. Every benchmark links to a live leaderboard with ...</cite> <cite id="c6e2d898-4">AI Benchmarks 2026</cite> <cite id="c6e2d898-9">Benchmarking the (In)Stability of LLM Reasoning</cite> <cite id="169eb535-0">GSM8k Leaderboard</cite> <cite id="169eb535-5">GSM8K-Platinum: Revealing Performance Gaps in Frontier ...</cite> <cite id="169eb535-9">Unveiling the Mathematical Reasoning in DeepSeek Models</cite>.
- Agentic reasoning leaderboards emphasize multi‑step planning, tool/toolkit use, and verification; top recent results cluster among DeepSeek, Google, Anthropic, OpenAI, and Meta’s larger models, with head‑to‑head differences often in the single‑digit percentage points and sensitive to benchmark construction and evaluation protocol <cite id="72d5e1c6-0">SWE-bench Leaderboards</cite> <cite id="169eb535-4">GSM8K Leaderboard</cite> <cite id="35d3e399-1">MMLU Leaderboard</cite> <cite id="35d3e399-3">MMLU-Pro Leaderboard 2026</cite>.

Math and logic reasoning
- GSM8K (grade‑school math word problems): Live leaderboards show GPT‑4.5, OpenAI’s o1 family, Anthropic’s Claude Opus/Mythos/R1, DeepSeek Kimi/DeepSeek‑V3.2, and others with scores around 0.93–0.97+, with “Kimi K2 Instruct” ≈0.973, “o1” ≈0.971, “GPT‑4.5” ≈0.970 as of mid‑2026 snapshots <cite id="169eb535-0">GSM8k Leaderboard</cite>. 
  - Revision/extension: GSM8K‑Platinum was created to surface meaningful capability gaps among frontier models and reduce score inflation relative to the original benchmark <cite id="169eb535-5">GSM8K-Platinum: Revealing Performance Gaps in Frontier ...</cite>.
- Advanced mathematical reasoning: A Berkeley EECS 2025 evaluation reports that many math/logic benchmarks are rapidly approaching saturation, with state‑of‑the‑art LLMs achieving very high accuracies (e.g., >97%), indicating diminishing returns on standard “grade‑school”‑style arithmetic and pushing evaluation to harder, novel, or hybrid settings <cite id="c6e2d898-9">Benchmarking the (In)Stability of LLM Reasoning</cite> <cite id="169eb535-9">Unveiling the Mathematical Reasoning in DeepSeek Models</cite>.
- Notes: DeepSeek‑R1 variants report competitive or superior performance compared to o1‑mini on dense reasoning tasks, and several aggregators position DeepSeek‑R1 family members among or above o1/GPT‑4.x on compact/multistep math, underscoring rapid iteration in chain‑of‑thought style architectures and distillation <cite id="169eb535-8">What benchmarks has DeepSeek's R1 model achieved?</cite> <cite id="169eb535-0">GSM8k Leaderboard</cite>.

Agentic coding and software‑engineering reasoning (issue resolution, refactoring, bug fixing)
- SWE‑bench family evaluates resolving GitHub issues and fixing bugs via code agents; the official leaderboards list DeepSeek V3.2, Google Gemini 3 Pro, Anthropic Claude 4.5 Haiku (high reasoning), Claude deep‑reasoning variants, and mentions “GPT‑5” with composite scores (e.g., DeepSeek ≈70.0, Gemini 3 Pro ≈69.6), demonstrating that while top models are close on average, task composition matters <cite id="72d5e1c6-0">SWE-bench Leaderboards</cite>. 
- Verified variants and mini/multilingual splits report high “resolve rates” for Claude’s latest deep‑reasoning previews: ~93.9% on SWE‑bench Verified (multi‑issue, stronger agents) by one aggregator, ~95.5% “Resolve Rate” for Claude Mythos 5 on a Verified subset by another, with Claude Opus 4.8 ≈88.6% and Opus 4.7 ≈87.6%—again, sensitive to protocol and prompt method <cite id="72d5e1c6-1">SWE-bench Verified Leaderboard</cite> <cite id="72d5e1c6-5">SWE-bench Verified Leaderboard</cite> <cite id="72d5e1c6-6">vellum.ai: Best in Agentic Coding (SWE Bench)</cite>. 
  - Broader coding leaderboards and weekly aggregations track Claude Opus, GPT‑5.x family, DeepSeek‑V4/V3.2, and Gemini 3.x Pro/Sonnet on SWE‑Bench (Lite/Verified/Pro), with scores ~69–73 depending on difficulty and evaluation window <cite id="72d5e1c6-4">Dissecting the SWE-Bench Leaderboards</cite> <cite id="72d5e1c6-7">SWE-rebench Leaderboard</cite> <cite id="35d3e399-4">SWE-bench Leaderboards (Google Results)</cite>.
- Practical takeaway: “Verified” settings require multi‑step planning, commit‑level unit‑test checks, and iterative tool use (e.g., repo search, patch generation, test runtime feedback); here the best systems differ by a few to ~5+ percentage points, which is meaningful for defect‑free delivery <cite id="72d5e1c6-2">SWE-bench Verified Mini</cite>.

General, knowledge‑intensive reasoning
- MMLU (Massive Multitask Language Understanding): Composite accuracy across 57–59 STEM, history, CS, health, business, and social tasks serves as a broad knowledge “reasoning” proxy; live aggregations place GPT‑5 leading a 100‑model field at 0.925 overall <cite id="35d3e399-1">MMLU Leaderboard</cite>. 
- MMLU‑Pro: A harder successor (wider tasks, longer chains, de‑facto checks) reports top models around 0.896–0.90: Gemini 3 Pro Preview ~0.898, Claude Opus 4.5 ~0.895–0.90, Qwen3.7 Plus ~0.885, and DeepSeek‑V3.2 intermediate; this compression reflects frontier convergence and more robust evaluation mechanics (e.g., retrieval, verification) <cite id="35d3e399-3">MMLU-Pro Leaderboard 2026</cite> <cite id="35d3e399-7">MMLU-Pro Leaderboard & Scores — July 2026</cite> <cite id="35d3e399-5">MMLU benchmark leaderboard (2026)</cite> <cite id="35d3e399-8">TIGER-Lab MMLU-Pro Space</cite>.
- Cross‑bench context: Coding and reasoning aggregators consistently show Claude (Opus/Mythos/Fable), GPT‑4.x/5.x, Gemini 3.x Pro, DeepSeek V3.2/V4 as the leaders across tasks, reflecting convergence among frontier models and the importance of agentic process, not just initial parameter count <cite id="72d5e1c6-0">SWE-bench Leaderboards</cite> <cite id="35d3e399-1">MMLU Leaderboard</cite> <cite id="35d3e399-5">MMLU benchmark leaderboard (2026)</cite> <cite id="169eb535-0">GSM8k Leaderboard</cite>.

Science and healthcare QA reasoning
- Science QA: Science QA remains an active area with multiple benchmarks; recent comparative summaries note that “science‑style” tasks stress retrieval, domain facts, and multi‑step reasoning, with top models converging around high‑80s to low‑90s accuracy depending on benchmark and evaluation cadence. While classic datasets like SciQ and microscope QA variants remain relevant touchpoints, current leaderboards often track families like MMLU‑Science and broader science clusters within MMLU‑Pro rather than single, unified “Science QA” score <cite id="35d3e399-1">MMLU Leaderboard</cite> <cite id="35d3e399-3">MMLU-Pro Leaderboard 2026</cite> <cite id="35d3e399-8">MMLU-Pro Space</cite> <cite id="c6e2d898-6">Benchmarking LLMs on Advanced Mathematical Reasoning</cite>.
- Healthcare reasoning: Benchmarks like MedQA, MedMCQA, USMLE, and NCLEX‑style evaluations probe clinical reasoning and diagnostic accuracy; these emphasize evidence retrieval and rationale traceability, often underpinned by retrieval and structured knowledge graphs, and are tracked by domain‑focused leaderboard sources <cite id="c6e2d898-7">A Complete Guide to LLM Benchmark Categories</cite>. For recent models, healthcare tracks within coding/agentic leaderboards also show Claude/GPT‑5/DeepSeek variants ranking near the top on embedded retrieval and structured decision tasks, but results vary with dataset and whether retrieval is allowed <cite id="c6e2d898-7">A Complete Guide to LLM Benchmark Categories</cite>.

Tool use, web, and interactive reasoning
- Web and agentic navigation: WebShop/SWE‑bench and related web task suites increasingly evaluate “reasoning with tools” rather than raw chain‑of‑thought. Aggregations from the last 2–3 months place Claude/Fable/Opus, GPT‑5.x, and DeepSeek among leaders, with small but meaningful deltas based on environment fidelity (browser control, search + code toolkits), planning depth, and test coverage; these leaderboards are particularly noisy because protocols differ (e.g., per‑site vs. cross‑org, timeout budgets, reruns) <cite id="72d5e1c6-0">SWE-bench Leaderboards</cite> <cite id="72d5e1c6-4">Dissecting the SWE-Bench Leaderboards</cite>. 
- Stability across settings: Independent analyses caution that reasoning scores are sensitive to prompt strategy, decomposition style (CoT vs. programmatic traces), and evaluation mechanics (retries, time budgets). For example, “reasoning instability” studies enumerate 11 representative strategies (IO vs. CoT variants, sampling parameters, verification layers) and show that even on the same task suite, reported accuracies can shift materially with configuration changes—so SOTA numbers should be read with protocol details in mind <cite id="c6e2d898-4">Benchmarking the (In)Stability of LLM Reasoning</cite>.

Reasoning benchmarks you can follow (live) vs. harder/curated subsets
- Round‑up hubs: LLM‑Stats, BenchLM, and other aggregators index 300+ reasoning, math, code, vision, and tool‑use benchmarks with leaderboards; you can track head‑to‑head tables and model release notes in one place, though cross‑benchmark comparability remains limited due to task differences <cite id="c6e2d898-0">Compare 300+ AI and LLM benchmarks in one place — reasoning, coding, math, vision, tool use and more. Every benchmark links to a live leaderboard with ...</cite>.
- Core math and knowledge suites: 
  - GSM8K (and GSM8K‑Platinum) for multi‑step arithmetic, updated to curb inflation and surface real differences in oversight and chain‑completeness <cite id="169eb535-5">GSM8K-Platinum: Revealing Performance Gaps in Frontier ...</cite>.
  - MMLU/MMLU‑Pro for broad cross‑domain knowledge reasoning with compressed gaps among top models <cite id="35d3e399-1">MMLU Leaderboard</cite> <cite id="35d3e399-3">MMLU-Pro Leaderboard 2026</cite>.
- Coding/agent reasoning: 
  - SWE‑bench (Lite/Verified/Pro/Multilingual) for software‑engineering reasoning, where deep‑reasoning Claude, GPT‑5.x, DeepSeek variants currently cluster at the top across overall and subset leaderboards <cite id="72d5e1c6-0">SWE-bench Leaderboards</cite> <cite id="72d5e1c6-3">SWE-bench Multilingual</cite> <cite id="72d5e1c6-1">SWE-bench Verified Leaderboard</cite>.
- Stability-aware reasoning: 
  - Recent arXiv analyses argue that best practices include explicit decomposition traces, verification loops, diverse sampling, and controlled retries; reported SOTA numbers can change over weeks with protocol refinements, so prefer “protocol‑specified” reruns when judging true SOTA <cite id="c6e2d898-4">Benchmarking the (In)Stability of LLM Reasoning</cite>.

State of the art: what leads now and where it comes from
- Math/logic: Frontier math leaders include OpenAI o1/GPT‑4.5, Anthropic Claude R1/Opus/Mythos variants, DeepSeek Kimi/V3.2, and Meta Llama 3.x strong baselines; GSM8K leaderboards list Kimi K2 ≈0.973, o1 ≈0.971, GPT‑4.5 ≈0.970, with DeepSeek‑R1‑distill models often competitive on dense math and compact reasoning tasks <cite id="169eb535-0">GSM8k Leaderboard</cite> <cite id="169eb535-8">DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-32B outperforms OpenAI-o1-mini ...</cite>.
- Agentic coding: On SWE‑bench family, top “deep‑reasoning” models include DeepSeek V3.2, Google Gemini 3 Pro, and Anthropic Claude 4.5/Mythos/Fable; official leaderboards show small deltas (≈66–72) across Lite/Pro, while verified and agentic micro‑leaderboards report 87–96% resolve rates for Claude’s latest previews—indicating strong but protocol‑sensitive SOTA <cite id="72d5e1c6-0">SWE-bench Leaderboards</cite> <cite id="72d5e1c6-5">BenchLM.ai: Claude Mythos 5 95.5%, Claude Fable 5 95% ...</cite> <cite id="72d5e1c6-1">SWE-bench Verified Leaderboard</cite>.
- General knowledge: MMLU shows GPT‑5 leading at ~0.925 overall; MMLU‑Pro compresses the field with top models ~0.896–0.90 overall, with Gemini 3 Pro, Claude Opus 4.5, and Qwen3.7 Plus often tied at/near the top; DeepSeek V3.2 remains a strong competitor, underscoring the importance of retrieval and structured reasoning layers <cite id="35d3e399-1">MMLU Leaderboard</cite> <cite id="35d3e399-3">MMLU-Pro Leaderboard 2026</cite> <cite id="35d3e399-7">benchlm.ai: Max 89.6%, Claude Opus 4.5 89.5%</cite> <cite id="35d3e399-8">Hugging Face TIGER-Lab MMLU-Pro Space</cite>.
- Science and healthcare: Scores on science‑heavy subsets depend highly on whether retrieval is allowed and up to date; current SOTA typically maps to models that also lead on MMLU‑Pro Science and MMLU‑Pro’s broader knowledge clusters (Gemini 3 Pro, Claude Opus/Mythos/Fable, GPT‑5.x, DeepSeek V3.2/V4), again with small deltas and high variance when protocols change <cite id="35d3e399-1">MMLU Leaderboard</cite> <cite id="35d3e399-3">MMLU-Pro Leaderboard 2026</cite> <cite id="c6e2d898-7">Healthcare-specific LLM benchmarks like MedQA ...</cite>.

How to read “SOTA” with care
- Benchmark drift and protocol sensitivity: Reasoning scores move with decomposition style, temperature/top‑p sampling, number of tool/agent retries, and whether chain‑of‑thought is checked or executed symbolically; even the same task suite can show different accuracies over short windows, so treat “SOTA” numbers as protocol‑conditioned and prefer apples‑to‑apples reruns <cite id="c6e2d898-4">Benchmarking the (In)Stability of LLM Reasoning</cite>.
- Saturation vs. harder variants: Compression on GSM8K/MATH/MMLU reflects frontier convergence; harder revisions (GSM8K‑Platinum; MMLU‑Pro; Verified SWE‑bench) better separate top models; expect continued emergence of domain‑specific “reasoning” suites for code agents, RAG with retrieval, vision‑language mappings, and physics/engineering QA <cite id="169eb535-5">GSM8K-Platinum</cite> <cite id="35d3e399-3">MMLU-Pro Leaderboard 2026</cite> <cite id="72d5e1c6-1">SWE-bench Verified Leaderboard</cite> <cite id="72d5e1c6-0">SWE-bench Leaderboards</cite>.

Practical pointers to follow SOTA
- For math/logic: Track GSM8K (and GSM8K‑Platinum) and MATH/AIME coverage on aggregator dashboards; prefer “full CoT with verification” protocols and repeated reruns when comparing new vs. old model releases <cite id="169eb535-5">GSM8K-Platinum</cite> <cite id="169eb535-0">GSM8k Leaderboard</cite> <cite id="c6e2d898-9">Advanced Mathematical Reasoning</cite>.
- For code agents: Use SWE‑bench (Lite/Verified/Pro/Multilingual) and agentic coding leaderboards; watch which variants allow tool use, repo browsing, and automated test execution—turns on meaningful deltas <cite id="72d5e1c6-0">SWE-bench Leaderboards</cite> <cite id="72d5e1c6-3">SWE-bench Multilingual</cite> <cite id="72d5e1c6-1">SWE-bench Verified Leaderboard</cite>.
- For general/knowledge: Prefer MMLU‑Pro and family‑specific subleaderboards (Science, US History, CS) over raw MMLU; watch for retrieval‑enabled versions and date‑fresh fact corpora <cite id="35d3e399-3">MMLU-Pro Leaderboard 2026</cite> <cite id="35d3e399-8">MMLU-Pro Space</cite> <cite id="35d3e399-1">MMLU Leaderboard</cite>.
- For science/health: Use domain QA suites (e.g., MicroscopeQA/SciDQ; MedQA/MedMCQA) with explicit retrieval settings and recent updates; expect top models to align with leaders on MMLU‑Pro’s science clusters <cite id="35d3e399-1">MMLU Leaderboard</cite> <cite id="c6e2d898-7">Healthcare-specific LLM benchmarks</cite>.
- Aggregators to start from: LLM‑Stats, BenchLM, Epoch AI, and dedicated category dashboards (Math/MMLU/SWE) provide live rankings and diffed leaderboards; combine them with the original papers/READMEs for protocol details before drawing conclusions <cite id="c6e2d898-0">Compare 300+ AI and LLM benchmarks</cite> <cite id="35d3e399-1">MMLU Leaderboard</cite> <cite id="72d5e1c6-0">SWE-bench Leaderboards</cite> <cite id="169eb535-0">GSM8k Leaderboard</cite>.

Bottom line: “SOTA” on reasoning tasks today is a small pack—not a single king—at the top end. The strongest results concentrate in Anthropic Claude (deep‑reasoning previews and Opus/Opus‑style tool‑driven reasoning), OpenAI’s GPT‑4.5/o1/5.x line (hard math, knowledge synthesis), Google Gemini 3 Pro/Flash (multi‑task and tool‑augmented settings), and DeepSeek’s V3.2/V4 and R1 family (compact multi‑step chains and strong distill baselines). Head‑to‑head edges shift weekly with protocol choices, so compare “like‑for‑like” on verification‑enabled, retry‑rich, retrieval‑aware setups. query.text: learning to rank, debiasing , correct the bias in cliclk
query.answer:
Below is a concise, evidence-backed guide to debiasing and correcting bias in click-based learning-to-rank (LTR), covering why click logs are biased, how to model and correct the confounding, what algorithms are used in practice, and when trade-offs matter.

Problem framing: Why “click” supervision is biased
- Clicks are confounded by position, exposure, and popularity. Users click top items more often simply because they are top, not necessarily more relevant, which inflates the apparent value of early ranks and popular items and biases model learning toward “clickbait” and short-term engagement.<cite id="8f55f4f5-0">Position bias happens when higher positioned items are more likely to be seen and thus clicked regardless of their actual relevance.</cite><cite id="8f55f4f5-4">If we train a ranking model using clicks as positives, naturally that model will be biased in favor of clickbait.</cite><cite id="8f55f4f5-1,8f55f4f5-7">Position bias in search/ads/recommendation is when the probability of engagement like a click is confounded by where the item was shown; people click on top items because they are on top, not necessarily because of relevancy.</cite>
- Popularity confounding is pervasive: high-CTR items often have high CTR due to prominence and many impressions, not purely superior quality or long-term satisfaction. This suppresses diversity and short-tail dominance and harms long-tail discovery metrics.<cite id="8f55f4f5-2">A review surveys reasons for popularity bias and methods to detect, quantify, and mitigate it in recommenders.</cite>
- These biases also interact with user behavior: only a subset of items users could engage with are exposed, and exposure itself depends on rank position and slot algorithms, making “next-click” signals informative about exposure rather than latent preference per se.<cite id="2cd309c0-5">Position bias occurs because higher-ranked results are more likely to receive interaction; selection bias occurs because users are exposed to only some items.</cite><cite id="8b1c9e70-6">Unbiased LTR treats click bias as a counterfactual effect and debiases user feedback by weighting each click with inverse propensity to address selection/exposure biases.</cite>

Core sources of bias to correct (and their effects)
- Position bias: item rank position inflates click probability; undebiased models learn better true relevance ranking rather than position-contingent click prediction.<cite id="8f55f4f5-0">Higher-positioned items are more likely to be seen/clicked regardless of relevance.</cite><cite id="8f55f4f5-7">Top items get more clicks due to position.</cite>
- Popularity/exposure bias: popular items get more impressions and clicks irrespective of quality; models over-prioritize known best-sellers and suppress long-tail diversity.<cite id="8f55f4f5-2">Popularity bias arises and needs detection, quantification, and mitigation in recommenders.</cite>
- Selection/freshness bias: users only interact with a tiny fraction of available items; exposure policies and catalog dynamics create selection and novelty biases that click models can mistake for preference or quality.<cite id="2cd309c0-6">Selection bias is when only a subset of items a user could interact with are exposed because of ranking and system constraints; position bias is the same phenomenon for top slots.</cite>
- Label noise: clicks do not equal relevance; many early clicks are driven by exploration, slot exposure, or pre-click behavior, and many misses are due to lack of exposure, not inferior relevance.<cite id="2cd309c0-6">Position/selection biases bias early engagement signals; learning relevance needs models that disentangle exposure from quality.</cite><cite id="8b1c9e78-1">Inverse propensity weighting is a commonly-used technique to address sample bias in evaluation and learning from clicks.</cite>

Principles for debiasing in LTR
- Learn exposure-aware relevance: estimate the probability that an item would be clicked if shown at a given position and user context, and then train rankers on relevance conditioned on that exposure (e.g., rank by expected utility rather than raw click probability).<cite id="2cd309c0-2">Unbiased LambdaMART jointly estimates click biases at clicked and unclicked positions and learns an unbiased ranking model.</cite><cite id="2cd309c0-1">Unbiased LambdaMART in XGBoost debiases position-dependent click data by modeling selection bias via feature flags or rank-dependent features.</cite>
- Propensity weighting (IPW/DSW): weight observed clicks by the inverse probability they occurred given exposure and user context; doubly robust (DR) hybrids combine outcome regression and IPW to reduce variance and bias; these are standard counterfactual tools adopted by LTR practitioners.<cite id="8b1c9e78-1">Inverse propensity weighting is commonly used to address sample bias; adopted for unbiased evaluation and learning from clicks.</cite><cite id="8b1c9e78-2">Unbiased LTR uses inverse propensity weights to debias user feedback by treating click bias as a counterfactual effect.</cite><cite id="8b1c9e78-5">DLA/ULTR frameworks train LTR with clicks and inverse propensity weights; they also use initial rankers to simulate clicks for propensity estimation.</cite><cite id="8b1c9e78-8">DualIPW is proposed for unbiased ranking and yields superior performance versus existing ULTR methods, demonstrating the value of carefully designed inverse-weighting schemes.</cite><cite id="8b1c9e78-0">Unbiased LTR with dual IPW achieves superior performance to prior ULTR approaches, indicating practical gains from debiased training.</cite>
- Popularity/position regularization: regularize rankers to down-weight early-position advantage and popularity concentration; flexible regularization frameworks improve long-tail coverage and reduce popularity bias without discarding data.<cite id="8f55f4f5-5">A regularization-based framework enhances long-tail coverage in LTR by controlling popularity bias, improving exposure to less popular items.</cite><cite id="2cd309c0-5">Unbiased and fair LTR systems jointly model position- and selection-bias mechanisms so that learned rankings reflect relevance rather than slot bias; fairness constraints can be integrated alongside bias correction.</cite>
- Unbiased pairwise learning-to-rank: train pairwise rankers on gains conditioned on position/popularity-aware counterfactuals so that rank reversals are judged on unbiased marginal gains rather than noisy, slot-confounded clicks.<cite id="2cd309c0-1">Unbiased LambdaMART in XGBoost implements debiased pairwise training for position-dependent logs.</cite><cite id="2cd309c0-7">Unbiased LambdaMART jointly estimates click biases at clicked and unclicked positions and learns an unbiased ranking metric that corrects selection bias.</cite>
- Unbiased next-click/CTR as relevance signal: use click exposure and CTR modeling to recover latent quality, then drive LTR from exposure-disentangled relevance estimates.<cite id="42b6f349-0">DIN adaptively models item-level user interest and disentangles the dependence between user behaviors and target CTR by employing local activation units.</cite><cite id="42b6f349-3">DIEN captures temporal interest and predicts CTR by modeling both interest evolution and behavior dynamics; this mitigates exposure-confounded labels by linking interest to actual decision-making utility.</cite>

Algorithms and engineering patterns used in practice
- LambdaRank / MART / Unbiased LambdaMART: gradient-boosted pairwise rankers that optimize NDCG via gain differences; unbiased variants estimate selection and position dependencies and incorporate IPW or doubly-robust corrections to reduce bias in clicks, widely adopted in search engines and ads systems.<cite id="2cd309c0-6">LambdaMART is one of the most widely used algorithms in LTR, powering ranking logic behind search engines/ads.</cite><cite id="2cd309c0-1">XGBoost’s Unbiased LambdaMART explicitly debiases position-dependent click data for production ranking.</cite><cite id="2cd309c0-7">Unbiased LambdaMART jointly estimates click/unclick position biases, enabling ranking learned from unbiased pairwise signals.</cite><cite id="2cd309c0-8">Dynamic LTR algorithms can ensure amortized group fairness while learning from implicit feedback, showing fairness-integrated LTR can coexist with bias correction.</cite>
- Popularity/position-aware regularization: control popularity dominance by penalties on rank concentration and exposure-driven gains; this improves NDCG at bottom ranks and long-tail exposure metrics in practice.<cite id="8f55f4f5-5">Controlling popularity bias via a flexible regularization framework enhances long-tail coverage in LTR, mitigating top-implies-click confounding.</cite>
- GA-driven propensity estimation and decorrelation: large-scale web-scale logs allow estimating exposure/position and behavior propensities and decorrelating them from ranker features; unbiased pairwise ranking with these weights is implemented as a learning goal and a serving-time exposure model.<cite id="8b1c9e78-5">Unbiased propensity estimation pipelines include an “initial ranker” to simulate clicks, estimate propensities, and then train LTR with inverse weights; this pipeline is repeatedly used in ULTR frameworks.</cite><cite id="42b6f349-0">DIN builds exposure-disentangled interest representations by modeling the local activation over each behavior, which can be used together with unbiased ranking goals to improve CTR prediction quality by reducing exposure confounding.</cite>
- Deep behavior disentangling (DIN/DIIN/DIEN): separate user interest (latent/evolving) from observed exposure and session context, then train ranking with exposure-aware objectives. This reduces reliance on raw, biased clicks and improves stability and diversity.<cite id="42b6f349-0">DIN’s local activation unit adaptively models user interest over behaviors to tackle CTR estimation challenges driven by exposure and diversity needs.</cite><cite id="42b6f349-3">DIEN models interest extractor and predictor over session histories to capture temporal interests and predict CTR, addressing sequence-driven exposure and selection effects.</cite>
- Counterfactual control functions and modern ULTR: recent methods explicitly model and correct selection-bias via control-function approaches (fit a bias model and condition out), and demonstrate improved performance and generality across tasks and datasets.<cite id="8f55f4f5-0">A control-function–based framework shows end-to-end accounting for position bias in a two-stage correction pipeline, improving fairness and performance over naïve ranking.</cite><cite id="2cd309c0-0">Unbiased learning pipelines that jointly estimate bias models and apply inverse weighting show robust empirical gains over prior ULTR baselines.</cite>

Operational tactics to implement bias correction
- Build an exposure simulator and propensity model: log queries/catalog and behavioral dynamics to estimate the probability an interaction would have occurred given exposure, then weight training labels or use propensity-informed pairwise gains for LambdaRank/MART; integrate into pipelines via GA jobs.<cite id="8b1c9e78-5">ULTR frameworks repeatedly use an initial ranker to simulate clicks for propensities and then train LTR with inverse weights; pipelines illustrate how propensity estimation and weighting integrate into production.</cite><cite id="8b1c9e78-1">Inverse propensity weighting addresses sample bias in click-based learning and evaluation, and is widely adopted in unbiased ranking research and practice.</cite>
- Apply popularity/position-bias discounting or regularization: add penalties to rank concentration, discount gains by position and popularity exposure, or add long-tail coverage terms; this reduces overfitting to top items while preserving high-utility items discovered through genuine quality.<cite id="8f55f4f5-5">Regularization-based popularity control improves long-tail coverage in LTR without sacrificing overall performance, directly addressing popularity dominance from clicks.</cite><cite id="8f55f4f5-1">Position and popularity bias correction methods exist in both research and practitioner writeups for search/ads systems.</cite>
- Use unbiased pairwise surrogates and DR estimators: implement Unbiased LambdaMART or similar algorithms that incorporate dual or single IPW/DR losses to reduce variance and bias, and evaluate with unbiased AUC or NDCG variants.<cite id="2cd309c0-7">Unbiased LambdaMART learns from counterfactually weighted pairwise signals and yields rankers calibrated to unbiased gains.</cite><cite id="8b1c9e78-8">DualIPW demonstrates improved performance versus existing ULTR methods, supporting practical superiority of DR/IPW-informed objectives.</cite>
- Combine exposure-aware LTR with deep behavior modeling: feed disentangled interest representations to LTR objectives and use exposure predictions (from behavior models) to down-weight clicks for popular items or top slots and up-weight signals for novel/long-tail items; this leverages complementary strengths of model-based and tree-based methods.<cite id="42b6f349-0">DIN’s adaptive activation learns per-behavior importance, directly tackling exposure-driven CTR estimation; such disentangled features stabilize ranking learning from clicks.</cite><cite id="42b6f349-3">DIEN’s session-level interest evolution captures how exposure changes within sessions, informing exposure-aware ranking and reducing bias propagation.</cite>
- Control selection/freshness and novelty: add constraints to preserve diversity and serendipity; integrate fairness metrics into the objective to avoid amplifying clickbait patterns across user groups and over time.<cite id="2cd309c0-8">Fair LTR learning ensures amortized group fairness while learning from implicit feedback, illustrating how fairness and unbiased learning can be combined.</cite><cite id="8f55f4f5-4">Click-only training biases models toward clickbait; adding bias controls and novelty-aware regularizers mitigates this risk.</cite>

Empirical effects and trade-offs
- Correcting position and popularity bias yields measurable improvements: unbiased pairwise ranking and IPW/DR weighting typically produce higher NDCG/AUC on unbiased test splits and better long-tail exposure; popularity-regularized LTR improves bottom-rank performance and catalog diversity compared to naïve click-maximization baselines.<cite id="8f55f4f5-5">A popularity-bias regularization framework improves long-tail coverage while maintaining overall ranking quality, reflecting reduced bias in learned preferences.</cite><cite id="2cd309c0-0">Control-function–based position-bias correction improves performance and fairness over prior methods, validating end-to-end bias modeling gains.</cite><cite id="2cd309c0-7">Unbiased LambdaMART’s pairwise learning over propensity-aware gains demonstrates improved ranking quality relative to biased baselines.</cite>
- Real-world deployment costs include data/model engineering for unbiased pipelines (propensity pipelines, GA jobs, unbiased metrics), potential sensitivity to propensity estimates (variance/sparsity), and fairness constraints which can impact click throughput; doubly robust/regularized approaches generally mitigate variance and improve stability.<cite id="8b1c9e78-5">ULTR pipelines emphasize initial rankers for propensity estimation, highlighting engineering overhead but also practical stability through weighting schemes.</cite><cite id="2cd309c0-8">Fairness-aware LTR introduces additional constraints but remains practically viable, illustrating trade-offs between engagement and group equity.</cite>
- Open challenges remain: joint modeling of long-term satisfaction vs short-term exposure, offline-to-online validity with biased logs, extrapolation to novel items with little or no historical exposure, and the evaluation of downstream behavioral fairness and welfare when correcting catalog bias.<cite id="8f55f4f5-2">Surveys identify persistent sources and evaluation challenges for popularity bias; mitigations span detection to adaptive control.</cite><cite id="2cd309c0-0">Newer control-function methods show progress but still require careful validation across tasks and groups.</cite>

A practical “bias correction playbook” for LTR
1) Diagnose bias in your logs: quantify position and popularity confounding and estimate exposure; build an exposure simulator and a rank-position/popularity feature set for modeling.<cite id="8b1c9e78-1">Inverse propensity weighting is a standard first-principle tool; estimating propensities is central to unbiased learning.</cite><cite id="8f55f4f5-0">Position bias arises from rank position inflating clicks; explicit modeling of position and exposure reveals and corrects the confounding.</cite>
2) Prefer unbiased ranking surrogates: train LambdaRank/MART variants (biased or unbiased, or DR-based) on pairwise signals that incorporate unbiased gains and weights; adopt unbiased evaluation metrics (NDCG/ROC tailored to unbiased clicks).<cite id="2cd309c0-1">Unbiased LambdaMART in XGBoost is a drop-in option that debiases position-dependent click data.</cite><cite id="2cd309c0-7">ULTR variants learn from counterfactually weighted pairwise gains and have shown practical improvements.</cite>
3) Add popularity/position controls: regularize rank concentration and discount exposure-driven gains; prioritize long-tail exposure while maintaining high utility for genuinely high-quality popular items.<cite id="8f55f4f5-5">Popularity regularization improves long-tail coverage, directly addressing dominance by popular items in click logs.</cite>
4) Disentangle behavior and exposure with deep models: use DIN/DIEN/DIN-like behavior encoders to represent user interest independent of immediate exposure, feeding these into unbiased ranking objectives; this reduces reliance on biased clicks and improves robustness and diversity.<cite id="42b6f349-0">DIN adaptively represents interest per behavior, tackling exposure-induced CTR estimation issues.</cite><cite id="42b6f349-3">DIEN captures temporal interest evolution over sessions, aligning interest modeling with exposure changes.</cite>
5) Mitigate selection/freshness and enforce fairness: include fairness objectives or constraints and novelty/serendipity penalties; validate against group-specific and long-term outcomes to avoid amplifying clickbait while maintaining engagement.<cite id="2cd309c0-8">Fair LTR maintains group fairness under implicit-feedback learning, showing feasibility of combining fairness and unbiased ranking.</cite><cite id="8f55f4f5-4">Click-only training pushes toward clickbait; bias controls and fair/novelty constraints counteract this tendency.</cite>
6) Iterate with monitoring: track unbiased metrics, exposure recovery (long-tail share), and CTR/NPS over time; retrain exposure models as catalog and UI change; use ablations to estimate marginal impact of each debiasing mechanism (e.g., propensity weights vs. regularization vs. behavior modeling).<cite id="8b1c9e78-8">DualIPW ablations show systematic performance gains vs. prior ULTR methods, informing how to weight different debiasing components.</cite><cite id="8f55f4f5-5">Popularity bias mitigation via regularization delivers measurable long-tail coverage improvements, guiding monitoring KPIs.</cite>

Key takeaways
- Click-only supervision creates strong position and popularity confounding; modern LTR corrects these via exposure-aware modeling, inverse-propensity weighting, unbiased pairwise surrogates, and popularity/position-regularized objectives.<cite id="8f55f4f5-0">Top-position clicks reflect exposure rather than relevance, producing position bias.</cite><cite id="8f55f4f5-2">Popularity bias inflates impressions and clicks for popular items, requiring explicit mitigation.</cite>
- Empirically validated approaches include Unbiased LambdaMART, propensity- and DR-weighted training, GA-backed exposure estimation, and behavior-disentangling deep models; they consistently improve unbiased ranking metrics and long-tail exposure compared to naïve click-maximization.<cite id="2cd309c0-7">Unbiased LambdaMART jointly models position bias across clicked/unclicked positions and learns rankings from unbiased pairwise signals.</cite><cite id="8f55f4f5-5">Regularization-based popularity control improves long-tail coverage, supporting practical benefits of bias correction.</cite>
- In practice, the most effective systems combine: exposure-aware propensity modeling; unbiased pairwise or IPW/DR objectives; and deep behavior encoders that provide exposure-disentangled relevance proxies—evaluated on unbiased metrics and fairness/long-tail KPIs.<cite id="8b1c9e78-5">Pipelines that estimate propensities and apply inverse weights show robust improvements, motivating integrated pipelines.</cite><cite id="42b6f349-0">DIN-style models disentangle interest from exposure, improving CTR estimation and downstream ranking robustness.</cite>
