without_term.text: When performing the algorithm how does the solution use previous time step solutions to advance the solution in time?
without_term.answer:
# Short Answer Up Front

- In time-marching methods, the new state at time t_{n+1} is computed from known or iteratively updated values at earlier times (most commonly t_n, and sometimes t_{n−1}, t_{n−2}, etc.) via a recurrence that combines the solution at the current/previous time steps with a time-integrated contribution of the right‑hand‑side f (or residual) evaluated at those states. The exact recipe depends on the scheme:
  - Forward (explicit) Euler: u_{n+1} = u_n + Δt f(u_n, t_n). <cite id="10150845-0">The Euler method is a first-order procedure where the next value is obtained by advancing one step of size h along the tangent at the current point, yielding u_{n+1} = u_n + h f(u_n, t_n).</cite> <cite id="10150845-3">An explicit Euler implementation defines y_{n+1}^* = y_n + h f(x_n, y_n), i.e., the next state is a first‑order Taylor step from the present state.</cite>
  - Backward/implicit Euler: a linear (or nonlinear) system involving u_{n+1} is solved, using f evaluated at u_n as a driver, i.e., (I + Δt A)u_{n+1} = b(u_n). <cite id="ab6bafc2-6">Implicit time steps form systems coupling future and present states; error contributions per step are O(h^2) but stability is improved because the stepsize can be chosen independent of high-frequency modes.</cite>
  - Crank–Nicolson (θ=1/2): averages the forward and backward increments, so u_{n+1} is computed from both u_n and a predicted/implied value at t_{n+1}, often solved implicitly; it is second‑order and unconditionally stable for linear problems. <cite id="fc8e4f9b-1">Crank–Nicolson is a 2‑level scheme producing a system to be solved implicitly, designed to be second order in both space and time and to avoid a Courant condition.</cite> <cite id="fc8e4f9b-4">Backward Euler is monotone; Crank–Nicolson gives the most accurate results among the two for linear ODEs.</cite> <cite id="fc8e4f9b-1">The θ‑scheme generalizes: at each step you solve for the unknown u_{n+1} using a linear combination of known and predicted values (implicit) to achieve second‑order accuracy and unconditional stability when the problem is linear and θ is chosen appropriately.</cite>

Across schemes, implementations maintain prior‑time snapshots (u_n, sometimes u_{n−1}) and reuse them to form the new right‑hand‑side and/or boundary conditions for the next step's linear/nonlinear solve; in multiphysics or spatially split PDEs, a "staggered" time coupling (e.g., x‑then‑y) reuses the completed x‑update as the initial condition for the y‑update at the same global time step. <cite id="ab6bafc2-0">Step‑by‑step (time‑marching) methods build each new solution only from previously computed time levels, proceeding serially in time.</cite> <cite id="ab6bafc2-5">General linear methods, IMEX, and multirate algorithms explicitly layer multiple solver stages where each stage consumes prior‑time data (fields or state) to produce the next.</cite>

# How the Advance-from-Previous-Steps Works in Major Scheme Families

## 1) Explicit (Forward) Euler
- Mechanism: Use the known u_n at t_n to form one step of the local ODE tangent; set u_{n+1} = u_n + Δt f(u_n, t_n). No need to solve a system; only one function evaluation per step is required (up to quadrature in PDEs). <cite id="10150845-0">The next iterate is computed by stepping along the slope at the current point.</cite> <cite id="10150845-3">In explicit Euler implementations, the update is y_{n+1}^* = y_n + h f(x_n, y_n).</cite>
- Practical usage: For ODE systems, you store y_n and reuse it to compute y_{n+1}; for PDE semidiscretizations, you assemble the right‑hand‑side using u_n's spatial snapshots and advance all DOFs together. <cite id="10150845-2">Forward Euler for ODEs updates the state from the present value and derivative, with first‑order local/truncation error.</cite>
- Cost/stability: Low cost per step, but stability-limited unless small Δt satisfies a Courant–Friedrichs–Lewy (CFL) condition; it is suitable for non‑stiff problems with sufficient time resolution. <cite id="10150845-7">Forward Euler is a first‑order method; its local truncation error is O(h^2), hence global error ~O(h).</cite>

## 2) Implicit (Backward) Euler and θ/Trapzoidal/Crank–Nicolson
- Mechanism: Define a two‑level formula that equates the increment to the average of forward/backward slopes or a linear combination of u_n and u_{n+1}. In matrix form, (I − αΔt A)u_{n+1} = b(u_n) for small α (implicitness), and α=1 gives fully implicit; α=0.5 gives Crank–Nicolson. <cite id="fc8e4f9b-4">Backward Euler is monotone and stable over large timesteps; Crank–Nicolson yields the most accurate results for linear problems.</cite> <cite id="fc8e4f9b-1">Crank–Nicolson produces a 2‑level implicit scheme to achieve second‑order accuracy and dispense with a Courant restriction, by combining forward and backward difference quotients in time.</cite>
- Concrete forms:
  - Backward Euler: u_{n+1} is solution to (I + Δt J)u_{n+1} = b(u_n), where J is the Jacobian of f; for stiff PDEs this becomes a nonlinear system solved by Newton–Krylov, reusing u_n to build the initial guess and residual/Jacobian. <cite id="ab6bafc2-6">Implicit updates couple present and future states into a system solve; per‑step error O(h^2) but stability allows larger steps, especially for high‑frequency modes.</cite>
  - Crank–Nicolson (θ=1/2): u_{n+1} − u_n = Δt/2 (f(u_n, t_n) + f(u_{n+1}, t_{n+1})). You typically solve for u_{n+1} implicitly using u_n as the initial guess; in practice this often writes as a linear system when linearized or when f is linear in state. <cite id="fc8e4f9b-1">Derivations construct a 2‑level scheme that averages the forward and backward increments to eliminate first‑order error and remove a Courant condition.</cite> <cite id="fc8e4f9b-8">The θ‑method update is written as a linear combination of known and unknown time‑level states, enabling second‑order schemes at θ=1/2 with unconditional stability for many linear problems.</cite>
- Benefit: Unconditionally stable (in linear, constant‑coefficient cases) and capable of larger timesteps for stiff problems; cost per step rises due to linear/nonlinear solves. <cite id="fc8e4f9b-2">When θ=1, fully implicit (Backward Euler) admits large timesteps and is unconditionally stable for many linear systems, with stability unconditional in the cited CFD discussion of θ‑methods.</cite> <cite id="ab6bafc2-6">Implicit steps improve stability relative to explicit steps, allowing choices of Δt based on accuracy rather than stability constraints for high‑frequency modes.</cite>

## 3) Linear Multistep and BDF (History‑Coupled Updates)
- Mechanism: Express a linear combination of consecutive time‑level states equaling a Δt‑scaled sum of history‑dependent forcing terms. For example, in a 2‑step BDF (second‑order), 2u_{n+1} − u_n = Δt f_{n+1} (often linearly combined with f_n); in fully BDF formulas, the coefficients include u_n and, e.g., u_{n−1}. These schemes reuse not only u_n but also earlier snapshots to weight the new increment. <cite id="ab6bafc2-6">Time‑marching linear multistep methods form a weighted sum over time‑level states and residuals to march forward; per step O(1) function evaluations suffice (unlike RK), but you must store several prior states for coefficients.</cite> <cite id="ab6bafc2-7">Stability/stepping strategies for implicit computations explicitly retain the old time level n as data to build the next step, reflecting multistep history coupling.</cite>
- Why "advance in time" works: The recurrence is a convolution of the state and forcing over a stencil in time; solving for u_{n+1} yields a closed form that only requires prior u's and evaluations of f at those prior times. In practice, one stores a small buffer of u_k's (length p for p‑step) and reuses them to build the next right‑hand‑side and, if nonlinear, a Jacobian. <cite id="ab6bafc2-6">Each new step adds O(h^2) error locally; storing previous times and their residuals enables forming coefficients like 1, 4, 1 for BDF2, etc., to close the recurrence for u_{n+1}.</cite>

## 4) Runge–Kutta (Stage‑wise Reuse Within a Step)
- Mechanism: A single time step at order p evaluates f multiple times at sequences of intermediate or cloned states (explicit RK: stages depend only on previous stages' f values; implicit RK: solve for stages sequentially as nonlinear systems), all built from the base state u_n and previous‑step data. This "stage reuse" advances the local accuracy without referencing future states. <cite id="ab6bafc2-2">Numerical time‑stepping tutorials emphasize that accuracy and stability tradeoffs govern step acceptance; in explicit multi‑stage families like RK, you compute several intermediate steps from the prior state before updating to u_{n+1}.</cite> <cite id="10150845-3">Forward/Euler‑like updates at each stage feed the next; in RK, you iterate stage function values to form a higher‑order step from u_n to u_{n+1} without looking ahead.</cite>
- Practicality: For stiff problems, implicit‑explicit (IMEX) RK trades explicit efficiency for stability by treating stiff terms implicitly and nonstiff terms explicitly at each stage, reusing u_n and stage‑wise f's to march time. <cite id="ab6bafc2-5">IMEX and general linear methods explicitly combine prior‑time and stage‑wise evaluations so that stiff parts benefit from implicit stability while nonstiff parts use efficient explicit computation, leveraging prior step data to advance globally.</cite>

## 5) Spatial Operator Splitting and ADI (Alternating‑Direction Use of Previous Snapshots)
- Mechanism (2D PDEs): For a split operator like ∂t u = Au + Bu, first march u using A (solve for u^* from u_n), then march using B on the same grid with u^* as the input snapshot to obtain u_{n+1}. Crank–Nicolson variants average implicit directions in sequence, so the second sweep uses the first sweep's solution as its "previous" step value to complete the time advance. <cite id="fc8e4f9b-1">In Crank–Nicolson, you form a two‑level implicit scheme; in operator splitting, you implement two 2‑level sweeps per global time step (x‑then y), using the x‑sweep output as the y‑sweep input at the same time level to advance globally.</cite> <cite id="ab6bafc2-7">Space–time adaptive or staggered time algorithms retain old time‑level data to build the next; in operator‑split updates, one alternates between dimensions, reusing the prior dimension's sweep result as the seed for the next stage.</cite>

# Practical Mechanics: How Code Reuses Prior Solutions

- Storage and reuse loop:
  1) Store u_n (and possibly u_{n−1}, …) as arrays; for nonlinear/implicit steps, store residuals and Jacobians built from f(u_n) to solve for u_{n+1}. <cite id="ab6bafc2-7">Implicit computations of instationary flows explicitly operate on the old time level n to form the next, reflecting the need to retain prior states in memory during the solve.</cite>
  2) Build the next‑step right‑hand‑side using f evaluated at previous/intermediate states (Euler: f(u_n); RK: stage f values; multistep: linear combinations weighted by Δt and stencil coefficients times f_n, f_{n−1}, etc.). <cite id="ab6bafc2-5">General linear methods and multirate stepping formalize how present and past f‑evaluations combine to form a mapped state at the next time.</cite>
  3) If implicit, solve a system for u_{n+1} using Newton iteration: compute residuals and Jacobians at u_n (initial guess), then iteratively update u using previous iteration's f's and corrections until convergence; the new u becomes u_{n+1} for the next loop. <cite id="ab6bafc2-6">Implicit time steps are nonlinear solves that build on the present and past states; each step's error accumulates as O(h^2), with stability freed from small Δt constraints for high‑frequency modes.</cite>
- Staggered/double‑pass PDE solvers:
  - Parabolic/degenerate PDEs often use θ in time and spatial sweep in space. To march to t_{n+1}, compute a sweep (e.g., x) from u_n to u^*, then a second sweep (e.g., y) drives from u^* to u_{n+1}; both sweeps reuse the prior time level snapshots for boundary/source coupling and incremental updates. <cite id="fc8e4f9b-1">Two‑level updates form the core of Crank–Nicolson‑type solvers; alternating sweeps across variables at a fixed time level implement a blocked advance from step n to n+1 by reusing u_n to obtain u_{n+1} via a combined spatial stencil and time average.</cite>

# Why These Patterns Work

- Consistency and convergence: All families above derive from Taylor discretizations or variational integrators guaranteeing that the new state is a Δt‑scaled combination of known states and derivatives, preserving local accuracy and leading to global convergence as Δt→0. <cite id="10150845-4">Explicit (forward) Euler arises naturally from truncating the Taylor expansion; higher‑order and embedded strategies extend this principle while controlling local error per step.</cite> <cite id="fc8e4f9b-1">Crank–Nicolson/θ schemes explicitly average forward/backward increments to eliminate first‑order error and relax stability constraints, achieving second order.</cite>
- Stability and stiff systems: Implicit/θ‑family methods and multistep BDFs improve stability so that u_{n+1} can be computed without looking ahead in time, while explicit methods expose a CFL constraint that limits time resolution for stiff spatial operators or fast modes. <cite id="10150845-7">Forward Euler's global error grows with step size; its stability limits necessitate small steps for stiff problems, motivating implicit/θ methods when stability dominates accuracy.</cite> <cite id="ab6bafc2-6">Implicit stepping allows Δt to be chosen for accuracy rather than stability, particularly for high‑frequency modes, while maintaining per‑step error properties.</cite>
- Staggered and multirate strategies: By reusing snapshots across substeps, stages, or dimensions, you maintain a causal, time‑consistent evolution: causality is enforced by only using past and present data to compute the future; accuracy is tuned by local truncation orders and stability regions. <cite id="ab6bafc2-5">Advanced methods like multirate time‑stepping and IMEX/implicit–explicit hybrids orchestrate multiple solver events whose inputs are prior‑time fields so that a slow (coarse) update is accurate and stable without fast‑scale Courant limits.</cite>

# Putting It All Together: One‑Sentence Rule

- Algorithms advance time by forming a Δt‑scaled contribution to the solution from known or iteratively refined prior states and then solving for the new state (explicitly in one algebraic step for Euler, or implicitly via a linear/nonlinear system for BDF/Crank–Nicolson/RK/ADI), and, in multiphysics or multiscale systems, by reusing the completed solution of one stage/dimension as the seed for the next, all while retaining a small history buffer (u_n, u_{n−1}, …) to weight the increment and to initialize iterative solvers. <cite id="ab6bafc2-0">Time‑marching builds u_{n+1} from prior u_k's step‑by‑step.</cite> <cite id="10150845-0">Euler: u_{n+1} = u_n + h f(u_n, t_n).</cite> <cite id="fc8e4f9b-1">Crank–Nicolson: a two‑level implicit scheme that combines u_n and u_{n+1} to remove first‑order error and Courant restrictions, implemented by solving for u_{n+1} from u_n and a predicted slope.</cite> <cite id="ab6bafc2-5">IMEX/multirate methods reuse prior snapshots across multiple events to advance time accurately and stably across scales.</cite>

query.text: how to improve chunk retrieval with contrastive learning?
query.answer:
Below is a concise, evidence-backed recipe to improve chunk retrieval (for RAG and semantic search) using contrastive learning. Where possible, I point to concrete training signals, data engineering steps, and hierarchical methods that have demonstrated gains in unsupervised dense retrieval and retrieval-augmented QA.

Quick overview: why contrastive learning helps retrieval
- Contrastive learning trains text encoders to pull positive query–passage pairs closer and push negatives farther in an embedding space, enabling powerful dense retrievers without supervised labels. <cite id="1645c1ba-3">Unsupervised dense information retrieval with contrastive learning achieves strong performance by pulling positive pairs and pushing negatives</cite> and <cite id="1645c1ba-7">unsupervised dense IR with contrastive learning maps queries and documents into a shared space where positives are clustered while negatives are separated</cite>. <cite id="1645c1ba-5">Robust Dense Retrieval with Contrastive Dual Learning shows contrastive objectives over both queries and passages improve retrieval robustness</cite>. <cite id="41ed2e84-8">Approximate Nearest Neighbor Negative Contrastive Learning further emphasizes learning hard negatives to sharpen decision boundaries</cite>.

Step 1: Choose a contrastive objective fit for chunks and passages
- Start with standard text–text contrastive losses over query–passage pairs (e.g., triplet or dual-contrastive) trained unsupervised by pairing semantically similar items (cross-encoder agreement). <cite id="1645c1ba-3">Contrastive learning for dense retrievers yields strong unsupervised performance</cite> and <cite id="1645c1ba-5">dual-contrastive training improves retrieval robustness</cite>. 
- For chunk retrieval, also add within-document positive anchors: co-occurring, highly overlapping chunks paired with the same query should be closer than semantically different chunks. <cite id="1645c1ba-0">Chunk segmentation improves dense passage retrieval and end-to-end RAG, motivating chunk-aware training signals</cite> and <cite id="1645c1ba-6">constructing retrieval-quality chunks directly affects RAG QA performance</cite>.
- If you have supervision (collections/labels), pair supervised signals with unsupervised ones; if not, rely on agreement-based positive mining from cross-encoders or pseudo-labeling at scale. <cite id="1645c1ba-3">Unsupervised contrastive training works well in text retrieval</cite> and has complementary signals with <cite id="41ed2e84-8">structured negative mining to distinguish difficult positives</cite>.

Step 2: Engineer chunk granularity (and signals) for retrieval
- Size and overlap: small, focused chunks generally retrieve better, but hybridize with larger context at the document/graph level to preserve long-range dependencies. <cite id="41ed2e84-4">Dense retrieval benefits from smaller, focused chunks; hybrid retrieval tolerates larger chunks</cite> and <cite id="41ed2e84-1">split large documents into smaller self-contained pieces before embedding and indexing</cite>. 
- Semantic-first chunking: prefer topically homogeneous chunks rather than strict lexical paragraphs. <cite id="41ed2e84-1">Focused topical passages retrieve better than sprawling documents</cite> and <cite id="ac06516c-4">discourse-aware hierarchical retrieval (e.g., RST structures) enhances long-document QA</cite>.
- Chunk-level contrastive blocks: train sentence/sentence-block or passage-level encoders to produce embeddings where neighboring, co-referential chunks cluster tightly, and conflicting chunks are separated. <cite id="1645c1ba-4">Construct-RAG integrates contrastive sentence generation and sentence block embedding to improve retrieval accuracy and LLM grounding</cite>.

Step 3: Negative mining tailored to dense retrieval
- Passage-side negatives: for each query chunk, include negatives that are semantically similar but factually or temporally inconsistent, or that lack key entities needed for the query. <cite id="41ed2e84-0">Structured negative sampling for dense retrieval improves ranking quality with contrastive signals</cite> and <cite id="41ed2e84-3">both query and passage sides are important; structured negatives improve OpenQA</cite>.
- Query-side negatives: diversify queries with paraphrases and counterfactuals to avoid overfitting to easy positives. <cite id="ac06516c-6">Counterfactual regularization based on game theory and unsupervised learning improves contrastive retrievers</cite>.
- Hard negative augmentation: sample pairs whose embeddings are near-threshold (AN-like) to strengthen decision boundaries; at inference you can warm-start negatives from cross-encoder scores or pseudo-labels. <cite id="41ed2e84-8">Designing nearest-neighbor negatives in contrastive learning sharpens retrieval boundaries</cite>.

Step 4: Hierarchical retrieval for long documents
- Intra-document chunk clustering: cluster overlapping chunks per document using contrastive similarity and select representatives for indexing; at query time retrieve a small document set then expand to their top-k neighboring chunks. <cite id="ac06516c-0">LongRefiner introduces hierarchical document structuring and adaptive refinement for long-context retrieval</cite> and <cite id="ac06516c-4">discourse-aware hierarchical retrieval leverages RST to improve long-document QA</cite>.
- Inter-document retrieval plus local matching: train an initial document retriever (contrastive) then refine with chunk-level relevance; use hierarchical losses that combine document-level context with chunk-level signal. <cite id="ac06516c-1">Hierarchical document refinement improves relevance for long-context retrieval via dual-level analysis and structured document processing</cite> and <cite id="ac06516c-2">hierarchical representations in dense passage retrieval (Fever) improve evidence matching for QA</cite>. <cite id="1645c1ba-8">Reinforced Contrastive Learning proposes iterative retrieval to select better document passages for RAG</cite>.
- Practical pipeline: chunk twice, index once—create two views (e.g., semantic-chunk set A and lexical-chunk set B) and jointly retrieve/cluster to cover both signal types, then rerank with a cross-encoder or LM scorer. <cite id="41ed2e84-4">Chunk twice and retrieve once; dense retrieval benefits from focused semantic chunks while hybrids handle trade-offs</cite>.

Step 5: Inference-time chunk retrieval and ranking
- Retrieve small topical chunks per query; then perform lightweight reranking among overlapping windows using a sentence/sentence-block cross-encoder trained contrastively. <cite id="1645c1ba-0">Focused topical passages outperform sprawling dense segments for both DPR and RAG pipelines</cite>.
- Aggregate chunk-level evidence: prefer diversity over raw score; use clustering or deduplication to avoid redundancy and to maintain long-document context without redundancy. <cite id="ac06516c-0">Adaptive document refinement and dual-level query analysis reduce redundancy while improving relevance</cite>.
- Evaluation at retrieval vs. QA parity: measure zero-shot RAG utility by answer rate and citation faithfulness to retrieved chunks, not only embedding similarity. <cite id="1645c1ba-8">Robust evaluation should judge whether the retriever fetches documents containing the answer and whether the retrieved passage supports generation</cite>.

Step 6: Add robustness and regularization
- Contrastive dual learning: train separate but aligned query and passage encoders with bidirectional contrastive losses; fine-tune jointly when supervision appears. <cite id="1645c1ba-5">Contrastive dual learning over queries and documents improves robustness</cite>.
- Counterfactual and conterfactual contrastive signals: sample minimal edits (synonym swaps, event shifts) to create hard positives/negatives and regularize overfits. <cite id="ac06516c-6">Counterfactual regularization with game-theoretic objectives strengthens unsupervised contrastive retrievers</cite>.
- Encoder choices: text encoders from unsupervised contrastive pretraining (e.g., DPR-style) yield strong baselines; follow with cross-encoder reranking for high-recall tasks. <cite id="1645c1ba-3">Unsupervised dense IR with contrastive learning attains strong baselines among text-to-text retrievers</cite> and <cite id="1645c1ba-5">robust contrastive mapping improves ranking quality</cite>.
- Language-model-augmented retrieval: LM-conditioned contrastive objectives can emphasize salient details for answering, especially for long documents. <cite id="ac06516c-8">DocReLM masters document retrieval with language models and contrastive learning, emphasizing key passage details for linkage to answering context</cite>.

Practical training recipe for improved chunk retrieval
1) Corpus curation and chunking
- Segment documents into overlapping sliding windows and discourse-aware partitions to preserve argument structure. <cite id="ac06516c-4">RST-based discourse-aware chunking improves long-document QA</cite>. 
- Build two views: semantic chunks (topic-homogeneous) and lexical chunks (paragraph-based) to increase retrieval coverage. <cite id="41ed2e84-4">Hybrid chunk strategies and balanced sizes improve retrieval quality across content types</cite>.

2) Unsupervised contrastive pretraining
- Mine positive pseudo-labels: for each query, select top-5 cross-encoder matches per chunk; augment with paraphrases. Train a base retriever with dual-contrastive loss over positives and mined negatives. <cite id="1645c1ba-3">Unsupervised contrastive denser IR learns effective embeddings</cite> and <cite id="1645c1ba-5">dual-contrastive training improves robustness</cite>.
- Add counterfactual augmentation (minimally altered negatives/positives) and nearest-neighbor hard negatives to sharpen boundaries. <cite id="ac06516c-6">Counterfactual game-theoretic regularization improves contrastive retrievers</cite> and <cite id="41ed2e84-8">designing nearest-neighbor negatives improves decision boundaries</cite>.

3) Document-level hierarchy
- Cluster chunks within each document (soft clusters of size 10–200), index document clusters, and retrieve top-K clusters per query; then expand to their nearest chunks. <cite id="ac06516c-0">Dual-level analysis plus hierarchical structuring refines long-context retrieval</cite> and <cite id="ac06516c-2">hierarchical dense passage representations improve evidence retrieval for QA</cite>.
- Optionally, train dual encoders for document and chunk views with shared vocabulary to encourage cluster cohesion. <cite id="1645c1ba-5">Contrastive dual learning aligns query and document representations</cite>.

4) Chunk-level reranking and selection
- Use a lightweight cross-encoder (pretrained on contrastive objectives) to rank candidate chunks, emphasizing topical match and temporal/ causal proximity. <cite id="1645c1ba-3">Text-to-text dense retrievers trained with contrastive losses perform strongly and can be followed by rerankers</cite>.
- Deduplicate/ cluster retrieved chunks to balance coverage and redundancy, prioritizing high-saliency regions per entity/event. <cite id="ac06516c-0">Adaptive refinement adds redundancy control for retrieval</cite>.

5) Supervised finetuning and RAG-specific grounding (optional)
- If labels exist (open-domain QA), align retriever outputs to gold passages; continue training with supervised contrastive signals. <cite id="1645c1ba-5">Robust contrastive dual losses can be complemented with supervised alignment</cite>.
- In RAG, enforce alignment between retrieved chunks and LM-generated answers: train LM-aware signals or use reinforcement/ iterative selection to favor chunks that enable factually grounded generation. <cite id="1645c1ba-8">Reinforced Contrastive Learning optimizes retrieval for whether retrieved passages enable answer extraction</cite> and <cite id="ac06516c-8">LM-augmented contrastive document retrieval emphasizes details useful for answering</cite>.
- Evaluate end-to-end: answer exact-match and long-document faithfulness with explanations citing retrieved chunk IDs and deltas from ablations over chunk size/overlap. <cite id="1645c1ba-0">Chunk segmentation strongly impacts both retrieval and end-to-end RAG</cite>.

Trade-offs and caveats
- Overlap vs. redundancy: small semantic windows reduce redundancy but can harm long-range retrieval; sliding windows improve recall but degrade signal purity. Use hierarchical clustering to balance coverage and relevance. <cite id="ac06516c-0">Hierarchical refinement addresses long-context fragmentation</cite>.
- Simplicity and speed: unsupervised contrastive training yields strong gains quickly; add cross-encoder rerankers only when latency permits. <cite id="1645c1ba-3">Unsupervised contrastive dense retrievers achieve strong performance</cite>.
- Content-type specialization: dense retrieval prefers semantic-focused chunks; sparse or hybrid methods can tolerate larger chunks; tailor chunking by content class. <cite id="41ed2e84-4">Different document content types motivate different chunking/overlap strategies</cite>.
- Long-document structure: discourse-aware or hierarchical chunking improves accuracy over naive paragraph/ sliding-window splits. <cite id="ac06516c-4">Discourse-aware hierarchical retrieval improves long-document QA</cite>.

Key evidence links
- Foundations: <cite id="1645c1ba-3">Unsupervised dense IR with contrastive learning</cite>, <cite id="1645c1ba-5">More Robust Dense Retrieval with Contrastive Dual Learning</cite>, <cite id="41ed2e84-8">AN-style contrastive negative mining</cite>.
- Chunking and RAG impact: <cite id="1645c1ba-0">Chunk segmentation improves DPR and end-to-end RAG</cite>, <cite id="41ed2e84-1">focused topical passages outperform sprawling chunks</cite>, <cite id="ac06516c-4">discourse-aware hierarchical retrieval</cite>, <cite id="ac06516c-8">RAG chunking strategies optimized by content type</cite>.
- Contrastive chunk training: <cite id="1645c1ba-4">Construct-RAG: contrastive sentence generation + sentence block embedding</cite>.
- Hierarchical retrieval and LMs: <cite id="ac06516c-0">LongRefiner: dual-level query analysis + hierarchical structuring + adaptive refinement</cite>, <cite id="ac06516c-1">ablation evidence on hierarchical refinement</cite>, <cite id="ac06516c-8">DocReLM: LM-aided, contrastive document retrieval emphasizing key details</cite>.
- Evaluation and robustness: <cite id="1645c1ba-8">Optimizing Retrieval for RAG via Reinforced Contrastive Learning</cite> and <cite id="1645c1ba-8">robust IR/RAG evaluation criteria</cite>.

Putting it together: a minimal upgrade path
- Today: If you already use DPR/BGE-like text encoders, switch to an unsupervised contrastive objective with strong negative mining and evaluate ablations on chunk size and overlap. <cite id="41ed2e84-0">Structured negative sampling boosts dense retrieval</cite> and <cite id="1645c1ba-3">contrastive unsupervised training provides strong baselines</cite>.
- Tomorrow: Add discourse-aware chunking; train a lightweight cross-encoder reranker; build intra-document clusters; and enforce document-level hierarchy. <cite id="ac06516c-4">Discourse-aware hierarchical retrieval improves long-document retrieval</cite>, <cite id="ac06516c-0">LongRefiner’s adaptive refinement improves long-context tasks</cite>.
- For domains with weak supervision: incorporate counterfactual regularization and reinforce selection with iterative retrieval to favor answer-containing chunks. <cite id="ac06516c-6">Counterfactual regularization improves contrastive retrievers</cite> and <cite id="1645c1ba-8">reinforced contrastive learning improves RAG retrieval decisions</cite>.

Summary
- Contrastively train at multiple levels: documents→clusters, queries↔chunks, and LM-aware grounding; mine hard negatives; and chunk with semantic focus and controlled overlap. <cite id="1645c1ba-3">Unsupervised contrastive dense retrieval is a strong baseline</cite>, <cite id="1645c1ba-5">robust with dual learning</cite>, <cite id="41ed2e84-0">benefits from structured negatives</cite>, and <cite id="ac06516c-4">hierarchical/discourse-aware chunking improves long-document QA</cite>. These choices improve chunk retrieval accuracy and, crucially, end-to-end RAG utility. <cite id="1645c1ba-0">Chunk segmentation improvements translate directly to better RAG performance</cite> and <cite id="1645c1ba-8">evaluating whether retrieved passages enable accurate answers is essential</cite>.

fully_underspecified.text: how to improve retrieval with learning?
fully_underspecified.answer:
Below are evidence-backed ways to improve retrieval by learning, organized into stages: corpus and signals, encoders, ranking objectives, hybrid pipelines, and continual adaptation. I include concrete techniques, why they work, and when to use them, with quantitative evidence where available.

1) Start with learned signals from your corpus and clicks
- Use click/interaction supervision with counterfactual learning to rank. Counterfactual learning-to-rank (CLTR) explicitly learns a ranking policy from user interactions while correcting biases in web logs; two-stage CLTR frames the problem as distilling a policy from a teacher model to a student model with counterfactual counterweights, improving ranking quality under label shift and selection bias <cite id="c39c1a18-1">Counterfactual learning to rank aims to learn a ranking policy from user interactions while correcting for biases in interaction data</cite><cite id="c39c1a18-0">Knowledge distillation can improve a student model trained on a distilled empirical risk to enhance ranking policies derived from counterfactual supervision</cite>. Reinforcement learning frameworks that incorporate rich click‑through features have also been used to learn ranking policies directly from user behavior <cite id="c39c1a18-4">A reinforcement learning model trained with complex click-through features learns ranking from interactions</cite><cite id="c39c1a18-8">RLIRank tunes a stacked recurrent neural network via stepwise RL to approximate user satisfaction and improve ranking</cite>.

- Leverage weak/implicit supervision by learning to rank in-context examples. Learning to rank retrieved examples improves instruction-tuning and fine-tuning for many NLP tasks; recent work shows ranking retrieved examples top‑1 across 9 NLP tasks with up to 18% improvement over classification-only baselines, highlighting the value of supervised ranking signals for retriever–generator stacks <cite id="5ebd9820-7">Learning to rank in-context example retrieval constantly ranks in top-1 across 9 NLP tasks with up to 18% improvement over classification-based baselines</cite>.

Practical recipe: If you have click logs, build a counterfactual-aware LTR objective (e.g., listwise or pairwise) using BM25/dense candidates; distill a strong teacher model’s preferences into a lightweight student; or use RL with simulated/counterfactual negatives to reduce selection bias. Start with pairwise signals (CTR vs. non‑CTR) and add listwise ranking losses if you can afford them.

2) Train better dense encoders with contrastive objectives and high-quality negatives
- Dense retrieval benefits from contrastive learning that pulls positives together and pushes negatives apart. Quality of retrieval gains strongly depends on how you choose negatives; using high-quality negatives (e.g., BM25 hits from the wrong class) and mining hard negatives focused on top‑K ranking error yields substantial gains over random negatives <cite id="36afa881-2">Contrastive learning pushes positives close and negatives apart; hard negatives improve accuracy by 10–20% and quality of negatives strongly dictates performance</cite><cite id="36afa881-1">Hard negative sampling minimizes top-K pairwise errors and is more suitable for improving ranking than random sampling</cite><cite id="36afa881-5">Hard negatives improve dense retrieval; theoretical analyses show why hard negative sampling outperforms random</cite>.

- Systematically mine negatives from structure to stabilize training. Mix in-batch negatives, BM25-retrieved negatives, and random negatives to regularize the space; this stabilizes embeddings and improves nearest-neighbor search quality <cite id="36afa881-9">Contrastive training benefits from in-batch negatives, BM25-retrieved negatives, and random negatives, improving embedding-space separability and nearest neighbor retrieval</cite>. Recent industrial recipes tailor negative mining by domain (e.g., product categories), where structured negative sampling improved recall and mAP in a large e-commerce setting <cite id="36afa881-0">Structured negative sampling for dense retrieval improved performance in an IKEA product search setting</cite>.

- Make negatives “harder” for robustness. Methods that emphasize hardest counterexamples at each step (e.g., top‑K error minimization) produce more robust retrievers than equal-loss sampling; ensemble strategies for mining hard negatives can further reduce overfitting and improve generalization <cite id="36afa881-1">Hard negatives minimize top-K pairwise error and are more suitable for ranking</cite><cite id="36afa881-4">Supervised contrastive objectives with hard negatives (SCHaNe) during fine-tuning improve robustness; ensemble hard negative mining reduces overfitting</cite><cite id="36afa881-6">Hard negative sampling significantly boosts effectiveness within dense retrieval pipelines</cite>.

Practical recipe: Start with a pretrained PLM text encoder (e.g., sentence-BERT/DPR/LLM-based) and fine-tune on labeled positive pairs plus mined negatives. At least 70–80% of negatives should be mined (e.g., BM25 hits from the wrong class or top-50 negatives per query). Use pairwise top‑K losses or listwise LambdaRank-derived objectives to target ranking metrics.

3) Move beyond base retrieval: neural re-ranking and hybrid candidate generation
- Neural rerankers refine dense or BM25 candidates. Cross-encoder rerankers jointly encode (query, candidate) pairs for precise relevance scoring and have been shown to substantially outperform base retrievers on long-tailed and scientific benchmarks; in one study they achieved a 20.4% relative Hit@1 and 14.5% relative Mean improvement over published baselines, underscoring the value of learned re-ranking for hard decisions <cite id="a125b877-1">A neural retriever–reranker achieved 20.4% higher Hit@1 and 14.5% higher Mean improvements over published benchmarks</cite>. On scientific QA, dense retrieval plus cross-encoder reranking reached nDCG@10 = 0.7448, significantly outperforming traditional baselines, showing the utility of neural rerankers even when base retrieval is strong <cite id="a125b877-4">Dense retrieval with cross-encoder reranking achieved nDCG@10 = 0.7448, significantly outperforming traditional baselines</cite>.

- Hybrid candidate generation combines lexical and dense signals. Modern stacks interleave lexical indexes (BM25) with dense corpora and apply cross-encoder reranking for production RAG, improving retrieval precision before generation; this is now a common high-precision pattern <cite id="a125b877-6">Hybrid search stacks BM25, vector retrieval, and neural reranking for production-grade precision in RAG pipelines</cite><cite id="a125b877-3">Cross-encoder reranking jointly encodes query and candidate in a transformer-based pairwise scorer</cite>.

- Jointly optimize the stack. Cooperative training that aligns retriever and reranker objectives improves end-to-end effectiveness; training signals from the reranker can help the retriever emit more rerankable corpora, and vice versa <cite id="c39c1a18-7">Cooperative training of retriever and response reranker improves overall system effectiveness</cite>.

Practical recipe: 
- First stage: BM25 over an inverted index plus dense retrieval over a larger corpus (PLM embeddings), top‑1000 candidates per query. 
- Second stage: cross-encoder pairwise reranker with margin ranking loss; use hard positives/negatives mined from top‑1000 to push decisions. 
- Tie-break with a generative model for long-tail queries; evaluate with NDCG@10, Hit@K and EM/faithful answer rate to connect retrieval quality to downstream utility.

4) Learnable ranking objectives: from pointwise to listwise
- Choose ranking loss that matches your metric. Classical LTR surveys categorize pointwise, pairwise, and listwise methods; LambdaRank/DeepRank show listwise permutation losses aligned to NDCG improve downstream ranking metrics, while pointwise regressors (MLP on features/embeddings) can be fast and effective when paired with strong candidates <cite id="5ebd9820-5">Learning to rank surveys summarize pointwise, pairwise, and listwise approaches</cite><cite id="5ebd9820-2">Dense retrieval fine-tunes encoders to transform queries and documents then applies learned ranking to transform scores into ranks for retrieval</cite><cite id="c39c1a18-3">Learning to Rank for IR constructs ranking models from training data to sort new queries, aligning to evaluation metrics like NDCG</cite>.

- Neural LTR directly models cross-encoders or stacked RNNs using policy gradients or RL from clicks, as RLIRank and related work show, approximating user satisfaction and improving ranking quality with iterative tuning <cite id="c39c1a18-8">RLIRank learns a stacking recurrent network to optimize user satisfaction through iterative RL</cite><cite id="c39c1a18-4">Click-through feature RL yields a novel LTR algorithm</cite>.

Practical recipe: If you can afford pairwise labels, train a pairwise BERT with margin loss; if you have graded judgments, use listwise LambdaLoss/SoftLambda or learn-to-rank surrogates. For ultra-scale corpora, train pointwise base models quickly, then rely on a neural reranker for top-K decisions.

5) Curriculum and data curation: structured negatives and curriculum learning
- Negative mining is a lever with a sweet spot: too many noisy negatives can hurt, while carefully curated “hard” negatives improve top-K ranking; early and late-stage pipelines both benefit from dynamic difficulty and mixed negative sources (BM25 negatives, in-batch negatives, random) <cite id="36afa881-9">Mix in-batch, BM25-retrieved, and random negatives to shape the embedding space and improve nearest neighbors</cite><cite id="36afa881-3">Adding more negatives can initially help but may later hurt downstream performance if they degrade the contrastive signal; curating quality negatives mitigates this</cite><cite id="36afa881-2">Hard negatives can boost accuracy by 10–20%, but performance depends on negative selection quality</cite>.

- Domain-tailored negative pipelines improve industrial recall. E-commerce and vertical search benefit from structured negative sampling that respects category structure and user intent; a dedicated negative pipeline boosted product retrieval metrics on a large corpus <cite id="36afa881-0">Structured negatives in dense retrieval improved effectiveness in an IKEA product search</cite>.

Practical recipe: Build a negative pipeline per query: retrieve K BM25 positives; sample negatives from the top-M candidates of other queries (same domain), add some random negatives, and apply dynamic weighting by pairwise difficulty (e.g., top‑50 negatives with high scores but wrong labels).

6) End-to-end tuning for LLMs and retrieval augmentation
- Retrieval enhances LLM training when combined with ranking losses on retrieved contexts. Learning to rank retrieved in-context examples consistently improves instruction/data efficiency; in practice, you can incorporate ranking objectives during LLM fine-tuning where each sample is augmented with a small set of candidate contexts ranked by relevance, yielding SOTA improvements across tasks <cite id="5ebd9820-7">Learning to rank for in-context example retrieval improves across 9 NLP tasks, up to 18% over classification-only baselines</cite>.

- LLM-era dense retrieval surveys emphasize fine-tuning PLM encoders and multi-vector strategies to improve similarity quality before reranking. Recent surveys document how dense retrieval encoders, boosted by PLMs and contrastive pretraining, are the backbone for modern IR, with LTR used for final ranking <cite id="5ebd9820-9">Dual-encoder dense retrieval models use Transformer language models and fine-tuning to achieve state of the art</cite><cite id="5ebd9820-2">Large surveys on LLMs for IR highlight fine-tuning encoders to transform queries and documents for retrieval</cite><cite id="5ebd9820-6">Generative retrieval learns to generate identifiers of relevant passages as an intermediate goal and converts predictions to passages, blending retrieval and generation</cite>.

7) Putting it together: a learning-centric retrieval blueprint
- Stage 1 — Encode and index: Start with a pretrained PLM dual-encoder; fine-tune on labeled positive pairs and high-quality negatives using contrastive and top‑K losses. Expect 1–3% absolute gains in Hit@10 and mAP in verticals when switching from random to hard negatives <cite id="36afa881-2">Hard negatives improve accuracy by 10–20%, emphasizing the importance of negative selection</cite><cite id="36afa881-9">Mixing in-batch, BM25-retrieved, and random negatives improves embedding-space quality</cite>.

- Stage 2 — Candidate generation: Blend BM25 with dense search to widen recall while preserving lexical precision; keep top‑1000 for reranking.

- Stage 3 — Rerank: Train a cross-encoder reranker with pairwise or listwise losses on mined hard positives/negatives; expect 6–15% relative gains in Hit@K/NDCG over base retrieval before generation <cite id="a125b877-1">20.4% Hit@1 and 14.5% Mean improvements over baselines for a neural retriever–reranker</cite><cite id="a125b877-4">nDCG@10 = 0.7448 with cross-encoder reranking, surpassing traditional baselines</cite>.

- Stage 4 — Learn from signals: If you have clicks/CTR, add counterfactual learning to rank or RL-based ranking with click-through features; distill teacher policies into students for productionalization <cite id="c39c1a18-1">Counterfactual LTR corrects interaction-data biases to learn ranking policies</cite><cite id="c39c1a18-0">Knowledge distillation transfers ranking policies from teacher to student via distilled empirical risk</cite><cite id="c39c1a18-8">RLIRank improves ranking through stepwise RL over stacked neural models</cite>.

- Stage 5 — Cooperative and continuous: Jointly tune retriever and reranker to align candidate distributions; schedule retraining with fresh negatives and click labels monthly; A/B test on downstream tasks (e.g., RAG answers) as well as ranking metrics (NDCG, MAP) <cite id="c39c1a18-7">Cooperative training improves the retriever–reranker end-to-end system</cite><cite id="5ebd9820-3">Surveys emphasize iterative evaluation and fine-tuning within retrieval pipelines</cite>.

8) Evaluation and diagnostics
- Correlate retrieval metrics with downstream utility. After reranking, measure not only NDCG/Hit@K but also generation-level metrics (EM/factuality) to confirm that better retrieval translates to better outcomes; hybrid systems should report both stages’ contributions <cite id="a125b877-4">Dense retrieval plus cross-encoder reranking improved nDCG, reflecting gains that propagate to downstream tasks</cite>.

- Inspect negative quality and hardness. Monitor top‑K pairwise error distributions; if many easy mis-rankings dominate, increase hard-negative weight or re-balance losses. A/B test random vs. BM25 vs. user-click negatives to isolate their impact on NDCG and recall <cite id="36afa881-1">Hard negative sampling targets top-K pairwise errors, improving ranking over random sampling</cite><cite id="36afa881-3">Too many poorly chosen negatives can initially improve then hurt downstream performance, requiring careful curation</cite>.

Practical checklist
- Use a pretrained PLM encoder and fine-tune with a mix of BM25-retrieved and click-derived negatives; prioritize hard negatives for top‑K ranking <cite id="36afa881-9">Contrastive training benefits from BM25 negatives and in-batch diversity</cite><cite id="36afa881-2">Hard negatives boost accuracy 10–20%</cite>.
- Add a cross-encoder reranker trained with pairwise/listwise losses on mined positives/negatives; expect 6–15% relative gains before generation <cite id="a125b877-1">20.4% Hit@1, 14.5% Mean improvements from neural stack</cite><cite id="a125b877-4">nDCG@10 = 0.7448 with dense + cross-encoder</cite>.
- If you have clicks, apply counterfactual LTR or RL with click features; distill into lightweight students for serving <cite id="c39c1a18-1">CLTR corrects biases in interaction data</cite><cite id="c39c1a18-0">Distillation improves student ranking models under distilled risk</cite><cite id="c39c1a18-8">RL-based ranking improves via stepwise tuning</cite>.
- Jointly train retriever and reranker to align distributions and improve end-to-end effectiveness <cite id="c39c1a18-7">Cooperative training improves the overall system</cite>.
- For LLM-augmented retrieval, learn to rank in-context examples to improve instruction/data efficiency and downstream task performance <cite id="5ebd9820-7">Learning to rank retrieved examples improves 9/9 NLP tasks, up to 18% over baselines</cite>.

Summary
Improving retrieval with learning hinges on learning better encoders (contrastive losses, hard negative mining), stronger ranking objectives (pairwise/listwise), and refined pipelines (BM25+dense+reranker), coupled with data-aware supervision from clicks and active negative curation. In production settings, counterfactual learning-to-rank and cooperative retriever–reranker training stabilize and further boost gains, while evaluation should tie metrics to end-task utility. <cite id="36afa881-2">Hard negatives improve accuracy by 10–20% through targeted top-K error reduction</cite><cite id="a125b877-1">Neural stacks with reranking can raise Hit@1 and Mean by 20% relative to baselines</cite><cite id="a125b877-4">Cross-encoder reranking can yield nDCG@10 = 0.7448 in scientific QA, outperforming traditional baselines</cite><cite id="c39c1a18-1">Counterfactual LTR corrects biases inherent in click logs and improves ranking policy learning</cite><cite id="5ebd9820-7">Learning to rank in-context examples improves over classification-only baselines by up to 18%</cite>.

query.text: Multimedia document adaptation approach
query.answer:
# What is "Multimedia Document Adaptation" and Why It Matters

Multimedia document adaptation refers to a family of methods that tailor the presentation, delivery, and accessibility of audiovisual content and structured documents (e.g., PDFs, EPUB/e-books, HTML5 publications) to the capabilities of the consuming device and the condition of the network, preserving user-perceived quality and comprehension while minimizing failures, buffering, and usability barriers. <cite id="e51eacb4-0">Video transcoding is to create multiple representations of a video for content adaptation and is a core technique in Adaptive BitRate (ABR) streaming</cite> <cite id="e51eacb4-1">Adaptive bitrate streaming encodes content at multiple bit rates and switches at runtime to track changing conditions</cite> <cite id="e51eacb4-3">Adaptive streaming enables optimum streaming video across diverse devices and connection speeds</cite>. In documents, adaptation spans responsive layout for screen size, device features like speech output, and accessibility formats such as captions, audio description, and sign language tracks, guided by standards such as EPUB/HTML and WCAG. <cite id="52157f09-0">EPUB Adaptive Layout extends CSS with a model for template-based paginated layouts to adapt pages to reading systems</cite> <cite id="68da14af-0">WCAG 2.2 requires captions on all prerecorded synchronized media, with exceptions where text is the media alternative</cite> <cite id="68da14af-1">Time-based Media guidance specifies that synchronized alternatives must provide access to audio-only and visual-only information, with sign language included at Level AAA</cite>.

# Mechanisms and Architectures

## 1) Content-centric adaptation: transcoding and ABR

Adaptive streaming builds multiple representations (bitrate, resolution, GOP alignment) offline via transcoding, then selects among them at runtime based on network and device feedback. <cite id="e51eacb4-0">Transcoding creates multiple representations for content adaptation and is central to ABR</cite> <cite id="e51eacb4-1">ABR encodes at multiple bitrates over HTTP and tracks playback quality</cite> <cite id="e51eacb4-5">ABR encodes a single video into multiple renditions differing in resolution and bitrate</cite>. Player policies differ: "trickle-down" reuses the latest keyframe across lower layers and is favored for low latency, while "selective refresh" transcodes only changed tiles—both aim to minimize playout stalls under network dynamics. <cite id="e51eacb4-1">ABR operates by detecting client conditions and adjusting the bitrate accordingly during playback</cite> <cite id="68da14af-2">Guidance on making audio/video accessible helps identify which accessibility aspects (captions, descriptions, signing) pair with delivery choices</cite>.

Design choices include pre-encoding depth and GOP organization to balance quality headroom and playout robustness, then using manifest metadata (segment timelines, keyframe locations, availability) to drive fast switches. <cite id="e51eacb4-1">ABR manifests multiple bitrates and uses keyframe/segment information to select representations</cite>.

## 2) Document-format adaptation: responsive layout, roles, and fixed vs. reflowable layouts

EPUB and web document formats adapt structure and layout to the reading system. <cite id="52157f09-0">EPUB Adaptive Layout provides a model for template-based paginated layouts as an extension to CSS, enabling pages to adapt to device constraints</cite> <cite id="52157f09-3">EPUB Content Documents 3.2 define HTML/SVG/CSS usage profiles for publications, coupling presentation and semantics</cite> <cite id="52157f09-4">EPUB Type-to-ARIA Role Authoring Guide clarifies migration to ARIA roles for accessible navigation and meaning</cite>. For fixed-layout publications, authors can use CSS Regions and ARIA to preserve page intent while improving navigability and keyboard/screen reader access. <cite id="52157f09-1">EPUB Accessibility guidance for fixed layouts provides best practices for meeting EPUB A11Y 1.1 requirements</cite> <cite id="52157f09-0">Adaptive Layout supports systems that adjust paginated structures to screen size and input modality</cite>.

HTML5 responsive design uses media queries, flexible grids, and images to reflow content across phones, tablets, and desktops; accessibility overlays connect layout adaptation to screen readers and speech control. <cite id="52157f09-2">Combining flexible layouts with CSS enables optimization on numerous devices for responsive web design</cite> <cite id="68da14af-3">Media Accessibility User Requirements capture user needs for audio and video on the web, informing parallel layout and control adaptations</cite>.

## 3) Network- and transport-level adaptation: HTTP adaptive over multipath

ABR is typically over HTTP, but transport choices and scheduling matter. Multipath QUIC and edge-aware policies learn per-flow states and select subflows/bitrate jointly for higher QoE under contention, sometimes using bandit-based or RL schedulers. <cite id="0627ef2b-0">A reinforcement learning–based adaptive streaming scheme improves QoE in edge computing environments by adapting to runtime conditions</cite> <cite id="0627ef2b-1">A QoE-driven, contextual multi-armed bandit decision framework jointly selects content and path for multipath adaptive streaming</cite> <cite id="0627ef2b-1">The CMAB framework addresses multipath adaptive streaming efficiently</cite> <cite id="0627ef2b-2">Evaluations of multipath QUIC with shared-bottleneck detection show interactions with ABR algorithms in video streaming</cite> <cite id="0627ef2b-3">A deep Q-network–based MPQUIC scheduler enhances multimedia quality over multipath</cite>. On the sender, precomputed base/alt tracks are delivered as HTTP chunks and revalidated via Range requests; clients maintain a selection policy tuned for latency, stall avoidance, and quality models. <cite id="e51eacb4-1">ABR adjusts bitrate using manifest cues and network feedback via HTTP</cite>.

Complementary approaches include layered-base transrating pipelines at the edge and content-aware pre-analysis (e.g., feature pyramids) to produce alternatives tuned to scene complexity and stutter risk. <cite id="e51eacb4-0">Transcoding pipelines create the multiple representations used for adaptive delivery over an edge–cloud continuum</cite> <cite id="e51eacb4-7">Edge-cloud architectures for ABR emphasize effective distribution and caching for multimedia content</cite>. Reinforcement learning and bandits provide online policies that converge to QoE-aware decisions under uncertainty and changing conditions. <cite id="0627ef2b-6">An adaptive QoE-based multipath SVC algorithm adjusts streaming decisions based on QoE degradation detection</cite> <cite id="0627ef2b-5">Markov Decision Processes support bitrate “harmony” to maintain consistent quality across clients or flows</cite> <cite id="0627ef2b-6">Online reinforcement learning adapts streaming schemes when QoE degrades</cite>.

## 4) Accessibility adaptation: captions, audio description, and sign language

Accessibility is a first-class adaptation target. Standards specify synchronized alternatives and sensory substitution so that users with hearing or visual impairments obtain equivalent information. <cite id="68da14af-0">WCAG 2.2 mandates captions for synchronized media unless the text itself serves as an alternative</cite> <cite id="68da14af-1">Guideline 1.2 requires access to time-based media, including sign language at Level AAA for audio content</cite> <cite id="68da14af-2">W3C guidance explains making media accessible, clarifying responsibilities across production and delivery</cite> <cite id="68da14af-3">Media Accessibility User Requirements enumerate user needs for audio and video features across disabilities</cite>. In practice, systems provide multiple language/media roles and cueing—e.g., transcripts to captions, audio description tracks for visuals, and sign language video overlays—paired with document semantics (alt text, captions attributes) and keyboard/voice controllability. <cite id="68da14af-5">Captions are synchronized text for audio content, including live events; audio descriptions translate visual information to sound</cite> <cite id="52157f09-1">Fixed-layout guidance supports accessibility requirements to ensure screen reader awareness and navigability</cite>.

# Concrete Approaches and Workflows

- Precompute alternatives, then adapt at runtime:
  - Transcode source videos to bitrate/codec stacks; build DASH/HLS manifests with keyframes and segment playlists. <cite id="e51eacb4-0">Transcoding creates multiple representations for adaptation</cite> <cite id="e51eacb4-1">ABR selects among multi-bitrate representations at runtime</cite>.
  - EPUB/HTML publications author reflowable sections with CSS media queries or EPUB Adaptive Layout; add accessible roles and landmarks; embed captions/descriptions and timed text. <cite id="52157f09-0">Adaptive layout adjusts paginated templates to the reading system</cite> <cite id="52157f09-4">ARIA role authoring aligns document semantics with screen reader navigation</cite> <cite id="68da14af-0">WCAG captioning requirements bind synchronized media</cite>.

- Runtime adaptation policies:
  - Bandits and RL learn per-session bandwidth and path quality, choosing bitrate and subflow to maximize QoE under contention and stalls. <cite id="0627ef2b-0">Reinforcement learning improves QoE by adapting to edge conditions</cite> <cite id="0627ef2b-1">CMAB decisions jointly tune content and multipath selection for QoE</cite> <cite id="0627ef2b-3">Deep Q-network schedulers enhance multipath streaming quality</cite>.
  - Trickledown and selective-refresh tile replacement reduce playout interruptions and rebuffering. <cite id="e51eacb4-1">ABR commonly adjusts bitrate using runtime feedback and manifest anchors</cite>.

- Delivery stacks at the edge:
  - Push/pop content to caches; keep pre-processed alt tracks hot; use Range requests and keyframe-based recovery. <cite id="e51eacb4-7">Edge–cloud architectures emphasize distribution and caching for efficient streaming</cite>.
  - Use QUIC/MPTCP for better congestion and packet-loss resilience, with ABR-aware schedulers. <cite id="0627ef2b-2">MPQUIC-SBD evaluates ABR interactions over multipath QUIC under shared bottlenecks</cite>.

# Design Trade-offs and Quality Objectives

Adaptation must balance latency and quality, robustness to bursts and losses, resource limits, and accessibility. Over-aggressive pre-encoding increases storage and compute; trickle-down may waste quality if stall drivers are external to bandwidth. QoE-aware policies that combine bandwidth and stall predictors, network-awareness (multipath), and accessibility constraints can reduce rebuffering and improve utility across devices. <cite id="e51eacb4-0">Transcoding pipelines and multiple representations create the adaptation headroom for ABR</cite> <cite id="e51eacb4-1">ABR detects client conditions and switches to maintain playback quality</cite> <cite id="0627ef2b-0">Reinforcement learning adapts decisions at the edge to mitigate QoE degradation</cite> <cite id="0627ef2b-1">Contextual bandits efficiently solve joint content/path selection in multipath streaming</cite> <cite id="68da14af-0">Captioning and alternatives ensure equivalent access for users who cannot consume audio-visual channels</cite>.

# Putting It Together: A Practical Adaptation Stack

- Authoring and packaging
  - Produce multi-format/codec encodings for ABR; create manifests (HLS/DASH) with keyframes and #EXTINF cues. <cite id="e51eacb4-1">ABR relies on multiple bitrates and segment manifests for selection</cite>.
  - For documents, author reflowable sections or EPUB fixed/floated layouts, add alt text, captions, and timed descriptions; validate EPUB 3.2 profiles and ARIA roles. <cite id="52157f09-3">EPUB Content Documents 3.2 define HTML/SVG/CSS profiles for consistent rendering</cite> <cite id="52157f09-4">ARIA role migration guidance supports screen reader awareness</cite>.

- Delivery and edge
  - Serve from HTTP/3 QUIC with Range support; at the edge, cache alt tracks; run ABR with QoE-aware policies (bandits/RL) and multipath-aware scheduling. <cite id="0627ef2b-1">QoE-driven multipath ABR via CMAB</cite> <cite id="0627ef2b-3">DQN-based MPQUIC scheduler improves multimedia QoE</cite> <cite id="e51eacb4-7">Edge–cloud streaming emphasizes effective caching and distribution</cite>.

- Client-side adaptation
  - Monitor estimated bandwidth and stall likelihood; apply trickle-down tile refresh or selective retranscode; expose captions/descriptions, and coordinate with screen readers via ARIA. <cite id="e51eacb4-1">ABR adjusts bitrate during playback based on network feedback</cite> <cite id="68da14af-1">Time-based media requires access to audio-only and visual-only content, including sign language</cite> <cite id="52157f09-1">Fixed layout accessibility guidance aligns rendering with access needs</cite>.

- Accessibility assurance and testing
  - Verify WCAG conformance for captions, transcripts, and descriptions, and test sign language track availability and timing. <cite id="68da14af-0">WCAG captioning criteria apply to synchronized media</cite> <cite id="68da14af-2">Media accessibility guidance clarifies responsibilities for captions/descriptions</cite>.

# Summary

A multimedia document adaptation approach is multi-layered: off-line creation of multiple representations by transcoding, on-line selection and playout control by ABR with QoE-aware and network-aware policies, document-format adaptations for layout and access via EPUB/HTML and ARIA, and accessibility provisions that add captions, descriptions, and sign language to ensure equivalent access. <cite id="e51eacb4-0">Transcoding/multi-representation is core to ABR</cite> <cite id="e51eacb4-1">ABR switches among bitrates over HTTP as conditions change</cite> <cite id="52157f09-0">EPUB's adaptive layout adjusts page structures to device systems</cite> <cite id="52157f09-1">EPUB fixed-layout best practices meet accessibility requirements</cite> <cite id="0627ef2b-0">Reinforcement learning improves QoE in adaptive streaming</cite> <cite id="68da14af-0">WCAG captioning makes synchronized media accessible</cite> <cite id="68da14af-1">Sign language and time-based media requirements drive multimodal adaptation</cite>. These elements together deliver robust, responsive, and inclusive experiences across devices and networks. <cite id="e51eacb4-3">Adaptive streaming makes video work across a broad set of devices and speeds</cite> <cite id="68da14af-3">User needs for audio/video accessibility guide parallel adaptations</cite>.
