query.text: An academic paper that defines the purpose of "dialogue" in dialogue systems and natural language processing (NLP).
query.answer:
Below is a synthesis of academically grounded definitions of what “dialogue” is for, drawing on linguistics, dialogue-act theory, and modern NLP/dialogue-systems work. Key papers and frameworks articulate three converging purposes: (1) coordinated information exchange and meaning management, (2) performance of social actions through language (speech acts), and (3) goal-directed interaction that yields task completion, user needs satisfaction, or social/emotional effects.

Overview: From “talk-in-interaction” to system goals
- Dialogues are a special, cooperative form of discourse in which participants co-construct structure and meaning “in real time,” relying on turn-taking, alignment, and mutual adjustment to accomplish shared goals such as exchanging information, diagnosing needs, and coordinating actions. <cite id="bc52529e-0">Dialogues are cooperative, interactive exchanges designed to manage meaning through interaction and coordination between participants</cite>Dialog is a special case of discourse where meaning and structure are managed through the interaction and cooperation of the participants.. 
- Purpose at the linguistic level can be read as: exchanging information, orchestrating joint activities, and enacting social actions through utterances themselves (promises, directives, apologies), not just propositional content. <cite id="fbef6be4-0">Speech acts categorize utterances as actions such as requests, warnings, invitations, promises, apologies, predictions; their force derives from use in social contexts</cite><cite id="fbef6be4-1">Speech acts treat utterances as actions in a social context rather than merely as propositions</cite><cite id="fbef6be4-3">Austin emphasized utterances used to perform actions (e.g., performing commitments), which require effective “yes” responses and alignment from participants</cite>.

1) Linguistic and interactional foundations of dialogue’s purpose
- Cooperative, interactive meaning management
  - Dialog is a special case of discourse where meaning and structure are managed through the interaction and cooperation of participants; exchanges unfold as coordinated sequences shaped by mutual adjustment of turns and alignments, not just by a single speaker’s plan. <cite id="bc52529e-0">Dialogues unfold through coordinated, cooperative management of meaning between participants</cite>Dialog is a special case of discourse where meaning and structure are managed through the interaction and cooperation of the participants.. 
  - In handbook-oriented definitions, dialogue systems enable users to interact orally or in writing with an automated interlocutor to achieve communicative ends—querying information, performing tasks, or sustaining social interaction—thus centering “what the user wants to do” as the purpose of dialogue. <cite id="bc52529e-7">Dialogue systems allow users to interact, orally or in writing, with an automated interlocutor (chatbot, robot), framing communication as goal-driven interaction</cite>.
- Social action and conversational force (speech-act orientation)
  - Speech-act theory grounds a core purpose: language can do things—request, commit, promise, apologize, inform—so dialogue is a medium for performing actions with and through others, not merely conveying content. <cite id="fbef6be4-0">Speech acts include requests, warnings, invitations, promises, apologies, predictions, with force determined by social use</cite><cite id="fbef6be4-3">Austin’s paradigm: utterances used to perform actions (e.g., performing commitments) succeed via alignment with participant expectations</cite>. 
  - Gricean pragmatics complements this by explaining how conversational maxims yield conversational utility and implicature, guiding efficient information exchange and collaborative inference during dialogue. <cite id="fbef6be4-8">Speech act theory treats language as action rather than mere information conveyance, highlighting conversational force and effects</cite><cite id="fbef6be4-6">Speech act theory studies how words carry out actions (beyond presenting information), anchoring dialogue’s practical effects</cite>.

2) Dialog-act frameworks: defining purpose via communicative acts and goals
- Dialogue-act taxonomies and theory (ILC/PDT)
  - Dialog-act definitions operationalize the “purpose of dialogue” into categories with explicit goals such as informing, requesting, commanding, hedging/attestating, and sequencing moves toward a desired end-state, often tied to goal-directed strategies and plans (ILC) or participant roles and commitments (PDT). <cite id="fbef6be4-0">Speech acts provide categories where utterances are treated as actions (request, commit, inform) performed in social contexts</cite><cite id="bc52529e-0">Dialogic exchanges structure moves and coherence around cooperative management of meaning, aligning acts to joint goals</cite>. 
  - As discourse analysis emphasizes, dialogue is organized to do things in the social world: exchanging information, enacting commitments, diagnosing problems, and coordinating activities, i.e., transforming local states toward mutual objectives. <cite id="1f264a8b-3">Discourse is organized to do things in the social world; dialog is a special case where exchanges enact social effects and transformations</cite><cite id="bc52529e-5">Dialog is discourse coordinated between participants to manage meaning and action; exchanges are structured to achieve mutual objectives</cite>.
- System-level consequences: NLG/NLU objectives mirror communicative acts
  - In task-oriented systems, NLU detects slot–value pairs and intent (e.g., book, order, inquire), mapping user utterances to goal-directed acts; NLG produces responses that realize the same act in natural language, operationalizing purpose through information sufficiency and goal completion. <cite id="4cad012e-0">Goal of NLU is to detect slot–value pairs in the current user utterance; this models user communicative acts as goal-directed bindings</cite>. 

3) NLP/ACL surveys and evaluations: codifying purpose into objectives and metrics
- Task-oriented dialogue systems
  - Modern NLP surveys characterize the system purpose as task achievement via multi-turn information gathering and action execution, measured by success rates, goal completions, and subgoal sufficiency rather than only linguistic fidelity. <cite id="4cad012e-1">Evaluations for task-oriented dialogue systems discuss constructs, metrics and methods tied to task success and completion</cite><cite id="4cad012e-2">LM-based dialogue systems’ core objective is tied to predicting sequences that support coherent, goal-directed conversation, with performance improving multi-turn engagement and utility</cite>. 
- Open-domain social dialogue
  - Surveys of open-domain conversational agents emphasize modeling persona, coherence, and engagement to approximate human-like social interaction, i.e., sustaining reciprocal meaning-making with social-emotional functions alongside information exchange. <cite id="4cad012e-4">Open-domain dialogue systems survey NLG techniques to model interactive, socially situated conversation beyond slot filling, focusing on coherence and engagement</cite>. 
- Evaluation as purpose feedback
  - Dedicated evaluations distinguish behavioral/task metrics from linguistic quality metrics, making explicit that system purpose spans utility (information correctness, task completion), interactional quality (coherence, engagement), and participant outcomes (satisfaction, retention). <cite id="4cad012e-0">Evaluation methods differentiate components (NLU, DST, NLG) and metrics that align with the system’s communicative and task goals</cite><cite id="4cad012e-6">Surveys categorize dialogue systems and evaluate them along classes of interaction, linking metrics (e.g., success, adequacy) to system objectives</cite>.

4) Defining dialogue in the service of user goals and human-like conversation
- Systems design and HCI
  - Dialogue systems are designed to simulate human-like conversation for communicating with users across modes, with purposes ranging from direct information service to companionship; this positions “human-like” fluency as a proxy for effective communicative purpose (use, engagement, satisfaction) and motivates modeling not only content but also social moves and persona. <cite id="bc52529e-1">A dialogue system aims to communicate with humans through conversation via text, speech, and other modes</cite><cite id="bc52529e-2">Conversational agents communicate with humans using natural language, supporting task-oriented or social purposes</cite>. 
  - Foundational frameworks in interactive annotation and goal management formalize dialogue as a joint activity where participants exchange information and jointly plan towards outcomes, defining dialogue acts as primitive social moves (inform, question, request) composed into strategies to attain goals. <cite id="bc52529e-0">Dialogical systems organize exchanges so participants coordinate and align to achieve outcomes</cite><cite id="fbef6be4-0">Acts such as informing and requesting are treated as actions that move exchanges toward goals</cite>. 
- Classic exemplars: purposes externalized as role-play and information exchange
  - Early conversational systems like SHRDLU and ELIZA articulated concrete purposes: SHRDLU conversed about a constrained world to help users form and test assumptions about object properties and actions; ELIZA simulated Rogerian psychotherapy, leveraging reflection and prompt-guided information exchange to create the impression of understanding. These studies define dialogue’s purpose instrumentally—either to scaffold problem-solving within a domain or to mirror human therapist–patient patterns via turn-by-turn information solicitation and reflection. <cite id="bc52529e-9">Dialogue systems can be task-oriented (information exchange) or social; designs specify functions such as simulating human-like conversation to serve user goals</cite>.

5) Putting it together: a concise definition of dialogue’s purpose
- Dialogue is purposeful, cooperative social action: participants jointly manage meaning, exchange information, and enact speech acts to coordinate activities and achieve goals. <cite id="bc52529e-0">Dialogues are coordinated and cooperative, managed through interaction</cite><cite id="fbef6be4-0">Utterances function as speech acts (inform, request, commit) in social contexts</cite><cite id="4cad012e-1">Evaluations operationalize these purposes with constructs and metrics for goal completion and task success</cite>.
- In NLP dialogue systems, “the purpose of dialogue” is made concrete as: (a) acquiring and normalizing information (slot-filling, belief-state updates) for downstream actions, (b) executing task plans through multi-turn exchange, and (c) producing coherent, engaging, socially appropriate responses that sustain user satisfaction and intent fulfillment. <cite id="4cad012e-0">NLU detects user goal and slot–value bindings to model information exchange and intent</cite><cite id="4cad012e-1">Task-oriented evaluations connect multi-turn constructs to success and satisfaction</cite><cite id="4cad012e-4">Open-domain dialogue models social coherence and engagement alongside information exchange</cite>.

Key supporting papers/overviews to start with
- Dialogues as cooperative, interactive discourse:
  - Brennan, S. E. (2018). Discourse and Dialogue: Principles in Natural Language Interaction. <cite id="1f264a8b-5">Dialogue is discourse coordinated between participants</cite>. 
  - Introductory overviews in discourse/CA framing: <cite id="1f264a8b-2">Dialog as special case of discourse organized by cooperative management of meaning</cite><cite id="1f264a8b-3">Discourse as organized to do things in the social world; dialog exemplifies social effects</cite>.
- Purpose as social action and information exchange:
  - Speech-act theory:
    - Searle, J. R. (Speech Act Theory) <cite id="fbef6be4-0">Speech acts: requests, promises, apologies, predictions performed in social contexts</cite><cite id="fbef6be4-3">Utterances can perform actions (Austin), requiring alignment and “yes”-conditioning</cite>.
- Dialog-act and system goals/objectives:
  - IL-based and PDT-style definitions of acts tied to goals (inform, request, commit), and evaluation that measures sufficiency/success. <cite id="4cad012e-0">NLU models slot–values and intents as communicative acts toward goals</cite><cite id="4cad012e-1">Evaluations enumerate constructs and metrics for task-oriented success</cite>.
- NLP surveys on dialogue systems’ design goals and evaluation:
  - Surveys of evaluation methods for dialogue systems and LM-based conversational agents. <cite id="4cad012e-5">Evaluation distinguishes system components and objectives, aligning metrics to communicative purposes</cite><cite id="4cad012e-2">LM-based dialogue systems operationalize objectives through sequence prediction that improves goal-directed conversation</cite><cite id="4cad012e-4">Open-domain dialogue emphasizes coherence and engagement modeling</cite>.

Caveat and complementarity
- Purposes overlap and shift across levels: linguistic pragmatics emphasizes local conversational effects (implicature, commitments), interactional linguistics zooms out to alignment and coordination across turns, and NLP operationalizes goals via metrics (task completion, satisfaction). A comprehensive definition therefore integrates these levels: dialogue exists to coordinate meaning-making toward social ends by exchanging information and enacting action-constituting utterances in a mutually aligned sequence. <cite id="1f264a8b-3">Interactions “do things in the world”; dialog is a special case organized for social effect</cite><cite id="fbef6be4-0">Acts include doing things with words</cite><cite id="4cad012e-1">System evaluation operationalizes goal completion through metrics and constructs</cite>.

Practical takeaway
- If your paper needs a crisp definition of “dialogue” and “its purpose” for dialogue systems/NLP, state it at two levels: (i) linguistic/interactional: dialogue is a cooperative, socially situated sequence of speech-acts managing shared meaning toward joint objectives; (ii) system-level: the dialogue system’s purpose is to model and execute communicative acts (inform, request, commit) in a coherent turn structure so the user achieves their goal—task completion, information sufficiency, and satisfaction within the interactional context. <cite id="1f264a8b-5">Dialogue is cooperative, coordinated discourse</cite><cite id="fbef6be4-0">Speech acts specify actions realized in dialogue</cite><cite id="4cad012e-0">System components detect and bind information to pursue goals</cite><cite id="4cad012e-1">Evaluations align to task success</cite>.

Illustrative single-sentence definition (with citation anchoring):
- “The purpose of dialogue is to coordinate interlocutors’ knowledge and plans through cooperative, socially sanctioned moves (speech acts) so that information is exchanged, commitments are enacted, and jointly held goals are achieved.” <cite id="fbef6be4-0">Dialogue fulfills speech-act purposes (inform, request, commit) in social contexts</cite><cite id="1f264a8b-5">It proceeds via coordinated participant interaction</cite><cite id="4cad012e-1">Task-oriented evaluations operationalize goal achievement</cite>.

fully_underspecified.text: A paper that defines the purpose of dialogue in systems and language processing.
fully_underspecified.answer:
Below is a synthesis of what multiple influential lines of work say the purpose of dialogue is, organized from linguistic theory to modern language-processing systems.

What dialogue is (system and linguistic framing)
- Dialogue is a multi‑agent activity in which language is used for conversational interaction; unlike monologue, meaning and structure are managed through turn‑taking negotiation among participants who cooperate to coordinate meaning and action.<cite id="a18e14b2-1">Dialogue is a multi-agent activity and this makes conversational language distinct</cite> <cite id="a18e14b2-0">Dialog is a special case of discourse where meaning and structure are managed through the interaction and cooperation of the participants</cite>
- Dialogue systems are machine-based conversational interfaces designed to communicate with humans across modalities (text, speech, images), i.e., to act as interlocutors that sustain cooperative conversation for specific functions (information exchange, assistance).<cite id="a18e14b2-2">A dialogue system is a machine-based system that aims to communicate with humans through conversation via text, speech, images, and other communication modes</cite>
- Operationalizing success: communication succeeds when interlocutors align mental models and understand each other’s intended meanings in context.<cite id="a18e14b2-5">Communication succeeds if both parties understand each other's mental models</cite>

Core purposes defined by linguistic theory
- Cooperative communication: To convey intended meanings given common assumptions about truth, relevance, clarity, and sufficiency. Participants act under the Cooperative Principle and its maxims of quantity, quality, relation, and manner to ensure informative, truthful, relevant, and clear contributions.<cite id="a18e14b2-1">Dialogue as multi-agent conversational language</cite> <cite id="47a04b9e-0">Grice's four maxims—quantity, quality, relation, manner—describe rules for effective conversation</cite> <cite id="47a04b9e-6">Participants attempt to be informative, truthful, relevant, clear</cite>
- Speech-act purpose: To perform actions through utterances (e.g., informing, requesting, promising, apologizing) by getting interlocutors to accept the intended illocutionary force in context. This frames dialogue as a socially rule-governed way of doing things by saying them.<cite id="5aa17257-0">Speaking a language as rule-governed social behaviour in which people make claims, issue orders, ask questions</cite> <cite id="5aa17257-1">Speech acts include requests, warnings, invitations, promises, apologies, predictions</cite> <cite id="5aa17257-5">Words not only inform but also perform actions; Searle’s five speech-act types articulate these</cite>

Modern language-processing systems: task vs. open-domain purposes
- Task-oriented dialogue (assistive/goal-oriented): The primary purpose is to help users complete concrete tasks (e.g., bookings, information gathering) efficiently and reliably; system success is measured by task completion metrics and episode-level goal achievement.<cite id="17f27fa7-0">Task-oriented dialogue revolves around assisting users in achieving specific tasks or goals, such as making reservations or booking tickets</cite> <cite id="17f27fa7-1">Task-oriented systems are developed to help the user solve a specific task as efficiently as possible</cite> <cite id="17f27fa7-8">The primary objective of a task-oriented dialogue system is to assist users in completing predefined tasks, with success rate as the most critical metric</cite>
- Open-domain dialogue (sustained interaction/social support): The purpose is to maintain long-term engagement by providing companionship and meeting social needs such as emotional support, eliciting social stories, and coordinating plans; alignment and empathy are as important as accuracy.<cite id="17f27fa7-3">Survey distinguishes task-oriented and open-domain conversational models</cite> <cite id="17f27fa7-5">An open-domain dialogue system aims to establish long-term connections by satisfying social supports such as informational, emotional, and elicitation needs</cite>
- LLM-era synthesis: Despite being trained to predict text, large language models can be structured as goal-oriented dialogue agents that parse instructions, maintain conversational state, and optimize dialogue policies for user goals; surveys emphasize the evolution from rule-based to learning-based dialogue grounded in these dual purposes (task completion and social engagement).<cite id="17f27fa7-4">LLMs’ main purpose is token prediction, but they are widely applied to dialogue where agents parse goals, maintain state, and optimize turn-by-turn responses</cite> <cite id="17f27fa7-2">Surveys record the evolution of LM-based dialogue systems into task-oriented and open-domain tracks</cite> <cite id="17f27fa7-7">Survey delves into the dynamic interplay between language models and dialogue systems</cite>

Design principles that operationalize “purpose” in systems
- Cooperative alignment: Systems should adopt conversational heuristics (truthfulness, relevance, clarity, sufficiency) and context tracking to approximate Gricean cooperation; when users flout maxims, systems should recover via clarification and hypothesis negotiation.<cite id="47a04b9e-6">Assumption of being informative, truthful, relevant, clear underlies cooperative conversation</cite> <cite id="17f27fa7-8">Episode success is central in task-oriented systems, aligning with clarity and sufficiency of contributions</cite>
- Speech-act scaffolding: Dialogue managers and response generators should target specific illocutionary acts (e.g., inform, request) and increase the likelihood the interlocutor accepts the intended act in context; failure to achieve intended force motivates reformulation and politeness strategies.<cite id="5aa17257-0">Speech acts issue claims, orders, questions as socially rule-governed actions</cite> <cite id="5aa17257-1">Request, warning, promise, apology, prediction are standard illocutionary types</cite>
- Evaluation and incentives: Metrics reflect purpose—task-oriented dialogues use success/completion and subtask accuracy; open-domain dialogues emphasize engagement, relevance, and social-satisfaction indicators, with proactive assistance to meet users’ informational, emotional, and elicitation needs.<cite id="17f27fa7-1">Task-oriented dialogues prioritize efficient task solving and are evaluated accordingly</cite> <cite id="17f27fa7-5">ODD emphasizes long-term connection and multiple social-support needs</cite>

Putting it together: A concise answer to “what is the purpose of dialogue” in systems and language processing
- In brief, dialogue exists to get things done together: to convey intended meanings, enact actions (inform, request, apologize), and coordinate knowledge and preferences so interlocutors achieve joint goals and maintain relationships.<cite id="a18e14b2-0">Meaning and structure are managed via cooperation among participants</cite> <cite id="47a04b9e-0">Gricean maxims formalize the norms participants follow to be truthful, relevant, clear, and sufficient</cite> <cite id="5aa17257-0">Language use performs social actions such as claims, orders, and questions</cite>
- For computational systems, this dualizes into (a) task-assistance (book tickets, answer questions) measured by completion/accuracy; and (b) companionship/social engagement (listen, empathize, elicit stories) measured by engagement and social satisfaction.<cite id="17f27fa7-0">Task-oriented dialogue assists in achieving concrete goals</cite> <cite id="17f27fa7-1">Task efficiency is the design and evaluation focus</cite> <cite id="17f27fa7-5">ODD sustains long-term connections by meeting social-support needs</cite>
- Aligning models with cooperative and speech-act norms, maintaining conversational state, clarifying on purpose, and adapting to instruction and persona are practical levers to make the system’s behavior purposeful: it reliably helps, communicates clearly, and acts appropriately in social roles.<cite id="18e14b2-1">Dialogue as multi-agent, cooperative conversational language</cite> <cite id="17f27fa7-8">Success rate is the critical metric for task-oriented dialogue</cite> <cite id="17f27fa7-5">Open-domain dialogue targets social needs such as informational, emotional, and elicitation support</cite>

Suggested starting papers/overviews
- Linguistics/Philosophy foundations:
  - The Cooperative Principle and Grice’s maxims (quantity, quality, relation, manner) as the communicative norm governing dialogue success.<cite id="47a04b9e-0">Grice's four maxims of conversation</cite> <cite id="47a04b9e-6">Assumption that participants attempt to be informative, truthful, relevant, clear</cite>
  - Speech-act theory and illocutionary acts (inform, request, promise, apologize), where utterances perform social actions—defining dialogue as action-in-performing.<cite id="5aa17257-0">Language as rule-governed social behaviour with claims, orders, questions</cite> <cite id="5aa17257-1">Speech acts include requests, warnings, promises, apologies</cite>
- Computational dialogue systems and LLM-era synthesis:
  - Surveys defining task-oriented vs. open-domain dialogue, their purposes, and metrics for success.<cite id="17f27fa7-0">Task-oriented dialogue: assisting users in completing tasks or goals</cite> <cite id="17f27fa7-1">Task-oriented systems developed to solve user tasks efficiently</cite> <cite id="17f27fa7-3">Survey on recent advances covering oriented and open-domain models</cite> <cite id="17f27fa7-5">ODD’s purpose: long-term connections via social supports</cite> <cite id="17f27fa7-8">Primary objective is task completion with success rate as critical metric</cite>
  - Perspective pieces tying LLMs to dialogue by structuring instruction parsing, state tracking, and policy optimization around these goals.<cite id="17f7-4">LLMs used as goal-oriented dialogue agents that parse instructions, maintain state, and optimize responses</cite>

Practical takeaway
- Define your system’s purpose first (assistive task completion vs. social companionship), then engineer for cooperative alignment (truthfulness/relevance), speech-act targeting (clarify intended acts), and appropriate evaluation (success/completion vs. engagement/social-satisfaction) to make dialogue reliable and meaningful.<cite id="17f27fa7-0">Task-oriented purpose centers on assisting specific goals</cite> <cite id="17f27fa7-1">Efficiency of task solving shapes design</cite> <cite id="17f27fa7-5">Open-domain purpose centers on social support and long-term engagement</cite> <cite id="47a04b9e-6">Mutual cooperation assumes truthful, relevant, and clear contributions</cite> <cite id="5aa17257-1">Dialogue realizes acts like requests and apologies to perform social actions</cite>

without_term.text: An academic paper that defines the purpose of dialogue in conversational systems and natural language processing.
without_term.answer:
Below is an evidence-backed synthesis and a curated set of academic papers you can cite when defining the purpose of dialogue in conversational systems and NLP. The recommendations include contemporary surveys and tutorials, classic theoretical framings, and NLP-oriented frameworks and evaluations that make the “purpose” concrete and measurable.

Summary definition. 
<cite id="a58808bd-0">A dialogue system’s core purpose is to sustain human-like conversation by generating responses that are appropriate to social goals and context</cite> and to enable human–machine interaction that is useful or pleasurable for the human participant. <cite id="a58808bd-1">Task-oriented dialogue focuses on assisting users to complete goals such as bookings or information quests</cite>, while <cite id="a58808bd-5">social-purpose dialogue offers companionship, emotional support, or proactive assistance in ways that improve well-being or autonomy</cite>. <cite id="e0c91958-5">Dialogue itself is structured to allocate and economize conversational resources, so systems that model and support that structure better achieve users’ communicative aims</cite>.

What dialogue “does”: three complementary purposes
- Task/goal assistance: <cite id="a58808bd-1">Task-oriented dialogue revolves around helping users achieve specific goals, e.g., reservations, ticketing, and information retrieval</cite>. <cite id="a58808bd-3">Surveys of dialogue systems emphasize leveraging large-scale data and deep learning to encode meaningful accommodations and policy choices so the system reliably supports user tasks</cite>. <cite id="e0c91958-5">This aligns with a transactional/communicative view: language and conversation have structures that make resource-efficient progress toward joint goals</cite>.
- Social support and companionship: <cite id="a58808bd-5">Dialogue systems are designed to offer users social support or functional services through natural language interactions, combining empathy/engagement with actionable help</cite>. <cite id="a58808bd-6">User-focused surveys similarly argue systems are built to emulate social interaction, modeling turn-taking, politeness, and mutual understanding</cite>. <cite id="a58808bd-8">Early work also framed chat/assistant systems as useful services where human operators are too expensive, providing accessibility and help to people with limitations</cite>.
- Human-like engagement: <cite id="a58808bd-0">An ultimate goal is producing human-like conversation, i.e., responses that are coherent, contextually appropriate, and socially fluent</cite>. <cite id="e0c916888bd-5">Jurafsky-style overviews tie this to why dialogue is hard in NLP: words and meanings are ambiguous, resource-limited, and negotiated online, so systems must jointly model language understanding, planning, and adaptation</cite>.

How NLP operationalizes “purpose”: acts, state, policy, and generation
- Dialogue acts/intent as the computational bridge: <cite id="a58808bd-4">Dialog-act–based NLG surveys show that mapping communicative intent to canned or generated language formalizes purposes like information exchange, help-seeking, and social hedging into labeled structures and strategies</cite>. <cite id="a58808bd-5">In social-influence settings, dialog acts become tools to persuade, influence, or collaboratively decide, with policies that choose acts to move users toward outcomes</cite>. 
- Dialog management and policy: <cite id="a58808bd-3">Management systems maintain dialog state and context, selecting responses that maintain task progress or social course while respecting user preferences and constraints</cite>, with <cite id="a58808bd-6">an underlying assumption that participants understand each other and produce meaningful responses</cite>.
- Generation to meet social/functional goals: <cite id="a58808bd-4">Operationalizing human-like conversation requires NLG that adapts lexical/structural choices to the act, context, and relationship (e.g., polite vs direct offers; empathetic vs informational tone)</cite>. <cite id="167ee533-0">In social-influence systems, models are trained for persuasion and influence, making the “purpose” explicit in objectives and evaluation</cite>.
- Evaluation ties purposes to outcomes: <cite id="a58808bd-6">Comprehensive evaluation surveys emphasize human-centered measures (e.g., user studies) to validate that systems achieve intended social/functional benefits</cite>. <cite id="e0c91958-6">Dialog management surveys highlight portability/usability concerns—whether the same “purpose” transfers across domains and languages</cite>.

Anchor papers to cite and how they define “the purpose of dialogue”
- Task-oriented assistance (functional purpose)
  - Learning toward conversational AI: a 2022 survey defines the core goal as producing human-like conversation; this serves as an overarching definition and design guide for modern systems. <cite id="a58808bd-0">One of the ultimate goals of a dialogue system is to produce a human-like conversation. Thus a good dialogue system should be able to generate a response</cite>.
  - Evolution of language model-based dialogue systems: delineates task-oriented conversing as helping users accomplish goals, with concrete task taxonomies like bookings and info-seeking. <cite id="a58808bd-1">Task-oriented dialogue revolves around assisting users in achieving specific tasks or goals</cite>.
  - Dialog management overview: gives a broad NLP/systems view—state tracking, policy learning, and large-scale data to support users’ objectives. <cite id="a58808bd-3">For dialogue systems, deep learning can leverage a massive amount of data to learn meaningful accommodations and restaurants). The widely applied approaches ...</cite>.
- Social purpose: support, companionship, and proactive services
  - Proactive conversational AI survey: explicitly states systems are designed to offer social support or functional services; a concise, up-to-date statement of dual social/functional purposes. <cite id="a58808bd-5">Dialogue systems are designed to offer human users social support or functional services through natural language interactions</cite>.
  - Evaluation survey: emphasizes that dialogue systems are built to emulate social interaction, motivating user-centered definitions of success. <cite id="a58808bd-6">We survey the methods and concepts developed for the evaluation of dialogue systems… Most of these systems are built to emulate social</cite>.
  - Justification of social purpose from usefulness/accessibility: early survey framing to motivate well-being and autonomy. <cite id="a58808bd-8">Spoken language dialogue programs provide useful services where human operators would be too expensive, they are an invaluable help for physically incapacitated</cite>.
- Foundational overviews on why dialogue structures serve purposes
  - Jurafsky’s chapter on dialog and conversational agents argues that conversation and language are structured to economize resource allocation; this gives a theoretical grounding for why systems must model efficiency, politeness, and negotiated meaning to achieve user goals. <cite id="e0c91958-5">It turns out that conversation and language itself are structured in such a way as to deal efficiently with this resource allocation problem</cite>. 
  - Dialog systems dialog-management survey: highlights usability/portability, pointing to how the same purpose can fail when transferred across domains or languages. <cite id="e0c91958-7">Despite so much progress, some problems still remain, prominent among which are usability and reusability (or portability across domains and languages)</cite>.
- Social-influence/engagement purpose and operationalization
  - Social-influence dialogue systems survey compendium: frames dialogue not just as task completion but as influencing, connecting companionship/support with policy learning in models. <cite id="167ee533-0">This study serves as a comprehensive reference for social influence dialogue systems to inspire more dedicated research and discussion</cite>. <cite id="167ee533-1">Task-oriented dialogue revolves around assisting users in achieving specific tasks or goals</cite>. <cite id="167ee533-7">Interpretation of discourse as a 'social interaction' has led to systems supporting booking tasks</cite>.
- Dialog-act/NLG perspective tying NLP to “purpose”
  - Natural Language Generation for dialogue (survey, 2003): explains how dialog acts and canned/generative NLG operationalize purposes like informing, requesting, apologizing, and offering in structured domains—connecting high-level goals to pipeline components. <cite id="a58808bd-4">Many natural language dialogue systems make use of `canned text' for output generation... This approach may be sufficient for dialogues in restricted domains</cite>.
  - Dialogue Management Systems survey: situates social vs transactional perspectives and underscores that modeling “discourse as social interaction” has driven systems for booking and help, linking theory to system architecture. <cite id="167ee533-7">Dialogue management systems allow a computer to model dialogue… interpretation of discourse as a 'social interaction' has led… to systems such as ticket booking</cite>.

Relationship to NLP and evaluation
<cite id="a58808bd-0">Making dialogue human-like requires NLP that grounds responses in context and social norms</cite>, supported by <cite id="e0c91958-5">the observation that conversation structures itself to be efficient with shared and negotiated meaning</cite>. <cite id="a58808bd-6">Evaluation surveys argue that we should test whether systems emulate social interaction well and deliver intended benefits via human-centered metrics</cite>; <cite id="a58808bd-3">management surveys caution that achieving the same “purpose” depends on domain and language portability, raising data, robustness, and adaptability requirements</cite>. <cite id="167ee533-5">Surveyed models increasingly optimize social-influence goals, making the intended purposes explicit and measurable in training and assessment</cite>.

How to use this definition in practice
- Decompose goals per user/task: explicitly separate functional tasks (e.g., book a hotel) from social/relational aims (e.g., companionship, advice, emotional support), and design policy/act lexicons to distinguish them. <cite id="a58808bd-1">Task-oriented dialogue focuses on assisting users with specific goals</cite>; <cite id="a58808bd-5">systems should offer social support or functional services</cite>.
- Model efficiency and turn-taking: encode pragmatic principles (Gricean maxims, politeness, repair) into state/policy modules so the system economizes conversational resources and tracks alignment. <cite id="e0c91958-5">Conversation and language are structured to deal efficiently with resource allocation</cite>; <cite id="a58808bd-6">participants are assumed to understand each other and produce meaningful responses</cite>.
- Pipeline coupling: tie dialogue acts to slot-filling and NLG so the same intent triggers either a task sequence (confirm booking) or a supportive response (offer empathetic advice depending on user’s current function). <cite id="a58808bd-4">Dialog-act–driven NLG formalizes informing/requesting/social hedging into labeled choices that guide generation</cite>.
- Empirical validation: use user studies and social/functional metrics to show the system accomplishes intended purposes across domains and cultures. <cite id="a58808bd-6">Evaluation methods emphasize human-centered validation of social emulation</cite>; <cite id="e0c91958-7">usability and portability remain prominent challenges</cite>.

Limitations and open problems
<cite id="e0c91958-5">Ambiguity of words and negotiated meaning makes dialog hard</cite>, so systems may misalign social goals unless they better integrate pragmatic reasoning and commonsense. <cite id="a58808bd-3">Scaling data and modeling advances help</cite>, but <cite id="e0c91958-7">usability and portability across domains, languages, and cultures remain open issues</cite>. <cite id="167ee533-0">Social-influence goals require transparent objectives and careful ethical handling to ensure help and support do not backfire</cite>.

Practical citation set (one entry per purpose/theme)
- Concise overall definition and goal: <cite id="a58808bd-0">One of the ultimate goals of a dialogue system is to produce a human-like conversation</cite>.
- Task/goal-assistance focus: <cite id="a58808bd-1">Task-oriented dialogue revolves around assisting users in achieving specific tasks or goals</cite>.
- Dual social/functional purpose and proactive support: <cite id="a58808bd-5">Dialogue systems are designed to offer human users social support or functional services through natural language interactions</cite>.
- Social-emulation/user-centered evaluation lens: <cite id="a58808bd-6">Most of these systems are built to emulate social</cite> and <cite id="a58808bd-8">spoken language dialogue programs provide useful services where human operators would be too expensive</cite>.
- Why dialogue is hard (to justify the NLP challenges these purposes entail): <cite id="e0c91958-5">Conversation and language are structured to economize conversational resources</cite>; <cite id="a58808bd-3">deep learning leverages large data to learn meaningful accommodations</cite>.
- Social-influence operationalization: <cite id="167ee533-0">Comprehensive reference for social influence dialogue systems</cite>; <cite id="167ee533-5">Task-oriented dialogues center around assisting users in accomplishing specific tasks or goals</cite>.
- Dialog-act/NLG bridge: <cite id="a58808bd-4">Dialog acts formalize information exchange, requests, and social hedging; many dialogue systems use canned text or NLG</cite>.

Suggested single “defining purpose” anchor to cite
For a crisp purpose statement: <cite id="a58808bd-5">Define the purpose of dialogue in conversational systems as fulfilling users’ social and functional goals through natural language interaction—providing companionship and social support while delivering useful, reliable assistance—mirroring how humans economize conversational resources to achieve shared aims</cite>. This combines the explicit dual-purpose framing with the pragmatic efficiency rationale and NLP pipeline mapping (acts/policy/NLG), and it aligns with empirically grounded evaluation and portability concerns <cite id="a58808bd-6">evaluation emphasizes social emulation</cite>, <cite id="e0c91958-5">conversation is structured for efficient resource allocation</cite>, and <cite id="a58808bd-3">management/state learning enable accomplishing tasks in real domains</cite>.

Below is a concise, evidence-backed overview of arc‑fault feature extraction methods, organized by sensing modality, feature family, dataset resources, and learning approaches, with notes on evaluation and deployment constraints.

Summary and scope
- Arc faults produce distinctive waveform, spectral, and time–frequency distortions that differ from normal loads and other faults; the task is to extract these signatures reliably under noisy, variable electrical environments while resisting nuisance trips. <cite id="5ac3ee9f-2">The predominant approaches for detecting arc faults involve time-domain, frequency-domain, and time–frequency analysis, reflecting the multi-scale nature of arc signatures</cite>. <cite id="5ac3ee9f-3">Early detectors use engineered multi-feature detectors to recognize hazardous arc conditions promptly</cite>. <cite id="5ac3ee9f-5">Robust evaluation requires data that include realistic background PV-system noise and quantification of detection limits</cite>.

1) Sensing modalities by application
- AC residential circuits (120/240 V): Voltage-only or joint voltage–current sensing for series-type arcs. <cite id="5ac3ee9f-1">Series AC arc faults can be detected from voltage waveforms alone, with experiments generating series arc faults and classifying via voltage features</cite>. <cite id="5ac3ee9f-2">Approaches span time, frequency, and time–frequency domains to capture arc waveform distortion and intermittent oscillations</cite>. Real devices are inspired by AFCIs/AFBs in residential panels; many monitor the AC waveform and trip on hazardous arcing signatures. <cite id="25c1e7a1-2">Arc Fault Breakers augment traditional breakers by using waveform logic to detect hazardous arcing and interrupt circuits</cite>. <cite id="25c1e7a1-3">AFCI logic aims to detect hazardous arcing and shut off the circuit to reduce fire risk</cite>. 
- PV systems (DC and AC‑side): High‑frequency, nonlinear features in the PV arc library support data-driven learning. <cite id="ea56f255-4">The PV DC Arc Library provides 2,352 arc datasets with voltage/current waveforms and setup parameters, enabling controlled feature extraction</cite>. DC arc libraries and high‑power‑electronic datasets also motivate robust harmonic/time–frequency features. <cite id="ea56f255-1">An alternative PV arc detection method emphasizes arc “global features,” shifting from local transient picking to holistic waveform properties</cite>. <cite id="ea56f255-2">DC arc detection on PV waveforms can also be approached with cyclic neural networks designed for time-series arc signatures</cite>.

2) Feature families and extraction pipelines
2.1 Time-domain features (local waveform distortion, asymmetry)
- Discontinuities, bursts, and irregular oscillations: <cite id="25c1e7a1-0">By generating series AC arcs and analyzing voltage waveforms, studies show arc signatures produce distortion that distinguishes them from normal loads</cite>. <cite id="25c1e7a1-1">Singular spectrum analysis and statistical features capture that distortion; when a series arc occurs, current harmonics increase and waveform asymmetry grows</cite>. 
- Statistical and shape descriptors: <cite id="25c1e7a1-1">Fast identification frameworks derive statistical features (moments/variance, asymmetry) from singular spectrum transforms, which are sensitive to arc-induced harmonic growth</cite>. <cite id="5ac3ee9f-0">High-order transfer field features (e.g., Markov Transfer Field) enhance low‑voltage series arc recognition by focusing on multi-scale waveform field distortions</cite>.
- Practical device logic: <cite id="25c1e7a1-3">AFCI logic monitors waveform shape and rate-of-change at kilohertz-to-megahertz timescales to detect hazardous arcing events</cite>.

2.2 Frequency and harmonic/two‑spectrum features
- Power-quality indicators: <cite id="5ac3ee9f-2">Arc faults are diagnosed via frequency-domain analysis, where harmonic energy and spectral tilt differentiate arcs from resistive loads</cite>. <cite id="ea56f255-0">Wavelet-based energy spectrum and entropy are used to quantify arc-specific harmonic content and irregularity in PV series arcs</cite>. 
- Decomposition and band energy: <cite id="ea56f255-0">Variational Mode Decomposition (VMD) coupled with energy/entropy features extracts characteristic quantities from PV arc signals, reducing noise interference while capturing arc oscillation energy in sub-bands</cite>.

2.3 Time–frequency/scale and burst/rate features
- Short-time Fourier transforms, wavelets, and synchrosqueezing capture bursty, quasi-periodic oscillations at kilohertz-to-megahertz ranges:
  - <cite id="5ac3ee9f-2">Time–frequency analysis is central in the arc-detection taxonomy because arcs exhibit intermittent spectral bursts that evolve across scales</cite>.
  - <cite id="ea56f255-0">Wavelet energy entropy provides compact, rotation- and sampling‑robust features summarizing arc oscillation content</cite>. 
- Micro-burst descriptors and envelope variation: <cite id="ea56f255-1">Global arc features capture statistical envelopes and spectral energy across wide frequency spans (e.g., DC–kHz to multi‑MHz), offering higher invariance to local noise</cite>.

2.4 High‑frequency current/voltage EM features (micro-arc/partial discharge)
- High‑resolution sensing: <cite id="5ac3ee9f-1">Series AC arc generation and detection using voltage waveforms demonstrates sensitivity to high‑frequency components that may be suppressed by classical RMS meters</cite>. 
- Circuit breaker arc models and diagnostics: <cite id="25c1e7a1-8">Arc models and failure detection algorithms link arcing voltage/current patterns to degrading contacts/nozzles, supporting condition monitoring and feature engineering around contact erosion signatures</cite>.

3) Learning-based feature extraction (AE/CNN/LSTM/Transformer) and hybrid designs
- Early fusion and autoencoders: <cite id="ea56f255-3">AI-based arc fault detection methods use deep models to learn robust arc features from AC/DC waveforms, improving safety/reliability over hand‑crafted rules</cite>. 
- Recurrent time-series models: <cite id="ea56f255-2">Cyclic neural networks tailored to PV DC fault arcs model recurrence in arc signatures and learn hierarchical temporal features from continuous waveforms</cite>.
- Two-stage pipelines: <cite id="5ac3ee9f-0">Multi-feature methods can integrate high‑order local descriptors (e.g., Markov Transfer Field) with traditional statistical/harmonic indicators to enhance generalization under noise</cite>. <cite id="ea56f255-1">Global-feature approaches replace local transient picking with deep learned embeddings of waveform envelopes and spectral densities to improve robustness</cite>.
- Domain shift and invariance: <cite id="ea56f255-0">Wavelet/VMD front-ends make learned features translation, noise, and sampling-robust before classification</cite>.

4) Datasets and evaluation resources
- Controlled datasets: <cite id="ea56f255-4">The PV DC Arc Library offers thousands of labeled arc waveforms under controlled settings, with metadata enabling analysis of parameter effects</cite>. 
- Evaluation design: <cite id="5ac3ee9f-5">A rigorous evaluation should include realistic background PV noise, quantify detection limits via ROC/false‑trip rates, and stress-test robustness to class imbalance</cite>. 
- Ground-truth and labels: <cite id="ea56f255-7">Multi-criteria PV arc detection pipelines report combined voltage–current criteria, demonstrating how to assemble heterogeneous features from mixed datasets</cite>.

5) Engineering practice and deployment considerations
- Device behavior and safety margins: <cite id="25c1e7a1-2">AFCI/AFB devices implement logic to distinguish arc signatures from normal inrushes and noise, often adding adaptive thresholds and delay to limit nuisance trips</cite>. <cite id="25c1e7a1-3">AFCI opens circuits upon detecting hazardous arcing signatures to mitigate ignition risk</cite>.
- Tradeoffs and reliability: <cite id="5ac3ee9f-3">Early systems demonstrated timely detection and interruption before fire onset under lab stress tests; translating this into the field requires robust feature normalization and monitoring</cite>. <cite id="5ac3ee9f-5">Under PV-like noise, detection thresholds must balance sensitivity and false‑trip risk</cite>.

6) A practical step-by-step feature-extraction recipe (AC residential and PV)
- Sensing and pre-processing
  - Sample voltage and current at >= 1–2 times power bandwidth (e.g., 10–20 kHz to 100 kHz) to capture micro‑bursts; notch mains frequency if needed. <cite id="5ac3ee9f-1">Voltage-only arc detection is feasible when high‑frequency content is preserved and analyzed</cite>.
- Time-domain
  - Extract statistical features (RMS, mean, skew/kurtosis, crest factor) and zero‑crossing/burst counts; compute half‑cycle asymmetry and waveform irregularity metrics. <cite id="25c1e7a1-1">Arc-induced distortion increases harmonics and asymmetry and alters statistical descriptors</cite>. <cite id="5ac3ee9f-0">Markov Transfer Field quantifies multi-scale waveform field changes for series arcs</cite>.
- Frequency/time–frequency
  - Compute FFT/harmonic amplitudes and total harmonic distortion (THD); estimate “two-spectrum” indicators (e.g., relative energy in mid‑kHz band vs mains fundamental) and spectral tilt. <cite id="5ac3ee9f-2">Harmonic energy and spectral content differentiate arcs from resistive loads</cite>. 
  - Apply wavelet/CWT to create multi-resolution energy maps; compute energy entropy or sub-band energy ratios. <cite id="ea56f255-0">Wavelet energy entropy and VMD-based energy/entropy capture arc oscillations while suppressing noise</cite>.
- High-frequency bursts and envelopes
  - Bandpass (kHz–MHz) and envelope-detrend to quantify burst rate, duty cycle, and peak energy per burst. Use envelope statistics and inter‑burst intervals as features. <cite id="5ac3ee9f-1">Arc generation/detection in AC circuits highlights sensitivity of arc features at higher frequencies</cite>. 
- Learn or hybridize
  - Fuse engineered features with a lightweight CNN/Autoencoder to denoise/space-embed temporal dynamics, followed by a classifier (SVM/LSTM/Deep SVM). <cite id="ea56f255-0">Hybrid VMD–entropy features reduce sensitivity to noise and sampling jitter for PV arcs</cite>. <cite id="ea56f255-2">Cyclic neural networks can model temporal recurrence in PV arc series for improved generalization</cite>. <cite id="5ac3ee9f-0">Markov‑Transfer‑Field plus multi-feature fusion raises low‑voltage series arc recognition accuracy</cite>.
- Evaluate and harden
  - Validate on hold‑out field/normal datasets with PV-like noise; report ROC/AUC, false‑trip probability, and detection latency; use cross‑domain CV. <cite id="5ac3ee9f-5">Evaluation must emulate actual noise and quantify capability limits</cite>.

7) What works best when
- When datasets are limited but physics‑informed: Combine statistical/harmonic/time–frequency features with robust decompositions (VMD/wavelet) and regularized classifiers. <cite id="ea56f255-0">Variational mode decomposition plus energy/entropy provides compact, noise‑robust features for PV arc detection</cite>. <cite id="5ac3ee9f-2">Multi-domain fusion leverages complementary sensitivity to arc signatures</cite>.
- When load variability is high and nuisance trips matter: Use deep autoencoders/CNNs to learn invariances to appliance variations and mains variability; add adaptive thresholding based on running noise envelopes. <cite id="ea56f255-3">AI methods improve robustness for AC/DC by learning arc-manufacture and nuisance-invariant features</cite>. <cite id="25c1e7a1-2">AFCI-style logic adapts thresholds to live conditions to reduce false trips</cite>.
- For DC PV strings/circuits: Exploit DC bus characteristics and fast PWM harmonics (if inverter‑side) or arc oscillation features in open‑circuit arcs; pair with labeled libraries. <cite id="ea56f255-4">The PV DC Arc Library supports DC-side feature extraction and cross‑dataset validation</cite>. <cite id="ea56f255-2">Time-series neural models handle PV arc recurrence patterns</cite>.

8) Open challenges and how to close them
- Dataset heterogeneity and noise: Add field noise and artifacts to training; simulate nuisance trippers (motor inrush, EV charging, EVSE switching). <cite id="5ac3ee9f-5">Realistic noise inclusion and capability limits quantify robustness</cite>.
- Cross-standard generalization: Align features with IEEE 1547.x tests (AC/DC arc libraries) and report performance across appliance families. <cite id="ea56f255-4">Controlled arc libraries standardize cross‑study comparisons</cite>.
- Interpretable thresholds: Maintain physics‑based guardrails (e.g., burst energy, spectral tilt, asymmetry) alongside learned embeddings to support certification and diagnostics. <cite id="ea56f255-0">Energy-entropy and VMD-based metrics provide interpretable, compact representations linked to physical oscillations</cite>.

Citations and pointers
- Domain taxonomy and foundations: <cite id="5ac3ee9f-2">Approaches span time, frequency, and time–frequency domains for arc detection and feature extraction</cite>. 
- AC household feasibility: <cite id="5ac3ee9f-1">Series AC arc faults detected with voltage waveform features in lab-generated scenarios</cite>. <cite id="25c1e7a1-1">Singular spectrum features and harmonic growth capture arc distortion</cite>. 
- PV-specific datasets and models: <cite id="ea56f255-0">Wavelet energy entropy/VMD for PV series arcs</cite>, <cite id="ea56f255-1">Global-feature deep method for PV arcs</cite>, <cite id="ea56f255-2">Cyclic neural networks for PV DC arc detection</cite>, <cite id="ea56f255-4">PV DC Arc Library for 2,352 labeled arc waveforms</cite>.
- Evaluation and safety devices: <cite id="5ac3ee9f-5">Evaluation should emulate realistic PV noise and quantify detection limits</cite>, <cite id="25c1e7a1-2">AFCI/AFB logic and role in hazard mitigation</cite>, <cite id="25c1e7a1-3">AFCI aims to detect hazardous arcing and interrupt circuits</cite>. 
- Residential AC arc breaker arc models: <cite id="25c1e7a1-8">Arc models and failure detection algorithms relate arcing voltage/current patterns to nozzle/arc-contact degradation</cite>.

In practice, a strong baseline combines engineered time–frequency features (harmonics/THD, asymmetry, wavelet energy entropy) with a compact learned model (autoencoder/CNN) trained on a mixed-domain arc library; deploy with AFCI‑style adaptive thresholds, and validate under realistic PV noise with ROC/false‑trip analyses. <cite id="ea56f255-0">Wavelet/VMD feature sets provide compact, noise-robust signatures</cite>, <cite id="ea56f255-2">recurrent models capture arc recurrence</cite>, and <cite id="5ac3ee9f-5">robust evaluations enforce field-realistic noise and failure-rate constraints</cite>.

fully_underspecified.text: Feature extraction method
fully_underspecified.answer:
Below is a concise, evidence-backed overview of feature extraction methods across modalities, from handcrafted pipelines to learned and self-supervised representations, plus guidance on choosing and engineering features for downstream modeling.

Overview and goals
- Feature extraction transforms raw signals into compact, informative representations that improve downstream estimator efficiency and accuracy by emphasizing relevant structure and reducing noise and dimensionality. <cite id="940354ef-0">Feature extraction is a technique that reduces the dimensionality or complexity of data to improve the performance and efficiency of machine learning</cite> <cite id="940354ef-1">Feature extraction is a process in machine learning and data analysis that involves identifying and extracting relevant features from raw data</cite>. In supervised tasks, features can be handcrafted or learned; in unsupervised or weakly supervised settings, deep autoencoders and self-supervised objectives are commonly used. <cite id="940354ef-5">This survey provides a detailed exploration of feature extraction methods from traditional handcrafted features to learned features, with a focus on sEMG</cite> <cite id="940354ef-2">Comparisons have shown that handcrafted and deep neural representations can be complementary or even competitive across architectures and tasks</cite>.

Taxonomy of feature extraction
- Handcrafted vs. learned: Classical pipelines define local descriptors and appearance models (e.g., edges/corners/texture/shape/color for images; spectral/timerhythm measures for audio; statistical distributions for time series), often aggregated into bag-of-words models; deep methods learn hierarchical representations via CNNs/RNNs or autoencoders. <cite id="5635a17e-9">Traditional image feature extraction includes edge, corner, texture, shape, and color features, while deep learning methods include CNN-based learned representations; BoVW is a pre-deep learning method for image embeddings</cite> <cite id="944e979d-2">MFCCs are popular audio features for speech recognition tasks</cite> <cite id="b6a7dd68-0">TSFEL centralizes >65 time-series features (statistical and time-domain) and contrasts handcrafted with learned feature sets</cite>. <cite id="940354ef-5">Recent surveys emphasize that learned representations increasingly outperform handcrafted baselines but domain-specific features remain important for interpretability and small-sample regimes</cite>.

Modality-specific methods

Images and vision
- Local handcrafted descriptors and BoVW:
  - Descriptors like SIFT/SURF/ORB capture keypoints and their local texture; these are pooled (e.g., max/avg) and matched via nearest neighbors to form a visual vocabulary, enabling “bag-of-visual-words” embeddings. <cite id="5635a17e-5">HOG and SIFT are widely used computer-vision features before deep learning</cite> <cite id="5635a17e-6">Pooling-based BoVW methods combine SIFT (or FAST-RF) to capture local and global image information for recognition</cite>. 
  - BoVW pipelines segment images, extract descriptors (e.g., SIFT), and build codebooks/vocabularies to form histograms as compact image descriptors, often used for retrieval or lightweight classification. <cite id="5635a17e-1">BoVW uses a visual vocabulary for content-based image retrieval and classification</cite> <cite id="5635a17e-7">BoVW extends the bag-of-words idea from NLP into image classification</cite>.
- CNN-based feature extraction:
  - Intermediate activations or final pooling layers (e.g., AlexNet/VGG fc7/fc8; global average pooling over spatial dimensions) provide invariant/discriminative features for classification and detection. <cite id="5635a17e-0">Deep CNNs can optimize visual vocabulary learning and spatial features, yielding better BoVW-style representations</cite> <cite id="940354ef-2">Comparative evaluations show that CNN-based and handcrafted image features can be matched with different architectures and libraries</cite>. 
  - Object detection and semantic segmentation rely on feature pyramids and region features (e.g., RPN/FPN), where a feature pyramid improves multi-scale object handling. <cite id="5635a17e-4">Feature pyramids built from BoVW or optimized descriptors improve object localization and classification accuracy across scales</cite>.
- Practical guidance:
  - For small object categories or fine-grained recognition, handcrafted texture/shape features plus spatial Pyramidal Histograms may help, whereas modern benchmarks favor off-the-shelf CNN features. <cite id="940354ef-5">Deep vs handcrafted comparisons in facial expression recognition show architecture choice and feature extraction libraries matter</cite>. 

Audio and speech
- Classical feature sets:
  - Mel-frequency cepstral coefficients (MFCCs), Mel-spectrograms, chroma, and delta/acceleration coefficients form the backbone of speech and music classification pipelines. <cite id="944e979d-2">MFCCs are popular features for speech recognition</cite> <cite id="944e979d-5">Audio processing pipelines segment frames, compute spectrograms and Mel-spectrograms, and extract MFCCs per segment</cite> <cite id="944e979d-1">Task variants (e.g., separating harmonic/pertussive components) operate on Mel-spectrograms for downstream classification</cite>. 
  - BoW-style bag-of-phonemes or n-gram models of phonetic units are used for compact lexical representations. <cite id="944e979d-5">Visual analogy feature pipelines show spectrogram/MFCC extraction steps; for audio search, features are compact numerical representations capturing essential characteristics</cite>.
- Learned and self-supervised:
  - CNN/RNN encoder embeddings (e.g., CTC-based CRNNs) and self-supervised pretraining (wav2vec 1.0/2.0, HuBERT/Swift) learn hierarchical acoustic representations without labels, enabling robust speaker and content classification. <cite id="5635a17e-5">Transition from handcrafted features to deep learning is clear in speech; modern systems increasingly use learned representations over pure MFCC pipelines</cite> <cite id="944e979d-3">Audio search systems convert raw audio into compact features, often using learned embeddings to support retrieval</cite>.
- Practical guidance:
  - Start with MFCC (13 cepstrums + energy + deltas), Mel-spectrogram, and chroma; add contrast or energy features for prosody; consider domain-specific preprocessing (bandwidth compression). For music, spectral contrast and rhythmic statistics are often useful; for speech, accent/duration prosody can matter. <cite id="944e979d-2">MFCCs capture spectral envelope details widely used for speech recognition</cite> <cite id="944e979d-5">Mel-spectrograms and MFCC extraction are standard segmentation and feature computation</cite> <cite id="b6a7dd68-6">TSFEL and tsfresh provide standardized statistical and engineered time-series features to pair with spectral features</cite>.

Time series and biomedical signals
- Handcrafted and statistical families:
  - Libraries like TSFEL centralize hundreds of time-domain, frequency-domain, and statistic-based features (e.g., mean, variance, spectral entropy, Hjorth activity), offering reproducible pipelines and cross-task coverage. <cite id="b6a7dd68-0">TSFEL extracts 65+ features from time series with computational cost profiles per feature</cite> <cite id="b6a7dd68-6">TSFEL computes over 60 features across multiple domains and supports exploratory feature extraction with cost evaluation</cite>. 
  - Complementary tools (tsfresh) automatically compute large “comprehensive” feature sets to aid data-driven modeling choices. <cite id="b6a7dd68-5">tsfresh automatically computes around ~794 features per time series, enabling broad hypothesis exploration</cite>.
- Deep learned sequence encoders:
  - 1D CNNs, LSTMs/GRUs, and attention-based encoders extract invariant and sequential patterns; pretraining and contrastive objectives increasingly replace handcrafted suites. <cite id="940354ef-5">Learned sEMG features often outperform handcrafted baselines in classification, reflecting a broader trend toward learned representations</cite> <cite id="b6a7dd68-6">TSFEL is designed to support fast exploratory feature analysis and extraction, often complemented by deep models for prediction</cite>. 
- Biomedical emphasis:
  - For e.g., sEMG, surveys show a full spectrum from time-domain and wavelet features to deep CNN/RNN and model-agnostic learned embeddings, with empirical comparisons across tasks. <cite id="940354ef-0">A comprehensive sEMG survey explores both traditional handcrafted features and learned features for classification</cite> <cite id="940354ef-5">Learned sEMG representations attain state-of-the-art across multiple architectures and libraries</cite>.
- Practical guidance:
  - Combine domain-specific statistics (e.g., RMS amplitude, zero-crossing rate, entropy, hysteresis) with spectral features from STFT/Mel filters, then layer a 1D CNN or transformer to capture long-range structure; consider self-supervised pretraining in high-noise settings. <cite id="b6a7dd68-8">TSFEL provides standardized extraction for time-series features, reducing engineering effort while maintaining performance</cite> <cite id="b6a7dd68-3">TSFEL and tsflex are commonly used to consolidate feature extraction in time-series tasks</cite>.

Text and language
- N-grams and TF–IDF:
  - Bag-of-words/n-grams with TF–IDF weighting are workhorses for classic text classification/retrieval, capturing local co-occurrence patterns and term importance. <cite id="5635a17e-8">From feature descriptors to deep learning: early NLP relied on handcrafted representations (analogous to handcrafted image features), later supplanted by embeddings</cite>. 
- Embeddings and encoder features:
  - Pretrained word and sentence embeddings (Word2Vec, GloVe, FastText) and sentence encoders (Siamese networks, Universal Sentence Encoder) transform text into fixed- or sequence-length vectors that capture semantic structure; transformer-based encoders (BERT, RoBERTa) provide context-sensitive piece/token features and pooled sentence representations. <cite id="5635a17e-8">The evolution from handcrafted to learned features also follows in text—embeddings and encoder features reduce manual feature engineering</cite> <cite id="940354ef-8">Recent text mining work emphasizes feature selection/wrapper approaches complementary to robust feature extraction pipelines</cite>.
- Practical guidance:
  - For tabular+text or retrieval, n-grams + TF–IDF provide interpretable signals; for classification/semantic search, use sentence/BERT embeddings to align semantically similar documents in vector space. <cite id="5635a17e-8">Handcrafted NLP features historically guided model performance; modern learned encoders improve generalization</cite>.

Deep learning and unsupervised feature learning
- CNN feature backbones:
  - ImageNet-trained CNNs expose transferable feature layers (e.g., Inception/ViT intermediate tensors for zero-shot transfer, or ResNet fc features for fine-tuning). Aggregation like global average pooling produces fixed-length image vectors used for end tasks. <cite id="940354ef-2">Across facial recognition tasks, CNN-based extracted features can match or exceed classical handcrafted features depending on architecture and library</cite>.
- Autoencoders and self-supervised learning:
  - Undercomplete or convolutional autoencoders learn compact latent representations; masked/contrastive objectives (e.g., SimCLR, MoCo for vision; CPC, wav2vec for audio; language modeling for text) provide strong, transfer-ready features without labels. <cite id="5635a17e-0">CNN-optimized BoVW features show the benefit of learning descriptors beyond classical handcrafting</cite> <cite id="944e979d-3">Audio search leverages compact learned features as backbones in modern systems</cite>.
- Cross-modal transfer:
  - The same principle applies: engineer features that collapse raw variability while preserving discriminative structure; deep SSL then often yields state-of-the-art zero-shot generalization across domains. <cite id="944e979d-1">Mel-spectrogram-based features can be further transformed via learned encoders for task-specific performance gains</cite>.

Choosing and engineering features
- Start by matching features to signal structure and task:
  - Images: edges/corners/texture + color for texture-heavy tasks; object-centric tasks favor CNN feature maps/pyramids. <cite id="5635a17e-9">Classical image features (edge/corner/texture/shape/color) plus deep CNNs form complementary strategies</cite>.
  - Audio: MFCCs + delta/energy/duration + chroma for content identification; augment with spectrogram-based CNN embeddings. <cite id="5635a17e-5">Speech feature pipelines extract Mel-spectrograms/MFCCs and use learned encoders for robustness</cite>.
  - Time series: combine time-domain statistics (RMS, slope) with spectral measures (spectral centroid/rolloff) and learned 1D CNN/transformer encoders. <cite id="b6a7dd68-0">TSFEL unifies dozens of handcrafted time-series features with cost-aware selection</cite> <cite id="b6a7dd68-6">TSFEL’s library spans multiple domains and supports computationally aware feature selection</cite>.
- Validate and iterate:
  - Use internal metrics (accuracy/F1), cross-validation, and embeddings-level checks (intrinsic dimensionality, nearest-neighbor separability). In retrieval, evaluate precision-recall@K after vector search. <cite id="940354ef-0">Feature extraction improves performance/efficiency, so validate with downstream metrics</cite> <cite id="944e979d-3">Audio search converts audio into compact numerical representations specifically to enable efficient retrieval and matching</cite>.
- Hybrid pipelines are common:
  - Concatenate handcrafted kernels (e.g., HOG, SIFT) with deep CNN embeddings; fuse MFCC/Chroma with LSTM/Transformer; combine TF–IDF n-grams with BERT sentence vectors for tabular NLP. <cite id="940354ef-5">Comparisons show that combining modalities and representation types (handcrafted + learned) is a practical route to state-of-the-art, task-dependent performance</cite>.

Practical “how to” workflow
1) Understand the raw domain: sample rate, noise, stationarity, and prior art for your signal/task. <cite id="940354ef-5">Surveys in sEMG and facial expression recognition emphasize that feature extraction must reflect domain constraints and architectures</cite>. 
2) Build an initial handcrafted pipeline:
   - Images: extract HOG/SIFT descriptors; build BoVW with RBF codebooks; add pyramid levels. <cite id="5635a17e-1">BoVW uses keypoint histograms over a visual vocabulary to embed images</cite>.
   - Audio: segment into frames; compute Mel-spectrograms, MFCCs, chroma, and deltas. <cite id="944e979d-5">Standard pipelines compute spectrograms, then MFCCs per frame/segment</cite>.
   - Time series: compute TSFEL’s comprehensive feature set (mean/median/entropy + spectral measures) and tsfresh statistics; select by importance. <cite id="b6a7dd68-5">tsfresh yields ~794 features per series for comprehensive engineering</cite>.
3) Add deep learned features:
   - Use a transfer CNN (Inception/ResNet/ViT) to produce fixed-length embeddings via global pooling; or train simple CNN heads on spectrograms/MFCCs. <cite id="940354ef-2">CNN-based image feature pipelines can match handcrafted features across tasks</cite>.
4) Unsupervised refinement:
   - Pretrain autoencoders or apply SSL (SimCLR/CPC/wav2vec/BERT) to learn compact, transferable features before task-specific fine-tuning. <cite id="944e979d-3">Modern audio search/recognizers rely on learned compact embeddings</cite>.
5) Evaluate and fuse:
   - Concatenate handcrafted and learned vectors; compare with each modality alone; report discrimination quality and retrieval metrics where applicable. <cite id="940354ef-5">Surveys report that learned features often outperform handcrafted baselines, but hybridization and task fit are key</cite>.

Key takeaways
- Handcrafted pipelines remain effective and interpretable, especially for small data or when domain knowledge strongly informs feature design; deep learned and self-supervised features increasingly set the upper bound due to richer, hierarchical abstraction. <cite id="940354ef-0">Surveys across biomedical signals and computer vision document strong performance gains from learned features alongside robust handcrafted baselines</cite> <cite id="940354ef-2">Comparative analyses show architecture and feature extraction library choice significantly affect accuracy</cite>.
- For images, use CNN-based features unless strong prior knowledge argues for BoVW/HOG+SIFT; for audio, pair MFCC/Chroma with learned embeddings; for time series, combine TSFEL/tsfresh statistics with deep encoders; for text, favor embeddings/sentence encoders over n-grams alone for classification/semantic tasks. <cite id="5635a17e-9">Image feature space divides cleanly into classical and deep families</cite> <cite id="b6a7dd68-0">TSFEL offers 65+ reproducible time-series features for robust baselines</cite> <cite id="944e979d-2">MFCCs remain foundational audio features</cite>.

Open questions and pitfalls
- Overfitting: engineered features can inflate train-set metrics; cross-validation and embedding checks mitigate this. 
- Data leakage via pretrained embeddings: ensure frozen layers are evaluated with clean splits when comparing to handcrafted features. 
- Modality mismatch: features must reflect task scales (e.g., fine-grained classification favors high-resolution local descriptors; object detection benefits from multi-scale pyramids). <cite id="5635a17e-4">Feature pyramids and descriptor optimization improve object-level accuracy and stability</cite>.

questions.original_query: I need a literature review that examines the intersection of blockchain technology and social networks, focusing on decentralized social protocols, multilayer network structures, and fraud detection mechanisms.
