query.text: I need a literature review that examines the intersection of blockchain technology and social networks, focusing on decentralized social protocols, multilayer network structures, and fraud detection mechanisms. We analyze the evolution of blockchain applications beyond decentralized finance, particularly in social networking contexts, and evaluate current approaches to crypto fraud detection using deep neural networks (DNN).
query.answer:
Title: Blockchain and Social Networks Converge: Decentralized Social Protocols, Multilayer Structures, and Deep Neural Fraud Detection

Summary
Decentralized social protocols embed user identity, content addressing, and participation logic into blockchains to reduce reliance on centralized intermediaries, enabling verifiable provenance, tokenized incentives, and on-chain governance in social applications beyond finance. <cite id="78710d9a-6">Surveys of blockchain-based secure social networks report that on-chain architectures provide privacy, security, data integrity, and user empowerment for social networking use cases</cite>. <cite id="78710d9a-4">Ethereum’s social-networking page frames decentralized social networks as blockchain-based platforms where users exchange and publish content directly</cite>. <cite id="78710d9a-1">Recent work proposes DeSocial, a framework for integrating distributed data and learning within Ethereum-based decentralized social networking</cite>. These systems are complemented by DAO governance and reputation layers that align participation and moderation, but they face persistent challenges in voter apathy, incentive design, and governance attack surfaces. <cite id="372148ff-1">Communication research finds decentralized social media reshape participatory communication and platform governance, shifting power and participation to token-based mechanisms</cite>. <cite id="372148ff-3">DAO meta-analyses note governance favors majority token holders and lacks reputation-based incentives</cite>. 

Concurrently, multilayer network science and blockchain-specific designs articulate the on-chain/off-chain interaction, multiplex identity/graph layers, and reputation overlays underpinning decentralized social ecosystems. <cite id="eb8ecf67-0">Multilayer network science provides a unifying framework for systems with interconnected and interdependent relationships</cite>. <cite id="eb8ecf67-3">Formal multilayer analysis defines multiple relationship layers within a single mathematical structure</cite>. <cite id="eb8ecf67-2">Blockchain self-sovereign identity work proposes a multi-layer trust framework leveraging verifiers and issuers, integrating cryptographic credentials with on-chain accountability</cite>. <cite id="eb8ecf67-7">Blockchain governance blends norms, legal/organizational constructs, and code, creating multi-scalar decision layers</cite>. 

Fraud detection is a central evaluation challenge for these protocols and for DeFi more broadly. While classical rule-based and ML classifiers achieve strong performance, DNN-based models that incorporate transaction, contract, and social-graph signals have become state of the art. <cite id="2b55cade-0">Taxonomies of DeFi fraud organized by the project lifecycle enumerate attack classes that span pre-launch fundraising, deployment, and post-launch interaction layers</cite>. <cite id="2b55cade-2">Comparative systematics of blockchain-based fraud detection report supervised methods such as XGBoost achieve high accuracy on labeled datasets, with federated learning pipelines achieving around 91% accuracy</cite>. <cite id="2b55cade-1">Latest knowledge-grounded LLM frameworks for cryptocurrency scam detection use retrieval to fuse textual artifacts and knowledge graphs, improving detection over baselines</cite>. <cite id="2b55cade-5">GNN-enhanced deep models on the Elliptic Bitcoin dataset demonstrate strong performance in distinguishing illicit from legitimate actor graphs, supporting scalable detection pipelines</cite>. 

Below we synthesize the literature along three axes and assess the evolution beyond DeFi into social networking, then evaluate DNN-based detection approaches.

1. Decentralized Social Protocols: Design, Governance, and Incentives
Decentralized social protocols are designed to internalize social graph primitives—handles, following/publishing, moderation votes, and reputation—into smart-contractible state and cryptographic identity, aiming to reduce censorship and increase user control. <cite id="78710d9a-4">Decentralized social networks allow users to publish and distribute content directly on blockchains, removing central content hosts</cite>. <cite id="78710d9a-6">Surveys emphasize improved privacy/security and data integrity via cryptographic guarantees and permissionable access</cite>. <cite id="78710d9a-1">DeSocial demonstrates an integration path where social data and learning are distributed across nodes, with smart contracts managing access and incentives</cite>. 

Protocol-level governance and content curation are typically delegated to DAOs, but incentive misalignment persists. <cite id="372148ff-3">Meta-analyses find governance tokenization tends to privilege majority token holders and lacks reputation-based accountability</cite>. <cite id="372148ff-4">Empirical work notes long-standing challenges in aligning participation, accountability, and decision/voting with incentive structures</cite>. <cite id="78710d9a-5">Recent commentary argues decentralized social platforms are reshaping digital interactions by restoring privacy and user control, while also requiring robust governance design</cite>. <cite id="372148ff-8">Practical guidance documents warn of governance-attack vectors and propose framework designs to harden voting and proposal mechanisms</cite>. Communication- and sociology-focused analyses further stress that tokenized communicative power alters participation dynamics and deliberation quality. <cite id="372148ff-1">Frontiers research finds decentralized social media reshape participatory communication and platform governance, evidencing new communicative power hierarchies based on tokenization</cite>. <cite id="372148ff-9">A chapter on DAO governance outlines incentive alignment and rapid coordination benefits alongside structural vulnerabilities in accountability and democratic participation</cite>. 

Practical deployments illustrate two complementary models: identity-first (on-chain profile graphs) like Farcaster, and substrate-based “social graph” stacks that externalize moderation and indexing. <cite id="78710d9a-3">Guides to decentralized social apps leverage Farcaster’s protocol to handle identity and data management, allowing application builders to focus on social features</cite>. <cite id="78710d9a-2">Developers also reference Lens as a composable social protocol, though adoption timelines and general availability remain variable</cite>. <cite id="78710d9a-8">Explainer pieces highlight how decentralized social media can enable communities organized around diverse interests and goals, emphasizing user-centric control</cite>. These protocols can be layered with reputation and trust frameworks to support content moderation and access control. <cite id="eb8ecf67-2">A multi-layer SSI trust framework integrates issuers and verifiers to represent heterogeneous trust relationships</cite>. <cite id="eb8ecf67-8">Blockchain reputation systems propose tokenization and smart contracts to establish trustworthy collaboration graphs for business interactions</cite>. 

2. Multilayer Network Structures: From Identity and Graphs to Governance and Risk Propagation
Decentralized social systems exhibit multilayer structures: identities and social edges (layer 1), cryptographic credentials and claims (layer 2), reputation scores (layer 3), and governance/voting flows (layer 4), with cross-layer dependencies. <cite id="eb8ecf67-0">Multilayer network science frames interconnected and interdependent systems as coupled layers with distinct relationship types</cite>. <cite id="eb8ecf67-3">Formally, multiple sets of relationships can co-exist in one structure, enabling cross-layer analysis of influence, resilience, and fraud propagation</cite>. <cite id="eb8ecf67-1">Shifts from single-layer to multilayer social network models better capture complex, multiplexed interactions</cite>. <cite id="eb8ecf67-7">Governance layers integrate code and social norms, making governance dynamics a coupling surface between technical and organizational layers</cite>. 

Self-sovereign identity and trust composition articulate how social graphs can be anchored in verifiable credentials and on-chain proofs, enabling decentralized authentication and privacy-preserving graph traversal. <cite id="eb8ecf67-2">A multi-layer SSI framework defines issuer–verifier relationships as a trust graph overlay on top of social and contract states, supporting fine-grained permissioning</cite>. <cite id="eb8ecf67-8">Reputation layers add token-based scoring and slashing to deter bad behavior and align incentives</cite>. Governance games model participation costs and attack incentives across layers. <cite id="eb8ecf67-5">Multi-layered blockchain governance games analyze strategy spaces to protect safety under attacker budgets and cross-layer coordination failures</cite>. <cite id="78710d9a-6">Surveyed blockchain social solutions leverage these layered architectures to combine privacy, integrity, and user empowerment</cite>. In practice, developers are building “reputation layers” and cross-chain identity bridges to interlink disparate social-graph instances. <cite id="eb8ecf67-4">Community projects describe reputation substrates that ease the construction of internet-wide identity graphs</cite>. 

These multilayer stacks have implications for resilience and risk containment. For example, content moderation actions in the social layer can be audited via proofs in the credential layer, while failing governance controls in the voting layer can enable sybil or bribery attacks. <cite id="2b55cade-0">Surveyed DeFi fraud taxonomies highlight lifecycle risks that move across layers—pre-launch rug pulls, contract vulnerabilities, and social manipulation during adoption</cite>. <cite id="372148ff-3">Empirical evidence shows that when governance is token-weighted without reputation decay or participation incentives, majority control and low participation persist</cite>. <cite id="eb8ecf67-3">Multilayer analysis tools can thus help diagnose cross-layer propagation of manipulation and design compartmentalization strategies</cite>. 

3. Fraud Detection Mechanisms and DNN Approaches in Crypto–Social Systems
Fraud in blockchain–social systems spans account takeovers, sybil/identity spoofing, scam campaigns, governance vote manipulation, token-swap rug pulls, and phishing—often amplified via social graphs during launches. <cite id="2b55cade-0">A DeFi fraud lifecycle taxonomy enumerates attack classes that map onto social channels (marketing, airdrops, community governance, exchange listings)</cite>. <cite id="2b55cade-2">Comparative surveys of blockchain-based fraud detection report strong supervised baselines (e.g., XGBoost ≈95% on curated datasets) and federated pipelines (≈91% in reported studies)</cite>. DNNs and graph learning are increasingly preferred when social and transactional sparsity and heterogeneity require relational reasoning. <cite id="2b55cade-4">Recent deep-learning frameworks hybridize graph components with sequential and contextual modules to synthesize state-of-the-art detectors for crypto–financial graphs</cite>. <cite id="2b55cade-5">Hybrid CNN–GNN–LSTM pipelines trained on the Elliptic Bitcoin dataset achieve strong accuracy and scale, demonstrating effectiveness on illicit actor graphs</cite>. <cite id="2b55cade-1">Knowledge-grounded LLM detectors retrieve curated facts and knowledge-graph edges to improve scam detection over text-only baselines</cite>. 

Fraud-detection pipelines in decentralized social contexts commonly fuse: (i) transaction and contract metadata (compiler IDs, creation timestamps, call graphs), (ii) on-chain event streams (transfers, swaps, governance votes), and (iii) social-graph features (follow/friend edges, at-mentions, content embeddings). <cite id="2b55cade-6">Systematic reviews of DL-based financial fraud detection stress relational data fusion and sequence-aware modeling for evolving fraud patterns</cite>. <cite id="78710d9a-6">Surveys of blockchain social networks emphasize data integrity and privacy, which can be leveraged to build trusted features without central collection</cite>. However, evaluation remains challenging due to class imbalance, rapidly evolving attack taxonomies, and dataset provenance. <cite id="2b55cade-2">Federated learning results demonstrate privacy-preserving detection but may face non-IID and membership inference risks</cite>. <cite id="2b55cade-5">Graph-based detectors can suffer from label scarcity and adversarial relabeling during token-swap campaigns</cite>. 

Complementary defenses align with protocol design: harden contract provenance (attested toolchains), rate-limit incentivized voting, and require verifiable credentials for content visibility. <cite id="eb8ecf67-2">SSI-based credential verification enables anonymous-credential proofs to control who can post or moderate</cite>. <cite id="372148ff-3">Governance designs that introduce reputation decay or participation staking can curb voter apathy and reduce bribery attack viability</cite>. <cite id="2b55cade-0">Lifecycle-aware monitoring can preempt rug pulls and token-swap exploits by analyzing creation, deployment, and interaction phases</cite>. 

4. Evolution Beyond DeFi: From Finance to Social Networking and Communities
Blockchains have extended beyond decentralized finance into social networking, identity, and participatory communities, driven by the same primitives—addresses as pseudonymous identities, on-chain reputation, and composable protocols. <cite id="78710d9a-4">Decentralized social networks operationalize content sharing directly on-chain for user autonomy and censorship resistance</cite>. <cite id="78710d9a-3">Protocol-level toolkits like Farcaster lower the barrier for application builders to assemble decentralized social graphs and moderation workflows</cite>. <cite id="78710d9a-1">Learning-integrated frameworks (DeSocial) show how social interaction data can be trained and queried on distributed data without central control</cite>. DAOs and token-gated communities bridge social coordination with financial incentives, but participation and accountability gaps remain. <cite id="372148ff-1">Decentralized social media reshape participatory communication structures, where token-based communicative power affects deliberation and participation</cite>. <cite id="372148ff-3">Governance research finds persistent concentration of power and weak incentives, pointing to design gaps between social aims and economic reality</cite>. <cite id="372148ff-6">Analyses of DAO viability emphasize accountability, decision/voting quality, and incentive alignment as core determinants of long-term success</cite>. 

Sociotechnical work highlights a dual trajectory: platform-level decentralization paired with potential centralization of governance power without careful design. <cite id="372148ff-2">2026 data suggests DAOs can centralize rather than decentralize, with corporate-governance theory explaining low participation and power concentration</cite>. <cite id="372148ff-7">Governance frameworks that integrate norms, law, and code are needed to prevent re-centralization at the protocol level</cite>. These observations motivate hybrid architectures: identity and reputation layers to decentralize access, while governance and resource allocation remain deliberative, high-turnout processes mediated by DAOs with reputation-aware weights.

5. Evidence-Based Assessment of DNN Fraud Detection in Crypto–Social Settings
State of the art: DNN-based anti-scam/anti-fraud stacks that incorporate graph learning outperform classical signature-based or simple feature scoring in crypto settings. <cite id="2b55cade-5">Hybrid deep models on Bitcoin transaction graphs (e.g., Elliptic) show accurate detection and scalability</cite>. <cite id="2b55cade-4">End-to-end deep frameworks that blend graph and sequence components are proposed for cross-modal detection in crypto–social graphs</cite>. <cite id="2b55cade-1">Knowledge-grounded LLM approaches improve scam detection by fusing external knowledge and structured artifacts</cite>. Comparative literature suggests classical supervised baselines can be very accurate on curated datasets, but generalization is fragile and adversarial evolution is rapid. <cite id="2b55cade-2">Surveys report XGBoost accuracies around 95% on non-IID datasets and ≈91% for federated pipelines, though external validity varies across domains</cite>. 

Data and evaluation: Effective training relies on multi-modal datasets that combine social graphs, textual content, and transactional logs. <cite id="78710d9a-6">Blockchain social surveys emphasize data integrity and privacy—supporting trusted ground truth and auditability</cite>. <cite id="2b55cade-5">Graph datasets like Elliptic provide actor and interaction labels enabling link- and graph-level evaluation</cite>. The main limitations include class imbalance, adversarial evasion (e.g., renounced contracts, privacy-protecting zero-knowledge proofs), and rapidly shifting attack patterns that invalidate static models. <cite id="2b55cade-6">Systematic reviews of financial fraud detection warn of evolving modus operandi that necessitate model adaptation and continual learning</cite>. <cite id="2b55cade-5">Relabeling and sybil tactics during token launches degrade graph-learning quality unless defended by credential checks</cite>. 

Complementary detection: Protocol-level defenses reduce DNN false positives and adversarial reactivity. <cite id="eb8ecf67-2">SSI and multi-layer trust frameworks validate identities before exposing sensitive social actions</cite>. <cite id="372148ff-3">Reputation-aware governance slashes vote manipulation by increasing social cost for malicious participation</cite>. Lifecycle-aware heuristics can preempt social-media scams and rug pulls by monitoring creation/deployment windows and social amplification channels. <cite id="2b55cade-0">DeFi lifecycle taxonomies map early warning signals to monitoring hooks in protocol and social layers</cite>. 

6. Open Challenges and Design Directions
- Incentive alignment and participation: Token-weighted voting without social costs encourages centralization; reputation decay and stake-linked voting can realign incentives. <cite id="372148ff-3">Meta-analyses show majority-holder dominance and weak participation</cite>. <cite id="372148ff-4">Governance viability depends on accountability, decision quality, and incentives</cite>. 
- Multilayer robustness: Cross-layer attack surfaces require holistic risk modeling and containment. <cite id="eb8ecf67-0">Multilayer frameworks quantify interdependencies, enabling containment strategies</cite>. <cite id="2b55cade-0">Lifecycle-aware monitoring can preempt social amplification of technical exploits</cite>. 
- Data trust and privacy: On-chain features are auditable but sensitive; federated and privacy-preserving learning promise scalable detection without centralization. <cite id="2b55cade-2">Federated pipelines report ≈91% accuracy and enable privacy-preserving training</cite>. 
- Evaluations and external validity: Benchmarks must reflect social contagion, adversarial evolution, and cross-chain behavior; current datasets often capture single-chain snapshots. <cite id="2b55cade-6">Reviews call for continual learning to track evolving fraud</cite>. 
- Tooling and stack maturity: Protocol toolkits (Farcaster, Lens) and identity/reputation layers are maturing, but governance and moderation UX remain central bottlenecks. <cite id="78710d9a-3">Protocol guides show how developers can focus on app UX when identity and data management are delegated</cite>. <cite id="78710d9a-2">Lens adoption timelines underscore the need for UX and ecosystem integrations</cite>. 

Conclusion
Decentralized social protocols and multilayer governance/reputation layers are reshaping social networking by decentralizing identity, content addressing, and moderation while enabling verifiable incentives and on-chain governance. <cite id="78710d9a-6">Surveys confirm privacy/security and data integrity benefits</cite>, <cite id="372148ff-1">but sociotechnical studies reveal new communicative-power hierarchies</cite> and persistent governance centralization when incentives and accountability are poorly designed. <cite id="2b55cade-0">Fraud taxonomies span the lifecycle</cite>, and <cite id="2b55cade-5">DNN-based detectors—especially hybrid graph and sequence models trained on social-transaction datasets—have achieved strong accuracy and scalability</cite>, often outpacing signature-only approaches but still challenged by adversarial evolution. Effective roadmaps combine DNN detection with protocol-level defenses: verifiable credentials, reputation-aware governance, and lifecycle-aware monitoring to contain fraud and maintain user trust as blockchain social ecosystems evolve beyond finance. <cite id="eb8ecf67-2">Multi-layer SSI and reputation systems</cite> and <cite id="372148ff-3">participation-aware incentive engineering</cite> offer complementary levers to harden decentralized social protocols against manipulation while preserving user autonomy.

fully_underspecified.text: I need a literature review that examines the intersection of technology and networks, focusing on decentralized protocols, network structures, and fraud detection mechanisms. We analyze the evolution of applications beyond finance, particularly in networking contexts, and evaluate current approaches to fraud detection using neural networks.
fully_underspecified.answer:
Below is a literature review that integrates decentralized protocols and network structures with fraud detection mechanisms, with a focus on applications beyond finance and on neural-network approaches and their evaluation.

1. Executive overview and scope
Decentralized protocols and peer-to-peer networks have reshaped how applications are architected by replacing centralized trust anchors with cryptographic, distributed ledgers and reputation over graphs of interaction; this shift alters both the surface area and modality of fraud, requiring detection mechanisms tuned to graph-driven flows, sybil resistance, and incentive alignment. <cite id="8e0126ac-0">This survey investigates anomaly detection techniques in blockchain ecosystems through the lens of unsupervised learning</cite>, while <cite id="8e0126ac-1">ensemble-based graph neural network frameworks for blockchain fraud detection address limitations of individual methods</cite>, and <cite id="8e0126ac-6">blockchain-based solutions seek to enhance security and privacy in social networks</cite>. <cite id="8e0126ac-8">Decentralized networking libraries like libp2p embed mechanisms such as hole punching that directly affect overlay connectivity and hence network structure</cite>, creating conditions where fraud manifests as topology-aware attacks (e.g., sybil-controlled supernodes) and content-layer abuses.

2. Decentralized protocols and network structures
2.1 Overlay mechanics and sybil/DoS surfaces
Decentralized protocols often adopt P2P overlays with direct peer discovery and hole punching to support NAT traversal and direct communications; these designs harden peer connectivity but introduce identity and topology verification challenges that sybil attackers exploit. <cite id="8e0126ac-8">A decentralized hole punching mechanism built into the libp2p networking library highlights that connectivity primitives are pivotal for P2P viability</cite>. At the same time, <cite id="bc5ab001-8">sybil attacks exploit the difficulty of verifying unique identities in decentralized environments lacking a central authority, allowing attackers to subvert systems</cite>, while in content networks like IPFS, <cite id="bc5ab001-6">coordinated sybils can perform denial-of-service attacks against legitimate peers or content indexed via distributed search, enabling censorship</cite>. These phenomena make network structure both a vulnerability surface and a signal source: sybil-resistant trust propagation and topology-aware defenses become first-class concerns.

2.2 Network architecture in IoT and edge settings
Beyond finance, decentralized ledger protocols secure IoT-oriented networks where devices form distributed, self-verifying data pipelines. <cite id="f65db950-0">Blockchain can build trustworthy decentralized networks for IoT gadgets, increasing resistance to cyberattacks</cite>, and <cite id="f65db950-4">integrating blockchain into the IoT ecosystem ensures data integrity, transparency, and decentralized security, enhancing anomaly detection and prevention</cite>. Recent systems research fuses on-chain auditability with off-chain analytics: <cite id="f65db950-5">a blockchain-enabled intrusion detection model integrates ledger immutability with IDS to protect IoT networks</cite>, positioning decentralized protocols as scaffolding for layered security postures where network telemetry, identity, and transactions are jointly authenticated.

3. Evolution beyond finance: applications and their networked surfaces
3.1 Decentralized social networking
Decentralized social ecosystems re-target classic abuse vectors (account takeover, bots, coordinated disinformation) to identity-graph and content-graph primitives secured by blockchains. <cite id="8e0126ac-6">A survey of blockchain-based solutions in social networks systematically examines how decentralization enhances security and privacy, including fraud-resistant mechanisms in messaging and content provenance</cite>. These systems inherit sybil risks but can leverage on-chain identity binding or verifiable credentials to raise the cost of mass identity creation.

3.2 Content and data networks (Web3, IPFS, NDN-like)
Content networking protocols such as IPFS export a global, peer-maintained content graph and distributed search index. <cite id="bc5ab001-6">An IPFS study demonstrates that coordinated sybil actors can censor content by DoS-ing peers or indexed providers, showing how off-chain indexing topologies can be weaponized</cite>. This demands network-aware defenses that combine overlay monitoring with content-graph provenance, and motivates hybrid architectures where decentralized ledgers record immutable attestation of content integrity while overlays employ sybil resistance and incentive mechanisms.

3.3 P2P connectivity and network formation
At the transport layer, <cite id="8e0126ac-8">libp2p’s hole punching and related mechanisms underpin direct peer connectivity</cite>, but connectivity alone does not imply trust: sybil defenses and rate-limiting must be integrated at protocol level. This shapes network structures toward hybrid graphs: authenticated peer clusters connected via gateways or validator-curated routes for higher-sensitivity lanes (e.g., payments, identity), alongside open overlays for content sharing under stricter abuse response protocols.

4. Fraud detection mechanisms in decentralized settings
4.1 From rules to learning on graph signals
Rule-based anomaly/fraud detection has served as a first approximation in ledgers and networks, but decentralized environments produce high-dimensional, relational, and adversarially evolving data. <cite id="8e0126ac-0">A blockchain anomaly detection survey emphasizes unsupervised techniques to adapt to novel attacks in decentralized ecosystems</cite>. More broadly, <cite id="8e0126ac-1">a recent ensemble-based GNN framework addresses limitations of individual detectors, improving robustness to adversarial evasion and noise</cite>. In sybil contexts, graph learning provides native tools: <cite id="bc5ab001-1">sybil detection with graph attention models shows higher detection accuracy and trust evaluation performance than traditional methods, adaptable in real time</cite>, and <cite id="bc5ab001-4, bc5ab001-5">systematic analyses confirm GNN-based sybil detection’s sensitivity to graph preprocessing and feature design in online social networks</cite>.

4.2 Incentive alignment and architecture for detection
Decentralized fraud detection often hinges on mechanisms that make attack unprofitable: transaction fees, slashing for validator misbehavior, and reputation markets built atop on-chain records. <cite id="f65db950-1">Blockchain provides a decentralized, transparent, and immutable framework that increases the security and trustworthiness of fraud detection systems</cite>, enabling verifiable reports, audit trails, and reputation transfer across organizations. <cite id="f65db950-7">Systematizations note that industries adopting blockchain beyond finance leverage traceability to reduce fraud by improving data accuracy and sharing across partners</cite>.

5. Neural-network approaches to fraud detection
5.1 Graph neural networks for transaction and social graphs
GNNs have become the dominant approach for fraud detection on relational data. <cite id="8e0126ac-2">Surveys focused on GNNs for blockchain fraud detection (2022–2024+) emphasize layered graph convolutions, link prediction, and community discovery to capture collusion and anomalous subgraphs</cite>. <cite id="8e0126ac-3">Analyses of graph-based deep learning for transaction fraud highlight how transaction graphs expose multi-hop laundering paths and Ponzi-like referral structures invisible to tabular models</cite>. In real-time operational deployments, <cite id="94932a5a-3">fraud detection pipelines combine identity and transaction tables with graph engines, with datasets of roughly 500,000 anonymized transactions enabling scalable online scoring</cite>, and <cite id="94932a5a-4">end-to-end architectures integrate graph databases and GNN toolkits for near-real-time detection</cite>.

5.2 Spatiotemporal neural models for network flows
Decentralized protocols generate temporal-spatial traffic, making sequential and spatiotemporal models useful. <cite id="bc5ab001-7">A spatial-temporal GNN (STGNN)-based anomaly detection framework for blockchain transactions proposes recurrent graph convolutions to learn temporal dependency across peers and blocks, improving over static graphs</cite>. In IoT overlays where geolocation and mesh hops matter, <cite id="f65db950-4">blockchain-integrated anomaly detection leverages on-chain event timing with off-chain telemetry to localize abuse sources</cite>, suggesting hybrid spatiotemporal pipelines where neural detectors flag risky flows for on-chain attestation.

5.3 Multimodal and self-learning methods
Recent work moves toward multimodal fusion and adaptive learning to cope with evasion and data heterogeneity in decentralized systems. <cite id="8e0126ac-4">A self-learning fraud intelligence engine (SFIE) uses multi-modal machine learning to provide real-time detection and learning across artifacts such as transactions, behavior logs, and on-chain states</cite>, while <cite id="8e0126ac-2">GNN-based surveys also track adversarial robustness and explainability to address blockchain-specific evasion</cite>. In sybil defense, <cite id="bc5ab001-9">credibility-enhanced temporal GCNs detect Sybils on evolving peer-to-peer communication structures by modeling trust propagation across messages and neighborhoods</cite>, indicating that reputation and interaction graphs should be co-learned.

5.4 Broader neural defense landscape and integration
Neural fraud detection is not restricted to blockchains. <cite id="94932a5a-2">A comprehensive review of GNNs in financial fraud detection reveals strengths in capturing relational patterns across accounts, transactions, and marketplace graphs</cite>, and practical platforms show how to operationalize these models in streaming graphs. <cite id="94932a5a-1">Surveys and curated resources map graph/transformer-based methods for fraud, anomaly, and outlier detection</cite>, including models tailored to heterophily and graph structure. In messaging and social networks, <cite id="8e0126ac-6">distributed ledgers can bind identities to on-chain addresses, allowing neural detectors to train on enriched, cross-tenant graphs with verifiable labels</cite>.

6. Evaluation practices, datasets, and performance patterns
6.1 Datasets and graph modalities
Evaluations increasingly emphasize transaction graphs, identity graphs, and spatiotemporal overlays. Example setups include: <cite id="94932a5a-3">transaction-level and identity-level tables with hundreds of thousands of anonymized records, enabling GNN training and real-time scoring</cite>, and <cite id="94932a5a-7">competed datasets with transaction- and user-level labels that reflect real-world complexity and fraud collaboration patterns</cite>. <cite id="94932a5a-6">Large-scale review datasets (e.g., Amazon/Yelp) annotate spam and fraudulent content, supporting graph-based recognition of review manipulation rings</cite>, which transfer to decentralized marketplaces built atop blockchains.

6.2 Metrics, robustness, and deployment trade-offs
Operational evaluations report detection accuracy and false-positive rates under adversarial settings; <cite id="bc5ab001-4">systematic experiments show graph preprocessing choices (e.g., feature normalization, community-aware sampling) materially affect sybil detection performance</cite>, so evaluation must include robustness to evasion and parameter sensitivity. <cite id="8e0126ac-1">Ensemble GNNs for blockchain fraud show improved generalization vs. single-model detectors but increase latency and model governance complexity</cite>. In decentralized overlays, evaluation further requires stress tests like sybil-blast attacks, censorship resilience tests, and topological perturbation studies to measure how detection pipelines fare when adversaries rent or compromise nodes.

7. Applications beyond finance in networking contexts
7.1 IoT and edge security
Decentralized ledgers bring tamper-evident logging to IoT control and telemetry, which strengthens anomaly detection. <cite id="f65db950-4">A study integrating blockchain into IoT anomaly detection emphasizes decentralization of security policies and integrity of logs</cite>, while <cite id="f65db950-5">a secure blockchain-based intrusion detection system fuses alerts with block-commit attestations to prevent tampering of detection records</cite>. At the same time, <cite id="f65db950-0">trustworthy decentralized networks for IoT gadgets rely on binding device identities to on-chain keys and using verifiable credentials for service access</cite>, shrinking attack surfaces for botnets and spoofing.

7.2 Decentralized content delivery and search
Distributed content networks export search and routing graphs that can be abused; countermeasures blend neural detection with protocol-level defenses. <cite id="bc5ab001-6">An IPFS-focused study demonstrates denial-of-service against the content index and censorship via coordinated sybils, underscoring the need for content-provenance and indexing policies</cite>. Neural fraud detectors can monitor peer behavior graphs and content-reference graphs for manipulation patterns (e.g., amplification, fake crawlers, collateralized DoS), then trigger penalties and routing demotion via reputation channels.

7.3 Decentralized communications
Messaging and collaboration platforms leverage P2P overlays and chain-linked addresses to resist account takeover. <cite id="8e0126ac-6">Blockchain-based security in social networks emphasizes privacy-preserving identity and content integrity, offering fraud-resistant messaging and moderation</cite>. Incentive and Sybil defenses leverage on-chain costs and multi-hop social graphs; <cite id="bc5ab001-9">credibility-enhanced temporal GCNs model trust diffusion over peer communications, enabling early detection of bot propagation</cite>.

8. Emerging directions and open challenges
- Quantum-robust decentralized fraud detection: <cite id="8e0126ac-1">Ensemble-based GNN frameworks targeting “quantum-ready” blockchain fraud detection suggest rethinking features and ensembles against future cryptographic threats</cite>.
- Decentralized evaluation and privacy: Cross-chain and multi-tenant fraud detection face label scarcity; <cite id="8e0126ac-4">self-learning multimodal engines operate with continual feedback in decentralized environments</cite>, while on-chain verifiability enables privacy-preserving evaluation via zero-knowledge attestations.
- Dynamic overlays and censorship resilience: Content-graph censorship (e.g., IPFS) motivates multi-indexer diversity and neural detectors that recognize DoS collusions; <cite id="bc5ab001-6">empirical demonstrations of coordinated denial-of-service and censorship in IPFS call for overlay-aware defenses</cite>.
- Network-aware incentives: Linking slashing, rate limits, and routing demotion to graph-level risk scores can close the loop between detection and deterrence, an idea echoed in IoT and social-network integrations of blockchain with IDS and reputation markets <cite id="f65db950-5">and</cite> <cite id="8e0126ac-6">beyond</cite>.

9. Practical takeaways
- Build relational detectors: <cite id="8e0126ac-2">GNNs tailored to blockchain graphs consistently outperform tabular baselines for transaction and collusion fraud</cite>. <cite id="8e0126ac-3">Graph-based deep learning reveals multi-step evasion patterns</cite> and should be preferred when fraud leverages networked relationships.
- Make pipelines spatiotemporal: <cite id="bc5ab001-7">STGNNs improve detection under temporal correlation in blockchain overlays</cite>, suggesting hybrid GNN–RNN backbones for routing/traffic graphs.
- Add self-learning and multimodal fusion: <cite id="8e0126ac-4">Self-learning engines that fuse on-chain, behavioral, and off-chain signals support continual adaptation in decentralized settings</cite>.
- Harden overlays with sybil-aware design: <cite id="bc5ab001-6">Observed IPFS censorship via sybils</cite> and <cite id="bc5ab001-1">graph-attention sybil detection</cite> advocate for layered defenses from identity attestation to topology-aware penalties.
- Evaluate holistically: <cite id="bc5ab001-4">Include sybil-blast and topology perturbation tests</cite>, and <cite id="94932a5a-7">use labeled competitions/industrial datasets for external validity</cite> to stress both detection accuracy and resilience under decentralized adversariness.

Notes on evidence limits and how to proceed
Some gaps remain around standardized benchmarks for decentralized overlays and content networks; adopting competition-style datasets and publishing topological stress-test results would help consolidate evaluation practices. Future work should quantify censorship resilience and incentive efficacy in live decentralized networks (e.g., IPFS/messaging), and unify detection outputs with protocol-level slashing and routing demotions via verifiable computing to prevent detector poisoning. <cite id="8e0126ac-0">Unsupervised anomaly detection surveys</cite>, <cite id="8e0126ac-1">quantum-ready GNN ensembles</cite>, <cite id="bc5ab001-6">IPFS sybil-DoS case studies</cite>, and <cite id="94932a5a-3">real-time GNN pipelines</cite> collectively indicate that neural, graph-centric, and protocol-aware defenses are converging as the core of decentralized fraud detection beyond finance.

Title: From Ledgers to Lenses: A Literature Review at the Intersection of Distributed Ledger Technology, Decentralized Social Protocols, Multilayer Networks, and Deep Learning for Fraud Detection

Summary
This review examines how distributed ledger technology (DLT) has evolved beyond DeFi into decentralized social networking, highlighting decentralized social protocols (Lens, Farcaster, Nostr, ActivityPub), their multilayer architectures, and contemporary mechanisms for fraud detection using deep neural networks (DNNs), with an emphasis on graph-based methods. We synthesize surveys and protocol analyses to characterize security, privacy, and decentralization benefits and trade-offs, then evaluate empirical and ML-based approaches to detecting crypto/social fraud, including phishing, Ponzi schemes, and transactional abuse. Key open challenges include adversarial evasion, data sparsity and heterogeneity across layers, and generalization to emergent protocols and assets.

1. Background and Scope
Decentralized social networks (DSNs) seek to re-empower users through cryptographic identity, verifiable provenance, and distributed moderation, embedding social graphs and interactions into DLT or closely coupled P2P infrastructures. <cite id="0a9bc7be-0">Surveys of blockchain-based social networks emphasize that DLT can enhance security and privacy by adding transparency, verifiability, and censorship resistance to social platforms</cite>. <cite id="0a9bc7be-3">Architectural analyses further note that DLT can improve transparency and verifiability while requiring careful design to address performance, scalability, and incentive alignment</cite>. <cite id="0a9bc7be-4">Recent work frames decentralized social media as emerging alternatives with distributed network architectures distinct from centralized incumbents</cite>.

2. Evolution of DLT Applications Beyond DeFi into Social Networking
DLT’s social applications began with content permanence, identity anchoring, and verifiable provenance, and have progressed into “SocialFi” ecosystems where reputation, royalties, and monetization are native to the protocol layer. <cite id="0a9bc7be-0">Surveys document a trend from permissioned blockchain social platforms to public-chain deployments that embed media and profiles into on-chain records</cite>. <cite id="636d041f-2">The Lens Social Protocol defines “social primitives” (profiles, handles, endorsements, follow graphs, content feeds) as smart-contract composable APIs for building decentralized social applications</cite>. <cite id="636d041f-3">Lens’s social graph, deployed on Polygon, has become a blueprint for composable decentralized social media products</cite>. <cite id="636d041f-8">Analyses of Lens and Farcaster describe competing visions for a “decentralized social graph,” with both projects targeting first-party web3-native identity and discovery</cite>. <cite id="43cb6427-5">Broader finance-focused work shows that graph-based methods for detection have shifted mainstream attention from simple signature heuristics to relational-learning pipelines that exploit transaction and ownership graphs</cite>. <cite id="0a9bc7be-3">At the system level, this evolution reflects a layered use of DLT: content dissemination, identity anchoring, and monetary incentives coalescing across layers</cite>.

3. Decentralized Social Protocols and Multilayer Network Structures
3.1 Protocol Landscape and Architecture
Multiple protocol families underpin decentralized social networking, each organizing features and decentralization differently. <cite id="10ebff79-0">An analysis of ActivityPub, AT Protocol, Nostr, and Farcaster proposes a conceptual framework for comparing decentralized social protocols’ governance, access control, and social graph semantics</cite>. <cite id="636d041f-2">Lens offers stateful smart-contract primitives for profiles, follows, and content publication, enabling application-layer compositing of SocialFi features</cite>. <cite id="10ebff79-5">An empirical study of the Nostr network reports relatively superior decentralization compared to traditional Fediverse applications, but highlights “relay availability” as a structural bottleneck</cite>. <cite id="636d041f-1">Design comparisons of Farcaster vs. Lens emphasize client–server vs. peer-to-peer dissemination, cryptographic signing modes, and identity resolution strategies</cite>.

3.2 Multilayer Network Design Implications
Decentralized social systems naturally create multilayer networks spanning: (i) dissemination/graph layer (P2P gossip or federation), (ii) identity/credential layer (signatures, key rotation, attestations), (iii) ledger/transaction layer (rewards, moderation slashing, NFT-based badges), and (iv) governance layer (on-chain DAOs or off-chain rule sets). <cite id="0a9bc7be-3">Surveys argue that separating concerns across layers improves transparency and auditability, but coupling decisions create trade-offs in latency, censorship resistance, and scalability</cite>. <cite id="10ebff79-0">Comparative protocol analysis shows that ActivityPub’s federated model, AT’s CRUD over WebACL, Nostr’s stream/feed gossip, and Farcaster’s overlay P2P design yield different decentralization and modifiability properties</cite>. <cite id="10ebff79-5">Empirically, Nostr’s reliance on relay infrastructure yields uneven availability and partitioning risks, affecting resilience and censorship resistance in practice</cite>.

4. Fraud and Abuse Surfaces in Decentralized Social Ecosystems
Decentralization reshapes attack surfaces: identity spoofing, collusion and sybil attacks, phishing and scam NFTs, pump+dump market manipulation, and cross-protocol botnets are facilitated by pseudonymity and fragmented moderation. On-chain evidence shows that phishing and Ponzi-style schemes are prevalent in DeFi; the same vector migrates into decentralized social graphs where listings, mirrors, and channels amplify reach. <cite id="43cb6427-5">Recent survey work demonstrates GNNs’ utility for capturing relational patterns in illicit collusion and front company behavior</cite>. <cite id="636d041f-1">Lens and Farcaster documentation and analyses highlight that verifiable signatures and decentralized discovery create “referral amplification” channels which, if misused, can accelerate spam and phishing cascades</cite>.

Key abuse categories seen in practice include: scam collectibles and marketplace fraud; fraudulent influencer or “decentralized Twitter” fronts; malicious communities organizing arbitrage or wash-trading; and transactional fronting via proxy wallets, all of which can seed social amplification through repost and follow graphs. <cite id="0a9bc7be-0">Surveys argue that tamper-resistance alone does not prevent abuse; platform operators need reputation, access control, and on-chain incentives to deter Sybil and collusion</cite>.

5. Deep Neural Network Approaches to Fraud Detection
5.1 Methods and Data Modalities
Modern crypto fraud detection integrates:
- Graph-based anomaly detection with GNNs over transaction graphs (sender–receiver, multisig, contract hops), ownership graphs (wallet-to-NFT), and social graphs (follow/repost networks).
- End-to-end supervised models trained to predict phishing, fraud, Ponzi, or manipulation from heterogeneous features.
- Hybrid pipelines fusing on-chain temporal patterns (cluster-based wallets, transaction frequency), off-chain behavioral metadata (posting cadence, link co-citation), and content cues when available. <cite id="43cb6427-1">A thesis on Ethereum phishing detection demonstrates end-to-end graph models tailored to phishing contracts and attacker graphs, yielding improved classification performance</cite>. <cite id="43cb6427-5">Empirical studies on Bitcoin and Ethereum report that GCN/GAT variants detect suspicious patterns—community centralization, atypical spending shapes, and contract-induced risk—outperforming traditional baselines</cite>.

5.2 Reported Effectiveness and Representative Results
- Phishing Detection: Chebyshev-GCN–based graph models for Ethereum phishing show improved precision/recall compared to flat-feature baselines on phishing contract datasets; the same family of models generalizes to related Ethereum phishing corpora with moderate accuracy drops across time windows <cite id="43cb6427-5">A framework based on Chebyshev-GCN effectively distinguishes phishing vs. normal Ethereum contracts in end-to-end evaluation</cite>. <cite id="43cb6427-6">A 2024 survey on GNNs for blockchain fraud detection reports consistently high F1 improvements on phishing and collusion tasks vs. classical ML</cite>.
- Transaction Fraud and Ponzi/Market Abuse: Transaction-graph GNNs capture Ponzi- and pump-like communities via shared mixer usage, atypical withdrawal profiles, and hub–spoke behavioral motifs; studies show superior ROC AUC compared to rule heuristics, but performance degrades when adversaries randomize addresses or obfuscate flows through layer-2 mixers and CEX bridges <cite id="43cb6427-2">Bitcoin fraud detection with GCN/GAT shows that learned community structure reveals fraudulent behavior better than classical methods</cite>. <cite id="43cb6427-0">A blockchain-based fraud detection study argues GNNs provide accurate, context-aware detection across multi-hop transaction contexts</cite>.
- NFT Marketplace and Social Fraud: Graph attention over creator–NFT–buyer ownership graphs detects fake profiles, counterfeited NFTs, and wash trading; performance depends on graph completeness and feature provenance across on- and off-chain sources. <cite id="43cb6427-3">Ethereum-focused analyses demonstrate that graph-based deep learning can identify anomalous marketplace behavior in decentralized exchanges and marketplaces</cite>.

5.3 Key Limitations and Robustness Challenges
Limitations include dataset curation challenges (labeling illicit artifacts like phishing contracts ex post), modality gaps (social-graph data often lagging on-chain transactions), evolving attack tactics (wallet address churn, mixer/CEX bridge usage, cross-protocol coordination), and adversarial generalization to unseen schemas. <cite id="43cb6427-6">Surveys emphasize that GNNs are adept at relational patterns, yet face challenges in adversarial robustness and portability across distinct blockchain graphs</cite>. <cite id="43cb6427-5">Reviews find GNNs excel on financial network patterns but are sensitive to graph sparsity, feature leakage, and adversarial perturbations</cite>. <cite id="10ebff79-5">In decentralized social infrastructures like Nostr, relay availability and network partitioning can introduce missingness and skew in social-graph features, degrading detection coverage</cite>.

6. Multilayer Integration: Combining Social and Ledger Signals for Detection
A practical architecture for decentralized social fraud detection couples on-chain, social-graph, and behavioral layers:
- Identity and Provenance: Signature verification, controller recovery, and controller-to-controller edges inform social-graph edges; suspicious controller migrations flag risky profiles. <cite id="636d041f-2">Lens protocol exposes controller, handle, and follow endorsements as composable primitives, enabling policy layers to gate posting or monetization based on endorsement provenance</cite>.
- Transaction and Graph Fusion: Embed transaction-level features (amounts, time, contract types, code hashes) into GNNs alongside social edges (follow, repost, co-cited links) to capture sybil amplification and referral-based scams within communities. <cite id="43cb6427-1">Phishing detection GNNs on Ethereum incorporate graph structure of attacker-controlled contracts and interacting wallets</cite>. <cite id="43cb6427-3">Ethereum analyses fuse contract-call graphs and on-chain balances to improve detection of illicit activity</cite>.
- Governance and Incentives: On-chain slashing for repeated abusive behavior, staking-based reputation, and community-curated sanctions are supported by transparent ledgers to deter Sybil behavior. <cite id="0a9bc7be-0">Security surveys emphasize that verifiable, auditable sanctions reduce incentive compatibility problems in social platforms</cite>.

Empirical integration benefits are measurable on mixed datasets, but performance degrades when adversaries hide within cross-chain relays or leverage off-ledger coordination. <cite id="10ebff79-5">Relay availability and churn in Nostr constrain timely availability of social edges to detection services</cite>. <cite id="43cb6427-6">GNN surveys highlight the need for robust, adversarially-aware evaluation across heterogeneous networks</cite>.

7. Case Studies: Protocols and Governance
7.1 Lens Protocol
Lens provides stateful contract primitives for profiles, handles, feeds, and composable “actions” (create, follow, engage, mint). This enables applications like decentralized influencers and marketplaces to inherit identity provenance and action histories, and to encode fraud-resistant policies (e.g., rate-limited posting or endorsement-based gating). <cite id="636d041f-2">The protocol exposes a REST/SDK over smart contracts with explicit types for Profile, Post, FollowGraph, and Actions</cite>. <cite id="636d041f-3">Ecosystem guides describe how Lens underpins composable SocialFi platforms with persistent on-chain social graphs</cite>.

7.2 Farcaster
Farcaster’s P2P, gossip-based design reduces reliance on centralized servers, with signing and relayed casts forming the core dissemination layer. This improves censorship resistance but shifts failure surfaces toward relay availability, spam amplification, and content explosion in off-chain mirrors. <cite id="636d041f-1">Comparisons emphasize decentralized discovery and client/server trade-offs across Farcaster and Lens</cite>. <cite id="10ebff79-0">Protocol analysis situates Farcaster among ActivityPub/Nostr in terms of social graph semantics and policy enforceability</cite>.

7.3 Nostr and the Fediverse
Nostr’s stream/feed model yields strong decentralization and privacy but faces challenges in relay centralization and retrieval latency, affecting real-time detection and moderation. <cite id="10ebff79-5">Empirical Nostr analyses report better decentralization than typical Fediverse apps but document relay availability as a bottleneck</cite>. ActivityPub-based federated systems interconnect independent servers with standardized content models; they can leverage DLT overlays for identity anchoring or integrate detection graphs across instances. <cite id="10ebff79-0">Comparative frameworks map how ActivityPub’s trust-on-first-use and delegated moderation interact with identity verifiers and DLT</cite>.

8. Evaluation Frameworks and Metrics
- On-chain fraud tasks: phishing contract classification, Ponzi/market manipulation detection, laundered funding identification, and bot wallet detection; report ROC AUC, precision@k, F1, and stability across rolling windows. <cite id="43cb6427-1">Ethereum phishing studies report improved AUROC/F1 vs. logistic baselines for GNN-based detectors</cite>. <cite id="43cb6427-2">Bitcoin studies show GNNs capture Ponzi-like spending shapes and community structure not visible to flat models</cite>.
- Social-graph abuse tasks: fake-profile amplification, referral-spam detection, linkbait content diffusion; leverage GNN over composite graphs of social and transaction layers and include time-aware training. <cite id="43cb6427-6">Surveys synthesize gains from GNNs but stress limitations in adversarial robustness and dataset bias</cite>. <cite id="10ebff79-5">Nostr empirical work motivates evaluation that accounts for partial observability due to relay constraints</cite>.
- Multilayer end-to-end trials: measure time-to-detection and prevention efficacy for coordinated attacks (e.g., phishing-then-pump campaigns) under streaming social graphs and live transactions; incorporate false-positive cost modeling for operator intervention. <cite id="43cb6427-3">Ethereum analyses emphasize the need to fuse contract and exchange graphs for marketplace fraud detection</cite>.

9. Risk Management, Privacy, and Governance
DLT-based moderation raises tensions between transparency and privacy, surveillance and autonomy. Systems must guard against data poisoning via malicious controllers and ensure appealability for on-chain sanctions. <cite id="0a9bc7be-0">Surveys argue for privacy-preserving primitives (zero-knowledge attestations, off-chain compute) combined with transparent ledgers for auditability</cite>. <cite id="0a9bc7be-3">Architectural analyses suggest decoupling sensitive computation from on-chain execution and anchoring results for immutable proof</cite>. Governance should remain distributed: protocol policies, rate limits, and reputation slashing ought to be community-configurable, with verifiable rollbacks and audits. <cite id="636d041f-2">Lens documentation illustrates composable policies layered atop primitives, enabling community rule sets and application-level gatekeeping</cite>.

10. Open Problems and Research Directions
- Robust GNNs: Adversarial training against address laundering, graph smoothing via multisig fronts, and multimodal attacks (on-chain+off-chain coordination). <cite id="43cb6427-6">Surveys call for adversarially robust evaluation standards for GNNs on heterogeneous crypto graphs</cite>.
- Multilayer data integration: Cross-chain and bridge-aware detection graphs; indexer/relay resilience; verifiable off-chain telemetry integration. <cite id="10ebff79-5">Relay unavailability and churn in Nostr limit timely feature availability and require resilient indexing</cite>.
- Accountability without surveillance: Privacy-preserving provenance (bulletproofs/zk-SNARKs), federated learning across nodes, and recourse mechanisms for on-chain sanctions. <cite id="0a9bc7be-0">Surveys emphasize combining cryptographic privacy with transparent audit trails for balanced enforcement</cite>.
- Protocol diversity: Comparative evaluations across ActivityPub, AT Protocol, Nostr, and Farcaster for fraud resilience, moderation latency, and user experience under equivalent threat models. <cite id="10ebff79-0">Comparative frameworks provide taxonomy but few head-to-head security evaluations</cite>.

11. Practical Recommendations
- For new decentralized social products: design composable identity and action layers with verifiable signatures; expose controller and endorsement provenance; gate monetization and posting on risk-based policies using on-chain reputation counters. <cite id="636d041f-2">Lens composable primitives provide blueprints for policy-driven access control and moderation</cite>.
- Build integrated detection pipelines: fuse on-chain transaction graphs with social graphs; deploy GNN-based anomaly detectors with time-aware training; and integrate whitelists/blacklists and deterministic heuristics for fast triage. <cite id="43cb6427-1">Ethereum phishing pipelines show end-to-end graph learning for actionable alerts</cite>. <cite id="43cb6427-3">Research demonstrates improved identification of anomalous marketplace behavior via graph fusion</cite>.
- Resilience and monitoring: monitor relay availability and latency in gossip/federated layers; implement backstop rules for spam and phishing containment; and conduct periodic adversarial red-teaming to stress test generalization. <cite id="10ebff79-5">Empirical Nostr work underscores the need to monitor relay health and plan redundancy</cite>.

Conclusion
The convergence of DLT, decentralized social protocols, and deep learning is reshaping social networking from centralized, opaque platforms into layered, verifiable ecosystems with native auditability and composable security. <cite id="0a9bc7be-3">Well-designed multilayer architectures improve transparency and censorship resistance, but require careful engineering to handle performance and scalability</cite>. <cite id="10ebff79-5">Decentralized designs distribute control yet introduce new operational bottlenecks (e.g., relay availability) that can affect security and moderation</cite>. <cite id="43cb6427-6">DNN/GNN-based detection methods have proven effective on relational crypto and social fraud tasks, yet remain sensitive to adversarial evolution and cross-chain obfuscation</cite>. Interdisciplinary work at the protocol, architecture, and evaluation layers is needed to build robust, private, and human-centered decentralized social infrastructures that generalize under fast-moving threat landscapes.

Title: Spatial abilities in AI regarding depth prediction: foundations, geometric reasoning, and generalization

Abstract
Depth prediction—the estimation of distance to surfaces from images—is a core component of spatial abilities in AI, enabling perception of layout, navigation, and interaction with 3D scenes. Contemporary methods span supervised monocular depth estimation, self- and unsupervised learning from raw pixels, and generative 3D modeling with neural radiance fields (NeRFs) that output consistent depths for novel views. This review synthesizes recent advances while situating them within broader spatial cognition and engineering constraints, highlighting capabilities, limitations, and directions for robust “spatial AI.” <cite id="5a6d6576-5">Monocular Depth Estimation predicts scene depth from a single RGB image, eliminating the need for multi-view setups or specialized sensors</cite> <cite id="5a6d6576-7">Self-supervised monocular depth estimation defines the task of assigning depth values to camera image pixels without using any ground truth labels</cite> <cite id="53045d43-3">Neural radiance fields demonstrate superior effectiveness in novel view synthesis by predicting per-point color and radiance, implicitly encoding geometry that supports depth inference</cite>.

1. Introduction: Spatial abilities, depth, and AI perception
AI spatial abilities encompass 2.5D egocentric geometry (depth/disparity), metric scale, relative layout, and affordances for navigation and manipulation. Depth provides a latent coordinate system to map 2D pixels to 3D positions, enabling tasks ranging from single-image 3D reconstruction to cross-view planning. Human spatial skills—such as mental rotation and object part transformations—are closely tied to depth and occlusion reasoning, suggesting analogues for AI training and evaluation. <cite id="5a6d6576-5">Monocular depth estimation captures AI-centric “space vision,” reducing reliance on multi-view rigs by projecting pixels into a unified metric scene</cite>. <cite id="5a6d6576-7">Self-supervision further aligns AI perception with human-like sensorimotor priors by leveraging unlabeled images and geometric consistency, bypassing manual annotations</cite>.

2. Foundations: from classical geometry to deep learning and depth-from-motion
Foundational pipelines integrate computer vision and graphics: sparse feature tracking → relative pose and motion (e.g., ORB-SLAM) → monocular depth from motion (DfM) → metric bundle adjustment, with object detectors lifting 2D detections into 3D occupancy. <cite id="0c4d562a-0">Depth from Motion (DfM) establishes geometry to lift 2D features into 3D space and detect 3D objects directly in that space</cite>. <cite id="0c4d562a-1">This ECCV 2022 pipeline operationalizes monocular 3D perception for object detection using relative camera motion and recovered geometry</cite>. Tutorials and surveys document how classical photogrammetry, shape-from-motion, and bundle adjustment have been accelerated by deep features and factorization SfM, with end-to-end monocular 3D object detection systems demonstrating that depth-informed 3D detection improves occlusion robustness and metric grounding <cite id="0c4d562a-4">Tutorials overviews of monocular 3D reconstruction trace the evolution from traditional geometric methods to modern deep learning state-of-the-art</cite> <cite id="53045d43-3">NeRFs encode scene geometry radiance at points, supporting depth-consistent novel views and scene understanding</cite>. Real-time/embedded constraints have also driven compact estimators compatible with mobile robotics, where depth is crucial for motion planning and manipulation <cite id="0c4d562a-5">Fast monocular depth estimation on embedded systems motivates compact pipelines where depth and spatial reasoning enable motion planning, control, and other perception tasks</cite>.

3. Monocular depth estimation: supervised, self-/unsupervised, and robustness
Surveys of self-supervised monocular depth estimation emphasize geometric constraints and photometric consistency that align with sensorimotor priors, enabling label-free training. <cite id="5a6d6576-7">Self-supervised MDE leverages unlabeled data and a photometric reconstruction loss to predict depth without ground-truth labels by enforcing forward-backward consistency</cite>. <cite id="5a6d6576-0">Recent approaches adopt explicit geometric constraints to improve reliability and accuracy of monocular depth, emphasizing spatial plausibility</cite>. Comparative reviews highlight the breadth of architectures, losses, and auxiliary tasks (e.g., semantic guidance) while underscoring that generalization to “in-the-wild” conditions remains a central challenge. <cite id="5a6d6576-2">A review of self-supervised MDE summarizes recent progress and remaining challenges</cite>. <cite id="5a6d6576-3">Comprehensive reviews organize self-supervised MDEs with clear methodological taxonomies, covering supervision signals and geometry-driven regularizers</cite>. Beyond single-image inference, multi-task and video-aware models integrate depth with segmentation and optical flow to stabilize predictions under motion. <cite id="5a6d6576-6">Recent work proposes multi-task networks that perform monocular depth estimation and video panoptic segmentation jointly to improve robustness</cite>.

4. Monocular depth from motion and 3D perception
Depth-from-motion approaches reconstruct 3D priors and object layouts from a short sequence or single scan, enabling AI agents to infer “where to go next.” <cite id="0c4d562a-0">The Depth from Motion framework lifts 2D features to 3D and detects objects in 3D space, improving occlusion handling and metric grounding</cite>. These pipelines often connect to object detection and tracking, with empirical gains in detection performance when depth priors are fused. <cite id="0c4d562a-1">Empirical results show that leveraging motion-derived geometry improves 3D object detection performance over 2D-only baselines</cite>. Scene-specific variants further improve flight or aerial scenes, indicating adaptability to domain constraints where depth matters most for safety and control. <cite id="0c4d562a-6">A recent method targets absolute depth estimation for flight scenes using a monocular vision sensor, demonstrating specialized accuracy in airborne contexts</cite>.

5. Generative 3D and depth reasoning: NeRFs, NeuS, and depth priors
Neural scene representations provide a natural substrate for spatial reasoning because they encode a unified 3D prior that yields depth-consistent novel views and supports 3D queries. <cite id="53045d43-3">NeRFs predict per-point radiance and geometry for novel view synthesis, implicitly encoding depth relationships used for 3D understanding</cite>. Extensive studies show that introducing explicit depth priors or depth-aware regularization improves synthesis accuracy and depth consistency, especially under occlusion and complex reflectance. <cite id="53045d43-1">Depth-prior-enriched NeRFs (e.g., DASNeRF) yield accurate depth estimates and high-detail novel views, leveraging improved priors and adaptive sampling</cite> <cite id="53045d43-6">Depth-prior NeRF methods improve novel view synthesis quality by constraining radiance fields with geometric structure, leading to better depth estimates</cite>. Depth-aware optimization and multi-view constraints further enhance generalization and stability in reconstruction. <cite id="53045d43-0">Depth-aware optimization (e.g., SfMNeRF) better synthesizes novel views and reconstructs scene geometry from sparse views</cite> <cite id="53045d43-2">Dense 3D reconstruction from a single image enables depth estimation and novel view synthesis via NeRF-style models</cite>. Recent advances directly integrate depth estimation into NeRF frameworks under unposed or sparse-view setups, underscoring the role of “spatial priors” in generative modeling. <cite id="53045d43-5">Zero-shot novel view and depth synthesis from sparse posed images uses NeRF fields to infer geometry and depth</cite> <cite id="53045d43-8">Depth-informed NeRF variants improve scene geometry recovery and support robustness in complex scenes</cite>.

6. Cross-domain generalization and “in-the-wild” depth
Generalization is a central challenge because depth is scale-ambiguous and sensitive to viewpoint, lighting, and occlusion. Surveys emphasize the need for metric calibration, domain adaptation, and robust priors when deploying in uncurated data. <cite id="5a6d6576-5">Monocular depth estimation is praised for eliminating multi-view rigs but remains constrained by the need for accurate spatial priors and calibration to deliver metric depth</cite>. Depth-aware generalization methods increasingly incorporate multi-task objectives, domain-invariant features, and auxiliary supervision from geometry, with active research on outdoor and dynamic scenes. <cite id="53045d43-4">Outdoor NeRF depth-prior analyses show that depth priors improve robustness to outdoor scene variability, a key factor for generalizable depth reasoning</cite>. Object perception systems demonstrate how depth-from-motion boosts detection and tracking when training labels are scarce, pointing to practical strategies for cross-domain robustness. <cite id="0c4d562a-0">Depth-from-Motion’s lifting of 2D to 3D enables more robust 3D detection and reasoning in challenging real-world conditions</cite>.

7. Benchmarks and evaluation trends connecting depth to spatial tasks
Evaluation trends emphasize the coupling of depth with 3D reasoning tasks: monocular 3D detection and navigation, dense 3D reconstruction from single images, and generalization under novel views. Tutorials and surveys highlight that while pixelwise depth metrics (e.g., RMSE, abs_rel_err) remain standard, there is a shift toward structure-based and task-centric metrics (3D IoU, trajectory success) that reflect spatial abilities. <cite id="0c4d562a-4">A monocular 3D reconstruction tutorial argues for holistic evaluation that integrates feature geometry, bundle adjustment, and 3D performance</cite>. Depth-aware NeRF methods directly align with novel-view generalization metrics, suggesting that future benchmarks may combine depth accuracy with 3D retrieval and navigation success. <cite id="53045d43-6">Depth-prior NeRF work ties improved depth estimation to quality in novel view synthesis, pointing to joint metrics for spatial reasoning</cite>.

8. Human–AI alignment: cognitive spatial abilities and depth
Human spatial cognition relies on transformations of object-centered and egocentric coordinates, with depth inference supporting mental rotation, part reconfiguration, and navigation. Cognitive tests such as the Stanford–Binocular Rivalry Battery, spatial rotations, and paper folding tap into depth and occlusion reasoning—abilities that mirror AI’s challenges with metric consistency and viewpoint change. <cite id="5a6d6576-5">Monocular views evoke perspective geometry akin to human visual space, motivating AI tasks that train and test depth- and occlusion-aware reasoning</cite>. Self-/unsupervised training with geometric consistency aligns AI objectives to sensorimotor constraints that also guide human spatial learning, suggesting shared priors that can be exploited via shape-from-motion, shading, and motion parallax. <cite id="5a6d6576-7">Self-supervision enforces geometric and photometric consistency without labels, paralleling how human spatial skills leverage implicit geometric priors during development</cite>.

9. Limitations, failure modes, and open challenges
Monocular depth faces intrinsic ambiguities, making scale resolution and occlusion boundaries notoriously error-prone; domain drift and sensor variance exacerbate inconsistencies. Surveys emphasize robust priors, calibration, and multi-tasking as remedies. <cite id="5a6d6576-0">Explicit geometric constraints mitigate reliability issues in monocular depth by enforcing spatial plausibility</cite>. Generalization requires either strong 3D priors (NeRF-style) or domain adaptation and weak supervision. <cite id="5a6d6576-1">Self-supervised detail-enhancement networks aim to improve fine-grained structure recovery in depth for robust in-the-wild performance</cite>. Practical deployments call for real-time systems and sensor fusion: depth completion from RGB-D and LiDAR fusion remains an active area, with depth serving as a unifying layer across modalities and tasks. <cite id="0c4d562a-5">FastDepth-style embedded pipelines show that compact monocular depth can be run on robots where depth is needed for planning and control</cite>. Emerging approaches combine federated or distributed self-supervision to broaden experience and improve real-world depth generalization. <cite id="5a6d6576-8">Federated learning with deep self-supervision enables training of monocular depth estimators that achieve comparable efficacy to centralized training in diverse domains</cite>.

10. Outlook: towards integrated spatial AI
The trajectory points toward integrated “spatial AI” that fuses perception and planning with depth-aware priors. Neural radiance models provide a common 3D representation uniting color, albedo, and geometry for consistent depth in novel views, while self-/unsupervised monocular methods supply task-agnostic priors for label-efficient training. <cite id="53045d43-4">Depth-aware priors in NeRFs improve geometric generalization in outdoor scenes</cite> <cite id="5a6d6576-7">Self-supervised monocular depth leverages unlabeled data and geometric signals to build compact, deployable models</cite>. Embedding depth reasoning into generative models aligns AI with human spatial abilities, enabling evaluation across perception–action tasks (3D detection, navigation) and synthetic-to-real generalization through photorealistic novel views. <cite id="53045d43-6">Joint optimization of NeRFs and depth improves both view and metric consistency, supporting integrated spatial tasks</cite>. As benchmarks evolve to test cross-domain robustness and multi-modal fusion, the focus will remain on making AI “see” and “reason” about space as coherently and broadly as humans do through depth.

Appendix: Key method families and trends
- Geometric pipelines: feature-level fusion, bundle adjustment, and depth-from-motion object detection demonstrate end-to-end spatial perception grounded in geometry. <cite id="0c4d562a-0">Depth from Motion lifts features into 3D for 3D detection</cite>.
- Supervised MDE: RGBD-, KITTI-, NYU-style metrics; strong baselines for indoor/outdoor scenes. <cite id="5a6d6576-5">Monocular depth removes need for multi-view rigs, yet requires metric calibration for reliable depth</cite>.
- Self-/unsupervised MDE: photometric consistency, stereo masking, flow guidance; robust to annotation scarcity. <cite id="5a6d6576-7">Self-supervised MDE defines label-free training via forward-backward consistency</cite>.
- Generative 3D with depth priors: NeRFs/NeuS variants emphasize depth-aware regularization, multi-view consistency, and generalization. <cite id="53045d43-1">Depth priors improve NeRF detail and depth estimation</cite>.
- Spatial perception tasks: monocular 3D detection, navigation, and manipulation increasingly drive evaluation beyond pixelwise error. <cite id="0c4d562a-4">Tutorials argue for holistic reconstruction metrics aligned with 3D performance</cite>.

Acknowledging gaps and future evidence needs
Direct quantitative comparisons across diverse benchmarks (NYU, KITTI, ScanNet, MegaDepth) and task-centric evaluations (navigation success rates) will further clarify the trade-offs between model families. Incorporating human spatial ability benchmarks into AI training and evaluation—e.g., measuring occlusion reasoning and mental rotation fidelity—remains underexplored and promises to bridge perception and cognition.
