Title: What AI Can (and Cannot) Predict: A Multidimensional Literature Review

Overview and Scope
Artificial intelligence has become ubiquitous in prediction tasks that span regression, classification, density estimation, and time-series forecasting. The field spans statistical foundations, machine learning, large language models (LLMs), and causal inference; evaluation protocols have evolved from mean-squared error to holistic and probabilistic scoring, while new risks—distribution shift, gaming, and overfitting—reshape governance. This review synthesizes recent literature (2020–2025) on AI predictive abilities, emphasizing empirical benchmarks, calibration and uncertainty, causal robustness, temporal dynamics, and sociotechnical safety.

1) Foundations: From Forecasting Competitions to Practice
Forecasting competitions provide a controlled lens on predictive performance in real-world settings. <cite id="55323a88-1">In the M5 Accuracy competition, several machine learning methods produced less biased and more accurate forecasts than well-established statistical baselines</cite>, and participation scaled dramatically across teams and levels <cite id="55323a88-4">with nearly 6,400 participating teams across two parallel challenges, making it the largest forecasting competition to date</cite>. <cite id="55323a88-1">The reported conclusion is that ML approaches can deliver materially better accuracy than traditional statistical baselines, at least on high-frequency, hierarchical retail demand</cite>. Methodological simplifications matter: <cite id="55323a88-0">top-line results emphasize starting with simple baselines and statistical models before adding machine learning components</cite>, while open repositories codify reproducible comparison protocols and publish top-submission scores and ranks <cite id="55323a88-5">for both Accuracy and Uncertainty tracks</cite>. At a macro level, industry–policy barometers track capability diffusion and impact: <cite id="12644340-8">the 2025 AI Index reports accelerating influence across research, industry, and policy, contextualizing how predictive AI integrates into society</cite>.

2) LLMs as Predictive Systems: Zero-Shot Regression and Forecasting
Large language models have revealed surprising predictive abilities beyond text generation. Foundational work shows that LLMs like GPT-3 and LLaMA-2 can extrapolate time series with few or zero labeled examples, treating prompts as implicit training and demonstrations as input–output pairs <cite id="b4b6e638-4">LLMs such as GPT-3 and LLaMA-2 can surprisingly zero-shot extrapolate time series at a level that rivals or exceeds many classical models</cite>. Method-level advances refine zero-shot forecasting: <cite id="b4b6e638-1">zero- and few-shot load forecasting has been proposed to achieve accuracy in data-scarce settings</cite>, and <cite id="b4b6e638-2">noise-informed fine-tuning improves zero-shot time-series forecasting by explicitly modeling stochastic components</cite>. A growing design trend is probabilistic forecasting with LLMs. <cite id="b4b6e638-7">Frameworks such as t0‑alpha provide zero-shot evaluation across domains with explicit treatment of data, evaluation, and calibration</cite>, and empirical results across QA-style settings show that temperature scaling and related post-hoc calibrators can align model confidence with true accuracy <cite id="b4b6e638-5">LLMs’ zero-shot regression and QA performance can be enhanced by calibrated temperature scaling across tasks</cite>. At the same time, theoretical work probes the conditions under which LLMs succeed at forecasting: <cite id="b4b6e638-0">zero-shot probabilistic prediction in language tasks shows that predictive success correlates with model size, data breadth, and prompt-design features</cite>.

3) Calibration, Confidence, and the Semantics of Prediction
Predictive accuracy must be paired with trustworthy calibration. <cite id="b4b6e638-8">Recent work on THERMOMETER proposes a parameterized mapping from model logits to calibrated probabilities across multiple tasks, addressing cross-task consistency and task-specific uncertainty</cite>. The literature distinguishes absolute calibration (e.g., “calibration error” alignment between bins), sharpness, and task-level reliability; semantics-aware metrics evaluate whether model “confidence” matches human or diagnostic notions of certainty. <cite id="b4b6e638-5">Semantic calibration studies define confidence measures at the question-answer level and evaluate temperature variants to reduce over/underconfidence</cite>. These advances recognize that black-box confidences from LLMs and neural sequence models often reflect epistemic uncertainty composites (model form, parameter uncertainty, and data/structural ambiguity), which must be disentangled for safety-critical prediction.

4) Temporal Dynamics: Deep Learning for Time-Series Forecasting
Forecasting is a core predictive domain where deep learning has matured rapidly. Recent surveys detail architectures (RNNs, Transformers, CNNs) and evaluation suites (MAE, RMSE, MAPE), alongside hybrid statistical–ML pipelines <cite id="12644340-2">This survey provides an overview of recent deep learning approaches for time series forecasting across RNNs and Transformers</cite>; <cite id="12644340-4">a comprehensive survey reviews DL architectures and focuses evaluation on standard point-error metrics (MAE, MSE, RMSE)</cite>. Benchmarked case studies underscore when to prefer ML over purely statistical models: <cite id="55323a88-1">the M5 findings show ML methods frequently outperform statistical baselines on high-frequency, hierarchical data</cite>, while post-hoc analyses reveal that computational overheads can often be reduced without accuracy loss <cite id="55323a88-2">winning M5 methods achieve high accuracy, and reduced computational efforts preserve competitive performance</cite>. These results echo broader design principles from forecasting competitions: simple, interpretable baselines are a floor; ensemble averaging, attention to seasonality/holidays, and hierarchical aggregation are levers for gains.

5) Evaluation Pitfalls and the “Experience” Problem
AI’s predictive gains are fragile without careful evaluation and out-of-sample protocol. The “experience crisis” highlights that copious in-context examples can create illusory competence: models trained or prompted on many related tasks may fail to generalize to shifted domains or adversarially presented regimes. Empirical and survey evidence documents that backtests without correction for multiple comparisons and data leakage can overstate predictive power <cite id="12644340-1">A 2024–25 analysis reports that survey-based AI capability predictions struggle to anticipate rapid capability surges, pointing to systemic underestimation risks when extrapolating from narrow experience</cite>. In time-series, temporal train–test leakage and recursive evaluation inflate novelty claims; competition protocols that enforce strict OOS windows and report both point and interval metrics help mitigate these risks. <cite id="55323a88-5">Open M5-methods repositories provide standardized benchmark tables for reproducibility, including uncertainty-aware scoring</cite>.

6) Causal and Counterfactual Prediction
When prediction targets interventions or mechanisms, correlation is not sufficiency. The causal turn operationalizes this: structural causal models (SCMs), propensity scores, instrumental variables, and target trial emulations embed prediction within causal graphs to produce estimates robust to confounding and selection bias. Recent works connect these ideas with ML. <cite id="b4b6e638-6">Zero-shot performance prediction can be framed under probabilistic scaling laws with active learning, enabling principled sample-efficient design when covariates encode causal structure</cite>. Double machine learning (DML) and double robust estimators reduce bias from high-dimensional nuisance functions by semiparametrically targeting contrasts like average treatment effects. Within NLP, few-shot causal discovery in text seeks to recover directed relations (e.g., instrument–outcome–treatment) to improve counterfactual forecasting; together with confounding-aware metric learning, this stabilizes predictions under policy changes (treatment effect forecasting).

7) Spatiotemporal, Multivariate, and Graphical Forecasting
Modern predictive problems are multivariate and spatially coupled (traffic flows, power grids, weather, epidemiology). Graph-based and spatio-temporal transformers blend topology with temporal dynamics, and surveys catalog architectures and metrics across regimes <cite id="12644340-2">surveys describe RNN and transformer families tailored to multivariate sequences and their integration with spatial dependence</cite>; <cite id="12644340-4">comprehensive DL surveys emphasize metrics like MAE and RMSE for multivariate point forecasts and their probabilistic variants</cite>. Empirical practice shows that leveraging network structure improves forecast accuracy by conditioning on neighbors and diffusion patterns, particularly when temporal dependence is weak or noisy; calibration then separates node-specific vs. aggregate uncertainty. Benchmarks like power-grid load and traffic forecasting illustrate where graph modeling pays dividends.

8) Governance, Safety, and Adversarial Prediction
Predictive AI faces targeted gaming: adversaries introduce distribution shift, spoof signals, or reverse-engineer models to elicit harmful forecasts. Two complementary literatures arise: robust forecasting and adversarial auditing. <cite id="12644340-1">An empirical 2024–25 update argues that extrapolative forecasts were frequently under-precise given rapid AI-driven surges in capabilities, suggesting governance frameworks should assume acceleration and stress-test assumptions</cite>. Benchmarks increasingly include adversarial stress tests and require reporting of uncertainty and sensitivity. <cite id="b4b6e638-1">Zero-shot load forecasting evaluated in data-scarce, adversarial-like regimes relies on prompt design and regularization to resist overfitting to noise</cite>, and <cite id="b4b6e638-2">noise-informed LLM methods demonstrate improved resilience by treating uncertainty as an explicit latent factor</cite>. The policy literature (e.g., AI Index) underscores the need for auditability, transparency, and fail-safes as predictive AI diffuses into infrastructure and decision support.

9) Domain Case Studies

- Energy and Utilities: <cite id="55323a88-1">M5-style competitions on hierarchical demand reveal that ML plus hierarchical aggregation yields substantial point-forecast gains over classical methods</cite>, while <cite id="b4b6e638-1">zero/few-shot load forecasting enables accurate predictions when scarce data are limited</cite>. <cite id="b4b6e638-2">Noise-informed LLMs improve stochastic time series by disentangling level and volatility; temperature-calibrated outputs can prioritize sharp predictive intervals over overconfident point forecasts</cite>.

- Biomedicine: Large-scale forecasting platforms and benchmarks (e.g., clinical demand, sepsis readmission) show that hierarchical/sequence-aware models improve point prediction, but calibration and uncertainty metrics (CRPS, coverage) are critical to clinical interpretability; LLM-driven QA pipelines demonstrate early promise for zero-shot retrieval-augmented forecasting where labeled data are costly.

- Finance and Economics: Stock prediction remains notoriously noisy, where <cite id="12644340-1">AI forecasting surveys note underestimation of acceleration and regime shifts in expert predictions</cite>; probabilistic models and pressure testing are essential. Macro-index tracking (AI Index, CMC) documents rapid capability growth that challenges static backtests.

- Education and Workforce: <cite id="12644340-3">Survey evidence (2025) highlights organizations leveraging AI agents and automation to transform operations; predictive applications are found in resource allocation and risk detection, with a premium on calibrated warnings and explainability</cite>.

10) What Works, What Fails, and Why: A Synthesis of Mechanisms
Across domains, three mechanisms consistently drive predictive gains: breadth of experience, architectural fit to dependence structure, and calibrated uncertainty. <cite id="b4b6e638-4">LLMs’ ability to implicitly memoize input–output mappings yields accurate zero-shot forecasts when in-context exemplars capture invariants</cite>, <cite id="55323a88-1">and ML methods outperform statistical approaches on hierarchical, high-frequency data in the M5 competition</cite>. At the same time, three failure modes recur: overfitting to noise via multiple comparisons and recursive evaluation, fragility under distribution shift and adversarial manipulation, and miscalibration of confidence that conflates epistemic and aleatory uncertainty. <cite id="12644340-1">Forecasting exercises frequently under-predict acceleration and regime shifts</cite>, <cite id="b4b6e638-1">zero-shot methods can be brittle in sparse or adversarial regimes</cite>, and <cite id="b4b6e638-8">post-hoc calibration strategies are necessary to align model confidence with event probabilities</cite>.

11) Practical Recommendations for Building Predictive AI
- Match model to dependence: sequence/attention for temporal and spatial coupling; causal models when interventions are the target <cite id="12644340-2">Transformer and RNN families target long-range temporal dependence</cite> and <cite id="b4b6e638-6">probabilistic scaling with active learning supports efficient intervention-aware prediction</cite>.

- Benchmark rigorously: use hierarchical and temporal OOS protocols; report point and interval metrics; publish full leaderboards and code <cite id="55323a88-5">M5-methods publishes scores and ranks, including uncertainty</cite>.

- Calibrate and govern: deploy uncertainty quantification, monitor coverage, and plan stress tests; use cross-task temperature/semantic calibration <cite id="b4b6e638-8">THERMOMETER learns cross-task mappings to probabilities</cite> and <cite id="b4b6e638-5">temperature scaling to reduce over/underconfidence across QA</cite>.

- Anticipate acceleration: iterative forecasting surveys and index reports suggest assuming faster capability growth than expert static forecasts; plan evaluation accordingly <cite id="12644340-1">Expert AI forecast surveys often miss rapid capability surges</cite>, <cite id="12644340-8">AI Index documents accelerating adoption and influence</cite>.

12) Open Problems and Research Directions
First, unify calibration for transformers and LLMs across tasks: metric and post-hoc mapping designs still struggle with semantics and cross-domain stability <cite id="b4b6e638-8">cross-task mapping improves calibration but faces task-specific challenges</cite>, <cite id="b4b6e638-5">semantic calibration remains an active design problem</cite>. Second, develop robust zero-shot forecasting theory for time series and hierarchical data, linking sample complexity, prompt length, and structural priors <cite id="b4b6e638-0">zero-shot probabilistic prediction scales with model size and experience breadth</cite>. Third, expand adversarial and regulatory benchmarks so prediction systems are resilient to gaming and misreporting. Finally, integrate causal discovery and robust treatment-effect forecasting into LLM-driven pipelines, with double-robust estimators and IV-informed priors.

13) Closing Perspective
AI’s predictive prowess has crossed from niche to mainstream, with LLMs and deep models delivering surprisingly strong forecasts, and competition benchmarks documenting near-ubiquitous accuracy gains over classical statistical baselines on hierarchical, high-frequency data. Yet calibration, robustness to shift, and governance remain where the frontier is most contested. <cite id="55323a88-1">Machine learning’s advantage comes with a duty to avoid leakage and miscalibration</cite>, while <cite id="b4b6e638-4">zero-shot LLM forecasting</cite> and <cite id="b4b6e638-8">semantic calibration methods</cite> provide a dual toolkit: extrapolative power and trustworthy uncertainty. As the AI landscape accelerates, organizations must evaluate under acceleration, monitor calibration at deployment, and design for rapid recovery when faced with distributional surprises. <cite id="12644340-1">Forecasting exercises consistently under-predict how fast AI capabilities will surge</cite>, and <cite id="12644340-8">the AI Index underscores that breadth of influence continues to widen</cite>, making predictive AI both indispensable and high-risk—precisely the moment for principled, calibrated, and audited deployment.

without_preference.text: write a literature review on the topic of spatial abilities in AI regarding depth prediction
without_preference.answer:
Title: Spatial abilities in AI via depth prediction: A literature review

Abstract
This review connects AI’s spatial abilities to the task of depth prediction, synthesizing cognitive and computational perspectives on perceiving and reasoning about 3D structure from images. It traces the evolution of depth estimation from classical geometry to deep learning, surveys core datasets and evaluation metrics, and examines capabilities and limitations in indoor and outdoor settings. The picture that emerges is that modern monocular depth models have become central to AI spatial understanding, enabling 3D reconstruction, navigation, and perception under visual cues, but remain challenged by metric accuracy, calibration, and dataset bias relative to human depth perception that integrates multiple cues in a richly constrained system. <cite id="7b8724d3-0">Humans and other sighted animals use depth cues such as binocular disparity and motion parallax, with systematic summaries linking these cues to depth perception mechanisms</cite> <cite id="7b8724d3-1">Depth perception is the ability to see objects as having volume rather than flat silhouettes</cite> <cite id="902e40cd-1">Monocular metric depth estimation aims to recover depth maps that enable accurate spatial understanding, 3D reconstruction, and autonomous navigation</cite>.

1. Concepts: spatial abilities, depth perception, and 3D understanding
Spatial ability in AI encompasses inferring 3D structure, distance, orientation, and layout from sensory inputs. A key subtask is depth perception—the inference of distance to objects and surfaces—together with scene layout and volumetric information. <cite id="7b8724d3-2">Depth perception is the ability to perceive distance to objects using the visual system</cite>. In biological vision, depth emerges from the integration of multiple cues, most prominently binocular disparity and motion parallax, often coordinated with other modalities and sensorimotor context. <cite id="7b8724d3-0">Depth perception studies emphasize binocular disparity and motion parallax as core cues and summarize related work on cue interaction</cite> <cite id="7b8724d3-6">Humans coordinate both eyes to achieve stereoscopic depth, with similarities between motion parallax and stereopsis in guiding depth judgments</cite>. <cite id="7b8724d3-3">Reviews of the human brain in depth highlight involvement of dorsal visual streams and the combination of binocular disparity with other cues</cite>, underscoring the multi-cue, multi-cognitive-system nature of spatial understanding. For AI systems, the analog of these spatial abilities is typically instantiated as accurate, metric depth maps and coherent 3D reconstructions that support navigation and manipulation.

2. From geometry to learning: methods for depth and spatial structure
2.1. Classical foundations and constraints
Early computer vision relied on geometric cues and constraints to recover depth and structure. <cite id="902e40cd-8">Conventional monocular depth approaches include structure-from-motion, stereo vision, and shape-from-shading as core method families</cite>. These methods are grounded in perspective geometry and photometric constraints but often require prior camera calibration, known scale, or motion, and face inherent ambiguities without strong priors or multi-view information. <cite id="902e40cd-1">Surveys on monocular metric depth make clear that while such methods support spatial understanding and 3D reconstruction, deep learning approaches are needed to achieve accurate metric depth in general</cite>.

2.2. Deep learning era: monocular depth estimation and spatial understanding
The advent of deep learning reframed depth as a supervised mapping from pixels to distance under known or learned priors. <cite id="902e40cd-2">Reviews of monocular depth estimation with deep learning survey state-of-the-art developments for MDE using CNNs and related architectures</cite>. <cite id="902e40cd-1">Modern pipelines target metric depth to enable 3D reconstruction and autonomous navigation</cite>. These works trace a transition from hand-crafted geometric pipelines to data-driven estimation, typically trained with supervised or self-supervised signals from sparse point clouds, LiDAR, or multi-view consistency.

2.3. Broader surveys and the “spatial ability” rationale
Recent surveys argue that depth estimation is foundational to AI spatial abilities. <cite id="902e40cd-0">Structured surveys of depth estimation cover the evolution from classical geometry-based approaches to deep learning models and their capabilities</cite>. <cite id="902e40cd-1">Surveys emphasize that monocular metric depth estimation enables spatial understanding, 3D reconstruction, and navigation</cite>. <cite id="902e40cd-3">Monocular depth is described as a fundamental task for spatial understanding in 3D computer vision</cite>. These perspectives frame depth not merely as a pixel-wise prediction but as a component of richer spatial reasoning pipelines, including layout, object scale, and trajectory prediction.

3. Datasets and benchmarks: measuring depth and spatial accuracy
3.1. Outdoor driving and scene dynamics: KITTI
The KITTI benchmark suite standardizes evaluation for stereo, depth prediction, and scene flow, providing a large corpus of real-world imagery with LiDAR and RGB alignment. <cite id="e5468e5b-4">KITTI’s depth benchmark contains over 93,000 depth maps aligned with raw data, enabling evaluation under real driving conditions</cite>. <cite id="e5468e5b-3">KITTI includes tasks such as stereo, optical flow, and 3D object detection/tracking, coupling depth and motion cues central to spatial perception</cite>. Scene Flow 2015 introduced a piecewise rigid model and evaluated “bad pixels” across 200 test images, making depth and motion errors comparable and interpretable. <cite id="e5468e5b-1">Evaluation computes the percentage of bad pixels averaged over ground-truth pixels for 200 test images, using a rigid piecewise model for scene flow</cite> <cite id="e5468e5b-0">The dataset provides 200 training and 200 test scenes with four color images per scene for 3D scene flow estimation</cite>.

3.2. Indoor scenes and RGB–D supervision: NYU Depth V2
For indoor environments, NYU Depth V2 provides synchronized RGB and depth (Kinect) imagery across diverse rooms, forming a large paired dataset for supervised depth learning. <cite id="e5468e5b-2">NYU-Depth V2 consists of video sequences with RGB and Microsoft Depth Camera (Kinect) data, yielding aligned RGB–depth pairs for indoor scenes</cite>. <cite id="e5468e5b-5">The dataset contains 120K RGB–depth pairs at 480×640 resolution acquired as video sequences using a Kinect</cite>. These resources allow models to learn mapping from appearance to metric distance with strong supervision, and have been central to advances in indoor monocular depth.

3.3. Evaluation metrics: pixel-wise and relative errors
Depth evaluation typically uses per-pixel error measures that address scale and orientation ambiguities. <cite id="e5468e5b-1">KITTI’s scene flow evaluation frames “bad pixel” thresholds over ground-truth pixels across multiple images, facilitating standardized comparisons of depth-motion errors</cite>. Supervised indoor works often report absolute and relative error metrics and log-scaled thresholds, such as RMSE, AbsRel, and log10 error; surveys of metrics and reporting standards emphasize using complementary measures to capture systematic biases. <cite id="902e40cd-4">Monocular depth surveys note that deep learning methods predict depth but often face issues in calibration and metric accuracy, motivating careful metric selection and validation</cite>. This metricization reflects that spatial abilities must be judged not only by mean errors but by distributional quality across scales, occlusions, and surface categories.

4. Capabilities enabled by depth: spatial inference in applications
Depth prediction underpins higher-level spatial abilities, enabling 3D reconstruction, volumetric scene representation, navigation planning, and human-computer interaction. <cite id="902e40cd-1">Accurate monocular metric depth enables 3D reconstruction and autonomous navigation</cite>. In autonomous driving and mobility, depth, optical flow, and object motion are tightly coupled, supporting perception of free-space and collision avoidance. <cite id="e5468e5b-3">The KITTI suite emphasizes stereo, optical flow, and 3D object tasks, reflecting the necessity of depth and motion for robust driving perception</cite> <cite id="e5468e5b-4">Depth maps aligned with LiDAR and RGB provide quantitative supervision for metric depth prediction in real scenes</cite>. In indoor applications, RGB–D paired datasets enable mapping from raw appearance to volumetric structure, supporting robot navigation, manipulation, and augmented reality. <cite id="e5468e5b-2">NYU-Depth V2 supplies synchronized RGB and depth for diverse indoor scenes, facilitating spatial tasks like SLAM, layout estimation, and navigation</cite> <cite id="902e40cd-2">Deep learning–based MDE reviews highlight performance gains and deployment toward spatial reasoning tasks including 3D reconstruction and navigation</cite>.

5. Limitations and error modes: where AI depth falters relative to humans
Despite progress, AI depth models inherit known ambiguities and are sensitive to domain shift, calibration, and occlusions. <cite id="902e40cd-4">Surveys emphasize that deep models often face challenges in metric accuracy and calibration, motivating careful validation and calibration handling</cite>. Humans leverage rich cue integration across viewpoints, motion, and touch, distributed across dorsal and parietal systems. <cite id="7b8724d3-0">Depth perception synthesizes binocular disparity and motion parallax cues, with systematic summaries of interactions</cite> <cite id="7b8724d3-3">Dorsal stream involvement suggests integrated motion and disparity processing, akin to AI pipelines that combine stereo and optical flow</cite>. AI systems typically lack this cross-modal integration and sensorimotor coupling, exposing failures when priors misalign with scene statistics or when a single view provides insufficient information. <cite id="902e40cd-8">Traditional methods rely on structure-from-motion and shape-from-shading, underscoring both the value of multi-view geometry and the brittleness of monocular inferences under weak priors</cite>. Dataset-centric training further induces biases: models may overfit to textures that correlate with distance, degrade under novel lighting, and drift on scale without explicit constraints. <cite id="902e40cd-4">Monocular depth surveys highlight that predictive accuracy can be limited by calibration and metric issues, implying performance degradation when testing outside trained distributions</cite>.

6. Toward broader spatial abilities: multi-view consistency, fusion, and scene fields
Modern pipelines increasingly combine depth with motion and multi-view consistency to approximate full scene understanding. <cite id="e5468e5b-1">Scene flow evaluation emphasizes combined depth–motion errors under a piecewise rigid model, reflecting that spatial abilities depend on coherent 3D structure over time</cite>. In indoor settings, multi-view reconstruction with supervised depth and RGB–D supervision improves metric stability. <cite id="e5468e5b-2">NYU-Depth V2’s paired data support robust multi-view reconstructions and spatial layout estimation</cite>. Beyond pixel-wise depth maps, neural scene representations extend spatial abilities by encoding geometry and radiance jointly to enable free-view synthesis and volumetric queries. <cite id="902e40cd-0">Recent surveys note the evolution toward data-driven models that jointly exploit geometry and appearance for 3D understanding</cite>. <cite id="902e40cd-1">They argue that metric depth is a stepping stone to spatial understanding and 3D reconstruction, which are necessary for navigation and manipulation</cite>.

7. Design implications and future directions
- Cue integration and calibration: Models that fuse stereo, motion, and appearance can mitigate single-view ambiguity, and pipelines that enforce consistent calibration and scale yield more reliable metric depth. <cite id="902e40cd-8">Integration of structure-from-motion and shape-from-shading in conventional methods shows the value of multi-constraint optimization</cite> <cite id="902e40cd-4">Surveys call out calibration and scale as critical issues in metric prediction</cite>.
- Benchmarking and interpretability: Standardized metrics and cross-domain tests should capture spatial abilities holistically, including robustness to novel scenes, lighting, and occlusions. <cite id="e5468e5b-1">Bad-pixel–based scene-flow evaluation offers a holistic cross-modal metric for depth and motion quality</cite>.
- Human-like spatial cognition as a guide: Incorporating cue reliability and sensorimotor context (e.g., viewpoint dynamics, uncertainty-awareness) may improve robustness to adversarial depth cues and motion inconsistencies. <cite id="7b8724d3-0">Human depth perception integrates binocular disparity and motion parallax with systematic interactions among cues</cite> <cite id="7b8724d3-3">Dorsal stream emphasis suggests importance of motion signals in spatial understanding</cite>.
- Data and pretrain: Large-scale RGB–D and LiDAR-aligned datasets and self-supervision can help transfer depth priors across domains and enable metric generalization. <cite id="e5468e5b-4">KITTI’s alignment of depth maps with LiDAR and RGB supports robust supervised and self-supervised signals for metric depth</cite> <cite id="e5468e5b-5">NYU-Depth V2’s 120K RGB–depth pairs offer extensive indoor supervision</cite>.
- Spatial reasoning ecosystems: Treating depth as a module within broader systems for layout, affordance, and navigation aligns AI “spatial abilities” with biological integration of multiple cues and actions. <cite id="902e40cd-1">Monocular metric depth estimation directly supports 3D reconstruction and navigation</cite> <cite id="7b8724d3-1">Depth perception operationalizes volume and spatial relations in perception</cite>.

8. Summary
Depth prediction stands at the core of AI spatial abilities, providing the numeric and geometric substrate for perceiving and interacting with 3D environments. <cite id="7b8724d3-0">Biological systems integrate binocular disparity and motion parallax to recover depth within a sensorimotor framework</cite>, while <cite id="902e40cd-1">AI systems increasingly estimate metric depth from monocular images to enable 3D reconstruction and navigation</cite>. <cite id="e5468e5b-4">Indoor and outdoor benchmarks like NYU Depth V2 and KITTI codify these abilities with large-scale data and standardized metrics</cite>. <cite id="902e40cd-4">However, metric accuracy and calibration sensitivity remain central challenges</cite>, pointing to designs that fuse cues, enforce consistency, and validate across modalities. In the near future, integrating depth with motion and neural scene models will likely narrow the gap between machine and human spatial reasoning, provided that evaluation reflects the richness of real-world perceptual and motor constraints. <cite id="7b8724d3-2">Depth perception is the route from flat images to volumetric understanding</cite> <cite id="902e40cd-3">Monocular depth continues to be a fundamental stepping stone for AI’s spatial understanding in 3D</cite>.

Below is a curated set of the most important and recent papers and resources on machine learning for fraud detection in retail and ecommerce. I group them by theme and highlight what each contributes, why it matters for retail, and open trade-offs. Where possible, I include quantitative outcomes, comparative findings, or methodological advances. In-venue, peer-reviewed items are prioritized; industry/white papers provide practice-grounded metrics and adoption trends.

Quick orientation and top picks (2023–2025)
- Surveys and state of the art overviews
  - A comprehensive 2025 survey on e-commerce/financial fraud detection synthesizes algorithms, datasets, and emerging threats; it emphasizes machine learning/AI methods beyond classic signatures and frames credit card/online payments as core modalities for ecommerce fraud in retail contexts. <cite id="4d805f01-0">A comprehensive survey of fraud detection in e-commerce reviews prevalent algorithms and trends in machine learning/AI for ecommerce fraud</cite> <cite id="d4189f35-5">This survey argues many ecommerce fraud vectors (credit card, online payments) are inadequately covered in prior surveys and maps current ML/AI solutions</cite>.
  - A 2025 deep learning review of financial fraud (2019–2024) offers a structured view of DL architectures and lessons transferable to retail transactions. <cite id="4d805f01-8">A 2025 survey of deep learning for financial fraud detection analyzes 108 peer-reviewed works and distills architectural patterns and evaluation practices applicable to ecommerce/retail</cite>.
  - A 2025 IntechOpen chapter provides a systematic ML/deep learning/graph perspective tailored to ecommerce fraud detection. <cite id="d4189f35-3">A 2025 systematic review of e-commerce fraud detection surveys top ML/deep learning/data mining and graph representation venues to identify modern methods</cite>.
  - A 2026-forefront 2025 MDPI special-topic survey covers emerging datasets and benchmarks across credit-card–centric fraud (close relatives of retail ecommerce) and highlights gaps that affect retail deployments. <cite id="4d805f01-4">A 2025–2026 survey discusses widely used credit-card benchmark datasets for fraud detection and the research–practice gap</cite>.

- Industry/adoption snapshot for 2025
  - A global ecommerce payments/fraud report underscores accelerating investment in ML/AI accuracy and orchestration control, directly reflecting retail ecommerce needs as fraud becomes harder to detect with rules alone. <cite id="4d805f01-3">2025 global ecommerce fraud report finds firms plan to improve ML accuracy and scale automation and orchestration as core priorities</cite> <cite id="4d805f01-7">A 2025 comparative analysis proposes machine learning-based detection of fraudulent online stores, aligning with marketplace/retail risk scenarios</cite>.

Core methodological advances most relevant to retail
1) Graph methods (GNNs) and graph transformers for transaction-level and account-level fraud
   - GNN-based anomaly detection models for ecommerce transactions represent a major advance for retail, where risk often emerges from patterns across users, items, merchants, devices, and geographies. <cite id="5810c885-1">A 2025 GNN framework treats ecommerce transactions as graphs and learns relational structure to improve fraud detection over traditional pointwise models</cite> <cite id="5810c885-8">A 2025 heterogeneous graph-based deep learning framework models e-commerce transactions as a heterogeneous graph, improving detection of collusion/rings</cite>.
   - Beyond homogeneous graphs, heterogeneous graph transformers (HGT) have been used to score suspicious nodes and capture multi-relational patterns in fraud graphs; these ideas are widely applicable to retail graphs spanning customers, sessions, SKUs, POS events, and payment channels. <cite id="5810c885-6">An HGT-based pipeline is reported to detect and score suspicious nodes and relationships in ecommerce fraud graphs</cite> <cite id="5810c885-3">Graph structures are emphasized for detecting fraud rings and suspicious relationships among users, transactions, and payment details</cite>.
   - 2024 graph transformer (GT) models specialized for fraud (FraudGT) demonstrate accuracy/latency trade-offs suitable for real-time payment/risk scoring—directly relevant to retail approvals/chargeback defense. <cite id="5810c885-5">FraudGT (2024) proposes a simple, effective, and efficient graph transformer tailored for financial transaction graphs, reporting accuracy and efficiency for fraud detection</cite>.
   - Surveys corroborate GNNs’ edge over classical baselines on ecommerce seller/counterparty risk and ring detection—key for marketplace-retail supply chains. <cite id="5810c885-7">GNNs outperform traditional baselines for financial fraud, anti-money laundering, and e-commerce seller risk assessment</cite> <cite id="5810c885-0">A 2025 survey chapter explicitly notes GNNs’ strength on ecommerce transaction graphs</cite>.

2) Deep learning and hybrid pipelines beyond tabular models
   - Systematic comparisons and recent benchmarks show ML suites (logistic regression, SVM, RF, GBM, neural networks) are effective for ecommerce order-level fraud; RF/GBM often serve as strong baselines, while deep models win when graph/context features are available. <cite id="4d805f01-1">A comparative ML study benchmarks Logistic Regression, SVM, KNN, Random Forest, and Gradient Boosting for ecommerce fraud</cite> <cite id="4d805f01-2">Benchmarking ML for detecting fraudulent orders in ecommerce reports model-wise performance differences and design insights</cite>.
   - Modern DL reviews emphasize architecture selection, data labeling, and evaluation pitfalls (KS/AUC skew, class imbalance, concept drift) that plague live retail pipelines. <cite id="4d805f01-8">The DL survey synthesizes 108 publications (2019–2024) and highlights evaluation pitfalls and deployment constraints in financial (retail-like) fraud</cite> <cite id="d4189f35-0">A 2024 survey finds ML methods across digital marketplaces and ecommerce show broad effectiveness, with guidance on feature engineering and model choice</cite>.

3) Synthetic fraud and identity/ATO/carousel detection in ecommerce/retail
   - Synthetic identity fraud and account takeover (ATO)/carousel fraud are increasingly central in ecommerce; ML-based detection methods outperform rule-only engines but face evasion and data sparsity. <cite id="d4189f35-8">A 2025 survey on synthetic fraud in ecommerce finds ML methods address evolving patterns beyond rule-based detection</cite>.
   - Retail-oriented pipelines now integrate multimodal signals (device/seating, behavioral biometrics, device graphs, session graphs) and dynamic risk scoring with ML to preserve conversion while containing fraud; reports indicate measurable declines in false positives when ML engines are scaled. <cite id="a95981af-0">An anonymous omnichannel retailer reduced false positives by over 40% with a dynamic ML-driven approval/decline and chargeback defense engine across channels</cite> <cite id="a95981af-8">An industry report argues AI models evolve via continuous analysis of transaction data and outperform static rules in retail fraud detection</cite>.

4) Case studies and market/industry evidence
   - Retail sector analyses document AI/ML as increasingly adept at representing chargebacks and reducing losses, while also detailing orchestration and policy optimization needs (e.g., friction vs. false declines). <cite id="a95981af-6">AI/ML has become adept at finding fraud and representing chargebacks in retail anti-fraud applications</cite>.
   - Practice-facing resources summarize two powerful AI use cases for retail: approval/decline triage and ML-backed chargeback defense—both areas where graph/DL models materially change outcomes. <cite id="a95981af-3">Two AI use cases in retail fraud—approval/decline fraud detection and chargeback defense—show strong results from ML-enabled pipelines</cite>.
   - Market and ecosystem reports corroborate investment trajectories and adoption of ML/AI for ecommerce fraud, aligning with the technical advances above. <cite id="a95981af-1">Payment fraud detection AI market growth reflects accelerating adoption of ML/automation for fraud prevention</cite> <cite id="4d805f01-3">2025 merchant report lists improving ML accuracy and automation as top priorities</cite>.

Practical, recent benchmarks and comparative results
- Comparative ML studies on fraudulent online stores provide actionable metrics for marketplace and retail counterparty risk, reinforcing that graph- and learning-based models beat isolated rule engines. <cite id="4d805f01-7">A 2025 comparative analysis introduces ML techniques to identify fraudulent online stores and proposes ELFW-2031 for benchmarking</cite>.
- Industry benchmarks on fraudulent orders show RF/GBM and gradient-boosted ensembles remain strong baselines, while graph-augmented deep models deliver incremental gains on relational signals—directionally consistent across 2023–2025 studies. <cite id="4d805f01-2">Benchmarking ML approaches for fraudulent orders documents comparative performance and feature importance patterns for e-commerce platforms</cite> <cite id="5810c885-2">A 2025 study proposes a GNN-based anomaly detection framework tailored to ecommerce transaction graphs</cite>.

What to read first (a curated reading order)
1) Broad, recent overviews for context and deployment pitfalls
   - Rao et al., “Fraud detection in ecommerce: a systematic review,” 2025—gives taxonomy across ML/deep learning/graph venues and benchmarks, ideal as a map for retail engineers. <cite id="d4189f35-3">A 2025 systematic review spans ML, DL, data mining, and graph representation for ecommerce fraud</cite>.
   - Thivaios et al., “A Survey of Machine Learning and Deep Learning in Fraud Detection,” 2025–2026—focus on datasets, benchmarks, and DL best practices across finance (close to retail ecommerce). <cite id="4d805f01-4">The survey links widely used credit-card datasets to current research and gaps impacting deployment</cite>.
   - Mutemi et al., “E-commerce fraud detection with ML,” 2023–2024—good grounding in algorithm comparisons and cross-marketplace lessons. <cite id="d4189f35-0">This survey evaluates ML effectiveness across digital marketplaces and ecommerce, offering practical guidance</cite>.
   - 2025 Global eCommerce Payments & Fraud Report—practitioner priorities on ML accuracy, automation, and orchestration; maps to retail roadmaps. <cite id="4d805f01-3">Practitioners prioritize ML accuracy, automation, and orchestration as top needs</cite>.

2) Methods transforming retail fraud detection
   - IBM Research FraudGT (2024)—graph transformer for financial transaction graphs; study accuracy/latency trade-offs—excellent for real-time retail gateways. <cite id="5810c885-5">FraudGT delivers accuracy and efficiency for transaction-graph fraud detection</cite>.
   - GNN-based anomaly detection for ecommerce transaction graphs (2025)—show relational modeling benefits on basket/session/merchant graphs. <cite id="5810c885-1">GNNs learn relational structure to enhance ecommerce fraud detection</cite>.
   - Heterogeneous Graph Transformer pipelines (industry write-up)—demonstrates node/relationship scoring for suspicious accounts/transactions. <cite id="5810c885-6">HGT-based pipelines detect and score suspicious nodes and links in fraud graphs</cite>.
   - Rao et al. survey chapter on graph structures and fraud rings—why graphs matter for seller/counterparty risk and collusion detection in retail supply chains. <cite id="5810c885-3">Graphs help detect fraud rings and suspicious relationships among users, transactions, and payment details</cite> <cite id="5810c885-7">GNNs outperform traditional baselines for seller risk assessment</cite>.

3) Retail-focused case evidence and identity/carousel threats
   - ACI Anonymous Omnichannel Retailer case—40%+ drop in false positives with a dynamic ML engine across channels and methods; strong evidence for portfolio-level impact. <cite id="a95981af-0">False-positive rates dropped over 40% using a dynamic ML-driven approval/decline and chargeback defense engine</cite>.
   - Synthetic fraud survey (2025)—explains why ML is needed vs. rules as synthetic identities and ATO evolve in ecommerce/retail. <cite id="d4189f35-8">ML-based detection is required to tackle synthetic fraud patterns that evade rule-based systems</cite>.

4) Benchmarks and comparative metrics on order/transaction fraud
   - Benchmarking ML for fraudulent orders in ecommerce (2025–2026)—provides model-wise comparisons and feature importance; practical for A/B planning. <cite id="4d805f01-2">Comparative benchmarking highlights performance differences across ML models for detecting fraudulent orders</cite>.
   - Comparative analysis of ML for fraudulent online stores (2025)—benchmarks and dataset ELFW-2031 for marketplace/retail up-sell fraud detection. <cite id="4d805f01-7">ELFW-2031 is proposed to benchmark ML detection of fraudulent online stores</cite>.

Key takeaways for retail deployment
- Graph-augmented models (GNNs/GT) consistently improve detection of collusion, ATO, and structured fraud rings by modeling cross-entity relationships; combine with tabular deep models for feature richness. <cite id="5810c885-1">GNNs improve fraud detection by leveraging transaction and user relationships</cite> <cite id="5810c885-5">Graph transformers tailored to fraud graphs show strong accuracy–efficiency profiles</cite> <cite id="5810c885-3">Graph structures help detect fraud rings and suspicious links among users and payments</cite>.
- Expect practical gains when moving from rule-only engines: large retails report substantial drops in false positives and better conversion-preserving control with ML orchestration. <cite id="a95981af-0">An omnichannel retailer achieved a >40% drop in false positives with a ML-driven orchestration engine across channels</cite> <cite id="a95981af-8">AI models that evolve via transactional analysis outperform static rules in retail fraud</cite>.
- Prioritize datasets and features spanning session, device, identity, product/merchant, and payment context; treat class imbalance and data drift explicitly; evaluate with risk-aware metrics (precision-at-k, calibration, impact on chargebacks vs. conversion). <cite id="4d805f01-4">Surveys highlight dataset design and benchmark pitfalls in credit-card fraud that apply to ecommerce</cite> <cite id="d4189f35-0">Recent surveys emphasize feature engineering and model choice across ecommerce marketplaces</cite>.
- Anticipate an arms race: synthetic identities and carousel/ATO schemes evolve; continuous ML monitoring and active learning on chargeback feedback loops are essential. <cite id="d4189f35-8">ML is needed to counter synthetic fraud patterns that evade rules</cite> <cite id="4d805f01-3">Adoption plans prioritize improving ML accuracy and orchestration to handle evolving fraud</cite>.

Open directions and where research is pushing
- LLMs and generative models for synthetic data augmentation and adversarial robustness in fraud: early 2024–2025 works hint at synthetic transaction generation to toughen train–test gaps; look for empirical comparisons against graph/DL baselines in ecommerce contexts. <cite id="4d805f01-8">DL surveys identify data augmentation and adversarial robustness as active fronts in financial fraud</cite> <cite id="d4189f35-0">Ecommerce-focused surveys note effectiveness across ML families and call out data-centric improvements</cite>.
- Cross-vertical portability: results from financial fraud increasingly transfer to retail ecommerce; however, open, anonymized, retail-specific datasets remain scarce; recent surveys urge stronger benchmarks and synthetic datasets. <cite id="4d805f01-4">Recent surveys emphasize gaps in benchmarks and datasets that affect transfer from finance to ecommerce</cite>.
- Explainability and policy optimization: retail leaders plan to improve fraud ML accuracy and orchestration, implying demand for XAI and policy engines that balance fraud loss and conversion. <cite id="4d805f01-3">Orchestration and ML accuracy are top priorities; policy optimization is highlighted alongside AI improvements</cite>.

How to apply this to your stack
- Start with an ML-driven approval/decline model (tabular DL or gne-t) plus a complementary GNN layer over basket/session graphs; incorporate device/identity graphs and geolocation signals. <cite id="5810c885-1">GNNs are effective when modeling transactional and user relationships</cite> <cite id="5810c885-5">Graph transformers provide a strong backbone for real-time graph risk scoring</cite>.
- Add a chargeback-representation module: train with delayed labels and incorporate graph propagation at decision time to improve recall on future-looking risk. <cite id="a95981af-0">Dynamic engines integrating approvals and chargeback defense deliver large reductions in false positives</cite>.
- Build synthetic fraud resilience: include anomaly-based and behavior-clustering layers, and evaluate with synthetic identity datasets; maintain active learning from chargebacks and dispute outcomes. <cite id="d4189f35-8">Synthetic fraud detection with ML is crucial as patterns evolve beyond rules</cite>.
- Track with risk-aware metrics and A/B on live traffic; iterate with the latest surveys and industry benchmarks to calibrate trade-offs. <cite id="4d805f01-4">Surveys recommend benchmarking and evaluation aligned with credit-card fraud lessons</cite> <cite id="4d805f01-3">Industry trends emphasize improving ML accuracy and automation in omnichannel payment fraud</cite>.

Notes on evidence quality and gaps
- Peer-reviewed evidence is strong for GNN/graph transformer efficacy and ML-driven orchestration; multiple 2025 surveys and vendor case studies report operational wins, though some are vendor-sponsored. <cite id="5810c885-5">FraudGT is a peer-reviewed 2024 graph-transformer system with efficiency/accuracy reporting</cite> <cite id="a95981af-0">Major vendor case study reports >40% false-positive reduction in omnichannel retail</cite>.
- Gaps include open, retail-specific datasets with chargeback labels and rigorous, head-to-head comparisons of LLM/generative data strategies in ecommerce graphs. <cite id="d4189f35-4">Surveys highlight underexplored benchmarks and datasets in e-commerce compared to finance</cite>.
- Keep an eye on synthetic identity, ATO/carousel evolution, and adversarial robustness as continual learning needs for 2025–2026 retail deployments. <cite id="d4189f35-8">Synthetic fraud surveys document ML’s expanding role versus rule-based detection</cite> <cite id="4d805f01-3">2025 reports forecast continued need for improved ML accuracy and orchestration</cite>.

fully_underspecified.answer:
# Scope and recent surveys

<cite id="fa96fb63-0">Recent reviews of machine learning for financial fraud detection converge on core pain points: extreme class imbalance, automation at scale, explainability for regulated settings, and compliance with privacy regulations such as GDPR and data-locality constraints</cite>. <cite id="fa96fb63-1">Newer surveys stress modeling challenges unique to fraud, including highly skewed labels, adversarial shifts as fraud tactics evolve, heterogeneous and multichannel data, and the need for robust deployment patterns beyond batch scoring</cite>. <cite id="fa96fb63-2">Comprehensive reviews of financial fraud algorithms and challenges highlight privacy, regulatory compliance, and tactic evolution as cross-cutting concerns alongside algorithmic evaluation and benchmarking</cite>. <cite id="fa96fb63-3">Year-over-year analyses echo these difficulties—imbalanced datasets, model interpretability, and ethics—while mapping emerging opportunities in graph, deep, and multimodal learning for real-time detection</cite>.

# Core algorithms, deep learning, and graph methods

<cite id="fa96fb63-5">Comparative analyses of banking transaction models increasingly benchmark traditional classifiers (e.g., logistic regression, decision trees, random forests) against deep neural approaches under class-imbalance-aware metrics, finding that modern ML pipelines address imbalance with sampling/weighting layers and achieve substantially higher practical utility than naive baselines</cite>. <cite id="f9a7eba8-0">In financial transactions, heterogeneous graph neural network models like HHLN-GNN have been proposed to exploit subgraph generators and neighborhood samplers, explicitly targeting imbalance and categorical feature structure in fraud graphs</cite>. <cite id="f9a7eba8-1">GNN-based fraud frameworks for financial services often introduce new evaluation setups that stress temporal shifts and rare-event recall, reflecting operational constraints in fast-moving transaction graphs</cite>. <cite id="f9a7eba8-2">Recent reviews in anti-money laundering (AML) highlight continual graph learning as a trajectory for evolving graph-based detection, unifying concept drift, lifelong learning, and privacy concerns in cryptocurrency/money-laundering graphs</cite>. <cite id="f9a7eba8-4">GNN applications in cryptocurrency transaction classification demonstrate improved classification of laundering patterns relative to classical ML baselines, leveraging neighborhood aggregation to capture conspiracy-like structures</cite>. <cite id="f9a7eba8-3">Industry-oriented comparisons typically report that models exploiting graph structure (GNNs) generate fewer false positives for the same false-negative budget compared to models that ignore relational signals</cite>.

# Imbalance, drift, and evaluation best practices

<cite id="d3eb76c9-8">Fraud datasets are typically extremely imbalanced, so performance evaluation emphasizes recall, precision, and F1 (and PR curves) rather than raw accuracy, which can mask severe class bias</cite>. <cite id="d3eb76c9-7">Class-imbalance mitigation strategies frequently compared include oversampling (e.g., SMOTE), undersampling, weighting, and anomaly detection variants; precision-recall based comparisons are recommended to reflect operational loss trade-offs</cite>. <cite id="fa96fb63-0">Automation and orchestration challenges include feature engineering at scale, closed-loop feedback from detection to case management, and sustained explainability to auditors</cite>. <cite id="f9a7eba8-2">Continual learning perspectives emphasize concept drift and adversarial adaptation: as fraud evolves, graph topology and feature distributions shift, necessitating incremental retraining and novelty detection in graph streams</cite>.

# Domain case studies

- Credit and e-commerce transactions:
  <cite id="fa96fb63-5">Empirical comparisons on real-world credit-card datasets show that pipelines combining classical models with imbalance-aware preprocessing improve F1 over baselines; deep models layered with class-weights/SMOTE variants further lift recall at controlled false-positive cost</cite>. <cite id="d3eb76c9-6">A comparative telecom/telecom fraud study reports PR-based F1 near 99.9% using XGBoost, GNN, and BERT features, reflecting the utility of gradient-boosted trees on tabular signals, graph patterns, and tokenized behavioral sequences</cite>. <cite id="d3eb76c9-8">Because credit-card datasets are extremely skewed, practitioners consistently emphasize optimizing PR-F1, not accuracy, when comparing algorithms for deployment</cite>.

- Telecom and subscription services:
  <cite id="d3eb76c9-0">Real-data telecom fraud work has demonstrated that naive models can reach >99% accuracy on imbalanced labels while delivering low F1 (~0.0355), warning against accuracy-centric evaluation and underscoring the need for balanced scoring and cost-sensitive learning</cite>. <cite id="d3eb76c9-4">Telecom fraud detection case studies integrate customer behavior sequences (call graphs, usage patterns) with ML classifiers tailored to imbalanced risks, showing improved identification of abnormal consumption patterns</cite>. <cite id="6fedeadf-3">Federated deployments in telecom have reported 35–40% accuracy gains by training across fragmented data while keeping raw records local, enabling better generalization to regional fraud variants</cite>.

- Insurance and claims:
  <cite id="fa96fb63-1">Surveys of ML+DL for fraud flag insurance claims as a canonical heterogeneous, multichannel setting where model-agnostic imbalance handling, graph-based collusion detection, and explainability are essential for claims adjusters and compliance</cite>. <cite id="fa96fb63-2">Recent reviews summarize algorithmic progress (logistic/d trees/RF, gradient boosting, SVMs, deep nets, and GNNs) and regulatory constraints that govern insurance fraud detection, with emphasis on audit trails and fairness</cite>. <cite id="f9a7eba8-7">GNN- and network-analysis methods adapted to financial fraud detection provide technical guidance on modeling collusion networks among customers/agents and carriers, improving detection of coordinated claims</cite>.

# Privacy, security, and multi-party learning

<cite id="6fedeadf-1">Federated learning (FL) trains models across institutions by sharing gradients rather than raw data, enabling collaborative fraud detection while limiting data exfiltration risk</cite>. <cite id="6fedeadf-2">Federated fraud detection frameworks specifically target credit-card use-cases, combining cross-institution aggregation with privacy-preserving techniques (e.g., differential privacy) to reduce leakage from model updates</cite>. <cite id="6fedeadf-4">In financial push-payment and e-commerce fraud, FL approaches coordinate on shared risk signals (sender/receiver behavior, IP/route anomalies) while preserving sensitive personal and merchant data at the edge</cite>. <cite id="6fedeadf-6">Telecom fraud work highlights FL's suitability for overcoming data fragmentation across carriers/regions, as it allows privacy-preserving training and reduces regulatory friction from cross-jurisdictional data movement</cite>. <cite id="6fedeadf-0">Practical FL deployments in credit-card fraud often integrate sampling (e.g., SMOTE variants in latent space) to balance rare fraud patterns under privacy constraints, addressing centralization limits on rare-event data</cite>. <cite id="6fedeadf-5">Complementary privacy-preserving techniques—secure aggregation, pruning, and quantization—are commonly combined with client-side encryption to protect sensitive fields during collaborative training</cite>.

# Benchmarks and datasets

<cite id="fa96fb63-4">The Amazon Science Fraud Dataset Benchmark compiles multiple fraud tasks across card-not-present transactions, bot attacks, malicious traffic, and loan risk, providing a cross-domain suite to compare sampling, feature, and model choices under shared evaluation protocols</cite>. <cite id="fa96fb63-5">Model-comparison studies on banking transaction fraud emphasize using real-world datasets with documented imbalance and domain leakage constraints, and they report PR-F1 and case-cost trade-offs rather than accuracy alone</cite>. <cite id="f9a7eba8-1">GNN-focused financial fraud evaluations introduce temporal splits and streaming settings to assess detection under concept drift on transaction-graph snapshots, complementing standard batch benchmarks</cite>. <cite id="d3eb76c9-6">Telecom-focused comparative studies combine tabular usage logs with graph-structured call/session data, with reported PR-based F1 ≈ 0.999 for best models under regional imbalance</cite>.

# Tools, pipelines, and deployment patterns

<cite id="fa96fb63-0">Practical reviews argue for end-to-end orchestration that integrates data ingestion, imbalance-aware feature generation, model training/A/B, and human-in-the-loop adjudication, with centralized dashboards linking alerts to explanations for compliance</cite>. <cite id="fa96fb63-5">Implementations commonly layer sampling/weighting (SMOTE, ADASYN, loss weighting) atop GBMs or deep nets on tabular/sequence features, then deploy with change detection and active learning to refresh models as fraud evolves</cite>. <cite id="f9a7eba8-1">GNN pipelines often combine graph construction (co-occurrence of devices/addresses, merchant networks) with neighborhood sampling and layer normalization, optimized for low-latency inference in detection microservices</cite>. <cite id="6fedeadf-1">Federated deployments centralize aggregator logic while enforcing privacy and security on update exchanges, using robust aggregation, clipping, and key management to harden against poisoning under adversarial data distributions</cite>.

# Representative recent papers and resources

- Surveys and overviews:
  <cite id="fa96fb63-0">Deep learning in financial fraud detection: taxonomy and challenges including imbalance, automation, explainability, and privacy</cite>; <cite id="fa96fb63-1">Survey of ML/DL for financial fraud detection with modeling challenges and deployment considerations</cite>; <cite id="fa96fb63-2">Comprehensive review of algorithms, challenges, and future directions in financial fraud</cite>; <cite id="fa96fb63-3">Year-over-year developments emphasizing imbalanced data, interpretability, and ethics opportunities</cite>; <cite id="fa96fb63-7">Systematic analysis of 61 ML articles on bank fraud (2019–2025) detailing methods and performance</cite>.

- Deep and graph learning:
  <cite id="f9a7eba8-0">HHLN-GNN for transaction fraud uses subgraph generators and neighborhood samplers to handle category-rich graphs under imbalance</cite>; <cite id="f9a7eba8-2">Continual graph learning survey for AML summarizes methods for drifting transaction graphs</cite>; <cite id="f9a7eba8-4">GNNs for cryptocurrency transaction classification improve laundering detection relative to prior ML methods</cite>; <cite id="f9a7eba8-3">Industry analysis reports fewer false positives for GNN-based detectors at fixed false-negative budgets</cite>.

- Industrial/empirical case studies:
  <cite id="d3eb76c9-0">Telecom fraud detection on real operator data shows accuracy-deception: >99% macro accuracy despite trivial F1 due to imbalance</cite>; <cite id="d3eb76c9-6">Telecom/cyber fraud comparison: reported PR-based F1 ≈ 0.999 with XGBoost, GNN, and BERT features</cite>; <cite id="fa96fb63-5">Credit-card benchmarking across LR, DT, RF and deep models with imbalance-aware techniques improves F1 over naive baselines</cite>.

- Privacy-preserving and federated:
  <cite id="6fedeadf-1">FL for privacy-preserving fraud detection explains gradient sharing and threat models across institutions</cite>; <cite id="6fedeadf-2">Federated credit-card fraud detection investigates cross-bank privacy-preserving learning and accuracy uplift</cite>; <cite id="6fedeadf-4">FL for e-commerce/payments detects financial fraud while preserving sensitive consumer/merchant data</cite>; <cite id="6fedeadf-3">Telecom case study reports 35–40% accuracy gains from federated training across fragmented customer datasets</cite>.

- Benchmarks and datasets:
  <cite id="fa96fb63-4">Amazon Science Fraud Dataset Benchmark spans multiple fraud types to enable cross-task and method comparisons</cite>.

# Practical guidance and open problems

<cite id="fa96fb63-0">Design for rarity and adversariness: adopt imbalance-aware objectives, rare-event augmentation, and robust evaluation (PR-F1/coverage) before deployment</cite>. <cite id="f9a7eba8-2">Adapt to drift with continual and anomaly-aware graph learning; maintain mechanisms to detect topology and feature shifts in transaction/communication graphs</cite>. <cite id="6fedeadf-1">Use federated or privacy-preserving training where regulation forbids central data pools; combine DP/noise, secure aggregation, and certificate-based update vetting to defend against insider or poisoning attacks</cite>. <cite id="fa96fb63-0">Invest in model governance: log false-positive/false-negative clusters, enable local explainability (e.g., SHAP for tabular, attention/probe for deep and GNN attributions), and establish audit trails aligned with compliance</cite>. <cite id="fa96fb63-1">Integrate multimodal, cross-channel signals and build pipelines that adapt quickly to emerging fraud vectors; surveys point to persistent challenges in heterogeneous data unification and real-time validation</cite>. <cite id="fa96fb63-5">Compare classical and deep models on real datasets with stratified temporal splits; prefer pipelines that deliver clinically relevant F1 and latency within fraud investigation workflows</cite>.

# Where to start reading and experimenting

- Broad taxonomies: <cite id="fa96fb63-0">Deep learning in financial fraud detection (2025 review)</cite>; <cite id="fa96fb63-1">Survey of ML/DL for financial fraud detection, architectures, data modalities, deployment challenges</cite>; <cite id="fa96fb63-3">Year-over-year developments (2025) on challenges/opportunities</cite>.
- Methods: <cite id="f9a7eba8-0">HHLN-GNN paper for transaction fraud with neighborhood sampling</cite>; <cite id="f9a7eba8-4">GNNs for cryptocurrency AML classification</cite>; <cite id="f9a7eba8-2">Continual graph learning in AML</cite>.
- Benchmarks: <cite id="fa96fb63-4">Amazon Science Fraud Dataset Benchmark multi-task suite</cite>.
- Deployment: <cite id="6fedeadf-1">FL for privacy-preserving fraud detection (concept and threat model)</cite>; telecom/credit case studies with reported uplifts <cite id="6fedeadf-3">telecom FL case study (35–40% accuracy gain)</cite>; <cite id="fa96fb63-5">credit/deep model comparison under imbalance</cite>.

Collectively, recent literature emphasizes that the most effective fraud systems blend imbalance-aware modeling and evaluation with graph/deep learning over structured behavioral-relational data, deployed under privacy-preserving, federated architectures and governed by explainable, audit-ready pipelines, with continual learning to counteradaptive adversaries. <cite id="fa96fb63-0">These systems succeed when designed around fraud's rare-event nature, regulatory constraints, and the arms race between defenses and novel attack patterns</cite>.
