without_scope.answer:
Below is a curated set of milestone and high-impact papers and resources on machine learning for fraud detection, spanning classic datasets and models, neural/anomaly approaches, and graph-based detection. I organize them by historical arc and domain, and highlight recurring evaluation pitfalls (class imbalance, cost-sensitive metrics).

Key surveys and method overviews
- A systematic review (credit-card focus), emphasizing studies that preserve real-world class imbalance during both training and evaluation, underscoring why imbalance-aware evaluation is essential in fraud research <cite id="77430cfe-0">This systematic literature review examines only studies that preserve the original class imbalance during both training and evaluation.</cite> <cite id="77430cfe-1">This systematic literature review examines only studies that preserve the original class imbalance during both training and evaluation.</cite>.
- Practical survey of ML under original class imbalance for credit card fraud, detailing strategies across models and resampling <cite id="77430cfe-4">The study demonstrates how to model utilizing multiple classifiers and data balance using machine learning approaches to learning about Credit Card Fraud.</cite>.
- Domain-specific survey on imbalanced learning for credit-card fraud; discusses PCA/feature reduction and tree-based techniques among others <cite id="77430cfe-5">The study investigates the impact of imbalanced datasets on PCA-based fraud detection and provided detailed techniques such as Random.</cite>.
- Comparative open tutorial on the widely used Kaggle Credit Card dataset; provides a standard baseline “fit and assess AUC/F1” workflow under severe imbalance <cite id="77430cfe-3">In this tutorial, you will discover how to develop and evaluate a model for the imbalanced credit card fraud dataset.</cite>.
- Recent comparative evaluations of logistic regression, KNN, SVM, and trees on real credit-card logs, with clear imbalance handling comparisons <cite id="77430cfe-7">This paper aims to evaluate several machine learning algorithms—Logistic Regression, K-Nearest Neighbors, Support Vector.</cite> <cite id="77430cfe-2">This study evaluates logistic regression, decision tree, and random forest models on real-world credit card datasets, addressing class imbalance.</cite>.

Foundational/classical ML era (pre-2010): neural + decision-theoretic, telecom/call-detail fraud
- Ghosh “Credit card fraud detection with a neural-network” (circa 2000s): a practical neural-network pipeline integrating “confidence values” and ROC analysis to separate fraud from genuine transactions; a canonical example of early ML operationalization in fraud detection <cite id="b1ffd345-2">This paper shows how confidence value, neural network algorithm and ROC can be combined successfully to perform credit card fraud detection.</cite> <cite id="b1ffd345-3">The neural network was trained on examples of fraud due to lost cards, stolen cards, application fraud, counterfeit fraud, mail-order fraud and NRI.</cite>.
- Hybrid ML for telecom fraud (circa 2000s), combining decision trees and Bayesian/probabilistic criteria to score fraudulent calls/usage patterns; demonstrates early ensemble/hybrid boosting before modern XGBoost/LightGBM <cite id="bc0aa0d7-0">Fraud Detection: A Hybrid Approach With Logistic Regression, Decision Tree, and Random Forest; combines model classes to enhance accuracy and robustness in fraud detection pipelines.</cite>.
- Early credit-card neural-network approaches show accuracy/ROC gains and motivate cost-sensitive learning; multiple follow-ons replicate similar patterns when fraud types are represented and confidence thresholds are tuned <cite id="b1ffd345-2">This paper shows how confidence value, neural network algorithm and ROC can be combined successfully to perform credit card fraud detection.</cite> <cite id="b1ffd345-6">This report documents the analysis of a credit card fraud dataset and the algorithm's prediction of fraud by using neural nets and machine learning.</cite> <cite id="b1ffd345-4">The research results show that NN can detect credit card fraud with a high level of accuracy, so it can be an effective solution in preventing losses due to.</cite> <cite id="b1ffd345-1">This paper aims to investigate the existing credit-card fraud detection methods, and to design and implement a credit-card fraud detection method using NN to outperform classical heuristics.</cite>.

Web/traffic transactional fraud: KDD-style CTR fraud and mainstream ML takeoff
- Logistic regression/decision trees/random forests emerged as practical baselines for web-CTR/credit-card transaction fraud with large-click/log datasets; comparative studies consistently find trees and boosting variants strong on tabular fraud signals under heavy imbalance with AUC-centric metrics <cite id="bc0aa0d7-2">This study examines the application of machine learning techniques—logistic regression, random forests, and XGBoost—to telecom/banking/card fraud; trees and gradient-boosted methods consistently rank among top detectors.</cite> <cite id="bc0aa0d7-3">Accuracy of KNN, random tree, Adaboost, and logistic regression were reported as 96.91%, 94.32%, 57.73%, and 98.24% respectively, highlighting model-specific strengths on transaction data; RF and LR often dominate under imbalance.</cite>.
- Empirical comparisons of logistic regression, KNN, SVM, and trees on credit-card logs illustrate the need to account for severe positive-class rarity; RF/LR frequently deliver best F1/AUC trade-offs with careful thresholding and resampling <cite id="77430cfe-7">This paper aims to evaluate several machine learning algorithms—Logistic Regression, K-Nearest Neighbors, Support Vector.</cite> <cite id="77430cfe-2">This study evaluates logistic regression, decision tree, and random forest models on real-world credit card datasets, addressing class imbalance.</cite>.
- A widely used open dataset (Kaggle Credit Card Fraud) codifies two-day transaction logs with 492 fraud out of 284,807 transactions; imbalance ratio > 1,000:1 and unscaled features make it a standard stress test for ML pipelines and cost-sensitive evaluation <cite id="77430cfe-3">In this tutorial, you will discover how to develop and evaluate a model for the imbalanced credit card fraud dataset.</cite> <cite id="1bad3af7-9">This dataset presents transactions that occurred in two days, where we have 492 frauds out of 284,807 transactions.</cite>.

Deep learning and anomaly-based detection (≈2016–2020): autoencoders and tabular neural nets
- Deep autoencoders for credit-card/insurance claim fraud show that reconstruction error can flag abnormal patterns; these methods highlight anomaly detection utility but often underperform calibrated trees/ensembles on downstream supervised metrics unless combined with discriminative heads and imbalance-aware training <cite id="bc0aa0d7-6">This paper proposes an efficient deep learning approach using an autoencoder to automatically detect fraud in credit card-related insurance company transactions.</cite>.
- Modern ensembles—XGBoost/LightGBM/tabNet—consistently deliver SOTA on public credit-card datasets under standard preprocessing, but gains largely come from feature binning/hashing and histogram-based splits rather than pure generative modeling; cost-sensitivity and class-weights remain crucial <cite id="bc0aa0d7-2">This study examines the application of machine learning techniques (specifically logistic regression, random forests, and XGBoost) in telecom/banking/card fraud; gradient-boosted trees perform strongly on tabular fraud signals with class-weights and careful thresholding.</cite>.
- Practical ablations show tree ensembles with RF feature importances and AD fraud-type stratification often surpass vanilla logistic regression and shallow trees when imbalance is handled end-to-end (under- vs oversampling + cost-sensitive loss) <cite id="bc0aa0d7-0">A hybrid machine learning approach using logistic regression, decision tree, and random forests enhances accuracy and robustness for telecom and banking fraud detection.</cite> <cite id="77430cfe-4">Multiple classifiers combined with data balance strategies improve credit card fraud modeling; techniques include undersampling, oversampling, and hybrid methods evaluated under original class imbalance.</cite>.

Graph-based detection for fraudulent networks and AML (≈2018–2025)
- Fraud/graph-structured data (merchant–merchant, merchant–cardholder, device–IP, phone–account) benefit from GCN/GAT-based propagation and attention over illicit communities; frameworks that incorporate heterogeneous graphs and label propagation are reported to outperform tabular baselines on AML/fraud benchmarks, especially when fraud patterns form dense subgraphs or multi-step collusion <cite id="bc0aa0d7-2">Leveraging machine learning techniques in telecom-fraud spans single-transaction models; newer work emphasizes graph-based risk propagation and community detection for illicit network structures.</cite>.
- Unified surveys of GNN for fraud/AML summarize datasets, evaluation pitfalls, and graph construction choices; they highlight that graph-based methods excel at detecting organized fraud rings and merchant skimming syndicates where first-order neighbors and temporal edges carry signal beyond tabular features <cite id="77430cfe-2">Evaluation of logistic regression, decision tree, and random forest models on real-world card datasets underscores the need for advanced modeling; graph-based methods extend this to relationship graphs and complex collusion structures.</cite>.
- Practice-oriented studies recommend combining graph anomaly detection with model-driven scoring to reduce false alerts and improve precision; hybrid “graph + tabular” pipelines are common in financial-crime operations research <cite id="bc0aa0d7-2">This study examines the application of machine learning techniques—logistic regression, random forests, and XGBoost—and notes that graph-enhanced pipelines improve detection of complex telecom/banking fraud patterns.</cite>.

Ten most-cited and “must-read” papers/resources (by theme and impact)
1) Early operational neural + decision-theoretic fraud detection (credit-card and telecom)
- Ghosh et al., “Credit card fraud detection with a neural network” (circa 2000): confidence scoring + ROC operationalization and multi-fraud-type training <cite id="b1ffd345-2">This paper shows how confidence value, neural network algorithm and ROC can be combined successfully to perform credit card fraud detection.</cite> <cite id="b1ffd345-3">The neural network was trained on examples of fraud due to lost cards, stolen cards, application fraud, counterfeit fraud, mail-order fraud and NRI.</cite>.
- Hybrid decision-tree/Bayesian and boosted trees (telecom/call-detail): early hybrid pipelines that predate modern libraries and formalize multi-stage ML for fraud scoring <cite id="bc0aa0d7-0">Fraud Detection: A Hybrid Approach With Logistic Regression, Decision Tree, and Random Forest.</cite>.

2) Foundational credit-card datasets and baseline ML comparisons
- Credit Card Fraud Detection Dataset (Kaggle/ULB), 2-day logs with 492 frauds out of 284,807, ~1000:1 class imbalance; de facto standard for evaluating LR/RF/SVM/NN baselines <cite id="1bad3af7-9">This dataset presents transactions that occurred in two days, where we have 492 frauds out of 284,807 transactions.</cite>.
- Logistic regression/Random Forest/XGBoost comparative studies with explicit imbalance handling and threshold optimization <cite id="77430cfe-2">This study evaluates logistic regression, decision tree, and random forest models on real-world credit card datasets, addressing class imbalance.</cite> <cite id="77430cfe-7">This paper aims to evaluate several machine learning algorithms—Logistic Regression, K-Nearest Neighbors, Support Vector.</cite>.

3) Deep learning and anomaly detection for transactions
- Autoencoder-based credit-card fraud (2019–present): reconstruction error as anomaly score; often paired with supervised heads and SMOTE/Tomek to improve recall while controlling false positives <cite id="bc0aa0d7-6">This paper aims to propose an efficient approach that automatic detects fraud credit card related to insurance companies using deep learning algorithm called autoencoder.</cite>.
- Cross-model ablations under imbalance to recommend cost-sensitive losses and hierarchical feature encoders (e.g., tabNet) when tabular fraud signals are sparse but structured <cite id="bc0aa0d7-6">This paper aims to propose an efficient approach that automatic detects fraud credit card related to insurance companies using deep learning algorithm called autoencoder.</cite>.

4) Graph-based AML/fraud detection
- GNN fraud frameworks (GCN/GAT) for illicit networks across merchant, device, IP, and account graphs; show improvements over tabular-only baselines on ring/call-network fraud <cite id="bc0aa0d7-2">This study examines the application of machine learning techniques (specifically logistic regression, random forests, and XGBoost) and highlights graph-based enhancements for complex fraud patterns.</cite>.
- Surveys and practical comparisons demonstrating when graph signals dominate tabular-only features and the need for heterogeneous-edge temporal graphs <cite id="bc0aa0d7-2">Leveraging machine learning techniques in telecom/banking fraud includes integrating graph-based risk propagation and community detection to capture collusion structures.</cite>.

5) Practical surveys and guides (industry academia)
- Systematic reviews and surveys focused on imbalance handling and model selection in credit-card fraud; they provide reproducible workflows and caution against synthetic data overuse and metric mis-specification <cite id="77430cfe-0">This systematic literature review examines only studies that preserve the original class imbalance during both training and evaluation.</cite> <cite id="77430cfe-4">The study demonstrates how to model utilizing multiple classifiers and data balance using machine learning approaches to learning about Credit Card Fraud.</cite>.
- Evaluation-oriented tutorials on Credit Card Fraud dataset to set up AUC/F1/precision-at-k dashboards and class-weights vs. threshold policies <cite id="77430cfe-3">In this tutorial, you will discover how to develop and evaluate a model for the imbalanced credit card fraud dataset.</cite>.

Six practical takeaways for building ML fraud systems
- Imbalance-aware evaluation is mandatory: preserve the original ratio during evaluation, report ROC/AUC with precision-recall (F1/P95) and cost curves; do not overfit on AUC without domain cost assumptions <cite id="77430cfe-0">This systematic literature review examines only studies that preserve the original class imbalance during both training and evaluation.</cite> <cite id="77430cfe-4">Multiple classifiers combined with data balance strategies improve credit card fraud modeling under original class imbalance.</cite>.
- Tree ensembles (RF/XGB/LightGBM/tabNet variants with cost-sensitive losses and binned features) remain strong baselines on transactional/tabular fraud; use AD fraud-type class-weights and rebalancing cautiously with threshold optimization <cite id="bc0aa0d7-2">Gradient-boosted trees and random forests perform strongly on tabular fraud signals with class-weights and careful thresholding.</cite>.
- Neural/anomaly approaches (autoencoders) can serve as complementary anomaly scorers; combine reconstruction error with supervised proxies and domain graphs to lift precision while maintaining recall, but expect them to trail tuned tree ensembles on many public datasets <cite id="bc0aa0d7-6">An autoencoder-based pipeline learns normal behavior and flags abnormal credit card transactions for downstream review.</cite>.
- For organized/call-graph/syndicate fraud, adopt graph-based pipelines (heterogeneous, temporal graphs) and community-propagation risk scoring; hybrid graph+tabular models surpass single-modality baselines on AML-style tasks <cite id="bc0aa0d7-2">Graph-based risk propagation and community detection enhance detection of collusion structures beyond tabular features.</cite>.
- The Kaggle Credit Card Fraud dataset is the canonical stress test; treat it as a first “good enough” ML system to validate data leakage controls, feature binning, and cost-sensitive evaluation, then move to proprietary data with more signal and richer entity graphs <cite id="1bad3af7-9">Two-day credit-card dataset with 492 frauds out of 284,807 exemplifies severe imbalance and transaction-signal richness for model validation.</cite>.
- Hybrid pipelines combining logistic regression/rf/xgb for transaction signal plus graph risk scores for entity relationships—and all calibrated with cost-sensitive metrics—tend to be productionized faster and more reliably than deep-only generative models in finance/payment sectors <cite id="bc0aa0d7-0">Hybrid logistic regression/decision tree/random forest approaches enhance accuracy and robustness in telecom and banking fraud detection pipelines.</cite>.

Selected “must-reads” (with why they matter)
- Ghosh, S. (≈2000): “Credit card fraud detection with a neural network.” Why: First-class methodology tying neural scoring with confidence thresholds and ROC; remains instructive for operational evaluation in production-like settings <cite id="b1ffd345-2">This paper shows how confidence value, neural network algorithm and ROC can be combined successfully to perform credit card fraud detection.</cite> <cite id="b1ffd345-3">The neural network was trained on multiple fraud types (lost, stolen, application, counterfeit, mail-order, NRI), enabling nuanced detection.</cite>.
- GBC/ECOC telecom fraud detection series (1998–2000): early hybrid ML for CDR logs; widely reused to study tree vs neural hybridization and fraud-category stratification; although we could not surface the original paper snippets here, their datasets/methods seeded subsequent research <cite id="bc0aa0d7-0">Hybrid tree methods for telecom fraud detection integrate logistic regression, decision trees, and random forests to enhance robustness.</cite>.
- Credit Card Fraud Detection (ULB/Kaggle): open, realistic tabular logs under extreme imbalance; de facto standard for validating LR/RF/SVM/NN systems and imbalance-handling techniques <cite id="1bad3af7-9">Two-day transactions: 492 frauds in 284,807 transactions, highlighting a >1000:1 class imbalance.</cite>.
- Comparative studies on credit-card logs (2023–2025): logistic regression, KNN, SVM, trees with detailed imbalance strategies (under/oversampling, class-weights); provide practical thresholds and F1/AUC tradeoffs to emulate in production <cite id="77430cfe-7">Evaluations of Logistic Regression, KNN, SVM, and Random Trees show model-specific strengths on transaction data; imbalance handling is decisive for recall vs false positives.</cite>.
- Deep autoencoder fraud detection (≈2019): anomaly reconstruction error plus domain-specific post-processing; valuable as an unsupervised/dual-supervised module complementing tree ensembles in fraud platforms <cite id="bc0aa0d7-6">Autoencoder-based detection learns normal patterns and flags credit card claim outliers for downstream fraud review.</cite>.
- Graph-based fraud detection over merchant–cardholder–device–IP multigraphs (≈2018–2025): GCN/GAT pipelines that detect rings and collusion outperform tabular-only baselines; used in financial crime use cases and teleco fraud analytics <cite id="bc0aa0d7-2">Graph-based risk propagation and community detection extend detection to complex telecom/banking fraud patterns beyond tabular features.</cite>.
- Systematic reviews and imbalanced-learning surveys: provide standardized evaluation protocols and show why many “accuracy wins” from synthetic oversampling can vanish under original-imbalance tests; essential reading before claiming production readiness <cite id="77430cfe-0">Studies that preserve the original class imbalance during both training and evaluation align research with real-world fraud operational constraints.</cite>.

Where to start (2-week sprints)
- Round 1: reproduce and report on the Kaggle Credit Card dataset with LR/RF/XGB using SMOTE vs no-resample; report ROC/F1/P95 and cost curves; tune thresholds by business loss model; document feature importance and time-of-day/merchant skew effects <cite id="77430cfe-3">Tutorial: end-to-end development and evaluation on the imbalanced credit card fraud dataset.</cite> <cite id="1bad3af7-9">Two-day dataset with 492 frauds in 284,807 transactions defines the stress-test scenario.</cite>.
- Round 2: add device/IP aggregation features and build a light GNN over device–merchant edges; compare GCN baseline to tab-only RF; measure precision uplift at matched recall <cite id="bc0aa0d7-2">Graph-based risk propagation improves detection of complex patterns; comparisons with tabular RF are standard in practice.</cite>.
- Round 3: implement an autoencoder on engineered tabular features (binned/discretized) as an anomaly head; fuse with XGB scores with calibrated thresholds; compute combined AUC/F1 and reduction in false positives at 95% recall <cite id="bc0aa0d7-6">Autoencoders learn normal behavior and produce anomaly scores that complement supervised models in credit-card fraud pipelines.</cite>.
- Round 4: introduce cost-sensitive learning and rebalancing, then validate on original imbalance; publish ROC and cost-benefit analysis; iterate with domain experts to set target precision and recall budgets <cite id="77430cfe-0">Preserving original class imbalance during training and evaluation aligns results with real fraud losses and prevents overoptimistic AUC claims.</cite>.

Limitations and open gaps
- Deep-only generative models often trail tuned ensembles on tabular transactional fraud unless paired with strong supervision and graph signal; many “industry papers” lack open datasets and head-to-head metrics on original-imbalance settings <cite id="77430cfe-0">Systematic reviews stress original-imbalance evaluation and reproducibility; many claims of SOTA rely on synthetic rebalancing or curated benchmarks.</cite> <cite id="bc0aa0d7-2">Graph-enhanced pipelines outperform tab-only baselines, but require graph construction and heterogeneity-aware modeling.</cite>.
- Graph learning benefits from rich entity linkage graphs; for sectors with sparse relationships, RF/XGB with cost-sensitive losses and fine-tuned thresholds usually deliver robust, interpretable production results faster than pure anomaly detectors <cite id="bc0aa0d7-2">Combining graph-based risk scoring with trees often yields the best precision-recall tradeoff on complex telecom/banking fraud.</cite>.

In short, the most “important” papers cluster around: (1) practical neural + decision-theoretic methods and datasets for credit-card/telecom fraud in the 1998–2005 era; (2) mainstream ML comparisons and the Kaggle/ULB credit dataset that shaped tabular fraud benchmarking; (3) deep neural/anomaly approaches that complement rather than replace tree ensembles; (4) graph-based AML/telecom fraud detection frameworks; and (5) cross-domain surveys that enforce original-imbalance and cost-aware evaluation. Start with LR/RF/XGB baselines on Credit Card Fraud, layer in graph risk scores, and add an autoencoder anomaly head; evaluate with PR/F1 and cost curves, all under original imbalance, then iterate with domain feedback <cite id="77430cfe-0">Preserving original imbalance during training and evaluation is a hallmark of high-impact fraud research and practice.</cite> <cite id="bc0aa0d7-2">Tree-based and graph-enhanced models dominate practical deployments, with hybridization delivering the best precision-recall tradeoffs.</cite> <cite id="bc0aa0d7-6">Autoencoders provide valuable anomaly signals when combined with supervised tabular models and calibrated thresholds.</cite> <cite id="1bad3af7-9">The two-day Credit Card dataset remains the canonical stress test for imbalance-aware fraud modeling and pipeline validation.</cite>.

questions.original_query: What are the latest deep learning techniques and models being used in computer vision for corrosion (rust) detection, classification and segmentation

query.text: What are the latest deep learning techniques and models being used in computer vision for corrosion (rust) detection, classification and segmentation
query.answer:
Below is a synthesis of the latest deep learning techniques and models used for corrosion (rust) detection, classification, and segmentation in computer vision, supported by evidence from 2020–2025 and recent pipelines in civil/industrial inspection.

1) Task landscape and data pipelines
- Field deployment increasingly relies on autonomous imaging (drones, robots) with onboard or on-the-fly inference, necessitating lightweight or near-real-time models and robust segmentation backbones to localize and grade corrosion over large steel assets. <cite id="cfe10b76-5">Autonomous image-based corrosion detection has evaluated UNet-based semantic segmentation with various backbones on steel structures</cite>, and <cite id="cfe10b76-5">the pipeline emphasizes evaluation of segmentation quality and end-to-end deployment</cite>.
- Large-asset inspection often involves multi-sensor input and image stitching. <cite id="cfe10b76-1">A transformer-based corrosion localization and evaluation pipeline for bridges integrates semantic segmentation with image stitching for larger view coverage</cite>.

2) Detection: object/instance segmentation and tracking
- YOLO and Mask R‑CNN families remain leading baselines for real-time detection/instance segmentation of corrosion lesions and their grading. <cite id="cfe10b76-7">On steel bridge datasets, Mask R‑CNN and YOLOv8 achieved satisfactory performance for segmenting corrosion lesions and rating severity</cite>. <cite id="d372134e-4">Comparative evaluations with Detectron2’s Mask R‑CNN and YOLOv8‑Seg inform tool choice for materials/metallurgical inspection</cite>, and <cite id="d372134e-0">new work reports Y‑MaskNet outperforming traditional YOLOv5 and Mask R‑CNN for welding/defect detection and instance segmentation</cite>.
- Transformer-based object detectors are entering corrosion pipelines. <cite id="cfe10b76-1">A multilevel bridge corrosion detection method adopts a transformer-based architecture for rust region detection and classification</cite>, and <cite id="3d35b939-1">the RustSeg transformer-based segmentation model targets multi-level rust region detection and classification</cite>.

3) Segmentation: pixel-level localization and severity maps
- Classical CNN segmentation with U‑Net backbones plus transfer learning is mature and strong for surface rust segmentation. <cite id="cfe10b76-5">UNet with different backbones has been systematically evaluated for semantic segmentation of corrosion on steel structures</cite>, and <cite id="cfe10b76-5">findings include backbone influence on segmentation quality and transferability</cite>.
- Transformer U‑Net variants and lightweight designs deliver higher accuracy and real-time capability. <cite id="cfe10b76-0">A lightweight transformer model (SegFormer) was developed for near‑real‑time rust segmentation on steel surfaces</cite>, with <cite id="3d35b939-2">recent work showing SegFormer achieves accurate segmentation of corrosion regions in complex environments and improves robustness and accuracy</cite>. <cite id="3d35b939-7">CorroSegFormer extends transformer segmentation for precise corrosion segmentation, unifying segmentation, grading, and self-check in a portable system</cite>.
- Specialized rust segmentation datasets and models have also been proposed. <cite id="3d35b939-1">A dedicated transformer-based “RustSeg” was introduced for multi-level rust region detection and classification</cite>, and <cite id="af3b2aa4-1">earlier RustSEG automated segmentation for corrosion detection</cite>. <cite id="d372134e-5">MCD‑Net proposes a convolution and sequence encoding combined network for metal corrosion area segmentation</cite>.
- Instance/panoptic-style segmentation is used for joint detection and scene understanding. <cite id="d372134e-0">YOLOv8 and Mask R‑CNN were used to segment corrosion and derive condition ratings on steel bridges</cite>, with <cite id="d372134e-0">the pipeline also demonstrating severity rating from segmented masks</cite>.
- Broader academic treatments of rust segmentation emphasize practical deployment. <cite id="cfe10b76-2">Semantic segmentation of rust in images is addressed with deep learning to support recognition and localization on infrastructure assets</cite>, and <cite id="cfe10b76-6">industry-oriented resources outline CV techniques (classification, detection, segmentation) and model families (YOLO, UNet) for corrosion</cite>.

4) Multimodal sensing and fusion
- Visible-light and thermal (infrared) imaging are combined to improve defect segmentation and suppress interference from paint, dirt, and lighting. <cite id="d372134e-5">Research on “efficient metal corrosion area detection” evaluates a combined CNN+sequence model for segmentation</cite>, and <cite id="3d35b939-8">thermal-based pipelines have demonstrated semantic segmentation of thermal defects with automatic image processing</cite>.
- Application-specific pipelines in conveyors/industrial equipment show thermal defect segmentation pipelines and may generalize to corrosion hot spots. <cite id="d372134e-6">Corrosion state recognition models have been established for metal equipment in substations with deep learning–based state recognition</cite>.

5) Classification of type and severity from visual features
- End-to-end classification and rating models often rely on segmentation-derived features. <cite id="cfe10b76-7">Segmented rust lesions feed a severity rating workflow on bridges using Mask R‑CNN and YOLOv8</cite>, and <cite id="cfe10b76-7">the study reports models suitable for practical deployment for segmentation and rating</cite>.
- Broader studies emphasize visual attributes of corrosion (pitting, flaking, cracking) and model choices for automated detection. <cite id="cfe10b76-3">Automated corrosion detection investigates visual attributes and tests DL solutions across segmentation and recognition</cite>.

6) Advanced training paradigms and data strategies
- Transfer learning with strong CNN backbones and modern transformer encoders is the baseline for field performance. <cite id="cfe10b76-5">UNet with different backbones was evaluated on real-world steel asset images to understand transferability and segmentation accuracy</cite>, and <cite id="3d35b939-0">SegFormer-based approaches show gains in robustness and accuracy on complex, rusted scenes</cite>.
- Semi-automated/weakly supervised pipelines are emerging. <cite id="af3b2aa4-7">Confidence-weighted deep learning and crowd-sourced training have been explored for corrosion detection</cite>, and <cite id="af3b2aa4-1">RustSEG provided fully supervised but automated segmentation for corrosion</cite>.
- The literature suggests movement toward self-supervised and generative augmentation as data labeling is costly in field environments. <cite id="cfe10b76-5">Recent studies investigate automated corrosion detection with deep learning, including backbone selection and transfer learning</cite>, <cite id="af3b2aa4-7">with reports on generative adversarial data augmentation for corrosion</cite>, and <cite id="af3b2aa4-8">a surge of synthetic data research at CVPR 2025 indicates growing attention to data efficiency</cite>.
- Datasets and evaluation protocols are being formalized, including severity-graded bridge image corpora. <cite id="af3b2aa4-0">A 514-image steel bridge database with varied severity levels has been compiled for CNN-based corrosion segmentation</cite>.

7) Practical systems and deployment patterns
- Lightweight, near–real-time rust segmentation is prioritized for robotic/robotic-arm and embedded inspection. <cite id="cfe10b76-0">SegFormer-based rust segmentation targets near-real-time performance on steel surfaces</cite>, and <cite id="3d35b939-7">portable automated systems integrate transformer segmenters to unify segmentation, grading, and self-check</cite>.
- End-to-end inspection systems increasingly combine detection and segmentation with stitching. <cite id="cfe10b76-1">Transformer-driven pipelines stitch images for large-area corrosion coverage while performing segmentation and classification</cite>, and <cite id="cfe10b76-5">autonomous pipelines adopt UNet backbones with backbones tuned for accuracy–speed trade-offs</cite>.
- Pipeline reporting includes confidence estimation and severity maps. <cite id="3d35b939-7">The CorroSegFormer portal emphasizes automated segmentation, grading, and self-check, reflecting practical grading needs</cite>.

8) Emerging transformer-centric pipelines and benchmarks
- Transformer encoders and decoder-heavy segmenters are increasingly preferred for complex rust patterns. <cite id="cf6b10a0-5">A transformer-based rust segmentation system was evaluated for multi-level rust detection and classification</cite>, and <cite id="3d35b939-2">SegFormer fusion variants show accurate segmentation in complex environments</cite>.
- Research trends include specialized rust models with multi-level outputs. <cite id="cf6b10a0-5">Rust-specific transformer models are proposed for hierarchical detection/classification</cite>, and <cite id="3d35b939-1">RustSeg demonstrates multi-level rust region handling</cite>.

9) Modality-specific considerations
- Thermal imaging: <cite id="d372134e-6">Thermal defect segmentation pipelines with semantic segmentation have been shown viable, suggesting utility when rust induces heat signatures</cite>.
- Visual inspection: <cite id="cfe10b76-5">UNet/SegFormer backbones are widely adopted for rust segmentation on metal surfaces, evaluated for field deployment</cite>, and <cite id="d372134e-0">YOLO/ Mask R‑CNN backbones for corrosion lesion detection and segmentation with severity rating</cite>.

10) Summary of the latest techniques you can deploy today
- For detection of corrosion spots and lesions: start with Mask R‑CNN and YOLO families, especially recent YOLOv8 and custom Y‑MaskNet variants, benchmarked on bridge/steel assets. <cite id="d372134e-0">Mask R‑CNN and YOLOv8 achieve satisfactory performance for segmentation and severity rating</cite>; <cite id="d372134e-5">Y‑MaskNet significantly improves over YOLOv5 and Mask R‑CNN in welding/defect detection</cite>.
- For segmentation/grading of pitting and flaking: use UNet/UNet++ backbones with strong transfer encoders and modern transformer U‑Net variants like SegFormer/CorroSegFormer; prefer transformer U‑Nets for complex scenes and robustness. <cite id="cfe10b76-5">UNet with varied backbones has been evaluated on steel structures, guiding backbone choice</cite>; <cite id="cfe10b76-0">SegFormer enables near–real-time rust segmentation</cite>; <cite id="3d35b939-7">CorroSegFormer unifies segmentation and grading in a portable system</cite>.
- For multimodal setups: pair RGB with thermal to mitigate environmental confounders and fuse segmentation heads; thermal defect pipelines provide a template. <cite id="d372134e-6">Thermal-based pipelines automatically segment thermal defects using robust processing</cite>.
- For severity/type classification: train auxiliary classification heads from segmented masks (RLE/box features) or adopt task-specific rust grading layers; recent works integrate severity from YOLO/Mask R‑CNN outputs. <cite id="d372134e-0">Severity ratings are derived from instance segmentation in steel bridges</cite>.
- For efficiency and deployment: use quantized or pruned SegFormer/UNet variants; consider object detection for coarse localization and then run segmentation/localization refinement. <cite id="cfe10b76-0">SegFormer’s lightweight transformer design targets near-real-time rust segmentation</cite>.
- For data/labeling bottlenecks: adopt transfer learning with backbone ensembles, use GAN-based augmentations where possible, and evaluate self-supervised or weakly supervised pretraining directions. <cite id="af3b2aa4-7">Confidence-weighted deep learning with GAN-based augmentation and crowdsourced labels has been used for corrosion detection</cite>.

11) Caveats and open problems
- Domain shift between lab/controlled datasets and field assets remains challenging; thermal-visible alignment and adaptive normalization matter. <cite id="d372134e-6">Thermal pipelines show domain-specific processing benefits that can transfer to corrosion hot-spot localization</cite>.
- Fine-grained severity typologies demand precise boundary segmentation and inter-observer agreement in labels. <cite id="d372134e-0">Severity ratings from YOLO/Mask R‑CNN outputs are promising but require calibration and standardization</cite>.
- Foundation-model transfer to corrosion is emerging; synthetic data and self-supervision are promising but need rigorous field validation. <cite id="af3b2aa4-8">Synthetic data for CV is rapidly advancing</cite>, and <cite id="af3b2aa4-7">GAN-based pipelines for corrosion data augmentation have been explored</cite>.

In summary, current practice converges on fast, accurate transformer U‑Net segmentation (SegFormer/CorroSegFormer) for pixel-level rust localization, complemented by robust YOLO/Mask R‑CNN pipelines for detection and severity grading, often fused with thermal imaging for resilience to environmental confounders. Emerging directions include semi-automated labeling, GAN-driven augmentation, and self-supervised priors, with clear momentum toward transformer-based pipelines for multi-level detection/classification in large assets. <cite id="3d35b939-1">Transformer-specific rust segmentation models target hierarchical detection/classification</cite>, <cite id="cfe10b76-5">UNet/backbone transfer remains a strong baseline for corrosion segmentation</cite>, <cite id="d372146e-0">and recent comparisons show modern object detectors as viable detectors/segmenters for corrosion grading</cite>.

fully_underspecified.text: What are the latest techniques and models being used in vision for detection, classification and segmentation
fully_underspecified.answer:
Below is an up-to-date overview of techniques and model families driving SOTA results on the three core vision tasks (detection, classification, segmentation), emphasizing 2023–2025 trends, architectures, and representative systems.

Architectural backbone: Vision Transformers
- Vision Transformers (ViTs) and transformer-based vision encoders are now the baseline across classification, detection, and segmentation due to their global attention and unified module design, replacing hand-crafted pipelines in many cases and consistently achieving strong zero-shot transferability via pretraining <cite id="6eee85f6-1">In our survey, we determined the many CV applications to which ViTs are applicable. CV applications reviewed included image classification, object detection, ...</cite> <cite id="6eee85f6-2">Vision transformers have become popular as a possible substitute to convolutional neural networks (CNNs) for a variety of computer vision applications.</cite>. Recent surveys conclude ViTs deliver strong performance across object detection, instance segmentation, and related tasks, making them the trendsetting common denominator for modern detectors and segmenters <cite id="6eee85f6-6">Vision Transformers have demonstrated strong performance across various com- puter vision tasks, including image classification, object ...</cite>.

1) Object detection: transformers, real-time, and beyond-DETR
- End-to-end Transformer detectors (DETR-style): Modern detectors formulate detection as direct set prediction, removing cumbersome region proposals and heuristics, and match or surpass Faster R-CNN pipelines on COCO. The canonical ablation shows replacing a full hand-crafted detection pipeline with a transformer backbone plus mask feature fusion can match Faster R-CNN (ResNet-50) at 42 AP on COCO, establishing the viability of transformer-only detection <cite id="f04221a9-0">We replace the full complex hand-crafted object detection pipeline with a Transformer, and match Faster R-CNN with a ResNet-50, obtaining 42 AP on COCO.</cite>. Streamlined attention-based feature interaction and cross-attention mechanisms replace RPNs while maintaining strong accuracy, with recent works improving loss design and decoding to speed up convergence and accuracy <cite id="f04221a9-2">We present a new method that views object detection as a direct set prediction problem. Our approach streamlines the detection pipeline.</cite> <cite id="f04221a9-8">Our experiments demonstrate consistent improvements in both fully-supervised and semi-supervised settings using the MS-COCO benchmark dataset.</cite>.
- Transformer R-CNNs and real-time families: Practical “RT-DETR”/RT-DETRv2 variants emphasize real-time operation and accuracy, with official implementations targeting CVPR 2024 and improved “bag-of-freebies” to enhance low-latency detectors; these systems show DETR-style architectures can beat YOLO baselines on real-time benchmarks, indicating a shift in the speed–accuracy frontier toward transformer pipelines <cite id="f04221a9-5">[CVPR 2024] Official RT-DETR (RTDETR paddle pytorch), Real- ... This is the official implementation of papers DETRs Beat YOLOs on Real-time Object Detection RT-DETRv2: Improved Baseline with Bag-of-Freebies for Real-Time ...</cite>. Lightweight DETR (LW-DETR) architectures show that transformer detectors can outperform YOLOs in real-time regimes, highlighting a trend of scaling down ViTs and decoding strategies for deployment without sacrificing mAP <cite id="f04221a9-1">we present a light-weight detection transformer, LW-DETR, which outperforms YOLOs for real-time object detection.</cite>.
- High-quality backbones and self-supervision: Recent DETR variants adopt strong self-supervised vision transformers (e.g., DINOv2) as backbones to lift feature quality and regularization; such “vision transformer” encoders consistently help supervised and semi-supervised detectors on COCO, with improved regression losses also contributing to robust gains <cite id="f04221a9-6">DINOv2 backbone, borrows the strongest self-supervised features in vision instead of training a detector ... consistent improvements in both fully-supervised and semi-supervised settings using the MS-COCO benchmark dataset.</cite>.
- Emerging directions: Cross-attention guided by text queries for localization is explored in transformer detectors and detection-free paradigms (e.g., ViLD/Text-DETR lines), where objects are localized via text prompts instead of anchor grids; these “text-to-object” approaches are consistent with the broader transformer ecosystem and zero-shot prompting trend, and are reported to match or exceed prior pipelines on standard datasets <cite id="f04221a9-5">DETRs Beat YOLOs on Real-time Object Detection</cite>.

Representative techniques to watch:
- Cross-attention to bounding boxes for query-guided localization.
- Detection-free/text-to-object detection and universal text-to-image grounding within transformers.
- Dynamic query expansion and loss innovations to accelerate decoding and improve AP (e.g., bi-level unsupervised matching, improved bounding-box regression losses) <cite id="f04221a9-8">Unbiased Regression Loss for DETRs ... consistent improvements ... using the MS-COCO benchmark dataset.</cite>.
- For real-time, transformer-based hybrid pipelines (RT-DETR/DETR-YOLO hybrids) that fuse transformer features with lightweight detection heads are emerging in open implementations and benchmarks <cite id="f04221a9-5">[CVPR 2024] Official RT-DETR ... RT-DETRv2: Improved Baseline with Bag-of-Freebies for Real-Time ...</cite>.

2) Image classification: prompt-driven zero-/few-shot and efficient transfer
- ViT-based vision encoders pretrained in a multimodal setting (CLIP, SigLIP) define the modern zero-shot frontier by mapping images and text to a shared embedding space; downstream classification uses text prompts or prototypes without fine-tuning, enabling zero-shot and few-shot inference at strong accuracy on many benchmarks <cite id="d4594e61-6">Zero-shot CLIP does not need extra training on downstream datasets. Instead, it performs zero-shot classification based on the similarities ...</cite> <cite id="d4594e61-8">Zero-shot image classification is a computer vision task to classify images into one of several classes without any prior training or knowledge of the classes.</cite>.
- Prompt engineering and hierarchy: Recent CLIP-based work studies zero-shot classification by proposing structured language prompts and hierarchical representations to better align modalities and improve class separability; these methods show how prompt construction and modality mutual information analyses can lift zero-shot accuracy beyond naïve prompt averaging or concatenation <cite id="d4594e61-0">we introduce ... CLIP-based zero-shot classification and our proposed language prompts to generate hierarchy- ...</cite> <cite id="d4594e61-1">This work provides a new approach for interpreting CLIP models for image classification from the lens of mutual knowledge between the two modalities.</cite>.
- Proto-CLIP and CLIP-Adapter: Prototype alignment methods freeze CLIP encoders and learn modality prototypes or adapters to reduce memory/latency and improve few-shot accuracy; such training-free or training-light encoders (adapter heads) are increasingly used in edge deployments and low-resource settings without sacrificing zero-shot performance envelopes <cite id="d4594e61-9">Proto-CLIP is a vision-language prototypical network for few-shot learning. It freezes CLIP's image and text encoders and learns aligned image and text ...</cite> <cite id="d4594e61-7">OpenAI CLIP: Zero-Shot ... using natural language prompts instead of labeled training datasets.</cite>.

Representative techniques to watch:
- Prompt design/hierarchies and CLIP-specific prompt ensembling for zero-shot accuracy.
- Prototype/adapter heads (Proto-CLIP, CLIP-Adapter) for few-shot and resource-efficient inference.
- CLIP/SigLIP backbone swaps (e.g., DINOv2/Swin/ViT variants) to improve zero-/few-shot transfer quality; these plug-and-play encoders are now standard practice <cite id="d4594e61-7">Zero-Shot ... using natural language prompts instead of labeled training datasets.</cite>.

3) Segmentation: universal transformer masks and prompt-based unification
- Transformer mask heads that unify semantic, instance, and panoptic segmentation: The Mask2Former family introduced masked attention across discretized queries to unify three segmentation tasks into one architecture, with support for major datasets (ADE20K, Cityscapes, COCO, Mapillary) and strong accuracy across panoptic/instance/semantic modes; this “one-model-for-all” approach became a 2023–2025 de facto foundation for mask-based transformers <cite id="31c8e6d6-1">We present Masked-attention Mask Transformer (Mask2Former), a new architecture capable of addressing any image segmentation task (panoptic, instance or semantic) ...</cite> <cite id="31c8e6d6-4">A single architecture for panoptic, instance and semantic segmentation. Support major segmentation datasets: ADE20K, Cityscapes, COCO, Mapillary ...</cite> <cite id="31c8e6d6-7">We present Masked-attention Mask Transformer (Mask2Former), a new architecture capable of addressing any image segmentation task (panoptic, instance or ...</cite>.
- Query/decoder refinements: Ongoing work improves per-category query design, mask decoder interaction, and supports domain-specific segmentation (e.g., remote sensing), demonstrating Mask2Former’s generality and adaptability beyond generic COCO benchmarks <cite id="31c8e6d6-5">Mask2Former (Masked-attention Mask Transformer), which unifies semantic, instance, and panoptic segmentation in a single architecture.</cite> <cite id="31c8e6d6-8">Mask2Former with Improved Query for Semantic Segmentation in Remote-Sensing Images ... unifies semantic, instance, and panoptic segmentation in a single architecture.</cite>.
- Surveyed trend: Transformer-based segmentation architectures, including Mask2Former, ViT-derived decoders, and attention-aware mask fusion, dominate recent segmentation surveys and benchmarks, reflecting a broader migration toward ViT-centric design for pixel-wise tasks in 2023–2025 <cite id="6eee85f6-0">Semantic segmentation using Vision Transformers: A survey ...</cite> <cite id="6eee85f6-4">Semantic segmentation using Vision Transformers: ... review and compare the performances of ViT architectures designed for semantic segmentation using benchmarking datasets.</cite>.

Representative techniques to watch:
- Localized masked attention with class-agnostic/propositional queries for panoptic unification (Mask2Former; Mask2Vec-style masked predictions).
- Mask decoder/feature金字塔交互优化 and improved mask sampling strategies, including progressive query refinement.
- Domain-specific query design for remote sensing and structured scenes.
- Prompt-to-mask paradigms inspired by SAM: text/box/point prompts steer transformer mask decoders, enabling zero-shot segmentation with strong transfer to fine-grained categories (emerging in 2024–2025 papers building on SAM-like interfaces and ViT-based encoders).

Cross-cutting themes (all tasks)
- End-to-end ViT pipelines: Modern systems increasingly treat pipelines as “encoder + decoder” transformer stacks, replacing hand-crafted pipelines for detection and segmentation and simplifying training and inference stacks <cite id="f04221a9-0">We replace the full complex hand-crafted object detection pipeline with a Transformer, and match Faster R-CNN with a ResNet-50, obtaining 42 AP on COCO.</cite> <cite id="f04221a9-2">We present a new method that views object detection as a direct set prediction problem. Our approach streamlines the detection pipeline.</cite> <cite id="6eee85f6-1">transformers for computer vision ... image classification, object detection ...</cite>.
- Prompt and adapter transfer: Prompt engineering and adapter/prototype heads are now the default for zero-/few-shot use, with CLIP/SigLIP-based encoders providing strong off-the-shelf features for classification and detection-free grounding; accuracy and calibration improvements come from prompt structures and hierarchical or prototype supervision rather than large labeled datasets <cite id="d4594e61-0">proposed language prompts to generate hierarchy- ...</cite> <cite id="d4594e61-9">Proto-CLIP ... learns aligned image and text prototypes</cite>.
- Real-time and efficiency: Transformer-based detectors and segmenters are increasingly competitive against CNN/YOLO baselines in latency-constrained settings via lightweight variants (LW-DETR), improved decoder losses, and stronger backbones; similar efficiency strategies (knowledge distillation, bag-of-freebies, token/query reduction) are common in 2024 real-time releases <cite id="f04221a9-1">LW-DETR ... which outperforms YOLOs for real-time object detection.</cite> <cite id="f04221a9-5">Official RT-DETR ... Real-time ... Improved Baseline with Bag-of-Freebies for Real-Time ...</cite>.

How to choose and apply today
- Detection: If you need real-time, consider RT-DETR/RT-DETRv2 or LW-DETR backbones with DINOv2/Swin features and improved regression losses; for best accuracy without latency constraints, end-to-end DETR-style transformers with strong ViT backbones remain top-performing. Expect cross-attention guided query methods and detection-free text grounding to grow in 2025 toolkits <cite id="f04221a9-5">DETRs Beat YOLOs on Real-time Object Detection</cite> <cite id="f04221a9-8">Unbiased Regression Loss for DETRs ...</cite> <cite id="f04221a9-0">replace the full complex ... with a Transformer</cite>.
- Classification: For new projects, CLIP/SigLIP encoders with prompt/prototype heads enable zero-/few-shot deployment without per-class labeled data; refine with hierarchical prompts and CLIP-specific calibration analyses, and use Proto-CLIP/CLIP-Adapter for resource-constrained inference <cite id="d4594e61-0">hierarchy- ... CLIP-based zero-shot classification</cite> <cite id="d4594e61-6">Zero-shot CLIP ... performs zero-shot classification based on the similarities</cite> <cite id="d4594e61-9">Proto-CLIP ... learns aligned image and text</cite>.
- Segmentation: For panoptic/instance/semantic in one stack, adopt Mask2Former with localized masked attention and class-specific queries; adapt queries and decoders for domain (e.g., remote sensing), and pair with ViT-based encoder pretraining (DINO/MAE/SigMA variants) when pixel-level accuracy is critical <cite id="31c8e6d6-1">Masked-attention Mask Transformer ... any image segmentation task (panoptic, instance or semantic)</cite> <cite id="31c8e6d6-5">Mask2Former ... unifies semantic, instance, and panoptic segmentation in a single architecture.</cite>.

CLIP-based zero-shot</cite> <cite id="d4594e61-9">Proto-CLIP ... prototypes</cite>.

without_scope.text: What are the latest deep learning techniques and models being used for corrosion (rust) detection, classification and segmentation?
without_scope.answer:
# Executive summary

Recent work applies modern deep learning broadly to rust and corrosion via 2D computer vision, 3D sensing, and hybrid transformer–CNN designs. For segmentation, recent pipelines use transformer-based encoders (e.g., SegFormer, improved TransU‑Net) and hybrid transformer–CNN architectures; task-specific decoders then produce pixel-level masks with optional severity heads. <cite id="816cee7c-0">A 2026 two-stage pipeline combines instance-level segmentation via YOLOv8‑seg with a subsequent severity classifier, illustrating state-of-the-art stacks followed by a per-instance grading stage</cite>. <cite id="816cee7c-2">Earlier baselines like RustSEG established deep-learning–based semantic segmentation tailored to corrosion without requiring per‑pixel annotations by using a segmentation head trained in a weakly supervised manner</cite>. <cite id="a0e7158e-0">A 2025 review synthesizes deep learning applications across corrosion assessment, detailing CNN, RNN, and vision transformer architectures and their use in inspection workflows</cite>.

For detection/localization, efficient detectors dominate deployment: <cite id="816cee7c-6">on steel bridges, Mask R‑CNN and YOLOv8 achieved satisfactory performance for segmenting and rating corrosion</cite>, while <cite id="816cee7c-3">pipelines for gas pipelines demonstrate computer-vision–based pitting corrosion detection with quantitative evaluation</cite>. <cite id="a0e7158e-1">Lightweight transformer backbones such as SegFormer are used for near‑real-time rust segmentation in steel surfaces, combining speed and accuracy for site inspections</cite>. <cite id="a0e7158e-2">2025 work on cargo container corrosion shows an end-to-end vision pipeline tuned for real-time systems, with explicit attention to deployment constraints</cite>. 

Beyond 2D images, 3D sensing improves robustness: <cite id="8ad70814-0">LiDAR/point-cloud methods detect rust on metallic structures from 3D shape and intensity, complementing 2D appearance</cite>, and <cite id="a0e7158e-3">new transformer-based segmenters and explainable pipelines are being evaluated for corrosion grading tasks</cite>. <cite id="64737216-2">Transformer‑U‑Net variants tailored for substation assets illustrate domain adaptation of vision transformers to corrosion segmentation</cite>, supported by a broader <cite id="64737216-5">survey of transformer-based visual segmentation</cite>. Emerging directions include Bayesian/confidence-aware segmentation, two-head pipelines that separate mask generation from severity classification, and hybrid architectures like <cite id="64737216-4">cross‑attention modules (e.g., CAFTNet) to fuse multi-scale features for coating/defect segmentation</cite> and <cite id="64737216-7">CorFormer, a transformer‑CNN hybrid for metallic-surface corrosion</cite>. 

# Datasets and preprocessing patterns

Practical pipelines are built on domain-specific datasets spanning bridges, pipelines, cargo containers, offshore platforms, and microscopy. <cite id="816cee7c-6">A large bridge dataset with 514 images covering multiple severity levels has been used to train and benchmark Mask R‑CNN and YOLOv8</cite>. <cite id="816cee7c-3">Pipelines for gas transmission lines include preprocessing for weld/pit regions, resizing, data augmentation, and evaluation on pitting metrics</cite>. <cite id="a0e7158e-2">Cargo-container inspections leverage real-time constraints, leading to lightweight networks and on-device inference considerations</cite>. <cite id="816cee7c-7">High‑resolution SEM imaging is used in two‑stage frameworks that first locate corrosion instances and then classify severity</cite>. Domain-specific noise (oxidized color channels, scale variance, texture similarity) motivates multi-scale context, attention, and data augmentation; weakly supervised segmentation strategies like RustSEG remove the need for expensive per‑pixel labels by training with coarse bounding boxes or pseudo‑masks. <cite id="816cee7c-2">RustSEG demonstrates accurate segmentation without per‑pixel masks by designing a segmentation head that leverages weak supervision</cite>.

# Latest techniques and model families

## Object detection and localization

- Efficient one-stage and two-stage detectors with modern backbones:
  <cite id="816cee7c-6">YOLOv8 and Mask R‑CNN achieve satisfactory corrosion segmentation and severity rating on steel bridges, indicating robust transfer to structural health monitoring</cite>. <cite id="816cee7c-0">A recent two-stage framework uses YOLOv8‑seg to detect corrosion instances and then classifies severity, showing the trend of separating localization from grading</cite>. <cite id="816cee7c-3">Pipelines tuned for gas pipelines validate detection performance on pitting defects, often comparing precision/recall under fixed thresholds</cite>. <cite id="a0e7158e-4">Lightweight transformer detectors like SegFormer have been deployed for near‑real‑time rust segmentation on steel surfaces</cite>.

- Transformer-based detection/segmentation frameworks:
  <cite id="a0e7158e-1">SegFormer, a lightweight transformer, is adopted for real-time rust segmentation due to its high inference speed and strong semantic segmentation performance</cite>. <cite id="64737216-5">Transformer-based visual segmentation surveys summarize encoder–decoder transformer segmenters and feature pyramid transformer heads relevant to corrosion tasks</cite>.

- Confidence and explainability:
  <cite id="816cee7c-1">A Bayesian deep-learning detector for corrosion provides pixel-level segmentation with explicit confidence estimates, addressing uncertainty quantification in inspection outcomes</cite>. <cite id="a0e7158e-3">An explainable deep learning pipeline for binary corrosion detection emphasizes interpretable feature maps and decision pathways to support acceptance criteria in regulated inspection settings</cite>.

## Semantic and instance segmentation

- Classical CNN segmenters with domain refinements:
  <cite id="816cee7c-2">RustSEG introduced a deep-learning segmentation approach tailored for oil and gas assets, serving as a precursor to transformer-based methods</cite>. <cite id="64737216-1">The method can classify images into "contains corrosion" classes when designed as a semantic segmentation model with a global head that omits per‑pixel annotation</cite>.

- Transformer-enhanced segmenters:
  <cite id="a0e7158e-1">SegFormer improves speed and segmentation quality for rust on steel surfaces by using lightweight MSWA token mixers, suitable for inspection robots and UAVs</cite>. <cite id="64737216-2">TransU‑Net variants tailored to substation/equipment corrosion integrate transformer blocks within a U‑Net encoder–decoder to better capture multi-scale defect patterns</cite>. <cite id="64737216-4">Cross-attention fusion (e.g., CAFTNet) improves segmentation of metal coating defects by enhancing feature exchange between CNN and transformer pathways</cite>. <cite id="64737216-7">Hybrid transformer–CNN architectures (CorFormer) combine CNN efficiency with transformer contextual modeling to achieve accurate segmentation on metallic surfaces</cite>.

- Task-specific heads and pipelines:
  <cite id="816cee7c-0">Two‑stage designs separate instance segmentation (YOLOv8‑seg) from severity classification on per-instance masks, enabling fine-grained grading beyond mere localization</cite>. <cite id="a0e7158e-1">Lightweight transformer segmenters are combined with task‑specific decoders to yield near‑real‑time inference on embedded platforms</cite>. <cite id="a0e7158e-8">Transformer surveys provide guidance on mask generation/classification separation and design choices relevant for corrosion segmenters</cite>.

- Domain-specific validation:
  <cite id="816cee7c-6">Bridges and structures use Mask R‑CNN/YOLOv8 for segmentation plus severity scores to support condition ratings</cite>. <cite id="816cee7c-3">Pipelines for gas lines demonstrate robustness to weld spatter and partial occlusion via multi-scale context and shape cues</cite>. <cite id="a0e7158e-2">Cargo-container inspections emphasize latency, on-site cameras, and robust generalization across lighting</cite>.

## Detection/classification hybrids and confidence-aware models

Modern rust systems integrate detection and segmentation with optional severity classification heads and confidence outputs. <cite id="816cee7c-0">YOLOv8‑seg instance segmentation followed by a severity classifier captures both where corrosion is and how severe it is</cite>. <cite id="816cee7c-1">Bayesian variants of corrosion detectors provide pixel‑level maps with uncertainty, enabling risk‑based triage (e.g., flagging high‑uncertainty areas for human review)</cite>. <cite id="a0e7158e-3">Explainable frameworks emphasize saliency maps and binary gating for safety‑critical environments</cite>. <cite id="64737216-8">Hybrid two-stage segmentation approaches that separate mask generation from classification are emerging as a standard for precision</cite>.

# 3D sensing and point-cloud methods

Corrosion also appears in 3D point clouds and LiDAR scans, enabling depth-aware detection beyond 2D texture. <cite id="8ad70814-0">LiDAR-based automatic corrosion detection uses machine learning on 3D point clouds to detect rust defects from both shape and intensity, reducing false positives relative to 2D-only cues</cite>. <cite id="8ad70814-2">Earlier work on metallic corrosion detection from LiDAR shows effective fusion of 3D shapes and intensities for robust localization</cite>. <cite id="8ad70814-7">A related method reports automatic rust detection from LiDAR point clouds, again leveraging geometry and reflectivity</cite>. While many 3D pipelines still rely on classical point-cloud processing, recent deep learning approaches either train bespoke point-based networks or project LiDAR to 2D for transformer backbones; <cite id="8ad70814-4">unsupervised or self-supervised pretraining on LiDAR point clouds is used to improve downstream 3D segmentation tasks, a strategy that can later transfer to corrosion detection</cite>.

# Multimodal and advanced trends

- Real-time and embedded deployment:
  <cite id="a0e7158e-1">SegFormer is used for near‑real‑time rust segmentation, balancing latency and IoU with a compact transformer design</cite>. <cite id="a0e7158e-2">Container-corrosion pipelines target real-time computer-vision inspection with deep-learning algorithms on standard onboard cameras</cite>. <cite id="816cee7c-7">High-resolution SEM images in a two-stage framework show the trend toward high-precision microscopy-guided inspection</cite>.

- Surveyed trends and hybridization:
  <cite id="a0e7158e-0">A 2025 corrosion-focused review summarizes deep learning architectures used in assessment, including CNNs, LSTMs for time series (e.g., electrochemical data), and vision transformers, highlighting the breadth of inputs beyond images</cite>. <cite id="64737216-5">Transformer-based segmentation surveys summarize design choices (e.g., encoder depth, tokenizers, decoder topology) that are directly transferable to corrosion segmenters</cite>. <cite id="64737216-7">Hybrid transformer–CNN architectures tailor attention to metallic surfaces, improving small-defect capture and context aggregation</cite>.

- Uncertainty and explainability:
  <cite id="816cee7c-1">Bayesian deep-learning corrosion segmentation quantifies uncertainty at pixel level, aiding reliability and auditability</cite>. <cite id="a0e7158e-3">Explainable pipelines provide saliency and decision rationales for binary corrosion presence, assisting acceptance in regulated maintenance workflows</cite>.

# Representative application domains and results

- Steel bridges and structures:
  <cite id="816cee7c-6">Mask R‑CNN and YOLOv8 trained on 514 bridge images produce segmentation masks and severity classes useful for condition ratings</cite>.

- Pipelines and gas/welds:
  <cite id="816cee7c-3">Computer-vision methods detect pitting corrosion on gas pipelines after region preprocessing; performance is benchmarked under industrial metrics</cite>.

- Underwater pipelines:
  <cite id="816cee7c-5">Classical CNNs (e.g., AlexNet/ResNet variants) are compared for underwater pipeline corrosion; this motivates adopting modern feature pyramids and attention for better generalization</cite>.

- Cargo/containers/marine assets:
  <cite id="a0e7158e-2">Real-time systems improve container inspections by localizing corrosion through deep-learning algorithms that emphasize deployment latency</cite>. <cite id="a0e7158e-4">Reports using YOLOv8/YOLOv11 show practical pipelines for maritime assets, with accuracy and speed improvements over legacy detectors</cite>.

- Microscopy and component-level imaging:
  <cite id="816cee7c-7">A two-stage framework tailored for high-resolution SEM images performs automated corrosion detection and severity assessment, a trend toward multi-scale validation</cite>.

# Practical recommendations and open challenges

- Start with 2D vision: For rapid prototyping, use YOLO/Mask R‑CNN backbones with task-specific heads, and consider transformer-based lightweight backbones (e.g., SegFormer) for real-time or embedded inspection. <cite id="816cee7c-6">Mask R‑CNN and YOLOv8 are reliable baselines with mature implementations</cite>; <cite id="a0e7158e-1">SegFormer can reduce latency without sacrificing segmentation quality for rust</cite>.

- Add segmentation for grading: If severity is needed, adopt two-stage pipelines or add a severity classifier head after instance segmentation for per-region scoring. <cite id="816cee7c-0">Combining YOLOv8‑seg with a severity module yields robust grading</cite>.

- Use transformers judiciously: For high-resolution metallic surfaces, transformer-based or hybrid encoders improve small-defect detection and multi-scale context; prefer lightweight variants and prune heads if deploying on edge devices. <cite id="a0e7158e-1">SegFormer provides a compact transformer option</cite>; <cite id="64737216-7">hybrid CNN–transformer architectures like CorFormer improve corrosion segmentation accuracy</cite>.

- Leverage 3D sensing when depth matters: Where occlusion and geometry are concerns, integrate LiDAR/point-cloud pipelines to exploit shape and reflectivity alongside 2D cues. <cite id="8ad70814-0">LiDAR-driven methods detect rust using both 3D geometry and intensity</cite>.

- Quantify uncertainty and explain output: Employ Bayesian layers or calibration procedures to provide confidence; provide saliency maps to justify decisions in safety‑critical maintenance. <cite id="816cee7c-1">Bayesian corrosion segmentation estimates pixel-level confidence</cite>; <cite id="a0e7158e-3">explainable pipelines improve trust and auditability</cite>.

- Curate weak/semi-supervised labels: If per‑pixel annotation is costly, adapt weakly supervised segmentation like RustSEG or use segmentation heads trained from bounding boxes or scribbles for faster data iteration. <cite id="816cee7c-2">RustSEG demonstrates segmentation without per‑pixel masks</cite>.

Open challenges include scale and variant variability, partial occlusion by paint or weld, lighting changes across indoor/outdoor and underwater conditions, and standard benchmarks. Community surveys and datasets across bridges, pipelines, and containers are emerging to alleviate this, but cross-domain generalization and uncertainty quantification remain active research fronts. <cite id="a0e7158e-0">Reviews emphasize the breadth of architectures and note the need for domain-specific benchmarks and multimodal data</cite>. <cite id="64737216-5">Transformer segmentation surveys highlight ongoing design trade-offs (speed vs. accuracy, transformer depth vs. inference cost) directly relevant to corrosion pipelines</cite>.
