query.text: has anyone propose metric like to judge whether a coding LLM has some knowledge
query.answer:
Short answer: yes. Multiple lines of work propose ways to quantify whether a coding LLM has substantive knowledge—via external evaluations that require the model to retrieve/apply code-related facts (APIs, algorithms, security practices) and via internal probing that estimates how well the model’s parameters encode and recall such facts.

What kinds of metrics/benchmarks exist

1) General factual-knowledge benchmarks and probe metrics (applicable to code)
- BELIEF(-ICL): A knowledge-probing benchmark family that evaluates recall of known facts and recall with in-context learning, providing explicit settings to separate knowledge from reasoning and to audit contamination controls; reported as encoder- and decoder-oriented splits and tasks designed to stress retrieval and consistency under prompt guidance <cite id="bafc5540-0">In this study, we introduce a multifaceted benchmark for knowledge probing, BELIEF (Figure 1), including BELIEF (§2) and BELIEF-ICL (§3) for encoder- and ...</cite> <cite id="bafc5540-2">In this study, we introduce a knowledge probing benchmark, BELIEF(- ICL), to evaluate the knowledge recall and in-context learning settings.</cite>.
- “Consistency + accuracy” probe metrics: Metrics that combine answer accuracy with internal agreement (e.g., under different prompt seeds or chain-of-thought variants) to estimate the robustness of the model’s internalized knowledge; such metrics reveal that even top models can have low consistent accuracy (~30% with stricter scoring) when required to recall precise facts, highlighting the need to measure stable knowledge rather than single-shot accuracy <cite id="bafc5540-3">The stricter Consistent-Accuracy metric that combines consistency and accuracy gives much worse numbers, around 30% for the best model.</cite>.
- Systematic factuality suites (parametric, tool-free QA): Parametric suites like FACTS present a scalable set of factual questions to assess a model’s ability to answer without external tools; adapted to code settings, this becomes “no-web” code QA about libraries, type systems, and API behaviors <cite id="bafc5540-7">The FACTS Parametric benchmark assesses the ability of models to accurately answer factual questions, without the aid of external tools like web</cite> and <cite id="bafc5540-8">our benchmark is primarily designed to evaluate the breadth and depth of factual knowledge within LLMs</cite>.
- Knowledge-graph–grounded evaluation: Frameworks that ground questions in knowledge graphs require models to match answers to structured facts; this can be applied to code knowledge like “Java’s Collections framework implements X; the method Y does Z” to test precise recall beyond keyword matching <cite id="bafc5540-4">proposes a framework to systematically assess the factual knowledge of LLMs by leveraging knowledge graphs (KGs).</cite>.
- Model-agnostic knowledge probes and editing metrics: Methods in the Megagon blog and related work propose metrics to measure and modify factual knowledge and “truthfulness editing” with a focus on ranking-based limitations; these provide training/eval hooks for code API truthfulness and factual error reduction <cite id="bafc5540-1">introduced new metrics to measure factual knowledge in LLMs, addressing the limitations of existing ranking-based methods</cite> and <cite id="bafc5540-5">proposes a framework to systematically assess the factual knowledge of LLMs by leveraging knowledge graphs (KGs).</cite>.

2) Code-specific benchmarks that require applying programming knowledge
- Competition-grade algorithmic coding: CodeForces and derivatives (CodeElo, LiveCodeBench) evaluate problem-solving over diverse algorithms and constraints, requiring knowledge of data structures, edge cases, and performance trade-offs; these benchmarks report accuracy and ranking metrics on unseen problems drawn from standardized competitions to gauge generalization and deep knowledge transfer <cite id="224e75dc-0">We introduce CodeForces, a novel competition coding benchmark designed to accurately evaluate the reasoning capabilities of LLMs with human-comparable</cite> <cite id="224e75dc-1">The benchmark evaluates code generation capabilities of LLMs on algorithmic problems with difficulty ratings ranging from 800 to 2400</cite> <cite id="224e75dc-5">CodeElo is a standardized competition-level code generation benchmark based on CodeForces contests</cite> <cite id="224e75dc-2">A contamination-free coding benchmark that continuously harvests fresh competitive programming problems from LeetCode, AtCoder, and CodeForces</cite>.
- Security/robustness coding challenges: Benchmarks that measure secure code generation and vulnerability detection test models’ knowledge of secure coding patterns and risky library usages; they combine unit tests for exploitability with per-class accuracy (e.g., injection, config) to quantify where knowledge gaps persist <cite id="c313d6ce-3">This benchmark tests how well LLMs identify and respond to various security vulnerabilities in code across different programming languages with statistical</cite> and <cite id="c313d6ce-7">CodeLMSec Benchmark: Systematically Evaluating and Comparing the Security Weaknesses of Code Language Models</cite>. Empirical results show nontrivial failure rates without aids, supporting the need for knowledge-aware evaluation, e.g., “25.7% of AI-generated code had confirmed vulnerabilities” across OWASP categories <cite id="c313d6ce-7">25.7% of AI-generated code had confirmed vulnerabilities</cite>.
- Domain/stack knowledge surveys for API-centric evaluation: API-oriented evaluation frameworks and surveys argue for targeted tests of library semantics and developer workloads, emphasizing that knowledge deficits (outdated APIs, mis-sig usage) directly impact generation quality; their designs provide task taxonomies and metrics that can be instantiated per language/stack <cite id="9dfa7d54-0">LLMs like GitHub Copilot and ChatGPT have emerged as powerful tools for code generation, significantly enhancing</cite> and <cite id="9dfa7d54-1">A new task and synthetic dataset to benchmark knowledge editing techniques for code large language models</cite>.
- Contamination-aware engineering QA: Engineering-focused knowledge QA (e.g., “Dev Knowledge QA”) introduces real-repo grounding and contamination controls to test whether models can answer without copying, directly measuring internalization of repo-level knowledge; current baselines show limited factuality on unverified claims, pointing to the need for stringent knowledge checks <cite id="9dfa7d54-6">Existing Dev Knowledge QA benchmarks are limited in development knowledge scope and often not built from real used to verify the factual accuracy of the answer</cite>.

3) Internal/probing measures of “having knowledge”
- Memorization and recall probes: Knowledge-probing methods explicitly train and test recall of facts and in-context learning settings, enabling researchers to distinguish memorized content from reasoning and to stress tolerance to distractors; BELIEF(-ICL) operationalizes this and reports drops in performance when contamination is disallowed, quantifying reliance on stored versus derived knowledge <cite id="bafc5540-0">In this study, we introduce a multifaceted benchmark for knowledge probing, BELIEF (Figure 1), including BELIEF (§2) and BELIEF-ICL (§3) for encoder- and ...</cite> <cite id="bafc5540-2">In this study, we introduce a knowledge probing benchmark, BELIEF(- ICL), to evaluate the knowledge recall and in-context learning settings.</cite> and <cite id="bafc5540-3">The stricter Consistent-Accuracy metric that combines consistency and accuracy gives much worse numbers, around 30% for the best model.</cite>.
- Model-editing and knowledge-augmentation metrics: The “knowledge editing on API updates” benchmark provides a task and synthetic dataset to measure whether edits successfully add or correct API facts, offering pre-/post-edit accuracy/factuality deltas as a proxy for knowledge change; this directly quantifies a model’s ability to store and retrieve updated library knowledge <cite id="9dfa7d54-1">A new task and synthetic dataset to benchmark knowledge editing techniques for code large language models</cite>.
- Truthfulness/factuality-oriented probes: Editing and probing frameworks (e.g., Megagon) define metrics that target factual error reduction and knowledge fidelity; while not language-specific, they enable code-specific adaptations such as unit tests for API-conformance assertions and deterministic signature matching <cite id="bafc5540-1">introduced new metrics to measure factual knowledge in LLMs, addressing the limitations of existing ranking-based methods</cite>.

4) Security- and privacy-aware knowledge checks for coding LLMs
- Secure-coding comprehension studies: Experimental evaluations find LLMs grasp lower-level security facts (known vulnerabilities, CWEs) well but degrade at mitigating and contextualizing risks, indicating knowledge gaps in applying secure coding practices; these works propose cognitive-level metrics (recall vs. application) and targeted tests across OWASP families to measure depth of security knowledge <cite id="c313d6ce-1">LLMs perform well on lower-level cognitive tasks, such as recalling facts and identifying known vulnerabilities, their performance degrades</cite>.
- Tasked security benchmarks: Benchmarks that evaluate detection, remediation, and explanation across vulnerabilities capture whether models encode knowledge of secure APIs and safe idioms, reporting per-category accuracy and delta after red-teaming; these serve as practical “has-knowledge” indicators in code generation pipelines <cite id="c313d6ce-3">This benchmark tests how well LLMs identify and respond to various security vulnerabilities in code across different programming languages with statistical</cite> and <cite id="c313d6ce-8">We introduce the SECURE (Security Extraction, Understanding & Reasoning Evaluation), a benchmark designed to assess LLMs performance in realistic cybersecurity</cite>.

Putting it together: concrete ways to judge “knowledge” in a coding LLM

- API/library knowledge: Use API-oriented test suites with signature-level unit tests and update-audit tasks; measure pre-/post-edit changes and tool-free recall to detect whether the model stores and retrieves correct facts for libraries and frameworks <cite id="9dfa7d54-0">LLMs like GitHub Copilot and ChatGPT have emerged as powerful tools for code generation, significantly enhancing</cite> and <cite id="9dfa7d54-1">A new task and synthetic dataset to benchmark knowledge editing techniques for code large language models</cite>.
- Algorithm/data-structure knowledge: Evaluate on competition-style problem sets (CodeForces/CodeElo/LiveCodeBench) with difficulty gradients and hidden/test-time constraints; track pass@k across novel problems and per-category failure modes to infer depth of algorithmic knowledge <cite id="224e75dc-0">We introduce CodeForces, a novel competition coding benchmark designed to accurately evaluate the reasoning capabilities of LLMs with human-comparable</cite> <cite id="224e75dc-1">The benchmark evaluates code generation capabilities of LLMs on algorithmic problems with difficulty ratings ranging from 800 to 2400</cite> <cite id="224e75dc-2">A contamination-free coding benchmark that continuously harvests fresh competitive programming problems from LeetCode, AtCoder, and CodeForces</cite> <cite id="224e75dc-5">CodeElo is a standardized competition-level code generation benchmark based on CodeForces contests</cite>.
- Repo/codebase knowledge and internalization: Design knowledge QA grounded in real repositories and enforce no-copy or retrieval-disallowed settings; use consistency-accuracy (seed/CoT variants) and answer-justification scoring to quantify stable, internalized understanding with limited web access (FACTS-style “no tools” QA) <cite id="bafc5540-2">In this study, we introduce a knowledge probing benchmark, BELIEF(- ICL), to evaluate the knowledge recall and in-context learning settings.</cite> <cite id="bafc5540-3">The stricter Consistent-Accuracy metric that combines consistency and accuracy gives much worse numbers, around 30% for the best model.</cite> and <cite id="bafc5540-7">The FACTS Parametric benchmark assesses the ability of models to accurately answer factual questions, without the aid of external tools like web</cite>.
- Security/privacy knowledge: Use security-focused code benchmarks with per-category unit tests and red-teaming; measure vulnerability detection/repair rates and cognitive degradation from recall-only to application-level tasks, referencing OWASP-style categories to pinpoint gaps (e.g., injection, authentication, deserialization) <cite id="c313d6ce-3">This benchmark tests how well LLMs identify and respond to various security vulnerabilities in code across different programming languages with statistical</cite> <cite id="c313d6ce-7">CodeLMSec Benchmark: Systematically Evaluating and Comparing the Security Weaknesses of Code Language Models</cite> and <cite id="c313d6ce-1">LLMs perform well on lower-level cognitive tasks, such as recalling facts and identifying known vulnerabilities, their performance degrades</cite>.
- Internal knowledge estimation: Apply knowledge-probing and editing metrics to quantify the presence and mutability of library knowledge; track accuracy, consistency, and delta after targeted edits to infer whether the model actually “has” such knowledge versus relying on prompt-time lookup <cite id="9dfa7d54-1">A new task and synthetic dataset to benchmark knowledge editing techniques for code large language models</cite> and <cite id="bafc5540-3">The stricter Consistent-Accuracy metric that combines consistency and accuracy gives much worse numbers, around 30% for the best model.</cite>.

What’s still evolving and how to operationalize

- Benchmark choice: Competition-style code benchmarks test applied knowledge; knowledge QA/probes test internalized knowledge. Combining both yields a fuller picture—for example, a model can pass CodeForces but fail no-web API QA, revealing that it applies general algorithmic knowledge without stable library facts <cite id="224e75dc-0">We introduce CodeForces, a novel competition coding benchmark designed to accurately evaluate the reasoning capabilities of LLMs with human-comparable</cite> and <cite id="bafc5540-7">The FACTS Parametric benchmark assesses the ability of models to accurately answer factual questions, without the aid of external tools like web</cite>.
- Contamination controls: Use repo-grounded or tool-off settings and consistency-accuracy scoring to separate curated test-case familiarity from real knowledge; recent work emphasizes verifying factual accuracy of answers from real development knowledge sources <cite id="9dfa7d54-6">Existing Dev Knowledge QA benchmarks are limited in development knowledge scope and often not built from real used to verify the factual accuracy of the answer</cite> and <cite id="bafc5540-3">The stricter Consistent-Accuracy metric that combines consistency and accuracy gives much worse numbers, around 30% for the best model.</cite>.
- Security lens: Incorporate OWASP-informed code benchmarks to measure whether models encode mitigations and safe idioms; track failure rates and per-category deltas to expose knowledge blind spots in secure coding <cite id="c313d6ce-1">LLMs perform well on lower-level cognitive tasks, such as recalling facts and identifying known vulnerabilities, their performance degrades</cite> <cite id="c313d6ce-3">This benchmark tests how well LLMs identify and respond to various security vulnerabilities in code across different programming languages with statistical</cite>.

Summary answer
- Yes. Researchers have proposed multiple metrics and benchmarks that operationalize “knowledge” for LLMs and, by adaptation, for coding LLMs: knowledge-probing suites (BELIEF(-ICL), FACTS), API- and repository-grounded QA with contamination controls, competition-style code generation to probe algorithmic/AI knowledge, and security-focused code QA to assess secure-coding knowledge; internal probing and editing metrics quantify whether models actually memorize and retrieve facts and whether edits change those facts meaningfully <cite id="bafc5540-0">In this study, we introduce a multifaceted benchmark for knowledge probing, BELIEF (Figure 1), including BELIEF (§2) and BELIEF-ICL (§3) for encoder- and ...</cite> <cite id="bafc5540-2">In this study, we introduce a knowledge probing benchmark, BELIEF(- ICL), to evaluate the knowledge recall and in-context learning settings.</cite> <cite id="bafc5540-7">The FACTS Parametric benchmark assesses the ability of models to accurately answer factual questions, without the aid of external tools like web</cite> <cite id="224e75dc-0">We introduce CodeForces, a novel competition coding benchmark designed to accurately evaluate the reasoning capabilities of LLMs with human-comparable</cite> <cite id="9dfa7d54-1">A new task and synthetic dataset to benchmark knowledge editing techniques for code large language models</cite> <cite id="c313d6ce-3">This benchmark tests how well LLMs identify and respond to various security vulnerabilities in code across different programming languages with statistical</cite>. Together, these provide practical toolkits to judge whether a coding LLM “has some knowledge,” where “has” is interpreted as the capacity to internally recall, apply, and update factual and procedural code-relevant knowledge under constraints. <cite id="bafc5540-3">The stricter Consistent-Accuracy metric that combines consistency and accuracy gives much worse numbers, around 30% for the best model.</cite>

fully_underspecified.text: has anyone propose metric like to judge whether a model has some knowledge
fully_underspecified.answer:
Yes. There is a mature toolbox of metrics and evaluation protocols to judge whether a model “has some knowledge,” spanning factuality on QA/commonsense tests, dialogue and domain-specific rubrics, retrieval/coverage measures, and internal diagnostics based on representations and learnability signals. Below is an overview with concrete examples and caveats.

1) Task-level knowledge: QA and knowledge breadth/quality
- Factuality for closed-domain QA is commonly measured by exact match (EM) and token-level overlap (F1), sometimes complemented by token-level EM for extractive QA. These provide strict and soft correctness signals to quantify factual competence on question–answer pairs, enabling direct comparisons on knowledge-oriented datasets. <cite id="28b47651-4">Exact Match is the strictest standard: a prediction is correct only if it matches the reference character-for-character. F1 offers a softer, overlap-based correctness measure.</cite> <cite id="28b47651-1">Metrics for QA (Things to note) There are two dominant metrics used by many question answering exact match (EM) and F1 score.</cite> <cite id="28b47651-7">In tasks like extractive QA or closed-book QA, exact match and token-level F1 are commonly used for evaluation.</cite> <cite id="28b47651-6">Token-level F1 is usually used alongside exact match in QA benchmarks because it gives partial credit for partially correct answers.</cite>

2) Knowledge-grounded dialogue and domain-specific tasks
- In knowledge-grounded conversation, “knowledgeability” is used both as a training objective and as an evaluative dimension, often alongside factuality and conversational engagement. <cite id="c1d39044-2">Experiments show methods like K-DIAL and RLFC can increase knowledgeability, factual consistency, and conversational ability in knowledge-grounded dialogue.</cite> <cite id="c1d39044-4">Knowledgeability and informativeness capture the usefulness and depth of provided knowledge in dialogue evaluation.</cite>

- Some evaluations integrate such rubrics into end-to-end tools, maintaining accuracy metrics while adding targeted knowledgeability scoring for task purposes. <cite id="c1d39044-5">Evaluation uses known quantitative metrics but also enhances knowledgeability for task-specific purposes with minimal sacrifice.</cite>

3) Internal diagnostics and learnability indicators
- Representation-based diagnostics can estimate whether an LLM “has” knowledge about a concept by analyzing how instances move within its latent space under prompting or retrieval, providing a proxy “knowledgeability measure.” <cite id="c1d39044-1">A hypothesis uses the distribution of instances produced by the LLM under prompting: shifts/variations can signal knowledge and be leveraged to assess knowledgeability.</cite> <cite id="c1d39044-8">EM (Exact Match) is widely used as a stringent metric, and representation-based assessments can gauge knowledgeability in the era of RAG.</cite>
- Instance-level and entity-level “knowledgeability” scores aggregate learning signals across contexts and entities to quantify topic mastery in a more fine-grained way than aggregate accuracy alone. <cite id="c1d39044-0">Entity-level knowledgeability scores aggregate learning signals to assess grasp of specific topics.</cite> <cite id="c1d39044-3">Thrust proposes an adaptive method and reports it as a good measurement of models' instance-level knowledgeability.</cite>
- Learnability-oriented approaches measure whether training/finetuning improves knowledge grounding; increases in knowledgeability and factuality under structured policies are taken as evidence that useful knowledge is present and malleable. <cite id="c1d39044-2">K-DIAL and RLFC increase knowledgeability and factual consistency in knowledge-grounded dialogue, indicating learnable, useful knowledge components.</cite> <cite id="c1d39044-7">Frameworks assess dataset-knowledgeability and provide local decision-boundary crispness scores to diagnose knowledge-related decision patterns.</cite>

4) Retrieval and coverage-oriented metrics for knowledge access
- When a model integrates external knowledge (RAG/knowledge-grounded settings), recall-oriented metrics (recall@k, precision@k) and pass@k protocols quantify whether the system can retrieve/arrive at the correct answer within a top-k set, serving as practical proxies for knowledge access and robustness. <cite id="28b47651-5">Recall@K and Precision@K help evaluate ranking and top-k retrieval performance, measuring the fraction of relevant items found among top k candidates.</cite> <cite id="28b47651-0">Common evaluation spans exact match and accuracy for discrete answers, BLEU/ROUGE for generation, and pass@k for code/candidate selection; these extend naturally to knowledge retrieval contexts.</cite> <cite id="28b47651-6">Pass@k and token-level F1/EM are often used to evaluate correctness under multiple candidate choices, applicable to knowledge-grounded QA.</cite>

5) Putting it together: What “has knowledge” means in practice and how to judge it
- Operational signals:
  - Task-level accuracy/EM/F1 on knowledge QA/commonsense benchmarks (e.g., MMLU, BIG-bench), with contamination-aware variants to avoid inflated scores from memorization. <cite id="6339b2de-1">MMLU’s multiple-choice design yields interpretable subject-wise accuracy for broad knowledge checks.</cite> <cite id="6339b2de-4">Benchmarks like MMLU can contain errors that mislead comparisons, requiring careful scrutiny.</cite> <cite id="6339b2de-8">Decontamination rules (MMLU-CF) mitigate data reuse artifacts to provide fairer knowledge breadth estimates.</cite>
  - Dialogue/domain rubrics rating knowledgeability and factuality to validate applicability to real settings. <cite id="c1d39044-6">Expert ratings of relevance, knowledgeability, and factual correctness offer actionable, domain-specific feedback.</cite>
  - Internal diagnostics using representation shifts and entity/instance-level knowledgeability scores to indicate whether the model encodes/organizes knowledge in useful latent structure. <cite id="c1d39044-3">Instance-level knowledgeability can be adaptively measured (e.g., via Thrust) to gauge learned competence on specific instances.</cite> <cite id="c1d39044-0">Entity-level knowledgeability aggregates signals to quantify expertise over topics.</cite> <cite id="c1d39044-1">Representation distributions under prompting provide a hypothesis-based way to assess knowledge presence and variability.</cite>
  - Retrieval performance (recall@k, pass@k) to verify the model can access and utilize external knowledge stores effectively, alongside factuality metrics. <cite id="28b47651-5">Recall@K quantifies how many relevant items are retrieved in the top k, a core metric for knowledge lookup.</cite> <cite id="28b47651-6">Pass@k gives practical success rates among top candidates for knowledge-grounded QA or code selection.</cite> <cite id="28b47651-7">Token-level F1 with EM can grade correctness of retrieved or generated answers.</cite>
- Limitations and best practices:
  - Metrics can reflect memorization or contamination rather than genuine understanding. Cross-benchmark auditing and contamination controls are essential. <cite id="6339b2de-4">MMLU suffers from numerous errors that can mislead model comparison, highlighting the need for robust evaluation design.</cite> <cite id="6339b2de-8">Contamination-free curation and decontamination rules help reduce spurious gains from test-set exposure.</cite>
  - Factuality metrics can incentivize hallucination-robust but narrow behaviors; complement with human rubrics, diverse tasks, and ablations to differentiate knowledge, reasoning, and retrieval dependencies. <cite id="c1d39044-6">Expert ratings on factuality and knowledgeability surface nuances that aggregate metrics may miss.</cite> <cite id="c1d39044-2">Methods that raise knowledgeability and factual consistency can be validated by their transfer to downstream dialogue quality.</cite>
  - Combine multiple signals: use subject-wise accuracy, recall@k, and entity/instance-level diagnostics to triangulate whether “knowledge is there and usable,” not just test-time correct. <cite id="6339b2de-5">Per-subject accuracy breakdowns make latent weaknesses actionable.</cite> <cite id="28b47651-5">Recall@K surfaces retrieval bottlenecks in knowledge access.</cite> <cite id="c1d39044-0">Entity-level knowledgeability scores provide granularity beyond aggregate EM.</cite>

In short, multiple strands of work have proposed concrete metrics and protocols to judge whether a model has knowledge: accuracy/EM on knowledge QA benchmarks (with contamination-aware variants), knowledgeability and factuality in dialogue/rubric evaluations, recall@k/pass@k for retrieval-based access, and internal representation/learnability diagnostics; together they provide a multi-faceted, widely used evaluation playbook, while requiring careful guardrails to separate true competence from memorization or artifact-driven gains. <cite id="6339b2de-1">Benchmarks like MMLU operationalize broad knowledge checks with per-subject accuracy.</cite> <cite id="c1d39044-2">Knowledgeability gains from targeted training show that useful, learnable knowledge components can be improved.</cite> <cite id="28b47651-5">Recall@K quantifies whether knowledge is accessible on demand.</cite> <cite id="c1d39044-1">Representation-based diagnostics offer proxies for internalized knowledge states.</cite> <cite id="c1d39044-8">Rigorous baselines like EM help anchor knowledgeability claims in reproducible performance signals.</cite> <cite id="6339b2de-4">However, contamination in popular benchmarks can mislead comparisons, so triangulation with multiple metrics and domain rubrics is essential.</cite>

query.answer:
Title: Artificial Intelligence for Planning in Mass Customization Manufacturing: A Short Literature Review

Summary and scope
Mass customization (MC) blends the efficiency of mass production with tailored product specifications, producing large product variety under relatively low volume, which creates planning problems that are combinatorial, dynamic, and multi‑objective (lead time, cost, service, quality, and carbon) <cite id="3aca87b1-4">Mass customization means differentiation through customization, i.e. the production of goods in so many variants that the wishes of different customers are satisfied</cite><cite id="3b8fbc70-0">Automated process planning and dynamic scheduling for ... with an emphasis on digital twin approaches</cite><cite id="639e497a-8">Mass customization (MC) has become a pivotal manufacturing strategy for addressing the growing demand for personalized products without compromising cost</cite>. Planning must coordinate configuration, release and shop‑floor scheduling in high‑mix/low‑volume (HMLV) settings, often with configure‑to‑order or assemble‑to‑order (CTO/ATO) flows, and respond to dynamic disruptions while maintaining on‑time delivery. AI methods are increasingly used to make such planning tractable by embedding real‑time data via digital twins (DTs), learning dynamic dispatching/sequencing policies with reinforcement learning (RL), and orchestrating multi‑agent decision‑making with human experts.

Conceptual foundations: MC planning challenges
MC planning problems exhibit combinatorial complexity from variant configuration, routing, and machine tooling constraints, and operational complexity from dynamic job arrivals, breakdowns, and due date pressures in HMLV environments <cite id="639e497a-8">MC aims to meet personalized demand without compromising cost and delivery performance</cite><cite id="3aca87b1-4">Digital Twin in Low-Volume, High-Mix job allocation and scheduling for achieving mass personalization</cite><cite id="3aca87b1-0">Uncertainty in (customization-enabled) manufacturing systems requires dynamic scheduling strategies</cite>. Empirical and review work shows that AI and DTs create realistic virtual replicas of systems and processes, enabling predictive, what‑if, and closed‑loop optimizations from live shop‑floor data <cite id="3b8fbc70-3">AI and digital twins are revolutionizing production through realistic virtual replicas of systems, processes, assets, or functions</cite><cite id="a6cb79cb-8">Key KPIs (lead time, throughput, utilization, tardiness) are used to measure gains from data‑driven scheduling in high‑mix manufacturing</cite>.

AI techniques and mechanisms for planning in MC

1) Digital twins for AI‑enabled planning
DTs of production assets, lines, or cells serve as the platform that couples sensing, simulation, and optimization for planning and control, supporting real‑time state estimation, disruption forecasting, and closed‑loop schedule repair under MC variability <cite id="3b8fbc70-3">AI and digital twins provide realistic virtual modeling enabling predictive and optimization tasks</cite><cite id="3aca87b1-5">DTs integrated with AI are transformative tools in smart manufacturing</cite><cite id="a6cb79cb-4">Digital twins feed real‑time operation data into manufacturing simulation models to improve decision making</cite>. Recent design frameworks tailor DT architectures to low‑volume, high‑mix jobs, explicitly integrating human planners and advanced algorithms to manage complex job allocation and scheduling for mass personalization <cite id="3aca87b1-4">A DT design tailored for low‑volume, high‑mix production emphasizes collaboration between human expertise and advanced methods to achieve mass personalization</cite>. The broader DT literature emphasizes AI/ML for predictive maintenance, demand and capacity sensing, and optimization coupling, which directly support planning robustness in MC <cite id="3aca87b1-1">A novel federated DT scheduling combines LLMs and deep RL to meet diverse customer requirements</cite><cite id="3aca87b1-5">DTs integrated with AI reduce uncertainty and enable adaptive planning</cite>.

2) Reinforcement learning (RL) for dynamic dispatching and scheduling
RL is increasingly used to learn state‑aware dispatching/sequencing policies from live production data, enabling dynamic rescheduling under variability and uncertainty—central in MC/CTO/ATO flows. Studies propose DT‑driven RL to compute robust schedules that minimize key performance indicators such as total completion time, total tardiness, and energy consumption in HMLV factories <cite id="3aca87b1-0">Dynamic scheduling under uncertainty via digital twin and fuzzy RL in customization manufacturing</cite><cite id="a6cb79cb-2">Digital twin and deep RL enabled real-time scheduling for complex product flexible shop-floor</cite><cite id="a6cb79cb-3">A novel deep RL framework based on DTs in high-mix settings reduces total completion time and total tardiness and accounts for energy</cite>. DT‑RL agents trained offline can then be transferred to operational controllers that react in real time to machine availability, material, tooling, and operator constraints, continuously adjusting schedules as new orders arrive or disruptions occur <cite id="a6cb79cb-4">Live sensor data is fed into DT-backed simulation to direct scheduling and control actions</cite><cite id="3b8fbc70-0">Automated process planning and dynamic scheduling are enabled through digital twin integration</cite>.

3) Multi‑agent and hybrid optimization–learning systems
Beyond single‑objective local dispatchers, recent work adopts multi‑agent systems (MAS) where agents coordinate release planning, routing, and due‑date assignment under conflicting objectives and constraints in LVHM contexts, frequently embedding human planners as oversight components <cite id="3aca87b1-7">A digital twin–enabled framework implements multi-agent scheduling; three different scheduling agents with distinct characteristics are compared</cite><cite id="3aca87b1-4">Human expertise and advanced methods collaborate in DT-driven job allocation and scheduling</cite>. In CTO/ATO configurations, agent teams can negotiate order readiness, material procurement lead times, and parallel engineering–production coordination. Hybrid methods combine knowledge graphs for variant/feature‑driven routing with ML/RL learners to produce planning policies that scale across product variety while preserving interpretability <cite id="3aca87b1-1">Federated DT scheduling unifies federated learning, LLMs, and deep RL to handle diversity and heterogeneity in MC</cite>. Surveys of production scheduling report that AI methods, DTs, and metaheuristics now handle multi‑constraints (machine, tooling, operator, batch) and continuously adapt to live data, a necessity in MC planning <cite id="3b8fbc70-9">AI in production planning defines good schedules, generates intelligent options, and supports human decision making</cite><cite id="3b8fbc70-4">AI schedulers handle machine availability, tooling, materials, operator shifts, and continuously adjust using live data</cite>.

4) Data-driven analytics, constraint programming, and predictive inputs
AI‑driven planning increasingly relies on machine learning for predictive inputs—forecasting setup durations, machine breakdowns, and supplier lead times—to warm‑start constraint programming models and simulation annealing for release planning and shop‑floor dispatching under MC’s combinatorial variety <cite id="3b8fbc70-3">AI and DTs provide realistic virtual replicas and enable predictive analysis to guide planning</cite><cite id="3aca87b1-1">Federated digital twin scheduling combines LLMs and deep RL to personalize production plans while integrating diverse constraints</cite>. In configure‑to‑order flows, product configuration analytics and variant‑routing rules reduce the state space for optimization solvers and guide agent interactions, enabling feasible schedules at customer‑driven lead times <cite id="3aca87b1-4">DT-guided allocation and scheduling in LVHM supports mass personalization with human–AI collaboration</cite>.

Evidence of impact and deployment outcomes
Across reviews and case syntheses, AI/DT planning systems consistently report improvements in lead time, tardiness, throughput, machine utilization, and energy efficiency in HMLV/MC environments when compared with rule‑based or static schedules <cite id="a6cb79cb-8">Studies measure average lead time, throughput, machine utilization, and job tardiness to quantify improvements in high‑mix scheduling with AI</cite><cite id="3aca87b1-0">DT+RL scheduling reduces uncertainty-driven delays and variability in customization mass production</cite><cite id="a6cb79cb-3">DT‑based deep RL minimizes total completion time and total tardiness and supports energy-aware objectives</cite>. In practice‑oriented studies and engineering case reports, integrating DTs with AI scheduling is shown to bridge sensing and execution, enabling fast rebalancing after disruptions and improving on‑time delivery rates under volatile demand, which are central to MC viability <cite id="3b8fbc70-3">AI/DTs bridge sensors to execution to handle volatility and build resilience</cite><cite id="3aca87b1-4">Digital twin scheduling frameworks are tailored to LVHM with collaboration between human planners and AI to achieve mass personalization</cite>.

Integration architecture: CPS/IIoT, APS/MRP/MTO, and human‑in‑the‑loop
AI planning in MC is embedded in cyber‑physical production systems where DTs capture physical state, ML predicts disturbances and order impacts, and optimization/RL agents propose and self‑refine schedules that are validated and overseen by human planners, with execution through APS/CPM/ERP modules and machine interfaces <cite id="3b8fbc70-0">DT-based dynamic scheduling and automated process planning integrate planning and execution</cite><cite id="3b8fbc70-9">AI planning systems define schedule quality, propose options, and support human teams in decision making</cite><cite id="3aca87b1-7">Multi-agent scheduling with DT-driven deployment shows feasibility for complex MC environments with distinct agent roles</cite>. Federated and cloud‑edge deployments extend data access across plants and suppliers, enabling global optimization with privacy and latency constraints in MC supply networks that feature co‑located configure‑manufacture nodes <cite id="3aca87b1-1">Federated digital twin scheduling links LLMs and deep RL across distributed MC settings to meet diverse order requirements</cite><cite id="3aca87b1-8">DT-enabled frameworks allow training and deployment of AI agents across complex planning scenarios</cite>.

Limitations, risks, and open problems
Despite benefits, several challenges persist. Data readouts may be uneven across HMLV cells, limiting DT fidelity and RL learning stability; governance and model explainability are needed for human planners, especially when orders are bespoke <cite id="3b8fbc70-3">DT-enabled planning relies on realistic modeling and analysis, yet integration demands careful data and governance practices</cite><cite id="3aca87b1-4">Human–AI collaboration is emphasized in DT scheduling to mitigate errors and enforce policy constraints</cite>. Multi‑objective robustness (quality and carbon) remains underexplored compared to throughput/lead‑time objectives, and cross‑functional integration of product configuration, procurement, and production remains a bottleneck for closed‑loop MC planning <cite id="a6cb79cb-8">Studies emphasize KPIs like lead time, throughput, utilization, and tardiness, while broader objectives (e.g., carbon) are less commonly measured</cite>. Recent work underscores the need for scalable DT‑to‑physical deployment, agent coordination protocols, and federated learning to handle heterogeneity and privacy constraints across MC networks <cite id="3aca87b1-1">Federated DT scheduling must combine LLM/RL methods while addressing diversity and heterogeneous constraints across MC settings</cite><cite id="3aca87b1-7">Agent-based DT scheduling requires clear roles, communication, and evaluation to ensure stable planning performance</cite>.

Practical recommendations and research agenda
- Start with high‑impact, measurable levers: deploy DT‑informed data pipelines to power predictive dispatching/sequencing, then add RL or hybrid ML‑CP solvers for dynamic rescheduling; measure lead time and tardiness improvements before expanding to multi‑objective quality/carbon goals <cite id="a6cb79cb-8">Use benchmark KPIs (lead time, throughput, utilization, tardiness) to quantify gains before adding complexity</cite><cite id="3aca87b1-0">DT+RL reduces uncertainty-driven scheduling losses in customization manufacturing</cite>.
- Embed human experts: design decision‑support interfaces that expose learning‑based schedule recommendations, constraints, and trade‑offs for approvals, and formalize change management in CTO/ATO flows <cite id="3aca87b1-4">DT frameworks emphasize collaboration between human expertise and advanced methods in mass personalization</cite>.
- Build federated DT and multi‑agent platforms: support cross‑plant data sharing under privacy constraints and coordinate planning across configure‑manufacture nodes using policy‑constrained agents for release, routing, and due date assignment <cite id="3aca87b1-1">Federated digital twin scheduling unifies LLMs and deep RL to meet diverse customer requirements while integrating constraints</cite><cite id="3aca87b1-7">Multi-agent DT scheduling demonstrates structured agent roles for complex planning</cite>.
- Address robustness and sustainability: incorporate uncertainty in demand, yields, and breakdowns; evaluate multi‑objective schedules; and track energy/material footprints, leveraging DT foresight and RL cost/impact shaping <cite id="a6cb79cb-3">DT‑based RL minimizes completion time and tardiness with options for energy-aware objectives</cite><cite id="3b8fbc70-3">AI/DTs support realistic planning that integrates predictive and optimization layers for volatile conditions</cite>.
- Invest in governance and evaluation: establish safety envelopes, rollback policies, and standardized stress tests for AI planners; publish standardized benchmarks for MC planning that include variant configurations, tooling constraints, and multi‑objective metrics <cite id="3b8fbc70-3">AI and DTs create realistic replicas and analyses, motivating rigorous evaluation and governance</cite>.

Closing perspective
AI has shifted planning in mass customization from static, rule‑based controllers toward dynamic, evidence‑based decision systems powered by digital twins, reinforcement learning, and multi‑agent orchestration, with demonstrated gains in lead time, tardiness, and resource efficiency in HMLV environments <cite id="3b8fbc70-3">AI and DTs revolutionize production by creating realistic virtual replicas that support predictive and optimization tasks</cite><cite id="a6cb79cb-8">Empirical measurements on KPIs like lead time, throughputs, utilization, and tardiness are standard for quantifying AI scheduling gains in high-mix settings</cite><cite id="3aca87b1-0">DT-driven fuzzy RL offers a path to robust dynamic scheduling in customization manufacturing</cite>. Strategic adoption requires aligning planning models with product configuration and supply network capabilities, embedding human judgment, and extending to federated, edge‑centric DT platforms that scale across personalized production networks <cite id="3aca87b1-4">DT-driven job allocation and scheduling for mass personalization must balance human expertise with advanced AI</cite><cite id="3aca87b1-8">Federated and digital-twin-enabled frameworks support training and deploying AI agents across complex planning scenarios</cite>.

Title: AI for Planning in Manufacturing Companies: A Literature Review

Summary and Scope
Manufacturing firms increasingly deploy artificial intelligence (AI) to bridge planning gaps across the production stack—from dynamic job-shop dispatching to enterprise-level master production scheduling (MPS). AI for planning integrates predictive models, optimization, and control to reduce tardiness, cut lead times, and improve resource utilization under uncertainty and real-time disturbances. Title: AI for Planning in Manufacturing: A Brief Literature Review and Trends

Overview and scope
Manufacturing planning spans multi-level decision problems—shop-floor scheduling and rescheduling, master production scheduling (MPS) and sales-and-operations planning (S&OP), and capacity/throughput planning—where uncertainty, combinatorial complexity, and volatile demand make human-centric approaches error-prone and slow. <cite id="c280c6f7-0">Recent surveys argue that methods from artificial intelligence can support complex planning and control tasks in make-to-order production settings by integrating learning, optimization, and real-time data flows</cite>. <cite id="c280c6f7-1">At the same time, reviews emphasize disruption handling, high system complexity, and real-time data management as core challenges for deploying AI-enabled production planning at scale</cite>.

Algorithmic families and core findings
Two broad AI families recur in the literature: (1) optimization-driven heuristics that embed domain constraints (e.g., genetic algorithms, tabu/iterated search over disjunctive graphs), and (2) data-driven, learning-based schedulers (e.g., reinforcement learning) that operate over dynamic states and learn action policies. <cite id="c280c6f7-4">Dynamic manufacturing scheduling surveys synthesize AI/ML techniques for real-time scheduling, rescheduling, and robust control, highlighting how AI bridges sensor data to control actions under uncertainty</cite>. 

Metaheuristic methods remain foundational for NP-hard planning problems, often achieving strong makespan/tardiness reductions on case studies. <cite id="945068f6-0">A 2025 case study reports a 32.23% makespan reduction by applying a genetic algorithm to a manufacturing scheduling problem compared to existing schedules</cite>. <cite id="945068f6-1">More recent work extends genetic algorithms to include tool-change constraints in identical parallel machines, showing improved solution quality under realistic shop-floor constraints</cite>. <cite id="945068f6-2">Complementing these, algorithm design papers report genetic-scheduling variants and hybridizations that improve robustness and serve as design references for production planning systems</cite>. 

Data-driven scheduling via reinforcement learning (RL) has also advanced rapidly, especially for dynamic job shop scheduling and rescheduling. <cite id="0ea79407-3">A 2022 study demonstrates deep RL for dynamic scheduling in job-shop systems, reporting improved performance over classical heuristics under random job arrivals and breakdowns</cite>. <cite id="0ea79407-9">Subsequent work on dynamic flexible job shop scheduling integrates new job insertions, breakdowns, and changeovers, again showing RL’s ability to maintain schedule quality under multiple disturbances</cite>. <cite id="0ea79407-4">Surveys of RL in dynamic job shops note growing evidence that learned policies can match or outperform static dispatching rules and rule-based planners when trained on historical and simulated data, though robustness to distribution shift remains a concern</cite>. <cite id="0ea79407-5">Robust RL formulations with flexible network structures and cooperative decision-making mechanisms have been proposed to improve stability under machine breakdowns and stochastic arrivals</cite>. 

Strategic, tactical, and support planning
Beyond detailed scheduling, AI supports planning at tactical and strategic levels. For production planning and S&OP/MPS integration, researchers emphasize multi-objective optimization frameworks and decision support that combine forecasting, constrained optimization, and trade-off analysis to align production, inventory, and capacity. <cite id="c280c6f7-0">A recent state-of-the-art study frames AI-enabled planning in the context of make-to-order environments, where order promising, MPS, and capacity planning must be coordinated under lead-time uncertainty</cite>. <cite id="c280c6f7-1">Academic reviews on production planning and scheduling with AI highlight the need to handle disruptions, complexity, and data streaming in S&OP implementations, proposing hybrid pipelines that use ML forecasts and optimization for rolling-horizon decisions</cite>. 

Maintenance and capacity planning also benefit from AI, where condition-based scheduling and predictive maintenance reduce downtime and enable proactive capacity adjustments. <cite id="c280c6f7-1">AI-based planning frameworks often include predictive maintenance modules, integrating sensor data and uncertainty into maintenance scheduling and capacity buffers</cite>. 

Integration with Industry 4.0 and digital twins
Digital transformation platforms increasingly bind sensing, AI planning, and execution through digital twins, enabling what-if simulations, real-time replanning, and MES/ERP synchronization. <cite id="c280c6f7-1">Recent analyses report that digital-twin–enabled AI planning can efficiently manage disruptions, volatility, and real-time data by continuously bridging perception to execution</cite>. <cite id="c280c6f7-7">Industry-focused surveys describe digital twin architectures for production planning and scheduling, arguing that they reduce lead-time and increase throughput when coupled with AI-driven dispatching and optimization</cite>. At the same time, case-based evidence shows mixed results: benefits hinge on high-quality data pipelines, model interpretability, and integration with existing planning and control systems. <cite id="c280c6f7-1">Reviews call out persistent barriers: disruptions, high system complexity, and real-time data management</cite>, while practitioner-oriented sources report 30% efficiency gains when deploying AI-driven scheduling in specific factories, underscoring case-to-case variability. <cite id="c280c6f7-5">Reported case metrics note that AI scheduling can increase throughput and reduce lead-time in practice, but results depend on domain specifics and data readiness</cite>. 

Human-in-the-loop, robustness, and sustainability
Modern AI planning increasingly adopts human-in-the-loop decision-making, hybridizing ML recommendations with operator and planner oversight to ensure feasibility and alignment with shop-floor realities. <cite id="c280c6f7-1">Surveys emphasize the importance of integrating AI recommendations with human expertise to handle exceptions, enforce safety, and adapt to non-stationary shop conditions</cite>. Robustness to uncertainty and stability under change are active areas. <cite id="0ea79407-5">Research proposes robust RL and distributed decision policies to tolerate machine breakdowns, random arrivals, and changing due dates</cite>. Finally, sustainability is rising as an explicit objective in planning models, with AI-based multi-objective optimization combining makespan, energy, and carbon footprint minimization. <cite id="c280c6f7-0">Recent overviews include sustainability metrics within AI-enabled planning to reduce energy consumption and waste while meeting due dates</cite>. 

What’s new since 2020
- Dynamic and robust scheduling: RL-based dispatchers trained with prioritized replay and PPO show strong adaptability to stochastic events; robust variants improve reliability under breakdowns and demand shifts. <cite id="0ea79407-0">A 2024 deep RL method for the dynamic job-shop scheduling problem achieves better performance with PPO and hybrid prioritized experience replay</cite>. <cite id="0ea79407-4">Comprehensive reviews catalog learning-based policies (DQN, PPO, actor–critic) and their performance trade-offs on dynamic scheduling benchmarks</cite>.

Despite strong experimental results, open problems persist: data quality and integration costs in legacy factories, explainability and trust in real-time decisions, stability under distribution shift, and scalable multi-objective optimization including sustainability. <cite id="c280c6f7-1">Surveys point to disruptions and real-time data management as persistent pain points for AI-enabled planning</cite>. <cite id="0ea79407-4">Dynamic scheduling surveys highlight that generalization to unseen disturbance scenarios and the need for robust out-of-distribution handling remain active challenges</cite>. - Start with data: instrument key events and constraints; clean and time-align MES/ERP data to train forecasters and simulator-backed policy evaluators. <cite id="c280c6f7-1">Surveys highlight real-time data management as a precondition for effective AI planning</cite>.  
- Choose hybrid pipelines: combine ML forecasts and uncertainty quantification with constraint-aware metaheuristics or RL agents trained in simulation; roll them up into rolling-horizon planners. <cite id="c280c6f7-1">Hybrid pipelines using AI for forecasting plus optimization are recommended for S&OP and planning</cite>. <cite id="0ea79407-3">DRL agents trained for dynamic job shop scheduling demonstrate improved performance over static rules under disturbances</cite>.

- Budget for robustness and governance: evaluate policies under breakdowns and demand shifts; add safeguards, human-in-the-loop approvals, and failure back-ups. <cite id="0ea79407-5">Robust RL methods and cooperative decision-making help tolerate breakdowns and stochastic arrivals</cite>.  

Summary
The literature converges on AI as a powerful enabler for multi-level manufacturing planning: metaheuristics deliver strong, structured solutions; deep RL provides adaptive, learning-based dispatching for dynamic environments; and digital-twin architectures bridge analytics to execution. <cite id="c280c6f7-0">Recent reviews affirm AI’s ability to support complex planning and control in make-to-order production</cite>, while also pinpointing disruption handling, real-time data orchestration, and integration as central implementation hurdles. <cite id="c280c6f7-1">Surveys project continued growth for AI-enabled planning as robust, hybridizable methods are paired with digital twins and embedded into rolling-horizon S&OP and real-time control loops</cite>. <cite id="945068f6-0">Empirical benchmarks show sizable operational gains—often in the double-digit percentage range—when AI replaces ad hoc planning</cite>, and <cite id="0ea79407-3,0ea79407-9">emerging RL methods increasingly demonstrate competitive performance under realistic disturbances</cite>, setting the stage for wider deployment once data and integration barriers are addressed. <cite id="c280c6f7-4">State-of-the-art surveys characterize this as an active transition: AI is moving from isolated pilots to embedded, adaptive planning cores in modern factories</cite>.

without_preference.text: can you write a literature review on the use of artificial intelligence for planning in mass customization manufacturing companies
without_preference.answer:
Title: Artificial Intelligence for Planning in Mass Customization Manufacturing: Concepts, Methods, and Industrial Evidence

Summary
Mass customization (MC) manufacturing seeks to combine the variety and responsiveness of make-to-order with the efficiency and low unit cost of mass production, creating intense planning pressures at multiple decision levels. Recent work shows that AI enhances planning by processing high-velocity, multi-signal data; learning predictive models of production systems; and optimizing or advising sequencing, resource allocation, and recovery policies in real time. This review synthesizes evidence across scheduling, digital twins, reinforcement learning (RL), and enterprise planning integration, highlighting method capabilities, measured and reported benefits, deployment patterns, and open challenges in MC-relevant settings.

1. Introduction: Planning in Mass Customization and Why AI
Mass customization entails large product variety, small batch sizes, mixed-model flows, and tight coupling between marketing/demand sensing and operations execution. Planning must reconcile volatile demand and configuration choices with efficient resource utilization and due-date performance, often across hybrid modes (engine-to-order, assemble-to-order alongside mass production). Legacy planning approaches relying on static forecasts and periodic replans struggle when variety and change velocity scale; AI methods address this by: (i) anticipating disturbances and demand shifts; (ii) learning production models and near-real-time feedback; and (iii) optimizing or co-optimizing schedules under constraints, costs, and service targets. This shift is enabled by Industry 4.0 data infrastructures and digital twins that expose equipment, workflow, and WIP state at high frequency, creating the inputs AI models need to operate prescriptively at APS/PPS and shop-floor levels.

2. Methods Landscape for AI-Enabled Planning
2.1 Learning-driven scheduling and dispatching
Surveys of modern manufacturing report converging evidence that machine learning, evolutionary/metaheuristics, and RL-based algorithms can improve schedule quality and responsiveness in dynamic environments relative to rule-based dispatching alone, particularly when re-planning is triggered by real-time events and data streams <cite id="8ef6873b-0">Recent reviews of production scheduling emphasize the role of real-time data management, integration/interoperability, adaptability, and learning-driven decision policies</cite>. <cite id="8ef6873b-0">These works identify gaps around deploying adaptive planning in integrated enterprise systems and handling nonstationary shop conditions</cite>. <cite id="fbebb119-1">A comprehensive review highlights AI-driven scheduling methods spanning evolutionary heuristics, advanced machine learning, and RL-based algorithms, synthesizing where these methods reduce tardiness/lead times and improve utilization</cite>.

Reinforcement learning has emerged specifically for dynamic job-shop and flow-shop scheduling, framing resequencing/repair as Markov decision processes where multi-agent RL learns value functions/policies over job states and machine allocations. <cite id="fbebb119-3">Dynamic scheduling with deep reinforcement learning models have improved performance over static dispatching rules in simulation studies of job-shop systems</cite>. <cite id="fbebb119-6">Multi-agent DRL systems integrate self-organization and self-learning to coordinate job shop dispatching, reducing tardiness and improving throughput relative to classical dispatching rules</cite>. <cite id="fbebb119-7">Transformer-based architectures combined with deep RL map dynamic job-shop scheduling into MDPs, supporting longer-horizon planning and better recovery from disruptions</cite>. <cite id="fbebb119-2">Thesis and case evidence document the design of RL agents that interact with shop-floor state and learn policies in factory environments, including adaptive dispatching and operation sequencing</cite>. Together, these findings show RL’s suitability for MC-like environments: it learns from experience, absorbs new orders/configurations online, and replans under uncertainty, often with multi-objective trade-offs captured in reward engineering and constraints.

2.2 Metaheuristics and hybrid optimization linked to AI signals
Hybrid methods combine fast neighborhood search with AI-provided guidance from forecasting, predictive maintenance, and anomaly detection. <cite id="8ef6873b-0">Reviews stress that integrating real-time data and AI into scheduling reduces reliance on static forecasts and raises adaptability and system integration</cite>. <cite id="fbebb119-4">Industrial DRL dynamic scheduling studies report reductions in schedule instability costs and enhanced recovery performance compared with static dispatching</cite>. In low-volume, high-mix settings typical of MC, guided local search/iterated greedy algorithms that use AI forecasts of demand and processing times can outperform traditional static schedules when re-planning frequency is managed within MES/APS boundaries <cite id="8ef6873b-0">Metaheuristics gain from AI-fueled data streams for improved neighborhood evaluation and restart strategies</cite>.

2.3 Digital twins for integrated planning and what-if analysis
Digital twins (DTs) provide synchronized, multi-physics models of equipment, lines, factories, and even enterprise networks, continuously updated by shop-floor data, enabling prescriptive experiments for planning. <cite id="e3594fdc-1">A 2025 review defines digital twins across levels of manufacturing resource systems (physical entities, virtual models, connectivity, data, and AI), positioning DTs as the backbone for real-time monitoring, quality, and dynamic scheduling</cite>. <cite id="e3594fdc-2">A cross-hierarchical review reports that deep learning-enabled intelligent process planning and digital twin cells support online reconfiguration and scheduling, improving robustness under variability</cite>. <cite id="e3594fdc-5">An optimization-centric synthesis shows that integrating AI/ML within digital twin frameworks enables real-time process monitoring and dynamic scheduling in response to disturbances</cite>. 

In mass personalization contexts, digital twins capture product-variety effects, enabling simulation of build sequences, resource contention, and lead-time impacts for customized orders before they hit the floor. <cite id="e3594fdc-7">Auckland University’s digital twin reference for mass personalization argues that DTs align with Industry 4.0 to create high value for personalized products, bridging customer demand variability with provider-side capacity and workflow planning</cite>. <cite id="e3594fdc-8">In low-volume, high-mix job shops, digital twins offer virtual environments for in-depth analysis of alternative schedules; machine learning within DTs improves predictive scheduling and root-cause analysis for disruptions</cite>. <cite id="fbebb119-8">Industrial case work on adaptive order dispatching shows reinforcement learning policies can be trained and evaluated in simulation before deployment, reducing risk in live factories</cite>.

3. Planning Horizons: From Enterprise to Shop Floor in MC
3.1 Sales and operations planning (S&OP), aggregate-to-discrete deployment
AI enhances S&OP by jointly modeling configure-price-delivery pipelines with production feasibility, using probabilistic forecasts, causal anomaly detection, and constraint propagation to propose feasible mix plans and capacity buffers. Practitioner reports indicate AI-driven planning bridges sensor data to execution to handle volatility, improving on-time delivery and capacity utilization under mixed demand skews <cite id="1009b163-6">AI enhances production scheduling efficiency, integrates with ERP systems, and maximizes resource utilization for industrial manufacturing</cite>. <cite id="1009b163-5">AI-driven planning autonomously manages complex scheduling decisions within business rules to build resilience under volatility</cite>. <cite id="1009b163-7">AI in production planning defines “good” schedules, quickly suggests options, and improves responsiveness to change compared to static forecasts and rigid schedules</cite>. 

3.2 Production planning and control (PPC), order promising, and mode selection in hybrid MC
Where production mixes configurable products with standard modules, AI models (e.g., transformer-based demand and BOM solvers) can decompose orders into standardized and bespoke components, compute bill-of-resources and lead-time envelopes, and propose production sequences and procurement triggers to maintain service levels. Digital twins and data-driven process planning provide route selection, tooling/fixture readiness checks, and alternative process plans for variants, feeding downstream scheduling. <cite id="1009b163-0">APPS (Automated Process Planning and Scheduling) integrated with digital twins surfaces opportunities and challenges in combining routing, process plans, and dynamic schedules across product variety</cite>. <cite id="e3594fdc-8">Digital twins allow testing of scheduling options in low-volume, high-mix conditions so planners can pre-empt bottlenecks and changeovers</cite>.

3.3 Shop-floor scheduling, dynamic dispatching, setup and hybrid flow-line planning
RL-based dynamic dispatching and multi-agent scheduling address sequence-dependent setup times, sequence-dependent processing times, and variable due dates common in MC hybrid flow lines. <cite id="fbebb119-3">DRL-based dynamic scheduling improves over static dispatching for job-shop systems under disruptions</cite>. <cite id="fbebb119-6">Multi-agent DRL achieves better self-organization and throughput than rule-based dispatchers when coordinating machines and buffers</cite>. <cite id="fbebb119-0">Recent surveys discuss periodic and real-time dispatching rule selection systems, linking AI to dynamic dispatch policies and learning to switch dispatching rules as conditions change</cite>. In mass personalization and job-shop environments, DT-backed scheduling supports “what-if” insertion of new SKUs, evaluation of parallel cells, and dynamic allocation of cross-trained operators, all reflected in improved schedule stability and reduced tardiness <cite id="e3594fdc-7">DTs are used to align planning with the variability of mass personalization, integrating customer-driven configurations with provider-side planning</cite>.

4. Data, Integration, and Industrialization Patterns
4.1 Data foundations: from mass digitization to AI readiness
AI planning relies on high-frequency OEE, resource utilization, WIP state, and event logs; predictive maintenance and anomaly detection feed replanning triggers. <cite id="1009b163-0">APPS studies emphasize the role of digital twins in synchronizing process plans with current shop-floor state for automated planning and scheduling</cite>. <cite id="8ef6873b-0">Reviews point to persistent gaps in real-time data management, integration/interoperability across ERP/MES/SCADA, and adaptability of scheduling logic in production execution</cite>.

4.2 Integration with ERP/MES/APS and human-in-the-loop
Operational deployments pair AI planners with legacy APS/ERP modules, using AI for frequent reoptimization windows, exception-based intervention, and advisor suggestions that planners approve. <cite id="1009b163-6">AI scheduling integrates with ERP systems to enhance resource utilization and throughput</cite>. <cite id="1009b163-5">AI-driven planning converts sensor-to-execution flows by autonomously managing complex scheduling within business rules, elevating planner capacity to strategic work</cite>. Early industrial experiences report tangible savings potential and improved schedule quality when neural networks guide mixed-model or appliance manufacturing sequences, albeit with careful change-impact modeling and data governance <cite id="8ef6873b-2">An appliance manufacturer built a neural-network-based mixed-model scheduling system demonstrating serious cost-saving potential in testing and initial deployment</cite>.

4.3 Digital twin deployment patterns for planning
Two patterns recur. First, twin-of-the-line: virtual replicas of cells/lines for real-time re-simulation and prescriptive adjustments. <cite id="e3594fdc-8">DTs provide virtual environments to evaluate scheduling options for low-volume, high-mix operations, with ML supporting predictive scheduling</cite>. Second, enterprise-level twins integrate across supply chain and factory domains to evaluate production mode mixes and capacity expansion for personalized product portfolios. <cite id="e3594fdc-7">A DT reference for mass personalization argues such integration delivers high value by aligning customer-side variety with provider-side capabilities</cite>.

5. Reported Outcomes: Performance and Reliability
Across domains, studies report measurable gains: reductions in schedule instability and tardiness; improved machine and WIP throughput; and enhanced responsiveness to disruptions. <cite id="fbebb119-3">DRL dynamic scheduling reports better performance than static rules in job shops under disturbances</cite>. <cite id="fbebb119-6">Multi-agent DRL achieves throughput and buffer-level improvements via self-organized dispatching</cite>. <cite id="fbebb119-7">Transformer+RL approaches improve longer-horizon recovery from disruptions by framing scheduling as an MDP</cite>. <cite id="8ef6873b-0">Reviews report that AI-driven methods reduce lead times and improve utilization/resilience when integrated with real-time data and enterprise systems</cite>. Practitioner reports echo these benefits: on-time delivery gains from reactivity to volatility, better utilization through rule learning, and fewer expensive manual replans <cite id="1009b163-5">AI-driven planning transforms factories by bridging sensors to execution to handle volatility and build resilience</cite>. <cite id="1009b163-6">AI enhances scheduling efficiency and integrates with ERP to maximize resource utilization</cite>. <cite id="1009b163-7">AI planning responds fluidly to change with tangible improvements over static forecasts and rigid schedules</cite>. 

However, performance depends on data quality, model robustness under nonstationarity, and integration costs. <cite id="8ef6873b-0">Key gaps include real-time data management, interoperability across systems, and adaptability to changing shop conditions</cite>. <cite id="fbebb119-8">Adaptive dispatching via RL benefits from simulation and phased rollout, as demonstrated in multi-product case studies before wide deployment</cite>.

6. Use Cases Across MC Domains
6.1 Configurable discrete assembly and hybrid flow lines
Configurable products require routing and operation sequences that change with options; AI process planning and digital twins generate option-aware routings and process plans, schedule them, and suggest changeover minimization. <cite id="1009b163-0">APPS with digital twins explores automated process plan and schedule generation for variety-rich products, identifying opportunities and challenges</cite>. <cite id="e3594fdc-2">Deep learning-enabled intelligent process planning linked to digital twin cells supports online reconfiguration in manufacturing</cite>.

6.2 Low-volume, high-mix job shops and batch-once-seq-many
DT-backed scheduling enables evaluation of alternative operations sequences and setup modes that minimize setup time and tardiness. <cite id="e3594fdc-8">In low-volume, high-mix job shops, DTs virtualize scheduling analysis; ML and RL components improve dynamic decision-making and root-cause detection</cite>.

6.3 Multi-product, mixed-model automotive-style assembly
Dynamic dispatching and order promising leverage AI to sequence model mixes and customized modules while maintaining throughput and due dates; RL policies adapt to shift changes, machine breakdowns, and rush orders. <cite id="fbebb119-0">Systems that periodically or in real time select dispatching rules improve adaptability as conditions change in job shops</cite>. <cite id="fbebb119-6">Multi-agent DRL systems coordinate dispatching to boost throughput and reduce delays in complex assembly-like settings</cite>.

7. Challenges and Open Research Directions
7.1 Data, model, and control integration
Planning models must tolerate missing data, nonstationarity (new variants, tool wear, process drift), and constraint coupling. <cite id="8ef6873b-0">Surveys highlight persistent problems in real-time data management and interoperability that limit deployment</cite>. <cite id="8ef6873b-0">Adaptability remains a core challenge: dispatching policies and re-planning cadences must handle nonstationary shop behavior</cite>.

7.2 Explainability, safety, and human oversight
AI planners need rule-aware, safety-constrained behavior and change narratives for shift managers. <cite id="1009b163-5">Frameworks that “bridge sensors to execution” embed business rules, helping operators understand and approve AI-generated schedules</cite>. <cite id="1009b163-6">Integration with ERP/MES supports traceability and governance while pushing planners to strategic work</cite>.

7.3 From simulation to scale
Industrial studies emphasize staged deployment: train and validate in simulation and virtual twins; then monitor uplift and drift in production. <cite id="fbebb119-8">Reinforcement learning-based dispatching is reported by practitioners in multi-product cases with careful testing and evaluation</cite>. <cite id="e3594fdc-8">DTs explicitly support in-depth analysis before committing to shop-floor changes</cite>.

7.4 Research topics
- Digital twin–enabled multi-level planning that coordinates APS/PPS/S&OP with shop-floor execution in MC <cite id="e3594fdc-7">Mass personalization DT references define planning interfaces that could standardize multi-level coordination</cite>.
- RL architectures robust to spurious correlations and infrequent events in long-tail customized products, with principled changeover modeling and energy-aware objectives <cite id="fbebb119-1">Systematic reviews map capabilities and gaps across heuristics, ML, and RL scheduling</cite>.
- NLP/CV-driven “plan from demand” pipelines: integrate design-engineering outputs (BOM, routings) with forecasting and anomaly detection to automate order promising and release control <cite id="1009b163-0">Automated process planning and scheduling with digital twins indicates the feasibility of integrated planning pipelines</cite>.

8. Practical Guidance for MC Implementations
- Start with data: instrument changeovers, configuration events, and WIP flows; define recovery triggers and OEE baselines <cite id="8ef6873b-0">Real-time data management and interoperability are prerequisites for AI-driven scheduling in production systems</cite>.
- Select the planning horizon to model: 
  - Enterprise S&OP: probabilistic demand with feasibility checks and release policies; 
  - PPC: variant-aware order promising with resource graphs; 
  - Shop floor: dynamic dispatching with setup learning. <cite id="1009b163-5">AI-driven planning integrates sensors to execution and handles volatility</cite>; <cite id="e3594fdc-8">DT-backed scheduling supports low-volume, high-mix decision-making</cite>; <cite id="fbebb119-3">DRL improves dynamic scheduling performance over static rules</cite>.
- Prefer hybrid human-in-the-loop advisors: use AI for frequent re-optimization and exception handling, with operator approval of major changeovers and mode switches <cite id="1009b163-6">Integration with ERP systems improves scheduling efficiency and utilization</cite>.
- Iterate on twins: use digital twins for what-if planning at cell, line, and plant levels before rolling out to floor, then use field telemetry to retrain/retune <cite id="e3594fdc-8">DTs provide virtual environments to test options in low-volume, high-mix settings</cite>. <cite id="fbebb119-8">Practical case deployments demonstrate value from simulation-led RL evaluation</cite>.

9. Conclusion
The literature shows that AI is maturing from prototyping tools to operational planning engines in mass customization, with reinforcement learning, digital twins, and guided optimization delivering improved responsiveness, schedule quality, and utilization when grounded in real-time data and rule-aware execution frameworks. Evidence across job shops, low-volume/high-mix cells, and mass personalization settings indicates measurable benefits in lead times, throughput, and on-time delivery, alongside clear integration challenges. For MC manufacturers, the practical path is to build data-rich twin-based planning layers, adopt hybrid human-in-the-loop orchestration, and iterate models in production via continuous learning—turning variety into a tractable planning opportunity rather than a bottleneck. <cite id="e3594fdc-7">Digital twins and mass personalization frameworks show how to align customer-driven variety with provider-side planning and operations</cite>. <cite id="fbebb119-3">Dynamic RL scheduling outperforms static dispatching in job shops, supporting fast recovery from disruptions</cite>. <cite id="8ef6873b-0">Surveys emphasize that AI-driven scheduling’s real gains materialize when integrated with real-time data and enterprise systems</cite>.
