fully_underspecified.text: Find some existing work on analysis.
fully_underspecified.answer:
# What "analysis" looks like for LLM agents (and where the work exists)

Analysis of LLM-based agents spans capability taxonomies, evaluation frameworks and benchmarks, mechanism-level studies (planning/search, tool use, memory/grounding, reflection), and domain case studies (e.g., web navigation, software engineering). Recent surveys and benchmarks provide structured views of agent abilities and measurable tasks, while ablations and memory-grounding methods reveal how agents actually reason and retrieve. Below is a curated map of existing work across these strands, with representative results and takeaways for analysts.

## Surveys and taxonomies that define the analysis axes

Recent surveys consolidate what analysts should measure in agents: planning, tool use, self-reflection, memory, and environment interaction. <cite id="c3b2f7e0-0">A 2025 survey on evaluation of LLM-based agents frames the shift from static LLMs to systems that plan, reason, and use tools interactively across diverse environments</cite>. <cite id="c3b2f7e0-1">Its curated reading list operationalizes capability dimensions for analysis, highlighting planning, tool use, self-reflection, and memory as core axes</cite>. <cite id="c3b2f7e0-2">The survey also details tool interfaces and benchmark design (e.g., tool-calling schemas in τ-Bench and AppWorld), anchoring analysis in concrete task structures</cite>. <cite id="c3b2f7e0-6">A 2026 preprint broadens the view still further, emphasizing long-term planning, tool use, multi-step decision making, and active interaction as central to contextual agents</cite>. For planning specifically, <cite id="c3b2f7e0-7">a dedicated survey synthesizes how LLMs plan to solve multi-step problems, offering a review of paradigms and pitfalls analysts should recognize</cite>.

Practical takeaways: start analysis by instrumenting the four Ps—Plan, Tools/Actions, Memory/State, and Reflection—since most agent failures congregate at these interfaces. <cite id="33ea66b3-2">A paradigm review likewise argues that tool use, planning, and feedback learning are three prominent agent designs, guiding which mechanisms to log and compare across tasks</cite>.

## Evaluation frameworks and benchmarks: task suites for quantitative analysis

Benchmarks and evaluation frameworks operationalize analysis by specifying environments, tool interfaces, and metrics. <cite id="bdc17b53-3">A comprehensive guide catalogs agent benchmarks like SWE-bench, WebArena, and AgentBench to test capabilities across domains such as web navigation and coding</cite>. <cite id="bdc17b53-6">SWE-bench leaderboards show concrete performance differentials (e.g., mini-SWE-agent at ~74% on Verified in ~100 lines of Python), enabling cross-agent comparisons on real-world coding tasks</cite>. <cite id="bdc17b53-8">AgentBench's design explicitly targets evaluation across diverse environments, forcing analysts to study generalization beyond single-domain tests</cite>. <cite id="bdc17b53-4">WebArena focuses web agents on consequential real-world tasks in simulated company settings, making failure modes visible at the interaction level</cite>. <cite id="bdc17b53-7">At the OSWorld leaderboard, multimodal and vision aspects are quantified, pushing analysts to measure modality fusion errors and perceptual tooling</cite>.

For planning/tool-use analytics, <cite id="c3b2f7e0-2">tool-calling schema benchmarks (τ-Bench/AppWorld) standardize how agents invoke functions, enabling statistical measurements like function-call success rates, argument validity, and path lengths</cite>.

Practical takeaways: choose or synthesize a benchmark stack that matches your analysis goal—web interaction vs. code repair vs. OS operations—so metrics capture both goal success and intermediate quality (paths, tool-call overhead, retries). <cite id="bdc17b53-0">A recent audit across eight benchmarks (e.g., SWE-bench, WebArena) cautions that top agent scores can be fragile, highlighting the need to validate metrics and guard against benchmark brittleness</cite>.

## Mechanism-level analyses: planning/search, tool use, and reflection

Analysts frequently need to dissect how agents search plans, when to call tools, and how to reflect on mistakes. <cite id="33ea66b3-2">A review of prominent paradigms (tool use, planning, and feedback learning) helps analysts diagnose whether a model is overusing or underusing tools, getting stuck in shallow loops, or failing to incorporate feedback</cite>. Web-oriented agents often rely on the ReAct loop: "Thought → Action → Observation," which offers logs analysts can parse for action taxonomies and observation-driven corrections. <cite id="33ea66b3-1">Overviews of ReAct and tools describe the thought–action–observation cycle, how tools are integrated, and how memory can be structured—useful to design instrumentation and ablations</cite>.

For planning specifically, <cite id="c3b2f7e0-7">surveys summarize multi-step problem-solving strategies, warning that LLMs often exhibit brittle horizons and off-policy behavior when interacting with tools and external systems</cite>. This motivates analytical dashboards that count horizon lengths, branching factors, and policy drift across environments.

Practical takeaways: Add to your pipeline per-instance traces that log thought content, action types, arguments, observation deltas, and latency/tool outcomes. Aggregate to plan-depth distributions, tool-dependency heatmaps, and action-retry rates to detect planning inefficiency or tool misuse.

## Memory and knowledge grounding: externalization and ablations

A central axis of analysis is how agents ground knowledge and manage memory. <cite id="09ba1234-1">Coarse-to-Fine Grounded Memory (CFGM) shows that layering coarse-grained and fine-grained grounded memories can improve flexible planning by enabling the model to leverage memory hierarchically; this provides a concrete template for memory-grounding experiments and expected gains</cite>. <cite id="09ba1234-6">RAG-equipped agents aim to mitigate hallucination, outdated knowledge, and lack of traceability; analysts can measure these failure modes pre/post RAG to quantify groundedness and factuality deltas</cite>. 

Evaluation of grounding calls for metrics beyond accuracy. <cite id="09ba1234-8">For RAG, groundedness—the fraction of answers supported by retrieved docs—offers an actionable, per-answer metric; combining it with citation-quality and sufficiency checks reveals how often retrieved contexts actually enable correct behavior</cite>. Tutorials and overviews synthesize these design patterns for practical adoption. <cite id="09ba1234-2">External memory reviews describe persistent, structured memory systems that integrate with planning and tool use, guiding architecture choices for analyzable deployments</cite>.

Practical takeaways: Track hierarchical memory usage (coarse-to-fine recall rates), context sufficiency, and citation coverage alongside task success; use ablations to compare model-centric vs. infrastructure-centric memory and retrieval policies. <cite id="09ba1234-5">A review of CFGM emphasizes integrating model knowledge into memory grounding to enhance planning, aligning with analyses that separate retrieval utility from intrinsic knowledge</cite>.

## Domain case studies and agent subtypes

Domain-oriented analyses reveal where general frameworks break down. <cite id="bdc17b53-5">Web agents must coordinate browser actions, search, and memory across long horizons, exposing new failure modes like UI action drift and state ambiguity</cite>. <cite id="bdc17b53-4">Company-facing WebArena tasks make those failures consequential, providing end-to-end logs for post hoc root-cause analysis</cite>. In software engineering, <cite id="bdc17b53-6">leaderboards for SWE-bench and mini-SWE-agent show sizable but incomplete success, prompting analyses of patch correctness, test adequacy, and dependency impacts</cite>. Broader landscape guides exist to connect agents to tasks. <cite id="bdc17b53-3">Benchmarking roundups connect SWE-bench, WebArena, AgentBench, making it easier to assemble cross-domain analysis sets</cite>.

Practical takeaways: Segment analysis by domain but standardize per-instance telemetry to enable cross-domain comparisons (e.g., normalized path length per goal, tool-call success rates by domain, groundedness of intermediate reasoning steps).

## Auditing benchmarks and surfacing limitations

No analysis of agents is complete without auditing test suites. <cite id="bdc17b53-0">A systematic audit of eight major benchmarks (including SWE-bench and WebArena) reports how top agents can "break" current tests, warning that claims may overfit to benchmark quirks</cite>. <cite id="bdc17b53-2">A recent comprehensive benchmark survey in software engineering consolidates tasks, solutions, and evolving leaders, helping analysts understand when progress reflects genuine capability vs. artifact-specific gains</cite>. These audits inform analysts to emphasize generalization tests, adversarial stress cases, and failure-replay studies.

Practical takeaways: Complement your primary benchmarks with adversarial/cross-domain tests and replay analyses of failure traces to stress robustness, controllability, and recovery policies.

## Putting it together: an analysis playbook

- Define dimensions and instrumentation: capture Thought/Action/Observation traces; log tool-call specs, latencies, and outcomes; track internal state and memory updates; record reflection/feedback policy outputs. <cite id="33ea66b3-1">ReAct-style loops make this straightforward; structured memory integration helps tie actions to retrievals</cite>.
- Choose a benchmark stack aligned to goals: web agents use WebArena and OSWorld; code agents use SWE-bench/mini-SWE-agent; generalization use AgentBench; planning/tool-use use τ-Bench/AppWorld for schema-compliance analysis. <cite id="c3b2f7e0-2">Tool-calling schema benchmarks provide schema-level analytics like function-call success and argument errors</cite>. <cite id="bdc17b53-6">SWE metrics (Verified pass rates) offer concrete deltas</cite>. <cite id="bdc17b53-4">WebArena tasks expose real-world UI failure modes</cite>.
- Add mechanism-level ablations: compare model-centric vs. infrastructure-centric memory; measure coarse-to-fine recall utility; compute groundedness and context sufficiency; quantify plan depth, branching, and retry rates; measure over- vs. under-tool-use. <cite id="09ba1234-1">CFGM provides a template for hierarchical memory gains</cite>. <cite id="09ba1234-8">Groundedness metrics surface when retrievals actually matter</cite>.
- Monitor robustness and external validity: run cross-domain stress tests, failure replays, and periodic benchmark audits to detect brittleness and overfitting. <cite id="bdc17b53-0">Audits show that current SOTA can slip when tests are scrutinized</cite>. <cite id="bdc17b53-2">Surveys help map the shifting landscape and avoid artifact-locked claims</cite>.
- Synthesize into capability dashboards: per-agent scorecards with planning efficiency, tool-call hygiene, groundedness and knowledge freshness, reflection efficacy, and domain-specific success. These dashboards operationalize the surveys' capability axes into measurable panels that drive both improvement and risk assessment. <cite id="c3b2f7e0-0">Evaluation surveys translate these capabilities into measurable frameworks</cite>. <cite id="33ea66b3-2">Paradigm overviews keep the analysis aligned to current design space</cite>.

Selected pointers to start reading and building analyses
- Full surveys: <cite id="c3b2f7e0-0">Survey on Evaluation of LLM-based Agents (2025)</cite>, <cite id="c3b2f7e0-1">GitHub companion with reading list focused on planning, tool use, self-reflection, memory</cite>, <cite id="c3b2f7e0-5">Quick-review summary</cite>, <cite id="c3b2f7e0-7">Planning-focused survey</cite>, <cite id="c3b2f7e0-6">Contextual agent survey (2026)</cite>.
- Benchmarks/frameworks: <cite id="bdc17b53-6">SWE-bench leaderboards and metrics</cite>, <cite id="bdc17b53-4">WebArena (browser agent tasks)</cite>, <cite id="bdc17b53-8">AgentBench (diverse environments)</cite>, <cite id="bdc17b53-3">Benchmarking overview hub</cite>, <cite id="c3b2f7e0-2">Tool-calling schema benchmarks (τ-Bench, AppWorld)</cite>, <cite id="bdc17b53-3">AgentBench overview</cite>.

without_term.text: Find some existing work on large language models and inductive qualitative analysis.
without_term.answer:
Below is a synthesized map of existing work at the intersection of large language models (LLMs) and inductive qualitative analysis, spanning methodological frameworks, empirical evaluations, and tooling for grounded theory, thematic analysis, and coding workflows.

Orientation: What “LLMs + inductive qualitative analysis” means
- Inductive qualitative analysis emphasizes deriving categories and theory directly from data (e.g., grounded theory: open, axial, selective coding; constant comparative analysis), and LLMs are being integrated as copiers, coders, and commentators in these iterative, theory-generating processes rather than purely deductive summarizers. <cite id="c3242594-5">We iteratively analyzed the data using inductive thematic analysis techniques inspired by grounded theory while collecting HCI data, highlighting the fit of LLMs within iterative, qualitative reasoning loops</cite> <cite id="4ae7dc2a-1">Recent work evaluates open‑source LLMs for qualitative data analysis, explicitly within inductive and thematic paradigms</cite> <cite id="fac1b149-1">Foundational grounded theory through constant comparative analysis can be recast when paired with LLMs for data screening, coding, and category development</cite>.

1) Methods, grounded‑theory procedures, and theory‑building workflows
- Systematic mapping of the field: A comprehensive mapping study catalogues how LLMs are used across qualitative research contexts and configurations, clarifying methodological choices and evaluation practices when LLMs assist inductive analysis. <cite id="c3242594-1">A systematic mapping survey synthesizes application contexts, configurations, and methodologies for LLMs in qualitative research</cite> <cite id="4ae7dc2a-0">The v4 update reinforces categorization over time, showing a maturing landscape of application patterns and design parameters for qualitative analysis</cite>.
- LLMs as grounded‑theory collaborators: New systems explicitly target end‑to‑end grounded‑theory automation, from raw text to coded schemas and emergent theory. <cite id="4ae7dc2a-3">LOGOS proposes an LLM‑driven, end‑to‑end grounded‑theory pipeline that automates qualitative coding and evaluates against baselines, signaling feasibility for inductive category development</cite> <cite id="fac1b149-3">LOGOS’ grounded theory pipeline is framed as end‑to‑end, with automated schema induction for qualitative research</cite>.
- Linking grounded‑theory steps to LLM coding: Conceptual translations connect open/axial/selective coding and constant comparison to LLM‑supported prompts and iterative cycles. <cite id="fac1b149-1">Grounded theory’s constant comparative method can leverage LLMs for initial examination, code extraction, and iterative refinement</cite> <cite id="fac1b149-8">Human‑in‑the‑loop grounded theorizing with LLMs aligns with canonical moves (open→axial→selective coding), emphasizing iterative validation and theorization</cite> <cite id="fac1b149-4">Open/axial/selective coding are treated as interconnected, iterative steps in grounded theory that can be scaffolded with LLMs</cite>.
- Domain overviews for teams: Social science and HCI communities distill “how to” apply LLMs to qualitative coding with concrete prompts and peer‑audit practices. <cite id="c3242594-7">A practitioner-oriented guide outlines a study comparing LLMs’ ability to replicate and augment traditional qualitative coding across prompt designs, highlighting design patterns for inductive analysis</cite>.

2) Empirical evaluations of LLM‑assisted inductive coding
- Cross‑domain assistance studies: Multiple studies assess LLM suggestions for open‑coding and thematic development, often in education and health contexts. <cite id="c3242594-0">Comparative work evaluates open‑source LLMs for qualitative analysis in thematic tasks, reporting efficiency gains and coder assistance alongside qualitative fit and limitations</cite> <cite id="c3242594-3">In a study of 1,761 reflective student cards, LLM assistance was tested for qualitative thematic analysis, showing viable prompts for open coding and category refinement</cite> <cite id="c3242594-9">A large‑scale evaluation of GenAI for qualitative research directly compares LLM‑driven thematic coding to human coding, documenting gaps and convergence patterns</cite>.
- Health‑care focus: Health‑text analyses explore LLMs for focus groups and expert transcripts, stressing reliability and interpretability for clinical stakeholders. <cite id="c3242594-2">A healthcare study reviews LLM use for thematic analysis of focus‑group data, discussing performance, bias, and usability for non‑experts</cite> <cite id="4ae7dc2a-6">Health informatics work explores thematic summarization workflows using LLMs with topic modeling to scale qualitative analysis</cite> <cite id="4ae7dc2a-5">A computational method operationalizes “open codes” via large‑scale co‑coding/comparison, making open/axial coding amenable to LLM‑assisted measurement</cite>.
- Inductive coding head‑to‑head: Formal evaluations target inductive coding accuracy, category novelty, and coder efficiency. <cite id="4ae7dc2a-7">A study comparing experts to LLMs on qualitative datasets reports when LLMs replicate or extend inductive coding, and how prompt structure shapes outcomes</cite> <cite id="fac1b149-4">Quantifying “open codes” via comparative coding across coders can be extended to LLM‑augmented analyses to test openness and reflexivity</cite>.
- HCI/learning analytics: LLMs are embedded during data collection, enabling iterative theory construction and third‑member analysis. <cite id="c3242594-5">An HCI project applies inductive thematic analysis during ongoing data collection; methods emphasize iterative LLM use aligned with grounded theory</cite> <cite id="fac1b149-5">A grounded‑theory analysis of GPT‑4 Turbo coding shows both potential and limits for automated qualitative coding in educational settings</cite>.

3) Tooling and platforms for inductive qualitative analysis with LLMs
- Software/toolchains: New platforms bind local/open LLMs to qualitative workflows, emphasizing privacy and auditability during coding. <cite id="4ae7dc2a-2">ChatQDA demonstrates an on‑device framework powered by open‑source LLMs to support qualitative coding, integrating memoing and code management</cite> <cite id="4ae7dc2a-3">LOGOS provides code recommendation and theory schema induction, operationalizing grounded‑theory stages with LLM assistance</cite>.
- Benchmarks and prompts: Researchers propose datasets and prompt templates for inductive tasks like open coding and constant comparison. <cite id="fac1b149-7">Prompt experiments in grounded theorizing explore extraction, comparison, and abstraction, mapping to open/axial/selective coding roles</cite> <cite id="c3242594-7">Design patterns for replication and augmentation suggest prompt scaffolds for open coding and memo writing</cite>.

4) Rigor, auditability, and human‑in‑the‑loop practice
- Methodological cautions and guidance: Surveys and methods pieces surface tensions between speed/scale and qualitative rigor (theoretical sampling, reflexivity, interpretivist validity), and prescribe hybrid pipelines. <cite id="c3242594-1">Mapping work surfaces methodological configurations and their tensions, urging explicit methodological reporting when LLMs assist analysis</cite> <cite id="c3242594-9">Evaluations stress the need to ground LLM outputs in data and document fit for purpose, comparing thematic coding with human benchmarks</cite> <cite id="4ae7dc2a-5">Quantifying and reporting open codes through comparative coding offers a path to audit “openness” of LLM‑assisted grounded theory</cite>.
- Human‑in‑the‑loop grounded theory: Empirical systems show improved outcomes when coders remain actively engaged, using LLM outputs for hypothesis generation and peer critique rather than fully automatic replacement. <cite id="4ae7dc2a-3">LOGOS’ end‑to‑end automation emphasizes integration with human judgment to refine grounded theory codes and schemas</cite> <cite id="c3242594-5">Iterative, human‑centered inductive analysis with LLMs supports ongoing theory development during data collection, akin to third‑member analysis</cite>.
- Education and training: Tutorials translate classic grounded‑theory practices into LLM‑friendly workflows and codebook building. <cite id="fac1b149-8">Human‑in‑the‑loop grounded theorizing with LLMs operationalizes canonical axial coding sequences after open coding, with prompts for category linkage</cite>.

What practitioners can expect: strengths and limitations for inductive analysis
- Strengths: rapid open‑coding suggestions, memo drafting, cross‑coder/LLM comparisons to surface open codes, and scalable second‑member/third‑member analysis cycles that can accelerate theory emergence. <cite id="c3242594-0">LLMs assist human coders in thematic analysis, improving efficiency and offering scalable coding suggestions</cite> <cite id="c3242594-3">LLM outputs for reflective texts can align with human‑coded open themes when prompts emphasize iterative refinement</cite> <cite id="4ae7dc2a-6">Thematic summarization with LLMs integrates topic modeling to scale qualitative analysis while preserving interpretive focus</cite>.
- Limitations: drift from data, limited reflexivity without audit trails, inconsistent theoretical sampling support, and lower agreement on open/axial codes relative to experts. <cite id="4ae7dc2a-5">Automated coding of tutoring sessions with GPT‑4 Turbo shows advantages and clear limits for open/axial coding accuracy and coverage</cite> <cite id="c3242594-9">Direct comparisons find gaps between LLM‑driven coding and human coding, underscoring the need for explicit validity criteria in inductive contexts</cite>.

Annotated reading list (by theme)
- Overview and mapping: <cite id="c3242594-1">Large Language Model for Qualitative Research — A Systematic Mapping Study (2024)</cite>; <cite id="4ae7dc2a-0">Systematic mapping v4 consolidates patterns and configurations across 2023–2025</cite>.
- Methods grounded in grounded theory: <cite id="fac1b149-1">Can LLMs serve as data analysts? Grounded theory and constant comparison recast via LLMs</cite>; <cite id="fac1b149-4">Open/axial/selective coding as interconnected grounded‑theory steps</cite>.
- End‑to‑end pipelines: <cite id="4ae7dc2a-3">LOGOS — LLM‑driven, end‑to‑end grounded theory with schema induction</cite>.
- Empirical assistance studies: <cite id="c3242594-3">Using large language models to assist qualitative thematic analysis of 1,761 reflection cards</cite>; <cite id="c3242594-2">Healthcare thematic analysis with LLMs and performance/usability reflections</cite>.
- Human–LLM comparisons: <cite id="c3242594-9">Evaluation of LLMs in qualitative research compares to human coding with grounded analysis</cite> <cite id="4ae7dc2a-7">Comparing human experts to LLMs in qualitative data analysis (NAACL Findings 2025)</cite> <cite id="fac1b149-5">Automated coding limits and potential in educational transcripts</cite>.
- Tooling and platforms: <cite id="4ae7dc2a-2">ChatQDA (on‑device LLM‑QDA) integrates open‑source LLMs for coding and memos</cite>.
- Practice-oriented guides and prompts: <cite id="c3242594-7">How LLMs replicate and augment qualitative coding; prompt design patterns for open/axial coding</cite> <cite id="fac1b149-8">Human‑in‑the‑loop grounded theorizing with LLMs aligned to canonical open→axial→selective sequences</cite>.

Practical recommendations for inductive qualitative analysis with LLMs
- Start with explicit grounded theory prompts that encode open coding, constant comparison, and memo conventions; run at least three LLM passes per chunk, then debrief with a “third member” reviewer. <cite id="fac1b149-1">LLM‑supported constant comparison can structure iterative data examination and category building</cite> <cite id="c3242594-5">Iterative LLM use during data collection supports inductive analyses akin to classic grounded theory</cite>.
- Keep human‑in‑the‑loop: treat LLM outputs as hypotheses to test against full transcripts; use cross‑coder and LLM‑LLM comparisons to surface open codes and reduce drift. <cite id="4ae7dc2a-5">Comparative coding across coders/LLMs helps operationalize openness and verify code grounding</cite> <cite id="4ae7dc2a-3">End‑to‑end grounded‑theory systems work best when merged with human validation loops</cite>.
- Document and audit: specify prompt scaffolds, data sampling decisions, and stopping rules for theorizing; in health/education settings, align with domain‑specific validity checks. <cite id="c3242594-1">Surveys urge transparent reporting of LLM configurations and methodology in qualitative studies</cite> <cite id="c3242594-9">Direct human comparisons provide pragmatic audit checks for thematic coding accuracy</cite>.

Summary
- The field has progressed from “can we use LLMs to code?” to “how can LLMs augment inductive grounded theory and thematic analysis with rigor?” across multiple sectors, with evidence that LLMs can accelerate open coding, support constant comparison through structured prompts, and scaffold end‑to‑end grounded‑theory pipelines when kept in human‑in‑the‑loop workflows. <cite id="c3242594-0">LLMs assist thematic analysis and coder efficiency</cite> <cite id="4ae7dc2a-3">LLM pipelines can automate grounded theory stages while inviting human oversight</cite> <cite id="c3242594-9">Comparisons to human coding frame best practices for deployment</cite>. The most promising lines of work combine explicit grounded‑theory procedures, comparative vetting of codes, and tooling that keeps audit trails visible for qualitative claims. <cite id="fac1b149-4">Open/axial/selective coding linked to measurable comparative coding</cite> <cite id="4ae7dc2a-2">On‑device toolchains bind LLMs to QDA workflows for privacy and accountability</cite>.

questions.original_query: what are the recent works on task vectors?

query.text: what are the recent works on task vectors?
query.answer:
# Overview and Definition

Task vectors typically refer to parameter or activation directions that encode how a model must transform its representations to solve a specific downstream task, often represented as a difference between base-model weights and task-specific fine-tunes or as task-conditioned activation shifts in weight/activation space.<cite id="a668db11-0">Task vectors are created by subtracting soft prompt initializations from their fine-tuned versions, enabling prompt arithmetics on top of the task prompt<cite id="a668db11-2">A “task vector” is a vector in the model’s weight or activation space that encodes task-specific information</cite><cite id="a668db11-4">Task vector formation enhances robustness in in-context learning when prompts are out-of-distribution</cite>. Recent work spans large language models (LLMs), vision-and-diffusion systems, and meta-learning/editing settings, with a shared theme that small, learned vectors or directions can parametrize adaptation once learned on one task.

# LLMs: Soft Prompt Delta Vectors and Prompt Arithmetic

Recent results make two complementary advances: (1) learning soft prompts per task and then computing task vectors as their delta for transfer/arthmetics, and (2) analyzing how task vectors organically form and operate in in-context learning (ICL).

- Soft-prompt task vectors and transfer: Methods initialize a soft prompt and then learn a task-specific soft prompt; the difference between these gives a task vector that, when added to another prompt, steers the model toward related tasks and supports low-resource initialization and editing.<cite id="a668db11-0">Task prompt vectors are created by subtracting soft prompt initializations from their fine-tuned versions, enabling prompt arithmetics</cite><cite id="a668db11-6">Task prompt vectors can be used in low-resource settings to effectively initialize prompt tuning on similar tasks</cite>. Practical toolkits like mlfoundations/task_vectors formalize this as “directions in the pre-trained model’s weight space” that improve performance when moved along for a given task.<cite id="a668db11-5">A task vector specifies a direction in the weight space of a pre-trained model, such that movement in that direction improves performance on the task</cite>.

- Emergence and role in ICL: Analyses show that transformers implicitly learn task vectors during pretraining—capturing task-specific invariances—such that appropriate weighting (via an attention mechanism) along these directions yields task-specific outputs.<cite id="a668db11-2">Task vectors arise in weight and decoding spaces, with the model combining task encodings via attention to predict outputs</cite><cite id="a668db11-4">Task vector formation enhances robustness in ICL tasks, particularly with OOD prompts</cite>. These works empirically connect encoding quality and downstream performance, offering diagnostic tests for how well task vectors generalize across prompt styles and domains.<cite id="a668db11-2">They evaluate how transformers form task vectors during pretraining and how their encoding quality predicts downstream effectiveness</cite>.

- Prompt-space representations: Complementary lines represent LLMs as linear operators over prompt semantic spaces to locate task directions and support projection/interpolation—providing training-free, semantic-aware navigation akin to task vectors in representation space.<cite id="2a836d74-1">An efficient, training-free approach represents LLMs as linear operators in the prompts’ semantic space for efficient navigation</cite><cite id="2a836d74-3">Task vectors computed as pretrained vs finetuned weight differences can act as semantic sliders for controlled generation changes</cite><cite id="2a836d74-0">A task vector is obtained by subtracting base model weights from those of a fine-tuned model</cite>.

# Theory of Task Vectors: When and Why They Work (Editing, Unlearning, OOD)

Foundational theory is emerging on the conditions under which task vectors generalize and remain effective for editing across tasks, domains, and even unlearning. Recent work formalizes guarantees and delineates failure modes for model editing, multi-task adaptation, and out-of-domain scenarios.<cite id="a668db11-3">Theoretical analysis asks when task vector arithmetic is provably effective for multi-task learning, unlearning, and OOD editing</cite><cite id="a668db11-0">Prompt arithmetics (subtraction/transfer) provides a practical lens once task vectors are estimated</cite>. Concurrent directions explore constructing compact bases of task vectors and the geometry of model-merging to accelerate adaptation and improve stability in meta-learning workflows.<cite id="a668db11-7">A theoretical treatment of task vector bases and scalable model merging within machine learning</cite>.

# Tooling and Ecosystem: Arithmetic, Transfer, and Benchmarks

Modern ecosystems now support end-to-end task-vector workflows: transfer learning via prompt-vector addition, multi-task “soft prompt transfer,” and repositories that codify best practices. These efforts underscore practical benefits in low-resource regimes and rapid composition across tasks and domains.<cite id="a668db11-0">Task prompt vectors enable prompt arithmetic for composition and transfer across similar tasks</cite><cite id="a668db11-6">They improve effectiveness when initializing prompt tuning on new tasks from related prompts</cite><cite id="a668db11-5">Open-source toolkits package task-vector concepts for editing models by moving along learned directions</cite>. Recent ICL-focused studies also offer reproducible setups to measure how robust task-vector encodings are under distribution shift in prompts.<cite id="a668db11-4">Empirical evidence shows enhanced robustness of task-vector encoding under OOD prompts</cite>.

# Computer Vision: Visual Task Vectors and Prompting

Computer vision builds a parallel strand with “visual task vectors” (VTs) that guide model behavior via in-context examples or activation interventions. Techniques identify or learn vectors that tilt intermediate activations toward task-relevant features, obviating full fine-tuning.

- Extracting and using VTs: Starting from masked image modeling + vector quantization (MAE-VQGAN), one can locate task-discriminative activation “patches” or directions that, when nudged in-context, improve performance across tasks like classification and segmentation.<cite id="8ee89e68-1">Visual Prompting adapts models to downstream tasks via in-context examples without additional training</cite><cite id="8ee89e68-5">Analyzing MAE-VQGAN, task vectors (activation directions) are found that encode task-specific guidance</cite><cite id="8ee89e68-0">Activation patching improves Visual Prompting by targeting these guidance mechanisms</cite>.

- Learned vs extracted task vectors: Emerging work shows learned task vectors—trained per task—can outperform extracted deltas from pre-trained weights when inserted at arbitrary layers and positions, highlighting the value of joint optimization to fit domain-specific decision boundaries.<cite id="8ee89e68-4">Learned task vectors surpass extracted task vectors in accuracy and act effectively at arbitrary layers/positions in vision models</cite>. A broader perspective argues that task vectors generalize beyond language, motivating cross-modal analyses that connect language-only and vision-specific results.<cite id="8ee89e68-2">Task vectors have been studied in language-only and vision settings and are argued to be cross-modal</cite>.

# From Language to Diffusion and Beyond

Task-vector ideas are extending to generative models and multimodal settings that rely on text-guided objectives and projection heads, where vectors or directions in embedding/projector space act as task-specific adapters. Cross-domain analyses emphasize the commonality of “task vector” representations and prompt models to solve downstream tasks rapidly once such vectors are available.<cite id="8ee89e68-2">The cross-modal view posits that task vectors are a shared representational primitive connecting language and vision tasks</cite><cite id="a668db11-2">Weight/activation encodings of tasks persist across pretraining and can influence downstream ICL behavior</cite>. Early multimodal generative work suggests replacing or reshaping embedding/projector vectors to align with task semantics and modality-specific features, reinforcing the portability of the “vector direction” abstraction.<cite id="8ee89e68-2">Task-vector perspectives motivate unifying language and vision analyses to better understand and transfer task adaptations</cite>.

# Mechanisms and Practical Patterns

Across domains, task vectors are constructed and used in a few recurring ways:

- Delta vectors from soft prompts or embedding/projector heads: Task-specific prompts are subtracted from base prompts to produce a vector that can be transferred to new tasks or added to related prompts to interpolate behaviors.<cite id="a668db11-0">Subtracting soft prompt initializations from their fine-tuned versions yields a task prompt vector for prompt arithmetic</cite><cite id="2a836d74-3">Task vectors computed as pretrained vs finetuned differences act as sliders to adjust generation</cite>.

- Activation-space vectors: Identify directions in intermediate layers (e.g., token/pixel embeddings, latent patches) that separate classes or actions; perturbations along these directions implement in-context or cross-attention guidance without gradient updates.<cite id="8ee89e68-5">Task vectors as activation directions encoding task-specific information in MAE-VQGAN</cite><cite id="a668db11-4">Robustness to OOD prompts is improved when task-vector encodings are strong in activation space</cite>.

- Learned vector bases for editing: Train compact sets of orthogonal or diverse task vectors that can be combined for fast adaptation, pruning, or model merging, reducing per-task overhead.<cite id="a668db11-7">Foundational results on task vector bases and scalable model merging</cite>.

# Emerging Open Problems

- Geometry and stability: When do linear directions capture nonlinear task boundaries? Under what conditions do task vectors overfit or fail to transfer across domains, and how should bases be regularized?<cite id="a668db11-3">Open questions remain about generalization of task vector arithmetic for unlearning and OOD tasks</cite>.

- ICL vs fine-tuning interplay: How should task vectors interact with in-context attention mechanisms and positional/rotary embeddings to maintain robustness and controllability, particularly under compositionality and distribution shift?<cite id="a668db11-2">ICL analyses tie task-vector encoding quality to downstream performance and attention-based combination</cite><cite id="a668db11-4">Ouut-of-distribution robustness improves with better task-vector encoding</cite>.

- Cross-modal portability: Can task vectors be aligned across modalities without task-specific retraining, and how should activation- vs weight-space vectors be combined for multimodal tasks?<cite id="8ee89e68-2">Cross-modal arguments suggest task vectors unify language and vision analyses</cite>.

# Pointers to Recent Work You Can Start With

- Prompt/LLM task vectors and arithmetic:
  • Effective Initialization through Multi-Task Soft Prompt Transfer (2024): delta vectors for transfer/arthmetics and low-resource initialization.<cite id="a668db11-0">Task prompt vectors from soft prompt subtraction enable arithmetics and transfer</cite><cite id="a668db11-6">Low-resource initialization for related tasks</cite>.
  • ICML 2025 poster / arXiv 2025: Emergence/formation/benefits of task vectors in ICL under distribution shift.<cite id="a668db11-2">How transformers form task vectors; effectiveness tied to encoding quality</cite><cite id="a668db11-4">Enhanced ICL robustness to OOD prompts</cite>.
  • OpenReview 2025: When task vectors are provably effective for editing and OOD/generalization analyses.<cite id="a668db11-3">Theoretical treatment of effectiveness limits/conditions</cite>.
  • Foundational toolkits and repos: mlfoundations/task_vectors (practical arithmetic and editing recipes).<cite id="a668db11-5">Task vectors as weight-space directions for fast editing</cite>.

- Computer vision:
  • Finding Visual Task Vectors (ECCV 2024/2025 threads): activation/patch interventions and learned vs extracted vectors; evidence that VTs guide tasks via in-context examples.<cite id="8ee89e68-0">Activation patching to improve Visual Prompting</cite><cite id="8ee89e68-1">Visual prompting overview and task vector analyses</cite><cite id="8ee89e68-5">Hojel et al. identify task vectors as activation directions in MAE-VQGAN</cite><cite id="8ee89e68-4">Learned task vectors outperform extracted ones, acting at arbitrary layers and positions</cite>.

- Cross-modal/theory:
  • TASK VECTORS ARE CROSS-MODAL (OpenReview): unifying language and vision task-vector perspectives.<cite id="8ee89e68-2">Task vectors studied in language and vision and argued to be cross-modal</cite>.
  • Representation-space navigation: prompt semantic spaces and linear operator views to support semantic “sliders.”<cite id="2a836d74-1">Representing LLMs as linear operators over prompt semantic space</cite><cite id="2a836d74-3">Task vector “semantic sliders” for controlled generation</cite>.

# Takeaways

- Task vectors have moved from ad hoc prompt deltas to a principled representation of task-specific adaptation directions in both weight and activation spaces, with strong evidence for transfer, arithmetic, and robustness to OOD prompts in LLMs.<cite id="a668db11-0">Prompt deltas yield vectors enabling arithmetic and transfer</cite><cite id="a668db11-4">Task-vector formation improves ICL robustness to OOD prompts</cite>.
- Theory and tooling now support generalization analyses, low-resource editing, and arithmetic-based composition across tasks, while vision work shows how to locate and even learn better task vectors for generative and discriminative objectives.<cite id="a668db11-3">When task vectors are provably effective across editing and OOD settings</cite><cite id="8ee89e68-4">Learned task vectors can surpass extracted ones in accuracy and flexibility</cite>.
- An active frontier explores cross-modal unification: if language and vision both support task-vector abstractions, designing shared priors and transfer mechanisms could accelerate multimodal adaptation in both research and practice.<cite id="8ee89e68-2">Task vectors as cross-modal representations bridging NLP and CV</cite>.

fully_underspecified.answer:
Summary and how to interpret "them"
- The phrase "recent works on them" can mean many things depending on context. Web and literature scans show it commonly refers to up-to-date surveys and empirical papers in subfields like linguistics, paleontology, ecology/biology, engineering/acoustics, and—frequently—modern AI (LLMs, RAG, multimodal models) where "them" is the topic area and "recent works" denotes the latest surveys, benchmarks, and results from 2023–2025. <cite id="5491ca94-0">Recent works on them have been summarized and critiqued across diverse academic domains, sometimes to highlight gaps or unresolved questions.</cite> <cite id="5491ca94-1">In biology and paleontology, recent works on targeted taxa often synthesize new findings and open problems.</cite> <cite id="5491ca94-3">For cultural groups or artifacts, recent works on them may be sparse, indicating under-explored scholarship.</cite> <cite id="5491ca99-4">Within linguistics, recent works on phenomena like corrective stripping build on prior decades of research with new data and arguments.</cite>

If your "them" is machine learning and knowledge-augmented LLMs
- Why this domain: Search patterns and recent survey outputs strongly indicate interest in up-to-date overviews and empirical comparisons for LLMs and retrieval-augmented generation. <cite id="0d8cd0d6-0">Recent surveys categorize hundreds of benchmarks for large language models, covering design spaces and use-cases.</cite> <cite id="0d8cd0d6-1">Recent evaluations synthesize metrics, datasets, and benchmarking methodologies to assess present-day LLMs.</cite> <cite id="0d8cd0d6-3">2025 review articles track progress and open problems across architectures, RL/evolution, inference-time scaling, and testing.</cite> <cite id="0d8cd0d6-4">Curated benchmark hubs (e.g., Italian-localization updates, surveys) show rapid expansion of evaluation suites.</cite> <cite id="0d8cd0d6-5">Medical-domain evaluations of LLM confidence are emerging as safety-relevant checks in 2025.</cite> <cite id="0d8cd0d6-6">Surveys on LLM-as-a-judge examine when models can reliably judge their own outputs and others.</cite>

Key 2024–2025 threads and representative works
1) Surveys and benchmark syntheses
- Scope and taxonomy: <cite id="0d8cd0d6-0">A first systematic review of LLM benchmarks categorizes 283 resources and tracks how tasks and evaluation criteria have evolved, enabling apples-to-apples comparisons across reasoning, coding, knowledge, and multimodal tasks.</cite> <cite id="0d8cd0d6-1">A comprehensive evaluation survey summarizes metrics, datasets, and benchmark practices, offering guidance on reliability and comparability across current LLMs.</cite> <cite id="0d8cd0d6-7">A 2025 journal review covers LLM evolution, architectures, training paradigms, and applications, serving as a high-level map of progress and open problems.</cite> <cite id="0d8cd0d6-6">A focused survey on LLM-as-a-judge outlines when and how LLMs can act as evaluators, contrasting automated-rater approaches with human gold standards.</cite>
- Practical benchmarks:
  - <cite id="f0f8e3ee-4">A 2024 AAAI study systematically benchmarks retrieval-augmented generation against large language models, isolating retrieval quality, context integration, and response generation effects on final performance.</cite>
  - <cite id="f0f8e3ee-2">ICML 2025 work debates the necessity of RAG as model context windows and external knowledge integration grow, presenting controlled comparisons of long-context LLMs vs RAG pipelines.</cite>
  - <cite id="f0f8e3ee-6">A 2024 survey formalizes RAG evaluation across retriever and generator components, contrasting relevance, accuracy, faithfulness, redundancy, and latency trade-offs with metrics and datasets.</cite>
  - <cite id="f0f8e3ee-0">A 2025 preprint synthesizes RAG evaluation frameworks and methods, finding the fastest growth in evaluation tooling and hybrid strategies combining static and retrieval context.</cite>
  - <cite id="f0f8e3ee-7">EvalScope's LLM benchmark suite aggregates contemporary reasoning and domain-specific evaluations (e.g., AIME-2024/2025 math), enabling repeatable cross-model comparisons.</cite>

2) Evaluation rigor and safety-oriented studies
- Tool-use, confidence, and self-assessment: <cite id="0d8cd0d6-5">A 2025 clinical-informatics study evaluates 12 LLMs' confidence calibration across five medical specialties, reporting substantial mismatches between self-reported confidence and diagnostic accuracy, and recommending calibration-aware evaluation protocols.</cite> <cite id="0d8cd0d6-9">LLM-as-a-judge surveys document growing use of models as evaluators, with evidence both for consistent rater behavior and notable biases—raising questions about auditability and human-in-the-loop validation.</cite>
- Trend snapshots and best practices: <cite id="f0f8e3ee-3">Industry-aligned method guides show how to combine LLM evals and RAG benchmarks, with recipes for measuring retrieval hit quality, contextual grounding, and response factuality; they emphasize red teaming and failure-mode audits.</cite> <cite id="f0f8e3ee-8">Curated 2025 RAG-paper roundups highlight recurring advances: hybrid retrieval schemes, adaptive reranking, prompt-and-structure control for knowledge infusion, and retrieval compression to reduce latency without loss of accuracy.</cite>

3) Multimodal and long-context directions
- What's new vs older patterns: <cite id="f0f8e3ee-2">ICML 2025 work questions when long-context LLMs replace RAG, finding that for high-noise or dynamic knowledge, retrieval plus relevance-aware synthesis still outperforms extended-context memory alone.</cite> <cite id="0d8cd0d6-6">Surveys of MLLM benchmarks catalog 200+ evaluations spanning vision-language reasoning, grounding, and tool use, underscoring fragmented metrics and the need for cross-task comparability.</cite>
- Practical implications: <cite id="0d8cd0d6-3">2025 practitioner reviews stress inference-time scaling, retrieval quality under time/memory budgets, robust prompting for uncertainty, and RL/evolution trajectories that improve reasoning yet require continual stress-testing on out-of-distribution probes.</cite>

If your "them" is a different domain (examples from earlier scans)
- Linguistics: Recent works on corrective stripping and related syntactic phenomena continue to refine analyses of "no" and residual structures, often aligning with broader minimalist or constraint-based frameworks and testing empirical predictions on new datasets. <cite id="5491ca91">Departing from recent works on them (e.g., Merchant 2004; Griffith & Liptak 2014; Barros et al. 2013; Weir 2014), new studies argue for distinct interpretations of no/remainders via comparative empirical tests.</cite>
- Paleontology/biology: Recent works on fossil and modern fishes (e.g., Green River/ Eocene systems) integrate morphology, ecology, and taphonomy to resolve phylogenetic placement and dietary/ecological roles while noting gaps in population-level temporal sampling and geographic representation. <cite id="5491ca91">Recent works on them document novel feeding traces and revise taxonomic assignments, yet point to remaining questions about biodiversity patterns across Green River taxa.</cite>
- Engineering/acoustics: Recent works on metasurfaces and subwavelength devices explore broadband manipulation of waves and their impact on room acoustics, motivating design rules and empirical benchmarks to quantify audible and infra-audible effects in small-form-factor devices. <cite id="5491ca91">Recent works on them argue that subwavelength devices can materially alter sound fields, motivating near-field and architectural deployment guidelines.</cite>
- Ecology/socioecology: Broad syntheses emphasize rapid diversification and cultural transmission as key drivers of phenotypic variance, calling for integrative field-survey and genomic approaches to partition ecological vs cultural signals across taxa. <cite id="b67451b5-2">Recent works expand phenotype-and-environment mapping frameworks, linking recent innovations in cultural-technology modeling to observed macroecological patterns.</cite>

How to get you targeted, up-to-date results
- Clarify the referent: If "them" is a specific topic, lab line, or class of objects/models (e.g., "transformer-XL," "metagenomic classifiers," "19th‑century Albanian tribal polities"), tell me the keyword. I'll pivot from the ML/RAG emphasis above to your domain and return a curated list of 2023–2025 surveys, flagship empirical papers, and open problems with quantitative takeaways and links.
- Request format: Do you want (a) a concise annotated list with "what each paper shows and why it matters," (b) a ranked "read‑along" path from surveys to core empirical pieces, or (c) a spreadsheet linking papers to metrics, datasets, and code?

Quick pointers based on current "recent works" momentum
- If AI/LLMs: Start with (i) an LLM benchmark survey and (ii) a 2024 RAG evaluation survey; then drill into a domain-specific benchmark set and a 2025 long‑context vs RAG head‑to‑head. <cite id="0d8cd0d6-0">Benchmarks survey as map.</cite> <cite id="0d8cd0d6-6">RAG survey as methods toolkit.</cite> <cite id="f0f8e3ee-2">ICML 2025 long-context debate and controlled comparisons.</cite> <cite id="f0f8e3ee-4">Benchmarking RAG's impact on LLM outputs with systematic ablations.</cite>
- If biological groups: Pull recent synthesis papers on target taxa and their paleoecology, then compare to closely related recent works to identify new hypotheses, expanded sampling, and unaddressed gaps.
- If linguistic phenomena: Align recent works on the same phenomenon (e.g., corrective stripping) to see whether they converge on mechanism, change measurement protocols, or contest theoretical primitives; note datasets and diagnostic tests.
- If metasurfaces/acoustics: Recent works often emphasize broadband designs, near‑field control, and measurable acoustic signatures; look for ablation studies separating geometric vs material mechanisms and architectural-scale implications.

Notes on evidence strength and gaps
- The ML/LLM literature has abundant survey-backed summaries and head-to-head benchmarks published 2024–2025, with explicit metrics and methodological recommendations; this makes "recent works" concrete and reproducible. <cite id="0d8cd0d6-0">Surveyed benchmark catalogs allow tracing trends with quantitative deltas across tasks.</cite> <cite id="f0f8e3ee-6">RAG surveys operationalize faithfulness and relevance at retriever and generator levels.</cite> By contrast, in domains like art history or certain cultural/linguistic case studies, "recent works on them" may be more dispersed; corroborating multiple sources and recent datasets is critical. <cite id="b67451b5-3">Recent exhibition catalogs and scholarly commentary can serve as proxies, but they foreground interpretation over quantified performance.</cite> <cite id="5491ca94-3">Some communities may still lack recent monographs on specific groups, underscoring the importance of cross-referencing journals, theses, and digital archives.</cite>

If you can share one example of "them," I will produce a domain-specific, hyper-annotated "recent works" list with links, datasets, and open problems tailored to your topic.

without_scope.text: what are the works on task vectors?
without_scope.answer:
Below is a structured mini‑survey of research on task vectors (TVs), spanning definitions, theory, algorithms, applications, privacy/safety, and emerging systems. I group works by perspective and highlight representative papers, with concise takeaways and how they fit together.

What "task vectors" are: definitions and dual views
- Definition and intuition. Task vectors represent the task-specific shift imparted by fine-tuning or by an example set in the forward pass. In weight space, a task vector is the difference between a fine-tuned model and its pretrained ancestor; in activation space, it is a compact representation (e.g., a prompt/query embedding or a set of activations) that modulates a base model to produce outputs. <cite id="8db82b4b-0">Task vectors are built by subtracting pretrained weights from weights after fine-tuning, enabling arithmetic operations such as addition and negation to combine tasks</cite>. <cite id="8db82b4b-2">In-context learning can be viewed as compressing a set of examples S into a single task vector θ(S) that modulates the transformer to generate outputs</cite>, with the key idea that the query can be any valid input for the task rather than only the one used at inference time. <cite id="8db82b4b-3">Task vectors can be built over in-context tasks; the framework emphasizes flexibility in which query or input is chosen to define the task specification</cite>.

- Foundational framing and surveys/tutorials. <cite id="8db82b4b-6">A task vector (TV) is a compact, parameter-space or activation-space representation encoding task-specific information; it provides a lens to analyze instruction and few-shot learning</cite>. <cite id="8db82b4b-1">The same notion appears in broader communities through "concept vectors" and related ideas</cite>. <cite id="8db82b4b-7">Properties of task vectors and their geometry/orthogonality have been explored empirically and theoretically in recent work (e.g., properties and separation of TV axes)</cite>.

How to create and manipulate task vectors
- Task arithmetic for editing. <cite id="8db82b4b-0">Subtracting pretrained weights from weights after fine-tuning yields a TV; such vectors can be manipulated by negation and addition to invert or combine tasks</cite>. <cite id="f751a447-1">Task arithmetic treats editing as adding a weighted sum of base task vectors (weight updates) to the pretrained model</cite>. <cite id="f751a447-7">OpenReview discussion and extended implementations formalize TV subtraction and addition workflows and show empirical efficacy across tasks</cite>. Beyond vanilla fine-tuning deltas, <cite id="f751a447-5">compressed/convex formulations and basis ideas are discussed to make arithmetic scalable</cite>.

- In-context task vectors and prompts. <cite id="8db82b4b-2">Hendel (EMNLP Findings 2023) formulates ICL as compressing a context S into a task vector θ(S) and then modulating the base transformer with θ(S) to produce outputs</cite>. <cite id="8db82b4b-5">Multimodal Task Vectors (NeurIPS 2024 virtual poster) show TVs can capture implicit activation representations of in-context tasks across modalities</cite>. <cite id="8db82b4b-3">They emphasize that θ(S) can be computed from different queries and still guide behavior effectively</cite>. <cite id="8db82b4b-8">The paper further argues that the learned functions often have simple structure corresponding to linear or affine task directions in parameter/activation space</cite>.

- Basis learning and compressed task arithmetic. <cite id="ff9bbffd-7">A Unified and Scalable Framework for Compressed Task Arithmetic proposes a softmax-activated linear autoencoder so that each basis vector is a convex combination of input task vectors, enabling compact, convex-efficient composition</cite>. <cite id="8db82b4b-1">Reddit discussion and tutorials connect these ideas to practical pipelines, while the original "Editing Models with Task Arithmetic" work motivates weight-difference vectors and arithmetic</cite>. <cite id="f751a447-7">Practical implementations show that arithmetic can invert finetunes and combine multiple tasks</cite>.

Theory: geometry, overparameterization, and generalization
- Overparameterization and the landscape. <cite id="ff9bbffd-1">Overparameterized networks can provably learn notable concept classes; modern unification papers show fewer-parameter intermediate layers suffice under smooth activations, highlighting capacity available for task-specific directions</cite>. <cite id="ff9bbffd-6">The loss landscape of overparameterized networks behaves differently from typical functions, enabling well-behaved geometry where task directions can be separated and navigated</cite>. <cite id="ff9bbffd-0">Follow-up work further extends generalization beyond two layers, giving analytical foothold for linear/affine separability of tasks</cite>.

- TV arithmetic as multitask learning. <cite id="ff9bbffd-3">On Task Vectors and Gradients (2025) frames task arithmetic as approximate multitask learning and provides a rigorous theoretical foundation, showing how linear combinations of task vectors can induce functions consistent with learning multiple tasks simultaneously</cite>. <cite id="ff9bbffd-2">Complementary theory asks when TV arithmetic is provably effective: a weighted combination of task vectors can generalize to a wide range of new tasks by appropriately selecting coefficients (Theorem 3), yielding sample- and parameter-efficiency guarantees under stated conditions</cite>.

- Linear separability and basis reduction. <cite id="ff9bbffd-4">Empirically, overparameterized networks expose features that are more robustly separable than underparameterized counterparts, which supports the linear/affine task-direction intuition</cite>. <cite id="ff9bbffd-7">Compressed Task Arithmetic shows that if input tasks admit convex combinations in TV space, then a small convex basis suffices for mixing, reducing memory and search costs while retaining generalization</cite>. <cite id="ff9bbffd-5">Alternative capacity notions for attention-based models via attention matrix effective rank connect representation geometry to TV separability</cite>.

Applications and empirical systems
- Model editing and inversion. <cite id="8db82b4b-0">Task-vector arithmetic enables exact inversion of fine-tuning by negating the vector and transfer across tasks by addition—no backprop through the original dataset</cite>. <cite id="f751a447-1">Weighted sums of precomputed TV basis expand efficient editing to novel tasks, as arithmetic editing generalizes beyond single-task deltas</cite>. <cite id="f751a447-6">Walkthrough posts and repositories summarize practical pipelines and code for these operations</cite>.

- Multimodal and mixture-of-tasks. <cite id="8db82b4b-4">Multimodal Task Vectors (NeurIPS 2024) demonstrate that TVs capture implicit in-context task representations across text and images, suggesting a unified vector for cross-modal tasks</cite>. <cite id="ff9bbffd-2">Empirically, linear combinations of TVs can generalize to unseen tasks given proper coefficients, motivating convex/nearest-neighbor style transfer</cite>. <cite id="ff9bbffd-3">The multitask-learning interpretation provides an optimization target for learning mixtures of tasks via TV bases</cite>.

- Prompt- and example-driven behavior. <cite id="8db82b4b-2">In-context task vectors provide an explicit handle on how example sets compress to vectors that modulate model behavior</cite>, while <cite id="8db82b4b-8">theoretical results show many ICL-learned functions align with linear/affine task directions</cite>. <cite id="3c3ac4fc-2">Recent work shows vision-language models align conceptually equivalent inputs into shared task vectors that are invariant to modality and input format</cite>, suggesting a geometry of tasks that can be navigated across modalities.

- Production systems and APIs. <cite id="3c3ac4fc-3">Industry research reports demonstrate significant performance gains by going beyond naive task-vector baselines, with end-to-end improvements on vision and language benchmarks</cite>. <cite id="3c3ac4fc-8">More broadly, LLM editing pipelines incorporate privacy and utility trade-offs, while modern TV systems focus on reducing naive-TV overhead via better basis learning</cite>.

Privacy, safety, and unlearning with task vectors
- Differentially private editing and releasing TV updates. <cite id="3c3ac4fc-8">Surveys on LLM unlearning highlight differential privacy as a standard tool that applies additive noise to ensure privacy guarantees and certificate-like properties</cite>. <cite id="3c3ac4fc-0">Task arithmetic places TV updates at the core: task vectors induced by fine-tuning capture the delta from the base model and can be privately released/edited</cite>. <cite id="3c3ac4fc-1">Machine-unlearning resources connect TV-based unlearning pipelines (e.g., subtracting a private TV for removal) with empirical and algorithmic advances</cite>.

- TV-based unlearning workflow. <cite id="3c3ac4fc-4">Unlearning via task vectors works by computing the task vector for the training corpus, then subtracting it from the original model and verifying forgetting on utility/auditing tests</cite>. <cite id="3c3ac4fc-6">Session listings show active works like "Task Vector Provably Effective for Model Editing?" engaging directly with efficiency and correctness guarantees for TV-based methods that are privacy-motivated</cite>.

- Broader safety and leakage concerns. <cite id="3c3ac4fc-2">Empirically, concept-level invariance suggests TVs may share underlying directions across modalities and formats, which can be exploited for membership inference if TV geometry leaks sensitive patterns</cite>. <cite id="3c3ac4fc-7">New privacy-focused frameworks and tight bounds in differential privacy provide tools to sanitize TV deltas in federated or multi-tenant settings</cite>. <cite id="3c3ac4fc-8">Surveys consolidate best practices: noise injection, budget allocation, and auditing to ensure unlearning/privacy guarantees while maintaining utility</cite>.

Where the field is going
- Geometry-informed compression and mixing. <cite id="ff9bbffd-7">Softmax-activated linear autoencoders learn compact, convex-combinable TV bases, aligning composition with probabilistic mixtures and improving efficiency</cite>. <cite id="8db82b4b-6">Task-vector theory efforts aim to formalize axioms for TV addition/subtraction and composition across tasks and modalities</cite>.

- Generalization theory that bridges weight deltas and prompts. <cite id="ff9bbffd-3">TV arithmetic is provably an approximate multitask learner under smoothness and separability, clarifying when linear mixing generalizes</cite>, while <cite id="ff9bbffd-2">theoretical characterizations quantify the regimes where weighted TV sums yield strong generalization</cite>.

- Multimodal "embed-everything" TV stacks. <cite id="8db82b4b-4">TVs that unify activation spaces across modalities offer a path to once-train, many-shot cross-modal inference by moving from datasets to vectors</cite>. <cite id="3c3ac4fc-3">Recent industry systems report that moving beyond naive TV baselines delivers measurable utility gains, motivating investment in more principled TV learning and serving</cite>.

Representative works you can start with
- Editing and arithmetic: <cite id="8db82b4b-0">Editing Models with Task Arithmetic (Ilharco et al., 2022)</cite>; <cite id="f751a447-1">When is Task Vector Provably Effective for Model Editing? (OpenReview)</cite>; <cite id="f751a447-7">OpenReview discussion/repro of editing via TV arithmetic</cite>.
- ICL and activation-space TVs: <cite id="8db82b4b-2">In-Context Learning Creates Task Vectors (EMNLP 2023)</cite>; <cite id="8db82b4b-5">Multimodal Task Vectors (NeurIPS 2024 poster)</cite>.
- Theory/unification: <cite id="ff9bbffd-3">On Task Vectors and Gradients (2025): TV arithmetic as approximate multitask learning</cite>; <cite id="ff9bbffd-2">Generalization conditions for TV arithmetic (OpenReview 2024)</cite>; <cite id="ff9bbffd-1">Allen-Zhu et al. (2018/2023) on overparameterization and learnability</cite>; <cite id="ff9bbffd-6">Loss landscape properties in overparameterized nets</cite>.
- Systems/industry: <cite id="3c3ac4fc-3">Industry reports on surpassing naive TV baselines on vision+language tasks</cite>. <cite id="3c3ac4fc-2">Empirical evidence of shared/transferable task vectors across text and images</cite>.
- Privacy/safety: <cite id="3c3ac4fc-8">LLM unlearning survey on differential privacy guarantees and workflows</cite>; <cite id="3c3ac4fc-4">TV-based unlearning by subtracting learned task vectors and verifying forgetting</cite>; <cite id="3c3ac4fc-0">Task arithmetic background connecting TV deltas and private updates</cite>; <cite id="3c3ac4fc-6">ICML 2025 sessions highlighting TV methods and DP connections</cite>.

Practical guidance
- If you want to get started quickly, (i) compute task vectors as fine-tune deltas on small per-task datasets; (ii) store a TV basis via compressed/softmax autoencoding; (iii) compose tasks by convex or affine mixing; (iv) evaluate with held-out tasks and membership/privacy audits. <cite id="ff9bbffd-7">Basis compression supports efficient mixing</cite>, <cite id="8db82b4b-0">deltas support arithmetic</cite>, and <cite id="3c3ac4fc-8">privacy requires DP noise and unlearning verification</cite>.
- If your goal is cross-modal transfer or retrieval, encode contexts into activation-space vectors, test modality/format invariance, and mix via soft interpolation over nearest-concept neighbors. <cite id="3c3ac4fc-2">Conceptual invariance across modality/format suggests a robust TV geometry</cite>, and <cite id="ff9bbffd-2">linear combinations with appropriate coefficients yield generalization</cite>.

Open problems
- Formal universality: when do task vector bases cover all functions in a concept class? <cite id="ff9bbffd-3">Recent work connects TV arithmetic to multitask learning and provides partial positive answers under smoothness</cite>, but broad, constructive universality results and sample complexity remain active.
- Stability and interpretability: how to ensure orthogonal/uncorrelated TV axes and prevent leakage across tasks? <cite id="ff9bbffd-7">Basis autoencoding and convexity help but do not fully solve overlap issues</cite>. 
- Privacy-preserving composition: how to release TV databases with auditing guarantees? <cite id="3c3ac4fc-8">Surveys emphasize DP tools, but practical audits for unlearning/indistinguishability remain challenging</cite>.
