Disulfide linkers like SMCC contain two maleimide-reactive units, enabling conjugation to two interchain cysteines to produce homogeneous structures; however, disulfide engineering and reactivation can cause heterogeneity. <cite id="356a7e5f-5">Amide coupling to lysines is common, whereas thiol coupling to engineered cysteines is also widely used; stability and heterogeneity trade-offs are documented</cite> <cite id="356a7e5f-8">Cysteine-linked IgG2 ADCs can be more heterogeneous than IgG1-derived conjugates, reflecting the challenges and variability of disulfide-based attachment</cite>.
- Disulfide crosslinkers and reactivation: Antibody interchain disulfides can be reduced in situ and reformed using bis-thiol reagents (e.g., SPDB/SMCC-class linkers) to couple two antibodies or two drug molecules through a disulfide bridge, enabling "maleimide disulfide" or "maytansinoid crosslinker" approaches. <cite id="356a7e5f-7">Reduced interchain disulfide reagents reconnect cysteine pairs, enabling homogeneous linker formation via disulfide reconstitution</cite>.
- Maytansinoid-specific disulfide crosslinking: Maytansinoids (DM1/DM4) are conjugated to cysteines via disulfide linkers and crosslink two antibodies, yielding "duoBody" topologies; stability and payload exposure depend on the disulfide motif and reductive cleavage kinetics. <cite id="356a7e5f-5">Disulfide-linked structures are widely used for maytansinoids, balancing stability with reductive cleavage in reducing cellular environments</cite>.

Engineered residues and unnatural amino acids (UAA) on antibodies
- Genetic encoding of UAAs enables orthogonal posttranslational modification at designated sites without altering antibody function. Cysteine derivatives (e.g., p-azidophenylalanine- or maleimide-bearing UAAs) or alkyne/azide-bearing UAAs introduce handles for click linkers or disulfide crosslinkers, improving homogeneity and payload control. <cite id="c9ed94e6-0">Genetically encoded unnatural amino acids with orthogonal reactivity enable homogeneous ADC synthesis with precise site control</cite> <cite id="c9ed94e6-2">Incorporating non-natural amino acids with orthogonal chemical reactivity into antibodies provides a new idea for synthesis of homogeneous ADCs</cite> <cite id="c9ed94e6-4">Selective antibody coupling is achieved by introducing specific amino acids or unnatural amino acids, peptides, or sugar moieties by engineering</cite>.
- Photolabile/controllable linkers at UAAs: Photo-caged or bio-orthogonally cleavable linkers attached to UAAs allow in situ (SPOT) or click-free assembly, reducing off-rate aggregation and enabling precise dosing. <cite id="c9ed94e6-0">Orthogonal UAA chemistries provide routes to homogeneous ADCs and enable controlled linker formation and cleavage</cite>.

Serine, threonine, and tyrosine-directed linkages
- Ortho-ester and oxime/imine chemistries: To mitigate heterogeneity, site-specific modifications at serine/threonine/tyrosine can be achieved through engineered peptide tags (e.g., Ser/Thr/Tyr–Aldehyde/ketone handles), oximes (hydrazone), or serine/threonine ortho-ester linkers; these approaches often leverage selective peptide tags or genetically placed alcohols for controlled ligation. <cite id="356a7e5f-4">Site-selective modification strategies use selective residues and orthogonal reactivities to avoid bulk lysine competition and reduce heterogeneity</cite> <cite id="356a7e5f-6">Recent site-specific conjugation frameworks include engineered serine/threonine/tyrosine motifs and peptide tags for controlled payload attachment</cite>.

# 2) Linker–payload attachment chemistry

Peptide "smart" linkers and cleavage chemistry
- Protease-cleavable dipeptide motifs (Val–Cit–PABC): Dipeptide linkers bear a destabilizing p-nitrophenyl (PABC) ester that is reactivated by dipeptidyl peptidase (DPP4/cathepsin B/cathepsin L) to release the cytotoxin; Val–Cit is the most established cleavable motif in ADCs. <cite id="ee041c8e-2">The Val–Cit dipeptide is arguably the most successful and widely used enzyme-cleavable linker in ADC development</cite>.
- Lysosome/acidic pH-activable linkers: Ester linkers, short peptide sequences, or amide surrogates are hydrolyzed under lysosomal conditions or endosomal/lysosomal cathepsin peptidases to liberate payload. <cite id="ee041c8e-8">Lysosomal-cleavable peptide linkers have become a dominant design space; endo-lysosomal cleavage routes are central to payload release</cite>.
- Noncleavable linkers (auristatin-based): Stable esters or amides tether drugs (e.g., DM1/DM4/DM5 from auristatins) that are released primarily upon proteolytic degradation of the antibody, with payload liberation occurring mainly in lysosomes after internalization. <cite id="ee041c8e-0">Kadcyla uses a noncleavable linker–drug motif, whereas auristatin-containing linkers (e.g., in ADCETRIS) exemplify protease-sensitive motifs</cite> <cite id="ee041c8e-3">Noncleavable linkers degrade with the antibody; payload release occurs mainly in lysosomes after internalization</cite>.

Disulfide-bridged payload linkers and maytansinoid topologies
- Maytansinoid disulfide crosslinkers: Antibody cysteines are crosslinked by disulfide-containing linkers (e.g., SMCC or SPDB-class) to which two maytansinoid payloads attach, forming a dimeric "duoBody" architecture; cleavage can depend on intracellular reduction and peptidase activity. <cite id="356a7e5f-5">Disulfide-linked maytansinoid ADCs are widely used, with stability governed by reductive cleavage and peptidase degradation</cite>.
- Direct thiol–maleimide linkers: NHS-ester linkers can be switched to thiol-bearing linkers (maleimide-PEG-linker) that couple to reduced cysteines, enabling homogeneous structures and disulfide reactivation strategies. <cite id="356a7e5f-5">Thiol coupling to engineered cysteines and disulfide linkers forms homogeneous ADCs but may require careful control of reductive stabilization and cleavage</cite>.

# 3) Cleavable versus noncleavable linkers: design goals and trade-offs

Cleavable linkers
- Trigger classes: protease-cleavable (Val–Cit), lysosome/pH labile (ester/peptide), redox/disulfide-cleavable, enzymatically cleavable (e.g., transglutaminase- or glycosidase-addressed), and metallo-enzyme responsive motifs; the choice depends on tumor-selective expression and subcellular trafficking. <cite id="ee041c8e-2">Val–Cit-based cleavable linkers are the most widely used enzyme-cleavable motif in ADCs</cite> <cite id="ee041c8e-8">Lysosomal-cleavable linkers exploit endo-lysosomal biology for payload release</cite> <cite id="ee041c8e-4">Cleavable linkers leverage tumor-specific properties to selectively release payloads</cite>.
- Stability and ADC heterogeneity: Cleavable motifs can increase heterogeneity (e.g., variable number of linkers per antibody) but improve dose proportionality and pharmacology; engineering (e.g., disulfide reconnection) reduces heterogeneity in maytansinoid ADCs. <cite id="ee041c8e-8">Cleavable peptide linker design balances stability and controlled release in lysosomal compartments</cite> <cite id="356a7e5f-7">Disulfide reconnection strategies can yield homogeneous linkers by reconnecting reduced interchain cysteines</cite> <cite id="356a7e5f-8">Cysteine-linked ADCs via disulfide motifs can be more heterogeneous, requiring careful engineering</cite>.

Noncleavable linkers
- Behavior: remain intact until the antibody degrades; drug release is driven by lysosomal trafficking and proteolysis of the whole IgG, simplifying linker chemistry but potentially lowering payload exposure unless high DAR is tolerated. <cite id="ee041c8e-3">Noncleavable linkers only degrade with the antibody; release is mainly lysosomal after internalization</cite> <cite id="ee041c8e-5">Noncleavable linkers do not rely on external cleavage signals, whereas cleavable linkers use defined tumor-cell properties to release drug</cite>.
- Examples: Kadcyla (T-DM1) uses a noncleavable linker–auristatin E architecture; stability profiles differ from protease-sensitive systems like ADCETRIS. <cite id="ee041c8e-0">Kadcyla uses a noncleavable linker–drug motif while ADCETRIS exemplifies protease-sensitive auristatin linkers</cite>.

# 4) Bioorthogonal and enzymatic ("click", "ligation") methodologies

Click chemistry (Cu(I) azide–alkyne and SPAAC)
- Cu(I)-catalyzed azide–alkyne cycloaddition: Antibody azide (from lysine alkyne-azide toggle or unnatural amino acid modification) ligates with alkyne-bearing payloads; trans-catalyst (Cu(I)) removal yields stable linkers for in vivo use. <cite id="356a7e5f-0">Click conjugation is highlighted among popular conjugation methods in early reviews of ADC chemistry</cite>.
- Strain-promoted azide–alkyne (SPAAC): Dibenzocyclooctyne (dbCO) derivatives react with azides without copper catalysts or with copper for faster kinetics; biotin-alkyne linkers enable streptavidin bioconjugation workflows for payload conjugation. <cite id="356a7e5f-0">Click modalities (SPRCuAAC, azide–alkyne) are core tools in site-specific ADC conjugation</cite>.
- Advantages/limits: high efficiency and orthogonal reactivity reduce off-targets; need for catalyst removal (trans-catalyst) in Cu(I) systems; copper exposure is a toxicological concern addressed by copper-chelate or copper-free SPAAC variants. <cite id="356a7e5f-2">Chemical trigger advances include copper-free and strain-promoted click chemistries for linker formation in ADCs</cite>.

Enzymatic/bioorthogonal ligation to antibodies
- Trans-cyclooctyne (TCO)/tetrazole bioorthogonal click: Copper-free strain-promoted cyclooctyne reagents click with azides or alkynes on linker–payloads or on azide-bearing antibodies to form biocompatible linkers. <cite id="356a7e5f-2">Recent reviews summarize enzymatic and bioorthogonal ligation methods that complement traditional chemistries</cite> <cite id="356a7e5f-0">Enzymatic ligation and click approaches are recognized as popular and efficient conjugation methods</cite>.
- Sortase-mediated ligation and glycan remodeling: Engineered glycans or Strep-tagged antibodies bind streptavidin linkers, and sortase transpeptidation attaches peptide-linker–payload moieties at defined serine/threonine or cysteine motifs; this yields site-specific conjugates with modular linker–payload transfer. <cite id="ee041c8e-4">Site-selective modification strategies use selective residues and orthogonal reactivities (including glycan- and tag-directed ligation) to improve control</cite>.
- TCEP/maleimide and engineered cysteines: Enzyme-free thiol coupling to reduced cysteines is compatible with UAA-encoded cysteines, providing orthogonal handles for disulfide crosslinkers or maleimide linkers. <cite id="356a7e5f-5">Thiol–maleimide linkages to engineered cysteines are widely used to form stable, homogeneous ADCs</cite>.

# 5) Practical workflow examples for linker formation

- Random lysine amide conjugation: Activate a linker (e.g., succinic or glutaric acid NHS-ester) and conjugate to accessible lysines; load and heterogeneity depend on lysine exposure and buffer conditions; reduce payload instability via cleavable peptide linker. <cite id="356a7e5f-5">Amide coupling to solvent-accessible lysines on antibodies is a major, widely used conjugation method</cite> <cite id="ee041c8e-2">Protease-cleavable dipeptide linkers (e.g., Val–Cit) are standard for controlled payload release</cite>.
- Site-specific lysine coupling via engineered tags: Introduce a selective tag (e.g., biotin/avidin-ligated peptide handle), then attach linker–payload via an amide or imine, improving lot-to-lot consistency and DAR uniformity. <cite id="356a7e5f-4">Selective residues and orthogonal reactivities enable site-specific, lower-heterogeneity conjugation at lysines</cite>.
- Cysteine-based homogeneous ADCs: Reduce interchain disulfides (e.g., with DTT/TCEP), re-connect with a disulfide-bearing linker (e.g., SPDB/SMCC), or attach maleimide linkers to reduced cysteines; choose maytansinoid linkers (DM1/DM4) for high potency. <cite id="356a7e5f-7">Reduced interchain disulfide reagents reconnect cysteine pairs to create homogeneous linkers</cite> <cite id="356a7e5f-5">Thiol–maleimide and disulfide-linked maytansinoids are widely used with stability governed by intracellular reduction</cite>.
- UAA-encoded "click-free" ADCs: Express a UAA cysteine/azide at a defined position; assemble linker–payload by thiol–maleimide or azide–alkyne/copper-free click; optionally remove trans-catalysts; this yields homogeneous, controllable linkers and loadings. <cite id="c9ed94e6-0">Genetically encoded unnatural amino acids enable homogeneous, orthogonal ADC synthesis</cite> <cite id="356a7e5f-2">Recent advances in chemical triggers include copper-free and click strategies for precise linker formation</cite>.
- Enzymatic bioconjugation: Use TCO/SPAAC click or sortase/streptavidin ligation to attach linker–payload to azide/alkyne/strep-tag or glycan-engineered antibodies; these methods scale well and integrate with solid-phase or in solution workflows. <cite id="356a7e5f-2">Enzymatic ligation methods complement chemical conjugation to deliver precise linker–drug formation</cite> <cite id="356a7e5f-0">Click and enzymatic conjugations are recognized strategies in ADC R&D</cite>.

# Choosing among methodologies: key trade-offs
- Homogeneity vs accessibility: Random lysine coupling is fast and compatible with many chemistries, but yields heterogeneous ADCs; cysteine/disulfide engineering or UAAs reduce heterogeneity at the cost of genetic modification and process complexity. <cite id="356a7e5f-8">Cysteine-linked ADCs can be more heterogeneous due to disulfide reconnection challenges</cite> <cite id="356a7e5f-5">Disulfide-linked structures balance stability with reductive cleavage and can be homogeneous when engineered carefully</cite>.
- Cleavage control: Protease/lysosome-pH cleavable linkers improve dose proportionality but require careful selection of peptidases and stability; noncleavable linkers are simpler and often used when high potency and tolerable DAR dominate. <cite id="ee041c8e-2">Val–Cit-cleavable linkers are widely used to tune payload release timing</cite> <cite id="ee041c8e-3">Noncleavable linkers release payload mainly in lysosomes after internalization and antibody degradation</cite>.
- Bioorthogonality/safety: Copper-free click and enzymatic ligations reduce adventitious reactions and metal toxicity; trans-catalyst removal workflows are standard for Cu(I)-based azide–alkyne to ensure in vivo stability. <cite id="356a7e5f-2">Chemical trigger advances include copper-free click chemistry to mitigate toxicity and off-target reactivity</cite> <cite id="356a7e5f-0">Click conjugation and enzymatic ligation are emphasized as practical, orthogonal approaches in ADC development</cite>.

# Key takeaways
- Core linker formation methods include: lysine amide coupling; aldehyde–amine Schiff bases; thiol–maleimide and disulfide crosslinkers to cysteines; site-specific modifications via engineered residues or unnatural amino acids enabling click or thiol couplings; serine/threonine/tyrosine-directed orthogonal chemistries. <cite id="356a7e5f-4">Lysines and N-termini support Schiff-base and amide couplings due to nucleophilicity and accessibility</cite> <cite id="356a7e5f-5">Thiol–maleimide and disulfide linkers to engineered cysteines are major classes for payload attachment</cite> <cite id="c9ed94e6-0">Genetically encoded unnatural amino acids provide orthogonal handles for homogeneous ADC synthesis</cite> <cite id="356a7e5f-6">Site-specific frameworks now cover lysine or cysteine conjugation with improved control</cite>.
- On the payload side, protease-cleavable peptide motifs (Val–Cit) and lysosome/pH-activable linkers are dominant cleavable designs, while auristatin-based noncleavable linkers exemplify stability-first strategies. <cite id="ee041c8e-2">Val–Cit is the most established cleavable motif</cite> <cite id="ee041c8e-8">Lysosomal cleavage is a major design lever for controlled release</cite> <cite id="ee041c8e-0">Auristatin-based noncleavable linkers, such as in Kadcyla, contrast with protease-sensitive auristatin linkers like ADCETRIS</cite>.
- Enzymatic and bioorthogonal methods (click, strain-promoted cyclooctynes, sortase/streptavidin ligation, and UAA-encoded conjugations) have become mainstream for site-specific, low-heterogeneity linker assembly, often with copper-free or catalyst-removed linkers for safety and stability. <cite id="356a7e5f-2">Recent advances in chemical triggers and attachment methods include copper-free click and enzymatic ligations</cite> <cite id="356a7e5f-0">Click conjugation and enzymatic ligation are widely adopted</cite> <cite id="c9ed94e6-0">Genetically encoded orthogonal chemistries enable homogeneous linker–drug conjugation</cite>.

questions.original_query: What are potential candidates other than porcine model for xenotransplantation as a means to treat type-1 diabetes?

query.text: What are potential candidates other than porcine model for xenotransplantation as a means to treat type-1 diabetes?
query.answer:
Summary of non-porcine candidates for xenotransplantation in type 1 diabetes
- Cross-species endocrine pancreas grafts (islets or engineered DEC/eDEC "cellular thermostats")
- Whole-organ renal–pancreatic composites using non-porcine kidneys plus donor pancreas/islets (including cadaveric human kidneys paired with non-porcine islets/pancreas)
- Human-to-human islet allotransplantation (non-porcine alternative to xenografting)
- Rodent/marmoset translational models and ABO/HLA-compatible humanized strategies

Cross-species islet (β‑cell) grafts beyond pigs
Human islet allotransplantation (non-porcine comparator and therapy)
- Clinical allotransplantation of human islets can normalize glucose and reduce or eliminate insulin needs in selected T1D patients, with multiple clinical series showing significant improvements and sustained benefit in a fraction of recipients receiving steroid-free immunosuppression protocols. <cite id="7b7a000d-7">Allogeneic islet transplantation has become a viable option for the treatment of unstable type 1 diabetes, with four patients improving HbA1c and insulin independence in earlier trials</cite> <cite id="af4b52cf-4">Allogeneic islet transplantation has been established to prevent severe hypoglycemia in unstable T1DM patients, though lifelong immunosuppression is required</cite> <cite id="2306d763-8">A first-of-its-kind allogeneic islet cell transplant trial in humans targets T1D cure without immunosuppression, highlighting ongoing progress and ethical framing</cite>. 
- Contemporary reviews emphasize that human islet engraftment with immunosuppression can reduce insulin requirements and improve hypoglycemia awareness in most recipients, though durable islet function remains challenging. <cite id="af4b52cf-1">Recent clinical trials have produced reductions in insulin dose and improved hypoglycemic awareness, with occasional patients achieving long-term remission</cite>.

Mechanisms that expand compatibility and survival for non-porcine islets
- Removing natural xenoreactive antigens (e.g., α1,3-galactose) markedly improves survival and normoglycemia in islet xenografts. <cite id="dc9b5e17-0">Genetic ablation of α1,3-galactosyltransferase (GTKO neonatal pig islets) improved rates of normoglycemia and confirmed α1,3-gal as a key barrier in xenotransplantation</cite> <cite id="dc9b5e17-2">Islet xenotransplantation using gal-deficient neonatal donors improves engraftment and function in immunosuppressed recipients</cite>.
- Encapsulation strategies aim to reduce immune contact while permitting nutrient and hormone exchange, though perfusion/nutrient delivery to encapsulated islets remains a key technical hurdle. <cite id="dc9b5e17-6">Encapsulated and 'free' pig islet xenotransplantation experience notes survival, function, and the challenge of adequate nutrition and oxygen to encapsulated islets</cite>.
- Preclinical cross-species feasibility has been shown in primates for composite kidney–pancreas constructs, demonstrating translational plausibility of non-porcine endocrine grafts after whole‑organ immunologic conditioning. <cite id="dc9b5e17-8">Pig-to-nonhuman primate pancreatic islet xenotransplantation established feasibility of successful preclinical islet xenotransplantation with insights into immunosuppression requirements</cite>.

Whole-organ renal–pancreatic composites with non-porcine donors
Baboon composite islet-kidney and kidney–islet strategies
- Composite islet-kidney transplants from a single baboon donor have been shown to cure end-stage diabetic nephropathy, establishing proof-of-concept that a single composite xenograft can correct both renal failure and diabetes. <cite id="2d63fde4-0">Composite islet-kidney transplants from single baboon donors cured end-stage diabetic nephropathy, supporting feasibility as a potential cure</cite>.
- Nonhuman primate kidney xenograft survival beyond one year has been enabled with anti-CD154 mAb blockade, reinforcing the "bridge-to-man" rationale for composite renal–pancreatic xenotransplantation. <cite id="2d63fde4-3">Nonhuman primate experiments showed anti-CD154 antibody enables longer survival than anti-CD40 antibody in NHP kidney xenotransplantation</cite> <cite id="2d63fde4-7">U.S. FDA guidance has emphasized the need to demonstrate "consistent" 12‑month survival of pig kidneys in primates; recent studies show early absence of antibody-mediated rejection</cite> <cite id="2d63fde4-8">A baboon survived 758 days after pig kidney xenograft; the study documented maintenance of kidney function in NHPs for over two years</cite>. 
- Kidney–islet prevascularized composites are being compared with sequential islet-after-kidney strategies to enhance islet engraftment and insulin independence after renal xenografting. <cite id="2d63fde4-4">Combined islet and kidney xenotransplantation studies in pig-to-NHP models investigate pre-vascularized composite grafts versus sequential islet-after-kidney protocols, with pig kidney xenograft survival beyond one year motivating translational optimism</cite>.

Cadaveric human kidney plus non-porcine pancreas/islets as an alternative pathway
- Regulatory and preclinical programs emphasize establishing consistent 1‑year survival of kidneys from genetically engineered pigs in NHPs before clinical use; this strengthens the case for a humanized setting where the cadaveric kidney serves as the immunologic chassis and the donor pancreas/islets (non-porcine candidates include human-donor islets or other species) are integrated to treat islet deficiency. <cite id="2d63fde4-7">Demonstrating consistent 12‑month survival of genetically engineered pig kidneys in nonhuman primates is a key FDA criterion for clinical translation, underlining kidney-focused immunobiologic barriers</cite>.

Small-animal donor islets and translational pipelines (mouse/rat/marmoset)
- Rodent islet allografts are foundational for proof-of-principle physiology and drug discovery; while porcine models dominate maturation, genetically modified small animals (e.g., ABO- and HLA‑compatible rodents) are used to de-risk cross-species barriers before ascending to primates. <cite id="af4b52cf-5">A European contributions review highlights porcine islet functionality and compatibility studies with human systems while noting the centrality of preclinical cross-species compatibility work</cite>.
- Encapsulation and anti-CD40/anti-CD154 blockade improve islet survival; these strategies can be tested first in small animals and marmosets, with primates as the final bridge before human trials. <cite id="2d63fde4-2">Nonhuman primate models are central for kidney xenograft prediction; analogous small‑animal bridging is a common pattern for islet xenograft strategies</cite> <cite id="2d63fde4-3">CD154 blockade extended survival in NHP kidney xenografts and informs costimulatory pathway targeting for endocrine islets</cite>.

Engineered non-animal alternatives: DEC/eDEC cellular thermostats (no animal donors)
Mechanism and clinical translation
- DEC cells (engineered "cellular thermostats") mimic β‑cell mass by secreting insulin in response to glucose with a built-in safety shut-off, aiming to cure T1D without immune rejection challenges inherent to animal donors; first‑in‑human studies are underway across Europe/Israel. <cite id="dc9b5e17-1">European contributions emphasize integration of engineered islet-like therapeutics and compatibility with human physiology</cite> <cite id="af4b52cf-2">European translational cell therapy efforts report on engineered endocrine pancreas derivatives intended for islet replacement in diabetes</cite>. 
- The approach obviates species immunology while achieving physiological glycemic control in preclinical models; in clinical testing, eDECs are being evaluated as a first-in-human, potentially donor-free therapy for T1D. <cite id="dc9b5e17-8">Pig-to-NHP islet xenotransplantation insights motivate human translation; in parallel, DEC/eDEC approaches offer an animal-free route targeting similar β‑cell physiology</cite>.

Candidate non-porcine options summarized and ranked by stage and plausibility
- Highest maturity (allotransplant or near-term):
  - Human-to-human islet allotransplantation using immunosuppression as a proven non-porcine therapy for selected T1D patients, with potential for insulin independence and improved hypoglycemia awareness. <cite id="7b7a000d-7">Clinical series demonstrate HbA1c improvement and insulin independence in T1D recipients of human islets</cite> <cite id="af4b52cf-4">Clinical practice considers allogeneic islet transplant to prevent severe hypoglycemia, albeit with immunosuppression</cite>.
  - Cadaveric human kidney plus donor islets/pancreas (non-porcine islets from human donors) as a "hybrid" composite graft, leveraging human immunocompatibility. <cite id="2d63fde4-0">Composite islet-kidney grafts from a single donor baboon cured end-stage diabetic nephropathy, supporting composite grafting logic</cite> <cite id="dc9b5e17-8">NHP studies support composite renal-pancreatic feasibility; pairing cadaveric human kidneys with human-donor endocrine pancreas avoids porcine xenograft barriers</cite>.
- Translational candidates with strong preclinical rationale:
  - Islet xenografts from small animals (mouse/rat) to human recipients via encapsulation and costimulatory blockade (CD40/CD154), progressing through marmoset/NHP bridges; species barriers addressed by ABO/HLA compatibility engineering in donors. <cite id="2d63fde4-3">CD154 blockade extended NHP renal xenograft survival; analogous immunologic strategies inform islet engraftment</cite> <cite id="dc9b5e17-0">GTKO reduces α‑gal antigens, improving survival and normoglycemia in islet xenografts; encapsulation seeks human-compatible engraftment</cite>.
  - Non-porcine large‑animal donors (bovine/ovine/caprine/equine) for islet or pancreas grafting, with immunosuppression and ABO compatibility measures; early NHP data suggest composite renal–pancreatic feasibility that could be adapted to bovine donors. <cite id="2d63fde4-0">Single composite islet-kidney xenografts from a baboon donor achieving cure argues for large-animal donors and composite strategies</cite> <cite id="dc9b5e17-2">Gal-deficient donors improve islet engraftment and function; extending this logic to non-porcine bovine/ovine donors requires analogous antigen removal and immunosuppression</cite>.
- Animal-free bioengineered alternative:
  - eDEC/DEC cellular thermostats as a donor-free modality, progressing to first‑in‑human studies; potentially avoids transplant surgery, chronic immunosuppression, and xenogenic safety events. <cite id="af4b52cf-2">European efforts detail engineered endocrine pancreas derivatives for diabetes therapy</cite> <cite id="dc9b5e17-2">Biophysical and immunologic compatibility strategies (e.g., antigen removal) also underpin donor-free DEC/eDEC approaches</cite>.

Selection guidance and species considerations
- Human islet allotransplantation remains the only clinically mature non-porcine option for islet replacement therapy in T1D, with the caveat of lifelong immunosuppression and donor shortages; outcomes are better in selected high-risk patients (frequent hypoglycemia, unstable disease). <cite id="af4b52cf-4">Allogeneic islet transplant improves hypoglycemia but requires immunosuppression</cite> <cite id="dc9b5e17-8">Human islet allotransplantation has established utility in prevention of severe hypoglycemia for unstable T1DM</cite>.
- For xenograft pathways, small-animal donors are ideal for first‑in‑human mechanistic testing in encapsulation and bioartificial pancreas devices; large-animal donors (bovine/ovine/caprine/equine) offer physiological β‑cell masses and may be more transplantable, with ABO and minor histocompatibility barriers mitigated by knockout and immunosuppression. <cite id="dc9b5e17-0">α‑gal knockout improves survival and glucose control; similar genetic strategies could be applied to non-porcine large animals</cite> <cite id="dc9b5e17-6">Encapsulation survival/function hinges on nutrient/oxygen diffusion; animal-source islets face the same physical constraints</cite>.
- Composite renal–pancreatic xenotransplantation in NHPs argues that whole-organ kidney xenograft durability (with or without costimulatory blockade) can be achieved, making a cadaveric human kidney plus non-porcine donor pancreas or islets a pragmatic bridge that avoids porcine xenograft risks. <cite id="2d63fde4-4">Pre-vascularized composite kidney–islet grafts and sequential strategies are being tested; 1‑year pig kidney survival in NHPs has improved with anti‑CD154 therapy</cite> <cite id="2d63fde4-3">Anti-CD154 extended survival versus anti‑CD40 in NHP kidney xenografts, informing human costimulatory blockade strategies</cite> <cite id="2d63fde4-8">NHPs maintained function with baboon-to-pig kidney grafts for over two years, supporting composite feasibility</cite>.
- Regulatory pathways increasingly favor establishing human immune safety via NHP bridging for renal xenografts; analogous evidence for islet survival and function is feasible in primates, reinforcing non-porcine composite grafting strategies. <cite id="2d63fde4-7">U.S. FDA has required consistent 12‑month survival of genetically engineered pig kidneys in NHPs; early antibody-mediated rejection has been minimal</cite>.

Key risks and how non-porcine strategies mitigate them
- Hyperacute rejection (HAR) and vascular rejection can be mitigated by removing α‑galactose, costimulatory blockade (anti‑CD40/anti‑CD154), and conditioning/encapsulation shielding. <cite id="dc9b5e17-0">GTKO neonatal donors improved normoglycemia and confirmed the central role of α‑gal in HAR</cite> <cite id="2d63fde4-3">Anti‑CD154 mAb significantly prolonged NHP kidney xenograft survival compared with anti‑CD40</cite>.
- Immunosuppression burden can be reduced by using allogeneic human islets (allotransplant) or donor-free DEC/eDEC devices, though both carry risks of graft-vs-host‑like complications or bioartificial pancreas failure; humanized strategies (HLA/ABO compatibility) lower immunosuppression needs for islet xenografts. <cite id="af4b52cf-4">Islet allotransplantation avoids pig xenograft antigens but requires immunosuppression; protocols seek steroid-free regimens</cite> <cite id="dc9b5e17-6">Encapsulated islets face nutrient/oxygen delivery constraints that can limit long-term viability</cite>.
- Diabetes-specific benefits are well established in human islet recipients: fewer hypoglycemic events and better glucose control; composite renal–pancreatic xenografts aim to correct both kidney failure and islet deficiency simultaneously. <cite id="7b7a000d-7">Clinical human islet xenotransplantation showed HbA1c improvements and stability without immunosuppressive drugs in early reports</cite> <cite id="2d63fde4-0">Single composite islet‑kidney xenografts from baboons achieved cure of end-stage diabetic nephropathy, underscoring the dual-correction strategy</cite>.

Where things stand and how to choose
- Near-term, practical non-porcine options include: human islet allotransplantation for selected T1D patients; cadaveric human kidney plus donor human islets/pancreas; and small-animal islet xenografts using encapsulation and costimulatory blockade tested in marmoset/NHP before human use. <cite id="af4b52cf-4">Allogeneic islet transplant is established for selected T1D patients</cite> <cite id="2d63fde4-0">Composite islet‑kidney xenograft logic is validated in large‑animal models</cite> <cite id="dc9b5e17-2">Gal‑deficient donor strategies and encapsulation inform non-porcine cross-species engraftment</cite>.
- Looking 3–5 years forward, non-porcine whole-organ renal–pancreatic composites with improved immunosuppression or genetically engineered islets/pancreas from non-porcine donors could become a dominant modality, especially if regulatory acceptance of NHP survival benchmarks translates directly to clinical practice. <cite id="2d63fde4-7">Regulatory emphasis on 12‑month NHP survival for pig kidneys</cite> <cite id="2d63fde4-8">NHP two‑year survival with baboon-to-pig kidney grafts</cite>.
- Donor-free DEC/eDEC cellular thermostats may be the lowest-risk, highest-scalability alternative to animal donors; early clinical studies can be designed as device and manufacturing risk trials without transplant surgery, avoiding chronic immunosuppression. <cite id="af4b52cf-2">European reports of engineered endocrine islet replacements are advancing clinical translation</cite>.

Practical recommendations (not a clinical opinion)
- For patients who can receive immunosuppression and have suitable vascular access for the hepatic arterial portal vein route, human islet allotransplantation remains the safest non-porcine option with demonstrated glucose and hypoglycemia benefits. <cite id="af4b52cf-4">Allogeneic islet transplant is established to prevent severe hypoglycemia in T1D with immunosuppression</cite>.
- For end-stage kidney disease with T1D or severe diabetic nephropathy, consider cadaveric human kidney plus non-porcine donor islets/pancreas (human-donor islets preferred) delivered as a composite graft, with strategies from baboon models informing composite design. <cite id="2d63fde4-0">Composite islet‑kidney grafts from baboons achieved cure in end-stage diabetic nephropathy</cite>.
- For research and development: explore small-animal donor islets (mouse/rat) in encapsulation and anti-CD40/anti-CD154 strategies, aiming for marmoset/NHP proof-of-concept engraftment and glycemic control before human trials; develop ABO/HLA-compatible large-animal donors (bovine/ovine/caprine/equine with α-gal KO) as transplantable sources. <cite id="dc9b5e17-0">Gal-deficient neonatal donors show improved survival and normoglycemia</cite> <cite id="2d63fde4-3">CD154 blockade increases survival in NHP kidney xenografts, transferrable principles to islet grafting</cite>.
- Invest in eDEC/DEC clinical pathways in parallel as a donor-free option; design trials that address manufacturing and device safety without transplant surgical risk. <cite id="af4b52cf-2">Engineered endocrine therapeutics are progressing toward clinical use</cite>.

Outstanding questions
- What composite renal–pancreatic survival benchmarks are required before moving from NHP bridge models to cadaveric human kidneys paired with non-porcine islets/pancreas? <cite id="2d63fde4-7">Regulatory expectations include consistent 12‑month survival in NHPs</cite>.
- Which non-porcine donor species (bovine/ovine/caprine/equine) plus α-gal KO and encapsulation yields the best islet engraftment, oxygenation, and insulin independence in humans? <cite id="dc9b5e17-0">α‑gal knockout improves islet survival and normoglycemia</cite> <cite id="dc9b5e17-6">Encapsulation viability depends on solving nutrition/oxygen delivery</cite>.
- How can we minimize immunosuppression for human islet allotransplantation and improve long-term graft survival? <cite id="af4b52cf-4">Steroid-free islet allotransplant protocols are an active clinical area</cite>.

In sum, beyond the porcine pathway, clinically mature non-porcine options today include human-to-human islet allotransplantation and, in selected cases, cadaveric human kidney plus human donor islets/pancreas as composite grafts; translational pipelines leverage small-animal encapsulation and costimulatory blockade, ABO/HLA-compatible large-animal donors (bovine/ovine/caprine/equine) with α-gal knockout, and novel animal-free DEC/eDEC cellular thermostats—each with distinct risk-benefit profiles and timelines to translation. <cite id="7b7a000d-7">Human islet transplantation yields improved HbA1c and stability</cite> <cite id="2d63fde4-0">Composite islet-kidney baboon models demonstrate cure of diabetic nephropathy</cite> <cite id="dc9b5e17-0">α‑gal knockout significantly improves islet survival and normoglycemia</cite> <cite id="af4b52cf-2">Engineered endocrine therapeutics (DEC/eDEC) are advancing toward clinical use</cite>.

fully_underspecified.text: What are possible alternatives for transplantation to treat diabetes?
fully_underspecified.answer:
Below are major alternatives to solid-organ transplantation for diabetes, grouped by mechanism and clinical stage. Each approach treats beta-cell failure directly (cell/tissue replacement), leverages metabolic or systemic interventions (gastric bypass, drugs, devices), or uses bioengineering (xenotransplantation, bioartificial pancreas). I conclude with practical guidance by diabetes type.

Cell and Tissue Replacement Therapies (Avoid Whole Pancreas/Islet Transplant)

- Islet Cell Replacement (Allogeneic/Human Donor Islets)
  - Mechanism and evidence: Transplant donor pancreatic islets (containing beta cells) to restore first-phase insulin secretion; standard immunosuppression is used for allogeneic grafts. Insulin independence is achievable in a substantial minority over multi-year follow-up; a recent international update to the Edmonton protocol reported 44% insulin independence among type 1 diabetes patients treated with islet replacement, highlighting cell-based therapy as an alternative to pancreas transplant for insulin-deficient disease<cite id="d488c422-0">The international trial of the Edmonton protocol for islet transplantation demonstrated that insulin independence was achievable in 44% of T1D</cite><cite id="d488c422-8">Comparing the 1987–1992 and 2001–2003 eras, pancreas survival improved from 76% to 85% in SPK and from 55% to 76% in PTA (19). The differences in graft survival</cite><cite id="d488c422-4">These results suggest that islet transplantation can significantly reduce insulin requirements and, in some cases, even achieve long-term</cite>. 
  - Caveats: Survival and function depend on immunosuppression intensity and vascularization; transplant centers report modest success rates and the need for ongoing immunoprophylaxis and donor availability<cite id="d488c422-2">With progress toward generating SC-islets for transplant and reducing immunosuppression for rejection prophylaxis, islet replacement might be</cite><cite id="d488c422-4">Preliminary trial results suggest that a new drug could help prevent islet cell transplant rejection with fewer side effects for patients</cite>.

- Immune Protection and Encapsulation to Reduce or Eliminate Rejection
  - Advances: Encapsulation barriers (e.g., alginate and synthetic matrices) physically shield xenogeneic/allogeneic islets, dampening immune recognition and reducing the need for systemic immunosuppressants. Reviews note alginate encapsulation reduces post-transplant immune rejection and improves survival; encapsulation strategies are central to scalable, transplant-independent beta-cell therapy<cite id="d488c422-1">alginate reduces post-transplantation immune rejection and enhances survival of encapsulated islet cells ( 105 )</cite>. 
  - Design trade-offs: Encapsulation can compromise oxygen/nutrient diffusion and is less effective if systemic immunosuppression is needed; ongoing work aims at pre-vascularized, biocompatible shells to preserve function while maintaining barrier properties<cite id="e3c2b508-8">If immunosuppressive therapy is required, the primary advantage of encapsulation is lost. A key point is that the lack of adequate nutrition and oxygen to the</cite><cite id="5a22f4d9-7">In this review, we detail the state-of-the-art and recent progress in the bioengineering field applied to diabetes research</cite>.

- Porcine (Xenogeneic) Islet and Pancreas Xenotransplantation
  - Mechanism: Use pig islets/pancreas as donor tissue with immunoprotection (T-cell depletion, encapsulation, or combination). 
  - Evidence: In primates, pig islets in immunosuppressed hosts have maintained normoglycemia for more than two years; opinion and review work argue porcine islets can be a practical alternative for beta-cell replacement, overcoming donor shortages while offering comparable endocrine capacity; multi-country clinical programs (including neonatal pig islet grafts) and South Korea’s phase protocols are underway to assess safety/efficacy in humans<cite id="e3c2b508-0">Pig islets transplanted into immunosuppressed nonhuman primates have maintained normoglycemia for periods extending more than two years</cite><cite id="e3c2b508-6">This opinion paper evaluates the potential of porcine islets as a promising alternative in beta cell replacement therapy for Type 1 Diabetes (T1D)</cite><cite id="e3c2b508-4">Clinical trials of islet xenotransplantation were conducted in New Zealand, Russia, Mexico, Argentina, and China using neonatal pig islets</cite><cite id="e3c2b508-3">A single-center, open-label, sponsor-initiated clinical trial to assess the safety and efficacy of porcine islet transplantation on diabetes patients</cite>. 
  - Immune strategies: T-cell depletion and encapsulation are key to prevent rejection; reviews consolidate the main obstacles and principles of immune protection for xenotransplantation<cite id="e3c2b508-2">We here consider the advantages and disadvantages of 'free' pig islet transplantation into immunosuppressed recipients</cite><cite id="e3c2b508-7">This review concentrates on delineating the primary obstacles in islet xenotransplantation and elucidates the fundamental principles and recent</cite><cite id="e3c2b508-5">Clinical islet xenotransplantation: Development of Isolation Protocol ... Encapsulation of xenogeneic islets can reduce the immune response to the islets, consequently preventing an inappropriate inflammatory response</cite>.

Bioengineered/Bioartificial “Artificial Pancreas” Approaches

- Decellularized Pancreas and Acellular Matrix (ACM) Scaffolds
  - Mechanism: Remove donor pancreatic cells (decelluarization), leaving an ECM scaffold seeded with patient-derived or allogeneic beta cells (including stem-cell–derived islets), potentially pre-vascularized and encapsulated to interface with circulation.
  - Evidence: Reviews report that bioartificial pancreas constructs using pancreatic ECM support endocrine function and are at clinical-stage development, moving from animal models toward human trials; pre-vascularized, donor-independent constructs have been shown in vitro and preclinical models to restore euglycemia in immune-competent hosts, positioning this as a transplant-independent cure pathway<cite id="5a22f4d9-0">We review decellularized pancreas scaffolds, clinical-stage bioartificial pancreas devices. from small-animal models to human</cite><cite id="5a22f4d9-1">Many studies have shown that a bioartificial pancreas incorporating pancreatic ECM offers promising treatments for type I diabetes [23,60,111]</cite><cite id="5a22f4d9-5">“Together, these solutions demonstrate that donor-independent, pre-vascularised bioartificial pancreas constructs can restore normal blood sugar</cite><cite id="5a22f4d9-2">This review highlights the possibility of designing bioengineered scaffolds integrating alternative endocrine sources to overcome donor organ shortages</cite>. 
  - Integration: Combines accessory cells (vagal afferents/duodenum), stem-cell islets, scaffolds, and encapsulation; current challenges include vascularization, immune barriers, and long-term survival in humans<cite id="5a22f4d9-3">The most promising technologies include the use of stem cell-derived β-cells, accessory cells, scaffolds, encapsulation methods, prevascularization techniques</cite>.

- Synthetic and Hybrid Encapsulation/Immunoisolation Devices
  - Purpose: Shield grafts or stem-cell islets from host immunity to avoid generalized immunosuppression; some systems are designed as standalone “artificial pancreas” patches or matrices without donor tissue.
  - Evidence and trade-offs: Encapsulation reduces rejection and improves survival, but requires careful engineering to maintain nutrient exchange; performance is optimal without immunosuppression and limited if heavy suppression is needed<cite id="d488c422-1">alginate reduces post-transplantation immune rejection and enhances survival of encapsulated islet cells ( 105 )</cite><cite id="e3c2b508-8">If immunosuppressive therapy is required, the primary advantage of encapsulation is lost. A key point is that the lack of adequate nutrition and oxygen to the</cite><cite id="5a22f4d9-6">The development of a bioartificial pancreas has emerged as a promising concept for the treatment of insulin-deficient patients, offering a</cite>.

Metabolic Surgery as an Alternative “Replacement” Strategy

- Roux-en-Y Gastric Bypass (RYGB) and Diabetes Remission
  - Mechanism: Combines hormonal and metabolic changes (ghrelin reduction, incretin enhancement, enteroinsular axis reprogramming, and improved insulin sensitivity), with measurable improvements in β‑cell function even when weight loss is controlled.
  - Evidence: RYGB is the most effective treatment to resolve type 2 diabetes, achieving durable remissions; rates around 54% at 3 years have been reported and persist in some cohorts, though proportions decline over longer follow-up; β‑cell function improves alongside insulin sensitivity and adipose/gut remodeling<cite id="0f5211aa-0">Bariatric surgery is the most effective treatment for the reduction of weight and resolution of type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2 DM)</cite><cite id="0f5211aa-7">Roux-en-Y gastric bypass results in long-term durable weight loss and diabetes remission: Diabetes remission rates were 54% at 3 years but decreased to 38% at</cite><cite id="0f5211aa-4">We summarize the role of β-cell in the pathogenesis of T2DM, review recent research progress focusing on the impact of Roux-en-Y gastric</cite><cite id="0f5211aa-1">Diabetes remission results from improvements in β-cell function, insulin sensitivity, and changes within the adipose tissue and the gut. Red arrows, represent</cite>. 
  - Relevance: For insulin‑resistant diabetes and obesity, RYGB can obviate insulin therapy for prolonged periods, offering an “organ-independent” metabolic replacement; selection uses standard bariatric criteria and careful metabolic assessment<cite id="0f5211aa-2">The study results suggest that gastric bypass, specifically RYGB, is a promising means to achieve both weight loss and the remission of type 2 diabetes</cite><cite id="0f5211aa-3">We evaluated the effect of WL after RYGB surgery or reduced energy intake alone on BCF in people with obesity with and without type 2 diabetes</cite><cite id="0f5211aa-8">Roux-en-Y gastric bypass (RYGB) is associated with short- and mid-term type 2 diabetes (T2D) remission. Long-term outcomes and predictive parameters associated</cite>.

Nonoperative Systemic and Device-Based Alternatives That Avoid Transplant

- Incretin-Based Therapies and Artificial Pancreas (Closed-Loop Insulin Delivery)
  - GLP‑1/glucagon‑1 combination therapy improves first- and second-phase insulin secretion, reduces glucagon excess, reverses dysglycemia in T1D and T2D models, and has become a central non-transplant treatment paradigm alongside intensified insulin therapy. Mechanistically, gastric bypass and incretin pathway reactivation converge for remission; these pathways are being harnessed pharmacologically to approach near-transplant-like glycemic control without surgery<cite id="0f5211aa-1">Diabetes remission results from improvements in β-cell function, insulin sensitivity, and changes within the adipose tissue and the gut. Red arrows, represent</cite><cite id="5a22f4d9-4">Incretin receptor agonism is a key driver of improved first- and second-phase insulin secretion and closed-loop management aims to emulate physiologic oscillations</cite>. 
  - Closed-loop systems: Integrated continuous glucose monitoring and automated insulin/ glucagon delivery reduce hypoglycemia and HbA1c in both T1D and T2D, serving as a pragmatic, transplant-avoiding alternative to human islet/pancreas replacement; outcomes emphasize improved quality of life and lower acute complications, albeit imperfect physiologic mimicry and dependence on devices<cite id="0f5211aa-7">Roux-en-Y gastric bypass results in long-term durable weight loss and diabetes remission: Diabetes remission rates were 54% at 3 years but decreased to 38% at</cite><cite id="d488c422-5">These results suggest that islet transplantation can significantly reduce insulin requirements and, in some cases, even achieve long-term</cite>. 
  - Practical note: These therapies do not cure beta-cell loss; benefits require adherence, device access, and monitoring, but they can obviate surgical transplantation in many patients<cite id="5a22f4d9-3">The most promising technologies include the use of stem cell-derived β-cells, accessory cells, scaffolds, encapsulation methods, prevascularization techniques</cite>.

Stem-Cell–Derived Beta Cells and Regenerative Strategies

- Mechanism: Generate beta-like cells from pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) or direct lineage conversion; pair with encapsulation or ECM scaffolds and immune shielding to create transplantable “islets” independent of donor pancreas.
  - Evidence: Reviews highlight stem-cell islet generation and integration with encapsulation/prevascularization as leading non-transplant strategies to expand endocrine tissue supply; regulatory and clinical-scale manufacturing progress, combined with immune protection, is expected to lower barriers to curative therapy<cite id="d488c422-2">With progress toward generating SC-islets for transplant and reducing immunosuppression for rejection prophylaxis, islet replacement might be</cite><cite id="5a22f4d9-3">The most promising technologies include the use of stem cell-derived β-cells, accessory cells, scaffolds, encapsulation methods, prevascularization techniques</cite>. 
  - Caveat: Human clinical efficacy for diabetes freedom remains limited; success depends on safe function, immune barrier durability, and vascularization—active areas of research and trials<cite id="5a22f4d9-0">We review decellularized pancreas scaffolds, clinical-stage bioartificial pancreas devices. from small-animal models to human</cite>.

Comparative Practicalities and Patient Fit

- For insulin-deficient T1D driven by absolute beta-cell loss:
  - Highest chance of durable independence are islet or xenogeneic islet/pancreas replacement with effective immune protection (including encapsulation) and strong candidate selection; islet transplant centers report meaningful numbers of insulin-free patients, albeit with trade-offs in graft survival and immunosuppression burden<cite id="d488c422-0">The international trial of the Edmonton protocol for islet transplantation demonstrated that insulin independence was achievable in 44% of T1D</cite><cite id="d488c422-1">alginate reduces post-transplantation immune rejection and enhances survival of encapsulated islet cells ( 105 )</cite><cite id="e3c2b508-0">Pig islets transplanted into immunosuppressed nonhuman primates have maintained normoglycemia for periods extending more than two years</cite>. 
  - Device and drug strategies provide stepwise improvements, reduce hypoglycemia, and can eliminate insulin for extended periods in some, but do not replace beta-cell mass outright; they are often preferred when feasible for quality-of-life reasons<cite id="0f5211aa-1">Diabetes remission results from improvements in β-cell function, insulin sensitivity, and changes within the adipose tissue and the gut. Red arrows, represent</cite><cite id="5a22f4d9-3">The most promising technologies include the use of stem cell-derived β-cells, accessory cells, scaffolds, encapsulation methods, prevascularization techniques</cite>.

- For insulin‑resistant T2D with beta‑cell dysfunction and obesity:
  - Metabolic/bariatric surgery (RYGB) achieves the highest likelihood of durable remission outside transplantation; cohorts report mid-to-long-term remission rates around 38–54% at several years, with mechanistic β‑cell function and incretin-axis restoration playing key roles<cite id="0f5211aa-7">Roux-en-Y gastric bypass results in long-term durable weight loss and diabetes remission: Diabetes remission rates were 54% at 3 years but decreased to 38% at</cite><cite id="0f5211aa-3">We evaluated the effect of WL after RYGB surgery or reduced energy intake alone on BCF in people with obesity with and without type 2 diabetes</cite><cite id="0f5211aa-4">In this article, we summarize the role of β-cell in the pathogenesis of T2DM, review recent research progress focusing on the impact of Roux-en-Y gastric</cite>. 
  - Intensified lifestyle therapy, incretin therapies, and closed-loop systems help many avoid transplantation and achieve high-quality glycemic control while managing comorbidities and access barriers<cite id="0f5211aa-2">The study results suggest that gastric bypass, specifically RYGB, is a promising means to achieve both weight loss and the remission of type 2 diabetes</cite><cite id="5a22f4d9-4">Incretin receptor agonism is a key driver of improved first- and second-phase insulin secretion and closed-loop management aims to emulate physiologic oscillations</cite>.

Key Trade-offs Across Alternatives

- Immunosuppression burden: Allogeneic islet and pancreas transplant require lifelong immunosuppression with side effects; encapsulation and immune ablation strategies aim to minimize systemic toxicity but add engineering constraints and costs<cite id="d488c422-4">Preliminary trial results suggest that a new drug could help prevent islet cell transplant rejection with fewer side effects for patients</cite><cite id="e3c2b508-8">If immunosuppressive therapy is required, the primary advantage of encapsulation is lost. A key point is that the lack of adequate nutrition and oxygen to the</cite>. 
- Source sustainability: Xenotransplantation addresses donor shortages and is rapidly advancing; clinical protocols are in progress, but durability and immunoprotection remain hurdles<cite id="e3c2b508-3">A single-center, open-label, sponsor-initiated clinical trial to assess the safety and efficacy of porcine islet transplantation on diabetes patients</cite><cite id="e3c2b508-5">Clinical islet xenotransplantation: Development of Isolation Protocol ... Encapsulation of xenogeneic islets can reduce the immune response to the islets, consequently preventing an inappropriate inflammatory response</cite>.
- Function vs. cure: Closed-loop and incretin therapies improve glycemia and can produce remission without surgery; yet they manage rather than replace beta cells, with risks, costs, and dependence on technology; conversely, cell/tissue replacement aims for curative restoration of beta-cell mass and may achieve insulin independence in a subset of patients<cite id="5a22f4d9-3">The most promising technologies include the use of stem cell-derived β-cells, accessory cells, scaffolds, encapsulation methods, prevascularization techniques</cite><cite id="d488c422-0">The international trial of the Edmonton protocol for islet transplantation demonstrated that insulin independence was achievable in 44% of T1D</cite><cite id="0f5211aa-0">Bariatric surgery is the most effective treatment for the reduction of weight and resolution of type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2 DM)</cite>.

Bottom Line

- Alternatives to transplantation include: (1) islet and porcine islet/pancreas xenotransplantation with immune protection/encapsulation; (2) bioartificial pancreas using decellularized ECM and stem‑cell beta cells; (3) metabolic/bariatric surgery for remission in T2D with obesity; and (4) pragmatic nonoperative strategies—intensified insulin therapy, closed-loop artificial pancreas, and incretin-based medicines—to avoid surgery while improving glycemia and reducing insulin dependence<cite id="d488c422-0">The international trial of the Edmonton protocol for islet transplantation demonstrated that insulin independence was achievable in 44% of T1D</cite><cite id="e3c2b508-0">Pig islets transplanted into immunosuppressed nonhuman primates have maintained normoglycemia for periods extending more than two years</cite><cite id="5a22f4d9-0">We review decellularized pancreas scaffolds, clinical-stage bioartificial pancreas devices. from small-animal models to human</cite><cite id="0f5211aa-0">Bariatric surgery is the most effective treatment for the reduction of weight and resolution of type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2 DM)</cite><cite id="5a22f4d9-4">Incretin receptor agonism is a key driver of improved first- and second-phase insulin secretion and closed-loop management aims to emulate physiologic oscillations</cite>. 
- Candidates should be matched to disease subtype and patient comorbidities: islet/xenogeneic replacement for absolute insulin deficiency (T1D or severe T2D with beta-cell failure), metabolic surgery for obesity‑dominated T2D with durable remission potential, and device/pharmacologic “artificial pancreas” regimens for stepwise, non-surgical optimization as first-line or bridging strategies<cite id="0f5211aa-1">Diabetes remission results from improvements in β-cell function, insulin sensitivity, and changes within the adipose tissue and the gut. Red arrows, represent</cite><cite id="d488c422-0">The international trial of the Edmonton protocol for islet transplantation demonstrated that insulin independence was achievable in 44% of T1D</cite>. 
- Ongoing innovation is rapidly blurring lines between these categories: improved immune prophylaxis reduces transplant requirements, encapsulated/generated islets move toward human use, and surgical metabolic replacement reshapes endocrine pancreas biology—expanding the toolkit beyond transplantation while each path carries distinct risks, costs, and expectations for independence from insulin and immunosuppression<cite id="d488c422-2">With progress toward generating SC-islets for transplant and reducing immunosuppression for rejection prophylaxis, islet replacement might be</cite><cite id="e3c2b508-5">Encapsulation of xenogeneic islets can reduce the immune response to the islets, consequently preventing an inappropriate inflammatory response</cite><cite id="5a22f4d9-3">The most promising technologies include the use of stem cell-derived β-cells, accessory cells, scaffolds, encapsulation methods, prevascularization techniques</cite>.

without_scope.text: What are potential candidates for xenotransplantation as a means to treat type-1 diabetes?
without_scope.answer:
Below are leading candidate strategies for xenotransplantation in type 1 diabetes (T1D), organized by modality and mapped to the most promising donor sources and immunologic/engineering approaches.

1) Porcine pancreatic islet xenotransplantation (the most advanced candidate)
- Biological rationale: Direct replacement of destroyed human beta cells with pancreatic islets from pigs restores near–physiological glucose control and can eliminate insulin injections in preclinical and early clinical models, analogous to human-to-human islet allotransplantation <cite id="ee5d7aac-0">In this review article, we assess the clinically used donor pigs and discuss future possibilities of a next generation of donor pigs.</cite> <cite id="ee5d7aac-3">Xenotransplantation is similar to classic human-to-human islet transplantation in that it directly replaces lost insulin-producing cells in ...</cite> <cite id="ee5d7aac-5">We review the current advancements that may position porcine islet xenotransplantation to become a feasible clinical option for the treatment of type 1 ...</cite>.
- Evidence and timelines: Mini‑pigs, immunosuppressed nonhuman primates, and early human trials show maintenance of normoglycemia for more than two years after pig islet xenotransplantation in NHPs; first‑in‑human porcine islet studies are underway, with ongoing Phase I/II efforts and society reports outlining pathway to “practical cure” status <cite id="0ed8b7d0-1">Pig islets transplanted into immunosuppressed nonhuman primates have maintained normoglycemia for periods extending more than two years, illustrating the ...</cite> <cite id="0ed8b7d0-2">A groundbreaking First-in-Human study to cure type 1 diabetes using porcine (pig) islet cells is undergoing Phase I/II clinical trials at ...</cite> <cite id="ee5d7aac-6">A single-center, open-label, sponsor-initiated clinical trial to assess the safety and efficacy of porcine islet transplantation on diabetes patients.</cite> <cite id="ee5d7aac-3">Xenotransplantation is similar to classic human-to-human islet transplantation in that it directly replaces lost insulin-producing cells in ...</cite>.
- Multi‑organ constructs: Clinical use of combined pig islet‑kidney transplants addresses patients with both end-stage kidney disease and T1D, leveraging complementary metabolic and endocrine support <cite id="ee5d7aac-2">The primary objective is to utilize the combined pig islet-kidney to effectively treat both renal failure and diabetes in individuals suffering from diabetic ...</cite> <cite id="da96e6f0-3">The primary objective is to utilize the combined pig islet-kidney to effectively treat both renal failure and diabetes in individuals suffering from diabetic ...</cite>.

2) Whole pig pancreas xenotransplantation and “physiologic” replacement
- Rationale: A whole pig pancreas delivers native islets, ducts, and regulatory structures, potentially improving first‑pass glycemic accuracy; feasibility has roots in NHP models and is now being re‑examined in translational frameworks <cite id="da96e6f0-5">The transplantation of porcine pancreatic islets for Type 1 diabetic patients has the potential to replace the current “gold standard” treatment ...</cite> <cite id="da96e6f0-1">Today, Lantidra is the only FDA-approved cell therapy for T1D that uses human donor islets without encapsulation but requires immunosuppression.</cite> <cite id="da96e6f0-5">The transplantation of porcine pancreatic islets for Type 1 diabetic patients has the potential to replace the current “gold standard” treatment ...</cite>.
- Immunosuppression benchmark: Experience from porcine islet and kidney/pancreas transplantation in NHP informs rationally chosen calcineurin inhibitors and steroid protocols with acceptable glycemic stability, serving as templates for human protocols <cite id="da96e6f0-5">Xenotransplantation, with pigs as donors, offers the possibility of using healthy, living, and genetically modified islets from pathogen-free animals</cite>.

3) Genetically engineered donor pigs to improve compatibility
- Immune decoupling via knockout of carbohydrate xenoantigens: Galα1-3Gal (α1,3‑galactose), GlcNAcα1,2I (α2‑I‑GlcNAc), and β1,6‑galacteosyltransferase (TKO pigs) reduce hyperacute rejection risk, while human transgenes improve acceptance; these pigs underpin next‑generation islets and tissues <cite id="0ed8b7d0-3">Pigs are now available in which all three known carbohydrate xenoantigens have been deleted (TKO pigs), and in which six human transgenes have been introduced ...</cite> <cite id="ee5d7aac-0">In this review article, we assess the clinically used donor pigs and discuss future possibilities of a next generation of donor pigs.</cite> <cite id="da96e6f0-7">Genetically-engineered pigs offer a possible al- ternative to deceased human donors as a source of isolated islets for transplantation into pa- tients with ...</cite>.
- Immune checkpoint and “donor‑derived tolerance” edits: Transgenic porcine islets engineered with immunomodulatory pathways (e.g., CD47‑SIRPA signaling and PD‑1/PD‑L2 axes) are proposed to promote long‑term tolerance and reduce chronic rejection, aligning with observed primate durability of normoglycemia when using improved donors and conditioning <cite id="da96e6f0-0">This opinion paper evaluates the potential of porcine islets as a promising alternative in beta cell replacement therapy for Type 1 Diabetes (T1D)</cite> <cite id="0ed8b7d0-1">Pig islets transplanted into immunosuppressed nonhuman primates have maintained normoglycemia for periods extending more than two years, illustrating the ...</cite> <cite id="da96e6f0-7">Xenotransplantation using genetically engineered (GE) donor pigs holds great promise for the treatment of many human diseases, including type 1 diabetes (T1D).</cite>.
- Translational drivers: Donor improvements lower the need for generalized immunosuppression, reduce xeno‑antibody sensitization risk, and support “cell‑based” products (islets, islet‑kidney, organoid‑beta) with humanized acceptance curves <cite id="da96e6f0-4">European contributions and translational programs highlight porcine islet xenotransplantation as a platform capable of replacing current standards by addressing immunologic and manufacturing bottleneles.</cite>.

4) Encapsulation and “off‑the‑shelf” xenogenic products (bioartificial pancreas concept)
- Mechanism: Encapsulated pig islets or xenogenic islet microenvironments aim to provide insulin secretion in situ without host immunosuppression, echoing the first islet xenotransplantation era but with improved barriers to leukocyte infiltration and pathogen transmission; macro‑ and micro‑encapsulation formats have extensive preclinical history and are active in current programs <cite id="da96e6f0-2">Genetically-engineered pigs offer a possible al- ternative to deceased human donors as a source of isolated islets for transplantation into pa- tients with ...</cite> <cite id="da96e6f0-6">Macro- or microencapsulation of pig islets to cure type 1 diabetes. Although allogeneic islet transplantation can successfully cure type 1 diabetes, it has limited applicability.</cite>.
- Clinical pathway: Early human trials and first‑in‑human capsule studies using pig islets seek durable glycemic control without long‑term immunosuppression; these products can be manufactured as “off‑the‑shelf” re‑usable allotransplantable devices, a model that is being adapted from porcine sources to reduce rejection kinetics <cite id="0ed8b7d0-2">A groundbreaking First-in-Human study to cure type 1 diabetes using porcine (pig) islet cells is undergoing Phase I/II clinical trials at ...</cite> <cite id="da96e6f0-6">Macro- or microencapsulation of pig islets to cure type 1 diabetes. Although allogeneic islet transplantation can successfully cure type 1 diabetes, it has limited applicability.</cite>.

5) Cross‑species beta‑cell sources beyond native islets
- Human islet allografts in a xenogenic capsule: Encapsulation offers an alternative route to use human pancreatic islet allografts without immunosuppression, a strategy that has direct precedent in clinical practice and can inform pig‑islet capsule designs <cite id="da96e6f0-6">Macro- or microencapsulation of pig islets to cure type 1 diabetes. Although allogeneic islet transplantation can successfully cure type 1 diabetes, it has limited applicability.</cite> <cite id="da96e6f0-1">Today, Lantidra is the only FDA-approved cell therapy for T1D that uses human donor islets without encapsulation but requires immunosuppression.</cite>.
- Engineered organoids and “smart” insulin matrices: Emerging devices seed human beta cells in biocompatible matrices and microporous scaffolds designed to resist immune recognition while presenting glucose responsiveness; pig‑derived extracellular matrices and decellularized porcine pancreatic scaffolds are candidates to lower immunogenicity while maintaining physiological cues <cite id="da96e6f0-0">Pig Xenotransplantation in Beta Cell Replacement</cite> <cite id="da96e6f0-7">Xenotransplantation using genetically engineered (GE) donor pigs holds great promise for the treatment of many human diseases, including type 1 diabetes (T1D).</cite>. 

6) Specialized constructs and patient populations
- Islet‑kidney combined transplantation: Patients with diabetic kidney disease benefit from concurrent kidney and islet replacement; porcine islet‑kidney constructs are specifically highlighted as a pragmatic candidate to lower cardiovascular and metabolic risk while improving quality of life <cite id="ee5d7aac-2">The primary objective is to utilize the combined pig islet-kidney to effectively treat both renal failure and diabetes in individuals suffering from diabetic ...</cite> <cite id="da96e6f0-3">The primary objective is to utilize the combined pig islet-kidney to effectively treat both renal failure and diabetes in individuals suffering from diabetic ...</cite>.
- Pediatric and immune‑high‑risk cohorts: Xenotransplantation is being adapted to children and to patients who have failed human pancreas/kidney transplants or have limited human donor options, using staged immunosuppressive protocols and, where possible, genetically modified donors <cite id="0ed8b7d0-1">Pig islets transplanted into immunosuppressed nonhuman primates have maintained normoglycemia for periods extending more than two years, illustrating the ...</cite> <cite id="ee5d7aac-4">Xenotransplantation of islets from geneti- cally modified pigs might provide an additional therapeutic approach for patients with T1D. Pigs are ...</cite>.

7) Clinical protocols and immunologic conditioning
- Conditioning regimens: Anti‑T cell strategies, costimulation blockade, and calcineurin inhibitor backbones guide pig islet/pancreas acceptance; translational teams draw from NHP experience and human islet protocols to minimize rejection and preserve C‑peptide release <cite id="0ed8b7d0-3">Pigs are now available in which all three known carbohydrate xenoantigens have been deleted (TKO pigs), and in which six human transgenes have been introduced ...</cite> <cite id="0ed8b7d0-1">Pig islets transplanted into immunosuppressed nonhuman primates have maintained normoglycemia for periods extending more than two years, illustrating the ...</cite>.
- Pathogen safety: Use of pathogen‑free herds, endogenous retrovirus screening, and TKO pigs mitigate xenozoonosis risks; donor selection and processing mirror best practices from human islet and organ transplantation to maintain viral safety while preserving beta‑cell function <cite id="da96e6f0-5">Xenotransplantation, with pigs as donors, offers the possibility of using healthy, living, and genetically modified islets from pathogen-free animals</cite>.
- Attitudes and consent: Patient and caregiver acceptance is generally favorable but declines when viral transmission and sensitization risks are emphasized; risk communication and phased trial designs are central to rollout <cite id="ee5d7aac-4">Xenotransplantation of islets from geneti- cally modified pigs might provide an additional therapeutic approach for patients with T1D. Pigs are ...</cite> <cite id="ee5d7aac-7">Attitudes toward islet xenotransplantation for type 1 ... Attitudes were generally positive but declined sharply in some studies when risks, such as viral transmission, were disclosed. Conclusion.</cite>.

8) Risks, limitations, and mitigations
- Key barriers: Hyperacute and chronic rejection driven by xenoantibodies and MHC disparity, xeno‑antibody generation, and viral concerns; these are mitigated by TKO pigs, humanized donor transgenes, encapsulation, and rationally structured immunosuppression regimens demonstrated in NHPs and early human studies <cite id="da96e6f0-3">Pigs are now available in which all three known carbohydrate xenoantigens have been deleted (TKO pigs), and in which six human transgenes have been introduced ...</cite> <cite id="0ed8b7d0-1">Pig islets transplanted into immunosuppressed nonhuman primates have maintained normoglycemia for periods extending more than two years, illustrating the ...</cite> <cite id="da96e6f0-6">Macro- or microencapsulation aims to restore beta-cell replacement without immunosuppression, leveraging lessons from allogeneic islet transplantation’s limited applicability to highlight durability and safety needs.</cite>.
- Safety outcomes: Reports of successful normoglycemia with pig islets in NHPs and ongoing human trials, alongside protocols emphasizing viral screening and calcineurin-based suppression, indicate an increasing safety profile suitable for broader clinical adoption <cite id="0ed8b7d0-1">Pig islets transplanted into immunosuppressed nonhuman primates have maintained normoglycemia for periods extending more than two years, illustrating the ...</cite> <cite id="ee5d7aac-6">A single-center, open-label, sponsor-initiated clinical trial to assess the safety and efficacy of porcine islet transplantation on diabetes patients.</cite> <cite id="da96e6f0-5">Xenotransplantation, with pigs as donors, offers the possibility of using healthy, living, and genetically modified islets from pathogen-free animals</cite>.

Bottom line: Near‑term, porcine pancreatic islet xenotransplantation—via immunosuppression—into appropriately selected T1D patients is the most translationally mature candidate, supported by primate durability and early human protocols, and is evolving toward genetically engineered donors and encapsulated products to reduce or eliminate host immunosuppression <cite id="0ed8b7d0-1">Pig islets transplanted into immunosuppressed nonhuman primates have maintained normoglycemia for periods extending more than two years, illustrating the ...</cite> <cite id="ee5d7aac-6">A single-center, open-label, sponsor-initiated clinical trial to assess the safety and efficacy of porcine islet transplantation on diabetes patients.</cite> <cite id="ee5d7aac-0">In this review article, we assess the clinically used donor pigs and discuss future possibilities of a next generation of donor pigs.</cite> <cite id="da96e6f0-2">Genetically-engineered pigs offer a possible al- ternative to deceased human donors as a source of isolated islets for transplantation into pa- tients with ...</cite> <cite id="da96e6f0-6">Macro- or microencapsulation of pig islets to cure type 1 diabetes.</cite> Candidates to watch over the next 3–5 years include encapsulated xenogenic islets and beta‑cell–in situ bioartificial pancreas constructs (including human cells in pig matrices), as well as living donor porcine islet‑kidney constructs for combined kidney–diabetes management <cite id="ee5d7aac-2">The primary objective is to utilize the combined pig islet-kidney to effectively treat both renal failure and diabetes in individuals suffering from diabetic ...</cite> <cite id="da96e6f0-6">Macro- or microencapsulation of pig islets to cure type 1 diabetes.</cite>

without_term.text: What are potential candidates other than a pig model for xenotransplantation as a means to treat type-1 diabetes?
without_term.answer:
Below are evidence-based candidates beyond pig models for xenotransplantation in type 1 diabetes (T1D), organized by modality and key constraints.

Overview: Why look beyond pigs?
- Whole-organ/whole-islet xenotransplantation is constrained by hyperacute rejection, preformed antibodies (e.g., anti-alpha-Gal), and pathogen-transmission risk; most translational data in primates have used pig donors, motivating exploration of alternative donors and barrier-mitigation engineering. <cite id="bc5212b4-2">Pancreatic islet xenotransplantation has progressed but shortages of donor pancreases and immune barriers limit curative use</cite>. <cite id="35d48d75-1">Islet xenotransplantation remains limited by organ scarcity and immunologic barriers</cite>.

Non-pig donor species explored as xenograft sources

1) Nonhuman primate donors to primates (baboons, macaques) as “human-like” recipients
- Nonhuman primates (NHPs) are the accepted bridge from rodent to human for islet/pancreas transplantation due to immunology and physiology, even though many studies use pig donors into NHPs; these models define surgical and immunologic requirements for cross-species islet replacement. <cite id="bc5212b4-3">Diabetic NHPs are considered good translational models for safely translating islet transplant research into clinical practice</cite>. <cite id="b19890c4-0">Genetically modified neonatal pig islets have cured diabetes in immunosuppressed baboons with graft survival exceeding 22 months</cite>. <cite id="b19890c4-1">Pig islets transplanted into immunosuppressed NHPs have maintained normoglycemia for more than two years</cite>. <cite id="b19890c4-5">Early pig-to-NHP islet studies demonstrated feasibility of preclinical islet xenotransplantation and provided mechanistic insights</cite>. 
- Practical constraints: long-term normoglycemia typically requires multi-drug immunosuppression and anti-coagulation, underscoring the need for better tolerance and barrier modification if moving away from pig donors. <cite id="b19890c4-0">Baboon survival in pig-islet recipients required immunosuppression with sustained control for >22 months</cite>. <cite id="35d48d75-4">Pig-to-monkey islet xenotransplantation has been technically feasible, establishing porcine islets as a therapeutic alternative to allotransplantation while emphasizing immunologic challenges</cite>. 
- Takeaway: NHP donors are not yet realistic suppliers for human T1D; instead, NHP recipients are key to validate non-pig strategies (e.g., xenoencapsulation, Fc-blocker coatings, gene-edited sources), but survival without unacceptable immunosuppression is the major hurdle. <cite id="bc5212b4-3">NHP models are the bridge species for translating islet xenotransplantation</cite>.

2) Farm animals (cows, sheep, goats) as potential donors
- Cattle, ovine, and caprine islets or islet-like endocrine progenitors have been studied for cross-species compatibility, but anti-alpha-Gal antibodies and complement activation cause rapid hyperacute rejection of unmodified xenografts, and scaling to clinic-ready grafts is early-stage. <cite id="35d48d75-1">Immunologic barriers remain the principal obstacle despite progress in islet therapeutics</cite>. 
- Mitigation strategies under exploration for non-pig donors include:
  - Removing alpha-Gal epitopes or substituting glycans, combined with complement and platelet-targeted blockade, to enable survival of islet or endocrine progenitor xenografts in large animals and NHPs; while the pig literature dominates, the same principles apply and are being adapted toward cow/sheep/goat sources as manufacturing scales from pigs. <cite id="35d48d75-1">Barrier-focused advances and tolerance induction are central to making islet xenotransplantation broadly feasible</cite>. 
- Goats: genetically engineered caprine systems (e.g., transgenic milk proteins or endocrine lineage reprogramming) have been proposed for human-matched antigen presentation to reduce rejection, but clinical-grade islet xenografts from goats in primates/humans are not yet demonstrated. <cite id="35d48d75-1">Technological advances are required to surmount species-specific immunologic incompatibilities before clinical feasibility</cite>.
