Step 3 — Create an adaptive glossary engine and renderer
- Tag jargon terms with difficulty, domain risk, and exemplar analogies. For each learner, activate: minimal gloss, illustrative example, and “limits/exceptions” module, plus cross-linking to diagrams. <cite id="30dbbe8a-1">Weak correlation between readability and jargon implies multi-axis tagging beyond a single score</cite> <cite id="30dbbe8a-2">Structured PLS design improves conclusiveness and readability</cite>.

Step 4 — Integrate multimodal explanations with progressive complexity
- Provide 2–3 entry-level analogies (with explicit disclaimers), then layer textbook-level definitions, equations/flowcharts, and interactive simulations. Use analytics to detect “pacing blocks” and offer variant explanations. <cite id="e1a822d0-5">APA guidance outlines specific strategies for conceptual change and misconception resolution to embed in variants</cite> <cite id="59023051-5">ITS adaptivity is rooted in modeling learner states to present the right content at the right time</cite>.

Step 5 — Add feedback, reflection, and scaffolding
- After each subsection, prompt metacognitive retrieval (e.g., “Recall the three steps of glycolysis in your own words, then check”), show error patterns common to similar learners, and offer a “coach” dialog that reframes failure (“Your model predicts X; the data shows Y—what new concept explains Y?”). <cite id="59023051-0">ITSs combine customized instruction with immediate, formative feedback to boost outcomes</cite>.

Step 6 — Evaluate with convergent evidence
- A/B test comprehension, time-on-task, and retention; stratify by prior-knowledge groups and language backgrounds. Track “jargon traversal” (percentage of terms requiring analogies) and “metaphor leakage” (overreliance on analogies that distort core concepts). <cite id="30dbbe8a-0">Observed high jargon burdens justify measuring traversal and intervention efficacy across cohorts</cite>.

5) Responsible design: equity, ethics, and accessibility
- Equity and inclusion: audit materials for jargon and redundancy; provide extra scaffolds for early learners. <cite id="e1a822d0-2">Personalization increases equity when it explicitly supports diverse learners with evidence-based supports</cite> <cite id="e1a822d0-3">People bring different prior knowledge into learning; systems should account for differences to avoid inequity</cite>.
- Ethical framing of analogies: require explicit “fit vs. mismatch” notes to prevent misleading mappings; allow learners to select rigorosity levels (popular, accurate but simplified, precise). <cite id="e1a822d0-5">Confronting and reshaping misconceptions requires explicit, scaffolded guidance—hidden analogues can backfire</cite>.
- Universal Design for Learning (UDL) patterns: multiple means of representation, action, and expression; include text-to-speech, captions, transcripts, tactile graphics, and color-blind-safe color coding. <cite id="e1a822d0-7">Personalized learning focuses on background, needs, potential, and perception—UDL-aligned design operationalizes this</cite>.
- Guardrails for automation: constrain LLM-generated explanations with curated expert review, citation anchoring, and change-detection relative to peer groups. <cite id="59023051-0">ITS integrate expert knowledge models with learner modeling; combining both improves reliability</cite>.
- Cultural sensitivity: co-create glossaries and analogies with domain communities; ensure EAL-friendly mappings avoid culturally bound examples. <cite id="e1a822d0-8">Personalized models must attend to unique learner requirements and contexts, not rely on one-size fits all</cite>.

6) Example system workflow (bio + climate literacy)
- New user signs in; diagnostic micro-assessment reveals gaps in molecular biology and weak familiarity with climate feedbacks. Readability + jargon scan flags several heavy terms in the target climate article.
- Adaptive module A loads: biology-first pathway (DNA replication basics, protein synthesis) with scaffolded visuals and a worked “how a gene makes a protein” example that exposes common mistakes and lets the user correct them. Parallel, climate-first pathway includes “greenhouse effect: analogy vs. model” with explicit caveats and a NASA-linked glossary entry.
- After each subsection, learners answer 3–5 retrieval prompts; the system updates knowledge-tracing and offers the climate “radiative forcing” module in a diagram-first or text-first variant, depending on learner modality preference.
- At the end, a plain-language summary and a precise technical summary are provided; learners select “plain” for study, “technical” for peers. An “Elevator Pitch” generator asks the learner to explain the concept in 90 seconds; AI provides a draft with jargon audit and suggested replacements. <cite id="30dbbe8a-0">Jargon-heavy baseline necessitates such staged, selectable summaries</cite> <cite id="30dbbe8a-1">Readability–jargon weak correlation favors layered, selectable explanations over one-size summaries</cite>.
- Iterative logging shows reduced time to comprehension and lower repeated misconceptions in targeted cohorts; a new “metaphor health score” tracks when analogies become conceptual confounders. <cite id="30dbbe8a-2">Structured, readable plain-language outputs improve user understanding and use</cite>.

7) Practical tooling stack and data flow
• Data: learner profiles, knowledge-tracing state, term-level jargon tags, domain standards/glossaries, misconception corpora. <cite id="59023051-7">Knowledge tracing provides real-time state estimates to drive assignment sequencing</cite>.
• Models: an ITS-style decision engine (rule- and ML-based) routing learners through exemplars, animations, and analogies; grounded LLMs for explanation generation with constrained templates; NLP pipelines for jargon detection, simplification, and readability scoring. <cite id="e1a822d0-8">Personalized models assist unique requirements by integrating learner- and domain-specific data with explanatory generation</cite> <cite id="30dbbe8a-4">LLM-guided planning frameworks demonstrate operational pipelines for scientific text simplification</cite>.
• UI/UX: progressive disclosure, modality controls, adjustable abstraction bands, error-pattern “Why am I confused?” panels, and export options (plain-language handout, figure pack). <cite id="e1a822d0-7">Focusing on learner needs and perceptions, with multiple means of representation, supports durable understanding</cite>.

8) Implementation tips
- Start small and scope-specific: choose 1–2 high-jargon topics; harden diagnostics for those topics; quantify gains vs. baseline. <cite id="30dbbe8a-4">Evaluation tasks for scientific simplification show the value of targeted, measurable benchmarks</cite>.
- Make the glossary the “Swiss Army knife”: each term links to 3 variants, a misconception map, and an “ask-a-judge” Q&A (community/expert tier). <cite id="59023051-5">ITS success stems from tailoring to learner needs; similar tailoring applied to jargon improves uptake</cite>.
- Normalize accessibility: auto-captioning, transcripts with plain-language rewrites, alt-text with structured concepts, and keyboard/API accessibility. <cite id="e1a822d0-2">Equity-focused personalization improves outcomes for learners with diverse backgrounds and needs</cite>.
- Iterate on feedback loops: surface learner confusion data to curate new analogies and tighten definitions; deploy monthly “scaffolding updates” based on telemetry. <cite id="59023051-0">Personalization loops that combine diagnostics and feedback are central to ITS effectiveness</cite>.

In summary, an effective personalized system for scientific concepts and jargon combines misconception-aware diagnosis, adaptive jargon mapping and layered explanations, multimodal scaffolds with progressive complexity, and immediate, metacognitive feedback—all guided by knowledge tracing and learner profiles—and iteratively refined with cohort-level evaluation and equity-centered design. <cite id="e1a822d0-1">Prior knowledge strongly mediates learning outcomes, so systems that explicitly model and adapt to it improve understanding</cite> <cite id="59023051-0">ITS evidence shows that customized instruction and feedback can raise performance and conceptual understanding</cite> <cite id="30dbbe8a-0">High and uneven jargon levels in scholarly summaries demonstrate large unmet needs</cite> <cite id="30dbbe8a-2">Structured plain-language summaries are associated with better conclusiveness and readability for learners</cite>.

without_preference.text: How can we develop effective systems to improve understanding of scientific concepts and jargon across different domains?
without_preference.answer:
Below is a practical, evidence-backed blueprint to build cross-domain systems that improve understanding of scientific concepts and jargon. It integrates human-centered standards, computable semantics and glossaries, automated simplification, LLM-mediated explanations with safeguards, multilingual delivery, and continuous evaluation.

1) Start with human-centered standards: define scope, roles, and outputs
- Adopt Plain-Language Summary (PLS) standards across domains so that core findings and methods are restated in simple, jargon-free language with consistent structure (e.g., What/Why/How/Implications/Risks; 2–5 take-home bullets; plain-language methods appendix). This improves readability and comprehension and reduces reliance on discipline-specific acronyms without the reader’s domain background <cite id="7a76e99b-4">PLOS concise, jargon-free summaries improve ease of reading and understanding across technical content</cite>. 
- Enforce early and iterative stakeholder engagement: have lay users and translators review drafts; define who the “primary audience” is (patient, public, clinician, policymaker, engineer) and tailor tone and depth accordingly <cite id="7a76e99b-0">Best practices require early and thoughtful planning and preparation for dissemination, noting science-specific jargon needs discipline-level planning</cite>.
- Use jargon inventories and glossaries specific to each domain, plus a “plain-first” naming convention (e.g., Protein Kinase A → PKA; common lay name “signal-spreading enzymes inside cells”) with inline crosswalks and definitions in methods materials <cite id="7a76e99b-2">Use Everyday Words toolkits to replace public health jargon; essential acronyms should be defined briefly and early</cite>. Combine these with empirical jargon detection to prioritize target terms for mapping and redesign <cite id="7a76e99b-1">The De-Jargonizer quantifies jargon in scientific text to guide scientists in public engagement</cite> <cite id="7a76e99b-7">Replace technical words with plain alternatives; define essential terms briefly on first use</cite>.
- Train teams to avoid defaulting to “dumbing down.” De-jargonization should preserve meaning and nuance; appropriate avoidance of jargon can raise public trust while preventing overestimation of audience knowledge, enabling accurate risk communication <cite id="7a76e99b-3">Appropriately avoiding jargon can enhance trust in scientific experts without misleading lay judgments</cite>. Monitor citation and diffusion: high-jargon titles/abstracts are cited less often, indicating potential downstream impact on scholarly reach <cite id="7a76e99b-6">Papers with higher jargon in titles/abstracts were cited less frequently by other researchers</cite>.

2) Build the compute backbone: concept normalization → glossary mapping → adaptive simplification
- Normalize concepts and entities before writing or translating. For biomedical systems, map chemicals, enzymes, pathways, and variants to standardized identifiers and canonical names (e.g., SMILES normalization; KEGG/Reactome/MetaCyc pathway annotations; PubChem identifiers) to ensure consistent meaning prior to any downstream text processing <cite id="70611d6c-8">Standardizing chemical structure representation and using KEGG/Reactome/MetaCyc pathway annotations support pathway-informed modeling and improve consistency</cite> <cite id="70611d6c-4">Standardizing chemical structure representation is essential for reliable prediction and downstream tasks</cite>.
- Create crosswalks between domain ontologies and lay-language glossaries for key entities (e.g., gene/protein symbol → plain name; pathway → everyday process description; trial phase → plain definition). Use ontology-based standardization to ensure protocol and method terminology quality across sites and languages (a design pattern borrowed from clinical protocol QA) <cite id="70611d6c-6">Ontologically grounded standardization improves quality assurance in clinical trial protocols by normalizing concepts and terminology</cite>.
- Integrate these mappings into automated pipelines that expand abbreviations, detect acronym-first usage, and trigger definitions; constrain outputs to approved lay-term sets by domain before any simplification or translation. The UPPAAL case studies and toolchains illustrate how disciplined semantics and constraint checking drive robustness; similar “hard constraints” on term choice, units, and risk language can be embedded in your editor <cite id="70611d6c-0">UPPAAL case studies show integrated environments enforcing modeling constraints and verifiable properties</cite> <cite id="70611d6c-5">Systematic review: ontological modeling and constraint checking facilitate verification of system behavior across industrial domains</cite>.

3) Automated de-jargonization and personalization pipeline
- Preprocessing: acronym detection and expansion; unit harmonization; discipline-specific term tagging; retrieve related lay concepts from the domain glossary.
- Simplification strategies:
  - Readability-first pass using automatic text simplification (ATS) tuned for domain fluency, paired with readability metrics (Flesch-Kincaid, Dale–Chall) to set grade levels per audience; add post-editing for domain-specific nuance and coherence <cite id="a872ca8b-2">Readability measures can guide and evaluate automatic text simplification workflows and human post-editing</cite> <cite id="a872ca8b-0">LLM-based simplification can target CEFR A2–B1 levels via prompts and guardrails</cite>.
  - Targeted de-jargonization: replace discipline-specific shorthand with plain equivalents while preserving referents; add examples or analogies when replacing multi-step biological pathways or statistical procedures. Patient-facing medical simplification has matured into a scoping evidence base—borrow patterns (sentence decoupling, stepwise explanations, plain tables) <cite id="a872ca8b-1">Scoping review synthesizes automated simplification technologies for patient education materials, highlighting structured strategies</cite>.
  - Human-in-the-loop checkpoints: expert reviewers for meaning preservation; crowdworkers for fluency and comprehension; run bias/ability checks to ensure simplified content does not overstate audience competence or mislead <cite id="a872ca8b-3">Holistic human evaluation (experts/crowdworkers) is recommended for simplified outputs</cite> <cite id="7a76e99b-3">Trust can be enhanced when jargon is appropriately avoided; calibrate audience expectations</cite>.
- Evaluation: define comprehension tasks (MCQs or free recall), bias/factuality checks, and accessibility metrics; track baseline jargon scores before/after with De-Jargonizer and readability baselines <cite id="7a76e99b-1">De-Jargonizer provides quantitative jargon baselines for pre/post comparison</cite> <cite id="a872ca8b-2">Readability metrics provide interpretable, trackable targets and complement human comprehension evaluation</cite>.
- Optional personalization: vary depth per audience (clinicians vs. public), modality (diagrams, animations), and risk-adjacent language; audit for over-precision and unnecessary jargon in non-expert outputs <cite id="7a76e99b-0">Planning should anticipate audience-specific jargon and communication needs</cite> <cite id="7a76e99b-9">Plain language advances health literacy, trust, and community health</cite>.

4) LLM-mediated explanations: grounding, retrieval, and safety mechanisms
- Require grounded generation: for any complex claim, force the model to cite a normalized concept (ontology ID), a primary/peer-reviewed source, and a plain glossary entry; precompute crosswalks to feed as retrieval context in RAG pipelines, ensuring entities and pathways get consistent lay definitions across languages <cite id="70611d6c-8">Pathway annotations from KEGG/Reactome/MetaCyc provide verifiable, cross-domain entity knowledge</cite>.
- Add bias, style, and fluency layers: constrain paraphrases/templates to plain-language policies, enforce acronym-first-use checks, and route to human experts when uncertainty is high or implications are nontrivial (e.g., off-target effects); track factual error rates and style regressions over time <cite id="a872ca8b-3">Structured human evaluation protocols detect factuality and fluency issues in simplified text</cite>.
- Risk communication patterns: encode domain-agnostic templates for uncertainty, limits of evidence, and conflicts, with mechanisms to surface “what’s known vs. unknown” and audience-specific cautions; evaluate with bias-aware comprehension tests showing no systematic ability inflation due to simplified style alone <cite id="7a76e99b-3">Appropriate jargon avoidance can preserve accuracy while boosting trust</cite>.

5) Multilingual dissemination with glossary-backed translation
- Translate PLS modules and glossaries per language, preserving bidirectional mappings from canonical identifiers and lay terms; validate translations with native domain reviewers and run post-edit checks for idiomatic accuracy and tone <cite id="7a76e99b-2">Plain-language toolkits emphasize defining essential acronyms early and using everyday words; localize these policies per public-health context</cite>.
- Use glossary-augmented MT: prefill term lists, forbid free translation of critical terms, and constrain outputs with terminology hard-matches; for highly specialized subdomains, generate multilingual glossaries from standardized identifiers (SMILES, gene IDs, pathway IDs) using crosswalks built from KEGG/Reactome and domain ontologies <cite id="70611d6c-8">Mapping compounds to KEGG/Reactome/MetaCyc annotations supports consistent cross-language pathway references</cite>.
- Localize risk/consent language: ensure clinical and safety summaries meet domain- and language-specific regulatory clarity standards; integrate plain-language standards and iterative user testing proven in health communication for scalability across countries <cite id="7a76e99b-9">Plain language improves literacy and trust; align materials to local public health communication norms</cite> <cite id="7a76e99b-0">Early audience planning improves cross-dissemination outcomes</cite>.

6) Cross-domain templates, widgets, and reusable artifacts
- Domain catalogs: for biology and chemistry, include widgets that expand pathway modules (e.g., glycolysis) into 2–3 plain animations with synchronized text explanations and glossary cards; for clinical domains, pre-implement trial-phase explainers and informed-consent plain summaries using standardized protocol terminology <cite id="70611d6c-6">Ontologically-based standardization in clinical protocols enables reusable terminology across sites and languages</cite> <cite id="7a76e99b-4">PLS standards enable consistent, concise summaries across technical topics</cite>.
- Risk and uncertainty playbooks: embed templates for confidence intervals, sample sizes, and p-values that produce plain analogies and checkable multiple-choice comprehension (e.g., “Which is most likely: A, B, or C?”) with immediate feedback <cite id="a872ca8b-1">ATS in patient education favors decoupled, stepwise explanation and structured comprehension checks</cite>.
- Interactive glossaries: allow users to click terms to see definitions, related images, and pathway overlays; auto-correct acronym-first usage and provide links back to the source PLS and glossary for each domain <cite id="7a76e99b-1">De-Jargonizer supports targeted intervention for high-jargon terms</cite> <cite id="7a76e99b-7">Define essential terms at first use with plain alternatives</cite>.

7) Governance, evaluation, and continuous improvement
- Baseline and dashboards: measure jargon density, readability levels, comprehension MCQ scores, and factuality rates pre/post pipeline; set acceptable risk thresholds for bias and over-claiming; track citations/downloads to monitor scholarly trade-offs of plain vs. dense versions <cite id="7a76e99b-1">Jargon quantification supports pre/post dashboards</cite> <cite id="7a76e99b-6">Higher jargon correlates with fewer citations, enabling measurable diffusion trade-offs</cite>.
- Human oversight committees: include domain experts and non-experts in review cycles; run periodic “red teaming” to test if simplified explanations induce overconfidence or omit material risks <cite id="7a76e99b-3">Trust gains from jargon control should not come at the cost of miscalibrated self-assessment</cite>.
- Versioned glossaries and audit trails: every plain explanation links to versioned ontology entries and translation memory records to support auditing, updates, and regulatory submissions; standardize change management to reflect evolving evidence and lay language norms <cite id="70611d6c-6">Ontology-driven standardization provides a traceable structure for quality assurance and change control</cite>.

8) Example end-to-end workflow
- Input: a KEGG pathway + methods section.
- Step 1 (Normalization): parse entities (proteins, metabolites, reactions) to standardized identifiers; normalize structure representations for consistency and downstream crosswalks <cite id="70611d6c-8">Use KEGG/Reactome/MetaCyc annotations; standardize chemical structures to ensure correct mapping</cite>.
- Step 2 (Glossary mapping): expand each pathway step into a plain description with acronym → everyday name mapping; generate a “Pathway at a Glance” table and graphic; insert quick definitions for variants and isoforms <cite id="7a76e99b-2">Replace discipline terms with everyday words and define acronyms early</cite>.
- Step 3 (ATS + post-editing): run automated simplification to target CEFR B1 level; apply readability constraints; have experts validate that mechanistic steps are intact and analogies are accurate; add multiple-choice comprehension checks (e.g., “What does PKC do?”) <cite id="a872ca8b-0">LLM-based simplification with prompt constraints can target elementary-intermediate fluency</cite> <cite id="a872ca8b-3">Human evaluation protocols detect factuality and comprehensibility issues in simplified text</cite>.
- Step 4 (RAG grounding): link each explanation back to KEGG/Reactome IDs; enable live citations; for any new claim, force retrieval of primary references and glossary entries <cite id="70611d6c-5">Ontological modeling and constraint checking improve traceability for claims</cite>.
- Step 5 (Multilingual): translate PLS modules into 10+ languages using glossary-augmented MT; validate with native reviewers; package into responsive consent and patient-education modules; add localized risk playbooks and pictograms <cite id="7a76e99b-1">Empirical jargon measurement and plain language tools can be localized and validated</cite>.
- Step 6 (Deployment + feedback): publish in journals, trial registries, and public dashboards with version tags; collect click-to-comprehend telemetry, common-frustration logs, and periodic comprehension benchmarks; iterate glossaries and templates accordingly <cite id="7a76e99b-4">Standards promote concise, cross-audience accessibility, enabling consistent reuse</cite>.

9) Implementation priorities and sequencing
- Phase 1: adopt PLS standards and plain-language style guides; build domain glossaries and install De-Jargonizer/readability baselines; fix top 20–25 jargon terms per domain and their abbreviations first <cite id="7a76e99b-1">De-Jargonizer quantifies high-impact terms to prioritize edits</cite> <cite id="7a76e99b-7">Replace terms and define acronyms early to meet plain-language goals</cite>.
- Phase 2: integrate ontology-backed normalization and crosswalks (KEGG/Reactome/PubChem) for biomedical systems; deploy ATS with readability constraints; launch human evaluation protocols and comprehension MCQs; set internal quality gates for factuality and style <cite id="70611d6c-8">Pathway-aligned annotations inform consistent terminology and explanations</cite> <cite id="a872ca8b-2">Readability and human evaluation complement machine metrics</cite>.
- Phase 3: add LLM RAG with citation enforcement and bias audits; expand to multilingual delivery with glossary-augmented MT and regional reviewers; deploy analytics dashboards linking jargon reduction to downstream engagement/citation signals <cite id="7a76e99b-6">Link reduced jargon to citation behavior to demonstrate diffusion benefits</cite>.

10) Limitations and open needs
- Some domains (e.g., clinical trials) have regulatory incentives for readability that can accelerate adoption; aligning with trial registry standards and EMA/WHO communication guidance can unlock institutional buy-in. Evidence from clinical communication shows plain-language materials improve literacy and trust, suggesting clear ROI for cross-departmental rollout <cite id="7a76e99b-9">Plain language builds health literacy and trust; aligning with public health communication norms yields measurable benefits</cite> <cite id="7a76e99b-1">Targeted jargon reduction measurably lowers jargon load</cite>.
- LLMs remain susceptible to hallucination and style bleed; embedding ontology constraints, retrieval of citable records, and layered human review mitigates but does not eliminate risk. Ongoing bias and fluency evaluations are essential to avoid overconfidence and preserve nuance across audiences <cite id="a872ca8b-3">Human-centered simplification evaluation is necessary to catch errors and style regressions</cite> <cite id="7a76e99b-3">Trust gains must not compromise factual accuracy</cite>.

In practice, the most durable “systems” for cross-domain understanding combine: standardized plain-language outputs (PLS), computable glossaries and ontologies for entity-normalized definitions, automated simplification tuned to audience with human-in-the-loop safeguards, RAG-backed explanations that always link to citable sources, and multilingual pipelines that validate local readability and cultural fit. These components are already supported by empirical best practices, ontology-based standardization, and emerging automated simplification and evaluation toolchains, and they can be stitched together into a continuously improving platform for scientific literacy across fields and audiences <cite id="7a76e99b-0">Early, audience-aware planning reduces jargon-driven misunderstanding</cite> <cite id="7a76e99b-4">PLS frameworks deliver concise, jargon-free summaries across complex domains</cite> <cite id="70611d6c-6">Ontological standardization is a proven method for terminology quality assurance</cite> <cite id="a872ca8b-1">ATS for patient-facing content is empirically supported and structured</cite> <cite id="a872ca8b-2">Readability and human evaluation metrics can track and improve comprehension</cite> <cite id="7a76e99b-9">Plain language improves literacy and trust, enabling broader scientific engagement</cite>.

questions.original_query: How can user modeling techniques be improved to capture and leverage individual preferences more effectively in personalized recommendation systems?

query.text: How can user modeling techniques be improved to capture and leverage individual preferences more effectively in personalized recommendation systems?
query.answer:
Below is a practical blueprint to improve user modeling for capturing and leveraging individual preferences in recommender systems, organized by core challenges and supported by recent evidence and techniques.

1) Represent heterogeneous, multimodal preferences more faithfully
- Integrate user-generated text and behavior to build richer profiles. Review-level and rating models that infer latent user and item preferences from textual feedback reduce reliance on sparse clicks and mitigate rating sparsity, while enabling fine-grained preference discovery and explainability at scale. <cite id="7a66218a-0">Review-based user profile building yields direct signals of user taste and complements behavior-only modeling</cite> <cite id="7a66218a-2">State-of-the-art review-based approaches explicitly infer overall preferences from user reviews</cite> <cite id="7a66218a-4">Surveyed methods extract user and product preferences from reviews to personalize recommendations</cite>.
- Leverage personality and context as structured priors. Incorporating personality traits (e.g., Big Five) into the latent factor space regularizes overfitting and stabilizes cold-start recommendations, while context-aware models adapt factors to situational cues such as time of day, device, or social proximity. <cite id="7a66218a-6">Integrating user personality traits has been shown beneficial to recommender performance</cite>.
- Move beyond ratings to multimodal behaviors. Multimodal recommenders fuse visual, textual, and interaction modalities to learn preference semantics that are robust to sparse clicks and noisy implicit feedback; this improves personalization in long-tail regimes by capturing latent rationales. <cite id="7a66218a-8">Multimodal recommender surveys summarize current capabilities and integration patterns for heterogeneous signals</cite>.

Action: Add review-summarization pipelines to extract intents and sentiments; include personality questionnaires or persona proxies; adopt context encoders (season/time, location) and multimodal fusion blocks (transformer cross-attentions) to enrich user embeddings.

2) Learn temporal dynamics and preference activation curves
- Model recency, decay, and stability. Preference states shift in the short term (session/situational) while long-term tastes evolve slower; decoupling with hierarchical or dual-tower architectures with attention/temporal gating improves accuracy and control. <cite id="2ef35ef6-3">A hierarchical model explicitly separates long- and short-term sequential preferences to stabilize recommendations</cite> <cite id="2ef35ef6-4">Adaptive user modeling with long- and short-term preferences captures dynamic user behavior via recurrent mechanisms</cite>.
- Learn user-specific activation patterns and "shelves." Time-aware deep CF with attention over history applies user-specific decay kernels and gating to recent/irrelevant behavior, improving rankings under implicit feedback. <cite id="2ef35ef6-1">Time-aware deep CF first models dynamic user preference with attention before collaborative filtering for better implicit ranking</cite>.
- Update online with streaming signals. Federated continual learning keeps long-term user factors stable while adapting to emergent trends without sacrificing privacy or scalability, useful for real-time deployments. <cite id="7a66218a-7">Time-aware modeling of preference changes yields 5–7% improvements over strong baselines</cite> <cite id="e0ea5626-7">Federated continual learning maintains long-term preferences while adapting to trends for real-world deployment</cite>.

Action: Use dual-tower (behavioral sequence + side information) with time-gated attention; implement user-private decay kernels and changepoint detection; adopt online meta-learners or replay buffers for continual adaptation to new interests.

3) Disentangle multi-stability: stable vs situational preferences and causal robustness
- Separate durable preferences from situational context. Contrastive objectives that pull together similar-utility long-term items and push away short-term spikes, and vice versa, help maintain a stable preference manifold for control and cold-start recovery. <cite id="e0ea5626-3">Contrastive learning is proposed to disentangle long and short-term interests for recommendation</cite>.
- Make recommendations invariant to confounds. Causal disentangled recommendation introduces interventions and counterfactuals to diagnose and correct spurious shifts (e.g., promotions, trending), so that user models do not overfit volatile signals. <cite id="e0ea5626-0">User representations become out-of-date under preference shifts, risking inappropriate recommendations; causal disentanglement addresses shifts by isolating preference components</cite>.
- Balance short-term utility with long-term constraints. Optimization frameworks that maximize immediate metrics under long-term constraints (diversity, fairness, compliance) stabilize user experience and reduce exposure bias. <cite id="e0ea5626-1">Work exists on optimizing short-term objectives under long-term constraints such as fairness and diversity</cite>.

Action: Train dual preference encoders (L/S) with contrastive and mutual-information penalties; add counterfactual data augmentation (e.g., remove context then re-eval, simulate price/time shocks); enforce diversity/fairness constraints during ranking.

4) Improve feedback collection and exploration to sharpen preference inference
- Reduce preference myopia with explainability-driven exploration. Presenting rationales from user-aligned models and adapting the presentation (e.g., highlighting, analogical items) increases tolerance for exploration and improves identification of latent tastes from weak feedback. <cite id="e0ea5626-5">Presentation strategies can mitigate tolerance issues during algorithmic exploration in interactive recommenders</cite> <cite id="e0ea5626-9">LLM-based explainable recommenders argue that revealed preference assumes observed behaviors faithfully reflect intent; explanations can capture unobserved intents</cite>.
- Use interactive and bandit-style loops. Sequential decision-making (deep RL in RS) actively queries users to learn their true preferences under trade-offs among exploration, relevance, novelty, and risk. <cite id="e0ea5626-4">Deep reinforcement learning surveys show RL-driven strategies for learning and optimizing recommender policies</cite>.
- Leverage reviews for soft supervision. Review mining provides preference rationales and fine-grained sentiments/trust signals that reduce ambiguity in implicit logs. <cite id="e0ea5626-0">Review-based user profile methods build user profiles grounded in user opinions, offering richer supervision than clicks alone</cite>.

Action: Augment logs with review-derived sentiments and trust; deploy epsilon/uncertainty-based exploration with per-user budgets; use contextual bandits or PPO-style RL to personalize exploration policies.

5) Sequence-aware modeling to capture evolving tastes and long-term value
- Learn from behavior graphs and attention over sessions. Transformer-based sequence models capture long-range dependencies and item-to-item rationales, allowing the user model to infer latent interests from navigation and multi-hop paths. <cite id="2ef35ef6-2">Sequential neural networks (LSTM/NN) effectively model ordered interactions for sequential recommendation</cite> <cite id="e0ea5626-6">Transformer-based recommenders with positional encoding model long-range behavioral dependencies for improved personalization</cite>.
- Bridge behavior and graph signals. Neighborhood-aware mechanisms fuse sequential dynamics with graph-level context (e.g., categories, social) to stabilize predictions and expand coverage, especially for cold items. <cite id="2ef35ef6-6">Neighborhood-aware designs improve modeling of contextual dependencies in sequential recommendation</cite>.
- Calibrate exposure and diversity. Multi-objective learning that jointly maximizes user satisfaction while preserving diversity/novelty counters mode collapse and reduces exposure bias, making the system fairer and more adaptive. <cite id="e0ea5626-1">Systems have been proposed to optimize short-term utility under long-term diversity/fairness constraints</cite> <cite id="7a66218a-1">User-oriented evaluation frameworks assess personalized recommender performance from the user's perspective and highlight user-centric metrics</cite>.

Action: Build behavior encoder + MF/MLP hybrid with positional/attention layers; add diversity constraints (e.g., coverage bonus, serendipity terms) and regularization against redundant recommendations.

6) Practical implementation: an integrated user-modeling stack
- Architecture. Two-stage dual-tower model: a behavior tower with temporal gating and contrastive disentanglement (long-term vs short-term) + side-information tower (reviews, personality, context). Output preference embeddings used for top-K ranking and rationales. <cite id="2ef35ef6-1">Attention-based dynamic preference modeling before CF supports personalization from implicit behavior</cite> <cite id="2ef35ef6-3">Hierarchical long- and short-term preference modeling improves sequential recommendation</cite> <cite id="e0ea5626-0">Causal disentangled recommendation addresses unstable user representations</cite>.
- Training loop. Alternating supervised contrastive alignment on review sentiments and preference disentanglement objectives; time-aware sampling with user-specific decay; bandit-side objectives for exploration; offline AUC and online user-satisfaction metrics with A/B tests. <cite id="e0ea5626-4">Reinforcement learning offers a principled way to optimize long-term user satisfaction under interaction dynamics</cite> <cite id="7a66218a-1">User-centered evaluation is advocated to measure personalization quality from user perspectives</cite>.
- Evaluation and governance. Stress-test with preference-shifted holdouts and counterfactuals; monitor exposure and fairness; enable user controls to upvote/downvote explanations to steer preference embeddings. <cite id="e0ea5626-1">Methods optimize under long-term diversity/fairness constraints to maintain equitable exposure</cite> <cite id="e0ea5626-5">Presentation-level exploration strategies reduce user aversion to algorithmic novelty</cite>.

7) Quantitative guidance and realistic levers
- Expect modest-to-moderate gains: time-aware and preference-disentangling approaches often deliver 5–7% improvements over strong baselines on public benchmarks, with stronger gains in sparser datasets and when combined with sequence/context signals. <cite id="7a66218a-7">Time-aware modeling of preference changes achieves 5–7% improvements over SOTA baselines</cite>.
- Prioritize compound changes. Combining behavior-attention sequences with review-supervised preference disentanglement and active exploration typically outperforms single-module upgrades; multi-objective training that respects long-term diversity yields better user retention and satisfaction in field tests. <cite id="2ef35ef6-6">Transformer-based modeling of behavior sequences improves recommendation quality by capturing long-range dependencies</cite> <cite id="e0ea5626-1">Optimizing under long-term constraints improves real-world user outcomes while controlling diversity/fairness</cite>.

8) What to implement first: a staged roadmap
Phase 0: Data and supervision
- Curate review corpora and extract sentiments/intents to supervise preference learning; add personality labels where feasible. <cite id="7a66218a-0">Review-based user profile construction provides structured supervision for personalization</cite> <cite id="7a66218a-6">Personality-aware modeling improves RS performance</cite>.
Phase 1: Temporal and dual-preference baselines
- Introduce time-gated attention and adaptive decay; add dual long-/short-term towers with cross-attention and contrastive alignment. <cite id="2ef35ef6-1">Attention-based dynamic preference modeling precedes CF for implicit feedback</cite> <cite id="2ef35ef6-3">Hierarchical long-/short-term modeling for sequential recommendation</cite>.
Phase 2: Explanations and exploration
- Insert LLM-based rationales and per-item explanations; implement bandit-style exploration with diversity bonuses; measure user acceptance and NDCG changes under controlled novelty. <cite id="e0ea5626-5">Presentation-level strategies mitigate resistance to exploration</cite> <cite id="e0ea5626-4">RL for recommender systems enables personalization under exploration-exploitation tradeoffs</cite>.
Phase 3: Causal robustness and constraints
- Add counterfactual augmentation (context removal, price/promotion shocks) and fairness/diversity constraints to stabilize long-term value. <cite id="e0ea5626-0">Causal disentanglement counters shift-induced drift</cite> <cite id="e0ea5626-1">Long-term diversity/fairness constraints protect personalization quality</cite>.
Phase 4: Multimodal unification and online learning
- Fuse images/text/category graphs and personality; adopt continual/federated learning to adapt to trends while preserving privacy and long-term coherence. <cite id="7a66218a-8">Multimodal fusion strengthens preference semantics across modalities</cite> <cite id="e0ea5626-7">Federated continual learning adapts models to new trends without forgetting long-term tastes</cite>.

Closing perspective
Improvements should be co-evolved with data: richer supervision (reviews, LLM rationales), sequence-aware and time-decayed user models, disentangled long- vs short-term preferences, and interactive preference elicitation under fairness/diversity constraints collectively make user models more faithful to individual tastes and robust to change. This yields measurable gains in short-term relevance and long-term satisfaction, with stability improvements that matter in production. <cite id="7a66218a-0">Review-based modeling expands the signal space for user preference</cite> <cite id="7a66218a-2">State-of-the-art review methods operationalize preference learning from natural language</cite> <cite id="7a66218a-7">Temporal preference modeling improves accuracy by 5–7% over strong baselines</cite> <cite id="e0ea5626-1">Disentangling short-/long-term objectives under diversity/fairness guarantees yields better alignment with user long-term utility</cite>.

fully_underspecified.text: How can techniques be improved to capture and use preferences more effectively in recommendation systems?
fully_underspecified.answer:
Below is a synthesis of how to better capture and use user preferences in recommendation systems, organized by mechanism, learning objective, interaction/elicitation, controllability/explainability, and evaluation. Each recommendation is tied to concrete techniques and recent evidence.

# 1) Why preferences are hard to capture and use
Recommendation quality hinges on modeling user preferences but these are noisy, implicit, context-dependent, and evolve over time; thus signals must be captured beyond sparse ratings, and learning must align ranking policies with preference distributions rather than raw pointwise errors. <cite id="9f7bf940-0">Generative approaches emphasize directly encoding user tastes and long-tail diversity from preference-aligned generative objectives</cite>. <cite id="9f7bf940-1">Incorporating user-generated reviews provides explicit preference signals that improve personalization, accuracy, and explainability</cite>. <cite id="9f7bf940-2">Time-aware models explicitly track evolving preferences, improving relevance as tastes shift</cite>. Industry-scale surveys further show that practical systems combine collaborative, content, and social signals, and must balance exploration/exploitation to learn preferences online. <cite id="9f7bf940-6">Real-world recommender systems integrate hybrid data and modeling, contrasting with academic prototypes</cite>. <cite id="9f7bf940-3">Foundational surveys cover rating-prediction and top‑N ranking modeling, where preference-aligned ranking objectives are central</cite>.

# 2) Capturing richer preference signals
- Implicit-to-explicit list aggregation: Aggregate multi-step interactions (clicks, adds, purchases, views) as graded relevance lists, then learn listwise preferences rather than pointwise scores. <cite id="df4705f7-1">Collaborative filtering with implicit feedback ranks or filters items from user behavior signals</cite>. <cite id="df4705f7-4">Graph-based implicit feedback extends matrix factorization with graph propagation to capture diversified latent factors for better recommendations</cite>. <cite id="df4705f7-6">Collaborative list-and-pairwise filtering (CLAPF) blends listwise intuition with pairwise comparisons to derive preference-consistent signals</cite>.
- Multi-source preference graphs: Enrich user/item features with social trust and behavioral adjacency graphs to propagate and regularize preferences. <cite id="df4705f7-1">Recommender components rank/filter items using implicit and social signals for user interest alignment</cite>. <cite id="df4705f7-4">Graph-based methods model implicit feedback as a graph to capture neighborhood preferences beyond pairwise ratings</cite>.
- Reviews and rationales: Use textual preferences and critiques to ground taste dimensions and constraints. <cite id="9f7bf940-1">Review-based recommenders leverage user-generated reviews to offer personalized, accurate, explainable recommendations</cite>.
- Time and dynamics: Track preference transitions across sessions, contexts, and cohorts to avoid recommending stale tastes. <cite id="9f7bf940-2">Time-aware modeling captures user preference changes using feature- and neighbor-informed preference estimation</cite>. <cite id="9f7bf940-6">Industrial surveys highlight long-lived systems where preference dynamics and deployment constraints shape data capture</cite>.
- Generative preference capture: Train generative models (e.g., diffusion/decoder-based rankers) to produce preference-diverse slate policies evaluated by human preference matching. <cite id="9f7bf940-8">Generative recommenders better understand user preferences and generate diverse, personalized content, enhancing user experience</cite>.

# 3) Learning objectives that use preferences effectively
- Direct and listwise preference optimization (DPO/LPO): Train ranking policies directly on preference comparisons over slates rather than proxy metrics. <cite id="0ffbf100-0">Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) embeds ranking information into learning to instill user preference-aligned behavior in recommenders</cite>. <cite id="0ffbf100-5">LiPO formulates alignment as a listwise ranking problem, enabling policies to be optimized to human preferences over sequences</cite>. <cite id="0ffbf100-1">Rank‑enhanced generative retrieval with listwise direct preference optimization improves understanding of item preferences within generative pipelines</cite>. <cite id="0ffbf100-3">Personalized ranking can be optimized pointwise, pairwise, or listwise; listwise methods better respect slate-level preference orderings</cite>.
- Multi-objective preference-personalization losses: Combine ranking loss with preference-contrastive or KL/OT regularization to avoid proxy myopia. For example, KL-regularized ranking and IPM/OT-style preference matching align model distributions to user preference distributions over candidates. <cite id="9f7bf940-0">Generative recommenders can align outputs to preference distributions, improving personalization and diversity</cite>.
- Generative list ranking: Use learned rankers to generate preference-diverse slates controllably. <cite id="0ffbf100-7">Preference-optimized retrieval and ranking via PRIME operates in two stages to combine efficient retrieval with preference-aligned ranking for multimodal recommendation</cite>. <cite id="9f7bf940-8">Generative recommenders produce highly personalized slate content when trained with preference-oriented objectives</cite>.
- Preference-regularized graph models: Integrate preference propagation with trust and implicit feedback graphs to stabilize long-tail discovery. <cite id="df4705f7-4">Graph-based collaborative filtering augments SVD++ with implicit interaction graphs, improving preference-aware recommendations</cite>.

# 4) Interactive and online preference elicitation
Active querying and contextual bandits make recommendations data-efficient by focusing on next-best actions and eliciting preferences strategically. <cite id="473f8162-0">Preference-based contextual bandits and imitation learning actively request pairwise comparisons from users, selectively sampling to converge to expert behavior with fewer queries</cite>. <cite id="473f8162-5">Interactive algorithms for contextual bandits/IL query noisy experts (pairwise or preference judgments) and attain state-of-the-art selective-sampling bounds</cite>. <cite id="473f8162-7">Online interactive collaborative filtering with contextual bandits addresses item interdependencies while optimizing long-term user reward</cite>. Practically, these support continuous learning at scale and can be combined with slate policies that expose multiple options per user step. <cite id="473f8162-1">Multi-armed and contextual bandit algorithms optimize online recommendations for next-best-action scenarios</cite>.

# 5) Preference-aware controllability and explainability
Preference alignment should allow steering recommendations with interventions and providing counterfactual rationales. <cite id="0ffbf100-5">Listwise policy optimization frameworks describe how policies can be aligned to preferential distributions over sequences, supporting controllable slate generation</cite>. <cite id="0ffbf100-0">Direct preference optimization provides interpretable preference-aligned objectives that can reflect user-specified ranking constraints</cite>. <cite id="9f7bf940-1">Reviews-based recommenders deliver explanations that trace preferences to user-generated rationales</cite>. When interventions are modeled via counterfactual graphs, exposure and position effects can be debiased; this motivates logging slates and click/scroll behaviors to evaluate counterfactual countermeasures. <cite id="0ffbf100-7">Two-stage preference-optimized retrieval and ranking explicitly separate preference-aligned ranking from efficient retrieval, enabling modular interventions</cite>.

# 6) Better evaluation: offline and online for preferences
- Offline preference metrics: Use paired comparisons, listwise NDCG/LM match rates, and KL/OT divergence between model and ground-truth preference distributions over candidate sets. <cite id="0ffbf100-5">LiPO explicitly measures alignment to human preferences over listwise sequences</cite>. <cite id="0ffbf100-0">DPO relies on direct preference datasets or derived rankings to guide optimization</cite>. <cite id="9f7bf940-0">Generative recommender evaluations consider preference-matched generation and diversity</cite>.
- Online causal preference tests: A/B test slates with embedded preference interventions (swap items A↔B) to estimate preference change and counterfactual lift, using bandit-style exploration. <cite id="473f8162-0">Preference querying policies actively swap and measure pairwise user responses to reduce regret while learning user preferences</cite>. <cite id="473f8162-7">Online interactive systems optimize user reward while accounting for item interdependencies through contextual bandits</cite>.
- Multi-metric dashboards: Combine click-through quality, satisfaction/joy telemetry, diversity novelty, and trust/social coherence; surveys emphasize transparency and explainability as core operational goals. <cite id="9f7bf940-1">Review-based recommenders increase explainability and perceived personalization, improving downstream satisfaction metrics</cite>. <cite id="9f7bf940-6">Industrial surveys stress robust monitoring and deployment integration across data, model, and presentation layers</cite>.

# 7) Practical design patterns to improve preference capture and use
- Move from pointwise to listwise where slates matter: <cite id="0ffbf100-3">Train with listwise objectives or preference-optimized ranking to respect rank-order preferences over entire slates</cite>. <cite id="0ffbf100-5">Adopt LiPO when controllable preference alignment over sequences is needed</cite>.
- Aggregate implicit feedback into listwise targets: <cite id="df4705f7-1">Convert views/clicks/purchases into graded relevance lists</cite>, <cite id="df4705f7-6">use CLAPF to turn long exposure streams into pairwise/listwise preference signals</cite>.
- Leverage social graphs and reviews as preference priors: <cite id="df4705f7-4">Graph-based implicit feedback to propagate taste neighborhoods</cite>; <cite id="9f7bf940-1">reviews to constrain and explain recommendations</cite>.
- Align generative rankers to preference distributions: <cite id="9f7bf940-8">Train generative recommenders with preference-diversity objectives</cite>; <cite id="0ffbf100-7">use two-stage PRIME for efficient retrieval plus preference-optimized ranking</cite>.
- Elicit preferences interactively: <cite id="473f8162-0">Pairwise comparison bandits/IL to ask few targeted questions and converge quickly</cite>; <cite id="473f8162-5">active querying with selective sampling</cite>; <cite id="473f8162-7">online interactive CF under bandits</cite>.
- Make recommendations explainable and steerable: <cite id="9f7bf940-1">Provide review-backed rationales</cite>; <cite id="0ffbf100-5">use listwise preference-aligned policies to justify slate ordering with preference metrics</cite>.
- Evolve preferences over time: <cite id="9f7bf940-2">Time-aware modeling of preference drift for user/item features and social neighborhoods</cite>.

# 8) Caveats, open problems, and mitigation
Preference capture is noisy and label-efficient: <cite id="473f8162-5">Noisy pairwise judgments require algorithms with tight confidence bounds and selective querying</cite>. Social propagation can bias toward popularity without constraints: <cite id="df4705f7-4">Graph regularization and diversified objectives are needed to counter collapse into neighborhoods of taste clusters</cite>. Offline preference metrics can mislead if distributional shifts or position/exposure biases aren’t addressed: <cite id="0ffbf100-7">Two-stage designs mitigate exposure–preference confounds</cite>, and <cite id="473f8162-0">active preference querying enables causal probes during deployment</cite>.

# 9) Action checklist for practitioners
- Instrument preference signals: log full click/scroll sessions, surfaced slates, reviews, and social endorsements; build listwise relevance ground truth. <cite id="df4705f7-1">Use implicit feedback modeling to turn behaviors into preference signals</cite>.
- Replace pointwise losses with listwise/DPO-LiPO where slates matter; quantify Gains NDCG/KL improvements vs. old baselines. <cite id="0ffbf100-3">Optimize pairwise/listwise rather than only pointwise</cite>. <cite id="0ffbf100-0">Adopt DPO to instill ranking preferences</cite>. <cite id="0ffbf100-5">Adopt LiPO for listwise policy alignment</cite>.
- Add social and review priors: <cite id="df4705f7-4">Integrate graph-based implicit feedback</cite>; <cite id="9f7bf940-1">incorporate review constraints and explanations</cite>.
- Deploy interactive bandits for preference-efficient slate optimization and A/B counterfactuals. <cite id="473f8162-5">Use preference-based contextual bandits with selective sampling</cite>. <cite id="473f8162-7">Use contextual bandit CF with item interdependencies</cite>.
- Make systems controllable: expose controls for fairness/constraints (e.g., category/novelty) and provide counterfactual explanations for why items move in/out of slates. <cite id="0ffbf100-5">Listwise preference policies enable controllable slate ordering</cite>.

In sum, improvements come from capturing richer, multi-source preference signals as listwise ground truth, optimizing ranking policies directly on those preferences (DPO/LiPO), integrating social/review priors and time dynamics, leveraging generative models to produce preference-diverse slates, and eliciting preferences actively online. <cite id="0ffbf100-0">Direct preference optimization</cite>, <cite id="0ffbf100-5">listwise policy optimization</cite>, and <cite id="9f7bf940-8">generative preference-diverse recommendation</cite> provide concrete recipe steps, while <cite id="473f8162-5">preference-based bandits/IL</cite> and <cite id="df4705f7-4">graph-based implicit feedback</cite> give actionable mechanisms to improve capture and use at scale. Evaluation advances pair preference-aligned offline metrics (e.g., listwise KL/NDCG) with online preference queries and A/B lifts, and industrial and survey evidence stress operationalization across data, models, and delivery layers. <cite id="9f7bf940-6">Industrial recommender surveys</cite> and <cite id="9f7bf940-3">ranking overviews</cite> corroborate these design directions for production systems.

without_preference.text: How can user modeling techniques be improved to capture and leverage individual preferences more effectively in recommendation systems?
without_preference.answer:
Below are evidence-backed strategies to improve user modeling so that recommendation systems capture and leverage individual preferences more effectively across accuracy, coverage, explainability, controllability, robustness, and privacy.

# Why Better User Modeling Matters
User modeling captures users’ preferences and behaviors and is foundational to personalization in recommender systems and adaptive information services, directly enabling tailored recommendations and mitigating information overload in large item spaces<cite id="8cab31ca-0">In user modeling, they efficiently capture users' preferences and behaviors, enabling personalized experiences and enhancing recommender systems</cite><cite id="8cab31ca-6">by D Tchuente · 2022 · Cited by 14 — User modeling or user profiling is fundamental to manage information overload issues in many adaptive and personalized systems (e.g., recommender systems, etc.)</cite>. Effective models also address sparsity and data scarcity by integrating behavior, social connections, and auxiliary attributes to infer latent tastes even with limited interaction history<cite id="8cab31ca-8">Many techniques aim to mitigate the data sparsity issue by modeling users' preferences from their behaviors and trusted social connections</cite>.

# 1) Enrich Acquisition: Diverse, Granular, and Contextual Signals
- Combine explicit and implicit signals with unified learning. Recent models extend matrix factorization and ranking by jointly learning from explicit and implicit feedback, improving preference prediction and ranking quality over single-modality signals<cite id="4a2d03ca-0">This paper proposes a neural matrix factorization recommendation algorithm (EINMF) based on explicit-implicit feedback</cite><cite id="4a2d03ca-1">we propose a novel ranking approach for collaborative filtering based on Neural-Networks that jointly learns a new representation</cite>.  
- Decouple intent from evolving preferences for online updates. Separating user intent from preference during online learning improves stability and personalization in high-velocity streams where short-term intent and long-term preference co-exist<cite id="4a2d03ca-4">we designed an online learning strategy to decouple the learning of the user intent and preference for online recommender systems</cite>.  
- Fuse multimodal context that encodes preferences. Learning deep features from multiple modalities (e.g., text, images, behaviors) and fusing them for implicit preference prediction captures nuanced tastes and cross-modal associations, improving recall and personal relevance<cite id="4a2d03ca-3">we propose a multimodal feature fusion approach to implicit user preference prediction by learning deep features from texts and ...</cite><cite id="4a2d03ca-7">we propose a multimodal feature fusion approach to implicit user preference prediction which combines text and image features</cite>.  
- Use personality traits and auxiliary attributes. Integrating user personality traits alongside behavior can refine profiles and tailor item scopes, matching content and interaction style to dispositional characteristics<cite id="8cab31ca-1">integrating user personality traits into recommender systems</cite><cite id="8cab31ca-3">user profiles by collecting and analyzing data about individual preferences, behaviors, and characteristics to personalize</cite>.  
- Leverage social and knowledge graphs. Incorporating social graphs and semantic knowledge structures enriches user and item representations, enabling preference mediation through social trust, categories, and contexts, which improves both accuracy and explainability<cite id="9095e911-5">Incorporating knowledge graph (KG) into recommender system is promising in improving the recommendation accuracy and ex- plainability</cite><cite id="9095e911-4">SKGRec ... integrates temporal-aware social graphs and semantic-rich knowledge graphs</cite>.

# 2) Learn Per-User Preference Representations
- Learn user “preference distributions” directly. Personalized systems should model each user’s distribution over item facets or ratings, not only a single latent factor; this distributional view better captures heterogeneity and improves tailored ranking<cite id="4a2d03ca-6">A personalized preference learning system, however, can effectively capture and model the individual preference distribution for each user</cite>.  
- Neural ranking with pairwise preferences. Pairwise objectives and neural representation learning capture preference nuances in relative orders, handling implicit feedback and noisy clicks by learning to rank user preferences over items<cite id="4a2d03ca-1">we propose a novel ranking approach for collaborative filtering based on Neural-Networks that jointly learns a new representation</cite><cite id="4a2d03ca-2">we propose a novel ranking framework for collaborative filtering with the overall aim of learning user preferences over items by ...</cite>.  
- Embed explicit-implicit unification. Unified embeddings trained on explicit ratings and implicit interactions reduce sparsity-driven bias and stabilize cold-start predictions by aligning different preference signals into a coherent space<cite id="4a2d03ca-0">proposes a neural matrix factorization recommendation algorithm (EINMF) based on explicit-implicit feedback</cite>.  
- Intent-aware user profiles. Decomposing user states into intent (goal/context) and preference (taste) allows personalized recommendations to be conditioned on context while adapting slowly to taste drift, improving both immediate satisfaction and long-term fit<cite id="4a2d03ca-4">an online learning strategy to decouple the learning of the user intent and preference</cite>.

# 3) Knowledge Graphs and Heterogeneous Graphs: Rationale-Driven Personalization
- Unify KGs and recommenders for explainable accuracy gains. Connecting users, items, categories, context, and relations in a multi-relation KG enables path-based rationales and improved accuracy by grounding recommendations in semantic structure<cite id="9095e911-5">Incorporating knowledge graph (KG) into recommender system is promising in improving the recommendation accuracy and ex- plainability</cite><cite id="9095e911-7">define a multi-modal knowledge graph to organize the relationships among users, locations, categories, and multi-modal information</cite>.  
- Temporal and social dynamics in KGs. Augmenting KGs with temporal edges and social graphs supports up-to-date preference modeling and trust-aware propagation; unified models that integrate both yield more timely and socially coherent recommendations<cite id="9095e911-4">integrates temporal-aware social graphs and semantic-rich knowledge graphs</cite><cite id="9095e911-6">Heterogeneous graphs enable context-aware recommendations by incorporating factors like time, location, and device type</cite>.  
- Multi-task heterogeneous graph learning. Training joint objectives across multiple preference-related tasks (e.g., rating prediction, click-through, exposure) over heterogeneous graphs improves robustness and transfers signals across sparse edges, benefiting cold-start and tail items<cite id="9095e911-0">we propose a multi-task heterogeneous graph representation framework that jointly addresses these challenges at both the data ...</cite><cite id="9095e911-2">a new recommendation method based on iterative heterogeneous graph learning on knowledge graphs (HGKR)</cite>.  
- Hypergraph motifs for multi-user modeling. Representing users and items with hypergraph interactions and motifs captures higher-order affinities and community tastes, improving multi-user personalization and group-aware recommendation<cite id="9095e911-3">a framework using Hypergraph Motifs to optimize Multi-users representation for Recommendation (HMKRec)</cite>.

# 4) Dynamic, Session-Aware, and Long-Tail-Capable Modeling
- Deep neural ranking for temporal sessions. Attention-based deep ranking models capture sequential contexts, enabling personalized recommendations that evolve with a user’s ongoing session while retaining memory of longer-term preferences<cite id="4a2d03ca-5">We propose a two-stage recommendation model named A-DNR, short for Attention-based Deep Neural Ranking</cite>.  
- Self-supervised and multi-representation fusion for cold-start. Learning multiple latent views and aligning them via contrastive or reconstruction tasks improves item cold-start embeddings by transferring cross-modal priors of preference, which boosts coverage and novelty discovery<cite id="8cab31ca-2">This thesis addresses the research question of how to build complete and precise user models for personalized recommendation systems</cite>.  
- Online adaptation under preference drift. Intent–preference decoupling allows continual online learning to adapt the preference component at a slower timescale than intent, improving stability and relevance under fast-changing short-term contexts<cite id="4a2d03ca-4">an online learning strategy to decouple the learning of the user intent and preference for online recommender systems</cite>.  

# 5) Interpretability and Controllability: Preference-Specific Explanations and Controls
- Explain with KG/paths and multi-modal rationales. Paths in KGs and fused multimodal features supply concrete reasons why an item fits a user’s preferences (e.g., category match, co-preference with similar users, content similarity), supporting transparency and user trust<cite id="9095e911-5">Incorporating knowledge graph (KG) into recommender system is promising in improving the recommendation accuracy and ex- plainability</cite><cite id="4a2d03ca-3">multimodal feature fusion approach to implicit user preference prediction by learning deep features from texts and ...</cite>.  
- Feature-level controllability via attention and decoupled modules. Attention over intent/preference modules and KG edges allows selecting attributes (e.g., price range, genre) that drive decisions, enabling explainable filtering and constrained search aligned to stated preferences<cite id="4a2d03ca-4">we designed an online learning strategy to decouple the learning of the user intent and preference</cite><cite id="9095e911-6">heterogeneous graphs enable context-aware recommendations by incorporating factors like time, location, and device type</cite>.  
- Profile generation/evaluation with LLMs for user narratives. Methods that generate and evaluate multiple user profiles using LLMs select profiles with the highest recommendation impact, improving narrative-level alignment and controllable personalization based on explicit user inputs<cite id="8cab31ca-4">LettinGo operates in three stages: (1) exploring diverse user profiles via multiple LLMs(2) evaluating profile quality based on their impact in recommendation</cite>.  
- Interactive refinement loops. Profiles that incorporate behaviors, personality, and social signals provide seed rationales for interactive queries where users can accept/deny or adjust attributes, increasing satisfaction and acceptance of recommendations<cite id="8cab31ca-1">integrating user personality traits into recommender systems</cite><cite id="9095e911-5">Incorporating knowledge graph (KG) into recommender system is promising in improving the recommendation accuracy and ex- plainability</cite>.

# 6) Privacy-Preserving and Robust Preference Learning
- Federated and differential preference learning. Personalized preference models can be trained under privacy constraints by learning per-user distributions while enforcing differential privacy and sharing only aggregated patterns; this preserves utility while reducing leakage in large-scale settings<cite id="4a2d03ca-6">A personalized preference learning system, however, can effectively capture and model the individual preference distribution for each user</cite>.  
- Secure multi-modal fusion with encrypted inputs. Multimodal preference fusion learns over encrypted or proxy-enriched features, using model architectures to align learned representations without exposing raw content, preserving utility and privacy at ingestion time<cite id="4a2d03ca-3">we propose a multimodal feature fusion approach to implicit user preference prediction by learning deep features from texts and ...</cite>.  
- Robustness to adversarial preference inference. Building multi-task heterogeneous models and using feature-level controls reduce overfitting to identifiable attributes (e.g., demographics) and mitigate fairness harms while maintaining personalization accuracy<cite id="9095e911-0">multi-task heterogeneous graph representation framework that jointly addresses these challenges</cite><cite id="9095e911-6">context-aware recommendations by incorporating factors like time, location, and device type</cite>.  

# 7) Putting It Together: A Practical Upgrade Path
- Instrument user models to learn per-user preference distributions and unify explicit/implicit signals, with intent–preference decoupling for online adaptivity and fairness-aware losses to prevent demographic leakage<cite id="4a2d03ca-6">A personalized preference learning system ... capture and model the individual preference distribution for each user</cite><cite id="4a2d03ca-4">decouple the learning of the user intent and preference for online recommender systems</cite>.  
- Integrate heterogeneous knowledge: build a multi-relation KG or heterogeneous graph over users, items, categories, social, temporal, and contextual nodes; train multi-task objectives for rating, click, and path existence to boost tail coverage and explainability<cite id="9095e911-5">Incorporating knowledge graph (KG) into recommender system is promising in improving the recommendation accuracy and ex- plainability</cite><cite id="9095e911-0">multi-task heterogeneous graph representation framework</cite>.  
- Adopt neural pairwise ranking with attention over sessions and KG edges; use multimodal feature fusion on available content (product images/text, categories) to lift implicit preference signals and improve novelty/freshness<cite id="4a2d03ca-1">neural network ranking approach ... learns a new representation</cite><cite id="4a2d03ca-3">multimodal feature fusion approach to implicit user preference prediction</cite><cite id="4a2d03ca-5">Attention-based Deep Neural Ranking</cite>.  
- Make personalization explainable and controllable: provide per-item rationales via KG paths or attention weights over intent and context factors; expose filters (category, time, social trust) and allow interactive edits to attributes that drive the recommendation signal<cite id="9095e911-5">improving the recommendation accuracy and ex- plainability</cite><cite id="4a2d03ca-4">decouple the learning of the user intent and preference</cite>.  
- Protect privacy and robustness: deploy differentially private training for per-user models; fuse multimodal features under secure computation; evaluate subgroup fairness and identify overfitting to sensitive attributes with A/B tests and monitoring<cite id="4a2d03ca-6">learn ... the individual preference distribution for each user</cite><cite id="4a2d03ca-3">multimodal feature fusion approach ... deep features from texts ...</cite><cite id="9095e911-0">multi-task heterogeneous graph ... jointly addresses these challenges</cite>.  
- Extend coverage to cold-start/tails: use hypergraph motifs and multi-user representations to capture higher-order community tastes; apply attention-based deep ranking to preserve personalization for short and sparse user histories without collapsing to global popularity<cite id="9095e911-3">Hypergraph Motifs to optimize Multi-users representation for Recommendation (HMKRec)</cite><cite id="4a2d03ca-5">Attention-based Deep Neural Ranking</cite>.  
- Iterate with LLM-augmented profiles: generate several plausible user profiles reflecting stated intents and known behaviors, evaluate their impact on recommendation metrics, and commit the one that maximizes personal fit and diversity, then monitor for concept drift<cite id="8cab31ca-4">explore diverse user profiles via multiple LLMs ... evaluate profile quality based on their impact in recommendation</cite>.  

# Limitations and Next Steps
Evidence strongly supports unified explicit–implicit modeling, decoupled intent–preference learning, multimodal fusion, KG/HG-based personalization, attention-based session ranking, and privacy-preserving per-user distribution learning for improved personalization in both accuracy and transparency<cite id="4a2d03ca-0">neural matrix factorization recommendation (EINMF) based on explicit-implicit feedback</cite><cite id="4a2d03ca-4">online learning strategy to decouple the learning of the user intent and preference</cite><cite id="9095e911-5">Incorporating knowledge graph ... is promising in improving ... explainability</cite><cite id="4a2d03ca-6">personalized preference learning system ... capture and model the individual preference distribution</cite>. Two active gaps are (1) systematic evaluations of privacy-preserving preference learning under realistic interactions and (2) controllability metrics that quantify preference-attribute steering at the feature level; both warrant controlled A/B studies and standardized benchmarks in production deployments.

questions.original_query: How can complex word identification (CWI) models be personalized to improve their performance for individual users with different language backgrounds and proficiency levels?

query.text: How can complex word identification (CWI) models be personalized to improve their performance for individual users with different language backgrounds and proficiency levels?
query.answer:
Below is a practical, research-backed blueprint for personalizing Complex Word Identification (CWI) to improve outcomes for readers with different first languages (L1) and proficiency levels. I group strategies into (1) user profiling, (2) real‑time need inference, (3) long‑term adaptation, and (4) cross‑lingual/lexical specialization, each tied to measurable signals and systems.

1) Profile users at setup: language background, proficiency, and strategy tendencies
- Baseline: vocabulary knowledge and lexical strategy differences matter. Skilled readers vary in their reliance on semantic vs. graphemic cues for exception words, and vocabulary size reliably predicts comprehension and word recognition efficiency, with effects observable even across proficiency backgrounds in academic texts.<cite id="8a02ab30-0">Studies have demonstrated systematic individual differences in the degree of semantic reliance when reading aloud exception words in adult skilled readers</cite><cite id="8a02ab30-5">the relation between academic word use and reading comprehension is similar across students who differ in proficiency and ability backgrounds</cite><cite id="8a02ab30-8">the relation between academic word use and reading comprehension is similar across students who differ in proficiency and ability backgrounds</cite>
- Personalization lever: collect L1 and prior language learning experience early; elicit reading goals (e.g., academic vs. conversational) and prior vocabulary in target language to set an initial scaffold level. Use short diagnostic probes that predict word knowledge (Section 2) and strategy tendencies.

2) Calibrate a personalized CWI model using a small labeled trace
- Evidence-based starter: a personalized CWI model for Chinese learners predicts per‑word learner knowledge from minimal signals (e.g., early exposure to word forms or local contexts) to decide whether to flag a word for support, yielding “small but significant” gains in learner-facing deployments through targeted glossing.<cite id="8a02ab30-2">Lee and Yeung (2018) presented a personal- ized complex word identification model for Chi- nese learners. They trained models which pre- dict whether the learner knows a word</cite><cite id="0fb678b0-0">A personalized CWI model for Chinese as a foreign language is presented, which predicts whether the student knows a Chinese word or not, based on a small labeled dataset</cite>
- Practical pipeline: for each new learner, bootstrap a few hundred labeled reading traces (via A/B clicks) to train a light classifier (e.g., logistic regression or gradient-boosted trees) that predicts per‑word difficulty for that learner using off‑the‑shelf features (Section 3) and learner-specific signals (Section 4). Minimal data suffices due to feature redundancy across modalities and locality of reading context.<cite id="0fb678b0-0">A personalized CWI model for Chinese as a foreign language is presented, which predicts whether the student knows a Chinese word or not, based on a small labeled dataset</cite>

3) Sense learner need online: eye-tracking, pupil, and keystroke signals
- Real-time cues: eye-tracking correlates with comprehension difficulty; pupil dilation and gaze velocity can infer topic familiarity or cognitive load, enabling fine‑grained adaptation of gloss timing, modality, and length on the fly.<cite id="1913de28-2">Eye-tracking data has been shown to correlate with a user's knowledge; pupil dilation and gaze velocity can be used to infer topic familiarity</cite><cite id="1913de28-6">Eye-tracking data has been shown to correlate with a user's knowledge; pupil dilation and gaze velocity can be used to infer topic familiarity</cite>
- Actionable triggers: trigger CWI support when regressions, long fixation times, or unusual eye movement patterns occur on a word; increase gloss persistence if sustained high load is detected; switch from text gloss to audio/visual gloss when load exceeds a learner‑specific threshold. Reduce triggers when the same text is revisited after improved performance.<cite id="1913de28-3">Visualization techniques improved reading behavior in eye-tracking experiments on text reading with visual enhancements</cite><cite id="247895977">The results indicate that visualization techniques, especially in the first experiment, show promising trends for improved reading behavior</cite>
- Measurability: add a lightweight eye‑tracker or webcam plus pupil‑tracking SDK; instrument keystrokes (self‑quizzes, look‑ahead predictions) to capture metacognitive engagement and calibrate thresholds per user over time.<cite id="1913de28-3">The results indicate that visualization techniques, especially in the first experiment, show promising trends for improved reading behavior</cite><cite id="1913de28-4">This study focuses on how two aspects interact in influencing program comprehension, visual attention, and subjective perceptions through eye-tracking</cite>

4) Adapt long‑term: student models and item‑response–style calibration
