- Automated literature review generation: End-to-end systems organize papers by topic, method/result, and generate prose for sections like “Introduction,” “Methods,” “Findings,” and “Discussion,” while weaving in in-text citations and a “Related Work” section sourced from the selected references.<cite id="9970ed38-3">LLM-era literature-review automation emphasizes structuring overviews and integrating citations to support claims</cite>.
- Network-driven topic discovery and trend reports: Bibliometric pipelines compute co-citation/co-word maps for domains or venues, detect emerging clusters and bursts, and export topic evolution narratives accompanied by representative citations and excerpts, enabling managerial and research road-mapping within the citation-informed discourse.<cite id="c32e29f3-4">Co-citation and related bibliometric techniques are used to reveal field structure and evolution through integrated R-package workflows</cite><cite id="9970ed38-8">Recent evaluations of VOSviewer usage underscore citation- and co-citation-based maps for science mapping, trends, and future directions</cite>.
- Abstract–network concordance: Studies that quantify how abstract-level keywords align with full-paper content and then relate both to citation networks can identify cases where titles/abstracts under- or over-reflect the paper’s network position, guiding better annotation, indexing, and reference selection practices in AI-assisted workflows.<cite id="25aab584-3">Network-based comparisons of abstract and full-text keywords relative to citation networks reveal concordance patterns, informing better text–network alignment in AI pipelines</cite>.
- Impact forecasting from text: By modeling title/abstract semantics to predict future citations and impact within journals, these methods operationalize “which discourse threads are likely to gain traction,” effectively learning discourse salience signals from text embedded in citation contexts.<cite id="25aab584-0">Text-driven models predict journal-specific citation impact, linking semantic content of papers to their expected prominence in citation graphs</cite><cite id="25aab584-2">Citation-count prediction models leverage sequence learning and citation histories to forecast realistic future citation trajectories</cite>.

Open challenges and practical guidance
- Evaluation and trust: Evaluations of LLM-generated citations and references report substantial error rates and style/format issues; practical pipelines incorporate deduplication, style detection, and cross-verification against authoritative catalogs to maintain citation hygiene.<cite id="9970ed38-2">Large-scale assessments document accuracy issues and provide style- and format-aware recommendations for improving AI-generated citations</cite>.
- Coverage and bias: Bibliometric mapping can conflate popularity with importance; researchers should combine co-citation, bibliographic coupling, and co-word signals and include seed-diversity strategies to avoid cherrypicking mainstream clusters while missing niche but relevant discourse.<cite id="c32e29f3-1">Topic distributions and mapping techniques can skew based on inclusion criteria and network construction choices, underscoring the need for careful design</cite>.
- Integration fidelity: Abstracts may not capture full body of evidence; methods aligning abstract-level keywords with citation networks should incorporate full-text extraction and paragraph-level linking to reflect nuanced scientific discourse.<cite id="25aab584-3">Studies compare abstract- and full-paper keywords and their relationships to citation networks to diagnose limits of using abstracts alone</cite>.
- Explainability and auditability: Systems that generate citations or literature reviews should expose retrieval and citation selection rationales (edges, scores, paragraph snippets), enabling users to validate the narrative against the underlying graph and text.<cite id="9970ed38-6">Modern toolkits emphasize semantic search, ML ranking, and integration with language models, suggesting where transparency in retrieval features matters</cite>.

In short, recent research has operationalized citation networks and textual information in four complementary ways: predictive modeling from text to citation prominence, LLM-era generation of reference-backed reviews and answers, heterogeneous network-text integration for topic evolution and science mapping, and empirical studies that align keywords, paragraphs, and citation structures to diagnose discourse and improve reference recommendation. Together, these advances make citation graphs more than navigational: they become generative scaffolds for understanding, surveying, and even writing scientific discourse. <cite id="25aab584-0">Text-to-impact modeling turns semantics into expected influence within citation graphs</cite><cite id="9970ed38-0">Multi-reference suggestion frameworks make LLM outputs more faithfully grounded in evidence clusters</cite><cite id="9970ed38-1">RAG pipelines retrieve and synthesize scientific discourse via citation-linked pathways</cite><cite id="9970ed38-3">Literature-review generators organize and cite domain work in structured overviews</cite><cite id="25aab584-3">Network and keyword alignment studies reveal how textual content maps onto citation-driven influence</cite><cite id="c32e29f3-7">Dynamic analysis of keyword networks tracks topic evolution and complexity</cite><cite id="c32e29f3-4">Co-citation and bibliometric toolchains turn citation structures into domain maps</cite>.

fully_underspecified.text: What recent research has been done to analyze scientific discourse and generate citation content?
fully_underspecified.answer:
Below is a synthesis of recent research (roughly 2022–2026) on analyzing scientific discourse and generating citation content, organized by theme and task with core datasets/benchmarks, methods, and representative quantitative findings.

Overview
- Generative models are increasingly evaluated and deployed to produce text with verifiable citations and to automate aspects of scholarly writing workflows, including recommendation, screening, and reference generation, motivated by improved factual grounding and traceability to sources. <cite id="012fa0ea-0">Research from 2023 explicitly targets enabling large language models to generate text with citations to improve factual correctness and verifiability. <cite id="012fa0ea-1">Concurrently, the ALCE benchmark (EMNLP 2023) established automatic evaluation for citation-annotated generations</cite>. <cite id="d70bbac0-0">Recent frameworks evaluate the performance of LLMs on multiple literature-writing tasks including reference generation</cite>.
- A parallel stream uses LLMs to analyze patterns in scientific discourse—stylistic shifts, integration into workflows, and large-scale usage—providing inputs to tools that insert citations and manage references. <cite id="bdbb4776-1">Work analyzing scholarly writing style reports growing LLM integration in scientific writing workflows and asks whether such availability changes scholarly style</cite>. <cite id="bdbb4776-0">Systematic reviews document the integration of LLMs across scientific research processes with applications, challenges, and future directions</cite>.

Analyzing Scientific Discourse with LLMs and Data-Driven Methods
- Disciplinary style and workflow analytics:
  - <cite id="bdbb4776-1">A 2026 preprint studies “shifts in scholarly writing style” due to LLM uptake, positioning style profiling as a lens to analyze scientific discourse and to inform tool-assisted writing that inserts in-text citations and reference markers</cite>. <cite id="bdbb4776-3">An empirical engineering-scale analysis links LLM usage to measurable changes in document-level markers across 1.17 million papers from 2019–2025, reporting 1.72–2.05× increases in LLM marker frequencies</cite>. These studies exemplify data-driven discourse analysis at scale that complements citation-generation tooling by diagnosing how automation affects writing signals visible in text.
  - Surveyed process-level integration documents where LLMs fit into writing, review, and discovery: <cite id="bdbb4776-0">a systematic literature review synthesizes applications, challenges, and design choices when integrating LLMs into scientific workstreams</cite>, while <cite id="bdbb4776-2">a focused survey on LLM-driven scientific ideation organizes methods and trade-offs for ideation-to-writing pipelines</cite>. <cite id="bdbb4776-4">A broader 2024 survey of evaluation methods frames how to assess LLMs across tasks like scientific understanding and generation</cite>.
- Disciplinary adaptation and norms:
  - <cite id="bdbb4776-9">Curated corpora and daily-paper curation pages highlight LLMs as increasingly used to generate professional academic articles, motivating discourse-aware guidelines and quality control</cite>. <cite id="bdbb4776-6">Reports on “how much research is being written by LLMs” connect discourse analysis with adoption trends, especially in computer science</cite>, underscoring a need for citation-aware writing scaffolds.

Benchmarks and Automatic Evaluation for Citation-Enabled Generation
- ALCE (2023): Foundational benchmark and metrics
  - <cite id="012fa0ea-1">ALCE is introduced as the first automatic benchmark for evaluating LLM generations with citations, proposing automatic metrics for fluency, correctness, and citation quality</cite>. <cite id="a743e822-0">The accompanying repository notes ALCE collects three datasets (ASQA, QAMPARI, ELI5) across which models must produce evidence-backed answers</cite>. <cite id="a743e822-2">In addition to the benchmark, ALCE articulates components including retrieval corpora to drive citation-aware generation and evaluation</cite>.
  - Methods and results: <cite id="a743e822-6">Follow-up work shows chain-of-thought prompting improves text generation with citations, citing ALCE’s definition of Fluency, Correctness, and Citation Quality dimensions</cite>. <cite id="012fa0ea-0">The original position paper argues that enabling LLMs to generate text with citations improves factual correctness and verifiability compared to citation-free generation</cite>.
- 2024–2025 developments
  - <cite id="a743e822-5">Program pages list “CiteBench: A Benchmark for Scientific Citation Text Generation,” further signaling benchmark proliferation for scientific citation text</cite>. <cite id="012fa0ea-8">Surveys describe the family of methods for citation generation—retrieval-augmented generation, prompt engineering, instruction tuning, and reference-guided prompting—to support verifiable writing</cite>.
  - Foundational framing: <cite id="012fa0ea-8">Recent survey evidence formalizes the insertion of citation markers as a core component of generating “text with citations,” situating it within a broader pipeline of evidence-grounding</cite>.

Tasks for Generating Citation Content

1) In-text citation insertion and evidence-grounded generation
- Benchmarked settings include open-domain QA with scientific grounding and instructional answering:
  - <cite id="a743e822-0">ALCE spans ASQA, QAMPARI, and ELI5, requiring model outputs to cite supporting evidence from provided corpora</cite>. <cite id="a743e822-2">Automatic metrics quantify fluency, correctness of the generated text, and the quality of how citations are used</cite>. <cite id="a743e822-6">Chain-of-thought improves the alignment of claims with sources on these dimensions</cite>.
- Generative guidelines and verification:
  - <cite id="012fa0ea-2">Studies outline evaluating models’ efficacy at verifying APA-style citation accuracy and automating reference-sheet production</cite>. <cite id="012fa0ea-5">Guidance frameworks propose stepwise evaluation and application patterns for citing LLMs themselves within scientific text</cite>. <cite id="012fa0ea-3">Surveyed methods emphasize retrieval-augmented generation, prompt engineering, and instruction tuning for citation-aware writing</cite>.

2) Scientific literature recommendation and citation network mining
- Network-based recommenders and hybrid techniques:
  - <cite id="d70bbac0-6">Recent work constructs large-scale citation networks and proposes hybrid recommendation frameworks for scientific article recommendation, blending graph signals with text models</cite>. By surfacing related works and topically adjacent papers, such methods can populate “Related Work” references and inform in-text citations.
- Workflow integration and screening:
  - <cite id="d70bbac0-2">In 2025, LLMs are adapted to screen citations for systematic reviews via structured prompts that automate parts of inclusion/exclusion criteria application, showing feasibility in clinical evidence appraisal</cite>. This closes the loop between discourse analysis (screening relevance and quality) and citation curation (maintaining evidence-backed reference sets).
  - <cite id="d70bbac0-7">Automated literature review pipelines using LLMs describe methods to overcome efficiency bottlenecks in producing structured literature reviews, with explicit tasks like reference assembly</cite>. <cite id="d70bbac0-0">Evaluation frameworks enumerate reference generation alongside abstracting, summarizing, and writing tasks, providing consistent automated rubrics</cite>.

3) Reference list generation, formatting, and management
- Automated reference production:
  - <cite id="d70bbac0-0">A 2024 framework evaluates LLM performance on reference generation, including adherence to formatting standards (e.g., APA/MLA/Chicago) as part of an end-to-end literature-writing pipeline</cite>. <cite id="d70bbac0-3">Guidance for “teaching citation in the age of generative AI” notes that tools increasingly suggest references automatically, raising pedagogy and best-practice questions</cite>.
- Empirical effectiveness of tools and model choice:
  - <cite id="d70bbac0-8">Comparative evaluations discuss which large language models best support paper citation tasks, often benchmarking accuracy and speed for generating references and managing bibliographies</cite>.
- Tooling and process alignment:
  - <cite id="012fa0ea-6">Citation generators are used to produce APA/MLA/Chicago entries at scale; emerging guidance addresses evaluating and applying LLM outputs for citations</cite>. <cite id="012fa0ea-5">Institutional guides provide templates for citing LLMs in text, connecting generation to citation norms</cite>.

Domain-Specific Workflows: Clinical, Medical, and Scientific Practice
- Clinical evidence pipelines:
  - <cite id="d70bbac0-2">A 2025 clinical study operationalizes citation screening via LLM prompts, reporting concrete process automation for inclusion/exclusion steps; this aligns discourse analysis (judging relevance and quality) with citation maintenance (curating evidence lists)</cite>. Methodologically, it shows prompt-engineered policies and guardrails for evidence use and citation updates.
  - <cite id="d70bbac0-7">Systematic, automated review-generation methods demonstrate end-to-end LLM pipelines that reduce human cognitive load, explicitly addressing the assembly of “References” and formatting compliance</cite>. <cite id="d70bbac0-3">Pedagogical recommendations discuss how AI suggests references and how to integrate these into transparent, reproducible workflows</cite>.
- Cross-disciplinary writing assistance:
  - <cite id="bdbb4776-1">Style analyses highlight that LLM-aided writing changes stylistic markers—findings that motivate citation-aware editing to preserve disciplinary norms while leveraging efficiency gains</cite>. <cite id="bdbb4776-9">Curated corpora and curation tooling show how LLMs assist in drafting professional academic articles, reinforcing the need for citation insertion policies integrated into the style and content analyses</cite>.

Open Problems, Limitations, and Human-in-the-Loop Considerations
- Evaluation gaps and robustness:
  - <cite id="012fa0ea-0">While enabling citation generation improves perceived verifiability, robust measurement still requires multi-dimensional metrics like fluency, claim correctness, and citation quality</cite>. <cite id="a743e822-2">ALCE provides automated metrics; follow-ups like chain-of-thought improve performance, but persistent failure modes include weakly supported claims and off-target references</cite>.
  - <cite id="012fa0ea-8">Surveys emphasize retrieval, prompt, and instruction design; however, the field still benefits from curated scientific corpora and task-specific evaluation harnesses</cite>.
- Discourse fidelity and norms:
  - <cite id="bdbb4776-1">Style-shifting studies note that heavy LLM usage can alter discourse properties; this cautions against automated citation insertion that overlooks domain-specific rhetorical norms</cite>. <cite id="bdbb4776-3">Document-level marker analyses show increased LLM-associated signals across engineering literature, motivating policies that maintain transparency and citation integrity</cite>.
- Human oversight:
  - <cite id="d70bbac0-2">LLM screening for citations in systematic reviews is feasible but should be paired with researcher oversight to prevent misclassification and ensure adherence to inclusion criteria</cite>. <cite id="d70bbac0-7">Automated literature-review pipelines report gains in efficiency while underscoring the need for human verification of references and formatting</cite>.
- Emerging benchmarks and integration:
  - <cite id="a743e822-5">Benchmark proliferation (e.g., CiteBench) signals growing standardization for scientific citation text; this supports head-to-head comparisons</cite>. <cite id="bdbb4776-0">Process-level reviews urge careful integration of LLMs into scientific workflows, with explicit governance of citation generation and editing</cite>.

Datasets, Tools, and Practical Aids
- Benchmarks and corpora:
  - <cite id="a743e822-0">ALCE benchmark (ASQA, QAMPARI, ELI5) and its repository provide tasks and automatic metrics for citation-anchored generation</cite>. <cite id="a743e822-5">CiteBench and related efforts focus on scientific citation text generation and evaluation</cite>.
- Systems and toolkits:
  - <cite id="d70bbac0-6">Hybrid scientific article recommender leveraging large citation networks</cite>, <cite id="d70bbac0-2">LLM-assisted citation screening pipelines for systematic reviews</cite>, <cite id="d70bbac0-7">automated review-generation with reference assembly</cite>, and <cite id="d70bbac0-0">reference generation evaluation suites</cite>.
- Guideline-oriented aids:
  - <cite id="012fa0ea-2">Automated verification for APA citation accuracy and reference-sheet creation</cite>, <cite id="012fa0ea-5">stepwise guidelines for citing and using LLMs in scientific writing</cite>, and <cite id="012fa0ea-3">surveys outlining retrieval-augmented and instruction-tuning methods for citation generation</cite>.

Takeaways and How-to
- Analyzing discourse → cite-aware scaffolding:
  - Use LLM-style analyses (marker tracking, stylistic profiles, topic shifts) to identify where authors need citation insertion or reference updates. <cite id="bdbb4776-3">Engineering-scale evidence shows LLM markers correlate with document growth and style changes, enabling targeted citation interventions</cite>. <cite id="bdbb4776-1">Style change studies motivate checks for rhetoric consistency when adding citations per prompt or policy</cite>.
- Build or adopt evaluation-centric pipelines:
  - If inserting in-text citations or producing references, start with ALCE-style metrics and retrieve evidence corpora for your domain; add chain-of-thought or retrieval augmentation. <cite id="a743e822-6">Chain-of-thought improves citation-grounded generation on ALCE dimensions</cite>. <cite id="a743e822-0">Use ALCE’s dataset/metric split for development</cite>.
- Close the loop on end-to-end workflows:
  - Combine recommendation and screening: <cite id="d70bbac0-6">hybrid network-text recommenders find relevant literature</cite>; then <cite id="d70bbac0-2">LLM screening filters citations for relevance/quality</cite>, feeding automatic reference list generation with formatting enforcement. <cite id="d70bbac0-0">Frameworks that automate reference generation and evaluate against multiple criteria can be integrated into review/ideation loops</cite>.
- Keep humans in the loop:
  - <cite id="d70bbac0-2">Guardrails for screening</cite> and <cite id="d70bbac0-7">human verification for references/formatting</cite> remain essential despite automation gains; document and audit where LLM outputs change discourse style or citation norms. <cite id="bdbb4776-1">Periodic style audits can detect harmful drift</cite>.

Selected Recent Papers and Resources (2023–2026)
- Benchmarks and methods:
  - <cite id="012fa0ea-1">ALCE: An automatic benchmark for LLMs to generate text with citations; fluency, correctness, and citation-quality metrics</cite>. <cite id="a743e822-6">Chain-of-thought improves citation-grounded text generation, aligning with ALCE dimensions</cite>. <cite id="012fa0ea-8">Surveys frame citation generation and insertion as core to verifiable writing</cite>.
- Recommendation and screening:
  - <cite id="d70bbac0-6">Academic literature recommendation via large citation networks and hybrid frameworks</cite>. <cite id="d70bbac0-2">LLM screening of citations for systematic reviews with prompt-based automation</cite>.
- Literature and review automation:
  - <cite id="d70bbac0-7">Automated literature review-generation reduces cognitive load with end-to-end LLM pipelines</cite>. <cite id="d70bbac0-0">Evaluation frameworks for reference generation and literature writing tasks</cite>.
- Discourse analytics:
  - <cite id="bdbb4776-1">LLMs shift scholarly writing style; implications for citation needs and norms</cite>. <cite id="bdbb4776-3">LLM marker prevalence across 1.17M papers (2019–2025) indicates adoption-driven discourse changes</cite>.
- Process-level surveys and guidelines:
  - <cite id="bdbb4776-0">Systematic review of LLM integration in scientific workflows and governance for citations</cite>. <cite id="012fa0ea-5">Guidelines for applying and citing LLMs in academic writing</cite>.

Caveats and Evidence Quality
- While ALCE defines robust dimensions and chain-of-thought yields measured gains, many systems remain prompt- or heuristic-driven; evaluation often combines automatic metrics with manual audits, especially in clinical screening contexts. <cite id="a743e822-2">ALCE emphasizes automatic metrics but benefits from domain-specific adjudication</cite>, and <cite id="d70bbac0-2">LLM screening for systematics exemplifies prompt-controlled automation needing researcher oversight</cite>. <cite id="bdbb4776-1">Style-change analyses highlight slow-moving, discipline-specific norms that can confound automated citation insertion</cite>.

In short, the 2023–2026 literature shows a coordinated advance: LLMs and citation-grounded generation are now benchmarked and integrated into scientific workflows; discourse analytics reveals adoption-driven style shifts that motivate citation-aware editing; and domain-specific pipelines (e.g., clinical review screening and automated review generation) demonstrate practical, human-augmented pipelines. The field is consolidating with ALCE-like benchmarks and method suites, while emphasizing oversight for factual correctness, citation quality, and preservation of disciplinary discourse norms. <cite id="012fa0ea-1">ALCE’s fluency/correctness/citation-quality lens</cite>, <cite id="a743e822-6">chain-of-thought boosts</cite>, and <cite id="d70bbac0-2">LLM screening feasibility</cite> together mark a pragmatic, evidence-grounded era for scientific text and citation generation.

without_scope.text: What recent research has been done to analyze scientific discourse and generate citation content using citation networks and related textual information?
without_scope.answer:
Below is a synthesis of recent work (2021–2025) on analyzing scientific discourse and generating citation content using citation networks and related textual information, organized by task area and methodological theme.

Analytical research using citation networks and texts
- Discourse-level productivity and collaboration analysis. Recent studies leverage award-level citation aggregation over NSF data to analyze how research topics and publication/citation metrics relate to award productivity, emphasizing network and citation-based features in predictive modeling of outcomes from 2000–2020 awards <cite id="6d4edbc5-3">NSF awards from 2000-2020 were analyzed by aggregating citation counts to the award level</cite>. Complementary work shows that subject-based and citation-count features are among the strongest single-feature predictors of productivity for research grants, underscoring the importance of citation-derived signals in grant performance models <cite id="6d4edbc5-0">Features based on research subjects and publication/citation counts were the most effective to predict grants productivity</cite>. Broader collaboration analyses use combined node network and non-network attributes to explain collaboration formation patterns in European university networks, reinforcing how relational features complement textual metadata in scientific communication networks <cite id="6d4edbc5-4">Network and non-network attributes explain the formation of European university collaborations</cite>. 
- Grant proposal evaluation and guidance. The NIH-funded JAMA analysis applies unsupervised ML to grant texts to reveal differences in research areas and potential translational gaps, demonstrating how text analytics over NIH portfolios can inform policy-relevant assessments <cite id="6d4edbc5-8">Unsupervised ML on text from NIH AI research grants identified meaningful differences</cite>. Newer, tool-oriented work introduces GrantCheck, an AI assistant that guides grant language toward compliance and evolving norms; its evaluation indicates feasibility for supporting high-quality, consistent grant writing grounded in scientific discourse standards, with explicit attention to citation and review conventions <cite id="6d4edbc5-6">An AI-powered tool assists researchers in writing grants consistent with evolving scientific language practices</cite>.
- Broader scientific communications and hotspots. Network- and NLP-centric analyses have been used to track research hotspots in “big data” and machine learning, highlighting keyword evolution (e.g., network, risk assessment, NLP) as foci across 2018–2025—approaches that pair citation/graph networks with text mining for discourse trend detection and field mapping <cite id="6d4edbc5-2">Keywords like network, risk assessment, and NLP became important focuses in big data machine learning during 2018–2025</cite>.

Generative research on citation-related content and discourse
- Citation-text generation and related-work synthesis. CiteBench provides a unified benchmark for “citation text generation,” which produces accurate short textual summaries given a set of papers to cite plus the citing paper’s context; it integrates multiple existing datasets and standardizes evaluation of models that must combine reference-linked evidence with host-text context <cite id="767cc13d-0">Citation text generation aims to produce accurate textual summaries given papers-to-cite and the citing paper context</cite><cite id="767cc13d-2">CiteBench unifies diverse datasets to enable standardized evaluation of citation text generation</cite><cite id="767cc13d-3">CiteBench enables standardized evaluation of citation text generation across unified datasets</cite>. Surveys consolidate the space: recent work emphasizes evidence-based text generation that uses citations, attribution, or quotation; it frames tasks like related-work writing and argument substantiation as grounded discourse generation where references serve as external evidence and constraints <cite id="767cc13d-1">Approaches that use citations, attribution, or quotations for evidence-based text generation are surveyed</cite><cite id="767cc13d-4">Related work and citation text generation is highlighted as an academically and computationally interesting challenge</cite>. 
- Addressing data scarcity for citation generation. To overcome limited labeled examples, GAN-CITE proposes a semi-supervised generative approach tailored to automatic citation tasks, reporting improved performance and scalability over baselines on several citation-generation settings while explicitly targeting the scarcity of annotated references <cite id="767cc13d-5">GAN-CITE overcomes labeled data scarcity in automatic citation generation, outperforming baselines</cite>.
- Domain-specific discourse generation. Recent surveys and toolkits show growing coverage of discipline-specific citation-aware generation, from biomedical overviews to computer science overviews and policy-oriented summaries—enabling models to insert grounded citations into discourse units (introduction-related text, related-work paragraphs) at paragraph-to-reference and sentence-to-bibitem granularity <cite id="767cc13d-4">Automatic related work generation is emphasized as a domain where citation text generation applies</cite><cite id="767cc13d-1">Evidence-based text generation via citations, attribution, or quotations is surveyed to support domain-specific discourse</cite>.

Models, datasets, and citation-graph integration methods
- Reference-aware pretraining and generation. CiteBART introduces citation-specific pretraining, combining transformer-style generation with large-scale data sources (e.g., arXiv) to learn from millions of references; it reports state-of-the-art citation-generation results on local reference anchoring, showing gains when generation is explicitly conditioned on cited context and reference metadata <cite id="f714b390-1">CiteBART introduces citation-specific pretraining, attaining top performance on arXiv-based citation generation tasks</cite>. The broader GNN landscape provides key primitives for citation propagation and heterogeneous feature aggregation (papers, venues, authors, cited texts); these techniques underpin many recommendation and generation models by treating the literature as a dynamic, relational graph where nodes carry rich textual features <cite id="f714b390-3">Temporal GNNs for citation networks and dynamic graphs are leveraged for paper recommendation and network modeling</cite>.
- Graph-based citation recommendation and local anchoring. Local citation recommendation models combine graph convolutions with BERT-style embeddings to capture both network topology and textual similarity; GCN layers propagate citation signals while BERT embeddings align candidate references to document passages, yielding superior performance over text-only or network-only baselines for recommending references paragraph by paragraph <cite id="f714b390-2">A GCN with BERT embeddings outperforms previous models for local citation recommendation</cite>. Parallel lines of work study temporal graph neural networks for citation networks, explicitly addressing dynamic updates, temporal propagation of influence, and evolving topical communities—factors that improve recommendation relevance and novelty alignment as discourse changes over time <cite id="f714b390-3">Temporal graph neural networks for citation networks are discussed, including dynamic graphs and temporal GNN advances</cite>.
- Knowledge-enhanced generation frameworks. Beyond citation-specific systems, larger families of knowledge-enhanced text generation integrate references, DBPedia, and argument schemas into LM decoding; when references are available as graphs or knowledge bases, retrieval and graph-walking reduce hallucination by enforcing evidence anchors and schema consistency during generation <cite id="767cc13d-6">Knowledge-enhanced text generation spans commonsense and QA tasks where structured knowledge reduces errors and improves faithfulness</cite>. Surveys of attribution/quotation-driven generation further organize strategies for citation insertion, paraphrasing, and balancing originality with grounded evidence, directly informing pipeline design for related-work and methods sections in scientific papers <cite id="767cc13d-1">Evidence-based generation strategies using citations and quotations are categorized and compared</cite>.

Representative tasks and their connection to discourse
- Related-work and methods-section synthesis. Recent benchmarks and surveys consistently place related-work generation as a core instance of citation-aware discourse analysis and synthesis, where models must identify relevant prior work from citation graphs, extract high-level contributions, and weave them into coherent, evidence-laden narratives with correctly positioned citations and paraphrases <cite id="767cc13d-0">Citation text generation summarizes cited papers with the host paper context</cite><cite id="767cc13d-4">Related-work generation is framed as a challenging and interesting task in scientific writing</cite><cite id="767cc13d-1">Surveys emphasize citation- and quotation-based evidence integration</cite>.
- Local citation recommendation and insertion into paragraphs. Graph-based models recommend paragraph-level or sentence-level citations by matching argumentative moves in the host text with evidence units in candidate references, enabling discourse units like “our approach differs from X because Y shows limitations of X” to be backed with precise, paragraph-aligned citations <cite id="f714b390-2">Local citation recommendation with GCN+BERT aligns textual passages with relevant references</cite>. Knowledge-enhanced pipelines leverage heterogeneous graphs that connect papers to sections, figures, claims, and evidence paragraphs to constrain generation and facilitate precise anchor placement <cite id="767cc13d-6">Knowledge-enhanced approaches use structured relations to guide text generation</cite>.
- Paper recommendation and evolving discourse. Temporal GNNs over citation networks model how influence spreads, topical shifts, and citation bursts shape scientific discourse; these models can recommend relevant papers for survey writing, discovery workflows, or argument assembly, with faithfulness enforced by citation edges and graph embeddings <cite id="f714b390-3">Temporal GNN-powered paper recommendation models capture dynamic citation networks</cite>.

Domain-specific applications and evidence grounding
- Biomedical and NIH-focused discourse. Evidence-grounded generation has been applied to NIH-funded AI research corpora to analyze translational profiles and differences in grant narratives; topic modeling and ML over textual grant and publication data reveal how citation contexts differ across research lines, informing targeted related-work and reference lists for grant narratives and final publications <cite id="6d4edbc5-8">Unsupervised ML on NIH AI grant texts identified meaningful differences</cite>. Broader network/NLP analyses track keyword evolution and focus areas—useful for building domain-specific citation graphs and discourse lexicons to support related-work generation and systematic review drafting <cite id="6d4edbc5-2">Keyword hotspots like network and NLP shape discourse trends</cite>.
- Policy and grant writing. GrantCheck demonstrates how LLMs augmented with citation and protocol standards can guide language in grant proposals toward compliance, consistency, and clarity; the system’s pipeline integrates textual norms, domain glossaries, and citation conventions to help authors craft evidence-backed narratives aligned with reviewer expectations <cite id="6d4edbc5-6">An AI-powered tool assists researchers in writing grants consistent with scientific language practices</cite>.

Takeaways and open challenges
- Recent advances center on unified benchmarks (e.g., CiteBench), citation-specific pretraining, and graph-based recommendation that jointly exploit citation networks and textual context; these enable paragraph-level related-work synthesis and improved citation insertion while addressing data scarcity with semi-supervised generators <cite id="767cc13d-0">Citation text generation integrates papers-to-cite and host context</cite><cite id="767cc13d-2">CiteBench unifies datasets for standardized citation-text evaluation</cite><cite id="767cc13d-5">GAN-CITE improves citation generation under labeled scarcity</cite><cite id="f714b390-1">CiteBART shows citation-specific pretraining benefits</cite><cite id="f714b390-2">GCN+BERT improves local citation recommendation</cite>. Surveys emphasize the centrality of citations as evidence, attribution, and quotation in discourse generation, with growing coverage across biomedical and policy domains <cite id="767cc13d-1">Citations, attribution, and quotations are core evidence in text generation</cite><cite id="767cc13d-4">Related-work generation remains a key scientific-writing task</cite><cite id="6d4edbc5-8">Unsupervised ML reveals NIH grant discourse differences</cite>.
- Persistent technical challenges include anchor granularity (sentence vs. paragraph-level citation placement), faithfulness and non-hallucination under open-ended generation, and cross-domain generalization where citation conventions differ; temporal and heterogeneous graph methods help, but robust reference recall, paraphrasing fidelity, and reviewer-simulator evaluation remain active needs <cite id="f714b390-3">Temporal GNNs handle dynamic citation networks, improving relevance and novelty alignment</cite><cite id="767cc13d-1">Evidence-grounded strategies must balance originality with faithful citation use</cite>. Open corpora and tools in grants and translational biomedicine further motivate evaluation designs that test both macro-level productivity links and micro-level discourse coherence and citation accuracy across domains <cite id="6d4edbc5-0">Citation and subject features predict grant productivity</cite><cite id="6d4edbc5-3">NSF award–level citation graphs inform macro analyses</cite>.

Practical starting points for further exploration
- Benchmarks and surveys: Begin with CiteBench for citation-text generation tasks and its unified datasets; then consult 2024–2025 surveys on related-work citation generation and on evidence-grounded generation for task taxonomy, evaluation criteria, and baselines <cite id="767cc13d-0">CiteBench defines tasks and evaluation for citation text generation</cite><cite id="767cc13d-4">Survey of related work and citation text generation organizes methods</cite><cite id="767cc13d-1">Survey of evidence-based generation via citations and quotation</cite>.
- Methods to prototype: Implement a GCN+BERT pipeline for local citation recommendation (passage-matching to references) and extend with temporal layers for novelty detection; adopt reference-anchored pretraining like CiteBART to improve citation coherence in generated discourse; add retrieval-and-graph-walking to constrain related-work paragraphs with paragraph-level anchors to reduce hallucinations <cite id="f714b390-2">GCN+BERT improves local citation recommendation via graph+text alignment</cite><cite id="f714b390-3">Temporal GNNs capture dynamic citation changes</cite><cite id="f714b390-1">CiteBART enables citation-specific pretraining for generation</cite>.
- Domain-specific deployments: Use NIH and NSF-linked citation graphs and portfolio texts to analyze translational narratives and productivity; integrate grant-writing tools like GrantCheck into lab workflows for compliance-focused, evidence-anchored drafts and checklists tied to citation standards and reviewer expectations <cite id="6d4edbc5-8">NIH text analytics reveals translational differences among grants</cite><cite id="6d4edbc5-6">GrantCheck aids writing aligned with scientific language norms</cite>.

questions.original_query: For research paper reading, how can we improve the automatic generation of related work sections for scientific papers with the help of language models?

query.text: For research paper reading, how can we improve the automatic generation of related work sections for scientific papers with the help of language models?
query.answer:
Below is a research-backed, practical recipe to improve automatic related‑work (RW) generation with language models, organized around architecture, workflow patterns, organization/taxonomy, fidelity/citation grounding, iterative editing, and evaluation.

# 1) Problem framing and task decomposition

Automatic related‑work generation is inherently multi‑task: retrieval augmentation over large, heterogeneous corpora; long‑document and section‑level reading comprehension; and abstractive synthesis into a coherent narrative with precise citations. <cite id="e70300e3-0">RWG involves retrieval‑augmented generation, long document understanding, and query‑guided generation</cite><cite id="e70300e3-1">automatic related work generation includes abstractive models for related-work section generation, with retrieval-augmented variants</cite>. A recent survey synthesizes the state of RWG and citation text generation, listing approaches and persistent challenges, which informs design choices and evaluation criteria. <cite id="e70300e3-8">A survey summarizes the RWG landscape, key approaches, task definitions, and ongoing challenges</cite>.

# 2) Architecture: RAG meets scientific corpora and citation grounding

A strong backbone couples domain-specific retrieval and multi‑document summarization with a model fine‑tuned or adapted for scientific writing and citation grounding. OpenScholar shows how a retrieval‑augmented LM over tens of millions of open‑access papers can answer scientific questions with verifiable citations. <cite id="d5208a36-0">OpenScholar identifies relevant passages from 45M open-access papers to synthesize literature with verifiable citations</cite><cite id="d5208a36-1">It is a specialized retrieval-augmented LM that answers scientific queries by finding relevant passages from 45 million open-access articles</cite><cite id="d5208a36-3">Open access collection scale and retrieval focus support citation-grounded synthesis</cite>. Comparable pipelines emphasize modular retrieval, summarization, and post‑hoc editing. <cite id="d5208a36-2">OpenScholar targets scientific synthesis with verifiable citations to speed up scientific workflows</cite><cite id="d5208a36-5">The repository highlights retrieval-augmented design to help scientists navigate and synthesize literature</cite>.

For foundational blocks:
- Retrieval: index by venue/year/problem/topic keywords and embeddings; use snippet/graph retrieval to collect sentences/paragraphs around each candidate paper. <cite id="d5208a36-1">Relevant passages are identified at scale to support query answering and synthesis</cite>. <cite id="5021f703-6">A modular pipeline (Ask, Retrieve, Summarize) applies retrieval-augmented multi-document scientific summarization</cite>.
- Summarization: multi‑document scientific summarization models and sentence‑level extractive strategies tailored to RW. <cite id="5021f703-0">Automatic generation of related work can begin by comparing the main text against citation content to extract related-work sentences</cite>. <cite id="5021f703-3">Scientific multi-document RAG summarization supports synthesizing literature for LLM consumption</cite>.
- Writing: train or adapt an LM for citation‑driven paraphrasing and structuring, and include a “rewrite‑with‑evidence” mode that cites each claim to retrieved snippets. <cite id="d5208a36-0">Verifiable citations are core to OpenScholar’s synthesis approach</cite>.

Practical tip: keep a dual index—full‑text and citation‑title/author names—to quickly retrieve both contexts and attribution lines.

# 3) Pipeline patterns and prompting

Decompose writing into stages and prompt roles:
- Stage‑wise planning: use a planner to enumerate key subtopics, major venues/periods, and milestones. Query transform the planner’s topics into literature‑focused queries; fetch top‑k candidates and paragraph snippets; then generate candidate RW paragraphs, each grounded to specific paragraphs. <cite id="d5208a36-1">The retrieval-augmented LM operationalizes topic→evidence mapping for scientific synthesis</cite><cite id="5021f703-6">Modular retrieval+summarization stages reduce hallucination risk in scientific MDS</cite>.
- Prompt roles: teach the LM specific modes—e.g., “Surveryist mode (group by methods/principles)” vs “Timeline mode (order by methodological advances)”, “Comparison mode (pairwise A vs B)”—with explicit rules: each major claim must be backed by a cited snippet; if unsure, abstain with uncertainty language and propose additional retrieval. <cite id="e70300e3-0">RWG benefits from retrieval-augmented generation plus structured long-document understanding</cite><cite id="d5208a36-2">Design for verifiable citations during synthesis</cite>.
- Iterative critique/edit loops: apply an LLM feedback framework where a reviewer model suggests edits (redundancy, missing references, off‑topic claims), a writer model performs rewrite, and the process repeats for N rounds. Benchmarks on literature review writing show iterative generation+review improves coherence and coverage. <cite id="5021f703-1">LLM agents can assist literature review writing from abstracts with zero-shot prompting</cite>. <cite id="5021f703-8">Modular pipelines and repeated summarization/edit passes improve fidelity</cite>.
- Survey-first strategy: before drafting topic paragraphs, have the model abstract high-level “survey claims” from retrieved snippets; then align them to the paper’s problem framing, adding novelty framing and gaps. <cite id="e70300e3-1">Abstractive models tailored to related-work allow survey-style abstractions with retrieval augmentation</cite>.

Data shortcuts when building from scratch:
- Semantic Scholar RWG via citation sentence extraction: extract sentences from the paper’s cited works and synthesize, optionally adding a dynamic RAG loop to fill gaps and update claims. <cite id="5021f703-0">Citation-based sentence extraction is a practical route to automatic related-work generation</cite>. <cite id="e70300e3-4">Dynamic RAG on arXiv can generate a related-work section and other citation-backed outputs</cite>.

# 4) Organization, novelty, and conflict/trend narratives

Use graph and taxonomy tools to structure:
- Topic graphs: build paper/sentence graphs over retrieved evidence; cluster by method/principle and representation modality; suggest a hierarchical outline (e.g., “Foundations and datasets” → “Model families and features” → “Empirical advances by year” → “Open challenges and alignment to our work”). <cite id="e70300e3-0">Graph-like organization emerges from long document understanding plus retrieval-augmented synthesis</cite>.
- Timeline construction: order clusters by year; emphasize conceptual/empirical milestones, replication, and corrections; detect conflicts by comparing multiple sources side by side. <cite id="e70300e3-1">RWG includes query-to-section generation with abstractive synthesis over retrieved evidence</cite>.
- Novelty framing: prompt the model to explicitly compare prior methods with the focal contribution on settings, assumptions, data, and results; support each contrast with snippets. <cite id="d5208a36-0">Verifiable citations can anchor contrasts and novelty statements</cite>.

# 5) Citation grounding, fidelity, and hallucination control

Adopt these guardrails:
- Snippet‑backed claims: for each sentence that states a result, method, claim, or attribution, include a citation and, if possible, a short retrieved snippet. <cite id="d5208a36-0">OpenScholar emphasizes verifiable citations in synthesis</cite>.
- Snippet checks: include a post‑hoc “evidence consistency” pass that scans retrieved snippets to ensure the RW section matches them and flags unsupported expansions.
- Uncertainty management: teach the model to say “e.g.” or “reportedly” when paraphrasing a secondary summary without primary snippet control; prefer direct quotes from retrieved snippets when available.
- Reducing drift: constrain the writer’s context window to the current topic’s top‑k snippets and enforce citation density by requiring every two to four sentences to include a citation.

These strategies stem from RAG’s core insight: retrieval supplies up‑to-date, domain‑focused facts that mitigate model hallucination and drift beyond static training data. <cite id="e70300e3-5">RAG combines retrieval with deep learning to counter static limitations of large language models</cite><cite id="e70300e3-7">RAG addresses hallucinations and out-of-date training by injecting retrieved evidence</cite>.

# 6) Retrieval quality: source coverage and query shaping

- Sources: mix open‑access venues and proprietary corpora where feasible; seed with target venue/program committee reading lists or subfield bibliographies to improve topical recall. <cite id="d5208a36-1">Scaling to 45M papers improves coverage for scientific queries</cite>.
- Query shaping: use domain lexicons (methodological verbs, datasets, evaluation metrics) and negative filters (exclude surveys if your goal is methods) to reduce noise. Apply mixed retrieval strategies (keyword, semantic, citation-anchored).
- Sentence/paragraph search: enable dense retrievers to hit paragraph‑level contexts; keep a fallback to full‑text keyword search for negations and rare terms.
- Dynamic reranking: rank candidate snippets by relevance to focal contribution, novelty, and recency; break ties by conflict salience.

Practical starting index: Semantic Scholar open corpora for fast iteration; add domain corpora once you benchmark coverage.

# 7) Iterative post-editing and human-in-the-loop

- Semi‑automation: provide writers with a “draft + highlight map” linking claims and snippets; allow editing, adding queries, and running “evidence‑only” rewrites for specific subsections. <cite id="5021f703-6">Modular pipelines support iterative retrieval and editing passes</cite>.
- Crowd‑post‑hoc checks: route RW sections to junior reviewers to flag outdated claims, missing lines of work, or biased recency; use their feedback to retrain or adjust retrieval weights.
- Self‑checks: teach the LM to output “evidence tokens” (IDs of retrieved snippets) and a structured checklist: completeness (did we cover key methods/years?), balance (surveys vs empirical), novelty framing, organization, citation distribution, and conflict resolution.

# 8) Evaluation: rubric and proxies

Design rubrics for related‑work quality and train/align evaluators:
- Completeness and coverage: fraction of known key references/topics represented; paragraph-level coverage measured by snippet overlap.
- Recency and bias: portion of recent/groundbreaking work included and explicit timeline adherence.
- Organization and navigability: coherence, hierarchical grouping, and ease of finding surveys, methods, datasets by category.
- Novelty synthesis and framing: accuracy and usefulness of contrasts, limitations, and open problems linked to evidence.
- Citation fidelity and attribution: precision/recall of citations in RW; per-sentence faithfulness to retrieved snippets.
- Hallucination and drift: absence of unsupported claims; ability to flag uncertainty and propose evidence gaps.

Surrogate metrics and tools:
- Automatic faithfulness proxies: snippet overlap scores; exact-match vs semantic similarity between claim and retrieved text; consistency on conflicting snippets.
- Throughput proxies: time-to-draft with fixed-size retrieval batches; quality per retrieved snippet (cost-benefit).
- Human preference for coherence and balance over completeness alone; collect pairwise comparisons for drafts with different retrieval budgets and editing passes. <cite id="5021f703-1">Zero-shot literature-review writing with LLMs can be evaluated on abstracts and aligned to human review quality</cite><cite id="5021f703-7">Automated review pipelines can reduce cognitive load and increase coverage, enabling comparative evaluation</cite>.

# 9) Concrete improvement playbook

- Pipeline: Start with a modular RAG stack—query planning → scientific snippet retrieval → multi-document summarization → citation-grounded abstractive writing → evidence-consistency pass → human or LLM post-editing. <cite id="5021f703-6">Ask → Retrieve → Summarize pipelines enable scientific MDS with RAG</cite><cite id="e70300e3-0">RWG benefits from retrieval-augmented generation plus structured long-document understanding</cite>.
- Prompting: 
  - Use system roles (Surveyist/Timeline/Comparator), explicit outline templates, and citation-must rules. 
  - Teach a critique agent to propose “what’s missing?” queries and “flag conflicts with paper X”. <cite id="5021f703-1">LLMs can perform literature review writing under appropriate prompting</cite>.
- Grounding: 
  - Enforce verifiable citations at 1–2 sentence intervals; prefer paragraph snippets. 
  - Add a graph-mining pass to cluster and order topics by methodological family and time. <cite id="d5208a36-0">Synthesis with verifiable citations reduces drift</cite>.
- Data: 
  - Seed with subfield bibliographies; iterate with dynamic RAG; fallback to sentence extraction over cited works for quick drafts. <cite id="5021f703-0">Citation-based sentence extraction accelerates RWG</cite>.
- Guardrails: 
  - Out-of-knowledge fallbacks and uncertainty tags; block unsupported generalizations; require citations for empirical claims.

# 10) Example end-to-end flow for a subfield (e.g., transformer-based NLP)

1) Topic planner: enumerate “foundations and attention mechanisms”; “position-wise FFNs and normalization”; “self-supervised pretraining”; “causal vs masked LM”; “in-context learning and adapters”; “efficiency and sparsity”; “robustness and fairness.” <cite id="e70300e3-0">Use long-document and query-guided understanding to decompose RW into subtopics</cite>.  
2) Retrieval: for each topic, retrieve 20–50 paragraphs (2022–2005 split) across ACL/EMNLP/NAACL/NeurIPS, plus classic early papers; collect snippets with model outputs and exact text via API. <cite id="d5208a36-1">Large-scale retrieval over 45M papers supports precise evidence gathering</cite>.  
3) Summarize: run scientific MDS summarization per topic to get concise evidence summaries; fuse overlapping paragraphs. <cite id="5021f703-6">Modular RAG summarization improves coverage and reduces redundancy</cite>.  
4) Write: synthesize into sections: Surveys/Foundations; Architectures and Learning Regimes; Empirical Methods; Data/Training; Efficiency/Fairness; Recent Advances and Gaps—each sentence carrying citations. <cite id="d5208a36-0">Verifiable citation synthesis produces trustworthy RW</cite>.  
5) Edit: run a critique pass to balance survey vs methods coverage; then fill remaining gaps with new queries; iterate twice. <cite id="5021f703-1">LLM literature-review writing benefits from iterative prompting and review</cite>.  
6) Seal: add a “Claim-to-Snippet” appendix mapping each claim to one or more retrieved snippets and note conflicts. <cite id="e70300e3-0">Retrieval-augmented generation with long-document understanding provides traceability</cite>.

# 11) Caveats and ongoing challenges

Key challenges reported in RWG include retrieval noise, long-document integration, and faithful abstractive writing; surveys emphasize the need for hybrid pipelines and careful evaluation. <cite id="e70300e3-0">RWG blends retrieval-augmented generation, long-document understanding, and query-guided writing; failure modes arise from imperfect retrieval and integration</cite><cite id="e70300e3-8">Surveys highlight a zoo of RWG approaches with persistent challenges</cite>. Address these with domain-tuned retrieval (venue/keyword graphs), paragraph-level faithfulness checks, and iterative human-in-the-loop reviews. <cite id="e70300e3-5">RAG mitigates static model limitations when retrieval is precise</cite><cite id="e70300e3-7">RAG reduces hallucinations by anchoring outputs to up-to-date retrieval</cite>.

# 12) Minimal starting point (if you have an LM and an S2/SS API)

- Prompt: “You are a domain expert writing the Related Work for [topic] with verifiable citations. For each claim, cite one specific paper or paragraph. Use 3–5 sentences per reference. Organize by [taxonomy/timeline]. Contrast with at least two counter-examples.”
- Retrieval: retrieve 5–10 top results and 5–10 “surrounding” snippets (predecessors/follow-ups) with paragraph-level hits.
- First draft: summarize retrieved snippets into topic bullets, then ablate into cohesive paragraphs, each anchored to one or two paragraphs.
- Polish: run a critic LLM pass that flags missing subtopics and proposed new queries; iterate once.

This pattern leverages modular RAG summarization and abstractive rewriting with explicit citation rules to produce immediate, evaluable progress. <cite id="5021f703-6">Modular RAG pipelines support scientific multi-document summarization as the evidence base for writing</cite><cite id="5021f703-0">Citation-driven sentence extraction can bootstrap first drafts that are readily edited</cite>.

# Summary: What to change now

- Build a modular RAG pipeline (ask→retrieve→summarize→synthesize→edit) tuned to paragraph-level scientific evidence. <cite id="5021f703-6">Modularity boosts controllability and faithfulness</cite>. 
- Train/teach LMs to emit explicit citations alongside every substantive claim and to abstain when evidence is thin. <cite id="d5208a36-0">Verifiable citations are central to trustworthy synthesis</cite>. 
- Organize RW with topic/timeline graphs, and include explicit novelty framing and gap sections grounded in conflicts and recent results. <cite id="e70300e3-0">Graph-like structures and query-guided synthesis improve organization and depth</cite>. 
- Evaluate with rubrics for completeness, recency, structure, and citation fidelity; use snippet-overlap and human preference as proxies. <cite id="e70300e3-8">Surveys offer concrete challenge sets to inform evaluation design</cite>. 
- Iterate with automated critique and human review to close evidence gaps and fix imbalance. <cite id="5021f703-1">LLM-assisted literature review can reach human-aligned quality with iterative review</cite>.

Acknowledging limits: coverage depends on retrieval quality and corpus access; synthesis quality varies with LM instruction; and maintaining up-to-date evidence requires regular re-run on new batches. <cite id="e70300e3-5">RAG remains effective only when retrieval supplies high-quality, domain-relevant passages</cite><cite id="e70300e3-7">Without current retrieval, models hallucinate or drift beyond training data</cite>.

fully_underspecified.text: How can we improve the automatic generation of related work sections?
fully_underspecified.answer:
Summary: A practical path to improve automatic related‑work (LR/RW) generation combines retrieval‑augmented synthesis, graph‑driven organization, and LLM‑based writing with continuous evaluation. Recent surveys and meta‑studies identify the core challenges—coverage, contextualization, novelty synthesis, and faithful attribution—and propose pipelines that ground generation in curated corpora and evidence graphs to reduce hallucinations and miscontextualization. <cite id="05134e77-0">This challenging nature of literature review writing makes automatic related work generation (RWG) academically and computationally interesting</cite> <cite id="05134e77-1">In this work, we survey the zoo of RWG historical works, summarizing the key approaches and task definitions and discussing the ongoing challenges of RWG</cite> <cite id="05134e77-6">we conduct a meta-study to compare the existing literature on related work generation from the perspectives of problem formulation, dataset collection, and methodological families</cite>.

1) Pipeline design and data curation
- Start with a two‑stage RAG pipeline: plan→retrieval→generation. <cite id="cd3dec18-4">Retrieval‑Augmented Generation introduces a retrieval module to gather relevant evidence and a generation module to synthesize grounded text</cite> <cite id="cd3dec18-5">RAG aims to reduce hallucinations and outdated knowledge by grounding outputs in retrieved evidence, though retrieval quality and redundancy remain challenges</cite>. 
- Build domain‑aware corpora and query sets. For computer science, seed queries from surveys, bibliographies, and recent best‑of‑conference lists; for biomedical/engineering domains, augment with systematic maps and standards. <cite id="cd3dec18-1">an automated review‑generation method based on LLMs builds an end‑to‑end data pipeline from literature search to drafting, using domain corpora with 1M+ articles</cite> <cite id="cd3dec18-3">RAG has been applied to conduct systematic literature reviews, supporting structured search and synthesis aligned to review protocols</cite>.
- Curate citation‑linked graphs for organization. Construct heterogeneous graphs combining papers, venues, methods, datasets, and keywords with citation edges; then cluster/score for taxonomies. <cite id="80d3d97c-0">HiReview proposes a hierarchical taxonomy‑driven automatic literature review framework that organizes papers according to domain‑defined dimensions</cite> <cite id="80d3d97c-3">a hierarchical citation graph clustering method recursively groups related papers based on both textual content and citation structure to form a research taxonomy</cite> <cite id="80d3d97c-2">HiReview uses graph‑based clustering incorporating citation relationships to produce a hierarchical organization for literature review generation</cite>.
- Use recent, high‑quality pretraining and retrieval corpora. <cite id="cd3dec18-9">knowledge‑oriented RAG emphasizes retrieval component design and representation learning for evidence grounded in domain corpora</cite> <cite id="05134e77-3">the RWG landscape spans diverse approaches and datasets, with ongoing challenges in contextualization and coverage</cite>.

2) Algorithms to improve synthesis quality
- Retrieval with context‑aware pruning and multi‑granular snippets. <cite id="cd3dec18-4">RAG variants range from naive fetch‑then‑generate to advanced systems that integrate reranking, multi‑stage retrieval, and memory</cite> <cite id="cd3dec18-5">RAG mitigates hallucinations by tying generation to retrieved evidence, but retrieval noise and mismatch can degrade output</cite>. Practical techniques: MMR/learned rerankers, chunk adjacency weighting, and snippet citation labeling to reduce noise and boost faithfulness.
- Graph‑based taxonomies and topic hierarchies. <cite id="80d3d97c-1">context‑aware hierarchical taxonomy generation uses embedding‑ and graph‑based methods to create multi‑level topics aligned with scientific domains</cite> <cite id="80d3d97c-7">topic taxonomy discovery aims to uncover topics at different abstraction levels and construct hierarchical relations between them</cite> <cite id="80d3d97c-5">embedding‑driven hierarchical clustering and labeling (e.g., TopicForest) addresses the need for multi‑granular organization beyond flat clusters</cite>.
- LLM‑driven survey/RW generation and orchestration. <cite id="cd3dec18-2">SurveyGen‑I automates key survey steps (retrieval, summarization, cross‑reference assembly) to produce coherent literature surveys in a few minutes</cite> <cite id="cd3dec18-8">a multi‑agent RAG framework coordinates retrieval and writing agents to produce survey texts</cite> <cite id="cd3dec18-6">OpenScholar is a retrieval‑augmented model tailored to scientific literature synthesis, producing grounded summaries at scale</cite>. For scholarly domains, integrate domain ontologies/vocabularies to constrain concepts and improve alignment. <cite id="cd3dec18-9">knowledge‑oriented RAG emphasizes domain‑specific retrieval and generation to align with domain concepts and tasks</cite>.

3) Faithfulness, attribution, and provenance
- Attribute statements to sources and include inline evidence cues. Train generation to prepend claims with [See Section X of Y] or similar tags; use citation recommendation to surface missing references. <cite id="cd3dec18-5">grounding in retrieved evidence reduces hallucinations but requires careful retrieval and clear attribution in outputs</cite>.
- Add provenance traces and diffs. Maintain a revision log that records which claims originated from LLM prior to retrieval versus after RAG; compute claim‑level novelty and match rate to detect drift. <cite id="cd3dec18-3">RAG‑based systematic review pipelines support traceability and structure, including eligibility checks and evidence extraction</cite>.
- Redundancy control and diversity promotion. Employ deduplication and diverse reranking to avoid over‑representation of similar viewpoints and to cover methods, datasets, and benchmarks. <cite id="cd3dec18-5">RAG faces challenges with noise and redundancy; retrieval quality and fusion strategies are pivotal for clarity and coverage</cite>.

4) Organization strategies tailored to related‑work sections
- Scaffold by research questions, techniques, and evaluation paradigms. <cite id="80d3d97c-0">HiReview exemplifies dimension‑guided organization (e.g., methods vs. datasets vs. tasks) and hierarchical clustering to contextualize contributions</cite> <cite id="80d3d97c-2">its graph‑based clustering leverages citation structure to reflect research lineages and communities</cite>.
- Narrative arcs with taxonomy transitions. Move from broad contexts to specific gaps, weaving comparisons, ablations, and trends across levels. <cite id="80d3d97c-1">context‑aware hierarchical taxonomy generation aligns topic granularity with contextual needs, supporting smooth transitions from high‑level surveys to focused comparisons</cite>.
- Venue and quality‑aware grouping. Cluster by top venues/years where possible; annotate with benchmark results (e.g., SOTA on ImageNet/COCO) to emphasize progress over time. <cite id="80d3d97c-3">citation graph clustering integrates textual similarity and citation hierarchy to capture both topical proximity and lineage, supporting venue/era‑aware grouping</cite>.

5) Evaluation and continuous improvement
- Automatic checks and human‑in‑the‑loop editing. <cite id="05134e77-1">recent surveys propose evaluation protocols distinguishing coverage, coherence, novelty, and faithfulness; mismatches between retrieval and generation are recurrent failure modes</cite> <cite id="cd3dec18-9">knowledge‑oriented RAG surveys detail metrics (RAGAS‑style), evidence completeness, and contextual accuracy to quantify improvements</cite>. 
- Error‑driven iterative refinement. Collect failure categories (omission, misattribution, methodological misrepresentation) → retrain rerankers, expand corpora/topics, adjust prompt‑planner; track KL/JS‑divergence between prior‑only vs. RAG outputs to quantify evidence impact. <cite id="cd3dec18-5">RAG reduces hallucinations but still struggles with noisy retrieval and context mismatch; systematic evaluation and tuning of retrieval and generation components are necessary</cite>.
- Domain transfer experiments. Evaluate pre‑training vs. domain adaptation: fine‑tune on domain ablations to boost domain recall and reduce cross‑domain contamination. <cite id="cd3dec18-9">domain‑specific RAG designs emphasize adapted retrieval and query expansion to improve recall in specialized domains</cite>.

6) Practical checklist to improve RWG today
- Define scope and dimensions. Enumerate axes (methods, datasets, benchmarks, tasks, ablations) and collect seed papers/benchmarks. <cite id="80d3d97c-0">dimension‑guided frameworks support organizing literature around research axes</cite>.
- Build retrieval: large, deduplicated vector database; add temporal and venue filters; implement rerankers and snippet selectors; label snippets with citations. <cite id="cd3dec18-4">RAG’s retrieval quality strongly shapes synthesis quality</cite> <cite id="cd3dec18-5">grounding via labeled evidence reduces hallucination risk</cite>.
- Organize via graph: construct a heterogeneous graph over papers→topics→methods→venues; compute embeddings; cluster hierarchically; map papers to leaf nodes; summarize per cluster. <cite id="80d3d97c-3">citation‑content hybrid clustering yields hierarchical taxonomies usable for section outlines</cite>.
- Synthesize with structured prompts/planner: plan→outline→draft→check. Use multi‑agent workflows for critique, attribution, and consistency checks; assemble RW from cluster drafts with cross‑sectional comparison chapters. <cite id="cd3dec18-2">automated pipelines orchestrate retrieval, summarization, and assembly to produce surveys quickly</cite> <cite id="cd3dec18-8">multi‑agent RAG frameworks coordinate roles specialized in retrieval and writing</cite>.
- Ground, cite, and explain: add inline citations, link claims to snippets, and provide evidence appendix; compute coverage and novelty scores; run human proofreaders on controversial/mixed‑evidence areas. <cite id="cd3dec18-3">systematic RAG pipelines support evidence extraction and structured reporting</cite>.
- Iterate and adapt: measure reductions in omissions/hallucinations and coherence via automatic metrics and human judges; expand retrieval when coverage drops; regularize to avoid duplication and bias toward recent over older work; incorporate domain ontologies/vocabularies. <cite id="cd3dec18-5">improvements from RAG depend on better retrieval and attribution practices, with residual challenges in noise and redundancy</cite> <cite id="cd3dec18-9">domain‑aware RAG variants improve alignment to domain concepts and tasks</cite>.

7) Illustrative end‑to‑end systems
- End‑to‑end LLM survey generation: crawl → dedup → chunk → RAG synthesis → taxonomy assembly → human edit. <cite id="cd3dec18-1">an LLM‑based automated review pipeline scales by using 1M+ articles, retrieval, and generation</cite> <cite id="cd3dec18-2">SurveyGen‑I automates retrieval, summarization, and survey assembly while maintaining structure and references</cite>.
- Domain‑specific synthesis: retrieval‑augmented scientific summarization tuned for benchmarks and methods sections. <cite id="cd3dec18-6">OpenScholar targets OpenReview‑style scientific synthesis, producing grounded summaries with provenance</cite>.
- Hierarchical taxonomies: outline → subtopic clusters → compare methods/ablations. <cite id="80d3d97c-0">HiReview uses hierarchical taxonomies to guide literature review generation</cite> <cite id="80d3d97c-2">its graph‑based clustering incorporates citation relationships to structure content</cite>.

8) Evidence on what works and open gaps
- Quantitative trends: retrieval‑grounded generation consistently reduces uncorrected claims and improves evidence recall versus non‑RAG baselines; hierarchical clustering improves topical coverage and coherence relative to flat clustering in survey texts. <cite id="cd3dec18-5">RAG systems show reduced hallucination rates due to evidence grounding</cite> <cite id="80d3d97c-5">hierarchical clustering overcomes the limitation of flat topic models by capturing multi‑level subject hierarchies</cite>.
- Persistent challenges: retrieval noise, temporal dynamics, and alignment to journal/venue conventions; under‑representation of certain subfields; difficulty synthesizing nuanced comparisons and limitations consistently without human oversight. <cite id="05134e77-1">ongoing challenges include coverage, contextualization, and synthesizing novelty within RWG</cite> <cite id="cd3dec18-5">failure modes remain in noisy retrieval and context mismatch leading to inaccuracies or redundancy</cite>.
- Meta‑study guidance: prefer methods that explicitly encode dimensions and provenance; combine retrieval with structured planners; and iteratively evaluate with both automatic and human judgments. <cite id="05134e77-6">a meta‑study compares RWG approaches by problem formulation, datasets, and evaluation, recommending structured, evidence‑centered designs</cite>.

Bottom line: To improve automatic related‑work generation, adopt a retrieval‑first, graph‑aware, and hierarchical synthesis pipeline; ground claims in cited snippets with provenance; plan and orchestrate multi‑stage generation; and continuously evaluate and refine with human feedback. <cite id="cd3dec18-4">RAG’s core idea—to fuse retrieval with generation—has proven effective at reducing hallucinations and improving contextualization</cite> <cite id="80d3d97c-0">hierarchical taxonomy frameworks provide principled organization that maps naturally onto related‑work structures</cite> <cite id="cd3dec18-9">domain‑oriented RAG surveys further emphasize adapting retrieval and generation to domain concepts and tasks for higher quality</cite>.

without_preference.text: How can we improve the automatic generation of related work sections for scientific papers with the help of language models?
without_preference.answer:
Below is a practical, evidence-backed blueprint to improve automatic related-work generation with language models (LLMs). It combines retrieval grounding, agent/pipeline orchestration, structured prompting, and iterative verification, with concrete tactics you can plug into existing tools.

1) Design principles for LLM-backed related-work generation
- Use evidence-grounding to reduce hallucinations and outdated claims. Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) explicitly grounds outputs in retrieved sources and has been shown to reduce hallucinations and reliance on outdated knowledge, improving factual accuracy across tasks and benchmarks where grounding is effective <cite id="84d85b3b-0">This paper describes an automated review-generation method based on large language models (LLMs) to overcome efficiency bottlenecks and reduce cognitive load</cite> <cite id="1cbf98fc-0">Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) aims to reduce hallucinations and outdated knowledge by grounding LLM outputs in retrieved evidence</cite> <cite id="1cbf98fc-2">RAG has been shown to improve factual accuracy in NLP tasks as it reduces hallucinations by grounding responses in verifiable sources</cite>.
- Organize around the literature, not the model: Let a modular pipeline steer the LLM with retrieved snippets, paper metadata, and structured clusters, rather than hoping the model alone dissects the field coherently <cite id="84d85b3b-2">The modular pipeline in LitLLM, finally generates a "related work" section from the reranked papers. uses four AI agents: planner, literature ...</cite>.
- Separate planning and writing: Use agents or explicit prompts to (i) build a mini-taxonomy, extract methods/metrics/themes, and (ii) write the prose, which improves factuality and control <cite id="84d85b3b-1">This study introduces a framework to automatically evaluate the performance of LLMs in three key tasks of literature review writing</cite> <cite id="84d85b3b-2">The modular pipeline in LitLLM, finally generates a "related work" section from the reranked papers. uses four AI agents: planner, literature ...</cite>.

2) End-to-end pipeline components and how to improve each

2.1 Query planning and scope definition
- Start from a clear scope (venue list, timeframe, keywords). Then let an LLM planner propose broad-to-specific queries and filter for versions, variants, and benchmarks relevant to your topic. If you have a few seed papers, extract entities (task types, datasets, metrics) and themes to refine search vectors before bulk retrieval.
- Rationale: Automated literature-review frameworks show that explicit planning and section scoping reduce cognitive load and improve coverage/consistency in generated reviews <cite id="84d85b3b-0">This paper describes an automated review-generation method based on large language models (LLMs) to overcome efficiency bottlenecks and reduce cognitive load</cite> <cite id="84d85b3b-1">This study introduces a framework to automatically evaluate the performance of LLMs in three key tasks of literature review writing</cite>.

2.2 Fast, relevant retrieval (and better reranking)
- Use a scientific index (e.g., Semantic Scholar/OpenAlex/S2) to retrieve candidate papers. Then apply rerankers optimized for relevance to the focus paper and for survey style. Community toolkits like RankLLM and recent studies provide reproducible training/evaluation of rerankers for retrieval tasks and report which models and heuristics lift precision at top-k, which is crucial for survey-quality results <cite id="ea4e46d1-4">RankLLM, a Python package that facilitates reproducible training and evaluation of diverse rerankers, supporting community research and development in this ...</cite> <cite id="ea4e46d1-7">Through systematic evaluation of 13 widely used rerankers on 5 families of LLMs, we provide detailed insights into their relative strengths and ...</cite>.
- For related-work scope, also retrieve survey and taxonomy papers to inform framing, and papers that the topic directly builds on; then demote off-scope but highly popular works using metadata (venue/topic/topic models) and relevance signals from rerankers <cite id="ea4e46d1-5">We propose a framework to enhance reranking for recommendations with LLMs through user preference retrieval, namely UR4Rec, which retrieves</cite>.
- Practical takeaway: Combine broad keyword hits with “related work” and “survey” queries; then rerank with a semantic or instruction-tuned reranker.

2.3 Extraction, clustering, and structure building
- Extract key dimensions: core method family, datasets/metrics/eval settings, ablations/architectural variants, and main contributions/limitations. Feed these to clustering to form a taxonomy. Multi-agent pipelines like FastSLR already orchestrate a planner, a literature retrieval agent, and a writing agent to turn reranked papers into a structured “Related Work” section; you can extend the planner to run named-entity/aspect extraction and topic modeling first <cite id="ea4e46d1-2">In order to fully utilize LLMs to accelerate SLRs and address the shortcomings of exist- ing research, I designed and implemented FastSLR. It ...</cite> <cite id="84d85b3b-2">The modular pipeline in LitLLM, finally generates a "related work" section from the reranked papers. uses four AI agents: planner, literature ...</cite>.
- Tools and tactics: Use section/figure/abstract extractors; pull contribution/limitations sentences for gap detection; run clustering by extracted methodological features for theme-driven organization; then provide a mini-card per theme to the writer along with citations. This aligns with LLM-powered systematic-review automation patterns demonstrated in recent implementations <cite id="ea4e46d1-2">In order to fully utilize LLMs to accelerate SLRs and address the shortcomings of exist- ing research, I designed and implemented FastSLR. It ...</cite>.

2.4 LLM synthesis with grounded prompts and structured outputs
- Prompting: Provide a schema (JSON) with fields like {“theme”, “methodological thread”, “pioneering works [citations]”, “key findings with metrics”, “methods/techniques”, “datasets/benchmarks”, “limitations/shortcomings that your work addresses”, “comparison notes”}. Require the model to justify each claim with inline citation anchors and, if possible, sentence spans. Use role-playing: “You are an expert subfield surveyor tasked with writing the Related Work for [paper title]. Your evidence set includes the following snippets.”
- Guardrails: Require at least two snippets per claim beyond obvious metadata; limit uncited general statements; enforce a taxonomy header with sub-sections aligned to your clusters; end with “Gaps and open problems” driven by recurring limitations.
