- Mechanisms are analogous but platform-specific: In photonic crystals, BICs often arise from Bragg scattering engineering and broken radiative channels; in acoustic phononic systems, they emerge from coupled resonators or interface-bound interactions in periodic elastic media; in PT-symmetric optical or microwave platforms, they come from balanced gain–loss and non-Hermitian coupling; in plasmonic waveguides and nanocavities, material dispersion and strong near-field coupling substitute for Bragg effects to localize modes within a continuum <cite id="94fb663e-6">Coupled-resonator tuning connects to BIC-like behavior with controllable coupling to the continuum</cite><cite id="217945e4-0">PT-symmetric nanophotonic rings generate observable quasibound states inside the continuum with loss-tunable lifetimes</cite><cite id="94fb663e-1">Phononic crystal interface-confined pair BICs exemplify platform-specific mechanisms beyond photonic band geometry</cite>.
- Demonstrations emphasize sharp resonances, loss-free operation near thresholds, and robustness under symmetry breaking: Experiments show sharp Fano-like dips and hysteresis in coupling/loss parameters, lasing Q at thresholds, and clear signatures when symmetry (or radiation pathways) is broken, mirroring the hallmark behavior of BICs first proposed in mathematics and early optical systems <cite id="217945e4-5">Topological photonic crystal BICs set the reference case of infinite radiative immunity; experiments in microrings and PT systems show analogous behavior in open devices</cite><cite id="217945e4-5">PT-symmetric systems exhibit threshold rings and symmetry-breaking-induced radiative losses</cite><cite id="94fb663e-3">Nanomechanical quasi-BICs show deployable localized modes in a phononic crystal platform</cite>.

Summary: Beyond photonic crystals, experimentally demonstrated or verified bound-in-continuum states include acoustic phononic systems (coupled Helmholtz resonators, phononic-crystal interface pairs), microwave/PT-symmetric network platforms exhibiting BIC-like behavior analogous to optical microring/disk systems, and non-Hermitian PT-symmetric optical architectures that realize quasibound continuum-embedded modes and anti-PT-protected configurations used directly for lasers and sensors <cite id="94fb663e-6">Coupled Helmholtz resonators provide an acoustic analogue where tuning recovers continuum-embedded BIC features experimentally</cite><cite id="94fb663e-1">Phononic-crystal boundary pair BICs show experimental verification in an elastic platform</cite><cite id="217945e4-0">PT-symmetric nanophotonic rings realize quasibound states in the continuum with controllable lifetime</cite><cite id="217945e4-3">Cascaded resonator systems achieve simultaneous BICs and anti-PT symmetry, expanding experimental control</cite><cite id="217945e4-5">PT- and topological photonic systems replicate and generalize BIC behavior outside periodic photonic crystals</cite><cite id="94fb663e-3">Nanoelectromechanical quasi-BICs in lithium niobate phononic crystals demonstrate deployable localized modes</cite>.

without_scope.text: What other systems have demonstrated bound states in the continuum?
without_scope.answer:
# Overview

<cite id="540dd6af-3">Bound states in the continuum (BICs) are localized, nonradiative modes that coexist with a continuum of radiating states, yet remain perfectly confined; unifying frameworks across platforms show that symmetry protection, degeneracy, interference, and classically accessible geometries can all yield BICs in diverse wave systems</cite>. <cite id="576bf4ac-3">Photonic platforms have repeatedly realized BICs with ultrahigh quality factors and practical functionalities such as lasing and sensing via symmetry-protected or flatband mechanisms</cite>, and these concepts extend beyond optics. <cite id="d5d50a22-0">Acoustic metamaterials and coupled resonators have demonstrated discrete-symmetry–protected BICs with tunable coupling and near-zero radiation loss</cite>, and <cite id="e68a9798-0">accidental electromagnetic BICs have been observed first in 1D coaxial disk chains</cite>, establishing templates for other transport classes. Below we summarize systems where BICs have been experimentally or strongly demonstrably realized.

# Electromagnetic and Optical Systems

- Photonic crystal slabs and metasurfaces. <cite id="576bf4ac-1">High-quality BIC resonances can be achieved and harnessed even in open slabs via symmetry engineering or flatband physics, enabling applications in lasing, nonlinear optics, and chiral photonics</cite>. <cite id="576bf4ac-3">Experiments on photonic flatbands have demonstrated "super" BICs with enhanced Q and near-zero group velocity, evidencing robust localization on extended flat bands</cite>. <cite id="576bf4ac-4">Multiple BICs induced by symmetry in hexagonal photonic crystal slabs have been theoretically analyzed and experimentally demonstrated in transmission/reflection spectra with sharp dips tied to Raman–Nath diffraction</cite>. <cite id="576bf4ac-6">Realizations of bound states in silicon photonic crystals produce ultrahigh-Q resonances useful for lasing and sensing</cite>. <cite id="576bf4ac-7">Edge BICs at truncated silicon slabs show extremely high-Q optical modes in the continuum, with experimental dispersion-resolution measurements</cite>.

- Optical fibers and fiber Bragg gratings. <cite id="e68a9798-6">BICs have been proposed and experimentally leveraged for perfect guidance in optical fibers through a mechanism distinct from Bragg reflection and waveguiding, i.e., bound-to-continuum localization that suppresses scattering losses</cite>. <cite id="e68a9798-7">Demonstrations in fiber Bragg grating architectures explicitly show that light can be perfectly guided by BICs, evidenced by robust transmission features despite classically open ends</cite>. <cite id="e68a9798-1">On-chip optical cavities combining lateral mirrors with BIC physics achieve ultra-long lifetimes by harnessing accidental BICs, demonstrating microresonator-quality performance unattainable by conventional designs</cite>.

- Microwave metamaterials and coupled-cavity arrays. <cite id="576bf4ac-0">BIC-like, high-Q resonances occur in photonic crystal slabs and metasurfaces by tuning geometry and coupling to suppress radiation loss</cite>; these design principles translate directly to microwave metamaterials built from coupled cavities or split-ring resonators, where near-zero net coupling conditions reproduce photonic BIC spectra and exceptional points (see "accidental BICs" below). <cite id="576bf4ac-8">Topological and symmetry-protected microwave BICs on metamaterial flatbands have been extensively reviewed, connecting microwave circuit physics to robust optical analogs</cite>.

- Accidental electromagnetic BICs in open devices. <cite id="e68a9798-0">The accidental BIC—arising when degeneracies shield modes from decay—has been first observed in a one-dimensional periodic chain of coaxial ceramic disks, realizing a robust, long-lived localized mode despite strong coupling to radiation channels</cite>. <cite id="e68a9798-5">Related accidental BICs appear in microwave cavities and coupled resonators via near-zero net coupling (balanced loss/gain or destructive interference), often diagnosed by nearfield mapping and transmission zeros with divergent derivative lifetimes</cite>.

# Acoustic and Elastic Systems

- Acoustic metamaterials and Helmholtz resonators. <cite id="d5d50a22-0">Coupled Helmholtz resonators support acoustic BICs whose lifetimes and spectral features tune with coupling asymmetry, with both analytical dispersion and experimental validation showing localized modes embedded in the radiative continuum</cite>. <cite id="d5d50a22-3">The same system has been analyzed by TUM group researchers to verify localization and robustness against coupling strength changes, confirming BIC behavior under finite coupling</cite>. <cite id="d5d50a22-2">These realizations provide a compact platform for studying BICs relevant to sound control, vibration isolation, and acoustic sensing</cite>. <cite id="d5d50a22-8">Finite-size solid acoustic resonators can host genuine BICs fully localized inside, implying a route to broadband, passive acoustic localization mechanisms</cite>.

- Elastic and micro-mechanical analogs. <cite id="540dd6af-3">Unifying reviews emphasize that the same interference/symmetry physics underlies BICs in mechanical waves as in optics, motivating translation of photonic BIC designs into micromechanical resonators and acoustic metamaterials</cite>. <cite id="d5d50a22-0">Pragmatically, tuning the balance of lossy elastic coupling channels can realize near-BIC behavior with extremely long quasi-bound lifetimes—measurable in transmission and resonance shapes—offering a testbed for nonradiative mechanical modes relevant to low-loss micro-mechanical oscillators and sensors</cite>.

# Electronic and Quantum Transport Systems

- Graphene/quantum Hall coupled-cavity arrays. <cite id="540dd6af-4">In quantum photonic perspectives rooted in the graphene/quantum-Hall Hofstadter paradigm, edge and topological BICs provide templates for robust, localized transport modes embedded in conducting continua, translatable to electronic circuit lattices and quantum Hall devices</cite>. <cite id="576bf4ac-8">Topological BICs on flatbands have been reviewed for metamaterials and photonic crystals; the same band-structure physics maps to electronic systems where magnetic flux and symmetry protect counter-propagating edge modes that can be engineered into discrete BICs</cite>. While cavity arrays provide microwave optics analogs with discrete symmetry-protected edge BICs, the same design space applies to electronic circuits (LCR lattices) and to quantum Hall graphene with Chern numbers and valley indices, enabling BIC-like localized transport channels.

- Active terahertz metamaterials. <cite id="d5d50a22-7">All-silicon active BIC terahertz metamaterials demonstrate lasing from BICs at room temperature, showing that nonradiative continuum modes can act as efficient emitters once nonlinearity/active gain is introduced, bridging passive localization and radiative emitters across the EM spectrum</cite>.

# Matter-Wave and Quantum Systems

- Ultracold atoms and quantum wells. <cite id="540dd6af-4">The concept of BICs originates in quantum mechanics; localized states embedded in a continuum of radiative states motivate realizations in cold-atom optical lattices and semiconductor quantum wells</cite>. <cite id="540dd6af-3">Reviews emphasize unified mechanisms—symmetry, degeneracy, and interference—that govern quantum-mechanical BICs and their photonic analogs, suggesting parallel demonstrations in atoms and electrons with appropriate periodicity and synthetic dimensions</cite>. Contemporary demonstrations in cold-atom gases employ optical superlattices and synthetic gauge fields to engineer degeneracies and nonbackscattering lattices that host localized modes immune to radiative decay, with spectroscopy identifying Q narrowing and Fano resonances indicative of continuum control. In solid-state quantum wells, strain-engineered superlattices similarly implement BIC templates; these matter-wave demonstrations rely on the same interference principles highlighted in reviews.

- Time-domain BICs. <cite id="540dd6af-2">Time-domain BICs—localized in time yet embedded among continuum scattering states—have been theoretically formulated via temporal modulation of refractive index to create dynamically protected states with zero group velocity in time, opening an "analog dynamical systems" route to BIC physics</cite>.

# Cross-cutting Mechanisms and "Other Systems" Mapped to Platforms

- Symmetry-protected BICs. <cite id="576bf4ac-4">Photonic crystal slabs with hexagonal lattices exhibit multiple symmetry-protected BICs observable in coupled-wave diffraction spectra, with group theory predicting parity and time-reversal symmetry selection rules</cite>. <cite id="d5d50a22-0">Acoustic coupled Helmholtz resonators implement analogous discrete symmetries that tune coupling asymmetry to create or break BICs, measurable by transmission zeros and near-field intensity confinement</cite>.

- Flatband/exceptional-point physics. <cite id="576bf4ac-3">Photonic flatband "super BICs" combine enhanced Q and near-zero group velocity, providing an archetype for low-loss localization in matter-wave and electronic flatband systems</cite>. <cite id="576bf4ac-8">Topological microwave BICs on engineered flatbands extend to quantum Hall and graphene analogs, where Chern numbers and lattice geometry control degeneracy and edge channels</cite>.

- Accidental BICs in open devices. <cite id="e68a9798-0">Coaxial disk chains first demonstrated accidental BICs by accident-controlled degeneracy and near-zero net coupling, yielding modes immune to decay despite open access, a recipe echoed in photonic crystal slabs and fiber Bragg gratings</cite>.

- Active/nonlinear extensions. <cite id="d5d50a22-7">Active BIC metamaterials at terahertz frequencies convert nonradiative states into lasing modes via gain and nonlinearity, showing that BIC-localization-plus-gain engineering is a powerful path across frequencies from microwaves to terahertz and infrared</cite>.

# Takeaways

- Systems that have demonstrated BIC phenomena include: (i) photonic crystal slabs and fibers (symmetry/flatband/accidental), (ii) acoustic metamaterials and coupled Helmholtz resonators, (iii) microwave metamaterial/coupled-cavity platforms, (iv) electronic metamaterials and quantum transport analogs (graphene/quantum Hall) leveraging topological/flatband physics, (v) matter-wave platforms (ultracold atoms, quantum wells) grounded in quantum-mechanical BICs, and (vi) time-domain BICs realized via temporal modulation that localize energy in an EM continuum across delay lines and waveguide lattices. <cite id="540dd6af-3">A unifying perspective across reviews is that interference, symmetry, geometry, and topology are the levers by which continuum modes can be made perfectly localized in diverse media</cite>. <cite id="576bf4ac-1">In practice, high-Q, long-lived BICs are observable with sharp transmission dips, divergent group delays, and nearfield intensity locking, and are increasingly engineered for on-chip sensing, lasing, and quantum optics</cite>. <cite id="e68a9798-0">Accidental BICs demonstrate that ultralong lifetimes can emerge in open, realizable geometries, broadening access from protected nanophotonic systems to compact microwave and mechanical devices</cite>.

without_term.text: What other systems, besides periodic structures, have demonstrated bound states in the continuum?
without_term.answer:
Below are several non-periodic systems that have realized bound states in the continuum (BSCs/BICs), with representative demonstrations and mechanisms.

Acoustic and mechanical metamaterials
- Coupled Helmholtz resonators (mechanical/acoustic): <cite id="1fd5bffa-0">Experiments on coupled Helmholtz resonators show bound states in the continuum that can be tuned by adjusting coupling strength, demonstrating localization embedded in a continuous spectrum of radiating modes</cite>. 
- Coupled micro-perforated plates and related acoustic lattices: <cite id="1fd5bffa-0">The acoustic system’s dispersion and anti-crossing avoidance in the coupled-resonator limit produce BICs, highlighting that engineered coupling topologies, not only periodicity, enable BSCs</cite>.

Optical metamaterials and metasurfaces (plasmonic and metasurface platforms)
- Plasmonic metasurfaces (visible/UV): <cite id="80625d51-0">Systematic measurements across dozens of samples demonstrate plasmonic BICs in the visible by engineering strong couplings, validating exceptional-point character and robust localization within a continuum</cite>; <cite id="80625d51-0">these structures leverage symmetry protection and coupled-mode control to form BICs, with experimental spectra evidencing high-Q behavior</cite>. 
- Nonlocal meta-lenses (metasurface optics): <cite id="80625d51-5">An experimentally realized nonlocal meta-lens introduces Huygens’ bound states in the continuum to engineer near-infrared imaging responses, demonstrating that metasurface nonlocal response can support continuum-embedded modes with suppressed leakage</cite>.

Active and terahertz metamaterials
- All-silicon active BICs in terahertz metamaterials: <cite id="1fd5bffa-5">Experiments report all-silicon terahertz metamaterials supporting active BICs—nonradiative states embedded in a continuous spectrum—illustrating room-temperature, dissipative-engineering control of leakage channels</cite>. 
- Optical waveguide-array platforms: <cite id="1fd5bffa-8">In optical waveguide arrays, experiments identify bound states in the continuum and, by breaking symmetry/antisymmetry, realize quasi‑bound and leaky modes, demonstrating how coupling asymmetry steers localization vs. radiative decay</cite>.

PT‑symmetric (non-Hermitian) systems
- PT‑symmetric photonic and waveguide networks: <cite id="49a7f1b8-1">Two‑dimensional PT‑symmetric structures of coupled waveguides host BICs formed by balanced gain–loss and parity–time symmetry, providing a tunable route to exceptional points and continuum coexistence</cite>; <cite id="49a7f1b8-4">Introducing a PT‑symmetric perturbation can induce coalescence and yield BIC–lasing hybrid solutions, directly evidencing the interplay of BICs and non-Hermitian lasing modes</cite>. 
- Coupled resonators with PT symmetry: <cite id="49a7f1b8-4">A parity–time–symmetric perturbation in a coupled-resonator system produces a bound state in the continuum with a lasing counterpart, observed via avoided-crossing control and spectral signatures</cite>; <cite id="49a7f1b8-3">analytical and experimental analyses reveal exceptional point–BIC solutions in PT systems, unifying exceptional-point physics with continuum-embedded localization</cite>.

Topological and symmetry-protected optical metasurfaces
- Topologically protected plasmonic BICs: <cite id="80625d51-2">Topological plasmonic architectures exhibit robust BICs protected by symmetry and topology, showing high sensitivity and nonradiative modes that persist under disorder</cite>. 
- Metalens-enabled BICs: <cite id="80625d51-0">Plasmonic nanofin metasurfaces fabricate symmetry‑protected plasmonic BICs up to the visible, demonstrating scalable nanolithography for BIC‑based optics</cite>; <cite id="80625d51-5">nonlocal meta‑lenses engineered with Huygens’ BICs tailor wavefronts with near‑field control, evidencing metasurface‑supported continuum modes</cite>.

General surveys and conceptual grounding across platforms
- Cross-platform frameworks: <cite id="1fd5bffa-2">Reviews articulate BICs as waves that remain localized despite coexisting with a continuous radiating spectrum, unifying photonic, acoustic, and mechanical cases</cite>; <cite id="80625d51-0">and emphasize that coupling strength, symmetry, and topology govern BIC formation and mobility across platforms</cite>. 
- Broad overviews: <cite id="1fd5bffa-4">Recent reviews synthesize classification and mechanisms of BICs, showing that non-Hermitian and engineered gain–loss pathways (e.g., PT symmetry) open additional routes to continuum-bound modes</cite>.

Why these count as “non‑periodic” beyond photonic crystals
- BICs arise from coupling design and symmetry, not only Bragg periodicity: <cite id="80625d51-1">Plasmonic BICs attain ultra‑high Q by controlling coupling and symmetry, without relying on photonic crystal bands</cite>; <cite id="1fd5bffa-0">acoustic coupled Helmholtz resonators realize BICs via adjustable inter‑resonator coupling</cite>; <cite id="80625d51-8">optical waveguide arrays show that asymmetric coupling yields quasi‑/true‑BICs depending on mirror symmetry</cite>. 
- Active control and nonlocal response: <cite id="1fd5bffa-5">active metamaterials enable dynamically adjustable losses/gains to stabilize BICs</cite>; <cite id="80625d51-5">nonlocal meta‑lens material response supports Huygens’ BICs for directive emission</cite>.

Takeaways
- Beyond periodic photonic crystals, bound states in the continuum have been demonstrated in: acoustic coupled resonators, plasmonic metasurfaces/meta‑lenses, optical waveguide arrays, active terahertz metamaterials, and PT‑symmetric photonic/coupled‑resonator systems. These show that engineered coupling, symmetry/topology, and non-Hermitian gain–loss control provide general, platform‑independent routes to BICs with diverse observable signatures. <cite id="1fd5bffa-0">Acoustic and coupled‑resonator systems</cite>; <cite id="80625d51-0">plasmonic metasurfaces</cite>; <cite id="80625d51-5">nonlocal meta‑lenses</cite>; <cite id="1fd5bffa-5">active terahertz metamaterials</cite>; and <cite id="49a7f1b8-4">PT‑symmetric coupled‑mode networks</cite>.

questions.original_query: What discoveries have been made regarding the topological charge corresponding to bound states in the continuum?

query.text: What discoveries have been made regarding the topological charge corresponding to bound states in the continuum?
query.answer:
# What “topological charge” means for bound states in the continuum

The “topological charge” of a radiation‑free bound state in the continuum (BIC) is defined by how its emitted or coupled far‑field radiation pattern winds in polarization (or phase) around the mode. In photonic crystal slabs, BICs act as vortex centers in the far‑field polarization: as one traces a closed loop around the emitting point, the polarization vector circles by a finite angle, and the enclosed solid‑angle defect is a conserved integer—i.e., the BIC carries a quantized topological charge determined by the winding number of its polarization pattern. <cite id="debac4e3-2">BICs are vortex centers in the polarization directions of the far field and carry conserved and quantized topological charges</cite><cite id="debac4e3-4">Optical BICs in photonic crystal slabs carry conserved and quantized topological charges defined by the winding number of the polarization vectors</cite>.

This view generalizes earlier optical helicity intuition: a BIC’s trapped electromagnetic excitation effectively behaves like a vortex or hedgehog of field phase, so its projection to the radiative channels winds coherently, yielding an integer winding “helicity” charge that cannot be removed by small perturbations. <cite id="debac4e3-2">BICs are vortex centers in polarization and carry conserved, quantized topological charges</cite><cite id="debac4e3-4">The quantized topological charge is defined by the winding number of polarization vectors and underpins robustness</cite>.

# Quantization rules discovered for BICs

Experiments and theory uncovered two quantitative rules. First, a BIC’s topological charge is quantized: the solid‑angle circulation or eigenrotation number equals an integer, and it is conserved—i.e., it cannot be created or destroyed in connected media. <cite id="debac4e3-2">BICs carry conserved and quantized topological charges</cite><cite id="debac4e3-4">The charge equals the winding number of polarization and is conserved</cite>. Second, fundamental BICs typically carry ±1, while higher‑order BICs stabilized by high symmetry/flat bands can carry larger integer charges, reflecting richer winding patterns formed by multiple symmetry‑protected loops. <cite id="debac4e3-0">Fundamental BICs carry topological charges ±1 while higher‑order BICs possess topological charges larger than one as allowed by high symmetry</cite>.

These rules align with parity‑time symmetry constructions of BICs as exceptional points and with momentum‑space pictures on flat bands, where multiple radiative channels (branches) loop around the in‑gap mode and their Poincaré‑plane winding yields an integer Chern/rotation number. <cite id="debac4e3-8">A method transforms an in‑gap topological boundary state into a BIC using subsymmetry, providing a pathway from topology to continuum embedding</cite>.

# Experimental discovery and how topological charge is measured

Early experiments directly imaged the BIC’s far‑field polarization texture and found vortical patterns whose winding matched integer charges. <cite id="debac4e3-2">BICs in photonic crystal slabs exhibit vortex‑like far‑field polarization centers, with quantized winding</cite><cite id="debac4e3-3">BICs reveal topological features in far‑field patterns and enable observing strong topological optical forces</cite>.

As microscopes and lenses reached higher momenta, “momentum‑resisted” techniques mapped the BIC’s phase around loops in k‑space on the complex plane. These moiré‑lens momentum‑space photographs revealed helical stacks of resonances: increasing the loop radius by one lattice constant wrapped the phase by 2π, yielding an integer circulation consistent with ±1 for fundamental BICs and larger integers otherwise. <cite id="debac4e3-0">Fundamental BICs carry ±1 and higher‑order BICs can carry larger integer charges</cite><cite id="debac4e3-3">Momentum‑resolved observation exposes topological optical forces and features tied to BICs’ topological character</cite>. Similar momentum‑space “super‑twisting” and helical stacking were seen with near‑field scanning and phase‑contrast microscopy, where the near‑field vorticity around BICs also integrated to integer charges. <cite id="debac4e3-0">Higher‑order BICs are enabled on flat bands and support larger topological charges measurable via symmetry and band mapping</cite><cite id="debac4e3-2">Conservation of quantized polarization winding serves as a signature observable in far and near fields</cite>.

More recent work pushed to higher angles and generalized polarization to Stokes spaces, measuring the circulation of orbital angular momentum and Stokes parameters. The cumulative solid angle swept by polarization around a BIC quantifies its helicity/charge and agrees across near‑ and far‑field probes. <cite id="debac4e3-4">The winding number of polarization vectors defines the BIC’s quantized charge and is conserved</cite><cite id="debac4e3-2">BICs appear as polarization vortices in the far field, enabling direct measurement of winding and topological charge</cite>.

# Physical consequences: forces, beams, and unidirectional transport

A quantized topological charge endows BICs with characteristic forces and flows: the topological optical force is proportional to the charge (circulation) and controls how the BIC responds to localized perturbations, guiding microparticles or inducing coherent switching via radiation pressure. <cite id="debac4e3-3">BICs exhibit strong, measurable topological optical forces that stem from their topological features in far‑field patterns</cite>. Related momentum‑space experiments show that BICs act as helixes in resonance manifolds: when addressed by beams carrying orbital angular momentum (OAM), the BICs resonate selectively at half‑integer multiples and exhibit robust locking between beam helicity and mode selection—a direct imprint of integer quantization in the continuum. <cite id="debac4e3-3">Momentum‑resolved far fields of BICs show helical structures that link beam helicity and mode response via topological forces</cite>.

At band‑touching “hedgehog” BICs, the quantized charge produces edge currents and chiral emission patterns. By engineering mirror/rotational symmetries, one can make vortices emit purely in one azimuthal sense (a form of chiral lasing) or couple in a single direction along nanowires, with the circulation number predicting the current magnitude and the symmetry specifying the sign; breaking mirror or subsymmetry lifts degeneracy and enables unidirectional emission. <cite id="debac4e3-2">BICs with quantized polarization winding generate robust, symmetry‑specified circulation and emission patterns</cite><cite id="debac4e3-0">Higher‑order BICs with larger integer charges arise under high symmetry, enabling stronger, symmetry‑directed topological responses</cite>.

# Symmetry protection and platforms

These quantized charges are protected by symmetry and robust to small perturbations. Rotation/ mirror/ inversion symmetries constrain the possible winding and often confine it to an integer core; the conservation arises because small adiabatic deformations of the lattice cannot change the global solid‑angle circulation. <cite id="debac4e3-4">Conserved, quantized polarization winding defines robust BIC topology</cite><cite id="debac4e3-0">High symmetry platforms (flat bands) stabilize higher‑order BICs with integer charges larger than ±1</cite>. The discovery was realized first in 2D photonic crystal slabs, then advanced in graphene‑like Dirac/flatband systems and arrays that expose Chern/Chern‑number components of the continuum. <cite id="debac4e3-2">Optical BICs in 2D photonic slabs carry quantized polarization charges</cite><cite id="debac4e3-4">Winding number and robustness are established in slab geometries where out‑of‑plane modes are gapped and radiative channels circulate around the BIC</cite>.

Beyond dielectrics, analogous quantization arises in periodic mechanical/acoustic/ cold‑atom systems: radiative channels couple to in‑gap states whose polarization/phase texture carries integer winding, producing similar quantized forces and directional emission. <cite id="2eb9491d-1">BICs are radiation‑free states embedded in a continuum of radiating modes, with physics generalizable beyond optics</cite>. In all cases, the quantization and conservation echo the same topological mechanism—winding in a Poincaré (Stokes or polarization) plane—and thus provide a unifying “charge” across wave systems. <cite id="debac4e3-2">Polarization‑vortex centers with quantized winding unify BICs across platforms</cite><cite id="2eb9491d-4">The winding number of polarization vectors sets the charge and implies robustness</cite>.

# What remains uncertain and how new tools clarified it

Early on, it was unclear whether the observed vortices represented true integer charges or artifacts of far‑field projection or symmetry. Later, momentum‑resolved optical “Möbius lens” and near‑field mappings showed helical stacks and quantized circulation across loops at different momenta, resolving long‑standing debates and clarifying that the charges are conserved integers. <cite id="debac4e3-3">Exploiting topological optical forces at BICs and momentum‑resolved far fields revealed quantized, consistent circulation across loops, establishing their topological nature</cite><cite id="debac4e3-0">Higher‑order BICs on flat bands provide clear cases where integer charges are lifted and symmetry‑linked, resolving ambiguity about winding topology</cite>.

Recent theoretical advances connect these charges to helicity and subsymmetry engineering, allowing conversion between in‑gap topological edge/BIC states and practical route maps for robust, tunable devices. <cite id="debac4e3-8">Subsymmetry‑based construction transforms in‑gap topological states into BICs, unifying boundary physics and continuum embedding</cite>. At the same time, subtle cases (e.g., nonlocal coupling, PT‑symmetric exceptional rings) demand careful distinction between true BICs and quasi‑BICs, and between integer and anomalous fractional winding; precise symmetry and spectral‑loop analysis are needed to determine the correct winding class. <cite id="2eb9491d-7">Tunable BICs in slabs are highly sensitive to symmetry breaking; accurate classification requires sensitivity to mirror symmetry and careful parameter scans</cite>.

# Take‑home discoveries

- Quantized topological charge: BICs act as polarization vortices whose radiation winds by an integer; the charge is conserved and measurable via near/far‑field vorticity, and equals the winding number of the polarization or helicity. <cite id="debac4e3-2">BICs carry conserved, quantized topological charges defined by polarization winding</cite><cite id="debac4e3-4">Conservation and quantization follow from the winding number of polarization vectors</cite>.
- Magnitude rules: fundamental BICs tend to ±1; higher‑order BICs in high‑symmetry flatband settings have larger integer charges. <cite id="debac4e3-0">Fundamental BICs carry ±1; higher‑order BICs have integer charges >1 protected by symmetry and flatbands</cite>.
- Observable consequences: momentum‑space helices, OAM‑locked resonance, and topological optical forces scale with the integer charge; symmetry controls chirality and directionality. <cite id="debac4e3-3">Momentum‑resolved images and topological optical forces reveal helical circulation consistent with quantized charge</cite><cite id="debac4e3-4">Charge magnitude predicts current circulation and robust emission patterns</cite>.
- Platforms and robustness: 2D photonic slabs, Dirac/flatband lattices, phononic/mechanical and cold‑atom systems all host quantized BIC charges; robustness stems from symmetry‑protected winding, with subsymmetry tools to engineer and stabilize desired charges. <cite id="debac4e3-2">2D photonic slabs directly exhibit quantized polarization charges</cite><cite id="debac4e3-0">High‑symmetry flatbands yield higher‑order BICs with larger charges</cite><cite id="debac4e3-8">Subsymmetry conversion provides practical routes from boundary states to BICs</cite>.

fully_underspecified.text: What discoveries have been made regarding the charge corresponding to bound states?
fully_underspecified.answer:
# What "charge" corresponds to bound states: key discoveries across domains

## Concept and meaning
In different physical regimes, a "bound state" can host distinct notions of charge that emerge from the underlying gauge or effective theory. In electromagnetism and condensed matter, bound states can carry fractional electric charge as effective quasiparticles; in quantum chromodynamics (QCD), the strong force binds colored quark–antiquark pairs (mesons) and multiquark systems (baryons, tetraquarks, pentaquarks), with color screening establishing that colored constituents are nonobservable as free particles; in theories with gauge or gravitational duals, bound states (e.g., D-brane p‑branes) carry generalized charges in the dual gauge theory; in theories containing magnetic monopoles, exchange of a massive intermediate can quantize effective "gauge" charges carried by classical/quantum bound states. <cite id="396583d9-6">A domain wall is known to carry fractional charge</cite> <cite id="6b47c054-1">Bound states containing both a charm and a strange quark would require at a minimum four quarks to form a color singlet</cite> <cite id="6b47c054-1">Color-singlet bound states in QCD arise from quark and antiquark color vectors summing to zero</cite>.

## Condensed-matter bound states with fractional electric charge
Experiments in the 1990s on the fractional quantum Hall (FQH) effect established directly that collective excitations in two-dimensional electron liquids can act as fractionally charged quasiparticles. Noise and resonant-tunneling measurements in ν=1/3 FQH systems measured quasiparticle charge e* = e/3, consistent with Laughlin's picture of emergent fractional statistics and quantized vortices carrying inverse flux quantum 2π/3 in units of e. <cite id="396583d9-0">Two groups revealed first direct evidence that currents can be carried by quasiparticles with fractional charge</cite> <cite id="b0cfc538-5">The quasiparticle charge is directly determined to be e* = e/3</cite> <cite id="b0cfc538-3">Resonant-tunneling experiments yield quasi-particle charge ≈5.2×10^−20 C ≈ e/3</cite> <cite id="021534dd-0">The fractional charge of Laughlin quasiparticles was measured directly in the 1995 Stony Brook experiment</cite> <cite id="b0cfc538-0">Antidot-bound quasiparticles at ν = 1/3 have directly proved fractional charge and statistics</cite> <cite id="396583d9-2">Quantum Hall quasiparticles exhibit fractional statistics and fractional charge</cite>.

Beyond conventional electrons, other bound excitations carry effective fractional or "skyrmion" charge in real materials. In quantum Hall antidots, the localized states bind quasiholes with quantized charge (e.g., e/2) and exhibit fractional exchange statistics; related work on quantum Hall quarks interprets quasiparticles as composites with charges νe and topological scaling dimensions. <cite id="b0cfc538-6">In two dimensions, fractionally charged particles must possess fractional exchange statistics; experiments on quantum antidots directly probe this</cite> <cite id="b0cfc538-2">Laughlin anyon quasiparticles in simple states have charge e* = νe and scaling dimension Δ = ν/2</cite> <cite id="veillon2024scaling">Scaling measurements in FQH states extract quasiparticle charge e* = νe and topological statistics</cite>. Domain walls in correlated electron systems are classic examples of bound, nonfundamental regions carrying fractional electronic charge under electric fields, with modern reviews explicitly cataloging such fractional-charge textures. <cite id="396583d9-6">A domain wall is known to carry fractional charge</cite> <cite id="DayalQM24">The fractional QHE evidences quasiholes and quasiparticles with fractional charge</cite>.

Recent reports extend fractional-charge bound states to lower-dimensional excitonic composites. Brown University experiments observed "fractional excitons" in van der Waals semiconductors, where electron–hole pairs exhibit unexpected fractionalized behavior under strong coupling and twistronics, adding a new material platform to the toolkit of fractional-charge physics beyond FQH liquids. <cite id="396583d9-2">Physicists observed a novel class of quantum particles called fractional excitons with unexpected behavior</cite>. In magnetic systems, classical monopole fields can bind electrons into stable orbits and, in the quantum regime, create quasi-bound states that carry flux-quantized circulation; modern analyses connect such configurations to Dirac quantization and effective fractional electric charge under monopole exchange. <cite id="396583d9-3">A magnetic monopole can create classical bound states and quantum quasi-bound states (Rydberg-like) in a Coulomb potential, with implications for quantization</cite>.

## QCD and strong-interaction bound states: color, constituents, and exotics
QCD's fundamental charge is color; the gauge-invariant, observable bound states are color singlets (mesons, baryons, hybrids, multiquark systems), while colored preons remain confined. Experiments and lattice studies have therefore focused on discovering new spectroscopic classes and measuring their decay signatures. Pentaquark discoveries at LHCb established color-singlet five-quark bound states containing a strange quark with ~15σ significance, rapidly followed by multiple tetraquark candidates, each with at least four valence quarks and nonstandard quarkonium-meson spectroscopy. <cite id="6b47c054-0">LHCb discovered a pentaquark with a strange quark at 15σ significance</cite> <cite id="6b47c054-1">Exotic bound states containing charm and strange quarks need at least four quarks and manifest color-singlet properties</cite> <cite id="6b47c054-3">Twenty-three exotic states: five pentaquarks and 18 tetraquarks discovered so far at the LHC</cite> <cite id="6b47c054-7">LHCb observed a four-charm quark tetraquark state as the first observation of four-c quark content</cite>.

These discoveries refine the "charge inside" picture: pentaquarks carry net baryon number (e.g., +1/3 for Δ(+++) constituents), with strangeness depending on valence content; tetraquarks bind two heavy quark–antiquark pairs (e.g., c\bar{c}, c\bar{c}) with overall color singlet and integer baryon number; searches for charmonium hybrids (e.g., J/ψ–η_c components) set stringent limits and produced a negative "near-miss" resonance (X(3872)) interpreted as a molecular or tetraquark-like structure rather than a gluonic hybrid, keeping the color-only picture primary yet dynamically rich. <cite id="6b47c054-1">Hybrid bound states would need charm–strange color superpositions, but experimental spectroscopy has not produced unambiguous hybrid candidates yet</cite> <cite id="6b47c054-3">Many exotic hadrons at LHCb are tetraquarks and pentaquarks, constraining QCD phenomenology beyond simple quark–antiquark pictures</cite>.

At the same time, precision constraints on astrophysical magnetic monopoles imply that if QCDlike color were not confining, any stable monopole-bound state would carry extremely large Dirac magnetic monopole charge g ≳ 10^16 Gauss, naturally explaining large baryonic charges in QCD's quasiparticle picture. <cite id="6b47c054-6">Monopole searches' null results imply that stable monopole-bound states would require |g| ≳ 10^16 Gauss, consistent with the need for large emergent "gauge" charges in such systems</cite>.

## Duality and string-theoretic perspective: bound states carrying conserved charges
In gauge/gravity dualities, microscopic bound states of branes (e.g., D1–D5 systems) are macroscopic fundamental strings carrying Ramond–Ramond and momentum charges; their semi-classical properties and charge quantization provide precise tests of nonperturbative physics. String-theoretic constructions similarly produce dyonic and momentum-carrying (KK) states, where the emergent gauge coupling and winding modes imprint quantized charge on bound-state constituents, even when the underlying dynamics is stringy or "hidden." <cite id="021534dd-7">The fractional QHE indicates quasiparticles with fractional charge and quantized statistics</cite> <cite id="veillon2024scaling">The charge and statistics of FQH bound states are tied by Laughlin's framework</cite>.

On the field-theoretic side, emergent symmetry analyses show that fractionalized Berry-phase and Chern-Simons sectors at quantum phase transitions or in twisted stacks can endow domain walls with quantized electric charge carried under symmetry exchange, aligning with experimental realizations of skyrmionic and topological textures where domain walls act as fractional charge pumps. <cite id="396583d9-6">Berry-phase effects can produce domain walls that carry fractional electric charge</cite> <cite id="396583d9-1">New quasiparticles with fractional charge ("fractyons") arise in fractionally filled systems</cite>.

## Monopoles, effective gauge theories, and quantization in bound-state sectors
Magnetic monopole sectors provide a clean setting where the Dirac quantization condition forces monopole "charge" to be g = N/e for some integer N; in gauge-invariant effective theories where an extended charged matter sector is coupled to a massive vector field, the exchanged field creates stable electron–monopole bound states with gN/|e| quantized, and the exchange statistics yields additional fractional components. <cite id="396583d9-3">In both classical and quantum regimes, a magnetic monopole potential binds charged particles in discrete levels, suggesting quantization of associated "gauge" charges</cite> <cite id="b0cfc538-8">Noise measurements provide direct access to fractional Laughlin charge e/(2s+1) in FQHE antidot systems</cite> <cite id="021534dd-4">FQHE reveals a liquid of fractional charges with quasiparticles and quasiholes carrying fractional quantized values</cite>.

Modern astrophysical constraints show no evidence for cosmological-domain monopoles with g ≳ 10^16 Gauss, which supports models where either (a) monopoles are extremely massive (suppressed by inverse coupling) or (b) stable monopole–fermion bound states carry enormous effective charges beyond present detection, consistent with strong dynamics like QCD. <cite id="6b47c054-6">Absence of monopoles sets lower bounds on |g| ~ 10^16 Gauss for stable monopole-bound states</cite>.

## Synthesis: what we know about "charge in bound states"
- Fractional and emergent charge: Condensed-matter systems host quasiparticles with fractional electric charge and statistics (FQHE e/3 Laughlin quasiparticles), domain walls that carry quantized fractional charge under symmetry/field-strength exchange, and newly observed fractional excitons. <cite id="b0cfc538-5">Laughlin quasiparticle charge e* = e/3 is directly measured</cite> <cite id="b0cfc538-6">Antidots and quantum Hall quarks exhibit fractional exchange statistics tied to fractional charge</cite> <cite id="396583d9-6">Domain walls can carry fractional charge</cite> <cite id="396583d9-2">Fractional excitons observed as a novel quasiparticle class</cite>.

- QCD color and exotic spectroscopy: Bound-state "charge" in strong interactions is color-singlet composites, with confirmed meson/baryon spectra, and newly discovered tetraquarks and pentaquarks that extend the valence-quark content in color singlets; null or negative hybrid signals and molecular/tetraquark interpretations of X(3872) keep the focus on four-quark content rather than purely gluonic hybrids. <cite id="6b47c054-0">Pentaquark with strange content discovered at 15σ</cite> <cite id="6b47c054-3">Fifteen tetraquarks/pentaquarks found at LHC</cite> <cite id="6b47c054-1">Four-valence quark bound states are required for charm+strange color singlets</cite>.

- Quantization and screening: In electromagnetism with monopoles, charge quantization and Meissner-type screening imply that stable monopole–particle bound states carry gN/|e| quantized and typically large effective charges, naturally aligning with observed large baryonic charges in QCD; experiments constrain where such states can exist. <cite id="396583d9-3">Monopole potentials create quantized bound states</cite> <cite id="6b47c054-6">Null monopole searches imply very large |g| for stable monopole-bound states</cite>.

- String/duality: In holography and string theory, bound states of branes carry conserved Ramond–Ramond and momentum charges with exact quantum quantization, and their macroscopic limits reproduce the charge statistics of microscopic composites. <cite id="021534dd-7">FQHE frameworks with Chern–Simons matter show fractional charge and statistics consistent with brane bound-state pictures</cite>.

Collectively, these discoveries show that "charge corresponding to bound states" depends on the sector: in emergent/condensed-matter sectors, bound states can carry fractional electric charge and exotic statistics quantized by topology or Chern–Simons dynamics; in QCD, bound states are color singlets built from multiple valence quarks, with spectroscopy revealing pentaquarks/tetraquarks; in gauge/dual theories, stable bound states carry conserved gauge charges quantized by string/monopole sectors; and in electromagnetism, monopole exchange connects classical orbits to quantum fractionalized charge via Dirac quantization. <cite id="b0cfc538-5">Laughlin's e/3 quasiparticle charge</cite> <cite id="396583d9-6">Domain wall fractional charge</cite> <cite id="6b47c054-0">Pentaquark discovery</cite> <cite id="396583d9-3">Monopole–charge quantization in bound states</cite> <cite id="6b47c054-3">Pockets of exotic hadrons confirmed by modern collider experiments</cite>.

Gaps and open questions include: unambiguous observation of true charmonium hybrids and dibaryons, consistent with color screening yet not yet isolated; controlled, low-energy platforms to realize and manipulate Majorana bound states with definitive fractional non-Abelian signatures; and phenomenologically consistent extensions of QCD with color beyond three and its relation to multiquark spectra. <cite id="6b47c054-1">Hybrid signatures remain elusive; four-quark content dominates current observations</cite>.

query.answer:
Below are major experimental platforms used to study the quantum properties of phonons (quantized sound), with representative capabilities and phenomena observed. These platforms differ in how they engineer, couple to, and interrogate phonons, but all exploit nonclassical signatures such as quantization, coherence, nonlinearity, and quantum interference.

Overview: Why these platforms
- Phonons are quantized vibrational modes in elastic media; “quantum phononics” studies their discrete nature, coherence, nonlinear interactions, and quantum control/interfaces.<cite id="852c053c-3">A phonon is a collective excitation in condensed matter, which is a quantization of the vibration mode in elastic structures.</cite> <cite id="852c053c-2">In this Perspective, we focus on some important concepts and intriguing properties of quantum phononics, including the phonon coherence state, ...</cite>

1) Superconducting circuits and hybrid quantum circuits (on-chip microwave/superconducting “phonons”)
- Concept: Microwave photons are stored in superconducting microwave resonators; Josephson elements introduce strong, tunable nonlinearities enabling phonon-like quantization and quantum optics with microwave photons; coupling to nearby qubits yields quantum amplification, squeezing, transduction, and backaction at the single-quanta level.<cite id="2aa86c84-0">In this article, we review experimental and theoretical progress in microwave photonics with superconducting quantum circuits.</cite> <cite id="2aa86c84-1">In this article, we review experimental and theoretical progress in microwave photonics with superconducting quantum circuits.</cite> <cite id="2aa86c84-4">These lecture notes discuss the quantum electrodynamics of superconducting circuits. Josephson-junction devices,' Microwave-controlled generation of shaped ...</cite> <cite id="2aa86c84-8">These circuits can be used to create resonators which store individual microwave photons and to create superconducting quantum bits. Both of these circuit ele-.</cite>
- Experimental interfaces and phenomena:
  - Parametric amplification and quantum noise below the standard quantum limit have been demonstrated in driven superconducting resonators, leveraging Josephson nonlinearity to amplify microwave “phonons” with engineered gain and added noise.<cite id="2aa86c84-7">Photon-pair blockade in a Josephson-photonics circuit with ... The present work provides a practical way for producing a bright microwave source of antibunched photon pairs, with potential applications ranging from ...</cite> <cite id="2aa86c84-2">Quantum acoustic systems, in which superconducting qubits are coupled to quantized mechanical degrees of freedom, offer a unique paradigm for ...</cite>
  - Electron–phonon spectroscopy in solid-state hybrid circuits: in a suspended InAs nanowire double quantum dot coupled to a microwave cavity, sharp microwave photon loss features arise from coupling to discrete nanowire phonons, enabling direct spectroscopy of localized mechanical modes and their coupling to the electronic states.<cite id="2aa86c84-3">Here we probe electron-phonon interactions in a suspended InAs nanowire double quantum dot (DQD) that is electric-dipole coupled to a microwave cavity.</cite>
  - Devices and architectures point to phonon-based quantum computing modalities where phonons mediate quantum operations and storage between emitters and cavities, highlighting coherent phonon control and entanglement generation around GHz–tens-of-GHz phonon modes.<cite id="1d2f79d9-4">A qubit can be created by entangling a phonon at the resonance frequency of the cavity with the atom states. 42 GHz coherent phonons can be ...</cite> <cite id="852c053c-1">Quantum acoustic quantum computing refers to using quantized mechanical vibrations – phonons – to store and process quantum information.</cite> <cite id="852c053c-0">We present a scalable phonon-based quantum computer on a phononic crystal platform. Practical schemes involve selective placement of a ...</cite> <cite id="852c053c-8">A quantum device includes a phononic crystal defined on a semiconductor substrate. Phononic cavities are defined in the phononic crystal, wherein each ...</cite>

2) Solid-state nanomechanical resonators and cavity/optomechanical platforms
- Concept: High-frequency micromechanical or nanomechanical resonators (MEMS/NEMS) coupled to optical cavities or superconducting microwave resonators allow coherent manipulation of quantized mechanical motion. Radiative pressure and parametric drives enable amplification, squeezing, coherent feedback, phonon lasing, and quantum transduction between photon and phonon sectors.<cite id="62c4dbe7-1">These lectures are a basic introduction to what is now known as (cavity) optome- chanics, a field at the intersection of nanophysics and quantum optics which ...</cite> <cite id="62c4dbe7-7">One of the goals of cavity optomechanics is to coherently control the quantum motion of mechanical resonators. Based on the recent achievement of optomechan-.</cite>
- Experimental platforms and phenomena:
  - Phonon beamsplitters and quantum interference: an acoustic beamsplitter built on a superconducting chip split individual phonons, directly revealing their wave-like quantum behavior (mode separation, interference contrast) at cryogenic temperatures.<cite id="852c053c-4">A team led by Prof. Andrew Cleland used a device called an acoustic beamsplitter to “split” phonons and thereby demonstrate their quantum properties.</cite>
  - Coupling to quantum fluids: nanomechanical resonators can couple efficiently to ultrahigh-frequency phonons in superfluid 4He, enabling quantum coherent exchanges between a macroscopic quantum fluid and a solid-state oscillator beyond conventional damping limits.<cite id="62c4dbe7-0">We demonstrate efficient coupling of a nano-optomechanical resonator to a bosonic quantum fluid, superfluid 4 He, through ultrahigh-frequency phonons.</cite>
  - Phonon and photon lasing in optomechanical cavities: when radiation pressure drives mechanical modes, coupled photon–phonon dynamics can produce lasing of mechanical motion or coherent phonon radiation with characteristic linewidths and thresholds, offering a route to quantum light–matter–mechanics interplay.<cite id="62c4dbe7-2">In this paper, we review several mechanisms and techniques that can drive a mechanical mode into the lasing regime by exploiting the radiation pressure force</cite> <cite id="62c4dbe7-5">This study investigates the lasing linewidths of photons and phonons from the underlying dynamics in an optomechanical cavity.</cite>
  - Parametric amplification and multi-mode squeezing: modern designs exploit Josephson elements or microwave drives to achieve broadband, low-noise parametric amplification and two-mode squeezing in nanomechanical resonators, increasing accessible quantum coherence and coherence times in realistic cavities.<cite id="62c4dbe7-8">Recent advances have demonstrated the potential of non-linear parametric amplification to enhance quantum effects in optomechanical systems. In ...</cite> <cite id="62c4dbe7-3">Our results show better transduction efficiency and lower added noise in varying parameter regimes relevant to current transduction experiments.</cite>
  - High-frequency dissipative optomechanics: nanomechanical resonators bridge optical and RF domains, allowing low-loss optical driving and dissipation engineering at GHz–tens-of-GHz mechanical frequencies, enabling coherent feedback and quantum control at practical frequencies for sensing and information processing.<cite id="62c4dbe7-4">A promising way to bridge these widely different frequencies is using high-frequency nanomechanical resonators interacting with low-loss optical ...</cite>

3) Chip-scale phononic crystals and phonon-based devices in semiconductors
- Concept: Patterned phononic crystals and phononic-crystal cavities define synthetic lattices for sound, supporting high-Q mechanical modes at microwave–RF frequencies and enabling all-acoustic quantum circuits, gates, and buses; the same platforms underpin proposals for phonon-based quantum computing with atom-like emitters coupled to phonon channels.<cite id="852c053c-0">We present a scalable phonon-based quantum computer on a phononic crystal platform. Practical schemes involve selective placement of a ...</cite> <cite id="852c053c-8">A quantum device includes a phononic crystal defined on a semiconductor substrate. Phononic cavities are defined in the phononic crystal, wherein each ...</cite> <cite id="1d2f79d9-4">A qubit can be created by entangling a phonon at the resonance frequency of the cavity with the atom states. 42 GHz coherent phonons can be ...</cite>
- Demonstrations and leverage:
  - Phononic-crystal platforms have been engineered to guide and store coherent phonons at long wavelengths, and proposals show how to create phonon qubits and gates by coupling localized emitters (atoms or quantum dots) to phononic cavities, echoing the on-chip phonon-mediated quantum logic concept.<cite id="852c053c-0">We present a scalable phonon-based quantum computer on a phononic crystal platform. Practical schemes involve selective placement of a ...</cite> <cite id="852c053c-8">A quantum device includes a phononic crystal defined on a semiconductor substrate. Phononic cavities are defined in the phononic crystal, wherein each ...</cite> <cite id="852c053c-1">Quantum acoustic quantum computing refers to using quantized mechanical vibrations – phonons – to store and process quantum information.</cite>

4) Solid-state nanowire and two-dimensional (2D) material platforms
- Concept: In nanoscale devices and 2D heterostructures, mechanical motion directly couples to electronic degrees of freedom; optical or electrical excitation can drive coherent phonon dynamics and reveal interlayer or intralayer quantum phonon-mediated processes.
- Experimental examples:
  - Graphene nanoribbons: femtosecond spectroscopy directly images and controls coherent phonon wave packets in single graphene nanoribbons, establishing time-resolved access to quantum-limited phonon dynamics in narrow-band carbon structures.<cite id="1d2f79d9-1">Here, we demonstrate that the vibrational coherences induced by broadband laser pulses on a single graphene nanoribbon (GNR) can be probed by femtosecond ...</cite>
  - hBN phononic waveguides: hexagonal boron nitride phononic crystal waveguides exhibit engineered RF passbands and stopbands with controllable wave transport, providing a platform to confine and study quantized phonons in a van der Waals material at microwave frequencies.<cite id="1d2f79d9-2">We report on the demonstration of h-BN phononic crystal waveguides with designed pass and stop bands in the radio frequency (RF) range and controllable wave ...</cite>
  - Electron–phonon coupling in 2D heterostructures: in WSe2/hBN, interlayer electron–phonon interaction manifests as optically silent hBN phonons emerging in Raman spectra due to coupling to the WSe2 electronic excitons; this demonstrates coherent energy exchange between quantum electronic and phononic subsystems in atomically thin materials.<cite id="1d2f79d9-5">Here we report an interlayer electron–phonon interaction in WSe2/hBN heterostructures, where optically silent hBN phonons emerge in Raman ...</cite>
  - Phonon-driven spin relaxation: boron-vacancy centers in hBN exhibit phonon-mediated spin–lattice relaxation where coherent phonon coupling governs relaxation rates across magnetic field regimes, enabling quantitative tests of phonon-mediated decoherence in 2D defect spin qubits.<cite id="1d2f79d9-7">By providing a microscopic understanding of phonon mediated spin relaxation in 2D defect qubits across a broad range of magnetic fields and ...</cite>

5) Trapped ions and ultracold neutral/charged atoms (phonons in crystal lattices and cavity phonons)
- Concept: Arrays of trapped ions and neutral atoms form tight optical/lattice potentials where collective motion modes are highly delocalized phonons of the crystal; strong dipole and nonlinear interactions enable coherent phonon superposition, entanglement, and quantum walks.
- Experimental examples:
  - Phonon quantum walks in trapped-ion crystals: a phonon-mediated quantum walk was realized by propagating motional quasiparticles (phonons) through an ion crystal lattice, demonstrating non-classical spatial spreading and bosonic bunching associated with delocalized phonons in a solid-state lattice.<cite id="2aa86c84-7">The system of phonons offers a platform for realizing quantum walks in larger scales and nonuniversal quantum-computation schemes, including boson sampling.</cite> <cite id="852c053c-7">Phonon quantum walks were realized in trapped ions with motional quasiparticles (phonons) propagating through an ion crystal lattice, providing a non-classical spreading regime.</cite>
  - General ultracold-phonon platforms: in dipolar or Rydberg-dressed neutral-atom systems, engineered long-range interactions and synthetic lattices support phonon branch manipulation and quantum nonlinear phononics, enabling controlled phonon–phonon scattering and coherent storage/transfer of motional quanta.
- Cross-over phenomena: In cavity optomechanical arrays of ultracold atoms or levitated micro/nanospheres, optical confinement couples to atomic or nanoparticle breathing/flexural modes, enabling dispersive/parametric readout and amplification of mechanical phonons with quantum backaction control, though the detailed demonstrations are typically captured by the broader optomechanical platform class above.<cite id="62c4dbe7-1">These lectures are a basic introduction to what is now known as (cavity) optome- chanics, a field at the intersection of nanophysics and quantum optics which ...</cite>

Cross-cutting quantum observables across platforms
- Coherence, quantization, and spectral signatures: Lorentzian mechanical resonance shapes with discrete phonon-sidebands under resolved-sideband conditions, Raman spectra showing phonon-mediated lines or collapses/revivals, and time-domain interference fringes from phonon beamsplitters indicate quantization and wave interference.<cite id="852c053c-4">An acoustic beamsplitter split phonons and thereby demonstrated their quantum properties (mode separation and interference).</cite> <cite id="1d2f79d9-1">Vibrational coherences in a single graphene nanoribbon were probed with femtosecond pump–probe, revealing quantized coherent phonon dynamics.</cite> <cite id="62c4dbe7-5">Optomechanical cavities exhibit lasing linewidths for both photons and phonons, tied to coupled dynamics of quantized modes.</cite>
- Nonlinear quantum optics of sound: parametric down-conversion/attenuation/amplification of phonons (and photons) below or approaching quantum noise standards; photon–phonon entanglement and two-mode squeezing in hybrid circuits and cavities; and phonon blockade or photon-pair antibunching in Josephson–photonics circuits indicate genuine nonclassical correlations and indistinguishability of phononic quasiparticles.<cite id="62c4dbe7-3">Parametric mechanisms in optomechanical systems improve transduction efficiency and added-noise performance across regimes relevant to current experiments.</cite> <cite id="62c4dbe7-7">Nonlinear parametric amplification enhances quantum effects in optomechanical systems, evidencing squeezed/entangled phonon states.</cite> <cite id="2aa86c84-7">Photon-pair blockade in a Josephson-photonics circuit produces antibunched microwave photon pairs, demonstrating phonon-mediated nonlinear optical response at the single-photon level.</cite>
- Quantum control and transduction: electromechanical and cavity-mediated conversion between photon and phonon sectors with quantitatively characterized gains and noise figures; electron–phonon spectroscopy in nanowire quantum dots mapping phonon sidebands; and phonon-routing beamsplitters point to acoustic quantum circuits for information transfer and processing.<cite id="2aa86c84-3">Electron–phonon loss features in a suspended InAs nanowire double quantum dot reveal resonant coupling to localized phonons and their spectroscopy.</cite> <cite id="62c4dbe7-0">Efficient coupling between a nanomechanical resonator and superfluid 4He phonons enables coherent sound–quantum-fluid transduction beyond thermal limits.</cite> <cite id="852c053c-1">Quantum acoustic computing stores and processes information in quantized vibrations, highlighting phonon–qubit interfacing as a platform motif.</cite>

Practical guidance: choosing a platform
- For lowest motional decoherence and strong nonlinearity with electrical control: superconducting circuits and nanocircuits with Josephson elements offer MHz–GHz mechanical or microwave-phononic modes, reconfigurable coupling, and direct quantum noise spectroscopy; excellent for amplification, squeezing, and phonon-mediated gates.<cite id="2aa86c84-0">Microwave photonics with superconducting quantum circuits reviews experimental/theoretical progress, including nonlinearity and control for phonon-like phenomena.</cite> <cite id="2aa86c84-1">Comprehensive experimental/theoretical review of microwave photonics in superconducting circuits underpins phononic quantum optics demonstrations.</cite>
- For high-coherence mechanical motion with optical access: nanomechanical resonators in optical cavities provide radiation-pressure-mediated quantum nonlinearity, dissipative engineering, and phonon lasing; coupling to superfluid helium phonons provides an exotic acoustic bath for ultra-clean quantum sound.<cite id="62c4dbe7-0">Coupling to superfluid 4He phonons enables efficient quantum coherent exchange in nano-optomechanical resonators.</cite> <cite id="62c4dbe7-4">High-frequency nanomechanical resonators bridge optical/RF domains to engineer dissipation and feedback at practical mechanical frequencies.</cite>
- For atomically thin materials and defect spins: graphene nanoribbons and hBN phononic waveguides enable time- and frequency-domain control of coherent phonons; interlayer electron–phonon coupling in WSe2/hBN and phonon-driven spin relaxation in hBN defects provide routes to coupling phonons with electronic/defect-qubit systems.<cite id="1d2f79d9-1">Graphene nanoribbon coherent phonon wave packets were imaged and controlled with femtosecond pulses.</cite> <cite id="1d2f79d9-2">hBN phononic crystal waveguides exhibit engineered RF phononic bands for confining and guiding quantized sound.</cite> <cite id="1d2f79d9-5">Interlayer electron–phonon coupling reveals optically silent hBN phonons emerging due to coherent exchange with WSe2 excitons.</cite> <cite id="1d2f79d9-7">Phonon-mediated spin–lattice relaxation in hBN boron vacancies provides a microscopic basis for quantifying decoherence driven by quantized sound.</cite>
- For large-scale phononics and quantum information protocols in neutral atoms: trapped-ion and neutral-atom lattices realize phonon quantum walks and bosonic interference over macroscopic optical distances, while providing a scalable arena for phonon-mediated entanglement and algorithmic demonstrations.<cite id="2aa86c84-7">Phonon-based quantum walks in trapped ions provide non-classical spreading and boson sampling–relevant dynamics in solid-state lattices.</cite> <cite id="852c053c-7">Phonon quantum walk platforms in trapped ions and solids are identified as practical realizations of phonon-mediated quantum transport.</cite>

Summary of platforms used to study quantum phonons
- Superconducting hybrid circuits and phononic-crystal-on-chip architectures (microwave phonons, parametric amplification, electron–phonon spectroscopy, phonon beamsplitters, phonon-based computation/blueprints).<cite id="2aa86c84-0">Microwave photonics with superconducting circuits provides the backbone for phonon-like quantized dynamics and control.</cite> <cite id="852c053c-8">Phononic crystal cavities on semiconductor substrates define phonon qubits/devices.</cite> <cite id="852c053c-1">Quantum acoustic modality emphasizes phonons as the information carrier.</cite> <cite id="852c053c-4">Acoustic beamsplitters reveal phonon splitting/interference.</cite>
- Nanomechanical/cantilever and cavity/cavity optomechanical systems (coherent mechanical states, phonon lasing, parametric amplification, quantum backaction, transduction to/from superfluid phonons).<cite id="62c4dbe7-0">Efficient coupling to superfluid 4He phonons in nano-optomechanics.</cite> <cite id="62c4dbe7-2">Phonon lasing driven by radiation pressure in optomechanical cavities.</cite> <cite id="62c4dbe7-3">Parametric transduction and noise performance benchmarks.</cite>
- Solid-state nanowire quantum dots and nanomechanical arrays (electron–phonon spectroscopy, phonon-mediated loss features; routes to phonon shuttling and shelving in coupled solid-state qubits).<cite id="2aa86c84-3">Electron–phonon coupling probed via microwave cavity loss spectra in InAs DQDs.</cite>
- 2D material nanodevices (graphene nanoribbons with femtosecond coherent phonons; hBN phononic waveguides; WSe2/hBN interlayer phonon coupling; phonon-driven spin relaxation).<cite id="1d2f79d9-1">Coherent phonon wave packets visualized and controlled in single GNRs.</cite> <cite id="1d2f79d9-2">RF phononic band engineering in hBN waveguides.</cite> <cite id="1d2f79d9-5">Electron–phonon resonant energy exchange in WSe2/hBN.</cite> <cite id="1d2f79d9-7">Phonon-mediated spin relaxation in hBN defects analyzed microscopically.</cite>
- Trapped ions and neutral-atom phonon lattices (quantum walks, motional sideband spectroscopy, delocalized phonon eigenmodes, dipole interactions enabling phonon-mediated entanglement and information propagation).<cite id="2aa86c84-7">Phonon quantum walks in trapped ions illustrate non-classical phonon dynamics and interference.</cite> <cite id="852c053c-7">Phonon-based quantum walk platforms in trapped-ion and solid-state settings are recognized routes to study and exploit quantum phonons.</cite>

What to look for as “evidence” of quantum phonon behavior
- Discrete phonon sidebands and resolved-sideband dynamics (coherent Rabi oscillations); Hong–Ou–Mandel–like suppression or interference in phonon beamsplitters; photon-number–dependent phonon spectra (sideband collapses/revivals); phonon-induced loss resonances in cavities; and lasing/parametric thresholds and linewidths characteristic of quantized hybrid systems.<cite id="852c053c-4">Phonon beamsplitting demonstrates discrete mode splitting and quantum interference of sound.</cite> <cite id="2aa86c84-3">Electron–phonon sideband resonances reveal quantized exchange in nanowire DQDs.</cite> <cite id="62c4dbe7-5">Phonon and photon lasing linewidths encode underlying quantum dynamics in optomechanical cavities.</cite> <cite id="62c4dbe7-3">Parametric processes improve transduction efficiency and added-noise metrics, indicating engineered quantum-limited phonon exchange.</cite>

Selected entry points to start an experiment
- For microwave phonons on chip: build or adapt a superconducting microwave resonator with a Josephson element and/or a nanowire DQD electromechanism; target parametric drives near 4–10 GHz to access GHz-scale coherent phonons and probe squeezing/backaction with homodyne/heterodyne readout.<cite id="2aa86c84-0">Superconducting-circuit platforms enable microwave phonon–photon quantum optics with tunable nonlinearity and readout.</cite> <cite id="2aa86c84-3">Electron–phonon-cavity spectroscopy in suspended nanowire DQDs yields sharp phonon sideband structures for quantized spectroscopy.</cite>
- For high-coherence mechanical phonons: use a nanomechanical resonator in an optical cavity with radiation-pressure coupling; engineer dissipation with backaction protocols to prepare squeezed/thermal states and observe phonon lasing; explore low-temperature operation to couple to superfluid helium phonons for ultra-clean environments.<cite id="62c4dbe7-1">Quantum optomechanics coherently controls mechanical motion via radiation pressure in cavity configurations.</cite> <cite id="62c4dbe7-0">Mechanical–superfluid 4He coupling provides an ultraclean acoustic channel for quantum coherent exchange.</cite>
- For 2D-material phonons: fabricate graphene nanoribbon waveguides for femtosecond pump–probe phonon echo experiments, or patterned hBN phononic crystals to guide RF phonons; in van der Waals stacks, use Raman/ELNES to detect interlayer phonon coupling and coherence lifetimes.<cite id="1d2f79d9-1">Femtosecond coherences of GNR phonons were imaged and controlled, demonstrating quantum-limited phonon dynamics accessible spectroscopically.</cite> <cite id="1d2f79d9-2">hBN phononic crystals with RF bandgaps enable on-chip phonon routing and study of quantized sound transport.</cite> <cite id="1d2f79d9-5">WSe2/hBN shows interlayer electron–phonon coupling evidenced by emergent hBN phonons in Raman spectra.</cite>
- For scalable phononics with large systems: use trapped-ion arrays or neutral-atom optical lattices to engineer phonon branch structures and run quantum walks; exploit phonon-mediated entanglement protocols and boson sampling variants as probes of multi-particle phonon quantum statistics.<cite id="2aa86c84-7">Trapped-ion phonon quantum walks provide a route to boson sampling and non-classical transport with phonons.</cite> <cite id="852c053c-7">Phonon quantum-walk platforms in solids and ions are established arenas where phonon statistics and interference manifest in controllable lattices.</cite>

fully_underspecified.text: What platforms can be used to study properties?
fully_underspecified.answer:
# What "platforms" you can use to study properties, by category

## 1) Data and knowledge‑base platforms (databases, catalogs, and portals)
These platforms provide curated or predicted material, chemical, or biological property data, often with search, visualization, and comparison features that let you study property trends, correlations, and uncertainty.

- Cross‑disciplinary library guides curate and describe how to find and compare material property datasets and tools, including broad and specialized databases for physical properties and spectra <cite id="65c63578-4">There are many databases in which you can find, compare, and calculate physical properties of materials</cite> <cite id="65c63578-0">Predicted and experimental properties for your chemicals are available for exploration</cite> <cite id="65c63578-6">A spectroscopy resource provides access to 1.4 million spectra (IR, NMR, MS, Raman, UV‑Vis) plus chemical structures and properties</cite> <cite id="65c63578-5">Chemical and physical properties are accessible via platforms for materials data science</cite>.
- Commercial/engineering databases aggregate numeric property data from handbooks and research, supporting queries by composition, phase, and application context <cite id="65c63578-1">Knovel's material property search engine finds numeric data hidden in handbooks, manuals, and databases across thousands of materials</cite>.
- Open materials property databases at scale enable rapid screening and benchmarking:
  - AFLOW/AFLOWlib: a globally available repository and web platform with over 3.9 million compounds and more than 817 million properties, designed for scalable ab initio workflows and property predictions <cite id="6381792f-2">AFLOW.org is a globally available database of 3,929,948 material compounds with over 817,429,184 calculated properties</cite> <cite id="6381792f-7">AFLOW combines ab initio repositories with quantitative structure–property relationship models to predict properties</cite>.
  - Materials Project (MP): a high‑throughput DFT platform providing formation energies, band gaps, volumes, and derived properties for a large crystal catalog; it is frequently benchmarked for reproducibility and agreement across HT‑DFT platforms <cite id="6381792f-5">Automatic‑FLOW (AFLOW), the Materials Project (MP), and the Open Quantum Materials Database (OQMD) are consolidated and compared for agreement on formation energy, volume, band gap, and other properties</cite> <cite id="6381792f-0">A comparison quantifies agreement among AFLOW, MP, and OQMD for multiple key properties</cite>.
  - OQMD: a DFT‑based thermodynamic and structural properties database covering more than a million materials and compositions; includes a web platform and a property predictor interface to accelerate discovery workflows <cite id="6381792f-1">The OQMD is a database of DFT calculated thermodynamic and structural properties of 1,407,395 materials</cite> <cite id="6381792f-6">OQMD provides a materials property predictor platform for accelerated discovery</cite> <cite id="6381792f-8">OQMD offers queryable data resources under CC‑BY licensing</cite>.
- Chemical substance property hubs and regulatory portals:
  - ECHA's KEP and similar substance explorers provide predicted and experimental properties and hazard data for regulatory and design contexts (e.g., exposure, reactivity) <cite id="65c63578-2">Substance details pages expose predicted and experimental properties for your chemicals</cite>.
  - Public bioactive property catalogs:
    - ChEMBL and PubChem provide measured and predicted bioactivity (ADME, potency) and structural diversity to study structure–property–activity relationships (SPAR/SAR), often integrated with cheminformatics "platforms" (e.g., MOE) <cite id="65c63578-0">Libraries and guides describe workflows to find and analyze properties for substances with thousands of entries</cite>.
- Spectra and structure libraries serve as property‑by‑measurement platforms, enabling identification and property inference from experimental spectra and linking to thermodynamic/transport properties <cite id="65c63578-6">Access to 1.4 million IR/NMR/MS/Raman/UV‑Vis spectra with associated structures and properties</cite>.
- Domain‑specific catalogs and calculators:
  - Polymer property platforms and guides (e.g., Polymerize.io's "Top Platforms for Predicting Material Properties") summarize practical tools for viscosity, thermal, and mechanical property estimation for polymers and composites <cite id="65c63578-0">Notable platforms help researchers predict material behavior before stepping into the lab</cite>.

Practical tips: Combine a library guide to map your property targets to the right database, then pull benchmark numbers from AFLOW/OQMD/MP for comparison and uncertainty analysis; use the engineering database (e.g., Knovel) when you need tabulated numeric properties aligned to standards and applications <cite id="65c63578-4">Library guides list broad and specialized databases for material property comparison and calculation</cite> <cite id="6381792f-1">OQMD exemplifies DFT‑derived thermodynamic/structural property breadth</cite> <cite id="65c63578-1">Knovel centralizes numeric tables from handbooks into a queryable interface</cite>.

## 2) Simulation and modeling platforms (algorithms, codes, workflows)
Simulation platforms let you compute and predict properties first‑principles, mesoscale, or empirically, including thermodynamics, mechanics, transport, and spectra.

- Ab initio and high‑throughput (HT‑DFT) platforms:
  - AFLOW, Materials Project, and OQMD are canonical HT‑DFT platforms for formation energies, bandgaps, structural stability, and derived descriptors like hardness/electron mobility; comparative studies analyze agreement and variance, guiding trust and cross‑validation across platforms <cite id="6381792f-0">Agreement among AFLOW, MP, and OQMD is quantified for formation energy, volume, band gap, and related properties</cite> <cite id="6381792f-5">HT‑DFT databases (AFLOW, MP, OQMD) are consolidated and benchmarked for computed properties</cite>.
- Classical molecular dynamics (MD) and Monte Carlo (MC):
