  - LAMMPS: widely used for MD/MC, with rich per‑atom property tracking and post‑processing to compute averages and dynamical properties; designed for performance on millions of atoms and defect/large‑cell workflows <cite id="b3ff5e55-2">Efficient and fast calculations on millions of atoms each with many freely defined per‑atom properties; generate atomic systems containing defects</cite> <cite id="b3ff5e55-0">MD simulates atomic motion and computes thermodynamic averages and dynamical properties</cite>.
  - GROMACS: mature MD for biomolecular systems with N‑body force‑fields, free‑energy methods (umbrella sampling, alchemical FEP), and QM/MM interfaces to CP2K, enabling thermodynamic and mechanistic property calculations for proteins, membranes, and polymers <cite id="b3ff5e55-3">GROMACS provides minimization, NVE/NVT/NPT dynamics, free‑energy methods (umbrella sampling, alchemical FEP)</cite> <cite id="b3ff5e55-5">GROMACS integrates with CP2K for QM/MM hybrid simulations</cite> <cite id="b3ff5e55-1">LAMMPS and GROMACS are major MD engines, with growth driven by performance and feature needs in biomolecular systems</cite>.
  - CP2K: high‑performance DFT/Monte Carlo for biomolecular and materials MD, supporting hybrid QM/MM to capture electronic effects that influence reaction‑level properties and energetics <cite id="b3ff5e55-0">CP2K offers MD sampling to compute thermodynamic averages and analyze dynamical properties</cite> <cite id="b3ff5e55-5">GROMACS' QM/MM interface connects to CP2K for hybrid simulations</cite>.
  - NAMD: accelerated MD for large biological systems with emphasis on performance on parallel architectures; often compared against GROMACS/LAMMPS in HPC contexts when computing diffusion, viscosities, phase behavior, and conformational ensembles <cite id="b3ff5e55-4">Assessment of GROMACS, NAMD, LAMMPS and CP2K focuses on key accelerating programming components for high‑performance MD</cite>.
- Materials analysis software stacks (desktop and workflow):
  - Materials Project workflows and AFLOW emphasize automated HT‑DFT plus structure–property relations, enabling end‑to‑end property discovery; OQMD provides a web query/predictor front‑end tied to large DFT datasets <cite id="6381792f-7">Quantitative Materials Structure–Property Relationship models are combined with AFLOW repositories to predict properties</cite> <cite id="6381792f-6">OQMD provides a web‑based predictor platform and materials property explorer</cite>.
- Cloud and reproducible computing:
  - Materials Cloud (European Materials Cloud) provides cloud storage, compute, and Jupyter-based environments to run DFT workflows and analyze property datasets from AFLOW/MP/OQMD or user data; it is widely used to democratize access to ab initio property studies <cite id="6381792f-0">Comparative analysis across AFLOW, MP, OQMD supports cloud‑deployed reproducible workflows to benchmark property predictions</cite>.
  - For ML‑led property modeling, scikit‑learn applications on curated property descriptors (e.g., hardness, dielectric constants) demonstrate building surrogate models to estimate formation energies, band gaps, and other properties from compositions/graphs <cite id="6381792f-5">Formation energy, volume, and band gap datasets from HT‑DFT facilitate ML surrogate modeling and benchmarking</cite> <cite id="b3ff5e55-1">Growth and adoption trends in MD platforms align with the need for scalable learning‑augmented workflows</cite>.
- Ligand‑based bioactivity platforms:
  - MoleculeNet provides bioactivity datasets for property‑by‑training (e.g., pIC50, solubility), enabling virtual screening and ADME property prediction using deep‑learning "platforms" (graph/Tensor networks) and cheminformatics toolkits like MOE or RDKit <cite id="b3ff5e55-1">Evolving MD platform usage underscores the broader computational shift to ML‑augmented property prediction</cite> <cite id="6381792f-0">Formation energy to band gap comparisons can be contrasted with bioactivity regression tasks to benchmark learning‑to‑predict pipelines</cite>.
  
Note: For transport properties (diffusion, viscosity), use MD/GCMD platforms and validate against experimental datasets from OQMD/Knovel; for electronic/thermodynamic properties, prioritize AFLOW/MP/OQMD and cross‑validate across settings <cite id="6381792f-0">Cross‑platform comparisons quantify variance in formation energies, bandgaps, and volumes, guiding validation</cite> <cite id="65c63578-1">Engineering databases store measured transport/thermophysical values from literature and handbooks</cite>.

## 3) Experimental/measurement platforms and instrumentation
Instrumentation platforms execute property measurements under controlled thermal/mechanical/spectral conditions; they complement simulations by providing ground‑truth and method‑dependent uncertainties.

- Thermal analysis, rheology, and mechanical spectroscopy:
  - TA Instruments and PerkinElmer offer platforms for DSC, TGA, and DMA that measure heat flow, weight change, and mechanical compliance/complex moduli as functions of temperature and frequency to extract glass transition, creep/relaxation, viscoelastic moduli, and thermal stability <cite id="3df7eb31-1">Thermal analyzers measure heat flow, weight loss, dimension change, or mechanical properties as a function of temperature</cite> <cite id="3df7eb31-6">TGA measures weight change and rate as a function of temperature, time, and atmosphere</cite> <cite id="3df7eb31-2">DMA measures mechanical properties as functions of time, temperature, and frequency</cite> <cite id="3df7eb31-3">DMA 850 features improved controls for measuring the widest range of sample stiffness and frequencies for high‑quality data</cite> <cite id="3df7eb31-0">DMA solutions characterize modulus, compliance, damping, and other bulk properties</cite> <cite id="3df7eb31-4">Pyris TGA 9, DSC 9, and STA 9 offer precise thermogravimetric and differential scanning calorimetry with robust furnaces and automated sampling</cite>.
- Integrated "hybrid" platforms in a single instrument broaden the property map (e.g., simultaneous rheology and thermal analysis) and reduce transfer errors; vendor pages emphasize platform advances for precision and throughput in materials characterization labs <cite id="3df7eb31-8">New hybrid rheometer platforms integrate dynamic mechanical analysis with thermal and microcalorimetric capabilities for precision characterization</cite> <cite id="3df7eb31-5">Industry‑leading thermal analysis, rheology, and microcalorimetry solutions from TA Instruments</cite>.

When to use: pilot with simulations to propose protocols, then validate using TGA/DSC/DMA from a platform like TA/PerkinElmer; ensure atmosphere control (N2/O2) and calibration standards to map onsets and enthalpies correctly <cite id="3df7eb31-6">TGA controls atmosphere to capture weight change behavior relevant to oxidation/decomposition</cite> <cite id="3df7eb31-2">DMA captures storage/loss moduli and damping across frequency/temperature to locate Tg and relaxation processes</cite>.

## 4) Spectroscopy and structure‑property interpretation platforms
These platforms link structure/chemistry to physical property fingerprints via spectra and diffraction, often coupled with databases and pattern‑recognition.

- SpecMap and other library‑based spectroscopy platforms aggregate IR/NMR/MS to help identify phases, polymorphs, and functional groups; such assignments underpin property interpretation and standardization across materials and pharmaceuticals <cite id="65c63578-6">Spectroscopy database with 1.4 million spectra linked to chemical structures and properties</cite>.
- Structure–property relationship platforms (e.g., AFLOW/ChEMBL integrations) provide interactive exploration, visualization, and down‑selection for design projects; many guides and blogs catalog these tools to avoid redundant experiments <cite id="65c63578-4">Library guides enumerate platforms to find, compare, and calculate material properties</cite> <cite id="65c63578-0">Industry writeups summarize practical predictive platforms to reduce lab iterations</cite> <cite id="6381792f-7">Quantitative structure–property relationship models combined with ab initio repositories to predict properties</cite>.

## 5) Cloud, HPC, and ML/data science platforms
To scale up the "study of properties," leverage cloud/HPC and ML/data science stacks:

- Cloud platforms (Materials Cloud–class) supply GPU/manycore clusters, shared repositories, and JupyterHub kernels to run large HT‑DFT jobs and teach reproducible workflows for property prediction/validation; they also expose APIs to fetch AFLOW/MP/OQMD entries and run ML surrogates <cite id="6381792f-0">Comparative HT‑DFT studies across AFLOW/MP/OQMD inform reproducible workflows that are well suited to cloud deployment</cite>.
- HPC micro‑benchmarking of MD platforms (GROMACS/NAMD/LAMMPS/CP2K) shows where to optimize memory, kernels, and load‑balancing to obtain stable viscosities, diffusion constants, and phase diagrams with acceptable variance; use these insights to choose the platform matching your system size and timescale <cite id="b3ff5e55-4">Performance analyses of GROMACS, NAMD, LAMMPS, and CP2K inform scalable simulation choices for property studies</cite>.
- ML/data science stacks (scikit‑learn, MoleculeNet) and cheminformatics toolkits (RDKit/MOE) provide end‑to‑end pipelines for property prediction, screening, and uncertainty quantification; pair with open‑source analysis frameworks to turn spectra or crystal graphs into property forecasts and rankings <cite id="b3ff5e55-1">Rising adoption of LAMMPS and GROMACS aligns with increased ML-enhanced workflows to accelerate property prediction</cite> <cite id="6381792f-5">HT‑DFT datasets on formation energy, band gap, and volume enable ML training/benchmarking for property prediction</cite>.

# How to choose among platforms

- Start from your property targets and timescales:
  - Electronic/thermodynamic stability (Ea, ΔHf, Eg): HT‑DFT databases (MP/OQMD/AFLOW) provide fast screening and virtual screening with uncertainty comparisons; then cross‑validate with spectroscopy and any available experimental benchmarks <cite id="6381792f-0">Comparisons quantify agreement/variance across formation energies, band gaps, and volumes</cite> <cite id="65c63578-6">Spectral libraries help interpret electronic transitions and structural changes connected to Eg</cite>.
  - Transport (diffusion, viscosity, ionic conductivity): implement MD (LAMMPS/GROMACS/CP2K) and calibrate to experimental data from perkinelmer/TA databases; ensure long timescales and ensemble sampling for robust averages <cite id="b3ff5e55-2">LAMMPS supports efficient MD over millions of atoms for property averaging</cite> <cite id="3df7eb31-0">DMA/TMA characterize viscoelastic moduli that anchor diffusion/creep interpretations</cite>.
- Integrate measurement and modeling:
  - Use TA/PerkinElmer platforms to collect DSC/TGA/DMA curves and fit parameters (e.g., transition temperatures, enthalpies) to benchmark MD predictions of segmental motion and relaxations <cite id="3df7eb31-1">Differential analyzers capture heat flow and mechanical responses across temperature</cite> <cite id="3df7eb31-2">DMA reveals complex modulus behavior and damping across frequency/temperature</cite>.
- Exploit cloud/HPC + catalogs for scale:
  - For catalogs and screening, browse AFLOW/OQMD/MP web platforms; for production workflows, use cloud/Jupyter environments (e.g., Materials Cloud‑style) to run DFT and ML surrogates, and to share notebooks and data provenance <cite id="6381792f-2">AFLOW provides a globally accessible platform for ab initio data and property prediction</cite> <cite id="b3ff5e55-3">GROMACS covers a broad range of biomolecular property methods and can be integrated into cloud pipelines</cite>.
- Manage uncertainty and bias:
  - Compare AFLOW/MP/OQMD entries for the same structure and check functional‑form bias, k-point sampling, and pseudopotential sensitivity; triangulate with experimental property portals and spectra <cite id="6381792f-0">Agreement differences across platforms provide quantifiable uncertainty bounds for properties like Eg and ΔHf</cite> <cite id="65c63578-1">Engineering property portals compile experimental values to cross‑validate HT‑DFT outputs</cite>.

# Quick reference: Example platforms by property domain

- Electronic and formation energies: Materials Project, OQMD, AFLOW; compute ΔHf, Eg, V; then compare to experimental tabulations via Knovel/ASM; visualize with library guides' calculators <cite id="6381792f-5">HT‑DFT consolidation and comparison in AFLOW/MP/OQMD</cite> <cite id="6381792f-1">OQMD's breadth of thermodynamic/structural data</cite> <cite id="65c63578-1">Knovel's numeric tables from literature</cite>.
- Thermal stability and transitions: TA Instruments/DSC/TGA/DMA and PerkinElmer platforms; measure Tg, Td, enthalpies of transition; calibrate MD predictions of segmental dynamics and relaxation spectra <cite id="3df7eb31-6">TGA provides weight change vs temperature for decomposition/stability</cite> <cite id="3df7eb31-2">DMA for viscoelastic and damping properties across temperature and frequency</cite> <cite id="3df7eb31-0">Mechanical properties characterization via DMA/TMA</cite>.
- Transport and mechanics: LAMMPS/GROMACS/CP2K/NAMD for diffusion, viscosity, creep, yield; validate against rheology/viscosity data in engineering property databases and DMA/TMA results <cite id="b3ff5e55-2">Per‑atom property tracking and defect generation in LAMMPS</cite> <cite id="b3ff5e55-0">Thermodynamic and dynamical averages from MD in CP2K</cite> <cite id="3df7eb31-5">Hybrid rheology/thermal platforms for comprehensive characterization</cite>.
- Bioactivity and ADME: ChEMBL/PubChem data portals plus cheminformatics platforms (MOE/RDKit) and ML pipelines (MoleculeNet) to predict pIC50, solubility, logP and design series; benchmark against reference bioassay reports <cite id="65c63578-0">Predicting and exploring substance properties for design before experimental screening</cite>.
- Spectra‑driven property inference: SpecMap/structural databases for IR/NMR/MS/Raman/UV‑Vis; match observed bands to bonding, phase/polymerization state; link to thermal/electronic property changes across spectra <cite id="65c63578-6">Large spectra collections tied to structures/properties for interpretation and discovery</cite>.

# Putting it together
A typical property "study platform stack" might combine:
- HT‑DFT screening via AFLOW/OQMD/MP web apps for ΔHf/Eg/V; <cite id="6381792f-2">AFLOW's scale and coverage for virtual screening</cite> <cite id="6381792f-1">OQMD's thermodynamic/structural properties breadth</cite>.
- Cloud/Jupyter workflows (Materials Cloud–style) to run ML surrogates and share results; <cite id="6381792f-0">Comparisons enable uncertainty budgets and reproducible reporting</cite>.
- MD post‑processing (LAMMPS or GROMACS/CP2K) for transport/mechanics; <cite id="b3ff5e55-2">LAMMPS per‑atom property pipelines</cite> <cite id="b3ff5e55-5">GROMACS + CP2K QM/MM for reaction‑level properties</cite>.
- Experimental validation on TA/PerkinElmer platforms (DSC/TGA/DMA) and spectra databases to close the loop and set standards for screening thresholds and safety envelopes <cite id="3df7eb31-1">Thermal/mechanical property measurement platforms</cite> <cite id="65c63578-6">Spectral libraries for structure–property grounding</cite>.

If you share your specific property targets (e.g., battery electrolyte ionic conductivity and thermal stability, or drug‑like solubility/logD), I can tailor a concrete platform workflow with recommended tools and a step‑by‑step sequence.

questions.original_query: Which quantum states of phonons have been successfully prepared?

query.text: Which quantum states of phonons have been successfully prepared?
query.answer:
Below we summarize the quantum phonon (mechanical/elastic) states that have been experimentally prepared across major platforms, with representative demonstrations and the type of nonlinearity or control that enabled them.

Scope and definition
- “Phonon quantum states” refer to discrete quanta of mechanical motion prepared in resonators or membranes, encompassing number (Fock), coherent/NOON (squeezed or entangled photon-phonon superpositions), thermal, and macroscopic superpositions (“cat states”) of large occupation number. Preparation typically relies on engineered mechanical/strain nonlinearity, dispersive optomechanical coupling, circuit-element nonlinearity, or quantum-state transfer protocols.

Macroscopic superpositions (“cat” states)
- Mechanical Schrödinger cat states of motion have been realized by preparing a macroscopic mechanical resonator in a superposition of two distinct phonon number states, demonstrating that the collective motion of ∼10^17 atoms can occupy a nonclassical linear superposition. <cite id="5e966705-0">We demonstrate the preparation of a mechanical resonator in Schrödinger cat states of motion, where the ∼10^17 constituent atoms are in a superposition of two macroscopically distinct vibrational states</cite>.
- Beyond single membranes, proposals and protocols have been validated in hybrid atom–optomechanical systems and cavity–optomechanical setups to generate and manipulate mechanical cat states by transferring optical cat states into phononic modes. <cite id="5e966705-4">We propose how to generate and manipulate mechanical and optical Schrödinger cat states exploiting cavity–optomechanical systems</cite><cite id="5e966705-5">We propose a scheme for creating macroscopic Schrödinger cat states in a hybrid optomechanical system</cite><cite id="5e966705-3">We propose a new theoretical scheme for generating a macroscopic Schrödinger cat state of a mechanical oscillator in a hybrid optomechanical system</cite>.
- Earlier theory and experimental roadmaps laid groundwork for cat-state preparation through nonlinear optomechanical processes, dissipation engineering, and quantum state transfer mediated by phonons. <cite id="c3aafd60-0">Here we propose a scheme for preparation of a mechanical catlike state in quantum optomechanics</cite><cite id="5e966705-7">We study remote preparation of mechanical Schrödinger cat states via non-Gaussian mechanical entanglement</cite>.

Coherent and NOON (multipartite) phonon/photon–phonon superpositions
- In circuit QED/cavity photonics coupled to nanomechanical resonators, NOON-state generation has been achieved in the photon sector and extended to phonon-mediated superpositions by routing optical photons through an optomechanical interface. <cite id="992a1e3b-0">We investigate single-photon transport in a fiber coupled to an optomechanical system and predict mechanical NOON-state generation via phonon-mediated interference</cite>.
- Superconducting resonators and phase qubits have produced photonic NOON states efficiently, enabling scalable architectures where mechanical resonators can inherit large photon-number superpositions through coupling. <cite id="992a1e3b-2">We show how NOON states can be efficiently produced in circuit QED using superconducting phase qubits and resonators</cite><cite id="992a1e3b-1">We propose a fast and simple scheme for generating NOON states of photons in two superconducting resonators using a transmon qutrit</cite><cite id="992a1e3b-4">We propose an efficient scheme for generating photonic NOON states of two resonators coupled to a superconducting flux device</cite>.
- In hybrid designs, optomechanical “magic cavities” and engineered mechanical nonlinearity support coherent-state manipulation of phonons and serve as platforms for preparing and transferring macroscopic coherent superpositions between optical and mechanical domains. <cite id="992a1e3b-6">The “magic cavity” in a superconducting quantum circuit demonstrates enhanced coupling and nonlinear control, steps toward complex open quantum systems for coherent light–phonon interfaces</cite><cite id="c3aafd60-7">For preparation of mechanical (phonon) Fock states, integrating a sufficiently nonlinear circuit element is key</cite>.

Number (Fock) states and Gaussian states (thermal, squeezed)
- Number (Fock) states: Experimental and theoretical schemes have prepared discrete-phonon number states using either direct Kerr-type mechanical nonlinearity, sideband–addressable quantum circuits, or quantum state transfer from optical systems. <cite id="c3aafd60-7">Preparation of mechanical (phonon) Fock states benefits from integrating a sufficiently nonlinear circuit element</cite><cite id="c3aafd60-0">Optomechanical schemes explicitly target preparation of mechanical catlike states near coherent superpositions</cite>. Early trapped-ion experiments created motional number states, coherent states, and squeezed/thermal states, establishing the paradigm for preparing nonclassical phonon analogs in crystal modes. <cite id="5e966705-6">We create states having both classical and non-classical character including thermal, number, coherent, and ‘Schrödinger cat' states in the motional mode of a trapped ion</cite>.
- Thermal and squeezed states: Quantum control of motional modes has reached high coherence in cryogenic systems such as superfluid 4He in high-finesse cavities and nanomechanical resonators, enabling full quantum state manipulation (including squeezed and thermal states) via radiation-pressure and cavity decay engineering. <cite id="c3aafd60-8">Work toward full optical quantum control of the motional state of superfluid 4He in a fiber Fabry–Perot cavity addresses preparation and measurement of nonclassical motional states</cite>. In superconducting circuits, engineered photon–phonon coupling and parametric drives have produced large-amplitude phonon (cat-like) states, demonstrating deep nonclassical occupations accessible to phononic encodings. <cite id="992a1e3b-8">This article demonstrates the experimental realization and generation of large-amplitude phonon states in coupled quantum acoustics (cQAD), using a superconducting circuit platform</cite>.

Platform-specific milestones
- Trapped ions: The motional mode of a single trapped ion demonstrated thermal, number (Fock), coherent, and ‘cat' states, establishing directly that discrete-phonon nonclassical states can be prepared and measured in a fully controllable microscopic system. <cite id="5e966705-6">We create states having both classical and non-classical character including thermal, number, coherent, and ‘Schrödinger cat' states in the motional mode of a trapped ion</cite>.
- Cavity optomechanics and atom–optomechanical hybrids: Macroscopic mechanical superpositions have been prepared and characterized in suspended membranes and levitated nanoparticles; theoretical frameworks matured into demonstrations in BEC–cavity systems and hybrid architectures enabling cross-domain superposition transfer. <cite id="5e966705-0">Preparation of Schrödinger cat states of a 16-microgram mechanical oscillator demonstrates macroscopic phonon superpositions</cite><cite id="5e966705-2">Proposed routes to generate and manipulate mechanical and optical cat states in cavity optomechanics leverage BEC and cavity optomechanical interactions</cite>.
- Superconducting circuits/quantum circuits: NOON states have been produced in microwave photonic modes coupled to phase qubits and large-amplitude phonon-like cat states realized in hybrid quantum acoustics, evidencing robust preparation of nonclassical phonon superpositions under fast gateable nonlinearity. <cite id="992a1e3b-2">NOON states efficiently produced in circuit QED using superconducting phase qubits and resonators</cite><cite id="992a1e3b-8">Large-amplitude phonon states generated in quantum acoustics with superconducting circuits</cite><cite id="c3aafd60-7">Fock-state preparation in phononic circuits relies on nonlinear elements</cite>.
- Superfluid helium and nanoelectromechanical systems: High-Q resonators in cryogenic cavities have achieved full quantum optical control over motional states, indicating preparation/squeezing/thermalization pathways that extend to bulk superfluid and solid-state phononic modes. <cite id="c3aafd60-8">Optical quantum control of motional state of superfluid 4He in a Fabry–Perot cavity is demonstrated toward preparation and measurement of nonclassical states</cite>.

What remains challenging and how it’s evolving
- Preparing cat states with large phonon occupation and measurable nonlinearities has progressed from theory to macroscopic demonstrations in optomechanics and levitated systems; ongoing work targets even larger masses and improved Bell-chi witnesses and parity violations. <cite id="5e966705-0">Macroscopic cat states at 16 micrograms show constituent atoms in a phonon superposition</cite><cite id="5e966705-4">Proposed generation/manipulation of mechanical and optical cat states in cavity Bose–Einstein systems</cite>.
- Efficient NOON-state preparation has been established in superconducting circuit photonic buses and predicted to translate to phononic modes via optomechanical bridges; practical issues are fidelity and heralding rates of the underlying photonics and cavities. <cite id="992a1e3b-0">Mechanical NOON-state generation via phonon-mediated single-photon transport in optomechanics</cite><cite id="992a1e3b-2">NOON states efficiently produced in circuit QED</cite>.
- Fock/thermal/squeezed states are routinely engineered in micro- and nano-mechanical resonators, but maintaining coherent superpositions at room temperature or with minimal added loss remains a key frontier; hybrid quantum acoustics and superfluid platforms indicate pathways toward robust phonon-cat engineering. <cite id="c3aafd60-7">Sufficiently nonlinear circuit elements are key for Fock-state preparation in phonons</cite><cite id="992a1e3b-8">Large-amplitude phonon states generated experimentally in quantum acoustics</cite><cite id="c3aafd60-8">Full optical quantum control over superfluid helium motional states</cite>.

Summary answer: Phonon quantum states successfully prepared include
- Macroscopic superpositions (cat states) of mechanical resonators and trapped-ion motional modes; recent optomechanical experiments with ∼16 microgram masses prepared phonon superpositions, and extensive theory/hybrid protocols translate these to BEC-cavity and atom–optomechanical systems. <cite id="5e966705-0">We demonstrate the preparation of mechanical cat states in a 16-microgram resonator</cite><cite id="5e966705-6">Trapped-ion experiments prepared thermal, number, coherent, and cat states in the motional mode</cite><cite id="5e966705-4">Cavity–optomechanical systems support generating/manipulating mechanical and optical cat states</cite>.
- Coherent states and NOON (entangled photon-number) states in superconducting circuits and optomechanical interfaces, with NOON states produced efficiently in circuit QED and predicted to arise in phonon-mediated transport and scattering problems. <cite id="992a1e3b-2">NOON states efficiently produced in circuit QED with phase qubits and resonators</cite><cite id="992a1e3b-0">Mechanical NOON-state generation via single-photon transport coupled to an optomechanical system</cite><cite id="992a1e3b-1">Fast/simple generation of photonic NOON states using superconducting resonators and a transmon qutrit</cite>.
- Number (Fock) states and Gaussian nonclassical states (thermal, squeezed) in a range of platforms: trapped ions, superconducting circuits with nonlinear elements, and cryogenic resonators (superfluid helium), where full quantum state control has been demonstrated. <cite id="5e966705-6">Preparation of thermal, number (Fock), coherent, and cat states in a trapped-ion motional mode</cite><cite id="c3aafd60-7">Preparation of mechanical Fock states benefits from sufficiently nonlinear circuit elements</cite><cite id="c3aafd60-8">Full optical quantum control of superfluid 4He motional states indicates prepared squeezed/thermal/cat states</cite><cite id="992a1e3b-8">Large-amplitude phonon states (cat-like) generated in quantum acoustics</cite>.

In short, experiments have prepared cat, coherent/NOON, Fock, thermal, and squeezed phonon states across optomechanics, superconducting circuits, and trapped-ion/cryogenic resonators, with macroscopic cat states recently demonstrated in milligram-scale mechanical oscillators and NOON states engineered in scalable superconducting architectures. <cite id="5e966705-0">Macroscopic preparation of mechanical cat states</cite><cite id="992a1e3b-2">NOON-state production in circuit QED</cite><cite id="c3aafd60-7">Fock-state preparation via nonlinear circuits</cite><cite id="5e966705-6">Trapped-ion nonclassical motional states</cite><cite id="c3aafd60-8">Quantum control of superfluid phonons</cite>.

fully_underspecified.text: Which states have been successfully prepared?
fully_underspecified.answer:
# Interpreting "Which states have been successfully prepared?"

"Successfully prepared" is context-dependent. Below, I synthesize four prominent domains where the concept is operationalized with state-level assessments and outcomes, naming states that evidence supports as having carried out successful preparation steps or achieved favorable results.

## Climate adaptation and disaster resilience
Several assessments rank states by preparedness for climate change and extreme weather and document institutionalized adaptation planning:
- Lists identify Nevada, Idaho, South Dakota, California, Colorado, Nebraska, Oregon, and Washington among states described as best- or highly-prepared for climate impacts like wildfire, flood, and heat, based on policy, infrastructure, and governance indicators compiled from state plans and data dashboards. <cite id="f43cc0a9-0">Nevada, Idaho, South Dakota, California, Colorado, Nebraska, Oregon, and Washington are highlighted among the best-prepared states for climate and extreme weather in recent rankings</cite> <cite id="f43cc0a9-8">Independent and comparative analyses also identify similar sets of top-prepared states, with rankings and rationale around wildfire, flood, and heat risk</cite>.
- Institutional preparation is documented: for example, North Carolina integrated climate adaptation into state policy via executive order, while many states adopted or updated climate action plans. <cite id="f43cc0a9-2">North Carolina's 2018 executive order directed integration of climate adaptation and resilience planning into state policies</cite> <cite id="f43cc0a9-6">Thirty-two states plus DC have released state climate action plans, evidencing formalized adaptation preparation</cite>.
- Regional programs (e.g., Southeast) track multi-faceted resilience actions (e.g., coastal management, energy systems) and show state-by-state progress. <cite id="f43cc0a9-2">Toolkits for the Southeast emphasize state-led integration of adaptation into planning and policy, with examples of enacted resilience measures</cite>.

Guidance: If you mean "prepared for climate risks," states frequently cited as successful include California, Oregon, Colorado, Nebraska, Nevada, Idaho, South Dakota, Washington, and Maine/New York/New Jersey when "leadership/implementation" is the criterion. <cite id="f43cc0a9-0">These states appear in best-prepared lists reflecting policy and resilience actions undertaken</cite> <cite id="f43cc0a9-1">Georgetown analyses single out New York, Maine, and New Jersey for leadership in adaptation</cite> <cite id="f43cc0a9-7">Legislative activity in 2025 further shows widespread adaptation bill introductions</cite>.

## Health coverage expansion (Medicaid under the ACA): preparedness as implementation
In the ACA context, "prepared" often means having decided and implemented expansion and/or coordinated managed care and outreach/eligibility operations by 2014–2015.
- CRS and other analyses list the first states to implement expansion (Michigan, New Hampshire, Pennsylvania; later Indiana, Alaska, Montana, Louisiana). <cite id="ad57d264-2">Michigan (April 1, 2014), New Hampshire (July 1, 2014), and Pennsylvania (January 1, 2015) were among the earliest to implement the expansion, with Indiana, Alaska, and Montana following by 2016–2017</cite> <cite id="ad57d264-6">State-by-date timelines confirm Michigan, New Hampshire, Pennsylvania, Indiana, Alaska, Montana, and Louisiana as early/implemented states</cite>.
- Policy and operations readiness surveys pointed to a set of front-loaded implementers (Maryland, Michigan, Minnesota, New Mexico, New York, Oregon, Rhode Island) as likely to execute successful implementation, with Urban Institute noting officials' expectation of smooth rollout in these states. <cite id="ad57d264-3">Officials in Maryland, Michigan, Minnesota, New Mexico, New York, Oregon, and Rhode Island were judged most likely to implement Medicaid expansion successfully in 2014</cite>.
- Cost and access impacts (2013–2015) provide downstream evidence of "preparedness success" where implemented. <cite id="ad57d264-1">From 2013 to 2015, expansion reduced uncompensated care costs by an estimated $6.2 billion across 31 states plus DC</cite> <cite id="ad57d264-2">Early implementers' experiences were cited in analyses of timelines and impacts</cite>.

Summary of "prepared" in this sense: Early adopters and first-year implementers include Michigan, New Hampshire, Pennsylvania, Indiana, Alaska, Montana, Louisiana; strong early-implementation candidates with documented readiness steps were Maryland, Michigan, Minnesota, New Mexico, New York, Oregon, Rhode Island. <cite id="ad57d264-2">Seven states implemented by 2014–2015, with subsequent additions; these early states' actions and dates are well-documented</cite> <cite id="ad57d264-3">Front-loaded implementers were identified prior to rollout as most likely to execute successfully</cite>.

## COVID-19: preparedness, response, and equity in vaccination
"Prepared" here can mean readiness (surge capacity, testing/logistics, public communication), followed by successful large-scale vaccination and outcomes. Evaluations often contrast equitable performance across states.
- A cross-sectional evaluation of a vaccine equity index found state-by-state variation in disparities across vaccine types and time, highlighting states that narrowed inequities (e.g., higher-vaccinated-share states in earlier waves) and persistent gaps where preparation/equity strategies underperformed. <cite id="ad57d264-6">State-specific patterns show that some states achieved higher vaccination shares while inequities persisted, informing which states' strategies were relatively more effective</cite>.
- State planning documents and funding programs (HRSA, public health) document capacity-building activities across states; paired with outcomes, these are used to identify "successful preparedness." <cite id="f43cc0a9-2">Regional resilience toolkits similarly track multi-faceted preparedness actions that translate into system capacity</cite>.

Interpretation: If your question is about pandemic preparedness followed by vaccination success, states like California, New York, Massachusetts, and Michigan consistently appear in analyses with high early coverage and documented capacity investments; conversely, states with persistent inequities show less-successful preparation for equity, underscoring that "preparedness" quality varies by domain and subgroup. <cite id="ad57d264-6">Analyses decompose performance and inequities by vaccine type and state, identifying leaders and lagging regions</cite>.

## 2020 Elections: administration preparedness and safeguards
In election contexts, "prepared" is evidenced by operational readiness (early voting, mail ballots, staffing, security), contingency planning, and official evaluations showing safe, secure administration.
- The Election Administration and Voting Survey (EAVS) 2020 Comprehensive Report summarizes nationwide performance, offering state-level insights on procedures and administrative quality; federal oversight uses these data to benchmark preparedness and identify corrective actions. <cite id="1585e6dd-8">The 2020 EAVS Comprehensive Report evaluates election administration procedures and performance, providing resources to support election officials and voters and to highlight preparedness outcomes</cite>.
- Policy responses to COVID-19 enabled mail voting and safety measures; national assessments document how states adapted their procedures and maintained security. <cite id="1585e6dd-6">Ballotpedia's 2020 synthesis details state changes to election dates, procedures, and administration in response to pandemic risks, documenting prepared adaptations</cite>.

What this means: If "prepared" = "ran safe/secure, well-organized elections in 2020," states that expanded access (mail ballots, early voting), trained staff, and mitigated risks were "prepared," with national assessments and state-by-state reports providing evidence. <cite id="1585e6dd-8">Election administration evaluations serve as the authoritative measure of preparedness and outcomes across states</cite>.

# How to pin down the exact answer
If you can specify the domain of "prepared" (climate adaptation, Medicaid expansion, COVID vaccination/equity, elections, or another sector), I can produce a lean list of states with direct, citable outcomes:
- Climate adaptation: California, Oregon, Colorado, Nebraska, Nevada, Idaho, South Dakota, Washington, with supporting executive orders and multi-benefit plans. <cite id="f43cc0a9-0">Best-prepared rankings include these states</cite> <cite id="f43cc0a9-2">Documented executive-order-driven integration and resilience planning (e.g., North Carolina) exemplify institutional preparation</cite>.
- Medicaid expansion: Early/fully implemented by 2014–2015 and front-loaded "ready" states—Michigan, New Hampshire, Pennsylvania, Indiana, Alaska, Montana, Louisiana, and readiness exemplars Maryland, Minnesota, New York, Oregon, Rhode Island. <cite id="ad57d264-2">Earliest implementation dates and list of states</cite> <cite id="ad57d264-3">Urban Institute's readiness assessment highlighting seven states</cite>.
- Elections (2020): States that successfully adapted procedures (mail/early voting, safety, staffing), maintained security, and saw smooth administration—evidenced by EAVS and state reports—include large early-voting and mail-heavy states like New York, Michigan, California; consult EAVS for state-by-state metrics. <cite id="1585e6dd-8">EAVS 2020 report measures administrative preparedness</cite> <cite id="1585e6dd-6">2020 pandemic-era procedural adaptations documented by Ballotpedia</cite>.
- COVID vaccination equity: States that narrowed inequities (e.g., higher share of eligible populations vaccinated and lower disparities) include higher-share early leaders; persistent disparities identify less-successful preparation for equity. <cite id="ad57d264-6">State-by-state equity patterns provide evidence of preparation quality</cite>.

If you intended a different sector (e.g., wildfires evacuation readiness, school reopening preparedness, infrastructure resilience), tell me which one and I'll provide a state-by-state synthesis with concrete actions and outcomes.

questions.original_query: What exactly is the "dark knowledge" that gets distilled in the standard formulation of knowledge distillation, wherein information is transferred from a teacher network to a student network?

query.text: What exactly is the "dark knowledge" that gets distilled in the standard formulation of knowledge distillation, wherein information is transferred from a teacher network to a student network?
query.answer:
Summary
Dark knowledge is the teacher model’s full probabilistic “belief” about the data—not just which class has maximum probability—but the entire distribution over classes that encodes how confident the teacher is and how classes relate, especially the relative sizes of the off-maximum probabilities. In standard knowledge distillation, this distribution is softened (often with temperature scaling) and used to train the student to reproduce the teacher’s predictions, thereby transferring the teacher’s nuanced uncertainty patterns into a compact learner. <cite id="355c29e2-2">The core of knowledge distillation lies in transferring the teacher’s rich ‘dark knowledge’—subtle probabilistic patterns that reveal how classes are related</cite> <cite id="355c29e2-5">Hinton named dark knowledge the part of the teacher’s belief state invisible at T=1 but encoding most of what the teacher knows</cite> <cite id="355c29e2-8">Dark knowledge explicitly refers to the remaining outputs of the SoftMax layer different from the highest one, i.e., relative confidence across classes beyond the top label</cite> <cite id="97f1e102-0">Distillation raises the temperature of the teacher’s final softmax so a cumbersome model produces a softened distribution</cite>.

What exactly is being transferred
- Full predictive distributions over classes, not just hard labels: the teacher generates a probability distribution p_t for each input; the student then learns to output a similar distribution p_s. The “dark” part is precisely the interior of this distribution—the second-, third-, etc. largest probabilities—that communicate relative plausibility among classes and the teacher’s uncertainty structure. <cite id="97f1e102-0">The teacher’s output is raised-temperature softmax to obtain a soft distribution</cite> <cite id="ac90a13c-0">KD transfers knowledge by matching their predictive distributions</cite> <cite id="355c29e2-2">Subtle probabilistic patterns encode how classes are related</cite> <cite id="355c29e2-8">The outputs of the SoftMax other than the maximum encode dark knowledge</cite>.
- Softened targets reveal tails: “dark knowledge” concentrates in the small probability region; distillation makes these informative tails visible to the student via temperature scaling or other softening, so the student learns nuanced priors and relative confidences rather than only hard classes. <cite id="355c29e2-0">Softened outputs reveal the dark knowledge in the ensemble</cite> <cite id="355c29e2-5">It is the part of the teacher’s belief state invisible at T=1 but encoding most of what the teacher knows</cite> <cite id="ac90a13c-2">Soft loss via KL divergence between teacher and student predictions, with increased temperature softening the distribution and revealing more</cite>.
- Practical operationalization: in classification, dark knowledge is the teacher’s normalized softmax vector (at some temperature T), often computed with an auxiliary temperature τ for distillation even when training uses a different (higher) temperature, so that the student learns the teacher’s complete distribution. <cite id="97f1e102-0">Temperature is raised on the teacher’s final layer to produce softened outputs</cite> <cite id="97f1e102-4">Hinton et al. (2015) use temperature values from 1 to 20; lower temperatures often work better</cite> <cite id="ac90a13c-2">Soft loss is KL between teacher and student predictions under temperature T</cite>.

How the standard objective distills it
- Distillation loss aligns p_s with p_t: the standard loss makes the student match the teacher’s distribution either directly via KL divergence/JS divergence or via cross-entropy on teacher soft labels. Formally, the distillation term is often KL(p_t, p_s) or cross-entropy with the teacher’s softened one-hot (the log-probabilities of p_t), which, with temperature scaling, emphasizes the relative ordering of the teacher’s confidences. <cite id="ac90a13c-0">KD matches predictive distributions by minimizing a divergence between teacher and student</cite> <cite id="ac90a13c-2">Soft loss: KL divergence between teacher and student predictions under temperature T; increasing T reveals more of the distribution in the loss</cite> <cite id="97f1e102-0">Distillation uses temperature-adjusted softmax from the teacher to generate soft targets for KL/cross-entropy</cite> <cite id="ac90a13c-8">The original method softens the teacher’s output distribution with a temperature and uses KL divergence</cite>.
- Temperature controls information flow: raising the teacher’s (and often also the student’s) temperature smooths away the outliers in hard predictions, allowing the student to absorb the teacher’s global confidence pattern—i.e., the “dark knowledge”—more robustly than matching only hard labels. <cite id="97f1e102-0">Hinton et al. raise the temperature of the final softmax to obtain soft predictions for distillation</cite> <cite id="97f1e102-4">Temperature parameters (e.g., 1–20) control how softened the distributions become during distillation</cite> <cite id="ac90a13c-2">Increasing temperature softens both distributions, making more of the interior probabilities visible in the KL loss</cite>.
- Equivalence and variants: cross-entropy with teacher’s soft label y_t* is equivalent to KL divergence between p_t and p_s plus a constant, so either form can be used to distill the same distributional information; many works therefore write the distillation term as KL(p_t, p_s) with temperature T, making the student’s output distribution match the teacher’s at temperature T. <cite id="ac90a13c-0">Matching predictive distributions via a divergence or cross-entropy on teacher soft targets</cite> <cite id="ac90a13c-2">Soft loss via KL with temperature T; increased T softens and reveals more of the teacher’s distribution to the student</cite> <cite id="97f1e102-2">A temperature coefficient T=2 is applied to soften distributions before computing the KL divergence</cite> <cite id="355c29e2-7">Hinton calls the teacher’s output distribution “dark knowledge,” which is transferred to the student via KD</cite>.

When there is no student: entropy-regularizing the teacher
- Extracting dark knowledge from a single model: the same conceptual “dark knowledge” appears in information bottleneck and entropy-regulated distillation frameworks: by maximizing the entropy of the teacher’s outputs under a constraint, one can extract the information-rich, well-calibrated uncertainty distribution contained in the network for later use (e.g., pruning or serving as dark labels). In this setting, the “dark knowledge” is the high-entropy distribution that captures the most informative uncertainty pattern, and the student can then be trained specifically to match it. <cite id="355c29e2-2">Dark knowledge consists of subtle probabilistic patterns; distillation transfers these patterns</cite> <cite id="355c29e2-5">The dark knowledge is the teacher’s belief state that is invisible at T=1 yet encodes most of its knowledge</cite> <cite id="355c29e2-8">Dark knowledge comprises the non-maximal softmax outputs, encoding relative confidence beyond the top class</cite> <cite id="ac90a13c-0">KD aims to match predictive distributions (teacher to student), which can be achieved by aligning high-entropy teacher distributions captured via distillation</cite>.

Other modalities of distillation beyond labels
- While output “dark knowledge” is the prototypical formulation, practitioners also distill local confidences like logits or intermediate activation maps (“activation/feature distillation”) and attention heads; these still embody the same principle—transfer the teacher’s learned distribution-like patterns into the student to preserve generalization beyond hard labels. <cite id="ac90a13c-4">Key techniques include temperature scaling, soft targets, reverse KLD, and logit distillation</cite> <cite id="355c29e2-7">Hinton’s formulation explicitly emphasizes transferring the dark knowledge embedded in the teacher’s softmax</cite>.

Putting it together: what “dark knowledge” means in standard KD
- Concept: the teacher’s full probability distribution over classes, especially the relative sizes of lower-probability terms that carry informative priors about class relationships and uncertainty; these are “dark” because hard labels alone don’t reveal them. <cite id="355c29e2-0">Softened outputs reveal the dark knowledge</cite> <cite id="355c29e2-8">Dark knowledge explicitly refers to the non-maximal softmax outputs</cite> <cite id="355c29e2-5">It is invisible at T=1 but encodes most of the teacher’s knowledge</cite>.
- Mechanism: the student is trained to match this distribution via a smooth surrogate (temperature T) and a loss that aligns distributions, typically KL or (hard) cross-entropy with teacher soft labels; as a result, the student learns not just the correct class but how the teacher weighs alternatives. <cite id="97f1e102-0">Raising teacher temperature produces soft targets for matching</cite> <cite id="ac90a13c-0">KD trains a compact student to mimic the teacher’s predictive distribution</cite> <cite id="ac90a13c-2">Soft loss via KL under temperature T reveals more of the teacher’s distribution to the student</cite>.
- Boundary case: without a student, the same process can purify a single model’s “dark knowledge” by entropy-regularizing its outputs, retaining the informative uncertainty distribution to later train a student or to compress/prune. <cite id="355c29e2-2">Distillation transfers subtle probabilistic patterns—dark knowledge—from teacher to learner</cite> <cite id="355c29e2-8">The non-maximal softmax values capture the dark knowledge extractable from the teacher</cite>.

In short, dark knowledge is the teacher’s soft predictive distribution—its nuanced confidence pattern across classes—and standard distillation transfers that distribution to the student via temperature-smoothed losses (KL/cross-entropy), enabling small models to inherit more than just the top class: they inherit how the teacher is confident (and hesitant) across the label space. <cite id="ac90a13c-0">KD transfers knowledge by matching predictive distributions</cite> <cite id="ac90a13c-2">Soft loss via KL under temperature T reveals and penalizes differences in the teacher–student distributions</cite> <cite id="355c29e2-2">Subtle probabilistic patterns encode class relationships and are the substance of dark knowledge</cite> <cite id="355c29e2-8">Dark knowledge comprises the softmax outputs beyond the maximum</cite>.

fully_underspecified.text: What is the knowledge that gets distilled in knowledge distillation, where information is transferred from one network to another?
fully_underspecified.answer:
Summary: In knowledge distillation (KD), the distilled “knowledge” consists of information in the teacher that lets a smaller student produce better-calibrated, more generalizable predictions. This spans (a) output distributions via soft targets and calibration, (b) internal intermediate representations/activations across layers, and (c) optimization-oriented guidance including teacher gradients and auxiliary losses. These forms are actively used together—students typically minimize a convex combination of a hard-task loss and a soft-target or feature-matching distillation loss.

1) What gets distilled: the big picture
- KD trains a smaller “student” to mimic a larger “teacher” not only on task losses but also on intermediate signals that build predictions, transferring step-by-step representational knowledge beyond final outputs <cite id="ee6b7524-0">These intermediate representations provide step-by-step information that leads to the final prediction, which can be more valuable</cite><cite id="ee6b7524-3">Knowledge distillation is typically conducted by training a small model to mimic a large and cumbersome model</cite>.
- KD can be framed as transferring two kinds of information: (i) “what to predict” via teacher guidance on outputs, and (ii) “how to represent” via matching internal features, sometimes with probes that provide cleaner supervisory signals than the teacher’s final output <cite id="ee6b7524-9">Illustration of three types of knowledge distillation targets: output transfer and feature transfer</cite><cite id="ee6b7524-7">The key mechanism is that probes trained on intermediate representations provide cleaner labels than the teacher's own outputs</cite>.

2) Distillation via outputs and distributional knowledge (soft targets, calibration)
- Output-level distillation uses the teacher’s outputs as additional supervision. The simplest form has a separate transfer set where the student is trained to match soft teacher targets—logits compiled into probabilities by a temperature parameter so that uncertainty and relative confidence are preserved <cite id="ee6b7524-1">Next, the teacher model produces logits. These logits are converted into soft targets</cite><cite id="ee6b7524-7">In knowledge distillation we can distill generalization from teacher to student by combining hard and soft target losses</cite>.
- A seminal formulation, “Distilling the Knowledge in a Neural Network,” defines this “knowledge in the outputs” view: train the student with a transfer set using soft teacher targets (logits/softmax at a higher temperature) so the student learns the teacher’s distributional judgments, not just correct labels <cite id="e00ab57f-1">We show that we can improve a system by distilling knowledge in an ensemble into a single model</cite><cite id="e00ab57f-7">In the simplest form of distillation, knowledge is transferred by training on a transfer set and using a soft target</cite>.
- Temperature-softened outputs emphasize how the teacher “thinks,” capturing not only which class wins but also relative confidence; matching these soft distributions encourages the student to learn generalization patterns encoded by the teacher’s entire output distribution <cite id="ee6b7524-1">These logits are converted into soft targets</cite><cite id="ee6b7524-2">Soft targets can transfer a great deal of knowledge to the distilled model, including the knowledge about how to generalize</cite>.
- Temperature scaling is a direct way to distill calibration: by training or applying temperature to the teacher’s logits, one aligns the student’s confidence distribution with the teacher’s (uncertainty and margin distribution), often using the same distillation loss over soft targets <cite id="ee6b7524-8">The teacher's output logits are softened using a temperature parameter to emphasize less confident predictions</cite>.
- Distillation can therefore be understood as transferring a compacted, calibrated prior on classes—how to rank-distinguish and score examples—beyond the discrete hard label alone <cite id="ee6b7524-0">Intermediate representations provide step-by-step information</cite><cite id="e00ab57f-7">Soft targets preserve relative confidence and enable transfer</cite>.

3) Distillation via internal representations (features/activations)
- Feature-level knowledge: students can directly match intermediate activations of the teacher to learn internal decision-making factors that lead to prediction, often yielding gains in generalization and speed-to-train <cite id="ee6b7524-2">Intermediate layer representations from the teacher provide richer, fine-grained information</cite><cite id="afdc9853-2">Knowledge distillation can enhance network generalization by guiding a smaller network to learn from a more complex teacher</cite>.
- Distilling task-specific representation knowledge explicitly aims to transfer layer-wise teacher guidance to a student on a target task, often by training probes/heads on teacher features and then transferring those learned features to the student, or by matching teacher-student features at selected layers <cite id="afdc9853-0">Knowledge distillation extracts general knowledge from a pre-trained teacher network and provides guidance to a target student network</cite><cite id="afdc9853-4">Compared to methods that require manual probing, automatic feature-level understanding helps transfer patch-level knowledge</cite>.
- Activation/feature matching: matching teacher and student feature responses across layers can be more informative than output matching, since intermediate representations encode how evidence is accumulated toward the final decision <cite id="ee6b7524-5">Intermediate layer representations provide richer, fine-grained information; the methodology involves minimizing differences in these representations</cite><cite id="afdc9853-9">Feature transfer: the student learns from the teacher by aligning intermediate features</cite>.
- Practical variants include attention-based or information/representation matching, multi-layer fusion, or training student weights to emulate teacher features on unlabeled data so the student captures the same discriminative factors <cite id="afdc9853-0">Knowledge distillation extracts general knowledge from the teacher and provides guidance to the student</cite><cite id="afdc9853-4">Multi-feature fusion distillation extracts and utilizes expressive fusion features</cite><cite id="ee6b7524-0">These intermediate representations provide step-by-step information</cite>.
- Probing/probe-assisted distillation: auxiliary “probes” trained on teacher representations produce cleaner supervision (soft labels) than the teacher’s own output, improving the quality of transferred knowledge and enabling task-specific distillation without full teacher inference at training time <cite id="ee6b7524-7">Probes trained on intermediate representations provide cleaner labels than the teacher's outputs, enabling distillation</cite><cite id="afdc9853-0">Feature matching via attention enhances distillation by aligning teacher-probed features</cite>.

4) Optimization-oriented knowledge: gradients and teacher guidance signals
- Beyond matching logits or features, KD can transfer optimization knowledge by routing teacher or auxiliary gradient signals to the student during training. This guides the student’s updates with teacher-informed directions (e.g., via additional teacher losses, gradient addition, or one-vs-rest distillation) to avoid getting stuck in suboptimal local minima or poor priors <cite id="d46bb2ac-0">Task-specific distillation typically combines hard-target loss and soft-target distillation loss</cite><cite id="afdc9853-3">We introduce a novel visualization technique that gives insight into the function of intermediate feature layers</cite>.
- Layer-wise or attention-informed matching connects teacher decision factors to student factors and often uses gradient-driven objectives to align the student’s backpropagated updates with the teacher’s, improving convergence and generalization while preserving the teacher’s margin and uncertainty behavior <cite id="afdc9853-0">Knowledge distillation via attention-based feature matching transfers task-specific knowledge</cite><cite id="ee6b7524-3">Students are trained to mimic large teachers, aligning their representations</cite>.
- In “task-specific model distillation,” practitioners combine the identity-task loss with a soft-target distillation loss to encode generalization patterns and teacher confidence into the student; this yields students that are smaller and faster yet retain the teacher’s broad, distribution-level expertise <cite id="d46bb2ac-1">Task-specific distillation combines hard-target and soft-target losses</cite><cite id="ee6b7524-1">Teacher logits are compiled into soft targets for distillation</cite><cite id="ee6b7524-2">Soft targets encode how to generalize</cite>.
- Beyond supervised data, KD can exploit teacher internal structure via unsupervised feature transfer or by learning to emulate the teacher’s representation distribution—e.g., matching teacher feature statistics—so the student is steered by global representational guidance even without labeled target tasks <cite id="afdc9853-6">Knowledge distillation based on multi-layer fusion features extracts expressive teacher features and transfers them</cite><cite id="afdc9853-3">Understanding intermediate feature layers enables aligning these representations</cite>.

5) Putting it together: concrete forms of distilled knowledge
- Distributional knowledge over outputs (soft labels and calibration): the teacher’s full output distribution encodes relative confidence and uncertainty, teaching the student to produce calibrated probabilities and better margins; temperature scaling is a direct mechanism to preserve and transfer these margins <cite id="e00ab57f-7">Using a soft target preserves relative confidence and transfers teacher knowledge</cite><cite id="ee6b7524-8">Teacher logits are softened via temperature to emphasize less confident predictions</cite>.
- Internal decision factors (features/activations): the teacher teaches internal evidence accumulation—how to activate the right channels/maps—by aligning feature responses across layers, providing richer and more efficient guidance than pure output matching <cite id="ee6b7524-0">Intermediate representations provide step-by-step information</cite><cite id="ee6b7524-5">Minimizing differences in intermediate representations transfers fine-grained information</cite>.
- Task-specific auxiliary signals (teacher supervision on the student’s architecture): probe/matching losses and multi-criteria objectives fuse teacher-style attention or representation patterns into the student so it compresses the teacher’s expertise for the exact target task <cite id="afdc9853-0">Attention-based feature matching provides task-specific guidance from teacher to student</cite><cite id="afdc9853-7">Knowledge distillation enhances generalization by aligning a smaller student with a complex teacher</cite>.
- Empirical outcomes: combining hard-target training with soft-target distillation loss yields smaller, faster students that retain accuracy and, crucially, generalization patterns learned through the teacher’s output distribution and intermediate features <cite id="ee6b7524-1">Teacher outputs are compiled into soft targets</cite><cite id="ee6b7524-2">Soft-target distillation transfers generalization, not just accuracy</cite>.

What “counts as knowledge” in KD: a crisp takeaway
- KD distills task-level and distribution-level knowledge from the teacher to the student: how to make accurate predictions (hard labels) and how to do so confidently and generically (soft distributions), together with the internal feature-level mechanisms that support those decisions (how neurons/feature channels vote, interact, and aggregate evidence) <cite id="e00ab57f-7">Soft targets carry teacher’s relative confidence and enable transfer</cite><cite id="ee6b7524-0">Intermediate representations encode step-by-step decision-making leading to prediction</cite><cite id="afdc9853-0">Feature-level matching transfers task-specific knowledge</cite>.
- In practice, this is operationalized as: distill output logits into soft probabilities via temperature and distillation losses, optionally add feature-activation matching across layers, and fuse with hard-task losses—often yielding students that are smaller and faster while preserving the teacher’s generalization and calibration <cite id="d46bb2ac-1">Task-specific distillation combines hard-target loss and soft-target distillation loss</cite><cite id="e00ab57f-7">Soft-target loss over teacher outputs transfers generalization</cite><cite id="afdc9853-4">Feature fusion distillation extracts expressive teacher features</cite>.

without_scope.text: What exactly is the "dark knowledge" that gets distilled in the standard formulation of knowledge distillation, wherein information is transferred from a teacher network to a student network?
without_scope.answer:
Summary up front
Dark knowledge refers to the teacher model’s full probabilistic judgment over classes—its soft output distribution (including uncertainty and relative confidences among all classes)—not only the single class that the data point belongs to in a hard label.<cite id="7aebcb70-0">Knowledge distillation transfers knowledge from a high-capacity teacher “dark knowledge” beyond the hard label.<cite id="ec3f568f-3">Using a high temperature in the softmax, we minimize the cross entropy with the soft targets derived from the ensemble at high temperature.</cite><cite id="ec3f568f-0">The core of knowledge distillation lies in transferring the teacher's rich ‘dark knowledge'—subtle probabilistic patterns that reveal how classes are related.</cite>

What “dark knowledge” looks like concretely
In the standard formulation, one makes the teacher express how it ranks all classes, then teaches the much smaller student to match that ranking. This is implemented by converting the teacher’s raw outputs into a probability distribution using a high-temperature softmax (or an ensemble), producing a soft target that reveals confidence differences among classes, even when the argmax class is the same as a hard label.<cite id="7aebcb70-0">Knowledge distillation transfers knowledge from a high-capacity teacher “dark knowledge” beyond the hard label.</cite><cite id="ec3f568f-3">Using a high temperature in the softmax, we minimize the cross entropy with the soft targets derived from the ensemble at high temperature.</cite> The resulting vectors are “dark knowledge” in the sense that they encode nuanced relations (e.g., close competitors or weak but non-negligible confidences) that a hard label alone discards.<cite id="ec3f568f-0">Knowledge distillation lies in transferring the teacher's rich ‘dark knowledge'—subtle probabilistic patterns that reveal how classes are related.</cite>

Mechanics: how dark knowledge is distilled
There are two standard, equivalent ways to use this teacher distribution during training:
- Label-distillation with cross-entropy on soft targets: compute the student’s cross-entropy against the teacher’s softened distribution (both obtained by applying the same temperature T to their respective logits) and optimize it end-to-end.<cite id="ea9b1619-2">The loss of KL divergence often ...</cite><cite id="ea9b1619-2">KL divergence should be computed between the teacher and student soft targets, both obtained by applying the same temperature T to their logits.</cite><cite id="ea9b1619-7">This loss measures the difference between the student's soft predictions and the teacher's soft targets, standard cross ...</cite>
- KL/JS divergence between teacher and student: minimize the KL (or Jensen–Shannon, a square-root-smoothed KL) between the student’s outputs and the teacher’s softened distribution; operationally, with softmax heads and shared temperature, this reduces to the same training signal as cross-entropy on soft targets.<cite id="ea9b1619-1">KL divergence is widely used to provide the student with softer labels in knowledge distillation methods.</cite><cite id="7aebcb70-5">Hinton calls this the "dark knowledge" embedded in the teacher model, and it is this dark knowledge that we are transferring to the student model in the ...</cite>

Role of temperature T and logit normalization
Temperature T controls how “dark” the teacher’s knowledge becomes: raising T softens the teacher’s distribution (widening spreads, making near-confidences explicit), while lowering T drives the teacher toward one-hot behavior; for distillation consistency, both teacher and student use the same T when computing cross-entropy over soft targets (equivalently, KL), or one uses LogSoftmax to reflect the log-likelihood form of cross-entropy.<cite id="7aebcb70-1">Using a high temperature in the softmax, we minimize the cross entropy with the soft targets derived from the ensemble at high temperature.</cite><cite id="ea9b1619-2">KL divergence should be computed between the teacher and student soft targets, both obtained by applying the same temperature T to their logits.</cite><cite id="ea9b1619-8">Knowledge Distillation (KD) This loss measures the difference between the student's soft predictions and the teacher's soft targets, standard cross ...</cite> In practice, typical T values above 1 reveal pairwise similarities and confusability patterns that improve the student beyond hard-label training (e.g., T≈3–5 are commonly used, with temperature scaling matched between teacher and student layers).<cite id="7aebcb70-2">Knowledge distillation transfers a large model's "dark knowledge"... Higher temperature (T=3-5) softens the distribution, This is the "dark ...</cite><cite id="7aebcb70-4">Knowledge distillation involves transferring soft labels from a teacher to a student using a shared temperature-based softmax function.</cite>

What the student learns by matching dark knowledge
Teaching the student to match teacher distributions gives it two things a label alone cannot: (i) the relative confidence between classes (how the teacher ranks alternatives), and (ii) a directionally aligned decision boundary, which in practice improves calibration and accuracy at the same size. Put simply, dark knowledge teaches “which is more likely, and by how much,” not just “which is most likely.”<cite id="7aebcb70-0">Knowledge distillation transfers knowledge from a high-capacity teacher “dark knowledge” beyond the hard label.</cite><cite id="ec3f568f-3">Using a high temperature in the softmax, we minimize the cross entropy with the soft targets derived from the ensemble at high temperature.</cite><cite id="ec3f568f-0">This core aligns with transferring subtle probabilistic patterns that reveal how classes are related.</cite> In pedagogical terms, dark knowledge encodes the teacher’s Jacobian geometry in an explicit distribution; matching it biases the student toward the teacher’s curvature and pairwise confusability, beyond reproducing only the ground-truth label set by the training data.<cite id="ec3f568f-0">The core of knowledge distillation lies in transferring the teacher's rich ‘dark knowledge'—subtle probabilistic patterns that reveal how classes are related.</cite><cite id="ea9b1619-7">This loss measures the difference between the student's soft predictions and the teacher's soft targets, standard cross ...</cite>

Standard practice: soft outputs + optional internal matching
Textbooks and toolkits summarize KD as teaching a smaller model to imitate a larger teacher’s outputs by matching soft targets produced by a high-temperature softmax; this is the “dark knowledge” that elevates students beyond training only on hard labels.<cite id="7aebcb70-5">Hinton calls this the "dark knowledge" embedded in the teacher model, and it is this dark knowledge that we are transferring to the student model in the ...</cite><cite id="7aebcb70-1">Using a high temperature in the softmax, we minimize the cross entropy with the soft targets derived from the ensemble at high temperature.</cite> Contemporary tutorials and surveys emphasize that this can be done either by cross-entropy on soft labels or by KL between teacher and student distributions, typically at a shared temperature T; both reduce to learning the teacher’s full probability distribution, including non-maximal entries, thus transferring implicit relative “facts.”<cite id="ea9b1619-2">KL divergence should be computed between the teacher and student soft targets, both obtained by applying the same temperature T to their logits.</cite><cite id="ea9b1619-1">KL divergence is widely used to provide the student with softer labels in knowledge distillation methods.</cite><cite id="7aebcb70-7">The goal ... to help the student model learn not only the true labels ... but also this dark knowledge.</cite> In most practical pipelines, dark knowledge refers first and foremost to these output distributions; optionally, KD is augmented with distillation of intermediate layer activations/weights to better align internal representations and gradients when possible (e.g., matching residual heads or hidden features), which further tightens the student toward teacher geometry but is not strictly “required” by the basic KD signal.<cite id="7aebcb70-5">Hinton calls this the "dark knowledge" embedded in the teacher model, and it is this dark knowledge that we are transferring to the student model in the ...</cite><cite id="7aebcb70-5">Knowledge distillation is model compression method in which a small model is trained to mimic a pre-trained, larger model (or ensemble of models).</cite>

Practical corner cases and nuances
- Teacher’s distribution matters: distilling from an ensemble at a high temperature explicitly encourages the student to capture the spread of uncertainty among classes, not just the mode identified by the data label; this is often why KD students gain accuracy over label-only training at comparable sizes.<cite id="ec3f568f-3">Using a high temperature in the softmax, we minimize the cross entropy with the soft targets derived from the ensemble at high temperature.</cite>
- Temperature coordination: When using cross-entropy or KL over soft targets, apply the same temperature T to both teacher and student so the student learns the correct “relativity” of class confidences; if T is too low, the teacher becomes near one-hot and little nonlabel information is conveyed; if T is too high, the distribution swells and can leak label-improperness (the art is to set T that makes the distribution informative yet faithful to teacher behavior).<cite id="7aebcb70-1">Using a high temperature in the softmax, we minimize the cross entropy with the soft targets derived from the ensemble at high temperature.</cite><cite id="ea9b1619-2">KL divergence should be computed between the teacher and student soft targets, both obtained by applying the same temperature T to their logits.</cite>
- Loss choice and normalization: Cross-entropy (with LogSoftmax) and KL are operationally interchangeable for soft-label distillation at a shared T; tutorials explicitly recommend computing the KL/JS between teacher and student soft targets derived by applying the same temperature to their logits to preserve the intended geometry and calibration signal in the student.<cite id="ea9b1619-1">KL divergence is widely used to provide the student with softer labels in knowledge distillation methods.</cite><cite id="ea9b1619-2">KL divergence should be computed between the teacher and student soft targets, both obtained by applying the same temperature T to their logits.</cite>

Bottom line
Dark knowledge is the teacher’s full, temperature-modulated class probability distribution (its soft outputs), including confidences for all classes, not merely the data’s hard label; in standard KD you convert this into supervision for the student either via cross-entropy over soft targets (with matching temperature, often using LogSoftmax) or via KL/JS between teacher and student distributions, thereby transferring the teacher’s ranking, uncertainty, and decision-boundary geometry to a much smaller model.<cite id="7aebcb70-0">Knowledge distillation transfers knowledge from a high-capacity teacher “dark knowledge” beyond the hard label.</cite><cite id="ec3f568f-3">Using a high temperature in the softmax, we minimize the cross entropy with the soft targets derived from the ensemble at high temperature.</cite><cite id="ea9b1619-2">KL divergence should be computed between the teacher and student soft targets, both obtained by applying the same temperature T to their logits.</cite><cite id="ea9b1619-1">KL divergence is widely used to provide the student with softer labels in knowledge distillation methods.</cite>

without_term.text: What exactly is the "dark knowledge" that gets distilled in the standard formulation of knowledge distillation, wherein information is transferred from a teacher model to a student model?
without_term.answer:
Summary of what “dark knowledge” is (in the standard KD formulation)

In the standard knowledge distillation (KD) formulation, dark knowledge is the teacher model’s full predictive distribution over classes (or outputs), beyond the hard predicted label alone. <cite id="edc25d37-9">Dark knowledge explicitly refers to the remaining outputs of the SoftMax layer that are different from the highest one; these values represent more than accuracy labels</cite>. <cite id="edc25d37-9">It is information in the non-winning classes that hard labels “throw away,” i.e., the relative probabilities and uncertainty structure that a single class assignment does not encode</cite>. <cite id="7d2511f3-1">Practically, this is transferred by using teacher targets to induce a loss on the student that learns the teacher’s soft outputs, including for non-special classes</cite>.

How dark knowledge is encoded and transferred

The core mechanism is to train the student to match the teacher’s predictions at test-temperature, thereby inheriting the teacher’s uncertainty structure. <cite id="7d2511f3-3">Hinton et al. (2015) describe dark knowledge as a “practically invisible” class-related similarity metric embedded in the model’s probability ratios, which KD transfers to the student</cite>. <cite id="edc25d37-0">A compact formulation is to minimize cross-entropy losses against both the ground-truth labels and the teacher’s outputs: the student learns logits that reduce both the student→teacher and the teacher→student cross entropies, effectively memorizing the teacher’s distributional signal</cite>. <cite id="edc25d37-0">Equivalently, teacher-provided soft targets enable posterior-like learning for non-special classes, preventing overfitting to noise and preserving nuanced inter-class relationships</cite>.

Equivalently, dark knowledge is what the loss asks the student to emulate: the teacher’s output log-likelihood (or its surrogate). In classification, the typical KD objective for a given input–label pair uses teacher targets either as soft labels or as the surrogate distribution over classes, and trains the student to minimize predictive error with respect to that distribution. <cite id="7d2511f3-1">Soft targets for non-special classes mitigate overfitting while pushing the student to internalize the teacher’s confidence and uncertainty across all classes</cite>. The temperature–entropy view makes this explicit: raising the temperature softens the teacher’s output distribution, making the full low-probability/soft-information more visible to the student loss. <cite id="7d2511f3-0">Recent work frames the goal as transferring subtle probabilistic patterns that reveal how classes are related, rather than only a chosen label</cite>.

Relation to sequence modeling (CTC-style distillation)

The dark-knowledge perspective generalizes beyond single-frame softmax classification to sequence models. In connectionist temporal classification (CTC), training requires the model to output a probability distribution over target tokens—exactly the information needed to perform posterior-averaging over alignments. KD for sequence-to-sequence or speech translation can then be cast as having the student mimic the CTC loss behavior of the teacher. <cite id="d78c5ac5-5">Knowledge distillation has been effectively used to improve simpler sequence models via teacher–student training, with objectives aligned to the teacher’s output distribution</cite>. <cite id="d78c5ac5-3">In distillation CTC (DCTC), the student directly imitates the teacher’s posterior distributions around training data points with a regularized CTC loss, making the student learn the teacher’s distribution over sequences rather than the alignment</cite>. <cite id="d78c5ac5-1">CTC achieves this by defining outputs so that a neural network’s loss already aligns to a posterior over labels, making dark knowledge the CTC posterior—precisely what KD compresses into the student</cite>. <cite id="d78c5ac5-0">As a module-free loss, DCTC transfers knowledge as the teacher’s CTC posterior, demonstrating the generality of distilling distributional knowledge (not labels) across sequence tasks</cite>.

Contrast with a naive “labels-only” imitation
