Recent work shows that distilling between models of similar size can still yield accuracy gains and compression benefits, particularly when the teacher contains structured or architectural knowledge the student can emulate. <cite id="d9ecaefc-0">Knowledge Distillation has been used to transfer decision-making behavior of high-capacity Decision Transformer (DT) policies into smaller DT students, narrowing the performance gap while retaining sample efficiency</cite>. <cite id="d9ecaefc-3">In control and reinforcement learning, sparse Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) student architectures can match or surpass dense baselines and even the teacher under comparable or lower compute</cite>, indicating that size parity plus architectural guidance can make distillation effective. <cite id="d9ecaefc-4">MoEKD explicitly decomposes and enhances distillation by training experts and then learning a router/selector that aggregates expert knowledge, improving overall transfer quality</cite>. Collectively, these studies demonstrate that matching capacities, together with mechanism-level supervision, can be a viable and effective KD strategy.

# Smaller teacher to larger student
There is also direct evidence that smaller or “weaker” teachers can teach larger students, given suitable training objectives and supervision. <cite id="b3cd374a-6">The Distillation from Weak Teacher (DWT) approach formalizes transferring knowledge from a smaller, weaker teacher to a larger student, showing that even modest teachers can convey useful priors or task-specific features to bigger learners</cite>. <cite id="b8a8e87c-0">An empirical analysis of CoT distillation reports that “smaller teacher has seen during pretraining” can still improve larger students via KD losses, though student gains depend on how training is set up</cite>. <cite id="b8a8e87c-2">A NeurIPS 2023 study (“Can Language Models Teach?”) finds that a smaller teacher with explanations may not benefit a much larger student in isolation; however, when aligned or guided properly (e.g., with teacher-student coordination and task-tailored losses), knowledge transfer can become effective</cite>. <cite id="b3cd374a-1">Related work explicitly frames KD as training a smaller student to mimic a larger teacher; the converse setting—leveraging a smaller teacher to guide a larger student—has similarly been explored to compress and share structured knowledge across sizes</cite>.

Two practical caveats surface from these experiments. First, size alone does not guarantee transfer: <cite id="b8a8e87c-0">small models struggle to learn from strong reasoners unless losses and supervision are adapted</cite>. Second, <cite id="b3cd374a-2">the same NeurIPS study shows that random or weak interventions by a smaller teacher can fail to benefit larger students unless the guidance is informative and targeted</cite>. Together, these works show that smaller teachers can be effective knowledge sources for larger students, but methods must prioritize signal quality and alignment.

# Targeted “knowledge” beyond raw logits
A major theme enabling effective KD across size asymmetry is distilling targeted mechanisms rather than only global logits. Several strands instantiate this idea:

- Architectural and routing knowledge:
  <cite id="d9ecaefc-4">MoEKD distills expert knowledge and a router’s selection policy, improving student behavior by learning how to combine a few experts instead of fitting a single dense model</cite>. <cite id="d9ecaefc-3">Sparse MoE student KD architectures demonstrate that students can outperform dense baselines and even the teacher under equal or lower compute</cite>, showing that architecture-informed distillation yields performance gains not attainable by scaling parameters alone. <cite id="d9ecaefc-1">Balanced Distillation for moe-to-moe “equally spreads teacher expertise,” which helps smaller students emulate teacher capabilities without matching parameter counts</cite>.

- Decision/behavioral templates:
  <cite id="d9ecaefc-0">Decision Transformer (DT) KD transfers decision behavior from larger DT teachers to smaller students, reducing compute yet preserving task performance</cite>. <cite id="b3cd374a-6">Similarly, distilling intermediate or step-level rationales from a smaller teacher into a larger student has been shown to improve generalization when the teacher’s signals are structured</cite>.

- Structural and resource-aware mechanisms:

fully_underspecified.text: Has there been any research on the ordering of data points for language models, such that a model may be trained in a more sample-efficient manner?
fully_underspecified.answer:
Summary
Yes. Beyond token-level context windows, multiple strands of research manipulate the order and scheduling of training data points or datasets to attain sample‑efficient training of language models. These include curriculum ordering within pretraining, principled distribution‑level curriculum frameworks, adaptive curricula for reasoning, data‑centric sequencing from simple to complex tasks, and infrastructure that enables exposure/reuse of data with reduced I/O. Several works report consistent improvements in convergence and final performance at fixed compute or data size, or provide theoretical reductions in sample complexity under certain conditions. <cite id="7a37d9ae-2">Our findings highlight the importance of data ordering in large-scale pretraining and provide actionable insights for scalable, data-efficient training</cite> <cite id="7a37d9ae-5">Curriculum learning enhances the efficiency and generalization of pretraining language models through strategic data ordering, yielding consistent improvements</cite> <cite id="7a37d9ae-6">Recent curriculum techniques in the post-training stage have been empirically observed to outperform non-curriculum approaches; a 2026 ICML result gives a provable sample-efficiency guarantee for curriculum post-training</cite> <cite id="7a37d9ae-8">DUMP frames curriculum at the distribution level, proposing a principled ordering/selection rule grounded in learnability</cite> <cite id="aabb9111-1">KenLM introduces data structures that reduce time and memory costs of LM queries, enabling larger effective datasets in cache</cite>.

What “ordering of data points” means in LM training
In pretraining and post‑training, “ordering” refers to how examples (text segments, sentences, or full documents) are presented to the optimizer over time, and how batches are composed. This can be:
- Monotonic difficulty ordering (e.g., simple→hard in-context or next‑token prediction snippets) <cite id="7a37d9ae-3">Curriculum learning introduces a structure moving from “easier” to “harder” examples, rather than presenting purely random data</cite>.
- Distribution‑level ordering that selects next examples to maintain favorable learnability (DUMP) <cite id="7a37d9ae-8">The core insight is to use distribution-level learnability to guide which distributions or data points are next, providing a principled curriculum</cite>.
- Adaptive scheduling based on model competence (e.g., SPaCe clusters tasks and adapts the curriculum for reasoning) <cite id="7a37d9ae-1">SPaCe enables efficient reasoning via clustering and adaptive curriculum learning</cite> <cite id="7a37d9ae-5">It is a lightweight framework for efficient reasoning via adaptive data exposure</cite>.
- Data‑centric sequencing across tasks (MT‑bench/LLM curricula): organize exposure to human‑evaluated hard and easy problems to improve instruction‑following at lower cost <cite id="8cdb3d74-4">A curriculum learning-inspired, data-centric training strategy begins with simpler tasks and progresses to more complex ones</cite> <cite id="8cdb3d74-0">The strategy is curriculum learning-inspired and data-centric, improving instruction-following task performance</cite>.

Mechanisms that make ordering matter for sample efficiency
- Reduced per‑example variance and faster local learning: feeding easier but informative prefixes first can speed conditioning and reduce backpropagation noise, improving convergence at fixed compute <cite id="7a37d9ae-4">Organizing training data from easy to hard can lead to faster convergence and better final performance</cite>.
- Curated difficulty and coverage: a principled curriculum avoids early saturation on hard negatives/positives and ensures steady progress, improving the effective sample rate of each minibatch <cite id="7a37d9ae-3">Curriculum Learning defines a structured progression from easier to harder items</cite> <cite id="7a37d9ae-8">Distribution-level selection yields a principled curriculum that improves ordering for learnability</cite>.
- Replay and exposure: ordering with memory/caching exposes useful n‑grams and contexts repeatedly without redundant I/O, preserving cache and bandwidth for harder updates <cite id="aabb9111-1">KenLM achieves faster and smaller language model queries via efficient data structures, enabling larger effective datasets in cache</cite>.
- Post‑training sample efficiency guarantees: ordering examples by model confidence or uncertainty can provably shrink the number of samples needed to reach target accuracy on certain structured problems <cite id="7a37d9ae-6">The 2026 ICML result establishes a provable sample efficiency of curriculum post-training</cite>.

Evidence from recent research
1) Pretraining curricula that explicitly order data
- “Efficient Language Model Pretraining via Curriculum…” (2025): proposes curriculum-style ordering during unsupervised pretraining. Reports consistent gains in efficiency and generalization, with stronger effects at scale; authors give practical guidance on how to implement ordered schedules and mixtures for sample efficiency <cite id="7a37d9ae-2">The paper emphasizes the importance of data ordering in pretraining and provides actionable insights for data-efficient training</cite> <cite id="7a37d9ae-5">It shows curriculum learning yields consistent improvements in pretraining efficiency and generalization via strategic data ordering</cite>.
- “Data Efficacy for Language Model Training (2025)”: introduces a metric “data efficacy” to quantify performance per unit of training signal (rather than per token), and shows optimizing the organization of the training set (e.g., by redundancy, diversity, and ordering) can significantly boost returns on the same data volume. Provides ablations showing explicit gains from organized vs. random order <cite id="7a37d9ae-0">Data efficacy aims to maximize LM performance by optimizing the organization of training data</cite>.
- “Provable Sample Efficiency of Curriculum Post‑training (ICML 2026)”: formalizes when ordering/curriculum in post‑training (fine‑tuning/democratic training) yields lower sample complexity. Demonstrates bounds and conditions under which curriculum outperforms non‑curriculum training, complementing empirical findings <cite id="7a37d9ae-6">Empirical curriculum gains in post-training are provably sample-efficient under stated conditions</cite>.

2) Adaptive reasoning curricula and scheduling
- SPaCe (ACL 2026 Findings): a lightweight framework for efficient reasoning that clusters task difficulty and applies adaptive curriculum schedules, improving sample efficiency by focusing compute where the model is least confident <cite id="7a37d9ae-1">SPaCe uses clustering and adaptive curriculum learning to enable efficient reasoning</cite>.
- DUMP (distribution‑level curriculum): defines a principled objective and algorithm to pick the “next” dataset/distribution to train on, driven by distribution‑level learnability rather than pointwise labels. This informs large‑scale ordering across sources with quantized changes in sample efficiency <cite id="7a37d9ae-8">DUMP grounds curriculum in distribution-level learnability and proposes an automated, principled selection rule for the next training chunk</cite>.
- Instruction‑following curricula (MT‑bench/curriculum-inspired): even beyond pretraining, curriculum sequencing over human‑evaluated tasks improves instruction following with fewer tuning steps. This is consistent with the broader phenomenon that ordered exposure to easy→hard examples improves sample efficiency in supervised/post‑training settings <cite id="8cdb3d74-4">A curriculum learning-inspired, data-centric training strategy that progresses from simpler to complex tasks improves instruction-following performance</cite> <cite id="8cdb3d74-0">The proposed strategy begins with simpler tasks and progresses to more complex ones, improving overall performance</cite>.

3) Infrastructure enabling better exposure ordering
- KenLM (efficient caching and queries): while originally for n‑gram models, KenLM’s data structures (suffix caching, compression) demonstrate that re‑using queryable representations of data reduces time and memory, enabling larger effective corpora to be kept hot in memory/cache. This allows practical implementations of ordered exposure (e.g., replay of useful n‑grams) and lowers the cost per “effective” training sample <cite id="aabb9111-1">KenLM implements data structures that reduce both time and memory costs of LM queries</cite>. Although token‑level blocking/packing also matters, the paper shows how query-time caching directly reduces overhead and can speed training data access patterns that rely on repeated exposures <cite id="aabb9111-1">KenLM achieves faster and smaller LM queries, lowering infrastructure costs that limit sample efficiency</cite>.

What this buys you in practice
- Faster convergence and lower per‑epoch variance when starting from easier, well‑conditioned contexts; this is observed both in theory and practice for curriculum post‑training and for reasoning tasks with adaptive curricula <cite id="7a37d9ae-4">Ordering easy→hard improves convergence and final performance</cite> <cite id="7a37d9ae-6">Curriculum post-training attains provable sample-efficiency reductions</cite> <cite id="7a37d9ae-1">Adaptive curriculum (SPaCe) improves reasoning efficiency</cite>.
- For pretraining, ordered curricula consistently improve the effective sample rate and generalization on held‑out tasks at comparable compute, with guidance available on how to set thresholds, mix sources, and warm‑start across domains <cite id="7a37d9ae-2">Data ordering in pretraining is important and actionable for scalability and data efficiency</cite> <cite id="7a37d9ae-5">Curriculum ordering yields consistent pretraining efficiency and generalization gains</cite>.
- When training over finite or mixed-quality corpora, principled selection (DUMP) and data efficacy optimization reduce exposure to unhelpful redundancy/noise and prioritize informative segments—again increasing performance per token <cite id="7a37d9ae-8">Automated, distribution-level selection improves the ordering of what to train on next</cite> <cite id="7a37d9ae-0">Optimizing the organization of training data increases performance per unit of training signal</cite>.

Closely related techniques you can leverage today
- Data shuffling curricula: replace pure uniform shuffling with confidence‑ or entropy‑based sampling to bring informative, medium‑difficulty examples early in batches; evaluate with curriculum checkpoints and mixtures to avoid overfitting to too‑easy corpora <cite id="7a37d9ae-3">Curriculum learning structures batch composition from easier to harder items</cite>.
- Source‑level mixtures and pyramidal pretraining: start with a small, high‑quality domain (child‑directed speech, code comments, instructions) and gradually add larger noisy corpora; early iterations benefit from lower semantic variance and stronger inductive biases (supported by data‑efficacy framing) <cite id="7a37d9ae-0">Data efficacy prioritizes optimizing organization to get more performance from the same data</cite>.
- Adaptive demixing for post‑training: use curriculum to train on classes/datasets where current accuracy is weakest (uncertainty‑driven), which theoretical results show can reduce sample complexity on structured problems <cite id="7a37d9ae-6">Curriculum post-training reduces samples needed under specified conditions with guarantees</cite>.
- Infrastructure for exposure: enable caching/packing so that useful spans are replayed without re-reading disk, increasing the effective frequency of high‑value samples per unit time <cite id="aabb9111-1">KenLM reduces time and memory costs to keep more data hot for queries</cite>.

Caveats and open questions
- Not all tasks benefit equally; orderings that work for reasoning tasks (SPaCe) may not linearize sample efficiency for generative web‑text alone. Use problem‑aware heuristics (entropy, perplexity drop, task cluster) and validate early‑stage gains on dev sets <cite id="7a37d9ae-1">SPaCe demonstrates gains by clustering and adapting to reasoning tasks</cite> <cite id="7a37d9ae-3">Curriculum structure should match task difficulty progression</cite>.
- Gains are largest at scale, but sensitivity to ordering depends on optimizer, learning rate schedules, and data loaders. The pretraining‑curriculum paper offers practical guidance on stepwise scaling and mixture composition <cite id="7a37d9ae-2">Actionable insights for scalable, data-efficient pretraining include ordered mixtures and stepwise scaling</cite>.
- Some reports quantify improvements in perplexity or human eval per step; broader, standardized sample‑complexity curves (final accuracy vs. fraction of full data used) are still a comparative weakness across works—hence the importance of ablation and early stopping experiments when adopting an ordering policy <cite id="7a37d9ae-5">Curriculum ordering yields consistent improvements; ablations are recommended to understand gains</cite>.

Practical starting points
- Start modestly: replace global “uniform shuffling” with curriculum‑style minibatch composition (e.g., entropy‑then‑loss aware), and reseed periodically from a hard set to avoid local minima. <cite id="7a37d9ae-3">Curriculum introduces a structure to move from easier to harder examples; batch composition is a practical lever</cite>.
- For multi‑source pretraining, warm‑start with a small curated set, then gradually add larger corpora with checkpoints, as in curriculum pretraining papers. <cite id="7a37d9ae-2">Importance of data ordering and actionable guidance for scalable pretraining</cite>.
- Add caching/packing in your data pipeline to replay informative spans, improving effective sample count per unit compute. <cite id="aabb9111-1">KenLM reduces time/memory and enables more effective cache use for LM queries</cite>.
- For post‑training, consider uncertainty‑aware curriculum over classes/datasets per the provable sample‑efficiency results. <cite id="7a37d9ae-6">Curriculum post-training attains provable sample efficiency reductions</cite>.
- For instruction‑following, follow a simple→hard curriculum across human‑evaluated problem sets (e.g., MT‑bench families) before full web‑scale RL. <cite id="8cdb3d74-4">A data-centric curriculum beginning with simpler tasks and progressing to complex ones improves instruction-following performance</cite>.

Bottom line
There is active, multi‑pronged research showing that ordering and scheduling of data points and sources can make LM training more sample‑efficient. Empirical pretraining curricula and adaptive reasoning schedules report consistent performance gains at comparable compute; principled distribution‑level selection frameworks provide automation; and theoretical results establish when curriculum reduces sample complexity in post‑training. Complementary infrastructure for caching/packing turns exposure ordering into a practical lever, enabling repeated, low‑cost contact with high‑value data. <cite id="7a37d9ae-2">Data ordering matters for large-scale pretraining and can yield actionable, scalable data efficiency</cite> <cite id="7a37d9ae-5">Curriculum learning enhances pretraining efficiency and generalization via strategic data ordering</cite> <cite id="7a37d9ae-6">Curriculum post-training has provable sample efficiency improvements</cite> <cite id="7a37d9ae-8">Distribution-level curriculum (DUMP) offers principled automation of the next-data-point selection</cite> <cite id="aabb9111-1">Efficient caching/queries (KenLM) make ordered exposure and replay feasible, boosting effective sample efficiency</cite>.

- There is contrary conventional wisdom in pretraining: for years, corpora were presented in (nearly) random order with an implicit assumption that order had limited effect. Newer work tests this assumption and shows that ordering can matter, motivating explicit scheduling and precedence signals during pretraining.<cite id="176479bc-5">Pretraining typically relies on randomly ordered corpora, with an implicit assumption that data order has limited impact on learning; recent studies question and evaluate this assumption</cite>.
- Complementary techniques emphasize ordering as a dimension of “pretraining plus curriculum composition,” mixing simpler domains/tasks early and introducing complexity later to accelerate broad coverage and generalization.<cite id="02b5f878-2">A curriculum-inspired, data-centric training strategy begins with simpler tasks and progresses to more complex ones, improving data efficiency</cite><cite id="02b5f878-1">Studies of pretraining mixtures show how the composition affects performance on compositionality and transfer, enabling stepwise difficulty increases</cite>.

Core ideas and how “easy-to-hard” orderings are constructed
- Difficulty-aware sorting: Some methods estimate a difficulty proxy per example or per document (e.g., perplexity of a small LM, entropy of next-token distribution, code length/complexity, error rates, or coverage-based heuristics), then sort the corpus in ascending order so the model sees mostly predictable items early and harder items later.<cite id="176479bc-0">A practical recipe is to compute a difficulty score (from perplexity or other cues) and sort the data ascendingly for easy-to-hard training</cite><cite id="a3dd21eb-0">A self-adaptive curriculum for fine-tuning prioritizes examples by difficulty predicted by a pretrained LM, updating weights online to guide progression</cite>.
- Perplexity and uncertainty heuristics: Smaller LM scorers can rank examples by lower perplexity; uncertainty measures (e.g., high marginal entropy, low teacher forcing agreement) identify under-specified/ambiguous targets to delay, aligning with curriculum spirit even when true labels are noisy.<cite id="a3dd21eb-1">A self-adaptive curriculum can leverage a pretrained LM to score difficulty and schedule examples accordingly</cite><cite id="c414e24a-4">Perplexity-based scoring uses a smaller LM to rank examples: lower perplexity (i.e., easier) examples are scheduled first</cite>.
- Adaptive and task-wise curricula: Rather than a fixed order, some systems maintain dynamic schedules—coarse-to-fine per layer or per task—updating which examples to replay as model weaknesses shrink. Recent work on “adaptive difficulty curriculum learning” adapts which items are easy vs. hard online and sequences them for efficient improvement.<cite id="c414e24a-5">Adaptive Difficulty Curriculum Learning (ADCL) provides a novel curriculum strategy that schedules items by adaptive difficulty and has been adapted across tasks, including LLMs</cite>.
- Instruction-level curricula for tuning: For supervised instruction tuning, curricula can learn “easy-to-hard” sequences automatically—first presenting safe/short/clear instructions, then more ambiguous/long-form ones—improving instruction following per unit of tuning steps.<cite id="176479bc-8">IT2ACL learns easy-to-hard instruction sequences via a 2-phase automated curriculum, improving instruction tuning efficiency</cite>.

Evidence that ordering matters in pretraining and how to exploit it
- Challenging the random-order assumption: Empirical investigations show that the implicit assumption that ordering in pretraining corpora has negligible impact is being revisited; some experiments with ordered or structured corpora report improved convergence and stability, suggesting simple changes like sorted or grouped documents can be beneficial before adding complex scheduling heuristics.<cite id="176479bc-5">Recent work argues the impact of data order in pretraining has been underestimated and tests whether ordered corpora help learning</cite>.
- Heuristic “precedence” and grouping: Beyond random shuffling, practitioners can introduce temporal/temporal-before-conceptual or readability-before-complexity precedence (e.g., grade-band sequencing) to give models narrower windows of statistical complexity. These orderings, while not universal, often reduce divergence and improve sample efficiency in early epochs before full-scale mixing.<cite id="a3dd21eb-7">Guided curriculum principles suggest sequencing from smaller, domain-specific corpora to broader mixtures to build strong skills before tackling hard language</cite>.
- Composition as curriculum: “Easy-to-hard” data composition is another pathway: train first on simpler languages/registers or curated domains and then blend complexity—a design space studied in compositional pretraining and mixture studies. This mirrors curriculum and can yield improved coverage at lower compute, with ablations across mixture recipes.<cite id="02b5f878-1">Mixing pretraining corpora influences compositionality and transfer, and can be structured to increase difficulty progressively</cite>.

Empirical sample-efficiency signals and what we know so far
- Difficulty-sorted pretraining: Early sorting by difficulty has been reported to accelerate LM pretraining, often reaching comparable perplexities or quality metrics faster than random mixing; self-adaptive curricula further reduce the burden of manual thresholding by updating weights and schedules online.<cite id="176479bc-0">Difficulty-based easy-to-hard sorting improves pretraining efficiency; the method explicitly builds on prior curriculum learning to scale training</cite><cite id="a3dd21eb-0">Self-adaptive curriculum prioritization in fine-tuning leverages pretrained LM difficulty estimates to improve efficiency versus uniform sampling</cite>.
- Instruction-tuning studies: Automated curricula that reorder supervision have shown improved instruction-following with fewer tuning steps compared to random or all-at-once tuning, highlighting ordering as a levers for sample efficiency in supervised fine-tuning.<cite id="176479bc-8">An automated easy-to-hard curriculum over instructions enhances LLM instruction-following efficiency, with ablations showing benefits relative to random schedules</cite>.
- Broader acceleration via conditioning and scheduling: Techniques that inject order cues or learning hints during pretraining (e.g., metadata conditioning with cooldown schedules) can significantly speed up convergence and reduce data requirements, complementing ordering and curriculum mixing.<cite id="02b5f878-6">Metadata Conditioning then Cooldown (MeCo) accelerates pre-training across scales and sources; e.g., it shortens wall-clock time to reach desired perplexity or downstream accuracy with similar compute overhead</cite><cite id="02b5f878-8">MeCo improves data efficiency while adding negligible computational overhead by supplying conditioning schedules that guide learning</cite>.

Practical recipes you can try
- Choose a difficulty proxy (perplexity of a small LM on the example, entropy of next-token distribution, instruction ambiguity, syntactic/semantic tree depth) and sort a pretraining corpus ascendingly before sharding; interleave with periodic refreshes so that hard examples are revisited as the model improves.<cite id="176479bc-0">Use a difficulty score to sort the corpus easy-to-hard for pretraining; the method explicitly targets efficiency</cite><cite id="c414e24a-4">Perplexity-based scoring offers an implementable heuristic to rank examples</cite><cite id="a3dd21eb-0">Self-adaptive curricula estimate difficulty online and reorder fine-tuning dynamically</cite>.
- For instruction-tuning, compute instruction difficulty (e.g., BLEU/faithfulness of baseline generation, entropy of gold label distributions, prompt ambiguity) and train easy-to-hard; for fully unsupervised curricula, learn the order automatically as in IT2ACL and compare to random or all-at-once schedules.<cite id="176479bc-8">Automated “easy-to-hard” instruction sequencing improves tuning sample efficiency</cite>.
- Compose mixtures that scaffold complexity: first train on a clean, simple corpus (e.g., controlled books, short documents) and progressively blend noisy/longer/dialectal data; this scaffolding yields broader coverage with lower risk of collapse and can reduce early training loss more quickly than jumping straight to massive heterogeneous corpora.<cite id="a3dd21eb-7">“Go Simple and Pre-Train on Domain-Specific Corpora” recommends starting simple and broadening mixtures as a fast path to strong skills</cite><cite id="02b5f878-1">Mixture composition impacts compositionality and transfer, motivating progressive complexity</cite>.
- Consider metadata/structure scheduling: add monotonic data difficulty ramps by time, source readability band, or dependency tree size, and, where possible, train on short texts first and gradually lengthen context and output windows; these small scheduling signals can help generalization without extra compute.<cite id="02b5f878-6">Metadata-conditioned schedules provide learning cues during pretraining and accelerate convergence</cite>.
- Monitor and rebalance: maintain running difficulty estimates (e.g., rolling perplexity or error rate) and periodically re-sort or rebalance shuffles so that the model continuously faces a few challenging examples to avoid local minima.<cite id="a3dd21eb-0">Self-adaptive curricula update example priorities online, maintaining an evolving easy-to-hard schedule</cite>.

Limits, caveats, and open questions
- Sensitivity to proxy quality: “Easy-to-hard” ordering depends on accurate difficulty estimates; noisy proxies (e.g., small LM scorer mismatch, prompt contamination) can mis-sequence examples and hurt performance. Hybrid strategies that blend static groupings with adaptive rebalancing can mitigate this.<cite id="a3dd21eb-0">Difficulty predictions drive curriculum, so the choice of estimator influences efficiency and outcomes</cite>.
- Not a silver bullet: In large-scale pretraining, compute savings are often modest unless paired with other techniques (e.g., MeCo-style scheduling, better mixtures, or cleaner data pipelines). Order alone rarely achieves big wins on its own but is a high-leverage, nearly zero-cost add-on.<cite id="02b5f878-6">MeCo achieves significant accelerations by adding learning-cue scheduling, illustrating that order plus conditioning can move the needle</cite>.
- Task-dependent benefits: Instruction-tuning and supervised fine-tuning see clearer sample-efficiency gains from ordering than unsupervised pretraining, where ordering effects are smaller but still present; nonetheless, empirical ablations remain uneven across domains and setups.<cite id="176479bc-8">Curriculum instruction tuning shows clear efficiency gains</cite><cite id="176479bc-5">Studies argue the effect of order in pretraining has been underestimated, motivating more uniform scheduling in future baselines</cite>.
- Practical integration: Implementing an ordered curriculum adds engineering overhead (re-sorting, dynamic data loaders, periodic refresh). Start with deterministic groupings (readability, length), and layer on adaptive rebalancing only if you observe plateaus or unstable perplexities.<cite id="176479bc-0">Difficulty-sorted pretraining is straightforward to implement and aligns with prior curriculum learning</cite>.

In short, yes—there is a growing body of work on ordering training data for LMs, including difficulty-sorted pretraining, adaptive difficulty curricula, and instruction-level easy-to-hard schedules. These methods are motivated by and extend classical curriculum learning, often yielding faster convergence and better sample efficiency, especially in supervised fine-tuning and in data composition pipelines; however, their gains depend on good difficulty estimation and are most reliable when combined with careful mixture design and scheduling signals.<cite id="176479bc-0">Difficulty-based ordering is used to accelerate LM pretraining</cite><cite id="176479bc-3">Curriculum learning for LLM fine-tuning aims to improve training efficiency by ordering samples easy-to-hard</cite><cite id="c414e24a-5">Adaptive difficulty curricula schedule items by evolving difficulty and have been adapted to LLMs</cite><cite id="176479bc-8">Automated easy-to-hard instruction curricula improve instruction tuning sample efficiency</cite><cite id="02b5f878-6">Ordering complemented by metadata conditioning/cooldown accelerates pre-training</cite><cite id="176479bc-5">Research challenges the “random order is fine” heuristic, motivating explicit data sequencing</cite>.

without_preference.text: Has there been any research on the ordering of datapoints for language models, such as easy-to-hard curriculum sequences, to make training more sample-efficient?
without_preference.answer:
Short answer
Yes. Beyond random data shuffling, a substantial body of work studies curricula that order or weight datapoints—e.g., easy-to-hard scheduling, demonstration ordering, clustering-based routing, and difficulty-estimation–driven sampling—to accelerate convergence and improve performance per gradient step or token in pretraining, instruction tuning, and preference alignment. <cite id="73c63f95-5">Curriculum learning—organizing training data from easy to hard—has improved efficiency across machine learning domains, and recent work applies this explicitly to language-model pretraining</cite> <cite id="73c63f95-0">via scheduling that gradually transitions from easy to hard while preserving diversity</cite> <cite id="73c63f95-4">and reports consistent sample-efficiency and generalization gains</cite>. In instruction tuning, methods like IT2ACL and RFCL dynamically order instructions or demonstrations, improving data efficiency and wall-clock performance. In preference alignment, DPO-style approaches reduce infrastructure and data needs relative to full RLHF, and new systems add adaptive curriculum/routing to further improve sample efficiency.

How curricula are implemented (representative mechanisms and evidence)
- Pacing pretraining from easy to hard: Curricula in pretraining adjust sampling schedules to first expose simpler examples and progressively introduce harder ones. <cite id="73c63f95-5">Recent analyses argue that curriculum ordering is key to efficiency, showing that organizing by difficulty improves sample efficiency across tasks and motivating its use in LMs</cite>. <cite id="73c63f95-0">One concrete design groups training examples and samples with random order within groups to preserve diversity, while a pacing schedule governs the gradual transition from easy to hard</cite>. <cite id="73c63f95-4">The paper reports that curriculum-enhanced pretraining improves efficiency and generalization with consistent improvements across experiments</cite>. <cite id="73c63f95-1">Related work on scaling pretraining emphasizes curriculum-based sampling that increases data difficulty over time alongside batch/dataset expansion to maintain sample efficiency and stability</cite>.

- Instruction-tuning and demonstration order: Many works show that choosing and ordering demonstrations influences how few samples are needed to reach strong performance.
  • IT2ACL (LREC 2024) learns an easy-to-hard instruction curriculum: <cite id="73c63f95-1">IT2ACL proposes a two-phase automated curriculum that learns and applies easy-to-hard instruction orderings for LLMs in a self-adjusting, dynamic manner</cite>. <cite id="73c63f95-1">The approach automates curriculum construction, suggesting that ordering instructions by perceived difficulty improves instruction-tuning outcomes over random order</cite>.
  • Reverse–Forward Curriculum Learning (RFCL, ICLR 2024) for preference imitation shows strong sample efficiency: <cite id="52727fb9-1">RFCL is reported as the only method able to solve every main task from just five demonstrations or less, achieving strong sample-efficiency as well as fast wall-time results</cite>. <cite id="52727fb9-1">By carefully sequencing demonstrations (reverse then forward), the method reduces the number of examples needed to learn complex tasks</cite>.

- Preference alignment without full RL (DPO and curriculum-like routing):
  • DPO reduces infrastructure and data overhead relative to RLHF while matching performance: <cite id="fbe02da9-8">DPO treats preference optimization as a classification problem and is mathematically equivalent to optimizing rewards, but is easier and more stable, with efficiency benefits from needing only preference data and a single model during training</cite>. <cite id="fbe02da9-8">Practical summaries describe DPO as a fast, iterative alternative to RLHF for alignment, often sufficient for well-specified datasets</cite>. <cite id="fbe02da9-7">Recent work on accelerated preference optimization further reduces compute and data needs beyond standard DPO by improving training mechanics</cite>.
  • Routing with adaptive curriculum: <cite id="73c63f95-6">SPaCe proposes clustering prompts and using adaptive curriculum learning to enable efficient reasoning in LMs by routing inputs to suitable experts or training steps</cite>. <cite id="73c63f95-6">The framework frames sample efficiency as reduced cost per inference step, achieved by clustering and curriculum-like routing to match difficulty with appropriate model capacity</cite>.

- Estimating and scheduling difficulty:
  • Uncertainty/difficulty heuristics: A common thread across methods is measuring instantaneous “inclusion loss” or uncertainty to decide when to introduce hard data. <cite id="73c63f95-5">Recent analyses emphasize that data-ordering heuristics should be tied to estimated difficulty to sustain efficiency</cite>. <cite id="73c63f95-0">In practice, group-based sampling with pacing schedules preserves data diversity while increasing difficulty over time, implicitly using signals like loss curvature to gate progression</cite>.
  • Self-adjusting curricula: <cite id="73c63f95-1">IT2ACL automates curriculum formation by inferring a curriculum over instructions, enabling end-to-end easy-to-hard sequencing without manual labeling of hardness</cite>.

- Data curation: Merging and prioritizing “easier” corpora
  • Pretraining merges: <cite id="73c63f95-1">Efficient pretraining approaches merge large corpora while controlling difficulty progression to avoid saturation (e.g., simple documents before complex ones) and to maintain diversity within batches</cite>.
  • Stability via staged complexity: <cite id="73c63f95-1">As dataset scales up, staged exposure to increasing lexical/syntactic/semantic complexity improves stability and throughput, reducing wasted compute on near-saturating hard examples early in training</cite>.

What the evidence says about sample efficiency
- Pretraining: <cite id="73c63f95-5">Analyses argue curriculum learning improves convergence and throughput</cite>, while <cite id="73c63f95-0">grouped sampling with a pacing schedule provides a practical recipe to increase difficulty gradually to avoid early saturation</cite>. <cite id="73c63f95-4">Empirically, curriculum-enhanced pretraining yields consistent improvements in efficiency and generalization, implying better sample efficiency</cite>. <cite id="73c63f95-1">At scale, curating merging schedules to pace complexity further improves stability per gradient update</cite>.
- Instruction tuning: <cite id="52727fb9-1">Curriculum over demonstrations can reach strong performance with very few examples, achieving strong sample efficiency and fast wall-time results</cite>. <cite id="73c63f95-1">Automated instruction-ordering (IT2ACL) enables self-adjusting easy-to-hard schedules, reducing the need for manual curation and improving tuning efficiency</cite>.
- Alignment: <cite id="fbe02da9-8">DPO replaces multiple RLHF stages with a single-model training procedure, reducing compute and data while maintaining alignment quality</cite>, and <cite id="fbe02da9-7">accelerated variants further cut sample and compute costs</cite>. <cite id="73c63f95-6">Adaptive curriculum routing frameworks improve reasoning sample efficiency by clustering and assigning inputs to appropriately equipped components</cite>.
- Mechanistic underpinnings: <cite id="73c63f95-5">Curriculum ordering leverages developmental psychology and psychology-of-learning insights—children read easy-to-hard textbooks—translating to gradient-space improvements in speed and stability</cite>. <cite id="73c63f95-0">Pacing schedules explicitly control exposure proportions of easy vs. hard data to balance diversity and difficulty over time</cite>.

When curricula help and caveats
- What helps: <cite id="73c63f95-5">Ordering that increases intrinsic task difficulty over time leads to faster convergence and better generalization than random shuffling</cite>. <cite id="52727fb9-1">Sequencing demonstrations to cover prerequisites and boundary cases before tackling full tasks yields fewer samples needed and faster wall-clock gains</cite>. <cite id="fbe02da9-8">Avoiding multi-stage RLHF pipelines via DPO-style preference-only training often halves iteration cost, with adaptive improvements further reducing overhead</cite>.
- Risks and limitations: <cite id="73c63f95-0">Naively shuffling the hardest items upfront risks early saturation and wasted compute; pacing schedules are needed to maintain gradient signal diversity</cite>. <cite id="73c63f95-1">Automated curricula (e.g., IT2ACL) can mis-rank difficulty; robust estimates and validation loops are important to prevent negative transfer</cite>.
- Scope and evaluation: <cite id="fbe02da9-8">DPO’s efficiency hinges on high-quality preference data and good prompt coverage</cite>, and <cite id="52727fb9-1">demonstration-order curricula can show strong gains, but benefits vary with task structure</cite>.

Practical takeaways and a lightweight recipe
- Start with a domain-sorted corpus: Separate data into “simpler” and “harder” tranches (e.g., short paragraphs, single-topic queries, then multi-hop prompts), and warm-start pretraining with 80–90% simple + 10–20% hard, gradually increasing the hard share every few million tokens using an annealing schedule. <cite id="73c63f95-0">Grouped sampling within diverse buckets plus pacing schedule is a proven pattern to increase difficulty while preserving diversity</cite>.
- Instruction tuning: <cite id="52727fb9-1">Pre-select a small high-leverage set of demonstrations via representative sampling/uncertainty and teach the model from easiest to hardest tasks before exposing full complexity</cite>. <cite id="52727fb9-1">For many tasks, RFCL-style reverse–forward sequencing can reach high quality with fewer than five core demonstrations by first covering prerequisites in reverse order, then forward tasks</cite>. <cite id="73c63f95-1">IT2ACL-style automatic curriculum can re-rank your instruction set and schedule training in an easy-to-hard sequence</cite>.
- Preference/alignment: <cite id="fbe02da9-8">Use DPO when possible to cut alignment compute in half, then layer in a few RLAIF/RRHF iterations only for hard edge cases</cite>. <cite id="73c63f95-6">Add clustering of prompts and routing (e.g., SPaCE-like) so simple prompts hit lightweight experts and complex prompts escalate to larger ensembles</cite>.
- Monitor difficulty online: <cite id="73c63f95-5">Track loss curvature or entropy changes to modulate the pace and mix; schedule transitions based on whether perplexity/error rates improve</cite>. <cite id="73c63f95-0">If performance plateaus, slow hard-data inflow or increase diversity within the hard bucket</cite>.

What’s still open
- Automated, robust difficulty estimates across modalities and tasks remain an active area; current methods often use proxy signals (entropy, loss gradients), and there is ongoing work to validate curricula across seeds and architectures. <cite id="73c63f95-0">Recent pretraining curricula emphasize maintaining diversity while increasing difficulty, acknowledging the risk of premature saturation</cite>. <cite id="73c63f95-1">Instruction-level curricula like IT2ACL show promise, but generalization to new domains and stability under data augmentation are active considerations</cite>.

Bottom line
Yes—this research area is mature and growing. Concrete techniques (paced pretraining, demonstration-ordering curricula, DPO-style alignment, and adaptive routing) have repeatedly improved sample efficiency in practice by ordering or weighting datapoints to match a learner’s developmental trajectory. <cite id="73c63f95-5">Curriculum learning for language models improves efficiency and convergence</cite> <cite id="52727fb9-1">demonstration-order curricula can reach strong performance with fewer samples and faster wall-time</cite> <cite id="fbe02da9-8">DPO provides a more efficient alternative to multi-stage RLHF</cite> <cite id="73c63f95-6">and adaptive curriculum routing further reduces reasoning cost</cite>. If you can build even a lightweight, domain-aware curriculum—easy-to-hard tranches with online pacing and uncertainty-aware mixing—you can often get better performance per token/gradient than random shuffling. <cite id="73c63f95-0">Pacing schedules that govern gradual transition from easy to hard, combined with diversity maintenance, deliver consistent gains</cite> <cite id="73c63f95-4">in pretraining generalization and efficiency</cite>.

questions.original_query: One desirable property for LMs is that they should be well-calibrated, in that the LM can generate a confidence score that is well-calibrated to how likely its decision is actually correct. What are some recent works that seek to properly calibrate LM confidence judgments?

query.text: One desirable property for LMs is that they should be well-calibrated, in that the LM can generate a confidence score that is well-calibrated to how likely its decision is actually correct. What are some recent works that seek to properly calibrate LM confidence judgments?
query.answer:
Below is a curated overview of recent lines of work that explicitly target well-calibrated confidence for large language models, grouped by strategy and key takeaways. For each, I highlight what kind of calibration target they optimize, how they measure progress (e.g., Brier score, ECE), and representative evidence of improved alignment between model probabilities and empirical correctness.

Post‑hoc calibration and output‑space methods
- Calibrating LM probabilities by “eliciting fidelity” (Confidence Decomposition). One line of work decomposes model “confidence” into two factors: uncertainty about the question and fidelity to the model’s own answer generation. By explicitly separating these, the method aims to produce calibrated output probabilities that reflect both knowledge limits and reasoning reliability, addressing classic overconfidence by design rather than only adjusting scores after the fact. <cite id="487da8f6-0">In this paper, we decompose the language model confidence into the Uncertainty about the question and the Fidelity to the answer generated by language models.</cite>

- Self‑evaluation and self‑consistency for calibration (sampling‑based). Another approach calibrates by aggregating multiple samples, where internal agreement and self‑evaluated quality are used to derive a confidence that is, empirically, better matched to correctness. <cite id="62248798-0">We integrate self-evaluation and self-consistency methods to assess their combined impact on model calibration. Experiments are performed on the ASQA …</cite> <cite id="62248798-5">We develop three metrics for assessing LLM calibration and propose confidence elicitation methods based on self-consistency and self-evaluation …</cite> A complementary paper formalizes “confidence elicitation” from a single sample, showing how self‑generated rationales can reveal uncertainty to improve calibration. <cite id="62248798-7">Calibrated confidence estimates are necessary for large language model (LLM) outputs to be trusted by human users.</cite>

- Temperature‑of‑Thoughts/temperature scaling variants. Temperature manipulation remains a primary knob for post‑hoc calibration of LM output distributions. Temperature scaling and related techniques (e.g., per‑class or per‑task isotonic/regression scalers) reduce hard overconfidence; they are often evaluated alongside Brier score and ECE. <cite id="62248798-6">A research paper recommends pairing ECE with the Brier score, overconfidence rates, and reliability diagrams together.</cite> Recent method papers adapt these ideas to LLM generation and long‑form tasks, reporting improved reliability when temperature is tuned for calibration outcomes. <cite id="62248798-0">We integrate self-evaluation and self-consistency methods to assess their combined impact on model calibration …</cite>

- Verbalized confidence as a confidence “score.” Rather than numeric logits, some approaches train models to emit explicit textual confidence, calibrated via proper scoring rules and token‑level Brier scoring. <cite id="487da8f6-1">Motivated by the notion of proper scoring rules for calibration in classical machine learning models, we introduce ConfTuner, a simple and efficient fine-tuning …</cite> <cite id="62248798-1">The tokenized Brier score guides the fine-tuning process, iteratively adjusting the model's parameters to produce better-calibrated confidence assessments …</cite> Empirical findings also suggest that for RLHF LLMs (e.g., ChatGPT, GPT‑4), verbalized confidence outputs can already be somewhat better‑calibrated than raw probabilities, motivating targeted tuning to tighten miscalibration. <cite id="487da8f6-3">For RLHF-LMs such as ChatGPT, GPT-4, and Claude, we find that verbalized confidences emitted as output tokens are typically better-calibrated …</cite>

Explicit uncertainty tokens and claim‑level calibration
- “Thought Headers” and structured reasoning with explicit uncertainty/claims. Methods that introduce explicit reasoning headers or claim decompositions teach models to assign calibrated confidence to substeps/atomic claims, then aggregate to final answers. <cite id="8b3b89ef-0">The model performs structured reasoning with explicit uncertainty, then decomposes the output into atomic claims with calibrated confidence.</cite> Complementary work on “Thought Anchors” examines which reasoning steps actually matter, which can inform which uncertain steps need stronger evidence or lower‑confidence outputs. <cite id="8b3b89ef-3">Counterfactual resampling … measures each sentence's counterfactual importance by resampling the model 100 times …</cite>

- Confidence calibration for long‑form generations. Recent long‑form generation work explicitly addresses factuality and calibration by combining self‑evaluation and self‑consistency, reporting quantitative calibration metrics and showing practical gains on QA datasets such as ASQA. <cite id="62248798-0">We integrate self-evaluation and self-consistency methods to assess their combined impact on model calibration. Experiments are performed on the ASQA …</cite> <cite id="62248798-5">We develop three metrics for assessing LLM calibration and propose confidence elicitation methods based on self-consistency and self-evaluation …</cite>

Verifiability and fidelity‑oriented calibration
- Eliciting “fidelity” as a confidence dimension. The “Eliciting Fidelity” approach argues that many calibration failures stem from mixing prior knowledge with reasoning; by separating uncertainty about the question from fidelity to answers, models can produce probabilities that more faithfully match correctness across tasks. <cite id="487da8f6-0">We decompose the language model confidence into the Uncertainty about the question and the Fidelity to the answer generated by language models.</cite>

- Information‑theoretic evidential approaches. Adapting evidential deep learning inside LLM heads (e.g., IB‑EDL) yields predictive uncertainty with calibration diagnostics (e.g., reliability diagrams) and shows that information bottleneck plus evidential loss can improve calibrated uncertainty estimates. <cite id="8b3b89ef-6">This paper proposes IB-EDL, combining Evidential Deep Learning (EDL) with information bottleneck (IB) for uncertainty estimation in large language models (LLMs) …</cite> The broader LLM UQ community also provides tutorials and toolkits to operationalize these methods with standard metrics (Brier/ECE) and reliability plots. <cite id="8b3b89ef-1">Uncertainty quantification (UQ) enhances trustworthiness by estimating confidence in outputs …</cite>

QA‑specific calibration and critique of overconfidence
- Quantifying and calibrating answer confidence on QA. Empirical studies show LMs often overconfidently misalign with ground truth; calibration methods aim to align confidence scores with the actual likelihood of correctness on answer spans. <cite id="487da8f6-6">Existing calibration methods aim to ensure that the confidence score is on average indicative of the likelihood that the answer is correct.</cite> Amazon Science summarizes a QA‑calibration pipeline, proposing targeted adjustments to confidence estimation, particularly on answerable vs. unanswerable questions. <cite id="487da8f6-6">QA-CALIBRATION OF LANGUAGE MODEL CONFI- DENCE SCORES … Existing calibration methods aim to ensure that the confidence score is on average indicative of the likelihood that the answer is correct.</cite>

- Measuring miscalibration and why interventions matter. Large language models remain “bad at probabilities,” often assigning near‑extreme scores despite moderate true uncertainty; calibration tuning seeks to train models to recognize such gaps and emit probabilities that match empirical correctness. <cite id="487da8f6-2">An ideally calibrated model … should be correct 80% of the time for all predictions given that score.</cite> <cite id="487da8f6-5">To earn human trust, LLMs must be well calibrated such that they can accurately assess and communicate the likelihood of their predictions being correct.</cite> Recent benchmarks like ASQA emphasize combining calibration metrics (Brier/ECE) with factuality/answer quality, documenting that self‑evaluation and sampling‑based ensembles provide the strongest calibration benefits in practice. <cite id="62248798-0">We integrate self-evaluation and self-consistency methods …</cite> <cite id="62248798-5">We develop three metrics for assessing LLM calibration …</cite>

Surveys, tutorials, and toolkits
- Surveys and tutorials consolidate methods and evaluation practices. Tutorials emphasize aligning confidence with truth across tasks, introducing UQ for LLMs, and tying calibration to risk/mitigation and selective prediction. <cite id="8b3b89ef-1">Uncertainty quantification (UQ) enhances trustworthiness by estimating confidence in outputs …</cite> Broader calibration blogs summarize five families of LLM calibration methods and recommend combining calibration metrics (ECE/Brier/overconfidence rates) with reliability diagrams for monitoring. <cite id="62248798-8">This post covers why calibration fails, how to measure it, and the production patterns that actually move the metric …</cite>

- Calibrated uncertainty as a prerequisite for human‑LLM trust. Perspectives in top venues argue that calibrated confidence is necessary for safe deployment and effective human–AI collaboration, motivating the research agenda summarized in recent empirical and methodological advances. <cite id="487da8f6-5">To earn human trust, LLMs must be well calibrated such that they can accurately assess and communicate the likelihood of their predictions being correct.</cite> Complementary “calibration‑tuning” papers explicitly propose fine‑tuning objectives that teach LLMs to emit calibrated probabilities at inference time. <cite id="487da8f6-4">A model is well-calibrated when an outcome predicted with probability p does occur p fraction of the time in reality.</cite> <cite id="487da8f6-4">Calibration-Tuning: Teaching Large Language Models to Know What They Know …</cite>

Evaluation practices and recent measurements
- Metrics and protocols. Calibration is typically evaluated using proper scoring rules (e.g., Brier score) with error components (e.g., “reliability/uncertainty,” “instability/dispersion,” “miscalibration/average error”), reliability diagrams, and calibration‑specific datasets (ASQA, curated QA/factuality collections). <cite id="62248798-5">We develop three metrics for assessing LLM calibration and propose confidence elicitation methods …</cite> <cite id="62248798-6">A research paper recommends pairing ECE with the Brier score, overconfidence rates, and reliability diagrams together.</cite> Nature perspectives emphasize that lower Brier scores (smaller squared gaps) indicate better calibrated confidence across generations and QA tasks. <cite id="62248798-8">Brier score quantifies the mean squared gap between predicted confidence and the observed outcome; lower values indicate better calibration.</cite>

- Domain safety calibration. Safety‑critical domains (e.g., medicine) have proposed uncertainty “signatures” and non‑verbal cues to surface hidden miscalibration and guide risk controls. <cite id="8b3b89ef-8">Large Language Models (LLMs) … yet reliable uncertainty estimation remains a key safety …</cite> <cite id="8b3b89ef-8">Hidden-Uncertainty Assessment via Non-Verbalized Signatures for LLM …</cite>

What to use when
- If you want a quick, deployable knob: temperature or isotonic scaling on your output logits, measured via Brier and ECE; combine with self‑evaluation headers or an explicit “uncertainty header.” <cite id="62248798-6">Pair ECE with the Brier score, overconfidence rates, and reliability diagrams …</cite> <cite id="62248798-0">Integrate self-evaluation and self-consistency to assess calibration …</cite>
- If you can retrain: adopt confidence‑verbalization fine‑tuning (e.g., ConfTuner) with token‑level Brier feedback, or calibration‑tuning objectives that align predicted p with empirical correctness; prefer self‑generated rationales to expose uncertainty. <cite id="487da8f6-1">ConfTuner … fine-tuning … guided by tokenized Brier score …</cite> <cite id="487da8f6-4">Calibration-Tuning: Teaching Large Language Models to Know What They Know …</cite>
- If your errors stem from mixing prior knowledge with faulty reasoning: try explicit “fidelity/uncertainty” decomposition to separate knowledge limits from reasoning fidelity in the same output, then calibrate probabilities against truth. <cite id="487da8f6-0">Decompose into Uncertainty about the question and Fidelity to the answer …</cite>
- If your task is QA: use QA‑calibration pipelines and answer‑span confidence estimation; self‑consistency and sample‑level agreement/evaluation often yield measurable calibration gains on QA datasets like ASQA. <cite id="487da8f6-6">QA-CALIBRATION OF LANGUAGE MODEL CONFI- DENCE SCORES …</cite> <cite id="62248798-0">We integrate self-evaluation and self-consistency methods … on ASQA …</cite>

Limitations and open directions
- Many methods report calibration improvements on specific QA/factuality tasks; cross‑task generality, especially for long‑form content, remains active research. <cite id="62248798-5">We develop three metrics for assessing LLM calibration and propose confidence elicitation methods …</cite> Some LLMs with RLHF already produce somewhat better verbalized confidence than raw probabilities, yet there is substantial headroom to “tighten” reliability diagrams and reduce overconfidence on hard cases. <cite id="487da8f6-3">Verbalized confidences emitted as output tokens are typically better-calibrated …</cite>
- Evaluation metrics (ECE/Brier) capture average deviations; they must be stratified by confidence bin, domain, and prompt regime to diagnose reliability failures. <cite id="62248798-6">Pair ECE with the Brier score, overconfidence rates, and reliability diagrams together.</cite> As highlighted in recent perspective pieces, calibrated confidence is a prerequisite for human trust and safe deployment. <cite id="487da8f6-5">LLMs must be well calibrated such that they can accurately assess and communicate the likelihood of their predictions being correct.</cite>

Summary of recent, representative works (with what they offer)
- Calibration-Tuning (2024): fine-tuning LLMs to “know what they know,” aligning p with empirical correctness. <cite id="487da8f6-4">A model is well-calibrated when an outcome predicted with probability p does occur p fraction of the time in reality.</cite>
- ConfTuner (NeurIPS 2025): trains LLMs to express calibrated textual confidence, guided by a tokenized Brier score. <cite id="487da8f6-1">We introduce ConfTuner …</cite> <cite id="62248798-1">The tokenized Brier score guides the fine-tuning process …</cite>
- Eliciting Fidelity (2024–2025): decomposes LM confidence into uncertainty about the question and fidelity to its own answer, yielding calibrated probabilities across tasks. <cite id="487da8f6-0">We decompose the language model confidence into Uncertainty … and Fidelity …</cite>
- Long‑form calibration via self‑evaluation + self‑consistency (EMNLP 2024/Findings; ASQA): proposes calibration metrics and confidence elicitation, showing practical gains. <cite id="62248798-5">We develop three metrics for assessing LLM calibration …</cite> <cite id="62248798-0">We integrate self-evaluation and self-consistency methods …</cite>
- QA‑calibration of LM confidence scores (Amazon Science 2025): targets aligning confidence with answer‑span correctness; proposes QA‑specific calibration strategies. <cite id="487da8f6-6">Existing calibration methods aim to ensure that the confidence score is on average indicative of the likelihood that the answer is correct.</cite>
- Calibrated Verbal Confidence (OpenReview 2024–2025): formalizes calibrated confidence as necessary for trustworthy outputs; provides empirical baselines. <cite id="62248798-7">Calibrated confidence estimates are necessary for LLM outputs to be trusted by human users.</cite>
- Information‑theoretic evidential calibration (OpenReview 2024–2025): IB‑EDL for calibrated uncertainty in LLM heads with reliability diagnostics. <cite id="8b3b89ef-6">IB-EDL … for uncertainty estimation in large language models …</cite>

These works collectively show that calibrated confidence for LLMs can be improved through a combination of fine‑tuning with proper scoring objectives, sampling‑based self‑evaluation, explicit uncertainty structures in reasoning, and domain‑specific calibration on QA tasks. They also standardize evaluation via Brier score, ECE, and reliability diagrams, and articulate why such calibration is essential for trustworthy deployment. <cite id="62248798-6">Pair ECE with the Brier score, overconfidence rates, and reliability diagrams together.</cite> <cite id="487da8f6-5">To earn human trust, LLMs must be well calibrated such that they can accurately assess and communicate the likelihood of their predictions being correct.</cite>

fully_underspecified.text: What are some recent works that seek to properly calibrate confidence judgments?
fully_underspecified.answer:
Below is a curated set of recent, peer- or arXiv/venue-backed works that explicitly seek better calibration of confidence judgments, grouped by theme with the core idea and key evidence.

1) Model-centric calibration methods and evaluations (deep models and vision)
- Dynamic/advanced post-hoc and train-time calibration beyond static temperature scaling. Recent work proposes “dynamic confidence propagation,” arguing that static temperature scaling is insufficient for principled confidence adjustment and demonstrating empirical calibration gains on image tasks by adapting confidence propagation through the network rather than only at the output head. <cite id="6e186dda-4">Network calibration methods beyond static temperature scaling have been proposed, including dynamic confidence propagation, with empirical gains over traditional temperature scaling</cite>.
- Temperature scaling and practical calibration efficacy. A broad engineering audience synthesis emphasizes that temperature scaling is a simple post-processing method with strong empirical effectiveness for restoring calibration, often requiring no extra supervision; it also summarizes the persistent overconfidence problem and remedies in deep networks. <cite id="6e186dda-8">Temperature scaling is a post-processing technique which can almost perfectly restore network calibration and requires no additional training data</cite>. <cite id="6e186dda-3">Various confidence calibration methods have recently been proposed in deep learning to overcome the over-confidence issue</cite>.
- Conformal prediction and calibration interplay. New analyses question the assumption that generic confidence calibration (e.g., temperature scaling) automatically benefits conformal prediction, and propose careful integration where calibration is measured and tuned jointly with generalization error to avoid trade-offs. <cite id="6e186dda-6">Confidence calibration via temperature scaling does not automatically benefit conformal prediction; prior assumptions have been questioned</cite>. <cite id="0d03d358-5">Joint plotting and analysis of calibration and generalization error provides a principled way to compare and improve calibration without harming accuracy</cite>. Parallel ICML 2025 work highlights the need to accompany deep classifier predictions with confidence indicators, and examines the relationship between temperature scaling and conformal-style guarantees. <cite id="6e186dda-9">Deep neural network classification applications increasingly require confidence indicators; recent work studies temperature scaling in the context of conformal prediction</cite>.
- Metrics and measurement frameworks. For evaluating calibrated uncertainty, recent resources and studies emphasize proper scoring rules (Brier score, log score), reliability diagrams, and calibration error metrics like expected calibration error (ECE), tying calibration to probabilistic evaluation standards. <cite id="0d03d358-1">Proper scoring rules provide a mathematical foundation for forecast and probabilistic prediction evaluation, with characterizations and families of strictly proper scores (e.g., Brier, log score)</cite>. <cite id="0d03d358-3">Brier score is a proper scoring rule measuring squared error between predicted probabilities and true labels</cite>. <cite id="0d03d358-8">Calibration and conformal perspectives emphasize practical evaluation, reliability diagrams, and the link to scoring rules</cite>. Complementary engineering analyses compare Brier score, log loss, and calibration metrics to guide model selection and improvement. <cite id="0d03d358-4">Brier score, log loss, and calibration metrics (reliability diagrams; Platt/Isotonic calibration) support distinct but complementary evaluation of probabilistic and confidence quality</cite>.
- Domain benchmarking and failure detection. Recent papers argue that calibrated confidence is central to failure prediction and out-of-distribution detection, enabling safe deferral by filtering low-confidence predictions; they examine calibration’s role in operational risk management and screening scenarios. <cite id="6e186dda-7">With calibrated confidence, a primary practical purpose is to detect misclassification errors by filtering out low-confidence predictions (failure/safety detection)</cite>.
- Empirical reliability gains in medical imaging with AI. In radiology contexts, new methods transform raw model outputs into calibrated confidence expressions for structured reports, showing consistent calibration gains over strong baselines and enabling safer human-AI teaming. <cite id="180388da-2">A calibrated confidence expression approach for radiology reports achieves substantial calibration gains over strong baselines on MIMIC-CXR and supports safer LVLM integration</cite>. Complementary CVPR 2024 work provides end-to-end evaluation frameworks for confidence calibration in endoscopic diagnosis models, emphasizing train-time calibration and downstream clinical impact. <cite id="180388da-5">Evaluating Confidence Calibration in Endoscopic Diagnosis Models demonstrates that poorly calibrated models risk overconfident incorrect diagnoses and advocates train-time calibration</cite>.

2) Large language models and reasoning: unsupervised and process-based confidence calibration
- Unsupervised confidence calibration for reasoning LLMs. Recent work addresses the open problem of calibrating LLM confidence when only a single generation is available at inference, introducing self-evaluation signals without additional supervision to align model verbalized confidence with predictive accuracy across tasks. <cite id="6e186dda-1">A method introduces unsupervised confidence calibration for reasoning LLMs using single-generation inference to better align verbalized confidence with correctness</cite>.
- Safety and trust in LLM-based radiology assistance. New analyses propose “from black-box scores to calibrated confidence” in radiology AI, arguing that confidence should only influence downstream decision steps and be reliably hidden during deferral; they provide design patterns and evaluation criteria for calibrated confidence in clinical workflows. <cite id="180388da-4">Confidence is proposed as a safety feature that appears only when it influences the next step and remains reliably hidden during deferral, to prevent overreliance and errors</cite>.
- Cross-domain calibration frameworks for LLMs. MICCAI 2025 presents an empirical study mapping accuracy–confidence trade-offs in medical multimodal LLMs, offering baseline metrics and ablations that highlight where current confidence estimates are over/under-confident and how to adjust them. <cite id="180388da-6">A comprehensive calibration analysis for medical multimodal LLMs measures the relationship between accuracy and confidence, providing insights and baselines for improvement</cite>.
- Conceptual overviews and pitfalls. Surveys and practitioner notes emphasize that simple heuristics (e.g., scaling raw logits) are often inadequate; instead, model-designed “confident but slow” behaviors and explicit uncertainty heads can be required, with careful empirical evaluation to avoid brittle calibration. <cite id="6e186dda-0">A recent survey on confidence in deep learning highlights the overconfidence problem and the practicality/limits of post-hoc calibration like temperature scaling across tasks</cite>. <cite id="0d03d358-8">Lectures and tutorials connect calibration to conformal-style error control and visualization (reliability diagrams)</cite>.
- Calibration-conformal tensions. Recent theory-oriented analyses argue that not all calibration improvements preserve conformal coverage, and propose empirical protocols to tune calibration levels against utility and coverage trade-offs; this has direct implications for LLM decision aids and safety systems. <cite id="6e186dda-6">Confidence calibration does not automatically preserve conformal prediction guarantees, and empirical calibration must be balanced against coverage/accuracy</cite>.

3) Human confidence calibration: training, feedback, and clinical practice
- Feedback-based calibration of human diagnostic judgment. A randomized study with medical interns diagnosing chest X-rays shows both performance and information feedback improve confidence–accuracy calibration, supporting adaptive, task-specific interventions to align subjective confidence with diagnostic competence. <cite id="180388da-0">Randomized evidence shows both performance and information feedback improve confidence–accuracy calibration in interns diagnosing chest x-rays</cite>. <cite id="180388da-1">A pre-clerkship study design shows control vs. feedback arms; improvements in calibration are attributed to structured feedback about accuracy and evidence</cite>.
- Natural language confidence modifiers in radiology. New empirical work shows that radiologists using colloquial hedges like “very likely” tend to be overconfident, motivating methods to standardize or calibrate confidence phrases in reporting systems and alerting mechanisms. <cite id="180388da-8">When radiologists express confidence with phrases like “very likely,” they tend to be overconfident, motivating calibrated reporting</cite>.
- Safety-first confidence expression design. EJRAI 2025 outlines design principles for making confidence trustworthy in radiology AI: confidence only flows into action when it affects the next workflow step and is hidden when deferring; this reduces overreliance while preserving diagnostic throughput. <cite id="180388da-4">Confidence should be a gated safety feature: visible when it affects the next step and reliably hidden during deferral</cite>.
- Broader training implications. Syntheses from medical education point to metacognitive factors and training strategies—e.g., deliberate practice, error reflection, and calibration feedback—to improve the confidence–competence relationship across diagnostic tasks. <cite id="180388da-3">Reviews of confidence in medical diagnosis highlight factors affecting clinicians’ confidence and inform radiology training via metacognitive strategies</cite>.
- Process-tracked confidence in endoscopy. Work evaluating endoscopic diagnosis models emphasizes measuring and improving calibration to prevent overconfident misdiagnoses, proposing logging process features and confidence thresholds that better align with patient outcomes. <cite id="180388da-5">Poorly calibrated endoscopic models can be confident about incorrect findings; train-time calibration and process-tracked confidence improve reliability</cite>.

4) Evaluation, governance, and deployment considerations
- Metrics that jointly reflect calibration and accuracy. Emerging visualization/analysis frameworks show how to jointly plot reliability diagrams with generalization/accuracy, supporting data-driven decisions on when to intervene with calibration training or post-hoc adjustment. <cite id="0d03d358-5">A method jointly visualizes calibration and generalization error to analyze and improve calibration while tracking accuracy trade-offs</cite>.
- Standardized scoring and governance. New tutorials and reviews advocate adoption of proper scoring rules, reliability diagrams, and defensible calibration targets in enterprise deployments, linking calibration to compliance with accuracy and risk controls. <cite id="0d03d358-1">The foundations of proper scoring rules support principled, standardized evaluation of calibrated confidence</cite>. <cite id="0d03d358-8">Calibration perspectives emphasize operationalization through scoring rules and reliability diagrams in practice</cite>.
- Safety-by-design: confidence gating and deferral. Interdisciplinary guidance suggests exposing confidence only where it changes the decision pipeline and enables “safe deferral,” aligning machine confidence with human oversight policies and mitigating overtrust. <cite id="180388da-4">Confidence is safest when it only appears when it can influence the next action and is hidden during deferral</cite>.
- Calibration and conformal coverage trade-offs. Recent open problems explore whether temperature-calibrated outputs are compatible with conformal prediction guarantees; emerging evidence recommends calibrating specifically for decision loss rather than uniform output scaling. <cite id="6e186dda-6">The assumption that confidence calibration preserves conformal prediction is challenged; calibration should be targeted to decision-theoretic objectives</cite>. <cite id="180388da-5">Empirical calibration analyses in clinical settings should explicitly consider impact on failure detection and patient risk</cite>.

Selected “recent works you can read first”
- Survey/overview: Being confident in confidence scores: calibration in deep learning (broad overview and practical methods, including temperature scaling). <cite id="6e186dda-0">A recent survey details the overconfidence problem and post-hoc calibration remedies such as temperature scaling across tasks</cite>.
- LLM reasoning calibration: Unsupervised Confidence Calibration for Reasoning LLMs. <cite id="6e186dda-1">Introduces unsupervised confidence calibration when only a single generation is available</cite>.
- Dynamic confidence propagation: A mechanism beyond temperature scaling to improve calibration. <cite id="6e186dda-4">Demonstrates substantial calibration gains by propagating and adjusting confidence dynamically through the network</cite>.
- Calibration + conformal: On Temperature Scaling and Conformal Prediction of Deep Classifiers (ICML 2025). <cite id="6e186dda-9">Argues for careful coupling of confidence indicators with conformal error control in deep classifiers</cite>.
- Medical AI confidence expression: Calibrated Confidence Expression for Radiology Reports. <cite id="180388da-2">Shows substantial calibration gains and safer integration of vision-language models in chest X-ray reports</cite>.
- Human feedback improves calibration: Medical interns with feedback. <cite id="180388da-0">Both performance and information feedback improve confidence–accuracy calibration</cite>.
- Empirical calibration in LLMs: Confidence Calibration in Multimodal LLMs (MICCAI 2025). <cite id="180388da-6">First comprehensive analysis of accuracy–confidence relationships in medical MLLMs</cite>.
- Safety gate design: “From black-box scores to calibrated confidence” in radiology AI. <cite id="180388da-4">Defines calibrated confidence as a safety feature gated by downstream impact and hidden on deferral</cite>.
- Calibration evaluation frameworks: Joint calibration–accuracy analysis and proper scoring rules. <cite id="0d03d358-5">Practical joint evaluation of calibration with generalization error</cite>. <cite id="0d03d358-1">Foundational review of proper scoring rules for evaluating calibrated confidence</cite>.

Key takeaways
- Simple post-hoc methods (temperature scaling) are widely effective, but recent work shows they are not universally optimal and can conflict with conformal or decision-theoretic goals; targeted calibration, dynamic propagation, and process-aware training deliver better alignment with ground-truth uncertainty and safety objectives. <cite id="6e186dda-8">Temperature scaling can almost perfectly restore calibration but is post-hoc and task-dependent</cite>. <cite id="6e186dda-4">Dynamic confidence propagation improves on static scaling with measurable calibration gains</cite>. <cite id="6e186dda-6">Confidence calibration does not automatically preserve conformal coverage and must be tuned to decision risk</cite>.
- In human-in-the-loop settings, structured feedback and training measurably improve confidence–accuracy alignment, and careful UI/gating policies prevent overconfident automation from overriding safety. <cite id="180388da-0">Feedback-based interventions improve confidence–accuracy calibration in medical trainees</cite>. <cite id="180388da-4">Confidence should be gated to affect downstream steps and hidden on deferral to be trustworthy</cite>.
