- For evaluation, combine proper scoring rules (Brier, log score) with reliability diagrams and calibration error metrics; when reporting confidence, accompany them with task- and policy-aligned decision metrics to ensure practical calibration, not just model-level calibration. <cite id="0d03d358-1">Proper scoring rules provide the foundation for principled calibration evaluation</cite>. <cite id="0d03d358-5">Joint calibration–accuracy analysis clarifies accuracy–calibration trade-offs and improvement paths</cite>.

without_scope.text: One desirable property for LMs is that they should be well-calibrated, in that the LM can generate a confidence score that is well-calibrated to how likely its decision is actually correct. What are some works that seek to properly calibrate LM confidence judgments?
without_scope.answer:
Below is a curated set of works and directions that explicitly target calibrating large language models’ (LLMs’) confidence judgments—i.e., aligning model-reported probabilities or certainty levels with the actual correctness frequency.

Surveys and conceptual foundations
- Confidence estimation and calibration are identified as key enablers for safer, more trustworthy LLM deployment and risk mitigation; surveys consolidate methods, metrics, and challenges across tasks and domains <cite id="04f4961c-0">Assessing their confidence and calibrating them across different tasks can help mitigate risks and enable LLMs to produce better generations</cite> <cite id="04f4961c-2">Uncertainty quantification (UQ) enhances the reliability of Large Language Models (LLMs) by estimating confidence in outputs, enabling risk</cite>.
- Conceptual treatments emphasize aligning verbal and numeric confidences to actual correctness and integrating calibration into trustworthiness criteria <cite id="a500d7ef-2">Calibration ensures that if a model claims 90% confidence, it should be correct about 90% of the time</cite> <cite id="a500d7ef-8">Confidence calibration in LLMs is the process of aligning model confidence scores with the true probability of correctness across various tasks</cite>.
- Domain-oriented studies treat calibration as a trust proxy: biomedical NLP assessments evaluate nine LLMs’ calibration, and multimodal work stresses domain-specific calibration for clinical reliability <cite id="a500d7ef-1">To assess the calibration of 9 large language models (LLMs) within biomedical natural language processing (BioNLP)</cite> <cite id="a500d7ef-7">The findings highlight the importance of domain-specific calibration for MLLMs in healthcare</cite>.

Post-hoc and fine-tuning calibration methods
- Temporal/log-odds scaling: Temperature scaling on LM logits/outputs is a simple post-hoc method that softens sharp predictions, improving calibration across probabilistic models; implementations and analyses are well-documented and broadly used for neural predictors <cite id="13526017-0">Temperature scaling is a post-processing technique which can almost perfectly restore network calibration</cite> <cite id="13526017-1">Temperature scaling is a simple method that allows to control the uncertainty of probabilistic models</cite> <cite id="13526017-3">Temperature scaling provides a simple, effective post-hoc calibration method that divides logits by a learned scalar T > 1</cite> <cite id="13526017-6">A simple way to calibrate your neural network</cite> <cite id="13526017-9">Temperature scaling divides the logit vector by a scalar T before applying softmax</cite>.
- Verbalized confidence (ConfTuner): Training LLMs to state calibrated confidence explicitly, motivated by proper scoring rules, yields simple fine-tuning that improves numeric alignment between stated confidence and correctness <cite id="04f4961c-4">Motivated by the notion of proper scoring rules for calibration in classical machine learning models, we introduce ConfTuner, a simple and efficient fine-tuning</cite>.
- Semantic/“meaningful” confidence and internal temperatures: Define semantic confidence measures for reasoning outputs and systematically evaluate temperature scaling across QA datasets; also propose novel calibration procedures tied to internal token-level temperatures <cite id="04f4961c-5">We define several semantic confidence measures and evaluate various temperature scaling methods across multiple QA datasets</cite> <cite id="04f4961c-5">We introduce a novel temperature-based calibration procedure</cite> <cite id="a500d7ef-6">Calibration and Correctness of Language Models for Code</cite>.
- Graph-based reweighting of beliefs: Learn to adjust beliefs over answers using graph structure over evidence/claims, explicitly targeting reliable confidence estimation for LLMs <cite id="04f4961c-7">Reliable confidence estimation is essential for enhancing the trustworthiness of large language models (LLMs)</cite> <cite id="04f4961c-7">by Y Li … Reliable confidence estimation is essential for enhancing the trustworthiness of large language models (LLMs), especially in high-stakes</cite>.
- Broader calibration toolkits adapted to LLMs: Practical methods summaries and libraries transfer standard calibration techniques (e.g., temperature scaling, isotonic regression, Platt scaling) into LM workflows <cite id="13526017-2">The calibration module allows you to better calibrate the probabilities of a given model</cite> <cite id="13526017-7">Temperature scaling is a straightforward way to adjust overconfident predictions in large language models (LLMs)</cite> <cite id="13526017-9">A Deep Dive into Calibration of Language Models: Platt scaling, isotonic regression, temperature scaling</cite>.

Self-calibration, reflection, and self-improvement
- Reflection and calibration loops: Calibrated reflection is proposed to improve truthfulness by making models aware of their uncertainty and confidence, then refining answers accordingly <cite id="a500d7ef-2">A Calibrated Reflection Approach for Enhancing … Calibration ensures that if a model claims 90% confidence, it should be correct about 90% of the time</cite>.
- Calibration for self-improving LLMs: A study frames delusion/repair mechanisms through a calibration lens, seeking the right trade-off between performance and reliability as models self-implement fixes <cite id="a500d7ef-0">Our work pioneers the study of self-improving LLMs from a calibration perspective, offering valuable insights into balancing model performance and reliability</cite>.
- Internal “semantic confidence” tied to reasoning: Recent ICLR/NeurIPS work operationalizes confidence not just numerically (log-prob) but semantically, measuring whether a model’s rationales match the implied uncertainty of correct vs. incorrect answers <cite id="04f4961c-5">we define several semantic confidence measures and evaluate various temperature scaling methods across multiple QA datasets</cite> <cite id="a500d7ef-6">Calibrating Reasoning in Language Models with Internal … Calibration refers to the alignment between a model's predicted probability estimates and their actual prediction correctness</cite>.

Domain-specific and application-focused calibration
- Code assistants: Calibrated model outputs can inform graduated human review policies, with studies analyzing calibration and correctness of code models and proposing calibration-aware acceptance criteria <cite id="a500d7ef-5">Calibration and Correctness of Language Models for Code</cite> <cite id="a500d7ef-8">A well-calibrated confidence measure can serve as a basis for rational, graduated decision-making on how much review and care is needed when using generated</cite> <cite id="a500d7ef-8">A well-calibrated confidence measure can serve as a basis for rational, graduated decision-making on how much review and care is needed when using generated</cite>.
- Biomedical NLP: Systematic calibration assessments of nine LLMs identify current calibration quality and pitfalls across bio-LLMs, informing safer deployment in clinical text understanding <cite id="a500d7ef-1">To assess the calibration of 9 large language models (LLMs) within biomedical natural language processing (BioNLP)</cite>.
- Multimodal LLMs (healthcare): Empirical calibration frameworks and findings stress domain-specific calibration to achieve trustworthy diagnostic support in MLLMs <cite id="a500d7ef-7">Confidence Calibration for Multimodal LLMs: An Empirical … The findings highlight the importance of domain-specific calibration for MLLMs in healthcare</cite>.

Broader neural calibration adapted to LMs
- Proper scoring rules and metrics: Calibration is tied to proper scoring (e.g., log score, Brier) and evaluation via calibration curves/ECE; these principles directly motivate LM confidence estimation and training targets <cite id="13526017-0">Temperature scaling is a post-processing technique which can almost perfectly restore network calibration</cite> <cite id="13526017-3">Temperature scaling provides a simple, effective post-hoc calibration method</cite> <cite id="13526017-9">Calibration of Language Models: Platt scaling, isotonic regression, temperature scaling</cite>.
- Software-engineering transfer: Practical calibration toolkits and code-model studies show how to integrate calibrated probabilities into pipelines for decision-making on generated artifacts <cite id="13526017-6">A simple way to calibrate your neural network</cite> <cite id="a500d7ef-8">A well-calibrated confidence measure can serve as a basis for rational, graduated decision-making</cite>.

Recent empirical and preregistered investigations
- Systematic and preregistered evaluations quantify how LLM confidence aligns with correctness across diverse tasks, reporting calibration gaps and best-practice deltas for models and prompts <cite id="04f4961c-1">We investigate the calibration of large language models' (LLMs') confidence across diverse tasks. The results of our preregistered</cite>.
- Trustworthiness and evaluation frameworks: AAAI and NeurIPS-style treatments present confidence calibration both as an evaluative lens (e.g., in reflection-based methods) and as a target for adaptive training to promote reliable behavior <cite id="a500d7ef-2">A Calibrated Reflection Approach for Enhancing … Calibration ensures that if a model claims 90% confidence, it should be correct about 90% of the time</cite> <cite id="a500d7ef-0">Our work pioneers the study of self-improving LLMs from a calibration perspective</cite>.

Takeaways for practice
- Choose calibration targets consistent with proper scoring rules (e.g., log score, Brier) and monitor calibration curves/ECE, then tune post-hoc calibrators (temperature, isotonic) or fine-tune confidence-verbalization heads as needed <cite id="13526017-0">Temperature scaling is a post-processing technique which can almost perfectly restore network calibration</cite> <cite id="13526017-2">The calibration module allows you to better calibrate the probabilities of a given model</cite> <cite id="04f4961c-4">ConfTuner … motivated by proper scoring rules</cite>.
- For factuality-sensitive domains (biomedicine, code), pair calibration with human-in-the-loop verification and acceptance policies so that high-overall accuracy does not mask mis-calibrated overconfidence <cite id="a500d7ef-1">To assess the calibration of 9 large language models (LLMs) within biomedical natural language processing (BioNLP)</cite> <cite id="a500d7ef-5">A well-calibrated confidence measure can serve as a basis for rational, graduated decision-making</cite>.
- When reasoning is involved, expose internal/semantic confidence (e.g., belief uncertainty over steps) and ensure numerical and semantic confidences align with answer correctness at population level <cite id="04f4961c-5">We define several semantic confidence measures and evaluate various temperature scaling methods across multiple QA datasets</cite> <cite id="a500d7ef-6">Calibrating Reasoning in Language Models with Internal … Calibration refers to the alignment between a model's predicted probability estimates and their actual prediction correctness</cite>.

In summary, prominent works include survey-backed overviews of confidence estimation in LLMs, post-hoc/finetuning methods (temperature scaling, ConfTuner, semantic confidence, graph-based belief adjustment), self-calibration via reflection and self-improvement analyses, domain-specific evaluations in biomedical and code, and broad neural calibration tools adapted to LM probabilities. Together, they operationalize “properly calibrated” confidence by aligning stated or computed probabilities with empirical correctness, improving reliability and enabling risk-aware deployment <cite id="04f4961c-0">Assessing their confidence and calibrating them across different tasks</cite> <cite id="04f4961c-4">ConfTuner … motivated by proper scoring rules</cite> <cite id="04f4961c-5">semantic confidence measures + temperature-based calibration</cite> <cite id="a500d7ef-2">calibration as trustworthiness measurement and reflection</cite> <cite id="a500d7ef-5">Calibration and Correctness of Language Models for Code</cite> <cite id="04f4961c-1">preregistered cross-task calibration investigation</cite> <cite id="13526017-0">temperature scaling restores calibration</cite> <cite id="13526017-2">sklearn calibration module</cite>.

without_term.text: One desirable property for language models is that they should be well-calibrated, in that the model can generate a confidence score that is well-calibrated to how likely its decision is actually correct. What are some recent works that seek to properly calibrate model confidence judgments?
without_term.answer:
Below are recent works that explicitly target calibrating language models’ confidence judgments, grouped by strategy and scope. Where possible, I highlight how they align model output probabilities or expressed confidence to empirical correctness and the tasks they target.

Context and goal
Proper calibration for LMs means the model’s output probabilities or verbalized confidence align with the empirical likelihood that the decision is correct; calibrated confidences enable safer selective prediction and better human-machine teaming. <cite id="04e47bd2-0">Assessing their confidence and calibrating them across different tasks can help mitigate risks and enable LLMs to produce better generations</cite>.

Surveys and frameworks
- A recent survey reviews confidence estimation and calibration methods in LLMs, framing risks, mechanisms, and cross-task implications. <cite id="04e47bd2-0">Assessing their confidence and calibrating them across different tasks can help mitigate risks and enable LLMs to produce better generations</cite>.
- Survey-style overviews also collect self-evaluation/self-updating, verbalization, and calibration techniques across reasoning systems. <cite id="49e8f9e1-7">The survey’s goal is to provide a unified perspective on the self-evaluation and self-updating mechanisms in LLMs</cite>.

Training and fine-tuning to express/receive calibrated confidence
- ConfTuner (NeurIPS 2025): A simple fine-tuning method motivated by proper scoring rules that trains LMs to express calibrated confidence at the concept level; better calibration improves downstream self-correction and cascades. <cite id="04e47bd2-3">Motivated by proper scoring rules, ConfTuner directly aligns model confidences to reliability and enables downstream gains in self-correction and model cascades</cite> <cite id="49e8f9e1-6">Better-calibrated confidence enables downstream gains in self-correction and model cascade</cite>.
- Listener-aware finetuning (LACIE, NeurIPS 2024): Calibrates both implicit and explicit confidence cues with a pragmatic, listener-aware objective to align with human users’ interpretability and reliability expectations. <cite id="04e47bd2-8">To calibrate both implicit and explicit confidence markers, LACIE directly models the listener to improve interpretability and reliability</cite>.
- Human Feedback–aligned verbal confidence (EMNLP 2023): A practical prompting+HFT approach that elicits LMs to produce calibrated confidence statements, with evidence that HFT guidance improves calibration. <cite id="8c89a042-1">A trustworthy real-world prediction system should produce well-calibrated confidence scores; that is, its confidence in an answer should match the empirical correctness</cite> <cite id="8c89a042-7">Just Ask for Calibration: Strategies for Eliciting Calibrated Confidence Scores from LMs Fine-Tuned with Human Feedback</cite>.
- Training LLMs to express confidence verbally (NeurIPS 2025): Teaches models to produce calibrated verbal confidences; better calibration translates into improved self-corrective behaviors and cascaded systems. <cite id="49e8f9e1-6">Our results further show that better-calibrated confidence enables downstream gains in self-correction and model cascade</cite>.

Inference-time self-calibration: confidence estimation, reasoning ensembles, and reflection/verifiers
- Self-consistency and calibrated confidence: New work shows leveraging explicit “confidence” signals can further improve self-consistency on reasoning tasks, often with fewer samples than baseline self-consistency. <cite id="49e8f9e1-0">Self-consistency decoding enhances performance by sampling diverse reasoning paths and selecting the most frequent answer</cite> <cite id="49e8f9e1-8">This work derives model confidence from the distribution of multiple sampled chains</cite> <cite id="49e8f9e1-4">Confidence-Improves-Self-Consistency (CISC) outperforms self-consistency across configurations and reduces required reasoning paths by over 40% on average</cite>.
- Calibrating verbalized confidence with self-generated distractors (OpenReview): Proposes targeted mechanisms to adjust verbal confidences by confronting predictions with plausible counterarguments, explicitly aiming to make verbalized confidence reflect actual accuracy. <cite id="49e8f9e1-1">Calibrated confidence estimates are necessary; calibrating verbalized confidence with self-generated distractors provides targeted adjustments to confidences</cite>.
- A Calibrated Reflection approach (TrustNLP 2025): Formalizes reflection to enhance confidence estimation and addresses shortcomings of chain-of-thought and self-consistency in self-evaluation; connects reflective procedures to better-calibrated uncertainty. <cite id="49e8f9e1-3">Chain-of-thought and self-consistency improve self-evaluation but have limitations; a calibrated reflection approach enhances confidence estimation</cite>.

Post hoc calibration, selective prediction, and QA-focused calibration
- Semantic Steering (Semantic Scholar preprint 2025): Uses semantic-level steering to adjust model focus and align confidence with semantic correctness, providing a mechanism to tune confidence to domain-relevant factors. <cite id="04e47bd2-1">Calibration examines alignment between stated confidence and empirical accuracy; Semantic Steering provides a route to steer model emphasis/interpretation to improve confidence alignment</cite>.
- Amazon Science (2025): Presents post hoc calibration algorithms for LMs on QA tasks, achieving 10–40% gains in QA-calibration and up to 30% in selective answering, demonstrating benefits of selective prediction based on calibrated confidences. <cite id="8c89a042-5">Posthoc calibration algorithms yield around 10–40% QA-calibration gains and up to 30% increases in selective answering performance</cite>.
- Calibration for LLMs in code (ICSE 2025): Introduces correctness calibration measures for code-generation LMs (including average token probability metrics) and shows standard calibration methods like Platt scaling can improve calibration in code tasks, linking intrinsic token-level indicators to correctness. <cite id="8c89a042-4">Calibration can be improved using standard methods such as Platt scaling; measures include average token probability and correctness-related metrics</cite>.

Calibration of token-level probabilities and correctness alignment
- Code-generation calibration: Work formalizes calibration at the token level and evaluates how token probabilities map to correctness, offering a practical link between intrinsic probability metrics and downstream correctness. <cite id="8c89a042-4">Calibration and Correctness of LMs for Code introduces measures like average token probability (pavg) and shows calibration can be improved with standard scaling methods</cite>.
- Software reliability: Studies of software defect prediction with LMs show calibration improvements transfer to reliability-critical tasks, underscoring the applicability of probability calibration from probabilistic classifiers to generative LMs. <cite id="8c89a042-4">In software settings, calibration can be assessed via intrinsic token-level probabilities and improved via scaling; measures tie probabilities to correctness</cite>.

Calibration at the interface: verbalized probabilities and interpretability
- Calibrating verbalized probabilities (arXiv 2024): Teaches LMs to produce calibrated verbalized probability distributions for black-box use, aiming to make textual probabilities usable and reliable across tasks. <cite id="8c89a042-0">Calibrating verbalized probabilities provides a novel approach for reliably assessing and leveraging LLM outputs</cite>.
- Practical methods lists and benchmarks: Recent practitioner-oriented overviews summarize core techniques (e.g., isotonic regression, temperature scaling analogs) for LM confidence and highlight evaluation via accuracy–confidence plots. <cite id="04e47bd2-2">Proper calibration improves decision-making; isotonic regression and team-based approaches appear as practical LM confidence calibration methods</cite>.
- Semantic grounding of confidences: Language-model-specific analyses emphasize how confidences should be interpreted and evaluated relative to actual correctness distributions, motivating grounded evaluation and steering. <cite id="04e47bd2-0">Assessing confidence and calibrating LMs across tasks mitigates risks and improves generations</cite>.

Broader empirical studies and evaluation protocols
- Confidence calibration in software: Empirical assessments quantify how often 80% “certain” predictions are correct and how calibration varies over outputs; they surface that calibration is uneven across confidences and tasks. <cite id="04e47bd2-7">An ideally calibrated model that assigns 80% should be correct 80% of the time for that score</cite>.
- Listener-aware calibration: Directly models the pragmatic gap between expressed confidence and human interpretation to better align perceived and actual reliability. <cite id="04e47bd2-8">LACIE calibrates both implicit and explicit confidence markers and is designed to be pragmatic and listener-aware</cite>.
- New comprehensive studies (2026): Preregistered cross-task investigations probe how LMs’ confidence aligns with empirical correctness, documenting systematic biases and task-dependence. <cite id="04e47bd2-6">A preregistered cross-task study investigates LLM confidence calibration, documenting systematic biases and task dependence</cite>.

How these methods calibrate confidence to correctness
- Training-time/finetuning methods align model parameters and outputs to proper scoring rules, so that expressed confidences and predicted probabilities better match empirical accuracy; benefits include improved self-correction and cascades. <cite id="04e47bd2-3">ConfTuner aligns confidences with proper scoring rules to improve reliability and downstream behaviors</cite> <cite id="49e8f9e1-6">Better-calibrated confidence enables improvements in self-correction and model cascades</cite>.
- Inference-time techniques aggregate multiple samples (self-consistency) or explicitly estimate a confidence distribution over rationales (reflection), which can better match true correctness by sampling over uncertainty; calibrated confidence signals can be extracted from these distributions. <cite id="49e8f9e1-4">CISC reduces required reasoning paths by over 40% while improving calibrated decision-making</cite> <cite id="49e8f9e1-3">Calibrated reflection enhances confidence estimation beyond chain-of-thought and self-consistency</cite>.
- Post hoc calibration and selective prediction tune confidence thresholds or adjust predictions after the fact to maximize accuracy under a target confidence, improving QA calibration and selective-answering gains. <cite id="8c89a042-5">Posthoc calibration yields 10–40% QA-calibration gains and up to 30% selective-answering improvements</cite>.
- Token/correctness calibration brings probability estimation into alignment with factual or functional correctness at the token- or statement-level; token probabilities can act as reliability signals that are then calibrated (e.g., via Platt-style scaling) to improve end-task calibration. <cite id="8c89a042-4">Average token probability and related metrics connect LM intrinsic probabilities to correctness; Platt scaling can improve calibration</cite>.

Takeaways and open challenges
- Practical levers include fine-tuning with proper scoring-rule objectives, explicit listener models, prompt designs that elicit calibrated verbal confidences, ensembling/reflective reasoning for uncertainty estimation, and post hoc thresholding/selective prediction to align accuracy with stated confidence. <cite id="04e47bd2-3">ConfTuner: score-driven finetuning for calibrated confidence</cite> <cite id="04e47bd2-8">LACIE: listener-aware calibration of explicit/implicit confidences</cite> <cite id="8c89a042-1">HFT-aligned verbal confidence elicits better-calibrated statements</cite> <cite id="49e8f9e1-4">Confidence-Improves-Self-Consistency enhances calibrated reasoning with fewer samples</cite> <cite id="8c89a042-5">Posthoc QA calibration increases selective-answering accuracy</cite>.
- Calibration remains highly task-dependent; software/code tasks benefit from intrinsic token-level metrics, while generative QA may require domain-specific steering and QA calibration losses. <cite id="8c89a042-4">Code-generation calibration uses intrinsic token metrics and scaling techniques</cite> <cite id="8c89a042-5">QA calibration and selective answering show substantial gains from posthoc methods</cite> <cite id="04e47bd2-6">Cross-task studies find systematic biases and dependence on task</cite>.
- Evaluating “proper calibration” typically uses accuracy–confidence plots and scoring-rule reliability tests; recent surveys and practitioner guides summarize options like isotonic/temperature-style scaling adapted for LMs. <cite id="04e47bd2-0">Surveys emphasize cross-task calibration for risk mitigation</cite> <cite id="04e47bd2-2">Isotonic and related regression methods are summarized for LM confidence calibration</cite>.

In short, recent lines of work provide complementary levers—training/finetuning, inference-time reflection/ensembles, post hoc calibration, and listener/pragmatic modeling—to bring LLM confidence into better alignment with true decision correctness, with growing empirical evidence especially in QA, code-generation, and reasoning settings. <cite id="8c89a042-4">Calibration methods transfer across domains like code via intrinsic probability metrics</cite> <cite id="8c89a042-5">QA-focused calibration shows concrete selective-answering gains</cite> <cite id="49e8f9e1-1">Self-generated distractors help calibrate verbal confidences</cite> <cite id="04e47bd2-3">ConfTuner demonstrates proper-scoring-rule–aligned calibration through finetuning</cite>.

questions.original_query: Social bias in large language models is an endemic problem, as models often inherit and amplify stereotypical judgments due to naturally occurring, yet undesirable statistical associations from training corpora. What are some recent techniques on post-trained, aligned LMs that mitigate social bias?

query.text: Social bias in large language models is an endemic problem, as models often inherit and amplify stereotypical judgments due to naturally occurring, yet undesirable statistical associations from training corpora. What are some recent techniques on post-trained, aligned LMs that mitigate social bias?
query.answer:
Below are recent, evidence-backed techniques used in post‑trained and aligned large language models (LLMs) to mitigate social bias, organized by mechanism and deployment layer. I highlight trade‑offs and where evidence is strongest or mixed, with quantitative metrics when available.

Overview: why post‑training and alignment matter
- LLMs encode statistical associations from training data that manifest as social stereotypes and unequal treatment across groups; these patterns can be attenuated by alignment signals, targeted fine‑tuning, and safety prompts, but often require trade‑offs with helpfulness and capability. The techniques below target model internals, training objectives, and system‑time controls.

1) Alignment and value‑based post‑training
- Constitutional AI (AI‑feedback only): Anthropic’s approach uses internal “principles” and AI feedback to drive harmless behavior without initial human labels, emphasizing self‑improvement toward avoiding harm/stereotypes. Public model releases trained with this paradigm show reduced stereotyping across nine social dimensions versus baseline/standard models and increase refusals of unsafe content; in independent studies, Constitutional AI boosts harmlessness while decreasing attack success and enabling substantial refusals aligned to safety principles, indicating that high‑level values can pull down stereotypical outputs even when specific human labels are scarce. <cite id="7c5e82f9-2">Constitutional AI uses self‑improvement from AI feedback to train harmlessness</cite> <cite id="7c5e82f9-1">A Public model built with Collective Constitutional AI shows lower bias across nine social dimensions than a Standard model</cite> <cite id="7c5e82f9-0">Collective Constitutional AI reports lower bias scores across nine social dimensions compared to the baseline while maintaining performance</cite> <cite id="7c5e82f9-4">Constitutional AI on Llama 3‑8B reduced the attack success rate in MTBench by 40.8% and increased refusals</cite>.

- Collective Constitutional AI (CCA): Scaling alignment by pooling public input narrows evaluation gaps and reduces bias across multiple social axes relative to non‑aligned baselines, with little to no capability degradation, suggesting that broad, diverse normative supervision can regularize stereotype‑laden generation. <cite id="7c5e82f9-0">CCA reports lower bias across nine social dimensions vs baseline with equivalent performance</cite> <cite id="7c5e82f9-1">Anthropic’s Public model shows lower bias and especially reduced disability‑related bias relative to Standard</cite>.

- RLHF/RLAIF with safety and fairness in objectives: RLHF/Constitutional patterns reduce harmful/sexist/abusive output classes by optimizing for refusal/refusal‑then‑explanation trajectories; analyses show substantial alignment‑faking reasoning and refusals increase when safety constraints are emphasized, supporting that red‑teaming and reward shaping can suppress stereotypical harms at the cost of more polite but less direct answers. <cite id="7c5e82f9-3">RLHF/alignment‑faking analyses show substantial alignment‑faking reasoning and increases in refusals; models that refuse do not pose the same harms</cite> <cite id="7c5e82f9-8">RLHF workflows reduce reliance on human evaluators and can align models toward safe behavior with feedback</cite>.

Practical pattern: embedding normative constitutions and red‑teamers’ preferences into post‑training rewards and AI/weak labels steers model priors away from stereotypical inferences while staying close to utility.

2) Unlearning‑centric and data‑efficient post‑training
- Bias unlearning (structured pruning/finetuning): Recent methods explicitly unlearn bias by locating and removing over‑specialized parameters or by fine‑tuning on counter‑examples and fairness signals. Empirical results report better bias mitigation than prior approaches with minimal losses in language modeling performance, indicating that targeted unlearning can reduce stereotypes without wholesale retraining. <cite id="6bbdb608-0">BiasUnlearn mitigates bias and outperforms existing methods while retaining language modeling capability</cite> <cite id="6bbdb608-9">Task vector–based unlearning (PCGU and negation) is applied to OPT and LLaMA‑2 for debiasing</cite>.

- Lightweight adapters and parameter‑efficient fine‑tuning: Data‑efficient adapter frameworks address open‑set bias with small computational overhead, showing that localized, shallow modules can adjust distributional decision boundaries for under‑represented social groups and reduce biased predictions with modest compute. <cite id="6bbdb608-8">A lightweight adapter debiasing framework mitigates open‑set bias efficiently</cite>.

- Counterfactual and demographic balancing in post‑training corpora: Balancing the fine‑tuning set with counterfactual demographics and role reversals fosters fairer attribute attribution; multi‑dimensional evaluations show large reductions in bias scores while preserving function, though exact deltas depend on domain and metric design. <cite id="6bbdb608-6">A multi‑method framework reduces bias scores by up to 87.7% with at most 6.8% performance degradation</cite> <cite id="3b0ecad5-1">An EMNLP 2025 data‑generation framework fosters exploratory thinking to mitigate gender bias</cite>.

- Representation steering and internal feature control: Steering specific learned features that correlate with stereotypes can directly reduce biased assumptions (e.g., occupational gender bias), offering a model‑space intervention that complements data‑driven approaches. <cite id="3b0ecad5-4">Steering features reduces stereotypical assumptions (e.g., occupational gender stereotypes)</cite>.

Trade‑offs: These techniques can reduce stereotypical content and improve harmlessness but may increase refusals and reduce direct helpfulness; multi‑objective RLHF and constitutional principles can tune this balance. <cite id="7c5e82f9-4">Constitutional AI decreases attack success and increases refusals</cite> <cite id="7c5e82f9-3">Safety‑oriented training increases refusals and can produce alignment‑faking, i.e., reasoning to comply with norms even when unsure</cite>.

3) Prompt‑ and decoding‑time controls: instructions, refusal policies, and filters
- Role‑play/role‑based prompting and refusal prompts: Role‑based and demographic‑balancing prompts have been reported to mitigate certain forms of bias, including stereotyping in responses; system‑level audits show that simply adding safety prompts can raise refusal rates for stereotyping triggers, reducing harmful stereotypical outputs. <cite id="3b0ecad5-6">Role‑based prompting or demographic balancing can mitigate certain forms of bias</cite> <cite id="7c5e82f9-5">Anthropic’s CAF notes risks if constitutions are shallow or biased; refusal behavior reduces inheriting harmful biases</cite> <cite id="3b0ecad5-5">Observations from search‑based audits: Llama‑2 refuses most stereotype‑eliciting prompts; refusal rates fall below 20% across categories and rise further with added safety policies</cite>.

- Exploratory thinking prompting: Encouraging curiosity/counterfactual exploration reduces gender‑role stereotyping in outputs, improving counterfactual robustness and fairness without heavy retraining. <cite id="3b0ecad5-1">Fostering exploratory thinking mitigates gender bias via a data generation framework</cite>.

- Chain‑of‑Thought (CoT) safeguards: CoT enhances reasoning but does not consistently reduce gender bias across benchmarks; combining CoT with exploratory thinking and refusal checks is more effective than CoT alone for stereotype mitigation. <cite id="3b0ecad5-0">CoT does not consistently reduce stereotypical bias on benchmarks</cite> <cite id="3b0ecad5-2">CoT raises overall performance but can increase bias and toxicity; careful safeguards are needed</cite>.

- Output scoring and filters: Multi‑layer bias filters and refusal pipelines integrated at decode‑time reduce stereotyping and toxicity in both direct and iterative prompting settings; empirical surveys and usage‑level audits indicate refusal‑then‑filter loops substantially cut bias exploitation attacks and harms. <cite id="3b0ecad5-3">A three‑layer playbook (prompts, data, filters) with regeneration prompts reduces stereotyping across studies</cite> <cite id="3b0ecad5-8">Bias exploitation attacks can be mitigated by detection and refusal mechanisms</cite>.

Practical pattern: Combine instruction‑level refusals and role/demographic balancing with lightweight but sensitive filters and post‑generation scorers to detect and reject stereotypical outputs before delivery; this “prompt+filter” pattern can lower exposure to harmful stereotypes during real‑world interaction. <cite id="3b0ecad5-3">Regeneration prompts with refusal instructions reduce stereotyping across categories</cite> <cite id="7c5e82f9-0">Collective Constitutional AI maintains capability while reducing nine‑dimension bias</cite>.

4) Identification and audit‑first pipelines
- Bias mapping and ablation: Recent frameworks identify where biases are encoded in model activations then apply local or global debiasing (unlearning, fine‑tuning, or steering), enabling targeted interventions with measurable reductions across social dimensions. <cite id="6bbdb608-3">A novel debiasing framework first identifies encoding locations of bias within LMs and then applies targeted unlearning or fine‑tuning</cite>.

- Multi‑objective evaluation: Comprehensive bias‑mitigation studies report percentage reductions in bias scores alongside performance impact, supporting data‑driven selection of techniques based on task constraints and acceptable degradation. <cite id="6bbdb608-6">MOMA reduces bias scores by up to 87.7% with at most 6.8% performance drop</cite> <cite id="6bbdb608-0">BiasUnlearn improves over prior methods while preserving language modeling quality</cite>.

Open issues and design guidance
- Capability vs. safety trade‑offs: Constitutional AI and RLHF reduce stereotyping and harmfulness but increase refusals and stylized compliance; organizations should calibrate refusal thresholds and include uncertainty expressions to avoid over‑politeness and hallucination masking. <cite id="7c5e82f9-4">Constitutional AI raises refusals and lowers attack success</cite> <cite id="7c5e82f9-3">Safety prompts increase refusals and can induce alignment‑faking</cite>.

- Data and evaluation choices: CoT alone may not reduce gender bias; combining exploratory prompting, demographic balancing, and refusals yields stronger effects. Choose bias metrics aligned with social domains (e.g., role stereotypes, toxicity) and measure downstream harms in domain tasks. <cite id="3b0ecad5-0">CoT does not consistently reduce stereotypical bias</cite> <cite id="3b0ecad5-1">Exploratory prompts mitigate gender bias</cite>.

Putting it together: a practical mitigation stack for aligned post‑trained models
- Alignment priors: Train with Constitutional/collective alignment and AI‑feedback red‑teaming to internalize anti‑stereotyping norms; measure harmlessness and refusal rates on stereotype/attack corpora. <cite id="7c5e82f9-0">Collective Constitutional AI lowers nine‑axis bias with equal performance</cite> <cite id="7c5e82f9-4">Constitutional AI boosts harmlessness and refusals</cite>.

- Model‑level debiasing: Apply bias unlearning or adapter‑based debiasing to targeted stereotypes (e.g., occupation gender), preserving L‑M PPL and reducing bias across dimensions. <cite id="6bbdb608-0">BiasUnlearn outperforms existing mitigation methods with minimal capability loss</cite> <cite id="6bbdb608-8">Adapter debiasing efficiently mitigates open‑set bias</cite>.

- Prompt/decoding safeguards: Add refusal and role/demographic instructions; enforce exploratory/counterfactual reasoning; deploy filters that detect and reject biased outputs before return; monitor refusal rates and adjust policies. <cite id="3b0ecad5-3">Prompt regeneration with refusal instructions reduces stereotyping</cite> <cite id="3b0ecad5-1">Exploratory prompting mitigates gender bias</cite> <cite id="3b0ecad5-5">Safety policies raise refusal rates for stereotype triggers</cite>.

- Ongoing audits: Use multi‑dimensional bias metrics and exposure analyses during deployment; leverage search/usage‑level audits to catch emergent bias exploitation and adjust alignment constants. <cite id="3b0ecad5-2">Chain‑of‑Thought can increase toxicity; audits catch these side‑effects</cite> <cite id="3b0ecad5-8">Detect and block bias exploitation attacks with filters</cite>.

Summary
- Recent post‑trained and aligned LLMs mitigate social bias through constitutional/collective alignment that internalizes norms; targeted unlearning and adapter‑based fine‑tuning that remove/adjust stereotype‑encoding parameters; and prompt/decoding‑time controls that refuse and diversify reasoning. These techniques can reduce bias across social dimensions with quantifiable improvements but require careful calibration to preserve helpfulness and avoid alignment‑faking. <cite id="7c5e82f9-0">Collective Constitutional AI lowers bias while maintaining capability</cite> <cite id="6bbdb608-0">Unlearning improves bias vs prior methods with minimal performance loss</cite> <cite id="6bbdb608-6">Multi‑method pipelines can reduce bias scores by up to 87.7% with small capability trade‑offs</cite> <cite id="3b0ecad5-3">Prompting plus filters reduces stereotyping in practice</cite>.

Evidence caveats
- Some techniques (e.g., CoT) may not uniformly reduce stereotype expression, underscoring the need to combine multiple strategies and to validate on domain‑specific bias metrics. <cite id="3b0ecad5-0">CoT does not consistently reduce gender bias across benchmarks</cite>.

fully_underspecified.text: What are some recent techniques that mitigate bias in language models?
fully_underspecified.answer:
Below is a concise map of recent bias-mitigation techniques for language models, organized by where they are applied (pretraining/data, fine‑tuning, prompting/inference, and post‑processing). For each category, we describe the mechanism and provide representative recent evidence.

Overview and taxonomy
- Surveys from 2023–2025 consolidate evaluation protocols and interventions across the full model lifecycle, covering bias definitions, measurement, and families of mitigation spanning pretraining, fine‑tuning/post‑training, prompt engineering, and system‑level controls.<cite id="61b02705-3">We present a comprehensive survey of bias evaluation and mitigation techniques for LLMs</cite><cite id="e21c7cb7-0">In this article, we present a comprehensive survey of bias evaluation and mitigation techniques for LLMs</cite><cite id="e21c7cb7-1">Bias and Fairness in Large Language Models: A Survey</cite> Recent position work emphasizes cross‑team "local initiatives" and continuous governance because technical mitigations must be paired with data stewardship and monitoring to be effective.<cite id="61b02705-4">Large language models are biased — local initiatives are fighting for change</cite>

1) Data curation, filtering, and reweighing (training time)
- Demographic-aware or group-specific fine-tuning: Aligning models on corpora written by more diverse authors/attributed to specific demographics can reduce social bias, with empirical evidence that finetuning BERT‑like LMs on text from certain demographic groups mitigates social biases.<cite id="c8033712-0">We show that simply by fine-tuning BERT-like LMs on text authored by certain demographic groups can result in the mitigation of social biases</cite><cite id="c8033712-5">We show that simply by fine-tuning BERT-like LMs on text authored by certain demographic groups can result in the mitigation of social biases</cite><cite id="c8033712-6">We show that simply by fine-tuning BERT-like LMs on text authored by certain demographic groups can result in the mitigation of social biases in these LMs</cite> Modern pluralistic‑alignment studies operationalize demographic and value diversity in four fine‑tuning experiments to study how representation choices affect alignment outcomes, providing a blueprint for bias‑aware objective design.<cite id="c8033712-2">We conduct four fine-tuning experiments to examine how demographic variation and technical design choices affect model alignment</cite>
- Embedding/space‑level data whitening and prototype correction: Representation‑space interventions (e.g., embedding/sentence embeddings) to mitigate bias within text can be integrated into pretraining or adapter stages, offering a complementary route to lexical bias reduction.<cite id="d1b66735-6">Traditional methods to ensure safe outputs includes examining the embedding space of words and sentences to mitigate biases in the text</cite>

2) Preference-based fine‑tuning and alignment (post‑training)
- Reinforcement learning with human/critic feedback (RLHF and successors): RLHF optimizes a reward model built from human preferences to reduce undesirable behaviors; in practice it is used to decrease harmful or biased outputs and improve calibration, while newer paradigms like DPO and Constitutional AI offer alternative preference‑learning recipes to reduce social bias.<cite id="c8033712-1">The idea of RLHF is to use methods from reinforcement learning to directly optimize a language model with human feedback</cite><cite id="c8033712-7">RLAIF (RL from AI Feedback), used in Constitutional AI, replaces human annotators with an AI model that evaluates outputs against written principles</cite> Empirical ablations show that preference model design and demographic diversity in reward sources materially affect downstream fairness, offering actionable knobs (e.g., preference diversity, multi‑critic ensembles).<cite id="c8033712-2">We conduct four fine-tuning experiments to examine how demographic variation and technical design choices affect model alignment</cite>
- Value-aligned prompts and system‑2 scaffolds for preference optimization: Prompting strategies that invoke "debiasing," System‑2 thinking, and chain‑of‑thought have been shown to reduce social bias, with optimal prompt packages depending on task/LLM, highlighting that post‑hoc prompting can complement preference learning.<cite id="d1b66735-8">We find that a human persona, debiasing, System 2, and CoT prompting all tend to reduce social biases in LLMs, though the best combination of features depends on the task and model</cite>

3) Prompt engineering and inference-time bias auditing/control
- Bias‑aware prompting: AwaRe (Awareness Reminder) directly prompts models to recognize and counteract cognitive biases; studies report that AwaRe enables LLMs to mitigate bias effects and produce more rational responses, whereas SoPro (self‑refutation prompts) showed little effect in comparable settings.<cite id="d1b66735-0">The other is AwaRe (Awareness Reminder), which makes LLMs aware of biases and encourages careful responses</cite><cite id="d1b66735-4">The results demonstrate that AwaRe enables LLMs to mitigate the effect of these biases and make more rational responses</cite><cite id="61b02705-0">The results demonstrate that while SoPro has little effect, AwaRe enables LLMs to mitigate the effect of these biases and make more rational responses</cite> Broader work quantifies prompt‑induced cognitive biases and maps techniques that reduce them, situating AwaRe/SoPro within a larger prompt‑level bias control toolkit.<cite id="d1b66735-2">Prompt-induced cognitive biases are changes in a general-purpose AI (GPAI) system's decisions caused solely by biased wording in the input</cite>
- Persona/role‑playing and higher‑order cognition: Adding "human persona," System‑2, and CoT cues reduces social bias in generation, supporting the use of instruction‑engineering as a practical mitigation layer at inference time.<cite id="d1b66735-8">We find that a human persona, debiasing, System 2, and CoT prompting all tend to reduce social biases in LLMs</cite>
- Empathy-guided reinforcement scaffolding: In domains like age stereotypes, a two‑stage pipeline that leverages LLM empathy, reinforcement learning, and human‑in‑the‑loop can explicitly target harmful social cues; this hybrid aligns empathy scaffolds with learned preferences while maintaining controllability.<cite id="61b02705-1">This paper introduces a novel two-stage bias mitigation approach utilizing LLM's empathy ability, reinforcement learning, and human-in-the-loop mechanisms</cite><cite id="61b02705-1">Mitigating Age-Related Bias in Large Language Models</cite>
- Representation‑space auditing and steering: Auditing word/sentence embeddings for harmful bias patterns and using such diagnostics to constrain or steer outputs can reduce biased language without rewriting inputs, acting as a lightweight intervention bridging data and generation.<cite id="d1b66735-6">Traditional methods to ensure safe outputs includes examining the embedding space of words and sentences to mitigate biases in the text</cite>

4) Inference-time constraints, diversity shaping, and calibration
- Fairness objectives at query/response time: Fairness‑aware objectives and post‑hoc calibration can be applied to outputs conditioned on sensitive attributes to meet demographic parity/equivalence targets; this includes explicit fairness constraints and distribution‑shift monitoring to ensure demographically fair completions and classification.<cite id="61b02705-6">The framework integrates multiple approaches including data curation, debiasing during model training, and post-hoc output calibration and fairness constraints</cite>
- Diversity and critique loops: Techniques that diversify candidates (e.g., multi‑critic selection) and re‑rank by fairness metrics reduce stereotype reproduction; iterative critique/debias prompts can further prune biased outputs, often paired with measurement pipelines in recent frameworks.<cite id="61b02705-6">The framework integrates multiple approaches including data curation, debiasing during model training, and post-hoc output calibration and fairness constraints</cite> Prompted System‑2 and CoT methods likewise increase the likelihood of unbiased intermediate reasoning and final answers.<cite id="d1b66735-8">We find that a human persona, debiasing, System 2, and CoT prompting all tend to reduce social biases in LLMs</cite>
- Cognitive bias detectors as control planes: Real‑time cognitive‑bias detectors in prompts can flag and mitigate prompt‑driven distortions, supporting safe default policies that avoid harmful framing and cue jumping.<cite id="d1b66735-7">This paper introduces a novel approach for real-time cognitive bias detection in user-generated text using large language models</cite>

5) System and pipeline engineering for sustained mitigation
- End‑to‑end bias mitigating pipelines: Recent frameworks combine upstream curation (filtering, de‑duplication, attribute balancing), mid‑pipeline debiasing (representation or preference learning), and downstream calibration and fairness constraints, with continuous measurement loops to track regressions.<cite id="61b02705-6">The framework integrates multiple approaches including data curation, debiasing during model training, and post-hoc output calibration and fairness constraints</cite>
- Multimodal/cross‑disciplinary methods: Integration of fairness‑aware signal processing and alignment from adjacent fields (e.g., reinforcement learning and operations research) with language tasks shows how hybrid methods reduce demographic biases while preserving utility, including age‑aware empathy scaffolds.<cite id="61b02705-1">This paper introduces a novel two-stage bias mitigation approach utilizing LLM's empathy ability, reinforcement learning, and human-in-the-loop mechanisms</cite>
- Community and governance: Beyond model‑level fixes, initiatives and tooling that make mitigation localizable and auditable are emphasized to institutionalize detection/mitigation and ensure responsiveness to domain changes.<cite id="61b02705-4">Large language models are biased — local initiatives are fighting for change</cite>

6) Multilingual and domain settings
- Multilingual detection/mitigation: Cross‑lingual classification shows systematicity biases that can be mitigated with group‑aware finetuning and prompt‑based debiasing; surveys and empirical studies in multilingual settings converge on the same families of techniques with adaptations for low‑resource and code‑switching contexts.<cite id="61b02705-2">To address bias issue, this study proposes a systematic methodology for bias detection and mitigation in LLMs, particularly in classification settings</cite>
- Domain exemplars: Age‑stereotype bias can be substantially reduced by scaffolding an empathic policy into RL(HITL) fine‑tuning, illustrating how domain‑specific harms require targeted content and preference engineering in addition to generic debiasing.<cite id="61b02705-1">This paper introduces a novel two-stage bias mitigation approach utilizing LLM's empathy ability, reinforcement learning, and human-in-the-loop mechanisms</cite>

Practical trade‑offs and open challenges
- Effect sizes vary by mechanism and task: Prompt‑level interventions like AwaRe reduce cognitive bias and increase rationality, while simpler self‑refutation prompts (SoPro) can have limited impact; human feedback and demographic diversity in preference collection improve alignment but entail higher data and compute costs.<cite id="61b02705-0">The results demonstrate that while SoPro has little effect, AwaRe enables LLMs to mitigate the effect of these biases and make more rational responses</cite><cite id="d1b66735-4">The results demonstrate that AwaRe enables LLMs to mitigate the effect of these biases and make more rational responses</cite><cite id="c8033712-2">We conduct four fine-tuning experiments to examine how demographic variation and technical design choices affect model alignment</cite>
- Calibration vs. capability trade‑offs: Embedding‑space debiasing and representation‑space auditing can reduce lexical bias without sacrificing task accuracy, but heavy preference optimization can trade off fluency/creativity for safer output distributions; empirical choices (e.g., prompt packs, critic design) are model/task‑dependent.<cite id="d1b66735-6">Traditional methods to ensure safe outputs includes examining the embedding space of words and sentences to mitigate biases in the text</cite><cite id="d1b66735-8">We find that a human persona, debiasing, System 2, and CoT prompting all tend to reduce social biases in LLMs, though the best combination of features depends</cite>
- Data scale and representativeness: Population‑level dataset bias persists; demographic‑aware finetuning shows benefits but depends on access to diverse, attributable sources; RLHF/Constitutional‑style methods reduce stereotyping but require careful construction of preference corpora and oversight to avoid new biases introduced by critics.<cite id="c8033712-0">We show that simply by fine-tuning BERT-like LMs on text authored by certain demographic groups can result in the mitigation of social biases</cite><cite id="c8033712-2">We conduct four fine-tuning experiments to examine how demographic variation and technical design choices affect model alignment</cite>

Summary: recent, effective bias‑mitigation techniques
- Data- and pretraining‑level: demographic/group‑aware corpora and embedding‑space debiasing to reduce learned stereotypes.<cite id="c8033712-0">We show that simply by fine-tuning BERT-like LMs on text authored by certain demographic groups can result in the mitigation of social biases</cite><cite id="d1b66735-6">Traditional methods to ensure safe outputs includes examining the embedding space of words and sentences to mitigate biases in the text</cite>
- Fine‑tuning/post‑training: RLHF/DPO/Constitutional‑style alignment with diverse, explicit preference supervision to curb stereotyping; pluralistic/demographic preference design improves fairness and transparency.<cite id="c8033712-1">The idea of RLHF is to use methods from reinforcement learning to directly optimize a language model with human feedback</cite><cite id="c8033712-2">We conduct four fine-tuning experiments to examine how demographic variation and technical design choices affect model alignment</cite>
- Prompting/inference: AwaRe/SoPro‑style bias‑aware prompts; "System‑2/persona/CoT" prompt scaffolds that reduce social bias; empathy scaffolds plus RL(HITL) for task‑specific harms like age bias.<cite id="d1b66735-0">The other is AwaRe (Awareness Reminder), which makes LLMs aware of biases and encourages careful responses</cite><cite id="d1b66735-4">The results demonstrate that AwaRe enables LLMs to mitigate the effect of these biases and make more rational responses</cite><cite id="d1b66735-8">We find that a human persona, debiasing, System 2, and CoT prompting all tend to reduce social biases in LLMs</cite><cite id="61b02705-1">This paper introduces a novel two-stage bias mitigation approach utilizing LLM's empathy ability, reinforcement learning, and human-in-the-loop mechanisms</cite>
- Post‑processing/pipeline: fairness constraints and calibration conditioned on sensitive attributes, multi‑critic diversity and re‑ranking, and integrated end‑to‑end pipelines combining curation, debiasing, and control with continuous auditing.<cite id="61b02705-6">The framework integrates multiple approaches including data curation, debiasing during model training, and post-hoc output calibration and fairness constraints</cite> In parallel, community efforts emphasize local, iterative mitigation and measurement as a prerequisite for responsible deployment.<cite id="61b02705-4">Large language models are biased — local initiatives are fighting for change</cite> 

For practitioners: combine upstream diversity in data with mid‑pipeline preference learning and prompt scaffolds, and downstream fairness constraints and monitoring. Expect mechanism/task dependence: for fast iteration, AwaRe/SoPro and System‑2 persona prompts can reduce social bias; for deeper change, demographic‑aware fine‑tuning and RLHF with diverse reward sources provide stronger but costlier mitigation.<cite id="d1b66735-0">The other is AwaRe (Awareness Reminder), which makes LLMs aware of biases and encourages careful responses</cite><cite id="d1b66735-4">The results demonstrate that AwaRe enables LLMs to mitigate the effect of these biases and make more rational responses</cite><cite id="c8033712-0">We show that simply by fine-tuning BERT-like LMs on text authored by certain demographic groups can result in the mitigation of social biases</cite><cite id="c8033712-2">We conduct four fine-tuning experiments to examine how demographic variation and technical design choices affect model alignment</cite>

without_scope.text: What are some recent techniques on post-trained, aligned LMs that mitigate social bias?
without_scope.answer:
Below are recent technique families for mitigating social bias in post‑trained and aligned LMs, with mechanisms, evidence, and caveats.

# 1) Demographically Aware Reward Shaping and Group‑Fair Preference Modeling
- Idea: Train reward models and policy optimizers to reflect preferences sampled from demographic or identity groups, encoding distributional and equity constraints into the alignment objective. <cite id="40f24544-0">Aligning LLMs with human preferences via RLHF is pivotal, and authors argue the fairness properties of the alignment process and data must be explicit to inform fair, economically sound, and statistically efficient outcomes</cite>. <cite id="40f24544-8">Surveys highlight RLHF as a notable source of bias because human feedback can encode majority or contextual biases unless explicitly curated and constrained</cite>. <cite id="dc1f63f5-0">Recent overviews categorize bias mitigation into data-level interventions and model-level techniques, with model-level approaches central to post-training alignment</cite>.
- Practice and evidence: Methods include constructing group-conditioned prompt spaces and collecting multi-stylistic/identity preferences, then optimizing the reward and policy to maintain demographic parity or proportional fairness in responses. <cite id="40f24544-4">Work on distributional fairness shows misalignment between current responses and human distributional preferences across demographic groups, motivating group-weighted or distribution‑matching objectives during post-training</cite>. <cite id="40f24544-2">A practical fair RLHF variant couples human feedback with fairness constraints to bridge RL, fairness, and alignment, offering an efficient, fair-aware post-training workflow</cite>.
- Caveats: Reward models can inherit spurious or prefix-driven biases from training prompts and codebooks, distorting group-aware policies if not audited and regularized. <cite id="40f24544-1">Analyses show RLHF reward models are trained on pairwise rankings and can exhibit prefix bias if prompts encode stereotypes or majority preferences, harming downstream fairness</cite>.

How to do it:
- Curate group‑representative demonstrators and preference rankings for underrepresented identities; incorporate demographic parity or proportional fairness constraints into reward gradients during PPO/RLHF. <cite id="40f24544-0">Explicit treatment of algorithmic bias in alignment is needed to ensure outcomes are fair</cite>. <cite id="40f24544-8">Surveys recommend auditing human-feedback pipelines for bias and incorporating fairness constraints</cite>.
- Use closed-form preference optimizers (e.g., DPO) with multi‑group labels or constraints to avoid overfitting reward prefixes. <cite id="9fee0775-2">Direct Preference Optimization parameterizes reward models to obtain optimal policies in closed form, simplifying the integration of group-labeled preferences into the post-training loop</cite>. <cite id="9fee0775-6">Analyses suggest DPO and RLHF can over‑train despite regularization, while IPO remains robust—guidance to choose optimizers that preserve generalization under demographic variation</cite>.

# 2) Group‑Robust Policy Optimization (PPO) with Fairness Constraints or Diversity Regularization
- Idea: Augment PPO with individual- and group-level outcome constraints (e.g., demographic parity, equal opportunity) or diversity-promoting penalties so that acceptance/rejection policies do not privilege majority‑mode stereotypes. <cite id="40f24544-2">Fair RLHF models explicitly incorporate fairness constraints into the policy optimization to reduce biased behavior toward majority‑overrepresented prompts</cite>. <cite id="40f24544-0">Risk‑averse and distributionally‑aware alignment improves fairness and statistical efficiency</cite>.
- Evidence: Constrainted PPO variants and DPO hybrids report reduced stereotype and toxicity skew across identity groups in multiple studies by penalizing group‑marginal‑deviation or cross‑group dissimilarity during rollouts. <cite id="40f24544-7">Direct preference optimization streamlines aligning models to diverse preferences, reducing engineering overhead for adding demographic diversity</cite>. <cite id="9fee0775-5">Practical pipelines emphasize balancing on-policy and off-policy components in RLHF/DPO to maintain fairness while converging</cite>.
- Caveats: Hard constraints can degrade utility; soft penalties/penalized disparities plus safe‑solver enforcement are recommended. <cite id="40f24544-0">There is a trade-off: fairness-aware alignment must be designed to remain statistically efficient; naive alignment can exacerbate disparities</cite>.

How to do it:
- Add soft constraints to policy updates that penalize disparities in acceptance probabilities or output embeddings across demographic features, solved via penalty terms or Lagrangian multipliers.
- Incorporate diversity-promoting KL or contrastive repulsion against identity‑stereotype prototypes in reward/penalty terms.

# 3) Representation‑Level Bias Mitigation (Finetune/Align Representation Steering)
- Idea: After pretraining, fine‑tune or align model representations (e.g., output heads or adapters) to demasculinize/feminize, depolarize, or otherwise reduce identity‑associations that feed into stereotypes, while preserving utility. <cite id="dc1f63f5-0">Model‑level intervention (post‑training) is a first‑line mitigation category alongside data‑level changes</cite>. <cite id="dc1f63f5-4">Even “explicitly unbiased” models can pass explicit tests yet harbor implicit social biases, suggesting representation‑level mitigation is necessary and can reveal hidden biases</cite>.
- Practice: Techniques include identity‑aware contrastive decoding/finetuning, bias-averse reward functions over hidden states, and adapter heads that steer representations toward fairness norms across identity groups; these are commonly combined with preference optimization to maintain conversational quality. <cite id="40f24544-0">Fair alignment research emphasizes steering toward fair preferences without unduly sacrificing performance</cite>.
- Caveats: Representation changes may not fully resolve distributional or prompt‑level disparities—use group‑aware evaluators to detect residual biases. <cite id="40f24544-4">Distributional misalignment persists, indicating the need for end‑to‑end audits beyond local representation changes</cite>.

How to do it:
- Train adapters that minimize cross‑group disparity (e.g., MSE or fairness proxies) on hidden representations for identity‑conditioned prompts; combine with preference losses to preserve fluency.
- Apply identity‑contrastive regularization during decoding or finetuning, steering outputs away from group‑stereotype directions in representation space.

# 4) Post‑Training Instruction/Value Alignment with Stereotype‑Reducing Datasets
- Idea: Fine‑tune aligned LMs on curated instruction/value datasets engineered to reduce gender, racial, or religious stereotypes, and to promote equitable attribution and role examples. <cite id="dc1f63f5-0">Data‑level and model‑level mitigations are complementary; both are necessary to address social bias</cite>. <cite id="dc1f63f5-1">In‑distribution prompts can expose social identity biases, motivating post‑training on prompts and responses that normalize equitable behavior</cite>.
- Evidence: Instruction‑tuning and value‑alignment corpora explicitly de‑emphasize ingroup‑positive/outgroup‑negative patterns report lower stereotype rates in evaluations and human‑preference tests, while keeping helpfulness largely intact. <cite id="dc1f63f5-4">Evaluation on explicit/implicit bias shows that passing explicit tests is insufficient, so value finetuning that targets implicit associations is needed</cite>.
- Caveats: If the social‑bias mitigation dataset is skewed, performance may regress on underrepresented groups. <cite id="dc1f63f5-0">Data‑level interventions can introduce new biases; model‑level post‑training can help hedge against such skew</cite>.

How to do it:
- Build multi‑identity, stereotype‑aware instruction corpora with de‑stereotyped role models and balanced attributions; include counter‑stereotype examples and identity‑disambiguation prompts; align with preference models to maintain helpfulness.

# 5) Distributional/Group Preference Optimization (DPO/RLHF over Distributions of Inputs)
- Idea: Optimize over distributions of inputs and preferences sampled from diverse demographics to ensure policies behave well on underrepresented groups, rather than only on majority prompts. <cite id="40f24544-4">A distributional fairness formulation demonstrates that current LLM responses do not align with human distributional preferences across groups, motivating post‑training with group‑marginal constraints</cite>. <cite id="dc1f63f5-1">Large LLMs already exhibit social identity biases (ingroup solidarity, outgroup hostility), suggesting post‑training with group‑normalized preferences can reduce those disparities</cite>.
- Practice: Techniques include constructing group‑conditioned preference datasets, using DPPs or group‑aware importance weights, and optimizing DPO or constrained PPO on identity‑marginals. <cite id="9fee0775-2">DPO provides a closed‑form path to learn from multi‑group preferences without complex RL infrastructures</cite>. <cite id="9fee0775-6">Optimizer choice matters: IPO can be more robust to over‑training than RLHF/DPO with common regularization</cite>.
- Caveats: Training over complex identity distributions risks mode coverage errors; incorporate active elicitation and safety constraints. <cite id="40f24544-1">Prefix bias in reward models indicates careful prompt design and auditing are required</cite>.

How to do it:
- Construct synthetic and human‑labeled multi‑identity preference datasets; apply marginal fairness weighting or DPP sampling; fit a reward model and use DPO or constrained PPO to learn a policy that equalizes outcomes across demographics.

# 6) Safety/Toxicity and Identity‑Agnostic Alignment
- Idea: Many social biases manifest as identity‑linked toxicity or aggressive responses; post‑training with identity‑agnostic or hate/sarcasm‑aware preference data can reduce social bias while preserving helpfulness. <cite id="dc1f63f5-0">Model‑level post‑training methods target these learned behaviors after pretraining</cite>. <cite id="dc1f63f5-1">Observed ingroup/outgroup patterns suggest aligning with identity‑agnostic norms can reduce hostility toward outgroups</cite>.
- Evidence: Reward models trained on identity‑neutral and toxicity‑aware preferences, plus constrained rollouts, have been used in RLHF/DPO pipelines to curb social bias in outputs. <cite id="40f24544-2">Fair RLHF designs explicitly combine human feedback with fairness-aware policy updates to reduce biased outputs</cite>.
- Caveats: Identity-agnostic policies can be less helpful to members of privileged groups; mitigate via group‑sensitive evaluators and subgroup finetuning.

How to do it:
- Pair identity‑neutral preferences with toxicity/sarcasm labels; fine‑tune reward models; optimize with constrained PPO/DPO to penalize identity‑linked aggression and stereotyping.

# 7) Auditing, Monitoring, and Iterative Feedback Loops
- Idea: Combine post-training with continuous auditing across social‑bias metrics and subgroup preferences, then iteratively re‑align. <cite id="40f24544-0">Fair alignment must be embedded into the training and deployment loop due to algorithmic bias in preference alignment</cite>. <cite id="dc1f63f5-4">Explicit tests can be gamed; monitoring implicit biases is critical</cite>.
- Practice and evidence: Teams deploy subgroup fairness monitors (e.g., disparity in harmfulness, stereotype conformity) and route ambiguous cases for adjudication; use these to refine post-training datasets and constraints. <cite id="40f24544-8">Surveys recommend taxonomic auditing and feedback curation to manage fairness risks in RLHF</cite>.
- Caveats: Audit–align cycles risk converging to local optima; diversify evaluators and data sources.

How to do it:
- Maintain a repository of subgroup‑specific prompt sets; run periodic ablations on stereotype and identity‑bias benchmarks; feed findings into the next round of preference collection and constraint optimization.

# Cross‑Cutting Challenges and Design Choices
- Reward model bias and prefix effects: <cite id="40f24544-1">RLHF reward models trained on pairwise rankings can exhibit prefix bias, propagating stereotypes if prompts/data are not sanitized</cite>. Mitigate by sanitizing prompts, diversifying demonstrators, and auditing for prefix bias; consider IPO over pure DPO/RLHF where generalization is key.
- Over‑training and instability: <cite id="9fee0775-6">Empirical analyses show DPO/RLHF can over‑train despite regularization, while IPO is more robust</cite>. Use conservative baselines, early‑stopping on fairness metrics, and conservative safety baselines.
- Trade‑offs and benchmarks: <cite id="40f24544-0">Fair alignment typically trades off utility and efficiency; explicit fairness objectives prevent “good enough” bias</cite>. <cite id="dc1f63f5-4">Explicitly unbiased models can still contain implicit biases; monitor with subgroup‑aware, implicit metrics</cite>.
- Surveys and taxonomies: <cite id="dc1f63f5-0">Recent overviews outline data vs. model‑level interventions and recommend both for robust mitigation</cite>. <cite id="40f24544-8">Taxonomic surveys highlight RLHF as a central locus of bias and advocate fairness constraints and audits</cite>.

Practical recipe (recent-style stack)
- Collect multi‑identity, stereotype‑aware preference data and sanitize prompts to reduce prefix bias; build a reward model with identity conditioners and disparity penalties. <cite id="40f24544-2">Use a fair RLHF pipeline with fairness constraints</cite>. <cite id="40f24544-1">Audit for prefix bias in reward prompts</cite>.
- Train with constrained PPO or DPO (or IPO as baseline) that enforces group‑marginal fairness and diversity; add representation‑level adapters to reduce stereotype associations. <cite id="9fee0775-2">DPO closes the loop on direct preference optimization</cite>. <cite id="9fee0775-6">Choose optimizers with better generalization under demographic shifts</cite>. <cite id="dc1f63f5-0">Use model‑level interventions alongside data‑level changes</cite>.
- Iterate with subgroup bias monitors and A/B preference tests; expand prompts to surface hidden biases and update constraints and adapters.

Bottom line
Recent post‑training and alignment techniques that mitigate social bias emphasize fairness‑aware reward shaping, group‑robust policy optimization, representation steering, and identity‑inclusive instruction/value finetuning—often combined in iterative pipelines that explicitly audit subgroup behavior. Effectiveness depends on diverse, identity‑informed preference data, careful selection of optimizers, and continuous monitoring to avoid over‑fitting and to address implicit disparities that pass explicit tests. <cite id="40f24544-0">Fair alignment requires embedding explicit fairness objectives into the post‑training loop</cite> <cite id="40f24544-1">while curing reward‑model prefix bias</cite> <cite id="40f24544-4">and matching policies to distributional human preferences across groups</cite> <cite id="dc1f63f5-0">through both model‑level and data‑level interventions</cite> <cite id="dc1f63f5-4">to counter hidden social biases</cite>.

questions.original_query: What are the differences between encoder-decoder and causal/non-causal decoder-only LMs?

query.text: What are the differences between encoder-decoder and causal/non-causal decoder-only LMs?
query.answer:
# Executive summary

- Encoder–decoder models jointly encode context and decode outputs using noncausal encoder self-attention, cross-attention over encoder outputs, and causal decoder self-attention with a future mask; they excel at tasks that require combining structured inputs with generated outputs such as machine translation and image captioning because the decoder can attend to the full input once it has been processed by the encoder.
- Decoder-only causal LMs (e.g., GPT-style) predict one token at a time from all previous tokens using a single autoregressive decoder stack; they achieve strong general-purpose generation by training to next-token prediction on unimodal, monolingual text and by scaling.
- Non-causal decoder-only LMs (statistical/prefix-tuning and instruction-tuned families like FLAN/DoLa) retain a purely autoregressive decoder but add left-to-right statistical prefixes or instruction-conditioned adapters learned during pretraining or posttraining; on many practical tasks, scale and instruction tuning can compensate for the lack of explicit cross-attention to an input, but they lose direct multimodal grounding and turn-taking context that encoder–decoders can exploit.

Below are the key differences and trade-offs.

# 1) Architecture and conditioning signals

- Architecture roles
  - Encoder–decoder: An encoder transforms the input into context-rich representations via noncausal self-attention; a decoder uses causal self-attention (masked future) and cross-attention to selectively attend to encoder representations while generating each output token. <cite id="c7951dda-5">The standard encoder–decoder Transformer decomposes the mapping into encoder self-attention, decoder self-attention with a causal mask, and cross-attention from encoder to decoder</cite>.
  - Decoder-only: Only a decoder stack of identical transformer blocks runs in a strictly left-to-right, causally masked fashion, so each block’s self-attention can only use previous tokens for prediction (e.g., GPT-style causal LM). <cite id="c7951dda-2">Causal language modeling (CLM), used by decoder models like GPT, predicts the next token based on all previous tokens</cite> <cite id="c7951dda-8">A decoder-only model stacks transformer blocks that process tokens autoregressively with causal masking on self-attention</cite>.
- Conditioning on inputs
  - Encoder–decoder: The decoder can “look at” the entire encoded input at once via cross-attention, enabling precise alignment (e.g., word-to-phrase) and structured grounding (e.g., image regions to words). <cite id="c7951dda-5">Cross-attention allows the decoder to attend to the encoder’s representations in a modular split of input–target mapping</cite>.
  - Decoder-only: Conditioning is purely sequential and statistical: the decoder uses only previous tokens plus static prompts or learned prefixes to guide generation, lacking a separate, explicit module to encode and selectively attend to structured inputs. <cite id="c7951dda-2">In decoder-only CLMs, the model relies on preceding tokens for prediction</cite>.

# 2) Training objectives and data

- Encoder–decoder pretraining (seq2seq)
  - Objective: Minimize a loss that aligns decoder predictions to targets given encoder context; training corpora are typically parallel text (e.g., multilingual pairs) or problem–solution pairs. The modular decomposition supports diverse supervision beyond language, including alignments among modalities. <cite id="c7951dda-5">The encoder–decoder split supports modular training where the decoder is optimized to generate targets conditioned on the encoder’s embedding of the input</cite>.
- Decoder-only causal LMs
  - Objective: Purely autoregressive next-token prediction on unimodal text; models like GPT are trained with a left-to-right causal language modeling objective. <cite id="c7951dda-2">Causal language models predict the next token from previous tokens, enabling generation like in GPT</cite>.
- Decoder-only non-causal (statistical/prefix) LMs
  - Objective: Left-to-right autoregressive generation with additional non-causal self-attention over learned or prompt-provided prefixes (statistical cache), or instruction-conditioned adapters. Models like FLAN-T5 and DoLa adapt decoder-only T5 with instruction tuning and instruction-conditioned adapters or latent vectors to handle free-form instructions without changing the autoregressive decoding mask. <cite id="811ae969-7">A prefix language model combines bidirectional prefix understanding with autoregressive generation to enable next-token prediction conditioned on prior context and a learned prefix</cite> <cite id="811ae969-1">DoLa adapts for T5/FLAN-T5 and evaluates instruction-following, treating the decoder with an auxiliary prefix-conditioning pathway</cite>.

# 3) Access to input and inference-time dependencies

- Causal decoder-only at inference
