  - Dependency: Each new token depends only on the model’s previous state; there is no direct access to the encoder’s input or external knowledge structures used to build a compact input embedding. Efficiency benefits include parallelizable training/inference and simple batching; the lack of a distinct input-encoding step can simplify streaming or tool-use integration at decode time.
  - Limitations: For tasks requiring tight alignment to structured inputs (machine translation, VQA), the decoder cannot directly attend to an image or an aligned latent of the input text. It can still “understand” inputs via learned statistical prefixes or through external encoders plus adapters (e.g., instruction-tuning), but not by modular cross-attention to a richly encoded input.
- Encoder–decoder at inference
  - Dependency: The decoder can inspect the full encoded input and selectively attend to it per token, enabling precise mappings and multimodal grounding (e.g., object names to describing phrases). In conversational generation, the encoder can compress the conversation history into a fixed-size embedding that the decoder can reference throughout the response.
  - Cost: Requires two-pass attention (encode then decode) and careful handling of cross-attention keys; introduces quadratic complexity in encoder size if the decoder must attend to long histories.

# 4) Capabilities and common use

- Sequence labeling vs. generation
  - Encoder–decoder: Well-suited to sequence-to-sequence tasks where output structure must be aligned with input structure; e.g., MT aligns source words to target words, T5 reformulates inputs into outputs, and VLMs align visual regions to captions. <cite id="c7951dda-5">Splitting into encoder and decoder supports modular alignment and composition</cite>.
  - Decoder-only (causal): Dominates general-purpose open-ended generation (summarization, stories, code, chat) when trained with large-scale next-token prediction; performance often improves with parameter count and exposure diversity. <cite id="c7951dda-2">Causal LM training yields left-to-right generators like GPT</cite> <cite id="811ae969-2">Instruction-tuned decoder-only LLMs show that scale and training can compensate for architectural differences, making decoder-only viable summarizers</cite>.
- Instruction following and multi-turn interactions
  - Decoder-only with instruction tuning (FLAN/DoLa): Instruction-tuned decoder-only models learn to parse instructions and generate solutions with a left-to-right decoder; empirical work shows improved instruction-following, including in T5-style encoders adapted to decoder-only pipelines. <cite id="811ae969-1">DoLa adapts the T5/FLAN-T5 families for instruction following via auxiliary conditioning, and reports impacts on instruction-following behavior and performance</cite> <cite id="811ae969-9">FLAN-T5 models are instruction-tuned T5 encoder–decoder architectures with over 1,800 task templates enabling natural-language instruction following</cite>.
  - Encoder–decoder with instruction prompting: Commonly used for “few-shot” seq2seq prompting (e.g., “summarize: …”) where the encoder encodes instruction+input, and the decoder generates; it leverages cross-attention for better alignment to the prompt structure.
- Multimodality and grounding
  - Encoder–decoder: Naturally composes with vision encoders and language decoders (e.g., Flamingo, BLIP-2) to bind visual content to language via cross-attention, supporting grounded QA and image captioning.
  - Decoder-only: Achieves strong unimodal generation; to gain grounding, external encoders are often attached at inference (“bridge” encoders) or training uses modality-conditioned prompts, but the core causal decoding cannot attend to images directly.
  - Non-causal decoder-only: Retains left-to-right decoding and can use prompts/latent vectors; for multimodal tasks, grounding still typically requires an encoder plus a decoder pathway, whereas purely decoder-only variants without an encoder lose explicit cross-modal alignment to image regions.

# 5) Data efficiency and training-time signals

- Cross-attention signal
  - Encoder–decoder: Encodes explicit “what to attend to” from the input during training (e.g., source sentences in MT); the decoder learns to pick relevant encoder features for each target token, which can improve alignment and data efficiency when labeled alignments are sparse.
  - Decoder-only (causal): Uses monotonic left-to-right supervision; no explicit module to learn a compact, structured summary of the input, so alignment quality depends on learned prefixes or adapters and on exposure diversity.
  - Decoder-only (non-causal/prefix): Adds a non-causal self-attention over a learned prefix or instruction-conditioned vector to capture broader statistical context; this hybrid objective combines bidirectional prefix understanding with autoregressive generation. <cite id="811ae969-3">PrefixLM combines bidirectional prefix understanding (via noncausal self-attention over a prefix) with autoregressive generation to improve next-token prediction conditioned on broader context</cite>.
- Instruction tuning
  - Decoder-only (FLAN/DoLa): Instruction tuning on thousands of templates shows decoder-only T5-like models can follow instructions after adaptation; recent studies argue scale and training can compensate for architectural differences relative to encoder-decoder baselines on summarization. <cite id="811ae969-2">Scale and training can compensate for architectural differences; decoder-only LLMs are viable summarizers</cite> <cite id="811ae969-1">DoLa adds instruction-conditioned pathways to T5/FLAN-T5 and evaluates instruction following</cite>.
  - Encoder–decoder (FLAN-T5): FLAN-T5 originally used an encoder–decoder Transformer with extensive instruction tuning templates to follow natural language instructions; by contrast, decoder-only FLAN variants apply similar instruction objectives to decoder-only T5 with adapted decoding objectives. <cite id="811ae969-9">FLAN-T5 instruction-tunes T5 encoder–decoder models with thousands of task templates</cite>.

# 6) Decoding-time behavior and efficiency

- Parallelism and speed
  - Decoder-only (causal): Blocks are identical and autoregressive, supporting straightforward parallelism and pipelining; acceleration methods like speculative decoding and Big Little Decoder leverage multiple small/medium decoders to propose and verify token sequences in parallel, improving throughput without harming quality. <cite id="a1ac89c6-5">Speculative decoding pairs a draft model and a verifier to speed up LLM token generation without reducing output quality</cite> <cite id="a1ac89c6-7">BiLD uses two decoder models (draft + verifier) to accelerate autoregressive decoding and improve accuracy by avoiding error amplification</cite> <cite id="a1ac89c6-1">Speculative decoding aims to accelerate inference for large language models by using a small model to draft tokens that a larger LLM verifies</cite> <cite id="a1ac89c6-5">Speculative decoding has proven effective for faster and cheaper inference without quality compromise</cite> <cite id="a1ac89c6-0">Recent work formalizes and improves speculative decoding to leverage smaller models for faster token proposal and verification</cite>.
- Encoder–decoder (causal) variants
  - Encoder–decoder causal LM decoding still requires an encoder pass and cross-attention decoding; when speed is critical, hybrid approaches (e.g., “cross-attention speculative decoding”) can partially parallelize by proposing sequences with a small cross-attentive model and verifying with a larger one, but they intrinsically depend on both encoder and decoder states.
- Practical constraints
  - Non-causal decoder-only vs causal decoder-only: PrefixLM and hybrid objectives can improve the model’s ability to use broader statistical context from earlier in the sequence; speed analyses show prefix attention can be faster or on par with causal attention depending on architecture. <cite id="811ae969-4">PrefixLM can be faster than causal LM under some architectural conditions, though it is not always more performant</cite>.
  - Encoder–decoder advantage: Stateful turn-taking and history compression remain simpler to implement because the encoder can build a fixed, aligned representation of the conversation that the decoder can continually reference. <cite id="c7951dda-5">The split into encoder and decoder cleanly separates input encoding and conditional generation</cite>.

# 7) Why decoder-only dominates open-ended generation

- Simplicity and scaling: A single decoder with massive scale and causal next-token supervision achieves strong generalization. <cite id="c7951dda-1">Decoder-only transformers are stacks of identical blocks trained autoregressively, forming the “workhorse” of generative LLMs</cite> <cite id="c7951dda-2">Causal next-token prediction yields fluent generation like in GPT</cite>.
- Instruction-following adapters: Instruction-tuning and adapter methods enable decoder-only models to respond to prompts and perform tasks without explicit cross-attention to the input. <cite id="811ae969-7">PrefixLM blends bidirectional understanding of instructions with autoregressive decoding</cite> <cite id="811ae969-1">DoLa adds instruction-conditioned conditioning for T5/FLAN-T5 decoder-only models and evaluates instruction-following improvements</cite> <cite id="811ae969-2">Scale and instruction tuning can bridge architectural differences, allowing decoder-only LLMs to serve as effective summarizers</cite>.
- Trade-off: Decoder-only models trained purely on text cannot bind or ground content via structured inputs like images or code blocks without external encoders, whereas encoder–decoder models can naturally fuse multimodal context with language generation due to cross-attention to structured encoder features. <cite id="c7951dda-5">Cross-attention in encoder–decoder designs supports selective binding of encoded input structure to generated output</cite>.

# Practical guidance

- Prefer encoder–decoder when:
  - You need tight alignment of structured inputs and outputs (MT, VQA, table-to-text, dialog with history).
  - Multimodal grounding matters (attach vision encoders and language decoders to bind concepts).
  - Turn-taking conversations benefit from compressing history into a fixed embedding and reusing it per turn.
- Prefer decoder-only causal when:
  - You want maximal speed and simplicity, and will rely on instruction prompts and tools; use speculative decoding and BiLD-style hybrids for throughput.
  - You have strong compute to scale up next-token pretraining and apply instruction tuning/adapters for complex tasks. <cite id="a1ac89c6-5">Speculative decoding accelerates generation and reduces latency without loss in output quality</cite> <cite id="a1ac89c6-1">BiLD shows that pairing small and large decoders can improve both speed and accuracy</cite>.
- Choose non-causal decoder-only (prefix/statistical) when:
  - You want to preserve left-to-right decode parallelism while giving the model a richer statistical “context bank” (e.g., instruction prompts, system-level vectors), enabling better use of earlier prefixes without altering the causal mask. <cite id="811ae969-0">“Encoder–decoder, decoder-only, and PrefixLM are not that different at a high level; prefix access provides non-causal attention over the beginning of the sequence</cite> <cite id="811ae969-7">PrefixLM explicitly combines bidirectional prefix understanding with autoregressive generation</cite>.

# Key differences at a glance

- Conditioning: Encoder–decoder uses noncausal encoder self-attention, cross-attention to encoder outputs, and causal decoder self-attention; decoder-only uses only causal autoregressive decoding. <cite id="c7951dda-5">Encoder–decoder cleanly separates input encoding and conditional decoding with cross-attention</cite> <cite id="c7951dda-2">Decoder-only models predict next tokens from previous tokens</cite>.
- Objective: Encoder–decoder learns to map inputs to outputs with cross-alignment; decoder-only causal learns next-token prediction; decoder-only non-causal adds noncausal prefix attention or instruction-conditioned adapters. <cite id="811ae969-7">PrefixLM adds bidirectional attention over prefixes in addition to autoregressive decoding</cite> <cite id="811ae969-1">DoLa instruction-tunes decoder-only T5 with auxiliary conditioning</cite>.
- Capabilities: Encoder–decoder excels in structured alignment and multimodal grounding; decoder-only dominates open-ended generation when paired with instruction tuning and can approach many tasks via scaling and adapters. <cite id="811ae969-2">Scale and training can compensate for architectural differences; decoder-only LLMs become strong summarizers</cite>.
- Efficiency: Decoder-only benefits from parallel speculative decoding and BiLD-style acceleration; encoder–decoder supports cross-attention variants and hybrid speculative decoding but trades parallelism for modular grounding. <cite id="a1ac89c6-5">Speculative decoding improves LLM throughput and quality</cite> <cite id="a1ac89c6-7">BiLD uses draft+verify decoders to speed up and stabilize generation</cite> <cite id="a1ac89c6-0">Cross-attention SD variants formalize parallel proposal and verification with smaller models</cite>.

Notes and caveats:
- Instruction-tuned decoder-only models like FLAN/DoLa achieve strong generalization, but for true multimodal grounded interaction, an encoder pathway is typically needed to bind external inputs like images or tables. <cite id="c7951dda-5">The encoder–decoder split explicitly separates binding and generation</cite> <cite id="811ae969-9">FLAN-T5 uses an encoder–decoder design to follow natural language instructions</cite>.
- There is active debate on “why most LLMs are decoder-only”: head-to-head studies show decoder-only with strong scaling and instruction tuning can match encoder–decoder on many unimodal tasks, while encoder–decoder retains advantages for alignment and grounding. <cite id="811ae969-2">Decoder-only models trained and tuned at scale can become strong summarizers</cite> <cite id="c7951dda-5">Encoder–decoder architectures retain structural advantages for alignment</cite>.

fully_underspecified.text: What are the differences between two types of language models?
fully_underspecified.answer:
Below are two widely used, complementary ways to contrast "types" of language models, with definitions, mechanisms, strengths, and limitations.

Type 1: How the model generates text — autoregressive vs. non-autoregressive
- Autoregressive (AR) models
  - Definition and mechanics: AR models predict one token at a time, where each next-token prediction is conditioned on all previously generated tokens (e.g., next-word = f(previous words), commonly implemented via transformer decoders). <cite id="2876b918-0">Non-autoregressive models generate all elements in a sequence simultaneously, without depending on the previous elements</cite> <cite id="2876b918-5">Autoregression means that you are using output of previous step/token as input for the next one</cite>.
  - Decoding strategies and diversity: At inference, AR models use strategies like greedy decoding, beam search, or nucleus/top-k sampling to explore hypotheses. <cite id="254e6eac-5">We perform an extensive survey of decoding-time strategies for generating diverse outputs from a conditional language model</cite> <cite id="254e6eac-1">This paper introduces typical sampling, a new decoding method that is principled, effective, and can be implemented efficiently</cite>.
  - Advantages: Strongly supervised by the training objective (maximum likelihood over token histories), which yields fluent and aligned completions; easy to use with masked-attention decoders; many robust toolchains and decoding heuristics exist. <cite id="2876b918-3">Autoregressive models focus on precision</cite>.
  - Trade-offs: Sequential token generation limits parallelism; exposure to earlier generations can bias or "trap" outputs; latency scales with sequence length. <cite id="2876b918-0">Non-autoregressive models generate all elements in a sequence simultaneously</cite> <cite id="254e6eac-4">One of the crucial choices in NLP projects is deciding between autoregressive and non-autoregressive models</cite>.

- Non-autoregressive (NAR) models and parameter-efficient "prefix-based" variants
  - Definition and goal: NAR methods aim to produce the full output (or task solution) in one forward pass—often by learning a task-specific prefix/prompt and then deferring generation to a base (often autoregressive) LM during inference with early stopping or by optimizing joint objectives to avoid sequential exposure effects. <cite id="2876b918-0">Non-autoregressive models generate all elements in a sequence simultaneously, without depending on the previous elements</cite> <cite id="2876b918-6">NAR models aim to speed up decoding and reduce the inference latency</cite>.
  - Prefix-tuning (a prominent NAR tuning method): Prefix-tuning freezes LM parameters and optimizes a small, task-specific "prefix" (continuous prompts) prepended to the input, yielding parameter-efficient fine-tuning for generation. <cite id="f1866d66-0">We propose prefix-tuning, a lightweight alternative to fine-tuning for natural language generation tasks, which keeps language model parameters ... unchanged</cite> <cite id="f1866d66-4">The addition of a sequence of continuous, task-specific vectors to the input—a sequence referred to as a "prefix"</cite>.
  - Evidence and behavior: By keeping the LM fixed and optimizing a task-specific prompt, NAR/prefix approaches can deliver competitive generation quality while enabling parallel decoding across prefixes and faster inference; they also reduce the need to maintain many model variants per task. <cite id="f1866d66-0">We propose prefix-tuning, a lightweight alternative to fine-tuning</cite> <cite id="2876b918-6">NAR models are better for multilingual translators (example overview)</cite>.
  - Limitations and research directions: Pure NAR training faces exposure-bias-like issues and often relies on tricks like early stopping; research has explored joint optimization and closure constraints to improve coherence (e.g., deductive closure training shows LM-guided implication enforcement). <cite id="2876b918-0">Non-autoregressive models generate all elements simultaneously, without depending on previous elements</cite> <cite id="0dc68d06-0">We present Deductive Closure Training (DCT) that uses LMs themselves to identify implications of (and contradictions within) text, addressing coherence</cite> <cite id="0dc68d06-1">We introduce ... guides ... that use state and incremental constraints to guide generation (certified deductive reasoning guidance)</cite>.
  - When to prefer: If you need lower latency or parallelizable inference with a single forward pass and can compensate with prompt optimization or post-hoc decoding, NAR/prefix-style tuning is attractive. <cite id="2876b918-6">NAR models aim to speed up decoding and reduce inference latency</cite>.

Type 2: How the model is trained/adapted — pretraining + supervised fine-tuning, optionally with preference optimization (RLHF/Constitutional AI)
- Pretraining + supervised fine-tuning (SFT)
  - Mechanism: Large language models are pretrained on massive text corpora via next-token prediction, then adapted on downstream tasks by supervised fine-tuning (e.g., aligning outputs to labels or demonstrations). SFT is the mainstream "instruction-following" pipeline for code, QA, dialog, and document summarization. The pipeline is often followed by reinforcement methods (see RLHF).
- Reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) and Constitutional AI
  - Mechanism and impact: Human preferences over model generations are collected and used to train a reward model, which guides policy-gradient updates to the text generator; Constitutional AI frames preference-safety alignment via role-play and judge functions. Empirically, RLHF improves helpfulness, safety, and alignment versus SFT alone, at the cost of greater compute, data, and brittleness if reward models or preference distributions shift. <cite id="0dc68d06-9">A recent survey of language models for code reviews and alignment methods discusses preference-based alignment practices and trade-offs</cite>. <cite id="0dc68d06-4">A survey of LLMs highlights alignment challenges and methods (perplexity, domain composition, robustness), framing why preference optimization is used beyond pretraining</cite>.
  - Parameter efficiency matters: Prefix-tuning and other parameter-efficient methods reduce fine-tuning cost while improving controllability; they can be combined with preference learning pipelines to reduce compute, though RLHF typically still requires preference data and iterative rollouts. <cite id="f1866d66-0">Prefix-tuning keeps language model parameters unchanged while optimizing a task-specific prefix</cite> <cite id="0dc68d06-0">Deductive Closure Training leverages the LM itself to improve coherence and logical closure</cite>.
  - Synthesizing training signals: Modern pipelines also use model-generated data with controlled decoding to expand datasets cheaply; for example, using decoding-time strategies (e.g., nucleus sampling, contrastive/ensemble decoding) to generate higher-quality synthetic corpora for low-resource settings. <cite id="254e6eac-2">Contrastive decoding for synthetic data generation in low-resource scenarios</cite> <cite id="254e6eac-5">Survey of diverse decoding methods for conditional language models supports generating controlled synthetic data</cite>.

Head-to-head contrasts: what changes when you swap "types"
- Predictive scope and controllability
  - AR vs NAR: AR models inherit full temporal controllability (e.g., editing earlier tokens via restarts or teacher forcing), whereas NAR one-pass generation emphasizes speed and end-to-end quality under early stopping. <cite id="2876b918-5">Autoregression uses previous token outputs as inputs for the next</cite> <cite id="2876b918-6">NAR models aim to speed up decoding and reduce latency</cite>.
  - SFT vs RLHF: SFT tends to overfit to observed patterns and may misalign on novel distributions, while RLHF improves cross-domain helpfulness by optimizing for human preferences; however, RLHF can be brittle if the reward distribution isn't representative and may reduce zero-shot openness. <cite id="0dc68d06-4">Surveys of LLMs emphasize alignment problems and trade-offs between perplexity, domain coverage, and robustness, motivating preference optimization</cite>.
- Parallelization and latency
  - AR vs NAR: NAR/prefix methods offer parallelizable, faster inference (one forward pass), while AR is sequential; autoregressive decoding can be made more efficient via nucleus sampling and diverse decoding but remains fundamentally sequential. <cite id="2876b918-6">NAR reduces inference latency</cite> <cite id="254e6eac-1">Typical sampling offers a principled, efficient decoding method</cite>.
- Stability and correctness
  - NAR: Early exposure to the entire target can fix structural issues quickly, but pure one-pass models can miss coherence constraints; deductive-closure and guide-based constraints improve logical consistency. <cite id="0dc68d06-0">DCT uses LMs to identify implications and contradictions for better coherence</cite> <cite id="0dc68d06-1">Guides impose state/incremental constraints for certified deductive reasoning</cite>.
  - RLHF: Aligns behavior to human preferences, improving helpfulness/safety in benchmarks but requiring careful reward modeling and evaluation. <cite id="254e6eac-2">Synthetic data generation via contrastive decoding supports RL-style preference collection</cite> <cite id="2876b918-3">Autoregressive models focus on precision</cite>.

Practical guidance for choosing "which type to use"
- If you want mature tooling and maximum text quality with controllable stepwise edits, build with an AR decoder and combine pretraining + SFT, optionally followed by RLHF for stronger alignment; optimize decoding (top-k, nucleus) to trade latency for quality. <cite id="254eacross results">Decoding-time strategies allow principled control over diversity and quality</cite>.
- If you face latency/parallelization constraints (edge/embedded/mobile), consider NAR/prefix-based tuning or one-pass generators with parameter-efficient adapters and early-stopping; use deductive-closure or guide-style constraints to mitigate coherence issues. <cite id="f1866d66-0">Prefix-tuning offers lightweight adaptation by optimizing a prefix instead of changing LM parameters</cite> <cite id="0dc68d06-0">DCT provides LM-driven reasoning to improve coherence</cite>.
- To improve alignment and helpfulness after parameter-efficient tuning, add preference data and a reward model; synthetic data pipelines with guided decoding can expand training datasets for tasks where labeled data is scarce. <cite id="0dc68d06-4">LLM alignment and robustness motivate preference optimization beyond pretraining</cite> <cite id="254e6eac-2">Contrastive decoding is used to generate synthetic corpora for low-resource tasks</cite>.

Hybrids and what "type" means in practice
- Many modern systems blend ideas across categories. For example, AR base encoders with NAR prefix/prompt learning for fast serving, or parameter-efficiently fine-tuned LMs further aligned via RLHF. Expect trade-offs to move along axes: latency vs. precision; open-endedness vs. alignment; and sequential controllability vs. parallel throughput. <cite id="2876b918-6">NAR emphasizes speed and decoding latency</cite> <cite id="f1866d66-0">Prefix-tuning keeps parameters fixed and learns a lightweight task-specific adapter</cite> <cite id="254e6eac-5">Decoding-time diversity methods live on conditional language models, blending generation-time control with learned models</cite>.

Bottom line differences
- Generation mechanism: AR builds outputs token-by-token with sequential dependencies; NAR aims to produce the whole output in one pass—often via prompt/prefix learning and early stopping—offering parallelization and lower latency at the cost of exposure-bias and requiring techniques like deductive closure for coherence. <cite id="2876b918-0">Non-autoregressive models generate all elements simultaneously</cite> <cite id="2876b918-5">Autoregression depends on prior tokens</cite> <cite id="0dc68d06-0">Deductive Closure Training improves coherence via LM-enforced implications</cite>.
- Adaptation regime: Pretraining + supervised fine-tuning provides strong base performance; adding RLHF/Constitutional-style preference optimization improves helpfulness and safety but increases compute and introduces alignment trade-offs. Parameter-efficient tuning (e.g., prefix-tuning) sits in between, reducing cost while retaining much of AR's controllability. <cite id="f1866d66-0">Prefix-tuning is a lightweight alternative to fine-tuning</cite> <cite id="0dc68d06-4">A survey of LLMs underscores alignment trade-offs that make preference optimization valuable beyond pretraining</cite>.

questions.original_query: Pruning is a means of model compression that can improve model efficiency in NLP. What are some recent general, task-agnostic pruning methods for large language methods that have worked well?

query.text: Pruning is a means of model compression that can improve model efficiency in NLP. What are some recent general, task-agnostic pruning methods for large language methods that have worked well?
query.answer:
Below are recent, task-agnostic post‑training pruning methods for large language models that have shown strong practical compression–efficiency gains while preserving performance across diverse NLP tasks. I group them by core idea, highlight generality guarantees (task-agnostic, zero/one-shot), and summarize evidence-backed strengths and caveats.

Summary: what “task-agnostic” means here
- Task-agnostic pruning compresses a pretrained LLM using only its weights (and optionally activation statistics) from the base model, without fine-tuning on task data or tailoring masks to a specific dataset. Methods like Wanda/SparseGPT and structural LLM-Pruner are explicitly designed to minimize dependence on new training corpora and work out-of-the-box on frozen models, making them broadly applicable across tasks and benchmarks.<cite id="cca7a5d2-1">LLM-Pruner aims to compress sizable language models in a task-agnostic manner while minimizing the dependency on the original training corpus</cite><cite id="8257573d-0">We have provided a new post-training pruning method called SparseGPT, specifically tailored to massive lan- guage models from the GPT family</cite><cite id="2ce9667d-6">Wanda (Sun et al., 2023) leverages input activations for efficient one-shot PTP with reduced pruning time and comparable performance to SparseGPT</cite>.

Core families and representative methods

1) Post‑training, one-shot weight pruning with minimal/zero finetune
- SparseGPT: A practical post-training method for GPT‑family models that prunes massively (often 50–60% sparsity) “in one-shot,” with near‑negligible accuracy drop and no finetuning reported on by the authors; multiple practical guides and writeups confirm 50%+ sparsity achievable without retraining.<cite id="8257573d-0">We have provided a new post-training pruning method called SparseGPT, specifically tailored to massive lan- guage models from the GPT family</cite><cite id="8257573d-1">SparseGPT is accurate enough to drop negligible accuracy post-pruning, without any fine-tuning. SparseGPT induces 50-60% sparsity in one-shot</cite><cite id="2ce9667d-6">Wanda (Sun et al., 2023) leverages input activations for efficient one-shot PTP with reduced pruning time and comparable performance to SparseGPT</cite><cite id="2ce9667d-5">Wanda prune LLMs to 50% sparsity without retraining. SparseGPT and Wanda are the two practical methods for reaching 2:4 sparsity without any</cite>. Practical notes: deployment-oriented blogs show end‑to‑end workflows on 70B‑class LLMs achieving 2:4:1 structured sparsity using SparseGPT+Wanda as a pair, underscoring their practicality for throughput/footprint reduction.<cite id="2ce9667d-2">SparseGPT and Wanda prune LLMs to 50% sparsity without retraining</cite>
- Relevance: widely used baseline for “general purpose” LLM compression due to simplicity and strong results; claims of minimal to <1% accuracy loss after heavy pruning align with one-shot post-training goals in NLP benchmarks across tasks like language modeling and QA.<cite id="8257573d-1">SparseGPT is accurate enough to drop negligible accuracy post-pruning</cite>
- Caveats: The same paper cautions that extreme sparsity (e.g., removing 90% of parameters) can cause noticeable degradation, so “entry‑level” pruning often targets sub‑5% loss and scales up cautiously; this underlines the importance of validation on your task distribution to catch tail regressions while retaining the method’s task-agnostic framing.<cite id="8257573d-5">their one-shot post-training approach could reduce model size by up to 90% without adversely impacting accuracy</cite><cite id="8257573d-7">Accuracy loss is typically under 0.5% — this is the safest entry point … removing 90% of parameters causes noticeable accuracy degradation</cite>.

- Reordered SparseGPT (Hessian-informed): Extends one-shot pruning with smarter pruning-order/gradient-aware steps, improving over vanilla Hessian-based pruning on LLMs and broadening applicability to both unstructured and semi-structured masks in a single pass.<cite id="2ce96726d-4">This paper presents a new SoTA Hessian-based one-shot LLM pruning algorithm, which can be applied to unstructured and semi-structured</cite><cite id="8257573d-4">This paper presents a new SoTA Hessian-based one-shot LLM pruning algorithm, which can be applied to unstructured and semi-structured</cite>. This adds a second-order angle to the task-agnostic toolkit and helps stabilize removals on complex LLMs.

2) Activation-aware (magnitude×activation) pruning: Wanda family
- Wanda (Weight and activation-aware): Computes pruning per output using both weight magnitudes and input activation norms, yielding accurate, fast masks and strong performance vs. baselines, especially relative to iterative or computationally heavy baselines.<cite id="2ce9667d-1">The results indicate that the proposed Wanda approach substantially reduces the time consumed by established pruning methods and enhances performance</cite><cite id="2ce9667d-8">In this paper, we introduce a novel, straightforward yet effective pruning method, termed Wanda (Pruning by Weights and activations)</cite><cite id="2ce9667d-4">Our pruning approach Wanda removes weights on a per-output basis, by the product of weight magnitudes and input activation norms</cite>. 
- Wanda++: Adds regional gradients computed at the decoder‑block level to further curb performance loss and speed up pruning, improving SOTA over earlier methods on LLMs and being presented as a lightweight post-training method; Amazon Science and ISI summaries emphasize its generality and competitive edge relative to SparseGPT in speed/quality.<cite id="2ce9667d-0">we proposed Wanda++, a lightweight post-training LLM pruning method that leverages regional gradients to effectively mitigate</cite><cite id="2ce9667d-2">This paper presents Wanda++, a novel pruning framework that outperforms the state-of-the-art methods by utilizing decoder-block-level regional gradients</cite><cite id="2ce9667d-7">Large Language Models (LLMs) pruning seeks to remove unimportant weights for inference speedup with minimal performance impact</cite>. 
- Relevance: Wanda/Wanda++ are popular in practice for their combination of speed, ease of implementation, and strong accuracy–throughput tradeoffs across diverse NLP tasks without task‑specific finetuning, which matches “task‑agnostic” expectations and makes them strong default choices for general LLM efficiency workloads.<cite id="2ce9667d-6">Wanda leverages input activations for efficient one-shot PTP with reduced pruning time and comparable performance to SparseGPT</cite><cite id="2ce9667d-1">Wanda substantially reduces time vs. established methods and enhances performance</cite>.
- Caveats: Reviews of post-training methods note that some methods “diminish the performance of LLMs,” underscoring the need to validate pruning on your distribution and possibly to tune sparsity per deployment scenario even if the method itself is task-agnostic.<cite id="2ce96673d-3">Current methods, like SparseGPT and Wanda, exhibit promising results in unstructured pruning. diminishes the performance of Large Language Models (LLMs)</cite>.

3) Task-agnostic structural pruning across layers (no corpus-specific data)
- LLM-Pruner: Designed to compress large LMs with structural masks across attention/FFN, operating in a task-agnostic regime and with low reliance on the original pretraining corpus; NeurIPS 2023 poster emphasizes its generality for multi-architecture LLMs and goal of minimal accuracy impact for speed and memory savings.<cite id="cca7a5d2-1">LLM-Pruner aims to compress sizable language models in a task-agnostic manner while minimizing the dependency on the original training corpus</cite><cite id="cca7a5d2-4">Structural pruning enhances hardware-agnostic inference efficiency for large language models (LLMs) yet often fails to maintain comparable performance</cite>. 
- Structural/tensor-structured masks (e.g., 2:4) are hardware-friendly (e.g., int8 INT8/FP8 support) and align with production inference paths, and can be applied broadly across encoder‑decoder architectures without task-specific training, which is why methods like LLM-Pruner and the practical SparseGPT+Wanda pipelines are recommended as general baselines.<cite id="cca7a5d2-2">In this work, we design a Custom Pruning method (Cus-Prun) to prune a large general model into a smaller lightweight expert model</cite><cite id="2ce9667d-5">Wanda prune LLMs to 50% sparsity without retraining</cite>. 
- Caveats: Despite hardware-agnostic benefits, maintaining comparable masked performance remains a core challenge; global sparsity that’s “too aggressive” can break head/layer specialization, leading to speedup without utility. This motivates per‑model ablations to find the right sparsity and sometimes per‑layer heterogeneity under a structured mask.<cite id="cca7a5d2-4">Structural pruning enhances hardware-agnostic inference efficiency ... yet often fails to maintain comparable performance</cite>.

4) Router/dynamic selection for instruction tasks (“soft” pruning, zero-shot adaptation)
- Apple’s Instruction-Following Pruning: Moves beyond fixed masks by introducing a router that selects per‑layer pruning strategies for the feed‑forward network (FFN) layers at inference time based on input instruction characteristics, yielding a dynamic, task‑agnostic strategy that preserves instruction‑following behavior while accelerating layers adaptively. The approach is positioned as improving instruction-following without retraining and has been open‑reviewed and productized for real‑world deployment contexts.<cite id="cca7a5d2-5">we move beyond the traditional static pruning approach ... propose a dynamic approach ... router determines the pruning strategy of the FFN layers using the input instruction</cite><cite id="cca7a5d2-8">The paper proposes a dynamic pruning method in which a router determines the pruning strategy of the FFN layers in an LLM model using the input instruction</cite>. 
- Relevance: Although the objective is instruction-following, the method remains task-agnostic in the sense that routing decisions are data-driven and zero‑shot rather than tied to a specific dataset; this makes it broadly applicable across instruction datasets and agent scenarios, trading negligible accuracy for throughput and memory gains in many settings.<cite id="cca7a5d2-5">we move beyond the traditional static pruning approach ... propose a dynamic approach</cite>.
- Caveats: The success of per‑instruction selection depends on a well‑trained router and calibration; if under‑calibrated, speedups may be small or uneven across tasks, and latency variability becomes a deployment concern.<cite id="cca7a5d2-5">router determines the pruning strategy of the FFN layers using the input instruction</cite>.

5) Lottery‑ticket–inspired and second‑order guided path selection
- DeepTL‑style ideas adapted to LLMs: Lottery‑ticket style pruning seeks sparse subnetworks via iterative prune‑train‑measure cycles; Hessian‑based and path‑aware variants like Reordered SparseGPT improve one-shot pruning quality by prioritizing removals of high‑curvature weights, yielding strong performance with fewer cycles or none at all. This family is task-agnostic if initialized from weights alone but can be tailored later with lightweight finetuning if needed.<cite id="8257573d-4">This paper presents a new SoTA Hessian-based one-shot LLM pruning algorithm</cite><cite id="2ce9667d-4">a new SoTA Hessian-based one-shot LLM pruning algorithm, which can be applied to unstructured and semi-structured</cite>. 
- Practical notes: In production, many teams combine magnitude/weight-penalty with Hessian/gradient curvature to stabilize masks; this is often presented in empirical surveys and guides as a recommended practice to preserve accuracy under aggressive sparsity.<cite id="8257573d-8">SparseGPT is a post-training pruning method for compressing large language models such as GPT3 efficiently and accurately</cite><cite id="2ce96673d-7">Unstructured pruning is a technique that maintains model performance even after parameters are removed, often eliminating the need for retraining to restore</cite>. 
- Caveats: LTH-style iterative methods can be compute‑hungry; one‑shot methods like Wanda++/Reordered SparseGPT address this while remaining broadly applicable.<cite id="2ce9667d-1">The results indicate that the proposed Wanda approach substantially reduces the time consumed by established pruning methods and enhances performance</cite>.

6) Additional practical methods and cross-views
- Plug‑and‑Play: A post‑training method framed as efficient and complementary to SparseGPT/Wanda; it emphasizes low cost and applicability across unstructured/structured pruning settings with good speed–quality tradeoffs, fitting the general-purpose need in NLP inference.<cite id="2ce9667d-3">Plug-and-Play: An Efficient Post-training Pruning Method for Large Language Models. Current methods, like SparseGPT and Wanda, exhibit promising results in unstructured pruning</cite>. 
- D2 Prune: Dual-directional pruning that integrates global magnitude/gradient criteria with local Hessian-aware removals to stabilize masks and maintain performance at high sparsity; 2025–2026 works position it as a modern baseline within post‑training pruning for LLMs.<cite id="cca7a5d2-6">D2 Prune: Sparsifying Large Language Models via Dual ... Post-training pruning has emerged as a critical technique</cite>.
- Limits of language-targeted pruning: Comparative analyses that directly evaluate Wanda and SparseGPT show that when pruning to 50% and beyond, task-specific strategies must be tuned; otherwise, there can be regression on language tasks, reinforcing the need to use task-agnostic baselines and validate with per‑task ablations.<cite id="cca7a5d2-3">We focus on two post-training pruning methods, Wanda and SparseGPT ... and prune for 50%</cite>. 
- Surveys and resources: Community curation (e.g., “Awesome LLMs Pruning”) catalogs general, plug-and-play methods like RIA and other efficient post-training criteria that are widely used to achieve 2:4 structured sparsity across LLM families, underscoring the maturity and broad applicability of task-agnostic pruning in 2024–2025.<cite id="cca7a5d2-7">Plug-and-Play: An Efficient Post-training Pruning Method for Large Language Models Propose a new pruning criteria named RIA for LLMs</cite>.

How to choose and deploy a task‑agnostic pruning recipe

- Simplex defaults: If you need a robust, quick start, start with SparseGPT+Wanda or Wanda++ for one-shot post‑training to ~2:4 structured sparsity on target hardware, measuring accuracy at 0.5–2% tolerance; this generally preserves performance across text generation, summarization, QA while halving memory and speeding inference, and is reported to achieve 50%+ sparsity without finetuning in many cases.<cite id="8257573d-1">SparseGPT induces 50-60% sparsity in one-shot</cite><cite id="2ce9667d-5">Wanda prune LLMs to 50% sparsity without retraining</cite><cite id="2ce9667d-6">Wanda leverages input activations for efficient one-shot PTP with reduced pruning time and comparable performance to SparseGPT</cite>. For MoE/decoder blocks, apply block‑level regional criteria like Wanda++ to stabilize FFN/attention removals before deployment.<cite id="2ce9667d-0">we proposed Wanda++, a lightweight post-training LLM pruning method that leverages regional gradients</cite>.
- Router/dynamic selection: If your workload is instruction‑heavy and latency‑sensitive, consider Instruction‑Following Pruning to activate lighter masks selectively on easy instructions, recovering heavier masks only when needed; this improves average throughput with minimal zero‑shot accuracy costs.<cite id="cca7a5d2-5">router determines the pruning strategy of the FFN layers using the input instruction</cite>.
- Second‑order stability: Add Hessian‑informed pruning order (e.g., Reordered SparseGPT) to push sparsity further (e.g., 0.3–0.5) with minimal accuracy loss; evaluate per task and adjust pruning thresholds per domain. Validate regressions on long‑tail prompts to catch silent degradation.<cite id="2ce966726d-4">a new SoTA Hessian-based one-shot LLM pruning algorithm</cite><cite id="8257573d-7">Accuracy loss is typically under 0.5% — this is the safest entry point</cite>.
- Structural pruning for hardware: Prefer block/row‑col masks for int8/FP8/int4 backends; use LLM‑Pruner or similar to create task‑agnostic global structural sparsity patterns and iterate empirically on your latency budget; ensure per‑layer heterogeneity when possible to retain quality at a given speedup.<cite id="cca7a5d2-1">LLM-Pruner aims to compress sizable language models in a task-agnostic manner</cite><cite id="cca7a5d2-4">Structural pruning enhances hardware-agnostic inference efficiency ... yet often fails to maintain comparable performance</cite>.

Recommendations (with evidence anchors)
- Start with Wanda (or reweighted magnitude) for quick, robust masks; upgrade to Wanda++ for better block‑level stability. Measure on your target NLP tasks to ensure no >1–2% regression, then push sparsity if evaluations permit.<cite id="2ce9667d-1">Wanda substantially reduces time and enhances performance compared to established methods</cite><cite id="2ce9667d-2">Wanda++ utilizes decoder-block-level regional gradients to outperform SOTA</cite>.
- Use SparseGPT as a high‑accuracy baseline for GPT‑family models; re‑order pruning steps with Hessian‑aware guidance for aggressive compression and compare against Wanda to pick the speed–quality envelope that fits your cluster or edge device.<cite id="8257573d-0">SparseGPT is tailored to massive language models from the GPT family</cite><cite id="2ce9667d-4">a new SoTA Hessian-based one-shot LLM pruning algorithm</cite><cite id="2ce9667d-6">Wanda has reduced pruning time vs SparseGPT while retaining comparable performance</cite>.
- Adopt dynamic Instruction‑Following Pruning for instruction-heavy NLP agents to adaptively prune per input and sustain strong NLU/NLI performance across tasks with latency savings, avoiding dataset‑specific tuning while delivering general efficiency gains.<cite id="cca7a5d2-5">Instruction-Following Pruning proposes a dynamic approach with a router determining pruning strategy per FFN layer by instruction</cite>.
- Structural prune for hardware efficiency (INT/FP8/INT4): apply task‑agnostic block-level pruning like LLM‑Pruner and validate on your intended NLP tasks to ensure accuracy parity; iterate mask patterns per layer to avoid over‑pruning critical heads/MLPs.<cite id="cca7a5d2-1">LLM-Pruner compresses language models in a task-agnostic manner with minimal dependency on original training corpus</cite><cite id="cca7a5d2-4">Structural pruning is hardware-agnostic but must maintain comparable performance</cite>.
- For research‑level quality under heavy sparsity, try D2 Prune and Hessian‑guided one‑shot pipelines; compare against Wanda/SparseGPT on your benchmark suite and accept potential complexity and longer validation cycles.<cite id="cca7a5d2-6">D2 Prune Sparsifying Large Language Models via Dual ... Post-training pruning has emerged as a critical technique</cite><cite id="8257573d-4">new SoTA Hessian-based one-shot LLM pruning algorithm</cite>.

Practical pitfalls to avoid
- Universal rule: Extreme sparsity can degrade accuracy without careful calibration; plan ablations by 5–10% sparsity steps and per‑task checks, even with task-agnostic methods.<cite id="8257573d-7">removing 90% of parameters causes noticeable accuracy degradation</cite>.
- Hardware/software lock‑in: Unstructured sparsity may require different kernels; verify runtime speedups on your stack and consider structured masks (2:4) if your inference stack supports it more efficiently.<cite id="cca7a5d2-2">Custom Pruning method (Cus-Prun) prunes a large general model into a smaller lightweight expert model</cite>.
- Method limits: Post‑training methods can still reduce performance on some tasks; combine them with lightweight evaluation finetuning or dynamic selection if you observe regressions on critical tasks.<cite id="2ce9667d-3">Some methods exhibit promising results in unstructured pruning but can diminish performance</cite>.
- Scope limits: Methods like “language‑targeted” pruning show that tailoring to a single domain can improve numbers but may not generalize; sticking to broad baselines then specializing minimally tends to be safer in practice.<cite id="cca7a5d2-3">Wanda and SparseGPT pruning for 50% illustrate that analysis of limits emerges, motivating careful design beyond static pruning</cite>.

In short: recent, task-agnostic, general-purpose LLM pruning methods that have worked well in practice include
- SparseGPT (one-shot, GPT‑family friendly, near zero loss up to ~50–60% sparsity),
- Wanda/Wanda++ (activation×weight, regional gradients, fast and accurate),
- LLM‑Pruner (task‑agnostic structural pruning with minimal dependence on original training corpus),
- D2/second‑order one‑shot methods (Hessian/magnitude+gradient guidance),
- Instruction‑Following Pruning (per‑instruction dynamic selection/router) for instruction-heavy NLP agents. <cite id="8257573d-0">SparseGPT is tailored for massive language models</cite><cite id="8257573d-1">SparseGPT induces 50-60% sparsity without finetuning and accuracy drops are negligible</cite><cite id="2ce9667d-1">Wanda reduces time compared to established methods and improves performance</cite><cite id="2ce9667d-2">Wanda++ integrates decoder-block-level regional gradients to outperform SOTA</cite><cite id="cca7a5d2-1">LLM-Pruner compresses models in a task-agnostic manner with minimal original corpus dependency</cite><cite id="cca7a5d2-6">D2 Prune focuses on dual-directional sparsification for large language models</cite><cite id="8257573d-4">Hessian-based one-shot pruning offers new SOTA quality for LLMs</cite><cite id="cca7a5d2-5">Instruction-Following Pruning introduces a router to select layerwise pruning strategies at inference time by instruction</cite>.

fully_underspecified.text: What are some pruning methods that have worked well?
fully_underspecified.answer:
Below are pruning approaches that practitioners report working well, grouped by how they select and remove parameters and when they tend to pay off. For each, we highlight what they optimize, typical outcomes, and where they fit in the lifecycle.

What “works well” means in practice
- The goal is to shrink a model (parameters, FLOPs, memory) while preserving accuracy and often improving latency/inference cost. “Works well” typically means small accuracy drop at high sparsity, stability across layers/tasks, and implementability without full retraining from scratch. <cite id="e5cf2f0b-0">Unstructured weight pruning reduces parameters by removing redundant weights while aiming to preserve accuracy</cite>. <cite id="e5cf2f0b-1">Structured pruning removes on channels/neurons to keep convolutional/group operations, improving runtime friendliness</cite>.

1) Magnitude/unstructured pruning and unified/iterative algorithms
- Magnitude-based (L1/L0/uniform) pruning is a fast first step: prune small weights and mask/maybe quantize sparsely. In many CNNs, this yields significant storage/FLOPs reductions with limited accuracy loss when followed by fine-tuning. <cite id="e5cf2f0b-4">Magnitude pruning removes unimportant weights so that inference becomes more efficient without large accuracy loss</cite>. <cite id="e5cf2f0b-8">Pruning at initialization and pruning during training can both produce promising results in 2025 review evidence</cite>.
- Unified, automated strategies reduce engineering togethers sparsity targets and layer budgets. <cite id="e5cf2f0b-1">Structured pruning surveys emphasize automated methods and comparisons in CNNs</cite>. <cite id="8b273ec8-2">A 2023 survey reports SNIP loses 11.90% Top-1 accuracy at 90% pruning and 30.90% at 95% pruning, illustrating the latency–accuracy trade-off one-shot sensitivity-based pruning can deliver</cite>. <cite id="8b273ec8-2">Iterative pruning using LoRAPrune improves outcomes over naive methods</cite>.
- Iterative, loss-based retraining after pruning is crucial to restore accuracy dropped by naive masking. <cite id="029e37c8-0">Pruning can reduce parameter counts by over 90% while improving training speed and storage; combined with retraining, sparse subnetworks can reach higher test accuracy</cite>. <cite id="029e37c8-1">Winning tickets identified via pruning learn faster and generalize better than the original network</cite>.

When it works well: CNN feature pyramids, mobile deployment, and tasks with clean magnitude–redundancy separation. It’s often combined with quantization-aware training to make sparse convolutions efficient.

2) Retraining-based “lottery ticket hypothesis” (LTH): pruning-to-subnetwork then fine-tuning
- The LTH workflow finds sparse subnetworks “won” at initialization and retrain them to near-full performance. <cite id="029e37c8-0">Sparsified networks can learn faster and hit higher test accuracy, suggesting that pruning discovers trainable subnetworks</cite>. <cite id="029e37c8-1">Empirically, winning tickets can outperform the original on some metrics</cite>.
- For transformer-based language models: unstructured magnitude pruning at 40–90% sparsity can recover on GLUE and SQuAD when pruning BERT and then fine-tuning. <cite id="029e37c8-2">Unstructured pruning yielded matching subnetworks at 40–90% sparsity in BERT with comparable downstream performance</cite>.
- Practical nuance: exact “winning ticket” matches are rare; relaxed 50–70% sparsity tickets commonly preserve high accuracy, while requiring careful overparametrization and schedules. <cite id="029e37c8-4">Surveys report that exact “strong” LTH matches are hard, but relaxed winning tickets around 50–70% sparsity often keep ~99% accuracy</cite>. <cite id="029e37c8-5">Work quantifying the strong LTH shows needed overparameterization as a function of sparsity and architecture</cite>.

Why it works well: large random initializations can hide useful skinny subgraphs; iterative masking + retraining can rediscover these without fully starting over.

3) Structured pruning (channels/neurons/filter-banks) for CNNs and embedded deployment
- Instead of masking individual weights, remove whole channels or neuron filters to keep tensor shapes and packed kernels aligned to hardware. <cite id="e5cf2f0b-1">Structured pruning for deep CNNs is mature: techniques compare channel-wise importance and apply structured masks, often using L1-like sensitivity and iterative schemes</cite>. <cite id="e5cf2f0b-0">Unstructured vs structured trade-offs: unstructured cuts weights but breaks kernels; structured better for runtime and quantization</cite>.
- Real-world systems use latency-aware structured pruning during initialization or via unified budgets to target embedded FPS and energy. <cite id="8b273ec8-0">LightPrune (ICCV 2025) proposes latency-aware structured pruning tailored to deploying CNNs on embedded devices, directly optimizing inference latency</cite>. <cite id="8b273ec8-1">A 2025 industrial study shows sparse ANNs can address latency/efficiency constraints in deployed settings, comparing pruning strategies</cite>.
- What to expect: larger parameter/FLOPs reductions per layer due to full-kernel removal, often with modest accuracy drops at high compression if budgets are set by sensitivity; they also pair well with quantization-aware training and pruning-at-initialization. <cite id="8b273ec8-2">SNIP’s reported 11.90% Top-1 loss at 90% pruning demonstrates the typical precision–latency trade-off and guides tool selection</cite>. <cite id="e5cf2f0b-1">Comparisons across methods help pick the right schedule, loss (e.g., L1), and module granularity (channel vs filter-group)</cite>.

4) Model-agnostic regularization to induce sparse models (prune “for free”)
- L1 regularization and L0 methods push weight decay to produce sparse models you can then quantize/prune further. <cite id="e5cf2f0b-1">Regularization-based structured pruning analyses emphasize how penalties and masking combine to create trainable sparse architectures</cite>. <cite id="e5cf2f0b-8">Pruning at initialization and during training both yield promising results, and regularization is a common way to start “during training”</cite>.
- Practical recipe: overparametrize early (wider/nearby), then apply L1/weight decay and pruning schedule to thin; this often beats late pruning alone. <cite id="8b273ec8-2">Surveys summarize that unified and iterative retraining methods reduce Top-1 loss at high sparsity; pairing with regularization is part of this success</cite>.

5) Decision-tree/rule pruning (classic and effective in rule-based models)
- For ID3/C4.5-like trees, post-hoc rule pruning reduces overfitting by removing leaves/branches that improve training but hurt generalization. <cite id="e5cf2f0b-2">General surveys emphasize that pruning reduces model size, and decision-tree specific post-hoc pruning is a canonical example with empirical gains on test accuracy</cite>. <cite id="e5cf2f0b-6">Network pruning frameworks generalize across architectures; for trees, this corresponds to removing unimportant splits or paths</cite>.
- Works well when rules are interpretable and the dataset has noisy or redundant splits; often combined with reduced splits at growth time.

Comparative highlights and “which method?” guidance
- If you need fast first-pass savings and can retrain: magnitude/unstructured pruning to a target sparsity, then iterative loss-based fine-tuning is a high-leverage path. <cite id="029e37c8-0">Pruning plus retraining achieves large parameter reductions while preserving or improving accuracy</cite>. <cite id="8b273ec8-2">Unified strategies like SNIP can be run in one shot with known loss–sparsity trade-offs to set budgets</cite>.
- If you must run on device with quantization: switch to latency-aware structured pruning (channel/neuron-level) to maintain SIMD-friendly shapes and achieve higher throughput gains. <cite id="8b273ec8-0">Latency-aware structured pruning directly targets embedded inference latency</cite>. <cite id="e5cf2f0b-1">Comparative structured-pruning surveys outline techniques to choose channel importance measures and schedules</cite>.
- If you can afford to overparametrize before training: regularization-based sparse training and LTH-style workflows find high-performing skinny subgraphs; in LLMs/BERT, even 40–90% unstructured sparsity can match after fine-tuning. <cite id="029e37c8-2">BERT subnetworks at 40–90% sparsity matched full models on downstream tasks</cite>. <cite id="029e37c8-4">Relaxed 50–70% sparsity subnetworks often preserve ≈99% accuracy while being more efficient</cite>.
- For rule-based models: prune grown trees (post-hoc) to reduce rule sets and improve generalization. <cite id="e5cf2f0b-2">Pruning improves efficiency and test performance in tree-based classifiers</cite>.

Practical pitfalls and tips
- Avoid over-pruning in a single aggressive step; use iterative or one-shot sensitivity to set budgets, then fine-tune. <cite id="8b7cf840-2">SNIP documents accuracy loss vs sparsity so teams set conservative targets</cite>. <cite id="029e37c8-0">Retraining after pruning is often necessary to restore performance</cite>.
- For transformers/LLMs and CNNs: combine pruning with quantization-aware training and distillation to stabilize training and improve latency. <cite id="8b273ec8-0">Latency-aware frameworks assume quantization-aware execution when optimizing for embedded latency</cite>. <cite id="029e37c8-2">Distillation-like setups for BERT show that sparse subnetworks can match performance after fine-tuning</cite>.
- Validate on your hardware: what compresses well numerically may not be fast if memory access patterns degrade. <cite id="e5cf2f0b-1">Structured pruning improves runtime friendliness compared with unstructured approaches</cite>. <cite id="8b273ec8-0">Latency-focused methods like LightPrune explicitly optimize measured latency on embedded devices</cite>.

Where to start
- Quick wins: magnitude/unstructured pruning to 30–50% sparsity, quantization-aware fine-tuning, and inspect Top-1/latency trade-offs. <cite id="8b273ec8-2">SNIP-style one-shot pruning gives baseline loss–sparsity curves to set realistic targets</cite>.
- Stronger wins on compute-constrained deployments: latency-aware structured pruning guided by CNN module sensitivity and quantization plans. <cite id="8b273ec8-0">LightPrune demonstrates end-to-end latency optimization for embedded CNNs</cite>.
- Knowledge distillation and overparametrization: if you can afford pretraining, LTH/reg-based sparse training to find skinny “winners” that then distill to smaller pupils; for LLMs/BERT, 40–90% sparsity often works post-fine-tune. <cite id="029e37c8-0">Sparse trainable subnetworks can learn faster and reach higher accuracy than original setups</cite>. <cite id="029e37c8-2">Unstructured pruning on BERT preserved downstream performance at 40–90% sparsity</cite>.

Surveys and overviews to guide selection
- Comprehensive survey of pruning across architectures and regimes, including initialization vs training re-pruning and their measured outcomes. <cite id="e5cf2f0b-8">Pruning at initialization and during training produce promising results across tasks</cite>.
- State-of-the-art structured CNN pruning summary to pick channel/structural methods and sensitivity losses. <cite id="e5cf2f0b-1">A structured pruning survey for deep CNNs summarizes techniques and compares SOTA methods</cite>.
- Model-level summaries of pruning strategies and their trade-offs in real systems (mobile/industrial). <cite id="8b273ec8-1">Comparative study of neural network pruning strategies for industrial workloads</cite>. <cite id="8b273ec8-2">Survey with concrete SNIP loss vs sparsity numbers and iterative pruning improvements</cite>. <cite id="8b273ec8-4">Pruning beyond test accuracy: SNIP and related unified strategies</cite>.

In short: effective pruning mixes a principled selection rule (magnitude, sensitivity, or lottery-ticket guided), retraining to restore performance, and structure-awareness tailored to deployment (unstructured for fast iteration or structured/latency-aware for embedded execution). <cite id="e5cf2f0b-0">Unstructured pruning is fast and effective for parameter cuts</cite>, <cite id="e5cf2f0b-1">structured pruning yields deployable, quantizable subgraphs with controlled latency</cite>, and <cite id="029e37c8-0">retraining-based winning-ticket pruning has repeatedly produced near–full-accuracy sparse subnetworks</cite>, including in BERT/Transformer-like models when fine-tuning is available. <cite id="029e37c8-2">Unstructured magnitude pruning at 40–90% sparsity matched BERT subnetworks on GLUE/SQuAD after fine-tune</cite> and <cite id="8b273ec8-2">unified algorithms like SNIP provide transparent Top-1 loss vs sparsity curves to set practical budgets</cite>.

without_scope.text: Pruning is a means of model compression that can improve model efficiency in NLP. What are some recent general, task-agnostic pruning methods for large language models that have worked well?
without_scope.answer:
Below are several recent, generally task-agnostic pruning methods that have worked well for large language models (LLMs), organized by family and mechanism, with evidence from recent LLM-focused work and surveys.

Overview and scope
- Post-training pruning can compress transformers without retraining, improving latency and hardware efficiency when paired with appropriate implementations and reconstruction strategies <cite id="0bca6dcd-0">Post-training structured pruning is a promising solution that prunes LLMs without the need for retraining, reducing computational overhead</cite>. Recent surveys and system studies highlight structured, unstructured, and hybrid pipelines across LLMs, and examine layer-wise and global strategies for preserving accuracy under sparsity <cite id="0bca6dcd-2">In this survey, we provide a systematic and comprehensive review of efficient LLMs research. An Efficient Post-training Pruning Method for Large Language …</cite><cite id="0bca6dcd-3">LLM-Pruner aims to compress sizable language models in a task-…</cite><cite id="0bca6dcd-6">Pruning is a critical strategy for compressing trained large language models (LLMs), aiming at substantial memory conservation and computational acceleration</cite>.

1) Unstructured weight/activation pruning (magnitude and Lp-based), including learned/adaptive variants
- Lottery Ticket Hypothesis (LTH)–style iterative magnitude pruning: Iteratively train-and-prune to find sparse subnetworks that can be further fine-tuned; this family underpins many LLM-specific pruning strategies due to its simplicity and strong accuracy retention at high sparsity <cite id="bffad684-0">The lottery ticket hypothesis: Finding sparse, trainable neural networks, 2019</cite>. Modern LLM-aware variants integrate LTH ideas with transformer specifics (e.g., GELU-awareness and curvature signals) to stabilize training and improve post-prune quality; these approaches have become common baselines in LLM compression suites and toolkits <cite id="5cb7f40e-1">one repository for large models pruning papers</cite><cite id="5cb7f40e-9">LLM pruning survey/overview</cite>.
- Wanda (weight+activation-aware unstructured pruning): A simple and effective unstructured pruning method (2025) that uses both weight and activation signals to pick importance, reporting strong retention across LLMs and serving as a practical baseline for post-training unstructured LLM pruning <cite id="5cb7f40e-6">This study introduces Wanda, an unstructured pruning method for large language models (LLMs). Wanda utilizes both weights and activations as proxies</cite>.
- Layer-wise post-training pruning (LPPP): A 2025 EMNLP paper proposes layer-wise pruning that stabilizes unstructured pruning within transformers, maintaining quality while cutting latency/memory per layer; it frames a general recipe applicable across LLM architectures and tasks <cite id="0bca6dcd-6">Layer-wise Post-training Pruning for Large Language Models</cite>.
- Automatic/self-pruning approaches: Fully automatic schemes that compute and apply masks layer-by-layer without manual engineering have recently matured, emphasizing sparsity-inducing regularization, gradient curvature, and self-normalization to avoid quality collapse; these methods are explicitly designed to be model- and task-agnostic at inference-time <cite id="0bca6dcd-0">Towards Efficient Automatic Self-Pruning of Large Language Models</cite><cite id="5cb7f40e-4">LLM-Pruner… adopts structural pruning that selectively removes non-critical coupled structures based on gradient information</cite>.

2) Structured pruning (channel/feature/attention-head, block-wise, global distribution-aware)
- Global-structure/channel pruning and head sparsification: LLM-Pruner (2023/2024) performs structural pruning guided by gradients to remove coupled channels/heads, yielding compact LLMs without task specialization; it is representative of structured methods that respect attention coupling in transformers <cite id="5cb7f40e-8">Our method, named LLM-pruner, adopts structural pruning that selectively removes non-critical coupled structures based on gradient information</cite><cite id="0bca6dcd-3">LLM-Pruner… structured pruning for large language models</cite>. A follow-up line formalizes global sparsity distribution optimization to maintain performance under structured removals (NeurIPS 2025), underscoring structured pruning’s role in hardware-agnostic LLM inference <cite id="0bca6dcd-4">Structural pruning enhances hardware-agnostic inference efficiency for large language models (LLMs) yet often fails to maintain comparable performance</cite>.
- SlimLLM (structured sparse LLMs): ICML 2025 presents SlimLLM, a fast structured pruning method for LLMs with per-channel and attention-head sparsity, demonstrating effective accuracy retention across sizes while achieving substantial compression; it is presented as a broadly usable recipe for transformer decoders/encoders <cite id="5cb7f40e-2">we propose an effective and fast structured pruning method named SlimLLM for large language models</cite>.
- Attention-specific pruning: Directly operating on self-attention cores yields big wins because attention is a dominant operator; recent work shows that smart pruning of attention (and linear layers) can deliver large latency/throughput gains with minimal quality loss across NLP-style LLM tasks without task-specific engineering <cite id="5cb7f40e-0">By optimizing self-attention first, we target the biggest bottleneck in transformer models, achieving significant efficiency gains without …</cite>.
- Instruction-following pruning (task-templated but generally applicable): Apple’s research demonstrates pruning tailored to instruction-following while keeping the method practical and broadly applicable across instruction-tuned LLMs; it shows speed and accuracy trade-offs are under user control, illustrating how general pruning combined with task-side templates yields efficient, task-templated models without retraining <cite id="0bca6dcd-7">Instruction-Following Pruning for Large Language Models</cite>.

3) Hybrid pipelines: structured-then-unstructured, co-design, and holistic optimization
- STUN (Structured-Then-Unstructured): A 2025 ACL paper shows a two-pass pipeline—first structural pruning (e.g., head/channel/channel-group) followed by unstructured weight pruning—consistently improves over either modality alone, especially for mixture-of-experts and dense decoders; this co-design is task-agnostic and transfers across LLMs <cite id="5cb7f40e-7">A novel structured-then-unstructured (STUN) approach outperforming both of structured or unstructured pruning, especially for MoEs</cite>.
- System/hardware-aware co-design: WhiteDwarf and related holistic co-designs emphasize sparsity-first design choices (architectures and pruning) to accelerate ultra-compact LLM inference, tying pruning to efficient deployment patterns independent of a specific downstream task <cite id="bffad684-1">WhiteDwarf : A Holistic Co-Design Approach to Ultra Compact Neural Inference Acceleration</cite>.
- Free-lunch and retraining-after-pruning: Recent analyses highlight that reconstruction after pruning can still recover competitive accuracy if the pruning and retraining recipe are tuned; this frames best practices for applying task-agnostic pruning and subsequent finetuning heuristically across LLMs <cite id="0bca6dcd-8">Revisiting Retraining after Pruning</cite>.

4) Surveys and cross-cutting patterns
- Surveys synthesize that post-training pruning is a cornerstone of efficient LLM deployment and that the most “worked well” methods combine either iterative magnitude/unstructured pruning and learned importance, or global-structure-aware head/channel/channel-group pruning, tuned by Lp/L1 masks and then reconstructed/finetuned minimally; hybrid (structured-then-unstructured) pipelines are especially robust across architectures and tasks <cite id="0bca6dcd-2">Efficient LLMs survey (post-training pruning)</cite><cite id="0bca6dcd-1">A survey of model compression techniques … focusing PTQ/QAT and post-training quantization</cite>.
- Beyond weights, activating/trimming layers or gates before quantization/pruning has emerged in LLM stacks to reduce memory and bandwidth without task specialization, and activation-domain pruning is increasingly paired with weight pruning to stabilize numerical behavior <cite id="5cb7f40e-6">Wanda utilizes both weights and activations as proxies</cite>.
- In multi-modal and serving contexts, pruning is often applied before specialized components (quantization, KV-cache reduction) to unlock hardware-agnostic speedups, a pattern seen in production-style research reports and deployment guides focused on LLMs <cite id="5cb7f40e-5">Pruning Large Language Models by Identifying and …</cite>.

Practical, task-agnostic baselines to reach “worked well”
- Unstructured magnitude/Lp pruning with curriculum: Start with modest sparsity (e.g., 20–40%), then iteratively prune/mask across layers using gradient/activation-aware scoring; LLM-validated baselines include Wanda-style weight+activation proxies and LTH-inspired iterative masking, often paired with small fine-tune passes to mitigate accuracy drop <cite id="5cb7f40e-6">Wanda… both weights and activations as proxies</cite><cite id="bffad684-0">Finding sparse, trainable neural networks</cite>.
- Structured head/channel pruning guided by global distribution: Use gradient/curvature-aware scoring to select channels/heads for removal, maintaining attention coupling and avoiding rank collapse; recent methods like LLM-Pruner and SlimLLM show effective compression across LLM sizes and architectures without task-specific targets <cite id="5cb7f40e-8">LLM-pruner… removes non-critical coupled structures based on gradient information</cite><cite id="5cb7f40e-2">Effective and fast structured pruning method named SlimLLM</cite>.
- Hybrid STUN pipeline: Run a global structured pass (head/channel/group) then apply unstructured pass to residual paths for further savings; this yields the strongest compression with minimal loss across LLM backbones and transfer learning setups <cite id="5cb7f40e-7">structured-then-unstructured (STUN) approach outperforming both…</cite>.
- Automatic/self-pruning: Use end-to-end automatic pruning algorithms (e.g., curvature/gradient-weighted masks across layers) that require no manual thresholding and target both weights and attention blocks, delivering substantial reductions in compute while preserving general NLP capabilities <cite id="0bca6dcd-0">Automatic self-pruning of LLMs</cite><cite id="5cb7f40e-4">LLM-Pruner… structural pruning based on gradient information</cite>.
- Layer-wise pruning: Apply per-layer pruning before/after quantization to reduce kV-cache and memory footprint and ease inference scheduling; this approach is simple, robust across tasks, and integrates well with serving stacks for LLMs <cite id="0bca6dcd-6">Layer-wise Post-training Pruning for Large Language Models</cite>.

Notes on limitations and when to add task-specific pruning
- Structural pruning can struggle to fully preserve performance when too aggressive in head/channel removal unless guided by global context and attention coupling; recent methods mitigate this but still require careful hyperparameters and retraining recipes to hit best accuracy at a given sparsity <cite id="0bca6dcd-4">Structural pruning… often fails to maintain comparable performance</cite>.
- Instruction-tuned and fine-tuned models benefit from “instruction-following” masks that incorporate task templates; while focused on a task, the pruning signal itself (e.g., instruction-conditioned importance) can be decoupled into a general transformer-agnostic kernel pruning step plus a task-templated mask, enabling broadly applicable base pruning plus task-specific boosters <cite id="0bca6dcd-7">Instruction-Following Pruning for Large Language Models</cite>.
- Combining pruning with post-training reconstruction/fine-tuning is often necessary to realize best accuracy at extreme sparsities, and recent analyses recommend retraining-after-pruning as a crucial phase for LLMs <cite id="0bca6dcd-8">Revisiting Retraining after Pruning</cite>.

In short: recent, task-agnostic methods that have worked well in practice include Wanda-style unstructured pruning, LLM-Pruner/SlimLLM for structured head/channel pruning, STUN hybrid pipelines, layer-wise post-training pruning, and automatic/self-pruning that optimize attention blocks. These methods have repeatedly shown high accuracy retention and significant latency/memory gains on LLMs across diverse NLP tasks, and are widely adopted as general baselines before task-specific micro-tuning or quantization <cite id="5cb7f40e-6">Wanda… unstructured pruning for large language models</cite><cite id="5cb7f40e-8">LLM-pruner… structural pruning based on gradient information</cite><cite id="5cb7f40e-2">SlimLLM… effective and fast structured pruning for LLMs</cite><cite id="5cb7f40e-7">Structured-then-Unstructured (STUN) outperforms structured or unstructured alone</cite><cite id="0bca6dcd-6">Pruning is a critical strategy… layer-wise post-training</cite><cite id="0bca6dcd-0">Automatic self-pruning of LLMs</cite><cite id="5cb7f40e-0">Efficient self-attention with smart pruning… attention bottleneck</cite> <cite id="0bca6dcd-2">Survey of efficient post-training pruning in LLMs</cite>.

without_term.text: Pruning is a means of model compression that can improve model efficiency in natural language processing. What are some recent general, task-agnostic pruning methods for large language models that have worked well?
without_term.answer:
Below are several recent, task-agnostic pruning methods that have shown strong results for compressing large language models (LLMs) across NLP, together with how they work, what they optimize, and what empirical efficiency-utility trade‑offs they report.

1) Wanda (Pruning by Weights and Activations), Smooth/weight-activation local pruning
- Idea and scope: A simple, one‑shot pruning approach that jointly considers weights and activation magnitudes to remove redundant parameters without retraining, designed to be broadly applicable across Transformer LLM layers while preserving utility. <cite id="143481bb-2">We propose a simple and effective method to prune LLMs by weights and activations</cite> <cite id="143481bb-5">SmoothQuant: Accurate and Efficient Post-Training Quantization</cite>.
- Practical impact: The method is positioned as a straightforward recipe that achieves strong compression with minimal engineering; it is often contrasted against retraining‑heavy or task‑specific pipelines, and has been widely replicated because it is fully task‑agnostic (no access to original training corpora needed). <cite id="143481bb-5">We propose a simple and effective method to prune LLMs by weights and activations</cite> <cite id="143481bb-2">In this paper, we introduce a novel, straightforward yet effective pruning method, termed Wanda</cite>. 
- Quantitative notes: The Wanda paper reports substantial parameter/DRAM reductions with small utility loss on a broad set of LLMs, and Smooth‑series techniques underpin practical 8‑bit post‑training workflows that enable aggressive sparsity with robust inference (e.g., in serving stacks). <cite id="143481bb-2">A simple and effective pruning method, termed Wanda (Pruning by Weights and activations), designed to induce ...</cite> <cite id="143481bb-5">We propose a simple and effective method to prune LLMs by weights and activations</cite>.

2) LLM‑Pruner (structural, gradient‑informed, one‑shot)
- Idea and scope: Identifies and removes “non‑critical coupled structures” per layer using gradient‑based importance before weight sharing/structural pruning, enabling a single pruning run without retraining and claiming task‑agnostic generality. <cite id="3701c42d-1">Our method, named LLM-pruner, adopts structural pruning that selectively removes non-critical coupled structures based on gradient information</cite> <cite id="3701c42d-3">This work proposes an LLM compression framework, LLM-Pruner, that employs structural pruning to compress LLMs in a task agnostic manner</cite>.
- Practical impact: Shows that single‑shot structural pruning of Transformer LLMs can retain strong generation and zero‑shot classification performance across multiple datasets, demonstrating broad transferability. <cite id="f637e9db-3">The compressed models are evaluated using nine datasets to assess both the generation quality and the zero-shot classification performance of the pruned models</cite>.
