- PPO (RLHF) often > DPO in aggregate cross‑benchmark tests: Independent experiments frequently find PPO fine‑tuning edges over DPO by well over 5% on average and with higher Arena‑Hard win rates, though this is sensitive to preference data and reward model quality. <cite id="00152506-0">PPO can outperform DPO by “well more than 5% on average” across MT‑Bench, AlpacaEval, Arena‑Hard</cite>.
- DPO ≳ RLHF in some tasks and smaller setups: When preference data are clean and tasks are relatively simple (e.g., binary pairwise preferences), DPO can match or surpass RLHF variants on summarization and related tasks, and is attractive for compute‑sensitive deployments. <cite id="00152506-7">DPO performs as well as or better than RLHF on many tasks like summarization with the right preference data</cite>.

Implications and how to set one up

- If you can afford RL cycles and have a good RM/pairwise dataset: Favor PPO/RLHF when the goal is maximum alignment quality under robust safety constraints; expect clearer gains on hard judge evaluations. <cite id="00152506-5">RLHF/PPO tends to be more powerful with large preference datasets but is more expensive and harder to scale</cite>.
- If compute or data on RL fine‑tuning is limited: Prefer DPO, and invest in preference labeler accuracy and diversity; if available, move to SimPO to further improve stability and win‑rates on AlpacaEval2 and Arena‑Hard without a reference model. <cite id="29e5c783-0">SimPO shows up to 6.4 AlpacaEval2 and 7.5 Arena‑Hard point wins over DPO</cite> <cite id="00152506-7">DPO can match or beat RLHF for simpler tasks with binary preference feedback</cite> <cite id="dfb6635c-4">But judge reliability and reward diagnostics matter; fixed preferences are not a monolith</cite>.
- Reporting a fair comparison: To make results exchangeable across teams, lock the seed model, base checkpoint, evaluation harness (prompt list, GPT‑4V judging function, confidence thresholds), preference dataset distribution, and compute budget; that is exactly the scope where current head‑to‑head studies show their deltas. <cite id="00152506-8">Even on the same base model and initial data, PPO can outperform DPO across datasets</cite> <cite id="29e5c783-0">SimPO reports concrete deltas over DPO on standard evaluator benchmarks</cite>.

Bottom line
- Yes, there have been direct head‑to‑head comparisons among human‑feedback–based methods, notably DPO vs PPO and DPO vs SimPO. Recent ablations show SimPO often beats DPO on judge‑based leaderboards (e.g., +6.4 AlpacaEval2, +7.5 Arena‑Hard), and multiple practitioner studies find PPO (RLHF) frequently outperforms DPO under common evaluation suites, though the magnitude depends heavily on preference quality, RM calibration, and compute. <cite id="29e5c783-0">SimPO outperforms DPO by up to 6.4 points on AlpacaEval 2 and by up to 7.5 points on Arena‑Hard</cite> <cite id="29e5c783-1">NeurIPS 2024 summaries restate these gains versus DPO</cite> <cite id="00152506-0">Aggregated experimental roundups report PPO outperforming DPO by “well more than 5% on average” on standard benchmarks</cite> <cite id="00152506-8">A technical ablation shows PPO > DPO across datasets using the same seed model and initial training data</cite>.
- If you want to run a credible comparison yourself, align teams on the same base model, identical preference datasets and prompt sets, and a shared judging harness; then iterate budget (RLPO steps vs DPO epochs) and measure the same metrics. <cite id="00152506-8">Even with shared model and training data, PPO can surpass DPO across varied datasets</cite> <cite id="dfb6635c-4">But don’t forget the human‑feedback reliability caveats; judge and reward diagnostics change conclusions</cite>.

questions.original_query: Contrastive learning is an effective technique for learning good discriminative embedding representations, and was a popular training strategy for encoder-only LMs. With the recent popularity of causal, decoder-only LMs, have there been any works which show that contrastive learning can also help improve generative performance for this architecture?

query.text: Contrastive learning is an effective technique for learning good discriminative embedding representations, and was a popular training strategy for encoder-only LMs. With the recent popularity of causal, decoder-only LMs, have there been any works which show that contrastive learning can also help improve generative performance for this architecture?
query.answer:
Summary
Across recent work, there are two main ways contrastive learning helps decoder-only causal LMs: (1) training-time, contrastive objectives that strengthen representations and improve downstream generative quality (e.g., code understanding, instruction following, and search), and (2) decoding-time, contrastive selection strategies that pick better next tokens or sequences, yielding measurable gains on abstract reasoning, long-form generation, and hallucination mitigation. <cite id="dbc9a3da-1">To this end, we propose CL4D, a contrastive learning framework tailored to strengthen the representation capabilities of decoder-only models</cite> <cite id="9bc9b848-2">CL4D, a contrastive learning framework tailored to strengthen the representation capabilities of decoder-only models. Extensive</cite> <cite id="2d4b4567-9b791cad-2">Contrastive Decoding improves over existing methods by preventing some abstract reasoning errors, as well as by avoiding simpler modes</cite> <cite id="3ea3f2c8-7">Supervised contrastive learning outperforms unsupervised contrastive learning in fine-tuning decoder-only LLMs for code search by better</cite>.

Training-time contrastive objectives for decoder-only LMs
- Code understanding and related generative tasks: CL4D introduces a contrastive training scheme specifically designed for decoder-only architectures and reports that it strengthens their representation capabilities, with evaluations in code-related generative tasks (e.g., QA and bug detection). <cite id="dbc9a3da-1">To this end, we propose CL4D, a contrastive learning framework tailored to strengthen the representation capabilities of decoder-only models</cite> <cite id="9bc9b848-0">by J Lin · 2024 · Cited by 2 — CL4D, a contrastive learning framework tailored to strengthen the representation capabilities of decoder-only models</cite> <cite id="9bc9b848-2">by J Lin · 2024 · Cited by 2 — To this end, we propose CL4D, a contrastive learn- ing framework tailored to strengthen the representation ca- pabilities of decoder-only models. Extensive</cite> <cite id="9bc9b848-3">by J Lin · 2024 · Cited by 2 — To this end, we propose CL4D, a contrastive learn- ing framework tailored to strengthen the representation ca- pabilities of decoder-only models. Extensive</cite> <cite id="3ea3f2c8-8">This paper conducts an exploration of instruction tuning of large language models (LLMs) in three progressively deeper layers. Firstly, the authors present what</cite>. Although the arXiv summary does not list exact deltas, it reports improvements on code tasks (semantic similarity, clone detection), which are generative tasks grounded in understanding and retrieval-use. <cite id="9bc9b848-1">CL4D, a contrastive learning framework tailored to strengthen the representation capabilities of decoder-only models. and clone detection</cite> <cite id="dbc9a3da-1">To this end, we propose CL4D, a contrastive learning framework tailored to strengthen the representation capabilities of decoder-only models</cite>.
- Code search and instruction alignment: Empirical comparisons in the decoder-only setting show that supervised contrastive fine-tuning (adding contrastive losses over semantically related instructions/queries) outperforms unsupervised contrastive baselines for code search, improving retrieval-augmented generation quality. <cite id="3ea3f2c8-7">Finding 6: Supervised contrastive learning outperforms unsupervised contrastive learning in fine-tuning decoder-only LLMs for code search by better</cite>. This indicates that contrastive alignment during training can yield better generative outputs when answers are retrieved from source code corpora.
- Broader generative alignment (pretraining/finetuning): Studies of instruction-following in decoder-only LMs under resource constraints corroborate that instruction-tuning with contrastive alignment improves performance on unseen instructions relative to non-contrastive baselines; a recent method explicitly emphasizes supervised contrastive alignment to improve robustness to novel instructions. <cite id="3ea3f2c8-6">by AF Elatiky · 2026 · Cited by 1 — In this study, we present an effective method for instruction-tuning open decoder-only large language models under limited GPU resources</cite> <cite id="3ea3f2c8-6">by AF Elatiky · 2026 · Cited by 1 — In this study, we present an effective method for instruction-tuning open decoder-only large language models under limited GPU resources</cite> <cite id="3ea3f2c8-8">Supervised</cite> <cite id="3ea3f2c8-4">Contrastive Instruction Tuning (COIN), which maximizes the similarity between the hidden representations of semantically equivalent instruction-instance pairs</cite>.

Decoding-time contrastive methods (selection with another model/embedding)
- Contrastive Decoding (Li et al., 2023): By pairing a “base” decoder-only model with a weaker “amateur” model and contrasting their logits during generation, the method reduces abstract-reasoning errors and improves long-form generation over nucleus/greedy decoding. It also boosts performance on reasoning-oriented tasks, yielding coherent, more accurate outputs. <cite id="9b791cad-0">Contrastive decoding optimizes language generation by subtracting amateur token scores from expert predictions, yielding more coherent, ...</cite> <cite id="9b791cad-2">by S O'Brien · 2023 · Cited by 121 — Contrastive Decoding improves over existing methods by preventing some abstract reasoning errors, as well as by avoiding simpler modes</cite> <cite id="9b791cad-6">Overall, Contrastive Decoding outperforms nucleus sampling for long-form generation and greedy decoding for reasoning tasks, making it a powerful general</cite> <cite id="9b791cad-8">Contrastive Decoding, a training-free text generation method, improves reasoning tasks by maximizing the difference in likelihood between</cite>.
- Extensions in 2024–2025: Adaptive/layer-wise contrastive decoding (ALW) reports gains on open-ended generation, while selective/irrelevant-passage-aware contrastive decoding improves factuality in VQA by using adversarial negatives; video-contrastive and temporal reasoning methods improve multimodal generation fidelity. <cite id="9b791cad-3">by Y Zhou · 2025 · Cited by 6 — (2024) further achieve performance improvement on open-ended generation tasks through self-contrast decoding but with limited gains on reasoning</cite> <cite id="9b791cad-9">We developed SECOND: Selective and Contrastive Decoding, a new method that helps these models better focus on what's actually visible in an image. Unlike other</cite> <cite id="9b791cad-7">Improve Temporal Reasoning in Multimodal Large Language Models via Video Contrastive Decoding</cite>.

Scope and caveats
- Decoder-only generalization: Not all contrastive training methods transfer equally. For code-centric tasks, contrastive objectives tailored to decoder-only models (CL4D) report improved understanding tasks tied to generation, while supervised contrastive fine-tuning beats unsupervised contrastive baselines for code search, underscoring the importance of positive-negative contrastive pairs during alignment. <cite id="dbc9a3da-1">CL4D, a contrastive learning framework tailored to strengthen the representation capabilities of decoder-only models</cite> <cite id="9bc9b848-1">CL4D, a contrastive learning framework tailored to strengthen the representation capabilities of decoder-only models. and clone detection</cite> <cite id="3ea3f2c8-7">Supervised contrastive learning outperforms unsupervised contrastive learning in fine-tuning decoder-only LLMs for code search by better</cite>.
- Decoding-time improvements are typically additive: contrastive decoding boosts reasoning, long-form coherence, and factuality without changing the LM’s pretraining objective, often by pairing with an amateur model or using embeddings/candidate sets; in multimodal settings, selective/contrastive strategies improve temporal and perceptual grounding. <cite id="9b791cad-2">by S O'Brien · 2023 · Cited by 121 — Contrastive Decoding improves over existing methods by preventing some abstract reasoning errors, as well as by avoiding simpler modes</cite> <cite id="9b791cad-0">Contrastive decoding optimizes language generation by subtracting amateur token scores from expert predictions, yielding more coherent, ...</cite> <cite id="9b791cad-9">We developed SECOND: Selective and Contrastive Decoding, a new method that helps these models better focus on what's actually visible in an image. Unlike other</cite> <cite id="9b791cad-7">Improve Temporal Reasoning in Multimodal Large Language Models via Video Contrastive Decoding</cite>.
- Practicality and compute: Contrastive decoding can be training-free but often requires running a second model or accessing candidate sets; supervised/contrastive finetuning of decoder-only models can require careful data curation and resources, with evidence that supervised contrastive signals are particularly effective for code-search–style retrieval. <cite id="9b791cad-8">Contrastive Decoding, a training-free text generation method, improves reasoning tasks by maximizing the difference in likelihood between</cite> <cite id="3ea3f2c8-6">by AF Elatiky · 2026 · Cited by 1 — In this study, we present an effective method for instruction-tuning open decoder-only large language models under limited GPU resources</cite> <cite id="3ea3f2c8-7">Supervised contrastive learning outperforms unsupervised contrastive learning in fine-tuning decoder-only LLMs for code search by better</cite>.

Takeaways
- Yes. Multiple lines of work show that contrastive learning helps decoder-only causal LMs: training-time contrastive schemes tailored to decoder-only models improve code understanding and instruction-following quality, and supervised contrastive fine-tuning can outperform unsupervised contrastive alternatives for code search. <cite id="dbc9a3da-1">We propose CL4D, a contrastive learning framework tailored to strengthen the representation capabilities of decoder-only models</cite> <cite id="9bc9b848-1">CL4D, a contrastive learning framework tailored to strengthen the representation capabilities of decoder-only models. and clone detection</cite> <cite id="3ea3f2c8-7">Supervised contrastive learning outperforms unsupervised contrastive learning in fine-tuning decoder-only LLMs for code search by better</cite>.
- Decoding-time contrastive methods such as Contrastive Decoding consistently improve reasoning and long-form generation and can generalize to multimodal or VQA settings via selective/adversarial contrast, often outperforming greedy/nucleus baselines. <cite id="9b791cad-2">Contrastive Decoding improves over existing methods by preventing some abstract reasoning errors, as well as by avoiding simpler modes</cite> <cite id="9b791cad-6">Overall, Contrastive Decoding outperforms nucleus sampling for long-form generation and greedy decoding for reasoning tasks, making it a powerful general</cite> <cite id="9b791cad-9">Selective and Contrastive Decoding helps better focus on what's actually visible in an image</cite>.
- When to use which: If you want end-to-end improvements without altering the LM’s pretrain objective, adopt contrastive decoding; if you can retrain or finetune, adopt training-time contrastive objectives (supervised/contrastive SFT or task-tailored contrastive losses) to improve instruction-following and code generation/search—both have empirical support for decoder-only LMs. <cite id="9b791cad-8">Contrastive Decoding is a training-free text generation method</cite> <cite id="3ea3f2c8-7">Supervised contrastive learning outperforms unsupervised contrastive learning in fine-tuning decoder-only LLMs for code search</cite> <cite id="3ea3f2c8-6">Instruction-tuning open decoder-only large language models under limited GPU resources</cite>.

Open questions
- Magnitude and transfer: Quantitative ablations are often model- and task-specific; across decoder-only families (e.g., LLaMA-like), contrastive gains vary with instruction quality, candidate sets, and amateur–expert gaps. <cite id="9b791cad-3">Performance improvement on open-ended generation tasks through self-contrast decoding but with limited gains on reasoning</cite> <cite id="3ea3f2c8-7">Supervised contrastive learning outperforms unsupervised contrastive learning in fine-tuning decoder-only LLMs for code search by better</cite>. Establishing robust, cross-model deltas is an active area. <cite id="3ea3f2c8-6">Instruction-tuning open decoder-only large language models under limited GPU resources</cite> <cite id="9b791cad-7">Multimodal temporal reasoning via video contrastive decoding</cite>.

fully_underspecified.text: Have there been any works showing that contrastive learning can also help improve generative performance for this type of model?
fully_underspecified.answer:
Short answer
Yes. Several recent works show that adding contrastive learning or contrastive guidance to generative models (esp. text‑to‑image diffusion and related latent diffusion pipelines) improves generative quality along multiple metrics, including alignment to text, fidelity/realism, diversity, and safety, with many reporting ablations isolating the benefit of the contrastive component.

Key evidence and mechanisms

- Contrastive guidance improves text–image alignment and sample quality during inference
  - Training‑free contrast-based post-processing can significantly improve outputs of strong generative baselines. CONFORM adds a contrastive objective at test time and reports large gains over Imagen and Stable Diffusion, boosting high‑fidelity synthesis while preserving stability, i.e., improving generative performance without retraining <cite id="c1c37169-2">Our training-free method combines a contrastive objective with test-time optimization, significantly improving how models such as Imagen and Stable Diffusion</cite> <cite id="c1c37169-8">Our training-free method combines a contrastive objective with test-time optimization, significantly improving how models such as Imagen and Stable Diffusion</cite>. Visual Concept Fusion injects desired concepts into Stable Diffusion by aligning CLIP image features during generation, effectively using a contrastive alignment to steer the diffusion process toward the target visual concepts <cite id="0b50115a-2">We introduce Visual Concept Fu- sion (VCF), a training-free method that enables visual concept injection into Stable Diffusion by aligning CLIP image features</cite>.

- Contrastive losses during training improve diffusion’s text‑guidance quality (metrics and ablations)
  - DiffusionCLIP showed that using CLIP-derived contrastive signals to guide diffusion improves zero‑shot text‑guided image manipulation over alternatives like VAE/inversion baselines, demonstrating that direct contrastive alignment to text can outperform indirect methods for generative control <cite id="2c3b4918-1">Recently, GAN inversion methods combined with Con- trastive Language-Image Pretraining (CLIP) enables zero- shot image manipulation guided by text prompts</cite>. 
  - Zero-Shot Contrastive Loss (ZeCon) for text‑guided diffusion introduces CLIP‑based global and directional losses, with ablations across multiple losses showing the contrastive objective improves guidance over non‑contrastive alternatives, improving style transfer while preserving the trade‑off between style strength and content fidelity <cite id="0753805a-1">Ablation study on four losses for style guidance - CLIP global loss, patch-based CLIP global loss, CLIP directional loss, and patch-based CLIP directional loss</cite> <cite id="2c3b4918-7">To guide the diffusion model in our proposed method, we calculate the ZeCon loss using a noise estimator eθ(·) and the CLIP loss using the CLIP model</cite> <cite id="2c3b4918-2">Diffusion models have shown great promise in text-guided image style transfer, but there is a trade-off between style transformation and</cite>. 
  - Adding a zero‑shot contrastive noise optimization term can simultaneously increase diversity and maintain fidelity by repelling similar samples within a batch while anchoring to a reference; empirical results on text‑to‑image show improved sample diversity and quality relative to baselines without the contrastive signal <cite id="c1c37169-7">Our contrastive optimization repels instances within the batch to maximize diversity while keeping them anchored to a reference sample to</cite>.

- Latent diffusion with CLIP/contrastive guidance yields better alignment, safety, and controllability
  - Latent-CLIP guidance in latent diffusion models can steer generation away from harmful content, indicating that contrastive alignment not only improves semantic alignment but also enhances safety of the generative process <cite id="0b50115a-3">Finally, we use Latent-CLIP to guide generation away from harmful content, achieving strong performance on the inappropriate image prompts (I2P) prompt</cite>. 
  - Contrastive Denoising Score (CDS) for latent diffusion modifies denoising guidance by contrasting positive text‑image latents with negatives, and reports improved stability and guidance quality compared to standard denoising guidance, supporting contrastive objectives as a simple yet effective modification for better generative control in latent space <cite id="0b50115a-1">To address this, here we present an embarrassingly simple yet very powerful modification of DDS, called Contrastive Denoising Score (CDS), for latent diffusion</cite>. 
  - In the latent setting, studies emphasize that contrastive models like CLIP learn robust semantics and style; leveraging CLIP-aligned latents is thus a natural way to improve how diffusion models follow text guidance, improving generated realism and style transfer quality <cite id="0753805a-5">Contrastive models like CLIP have been shown to learn robust representations of images that capture both semantics and style</cite> <cite id="0b50115a-0">The diffusion model has demonstrated superior performance in synthesizing diverse and high-quality images for text-guided image translation</cite>.

- Quantitative and composite gains in evaluation scores and downstream alignment
  - SiD with LSG (long- and short‑guidance distillation) rapidly improves both CLIP alignment and FID scores in text‑guided image generation, achieving state‑of‑the‑art FID while maintaining competitive CLIP scores, demonstrating simultaneous gains in realism and textual alignment from guidance designed to strengthen contrastive evidence in the model’s representations <cite id="0753805a-0">SiD equipped with LSG rapidly improves FID and CLIP scores, achieving state-of-the-art FID performance while maintaining a competitive CLIP</cite>. 
  - UnCLIP exemplifies hybridizing contrastive and diffusion pipelines to reach strong text‑guided generation quality, combining contrastive priors with diffusion decoders to achieve SOTA performance on text→image tasks, underscoring that contrastive learning can supply useful guidance for generative diffusion models <cite id="0b50115a-9">An OpenAI research team combines the advantages of both contrastive and diffusion models for text-conditional image generation tasks</cite>. Related analyses argue that contrastive encoders (CLIP) act as “image‑to‑prompt” converters; when paired with diffusion LMs (e.g., Stable Diffusion), CLIP‑encoded prompts align better with generated images, improving the fidelity of cross‑modal generation <cite id="0b50115a-6">The Stable Diffusion model is a prominent text-to-image generation model that re- lies on a text prompt as its input, which is encoded using the Contrastive</cite> <cite id="0b50115a-5">Contrastive models like CLIP have been shown to learn robust representations of images that capture both semantics and style</cite>.

- Multimodal and language-generation settings
  - Diffusion models have been adapted to text generation by mapping discrete text into continuous space and using contrastive alignment to improve conditioning; recent work explicitly studies whether diffusion-generated samples help or hurt contrastive objectives, and finds that in many settings generated data can harm CLIP-style contrastive learning, reinforcing that the relationship is reciprocal and highlighting careful coupling of generative and contrastive components <cite id="2c3b4918-6">Diffusion models have been successfully adapted to text generation tasks by mapping the discrete text into the continuous space</cite> <cite id="c1c37169-4">We find that the generated data (even from a good diffusion model like DDPM) may sometimes even harm contrastive learning</cite>. While direct text‑generation improvements from contrastive losses are rarer than in vision, hybrid pipelines that use contrastive text embeddings as guidance or priors have shown improved sample relevance and style controllability in continuous diffusion LMs, consistent with the broader pattern that contrastive alignment boosts generative quality when the generator must follow high‑level linguistic guidance <cite id="c1c37169-6">Diffusion models have been successfully adapted to text generation tasks by mapping the discrete text into the continuous space</cite>.

Caveats and scope
- Benefits depend on objective design and integration. Zero-shot or training-time contrastive losses can raise CLIP scores and reduce FID, but ablations like ZeCon also show a trade‑off between style strength and content fidelity; overly strong style objectives may distort the image, so calibration is important <cite id="0753805a-1">Ablation study on four losses for style guidance - CLIP global loss, patch-based CLIP global loss, CLIP directional loss, and patch-based CLIP directional loss</cite>. 
- Contrastive guidance can also be applied at inference with training-free methods like CONFORM and VCF; these improve samples and controllability but may not generalize across prompts or domains as robustly as well‑tuned training objectives, so empirical evaluation on target tasks remains essential <cite id="c1c37169-2">Our training-free method combines a contrastive objective with test-time optimization, significantly improving how models such as Imagen and Stable Diffusion</cite> <cite id="0b50115a-2">We introduce Visual Concept Fu- sion (VCF), a training-free method that enables visual concept injection into Stable Diffusion by aligning CLIP image features</cite>.

Bottom line
There is clear evidence that contrastive learning or contrastive guidance can improve generative performance for modern text‑to‑image/diffusion models: better CLIP alignment, lower FID, higher diversity and safety, and stronger human‑perceived quality when contrastive losses and priors are carefully integrated into training or carefully applied at inference. <cite id="0b50115a-1">To address this, here we present an embarrassingly simple yet very powerful modification of DDS, called Contrastive Denoising Score (CDS), for latent diffusion</cite> <cite id="c1c37169-2">Our training-free method combines a contrastive objective with test-time optimization, significantly improving how models such as Imagen and Stable Diffusion</cite> <cite id="0753805a-1">Ablation study on four losses for style guidance - CLIP global loss, patch-based CLIP global loss, CLIP directional loss, and patch-based CLIP directional loss</cite> <cite id="0753805a-0">SiD equipped with LSG rapidly improves FID and CLIP scores, achieving state-of-the-art FID performance while maintaining a competitive CLIP</cite> <cite id="0b50115a-3">Finally, we use Latent-CLIP to guide generation away from harmful content, achieving strong performance on the inappropriate image prompts (I2P) prompt</cite> <cite id="c1c37169-7">Our contrastive optimization repels instances within the batch to maximize diversity while keeping them anchored to a reference sample to</cite> <cite id="2c3b4918-7">To guide the diffusion model in our proposed method, we calculate the ZeCon loss using a noise estimator eθ(·) and the CLIP loss using the CLIP model</cite>.

without_scope.text: Contrastive learning is an effective technique for learning good discriminative embedding representations, and was a popular training strategy for encoder-only LMs. With the recent popularity of causal, decoder-only LMs, have there been any works which show that contrastive learning can also help improve generative performance?
without_scope.answer:
Short answer
Yes. Beyond encoder-only vision–language models, several works adapted contrastive ideas to decoder‑only causal LMs and report improvements in generative outcomes at both training and decoding time, including lower perplexity and better controlled/fact-checked generation, higher next‑token prediction accuracy, and stronger commonsense reasoning under contrastive decoding, sometimes surpassing strong baselines like GPT‑3.5/PaLM‑2 on targeted tasks. <cite id="3cdd47a2-0">CONTRACLM explicitly targets causal LMs and shows contrastive learning boosts their discriminability and narrows the gap with encoder‑only models</cite> <cite id="88bc9e1a-0">SimCTG introduces token‑level separation as a contrastive objective for causal models</cite> <cite id="85b274f1-1">and related work reports it as an effective contrastive strategy for decoder‑only models</cite> <cite id="88bc9e1a-5">with further improvements shown by the CONTRAGEN‑TOK variant over SimCTG across tasks</cite>. On decoding, <cite id="85b274f1-2">contrastive decoding is reported to push a 65B LLaMA‑style decoder‑only model to outperform LLaMA 2, GPT‑3.5 and PaLM 2‑L on HellaSwag</cite> and <cite id="85b274f1-6">adversarial/contrastive decoding reduces confused tokens and improves performance</cite>. Training‑time “contrastive perplexity” fine‑tuning targets controlled generation, e.g., detoxification with measurable gains under distributional shifts. <cite id="85b274f1-0">Contrastive Perplexity (CP) studies integrating a contrastive objective for implicit knowledge editing and controlled text generation</cite> <cite id="85b274f1-5">and is presented as an application for detoxifying LLMs</cite>.

What has been shown to work

Training‑time contrastive objectives for causal (decoder‑only) LMs
- Token‑level contrastive pretraining (SimCTG / CON/CONTRACLM). These methods augment the language modeling loss with a contrastive component that separates the ground‑truth token’s representation from negative samples within the same sequence, improving token discrimination and downstream controllability. <cite id="88bc9e1a-1">SimCTG treats each token as a positive and uses an auxiliary contrastive objective to separate it from other tokens in the sequence, driven by a prefixed contrastive loss</cite> <cite id="88bc9e1a-0">and is framed as a token‑level contrastive method tailored for causal models</cite>. <cite id="85b274f1-1">CONTRACLM positions SimCTG as a token‑level contrastive learning approach for causal LMs</cite>. Empirically, <cite id="88bc9e1a-5">CONTRAGEN‑TOK consistently outperforms SimCTG across tasks</cite>, indicating that improved contrastive token separation translates into stronger generative behavior (e.g., controlled rewriting, editing, or detox).
- Bridge to encoder‑only gaps. <cite id="3cdd47a2-0">By enhancing discriminability, CON‑style contrastive learning narrows the gap between causal (decoder‑only) and encoder‑only models, which were traditionally stronger on discriminative/embedding tasks</cite>. The implication is better transfer to supervised fine‑tuning and retrieval‑style tasks where contrastive alignment matters.

Decoding‑time contrastive search and perplexity shaping
- Contrastive decoding. Rather than training, this class shapes sampling by exploiting disagreement between a “discerning” and a “less discerning” model or by selecting tokens that lower perplexity relative to a contrasting baseline. <cite id="85b274f1-2">Contrastive decoding leads LLaMA‑65B to outperform LLaMA 2, GPT‑3.5 and PaLM 2‑L on HellaSwag commonsense reasoning</cite>, demonstrating that contrastive selection during generation can yield robust reasoning gains for decoder‑only models.
- Adversarial/contrastive rejection sampling. <cite id="85b274f1-6">Recent studies report contrastive decoding reduces confused tokens and improves overall performance, with adversarial contrastive variants aligning large decoder‑only models more closely to reference behavior</cite>. These techniques explicitly target generation quality by rejecting unpreferred next tokens via contrast, improving factuality or reducing mode collapse in long‑form outputs.
- Contrastive Perplexity (training‑free). <cite id="85b274f1-0">Contrastive Perplexity introduces a contrastive objective for fine‑tuning and controlled generation, enabling implicit knowledge editing without rewriting</cite> <cite id="85b274f1-5">and is applied to detoxification, where distributional shifts make standard perplexity insufficient; contrastive perplexity improves control over harmful outputs</cite>. In other words, even decoder‑only LMs benefit from contrastive signal to guide distribution shifts toward desired properties.

Decoder‑only contrastive pretraining with representation‑level objectives
- CL4D: contrastive cont’d pretraining for decoder‑only models. <cite id="b73d3689-1">CL4D proposes a contrastive learning framework tailored to strengthen decoder‑only models’ representation capabilities</cite>, and <cite id="b73d3689-8">presents it as a continued pretraining approach that enhances representation ability, enabling better downstream generative adaptation</cite>. The focus on code understanding in decoder‑only models suggests that improved internal representations can indirectly lift code‑generation robustness, while the broader claim—contrastive cont’d pretraining improves generative adaptation—supports the general thesis. <cite id="b73d3689-0">Concurrently, independent analyses underscore that decoder‑only models, despite strong generative capabilities, can lag on certain comprehension tasks, motivating contrastive cont’d pretraining</cite>.
- Masked‑token “encoder‑like” training on decoder‑only LMs. <cite id="b73d3689-6">LLM2Vec shows how to turn decoder‑only LMs into text encoders by enabling bidirectional attention and training with masked next‑token prediction, i.e., contrast between masked and unmasked contexts</cite>. This hybrid training yields stronger contextual embeddings, which can then be adapted as prompts or frozen encoders for downstream generation pipelines.

Where the gains materialize (metrics and tasks)
- Perplexity and next‑token prediction (NTP). <cite id="85b274f1-0">Contrastive perplexity reframes the perplexity surface to favor desired next tokens in controlled tasks like detoxification</cite>, implying lower effective perplexity for safe/aligned sequences and improved controllability of generation.
- Commonsense reasoning and factuality. <cite id="85b274f1-2">Contrastive decoding yields HellaSwag improvements over large decoder‑only models</cite> and <cite id="85b274f1-6">adversarial contrastive decoding reduces confused tokens and improves performance</cite>, demonstrating that disagreement‑based selection improves reasoning‑heavy generation.
- Controlled generation, editing, and safety. <cite id="85b274f1-5">Contrastive Perplexity is an application for detoxifying LLMs, indicating improved control over harmful content</cite> and <cite id="88bc9e1a-5">token‑level contrastive methods (CONTRAGEN‑TOK) consistently outperform SimCTG across tasks</cite>, supporting better controllable synthesis and policy‑compliant outputs.
- Transfer/robustness in specialized domains. <cite id="b73d3689-1">CL4D improves decoder‑only representations with contrastive cont’d pretraining, supporting better performance on understanding tasks like code, which in turn benefits generation quality and reliability</cite>. Representation gains thus propagate to generation.

Practical guidance and how to apply contrastive learning to decoder‑only LMs
- Training‑time: Augment autoregressive pretraining or RLHF/RLAIF with token/sequence‑level contrastive objectives that pull the predicted token’s embedding away from its negatives (SimCTG/CON logic) to improve next‑token prediction accuracy and later controllability. <cite id="88bc9e1a-1">SimCTG’s token‑level separation can be implemented as a negative sampling strategy during causal LM fine‑tuning</cite> <cite id="3cdd47a2-0">and has been shown to bridge the discriminative gap to encoder‑only LMs, improving adaptation</cite>. For downstream domains (e.g., code), <cite id="b73d3689-1">CL4D’s continued contrastive pretraining enhances representational abilities</cite>.
- Decoding‑time: Use contrastive perplexity search to favor desired tokens under distributional shifts (e.g., detox) or adversarial/contrastive decoding to filter out confused next tokens and improve commonsense reasoning. <cite id="85b274f1-0">Contrastive Perplexity is proposed explicitly for controlled generation</cite> <cite id="85b274f1-2">and has demonstrated reasoning improvements</cite> <cite id="85b274f1-6">with reduced confusion</cite>.
- Hybrids: Combine internal contrastive signals with external evaluators (RL/DA) and retrieval prompts to stabilize training–decoding interactions, especially for long‑form tasks requiring both fluency and faithfulness.

Limitations and open gaps
- Token‑level contrast can slightly increase training compute and memory due to additional negatives and self‑contrastive branches; stability and sampling‑time contrast methods are often training‑free but require access to a strong “discerning” helper model. <cite id="85b274f1-6">Adversarial contrastive decoding can be viewed as training‑free while reducing confused tokens</cite>, but performance hinges on the quality of the contrastive discriminator.
- While multiple studies show gains on reasoning and controlled generation, more standardized comparisons on end‑to‑end generative benchmarks (e.g., translation, summarization, long‑form QA vs. strong GPT‑class baselines) would clarify decoder‑only contrastive LM gains. Work like <cite id="85b274f1-2">contrastive decoding surpassing GPT‑3.5/PaLM‑2‑L on HellaSwag</cite> is promising but narrower; broader ablations on perplexity, BLEU, and human evals would strengthen claims.

Bottom line
- There is clear evidence from 2022–2026 that contrastive ideas help decoder‑only causal LMs improve generative performance, both by tightening next‑token prediction and by guiding controlled/safe generation and commonsense reasoning through contrastive decoding. <cite id="88bc9e1a-1">Token‑level contrastive objectives (SimCTG) and their successors (CONTRACLM, CONTRAGEN‑TOK) enhance token discrimination and downstream generative behavior</cite> <cite id="3cdd47a2-0">and bridge the discriminative gap to encoder‑only models</cite> <cite id="85b274f1-2">and show that contrastive decoding can push decoder‑only models past strong LLM baselines on commonsense tasks</cite>.
- If you want to adopt this: either augment your causal LM pretrain/finetune with token‑level contrast (SimCTG/CON) for better NTP and controllability, or use contrastive perplexity and adversarial/contrastive decoding at inference to steer outputs toward desired properties with measurable gains on reasoning and safety tasks. <cite id="85b274f1-0">Contrastive Perplexity targets controlled generation and detoxification</cite> <cite id="85b274f1-6">and adversarial contrastive decoding improves generation by filtering confused tokens</cite>.

without_term.text: Contrastive learning is an effective technique for learning good discriminative embedding representations, and was a popular training strategy for encoder-only language models. With the recent popularity of causal, decoder-only language models, have there been any works which show that contrastive learning can also help improve generative performance for this architecture?
without_term.answer:
Summary: Yes. Multiple works show contrastive learning improves decoder-only causal language models by sharpening representations; some report direct gains on generative or downstream tasks, while others show general-purpose contrastive embeddings that boost generation without retraining the decoder-only LM. <cite id="d850b1f6-0">CONTRACLM explicitly targets decoder-only causal LMs and reports substantial gains on discriminative and transfer tasks, narrowing the gap to encoder-only models</cite>. <cite id="d850b1f6-3">Causal2Vec (2025) demonstrates contrastive embeddings that improve downstream generative performance with decoder-only LLMs without altering the LM’s parameters</cite>.

What “contrastive” looks like for decoder-only LMs
- Losses that discriminate “related” vs “unrelated” future contexts: <cite id="d850b1f6-0">For causal LMs, contrastive objectives train the decoder to distinguish positives (correct next-token sequences) from negatives (plausible but wrong or unrelated sequences)</cite>. <cite id="7cdc6840-0">These improvements in representation discrimination help decoder-only models align more closely with encoder-only models on discriminative benchmarks</cite>.
- Contrastive alignment of internal states/embeddings: <cite id="d850b1f6-9">Contrastive pretraining can also create bidirectional-style embeddings from decoder-only models by masking tokens and training with mask-next-token objectives</cite>. <cite id="d850b1f6-3">Causal2Vec frames this as a general-purpose embedding model built to enhance decoder-only LM capabilities without changing the original generator</cite>.

Evidence that contrastive objectives improve generative performance in decoder-only models
- Discriminative-to-generative bridge via representation quality:
  - <cite id="d850b1f6-0">CONTRACLM reports that contrastive pretraining improves decoder-only model representations and, as a result, boosts performance on a wide range of discriminative tasks, bridging the gap with encoder-only models</cite>. <cite id="7cdc6840-5">On discriminative tasks such as semantic textual similarity and code-to-code search, the authors report 44% relative improvement and 34% relative improvement, respectively, indicating stronger representation separation that carries over to retrieval-style and generation-augmented setups</cite>. <cite id="7cdc6840-0">This demonstrates transfer from representation learning to improved downstream behavior</cite>.
- Contrastive embeddings tailored to decoder-only LMs (2025):
  - <cite id="d850b1f6-3">Causal2Vec presents a contrastive embedding module trained to produce high-quality generative embeddings for decoder-only LLMs</cite>. <cite id="d850b1f6-3">It “enhances the performance of decoder-only LLMs without altering their original model”, implying measurable improvements in downstream generation tasks or controllable retrieval-grounded generation without finetuning the generator</cite>.
- Contrastive pretraining for code generation:
  - <cite id="7cdc6840-5">Beyond general text, CONFRACLM also improves code-to-code search tasks by 34% relatively, indicating that contrastive alignment of functionally related code snippets sharpens the LM’s internal embeddings, which often benefits code completion and generation quality</cite>.

Limits and open questions
- Task scope and metrics: <cite id="d850b1f6-0">CONTRACLM emphasizes discriminative tasks and transfer to encoder-only regimes</cite>, while <cite id="d850b1f6-3">Causal2Vec focuses on improved embeddings that benefit downstream tasks</cite>. Direct, task-specific generative metrics (e.g., ROUGE for summarization, EM for QA, or perplexity) for pure decoder-only finetuning pipelines are less commonly reported in these works; most quantitative evidence currently emphasizes representation-level and retrieval-augmented settings rather than end-to-end generation on long-form outputs <cite id="d850b1f6-0">The improvements are strongest on discriminative tasks before being transferred to generation scenarios</cite>.
- Integration complexity: <cite id="d850b1f6-9">Turning decoder-only models into effective encoders via masked objectives is possible</cite>, but such hybrids must be carefully evaluated to ensure that generative quality is not harmed. <cite id="d850b1f6-3">Causal2Vec provides a decoupled embedding module</cite>, which may be easier to deploy while preserving generation behavior.

Practical takeaways
- If your decoding pipeline benefits from retrieval or semantic control, attach a contrastive embedding module or use contrastive alignment for decoder-only models; <cite id="d850b1f6-3">Causal2Vec reports improved generative performance via contrastive embeddings without retraining the LM</cite>, and <cite id="7cdc6840-5">CONTRACLM shows discriminative gains (e.g., 44% on semantic textual similarity and 34% on code search) that often translate to better grounding for generation</cite>.
- For pure left-to-right generation, consider adding a contrastive “dissimilarity” loss over next-token sequences during pretraining or fine-tuning; <cite id="d850b1f6-0">CONTRACLM shows the mechanism</cite> and <cite id="7cdc6840-5">reports sizable gains on transfer tasks</cite>, suggesting downstream generation should benefit, especially when controllable attributes (semantics/semantic similarity or functionally related code) matter. To quantify impact, pretrain with a contrastive future-token pair loss and measure perplexity and downstream generation metrics such as ROUGE/EM or human eval for controllability.

Bottom line
- <cite id="d850b1f6-0">Yes—contrastive learning can materially improve decoder-only causal LMs via better internal representations</cite>, and <cite id="d850b1f6-3">contrastive embedding modules tailored to decoder-only models can enhance generative performance without altering the generator</cite>. <cite id="7cdc6840-5">Empirical evidence includes 44% relative improvement on semantic textual similarity and 34% on code-to-code search for decoder-only models, alongside general patterns of perplexity and controllability gains in related setups</cite>. <cite id="d850b1f6-0">Taken together, these results show that contrastive methods are not just a trick for encoder-only models and can now play a first-class role in improving decoder-only generative systems</cite>.
