- Representative result: <cite id="c9467535-8">A recent study demonstrated statistical separation of single- and multiple-scattering components based on a Wishart random matrix, enabling discrimination and potential suppression of the multiple-scattering component in imaging</cite>. <cite id="c9467535-1">Cross-correlation techniques can discriminate photons multiply scattered from a single illuminating beam, attenuating MS contamination</cite>. <cite id="c9467535-6">Dynamic light-based imaging with digital camera detection can be designed for multiple-scattering suppression</cite>.
- Takeaway: Nonparametric/statistical characterization provides a route to suppress multiple-scattering contamination, complementing engineering methods in both static and dynamic light scattering imaging. <cite id="c9467535-8">Single- vs multiple-scattering components were statistically separated via Wishart analysis</cite>. <cite id="c9467535-1">Cross-correlation can discriminate multiply scattered photons</cite>.

3) Time-gating, streak imaging, and depth-resolved/confocal strategies
- Principle: Use temporal or angular diversity to separate ballistic or few-scatter components from multiply scattered/diffuse photons, often via time-resolved detection or streak imaging; in confocal/multiphoton microscopes, temporal/interferometric gating of coherence enhances axial discrimination.
- Representative results: <cite id="06c084e9-0">Depth-resolved imaging through turbid media can implement confocal discrimination combined with coherent time gating (via interferometry) to select singly-scattered photons and suppress multiple scattering</cite>. <cite id="06c084e9-3">To enhance delivery/focusing in turbid media, methods emphasize multiple scattering as the major limitation, with strategies including coherence and time gating</cite>. <cite id="06c084e9-2">Controlling multiple scattering via coherence/time gating improves deep imaging and focusing in turbid media</cite>. <cite id="06c084e9-1">Recent work on depth-resolved imaging shows that alternatives to streak cameras can expand the repertoire of turbid medium imaging strategies</cite>. <cite id="06c084e9-5">All-Photons Imaging uses a time-resolved measurement and novel signal processing to recover “all photons,” enabling imaging through volumetric scattering</cite>. <cite id="06c084e9-7">Ballistic imaging through strongly scattering media suppressed speckles via a supercontinuum source, indicating that spectral/spatial diversity can support cleaner detection of ballistic components</cite>. <cite id="c9467535-4">Harnessing forward multiple scattering allows local compensation of MS paths and produces 3D confocal-like images, demonstrating an algorithmic pathway to mitigate MS rather than simply suppress it</cite>.
- Takeaway: Time and angular diversity—via confocal, coherence-gated, time-resolved/streak imaging, and advanced processing—selectively attenuate multiply scattered components and restore effective depth resolution, with reports of improved signal quality and suppressed speckles in strongly scattering media. <cite id="06c084e9-0">Confocal discrimination plus coherent time gating suppresses multiply scattered components</cite>. <cite id="06c084e9-2">Coherence and time gating directly target multiple scattering limits</cite>. <cite id="06c084e9-1">Depth-resolved imaging methods reduce reliance on streak cameras while coping with scattering</cite>. <cite id="06c084e9-5">Time-resolved ‘All Photons’ processing mitigates scattering to see through objects</cite>. <cite id="06c084e9-7">Speckles are suppressed by supercontinuum-based collection of ballistic components</cite>.

4) Transport-of-Intensity/Phase Retrieval (TIE/OTF) and quantitative phase imaging under scattering
- Principle: Acquire intensity projections along defocus and solve a non-interferometric phase retrieval (TIE) to reconstruct weak phase from multiple scattering; modern formulations incorporate intensity variations and unknown boundaries for improved robustness.
- Representative evidence: <cite id="eb126e05-2">An improved TIE reconstruction algorithm properly considers intensity variations and unknown boundary conditions, addressing practical issues in phase retrieval under non-ideal illumination</cite>. <cite id="eb126e05-4">TIE-based phase retrieval uses the paraxial wave equation continuity to connect intensity defocus to phase, allowing recovery in challenging conditions</cite>. <cite id="eb126e05-3">Combining TIE with a transport-of-phase approach enables quantitative phase access without recursive assumptions, broadening applicability</cite>. <cite id="eb126e05-6">Zuo's tutorial summarizes that TIE provides a non-interferometric way to obtain quantitative phase from intensity-only measurements</cite>. <cite id="eb126e05-5">Early applications to electron microscopy showed how TIE-based phase measurement reconstructs weak phase despite strong noise, illustrating the robustness of phase retrieval to scattering conditions</cite>.
- Takeaway: In scattering media, TIE/phase retrieval can recover weak, sparse phase structures that carry diagnostic content (e.g., refractive index contrast), effectively suppressing the overwhelming diffuse MS background by focusing on defocus-linked phase information and advanced solvers. <cite id="eb126e05-2">Improved TIE solvers handle intensity inhomogeneities and boundary ambiguity</cite>. <cite id="eb126e05-4">Defocus-linked phase-intensity relations enable MS-robust phase retrieval</cite>. <cite id="eb126e05-6">Non-interferometric quantitative phase imaging via TIE is feasible from intensity-only data</cite>.

5) Nonlinear microscopy (two-photon, multiphoton) with time gating in turbid tissue
- Principle: Use near-infrared multiphoton excitation to increase scattering mean-free-path and axial selectivity while applying time or confocal gating to suppress out-of-focus multiple scattering.
- Representative evidence: <cite id="06c084e9-3">Microscopic imaging in turbid media points out that when optical scattering is weak, two-photon excitation improves imaging; for highly scattering media, time-gated optical detection is recommended to suppress scattered photons</cite>. <cite id="06c084e9-4">Tissue-compatible two-photon excitation enables deep intact-tissue imaging, leveraging longer wavelengths relative to scattering</cite>. <cite id="c9467535-5">Surveys on multiple light scattering describe its role in optical imaging modalities (medical imaging and random lasers), underscoring how scattering dictates contrast and depth</cite>.
- Takeaway: Tuning excitation wavelength and adding time-domain gating within multiphoton architectures increases effective penetration and reduces MS blurring, enabling higher-quality volumetric imaging in strongly scattering biological media. <cite id="06c084e9-3">Two-photon excitation excels at weak scattering; time-gated detection is crucial in highly scattering media to suppress scattered photons</cite>. <cite id="06c084e9-4">Two-photon microscopy enables whole-organ imaging despite scattering</cite>.

6) Coherence gating and interferometric variants for suppression
- Principle: Discriminate path lengths via interference within a gating window (autocorrelation/low-coherence), attenuating multiply scattered paths that fall outside the coherence time window.
- Representative results: <cite id="06c084e9-0">Coherence-gated imaging (often confocal) gates singly scattered photons by interferometry to reduce MS contributions</cite>. <cite id="06c084e9-2">Coherence and time gating are highlighted as central to overcoming multiple scattering as the dominant limitation for deep imaging and focusing</cite>.
- Takeaway: Interferometric or noninterferometric coherence-domain gating narrows temporal/axial support, which suppresses MS and stabilizes axial resolution and lateral image quality at depth. <cite id="06c084e9-0">Interferometric time gating selects singly scattered photons and suppresses multiple scattering</cite>.

7) Algorithmic “harnessing” of forward multiple scattering for imaging
- Principle: Rather than purely suppressing, forward MS can be modeled and compensated locally to reconstruct high-fidelity images. In turbid layers or 3D particle fields, learned or physics-informed models recover structure by accounting for scattering transport locally.
- Representative evidence: <cite id="c9467535-4">A 2024 Nature Communications method harnesses forward multiple scattering to enable local compensation of forward MS paths, producing a 3D confocal image of the sample—effectively mitigating MS without discarding it</cite>.
- Takeaway: Learned/inverse-scattering models and forward-scattering-aware priors can reconstruct images by explicitly compensating MS, achieving confocal-like quality under strong scattering conditions. <cite id="c9467535-4">Local compensation of multiple-scattering paths yields 3D confocal-like images</cite>.

8) Application-focused: OCT and in vivo optical imaging under MS
- Principle: Use specialized detection and modeling to remove MS-induced noise and restore image fidelity in tissue.
- Representative example: <cite id="c9467535-2">A 2024 in vivo optical coherence tomography study demonstrates a method that reduces the noise caused by multi-scattering photons in OCT images, directly targeting MS artifacts in clinical-relevant conditions</cite>.
- Takeaway: For label-free microscopy and tomography in complex media, MS noise can be reduced through tailored signal processing or model-based denoising, improving structural visibility in vivo. <cite id="c9467535-2">Multi-scattering photon noise is reduced in in vivo OCT images</cite>.

Cross-cutting notes and practical recommendations
- Combining modalities often yields the best suppression. For example, structured-illumination contrast control paired with time gating or phase reconstruction can suppress diffuse MS while retaining weak phase/axial information. <cite id="c9467535-0">Speckle-contrast–based suppression of diffuse light can raise image contrast by up to 25 percentage points</cite>; <cite id="06c084e9-0">coherence/time gating then further filters out non-ballistic components</cite>; <cite id="eb126e05-2">and robust TIE solvers recover phase even with intensity inhomogeneities</cite>.
- Recent algorithmic/hardware advances emphasize choosing between suppression and compensation. <cite id="c9467535-4">Forward-scattering compensation can recover 3D structure</cite>, while <cite id="06c084e9-7">spectrally broad, speckle-suppressed collection</cite> or <cite id="06c084e9-5">time-resolved ‘All Photons’ processing</cite> preferentially retain useful components.

Representative papers to start with (across categories)
- Structured illumination and contrast control: <cite id="c9467535-0">Structured-illumination imaging: suppression of diffuse (multiple-scattered) light boosts contrast from 55% to 80%</cite>; <cite id="c9467535-9">SLIPI: multiply scattered light is diminished, improving contrast and quality in scattering media</cite>.
- Statistical separation: <cite id="c9467535-8">Statistical separation of single- vs multiple-scattering via Wishart matrix analysis</cite>; <cite id="c9467535-1">Cross-correlation discrimination of multiply scattered photons</cite>; <cite id="c9467535-6">Multiple-scattering suppression with digital camera-based DLS detection schemes</cite>.
- Time gating, confocal, streak: <cite id="06c084e9-0">Confocal plus coherent time-gated interferometric discrimination suppresses MS</cite>; <cite id="06c084e9-2">Coherence and time gating overcome MS limits for deep imaging/focusing</cite>; <cite id="06c084e9-1">Depth-resolved imaging via non-streak strategies for turbid media</cite>; <cite id="06c084e9-5">All-Photons Imaging: uses time-resolved acquisition and processing to see through scattering</cite>; <cite id="06c084e9-7">Ballistic imaging through strong scattering with speckle suppression</cite>.
- Phase/TIE under scattering: <cite id="eb126e05-2">Improved TIE reconstruction considering intensity variations and boundaries</cite>; <cite id="eb126e05-4">TIE formalism for phase retrieval from intensity defocus in scattering environments</cite>; <cite id="eb126e05-6">Tutorial on TIE for noninterferometric quantitative phase imaging</cite>; <cite id="eb126e05-5">Electron TIE illustrates phase recovery with strong noise</cite>.
- Multiphoton with time gating: <cite id="06c084e9-3">Two-photon excitation excels in weak-scattering regimes; time-gated detection is necessary in highly scattering media to suppress scattered photons</cite>; <cite id="06c084e9-4">Multiphoton microscopy surveys</cite>.
- Algorithmic compensation of MS: <cite id="c9467535-4">Harness forward multiple scattering to locally compensate paths and obtain 3D confocal-like images</cite>.
- In vivo OCT denoising under MS: <cite id="c9467535-2">Method reduces MS-induced noise in in vivo OCT</cite>.

How to choose among methods
- For quantitative phase and nano/micro-structural imaging of weakly scattering samples, use TIE/phase retrieval with intensity-robust solvers. <cite id="eb126e05-2">Robust TIE accounts for intensity variations and unknown boundaries</cite>.
- For turbid biological tissue where depth matters, combine time-domain discrimination and structured illumination or coherence gating. <cite id="06c084e9-0">Confocal coherent time gating selects single-scattered photons</cite>, <cite id="06c084e9-2">coherence/time gating alleviates MS</cite>, <cite id="c9467535-9">SLIPI boosts contrast</cite>.
- For speckle-dominated imaging of complex media, apply statistical separation and/or decorrelation strategies. <cite id="c9467535-8">Wishart-based separation of single vs multiple scatterers</cite>, <cite id="c9467535-1">cross-correlation to filter MS</cite>, <cite id="c9467535-6">dynamic light camera-based MS suppression</cite>.

In summary, modern suppression strategies span illumination engineering (SLIPI), temporal/interferometric gating (confocal/OCT), statistical phase separation, time-resolved/streak and speckle-aware imaging, and non-interferometric phase retrieval—often combined to recover useful signal while attenuating multiply scattered light. <cite id="c9467535-0">Speckle-contrast–based suppression has shown quantitative gains in contrast</cite>, <cite id="06c084e9-0">coherent time gating provides single-path selectivity</cite>, <cite id="eb126e05-2">TIE solvers recover weak phase in non-ideal conditions</cite>, and <cite id="c9467535-4">forward-scattering compensation can reconstruct confocal-like 3D images</cite>. For biomedical and industrial scattering imaging, selecting a combination of these methods—tuned to scattering strength, depth, and required contrast—yields practical suppression of multiple scattering effects. <cite id="c9467535-2">In vivo OCT demonstrates MS noise reduction in real conditions</cite>.

fully_underspecified.text: Find some papers about methods to reduce scattering effects on imaging
fully_underspecified.answer:
Below is a curated set of papers and reviews on techniques to reduce scattering effects in imaging, organized by modality and method family. Each entry highlights what kind of scattering is targeted, the method, and typical strategies for mitigation with concrete evidence where available.

Optical and microscopy imaging (single-photon and polarimetric)
- Surveys and principles in scattering media
  - Polarimetric Imaging Through Scattering Media: A Review. <cite id="fda466f8-0">Results show that scattering decreases with increased wavelength; based on this wavelength dependence, the authors propose wavelength-selection strategies to improve image formation through scattering media</cite>. <cite id="fda466f8-5">The review synthesizes recent development in polarimetric imaging techniques aimed at tackling scattering-induced blurring and loss of polarization contrast</cite>.
  - Imaging in Scattering Media (Boston University Tian Lab overview). <cite id="fda466f8-4">Beam-propagation-method (BPM) reconstruction significantly outperforms single-scattering models when object/scene changes or scatterer displacements are present, indicating that full or physical-model-based reconstructions can recover structure that simple single scattering models miss</cite>.
  - Microscopic Imaging and Spectroscopy with Scattered Light (review). <cite id="fda466f8-2">Describes methodologies that exploit scattered light (e.g., transport-of-intensity equation, speckle correlation) and how to separate useful signal from excess scattering, including biological demonstrations</cite>.
  - Polarimetric Imaging Through Scattering Media review (cross-reference). <cite id="fda466f8-5">Covers how polarimetry provides channels that are less degenerate under scattering and how algorithms and hardware can be co-designed to suppress scattering-induced degradation</cite>.

- Hardware and wavefront control to conquer multiple scattering
  - Wavefront shaping as a versatile toolkit (The Innovation). <cite id="f18f75f6-0">Wavefront shaping can restore optical focusing and imaging through multimode scattering media by optimally controlling the input field; reported applications include optical focusing and imaging through strongly scattering fibers and tissues</cite>.
  - Wavefront shaping improves transparency of scattering media (PMC). <cite id="f18f75f6-2">By optimizing the input wavefront or inverting the transmission matrix, wavefront shaping compensates distortions and increases penetration and image quality in diffusive media</cite>.
  - Wavefront shaping practical performance. <cite id="f18f75f6-3">A practical wavefront shaping method controls thousands of incident modes and can form a focus up to 1000× stronger in a thick scattering medium, indicating strong suppression of multiple scattering losses en route to the focal spot</cite>.

- Computational optics for scattering suppression and imaging deeper layers
  - Scattering-reduced imaging of spheroids via refractive index engineering (Optica BOE). <cite id="fda466f8-3">Refractive-index–based scattering management allows resolving deep spheroid structures that are otherwise invisible in confocal laser scanning microscopy, requiring no additional hardware and effectively mitigating out-of-focus/long-path scattering</cite>.
  - Scattering-suppressed optical imaging concepts. <cite id="f18f75f6-1">Turbidity from multiple light scattering can be harnessed with tailored phase elements (“scattering lens/plate”) to achieve optical imaging through thick or turbid media</cite>.
  - Computational optics framing. <cite id="f18f75f6-4">A computational optics analysis shows that combining spatial, angular, and spectral degrees of freedom with appropriate constraints can effectively “inpaint/regularize” through-scattering images</cite>.

Ultrasound imaging
- Speckle and multiple-scattering mitigation via compounding and motion
  - Frequency and angular compounding for multiplicative speckle reduction. <cite id="cda3cfdd-0">Combining frequency and angle compounding provides a multiplicative reduction in speckle, addressing both Rayleigh scatterer fluctuations and angle-dependent speckle decorrelation to improve contrast</cite>. <cite id="cda3cfdd-2">Spectral compounding reduces speckle noise by about 2–3× and markedly improves image quality in motion sequences</cite>.
  - Motion-compounding method. <cite id="cda3cfdd-1">A motion-compounding technique fuses ultrasound frames acquired under controlled motion to suppress speckle while preserving flow/strain information</cite>. <cite id="cda3cfdd-4">Compound images enable accurate motion assessment with improved visualization versus single-frame images</cite>.
  - Quantitative synthesis of ultrasound speckle suppression. <cite id="cda3cfdd-5">A review of 97 studies concludes that both conventional filters and modern machine learning can reduce speckle, with trade-offs in preserving tissue boundaries and introduction of bias</cite>. <cite id="cda3cfdd-6">An unsupervised deep-learning framework (speckle-to-speckle) demonstrates speckle and noise suppression on clinical ultrasound without paired ground truth</cite>. <cite id="cda3cfdd-7">A holistic enhancement approach simultaneously improves ultrasound resolution and noise suppression, addressing both blur and speckle artifacts from scattering and limited aperture</cite>.

- Polarization and scattering matrix approaches
  - Speckle-covariance/Scattering Matrix Methods. <cite id="cda3cfdd-3">Speckle–correlation scattering matrix (SSM/SSCM) techniques provide a principled framework to separate specular/structured scatter from isotropic speckle and can be implemented with holography/microscopy to improve contrast</cite>.

X-ray and CT imaging (beam hardening and scattering artifact reduction)
- Beam hardening vs. scattering in polychromatic CT
  - Mechanism and impact. <cite id="9bd6ce4f-8">Beam hardening arises when a polychromatic X-ray beam passes through an object, preferentially transmitting higher energies and causing cupping, stripe, and streak artifacts that resemble or co-occur with scattering-induced blurring</cite>.
  - Practical correction overview. <cite id="9bd6ce4f-9">Projection- or sinogram-domain beam-hardening correction maps polychromatic projections to an ensemble of monochromatic ones to remove energy dependence before reconstruction</cite>.

- Energy-resolved and virtual monochromatic imaging to mitigate beam hardening
  - Dual-energy and monochromatic imaging. <cite id="9bd6ce4f-0">Virtual monochromatic imaging (VMI) reduces beam-hardening artifacts and enables more quantitative attenuation (e.g., iodine quantification), with clinical utility reported across applications</cite>. <cite id="9bd6ce4f-6">Virtual monochromatic CT synthesized in the projection domain can, in principle, fully eliminate beam-hardening artifacts</cite>. <cite id="9bd6ce4f-5">VMI approaches that minimize CT number variations show improved beam-hardening reduction in practice</cite>. <cite id="9bd6ce4f-3">Dual-energy CT uses two energies to derive virtual monochromatic images and reduce beam hardening</cite>.
  - Novel algorithms for beam-hardening correction. <cite id="9bd6ce4f-1">A new beam-hardening correction in the projection domain addresses polychromatic effects and reduces artifacts in reconstructed images by better modeling and mapping lower-energy absorption</cite>.

- Anti-scatter hardware/software strategies
  - Anti-scatter grids and system trade-offs. <cite id="fda466f8-8">Anti-scatter grids reduce scattered X-rays in radiography but introduce their own artifacts and modulate primary beam; proper design and calibration are needed to optimize SNR and spatial resolution</cite>. <cite id="fda466f8-1">A scoping review of X-ray scatter correction software summarizes algorithmic approaches to model and subtract Compton-scatter components, complementing hardware-based grids and collimation</cite>.
  - Practical workflow guidance. <cite id="fda466f8-8">Beam geometry adjustments (incident angle, collimation) can reduce scatter-induced artifacts; selecting appropriate grid types and distances mitigates grid shadowing and resolution loss</cite>. <cite id="fda466f8-7">Optimizing beam collimation/angle and material/energy selection reduces beam hardening and scattering simultaneously</cite>.

- Practical and didactic resources
  - Mechanism-focused overviews. <cite id="9bd6ce4f-8">Beam hardening is a polychromatic effect producing cupping/streaks that can overlap with geometric and multiple scattering streaks; recognition is key to choosing corrective measures</cite>. <cite id="9bd6ce4f-2">Beam hardening is a pervasive artifact across CT scales (micro to clinical), requiring careful calibration, dual-energy strategies, or energy-resolved detectors</cite>.

Computational and deep-learning mitigation across modalities
- Regularized and model-based inverse methods
  - Physical-model reconstruction for scattering media. <cite id="fda466f8-4">BPM-based reconstructions better capture multiple scattering transport and can track changes in scatterer distribution, improving restoration beyond single-scattering approximations</cite>.
  - In-scattering imaging and denoising. <cite id="fda466f8-3">Refractive index–designed scattering management enables denoising-like effects on deep layers by engineering how light is collected/filtered through the specimen</cite>.
  - Speckle-covariance based filtering. <cite id="cda3cfdd-3">Speckle-correlation scattering matrix frameworks can filter multiplicative speckle while preserving structured features, providing strong contrast improvements in coherent-scattering-limited imaging</cite>.
  - Deep-learning for ultrasound speckle. <cite id="cda3cfdd-6">An unsupervised S2S framework reduces speckle and noise on clinical ultrasound without reference data, showing practical applicability</cite>. <cite id="cda3cfdd-7">Joint resolution–noise enhancement improves both sharpness and noise properties, suggesting learned priors tailored to speckle physics</cite>.

- Cross-modal practical mitigation strategies (microscopy)
  - Design-of-experiment mitigation. <cite id="fda466f8-9">Reducing excitation numerical aperture, using differential interference contrast or confocal confocal strategies, adding pinholes or spectral filters, and optimizing detector bandwidth are standard methods to mitigate scattered light, reduce blooming, and improve axial separation</cite>.

Representative “hardware trick” and algorithm co-design
- Scattering-managed optics for biological imaging. <cite id="fda466f8-3">Refocusing deep layers in spheroids via refractive-index engineering demonstrates that tailored phase/scattering elements can selectively attenuate harmful multiple-scattering paths while preserving useful rays, improving axial resolution and contrast</cite>. <cite id="f18f75f6-1">Optical systems using a “scattering lens/plate” demonstrate that carefully controlled multiple scattering can actually deliver usable images in turbid conditions</cite>.
- Wavefront shaping for deep focus. <cite id="f18f75f6-3">By shaping incident modes to match the inverse of the medium, wavefront shaping can create foci up to 1000× stronger inside thick scattering media, effectively countering extinction due to multiple scattering</cite>. <cite id="f18f75f6-2">In practice, transmission-matrix inversion yields improved transmission and image fidelity through diffusers</cite>.

Selected practical/algorithmic checklists by modality

Optical microscopy and endoscopy
- Choose lower scattering excitation (longer wavelength) within tissue windows, but account for absorption and autofluorescence trade-offs. <cite id="fda466f8-0">Scattering decreases with wavelength; wavelength selection improves imaging through scattering media</cite>.
- Use polarization-aware detection or encoding to separate channels less affected by scattering. <cite id="fda466f8-5">Polarimetric channels are less degenerate under scattering; algorithms and hardware exploit this to suppress artifacts</cite>.
- Apply model-based or deep learning reconstructions with total variation or scattering-transport models. <cite id="fda466f8-4">BPM reconstructions outperform single-scattering models</cite>. <cite id="fda466f8-3">Refractive-index–based scattering management yields deep-layer visibility</cite>.
- Control the NA and collect/weight multi-angle information to trade speckle for depth discrimination. <cite id="fda466f8-9">Reduced NA, angular compounding, spectral selection mitigate scattered light and improve separation of layers</cite>.

Ultrasound
- Use spectral/angular compounding to decorrelate speckle and lower variance, with quantitative gains up to 2–3× in speckle reduction. <cite id="cda3cfdd-0">Frequency and angle compounding yields multiplicative speckle reduction</cite>. <cite id="cda3cfdd-2">Spectral compounding reduces speckle 2–3× while preserving dynamics</cite>.
- Fuse motion (mechanical/thermal or tracking) to average over speckle and recover structure. <cite id="cda3cfdd-1">Motion compounding improves visualization and accurate motion estimation</cite>.
- Combine physics-aware pre-processing (speckle covariance) with deep networks when ground truth is unavailable. <cite id="cda3cfdd-3">SSC/SSCM methods provide robust subtraction of multiplicative speckle</cite>. <cite id="cda3cfdd-6">Unsupervised deep networks reduce speckle in clinical data</cite>.
- For diagnostic or interventional use, consider polarization-contrast techniques to reduce backscatter dominance. <cite id="cda3cfdd-3">Polarization-sensitive scattering models improve contrast</cite>.

X-ray/CT
- Recognize beam hardening as a primary source of cupping/streaks and separate it from geometric/multiple scattering. <cite id="9bd6ce4f-8">Beam hardening requires energy- or material-sensitive corrections</cite>.
- Move to dual-energy or energy-resolved acquisition and synthesize virtual monochromatic images; expect 40–90% reductions in beam-hardening artifacts depending on protocol and materials. <cite id="9bd6ce4f-0">VMI reduces beam-hardening and improves quantitative attenuation</cite>. <cite id="9bd6ce4f-6">Projection-domain virtual mono can eliminate hardening artifacts in principle</cite>.
- Use anti-scatter grids and scatter simulation/estimation software with careful calibration to avoid introducing new artifacts. <cite id="fda466f8-8">Anti-scatter grids reduce scatter but alter primary beam; optimization is required</cite>. <cite id="fda466f8-1">Scatter correction software models and subtracts scattered components via Monte Carlo and statistical models</cite>.

Open problems and emerging directions
- Through-scattering imaging with deep networks and wavefront shaping: joint design of acquisition (spatio-temporal, multi-wavelength) and reconstruction (TM inversion, BPM) to maximize contrast at depth. <cite id="f18f75f6-0">Wavefront shaping restores focusing and imaging through scattering</cite>. <cite id="fda466f8-4">Model-based reconstructions recover multi-scattering dynamics</cite>.
- Speckle reduction without losing diagnostic content in ultrasound and optical coherence imaging: hybrid physics-learned priors and multiplexed acquisitions (angle, frequency, polarimetry) to maintain microstructure while lowering variance. <cite id="cda3cfdd-0">Frequency and angle compounding yields multiplicative speckle reduction</cite>. <cite id="cda3cfdd-3">SSM/SSCM provides physically grounded denoising</cite>.
- Energy-resolved sensing in portable and preclinical CT: advanced beam-hardening modeling and VMI to deliver artifact-free quantitative imaging under lower dose and wider energy ranges. <cite id="9bd6ce4f-1">Projection-domain correction maps polychromatic data to monochromatic equivalents before reconstruction</cite>. <cite id="9bd6ce4f-6">Virtual mono imaging can fully remove beam-hardening artifacts with proper synthesis</cite>.

Quick-start reading list (by area)
- Optical/through-scattering imaging: “Polarimetric Imaging Through Scattering Media: A Review,” “Imaging in Scattering Media (Tian Lab overview),” “Wavefront shaping… versatile tool” (The Innovation), “Wavefront shaping improves transparency” (PMC). <cite id="fda466f8-0">Wavelength-selection strategies address scattering</cite><cite id="fda466f8-4">BPM reconstruction surpasses single-scattering models</cite><cite id="f18f75f6-0">Wavefront shaping restores focus and imaging through scattering</cite><cite id="f18f75f6-2">Transmission-matrix inversion mitigates multiple scattering</cite>.
- Ultrasound speckle/multiple-scattering reduction: “Multiplicative frequency and angular speckle reduction,” “Spectral compounding for speckle reduction,” “Motion-compounding method,” “Unsupervised deep learning for speckle suppression,” “Speckle-correlation scattering matrix review.” <cite id="cda3cfdd-0">Multiplicative speckle reduction via frequency and angle compounding</cite><cite id="cda3cfdd-2">2–3× speckle reduction with spectral compounding</cite><cite id="cda3cfdd-1">Motion compounding improves visualization and accuracy</cite><cite id="cda3cfdd-6">Unsupervised deep learning reduces speckle in clinical US</cite><cite id="cda3cfdd-3">SSM/SSCM provides physically grounded speckle reduction</cite>.
- X-ray/CT beam hardening and scatter reduction: “Dual-energy CT–Based Monochromatic Imaging,” “Beam hardening artifacts in CT,” “Virtual monochromatic imaging can eliminate beam-hardening in principle,” “Scatter correction software principles,” “Anti-scatter grid trade-offs.” <cite id="9bd6ce4f-0">VMI reduces beam hardening and improves quantification</cite><cite id="9bd6ce4f-8">Beam hardening mechanisms and artifacts</cite><cite id="9bd6ce4f-6">Projection-domain VMI can fully eliminate hardening artifacts</cite><cite id="fda466f8-1">Scatter correction software surveys</cite><cite id="fda466f8-8">Anti-scatter grid design/impact</cite>.

Notes and practical tips
- Cross-talk between scattering types: beam hardening can produce streaks/cupping that mimic or exacerbate geometric/multiple scattering; correcting polychromatic energy dependence often reduces “scattering-like” artifacts. <cite id="9bd6ce4f-8">Beam hardening produces streaks and cupping</cite><cite id="9bd6ce4f-9">Energy mapping from polychromatic to monochromatic projections corrects scatter-like effects</cite>.
- Multi-scan methods (e.g., spectral, angular, motion) trade dose/time for speckle reduction; plan protocols to maintain temporal dynamics (e.g., cardiac) and spatial resolution. <cite id="cda3cfdd-2">Spectral compounding preserves dynamics while reducing speckle</cite>. <cite id="cda3cfdd-0">Angular compounding decorrelates speckle across views</cite>.
- Model-based or deep-learning corrections should be validated against task- and anatomy-specific metrics rather than only PSNR; use prior-informed priors grounded in scattering physics. <cite id="fda466f8-4">Physical-model reconstruction better captures multiple-scattering transport and changes</cite>. <cite id="fda466f8-3">Refractive-index–designed elements act as tailored high-pass/low-pass filters for deep layers</cite>.

How to use this list
- For optical sectioning/tissue imaging: start with wavelength-selection and wavefront shaping; add polarization encoding; adopt model-based reconstruction when possible. <cite id="fda466f8-0">Wavelength selection reduces scattering</cite><cite id="f18f75f6-0">Wavefront shaping restores imaging through scattering</cite><cite id="fda466f8-5">Polarimetric techniques reduce scattering-induced ambiguity</cite>.
- For ultrasound labs: combine spectral and motion compounding for strong speckle suppression; adopt SSM/SSCM or learned denoisers; quantify contrast-to-noise improvements. <cite id="cda3cfdd-2">2–3× speckle reduction with spectral compounding</cite><cite id="cda3cfdd-1">Motion compounding enhances visualization</cite><cite id="cda3cfdd-3">SSM/SSCM improves contrast while preserving structure</cite><cite id="cda3cfdd-6">Unsupervised deep learning suppresses speckle in clinical images</cite>.
- For CT/MRI: move to dual-energy or add energy-resolved detectors and synthesize VMI to eliminate beam hardening; pair with scatter correction software and anti-scatter grids calibrated for task. <cite id="9bd6ce4f-0">VMI reduces beam-hardening artifacts and improves quantification</cite><cite id="9bd6ce4f-6">Projection-domain VMI can remove beam hardening</cite><cite id="fda466f8-1">Scatter correction software models and subtracts scatter</cite><cite id="fda466f8-8">Anti-scatter grids reduce scatter with trade-offs</cite>.

without_preference.text: Find some papers that discuss methods to suppress multiple light scattering effects in light scattering imaging.
without_preference.answer:
Below is a curated set of papers that discuss and demonstrate strategies to suppress or mitigate multiple light scattering (MS) in light-scattering imaging. Each entry highlights the method idea and how MS is addressed, with links and citations to specific paragraphs.

Foundational theory and limits (to motivate suppression)
- Multiple-scattering limit in optical microscopy (Optica/OSA, 2017). Provides a compact theoretical framework for how MS sets depth and resolution limits in confocal and related modalities, directly informing suppression strategies such as aperture/detection design or coherence control. <cite id="8e24ce3e-0">The multiple scattering limit is deduced for various microscopic imaging techniques such as confocal microscopy, optical coherence tomography and related techniques</cite>.

Wavefront shaping and path control
- Wavefront shaping techniques for controlling multiple light scattering: a perspective (AIP, 2020). Surveys deterministic control of MS via angular and polarization coding to select or focus specific multiply scattered paths; practical for optical sectioning and deep-tissue imaging. <cite id="8e24ce3e-7">Recent progress in the field has focused on utilizing the deterministic nature of elastic light scattering to control multiple scattering in microscopic imaging</cite>.
- Wavefront shaping as a versatile tool to conquer multiple scattering (ScienceDirect perspective, 2022). Emphasizes focusing and imaging deep in scattering media, with methods applicable to biomedical imaging—e.g., transport-of-intensity/phase retrieval to reverse MS-induced blurring. <cite id="4bd57b71-5">Wavefront shaping can be used to achieve optical focusing deep inside scattering media for biomedical imaging, sensing, stimulation, and treatment</cite>.

Confocal/OCT imaging: detection-based suppression and algorithmic improvements
- Confocal microscopy of colloids (review, 2007). Explains how axial pinhole/confocal detection suppresses out-of-focus MS in turbid samples, recovering optical sectioning despite scattering; highlights decoherence due to MS and how confocality mitigates it. <cite id="8e24ce3e-4">However, conventional microscopy suffers from the same problem as light scattering, namely multiple scattering from objects that are out of focus</cite>.
- Multiple scattering suppression for in vivo optical coherence tomography (OCT; PMC 2024). Presents a method to reduce noise from MS photons to enhance OCT image quality in deep, in vivo tissues. <cite id="4bd57b71-1">We demonstrate a method that reduces the noise caused by multi-scattering (MS) photons in an in vivo optical coherence tomography image</cite>.
- Multi-focus averaging (MFA) for MS suppression in deep OCT (PMC 2023). Demonstrates that averaging multiple focus planes suppresses MS signals and improves contrast at greater depths. <cite id="4bd57b71-7">We propose a method termed multi-focus averaging (MFA) to suppress the multiple-scattering signals and improve the image contrast of OCT in deep regions</cite>.
- Multiple scattering low-coherence interferometry (review/Wikipedia entry). Shows how depth-resolved imaging can be achieved by analyzing MS in low-coherence interferometry—useful when constructive suppression of MS is leveraged as a computational advantage. <cite id="4bd57b71-2">ms/LCI is an imaging technique that relies on analyzing multiply scattered light in order to capture depth-resolved images from optical scattering media</cite>.

Speckle and crosstalk suppression via interference and correlation
- Multiple scattering suppression in laser light scattering via cross-correlation (Tech Briefs summary; method based on Nobbmann, 1997). Uses cross-correlation of two slightly tilted single-mode fibers to discriminate multiply scattered photons, reducing MS-induced noise—principles that carry over to imaging with angularly separated detection arms. <cite id="4bd57b71-3">In the present method, cross-correlation is used to discriminate against photons multiply scattered from a single illuminating laser beam</cite>.
- Homodyne cross-correlation suppression in quasiscattering/profiling (Institut Langevin/Langmuir-style paper; referenced from the measurement paper list). Shows suppression of MS effects in quasielastic light scattering through phase-locked correlation, which reduces speckle/crosstalk by emphasizing correlated, phase-maintaining components over disordered MS. <cite id="8e24ce3e-3">Suppression of multiple scattering effects in quasielastic light scattering by homodyne cross- correlation techniques</cite>.

Time-domain and path-decoding approaches
- Imaging through volumetric scattering media by decoding angular light paths (2025 preprint). Addresses MS-driven blur with high-dimensional angular path decoding, recovering microscopic contrast at depth—demonstrates suppression via angular path identification and suppression of nonback-scattered paths. <cite id="473f7fbb-2">High-resolution optical microscopy has transformed biological imaging, yet its resolution and contrast deteriorate with depth due to multiple light scattering</cite>.
- Time-gated multiple light scattering focusing (biorxiv 2026 preprint, referenced via Emory “Confocal” paper’s citations). Describes time-gated control of MS to concentrate energy at the focal plane or target depths; applicable to suppression when temporal coherence is available. <cite id="8e24ce3e-5">Focusing of light energy inside a scattering medium by controlling the time- gated multiple light scattering</cite>.

Angle-resolved and polarization-resolved suppression
- Imaging scattering orientation with spatial frequency domain imaging (SFDI); review by Konecky (2011). Notes that baseline scattering imaging has poor sensitivity to microscopic scattering orientation due to MS; angle-resolved/SFDI leverages angular and spectral decorrelation to extract microstructural orientation—effectively suppressing MS-dominated isotropic scattering to recover anisotropy. <cite id="473f7fbb-0">Optical imaging techniques based on multiple light scattering generally have poor sensitivity to the orientation and direction of microscopic light scattering</cite>.
- Polarization control in scattering imaging (MDPI Sensors, 2023; arXiv 2023). Demonstrates how controlling illumination and detection polarization suppresses scattered-field ambiguity and enhances contrast in scattering near-field microscopy by selecting polarized paths and reducing isotropic MS contributions. <cite id="473f7fbb-6">In this paper, we theoretically and experimentally explore how linear polarization control of both near-field illumination and detection, can constructively be used to improve scattering imaging</cite>.
- Polarized multispectral imaging in rigid endoscopes (PMC 2012). Describes angle-resolved/goniometric acquisition per wavelength and post-processing to reconstruct micro-structure—these methods suppress MS-induced isotropy by enforcing angular/polar constraints in reconstruction. <cite id="473f7fbb-8">There are two approaches to achieving this: the first collects angle-resolved scattered light over a large range of angles for one wavelength</cite>.

Model-based suppression: diffusion/transport constraints and focusing limits
- Diffusion-limit perspective on focusing in scattering media (Caltech NIHMS 2010). Establishes the fundamental optical diffusion limit: MS diffuses focus, so direct coherent focusing fails at high turbidity; this motivates suppression via detection aperturing, coherence control, wavefront shaping, or averaging. <cite id="8e24ce3e-6">However, multiple scattering imposes a fundamental optical diffusion limit on direct light focusing in scattering media</cite>.
- Modeling multiply scattered light in full-field optical microscopy (2024 SciDirect). Builds explicit forward models of MS within full-field systems; such models underpin deblurring/regularization or design of suppression filters and detection masks. <cite id="8e24ce3e-2">As for optical microscopy such as confocal microscopy and optical coherence tomography (OCT), multiple scattering poses a big challenge in the case of the full-field optical microscopy</cite>.

Selected application papers and demonstrations
- Targeted references for OCT-specific MS suppression (recent clinical and engineering work): <cite id="4bd57b71-1">We demonstrate a method that reduces the noise caused by multi-scattering (MS) photons in an in vivo optical coherence tomography image</cite>; <cite id="4bd57b71-7">Multi-focus averaging (MFA) improves image contrast of OCT in deep regions by suppressing MS signals</cite>.
- Confocal single-pixel imaging via double-path geometry (2023, MDPI Micromachines). Uses confocal detection with single-pixel architectures to reduce deleterious scattering artifacts while maintaining sectioning—demonstrates hardware-level suppression of out-of-focus MS. <cite id="4bd57b71-9">Here, we describe the use of a double path single-pixel imaging geometry which we call confocal single-pixel imaging to reduce the deleterious effects of multiple scattering</cite>.
- Confocal imaging in colloids/complex suspensions (Prasad review, 2007). Explains the decoherence and scattering crosstalk mechanisms in turbid samples and why confocality remains effective; useful for method selection and limitations. <cite id="4bd57b71-4">For relatively turbid samples, multiple scattering causes decoherence of the incident beam, about structure and dynamics present in the sample</cite>.
- Experimental and conceptual goniometer systems for controlled angular sampling (UT Austin). While hardware-centric, angle-resolved setups enable suppression of MS-dominated isotropy by constraining the forward model with measured angular distributions. <cite id="473f7fbb-1">It is a precision instrument designed for exacting scattering measurements [for angle-resolved light scattering]</cite>.

How to apply these across modalities
- Confocal/microscopy: Use pinhole/aperture, polarization, time-gating, or multi-focus averaging to exclude or decorrelate multiply scattered paths; combine with wavefront shaping when possible for deeper optical sectioning. <cite id="8e24ce3e-4">Multiple scattering from out-of-focus objects degrades contrast; confocal’s axial aperture improves suppression</cite><cite id="4bd57b71-7">Averaging multiple focus positions reduces MS noise and deepens useful imaging</cite><cite id="8e24ce3e-7">Wavefront shaping provides deterministic control of MS for focusing/sectioning</cite>.
- OCT/reflectance imaging: In vivo MS-noise separation and averaging, coherence-gating (CRI), and path-decoding to mitigate blur; these are discussed in the OCT-specific suppression papers. <cite id="4bd57b71-1">MS-noise reduction with coherence/processing improves OCT images in vivo</cite><cite id="4bd57b71-7">Multi-focus averaging suppresses MS and boosts deep-region contrast</cite>.
- Wide-field/large-area scattering imaging: Use angle-resolved goniometry and polarization constraints; reconstruct with models that penalize MS-dominated isotropy or enforce angular/polar consistency. <cite id="473f7fbb-0">Baseline MS-based imaging has poor sensitivity to microstructure orientation; angle/SFDI methods recover it</cite><cite id="473f7fbb-8">Angle-resolved per-wavelength acquisition followed by reconstruction mitigates MS isotropy</cite>.
- Speckle/noise suppression: Employ homodyne/cascaded cross-correlation with dual-beam or tilted-fiber geometry to filter out MS components, reducing speckle while preserving dynamics. <cite id="4bd57b71-3">Cross-correlation with tilted single-mode fibers suppresses multiply scattered photons</cite><cite id="8e24ce3e-3">Homodyne cross-correlation reduces MS effects via phase-locked correlation</cite>.
- Fundamental bounds: Check diffusion limits when designing protocols; if limits are exceeded, shift to wavefront shaping, multi-angle/polar reconstructions, or hybrid labelling. <cite id="8e24ce3e-6">Multiple scattering imposes a fundamental optical diffusion limit on focusing; imaging strategies must respect it</cite>.

Open access and practical starting points
- A good starting survey for imaging-focused suppression is the Optica/OsA “multiple-scattering limit in optical microscopy” and AIP perspectives on wavefront shaping. <cite id="8e24ce3e-0">The multiple scattering limit is deduced for various microscopic imaging techniques</cite><cite id="8e24ce3e-7">Wavefront shaping can be used to control multiple light scattering in microscopic imaging</cite>.
- For OCT and clinical turbidity: search combinations of “multiple scattering suppression” + “optical coherence tomography” + “wavefront shaping,” “multi-focus averaging,” “coherence gating,” or “speckle reduction.” <cite id="4bd57b71-1">An in vivo OCT method reduces MS photon noise</cite><cite id="4bd57b71-7">Multi-focus averaging improves deep OCT contrast via MS suppression</cite>.
- For angle-resolved/polarization-aware imaging of turbid media: look into SFDI (Konecky, 2011), goniometer-based systems, and polarization-controlled near-field approaches to suppress isotropic MS and recover anisotropy or phase. <cite id="473f7fbb-0">MS limits orientation sensitivity; angle-resolved/SFDI improves it</cite><cite id="473f7fbb-6">Polarization control enhances scattering imaging contrast by suppressing uncontrolled MS</cite><cite id="473f7fbb-8">Angle-resolved light collection per wavelength and reconstruction reduces MS isotropy artifacts</cite>.

Notes and caveats
- Confocal’s optical sectioning primarily suppresses out-of-focus but does not eliminate MS within the focal plane; consider polarization, angle-resolved detection, or wavefront shaping for in-plane suppression. <cite id="8e24ce3e-4">Multiple scattering from out-of-focus objects is the main decoherence source even in confocal systems</cite>.
- Any MS-suppression method trades speed, SNR, or depth for resolution/contrast; the diffusion limit provides a ceiling to expect. <cite id="8e24ce3e-6">Direct coherent focusing suffers due to diffusion imposed by multiple scattering</cite>.

If you share your specific modality (confocal widefield vs OCT vs widefield reflectance) and constraints (depth, speed, polarization access), I can tailor a short, implementable reading list and method sequence with parameter pointers.

questions.original_query: Find papers discussing phantom fabrication for bio tissues for imaging

query.text: Find papers discussing phantom fabrication for bio tissues for imaging
query.answer:
Below is a curated cross-modality guide to papers on phantom fabrication for biological tissues used in imaging, with fabrication themes, key materials, and modality validation.

Overview: Why tissue-mimicking phantoms?
- Tissue-mimicking materials (TMMs) are foundational for realistic ultrasound phantoms used in training, device calibration, and cross-modality development, supporting the need to reproduce acoustic, mechanical, and structural properties of soft tissues with tunability and longevity for repeatable imaging evaluation. <cite id="ccd4d171-0">Tissue-mimicking materials are essential for developing realistic ultrasound phantoms in medical training and device calibration</cite> <cite id="ccd4d171-1">Tissue mimicking materials ... have been used for many decades in both imaging and therapeutic applications</cite> <cite id="1dfdd8f1-1">The ideal ultrasound TMM should have: independently tuneable acoustic properties, tuneable mechanical properties, good longevity and structural integrity</cite>.

Cross-Modality Reviews and Surveys
- Broad reviews synthesizing materials, properties, and design criteria
  - <cite id="ccd4d171-1">A comprehensive review details tissue-mimicking materials across many decades, including specifications used in modern phantom development, and provides a reference for imaging- and therapy-phantom design</cite> <cite id="ccd4d171-3">This review investigates the specifications typically used in development of latest TMMs</cite> <cite id="ccd4d171-4">An IOP review reports a 3D-printed anthropomorphic pelvis phantom that provides tissue-like contrast on MRI and CT and can validate MRI-based processes</cite>.
  - <cite id="ccd4d171-2">A 2024 systematic analysis of tissue-mimicking materials for ultrasound phantoms synthesizes 234 studies into material classes, tunability, and application guidance</cite>.
  - <cite id="03583ecf-0">A 2018 PMC survey describes how 3D printing enables relatively low-cost phantoms with controllable complexity for imaging and dosimetry, highlighting rapid development of anatomically shaped structures</cite>.
  - <cite id="03583ecf-2">A 2025 International Journal of Biometrics paper reports silicone 3D-printed phantoms achieving MRI signal properties corresponding to a range of soft tissues</cite>.

Soft-tissue mimicking materials and fabrication strategies (across modalities)
- Hydrogels and organo-gels: Gelatin-, agar-, and alginate-based matrices are widely used to tune speed of sound, attenuation, and echogenicity; multi-material blends and 3D printing add structural realism and mechanical stratification. <cite id="ccd4d171-1">Gel-based breast phantoms have been designed for CT, MRI, and ultrasound, with 3D-printed materials used to produce heterogeneous tissue-like features</cite> <cite id="ccd4d171-6">A protocol details fabrication of an agar-based tissue-mimicking phantom with practical steps to ensure consistent properties under a CC license</cite> <cite id="ccd4d171-5">3D printing of gelatin phantoms is feasible, with reports on workflow and challenges including acoustic bubble control</cite> <cite id="03583ecf-4">A 3D-printed head phantom was made from agar-evaporated milk-silica gel to achieve MRI compatibility, reflecting multi-material printing strategies</cite>.
- Acoustic and mechanical tunability: Dual-tuning is a central design criterion especially for ultrasound phantoms; composition, porosity, and filler selection (e.g., silica, microbubbles) modulate speed of sound, attenuation, Young’s modulus, and damping. <cite id="1dfdd8f1-1">Specifying target properties (Young’s modulus, density, speed of sound, acoustic attenuation) and their independence is key for ultrasound TMMs</cite> <cite id="1dfdd8f1-7">A dynamic phantom study defines material targets for each tissue-mimicking region and demonstrates co-mapping of mechanical and acoustic properties</cite> <cite id="1dfdd8f1-2">A 2025 echogenicity study evaluates 3D-printed composite cardiac-tissue phantoms, quantifying matching of acoustic properties relevant to echocardiography</cite>.
- Multi-material/3D-printed organ phantoms: Freeform printing allows anatomically realistic shapes (e.g., pelvis, breast, head/face), with multi-material regions to mimic fat/water contrast and mechanical stratification for MRI/CT/US. <cite id="03583ecf-2">The 2025 silicone MRI phantoms show controllable R1/R2* and proton density to match soft tissues</cite> <cite id="03583ecf-4">Agar-evaporated milk-silica gel composites printed from a brain CT produced MRI-compatible phantoms</cite> <cite id="ccd4d171-3">Breast phantoms can bridge CT, MRI, and ultrasound, enabling cross-modality QA with controlled inclusions</cite>.

Ultrasound-specific phantom fabrication
- Materials and tunability: Hydrogels (gelatin/agar/PVA), microbubbles (for echogenicity), and layered composites are used to match ultrasound propagation and backscatter statistics of cardiac/soft tissues; post-processing and curing protocols, bubble management, and interfaces to electronics are reported. <cite id="ccd4d171-5">Gelatin phantoms printed for ultrasound achieved suitable acoustic properties when air bubble content was reduced, indicating manufacturability via additive workflows</cite> <cite id="1dfdd8f1-5">A 3D-printed gelatin-based cardiac-tissue phantom showed suitable acoustic properties when manufacturing defects were minimized</cite>.
- Echogenicity engineering: Embedding polymeric or gas-filled microspheres and optimizing size distributions improves backscatter spectra to resemble biological tissues. <cite id="1dfdd8f1-2">A synthetic composite cardiac-tissue phantom achieved echogenicity aligned with cardiac biological tissues, supporting ultrasound validation</cite> <cite id="1dfdd8f1-7">Mechanical-acoustic co-mapping frameworks guide selection of Young’s modulus and acoustic attenuation targets per region to match ultrasound response</cite>.
- Validation and use cases: Phantoms are used for transducer calibration, speckle characterization, elastography, contrast-agent evaluation, and surgical planning, with known challenges around speed-of-sound mismatch, attenuation, and anisotropy. <cite id="ccd4d171-0">Realistic ultrasound phantoms are central for device calibration and training</cite> <cite id="1dfdd8f1-8">Anatomically correct models composed of materials mimicking tissue acoustic properties support applications in ultrasound QA, interventional planning, and education</cite>.
- Practical notes: Multi-material printing, embedded vascular networks, and heterogeneous layering increase realism but require careful parameter sweeps and non-destructive testing for speed/attenuation. <cite id="03583ecf-1">Recent MRI phantom materials reviews emphasize hydrogel and composite systems with tunable optical and acoustic properties for multi-modality QA</cite>.

MRI- and CT-oriented soft-tissue phantoms
- MRI phantoms that emulate fat/water separation, T1/T2 contrast, proton density, and diffusion are produced from silicone/agar/silk fibroin composites with embedded magnetic nanoparticles or oxygen/short-T2 fillers, and validated with in-vivo protocols. <cite id="03583ecf-2">Silicone 3D-printed phantoms achieved MRI signal properties that correspond to a range of soft tissues, facilitating quantitative QA</cite> <cite id="03583ecf-4">A 3D-printed brain-like phantom constructed from agar-evaporated milk-silica gel offers MRI-compatible tissue-mimicking signal behavior</cite>.
- Dual-modality CT/MRI: Phantoms are engineered so HU and signal intensity correlate with tissue-like attenuation and MR contrast in the same specimen, enabling cross-modality algorithm validation. <cite id="ccd4d171-3">Gel-based breast phantoms designed for CT, MRI, and ultrasound provide a shared ground-truth structure for multimodal imaging validation</cite> <cite id="ccd4d171-4">A 3D-printed anthropomorphic pelvis phantom exhibits tissue-like MRI and CT contrasts and supports validation of MRI-based workflows</cite>.
- Disease-feature mimicking: In-vivo–like phantoms include inclusions to model lesions, calcification, or fat-rich regions, enabling reproducible testing of segmentation and plaque characterization methods across imaging modalities. <cite id="ccd4d171-3">Breast phantoms with controlled inclusions have been used to study CT, MRI, and ultrasound behavior in a unified model</cite>.

Examples of specific phantom families and fabrication workflows
- Cardiac tissue-mimicking phantoms (ultrasound/MRI focus): Hydrogel matrices (e.g., gelatin/silica composites) with echogenic microspheres or gas bubbles; 3D-printed anatomical shapes for heart chambers and valves, evaluated for speed of sound, attenuation, and speckle metrics. <cite id="1dfdd8f1-2">A 3D-printed composite cardiac-tissue phantom demonstrated echogenicity comparable to biological cardiac tissue</cite> <cite id="1dfdd8f1-5">Gelatin-based cardiac phantoms achieved suitable acoustic properties with optimized printing parameters to reduce air bubbles</cite>.
- Skin/tissue interfaces and superficial structures: Multilayer phantoms matching epidermis–dermis acoustics/optics; long-lasting designs balance acoustic and optical similarity to enable combined ultrasound/photoacoustic/OCT validation. <cite id="1dfdd8f1-3">A multilayer, long-lasting skin–radial phantom reports matching of optical and acoustic properties in a dermatology-relevant region</cite>.
- Anthropomorphic organ phantoms (pelvis/head/breast): From CT-derived shells printed in TMMs, filled with organ-specific mixtures for MRI/CT/US; used to train, test algorithms, and simulate interventions with repeatable geometry and tissue-like signal behavior. <cite id="03583ecf-4">A pelvis phantom printed from a brain CT scan and filled with agar-evaporated milk-silica gel composite shows MRI-compatible phantoms and realistic CT attenuation</cite> <cite id="ccd4d171-3">Breast phantoms designed for CT, MRI, and ultrasound can embed features to study multimodal imaging performance</cite>.

Selected papers and resources (with emphasis on fabrication and validation)
- Reviews and design compendia
  - <cite id="ccd4d171-1">Tissue mimicking materials for imaging and therapy phantoms (IOP Science, 2020): criteria, material families, and decades-long applications</cite>.
  - <cite id="ccd4d171-2">Tissue-Mimicking Materials for Ultrasound Phantoms (MDPI Sensors, 2024): 234-study analysis and practical design guidance</cite>.
  - <cite id="1dfdd8f1-1">Tissue mimicking materials (2020): articulates dual-tunability targets and longevity requirements for ultrasound applications</cite>.
  - <cite id="1dfdd8f1-7">Dynamic ultrasound phantom paper (MIT Media Lab): co-optimizes mechanical and acoustic properties per region with literature-derived targets</cite>.
  - <cite id="03583ecf-1">Narrative review of tissue-mimicking materials for MRI phantoms (2024): materials, composition, fabrication</cite>.
- 3D-Printed, multi-material organ phantoms
  - <cite id="03583ecf-2">3D-printed silicone phantoms with controllable MRI signal properties (2025): demonstrate realistic soft-tissue contrast across T2*/PD/R1</cite>.
  - <cite id="ccd4d171-4">3D-printed anthropomorphic pelvis phantom used to validate MRI-based processes with tissue-like MRI/CT contrast</cite>.
  - <cite id="03583ecf-4">CT-derived 3D print with agar-evaporated milk-silica gel composite to match MRI compatibility for a brain-like phantom</cite>.
  - <cite id="ccd4d171-3">Gel-based breast phantoms designed for CT, MRI, ultrasound with 3D-printed heterogeneous fillings</cite>.
- Hydrogel/agar/gelatin fabrication protocols and challenges
  - <cite id="ccd4d171-5">3D printing gelatin ultrasound phantoms: workflow, acoustic validation, and bubble management</cite>.
  - <cite id="ccd4d171-6">Agar-based tissue-mimicking phantom protocol emphasizing repeatable fabrication and open-licensing for use</cite>.
  - <cite id="1dfdd8f1-5">Stable multi-layer skin phantoms with controlled acoustic/echoic behavior and practical 3D printing considerations</cite>.
- Specialty targets: echogenicity, cardiac, and dual-modality validation
  - <cite id="1dfdd8f1-2">Echogenicity-focused cardiac phantom using 3D-printed composite with matched tissue-like acoustic response</cite>.
  - <cite id="1dfdd8f1-8">Additive manufacturing applications in ultrasound yield anatomically correct models of tissue acoustic properties for multiple use cases</cite>.

Practical guidance for choosing and building tissue-mimicking phantoms
- Start from modality requirements: For ultrasound QA, select hydrogels with matched speed of sound and attenuation; add echogenic fillers (microbubbles/metal-coated spheres) to replicate backscatter spectra; layer or co-print regions for mechanical variation and flow simulations. <cite id="1dfdd8f1-1">Ultrasound TMMs should independently tune acoustic and mechanical properties to match target speed, attenuation, and elasticity</cite> <cite id="1dfdd8f1-5">Reducing entrapped air bubbles improves acoustic fidelity in gelatin phantoms</cite> <cite id="1dfdd8f1-2">Composite echogenic phantoms can match backscatter behavior critical to echocardiography</cite>.
- For MRI/CT or multi-modal phantoms, engineer multi-material cores and shells to reproduce HU and MR contrast via filler composition and printing workflow; validate with quantitative T1/T2* maps and, where possible, functional metrics (e.g., diffusion). <cite id="03583ecf-2">Silicone phantoms with controllable relaxometry enable MRI-based comparisons across soft tissues</cite> <cite id="03583ecf-4">Agar-silica-gel composites provide MRI compatibility while supporting CT-like attenuation</cite> <cite id="ccd4d171-3">Breast phantoms designed for CT, MRI, ultrasound allow shared anatomical inclusions for cross-validation</cite>.
- Benchmark against tissue datasets: Use phantoms to calibrate segmentation pipelines for fat/water separation, elastography, plaque quantification, and contrast-agent detection, iterating material proportions and inclusion geometry based on imaging residuals. <cite id="ccd4d171-0">Phantoms are essential for device and algorithm calibration and training scenarios</cite> <cite id="ccd4d171-4">Anthropomorphic pelvis phantoms enable realistic validation of MRI-based imaging processes</cite>.

Open gaps and where to look next
- Photoacoustic and OCT tissue phantoms: Seek papers that match optical absorption/scattering (e.g., Intralipid-tissue phantoms) combined with acoustic contrast for photoacoustic-ultrasound co-registration and OCT-based structural QA.
- Disease-specific micro-structures (calcification, fibrosis, atherosclerotic plaques): Look for embedded micro-chips or mineralized matrices that reproduce echogenic/calcified layers for ultrasound/photoacoustic validation.
- Dynamic phantoms: Search for peristalsis/flow/viscoelastic behavior to evaluate strain-encoded imaging and microbubble kinetics under cyclic loading.

Summary
- Cross-modality phantom fabrication for bio tissues has converged on hydrogel-based matrices and 3D printing to realize tunable, anatomically realistic models; ultrasound emphasizes acoustic/echogenic fidelity, while MRI/CT phantoms focus on material-driven signal and attenuation realism. <cite id="ccd4d171-1">Tissue-mimicking materials have underpinned imaging phantoms across decades and modalities</cite> <cite id="ccd4d171-2">Contemporary reviews provide detailed design spaces for ultrasound phantoms</cite> <cite id="03583ecf-2">Recent work demonstrates 3D-printed silicone phantoms with soft-tissue-like MRI signals</cite> <cite id="ccd4d171-5">Gelatin systems are manufacturable into ultrasound-relevant phantoms with processing controls</cite> <cite id="03583ecf-4">Multi-material, CT-derived phantoms bridge MRI and CT validation in a unified model</cite>.

fully_underspecified.text: Find papers discussing fabrication for imaging
fully_underspecified.answer:
Below is a curated set of papers and reports across optical, acoustic, and integrated imaging device fabrication. Each item highlights concrete fabrication methods and how they enable new imaging capabilities or performance.

Optical metasurface/metalens and meta-optic fabrication for imaging
- Review: Optical metalens based on metasurfaces (fabrication and applications). This paper synthesizes fabrication strategies and imaging/non-imaging uses of metalenses, discussing practical challenges and commercialization prospects for nano-imaging systems. <cite id="1b4078de-0">This paper reviews fabrication, non-imaging and imaging applications of metalenses and discusses challenges and prospects in the commercialization of metasurface imaging</cite>.
- Manufacturing perspectives and process options. A broad manufacturing overview catalogs passive metasurface fabrication into direct-write lithography and related patterning routes, and links metasurface optics to microscopy and imaging workflows. <cite id="1b4078de-1">Passive metasurface fabrication methods can be divided into categories, notably direct-write lithography and pattern-based approaches</cite> <cite id="1b4078de-3">Methods and systems for metasurface-based nanofabrication include metasurface optics, direct laser writing, and microscopy</cite>.
- Process integration and industrialization. Reports emphasize compatibility with semiconductor fabs for nanometer-scale optics and the potential to fabricate complex optical functions with fewer lithography masks, directly benefiting compact, high-performance imaging systems. <cite id="1b4078de-2">Metasurface structures for nanometer-scale optics can be produced in the same semiconductor fabs that produce silicon chips</cite> <cite id="1b4078de-8">A single lithography stage enables fabrication in meta-optics, significantly reducing masks</cite> <cite id="1b4078de-6">Polarization-dependent meta-lenses support compact, high-contrast polarization imaging</cite>.
- Application-focused meta-optics. Roadmaps and group reports describe polarization detection/imaging with metalenses and compact, lightweight optics for end-use imaging. <cite id="1b4078de-5">Polarization detection and imaging based on polarization-dependent meta-lenses provide higher contrast ratios and more compact optics</cite>.
- Dual-band/near-IR imaging metasurfaces. Production-ready fabrication demonstrates dual-band infrared meta-optics, showcasing scalable nanofabrication for imaging windows relevant to sensing and biophotonic modalities. <cite id="1b4078de-7">Production-ready double-sided fabrication of dual-band infrared metasurface optics has been demonstrated, highlighting metasurface-based imaging advantages in size and weight</cite>.
- Performance sensitivity to fabrication errors. Studies quantify how nanofabrication errors impact optical performance of metasurface deflectors, informing yield-focused design and process controls for high-throughput imaging. <cite id="1b4078de-8">Nanofabrication errors in metasurfaces induce measurable performance degradation in fabricated meta-deflectors</cite>.

Acoustic and ultrasonic imaging metasurfaces, arrays, and additive fabrication
- Subwavelength acoustic transmission and focusing metasurfaces. Metasurface-enhanced ultrasonic transducers achieve extraordinary acoustic transmission with experimental validation, enabling higher-resolution ultrasound imaging beyond diffraction limits. <cite id="712beaa8-0">A subwavelength focused ultrasonic transducer with an acoustic metasurface demonstrates extraordinary acoustic transmission and enhanced focusing experimentally</cite>.
- High-frequency ultrasound 2D arrays with 3D-printed interposers. Interposer-based microfabrication at 200 μm pitch advances high-frequency array design, expanding options for high-resolution ultrasound imaging hardware. <cite id="712beaa8-2">High-frequency ultrasound 2D arrays at 200 μm pitch were fabricated using 3D-printed interposers</cite>.
- CMOS-compatible metasurface piezoelectric arrays. Integrated elastic metasurface ring arrays form subwavelength focal spots and enable compact beam shaping for imaging and non-destructive testing. <cite id="712beaa8-6">A metasurface piezoelectric ring array forms a needle-like subwavelength focal spot, demonstrating compact, engineered ultrasound focusing</cite> <cite id="712beaa8-8">Elastic metasurfaces localized phase/amplitude control to realize compact acoustic imaging optics</cite>.
- Additive manufacturing of transducer arrays. DMD-based projection lithography enables rapid fabrication of array apertures/holders, reducing prototyping time and cost for acoustic imaging systems. <cite id="712beaa8-5">An additive manufacturing process based on digital micromirror devices fabricates ultrasound transducer arrays</cite>.
- Laser/DMD micromachined acoustic lenses and coupling layers. Direct laser writing and projection processes fabricate spiral phase or vortex ultrasound structures and microscale coupling features that focus and steer waves for imaging. <cite id="712beaa8-4">Miniaturized vortex ultrasound transducers integrate spiral phase structures to generate orbital angular momentum waves</cite> <cite id="712beaa8-3">Phase-amplitude wavefront shaping combines plane-wave steering with passive acoustic meta-lens control for steerable high-resolution ultrasound imaging</cite>.
- Systems-to-transducer design exemplars. Published device designs and patents detail array architectures, manufacturing flows, and packaging choices for endoscopic or planar ultrasound imaging platforms. <cite id="712beaa8-1">A report details design and fabrication of an ultrasound endoscope imaging platform and a novel array transducer</cite> <cite id="712beaa8-7">A patent describes an ultrasonic transducer array architecture and its manufacturing method for imaging applications</cite>.

CMOS image sensors and backside-thinned photodiode fabrication for high-sensitivity imaging
- Backside-illumination (BSI) pixel isolation and scattering engineering. Trench-array and deep-trench-isolation strategies suppress dark current and enhance backside light capture, improving quantum efficiency and low-light imaging. <cite id="63b1368e-0">Surface-limited local trench array backside scattering enhances backside-illumination pixel performance for improved imaging</cite> <cite id="63b1368e-1">Standard IC flows can realize frontside or backside-illuminated image sensors with appropriate isolation and packaging</cite>.
- BSI process integration and reliability. DTI/BSI implementations report improved performance and reduced fabrication costs while maintaining reliability for high-sensitivity imaging sensors. <cite id="63b1368e-3">BSI image sensors with deep trench isolation show improved performance and reduced fabrication costs with enhanced reliability</cite> <cite id="63b1368e-4">Deep trench isolation encloses the photodiode from the backside to mitigate frontside light absorption and leakage</cite>.
- Commercial BSI advancements. Industry reports highlight BSI-driven sensitivity and ultra-high resolution/throughput imaging platforms, including ultra-high-speed TDI and backside-thinned InGaAs CMOS. <cite id="63b1368e-2">Back-illuminated CMOS image sensors are used to suppress dark current and achieve high pixel-level performance</cite> <cite id="63b1368e-5">CMOS and InGaAs sensors with backside thinning achieve high sensitivity, quantum efficiency, ultra-high resolution (100+ MP), and ultra-high speed via TDI</cite>.
- Shared-pixel/phase-detecting structures with isolation. 2×4 shared pixel arrays and phase-detecting pixels leverage deep-trench isolation to minimize optical cross-talk and maximize low-light performance. <cite id="63b1368e-6">A 2×4 shared pixel structure with deep trench isolation minimizes light absorption and suppresses cross-talk in high-sensitivity imaging</cite> <cite id="63b1368e-7">Phase-detecting pixels use deep-trench isolation patterns to block implant regions and improve phase measurement accuracy</cite>.
- Stacked BSI architectures and ultrafast imaging. 3D-stacked BSI sensors with integrated on-sensor memory demonstrate 100+ megapixel burst capture and millisecond-scale event recording. <cite id="63b1368e-8">A 3D stacked BSI sensor with pixel-wise Si trench capacitor memory achieves 125 Mfps and 368-frame record length, enabling ultrafast burst imaging</cite>.

Integrated optical/acoustic manufacturing and fabrication roadmaps
- Metamaterials/metasurfaces across UV–IR for imaging. Community roadmaps outline sustainable, wide-band manufacturing approaches that enable near-diffraction-limited imaging from UV to IR via patterned nanostructures. <cite id="1b4078de-4">Metamaterials and metasurfaces as nanostructured arrays enable near-diffraction-limit imaging from UV to infrared for sensing and imaging</cite> <cite id="1b4078de-5">Polarization-sensitive meta-optics provide compact, higher-contrast imaging</cite>.
- Process-level notes from device groups. Reports from meta-optics groups emphasize that single-stage or few-mask fabrication of polarization-dependent lenses reduces cost and aligns with system-level imaging integration. <cite id="1b4078de-6">Single-stage fabrication of polarization-dependent meta-lenses reduces masks and streamlines imaging optics integration</cite>.
- Practical device exemplars. CMOS-compatible metasurface arrays and printed interposers show production readiness and compatibility with existing microfabrication ecosystems, informing imaging hardware prototyping. <cite id="63b1368e-8">A 3D stacked BSI sensor with pixel-wise Si trench capacitor memory achieves 125 Mfps with 368-frame record length</cite> <cite id="712beaa8-2">High-frequency ultrasound 2D arrays with 200 μm pitch fabricated using 3D-printed interposers</cite>.

How to use these papers: practical guidance and cross-cutting themes
- From materials to performance: Optical fabrication routes that cut masks and tolerate wafer-level throughput (direct-write lithography, DMD projection, maskless etch/deposition) are highlighted as enabling lower-cost, CMOS-compatible imaging optics and arrays. <cite id="1b4078de-1">Direct-write lithography supports passive metasurface fabrication for compact imaging</cite> <cite id="1b4078de-2">Semiconductor compatibility makes nanometer-scale metasurface optics practical for mass manufacturing</cite> <cite id="712beaa8-5">DMD-based additive manufacturing accelerates ultrasound array prototyping</cite>.
- From design to yield: Backside-thinned and DTI-encased sensors show how geometry and isolation reduce dark current and cross-talk, directly increasing usable photons at pixel level; analogous process controls (trench scattering/edge passivation) can be applied to improve low-light imaging yield. <cite id="63b1368e-0">Backside scattering via trench arrays enhances back-illuminated pixel capture and performance</cite> <cite id="63b1368e-4">Deep trench isolation can be formed from the second side toward the first to encase the photodiode</cite>.
- Rapid translation for ultrasound: Spiral/vortex metasurface transducers and 3D-printed interposer arrays provide blueprints to reconfigure beam patterns and apertures quickly, enabling steerable focusing and engineered phase profiles without full foundry cycles. <cite id="712beaa8-4">Spiral phase integration in miniaturized transducers generates vortex beams for precise focusing</cite> <cite id="712beaa8-6">Metasurface piezoelectric ring arrays produce subwavelength focal spots with engineered phase</cite>.

Suggested starting points by need
- Prototyping compact, tunable optical systems: Optical metalens fabrication reviews and few-mask meta-optic design papers to select patterning flows and integration strategies for polarization-sensitive or wideband imaging. <cite id="1b4078de-0">An optical metalens review on fabrication and imaging applications helps select practical processes and device stacks</cite> <cite id="1b4078de-6">Few-mask meta-optic fabrication lowers barriers to polarization-aware imaging optics</cite>.
- High-resolution ultrasound platforms: Metasurface arrays (MPRA) and 3D-printed interposers provide end-to-end fabrication recipes; DMD/laser micromachining processes show cost-effective ways to iterate lenslet and phased-array geometry. <cite id="712beaa8-6">Metasurface ring arrays demonstrate subwavelength focusing and compact imaging</cite> <cite id="712beaa8-2">3D-printed 200 μm-pitch arrays show high-frequency array feasibility</cite> <cite id="712beaa8-5">DMD-based additive fabrication yields transducer arrays rapidly</cite>.
- High-sensitivity visible/NIR imaging: BSI sensors with DTI, backside scattering, and shared-pixel phase-detecting pixels offer concrete device-level changes to improve QE and reduce noise. <cite id="63b1368e-0">BSI pixel trench-array scattering improves low-light capture</cite> <cite id="63b1368e-6">Deep-trench isolation in shared-pixel arrays minimizes light absorption</cite> <cite id="63b1368e-5">Backside thinning yields high-sensitivity, ultra-high-speed CMOS imaging</cite>.
