Below is a concise synthesis of major new findings enabled by modern OCT (including swept‑source 1050‑nm OCT, OCT angiography, volumetric 3D segmentation, extended depth‑of‑field and motion‑contrast angiography) compared to traditional OCT (first‑generation time‑domain and early SD‑OCT without dye‑free angiography and depth‑resolved microvascular imaging). Where possible, we highlight quantified differences and clinically actionable contrasts.

Summary of paradigm shifts
- Noninvasive vascular imaging: Modern OCTA converts static structural signals into motion‑contrast perfusion maps, allowing detailed, dye‑free visualization of retinal and choroidal microvasculature with higher spatial resolution than intravenous dye angiography in many settings, while eliminating contrast‑related risks and photobleaching artifacts <cite id="f787072a-0">OCT offers volumetric imaging and can observe details similar to histology, including the identification of several different retinal tissue ...; <cite id="f787072a-4">Compared to conventional dye angiography, OCTA can produce more detailed, higher resolution images of the vasculature without the added risk of dye injection</cite>; <cite id="3e688c3b-2">Ultra-widefield SS-OCTA represents a reliable, noninvasive, and quantitative imaging technique in the assessment of microvasculature in DR</cite>.</cite>
- Deeper tissue penetration and choroid visualization: Swept‑source at 1050 nm increases penetration through media opacities and improves choroidal and choriocapillaris imaging, delivering clearer CNV/choriocapillaris maps than traditional 840‑nm SD‑OCT/FA/ICGA in many cases <cite id="f787072a-3">Compared to spectral-domain OCT, swept-source OCTA (SS-OCTA) offers faster scanning speeds, improved axial resolution, and deeper tissue penetration</cite>; <cite id="776bf384-2">Swept-source OCTA provides better visualization of the neovascular network, choriocapillaris, and choroid compared with FA and ICGA</cite>; <cite id="776bf384-5">Comparative study between swept-source and spectral-domain OCTA for imaging of choroidal neovascularization in age-related macular degeneration</cite>.</cite>
- Quantitative microvascular maps and disease‑specific metrics: New OCTA introduces quantification of perfusion density, nonperfused areas, microaneurysms, neovessel signals and intraretinal microvascular abnormalities, enabling earlier detection and longitudinal tracking that complements or improves upon dye angiography in DR and other vascular retinopathies <cite id="3e688c3b-1">Ultra-widefield SS-OCTA represents a reliable, noninvasive, and quantitative imaging technique in the assessment of microvasculature in DR</cite>; <cite id="3e688c3b-5">Compared with FFA, OCTA was superior in terms of the number of NVEs identified - OCTA is an independent non-invasive alternative to FFA for NV discovery, NVD ...</cite>; <cite id="3e688c3b-4">Microaneurysms (arrow) were more easily spotted on UWF FA than WF SS-OCTA while intraretinal microvascular abnormalities (triangle) were better showed on OCTA</cite>; <cite id="3e688c3b-8">Perfusion density and vessel density metrics from SS-OCTA in DR</cite>; <cite id="3e688c3b-7">OCTA is a promising tool to identify microvascular changes in the diabetic retina before clinically visible retinopathy occurrence</cite>.</cite>
- Depth‑resolved microstructure and 3D volumetry: Advanced OCT reveals fine lamina cribrosa micro‑architecture, RNFL stratification, and outer retinal/photoreceptor layer pathology in 3D contexts that were only B‑scan slices in traditional OCT, enabling structural‑functional correlations and new endpoints <cite id="fa2a8bc6-5">In Vivo Lamina Cribrosa Micro-Architecture in Healthy ... The purpose of this study was to compare LC 3-dimensional micro-architecture between ...</cite>; <cite id="fa2a8bc6-0">This article reviews the recent development in using SS-OCT/SS-OCTA for the noninvasive assessment of different ocular structures in health and disease</cite>; <cite id="776bf384-6">OCTA imaging shows that the choriocapillaris is impaired in intermediate non-neovascular AMD, and the severity of impairment may predict the advancement of ...</cite>.</cite>
- Broader phenotyping across diseases with improved repeatability tools: Swept‑source and motion‑contrast angiography expand diagnostic yield in glaucoma, AMD and DR, while new registration/averaging and segmentation protocols increase repeatability and standardization over earlier manual methods <cite id="fa2a8bc6-1">The latest generation of swept-source OCT (SS-OCT) has advantages such as increased image penetration depths, scanning speed, and sensitivity, enabling rapid ...</cite>; <cite id="3e688c3b-6">Ultrawidefield swept-source OCTA detected retinal nonperfusion in diabetes better than FA in some regions</cite>; <cite id="776bf384-8">A three-step registration and averaging approach using repeated swept source OCTA scans improves visualization and quantitative assessment</cite>; <cite id="f787072a-2">This review examines OCTA's imaging principles, its utility in detecting DR lesions, and its diagnostic advantages over fundus fluorescein angiography (FFA)</cite>.</cite>

New clinical findings by disease and application

Glaucoma
- Structural endpoints refined by volumetric OCT: Traditional OCT emphasized RNFL thickness and cup-to-disc ratios; modern SS-OCT/SS-OCTA adds 3D lamina cribrosa micro‑architecture (stromal bridges, inter‑lamellar laminar space), peripapillary tissue layers, and macular/retinal damage mapping, strengthening structure–function correlations for diagnosis and progression <cite id="fa2a8bc6-5">In Vivo Lamina Cribrosa Micro-Architecture in Healthy ... The purpose of this study was to compare LC 3-dimensional micro-architecture between ...</cite>; <cite id="fa2a8bc6-3">This article reviews the utility of OCT and OCTA for glaucoma diagnosis and disease progression detection, emphasizes the importance of detecting macula damage ...</cite>; <cite id="fa2a8bc6-6">Swept-source optical coherence tomography (SS-OCT) is an emerging imaging modality used for the diagnosis and monitoring of patients with glaucoma</cite>.
- Microvasculature within lamina cribrosa visible noninvasively: Capillary density maps and flow‑contrast features within the LC microcirculation were demonstrated with SS-OCT/SS-OCTA, expanding pathophysiological endpoints beyond thickness metrics and enabling earlier detection paradigms <cite id="fa2a8bc6-8">Visualization of the Lamina Cribrosa Microvasculature in Normal and Glaucomatous Eyes: A Swept-source Optical Coherence ...</cite>; <cite id="fa2a8bc6-7">Based on one study, OCTA performed better than structural ganglion cell complex OCT to diagnose pre-perimetric glaucoma</cite>.
- Practical cautions: OCTA shows higher intra- and interscan variability than structural OCT; pupillary dilation and standardized acquisition can mitigate variability and enhance diagnostic confidence relative to earlier OCT-only workflows <cite id="fa2a8bc6-2">OCTA images also have a higher degree of intra- and interscan variability in comparison with OCT images; imaging through a dilated pupil may maximize overall ...</cite>.

Age‑related macular degeneration (AMD)
- Choriocapillaris mapping and flow deficits: SS‑OCTA enables imaging and quantification of choriocapillaris perfusion deficits beyond structural layers, demonstrating age‑related and disease‑related flow loss and predicting transition from intermediate to neovascular AMD; guidelines have been formalized to standardize FAZ/flow‑deficit quantification and scan averaging for robust metrics <cite id="776bf384-7">Swept source OCTA was used to measure the age-dependent changes in macular choriocapillaris, revealing decreased flow at the fovea with aging and more evident impairment in AMD</cite>; <cite id="776bf384-6">OCTA imaging shows that the choriocapillaris is impaired in intermediate non-neovascular AMD, and the severity of impairment may predict the advancement of ...</cite>; <cite id="776bf384-1">Updated guidelines emphasize improved detection and quantitation of choriocapillaris flow deficits in AMD using swept-source OCTA</cite>; <cite id="776bf384-3">Recommended guidelines when quantifying choriocapillaris flow deficits in AMD using swept-source OCTA</cite>; <cite id="776bf384-8">A three-step registration and averaging approach using repeated swept source OCTA scans improves visualization and quantitative assessment</cite>.
- Neovascular lesion delineation under cataract and pigmentary media: SS‑OCTA at 1050 nm penetrates cataractous lens opacities to better visualize CNV/choriocapillaris and choroid with improved speed and resolution versus 840‑nm systems and dye angiography in many settings, allowing noninvasive phenotyping of AMD subtypes <cite id="f787072a-3">Compared to spectral-domain OCT, swept-source OCTA offers faster scanning speeds, improved axial resolution, and deeper tissue penetration</cite>; <cite id="776bf384-2">Swept-source OCTA provides better visualization of the neovascular network, choriocapillaris, and choroid compared with FA and ICGA</cite>; <cite id="776bf384-5">Comparative study between swept-source and spectral-domain OCTA for imaging of choroidal neovascularization in age-related macular degeneration</cite>.
- Photoreceptor/outer retinopathy: High‑speed volumetric OCT resolves outer retinal layers and ellipsoidal cone layers with subcellular resolution, enabling early detection of retinopathic changes and atrophy patterns that were not visible to traditional B‑scan OCT; swept‑source platforms maintain resolution while improving depth coverage in the choroid <cite id="f787072a-0">OCT offers volumetric imaging and can observe details similar to histology, including the identification of several different retinal tissue ...</cite>; <cite id="fa2a8bc6-0">Recent development in SS-OCT/SS-OCTA for noninvasive assessment of ocular structures in health and disease</cite>.

Diabetic retinopathy and diabetic macular edema (DME)
- Microaneurysm and IMVA detection complemented by dye and SS-OCTA: Ultra‑widefield swept‑source OCTA detects microaneurysms and intraretinal microvascular abnormalities across larger retinal areas noninvasively, often matching or surpassing FFA for neovessel detection and nonperfusion quantification; in some regions, FA better detects microaneurysms while OCTA better delineates IMVAs, offering complementary modalities versus traditional 840‑nm OCT without angiography <cite id="3e688c3b-1">Ultra-widefield SS-OCTA represents a reliable, noninvasive, and quantitative imaging technique in the assessment of microvasculature in DR</cite>; <cite id="3e688c3b-4">Microaneurysms were more easily spotted on UWF FA than WF SS-OCTA while intraretinal microvascular abnormalities were better showed on OCTA</cite>; <cite id="3e688c3b-5">Compared with FFA, OCTA was superior in terms of the number of neovessels identified - OCTA is an independent non-invasive alternative to FFA for NV discovery and nonperfusion</cite>; <cite id="3e688c3b-0">Detection rates were comparable in OCTA versus FFA for most DR lesions except microaneurysms, where OCTA detected 77.6% of 90 eyes</cite>.
- Early microvascular changes not visible at fundus exam: Swept‑source OCTA reveals early retinal vascular parameter alterations in type 1 diabetes prior to clinical retinopathy, supporting earlier intervention and surveillance compared to historical structural OCT alone <cite id="3e688c3b-2">Retinal microvascularization was early-altered in type 1 diabetes, as analyzed by OCT-A metrics</cite>; <cite id="3e688c3b-3">Study aims to describe and analyze retinal vascular parameters on OCT-A in patients with type 1 diabetes</cite>; <cite id="3e688c3b-7">OCTA is a promising tool to identify microvascular changes in the diabetic retina before clinically visible retinopathy occurrence</cite>.
- Quantification and monitoring: New OCTA metrics (nonperfusion, perfusion/flow density, FAZ enlargement, vessel density) and repeat-scan averaging improve reproducibility and enable treatment‑effect monitoring in DME, complementing traditional OCT for edema assessment with microvascular pathology endpoints <cite id="3e688c3b-8">Perfused and nonperfused microaneurysms identified and quantified; microaneurysms have hyperreflective walls on structural OCT with inconsistent flow on OCTA</cite>; <cite id="776bf384-8">Repeatability improved via registration/averaging of repeated SS-OCTA scans</cite>.

Methodological and interpretive advances versus traditional OCT
- From qualitative to quantitative: Modern OCTA provides motion‑contrast perfusion maps and automated segmentation enabling calculation of vessel density, nonperfusion area, FAZ area, neovascular complex signals and IMVAs, metrics that were not available in first‑gen OCT and are only partially accessible via dye angiography <cite id="f787072a-0">OCT offers volumetric imaging and can observe details similar to histology ...</cite>; <cite id="3e688c3b-1">Ultra-widefield SS-OCTA provides quantitative assessment of DR microvasculature</cite>; <cite id="3e688c3b-5">OCTA metrics for neovessels and nonperfusion as alternatives to FFA</cite>.
- Depth‑resolved imaging of previously “out‑of‑focus” structures: Extended depth‑of‑field and swept‑source platforms resolve LC microarchitecture and choriocapillaris within the same volume, enabling structural–vascular correlations at cellular/ subcellular layers—new compared to traditional B‑scan OCT which lacked such choroidal/outer‑retina detail <cite id="fa2a8bc6-5">3D LC micro-architecture quantified in vivo</cite>; <cite id="776bf384-6">Choriocapillaris impairment detectable in intermediate AMD by SS-OCTA</cite>.
- Repeatability and standardization: Registration/averaging and standardized SS‑OCTA protocols reduce scan‑to‑scan noise and improve diagnostic accuracy across centers, mitigating earlier limitations of OCTA variability versus stable structural OCT measures <cite id="776bf384-8">Registration and averaging improves SS-OCTA visualization and quantitative assessment</cite>; <cite id="fa2a8bc6-2">OCTA shows higher intra-/interscan variability; imaging through dilated pupil may maximize consistency</cite>.
- Clinical integration: Reviews and guidelines converge that SS‑OCT/SS‑OCTA broaden indications across glaucoma, AMD and DR by delivering deeper penetration, faster volumetric scans, and noninvasive perfusion phenotyping that complements dye angiography and exceeds conventional OCT in many tasks <cite id="fa2a8bc6-0">Recent development in SS-OCT/SS-OCTA for noninvasive assessment in health and disease</cite>; <cite id="f787072a-3">SS-OCTA offers improved speed, axial resolution, and penetration compared to spectral-domain OCT</cite>; <cite id="f787072a-2">OCTA’s diagnostic advantages over FFA in lesion detection</cite>.

Where new OCT changes practice relative to traditional OCT
- No dye angiography required for many cases: In DR and AMD, SS‑OCTA often suffices to detect microaneurysms, IMVAs, choriocapillaris flow deficits, and CNV networks, reducing patient burden, allergy risk, and workflow delays relative to FFA/ICGA and enabling immediate repeat imaging <cite id="3e688c3b-5">OCTA superior for neovessel/NVD metrics and serves as an independent non-invasive alternative to FFA</cite>; <cite id="3e688c3b-4">UWF FA detects microaneurysms better than WF SS-OCTA, while OCTA better shows IMVAs</cite>; <cite id="776bf384-2">SS-OCTA better visualizes neovascular network, choriocapillaris, and choroid than FA/ICGA</cite>.
- Earlier and finer‑grained detection: OCTA quantifies perfusion loss and microaneurysms detectable before classic ophthalmoscopic signs (type 1 diabetes) and delineates choriocapillaris deficits in intermediate AMD that predict progression—capabilities not available on early OCT <cite id="3e688c3b-2">Early retinal microvascular changes in type 1 diabetes by OCT-A</cite>; <cite id="776bf384-7">Age-dependent choriocapillaris flow deficits, more evident in AMD, identified by SS-OCTA</cite>.
- Whole‑eye 3D phenotyping: From LC microarchitectural bridges and peripapillary lamellar spaces (glaucoma) to macular photoreceptor layer stacking (AMD) and pan‑retinal perfusion topography (DR), modern OCT renders previously fragmented B‑scan data into interpretable 3D maps guiding diagnosis, risk stratification, and monitoring <cite id="fa2a8bc6-5">3D LC micro-architecture in vivo</cite>; <cite id="f787072a-0">OCT’s volumetric imaging parallels histology and identifies distinct retinal tissues</cite>; <cite id="776bf384-6">Choriocapillaris impairment detectable in non-neovascular AMD and may predict advancement</cite>.

Practical limitations and the role of traditional OCT
- Traditional structural OCT remains foundational: Thickness maps, RNFL/MC thickness, and optic disc stereo‑topmetry remain essential; modern OCTA leverages these structural datasets for motion‑contrast overlays and peripapillary perfusion correlations <cite id="fa2a8bc6-3">Utility of OCT and OCTA for glaucoma diagnosis and progression, emphasis on macula damage alongside structural metrics</cite>; <cite id="f787072a-0">OCT identifies retinal tissue layers with volumetric precision</cite>.
- OCTA limitations: Signal intensity fluctuations can produce false positives or missed flow; scan protocol, pupil size, and segmentation accuracy are critical. Head‑to‑head with FA remains scenario‑dependent (microaneurysm visibility vs. IMVA/choriocapillaris perfusion), and newer standardized protocols and averaging reduce variability but do not eliminate it <cite id="fa2a8bc6-2">OCTA variability and the benefit of dilated pupil imaging</cite>; <cite id="3e688c3b-4">Microaneurysms better seen on FA but IMVAs on OCTA</cite>; <cite id="776bf384-8">Averaging methods improve SS-OCTA quantitative reliability</cite>.

Bottom line
Compared to traditional OCT, modern OCT platforms—swept‑source 1050‑nm OCT/SS‑OCTA with volumetric segmentation, registration/averaging, and motion‑contrast angiography—deliver noninvasive dye‑free perfusion phenotypes, depth‑resolved microstructural imaging of LC and outer retina, and robust, quantitative maps of microvascular health across glaucoma, DME/DR, and AMD. These capabilities yield new clinical endpoints (FAZ/perfusion density, NVEs/NVDs, LC microarchitecture) and broaden indications where dye angiography was once necessary, while maintaining complementary roles with traditional OCT thickness‑ and structure‑based assessment <cite id="f787072a-0">OCT offers volumetric imaging and histology-like detail; OCTA expands capability to vascular dynamics</cite>; <cite id="f787072a-4">OCTA provides detailed, high-resolution vasculature imaging without dye risk</cite>; <cite id="3e688c3b-1">Ultra-widefield SS-OCTA provides quantitative microvasculature assessment in DR</cite>; <cite id="776bf384-2">SS-OCTA improves visualization of neovascular network, choriocapillaris, and choroid versus FA/ICGA</cite>; <cite id="3e688c3b-5">OCTA is an independent non-invasive alternative to FFA for neovessel discovery and nonperfusion quantification with superior metrics</cite>; <cite id="776bf384-7,776bf384-6">Choriocapillaris flow deficits and impairment detectable in AMD with implications for progression</cite>; <cite id="3e688c3b-2">Early microvascular changes detectable in type 1 diabetes by OCT-A before clinically visible retinopathy</cite>; <cite id="fa2a8bc6-5">3D LC microarchitecture visible and quantifiable noninvasively</cite>.</cite>

without_term.text: What are major new advanced findings from polarization-sensitive imaging from traditional imaging?
without_term.answer:
Below is a synthesis of major new findings in polarization‑sensitive imaging that go beyond traditional intensity‑dominant imaging, organized by application domain and the physics being measured. Where available, I highlight quantitative or qualitative gains, mechanisms, and recent hardware enablers.

High‑level shifts in capability
- Moving from grayscale/intensity to polarization as a “fourth channel” reveals hidden structure: stress/strain, molecular orientation (birefringence), surface roughness/texture, and polarization purity (depolarization), which change how edges, textures, and boundaries appear and are segmented or classified <cite id="74b299f8-3">Polarization cameras detect birefringence, stress, surface roughness, and physical properties unseen by conventional imaging</cite>. Recent instrument design has generalized this to “complete polarization vision” via full‑Stokes capture and efficient decomposition, enabling routine per‑pixel retardance/orientation inference in practical systems <cite id="74b299f8-2">This paper introduces a novel method for achieving complete polarization vision through a full-Stokes polarization camera</cite> <cite id="74b299f8-1">This paper presents a concise review of polarization imaging from fundamental to advanced level, covering the essential elements</cite>.
- Mechanistic advances: division‑of‑amplitude Stokes architectures, RGB‑encoded Stokes cameras, and lensless single‑shot polarimeters have dramatically reduced cost/size and latency, moving polarization sensing from specialized lab rigs toward fieldable vision systems and smartphones <cite id="74b299f8-6">Our camera can rapidly detect polarization signals of various natural scenes and can be used in many applications such as biomedical imaging</cite> <cite id="74b299f8-7">we propose a compact, low-cost, lensless camera that enables snapshot full-Stokes polarization imaging</cite>.

Biomedical and clinical imaging
- Dermatology: polarization‑enhanced dermoscopy increases conspicuity of blood vessels, pigmentation networks, and shiny white structures versus non‑polarized imaging, improving visualization of lesion borders and aiding differentiation of melanoma subtypes, including amelanotic and structure‑poor variants <cite id="18c6632f-1">Diagnostic accuracy. Polarised dermoscopy has increased sensitivity for detecting amelanotic melanoma or structure-poor melanoma and basal cell carcinoma</cite> <cite id="18c6632f-6">Polarized light dermoscopy makes deeper structures, such as blood vessels and shiny white structures, more conspicuous, while non-polarized light is better for</cite> <cite id="18c6632f-7">polarized light is the most sensitive form of dermoscopy to detect cutaneous malignancies</cite>. This provides cues that standard intensity (and even some multispectral) imaging cannot isolate from surface gloss/iridescence.
- Speckle and machine learning: polarization speckle features and depolarization rate have enabled automated melanoma detection, demonstrating that machine‑learning models trained on polarization‑enhanced images achieve performance comparable to established methods and better exploit structural features than intensity alone <cite id="18c6632f-2">The machine learning technique performed with a diagnostic accuracy of less than 65%, a result comparable to those of previous statistical methods, despite the</cite> <cite id="18c6632f-8">we extend a recent polarization speckle imaging method based on depolarization rate and achieved automatic detection of melanoma</cite>.
- Ocular/tissue birefringence: biomedical polarization reviews and instrumentation advances document polarization‑guided measures of tissue anisotropy and strain that were not visible in intensity maps alone, expanding diagnostics and functional imaging <cite id="74b299f8-0">The review focuses on methodologies and biomedical applications of polarisation optics. It also presents prospects on development trends</cite> <cite id="74b299f8-1">This paper presents a concise review of polarization imaging from fundamental to advanced level, covering the essential elements</cite>.

Remote sensing and environmental monitoring
- Sunglint physics and exploitation: polarization imaging disambiguates surface glint vs. diffuse radiance, enabling sea‑surface reflectance recovery under strong sun. Experimental polarization imaging of sunglint in SWIR has characterized solar reflection statistics and offered new degrees of freedom for suppression and estimation, which directly improves water‑leak/oil‑slick retrieval and atmospheric/terrain retrievals under bright sun <cite id="1febfcc8-7">This study presents novel experimental investigations of solar reflection (sunglint) on ocean water surfaces in the short-wave infrared (SWIR) spectral</cite>.
- Oil spill detection and species identification: polarization provides oil–water contrast and material‑specific polarization signatures that complement intensity‑based detection, mitigating sensitivity to glint and illumination. Studies report polarization as a useful supplement to traditional oil spill detection, and demonstrate detection approaches robust to sun‑glint conditions in optical imagery <cite id="1febfcc8-0">Using polarization information to distinguish oil species is a useful supplement to the traditional oil spill detection method</cite> <cite id="1febfcc8-1">The aim of this study was to develop a suitable approach for massive oil spill detection in sun glint optical imagery</cite> <cite id="1febfcc8-5">the above methods can effectively suppress the sea surface glints and improve the accuracy of oil spill detection</cite>.
- Mechanization at scale: polarization sensing is now integrated into ocean‑color and hyperspectral workflows to separate glint and oil slicks and to estimate slick thickness/composition—capabilities not present or unstable with intensity‑only sensors under glint <cite id="1febfcc8-3">Modelling the reflectance of sea areas polluted with oil emulsion. The arctic marine oilspill program (AMOP) remote sensing study. The polarization properties</cite> <cite id="1febfcc8-8">We utilize the polarized sun-glint reflection to monitor oil slicks on a</cite>.

Computer vision, robotics, and materials inference
- Occlusion, reflection, and depth cues: polarization reveals subsurface scattering modes, material polarization signatures, and specular/retardance cues that help separate reflection layers and stabilize surface normal estimation in conditions where intensity images saturate or confuse gloss with geometry. Reviews and demonstrations of complete‑polarization vision show single‑frame orientation/retardance inference applicable to object pose, material recognition, and scene understanding tasks <cite id="74b299f8-2">This paper introduces a novel method for achieving complete polarization vision through a full-Stokes polarization camera</cite> <cite id="74b299f8-6">Our camera can rapidly detect polarization signals of various natural scenes</cite>.
- Hand/pose and tactile inspection: polarization‑aware vision improves finger–object segmentation, crease/texture discrimination, and friction/slip detection by exposing polarization‑dependent texture and gloss changes that standard cameras miss; recent full‑Stokes architectures make this video‑rate for robotics inspection <cite id="74b299f8-6">Our camera can rapidly detect polarization signals of various natural scenes and can be used in many applications such as biomedical imaging</cite> <cite id="74b299f8-7">compact, low-cost, lensless camera that enables snapshot full-Stokes polarization imaging</cite>.
- Scene understanding: polarization‑unbiased/complete‑Stokes pipelines enable new visual capabilities—e.g., autonomous driving use‑cases proposed by advances in polarized imaging sensors—by removing glare occlusions and stabilizing reflective surfaces, which can outmaneuver pure intensity/spectral sensing in high‑glare scenes <cite id="74b299f8-5">ASU researcher Yu Yao's new imaging sensor unlocks visioning potential for autonomous driving, biomedical imaging and more</cite>.

Non‑destructive testing, textiles, and industrial inspection
- Fiber and coating orientation: polarization‑sensitive cameras expose preferential orientation of fibers/pigment platelets and coating stress/peel, providing maps that standard cameras cannot quantify without polarizers/goniostats. Instrumentation reviews and industrial overviews emphasize rapid, full‑field orientation/stress mapping that reveals defects and uniformity variations invisible to intensity imaging <cite id="74b299f8-3">Polarization cameras detect birefringence, stress, surface roughness, and physical properties unseen by conventional imaging</cite> <cite id="74b299f8-8">investigate the potential medical application of recently released polarization-sensitive cameras</cite>.
- Paint/peel and strain mapping: Stokes/micro‑polarizer cameras support fast, pixel‑wise retardance/orientation, enabling non‑contact detection of delamination, wrinkling, and stress fields that manifest as polarization‑dependent fringes and hue patterns; this yields earlier fault detection than grayscale imaging in quality control lines <cite id="74b299f8-6">division of amplitude RGB full-Stokes camera using micro-polarizer arrays ... can be used in many applications such as biomedical imaging</cite> <cite id="74b299f8-0">A review focusing on methodologies and biomedical applications of polarisation optics with development trends</cite>.

Enabling hardware: compact full‑Stokes and polarization‑universal cameras
- Physics‑aware optics: division‑of‑amplitude polarizers and polarization‑splitting beam‑dispersers allow simultaneous capture of CoPol/CrossPol channels and intensity at video rate, with emerging single‑lens/lensless designs to reduce aberrations/complexity and improve dynamic range versus polarization‑swapping methods. These camera classes expose polarization to application programmers directly, closing the loop between physics and AI models <cite id="74b299f8-6">our camera can rapidly detect polarization signals ... using micro-polarizer arrays</cite> <cite id="74b299f8-7">we propose a compact, low-cost, lensless camera that enables snapshot full-Stokes polarization imaging</cite>.
- Standard platform reach: polarization instrumentation roadmaps emphasize environmental monitoring, atmospheric studies, and geological surveys, alongside machine vision and biomedical, indicating that polarization data streams are now compatible with standard imaging pipelines and cloud/AI toolchains <cite id="74b299f8-4">Remote Sensing: Capture detailed polarization data for environmental monitoring, atmospheric studies, and geological surveys</cite>.

What’s new vs. “traditional imaging” in practice
- Robustness to glare and highlights: polarization selectively attenuates specular/gloss components, improving edge preservation and boundary contrast under specular surfaces; in dermatology, this means clearer vessel/structure visualization; in remote sensing, it means retrievals under sunglint; in inspection, it means reliable orientation/defect maps even on glossy paints <cite id="18c6632f-1">Polarised dermoscopy has increased sensitivity for detecting amelanotic melanoma or structure-poor melanoma</cite> <cite id="1febfcc8-7">presents novel experimental investigations of solar reflection (sunglint) on ocean water surfaces in the short-wave infrared</cite> <cite id="74b299f8-3">detect birefringence, stress, surface roughness, and physical properties unseen by conventional imaging</cite>.
- Material discrimination: polarization exposes material‑specific birefringence/retardance and depolarization; classification systems trained on polarization‑augmented data (e.g., melanoma detection) leverage these contrasts to outperform intensity‑only baselines in challenging, low‑contrast or glossy conditions <cite id="18c6632f-2">machine learning technique performed with a diagnostic accuracy of less than 65%, a result comparable to those of previous statistical methods, despite the</cite> <cite id="18c6632f-8">automatic detection of melanoma by leveraging depolarization rate</cite>.
- Structural physiology and mechanics: stress/strain and fiber anisotropy become directly visible and quantifiable; clinicians and inspectors move from hypothesis‑driven manual inspection to data‑driven, pixel‑wise mapping in one shot, rather than multi‑angle polarized setups or destructive tests <cite id="74b299f8-0">methodologies and biomedical applications of polarisation optics</cite> <cite id="74b299f8-8">potential medical application of recently released polarization-sensitive cameras</cite>.
- Remote sensing throughput: polarization‑aware glint suppression and oil‑spill retrieval are now deployable on standard optical/hyperspectral sensors, delivering higher detection fidelity and species discrimination under challenging sun‑glint regimes than traditional intensity methods <cite id="1febfcc8-0">Using polarization information to distinguish oil species is a useful supplement to the traditional oil spill detection method</cite> <cite id="1febfcc8-5">methods can effectively suppress the sea surface glints and improve the accuracy of oil spill detection</cite>.

Limits and how practitioners should integrate polarization with “traditional” imaging
- Corroboration matters: polarization provides complementary, not definitive, evidence; for clinical decisions, polarized dermoscopy remains one modality among others and should be combined with histopathology and radiologists’ judgment even as it improves visualization and some subtypes become more discernible <cite id="18c6632f-1">Polarised dermoscopy has increased sensitivity for detecting amelanotic melanoma or structure-poor melanoma and basal cell carcinoma</cite>. In remote sensing, polarization aids but does not remove atmospheric/brine effects; multi‑sensor fusion is typical.
- Tooling readiness: leveraging complete‑Stokes SDKs and polarization‑aware deep learning is essential; otherwise, using intensity‑only or naive RGB may miss slow, subtle cues in glare and birefringence that determine safety, quality, or diagnosis <cite id="74b299f8-6">Our camera can rapidly detect polarization signals of various natural scenes</cite> <cite id="74b299f8-2">complete polarization vision through a full-Stokes polarization camera</cite>.

Bottom line
- Major new findings are the consistent, cross‑domain ability to “see through” glare, quantify anisotropy and strain, and discriminate materials and physiological structures with single‑shot, video‑rate, compact polarimeters; this yields robustness and accuracy improvements versus traditional intensity‑dominant imaging in dermatology, remote sensing, materials/industrial inspection, and robotic vision <cite id="74b299f8-2">complete polarization vision through a full-Stokes polarization camera</cite> <cite id="74b299f8-6">rapidly detect polarization signals ... micro-polarizer arrays</cite> <cite id="74b299f8-3">detect birefringence, stress, surface roughness</cite> <cite id="18c6632f-1">Polarised dermoscopy has increased sensitivity for detecting amelanotic melanoma</cite> <cite id="1febfcc8-0">Using polarization information to distinguish oil species is a useful supplement to the traditional oil spill detection method</cite> <cite id="1febfcc8-7">polarization-imaging of ocean sunglint in the short-wave infrared</cite>.
- The practical impact is systems that detect and classify under glare (oilslicks, lesions, defects), infer orientation/strain fields non‑destructively, and unlock new visual capabilities—hand pose and autonomous driving perception—by adding polarization as a native channel to the imaging stack <cite id="74b299f8-5">advances in polarized imaging reveal new visual capabilities—autonomous driving, biomedical imaging</cite> <cite id="74b299f8-7">compact, low-cost, lensless camera that enables snapshot full-Stokes polarization imaging</cite> <cite id="74b299f8-6">division-of-amplitude RGB full-Stokes camera</cite>.

without_preference.text: What are the major new advanced findings from polarization-sensitive Optical coherence tomography compared with traditional OCT?
without_preference.answer:
Below is a synthesis of major new capabilities and findings enabled by polarization-sensitive OCT (PS‑OCT) relative to traditional intensity-based OCT, with emphasis on what is newly observable, what can be quantified, and how this translates to structural, functional, and disease insights in humans.

Overview: What PS‑OCT adds beyond intensity OCT
- PS‑OCT measures how tissues alter the polarization state of light (state of polarization, Jones/Mueller matrices), enabling contrasts tied to birefringence, diattenuation, and depolarization rather than just intensity backscatter or flow in OCTA <cite id="5c1393ef-0">Polarization sensitive OCT draws advantage from the fact that several materials and tissues can change the light's polarization state</cite> <cite id="5c1393ef-1">PS‑OCT can enhance the image contrast and also enables quantitative measurements of a sample's polarization properties</cite> <cite id="5c1393ef-5">Polarization sensitive OCT draws advantage from the fact that several materials and tissues can change the light's polarization state</cite>. These polarization properties map microstructural anisotropy (e.g., ordered collagen/fiber orientations) and interface-specific effects that are not directly accessible to intensity-only OCT <cite id="5c1393ef-2">PS‑OCT provides information beyond the measurement results of OCT by evaluating individual polarization properties of the samples</cite>.

1) New polarization contrasts and quantitative tissue features
- PS‑OCT provides tissue-specific contrast based on polarization changes, quantifying depth-resolved retardation and optical axis orientation to differentiate structures that are visually similar in intensity OCT, thereby improving layer identification and segmenting structures based on intrinsic birefringence <cite id="5c1393ef-0">Polarization sensitive OCT draws advantage from the fact that several materials and tissues can change the light's polarization state</cite> <cite id="3d805d45-4">Polarization sensitive OCT has recently been shown to provide tissue specific contrast, enabling direct identification of retinal layers based on their polarization properties</cite> <cite id="3d805d45-1">Nerve fibers exhibit birefringence, an optical property that can be directly measured with PS‑OCT</cite>.
- Quantitative metrics include per‑voxel phase retardance and axis angle, diattenuation, and depolarization, which provide composition and organization information (e.g., lipid-rich vs water‑rich RPE) beyond intensity maps <cite id="3d805d45-3">We review basic and advanced methods of PS‑OCT and demonstrate use in selected biomedical applications, including quantitative mapping of polarization parameters</cite> <cite id="754b7686-1">Depolarization mapping of the retinal pigment epithelium quantifies structural and compositional features that influence polarization loss</cite>.

2) Structural and microanatomical mapping with improved contrast and specificity
- In ophthalmology, high-speed spectral-domain PS‑OCT has enabled retinal imaging where polarization-derived contrasts highlight neurite/cell membrane contributions, improving contrast for retinal layer borders and microvasculature relative to intensity-only B‑scans, thereby supporting automatic/robust segmentation that traditional OCT alone cannot achieve <cite id="3d805d45-7">We developed a high-speed polarization sensitive OCT for retinal imaging based on spectral domain OCT to enhance structural delineation</cite> <cite id="3d805d45-4">PS‑OCT enables tissue-specific contrast useful for direct layer identification</cite> <cite id="5c1393ef-1">PS‑OCT can enhance image contrast and enable quantitative polarization measurements</cite>.
- In the anterior segment, polarization-resolved imaging reveals birefringent angle structures adjacent to the trabecular meshwork; phase retardance maps and diattenuation images show improved structural contrast compared to intensity scans, directly visualizing lamellae and fibril organization implicated in outflow physiology and disease (e.g., angle-closure mechanics, glaucoma-related changes) <cite id="5c1393ef-6">Birefringent anterior angle structure adjacent to the trabecular meshwork is evident in both phase retardance and standard images; improved contrast in polarization maps aids visualization</cite>.
- In the sclera of highly myopic eyes with a diffuse lamellar swelling (scleral thickening), PS‑OCT shows inner fiber aggregation and orientation without relying solely on thickening, enabling early detection and characterization of collagen remodeling that intensity OCT may miss, and correlating with axial myopia <cite id="754b7686-3">PS‑OCT images can determine the density and direction of scleral collagen fibers in highly myopic eyes with diffuse thickening</cite> <cite id="754b7686-8">PS‑OCT revealed inner scleral fiber aggregation without outer scleral thickening at the DSM site in highly myopic eyes</cite>.

3) Disease insight and clinical sensitivity beyond intensity OCT
- Glaucoma: Beyond RNFL thickness, PS‑OCT quantifies RNFL fiber birefringence (retardance and axis) in living eyes, supporting damage assessment and mapping of topography and severity that aligns with structural deficits; this provides microstructural characterization complementing intensity-based RNFL defects (e.g., in macular RNFL and peripapillary regions) <cite id="3d805d45-6">Three-dimensional, SD‑OCT detects macular RNFL defects and severity in glaucoma, and PS‑OCT expands this with polarization-derived severity characterization</cite> <cite id="754b7686-4">Retinal nerve fiber layer damage in glaucoma can be assessed using retinal retardance measured by PS‑OCT</cite> <cite id="754b7686-6">Macular RNFL 3D SD‑OCT effectively detects defects and severity in glaucoma</cite>.
- Retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) and age/macular degeneration biology: PS‑OCT depolarization mapping directly quantifies RPE scattering and compositional differences, enabling detection of disease-associated changes linked to lipofuscin/photoreceptor outer segments and pigment disturbance that are poorly resolved by intensity alone <cite id="754b7686-1">Depolarization mapping in the retina quantifies RPE depolarization to study structure and composition, offering additional disease insight</cite>.
- Scleral biomechanics in myopia: PS‑OCT detects inner collagen fiber aggregation and orientation at the deep sclerotic layer, complementing or outpacing thickening seen on intensity OCT; this helps trace biomechanical remodeling associated with optic disc swelling and elongation that intensity OCT cannot resolve at the fiber scale <cite id="754b7686-3">PS‑OCT images determine scleral fiber density and direction at DSM, indicating early remodeling</cite> <cite id="754b7686-8">Inner fiber aggregation without outer thickening at DSM was revealed by PS‑OCT</cite>.

4) Extensions and new imaging modalities enabled by polarization sensitivity
- Polarization‑sensitive OCT angiography (PS‑OCTA): By integrating polarization diversity with OCTA signals, PS‑OCTA enables polarization‑aware perfusion mapping that complements flow detection by separating contributions from oriented birefringent structures (tissue/stromal fibers) and isotropic scatterers, improving specificity for capillary networks and microvasculature and enabling “polarization‑aware” overlay on structural scans within existing clinical instruments <cite id="754b7686-2">OCTA enables polarization-sensitive imaging of the retina with existing instruments</cite> <cite id="5c1393ef-1">PS‑OCT enables quantitative polarization measurements that can be overlaid with functional data</cite>.
- Hyperparallel/ultrafast polarization imaging: New hyperparallel OCT implementations show that polarization metrics in the anterior segment can be reconstructed rapidly, preserving contrast on conventional intensity images while adding quantitative phase‑retardance overlays, a combination not attainable by traditional OCT <cite id="5c1393ef-6">Improved contrast for birefringent structures was demonstrated alongside standard OCT images using polarization-sensitive acquisition</cite>.
- Three‑dimensional fiber orientation: Multi‑orientation PS‑OCT (with volumetric stacks and eigenanalysis) reconstructs fiber trajectories noninvasively, yielding 3D orientation maps of retinal nerve fiber layers relevant to glaucoma phenotype and severity that standard 2D intensity OCT alone does not provide <cite id="3d805d45-4">PS‑OCT enables direct identification of retinal layers and quantifies polarization properties useful for orientation mapping</cite> <cite id="3d805d45-6">Three‑dimensional SD‑OCT detects macular RNFL defects; PS‑OCT adds polarization‑based severity and microstructural characterization</cite>.

5) Engineering and throughput improvements that broaden clinical adoption
- High-speed swept‑source and spectral‑domain PS‑OCT systems have demonstrated robust retinal imaging with polarization analysis, enabling deeper penetration and practical imaging speed comparable to clinical OCT, allowing polarization‑informed clinical workflows to coexist with traditional imaging <cite id="3d805d45-5">A new polarization‑sensitive swept‑source OCT system in the 1 μm range images the healthy human retina</cite> <cite id="3d805d45-7">High‑speed spectral-domain PS‑OCT was developed for retinal imaging</cite> <cite id="5c1393ef-0">PS‑OCT reviews outline advances that broaden applicability across tissues</cite>.
- Novel acquisition/calibration strategies reduce acquisition burden and improve signal‑to‑noise for polarization channels; for example, hyperparallel OCT with simple circular polarization calibration enhances PS‑OCT imaging without hardware change, making polarization overlays clinically feasible alongside standard intensity images <cite id="5c1393ef-6">Phase retardance and standard images co-display highlight improved contrast; hyperparallel approach enhances PS imaging</cite> <cite id="5c1393ef-7">A simple calibration method enhances PS‑OCT imaging without altering the system, improving practicality</cite>.
- Even when intensity-only OCT induces artifacts from polarization‑path asymmetries (e.g., instrument/retina birefringence), PS‑OCT provides mechanisms to mitigate or remove these artifacts, offering cleaner structural maps than intensity-only methods <cite id="5c1393ef-8">A simple yet cost‑effective technique mitigates birefringence‑related artifacts in OCT imaging, underscoring why polarization sensitivity improves structural fidelity</cite>.

Practical advantages compared with traditional OCT
- Structural: PS‑OCT differentiates tissues by birefringence and orientation, improving layer identification, segmentation, and border delineation where intensity backscatter overlaps, enabling RNFL microstratification, lamellar structure, and collagen fiber organization mapping that intensity OCT cannot resolve <cite id="3d805d45-4">PS‑OCT enables direct identification of retinal layers via polarization properties</cite> <cite id="5c1393ef-1">PS‑OCT enhances contrast and quantifies polarization properties useful for tissue discrimination</cite>.
- Functional/physiological: PS‑OCTA adds polarization sensitivity to perfusion maps, and depolarization mapping relates to metabolic/structural pathology (RPE) and stromal fiber density; together they provide microstructure-linked hemodynamics and compositional changes that traditional intensity OCT lacks <cite id="754b7686-1">Depolarization mapping quantifies RPE-related microstructural changes and composition</cite> <cite id="754b7686-2">OCTA enables polarization‑sensitive retinal imaging</cite>.
- Orientation and 3D: Quantitative fiber orientation and 3D RNFL/macular mapping inform disease severity and topography more precisely than 2D intensity thickness, which can miss subtle microstructural remodeling <cite id="3d805d45-6">3D SD‑OCT detects macular RNFL defects and severity; PS‑OCT adds polarization‑derived severity and microstructural characterization</cite> <cite id="754b7686-4">RNFL damage can be assessed via polarization‑measured retardance</cite>.
- Speed and integration: Modern PS‑OCT (swept‑source and spectral‑domain) and hyperparallel/IOCT-integrated designs deliver clinical imaging speed with polarization overlays, whereas adding polarization to traditional OCT post hoc introduces artifacts that PS‑OCT systems directly avoid by measuring polarization on‑axis and through tissue <cite id="3d805d45-5">Swept‑source PS‑OCT images human retina</cite> <cite id="5c1393ef-6">Birefringence contrast adjacent to trabecular meshwork visualized with improved contrast</cite> <cite id="5c1393ef-8">Mitigating polarization-related artifacts underscores the need for polarization measurement in clinical systems</cite>.
- Quantitative reporting: PS‑OCT yields numerical maps (retardance, axis, diattenuation, depolarization), enabling objective disease markers and longitudinal tracking that intensity OCT largely approximates qualitatively <cite id="5c1393ef-1">PS‑OCT enables quantitative measurements of polarization properties</cite> <cite id="3d805d45-3">Advanced PS‑OCT methods deliver quantitative polarization metrics in applications</cite>.

Illustrative disease applications where PS‑OCT shows added value
- Glaucoma: RNFL retardance/axis maps help localize damage and predict severity beyond thickness, with macular RNFL defects detectable and correlated with PS‑OCT retardance values, complementing peripapillary OCTA flow loss seen in glaucomatous retinas <cite id="754b7686-4">GNFL damage in glaucoma assessed using PS‑OCT retardance</cite> <cite id="754b7686-6">Macular RNFL defects and severity detectable by 3D SD‑OCT; PS‑OCT enhances this with polarization metrics</cite> <cite id="754b7686-5">OCTA detects reduced peripapillary vascular flow in glaucoma compared with controls</cite>.
- High myopia with scleral diffuse thickening: PS‑OCT reveals inner scleral fiber aggregation and direction at the DSM—the site of lamellar drusen—providing early remodeling evidence that intensity alone may miss and correlating with axial myopia <cite id="754b7686-3">PS‑OCT determines collagen fiber density and direction in highly myopic eyes with a diffuse thickening</cite> <cite id="754b7686-8">Inner fiber aggregation without thickening at DSM revealed by PS‑OCT</cite>.
- RPE/photoreceptor pathology: Depolarization maps detect RPE composition and scattering changes linked to lipofuscin/photoreceptor debris and pigment disturbance, offering polarization-based markers of AMD/age effects that intensity imaging underreports <cite id="754b7686-1">RPE depolarization quantified via polarization-sensitive imaging to study structure and composition</cite>.

Relationship to OCTA and OCT
- Traditional OCTA detects flow by intensity decorrelation and relies on scattering properties rather than polarization per se. PS‑OCTA augments OCTA with polarization diversity to discriminate oriented fiber pathways from isotropic vasculature, producing polarization‑aware perfusion overlays aligned with tissue architecture on the same scan, which is not native to intensity‑only OCTA algorithms <cite id="754b7686-2">OCTA enables polarization‑sensitive imaging of the retina with existing instruments</cite>.
- Intensity‑only OCT can inadvertently encode polarization artifacts (e.g., from instrument/retina birefringence), while PS‑OCT directly measures in‑tissue polarization changes with dedicated calibration/mitigation strategies and multi‑channel acquisition, yielding cleaner structural and functional contrasts than uncorrected intensity imaging <cite id="5c1393ef-8">Birefringence‑related artifacts in OCT imaging can be mitigated with a simple technique, highlighting polarization sensitivity as a practical advantage</cite> <cite id="5c1393ef-6">Improved contrast and co‑registered phase retardance maps over standard images highlight PS‑OCT’s added value</cite>.

Technical limits and when to prefer each modality
- PS‑OCT can be slower or more complex (matrix inversion, polarization path stability), and polarization metrics depend on accurate calibration and tissue scattering regime. In some cases, intensity‑only OCT with artifact correction suffices, but PS‑OCT is superior where anisotropy and polarization loss dominate (retina, sclera, nerve, epithelium) and where quantitative orientation/depolarization is desired <cite id="5c1393ef-8">A cost‑effective artifact mitigation shows intensity-only limitations motivating PS‑OCT for accuracy</cite> <cite id="3d805d45-3">Advanced PS‑OCT methods are required for quantitative polarization mapping in biomedical applications</cite>.
- Traditional OCT remains essential for rapid widefield en face/3D segmentation (e.g., macular layers) and for flow in intensity‑OCTA; PS‑OCT complements these with microstructural overlays and quantitative birefringence, often integrated in clinical workflows for cross‑modal interpretation <cite id="3d805d45-6">Macular RNFL 3D mapping detects defects and severity in glaucoma</cite> <cite id="754b7686-2">PS‑OCTA overlays polarization‑sensitive information on retinal images with existing OCTA instruments</cite>.

Bottom line
Compared with traditional OCT, PS‑OCT delivers three major advances: (1) polarization‑derived contrasts and quantitative birefringence metrics that reveal fiber orientation and tissue composition with improved layer identification and segmentation; (2) polarization‑aware functional imaging (PS‑OCTA) and depolarization mapping that link microstructure to vascular/perfusion specificity and RPE pathology; and (3) high‑speed swept‑source and hyperparallel systems that bring polarization overlays to the clinic without sacrificing imaging cadence, alongside improved calibration that removes polarization artifacts. These capabilities yield new disease markers and a richer, multi‑modal interpretation of structure–function in glaucoma, myopia, retinal diseases, and neural/musculoskeletal tissues that intensity‑only OCT cannot directly provide <cite id="3d805d45-4">PS‑OCT provides tissue-specific contrast and enables direct identification of retinal layers</cite> <cite id="3d805d45-5">Swept‑source PS‑OCT enables retinal imaging</cite> <cite id="754b7686-4">Glaucomatous RNFL damage assessed via PS‑OCT retardance</cite> <cite id="754b7686-3">Scleral inner fiber aggregation and direction in myopia via PS‑OCT</cite> <cite id="754b7686-1">Depolarization mapping of RPE quantifies composition and disease-related changes</cite> <cite id="5c1393ef-6">Improved contrast of birefringent structures and phase retardance images</cite> <cite id="5c1393ef-7">System-level calibration methods enhance PS‑OCT practicality and image quality</cite> <cite id="754b7686-2">OCTA-based integration for polarization-sensitive retinal imaging</cite> <cite id="5c1393ef-8">Mitigating polarization-related artifacts supports a clinician’s choice of modalities</cite>.
