- Noise modeling: OCT speckle multiplicity and log‑compression mean frequency‑domain and multiresolution strategies often outperform traditional filters at comparable computational cost; still, Wiener‑type filters calibrated to OCT statistics remain strong baselines where labeled data are scarce <cite id="d8bd6f6e-4">Log transform plus low-pass filtering is standard to mitigate noise in OCT images</cite> <cite id="d8bd6f6e-6">Wiener filtering shows superiority for multiple noise types in OCT compared to median/mode</cite>.
- Hybrid hardware–software: Averaging strategies benefit when hardware allows rapid acquisition; for clinical workflows with limited per‑frame SNR, add digital motion compensation and ML denoising to close remaining gaps without extra patient time <cite id="ec4e5152-0">High acquisition speed enables large SNR gains via averaging</cite> <cite id="ec4e5152-4">Deblurring and denoising raise SNR/CNR in practical times</cite>.

Summary: Representative digital SNR‑improving methods for OCT imaging include B‑scan volume/multi‑scan averaging; classical OCT‑aware filtering (band‑pass/Butterworth; Wiener; median/bilateral; multiresolution/shearlet); OCT‑specific sparse/adaptive denoising; and modern CNN/autoencoder and self‑supervised strategies integrated into pipelines, with OCTA‑specific variants (masking, background/phase subtraction, dual‑beam/angle compounding, few‑scan learning) that preserve vessel SNR at clinically practical speeds and compute budgets <cite id="ec4e5152-0">Signal averaging is a core digital lever for SNR gains</cite> <cite id="d8bd6f6e-0">Fourier Butterworth filtering reduces speckle in OCT</cite> <cite id="d8bd6f6e-6">Wiener and classical filters have OCT-specific strengths for noise suppression</cite> <cite id="ff837b01-2">Sparse representation with noise estimation improves OCT despeckling</cite> <cite id="ec4e5152-1">CNN-based SNR-Net OCT enhances brightness and speckle suppression</cite> <cite id="5135df93-5">Angular compounding improves SNR and reduces speckle</cite> <cite id="ff837b01-5">Few-scan learning approaches can match multi-scan averaging SNR</cite> <cite id="ff837b01-1">Live 4D-OCT denoising confirms real-time feasibility</cite> <cite id="ec4e5152-4">End-to-end deblurring+denoising improves SNR/CNR/SSIM rapidly</cite>.

without_term.text: What are representative SNR improvement digital methods in optical coherence tomography imaging
without_term.answer:
Below are representative digital methods that improve signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) and image quality in optical coherence tomography (OCT), grouped by mechanism and modality, with notes on trade‑offs and typical implementations.

1) Temporal averaging of A‑lines/B‑scans
- Multi‑line/B‑scan averaging is a foundational digital SNR enhancer: repeated A‑lines in the same location are co‑registered and averaged to reduce uncorrelated noise, with modern systems able to deliver "massive" SNR gains due to high acquisition speeds and large ensemble sizes. <cite id="5124795f-0">The high acquisition speed of state-of-the-art optical coherence tomography (OCT) enables massive signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) improvements by signal averaging</cite> <cite id="c7bcb45f-0">Signal averaging yields massive SNR improvements by repeated A-line acquisition and averaging</cite>. 
- In Fourier-domain OCT, averaging across ensembles of A-lines also reduces shot noise and detector noise in the complex spectrum prior to inverse FFT, improving depth profile SNR while preserving the underlying structure. <cite id="c7bcb45f-0">Signal averaging across A-line ensembles improves SNR in spectral-domain OCT</cite>.
- Practical considerations: the time constant of averaging is the dominant knob for SNR versus acquisition speed; aggressive averaging shortens temporal dynamics and increases motion sensitivity, motivating concurrent motion correction and averaging limits due to eye/biological motion. <cite id="c7bcb45f-2">Phase noise and system factors in swept‑source OCT imply that further SNR gains from averaging alone do not necessarily improve phase stability for phase-related tasks</cite> <cite id="5124795f-1">Software combining 2D filters and BM3D complements multi‑scan averaging to improve OCT SNR</cite>.

2) Motion artifact correction and registration-based enhancement
- Digital motion correction aligns A-scans across frames to suppress ghosting and blur, enabling effective co‑registration for averaging and improving both visual quality and quantitative reliability of derived measurements. <cite id="77d01cf4-0">A software-based, per-A-scan, per-B-scan motion compensation method corrects OCT raster-scan artifacts and improves reliability</cite> <cite id="77d01cf4-2">Motion correction improves the visual appearance and reliability of quantitative measurements in OCT volumes</cite>.
- In OCTA, automated motion-artifact correction using vessel/structural priors repairs scan misalignment, reducing artifacts that otherwise depress SNR and obscure flow signals. <cite id="77d01cf4-3">A tensor-based automated approach detects and corrects motion artifacts in OCTA by leveraging the microvasculature structure</cite> <cite id="77d01cf4-6">Self-supervised learning can simultaneously remove motion artifacts and noise in OCTA images</cite>.
- Eye-movement/scan jitter are pervasive; algorithmic frameworks for involuntary eye-movement correction summarize state-of-the-art registration and stabilization approaches to recover SNR-limited detail. <cite id="77d01cf4-1">State-of-the-art OCT eye-movement correction combines tracking models and registration to stabilize volumes and reduce motion-related signal loss</cite> <cite id="77d01cf4-5">Software-based per-A-/B-scan correction reduces artifacts and enhances signal in clinical-grade datasets</cite>.
- Trade-off: motion correction is necessary before multi-frame averaging/fusion; failure to correct prolongs artifact patterns and limits SNR gains. <cite id="77d01cf4-4">SELFF-OCT is highly sensitive to motion; automated detection of invalid volumes plus realignment increases effective SNR and measurement robustness</cite>.

3) Spectral-domain and swept‑source post‑processing for noise/phase stability
- Balanced-detection and spectral-domain processing suppress common‑mode noise; frequency-domain filters can remove high‑frequency spectral leakage, improving SNR of the complex signal before back‑propagation. <cite id="5124795f-2">Digital signal processing improves flexibility, functionality, and image quality of ultrahigh-resolution OCT</cite>.
- Swept‑source systems benefit from scan-averaging and spectral windowing/apodization to limit phase noise; however, increasing SNR via averaging alone has diminishing returns for phase‑related metrics unless the photonic/phase-noise sources are concurrently constrained. <cite id="c7bcb45f-2">Increasing SNR from averaging does not necessarily boost phase stability in SS-OCT; merits include improved sensitivity/penetration for phase tasks</cite> <cite id="c7bcb45f-6">Phase noise's origin and composition are separable in swept‑source OCT, supporting digital suppression via improved signal processing of the swept spectrum</cite>.
- Compressed sensing and noise-shaping in swept‑source OCT shorten the time required for repetitive scans and enable fewer‑scan averaging while preserving image quality, effectively improving temporal SNR efficiency. <cite id="c7bcb45f-3">Compressed sensing applied to swept‑source OCT reduces scan count for averaging through sparse domain noise reduction</cite> <cite id="c7bcb45f-5">Proposed noise-reduction plus averaging shortens repetitive-scan time, improving both imaging speed and average SNR over five scans</cite>.
- Comparative notes: swept‑source provides deeper penetration/sensitivity falloff benefits, often used with post-processing to maintain phase stability; spectral-domain OCT benefits strongly from multi‑scan averaging. <cite id="c7bcb45f-7">Swept-source OCT improves sensitivity and penetration versus spectral-domain; comparative SNR depends on system design and post-processing</cite>.

4) Speckle/noise suppression filters and OCTA denoising
- Linear/nonlinear filters (e.g., Wiener, 2D/3D filtering) reduce speckle and noise, with modern nonlocal and wavelet-based denoisers (e.g., BM3D, block-matching 3D) offering strong SNR/SSIM/CNR gains while preserving anatomy; GPU-accelerated variants are widely used clinically. <cite id="5124795f-1">Software-based 2D filter combination, BM3D, and related algorithms are standard OCT denoisers to improve SNR</cite> <cite id="5124795f-4">Denoising approaches are central for OCT image quality and downstream pathology segmentation</cite> <cite id="5124795f-7">One-Step Enhancer deblurring/denoising increases SNR, CNR, and SSIM in OCT with real-time speeds</cite>.
- In OCTA, where raw intensity SNR sets flow-detection thresholds, digital denoising plus motion correction reduces speckle and recovers weak flow signals across frames; deep networks and self-supervised methods learn joint artifact/noise suppression. <cite id="77d01cf4-3">Automated OCTA motion correction based on vascular structure improves artifact-free averaging and flow SNR</cite> <cite id="77d01cf4-6">Self-supervised networks remove motion artifacts and noise simultaneously in OCTA</cite> <cite id="5124795f-1">Deep-learning-based SNR enhancement in OCT demonstrates the viability of learned denoisers beyond classical filters</cite>.
- Hybrid strategies combine multi-scans plus learned priors; for swept-source OCT, sparse continuous deconvolution and other post-processing can sharpen structures while suppressing noise, with measured quality gains (PSNR/SSIM/SNR) reported in image-domain evaluations. <cite id="5124795f-8">Deep learning super-resolution and resolution enhancement in OCT improves both optical and digital resolution with denoising benefits</cite> <cite id="5124795f-5">A deep learning framework simultaneously improves optical and digital OCT resolution with reduced data size, implying denoised reconstructions</cite> <cite id="5124795f-7">Sparse deconvolution/deblurring enhances OCT image quality with quantifiable SNR/SSIM improvements</cite>.

5) Multi‑scan fusion, artifact-aware reconstruction, and registration
- Digital reconstruction pipelines integrate multiple adjacent scans: motion detection, gap-filling, and then weighted fusion/averaging to suppress speckle/noise while preserving edges, with automated rejection of invalid volumes to avoid artifact amplification. <cite id="77d01cf4-4">Automated detection of invalid volumes and rapid realignment in SELFF-OCT improve fusion quality and SNR</cite> <cite id="77d01cf4-0">Per-A-/per-B-scan motion compensation forms a prerequisite for robust multi-scan averaging and fusion</cite>.
- Artifact-aware denoisers in OCT leverage known OCT-specific artifacts (e.g., frequency-domain out-of-focus leakage, shadowing) to constrain filters and improve SNR of relevant layers without over-smoothing. <cite id="77d01cf4-8">Common OCT artifacts degrade effective SNR; artifact-aware processing restores reliability in various retinal conditions</cite>.

6) Domain-specific and hardware-bridging digital steps
- Frequency-domain phase unwrapping, windowing, and coherence-gating in swept‑source systems improve phase-SNR and reduce decorrelation noise in depth, enabling phase mapping with lower sampling rates in the RF domain. <cite id="c7bcb45f-2">Analysis of swept‑source phase noise shows the limits of SNR-increment-only approaches and guides use of digital phase suppression strategies</cite>.
- Balanced-detection DSP (e.g., subtraction and offset correction), spectral leakage control, and digital low-pass filtering are employed to maximize SNR at pixel/voxel level, often forming the baseline before any denoising. <cite id="5124795f-2">DSP techniques in OCT improve image quality by suppressing noise and leakage across the acquisition pipeline</cite>.
- Practical systems trade off sensitivity and speed: increasing averaging to raise SNR reduces frame rate; motion correction mitigates this constraint by maintaining usable frame rates while enabling effective averaging for deeper tissues or OCTA. <cite id="c7bcb45f-2">Phase-related tasks can be insensitive to raw SNR increases unless photonic/phase-noise sources are also addressed</cite>.

7) Deep learning for SNR/quality restoration
- Super-resolution and resolution enhancement models (e.g., deep networks) jointly improve SNR by exploiting inter-scale redundancy in OCT data, increasing effective contrast-to-noise and enabling clearer boundary delineation in low-dose or low-SNR scans. <cite id="5124795f-3">Deep learning-based resolution enhancement (SNR/SD improvements) shows that algorithms can recover detail otherwise lost to noise and blurring</cite> <cite id="5124795f-5">Simultaneous optical/digital resolution improvement with reduced data size supports denoising-driven SNR gains</cite>.
- Task-agnostic denoisers (e.g., BM3D-like, CNN-based, transformer-based) and plug-and-play priors tailored to OCT spectra and OCTA intensity/flow maps improve SNR/SSIM with real-time feasibility. <cite id="5124795f-1">Bilateral/bundle filters, BM3D, and deep nets serve as software tools to improve OCT SNR in clinical pipelines</cite> <cite id="5124795f-7">One-Step Enhancer demonstrates deblurring and denoising with quantifiable quality gains</cite>.

Representative "cookbook" recipes by scenario
- Routine clinical OCT images at adequate SNR: 
  - Enable multi-scan averaging (3–5×) and motion/autocorrection; apply anisotropic/directional 2D filtering (Gaussian–Laplacian) or nonlocal/BM3D if speckle remains high. <cite id="5124795f-0">Signal averaging is the cornerstone; modern systems support large ensembles for strong SNR gains</cite> <cite id="77d01cf4-0">Motion correction aligns scans for effective averaging</cite> <cite id="5124795f-1">2D filter combination + BM3D denoising boosts SNR beyond averaging alone</cite>.
- OCTA with low-contrast flow:
  - First correct global/local motion with vascular priors; then apply speckle/noise denoising, followed by multi-frame averaging and adaptive enhancement; combine with sparse deconvolution to sharpen vessels without speckle overflow. <cite id="77d01cf4-3">Automated OCTA motion correction uses microvasculature detection to fix large deformations</cite> <cite id="5124795f-1">BM3D/denoisers improve SNR in low-light OCT scenes</cite> <cite id="5124795f-7">Deblurring/denoising improves OCTA quality metrics</cite>.
- Swept‑source depth/phase mapping:
  - Use digital apodization/windowing, coherence gating, and multi‑scan averaging; for phase maps, add phase unwrapping and noise-aware filtering; exploit CS/shortened averaging to maintain speed/depth with acceptable phase SNR. <cite id="c7bcb45f-2">Phase noise analysis in swept‑source OCT informs windowing/averaging and phase filtering choices</cite> <cite id="c7bcb45f-3">Compressed sensing reduces scan count prior to averaging, improving effective SNR</cite>.
- Rapid scanning or unstable subjects:
  - Prioritize motion detection/autocorrection plus small-time-constant averaging; use artifact-aware denoising to fill in transient drops in intensity without smearing dynamics; for OCTA, integrate motion-informed flow regularization. <cite id="77d01cf4-4">Automated detection and realignment maintain valid frames under motion</cite> <cite id="77d01cf4-6">Self-supervised learning removes motion artifacts and noise simultaneously</cite>.

Key trade-offs and practical notes
- Averaging reduces temporal dynamics and increases motion sensitivity; pairing with motion correction is essential, especially in OCTA and dynamic tissues. <cite id="77d01cf4-2">Motion correction improves measurement reliability, enabling effective co-registration for averaging</cite>.
- In swept‑source OCT used for phase, raising SNR via averaging alone may not stabilize phase without addressing photonic/phase-noise sources; digital phase unwrapping, windowing, and coherence-gating are often required. <cite id="c7bcb45f-2">Further SNR increases do not necessarily boost phase stability; multimodal strategies are advised</cite>.
- Deep learning methods can deliver substantial quality/SNR gains but require careful priors to avoid over‑smoothing, and their performance depends on training data realism and artifact coverage. <cite id="5124795f-4">Denoising improves classification and segmentation, but method choice affects SNR and structure fidelity</cite>.

In summary, digital SNR-improving methods in OCT commonly combine multi-ensemble averaging, motion/autocorrection and artifact-aware registration, spectral-domain/swept-source post-processing (windowing, coherence gating, CS-based averaging), classical and modern denoisers (Wiener, nonlocal/BM3D), and deep-learning-enhanced deblurring/denoising and super-resolution. The best approach depends on modality (SD vs SS OCT/OCTA), phase vs intensity emphasis, and speed/throughput; integrating averaging with motion correction and OCT-specific denoising yields the most consistent SNR gains with minimal loss of diagnostic detail. <cite id="5124795f-0">Signal averaging provides the baseline SNR uplift</cite> <cite id="5124795f-2">DSP-based denoising and leakage control improve image quality</cite> <cite id="c7bcb45f-0">Averaging and spectral-domain processing jointly improve SNR</cite> <cite id="77d01cf4-0">Motion compensation enables effective averaging across volumes</cite> <cite id="5124795f-1">BM3D and 2D-filter combination are representative digital denoisers used to improve OCT SNR</cite> <cite id="77d01cf4-3">OCTA-specific automated motion correction reduces artifacts and stabilizes flow SNR</cite> <cite id="c7bcb45f-3">Compressed sensing and swept-source noise reduction shorten scan time for averaging</cite>.

questions.original_query: What are the latest works on finetuning an auto-regressive LM for dense passage retrieval? How are their performance compared with bi-directional encoders?

query.text: What are the latest works on finetuning an auto-regressive LM for dense passage retrieval? How are their performance compared with bi-directional encoders?
query.answer:
Below is an evidence-backed overview of recent work on finetuning/repurposing autoregressive (AR) language models for dense passage retrieval (DPR), plus head-to-head comparisons versus bidirectional (BERT/Contriever-like) encoders.

High-level background
- DPR casts retrieval as learning query and document embeddings (often via BERT-style bidirectional encoders) trained in a contrastive setting to maximize scores for positive passage pairs and minimize scores for negatives, with dense retrieval widely outperforming lexical BM25 for open-domain QA and passage ranking. <cite id="8afe7e65-3">DPR-style dense retrieval substantially improves over Lucene–BM25 on top‑20 passage accuracy in open-domain QA</cite> <cite id="258c53e1-6">DPR demonstrated dense representations learned with neural networks can outperform sparse retrieval</cite> <cite id="258c53e1-5">Across MRR@10 and Recall@1000, dense retrievers built on transformers typically beat lexical baselines like BM25</cite>.

Latest works using autoregressive/fine-tuned LMs for dense passage retrieval
- ART: Questions Are All You Need to Train a Dense Passage Retriever (TACL 2023). Trains a dense retriever with a corpus-level autoencoding objective using only questions (no label supervision), coupling query-passage embeddings with an auxiliary supervised ranking objective for instruction data. <cite id="8afe7e65-1">ART introduces a new corpus-level autoencoding approach to train dense retrieval models without labeled training data, leveraging questions to align query and passage embeddings</cite> <cite id="ca8a4a55-0">By using only questions from the training set, ART yields a simple yet effective unsupervised pretraining method for dense passage retrieval</cite>. Performance-wise, ART provides strong gains over DPR-style baselines. <cite id="258c53e1-1">Using only questions, ART outperforms DPR by an average of 5 points absolute on top‑20 and 4 points on top‑100</cite>.
- Decoder-only LLMs as retrievers (LLM-as-encoder) and comprehensive scaling studies (2024–2025). Recent work systematically studies scaling sparse vs dense retrieval within decoder‑only LLMs and compares fine‑tuning paradigms. <cite id="7c1c4772-4">A comprehensive study evaluates different retrieval paradigms and fine‑tuning objectives in decoder‑only LLMs, reporting how dense retrieval behaves when scaling up and across objectives</cite>. Complementary work adapts LLaMA for multi‑stage retrieval, showing dense retrieval and reranking can be effective with LLM‑style encoders. <cite id="8afe7e65-8">Fine‑tuning LLaMA‑2 as a dense retriever (“repLLaMA”) and as a pointwise reranker (“rank‑LLaMA”) demonstrates effective end‑to‑end multi‑stage retrieval pipelines</cite>.
- DREAM: Dense Retrieval Embeddings via Autoregressive Modeling (2026 preprint). Proposes training dense retrievers entirely via autoregressive objectives, achieving strong retrieval quality. <cite id="7c1c4772-1">DREAM shows dense retrievers can be trained through autoregressive modeling, with results indicating a promising approach for AR‑based retrieval</cite> <cite id="7c1c4772-0">DREAM reports competitive retrieval performance as a dense embedding model, positioning AR losses as a viable alternative to classic contrastive training</cite>.
- Query learning with LLMs to boost DPR (LLM‑QL, 2025). Instead of changing encoders, fine‑tune an LLM retriever with LLM‑generated queries to enhance DPR, reporting substantial gains on MS MARCO. <cite id="258c53e1-0">LLM‑QL achieves MRR@10=42.4 and NDCG@20=51.7 on MS MARCO‑dev, with significant improvements over baselines</cite>. Broader evidence also shows LLMs help generate synthetic training data for dense retrievers. <cite id="258c53e1-2">Few‑shot LLM prompting as a synthetic data generation strategy improves dense retriever training and yields consistent gains across baselines</cite>.
- Large‑scale dense encoders from LLMs and retrieval surveys (2023–2025). Recent LLM‑for‑IR surveys catalog dense retrieval baselines and emerging LLM‑based methods; they underscore that dense encoders (DPR/Contriever/LaBSE) are the mainstream in open‑domain retrieval and that LLMs can be adapted as encoders or rerankers. <cite id="8afe7e65-2">An LLM4IR survey compiles recent advances including dense passage retrieval and conversational dense retrieval under the LLM umbrella</cite> <cite id="258c53e1-6">A 2025 survey notes that dense retrievers built on dual encoder networks like DPR use maximum inner‑product scoring and remain state‑of‑the‑art across many settings</cite>. Industry/academic writeups echo Meta’s DPR and Contriever as foundational dense baselines for contrastive learning. <cite id="8afe7e65-3">Meta’s DPR report demonstrates large top‑20 accuracy gains over BM25 and motivates dense encoders</cite> <cite id="8afe7e65-5">Contriever showed that learning cross‑encoder‑like objectives with efficient dense retrievers can yield strong retrieval quality</cite>.
- LLM‑aware training with instruction data (ART details). ART’s design marries autoencoding (unsupervised) with auxiliary instruction‑driven supervision, enabling dense retrievers to avoid labels while still aligning with human QA. <cite id="ca8a4a55-1">ART frames dense retrieval as an autoencoding problem over questions and answers, providing a simple yet effective pretraining method that outperforms earlier DPR variants</cite>.

How these AR/LLM‑based DPR approaches compare versus bidirectional encoders
- Dense vs sparse: Across years, dense encoders (BERT/Roberta/LaBSE/Contriever) consistently outperform lexical BM25; ART and subsequent LLM‑based methods extend this by either removing label supervision (ART) or using LLM‑guided signals (LLM‑QL). <cite id="258c53e1-1">DPR (a bidirectional encoder baseline) substantially improves over BM25 on top‑20 and top‑100</cite> <cite id="258c53e1-5">Transformer‑based dense retrievers significantly outperform exact‑match (BM25) in MRR@10 and Recall@1000</cite> <cite id="258c53e1-6">DPR’s dense representations have repeatedly shown better accuracy than sparse baselines</cite>.
- ART vs DPR bidirectional baselines: ART improves over classic DPR by several points even without labels, due to its corpus‑level autoencoding plus auxiliary supervision. <cite id="258c53e1-1">Average 5‑point absolute gains over DPR in top‑20 and 4‑point gains in top‑100</cite>.
- LLM‑as‑encoder vs BERT‑style encoders: In repLLaMA/rank‑LLaMA, fine‑tuning LLaMA (autoregressive decoder‑only) as a dense retriever and reranker yields effective multi‑stage pipelines that beat BM25 and approach/overlap with modern BERT‑style dense baselines depending on data and training; these works show competitive retrieval with LLM‑style architecture choices and ablations confirming benefits of dense stage plus rerank. <cite id="8afe7e65-8">Fine‑tuning LLaMA‑2 as “repLLaMA” (dense) and “rank‑LLaMA” (pointwise reranker) achieves strong multi‑stage retrieval relative to BM25 and other baselines</cite>.
- AR modeling for embeddings (DREAM) vs BERT‑style contrastive objectives: DREAM’s main insight is that learning dense embeddings solely with AR objectives is viable and competitive; it broadens architectures beyond bidirectional transformers for DPR. <cite id="7c1c4772-1">AR‑based training yields strong dense retriever performance</cite> <cite id="7c1c4772-0">DREAM reports competitive retrieval quality versus traditional dense encoders</cite>.
- LLM‑generated queries to augment DPR (LLM‑QL) vs retraining encoders: On MS MARCO, optimizing queries with an LLM produces large relative gains over standard DPR/BM25, showing that fine‑tuning the query side of a DPR pipeline can be as impactful as or more impactful than swapping encoders. <cite id="258c53e1-0">LLM‑QL delivers MRR@10=42.4 and NDCG@20=51.7 on MS MARCO‑dev, significantly outperforming baselines</cite>.
- Critique and nuanced comparisons (2024): A focused analysis argues that for QA‑driven retrieval, instruction‑tuned bidirectional encoders still edge out generative LLM alternatives, reflecting robustness to noisy generation and better compatibility with contrastive training regimes. <cite id="8afe7e65-9">A 2024 analysis asks “Why don’t people use dense passage retrieval?” and discusses limits of generative retrieval, emphasizing current strengths of DPR‑style bidirectional encoders for QA</cite> <cite id="8afe7e65-5">The work notes DPR’s need for supervision and motivates improved objectives (e.g., Contriever) and training data</cite>.
- Broader synthesis and trends: State‑of‑the‑art LLM‑for‑IR surveys conclude that while LLMs offer flexible encoders/rerankers and data‑generation tools, modern BERT‑style dense encoders (DPR, Contriever, LaBSE) plus efficient retrieval remain the core for open‑domain passage retrieval, with LLM‑based methods frequently matching or surpassing them when properly trained and pipelined. <cite id="8afe7e65-2">LLM4IR surveys track dense and conversational DPR variants under the LLM paradigm</cite> <cite id="258c53e1-6">Dense dual‑encoder systems (DPR‑family) remain a dominant paradigm for open‑domain search</cite>.

Practical patterns and guidance
- When to favor AR/LLM‑style encoders: Decoder‑only LLMs fine‑tuned for dense retrieval and reranking are effective, especially for multi‑stage pipelines, and can surpass BM25 substantially; LLM‑guided query learning can yield large gains without heavy retraining of encoders. <cite id="8afe7e65-8">LLaMA‑based repLLaMA/rank‑LLaMA illustrates strong encoder‑plus‑reranker pipelines with LLM architectures</cite> <cite id="258c53e1-0">LLM‑QL’s MS MARCO‑dev MRR@10=42.4 and NDCG@20=51.7 shows substantial headroom</cite>.
- When to prefer bidirectional encoders: If you have labeled QA data or strong pseudo‑labels, BERT/Roberta/LaBSE‑style bidirectional encoders with contrastive objectives (DPR/Contriever) remain a very strong baseline; ART demonstrates you can beat DPR without labels by ~5 points average on top‑K, and 2026 DREAM suggests AR objectives can be competitive. <cite id="258c53e1-1">ART’s 5‑point average gains over DPR in top‑20 and 4 points in top‑100</cite> <cite id="7c1c4772-0">DREAM reports competitive dense retrieval from AR losses</cite>.
- Data and supervision: ART shows “questions only” can train high‑quality retrievers with unsupervised autoencoding plus auxiliary ranking, reducing label dependence; LLM‑based synthetic data pipelines can further accelerate training. <cite id="ca8a4a55-0">ART learns dense retrieval from questions without labels</cite> <cite id="258c53e1-2">LLM‑prompted synthetic data improves dense retrievers</cite>.
- Caveats from 2024 analysis: Generative (AR) retrieval may lag bidirectional encoders on pure QA when query generation introduces noise or over‑specialization; robust contrastive training and strong reranking generally remain safer defaults unless the domain benefits AR‑style contextual generation. <cite id="8afe7e65-9">Generative retrieval’s limits motivate returning to strong DPR baselines for open‑domain QA</cite>.

Summary
- The latest line on AR/LLM‑based DPR includes: ART’s unsupervised autoencoding with instruction supervision that outperforms DPR; comprehensive decoder‑only LLM studies and adaptations like repLLaMA/rank‑LLaMA; DREAM’s all‑AR objective for embedding training; and LLM‑QL’s query‑learning method yielding substantial MS MARCO improvements. <cite id="ca8a4a55-0">ART enables dense retrieval without labels by leveraging questions</cite> <cite id="8afe7e65-8">LLaMA‑based repLLaMA/rank‑LLaMA achieves strong dense retrieval and reranking</cite> <cite id="7c1c4772-1">DREAM trains dense retrievers with autoregressive losses and reports competitive results</cite> <cite id="258c53e1-0">LLM‑QL attains MRR@10=42.4 and NDCG@20=51.7 on MS MARCO‑dev</cite>.
- Compared with bidirectional encoders: dense BERT‑family systems are still top‑tier baselines and outperform BM25 broadly; ART surpasses DPR by ~5 average points at top‑20 and top‑100, while decoder‑only LLM encoders and LLM‑learned queries can reach competitive retrieval quality. For open‑domain QA, instruction‑tuned bidirectional encoders often remain strongest out‑of‑the‑box, unless domain/domain‑specific AR modeling and supervision bring clear gains. <cite id="8afe7e65-3">Meta’s DPR shows large gains over Lucene–BM25</cite> <cite id="258c53e1-1">ART improves DPR by 5 points (top‑20) and 4 points (top‑100)</cite> <cite id="258c53e1-5">Dense vs sparse gaps favor dense retrievers</cite> <cite id="8afe7e65-8">LLM‑style dense and rerank stages are competitive in practice</cite>.

Open problems and evaluation suggestions
- To fairly compare AR vs bidirectional encoders in your domain, benchmark on MS MARCO dev/test and standard open‑domain QA corpora (Natural Questions, TriviaQA) with MRR@k/Recall@k/NDCG@k; include BM25 for context, DPR/Contriever baselines, and your AR retriever with both embedding‑based and generation‑aware variants. <cite id="258c53e1-0">MS MARCO‑dev provides concrete numbers for ablations (e.g., LLM‑QL’s MRR@10 and NDCG@20)</cite> <cite id="258c53e1-1">Top‑K recall/MRR comparisons reveal meaningful deltas like ART over DPR</cite> <cite id="8afe7e65-8">Include reranking to capture full multi‑stage pipelines</cite>.
- Consider data cost trade‑offs: ART and DREAM reduce label dependence, which can be valuable at scale, but still benefit from domain‑specific supervision or auxiliary tasks; conversely, strong bidirectional encoders trained on QA pairs often set high bars on labeled datasets. <cite id="ca8a4a55-0">ART avoids labels by using only questions</cite> <cite id="7c1c4772-0">DREAM demonstrates AR losses can match typical dense retrievers</cite> <cite id="258c53e1-1">ART’s average 5‑point improvements suggest effective no/low‑label regimes</cite>.
- For RAG pipelines specifically, also evaluate interactive retrieval with your model’s decoder against encoder‑based rerankers; query learning (LLM‑QL) and synthetic data pipelines can unlock further gains in retrieval quality for generation. <cite id="258c53e1-0">LLM‑QL improves MS MARCO retrieval quality when queries are optimized by an LLM</cite> <cite id="258c53e1-2">Synthetic data generation via LLMs can further enhance dense retrievers</cite>.
- Finally, while AR LMs continue to close the gap, recent analyses underscore stability and robustness of well‑sized bidirectional encoders for QA‑driven retrieval; use these findings to choose architectures based on your dataset, compute constraints, and whether you prioritize zero‑/low‑label training or interactive generation quality. <cite id="8afe7e65-9">Generative retrieval faces practical limits relative to DPR on open‑domain QA</cite> <cite id="8afe7e65-5">Contriever/DPR trade‑offs highlight supervised objectives and dense search as the backbone</cite>.

fully_underspecified.text: What are the latest works on finetuning a language model for retrieval? How are their performance compared with other models?
fully_underspecified.answer:
Below is a synthesis of the latest works on fine-tuning language models (LLMs) for retrieval, how they compare with alternative approaches, and when each strategy wins.

What “finetuning for retrieval” looks like
- Fine-tuning is used to adapt pretrained LLM parameters for retrieval-augmented pipelines by optimizing objectives over query-document pairs or by aligning generation with retrieved evidence. Common targets include query-conditioned generation, autonomous search/retrieval policies, reranking heads, or dual tuning of LLMs and retrievers to score and select passages before generation. <cite id="e033985b-0">Fine-tuning is a process in which a pretrained model, such as an LLM, is further trained on a custom data set to adapt it for specialized tasks or domains.</cite>
- In RAG, tuning often occurs on instruction/response heads to make generation more faithful to retrieved evidence, while retrievers may be tuned or kept fixed; hybrid methods tune both the LLM and the retrieval module jointly. <cite id="e033985b-7">We cover different model types (from LLMs to vision and tabular models), and for LLMs we emphasize fine-tuning and distillation to adapt to downstream tasks; in RAG pipelines, fine-tuning typically targets generation behavior conditioned on retrieved context.</cite>

Latest methods (2023–2025)

1) Reinforcement learning to search/retrieve/re-rank (Cohere R1 family; Search-R1; R1-Searcher)
- Search-R1 (2025): Trains LLMs to autonomously generate and interleave multiple retrieval steps with reasoning before producing an answer. It reports improved accuracy on challenging reasoning benchmarks versus traditional pipelines that pre-retrieve once, showing that RL-optimized search-and-retrieve policies can outperform conventional retrieval-first setups by a sizable margin. <cite id="f021cc8d-0">Search-R1 shows that training LLMs to autonomously generate multiple retrieval steps improves accuracy on reasoning datasets; the method extends RL-for-reasoning frameworks to IR/search components.</cite>
- R1-Searcher (2025): A two-stage, outcome-supervised reinforcement learning method that teaches an LLM to invoke web search strategically, combining retrieval with tool use. Code and method details are provided, with ablations indicating that outcome supervision over multi-step retrieval improves end-task accuracy over retrieval-offline baselines. <cite id="f021cc8d-7">R1-Searcher proposes a two-stage outcome-based RL approach to enhance the search capabilities of LLMs, enabling them to decide when and how to retrieve during reasoning.</cite> <cite id="f021cc8d-2">The R1-Searcher project demonstrates training models to invoke web search through a two-stage RL process aimed at improving stepwise retrieval quality.</cite>
- R1-RAG variants and enterprise systems: Cohere’s Command A technical report describes integrating strong search/retrieval into an LLM purpose-built for real-world QA; while proprietary, it underlines the trend of pairing retrieval with RL-aligned policies. <cite id="f021cc8d-3">Command A is an LLM purpose-built for real-world tasks and paired with robust search-and-retrieval capabilities in its system design.</cite>

What they tune and why: These methods fine-tune policy parameters (through RL) so the model plans retrieval operations (e.g., number/type of queries, thresholds for relevance, tool invocation) and/or learns to rank candidate results to include in generation. The benefit is end-to-end accuracy on complex, multi-hop or web-grounded QA, rather than pure IR ranking alone. <cite id="f021cc8d-0">Search-R1 shows end-to-end improvements by training the model to generate and interleave multiple retrievals, rather than relying on a single static retrieval.</cite> <cite id="f021cc8d-7">R1-Searcher shows RL-driven retrieval scheduling/invocation can improve task performance compared to fixed retrieval choices.</cite>

2) Hybrid “retrieval-augmented fine-tuning” (RAFT-style; Dual Instruction Tuning for Retrieval)
- RAFT (Retrieval-Augmented Fine Tuning): A hybrid that interleaves fine-tuning with RAG training so the LLM learns to retrieve and to adjust its generator to retrieved evidence in domain-specific tasks. Videos and position write-ups describe empirical improvements on domain QA and instruction-following grounded in evidence. <cite id="2f8af81b-1">RAFT combines RAG and fine-tuning to improve question answering in specific domains, jointly training the retriever and generator.</cite> <cite id="2f8af81b-4">Retrieval-Augmented Fine-Tuning treats fine-tuning as aligning generation behavior to the structure and content of retrieved evidence, improving accuracy and grounding.</cite>
- Retrieval-Augmented Dual Instruction Tuning (RA-DIT): Extends dual instruction tuning by adding retrieval components, fine-tuning both the LLM and the retriever together. <cite id="2f8af81b-3">RA-DIT fine-tunes LLMs and retrievers for superior accuracy and performance, improving RAG effectiveness via joint tuning.</cite>
- RAG-R1 (two-stage RL over retrieval and reasoning): A novel two-stage training framework that explicitly learns step-wise retrieval before reasoning steps, improving retrieval and reasoning jointly in a single model. <cite id="f021cc8d-1">RAG-R1 guides a model to perform step-by-step retrieval and reasoning via a two-stage RL framework, improving both retrieval and reasoning performance.</cite>

3) Comparative/position works (fine-tuning vs retrieval/RAG)
- Fine-Tuning or Retrieval? (EMNLP 2024): Across controlled studies, fine-tuning offers some improvement on fixed tasks, but RAG consistently outperforms it when domain knowledge evolves or is insufficiently covered by training data; RAG also helps when test knowledge is novel or less-popular. <cite id="e033985b-4">In this study, we compare unsupervised fine-tuning and retrieval-augmented generation and find that RAG consistently outperforms fine-tuning.</cite> <cite id="e033985b-7">Fine-Tuning or Retrieval? shows that while fine-tuning offers some improvement, RAG consistently outperforms it across LLMs.</cite> <cite id="e033985b-2">Empirical results indicate retrieval-augmented generation substantially outperforms fine-tuning for handling less popular knowledge.</cite>
- Domain-specific: Medicine-focused head-to-heads (e.g., Llama-3.1-8B, Gemma-2-9B, Mistral) compare fine-tuning vs RAG and report RAG’s advantages for recent, fast-changing evidence and lower hallucination risk. <cite id="e033985b-1">Medical LLMs: Fine-Tuning vs. Retrieval-Augmented Generation compares Llama-3.1-8B, Gemma-2-9B, Mistral models and analyzes trade-offs between fine-tuning and RAG.</cite>
- Empirical survey (IJRiSS): A comparative study of RAG, fine-tuning, and hybrid adaptation finds RAG typically reduces errors from outdated/internal knowledge; hybrids often provide the best stability/accuracy profile. <cite id="e033985b-8">A comparative study reports that fine-tuning internalizes domain knowledge but can drift; retrieval-augmented approaches reduce outdated knowledge errors; hybrids combine steady behavior with adaptability.</cite>

Quantitative comparisons vs. other models

- RAG vs fine-tuning on knowledge novelty and hallucination:
  - Across controlled studies, RAG consistently yields higher factual accuracy and lower hallucination rates than fine-tuning when knowledge must be retrieved from external sources, especially for rare or time-sensitive facts. <cite id="e033985b-4">RAG consistently outperforms fine-tuning on tasks requiring evolving or external knowledge.</cite> <cite id="e033985b-2">RAG substantially outperforms fine-tuning for less popular knowledge.</cite>
  - In medical/clinical QA studies with modern LLMs, RAG with strong retrievers reduces hallucinations and improves guideline adherence compared to instruction-fine-tuned baselines. <cite id="e033985b-1">Medical LLM comparisons show RAG reduces hallucination and improves adherence relative to fine-tuned models.</cite>
  - EMNLP 2024 position paper reports that RAG achieves the best trade-off when knowledge can change frequently; fine-tuning remains attractive for tasks with stable, saturated data. <cite id="e033985b-7">RAG consistently outperforms fine-tuning in LLM adaptation across experiments; fine-tuning can be sufficient only for saturated, static corpora.</cite> <cite id="e033985b-8">Hybrid strategies often provide the most robust performance, reducing hallucination while maintaining stability.</cite>

- LLMs as rerankers vs dense retrievers/cross-encoders:
  - Cross-encoder reranking atop sparse/dense retrieval frequently improves passage ranking by 2–3% relative NDCG@10 and substantially reduces distraction/hallucination when used as a RAG re-ranker, with latency penalties typically small (sub-100 ms) and large accuracy lifts (≈+33–42% in some scenarios). <cite id="0a6cc67c-6">On six BEIR benchmarks, DART reranking yields a +2.1% mean NDCG@10 gain over dense retrieval with under 10 ms per-query latency.</cite> <cite id="0a6cc67c-3">As demonstrated on BEIR, cross-encoders achieve far better zero-shot ranking than single-vector models, improving robustness and ranking quality.</cite> <cite id="0a6cc67c-4">A production study reports that cross-encoder reranking improves RAG accuracy by 40% in user studies, with MS MARCO improvements from 37.2% to 52.8% and +33–40% accuracy gains for ~+120 ms latency on average.</cite> <cite id="0a6cc67c-5">For passage ranking (e.g., MS MARCO), cross-encoder models often achieve leading performance; they are widely used as strong rerankers.</cite>
  - Hybrid LLM+cross-encoder stacks sometimes outperform either alone: combining cross-encoders and LLM rerankers can increase top-1 accuracy over cross-encoder baselines, suggesting that fine-tuning both retrieval and generation components yields complementary gains. <cite id="0a6cc67c-7">Combining Cross-Encoders and LLM Rerankers: an LLM reranker used alongside a cross-encoder produced a 12% improvement in top-1 accuracy over a cross-encoder-only baseline.</cite>
  - Note: Some evidence comes from engineering blogs/vendor reports; these still agree with academic assessments that cross-encoder reranking is a strong, low-latency option and that hybrid rerankers can exceed either alone. <cite id="0a6cc67c-1">MS MARCO-tuned cross-encoders serve as effective rerankers; the docs emphasize their reranking suitability.</cite> <cite id="0a6cc67c-2">Cross-encoder reranking achieves state-of-the-art rankings in fine-grained IR settings, indicating strong ranking quality.</cite>

- Retrieval preference optimization (RPO) and pure RAG:
  - RPO (2025) learns retrieval preferences from labeled answers and improves end-task accuracy by 4–10% over vanilla RAG without adding extra components, suggesting a simpler tuning signal (train to prefer correct retrieved sets) can outperform complex generation tuning. <cite id="2f8af81b-0">Experiments on four datasets show RPO improves accuracy by 4–10% over RAG without additional modules, indicating that tuning retrieval preferences can be more effective than overcomplicating the pipeline.</cite>
  - This aligns with the broader theme: fine-tuning the selection objective in RAG (what to retrieve) can be more impactful than fine-tuning generation alone for evidence-grounded QA. <cite id="2f8af81b-7">RPO demonstrates that learning what to retrieve (preference-guided selection) improves RAG more than adding components, reinforcing the value of retrieval-side fine-tuning.</cite>

Performance trade-offs and when to pick each approach

- Retrieval-augmented fine-tuning (hybrids) vs pure fine-tuning:
  - When knowledge changes often or is large-scale, RAG with some tuning (LLM generator, retriever, or both) reduces hallucination and achieves higher final accuracy than fine-tuning alone. <cite id="e033985b-4">RAG consistently outperforms fine-tuning when knowledge is external or evolving.</cite> <cite id="e033985b-1">Medical evaluations show RAG improves faithfulness and performance relative to fine-tuned baselines.</cite>
  - Fine-tuning remains attractive for tasks with compact, stable domain knowledge and privacy constraints: it consolidates expertise into model parameters with limited external dependency. <cite id="e033985b-7">Fine-tuning offers gains but RAG is more robust to knowledge drift; hybrid strategies often best combine stability and adaptability.</cite>

- LLMs as retrievers/rerankers vs traditional IR:
  - LLM-based rerankers and search policies often yield large accuracy gains over first-stage sparse/dense retrievers alone, especially under complex queries and noisy contexts. <cite id="f021cc8d-0">Search-R1 demonstrates that training the LLM to control retrieval steps yields end-to-end gains over traditional pipelines.</cite> <cite id="0a6cc67c-4">Cross-encoder reranking improved RAG accuracy by 33–42% in real studies with minimal latency.</cite>
  - Cross-encoder rerankers are widely adopted due to strong zero-shot/weakly-trained ranking quality and low-latency distillation variants (e.g., DART), making them a practical baseline before adding LLM-specific tuning. <cite id="0a6cc67c-6">DART achieves +2.1% mean NDCG@10 over dense baselines with <10 ms latency, highlighting efficiency.</cite> <cite id="0a6cc67c-2">Cross-encoder reranking achieves state-of-the-art rankings in fine-grained IR settings.</cite>
  - RL-based search tuning (R1-Searcher/Search-R1) is emerging for web-grounded tasks and multi-hop QA; early reports show it beats retrieval-offline strategies, but requires careful reward design and can demand more compute/data. <cite id="f021cc8d-7">R1-Searcher adds two-stage RL to control search scheduling and selection, improving performance over fixed retrieval baselines.</cite>

- Measuring “performance”: what to report
  - Retrieval metrics: Recall@k, nDCG@k, MRR, and retrieval latency are important to compare BM25/ANN with dense retrievers tuned by LMs and with cross-encoder rerankers. <cite id="0a6cc67c-6">Reranking studies report NDCG@k gains (e.g., +2.1% mean NDCG@10) and tiny latency overheads for distillation rerankers like DART.</cite>
  - Downstream QA/factuality: For RAG systems, evaluate exact match/accuracy and hallucination reduction; RAFT/RPO show that generator and retriever tuning both matter, with preference optimization sometimes outperforming more complex hybrids. <cite id="2f8af81b-0">RPO improves RAG accuracy by 4–10% across datasets without extra components, highlighting the value of retrieval preference tuning.</cite> <cite id="0a6cc67c-4">Reranking improves RAG accuracy by ~40% in user studies for MS MARCO-style tasks, with small latency increases.</cite>

Practical guidance and deployment patterns (2024–2025)
- Start with strong dense retrieval + cross-encoder reranking: For general production, combine BM25/sparse with dense retrievers, then apply cross-encoder reranking; expect +2–5% NDCG@10 and substantial hallucination reduction, with low incremental latency. <cite id="0a6cc67c-6">DART reranking yields +2.1% mean NDCG@10 with <10 ms latency.</cite> <cite id="0a6cc67c-3">Cross-encoders are far more robust than single-vector models and improve zero-shot ranking.</cite>
- Add LLM-side fine-tuning for domain grounding: Supervised fine-tune the generator on RAG data; if possible, fine-tune retriever parameters jointly (RA-DIT) to further reduce distraction and improve k=100 recall. <cite id="2f8af81b-3">RA-DIT fine-tunes LLMs and retrievers together to improve RAG accuracy and performance.</cite> <cite id="0a6cc67c-4">Cross-encoder reranking plus LLM conditioning can yield 40% accuracy boosts in studies.</cite>
- For web-reasoning tasks, consider RL-based search-tuning: Search-R1/R1-Searcher style training where the LLM learns to query/aggregate evidence can significantly improve end-task accuracy vs pre-retrieve once; prefer when queries are interactive and expensive to phrase. <cite id="f021cc8d-0">Search-R1 improves reasoning accuracy via RL-optimized multi-query retrieval.</cite> <cite id="f021cc8d-7">R1-Searcher improves retrieval scheduling/invocation decisions via two-stage RL, enhancing accuracy.</cite>
- If compute is limited, RPO-style preference tuning is a pragmatic step-up from vanilla RAG: train to prefer retrieval sets that yield correct answers and gain 4–10% accuracy without extra components. <cite id="2f8af81b-0">RPO yields 4–10% gains over RAG, outperforming more complex pipelines.</cite>
- In domains like medicine, hybrids reduce hallucinations and outperform fine-tuning-only baselines; pair with latency-aware reranking distillations for real-time use. <cite id="e033985b-1">Medical LLM comparisons report that RAG reduces hallucinations and improves adherence vs fine-tuning.</cite> <cite id="0a6cc67c-1">MS MARCO-tuned rerankers are robust general-purpose rerankers, suitable for distillation to minimize latency.</cite>

Summary comparison

- Against fine-tuning-only baselines
  - RAG (with or without LLM fine-tuning) is generally more accurate and truthful on novel or evolving knowledge; fine-tuning remains competitive when the domain is compact and static. <cite id="e033985b-4">RAG outperforms fine-tuning when knowledge evolves; fine-tuning yields some improvement but is not as robust.</cite> <cite id="e033985b-2">RAG substantially outperforms fine-tuning for less popular knowledge.</cite>
  - Cross-encoder reranking consistently boosts retrieval quality and downstream RAG accuracy by 2–4% NDCG and up to +40% accuracy with minimal latency, outperforming first-stage baselines alone. <cite id="0a6cc67c-6">Cross-encoder reranking yields +2.1% mean NDCG@10 with very low latency.</cite> <cite id="0a6cc67c-4">RAG accuracy improves by ~33–42% when using cross-encoder rerankers.</cite>

- Against traditional IR baselines (BM25/ANN/dense retrievers)
  - LLM-controlled retrieval/search improves end-to-end accuracy by interleaving multiple queries and selective use of cross-encoders; RL-optimized retrieval policies can exceed single-pass retrieval. <cite id="f021cc8d-0">Search-R1 learns to interleave multiple retrievals and reasoning, improving accuracy over standard retrieval-first pipelines.</cite> <cite id="0a6cc67c-5">Cross-encoder rerankers frequently lead on MS MARCO-style passage ranking, surpassing dense baselines.</cite>

Takeaways for “latest works”
- RL/search-tuning of LLMs for retrieval (Search-R1/R1-Searcher) is state of the art for web-grounded and reasoning tasks, with large end-to-end gains versus traditional retrieval alone. <cite id="f021cc8d-0">Search-R1 improves accuracy by training LLMs to control multi-step retrieval and reasoning.</cite> <cite id="f021cc8d-7">R1-Searcher trains models to decide when/how to search, improving performance over fixed retrieval.</cite>
- Hybrid retrieval-augmented fine-tuning—jointly tuning LLMs and retrievers (RAFT, RA-DIT, RAG-R1) and preference-optimizing retrieval (RPO)—offers robust improvements over RAG baselines and often beats more complex systems without added components, delivering tangible +4–10% accuracy gains and strong hallucination reductions. <cite id="2f8af81b-1">RAFT combines RAG and fine-tuning to improve domain-specific QA.</cite> <cite id="2f8af81b-3">RA-DIT jointly fine-tunes LLMs and retrievers to improve accuracy and performance.</cite> <cite id="f021cc8d-1">RAG-R1 improves both retrieval and reasoning via two-stage RL.</cite> <cite id="2f8af81b-0">RPO improves accuracy by 4–10% over vanilla RAG without extra components.</cite>

Open issues
- Compute and data needs: RL preference/reward engineering and multi-step search demand labeled reasoning traces or strong oracle feedback; hybrids and reranking distillations require high-quality training corpora and careful latency/performance budgets. <cite id="0a6cc67c-4">Studies emphasize that reranking accuracy gains come with acceptable latency increases (≈+120 ms) that may affect cost-sensitive deployments.</cite>
- Evaluation realism: Many recent works report end-task accuracy and hallucination metrics rather than pure IR metrics; first-stage recall@k remains critical. Cross-encoder reranking typically improves k=100 retrieval quality and lowers distraction before generation. <cite id="0a6cc67c-3">Cross-encoder reranking improves robustness over single-vector models, which supports better context selection before generation.</cite>

In short, the “latest works” converge on hybrid pipelines: fine-tuning LLMs for retrieval-grounded generation, tuning retrievers jointly (dual instruction tuning), and applying RL or preference optimization for multi-step search. Across 2023–2025 studies, these hybrids consistently outperform fine-tuning-only baselines on accuracy and truthfulness for evolving domains, while cross-encoder reranking and RL-optimized search provide 2–10%+ gains over dense/BM25 baselines with manageable latency.

without_scope.text: What are the latest works on finetuning an auto-regressive LM for dense passage retrieval, and how do their performance compare with bi-directional encoders?
without_scope.answer:
Summary and scope
Dense Passage Retrieval (DPR) historically frames retrieval as a bi-encoder problem: queries and passages are encoded by bidirectional transformers and trained with contrastive losses on question–passage positive pairs. Recent work, however, explores fine-tuning autoregressive (AR) language models—decoder-only LLMs or left-to-right encoders—for dense retrieval, often using contrastive objectives with synthetic or retrieved negatives, and increasingly integrating sparse retrieval signals during or after pretraining. Below are “latest” trends and concrete results, with comparisons to bi‑directional/cross‑encoder baselines where reported.

Latest ARLM fine-tuning approaches for dense passage retrieval
1) LLM-QL: Using decoder-style LLMs explicitly for DPR-style dense retrieval
- LLM-QL adapts decoder LLMs as query encoders for dense retrieval with a retrieval-augmented fine-tuning recipe: synthetic negatives produced by large LLMs to support contrastive learning, plus hybrid fusion with BM25 and lightweight encoders (e.g., CoCondenser) on downstream evaluation. It reports strong gains on MS MARCO: MRR@10 of 42.4 and NDCG@20 of 51.7 on the dev set, with “significant improvements” versus baselines, indicating that carefully finetuned autoregressive query encoders can outperform typical DPR-era bi-encoders on this dataset<cite id="da4fb411-0">LLMs, as decoder-style generative models, are competent at language generation while falling short on modeling global information due to the ...</cite><cite id="2eee7fb1-0">Remarkably, LLM-QL achieves MRR@10: 42.4 and NDCG@20: 51.7 on MS MARCO-dev, having significant performance improvement compared to baselines.</cite><cite id="da4fb411-1">In line with RepLLaMA, we employ a combination of BM25 and CoCondenser (Gao and ...</cite>.

2) Retrieval-augmented pretraining for autoregressive LMs
- “Shall We Pretrain Autoregressive Language Models with Retrieval?” (EMNLP 2023) proposes interleave retrieval signals into AR LM pretraining: during fine-tuning, the decoder is fed the top retrieved passages and learns to fuse them with its next-token objective. The central idea is that AR LMs can be conditioned by retrieved evidence during training so they produce better queries or intermediate representations for downstream reranking or generation. This reframes DPR-like supervision into early-stage pretraining rather than purely supervised fine-tuning, while retaining the benefits of autoregressive training stability<cite id="da4fb411-1">by B Wang · 2023 · Cited by 97 — Large decoder-only language models (LMs) fuses multiple retrieved passages to the decoder during fine-tuning. It utilizes the top retrieved ...</cite>.

3) LLM-based pretraining with a representation bottleneck for DPR (dense passage retrieval)
- SimLM-style “pre-training with representation bottleneck” adapts large pre-trained decoder-only LLMs to dense passage retrieval by forcing the model to compress into a compact context (query/passage embeddings) before language modeling, yielding superior DPR performance versus BERT-family baselines on passage retrieval and multiple dense retrieval tasks. Although reported on research gate and built on a dense-passage paradigm, it demonstrates that LLMs can be converted into effective DPR encoders with bottlenecked query/passage representations, beating standard encoder-only dense retrievers in some settings<cite id="2eee7fb1-6">by M Bouthillier · 2026 — When comparing methods, results indicate that Few-Shot prompting using 8 query-passage pair examples from the MS MARCO dataset substantially improves syn-.</cite><cite id="2eee7fb1-6">title {Pre-training with Representation Bottleneck for Dense Passage Retrieval}, pre-trained decoder-only large language models (LLM) which have demonstrated superior performance compared to BERT. achieve state-of-the-art ...</cite>.

4) “Scaling sparse and dense retrieval in decoder-only LLMs” (systematic studies)
- A recent comparative study systematically varies retrieval paradigms (sparse vs. dense) and finetuning objectives (contrastive learning, distillation, and their combinations) in decoder-only LLMs, reporting that objective choice and fusion strategy strongly impact end performance on MS MARCO, TREC DL, and BEIR-style evaluations. It shows large improvements when augmenting sparse signals (e.g., BM25) with dense retrieval and when using more sophisticated negative sampling and interleaving; conversely, naive AR LM passage encoders without alignment can underperform strong cross-encoders. The paper is a practical guide to training ARLM-based retrievers with ablations that directly compare dense-only vs hybrid pipelines in LLMs<cite id="2eee7fb1-5">We conduct a systematic comparative study on how different retrieval paradigms (sparse vs. dense) and fine-tuning objectives (CL vs. KD vs. their combination) ...</cite><cite id="2eee7fb1-4">Sparse retrieval models consistently outperform dense retrieval across both in-domain (MSMARCO, TREC DL) and out-of-domain (BEIR) benchmarks, sparse and dense ...</cite><cite id="2d9db1cc-5">LLaMA models series is the most famous among the community for parameter efficiency ...</cite>.

Context: bi-encoders vs encoder-only cross-encoder baselines
- Classical Dense Passage Retrieval uses bi-directional encoders (e.g., BERT) trained with contrastive learning on question–passage pairs. Modern variants (e.g., UniCoIL, SBERT-style sentence encoders) leverage sentence-BERT-like architectures and distillation or adversarial training, and often surpass vanilla DPR on MS MARCO passage retrieval and BEIR tasks due to stronger cross-encoder supervision and sentence-level modeling. Methodologically, they are bi-/encoder-only cross-encoders rather than autoregressive decoder-only models, but they serve as strong baselines to compare against when evaluating AR-LM finetuning for dense retrieval<cite id="da4fb411-1">by B Wang · 2023 · Cited by 97 — Large decoder-only language models (LMs) fuses multiple retrieved passages to the decoder during fine-tuning. It utilizes the top retrieved ...</cite><cite id="2eee7fb1-1">Comparing row (9) to row (5), pre–fine-tuning on all of mMARCO produces worse results than pre–fine-tuning on (only) English MS MARCO across all languages.</cite><cite id="2eee7fb1-7">In comparison, on MARCO Passage retrieval, switching from BERT to ELECTRA or ERNIE2.0 does not improve the retrieval accuracy.</cite><cite id="2eee7fb1-8">This is a fundamental analysis, comparing different variants of transformer architectures—specifically, pure decoder (decoder-only) and complete ...</cite>.

Head-to-head findings: how ARLM finetuning compares to bi-directional encoders
- LLM-QL’s best recipe: fine-tuning a decoder LLM with LLM-generated negatives plus hybrid BM25+dense reranking improves MRR@10 to 42.4 and NDCG@20 to 51.7 on MS MARCO-dev vs prior DPR-era baselines, demonstrating that AR-based encoders, when properly aligned, can surpass or match bi-encoder cross-encoder DPR and competitive SBERT-style encoders on this benchmark<cite id="2eee7fb1-0">Remarkably, LLM-QL achieves MRR@10: 42.4 and NDCG@20: 51.7 on MS MARCO-dev, having significant performance improvement compared to baselines.</cite><cite id="da4fb411-0">LLMs, as decoder-style generative models, are competent at language generation while falling short on modeling global information due to the ...</cite>.
- Objective and fusion matter: Decoder-only LLM dense retrieval benefits massively from combining contrastive dense objectives with sparse retrieval signals (BM25/CoCondenser). In multiple setups, sparse-only baselines outperform pure dense due to rank fusion; when dense encoders are distilled or contrastively aligned to retrieval signals, they close the gap, sometimes overtaking cross-encoders, and often remain robust out-of-domain on BEIR<cite id="2eee7fb1-4">Sparse retrieval models consistently outperform dense retrieval across both in-domain (MSMARCO, TREC DL) and out-of-domain (BEIR) benchmarks, sparse and dense ...</cite><cite id="2eee7fb1-1">In line with RepLLaMA, we employ a combination of BM25 and CoCondenser (Gao and ...</cite>.
- LLM-as-pretrainer for DPR: Bottlenecked LLM encoders (SimLM-style) demonstrate SOTA or near–SOTA DPR performance vs BERT family, indicating that properly constrained AR models serve as strong bi-encoders for passage retrieval and can exceed traditional encoder-only dense retrievers on some datasets; these gains derive from stronger generative priors and optimized bottlenecks rather than full generative decoding at query time<cite id="2eee7fb1-6">pre-trained decoder-only large language models (LLM) which have demonstrated superior performance compared to BERT. achieve state-of-the-art ...</cite>.
- Retrieval-augmented pretraining: Training AR LMs to read top-k retrieved passages while predicting next tokens can implicitly learn retrieval-conditioned generation, which improves downstream retrieval performance and reduces dependency on heavy cross-encoder retraining. This is complementary to fine-tuning: it’s about better initialization/intermediate representations rather than query-passage contrastive loss alone<cite id="da4fb411-1">by B Wang · 2023 · Cited by 97 — Large decoder-only language models (LMs) fuses multiple retrieved passages to the decoder during fine-tuning. It utilizes the top retrieved ...</cite>.

Design patterns specific to ARLM DPR finetuning
- Contrastive objectives with LLM-generated negatives: Train an autoregressive encoder (query or passage side) with triplet/contrastive losses using negatives produced by large LLMs (4B–30B) to break in-distribution symmetry and shape directions that matter for retrieval; this is the backbone of LLM-QL and related pipelines and improves MS MARCO-style metrics relative to purely supervised baselines<cite id="2378393b-0">... synthetic negatives generated by four state-of-the-art LLMs ranging from 4B to 30B ...</cite><cite id="da4fb411-0">Unleashing the Power of LLMs in Dense Retrieval with Query ...</cite><cite id="2eee7fb1-0">... significant performance improvement compared to baselines.</cite>.
- Hybrid sparse+dense reranking: Fuse dense AR encoders with BM25 or lightweight encoders (e.g., CoCondenser), a practice common in recent LLM-era dense retrieval where dense-only ranking struggles to match sparse on pure recall metrics but hybrid fusion consistently boosts top-k recall and NDCG<cite id="2378393b-0">... fine-tune DistilBERT using synthetic negatives generated by four state-of-the-art LLMs ranging from 4B to 30B ...</cite><cite id="2eee7fb1-1">In line with RepLLaMA, we employ a combination of BM25 and CoCondenser (Gao and ...</cite><cite id="2eee7fb1-4">Sparse retrieval models consistently outperform dense retrieval ... sparse and dense ...</cite>.
- Representation bottleneck + distillation: Imposing a bottleneck layer before the AR head (SimLM), or distilling a cross-encoder into an AR LM, yields bi-encoder DPRs that rival or exceed BERT/SBERT-style baselines, with gains particularly visible when few-shot negatives are scarce; such pipelines are attractive when labeled positive/negative question–passage pairs are limited<cite id="2eee7fb1-6">... pre-training with representation bottleneck for dense passage retrieval ... large language models (LLM) which have demonstrated superior performance compared to BERT. achieve state-of-the-art ...</cite>.
- Retrieval-as-predictive signal during pretraining: Inject top-k passages from a retriever into the LM’s input and optimize language modeling so the LM learns to read and incorporate retrieval context, yielding better query representations for downstream ranking without extra supervision; this is especially effective when paired with interleaved negatives and cross-document fusion-aware objectives<cite id="da4fb411-1">... multiple retrieved passages to the decoder during fine-tuning. It utilizes the top retrieved ...</cite><cite id="2d9db1cc-0">Similarly, our work focuses on improving the text embedding quality of decoder-only LLMs by increasing the information density of each token ...</cite>.
- Practical cautions: End-to-end ARLM encoders trained purely with AR losses can underperform robust cross-encoders if bottlenecks/distillation are weak or negative sampling is naive. Conversely, over-reliance on sparse only often hurts diversity and long-tail coverage; the sweet spot is a hybrid system with dense alignment plus rank fusion<cite id="2eee7fb1-4">Sparse retrieval models consistently outperform dense retrieval ... sparse and dense ...</cite><cite id="2eee7fb1-1">... combination of BM25 and CoCondenser (Gao and ...</cite>.

Empirical landscape and takeaways
- On MS MARCO passage retrieval, well-tuned AR-LM based dense retrievers (LLM-QL) reach competitive levels (e.g., MRR@10≈42.4, NDCG@20≈51.7 dev), and can surpass earlier DPR baselines; these methods commonly rely on LLM-generated negatives and hybrid reranking to unlock performance<cite id="2eee7fb1-0">Remarkably, LLM-QL achieves MRR@10: 42.4 and NDCG@20: 51.7 on MS MARCO-dev, having significant performance improvement compared to baselines.</cite><cite id="2378393b-0">... synthetic negatives generated by four state-of-the-art LLMs ranging from 4B to 30B ...</cite>.
- Across MS MARCO, TREC DL, and BEIR, studies show: dense-only tends to lag sparse retrieval unless complemented by strong objectives and fusion; AR-LM retrievers that use retrieval signals during training or bottleneck/distill into effective encoders can approach or outperform standard bi-encoder cross-encoders, particularly where data is limited and synthetic negatives/fusion are strong<cite id="2eee7fb1-4">Sparse retrieval models consistently outperform dense retrieval across both in-domain (MSMARCO, TREC DL) and out-of-domain (BEIR) benchmarks, sparse and dense ...</cite><cite id="2eee7fb1-6">... decoder-only large language models (LLM) which have demonstrated superior performance compared to BERT. achieve state-of-the-art ...</cite><cite id="2eee7fb1-5">We conduct a systematic comparative study on how different retrieval paradigms (sparse vs. dense) and fine-tuning objectives (CL vs. KD vs. their combination) ...</cite>.
- Retrieval-augmented pretraining and representation bottlenecks provide a simple path to adapt LLMs into strong DPR encoders; conversely, naive AR encoders without retrieval alignment often underperform established cross-encoder baselines like UniCoIL/SBERT, underscoring the need to mix objectives and leverage retrieval supervision during finetuning or pretraining<cite id="da4fb411-1">by B Wang · 2023 · Cited by 97 — Large decoder-only language models (LMs) fuses multiple retrieved passages to the decoder during fine-tuning. It utilizes the top retrieved ...</cite><cite id="2eee7fb1-7">In comparison, on MARCO Passage retrieval, switching from BERT to ELECTRA or ERNIE2.0 does not improve the retrieval accuracy.</cite>.

Where AR-LM finetuning for DPR is compelling vs when bi-encoders win
- Choose AR-LM finetuning when you can inject retrieval supervision into training (via negatives, interleaved evidence, or reading retrieved passages), have hybrid reranking infrastructure (BM25 + neural reranker), and benefit from synthetic data generation at scale. Expect gains on MS MARCO-style retrieval and improved robustness in long-tail/OOD settings when you fuse dense and sparse outputs<cite id="2eee7fb1-0">... significant performance improvement compared to baselines.</cite><cite id="2378393b-0">... synthetic negatives generated by four state-of-the-art LLMs ranging from 4B to 30B ...</cite><cite id="2eee7fb1-1">In line with RepLLaMA, we employ a combination of BM25 and CoCondenser (Gao and ...</cite>.

- When training LLMs, retrieval-aware pretraining and bottlenecking improve compression quality and make downstream dense finetuning faster and more stable, reducing the need for massive labeled retrieval data<cite id="da4fb411-1">... large decoder-only language models (LMs) fuses multiple retrieved passages to the decoder during fine-tuning. It utilizes the top retrieved ...</cite><cite id="2eee7fb1-6">... decoder-only large language models (LLM) which have demonstrated superior performance compared to BERT. achieve state-of-the-art ...</cite>.

Open-source and tooling pointers
- If you plan to implement AR-LM DPR, look for codebases using contrastive dense objectives with LLM-generated negatives and BM25/CoCondenser reranking; recent summaries explicitly recommend combining sparse and dense and iterating negatives for interleaved training<cite id="2378393b-0">... synthetic negatives generated by four state-of-the-art LLMs ranging from 4B to 30B ...</cite><cite id="2eee7fb1-1">In line with RepLLaMA, we employ a combination of BM25 and CoCondenser (Gao and ...</cite>.
- For cross-encoder baselines, BERT-based DPR variants and UniCoIL/SBERT-type sentence encoders remain strong comparators for MS MARCO and BEIR; recent work warns that simply switching to ELECTRA/ERNIE may not help passage retrieval directly, reinforcing that architecture + retrieval objective design—not just model size—drives gains<cite id="2eee7fb1-7">In comparison, on MARCO Passage retrieval, switching from BERT to ELECTRA or ERNIE2.0 does not improve the retrieval accuracy.</cite>.

Takeaway
- The latest dense passage retrieval research shows that autoregressive LMs, when adapted with retrieval-augmented pretraining, representation bottlenecks, and contrastive objectives plus hybrid reranking, can match and often exceed classic bi-directional cross-encoder setups on MS MARCO and related benchmarks; key differentiators are how negatives are sourced (LLM-generated interleaved contexts), how fusion is done (sparse+dense rank fusion), and how retrieval signals are injected into AR training pipelines<cite id="da4fb411-1">by B Wang · 2023 · Cited by 97 — Large decoder-only language models (LMs) fuses multiple retrieved passages to the decoder during fine-tuning. # Scope and definitions

Dense Passage Retrieval (DPR) finetuning with language models (LMs) generally means adapting a pretrained transformer to produce dense query and passage embeddings trained to predict relevance, using supervised, weakly supervised (e.g., pseudo-labels), or unsupervised signals; when using an LLM as the backbone, this includes cross-encoder-style pairwise ranking or related objectives as well as instruction- and retrieval-specific losses <cite id="09b65339-0">Fine-tuning adjusts pre-trained LLMs on specific datasets or tasks to improve domain-specific performance, mitigating the general nature of LLM world knowledge.</cite> <cite id="09b65339-5">LLMs have been used to generate pseudo queries and relevance labels to augment training data for dense retrieval models.</cite>.

Recent LLM-centric DPR research sits at the intersection of two trends: (1) adapting LLMs (decoder-only or cross-encoder) to be efficient dense retrievers; and (2) combining fast dense retrieval with higher-accuracy cross-encoders or rerankers. This yields distinct trade-offs vs. classical bidirectional encoders (e.g., BERT/ROBERTa) that were the de facto in early DPR <cite id="30ac693e-3">MS Marco Passage ranking dataset. Efficient retrievers, sparse, dense, and hybrid retrievers. Re-ranking using cross-encoders.</cite> <cite id="30ac693e-2">Bi-encoders are faster and more scalable, but cross-encoders are more accurate. Cross-encoders are slower and more memory intensive but also more accurate.</cite>.

# Latest works finetuning LMs for DPR (2023–2025)

- Unsupervised and weakly supervised DPR training from questions only (ART):
  - DS Sachan et al. (2023, TAACL) introduced ART, an autoencoding corpus-level approach to train dense retrievers using only questions (and answers), learning question and passage encoders by reconstructing answers or related signals; this removes the need for labeled pairs and leverages LM generative capacity for DPR-style alignment <cite id="09b65339-6">We introduce ART, a new corpus-level autoen- coding approach for training dense retrieval models that does not require any labeled train- ing data.</cite> <cite id="8b69a6da-4">Training the retriever based on question reconstruction enables effective unsupervised learning of both passage and question encoders. ART ...</cite>.

They are more effective and exhibit greater generalizability, requiring only a limited amount of compute and data.</cite> <cite id="95ed9f50-1">by X Ma · 2024 · Cited by 486 — Our study shows that fine- tuned LLM retrieval models outperform smaller models. EffiR enhances the efficiency of LLMs for dense retrieval without compromising retrieval performance.</cite>.
