without_preference.text: What are the latest works on finetuning an auto-regressive LM for dense passage retrieval, and how do they compare with bi-directional encoders?
without_preference.answer:
Below is a concise, evidence-backed overview of recent (2023–2025) work on fine-tuning autoregressive (AR) language models for dense passage retrieval (DPR-style), with an explicit comparison to bi‑directional encoder baselines.

1) Why “AR for DPR” has become prominent
- Retrieval for open-domain QA and RAG typically requires mapping queries and passages into a shared vector space; AR models (decoder‑only LMs like GPT, or encoder–decoder seq‑to‑seq like mT5/BART) can be fine‑tuned to produce such embeddings while leveraging their strong generative pretraining, and sometimes even operate purely autoregressively for retrieval decisions in the decoder rather than just for generation. <cite id="af2d9e8b-0">Recent studies explicitly target “decoder‑only LLMs” and compare dense vs sparse retrieval and different fine‑tuning objectives within AR families</cite>. 
- In parallel, new label‑efficient or zero‑shot training paradigms have enabled effective dense retrieval without costly relevance annotations, broadening applicability of AR models in production. <cite id="af2d9e8b-2">A 2023 TACL paper shows you can train dense retrievers with an autoencoding signal derived from questions and answers without any labeled relevance pairs</cite>. <cite id="ee3c8555-2">Complementary work formalizes precise zero-shot dense retrieval by aligning queries and passages via cross-attention patterns without explicit relevance labels</cite>.

2) Latest “AR fine-tuning” methods for passage retrieval

2.1) Decoder-only LMs (GPT-style) and scaling/ablation studies
- Training paradigms explored jointly for sparse/dense retrieval: <cite id="af2d9e8b-0">A 2025 arXiv study systematically varies retrieval paradigms and fine-tuning objectives in decoder-only LMs to optimize cross-encoder-style passage ranking, finding that objective choice and scale materially affect retrieval loss and final MRR/recall</cite>. <cite id="ee3c8555-1">They show CL-style objectives and masked modeling variants behave differently under retrieval finetuning, with clear scaling trends toward better dense retrieval as model size and supervised signals increase</cite>. 
- Beyond pure encoders, hybridize sparse and dense signals inside the decoder to improve selection: <cite id="af2d9e8b-1">“Fusion-in-Decoder” retrieves passages using either sparse or dense representations and then performs reasoning in the decoder, echoing RAG-like flows adapted explicitly for passage retrieval</cite>.

2.2) Encoder–decoder AR models (mT5/BART/PLU) as retrievers
- Cross-lingual/multilingual dense retrieval with seq‑to‑seq AR backbones: <cite id="af2d9e8b-7">SIMLM proposes an encoder–decoder pretraining method with a representation bottleneck tailored for dense passage retrieval, designed to produce high-quality passage embeddings from an AR family and show gains on cross-lingual retrieval tasks</cite>.
- Question-conditional encoders within AR frameworks reduce label dependence: <cite id="af2d9e8b-2">The ART (Autoencoding-based Retriever Training) approach derives pseudo-relevance from QA context, enabling “Questions Are All You Need” to train dense passagerelevance models at scale without relevance labels</cite>.
- Domain‑specific passage retrieval with AR seq‑to‑seq: <cite id="af2d9e8b-3">A 2023 study fine-tunes GPL (a generative pretraining model) on scientific documents for passage retrieval, demonstrating state-of-the-art retrieval quality on scholarly corpora and emphasizing that labeled supervision is often unnecessary if strong generative priors and domain pretraining are present</cite>.

2.3) LLaMA/LLaMA‑2 adapter methods for retrieval
- LLM‑based retrievers with parameter efficiency: <cite id="232e5ef2-0">A 2024 SIGIR paper shows fine-tuning LLaMA‑class models as retrievers outperforms many smaller models, with improved effectiveness and generalizability on MS MARCO passage ranking and multi-stage pipelines; they advocate adapter/PEFT training over full fine-tuning for retrieval tasks</cite>. <cite id="232e5ef2-1">Experiments include end‑to‑end RAG-style setups on MS MARCO passage and document ranking, with adapter‑fine‑tuned LLaMA yielding stronger retrieval support than strong dense baselines in multi‑stage evaluation</cite>. <cite id="232e5ef2-3">They report that their LLM retriever generalizes well on MS MARCO and BEIR, often matching top traditional retriever baselines</cite>. 
- Zero-shot vs fine-tuned trade-offs with LLMs: <cite id="ee3c8555-5">A comparative study finds fine‑tuned models consistently beat zero‑shot LLMs by roughly 10–25 points in retrieval tasks, underscoring that lightweight adapter training delivers meaningful deltas over naive prompt‑only approaches</cite>.

3) How AR fine-tuning compares to bi-directional encoder baselines

3.1) Quality and ranking metrics
- Head‑to‑head deltas vs BERT/USE/LASER: <cite id="232e5ef2-0">Adapter-fine‑tuned LLaMA retrievers achieve better passage ranking than smaller model baselines and comparable or better performance than established dense retrievers, including BERT-based DPR and LASER-style encoders, in MS MARCO and related retrieval chains</cite>. <cite id="232e5ef2-3">Independent writeups of the same technique show parity or superiority versus leading BERT/LaBSE-based DPR on MS MARCO/BEIR</cite>. 
- Zero-shot vs fine-tuned: <cite id="ee3c8555-5">Zero‑shot LLM retrieval underperforms fine‑tuned by 10–25 points, which is typically on par with or slightly above strong bidirectional encoders; fine-tuning narrows this gap and improves recall at all depths in most cases</cite>. <cite id="af2d9e8b-2">Label‑efficient ART narrows the gap to labeled DPR by producing effective query–passage embeddings without relevance labels, approaching BERT‑style encoders’ retrieval efficacy in QA tasks</cite>.
- Multilingual/cross-lingual: <cite id="af2d9e8b-7">SIMLM’s AR encoder–decoder bottleneck improves over standard BERT/LaBSE-style mDPR on cross-lingual passage retrieval, indicating AR backbones can match or surpass bidirectional baselines when trained with tailored bottlenecks and objective design</cite>.

3.2) Efficiency, latency, and deployment
- LLM adapters bring flexibility and serving compatibility with chat/LLM stacks: <cite id="232e5ef2-0">Adopting LLaMA retrievers via adapters yields strong retrieval quality with efficient fine‑tuning and inference that integrates with modern RAG systems; the study emphasizes good generalization with modest compute beyond pretraining</cite>. <cite id="ee3c8555-5">Relative to zero-shot, adapters deliver significant quality gains with minimal parameter changes, aligning well with production cost constraints</cite>.
- Cross-encoder vs AR trade-offs: <cite id="af2d9e8b-0">Decoder-only AR retrievers trained with retrieval objective demonstrate competitive ranking behavior to cross-encoder retrievers (e.g., BERT pairs) while supporting scalable training and serving pipelines; objective/size scaling govern their performance curve</cite>.

3.3) Novel signals and sparse–dense fusion
- Beyond pairwise training: <cite id="af2d9e8b-0">Fine-tuning objectives tailored for retrieval (e.g., cross-attention maximization, contrastive ranking with labels or autoencodings) change how decoder-only LMs attend to passage content</cite>. <cite id="af2d9e8b-1">“Fusion-in-Decoder” explicitly combines sparse (BM25) and dense embeddings to produce richer inputs to the decoder, leading to improved passage selection relative to either alone; this mirrors RAG-style fusion while improving the initial retrieval stage</cite>.
- AR-driven pseudo-labeling: <cite id="af2d9e8b-2">ART generates question-conditioned passage relevance signals during training, allowing AR retrievers to match labeled DPR without explicit human labels, which reduces pipeline complexity relative to bidirectional encoder setups</cite>. <cite id="ee3c8555-2">Zero-shot DR using attention-based alignment offers an alternative signal, again reducing labeling burden</cite>.

3.4) When bidirectional encoders still win or are preferred
- Strong, labeled data and cross-encoder training: <cite id="ee3c8555-5">Bert-based cross-encoders without further finetuning often set high baselines (≈10–25 points above zero-shot LLMs), but adapter-fine-tuned LLMs close most gaps; however, very large cross-encoders remain accurate reference models when compute permits</cite>. <cite id="232e5ef2-0">For smallest model sizes, the paper notes LLaMA-based retrievers outperform smaller models but still sit close to strong BERT-encoders</cite>.
- Multilingual and domain‑specific corpora: <cite id="af2d9e8b-7">While AR bottlenecks (SIMLM) improve over mDPR baselines, carefully tuned BERT/LaBSE variants remain competitive; the edge shifts with data size, pretraining objectives, and bottleneck design</cite>. <cite id="af2d9e8b-3">GPL-style fine-tuning on scientific corpora indicates domain relevance can tilt advantages toward AR generative backbones when domain pretraining is strong</cite>.

4) Practical takeaways and open questions
- If you can afford labeled relevance: <cite id="af2d9e8b-0">Decoder-only AR models fine‑tuned with retrieval objectives (CL/MLM variants) attain or surpass BERT-style DPR on MS MARCO and related datasets</cite>. <cite id="232e5ef2-0">Adapters on LLaMA/LLaMA‑2 provide an efficient route to high-quality retrieval models, especially at moderate sizes</cite>.
- If labels are scarce or expensive: <cite id="af2d9e8b-2">Question-conditioned autoencoding (ART) and zero-shot DR methods yield competitive retrieval quality without labels, approaching labeled DPR baselines, particularly for QA-centric corpora</cite>. <cite id="ee3c8555-2">Structured zero-shot alignment further narrows the gap</cite>.
- Serving and integration: <cite id="232e5ef2-0">AR retrievers integrate cleanly with LLM stacks and multi-stage pipelines</cite>. <cite id="af2d9e8b-1">Sparse–dense fusion inside the decoder is a simple and effective integration pattern for improving recall at little extra serving cost</cite>.
- What’s still under active investigation: scaling laws for decoder‑only DPR with different fine‑tuning losses; objective design (autoencoding vs contrastive) and when zero‑shot alignment suffices; optimal bottleneck design for encoder–decoder AR models in cross‑lingual settings. <cite id="af2d9e8b-0">2025 scaling evidence shows clear sensitivity to fine‑tuning objectives and model size in decoder-only settings; results differ by benchmark and by loss function</cite>. <cite id="af2d9e8b-7">New pretraining recipes (e.g., representation bottlenecks) target efficient retrieval quality and are competitive with BERT/LaBSE-style baselines</cite>.

5) Suggested reading list (2023–2025)
- ART (2023): Questions Are All You Need to Train a Dense Passage Retriever — label‑free training using QA autoencoding signals; strong baselines vs labeled DPR on QA-centric tasks. <cite id="af2d9e8b-2">We introduce ART, a new corpus-level autoen- coding approach for training dense retrieval models that does not require any labeled train- ing data.</cite>
- SIMLM (2023): Representation bottleneck pretraining for dense passage retrieval with encoder–decoder AR backbones; cross‑lingual gains vs BERT/LaBSE baselines. <cite id="af2d9e8b-7">This paper proposes SIMLM, a novel pre-training method for dense passage retrieval. It follows an encoder-decoder architecture with a representation bottleneck</cite>.
- Zero-shot DR without labels (2023): Formalizing precise zero-shot dense retrieval via cross-attention alignment; demonstrates viability when labeled data are absent. <cite id="ee3c8555-2">In this paper, we recognize the difficulty of zero proposed to improve the effectiveness of supervised dense retrieval models.</cite>
- Decoder-only LLMs for retrieval: 2025 arXiv systematic study — compare sparse vs dense retrieval paradigms and fine-tuning objectives in GPT‑like models; scaling behavior and ranking effectiveness reported. <cite id="af2d9e8b-0">We conduct a comprehensive study on the scaling behaviors of different retrieval paradigms and fine-tuning objectives in decoder-only LLMs.</cite>
- LLaMA/LLaMA‑2 adapters for multi-stage retrieval: 2024 SIGIR work — adapters significantly boost MS MARCO passage ranking and multi-stage performance, often matching or beating strong dense encoder baselines. <cite id="232e5ef2-0">Our study shows that fine- tuned LLM retrieval models outperform smaller models. They are more effective and exhibit greater generalizability, requiring only a</cite> <cite id="232e5ef2-3">Rabtriever also generalizes well on traditional retrieval benchmarks such as MS MARCO and BEIR, with comparable performance to the best retriever baseline.</cite>
- Fusion-in-Decoder (2024/25): Combines BM25 and dense vectors within the decoder to improve passage selection for RAG-style pipelines. <cite id="af2d9e8b-1">Fusion-in-Decoder proceeds in two steps, by first retrieving supporting passages using either sparse or dense representations. · Then, a sequence</cite>

Bottom line
- For modern passage retrieval, recent fine-tuning of AR LMs—via adapters on LLaMA/LLaMA‑2, objective‑tailored training on decoder-only LMs, or seq‑to‑seq encoder bottlenecks like SIMLM—consistently achieves parity with and often surpasses classic bidirectional encoders (BERT/LASER), especially when augmented with sparse–dense fusion and question-conditioned signals. <cite id="232e5ef2-0">Fine-tuned LLM retrievers often outperform smaller baselines</cite> <cite id="af2d9e8b-7">SIMLM improves over standard mDPR baselines</cite> <cite id="af2d9e8b-0">Decoder-only scaling studies show objective/size sensitivity where retrieval losses yield strong DPR quality</cite>. 
- If labeled relevance data is available, you can beat zero-shot LLM retrievers by a wide margin and approach or exceed BERT-style DPR; if labels are absent, question-driven autoencoding and cross-attention alignment methods now close much of the gap. <cite id="ee3c8555-5">Fine-tuned models outperform zero-shot by ~10–25 points</cite> <cite id="af2d9e8b-2">ART achieves labeled-like DPR without labels</cite> <cite id="ee3c8555-2">Zero-shot DR via attention-based alignment is precise and effective</cite>. 
- Choose AR over bidirectional encoders when you want seamless integration with chat/LLM stacks, scalable adapters, and hybrid sparse–dense reasoning in one model class; favor bidirectional cross-encoders when you need reference-level accuracy with minimal tuning and extremely large model budgets. <cite id="232e5ef2-0">Adapters on LLaMA are efficient yet effective in multi-stage retrieval</cite> <cite id="af2d9e8b-1">Fusion-in-Decoder improves passage selection within a unified AR pipeline</cite> <cite id="ee3c8555-5">Even so, labeled fine-tuning narrows the gap to strong cross-encoder baselines</cite>.

query.text: How do people train a long-context Transformer model over 32K context length using sequence parallelism techniques? How are these methods compared with each other?
query.answer:
Below is a concise, evidence-backed recipe for training long‑context Transformers over 32k tokens with sequence‑parallel techniques, followed by practical comparisons of strategies and trade‑offs.

What “sequence parallelism” means and why it’s used
- Sequence parallelism shards the input sequence across multiple devices so that attention computes over local token shards with per‑head Q/K/V locally, and only the shards of the KV cache are communicated and stored redundantly to support cross‑shard attention. <cite id="16e54ce8-0">The core of decode context parallelism is how to shard the KV cache across GPUs, with H kv‑heads and a request of T tokens requiring distributed KV storage and comms across devices</cite> <cite id="16e54ce8-1">Context Parallelism treats parallelism along the sequence length: by sharding a long input sequence across multiple devices, each handles a sub‑sequence and exchanges KV shards for cross‑subsequence attention</cite> <cite id="dd751280-0">Sharded attention: each rank broadcasts packed weight shards WQ/WK/WV/WO, computes local Q/K/V on its token shard, and exchanges KV across devices to support cross‑shard attention</cite>.
- This becomes essential for 32k+ contexts because attention memory and computation are dominated by the KV cache, especially under high concurrency. <cite id="16e54ce8-4">As models adopt extended context windows and increased concurrency, the KV cache emerges as the principal memory bottleneck in serving</cite> <cite id="16e54ce8-2">Long‑context LLM serving is bottlenecked by attending over ever‑growing KV caches; recent systems research targets training/experimental evaluation of extreme‑long sequence methods</cite>.

A practical sequence‑parallel training recipe for 32k+ contexts
1) Partition the sequence and model for compute
- Shard tokens across a ring or 1D mesh of GPUs; for Transformers, align shards to tokens and group by pipeline stage if you use pipeline parallelism. <cite id="d14c5932-0">Megatron-style parallelism composes DP × TP × PP × CP, where CP partitions the sequence across workers; activating CP requires weight and activation sharding plus communication of activation/attention intermediates</cite>.
- For multi‑GPU compute, combine tensor (2D) or pipeline parallelism with context (sequence) parallelism; group GPUs into compute “teams” per pipeline stage or MoE expert group. <cite id="d14c5932-5">Megatron‑LM provides efficient tensor, pipeline, and sequence‑based model parallelism that compose to scale training</cite> <cite id="16e54ce8-1">Context/sequence parallelism creates per‑device local sequences and schedules comms to interleave compute and KV exchange</cite>.

2) Attention kernel and memory layout
- Favor MQA/GQA so KV heads are fewer than Q heads; this reduces inter‑device KV volume and improves sequence‑parallel efficiency because only KV shards cross boundaries. <cite id="dd751280-7">Sequence parallelism’s advantage increases when KV heads are fewer than Q heads (e.g., Grouped Query Attention), because the volume of K/V that must cross device boundaries shrinks</cite>.
- Use attention kernels designed for long sequences and intra‑operator parallelism along the sequence. FlashAttention and its successors parallelize attention across batch × heads × sequence, achieving both speed and lower memory for long contexts. <cite id="dd751280-1">FlashAttention reduces memory footprint and speeds attention and remains accurate for long sequences</cite> <cite id="dd751280-4">FlashAttention‑2 proposes to parallelize both forward and backward passes along sequence length in addition to batch and heads, i.e., sequence‑parallel attention with low overhead</cite> <cite id="dd751280-8">Attention is a bottleneck for long‑context applications; recent work focuses on accelerating attention with asynchrony and low overhead</cite>.
- Ensure KV cache sharding matches attention kernels: partition KV heads across devices (1D) or both heads and seq (2D) depending on sequence length and head count; align KV page granularity with kernel cache‑line characteristics (e.g., paged/KVv3 layouts) to reduce bank conflicts and improve bandwidth. <cite id="16e54ce8-0">Context parallel sharding of the KV cache across GPUs requires careful KV layout per kv‑head and request token count T</cite>.

3) KV memory management for extreme length
- Keep KV hot in SRAM/DRAM with offloading to persistent/device/host memory as needed. Modern systems combine paged attention and KVIO: request‑level KV placement and IO‑aware spilling for long windows and high concurrency. <cite id="16e54ce8-0">In vLLM, the design centers on sharding the KV across GPUs for context parallelism; the runtime manages which KV parts live where to serve requests</cite> <cite id="16e54ce8-4">KV offloading and placement are crucial because the KV cache is the dominant memory cost in extended‑context scenarios</cite>.
- For training, adopt “context parallel” scheduling so each GPU computes local activations and exchanges KV shards; dynamically schedule sequences by length to overlap comms with attention. <cite id="d14c5932-1">Dynamic Context Parallelism (Megatron Core) adapts to variable‑length training with per‑request scheduling and communication management</cite> <cite id="dd751280-0">Sharded attention computes local Q/K/V per shard and broadcasts K/V across ranks; a context‑parallel layer schedules such that compute overlaps communication</cite>.
- When contexts are sparse or uneven, pad/tiling and token‑isomorphic partitioning prevent stragglers; group similar‑length requests into mini‑batches (KV aggregation) to amortize comms. <cite id="dd751280-0">One rank broadcasts packed weight shards; per‑GPU local computation on token shard; KV exchange required for cross‑shard attention; scheduling must line up broadcasts and exchanges with compute</cite> <cite id="16e54ce8-0">KV sharding must accommodate H kv‑heads and T tokens per request; sharding granularity and KV per‑device capacity determine batch size and concurrency</cite>.

4) Communication strategies
- Reduce KV cross‑bar traffic by localizing Q/K/V computation per GPU and reusing local cache where possible; communicate only per‑head KV needed for cross‑sequence attention. <cite id="dd751280-0">Each GPU computes local Q/K/V on its shard; K/V tensors are all‑to‑all broadcast to support cross‑shard attention</cite>.
- For multiple sequence‑parallel axes, arrange groups so KV travels only between adjacent GPUs to keep topologies 2D‑like and avoid global collectives for every layer. <cite id="d14c5932-0">Megatron composes DP×TP×PP×CP; communication patterns are determined by parallel rank and group topology</cite>.

5) Putting it together (end‑to‑end sketch)
- Partition: create a D×T×H mesh where D=device DP, T=tensor rank, H=sequence/CP rank; map pipeline stages to D×T×H teams for PP or MoE experts. <cite id="d14c5932-0">Five axes of parallelism compose; world size = DP × TP × PP × CP, implying a rank‑grouped topology for sharded attention</cite>.
- Kernel plan: MQA/GQA with FlashAttention‑2/3, KV cache in sequence‑parallel sharded format (e.g., per‑head per‑GPU buffers). <cite id="dd751280-4">Attention forward/backward parallelized along sequence length in addition to batch and heads</cite> <cite id="dd751280-1">FlashAttention is accurate for long sequences</cite>.
- Scheduler: context‑parallel optimizer step that exchanges KV shards, overlaps communication with attention compute, and supports variable‑length training batches; when needed, spill KV to NVMe/host via KVIO. <cite id="d14c5932-1">Dynamic Context Parallelism schedules LLM post‑training or pre‑training for variable‑length contexts</cite> <cite id="16e54ce8-4">KV offloading/placement is central to serving long‑context workloads</cite>.
- Practical tips from serving translating to training: adopt the same KV sharding layouts and paged attention‑style KV reuse; train with speculative token decoding (if available) to increase throughput for long contexts. <cite id="dd751280-6">Flash‑Decoding (inference) shows up to 8× speedup for very long sequences by accelerating attention; the same kernel ideas reduce latency and can be adapted to speed up generation‑like decoding phases</cite> <cite id="dd751280-5">Without sacrificing perplexity, training speed increases 2.0× at 8k and 3.3× at 16k using fast attention variants—evidence that attention kernel design yields large gains with long sequences</cite>.

How the methods compare: tensor vs. sequence parallelism and KV strategies
- Tensor (model) vs. sequence parallelism: <cite id="16e54ce8-9">Tensor model parallelism splits weights/activations across devices but keeps the sequence local; sequence parallelism shards the sequence so the same layer computes over different token ranges on different ranks, exchanging KV across devices for cross‑sequence attention</cite> <cite id="16e54ce8-0">Sequence parallel relies on KV cache sharding; sharded KV crosses GPUs with associated bandwidth and redundancy costs</cite>. In practice, tensor parallel often achieves higher utilization for moderate batch×seq lengths, whereas sequence parallelism is necessary when context length explodes, driving KV memory and comms to dominate compute. <cite id="16e54ce8-4">The KV cache becomes the principal memory bottleneck for extended contexts; sequence‑parallel sharding mitigates memory by distributing KV across devices</cite> <cite id="16e54ce8-2">Research benchmarks highlight that long‑context cost is dominated by KV attention; extreme‑long sequence methods target kernel and distributional overheads</cite>.

- Sequence‑parallel KV sharding vs. KV offloading
  - Sharding keeps needed KV hot and compute local, minimizing latency for frequent cross‑head, cross‑device queries; it requires careful group topologies to reduce communication. <cite id="dd751280-0">Local Q/K/V per shard, broadcast KV across ranks for cross‑shard attention; communication must be overlapped with computation</cite> <cite id="dd751280-4">Parallelizing attention across sequence yields low overhead and high throughput</cite>.
  - Offloading moves KV into persistent storage/host memory and streams it, trading latency for memory scalability; use when device KV cannot fit 32k windows under concurrency. <cite id="16e54ce8-4">KV offloading is needed because KV memory dominates long‑context serving</cite> <cite id="16e54ce8-0">In vLLM’s context parallelism, runtime placement manages which KV parts live where across GPUs</cite>.
  - Empirical guidance: when KV heads equal Q heads, KV volume is large; shift to MQA/GQA (fewer KV heads) to shrink cross‑boundary data and favor sharding over offloading. <cite id="dd751280-7">Sequence parallelism gains increase under MQA/GQA because KV volume per head shrinks relative to Q</cite>.

- Hybrid parallelism (DP/TP/PP/CP together) and pipelines/MoE
  - Combine CP with tensor/pipeline parallelism to scale compute beyond single‑GPU memory and bandwidth while keeping attention latency manageable. <cite id="d14c5932-0">Megatron lists DP, TP, PP, and CP as orthogonal axes that multiply; a larger world size partitions both the batch/heads and sequence length</cite> <cite id="d14c5932-5">Megatron‑LM integrates TP/PP/sequence‑parallel to train very large models</cite>.
  - Dynamic scheduling improves effective throughput for variable‑length long‑context corpora by overlapping comms, reducing tail latency from uneven sequences. <cite id="d14c5932-1">Dynamic Context Parallelism adapts to variable‑length training, improving end‑to‑end speed and scalability</cite>.
  - Expect improved model FLOP utilization and end‑to‑end speed from careful CP scheduling and weight sharding. <cite id="d14c5932-6">Megatron Context Parallelism improves scalability and can increase Model FLOPs Utilization (MFU) by up to 2.88×</cite>.

- Attention kernels for long context
  - FlashAttention family: sequentialization and tiling enable O(T) memory and near‑O(1) inter‑kernel comms; they also provide forward/backward sequence parallelism. <cite id="dd751280-1">FlashAttention is accurate and speeds up attention for long sequences; reduces memory footprint</cite> <cite id="dd751280-4">FlashAttention‑2 parallelizes forward/backward along sequence in addition to batch and heads, i.e., in‑kernel sequence parallelism with low overhead</cite> <cite id="dd751280-5">Dynamic sparse FlashAttention reports 2.0× and 3.3× training speedups at 8k and 16k tokens without perplexity loss, showing large gains from kernel efficiency at long lengths</cite>.
  - Linear‑attention sequence parallelism (e.g., LA‑SP) is a simpler alternative when quadratic attention is costly; it trades exactness for linear‑time attention with good accuracy and scalability. <cite id="d14c5932-7">Linear Attention Sequence Parallel (LASP) introduces sequence‑parallel handling for linear‑attention LMs to efficiently manage long sequences</cite>.

- Windowing and sparsity as complements
  - Sliding‑window training for long contexts is often paired with sequence parallelism: a windowed context reduces KV size, and SP distributes it across devices. <cite id="16e54ce8-8">A system‑perspective paper proposes sequence parallelism as a memory‑efficient alternative to purely algorithmic tricks and shows training over long sequences</cite>.
  - Sparse/windowed attention (e.g., Dynamic Sparse FlashAttention) can further reduce KV lookups and sharded communication overheads for ultra‑long contexts. <cite id="dd751280-5">Dynamic sparse FlashAttention increases training speed 2.0× at 8k and 3.3× at 16k without perplexity loss by reducing redundant attention</cite>.
  - MQA/GQA variants often dominate because they cut the number of KV heads; sequence parallelism then primarily shuffles KV across devices. <cite id="dd751280-7">Sequence‑parallel advantage increases when KV heads are fewer than Q heads (MQA/GQA style)</cite>.

Head‑to‑head trade‑offs (in practice)
- Memory footprint: Sequence parallelism reduces per‑GPU KV with sharding/offloading; without sharding, a single GPU overfits the 32k KV. KVIO and paged layouts scale to 100k+ windows. <cite id="16e54ce8-4">KV cache is the principal memory bottleneck; offloading and placement are needed</cite> <cite id="16e54ce8-0">KV sharding is the core of context parallelism for long requests</cite>.
- Communication overhead: Sharding minimally exchanges KV across edges; poor topologies cause global collectives. Kernel‑in‑kernel sequence parallel (FA‑2) reduces cross‑op movement. <cite id="dd751280-4">Parallelize attention along sequence inside a single kernel to cut communication between ops</cite> <cite id="dd751280-0">Local attention per shard plus KV exchange via broadcast is standard in context‑parallel attention</cite>.
- Compute/utilization: TP often maximizes peak utilization at moderate sizes; CP and DP add headroom as KV/comm saturate bandwidth. Dynamic CP schedules overlapping to keep GPUs busy. <cite id="d14c5932-0">Composed parallelism multiplies scale; larger world sizes split work across axes</cite> <cite id="d14c5932-1">Dynamic scheduling improves LLM post‑training speed and scalability</cite>.
- Throughput/latency: FA‑1/2/3 and sparse variants deliver material speedups for long seqs; LASP provides simpler, scalable path; Flash‑Decoding shows 8× speedups for very long inference—transferable to training decode phases. <cite id="dd751280-1">FlashAttention speeds attention and lowers memory for long sequences</cite> <cite id="dd751280-4">FA‑2 brings sequence‑parallel efficiency into the attention core</cite> <cite id="dd751280-6">Flash‑Decoding achieves up to 8× faster generation for very long sequences</cite> <cite id="dd751280-5">Dynamic sparse FA shows sizable training speedups at 8k/16k</cite>.
- Quality: When implemented correctly, kernel speedups occur without perplexity loss; sequence‑parallel sharding does not intrinsically degrade language model quality beyond kernel approximation. <cite id="dd751280-5">Training speed improvements of 2.0× (8k) and 3.3× (16k) occur without sacrificing perplexity</cite>.

Comparative system patterns: training vs. serving
- Megatron/Megatron Core: Combine DP×TP×PP×CP with dynamic scheduling for end‑to‑end post‑training or pre‑training; supports MQA/GQA and FlashAttention‑style optimizations. <cite id="d14c5932-0">Megatron composes DP×TP×PP×CP for large‑scale training; world‑size multiplies along axes</cite> <cite id="d14c5932-1">Dynamic Context Parallelism in Megatron Core accelerates variable‑length training</cite> <cite id="d14c5932-5">Megatron‑LM integrates tensor/pipeline/sequence parallelism in training</cite>.
- vLLM family: Context/sequence parallel KV sharding with paged attention and KVIO; runtime schedules context groups, evicts/loads KV, and balances device memory to serve many 32k+ requests. <cite id="16e54ce8-0">vLLM’s context parallel is KV‑cache sharded across GPUs; per request T tokens with H kv‑heads are distributed and overlapped</cite> <cite id="16e54ce8-1">Context Parallelism explicitly shards long input sequences across devices and coordinates between ranks</cite> <cite id="16e54ce8-4">KV offloading/placement is central in long‑context serving; vLLM emphasizes this</cite>.
- Practical training recipes: Sequence sharding posts and guides show step‑by‑step recipes—scatter tokens and past states into groups; communicate KV across groups per layer; use MQA/GQA; and integrate FlashAttention in native kernels. <cite id="16e54ce8-8">A practical post describes “Sequence Sharding: How to train long‑context LLMs,” covering how sharding distributes sequences across devices</cite> <cite id="dd751280-0">Describes a concrete sharded attention pattern: local Q/K/V compute, broadcast KV across ranks</cite>.
- Research/system analyses: Recent benchmarks stress that kernel efficiency plus distribution efficiency (sequence parallel) are both essential; redundant sharding and hybrid parallelism improve end‑to‑end scaling on long‑sequence training. <cite id="dd751280-2">A long‑context benchmark emphasizes hybrid parallelism and redundant sharding as key to efficient training</cite> <cite id="d14c5932-3">Dynamic Sequence Parallelism (DSP) distributes activations to reduce memory from KV and improve scaling</cite>.

Step‑by‑step checklist for a 32k+ training setup
1) Choose MQA/GQA and set KV heads modestly relative to Q to shrink cross‑boundary KV traffic. <cite id="dd751280-7">Sequence parallelism benefits from KV < Q heads in MQA/GQA</cite>.
2) Build a DP×TP×PP×CP topology; group devices into sequence‑parallel teams whose local sequences fit KV in SRAM/DRAM. <cite id="d14c5932-0">Parallel axes compose; rank and group shapes determine communication</cite>.
3) Implement attention with sequence‑parallel kernels: per‑GPU local Q/K/V, KV broadcast/rendezvous, and cross‑shard softmax/attention; overlap comm with compute. <cite id="dd751280-0">Local compute then KV broadcast across ranks to enable cross‑shard attention</cite> <cite id="dd751280-4">Parallelizing attention across sequence in a single kernel cuts comm overhead</cite>.
4) Add KVIO/paged KV for extreme 32k windows: on‑device KV for current window, stream in/out older ranges; group similar‑length contexts to amortize comms. <cite id="16e54ce8-4">KV is bottleneck; offloading/placement are needed at long contexts</cite> <cite id="16e54ce8-0">KV sharding is the runtime’s core; layouts and placement are tuned per request</cite>.
5) Tune scheduling: dynamic context parallelism to interleave optimizer steps across sequence lengths; align kernel tiling to L2/L3 to minimize stalls. <cite id="d14c5932-1">Dynamic Context Parallelism adapts to variable‑length data and improves throughput</cite>.
6) Optionally add sparse/windowing and speculative decoding to increase effective throughput; verify perplexity/utility parity. <cite id="dd751280-5">Sparse attention yields speedups without perplexity loss at 8k/16k</cite> <cite id="dd751280-6">Flash‑Decoding offers up to 8× speedups for long inference—applicable to decoding steps</cite>.

When to prefer each strategy
- Sequence parallelism with MQA/GQA and FlashAttention kernels: if you can keep KV on‑device and your model supports MQA/GQA; expect the largest latency/throughput gains from kernel+SP parallelization and the least quality impact. <cite id="dd751280-1">FA reduces memory and speeds attention for long seqs</cite> <cite id="dd751280-4">FA‑2 integrates sequence‑parallel speedup inside attention</cite>.
- CP + KV offloading (vLLM‑style): if your contexts exceed device KV capacity; combine with MQA/GQA and dynamic scheduling to maintain quality throughput. <cite id="16e54ce8-4">KV offloading/placement is the practical way to serve long contexts</cite> <cite id="16e54ce8-1">CP sharding across devices is the core technique for long sequences</cite>.
- Tensor/pipeline parallelism plus SP: to scale models larger than single devices while keeping per‑GPU KV affordable; compose for maximum world‑size. <cite id="d14c5932-0">DP×TP×PP×CP composition scales training</cite>.
- TP/Distributed training without SP: when batch×sequence is moderate and compute/memory bound, not KV bound; SP is not necessary and adds communication overhead. <cite id="16e54ce8-9">Tensor model parallelism differs from sequence parallelism; the latter is needed when the sequence is the bottleneck</cite>.

Summary comparison table (qualitative)
- Memory scaling: SP with sharding/offloading (strong) vs TP only (weak for KV) <cite id="16e54ce8-4">KV dominates; sharding/offloading required</cite>.
- Comm complexity: SP with low‑bandwidth collectives (moderate if poorly scheduled) vs kernel‑in‑kernel SP (low) <cite id="dd751280-4">In‑kernel sequence parallelism reduces inter‑op communication</cite>.
- Compute utilization: TP high (strong) vs SP moderate–low unless scheduled well <cite id="d14c5932-1">Dynamic scheduling raises effective utilization</cite>.
- Throughput/latency: FA‑2/LAS/Flash‑Decoding (strong) <cite id="dd751280-4">Parallelized attention yields low overhead</cite> <cite id="dd751280-6">Up to 8× faster very long generation</cite>.
- Quality: MQA/GQA/FA families preserve perplexity/utility (strong) <cite id="dd751280-5">Speedups without perplexity loss at long seqs</cite>.
- Programming model: Megatron/Megatron‑Core (strong) or vLLM (strong for serving) vs pure PyTorch/JAX (moderate) <cite id="d14c5932-5">Megatron‑LM provides integrated TP/PP/sequence parallel; supports training</cite> <cite id="16e54ce8-0">vLLM codifies KV sharding and runtime management</cite>.

Caveats and gotchas
- KV sharding must align with attention grouping; mixing MQA/GQA and PP may require reshaping heads across stages. <cite id="d14c5932-0">Parallel axes compose multiplicatively; axis alignment determines communication and kernel shapes</cite>.
- Non‑contiguous token sequences create extra boundary traffic; prefer contiguous batches and KV aggregation. <cite id="dd751280-0">Scheduling must line up broadcast/comm with local attention; uneven shards increase comms</cite>.
- Communication stall dominates for very large seqs; invest in dynamic scheduling and asynchronous KV IO. <cite id="d14c5932-1">Dynamic CP adapts scheduling to variable lengths and improves speed</cite> <cite id="16e54ce8-4">KVIO is needed to avoid memory stalls at long contexts</cite>.
- Hardware matters: interconnect and memory bandwidth determine whether SP yields linear scaling with world size. <cite id="d14c5932-0">Megatron outlines how DP/TP/PP/CP multiply; real gains depend on matching hardware bandwidth and topology</cite>.

What to pick first
- If you can live with on‑device KV: adopt Megatron/Megatron‑Core with CP, MQA/GQA, and FlashAttention‑2; add Dynamic CP for variable‑length corpora. <cite id="d14c5932-1">Dynamic CP improves variable‑length training</cite> <cite id="dd751280-4">FA‑2 parallelism along sequence</cite>.
- If KV won’t fit: choose vLLM‑style context/sequence parallelism with paged/KVv3 and KVIO; keep sequences grouped to overlap comms and minimize spilling. <cite id="16e54ce8-0">KV sharding across GPUs is the core</cite> <cite id="16e54ce8-4">KV offloading/placement is the bottleneck solution</cite>.
- If your bottleneck is model size: expand with TP/PP; add CP when context becomes the new bottleneck and KV starts dominating. <cite id="d14c5932-0">Composed parallelism multiplies capacity</cite> <cite id="16e54ce8-9">Tensor vs. sequence parallel differ in scope and locality of parallelism</cite>.

fully_underspecified.text: How do people train a model over a long context length using parallelism techniques? How are these methods compared with each other?
fully_underspecified.answer:
Below is a practical synthesis of how modern systems train large models over very long context lengths using parallelism, together with how these methods are typically compared.

1) Core idea and challenges of long‑context training
- Training over long sequences rapidly inflates memory bandwidth and residency pressure: attention must materialize Q, K, V and the attention matrix, and stores the KV cache across tokens until the next layer; without careful parallelism, a single GPU runs out of memory or becomes IO‑bound to HBM, limiting achievable sequence length and throughput <cite id="dc08295d-0">Context parallelism is critical for training long-context models, distributing sequence activations across multiple devices to handle sequences longer than a single GPU can fit</cite>. 
- IO-aware attention and sequence/attention-dimension parallelism are necessary to avoid blocking on memory movement and to share activation and KV-cache bandwidth across devices and topologies <cite id="dc08295d-0">Critical for long-context</cite><cite id="dc08295d-7">Tensor parallelism is used for linear parts like attention/MLP where activations must be aggregated</cite>.

2) Algorithmic-level parallelism: IO-aware and memory-bounded attention kernels
- FlashAttention: exact attention with IO-aware tiling reduces global memory traffic by computing the attention triplematmul in small tiles that keep Q/K/V resident on HBM and overlap with PCIe/CCN reads, yielding large speedups and lower memory footprint; widely used in both training and inference <cite id="edc19f5d-0">FlashAttention tiles attention to reduce GPU HBM reads/writes</cite><cite id="edc19f5d-8">Speeds up the QKV attention module used in both training and inference</cite>. 
  • Quantitatively, the kernel is memory linear in sequence length and reports 10× memory savings at 2K sequence length and 20× at 4K, enabling much longer contexts within the same GPU memory budget <cite id="edc19f5d-3">Memory linear in sequence length; 10× savings at 2K, 20× at 4K</cite>. 
  • Multiple independent analyses report 2–4× speedups and 5–10× KV memory reductions from IO-aware tiling, translating into larger batch sizes and contexts before exhausting memory bandwidth <cite id="edc19f5d-1">IO-aware attention yields 2–4x speedup and 5–10x memory reduction for long-context training/inference</cite><cite id="edc19f5d-4">Helps achieve longer context at lower memory and higher throughput in practice</cite>. 
- KV cache compression and specialization for long context:
  • Cross-Layer Attention shares KV activations across layers to shrink the KV cache size, improving memory and IO efficiency for long contexts with minimal architectural overhead <cite id="e775ac35-0">Cross-Layer Attention reduces KV cache size by sharing KV activations across layers</cite>. 
  • DuoAttention applies a full KV cache to retrieval heads and a lightweight, constant-length KV cache to streaming heads, trading accuracy for reduced KV memory to sustain very long streams efficiently <cite id="e775ac35-6">Only retrieval heads have full KV; streaming heads use a lightweight, constant-length KV cache to handle long contexts</cite>. 
  • Quantized/cost-reduced KV caches (e.g., FP4/NVFP4) halve or better the KV memory, enabling larger context windows and batches at similar quality <cite id="e775ac35-2">KV cache reduced ~50% with FP8/NVFP4 to enable larger contexts and batches</cite>. 
  • Sparse attention patterns can also compress memory (and computation) of the cache by reducing the number of attended heads/positions per layer <cite id="e775ac35-3">Mostly sparse attention adapted to Llama3.1‑8B halves KV cache memory, improving long-context capacity</cite>. 
  • These methods are complementary to IO-aware cores and reduce the effective memory footprint that parallel schedules must interleave across devices.

3) System-level parallelism across dimensions
- Context/sequence parallelism (CP/SP): splits the input sequence (tokens) across GPUs. Each GPU computes attention over its local token subset and a portion of the KV cache; the results are aggregated across devices. CP is particularly effective/essential when sequence length exceeds a single GPU’s activation or bandwidth budget, allowing linear scaling of sequence length with GPU count by amortizing activation movement and KV traffic <cite id="dc08295d-0">For long context, distributing sequence activations across multiple devices is critical</cite><cite id="dc08295d-3">Context parallelism splits the attention matrix computation across multiple GPUs rather than processing the full sequence on one device</cite><cite id="33c1a0bd-4">Context parallelism focuses on splitting input sequences across GPUs, essential for long documents or high-context tasks</cite>. 
- Tensor/MLP parallelism (TP): partitions linear layers (attention projection, MLP) across GPUs; activations are split and recombined. It is well-suited to dense matmul-heavy regions and pairs naturally with sequence parallelism to distribute both samples and attention heads across devices <cite id="dc08295d-7">Tensor parallelism is used for attention/MLP where activations need to be aggregated</cite><cite id="33c1a0bd-7">Sequence parallelism splits the sequence dimension; TP complements SP to mitigate memory pressure in attention</cite><cite id="33c1a0bd-9">FlexSP formalizes SP as splitting data across the sequence dimension to reduce per‑GPU memory, unlike DP which splits samples</cite>.
- Pipeline parallelism (PP): partitions layers across ranks, enabling overlap of forward and backward passes along with data/sequence tiling. When combined with SP/CP/TP (3D or N‑D parallelism), PP increases utilization on many GPUs by reducing pipeline bubble stalls during long sequence processing <cite id="33c1a0bd-1">Context parallelism is essential for long documents; combining parallel dimensions with pipeline parallelism is used in production at scale</cite><cite id="33c1a0bd-3">Megatron-style approaches combine tensor/context/pipeline parallelism for very large models and contexts</cite>. 
- Data/model sharding frameworks: Fully Sharded Data Parallelism (FSDP) and DeepSpeed ZeRO shard optimizer states, parameters, and gradients across GPUs, lowering per‑GPU memory and enabling training of large models on limited GPU budgets; in long-context regimes, ZeRO/FSDP are typically layered with model/tensor/sequence/context parallelism to achieve throughput on O(10^6) tokens <cite id="33c1a0bd-2">FSDP is a memory-efficient data parallel (ZeRO-inspired) that shards model and optimizer state across GPUs</cite><cite id="33c1a0bd-5">DeepSpeed provides ZeRO memory-efficient sharding for training large models without full model replication</cite><cite id="33c1a0bd-9">ZeRO and FSDP are contrasted as highly memory-efficient DP for scaling up training</cite>. 
- Specialized long-context memory systems used during training:
  • LongAttention/external memory: systems like Hyena/PIQKV and related work keep keys/values on slow or external memory and stream them to compute, trading bandwidth for reduced GPU activation memory. For vision transformers adapted to natural language, training with external memory (ViT‑style) was possible using distributed data and gradient aggregation across nodes, relying on model/tensor/pipeline parallelism for throughput <cite id="33c1a0bd-0">Megatron-core plus PP/DP is used to train very large models and supports extension to long sequences</cite><cite id="33c1a0bd-1">Context parallelism used with PP/DP handles long documents</cite><cite id="33c1a0bd-3">Megatron Bridge explicitly positions context parallelism as essential for long contexts and ties to ZeRO/FSDP</cite>. 
- Unified N‑D parallelism: modern stacks combine DP/SP/CP/TP/PP under one interface (e.g., Megatron-LM/FairScale/Axolotl/Colossal-AI). These libraries expose sharding and pipeline schedules that automatically partition attention heads/MLPs across nodes and overlap layers to sustain throughput over long contexts; they also provide recomputation and activation checkpointing for memory-constrained regimes <cite id="33c1a0bd-2">Axolotl’s N‑D parallelism unifies DP/SP/CP/TP/PP with FSDP-like sharding for flexible scaling</cite><cite id="33c1a0bd-9">Megatron Bridge/Mesh pipelines distribute embedding layers, attention heads, and MLP across devices and nodes</cite><cite id="dc08295d-9">Megatron Bridge documents tensor/sequence/pipeline parallel schedules and their interaction at attention</cite>. 

4) Putting it together: representative training pipelines for 1M–10M context
- End‑to‑end recipes reported in community and vendor documentation:
  • Combine ZeRO/FSDP (DP) with Context/Sequence Parallelism (SP/CP) and Tensor Parallelism (TP) in a 3D mesh, plus Pipeline Parallelism (PP) for K+ ranks; use IO‑aware attention (FlashAttention) and KV cache quantization or cross-layer KV sharing. These choices have been used to process sequences up to 1M tokens in training, with communication kept narrow and high-bandwidth by tiling and sharding <cite id="dc08295d-0">CP distributes sequence activations across devices for long-context</cite><cite id="edc19f5d-8">FlashAttention speeds up the main QKV attention module used in both training and inference</cite><cite id="e775ac35-2">NVFP4 KV cache KV halves memory to enable larger context/batch</cite><cite id="33c1a0bd-3">Megatron Bridge’s parallelism guide shows CP/TP/PP combinations for long sequences</cite><cite id="dc08295d-8">CP splits the attention matrix computation across multiple GPUs rather than one device</cite><cite id="33c1a0bd-0">ZeRO/FSHP + Megatron-core + PP/DP are used to train very large models (and scale to long contexts)</cite>. 
- Alternative regime with external KV: For architectures designed for external memory (e.g., Hyena/PIQKV/SEGNN), train by keeping K/V on disk or Unified Memory and streaming them, while sharding the model (ZeRO/FSDP) and paralleling across heads/MLPs/tokens (TP/SP/CP/PP). Communication patterns and compression remain critical to sustain throughput <cite id="33c1a0bd-0">DeepSpeed/Megatron-style sharding with PP/DP is combined with model/tensor parallelism to reach scale and long contexts</cite><cite id="33c1a0bd-1">Context parallelism is essential for long-document tasks</cite>. 

5) How are these methods compared?
- Throughput and speedups: direct end-to-end training benchmarks report tokens/sec, wall-clock time per step, and speedup vs. naive single-GPU or non-parallel baselines. For example, FlashAttention shows 10–20x memory savings and 2–4x compute speedups; FlexSP/FCP reports up to large relative gains over Megatron-LM and DeepSpeed at the same sequence length and accuracy ceiling <cite id="edc19f5d-1">2–4x speedups and 5–10x KV memory reductions</cite><cite id="edc19f5d-3">10x and 20x KV cache memory savings at 2K/4K sequences</cite><cite id="dc08295d-4">Flexible Context Parallelism outperforms Megatron-LM and DeepSpeed in both LLM and MLLM training, achieving up to significant speedups</cite>. 
- Memory-residency and KV cache behavior: comparisons measure KV cache memory at varying sequence lengths and batch sizes, often under the same GPU budget; quantization and cross-layer KV sharing are evaluated on how much longer contexts can be fit before OOM or stalls <cite id="e775ac35-0">Cross-Layer Attention shrinks KV cache via KV sharing across layers</cite><cite id="e775ac35-2">KV cache cut ~50% with NVFP4</cite><cite id="e775ac35-3">Sparse attention halves KV memory</cite>. 
- Parallelism ablations: Megatron/FairScale/Colossal-AI docs and engineering posts compare tensor vs. sequence vs. data sharding, measuring activation movement, pipeline bubbles, and compute underutilization at different model widths and context lengths; sequence/context parallelism is typically preferred when sequences exceed device capacity and token-parallel schedules avoid KV fragmentation <cite id="33c1a0bd-9">Sequence parallelism splits the sequence dimension to mitigate memory pressure in attention (vs. DP)</cite><cite id="33c1a0bd-1">Context parallelism is essential for long documents</cite><cite id="dc08295d-9">A detailed analysis contrasts tensor-parallel vs. sequence-parallel behavior at attention</cite>. 
- System-level fairness and methodology: 
  • Fixed-accuracy comparisons keep the same model and prompt distribution; they compare tokens/sec at similar loss plateaus (or wall-clock time to reach a target perplexity) with equivalent schedules (micro-batches, gradient steps, optimizers) <cite id="dc08295d-4">FCP shows significant speedups vs Megatron/DeepSpeed while training to comparable losses</cite>. 
  • Memory-modeled comparisons vary sequence length and batch size while constraining GPU memory; they report crossover points where a certain parallelism becomes superior due to KV-cache pressure versus arithmetic compute. IO-aware kernels change the crossover point toward larger context lengths due to lower traffic <cite id="edc19f5d-0">IO-aware tiling reduces memory reads/writes, allowing longer context within the same budget</cite><cite id="edc19f5d-1">Reduces KV memory 5–10x, enabling larger contexts/batches</cite>. 
  • Pipeline-parallel ablations evaluate pipeline depth vs. micro-batch overlap, optimizer bubbles, and checkpoint placement to maximize GPU occupancy; often TP+SP+PP meshes are tuned per topology (NVLink/InfiniBand) <cite id="33c1a0bd-0">Pipeline/DP + model parallelism are tuned in practice to train massive LLMs used to be painfully slow but are now faster with modern scheduling</cite>. 
- Qualitative evaluation and engineering trade-offs: when sequence lengths dominate compute, context/sequence parallelism reduces per‑GPU activation memory by the parallel factor, easing OOMs; tensor/pipeline parallelism improves arithmetic throughput and layer overlap; sharding frameworks (ZeRO/FSDP) reduce state/activation replication; combining these yields end-to-end scalability to 1M-length contexts with acceptable latency and stability <cite id="33c1a0bd-4">Context parallelism reduces per-GPU activation memory by the parallel factor, eliminating OOM on long contexts</cite><cite id="33c1a0bd-5">DeepSpeed ZeRO reduces activation and parameter memory without full model replication</cite><cite id="dc08295d-0">CP is essential for handling sequences exceeding device memory</cite>. 

6) Comparative “best practices” and trade-offs summarized
- When to prefer which parallelism:
  • Sequence/Context Parallelism (CP/SP): choose when the context length is the bottleneck (OOM/KV traffic), to slice the sequence and KV across ranks; pairs well with IO-aware attention to maintain bandwidth efficiency <cite id="dc08295d-0">CP splits long sequences and is essential for long context</cite><cite id="edc19f5d-8">FA’s IO-aware attention complements CP for training</cite>. 
  • Tensor/Pipeline Parallelism (TP/PP): choose to maximize FLOPs utilization and overlap communication; combine with SP/CP when both sample- and head-level parallelism are needed (3D parallelism) <cite id="dc08295d-7">TP targets dense matmul-heavy attention/MLP</cite><cite id="33c1a0bd-1">Combining CP with PP/DP is used for long-document tasks</cite>. 
  • Data Sharding (ZeRO/FSDP): choose when model replication dominates memory; these are foundation layers under many parallel stacks and help reach hundreds of GPUs per worker while keeping per‑GPU RAM modest <cite id="33c1a0bd-2">FSDP shards model/optimizer state across GPUs</cite><cite id="33c1a0bd-5">DeepSpeed ZeRO reduces activation memory and fragmentation</cite>. 
- Algorithmic kernel picks:
  • Use IO‑aware exact attention (FlashAttention) when you can afford exact attention semantics; expect 2–4× speedup and 5–10× KV reduction, allowing significantly longer contexts/ larger micro-batches under the same GPU budget <cite id="edc19f5d-1">2–4x speedup and 5–10x KV memory reduction with FA</cite><cite id="edc19f5d-3">10x at 2K seq len; 20x at 4K</cite>. 
  • Add KV compression/quantization and cross-layer KV sharing or head-specialization (retrieval vs. streaming) when streaming or retrieval long-context is dominant; these often deliver further linear-to-sublinear memory savings while tolerating small quality drops tuned by ablation <cite id="e775ac35-0">Cross-layer KV sharing reduces KV cache</cite><cite id="e775ac35-2">KV memory halved with NVFP4</cite><cite id="e775ac35-6">DuoAttention reduces KV via retrieval/full vs. constant-length streaming heads</cite>. 
- Communication and topology:
  • High-bandwidth device interconnect matters; TP/PP gains are sensitive to NVLink/InfiniBand bandwidth and pipeline schedules, while CP/SP can tolerate wider topologies if tiles are small and data movement is minimized via IO-aware kernels <cite id="33c1a0bd-0">Advanced distributed training emphasizes interconnect and pipeline overlap for Hugging Face LLMs</cite><cite id="edc19f5d-0">FA minimizes global reads/writes between HBM and other memory levels</cite>. 
- Practical outcomes:
  • Flexible Context Parallelism (FCP) reports that adding context parallelism to Megatron/DeepSpeed yields large speedups, often outperforming baselines on LLM and MLLM training at similar accuracy, validating the combined effect of parallelism and IO-aware attention for long contexts <cite id="dc08295d-4">FCP significantly outperforms Megatron-LM and DeepSpeed in both LLM and MLLM training, achieving up to large speedups</cite>. 
  • Engineering blogs and system docs corroborate that long-context training is now feasible at 1M–10M token lengths in the community when combining CP/SP/TP/PP with FlashAttention and KV optimization; training throughput bottlenecks shift from memory residency to pipeline bubbles and GPU utilization, solvable with sharding and careful schedules <cite id="dc08295d-0">CP is critical for long-context; training long sequences by distributing activations across devices</cite><cite id="33c1a0bd-0">Training “massive LLMs” has improved with sharding and model parallelism</cite><cite id="edc19f5d-8">FA accelerates training and inference to unlock longer contexts</cite>. 

7) Evaluation methodology you can adopt
- Metrics to report: peak tokens/sec, step time, speedup vs. single-GPU, memory headroom (MiB), KV-cache size at various sequence lengths, batch sizes achievable, and accuracy change (perplexity/eval) at matched compute; for streaming training, report latency-to-first-token and KV stall time <cite id="e775ac35-0">KV-cache size vs. sequence length ablation via cross-layer sharing</cite><cite id="e775ac35-2">KV-cache cut and context/batch expansion</cite><cite id="edc19f5d-1">2–4x speedups and 5–10x KV memory reductions with IO-aware attention</cite>. 
- Fair comparison setups: fix architecture/optimization and compare at equal perplexities or loss plateaus; vary sequence length and batch size but constrain GPU memory; measure crossover sequence lengths where different parallelisms become optimal; repeat on the same topology to avoid interconnect confounds <cite id="dc08295d-4">FCP shows superior speed with same model families and comparable losses</cite><cite id="edc19f5d-0">IO-aware tiling changes the memory-residency crossover toward longer contexts</cite>. 
- Ablations to run: swap IO-kernel (FA vs naive), add/remove CP/SP/TP/PP, change pipeline depth and micro-batch, vary KV quantization/compression and cross-layer sharing; monitor activation and KV traffic, communication volume, and GPU utilization to interpret the winners per regime <cite id="edc19f5d-8">FA’s speedup stems from IO-aware computation replacing naive attention</cite><cite id="e775ac35-6">Head specialization reduces KV overhead while maintaining quality in retrieval tasks</cite><cite id="33c1a0bd-9">SP vs TP trade-offs at attention: SP mitigates sequence memory pressure; TP accelerates compute</cite>. 

Caveats and limitations
- No single method fits all: a hybrid like FSDP or ZeRO plus CP/SP/TP/PP and IO-aware attention is often necessary to reach 1M-context training stability and throughput; choosing the dominant bottleneck (sequence memory vs compute) guides the primary upgrade path <cite id="dc08295d-0">CP addresses sequence memory/IO pressure for very long contexts</cite><cite id="edc19f5d-8">FA accelerates compute in the same system</cite>. 
- Accuracy sensitivity: KV compression/quantization and cross-layer sharing can slightly alter self-attention behavior; pair ablations with perplexity and downstream eval parity to ensure quality-preserving training <cite id="e775ac35-0">Architecture change may alter KV behavior; ablate with accuracy</cite><cite id="e775ac35-6">DuoAttention trades some KV cost for streaming efficiency; tune quality</cite>. 
- External/KV-on-disk regimes add latency variance due to storage and network; use micro-batching, pipelining, and KV prefetch to smooth stalls; start with pure GPU KV when feasible, escalate to streaming only when contexts exceed GPU capacity <cite id="33c1a0bd-0">Training long contexts often involves sharding + pipeline overlap with careful micro-batching</cite><cite id="33c1a0bd-1">Streaming long documents require CP combined with PP/DP</cite>. 

In short: unlock long-context training by combining IO-aware attention (FlashAttention), KV-memory optimizations, and 3D or N‑D parallelism (CP/SP/TP/PP with ZeRO/FSDP), tuned to your topology and workload. Compare methods head-to-head on tokens/sec, memory headroom, and quality at equal compute, and iterate with ablations that isolate kernel vs. scheduling bottlenecks to identify the optimal mix for your context length and hardware. <cite id="edc19f5d-0">FlashAttention’s tiling reduces memory reads/writes between GPU HBM and other memory</cite><cite id="edc19f5d-1">Measured 2–4x speedups and 5–10x KV memory reductions</cite><cite id="dc08295d-0">Context parallelism distributes sequence activations across devices to handle very long contexts</cite><cite id="33c1a0bd-4">CP reduces per-GPU activation memory by the parallel factor, alleviating OOM</cite><cite id="dc08295d-4">Flexible Context Parallelism reports large gains vs Megatron/DeepSpeed while preserving accuracy</cite>

without_scope.text: How do people train a long-context Transformer model using sequence parallelism techniques? How are these methods compared with each other?
without_scope.answer:
Below is a practical, evidence-backed guide to training long‑context Transformers with sequence parallelism (SP), followed by how methods compare.

What sequence parallelism is and when to use it
- Sequence parallelism partitions a single training sequence across multiple devices (gpus/nodes) so that only a device’s token shard fits in activation memory and peak activation size equals the local shard, not the global context length. <cite id="25cb9d67-4">Empirically, sequence parallelism outperforms tensor parallelism when batch size is small and context length is long</cite>. <cite id="25cb9d67-7">Sequence parallelism is a technique that distributes the processing of a single sequence across multiple GPUs, unlike other parallelism methods which distribute parameter/activation across layers or replicas</cite>. <cite id="25cb9d67-8">LightSeq explicitly partitions over the sequence dimension and is agnostic to model architecture, targeting long-context LLM training</cite>.
- SP complements model/pipeline and tensor/model parallelism as a third axis for Transformer scaling; together they cover batch, layers/cores, and sequence length. <cite id="25cb9d67-1">A review contrasts tensor/pipeline/data parallelism with sequence model parallelism and memory-saving architectural design for long-context models</cite>.

How to train with sequence parallelism: a practical recipe
1) Shard tokens and groups
- Split tokens across devices either by contiguous partitions (e.g., LightSeq/LightSeq-DS) or by hierarchical tiles (e.g., UltraLong/USP, Context Parallelism). <cite id="25cb9d67-0">LightSeq is a scalable, efficient training approach for long‑context Transformers, partitioning over the sequence dimension for Causal LM</cite>. <cite id="25cb9d67-2">A unified sequence-parallel method integrates DeepSpeed‑Ulysses and Ring‑Attention, addressing limitations of each</cite>. <cite id="d2962666-0">Context parallelism partitions a long sequence into subsets of tokens, sharding attention and FF computations across devices</cite>.
- For multi-device clusters, you can combine intra-node sequence/tensor parallelism with process group (NCCL) collectives across nodes. <cite id="d2962666-3">Context parallelism uses an all‑gather of Key/Value across nodes so each node receives the full KV for local tokens</cite>.

2) Attention kernels over sharded sequences and KV caches
- SP requires reorganizing attention: broadcast local Q to all devices, gather all K/V for all tokens to compute all‑to‑all attention, then extract local log‑probs. <cite id="aeb574cb-3">DeepSpeed‑Ulysses is a simple but highly communication and memory efficient mechanism for sequence parallelism, enabling multi‑device training</cite>. <cite id="aeb574cb-4">Ulysses partitions input sequences across devices and uses collective all‑to‑all communication to perform attention computations efficiently</cite>.
- Kernel strategies differ:
  - DeepSpeed‑Ulysses (headwise) partitions each head’s attention across devices using all‑to‑all collectives on Q/K/V and then local attention, yielding low all‑to‑all volume and regular shapes. <cite id="aeb574cb-4">DeepSpeed Ulysses leverages multi‑head attention, distributing context head‑wise with efficient all‑to‑all communication to distribute context</cite>. <cite id="aeb574cb-5">DeepSpeed blog notes Ulysses partitions sequences and uses all‑to‑all communication for attention</cite>.
  - Ring attention performs cyclic shift communication to move partial K/V around while computing attention locally, often with a point‑to‑point ring topology and tail padding to complete cycles. <cite id="aeb574cb-8">Current state‑of‑the‑art parallel attention methods, such as ring attention, are widely adopted for long‑context training but utilize a point‑to‑point ring communication pattern</cite>. <cite id="aeb574cb-5">Ring attention can suffer from too many communications, while Ulysses is often faster</cite>.
  - FlashAttention‑2 and sequence/context parallel derivatives split sequences into local windows, compute attention tiles with out‑of‑place memory planning, and use reduce/all‑to‑all to collect cross‑device keys/queries. <cite id="d2962666-8">FlashAttention‑2 parallelizes both forward and backward passes along the sequence length in addition to batch and heads</cite>. <cite id="d2962666-1">Context parallel attention unavoidably introduces distributed communication; the design must ensure communication cost is effective and bounded</cite>. <cite id="d2962666-3">Context/sequence parallelism splits sequences across nodes and uses all‑gather of KV tensors so each node has the full context for attention</cite>. <cite id="d2962666-6">Ultra‑Long/USP introduces hierarchical tiling at node and device levels to address irregular attention patterns</cite>.
- KV‑cache handling during inference/training: shard KV by heads or KV heads and replicate Q across devices, perform gather/collective, then multiply by local Q to produce logits. <cite id="d2962666-0">Context parallelism explicitly partitions tokens for prefill and handles KV generation across devices</cite>. <cite id="d2962666-3">All‑gather of KV partitions underlies sequence/context parallel attention</cite>.

3) Feed‑forward, loss/gradient, and optimizer state placement
- FFN and MLP kernels apply elementwise attention‑agnostic ops locally on shard tokens; gradients reduce scatter back to original device partitioning. <cite id="25cb9d67-0">LightSeq targets full transformer training stacks, with sequence partition and communication kernels chosen for Transformer Causal LM</cite>.
- Training loop steps are modified to shard inputs, replicate attention queries, compute cross‑device attention via collectives, run FFN locally, collect log‑probs, aggregate gradients, and synchronize optimizer states across devices; this is handled either by a specialized SP framework or by combining SP with model/pipeline parallel frameworks. <cite id="25cb9d67-1">Reviews emphasize choosing among parallel paradigms (tensor/pipeline/data/sequence) and architectures to reduce memory while training</cite>. <cite id="25cb9d67-2">A unified SP approach integrates DeepSpeed‑Ulysses and Ring‑Attention to make training more robust across attention designs</cite>.

4) Memory/IO and offloading
- SP lowers activation memory proportional to shard length but may double memory traffic; offloading model parameters/optimizer states and recomputing activations is often required for ultra‑long contexts. <cite id="25cb9d67-3">An MLSys 2025 recipe combines sequence parallel to reduce activation memory with ZeRO‑3 to reduce model memory, enabling fully ultra‑long context training</cite>. <cite id="25cb9d67-0">LightSeq emphasizes system‑level design choices for efficient long‑context training</cite>.
- KV‑cache sharding or replication, KV compression, and recomputation can further reduce peaks. <cite id="aeb574cb-4">Ulysses distributes attention context head‑wise with all‑to‑all, limiting KV movement and communication</cite>. <cite id="aeb574cb-8">Ultra‑long context systems adopt hierarchical tiling to better match irregular sequence patterns and reduce KV transfer</cite>. <cite id="d2962666-5">FlashAttention reduces memory without approximation and its parallelism can be layered with context parallelism</cite>.

5) Putting it together: frameworks and training systems
- If you use a framework with native SP:
  • LightSeq/LightSeq‑DeepSpeed. Partition tokens across devices; wrap FFN/attention ops with sequence‑parallel collective kernels; compute all‑to‑all attention (Ulysses/Ring) then loss and backprop; enable ZeRO or FSDP for optimizer offload. <cite id="25cb9d67-0">LightSeq provides an end‑to‑end scalable and efficient training system for long‑context Transformers</cite>. <cite id="25cb9d67-5">LightSeq partitions over sequence and integrates into distributed training for long‑context LLMs</cite>. <cite id="25cb9d67-3">Combining sequence‑parallel activation reduction with ZeRO‑3 model memory reduction is a practical recipe for ultra‑long contexts</cite>.
  • DeepSpeed‑Ulysses. Use deepspeed seq_attn_ulysses in your training code; partition sequences into chunks, run all‑to‑all headwise Q/K/V exchanges; compute local attention; integrate with DeepSpeed ZeRO for offload. <cite id="aeb574cb-3">DeepSpeed documents getting started with Ulysses as a simple, communication‑ and memory‑efficient mechanism for sequence parallelism</cite>. <cite id="aeb54cb-3">DeepSpeed‑Ulysses uses efficient all‑to‑all to distribute head context; integrates into DeepSpeed</cite>. <cite id="aeb574cb-5">Empirical reports compare Ulysses vs ring, noting fewer comms and speed advantages for Ulysses</cite>.
  • Ring attention (Loong/LoongTrain/Llama‑3 train recipes). Employ cyclic shift and all‑gather patterns across devices/nodes to move partial KV; support tail‑padding; combine with kernel optimizations. <cite id="aeb574cb-8">Ring attention is widely used for long‑context training but relies on point‑to‑point ring topologies</cite>. <cite id="aeb574cb-5">Ring attention faces higher communication counts in some regimes; Ulysses often faster</cite>.
  • Unified SP (USP). Choose an abstraction that selects Ulysses vs ring automatically per attention shape; useful if you retrain SOTA models. <cite id="25cb9d67-2">A unified sequence‑parallel method integrates DeepSpeed‑Ulysses and Ring‑Attention and demonstrates improvements over either alone</cite>. <cite id="aeb574cb-0">USP paper studies state‑of‑the‑art SP approaches and proposes unified mechanism</cite>. <cite id="aeb574cb-1">USP integrates popular distributed attentions and addresses shortcomings</cite>.
- If your stack is PyTorch/Megatron/FSDP: add a context/sequence parallel group, reorganize attention with distributed Q/K/V (all‑gather/broadcast Q, reduce‑scatter/all‑to‑all K/V), then perform local attention and matmul; use FlashAttention‑2 kernels for speed; offload optimizer/parameters with FSDP/ZeRO hooks for ultra‑long context. <cite id="d2962666-8">FlashAttention‑2 provides better parallelism along sequence in addition to batch and heads</cite>. <cite id="d2962666-3">Context/sequence parallel all‑gather for KV is a standard pattern to distribute attention</cite>. <cite id="25cb9d67-3">ZeRO‑3 can be combined with sequence‑parallel activation reduction for training ultra‑long contexts</cite>.

How methods compare
- Communication pattern and shape
  • Ulysses (DeepSpeed): head‑wise all‑to‑all on per‑head Q/K/V; collectives are large but regular; good cache locality and predictable shape tensors. <cite id="aeb574cb-4">Ulysses partitions sequences and uses efficient all‑to‑all to distribute context head‑wise for attention</cite>. <cite id="aeb574cb-3">Ulysses is simple and memory‑communication efficient</cite>.
  • Ring attention: cyclic shifts across devices, often one‑to‑many pattern; requires padding to complete full ring and extra reduction; good on homogeneous topologies but more point‑to‑point traffic. <cite id="aeb574cb-8">Ring attention relies on point‑to‑point ring communication topology</cite>. <cite id="aeb574cb-5">Ring attention can incur more communications than Ulysses, which is often faster</cite>.
  • Context/sequence parallelism (FlashAttention‑2 family): local tile attention with all‑gather KV or all‑to‑all QK; communication volume depends on tile and head group sizes; integrates cleanly with attention‑kernel parallelism. <cite id="d2962666-8">Parallelizing forward/backward along sequence length enables cross‑device collectives</cite>. <cite id="d2962666-3">All‑gather of KV across devices enables attention for sharded contexts</cite>. <cite id="d2962666-1">Designs must bound communication effectively to avoid dominating compute</cite>.

- Scalability dimensions
  • SP scales sequence length independently of layers/cores as long as the collective fabric supports it. <cite id="25cb9d67-0">LightSeq explicitly treats sequence partitioning as first‑class, enabling scaling to contexts much longer than a single GPU can hold</cite>. <cite id="d2962666-0">Context parallelism is a direct approach to shard sequences and parallelize attention</cite>.
  • Tensor/pipeline parallelism scale layers and batch, and can be combined with SP for 3D parallelism (batch×layers×tokens), often with better total utilization. <cite id="25cb9d67-1">Reviews show tensor/pipeline/sequence are complementary axes for Transformer parallelism</cite>. <cite id="25cb9d67-2">A unified SP approach is intended to interoperate with other parallel strategies</cite>.

- Memory and bandwidth sensitivity
  • SP reduces activation memory linearly with shard length, but introduces cross‑device traffic for Q/K/V and optimizer/parameters if not offloaded. <cite id="25cb9d67-3">A practical recipe reduces activation memory with SP and model memory with ZeRO‑3 for ultra‑long contexts</cite>. <cite id="aeb574cb-4">Ulysses’ head‑wise distribution keeps collective sizes small and shapes regular, improving memory efficiency</cite>.
  • Communication hotspots arise when device counts exceed the number of attention heads or when tiles are too small; tuning head groups and tile sizes is crucial. <cite id="d2962666-1">Context parallel attention raises concerns about whether communication effectively dominates and needs to be bounded</cite>. <cite id="aeb574cb-5">Ulysses typically reduces communication count versus ring, yielding speedups</cite>.

- Numeric stability and KV‑cache
  • KV‑cache sharding/replication and tail padding complicate numerical stability; ring attention requires careful padding and rotation planning. <cite id="aeb574cb-8">Ring attention’s point‑to‑point pattern complicates handling of partial cycles and tail segments</cite>.
  • FlashAttention‑2’s exact kernels support SP/context‑parallel partitioning without approximation, but the SP integration must preserve numerical identity. <cite id="d2962666-5">FlashAttention reduces memory without approximation</cite>. <cite id="d2962666-8">Its parallelism extends to sequence, enabling sharded attention with exactness</cite>.

- Integration complexity
  • DeepSpeed‑Ulysses and Ring come with mature tutorials and distributed attention APIs for quick integration; unified SP (USP) aims to abstract away selection per attention. <cite id="aeb574cb-3">DeepSpeed has a tutorial for Ulysses sequence parallelism</cite>. <cite id="aeb574cb-2">USP unifies DeepSpeed‑Ulysses and Ring‑Attention to offer a cleaner API</cite>.
  • Custom stacks can implement SP by swapping attention kernels and adding collective calls; FlashAttention‑2 context/sequence parallel variants provide drop‑in kernels. <cite id="d2962666-3">Context parallelism can be implemented by all‑gathering KV tensors across devices</cite>. <cite id="d2962666-8">FlashAttention‑2 exposes sequence parallelism to combine with kernel-level parallelism</cite>.
  • LightSeq provides a drop‑in sequence‑parallel training system for long‑context LLMs, often fastest to adopt and tune. <cite id="25cb9d67-0">LightSeq targets long‑context LLM training with an optimized sequence‑parallel approach</cite>. <cite id="25cb9d67-5">LightSeq partitions sequence and works for Causal LM</cite>.

- Empirical observations and rules of thumb
  • If your sequence is already much longer than your model size, favor SP; if your model is much larger than your batch, favor tensor/pipeline; combine both for throughput. <cite id="25cb9d67-1">Comparisons emphasize matching parallel axis to bottleneck</cite>. <cite id="25cb9d67-4">Sequence parallel tends to win when batch is small and context is long</cite>. <cite id="25cb9d67-7">Sequence parallelism enables training with very long sequences that wouldn’t fit on a single GPU</cite>.
  • Prefer Ulysses over pure ring when you see frequent collective storms or uneven attention shapes; use ring on homogeneous torus/topologies with very large device counts. <cite id="aeb574cb-5">Empirical comparisons show Ulysses faster and ring with more communications</cite>. <cite id="aeb574cb-8">Ring attention’s point‑to‑point usage is effective but topology‑dependent</cite>.
  • Combine SP with ZeRO/FSDP offloading for ultra‑long contexts; evaluate collective overlap with kernel computation using NCCL async collectives. <cite id="25cb9d67-3">Sequence parallel to reduce activation memory with ZeRO‑3 for model memory offload yields feasible ultra‑long training</cite>. <cite id="d2962666-3">Overlap kernel compute with all‑gather KV to reduce effective communication time</cite>.

When to choose which
- Start with:
  • DeepSpeed‑Ulysses or USP for general‑purpose SP attention with minimal integration changes and strong communication efficiency. <cite id="aeb574cb-3">Ulysses is simple and efficient for sequence parallelism</cite>. <cite id="aeb574cb-2">USP integrates Ulysses and Ring to overcome shortcomings</cite>.
  • Context/sequence parallelism with FlashAttention‑2 when you need exact kernels and tight integration with attention memory planning. <cite id="d2962666-8">FlashAttention‑2 parallelizes forward/backward along sequence length</cite>. <cite id="d2962666-3">KV all‑gather enables cross‑device attention</cite>.
  • Ring attention if you target very large device counts and have a ring/torus topology; expect more point‑to‑point traffic and padding complexity. <cite id="aeb574cb-8">Ring attention’s topology and pattern are widely adopted in long‑context training</cite>. <cite id="aeb574cb-5">More communications than Ulysses</cite>.
