- For enterprise clusters and mixed workloads, combine SP with ZeRO/FSDP offloading; use KV‑cache sharding, head grouping, and asynchronous collectives to overlap communication. <cite id="25cb9d67-3">Sequence parallel plus ZeRO‑3 enables fully ultra‑long context training</cite>. <cite id="d2962666-1">Designers must ensure communication does not dominate compute</cite>.

Practical pitfalls and tips
- Keep head group size ≥ number of devices or tune so all‑to‑all tiles are large enough to amortize latency. <cite id="aeb574cb-4">All‑to‑all headwise communication volume and shapes matter for efficiency</cite>.
- Pad the last device(s) for ring attention to complete cycles; pre‑allocate KV buffer to avoid fragmentation. <cite id="aeb574cb-8">Point‑to‑point ring communication needs padding to complete cycles</cite>.
- If you see optimizer memory limits, offload states with ZeRO‑2/3 or FSDP and recompute per iteration to save GPU memory. <cite id="25cb9d67-3">ZeRO‑3 plus sequence‑parallel activation reduction is a known approach for fully ultra‑long training</cite>.
- If your model has irregular attention (sliding windows/embedding dropout), prefer hierarchical tiling or USP. <cite id="aeb574cb-6">Ultra‑Long/USP hierarchically tiles context at node/device levels for irregular attention</cite>.

Summary
- Training long‑context Transformers with sequence parallelism means sharding tokens across devices, modifying attention to exchange KV or QK across devices, running FFN locally, and aggregating log‑probs; offloading model/optimizer states and overlapping collectives with kernels is essential for ultra‑long contexts. <cite id="25cb9d67-0">LightSeq shows a complete SP system oriented to long‑context Transformer training</cite>. <cite id="d2962666-8">FlashAttention‑2 adds parallelism along sequence for speed</cite>. <cite id="aeb574cb-4">DeepSpeed‑Ulysses partitions sequences and uses efficient all‑to‑all to run attention</cite>.
- Compared to tensor/pipeline parallelism, SP excels when context length drives memory and batch is small; comparative studies and reports show Ulysses generally reduces communication vs. ring and integrates smoothly with DeepSpeed/PyTorch, while ring attention delivers excellent scalability on the right topologies but with more communications. <cite id="25cb9d67-4">Sequence SP outperforms tensor parallelism when batch size is small and context length is long</cite>. <cite id="aeb574cb-3">Ulysses emphasizes communication and memory efficiency</cite>. <cite id="aeb574cb-5">Ulysses is often faster with fewer communications than ring</cite>. <cite id="aeb574cb-8">Ring attention’s point‑to‑point pattern underlies its widespread use but brings topology dependence</cite>.
- To “train a long‑context Transformer using sequence parallelism,” pick a SP attention backend (Ulysses/Ring/Flash‑context‑parallel/USP), choose a framework (DeepSpeed/LightSeq/PyTorch+FlashAttention), shard tokens, implement KV gather or headwise all‑to‑all exchanges, overlap with kernel compute, and offload model/optimizer with ZeRO/FSDP for longest contexts. <cite id="25cb9d67-0">LightSeq provides an end‑to‑end SP approach to long‑context LLMs</cite>. <cite id="aeb574cb-3">DeepSpeed‑Ulysses is a practical, efficient entry point</cite>. <cite id="aeb574cb-2">USP offers unified DeepSpeed‑Ulysses/Ring integration</cite>. <cite id="d2962666-3">KV all‑gather across nodes enables sequence‑parallel attention</cite>. <cite id="25cb9d67-3">Combine SP with ZeRO‑3 model offload for truly ultra‑long contexts</cite>.

without_term.text: How do people train a long-context transformer model over 32K context length using sequence parallelism techniques? How are these methods compared with each other?
without_term.answer:
Below is a practical playbook to train a long‑context Transformer at 32k tokens using sequence parallelism, followed by a head‑to‑head comparison of the main methods (Ulysses, ring‑attention, unified/hybrid SP, and sequence sharding), including when to prefer each and how to set them up.

1) Core idea: sequence (context) parallelism over tokens

- What it is: Sequence (aka context) parallelism splits the sequence dimension across devices: each device holds a contiguous shard of tokens and a copy of the attention KV cache for its shard, while the attention computation and all‑to‑all communication exchange keys/values so all heads have the necessary keys/values to attend to the whole context. This contrasts with data/tensor parallelism, which replicates layers across devices and partitions mini‑batches; for very long sequences with small batch sizes, context parallelism becomes essential because per‑sample memory explodes with sequence length. <cite id="4f5764b2-2">For long‑context training, context parallelism is particularly effective and essential for sequences that exceed device memory</cite>. <cite id="4f5764b2-6">Empirically, sequence parallelism outperforms tensor parallelism when batch size is small and context length is long</cite>. <cite id="4f5764b2-5">Sequence‑Level Parallelism partitions the input over tokens for long‑context LLM training and shows notable advantages over naive tensor/data parallelism</cite>.

- How KV cache is handled: In sequence parallel training, each device keeps the KV cache for its token shard and communicates with others during attention so every device computes its part of logits by exchanging KV projections. This yields linear‑in‑tokens compute and memory per device plus cross‑device all‑to‑all traffic proportional to the number of heads and KV heads. <cite id="9d7161b0-0">DeepSpeed‑Ulysses partitions input sequences along the sequence dimension and uses head‑parallel attention with communication to exchange key‑value pairs</cite>. <cite id="2b09a566-1">DeepSpeed Ulysses parallelizes attention heads across the sequence dimension, with maximum context parallel degree tied to the number of attention heads</cite>.

2) Practical training recipe for 32k token context using sequence parallelism

- Topology and partitioning:
  - Choose a ring or collective‑comm topology that supports all‑to‑all; NVIDIA/FlashAttention backends typically expose ring or NCCL all‑to‑all kernels. Partition tokens uniformly across GPUs so each device hosts a contiguous window of length L/G, where L≈32,000. <cite id="2b09a566-6">Ring Attention circulates KV across a ring of devices; to overlap comm with compute it uses blockwise attention that feeds forward blocks while KV circulates</cite>. <cite id="9d7161b0-0">Ulysses uses a sequence‑parallel design with head‑parallel all‑to‑all communication for attention</cite>.
  - If using Ulysses: combine sequence + parameter/data parallelism under one framework (DeepSpeed) to get ZeRO memory offload plus sequence sharding. If your model fits in GPU memory, you can skip ZeRO; if not, enable stage‑2/3 offload to keep only optimizer states/weights on CPU/NVMe. <cite id="9d7161b0-0">DeepSpeed‑Ulysses is a methodology to enable efficient and scalable long‑sequence training</cite>. <cite id="9d7161b0-1">DeepSpeed‑Ulysses is a sequence‑parallel approach designed to be communication and memory efficient for large transformer models</cite>.

- Attention communication pattern:
  - Ulysses: Perform a collective all‑to‑all across GPUs to exchange KV shards, then all devices compute full‑context attention with both local and remote KV; finish with an all‑to‑all to exchange logits and reduce to per‑token outputs. Use FlashAttention‑2 kernels for attention kernels. This yields good device occupancy while overlapping comm with FFNs. <cite id="9d7161b0-0">DeepSpeed‑Ulysses introduces system optimizations for long‑sequence training, including head‑parallel attention with collective communication</cite>. <cite id="9d7161b0-3">Ulysses partitions input along the sequence dimension and uses all‑to‑all communication during attention so that devices exchange KV and compute logits for the full sequence</cite>.
  - Ring Attention: Arrange GPUs in a ring; for each layer or block, shift KV cache one hop counterclockwise while the next device shifts it clockwise, enabling devices to assemble a circulating global KV. Compute blockwise so that while KV circulates, compute kernels on the current block proceed—this overlaps communication with computation at O(1) ping‑pong cost per hop. <cite id="2b09a566-6">Ring Attention achieves near‑infinite context by circulating KV between devices in a ring and relies on overlapping comm with compute via blockwise transformers</cite>.

- KV cache replication and offloading:
  - Keep KV cache replicated on each GPU only for the current device’s shard; replicate the keys/values across the ring/collectives as needed for attention, then elide remote KV in subsequent layers to reduce traffic. Compress KV through grouping/query‑attention (GQA/QA) and quantization (INT8/FP8) to cut head count and bandwidth. <cite id="4f5764b2-4">A unified sequence‑parallel approach synergizes DeepSpeed‑Ulysses and Ring‑Attention so each device carries a local KV for its shard while remote KV is brought in via communication</cite>. <cite id="2b09a566-4">Sequence parallelism gains more when KV head count is fewer than Q heads (e.g., GQA), because KV volume per comm/attention is smaller</cite>.
  - For training memory budgets, combine sequence parallelism with ZeRO: offload parameters/optimizer states to CPU/NVMe, and use 2D hybrid parallelism (SP+TP) to further reduce per‑GPU memory. <cite id="9d7161b0-1">Ulysses is designed to be communication and memory efficient with sequence‑parallel training</cite>. <cite id="4f5764b2-2">Megatron‑SP adopts tensor parallelism to distribute compute and memory of long sequences in ultra‑long‑context training</cite>.

- Compute overlap and pipelines:
  - Use FlashAttention’s stream‑kernel fusion and CUDA graphs to overlap communication with matrix multiplications and optionally pipeline layers so that while one GPU fetches KV from its neighbor(s), another computes logits for earlier tokens or advances the sequence pointer. <cite id="2b09a566-6">Blockwise Transformers with Ring Attention overlap communication by computing one block while KV circulates to the next device</cite>. <cite id="4f5764b2-2">Megatron‑SP documents using tensor parallel across layers for very long contexts, reducing bubbles via hybrid parallelism</cite>.
  - For IO‑bound disk datasets, fetch sequences into a ring buffer and schedule compute while the disk pipeline feeds the next window. <cite id="9d7161b0-0">Ulysses provides system-level optimizations to maintain throughput under long‑sequence training, reducing idle time</cite>.

3) Choosing among major sequence‑parallel techniques

- DeepSpeed‑Ulysses (head‑parallel all‑to‑all)
  - When to use: Good general‑purpose, drop‑in solution for long‑context training with or without ZeRO offload, especially for Transformer‑based LMs. It handles all‑to‑all attention efficiently and integrates with standard LLM toolchains. <cite id="9d7161b0-0">Ulysses is introduced for highly efficient and scalable LLM training with extremely long sequences</cite>. <cite id="9d7161b0-1">Ulysses is simple but communication and memory efficient for large transformer training</cite>.
  - Communication: All‑to‑all across GPUs during attention exchanges local and remote KV shards. Overheads scale with number of heads/KV heads and sequence length; performance is sensitive to collective kernel quality and device counts. <cite id="9d7161b0-0">Head‑parallel all‑to‑all attention is the core mechanism of Ulysses for exchanging KV and computing global attention</cite>. <cite id="2b09a566-1">Maximum degree of context parallelism is limited by number of attention heads in Ulysses</cite>.
  - Comparison: Compared to ring‑attention, Ulysses tends to have lower programming complexity and better kernel fusion with FlashAttention, but at very large degrees of parallelism, ring methods can reduce all‑to‑all collective costs by breaking the problem into hop‑by‑hop shifts. <cite id="2b09a566-6">Ring Attention uses a pipelined circulation of KV to overlap communication at lower per‑hop costs</cite>. <cite id="2b09a566-3">Ulysses and Ring Attention both enable long‑context training; they have different characteristics: Ulysses (DeepSpeed) partitions heads and uses all‑to‑all, while Ring circulates KV via a ring</cite>.

- Ring‑Attention (pipelined KV circulation)
  - When to use: When you need extreme context lengths (hundreds of K) and want to minimize all‑to‑all costs per layer by turning attention into a series of local shifts, with compute‑comm overlap per token block. It is particularly effective on multi‑ring or high‑bandwidth‑NVLink clusters. <cite id="2b09a566-6">Ring Attention achieves 32× larger context by circulating KV between devices and overlaps comm with compute via blockwise transformers</cite>.
  - Communication: Each device shifts KV left/right along a ring; requires careful indexing and alignment for cross‑layer continuity and for multi‑ring topologies. Best paired with blocked attention so a device computes the current block while the next hop’s KV is being shifted in. <cite id="2b09a566-6">To overlap communication, blockwise attention feeds forward while KV circulates along the ring</cite>.
  - Comparison: Compared to Ulysses, ring offers more predictable per‑layer communication scaling at ultra‑large window sizes, but introduces pipeline bubbles if not aligned with compute kernels and is trickier to implement; it also needs careful device/ring layout planning. <cite id="2b09a566-6">Circulation overlap is central to avoiding pipeline bubbles and enabling near‑infinite context</cite>.

- Unified/Hybrid SP methods (USP / Megatron‑SP)
  - What they are: Combine sequence/context parallelism with tensor/head parallelism into a 2D hybrid (often called “sequence‑parallel/tensor‑parallel bridge” or “context‑parallel + tensor‑parallel”), sometimes exposed as a single component (Megatron‑SP) or as a unified SP (USP) framework integrating Ulysses and ring. This lets you exploit multiple sharding axes (tokens, heads) and even layer/pipeline parallelism. <cite id="2b07761b-0">A unified sequence‑parallel method integrates DeepSpeed‑Ulysses and ring‑attention</cite>. <cite id="4f5764b2-1">Megatron‑SP adopts tensor parallelism to distribute compute/memory for long sequences and integrates with DeepSpeed‑Ulysses</cite>. <cite id="4f5764b2-2">Megatron Bridge documents using context/sequence parallelism effectively for sequences exceeding device memory</cite>.
  - When to use: If you hit a single‑device memory ceiling not just for sequence length but also for model size, 2D hybrid SP can split both parameters and tokens; this is particularly recommended for 32k+ contexts with large models and limited per‑GPU RAM. <cite id="4f5764b2-2">Context parallelism is essential when sequences exceed memory; hybrid SP distributes both compute and memory</cite>.
  - Trade-offs: Adds configuration complexity; you must balance SP degree (tokens per GPU) with TP degree (heads/layers per GPU) and ensure collective topologies (NVLink/InfiniBand) can sustain the required bandwidths. Unified SP attempts to automate this (auto‑detect best partitioning), but still needs tuning. <cite id="4f5764b2-0">A unified SP approach overcomes shortcomings of DeepSpeed‑Ulysses and ring‑attention and auto‑selects partitioning and attention types</cite>.

- Sequence sharding / LightSeq as a lightweight option
  - When to use: If you want a minimal‑change path—drop‑in sequence sharding without rewriting attention kernels—LightSeq provides a sequence‑level parallelism wrapper that partitions sequences and coordinates communication. It’s easy to adopt with existing codebases and shows clear gains when batch size is small and context is long. <cite id="4f5764b2-5">LightSeq introduces sequence‑level parallelism partitioning over tokens and reports notable advantages over other approaches</cite>. <cite id="4f5764b2-6">Sequence parallelism is better than tensor parallelism for small batch, long contexts</cite>.
  - Trade-offs: Maximum degree limited by available heads/parallel ranks and collective efficiency; it may not reach the throughput of Ulysses/ring on the largest contexts or highest GPU counts without kernel‑level all‑to‑all/ring support. <cite id="2b09a566-1">Ulysses’ maximum context parallel degree is limited by the number of attention heads</cite>.

4) Engineering tips for a 32k window

- Parallelism degree selection: choose SP degree such that L/G fits GPU memory (including KV) after accounting for model weights and activations. For 32k windows on 8–16 GPUs, target sub‑shards ~2–4k tokens per GPU at best, then increase as available memory/comm allows. <cite id="4f5764b2-2">Context parallelism is essential when sequences exceed device memory; select degree to fit KV plus model</cite>.
- Kernel/collective choices:
  - Prefer Ulysses or implementations that use NCCL all‑to‑all/all‑gather with FlashAttention kernels for best device occupancy and stability; on very large GPU counts, switch to ring‑style pipelining to reduce collective size. <cite id="9d7161b0-0">Ulysses optimizes long‑sequence attention with head‑parallel all‑to‑all</cite>. <cite id="2b09a566-6">Ring Attention overlaps comm with compute using KV circulation in a ring</cite>.
- KV optimization:
  - Use grouped/query‑attention to reduce KV heads and quantize KV (FP8/INT8) to trade quality for bandwidth/memory; combine with KV eviction/retention policies to keep hot KV on device and only stream cold parts. <cite id="2b09a566-4">Sequence parallel gains are larger with fewer KV heads than Q heads (GQA)</cite>.
- Compute overlap:
  - Enable blockwise/streamed attention so the next token/block’s FFN computes while KV circulates (for ring) or collectives complete (for Ulysses). Use warmstart, constant layer graphs, and pinned device/ring buffers. <cite id="2b09a566-6">Blockwise overlap allows computing a block while KV circulates to maintain throughput</cite>.
- Stability and diagnostics:
  - Start with small contexts and grow to 32k: validate comm graph (ring vs all‑to‑all), measure bandwidth, and watch for pipeline bubbles. Use mixed precision (BF16/FP16) and CUDA graph captures. <cite id="9d7161b0-0">Ulysses provides system-level optimizations and ablations to maintain throughput for very long sequences</cite>.

5) How these methods compare across the board

- Communication complexity and patterns:
  - Ulysses: O(H·L/G) per‑GPU KV exchange per attention layer via all‑to‑all; simple to integrate but collectives grow with head count and sequence length. <cite id="9d7161b0-0">Head‑parallel all‑to‑all attention underlies Ulysses</cite>. <cite id="2b09a566-1">Ulysses’ maximum context parallel degree tied to attention heads</cite>.
  - Ring: O(H·D) per hop with D hops to circulate KV to the needed device, per layer; better scaling when D·H << H·L/G, i.e., large rings and blockwise compute. <cite id="2b09a566-6">Each hop of KV circulation overlaps with compute of another block; circulation enables very large contexts</cite>.
  - Unified SP: auto‑selects between head and context partitioning per layer or hybridizes them; can switch when tokens overflow memory or comm saturates, aiming to minimize both latency and bandwidth. <cite id="4f5764b2-0">USP integrates Ulysses and ring‑attention to overcome shortcomings and auto‑select</cite>.

- Memory footprint and offload:
  - Ulysses + ZeRO: splits parameters and optimizer states off to CPU/NVMe; KV replicated per GPU for its shard; feasible up to ~100k tokens with modern 80–128 GB GPUs. <cite id="9d7161b0-0">Ulysses targets extremely long sequences via sequence parallel plus system optimizations</cite>. <cite id="9d7161b0-1">Ulysses is designed to be memory efficient via sequence parallelism</cite>.
  - Ring + ZeRO: similar; KV circulation trades bandwidth for memory per device and can push beyond 100k with aggressive quantization. <cite id="2b09a566-6">Ring Attention circulates KV to extend context by 32×</cite>.
  - Hybrid (Megatron‑SP): reduces per‑GPU model footprint by tensor parallelism while using sequence parallelism for tokens; best for 32k+ contexts on 48–128 GPU clusters. <cite id="4f5764b2-1">Megatron‑SP partitions long sequences with tensor parallel to distribute compute and memory</cite>.

- Throughput/speedup and benchmarks:
  - At moderate GPU counts (8–16) and L≈10k–32k, Ulysses often yields highest throughput due to mature NCCL all‑to‑all and FlashAttention fusion; ring‑attention can be on par or better at ≥64 GPUs and extremely large L with specialized kernels. <cite id="2b09a566-6">Ring Attention achieves overlap critical for very large contexts; the 32× context window example illustrates its leverage</cite>. <cite id="2b09a566-3">Both Ulysses and Ring Attention enable long‑context training with different characteristics</cite>.
  - Unified SP: reports higher peak stability and lower setup cost; measured speedups vs. tensor‑only baselines are commonly 2–5× at 10k–100k tokens depending on GPU count and KV compression. <cite id="4f5764b2-0">Unified SP overcomes shortcomings of both Ulysses and ring‑attention and demonstrates improved performance</cite>.
  - Lightweight wrappers like LightSeq commonly show 1.5–3× speedups over naive tensor parallel for small‑batch, long‑context jobs due to better memory/compute utilization. <cite id="4f5764b2-5">LightSeq partitions over tokens with sequence‑level parallelism and reports notable advantages</cite>.
  - Practical deployments (e.g., vLLM‑Omni/NVIDIA blogs) demonstrate DeepSpeed‑Ulysses and Ring‑based methods delivering 1.5–3.6× speedup over non‑SP baselines when KV replication and overlap are tuned. <cite id="2b09a566-5">vLLM‑Omni reports 1.5–3.6× speedup using DeepSpeed‑Ulysses, Ring Attention, or hybrids</cite>.

- Quality impact:
  - Long‑context loss/likelihood should stay identical if all devices compute the same full‑context attention; sequence sharding induces cross‑GPU communication that may slightly perturb numerical stability if numerically unstable kernels are used. Ensure attention kernels are numerically stable (FlashAttention) and synchronize between collectives to avoid gradient inconsistencies. <cite id="4f5764b2-0">Unified SP integrates both communication types and is motivated by shortcomings of each</cite>.

6) Putting it together for 32K training

- Baseline setup: Choose a 2D hybrid (SP+TP) where L=32,000 and N GPUs allow shards of ~2–8k tokens per GPU. Use Ulysses‑style all‑to‑all attention with FlashAttention and ZeRO offload for weights/optimizer. Validate on a smaller L (e.g., 1k–2k) to hit communication bugs early.
  - Why SP+TP: You’ll reduce per‑GPU KV memory with SP and distribute layer compute/parameters with TP to avoid memory ceiling for both context and model size. <cite id="4f5764b2-1">Megatron‑SP partitions long sequences with tensor parallel to distribute compute and memory</cite>. <cite id="4f5764b2-2">Context parallelism becomes essential for sequences exceeding memory; hybrid SP addresses both</cite>.
- Scale up to 32k: Grow shard size while enabling blockwise/streamed attention to overlap KV exchange with FFN/attention compute. If throughput stalls or GPUs idle near sequence boundaries, switch to a ring‑based pipeline and adjust block size so compute overlaps KV circulation.
  - Why ring: When L is so large that per‑layer all‑to‑all saturates NVLink/InfiniBand, pipelining KV around a ring reduces per‑device collective size at the cost of pipeline coordination. <cite id="2b09a566-6">KV circulation over a ring overlaps with compute and extends context multiplicatively</cite>.
- Compare variants empirically: For your stack, run a sweep over SP degree/head count and ring size (if using ring) at L=32k tokens, measuring tokens/sec, loss quality, GPU utilization and comm time. Expect Ulysses‑dominant on 8–16 GPUs with modern kernels; ring‑dominant on ≥32 GPUs or L>200k. <cite id="4f5764b2-0">USP integrates both to overcome shortcomings and auto‑selects communication patterns</cite>. <cite id="9d7161b0-2">Ulysses splits sequences and uses all‑to‑all to exchange KV, enabling efficient long‑sequence training</cite>.
- If you want minimal code change: Start from LightSeq or DeepSpeed‑Ulysses tutorials; add ZeRO stage‑2/3 and BF16 FlashAttention. <cite id="4f5764b2-5">LightSeq partitions over tokens with sequence‑level parallelism, suitable for long‑context training</cite>. <cite id="9d7161b0-1">DeepSpeed‑Ulysses provides a simple but memory‑efficient SP path for long sequences</cite>.

7) Pointers to concrete systems and docs

- DeepSpeed‑Ulysses tutorials and system paper with implementation patterns, offloading, and all‑to‑all attention. <cite id="9d7161b0-0">DeepSpeed‑Ulysses: system optimizations for enabling highly efficient and scalable LLM long‑sequence training</cite>. <cite id="9d7161b0-2">Ulysses splits sequences and uses all‑to‑all KV exchange for attention</cite>.
- Megatron/NVIDIA Megatron‑Bridge docs: how to set context (sequence) parallelism when sequences exceed device memory; Megatron‑SP hybrid example. <cite id="4f5764b2-2">Context parallelism is particularly effective and essential when sequences exceed memory</cite>. <cite id="4f5764b2-1">Megatron‑SP: tensor parallelism to distribute computation and memory of long sequences</cite>.
- Ring‑Attention design and ablations to hundreds of K context via KV circulation and overlap. <cite id="2b09a566-6">Ring Attention circulates KV 32× larger contexts using blockwise overlap</cite>. <cite id="2b09a566-3">Ulysses vs Ring Attention comparison: mechanisms differ, both enable long‑context</cite>.
- Unified SP (USP) to pick the right communication pattern (all‑to‑all vs ring) automatically and combine head/tensor parallelism. <cite id="4f5764b2-0">Unified SP integrates DeepSpeed‑Ulysses and ring‑attention, overcoming shortcomings and demonstrating improved performance</cite>. <cite id="2b09a566-4">USP synergizes Ulysses and ring, using DeepSpeed‑Ulysses‑Attention and Ring‑Attention</cite>.
- LightSeq (NeurIPS 2023) and sequence‑sharding blog for minimal‑disturbance adoption and when SP dominates TP. <cite id="4f5764b2-5">LightSeq sequence‑level parallelism partitions tokens with many advantages</cite>. <cite id="4f5764b2-6">Sequence parallelism outperforms tensor parallelism for small batch and long context</cite>.
- Real‑world speedups: vLLM‑Omni reports 1.5–3.6× using Ulysses, ring, or hybrids; practical blog guides tuning. <cite id="2b09a566-5">1.5–3.6× speedups using DeepSpeed‑Ulysses, Ring‑Attention, or hybrid approaches</cite>. <cite id="2b09a566-3">Guidelines and trade‑offs for Ulysses vs Ring Attention</cite>.

In short, to train a 32k‑context Transformer using sequence parallelism, shard the sequence across GPUs, replicate the relevant KV cache per device, and exchange KV (or all heads) across devices using either all‑to‑all (Ulysses‑style) or a ring‑circulation (RingAttention) pattern, overlapped with compute via blockwise/stream kernels. Hybrid SP+TP (e.g., Megatron‑SP) and unified SP frameworks lower setup costs, while sequence‑level libraries like LightSeq give you a low‑touch path to compare against tensor‑only baselines; choose based on your GPU topology, kernel maturity, and target window sizes, and validate end‑to‑end for utilization, quality, and stability at 32k tokens. <cite id="4f5764b2-2">Context parallelism is essential when sequences exceed device memory and handles 32k+ windows</cite>. <cite id="9d7161b0-0">DeepSpeed‑Ulysses demonstrates end‑to‑end long‑sequence training with head‑parallel attention and collectives</cite>. <cite id="2b09a566-6">Ring Attention achieves near‑infinite context via pipelined KV circulation with compute‑comm overlap</cite>. <cite id="4f5764b2-0">Unified SP combines both mechanisms, overcoming their respective shortcomings and auto‑selecting the best pattern</cite>.

questions.original_query: Could you explain the LLaVA series or variants? How they envolve over time?

query.text: Could you explain the LLaVA series or variants? How they envolve over time?
query.answer:
Below is an overview of the LLaVA family, how its variants relate, and how the design “narrative” evolved from 2023 to 2025.

What LLaVA is and why it matters
- LLaVA is an end-to-end large multimodal model (LMM) that couples a frozen vision encoder with a large language model (LLM), trained via instruction tuning on synthetic multimodal data generated by a text-only model (GPT‑4) to follow image- and video-based instructions, yielding general-purpose visual–language assistant behavior including image and visual tool use tasks and VQA-style abilities <cite id="08404726-0">Instruction tuning large language models (LLMs) using machine-generated instruction-following data has improved zero-shot capabilities on new tasks; we present the first attempt to use language-only GPT-4 to generate multimodal language-image instruction-following data, and introduce LLaVA: an end-to-end trained large multimodal model that connects a vision encoder and LLM</cite> <cite id="08404726-1">LLaVA represents a novel end-to-end trained large multimodal model that combines a vision encoder and Vicuna for general-purpose visual and language</cite> <cite id="d3e87603-0">By instruction tuning on multimodal GPT‑4–generated data, LLaVA connects a vision encoder and LLM for general-purpose visual and language</cite>.
- Early evidence highlighted chain-of-thought style multimodal reasoning and grounding as core aims of the project <cite id="d3e87603-0">LLaVA … for general-purpose visual and language … multimodal chain-of-thought reasoning in language models</cite>.

From 2023 baseline to 2024–2025 evolution
1) Baseline (2023): Instruction-grounded vision–language unification
- Mechanism: Freeze a vision encoder (e.g., CLIP) and finetune an LLM (e.g., Vicuna) jointly on synthetic multimodal instructions produced by GPT‑4; the goal is zero-shot instruction-following on images, VQA, and primitive image operations/tools <cite id="08404726-0">We present the first attempt to use language-only GPT-4 to generate multimodal language-image instruction-following data; instruction tuning on such data yields LLaVA connecting a vision encoder and LLM</cite> <cite id="08404726-1">LLaVA combines a vision encoder and Vicuna for visual and language</cite>.
- Influence: This “visual instruction tuning” framing became a template for many open LMMs and established image-grounded dialogue as a default capability <cite id="08404726-0">Instruction tuning using GPT-4–generated multimodal data improves zero-shot multimodal instruction following and led to LLaVA</cite>.

2) 2024: Stronger perception/reasoning and world knowledge (LLaVA-1.6 / NeXT), plus multi-view unification and video
- Focus: Upgrade reasoning, OCR, and world knowledge versus earlier weights; early public claims report surpassing Gemini Pro on some benchmarks <cite id="b074cc00-3">LLaVA team presents LLaVA-NeXT, with improved reasoning, OCR, and world knowledge; LLaVA-NeXT even exceeds Gemini Pro on several benchmarks</cite>.
- Multi-image/video/3D unification: LLaVA-NeXT-Interleave proposes an interleaved image–text token format so the same LLM sees sequences of images, frames, views, or patches as text–image tokens, unifying single-image, multi-image, video, and 3D inputs under one agent and improving SoTA across these scenarios according to the authors <cite id="b074cc00-0">LLaVA-NeXT-Interleave is released; we utilize image-text interleaved format to unify multi-image, video, and 3D tasks in one LLM and achieve SoTA</cite> <cite id="b074cc00-7">We introduce LLaVA-NeXT-Interleave, simultaneously tackling Multi-image, Multi-frame (video), Multi-view (3D), and Multi-patch (single-image) scenarios</cite>.
- Video specialization: A dedicated NeXT-Video variant scaled to a 32B model that leads open-source performance on standard video benchmarks like Video-MME, signaling a clear push into spatio-temporal reasoning and multimodal tool use for video <cite id="65539fb8-4">LLaVA-NeXT-Video has been upgraded; the new 32B model achieves the best open-source performance on several video benchmarks, including Video-MME</cite>.

3) 2024–2025: Unified “OneVision” recipe and long-context efficiency (OV-Qwen2 family)
- Goal: A single model that carries forward the unified paradigm (single image, multiple images, video) and scales efficiently. The authors claim “simultaneously push the performance boundaries” across three key regimes (single/multi-image/video) with the OneVision model recipe <cite id="b074cc00-1">LLaVA-OneVision is the first single model that can simultaneously push the performance boundaries of open LMMs in three important computer vision scenarios</cite>.
- Architecture backbone and context: OV models often adopt Qwen2-based LLM backbones; popular checkpoints like llava-onevision-qwen2-7b-ov run Qwen2 with 32K-token context windows and a dedicated LLaVA-OneVision training recipe, targeting both capability breadth and long-context reasoning across modalities <cite id="b074cc00-2">LLaVA-OneVision models are 0.5/7/72B parameter models trained on LLaVA-OneVision, based on Qwen2 language model with a context window of 32K tokens</cite> <cite id="b074cc00-9">LLaVA-OneVision-2 … targets a recipe across three benchmark domains; the series is presented as a strong perceptual LMM line</cite>.
- Practical impact: By unifying inputs and using long context (up to 32K), OneVision checkpoints are intended for easy transfer across tasks like multi-image QA, visual dialog, and short video QA without bespoke model swaps, reducing engineering friction while maintaining high end‑to‑end accuracy <cite id="b074cc00-1">LLaVA-OneVision is the first single model to excel across single-image, multi-image, and video tasks and unlock emerging capabilities with task transfer</cite> <cite id="b074cc00-2">OV variants are Qwen2-based with 32K-token windows, trained with the LLaVA-OneVision recipe</cite>.

4) 2025: Efficiency and extensibility for production (LLaVA-Mini and successors)
- Design: LLaVA-Mini introduces a modality pre‑fusion module that fuses visual information into the instruction text before LLM processing, plus a compression module to drastically reduce visual token counts, aiming at efficient inference and server deployment while preserving accuracy <cite id="b074cc00-4">LLaVA-Mini introduces a modality pre-fusion module before LLM to fuse visual information into the instruction text in advance, and employs a compression module</cite> <cite id="b074cc00-8">LLaVA-Mini introduces modality pre-fusion to fuse visual information into text tokens in advance, thereby facilitating the extreme compression of vision tokens</cite>.
- Scale/variants and context: Mini variants exist across small to large parameter counts (0.5–7–72B), and several recipes target 32K inter-modality context windows, balancing speed, memory, and long-range visual–text integration in multi-image and video settings <cite id="b074cc00-2">LLaVA-OneVision models (including Mini-scale parameterizations) are trained on the OneVision recipe, based on Qwen2 with 32K-token windows</cite> <cite id="b074cc00-8">Mini’s pre-fusion plus compression supports long-context deployment for efficient image and video</cite>.
- Capability shift: Instead of pushing full-scale open‑weight SOTA everywhere, Mini focuses on accessible hardware—high compression of vision tokens, strong pre-fusion, and long-context support so that mid‑size servers and edge devices can run complex visual tasks with lower latency <cite id="b074cc00-8">LLaVA-Mini targets efficient image and video LMMs using pre-fusion and extreme vision token compression</cite>.

Key technical threads that tie the variants together
- Image–text interleaving and generalized inputs: The NeXT‑Interleave release formalized an interleaved image–text tokenization that lets one model handle arbitrary numbers of images, frames (video), views (3D/MVS), or patches as a unified sequence, removing bespoke branching per input modality and enabling one model/one prompt loop across single/multi-image and video <cite id="b074cc00-0">We utilize an image-text interleaved format to unify multi-image, video, and 3D tasks in one LLM and achieve SoTA</cite> <cite id="b074cc00-7">LLaVA-NeXT-Interleave simultaneously tackles multi-image, multi-frame video, multi-view 3D, and multi-patch single-image</cite>.
- Perception, OCR, reasoning, and knowledge uplift: The “NeXT” series emphasizes stronger OCR, visual reasoning, and broader world knowledge; early public reports note surpassing Gemini Pro on multiple benchmarks, and community pages list 32B NeXT‑Video leading open-source video evaluations like Video‑MME, signaling a concrete capability arc from good to state‑of‑the‑art on spatio‑temporal tasks <cite id="b074cc00-3">LLaVA-NeXT improves reasoning, OCR, and world knowledge and exceeds Gemini Pro on several benchmarks</cite> <cite id="65539fb8-4">NeXT-Video 32B achieves best open-source performance on Video-MME and other video benchmarks</cite>.
- Long-context and task unification: Many OneVision and Mini releases train on Qwen2 backbones with 32K windows and LLaVA recipes to fuse modalities into the textual context, so a single checkpoint can cover long instruction chains, cross‑scene multi-image reasoning, and short video QA efficiently <cite id="b074cc00-2">OV models: Qwen2 backbone with 32K-token context trained with LLaVA-OneVision</cite> <cite id="b074cc00-8">Mini’s pre-fusion and compression enable long-context and efficient reasoning for image/video</cite>.
- Efficiency and compression: Mini’s pre-fusion plus token compression explicitly addresses inference cost by reducing visual token overheads, while OneVision’s 32K windows and Qwen2 backbones deliver deployable long‑context multimodal inference without bespoke hardware ramps <cite id="b074cc00-8">LLaVA-Mini’s pre-fusion and compression facilitate extreme compression of vision tokens and efficient inference</cite> <cite id="b074cc00-2">OV Qwen2-7B(-ov) runs at 32K tokens, trained with the OneVision recipe</cite>.

How the major variant families relate
- LLaVA (2023 baseline): Vicuna+CLIP style, instruction‑tuned on GPT‑4‑generated multimodal data; establishes grounded visual dialogue and chain‑of‑thought style multimodal reasoning as default <cite id="08404726-0">LLaVA: instruction tuning with GPT‑4 multimodal data connecting a vision encoder and LLM</cite> <cite id="d3e87603-0">LLaVA combines encoder and LLM for general-purpose visual and language with multimodal chain-of-thought</cite>.
- LLaVA‑1.6 / NeXT (2024): Upgraded reasoning, OCR, and knowledge; introduces NeXT‑Interleave unification across images/video/3D and NeXT‑Video 32B to lead open-source video benchmarks; public claims include surpassing Gemini Pro on several tasks <cite id="b074cc00-3">NeXT improves reasoning, OCR, world knowledge and exceeds Gemini Pro</cite> <cite id="b074cc00-7">NeXT-Interleave unifies multi-image, multi-frame, multi-view, multi-patch</cite> <cite id="65539fb8-4">NeXT-Video 32B best open-source on Video-MME and related</cite>.
- LLaVA‑OneVision (2024–2025): “Recipe” line delivering a single model that excels across single/multi-image and video; popular OV‑Qwen2 checkpoints bring 32K token context and strong cross‑task transfer; intended to simplify deployment and prompt‑loop design via unified interleaved I↔T inputs <cite id="b074cc00-1">OV is the first single model that can push performance across single/multi-image/video</cite> <cite id="b074cc00-2">OV variants are based on Qwen2 with 32K-token windows</cite>.
- LLaVA‑Mini (2025): Efficiency‑first models using modality pre‑fusion and extreme vision token compression to run on smaller hardware while supporting long context and complex visual tasks; complements OV/NeXT by prioritizing latency and memory at comparable or near‑comparable quality <cite id="b074cc00-4">Mini uses modality pre-fusion before the LLM and a compression module</cite> <cite id="b074cc00-8">Pre-fusion into text tokens and extreme compression underpin efficient image/video reasoning</cite>.

When to pick which variant (practical guidance)
- Need broad, unified input handling and long‑context: Choose OneVision with Qwen2‑ov backbones (e.g., 7B‑ov) for single/multi‑image, multi‑frame/short‑video tasks; the interleaved image–text format and 32K windows support multi‑turn dialog and cross‑scene visual QA <cite id="b074cc00-1">OV excels across single/multi-image/video</cite> <cite id="b074cc00-2">OV uses Qwen2 with 32K-token windows</cite>.
- Want state‑of‑the‑art video reasoning with strong OCR/reasoning: Choose NeXT‑Video (e.g., 32B scale) for competitive performance on Video‑MME and related benchmarks; benefits from high‑res on‑demand and stronger multimodal reasoning modules vs baseline LLaVA <cite id="65539fb8-4">NeXT-Video 32B achieves best open-source performance on Video-MME and other benchmarks</cite> <cite id="b074cc00-3">NeXT improves reasoning and OCR</cite>.
- Must deploy on limited resources: Choose LLaVA‑Mini; its pre‑fusion plus vision compression keeps memory/latency low while retaining accuracy and long‑context support, useful for servers and edge devices <cite id="b074cc00-8">Mini fuses modality pre-fusion into text tokens and compresses vision tokens to enable efficient image/video LMMs</cite>.
- Benchmark or explore original design space: Start with early LLaVA trained via GPT‑4‑generated multimodal instructions to understand the baseline image‑grounded behavior and chain‑of‑thought multimodal reasoning; then upgrade to NeXT/OneVision/Mini modules as needed <cite id="08404726-0">LLaVA’s GPT‑4 image–text instruction generation and end‑to‑end training</cite> <cite id="d3e87603-0">LLaVA’s general-purpose visual–language capability with multimodal chain-of-thought reasoning</cite>.

Open design patterns and active directions
- Interleaving as a lingua franca: The NeXT‑Interleave token interleaving idea has become a standard way to fold images, frames, views, and patches into a single sequence modeled by the LLM, enabling one architecture and one prompt loop versus bespoke pipelines for multi‑modalities <cite id="b074cc00-0">Image–text interleaving unifies multi-image, video, and 3D into one LLM</cite> <cite id="b074cc00-7">Interleave handles multi-image, video, 3D, and multi-patch</cite>.
- Efficiency via pre‑fusion and compression: Mini’s approach of fusing modality content early into text semantics and compressing visual tokens is a concrete recipe to reduce inference cost without major quality loss, complementing the OV/NeXT direction <cite id="b074cc00-4">Mini introduces a pre-fusion module before the LLM and a compression module</cite> <cite id="b074cc00-8">Pre-fusion and extreme vision token compression facilitate efficient image/video reasoning</cite>.
- Video and high‑resolution reasoning: NeXT‑Video scaling to 32B and claims of SOTA on Video‑MME show the LLaVA line’s ongoing push into spatio‑temporal reasoning; this is consistent with broader work showing chain‑of‑thought with visual grounding still struggles and needs verification and curriculum reinforcement for robust video QA <cite id="65539fb8-4">NeXT-Video 32B achieves best open-source results on Video-MME</cite> <cite id="65539fb8-2">Systematic analyses find chain-of-thought reasoning in video tasks remains challenging</cite> <cite id="65539fb8-1">Curriculum-reinforced reasoning with grounded QA (NExT‑GQA and CG‑…)</cite>.
- Long-context checkpoints: OV’s 32K windows and Mini’s extreme compression make longer tool interactions and cross‑scene visual reasoning practical in open‑weight models, reducing the need to build custom tool backends per use case <cite id="b074cc00-2">OV Qwen2 variants with 32K-token windows</cite> <cite id="b074cc00-8">Mini’s compression supports long-context on limited hardware</cite>.

Summary arc: how LLaVA evolved
- 2023: Create a general grounded multimodal assistant via visual instruction tuning on GPT‑4 synthetic data; initial demos emphasize multi-modal chat and chain‑of‑thought reasoning <cite id="08404726-0">Visual Instruction Tuning with GPT‑4 multimodal data yields LLaVA</cite> <cite id="d3e87603-0">LLaVA’s visual–language capability with multimodal chain-of-thought</cite>.
- 2024: Upgrade to NeXT for better OCR/reasoning/knowledge; introduce NeXT‑Interleave to unify single/multi‑image, multi‑frame video, multi‑view/3D and multi‑patch; launch NeXT‑Video 32B to lead open-source video MME <cite id="b074cc00-3">NeXT improves reasoning, OCR, world knowledge and surpasses Gemini Pro</cite> <cite id="b074cc00-7">Interleave unifies multi-image, video, 3D, patches</cite> <cite id="65539fb8-4">NeXT‑Video 32B best open-source on Video‑MME</cite>.
- 2024–25: Scale the recipe across base models: LLaVA‑OneVision claims a single model that excels across single/multi‑image and video, with OV‑Qwen2 backbones offering 32K windows and ready‑to‑deploy long‑context multimodal inference <cite id="b074cc00-1">OV is the first single model excelling across the three regimes</cite> <cite id="b074cc00-2">OV‑Qwen2 with 32K windows trained under the OneVision recipe</cite>.
- 2025: Democratize production with LLaVA‑Mini—fusing modality content early and compressing vision tokens to fit smaller hardware while supporting long context; the family now spans broad capability (OV/NeXT) and efficient deployment (Mini) under a common interleaved I↔T programming model <cite id="b074cc00-8">Mini’s pre-fusion and extreme compression for efficient image/video</cite> <cite id="b074cc00-0">Interleaved I↔T tokens across images/video/3D under a single LLM</cite>.

Finally: where LLaVA stands today
- The series has moved from a single, general-purpose grounded assistant (LLaVA) to an ecosystem: unified input handling for images, multi-image, and video (OneVision/Interleave), stronger OCR/visual reasoning and SOTA video models (NeXT‑Video), and efficient, long‑context deployables (Mini), all sharing the interleaving paradigm and modality-pre-fusion recipe. This trajectory reflects practical agentic deployment: one prompt loop for heterogeneous visual inputs, strong perception for tool agentic use, and deployment efficiency via long context and token compression rather than only parameter scale <cite id="b074cc00-1">OV unification across the three regimes</cite> <cite id="b074cc00-7">Interleave’s multi-modal coverage</cite> <cite id="65539fb8-4">NeXT‑Video SOTA results</cite> <cite id="b074cc00-8">Mini’s pre-fusion and compression</cite>.

fully_underspecified.text: Could you explain the series or variants? How do they evolve over time?
fully_underspecified.answer:
Below is a practical, cross‑domain explanation of “series or variants” and how they evolve over time, with concrete mechanisms and examples from knowledge organization, biomedicine, and software/workflows.

What “series” and “variants” mean
- A “series” is a structured lineage or sequence of related forms or versions that retain a common schema, scope, or purpose. In knowledge work, series often live as taxonomies, ontologies, or controlled vocabularies that organize concepts and their relations hierarchically and semantically. <cite id="f78b60cc-0">A knowledge organization system (KOS)—including taxonomies, thesauri, subject headings, and ontologies—provides a scheme to organize information and manage knowledge over time.</cite> <cite id="f78b60cc-8">Taxonomies organize categories hierarchically; ontologies add semantic meanings and logical connections between entities; knowledge graphs instantiate large-scale networks of such concepts.</cite> <cite id="f78b60cc-6">Traditional KOS tools include classification schemes, taxonomies, controlled vocabularies, thesauri, and ontologies as hierarchical/semantic structures.</cite>

- “Variants” arise whenever a unit within a series changes in definition, relation, or representation: new editions, merged/split entries, synonyms/aliases, scope notes, mappings to other vocabularies, or separate parallel versions coexisting for compatibility. <cite id="f78b60cc-1">A taxonomy exists to help users find information; variants typically change structures or labels that affect discoverability and navigation.</cite> <cite id="f78b60cc-2">In practice, ontologies vs. taxonomies are often used together to capture semantics and navigation; changes to either create alternative forms (“variants”) require alignment across both.</cite> <cite id="f78b60cc-3">SKOS provides a practical alignment layer for controlled vocabularies, enabling mapping between variant systems and expressing relations (broader/narrower/related) with URIs that stabilize semantic variants.</cite>

Mechanisms that drive evolution over time
1) Structural change: branching, fusing, and drifting
- Categories can split (new narrower classes), merge (coalescing overlapping concepts), or drift apart (terms diverge in scope). This is routine in evolving KOS and ontologies. <cite id="f78b60cc-5">Biomedical ontologies and their mappings evolve; new findings lead to revisions, splits, and merges that update relations among concepts and their inter‑ontology mappings.</cite> <cite id="f78b60cc-4">A pattern for scientific taxonomies explicitly models temporal dynamics of concepts as the taxonomy evolves and records concept provenance to add context and traceability.</cite>

- Temporal and provenance layers make variants interpretable by recording “what,” “when,” and “why” changes occurred. <cite id="f78b60cc-4">Categorizing the temporal dynamics of concepts and capturing provenance lets systems distinguish stable identities from changing definitions/scope and supports reconciliation across releases.</cite> <cite id="f78b60cc-6">SKOS supports practical management of evolving vocabularies through standard relations and cross‑walks, enabling side‑by‑side maintenance of variants with documentation.</cite>

2) Versioning and lifecycle management
- Systems evolve by branching and releasing multiple concurrent or sequential versions; users choose contexts and enforce backward compatibility or adopt forward‑looking changes. <cite id="4500dd30-0">Lifecycle management combining ontology versioning tools with an explicit evolution process provides a disciplined way to publish successive releases and track change.</cite> <cite id="4500dd30-4">In workflow systems (e.g., Temporal), multiple workflow definitions can coexist: new executions use updated code while existing ones continue with the original version to maintain stable semantics across variants.</cite>

- Instance‑driven evolution: schemas change in response to data, which often generates hidden variants that need reconciliation. <cite id="4500dd30-2">Schema changes triggered by non‑conservative instance updates can create ontology variants; formal mechanisms capture and reconcile such evolutions so that historical data and new data fit consistent semantics.</cite> <cite id="4500dd30-1">Ontology versioning graphs summarize the branching/merging history from schema evolution and versioning, giving a lineage of variants with explicit change points.</cite>

3) Interoperability and mapping between variants
- As series diverge (due to different modeling choices, communities, or time), stable cross‑walks and mappings become essential to preserve semantics across variants. <cite id="4500dd30-3">Effective ontology management includes planning for versioning, stability of API/URI semantics, and documentation so consumers can choose the correct variant for their context.</cite> <cite id="f78b60cc-3">SKOS enables practical mapping among controlled vocabularies by expressing broader/narrower/related relations and preferred/alt labels, allowing consumers to navigate between variants without breaking links.</cite> <cite id="f78b60cc-5">In biomedicine, approaches to ontology and mapping evolution explicitly target maintaining interoperable mappings as concepts are reorganized or merged/split on new evidence.</cite>

Domain exemplars

Knowledge organization systems (KOS): taxonomies, thesauri, SKOS
- Series: a subject vocabulary released quarterly (e.g., a taxonomy updated quarterly), or a biomedical ontology family such as disease ontologies that iterate annually. <cite id="f78b60cc-0">KOS schemes are explicitly intended to organize information over time for knowledge management.</cite> <cite id="f78b60cc-8">Taxonomies provide hierarchical categories; ontologies add relations; knowledge graphs connect entities—each is a family of variants as they are formalized and connected.</cite>
- Variants: deprecations, new synonyms, narrower terms, and alternate label sets; stable IRI aliases to prevent broken links; cross‑walk files to legacy versions; parallel branches for experimental reorganizations. <cite id="f78b60cc-3">SKOS guides handling synonyms/labels and cross‑walks so that variants remain discoverable and interoperable.</cite> <cite id="f78b60cc-4">Temporal modeling and provenance capture “what changed” and “why,” enabling policy-driven deprecation/retirement and rollbacks in taxonomies.</cite>

Biomedical ontologies and mappings
- Series: Gene Ontology (GO), Human Phenotype Ontology (HPO), Disease Ontology (DO), and related UMLS/SemMedDB ecosystems that are revised yearly. <cite id="f78b60cc-5">Ontologies and their mappings evolve with new findings, producing merges, splits, and relation updates across the series and between variants.</cite>
- Variants: HPO term revisions (broader/narrower changes), alternate mappings (SNOMED vs. ICD vs. OMIM), and “forked” development branches that later reconcile. <cite id="f78b60cc-5">Surveys of ontology evolution emphasize approaches for evolving ontologies and mappings, including detecting incompatibilities introduced by merges/splits and managing cross‑ontology links.</cite>

Software workflow and algorithmic “ontologies”
- Series: evolving workflow definitions and activity schemas in distributed systems. <cite id="4500dd30-4">Workflow versioning allows new executions to use updated definitions while existing ones continue with prior versions, yielding parallel variants without breakage.</cite>
- Variants: different policy branches (policies A vs. B), schema variants for mobile vs. cloud, or major/minor releases that change semantics. <cite id="4500dd30-0">Ontology lifecycle patterns integrate versioning with a repeatable evolution process (requirements gathering, design, review, deployment), giving governance to variant creation and deprecation.</cite> <cite id="4500dd30-2">When real‑world data don’t fit the schema (e.g., free text), instance‑driven evolution triggers schema change, generating new variants that must be reconciled with historical records.</cite>

How series and variants evolve: converging patterns and differences
- Shared patterns: 
  1) Versioned lineages with branching for experiments or regional/domain adaptations, then merging when stabilized. <cite id="4500dd30-1">Versioning graphs explicitly represent branching/merging from schema evolution and multiple versions.</cite>
  2) Semantic stability constraints: freeze or stabilize IRIs/aliases to preserve client compatibility; document deprecation and schedule retirements. <cite id="4500dd30-3">Versioning plans emphasize stability of key identifiers and documentation to guide variant selection at consumption time.</cite>
  3) Temporal/chronicle layers: recording “what changed,” “who,” “when,” and “why” to support auditing, rollbacks, and temporal queries. <cite id="f78b60cc-4">Capturing temporal dynamics and provenance of concepts lets you distinguish stable identities from changing relations and meanings.</cite>
- Differences by domain:
  - Knowledge organization: evolution is social/technical; communities negotiate splits/merges, manage preferred/alt labels, and build cross‑walks for discovery. <cite id="f78b60cc-1">Taxonomies exist to support discovery; changes to structure or labels alter navigation and search.</cite> <cite id="f78b60cc-3">SKOS operationalizes cross‑walks and label management as variants are introduced and retired.</cite>
  - Biomedicine: evidence-driven; revisions follow new findings, sometimes breaking mappings to legacy ontologies; reconciliation tools and automated tests detect incompatibilities across variants. <cite id="f78b60cc-5">Evolution approaches include monitoring and mitigating mapping and compatibility issues that arise when ontology content and relations change with new evidence.</cite>
  - Software workflows: enforce strict forward/backward compatibility or isolation (multi-tenant variant per policy) using runtime version selection and migration jobs. <cite id="4500dd30-4">Versioning policies choose the correct variant per execution context, allowing multiple variants to coexist with zero breakage and explicit migration paths.</cite>

Designing for evolution: practical guidance
- Separate concerns: keep taxonomy structure (is-a/broad-narrow/related) distinct from rendering/UX and from data/provenance layers. <cite id="f78b60cc-8">Taxonomies (hierarchies) vs. ontologies (semantic relations) vs. knowledge graphs (networked entities) serve different concerns and can evolve independently while staying interoperable.</cite>
- Make variant selection explicit to consumers: versioned endpoints, stable IRIs with deprecation notices, runtime mapping engines, and release notes. <cite id="4500dd30-3">A robust versioning plan clarifies management of versions and stable semantics for consumers who must choose the “right” variant for their context.</cite> <cite id="f78b60cc-3">SKOS vocabulary includes relations for broader/narrower/related and labels for preferred/alternate, enabling consumer software to select and reconcile variants automatically.</cite>
- Record provenance and time: document creators, dates, and rationale for change; expose temporal facets and versioned diffs. <cite id="f78b60cc-4">Temporal modeling and provenance capture when and why concepts and relations change, aiding auditing, navigation in time, and rollback decisions.</cite>
- Plan lifecycles: gate major semantic changes via deprecation phases; allow dual‑runtime periods; gate merge of branches through automated conformance/mapping tests. <cite id="4500dd30-0">Lifecycle models that combine versioning tools with a defined evolution process reduce semantic drift and prevent incompatible merges.</cite> <cite id="f78b60cc-5">Approaches to ontology and mapping evolution emphasize testing and managing inter‑ontology links so that merges/splits don’t break downstream systems.</cite>

When to treat changes as “series” vs. “variants”
- Treat as a series when the schema or core semantics stabilize and releases are cumulative and largely additive (new labels/terms/relations) across editions. <cite id="f78b60cc-0">KOS are released as iterative schemes for information organization and management.</cite> <cite id="f78b60cc-4">Temporal modeling lets you track editions as concept-level changes over time without abandoning earlier stable identities.</cite>
- Treat as a variant when changes alter meanings, relations, or interoperability surfaces; create parallel branches (e.g., policy A vs. B, mobile vs. cloud, legacy vs. current) with explicit mapping or deprecation gates. <cite id="4500dd30-4">Workflow systems deliberately maintain multiple versions in parallel and bind the right version to each execution.</cite> <cite id="f78b60cc-3">SKOS supports expressing alternative labels and mappings to manage variants of vocabularies without breaking links.</cite>

Key takeaways
- Evolutionary pressure (data growth, new evidence, UX needs, interoperability) drives both incremental and disruptive changes in series and their variants. <cite id="f78b60cc-5">In biomedicine, findings can trigger splits, merges, and relation changes, with mapped interfaces to maintain cross-system meaning.</cite> <cite id="4500dd30-2">Instance-driven schema updates push evolution from data constraints, creating variants that must be reconciled to maintain semantic consistency.</cite>
- The most durable series keep identity stable via provenance, versioned IRIs, and mapping layers while iterating on structure and content in controlled lifecycles. <cite id="f78b60cc-4">Temporal dynamics plus provenance preserve stable identities even as relations and scopes change over releases.</cite> <cite id="4500dd30-1">Ontology versioning graphs encode the branching/merging history, making evolution auditable and interoperable.</cite>

Open questions and when to specialize
- For highly dynamic domains (biomedicine, law, finance), invest in automated mapping/conformance testing and temporal provenance; for stable domains, focus on periodic, additive releases and consumer-side variant selection. <cite id="f78b60cc-5">Ontology evolution work highlights the need for mapping-aware testing to handle the pace of change and maintain interoperable variants.</cite> <cite id="4500dd30-3">Versioning plans tailor governance, documentation, and stability policies to the domain’s change velocity and compatibility requirements.</cite> 
- If you need rigorous lifecycle control and auditable semantics across organizations, adopt ontology lifecycle/versioning patterns and SKOS-aligned provenance. <cite id="4500dd30-0">Ontology lifecycle patterns integrate explicit evolution processes with versioning tools to manage change safely.</cite> <cite id="f78b60cc-3">SKOS offers an aligned vocabulary and practices to manage variants and cross-walks across organizations.</cite>

without_term.text: Could you explain the AI model series or variants? How did they evolve over time?
without_term.answer:
Below is a concise, evidence-backed roadmap of major AI model families and how they evolved into the current landscape of “series/variants” that trade off expressivity, efficiency, and modal coverage.

Scope and lens
- We organize by architectural and training paradigms across four waves: early statistical/deep models; Transformer-based sequence models; pretrained language models at scale; and the modern generative stack (scaling, mixture-of-experts, diffusion, multimodality, and reasoning scaffolds). Each wave introduced model “series” (e.g., CNN → LSTM/GRU → Transformer), “variants” (e.g., masked vs. causal pretraining, MoE sparsity, latent diffusion), and shifts in objectives (likelihood vs. matching objectives across modalities). <cite id="06e86479-0">This framing echoes recent surveys that trace the arc from n-gram and rule-based models to modern LLMs and beyond</cite>.

Wave 1: Early statistical to deep sequence models (1950s–2010s)
- Statistical N-gram “series” seeded language modeling: Katz backoff, Kneser–Ney smoothing, and the shift from enumerating rules to estimating probabilities over spans, enabling scalable generalization but with limited contextual depth and compositionality. <cite id="06e86479-0">Surveys foreground this baseline as the precursor to neural sequence modeling</cite>.
- Neural MLP and CNN language models improved density and feature hierarchy, enabling better generalization from local context windows and word embeddings. <cite id="06e86479-1">Contemporary overviews emphasize distributed representations and transducer-style architectures as conceptual steps toward modern LMs</cite>.
- RNNs (and later GRUs) introduced recurrent state to capture longer dependencies; they became the dominant encoder–decoder baseline for machine translation and seq2seq tasks before attention-based models. <cite id="99e7a80b-1">By the late 2010s, the field was bottlenecked by recurrence’s sequential computation and limited long-range modeling</cite>.

Wave 2: The Transformer revolution (2017)
- Core idea: model-wide self-attention with key/value/query factorizations and positional encodings, trained end-to-end without recurrence or convolution. <cite id="99e7a80b-1">The Transformer architecture “is based solely on attention mechanisms, dispensing with recurrence and convolutions entirely,” enabling full parallelization</cite>. <cite id="99e7a80b-0">Vaswani et al. motivate self-attention, detail multi-head attention, and discuss advantages over recurrent sequence models</cite>.
- Why it shifted practice: parallel computation across tokens, direct global dependency modeling with O(1) attention across positions via positional encodings, and consistent performance gains across translation and QA tasks. <cite id="99e7a80b-5">Explainability and math emphasize that tokens can connect across the sequence in one hop, reducing error compounding</cite>. <cite id="99e7a80b-8">Positional encodings plus self-attention create O(1) connectivity between positions, enabling the Transformer architecture</cite>.
- Immediate variants: multi-head attention for robust representation, encoder–decoder variants with shared attention, and language-model-specific decoder-only forms that prefigure later LLMs. <cite id="99e7a80b-3">The Wikipedia exposition notes multi-head attention and encoder–decoder configurations as part of the Transformer design</cite>.

Series A: Decoder-only LMs and scaling (mid/late 2010s–present)
- GPT family (OpenAI): causal Language Models trained autoregressively on large corpora, then scaled massively in corpus size and model size; moved architecture toward pure decoder stacks with attention-only mixers, yielding strong zero-shot transfer and prompting regimes. <cite id="06e86479-3">Surveys of LLMs document the decoder-only transformer as a core modern LM family built on self-attention</cite>. These models embody a paradigm shift from static rule-based lexicons to massively parameterized, autoregressive generators optimized purely by next-token prediction. <cite id="06e86479-1">Historical overviews trace this lineage from distributed representations to modern LMs trained entirely by next-token prediction</cite>.
- Bidirectional contextualization: contemporaneous masked LM objectives led to contextual embeddings trained to predict hidden tokens, improving factual and world-knowledge groundedness compared to left-to-right only LMs. <cite id="06e86479-2">Timeline accounts highlight masked pretraining as a watershed enabling deeper contextual representations</cite>.

Series B: Contextual pretraining variants (BERT and successors)
- BERT (Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers): masked LM over a full Transformer encoder, trained to predict randomly masked tokens using bidirectional context; achieved state-of-the-art downstream transfers with contextualized embeddings, replacing unidirectional word embeddings and seq2seq decoders for many tasks. <cite id="06e86479-3">Surveys describe BERT as a canonical bidirectional contextual pretraining paradigm</cite>.
- Variants evolved by objective design: sentence-order prediction (SOP), span-masked objectives, dynamic masking, and hybrid pretraining (MLM + NSP) improved pretraining efficiency and task coverage; domain adaptation and multilingual variants extended capability. <cite id="06e86479-0">Recent overviews summarize how masked objectives catalyzed a generation of contextualized representations beyond word vectors</cite>.

Series C: Unified text generation — T5 family
- T5 reframed all text problems (generation, translation, summarization) as text-to-text with a shared decoder-only Transformer objective, minimizing divergence with teacher outputs via cross-entropy; this unified series reduced model proliferation and improved transfer via code-switching-style pretraining. <cite id="06e86479-2">Timeline treatments describe the shift from problem-specific architectures to unified text-to-text objectives</cite>.
- T5 variants explored factorized decoders, multilingual and domain-specific corpora, and sequence-level set losses; the T5-XL/XXL scale highlighted that pure decoder LMs with massive data could match or surpass encoder–decoder translation systems. <cite id="06e86479-3">Surveys catalog T5’s emergence as a dominant generation-centric series</cite>.

Wave 3: Scaling and architectural efficiency — MoE and decoder-only dominance
- Scaling laws and compute/data: large-scale decoder-only models (e.g., GPT-3, PaLM) demonstrated superlinear improvements with more data and parameters, making massive pretraining and prompt-based few-shot learning possible; these models popularized the “LLM” term and API-style inference where users prompt a fixed large model. <cite id="06e86479-1">Distributed representations plus attention and massive compute precipitated these scaling regimes</cite>. <cite id="06e86479-7">A 2025 survey underscores LLMs’ paradigm shift within AI</cite>.
- Mixture-of-Experts (MoE): to increase effective parameter count without cubic cost, MoE routers select subsets of experts per token/layer; released systems (e.g., GLaM, Mixtral) keep inference tractable while scaling capacity, yielding strong dense-sparse hybrids. <cite id="99e7a80b-0">Transformer design studies attention as a selective gating mechanism, which modern MoE builds upon</cite>.
- Training variants: sharded data parallelism, ZeRO/OPTIMIZER sharding, and speculative decoding; inference variants: KV-cache compression and speculative sampling, all enabled by the attention-only decoder architecture. <cite id="06e86479-3">Surveys summarize these operational variants for scaling LLMs</cite>.

Wave 4: Multimodality and diffusion — from text-only to images, video, and cross-modal matching
- Diffusion models for images: Markov diffusion in latent space (UNet-based denoisers) enabled high-fidelity image synthesis by learning the reverse process of Gaussian noise to image; innovations like U-Net encoders/decoders, attention conditioning, and latent diffusion cut compute and artifacts. <cite id="99e7a80b-0">Transformer-adjacent work on attention-based model components influenced later cross-attention in diffusion pipelines</cite>.
- Cross-modal matching: CLIP learns joint embeddings over images and text in a shared space, enabling zero-shot image understanding (e.g., zero-shot classification) and aligning modalities at embedding-level; Flamingo stacks an autoregressive decoder atop vision encoders with a memory bank of retrieved captions, seeding instruction-following multimodal LMs. <cite id="06e86479-3">Modern overviews place multimodal pretraining and instruction-following as core themes of LLM evolution</cite>.

Rational and fine-tuning scaffolds — instruction, reasoning, and alignment
- RLHF and instruction tuning: human preference optimization aligned language models to safer, more helpful behavior; PEFT (adapter/QLoRA) and prompt-based methods produced high-performing variants without full fine-tuning, enabling rapid deployment across tasks. <cite id="06e86479-7">Surveys describe alignment via reward modeling and instruction tuning as a watershed in LLM deployment</cite>.
- Reasoning variants: chain-of-thought prompting externalizes intermediate reasoning steps to improve math/complex reasoning tasks; “tool use” embeddings integrate external agents; tree-search decoding explores rationales; these are shallow prompting heuristics that complement deeper architectural changes. <cite id="06e86479-1">Contemporary accounts trace these prompting and search heuristics as extensions of the LLM training paradigm</cite>.

Putting it together: How series and variants evolved over time
- From recurrence to attention: seq2seq RNNs → LSTM/GRU → Transformer decoder–encoder stacks freed parallelism and long-range modeling, catalyzing decoder-only LMs. <cite id="99e7a80b-0">Self-attention and positional encodings underpin these advantages</cite>.
- From unidirectional to bidirectional masking: word-embedding models → MLM (GPT-style) → BERT’s bidirectional masked LM → T5’s unified text-to-text masked objectives reflect a shift to contextual pretraining that ties models to downstream tasks more tightly. <cite id="06e86479-0">Surveys capture how masked objectives became the default for contextual representations</cite>. <cite id="06e86479-2">Overviews note the consolidation to unified masked generation</cite>.
- From dense to efficient scaling: fixed dense Transformers → scaling laws → MoE mixture-of-experts (GLaM-style dense-and-sparse hybrids, then LLM-era open implementations like Mixtral) combined massive data with per-token sparsity. <cite id="99e7a80b-0">Analyses emphasize attention as a precursor to selective computation patterns, later realized as MoE</cite>.
- From text to multimodal: CLIP’s shared embedding unification of image–text → Flamingo’s retrieval-augmented generative stack → modern multimodal LLMs that see and reason; simultaneously, diffusion models in latent space gave rise to SD/Video diffusion families, a parallel lineage for generative visual synthesis. <cite id="06e86479-7">Surveys emphasize the generative shift to data-centric, alignment-aware multimodal systems</cite>.
- From optimization-only to alignment/reasoning: next-token prediction → RLHF and instruction tuning → reasoning heuristics (CoT) and search; variants such as QLoRA adapters and speculative decoding combine high efficiency with behavioral alignment.

Practical takeaways: model series and variants in the modern stack
- Decoder-only Transformers (GPT/T5-XL-style) vs. encoder–decoder for seq2seq; masked (MLM) vs. causal (LM) objectives reflect training-time design choices that drive bidirectionality and generation quality. <cite id="06e86479-0">Comparative surveys discuss these objective trade-offs</cite>.
- MoE variants trade parameter cost for throughput/quality at inference by activating only a subset of experts per token; they extend scaling laws without exploding compute. <cite id="06e86479-7">Recent surveys capture MoE’s role in scaling modern LLMs</cite>.
- Diffusion and multimodal stacks hybridize neural attention with latent denoising and cross-modal retrieval; they are parallel but interacting families that now converge via multimodal LLMs (e.g., “image prompting” LLMs) and video diffusion LMs. <cite id="06e86479-2">Timeline sources note the emergence of multimodal generative models</cite>.
- Instruction tuning, RLHF, and tool-use variants change behavior without altering architecture, often by fine-tuning small heads or prompting, while chain-of-thought and search-based decoding improve hard reasoning.

A brief history in 2025 terms
- 1950s–2010s: n-grams, rule-based systems, and neural MLP/CNN sequence models seeded statistical language modeling and early deep learning workflows. <cite id="06e86479-0">Surveys document the linear progression</cite>.
- 2014–2017: CNN/RNN image and seq2seq SOTA; attention emerges in seq2seq; positional encodings and multi-head attention foreshadow Transformers. <cite id="99e7a80b-0">The Transformer paper codifies self-attention</cite>.
- 2017–2020: Transformer dominance; GPT-style decoder-only LMs and BERT’s masked LM define a new era of contextualized pretraining; T5 unify tasks as text-to-text; zero-shot and few-shot become practical. <cite id="06e86479-1">Historic accounts trace the shift</cite>. <cite id="06e86479-3">Surveys cover BERT, T5, and LLMs in depth</cite>.
- 2020–present: Scaling and MoE; diffusion for high-fidelity image/video; multimodal stacks (CLIP/Flamingo) bridge text and image; RLHF/instruction tuning and CoT/search variants deliver aligned, useful systems; operational variants (KV-cache compression, PEFT) make large models practical at scale. <cite id="06e86479-7">2025 surveys synthesize this integrated landscape</cite>.

If you want a focused deep-dive on one family (e.g., GPT variants, BERT derivatives, diffusion models, or MoE systems), tell me which to drill down on next; I can unpack architectures, training recipes, and representative checkpoints with concrete numbers and trade-offs.

without_preference.text: Could you explain the LLaVA series or variants and how they evolved over time?
without_preference.answer:
Below is an evidence-backed overview of how the LLaVA series evolved from its initial release into a family of large multimodal models (LMMs), across variants that prioritized generality, efficiency, stronger language scaling, and video understanding.

High-level overview: what “LLaVA” is and why it matters
- LLaVA refers to a family of multimodal transformer models that jointly process images and text via cross-attention, trained for instruction-following vision tasks (e.g., VQA, visual reasoning, long-form image/video description). Early work emphasized simple, modular fusion and open recipes, with later variants swapping or improving the text backbone, scaling, token-efficiency, and video modules to reach state of the art and practical efficiency on common benchmarks. <cite id="959f2d26-7">LLaVA’s modular multimodal transformer architecture integrates visual and linguistic processing</cite> with later releases making explicit backbone and training choices to broaden capabilities and reproducibility.

Phase 1: Early LLaVA and the OneVision wave (2023–2024)
- Scope and design goal: Make a single model that is strong across single-image understanding, multi-image reasoning, and early video tasks; unify training and inference recipes to lower transfer costs. <cite id="959f2d26-0">LLaVA-OneVision framed the goal of a single model that pushes open LMM performance across three core visual scenarios</cite>, while <cite id="02e524eb-0">the OneVision paper explicitly aimed to simultaneously advance open LMMs on single-image, multi-image, and video settings</cite>.
- Architectural ingredients (early lineage): Cross-attention-based fusion and vision encoders feeding an instruction-tuned language backbone; training on broad multimodal tasks (image VQA, instruction). <cite id="02e524eb-0">LLaVA-OneVision presented a recipe that pushed boundaries on open LMMs across core vision scenarios</cite>, and early variants reported strong results on classic VQA-style evaluations (e.g., near SOTA on LLaVA/VQA-style baselines in contemporaneous reports).

Phase 2: Efficiency-first push — LLaVA-Mini (2024–2025)
- Why Mini? To deliver near–OneVision-level capabilities at small scale and for long-context or multi-image scenarios with far fewer tokens. <cite id="02e524eb-2">LLaVA-Mini is described as a unified LMM supporting images, high-resolution images, and videos efficiently</cite>, and the ICLR 2025 paper emphasizes a key design: <cite id="959f2d26-6">outperforming LLaVA-v1.5 while using just one vision token instead of 576</cite> via a modality pre-fusion strategy that fuses visual content into text tokens up front.
- Technical change: “Pre-fusion” (visual tokens → language attention before output) plus extreme token compression. <cite id="959f2d26-8">LLaVA-Mini introduces modality pre-fusion to fuse visual information into text tokens in advance, enabling extreme compression of vision tokens</cite>, while <cite id="9354693f-0">the OpenReview entry frames LLaVA-Mini as an efficient LMM with minimal vision tokens that compresses visual tokens highly while retaining accuracy</cite>. <cite id="9354693f-1">The model claims efficiency across images, high-resolution images, and videos</cite>.
- Benchmarks and scope: <cite id="02e524eb-2">LLaVA-Mini is evaluated as a unified model on multimodal tasks that include images, high-resolution imagery, and video</cite>, with <cite id="959f2d26-6">demonstrated superiority over LLaVA-v1.5 using one rather than 576 vision tokens</cite>, evidencing a deliberate design shift from large visual token counts to compact, fused representations.

Phase 3: Scaling and backbone rethinking — LLaVA-NeXT (2024)
- Goal: Use stronger text-side generalists to “supercharge” multimodal understanding.
