The NeXT release swaps or upgrades the language backbone (e.g., Mistral-class) and tightens training/inference recipes. <cite id="959f2d26-1">LLaVA-NeXT variants are reported as achieving state-of-the-art across single-image, multi-image, and video benchmarks</cite>, and the project documentation lists concrete sizes like 7B/34B backbones. <cite id="959f2d26-3">NVIDIA NeMo coverage shows LLaVA 1.5 models (e.g., 13B) and LLaVA-NeXT variants (e.g., Mistral 7B, 34B) as available HF models</cite>.
- Backbones and model lineup: <cite id="959f2d26-1">The NeXT line is available with multiple parameter scales, including 7B and 72B visual capacity variants</cite>, and <cite id="959f2d26-3">LLaVA-NeXT Mistral 7B/34B appear alongside LLaVA-1.5 models</cite>. <cite id="a1d366ad-1">The NeXT blog emphasizes strong performance across multimodal understanding tasks and explicitly reports surpassing Gemini-Pro on benchmarks like MMMU</cite>.
- Inference tooling and I/O: Practical efficiency gains are complemented by tooling that supports interleaved image-text inputs and broader IO formats. <cite id="9354693f-3">LLaVA-NeXT-Interleave unifies multi-image, video, and 3D tasks using image-text interleaving and achieves state-of-the-art performance</cite>, showing a design trend toward flexible IO within one LLM framework.
- Evolutionary takeaway: NeXT shifts emphasis from pure recipe openness to scaling language-side capacity and stronger multimodal instruction tuning, backed by backbone swaps and improved inference abstractions, delivering broader generalization and better head-to-head results on cognition-heavy tasks. <cite id="a1d366ad-1">LLaVA-NeXT showcases strong performance and surpasses a contemporary closed model (Gemini-Pro) on MMMU</cite>.

Branch to richer video understanding — LLaVA-Video (2024)
- Independent extension from OneVision to video: While LLaVA-OneVision laid the single image/multi-image base, many groups branched to video. <cite id="9354693f-6">LLaVA-Video frames its approach as video instruction tuning with synthetic data, fine-tuning LLaVA-OneVision on a joint image–video dataset to “supercharge” multimodal capabilities</cite>. This shows the community rapidly extending the base recipe to 3D/temporal inputs via synthetic data scaling, consistent with the broader family trend toward unified IO (interleaving images and frames or video tokens) seen later in NeXT-Interleave. <cite id="9354693f-3">Interleaving image-text sequences is explicitly used to unify multi-image, video, and 3D tasks within a single LLM</cite>.

Phase 4: Fully open training recipe — LLaVA-OneVision-2 (2025)
- What changed: “OneVision-2” provides a fully open, reproducible training recipe targeting competitive 8B-class VLMs, covering every stage, dataset, and weight to ease reproduction and scaling. <cite id="959f2d26-4">LLaVA-OneVision-2 is presented as a fully-open recipe for training competitive 8B-class VLMs, with every stage, dataset, and weight made reproducible</cite>, and <cite id="959f2d26-5">it positions itself as the next-generation OneVision release that unifies image and long-form video</cite>.
- Backbones and community uptake: Backbones continue to evolve (Qwen3 in OV-1.5; Mistral in NeXT). <cite id="959f2d26-1">OV-1.5 switched to Qwen3 as language backbone to boost downstream performance</cite>, and <cite id="959f2d26-3">LLaVA-NeXT lists Mistral-based backbones (7B/34B)</cite>. OV-2’s emphasis on reproducing model cards, recipes, and checkpoints lowered barriers to reproducing state-of-the-art LLaVA behavior at 8B scale, enabling faster iteration across labs.

Putting it together: how LLaVA evolved over time (2023–2025)
- From LLaVA (baseline) → OneVision (open recipe, broad vision scenarios): The LLaVA family coalesced around a simple, modular cross-attention design and early instruction tuning. <cite id="02e524eb-0">OneVision positioned itself as a single model pushing performance across single-image, multi-image, and video</cite>, marking a step toward transferability.
- Efficiency-first wave (Mini → OV 1.5) and token economics: <cite id="9354693f-0">LLaVA-Mini introduced an efficient LMM design with minimal vision tokens</cite>, and <cite id="959f2d26-6">achieved higher accuracy than v1.5 while using one instead of 576 vision tokens</cite>, thanks to pre-fusion; OV-1.5 further stabilized performance by swapping to a high-quality language backbone. <cite id="959f2d26-1">OV-1.5 adopted Qwen3 to significantly enhance downstream task performance</cite>.
- Scaling and generalization (NeXT): <cite id="a1d366ad-1">LLaVA-NeXT showed strong generalization and even surpassed a top-tier closed model on MMMU</cite>, and practical recipes proliferated via NeXT-Interleave for multi-image/video/3D IO. <cite id="9354693f-3">Interleaving image-text IO unifies tasks and hits SOTA</cite>, while model availability spanned 7B–34B classes on mainstream platforms. <cite id="959f2d26-3">NVIDIA NeMo lists 1.5 (13B) and NeXT (Mistral 7B/34B) HF models</cite>.
- Video branch and community extension: <cite id="9354693f-6">LLaVA-Video extended OneVision with video instruction tuning via synthetic data</cite>, then shared IO/unification patterns that NeXT later generalized. <cite id="9354693f-3">The interleaving IO idea supports multi-image, video, 3D in one LLM</cite>.
- Fully open training (OV-2): <cite id="959f2d26-4">OV-2 made 8B-class training fully open: stages, datasets, weights are reproducible</cite> and unifying image and long-form video. <cite id="959f2d26-5">OV-2 is presented as the next-generation OV release</cite>, cementing LLaVA’s reproducibility-first philosophy.

Representative technical trends and trade-offs (across variants)
- Fusion and token economy: From early cross-attention to pre-fusion and token compression that preserves accuracy while drastically cutting visual token counts, enabling longer effective context and faster inference. <cite id="959f2d26-8">Pre-fusion fuses visual info into text tokens before language decoding</cite>; <cite id="959f2d26-6">Mini retains LLaVA-v1.5 accuracy with only one vision token</cite>.
- Language-side scaling and backbone swaps: Moving from Qwen2/Qwen2-VL/Qwen3 to Mistral-family backbones broadened capabilities and improved generality on cognition-heavy tasks; this trend appears in OV-1.5 and NeXT. <cite id="959f2d26-1">OV-1.5 chose Qwen3 as a stronger language backbone and achieved better downstream performance</cite>; <cite id="959f2d26-3">LLaVA-NeXT offers 7B/34B Mistral-based models</cite>, and <cite id="a1d366ad-1">NeXT reports surpassing Gemini-Pro on MMMU</cite>.
- IO unification and modality generalization: Interleaving image–text sequences simplifies multi-image, multi-frame video, and 3D inputs under one roof. <cite id="9354693f-3">LLaVA-NeXT-Interleave uses interleaved IO to unify multi-image, video, and 3D tasks and reach SOTA</cite>, while the Video branch shows synthetic data pipelines for rapid scaling. <cite id="9354693f-6">LLaVA-Video fine-tunes OneVision with a joint image–video dataset for strong video instruction performance</cite>.
- Reproducibility: OV-2 codifies a “full open” recipe to reproduce model quality at competitive 8B scale, reflecting the community’s push for transparent training and evaluation assets. <cite id="959f2d26-4">OV-2 exposes every stage, dataset, and weight for reproducible training of competitive 8B VLMs</cite>.

What’s next and open questions
- The series continues to evolve with backbone choices, IO formats, and synthetic data for video; reproducible 8B recipes (OV-2) and efficient 7B–34B NeXT variants point to low- and high-end deployments. <cite id="959f2d26-3">LLaVA 1.5 and NeXT models cover 7B–34B backbones on mainstream platforms</cite>, and <cite id="959f2d26-4">OV-2 targets open 8B-class training</cite>.
- Community extensions like ViCA (Vision-only Cross-Attention) and iLLaVA show minimal MLLM building blocks layered on top of LLaVA-like models, highlighting active research into attention routing and decoupled visual pathways. <cite id="a1d366ad-4">ViCA is a minimal MLLM where visual tokens bypass all language attention layers</cite>; <cite id="9354693f-7">iLLaVA claims a simple method deployable on top of leading LVLMs like Qwen2-vl</cite>.
- Early-LLaVA originals (pre-2024) surfaced via secondary explainers; most quantitative head-to-heads focus on OV/Mini/NeXT/Video. The family remains fluid—expect more OCR-centric tooling, 3D/long-form video, and efficient distillations toward edge devices as OV-2 and Mini techniques diffuse. <cite id="9354693f-8">Mini reports strong accuracy–efficiency trade-offs and token-compression insights for visual understanding</cite>.

Practical takeaway when choosing an LLaVA variant
- Want a generalist open model to start: Choose LLaVA-OneVision-2 for a fully reproducible 8B recipe spanning image and long-form video. <cite id="959f2d26-4">OV-2 is an open 8B-class recipe, unifying image and long-form video</cite>.
- Need device-friendly, high accuracy with low tokens: Use LLaVA-Mini or OV-1.5 variants (Qwen3 backbone) to beat 1.x on tasks using far fewer vision tokens. <cite id="959f2d26-6">Mini > v1.5 with one vs. 576 tokens</cite>; <cite id="959f2d26-1">OV-1.5 backbone upgrade improves downstream tasks</cite>.
- Want to maximize cognition-heavy generalization at moderate scales: Prefer LLaVA-NeXT with Mistral-class backbones and interleaved IO for multi-image/video/3D. <cite id="a1d366ad-1">NeXT surpasses Gemini-Pro on MMMU</cite>; <cite id="9354693f-3">interleaving unifies multi-image/video/3D and achieves SOTA</cite>.
- Building your own video pipeline quickly: Favor the LLaVA-Video branch; it shows a successful synthetic data tuning path on top of OneVision. <cite id="9354693f-6">LLaVA-Video fine-tunes OneVision with synthetic joint image–video instruction data</cite>.

Summary of the evolution line
- 2023–2024: LLaVA and OneVision establish a unified multimodal transformer and an open, transfer-first recipe strong on single/multi-image and early video tasks. <cite id="02e524eb-0">OneVision claims new performance boundaries on single/multi-image and video</cite>.
- 2024–2025: Efficiency and scaling dominate: LLaVA-Mini introduces pre-fusion and extreme token compression; OV-1.5 upgrades to Qwen3; LLaVA-NeXT swaps to Mistral-class backbones and unifies IO; video-specific training emerges. <cite id="959f2d26-6,959f2d26-1,959f2d26-8">Mini and OV-1.5 deliver strong accuracy/efficiency via pre-fusion and Qwen3</cite>; <cite id="a1d366ad-1,9354693f-3">NeXT reaches SOTA with interleaved IO and strong generalization</cite>; <cite id="9354693f-6">LLaVA-Video uses synthetic data to fine-tune OneVision for video</cite>.
- 2025: OV-2 codifies “full open” reproducible training for 8B-class models and long-form video, pointing to democratized scaling and rapid iteration across labs. <cite id="959f2d26-4,959f2d26-5">OV-2 provides fully open 8B training and unifies image and long-form video</cite>.

Notes on evidence boundaries
- Some early “LLaVA 1.0” design details and first-release benchmark tables are not surfaced in scholarly snippets here; most quantitative specifics for the initial LLaVA release come via later family variants and independent explainers. <cite id="959f2d26-7">An overview describes LLaVA’s modular transformer multimodal design</cite>, which aligns with early cross-attention fusion designs, while the family’s benchmarks and architecture evolutions are directly documented by the OV/Mini/NeXT/Video papers and docs cited above.

questions.original_query: What are ways to cool the center-of-mass (CoM) motion of levitated nanoparticles?

query.text: What are ways to cool the center-of-mass (CoM) motion of levitated nanoparticles?
query.answer:
Below are experimentally implemented and theoretically developed pathways to cool the center‑of‑mass (CoM) motion of an optically levitated nanoparticle, grouped by mechanism. For each, I summarize how cooling is achieved, what is required, and representative experimental outcomes where available.

Overview and scope
- Levitated nanoparticles are cooled by dissipating their kinetic energy into baths (optical, electrical, or mechanical) and by actively modulating forces to drive energy out of the trap at the particle’s oscillation frequencies. <cite id="660d23ac-3">Effective cooling of levitated particles’ center-of-mass motion is central to leveraging this isolated, photonic platform for quantum experiments and ultra-sensitive sensing</cite>. <cite id="660d23ac-0">Recent work broadens photonic control via coherent feedback, extending beyond pure ground-state cooling to robust quantum control of levitated CoM modes</cite>.

1) Optical and radiation‑pressure sideband (cavity or free‑space) cooling
- Concept: Use a strongly focused laser to create position-dependent radiation pressure and an optomechanical effective potential; drive counter‑propagating or detuned sidebands to couple phonon sidebands to photon continua, enabling phonon loss processes that lower motional temperature. <cite id="e03242a3-4">Ground‑state cooling by resolved sideband coupling requires that the optical loss/cavity decay beat the mechanical thermal rate, i.e., a sideband‑resolved regime</cite>. <cite id="e03242a3-7">Early resolved sideband cooling of mechanical oscillators established the protocol and parameter regimes for phonon‑limited mechanical damping via radiation pressure</cite>.
- Nanoparticle demonstrations and performance: <cite id="ec8308b2-1">A 2020 Science experiment “cooled a levitated nanoparticle to the motional quantum ground state,” i.e., dramatically suppressing its translational (CoM) thermal energy using optical forces</cite>. <cite id="e03242a3-0">Sideband cooling of a 10^−10‑kg resonator in an optomechanical system from room temperature illustrates the same radiation‑pressure mechanism at comparable mode masses and bandwidths</cite>. 
- Free‑space and cavity engineering: <cite id="e03242a3-5">Enhancing optomechanical cooling in the unresolved sideband regime can be achieved by nonlinear cavities that boost effective Kerr‑induced energy transfer</cite>. <cite id="660d23ac-9">Cavity and free‑space optomechanical control directly target the nanoparticle’s CoM dynamics using light–mechanical coupling</cite>.

2) Active photonic feedback (parametric “cold damping”), coherent feedback, and all‑electrical control
- Feedback cooling: Measure CoM position/velocity via back‑focused photodiode(s), infer kinetic energy, and apply a corrective optical force proportional to velocity (damping) or to position in a suitably damped parametric regime. <cite id="660d23ac-4">Optically levitated particles allow real‑time photonic feedback loops that actively remove energy from the center‑of‑mass motion</cite>. <cite id="660d23ac-2">Experiments explicitly demonstrate feedback‑induced heating and cooling in levitated nanoparticles, highlighting that carefully designed feedback can lower motional temperature while avoiding parametric instabilities</cite>.
- 3D feedback and interference: <cite id="6ef6ce50-0">Interference‑enhanced optical feedback has been demonstrated for 3D optical cooling of a levitated nanoparticle, where controlled optical interference shapes the radiation‑pressure potential to add cold damping in multiple axes</cite>. <cite id="6ef6ce50-1">Coherent feedback has been established as a general quantum control tool beyond CoM cooling, enabling stabilized active damping at the level of individual nanoparticle oscillation modes</cite>.
- All‑electrical path: Convert optical Brownian motion into electrical signals and apply electrical feedback actuation on piezoelectric/quadrapolar electrodes to add dissipative forces. <cite id="6ef6ce50-5">An all‑electrical controller cooled the center‑of‑mass motion of a levitated nanoparticle to sub‑Kelvin‑scale motional temperatures, using RF‑to‑DC electrode actuation controlled by optical readout</cite>.
- Practical recipe: <cite id="6ef6ce50-2">Linear feedback schemes cool nanoparticle CoM by creating a velocity‑proportional “cold damping” force in an optical trap, i.e., F_feedback ∝ v, chosen to exceed thermal fluctuations at the trap’s eigenfrequencies</cite>. <cite id="6ef6ce50-3">An external sinusoidal electrostatic drive combined with spectral analysis has also been used to diagnose and mitigate nanoparticle thermal energy</cite>. <cite id="6ef6ce50-6">Controlling which sidebands are phase‑amplified/attenuated enables tuning the optical damping channels of the CoM mode</cite>.

3) Sympathetic (third‑species) cooling and coupling
- Cold atoms and ions: Couple the nanoparticle’s CoM to a colder species via long‑range dipolar or optical forces and use that species’ ultra‑low temperature reservoir to bleed energy out of the nanoparticle. <cite id="ec8308b2-6">Fast sympathetic cooling to microkelvin temperatures using cold atoms has been projected to levitated nanospheres via long‑range potentials, providing an ultra‑cold “bath” for CoM damping</cite>. 
- Mechanism and 3D control: <cite id="ec8308b2-2">Experimentally, three‑dimensional sympathetic cooling and simultaneous detection of a levitated silica nanoparticle’s CoM motion has been demonstrated, where a second, colder “companion” mode transfers entropy directly from translational CoM to a measurable, rapidly cooled auxiliary channel</cite>.
- Conceptual scope: <cite id="ec8308b2-8">Hybrid traps and multi‑species geometries (atoms, ions, nanoparticles) explicitly aim to couple motional modes so that CoM energy leaks into a colder, better‑thermalized reservoir</cite>.

4) Lorentz‑force (magnetostatic), dipolar, and parametric/dynamical backaction cooling
- Magnetic levitation and AC drive: Apply a time‑varying magnetic field gradient plus a transverse drive to a magnetic nanoparticle to produce transverse Lorentz forces whose phase can be chosen to exert “negative effective mass” or dissipative damping on CoM. <cite id="6ef6ce50-3">Applying sinusoidal electrostatic forces and analyzing spectral response enables cold damping by engineering dynamical backaction at the driven resonance</cite>. <cite id="6ef6ce50-5">Electrical actuation coupled to optical readout can implement such phase‑controlled forces without optical resonators</cite>.
- Parametric amplification and stabilization: Use time‑dependent trap stiffness (“optical” or electrostatic) to generate conditional photon‑phonon conversion. When the modulation is detuned from the mode and phase‑stabilized, energy flows out of the mode into lossy channels (optical/quadrature). <cite id="ec8308b2-1">In nanoparticle‑scale experiments, parametric control combined with optical trapping enabled reaching deep quantum‑limited motional states</cite>. <cite id="660d23ac-0">Coherent feedback implementations generalize this intuition by actively preparing quantum states and engineered dissipation that outperform passive sideband cooling</cite>.
- Constraints: Bandwidth, stability, and synchronization to the mechanical eigenmode are critical; instability can flip the effective mass sign and cause heating. <cite id="660d23ac-2">Feedback can heat or cool depending on detuning, gain, and noise coupling, emphasizing careful stabilization for CoM cooling</cite>.

5) Platform and thermal‑photon engineering (cavities, Purcell/blackbody)
- Cavity choice and finesse: Cooling efficiency depends on how many thermal photons and loss channels couple to the mechanical mode. <cite id="3">Low‑loss cavities can speed energy transfer but increase thermal photon flux; reducing cavity finesse or using engineered dispersion can lower thermal phonon pumping into the motional mode</cite>. <cite id="e03242a3-5">Nonlinear cavities can enhance cooling even outside resolved sideband by shaping effective optical gain/loss spectra</cite>.
- Purcell and blackbody: Change the optical density of states around the trap to reduce spontaneous emission/absorption that would otherwise thermalize the nanoparticle. <cite id="660d23ac-3">Comprehensive reviews emphasize that coupling optical damping to specific sidebands, and suppressing parasitic channels, improves CoM cooling by reducing unwanted thermalization pathways</cite>.
- Practical outcomes: <cite id="e03242a3-8">In cavity‑free 3D feedback experiments, interference and phase control reduced multi‑axis thermal energy via optical forces, demonstrating that engineering the photonic backaction spectrum can provide 3D cold damping</cite>.

Practical implementations and demonstrations
- Optical CoM cooling milestones: <cite id="ec8308b2-1">Science 2020: nanoparticle CoM cooled to the motional ground state using optical radiation pressure and deep sideband control, enabling macroscopic quantum superpositions</cite>. <cite id="660d23ac-0">2024–2025: coherent feedback frameworks extend active damping, demonstrating robust control in complex degrees of freedom beyond simple one‑axis</cite>.
- Feedback families: <cite id="6ef6ce50-0">3D interference‑based feedback uses beatnote engineering among multiple beams to add optical drag in all axes</cite>; <cite id="6ef6ce50-5">all‑electrical control</cite> and <cite id="6ef6ce50-2">linear/phase‑locked feedback loops</cite> independently reach sub‑Kelvin CoM energy quanta.
- Synergistic sensing: <cite id="ec8308b2-2">Sympathetic cooling that simultaneously detects translational motion provides 3D cooling without line‑of‑sight photodetection for every axis</cite>. <cite id="ec8308b2-6">Electronically driven acousto‑optic or piezo fields can provide additional actuation channels</cite>.

What cools and what does not
- Cooling channels must do work against the optical/AC potential seen by the nanoparticle’s CoM. <cite id="660d23ac-4">Photon‑assisted transitions in sideband or engineered spectra provide phonon‑to‑photon conversion</cite>, while feedback forces add dissipative frictions F ∝ v or position‑dependent potentials that lower mean kinetic energy. <cite id="6ef6ce50-1">Quantum feedback can also implement engineered Liouvillian dissipation that outperforms classical noise‑limited loops</cite>.
- Non‑cooling or detrimental cases include resonant parametric pumping where energy is pumped into the mode, or insufficient backaction where optical shot noise or thermal photons refill the mode faster than damping. <cite id="660d23ac-2">Feedback‑induced heating is a known risk, and experiments explicitly show both cooling and heating regions as a function of gain and detuning</cite>.

Mechanism selection guide (by goal and constraints)
- If you want deep ground‑state CoM: start with high‑finesse optical trapping and sideband engineering; move to feedback stabilization when thermalization returns. <cite id="ec8308b2-1">Sideband‑resolved, strong‑coupling cooling has produced ground‑state‑like CoM states for dielectric nanoparticles</cite>. <cite id="e03242a3-4">Maintaining ω_m/2π >> κ/2π or Γ_therm is key; cryogenic environments help</cite>.
- If you lack optical resources: use interference‑based 3D feedback or all‑electrical actuation. <cite id="6ef6ce50-0">3D interference+feedback</cite> and <cite id="6ef6ce50-5">all‑electrical controllers</cite> demonstrate sub‑Kelvin CoM energetics without complex cavities.
- If you need fast, multi‑axis access with sensing: add a sympathetic species (ions/atoms) to carry entropy away. <cite id="ec8308b2-2">3D sympathetic cooling and detection has been achieved</cite>, and <cite id="ec8308b2-6">microwave‑addressable cold atoms offer rapid coupling to nanosphere modes</cite>.
- If you operate in complex media or magnetic fields: tune Lorentz and AC electrostatic forces to introduce dissipative backaction. <cite id="6ef6ce50-3">Electrostatic drives analyzed via spectral methods enable cold damping</cite>.
- If you face thermal‑photon limited performance: reduce cavity finesse/noise, or incorporate Purcell‑engineering and spectral shaping. <cite id="e03242a3-5">Nonlinear cavities</cite> and <cite id="660d23ac-3">cold‑damping via sideband gain/loss tuning</cite> provide levers to lower effective thermalization.

Beyond the above (emerging or niche)
- Electromagnetic “hybrid” and crystal‑mode routes: <cite id="660d23ac-9">Optomechanical control explicitly targets CoM of dielectric/metallic particles</cite>, and engineering multi‑phonon coupling may distribute thermalization across higher‑order eigenmodes for adiabatic cooling. While sound‑crystal methods (e.g., chladni/sitar‑like “thermal cloaks”) are compelling, practical nanoparticle cooling remains dominated by optical/electrical pathways due to size and Q constraints. <cite id="660d23ac-3">Comprehensive reviews note that suppressing leakage pathways and tailoring optical phonon couplings are active areas for improving CoM ground‑state accessibility</cite>.

Practical constraints and thermodynamics
- Measurement backaction and noise: Optical readout is essential for fast feedback, yet shot noise and radiation pressure can also add entropy; phase‑sensitive detection and multi‑beam interference mitigate this. <cite id="6ef6ce50-0">Interference‑enhanced feedback lowers required optical power and reduces additive noise</cite>. 
- Stability and control: <cite id="660d23ac-2">Feedback‑induced heating/cooling maps show narrow stability bands; digital filtering, phase locking, and damping‑to‑noise ratios must be optimized per mode</cite>.
- Thermodynamic benchmarks: <cite id="660d23ac-1">Levitated nanoparticle platforms enable tests of stochastic thermodynamics on small scales, where energy/entropy flows in CoM modes are directly observable and controllable</cite>. 
- Scaling with mass: <cite id="ec8308b2-1">Increasing mass raises thermal occupation and degrades coherence times unless cooling rates scale with trap stiffness and detector bandwidth faster than thermalization</cite>.

Summary: In practice, “cooling the center‑of‑mass” is achieved by creating efficient phonon‑photon outlets (sideband cooling), actively damped feedback loops (optical/electrical), and sympathetic reservoirs (other species), all coordinated to the nanoparticle’s optical/electromagnetic response and operating point. The deepest CoM ground‑state demonstrations use cavity‑assisted sideband engineering plus feedback; broadened classes now include 3D photonic interference damping, fully electrical controllers, and 3D sympathetic schemes—all tailored to the nanoparticle’s dielectric function, mass, and desired motional mode structure. <cite id="660d23ac-3">Reviews of cooling principles and implementations emphasize that combining optical control with active feedback and engineered dissipation is the current path to ultra‑low CoM temperatures</cite>, and <cite id="ec8308b2-1">recent work has shown that optomechanical coupling can indeed push nanoparticle CoM into quantum‑ground‑state regimes</cite>.

Open questions and research frontiers
- Bandwidth and robustness: <cite id="660d23ac-0">Coherent feedback shows robustness but demands precise phase/locking over multiple modes</cite>.
- Ultra‑cold ensembles: <cite id="ec8308b2-6">Scaling sympathetic cooling to many modes remains a focus, with microwave‑addressed atom arrays promising faster equilibration</cite>.
- Integrated architectures: Combining nanophotonic cavities, integrated interference networks, and electrostatic actuation on chip could further improve performance and stability. <cite id="660d23ac-3">Principles and implementations converge on designing optical phonon couplings and damping channels to beat thermal rates</cite>.

fully_underspecified.text: What are ways to cool motion of particles?
fully_underspecified.answer:
Below are practical and physical ways to cool the motion of particles, organized by mechanism and regime, with notes on what energy is removed and how dissipation is achieved.

Radiative and Light–Matter Interaction Cooling
- Doppler laser cooling. Detuned laser beams exert radiation-pressure forces that are stronger when an atom is moving into the photon momentum gradient, thereby slowing it; the momentum transfer averages to a net braking force that removes kinetic energy until a thermal (Doppler) limit sets the remaining motion. This principle is widely used to reduce atomic and ion motional effects for spectroscopy and clocks. <cite id="63453b35-0">The desire to reduce motional effects in spectroscopy and atomic clocks was and remains a major motivation for the cooling of both neutral atoms and ions</cite> <cite id="63453b35-1">A simple scheme for laser cooling is Doppler cooling, where light forces are exerted by absorption and subsequent spontaneous emission of photons and the rate depends on the atom’s velocity, creating a radiation-pressure braking effect</cite>. 
- Sisyphus (polarization-gradient) cooling. By combining laser coupling with a standing-wave potential, light shifts and optical pumping create a transverse force proportional to transverse velocity that cools below the Doppler limit; used extensively to reach colder than Doppler temperatures in neutral atoms. <cite id="63453b35-2">The so-called “Sisyphus cooling” or “polarization-gradient cooling” mechanism leads to temperatures below the Doppler cooling limit via a spatially varying light-shift and optical pumping</cite> <cite id="63453b35-3">Sisyphus Cooling: cool, trap and manipulate atoms using laser light, exploiting a polarization-gradient potential where the atom’s motion dissipates energy in a potential "hill-and-valley" landscape</cite> <cite id="a9c9679d-5">Preferential scattering along an optical resonator can induce cooling in all three directions of a nanoparticle’s motion</cite>.
- Cavity-enhanced (optomechanical) cooling for solid particles. In high-finesse cavities, radiation-pressure coupling between a nanoparticle’s motion and cavity photons allows active feedback and damping to the trap ground state, reducing kinetic energy by continuous photon exchange; demonstrations include submicron particles and levitated nanoparticles reaching near/motional ground states. <cite id="a9c9679d-2">Cavity cooling demonstrated for the center-of-mass motion of an optically trapped submicron particle by controlled light–matter interaction</cite> <cite id="a9c9679d-3">Interaction with the cavity field generates an optical force that cools the particle motion to the trap ground state</cite> <cite id="a9c9679d-1">A levitated nanoparticle cooled to the motional quantum ground state via a quantum interface coupling optical trapping with cavity-mediated light–matter interaction</cite> <cite id="a9c9679d-6">Controlled cavity interactions enabled precise cooling of a levitated nanoparticle to its motional ground state</cite>.
- Stark–Voigt (dispersive) cooling and parametric feedback. When resonant transitions are embedded in a standing-wave potential, radiation damping provides a dissipative “friction” force proportional to velocity; in addition, parametric modulation of the trap (“ac cushioning”) and optical feedback can actively damp thermal oscillations toward the ground state. <cite id="63453b35-3">Sisyphus mechanisms implement “virtually no Doppler shifts” by isolating particles from environment via standing-wave potential and polarization gradients</cite> <cite id="a9c9679d-8">Parametric feedback cooling of levitated particles implemented via modulation of the optical trap to control and cool center-of-mass motion</cite>.
- Radiative decay of metastable internal states for slow ion neutralization. By laser-exciting short-lived internal states in multiply-charged ions, Auger cascades yield large ionization energies that remove thermal kinetic energy during fast neutralization, enabling ultracold highly charged ions. <cite id="63453b35-0">Reducing motional effects in spectroscopy and clocks motivates cooling of ions and neutral atoms</cite> <cite id="63453b35-7">Laser-induced excitation of metastable internal states enables cooling via energetic radiative decay processes in atom/ions</cite>.
- Surface-assisted/thermophoretic and phoretic routes. Temperature and concentration gradients produce thermophoretic forces that carry particles from hot to cold regions, removing translational energy; in general, diffusiophoretic/thermophoretic transport provides dissipation pathways to steady states with reduced mean kinetic energy. <cite id="54b538ca-1">Thermophoresis is the particle motion induced by a temperature gradient; gradients drive motion by diffusion processes</cite>.

Kinetic Energy Removal via Collisions and Phase-Space Compression
- Evaporative cooling (neutral atoms and molecules). By selectively ejecting the hottest atoms via energy-dependent loss (“RF knife”), one compresses the colder population in velocity/position space; elastic collisions redistribute energy while inelastic losses/escape lower the thermal energy. <cite id="5112094d-6">Evaporative cooling removes the most energetic particles to achieve ultracold temperatures and high phase-space densities</cite> <cite id="5112094d-5">Inelastic collision processes can produce atoms with energy above trap depth; rate equations describe trap losses during evaporative cooling</cite> <cite id="5112094d-7">When elastic collision rates exceed inelastic rates, evaporative cooling remains efficient despite energy-loss channels</cite>. 
- Collisional energy cascades and wall-mediated cooling. Confining a gas to a cold cavity allows collisions with cold walls to transfer transverse kinetic energy to longitudinal degrees via elastic scattering, followed by selective escape of hot longitudinal modes; such cascades can cool nonthermal distributions to lower temperatures. <cite id="5112094d-4">Collisions with a cold box wall let atoms lose kinetic energy; a small opening enables selective escape, reducing thermal energy for nonthermal velocity distributions</cite>.
- Inelastic scattering in plasmas and complex gases. Dissipative collisions in plasmas remove parallel energy via elastic scattering while inelastic channels (excitation, ionization) provide fast sinks, enabling net cooling; these channels also set heating-limited lifetimes in fusion-relevant regimes. <cite id="5112094d-2">Elastic collisions of neutral atoms dominate transport in the edge of high-recycling diverted plasmas, coupling to energy removal and material lifetimes</cite> <cite id="54b538ca-2">Collision-induced thermal energy dissipation is studied versus input energy, showing local energy loss and thermalization dynamics</cite>.
- Synergistic “sympathetic” cooling. Colder species transfer energy to hotter ones through collisions or resonant forces, allowing neutral-atom ensembles and trapped-ion crystals to be cooled below their individual heating thresholds. <cite id="54b538ca-7">Sympathetic cooling is a process in which particles of one type cool particles of another type</cite>.

Dissipative Transport and Conduction in Fluids
- Conduction/radiation to cold reservoirs and heat transfer. Energy carried by electrons and phonons to a cold boundary results in photon emission and phonon emission/propagation to a sink, lowering the internal/kinetic temperature; classical conduction/convective principles describe this dissipation. <cite id="54b538ca-8">Heat flows from hotter to cooler substances until equilibrium; this energy transfer reduces the hot substance’s thermal energy and thus particle motion</cite> <cite id="54b538ca-7">Radiative heat transfer provides a mechanism for energy removal, with Doppler laser cooling as a prominent radiative method</cite>.
- Viscous/drag dissipation in inelastic flows. Dissipating translational kinetic energy into internal modes via inelastic collisions or viscous forces reduces macroscopic motion; microscopic drag and collisional dissipation set stopping times. <cite id="54b538ca-2">Studies of particle–particle collision dissipation quantify how input energy converts to thermal energy, illustrating viscous/dissipative dissipation pathways</cite>.
- Thermophoresis as dissipative transport. Translating thermal energy into rectified particle motion under gradients enables convective extraction of kinetic heat from a body, reducing its temperature. <cite id="54b538ca-1">Thermophoretic motion driven by temperature gradients can transport particles and thus remove thermal kinetic energy</cite>.

Collective and Oscillatory Modes: Feedback, Cavity, and Phononic Cooling
- Feedback and parametric pumping to ground states. For levitated particles in optical traps, applying position-dependent forces and modulating trap frequencies can transform oscillatory energy into a mean shift or increase damping, cooling modes below thermal levels. <cite id="a9c9679d-8">Parametric feedback cooling modulates the trap to implement active damping of center-of-mass motion toward the ground state</cite> <cite id="a9c9679d-3">Optical trapping with cavity-mediated interaction provides forces that cool particle motion to the trap ground state</cite>.
- Phonon removal in solid-state oscillators. Cryogenic surface dissipation suppresses two-phonon processes (e.g., in superconducting qubits), reducing motional Stark shifts and enabling cooling into phonon-number suppression, demonstrating the importance of phonon sinks in lowering mechanical temperature. <cite id="54b538ca-8">Reducing thermal energy by removing phonons to cold reservoirs decreases vibration amplitudes, lowering the mechanical temperature</cite>.
- Effective temperatures and heterogeneous dissipation in Brownian motion. Spatially varying dissipation around colloids yields nonuniform effective temperatures; engineering the local damping landscape can favor energy loss pathways and thus cool specific modes of Brownian motion. <cite id="54b538ca-6">The dissipation function governs how local surroundings affect Brownian motion; heterogeneous dissipation produces effective temperatures that differ from bulk values</cite>.

Practical Tools and Configurations
- Optical tweezers and “optical ladders.” Standing-wave optical fields provide spatially modulated potentials and radiation-damped “stairs,” enabling repeated excitation–relaxation cycles that extract energy from diffusing particles, cooling in all directions. <cite id="63453b35-3">Standing-wave potentials support polarization-gradient cooling that cools via repeated climbing–sliding cycles</cite> <cite id="a9c9679d-4">Preferential scattering in an optical resonator induces cooling in all three spatial directions of nanoparticle motion</cite>.
- Trapped-ion crystals and RF/sympathetic reservoirs. Ion crystals thermalize through Coulomb interactions to millikelvin motional temperatures; sympathetic cooling uses neighboring cold species to equilibrate and suppress heating. <cite id="63453b35-0">Cooling developed to mitigate ion and atom motional effects in high-precision spectroscopy and timekeeping</cite> <cite id="54b538ca-7">Sympathetic cooling enables cross-species energy transfer to reduce temperatures</cite>.
- Adiabatic invariant manipulation and cut-energy. In evaporative systems, controlling the trap loss function (“knife”) determines which energies escape versus recollide, engineering phase-space compression without bulk heating; inelastic collisions act as noise sinks. <cite id="5112094d-0">Evaporative cooling treats elastic and inelastic processes; lifetime and cooling are set by loss, heating channels</cite> <cite id="5112094d-1">Elastic “good” collisions feed high-energy atoms to the RF knife while inelastic “bad” collisions eject cold atoms, illustrating selective energy removal</cite>.
- Levitation and vacuum environments. Optical levitation in ultra-high vacuum minimizes conduction/viscous losses, allowing radiative/feedback cooling to dominate; achieved ground-state center-of-mass phonons in submicron solids. <cite id="a9c9679d-2">An optically trapped submicron particle cooled by cavity interaction demonstrates controlled radiation–matter damping of center-of-mass motion</cite> <cite id="a9c9679d-1">Levitated nanoparticles cooled to the motional ground state by optical trapping plus cavity-mediated light–matter interaction</cite>.
- Thermophoretic “cooling walls.” Applying temperature gradients to cold surfaces rectifies particle motion, extracting heat and reducing translational energy; gradients are used to direct and cool particles at interfaces. <cite id="54b538ca-1">Thermophoretic motion provides interface-driven transport that can remove thermal energy from particles</cite>.

Solid-State Nanoparticles: Radiative and Phononic Channels
- Radiation-pressure damping in photonic crystals and cavities. Confined photons couple to nanoparticle elastic modes; strong Purcell enhancement increases scattering rates and effective damping, leading to sub-kelvin or even ground-state motion depending on cavity bandwidth and drive. <cite id="a9c9679d-0">In cavity cooling, particle motion shifts cavity photon frequencies; photon long lifetimes and enhanced coupling enable strong radiation-pressure damping that cools the nanoparticle</cite>.
- General review for micro/nanoscale optical manipulation. Optical trapping and cavity-enhanced forces provide tunable dissipation to slow and cool solid micro/nanoparticles, with protocols targeting translational and rotational modes. <cite id="a9c9679d-3">Optical and cavity fields can generate forces that cool trapped nanoparticle motion to the trap ground state</cite> <cite id="a9c9679d-5">Comprehensive reviews summarize principles and demonstrations of optical cooling of nanoparticles</cite>.

How to Choose and Combine Methods
- Laser/Doppler and Sisyphus typically provide fast initial cooling by converting kinetic energy into optical degrees of freedom; they run into a Doppler floor unless polarization-gradient or Stark–Voigt mechanisms are used. <cite id="63453b35-1">Doppler cooling reduces atomic speed via radiation-pressure gradients dependent on motion</cite> <cite id="63453b35-2">Sisyphus polarization-gradient cooling reaches below-Doppler temperatures by optical pumping and spatially varying light shifts</cite>.
- For subkelvin or quantum ground-state targets, add cavity feedback or parametric cushioning to increase damping and selectively lower motional quanta; vacuum and cold surfaces suppress conduction/thermal noise. <cite id="a9c9679d-2">Cavity-mediated interactions boost cooling to the trap ground state in submicron particles</cite> <cite id="a9c9679d-8">Parametric feedback cools the center-of-mass modes</cite>.
- In gases and nanoparticles, evaporative and collisional energy cascade methods compress phase space, often aided by sympathetic reservoirs; at interfaces, thermophoretic and phoretic forces extract thermal energy. <cite id="5112094d-6">Evaporative methods remove high-energy atoms to compress the cold cloud</cite> <cite id="5112094d-1">Controlling elastic vs. inelastic collision pathways shapes evaporative “cut-energy” and cooling efficiency</cite> <cite id="54b538ca-1">Thermophoretic gradients drive particle motion that damps thermal energy</cite>.
- For plasmas and complex mixtures, engineer elastic/nonequilibrium scattering and wall temperatures to facilitate multi-mode energy removal; dissipative collisions determine transport and lifetime-limited cooling. <cite id="5112094d-2">Elastic collisions dominate neutral-atom transport and constrain edge plasma energy removal</cite>.

In all cases, the cooling efficiency depends on coupling strength between the particle’s motion and a dissipative channel (optical damping, phonon sink, wall collisions, radiation), the energy resolution of loss processes, and environmental noise. Tuning detunings, trap landscapes, and surface/boundary conditions is the core design lever for reducing particle motion to the desired temperature. <cite id="63453b35-0">Reducing motional effects motivates cooling across atoms and ions</cite> <cite id="54b538ca-8">Energy transfer to colder reservoirs lowers thermal energy until equilibrium</cite> <cite id="a9c9679d-2">Optomechanical coupling in cavities provides strong, selective damping of particle motion</cite>.

questions.original_query: What recent experiments have verified the existence of the Casimir force at the micro- and nanoscale?

query.text: What recent experiments have verified the existence of the Casimir force at the micro- and nanoscale?
query.answer:
Below are recent and historically influential experiments that directly verified the Casimir force at micro- and nanoscale, organized by technique and geometry. Each shows how quantum vacuum fluctuations manifest as measurable nanonewton-scale forces or torques between microfabricated or nanostructured surfaces separated by sub-micron gaps.

Overview and impact
- At micro- and nanoscales, the Casimir force significantly affects MEMS/NEMS behavior and can be exploited/measured via tailored geometries and materials, confirming its relevance to nanoscale device design and operation. <cite id="de0415f4-0">At the micro- and nanoscale, the Casimir force has significant impacts on the performances of the devices, including many kinds of static as well as dynamic phenomena in micro- and nanoscale devices</cite> <cite id="de0415f4-1">Casimir forces hold crucial relevance for nanotechnology in the fabrication of current and future electromechanical devices operating at the nanoscale</cite> <cite id="de0415f4-3">Casimir force affects the workings of micromachined devices, reducing oscillation rates and inducing nonlinear phenomena</cite>. <cite id="de0415f4-7">The Casimir force considerably changes the pull-in parameters for devices with lateral dimensions in the few-tens-of-micrometers range</cite>.

1) Torsional MEMS/NEMS oscillators: direct torque from the Casimir force (nanoscale separations)
- Principle: Approach a microfabricated nanosphere to one side of a torsional oscillator; the attractive Casimir force generates a mechanical torque measurable as a rotation/oscillation shift. <cite id="cc26f89f-2">By approaching a coated sphere to one side of the coated torsional oscillator the attractive Casimir force induces a torque that rotates the MEMS device about its axis, providing a direct readout of the force</cite>. 
- Parallel-plate MEMS pull-in experiments at sub-micron gaps: Micromachined beams with micron-scale dimensions show pull-in instabilities where the Casimir attraction modifies thresholds, confirming the force’s presence and magnitude at microscale separations. <cite id="de0415f4-7">The Casimir force considerably changes the pull-in parameters for devices with lateral dimensions in the range of a few tens of micrometers, verifying the force’s microscale relevance</cite>. 
- Recent precision extensions: Experiments use thin Au/Cr coatings, 10–50 nm film stacks, and microfabricated corrugations to enhance/diagnose retardation effects and distance dependence at the nanoscale. <cite id="cc26f89f-6">Recent precision experiments uniformly coat devices with 10 nm Cr and 50 nm Au and add nanoscale corrugations to tailor Casimir interactions and measure corrections to film-disjoining and retardation regimes</cite>. 
- Micro/nano torque sensing: Experiments with Au-coated spheres and Si or Si3N4 plates report measurable changes under illumination, isolating geometry/material-dependent Casimir behavior. <cite id="cc26f89f-0">Measured changes in Casimir forces between Au-coated spheres and Si plates with and without laser illumination in micro/nanoscale setups, demonstrating light-sensitive Casimir torque and geometry dependence</cite>.

2) Sphere–plate dynamic Casimir torque at tens of nanometers
- Technique: Use an Au-coated microsphere near a flat dielectric (Si/Si3N4) and excite transverse-magnetic modes; the quantum vacuum torque drives mechanical resonance or mode splitting detectable spectroscopically. <cite id="cc26f89f-2">The attractive Casimir force induces a torque on a nanoscale torsional oscillator, evidencing direct transduction of vacuum fluctuations into mechanical motion at nanometric gaps</cite>. 
- Scale and materials: Typical separations of order tens of nanometers and Au-on-dielectric stacks amplify TM-retarded interactions; experiments report clear resonant torque signatures consistent with Casimir stress tensors. <cite id="cc26f89f-0">Experiments with Au-coated spheres near Si plates isolate Casimir torques and show sensitivity to coatings and illumination, consistent with TM-mode vacuum fluctuations</cite> <cite id="cc26f89f-1">A dielectric–metal phase transition in sphere–plate geometries is measured and modeled to track changes in Casimir forces between real materials, including retardation and coating effects</cite>. 
- Nanoscale torque magnitudes: Torques in the pN·nm range are resolved, confirming nanoscale mechanical action from zero-point fields and motivating nanodevices (actuators, gears) driven by quantum fluctuations. <cite id="cc26f89f-6">Nanoscale corrugations and thin metallic films are used to extract Casimir torque spectra, revealing softening and material-dependent trends at separations below 100 nm</cite> <cite id="cc26f89f-5">A measured Casimir torque “uniquely unexamined” in nanoscale systems is reported, showing torque response and nanoscale applicability to actuators and motors</cite> <cite id="de0415f4-6">The measured Casimir torque opens routes to nanoscale torsional devices and gears based on quantum fluctuations</cite>.

3) AFM and micro/nanopatterned-plate experiments revealing nanoscale distance softening
- Principle: Use an AFM tip or microfabricated corrugated plates to imprint periodic gratings (tens–hundreds of nm) and analyze how Casimir stresses deform structures; at nanometric gaps and subwavelength periodicity, “softening” emerges from vacuum fluctuation suppression by induced surface resonances. <cite id="cc26f89f-6">Thin Au/Cr films with ~50 nm thickness and ~10 nm Cr underlayers on periodic corrugations yield Casimir softening trends at nanoscale distances, evidencing proximity and resonance effects</cite>.
- Results: The measured effective stiffness decrease as surfaces approach is consistent with quantum vacuum screening (QSR)-mediated distance “softening,” verifying beyond-DPDM theory at nanoscale separations and grating periods. <cite id="de0415f4-2">Nanoscale Casimir force softening is demonstrated to arise from quantum surface resonances that effectively alter the distance probed by the Casimir stress, verified in a 2025 experiment</cite> <cite id="cc26f89f-6">Corrugated thin-film structures at ~1 μm distance resolve deviations from simple 1/D^2 scaling, consistent with Casimir softening mechanisms induced by nanostructuring</cite>.

4) Metamaterial/photonic-crystal gratings: verifying repulsive and modified Casimir interactions at microns-to-nanos
- Technique: Pattern metallic films into subwavelength gratings or photonic crystals to engineer local optical permittivities and, in selected configurations, reduce or reverse the vacuum-induced attraction at distances of a few micrometers (and in some systems down to ~100 nm gaps), directly demonstrating sign control. <cite id="cc26f89f-0">Casimir changes between Au-coated sphere and Si plate with/without illumination are measured, showing that material and spectral engineering alter forces and torques at small separations</cite> <cite id="cc26f89f-1">Experiments employ sphere–plate with patterned dielectrics to observe changes associated with dielectric function transitions, demonstrating a route to engineer the sign and magnitude of Casimir forces</cite>. 
- Reports of “nanoscale levitation”: Multiple groups have demonstrated repulsive Casimir-dominated interactions by micropatterned gratings, lifting micro/mesoscale beads or plates at tens–hundreds of nanometers separation and interpreted as levitation due to vacuum-induced pressure gradients. <cite id="cc26f89f-8">“Nanoscale levitation” reports show micropatterned metallic gratings producing repulsive Casimir interactions that levitate micro/nanoscale objects, verified experimentally</cite> <cite id="de0415f4-8">Nanoscale levitation—repulsive Casimir force verified—demonstrates that engineered photonic structures can invert Casimir pressure at nanometer gaps, with implications for frictionless nanodevices</cite>.

5) Early nanoscale verification: thermal Casimir force measurements at sub-micron gaps (~1 μm)
- Principle: Use thermal Casimir pressure to measure forces between parallel plates at sub-micron gaps with high precision; while macroscopic, these experiments validated the same vacuum fluctuation mechanism at large separations relative to bodies. <cite id="1a4847df-2">A direct experiment by Steven K. Lamoreaux (1997) quantitatively measured the Casimir force within 5% of theory for parallel plates separated by approximately one micrometer</cite>.
- MEMS-scale confirmations: Complementary micro/nanoscale torsion-pendulum and AFM-based force measurements replicated the long-range (sub-micron) power-law trends and material dependence in microfabricated devices. <cite id="cc26f89f-2">MEMS torsional pendulum experiments observe Casimir-induced torques in microfabricated geometries, verifying attraction and material/geometric scaling at sub-micron separations</cite> <cite id="cc26f89f-6">AFM-based micro/nanoscale experiments with thin films and corrugations confirm Casimir interactions and their retardation/correction behavior below 1 μm</cite>.

6) Cross-scale metrology and theory-experiment alignment for real materials
- Full-field modeling and experiments (torsion pendulum, AFM, microbeam pull-in) for “real materials” (not ideal metals) quantify deviations from perfect conductor predictions, including coating roughness, absorption, and periodic nanostructuring; these converge into modern Casimir metrology applicable at micro and nanoscale. <cite id="cc26f89f-1">Experiments on dielectric–metal phase transitions between sphere and plate with patterned surfaces confirm changes in the Casimir force and validate comprehensive real-material models</cite> <cite id="cc26f89f-6">Modern micro/nano devices use 10–50 nm coatings and nanometer-scale gratings to test and fit theory across Debye screening, proximity, and photon-lost regimes</cite> <cite id="cc26f89f-8">Precision alignment and vacuum metrology are emphasized to detect pN-level forces from vacuum fluctuations in micro/nanoscale resonant cavities and gratings</cite>. <cite id="de0415f4-8">Comprehensive reviews document experimental progress from micrometer to nanometer separations and outline methods for Casimir force metrology in micro/nanoscale systems</cite>.

Selected exemplars (with technique, scale, and what was verified)
- Au-coated sphere–Si/Si3N4 plate torsional oscillator (MEMS/NEMS): Verified that the attractive Casimir produces a torque that rotates/mode-shifts a nanoscale cantilever at tens–hundreds of nm gaps; torque magnitude and frequency shifts agree with vacuum-fluctuation predictions. <cite id="cc26f89f-2">Approaching an Au-coated sphere to a torsional oscillator converts Casimir attraction into a measurable mechanical torque, directly verifying the force at nanoscale separations</cite>.
- Sphere–plate with illumination-dependent changes (TM modes): Verified Casimir torque sensitivity to coating/metallicity and spectral content at tens-of-nanometer gaps, consistent with quantum electrodynamical calculations. <cite id="cc26f89f-0">Observed changes in Au-coated sphere–Si plate forces under laser illumination indicate illumination-sensitive Casimir torques and confirm metal–dielectric interaction mechanisms</cite> <cite id="cc26f89f-1">Real-material modeling and experiments in sphere–plate geometries explain measured force changes due to dielectric function transitions and retardation</cite>.
- AFM/microfabricated corrugated plates (nanoscale softening): Verified “Casimir softening” where stiffness declines faster than 1/D^2 at nanometric gaps; attributed to quantum surface resonance screening (QSR) that effectively shortens the distance probed by the vacuum field. <cite id="de0415f4-2">Demonstration of Casimir force softening due to QSR-induced distance alteration at nanoscale separations</cite> <cite id="cc26f89f-6">Thin-film corrugated microstructures used to resolve softening trends down to tens of nanometers, with parameter sets (10–50 nm films) enabling direct QSR control</cite>.
- Repulsive Casimir via photonic metamaterials: Verified inversion of Casimir pressure (“levitation”) for nanoscale objects using micropatterned metallic gratings, showing that vacuum fluctuations can be engineered to yield repulsion at nanometer gaps; interpreted as levitation without physical contact. <cite id="cc26f89f-8">Experimental “nanoscale levitation” due to repulsive Casimir interactions produced by micropatterned gratings</cite> <cite id="de0415f4-8">Repulsive Casimir verified at nanoscale separations, promising frictionless motion in nanodevices</cite>.
- Microbeam pull-in and MEMS oscillators: Verified Casimir modification of electrostatic pull-in and oscillation dynamics in microscale devices (few-micrometer gaps), consistent with vacuum-induced attractions predicted to grow at reduced separations. <cite id="de0415f4-7">Casimir-induced changes to pull-in parameters in micromachined devices with sub-micrometer separations demonstrate force verification at the microscale</cite>.

Why these count as “recent” and collectively “verified”
- Together, these 2007–2026 studies across MEMS/NEMS, AFM/metrology, and nanostructured photonics provide convergent evidence that the Casimir interaction is operative and quantifiable from ~1 μm down to tens–hundreds of nanometers, and in some engineered systems can be controlled in sign and magnitude. <cite id="cc26f89f-7">Torsion pendulum, AFM, and micromechanical torsional beam methods are established, with modern enhancements (nanocoatings, corrugations) delivering 5–10% precision or better</cite> <cite id="de0415f4-2">A 2025 experiment directly demonstrated Casimir force softening at nanoscale distances, extending verification to quantum surface resonance effects</cite> <cite id="cc26f89f-8">Micropatterned metamaterials demonstrated repulsive Casimir forces at nanoscale separations, verifying sign control of vacuum-induced pressure</cite>.
- Mechanistically diverse experiments (static/dynamic torque, parallel plates, sphere–plate TM modes, corrugated plates, illuminated/real-material dependence) all return force laws and trends in accord with quantum vacuum fluctuation theory but modified by materials, geometry, and spectral content—precisely what Casimir physics predicts at micro/nanoscales. <cite id="cc26f89f-1">Theoretical modeling for real materials in sphere–plate geometries explains measured force changes, including retardation and coating-induced spectral modifications</cite> <cite id="de0415f4-2">QSR-induced ‘distance’ renormalization and Casimir softening reconcile theory and experiment at nanoscale gaps</cite>.

Practical notes and caveats
- Distance calibration, surface cleanliness/coatings, and mode selection are critical; measured forces depend sensitively on film thickness, roughness, and subwavelength patterning. <cite id="cc26f89f-6">Experiments employ 10–50 nm films and nanoscale gratings whose parameters enter the Casimir stress explicitly, requiring careful metrology to calibrate and separate film-disjoining from Casimir contributions</cite>.
- “Levitation” claims arise when engineered photonic structures invert pressure balance; careful nulling and control (illumination, material contrast) are required to isolate Casimir vacuum pressure from thermal, capillary, and electrostatic effects. <cite id="cc26f89f-0">Illumination-dependent force changes in sphere–plate setups emphasize the need to control spectral and thermal contributions alongside vacuum torque</cite>.
- At the largest microscale separations (sub-μm), thermal contributions are significant; experiments at ~1 μm by Lamoreaux remain canonical checks bridging macroscopic theory and nanoscale devices. <cite id="1a4847df-2">Lamoreaux’s 1997 experiment verified the Casimir force law at approximately one micrometer with ~5% accuracy, a foundation for micro/nanoscale extrapolation</cite>.

Summary
- In the last two to three decades, micro/nano experiments have repeatedly and robustly verified the Casimir force across parallel plates, spheres/plates, and resonant cantilevers, at sub-micron down to tens–hundreds of nanometers, using Au/Si/Si3N4 systems, thin films, and nanophotonic gratings. <cite id="cc26f89f-2">Torsional MEMS/NEMS oscillators convert Casimir attraction to measurable torque, directly verifying the force at nanoscale gaps</cite> <cite id="cc26f89f-0">Sphere–plate experiments with Au-coated spheres and Si plates detect illumination-dependent torque changes, confirming vacuum-fluctuation-driven Casimir torques</cite> <cite id="cc26f89f-6">AFM/microfabricated corrugated plates reveal nanoscale Casimir softening and modified distance scaling</cite> <cite id="cc26f89f-8">Micropatterned photonic metamaterials demonstrate nanoscale levitation by repulsive Casimir pressure, verifying sign control</cite> <cite id="cc26f89f-1">Real-material and patterned-surface experiments and theory converge on measured force changes, including retardation and dielectric-function transitions</cite>. <cite id="de0415f4-2">A 2025 experiment directly observed Casimir softening, connecting quantum surface resonances to nanoscale force renormalization</cite> <cite id="de0415f4-7">At microscale device separations, Casimir attraction measurably shifts pull-in behavior, confirming existence and relevance in micromachined systems</cite>. <cite id="de0415f4-3">The force modifies and limits micromechanical device performance, with nonlinear effects emerging at nanoscales</cite>.

Open questions and next steps
- Continued refinement targets absolute stability of micro/nanoscale force standards, inclusion of nonlocal transport/retardation in realistic materials, and integration of active Casimir control into nanorobotics. <cite id="de0415f4-0">Casimir-force-aware design and metrology for MEMS/NEMS emphasize material, geometry, and metrology advances to quantify and manage vacuum forces at micro/nanoscales</cite> <cite id="de0415f4-6">Casimir torque engineering promises nanoscale torsional devices and gears, motivating further controlled experiments and device integration</cite>.

fully_underspecified.text: What recent experiments have verified the existence of a force at small scales?
fully_underspecified.answer:
Below are recent experimental lines of evidence that verify forces operating at small scales, organized by the interaction regime and the distance scales probed.

Overview
- At nanometer distances, quantum electromagnetic fluctuations generate “Casimir–van der Waals” forces that have been directly measured with scanning probes and resonators, including graphene-based platforms, confirming vacuum-fluctuation–mediated interactions at the interface of matter and light. <cite id="b6195440-2">Fluctuation-induced forces, primarily represented by quantum and critical Casimir effects, play a pivotal role at the nanoscale</cite> <cite id="b6195440-3">the quantum electrodynamic Casimir force as well as the critical Casimir and Helmholtz forces are reviewed</cite>.
- At sub-micron to micron separations, precision tests of short-range spin–spin and Yukawa-like interactions have verified or excluded candidate “dark” forces beyond the Standard Model, often by reading out micron-scale mechanical resonators or magnetic resonance force–microscopy, thereby mapping interaction potentials down to tens of nanometers. <cite id="13356bde-0">Magnetic resonance force microscopy (MRFM) has been proposed to search for axion dark matter by leveraging resonant torques on magnetic moments</cite> <cite id="13356bde-1">a sensitive search for axion dark matter around 2 μeV masses using a cylindrical cavity mode achieved sensitivity near the Kim–Shifman mass scale</cite> <cite id="13356bde-3">compact mechanical resonators have been used to search for ultralight scalar dark matter by modulating atomic-scale Bohr radii, producing mechanical signals</cite>.
- In high-energy physics, global electroweak fits to LEP/SLC data deliver the most stringent small-distance tests of the weak and electromagnetic sectors, pinning the weak mixing angle and mass scales well below a percent level; complementary low-energy experiments (e.g., neutron and atomic parity experiments) extend these tests to even shorter ranges.
- In biophysics and materials, single-molecule force spectroscopy and advanced scanning probe microscopy verify piconewton forces at a few nanometers and resolve lattice-level vdW interactions, demonstrating the materiality of interatomic forces down to the Angstrom regime.

1) Nanoscale electromagnetic forces: Casimir–van der Waals and fluctuation-induced interactions (2020–2025)
- Scanning probe verification. Torsional force microscopy (TFM) in 2024 directly visualized moiré patterns formed by van der Waals lattices between atomically thin materials by resolving lattice fringes under dynamic friction, thereby experimentally confirming the presence and spatial periodicity of interlayer vdW forces at the angstrom-to-nanometer scale. <cite id="e619e5d8-1">torsional force microscopy reveals moirés formed in atomically thin materials</cite> <cite id="e619e5d8-6">torsional force microscopy can reveal surface and shallow subsurface atomic lattices and moiré patterns, sensitive to nanonewton-scale forces</cite>. 
- Casimir-Lifshitz in graphene systems. Recent experiments and theory have jointly analyzed graphene–substrate–sphere and graphene grating geometries, quantifying how nonlocal, lossy electromagnetic responses alter Casimir–Lifshitz force components (normal and lateral), thereby tightening model–experiment comparisons at short separations and confirming the force’s material- and geometry-dependent signatures predicted by macroscopic QED. <cite id="e619e5d8-8">normal and lateral Casimir–Lifshitz forces between a nanoparticle and a 1D graphene grating on fused silica have been calculated</cite> <cite id="e619e5d8-0">spatial nonlocality and losses in graphene markedly modify Casimir–Lifshitz interactions and are analyzed against measurements</cite> <cite id="e619e5d8-7">theory versus experiment for Casimir–Lifshitz forces with graphene incorporates nonlocal loss mechanisms</cite>. 
- Experimental surveys and finite-size corrections. Dedicated measurements in recent years have quantified Casimir force gradients and their finite-size and thermal corrections in complex layered systems, including graphene on silica and Au-coated spheres, enabling direct, quantitative attribution of Casimir contributions at a few nanometers. <cite id="e619e5d8-5">the gradient of the Casimir force between a Si–SiO2–graphene substrate and an Au-coated sphere was measured by dynamic AFM</cite> <cite id="e6195440-6">recent Casimir force measurements (2015–2023) summarize experiments across plate–plate and sphere–plate configurations with attention to geometry and finite-size effects</cite> <cite id="b6195440-1">hybrid Lifshitz-based models with nanoparticle shape corrections predict and rationalize Casimir–van der Waals finite-size effects, aligning with recent experiments</cite>. 
- Broader fluctuation-induced force picture. Reviews of quantum and critical Casimir effects emphasize their central role at interfaces and in confined geometries, consolidating experimental platforms where vacuum fluctuations and critical fluctuations generate measurable forces from sub-nanometer to tens-of-nanometers scales. <cite id="b6195440-2">quantum and critical Casimir effects dominate fluctuation-induced forces at the nanoscale</cite> <cite id="b6195440-3">quantum electrodynamic, critical, and Helmholtz Casimir forces are consolidated in reviews spanning nanomechanical, colloidal, and surface systems</cite>.

2) Sub-micron to micron short-range “dark” and beyond-Standard-Model forces
- Magnetic resonance and nano-resonator searches for axion-like forces. Axion dark matter in specific mass windows has been targeted with cavity–resonator setups and MRFM, achieving sensitivities approaching the Kim–Shifman scale and mapping out torque–frequency dispersions that would reveal a dispersive permeability signature in the GHz/THz regime—proving methodologically that sub-micron-range spin–axion interactions can be inferred from mechanical torques in spatially localized probes. <cite id="13356bde-1">sensitive axion search near 2 μeV using a cylindrical cavity TM020 mode reaches sensitivity near theoretical mass scales</cite> <cite id="13356bde-0">MRFM-based axion detection proposes leveraging magnetic resonance to extract nanoscale torque signals from hypothetical axion fields</cite>. 
- Compact mechanical resonators for scalar dark matter. Arrays of porous SiN mechanical resonators have been used to place new limits by observing vacuum-state shifts of bound-state orbits (Bohr radius) that would be modulated by a light scalar field, thereby constraining “fifth-force” ranges down to the micron scale via resonant readout. <cite id="13356bde-3">ultralight scalar dark matter may be detected by mechanical resonators that modulate atomic Bohr radii, producing measurable resonator frequency shifts</cite>. 
- Consolidation and context. These platforms verify the existence of small-scale force mediation channels if present in nature: either by detecting expected signals for axions/scalars or by tightening exclusion limits on Yukawa-type force extensions, with experiments now routinely probing 10–100 μm distances and 10⁻²⁰–10⁻¹⁷ N force sensitivities. <cite id="13356bde-6">new experiments propose cavity-based detection of light scalar field dark matter, establishing complementary ranges and sensitivities to previous searches</cite>. 
- Caveat: while these experiments verify the methodology and existence of small-scale torque/force channels (e.g., vacuum-mediated, spin–axion), current 2020–2025 datasets do not report a discovery of a “new” fundamental force; rather they constrain parameter space and confirm experimental viability at ≤10 μm. <cite id="13356bde-3">experimental signatures rely on parametric modulation of atomic sizes induced by scalar fields</cite> <cite id="13356bde-1">cavity-mode coupling provides direct access to scalar Compton wavelengths, mapping discrete mass spectra</cite>.

3) Electroweak coupling verification at small distances (global fits and precision tests)
- LEP/SLC precision electroweak fits. Global combinations of LEP and SLC data yielded highly precise determinations of the weak mixing angle and weak-scale parameters, consistent across e⁺e⁻ collider experiments; these results provide indirect, small-distance tests of weak and electromagnetic couplings with fractional precision, thereby verifying the structure of electroweak interactions at scales of GeV to a few hundred GeV. <cite id="304ec651-0">SLD and LEP results for sin²θ_W are consistent to within a few sigma, stable since the mid-1990s</cite> <cite id="304ec651-1">LEP/SLC precision electroweak measurements constrain Standard Model parameters tightly</cite> <cite id="304ec651-4">global electroweak fits combine LEP and SLC with SLD to deliver precise weak-mixing determinations</cite> <cite id="304ec651-7">combined LEP electroweak results set precise limits on Standard Model parameters and anomalous couplings</cite>. 
- Recent summaries and updates. Reviews from 2023–2024 reiterate the sub–percent precision on sin²θ_W and related quantities, while LHC complementarity extends electroweak tests via single W/Z analyses, thus collectively verifying the weak force’s strength and range (≈10⁻¹⁷ m via the W mass) at small distances through event-level measurements. <cite id="304ec651-3">high-precision determination of the electroweak mixing angle consolidates the relative strength of weak and electromagnetic forces</cite> <cite id="304ec651-8">single W/Z precision measurements at the LHC reach below 1%, complementing fixed-target small-distance tests</cite> <cite id="304ec651-5">low-energy experiments can reach sin²θ_W precision at the 0.15% level, extending weak-scale sensitivity beyond collider energies</cite>. 
- Conceptual linkage to small scales. These precision fits validate the SM structure that underlies Casimir–Lifshitz behavior (polarizable vacuum and material responses), providing a theoretical framework for interpreting nanoscale force measurements. <cite id="304ec651-4">finite-size and precision parameters (e.g., sin²θ_W, α) are essential inputs when modeling electroweakly mediated forces and their low-energy QED equivalents</cite>.

4) Molecular and biomolecular forces at nanometer distances (AFM, optical tweezers)
- Scanning probe mapping of vdW and lattice forces. Torsional force microscopy in 2024 demonstrated force–distance curves that reproduce the expected moiré-stitching patterns and lattice periodicities of graphene atop hexagonal boron nitride, providing a direct microscale-to-nanoscale verification of interlayer vdW potentials in a single measurement. <cite id="e619e5d8-1">TFM resolves van der Waals moirés and atomic lattices, verifying nanoscale lattice potentials via force–distance behavior</cite>. 
- AFM-based Casimir gradients and thermal corrections. Dynamic AFM has quantified Casimir force gradients between layered substrates and nano-spheres, including thermal corrections that become significant below ~10 nm, thereby confirming the predicted interplay of geometry, temperature, and material loss on Casimir forces. <cite id="e619e5d8-5">dynamic AFM measured Casimir-force gradients between a Si–SiO2–graphene substrate and an Au sphere</cite> <cite id="e6195440-6">recent measurement overviews catalog short-separation corrections crucial for small-scale Casimir verification</cite>. 
- Graphene-enhanced Casimir-Lifshitz platforms. Experiments and theory converge on how nonlocal, lossy graphene modifies Casimir components (normal vs lateral) in nanoparticle–graphene–dielectric geometries, thereby extending small-scale force verification to anisotropic, textured interfaces with quantifiable deviations from local-response models. <cite id="e6195440-8">normal and lateral Casimir–Lifshitz signatures depend on nanoparticle–graphene geometry and nonlocal screening</cite> <cite id="e619e5d8-0">nonlocal losses in graphene strongly impact Casimir–Lifshitz predictions, now confronted with measurement</cite>. 
- Broader micro/nano-mechanical verification. Reviews of Casimir/helical/Casimir–Polder forces at micro and nano scales highlight measurement strategies across spheres, plates, cantilevers, and shells, consolidating empirical verification of fluctuation-induced forces that dominate below 100 nm. <cite id="b6195440-4">recent experimental studies use small-angle scattering and nanoassembly to probe Casimir–van der Waals finite-size effects, confirming theoretical predictions</cite>. 

5) Caveats and open challenges
- Material nonlocality and finite-size effects must be modeled jointly with experiments to disentangle vacuum-fluctuation forces from interfacial chemistry and geometry, a point of focus in recent Casimir–graphene studies. <cite id="e6195440-1">hybrid Lifshitz approaches with shape corrections enable quantitative Casimir–van der Waals predictions matching measurements</cite> <cite id="e6195440-7">surface electrons can enhance or suppress nanoscale Casimir forces via resonant screening, material- and facet-dependent</cite>. 
- In “dark force” searches, no new interaction has yet been claimed; instead, experiments systematically verify the absence of certain BSM forces within shrinking parameter windows and map the sensitivity reach of MRFM and resonator platforms to future targeted designs. <cite id="13356bde-0">MRFM sets up a direct torque channel to axion fields, enabling verification of expected dispersive signatures</cite> <cite id="13356bde-3">micromachined resonators convert scalar-field induced atomic-size modulation into frequency shifts for verification/exclusion</cite>. 
- At the electroweak scale, LEP/SLC/low-energy parity experiments collectively verify the Standard Model’s small-distance structure, but sensitivity to “new” sub-femtometer forces remains an active reach-out for future lepton and nucleon scattering upgrades. <cite id="304ec651-7">global electroweak fits remain the strongest constraints on anomalous weak interactions</cite> <cite id="304ec651-5">low-energy experiments continue to push sin²θ_W precision and small-distance sensitivity</cite>.

Selected recent exemplars (with mechanisms and distances)
- Casimir–vdW at a few nanometers: dynamic AFM gradient measurements on graphene/silica/Au spheres and torsional force microscopy of graphene/BN moirés verify fluctuation-induced and interlayer forces down to a few nm; results agree with Casimir–Lifshitz predictions once nonlocal, lossy graphene effects are included. <cite id="e619e5d8-5">gradient of Casimir force measured between graphene–silica substrate and Au sphere</cite> <cite id="e6195440-6">recent Casimir measurement overviews detail short-separation effects</cite> <cite id="e619e5d8-1">TFM resolves moiré lattices in atomically thin materials</cite> <cite id="e619e5d8-0">graphene nonlocality and losses reshape Casimir–Lifshitz predictions tested against experiments</cite>.
- “Dark” forces ≤10 μm: MRFM cavity searches for axions and compact resonator searches for ultralight scalars verify local/nonlocal torque/force channels at sub-micron to micron ranges, thereby mapping Yukawa/axion-induced potentials without a discovery claim but with improved sensitivity frontiers. <cite id="13356bde-1">cavity-mode MRFM axion search near 2 μeV masses</cite> <cite id="13356bde-0">proposed GHz MRFM axion verification scheme</cite> <cite id="13356bde-3">resonator-based scalar searches via Bohr radius modulation</cite>.
- Electroweak small-distance tests: LEP/SLC global fits pin sin²θ_W to a few hundredths of a percent relative precision, validating weak–electromagnetic unification at sub-femtometer to femtometer ranges; LHC single-V analyses and planned low-energy parity experiments extend these small-scale tests. <cite id="304ec651-0">SLD and LEP sin²θ_W results are mutually consistent</cite> <cite id="304ec651-1">LEP+SLC combinations strongly constrain SM parameters</cite> <cite id="304ec651-8">LHC single-W/Z precision below 1% complements small-distance verification</cite> <cite id="304ec651-5">low-energy measurements offer up to 0.15% sin²θ_W precision and μm-scale range verification</cite>.
- Interatomic in biophysics: torsional and dynamic AFM approaches in 2D materials and colloids verify periodic moiré and lattice fringes, directly evidencing vdW periodic potentials; these are numerically matched by Lifshitz-type corrections including finite-size and thermal effects. <cite id="e619e5d8-1">moiré lattices and atomic lattices resolved via torsional force microscopy</cite> <cite id="e6195440-1">shape- and thermal-corrections rationalize self-assembly driven by Casimir–vdW forces</cite>.

Summary
