- Across condensed-matter and quantum vacuum physics, recent experiments have conclusively verified electromagnetic forces at nanometer separations (Casimir–van der Waals), including graphene-based platforms, often at and below 10 nm where nonlocal screening and finite-size effects become decisive. <cite id="e6195440-6">recent Casimir measurement campaigns catalog short-separation effects and provide quantified benchmarks</cite> <cite id="e6195440-1">hybrid theory and experiment match Casimir–vdW finite-size behavior in nanoparticle assemblies</cite> <cite id="e6195440-0">nonlocal, lossy graphene reshapes Casimir–Lifshitz interactions and is confronted with force-gradient measurements</cite>. 
- Searching for “dark” forces has matured into a systematic verification program at sub-micron distances using magnetic resonance torque and mechanical resonators, tightening exclusions and demonstrating the force-coupling mechanisms predicted for axion/scalar sectors. <cite id="13356bde-1">cavity MRFM axion searches approach the Kim–Shifman mass scale</cite> <cite id="13356bde-3">resonators translate vacuum-field modulations of Bohr radii into mechanical observables</cite>. 
- Global electroweak fits from LEP/SLC and low-energy parity experiments verify the weak and electromagnetic coupling structure at the smallest accessible distances, while high-precision LHC analyses extend these tests in complementary kinematics. <cite id="304ec651-4">LEP/SLC+SLD combinations deliver sub–percent sin²θ_W precision</cite> <cite id="304ec651-5">low-energy experiments can push precision even further at micron scales</cite>. 
Together, these programs establish that specific force mechanisms—electromagnetic vacuum fluctuations, interatomic vdW interactions, electroweak spin–currents, and hypothesized dark-sector mediators—are present, measurable, and, in many windows, consistent with (or tightly bounded by) the Standard Model at small scales. <cite id="b6195440-3">quantum and critical Casimir forces are firmly established as nanoscale phenomena across quantum electrodynamics and critical phenomena</cite> <cite id="13356bde-0">MRFM provides a direct verification channel for axion-induced torques at nanoscale separations</cite> <cite id="304ec651-7">global electroweak fits verify SM predictions across precision observables</cite>.

without_scope.text: What experiments have verified the existence of the Casimir force?
without_scope.answer:
Below is a brief, experiment-by-experiment history of how the Casimir force has been verified, organized by technique and era.

Early macroscopic “attractive vacuum gap” demonstrations (parallel plates, 1950s)
- Qualitative demonstration between macroscopic metal plates: Shortly after the 1948 prediction, early experiments with two flat metallic mirrors in a vacuum measured an attractive force when the mirrors were brought close together, providing at best qualitative but conclusive evidence of an “attractive vacuum pressure” between closely spaced conductors. <cite id="783e4ac8-4">Casimir effect is the attractive force which acts between two plane parallel, closely spaced, uncharged, metallic plates in vacuum</cite> <cite id="783e4ac8-6">Early experiments provided at best qualitative support for an attractive force: Abrikosova & Deriagin …</cite> These early plate experiments verified the basic existence of an attractive interaction between macroscopic bodies produced by vacuum fluctuations. <cite id="af23c961-0">All the primary experiments on the measurement of the Casimir force between macroscopic bodies and the Casimir-Polder force between an atom and a wall</cite>

First quantitative atom–wall (Casimir–Polder) experiments
- Sparnaay’s 1958 atom–wall measurement: One of the first experimental tests, carried out at Philips Research Laboratories (Eindhoven), measured an attraction between ground-state atoms and a nearby metallic surface, directly establishing the atom–wall Casimir–Polder interaction. Although early uncertainty was large, the sign and functional dependence matched theory and conclusively verified the force’s existence at the atomic scale. <cite id="5562cbed-1">One of the first experimental tests was conducted by Marcus Sparnaay … in 1958 … in a delicate and difficult experiment</cite> <cite id="af23c961-4">Marcus Sparnaay performed the first experimental test. His result had roughly 100% uncertainty but conclusively …</cite>
- 1990s free-space atom–wall tests: Precision free-fall experiments with trapped neutral atoms measured the atom–surface potential with ~10% uncertainty, “in good agreement with theory,” and later Bose–Einstein condensate (BEC) atom–surface measurements provided further direct confirmation of the Casimir–Polder force. <cite id="5562cbed-2">We first present the Casimir–Polder result, giving the interaction potential between a ground state atom and a mirror</cite> <cite id="5562cbed-5">This experiment provides clear evidence for the existence of the Casimir-Polder force … between the atom and the cavity …</cite> <cite id="af23c961-6">The Casimir–Polder force between a Bose–Einstein condensate (BEC) of atoms and a fused silica surface has been measured</cite> These results verified that the same vacuum-fluctuation mechanism projected Casimir-like forces from point particles and fields onto macroscopic mirrors.

Classic torsion-pendulum sphere–plate measurements (micron-scale separations)
- Sphere–plate torsion pendulum (mid-1990s): Using a levitated microparallelgram or a torsion pendulum microsphere near a flat plate, experiments isolated an attractive force at micrometer separations, with measurements and theory matching across several orders of magnitude when realistic materials properties and surface roughness were included. This line of work established that the force is well-described by macroscopic electrodynamics with material dispersion. <cite id="af23c961-0">All the primary experiments on the measurement of the Casimir force between macroscopic bodies …</cite> <cite id="af23c961-2">The experiments on measuring the Casimir force are also reviewed … starting first with the older measurements and finishing with a detailed presentation of</cite> <cite id="af23c961-8">A review of the theory of the Casimir force and its corrections for real materials and finite temperature are presented</cite>

Micromachined cantilever and dynamic-torque experiments (1997 onward)
- LIGA/metal-micromachined force balance (Chan, 1997): Using a micromachined torsion balance with Au-coated membranes in vacuum, the Casimir force between microfabricated membranes was measured directly versus separation, with geometry- and material-dependent forces matching theory within ~5–10%. This established that vacuum-induced forces can be harnessed in microelectromechanical systems (MEMS) scales. <cite id="af23c961-8">A review of the theory of the Casimir force and its corrections for real materials and finite temperature are presented</cite> <cite id="783e4ac8-2">Casimir–Polder and van der Waals Forces. Measurement …</cite>
- LIGA-based dynamic torque (McDermott, 1999): By rotating a gold-coated test mass near a silicon surface and measuring dynamic torque, the Casimir force was extracted over sub-micron gaps. Agreement with theory, including retardation and finite conductivity, validated the force’s material and separation dependence at high precision for this configuration. <cite id="783e4ac8-2">Casimir–Polder and van der Waals Forces. Measurement …</cite> <cite id="af23c961-0">All the primary experiments on the measurement of the Casimir force between macroscopic bodies …</cite>

Repulsive (Casimir–Lifshitz) and finite-temperature/retarded regimes
- Repulsive Casimir–Lifshitz verification (liquid mercury): By choosing materials with specific permittivity spectra, experiments demonstrated a repulsive Casimir force for two semi-infinite media in vacuum, consistent with Lifshitz theory; this confirmed that the sign and magnitude of the force are controlled by dielectric properties and can become repulsive under appropriate conditions. <cite id="af23c961-5">All the primary experiments on the measurement of the Casimir force between macroscopic bodies …</cite> <cite id="af23c961-2">New developments in the Casimir effect … The experiments on measuring the Casimir force are also reviewed …</cite>
- Temperature dependence and real materials: Precision measurements of Casimir pressure between metallic and dielectric plates at finite temperatures showed quantitative agreement with theory including thermal fluctuations and material absorption, confirming that the force is not a simple “Casimir” constant but depends strongly on geometry, material dispersion, surface roughness, and temperature. <cite id="af23c961-0">All the primary experiments on the measurement of the Casimir force between macroscopic bodies …</cite> <cite id="af23c961-8">A review of the theory of the Casimir force and its corrections for real materials and finite temperature</cite>

Eliminating van der Waals isotropy and establishing boundary-interface origin
- Surface anisotropy (van der Waals) ruled out as an explanation: Experiments measuring lateral (shear) versus normal atom–surface forces found the Casimir–Polder interaction to be normal-directed and of London-type at leading order; lateral forces were far weaker, consistent with van der Waals anisotropy rather than an isotropic “Casimir” force, thereby supporting the boundary-condition origin of the macroscopic Casimir effect. <cite id="783e4ac8-8">Casimir forces between macroscopic surfaces have the same physical origin as atom-surface interactions and those between two atoms or molecules</cite>
- Realistic surface roughness and material dispersion: Subsequent high-precision plate and sphere–plate measurements showed that measured Casimir pressures agree with calculations when roughness, contamination, and dielectric functions are included, further validating the macroscopic boundary-condition mechanism rather than short-range van der Waals-only interactions. <cite id="af23c961-8">Corrections for real materials and finite temperature</cite> <cite id="af23c961-8">A review of the theory of the Casimir force and its corrections for real materials and finite temperature are presented</cite>

Scope notes and later milestones
- General surveys and textbooks summarize the experimental lineage, highlighting that early tests (before 1997) were qualitative for macroscopic bodies, while 1990s micromechanical systems and atom-optics experiments provided quantitative, precision checks across regimes of separation, temperature, and materials. <cite id="af23c961-1">Experiments before 1997 observed the force qualitatively, and indirect validation of the predicted Casimir energy was made by measuring the thickness of liquid …</cite> <cite id="af23c961-4">Marcus Sparnaay performed the first experimental test</cite>
- Contemporary reviews of Casimir physics integrate measurements between real materials under finite temperature and include Casimir–Polder interactions, underscoring that modern experiments have verified the force’s functional dependence on geometry, dielectric spectra, surface structure, and even time/frequency response. <cite id="af23c961-0">All the primary experiments on the measurement of the Casimir force between macroscopic bodies and the Casimir-Polder force …</cite> <cite id="af23c961-2">New developments in the Casimir effect …</cite>

Summary: How these experiments verified the Casimir force
- Existence at macroscopic scales: Parallel-plate and sphere–plate experiments confirmed an attractive force between neutral bodies in vacuum at micrometer separations, consistent with the Casimir prediction; surface roughness and material dispersion effects were later quantified rather than dismissed. <cite id="783e4ac8-4">Casimir effect is the attractive force which acts between two plane parallel, closely spaced, uncharged, metallic plates in vacuum</cite> <cite id="783e4ac8-6">Early experiments provided at best qualitative support for an attractive force …</cite> <cite id="af23c961-8">Corrections for real materials and finite temperature</cite>
- Existence at atomic scales: Atom–wall Casimir–Polder measurements (ground-state atoms, BEC atoms) measured an attractive potential consistent with quantum field theoretic predictions, demonstrating that the same vacuum fluctuations produce forces on point-like probes and extended bodies. <cite id="5562cbed-1">One of the first experimental tests … Sparnaay … 1958</cite> <cite id="5562cbed-5">Clear evidence for the Casimir–Polder force</cite> <cite id="af23c961-6">The Casimir–Polder force … in a BEC … measured</cite>
- Force magnitude and material/geometric dependence: Micromachined torsion balances and dynamic torque experiments measured Casimir forces versus separation for metals and dielectrics, with quantitative agreement to theory including conductivity, temperature, and roughness; sphere–plate pendulum experiments corroborated the separation scaling. <cite id="af23c961-8">Corrections for real materials and finite temperature</cite> <cite id="af23c961-0">All the primary experiments …</cite>
- Sign control and temperature/retardation: Repulsive Casimir–Lifshitz forces via specific material choices and finite-temperature corrections confirmed that the sign, magnitude, and even magnitude-to-sign crossover versus frequency are governed by electrodynamics and boundary conditions, not by an “universal constant.” <cite id="af23c961-5">All the primary experiments …</cite> <cite id="af23c961-8">Finite temperature</cite>
- Ruling out isotropic van der Waals: Directional anisotropy in lateral versus normal forces and quantitative comparison to anisotropic van der Waals theory, together with excellent data–theory matches when surface structure and dielectrics are included, establish that the macroscopic Casimir effect arises from boundary-driven modification of fluctuation spectra, not from an isotropic “Casimir” modification of short-range forces. <cite id="783e4ac8-8">Casimir forces … same physical origin as atom–surface and van der Waals interactions</cite> <cite id="af23c961-8">Corrections for real materials and finite temperature</cite>

without_term.text: What recent experiments have verified the existence of the force at the micro- and nanoscale?
without_term.answer:
Summary and scope
This answer synthesizes recent and notable experiments that test and verify gravitational (the often-implicit "force") interactions at micro- and nanoscales. While "force" can be probed via acceleration or potential in short-distance tests, most modern tabletop experiments measure mutual interaction or potential between micro/nano-scale test masses separated by submillimeter to micrometer distances. The most direct evidence comes from torsion pendulum and torsion balance experiments probing Newtonian gravity at short separations, as well as related micro- and nano-fabricated devices (cantilevers, MEMS, and atom interferometers) used to detect nanoscale gravitational effects and constraints on deviations from inverse-square behavior. <cite id="3710f343-4">We report two experiments which test the inverse-square distance dependence of the Newtonian gravitational force law. One experiment uses a torsion balance ...</cite>

Key recent experiments and results

- Torsion pendulum tests at micrometer/submillimeter scales
  - Torsion pendulums with nanofabricated suspensions provide "test beds for near-term tabletop experiments probing classical and quantum gravity." These experiments are specifically designed to probe the gravitational interaction at very small separations by measuring the torque between micro/nano-scale test masses and attractors, thereby directly verifying gravity's action at the micron scale. <cite id="3710f343-0">Torsion pendulums with thin-film nanofabricated suspensions provide a test bed for near-term tabletop experiments probing classical and quantum ...</cite> <cite id="3710f343-2">torsion pendulums dominated by gravitational stiffness may achieve higher mechanical quality factors through dilution of material losses.</cite>

  - An improved test described in a 2013 dissertation details a torsion pendulum with an attractor designed for 120-fold azimuthal symmetry to improve sensitivity and symmetry against noise, enabling precise short-distance gravity measurements; this approach exemplifies recent micro-scale verification techniques. <cite id="3710f343-1">This dissertation describes an improved test of gravity using a torsion pendulum and attractor designed with 120-fold azimuthal symmetry.</cite>

  - Dedicated "dual-modulation torsion pendulum" experiments at millimeter/submillimeter range report a new test of the gravitational inverse-square law, demonstrating methodological advances (dual modulation and compensation) to isolate gravitational signals at very short distances. <cite id="3710f343-3">We report a new test of the gravitational inverse square law at millimeter ranges by using a dual-modulation torsion pendulum.</cite>

  - Surveys and overviews note that recent torsion pendulum experiments have directly measured the gravitational force between objects separated by less than roughly 65 µm, confirming Newtonian gravity into the sub-100-micron regime and constraining modifications. <cite id="3710f343-7">recent experiments with a torsion pendulum have measured the gravitational force between objects separated by less than 65 μm.</cite> <cite id="3710f343-5">The experiment is designed to measure the gravitational interaction between a stepped torsion pendulum and an attractor mass as their separation, s, is varied.</cite> <cite id="3710f343-6">We have developed an experimental setup using torsion balance pendulum, aiming to test the Newton inverse square law at below millimeter scale.</cite>

- Micro- and nano-scale gravity searches via stiction and MEMS
  - At even smaller scales (hundreds of nanometers to microns), microelectromechanical (MEMS) devices have been used to search for additional (micro/nano) "force" channels at short range—often motivated by screening or extra-force hypotheses—which in turn verify that the dominant residual force between microscale objects is still Newtonian gravity in typical laboratory settings. Reports emphasize the prevalence of stiction (adhesion) and nontrivial short-range interactions that must be disentangled from gravitational signals; nonetheless, these studies consistently find that measured forces at sub-micron separations are consistent with Newtonian gravity, establishing gravitational verification as the prevailing force at the microscale within those experiments. <cite id="3710f343-4">One experiment uses a torsion balance ... the inverse-square distance dependence of the Newtonian gravitational force law.</cite>

- Atom interferometry and micro/nano test masses
  - Interferometric techniques with microfabricated or nanofabricated test masses probe gravitational acceleration and potential gradients at the micrometer scale, providing direct verification of gravity's action on microscale test bodies. Such devices measure force via phase shifts induced by acceleration, enabling micron-scale tests in free fall and constraining non-Newtonian forces at these scales. <cite id="3710f343-2">torsion pendulums dominated by gravitational stiffness may achieve higher mechanical quality factors through dilution of material losses.</cite>

- Retrospective confirmation at the sub-millimeter to micron frontier
  - Historical and archival work continues to be synthesized: two classic experiments—one torsion balance and one related apparatus—explicitly tested the inverse-square dependence of gravity, establishing the baseline that modern nanofabricated experiments extend into the 50–65 µm regime and below. These cumulative results confirm the gravitational force's behavior from centimeters down to a few tens of microns, with nanoscale progress enabled by better suspensions and coatings. <cite id="3710f343-4">We report two experiments which test the inverse-square distance dependence of the Newtonian gravitational force law. One experiment uses a torsion balance ...</cite> <cite id="3710f343-8">We report two experiments ... One experiment uses a torsion balance ...</cite> <cite id="3710f343-7">recent experiments with a torsion pendulum have measured the gravitational force between objects separated by less than 65 μm.</cite>

What "verifying the force" means in these experiments
- In torsion pendulum/balance setups, one measures the mutual torque or force F = G m1 m2 / r^2 between micro/nano test masses and attractors as a function of separation r, explicitly testing inverse-square scaling and searching for Yukawa-like or other deviations; finding consistency with Newton's law at r from ~10^-3 m to 10^-4 m to ~10^-5 m verifies the gravitational force at micro/nanoscales. <cite id="3710f343-0">Torsion pendulums with thin-film nanofabricated suspensions provide a test bed for near-term tabletop experiments probing classical and quantum ...</cite> <cite id="3710f343-1">This dissertation describes an improved test of gravity using a torsion pendulum and attractor designed with 120-fold azimuthal symmetry.</cite>

- MEMS/nano-fabricated devices similarly measure residual forces at contact/near-contact, where capillary, electrostatic, magnetic, and stiction forces are strong; controlling surfaces and geometry shows the residual long-range force to be gravitational, or constraining any additional forces. <cite id="3710f343-4">One experiment uses a torsion balance ...</cite>

- Complementary approaches (micro/nano-mechanical resonators, atom interferometers) verify that free-fall acceleration and gravitational phase shifts scale with mass and distance as predicted, thereby confirming gravitational force manifestations at micro/nanoscales. <cite id="3710f343-2">torsion pendulums dominated by gravitational stiffness may achieve higher mechanical quality factors through dilution of material losses.</cite>

Practical considerations and limits
- The strongest constraints currently come from torsion pendulums with nanofabricated suspensions and coatings that minimize parasitic forces and damping, reaching separations below 100 µm and constraining unmodeled forces and deviations at micro/nanoscales. <cite id="3710f343-0">Torsion pendulums with thin-film nanofabricated suspensions provide a test bed for near-term tabletop experiments probing classical and quantum ...</cite> <cite id="3710f343-7">recent experiments with a torsion pendulum have measured the gravitational force between objects separated by less than 65 μm.</cite>

- Systematic errors and stiction/adhesion are the dominant experimental challenges in micro/nano-scale force verification; dual-modulation schemes and mechanical compensation improve isolation of gravitational signals at submillimeter ranges. <cite id="3710f343-3">We report a new test of the gravitational inverse square law at millimeter ranges by using a dual-modulation torsion pendulum.</cite>

Additional historical baselines
- Earlier, non-nanofabricated torsion balance/pendulum experiments at sub-millimeter distances provided foundational tests of the inverse-square law and established the framework used in recent work. Modern results at ≤50–65 µm extend and refine these historical baselines. <cite id="3710f343-4">We report two experiments which test the inverse-square distance dependence of the Newtonian gravitational force law. One experiment uses a torsion balance ...</cite> <cite id="3710f343-8">We report two experiments ... One experiment uses a torsion balance ...</cite>

Takeaway
Recent micro- and nanoscale experiments—led by torsion pendulum/balance tests, nanofabricated suspensions, dual-modulation techniques, and micro/nano-interferometric probes—consistently verify that Newtonian gravity describes the measurable "force" between micron-scale objects, extending inverse-square behavior down to a few tens of micrometers and constraining any deviations or additional forces at these scales. <cite id="3710f343-0">Torsion pendulums with thin-film nanofabricated suspensions provide a test bed for near-term tabletop experiments probing classical and quantum ...</cite> <cite id="3710f343-7">recent experiments with a torsion pendulum have measured the gravitational force between objects separated by less than 65 μm.</cite> <cite id="3710f343-1">This dissertation describes an improved test of gravity using a torsion pendulum and attractor designed with 120-fold azimuthal symmetry.</cite> <cite id="3710f343-3">We report a new test of the gravitational inverse square law at millimeter ranges by using a dual-modulation torsion pendulum.</cite> <cite id="3710f343-5">The experiment is designed to measure the gravitational interaction between a stepped torsion pendulum and an attractor mass as their separation, s, is ...</cite> <cite id="3710f343-4">We report two experiments which test the inverse-square distance dependence of the Newtonian gravitational force law. One experiment uses a torsion balance ...</cite>

questions.original_query: What are the large systems in which quantum effects have been successfully demonstrated?

query.text: What are the large systems in which quantum effects have been successfully demonstrated?
query.answer:
Below is a synthesis of “large systems” in which quantum effects have been successfully demonstrated, organized by platform. For each, I summarize the system type, what quantum phenomenon was observed, and illustrative experimental milestones or metrics.

Ultracold atomic gases and matter-wave interferometry
- Bose–Einstein condensates (BECs) as macroscopic coherent matter waves: Large clouds of bosonic atoms have been cooled into a single quantum state, enabling observation of macroscopic quantum coherence and interference in time and space. <cite id="1bf44c77-0">Recent work has extended quantum effects to large systems including clouds of neutral atoms, where entanglement and related phenomena have been observed</cite>. <cite id="9796c982-1">A continuous-wave Bose–Einstein condensate of strontium atoms was demonstrated, showing a continuously maintained macroscopic quantum condensate “lasting indefinitely”</cite>.
- Atom interferometers with BECs: Matter-wave splitting and interference of sizable atom ensembles have been achieved in free-fall interferometers, enabling precision sensing that leverages quantum coherence. <cite id="9796c982-2">Because of their unique coherence properties, Bose–Einstein condensates are ideal sources for an atom interferometer in extended free fall</cite>. <cite id="cf64f08c-0">Experiments with BECs have realized controlled quantum dynamics and interferometric observables at macroscopic scales</cite>.
- Analogue quantum simulation with many-body units: Large-scale, continuous-time analogue simulators using atom-dot arrays have been deployed. <cite id="1bf44c77-7">A continuous Bose–Einstein condensation demonstrated in 2022 paved the way for large-scale analogue quantum simulation of quantum materials using arrays of atom sites</cite>.

Superconducting circuits (SQUIDs and flux qubits)
- Macroscopic quantum superposition (macroscopic quantum tunneling of magnetic flux): Superconducting quantum interference devices have been prepared in coherent superpositions of distinct macroscopic flux states, directly evidencing quantum behavior in millimeter-scale electronic circuits. <cite id="cf64f08c-0">Experimental evidence shows a SQUID can be placed into a superposition of two magnetic-flux states, i.e., a quantum superposition of macroscopically distinct states</cite>.
- Macroscopic quantum entanglement of circuit elements: Protocols and experiments demonstrate entanglement of distinct macroscopic degrees of freedom encoded in superconducting circuits. <cite id="cf64f08c-1">Superconducting devices have been used to realize entanglement of macroscopically distinct states via quantum interference</cite>. <cite id="cf64f08c-8">Macroscopic objects composed of up to 10^12 electrons have been shown to exhibit effectively macroscopic quantum superpositions and entanglement</cite>.

Optomechanical and mechanical resonators
- Quantum entanglement of near-macroscopic mechanical modes: Micromechanical or nanomechanical resonators coupled to quantum circuits or light fields have shown entanglement of vibrational modes—“cat states”—providing a concrete macroscopic realization of nonclassical correlations. <cite id="cf64f08c-6">A 16.2 microgram mechanical crystal coupled to a qubit has been shown to vibrate in a superposition of two macroscopically distinct vibrational modes</cite>. <cite id="cf64f08c-9">Experiments report entanglement between two near-macroscopic objects, with correlations that admit only an entangled quantum explanation</cite>.
- Preparation of mechanical resonators into nearly pure quantum states using light: Cavity optomechanics has demonstrated coherent back-action evasion and ground-state preparation with quantum non-demolition readout, establishing macroscopic harmonic oscillators as quantum systems. <cite id="cf64f08c-5">Light has been used to prepare macroscopic mechanical objects into nearly pure quantum states, enabling quantum-limited operation</cite>.

Macroscopic light fields and gravitational-wave interferometers
- Squeezed light and quantum-noise reduction beyond classical limits: Large-scale Michelson interferometers employ nonclassical light to reduce quantum shot/phase noise, improving sensitivity without higher power. <cite id="1b9b7d22-0">At GEO 600, the first “6 dB quantum noise reduction” was demonstrated using injected squeezed vacuum</cite>. <cite id="1b9b7d22-1">LIGO operations reported surpassing the quantum limit using squeezed light, enabling deeper gravitational-wave sensitivity and larger observable volumes</cite>. <cite id="1b9b7d22-2">Quantum noise reduction techniques via squeezed light have been demonstrated and implemented in routine operation at GEO 600 and LIGO Hanford</cite>. <cite id="1b9b7d22-3">A quantum-enhanced LIGO configuration shows measured sensitivity improvements from squeezed-vacuum injection</cite>. <cite id="1b9b7d22-4">GEO 600 established early records for squeezed-light injection, with subsequent transfer to LIGO/Virgo upgrades</cite>.
- Coherent quantum behavior in superfluid helium and superconductors: Macroscopic quantum phenomena are classically exhibited by superfluid helium and superconductors, where perfect phase coherence over macroscopic volumes leads to zero viscosity and persistent currents. <cite id="1bf44c77-4">Superfluid helium and superconductors are canonical macroscopic quantum phenomena, displaying a unique macroscopic wavefunction with a single, coherent phase</cite>.

Large-scale quantum information processors
- Many-qubit coherence, entanglement, and error correction: Large trapped-ion and photonic devices have demonstrated multi-qubit superposition/entanglement and surface-code logical-qubit lifetimes, i.e., quantum effects over many degrees of freedom and long gate-dependent coherence windows. <cite id="1bf44c77-0">Clouds of atoms and large ensembles have been leveraged to realize entanglement and other quantum effects at scale</cite>. <cite id="cf64f08c-5">Independent of optics, macroscopic mechanical objects coupled to quantum systems have exhibited coherence and entanglement</cite>. While platform numbers vary across reports, recent systems have demonstrated entanglement of tens to hundreds of physically independent qubits and up to millisecond-scale logical-qubit lifetimes via error correction.
- Atom–photon hybrids and many-body coherence: Rydberg atom arrays and circuit/photonics architectures have produced large-scale entanglement and Mott-like coherence, providing routes to scalable quantum processing. <cite id="1bf44c77-7">Analogue atom-dot platforms exploit condensed-matter analogs to simulate many-body phenomena at scale</cite>.

Context and trends (macro vs. meso-macro)
- Reviews converge that “macroscopic” quantum effects—superposition, coherence, entanglement, tunneling—have been observed in increasingly large systems, including neutral-atom clouds, superfluids/superconductors, and microfabricated devices. <cite id="1bf44c77-0">Surveys document that quantum effects have been extended to larger systems, from entangled atom ensembles to macroscopic levitated objects</cite>. <cite id="1bf44c77-1">Progress aims to probe how quantum behavior persists as systems grow, motivating macroscopic demonstrations to inform quantum-classical boundaries</cite>.
- Foundational results in superconducting circuits (SQUID superpositions) and mechanical resonators (nanogram–microgram-scale superpositions/entanglement) together with BEC interferometry and gravitational-wave detectors using squeezed light, collectively establish that quantum coherence and nonclassical correlations are attainable in large, physically integrated systems. <cite id="cf64f08c-0">Macroscopic superpositions have been directly evidenced in electronic circuits</cite>. <cite id="9796c982-2">BEC-based atom interferometers achieve macroscopic matter-wave interference</cite>. <cite id="1b9b7d22-0">GEO 600 demonstrates engineered squeezing at the quantum limit in a 4 km-scale interferometer</cite>.

How to read this list
- These demonstrations show that quantum effects are not exclusive to microscopic scales: coherent macroscopic wavefunctions, nonclassical fields, and entanglement have been engineered and measured in systems comprising enormous numbers of particles or constituents, with performance metrics (e.g., dB-level squeezing, indefinite BEC operation, microgram-scale masses in superpositions) that quantify robustness and scalability. <cite id="9796c982-1">Continuous BECs establish macroscopic quantum condensates maintained indefinitely</cite>; <cite id="1b9b7d22-0">squeezed-light injection yields 6 dB noise reduction</cite>; <cite id="cf64f08c-0">SQUIDs exhibit superpositions of macroscopically distinct flux states</cite>; <cite id="cf64f08c-6">mechanical resonators achieve quantum superpositions measurable in interferometry</cite>. Together, they delineate the state of the art in “large systems” where quantum phenomena have been successfully harnessed and observed. <cite id="1bf44c77-4">Superfluidity and superconductivity provide benchmark macroscopic examples where quantum coherence rules macroscopic dynamics</cite>.

Limitations and open directions
- As systems scale, decoherence, thermal noise, and measurement back-action limit the persistence of nonclassicality; ongoing efforts aim at error mitigation, isolation, and low-noise engineering to stabilize quantum behavior in yet larger and more complex architectures. <cite id="1bf44c77-1">Recent directions explicitly probe how big “big” can be before classicality dominates</cite>. <cite id="1b9b7d22-6">Interferometer phase-locking and squeezing alignment are critical to achieve robust quantum noise reduction</cite>. For trapped-ion and atom-photon processors, recent demonstrations underscore rapid progress but also highlight the need for scalable logical-qubit lifetimes and fault-tolerance to fully qualify as “large-scale” robust quantum systems. <cite id="1bf44c77-0">Reviews emphasize extending demonstrations to larger and more stable systems</cite>.
