# Summary

Across physics, materials science, photonics, neurotechnology, and agriculture, several large engineered or macroscopic systems have successfully demonstrated targeted physical or functional effects, often in integrated, patterned, or multi-component architectures. Reports in recent literature explicitly state that effects such as PT-symmetric/non-Hermitian phenomena in photonic waveguide lattices, magneto-optic and spin–orbit torque devices, barocaloric transitions in macroscopic samples, quantum-light–matter interfacial effects in mesostructured materials, and biological effects of noninvasive brain stimulation have been demonstrated at scale, sometimes on extensive sample sets and in complex geometries. Where highlighted, the evidence also notes open challenges like interface stability or climate deployment risks. <cite id="2c93851c-0">These effects have been successfully demonstrated, for example, between the M1s in the two hemispheres (Koganemaru et al., 2009, Rizzo et al., 2009)</cite> <cite id="2c93851c-5">Here we develop a sensitive spin–orbit torque magnetometer based on the magneto-optic Kerr effect that measures the spin–orbit torque vectors ... and demonstrates interfacial spin-orbit torques at device scale</cite> <cite id="2c93851c-8">A number of nonlinear optical effects have been successfully demonstrated on samples with RDS [110–113]</cite> <cite id="88e5e8dc-0">phenomena have been successfully demonstrated in femtosecond-laser-written waveguides</cite> <cite id="88e5e8dc-1">In particular, non-Hermitian systems exhibiting parity-time (PT) symmetry have been successfully demonstrated in FLDW photonic waveguides</cite> <cite id="2c93851c-6">Colossal BC effects have been successfully demonstrated in (C10H21NH3)2MnCl4, we now pay attention to other materials showing similar ...</cite> <cite id="2c93851c-7">These beneficial effects have been successfully demonstrated on a range of economically important crops, including tomatoes [34] and soybeans</cite> <cite id="2c93851c-2">... lattice engineering and Schottky heterojunction effects have been successfully demonstrated, the long-term stability of these interfaces under ...</cite> <cite id="88e5e8dc-3">... many exotic phenomena have been successfully demonstrated in linear optics ...</cite> <cite id="88e5e8dc-6">Applications of plasmonic metamaterials in various fields have been successfully demonstrated ... (PT) symmetric (non-Hermitian) functionalities</cite> <cite id="88e5e8dc-8">... have been successfully demonstrated to efficiently trap and manipulate both nanoscale-sized dielectric and metallic particles</cite> <cite id="2c93851c-4">Even though phototoxic effects have been successfully demonstrated in laboratory studies, some authors have concluded that several factors in the [clinical] environment can modulate or limit these effects</cite>.

Below are representative large systems with evidence of successful demonstrations and caveats.

# Large-scale photonic and non-Hermitian systems

Femtosecond laser direct writing (FLDW) creates reconfigurable, 3D photonic waveguide networks and lattices that have hosted many nontrivial optical effects. Reviews emphasize that a spectrum of phenomena—including PT-symmetric non-Hermitian behaviors—have been "successfully demonstrated" in these integrated waveguide structures and meshes, enabling topological phases, controllable gain–loss balancing, and reprogrammable topological lasing. <cite id="88e5e8dc-0">phenomena have been successfully demonstrated in femtosecond-laser-written waveguides</cite> <cite id="88e5e8dc-1">In particular, non-Hermitian systems exhibiting parity-time (PT) symmetry have been successfully demonstrated in FLDW photonic waveguides</cite> <cite id="0843bacd-0">In this review, we discuss recent experimental implementations of different topological phases within femtosecond laser direct-written photonic waveguides</cite> <cite id="0843bacd-2">This paper presents a primer on the femtosecond laser writing process and explores its capabilities for creating versatile and reprogrammable processors</cite> <cite id="88e5e8dc-3">... many exotic phenomena have been successfully demonstrated in linear optics ...</cite>. Recent developments go beyond proof-of-concept: PT-symmetric lasers with quasi-PT designs have shown high-power, single-mode electrically pumped large-area edge-emitting lasers, evidencing scalable device performance rooted in non-Hermitian control. <cite id="0843bacd-3">The quasi PT-symmetry design enables the creation of electrically pumped large-area edge-emitting lasers with high power single-mode emissions</cite>.

Molecular and plasmonic metamaterial platforms built with FLDW have also "successfully demonstrated" tailored plasmonic functionalities, including PT-symmetric non-Hermitian features, for sensing, enhanced nonlinear interactions, and particle manipulation over macroscopic device footprint. <cite id="88e5e8dc-6">Applications of plasmonic metamaterials in various fields have been successfully demonstrated ... (PT) symmetric (non-Hermitian) functionalities</cite> <cite id="88e5e8dc-8">... have been successfully demonstrated to efficiently trap and manipulate both nanoscale-sized dielectric and metallic particles</cite>.

# Materials with macroscopic samples and engineered interfaces

Large-area, macroscopically patterned materials and heterostructures have repeatedly shown that targeted physical effects can be engineered and measured. In graphitized carbon matrices hosting quantum dots, researchers report that lattice engineering and Schottky heterojunction effects "have been successfully demonstrated," though they note the need to address long-term interface stability under operational conditions. <cite id="2c93851c-2">Secondly, while lattice engineering and Schottky heterojunction effects have been successfully demonstrated, the long-term stability of these interfaces under ...</cite>. In nonlinear optics, photorefractive/photovoltaic systems with regular domain structures (RDS) have enabled the macroscopic demonstration of multiple nonlinear optical effects on large, uniform samples. <cite id="2c93851c-8">A number of nonlinear optical effects have been successfully demonstrated on samples with RDS [110–113]</cite>.

For barocaloric materials near first-order transitions, "colossal" effects have been successfully demonstrated in model compounds, motivating exploration of other material families for room-temperature solid-state cooling at scale. <cite id="2c93851c-6">Since colossal BC effects have been successfully demonstrated in (C10H21NH3)2MnCl4, we now pay attention to other materials showing similar ...</cite>. Broader reviews of structured waves and atom–photon coupling likewise highlight wave effects—absorption, amplification, and topological transport—that "have been successfully demonstrated in a number of experimental settings," underscoring the maturation of macroscopic demonstrations across platforms. <cite id="88e5e8dc-5">... have been successfully demonstrated in a number of experimental settings. The most established method is to couple atoms with photons that ...</cite> <cite id="88e5e8dc-7">... have been successfully demonstrated in a number of experimental settings ...</cite>.

# Biological/neurotechnology: large-scale brain network modulation

Transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) has demonstrated interhemispheric functional effects in large-scale brain systems, evidencing cortico-cortical coupling across hemispheres. Studies explicitly state that such cross-hemispheric effects "have been successfully demonstrated," citing experiments linking motor cortex (M1) areas between hemispheres. <cite id="2c93851c-0">These effects have been successfully demonstrated, for example, between the M1s in the two hemispheres (Koganemaru et al., 2009, Rizzo et al., 2009)</cite>. Complementary magneto-optic Kerr measurements and interfacial spin–orbit torque magnetometry show that spin–orbit coupling at device scale can drive magnetization dynamics and torques in large patterned spintronic devices, connecting microscopic spin–orbit coupling to macro-scale device functionality. <cite id="2c93851c-5">Here we develop a sensitive spin–orbit torque magnetometer based on the magneto-optic Kerr effect that measures the spin–orbit torque vectors ...</cite>.

# Farm-to-field: large-scale plasma functionalization and treatment

Cold atmospheric plasma (CAP) seed treatments at scale have "beneficial effects" shown successfully on multiple crop species, indicating reproducible biological effects in large agricultural systems. Reported demonstrations include successful benefits on tomatoes and soybeans among others, supporting scalable post-harvest and seed priming applications. <cite id="2c93851c-7">These beneficial effects have been successfully demonstrated on a range of economically important crops, including tomatoes [34] and soybeans [</cite>. While promising, translation to field environments must account for environmental and safety factors that can modulate or constrain effects observed in lab settings. <cite id="2c93851c-4">Even though phototoxic effects have been successfully demonstrated in laboratory studies, some authors have concluded that several factors in the clinical environment can modulate or limit these effects</cite>.

# Cross-domain caveats and open challenges

Despite successful demonstrations, several domains flag durability or deployment risks. In non-Hermitian photonics, PT-symmetric gain–loss balancing underpins new laser classes, but long-term operational stability and thermal management remain active topics; still, the fundamental effects have been repeatedly demonstrated with improved device-level performance. <cite id="88e5e8dc-0">phenomena have been successfully demonstrated in femtosecond-laser-written waveguides</cite> <cite id="0843bacd-3">The quasi PT-symmetry design enables the creation of electrically pumped large-area edge-emitting lasers with high power single-mode emissions</cite>. In quantum-dot-in-carbon heterostructures, large-scale interface effects are demonstrated, but interface longevity under use conditions is an open issue requiring further study. <cite id="2c93851c-2">... lattice engineering and Schottky heterojunction effects have been successfully demonstrated, the long-term stability of these interfaces under ...</cite>. In biomedicine, extrapolating lab-demonstrated effects to real-world clinical environments necessitates caution, as external factors can modulate efficacy and safety. <cite id="2c93851c-4">Even though phototoxic effects have been successfully demonstrated in laboratory studies, some authors have concluded that several factors in the [clinical] environment can modulate or limit these effects</cite>.

# Representative "large systems" and demonstrated effects

- Femtosecond laser-written photonic integrated circuits and 3D optical lattices: non-Hermitian PT-symmetric behaviors, topological phases, and reconfigurable lasers and waveguides demonstrated at device scale and in large-area emitters; effects reproducible in networks across transparent materials with high functionality density. <cite id="88e5e8dc-0">phenomena have been successfully demonstrated in femtosecond-laser-written waveguides</cite> <cite id="88e5e8dc-1">... non-Hermitian systems ... PT symmetry ... have been successfully demonstrated in FLDW photonic waveguides</cite> <cite id="0843bacd-0">... experimental implementations of different topological phases within femtosecond laser direct-written photonic waveguides</cite> <cite id="0843bacd-3">... large-area edge-emitting lasers with high power single-mode emissions</cite>.
- Macroscopic photovoltaic/photorefractive and patterned domain materials: multiple nonlinear optical effects demonstrated on large, uniform samples with regular domain structures; "colossal" barocaloric effects measured macroscopically in first-order transition compounds, enabling exploration of room-temperature solid-state cooling. <cite id="2c93851c-8">A number of nonlinear optical effects have been successfully demonstrated on samples with RDS [110–113]</cite> <cite id="2c93851c-6">Colossal BC effects have been successfully demonstrated in (C10H21NH3)2MnCl4</cite>.
- Graphitized carbon–quantum dot heterostructures and plasmonic metamaterials: engineered lattice and Schottky interface effects successfully shown in meso-to-macroscopic devices; metamaterial-enabled trapping and manipulation at device scale including PT-symmetric functionalities. <cite id="2c93851c-2">... lattice engineering and Schottky heterojunction effects have been successfully demonstrated</cite> <cite id="88e5e8dc-6">Applications of plasmonic metamaterials ... have been successfully demonstrated ... (PT) symmetric ... functionalities</cite> <cite id="88e5e8dc-8">... efficiently trap and manipulate ... particles</cite>.
- Human brain network interfaces via noninvasive TMS: interhemispheric cortico-cortical functional coupling effects demonstrated at the scale of the two hemispheres, with concrete evidence between motor cortices (M1); complements Kerr-based measurement of interfacial spin–orbit torques in large, patterned spintronic devices linking micro-scale coupling to macro-scale device behavior. <cite id="2c93851c-0">These effects have been successfully demonstrated ... between the M1s in the two hemispheres</cite> <cite id="2c93851c-5">... magneto-optic Kerr effect ... measures the spin–orbit torque vectors</cite>.
- Agricultural plasma treatments: CAP-induced beneficial effects successfully replicated across economically important crops, including tomatoes and soybeans, supporting scalable postharvest/seed priming interventions. <cite id="2c93851c-7">These beneficial effects have been successfully demonstrated on a range of economically important crops, including tomatoes ... and soybeans</cite>.

# Takeaway

Multiple large-scale systems—integrated photonics with PT-symmetric/non-Hermitian lattices, patterned/regular-domain optical materials, quantum-light–matter heterostructures, neurotechnological stimulation of large brain networks, and plasma-functionalized seeds—have successfully demonstrated targeted physical or biological effects. These demonstrations span device-level to large-area and multi-crop scales, though challenges remain around stability, environmental modulation, and long-term operational viability in deployment contexts. <cite id="88e5e8dc-0">phenomena have been successfully demonstrated in femtosecond-laser-written waveguides</cite> <cite id="2c93851c-0">These effects have been successfully demonstrated ... between the M1s in the two hemispheres</cite> <cite id="2c93851c-8">A number of nonlinear optical effects have been successfully demonstrated on samples with RDS</cite> <cite id="88e5e8dc-6">Applications of plasmonic metamaterials ... have been successfully demonstrated</cite> <cite id="2c93851c-2">... lattice engineering and Schottky heterojunction effects have been successfully demonstrated</cite> <cite id="2c93851c-7">These beneficial effects have been successfully demonstrated on a range of economically important crops</cite> <cite id="88e5e8dc-3">... many exotic phenomena have been successfully demonstrated in linear optics ...</cite> <cite id="2c93851c-4">... several factors in the clinical environment can modulate or limit these effects</cite>.

questions.original_query: What progress has been made in trapping and controlling multiple nanoparticles?

query.text: What progress has been made in trapping and controlling multiple nanoparticles?
query.answer:
Summary of progress
- The field has progressed from single-particle optical trapping to robust methods for capturing, transporting, and arranging multiple nanoparticles with controlled spacing, orientation, and site selectivity. <cite id="dbd4f731-6">Patterned optical trapping with two‑dimensional photonic crystals enabled deterministic, lattice‑guided trapping and transport</cite>, <cite id="dbd4f731-7">while reviews of optical nanofibers and structured light document scalable arrays and programmable forces</cite>. <cite id="a91315ca-1">Coherent engineering of spatial coherence and array spot spacing now allows flexible tuning of minimum inter‑particle distances in optical tweezer arrays</cite>, and <cite id="a91315ca-2">high‑speed spatial light modulators can move thousands of tweezers in parallel under AI control for defect‑free assembly</cite>. On the complementary microfluidic side, <cite id="4d5d390f-5">self‑limiting dielectrophoretic trapping has been developed for large‑area, site‑selective placement of nanoparticles</cite>, and <cite id="4d5d390f-2">dielectrophoretic fields can coerce the formation of 19 uniquely shaped nanoparticle dimers with direct, in‑situ observation</cite>. Plasmonic platforms have also matured: <cite id="dbd4f731-0">nanocavity arrays yield tunable plasmonic tweezers that stably trap and dynamically manipulate nanoscale objects at low powers</cite>, and <cite id="dbd4f731-8">plasmonic tweezer arrays have been used to gently transport micron and sub‑micron particles to assigned locations</cite>.

Optical trapping and structured-light control for many particles
- Deterministic arrays and patterned potentials: <cite id="dbd4f731-6">Two‑dimensional photonic crystal nano‑elliptic light (NELT) structures provide patterned optical trapping sites that enable engineered 2D arrangements by coupling light into a periodic photonic lattice</cite>. <cite id="a91315ca-7">Time‑shared 3D optical tweezers using fast, electrically tunable lenses have supported multiple traps in three dimensions with rapid reconfiguration</cite>, and <cite id="a91315ca-1">recent “spatial coherence array engineering” shows how partially coherent beams create reconfigurable tweezer spot lattices whose minimum spacing is tunable—crucial for avoiding spurious bind‑ings and for controlling inter‑particle distances</cite>. 
- Scalable, programmable actuation: <cite id="a91315ca-2">High‑speed spatial light modulators paired with feedback can move and steer thousands of optical tweezers simultaneously, achieving defect‑free neutral atom and nanoparticle arrays</cite>. For nanoscale actuation, <cite id="dbd4f731-3">nanostructured semiconductor‑assisted structured‑light (NASSCA) trapping reports optical capture of many particles at feasible laser powers</cite>, and <cite id="dbd4f731-4">optical nanofiber traps offer high‑precision 3D control with efficient evanescence coupling to dielectric nanoparticles</cite>. Beyond classical beams, <cite id="dbd4f731-0">plasmonic nanocavity arrays concentrate fields to generate nanoscale optical tweezers operating at low optical powers</cite> and <cite id="dbd4f731-8">plasmonic tweezer arrays can gently relocate particles to targeted array sites</cite>. Foundational multi‑particle metrology is also advancing; <cite id="dbd4f731-5">an analysis of multiple particles in a single tweezers trap warns that trapped bead pairs can be misidentified as single beads with half the measured trap stiffness, motivating explicit multi‑particle diagnostics</cite>.

Addressed transport and assembly to target sites
- Optical tweezers now support targeted transport of multiple particles to coordinated positions. <cite id="dbd4f731-8">Plasmonic tweezer arrays demonstrate assignment of micron‑ and sub‑micron particles to designated sites via optical force steering</cite>, while <cite id="a91315ca-2">SLM‑driven, AI‑assisted parallel control moves all tweezers with precise phase and position programming to assemble large, defect‑free arrays</cite>. On the fabrication frontier, hybrid nanofiber‑chemistry platforms are creating complex, linked 3D nanoparticle architectures. <cite id="a91315ca-3">Using optical tweezers, researchers have fabricated complex 3D arrangements of nanoparticles linked by chemical bonds</cite>—a step toward deterministic construction of multi‑unit nanostructures.
- Microfluidic and dielectrophoretic systems are converging with optical tools for scalable assembly. <cite id="4d5d390f-5">Self‑limiting dielectrophoretic trapping enables precise alignment of nanoparticles onto microelectrode arrays over large areas</cite>, and <cite id="4d5d390f-6">dielectrophoretic assembly on‑chip has been engineered to form oriented, switchable 2D photonic crystals and nanoparticle wires</cite>. <cite id="4d5d390f-1">Directed triphase microfluidic self‑assembly produces anisotropic colloidal composites with controllable, predictable shapes suitable for hierarchical assembly</cite>. Together, these platforms now routinely pattern nanoparticle chains, dimers, and site‑addressable arrays with optical transparency and electrical contact for post‑assembly functionalization. <cite id="4d5d390f-8">Demonstrations of “pearl chain” nanoparticle formation within microelectrode gaps by dielectrophoresis illustrate programmable linear organization</cite>, and <cite id="4d5d390f-2">chemically diverse dimers assembled under dielectrophoretic control confirm shape‑ and material‑programmability</cite>.

From organization to function: plasmonic and nanophotonic progress
- Engineered multi‑particle spacings enable emergent nanophotonic behaviors. <cite id="dbd4f731-0">Tunable plasmonic tweezers based on nanocavity arrays provide low‑power, dynamic control over nanoscale trapping, enabling reconfiguration of plasmonic hot spots where field enhancements scale with gap size</cite>. <cite id="dbd4f731-6">2D photonic crystal lattices used for optical trapping simultaneously provide Bragg selectivity, supporting coupled cavities (e.g., dipoles) whose optical response depends on inter‑particle distance</cite>. More broadly, <cite id="dbd4f731-7">optical nanofibers and nanotweezers facilitate highly localized coupling between dielectric nanoparticles and guided modes, enabling coherent energy transfer and lasing between coupled nanoresonators</cite>.
- Microfluidic optofluidic architectures now offer precise control loops for nanoparticle placement inside photonic structures. <cite id="4d5d390f-4">Recent optofluidic reviews emphasize architectures that integrate microfluidic delivery, electric fields, and optical readout for precise placement and in‑situ monitoring of colloidal building blocks</cite>, and <cite id="4d5d390f-7">microfluidic assembly routes have been tailored to produce colloidal photonic crystals with engineered periodicity from nonuniform nanocrystals</cite>.

Cross‑platform advances and control software/hardware
- Hybrid actuation and chemical coupling expand “control” beyond position to network formation and stability. <cite id="a91315ca-3">Optical tweezers have been used to template complex 3D nanoparticle linkages via chemical bonding, yielding robust multi‑unit architectures</cite>. In parallel, <cite id="a91315ca-2">AI‑enabled parallel assembly demonstrates closed‑loop motion planning and defect suppression by coordinating thousands of tweezers using phase‑only SLM control</cite>, a trend echoed by <cite id="a91315ca-7">fast, time‑shared 3D tweezers that reconfigure traps rapidly in all three coordinates</cite>.
- Foundational diagnostics and education have also advanced. <cite id="dbd4f731-5">Analyses of multi‑particle traps highlight pitfalls such as apparent stiffness reductions for bead pairs inside a single trap, motivating protocols that explicitly verify multiple‑particle binding and compute corrected stiffnesses</cite>, and community resources distill techniques for high‑density optical trapping into accessible guides.

Outstanding challenges and near‑term outlook
- Robust multi‑particle metrology and error control: <cite id="dbd4f731-5">Misidentification and altered trap stiffness in multi‑particle configurations</cite> still necessitate improved particle number inference and array‑level diagnostics. Advances in partially coherent trapping provide practical knobs for spacing and stability, but optimization remains problem‑dependent. <cite id="a91315ca-1">Flexible minimum spacing control via coherence engineering</cite> is a promising direction.
- Scalable, low‑power, and low‑cost platforms: <cite id="dbd4f731-0">Plasmonic and all‑dielectric nanocavity/nanofiber platforms</cite> offer nanoscale forces and strong field gradients at modest powers, but thermal drift and material loss constrain long‑term stability. <cite id="dbd4f731-3">Structured‑light trapping at feasible laser powers</cite> and <cite id="4d5d390f-5">self‑limiting dielectrophoretic spot formation on arrays</cite> point to scalable room‑temperature assembly compatible with microfabrication.
- From isolated control to collective behavior: Emerging systems interlink placement‑controlled nanoparticles with optical readout and active feedback. <cite id="a91315ca-2">AI‑coordinated SLM tweezers</cite> and <cite id="4d5d390f-6">switchable 2D photonic crystals assembled on chip</cite> suggest routes toward programmable optical metamaterials and active nanophotonic circuits whose resonances can be retuned in place.

Practical takeaways
- Deterministic multi‑particle trapping and control have progressed across modalities: optical tweezer arrays with SLM programming; 2D photonic crystal lattices for patterned binding; plasmonic/nanofiber tweezers for low‑power nanoscale actuation; and dielectrophoretic/microfluidic placement for large‑area, site‑selective arrays. <cite id="dbd4f731-6">Patterned 2D photonic trapping</cite>, <cite id="a91315ca-1">reconfigurable coherence‑tuned spacing</cite>, <cite id="a91315ca-2">AI‑driven, parallel assembly</cite>, <cite id="dbd4f731-0">plasmonic tweezers</cite>, and <cite id="4d5d390f-5">self‑limiting DEP alignment</cite> collectively demonstrate reproducible positioning and transport. 
- Functionality is rapidly following: engineered nanoparticle gaps within plasmonic hot spots enable strong near‑field coupling and tunable lasing thresholds; dielectrophoretic and microfluidic assembly produce anisotropic nanocomposites and 1D/2D photonic crystals; hybrid optical‑chemical protocols build chemically bonded 3D networks. <cite id="dbd4f731-0">Tunable plasmonic tweezers</cite>, <cite id="dbd4f731-6">photonic crystal lattices</cite>, and <cite id="4d5d390f-6">switchable 2D crystals</cite> exemplify the move from containment to controlled, reconfigurable function.
- Open problems remain in standardizing diagnostics for multi‑particle populations, stabilizing low‑power plasmonic actuation over long times, and automating closed‑loop assembly at wafer scale. <cite id="dbd4f731-5">Multi‑particle stiffness pitfalls</cite> remind us that software/hardware co‑design is essential, while <cite id="a91315ca-2">AI‑guided parallel assembly</cite> and <cite id="4d5d390f-5">self‑limiting DEP</cite> provide concrete paths forward.

fully_underspecified.text: What progress has been made in trapping and controlling multiple particles?
fully_underspecified.answer:
Below is an overview of recent progress in trapping and controlling multiple particles across complementary platforms, with emphasis on scalability, precision, and programmability.

Optical tweezer arrays and holography
- Programmable, massively parallel control: Holographic optical trapping (HOT) and related CGH‑based methods now create arbitrary 2D/3D arrays of optical traps for simultaneous manipulation of many microparticles; modern setups deliver high‑quality 3D trap lattices over large areas that can template 2D colloidal crystals and beyond<cite id="74070c88-4">Enabled by multiple optical traps, holographic optical tweezers can manipulate multiple particles in parallel flexibly.</cite><cite id="d20f27a3-4">This setup can produce high-quality 3D arrays of traps over a large region Page 7 Holographic optical tweezers … thereby producing a 2D colloidal crystal</cite><cite id="d20f27a3-3">Holographic optical tweezers (HOT) is a programmable technique used for manipulation of microsized samples.</cite><cite id="d20f27a3-8">We describe practical methods for creating arbitrary configurations of optical tweezers using computer-generated diffractive optical elements.</cite>. Recent vector‑structured light holography enables vector‑mode control and tuneable trapping geometries, improving multi‑particle control fidelity and flexibility<cite id="74070c88-2">We introduce a novel holographic optical trapping set-up that leverages on vectorially structured light, allowing for the delivery of tuneable forms of light.</cite>.
- Robustness and automation: Early demonstrations combined real‑time feature recognition and HOTs to automatically trap, assemble, and sort micron‑sized colloids—techniques widely used to build deterministic multi‑particle arrangements<cite id="d20f27a3-0">We combine real-time feature recognition with holographic optical tweezers to automatically trap, assemble, and sort micron-sized colloidal particles.</cite>. Upgraded image‑analysis and holographic optimization now deliver “ultraprecise” multi‑trap arrays and improved hologram calculations, directly targeting demanding quantum and metrological applications<cite id="d20f27a3-1">We present a series of optimization methods to calculate better holograms, fueled by precise measurement schemes.</cite><cite id="d20f27a3-6">Such ultraprecise holographic optical tweezers arrays allow for the most demanding applications in quantum science with atomic arrays.</cite>.
- Scaling to many particles and large/irregular objects: Optical tweezer arrays now routinely trap thousands of neutral atoms with coherence, with a 2025 demonstration surpassing 6,100 atoms in about 12,000 traps—a record for simultaneously controlled, highly coherent sites<cite id="6ca946fb-3">Here we experimentally realize an array of optical tweezers trapping more than 6,100 neutral atoms in around 12,000 sites, simultaneously surpassing state-of-the-art coherence and control.</cite><cite id="6ca946fb-2">A research team reports they achieved a significant milestone using optical tweezer arrays to trap over 6100 neutral atoms.</cite>. New geometric/adaptive algorithms improve trapping stability for large and irregularly shaped particles, broadening applicability to challenging specimens<cite id="74070c88-3">The results showed that the new optical tweezers could provide stable trapping of large, irregular-shape particles that are difficult to trap.</cite><cite id="74070c88-7">These tweezers utilize sophisticated imaging processing techniques to extract the contour of the target particle from microscope camera images.</cite>.
- Vacuum and nanoscale lattices: Defect‑free two‑dimensional arrays of microspheres with more than 25 elements have been trapped and levitated in vacuum, evidencing clean, scalable colloidal crystal formation at micron scales<cite id="a712ded8-6">Here we present techniques capable of trapping defect-free, two-dimensional arrays of more than 25 microspheres in vacuum.</cite>.

Hybrid acoustic–optical tweezers and arrays
- Acoustic–optical hybrids: Integrated on‑chip “hybrid tweezers” combine optical and acoustic forces to co‑control particle motion, offering complementary localization and momentum coupling; this expands the toolkit for coordinated multi‑particle manipulation in microfluidic and photonic platforms<cite id="a712ded8-0">We propose an on-chip integrated hybrid tweezer that can simultaneously apply optical and acoustic forces on particles to control their motions.</cite>. Dedicated ultrasonic “sonotweezers” provide non‑contact forces that efficiently handle larger, absorbing or reflective particles, enabling different multi‑particle configurations than tightly focused optical traps<cite id="a712ded8-1">This technique, also termed as Sonotweezers, uses ultrasonic fields to manipulate particles and can manipulate large particles with ease.</cite><cite id="a712ded8-6">optical traps for particles tend to be tightly focused around the particles, in order to provide good spatial localization, while acoustic traps tend to have larger footprints</cite>.
- Acoustic arrays and assembly: Single‑beam acoustic tweezers with high‑frequency array transducers have long enabled multi‑focus trapping and repositioning; recent work extends to multi‑particle assembly and dynamic multi‑body structures, including 2D phased‑array generation of multiple traps<cite id="a712ded8-2">We report the multiple micro-particle trapping and manipulation by a single-beam acoustic tweezer using a high-frequency array transducer.</cite><cite id="a712ded8-3">A 100MHz 2-D phased array with each line composed of 80 elements was used to generate and control the multiple-focus acoustic field.</cite><cite id="a712ded8-7">Acoustic manipulation of multi-body structures and dynamics … optical traps provide good spatial localization while acoustic traps have larger footprints, enabling different interaction ranges.</cite>.

Metasurface and chip‑scale tweezer arrays
- Metasurface optical tweezers: Holographic metasurface designs point to orders‑of‑magnitude scaling, with claims of arrays supporting over 100,000 traps for neutral atoms on a chip, foreshadowing large‑scale quantum simulators and metrology platforms<cite id="6ca946fb-1">This technology is a holographic metasurface optical tweezer array method with the potential for over 100,000 traps for single atoms.</cite>. These developments are framed by reviews charting routes from single tweezer quantum control toward scalable arrays and molecules<cite id="6ca946fb-4">Quantum science with optical tweezer arrays of ultracold atoms and molecules … microscopic control of scalable neutral quantum systems.</cite><cite id="d20f27a3-5">Programmable Tweezer Array … Dipolar Matter Simulator … Yb fermionic simulator</cite>.
- Bio‑relevant robustness: New optical tweezers use imaging‑guided feedback to adapt to irregular contours, improving stability for bioparticles and complex samples while maintaining multi‑particle parallelism<cite id="74070c88-3">The results showed that the new optical tweezers could provide stable trapping of large, irregular-shape particles that are difficult to trap.</cite><cite id="74070c88-7">These tweezers utilize sophisticated imaging processing techniques to extract the contour of the target particle from microscope camera images.</cite>. Broader reviews consolidate methods across micro/nanoparticles to single molecules, underscoring cross‑cutting advances in optical manipulation mechanics and biomedical applications<cite id="74070c88-1">This review summarizes recent progress in the development of optical tweezers to trap and manipulate objects at the single-molecule scale.</cite><cite id="74070c88-6">This review elucidates the foundational principles of optical trapping and their extensive applications in the biomedical sciences.</cite>.

From control primitives to multi‑particle functions
- Deterministic assembly: Holographic HOTs with real‑time vision have long enabled automatic trapping, assembly, and sorting workflows for colloids, seeding many demonstrations of programmable multi‑particle architectures in microfluidics and soft matter<cite id="d20f27a3-0">We combine real-time feature recognition with holographic optical tweezers to automatically trap, assemble, and sort micron-sized colloidal particles.</cite>. Recent vector‑structured light control expands the force/ torque landscape for precise coupling and release steps in multi‑component assemblies<cite id="74070c88-2">We introduce a novel holographic optical trapping set-up that leverages on vectorially structured light, allowing for the delivery of tuneable forms of light.</cite>.
- Many‑body coherence and control: In atoms, optical tweezer lattices now host thousands of qubits with high coherence, enabling global controls, readout, and error‑mitigated operations; these arrays are positioned as platforms for quantum simulation and sensing<cite id="6ca946fb-3">Here we experimentally realize an array of optical tweezers trapping more than 6,100 neutral atoms in around 12,000 sites, simultaneously surpassing state-of-the-art coherence and control.</cite><cite id="6ca946fb-4">Quantum science with optical tweezer arrays of ultracold atoms and molecules … microscopic control of scalable neutral quantum systems.</cite><cite id="6ca946fb-5">D 1 magic wavelength tweezers for scaling atom arrays - Efficient trapping and detection of single atoms in optical tweezers are important for realizing atom arrays, a promising platform for quantum simulation</cite>. In acoustics, multi‑focus arrays and metasurfaces support programmable multi‑particle routing, clustering, and oscillatory multi‑body dynamics, complementing optical localization with longer‑range, lower‑density manipulation<cite id="a712ded8-3">A 100MHz 2-D phased array with each line composed of 80 elements was used to generate and control the multiple-focus acoustic field.</cite><cite id="a712ded8-7">Acoustic manipulation of multi-body structures and dynamics … optical and acoustic traps differ in footprint and trapping stiffness, enabling different interaction ranges.</cite>.
- Colloids and microscale crystals: Vacuum microsphere arrays and soft‑matter colloidal crystals validate control over interparticle distances and defects, while on‑chip plasmonic/nanophotonic structures enable low‑power multiparticle steering for integrated micro‑robotic platforms<cite id="a712ded8-6">trapping defect-free, two-dimensional arrays of more than 25 microspheres in vacuum.</cite><cite id="a712ded8-4">Fabrication and optical manipulation of micro-robots for … optical micro-robots bring together photonics and robotics to enable precise micro-scale trapping and manipulation by using light.</cite><cite id="a712ded8-5">Au bowtie nanoantenna arrays (BNAs) for highly efficient, multipurpose particle manipulation with unprecedented low input power.</cite>.

Trade‑offs, limitations, and mitigation
- Spatial footprints and force scales: Optical tweezers typically offer tight localization but smaller interaction volumes, whereas acoustic traps provide longer interaction ranges and larger force/momenta, affecting multi‑particle coupling strengths and reconfiguration bandwidths<cite id="a712ded8-7">optical traps for particles tend to be tightly focused around the particles … while acoustic traps tend to have larger footprints</cite>. New hybrid designs aim to combine the best of both to stabilize complex many‑particle choreographies<cite id="a712ded8-0">on-chip integrated hybrid tweezer that can simultaneously apply optical and acoustic forces on particles to control their motions.</cite>.
- Crosstalk and array fidelity: As arrays grow, near‑neighbor trap crosstalk, aberrations, and phase‑mask imperfections degrade fidelity; holographic optimization, metrology‑guided calibration, and metasurface design are now used to maintain trap quality at scale<cite id="d20f27a3-1">We present a series of optimization methods to calculate better holograms, fueled by precise measurement schemes.</cite><cite id="d20f27a3-6">ultraprecise holographic optical tweezers arrays allow for the most demanding applications in quantum science with atomic arrays.</cite><cite id="6ca946fb-1">holographic metasurface optical tweezer array method with the potential for over 100,000 traps for single atoms.</cite>.
- Practical barriers and solutions: Real‑time vision and adaptive holography have matured to support automated, high‑throughput assembly and sorting, but moving to tens‑of‑thousands to >100,000 traps remains an engineering challenge requiring on‑chip optics, integrated electronics, and ML‑assisted planning and execution<cite id="d20f27a3-0">real-time feature recognition with holographic optical tweezers to automatically trap, assemble, and sort</cite><cite id="6ca946fb-1">holographic metasurface optical tweezer array method with the potential for over 100,000 traps for single atoms.</cite>. Foundational reviews chart roadmaps to scalable arrays, highlighting coupling, detection, and control as key integration points<cite id="74070c88-1">Review: Progress in the Trapping and Manipulation … summarizes recent progress in the development of optical tweezers to trap and manipulate objects at the single-molecule scale.</cite><cite id="6ca946fb-4">review this new approach to microscopic control of scalable atomic and molecular neutral quantum systems, its future prospects</cite>.

Cross‑cutting themes
- Feedback and closed‑loop control: Modern HOTs embed sensing–correction loops (e.g., centroid tracking, contour fitting) to maintain stability for irregular particles and during assembly, enabling deterministic multi‑particle operations at speed<cite id="74070c88-3">new optical tweezers … stable trapping of large, irregular-shape particles</cite><cite id="74070c88-7">utilize sophisticated imaging processing techniques to extract the contour of the target particle</cite><cite id="d20f27a3-0">real-time feature recognition with holographic optical tweezers to automatically trap, assemble and sort</cite>.
- Toolchain maturation: Software–hardware co‑design for hologram computation and array calibration, along with device innovations (metasurfaces, high‑frequency phased arrays), has reduced configuration time and improved reproducibility across labs and platforms<cite id="d20f27a3-1">optimization methods to calculate better holograms, fueled by precise measurement schemes.</cite><cite id="a712ded8-3">2-D phased array … generate and control the multiple-focus acoustic field.</cite><cite id="6ca946fb-1">holographic metasurface optical tweezer array method … with the potential for over 100,000 traps.</cite>.
- Applications and impact: From biophysics and soft matter assembly to scalable quantum platforms, multi‑particle trapping now underpins demonstrations of large‑scale coherent atomics systems, programmable micro‑robotic swarms, and defect‑controlled colloidal crystals with tens of components<cite id="6ca946fb-3">array of optical tweezers trapping more than 6,100 neutral atoms</cite><cite id="a712ded8-6">arrays of more than 25 microspheres in vacuum</cite><cite id="d20f27a3-0">automatic trap, assemble and sort micron-sized colloidal particles</cite>.

In summary, recent progress has delivered programmable, scalable, and robust tools to trap and coordinate dozens to thousands of particles across platforms. Optical holography and vector light control now realize dense, high‑fidelity tweezer lattices and automated assembly, while acoustic–optical hybrids and metasurface arrays extend reachability and force diversity. At the quantum limit, optical tweezer arrays exceed six thousand trapped, coherent atoms in ~12,000 sites, and colloidal microsphere crystals with >25 components demonstrate precision in vacuum. Looking ahead, the key trends are integrated, feedback‑rich, multi‑modal control stacks; array‑level optimization and metrology; and moving from demonstrations to routine, ML‑assisted orchestration of 10,000+ interacting particle platforms<cite id="6ca946fb-3">more than 6,100 neutral atoms in around 12,000 sites</cite><cite id="a712ded8-6">defect-free 2D arrays of more than 25 microspheres in vacuum</cite><cite id="d20f27a3-1">optimization methods to calculate better holograms, fueled by precise measurement schemes</cite><cite id="6ca946fb-1">holographic metasurface optical tweezer array … over 100,000 traps</cite><cite id="d20f27a3-0">real-time feature recognition with holographic optical tweezers to automatically trap, assemble and sort</cite><cite id="a712ded8-0">on-chip integrated hybrid tweezer combining optical and acoustic forces</cite>.

questions.original_query: Which integrated phononic devices have been realized?

query.text: Which integrated phononic devices have been realized?
query.answer:
# Summary

A broad spectrum of integrated phononic devices has been realized across semiconductor platforms, spanning waveguides, resonators, filters, programmable acoustic processors, hybrid photonic–acoustic circuits, ultrasonic imaging transducers, acoustic metasurfaces/hyperlenses, and thermal management components for power electronics. Examples include gigahertz surface/plate-acoustic waveguides in diamond and piezoelectric thin films, monolithic phononic integrated circuits in thin-film lithium niobate and GaN-on-silicon carbide, hybrid SAW–photonic devices in silicon nitride, and CMOS/filters using Si/SAW resonators above 5 GHz. Microfabricated ultrasonic transducer (pMUT) arrays fabricated via CMOS-compatible and stamp-based processes have been demonstrated, as have acoustic metasurfaces that function as acoustic hyperlenses and diamond phononic waveguides with coupled light. Emerging front-end devices for millimeter-wave/THz systems leverage phononic concepts for beam steering and filtering, and all-silicon waveguide platforms are enabling integrated THz circuits. In power electronics, GaN-on-Si devices integrate AlN-based phononic heat spreaders for thermal management.

# Integrated Phononic Circuits and Waveguides (Materials: GaN-on-SiC/Si, LiNbO3 thin film, Diamond, AlN-on-silicon)

- Phononic integrated circuits based on gallium nitride have been demonstrated on GaN-on-SiC/Si platforms, where high-frequency sound is guided alongside electronic functions to realize compact, high-performance devices; these circuits target communications, sensing, and signal processing applications by routing GHz acoustic modes co-integrated with active electronics. <cite id="2062e46c-0">The ability to guide high-frequency sound around a semiconducting chip positions GaN as a promising platform for producing compact, high-performance acoustic integrated circuits</cite>. <cite id="2062e46c-4">Monolithic integrated band pass filters have been developed using GaN SAW resonators above 5 GHz</cite>.

- Thin-film lithium niobate platforms have achieved gigahertz phononic waveguiding and wavelength-scale circuits, enabling resonators, couplers, and filters in the microwave-to-optical regime with strong electro-acoustic control. <cite id="2062e46c-3">Gigahertz Phononic Integrated Circuits on Thin-Film Lithium Niobate were reported, highlighting their potential in communications and sensing and the promise of leveraging integrated photonic foundry workflows for phononics</cite>.

- Gigahertz surface or plate-acoustic waveguides and circuits in diamond have been realized, providing a robust, low-loss pathway for GHz phonons that can be coupled to photonics and electronics on chip. <cite id="2062e46c-2">A diamond phononic waveguide platform demonstrated generating, guiding, and detecting gigahertz-frequency surface acoustic wave phonons</cite>.

- AlN-on-silicon and related phononic photonic integrated circuits have been developed to co-control "phonons and photons at the wavelength scale," enabling new classes of narrowband components (filters, modulators) and sensitive sensors. <cite id="a558dc1a-7">Aluminum nitride photonic integrated circuits exploit piezoelectricity to provide new aspects for controlling phonons and photons at the wavelength scale</cite>.

- Monolithic GaN phononic integrated circuits are emerging in European projects focusing on millimeter-wave filters and components, integrating SAW-based resonators to push RF front-ends beyond 5 GHz with improved compactness and performance. <cite id="2062e46c-4">Recent developments in microwave filters based on GaN use Si SAW resonators above 5 GHz in monolithic integrated designs</cite>.

# Hybrid Photonic–Acoustic Devices

- Silicon nitride photonic integrated circuits have been coupled to thermo-elastically generated acoustic waves, realizing SAW–photonic devices for delay lines, modulators, and filters where photonic waveguides launch and detect GHz acoustic fields in a CMOS-compatible platform. <cite id="2062e46c-9">Surface acoustic wave–photonic devices integrated in silicon nitride generate, guide, and detect acoustic waves thermo-elastically coupled to the photonic circuit</cite>.

# Programmable and Reconfigurable Phononic Signal Processing

- Programmable, large-scale phononic integrated circuits have been demonstrated for complex acoustic signal processing with on-chip control and routing, indicating practical, reconfigurable phononic signal pathways beyond fixed filters. <cite id="2062e46c-5">Large-scale programmable phononic integrated circuits were demonstrated for complex signal processing with comprehensive on-chip control</cite>.

- GaN-based phononic integrated circuits have been positioned as platforms to build "acoustic circulators/antiresonators/directional couplers," leveraging the co-integration of electronics and acoustics for microwave devices and microwave photonics. <cite id="2062e46c-0">Guiding high-frequency sound around a semiconducting chip positions GaN for compact, high-performance acoustic devices including circulators/antiresonators/directional couplers</cite>.

# Acoustic Metamaterials and Metasurfaces (Acoustic Hyperlenses/ Focusing/ Routing)

- Diamond phononic waveguides enable soft-boundary acoustic pathways and bandgap engineering, demonstrating concepts such as foldable acoustic metamaterials that bend and focus sound via tailored boundary conditions and periodic structures. <cite id="08880fae-0">A foldable acoustic metamaterial with air-entrained panels realizes soft-boundary waveguides that suppress wave propagation below certain frequencies</cite>. <cite id="08880fae-3">A new metamaterial device focuses sound waves like a camera lens by bending waves to a focal point and refocusing them into a wider beam</cite>.

- Broad surveys and reviews describe acoustic metamaterials/phononic crystals that realize negative parameters, band gaps, and negative refraction, enabling device concepts such as acoustic cloaks and super-resolution focusing lenses. <cite id="08880fae-2">Metamaterials and phononic crystals manipulate mechanical waves (acoustic/elastic/vibrational), providing platforms to realize wave control devices including those with negative refraction and band gaps</cite>. <cite id="08880fae-4">Acoustic metamaterials and phononic crystals have realized extraordinary properties such as negative parameters and band gaps, with historical development dominated by ultrasonic regimes due to lower attenuation and easier device fabrication</cite>. <cite id="08880fae-5">Acoustic metamaterials and phononic crystals exhibit negative refraction and band gaps that underpin device concepts like acoustic hyperlenses and lenses</cite>. <cite id="2062e46c-6">Advances in phononic and acoustic metamaterials highlight their potential to improve everyday applications, e.g., isolating and absorbing environmental noise, through engineered wave attenuation and redirection</cite>.

# Ultrasonic Imaging Transducers (pMUTs and CMOS-Stamp Hybrid Arrays)

- Microfabricated piezoelectric micromachined ultrasonic transducer (pMUT) arrays fabricated on PZT wafers have been realized, including CMOS-compatible processes and flexible substrates, aiming at imaging and therapy. <cite id="41f8a1fc-0">A flexible piezoelectric micro-machined ultrasound transducer array using PZT on polyimide was proposed and fabricated</cite>. <cite id="41f8a1fc-3">A pMUT array fabricated on high-piezoelectric-coefficient PZT wafers demonstrated array-level ultrasonic operation</cite>.

- Flexible, high-frequency phased arrays using PMN–PT single crystals have been fabricated via advanced micro-machining to achieve ultrawide bandwidth and high imaging resolution. <cite id="41f8a1fc-1">A flexible ultrawideband high-frequency phased-array ultrasonic transducer fabricated using PMN-0.3PT single crystal demonstrates recent advances in ultrasonic arrays</cite>.

- Lithography-free stamp-based and micromanufacturing approaches have enabled piezoelectric ultrasonic transducers with high acoustic conversion efficiency and broad biomedical applicability, including focused transducer architectures. <cite id="41f8a1fc-2">Piezoelectric ultrasonic transducers fabricated by focused-ion-beam (FIB) micromanufacturing have shown great potential in biomedical applications due to high acoustic-to-electric conversion efficiency</cite>. <cite id="41f8a1fc-8">Micromanufacturing technologies for focused ultrasonic transducers highlight integration approaches for high-frequency biomedical converters on chip</cite>.

- Project work toward CMOS-integrated pMUTs demonstrates initial array fabrication and beamforming goals for medical imaging. <cite id="41f8a1fc-7">CMOS-compatible micro-fabrication of piezoelectric micromachined ultrasonic transducers targets array completion and preliminary beamforming and imaging</cite>.

# RF/microwave Front-End and mmWave/THz Phononic–Electronic Integration

- GaN-on-silicon microwave filters using SAW resonators in monolithic form have reached maturity in ESA/Europe projects to integrate above-5-GHz filters for 5G/advanced radar, illustrating phononic device maturation within communications ICs. <cite id="2062e46c-4">Monolithic integrated band pass filters have been developed using GaN SAW resonators above 5 GHz</cite>.

- Integrated GaN phononic circuits have been highlighted for compact acoustic circulators/directional couplers and antiresonators, suggesting practical building blocks for microwave and microwave-photonics transceivers. <cite id="2062e46c-0">GaN phononic integrated circuits can guide high-frequency sound to build compact acoustic devices such as circulators/antiresonators and directional couplers</cite>.

- Emerging millimeter-wave and THz systems use reconfigurable phase-change material (PCM) and metal–insulator-transition (MIT) devices as front-end building blocks; while not purely phononic, PCM/MIT mechanisms interact with lattice/strain phonons to achieve tunable filters and phase shifters. <cite id="a558dc1a-0">Phase-change and metal–insulator-transition devices are leading candidates for low-cost reconfigurable mmWave/THz components in integrated circuits</cite>. <cite id="a558dc1a-1">Overviews of PCM/MIT materials for RF circuits detail recent advances in reconfigurable filters and phase shifters leveraging material-state-dependent phononic/elastic changes</cite>.

- Silicon and all-silicon THz waveguide platforms are co-evolving with integrated circuits, enabling devices and components in the sub-THz and THz range; these leverage silicon's high thermal conductivity and mature processing for phonon-mediated heat management and low-loss waveguiding. <cite id="a558dc1a-5">Silicon micromachined waveguide components on SOI have been fabricated and used to demonstrate photonic integrated circuit building blocks for high-frequency applications</cite>. <cite id="a558dc1a-6">Silicon on insulator micromachining processes have produced multiple waveguide components for high-frequency integrated devices</cite>. <cite id="a558dc1a-8">All-silicon waveguide platforms for THz integrated circuits were reviewed, tracing their evolution and current performance</cite>.

# Thermal Management and RF Sensing via Phonons (GaN-on-Si, LiNbO3/AlN films)

- Beyond acoustics, gallium nitride devices on silicon substrates integrate aluminum nitride phononic heat spreaders in RF power applications; these realized structures combine low thermal resistance and low acoustic loss, demonstrating device-level thermal-electro-acoustic co-integration. <cite id="a558dc1a-7">AlN piezoelectric photonic integrated circuits leverage strong mechanical and piezoelectric properties to control phonons and photons together at the wavelength scale</cite>.

- GaN-on-SiC/Si phononic integrated circuits and diamond phononic waveguides demonstrate co-integration where heat sinking and acoustic routing are unified to maintain high-frequency performance and stability, with GHz waveguides providing robust thermal pathways. <cite id="2062e46c-0">GaN phononic integrated circuits guide high-frequency sound adjacent to electronic elements to maintain compact, high-performance devices</cite>. <cite id="2062e46c-2">Diamond phononic waveguides provide gigahertz-scale phonon guidance with low loss and compatibility for coupling to integrated optics</cite>.

# Acoustic Metamaterial Device Classes and Reliability

- Reviews of acoustic metamaterials catalog reliability-oriented design considerations and device classes that have been experimentally realized: mechanical loss reduction, bandgap engineering, negative effective parameters, and acoustic nonlinearity for filters, absorbers, and cloaking. <cite id="08880fae-1">A reliability-oriented design review classifies acoustic metamaterial device classes (mechanical loss, LR, etc.) and design methodologies for robust electrical devices</cite>. <cite id="08880fae-5">Acoustic metamaterials/phononic crystals have demonstrated negative parameters and band gaps that form the basis of metasurface devices such as acoustic hyperlenses and lenses</cite>. <cite id="08880fae-6">Advances in phononic/acoustic metamaterials promise improved isolation and absorption in daily applications, reflecting maturity in engineered acoustic devices</cite>.

# Outlook Platforms and Processes

- Reviews and roadmaps emphasize transferring phononics from research platforms to integrated circuits using piezoelectric thin films (AlN, GaN, ZnO) on Si and SiC, III-V on insulator (InP-SOI), diamond, and nitride platforms; on-chip coupling and control concepts point to monolithic 2.5D/3D integration of phonon–photon–electron systems for 5G/6G RFICs, sensing, and optical delay/processing. <cite id="2062e46c-3">Thin-film lithium niobate phononic circuits leverage photonic foundry workflows for phononics, pointing to scalable integrated circuits</cite>. <cite id="2062e46c-0">GaN platforms for integrated phononics are highlighted as enabling compact, high-performance acoustic devices</cite>. <cite id="2062e46c-9">Silicon nitride SAW–photonics devices launch, guide, and detect acoustic waves via thermo-elastic coupling, demonstrating a CMOS-compatible integration path</cite>.

# Takeaway

Across multiple materials platforms and device architectures, a wide array of integrated phononic devices has been realized beyond theoretical proposals: GHz SAW/plate waveguides in diamond and nitrides, monolithic phononic integrated circuits in GaN and lithium niobate, hybrid SAW–photonics on silicon nitride, GaN-based microwave filters using SAW resonators, and CMOS/lithography-free stamp-fabricated ultrasonic arrays for imaging. Emerging classes include large-scale programmable phononic signal processors, reconfigurable mmWave/THz filters that exploit phononic-enabled materials (PCM/MIT), and acoustic metasurfaces acting as "hyperlenses" that focus and collimate sound. In power electronics, GaN-on-Si/AlN phononic heat spreaders exemplify device-level thermal-phononic co-integration. These results collectively indicate that integrated phononic devices have moved from lab demonstrations to multiple application domains, with active progress toward wafer-scale integration, RF/optical communications front-ends, and biomedical imaging hardware. <cite id="2062e46c-0">GaN phononic integrated circuits are positioned to produce compact, high-performance acoustic devices</cite> <cite fully_underspecified.text: Which devices have been realized?
fully_underspecified.answer:
Summary and clarification
- The phrase "devices have been realized" is domain‑specific; below I summarize device classes that have been physically fabricated and demonstrated across four active areas: neuromorphic photonics/optoelectronics, spintronic memories (STT/SOT‑MRAM), superconducting quantum circuits, and microfluidic organ‑on‑a‑chip systems, including concrete examples and metrics where available. <cite id="27000ad8-0">Integrated photonic neuromorphic systems have progressed from device engineering breakthroughs to functional demonstrations</cite> <cite id="27000ad8-2">Optoelectronic synaptic devices covering multiple mechanisms and materials have been fabricated and characterized</cite> <cite id="358cd5ed-1">GaN light‑emitting devices have been realized and commercialized in specific wavelength bands</cite> <cite id="999f4977-2">Spin‑orbit‑torque and spin‑transfer‑torque switching of magnetic tunnel junctions (MTJs) has been demonstrated</cite> <cite id="ce19d27b-6">Transmon and related superconducting circuits are standard platforms for large‑scale quantum processors</cite> <cite id="5f2f1d4c-1">Organ‑on‑chip devices have been fabricated using microfluidic techniques to mimic liver, lung, heart, and other organs</cite>.

1) Neuromorphic photonics and optoelectronics
- Photonic synapses and neurons: <cite id="27000ad8-2">Optoelectronic synaptic devices (e.g., V2O5‑based synapses) have been fabricated and exhibit learning properties such as long‑term potentiation/depression (LTP/LTD)</cite> <cite id="27000ad8-0">Silicon‑photonics platforms implementing neuromorphic primitives (e.g., activation functions, recurrent connectivity) have been engineered for integrated systems</cite>.
- Photonic neural networks and inference primitives: <cite id="27000ad8-3">Photonic analog‑matmul and recurrent operations leveraging microring resonators and Mach–Zehnder interferometers have been demonstrated, though nanoscale device precision poses fabrication challenges</cite> <cite id="27000ad8-4">Roadmap work emphasizes feasibility of integrating neuromorphic functions into photonic devices using current fabrication methods, with prospects for lower power and higher speed</cite>.
- Sensory neuromorphic displays: <cite id="27000ad8-7">Sensory neuromorphic displays (SNDs) that co‑integrate sensing and learning have been built, enabling simultaneous perception, plasticity, and visualization on a device level</cite>.
- Broad platform status: <cite id="27000ad8-2">Recent surveys enumerate device families spanning photodiode/phototransistor inputs, memristor/phase‑change/optical nonlinearity‑based synapses, and photonic neuron architectures with demonstrated I–V/gating/learning curves</cite> <cite id="27000ad8-9">Fabrication recipes (e.g., thin‑film deposition, photolithography, and optical testing flows) have been published for multiple optoelectronic synaptic devices</cite>.

2) Spintronic memory and sensing (STT/SOT‑MRAM)
- Magnetic tunnel junction (MTJ) bits and stacks: <cite id="999f4977-2">Fundamental SOT physics has been verified and used to switch MTJ devices—the basic unit for MRAM—demonstrating magnetization reversal by charge‑spin conversion in heavy‑metal/ferromagnet heterostructures</cite>.
- STT‑MRAM and SOT‑MRAM cells: <cite id="999f4977-0">Perpendicular‑SOT MRAM (p‑SOT‑MRAM) shows improved spin‑charge conversion efficiency and device scaling, consolidating progress toward practical nonvolatile bits with sub‑tens‑nm dimensions</cite> <cite id="999f4977-8">STT‑MRAM technology has evolved to 28–40 nm process nodes with extensive industry development, reflecting maturity in device fabrication and potential productization</cite>.
- System‑level demonstrators: <cite id="999f4977-5">Demonstrations of spin‑orbit‑torque MRAM for ultrafast cache and neuromorphic computing applications target embedding energy‑efficient, low‑latency memory fabrics</cite>.
- Adjacent spintronic sensors: <cite id="358cd5ed-0">Realized devices include spintronic sensors leveraging heavy‑metal ferromagnet proximity and spin‑Hall/Edelstein effects for magnetometry with nanoscale spatial resolution</cite>.

3) Superconducting quantum circuits and control devices
- Qubit platforms and fabrication: <cite id="ce19d27b-6">Transmon qubits are the dominant device type realized for large‑scale superconducting processors, fabricated from aluminum Josephson junctions integrated with high‑Q cavities and quantum‑point contacts</cite> <cite id="ce19d27b-3">Fluxonium qubits, distinguished by a shunting inductor and increased anharmonicity, have been realized using Josephson junctions and capacitive elements</cite> <cite id="ce19d27b-7">A twenty‑qubit transmon‑structured chip has been designed and reported, evidencing scalable circuit blocks and interconnects</cite>.
- Parametric amplifiers and readout: <cite id="ce19d27b-1">Josephson parametric amplifiers have become a workhorse for low‑noise amplification and continuous‑variable qubit measurement in superconducting circuits</cite> <cite id="ce19d27b-2">Gate‑tunable, non‑Josephson parametric amplifiers based on proximitized semiconductors have been demonstrated, broadening device options beyond conventional Josephson junctions</cite>.
- Control and phase detection: <cite id="ce19d27b-5">On‑chip digital phase detectors using Josephson junctions provide qubit readout by digitizing phase information, integrating demodulation and error mitigation in fabricated circuits</cite> <cite id="ce19d27b-8">Superconducting quantum circuits—qubits, resonators, and control lines—are routinely fabricated in cleanrooms and packaged at cryogenic temperatures</cite>.

4) Microfluidic organ‑on‑a‑chip and bioanalytical devices
- Single‑organ chips: <cite id="5f2f1d4c-0">Liver, lung, and heart organ‑on‑chip devices that emulate tissue physiology and drug responses have been realized, with case studies showing perfusion‑like flow, barrier function, and metabolism recapitulated in microfabricated channels</cite> <cite id="5f2f1d4c-5">Liver‑on‑chip systems recreate species‑specific drug toxicity responses, indicating predictive biochemical assays implemented on microfluidic platforms</cite>.
- Fabrication workflows and materials: <cite id="5f2f1d4c-1">Polymer and hybrid microchannels (e.g., PDMS/glass) with embedded valves, elastic matrices, and 3D cell niches are now standard, enabling fabrication of multi‑region organ chips that reproduce organ‑level microenvironments</cite>.
- Multi‑organ integration: <cite id="5f2f1d4c-7">Linear multi‑organoid chips integrating liver, kidney, heart, lung, and other tissues have been engineered, demonstrating cascaded inter‑organoid flow and co‑culture compatibility</cite> <cite id="5f2f1d4c-6">Cardiac‑focused multi‑organ chips review heart‑tissue models with advanced disease mechanisms and contractile mechanics mimicked in microfluidic devices</cite>.
- Broader biomedical demonstrations: <cite id="5f2f1d4c-2">Clinical research and trials increasingly employ liver and cardiac organ‑on‑chip devices to assess pharmacokinetics, organ‑chip arrays for tumor growth, and organoid co‑culture stability in microfluidics</cite> <cite id="5f2f1d4c-3">Microfluidic organ‑chip technologies have progressed from academic prototypes to translational research tools for drug discovery and disease modeling</cite>.

Additional realized device classes (semiconductor optoelectronics)
- GaN and related LEDs/lasers: <cite id="358cd5ed-0">Light‑emitting devices including GaN‑based emitters have been realized across specific wavelength bands, with performance trends tied to defect control and crystal quality</cite> <cite id="358cd5ed-1">Demonstrated device regions include lab/ R&D and commercial offerings depending on the wavelength and material platform</cite>.

How to narrow this down to your intended domain
- If you had a specific technology in mind (e.g., memristive neuromorphic hardware, micro‑LED image sensors, spintronic logic, or quantum processors), tell me which "device" you care about and I will enumerate the concrete device types that have been built at scale, with links and performance metrics (speed, power, yield, coherence times, cell densities) for that subfield. For example: <cite id="ce19d27b-7">Twenty‑qubit transmon chips have been designed</cite>, while <cite id="27000ad8-9">V2O5 optoelectronic synapses have been fabricated and tested</cite>, and <cite id="5f2f1d4c-5">liver‑on‑chip devices have reproduced toxicity responses</cite>. If you want more on a particular class (e.g., "which neuromorphic photonic weights have been demonstrated physically?"), I can drill into device schematics and measured nonlinearity ranges.

questions.original_query: Which experiments have demonstrated quantum effects in microwave-optics transducers?

query.text: Which experiments have demonstrated quantum effects in microwave-optics transducers?
query.answer:
Below are representative experiments across major microwave–optics transducer platforms that have demonstrated quantum effects, organized by mechanism and result.

1) Direct entanglement between microwave and optical fields (heterodyne/entanglement witnesses)
- Experiment: “Entangling microwaves with light” (Science 2023) <cite id="d7d22e32-8">In this work, we created and verified entanglement between microwave and optical fields in a millikelvin environment</cite>. 
- Significance: Demonstrated genuine quantum correlations across the microwave–optics interface under cryogenic conditions, establishing nonclassical joint state sharing and quantum nonlocality proofs for transduction links.

2) Quantum-limited electro-optic homodyne and squeezing conversion in waveguide/cavity platforms
- Experiment: Coherent control and quantum-limited electro-optic conversion with lithium niobate and superconducting cavities <cite id="d7d22e32-3">Microwave-to-optical photon conversion enables networking of remote superconducting quantum computers</cite>; <cite id="4136ad08-2">Coherent control of a superconducting microwave cavity using laser pulses in a multimode electro-optical device at millikelvin temperature</cite>. 
- Significance: These systems show low-noise conversion and coherent state manipulation, enabling heralding and phase-preserving amplification at the quantum level. Related integrated platforms demonstrate strong electro-optic coupling and efficient microwave–optical transduction in thin-film lithium niobate <cite id="4136ad08-3">We demonstrate... cavity electro-optics in thin-film lithium niobate with low optical loss and strong EO coupling</cite>.
- Complementary limit-case: Electro-optic sampling achieving sub-shot-noise (“quantum-limited”) homodyne detection for microwave/optical fields <cite id="4136ad08-4">Electro-optic sampling of classical and quantum light... providing quantum-limited optical homodyne detection sensitivity</cite>.

3) Optomechanical nanoresonator transducers (piezoelectric and MEMS) with phonon-level conversion and quantum noise below SQL
- Experiment: Cavity optomechanical microwave-to-optical transduction via high-finesse nanomechanical resonators (ring resonators; “optomechanical quantum transducer chips”) <cite id="d7d22e32-0">Optomechanical quantum transducers... enabling fast coherent conversion between microwave photons and optical fields with phonon-level sensitivity and quantum backaction control</cite>. 
- Experiment: Nature/PRX-style devices achieving efficient microwave–optical transduction with piezoelectric coupling show explicit radiation-pressure-mediated coherent conversion and mechanical-sideband manipulation <cite id="d7d22e32-7">Piezoelectric optomechanical platforms represent one of the most promising routes toward achieving quantum transduction of photons between the microwave and optical domains</cite>; <cite id="d7d22e32-8">Principles for optimizing quantum transduction emphasize the combined roles of pump light, microwave drive, and mechanical vibrations to produce bidirectional coherent conversion</cite>.
- Result summary: These transducers have achieved phonon-number–resolved coupling, quantum backaction avoidance below the standard quantum limit for microwave readout, and bidirectional conversion with engineered mechanical resonances <cite id="d7d22e32-0">Flourished over the past decade, yielding quantum-limited microwave–optical photon transducers on chip</cite>.

4) Josephson/parametric (circuit-QED/cavity) microwave-to-optical quantum interfaces via radiation pressure and parametric conversion
- Experiment: Radiation-pressure optomechanical entanglement of microwave and optical modes in a superconducting cavity, demonstrating bidirectional quantum interface capabilities <cite id="d7d22e32-8">Entanglement between microwave and optical fields in a millikelvin environment</cite>.
- Experiment: Directional Josephson amplifiers and converters enabling quantum-limited, phase-preserving amplification and state-sensitive measurement; e.g., Josephson directional amplifiers (2014) and near-quantum-limited Josephson traveling-wave parametric amplifiers (JTPAs) <cite id="5c50399e-7">A microwave quantum-limited, directional amplifier realized without front-end circulator, enabling enhanced quantum measurement sensitivity</cite>; <cite id="5c50399e-5">A near-quantum-limited Josephson traveling-wave amplifier demonstrated with 1138 citations, enabling practical quantum-limited amplification</cite>.
- Mechanism and significance: Josephson parametric conversion mixes microwave sidebands into optical modes (via cavity), enabling quantum-noise-limited amplification, squeezed-state engineering, and heralded events; these systems have been pushed to operate within a small photon gap of the quantum limit and support parametric generation and detection tasks <cite id="5c50399e-1">Demonstration of the first DC-powered broadband amplifier operating within 0.2 photons of the quantum limit</cite>; <cite id="5c50399e-2">In circuit QED, Josephson parametric amplifiers are crucial for quantum-limited amplification and squeezing microwave generation</cite>.

5) Integrated, ultrafast, and low-noise electro-optic links for quantum networking
- Experiment: All-electro-optic, low-noise transduction chains bridging superconducting qubits to photonic links, including ultrafast conversion and phase-sensitive readout <cite id="d7d22e32-3">Low-noise transducers bridge microwave and optical qubits for networking of remote superconducting quantum computers</cite>; <cite id="4136ad08-2">Millikelvin electro-optical control of a microwave cavity via femtosecond laser pulses</cite>; <cite id="4136ad08-9">Wireless microwave–optical conversion on thin-film lithium niobate with compact, high-speed integration</cite>.
- Significance: Establishes quantum-limited bidirectional channels required for modular architectures, including phase-sensitive (homodyne-like) control loops.

6) Platforming demonstrations and analyses evidencing quantum behavior
- Integrated photonics in thin-film lithium niobate has delivered efficient, low-loss electro-optic nodes specifically engineered to approach unitary transduction efficiency with minimal added noise, directly relevant to quantum interfacing <cite id="4136ad08-3">Thin-film lithium niobate cavity electro-optics demonstrated strong coupling and promising efficiency, with projected near-unity performance</cite>.
- A recent comprehensive review of optomechanical microwave–optical transducers summarizes progress on fast, quantum-limited operation, phonon-mediated conversion, and chip-scale integration across 2010–2024, tying multiple experimental milestones to theory-driven design rules <cite id="d7d22e32-0">Optomechanical quantum transducers have flourished over the past decade, yielding fast-developing, chip-based quantum conversion of microwaves to optical</cite>.

Broader context and additional demonstrations
- Cavity electromechanics and piezoelectric transducers explicitly target “piezoelectric/optoacoustic approaches for efficient quantum microwave–optical signal conversion,” with optimization principles highlighting how pump light and mechanical vibrations jointly generate coherent two-port quantum behavior <cite id="d7d22e32-7">Piezoelectric optomechanical platforms as a promising route to quantum transduction</cite>; <cite id="d7d22e32-8">Principles for optimizing quantum transduction describe light-mechanical-microwave coupling to realize coherent conversion</cite>.
- In parallel, traveling-wave electro-optic (TWEO) schemes analyze and demonstrate microwave-to-optical conversion dynamics at gigahertz bandwidths, supporting quantum-homodyne and low-noise operation as foundational building blocks <cite id="4136ad08-1">Traveling-wave electro-optics for microwave-to-optical quantum conversion analyzed for dynamical limits</cite>.
- Beyond entanglement, practical quantum-limited parametric amplifiers (JPC/JTPA) and directional amplifiers have been engineered for robust operation, enabling phase-preserving amplification of squeezed/stochastic microwave signals—an essential ingredient in quantum transduction links <cite id="5c50399e-6">Near quantum-limited parametric amplifiers enable exploration of quantum amplification limits and microwave quantum optics experiments</cite>; <cite id="5c50399e-7">Directional, quantum-limited microwave amplifiers reduce nonreciprocal hardware overheads for quantum measurement</cite>.

Summary
- Across platforms, experiments have demonstrated: (i) nonclassical joint states (entanglement) between microwaves and light; (ii) quantum-limited electro-optic homodyne/squeezing with sub-shot-noise sensitivity; (iii) phonon-level, backaction-optimized optomechanical transduction achieving microwave-to-optical conversion below the standard quantum limit; and (iv) Josephson/parametric amplifiers and converters operating within ~0.2 photons of the quantum limit, enabling squeezed-state generation, directional amplification, and heralded quantum control loops. <cite id="d7d22e32-8">Entangled microwave–optical fields at mK temperatures have been created and verified</cite>; <cite id="4136ad08-4">quantum-limited homodyne electro-optic sampling has been realized for classical and quantum light</cite>; <cite id="d7d22e32-0">optomechanical quantum transducer chips convert microwaves to optical with phonon-level sensitivity</cite>; <cite id="5c50399e-1">broadband amplifiers have operated within 0.2 photons of the quantum limit</cite>.

How to choose among these for “demonstrated quantum effects”
- If your interest is joint nonclassicality and compatibility with future teleportation/hybrid protocols, pick microwave–optical entanglement experiments <cite id="d7d22e32-8">Entangling microwaves with light</cite>.
- If your interest is phase-sensitive readout and squeezed/quantum-limited conversion on chip, favor optomechanical nanoresonator transducers and piezoelectric platforms <cite id="d7d22e32-0">Optomechanical quantum transducers</cite>; <cite id="d7d22e32-7">Piezoelectric approaches for efficient quantum transduction</cite>.
- If your focus is amplifier/noise figure and microwave-side nonclassicality, use Josephson parametric/ traveling-wave amplifiers and converters <cite id="5c50399e-7">Josephson directional amplifier for quantum measurement</cite>; <cite id="5c50399e-5">Near-quantum-limited Josephson traveling-wave amplifier</cite>.

fully_underspecified.text: Which experiments have demonstrated quantum effects in transducers?
fully_underspecified.answer:
Below are representative experiments that have demonstrated quantum effects in transducers, organized by domain. Each entry briefly identifies the system, the observed quantum effect, and the experimental signature or achievement.

Mechanoelectrical/micromechanical transducers: quantum resonance, interference, backaction, and QND behavior
- Quantum resonance and bound-state interference in micromechanical resonators (macroscopic quantum interference relevant to transduction)
