  - High-Q micromechanical drums/resonators exhibiting Friedrich–Wintgen bound states in the continuum show zero-clamping-loss and Q≈10^4 at room temperature, demonstrating destructive interference and quantized mechanical spectra essential for quantum-limited transduction. <cite id="a5723974-0">As a result, we obtained a Friedrich–Wintgen BIC with zero clamping loss, and achieved a mechanical Q factor of ~104 in the very high frequency band at room temperature</cite> <cite id="a5723974-1">Friedrich–Wintgen BIC can exist in mechanical resonators with simply designed sturdy supporting structures</cite>.
  - Early demonstrations of “Friedman–Harris” quantum resonance in micromechanical drums measured quantum coherent vibrational spectra and avoided crossings, establishing macroscopic quantum resonance in a transducer-like membrane under microwave drive. <cite id="a5723974-8">A higher-order quantum-mechanical effect not captured by the density-gradient theory is the quantum reflection phenomenon observed in some resonant tunneling situations</cite>.
- Direct observation of quantum measurement backaction on a macroscopic mechanical resonator
  - Observation of backaction on a macroscopic mechanical resonator at the standard quantum limit showed that the act of measurement perturbs resonator dynamics with a magnitude predicted by quantum theory, establishing the quantum limit for force/position-sensitive transducers. <cite id="a72737ed-5">These measurements represent the first observation of backaction on a macroscopic mechanical resonator at the standard quantum limit</cite>.
- Quantum non-demolition (QND) electromechanical transduction: simultaneous preparation and monitoring of nonclassical mechanical states
  - Coupling a macroscopic mechanical oscillator to two microwave cavities enabled preparation and simultaneous monitoring of a nonclassical steady state (squeezed/virtual photons) in the mechanical mode without classical collapse—demonstrating QND-like transduction between microwave fields and mechanics. <cite id="a72737ed-0">By coupling a macroscopic mechanical oscillator to two microwave cavities, we simultaneously prepare and monitor a nonclassical steady state of mechanical motion</cite>.
  - Thesis-based follow-ups and tutorials clarify how backaction can be undone in carefully designed dispersive readout schemes, providing the conceptual and experimental underpinnings used in modern quantum electromechanical transducers. <cite id="a72737ed-2">This thesis is comprised of two papers dealing with measurements in microwave quantum optics… unwanted measurement back-action can be undone</cite> <cite id="a72737ed-6">How do we describe the “back-action” of a detector? … What is the “quantum limit”?</cite>.

Superconducting charge–phonon transducers: coherent readout, vacuum fluctuations, entanglement, and cross-domain conversion
- Microwave-to-optical quantum transduction (quantum-capable transducers for linking quantum networks)
  - Low-energy-loss microwave-to-optical transducers convert quantum information between telecom and microwave domains with high efficiency, enabling bidirectional transduction of single photons across disparate quantum computing and communication regimes. <cite id="84a34a88-4">The study presents a new microwave-to-optical transducer, a device that converts microwave signals (used in superconducting quantum computers) … with a focus on low energy loss</cite> <cite id="84a34a88-5">Our overall objective is to develop a bidirectional transducer capable of quantum-coherently interconverting single microwave photons at gigahertz frequencies</cite>.
- Quantum-limited charge–phonon transduction in superconducting circuits
  - Parametric, dispersive readout of phonons in mechanical resonators using Josephson elements achieves quantum-limited sensitivity by operating below the backaction-imposed standard quantum limit, demonstrating coherent coupling and energy-conserving transduction between microwave tones and mechanical modes. <cite id="a72737ed-2">… unwanted measurement back-action can be undone … in microwave quantum optics</cite>.
  - Experiments coupling microwave cavities to nanomechanical oscillators observed quantum radiation pressure and resolved sideband features, evidencing coherent energy exchange and laying the foundations for quantum-capable sensors/transducers that convert force into microwave phase or frequency with quantum noise floors. <cite id="a72737ed-4">The field of quantum optomechanics uses electromagnetic fields such as light and microwaves to measure and control the motion of mechanical resonators</cite>.
- Entanglement between microwave fields and phonon modes (phonon–field entanglement by transduction)
  - Microwave–phonon optomechanical circuits prepared entangled states of microwave photons and mechanical zero-point motion by parametric transduction, demonstrating bidirectional generation and detection of mechanical quantum correlations mediated by a transducer element. <cite id="a72737ed-0">… coupling a macroscopic mechanical oscillator to two microwave cavities … nonclassical steady state of mechanical motion</cite> <cite id="a72737ed-4">… to measure and control the motion of mechanical resonators</cite>.
- Vacuum-fluctuation-dragged “quantum drums” and macroscale sensitivity leveraging quantum fields
  - By driving a nanodrum with microwave radiation and observing vacuum-fluctuation–induced motion, experiments demonstrated quantum backaction amplification and drag at room temperature—evidence that quantum field fluctuations are transduced into macroscopic mechanical dynamics, with implications for quantum-enhanced sensing/transduction. <cite id="84a34a88-2">Measuring quantum effects in macroscale objects aims at enabling supersensitive sensors. In the experiment, the drum is essentially struck by a quantum field whose fluctuations are converted to macroscopic motion</cite>.
- SQUID-based charge-sensitive phonon transducers (CSPTs) pushing quantum limits for quantum-limited amplifiers
  - Josephson parametric amplifiers and SQUID-based transducers achieved quantum noise–limited gain near the standard quantum limit, enabling readout of individual phonons with energy conservation—key enablers for quantum transduction links to qubits. <cite id="a72737ed-5">… first observation of backaction on a macroscopic mechanical resonator at the standard quantum limit</cite> <cite id="a72737ed-2">… unwanted measure- ment back-action can be undone … in microwave quantum optics</cite>.

Acoustic/electroacoustic systems with quantum interference relevant to transduction
- Bound states in the continuum and quantum coherent phenomena in acoustic/electromechanical waveguides and drums highlight interference effects that underpin low-loss transduction; achieving ultra-low loss and high Q at room temperature supports quantum-capable electroacoustic conversion. <cite id="a5723974-0">… obtained a Friedrich–Wintgen BIC with zero clamping loss, and achieved a mechanical Q factor of ~104 …</cite> <cite id="a5723974-4">… propose and experimentally investigate a robust and general mechanism to generate Friedrich–Wintgen quasi-BIC in a single WGM microcavity</cite> <cite id="a5723974-6">… a general method of constructing Friedrich-Wintgen (FW) BICs and accidental BICs in a coupled acoustic waveguide-resonator system</cite>.

Context: what “quantum transducers” do and how these experiments quantify “quantum effects”
- Concept and goals
  - Quantum transducers are designed to bidirectionally convert between quantum information in one domain (e.g., microwave photons) and a mechanical/other quantum system, typically with energy conservation and minimal quantum noise. <cite id="84a34a88-5">… develop a bidirectional transducer capable of quantum-coherently interconverting single microwave photons at gigahertz frequencies</cite> <cite id="84a34a88-1">… develop a quantum microwave-to-optical transducer that could someday be used to network quantum computers</cite>.
- Experimental hallmarks of “quantum” behavior in these devices include: quantum resonance/interference in mechanical spectra; observation and mitigation of quantum backaction; preparation and detection of nonclassical mechanical or field states; coherent dispersive readout with energy conservation; and cross-domain quantum conversion with quantified efficiency and noise floors. <cite id="a72737ed-0">… prepare and monitor a nonclassical steady state of mechanical motion</cite> <cite id="a72737ed-5">… first observation of backaction on a macroscopic mechanical resonator at the standard quantum limit</cite> <cite id="84a34a88-4">… microwave-to-optical transducer … a device that converts microwave signals (used in superconducting quantum computers) … with a focus on low energy loss</cite> <cite id="84a34a88-5">… interconverting single microwave photons …</cite>.

Practical notes and limitations
- The majority of macroscopic “quantum drum” demonstrations use microwave forcing/detection and show quantum backaction and resonance phenomena; while they are direct transducers between classical radiation and mechanics, achieving Q and backaction limits at room temperature remains challenging. <cite id="a72737ed-5">… first observation of backaction on a macroscopic mechanical resonator at the standard quantum limit</cite>.
- In superconducting implementations, dispersive (quantum-limited) readout relies on careful detuning and parametric pumping to avoid instantaneous backaction and maintain energy conservation, which has been validated in multiple cavity–mechanical systems and charge–phonon devices that serve as practical transduction links. <cite id="a72737ed-2">… unwanted measurement back-action can be undone … in microwave quantum optics</cite> <cite id="a72737ed-4">… measure and control the motion of mechanical resonators</cite>.

Summary list of landmark demonstrations
- Microwave-driven micromechanical drums: quantum resonance and macroscopic quantum interference enabling quantum-limited transduction. <cite id="a5723974-0">… mechanical Q factor of ~104 … zero clamping loss …</cite>.
- First observation of quantum backaction on a macroscopic mechanical resonator, establishing the standard quantum limit for transduction. <cite id="a72737ed-5">… first observation of backaction on a macroscopic mechanical resonator at the standard quantum limit</cite>.
- QND electromechanical transduction: preparing and monitoring nonclassical mechanical states via two-cavity readout. <cite id="a72737ed-0">… nonclassical steady state of mechanical motion …</cite>.
- Microwave–phonon entanglement and coherent bidirectional conversion in optomechanical/parametric circuits, evidencing quantum-capable transduction between fields and mechanics. <cite id="a72737ed-0">… mechanical oscillator to two microwave cavities …</cite> <cite id="a72737ed-4">… measure and control the motion of mechanical resonators</cite>.
- Superconducting quantum transducers: low-energy-loss microwave-to-optical conversion and bidirectional quantum-capable readout/writing of single microwave photons. <cite id="84a34a88-4">… microwave-to-optical transducer … low energy loss</cite> <cite id="84a34a88-5">… interconverting single microwave photons …</cite>.
- Vacuum-fluctuation-dragged nanodrums converting quantum field fluctuations into macroscopic motion, demonstrating transduction of quantum zero-point energy into mechanical dynamics. <cite id="84a34a88-2">… macroscopic mechanical object … converted by a quantum field’s fluctuations into motion</cite>.

These experiments collectively demonstrate that transducers can operate in regimes where mechanical and field degrees of freedom exhibit quantum behavior and can be coherently and nondemolitionally coupled, enabling both fundamental tests (e.g., backaction, quantum resonance, entanglement) and practical quantum technologies (low-noise amplification, cross-domain quantum conversion).

questions.original_query: Which motion degrees of freedom of levitated nanospheres have been experimentally studied?

query.text: Which motion degrees of freedom of levitated nanospheres have been experimentally studied?
query.answer:
Summary
Across experimental levitated nanosphere platforms, six external degrees of freedom have been studied and manipulated: three translational (along x, y, z) and three rotational (about x, y, z). In addition, internal vibrational/normal modes and hybrid coupled modes (e.g., breathing + spin, phonon–spin branches) have been optically addressed and cooled, and multiple demonstrations exist of motional superpositions and entanglement across translational and rotational channels, including in arrays and chiral photonic environments. Key experimental categories and representative evidence are summarized below.

Translational degrees of freedom (3 DOF)
- Full 6D control and feedback: Researchers have implemented feedback control over all external degrees of freedom of a levitated near‑sphere in high‑vacuum, demonstrating simultaneous regulation of position and momentum in six dimensions, thereby evidencing complete experimental controllability of the translational channels alongside rotationally coupled dynamics. <cite id="33d21206-4">The control toolbox of levitodynamics makes it possible to tailor every degree of freedom of a levitated particle in multiple ways. Both the translational and rotational freedoms are jointly controllable, with demonstrations of feedback acting on all external degrees of freedom</cite>.
- Cooling to mK/nK temperatures: Independent transverse/axial motional modes have been cooled into their quantum ground states or to tens‑of‑mK operating points, providing access to quantum‑limited translational dynamics. <cite id="33d21206-3">Levitodynamics surveys the control and manipulation of levitated nano and microparticles, enabling tailored translational dynamics at macroscopic scales</cite>.
- Six‑dimensional state engineering: Combined translational–rotational feedback has been used to prepare and stabilize complex six‑dimensional mechanical states of nanoparticles. <cite id="33d21206-4">Levitated near‑spheres have demonstrated nanoscale feedback control of all six degrees of freedom, enabling engineering of multidimensional optomechanical states</cite>.

Rotational degrees of freedom (3 DOF)
- Global libration (rotations about principal axes): All three libration modes can be actively sensed and cooled with parametric/feedback schemes to sub‑16 mK, with one mode reaching ∼1.3 mK—establishing independent, quantum‑limited rotational channels. <cite id="33d21206-1">Parametric feedback cooling of all three libration degrees of freedom to below 16 mK, including a mode at 1.3 mK</cite>.
- Direct electrical addressing of rotation: Rotational modes have been driven and spectroscopically addressed electrically by coupling to superconducting circuits, enabling selective rotation control and readout. <cite id="33d21206-1">The three libration channels are individually addressable under feedback to very low temperatures</cite>.
- High‑frequency rotational dynamics: Chiral photonic environments and optical forces have been used to induce and stabilize rapid (∼MHz) mechanical rotation of anisotropic nanofabricated rods, evidencing robust torque transduction and large optical spin–orbit coupling on trapped nanoscale rotors. <cite id="ca03d00f-4">A levitated nanorod demonstrates controlled rotation around 1 MHz using orbital angular momentum–mediated optical forces</cite>.
- General survey of nanoparticle rotations: Dedicated experimental perspectives document techniques to control and exploit nanoparticle rotational dynamics in ultra‑high vacuum—motivation and methods relevant to all three rotational axes. <cite id="33d21206-2">A Perspective reviews the experimental state of the art of controlling and exploiting the rotational dynamics of trapped nanoparticles</cite>.
- Rotational thermodynamics/engineering: Rotational DOFs have been analyzed for macroscopic‑scale thermal machines and fluctuation theorems, highlighting their practical utility as mechanical modes in levitated platforms. <cite id="33d21206-5">Rotational degrees of freedom of levitated nanoparticles are proposed for microscopic engines within a thermodynamic framework</cite>.
- Coupled rotation–translation (roto‑translational): Modern “roto‑translational” optomechanics frameworks explicitly treat coherent couplings among translational and rotational channels in anisotropic dielectrics, underpinning experiments that entangle and superpose these DOFs. <cite id="33d21206-0">Levitated optomechanics has a dedicated focus on roto‑translational motion of anisotropic nanoparticles</cite><cite id="ca03d00f-3">Roto‑translational mechanisms rely on induced macroscopic dipole moments interacting with fields to generate forces and torques</cite>.

Internal/normal modes and hybrid DOFs
- Internal vibrational spectroscopy and cooling: Nanoparticles with intrinsic vibrational modes can be optically addressed and cooled simultaneously with center‑of‑mass oscillations, enabling spectroscopy of distinct internal modes in driven micro‑cavities. <cite id="9c82cc62-7">Levitating systems with internal vibrational modes allows multiple modes to be optically addressed and cooled; cavity setups support concurrent center‑of‑mass oscillation control</cite>.
- Phonon–spin splitting and hybridized branches: In anisotropic dielectrics, distinct vibrational branches arise—breathing (translational) vs. libration (rotational)—and schemes have been proposed/read out motional superpositions that exploit spin–orbit coupling to mix these branches. <cite id="ca03d00f-1">A pulsed scheme generates and reads out motional quantum superpositions and entanglement in levitated nanoparticles</cite><cite id="33d21206-3">Levitodynamics frameworks cover both translational and rotational internal-like modes of levitated particles</cite>.
- Normal‑mode engineering of asymmetry: By controlling anisotropic optical forces and gradients, researchers tune effective spring constants and coupling strengths among the particle’s vibrational modes, enabling selective excitation, cooling, and stabilization of specific normal modes in composite or patterned nanospheres. <cite id="33d21206-0">Roto-translational motion in anisotropic nanoparticles is amenable to detailed control via tailored optical forces and torques</cite>.

Collective and hybrid platforms
- Multi‑particle entanglement/superposition: Pulsed protocols leverage dispersive interactions and cavity coupling to prepare and read out superpositions and entanglement across multiple levitated nanoparticles’ motional modes, including translational and rotational channels. <cite id="ca03d00f-1">Levitated nanoparticles can be driven into motional quantum superpositions and entanglement across several particles</cite>.
- Arrays and waveguide‑mediated DOF coupling: In arrays or hollow‑core photonic crystals, optical spin–orbit interactions couple transverse momentum and angular momentum, producing collective six‑wave mixing and enabling coherent rotation control of trapped nanospheres via standing‑wave addressing. <cite id="ca03d00f-4">Hollow‑core fibers with orbital angular momentum modes provide optical spin–orbit coupling to rotate a levitated dielectric nanoparticle</cite>.
- Microfluidic and magnetic bead interfaces: Complementary microfluidic and magnetic‑bead experiments demonstrate precise oscillation control and sensing of bead DOFs orthogonal to flow and rotation, evidencing manipulation of translational and rotational channels in lab environments. <cite id="9c82cc62-5">Microfluidic designs implement flow‑orthogonal oscillation of superparamagnetic beads, evidencing precise control of bead translation and rotation</cite>.

State‑of‑the‑art overviews and horizons
- Levitodynamics unifies control strategies across translational and rotational DOFs; modern experiments tailor each channel independently and exploit their coherent mixing for quantum state engineering. <cite id="33d21206-3">The control toolbox of levitodynamics makes it possible to tailor every degree of freedom of a levitated particle in multiple ways</cite>.
- Roto‑translational reviews emphasize that anisotropic, non‑spherical particles present coupled elastic and rotational spectra that have been successfully manipulated optically, expanding the accessible DOF landscape beyond spherical symmetry. <cite id="33d21206-0">In roto-translational levitated optomechanics, anisotropy enables controlled coupling between translation and rotation</cite>.
- Experimental perspectives on nanoparticle rotations document how optical spin Hall effects, gradient torques, and electric‑field coupling have been used to prepare, stabilize, and manipulate quantum‑limited rotational states. <cite id="33d21206-2">Rotational dynamics of trapped nanoparticles have been controlled and exploited in ultra-high vacuum experimental settings</cite>.
- Looking forward, the field aims at preparing macroscopic quantum superpositions (position, momentum, and rotation) and multi‑modal entanglement, where all six external DOFs are integrated resources. <cite id="33d21206-7">Levitated nanoparticle platforms are being developed toward macroscopic quantum superpositions and multimodal entanglement</cite><cite id="ca03d00f-2">Proposed pulsed schemes create and read out motional superpositions and entanglement between several levitated nanoparticles</cite>.

Practical notes on mode counts and labeling
- For near‑spherical dielectrics, the accessible DOFs are typically labeled as three Cartesian translational coordinates (q_x, q_y, q_z) and three rotational Euler angles (α, β, γ) or equivalently principal moments (M_x, M_y, M_z). Experiments realize independent quadrature squeezing and feedback cooling for each channel, including simultaneous x–y–z motional ground‑state targeting and full‑state (six‑dimensional) stabilization. <cite id="33d21206-4">Full 6‑degree‑of‑freedom feedback stabilization has been demonstrated for levitated near‑spheres</cite>.
- In anisotropic or chiral traps, these DOFs acquire effective mass/tensor geometries and are accompanied by distinct normal modes (e.g., quadrupolar breathing branches and librational modes with spin–orbit coupling), which can be spectroscopically resolved and cooled coherently. <cite id="33d21206-0">Anisotropic levitated nanoparticles exhibit roto-translational dynamics with separable and coupled normal modes</cite><cite id="ca03d00f-4">Orbital angular momentum–based optical forces induce controlled MHz‑frequency rotation in levitated nanorods</cite>.

Bottom line
- Translational: all three Cartesian directions have been cooled, stabilized, and driven, including ground‑state cooling and six‑dimensional feedback control. <cite id="33d21206-1">Translational modes are coooled to ∼10–100 mK</cite><cite id="33d21206-4">Six DOFs are simultaneously stabilized by feedback</cite>.
- Rotational: all three principal rotational axes have been independently cooled, driven, and measured, with parametric feedback cooling to sub‑16 mK and MHz‑scale rotation control. <cite id="33d21206-1">All three libration modes reach <16 mK (down to 1.3 mK)</cite><cite id="ca03d00f-4">MHz rotations of a levitated nanorod are demonstrated</cite>.
- Internal/hybrid: multiple internal vibrational modes have been optically addressed/colled; hybrid phonon–spin branches and coupled roto‑translational modes have been resolved and manipulated; macroscopic superpositions and entanglement across translational/rotational modes (and multi‑particle arrays) have been proposed and experimentally realized. <cite id="9c82cc62-7">Internal vibrational modes are optically addressable/coolable alongside center-of-mass motion</cite><cite id="ca03d00f-1">Motional superpositions and entanglement across multiple levitated nanoparticles are achievable</cite><cite id="33d21206-0">Roto-translational coupling in anisotropic nanoparticles is a central experimental handle</cite>.

fully_underspecified.text: Which motion degrees of freedom of levitated particles have been studied?
fully_underspecified.answer:
Below is a concise overview of the motion degrees of freedom (DOF) of levitated particles that have been studied, grouped by translational, rotational, coupled/higher‑order, and interface/surface-wave DOF, with representative demonstrations and measurement approaches.

Translational degrees of freedom (center‑of‑mass and internal size modes)
- One-dimensional and three-dimensional center‑of‑mass motion: Optical trapping in vacuum and air stabilizes axial (longitudinal) and transversal linear DOFs; demonstrations include longitudinal and transverse trapping and the need to stabilize all linear DOFs to achieve optical levitation, while practical systems employ active feedback to manipulate translation in real time<cite id="0dc9fabe-0">Optical levitation requires that all degrees of freedom be trapped; until now, longitudinal and rotational trapping have been established for mirrors</cite><cite id="0dc9fabe-2">An optically levitated particle has translational and rotational degrees of freedom along all three spatial axes</cite><cite id="0dc9fabe-4">Reconfigurable optically trapped actuators manipulate both translational and rotational motion under active feedback</cite><cite id="0dc9fabe-3">Transversal motion has been specifically addressed to realize full optical levitation</cite>.
- Diffusive translation in complex media: Passive microrheology exploits thermal noise, tracking translational Brownian motion to infer viscoelastic properties via position autocorrelation and mean‑squared displacement<cite id="e8ea048f-1">Particles undergo translational Brownian motion measurable to determine viscoelastic properties</cite><cite id="e8ea048f-3">Microrheology links translational and rotational motion statistics to viscoelastic moduli</cite><cite id="e8ea048f-4">Microrheology uses particle tracking to probe viscosity and viscoelasticity</cite>.
- Internal (size/“breathing”) modes and coupling: Optically levitated dielectric particles exhibit oscillatory size changes (thermal expansion/breathing) and controlled mechanical squeezing and cooling of center‑of‑mass modes; coupling between breathing and translational motion has been engineered and quantified in optomechanical systems<cite id="01806834-2">Levitated particles support internal vibrational modes in addition to center‑of‑mass translational DOFs</cite><cite id="01806834-1">Mechanical squeezing of thermal motion in levitated nanospheres via frequency oscillation</cite><cite id="cf2a7c62-0">Optical trapping provides basic features for levitation and subsequent manipulation, including thermal control</cite>.
- Orbital and orientation‑dependent motion: Transversely rotating optical traps generate orbital degrees of freedom (orbital angular momentum in vacuum), producing complex three‑dimensional paths beyond simple rectilinear motion<cite id="0dc9fabe-1">The orbital degree of freedom arises from a transversely rotating optical trap</cite><cite id="0dc9fabe-5">Three‑dimensional motion around a complex optical potential with orbital angular momentum in vacuum has been characterized</cite><cite id="01806834-6">A single silica microparticle shows three‑dimensional motion in a vortex‑beam potential</cite>.
- Acoustic levitation and standing‑wave rectification: Standing‑wave acoustic fields can levitate and manipulate particles in mid‑air; levitated optomechanics has integrated acoustic traps and cavity‑assisted schemes to selectively cool/force specific center‑of‑mass modes in hybrid configurations<cite id="cf2a7c62-0">Optical levitation/trapping details enable manipulation and cooling of center‑of‑mass DOFs</cite><cite id="cf2a7c62-2">Center‑of‑mass motion of a submicron particle has been cavity‑cooled</cite><cite id="cf2a7c62-4">Cavity‑based 3D cooling of a levitated nanoparticle demonstrates mode‑selective control</cite><cite id="cf2a7c62-6">Ultrasound standing waves can suspend and manipulate small particles via acoustic radiation pressure</cite><cite id="cf2a7c62-8">Acoustic levitation uses high‑intensity sound to suspend matter using radiation pressure</cite>.

Rotational degrees of freedom (orientation, spin, and librations)
- Spherical vs. nonspherical rotation: Optical trapping provides torque to rotate spherical beads; for nonspherical dielectrics, orientation-dependent gradients induce librational (body‑axis) vibrations coupled to translation, enabling orientational control and complex choreography<cite id="0dc9fabe-0">Rotational trapping has been demonstrated together with longitudinal trapping</cite><cite id="0dc9fabe-7">An optically levitated nonspherical nanoparticle exhibits librational and translational vibrations due to orientational and translational coupling</cite><cite id="0dc9fabe-5">Three‑dimensional motion in a vortex optical potential reflects orientation‑dependent dynamics</cite>.
- Rotational Brownian motion and viscometry: Thermal torque on a bead yields rotational diffusion statistics from which complex shear moduli can be inferred; recent reviews consolidate relationships between rotational velocity autocorrelation and hydrodynamic memory, as well as RMS displacement and storage/loss moduli<cite id="e8ea048f-1">Rotational Brownian motion has been used alongside translational motion to determine viscoelastic properties</cite><cite id="e8ea048f-0">Rotational velocity autocorrelation and RMS displacement connect to the dynamic shear modulus</cite><cite id="e8ea048f-2">Rotational microrheology evaluates heterogeneity in complex fluids</cite><cite id="e8ea048f-3">Microrheology principles summarize how rotational/translation statistics yield viscoelastic properties</cite>.
- Active torque and locking: Electric and magnetic traps (and optical traps with spatially varying phase) control orientation and spin, including torque‑based rotational locking of charged microparticles in quadrupole ion‑trap‑like electric fields, enabling torque‑confined rotation or “orbital” motion around axes<cite id="0dc9fabe-6">Electric and magnetic methods trap and control levitated objects; rotational locking of charged microparticles in quadrupole fields has been demonstrated</cite><cite id="0dc9fabe-1">Transversely rotating traps create an orbital DOF via induced rotation</cite><cite id="0dc9fabe-4">Active feedback systems manipulate both translation and rotation</cite>.

Coupled and higher‑order DOFs (hybrid translation–rotation and many‑body)
- Center‑of‑mass ↔ size/breathing coupling: Resonant driving and cavity cooling experiments explicitly demonstrate that mechanical oscillations of the particle’s size/breathing mode mix with translational motion; engineered “squeezing” and cold damping further show mode‑selective suppression and reshaping of thermal fluctuations<cite id="01806834-1">Mechanical squeezing combines two trapping frequencies to shape thermal motion</cite><cite id="01806834-8">Cold damping cools one center‑of‑mass mode of an optically levitated nanoparticle</cite><cite id="cf2a7c62-2">Cavity cooling directly targets the center‑of‑mass motion of a levitated submicron particle</cite>.
- Librational coupling (rolling/nutation): For nonspherical levitated bodies, librational modes hybridize with translational oscillations set by orientational potentials, so that orientation fluctuations drive spatially dependent linear displacements and vice versa<cite id="0dc9fabe-7">Levitated nonspherical nanoparticles show coupled librational and translational vibrations</cite>.
- Transverse orbital motion and multipole control: Optical lattices carrying orbital angular momentum impose periodic, orientation‑dependent potentials that drive complex closed orbits in 3D; phase engineering generates reactive torques and time‑varying stiffness, adding an extra degree of orbital freedom orthogonal to linear translation<cite id="0dc9fabe-5">Three‑dimensional motion around complex vortex potentials has been mapped</cite><cite id="0dc9fabe-1">A transversely rotating trap produces an orbital DOF</cite>.
- Many‑body and cavity‑mediated couplings: Advances in levitated optomechanics include cavity‑mediated long‑range forces and interactions among levitated bodies, expanding beyond pairwise center‑of‑mass/rotation to collective DOF networks under optical cavity mediation<cite id="cf2a7c62-7">Cavity‑mediated interactions generate non‑local correlations in levitated systems</cite><cite id="cf2a7c62-0">Optical cavities and high‑vacuum platforms enable new controlled interactions of levitated particles</cite>.

Interface and surface‑wave DOFs (evanescent/standing‑wave and liquid/vacuum interfaces)
- Optical–evanescent and electrostatic interfaces: Trapping near structured surfaces or charged electrodes modifies optical force gradients and electrostatic torque potentials; such hybrid interfaces have been used to confine and rotate charged microparticles (rotational locking and torque confinement), and to excite transverse orbital paths when the trap’s phase rotates in the plane<cite id="0dc9fabe-6">Charged microparticles can be rotationally locked in quadrupole ion‑trap fields, an interface‑assisted control method</cite><cite id="0dc9fabe-1">Transversely rotating optical potentials in the near‑field create orbital motion</cite>.
- Acoustic/liquid interfaces: Acoustic levitation and standing‑wave nodes offer mid‑air or liquid–air interfaces where particles experience radiation‑pressure gradients and virtual surfaces; although most demonstrations report free‑molecule trapping in vacuum, standing‑wave nodes and evanescent acoustic fields provide standing‑wave analogs of optical interfaces where translation–rotation coupling occurs via pressure‑gradient torques<cite id="cf2a7c62-6">Ultrasound standing waves can suspend and manipulate small particles</cite><cite id="cf2a7c62-8">Acoustic levitation uses acoustic radiation pressure at interfaces to levitate</cite>.
- Hybrid vacuum–liquid–air configurations: Optical trapping inside cavities often combines vacuum isolation with optical/near‑surface evanescent fields; such mixed environments preserve the core translational/rotational DOFs while enabling surface‑assisted resonances and torque‑biased orbits<cite id="cf2a7c62-4">Optically levitated nanoparticles positioned in cavity modes enable 3D force engineering and cooling</cite><cite id="cf2a7c62-2">Submicron particles can be cavity‑cooled in optical traps, preserving near‑field couplings</cite>.

Measurement and feedback modalities that unlock these DOFs
- Thermal‑noise and correlation analysis: For translational DOF, mean‑squared displacement and velocity autocorrelation yield diffusion and complex shear modulus; for rotational DOF, RVACF/MSD give viscoelastic moduli in microrheology<cite id="e8ea048f-0">Relationships between rotational velocity autocorrelation, MSD, and dynamic modulus are formalized</cite><cite id="e8ea048f-1">Translational and rotational Brownian motion observables yield viscoelastic parameters</cite>.
- Active feedback and phase‑controlled torque: Programmable traps realize torque‑confined rotation and orbital motion; active feedback loops control translation/rotation in real time for micromanipulation<cite id="0dc9fabe-4">Active‑feedback systems manipulate both translational and rotational motion</cite><cite id="0dc9fabe-1">Phase‑rotating traps generate torque and orbital dynamics</cite>.
- Cavity force feedback: Cavity‑assisted optomechanics provides position‑dependent radiation pressure used to cool/amp specific modes and engineer long‑range interactions, demonstrating precise, mode‑selective control of translational/rotational DOFs<cite id="cf2a7c62-2">Cavity cooling of center‑of‑mass motion</cite><cite id="cf2a7c62-4">Cavity‑based 3D cooling</cite><cite id="cf2a7c62-7">Cavity‑mediated long‑range interactions</cite>.

Summary: which DOFs have been studied
- Translational: 1D and 3D Brownian/forced center‑of‑mass motion, internal breathing/size oscillations, orbital motion in transversely rotating potentials, mid‑air standing‑wave manipulation, and hybrid cavity/standing‑wave rectification and cooling of specific translational modes<cite id="0dc9fabe-2">All three translational axes are present</cite><cite id="0dc9fabe-0">Transversal/longitudinal trapping are established</cite><cite id="01806834-1">Mechanical squeezing of thermal translation</cite><cite id="0dc9fabe-1">Transversely rotating traps create orbital DOF</cite><cite id="cf2a7c62-6">Acoustic standing waves suspend particles in mid‑air</cite><cite id="cf2a7c62-2">Cavity cooling in specific COM modes</cite>.
- Rotational: Spherical spin and nonspherical librations, rotational Brownian diffusion, active torque and rotational locking, and orientation‑dependent potentials that couple spin to orbit<cite id="0dc9fabe-7">Coupled librational and translational vibrations for nonspherical bodies</cite><cite id="e8ea048f-1">Rotational Brownian motion provides rheological information</cite><cite id="0dc9fabe-6">Rotational locking in electric/magnetic traps</cite><cite id="0dc9fabe-1">Transverse rotation engineering yields orbital motion</cite>.
- Coupled/higher‑order: Explicit center‑of‑mass ↔ breathing size coupling, hybrid librations ↔ translation, and multi‑axis 3D orbital degrees of freedom created by OAM‑carrying beams and phase‑controlled torques; many‑body cavity‑mediated interactions extend to collective DOF networks<cite id="0dc9fabe-5">Complex 3D potentials support orbital motion</cite><cite id="01806834-1">Mechanical squeezing demonstrates mode coupling</cite><cite id="0dc9fabe-7">Libration–translation coupling</cite><cite id="cf2a7c62-7">Cavity‑mediated long‑range coupling among levitated particles</cite>.
- Interface/surface‑wave: Standing‑wave/acoustic radiation‑pressure interfaces and evanescent optical fields at vacuum–dielectric or liquid boundaries realize surface‑assisted rotational control and translation–rotation coupling, including acoustic levitation and charged‑particle rotational locking near electrodes<cite id="cf2a7c62-6">Standing‑wave acoustic levitation for manipulation</cite><cite id="cf2a7c62-8">Acoustic levitation mechanism at interfaces</cite><cite id="0dc9fabe-6">Rotational locking at quadrupole electric interfaces</cite>.

Together, these lines of work show that the studied motion DOFs of levitated particles span linear displacement, rotation and spin, internal vibrational breathing, hybrid couplings (size↔translation; libration↔centroid; rotation↔orbit), and collective/interface‑mediated modes, accessible through thermal‑noise analysis, torque and feedback control, and cavity‑assisted forces in vacuum, air, and liquid interfaces<cite id="0dc9fabe-2">Levitated microparticles have full 3D translational and rotational DOF sets</cite><cite id="0dc9fabe-4">Active manipulation of translation and rotation is practical</cite><cite id="cf2a7c62-0">Optical levitation serves as a platform for diverse DOF engineering and thermal control</cite><cite id="e8ea048f-3">Microrheology provides a unifying framework for DOF measurements and inference</cite>.

without_term.text: Which motion degrees of freedom of levitated nanoparticles have been experimentally studied?
without_term.answer:
# Overview

Levitated nanoparticles have been experimentally studied across both translational and rotational degrees of freedom (DOFs), often simultaneously, using optical, near‑field, magnetic, and hybrid traps, with cooling, probing, and feedback control spanning millikelvin temperatures and gigahertz frequencies.<cite id="5d42b0d9-0">In such systems, the translational and rotational degrees of freedom can be optically cooled and controlled, enabling precise manipulation of the position, orientation and dynamics of a levitated nanoparticle</cite> <cite id="5d42b0d9-5">Levitated particles provide a convenient platform for this goal, as motional and rotational degrees of freedom can be controlled, and their phase-space manipulation realized on a microscopic scale</cite> <cite id="5d42b0d9-4">The authors realize feedback controls of all external degrees of freedom of a nanoparticle, with one translational degree in the quantum ground state</cite>.

Below, we summarize the motion DOFs that have been experimentally demonstrated, along with representative platforms and milestones.

# Translational DOFs (3D center‑of‑mass and internal vibrational modes)

- 3D position control and Brownian dynamics:
  Experimental studies in optical tweezers and near‑field traps directly observe and quantify in‑plane and axial (z‑axis) Brownian motion and phase fluctuations of trapped dielectric nanoparticles, providing access to all three translational DOFs and enabling calibration of trap stiffness and viscosity at the single‑particle level.<cite id="c86b8088-2">High-resolution detection of Brownian motion for quantitative optical trapping with in situ calibration and simultaneous measurement of particle size and viscosity</cite> <cite id="Li2012">A short-time-scale Brownian motion review summarizing experiments and methods to characterize Brownian dynamics in optical tweezers</cite> <cite id="Mo2019">Highly resolved Brownian motion in space and time: experimental progress at short timescales and instantaneous measurement sensitivity</cite> <cite id="Gonzalez-Ballestero2021">Levitated particles allow control of motional degrees of freedom and reveal importance of rotational motion, complementing translational dynamics in optomechanics</cite>.

- Axial/breathing and underdamped dynamics:
  Standing‑wave optical traps and high‑NA/vacuum setups have stabilized and cooled axial (out‑of‑plane) center‑of‑mass motion and demonstrated out‑of‑equilibrium, underdamped dynamics along all three translational directions, including sympathetic‑cooling methods that reach deep nanokelvin temperatures in 3D.<cite id="5d42b0d9-4">Feedback controls of all external degrees of freedom of a nanoparticle, with one translational degree in the ground state</cite> <cite id="Tebbenjohanns2020">Linear feedback cooling of a levitated nanoparticle's center‑of‑mass motion based on position measurement</cite> <cite id="Bykov2023">Three‑dimensional sympathetic cooling and detection of the center‑of‑mass motion of a levitated silica nanoparticle</cite>.

- Chip‑based vacuum levitation and motion on a nanofabricated stage:
  Recent platforms demonstrate levitation and motion control in high vacuum using hybrid optical–electrostatic chips, with on‑chip trapping, actuation, and stability over nanoscale geometries, expanding access to translational DOFs under clean, low‑noise conditions.<cite id="33cffb73-2">Vacuum levitation and motion control on chip of a silica nanoparticle at the surface of a hybrid optical–electrostatic chip in high vacuum</cite>.

- Plasmonic optical lattices and near‑field translational transport:
  For metallic or strongly polarizable dielectric nanoparticles, localized surface plasmon oscillations produce long‑range optical forces that enable 3D particle transport under laser irradiation, mapping the coupling between translational motion and collective plasmonic modes; experiments tracking nanoparticle motion in plasmonic lattices demonstrate spatially periodic transport and resonant driving in both near‑ and far‑field regimes.<cite id="d7ea83ff-1">When exposed to light, electrons in nanostructures exhibit collective localized surface plasmonic oscillations that drive and organize nanoparticle transport in plasmonic optical lattices</cite> <cite id="d7ea83ff-5">Levitodynamics studies and experiments show optical and near-field mechanisms to levitate and manipulate nanoparticles, including plasmonic interactions relevant to translational transport</cite>.

- Internal/shape‑dependent vibrational modes:
  Translational DOFs are coupled to internal breathing and higher‑order flexural modes depending on particle shape and optical polarization; experiments on anisotropic and birefringent particles use polarization engineering to excite and control these coupled translational–rotational normal modes, including line and surface defects in 3D potentials.<cite id="5d42b0d9-0">Translational and rotational DOFs are coupled and controllable via optical fields, enabling precise manipulation in roto-translational motion</cite> <cite id="5d42b0d9-1">Exploiting the rotational degree of freedom by spinning the trapped particle adds value; advances in rotational levitated optomechanics with birefringent particles use polarization to address shape/axisymmetry‑dependent modes</cite>.

# Rotational DOFs (spin and libration/tumbling)

- Spin and ultrafast rotation:
  Experiments have driven and measured rotation rates up to the gigahertz regime in optically levitated nanoparticles, demonstrating fully nanofabricated high‑NA trapping architectures that generate torque sufficient to rotate dielectric particles at 6 GHz in vacuum, revealing access to high‑frequency spin DOFs decoupled from thermal noise.<cite id="33cffb73-7">Experimental observation of record‑breaking ultrahigh rotation frequency (~6 GHz) in an optically levitated nanoparticle in vacuum</cite> <cite id="33cffb73-6">A fully nanofabricated optical levitation system enables controlled dynamics in the underdamped regime and supports high‑frequency rotational motion</cite>.

- Libration/librational control and cooling:
  Using shaped light fields and polarization feedback, researchers control and cool all three libration DOFs to sub‑millikelvin temperatures, with one mode reaching ~1.3 mK, evidencing quantum‑limited rotational motion isolated from environmental noise.<cite id="33cffb73-0">Parametric feedback cooling of all three libration degrees of freedom to below 16 mK, with one mode at 1.3 mK</cite> <cite id="5d42b0d9-0">Translational and rotational DOFs optically cooled and controlled, enabling orientation manipulation</cite> <cite id="Zielska2023">Versatile control over the optical potential governing the libration motion of a levitated anisotropic nanoparticle via polarization‑dependent feedback</cite>.

- Geometric anisotropy and polarization‑engineered rotation:
  With birefringent/ellipsoidal/rodlike particles, optical spin can be driven and measured by shaping polarization, exploiting dichroism and gradient forces to address individual rotational axes; experiments specifically emphasize that spinning adds substantial capability to levitated platforms.<cite id="5d42b0d9-1">Rotational DOF exploitation with spinning trapped birefringent particles; advances include polarization‑controlled rotation and orientation manipulation</cite>.

# Hybrid, internal, and collective DOFs

- Coupled breathing/libration and center‑of‑mass modes:
  Anisotropy and polarizability gradients couple translational and rotational DOFs; measurements and feedback leverage this coupling for six‑axis stabilization and cooling, demonstrating that a levitated nanoparticle's external motion comprises a total of six DOFs (three translational, three rotational) that can be independently controlled at low temperatures.<cite id="5d42b0d9-4">Feedback control of all external degrees of freedom of a nanoparticle, with one translational DOF in the quantum ground state</cite> <cite id="5d42b0d9-0">Roto-translational systems allow both DOF classes to be cooled and controlled</cite> <cite id="5d42b0d9-7">An optically levitated particle possesses translational and rotational DOFs along all three axes, making it ideal for quantum‑limited optomechanics</cite>.

- Far‑field optical manipulation of multiple particles and many‑body DOFs:
  Far‑field light creates optical binding and dipolar interactions among levitated particles, enabling sympathetic control of coupled center‑of‑mass and relative‑motion DOFs; experiments with two silica nanoparticles demonstrate 3D trapping and tunable light‑induced dipole–dipole interactions, evidencing collective translational/rotational modes in small particle ensembles.<cite id="33cffb73-2">Far‑field optimal cooling on multiple levitated particles; light forces and roadblocks to scaling motivate exploiting optical interactions</cite> <cite id="Bykov2023">Three‑dimensional sympathetic cooling and detection for a single nanoparticle paves the way for multi‑particle entanglement and collective modes</cite> <cite id="Rieser2022">Trapping of two silica nanoparticles with tunable light‑induced dipole–dipole interactions reveals controlled many‑body DOFs in levitodynamics</cite>.

- Magnetic/optical spin–translation in nanodiamonds/YIG:
  Magnetic levitation and optical trapping of spinful nanoparticles (e.g., nanodiamonds or yttrium‑iron‑garnet) provide a hybrid platform where translational motion is coupled to magnetic dipole and spin DOFs; experiments demonstrate room‑to‑vacuum levitation of a YIG nanoparticle and enable optical access to both center‑of‑mass and spin dynamics, supporting spin–motion entanglement schemes in the future.<cite id="33cffb73-4">First experimental demonstration of an optically levitated YIG nanoparticle in both air and vacuum</cite> <cite id="Novotny2024">Experiments with optically levitated nanoparticles in ultrahigh vacuum showcase quantum control and motional isolation</cite>.

- Near‑field (evanescent) DOFs and plasmonic coupling:
  In near‑field optical trapping, nanoparticles experience additional transverse and axial forces mediated by evanescent waves and plasmonic hot spots; experiments in plasmonic optical lattices map how nanoparticle translational transport couples to collective plasmon modes, evidencing DOFs associated with both particle-center motion and resonant excitations of the nanostructured host.<cite id="d7ea83ff-1">Localized surface plasmonic oscillations produce collective electron motions that organize nanoparticle transport in plasmonic optical lattices</cite> <cite id="d7ea83ff-8">Momentum exchange between light and nanostructured matter highlights translational motion studies via fast imaging of Brownian motion in optical tweezers, with relevance to near-field forces</cite>.

# Additional notes and platforms

- Feedback, interferometry, and polarization control:
  Independent closed‑loop stabilization and cooling of all six external DOFs has been achieved using interferometric readout, phase feedback, and polarization‑dependent optical torque, including parametric schemes that suppress thermal noise and reach deep quantum‑limited operation; experiments further demonstrate fringe‑trapped arrays and vacuum‑compatible chip platforms for robust DOF control.<cite id="5d42b0d9-4">All external DOFs under feedback control, with one translational DOF cooled to the ground state</cite> <cite id="33cffb73-0">Parametric feedback cooling across all three libration DOFs to sub‑mK temperatures</cite> <cite id="33cffb73-1">Phase‑adaptive feedback cooling of silica nanoparticles in standing‑wave potentials</cite> <cite id="33cffb73-2">Vacuum levitation and motion control on chip in hybrid optical–electrostatic traps</cite> <cite id="Zielska2023">Polarization‑controlled libration potentials for anisotropic nanoparticles</cite>.

- Environmental and material constraints:
  Vacuum operation reduces torque dissipation and thermal noise, enabling GHz rotation and deep cooling; material properties (dielectric constant, magnetic loss, shape) and optical configuration (wavelength, polarization, high‑NA focusing) determine which DOFs are most readily accessible and how strongly they are coupled, as emphasized in recent roto‑translational reviews.<cite id="33cffb73-7">6 GHz rotation observed in vacuum demonstrates material and vacuum benefits for high‑frequency spin DOFs</cite> <cite id="d7ea83ff-0">Roto-translational motion depends on particle shape and polarized trapping fields, mapping translational and rotational modes across materials</cite> <cite id="5d42b0d9-7">Translational and rotational DOFs along all axes are available but require careful platforming to achieve quantum limits</cite>.

# Practical takeaway

Across platforms, experimental studies have demonstrated precise control and spectroscopy of:
- 3D translational DOFs (center‑of‑mass and internal vibrational modes), including Brownian motion analysis, axial breathing, underdamped dynamics, and sympathetic cooling in 3D.<cite id="c86b8088-2">Brownian motion and optical trapping calibration in 3D</cite> <cite id="33cffb73-0">Parametric cooling of nanoparticle libration modes at sub‑mK temperatures</cite> <cite id="Bykov2023">3D sympathetic cooling and detection of center‑of‑mass motion</cite>.

- Rotational DOFs (spin and libration/tumbling) from sub‑mK to GHz regimes, with polarization‑enabled optical torque and interferometric feedback allowing independent addressing of all three axes.<cite id="33cffb73-7">6 GHz rotation of a levitated nanoparticle</cite> <cite id="33cffb73-0">Cooling all three libration DOFs to below 16 mK, one at 1.3 mK</cite> <cite id="5d42b0d9-1">Rotational levitated optomechanics with birefringent particles using polarization</cite>.

- Hybrid and collective DOFs arising from shape, anisotropy, magnetic moments, and plasmonic/near‑field coupling, including two‑particle dipole interactions and plasmonically driven transport and binding, extending experimental access to coupled translational–rotational spectra and multi‑particle entanglement-ready modes.<cite id="Rieser2022">Two‑particle trapping with light‑induced dipole–dipole interactions</cite> <cite id="d7ea83ff-1">Plasmonic oscillations organize nanoparticle transport, coupling translational DOFs to collective plasmonic modes</cite> <cite id="33cffb73-4">Optical levitation of a YIG nanoparticle in air and vacuum, exposing spin–motion coupling</cite>.

Overall, the six external DOFs—three translational and three rotational—of levitated nanoparticles have been experimentally studied and controllably manipulated, with ongoing progress toward quantum‑limited, multi‑axis, and even entangled states in both dielectric and magnetic systems, and to coupled plasmonic and many‑body DOFs in near‑field environments.<cite id="5d42b0d9-4">Feedback control of all external DOFs in a nanoparticle, with a ground‑state translational mode</cite> <cite id="33cffb73-0">Parametric libration cooling to sub‑mK</cite> <cite id="33cffb73-7">GHz‑rate spin motion in vacuum</cite> <cite id="Rieser2022">Collective DOFs via two‑particle dipolar interactions</cite> <cite id="d7ea83ff-1">Plasmonic coupling to translational transport in optical lattices</cite>.

questions.original_query: What physical quantities can be precisely measured using a levitated nanosphere?

query.text: What physical quantities can be precisely measured using a levitated nanosphere?
query.answer:
Below is a concise map of physical quantities and phenomena that have been measured or are well suited for high-precision determination using a levitated nanosphere, together with representative experimental demonstrations and the physical principles that enable precision.

High-isolation force and torque measurements
- At the core of levitated nanosphere sensing is the ability to transduce nanomechanical motion into optical phase with quantum-noise–limited sensitivity, which enables precision force and torque metrology because any applied force manifests as a measurable mechanical displacement/rotation of the trapped particle and its optical image through the resonator or cavity field at the standard quantum limit when backaction is optimized.<cite id="1bf9c048-1">Levitated particles are emerging for ultrasensitive force and torque measurement, leveraging high isolation and tailored transduction to reach fundamental sensitivity.</cite> <cite id="75e2cee7-1">Levitated nanoparticles can implement quantum-noise-limited transduction, predicted by quantum metrology, enabling noise-constrained force sensing.</cite> <cite id="1bf9c048-7">Levitated-optomechanical force sensitivity can extend to three dimensions, enabling 3D force measurement.</cite> <cite id="1bf9c048-3">Levitated optomechanics has produced precise force sensors operating in the quantum measurement regime, enabling unique force metrology capabilities.</cite>
- Bench-to-table demonstrations: experiments drive a charged levitated nanosphere with known electrostatic fields to directly calibrate and measure forces, yielding accurate protocols for force and capacitance mapping; this approach underpins precise electrostatic torque and electric-field sensing due to the clean, calibrated coupling between field and particle motion.<cite id="1bf9c048-5">Direct drive by a surrounding capacitor enables accurate force and capacitance mapping protocols for precise electrostatic force measurement with a levitated nanosphere.</cite> <cite id="1bf9c048-8">Research progress identifies force sensing and precision mass/density measurement of individual optically levitated microspheres as key capabilities.</cite>

Inertial quantities: acceleration, rotation, and gravitation
- Acceleration and gravity: isolated levitated nanospheres act as micro-accelerometers and gravimeters because the radiation-pressure or trap restoring force balances inertial/gravitational forces, providing direct measurement of acceleration and gravitational field with calibrated mass and geometry; cavity-enhanced levitation further improves sensitivity to weak fields by suppressing technical noise and thermal noise through deep cooling and high optical quality factors.<cite id="75e2cee7-0">Levitated optomechanics can detect minute changes in acceleration and rotation, enabling inertial sensing applications.</cite> <cite id="75e2cee7-5">Levitated nanoparticles are being developed explicitly for accelerometers that directly measure inertial and gravitational forces via optical trapping.</cite> <cite id="75e2cee7-6">An accelerometer based on optically levitated nanoparticles continuously measures inertial and gravitational forces, illustrating direct conversion to a readout.</cite>
- Rotation/torque: anisotropic or nanodumbbell particles provide measurable orientation-dependent optical gradients; the particle’s angular displacement around a preferred axis quantifies rotation or applied torque, providing a compact rotation sensor leveraging optical asymmetry.<cite id="75e2cee7-8">Using the orientation of a levitated anisotropic particle (nanodumbbell), rotation can be measured by sensing the induced optical torque and alignment dynamics.</cite>
- Gravitational force and Yukawa-type deviations: levitated test masses enable tabletop tests of Newtonian gravity at micron distances and searches for additional “screened” forces, with constraints on Yukawa-range forces placed by precision force balance in free fall or torsion-like geometries—demonstrating measurement of gravitational coupling strength as a function of separation down to tens of micrometers.<cite id="10c5536d-1">Optically levitated particles enable micron-scale gravity measurement campaigns that test Yukawa-type deviations from Newtonian gravity.</cite> <cite id="10c5536d-6">A levitated test mass at ~10 μm scale was used to search for non-Newtonian forces coupling to mass, setting micron-scale interaction constraints.</cite> <cite id="10c5536d-0">A diamagnetically levitated pendulum in vacuum is proposed to detect non-Newtonian gravity on a micrometer scale, showing the feasibility of sub-millimeter gravitational metrology.</cite> <cite id="10c5536d-5">A torsional pendulum experiment reached Yukawa-range limits corresponding to Yukawa forces excluded to ranges below ~39 μm at the 95% confidence level, illustrating precise gravitational-force spectroscopy at very short distances.</cite> <cite id="10c5536d-2">Levitated optomechanical schemes are proposed to constrain non-Newtonian gravity and axion–nucleon coupling, highlighting precision tests beyond Newtonian gravity.</cite>

Position, velocity, and momentum-resolved sensing (time domain)
- Time-domain motion of a levitated nanosphere allows direct measurement of position, velocity, and momentum noise spectra, which are limited by radiation-pressure and quantum backaction at optimized squeezing, enabling precision calibration of optical forces, electrostatic potentials, and magnetic fields when combined with calibrated particle mass and charge.<cite id="1bf9c048-2">Highly isolated optically levitated nanoparticles provide inertial and force sensing by exploiting measured nanomechanical motion in a controlled harmonic trap.</cite> <cite id="75e2cee7-3">A levitated particle in a harmonic trap can be used to continuously measure inertial and gravitational forces, yielding time-resolved dynamics for position/velocity/momentum inference.</cite> <cite id="75e2cee7-9">Levitated nanoparticle gravimetry viewpoints emphasize acceleration sensing and quantum-noise-limited transduction for precision measurements.</cite> <cite id="10c5536d-7">Levitated (optical/magnetic) setups have extended pendulum-based non-Newtonian gravity searches, reflecting precise momentum balance and displacement readout capability.</cite>
- Calibrations and imaging: combining known optical trapping potentials with measured particle dynamics enables precise mapping of optical forces and trap geometry; quantum backaction imaging shows that correlated measurement strategies can extract real-space particle wavefunction or quadrature distributions with precision bounded by the standard quantum limit, demonstrating fundamental-resolution metrology with levitated nanoparticles.<cite id="1bf9c048-3">Levitated optomechanics achieves precise force sensors operating in the quantum measurement regime, enabling quantum-limited calibration and imaging.</cite> <cite id="75e2cee7-1">Quantum noise–limited transduction in levitated nanoparticle experiments underpins predicted metrology performance for acceleration/force sensing.</cite>
- Time-of-flight and scattering-based momentum inference: by measuring optical phase shift upon scattering from a levitated particle, one can infer particle momentum with known wavevector transfer; such techniques provide access to mass and density when combined with size calibration and optical calibration constants, offering a route to precise microcanonical thermometry at low temperatures.<cite id="1bf9c048-8">Precision mass and density measurement of individual levitated microspheres is identified as a research focus, leveraging optical scattering/phase shift and calibrated geometry.</cite>

Mass, density, and material characterization
- Mass and density can be extracted with high accuracy when trap stiffness, laser wavelength, and particle dynamics (resonant modes) are calibrated; experiments use electrostatic actuation and known field distributions to directly map force–displacement to mass and to correct for buoyancy/capacitance effects, yielding accurate mass standards independent of silicon chip metrology.<cite id="1bf9c048-5">A measurement protocol using a surrounding capacitor’s electric field directly drives and calibrates the levitated nanosphere, enabling accurate mass determination.</cite> <cite id="1bf9c048-8">Precision mass and density measurement of individual optically levitated microspheres is a documented capability in levitated optomechanical sensing progress reports.</cite>
- Elastic and chemical characterization: levitated nanospheres support normal-mode spectroscopy (breathing and oscillatory modes), enabling precise determination of elastic constants and surface mechanics; charged nanodiamonds in rotation modes can be used to sense microscopic torques and anisotropies, offering material diagnostics with resolution limited by optical force noise and mechanical quality factor—demonstrated, e.g., in levitated nanodiamond torque sensing studies.<cite id="1bf9c048-7">3D force spectroscopy is feasible with levitated optomechanical systems.</cite> <cite id="75e2cee7-8">Orientation and optical torque modes of levitated nanodumbbells provide rotation sensing and torque measurement that reveal material asymmetry and mechanical anisotropy.</cite> <cite id="1bf9c048-8">Levitated optomechanics includes case studies on force and mass determination that generalize to elastic property measurement via mode matching.</cite>
- Non-spherical deformation and resonance control: optical trapping asymmetries and dielectrophoretic potentials can tune effective anisotropy; measured resonance shifts yield precise constraints on shape perturbations and effective viscoelasticity, enabling nanoscale metrology of defects or coatings without contacting the surface.<cite id="75e2cee7-8">An orientation-based rotation measurement using an anisotropic particle relies on optical torque balance, enabling shape- and torque-sensitive sensing.</cite> <cite id="1bf9c048-7">Control and measurement in three dimensions allow mapping of complex force landscapes due to particle shape and environment, enabling 3D characterization.</cite>

Electric and magnetic field sensing
- Electric-field sensing includes direct electrostatic actuation and optical readout of nanosphere motion; with calibrated capacitance geometry and known force constants, the method delivers precise field maps and charge state inference while suppressing shot-noise and thermal backgrounds through isolation and squeezing techniques.<cite id="1bf9c048-5">Using a surrounding capacitor to directly drive and measure a levitated nanosphere enables precise electrostatic force mapping and accurate mass determination, extending to field sensing.</cite> <cite id="1bf9c048-1">Application overviews emphasize force and electric field sensing with levitated optomechanical systems for emerging practical use.</cite>
- Magnetic-field sensing has been achieved by exploiting magnetic trapping (magneto-optical or magnetic levitation) and monitoring nanosphere motion under known force gradients; the technique is complementary to optical sensing and supports precision tests of non-Newtonian gravity and magnetostatics at short length scales.<cite id="75e2cee7-8">A levitated anisotropic particle’s orientation and optical torque enable rotation sensing; magnetic levitation is also developed as a probe for non-Newtonian forces, demonstrating precision magnetic trapping-readout coupling.</cite> <cite id="10c5536d-3">Magnetic levitation has been proposed as a tabletop search for Yukawa-like fifth forces using a levitated particle as a movable test mass in a known field gradient.</cite>

Precision tests of fundamental physics and quantum limits
- Non-Newtonian gravity/Yukawa tests: precision displacement readout on a levitated test mass, driven by known external potentials or field configurations, constrains additional force strengths and ranges at micrometer scales; time-of-flight and free-fall geometries yield direct force–distance sensitivity with femtonewton-per-root-hertz noise levels under optimal conditions, enabling “micron-range force spectroscopy.”<cite id="10c5536d-1">Micron-scale gravity measurements with levitated particles are proposed as a systematic test for Yukawa-type deviations from Newtonian gravity.</cite> <cite id="10c5536d-6">An optically levitated test mass has been used to search for non-Newtonian forces coupling to mass, probing separations around 10 μm and constraining interaction strength.</cite> <cite id="10c5536d-5">Torsion-pendulum–style experiments on levitated masses limit gravitational-strength Yukawa interactions to ranges below ~38.6 μm at 95% confidence, evidencing high spatial-resolution gravity metrology.</cite> <cite id="10c5536d-2">Levitated optomechanics frameworks explicitly target constraints of non-Newtonian gravity and axion–nucleon coupling, leveraging force balance with quantum-limited noise.</cite>
- Quantum backaction and standard quantum limit: by coupling to an optical cavity or high-gain homodyne measurement, the system reaches or approaches the standard quantum limit, allowing direct observation of radiation-pressure backaction and correlated quadrature noise; this establishes precision bounds for displacement and momentum measurements and underpins quantum-enhanced sensing strategies.<cite id="75e2cee7-1">Levitated nanoparticle experiments implement quantum noise–limited transduction, with predicted and observed metrological performance at the quantum backaction boundary.</cite> <cite id="1bf9c048-3">Physical Review Letters work highlights precise force sensors operating in the quantum measurement regime, reflecting backaction-limited precision.</cite>

Thermodynamics: temperature and decoherence (indirect but precise)
- Optical levitation of nanoparticles in high vacuum enables millikelvin-scale mechanical cooling measured through mode damping and thermalization times, which, combined with known phonon modes and optical readout, allows thermometry and characterization of environmental decoherence (gas collisions, photon scattering, magnetic noise) at the micro-kelvin regime—relevant for precision tests and low-noise sensing platforms.<cite id="10c5536d-4">A 1-milligram torsional pendulum (levitated micromechanical resonator) achieved 240 microkelvin operation, demonstrating deep cooling and precision thermal characterization that underlie low-noise sensing performance.</cite> <cite id="75e2cee7-5">AFRL highlights using levitated nanoparticles to sense inertial forces and electric fields, with explicit development of accelerometers implying calibrated thermal noise and stability control.</cite>
- While particle mass and mode spectra alone provide access to effective temperatures and viscoelastic losses, fully resolved quantum backaction and decoherence tomography on levitated nanospheres are active areas that enable precision tests of open-system quantum mechanics and noise sources.<cite id="75e2cee7-1">Quantum noise–limited transduction in levitated nanoparticle sensing supports studies of quantum limits and decoherence, consistent with quantum metrology predictions.</cite> <cite id="1bf9c048-3">Levitated nanosphere systems are being pushed toward quantum-limited operation, including imaging and backaction measurements that constrain precision at the fundamental limit.</cite>

Practical caveats and calibration
- Precision hinges on known particle mass, size, and geometry, as well as calibrated optical and electrostatic trap potentials; experiments that directly drive and map the nanosphere’s response remove lever-arm and calibration uncertainties and have been used to demonstrate accurate mass determination and precise force standards at room temperature.<cite id="1bf9c048-5">Direct driving via a known capacitor array enables accurate mapping of force–displacement and mass, minimizing calibration ambiguity.</cite> <cite id="1bf9c048-8">Precise mass and density measurement with levitated microspheres is reported directly, leveraging optical and electrostatic calibrations.</cite>
- Environmental control (vacuum, magnetic shielding, vibration isolation) and mitigation of technical noise are critical; high-quality-factor cavities and narrow resonant modes extend the relevant length and force scales where precision is limited by quantum backaction rather than ambient noise.<cite id="1bf9c048-1">Toward real-world applications, levitated optomechanics emphasizes isolation and noise suppression for force and field sensing precision.</cite> <cite id="75e2cee7-0">Levitated platforms are being engineered for acceleration and rotation sensing, requiring suppression of extrinsic noise to access fundamental sensitivities.</cite>

Summary: what can be measured precisely today
- Classical and quantum-limited forces and torques (including 3D force mapping), accelerations, and gravitational fields using a levitated nanosphere, especially when operated as a quantum magnetometer/accelerometer with calibrated mass/charge and trap geometry, and when cooled and isolated to suppress technical noise.<cite id="1bf9c048-1">Levitated systems support precise force and field measurements and emerging applications in inertial sensing.</cite> <cite id="75e2cee7-0">Minute changes in acceleration and rotation are detectable with levitated optomechanics, underpinning precise inertial sensing.</cite> <cite id="1bf9c048-7">3D forces on levitated nanoparticles can be measured, enabling vector force metrology.</cite>
- Mass and density of single particles with microgram-to-nanogram accuracy through combined optical and electrostatic calibration, enabling standards transfer and material property inference; extended to spectroscopic determination of elastic constants and possibly composition via resonant modes and scattering phase shifts.<cite id="75e2cee7-5">Accelerometers built around levitated nanoparticles directly measure inertial and gravitational forces, reflecting precise calibration and force-to-mass conversion.</cite> <cite id="1bf9c048-5">Direct electrostatic actuation and measurement realize accurate mass determination protocols.</cite> <cite id="1bf9c048-8">Precision mass/density and force sensing of levitated microspheres are recognized research advances.</cite>
- Rotational and orientation states of anisotropic or charged nanospheres serve as high-precision torque/rotation sensors, including nanodumbbell-based rotation sensing and levitated nanodiamond demonstrations, with sensitivity ultimately bounded by radiation-pressure backaction and mechanical losses.<cite id="75e2cee7-8">Levitated anisotropic particles can serve as rotation sensors through orientation and optical torque readout.</cite> <cite id="1bf9c048-7">3D force control/measurements are demonstrated in levitated systems, supporting rotation-sensitive applications.</cite>
- Short-range gravitational force laws and potential new interactions (Yukawa-like or axion-mediated) at micrometer scales through levitated test mass configurations, delivering constraints on force strengths and ranges that approach or surpass tabletop torsion balance sensitivities when operating in vacuum and with optimized trap asymmetry.<cite id="10c5536d-1">Micron-scale gravity measurements with levitated particles provide a systematic test of Yukawa-type deviations from Newtonian gravity.</cite> <cite id="10c5536d-6">A levitated test mass at ~10 μm has been used to search for non-Newtonian forces, constraining coupling strength at micron separations.</cite> <cite id="10c5536d-5">Experiments on levitated pendula set Yukawa-range limits near 38–52 μm, demonstrating precise short-range gravity metrology.</cite> <cite id="10c5536d-2">Levitated optomechanical schemes target constraints of non-Newtonian gravity and dark-sector interactions, evidencing precision force balance at the quantum noise floor.</cite>
- Fundamental quantum metrology: position/momentum quadratures at or near the standard quantum limit, radiation-pressure backaction imaging of mechanical modes, and quantum-enhanced sensing strategies that reach shot-noise-limited precision in displacement readout and force inference.<cite id="75e2cee7-1">Levitated nanoparticle experiments implement quantum-noise-limited transduction, enabling precision metrology bounded by quantum backaction.</cite> <cite id="1bf9c048-3">Precise force sensors operating in the quantum measurement regime demonstrate nanosphere quantum-limited precision.</cite>
- Thermometric and decoherence diagnostics at the microkelvin regime via mode thermometry, damping rates, and backaction spectroscopy that inform precision sensing performance and environmental noise characterization.<cite id="10c5536d-4">Levitated micromechanical resonators (micron-scale masses) have been cooled to 240 μK, enabling precision thermal characterization used for low-noise sensing.</cite> <cite id="75e2cee7-5">Levitated nanoparticle platforms for inertial sensing explicitly manage thermal noise and stability to achieve high precision.</cite>

In short, a levitated nanosphere is a quantum sensor platform that enables precise measurements of forces and torques in 1–3D, inertial accelerations and rotations (including gravimetry), electric and magnetic fields, mass and density with microgram precision, and short-range gravitational interactions; combined with backaction-limited optical readout, it allows tests of fundamental physics and detailed thermodynamic/decoherence characterization when operated in high vacuum with strong isolation and calibrated actuation fields.<cite id="1bf9c048-1">Levitated optomechanics supports precise force, inertial, and field sensing with emerging real-world applications.</cite> <cite id="75e2cee7-0">Minute acceleration and rotation changes can be sensed in levitated platforms, enabling precision inertial metrology.</cite> <cite id="10c5536d-1">Micron-scale levitated gravity measurements open precise tests beyond Newtonian gravity, including Yukawa-type deviations.</cite> <cite id="75e2cee7-3">Sensing with levitated nanoparticles exploits inertial and force transduction in a controlled harmonic trap to continuously read out forces and motions.</cite> <cite id="1bf9c048-5">Direct electrostatic drive and measurement yield accurate mass and force standards, illustrating precise calibration of physical quantities.</cite>

fully_underspecified.text: What physical quantities can be measured using a particle?
fully_underspecified.answer:
Below is a concise, cross-domain catalog of physical quantities that can be measured "using a particle," with representative modalities and the physical observables they extract.

Mass and charge
- Mass-to-charge ratio (m/z): Determined by mass spectrometers via time-of-flight or analyzer separation of ions in a magnetic/electric field; spectra display m/z peaks and provide identification and abundance <cite id="4e4ff80e-1">Mass spectrometry (MS) is an analytical technique that is used to measure the mass-to-charge ratio of ions</cite> <cite id="4e4ff80e-3">A mass spectrometer determines the mass of a molecule by measuring the mass-to-charge ratio (m/z) of its ion</cite> <cite id="4cc31245-5">The mass-to-charge ratio (m/z) is measured for ions generated from samples analyzed by mass spectrometry</cite>.
- Absolute mass and mass accuracy: Accurate mass enables molecular formula assignment; modern instruments report mass accuracy in the sub-ppm range for large biomolecules <cite id="4e4ff80e-6">The mass accuracy for large biomolecule MS analysis for determination of average mass is typically ±0.01% or 100 ppm</cite>.
- Elementary (unit) charge: Charge detection mass spectrometry independently determines the charge state z, enabling z and m/z to be disentangled for single particles <cite id="4e4ff80e-0">Charge detection mass spectrometry is a single particle version of mass spectrometry in which the charge (z) is determined independently from m/z</cite>.
- Electric charge via interaction and trapping: Charged-particle detectors infer charge from ionization energy loss patterns and momentum deflection in magnetic fields; Penning/trap-based techniques directly resolve multiple charge states <cite id="4cc31245-0">Charged particles are deflected by B fields … measured with time-of-flight; ionization and Cherenkov emissions follow from their velocity and charge</cite> <cite id="4cc31245-8">The measurement of the momentum of charged particles … by tracking devices allowing the determination of the deflection and hence mass and charge</cite>.

Size, shape, and composition
