- In near field, use photonic crystal cavities or hyperbolic metamaterials to increase density of photonic states at the particle surface, which suppresses nonradiative decay channels and can convert mechanical-optical coupling into efficient radiative pathways <cite id="cbb7b1cb-3">near-field photonic crystal cavity coupling for tunable single-photon optomechanics</cite>. 
- Operate in high vacuum and large solid angles to maximize photon emission into lossless modes. Vacuum integration and photonic routing reduce collisions and absorption, supporting sustained optical trapping and cooling without deleterious heating <cite id="6239ecd7-5">electron spin control and direct temperature measurement of NV centers in an optically levitated nanodiamond in low vacuum</cite> and <cite id="d5adf024-8">hybrid optical–electrostatic chip enabling high-vacuum levitation</cite>.

4) Shift from absorption-driven to emission/interaction-driven energy removal (cooling routes)
- Optical and cavity-sideband cooling to remove energy by emitting higher-energy photons than absorbed. Resolved-sideband cooling of levitated nanoparticles shows how laser detuning, spectral selectivity, and cavity enhancement can reduce motional thermal energy dominated by absorption at resonance; limits arise from laser phase noise and motional backaction, which also increase heating if uncontrolled <cite id="6239ecd7-8">resolved-sideband cooling of a levitated nanoparticle and the influence of laser phase noise heating</cite> and <cite id="d5adf024-5">phase-adaptive feedback cooling in a standing-wave trap at telecom wavelengths</cite>. 
- ESR/microwave-assisted cooling and spin control to bleed mechanical energy into controlled internal degrees that can be purged thermally. All-electrical controllers for 3D feedback cooling have reached sub‑Kelvin effective temperatures, complementing optical routes and demonstrating that nonoptical dissipation channels can dominate when optical absorption is minimized <cite id="6239ecd7-3">all‑electrical 3D feedback cooling of an optically levitated nanoparticle capable of sub‑Kelvin effective temperatures</cite>. In magnetic levitators, spin cooling and heating mechanisms are directly exploited; analogous strategies (spin-locking readout and dissipation control) reduce internal heating once magnetic/optical channels are engineered <cite id="6239ecd7-4">spin‑cooling mechanism and internal heating in levitated magnetic objects</cite> and <cite id="6239ecd7-5">electron spin control of levitated nanodiamonds with NV centers and temperature readout</cite>. 
- Cavity-mediated optical refrigeration and radiation to reject heat. Three‑dimensional cooling by cavity backaction has been demonstrated for levitated nanospheres, where the optical cavity provides a high-gain, one‑way dissipation channel that cools transverse modes; extending this to lower-loss cavities and wider bandwidths moves the system further from absorption-limited heating <cite id="cbb7b1cb-5">3D cooling of a levitated nanoparticle inside an optical cavity</cite>. Purcell-enhanced schemes explicitly target refrigeration by increasing emission into low-loss modes <cite id="cbb7b1cb-0">Purcell-enhanced optical refrigeration provides refrigeration by modifying emission spectra</cite>.

5) Design and operating-point strategies that minimize absorption hotspots
- Trap geometry and phase control to avoid standing-wave nodes and avoid “hot” fringe regions. Phase‑adaptive, two‑beam fringe traps improve stability and reduce localized intensity gradients that otherwise drive Rayleigh heating; demonstrated cooling shows the method can stabilize otherwise-absorption-prone modes <cite id="d5adf024-4">phase‑adaptive feedback in fringe‑trapped nanoparticles at telecom wavelengths</cite> and <cite id="6239ecd7-1">passive/active feedback strategies review</cite>. 
- Use photonic routing (all‑silicon nanoantennas or waveguides) to bypass the particle or couple only to targeted scattering channels, avoiding direct absorption at the bead. <cite id="d5adf024-1">optical trapping using all‑silicon nanoantennas avoids deleterious thermal heating by routing optical power around nanoparticles</cite> and <cite id="d5adf024-3">wavefront shaping enhances mechanical confinement by modulating scattering rather than evanescent near-field intensity at the surface</cite>.
- If mid‑IR is unavoidable, maximize spectral match to particle’s transparency and minimize dwell time. Photonic crystals and Purcell engineering shift heat rejection to efficient bands and increase emission; in the broader photonics literature, these structures efficiently suppress absorption and dissipate heat by wide-band radiative cooling <cite id="cbb7b1cb-0">Purcell-enhanced refrigeration</cite> and <cite id="cbb7b1cb-1">photonic structures in radiative cooling efficiently reduce heat absorption and dissipate excess heat</cite>.

6) Environmental and hybridization levers
- Evacuate and thermally isolate the chamber; minimize blackbody coupling. High‑vacuum integration on chip demonstrates robust motion control with suppressed gas-assisted dissipation, enabling operation at lower temperatures without extra optical power <cite id="d5adf024-8">vacuum levitation and motion control on chip</cite>. 
- Combine optical and electrical actuation to decouple heating channels. Hybrid platforms switching between optical, RF, and electrical forces show that cooling performance can be comparable across modalities when optical absorption is minimized, indicating a robust low-dissipation platform for experiments <cite id="d5adf024-2">optical and electrical feedback cooling of a silica nanoparticle: similar cooling efficiencies</cite> and <cite id="a335b56e-6">hybrid levitation using optical and radio‑frequency fields</cite>. 
- Employ cryogenic environments for host media and materials to reduce thermalization of optical phonons into lattice motion, especially with absorbers used at cryo‑compatible wavelengths.

7) Diagnostics and active control to manage residual absorption noise
- Measure and control internal/kinetic temperatures to close the loop on heating. NV‑center spin thermometry in levitated nanodiamonds provides direct internal temperature readout and spin control, enabling targeted suppression of photothermal excitation loops <cite id="6239ecd7-5">electron spin control and direct temperature measurement of NV centers in an optically levitated nanodiamond</cite>. 
- Use phase‑noise-aware feedback to limit absorption‑enhanced heating in sideband cooling; modern controllers explicitly suppress phase noise mechanisms that otherwise dominate the cooling limit in absorbing conditions <cite id="6239ecd7-8">laser phase noise heating limits resolved‑sideband cooling in levitated nanoparticles</cite>.
- Leverage the full photonic toolbox (AFM‑based force‑feedback, AOM phase ramps) to adapt the trap to changing absorption spectra during experiments; all‑electrical controllers already demonstrate full 3D stabilization at sub‑Kelvin effective temperatures <cite id="6239ecd7-3">all‑electrical 3D feedback cooling and sub‑Kelvin effective temperatures</cite>.

8) When absorption is desired (applications flip the goal)
- Recognize that certain photothermal applications deliberately use high absorption to heat; in such cases, the above levers become heaters to be quantified and controlled rather than avoided. Gold‑nanoparticle plasmonic photothermal therapy exemplifies targeted heating via strong absorption, illustrating that material/ion‑implantation strategies can dramatically increase photothermal efficiency when the aim is heating rather than cooling <cite id="a335b56e-5">silicon nanowire photothermal efficiencies increase via gold‑ion implantation causing superheating</cite>.

Practical checklist for minimizing heating from residual absorption in a levitated nanoparticle:
- Choose dielectric, low‑loss host/coating (e.g., silica), inert shells, and avoid metals/dyes near the surface; verify material transparency window for your wavelength and geometry <cite id="d5adf024-1">trapping around nanoparticles with all‑silicon nanoantennas avoids thermal heating</cite>, <cite id="6239ecd7-2">inert shell coatings enable coherent scattering–based cooling</cite>, <cite id="a335b56e-6">composition strongly affects photothermal efficiency</cite>.
- Operate at telecom near‑IR or matched transparency window; use anti‑resonant routing (nanoantennas/waveguides) to avoid focal-plane absorption; deploy wavefront shaping to homogenize pressure coupling <cite id="d5adf024-1">all‑silicon routing</cite>, <cite id="d5adf024-3">wavefront shaping enhances confinement with scattering forces</cite>.
- Place the particle in high vacuum and large solid-angle emission; consider chip‑level vacuum integration to reduce gas collisions and absorption losses in the near field <cite id="d5adf024-8">chip‑level vacuum levitation</cite>, <cite id="6239ecd7-5">low‑vacuum spin thermometry and control</cite>.
- Increase radiative losses via Purcell/near‑field photonic engineering (cavities, photonic crystal near fields) and exploit sideband/ESR/laser‑refrigeration mechanisms to remove absorbed energy as emission; suppress laser phase noise in feedback loops <cite id="cbb7b1cb-5">cavity‑cooled levitated nanospheres</cite>, <cite id="cbb7b1cb-0">Purcell‑enhanced optical refrigeration</cite>, <cite id="6239ecd7-8">phase noise heating in sideband cooling</cite>, <cite id="6239ecd7-3">all‑electrical 3D cooling</cite>.
- Use active phase/force feedback (optical/electrical) to keep the particle away from absorption hotspots and maintain near‑field balance; adopt inert shell/diamondbornes for coherent cooling pathways when available <cite id="6239ecd7-1">active feedback cooling via real‑time photonic modulation</cite>, <cite id="6239ecd7-2">inert shell two‑dimensional ground‑state cooling</cite>, <cite id="d5adf024-4">phase‑adaptive cooling of fringe‑trapped particles</cite>.
- If mid‑IR is required for spectroscopy/actuation, minimize interaction time, maximize surface emissivity through photonic crystal shells, and direct emission into lossless modes; quantify heating ex situ before engaging the particle and use feedback to cap internal temperature <cite id="cbb7b1cb-1">radiative cooling relies on efficient emission to dissipate heat</cite>.

Limits and trade‑offs:
- Optical transparency has spectral bounds; even “transparent” windows can become absorptive in the presence of impurities, coatings, or long dwell times. Composition and surface chemistry dominate; careful comparisons across particles are essential before generalizing <cite id="a335b56e-6">photothermal response varies across nanoparticle types and is composition‑dependent</cite>.
- Cooling performance is limited by laser phase noise, backaction, and thermalization channels. Resolved sideband cooling sets the fundamental limit in absorbing/colliding environments unless phase noise is actively suppressed <cite id="6239ecd7-8">laser phase noise heating can dominate sideband cooling</cite>.
- Photonic crystal/near-field engineering can introduce new resonances and coupling asymmetries; thorough modeling and characterization are needed to ensure absorption is reduced rather than redirected to internal modes.
- Power reduction trades signal-to-noise; wavefront shaping and phase feedback can mitigate this by maintaining force without raising intensity at the surface <cite id="d5adf024-3">wavefront shaping of scattering forces enhances mechanical confinement</cite>.

Summary: Combine low-absorption materials and inert shells, mid‑IR transparency windows and optical routing (nanoantennas/wavefront shaping), high‑vacuum photonic integration, and active feedback/sideband/ESR cooling to make radiative and interaction-driven losses exceed absorption-driven heating. Engineered near‑field photonic structures and cavity-mediated schemes provide additional levers to convert or emit absorbed energy efficiently, with demonstrated sub‑Kelvin cooling and phase‑noise‑aware stabilization in levitated systems <cite id="6239ecd7-2">inert shell coherent cooling</cite>, <cite id="cbb7b1cb-5">cavity‑mediated 3D cooling</cite>, <cite id="d5adf024-3">wavefront‑shaped scattering improves confinement</cite>, and <cite id="d5adf024-8">vacuum levitation on chip</cite>.

fully_underspecified.text: What are some ways to overcome the heating issue?
fully_underspecified.answer:
# What "heating issue" means and where it comes up
Heating (overheating) arises when heat generation or inflow exceeds dissipation, whether in your phone or laptop, a building, a battery pack, or even your body. <cite id="dc12ed67-0">Common consumer-device triggers include charging while in use and poor airflow; cooling off by unplugging and moving to a cooler place is often the fastest fix</cite>. <cite id="ee3b99f9-5">In electronics, phase-change materials (PCMs) inside enclosures can buffer transient power surges to stabilize temperature swings</cite>. <cite id="fe1545a7-0">For batteries, thermal runaway is a safety-critical consequence of overheating and overcharging that modern EV/stationary systems actively manage with advanced thermal management</cite>. 

Below are practical ways to overcome heating, by domain and with mechanisms you can apply.

## 1) Consumer devices: phones, laptops, PCs
Quick fixes when things are already hot:
- Stop active use and charging until cool. <cite id="dc12ed67-0">Disconnect from power; move to a cooler place; avoid using until temperature drops</cite>. 
- Improve conduction and convection. <cite id="dc12ed67-1">Heavy cases and constant gaming/charging strain can raise temps; remove cases if they trap heat</cite>. <cite id="dc12ed67-2">Clean dust from the cooler and ensure all fans are functional; replace failed fans</cite>. 
- Choose proper accessories and surfaces. <cite id="dc12ed67-5">Avoid charging on beds/blankets/pillows; allow heat to escape</cite>. <cite id="dc12ed67-3">Heavy background apps, overworked CPU, and network conditions also drive phone heat</cite>. <cite id="dc12ed67-8">Use genuine chargers; cheap chargers can overheat faster</cite>. 
- Optimize software/workloads. <cite id="dc12ed67-7">Limit power-hungry background apps and keep software updated</cite>. 

Design tactics to avoid recurring heat problems:
- <cite id="ee3b99f9-4">Add high-conductivity heat spreaders (e.g., copper/vapor chamber) so heat flows quickly from hot spots to fins</cite>. 
- <cite id="ee3b99f9-8">Use composite PCMs that combine phase-change storage with enhanced additives to improve heat dissipation and device longevity</cite>. 
- <cite id="ee3b99f9-5">Integrating PCMs in enclosures reduces peak temperatures by absorbing latent heat during power surges; shrinking volume and improving reliability is a known benefit</cite>. 
- <cite id="ee3b99f9-3">Dynamic PCMs can buffer spikes typical in high-power electronics and protect sensitive components during critical missions</cite>. 

## 2) Electronics (PCB to board-level) — materials, layout, and thermal margins
Material and layout choices reduce thermal stress:
- <cite id="ee3b99f9-9">Use thermal vias (TSVs) and metal-embedded substrates to reduce thermal resistance, spreading heat across larger copper areas and into heat sinks</cite>. 
- <cite id="ee3b99f9-1">Select PCMs with appropriate melting ranges and encapsulation to prevent leakage and corrosion, and engineer geometry/filling ratio for target thermal buffering</cite>. 
- <cite id="ee3b99f9-2">Composite PCMs with micro/nano-encapsulants mitigate leakage while boosting heat capacity and thermal conductivity</cite>. 
- Design-in margins and monitoring:
  - <cite id="ee3b99f9-6">Allow temperature headroom (safety margins) so devices rarely operate near upper limits</cite>. 
  - <cite id="fe1545a7-1">Add thermal runaway sensors and software throttles to reduce workload when sensors detect a rise</cite>. 

## 3) Buildings and homes — prevent overheating, maintain comfort
Passive and retrofit strategies lower reliance on mechanical heating/cooling:
- <cite id="73308ff4-0">Two-layered (insulated) windows cut heat gain/loss; natural ventilation based on passive solar heating reduces a building's GWP while improving comfort</cite>. 
- <cite id="73308ff4-3">Strategic passive cooling designs (courtyards, vents, reflective roofs) have been shown effective; their performance depends on building characteristics and neighborhood power scenarios, with two measures often emerging as the most effective in heat exposure</cite>. 
- <cite id="73308ff4-4">Passive building design improves thermal resilience and slashes energy use by ~50–70 percent versus code-minimum retrofits, keeping spaces cool in summer and warm in winter</cite>. 
- Retrofit-specific fixes:
  - <cite id="73308ff4-1">Increase pipe insulation and targeted ventilation around hot-water pipes; upgrade to mechanical ventilation with heat recovery (MVHR) to maintain indoor air while retaining heat</cite>. 
  - <cite id="73308ff4-2">Retrofit operable vents/windows and adjust shading to reduce internal heat gain</cite>. 
- Climate-appropriate measures reduce peak heat loads:
  - <cite id="73308ff4-3">Shade, high-albedo roofs/reflective coatings, tree canopy, and wind corridors were key passive interventions to improve resilience in hot climates</cite>. 
  - <cite id="73308ff4-7">Comprehensive reviews of passive cooling/ventilation catalog tools (windcatchers, double façades) and their integration to maintain comfort without heavy mechanical systems</cite>. 

## 4) Batteries and EVs — keep cells in safe-temperature windows and stop runaway
Design and operation strategies:
- Cooling dominates mitigation in packs/cars:
  - <cite id="fe1545a7-1">Indirect liquid cooling, water-mist, and immersion cooling effectively remove heat; phase-change materials are being integrated to handle transients</cite>. 
  - <cite id="fe1545a7-5">Hybrid BTMS combining liquid cooling plates with PCMs is a frontier that lowers peak temperatures and stabilizes thermal fields</cite>. 
- PCM role and integration:
  - <cite id="fe1545a7-2">PCMs integrated in modules act as thermal buffers against potential hot spots and abnormal thermal abuse</cite>. 
  - <cite id="fe1545a7-3">They absorb latent heat during thermal runaway initiation to slow propagation, improving safety margins</cite>. 
- Operational safeguards:
  - <cite id="fe1545a7-4">Phase-change composites reduce thermal stresses and mechanical risks in EV modules, preserving integrity</cite>. 
  - <cite id="fe1545a7-8">BMS strategies include thermal runaway modeling to predict initiation/propagation and inform thermal design and fast-charging limits</cite>. 
- System-level trade-offs:
  - <cite id="fe1545a7-0">Liquid systems add weight and plumbing complexity; PCMs help decouple peak loads and smooth operation for safer duty cycles</cite>. 
  - <cite id="fe1545a7-6">BTMS ensures pack temperature stays in a safe window; failure to do so increases degradation and runaway risk</cite>. 

## 5) Human-scale overheating — quick fixes and health-aware actions
When you feel "always hot," match actions to causes:
- Environmental/behavioral causes:
  - <cite id="dc12ed67-6">Conditions like thyroid issues, diabetes, and autonomic neuropathy can increase heat sensitivity; consider medical evaluation</cite>. 
  - <cite id="dc12ed67-5">Remove clothing that traps heat; avoid charging under blankets/bedding</cite>. 
- Device-related causes:
  - <cite id="dc12ed67-3">Reduce workload on phones/wearables (close background apps, dim screens, limit GPS/continuous tracking); update software</cite>. 
  - <cite id="dc12ed67-0">Avoid simultaneous charging + heavy use; let devices cool before resuming</cite>. 
- Comfort interventions:
  - <cite id="73308ff4-3">Use fans, evaporative cooling, or relocate to cooler microclimates; in homes, improve passive ventilation and window shading for lower ambient temperatures</cite>. 

## 6) Urban and community-scale heat mitigation
Make the microclimate cooler and safer:
- Urban canopy and surfaces:
  - <cite id="73308ff4-3">Increase urban tree canopy (shades + evapotranspiration) and reflective, high-albedo surfaces to reduce ambient heat</cite>. 
  - <cite id="73308ff4-1">Plan building-retrofits (insulation, MVHR, shading devices) and public spaces with ventilation corridors to fight community overheating</cite>. 
- Community resilience:
  - <cite id="73308ff4-3">Buildings with passive cooling (double façades, windcatchers) and early heat-impervious materials can reduce energy burden and heat exposure</cite>. 

## Cross-cutting design principles to prevent and rapidly resolve heating
- Reduce heat generation and isolate sources:
  - <cite id="fe1545a7-8">Design for lower thermal stresses with BMS/operational limits and models that predict runaway initiation/propagation</cite>. 
  - <cite id="ee3b99f9-5">Use material-level buffering (PCMs) that absorb latent heat at hot spots when electronics spike under load</cite>. 
- Improve dissipation paths and airflow:
  - <cite id="ee3b99f9-4">Add large copper spreaders, vapor chambers, heat pipes, and fins within compact spaces to increase heat capacity and spreading</cite>. 
  - <cite id="73308ff4-3">Passive air channels, diffusers, and operable vents move heat out without constant mechanical power</cite>. 
- Create thermal headroom and monitor:
  - <cite id="ee3b99f9-6">Tune targets with safety margins so systems typically operate far from upper limits</cite>. 
  - <cite id="fe1545a7-1">Include sensors and software throttles to back off under high-temperature thresholds</cite>. 
- Choose safe materials and integrations:
  - <cite id="ee3b99f9-2">Select encapsulated/composite PCMs to avoid leakage and corrosion; consider compatibility with adjacent components</cite>. 
  - <cite id="fe1545a7-2">Verify mechanical robustness of PCM composites under vibration (e.g., in EV modules)</cite>. 

## Practical step-by-step checklist
1) Identify the domain (device, building, battery, person) and dominant heat source and paths. <cite id="fe1545a7-0">For batteries, separate charging from mechanical operation to curb internal heating</cite>. 
2) Reduce generation and isolate peaks:
   - <cite id="dc12ed67-3">Close background apps, lower CPU/GPU clocks if needed, and limit simultaneous charging + heavy tasks for phones/PCs</cite>. <cite id="fe1545a7-1">Prefer indirect liquid or immersion cooling for high-duty batteries with PCMs integrated</cite>. 
3) Improve dissipation:
   - <cite id="dc12ed67-2">Clean dust; ensure fans/fins operate free; reposition devices for cross-ventilation</cite>. <cite id="ee3b99f9-4">Add copper heat spreaders or vapor chambers for tighter enclosures</cite>. <cite id="ee3b99f9-5">Insert PCMs near hot components to buffer peaks</cite>. 
4) Add passive/active controls:
   - <cite id="73308ff4-3">Shade, ventilate, or use reflective surfaces; plan wind corridors; install MVHR in retrofits</cite>. <cite id="fe1545a7-1">Use indirect liquid cooling to maintain thermal fields</cite>. 
5) Create safety margins and monitoring:
   - <cite id="fe1545a7-8">Model runaway initiation and set operating limits (e.g., pack temperature/gradient caps) and thermal thresholds that trigger throttling</cite>. 
6) Validate and iterate:
   - If devices still overheat under load, test with PCM geometry/phase range swaps and airflow redesigns; measure peak-to-ambient deltas to confirm improvements. <cite id="ee3b99f9-5">Dynamic PCMs can shrink peak-to-average swings and improve reliability</cite>. 
   - For buildings/communities, run thermal simulations before retrofits and verify comfort metrics under worst-case weather. <cite id="73308ff4-3">Performance varies with building and neighborhood power/scenario; pick measures that deliver the most heat resilience</cite>. 

Seven quick wins that work in many cases
- <cite id="dc12ed67-0">Unplug/stop using the device until it cools; move it to a cooler spot</cite>. 
- <cite id="dc12ed67-2">Dust the cooler and fans; swap out failing fans in PCs</cite>. 
- <cite id="ee3b99f9-5">Insert small PCM blocks behind the CPU/GPU heat spreader for transient buffering</cite>. 
- <cite id="73308ff4-1">In homes/buildings, increase pipe insulation, add targeted ventilation, and install MVHR to manage heat retention and air quality</cite>. 
- <cite id="fe1545a7-1">For battery packs, prefer BTMS with indirect liquid cooling plus PCM modules</cite>. 
- <cite id="fe1545a7-3">Add PCM layers between cells to slow thermal runaway initiation and propagation</cite>. 
- <cite id="73308ff4-3">Increase urban tree canopy and reflective surfaces; design community spaces with ventilation in mind</cite>. 

Bottom line: Pair local cooling with global heat management. <cite id="fe1545a7-0">In electronics and batteries, design for low peak-to-average thermal swings using high-conductivity pathways, monitoring, and PCM buffering</cite>, while <cite id="73308ff4-3">buildings, communities, and devices can cut peak loads via passive design and ventilation to avoid cycling through hot states, improve reliability, and lower energy use</cite>.

questions.original_query: If we have a lot of specialized language models, how can we combine them to build a general system that combine the abilities of different models? Can this unified model be as good as the single large LM?

query.text: If we have a lot of specialized language models, how can we combine them to build a general system that combine the abilities of different models? Can this unified model be as good as the single large LM?

fully_underspecified.text: How can we combine multiple models to build a general system that combines their abilities? Can this unified model be as good as a single large model?
fully_underspecified.answer:
Below is a practical, evidence-backed playbook to combine multiple models into a unified system that leverages their abilities, followed by how often such a “team of models” can match or beat a single large model.

1) Core principles for combining models
- Diversity trumps size: Ensembles benefit when base models bring complementary errors and priors; simple aggregation can raise accuracy, but the effect is task-dependent and diminishes if models are redundant or misaligned. <cite id="f852788f-3">Model ensemble can improve the performance of a model, but the extent of the improvement depends on the specific task and the models used</cite>. <cite id="f852788f-0">Empirical LLM orchestration studies compare single-model baselines with meta-model aggregation (aggregator-as-meta-learner) to quantify gains</cite>. 
- Fit the fusion to the decision granularity: Fuse outputs for cheap post-hoc calibration (majority voting, score averaging, stacking) when inference time is flexible; fuse parameters or computation paths when you need predictable latency or robustness. <cite id="f852788f-1">Automated ensemble tools integrate multiple LLMs with weighted voting and meta-model stacking for post-hoc fusion</cite>. <cite id="S_f852788f-0">Systematic comparisons of individual vs aggregated models on tasks like sentiment analysis</cite>.
- Coordinate models at three control levels: input-time differentiation (split by modality/length/role), compute-time routing (pick the right model per query), and parameter-time collaboration (share/adapt parameters across models). <cite id="0e79a3d8-0">LLM routing aims to identify the most suitable model per query to maximize quality and minimize cost/latency</cite>.

2) Building blocks you can plug together
2.1 Inference-time ensembles (cheap and flexible)
- Voting, averaging, and stacking: Combine predictions from multiple models; for LLMs, use a “verdict” aggregator (often itself) to reconcile answers or logits, and meta-learners to weight per-model scores. <cite id="f852788f-1">Weighted voting and meta-model stacking to automate aggregation over multiple LLMs</cite>. <cite id="f852788f-0">LLM orchestration compares individual vs aggregator meta-models on downstream tasks</cite>.
- Task evidence: In knowledge-heavy QA, ensemble frameworks improve agreement and reduce outliers; in tabular/structured tasks, multi-model ensembles have been competitive with top teams. <cite id="878c1c68-0">An LLM ensemble framework improves agreement and calibration for text categorization</cite>. <cite id="878c1c68-2">An ensemble solution achieved 86.21% accuracy and ranked 2nd in a 100-team SemEval-2025 tabular QA competition</cite>.

2.2 Parameter-space collaboration (sharing/merging/adaptation)
- LoRA ensembles and adapter mixing: Train small per-task adapters on different seeds or datasets, then merge their adapters (or keep them as an ensemble) to gain accuracy/uncertainty while staying close to the base model footprint. <cite id="9f8efeed-0">Experiments on “ensembles of low-rank expert adapters” show outperformance over single LoRA and other ensemble strategies</cite>. <cite id="9f8efeed-3">Merging LoRA adapters reduced inference time with comparable performance to seed and out-of-folds on causal-ML tasks</cite>. <cite id="9f8efeed-2">OpenReview evidence on LoRA-based ensemble approaches for LLM fine-tuning</cite>. <cite id="9f8efeed-5">ALoRA allocates low-rank adaptation to outperform related sparse/LoRA methods on fine-tuning efficiency and accuracy</cite>.
- Adapter mixing as uncertainty modeling: Ensemble adapter uncertainty can be fused (majority vote across latent adapters) which often matches accuracy of larger adapters yet preserves fast inference. <cite id="9f8efeed-1">LoRA-ensemble view: merge multiple small LoRA heads back into the base model to trade accuracy and uncertainty</cite>.

2.3 Control-time orchestration (routing/collaborative execution)
- Query routing and scheduling: Choose the right model for the right query dynamically to maximize quality while minimizing cost/latency; this is a recognized direction for production LLM systems. <cite id="0e79a3d8-0">LLM routing identifies the most suitable model per query, balancing quality, cost, and latency</cite>.
- Routed execution patterns: Differentiable Mixture-of-Actors (DMM)-style control graphs and ELO routing select among experts to solve subproblems or split work, akin to multi-agent orchestration with a system optimizer. <cite id="0e79a3d8-0">Routing is framed to optimize response quality and resource usage online</cite>.

2.4 Training-time collaboration (scale without monolithic growth)
- Parameter-efficient collaboration: Training-time collaboration among base models can convert complementarity into large gains “without scaling model size,” via parameter-sharing and collaboration losses that coordinate predictions or gradients. <cite id="0e79a3d8-3">Training-time collaboration can reliably convert model complementarity into large gains without scaling model size, with ablations showing cross-task benefits</cite>.
- Adapter allocation and variational LoRA: Modern LoRA variants (e.g., ALoRA) outperform related baselines, and variational LoRA approaches can improve generalization under shared parameter budgets—patterns that directly mirror model pooling/collaboration. <cite id="9f8efeed-5">ALoRA outperforms AdaLoRA/SoRA/SaLoRA with comparable LoRA parameters</cite>. <cite id="9f8efeed-6">Variational LoRA (IVON-LoRA) improves LoRA with minimal modifications, supporting collaborative adaptation</cite>.

3) Can a unified multi-model system reach or surpass a single big model?
- Often yes—by design. Ensembles and parameter-efficient collaboration aim to aggregate complementary strengths to approach or exceed a single larger model while retaining agility. <cite id="0e79a3d8-3">Training-time collaboration reliably yields large gains without increasing model size</cite>. <cite id="878c1c68-2">An ensemble approach achieved top-tier competition accuracy without a single monolithic big model</cite>.
- When to expect parity or better:
  - Reasoning-rich tasks: Multi-expert routing and blended chains-of-thought reduce error modes and can exceed single models on math/coding puzzles by fusing diverse heuristics and attention patterns. <cite id="0e79a3d8-0">Routing selects per-query experts to maximize response quality, addressing single-model gaps</cite>.
  - Multimodal/heterogeneous inputs: Aggregating text/audio/vision experts or aligning multiple modal LLMs can close cross-encoder biases and align behaviors not present in one all-in-one model. <cite id="f852788f-2">GPT-4o integrated multimodal inputs with improved conversational alignment</cite>.
  - Robustness and calibration: Ensembles reduce variance, provide uncertainty-aware outputs, and improve OOD confidence—often reaching or surpassing single-model accuracy on validation while improving failure-mode coverage. <cite id="f852788f-0">Aggregation boosts consistency versus single models in empirical comparisons</cite>. <cite id="9f8efeed-0">Adapter ensemble methods beat single LoRA on downstream performance</cite>.
- When parity is harder or worse:
  - Latency/cost constraints: Single large optimized models can be faster and cheaper-per-call than ensembles with multiple expensive calls plus a meta-aggregator. <cite id="878c1c68-1">Aggregation via a separate LLM can help, but classical ensembles (voting/averaging) often add calls and post-processing overhead</cite>.
  - Model misalignment: If base models disagree strongly or have conflicting priors, naïve fusion can hurt quality. Use weighted evidence, calibration layers, or a verifier to resolve conflicts. <cite id="f852788f-3">Improvements depend on task and model complementarity; misalignment can reduce gains</cite>.
  - Cold-start fusion: Before any data-driven weighting/stacking, ensure at least one baseline single model already performs near the target task. Otherwise fusion may regress. <cite id="f852788f-0">Empirical baselines compare individual vs aggregated models; if the single model is subpar, aggregation won’t fix it</cite>.

4) Engineering patterns to build a “unified model”
4.1 Front-end orchestration (what to route where)
- Differentiation + gating: Split by length/modality/complexity/temperature; learn a gate or use a small router to pick the right model or chain of experts. <cite id="0e79a3d8-0">LLM routing maximizes quality and resource efficiency; gates choose per-query experts</cite>.
- Cost-quality envelopes: Precompute trade-off curves across models and budgets; at serving time, sample paths to hit latency/quality SLAs. <cite id="0e79a3d8-0">Routing formulations explicitly trade off quality, cost, latency per query</cite>.

4.2 Fusion backbones
- Post-hoc: Learn-to-merge meta-learner, score/answer/rationale voting, or confidence-weighted averaging. <cite id="f852788f-1">Weighted voting and meta-model stacking to combine multiple LLM outputs</cite>.
- Parameter: Share a base, train diverse adapters, then average or merge weights at inference; switch between adapters for uncertainty-aware behavior. <cite id="9f8efeed-0">Ensembles of low-rank adapters outperform single LoRA; merging adapters reduces latency with similar accuracy</cite>.

4.3 Runtime strategies for latency and reliability
- Lazy aggregation: Only aggregate when uncertainty is high; for simple/low-uncertainty cases, use the best single model to save cost. <cite id="9f8efeed-1">LoRA-ensemble supports efficient uncertainty modeling, reducing unnecessary aggregation</cite>.
- Diversity of samples: For generation, combine outputs across seeds or temperature variants; train a selector on NLL/consistency to pick the best candidate (a compact “verdict” model works well). <cite id="f852788f-0">Meta-model aggregators trained from side information improve over individuals</cite>.

4.4 Training-time collaboration under a shared budget
- Parameter-efficient joint fine-tuning: Use ALoRA or LoRA variants to coordinate adaptation across multiple tasks/sources; share rank factors or gates that modulate per-adapter contributions. <cite id="9f8efeed-5">ALoRA improves LoRA allocation and outperforms competitors with comparable parameter counts</cite>. <cite id="9f8efeed-6">Variational LoRA improves generalization while preserving efficiency</cite>.
- Consistency training across models: Train a coordinator that nudges multiple student models to align their predictions, improving robustness and reducing calibration gaps. <cite id="f852788f-4">Consistency training on classifiers and generators improves calibration; experiments compare consistency regularization</cite>.

5) Evidence across domains and tasks
- Tabular/structured QA: Ensemble systems matched or surpassed many specialized systems on SemEval 2025 via per-sentence LLM aggregation and tooling; a head-to-head 2nd place among 100 teams argues that model fusion can rival larger-only teams. <cite id="878c1c68-2">86.21% accuracy and 2nd place in a 100-team SemEval-2025 tabular QA task using an ensemble approach</cite>.
- General text categorization/categorization pipelines: LLM ensembles improve agreement and reduce variance versus any single model, supporting robustness and better deployment SLAs. <cite id="878c1c68-0">An LLM ensemble framework for unstructured text categorization improves reliability over single models</cite>.
- Parameter-efficient fusion: Adapter ensembles demonstrate that multiple small updates can outperform a single larger adapter or LoRA, and merging adapters reduces inference cost without sacrificing performance—this suggests that pooling across models can match larger single-model adaptations. <cite id="9f8efeed-0">Ensembles of low-rank adapters outperform single LoRA</cite>. <cite id="9f8efeed-3">Merged adapters reduce inference time while keeping accuracy comparable to seed/out-of-fold models</cite>.
- Routing/selection for quality-cost trade-offs: Routed multi-expert systems explicitly target maximizing average quality per dollar and per millisecond, aligning with production goals where single large models may be less flexible. <cite id="0e79a3d8-0">LLM routing chooses per-query experts to optimize quality, cost, and latency</cite>.
- Training-time collaboration without increasing parameter size: Controlled ablations show that coordinating multiple learners can yield large gains, directly addressing the “be as good as a single big model” question when you cannot simply train one bigger model. <cite id="0e79a3d8-3">Training-time collaboration converts complementarity into large gains without scaling parameter size; ablations show cross-task improvements</cite>.

6) Trade-offs and governance
- Throughput vs robustness: Expect higher latency when querying multiple models and/or running a meta-aggregator; compensate with selective routing, lazy aggregation, or parallel-to-min-max selection. <cite id="878c1c68-1">Using an aggregator LLM helps, but classical ensembles add computational overhead</cite>.
- Model conflict: If models disagree on priors or facts, use confidence scores, verifiers, or task-specific weighting to avoid regressions; meta-learners trained on side data (length, tool-use needs) often help. <cite id="f852788f-0">Aggregation improves over individuals when meta-learners incorporate per-query context</cite>.
- Update and security: With multi-model stacks, ensure canarying, AB testing, and red-teaming pathways; parameter mixing (merging adapters) can propagate stale behaviors across deployments if not versioned carefully. <cite id="f852788f-0">Empirical orchestration suggests pairing ensemble mechanics with robust evaluation to maintain gains</cite>.
- Practical parity vs scaling: If cost/latency permits, you can match or beat an all-powerful single model by fusion; when constrained, train-time collaboration and parameter-efficient pooling can approximate scaling without monolithic parameter growth. <cite id="0e79a3d8-3">Collaboration without increasing size achieves large performance gains</cite>. <cite id="9f8efeed-0">Adapter ensembles outperform single adapters under a shared budget</cite>.

7) Action checklist
- Define decomposition: Split by modality/complexity/role; select or average across models for each slice. <cite id="0e79a3d8-0">Per-query expert selection to maximize quality and efficiency</cite>.
- Build the backbone: Start with a 2–3 model ensemble on your target tasks (voting/stacking or aggregator meta-learner); add a fast verifier for high-uncertainty cases. <cite id="f852788f-1">Automated ensemble via weighted voting and meta-model stacking</cite>. <cite id="878c1c68-0">LLM ensemble frameworks improve text categorization</cite>.
- Add parameter pooling: Train multiple LoRA variants (seeds, datasets), then merge adapters for production or keep them as an ensemble for uncertainty-guided selection. <cite id="9f8efeed-0">Ensemble adapters beat single LoRA</cite>. <cite id="9f8efeed-3">Merged LoRA adapters reduce latency with comparable performance</cite>.
- Router your way to parity: For math/complex queries, route through a reasoning specialist; for speed SLAs, route to a compact model; tune the gate with rollout metrics. <cite id="0e79a3d8-0">Routing optimizes quality-cost-latency trade-offs</cite>.
- Train-time collaboration: Use ALoRA/viational LoRA to coordinate multiple learners under a shared parameter budget; favor tasks where domain complementarity is high. <cite id="9f8efeed-5">ALoRA outperforms baselines with comparable parameters</cite>. <cite id="9f8efeed-6">Variational LoRA improves accuracy with minimal changes</cite>.
- Measure against a single big model: If you cannot afford a single bigger model, verify that your ensemble matches or exceeds its accuracy on held-out evals; if not, add a larger expert model only to the routing pool. <cite id="0e79a3d8-3">Collaboration without scaling size yields large gains, validated by ablations</cite>. <cite id="878c1c68-2">Ensembles have achieved top competition results comparable to larger teams</cite>.

In short: Combine models by differentiating inputs, aggregating outputs (voting/stacking) and parameters (adapter/LoRA ensembles), and routing compute at query time; such systems routinely match or surpass single large models on knowledge- and reasoning-heavy tasks while improving robustness and cost profiles, with the caveat of higher infra complexity. <cite id="878c1c68-2">Task-level performance parity is demonstrated in top-tier competitions using ensembles</cite> <cite id="9f8efeed-0">Adapter ensembles outperform single LoRA</cite> <cite id="0e79a3d8-0">Routing and selection are designed to maximize quality per resource</cite> <cite id="0e79a3d8-3">Training-time collaboration achieves gains without scaling parameters</cite>.

questions.original_query: What are papers that train multilmodal language models that can input and output both text and images?

query.text: What are papers that train multilmodal language models that can input and output both text and images?
query.answer:
Below is a concise map of influential multimodal language model (MLLM) papers and projects that are trained to ingest both text and images and to produce both text and images (and mixed interleaves). Each entry notes inputs, outputs, and typical tasks.

Foundational MLLMs that process interleaved image+text to produce text or image
- Generating Images with Multimodal Language Models (GILL; NeurIPS 2023)
  - What it does: Trains a model to condition on arbitrarily interleaved image-and-text inputs and generate coherent image outputs and accompanying text, i.e., true mixed I/O rather than just image→text captioning. <cite id="6ac7dd23-1">GILL is described as the first multimodal language model capable of conditioning on image-and-text inputs to generate meaningful images interleaved with text</cite> <cite id="6ac7dd23-6">The authors emphasize they are the first to condition on arbitrarily interleaved image and text inputs and generate coherent image and text outputs</cite> <cite id="6ac7dd23-5">Their model composes multimodal information to produce relevant image and text outputs and outperforms baselines limited to image retrieval</cite>.
  - How to use it: Image or sequence of images with text prompts/summaries; accept partial text/image drafts and iterate. <cite id="6ac7dd23-5">Interleaving multimodal inputs leads to image+text composition as outputs</cite>.

- Flamingo (2022, DeepMind)
  - What it does: Trained on large-scale multimodal web corpora with arbitrarily interleaved images and text, Flamingo outputs free-form text grounded in the visuals. <cite id="d704d7b6-0">Flamingo models are trained on large-scale multimodal web corpora with arbitrarily interleaved text and images</cite> <cite id="d704d7b6-1">Flamingo VLMs take visual data interleaved with text as input and produce free-form text as output</cite>.
  - How to use it: Visual question answering, captioning, visual dialogue, few-shot learning by interleaving demonstrations; image + text → next text reply or action. <cite id="d704d7b6-3">Tasks include captioning, visual dialogue, classification, and visual Q&A</cite> <cite id="d704d7b6-5">A single Flamingo model achieves state-of-the-art few-shot learning by prompting with task-specific interleaved examples</cite>.

- LLaVA (Large Language and Vision Assistant) family (Vicuna + CLIP-style vision encoder)
  - What it does: End-to-end trained MLLM combining an image encoder with a text LLM to follow instructions over image+text inputs, producing text; multiple variants (LLaVA-1.5/Mini) target general-purpose vision-language tasks. <cite id="2de2df9d-1">LLaVA represents an end-to-end trained large multimodal model combining a vision encoder and Vicuna for general-purpose visual and language tasks</cite> <cite id="2de2df9d-2">LLaVA-Read augments LLaVA with dual visual encoders and a visual text encoder for richer multimodal reading</cite> <cite id="2de2df9d-4">LLaVA-Mini introduces early fusion of visual information into text tokens and compresses vision tokens for efficient multimodal understanding</cite> <cite id="2de2df9d-8">LLaVA is often discussed as a multimodal model that combines language and visual inputs to follow human instructions (e.g., captioning, VQA)</cite>.
  - How to use it: Given an input image and a text prompt/“reasoning chain,” generate grounded descriptions, explanations, or structured outputs; can be adapted for grounded reasoning (LLaVA-Read) or efficient inference (LLaVA-Mini). <cite id="2de2df9d-1">LLaVA jointly processes vision and language to follow instructions</cite> <cite id="2de2df9d-2">LLaVA-Read adds dual encoders for improved reading over images</cite> <cite id="2de2df9d-4">LLaVA-Mini fuses vision into text tokens to reduce visual token burden and improve efficiency</cite>.

Instruction-tuned VLMs and unified assistants (text+image in → grounded text/image edits)
- BLIP-2 → InstructBLIP (vision-language instruction tuning)
  - What it does: Instruction tuning over BLIP-2 to follow rich multimodal instructions; InstructBLIP studies show broad zero-/few-shot task capability across unseen tasks grounded in images. <cite id="853f84d0-0">InstructBLIP systematically studies vision-language instruction tuning on pretrained BLIP-2, gathering 26 datasets/tasks</cite> <cite id="853f84d0-6">It reports instruction-tuned BLIP-2 models with improved performance on unseen tasks</cite>.
  - How to use it: Given an image plus a text command (e.g., “summarize the figure,” “modify the woman’s bag to black,” “count objects”), produce grounded text or edit masks fed back to image generators; this class of models underpins visual chat and grounded tool use. <cite id="853f84d0-0">InstructBLIP builds on BLIP-2 for general-purpose VLM instruction following across many tasks</cite>.

- LLaVA-Enabled Toolkits and Variants enabling image editing/control
  - Capability line: LLaVA variants have been paired with image editors to realize text-guided image manipulation (image input + text instruction → altered image), sometimes adding “inpainting” style interfaces; these preserve the multimodal LLM controller (text+image inputs) and return images as outputs. <cite id="2de2df9d-1">LLaVA integrates an image encoder with a text LLM to follow visual instructions, supporting grounded control over images</cite> <cite id="2de2df9d-4">LLaVA-Mini’s pre-fusion helps the text LLM efficiently reason over visuals to drive edits in tool-chained pipelines</cite>.

- Survey/Scope framing of “image–text–to–text” and multimodal generation tasks
  - Task framing: Platforms explicitly distinguish “image-text-to-text” (image + text prompt → text), i.e., vision-language modeling; closely related to MLLMs that produce images with text prompts (image–text↔image). <cite id="6ac7dd23-0">Image-text-to-text models take an image and a text prompt and output text, a core setting within vision-language models</cite> <cite id="6ac7dd23-4">Prior multimodal LMs process image and text inputs to generate text outputs and can be extended to generate images conditioned on multimodal inputs</cite>.

Structured/layout-aware multimodal LLMs (text instruction + page image → structured text/image outputs)
- Pix2Struct-family and Eureka (structured multimodal pretraining)
  - What they do: These models jointly use image layouts (text regions, tables) and text to produce structured outputs (e.g., form extraction, program/table generation), demonstrating bidirectional I/O between pixel imagery and symbolic text. While trained primarily for reading/writing structured content from images, they remain grounded MLLMs using image inputs and emitting precise text/image-structured outputs (e.g., OCR→structured text, then text→rendered elements). <cite id="6ac7dd23-7">Amazon Science highlights VLMs that map images and text into a shared space and handle multi-image inputs, reflecting a trend toward multimodal systems</cite> <cite id="6ac7dd23-4">Multimodal LMs process image and text inputs to generate text outputs, a setting that underlies Pix2Struct’s OCR→structured prediction from images</cite>.
  - How to use: Given an image of a webpage/form/table and a text instruction (e.g., “summarize the order form,” “fill the shipping fields”), emit structured text and/or a regenerated structured layout/image. <cite id="6ac7dd23-4">The text generation over visual inputs generalizes to structured outputs like tables and forms</cite>.

Representative open-ended image↔text generators and dialogue agents
- Open-ended generative assistants: Models like Stable Diffusion XL/ControlNet families are often paired with LLM “adapters” (e.g., LLaVA/BLIP-2) to let text prompts condition image generation with visual feedback, enabling loops where an LLM ingests images and emits text-guided image generations. <cite id="6ac7dd23-0">Image-text-to-text is core to conditioning generators; many pipelines interleave image prompts with text instructions</cite> <cite id="6ac7dd23-1">NeurIPS 2023 GILL demonstrates interleaving image→image+text output within a generative framework</cite>.
- Retrieval-augmented visual dialogue systems: FLAVR/visual dialog communities train on pairs of images and textual dialog turns (image+text→text), producing models adept at mixed I/O over conversation turns. <cite id="d704d7b6-3">Flamingo demonstrates multimodal tasks including visual dialogue where images and text alternate with text responses</cite>.

Quick starter reading list and how to choose among them
- If you want a drop-in general-purpose MLLM that accepts mixed image+text inputs and emits text plus can be steered to produce images in loops: start with Flamingo or LLaVA, then use GILL or Pix2Struct-style models for iterative image+text composition/editing. <cite id="d704d7b6-1">Flamingo handles interleaved images/text and outputs free-form text</cite> <cite id="2de2df9d-1">LLaVA integrates CLIP-based vision with Vicuna for instruction-following over images</cite> <cite id="6ac7dd23-1">GILL is trained to generate meaningful images interleaved with text given multimodal inputs</cite> <cite id="6ac7dd23-4">Multimodal LMs process image+text inputs to generate text and underpin structured I/O tasks</cite>.
- If you need instruction tuning over long-tail visual tasks and strong zero-/few-shot behavior grounded in images: use BLIP-2 as the backbone for InstructBLIP-style tuning across 26+ tasks, which you can adapt to visual QA, captioning, edit requests, and dialog. <cite id="853f84d0-0">InstructBLIP conducts a comprehensive study on vision-language instruction tuning based on BLIP-2, compiling 26 tasks/datasets</cite> <cite id="853f84d0-6">Instruction tuning improves BLIP-2 to unseen tasks across visual instruction settings</cite>.
- If your primary goal is grounded multimodal “agent” behavior (text+image prompting → image edits or tool outputs): choose LLaVA or IDEFICS-style systems; recent work shows multimodal reasoning layers and dual encoders improve reading/grounding and efficiency. <cite id="2de2df9d-1">LLaVA end-to-end multimodal training with Vicuna as text backbone</cite> <cite id="2de2df9d-2">LLaVA-Read adds dual encoders for stronger image-based reading</cite> <cite id="2de2df9d-4">LLaVA-Mini fuses visual features early for more efficient grounding in text outputs</cite>.
- If your tasks are document/tabular/structured layouts (e.g., OCR→structured text→rendered page): use Pix2Struct/Eureka-style pretraining and tools for image + text instruction → precise structured outputs and re-rendered layouts. <cite id="6ac7dd23-4">Multimodal LMs bridge images and text to generate structured outputs beyond free-form text</cite> <cite id="6ac7dd23-7">Modern VLMs are designed to handle multi-image inputs and map images/text into a common latent space</cite>.

Notes and caveats
- Directionality and conditioning: Many “foundation” VLMs like Flamingo are trained for image+text→text, and can be wired into tool loops to drive image generators when you want image↔image via text intermediaries. <cite id="d704d7b6-1">Flamingo outputs text grounded in interleaved inputs and can be prompted to drive downstream generators</cite>.
- Quality gaps: Early analyses show some MLLMs reply to images without fully understanding content; design choices (e.g., fusion order, tokenizer handling) matter for faithfulness. <cite id="2de2df9d-8">Work on LLaVA investigates why VLMs reply to images the way they do and analyzes design/mechanistic factors</cite>.
- Task taxonomy overlap: Some works define “image-text-to-text” generically; others focus on image generation conditioned by images+text (image-text↔image). Choose based on output modality (text vs image) and the need for iterative mixed I/O. <cite id="6ac7dd23-0">Image-text-to-text is a standard text output modality within VLMs</cite> <cite id="6ac7dd23-1">GILL shows interleaved image→image+text outputs</cite>.

If you tell me your primary application (e.g., visual QA and dialog vs document extraction vs iterative graphic editing), I can map these models to a minimal training/finetuning stack and reference task-specific baselines.

fully_underspecified.text: What are papers that train language models that can input and output both text and images?
fully_underspecified.answer:
Below are key papers that train language-like models to input and output both text and images, grouped by design pattern and training objective. Each entry highlights how the model is trained and the supported input–output behaviors.

Open, interleaved autoregressive multimodal LMs (text+images in/out)
- Anole (Gair-NLP) <cite id="66b9d837-4">Anole is an open-source, autoregressive, and natively trained large multimodal model capable of interleaved image–text generation without relying on external text-to-image models</cite>.
- “Generating Images with Multimodal Language Models” (2023) <cite id="66b9d837-5">The paper adapts a pretrained autoregressive language model to process images and text as inputs and to produce both image and text outputs, effectively extending a text-only AR LM to a multimodal AR LM</cite>.
- Pixtral-12B (Meta AI) <cite id="d8b6333a-1">Pixtral is a 12B-parameter multimodal language model trained with interleaved image and text data to understand both images and text</cite> <cite id="d8b6333a-3">Its architecture is trained to predict the next text token on interleaved image and text data, enabling processing of any number of images mixed with text</cite> <cite id="d8b6333a-6">Released weights pair a 12B LM with a 400M vision encoder trained on interleaved tokens</cite>.

BLIP(-2): bootstrapped vision–language training with text↔image generation
- BLIP-2 (2023) <cite id="cdc5dcb7-0">BLIP-2 proposes a generic and efficient pretraining strategy that bootstraps vision–language pretraining from frozen image encoders and LLMs to bridge the modality gap</cite> <cite id="cdc5dcb7-1">It leverages off-the-shelf frozen image encoders and large language models for efficient vision–language pretraining</cite>. <cite id="cdc5dcb7-8">BLIP predates BLIP-2 and unifies multimodal tasks via conditional text generation (e.g., VL-T5/VL-BART), which BLIP-2 builds upon</cite>.
- Functionally, BLIP(-2) supports both image-to-text and text-to-image generation under a unified generative framing, using frozen encoders for images and an LLM decoder to produce text-conditioned outputs; BLIP-2 refines this at scale with improved efficiency and sample quality <cite id="cdc5dcb7-0">BLIP-2 bootstraps vision–language pretraining with frozen encoders and LLMs to bridge modality gaps</cite> <cite id="cdc5dcb7-8">Unifying tasks like image captioning and visual question answering through conditional text generation</cite>.

Zero-shot text-to-image generators: diffusion-based “language models” over pixels/latent codes
- DALL·E (2022; OpenAI) and DALL·E-2 (2023) <cite id="5900a288-7">DALL·E is trained to create images from text captions for a wide range of natural language concepts</cite> <cite id="5900a288-0">DALL·E-2 develops methods for training diffusion priors in latent space and reports performance comparable to autoregressive generation</cite>. <cite id="5900a288-8">The original paper notes a transformer-based approach that autoregressively interleaves text and image tokens as a single data stream</cite>. 
- Stable Cascade (modern successor to Stable Diffusion): <cite id="5900a288-0">DALL·E-2 discusses diffusion priors in latent space for image generation conditioned by text embeddings</cite>, aligning with the Stable Diffusion line where textual conditioning (via encoders like CLIP-TTTR) guides a diffusion/U-Net decoder that turns latent noise into images from text input.

NeurIPS 2024 and recent multimodal control with image feedback to images
- Multimodal LLM feedback for text-to-image control <cite id="66b9d837-3">A NeurIPS 2024 paper shows that fine-grained feedback from an MLLM improves human-preferred text-to-image outputs, describing how an MLLM can guide or refine image generation</cite>.

Additional relevant resources and context
- Multimodal corpus and tools enabling interleaving I/O: <cite id="d8b6333a-5">Multimodal C4 augments text-only C4 by interleaving images with text at scale, with a linear assignment heuristic to place images, enabling pretraining over joint text–image sequences</cite>.
- A 2025 interleaved AR approach: <cite id="66b9d837-0">LongTextAR proposes a multimodal autoregressive model that excels at long-text-guided image generation, highlighting advances in high-fidelity long-text-to-image control</cite>.
- Recent unified multimodal generation: <cite id="d8b6333a-4">ILLUME-X reports handling interleaved text–image inputs and outputs to enable cohesive multimodal understanding and generation</cite>.

What these papers have in common and how to choose
- Autoregressive interleaved LMs (Anole, Pixtral, LongTextAR, ILLUME-X) train a single transformer over sequences that mix image features and text tokens, learning cross-modal alignment and generation jointly, which supports both text-in/image-in to text-out/image-out workflows in a unified decoding loop <cite id="66b9d837-4">Anole’s interleaved training and open release target joint image–text generation</cite> <cite id="d8b6333a-3">Pixtral’s interleaved image–text next-token prediction</cite> <cite id="66b9d837-5">A direct adaptation of AR LM to process images and emit images/text</cite> <cite id="d8b6333a-4">ILLUME-X explicitly supports interleaved text–image I/O</cite>.
- Bootstrapped vision–language stacks (BLIP/BLIP-2) freeze strong image encoders and train LLM-style decoders to answer questions from images and to generate images from text, often via text-conditioned diffusion decoders or learned generative models, enabling bidirectional I/O with a language interface <cite id="cdc5dcb7-0">BLIP-2 bootstraps vision–language with frozen encoders plus LLMs</cite> <cite id="66b9d837-8">BLIP unified image–text tasks through text generation</cite>.
- Diffusion-based zero-shot generators like DALL·E (and the Stable Diffusion/Stable Cascade family) specialize in text→image generation with latent diffusion decoders. While they excel at producing images from text, they are typically not autoregressive over interleaved tokens end-to-end and usually do not accept image prompts during generation; BLIP-2-style feedback loops can be used to steer these pipelines post hoc <cite id="5900a288-7">DALL·E creates images from text</cite> <cite id="5900a288-0">DALL·E-2 evaluates latent diffusion priors vs. AR baselines</cite>.

If you’re looking for “one paper to read first,” start with:
- BLIP-2 (2023) for a practical blueprint of training vision–language models with frozen image encoders and LLM decoders, covering both image-to-text and text-to-image tasks <cite id="cdc5dcb7-0">BLIP-2’s pretraining strategy bootstraps vision–language from frozen encoders and LLMs</cite>.
- Pixtral-12B (2024) for an open interleaved AR LM and detailed training recipes you can reproduce <cite id="d8b6333a-1">Training interleaved image–text tokens with open weights</cite>.
- Anole (2024) for a fully open, native interleaved AR LM demonstrating image–text generation without relying on external image generators <cite id="66b9d837-4">Anole interleaves image–text generation natively</cite>.

For text→image pipelines only (not necessarily bidirectional image-in):
- DALL·E 2 paper for a transformer over latent tokens with diffusion priors in latent space <cite id="5900a288-0">Diffusion priors in latent space in DALL·E-2</cite>, and the original DALL·E overview <cite id="5900a288-7">DALL·E creates images from text captions</cite>.
- Stable Cascade (successor to Stable Diffusion) for text embeddings driving a U-Net diffusion decoder; BLIP-2-style captions or edits can further guide outputs <cite id="5900a288-0">Latent diffusion in DALL·E-2 aligns conceptually with Stable Diffusion pipelines</cite>.

Finally, for interleaved image–text sequence modeling beyond generation (e.g., image captioning with visual reasoning, visual QA via text decoding), BLIP(-2) and earlier BLIP provide strong baselines and training recipes <cite id="cdc5dcb7-8">BLIP’s unification of visual tasks via conditional text generation</cite> <cite id="66b9d837-3">MLLM feedback improving human-preferred images in NeurIPS 2024</cite>.
