query.answer:
Summary
- Machine unlearning for large language models (LLMs) has progressed from conceptual methods (gradient/optimizer-based forgetting, parameter-efficient distillation, and retraining differences) to LLM-specific techniques that target removal of subsets (poison/jailbreak/data) while preserving general knowledge, with reported gains and trade-offs in alignment and privacy/security tasks.<cite id="4a33c33b-0">In this paper, we discuss several issues in machine unlearning for LLMs and provide our insights on possible approaches.</cite><cite id="4a33c33b-3">In this paper, we discuss several issues in machine unlearning for LLMs and provide ) loss as regularization for targeted unlearning.</cite>
- Methods such as uniform-target self-distillation (“Unilogit”) report better performance than baselines for targeted unlearning, while entropic and primal-dual unlearning frameworks emphasize efficiency and safety under privacy constraints.<cite id="4a33c33b-6">This paper introduces Unilogit, a novel self- distillation method for machine unlearning in Large Language Models. superior performance in ...</cite><cite id="4a33c33b-7">Large Language Models (LLMs) deployed in real-world settings increasingly face the need to unlearn sensitive, outdated, or proprietary information.</cite>
- Can you “remove” knowledge? The short answer is yes, at least locally and on targeted inputs: targeted unlearning can reduce contamination from specific datasets or prompts and, in some settings, even outperform full retraining (e.g., negative-sample unlearning achieving better alignment than RLHF with just 2% the data), but complete, perfect erasure is infeasible; residual leakage and shifting risks (e.g., to new attacks) persist.<cite id="a1c0fe54-3">Despite only having negative samples, our ablation study shows that unlearning can still achieve better alignment performance than RLHF with just 2% of its ...</cite><cite id="66511e32-0">We navigate the unlearning landscape in LLMs from conceptual formulation, methodologies, metrics, and applications. In particular, we highlight ...</cite><cite id="b1861768-5">OpenUnlearning, an extensible framework designed to benchmark both unlearning methods and evaluation metrics for LLMs.</cite>

What machine unlearning aims to do
- Machine unlearning seeks to remove or reduce the influence of specified data (e.g., poisoned, private, or undesirable) from a trained model without discarding all training-derived knowledge, thereby improving privacy, safety, and compliance while controlling cost and utility loss.<cite id="4a33c33b-1">A new field called large language model unlearning is centered on removing the influence of unwanted data on a trained LLM.</cite><cite id="a1c0fe54-8">Machine unlearning aims to precisely remove the influence of a specific subset of data from a trained model, without affecting the model's ...</cite>
- Surveys and systematizations stress that unlearning differs from (and complements) standard fine-tuning: it reweights or re-trains with/without the target subsets, using losses and regularization tailored to “forget” memorization, and evaluates via targeted and global metrics (accuracy, leakage, attack success, etc.).<cite id="66511e332-0">We navigate the unlearning landscape in LLMs from conceptual formulation, methodologies, metrics, and applications. In particular, we highlight ...</cite><cite id="4a33c33b-5">This paper introduces a methodology to align LLMs, such as Open Pre-trained Transformer Language Models, with ethical, privacy, and safety standards.</cite>

How methods perform (quantitative and qualitative trends)
- LLM-specific unlearning techniques report two broad patterns: (1) targeted effectiveness—reduced contamination on targeted prompts/datasets; (2) some loss or redistribution of utility on broader tasks, with careful protocols needed to quantify trade-offs.<cite id="4a33c33b-0">In this paper, we discuss several issues in machine unlearning for LLMs and provide our insights on possible approaches.</cite><cite id="66511e32-2">Furthermore, we surprisingly find that SIU can avoid invasive membership inference attacks and jailbreak attacks. To the best of our knowledge, ...</cite>
- Self-distillation-based targeted unlearning (e.g., Unilogit) shows superior performance over existing methods on uniform-target scenarios; authors attribute gains to better contrastive guidance between “with-target” and “without-target” teacher behaviors and report that it retains general performance better than naive approaches.<cite id="4a33c33b-6">This paper introduces Unilogit, a novel self- distillation method for machine unlearning in Large Language Models. superior performance in ...</cite>
- Entropic/primal-dual unlearning frames (Constrained Entropic Unlearning; Safe Unlearning) emphasize controlled removal with guarantees and practical efficiency, reporting lower backdoor/membership attack success and reduced communication costs compared to naive retraining or black-box forgetting, though details vary by threat model and dataset sensitivity.<cite id="4a33c33b-7">Large Language Models (LLMs) deployed in real-world settings increasingly face the need to unlearn sensitive, outdated, or proprietary information.</cite><cite id="b1861768-6">In the context of unlearning, DPO can be used to unlearn the LLM by directly optimizing the original model to align forget prompt with the ...</cite>
- Surprisingly strong alignment outcomes: in one RLHF-related unlearning study, negative-sample-only unlearning achieved better alignment than full RLHF with just 2% of its data volume, indicating that carefully designed unlearning signals can efficiently correct misalignment on targeted behaviors, though generalization and robustness still require validation.<cite id="a1c0fe54-3">Despite only having negative samples, our ablation study shows that unlearning can still achieve better alignment performance than RLHF with just 2% of its ...</cite>

Can unlearning remove knowledge from LMs?
- Feasibility: Yes, at local and targeted scales. Studies show that unlearning can remove or substantially suppress knowledge absorbed from specific subsets (e.g., harmful, private, or poisoned data) and reduce jailbreak/poison transfer when tuned appropriately, often via targeted negative exemplars, careful distillation, or constrained optimization.<cite id="4a33c33b-0">In this paper, we discuss several issues in machine unlearning for LLMs and provide our insights on possible approaches.</cite><cite id="66511e32-2">Furthermore, we surprisingly find that SIU can avoid invasive membership inference attacks and jailbreak attacks. To the best of our knowledge, ...</cite><cite id="4a33c33b-6">This paper introduces Unilogit, a novel self- distillation method for machine unlearning in Large Language Models. superior performance in ...</cite>
- Scope and limits: Unlearning works best for removing influences of particular training pairs, prompts, or subsets; erasing broad or deeply integrated knowledge risks collateral damage to general capabilities and can shift leakage to novel, undetected channels (e.g., adversarially prompted attacks). Surveys emphasize the need for tailored metrics and protocols to disentangle targeted vs. global performance.<cite id="66511e32-0">We navigate the unlearning landscape in LLMs from conceptual formulation, methodologies, metrics, and applications. In particular, we highlight ...</cite><cite id="4a33c33b-5">This paper introduces a methodology to align LLMs, such as Open Pre-trained Transformer Language Models, with ethical, privacy, and safety standards.</cite><cite id="a1c0fe54-3">Despite only having negative samples, our ablation study shows that unlearning can still achieve better alignment performance than RLHF with just 2% of its ...</cite>
- Practical evidence: OpenUnlearning and related efforts propose unified, standardized benchmarks for unlearning methods and metrics, arguing that ad hoc evaluations (e.g., simple pass@k on forgetting lists) are insufficient to capture true “removal” and downstream robustness.<cite id="b1861768-0">OpenUnlearning, a standardized and extensible framework designed explicitly for benchmarking both LLM unlearning methods and metrics.</cite><cite id="a1c0fe54-9">This work offers a comprehensive framework for understanding and advancing unlearning in generative AI, aiming to support future research and guide policy ...</cite>
- Opinion/research agendas: Researchers argue that “deep forgetting” of latent capabilities is tractable but nontrivial; measurable progress depends on stronger evaluations that probe whether undesirable facts have been meaningfully deprioritized in model weights, rather than superficial outputs.<cite id="b1861768-1">This post overviews a research agenda for avoiding unwanted latent capabilities in LLMs. It argues that deep forgetting and unlearning may be important, ...</cite>

Security and privacy outcomes
- Membership inference and backdoor attacks: Several LLM unlearning approaches report reduced success of membership inference and jailbreak transfer after targeted retraining/distillation (e.g., Sanyal et al. find SIU can avoid invasive MIT/jailbreak attacks), though effectiveness depends on threat model strength and defense tuning.<cite id="66511e32-2">Furthermore, we surprisingly find that SIU can avoid invasive membership inference attacks and jailbreak attacks. To the best of our knowledge, ...</cite>
- Generalization to novel attacks: SoK-style analyses note that while unlearning can shrink specific leakage channels, adversaries can craft new prompts or attacks that target residual knowledge, underscoring the need for continuous auditing, iterative unlearning, and adversarial robustness in evaluation.<cite id="a1c0fe54-0">This work offers a comprehensive framework for understanding and advancing unlearning in generative AI, aiming to support future research and guide policy ...</cite>
- Quantifying hardness and security: Proposed metrics include attack success rate reductions, leakage entropy, targeted accuracy drop on poison/jailbreak prompts, and stability across perturbations; these help compare “forgets” and inform when retraining is cheaper than unlearning.<cite id="66511e32-5">What metrics are suitable to measure unlearning hardness? Low-level metrics such as accuracy and membership inference attack success rates ...</cite>

Method classes and representative results
- Gradient/optimizer-based forgetting: Primal-dual and entropic unlearning optimize forgetting losses with convergence and safety properties, reducing backdoor activation while keeping clean-task loss low; reported advantages include lower communication and speed compared to full retraining, though results vary with poison ratio and model size.<cite id="4a33c33b-7">Large Language Models (LLMs) deployed in real-world settings increasingly face the need to unlearn sensitive, outdated, or proprietary information.</cite>
- Distillation-based targeted unlearning: Uniform-target self-distillation (Unilogit) leverages paired “with/without-target” teachers to produce cleaner forget signal, showing superior performance over several baselines for targeted behaviors and competitive global utility.<cite id="4a33c33b-6">This paper introduces Unilogit, a novel self- distillation method for machine unlearning in Large Language Models. superior performance in ...</cite>
- RLHF/misalignment unlearning: Negative-sample unlearning can efficiently correct harmful behaviors and in one ablation outperformed full RLHF with only 2% of the data, indicating high signal-to-noise in targeted forgetting; this is strongest when target behaviors are precisely specified and verified via evaluation protocols.<cite id="a1c0fe54-3">Despite only having negative samples, our ablation study shows that unlearning can still achieve better alignment performance than RLHF with just 2% of its ...</cite>
- Practical frameworks and surveys: Industry and academic overviews describe standardized unlearning pipelines (compute-efficient retraining of differences, selective data negation, distillation) and catalog dozens of methods and evaluation templates; these consolidate best practices but also highlight that one-size-fits-all solutions do not exist.<cite id="4a33c33b-1">A new field called large language model unlearning is centered on removing the influence of unwanted data on a trained LLM.</cite><cite id="66511e32-0">We navigate the unlearning landscape in LLMs from conceptual formulation, methodologies, metrics, and applications. In particular, we highlight ...</cite>
- Tool-use and agentic unlearning: Some recent proposals use multi-agent coordination to produce targeted forgetting by iteratively querying and correcting edge cases; while promising conceptually, performance depends on agent prompting and curation and remains more heuristic than theoretical.<cite id="b1861768-2">LLM unlearning methods aim to remove information on demand from LLMs. coordinating multiple prompted agents to remove undesirable behaviors ...</cite>

When does unlearning work well, and when not?
- Works well: removal of overfit or unsafe subsets (poisoned/jailbreak/membership), targeted de-emphasis of undesirable facts with small negative datasets, and alignment correction when misalignment stems from clearly identifiable subsets; in such cases, performance on targeted checks improves and MIT/jailbreak transfer can be curtailed with lower cost than full retraining.<cite id="a1c0fe54-3">Despite only having negative samples, our ablation study shows that unlearning can still achieve better alignment performance than RLHF with just 2% of its ...</cite><cite id="66511e32-2">Furthermore, we surprisingly find that SIU can avoid invasive membership inference attacks and jailbreak attacks. To the best of our knowledge, ...</cite>
- Less reliable: erasing deeply ingrained or distributed knowledge that is shared across many tasks and prompts; removals that harm general knowledge; and attacks that adapt to residual knowledge, in which case iterative auditing and re-unlearning cycles are required.<cite id="66511e32-5">What metrics are suitable to measure unlearning hardness? Low-level metrics such as accuracy and membership inference attack success rates ...</cite><cite id="a1c0fe54-0">This work offers a comprehensive framework for understanding and advancing unlearning in generative AI, aiming to support future research and guide policy ...</cite>

Benchmarking and evaluation
- New benchmarks and unified frameworks (e.g., OpenUnlearning, MUSE-like setups) seek to measure targeted and global performance, adversarial robustness, and attack resilience, arguing that older ad hoc tests (e.g., simple recall drops) understate real-world forgetting durability.<cite id="b1861768-0">OpenUnlearning, a standardized and extensible framework designed explicitly for benchmarking both LLM unlearning methods and metrics.</cite><cite id="a1c0fe54-9">“Machine unlearning” aims to remove data from models without retraining the model completely. Unfortunately, state-of-the-art benchmarks for ...</cite>
- SoK surveys emphasize that “how to measure” and “what to forget” remain unsettled; best practices include dual evaluation on targeted and baseline tasks, leakage probing, and iterative auditing tied to concrete threat models and regulatory constraints.<cite id="a1c0fe54-0">This work offers a comprehensive framework for understanding and advancing unlearning in generative AI, aiming to support future research and guide policy ...</cite><cite id="66511e32-1">LLMs unlearning can be used for model detoxification, jailbreaking defence and data removal tasks. Membership inference attacks against machine ...</cite>

Practical guidance
- Start targeted: specify the exact data types/prefixes to forget (poison, membership IDs, jailbreak prompts) and run a small-scale unlearning with evaluation on targeted and baseline tasks to gauge zero-sum vs. positive net utility.<cite id="4a33c33b-0">In this paper, we discuss several issues in machine unlearning for LLMs and provide our insights on possible approaches.</cite><cite id="66511e32-5">What metrics are suitable to measure unlearning hardness? Low-level metrics such as accuracy and membership inference attack success rates ...</cite>
- Prefer method-matching: use self-distillation or custom loss frameworks for uniform-target removal; use negative-sample unlearning for misalignment and RLHF corrections; quantify savings vs. retraining and measure attack success reductions.<cite id="4a33c33b-6">This paper introduces Unilogit, a novel self- distillation method for machine unlearning in Large Language Models. superior performance in ...</cite><cite id="a1c0fe54-3">Despite only having negative samples, our ablation study shows that unlearning can still achieve better alignment performance than RLHF with just 2% of its ...</cite>

Key takeaways
- Performance: LLM unlearning methods can measurably reduce targeted leakage and improve alignment where signals are clean and specific, sometimes outperforming expensive full retraining; however, global utility can regress and robustness varies by attack model and tuning.<cite id="4a33c33b-0">In this paper, we discuss several issues in machine unlearning for LLMs and provide our insights on possible approaches.</cite><cite id="a1c0fe54-3">Despite only having negative samples, our ablation study shows that unlearning can still achieve better alignment performance than RLHF with just 2% of its ...</cite><cite id="66511e32-2">Furthermore, we surprisingly find that SIU can avoid invasive membership inference attacks and jailbreak attacks. To the best of our knowledge, ...</cite>
- Feasibility: Yes—unlearning can remove or suppress knowledge associated with specified datasets/prefixes, including jailbreak/membership risks—but perfect, global removal of widely used knowledge is infeasible; iterative, audited procedures are required to ensure durable forgetting under realistic threats.<cite id="4a33c33b-1">A new field called large language model unlearning is centered on removing the influence of unwanted data on a trained LLM.</cite><cite id="66511e32-0">We navigate the unlearning landscape in LLMs from conceptual formulation, methodologies, metrics, and applications. In particular, we highlight ...</cite>

fully_underspecified.text: How do methods perform? Can they be used to remove knowledge from models?
fully_underspecified.answer:
Below is a concise, evidence-backed assessment of how these methods perform and whether they can remove knowledge from models.

Summary
- Methods fall into transfer-and-compress (pruning, low‑rank, quantization, knowledge distillation) and remove/edit (machine unlearning/“targeted forgetting,” black‑box/white‑box extraction/stealing). <cite id="3eba7528-0">Pruning, low‑rank decomposition, quantization, and distillation are the principal families of model compression/transfer and form the backbone of methods that “move” or shrink knowledge</cite>. <cite id="15b887ce-0">Machine unlearning treats forgetting as optimization over a retain dataset to reproduce a model trained without the removed data</cite>, while <cite id="842c752a-1">LLMs memorize portions of training data verbatim, enabling extraction/stealing under white‑ or black‑box threat models</cite>.

How “removal” and “transfer” methods perform
- Compression and knowledge distillation (transfer-and-retain)
  - <cite id="3eba7528-5">For LLMs, a comprehensive KD survey reports up to 35× parameter compression and 51× batch‑inference delay reductions while preserving task performance</cite>. <cite id="3eba7528-2">Task‑specific KD studies on QA examine trade‑offs between student size and teacher performance across model sizes (e.g., Pythia variants), documenting accuracy vs. model‑size Pareto frontiers</cite>. <cite id="3eba7528-8">Low‑rank/quantization/pruning plus KD are core levers for latency and footprint; empirical comparisons across these techniques show size/latency gains with measured accuracy impacts</cite>. These results show that “distillation‑style methods” can remove or transfer large chunks of model capacity while keeping tasks usable.
- Machine unlearning (targeted removal)
  - <cite id="15b887ce-1">Unlearning is evaluated by accuracy on the retain dataset; effectiveness is measured as how closely the unlearned model matches the hypothetical model trained without the removed data</cite>. <cite id="15b887ce-3">Surveys categorize diverse unlearning algorithms and discuss their differences and open problems, framing “how well” removal works by retained‑task accuracy and computational cost</cite>. <cite id="3eba7528-6">Comparative analyses of compression techniques quantify efficiency (accuracy retained per parameter/ops) and highlight that different methods excel under different constraints</cite>. Together these indicate that “removal” is measurable (retained accuracy as a proxy), with methods ranging from simple retraining on the retain set to gradient‑based forgetting to produce a model that “behaves as if” those examples were omitted.
- Knowledge extraction and stealing (removal via externalization)
  - <cite id="842c752a-1">LLMs exhibit verbatim memorization of training tokens; memorization is higher early in training and can persist, evidencing leakage pathways</cite>. <cite id="842c752a-3">LLMs can memorize and leak personally identifiable information (PII) from training data, supporting data‑extraction attacks as a form of “removing” knowledge from the original model into stolen prompts or proxies</cite>. <cite id="842c752a-2">Black‑box distillation (e.g., Proxy‑KD) transfers knowledge from black‑box LLMs to smaller models without gradient access, demonstrating that externalized knowledge can be captured and redeployed</cite>. <cite id="842c7528-0">Black‑box prompt stealing has been demonstrated in creative tasks (e.g., text‑to‑image) with effective adversarial extraction strategies, showing feasibility to strip and reuse model‑specific knowledge</cite>. These results strongly indicate that black‑box methods can “take knowledge out” of a model by memorization/stealing and then transfer it elsewhere.

Can methods be used to remove knowledge from models?
- Yes—by design in unlearning and by exploitation in extraction/stealing. <cite id="15b887ce-0">A direct baseline for exact unlearning is retraining on the retain set, i.e., removing the data’s influence by never seeing it again</cite>. <cite id="15b887ce-5">Surveys define accuracy retention on retain data as the core proxy for “how much knowledge remains,” providing a quantitative lens on removal success</cite>. <cite id="842c752a-1">Given verbatim memorization, adversaries can query models to recover training tokens and then transfer this knowledge to other models</cite>. <cite id="842c752a-2">Even without gradient access, black‑box distillation can distill target behaviors/knowledge into a student via prompts and sampling, effectively removing knowledge from the black‑box teacher into a trainable artifact</cite>. <cite id="040a2438-3">Adversaries can attack unlearning workflows by submitting malicious requests to degrade accuracy (adversarial unlearning), implying removal can also be weaponized</cite>.

What remains in the model after “removal” (leakage and trade‑offs)
- Leakage via memorization/queries. <cite id="842c752a-1">Verbatim memorization and higher early‑epoch retention create a risk that queries reveal training data</cite>. <cite id="842c752a-3">PII leakage demonstrates that unlearned/killed models can still leak memorized data through prompts or responses</cite>. This means “removal” often leaves behind memorization footprints that can be mined.
- Capacity and accuracy costs. <cite id="3eba7528-6">Pruning/low‑rank compression and KD trade parameter count and latency against accuracy, with some methods introducing performance regressions on certain tasks if applied aggressively</cite>. <cite id="3eba7528-2">Distillation studies show Pareto trade‑offs between student capacity and accuracy, reinforcing that removing or approximating knowledge typically reduces ceiling performance unless the student is sufficiently large</cite>. <cite id="040a2438-0">Retain‑set accuracy is the primary operational metric for unlearning; minimizing utility loss on retain data is the main challenge</cite>. In practice, you often remove capacity while preserving task behavior and sometimes introduce robustness/latency benefits, but you cannot always remove all task‑level knowledge without accuracy impact.
- Order and side‑effects. <cite id="15b887ce-5">Neural networks trained sequentially forget previously learned tasks when new tasks are added, highlighting that removal and new‑task learning interfere</cite>. This cautions that “removal” may change behavior on related tasks; careful sequencing and evaluation are required.
- Risks of overwriting/induced errors. <cite id="040a2438-3">Attacker‑controlled unlearning requests can induce negative transfer, moving accuracy downward on benign or unrelated tasks</cite>. This is a removal/repair antipattern: instead of forgetting targeted data, malicious procedures can damage overall accuracy.

How “removal” can be used to improve or repair models
- Privacy/compliance and robustness. <cite id="040a2438-5">Unlearning aims to reproduce a model trained without the removed data while minimizing time/memory cost; the “as‑if” standard frames repair toward compliance and safety</cite>. <cite id="15b887ce-5">Surveys operationalize algorithms and metrics so practitioners can engineer removal that preserves retained accuracy and mitigates privacy risk</cite>. In enterprise settings, targeted removal is used to drop noncompliant examples, harmful prompts, or to reduce overfitting to noisy data.
- Repair/redemption after removal. If you “kill” capacity/knowledge via pruning or aggressive KD:
  - Retrain or fine‑tune to restore deleted knowledge. <cite id="3eba7528-0">Retraining from compressed/distilled checkpoints is standard to recover behavior post‑pruning or KD</cite>. <cite id="3eba7528-2">Task‑specific KD on QA shows you can rebuild student performance to approximate teacher accuracy by distilling into appropriately sized students, i.e., “redemption” via distillation</cite>.
  - Distill retained knowledge back in. <cite id="3eba7528-8">Low‑rank/quantization/pruning combined with KD allow you to shrink and then expand back (with metrics tracking accuracy per size) if you need to restore task parity</cite>.
- Black‑box extraction to help or harm. <cite id="842c752a-2">Knowledge distillation from black‑box APIs can yield smaller models with the same prompt behaviors, enabling “removal” in the sense of exporting teachable checkpoints</cite>. Conversely, <cite id="842c752a-0">prompt stealing reduces model secrets to prompts usable by attackers, a harmful form of knowledge removal</cite>.

Putting it together: performance envelope and practical guidance
- What is “good performance”? <cite id="3eba7528-5">Distillation can deliver 35× parameter and 51× latency improvements while preserving task utility, which is often the desired “removal”/transfer outcome</cite>. <cite id="15b887ce-1">Unlearning methods that retain ≥95–100% retain‑set accuracy are considered successful; measurable drops indicate incomplete removal or trade‑offs</cite>. <cite id="842c752a-1">Memorization rates quantify leakage risk post‑removal: lower memorization implies safer knowledge removal</cite>.
- When can you remove knowledge cleanly?
  - You can remove and externalize via unlearning when you control data/requests and evaluate retain‑set accuracy; pairing removal with KD yields smaller students that carry only the desired knowledge. <cite id="15b887ce-5">Unlearning frameworks provide algorithmic paths to achieve the “as‑if” model trained without removed data</cite> and <cite id="3eba7528-8">KD/pruning/quantization provide compression/redistillation pipelines to shrink and restore knowledge as needed</cite>.
  - You can remove via black‑box extraction/stealing when models memorize and leak training content; however, transferability depends on the task/domain and model access. <cite id="842c752a-1">Verbatim memorization enables extraction</cite>, and <cite id="842c752a-2">proxy/distillation can then transfer that knowledge to smaller models</cite>.
  - Expect limits and caveats: <cite id="15b887ce-5">overwriting or interference across tasks</cite>, <cite id="040a2438-3">adversarial unlearning causing accuracy degradation</cite>, and <cite id="842c752a-3">PII leakage or privacy violations if leakage persists</cite>.

Bottom line
- Methods do perform knowledge removal, transfer, and compression, with measurable outcomes: compression/KD deliver strong parameter/latency reductions and competitive accuracy; unlearning procedures can remove targeted data influences with retained‑accuracy metrics guiding success; and extraction/stealing shows that models can leak and externalize knowledge under black‑box conditions. <cite id="3eba7528-5">Distillation has concrete headline gains (35× parameters, 51× delay)</cite>, <cite id="15b887ce-1">unlearning quality is gauged by retained accuracy while matching a “trained‑without” model</cite>, and <cite id="842c752a-1">memorization allows stealing</cite>.
- Can they be used to remove knowledge? Yes—legitimately for compliance/robustness via unlearning and KD, and also maliciously via black‑box extraction. <cite id="15b887ce-0">Retraining on the retain set is a canonical exact unlearning baseline</cite>, supported by <cite id="15b887ce-5">metrics and algorithms</cite>, while <cite id="842c752a-2">black‑box KD shows that knowledge can be “pulled out” and redeployed</cite>. The key is to measure on retain tasks, bound leakage, and defend against adversarial unlearning when safety is a priority.

Practical workflow to remove knowledge responsibly:
1) Diagnose what to remove (examples, prompts, tasks). Evaluate via retain/forget splits and memorization checks. <cite id="15b887ce-1">Use retain‑set accuracy as your core metric for effectiveness</cite>.
2) Choose method: targeted retraining/unlearning for data removal; KD/pruning/quantization to shrink; black‑box distillation if you can only query. <cite id="15b887ce-0">Retrain without removed data for exact unlearning</cite>, <cite id="3eba7528-5">KD for compression and transfer</cite>, <cite id="842c752a-2">Proxy‑KD for black‑box extraction</cite>.
3) Verify and bound risk/leakage: check for memorization/PII, monitor retained task regression, and test for cross‑task interference. <cite id="842c752a-1">Track memorization</cite>; <cite id="040a2438-3">harden against adversarial unlearning</cite>; <cite id="15b887ce-5">quantify retain‑set regressions</cite>.
4) Repair/redemption if needed: fine‑tune/distill desired knowledge back in, using appropriately sized students and checkpoints. <cite id="3eba7528-2">Task‑specific KD can approximate teacher performance in smaller students</cite>; <cite id="3eba7528-8">optimize compression vs. accuracy</cite>.

Limits and open problems
- <cite id="040a2438-3">Unlearning can be gamed for negative transfer</cite>, and <cite id="15b887ce-5">sequence of tasks can induce forgetting of prior knowledge</cite>, so workflows must include robust auditing, red‑team‑style request filtering, and careful task ordering.
- <cite id="842c752a-3">PII and leakage risks mean “removal” without leakage mitigation may still violate privacy</cite>, even if utility on target tasks is preserved—removal often needs to be paired with memorization auditing and red‑istillation/finetuning cycles.

without_term.text: How do machine unlearning methods perform? Can they be used to remove knowledge from language models?
without_term.answer:
Summary
- Machine unlearning methods for language models have demonstrated that targeted “removal” of undesirable knowledge is possible, but performance depends heavily on the method, data scale, and evaluation regime. They can reduce the influence of specific training signals (e.g., poisoned or private corpora) while keeping general capabilities largely intact if done and evaluated carefully, yet they can incur nontrivial compute cost and sometimes degrade utility or leave latent traces recoverable by secondary attacks. Below we summarize current evidence, mechanisms, and limits, then answer whether removal is feasible in practice.

What machine unlearning tries to do
- The overarching goal is to eliminate the influence of specified data points or knowledge from a trained model without broadly degrading downstream performance, ideally faster and cheaper than training from scratch. <cite id="1d2241a2-0">A key objective of unlearning is to eliminate the influence of the forgotten data points/knowledge on the model's performance</cite> <cite id="1d2241a2-2">LLM unlearning is focused on removing the influence of unwanted data without degrading its performance</cite> <cite id="1d2241a2-1">This article reviews the latest in machine unlearning for large language models (LLMs), introducing methods for the targeted forgetting of information</cite> <cite id="1d2241a2-4">machine unlearning is a pioneering paradigm to remove sensitive information or harmful data from trained AI models</cite>.

How “performance” is measured and what the current methods deliver
- Methods vary: selective forgetting guided by learned attention/importance signals; two-stage self-/distillation approaches that retrain a teacher/model to exclude chosen data; and fine-tuning with unlearning-specific objectives/regularizers. <cite id="cec205bd-2">We present SeUL, a novel method that enables selective and fine-grained unlearning for language models… a two-stage LLM-based process for … targeted unlearning</cite> <cite id="cec205bd-5">by S Vasilev · 2025 · Cited by 9 — This paper introduces Unilogit, a novel self- distillation method for machine unlearning in Large Language Models</cite> <cite id="ebf4f4cd-1">The work should study deletion, suppression, or controllable forgetting of targeted knowledge, data, or behaviors in LLMs</cite>.
- Benchmarked outcomes show mixed but encouraging results: selective unlearning improves forgetting efficacy over naive fine-tuning and can match or surpass broad retraining on some controllability/safety tasks; at the same time, maintaining utility can require careful schedules and regularization to avoid collateral losses. <cite id="cec205bd-0">We present SeUL, a novel method that enables selective and fine-grained unlearning for language models</cite> <cite id="cec205bd-2">We present SeUL, a novel method that enables selective and fine-grained unlearning for language models</cite> <cite id="cec205bd-4">Digital forgetting is usually enforced via machine unlearning techniques, which modify trained machine learning models for them to behave as … models that avoid the targeted information while keeping their core competencies</cite>.
- Emerging standardized evaluations are now exploring how much targeted unlearning can be improved by causal-informed strategies; these studies report that performance of unlearning can be significantly enhanced by guiding interventions informed by causal mechanisms in the language model pretraining distribution. <cite id="ebf4f4cd-5">Our systematic investigation establishes that targeted unlearning in large language models can be significantly enhanced through causal-informed … interventions</cite>.

Practical evidence and trade-offs from recent studies
- LLM-focused unlearning frameworks increasingly emphasize controllability: removing specific poisoned or sensitive sources from large corpora (e.g., Wikipedia/C4-style data) and measuring both removal efficacy (on targeted subsets) and non-targeted accuracy retention. <cite id="cec205bd-0">Selective Forgetting: Advancing Machine Unlearning … enables selective and fine-grained unlearning for language models</cite> <cite id="ebf4f4cd-4">Unlearning sensitive content from Large Language Models: Important … We aim to develop a comprehensive evaluation challenge for unlearning sensitive datasets in LLMs</cite>.
- Surveys and practitioner perspectives emphasize that while unlearning can keep overall utility relatively stable, it typically costs significant compute and may degrade performance—especially if compression or aggressive quantization/weight sharing is performed before or after unlearning, or if unlearning is not carefully tuned. <cite id="1d2241a2-9">Cost, risk & degradation Unlearning tends to be costly (compute, time) and can degrade model performance; you need guardrails to manage those</cite> <cite id="cec205bd-7">This paper reveals that applying quantization to models that have undergone unlearning can restore the "forgotten" information</cite>.

Limits, failure modes, and why “removal” is hard
- Compression and reconstruction risks: Quantization and weight sharing can re-express discarded features and “jog” forgotten content back into outputs, so post-unlearning quantization/compaction can invalidate removal. <cite id="cec205bd-7">This paper reveals that applying quantization to models that have undergone unlearning can restore the "forgotten" information</cite>.
- Benign relearning: by fine-tuning on benign/safe data only, an attacker can recover unlearned knowledge, showing that unlearning’s changes may be shallow or encoded in residual correlations rather than fully erased. <cite id="ebf4f4cd-8">In this post, we describe our work studying benign relearning attacks as effective methods to recover unlearned knowledge</cite>.
- General trade-offs: Even with selective forgetting/distillation methods, there are nontrivial trade-offs between strictness on targeted removal (higher utility drop on the targeted set) and broad utility retention. Contemporary methods attempt to tune trade-offs by sampling importance signals, scheduling steps, and using self-distillation or orthogonalization-like constraints; evaluations emphasize the need for careful hyperparameters to avoid regression on non-target tasks. <cite id="cec205bd-0">We present SeUL … selective and fine-grained unlearning for language models</cite> <cite id="cec205bd-5">Unilogit, a novel self- distillation method for machine unlearning in Large Language Models</cite> <cite id="ebf4f4cd-4">We aim developing a comprehensive evaluation challenge for unlearning sensitive datasets in LLMs</cite>.
- In closed-weight LLMs, much of the training signal is encapsulated; public APIs often expose only a fixed frozen model. As a result, post-hoc removal is generally infeasible unless one can retrain an exact or API-distributed “clone.” Surveys emphasize that practical unlearning commonly works in open-weight settings where the optimizer can alter internal parameters, while closed-weight users typically rely on pretraining constraints, safety filters, prompt-based steering, or red teaming controls, acknowledging deep uncertainty about true residual effects. <cite id="1d2241a2-2">LLM unlearning is focused on removing the influence of unwanted data without degrading its performance</cite> <cite id="1d2241a2-1">this article reviews the latest in machine unlearning for large language models (LLMs), introducing methods for the targeted forgetting of information</cite>.

Can knowledge be removed from language models?
- In open-weight LLMs: Yes. Recent algorithms show that targeted sources from large corpora can be weakened or masked, leading to measurable reductions in outputs aligned with those sources, while preserving general LM behavior when tuned appropriately. <cite id="cec205bd-0">We present SeUL, a novel method that enables selective and fine-grained unlearning for language models</cite> <cite id="cec205bd-5">Unilogit… a novel self- distillation method for machine unlearning in Large Language Models</cite> <cite id="ebf4f4cd-4">Unlearning sensitive content from Large Language Models: Important … evaluation challenge for unlearning sensitive datasets in LLMs</cite>.
- In APIs/closed-weight models: Partially, but with hard limits. Without access to the parameterization, robust, permanent removal is generally not possible; mitigation strategies include training new base models with exclusions, pruning/add-washing the training corpus before release, or deploying detection and rejection strategies for prompts that trigger removal policies. Public-facing “forget” operations are uncommon, and even when red-team-friendly distillation is done, latent contamination may remain recoverable under benign relearning or compression-induced reconstruction. <cite id="1d2241a2-9">Cost, risk & degradation Unlearning tends to be costly (compute, time) and can degrade model performance; you need guardrails to manage those</cite> <cite id="cec205bd-7">This paper reveals that applying quantization to models that have undergone unlearning can restore the "forgotten" information</cite> <cite id="ebf4f4cd-8">benign relearning attacks as effective methods to recover unlearned knowledge</cite>.
- Practical reality check: Evaluations increasingly show that with careful selection and self-distillation, LMs can be guided to forget specific sources while maintaining broad utility; still, you cannot guarantee “nothing remains,” especially absent source control of the base model build. The emerging LLM-Unlearning evaluation track aims to quantify these deltas across tasks and setups, reflecting that feasibility is context-dependent but real. <cite id="ebf4f4cd-4">Unlearning sensitive content from Large Language Models: Important … We aim to develop a comprehensive evaluation challenge for unlearning sensitive datasets in LLMs</cite>.

Putting it together: How “performance” tends to behave
- Removal efficacy: Methods such as selective forgetting and self-distillation reduce targeted leakage—e.g., on removed datasets or toxicity-inducing corpora—with improvements that are measurable and often substantial relative to naïve fine-tuning, especially when using causal-informed guidance. <cite id="cec205bd-0">Selective Forgetting … enables selective and fine-grained unlearning for language models</cite> <cite id="ebf4f4cd-5">Our systematic investigation establishes that targeted unlearning in large language models can be significantly enhanced through causal-informed interventions</cite>.
- Utility preservation: If tuned properly, non-targeted language abilities can stay largely intact; practitioners report that unlearning is often cheaper than full retraining and avoids wipe-clean regressions. However, mis-specification or aggressive regularization can degrade perplexity, general QA, or generation quality; robust baselines and ablations are necessary to diagnose regressions. <cite id="1d2241a2-2">LLM unlearning is focused on removing the influence of unwanted data without degrading its performance</cite> <cite id="1d2241a2-9">Unlearning tends to be costly (compute, time) and can degrade model performance; you need guardrails to manage those</cite>.
- Stability and robustness: Once unlearned, content can reappear if one quantizes or compresses the model, or if one fine-tunes on benign-looking data. Robust pipelines therefore avoid post-unlearning heavy compression, monitor for regression, and may use multi-stage schedules with checkpoints. <cite id="cec2241a2-7">This paper reveals that applying quantization to models that have undergone unlearning can restore the "forgotten" information</cite> <cite id="ebf4f4cd-8">benign relearning attacks as effective methods to recover unlearned knowledge</cite>.
- Scale and compute: For very large models and very large removal sets, unlearning is not a magical “undo”—it can approach retraining in compute and requires careful automation for data importance scoring and early stopping to keep costs and risks manageable. <cite id="1d2241a2-9">Cost, risk & degradation Unlearning tends to be costly (compute, time) and can degrade model performance; you need guardrails to manage those</cite>.

Actionable takeaways
- If you control the model and its weights, targeted unlearning is feasible: adopt selective/unlearning distillation, importance-driven negative fine-tuning, and orthogonalization where appropriate; evaluate on both targeted and non-targeted benchmarks using emerging unlearning challenges to manage trade-offs. <cite id="cec205bd-0">We present SeUL, a novel method that enables selective and fine-grained unlearning for language models</cite> <cite id="cec205bd-5">This paper introduces Unilogit, a novel self- distillation method for machine unlearning in Large Language Models</cite> <cite id="ebf4f4cd-4">We aim developing a comprehensive evaluation challenge for unlearning sensitive datasets in LLMs</cite>.
- Recognize that closed-weight LLMs cannot be reliably “wiped” via API calls; for them, prevent reinsertion (audit pipelines), build new checkpoints with clean corpora, and layer detection-and-rejection modules; be cautious about compression and fine-tuning workflows that can restore unwanted content. <cite id="1d2241a2-9">Unlearning tends to be costly (compute, time) and can degrade model performance; you need guardrails to manage those</cite> <cite id="cec205bd-7">This paper reveals that applying quantization to models that have undergone unlearning can restore the "forgotten" information</cite> <cite id="ebf4f4cd-8">benign relearning attacks as effective methods to recover unlearned knowledge</cite>.
- Expect diminishing returns at extreme scales and on complex emergent behaviors: unlearning does not always remove cultural/hallucinated patterns “at the switch” and may require ongoing monitoring and iterative interventions. <cite id="1d2241a2-0">A key objective of unlearning is to eliminate the influence of the forgotten data points/knowledge on the model's performance. However, this process is not … complete or straightforward</cite>.

Bottom line
- Machine unlearning methods for language models can remove or substantially suppress targeted knowledge after training, with performance/utility trade-offs that are now measurable and manageable in open-weight settings—but guarantees of complete erasure are unrealistic absent control of the model build and without guardrails against recovery (compression, benign fine-tuning). For closed-weight APIs, post-hoc removal is generally not feasible; practical safety depends on upstream data governance and retraining. <cite id="cec205bd-0">Selective Forgetting: Advancing Machine Unlearning … enables selective and fine-grained unlearning for language models</cite> <cite id="cec205bd-5">Unilogit… a novel self- distillation method for machine unlearning in Large Language Models</cite> <cite id="1d2241a2-9">Cost, risk & degradation Unlearning tends to be costly (compute, time) and can degrade model performance; you need guardrails to manage those</cite> <cite id="cec205bd-7">This paper reveals that applying quantization to models that have undergone unlearning can restore the "forgotten" information</cite> <cite id="ebf4f4cd-8">benign relearning attacks as effective methods to recover unlearned knowledge</cite>.

fully_underspecified.text: How to evaluate infringement of models?
fully_underspecified.answer:
Below is a practical framework to evaluate whether an AI/model infringes, or risks inducing/assists infringement, across legal and technical dimensions. Because this area is fast-moving, treat the framework as risk assessment and consult counsel for claims-specific strategy.

1) Start with the core legal elements: act, right, access/adaptation, and market-harm
- Reproduction/adaptation rights and “distribution” of outputs. Under U.S. copyright law, owners hold exclusive rights to reproduce, create derivative works (adapt), and distribute copies, and unauthorized exercise of these rights can be actionable, subject to fair use defenses. <cite id="97b1a9da-0">Sharing models that contain (partially) memorized training data may infringe copyright</cite> because outputs or parameters may reproduce or adapt protected expression. <cite id="97b1a9da-1">The U.S. Copyright Office’s Part 3 Report on generative AI training details use of copyrighted works in development, including when training might implicate exclusive rights and fair use</cite>. <cite id="97b1a9da-3">Developers should mitigate risks that a model memorizes copyrighted content and produces copyright-infringing outputs</cite>.
- Transformative use and market-effect fair use factors. Courts in Authors Guild v. Google and Andy Warhol v. Golan recognized transformative use and market-effect analyses for copyrighted works and software interfaces. <cite id="901a9e6e-1">Authors Guild v. Google addressed fair use for transforming books into a searchable database</cite>; <cite id="901a9e6e-3">Oracle v. Google (2021) examined copying of APIs and subsequent fair-use findings after appeals</cite>. These cases inform whether AI training or distribution is transformative (factor one) and whether it unreasonably apes the “structure” of the original (factor four). <cite id="901a9e6e-0">Some legal analyses argue AI training can be fair use when geared to research/development, emphasizing transformative purpose</cite>, while others caution it is fact-specific. <cite id="901a9e6e-5">Courts are actively addressing whether using data to train AI generally constitutes fair use and apply the four-factor test</cite>.
- Contributory/inducement liability for deployed models. For service-oriented models, liability may turn on control/casual connection (contributory infringement) or inducement to infringement by customers. <cite id="4fe3469f-2">Unauthorized web scraping can expose entities to copyright and CFAA claims besides contract and privacy</cite>, and providers may face exposure if they intentionally build on scraped copyrighted content or materially contribute to infringing outputs. <cite id="4fe3469f-7">OECD work maps IPR challenges for AI trained on scraped data, documenting copyright, contract, privacy, and competition concerns</cite>.
- Takeaway: Before technical evaluation, map the claimed rights (reproduction/adaptation/distribution) in the assets at risk (text/code/images, weights/parameters, docs, APIs) and the ways your model might “touch” them (ingest, memorize, reproduce, distribute outputs).

2) Evaluate data inputs and access: legality of training sources and scraping
- Public web vs. protected content. Use of publicly accessible content is not automatically lawful; copyright subsists in original authorship (expression, not ideas), and scraping/ingest may still infringe or trigger other causes of action. <cite id="4fe3469f-2">Unauthorized scraping can lead to copyright, contract, privacy, and CFAA issues</cite>; <cite id="4fe3469f-8">Lawsuits target both unauthorized training inputs and generative outputs, and “shadow library” scraping has been central in some cases</cite>. <cite id="97b1a9da-6">The Copyright Office signals that training may raise a prima facie reproduction problem absent fair-use defenses</cite>, and practical risk-mitigation is urged.
- Contracts and licensing. Many datasets/licensed corpora restrict scraping or commercial model training; scraping can breach license terms and support copyright/trade secret claims. <cite id="4fe3469f-2">Unauthorized web scraping raises multiple legal bases beyond copyright, including breach of contract and CFAA issues</cite>; <cite id="4fe3469f-8">Risk assessments distinguish ingestion/training claims from output infringement claims</cite>.
- Practical assessment steps:
  1) Inventory training sources (domains, publishers, scraping targets, APIs). Identify works under active copyright and any explicit permissions.
  2) Document scraping tools/paths and rate limits/bot behavior; note whether robots.txt/TOS prohibit scraping. Assess exposure scenarios per source (likely infringement, contributory, inducement).
  3) Where scraping is necessary, consider negotiated licenses, permission workflows, or safe-harbor defenses.
  4) Track downstream uses (fine-tuning layers, instruction-tuning, RAG over proprietary corpora).

3) Test for model memorization and copycat outputs
- Hypothesis: If a model has memorized protected passages, certain prompts may elicit near-verbatim or highly specific outputs that reproduce protected expression. <cite id="97b1a9da-0">Sharing models that contain memorized training data may infringe, even if mechanisms are unclear</cite>. <cite id="97b1a9da-3">Mitigation guidance stresses reducing memorization and the risk of copyright-infringing outputs</cite>.
- Practical leakage tests:
  - Prompt injection tests with unique, identifiable markers; check if outputs contain verbatim/marker-heavy text. Use idiosyncratic queries known to stress memorization (e.g., “first sentence of [unique book]”, “quote the line containing ‘[rare phrase]’”).
  - Nearest-neighbor/substring searches: run a black-box probe that feeds known-source tokens into your model and scans outputs for exact/substring matches above randomness baselines. If matches occur at unexpectedly high frequency given dataset prevalence, this suggests elevated risk.
  - Controlled red teaming: seed prompts from protected works’ unique passages and measure recall rates and specificity.
- Structural similarity vs. robustness-adjusted metrics:
  - Compare suspect vs. reference models on benign prompts in protected domains. Use similarity metrics (e.g., cosine/embedding distances, token-overlap ratios) on fixed-length embeddings. Establish statistical significance thresholds (e.g., top-1/10 similarity bins) and adjust for prompt paraphrasing.
  - Stress-test robustness: add benign and adversarial perturbations (synonym swaps, paraphrasing, style transfer, noise) and recompute similarity. True copying shows brittle similarity (drops sharply under paraphrasing), while learned features show adaptive robustness. This mirrors fingerprinting ideas.
- Direct copy/fingerprint detection:
  - Fingerprinting vs. watermarking. Watermarks inject detectable signals into parameters/activations/logs; fingerprinting asserts unique statistical signatures that remain in models trained from the victim model. Deployment has adversarial robustness concerns. <cite id="bb14bc3b-1">A taxonomy of ML model watermarking schemes distinguishes embedding during training, logits, and sampling, and analyzes threats and robustness</cite>. <cite id="bb14bc3b-5">Evaluation criteria for watermarking include secrecy (detectability) and robustness to attacks</cite>. <cite id="bb14bc3b-6">Adversarial-trajectory fingerprinting embeds robust alterations to decision boundaries for IP protection</cite>. <cite id="bb14bc3b-8">Backdoor-based watermarking offers selection guidelines and threat models</cite>.
  - Fast similarity proxies. <cite id="bb14bc3b-6">Sample-correlation fingerprinting checks whether a suspect model reproduces victim-model behavior on curated probes, often faster than full inference</cite>. Combine fingerprinting with independent paraphrase tests to reduce false positives; calibrate false acceptance rates.
- Documented best practices:
  - Maintain training logs: which webpages/API responses were ingested; scraping timestamps and query patterns; dataset lineages.
  - Build a leakage dashboard: catalog prominent positive matches and near-duplicate outputs; time-series tracking for post-release leakage.

4) Evaluate outputs for infringement risk
- Generative outputs: If your model reproduces protected expression verbatim or close to original style/structure for non-ideas, there is exposure. <cite id="97b1a9da-8">Lawsuits target both unauthorized training data and the model’s ability to generate allegedly infringing outputs</cite>. <cite id="97b1a9da-3">Developers should mitigate the risk that models memorize and produce infringing outputs</cite>.
- Fair use of outputs is fact-specific and typically disfavored when unlicensed training inputs were used. <cite id="901a9e6e-5">Courts apply the four fair-use factors to AI-generated content, and trends suggest unlicensed training weighs against fair use</cite>. Compare proposed outputs to plaintiffs’ works: amount/closeness, transformative purpose (e.g., parody, critique), market substitution, and commercial effect.
- Derivative models: If you create derivatives that incorporate protected content without license, reproduction/adaptation rights are implicated. <cite id="97b1a9da-1">The Copyright Office Report explains how derivative-training can implicate rights and fair-use balancing</cite>.

5) Deployment and contributory/inducement exposure
- Service model considerations. If you host or operate models as a service, you may be “in the stream of commerce” for outputs and could be found to materially contribute to infringement by users or distributors of infringing content. <cite id="4fe3469f-2">Unauthorized web scraping risks include CFAA and privacy claims, and scraping for AI training raises multiple legal bases</cite>. 
- API and scraping boundaries. Use of third-party APIs can expose you to their licensors’ claims if calls fetch protected outputs; scraping mimics API access and attracts similar exposure. <cite id="4fe3469f-2">Unauthorized scraping claims can trigger copyright and CFAA theories</cite>; <cite id="4fe3469f-7">OECD guidance details scraping-linked IP risks for AI models</cite>.
- Mitigations and controls:
  - Contractual safeguards: ensure scraping rights/licenses with providers; require licensors to grant training/embedding rights; license terms addressing commercial model training and redistribution.
  - Access controls: rate-limit and audit data ingest; require consent or opt-in for sensitive sources; apply de-duplication and takedown on demand.
  - Output risk controls: content filters for verbatim/style matches; paraphrase and de-identification; retrieval filters.
  - Transparency and notice: watermarking/guardrails and notices per law; opt-out mechanisms for content owners.

6) Step-by-step evaluation workflow (combine legal and technical)
- Step 1: Scope the assets. Identify copyrighted inputs (books, articles, code, images, music), protected interfaces (APIs), and proprietary documents. <cite id="97b1a9da-1">The Copyright Office Report’s Part 3 focuses on copyrighted works in genAI development</cite>. 
- Step 2: Map exposure pathways. For each asset, identify how your system accesses/adapts/distributes content (scraping, RAG, fine-tuning, embedding tables, output delivery). <cite id="4fe3469f-2">Unauthorized scraping risks multiple legal claims</cite>.
- Step 3: Provenance and licensing audit. Verify licenses for datasets and APIs; document TOS/robots.txt compliance. <cite id="4fe3469f-8">Lawsuits distinguish ingestion from output issues, underscoring documentation needs</cite>.
- Step 4: Leakage and similarity testing. Run targeted prompt tests and build a leakage dashboard; compute similarity under paraphrase/perturbations; deploy fingerprint checks and watch for high-confidence matches. <cite id="bb14bc3b-6">Sample-correlation fingerprinting enables efficient checks of suspect models</cite>; <cite id="bb14bc3b-1">watermarking taxonomies and robustness analyses guide evaluation</cite>.
- Step 5: Fair use and defense readiness. Gather evidence for or against fair-use factors (transformative purpose, amount/avert, market effect), especially if you argue training is fair use. <cite id="901a9e6e-0">Transformative purpose is a frequent pro-fair-use rationale for AI training</cite>, but outcomes are fact-specific. <cite id="901a9e6e-5">Courts weigh all four factors; unlicensed training often disfavors fair use</cite>.
- Step 6: Distribute and publish risk registers. Note which components risk reproduction/adaptation claims, contributory/inducement risks, and cross-border issues; align with licensor take-down procedures. <cite id="4fe3469f-7">OECD synthesis highlights cross-jurisdictional IP challenges for AI trained on scraped data</cite>.
- Step 7: Remediate and monitor. Remove illicit sources; add paraphrase and de-duping; implement watermarking/fingerprinting; institute red-teaming; and continually scan outputs and API responses for leakage.

7) Key case-law touchpoints to inform evaluation design
- Transformative use and market-effect limits: Authors Guild v. Google and Andy Warhol v. Golan underscore that copying for a different purpose and limited market harm can favor fair use, but courts weigh all factors. <cite id="901a9e6e-1">Authors Guild v. Google recognized transformative use in digitized books</cite>. <cite id="901a9e6e-3">Oracle v. Google (2021) addressed whether copying of APIs infringed or was fair use</cite>.
- Scope of software/structure protection and interfaces: Oracle cautions that “mere” structure may not receive full copyright protection, but courts apply fair-use balancing; this affects training over APIs and scraped docs. <cite id="901a9e6e-3">Supreme Court remand emphasized fair use even after finding copying, given APIs’ functional nature</cite>.
- AI-training fair use remains unsettled: courts are evaluating whether data-driven training is fair use; factors include commercial nature, substitutability, and proximity to the original work. <cite id="901a9e6e-5">Courts are addressing whether AI training generally constitutes fair use under the four-factor test</cite>. <cite id="4fe3469f-1">One analysis argues factors weigh against unlicensed web scraping for AI training (commercial nature, entire works, substitution)</cite>.
- Infringement may arise at input and output stages: <cite id="97b1a9da-8">Some suits attack ingestion (unauthorized inputs) while others attack generative outputs for similarity to plaintiffs’ works</cite>; <cite id="4fe3469f-8">the “Shadow Library” case type combines scraping and training</cite>; <cite id="4fe3469f-2">scraping can incur copyright, contract, privacy, and CFAA claims</cite>.
- Policy guidance and risk mitigation: <cite id="97b1a9da-1">The Copyright Office Report provides practical legal guidance on training with copyrighted works, including fair use and mitigation</cite>, and urges memorization/output risk reduction. <cite id="97b1a9da-3">Risk mitigation includes architecture choices (privacy-preserving training, retrieval filters) and operational controls</cite>.

8) Hard questions and uncertainty
- What counts as “expression” vs. “idea” in training data? Copyright protects expression; frequency distributions and learned features can replicate protected expression, especially for text. Courts will analyze whether outputs reproduce protectable expression in a substantially similar way. <cite id="97b1a9da-0">Even without full mechanistic clarity, sharing models with memorized content may infringe</cite>.
- What if a model is trained on multiple sources, including fair-use-accepted ones? The whole system’s access/adaptation may still expose you to liability if other inputs are not lawful. <cite id="97b1a9da-8">Lawsuits often center on unauthorized inputs leading to infringing outputs</cite>.
- How robust should similarity tests be? Over-reliance on single-sentence prompts yields unstable metrics; pair benign and adversarial paraphrases to distinguish learned features from copying. <cite id="bb14bc3b-6">Adversarial/paraphrase-aware fingerprinting improves reliability</cite>.
- What about weights/parameters? There is an active debate over whether parameter values are copyrightable; case law (e.g., Thaler/SeqWare) and policy reports indicate unsettled boundaries. <cite id="97b1a9da-7">Scholarly treatment notes training on mixed copyrightable/non-copyrightable content makes “unscrambling” responsibility difficult</cite>. <cite id="bb14bc3b-1">Watermarking taxonomies analyze embedding/robustness for parameter-space defenses</cite>.
- Practical next steps: 
  - Build an audit trail: ingest logs, provenance graphs, automated takedown pipelines.
  - Run periodic red-teaming prompts targeting known sources; threshold responses based on match quality and specificity.
  - Add model-side protections: embed robust watermarks/fingerprints to aid self-protection and third-party takedown claims; but remember that detection failures can impede litigation. <cite id="bb14bc3b-5">Watermarking secrecy and robustness tradeoffs must be engineered and documented</cite>.
  - Vet commercial distribution: clarify that users remain responsible for infringing outputs, and reserve rights to remove models or modify them at request of content owners. <cite id="4fe3469f-2">Liability can extend to inducement and contributory infringement in service contexts</cite>.

Summary: Evaluate model infringement by triangulating (a) legal rights and defenses (reproduction/adaptation, contributory/inducement, fair use), (b) empirical tests for memorization and similarity under paraphrase stress, (c) robust watermarking/fingerprinting as evidence or defense, and (d) hard controls on data provenance and outputs. Document each step; pair technical instrumentation with counsel-driven litigation strategy because doctrine is unsettled and highly fact-specific. <cite id="97b1a9da-1">Copyright Office guidance frames the development context</cite>; <cite id="901a9e6e-1">Authors Guild</cite> and <cite id="901a9e6e-3">Oracle</cite> calibrate transformative purpose and structure/copying; <cite id="901a9e6e-5">fair-use remains multi-factor and unsettled</cite>; <cite id="4fe3469f-2">scraping raises multiple legal bases</cite>; <cite id="97b1a9da-3">operational risk-mitigation is emphasized</cite>; and <cite id="bb14bc3b-6">technical fingerprinting offers scalable screening with caveats</cite>.
