fully_underspecified.text: How to detect or extract data from models? Are there related works on this topic?
fully_underspecified.answer:
Below is a concise, structured overview of how "detecting or extracting data from models" is studied, key methods and findings, and recent related work. I organize by problem type, attack setting (white-/black-/gray-box), model type (classic ML, deep nets, LLMs/diffusion), and complementary detection/defense themes like poisoning and provenance.

1) Problem framing and surveys: detecting data used to train a model
- Core idea: membership inference attacks (MIAs) aim to infer whether a specific record was used in training by exploiting differences in model behavior on train vs test data, under white-box (gradients/loss), gray-box (limited architecture/loss), or black-box (only predictions) access. <cite id="de6ec4c6-0">The survey reveals that attacks operate in both white-box settings, where attackers have full model access, and black-box settings, providing only prediction</cite> <cite id="de6ec4c6-5">ML models are vulnerable to membership inference attacks (MIAs), which aim to infer whether a data record was used to train a target model or not</cite> <cite id="de6ec4c6-8">We propose an attack-driven explainable framework by integrating the target and attack models to identify the most influential features of raw data</cite>. 
- LLM-specific directions emphasize gray-box/black-box MIAs, including adversarial prompts and auxiliary unlabeled samples: <cite id="de6ec4c6-2">Gray-Box Scenario This scenario lies between the Black-Box and White-Box settings, assuming the attacker has an extra limited understanding of the target</cite> <cite id="de6ec4c6-4">Membership inference attacks (MIAs) have emerged as a promising tool for identifying unauthorized data usage during model training</cite>. 
- Educational/overview resources summarize goals and mechanics: <cite id="de6ec4c6-6">The first, and simplest one is membership inference attack. This is when the attacker has a data point at hand and wants to know if it belonged</cite> <cite id="de6ec4c6-7">Membership inference attacks determine whether a data point is in the training set of an ML model</cite> <cite id="de6ec4c6-9">The main goal of this attack model is to learn the behavior of the target model with respect to training data compared to the data outside of trains</cite>.

2) Extracting training data from models (model inversion, feature inversion, reconstruction)
- Feasibility and guarantees: recent work shows that for some models, a significant fraction of training data can be reconstructed from parameters, establishing that deep nets can memorize/encode data in their weights; approaches leverage optimization on inputs given fixed network outputs and training losses. <cite id="b9fa7451-0">In this paper we show that in some cases a significant fraction of the training data can in fact be reconstructed from the parameters of a trained neural</cite> <cite id="b9fa7451-2">Many methods deal with extracting sensitive information from trained models. Perhaps the closest to our approach is model-inversion that aims to reconstruct</cite> <cite id="b9fa7451-7">In this paper we show that in some cases a significant fraction of the training data can in fact be reconstructed from the parameters of a trained neural</cite>. 
- Model inversion concept and practical demonstrations: inversion/stealing frameworks that map network features back to inputs to recover sensitive examples have been shown feasible in practice, and are often paired with privacy amplification via averaging to reduce leakage, yet remain effective under certain conditions. <cite id="b9fa7451-4">In this article, we will demonstrate one such method for extracting supposedly private information from a model, known as a model inversion attack</cite> <cite id="b9fa7451-5">Inverse problem goal: given observations y^, determine underlying hidden parameters. Invertible Neural Networks with Coupling Layers (= feature extraction) with</cite>. 
- Domain breadth: inverse-problem perspectives extend to physics and vision, highlighting connections between generative models and inverse mappings. <cite id="b9fa7451-8">In this paper we show that in some cases a significant fraction of the training data can in fact be reconstructed from the parameters of a trained neural</cite> <cite id="b9fa7451-5">Inverse problem goal: given observations y^, determine underlying hidden parameters. Invertible Neural Networks with Coupling Layers (= feature extraction) with</cite> <cite id="b9fa7451-6">In this work, we gain insights into the nature of the training data by extracting the model from the network parameters, thus bridging the gap between the</cite>.

3) Stealing or cloning models (model extraction) and extracting data by eliciting model functions
- API-based black-box stealing: adversaries can call a production API to query model responses and then train an emulating model or perform parameter recovery, sometimes via knowledge distillation, direct querying, or prompt-elicited features. <cite id="6315a0ae-0">In a model extraction attack, an adversary with query access to a ML model can steal the model's underlying functionality by systematically</cite> <cite id="6315a0ae-1">We analyze various attack methodologies including API-based knowledge distillation, direct querying, parameter recovery, and prompt stealing</cite> <cite id="6315a0ae-4">Recently, a series of works have demonstrated that attackers manage to steal or extract the victim models</cite>. 
- LLM/PaLM/ChatGPT case studies: partial extraction/affine transformation recovery from text queries shows that even cutting-edge language models leak structure; attacks combine membership elicitation and imitation learning to match distributional features or logits. <cite id="6315a0ae-3">We've just released a paper that shows it was possible to steal part of OpenAI's ChatGPT or Google's PaLM-2 (up to an affine transformation) by making queries</cite> <cite id="6315a0ae-5">This attack unveils precise, nontrivial information from black-box production language models such as OpenAI's ChatGPT or Google's PaLM-2</cite>. 
- Industry-oriented guides and practical tools summarize attack/defense surface: <cite id="6315a0ae-2">This repository contains a curated list of research papers on model extraction attacks and defenses in machine learning, organized by year of publication</cite> <cite id="6315a0ae-6">Model extraction attacks exploit a fundamental property of machine learning APIs: of $50-$500</cite> <cite id="6315a0ae-8">Model extraction attacks attempt to replicate a target machine learning model by querying its inference API. State-of-the-art attacks are</cite>. 
- Diffusion models: white-box MIAs exploit evaluation losses and gradients, while gray-box variants blend partial architecture/latent-space access with targeted prompts to reconstruct high-confidence latent directions. <cite id="de6ec4c6-3">The current state-of-the-art attacks on diffusion models are predominantly white-box, relying on the loss generated during the evaluation process</cite> <cite id="de6ec4c6-2">Gray-Box Scenario This scenario lies between the Black-Box and White-Box settings, assuming the attacker has an extra limited understanding of the target</cite>.

4) Poisoning detection, contamination, and memorization as related "data extraction" problems
- Poisoning detection operationalizes whether training points or labels were injected: by auditing outputs for telltale patterns or anomalies, one can detect contamination, which often implies data extractability or fingerprinting in downstream behaviors. <cite id="de6ec4c6-0">The survey reveals that attacks operate in both white-box settings, where attackers have full model access</cite> <cite id="de6ec4c6-6">Membership inference attack. This is when the attacker has a data point at hand and wants to know if it belonged</cite>. 
- LLM memorization and targeted extraction: adversarial extraction protocols show that memorized substrates or entities can be recovered with nonzero probability, motivating defenses like de-duplication, redaction, and training-time obfuscation. <cite id="01d6d87a-0">However, prior research has shown that LLM training data extraction is indeed feasible. A seminal study by Carlini et al. [18] proposed a method</cite> <cite id="01d6d87a-5">This paper introduces a probabilistic relaxation of discoverable extraction that quantifies the probability of extracting a target sequence within a set of</cite>. 
- Provenance and traceability: verifying derivative/based-on relationships and transparency about training modifications is an emerging detection/audit theme complementing extraction. <cite id="01d6d87a-1">The problem of model provenance testing is as follows: Determine whether a target model has been derived from a foundational model by lighter customization</cite> <cite id="01d6d87a-8">Tracing the Data Trail: A Survey of Data Provenance, Transparency and Traceability in LLMs</cite>. 
- Tooling and semantic guidance: LLM-driven systems can help interpret provenance artifacts, and agents can automate forensic analysis to extract evidence from model artifacts. <cite id="01d6d87a-2">In our design, the state-of-the-art LLM offers additional details in provenance data interpretation, leveraging their knowledge of system calls</cite> <cite id="01d6d87a-7">We introduce ProvSEEK, an LLM-powered agentic framework for automated provenance-driven forensic analysis and threat intelligence extraction</cite>.

Practical taxonomy: how to "detect" vs "extract", with typical signals, settings, and defenses
- Detecting data usage (membership/training-point membership or not):
  - White-box: use gradients/loss/activations to distinguish train vs test responses; binary classification of a single point. <cite id="de6ec4c6-0">The survey reveals that attacks operate in both white-box settings, where attackers have full model access</cite> <cite id="de6ec4c6-9">The main goal of this attack model is to learn the behavior of the target model with respect to training data compared to the data outside of trains</cite>.
  - Gray-box/black-box: only predictions (and sometimes confidence), use auxiliary unlabeled data and probing prompts; targeted MIAs show feasibility even on LLMs and large-scale data. <cite id="de6ec4c6-2">Gray-Box Scenario This scenario lies between the Black-Box and White-Box settings, assuming the attacker has an extra limited understanding of the target</cite> <cite id="de6ec4c6-4">Membership inference attacks (MIAs) have emerged as a promising tool for identifying unauthorized data usage during model training</cite> <cite id="01d6d87a-0">However, prior research has shown that LLM training data extraction is indeed feasible. A seminal study by Carlini et al. [18] proposed a method</cite>.
  - Defense: membership training/obfuscation (stochastic smoothing), membership-private aggregation, label-only supervision, privacy amplification by clipping/aggregation. <cite id="de6ec4c6-0">The survey reveals that attacks operate in both white-box settings, where attackers have full model access</cite>.
- Extracting training data (feature/hidden-state inversion or direct reconstruction):
  - Image/CNN/Vision transformers: optimize inputs to match model features/outputs when features map injectively to pixels; success depends on architecture invertibility, noise, and dataset distribution. <cite id="b9fa7451-0">In this paper we show that in some cases a significant fraction of the training data can in fact be reconstructed from the parameters of a trained neural</cite> <cite id="b9fa7451-2">Many methods deal with extracting sensitive information from trained models. Perhaps the closest to our approach is model-inversion that aims to reconstruct</cite>.
  - Diffusion: latent-space inversion and diffusion-specific white-box attacks can recover images given access to loss; defenses focus on denoising obfuscation, membership-private training, redacting/deterministic perturbations. <cite id="de6ec4c6-3">The current state-of-the-art attacks on diffusion models are predominantly white-box, relying on the loss generated during the evaluation process</cite> <cite id="b9fa7451-0">In this paper we show that in some cases a significant fraction of the training data can in fact be reconstructed from the parameters of a trained neural</cite>.
  - Text/LLMs: prompt- and gradient-based elicitation, training copy/steal models, or fitting latent affine transforms can yield useful features; partial model stealing demonstrates feasibility against ChatGPT/PaLM-2. <cite id="6315a0ae-3">We've just released a paper that shows it was possible to steal part of OpenAI's ChatGPT or Google's PaLM-2 (up to an affine transformation) by making queries</cite> <cite id="6315a0ae-4">Recently, a series of works have demonstrated that attackers manage to steal or extract the victim models</cite>.
- Stealing model functionality (clone/extract model behavior):
  - API-based: train an imitator via KD or direct search, leveraging prompt libraries and membership elicitation to match outputs; defenses include rate limiting, adversarial training on synthetic queries, randomized perturbations, and certificate-based constraints. <cite id="6315a0ae-0">In a model extraction attack, an adversary with query access to a ML model can steal the model's underlying functionality by systematically</cite> <cite id="6315a0ae-1">We analyze various attack methodologies including API-based knowledge distillation, direct querying, parameter recovery, and prompt stealing</cite> <cite id="6315a0ae-8">Model extraction attacks attempt to replicate a target machine learning model by querying its inference API. State-of-the-art attacks are</cite>.
  - Imitation learning: teach a model to behave like a target by selecting prompts/examples and matching outputs, sometimes via lightweight adapters or distillation. <cite id="6315a0ae-4">Beyond Model Extraction: Imitation Attack for Black-Box NLP APIs</cite> <cite id="6315a0ae-5">This attack unveils precise, nontrivial information from black-box production language models such as OpenAI's ChatGPT or Google's PaLM-2</cite>.
- Poisoning detection and data provenance:
  - Signature scanning, pattern reconstruction, and behavioral audits can detect contamination or derived status; transparency and provenance testing help verify lineage and customization scope. <cite id="01d6d87a-1">The problem of model provenance testing is as follows: Determine whether a target model has been derived from a foundational model by lighter customization</cite> <cite id="01d6d87a-8">Tracing the Data Trail: A Survey of Data Provenance, Transparency and Traceability in LLMs</cite>.

How-to workflow: choosing method by objective, access, and model type
- Decide objective and access:
  - Goal: detect if a specific record likely trained the model? Use MIAs (white-/gray-/black-box), adversarial prompts for LLMs, or targeted queries for large-scale data. <cite id="de6ec4c6-0">The survey reveals that attacks operate in both white-box settings, where attackers have full model access, and black-box settings, providing only prediction</cite> <cite id="de6ec4c6-4">Membership inference attacks (MIAs) have emerged as a promising tool for identifying unauthorized data usage during model training</cite>.
  - Goal: extract the actual data points? Use feature-inversion or reconstruction on deep nets/diffusion when architectures allow; add privacy noise removal or domain-specific constraints; validate with multiple restarts and similarity filtering. <cite id="b9fa7451-0">In this paper we show that in some cases a significant fraction of the training data can in fact be reconstructed from the parameters of a trained neural</cite> <cite id="b9fa7451-2">Many methods deal with extracting sensitive information from trained models. Perhaps the closest to our approach is model-inversion that aims to reconstruct</cite>.
  - Goal: steal/clone model behavior (for inference-like usage)? Use API-based imitations, KD, or latent affine matching; precompute large prompt/query libraries and tune via loss-matching. <cite id="6315a0ae-0">In a model extraction attack, an adversary with query access to a ML model can steal the model's underlying functionality by systematically</cite> <cite id="6315a0ae-3">We've just released a paper that shows it was possible to steal part of OpenAI's ChatGPT or Google's PaLM-2 (up to an affine transformation) by making queries</cite>.
- Cross-cutting: poisoning/traceability
  - Build poisoning detectors and provenance verifiers to flag contaminated data, track derivative models, and bound exposure from upstream sources; combine with MIAs and memorization tests to localize leakage. <cite id="01d6d87a-1">The problem of model provenance testing is as follows: Determine whether a target model has been derived from a foundational model by lighter customization</cite> <cite id="01d6d87a-0">However, prior research has shown that LLM training data extraction is indeed feasible. A seminal study by Carlini et al. [18] proposed a method</cite>.

Defenses and mitigations (pick and combine)
- Privacy-preserving training: differential privacy, clipping, noise injection, and aggregation amplify privacy and blunt MIAs/reconstruction. <cite id="de6ec4c6-0">The survey reveals that attacks operate in both white-box settings, where attackers have full model access</cite>.
- Architectural/algorithmic defenses: adversarial training for extraction (e.g., randomize features, denoise, obfuscate), membership-private optimization (randomize labels/noise), input/output clipping or perturbations for APIs. <cite id="6315a0ae-0">In a model extraction attack, an adversary with query access to a ML model can steal the model's underlying functionality by systematically</cite> <cite id="de6ec4c6-0">The survey reveals that attacks operate in both white-box settings, where attackers have full model access</cite>.
- Access control and rate limiting: restrict queries, add secret tokens/perturbations, and monitor anomalous query patterns to reduce API-based stealing risk. <cite id="6315a0ae-6">Model extraction attacks exploit a fundamental property of machine learning APIs: of $50-$500</cite> <cite id="6315a0ae-8">Model extraction attacks attempt to replicate a target machine learning model by querying its inference API. State-of-the-art attacks are</cite>.
- Transparency/provenance: document training data, derivative models, and patches; use provenance testing to verify lineage and detect unannounced derivatives. <cite id="01d6d87a-1">The problem of model provenance testing is as follows: Determine whether a target model has been derived from a foundational model by lighter customization</cite> <cite id="01d6d87a-8">Tracing the Data Trail: A Survey of Data Provenance, Transparency and Traceability in LLMs</cite>.

Quick start: choosing a method
- If you only need to detect whether a record likely trained the model: start with black-box MIAs (adversarial prompts + unlabeled data) and iterate to gray-box with small unlabeled batches; for LLMs, use prompt-based elicitation and targeted MI losses; for vision/diffusion, adapt white-box MIAs when possible and use latent-space features. <cite id="de6ec4c6-4">Membership inference attacks (MIAs) have emerged as a promising tool for identifying unauthorized data usage during model training</cite> <cite id="de6ec4c6-3">The current state-of-the-art attacks on diffusion models are predominantly white-box, relying on the loss generated during the evaluation process</cite> <cite id="de6ec4c6-2">Gray-Box Scenario This scenario lies between the Black-Box and White-Box settings, assuming the attacker has an extra limited understanding of the target</cite> <cite id="01d6d87a-0">However, prior research has shown that LLM training data extraction is indeed feasible. A seminal study by Carlini et al. [18] proposed a method</cite>.
- If you need to extract training data points: for deep nets, use feature-inversion with activation matching and regularization, and evaluate reconstruction fidelity by similarity filters and label checks; for diffusion, leverage white-box access to loss in latent space and denoising stability; for text, consider prompt elicitation and affine-parameter matching to recover distributional features. <cite id="b9fa7451-0">In this paper we show that in some cases a significant fraction of the training data can in fact be reconstructed from the parameters of a trained neural</cite> <cite id="b9fa7451-2">Many methods deal with extracting sensitive information from trained models. Perhaps the closest to our approach is model-inversion that aims to reconstruct</cite> <cite id="6315a0ae-3">We've just released a paper that shows it was possible to steal part of OpenAI's ChatGPT or Google's PaLM-2 (up to an affine transformation) by making queries</cite>.
- If you need to clone model behavior over an API: build an imitation model via KD or direct query search with a large prompt library; add membership/quality filters and use latent/affine matching to reduce sample complexity. <cite id="6315a0ae-0">In a model extraction attack, an adversary with query access to a ML model can steal the model's underlying functionality by systematically</cite> <cite id="6315a0ae-1">We analyze various attack methodologies including API-based knowledge distillation, direct querying, parameter recovery, and prompt stealing</cite>.

Related works and where to look
- General MIAs and surveys: recent surveys and tutorials that cover MI definitions, settings, datasets, and LLM-scale adaptations. <cite id="de6ec4c6-0">The survey reveals that attacks operate in both white-box settings, where attackers have full model access, and black-box settings, providing only prediction</cite> <cite id="de6ec4c6-5">ML models are vulnerable to membership inference attacks (MIAs), which aim to infer whether a data record was used to train a target model or not</cite>.
- Data extraction from neural networks: reconstruction and model inversion frameworks and their analyses. <cite id="b9fa7451-0">In this paper we show that in some cases a significant fraction of the training data can in fact be reconstructed from the parameters of a trained neural</cite> <cite id="b9fa7451-2">Perhaps the closest to our approach is model-inversion that aims to reconstruct</cite>.

fully_underspecified.text: What are the common model architectures for language models?
fully_underspecified.answer:
Below is a concise map of common language model architectures, how they are trained, and where they excel.

1) Core Transformer families

- Autoregressive decoder-only Transformers (the LLM workhorse)
  - Modern large language models often use a decoder-only Transformer stack, sometimes called the “LLaMA template,” with components like RoPE positional embeddings, SwiGLU activation functions, and RMSNorm pre-normalization; these models are trained to predict the next token one step at a time, i.e., as autoregressive causal language models. <cite id="13c9d7b5-0">The architectural template established by LLaMA, comprising a decoder-only Transformer with RoPE, SwiGLU activations, RMSNorm pre-normalisation</cite> <cite id="13c9d7b5-5">Large language models typically leverage only the decoder component of the Transformer architecture</cite> <cite id="13c9d7b5-2">Decoder-only transformer models are a specialized type of autoregressive language model designed to predict the next token in a sequence</cite> <cite id="13c9d7b5-4">Decoder models use only the decoder of a Transformer model</cite> <cite id="13c9d7b5-7">Decoder-only models may excel in tasks that are closer to unconditional language modeling – extremely open-ended generation</cite>.
  - Decoder-only Transformers are simple to scale by adding layers; many contemporary models (e.g., LLaMA-like) adopt this design for generative efficiency and quality, and can also be trained under masked variants to compress or summarize content before reconstruction on [EOS] tokens. <cite id="13c9d7b5-0">The architectural template established by LLaMA, comprising a decoder-only Transformer with RoPE, SwiGLU activations, RMSNorm</cite> <cite id="13c9d7b5-3">UniMAE compresses the semantic content of input text into the [EOS] token via an unsupervised masked approach</cite>.

- Sequence-to-sequence (encoder–decoder) Transformers
  - Encoder–decoder Transformers split processing into an encoder for the input and a decoder for generation; they are powerful for generation problems that benefit from separating understanding (encoder) and generation (decoder), such as translation, summarization, dialogue responses, and text-to-text completion. <cite id="13c9d7b5-6">The encoder-decoder architecture decomposes the input-target mapping into three separate modules – encoder self-attention, decoder self-attention, and encoder–decoder cross-attention</cite> <cite id="13c9d7b5-8">Decoder-only models may excel in open-ended generation, whereas encoder–decoder models often excel in tasks like summarization, translation, and QA</cite> <cite id="580ae962-2">T5's paper compared architectures and concluded the encoder–decoder architecture outperformed encoder-only or decoder-only models</cite>.
  - T5 exemplifies the “text-to-text” paradigm: an encoder–decoder Transformer trained on a vast corpus of text–text alignments with objectives like masked span corruption (a denoising variant), enabling transfer across diverse outputs. <cite id="580ae962-1">T5 uses relative position biases and span-corruption pretraining, fitting a unified text-to-text framework</cite> <cite id="580ae962-8">Pre-training objectives include fill-in-the-blank denoising and encoder–decoder models outperform decoder-only language models</cite> <cite id="580ae962-5">Encoder–decoder models often excel at summarization, translation, QA, and related tasks</cite>.

- Bidirectional encoder-only Transformers (context aggregation)
  - Encoder-only Transformers (the “encoder” half of the original Transformer) can be pretrained bidirectionally to capture full left/right context for representations. BERT is a canonical example, where an encoder processes entire inputs and excels at tasks requiring understanding of both preceding and following context. <cite id="580ae962-8">Pre-training objectives include fill-in-the-blank denoising-style objectives</cite> <cite id="d39b2345-3">The masked language modeling training objective predicts the original inputs for each masked token using a bidirectional encoder</cite> <cite id="d39b2345-5">BERT is a finetuning-based representation model that achieves state-of-the-art performance on sentence- and token-level tasks</cite>.
  - Encoder-only models are widely used as text encoders in modern pipelines (e.g., RAG and retrieval), where representations, not fluency, are the goal; they remain central in hybrid multimodal encoders that feed language decoders. <cite id="13c9d7b5-5">LLMs leverage only the decoder component, though many systems pair encoder representations with a decoder head</cite>.

2) Training objectives that shape the architecture

- Causal autoregressive LM (AR-CAUSAL)
  - Next-token prediction (unidirectional) is the classic autoregressive objective and underpins GPT-style, decoder-only LMs; it favors open-ended generation and chat, where coherence over long horizons is rewarded by fluent next-step prediction. <cite id="13c9d7b5-2">Decoder-only transformer models predict the next token in a sequence</cite> <cite id="13c9d7b5-4">Decoder models use only the decoder of a Transformer model</cite>.

- Masked Language Modeling (MLM, bidirectional)
  - In contrast, BERT-style MLM randomly masks tokens and trains a bidirectional encoder to reconstruct the original sequence, capturing both left and right context per token; this yields strong comprehension-like representations for QA, NLU, and text simplification. <cite id="d39b2345-3">The MLM objective predicts the original inputs for each of the masked tokens using a bidirectional encoder</cite> <cite id="d39b2345-0">In MLM-style pretraining, a portion of tokens is masked and the model learns to fill in the blanks</cite> <cite id="d39b2345-4">About 15% of tokens are masked with random noise and the model predicts missing tokens</cite>.
  - MLM-like pretraining variants have been explored and sometimes improve over traditional masking, with alternatives proposed to replace or complement MLM in pretraining. <cite id="d39b2345-2">Alternatives to MLM pretraining based on token-level classification tasks are explored as replacements for masking</cite> <cite id="d39b2345-8">Pretrained masked language models are commonly evaluated without full task-specific fine-tuning</cite>.

- Denoising/seq2seq objectives
  - Sequence-to-sequence and denoising objectives (span corruption, permutation/word replacement) further shape encoder–decoder models, often improving transfer to generation tasks through probabilistic reconstruction of altered inputs. <cite id="580ae962-1">T5 applies span corruption pretraining</cite> <cite id="580ae962-8">Fill-in-the-blank denoising objectives are central; encoder–decoder models outperform decoder-only ones</cite>.

3) Specialized and emerging architectures

- Decoder-only Transformers with mixture-of-experts (MoE)
  - MoE-LMs introduce sparse routing among many candidate experts per token; they keep the autoregressive decoder while scaling compute/token budgets by activating only a subset of experts per position, improving cost-accuracy efficiency. Google’s GLaM is a notable instance demonstrating both decoder-only and masked autoencoder variants for compression/generation under a unified autoregressive framework. <cite id="13c9d7b5-0">LLaMA decoder-only architecture details (RoPE, SwiGLU, RMSNorm) generalize to decoder-heavy systems</cite> <cite id="13c9d7b5-3">UniMAE shows decoder-only masked methods can compress content into EOS tokens</cite> <cite id="d39b2345-0">BART-like masked corruption pipelines train decoders to reconstruct random masked text</cite>.

- Multimodal (vision–language) encoder–decoder LMs
  - Large vision-language models use a vision encoder (e.g., vision transformer or CNN) plus a text decoder to interleave multimodal understanding with language generation, enabling tasks from image captioning to referring expression comprehension. These systems highlight the versatility of encoder–decoder Transformers across input modalities and text generation. <cite id="13c9d7b5-6">Encoder–decoder Transformers explicitly separate encoder self-attention, decoder self-attention, and cross-attention streams</cite> <cite id="13c9d7b5-8">Encoder–decoder models fit multimodal flows well and excel in tasks like QA over images and grounded generation</cite> <cite id="580ae962-5">Encoder–decoder models offer high inference efficiency and design flexibility for tasks like QA and multimodal transfer</cite>.

- RNN-based successors and controlled generation (historical/legacy)
  - Older LMs relied on RNNs/LSTMs, but memory/parallelization limits drove adoption of Transformers; more recent controlled-LM (CTRL-like) approaches embed RNN-style recurrence surrogates (e.g., SRU units) and prefix-based control signals to shape generation, offering intuition-preserving control compatible with large-scale pretraining. <cite id="13c9d7b5-7">Decoder-only structures visualize modern LLM blocks but the original decoder–encoder lineage highlights architectural evolution of recurrence and attention</cite>.

4) Practical guidance: when to use which architecture

- Choose decoder-only Transformers (AR-CAUSAL) when:
  - You want open-ended fluency, long-form reasoning, or chat, where next-step coherence dominates and large-scale autoregressive pretraining suffices. <cite id="13c9d7b5-0">Decoder-only LLaMA-style stacks with RoPE and SwiGLU reach strong generative quality</cite> <cite id="13c9d7b5-2">Next-token prediction is the core AR objective for LLMs</cite> <cite id="13c9d7b5-7">Decoder-only models excel in unconstrained language modeling and open-ended generation</cite>.
- Choose encoder–decoder Transformers (seq2seq, T5/BART-style) when:
  - Translation, summarization, dialog responses that benefit from a separate generator, or multilingual text-to-text tasks; the split helps disentangle understanding from generation and improves controllability and efficiency for many IO tasks. <cite id="580ae962-2">T5 reports encoder–decoder superior to encoder- or decoder-only</cite> <cite id="13c9d7b5-8">Encoder–decoder models often excel at summarization, translation, and QA</cite> <cite id="580ae962-5">Google’s encoder–decoder family highlights efficiency and flexibility for text generation tasks</cite>.
- Choose encoder-only bidirectional MLM (BERT-style) when:
  - Downstream tasks require strong contextual understanding with limited generation, such as QA, NLU, text simplification, or when you will fine-tune an encoder head after retrieval or conditioning. <cite id="d39b2345-3">BERT’s MLM trains bidirectional encoders to reconstruct masked tokens</cite> <cite id="d39b2345-5">BERT achieves state-of-the-art performance on many sentence- and token-level tasks</cite>.
- Consider MoE/Large-Mixture or decoder-only with masked compression when:
  - You need to scale compute efficiently and also support summarization/compression via masked objectives before final generation; modern masked autoencoders let decoders condense content at [EOS] for later expansion. <cite id="13c9d7b5-3">UniMAE performs unsupervised masked compression into EOS tokens for downstream use</cite> <cite id="13c9d7b5-5">Decoder-focused LLMs offer efficient generative inference, aided by architectural choices like RMSNorm and SwiGLU</cite>.
- Use multimodal encoder–decoder LMs when:
  - Input includes images/videos and output needs grounded natural language; leverage a vision encoder plus text decoder to jointly model vision concepts and linguistic fluency. <cite id="13c9d7b5-6">Encoder–decoder designs support cross-modal alignment via cross-attention</cite> <cite id="13c9d7b5-8">These models suit multimodal tasks like image captioning and referencing grounded on visual content</cite>.

5) Choosing among them: a quick decision rule

- Maximize generative quality and cost-efficiency on free-form text: pick decoder-only autoregressive Transformers (e.g., LLaMA/GPT-style) possibly with MoE to scale compute/token budgets. <cite id="13c9d7b5-0">Modern decoder-only templates (RoPE, SwiGLU, RMSNorm) set the LLaMA baseline</cite> <cite id="13c9d7b5-3">Masked variants like UniMAE can serve as efficient pre/post-processing for decoders</cite>.
- Need translation/summarization/dial-style IO: prefer encoder–decoder (T5/BART family) for modular separation and strong IO control. <cite id="580ae962-2">T5 showed encoder–decoder tends to outperform single-sided counterparts</cite> <cite id="580ae962-5">Encoder–decoder models excel in many generation tasks with flexible design</cite>.
- Focus on understanding and retrieval-augmented tasks: encoder-only BERT-style encoders supply strong representations for QA and document understanding, then drive generation via separate decoders if needed. <cite id="d39b2345-3">Bidirectional MLM trains encoders to reconstruct masked tokens</cite> <cite id="d39b2345-5">BERT’s pretraining yields strong representations for a broad suite of tasks</cite>.
- Grounded multimodal generation: use vision encoders + language decoders to align concepts and generate fluently. <cite id="13c9d7b5-6">Encoder–decoder decomposes into self-, cross-, and cross-attention flows conducive to multimodal fusion</cite> <cite id="13c9d7b5-8">Decoder-only excels at open-ended language; encoder–decoder excels with multimodal inputs</cite>.

Notes on evolution and trends
- Decoder-only Transformers have surged because they scale cleanly with layer count and self-attention, and are compatible with causal or masked training recipes; they underpin today’s leading chat and reasoning LLMs. <cite id="13c9d7b5-0">LLaMA exemplifies a decoder-only template with RoPE, SwiGLU, RMSNorm</cite> <cite id="13c9d7b5-2">They predict next tokens unidirectionally</cite> <cite id="13c9d7b5-5">Large language models often leverage only the decoder component</cite>.
- Encoder–decoder architectures remain essential where separate understanding and generation are advantageous, or where multimodal inputs require cross-attention; recent “text-to-text” unification (e.g., T5) shows how decoder stages can be trained generatively on diverse outputs. <cite id="580ae962-1">T5’s relative position biases and denoising pretraining support flexible text-to-text mapping</cite> <cite id="580ae962-8">Denoising objectives and encoder–decoder models often surpass decoder-only alternatives</cite>.
- Alternative recurrent designs (e.g., SRU-based CTRL) persist for controllable generation and interpretability bridges to sequence modeling history, while modern masked objectives (MLM and successors) broaden how models learn from corrupted or augmented inputs before task-specific adaptation. <cite id="d39b2345-2">Simple pretraining objectives beyond MLM are explored for improved representation pretraining</cite>.

fully_underspecified.text: What is an attack?
fully_underspecified.answer:
# Short answer
An attack is an act by a malicious actor who uses one or more exploitation paths ("vectors") against a target to achieve unauthorized effects—such as stealing data, disrupting service, or gaining elevated control—by leveraging weaknesses (vulnerabilities) in systems, applications, or processes and deploying mechanisms like payloads or commands that a normal authorization path should not allow. <cite id="49c10207-2">An authorized effect is an action that a subject is permitted to perform; a vulnerability is a weakness that can be accidentally triggered or intentionally exploited; when a threat source uses intent and method to exploit a vulnerability, that constitutes a threat acting on a system</cite>. <cite id="6cb13109-0">Injection and related web-bug classes are canonical examples where untrusted data is interpreted by a component (parser, DB, OS command) and executed against its trust boundary</cite>. <cite id="54885650-1">Physical-layer attacks such as GPS spoofing inject crafted radio signals to masquerade as legitimate satellites, demonstrating that "attack" spans beyond software to hardware and communications</cite>.

# How attackers and defenders frame it
- Core elements:
  - Actor and intent: Adversary seeks unauthorized impact (confidentiality, integrity, availability change) on a target system, network, or process, often after reconnaissance and planning. <cite id="49c10207-6">A threat source is characterized as the intent and method targeted at the exploitation of a vulnerability, or a situation and method that may produce a negative outcome</cite>.
  - Vector: Pathway used (input fields, network ports/protocols, physical radio links, API endpoints, etc.). <cite id="6cb13109-0">Injection attacks use inputs (forms, data submission) to coerce a code interpreter into executing attacker-controlled content</cite>. <cite id="54885650-1">GPS spoofing operates at the physical/RF and signal-trust layer</cite>.
  - Vulnerability: Flaw or misconfiguration enabling unintended behavior, often in trust boundaries, access control, validation, or serialization logic. <cite id="49c10207-0">A vulnerability is a condition or weakness in procedures, controls, or other defenses that could be triggered</cite>. <cite id="49c10207-2">It is a weakness that can be accidentally triggered or intentionally exploited</cite>.
  - Exploit/payload: Attacker's mechanism that, via the vector and against the vulnerability, achieves capabilities that proper authorization would block. <cite id="6cb13109-0">Database-side scripting via injected SQL (SQLi) or code execution via unsafe deserialization are exploit patterns where untrusted data is executed in a trusted context</cite>.
  - Effects: Unauthorized read, modify, create, delete, or DoS; lateral movement; persistence.

- When do incidents cross into "attack" versus "accident"? 
  <cite id="49c10207-7">Risk frameworks distinguish adversarial threats (deliberate exploitation) from accidental or structural causes, reflecting intent and method as hallmarks of an attack</cite>.

# In web and application security (OWASP-style)
Application-layer attacks focus on inputs, trust boundaries, and control/data flow. They include:
- Injection (SQLi, OSi, OS shell, script injection): untrusted data interpreted as commands in a different security context, subverting the target component's integrity and privileges. <cite id="6cb13109-0">Injection happens when untrusted data is sent to a code interpreter via forms or data submission, causing unintended execution</cite>. <cite id="6cb13109-3">In XSS, attacker uses the web app to send malicious browser-side script to another end user, often via reflected/stored DOM vectors</cite>.
- Data exposure and manipulation: unauthorized read or modify via insecure deserialization, directory traversal, file path traversal, or weak access control. <cite id="49c10207-2">Weaknesses that can be exploited to gain unauthorized effects are vulnerabilities; their intentional exercise by a threat source is an attack</cite>. <cite id="6cb13109-8">Classic examples include directory listing exposure, downloading compiled classes for decompilation and reverse engineering</cite>.
- Rate-based disruption and scraping: volume-based exploitation (e.g., brute-force forms or API abuse) or scraping capabilities to degrade service. <cite id="6cb13109-4">Web application attacks target apps by exploiting design/implementation vulnerabilities, including abuse surfaces</cite>. <cite id="6cb13109-6">Improper validation/sanitization of URLs and resources can allow attackers to redirect or abuse external resources through the app</cite>.
Practical takeaway: Treat an "attack" on web apps as any deliberate attempt to violate the app's stated policy—change data without auth, execute code in the browser/DB/OS behind the app, or exhaust defenses—rather than benign misuse, unless mitigations (validation, least privilege, serialization hardening) prevent exploitable conditions. <cite id="49c10207-6">A threat requires intent and method to exploit a vulnerability; without these, it is an exposure or accident, not necessarily an attack</cite>.

# In OS and system/network security
Systems and network defenses define a complementary layer:
- Vulnerability and exploit: <cite id="49c10207-0">A vulnerability is a condition in procedures or controls that could be triggered</cite>; <cite id="49c10207-2">a vulnerability that can be intentionally exploited indicates a potential attack path</cite>. <cite id="49c10207-6">A threat source is the intent plus method directed at exploiting a vulnerability</cite>.
- Defense and attack: The goal of an attack is to achieve unauthorized primitives (e.g., execute arbitrary code, gain root, eavesdrop on traffic, forge identities), typically by chaining reconnaissance, exploitation of a flaw, and payload delivery/execution. <cite id="49c10207-6">A situation with method that may produce a negative outcome is the framework's way of describing a threat acting through exploitation</cite>. 
Classic families include credential theft (formjacking, replay), buffer overflow and format string attacks causing code execution, man-in-the-middle (MITM) that forges or sniffs traffic between trust anchors, and denial-of-service (DoS/ DDoS) that exhausts resources. <cite id="54885650-3">DDoS taxonomies enumerate Lateral Movement, Privilege Escalation, Reconnaissance, Denial of Service, etc., emphasizing coordinated exploit families and defenses</cite>. <cite id="6cb13109-0">Injection and related patterns are crosscutting vectors that map to many attack families on the web</cite>.

# Physical, embedded, and cyber-physical settings
Attack is not limited to software:
- GPS/GNSS spoofing: <cite id="54885650-1">An attacker transmits specially crafted radio signals at the physical layer to impersonate satellites and fool receivers, altering perceived position/velocity/time (PVT) without cryptography</cite>. This is a trust-root compromise at the signal-authentication layer—an adversarial input to an embedded position module.
- Cyber-physical attack surfaces combine digital vulns with operational impacts (safety, environment, finances). <cite id="6cb13109-4">Web app attacks are malicious activities exploiting design/implementation flaws; analogously, embedded/IoT interfaces (APIs, protocols, UIs) expose attack vectors whose exploitation can directly alter physical processes</cite>. <cite id="54885650-3">Surveys of physics-based attack detection treat spoofing, jamming, intrusion, and anomaly detection as intertwined concerns in cyber-physical systems</cite>.

# Machine-learning adversarial perspective
In ML and AI, "attack" often means a carefully crafted perturbation that an adversary applies to inputs or models to cause misclassification or privilege elevation, while remaining imperceptibly small to benign users and defenses (adversarial examples). Though exploitability depends on model invariants and defenses, the conceptual parallel holds: an authorized user's access is to data/labels consistent with the model's trust invariance; an attacker crafts inputs that cross that boundary.
- ML attack patterns include evasion (poisoned inputs at inference), poisoning (poisoned training data), and model inference extraction; the effect is unauthorized prediction control or model reverse engineering. <cite id="6cb13109-3">Code execution and data exfiltration via browser-side scripts show how placing untrusted content into a trusted execution context achieves control or secrecy goals; ML adversarial examples generalize this idea to model trust boundaries</cite>.

# Putting it together: what distinguishes an attack?
- Intentionality and effect boundary: <cite id="49c10207-6">A threat is the potential for a threat-source to exercise (exploit) a specific vulnerability, implying intent and method</cite>. <cite id="49c10207-0">A vulnerability is a condition that can be triggered</cite>, and <cite id="49c10207-2">that can be exploited</cite>. If an actor causes a system to perform an action that policy disallows (e.g., unauthorized read/write/execute), that is an attack.
- Surface and pathway: <cite id="6cb13109-0">Application inputs, database queries, forms, and data submissions are common vectors when input validation is absent</cite>. <cite id="54885650-1">Radio interfaces and GNSS signals are vectors when cryptographic authentication is missing, enabling physical-layer spoofing</cite>.
- Outcome space: 
  - Exploitation succeeds: unauthorized effect achieved (data exfiltration, code execution, account takeover). <cite id="49c10207-2">A weakness that is intentionally exploited realizes the unauthorized effect</cite>.
  - Exploitation fails: a flaw or misconfiguration exists (vulnerability), and there is exposure or risk; but absent intent and method to act on it, it is not an attack per risk taxonomies. <cite id="49c10207-6">Risk characterizes intent/method as part of a threat source; without them, the situation is exposure or accident</cite>.

# Practical red flags and examples
- On web/app: unvalidated user-controlled data flowing into: 
  - SQL, NoSQL, or OS commands; <cite id="6cb13109-0">injection attacks</cite>.
  - Script contexts (HTML/DOM, browser APIs); <cite id="6cb13109-3">XSS</cite>.
  - Policy bypass via weak or path traversal; directory listing, class download exploits; <cite id="6cb13109-8">decompilation/reverse-engineering opportunities</cite>.
- On network/OS: unauthorized remote execution, credential theft (SSP replay, form capture), MITM, DDoS. <cite id="54885650-3">Classical DDoS and attack/defense taxonomies enumerate reconnaissance, privilege escalation, and denial-of-service families</cite>.
- Physical/IoT: spoofed signals to override sensors, replayed credentials to embedded controllers, supply-chain firmware implants. <cite id="54885650-1">GPS spoofing</cite>. <cite id="54885650-3">Physics-based attack surveys emphasize detection at the application, protocol, and control-system layers</cite>.
- ML: adversarial examples that fool classification, evasion under constraints. <cite id="6cb13109-3">Browser-script injection demonstrates control of a trusted execution environment; adversarial ML does the same relative to model decision boundaries</cite>.

# Key takeaways
- An attack is a deliberate act against a system's trust boundary and policy—any unauthorized effect achieved via vulnerabilities, vectors, and payloads. <cite id="49c10207-2">A vulnerability is a weakness that can be intentionally exploited</cite>, and <cite id="49c10207-6">that intentional exercise by a threat source is at the core of what makes an incident an attack</cite>.
- Across application, OS/network, embedded/GNSS, and ML, the pattern is consistent: attacker crafts and delivers an input or mechanism to a target whose defenses do not authorize it, producing confidentiality, integrity, or availability loss. <cite id="6cb13109-0">OWASP-aligned examples</cite>, <cite id="54885650-1">GPS spoofing</cite>, and <cite id="54885650-3">cyber-physical attack surveys</cite> show the cross-domain commonality.
- Defense posture: harden trust boundaries (validate/sanitize/allowlist), minimize privileged surfaces, monitor for intent+method and anomalous effect, and apply layer-appropriate protections (rate limiting, cryptographic authentication, WAF/IDS, ML robustness). <cite id="49c10207-6">Risk frameworks emphasize identifying adversary intent and methods targeting vulnerabilities to prioritize mitigations</cite>.

questions.original_query: Can you explain to me what is Visual programming?

query.text: Can you explain to me what is Visual programming?
query.answer:
Summary
Visual programming is a style of programming in which you create and modify programs by manipulating graphical elements (icons, blocks, nodes, or diagrams) rather than by writing text-based code. The goal is to make program structure, data flow, and logic more visible for easier design, understanding, and sometimes direct execution.

What it is and how it works
- Core idea: You “wire” operations and data through graphical nodes/edges and connect components by drag-and-drop, constraint-based alignment, or sockets that validate connections. This can be block-based (snap-together blocks), icon-based (dataflow graphs), or diagrammatic (UML activity/state machines). <cite id="05a1e003-0">Visual programming languages are static diagramming systems that aim to simplify the process of writing and understanding computer programs</cite> <cite id="05a1e003-3">Visual programming languages let users create programs by manipulating program elements graphically rather than textually</cite> <cite id="103be738-5">Visual programming is a high-level approach that uses visual metaphors to simplify complex concepts and details in programming</cite>.
- Execution models vary. Block-based and diagrammatic variants often compile or interpret at runtime into target code for execution. Dataflow variants evaluate signals/nodes when inputs arrive. <cite id="103be738-7">There has been great activity in dataflow visual programming languages</cite> <cite id="05a1e003-0">Visual programming languages are static diagramming systems</cite>.

How are they categorized?
- Education and beginner development: Block-based VPLs like Scratch/Blockly use snap-together blocks that enforce semantics and reduce syntax errors, enabling rapid prototyping of sequence, loops, conditions, and events. <cite id="05a1e003-3">Visual programming languages let users create programs by manipulating program elements graphically rather than textually</cite> <cite id="675d1b65-1">A two-year case study using Scratch in five schools analyzed outcomes and attitudes of 107 students and teachers</cite> <cite id="675d1b65-4">Reviews show generally positive educational effects of Scratch, while noting the need for more rigorous evaluation</cite> <cite id="675d1b65-6">Research indicates block-based languages are easier for novices and teach core concepts effectively</cite>.
- Dataflow/Node-graph: Languages like LabVIEW/NOIR and Web VPLs use nodes connected by edges to represent data flow or control. Wiring “type-checks” connections; evaluation is reactive to data arrival. <cite id="103be738-1">Graphical dataflow in LabVIEW provides a better way to solve problems than traditional lower-level alternatives</cite> <cite id="103be738-7">A survey of dataflow programming languages highlights advances and structures in data-flow visual programming</cite> <cite id="05a1e003-0">Visual programming presents a simplified way to write and understand programs</cite>.
- Visual modeling for design: UML (use-case, class, sequence, state machine, activity) and Petri nets describe behavior and concurrency as diagrams; sometimes these are compiled/transpiled into executable models or code. <cite id="4564a772-0">Modeling language surveys show techniques to specify comprehensive and consistent information systems modeling languages</cite> <cite id="4564a772-2">UML has difficulties/drawbacks in certain phases and activities and cannot represent time accurately</cite> <cite id="4564a772-8">Colored Petri nets extend basic nets to capture richer behavior and are widely used for concurrency, synchronization, and hierarchical modeling</cite>.
- End-user visual scripting in engines/tools: Unreal Blueprints and Unity Visual Scripting provide visual nodes/connections to script gameplay, systems, and interactions in creative pipelines. <cite id="05a1e003-4">Visual programming is a CAD-like technique used to design and document interactive software and hardware systems</cite>.
- Industry/enterprise VPLs: Systems like Microsoft Comidor expose a drag-and-drop interface for automations, integrating with backend code generation or interpreters. <cite id="05a1e003-4">Visual programming in low-code/automation lets users design and document workflows via graphical elements</cite>.

When are visual representations used?
- Teaching and learning: Blocks/dataflow simplify concepts, provide immediate feedback, and encourage decomposition. <cite id="675d1b65-1">Scratch classroom studies assess learning outcomes and attitudes of many students across schools</cite> <cite id="675d1b65-6">Block-based environments are easier for novices and effective for core programming concepts</cite> <cite id="675d1b65-8">Scratch is designed to introduce programming to children and teens in a more accessible way</cite>.
- Rapid prototyping and domain-specific engineering: Dataflow VPLs map naturally to hardware-in-the-loop, control, and simulation tasks. <cite id="103be738-1">Graphical programming in LabVIEW is presented as a better problem-solving approach for many tasks</cite> <cite id="103be738-7">Dataflow VPL activity highlights their utility and advancement</cite>.
- Software/game development pipelines: Blueprints/Unity Visual Scripting accelerate iteration for designers and artists who may not write text code. <cite id="05a1e003-4">Visual programming is used to design and document interactive systems</cite>.
- Business process automation and low-code/no-code: Drag-drop interfaces produce workflows and integrations; some are compiled to code, others run in interpreted engines. <cite id="05a1e003-0">Visual programming languages simplify writing and understanding programs</cite>.

Benefits
- Accessibility and learning: Graphical composition reduces syntax overheads and supports visual reasoning, which studies report improves engagement, creativity, and structured thinking for beginners; industry-oriented reviews are generally positive though they call for more rigorous evaluation. <cite id="675d1b65-1">A multi-school study analyzed outcomes and attitudes of 107 students using Scratch</cite> <cite id="675d1b65-4">Systematic review finds generally positive results of Scratch for K–12, with calls for more research</cite> <cite id="675d1b65-6">Block-based languages are easier for novices and teach fundamental programming effectively</cite> <cite id="05a1e003-3">Visual manipulation of program elements can make languages more accessible</cite>.
- Readability and documentation: Diagrams expose structure and dependencies; they aid onboarding, communication across disciplines, and later maintenance. <cite id="103be738-1">Graphical dataflow communicates flow and relationships more directly than traditional alternatives</cite> <cite id="05a1e003-4">Visual programming is used to design and document systems in a CAD-like manner</cite>.
- Rapid prototyping and cross-disciplinary design: Visual connectors enforce semantic constraints (e.g., only number to number), speed up iteration, and help discover design errors early in UX/control/game pipelines. <cite id="05a1e003-0">Static diagramming aims to simplify both writing and understanding programs</cite> <cite id="103be738-1">Benefits of graphical programming in LabVIEW emphasize solving problems in a more intuitive way for non-experts</cite>.

Trade-offs and limitations
- Runtime mapping and performance: Visual graphs are often compiled/interpreted at runtime; translation layers and abstractions can introduce overhead or suboptimal generated code. Mapping from graph semantics to efficient execution can be lossy. <cite id="103be738-8">Users note that dataflow tools like LabVIEW/Simulink expose the big picture but struggle with state machines, indicating modeling limits</cite> <cite id="4564a772-2">UML’s inability to represent time accurately shows that visual modeling can miss key runtime semantics</cite> <cite id="4564a772-0">Modeling language surveys emphasize ensuring consistency and comprehensiveness, which is challenging in practice</cite>.
- Expressiveness and fidelity: Some patterns (e.g., complex state machines, fine-grained concurrency, performance-critical code, formal timing) are hard to capture or optimize in visual metaphors; toolchains sometimes require hand-written code for performance. <cite id="103be738-8">Even in dataflow environments, state-machine complexity can be difficult to manage</cite> <cite id="4564a772-2">UML lacks precise modeling of time</cite> <cite id="675d1b65-4">Reviews also note limitations for more advanced learners and research needs</cite>.
- Learning curve paradox: For experts, visual metaphors can be constraining or unintuitive compared with text; for novices, they help—fit varies by domain and user background. <cite id="103be738-3">Community reports LabVIEW as a good fit for people with little to no programming experience, but harder for experienced programmers who already think they know how to program</cite>.
- Maintenance and evolution: As models grow, diagram clutter, consistency, and documentation maintenance can become burdens; rigorous modeling discipline and tooling support mitigate this. <cite id="4564a772-0">Surveys of modeling language specification emphasize consistency and comprehensiveness to avoid maintenance debt</cite>.

Design principles and good practice
- Orthogonality and progressivity: Combine a small, orthogonal set of primitives, progressively increasing abstraction to avoid runaway complexity. <cite id="103be738-7">Dataflow work emphasizes structure and orthogonality in data-flow visual programming languages</cite>.
- Semantic validation: Enforce legal connections and show live feedback to preserve the mental model. <cite id="103be738-1">Graphical programming emphasizes wiring semantics and problem-solving fit</cite>.
- Bridge to text/back-and-forth: Provide round-trip engineering from visual to code and vice versa to tap both cognitive styles and optimization capabilities. <cite id="05a1e003-4">Visual programming supports designing, documenting, and automating, sometimes integrating with code generation</cite>.

Frequently asked questions and examples
- “What kind of jobs/hardware can visual programming run on?” Dataflow and block-based VPLs typically run on desktop CPUs/GPUs or specialized runtime engines; they can target embedded systems through drivers and compilers. <cite id="103be738-1">LabVIEW presents a better way to solve problems and targets domains like measurement and control</cite>.
- “Is Scratch the same as ‘real programming’?” Scratch/Blockly compile to text languages (often JS) or execute in virtual machines; they teach core concepts but aren’t substitutes unless project constraints match the runtime. <cite id="675d1b65-1">Scratch classroom studies validate learning value, while reviews note it’s generally positive but not a full replacement</cite>.
- “When should I avoid visual programming?” Avoid for performance-critical kernels, tasks requiring precise formal timing, or advanced algorithms where linear control is essential; hybridize with text/code for bottlenecks. <cite id="4564a772-2">UML’s time limitations exemplify gaps at the core of runtime correctness</cite> <cite id="103be738-8">State-machine limitations show fit/limits for complex control logic in dataflow VPLs</cite>.

Why “visual”?
- Metaphors matter: icons, blocks, nodes, and arrows map to human spatial and causal reasoning, reducing abstraction tax and making implicit runtime behavior visible. <cite id="05a1e003-5">A tutorial and survey describes visual languages as an umbrella covering visual programming languages, highlighting their pedagogical and cognitive appeal</cite>.
- Domain-specific mappings: Each family (Scratch, LabVIEW, UML/Petri nets, Unreal Blueprints) tailors visuals to its problem space. <cite id="675d1b65-8">Scratch’s visual model targets K–12 programming literacy</cite> <cite id="103be738-1">LabVIEW focuses on dataflow for measurement, automation, and control</cite> <cite id="4564a772-5">Colored Petri nets give fine-grained modeling control over concurrency; UML has time modeling drawbacks</cite> <cite id="05a1e003-4">Visual programming can design and document interactive software and hardware</cite>.

Putting it together: When to use it
- Start with a visual metaphor if novices, prototyping speed, cross-disciplinary collaboration, or UX clarity is critical. Expect to fall back to text for performance/optimization hotspots and complex control logic. <cite id="675d1b65-6">Block-based visual languages are easier for novices and teach core programming</cite> <cite id="675d1b65-1">Classroom use shows measurable engagement and outcome benefits</cite> <cite id="103be738-1">For engineering/control tasks, graphical dataflow can be a more natural fit than text</cite>.
- Choose the family that matches your domain and stack. Education → Scratch/Blockly; control/simulation → LabVIEW/NOIR; system design → UML/Petri nets; games → Unreal/Unity Visual Scripting; automations → low-code enterprise VPLs. <cite id="675d1b65-8">Scratch targets beginner learning</cite> <cite id="103be738-1">LabVIEW targets dataflow problem solving</cite> <cite id="4564a772-5">Petri nets provide formal concurrency and synchronization modeling</cite> <cite id="05a1e003-4">Visual programming supports interactive systems design and documentation</cite>.
- Budget time for validation and hybrid workflows, because the biggest wins are visibility and speed-to-iteration; the costs are optimization gaps, modeling fidelity limits, and long-term diagram maintenance. <cite id="4564a772-0">Modeling language surveys stress consistent, comprehensive specifications to reduce maintenance and inconsistencies</cite> <cite id="4564a772-2">UML’s time modeling limits highlight runtime-semantics pitfalls that require hybrid solutions</cite>.

Open caveats and where research is active
Visual languages research spans cognitive effects, education outcomes, dataflow compilation, and metamodeling. Findings often depend on implementation and user profile; hybridization (visual-to-text round-trip) remains a best practice when high performance and formal guarantees are needed. <cite id="05a1e003-1">A survey outlines history and state of visual programming languages</cite> <cite id="05a1e003-7">A tutorial survey summarizes research and applications</cite> <cite id="103be738-7">Dataflow programming surveys document structures and constructs for dataflow VPLs</cite> <cite id="675d1b65-4">Systematic reviews in education confirm positives and remaining gaps</cite>.

Quick analogy
Think of text programming as “assembly for the mind”—precise but taxing. Visual programming is “sketching on a whiteboard,” letting you rapidly draft, test, and communicate ideas, then selectively retarget the most promising sketches into efficient code when and where you need it. <cite id="05a1e003-0">Visual approaches simplify both writing and understanding</cite> <cite id="675d1b65-6">Blocks make novices productive faster</cite> <cite id="103be738-1">Graphical dataflow presents a more intuitive problem-solving approach in many domains</cite>.

fully_underspecified.text: Can you explain to me what is programming?
fully_underspecified.answer:
# What is "programming," in plain terms?

Programming is the craft of writing precise instructions for computers so they can automatically perform tasks or solve problems. <cite id="b2a35718-0">A computer program is a detailed plan or procedure for solving a problem, specifically an unambiguous, ordered sequence of steps for a computer to execute</cite>. <cite id="b2a35718-1">A programming language is a notation to express those detailed instructions</cite>, and <cite id="b2a35718-8">tools like compilers translate human‑readable code into machine‑language instructions that the computer can run</cite>. <cite id="b2a35718-3">In practice, programming means crafting code that tells an application or software what to do</cite>, and <cite id="b2a35718-5">it's about instructing a computer which tasks to perform to solve problems</cite>. <cite id="b2a35718-7">At the core, a program is a sequence or set of instructions for a computer to execute as part of software</cite>.

## How computers execute your instructions

Modern general‑purpose computers are built around the von Neumann architecture: a processing unit (CPU) that executes instructions, memory to hold both instructions and data, and input/output for interaction. <cite id="4e9e4cf3-9">The "store program" von Neumann machine is the basic design of the modern computer, with instructions and data stored in the same memory space</cite>. <cite id="4e9e4cf3-6">Most general‑purpose computers use the fetch–decode–execute cycle: the CPU retrieves an instruction, decodes it to determine the operation, and executes it, repeating for the next instruction</cite>. <cite id="4e9e4cf3-5">In this architecture, the CPU fetches instructions and operates on data, step by step, to carry out a program</cite>.

From your code to running instructions: you write code in a high‑level language; a compiler (or interpreter) converts it into low‑level machine code that operates on binary data. <cite id="b2a35718-8">A compiler translates source code written in a high‑level language into machine‑language instructions that the CPU can execute</cite>. <cite id="4e9e4cf3-5">Once translated, the program runs on the CPU, manipulating data stored in memory through the fetch–decode–execute loop</cite>.

## Algorithms: the "what" and "how" of programs

Programs implement algorithms: step‑by‑step methods for computation. <cite id="7b76a44d-3">An algorithm is a specific procedure for solving a well‑defined computational problem; the development and analysis of algorithms is central to computer science</cite>. <cite id="7b76a44d-1">In everyday language, an algorithm is a specific step‑by‑step procedure for solving a problem or accomplishing an end</cite>. <cite id="7b76a44d-4">Algorithms take one or more inputs, process them systematically according to rules, and produce outputs</cite>. <cite id="7b76a44d-0">In code, conditionals and loops within algorithms let the steps adapt and repeat to handle diverse inputs</cite>. <cite id="7b76a44d-8">Analyzing algorithms lets us prove correctness and predict performance, which matters when choosing and optimizing a method for a program</cite>.

Think of a simple example: a recipe is like an algorithm. <cite id="7b76a44d-6">An algorithm is a list of rules in the right order to complete a task</cite>. A program is the computerized version of that recipe, using variables for quantities, loops for repetitive steps, and conditionals (if–else) to adapt based on measurements. <cite id="b2a35718-1">The programming language expresses the steps clearly enough that a machine can execute them reliably</cite>.

## The core abstractions you use every time you program

- Variables and values: names that refer to locations in memory holding numbers, text, or other structured data; programs manipulate these by name and through their addresses in memory. <cite id="134c8fe3-0">In low‑level code like C, working with pointers lets you directly manipulate memory addresses and structures, which underlies many data operations</cite>.
- Control flow: conditionals (if/else), loops (for/while), and branching let the computer make decisions and repeat work. <cite id="134c8fe3-3">Functions may be called recursively, enabling repeated subproblems to be solved via self‑invocation</cite>.
- Functions/procedures and modules: reusable chunks with inputs/outputs; programs decompose into functions that call one another. <cite id="134c8fe3-8">In C, functions are central: you define and use them to structure programs, encapsulate behavior, and reuse code</cite>.
- Data structures and objects: ways to organize related data and operations over it. <cite id="b2a35718-8">High‑level languages express these directly or via libraries; compilers translate them into efficient machine code</cite>.

These abstractions let you encode human‑scale ideas into tight, repeatable machine instructions. <cite id="b2a35718-8">Languages plus compilers/interpreters bridge human readability and machine execution, producing efficient, addressable instructions from your source code</cite>.

## The programming workflow (from idea to running software)

1) Understand the problem and requirements. <cite id="b2a35718-0">Programming is about producing a detailed, unambiguous plan (a program) for solving a specific problem</cite>. This requires eliciting inputs, outputs, constraints, and success criteria. 
2) Design the solution (algorithms and structure). <cite id="7b76a44d-3">Choose or design algorithms for core computations and analyze their correctness and efficiency</cite>. <cite id="b2a35718-8">Decompose into functions and data structures; plan how high‑level constructs map to machine code</cite>.
3) Implement the code. <cite id="b2a35718-1">Write instructions in a programming language</cite>, using variables, control, and functions to realize the design. <cite id="134c8fe3-3">Support recursion when appropriate and define parameters/return types</cite>.
4) Test, debug, and verify. <cite id="7b76a44d-8">Use algorithm analysis and testing to prove correctness and predict performance; accurate prediction lets you spot likely failures before deployment</cite>. <cite id="b2a35718-8">Compilers may catch syntax and type errors; runtime tests expose logical or environmental issues</cite>. <cite id="4e9e4cf3-6">Because execution follows the fetch–decode–execute loop step‑wise, many bugs appear as pathologies of control flow, memory access, or data handling that surface under test</cite>.
5) Maintain, deploy, and iterate. <cite id="4e9e4cf3-5">Production programs run on machines that fetch, decode, and execute your translated instructions continuously</cite>. When users find new needs or bugs, you update code, recompile, and redeploy; good abstractions and documentation make maintenance tractable.

Agencies and standards emphasize this lifecycle. <cite id="b2a35718-8">Compilers and language tooling are integral to implement and validate code</cite>, while <cite id="7b76a44d-8">analysis of algorithms underpins accurate performance prediction and correctness proofs</cite>. In large systems, rigorous testing and reviews are standard practice to catch errors early; this is reflected in software engineering handbooks' emphasis on verification and change control.

## Why programming matters, and how people and AI fit in

Programming automates both computation and control. <cite id="b2a35718-0">It encodes unambiguous procedures that machines can execute at high speed to solve problems too big, fast, or complex for humans to do by hand</cite>. <cite id="b2a35718-1">Because programs are written in languages designed for instruction clarity, they become reproducible, auditable, and sharable artifacts</cite>. <cite id="4e9e4cf3-9">At the hardware layer, the von Neumann design ties programs to the machine's cycle‑by‑cycle execution, enabling everything from spreadsheets to AI systems</cite>.

People program to transform information, build systems, and enable collaboration. <cite id="b2a35718-2">Computer science studies computers and their applications; programming is how you operationalize those abstractions (algorithms, data) into artifacts that solve real problems</cite>. <cite id="b2a35718-5">Modern explanations frame programming as the technological process for telling a computer which tasks to perform to solve problems</cite>. Tools and environments (IDEs) integrate writing, compiling, running, and debugging within a single workspace, lowering barriers and improving productivity.

AI is changing the role of programmers. <cite id="b2a35718-8">With compilers translating high‑level code into machine instructions, AI assistants can propose, review, and even optimize code by analyzing patterns and performance implications</cite>. <cite id="7b76a44d-8">Algorithm analysis informs when a rewrite can reduce time or memory; these are exactly the kinds of trade‑offs where AI support and human judgment complement each other</cite>. The outcome is still human‑centered design: you specify goals, AI suggests variants, and you choose, test, and integrate.

## Putting it together: a simple example

Suppose you want to compute the factorial of a number N. 
- Problem decomposition: "N!" = N × (N−1) × … × 1 for N ≥ 0, with 0! = 1; handle integers and N ≥ 0. <cite id="7b76a44d-6">This is an algorithmic problem solvable by a rule‑based process</cite>.
- Algorithm: iterative loop multiplying an accumulator, or recursive function calling itself with N−1 until the base case. <cite id="7b76a44d-0">Conditionals and recursion express the base case and step</cite>; <cite id="7b76a44d-8">analysis can confirm correctness and estimate steps (O(N) for iteration or O(N) for recursion, with stack overhead for recursion)</cite>.
- Code: write a loop with variables for result and counter, or define a recursive function with parameters and base case. <cite id="134c8fe3-3">C supports recursion and functions as first‑class building blocks</cite>.
- Execution: the compiler turns the loop/recursion into jumps, loads, multiplies, and stores; the CPU fetches each instruction and executes it, updating registers/memory until it returns the result. <cite id="4e9e4cf3-5">Execution proceeds via the architecture's instruction fetch/execute</cite>; <cite id="b2a35718-8">the machine‑code instructions are just arithmetic and control operations executed by the CPU</cite>.
- Test: try N=0, N=1, N=5, N=100 to confirm the output and edge‑case handling; check performance on large N if needed. <cite id="7b76a44d-8">Algorithm analysis and testing together support correctness and performance assurance</cite>.

## Key takeaways

- Programming is the art of encoding algorithms and problem‑solving steps into a language a computer can execute. <cite id="b2a35718-0">It is creating a plan or procedure for solving a problem on a computer—unambiguous and ordered</cite>, and <cite id="b2a35718-1">expressed via a programming language</cite>.
- Programs run inside von Neumann machines by being translated into machine code that is fetched, decoded, and executed stepwise. <cite id="4e9e4cf3-9">Modern computers use the stored‑program, von Neumann design</cite>, <cite id="4e9e4cf3-6">and execute through the fetch–decode–execute cycle</cite>, enabled by <cite id="b2a35718-8">compilers</cite>.
- Abstractions such as variables/pointers, control flow, functions, and data structures are how humans manage scale and repeatability. <cite id="134c8fe3-3">Functions and recursion are core C constructs; pointers directly manipulate memory</cite>.
- Engineering is iterative: design algorithms, implement, test/debug, and maintain. <cite id="7b76a44d-8">Algorithm analysis supports correctness and performance prediction</cite>; <cite id="4e9e4cf3-5">machine execution makes each step visible for debugging</cite>.
- People write programs to harness computation for real‑world tasks, and AI tools increasingly assist by suggesting and optimizing code; humans remain responsible for requirements, evaluation, and integration. <cite id="b2a35718-5">Programming instructs a computer which tasks to perform to solve problems</cite>, and modern tooling and analysis make that human‑machine collaboration practical at scale.

without_term.text: Can you explain to me what is visual programming?
without_term.answer:
What is “visual programming”?

• Core idea: Visual programming is a paradigm where programs or program logic are expressed through graphics rather than text, using icons, blocks, nodes, and connections to represent operations, data flow, and control flow. <cite id="3320c43b-4">In computing, a visual programming language (also called diagrammatic, graphical, or block coding) is a language in which programmers construct programs by manipulating graphical elements rather than writing text syntax</cite>. <cite id="3320c43b-2">Overviews describe visual programming languages as static diagramming systems that aim to simplify writing and understanding programs</cite>. <cite id="3320c43b-0">The “block diagram” is a classic example of a data-flow visual program, where blocks represent operations and连线 represent data movement</cite>.

• Origins and taxonomy: <cite id="3320c43b-7">Early work distinguished “visual programming” from “program visualization,” grouping systems by whether graphics are used as a primary means to write/structure programs (visual programming) or as an aid to understand running programs (visualization)</cite>. <cite id="3320c43b-1">Surveys later organized visual-programming systems by techniques used or by focus (e.g., manipulation, construction, or decoration of program structure)</cite>.

How it differs from text-based programming

Visual and text-based programming solve the same problem (specifying computation), but reverse the representation:
- Text-based programming encodes semantics in syntax (keywords, symbols, braces), which can be powerful and compact but demands memorization and precise grammar mastery.
- Visual programming encodes semantics in arrangement (placement, connectivity), often improving immediate readability of structure and flow, at the cost of scale and meta-operations when programs grow complex. <cite id="3320c43b-4">Visual languages include graphical/block syntaxes</cite>, and <cite id="3320c43b-7">are contrasted with program visualization tools that render execution as diagrams</cite>.

Major paradigms and examples

1) Block-based (learning, prototyping)
