- Scratch/Blockly-like editors represent logic as snap-together blocks (sequence, conditionals, loops), reducing syntax errors and making abstractions tangible for beginners. <cite id="31c49ff9-3">A systematic review reports Scratch-based media enhance conceptual understanding with an average comprehension improvement of 23.4%</cite>. <cite id="31c49ff9-5">Research and educator guides describe block-based languages as effective for teaching core CS concepts (algorithms, variables, conditionals, events)</cite>. <cite id="31c49ff9-7">Comparative analyses conclude both block-based and visual environments are powerful tools for supporting novices</cite>.
- General-purpose VPLs: Blockly (Google), BlocklyDuino (ARDUINO IDE), Tynker, Kodu.

2) Diagrammatic and dataflow programming
- Dataflow/block diagrams bind nodes (operations) with edges (dataflow), commonly used in scientific/engineering and embedded systems. <cite id="3320c43b-0">Data-flow models make block diagrams the “visual program” for procedures, where nodes compute values and edges carry data</cite>. <cite id="3320c43b-3">Iconic/dataflow programming emphasizes arranging operations whose outputs drive inputs of others, enabling parallel/concurrent thinking</cite>.
- Platform exemplars: LabVIEW (industry/academic research), MATLAB Simulink/Stateflow (model-based design), graphical SQL tools, Node-RED (IoT). <cite id="3320c43b-6">Comparisons of early Microsoft VPLs vs LabVIEW highlight differences in dataflow semantics and tooling on block diagrams</cite>.

3) Event-driven UI and application wiring
- Drag-and-drop UI logic and wiring (Qt Designer), web/mobile no-code/low-code flows (Webflow, Glide, OutSystems), and visual databases often “generate code under the hood,” hiding much syntax while exposing some text/code for extension. <cite id="3320c43b-5">VPLs generalize to icons, diagrams, and blocks, including domain-specific assemblers</cite>. <cite id="31c49ff9-1">Modern low-code platforms use drag-and-drop visual logic to accelerate application development</cite>.

4) Visual/scripting graphs in games and engines
- Unreal Engine Blueprints and Unity Visual Scripting expose event-driven graph editors for gameplay, animation, and interactions. <cite id="44540a6e-9">In Unreal’s Event Graph, most logic responds to events (input, animations, sounds), and Blueprints provide a visual language to build complex game behaviors without writing C++</cite>. <cite id="44540a6e-8">Blueprints target non-programmers, enabling complex logic via nodes and wiring</cite>. <cite id="e49cae8a-2">Node-based graph tools (e.g., Unreal, Unity Bolt) are widely used for rapid orchestration of systems and behaviors</cite>.
- Trade-offs: <cite id="44540a6e-3">Some find Unity visual graphs easier to read at a glance but less intuitive when wiring to game components</cite>, and <cite id="44540a6e-0">practitioners report performance/runtime workarounds (e.g., generating per-node C# and adopting new high-performance interpreted runtimes)</cite>.

5) IoT/dataflow “wiring”
- Node-RED is a flow-based programming tool for connecting devices, APIs, and cloud services. <cite id="e49cae8a-5">Its stated goal is to let anyone build applications that collect, transform, and visualize data via intuitive flows</cite>, and <cite id="e49cae8a-2">engineers use it to rapidly connect hardware, APIs, and cloud services, simplifying integration</cite>. <cite id="e49cae8a-3">Studies show it can handle real-time IoT sensor data collection and visualization with reasonable accuracy</cite>. <cite id="44540a6e-1">It’s also discussed in transitions from Unity visual scripting to Unreal-style blueprints for similar logic patterns</cite>.

6) Visual programming in machine learning and web automation
- Many ML playgrounds and web-automation tools use drag/drop or declarative visual UI to compose models or UI logic; these often auto-generate Python/JS code or DSLs (e.g., Microsoft’s “Visual DL,” Google Cloud AI Studio “AutoML Vision” UIs; no-code app builders). This blurs boundaries: the “visual” side is wiring and configuration, the “code” side handles execution and extensibility. <cite id="3320c43b-4">Visual programming languages span graphical block coding to diagrammatic program construction</cite>.

Benefits and common use cases

- Accessibility and learning: <cite id="31c49ff9-5">Block-based approaches help learners internalize algorithms, variables, and conditionals with reduced syntax overhead</cite>, with <cite id="31c49ff9-3">empirical gains in conceptual understanding</cite>. <cite id="31c49ff9-7">Reviews conclude both block-based and general visual environments support novices effectively</cite>. <cite id="31c49ff9-1">Low-code platforms accelerate application development via drag-and-drop wiring</cite>.
- Rapid prototyping and domain wiring: <cite id="e49cae8a-5">Event-driven flows (Node-RED) help assemble pipelines that collect, transform, and visualize data</cite>, useful for IoT, data pipelines, and dashboards. <cite id="e49cae8a-2">Visual graphs speed integrations among devices, APIs, and services</cite>.
- Readability of structure: <cite id="44540a6e-3">Node graphs can be more “at-a-glance” readable than long text scripts, aiding comprehension of event/response chains</cite>.
- Non-programmers and cross-functional teams can assemble features; programmers can use graphs for fast iteration and then drop into code for performance or extensibility. <cite id="3320c43b-0">Dataflow block diagrams explicitly represent inputs/outputs for composition</cite>, which can help cross-discipline alignment.

Trade-offs and limitations

- Scale and complexity: As visual programs grow, meta-operations (refactoring, conditional compilation, metaprogramming-like transformations) become awkward unless the tool supports structured abstractions and versioning. <cite id="31c49ff9-2">Static diagramming aims to simplify, but programs still need modularization, documentation, and testing</cite>. <cite id="e49cae8a-1">Practitioners note that flow-based programming requires a mindset shift from text editors, and that flows can become hard to manage as they grow</cite>.
- Debugging and observability: Flow graphs can be challenging to reason about when many nodes run in parallel or asynchronously; proper instrumentation and breakpoints matter. <cite id="e49cae8a-3">Educational and lab settings emphasize real-time dashboards and visualizations, but debugging often relies on logging/pinboards rather than text traces</cite>.
- Performance and runtime/runtimegen: <cite id="44540a6e-0">Unity noted a “new high-performance interpreted runtime” for visual nodes, with per-node C# generation to reach 10–12× speedups over older interpreted visual logic</cite>. This shows a common pattern: tooling interprets graphs and may need to emit or hybridize with code for performance.
- Security, diffing, and deployment: Visual assets may be harder to diff, review as text, or enforce via linters; integrating CI/CD and formal verification often requires code-generation or hybrid pipelines. <cite id="e49cae8a-4">Some practitioners warn Node-RED flows can become large and unwieldy, raising concerns about maintainability in bigger, “critical” environments</cite>. <cite id="31c49ff9-2">Visual languages are “static diagramming systems,” so tooling must bridge from diagram to executable artifact and back</cite>.
- When to prefer text/code: For complex control logic, metaprogramming, or tight performance, text-based languages with compile-time checks and mature tooling often win; visual tools can be less expressive or force workarounds. <cite id="44540a6e-7">Analyses note graphs work best for signal processing/AI wiring, while scripting is most efficient in text form</cite>. <cite id="44540a6e-0">Interpreted visual graphs may lag, prompting hybrids that generate per-node code</cite>.

When to use visual programming and how to choose

- Good fits:
  - Teaching/learning and introducing CS concepts to novices. <cite id="31c49ff9-3">Scratch-based approaches significantly improve conceptual scores</cite>.
  - Rapid prototyping or proof-of-concept pipelines and IoT integrations. <cite id="e49cae8a-5">Event-driven flows for collecting/translating/visualizing data</cite>. <cite id="e49cae8a-2">Quick wiring of devices and services</cite>.
  - Applications dominated by state/event machines and reactive logic (games, dashboards, audio/vis processing), where wiring and signals are natural. <cite id="44540a6e-9">Event graphs are idiomatic for game logic</cite>.
  - No/low-code delivery for internal tools, dashboards, or simple automations where maintenance by non-experts is required. <cite id="31c49ff9-1">Drag-and-drop visual logic speeds delivery</cite>.

- Trade-offs to plan for:
  - Add structured abstractions (custom nodes/subflows), templates, and documentation; export to code when possible for review/automation. <cite id="3320c43b-7">Taxonomies emphasize tooling by technique and focus; adding meta-operations is often necessary at scale</cite>.
  - Adopt best practices: modular flows, version control (even if generated), testing with simulated events, and monitoring/diagnostics tailored to graphs (node-level metrics/logs). <cite id="e49cae8a-3">Integrations commonly rely on dashboards and live visualizations, which also serve as debugging aids</cite>.
  - Use hybrid workflows: build with visual graphs, then “gradualism” down to code for hotspots, or let the tool auto-generate code for performance. <cite id="44540a6e-0">Interpreted node runtimes with per-node C# generation and high-performance updates demonstrate a productive hybrid path</cite>.

Quick examples that illustrate “visual programming” in practice

- Education and coding foundations: Scratch, Blockly/BlocklyDuino, Tynker. <cite id="31c49ff9-5">Blocks teach core CS concepts and improve accessibility</cite>.
- Scientific/industrial apps: LabVIEW, MATLAB Simulink/Stateflow, graphical SQL tools. <cite id="3320c43b-0">Dataflow blocks model operations and feedback loops</cite>.
- Game engines: Unreal Blueprints (event-driven graphs), Unity Visual Scripting (with paths to C# codegens/optimized runtimes). <cite id="44540a6e-9">Blueprints glue events to gameplay behaviors</cite>.
- IoT/data: Node-RED for device/API wiring, pipelines, and dashboards. <cite id="e49cae8a-5">Low-code flows automate data collection/visualization</cite>.
- Web and mobile no-code/low-code: Webflow, Glide, OutSystems, Power Apps; these expose visual editors and often auto-generate JS/React/PowerFx/CloudScript, switching to text for APIs or business logic. <cite id="3320c43b-2">Visual languages simplify both writing and understanding by mapping logic to diagrams</cite>.

Key takeaways

- Conceptually, visual programming is about expressing computation through graphical composition rather than text syntax; it’s not “not programming,” but a powerful alternative or complement whose value depends on the problem domain and team skill mix. <cite id="3320c43b-4">Visual languages use icons, blocks, or diagrams as executable artifacts</cite>, and <cite id="3320c43b-7">are often distinguished from visualization tools for inspecting running programs</cite>.
- Choose a paradigm and tool based on domain constraints (performance, concurrency, extensibility), stakeholder skills (novices vs experts), and lifecycle practices (testing, CI/CD, monitoring). Use hybrids when needed: visualize to wire, then code-generate or hybridize for critical paths and scale. <cite id="31c49ff9-7">Both block-based and general visual environments are powerful for novices</cite>, <cite id="e49cae8a-3">flows can deliver real-time data processing and visualization</cite>, and <cite id="44540a6e-0">interpreting/compiling visual nodes to native code resolves performance bottlenecks</cite>.
- If you’re deciding what to adopt, start small (proof of concept), define a governance plan (structured abstractions, versioning, tests), and plan a path to hybridization or code export—then expand to visuals wherever wiring and structure are clearer than text. <cite id="31c49ff9-1">Drag-and-drop visual programming accelerates delivery</cite> while <cite id="44540a6e-0">interpreters and codegens bridge readability and performance</cite>.

without_preference.text: What is visual programming?
without_preference.answer:
Summary definition
- <cite id="9ee8ad08-2">Visual programming is a programming paradigm in which users create programs by manipulating graphical program elements (e.g., blocks, icons, nodes, or diagrams), rather than by writing text syntax</cite>. <cite id="9ee8ad08-0">Visual programming languages are commonly conceived as static diagramming systems designed to simplify writing and understanding programs by leveraging visual representations</cite>. <cite id="9ee8ad08-4">They are a subfield of software visualization whose goal is to help development by replacing or complementing textual languages with visual notations</cite>.

Core mechanism: from diagrams to executable programs
- <cite id="9ee8ad08-8">In a typical workflow, programmers arrange icons or graphical representations into a visual structure (a diagram or graph), and the system subsequently debugs and executes that visual program</cite>. <cite id="d40ab1ba-3">Visual expressions and the spatial arrangement of text and graphic symbols function as elements of syntax or secondary notation, indicating how program structure is expressed</cite>. <cite id="9ee8ad08-4">Designers explicitly aim to balance consistent visual representation with usability, tailoring the mapping between diagram and semantics to the target users</cite>.
- Concrete execution models vary by domain. <cite id="eeb78829-0">Unreal Engine Blueprints provides a node‑based interface where nodes and connections encode gameplay logic; users create behavior by wiring nodes for events, actions, and control</cite>. <cite id="915f4875-1">LabVIEW's dataflow model executes when data arrives at node ports, supporting real‑time systems and embedded control/automation in deterministic environments</cite>. <cite id="80e413f9-0">Simulink block diagrams let engineers simulate and deploy multidomain systems without hand‑coding much of the implementation</cite>. <cite id="8d73d188-7">In Node‑RED, block-based "Blockly" nodes generate JavaScript code that is evaluated by Node.js, illustrating how browser-native visual programs compile/interpret into runtime logic in a sandbox</cite>.

How visual abstractions are structured
- <cite id="9ee8ad08-1">Block-based and graphical languages often provide drag‑and‑drop elements, graphical operators, and visual control structures whose semantics are grounded in a specified programming model</cite>. <cite id="d40ab1ba-1">Graphical programs may mix text and graphics (icons, connectors) to express operations, control flow, and data binding with spatial arrangement contributing to syntactic correctness</cite>. <cite id="9ee8ad08-3">Typical tools include graphical blocks, icons, connectors, and a canvas where programs are assembled as diagrams</cite>.
- <cite id="9189e71f-3">Scratch exemplifies event‑driven block‑based programming (developed by MIT), where actors, events, and blocks model behavior and interactions to produce stories, games, and animations</cite>. <cite id="915f4875-2">LabVIEW simplifies sensor data capture, real‑time processing (e.g., filtering, FFTs, waveform generation) and visualization within the dataflow canvas</cite>. <cite id="eeb78829-0">Blueprints integrates tightly with the Unreal Editor, providing a "complete gameplay scripting system" for authoring game systems interactively</cite>. <cite id="80e413f9-0">Simulink's block diagrams are used to simulate and deploy systems across domains without writing extensive code, shortening development and enabling virtual integration</cite>.

Who uses it and why: benefits and learning profiles
- <cite id="9ee8ad08-2">Visual representations reduce reliance on textual syntax, widening accessibility to non‑specialists and easing initial learning</cite>. <cite id="67387a91-1">Removing syntax barriers makes programming accessible to a broader audience, lowering the barrier to entry for novices and domain experts</cite>. <cite id="67387a91-5">Pros include an easy start for creating functional programs, as the visual mapping often conveys structure and intent more quickly than raw text</cite>. <cite id="8d73d188-5">Node‑RED is designed "to enable anyone to build applications that collect, transform and visualize their data," reflecting a hands‑on, flow‑centric approach</cite>.
- <cite id="67387a91-3">Usability research underscores a tension: tool designers must balance consistent visual representations with practical usability to support powerful models without overwhelming users</cite>. <cite id="67387a91-0">Surveys report practical gains: visual languages reduce manual typing and can accelerate building robust programs, especially via drag‑and‑drop composition</cite>. <cite id="67387a91-7">Empirical code-review methods tailored for visual languages have shown tangible usability improvements and task-load reductions in real tools, underscoring the benefits of targeted practices for maintainability</cite>.

Trade‑offs and limitations
- Readability, precision, and verification. <cite id="67387a91-5">A common limitation is that visualizations can degrade in readability and comprehensibility as programs scale, making long‑term maintenance harder than with textual idioms</cite>. <cite id="67387a91-2">Conversely, some resources caution that certain visual languages can be among the hardest to learn—illustrating that accessibility has trade‑offs and that mental models can become difficult to scale</cite>. <cite id="eeb78829-1">Anecdotal developer reports describe Blueprints/visual scripts as harder to maintain and more prone to inconsistencies, reflecting real-world friction in large teams</cite>. <cite id="80e413f9-6">Model‑based flows (Simulink) emphasize building virtual prototypes; while readable as models, fidelity and tooling constraints can complicate rigorous formal verification compared to typed textual code</cite>. 
- Execution model and performance/security. <cite id="67387a91-3">Because visual program graphs are often compiled or interpreted to machine code, run-time models (dataflow, event‑driven) influence determinism, latency, and resource usage</cite>. <cite id="915f4875-4">LabVIEW targets deterministic, real‑time systems and embedded control for fast response, reflecting industrial constraints and guarantees unavailable in generic web contexts</cite>. <cite id="8d73d188-6">In browser contexts like Node‑RED with Blockly, each visual program is transpiled to JavaScript and evaluated in a sandbox, imposing runtime overhead and requiring isolation and input sanitization to avoid breakage</cite>. <cite id="8d73d188-7">Because the Blockly node evaluates generated JavaScript similarly to a sandboxed large text blob, security boundaries and input validation are essential pitfalls to guard against</cite>.
- Scope creep and design debt. <cite id="9ee8ad08-4">Visual languages help early prototyping and rapid iteration, but unless backed by strong modeling discipline, diagrams can accumulate clutter and ambiguity</cite>. <cite id="9ee8ad08-8">As programs get large, visual graphs can become less inspectable than structured text for static analysis and long‑term refactoring</cite>. 

Where visual programming is used
- Education and creative arts. <cite id="9189e71f-3">Scratch is used for interactive stories, games, and animations, and serves as an introductory pathway for learners due to its event‑driven, block‑based semantics</cite>. <cite id="9ee8ad08-2">Its approach generalizes to other block‑based and icon‑based languages that let novices express behavior and control without mastering syntax</cite>.
- Engineering, control, and measurement. <cite id="915f4875-2">LabVIEW's dataflow canvas excels in test and measurement, data visualization, real‑time processing (e.g., filtering, FFTs) and deterministic embedded control</cite>. <cite id="915f4875-4">Applications demand fast, predictable responses, aligning with visual execution models suited to hardware interaction</cite>. <cite id="915f4875-8">Developers iterate on host computers and then deploy to real‑time targets, leveraging graphical constructs that map directly to device behavior</cite>.
- Game development. <cite id="eeb78829-0">Unreal Engine Blueprints provide an integrated node‑based visual scripting system for gameplay logic, level control, and interaction, enabling non‑programmers to build game systems</cite>. <cite id="eeb78829-2">Visual scripting is widely adopted to enable rapid logic assembly; however, performance‑critical systems often integrate with native code</cite>.
- Scientific and multidomain simulation. <cite id="80e413f9-0">Simulink supports block‑diagram modeling and deployment across domains (electronics, mechanics, control) before hardware implementation</cite>. <cite id="9ee8ad08-0">The diagrammatic nature aids cross‑disciplinary comprehension and early validation of system behavior</cite>.
- IoT, dataflows, and web/low‑code. <cite id="8d73d188-5">Node‑RED emphasizes wiring dataflows where components exchange messages, enabling automation, transformation, and visualization end‑to‑end</cite>. <cite id="8d73d188-6">It targets server‑side automation (Node.js) with node‑based wiring and visual function editors to assemble pipelines for devices and APIs</cite>. <cite id="9ee8ad08-3">The same "drag‑and‑drop nodes on a canvas" pattern permeates modern low‑code platforms, reducing text entry and supporting rapid wiring</cite>. <cite id="9ee8ad08-1">Surveys highlight practical productivity from visual composition and reuse via palette libraries</cite>.

How to choose or evaluate a visual language
- <cite id="9ee8ad08-4">Match the language's abstraction to the task and team: visual notations excel at exploratory design, human‑driven prototyping, and domains where spatial reasoning aids comprehension</cite>. <cite id="67387a91-3">Design for consistency: map visual shapes to semantics in ways that scale to larger programs, and provide affordances for reuse and documentation</cite>. <cite id="67387a91-5">Anticipate readability decline with program size; invest in naming, compartmentalization, and tool support</cite>.
- <cite id="67387a91-7">Adopt practices tailored to visual artifacts (e.g., visual code review, refactoring patterns) to sustain quality; studies report substantial usability gains from such methods</cite>. <cite id="8d73d188-7">When running in browsers or sandboxed interpreters, enforce security boundaries around generated code and validate all inputs</cite>.

Related concepts and boundaries
- <cite id="9ee8ad08-0">Visual programming overlaps with "visual programming languages" and broader "software visualization," but typically remains the primary notation and execution channel for authoring programs</cite>. <cite id="67387a91-8">Some research frames it alongside "big code" and ML overviews, but direct machine learning support isn't inherent and varies by toolchain</cite>.
- <cite id="9ee8ad08-8">Tooling ranges from integrated development environments (e.g., LabVIEW, Unreal Editor) to browser/low‑code runtimes (Node‑RED), each with distinct execution models (dataflow/event‑driven, imperative/JS evaluation)</cite>.

Bottom line
- <cite id="9ee8ad08-2">Visual programming is a way to author programs by manipulating graphical elements—blocks, nodes, and diagrams—to express structure, control, and dataflow</cite>. <cite id="9ee8ad08-8">These graphs are compiled or interpreted into executable logic, often with integrated debugging and runtime execution</cite>. <cite id="80e413f9-0">Across domains from education to engineering and web automation, the main appeal is accessibility and rapid composition</cite>, while <cite id="67387a91-5">scaling maintainability and rigorous verification demands discipline and complementary practices</cite>, and <cite id="8d73d188-7">security and runtime overheads must be managed in browser/JS backends</cite>. <cite id="9ee8ad08-4">In all cases, the core promise is greater productivity for certain problem classes by trading syntax mastery for visual reasoning</cite>.

questions.original_query: How should we analyze the training dynamics of language models?

query.text: How should we analyze the training dynamics of language models?
query.answer:
Below is an evidence‑backed workflow to analyze the training dynamics of language models, organized by goals, measurement choices, mechanisms to test, ablations that work in practice, and cross‑phase practices (pretraining, continued pretraining/mid‑training, and post‑training). It blends recent surveys, dynamical/geometry methods, and specific ablations reported in recent work.

1) Define your analysis goals and scope
- Decide whether you care about: convergence and loss behavior (including over‑fitting), internal representation geometry and specialization, memorization versus abstraction/generalization, optimization/mechanics of learning (SGD/momentum, feature‑space routing), or objective‑specific behavior (e.g., SFT/DPO changes). Then select methods accordingly. <cite id="a85a6a36-0">EvoLM proposes a systematic and transparent toolkit to analyze LM training dynamics across pretraining and continued pretraining, offering a blueprint to operationalize these goals</cite> <cite id="a85a6a36-1">Training dynamics aims to characterize how models change as they train, surveying visualizations and formalizing change as an emergent property to be measured</cite> <cite id="a85a6a36-6">Mid‑training/continued pretraining is motivated by shifting dynamics from memorization to abstraction</cite>.
- If you are in a resource‑efficient setting, surveys on data‑centric post‑training can inform what to monitor as you modify data, objectives, and schedules. <cite id="a85a6a36-3">A recent survey organizes efficient LLM post‑training from a data‑centric perspective, providing a taxonomy of objectives and procedures to audit</cite> <cite id="a85a6a36-7">The same survey is available in full text, outlining efficiency‑oriented post‑training methods</cite>.

2) Choose core measurement primitives and time resolution
- Loss and accuracy trajectories by epoch/step/task shard are the backbone; they diagnose divergence, overfitting, and scaling behaviors. Complement them with per‑layer/per‑head losses or activation norms to detect specialization or imbalance. <cite id="a85a6a36-0">A model suite like EvoLM emphasizes end‑to‑end transparent runs and change‑centric evaluations across pretraining and continued training</cite> <cite id="a85a6a36-1">Surveyed work frames dynamics as measurable model change across epochs, motivating per‑epoch checkpoints and visualizations</cite>.
- Internal geometry: track activation statistics (means/covariances), effective rank/spectral properties of hidden or cross‑attention layers, and per‑token or instance stability over epochs. <cite id="b44258a5-6">Spectral geometry tools like effective rank (RankMe) have been used to trace representation geometry across pretraining and post‑training</cite> <cite id="b44258a5-2">Work tracing this geometry reports warmup, memorization‑related entropy‑seeking, and compression phases as the geometry evolves</cite>.
- Optimization “state” observables: log optimizer‑state snapshots (grad norms, momentum directions, Fisher/inverse‑Hessian proxies) and analyze feature‑space routing and stability. <cite id="b44258a5-0">Spectral analyses reveal phases and emergent compression; these can be coupled with Fisher‑based probes in principle to connect loss reduction to representation stability</cite>.
- Instance/task‑level observables: per‑instance training‑loss rank stability, memorization of input sequences, and leakage across contexts to quantify memorization versus learning of generalizable factors. <cite id="b44258a5-7">There is a line of work explicitly analyzing memorization dynamics in transformers across epochs</cite>.
- Objective‑specific geometry: alignment and preference‑learning (e.g., SFT, PPO/DPO) produce entropy‑seeking dynamics in latent instruction/embedding space; measure how instruction distributions integrate and whether cross‑distribution interference degrades unrelated in‑distribution performance. <cite id="5c8c1206-4">Entropy‑seeking dynamics have been observed under SFT and DPO, improving in‑distribution performance while degrading others via integration of instruction/preference data</cite>.

3) Mechanisms to test: instability, compression, specialization, and abstraction
- Instability and growth in hidden manifolds: monitor singular values/eigen spectra and embedding/hiddenspace effective ranks; look for instability periods where activation manifolds expand, then compress later. <cite id="b44258a5-6">Effective‑rank measures (RankMe) can quantify geometry shifts before/after post‑training</cite> <cite id="b44258a5-2">A warmup phase, memorization phase with entropy‑seeking geometry, and compression phase are reported in pretraining</cite>.
- Specialization and feature routing: check layer/head‑wise activation sparsity, entropy, or rank changes to see if later layers specialize to task‑relevant features while earlier layers stabilize. Combine with per‑token attribution. <cite id="a85a6a36-1">Training‑dynamics research emphasizes measuring how parameters and activations change; per‑layer summaries are a central output</cite> <cite id="5c8c1206-3">Low‑dimensional latent models can summarize hidden dynamics across grokking and classification tasks, linking to specialization</cite>.
- Memorization vs abstraction: build small‑shard ablations where you add/remove hard examples; watch loss “swooping,” stability of partial solutions, and downstream contamination. Use instance‑stability over time and retrieval‑augmented checks for leakage. <cite id="b44258a5-7">Epoch‑wise memorization dynamics have been analyzed directly in transformer LMs</cite> <cite id="5c8c1206-7">Large‑scale studies of instance‑level stability quantify how much hidden states change across updates when models are accelerated or altered</cite>.
- Continual learning/instability control: if you perform continual finetuning or mid‑training, track catastrophic forgetting and cross‑task interference; mid‑training is explicitly proposed to steer dynamics from memorization toward abstraction. <cite id="a85a6a36-6">Mid‑training aims to shift LMs’ learning dynamics from memorization to abstraction, an explicit design goal in continual training</cite>.

4) Practical, testable ablations (order from cheap to deep)
- Loss/accuracy micro‑checks: shard the dataset and plot per‑shard loss/accuracy per epoch; look for divergence/swinging and rank changes. <cite id="a85a6a36-0">EvoLM’s transparent runs include dataset‑level tracking to expose changes over epochs</cite>.
- Activation geometry by epoch: compute activation norms and effective rank across layers/heads; compare warmup vs later epochs. <cite id="b44258a5-6">Effective rank has been used across pretraining/post‑training to detect compression/de‑compression</cite> <cite id="b44258a5-2">Phase transitions (warmup → entropy‑seeking → compression) can be read off geometry trajectories</cite>.
- Entropy‑seeking probes under alignment: run SFT/DPO and track entropy of representation draws for instruction prompts; test if integrating preferred trajectories reduces out‑of‑distribution costs. <cite id="5c8c1206-4">SFT/DPO produce entropy‑seeking integration dynamics in latent space, with measured in/distribution trade‑offs</cite>.
- Memorization dynamics: add/remove a few “hard” examples; plot loss surfaces over examples and measure stability of partial solutions and leakage to unrelated tasks. <cite id="b44258a5-7">Epoch‑level memorization analyses provide templates for such ablations</cite>.
- Continued pretraining/mid‑training: compare models at the same global step trained earlier vs later on the same curriculum to quantify drift and the benefit of mid‑interventions steering abstraction. <cite id="a85a6a36-6">Mid‑training is justified by its effect on learning dynamics, shifting from memorization to abstraction</cite> <cite id="a85a6a36-0">EvoLM frames continued training within a systematic analysis of model change</cite>.

5) Modeling and forecasting dynamics
- Learn latent dynamics models: fit low‑dimensional latent state models or autoencodings of activation/optimizer updates to summarize trajectory and predict “grokking” transitions or phase changes. <cite id="5c8c1206-2">Latent‑state models recover discrete regimes in grokking, classification, and masked language modeling, enabling regime‑aware forecasting</cite> <cite id="a85a6a36-0">A unified model‑suite approach can produce standardized latent trajectories for comparison</cite>.
- Phase classification and control: label dynamics into warmup, memorization/expansion, and compression phases; use these labels to design schedules or data filters that accelerate healthy compression or reduce harmful instability. <cite id="b44258a5-2">Warmup → entropy‑seeking memorization → compression provides a repeatable phase narrative across tasks</cite>.
- Optimization‑level lenses: even without full simulator access, record gradient norms, optimizer‑momentum directions, and curvature proxies to interpret feature‑space routing and saturation. <cite id="b44258a5-0">Spectral/geometry methods connect to Fisher‑curvature views, supporting routing/stability analyses</cite> <cite id="5c8c1206-0">Dynamical systems perspectives characterize training stability/instability at high dimensionality, offering a unified framework for empirical measures</cite>.

6) Cross‑phase guidance: when to use which analysis
- Pretraining: combine spectral activation geometry (RankMe/eigen) with per‑layer specialization, instance‑level memorization screens, and loss‑shard analyses; look for early instability and late compression, intervening with data balancing or mid‑training distillation if needed. <cite id="b44258a5-2">Pretraining exhibits warmup, memorization (entropy‑seeking), and compression phases that can be diagnosed and possibly steered</cite> <cite id="b44258a5-6">Effective‑rank tracks are effective for detecting compression</cite>.
- Continued pretraining/mid‑training: quantify off‑target drift and interference with in‑distribution objectives; deliberately schedule “abstraction” tasks, curriculum smoothing, or periodic consolidation to move the system toward abstraction and away from noise memorization. <cite id="a85a6a36-6">The rationale is to shift dynamics from memorization to abstraction during continued training</cite> <cite id="a85a6a36-0">EvoLM’s continued‑training analyses offer practical monitors for this shift</cite>.
- Post‑training (SFT, DPO, RLHF/CF/RL): track entropy‑seeking geometry in instruction space, KL/relative entropy to teacher, and cross‑objective interference; use data‑centric rejections/re‑weighting or preference‑routing to prevent integration of harmful out‑of‑distribution exemplars. <cite id="5c8c1206-4">Entropy‑seeking integration under SFT/DPO can improve in‑distribution while degrading others due to instruction/preference integration</cite> <cite id="a85a6a36-3">Data‑centric post‑training surveys supply operational levers (data selection/weighting) to control dynamics</cite>.

7) Visualization and reporting that make dynamics legible
- Epoch snapshots: side‑by‑side activation/eigen/spectral heatmaps; layer‑wise activation entropy; per‑shard loss surfaces; and stability matrices over consecutive epochs for key examples. <cite id="a85a6a36-1">Visualization is central in training‑dynamics surveys to expose how parameters/activations change</cite>.
- Phase dashboards: plot geometry ranks (RankMe), example‑instance stability Z‑scores, and specialization indices over time with regime labels (warmup/memorization/abstraction), allowing early intervention. <cite id="b44258a5-2">Phase labels grounded in entropy‑seeking behavior can annotate training curves and geometry</cite>.
- Comparative EvoLM style: run matched baselines with different schedules/data and compare latent trajectories, compression speeds, and stability under perturbation to answer “what‑if” design questions. <cite id="a85a6a36-0">Model suites designed for transparent dynamic analysis help compare conditions systematically</cite> <cite id="a85a6a36-6">Mid‑training interventions can be compared by their effect on abstraction vs memorization</cite>.

8) Caveats and how to address them
- Interpreting instability: instability can be healthy (learning new modes) or harmful (overfitting to noise/long‑tail). Use instance‑level stability tests and memorization screens and combine with downstream robustness checks and preference audits to distinguish them. <cite id="5c8c1206-4">Entropy‑seeking dynamics can improve some metrics while degrading others via integration of preference/instruction exemplars</cite> <cite id="b44258a5-7">Epoch‑wise memorization analyses help audit what the model actually stores</cite>.
- Scale and compute: large models’ dynamics unfold over many epochs; use stratified sampling of examples/parameters and instance‑level stability to make analyses scalable. Complement with spectral proxies (effective rank) to compress measurement cost. <cite id="5c8c1206-0">High‑dimensional dynamics admit low‑dimensional characterizations of stability/instability to make analysis tractable</cite> <cite id="b44258a5-6">Effective‑rank measures provide scalable geometry diagnostics across layers</cite>.
- Objective conflicts: during post‑training, in‑distribution gains may come with out‑distribution costs; monitor preference/embedding entropies and run targeted audits. <cite id="5c8c1206-4">Observed entropy‑seeking effects integrate instruction/preference data with measurable in/distribution trade‑offs</cite> <cite id="a85a6a36-3">Data‑centric post‑training strategies offer ways to bias objectives toward desired dynamics</cite>.

Practical checklist (put together a week‑long dynamic audit)
- Day 1: baseline loss/accuracy per shard and global loss/param norm trajectories; set checkpoints every epoch. <cite id="a85a6a36-0">Transparent, end‑to‑end runs are the backbone for change‑centric analysis</cite>.
- Day 2: activation/spectral geometry by layer across epochs; compute effective rank (RankMe) and per‑layer specialization indicators. <cite id="b44258a5-6">Effective rank is a practical geometry diagnostic</cite>.
- Day 3: run memorization dynamics ablations on small subsets; compute example‑level stability and leakage checks. <cite id="b44258a5-7">Epoch‑wise memorization analysis templates exist for transformers</cite>.
- Day 4: post‑training objective dynamics; plot entropy/representation distances for instruction prompts and quantify in/distribution trade‑offs. <cite id="5c8c1206-4">Entropy‑seeking and integration trade‑offs are diagnosable with embedding/latent geometry</cite>.
- Day 5+: mid‑training/continued pretraining intervention; compare to no‑intervention schedules on abstraction vs memorization metrics; use data/curriculum steering to steer dynamics. <cite id="a85a6a36-6">Mid‑training is explicitly used to shift dynamics toward abstraction</cite> <cite id="a85a6a36-0">Model‑suite style comparisons make intervention effects transparent</cite>.

In short, analyze LM training dynamics by combining change‑centric logging (loss/activations/geometry), spectral/optimization‑level probes (effective rank, optimizer/gradient state), and objective‑specific audits (entropy‑seeking geometry under alignment, instance‑level memorization screens). Connect these to mechanisms—instability/growth, compression, specialization, and abstraction—and use controlled ablations and dashboards to steer training toward desired behavior. This workflow is supported by recent surveys and empirical geometry studies that show distinct phases across training and by continued‑training frameworks designed to systematically expose model change over time. <cite id="a85a6a36-0">EvoLM</cite> <cite id="a85a6a36-1">Training dynamics survey</cite> <cite id="a85a6a36-6">Mid‑training rationale</cite> <cite id="a85a6a36-3">Efficient post‑training survey</cite> <cite id="b44258a5-6">Spectral geometry (RankMe)</cite> <cite id="b44258a5-2">Phases narrative (warmup → memorization → compression)</cite> <cite id="5c8c1206-4">Entropy‑seeking under SFT/DPO with in/distribution trade‑offs</cite> <cite id="b44258a5-7">Memorization dynamics ablations</cite> <cite id="5c8c1206-0">Low‑dimensional dynamical stability perspective</cite> <cite id="a85a6a36-0">Latent dynamic modeling and reporting for comparability</cite>.

fully_underspecified.text: How should we analyze training dynamics?
fully_underspecified.answer:
Below is a practical, evidence‑grounded workflow for analyzing training dynamics. It blends high‑level perspectives with concrete diagnostics and interventions you can add to existing training runs.

1) What “training dynamics” are and why they matter
- Training dynamics concern how model parameters and internal representations evolve with optimizer steps, how loss and validation metrics change over time, and why solutions generalize differently once training stops. <cite id="de1c016a-0">For modern deep networks, analyses are often descriptive, explaining why practitioners’ procedures (e.g., scheduling, regularization) seem to work in practice</cite>. <cite id="de1c016a-5">Understanding feedback inside feedforward layers (as in MLPs) helps reveal internal dynamics during training rather than only at inference</cite>. <cite id="de1c016a-1">Recent survey work frames neural‑network theory around approximation and training dynamics, surveying statistical theories that connect optimization trajectories, features, and generalization</cite>.
- Two contrasting lenses help structure analysis:
  - Mechanistic/statistical: how optimization, curvature, and representation geometry shape convergence and generalization. <cite id="de1c016a-1">A statistical view integrates approximation capacity, training dynamics, and inference behavior</cite>.
  - Descriptive/pragmatic: interpreting learning curves, instabilities, and credit‑assignment failures in current architectures and optimizers. <cite id="de1c016a-0">Modern deep training is frequently analyzed through practitioner procedures to explain observed behavior</cite>.

2) Instrument training runs to observe dynamics
- Logging and visualization
  - Plot the full training curve (train/valid loss, per‑epoch metrics), and break them down into components (classification loss, regression error, auxiliary heads), since different components may equilibrate at different timescales. <cite id="157154b0-3">Treating SGD as a dynamical system makes visible orbits in parameter space and allows diagnosing stability/oscillation issues under gradient‑descent optimizers</cite>.
  - Inspect per‑layer activations and gradients over time (e.g., PCA embeddings of hidden‑unit states across epochs), to detect slow feature emergence, dead neurons, or representation collapse. <cite id="de1c016a-7">PCA plus classical sequence models can reveal how networks learn different data subsets over time, yielding interpretable trajectories of representation usage</cite>.
- Sharpness and curvature monitors
  - Track loss curvature and sharpness proxies (e.g., Hessian/Eig or surrogate like squared gradient norm) to detect optimization bottlenecks and generalization trade‑offs. <cite id="de1c016a-1">Surveys explicitly connect sharpness, curvature, and generalization behavior in statistical theory of deep learning</cite>.
  - Evaluate flatness/edge-of-stability: compare test error vs. stability along small perturbations to assess minima quality. <cite id="157154b0-0">Sharpness‑aware minimization is designed to find flat minima by jointly minimizing loss and a proxy for sharpness</cite>. <cite id="157154b0-8">Experiments show SAM efficiently selects flatter minima late in training; even a few late epochs of SAM yield similar improvements and stability gains</cite>.
- Credit‑assignment diagnostics
  - Compute per‑layer Fisher information and log‑derivatives to understand how much each parameter “cares” about the loss and how natural‑gradient moves would change paths. <cite id="5d094d8c-0">Measuring Fisher information flow through layers reveals how input uncertainty is mapped to parameter uncertainty, providing a monitor for representational and identifiability issues</cite>. <cite id="5d094d8c-7">Natural gradient learning leverages the Fisher information metric to avoid inefficient optimizer paths; in random deep networks, online natural gradient dynamics can be Fisher‑efficient and speed learning</cite>.
- Dynamics‑aware optimization view
  - Add dynamics‑aware stabilizers or change of variables. <cite id="157154b0-3">Formulating training as a dynamical system enables analyzing convergence speed, limit cycles, and applying stabilizing transforms tailored to gradient‑based optimizers</cite>.

3) What to look for in the dynamics (patterns and signals)
- Phase separation and timescales
  - Early vs. late training: feature discovery vs. fine‑tuning. <cite id="de1c016a-0">Descriptive analyses of deep nets highlight stage‑wise behaviors (feature learning, optimization) that align with empirical practice rather than only theoretical convex settings</cite>. <cite id="157154b0-8">Late‑stage dynamics often exhibit selection among minima; interventions like SAM applied near the end can be surprisingly effective</cite>.
- Sharpness, curvature, and stability
  - Sharp valleys correlate with higher variance in test and adversarial vulnerability; flat minima tend to generalize better and are more stable to perturbations. <cite id="157154b0-0">SAM explicitly targets reduced sharpness through a modified loss</cite>. <cite id="5d094d8c-0">Monitoring Fisher information flows helps detect bottlenecks and layers with low Fisher (or high identity), signaling weak identifiability or limited sensitivity</cite>.
- Credit assignment and saturation
  - High gradient norms without reduction in loss can signal saturation or redundant updates; Fisher “hotspots” (high eigenvalue regions) suggest over‑parametrization or pathologies. <cite id="5d094d8c-7">Fisher‑efficient natural‑gradient updates avoid redundant directions implied by the metric</cite>.
- Representation drift and collapse
  - Activation subspaces that fail to diversify across classes or samples can lead to slow convergence and poor generalization. <cite id="de1c016a-7">PCA/sequence modeling of hidden units can reveal whether the network learns distinct subsets of data over epochs</cite>.
- Generalization vs. stability interplay
  - Flatness and stability do not fully replace accuracy: edge‑of‑stability regimes can yield high accuracy with sharp losses; SAM aims to trade a bit of accuracy for stability. <cite id="157154b0-1">General analysis shows SAM improves generalization by reducing sharpness, with convergence and sampling guarantees in unified settings</cite>.

4) Mechanism‑linked interventions and ablations
- Adjust optimizer/momentum/batch to stabilize trajectories
  - Stronger or Nesterov momentum can accelerate early‑stage movement and reduce oscillations; smaller batches amplify gradient noise and can increase instability. <cite id="de1c016a-0">Practitioners’ procedures are often explained via descriptive analyses: scheduler choices, damping, and momentum settings stabilize different phases of training</cite>.
- Structural simplifications for transparency
  - Two‑layer toy networks reveal internal dynamics; insights often transfer to deeper models. <cite id="de1c016a-2">A first theoretical analysis inside a convolutional neural network provided new insights into how properties and behaviors emerge during training</cite>.
- Regularizers and dynamics alignment
  - Weight decay, batch normalization, and other constraints shape curvature; sharpness‑oriented training changes the loss geometry. <cite id="157154b0-0">SAM modifies the loss to also penalize sharpness, effectively steering curvature and the optimizer’s effective noise</cite>. <cite id="5d094d8c-0">Fisher monitoring can guide choices that increase effective identifiability (e.g., adding pathways where Fisher is low)</cite>.
- Curriculum and data‑level controls
  - Scheduling exposure to difficult samples or adversarial perturbations can expose stability weaknesses. <cite id="de1c016a-7">By tracking which data subsets are activated over time, you can stage curricula that push the representations to diversify</cite>. <cite id="5d094d8c-8">Graph information bottleneck methods impose information constraints that yield robust, discriminative representations and reduce adversarial sensitivity</cite>.
- Natural‑gradient‑aware steps
  - When gradients are collinear or noisy, applying a Fisher‑aware rescaling to weights or Adam updates can improve effective learning rates along informative directions. <cite id="5d094d8c-7">In random deep networks, natural‑gradient online learning is provably Fisher‑efficient and can speed up dynamics</cite>.

5) Phases, generalization, and stability: tying the diagnostics together
- Flat vs. sharp minima and test behavior
  - Models in flat basins tend to generalize better and resist adversarial attacks; sharp losses correlate with unstable training and validation variance. <cite id="157154b0-1">SAM improves generalization by minimizing an explicit sharpness term, with broader convergence analyses</cite>. <cite id="5d094d8c-0">Fisher information flow diagnostics identify where Fisher is low or poorly distributed, suggesting where training can be made flatter and more identifiable</cite>.
- Dynamics across training epochs
  - Early optimization benefits from noise and step‑size matching; late‑stage credit assignment requires different tools. <cite id="157154b0-8">SAM’s late epochs can efficiently select flatter minima, indicating a late‑stage competition among nearby solutions</cite>.
- Stability and robustness monitors
  - Perturb weights slightly and re‑score; measure accuracy/stability along directions of low curvature to diagnose robustness–accuracy trade‑offs. <cite id="5d094d8c-0">A direct method to monitor Fisher information through layers links parameter uncertainty to data uncertainty and supports stability analyses</cite>.
- Edge‑of‑stability design
  - Some architectures exploit sharp edges to fit complex boundaries yet retain accuracy; SAM offers a knob to trade accuracy for stability when needed. <cite id="157154b0-0">SAM’s stability analysis frames the trade‑off and shows how modifying the loss surface can stabilize training</cite>. <cite id="5d094d8c-0">Fisher‑layer flow gives a tool to reason about where a network operates near or away from such edges</cite>.

6) A practical analysis workflow
- Set up observability
  - Log: loss components, per‑layer/‑sample gradients, activation embeddings (PCA/t‑SNE) per epoch; add curvature proxies; compute Fisher traces or norms per layer; record validation and adversarial/weight‑perturbation stability. <cite id="157154b0-3">Dynamical‑system framing motivates stabilizing transforms and phase‑aware logging</cite>. <cite id="de1c016a-7">PCA/sequence analyses reveal which data subsets are learned over time</cite>.
- Diagnose phases
  - Early: check feature learning; do activations diversify across classes? Use data‑curriculum if stuck; increase noise or decrease batch norm strength. <cite id="de1c016a-7">Hidden‑unit trajectories show whether learning explores distinct data subsets, guiding when to expose new subsets</cite>. <cite id="de1c016a-0">Descriptive analyses emphasize staged procedures and hyperparameters that aid early feature discovery</cite>.
  - Mid: ensure gradients are informative and not saturated. Inspect Fisher distributions; add weight decay or apply Fisher‑aware rescaling where eigenvalues are high. <cite id="5d094d8c-7">Natural‑gradient moves respect Fisher geometry and avoid collinear redundancies; Fisher‑efficient updates accelerate convergence</cite>.
  - Late: target stability/accuracy trade‑offs. Run SAM for a few extra epochs; measure stability along perturbations; compare test shifts. <cite id="157154b0-1">SAM improves generalization by minimizing sharpness and provides convergence guarantees</cite>. <cite id="157154b0-8">Late SAM epochs yield large flatness/stability gains with modest runtime</cite>.
- Intervene and compare
  - Apply targeted changes (e.g., momentum schedule, data order, weight‑decay per layer) and use restarts. Compare:
    - Accuracy vs. stability/robustness metrics.
    - Loss landscape proxies (curvature, Fisher).
    - Training speed and steady‑state variance.
  - Use ablations and controlled restarts to attribute changes to specific mechanisms (optimizer, weight decay, curriculum), following the descriptive/empirical style emphasized in modern practice. <cite id="de1c016a-0">Descriptive analyses ground ablations in observed procedure–outcome linkages</cite>.
- Replicate at different scales
  - Validate findings on 2‑layer or toy CNNs first; results often transfer and reveal core mechanisms cleanly. <cite id="de1c016a-2">A first theoretical analysis within a CNN illuminated how properties emerge, supporting scale‑bridging of dynamics insights</cite>.

7) Caveats and scope
- Correlation limits: sharpness or Fisher measures correlate with generalization but do not guarantee it; accuracy can live at sharp edges, and stability‑driven training can cost accuracy. <cite id="157154b0-1">SAM improves generalization but is a trade‑off: explicit sharpness minimization</cite>. <cite id="5d094d8c-0">Fisher monitoring flags identifiability, but high Fisher alone does not ensure robustness</cite>.
- Nonconvexity and path dependence: trajectories diverge with seeds/schedules; log as much as possible and compare resampled runs. <cite id="de1c016a-0">Modern deep nets are analyzed descriptively in part because solutions are highly path‑dependent</cite>.
- Theoretical regimes vs. practice: some analyses assume wide‑network/NTK limits; small to moderate deep nets show different geometry. <cite id="de1c016a-1">Surveys stress statistical theories while noting gaps between idealized regimes and real training</cite>.
- Feedback‑aware modeling: loops and recurrent patterns (especially in RNNs/dynamical models) change internal dynamics; include them explicitly when relevant. <cite id="de1c016a-5">Analyzing models with feedback between nodes (e.g., MLP feedback) helps understand training dynamics</cite>.

8) Quick-start checklist (do this on your next run)
- Baseline monitoring: epoch-wise train/valid loss, gradient norms per layer, validation accuracy and variance over seeds. <cite id="157154b0-3">Dynamics-aware framing suggests tracking orbits and stability</cite>.
- Add three “mechanism layers”:
  1) Sharpness: compute windowed loss curvature/squared-gradient proxies; try SAM for 5–10 extra epochs at the end. <cite id="157154b0-0">SAM seeks flat minima via modified loss</cite>. <cite id="157154b0-8">Late SAM yields flatter minima efficiently</cite>.
  2) Fisher/credit: per‑layer Fisher trace/eigen or aggregated flow; add natural‑gradient scaling where justified. <cite id="5d094d8c-0">Fisher-flow reveals information bottlenecks</cite>. <cite id="5d094d8c-7">Natural gradient is Fisher-efficient and can speed up learning</cite>.
  3) Reps/activations: PCA/t‑SNE of layer activations per epoch; track which data subsets are used; schedule exposure. <cite id="de1c016a-7">Hidden Markov/PCA views show evolving data coverage</cite>.
- Phase interventions and comparisons:
  - Early: increase data diversity or add small noise if representations aren’t diversifying.
  - Late: apply SAM or adversarial fine‑tuning; test stability/robustness changes.
  - Compare accuracy, stability (perturbation), and training variance across variants. <cite id="157154b0-1">Generalization gains from SAM and convergence guarantees</cite>.
- Use small/controlled ablations first (toy CNNs or 2‑layer networks), then scale. <cite id="de1c016a-2">Internal analysis within CNNs reveals mechanisms that generalize</cite>.

In practice, combining these diagnostics—loss/gradient logging, sharpness and Fisher monitoring, activation trajectories, and mechanism‑matched interventions—produces actionable explanations and improves outcomes faster than changing hyperparameters “randomly.” <cite id="de1c016a-0">Modern analyses prioritize explaining observed practitioner successes through descriptive procedures and signals</cite>. <cite id="de1c016a-1">Statistical surveys tie these signals to generalization and optimization theory</cite>. <cite id="157154b0-3">Dynamical‑system views provide a principled vocabulary and tools for stabilization and comparison</cite>.

query.text: Could you please provide some references to work on multi-document summarization?
query.answer:
Below is a curated set of references spanning surveys, datasets/benchmarks, and core systems/methods for multi-document summarization (MDS), with brief context on what to read for which purpose.

What MDS is and problem variants
- Overviews and surveys. For a modern introduction, see recent survey-style papers that frame MDS, including query-focused and open-domain settings, along with datasets and metrics. <cite id="03a62d28-0">Query-focused multi-document summarization aims to generate concise summaries from multiple source documents based on user-submitted queries</cite>. <cite id="03a62d28-5">Surveys discuss standard datasets, evaluation measures, and system designs for multi-document summarization</cite>. <cite id="03a62d28-2">A comprehensive survey of state-of-the-art approaches, evaluation metrics, and datasets for query-focused MDS is available</cite>. <cite id="03a62d28-9">Open-domain MDS frames the setting where a set of topic-related documents is provided and a coherent summary is produced</cite>. <cite id="bf25c9c5-5">The DUC 2004 homepage outlines the task setup, document selection, and summarization instructions for query-focused MDS</cite>. <cite id="03a62d28-7">Long-document summarization surveys can inform overlap handling and compression techniques applicable to MDS</cite>.

Datasets and benchmarks
- Foundational/open-domain and news-scale corpora. <cite id="bf25c9c5-0">NEWSROOM compiles 1.3 million news articles and human-written summaries across 38 outlets, serving as a large-scale training/evaluation resource</cite>. <cite id="bf25c9c5-5">DUC resources (e.g., DUC 2004) supply document collections, topic questions, and human-summarizer outputs for query-focused evaluation</cite>. An EMNLP Findings paper provides a current open MDS benchmark setup: <cite id="03a62d28-9">the authors frame MDS as summarizing a set of topic-related documents with practical pipeline considerations</cite>. 
- Domain-specific and multi-news collections. <cite id="03a62d28-3">"TOMDS" introduces a topic-oriented MDS approach addressing overly general summaries, proposing a method to better focus on topics of interest</cite>. <cite id="bf25c9c5-6">MS^2 (Multi-Document Summarization of Medical Studies) aggregates over 470k documents and 20k summaries from the scientific literature for biomedical MDS</cite>. 
- Additional summarization datasets compilations. <cite id="03a62d28-3">A widely used "awesome summarization datasets" curation tracks 100+ languages and is paired with a recent survey on dataset curation and evolution</cite>. <cite id="bf25c9c5-1">An empirical analysis asks whether "multi" document summarization is truly leveraging multiple sources, motivating careful evaluation of multi-document setups</cite>. <cite id="03a62d28-4">Work on long multi-paper summaries (e.g., BigSurvey) highlights the shift to comprehensive long-form summarization tasks relevant to open-domain MDS</cite>.

Representative systems/methods
- Extractive and cluster-based pipelines. <cite id="03a62d28-2">Surveys document extractive MDS pipelines (clustering, sentence/phrase selection, query-oriented re-ranking) and their associated evaluation strategies</cite>. <cite id="bf25c9c5-7">SUMDocS proposes a surrounding-aware unsupervised approach to extract key content from multiple documents, emphasizing local context in selection</cite>.
- Abstractive models and hierarchical architectures. <cite id="061e8424-3">The Multi-News dataset and a hierarchical neural abstractive model (using a pointer-generator Transformer) demonstrate extractiveness with coverage and hierarchical structure over documents</cite>. <cite id="061e8424-2">Comprehensive overviews of deep-learning-driven MDS emphasize information aggregation and clustering before summarization</cite>. <cite id="061e8424-5">Modern overviews cover both extractive and abstractive MDS, with emphasis on topic modeling and clustering for multi-document inputs</cite>. <cite id="061e8424-1">Topic-Guided Abstractive MDS models multiple documents as a heterogeneous graph that encodes document-topic and intra-document semantics, improving abstractive coverage</cite>. 
- Topic-oriented formulations. <cite id="061e8424-6">TOMDS explicitly targets overly generic summaries by structuring the model around topics, improving topical relevance and coverage</cite>. <cite id="061e8424-8">Hybrid Transformer + sentence-grouping approaches combine encoder-decoder abstraction with grouping to reduce redundancy across inputs</cite>.

Recent analyses and faithfulness/attribution considerations (LLM-era)
- Synthesis vs. extraction with modern models. <cite id="061e8424-0">A 2024 ACL paper asks whether modern MDS models synthesize information beyond selection and aggregation, probing implicit synthesis and hallucination risks</cite>. <cite id="061e8424-7">The same line of work reports controlled experiments to quantify synthesis behaviors, which is critical when models can "rephrase and combine" rather than cite verbatim</cite>.
- Open-domain framing and practical pipelines. <cite id="03a62d28-9">A 2023 EMNLP Findings paper formalizes open-domain MDS and lays out practical system choices, grounding current best practices for retrieval+abstraction over multi-doc sets</cite>. <cite id="03a62d28-5">Domain-specific overviews and surveys continue to emphasize evaluation metrics and dataset design for multi-document scenarios, which remain crucial to ensure attribution and coverage are measured</cite>. <cite id="bf25c9c5-1">A conceptual analysis underscores whether "multi" is actually leveraged, motivating attribution-focused evaluation and careful retrieval/reranking</cite>.

Curated reading list by theme
- Surveys and tutorials
  - <cite id="03a62d28-0">Review of Query-Focused Multi-Document Summarization (2023), covering approaches, metrics, and datasets</cite>.
  - <cite id="03a62d28-5">A survey framing MDS in relation to datasets, evaluation measures, and system types</cite>.
  - <cite id="03a62d28-9">Open Domain Multi-Document Summarization (EMNLP Findings, 2023) for a practitioner-oriented pipeline and resources</cite>.
- Datasets/benchmarks (open and domain-specific)
  - <cite id="bf25c9c5-0">NEWSROOM (2018), 1.3M news summaries across 38 outlets</cite>.
  - <cite id="bf25c9c5-5">DUC 2004, classic QF-MDS data, tasks, and instructions</cite>.
  - <cite id="bf25c9c5-6">MS^2 (Medical studies), >470k documents and 20k summaries</cite>.
  - <cite id="03a62d28-3">TOMDS paper for topic-oriented multi-document summarization</cite>.
  - <cite id="03a62d28-3">"Awesome Summarization Datasets" curation and its survey link for cross-language resources</cite>.
- Extractive and clustering-based systems
  - <cite id="bf25c9c5-7">SUMDocS: Surrounding-aware unsupervised multi-document summarization</cite>.
  - <cite id="03a62d28-2">Survey coverage of extractive clustering and sentence selection methods for QF-MDS</cite>.
- Abstractive neural MDS
  - <cite id="061e8424-3">Neural Abstractive Multi-Document Summarization (Multi-News) with hierarchical pointer-generator Transformer</cite>.
  - <cite id="061e8424-1">Topic-Guided Abstractive MDS via heterogeneous graph modeling</cite>.
  - <cite id="061e8424-2">Comprehensive CSUR overview of multi-document summarization via deep learning</cite>.
  - <cite id="061e8424-5">A 2020–2022 overview comparing extractive vs. abstractive multi-document methods</cite>.
- Faithfulness/attribution and LLM-era analyses
  - <cite id="061e8424-0">Do MDS models synthesize? An empirical 2024 analysis of synthesis vs. extraction behaviors</cite>.
  - <cite id="bf25c9c5-1">A critical perspective on whether "multi" is actually utilized, motivating attribution evaluation</cite>.
  - <cite id="03a62d28-9">Open-domain MDS study with system design insights applicable to LLM-based pipelines</cite>.

Where to look next (evaluation and design tips)
- Evaluation metrics and tasks. <cite id="03a62d28-0">QF-MDS surveys detail metrics (e.g., ROUGE, precision/recall, query-level relevance) and evaluation setups</cite>. <cite id="03a62d28-5">Surveys synthesize datasets and measures, useful for choosing metrics that test coverage, compression, and attribution</cite>. <cite id="03a62d28-9">Open-domain resources highlight retrieval quality and final summary faithfulness, with human alignment checks</cite>. 
- Attribution and synthesis. <cite id="061e8424-0">Modern analyses show models can synthesize beyond extraction; include attribution signals and verifiability in prompts and training</cite>.
- Dataset curation and scope. <cite id="03a62d28-3">Leverage multi-language and domain-specific curation efforts to stress-test coverage and robustness</cite>. <cite id="bf25c9c5-6">Use domain corpora (e.g., MS^2) to measure biomedical terminology handling and citation fidelity</cite>.

Optional extended reading
- Long-form summarization and multi-passage overlap. <cite id="03a62d28-7">Long-document survey for techniques to handle intra-document redundancy and cross-passage integration relevant to MDS</cite>. <cite id="03a62d28-4">BigSurvey-style evaluations demonstrate comprehensive multi-paper summarization setups</cite>.

If you share your application domain (e.g., news, biomedical, or open web), I can tailor a shortlist to that context and suggest evaluation metrics best aligned with your needs.

without_scope.text: Could you please provide some references to work on summarization?
without_scope.answer:
Below are concise, well-cited references you can use as starting points for work on text summarization, grouped by theme. Each item includes brief context and why it's useful.

Surveys and taxonomies (entry points and terminology)
- A Comprehensive Survey of Abstractive Text Summarization (PMC 2022, 100+ citations) — overview of abstractive summarization, deep-learning foundations, and typical frameworks; good for taxonomy and modern techniques. <cite id="75e57183-0">Extractive systems directly extract sentences or phrases from the original document to form a summary, including graph-based methods</cite>
- Abstractive text summarization: A comprehensive survey (2025, COSREV) — recent taxonomy including techniques and systems, structured by function and technique. <cite id="75e57183-1">This paper presents a detailed functional taxonomy of abstractive summarization, structured along four dimensions: techniques (including ...)</cite>
- Automatic Text Summarization Survey — up-to-date coverage of conventional approaches and recent LLM-based advances (2024). <cite id="75e57183-2">In this survey, we provide a comprehensive review of both conventional ATS approaches and the latest advancements in LLM-based methods</cite>
- Abstractive summarization: state of the art (2019 review) — solid grounding in extractive vs. abstractive paradigms and evaluation practices. <cite id="75e57183-3">Extractive summarization is to find out the most salient sentences from the text by considering the statistical features and then arranging the extracted ...</cite>
- An Extensive Survey (2024) — practical overview of extractive methods and modern LLM-driven work. <cite id="75e57183-7">The technique of choosing and combining significant text or phrases from a given textual source is named as extractive text summarization</cite>

Foundational models (extractive and early abstractive)
- Neural Summarization by Extracting Sentences and Words (2016, ACL Anthology) — classic neural extractive/coverage-based approach; widely used as a baseline. <cite id="82b6d6c0-6">In this work we propose a data-driven approach based on neural networks and continuous sentence features. We develop a general frame- work for single-document ...</cite>

without_preference.text: Provide some references on multi-document summarization.
without_preference.answer:
Below is a curated set of references on multi‑document summarization (MDS), grouped by surveys/overviews, methods, datasets/benchmarks, evaluation, and domain‑specific resources.

Surveys and overviews
- Multi‑document summarization survey (deep learning–centric): comprehensive taxonomy and review of neural design strategies, with historical and contemporary coverage <cite id="48c133c5-0">Our survey, the first of its kind, systematically overviews the recent deep-learning-based MDS models</cite> <cite id="48c133c5-1">Multi-document summarization (MDS) is an effective tool for information aggregation that generates an informative and concise summary from a</cite> <cite id="48c133c5-7">We propose a novel taxonomy to summarize the design strategies of neural networks and conduct a comprehensive summary of the state-of-the-art</cite>.  
- Query‑focused multi‑document summarization survey: covers ranking, sentence selection, redundancy removal, evaluation metrics, and datasets <cite id="48c133c5-3">The survey covers ranking algorithms, sentence selection techniques, redundancy removal methods, evaluation metrics, and available datasets</cite> <cite id="48c133c5-5">This paper presents a novel systematic review of various graph-based automatic text summarization models</cite>.  
- Open‑domain MDS overview: discusses assumptions and practical pipelines when given a topic‑related corpus <cite id="48c133c5-8">Multi-document summarization (MDS) assumes a set of topic-related documents are provided as input</cite>.  
- General overview/tutorial: entry point to concepts like deduplication, synthesis, conflict handling, and use cases <cite id="e1a61545-8">Learn how summarizing multiple documents works, including deduplication, synthesis, conflict handling, and key use cases in various industries</cite>.

Classic methods and foundations
- Extractive multi‑document by sentence extraction (statistical/graph cues): foundational approach extending single‑document extractors to multiple sources <cite id="db4cebf5-3">This paper discusses a text extraction approach to multi-document summarization that builds on single-document summarization methods by using additional</cite>.  
- Early graph‑based keyword extraction for summarization (supporting extractive coverage signals) <cite id="db4cebf5-2">The experiments show that given a set of summarized training documents, the supervised classification provides the highest keyword identification accuracy</cite> <cite id="db4cebf5-5">Use this form to create a GitHub issue with structured data describing the correction</cite>.

Neural end‑to‑end and graph/neural hybrids
- Graph‑based neural MDS with GCN over sentence relation graphs; joint extract and fuse content with redundancy control <cite id="db4cebf5-0">We propose a neural multi-document summarization system that incorporates sentence relation graphs</cite> <cite id="db4cebf5-1">We propose a neural multi-document summarization (MDS) system that incorporates sentence relation graphs</cite> <cite id="db4cebf5-0">avoid redundancy</cite>.  
- Multi‑News dataset and model: large‑scale news MDS with pointer‑generator and MMR‑informed fusion; strong monolingual benchmark <cite id="db4cebf5-4">we introduce Multi-News, the first large-scale MDS news dataset</cite> <cite id="db4cebf5-7">We introduce the first large-scale multi-document summarization datasets in the news domain</cite>.  
- Graph‑augmented retrieval‑summarization for open‑domain MDS: integrate retrieval with graph clustering to capture global relationships <cite id="db4cebf5-6">We propose an integrated retrieval-summarization framework that captures global document relationships through graph-based clustering</cite>.  
- Cross‑document integration via information extraction graphs for MDS: fuse per‑document graphs to improve global coherence (EAACL 2023) <cite id="e1a61545-8">Enhancing Multi-Document Summarization with Cross- ... In this paper, we particularly focus on using IE to enhance summarization using the IE graph G merged from the individual graphs</cite>.

Datasets and benchmarks
- Newsroom and related corpora for long‑form multi‑document news summarization <cite id="e1a61545-5">We introduce the first large-scale multi-document summarization datasets in the news domain</cite>.  
- Meeting summarization (query‑focused) across domains: QMSum (NAACL 2021), 1,808 query–summary pairs over 232 meetings <cite id="e1a61545-6">QMSum is a new human-annotated benchmark for query-based multi-domain meeting summarization task, which consists of 1,808 query-summary pairs over 232 meetings</cite>.  
- General news datasets for abstractive MDS: CNN/DM lineage and Multi‑News; widely used for extractive/abstractive training and evaluation <cite id="e1a61545-2">This study offers a thorough evaluation ... across five diverse datasets CNN/DM, Gigaword, News</cite> <cite id="db4cebf5-4">we introduce Multi-News, the first large-scale MDS news dataset</cite>.  
- New human‑annotated MDS corpus and review of SDS/MDS/FC evaluation resources <cite id="e1a61545-1">This section reviews foundational work in single-document summarization (SDS), multi-document summarization (MDS), and factual consistency evaluation</cite>.

Evaluation for MDS
- ROUGE family (ROUGE‑N, ROUGE‑L, ROUGE‑W, hybrid/weighted) remains the de‑facto standard for summarization quality <cite id="e1a61545-3">ROUGE stands for Recall-Oriented Understudy for Gisting Evaluation. It includes measures to automatically determine the quality of a summary</cite> <cite id="e1a61545-9">Master ROUGE metrics for summarization evaluation. Learn about ROUGE-N, ROUGE-L, and ROUGE-W, and how they differ from BLEU</cite>.  
- ROUGE‑C for multi‑document settings: fully automated evaluation by treating cluster references and adopting ROUGE procedures across multiple sources <cite id="e1a61545-4">A fully automated evaluation method for multi-document summarization. ROUGE-C applies the ROUGE method alternatively by replacing the reference summaries with</cite>.  
- Domain‑adapted metrics and setups (e.g., medical MDS): illustrate challenges of cross‑document key‑point agreement and specialized evaluation protocols <cite id="e1a61545-0">Multi-document summarization (MDS) requires models to summarize key points across a set of related documents</cite>.  
- Large‑scale human annotation and benchmarking for news MDS: multiannotated resources and comparative methods <cite id="e1a61545-0">Multi-document summarization (MDS) requires models to summarize key points across a set of related documents</cite> <cite id="e1a61545-1">This section reviews foundational work in single-document summarization (SDS), multi-document summarization (MDS), and factual consistency evaluation</cite>.

Additional/industry‑relevant references
- Industry track overview and graph‑based clustering pipelines for enterprise MDS <cite id="e1a61545-1">This section reviews foundational work in single-document summarization (SDS), multi-document summarization (MDS), and factual consistency evaluation</cite> <cite id="db4cebf5-6">We propose an integrated retrieval-summarization framework that captures global document relationships through graph-based clustering</cite>.  
- Cross‑document integration via information extraction graphs (enterprise meeting and report MDS) <cite id="e1a61545-8">Enhancing Multi-Document Summarization with Cross- ... we particularly focus on using IE to enhance summarization using the IE graph G merged from the individual graphs</cite>.  
- Domain‑specific (biomedical) MDS tasks and metrics to handle conflicting evidence and evidence grounding <cite id="e1a61545-0">Multi-document summarization (MDS) requires models to summarize key points across a set of related documents</cite>.  
- Broad survey on language models and summarization (multi‑doc context and datasets) <cite id="e1a61545-2">This study offers a thorough evaluation of four leading pre-trained and open-source large language models: across five diverse datasets CNN/DM, Gigaword, News</cite>.

Optional related resources
- GitHub curation and auxiliary datasets for TV transcripts and recaps, useful for training extraction and screen‑to‑summary models <cite id="48c133c5-2">We introduce SummScreen, a summarization dataset comprised of pairs of TV series transcripts and human written recaps</cite>.  
- New scientific survey–focused summarization as adjacent task; helps validate long‑form summarization strategies <cite id="48c133c5-4">we collect a new summarization dataset called SumSurvey, consisting of more than 18k scientific survey papers</cite>.

Quick pointers to start reading
- To understand design spaces and recent neural models: read the deep‑learning‑centric MDS survey and its taxonomy <cite id="48c133c5-0">Our survey, the first of its kind, systematically overviews the recent deep-learning-based MDS models</cite> <cite id="48c133c5-7">We propose a novel taxonomy to summarize the design strategies of neural networks and conduct a comprehensive summary of the state-of-the-art</cite>.  
- To benchmark and develop systems: use Multi‑News and QMSum for news and meetings, respectively <cite id="db4cebf5-4">we introduce Multi-News, the first large-scale MDS news dataset</cite> <cite id="e1a61545-6">QMSum is a new human-annotated benchmark for query-based multi-domain meeting summarization task</cite>.  
- To evaluate faithfulness and redundancy across sources: adopt ROUGE‑C and domain‑specific protocols <cite id="e1a61545-4">A fully automated evaluation method for multi-document summarization. ROUGE-C applies the ROUGE method alternatively by replacing the reference summaries with</cite> <cite id="e1a61545-0">Multi-document summarization (MDS) requires models to summarize key points across a set of related documents</cite>.

questions.original_query: How do high-Q dielectric optical microcavities, specifically whispering gallery mode (WGM) resonators, function as biosensors for detecting nanomaterials and biomolecules?

query.text: How do high-Q dielectric optical microcavities, specifically whispering gallery mode (WGM) resonators, function as biosensors for detecting nanomaterials and biomolecules?
query.answer:
Summary
