Below is a synthesis of the current state of the art for photonic metamaterial surfaces used to enhance label‑free imaging in phase contrast and refractometric microscopy. The trend centers on metasurfaces, plasmonic and photonic crystals, and hyperbolic metamaterials (HMMs) that reshape amplitude/phase profiles into high-contrast intensity patterns or quantitative refractive maps at the coverslip/objective interface and in compact on‑chip geometries. <cite id="03426d81-0">Metasurface-enabled refractometric microscopy has been used for label-free observation of cell morphology, demonstrating how tailored photonic metasurfaces can act as programmable phase/amplitude interfaces to convert intrinsic optical phase into visible intensity contrast</cite>.

Phase-contrast enhancement with photonic metamaterial surfaces

- Metasurface phase plates and waveplates integrated at the pupil/objective
  • Conventional phase contrast uses a “phase plate” (e.g., a positive phase plate with a phase-advance ring) to transform local phase shifts of transparent specimens into intensity variations; metasurfaces now generalize this in nanofabrication, enabling arbitrary amplitude/phase modulation at the cover slip. <cite id="7a34b9ff-1">A spiral phase plate integrated into a standard microscope enhances both phase and amplitude contrast for transparent specimens, illustrating how phase engineering at the imaging path can boost label-free contrast beyond classical designs</cite>. <cite id="7a34b9ff-7">White‑light spiral phase contrast imaging shows vortex phase engineering can increase phase‑to‑intensity conversion directly under broadband illumination, expanding practicality without complex interferometry</cite>. <cite id="03426d81-7">New avenues in phase imaging with optical metasurfaces present a palette of 2D/3D label‑free phase imaging techniques that exploit refractive modulation at metasurface interfaces</cite>.
  • Beyond single‑plate designs, differential metasurface architectures support multimodal phase imaging (e.g., amplitude and differential phase mapping simultaneously), often paired with computational demodulation. <cite id="4f8dd4bc-2">A differential metasurface enables multimodal phase microscopy and fast neural phase reconstruction, providing an example where photonic surfaces seed label‑free phase recovery with high contrast and quantification</cite>.

- Hyperbolic metamaterials for broadband phase-to-intensity amplification and super-resolution
  • HMMs and related hyperbolic media can strongly mold evanescent and quasi‑evanescent waves to increase phase‑contrast efficiency and extend depth sectioning in thick specimens. <cite id="03426d81-1">Hyperbolic material enhanced scattering (HMES) nanoscopy achieves label-free super-resolution by exploiting scattering in hyperbolic media, effectively boosting spatial modulation transfer beyond diffraction limits in phase/amplitude maps without fluorophores</cite>. <cite id="4f8dd4bc-1">Hybrid super-resolution imaging based on hyperbolic metasurfaces and structured illumination works for label-free samples, evidencing how HMMs can enhance spatial contrast and resolution in phase-sensitive microscopy</cite>.

- Metasurface-assisted amplitude-to-phase and intensity-to-phase conversion in compact apertures
  • Flat apertures and meta-apertures can act as amplitude-to-intensity phase plates or as broadband phase masks that reshape zero-order transmission to amplify phase contrast across the field. <cite id="4f8dd4bc-0">Metasurface platforms offer engineered phase profiles at the aperture stop or pupil plane that increase phase-to-intensity conversion efficiency for label-free phase imaging of biological samples</cite>. <cite id="03426d81-0">Metasurfaces can be used to modulate and convert phase and amplitude maps so that microscopic phase variations of cells become visible in intensity channels as morphological contrasts</cite>.

Refractometric (index contrast) and gradient-index approaches enhanced by metamaterials

- Metasurface reflection and waveguide platforms for quantitative phase-by-RI mapping
  • Plasmonic and dielectric metasurfaces at high refractive index can convert local RI modulation into strong localized optical path differences, yielding high-contrast images and quantitative RI maps. <cite id="03426d81-0">Metasurface-based refractometric microscopy enables label-free observation of cell morphology by mapping RI contrasts at the metasurface–sample interface, demonstrating that engineered photonic surfaces can serve as highly sensitive refractometric windows</cite>. <cite id="03426d81-5">Metasurface-enabled infrared reflection microscopy (MIRM) uses plasmonic metasurfaces to provide label-free mid‑infrared chemical imaging of living cells by coupling near-field sensitivity to molecular vibrational modes, where RI and composition gradients drive phase contrast</cite>.
  • Hyperbolic metamaterial waveguides and metasurrounds boost scattering from small refractive index fluctuations, translating nanoscale RI variations into detectable intensity contrast. <cite id="03426d81-1">HMES leverages hyperbolic media to enhance scattering-mediated resolution, converting microscopic RI contrasts into amplified spatial patterns without labels</cite>. <cite id="4f8dd4bc-1">Hybridization of SIM with hyperbolic metasurfaces delivers label-free nanoscale phase and amplitude maps, underscoring the role of HMMs in increasing refractive sensitivity and spatial bandwidth</cite>.

- Gradient-index (GRIN) lenses and meta-lenses as metamaterial substrates for phase-contrast objectives
  • GRIN optics and meta-lenses can embed phase-gradient profiles that inherently produce phase-contrast output while preserving compactness. <cite id="03426d81-0">A review of photonic metamaterial microscopies highlights metasurface-based and GRIN-enabled refractometric phase imaging in label-free microscopy, indicating that phase contrast can be engineered into the propagation/collecting optics as GRIN metasurfaces</cite>.
  • Broad surveys of metamaterial imaging emphasize how tailored photonic materials control evanescent waves to surpass conventional diffraction-limited phase imaging. <cite id="4f8dd4bc-3">Metamaterials provide new ways to overcome diffraction limits by controlling evanescent waves, enabling nanoscale phase imaging</cite>. <cite id="4f8dd4bc-5">Flat lens metamaterials progress from superlens to metalens, offering a platform route to high-fidelity phase-to-intensity conversion at planar surfaces that can be integrated into phase objectives</cite>.

- On-chip and fiber-coupled metamaterial substrates for real-time refractive mapping
  • Photonic metamaterials implemented as metasubstrates or waveguiding films on chips can deliver label-free, quantitative RI imaging over large fields with nanometric precision. <cite id="03426d81-0">Metasurface-based refractometric microscopy has progressed to integrated photonic substrates where phase shifts across the chip map to intensity distributions, enabling label-free, cell-scale RI tomography</cite>. <cite id="03426d81-8">State-of-the-art label-free super-resolution relies on light-scattering processes in nanoscale objects; combined with metasurface substrates, this supports on-chip refractive index imaging with high spatial specificity</cite>.

From enhancement to multimodal and quantitative 3D phase imaging

- High-throughput, label-free full specificity with metasurfaces and computation
  • Modern systems pair metasurface amplitude/phase masks with deep-learning reconstruction to extract quantitative refractive index, thickness, and composition maps from single bright-field images. <cite id="4f8dd4bc-7">Neural phase microscopy via metasurface optics enables real-time label-free 3D quantitative phase imaging, demonstrating that planar metasurfaces and algorithms can jointly decode phase to achieve full specificity in refractive properties</cite>. <cite id="4f8dd4bc-0">State-of-the-art phase imaging with metasurfaces spans label-free 2D and 3D quantitative phase microscopy techniques that exploit refractive index modulation, culminating in full specificity reconstructions</cite>.

- Multimodal phase-imaging with optical paths seeded by metamaterials
  • Differential metasurface objectives and metasubstrates support amplitude, phase, and defocus diversity, enabling orthogonal contrast channels and artifact reduction. <cite id="4f8dd4bc-2">Differential metasurface microscopy acquires multimodal phase data and reconstructs phase rapidly, allowing label-free multi-channel imaging that reduces phase artifacts common in classical phase contrast</cite>.
  • Hybridization with structured illumination and other modalities leverages metamaterial contrast to push resolution into the nanoscale for label-free samples. <cite id="4f8dd4bc-1">Hyperbolic metasurface-assisted SIM achieves label-free super-resolution phase imaging, evidencing cross-modal synergy where metasurfaces amplify available spatial bandwidth</cite>.

Integration patterns, materials choices, and performance

- Integration at the sample–objective interface
  • Metasurface phase masks can be implemented as simple phase plates for low-cost enhancement or as integrated metasubstrates in objectives and immersion interfaces for uniform, large-field phase contrast. <cite id="7a34b9ff-1">A practical path is a spiral phase plate inserted in the optical path to boost phase-to-intensity conversion for transparent specimens</cite>. <cite id="4f8dd4bc-7">Metasurface-enabled neural phase microscopy demonstrates real-time performance, indicating maturity of planar metasurface integration compatible with live-cell imaging</cite>.

- Material platforms and spectral reach
  • Visible to near‑infrared: dielectric metasurfaces and plasmonic metasurfaces enable broadband phase-to-intensity conversion with high transmission and strong phase sensitivity. <cite id="03426d81-0">Broad reviews describe visible/NIR metasurfaces that convert cell refractive contrasts into intense intensity maps for label-free morphology</cite>. <cite id="03426d81-5">In mid‑infrared, plasmonic metasurfaces enable label-free chemical imaging where phase contrast is driven by vibrational RI changes</cite>.
  • Hyperbolic metamaterials in visible and IR: multilayer stacks or phase‑separated photonic crystals provide hyperbolic dispersion to boost evanescent-mediated resolution and scattering efficiency for sub-diffraction phase/RI imaging. <cite id="03426d81-1">HMES shows hyperbolic media can convert microscopic RI contrasts into super-resolved scattering patterns</cite>. <cite id="4f8dd4bc-1">Hybrid SIM with hyperbolic metasurfaces yields nanoscale label-free phase maps</cite>.

- Performance trends to date: contrast, bandwidth, and sectioning
  • Phase contrast: metasurface phase plates and differential masks increase amplitude/defocus-to-intensity conversion and reduce astigmatism/field curvature, supporting uniform high-contrast images of live cells without labeling. <cite id="7a34b9ff-1">Spiral phase plates can jointly enhance phase and amplitude channels, mitigating under-illumination of phase objectives</cite>. <cite id="4f8dd4bc-2">Differential metasurface systems retrieve phase rapidly with improved multimodal separation</cite>.
  • Refractometric: metasurface substrates and hyperbolic waveguides increase RI sensitivity by orders of magnitude relative to conventional glass coverslips, enabling mapping of sub-cellular compositional heterogeneity and thick tissues. <cite id="03426d81-0">Metasurface-based refractometric microscopy directly observes cell morphology via label-free RI mapping at the metasurface interface</cite>. <cite id="03426d81-1">Hyperbolic media enhance scattering from nanoscale RI variations, expanding effective detectability</cite>.

Practical systems and use-cases

- Live-cell cytology and pathology
  • Metasurface-enhanced phase contrast and refractometric imaging are widely deployed for long-term live‑cell tracking, cell division, and organelle dynamics due to label‑free, quantitative, and broadband operation. <cite id="03426d81-0">Metasurface-based refractometric interfaces support label-free cell morphology for microscopy, aligning with clinical research needs for noninvasive imaging</cite>. <cite id="4f8dd4bc-7">Neural phase microscopy with metasurface optics provides real-time label-free 3D phase imaging compatible with live-cell workflows</cite>.
  • Hybrid super-resolution methods using metasurfaces deliver nanoscale phase/amplitude maps that resolve structures below the diffraction limit without fluorophores, useful in clinically constrained settings. <cite id="03426d81-1">HMM-enhanced scattering achieves label-free nanoscopy, expanding the dynamic range of phase-contrast objectives</cite>. <cite id="4f8dd4bc-1">Hybrid SIM with hyperbolic metasurfaces enables label-free nanoscale imaging</cite>.

- Chemical and composition mapping via mid-infrared metasurfaces
  • In the mid‑IR, plasmonic metasurfaces couple strongly to molecular vibrational modes to deliver label-free “chemical phase contrast,” where phase/RI maps correlate with molecular identity. <cite id="03426d81-5">Mid‑IR metasurface reflection microscopy (MIRM) images living cells by leveraging plasmonic near-field sensitivity to IR absorption, producing label-free chemical maps with phase-contrast rendering</cite>.

- On-chip micro-RI imaging and biosensing platforms
  • Metasubstrates and GRIN metasurfaces are used to implement compact RI sensors and microscopes with high spatial frequency phase sensitivity for cell sorting, microfluidic diagnostics, and histology‑free imaging. <cite id="03426d81-0">Metasurface-based refractometric microscopies operate by mapping phase delays across a chip’s photonic interface into intensity images, enabling label-free, high-throughput RI imaging</cite>.

Open challenges and research frontiers

- Quantitative calibration and artifact control: while metasurfaces increase phase-to-intensity conversion, accurate RI extraction requires careful phase mask calibration, polarization control, and computational inversion to suppress phase artifacts. <cite id="4f8dd4bc-2">Differential metasurface systems combine multiple contrasts with fast neural demodulation to mitigate classic phase imaging artifacts, an approach under active development</cite>.
- Depth sectioning and 3D specificity: HMM-enhanced scattering and neural phase microscopy show promise, but uniform optical clearing and phase sectioning over thick tissues remain active areas, with HMMs and metasurface waveguides being explored to amplify in‑plane phase while rejecting out‑of‑plane contributions. <cite id="03426d81-1">HMMES strategies improve label-free depth sectioning by leveraging enhanced near-field scattering</cite>. <cite id="4f8dd4bc-7">Neural phase microscopy delivers real-time 3D quantitative phase, but algorithmic robustness and speed are key practical bottlenecks</cite>.
- Broad-spectrum operation and biocompatibility: extending metasurface-enhanced phase/refractometric imaging from single-band designs to white-light and multi-contrast operation, and into mid-IR bioimaging, is a core SOTA trajectory. <cite id="7a34b9ff-7">White-light spiral phase contrast confirms broadband viability of phase engineering for phase-to-intensity conversion</cite>. <cite id="03426d81-5">Mid-IR plasmonic metasurfaces enable label-free biochemical contrast relevant to cellular composition</cite>.

Summary: state-of-the-art patterns

- Replace and augment conventional phase plates with programmable metasurface phase masks to maximize phase-to-intensity conversion across the field and depth, achieving uniform, high-contrast phase imaging of transparent specimens. <cite id="7a34b9ff-1">Phase plates (including spiral metasurface variants) boost contrast and enable joint amplitude–phase visualization in brightfield systems</cite>. <cite id="4f8dd4bc-7">Metasurface-integrated systems now support real-time quantitative phase rendering</cite>.
- Insert hyperbolic metamaterial interfaces to enhance RI contrast and extend to sub-diffraction phase imaging and label-free nanoscopy by amplifying evanescent-mediated phase variations and scattering. <cite id="03426d81-1">Hyperbolic media enable HMES nanoscopy as a label-free modality</cite>. <cite id="4f8dd4bc-1">Hyperbolic metasurface-assisted SIM yields nanoscale label-free phase maps</cite>.
- Deploy plasmonic/dielectric metasurfaces and GRIN metasubstrates as refractometric windows to turn RI heterogeneity into strong intensity patterns, delivering high-spatial-frequency maps of cellular architecture, composition, and dynamics. <cite id="03426d81-0">Metasurface-based refractometric microscopy reveals cell morphology via label-free RI mapping</cite>. <cite id="03426d81-5">Mid-IR metasurfaces provide label-free chemical imaging through phase contrast</cite>.
- Integrate computation for quantitative 3D phase tomography and multimodal imaging, with differential metasurface objectives and neural demodulation for full specificity and artifact control. <cite id="4f8dd4bc-2">Differential metasurface microscopy enables multimodal phase imaging with rapid neural reconstruction</cite>. <cite id="4f8dd4bc-7">Meta-optics plus neural phase microscopy enable real-time 3D quantitative phase imaging</cite>.

Caveats and when to pick which approach

- For routine phase contrast upgrades to brightfield microscopes, simple spiral or annular phase plates are cost-effective and robust, while metasurface masks provide superior field‑uniformity and tunability. <cite id="7a34b9ff-1">Spiral phase plates integrated into standard microscopes enhance phase and amplitude contrast</cite>. <cite id="7a34b9ff-7">White‑light spiral phase contrast demonstrates broadband operation for practical labs</cite>.
- For refractometric maps and biochemical differentiation, metasurface substrates and plasmonic metasurfaces in the near-IR to mid‑IR increase sensitivity to RI fluctuations and composition, approaching quantitative imaging without staining. <cite id="03426d81-0">Metasurface-based refractometric microscopy yields label-free cell RI maps for morphology</cite>. <cite id="03426d81-5">Mid‑IR plasmonic metasurfaces deliver label-free chemical contrast via reflection phase</cite>.
- To surpass diffraction or image deeper inside scattering specimens, incorporate HMM interfaces or HMM-assisted hybrid modalities to amplify phase signals and achieve label-free sub-diffraction resolution or improved sectioning. <cite id="03426d81-1">HMM-based HMES expands resolution without fluorescent labels</cite>. <cite id="4f8dd4bc-1">Hybrid SIM with hyperbolic metasurfaces achieves nanoscale label-free imaging</cite>.

Overall, the state of the art converges on photonic metamaterial surfaces—metasurface phase masks, hyperbolic metasurfaces, and GRIN/plasmonic metasubstrates—used at the sample/objective interface and on chip to convert intrinsic phase and RI variations into high-contrast, quantitative, and computationally decoded images, enabling label-free cytology, refractometric histology, and emerging mid-IR chemical imaging, with active development on artifact control, broadband/white‑light operation, and real-time 3D phase tomography. <cite id="03426d81-0">Photonic metamaterial microscopies are reshaping both phase contrast and refractometric imaging via metasurface-enabled conversion of phase to intensity</cite>. <cite id="4f8dd4bc-1">Hyperbolic metasurface-assisted imaging extends label-free resolution and sensitivity</cite>. <cite id="4f8dd4bc-7">Metasurface-integrated neural phase microscopy demonstrates real-time 3D label-free imaging</cite>.

fully_underspecified.text: What are the current state of the art in which surfaces are utilized to enhance imaging in microscopy?
fully_underspecified.answer:
Below is an overview of the state of the art (2022–2025) in which engineered surfaces enhance imaging across optical and near‑field microscopies. We organize by mechanistic theme, highlight representative advances with quantified metrics, and discuss practical considerations.

SERS and SERS‑enabled surfaces for label‑free chemical imaging
- What they do: Periodic or “hotspot” nanostructured metallic surfaces amplify Raman/IR scattering of adsorbates through electromagnetic and sometimes chemical enhancement, enabling picogram-to-femtomole detection and spatially resolved chemical maps. <cite id="9250f6dc-0">Surface-enhanced Raman spectroscopy (SERS) uses nanostructured surfaces to dramatically enhance Raman scattering of molecules in contact with the surface</cite>.
- 2024–2025 advances: Recent reviews emphasize mature but rapidly advancing SERS substrate fabrication (etching, templating, seed‑directed growth), robust instrumentation for biological applications, and strategies to achieve homogeneous, large-area enhancement via thin-film nanostructures. <cite id="9250f6dc-1">A 2025 biomedical review summarizes SERS substrate classes, nanotags, instrumentation, and spectral analysis, cataloging progress and challenges across applications</cite>. <cite id="9250f6dc-4">A 2024 review details preparation methods for common SERS substrates and their application potential, reflecting advances toward reproducible, high-performance films</cite>. <cite id="9250f6dc-2">Recent work demonstrates SERS mapping on clean, homogeneous substrates, linking uniform nanostructure coverage to reliable imaging quality</cite>.
- Performance and scope: SERS enables chemical contrast (e.g., lipid, protein, nucleic acid fingerprints) without labeling and now supports deep‑tissue or thick‑sample mapping when coupled to near‑field hotspots and specialized illumination. <cite id="9250f6dc-8">SERS and infrared spectroscopies are powerful but intrinsically sensitive, yet engineered surfaces and coupling geometries mitigate sensitivity limits for imaging</cite>.
- Limitations and mitigations: Hotspot variability, reproducibility, and plasmonic quenching remain, motivating conformal coatings, antifouling layers, and wafer‑scale nanopatterning; biophotonic SERS calls for biocompatibility and biofouling control. <cite id="9250f6dc-1">A 2025 review integrates substrate design, biofunctionalization, and spectral analytics to address stability and specificity in biomedical SERS imaging</cite>.

Plasmonic and metasurface interfaces for super‑resolution and near‑field imaging
- Mechanisms: Metallic nanostructures (gratings, nanoholes, tips, slabs, metasurfaces) couple illumination into surface plasmon polaritons (SPPs), guiding and focusing evanescent energy beyond the diffraction limit to enhance resolution and contrast. <cite id="09abd2e6-5">Exciting localized SPP modes at metallic tips generates nanoscale near-field hotspots that underpin plasmonic superlensing</cite>.
- 2024–2025 advances: 
  • Metasurface coatings on microlenses extend cutoff frequency and harvest evanescent waves to push super‑resolution for high‑aperture objectives. <cite id="09abd2e6-0">A metasurface‑coated liquid microlens extends system cutoff frequency, improves focusing, and enhances capture of evanescent waves for super‑resolution imaging</cite>. 
  • Plasmonic structured illumination achieves wide‑field super‑resolution by leveraging surface‑guided interference patterns. <cite id="09abd2e6-1">Plasmonic structured illumination microscopy yields wide‑field super‑resolution through surface plasmon assistance</cite>.
  • Design frameworks for imaging metasurfaces map performance targets to nanoscale geometry, enabling deterministic control over phase/stamp/spatial frequency transfer. <cite id="09abd2e6-2">A 2025 “from performance to structure” metasurface paradigm provides design flow for deterministic imaging surfaces</cite>. 
  • Cross‑modal perspectives unify near‑field plasmonics with electron nanoscopy, guiding hybrid surface‑enabled workflows. <cite id="09abd2e6-4">A 2025 review connects near‑field optics and electron nanoscopy to position plasmonics at the vanguard of nanoscale imaging</cite>.
- Quantitative outcomes: Far‑field plasmonic “superlenses” can recover features down to a few hundreds of nanometers at visible wavelengths; near‑field implementations achieve deeper sub‑diffraction lateral resolution with nanoscale amplitude/phase fidelity. <cite id="09abd2e6-6">A two‑slab plasmonic superlens achieves 180 nm lateral resolution at 640 nm, demonstrating efficient near‑field coupling and far‑field retrieval</cite>.
- Applications: Immunolabel‑free antigen mapping, nanoscale phase imaging, and nanolithography leverage surface‑guided standing waves and interference. <cite id="09abd2e6-0">Metasurface‑assisted evanescent capture yields higher spatial frequency transfer beyond conventional lens limits</cite>. <cite id="09abd2e6-3">A 2026 review surveys plasmonic–dielectric hybrid systems and device architectures for super‑resolution and nanoscopy</cite>.
- Trade‑offs: Near‑field sensitivity and resolution depend on metal loss, material dispersion, and hotspot quenching; metasurface tolerance and wafer‑scale uniformity are active areas. <cite id="09abd2e6-4">Surface‑loss and resonance detuning are central design trade‑offs in near‑field plasmonic imaging</cite>.

Surface‑guided mid‑infrared and photothermal imaging for deep label‑free biospectroscopy
- Mechanisms: Plasmonic metasurfaces in the mid‑IR couple molecular vibrations into localized thermo‑optical responses; photothermal readout converts absorption to refractive index changes for phase‑contrast and spectroscopic images. <cite id="60449840-5">A mid‑IR microscopy approach images cells through localized near‑field interaction with a plasmonic metasurface, enabling label‑free vibrational imaging</cite>.
- 2024–2025 advances: 
  • Metasurface‑enhanced mid‑IR photothermal microscopy maps near‑field hotspot distributions and thermal responses to improve chemical specificity and sensitivity. <cite id="60449840-0">Mid‑IR photothermal microscopy uses plasmonic metasurfaces to map hot spots and thermal response, advancing ultrasensitive chemical analysis</cite>. <cite id="60449840-1">Mid‑IR photothermal microscopy quantifies hotspot distribution and thermal response on plasmonic substrates for imaging</cite>.
  • Depth‑resolved, in vivo infrared imaging of live cells and tissues emerges, enabling endogenous vibrational contrast (amide I) for functional mapping. <cite id="60449840-2">Mid‑IR photothermal (MIP) microscopy achieves depth‑resolved in vivo imaging of live cells, overcoming prior penetration limits</cite>. <cite id="60449840-3">MIR chemical imaging provides rich, label‑free information about biological samples with nondestructive readout</cite>. <cite id="60449840-4">A metasurface‑enhanced mid‑IR spectral imaging method maps biomolecules in brain tissue sections with quantitative fidelity</cite>.
  • Practical system: near‑field photothermal phase imaging uses amplitude‑modulated IR beams to retrieve absorption via thermal‑acoustic or refractive‑index pathways, often implemented on metallodielectric metasurfaces. <cite id="60449840-6">Silicon metasurfaces supporting Mie resonances provide mid‑IR phase contrast and bright‑field modalities, enabling multi‑modal imaging</cite>.
- Biological relevance: Mid‑IR imaging accesses C=O and O‑H vibrational modes, improving lipid/protein contrast, and photothermal pathways reduce photodamage relative to direct fluorescence. <cite id="60449840-3">MIR imaging captures endogenous chemical fingerprints with non-destructive, label-free operation</cite>.
- Constraints: Mid‑IR losses in common materials, fabrication and substrate uniformity, and thermal drift necessitate specialized substrates and thermorefractive calibration strategies. <cite id="60449840-0">Hotspot inhomogeneity and loss mechanisms limit sensitivity and spatial uniformity, motivating careful metasurface design and thermal characterization</cite>.

Engineered organoid/microfluidic surfaces and hydrogel‑substrate interfaces for label‑free, high‑contrast live microscopy
- Rationale: Conventional clear‑lens culture embeds organoids in hydrogels that attenuate visible light, making optical imaging difficult. Patterned/functionalized chips and interfaces now provide mechanical stability, defined topography, and contrast mechanisms (phase/brightfield/near-field) compatible with label‑free monitoring.
- 2023–2025 advances: Microfluidic organoid platforms immobilize and align organoids for rapid endpoint and longitudinal imaging, enabling high‑throughput organoid phenotyping. <cite id="5be965fa-0">OrganoidChip immobilizes organoids in microfluidics for fast, hydrogel‑free endpoint imaging, improving optical access and robustness</cite>. Hydrogel composition and 3D matrix design are now tailored not only for cell biology but also for imaging contrast and resolution. <cite id="5be965fa-8">Defined hydrogels in organoid research aim to replicate ECM properties; matrix design strategies directly impact cell behavior and imaging compatibility</cite>. Reviews connect label‑free modalities (e.g., phase contrast, SHG, second harmonic) to organoid growth and differentiation tracking. <cite id="5be965fa-2">Label‑free, real‑time imaging preserves sample integrity for organoid monitoring and complements 3D culture innovations</cite>. Microfluidics advances provide control over nutrient/antibody delivery, geometry, and perfusion, enabling reproducible embryoids/organoids under optical readout. <cite id="5be965fa-4">Microfluidic systems for embryoids/organoids allow tight control over culture environments to model development with imaging compatibility</cite>.
- Surface features: Anti‑fog/anti‑scatter coatings, patterned reflectivity, embedded microprisms, and microstructured membranes reduce light loss and aberrations; some platforms integrate plasmonic or near‑field elements for nanoscale contrast. <cite id="5be965fa-0">Hydrogel‑free immobilization on microfluidic chips streamlines imaging access and throughput for organoid assays</cite>. <cite id="5be965fa-3">Engineered 3D culture environments reliably generate placental organoids and guide trophoblast differentiation, aligning culture and imaging needs</cite>.
- Outlook: Integration of biocompatible metasurfaces and label‑free nonlinear/near‑field contrast is expected to improve resolution and specificity in organoid imaging without perturbation. <cite id="5be965fa-2">Noninvasive label‑free imaging supports continuous monitoring while preserving organoid integrity</cite>.

Graphene and 2D‑material hybrid surfaces bridging electron and optical microscopy
- Mechanisms: Atomically thin conductors and semiconductors modify field distribution, reduce charging, and act as tunable plasmonic media. They also enable correlative workflows: same sample exposed to SEM/TEM after optical pre‑mapping, or metasurface‑assisted near‑field scanning.
- 2023–2025 synthesis and perspective: Cross‑disciplinary reviews link near‑field optics to electron nanoscopy, highlighting graphene/plasmonic hybrids as deterministic near‑field probes and sample carriers that preserve charge state across modality transitions. <cite id="09abd2e6-4">A 2025 review unifies near-field optics and electron nanoscopy, with plasmonics and 2D materials at the center of near-surface imaging mechanisms</cite>.
- Practical benefits: Reduced sample charging, improved phase contrast, tunable plasmonic resonances in the near‑IR/near‑UV, and mechanical robustness on chips. <cite id="09abd2e6-3">Hybrid plasmonic–dielectric systems survey material strategies where 2D materials and graphene act as scalable building blocks for near-field imaging</cite>.
- Gaps: Achieving wafer‑scale, defect‑controlled graphene metasurfaces with reproducible resonance lines and stable coupling at biophotonic wavelengths remains an engineering challenge. <cite id="09abd2e6-2">Deterministic mapping from performance (bandwidth, efficiency, depth) to surface geometry is needed for reproducible metasurface imaging</cite>.

Cross‑cutting quantitative impacts and design metrics
- Sensitivity/contrast: SERS substrates routinely deliver 10^2–10^6 Raman enhancements at single‑molecule levels for spatial mapping; metasurface hotspots extend this into spectrochemical imaging and depth‑resolved biology. <cite id="9250f6dc-1">SERS instruments now standardize nanotag design and spectral analytics to extract quantitative, spatially resolved signals in biomedicine</cite>. <cite id="60449840-0">Metasurface-enhanced mid-IR photothermal imaging quantifies hotspot-to-thermal conversion to improve chemical sensitivity</cite>.
- Resolution/scale: Plasmonic/metasurface systems achieve sub‑diffraction (≈180 nm) in far‑field optics; near‑field configurations resolve tens of nanometers with phase/amplitude sensitivity. <cite id="09abd2e6-6">A plasmonic superlens attains 180 nm resolution at 640 nm via near-field coupling and far-field reconstruction</cite>. <cite id="09abd2e6-1">Plasmonic structured illumination supports wide-field super-resolution beyond Abbe’s limit using surface-assisted interference</cite>.
- Throughput and uniformity: Wafer‑scale nanopatterning and conformal coatings are central to moving from single‑spot demonstrations to high‑throughput imaging; reviews emphasize reproducibility and stability for clinical/bioprocessing translation. <cite id="9250f6dc-4">Substrate preparation methods increasingly focus on scalability and homogeneity for reliable imaging over large surfaces</cite>. <cite id="9250f6dc-1">Instrumentation and spectral analysis frameworks are co-developing with substrate advances to standardize biomedical SERS pipelines</cite>.

Where the field is heading
- Designer metasurfaces and heterostructures: From performance metrics to nanoscale geometry, deterministic metasurface design now bridges theory, fabrication, and imaging benchmarks, with cross‑modal workflows spanning optical, IR, and electron domains. <cite id="09abd2e6-2">Deterministic “from performance to structure” design links imaging metrics to nanofabrication</cite>. <cite id="09abd2e6-4">Unified perspectives connect near-field plasmonics and electron nanoscopy for hybrid readouts</cite>.
- Functional imaging at bio‑relevant depths: Mid‑IR plasmonic metasurfaces and photothermal conversion open depth‑resolved chemical imaging in live cells and tissues with lower photodamage than fluorescence, poised for in vivo and longitudinal studies. <cite id="60449840-2">Mid-IR photothermal microscopy enables depth-resolved in vivo imaging of live cells, extending chemical imaging into biological depths</cite>. <cite id="60449840-4">Metasurface-enhanced IR imaging maps biomolecules in tissue sections with quantitative fidelity</cite>.
- Organoid‑on‑chip imaging interfaces: Standardized microfluidic platforms with engineered surfaces—anti‑scatter/reflective coatings, patterned membranes, and plasmonic/near‑field elements—are reducing artifacts and improving longitudinal, label‑free tracking of organoid development and disease modeling. <cite id="5be965fa-0">OrganoidChip demonstrates hydrogel-free immobilization for rapid, high-throughput imaging</cite>. <cite id="5be965fa-4">Microfluidic control over culture and structure advances organoid models aligned to optical readout</cite>.
- Practical engineering: Heat management, material loss at IR, hotspot stability, and fabrication tolerance are now co‑solved via metasurface topology optimization, antifouling/antireflection stacks, and thermorefractive calibration. <cite id="60449840-0">Metasurface thermal response mapping informs strategies to mitigate losses and enhance uniformity</cite>. <cite id="9250f6dc-1">Biomedical reviews capture instrument-software-substrate integration as the key to robust SERS imaging</cite>.

Key takeaways
- State‑of‑the‑art surface‑enabled imaging spans four pillars: SERS/IR metasurfaces for sensitive chemical mapping, plasmonic/metasurface optics for super‑resolution and near‑field contrast, mid‑IR photothermal/metasurface spectroimaging for deep, label‑free biospectroscopy, and engineered organoid/microfluidic surfaces for high‑contrast, longitudinal live‑sample imaging. <cite id="9250f6dc-1">SERS substrates and instrumentation now support biomedical-grade imaging with defined performance envelopes</cite> <cite id="09abd2e6-6">Plasmonic superlenses demonstrate 180 nm resolution at visible wavelengths</cite> <cite id="60449840-2">Mid-IR photothermal imaging achieves depth-resolved in vivo chemical mapping</cite> <cite id="5be965fa-0">Microfluidic organoid chips unlock label-free, high-throughput optical access to 3D tissues</cite>.
- Emerging surfaces—graphene and plasmonic–dielectric hybrids—are compressing the gap between electron and optical nanoscopy, while deterministic metasurface design makes performance and reproducibility predictable. <cite id="09abd2e6-4">Near-field optics–electron nanoscopy unification highlights the role of 2D materials and plasmonics at surfaces</cite> <cite id="09abd2e6-2">Performance-to-structure metasurface engineering provides reproducible imaging surfaces</cite>.
- Watch for convergence: coupling plasmonic hotspots with multiphoton/SWIR readouts and microfluidic organoid platforms to deliver quantitative, longitudinal, and chemically specific imaging with minimal perturbation. <cite id="60449840-4">Metasurface mid-IR spectrochemical imaging establishes quantitative tissue mapping</cite> <cite id="60449840-5">Plasmonic metasurfaces enable label-free MIR cell imaging via near-field coupling</cite> <cite id="5be965fa-2">Label-free, real-time imaging preserves organoid integrity for continuous monitoring</cite>.

Caveats and open problems
- Hotspot stability, reproducibility across wafers, and fouling resistance remain critical; mid‑IR losses and thermal drift require thermorefractive calibration and materials innovation. <cite id="09abd2e6-4">Plasmonic loss and resonance tolerance define near-field imaging performance envelopes</cite> <cite id="60449840-0">Hotspot heterogeneity and thermal response variability must be characterized and mitigated</cite>.
- Biocompatibility, biofouling, and sample viability in SERS/IR imaging demand antifouling coatings and biocompatible metals or dielectrics. <cite id="9250f6dc-1">Biomedical SERS reviews codify substrate/biofouling/compatibility design rules alongside spectral analytics</cite>.
- Benchmarking across modalities needs standardized quantitative metrics (resolution vs. penetration depth vs. SNR) and cross‑technology comparisons for fair integration into lab workflows. <cite id="9250f6dc-2">Homogeneous SERS substrates facilitate reproducible mapping yet call for standardized evaluation across areas</cite>.

without_term.text: What are the current state of the art in which photonic metamaterial surfaces are utilized to enhance label-free imaging in phase contrast microscopy and refractometric microscopy?
without_term.answer:
Below is a concise synthesis of how photonic metamaterial surfaces are being used to enhance label‑free imaging in phase‑contrast and refractometric (refractive‑index) microscopy, highlighting recent advances, quantitative performance, integration with conventional systems, and open challenges.

Summary: where the field is headed
- Photonic metamaterials—thin, patterned subwavelength metasurfaces and metasubstrates—enable efficient conversion of weak phase (and RI‑dependent) signals into brightfield‑compatible contrast without exogenous stains or dyes, boosting sensitivity and contrast for label‑free bioimaging and materials microscopy. <cite id="593461df-4">These phase‑contrast and bright‑field modalities have become essential for label‑free microscopy, with metasurface platforms now supporting multi‑modal operation and compact, integrable designs</cite>. <cite id="efcfee39-8">Importantly, metasurfaces that sense background medium refractive index can be tuned via surrounding liquid to modulate transmission and phase response, providing programmable contrast control in RI‑sensitive imaging</cite>.
- Recent work has pushed contrast and resolution to new levels in conventional microscopes by replacing bulky phase plates or Köhler components with ultrathin metasurfaces, and by introducing deep‑UV and mid‑IR implementations for high‑resolution label‑free imaging. <cite id="593461df-0">In visible, deep‑UV metasurfaces deliver ultra‑high extinction ratio and superior native‑contrast imaging, achieving high‑resolution label‑free microscopy by exploiting strong optical path differences in transparent specimens</cite>. <cite id="593461df-4">In the mid‑IR, metasurface phase plates have been engineered to interconvert phase and intensity for multimodal phase‑contrast and brightfield imaging, targeting point‑of‑care, label‑free diagnostics</cite>.

Metasurface augmentation of phase‑contrast microscopy
- Tunable phase‑to‑intensity conversion with standard objectives. Thin‑film metasurface phase plates can replace the traditional phase annuli in Zernike phase‑contrast systems, offering compact, mass‑producible alternatives that translate quantitative phase into intensity over broad fields of view. <cite id="593461df-4">Quantitative phase imaging techniques that retrieve phase from intensity rely on metasurface phase encoding to create efficient phase‑to‑intensity contrast in the back‑focal plane or pupil plane, enabling brightfield observation without stains</cite>. <cite id="593461df-5">High‑Q metasurface phase plates enable more convenient and tunable phase contrast imaging with improved spatial filtering properties compared to bulk optics</cite>.
- Real‑time, reconfigurable phase contrast for dynamic samples. Liquid‑crystal or azobenzene‑modulated metasurfaces integrated in or near the pupil allow “on‑demand” phase‑contrast control under Köhler illumination, useful for adapting contrast to specimen opacity and refractive heterogeneity. <cite id="593461df-2">An azobenzene‑liquid‑crystal Zernike filter in a phase‑contrast configuration demonstrated real‑time label‑free microscopy with adjustable phase contrast</cite>. <cite id="efcfee39-8">Metasurfaces whose response depends on surrounding refractive index have been shown to respond to solution concentration by modulating their optical transmission and phase, enabling remote, non‑mechanical tuning of contrast</cite>.
- High‑contrast deep‑UV platforms for cellular imaging. Shifting to 200–280 nm c‑band UV, metasurface coatings exploit higher refractive index contrasts and smaller feature scales to produce extinction ratios and phase‑to‑intensity conversion that greatly surpass conventional phase contrast, improving visualization of cytoskeleton, nuclei, and organelles without dyes. <cite id="593461df-0">Using c‑band UV metasurfaces with high extinction ratio achieved label‑free high‑resolution imaging in which cellular structures appear with enhanced contrast and fine detail</cite>. 
- Compact, efficient metasurface phase plates and spatial filters. Integration‑friendly metasurfaces can simultaneously perform phase contrast and spatial frequency filtering, simplifying alignment and reducing loss compared to multi‑element phase plates. <cite id="593461df-5">A high‑Q metasurface implemented as a compact, ultrathin plate delivers phase contrast and spatial filtering with favorable efficiency and mechanical robustness for practical systems</cite>.

Refractometric (refractive‑index) microscopy with metamaterial surfaces
- Metasurface RI sensing under standard microscopes. By patterning 2D arrays of subwavelength resonators (e.g., nanoholes, nanocrosses) on transparent substrates, the metasurface transmittance and phase shift become strongly dependent on the local and surrounding refractive index, enabling RI contrast in brightfield systems without specialized objectives. <cite id="efcfee39-8">The metasurface response is directly responsive to changes in surface refractive index induced by covering solutions; varying solution concentration tunes the transmitted intensity and resonance phase, providing a controllable, label‑free RI imaging pathway</cite>. 
- Gradient‑index (GRIN) and graded metasurfaces as refractive‑index prisms. Engineered spatial variation of refractive index across a metasurface can act as an on‑chip GRIN lens or prism, shaping wavefronts and converting modal phase gradients into spatially varying intensity patterns that map to specimen RI fields. <cite id="efcfee39-5">Fundamentally, inhomogeneous metasurfaces rely on dielectric meta‑atoms with high refractive index to realize spatially varying optical functions, enabling programmable phase‑to‑intensity conversion over graded index profiles</cite>. <cite id="efcfee39-6">Broader GRIN metamaterial theory shows how spatially varying effective index can be mapped to meta‑atom parameter changes, providing the design space for RI‑sensitive graded metasurfaces usable as integrated refractometric prisms</cite>. 
- Broadband and mid‑IR refractometry. Moving into the IR reduces water absorption and increases compatibility with aqueous biological samples; metasurface phase plates and apertures translate RI variations into intensity contrast compatible with conventional brightfield detectors. <cite id="593461df-4">Infrared metasurface phase plates have been designed for phase‑contrast and brightfield interconversion, with demonstrations pointing toward practical, label‑free microscopic RI mapping in physiological media</cite>. 
- Integration models: metasubstrates beneath coverslips. Thin‑film metasurfaces patterned on glass can serve as metasubstrates under the specimen/coverslip stack, where RI gradients across the cell or particle modulate the metasurface resonance and generate spatial RI maps in transmitted or reflected intensity. <cite id="efcfee39-8">Because metasurface transmission depends linearly (or approximately) on the effective refractive index of the overlayer, modulating overlayer refractive index via salt concentration produces distinct metasurface contrast changes, enabling noninvasive RI contrast control</cite>. <cite id="efcfee39-5">These inhomogeneous (graded) metasurfaces provide the mechanism to transform local RI variations into spatially resolved intensity fields observable through standard objectives</cite>.

What the numbers look like and reported gains
- Contrast and resolution: <cite id="593461df-0">Deep‑UV metasurface platforms reported “ultra‑violet extinction” with markedly higher extinction ratios than standard phase contrast, enabling high‑resolution label‑free imaging of cellular structures</cite>. <cite id="593461df-2">Azobenzene‑tunable phase contrast provided real‑time, label‑free imaging with adjustable phase‑to‑intensity conversion under Köhler illumination</cite>. <cite id="593461df-5">High‑Q metasurface phase plates improved practicality and tuning bandwidth for phase contrast compared to bulk equivalents</cite>. 
- RI sensitivity and tunability: <cite id="efcfee39-8">Metasurface transmittance shows strong dependence on surface refractive index; changing solution refractive index via concentration variation modulates transmission and resonance phase, enabling quantitative RI modulation without physical contact or staining</cite>. While reported RI sensitivity values range widely by geometry and wavelength, the principle has been validated across visible and IR, with practical tunability via ambient medium and solution handling. <cite id="efcfee39-5">Controlling meta‑atom scale and material refractive index allows tuning of phase sensitivity and bandwidth</cite>. 
- System‑level integration: <cite id="593461df-4">Metasurface platforms in the mid‑IR demonstrate phase‑contrast to brightfield interconversion with low loss and compactness—an essential step toward label‑free point‑of‑care microscopy</cite>. <cite id="593461df-5">Thin‑film, high‑Q metasurfaces mitigate alignment sensitivity while maintaining efficient phase‑to‑intensity conversion compatible with commercial objectives</cite>.

Practical considerations and limitations
- Bandwidth and dispersion. <cite id="593461df-0">Deep‑UV platforms achieve excellent contrast but introduce higher material loss and stricter fabrication tolerances; careful antireflection and UV‑resistant dielectrics are required</cite>. <cite id="593461df-4">IR implementations benefit from reduced absorption in water but require specialized materials and long‑wavelength detectors</cite>. 
- Sensitivity trade‑offs. <cite id="efcfee39-8">Metasurface RI contrast increases with refractive index detuning, but too large a mismatch reduces transmission and excites higher‑order resonances; practical systems tune immersion medium to target optimal transmittance sensitivity</cite>. <cite id="efcfee39-5">Using higher index dielectrics and compact unit cells increases phase gradient per RI unit but narrows bandwidth; designers balance sensitivity and working bandwidth</cite>. 
- Sample–substrate coupling and alignment. <cite id="593461df-4">Pupil‑plane or back‑focal metasurface phase plates interpose phase shifts between object and image, which can introduce nonlocal sensitivity to condenser and sample path aberrations; careful Köhler alignment or pupil‑plane access mitigates phase errors</cite>. <cite id="593461df-5">Compact metasurface plates simplify alignment while maintaining phase‑to‑intensity efficiency, easing adoption on existing microscopes</cite>. 
- Safety and materials compatibility. Deep‑UV exposure and ozone generation require protective enclosures and UV‑rated objectives; immersion liquids must be compatible with specimen biology and compatible with substrate materials to avoid biofouling or swelling that alters effective RI. <cite id="593461df-0">The deep‑UV metasurface designs emphasize safety and material stability while delivering high‑resolution, label‑free imaging</cite>. <cite id="efcfee39-8">Using aqueous or buffered immersion media and monitoring metasurface transmission provides a practical route to real‑time RI control</cite>.

Representative demonstrations and emerging tools
- Generalizable metasurface phase‑contrast. <cite id="593461df-5">High‑Q metasurface phase plates enable convenient phase contrast, with spatial frequency filtering integrated for improved noise rejection and artifact suppression</cite>. <cite id="593461df-2">Azobenzene‑liquid‑crystal Zernike filters allow live‑cell phase contrast adjustment; metasurface‑enabled designs extend this reconfigurability to nanofabricated, high‑efficiency plates</cite>.
- Label‑free multimodal IR imaging. <cite id="593461df-4">ACS Photonics work on metasurface phase plates for IR multimodal microscopy shows the path from principle to prototype, with demonstrations of phase‑to‑intensity conversion compatible with brightfield detectors and label‑free operation</cite>.
- Deep‑UV boosting of native contrast. <cite id="593461df-0">Nature Communications demonstrates extreme metasurface extinction at c‑band UV, yielding superior, stain‑free contrast in transparent biological specimens and nanomaterials</cite>.
- RI‑tunable metasurface layers. <cite id="efcfee39-8">Metasurface layers whose transmission varies with the surrounding refractive index can be tuned by solution concentration; this effect underpins refractometric contrast and allows closed‑loop adjustment of imaging contrast</cite>. <cite id="efcfee39-5">Gradient‑index metasurfaces translate local RI variations into spatial phase gradients, enabling intensity‑contrast mapping over graded index profiles</cite>.

How to deploy today
- Phase‑contrast enhancement: swap or add a metasurface phase plate at the condenser or pupil plane to convert quantitative phase to intensity for standard brightfield cameras; tune dynamically using immersion medium or liquid‑controlled samples for optimal contrast. <cite id="593461df-4">Metasurface phase plates interconvert phase and intensity efficiently in pupil/back‑focal planes</cite>. <cite id="593461df-2">Azobenzene‑based reconfigurable phase contrast shows feasibility; metasurface variants extend stability and efficiency</cite>. 
- Refractometric imaging: place a thin, transparent metasurface metasubstrate beneath the coverslip; image transmitted or reflected intensity over controlled immersion media to map RI fields of cells or colloids. <cite id="efcfee39-8">Metasurface transmission responds to surface RI changes induced by solution concentration</cite>. 
- Choose wavelength by sample and detector: visible for brightfield CCD/CMOS; deep‑UV for maximal extinction ratio and resolution; IR for aqueous samples and reduced scattering. <cite id="593461df-0">Deep‑UV metasurfaces achieve superior extinction, enabling high‑resolution label‑free imaging</cite>. <cite id="593461df-4">IR metasurface phases enable multimodal, label‑free operation compatible with standard objectives</cite>.

Outlook
- The state‑of‑the‑art converges on ultrathin, broadband, and reconfigurable metasurface platforms that deliver high‑fidelity phase‑to‑intensity conversion and RI‑sensitive contrast compatible with standard microscopes, with demonstrated gains in label‑free live‑cell imaging, dynamic contrast control, and chemical contrast via immersion tuning. <cite id="593461df-0">Deep‑UV metasurface platforms show the upper bound of extinction‑based contrast for transparent specimens</cite>, while <cite id="593461df-4">IR metasurface phase plates point toward clinical, point‑of‑care modalities</cite>. <cite id="efcfee39-8">Active control via surrounding refractive index opens closed‑loop RI imaging and diagnostic assays</cite>, and <cite id="efcfee39-5">graded/GRIN metasurfaces</cite> provide the route to high‑resolution RI maps from phase gradients. The principal challenges remaining are dispersion management across bandwidth, robust biocompatibility and stability at interfaces, and low‑cost, large‑area patterning to bring these to routine lab and bedside use. <cite id="593461df-4">System‑level integration for label‑free multimodal imaging</cite> is maturing rapidly, with multiple platforms ready to be incorporated into research and translational workflows.
